1.Limited discussion of clinical relevance of geometric variability:
While the method emphasizes robustness to varying geometries (e.g., different SIDs), the clinical motivation for such variability is not sufficiently explained. It would be helpful to clarify in which real-world scenarios such variations occur and why zero-shot adaptation is necessary. 
2.Potential issue in experimental setup (Section 3, S3 Mixed-Condition Robustness):
The authors state that baselines are trained on mixed geometries including parallel-beam with different SIDs (800/1200 mm). However, under parallel-beam geometry, changing SID does not affect the imaging formation, making this setting questionable and potentially unfair or misleading. 
3.Loss of high-frequency details compared to baseline:
In Fig. 2, ALFA shows improved reconstruction in certain regions (e.g., sagittal view, underbite and deep overbite cases). However, globally the results appear smoother compared to PerX2CT, suggesting a loss of high-frequency details.
It would be important for the authors to discuss: 
oWhy the method appears globally smoother, 
oWhy certain local regions still benefit despite the overall smoothing effect.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents an interesting idea by decoupling anatomical prior learning from geometry-specific adaptation using INR and test-time optimization, which enables zero-shot generalization across varying acquisition geometries. This is a meaningful direction with potential practical impact.
However, several key issues limit the strength of the contribution. In particular, the motivation and realism of the experimental setup are not sufficiently justified (e.g., the use of parallel-beam simulations for bi-plane imaging and the treatment of SID variations), raising concerns about the practical relevance of the evaluation. In addition, the proposed method appears to trade off high-frequency details for smoother reconstructions, and this behavior is not adequately analyzed or discussed.

The paper received overall positive reviews with scores of 4, 3, and 4.Reviewers appreciated the clean methodological design, the focus on geometry generalization, and the strong simulated results, especially under unseen geometry and robustness settings. author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the reviewers for recognizing ALFA’s conceptually clean framework, zero-shot generalization, and robustness. Below we address your concerns:
1.Imaging Physics & Setup (R2)
We agree that changing SID in parallel beams does not affect image formation and apologize for the ambiguous phrasing in Sec 3.2.To clarify: we did NOT vary SID for parallel beams. The S3 dataset simply merges three distinct subsets: (1) pure parallel-beam, (2) cone-beam (SID=800mm), and (3) cone-beam (SID=1200mm). Supervised baselines were trained on this mixed dataset solely to test their robustness to dataset-level geometric variance. No physical laws were violated, and we will explicitly clarify this.
2.Clinical Motivation & Simulated Data (R1, R2, R3)
Motivation (R2): In multi-center settings, SIDs vary widely (e.g., 1000-1800mm) due to vendor differences or patient positioning, causing end-to-end models to fail catastrophically. ALFA provides a zero-shot, plug-and-play solution across heterogeneous clinics.
Simulated Data (R1, R3): Acquiring paired biplanar X-rays and 3D CTs in identical poses is practically infeasible due to radiation hazards, making high-fidelity DRRs the standard benchmark. Crucially, baselines require paired data, whereas ALFA only needs unpaired CTs to learn the prior, ensuring high scalability to real clinical X-rays.
3.Efficiency & Multi-resolution (R1)
ALFA is highly lightweight (only 15.3M parameters). Inference via Test-Time Optimization (TTO) takes ~15s/case, which is a clinically acceptable overhead for pre-operative planning where accuracy is paramount. While we omitted multi-resolution results due to space limits, this is a proven inherent advantage of INR-based methods, which we will detail in future work.
4.Pathology Metrics (R3)
We agree that specialized pathological metrics provide deeper quantitative insights. Currently, our PSNR and SSIM metrics capture global similarity and reflect morphological distortions from pathologies. We will incorporate more specialized, in-depth quantitative pathological analyses in our subsequent work.
5.Smoothness vs. Topological Correctness (R2)
ALFA appears smoother due to the “spectral bias” of INRs, which prioritizes fitting low-frequency structural topologies over high-frequency noise. End-to-end models (e.g., X2CT-GAN) hallucinate sharp but anatomically incorrect average teeth. ALFA trades high-frequency texture for topological faithfulness, ensuring that critical macro-level deformations (e.g., underbite/overbite) are strictly and anatomically valid.
6.Hyperparameters & Baselines (R1)
Hyperparameters: During training, we randomly sample 51,200 points/subject per epoch. For rendering, we sample 1,024 rays/epoch and 128 points/ray to match real resolution. We will conduct detailed ablation experiments on the components and settings of the model in subsequent work.
Baselines: Swin-X2S and Diffusion methods target meshes/segmentations or lack open-source paired training scripts for our volumetric setup. ALFA’s core contribution is the decoupled paradigm; future advanced priors (e.g., diffusion) can seamlessly replace INRs within our framework.
7.Source of Gain: Prior vs. TTO (R3)
Both are indispensable. Without the learned prior, TTO is a severely ill-posed 2D-to-3D optimization, causing massive ray-aliasing artifacts. Without physics-guided TTO, performance drops drastically on unseen SIDs (matching S2 baseline failures). ALFA’s gain stems from restricting physical TTO strictly within the valid anatomical manifold defined by the prior.

title: Aligning Prototypes and Updating Null Spaces for Continual WSI Learning
abstract:
Whole Slide Image (WSI) analysis in digital pathology requires continual learning (CL) to adapt to growing data streams without catastrophic forgetting. Current CL methods for WSIs face challenges from large sample sizes and strict patient privacy constraints, risking either data leakage or limited performance on visually similar categories.
Existing methods suffer from inter-task class confusion due to insufficient discriminative supervision, and an inability to update prior class representations. 
To address these, we propose AlignMIL-NS with two innovations: (1) Prototype-Class Feature Alignment (PCFA), which enforces within-task alignment between class and visual features while promoting inter-task discrimination; and (2) Null Space Class Feature Update (NS-CFU), which refines previous task representations within their task-specific null spaces to mitigate interference from new tasks.
On a challenging five-dataset WSI benchmark, AlignMIL-NS achieves 89.1\% AACC on both task orders, outperforming all rehearsal-free methods and matching rehearsal-based approaches without storing any patient data.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces a rehearsal-free continual learning framework designed for digital pathology. It addresses the catastrophic forgetting that occurs when MIL models are sequentially trained on new WSI datasets.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Unlike conventional methods that typically freeze old representations to avoid forgetting, the proposed method allows the model to continuously refine previous-task class representations. This is achieved by constraining updates to the task-specific null space. 
2.The proposed method addresses the challenge of inter-task class confusion by enforcing alignment between class features and visual prototypes within a single task. Because historical visual features are inaccessible in a privacy-preserving setting, PCFA uses prototype features as a proxy to promote cross-task separability, which is particularly effective for distinguishing between visually similar disease categories across sequential data streams.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The stability of this framework is highly dependent on the fine-tuning of hyperparameters. To balance model plasticity (the ability to acquire new knowledge) with stability (the ability to preserve previously learned knowledge), users must configure specific settings for the null space threshold gamma, which serves as a margin hyperparameter, as well as the weights for various loss functions. The generalizability of these hyperparameters remains to be further validated when encountering different pathological tasks or more complex, multi-center data streams.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The recommendation is primarily based on the framework’s strong clinical utility and its ability to achieve performance comparable with rehearsal-based methods without storing raw patient data, thus strictly respecting medical privacy constraints. With competitive performance across a rigorous five-dataset benchmark, the proposed method proves highly effective at mitigating catastrophic forgetting by addressing the visual similarity and inter-task interference common in WSI analysis by enforcing discriminative supervision and allowing non-destructive updates to old knowledge. Additionally, the architecture is remarkably efficient.
However, there is a notable dependency on the fine-tuning of hyperparameters, which may hinder its robustness when applied to varying pathological tasks or multi-center data streams.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper focuses on the problem of pathology slide classification using a continual learning setting, specifically prototype-based multiple instance learning. In this setting, tasks are learned sequentially, and the feature extractor evolves over time. The feature embeddings are updated and class prototypes from earlier tasks are typically frozen. This leads to two problems: (i) a mismatch between outdated prototypes and current embeddings, and (ii) misalignment between learned prototypes and the true class feature distributions.
To address these issues, the paper proposes two main components. First, an alignment step that forces prototypes to closely match their corresponding class feature distributions (within-task alignment) while also explicitly separating features across different tasks (cross-task discriminability). This results in tighter class clusters and improved separation between classes from different tasks. Second, they introduce null space update that moves prototypes from previous tasks instead of freezing them. The updates are constrained to lie in the null space of the feature subspace associated with each previous task, i.e., the new information can be incorporated without altering the original task-specific representations. This allows prototypes to adapt to the evolving feature space while avoiding interference with previously learned knowledge.
The paper is well supported experimentally using five WSI datasets, ablation studies, and comparisons against baselines.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper identifies known issues with MIL and explains them well. Then, it proposed two natural solutions to handle these issues. It provides geometric interpretation of their solutions. The experimental results are also solid. The improvements are as expected.
reviews.text_weaknesses: I am not sure if there is any major weakness. Perhaps the paper assumes that a reader is well versed in continual learning but that is expected in such conferences.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I am not an expert in this field but based on my understanding this paper is definitely suggesting some natural and significant improvements to handle known problems in MIL.

meta_reviews.text: The consensus is positive, with two Weak Accepts and one Accept. The work addresses an important and clinically relevant problem: continual WSI learning under privacy constraints. The methodological contribution is reasonably clear and targeted, and the results appear competitive across a challenging multi-dataset benchmark. The main concerns are not fatal but should be clarified in rebuttal or revision. In particular, the technical validity of updating text-derived class representations in a visual null space needs stronger explanation, and the sensitivity of key hyperparameters should be better supported.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback. We address the major concerns below.
1.Hyperparameter Sensitivity (Meta-review, R1)
We tested $\gamma$ across different values. Although model performance is affected by this hyperparameter, it consistently brings positive gains over the baseline (AACC 77.3% without NS-CFU) within the range of [0, 0.6]. Moreover, the null space constraint (Sec. 3.3) guarantees $\langle f_q^j, f_c^j + \phi_j \alpha_j^\top \rangle = \langle f_q^j, f_c^j \rangle$, meaning $\gamma$ only affects cross-task discrimination and cannot degrade within-task performance. Loss weights ($\lambda_M$=0.5, $\lambda_{\text{PCFA}}$=1.0) remained fixed across both task orders and all five folds without per-task tuning.
2.Role of the Fixed Language Encoder (R2-Q3, Meta-review)
Fine-tuning the lightweight $\mathbf{v}_c$ requires far fewer parameters than fine-tuning $E_l$ (0.031M vs. 0.479M, Tab. 5). More importantly, in the CL setting, fine-tuning $E_l$ would alter all class features simultaneously, whereas updating $\mathbf{v}_c$ only modifies the target class feature, avoiding interference with previously learned classes.
3.Text-Visual Alignment (R2-Q4, Meta-review)
Our framework operates under CONCH (Sec. 4.1), where both patch features ($E_v$) and text templates ($E_l$) are encoded by the same vision-language model, which is explicitly trained with contrastive learning to align text and visual embeddings. Therefore, the alignment between text and visual spaces is an architectural property, not an unsupported assumption. We will clarify this more explicitly in the manuscript.
4.Ablation Metrics (R2-Q5)
AACC is the primary metric in class-incremental learning. Since the joint-training upper bound (90.3%) is the same across all configurations, a higher AACC directly indicates better forgetting resistance. The full model achieves BWT=-4.0 vs. -15.1 for QPMIL-VL (Tab. 2), confirming that both PCFA and NS-CFU contribute to reduced forgetting.
5.Notation and Figure Clarity (R2-Q1, R2-Q2)
We acknowledge that $P_i^x$ in Eq. 1 is not clearly defined. It refers to the keys $k_i$ in the prototype pool as described in the QPMIL-VL formulation. We will fix this notation. Regarding Fig. 1, we apologize for the confusion: the current figure only shows the QPMIL-VL heatmap. We will add the AlignMIL-NS heatmap and improve the in-figure annotations.
6.Accessibility (R3)
We will improve the exposition to be more accessible for readers less familiar with continual learning.

title: All-in-One Augmented Reality Guided Head and Neck Tumor Resection
abstract: Positive margins are common in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, yet intraoperative re-resection is often imprecise because margin locations are typically communicated verbally from pathology. We present an all-in-one augmented reality (AR) system that relocalizes positive margins from a resected specimen to the resection bed and visualizes them in situ using HoloLens 2 depth sensing and fully automated markerless surface registration. In a silicone phantom study with six medical trainees, markerless registration achieved target registration errors comparable to a marker-based baseline (median 1.8 mm vs. 1.7 mm; maximum < 4 mm). In a margin relocalization task, AR guidance reduced error from verbal guidance (median 14.2 mm) to a few millimeters (median 3.2 mm), with all AR localizations within 5 mm error. These results support the feasibility of markerless AR margin guidance for more precise intraoperative re-resection.
subject_areas: Modalities -> Mobile / Wearable / Point-of-Care Imaging & Sensors

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The document describes a markerless augmented reality guidance system that assists in tumor resection by precise in-situ visualization. A phantom study involving six participants providing qualitative and quantitative data shows that the markerless registration is, above all, objectively on par with the baseline using markers.
reviews.text_strengths: The entire paper is well written, and the novelty of markerless registration for in-situ AR visualization is clearly explained and demonstrated in a thorough evaluation. It is commendable that the evaluation does not only consider technical aspects but also subjective user feedback.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
After reading the document, I wonder how the results presented are to be contextualized in relation to similar work, including markerless approaches. In my opinion, the discussion does not go far enough in this regard. In particular, a connection should be established with the following two aspects, respectively references:
Regarding deformable registration (see section on future work): Yang, Q. , Li, F. , Xu, J. , Liu, Z. , Sridhar, S. , Jin, W. , . . . & Wu, J. Y. (2025, September). Augmented Reality-Based Guidance with Deformable Registration in Head and Neck Tumor Resection. In International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention (pp. 45-54). Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. 
Regarding markerless situs registration: Liebmann, F. , von Atzigen, M. , Stütz, D. , Wolf, J. , Zingg, L. , Suter, D. , . . . & Fürnstahl, P. (2024). Automatic registration with continuous pose updates for marker-less surgical navigation in spine surgery. Medical Image Analysis, 91, 103027.
In addition, I spotted redundant information which should be shortened (e. g. , quartile range in the text and in plots), and the statistical reports should be updated according to APA standards (i. e. , including all measures such as effect size). Non-significant aspects should be given less weight, especially given the relatively small sample size. In Figure 3, a significance bar could help to visualize differences, and in Figure 4, the similar color coding for different aspects creates potential for misunderstanding. I recommend that all metrics used should be listed before the Results section; otherwise, the questionnaires used simply appear surprisingly and confuse the reader. Also, the single qualitative quote in the Discussion and Conclusion sections is somewhat surprising; I assume it would be better to have a separate paragraph addressing this feedback within the Results section.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Given that it is clear, technically sound, and timely, I consider this submission highly suitable for the MICCAI conference. However, its somewhat unclear positioning relative to existing work and the need for minor optimization somewhat detract from the otherwise positive impression it makes. I hope my comments will help the authors address these points in a rebuttal, and I therefore recommend a “weak accept.”
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Having the read the authors’ rebuttal and the other reviews, my main points of criticism have been addressed. But I also recognize that R2’s and R3’s concerns remain significant and substantial (particularly regarding novelty and methodology). Since, to my understanding, the authors have addressed the ambiguities, I recommend, by a narrow margin, to accept the paper. However, I would also be okay with rejecting the paper if R2 and R3, who are more experts in this field, disagree.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a HoloLens 2 depth-sensor-based registration method to align specimen scans for in-situ visualization of positive margins, with the goal of guiding tumor resection in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. The method was evaluated on a cranial phantom with six users. Compared with verbal guidance, the proposed method improved re-localization accuracy, but only showed limited benefit in system usability and workload reduction.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper focuses on specimen re-localization, which is a clinically relevant application scenario that has rarely been addressed in previous AR navigation studies.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Methodological concerns
a. Practical usability: specimen deformation and shrinkage
Specimen deformation and shrinkage are major issues in the operating room. Although the authors mention these as future work, they are in fact central challenges for any real clinical deployment. Treating the specimen registration problem as rigid severely limits the practical usability of the proposed method.
b. Practical usability in iterative resection workflows
Re-localization is not a one-time procedure. In real surgical workflows, resection may be iterative. The proposed registration-based strategy appears applicable only to the initially resected specimen and does not seem able to support repeated or iterative re-localization during subsequent resections.
c. Depth sensing accuracy of the AHAT camera
Previous studies have shown that the depth error of the HoloLens 2 AHAT sensor is substantial and varies across different surface types [Ref 1]. This issue is not considered in the current study, although it may significantly affect both registration accuracy and visualization reliability.
d. Dependence on HoloLens SLAM stability
The proposed multi-frame stacking approach relies on HoloLens 2 pose estimation, which means that the overall system depends heavily on the stability of the device SLAM for both registration and in-situ visualization. In realistic scenarios, head movement may introduce spatial drift, which could substantially reduce usability and reliability.
e. Limited methodological novelty
Using a depth camera for point cloud registration has already been widely adopted in previous work [Ref 1]. The pipeline of FPFH-based coarse registration followed by ROI selection and ICP refinement is also a common approach in point-cloud-based registration pipelines [Ref 2]. Registration method difference between this paper and others are not clearly presented. Therefore, the technical novelty of the method itself appears limited, aside from the specific clinical use case.
2.Experimental concerns
a. Lack of clarity in the experimental setup
The paper does not clearly explain how marker-based registration was performed. As a result, it is difficult to understand the actual difference between the marker-based and markerless registration settings.
b. Lack of objective ground truth for registration accuracy
Since the authors used a cranial phantom with retro-reflective markers, it should be feasible to establish objective ground truth using CT scanning or an optical scanner. However, no direct objective evaluation of registration accuracy is provided.
c. Inappropriate use of expert performance as ground truth
The mean performance of experts was used as the ground truth in the evaluation. This is not appropriate for accuracy assessment, because it conflates user error with system error. Ground truth in an accuracy study should be defined independently and objectively.
d. Insufficient comparison baseline
In Experiment 2, the markerless AR method is compared only with verbal guidance. However, in actual practice, surgeons may also rely on specimen photographs or non-in-situ 3D holographic visualization. These would be more meaningful and clinically relevant baselines for comparison.
3.Writing
a. Writing
The paper is generally clearly written. However, the comparison with previous studies is insufficient. The manuscript does not clearly articulate its innovation beyond introducing a relatively uncommon use case. 
b. Figures
The figures do not sufficiently illustrate the proposed method. For example, the paper does not clearly show what the AHAT point cloud looks like, how the ROI is extracted, or how the registration pipeline operates in practice. In contrast, there are too many figures dedicated to NASA-TLX and SUS results. Given that only six users were included and limited distribution information is shown, these results could be more effectively summarized in tables rather than multiple separate figures.
__
__
__
__
__
__
__
Suggestions for improvement
1.The ground truth should be defined objectively. Expert performance should not be used as the ground truth in an accuracy evaluation. 
2.The proposed method should be compared against stronger and more clinically relevant baselines or current standard workflows, rather than only against a very naive verbal-guidance condition. 
3.Since the automatic registration procedure occupies a large portion of the method section, if the authors consider automation to be a core contribution, they should:
a. clearly explain why automatic registration is particularly important in this application;
b. clarify what limitations or ambiguities remain in prior automated approaches;
c. provide a clearer demonstration of how the proposed automated method works in practice;
d. objectively evaluate the automation result against a non-automated alternative, including both accuracy and efficiency;
e. analyze how much time is saved and how much accuracy is preserved over time, particularly under spatial drift or repeated use.

reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents an all-in-one augmented reality system designed to assist in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma resections. The system uses a Microsoft HoloLens 2 and its depth sensor to perform fully automated, markerless surface registration. By leveraging curvature-based keypoint sampling, FPFH descriptors, and a TEASER++ based coarse-to-fine registration pipeline, the system eliminates the need for manual region-of-interest selection or fiducial markers.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The proposed technical pipeline successfully removes the workflow burden of manual region-of-interest selection and physical markers. The combination of curvature-biased sampling, TEASER++ for robust global alignment, automatic bounding box construction for cropping, and point-to-plane ICP yields an impressive median TRE of 1.8 mm. 
2.The study provides a well-rounded assessment by incorporating human factors. The inclusion of a margin relocation task with six participants, alongside validated workload and usability metrics, strengthens the paper’s claims regarding the system’s practical viability.
reviews.text_weaknesses: 1.The current evaluation is conducted entirely on a rigid silicone face phantom. In actual surgical scenarios, tissue deformation, bleeding, and shrinkage of the resected specimen will heavily impact the rigid surface registration assumptions. 2.The user study relies on a very small sample size of six participants. The absence of experienced attending surgeons limits the generalizability of the baseline “verbal guidance” error.

N/A

This submission proposes a markerless AR system for tumor resection guidance. It is based on HoloLens 2 depth sensing, combined with a coarse-to-fine registration pipeline (curvature sampling, FPFH/TEASER++ initialization, ICP refinement). Evaluated was performed on a rigid phantom with a six-participant user study.
All reviewers recognize the clinical relevance and the value of eliminating markers and manual ROI selection. R1 and R3 additionally highlight manuscript clarity, automated workflow, user validation, and quantitative improvements over baselines./ R2 also acknowledges good motivation and potential clinical value.
The rebuttal clarified key methodological details: landmark-based evaluation, AHAT depth handling, markerless registration baselines, and workflow applicability.
However, reviewer concerns about methodological novelty, evaluation rigor, and clinical realism remain post-rebuttal. R2 argues that the method largely follows established depth-based registration pipelines with limited innovation. R2 also raises major issues about rigid phantom evaluation and weak baseline comparisons. R1 and R3 similarly note the small sample size and phantom-only validation l;imitations.
In summary, the rebuttal resolved several key issues, and the overall reviewer sentiment shifted positively. I recommend acceptance based on the clinical importance of the problem, the successful integration of a fully markerless AR workflow that removes manual registration steps, supporting evidence from the user validation. Of course, the work remains an early-stage CAI prototype and will require substantially broader validation under realistic clinical conditions, nevertheless, it represents a meaningful contribution.

Following the rebuttal, two reviewers noted that the authors clarified the objective landmark-based evaluation, the markerless registration baseline, AHAT correction procedure, and the intended iterative workflow. However, one reviewer is still concerned regarding deformation and shrinkage, iterative clinical applicability, the appropriateness of the verbal-guidance baseline, and the limited phantom-based evaluation. Overall, while the current study remains preliminary and should more clearly position its contribution relative to prior AR registration work, the rebuttal addressed several major ambiguities and the proposed HoloLens-only workflow demonstrates promising accuracy and translational relevance. I therefore recommend acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers.
Novelty
We agree prior deformable and markerless navigation work needs clearer contrast (R1, R2-1e, R2-3a). Our contribution is an all-in-one AR margin relocalization system using only the HoloLens POV AHAT sensor, without external RGB-D cameras, fiducials, or manual ROI selection (R1, R2-1e). This lowers OR burden by avoiding sensor installation (R1). Yang et al. model deformation but use ArUco and manual landmarks for AR registration [3], and Liebmann et al. study spine navigation with external sensing [4]. R2 Ref.1 concerns AHAT error correction with markers, not markerless specimen-to-bed registration [5]. Our Sec.2 uses curvature-biased sampling, TEASER++-style global alignment, automatic coarse-pose ROI cropping, and ICP for small HN specimens (R2-1e, R3). These choices gave markerless TRE comparable to a marker baseline, median 1.8 mm vs 1.7 mm and max <4 mm (R1, R3). Although we demonstrated our method on HN, our method is broadly applicable to open surgery solid malignancies.
Clinical scope
We agree deformation and shrinkage are crucial (R2-1a, R3-1). Clinical deployment needs deformation modeling plus markerless AR relocalization of the deformed model (R2-1a). This paper evaluates the second part, still required after deformation modeling (R2-1a). Iterative resections are supported because after any later positive-margin report, the same scan-register-visualize workflow can be rerun (R2-1b). The goal is to reduce repeated re-resections caused by coarse path-to-surgeon communication. [1,2] (R2-1b, R2-2d).
Evaluation, ground truth, and baselines
We apologize for the wording “expert measurements provided ground truth” (R2-2b, R2-2c). Targets were small physical ink landmarks on the phantom that were also identified on the structured-light specimen model (R2-2b). They were hidden among black marks for blinding participants, while the expert who created them could easily identify them with AR (R2-2c). Expert touching was only a measurement step for known physical landmarks, repeated twice and averaged (for tracking noise), so expert performance was not used as clinical ground truth (R2-2c). The marker baseline used the same STTAR retro-reflective tracking used for the stylus [6] (R2-2a). The study therefore reports registration accuracy versus a fiducial baseline and preliminary margin relocalization accuracy (R2-2d). We agree the phantom task does not capture all intraoperative information, but the verbal script was designed with experienced HN surgeon, and studies show surgeons often rely on verbal pathology communication [1,2] (R2-2d, R3-2).
AHAT, SLAM, reporting
We agree AHAT error is surface-dependent [5] (R2-1c). In our setup, an AHAT-tracked tool sampled the true local surface contour, nearest depth-sensor points were paired to tool points, and least-squares SVD corrected the local point cloud (R2-1c). This took <30 s and was applied once before experiments (R2-1c). For SLAM, acquisition took ~3s while users viewed the resection bed via AR, followed by noise reduction processing (R2-1d). The ground truth points were also collected right after each experiment to minimize drift. We will streamline statistics and figures, add effect sizes and APA reporting, deemphasize non-significant NASA-TLX and SUS results, clarify experiment setup, and release acquisition, depth correction, and ROI code (R1, R2-3b, R2 reproducibility).
[1] Quality in Surgical Pathology Communication and Reporting 2011
[2] How Often Is Cancer Present in Oral Cavity Re-resections After Initial Positive Margins? 2024
[3] Augmented Reality-Based Guidance with Deformable Registration in Head and Neck Tumor Resection 2025
[4] Automatic Registration with Continuous Pose Updates for Marker-less Surgical Navigation in Spine Surgery 2024
[5] EVD Surgical Guidance with Retro-reflective Tool Tracking and Spatial Reconstruction Using a Head-Mounted AR Device 2024
[6] STTAR Surgical Tool Tracking Using Off-the-Shelf AR HMDs 2023

title: ALSAnchorNet: Biologically Informed Multimodal MRI Fusion for Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Diagnosis
abstract: Deep learning–based multimodal MRI integration for Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) diagnosis remains largely unexplored. We present ALSAnchorNet, a biologically guided multimodal framework that integrates resting-state fMRI, diffusion tensor imaging, and structural MRI for ALS diagnosis. We introduce Frontal Anchor Attention to encode frontal lobe vulnerability by using intra-frontal functional connectivity as an anchoring query to modulate whole-brain connectivity interactions. This anchor-guided mechanism enhances disease-relevant feature amplification during cross-modal fusion. ALSAnchorNet applies modality-specific linear projections followed by anchor-based refinement to jointly model connectivity, glymphatic, and cerebral-spinal fluid (CSF) markers. Using one of the largest ALS cohort to date of 159 ALS and 107 healthy controls, ALSAnchorNet achieves 77% classification accuracy with AUC = 0.80, outperforming single-modality models and non-anchored fusion approaches. Ablation analyses demonstrate that glymphatic and CSF markers provide complementary diagnostic value beyond connectivity features. Interpretability analysis further reveals elevated contributions from the superior frontal gyri and paracentral lobule, consistent with established motor network involvement in ALS. These results establish an important first step toward biologically grounded deep learning for multimodal ALS modeling. Future work will incorporate biofluid markers and longitudinal data for more comprehensive disease modeling.
subject_areas: Special Topic -> AI for Neglected Diseases & Limited-Resource Settings

reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes ALSAnchorNet, a multimodal framework for classifying ALS and healthy controls. The claimed contributions are threefold. First, the paper introduces a multimodal framework for ALS versus HC classification, and it achieves SOTA performance. Second, it proposes a disease-guided attention mechanism that leverages intra-frontal connectivity to modulate whole-brain interactions. Third, the authors state that they will make their large ALS dataset publicly available upon acceptance.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The study is evaluated on one of the largest ALS cohorts reported to date.
2.The model architecture and input design are informed by prior biological knowledge, using a cross-attention mechanism to encode frontal lobe vulnerability.
3.The framework incorporates multimodal biomarkers, which help improve diagnostic performance and provide complementary information beyond connectivity features.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Baselines appear to be collapsing to the majority class since the recall is 1 for FC + SC only and MLP fusion. 
2.Weak baseline models. Classic connectome-specific baselines, such as BrainNetCNN, BrainGNN, Brain Network Transformer, etc., are not chosen. 
3.No variance reporting. Only mean 5-fold CV metrics are reported, standard deviations are not reported in tables 1 and 2.
4.Figure 1 inconsistency. FC and SC dimensions are visually different, while the text mentioned they are the same dimension. 
5.Poor methodological clarity.
The paper states that d_c = 60,516 is the vectorized upper-triangular dimension of a 246*246 matrix, which is contradictory.
In the Method section, the text “partition the connectivity embeddings” is misleading since the h_p and h_p,; appear to be created using different MLPs.
Eq 3 and Eq 4 define K and V with dimensions d_k and d_v, which is inaccurate since K and V need to be the same dimension
The implementation details describe a two-layer classifier (128 -> 64 -> 2), but Eq 10 only shows a single linear layer, which is contradictory
6.One of the claimed contributions, the Fusion Refinement Encoder, appears to be simply a concatenation operation followed by an MLP, which does not seem sufficiently novel.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses an underexplored problem and contributes one of the larger single-center ALS multimodal MRI cohorts to date, with a promised data release, which is a meaningful contribution to the field. Integrating glymphatic and CSF biomarkers with connectomes is also underexplored in the context of ALS. However, baseline comparisons are weak, the variance in the 5-fold experiment is not reported, and the method section contains several inconsistencies.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors honestly admitted to the methodological mistakes and promised to correct them in the camera-ready version. Baseline selection and the fusion novelty remain partially unresolved, but the application contribution and the promised data release could be meaningful to the field

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The authors introduced ALSAnchorNet, a biologically informed multimodal deep learning framework that integrates
connectivity, glymphatic, and CSF biomarkers for multimodal MRI-based ALS diagnosis. They proposed Frontal Anchor Attention (FAA), a disease-guided attention mechanism that leverages intra-frontal connectivity to modulate whole-brain interactions. This design improves diagnostic accuracy and interpretability while remaining parameter-efficient compared to Transformer-based fusion.
reviews.text_strengths:
The proposed FAA explicitly encodes known ALS vulnerability, making the model more meaningful than conventional DL fusion.
Their design combines connectivity with glymphatic and CSF biomarkers, demonstrating clear complementary gains beyond FC or SC alone.
Their approach shows increasing clinical credibility since region-level and connectivity analyses align with known motor network pathology.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The methodological contribution in this work seems incremental rather than fundamentally something new.
The proposed “anchor attention” is a simple adaptation of standard attention with a predefined region.
Additionally, fixing the frontal lobe as the anchor is not learned or validated and this may bias the proposed model and limit generalization to other ALS patterns.
In current work the fusion is largely MLP-based with simple concatenation and refinement. No strong comparison to more advanced cross-modal methods was reported which is very important.
The performed evaluation is limited to a relatively small cohort, with only moderate performance (accuracy: 77%), and without any external validation. It is unclear how well the proposed model generalizes.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper is well-motivated, but the overall contribution is limited by incremental novelty and a relatively simple methodological design. The proposed FAA is not sufficiently distinct from existing attention mechanisms, and key design choices are not justified. The fusion strategy is very basic, without strong comparison to more advanced multimodal approaches. Additionally, the evaluation is constrained to a small, single-center cohort with moderate performance, and no external validation was performed which leaves generalization unclear. These concerns limit the overall impact and strength of the work in this current form.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: While the rebuttal clarifies the clinical motivation and acknowledges several limitations, it does not sufficiently address my main concerns regarding the strength of the methodological contribution, limited validation, and generalization. The proposed attention mechanism remains closely related to standard attention with a fixed anatomical prior, while the multimodal fusion itself is relatively simple. External validation is also missing, and given the moderate performance and single-center evaluation, I do not feel the work is currently strong enough for acceptance.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper presents ALSAnchorNet, which combines an attention network for intra- and inter-frontal structural/functional connectivities with glymphatic and CSF biomarker features, to identify ALS (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis). The paper lacks statistical evaluation and comparison with advanced architectures, as all reviewers consistently pointed out. Although conducting more experiments is not asked during the rebuttal phase, they should be clarified in the rebuttal. The clarification questions about the methodology part need to be answered in the rebuttal.

The rebuttal sufficiently addressed reviewers’ questions regarding the clarification of the methodology and details of the experiments.
I recommend accept: post-rebuttal R1 and R2 both raised to Accept and the rebuttal addressed the primary AC’s methodology clarifications.

This paper’s main contribution is a biologically informed multimodal ALS diagnosis framework that combines connectivity features with glymphatic and CSF biomarkers, together with a clinically meaningful dataset that reviewers viewed as valuable to the field. The rebuttal did not eliminate every concern, yet it appears to have satisfactorily clarified several technical points and preserved positive reviewer support after rebuttal. On balance, the paper’s contribution to ALS imaging analysis and multimodal modeling is sufficient to justify acceptance despite some methodological limitations.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback and for recognizing our contributions: the biologically grounded design (all reviewers), one of the largest single-center ALS multimodal MRI cohort to date (R2), and the clinical credibility of our findings (R4). We address the main concerns below.
1.Methodological Clarifications (Meta, R2)
(1) d_c dimension (R2): We apologize for the typo. We use the full FC/SC matrix as input. We will remove the word “upper-triangular”. 
(2) Modality-specific encoders (R1-Q2, R2): h_p (FC) and h_{p} (SC) are produced by separate, modality-specific MLPs, not a shared encoder. We use different colors of MLP blocks in Figure 1 to indicate this, but provided the incorrect description in the Method section. We will rewrite the corresponding method section as “modality-specific embedding via two parallel MLPs.” and update equation (1) to reflect this.
(3) Eq. 3–4 (R2): We fully agree K and V matrix should share the same sequence length. We incorrectly use the same symbol for both the dimension of the K matrix and the normalization scale factor d_k, We will revise the method description to clarify.
(4) Eq. 10 (R2): Equation (10) will be corrected to reflect the two-layer classifier (128→64→2) used in implementation.
(5) Figure 1 (R2): FC and SC are indeed the same dimension; the visual difference was an illustration artifact and will be corrected. 
(6) Clinical variables (R1-Q1): The 93-dim vector comprises 3 ChP, 3 gBOLD, 70 FWF, 11 ALPS, and 6 PVS features. We will add this in Section 2.
2.Statistical Rigor (Meta, R1, R2)
Our 5-fold CV was stratified by class (R1-Q3); we will state this explicitly. Standard deviations across folds and paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests against each baseline will be added to Tables 1 and 2 in the camera-ready version.
3.Baselines (R2, R4)
Recall = 1.0 on weaker baselines (R2-Q1): This reflects collapse to the majority class (ALS), which actually highlights the difficulty of the task and the value of our biologically informed design — ALSAnchorNet avoids this collapse and achieves balanced sensitivity and specificity.
Connectome-specific baselines (R2-Q2, R4): We have compared SOTA methods in the ALS diagnosis task. Since the original papers did not provide specific names for their methodologies, we refer to them as CNN, GNN, and Transformer in the manuscript. Furthermore, the selected baselines include established CNN/GNN/Transformer-based frameworks, which represent the core innovations of BrainNetCNN, BrainGNN, and Brain Network Transformer, respectively. In contrast, our approach selects similar methodologies that are more specifically designed for ALS. To clarify that we have compared SOTA methods, we will update the naming of the baseline methods to ‘XXX et al.’ in the revised manuscript and include broader comparisons in the journal extension.
4.Novelty and Design (R4, R2-Q6)
We acknowledge that our contribution lies more in designing an appropriate method for an important and underexplored clinical application than in proposing fundamentally new machinery. To our knowledge, this is the first framework integrating connectomics with glymphatic/CSF biomarkers for ALS, and the first to encode frontal-lobe vulnerability as an architectural prior. FAA is not generic attention — its query is anatomically constrained to the frontal subnetwork, which is precisely what lets the biological prior shape whole-brain interactions. Fixing the anchor (R4) is intentional; learning it would discard the prior knowledge motivating the design.
5.Generalization (R1-Q5, R4)
We acknowledge the single-center limitation. Multimodal MRI ALS datasets are extremely scarce, which motivates our public data release of the processed data (159 ALS/107 HC). Cross-site validation will be reported in future work.
We will incorporate all clarifications and corrections in the camera-ready version.

title: AMFG: Anatomy-Grounded Multi-finding Guidance for Training-Free Chest X-Ray Generation
abstract: Text-conditioned diffusion models have enabled chest X-ray (CXR) synthesis, yet when prompted with multi-finding radiology reports they frequently omit findings or place them at anatomically incorrect locations. Existing approaches improve this through reinforcement learning or adapter training, but their reliance on additional training limits portability across base models. We propose AMFG (Anatomy-grounded Multi-Finding Guidance), a training-free framework applied at inference time to a frozen CXR diffusion model. AMFG comprises three complementary guidance signals: (1) finding presence guidance using a pretrained pathology classifier, (2) anatomical grounding guidance that constrains cross-attention maps to clinically correct regions via segmentation masks, and (3) finding interaction guidance that enforces spatial consistency among co-occurring findings. All components use only existing public models with no additional training. Experiments on MIMIC-CXR demonstrate that AMFG achieves the highest anatomical correctness among all compared methods and that this accuracy translates into superior downstream classifier performance, demonstrating that explicit anatomical grounding—rather than additional training alone—is key to clinically useful synthetic CXR data.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs
Machine Learning -> Reinforcement Learning / Control / Decision-Making

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper presents AMFG, a training-free guidance framework for generating multi-finding chest X-ray images at inference time using only public models. The main contributions include:
(1) Proposing a training-free framework that steers a frozen CXR diffusion model to generate anatomically faithful multi-finding CXR images at inference time, using only publicly available pretrained models without additional training. 
(2) Demonstrating through systematic ablation that the bottleneck in multi-finding CXR image generation is anatomical spatial supervision rather than model capacity. 
(3) Providing empirical evidence that anatomically correct synthetic CXR data directly improves downstream classifier performance with the largest gains on rare findings, suggesting that spatial accuracy determines clinical utility.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.AMFG guides a frozen diffusion model at inference using only publicly available pretrained models via three complementary signals. It requires no fine‑tuning or adapter training, making it easy to deploy across different base models.
2.AMFG directly addresses poor spatial calibration in CXR diffusion models by constraining cross‑attention to clinically correct regions via segmentation masks.
3.Comprehensive experiments evaluate AMFG’s generation quality through multiple complementary metrics (FID for image quality, mAUROC for finding presence, Dice and MF‑Acc for spatial localization), and demonstrate downstream clinical utility via classifier augmentation, collectively proving that AMFG improves both finding consistency and anatomical correctness.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.In latent diffusion models, x typically denotes the image, and z=enc(x) the VAE-compressed latent, with the diffusion process operating on z. While Fig. 1 and Eq. (6) use this convention correctly, Section 3.1 contains errors: it incorrectly mixes the predicted clean image x0 and zt through reversed diffusion formula​. Additionally, Section 3.2 and 3.3 use dec(x0), which is redundant since x0 should already be in pixel space. These inconsistencies may confuse readers and should be corrected.
2.Fig. 2 compares generated CXRs across methods, but no highlights (e. g. , arrows, bounding boxes, or overlaid masks) indicate where findings are correctly or incorrectly located. And it does not indicate what the baseline method is. Adding such annotations would better support the claimed advantages of AMFG.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses a critical problem in multi‑finding CXR image generation with a novel training‑free guidance framework. The method requires no fine‑tuning or adapter training, making it portable across base models. Comprehensive evaluation convincingly demonstrates generation quality and clinical utility. Minor weaknesses exist in presentation (e.g., notations, figure) but do not undermine the core contributions. Overall, the work is well‑structured, technically sound, and offers practical value for medical image synthesis.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes AMFG, a training-free inference-time guidance framework for steering a frozen chest X-ray (CXR) diffusion model to generate multi-finding images with anatomically correct placement. The method combines three complementary guidance signals: (1) a finding presence loss using a pretrained pathology classifier (CheXNet/TorchXRayVision), (2) an anatomical grounding loss that constrains cross-attention maps to clinically appropriate regions using a pretrained segmentation model (CheXmask) and a fixed finding-to-anatomy mapping, and (3) a finding interaction loss that penalizes attention overlap between distinct findings and enforces bilateral symmetry for bilateral findings. Experiments on MIMIC-CXR show that AMFG achieves superior anatomical correctness (Dice, MF-Acc) compared to both training-free and training-based baselines, and that this translates into improved downstream classifier performance.
reviews.text_strengths:
The core insight is compelling and clearly articulated: faithful multi-finding CXR generation requires not just ensuring findings are present, but controlling where they appear and how they interact spatially. This is a real limitation of existing methods that the paper addresses head-on.
The training-free design is a genuine practical advantage. By operating entirely at inference time on a frozen model, AMFG is portable across base models, which is a significant benefit over methods like XReal that require retraining adapters for each new model. This makes the approach broadly applicable.
The three-component guidance framework (what/where/how) is elegant and well-motivated. Each component has a clear purpose, and the ablation study (Table 2) convincingly shows the contribution of each, with the anatomical grounding loss (L_attn) being the dominant driver. This is a clean and interpretable result.
The evaluation is thoughtful. The authors introduce anatomical correctness metrics (Dice, MF-Acc) that go beyond standard FID/mAUROC, and they validate these metrics with cross-validation using an independent segmentor (PSPNet, r=0.94). The downstream classification experiment (Table 3) is particularly valuable because it connects generation quality to actual clinical utility.
The paper is well-written, concise, and clearly structured. The method section is easy to follow, and the figures effectively illustrate both the approach and the results.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The Dice evaluation metric shares the same segmentation model (CheXmask) used during guidance. Although the authors address this with a PSPNet cross-validation (r=0.94), this is a correlation check, not an independence guarantee. A stronger validation would be to evaluate Dice entirely with a segmentor that was never used during generation. The current setup risks inflating Dice scores even if the cross-validation suggests otherwise.
The finding-to-anatomy mapping (phi) is fixed and manually defined. The paper only demonstrates mappings for a limited set of findings, such as cardiac findings to heart and pulmonary findings to ipsilateral lung. What about findings that span multiple regions or don’t have a clear anatomical anchor (e.g., support devices, fractures)? The authors mention that such findings are guided by L_cls only, but this means the method effectively falls back to ungrounded guidance for a non-trivial subset of CXR findings.
The method is evaluated on a single base model (RoentGen) and a single dataset (MIMIC-CXR). The portability claim is a central selling point, but it remains unvalidated. Demonstrating AMFG on even one additional base model (e.g., a different CXR diffusion model) would substantially strengthen the paper.
The downstream classification experiment (Table 3) uses only 1,000 synthetic images for augmentation. It would be informative to see how performance scales with the number of synthetic images, and whether there is a saturation point or diminishing returns.
The inference time overhead (1.3x) is reported but not broken down by component. How much of this is from the segmentor, the classifier, and the gradient computation? This matters for practical deployment.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The noise-level-aware guidance schedule g(t) = sqrt(1 - alpha_bar_t) is a nice detail. The ablation showing it outperforms uniform guidance validates this design choice.
The bilateral symmetry loss (L_sym) is an interesting idea, but its impact seems modest in the ablation. Could the authors comment on how frequently bilateral findings appear in the test set?
Minor: The paper title is suppressed in headers (“Title Suppressed Due to Excessive Length”), which should be fixed for the camera-ready.
The qualitative examples in Figure 2 are helpful but limited to 4 cases. More examples (perhaps in supplementary) would be welcome.
How does AMFG handle conflicting guidance signals? For instance, if L_cls pushes the model toward a finding but L_attn constrains it to a region where the diffusion model struggles to render that finding?

This paper makes a clear and well-executed contribution to medical image synthesis. The insight that anatomical grounding, not additional training, is the key bottleneck for multi-finding CXR generation is convincingly demonstrated through both ablation and downstream evaluation. The training-free design offers genuine practical advantages. The evaluation is thorough, with appropriate metrics and a downstream task that validates clinical utility. The main limitations (shared segmentor between guidance and evaluation, single base model, fixed anatomy mapping) are real but do not undermine the core contribution. The method is simple, principled, and effective, which is exactly what makes for a good contribution.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This work addresses the gap of text-conditioned diffusion models for Chest X-Ray (CXR) image synthesis. The text conditions are provided by reports and these findings are usually more than one for each CXR report. The work focuses on the improvement of multi-finding text-conditioning that suffers from anatomically incorrect locations and the omission of findings present in the report. The training-free approach checks the presence of the finding and constrains it to an anatomical location. For example, pleural effusion can only exist in the lungs. Using a publicly available CXR synthesis model, they proved the free-training approach improved downstream pathological classification.
reviews.text_strengths: The methodology’s strength lies in the use of publicly available data and models to prove that a simple idea such as anatomical spatial constrains can improve models for other tasks, such as classification. The explanation of the architecture and used components for the training-free approach is solid and understandable and the experimental campaign includes varied approaches from other authors.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The non-overlap condition of the attention maps of the findings “must not excessively overlap”. This criteria is quite vague and I think it can change depending on the finding, so it needs further explanation. The evaluation metrics of Dice score brings up some doubts about the information leakage that the attention mask in the inference gives to the model, that it’s input later on is used for the classifier and it’s output GradCAM. Although the weights of these two models are not shared.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The work is well written and comprehensible, it seems to be reproducible due to it’s detailed description. And for the most part, the evaluation process seems robust. From the novelty point-of-view, the idea to condition text using spatial anatomical masks is interesting but can be seen in other fields as well. It is not a groundbreaking work but I would say it would an accept.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

meta_reviews.text: all reviewers agree the experiments are well thought and effective, the paper is clearly written. The remaining concerns can be addressed in rebuttal or camera-ready before acceptance

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their positive and constructive feedback. We clarify the main remaining concerns below.
(1) Central contribution and novelty. We agree that individual ingredients such as classifier guidance, attention guidance, and anatomical masks have precedents. AMFG’s contribution is the clinically grounded integration of these ingredients for the what/where/how failure modes in multi-finding CXR generation without additional training. The submitted ablation shows that the classifier guidance improves finding presence but the anatomical grounding guidance drives the localization gain, and Table 3 connects this anatomical correctness to downstream utility, with the largest improvement on rare findings. Thus, the key message is that anatomical grounding, not visual realism or additional training alone, is critical for clinically useful synthetic CXR data. Consistently, AMFG outperforms the trained XReal adapter on anatomical metrics (Dice .458 vs .421; MF-Acc 42.6% vs 38.4%).
(2) Dice evaluation and possible leakage. We agree that using CheXmask as the anatomical ROI source in both guidance and Dice evaluation is a limitation. However, the evaluated localization signal is not the guidance loss itself: Dice uses GradCAMs from an independent CheXpert-pretrained evaluation classifier, different from the NIH ChestX-ray14 classifier used for the classifier guidance. The PSPNet cross-validation reported in Sec. 4.2 (r=0.94, p<0.001) supports robustness to the mask source, although it is not a full independence guarantee. Importantly, the downstream classification experiment in Table 3 does not use segmentation masks at evaluation time and still shows AMFG’s largest gain, providing additional evidence that the improvement is not solely an artifact of the shared ROI source.
(3) Scope of the finding-anatomy mapping and the overlap regularizer. The mapping is intentionally conservative and transparent. AMFG grounds findings only when a reliable anatomical anchor is available; findings without a single target region are guided by the classifier guidance only, as stated in Sec. 3.3.We therefore do not claim universal anatomical grounding for every CXR label; expanding the mapping via radiology knowledge graphs remains future work. Likewise, the overlap regularizer is not a hard clinical assumption that pathologies cannot co-exist or overlap in the image. It is a soft attention-space regularizer that discourages multiple finding tokens from collapsing onto the same region. The ablation also shows that the anatomical grounding guidance is the primary driver, while the finding interaction guidance provides a smaller refinement. We will clarify this wording in the camera-ready.
(4) Empirical scope and presentation fixes. We agree that empirical validation currently uses one base model and one dataset, as acknowledged in Sec. 5.Our portability claim refers to AMFG being weight-preserving, requiring no base-model or adapter training, and using standard LDM interfaces, rather than completed empirical validation across CXR diffusion backbones; cross-architecture empirical validation remains future work. Systematic scaling of synthetic augmentation and per-component overhead profiling are also valuable follow-up directions. In the camera-ready, we will correct latent/image notation, running header, Figure 2 caption wording, and typographical issues. These are presentation and clarification fixes only and do not change the method, datasets, experimental protocol, evaluation protocol, or reported results.

title: An Artifact-Based Agent Framework for Adaptive and Reproducible Medical Image Processing
abstract: Medical imaging research is increasingly shifting from controlled benchmark evaluation toward real-world clinical deployment. In such settings, applying analytical methods extends beyond model design and requires dataset-aware workflow configuration and provenance tracking. Two requirements therefore become central: adaptability, the ability to configure workflows according to dataset-specific conditions and evolving analytical goals; and reproducibility, the guarantee that all transformations and decisions are explicitly recorded and re-executable. Here, we present an artifact-based agent framework that introduces a semantic layer to augment medical image processing.  The framework formalizes intermediate and final outputs through an artifact contract, enabling structured interrogation of workflow state and goal-conditioned assembly of configurations from a modular rule library.  Execution is delegated to a workflow executor to preserve deterministic computational graph construction and provenance tracking, while the agent operates locally to comply with most privacy constraints. We evaluate the framework on real-world clinical CT and MRI cohorts, demonstrating adaptive configuration synthesis, deterministic reproducibility across repeated executions, and artifact-grounded semantic querying. These results show that adaptive workflow configuration can be achieved without compromising reproducibility in heterogeneous clinical environments. Our code is available at https://github.com/MASILab/medimg-agent

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The proposed framework of this paper provides an agent-based architecture for integrating a semantic planning layer on top of a deterministic medical image processing workflow engine called Snakemake. In order to achieve reproducible executions of workflows and allowing for new datasets to be processed, this framework is based on the “artifact contract” concept: outputs from workflows are produced as type-based tuples (i. e. , type + attributes + provenance), which the long-lived, multipurpose agent interprets semantically via formalized artifact contracts to reason over artifact contract-compliant files, while simultaneously recording provenance for auditing purposes. By taking advantage of the structure of the state of the agent, the agent can complete two types of tasks: (1) generate configuration C = (π, θ) as a means of selecting rules from a modular rule library based on set of artifacts and desired analytical outcome at time of execution of workflow, and (2) respond to natural-language questions about contract-compliant artifacts (i. e. , structured output files produced by executing workflows) while allowing workflows to execute deterministically. The framework has been validated for use in three clinical cohorts (NLST, LungCaTrial, and BrainICU) and across 9 different workflows covering distinct analytical goals (curation, lung lobe/nodule segmentation, cancer risk estimation, harmonization of MRI images, and brain segmentation), and through the use of an ablation where access to the artifact contract was removed, the contribution of the structured basis provided by the artifact contract to the agent’s functioning was documented.
reviews.text_strengths:
S1.The authors aim at addressing a real issue related to the clinical translation of imaging techniques; in particular the authors have conducted research and implemented pipelines on actual PACS derived data and know that there is a large difference between the benchmarks of controlled environments and the clinical dataset, which include format differences, nested archives, planning/localizer images, inconsistent naming and missing metadata. The majority of work presented at MICCAI focuses primarily on the architecture of the model; however, this paper is focused on the infrastructure level, where most of the practical failures actually occur. 
S2.The decision to separate the semantic design (LLM-based, probabilistic) of a system from its deterministic execution (workflow engine) is an intentional and principled approach to achieving both a degree of flexibility as well as scientific repeatability in the final application of the system. The artifact contract is the interface between the two levels of the system architecture and is a very clever method of abstraction, since it is (a) representing the state of the artifact that can be queried, (b) gathering provenance data about the artifact that can be used for auditing purposes and (c) constraining the LLM reasoning to only the structured fields of data associated with the artifact rather than the raw filenames from which the artifact was created. This will help to alleviate a true risk with the use of LLM-driven pipeline tools. 
S3.The decision to run fully on-premise using Ollama with a DeepSeek-R1 14B system presents a significant engineering commitment that illustrates recognition of the impact of regulatory restrictions (HIPAA/GDPR/institutional agreements) applicable to clinical imaging research/data. This is crucial to be able to use the results derived using the constructed system in other clinical areas and differentiates the work from cloud-dependent agentic systems. 
S4.The ablation that removed access to the artifact registry (Section 3, Table 2) provides a direct quantitative measure of the value of the artifact contract. By demonstrating that filtering query accuracy drops from 90-95% down to 10-15% when the artifact contract is removed, the authors prove the observed accuracy is a function of structured grounding rather than solely LLM capabilities. The ablation design allows for the isolation of the contribution of structured grounding when producing the observed accuracy levels. 
S5.The three cohorts include research CT (NLST), clinical CT (LungCaTrial) with significant heterogeneity, and research MRI (BrainICU) with moderate heterogeneity. There are 9 different workflows, covering distinct analytical goals such as data curation, segmentation, risk estimation, and harmonization. This wide range of goals supports the framework nature of the paper, while also creating an opportunity for authors to fall into a common pitfall of evaluating only one curated dataset. 
S6.The authors have committed to making the code and report available using Snakemake for deterministic execution, which is also a well-established and auditable tool in bioinformatics. There is 100% DAG equivalence across repeated executions under all circumstances.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
W1.Only one existing workflow adaptation tool was compared in the study. Reference works such as Snakemake and NextFlow were mentioned; however, there were no time comparisons or calibration of performance against any of these systems (including your domain expert’s manual workflow assembly) or a “proof of correct operation” using the comparison with any of these systems or as a baseline. Findings from developing correct workflows indicate that the authors should have compared their own algorithm and tooling against a small but viable source of aggregated evidence including i) traditional manual scripting in Snakemake, ii) a conventional LLM, not using an artifact contract, and not using raw file listings, and iii) a basis for comparing against a BIDS formatted Pipeline Manager, would have provided substantial evidence to establish that the Artifact Contract architecture provides the greatest benefit to the user or workflows. 
W2.A small sample of semantic query brands for testing the audience of the model for providing statistics. Evaluating only 20 questions per category across these datasets provides a small sample size, and lacking a description of an independent generation protocol raises concerns of confirmation bias. The authors need to establish the method used for creating the question set to show their independence and defend against confirmation bias, as the system to establish the benchmarks and created the questions were written by the authors, thus leading to the possibility of the authors subconsciously designing the questions to enable the system to correctly answer all questions, thereby providing support for the authors of the system. At a minimum, the authors of the paper must include a sufficient description of the question generation protocol to establish its independence from bias and ideally include questions authored by an independent party (a collaborating clinician or radiologist). 
W3.Insufficient timing, latency, and cost analyses will hinder any framework paper that possesses dynamism being able to count any definite human labor saved; without knowing how long it takes to build a workflow in the framework compared with an expert manually, what the agent latency (LLM inference time) will be, and how many tokens are required for each query, we cannot determine whether the framework provides any real increase in operational efficiency or simply a better-structured abstraction of an essentially identical performance. 
W4.The true ground for determining adaptability metrics consists of a single domain expert’s opinion. Each of the metrics used (Initial Rule Match (IRM), Plan Iteration (PL), and Final Output (FO)) will be made against an “expert provided ground truth. “ The professional profile, years of experience, and institutional independence of the expert are not delineated, nor is there a measure of inter-rater reliability. Multiple valid ways exist to build a medical imaging workflow (i. e. , several valid strategies will exist to enclose intensity normalization, all may work in their respective applications). Since a single-domain-expert ground truth may lead to confusion, two or more experts’ agreement would greatly increase confidence in those metrics. 
W5.The scalability of the rule library within this evaluation is never stated. The total number of rules within each of the analytical goals as shown in figure A/C; each will contain 11 – 20 rules for this project; there will likely be a few dozen overall; an actual clinical workflow may run in the hundreds of rules across many modalities, and retrieval/planning over a large rule library is known to degrade agent performance due to context window constraints and selection ambiguity. The paper does not discuss how the framework scales, whether the rule library would be modularized or hierarchically indexed, or how performance degrades as the rule count grows. 
W6.The assertion that the method is reproducible is factually correct, but somewhat exaggerated. 100% Database Access (DAG) equivalence across multiple executions is anticipated when Snakemake is given control of the execution and replicability. The fact that an agent can repeatedly create the same configuration C when the same inputs are supplied is the true novel contribution of this procedure; the agent achieves this by being programmed with a defined Non-Fuzzy Metric (NFM) and defined inputs. Therefore, the LLM’s output is based on its sampling temperature and prompt consistency and is not based on Snakemake. 
To clarify the above statement, it is worth noting that the DAG equivalence of results is dependent on the probabilistic planning behavior, in which all planning is predetermined. The authors do not specify the decoding temperature for DeepSeek-R1 (e. g. , T=0.0 for greedy decoding), leaving the source of the agent’s deterministic output generation ambiguous. 
W7.Limited variations in LLM. The document only contains references to two different local LLMs, both 14 billion LLMs: DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen. If smaller local LLMs (7 billion) or larger local LLMs (70 billion, proprietary versions of GPT-4/Claude) were to undergo testing, or if an acknowledgment of the trade-off between localized privacy and capability was indicated, this would be beneficial for clinical facilities in the selection of their infrastructure. 
W8.The density of the information contained in Figure 2 (system overview) is difficult to read, as it contains a complete user layer, agent layer, execution layer, rule library, memory type, skill set, and an example configuration type all within the same diagram, therefore, at the time of first review, the reader is unable to systematically read the diagram. The diagram could easily be split into two (one depicting the ‘architectural depiction’ and the other depicting the ‘workflow action type’) to provide a clearer understanding. Similarly, the example dialog in Table 1 uses “[omit to save space]” several times, which reduces the transparency of the interaction loop. 
W9.There is a lack of discussion of agent-side failure modes other than missing metadata. Section 3 (Adaptability) discusses that most failures result from missing or flawed DICOM metadata. This is useful knowledge, but the submission also should discuss agent-side failure modes such as hallucinating nonsensical rules, selecting conflicting rules, or failing to terminate planning. All of these failure modes can easily occur in a real-world deployment of the framework; therefore, mechanisms to address how the proposed generally-constrained design can manage them would be worthwhile to include. 
W10.The submission does not propose any methodological innovation for image analysis. It’s a framework/systems paper, not a new algorithm/model for a specific medical imaging application. Therefore, this may present some discomfort to reviewers in an MIC-oriented venue; however, this is actually a positive in terms of the Clinical Translation track. Authors should make it clear in the rebuttal that the intention of this submission is to be part of the Clinical Translation track, not a pure methodology track.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Thank you for your submission. I appreciate that you are tackling a very relevant, underrepresented area at MICCAI. The artifact contract is also a neat representation of an accessible abstraction, as is your separation of semantic planning from deterministic execution. 
Here are some of my suggestions for enhancing your work:
1.In the ablation studies, provide a pure LLM agent (no artifact contract) as a baseline comparison to Tables 1 and 2, ideally alongside a manual Snakemake pipeline developed by a domain expert. Right now, your ablation studies in Table 2 are a good start, but represent against a degraded/less capable version of the tested system rather than against established workflows. 
2.Provide some quantification (in hours, for example) as to how much time/effort clinicians will save from using your system. This would give credibility to translating your work into the clinical setting, perhaps through the use of a plot of assembly time versus workflow complexity or at an average assembly time per workflow. 
3.Please disclose how the authors of the semantic query benchmark questions created them, and if possible, engage a clinician who will not be a co-author to draft some questions as well.
