4.Clarify your statement about reproducibility: DAG equivalence is a feature of Snakemake workflows, not of your agent. Your contribution should therefore not be described as reproducible but rather as producing configuration stability across LLM sampling (which is important). Did you use temperature=0?
5.Talk about how the rule library can grow; discuss ways that the agent might produce false (“hallucinated”) rules or fail to stop running conflicts when choosing which rule to run. 
6.Look at doing something like dividing Figure 2 into separate figures so that it is easier to view. Also, make changes to the example shown in Table 1’s conversation to shorten it up a bit. 
7.When presenting the rebuttal position to the clinical translation track, be sure to point out that this paper is providing an infrastructure, as opposed to algorithms. 
Overall, the paper has a lot of well-thought-out engineering and provides a validation of a real clinical translation issue. The above comments would enhance the paper’s overall contribution significantly.

I suggest Weak Accept (4). The manuscript presents an essential problem in clinical translation that is not as relevant as it could be at MICCAI, outlines an architectural solution (artifact contract + constrained agent + deterministic executor) that is based on principles, and validates that solution on three real clinical cohorts with a meaningful ablation. The artifact contract abstraction is a true contribution that goes beyond the “LLM + tool use” framing; placing a constraint on the agent to reason through structured artifact fields that contain explicit provenance is a fundamental solution to solving the critical grounding and reproducibility challenges that have made the use of LLMs for clinical pipeline tools limited. The ablation contained evidence of a 70% accuracy improvement, indicating that the artifact contract is actually producing useful results rather than just wrapping the results of the LLM. 
I have several greater evaluative concerns than conceptual for this submission. First, the baselines utilized are far too limited to a severely degraded self-baseline. Second, the semantic query benchmark appears not only small, but has a strong possibility of being constructed with author assistance from an as-yet-unreported author source, thereby creating substantial issues with its reliability. Third, the claim surrounding reproducibility conflates Snakemake’s (Container) deterministic outcomes with the agent’s own outcome stability, thus exhibiting a reduction in overall quality when making general conclusions about agent reproducibility. Finally, the scalability of the rule library has not been addressed. The overall strength of the authors’ claim of the artifact contract serving as the enabler to the proposed solution would be greatly enhanced with direct comparisons to either manual pipeline assembly or an unconstrained LLM agent. Additionally, I believe measurements of (and possibly statistics for) how long each of the tasks took, or how much effort was required to complete the tasks, would be imperative for any paper framed around adaptability and clinical translation.
All things considered, I think the paper has a strong enough contribution to the field, and the problem it addresses is of sufficient importance that I would recommend accepting it if the authors can adequately respond to the evaluation deficiencies in their rebuttal. I would not be against rejecting the paper, since there are very real issues with the evaluation; I would rather see it accepted than rejected, because the quality of clinical translation infrastructure papers submitted to MICCAI is not too high.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper addresses the important question of translating research imaging workflows to clinical practice. It proposes an agentic framework providing (1) adaptability to heterogeneous clinical environment, and (2) reproducibility through an integration with snakemake and test-retest experiments.
reviews.text_strengths:
The use of AI agents to address “technical” clinical heterogeneity (e.g., heterogeneous data organizations) is very thoughtful
Thorough problem formulation, unusual for a software tool contribution.
Open-source, local execution stack including Ollama and snakemake.
Broad evaluation including reproducibility, adaptability, semantic query and ablation.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Reproducibility experiments do not test DAG stability across multiple LLMs or LLM versions (e.g., DeepSeek versions)
Limited discussion of related work.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The proposed framework is very thoughtful, well described and evaluated overall. My main comment relates to the lack of depth of the reproducibility evaluation, as in my experience results tend to vary substantially across LLMs and LLM versions. Measuring the variability of the generated DAGs across LLMs and their versions would be very useful. In addition, the paper lacks a discussion of the related work on existing systems to deal with clinical heterogeneity.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose a novel, artifact-contract-based agent framework designed to enhance the adaptability and reproducibility of neuroimaging workflows. The core innovation is the introduction of a semantic layer atop deterministic execution (via Snakemake). This layer utilizes an artifact contract to encode intermediate and final workflow states into queryable records with explicit provenance. The system features a multi-agent architecture for workflow assembly, goal planning, and semantic querying, while maintaining a human-in-the-loop approval process for generated Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs). Notably, the framework is designed for local deployment to satisfy clinical privacy constraints.
reviews.text_strengths:
Novelty Use of Artifacts: Unlike many workflow managers that focus solely on the final output, this framework prioritizes the paper trail of intermediate results, making the entire processing pipeline transparent and queryable.
It is interesting how it keeps the agents from unfounded generation
The authors use ablation studies to highlight how it improves performance
Formal Rigor: The authors provide a clear mathematical formulation of the framework, which adds theoretical weight to the proposed architecture.
Adaptable Framework: A core strength of the framework is its ability to create workflow configurations dynamically based on specific analytical objectives and by using a modular rule library in response to user commands, heterogeneous datasets without manual reconfiguration.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Architectural Ambiguity: While the high-level theory is sound, the specific interactions between the workflow components (ex: the Knowledge, Semantic Querying, Workflow Planning Agent, Workflow Assembling Agent, and Snakemake) are underspecified.
Snakemake appears to be the foundation of the framework, but how it functions or the reason for its selection is not specified.
The paper lacks discussion of relevant neuroimaging workflow tools such as Nipoppy, Neurobagel or the BIDS app ecosystem, and provides no justification for the selection of Snakemake over other executors (e.g., Nextflow).
Very vague language is used. In Section 2.2 Adaptation via Workflow Assembly, it is unclear what the “planning component” is or how the “inspection skill” evaluates new datasets or how a feasible goal is established.
Is DeepSeek used for all the mentioned agents? Was there fine-tuning/training involved? This isn’t specified and little description is given for agents other than the Semantic Querying Agent.
Deterministic Paradox: There is a fundamental tension between the deterministic claim and the use of LLMs (DeepSeek/Qwen) for semantic querying and planning. The authors do not sufficiently address how the LLM is configured to control non-determinism or whether LLM hallucinations or non-deterministic sampling could compromise the contract.
While the presence of artifacts and rules are supposed to ground the LLMs in truth, it is not clear how that prevents hallucinations or a loss of reproducibility with introduction of subtle variations possibly from different computational environments
Incomplete Implementation Details: Crucial information regarding computational requirements is missing and the handling of competing tools (e.g., different brain segmentation algorithms/pipelines) is missing. It is unclear how a user defines the underlying toolsets within the configuration.
In brain MRI processing, multiple tools can perform the same task. It is unclear whether the framework restricts or supports specific tools, and at what level users are expected to specify them. It is also not specified whether the system relies on pre-written Snakemake wrappers or generates them dynamically. These details are not addressed in the paper.
Due to the framework’s use of several LLMs and GPUs for the experiments, it would be helpful to specify what computational resources a potential user might need (GPU, memory, etc.)
Nitpick: DeepSeek has been banned or is heavily regulated by some institutions. If the user isn’t legally allowed to use this model at work, is there a workaround?
Minor comment: In the experiments, 2 out of the 3 datasets are not cited, so it is unclear if it is possible to obtain them in order to replicate the paper. Moreover, besides describing them as moderate/high heterogeneity, it is unclear of their composition or file layout.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
With the emphasis on reproducibility in the introduction, why was the reproducibility experiment limited to only examining the DAGs for 2 repetitions?
The authors should clarify what constitutes “representative questions” for the querying agent and whether more rigid query structures (e.g., SQL-style) were considered to mitigate LLM miscommunication.

This paper introduces an interesting concept in the semantic layer for medical imaging provenance, addressing the urgent need for adaptable frameworks. The artifact contract is also a strong conceptual contribution. However, key components (the planning logic, tool-set integration, framework component interaction, and LLM non-determinism) are not described with enough detail to justify an “Accept” or to fully clarify how the proposed framework functions or why certain design choices were made. The limited experimental reproducibility repetitions (n=2) and the lack of clarity on dataset availability further weigh down the score.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper presents a novel AI Agent with semantic planning layers on top of a deterministic medical image processing workflow engine (Snakemake) to address the issues of adapting research workflows to clinical practice, where data heterogeneity and privacy constraints limit this transition. The paper reads easily and is well-organized. The problem formulation is clear and particularly remarkable for a software tool paper. In addition, the proposed framework has been designed to address clinical constraints: open-source models and local execution to meet privacy requirements. The authors provided a deep and broad evaluation of their framework across 3 datasets, including a real-world clinical dataset, along with relevant ablations. Overall, this paper presents a strong contribution that targets an unmet need in research-to-clinics transitions. I recommend its provisional acceptance, but would still like to suggest the authors address a few concerns raised by reviewers:
R1 and R3 pointed out a lack of clarity in model presentation, with only minor justifications of implementation parameters, model choices, etc. Please add a bit more detail about these.
For more insights on clinical usability, provide a few metrics on computation time, assembly time vs. workflow complexity, to better highlight the benefit of the proposed framework for clinical practice.
All reviewers were concerned about the non-deterministic nature of the workflow. While the authors claim that adding this semantic planning layer on top of an LLM leads to determinism and reproducible results, they should also discuss stability across multiple LLMs or versions, and how the introduction of subtle variations, possibly from different computational environments, would affect reproducibility.
The paper lacks discussion about how the proposed framework compares (theoretically) to relevant neuroimaging workflow tools such as Nipoppy, Neurobagel, or the BIDS app ecosystem. I strongly advise the authors to include a statement on related work and a literature review. 
In any case, as stated by R1, I believe this paper falls in the scope of “Clinical translation” rather than “MIC”. Since the aforementioned comments would be critical for a method paper, its positioning as a clinical translation paper encourages me to recommend acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank all three reviewers for their comments and the AC’s recommendation of early acceptance. We are especially grateful for the consistent recognition of the artifact contract, the semantic/deterministic separation, and the clinical-translation focus. This response clarifies major points raised by the AC & reviewers.
1.Determinism and stability across LLMs. Meta-Reviewer, R1 (W6), R2, R3
We appreciate this point and would like to clarify our framing. Snakemake provides DAG-level determinism once a configuration C is fixed. For a fixed C assembled by the agent, it is automatically stored as an artifact and can be re-executed to produce the exact output. This is verified in Tables 1 & 2.Independent user interaction with the agent may produce different configuration C, however, it will always check pre-existing configuration artifact. We will clarify our definition of reproducibility in the camera-ready version.
2.Related work: BIDS, Nipoppy, Neurobagel. Meta-Reviewer, R1, R3
Thank you for the suggestion. We would like to clarify that BIDS, Nipoppy, and Neurobagel are complementary standards/tools rather than alternative agent architectures, i.e., each can be registered as a rule (or set of rules) and incorporated in our modular library S (e.g., a BIDS-conversion rule, a Neurobagel-query rule). Our major contribution lies in the semantic agent layer and artifact contract that sit above such tools, i.e., prompting with users to decide which tools to use in which dataset. We will add a related-work paragraph making the complementary relationship between our work and these existing tools more explicit.
3.Report timing. Meta-Reviewer, R1 (W3)
This is a very valuable comment. Due to the page limit, we will include discuss this in the Discussion; more thorough time analysis will be included in our journal extension.
4.Other comments from R1
We sincerely thank R1 for the careful reading and valuable comments on strengths and weaknesses. Several points were already in the paper but can be stated more visibly, and we will tighten them in the camera-ready: stating decoding temperature explicitly (W6); positioning the paper as Clinical Translation (W10); elaborate on Figure 2 and Table 1 dialog (W8); and briefly noting agent-side failure modes and guardrails imposed by the contract (W9). The remaining comments (additional baselines, larger independently-authored query sets, rule-library scaling, broader LLM-size sweeps; W1, W2, W5, W7) are excellent directions, and we will include them in future work due to page limit.
5.Other comments from R2
We thank R2 for the positive evaluation. The cross-LLM reproducibility and related-work are addressed above, will be reflected in the camera-ready version.
6.Other comments from R3
We sincerely thank R3 and gently clarify a few points. We will incorporate clarifications in the camera-ready.
6a) DeepSeek-R1 the open-source model and the DeepSeek App are two different things: the former is a set of model weights and architecture released publicly, while the latter is a cloud-based service (e.g., ChatGPT). In our paper, we download the weights and run inference entirely on our local GPU (Sec. 2.2). Conceptually, it is not fundamentally different from downloading a pretrained nnU-Net and running inference locally.
6b) No fine-tuning was performed on any LLM, as such fine tuning is beyond clinical computational capabilities. The framework operates by prompting & artifact-contract grounding as inference mode, consistent with the single-A6000 footprint reported in the paper. 
6c) Competing tools (e.g., alternative brain-segmentation pipelines) are each registered as a separate rule in S; the agent selects among them based on goal, artifact state, and user preference upon request.
We again thank the meta reviewer and all reviewers; the feedback will help us improve this and our future work.

title: Anatomically Accurate 3D Vessel Generation via 3-Phase Chebyshev Curve Diffusion
abstract: Large-scale collection of 3D vascular data is inherently difficult, resulting in scarce publicly available datasets. Existing methods represent vessel edges as discrete point sequences, which cannot guarantee smoothness and lose millimeter-scale size information through normalization. We propose 3-Phase Chebyshev Curve Diffusion, a framework that generates vessel curves directly in a continuous polynomial coefficient space, an approach not previously explored for vascular generation. Chebyshev coefficients yield a fixed-dimensional, length-independent representation that inherently ensures C-infinity smoothness without post-processing. We further design auxiliary modules that recover mm-scale size lost due to normalization and a mechanism that preserves overall curve trajectories. On the ImageCAS coronary artery dataset, we achieve superiority over two existing methods across key anatomical metrics, including up to a 5.2-times reduction in curvature Wasserstein distance, while confirming mm-scale accuracy.
subject_areas: Applications -> Digital Twins / Simulation / Synthetic Data
Machine Learning -> Synthetic Data / Data-centric AI

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The core contribution lies in proposing a novel vessel curve representation (Chebyshev polynomial coefficient space) and a corresponding three-phase diffusion generation framework, which is primarily a methodological innovation.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Novel representing vessel centerlines as Chebyshev polynomial coefficients is an elegant choice. Chebyshev polynomials achieve minimax-optimal approximation on [−1,1], providing clear theoretical advantages over B-splines (knot-placement dependency) and Fourier bases (Gibbs phenomena at open endpoints). The K=48 expansion achieves 0.003–0.020 mm reconstruction error, far below the ~0.3 mm voxel resolution, demonstrating the compact efficiency of this representation.
2.It is very interesting for polar decomposition and three-phase diffusion. Decomposing Cartesian coefficient pairs (c_n,k, c_b,k) into magnitude r_k and angle θ_k enables diffusion in domain-appropriate spaces. The ablation study convincingly validates this design (removing polar decomposition degrades curvature Wasserstein by 11×). The decision to sample θ_k≥1 from von Mises distributions is data-driven (Pearson correlation <0.04), reflecting careful analysis of the data distribution
3.It presented the comprehensive and convincing evaluation of the method. The evaluation spans tree-level (CD), edge-level (Wasserstein distances for curvature, tortuosity, radius, tapering), physiological constraints (Murray law compliance), and statistical coverage (Bounds compliance). The improvement of Murray’s law compliance to 35–37% is particularly noteworthy for physiological plausibility. The ablation study clearly isolates each component’s contribution.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.For the presentation of topology, it is limited to tree structures. The method is constrained to binary tree topology by the Stage 1 RVAE, unable to handle loop structures (e. g. , circle of Willis) or more complex vascular networks. This severely limits generalizability. Discrete diffusion models [18,17] mentioned in related work already handle arbitrary network topologies, representing a notable regression. The authors should discuss specific technical challenges for extending to general graph topologies in more detail.
2.It somewhat unfairness of baseline comparisons. VesselGPT [8] was originally designed for cerebral vasculature, not coronary arteries, and supports only unconditional generation. Although the authors adapted it, cross-domain transfer may not represent VesselGPT’s true capabilities. VesselGPT supports only unconditional generation while this method and PartVessel use GT topology as conditioning, making qualitative comparison (Fig. 3) inherently unfair. The authors should provide more details about the adaptation and discuss its limitations. Moreover, with only two baselines (one being the foundation framework), the comparison lacks breadth. A comparison with diffusion in B-spline coefficient space, for instance, would more convincingly demonstrate the advantage of the Chebyshev representation.
3.With Stage training, the authors acknowledge a significant gap in mean bifurcation count for LCA (3.2 vs. GT 4.8), which directly affects tree-level CD and overall generation quality. However, the Stage 1 modifications are limited to auxiliary heads; the topology generation itself is not improved. Since Stage 1 topology constrains Stage 2 inputs, this upstream bottleneck may systematically limit overall quality and deserves deeper analysis. We would like to see the detail discussion about it in the revised version
4.The motivation emphasizes the value of generated vessels for segmentation training or endovascular robot simulation. While the experimental section validates no downstream applications. There is no demonstration that generated vessels improve segmentation via data augmentation, nor any evaluation of generated sample suitability in simulation environments. This leaves the practical clinical value without direct evidence.
5.Experiments are conducted only on ImageCAS coronary arteries (LCA and RCA). Given the relatively regular structure of coronary arteries (mainly binary trees), performance on more complex vascular structures such as cerebral and pulmonary vessels remains unknown. Cross-anatomical generalization is not validated.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1.Recommend reporting GT Murray’s law compliance: The ±20% threshold is used, but the GT compliance rate itself is not reported. If GT compliance is much higher than 35–37%, substantial improvement room exists; if GT is also low, the metric of clinical significance should be reconsidered.
2.We would like to see the sufficient discussion of generation diversity. The qualitative results mention “PartVessel” two samples are nearly identical while ours are visually distinct. A quantitative diversity metric such as average pairwise distance among generated samples would more rigorously support this claim.

The core contribution, performing vessel curve diffusion generation in Chebyshev polynomial coefficient space, is a genuinely novel and technically deep methodological innovation. This representation elegantly addresses fundamental problems of discrete point-sequence representations (no smoothness guarantee, length-dependent dimensionality) while providing minimax optimal approximation guarantees. The polar decomposition and three-phase diffusion design have clear physical motivation and statistical justification, supported by thorough ablation experiments. The mm-scale recovery via ScaleHead is unique among existing vessel generation methods, with clear clinical translation value.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The authors propose a vessel generation method based on the PartVessel framework. A 3-phase Chebyshev curve diffusion scheme is used to generate vessel curves while ensuring 
C^∞ smoothness. The method is evaluated on a public dataset and shows improved performance over two existing methods while preserving anatomical features.
reviews.text_strengths: The 3-phase Chebyshev curve diffusion and temperature-calibration mechanisms improve vessel generation, enhancing curve smoothness and mm-scale size consistency.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The use of public datasets demonstrates the performance of the proposed method in specific cases. The validation could be strengthened by further testing on synthetic data that represents extreme or challenging scenarios.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The 3-phase Chebyshev curve diffusion and temperature-calibration mechanisms improve vessel generation, showing good performance on public datasets, but validation could be strengthened with synthetic tests under extreme or challenging scenarios.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper builds on PartVessel, which generates synthetic vessels in three steps: generating a key graph representing overall vessel topology, generating each vessel edge, and assembling the full vessel tree. Unlike PartVessel, which represents each edge as a discrete point sequence, this paper represents each edge as a continuous polynomial function using Chebyshev polynomials. This gives C∞ smoothness by construction and a fixed 102-dimensional vector per edge regardless of edge length or complexity. These 102 coefficients are generated using three separate diffusion models, handling bending magnitude, bending direction, and radius profile independently. Auxiliary modules ScaleHead and EdgeRadiusHead recover mm-scale dimensions lost through normalization, which is applied during training to stabilize learning.
reviews.text_strengths:
Strengths:
1.Diffusing in Chebyshev coefficient space is genuinely new for vascular generation. Chebyshev polynomials achieve minimax-optimal approximation, giving 0.003–0.020mm reconstruction error against a 0.3mm voxel resolution using just 48 coefficients per edge.
2.Smoothness is guaranteed by the representation itself. This directly shows in results: curvature variance of 21.5 vs PartVessel’s 107.2, which nearly matches ground truth (23.9).
3.For actual medical use (surgical simulation, segmentation training), having real physical dimensions is important. Compared methods can’t be evaluated in mm at all. This method achieves within 5% error on length and 3% on radius.
Using Murray’s law compliance as a metric goes beyond geometric evaluation. The improvement is substantial: 0% (PartVessel), 17% (VesselGPT), 37% (theirs), suggesting the continuous radius representation produces genuinely more physiologically plausible vessels.
5.Every component of the pipeline is individually tested, including hint nodes, polar decomposition, phase decomposition, and temperature calibration.
6.Observing that higher-order angles have near-zero correlation with conditioning (Pearson < 0.04) and sampling them from von Mises distributions rather than a diffusion model is an efficient, empirically grounded architectural choice.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Weaknesses:
1.Stage 1 (key graph generation) is unchanged and is a clear bottleneck. The paper acknowledges that Stage 1 under-generates bifurcations for LCA (mean 3.2 vs ground truth 4.8). This directly hurts CD on LCA, which the paper attributes to Stage 1 rather than curve quality. Since Stage 1 determines the overall topology of the vessel tree, leaving it unimproved limits the clinical utility of the full pipeline regardless of how good Stage 2 is.
2.Murray’s law compliance is low in absolute terms. 35-37% means roughly two out of three bifurcations violate a known physiological law. The paper frames this as a win over baselines, which it is, but the absolute number is weak for any downstream clinical application. The paper does not discuss why compliance is still so low or how it could be improved.
3.The ScaleHead is a simple and expected engineering addition. Predicting a single scalar scale factor from the root hidden state is a straightforward MLP regression task. The more interesting question is whether the scale factor could be made a direct part of the latent space or sampled from a learned distribution rather than point-estimated, which would give control over tree size at inference. As implemented, ScaleHead always predicts the same deterministic scale for a given z, limiting size diversity in generated trees. This is a limitation worth discussing that the paper does not address.
4.The VesselGPT comparison is questionable. VesselGPT was designed for cerebral vasculature and is evaluated here on the coronary arteries out of domain. Despite this disadvantage, VesselGPT outperforms the proposed method on tapering (LCA) and radius (RCA). This raises questions about how competitive the proposed method would be against VesselGPT on its intended domain and weakens the validity of the comparison overall.
5.Single dataset and single anatomy. The method is evaluated exclusively on the ImageCAS coronary artery dataset with 855/861 samples. There is no evaluation on other vessel types such as cerebral, hepatic, or pulmonary vasculature, which have different geometric and topological properties. It is unclear whether the Chebyshev representation and the 3-phase decomposition generalise beyond coronary arteries.
6.K=48 coefficients is not justified beyond reconstruction error. The paper sets K=48 based on achieving low reconstruction error but provides no analysis of the tradeoff between K and generation quality. A smaller K would mean a lower-dimensional diffusion space, potentially easier to learn. It is possible that a much smaller K would achieve similar generation quality while being simpler, but this is never investigated.
7.The paper builds heavily on PartVessel but provides only a brief and difficult to follow description of it, making the paper hard to understand without referring to the original PartVessel work. A more complete description of PartVessel would make the paper more self-contained.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The paper would benefit from a brief introduction to Chebyshev polynomials, as readers unfamiliar with approximation theory may find it difficult to follow the core technical contribution without this background.

The primary factor in favour of acceptance is the representational shift from discrete point sequences to Chebyshev coefficient space, which is principled, novel, and demonstrably effective. The primary factors limiting the score are the unchanged Stage 1, which the paper itself acknowledges as a bottleneck, and the evaluation on a single dataset and single anatomy, leaving generalisability unclear. These open questions place the paper at Weak Accept.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text: Reviews are positive and note significant empirical improvements and a relatively novel vessel representation/learning method.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and AC. To our knowledge, vessel-centerline diffusion in Chebyshev coefficient space (Section 1) is novel; polar decomposition is validated by ablation (Table 2: 11× curvature degradation when removed). All quantities derive from existing data (no new training/generation).
1.VesselGPT comparison [R1, R3]. 
VesselGPT (MICCAI 2025), originally evaluated on cerebral vasculature, is autoregressive; we adapt it to ImageCAS coronary arteries and, since VesselGPT supports only unconditional generation, evaluate 1,000 samples (Section 4). Across 14 cells (Table 1), ours obtains the best in 11—curvature and tortuosity Wasserstein best on both arteries; Murray’s compliance (35–37%) surpasses PartVessel (0%) and VesselGPT (15–17%). VesselGPT leads on tapering (LCA) and radius (RCA), aligned with its B-spline cross-section parameterization (Section 2); our 3-phase design trades local radius fidelity for global geometry. CD: RCA best (Ours 59.0 / PartVessel 72.8 / VesselGPT 119.9), LCA close to PartVessel (Ours 59.1 / 57.0 / 99.0); the LCA gap is from Stage-1 bifurcation undercount, not curve quality.
2.Stage-1 bifurcation undercount [R1, R3]. 
Stage-1 extends PartVessel’s RVAE to additionally predict degree-2 hint nodes (intermediate trajectory waypoints, Section 3.3), used to condition Stage-2’s curve generation. Removing hint nodes degrades curvature Wasserstein by 11× (Table 2). Per-tree node count rises 11.45→23.87 (LCA, +12.42) and 7.21→16.79 (RCA, +9.58); hint nodes contribute +12.42 (LCA, all) and +9.33 (RCA, ~97% of the increase). Under the same RVAE capacity, this larger prediction target likely reduces bifurcation accuracy; a diffusion-based Stage-1 is a future direction.
3.Murray’s law and GT reference [R1, R3]. 
Following R1, we computed GT compliance on ImageCAS: strict (±20%) = 16.6%/15.9% (LCA/RCA); loose (±50%) = 53.1%/62.4%. Held-out 163 is consistent (16.6%/17.1%). GT mean of (Σr_child³)/r_parent³ is 1.46/1.40 vs ideal 1.0—reflecting that GT radii are skeleton-derived from standard centerline-extraction preprocessing (not direct mm measurements), inherited equally by all methods. Under this preprocessing-bounded reference, our 35–37% (2.2× GT, uniformly best) represents substantial movement toward physiological plausibility; closure to ideal Murray would require advances in centerline-radius estimation itself.
4.Diversity quantification [R1]. 
Manifold coverage on LCA (fraction of GT 6D-feature k-means clusters reached): Ours 0.70 vs PartVessel 0.50.Raw diversity (coefficient of variation of per-edge curvature/radius/length): +14% (LCA), +59% (RCA) over PartVessel.
5.ScaleHead determinism [R3]. 
ScaleHead is deterministic for fixed z. By design, Stage-2 operates in normalized coordinate space (Section 3.1); mm-scale recovery is architecturally confined to Stage-1’s root latent z, not an arbitrary choice. Tree-level scale diversity arises from different z; length/radius match GT within 5%/3% (Section 4.1). Decoupling scale from z would require two-stage redesign (future direction).
6.K=48 and B-spline baseline [R3, R1]. 
K=48 reconstruction error (0.003–0.020 mm) is well below voxel resolution (~0.3 mm, Section 3.3). Smaller K (e.g., K=24) also yields sub-voxel reconstruction; we chose K=48 since the model handles it stably with extra precision margin (K tunable to dataset/compute). We considered B-spline coefficient diffusion: per-curve adaptive knots would add a Stage-1 prediction target—and given the Stage-1 trade-off from hint nodes (Topic 2), would likely worsen bifurcation accuracy; fixed shared knots compound a hyperparameter with K. Chebyshev avoids both via an orthogonal global basis (Section 2).
Limitations. 
Loop-topology via graph diffusion (Section 5), downstream applications, cross-anatomy validation, and synthetic stress testing are future directions. A short Chebyshev intro and PartVessel-summary clarification fit within camera-ready limits.

title: Anatomically Consistent TMJ Disc Segmentation via Semantic Anchoring and Clinical Priors
abstract: Segmenting the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disc from MRI is essential for accurate diagnosis of internal derangement, yet it remains unreliable in practice due to its small size, low contrast, and morphological variability. Existing methods, primarily adapted from general segmentation architectures, often produce fragmented or anatomically inconsistent masks, leading to unstable measurements of disc position and shape for downstream diagnosis. To address these challenges, we propose TISC, a TMJ disc segmentation framework that integrates semantic anchoring with clinical metadata-guided boundary refinement. The framework first establishes robust disc localization in the foundation model feature space via a Prototypical Semantic Anchoring (PSA) module that aggregates adjacent-slice MedDINOv3 features and derives a prototype-driven similarity map. It then performs targeted boundary refinement through a Clinical-Metadata Point Refinement (C-MPR) module, with point-wise predictions modulated by Mouth Open Limitation (MOL), a clinical indicator associated with disc displacement without reduction. On a large-scale cohort of 2,488 PD MRI volumes from 1,300 patients, our method achieves up to a 4.96 Dice improvement over strong baselines across diverse architectures, delivering more anatomically coherent and clinically reliable TMJ disc segmentation.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The PSA module and C-MPR are well designed and integrated to cooperate to solve the targeted problem. The PSA module is responsible for anatomical consistency by utilizing the MedDINOv3 to extract semantic features to achieve stable localization of disc. And C-MPR is responsible for boundary refinement with the help form PSA module. In addition, clinical prior of MOL is cleverly utilized in both modules to improve the preformance.
reviews.text_strengths:
The targeted problem is practical and challeging. 
The module designs are very clear and interpretable, for example the use of MedDINOv3 in PSA module. 
MOL is effectively used to help with the performance improvment.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The explanation of some method designs and experimental settings is insufficient. , such as the temperature in softmax function, the ratios of sampled points. 
The proposed framework is a 2D segmentation model in essence, although the PSA module aggregate adjacent slices. As we know, 3D segmentation models are advantageous over 2D models in anatomical inconsistency performances. I suggest the authors add some metrics of continuity or topology accuracy to further prove the effectiveness of their method, such as, number of connected components, fragmentation score.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The method proposed in this paper exhibits a certain degree of novelty. And experiments results show the effectiveness
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors’ reply addresses my questions adequately. Although their method still has some limitations, the paper presents certain novelty.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: In this paper, the authors proposed TSIC, a TMJ disc segmentation framework that integrates semantic anchoring with clinical metadata-guided boundary refinement. Previous methods struggle with spatial uncertainty due to small target localization and precise boundary delineation after coarse localization. To address above problems, the proposed PSA module aggregates adjacent-slice MedDINOv3 features and generates a similarity-based localization map，stabilizing predictions and reducing false positives under pathological displacement. The C-MPR module adaptively adjusts boundary predictions at the point level conditioned on clinical metadata, enabling correction of ambiguous regions. Moreover, MOL, a binary indicator of limited mouth opening as auxiliary metadata, guides spatial attention in PSA and modulates refinement features via FiLM layers, promoting adaptive localization and boundary correction across pathological states. The quantitative and qualitative experimental results show the effectiveness of the proposed method.
reviews.text_strengths:
a) The writing of this paper is easy to understand and there are few spelling or grammatical error.
b) The quantitative and qualitative experimental results show the effectiveness of the proposed method, and the article achieves SOTA performance in comparative experiments.
c) The method tries to describe the network architecture as well as the objective functions thoroughly.
d) Considering the specific difficulties of the TMJ task, the proposed TSIC utilizes object detection foundation model and adjacent-slice features to produce an enhanced similarity based localization map, overcoming the challenge in localizing small targets. Besides, it adaptively adjusts boundary predicions at the point level to resolve the issue of boundary ambiguity.
e) The innovative introduction of auxiliary metadata effectively enchance the performance.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
a) In ‘Introduction’ section, the review of current methods is insufficient, lacking more detailed introduction of relevant specific approaches on TMJ task. Meanwhile, foundation models such as MedSAM and MedDINOv3 are mentioned. What’s the advantages and disadvantages of them compared to general model.
b) The comparison methods in experiments are not up-to-date. It only compares against old methods like the standard UNet and its very basic variants and new but less effective SAM-based model. If possible, more state-of-the-art methods specifically for TMJ Segmentation tasks should be included for comparison.
c) In ‘Application’ section, predicted masks and images are concatenated for downstream diagnostic tasks, the setting should be discussed. Besides, more state-of-the-art medical image classification methods should be taken into account, rather than very basic ResNet. Actually, more detailed experimental elaboration and corresponding tabulated comparison results should be included.
d) Although the writing of this paper is easy to understand, there are still some minor writing issues can be corrected. For example, the first line of ‘Ablation Study’ section references a non-existent ‘Table 2(a)’. The architecture diagram uses two different representations for the ground truth: ‘Mgt’ and ‘GroundTruth’, Although they are used in different modules, the notation should remain consistent if there is no change.
e) The submission does not mention open access to source code or data. Although it’s allowed, the ‘Method’ section should be more specific in the absence of source code. While the paper provides a detailed description of the implementation process, it lacks more intuitive mathematical formulations.

N/A

a) The proposed method is novel, utilizing popoular foundation model and multi-modal concepts. Futhermore, the network is designed to address specific research challenges with promising experimental results.
b) The comparison methods in experiments are not up-to-date. If possible, more state-of-the-art methods specifically for TMJ segmentation tasks should be included for comparison
c) The downstream diagnostic task lacks interpretability. More state-of-the-art medical image classification methods should be taken into account.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have fully addressed all my core concerns. For all the issues, they have provided a complete explanation and committed to release the code to ensure reproducibility. I recommend acceptance.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of this paper is the proposal of an anatomically consistent TMJ disc segmentation framework that integrates semantic anchoring and clinical metadata. Specifically, the method introduces a Prototypical Semantic Anchoring module to improve localization using foundation model features, and a Clinical-Metadata Point Refinement module to enhance boundary accuracy by leveraging clinical priors such as Mouth Open Limitation.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper addresses a clinically meaningful and challenging problem, namely TMJ disc segmentation, which is difficult due to small object size, low contrast, and high anatomical variability.
The proposed framework is well-motivated and technically sound. The combination of semantic anchoring in foundation model feature space and metadata-guided refinement is a thoughtful design that directly targets both localization and boundary ambiguity. The method effectively incorporates clinical prior knowledge. This adds interpretability and domain relevance.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The proposed method partially relies on empirical design choices and task-specific clinical priors. While these components are effective for the current dataset, it remains unclear whether the approach can generalize to external datasets. Therefore, validation on independent external datasets is necessary to demonstrate the robustness and generalizability of the method.
The current evaluation mainly focuses on integrating the proposed method into baseline models, rather than comparing with recent dedicated TMJ disc segmentation methods. As a result, it is difficult to properly assess the relative performance level of the proposed approach within the current state of the field.
We note that although the proposed method achieves notable improvements over the baselines, there is still room for further performance gains. Providing an analysis of failure cases or samples with large segmentation errors would be beneficial for better understanding the limitations of the method and guiding future improvements.
In the ablation study, we observe that the performance gains mainly stem from the MOL and PSA components, while the contribution of C-MPR appears relatively limited. Moreover, MOL also plays an important role in supporting PSA. This raises a practical concern for clinical deployment: whether MOL can be consistently obtained for all patients. In cases where MOL is partially missing, it remains unclear whether the model can still maintain stable performance.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Overall, this paper presents a well-designed framework for TMJ disc segmentation, addressing a clinically meaningful problem. The integration of semantic anchoring and clinical metadata is interesting and shows clear improvements over baseline models.
However, several issues limit a stronger recommendation. The method relies on empirical designs and task-specific priors, and its generalizability remains unclear due to the lack of external validation. The comparison experiments are also not sufficiently comprehensive, making it difficult to assess the method’s standing relative to recent TMJ segmentation approaches.
In addition, there is still room for performance improvement, and analysis of failure cases would help better understand the method’s limitations. The ablation study further suggests a strong dependence on MOL, raising concerns about robustness when such metadata is unavailable in real clinical settings.
Overall, the work is promising but slightly below the acceptance threshold. I would be open to a higher score if these concerns are addressed in the rebuttal.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
There is clear consensus among reviewers that the work presents a well-designed and interpretable framework with clinical relevance. There is strong empirical performance demonstrated with improvements over baselines and clear presentation. However, all reviewers also acknowledge limitations in evaluation of the work, the fact that the evaluation is limited to a single dataset with no external validation making the generalization potential unclear and there is a lack of comparison with strong baselines.
In rebuttal, the authors should focus on strengthening the state of the art comparison by clarifying why the given baselines were chosen and comparing with more reject relevant approaches. If additional experimental results on external datasets exist, these should be reported and if not the authors should give a strong justification for limiting the work to the single dataset, acknowledging the limitations of this. The authors should also clarify the dependence on MOL and whether this can be consistently obtained given the apparent strong need for it. The contributions of the components should also be clarified given the apparently small contributions of C-MPR.

R1 kept the same recommendation of Accept, while R2 changed from Weak Accept to Accept. Both reviewers were satisfied with the rebuttal, in which the authors addressed initial concerns regarding the paper.

TISC introduces an anatomically and clinically consistent framework for the challenging task of temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disc segmentation from MRI by coupling deep foundation feature anchoring with clinical metadata. The initial reviewer concerns regarding baseline rationale, missing external validation, and metadata dependency were comprehensively and convincingly resolved during the rebuttal phase. Specifically, the authors clarified that paper-level SOTA comparisons are structurally restricted due to the lack of a standardized public benchmark, while successfully demonstrating that their method degrades gracefully and maintains stable performance even if clinical metadata is completely absent.

author_feedback_text:
We thank Reviewers 1,2,3 (R1,R2,R3) and the Meta-Reviewer (M) for the constructive feedback.
[M,R2,R3: Baseline rationale] We agree that recent TMJ methods need more discussion. For example, Liu et al. use a topology-preserving multi-branch decoder with joint loss, and Hu et al. extend TransUNet with edge enhancement and cross-slice attention. However, without a public TMJ benchmark, paper-level SOTA comparison is unreliable due to different datasets/settings, and fair reproduction is difficult without released code/protocols. We therefore used strong, widely validated, reproducible baselines for a fair test across CNN, self-configuring, Transformer, and foundation-model families.
[M,R3: External validity] We acknowledge the lack of external TMJ validation as a limitation. Suitable cohorts are scarce because no public TMJ benchmark exists. As a sanity check, our pipeline improved Dice from 0.82 to 0.89 on a structurally similar knee meniscus task, but this was not treated as external validation due to anatomical/task mismatch. Within available TMJ data, we used patient-level 5-fold CV on a relatively large cohort for fair evaluation and observed consistent gains across backbones. Future work will pursue multi-institutional validation.
[M,R3: C-MPR] C-MPR is a boundary refinement module, not the main localization component, so its effect is clearer in HD95 than Dice. Comparing Exp. 3 and Exp. 6 in Table 2, adding C-MPR lowers HD95 from 6.01 to 5.27 (↓12.3%), supporting its role in reducing boundary outliers after localization.
[M,R3: MOL dependency] MOL is routinely assessed in TMJ evaluation [23] and is naturally recognized during closed/open-mouth MRI acquisition, so missingness is unlikely. Nevertheless, if unavailable, the model can operate as the no-MOL variant (Table 2, Exp. 5), which still outperforms the vanilla backbone, showing that MOL improves performance but is not strictly required.
[R1,R2,R3: Code] Model code will be released for implementation clarity and reproducibility.
[R1: Empirical design choices] Most method-specific settings were chosen through qualitative inspection and empirical validation. The actual softmax temperatures are τ=0.05 for MOL=0 and τ=0.1 for MOL=1, yielding sharper and broader localization, respectively (the reversed description will be corrected). For point sampling, we follow PointRend [11] with 75% uncertainty-based samples and a 25% coverage pool, where 25% is drawn from PSA-defined salient regions and the rest remains random. We will clarify these details.
[R1: Topology metrics] Thank you for the suggestion. We agree and will reflect topology metrics, such as CC, FS, and Euler, in the released evaluation code for additional verification.
[R2: Related-methods] We agree that these methods need better context, as they serve different roles rather than a direct pros/cons comparison. Prior TMJ-specific studies are mostly CNN-based adaptations to TMJ MRI and were too briefly summarized. MedSAM is a strong recent medical segmentation baseline, while MedDINOv3 is both a representative foundation model and the semantic feature source for PSA. We will clarify this distinction and expand the TMJ-specific discussion.
[R2: Application settings] This pilot study tested the diagnostic value of predicted masks while limiting classifier effects. We used ImageNet-pretrained ResNet18 as a simple baseline, trained for 50 epochs with learning rate 6e-5 and batch size 16.Masks were concatenated with close/open MRI pairs as 4-channel inputs and improved AUROC. SOTA-oriented classifiers remain future work.
[R2: Typos] Thanks for catching these. We will fix them.
[R3: Failures] Thank you for the suggestion. During qualitative analysis, we observed failures, including over-segmentation into adjacent retrodiscal tissue when the posterior disc margin appeared intermixed and hard to distinguish. Given the tiny disc size, even small spill-over can affect metrics under severe anatomical ambiguity.

title: Anatomy- and Site-Guided 3D Patch Diffusion for Robust MRI Harmonization
abstract: Pooling multi-site T1-weighted MRI increases power but introduces scanner-driven variability that can bias analyses. We propose a 3D patch-based conditional diffusion framework for MRI harmonization that preserves fine anatomical details while aligning image contrast across sites. Our method constructs site-invariant anatomical maps using gradient and high-frequency features, which guide patch-wise diffusion synthesis together with learnable site embeddings. Processing overlapping high-resolution patches avoids latent-decoder blurring and reduces memory requirements, enabling faithful preservation of fine anatomical detail. To further enhance anatomical fidelity, we employ manifold-constrained classifier-free guidance, stabilizing diffusion sampling while maintaining subject-specific structures. We evaluate our framework on a multi-site traveling-subject dataset and a clinically acquired pathological cohort, comparing against state-of-the-art harmonization methods. Results show that our approach effectively reduces site-related intensity variability, preserves anatomical and tissue-specific information, and maintains clinically relevant brain–cognition associations. These findings demonstrate that patch-based, anatomy-guided diffusion harmonization provides a robust, high-fidelity solution for multi-site MRI, with clear practical benefits for clinical datasets and downstream analyses. Code and model weights are available at https://github.com/barna-hache/PatchLevelDiffusionMRIHarmonization.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This work presents a 3D patch-based conditional diffusion framework for multi-site structural MRI harmonization. The framework leverages derived site-invariant anatomical maps to preserve structural details while harmonizing scanner-specific contrast. Evaluation is performed on robust, diverse datasets spanning international multi-site studies and a traveling subject study.
reviews.text_strengths:
The investigators appropriately generated a curated, robust training dataset assembled from multiple public repositories of multi-site international medical imaging studies and a robust clinical cohort of patients with Alzheimer’s disease for testing.
Methodological refinement is demonstrated in (1) performing ablation studies to optimize classifier-free guidance, (2) assessing site variability of supposedly site-invariant anatomical priors, and (3) assessing harmonization performance of clinically meaningful structure-cognition correlations. However, further methodological detail is needed as specified below.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Although the presented 3D patch-based conditional diffusion framework is intriguing, and training and testing datasets are robust, greater clarity is needed on methodological reasoning and details throughout the paper.
Derivation of anatomical representations that are supposedly site-invariant is a critical step in the proposed framework for structural MRI harmonization. As such, greater detail should be provided on how Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) tests in Ablation Study 2 demonstrate site-invariance of the anatomical conditioning map. What specific distribution pairs were MMDs calculated between? How was MMD averaged per site when MMDs were calculated on inter-site discrepancies? Presumably MMDs were calculated on same subject, same map (raw vs. anatomical map), between sites, e. g. , subject1-site1-raw histogram vs. subject1-site2-raw histogram or subject1-site1-anatomical histogram vs. subject1-site2-anatomical histogram. However, such detail should be explicitly specified for clarity and reproducibility in the paper. Visual or tabulated results, rather than single summary p-values, would also be helpful for interpretation. As is, the site-invariance of anatomical representations is questionable.
In Task 1, the dependent variable in the linear mixed-effects model is not stated – a model formula should be provided for clarity. Presumably, the site fixed effect and subject random effect predicted GM and WM volumes normalized to intracranial tissue volume. If so, why were whole tissue volumes chosen for site- and subject-effect modeling as opposed to more specific memory- or disease-related regional volumes as in Task 2? Gross whole-GM and whole-WM tissue volumes are likely less sensitive to small scanner-specific differences in tissue boundaries than small regional volumes like the hippocampus or entorhinal cortex. Normalizing GM and WM volume to total intracranial tissue volume (GM+WM) may have further reduced sensitivity to site or scanner effects. Why was normalization to whole tissue volume chosen?
Overall, it’s unclear if the proposed 3D patch-based conditional diffusion framework is a superior method or step forward for structural MRI harmonization, relative to existing published techniques. STGAN and HACA3 outperform the proposed framework in matched-subject harmonization performance (SSIM, WD, PCC). STGAN, HACA3, and basic preprocessing outperform the proposed framework in mixed-effects modeling of brain tissue volumes, albeit not consistently. HACA3 is also the best-performing method for cognitive associations in 3/8 regions assessed, whereas the proposed diffusion framework is the clear best-performer in only 2/8 regions (possibly 3/8 if including middle temporal, though it is difficult to discern a difference between STGAN and Diffusion for middle temporal in Fig. 3). For what tasks or under what circumstances would the authors recommend the proposed framework be utilized over STGAN or HACA3?
While the curated training and clinical datasets are robust in spanning multiple international sites and studies, re-training and evaluating methods on all full available datasets would increase confidence in results.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

While the presented harmonization framework is intriguing, additional methodological details are necessary, as specified in weaknesses above. Further, it is questionable that the proposed framework is a significant or impactful step forward in structural MRI harmonization, based on presented results.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors sufficiently clarified details on the site-invariance MMD and mixed-effects model analyses. Importantly, evaluation scripts will be made public upon acceptance, along with code and pretrained models, so analyses can be understood and reproduced even if specific details are missing from the manuscript text.
While the proposed method does not clearly outperform other techniques universally, the authors’ rebuttal that it is the most consistent and balanced across evaluations is true and well-received.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper presents a 3D patch-based diffusion framework for multi-site MRI harmonization. The key idea is to disentangle anatomical structure and site-specific contrast via a site-invariant anatomical map and learnable site embeddings, enabling harmonization without requiring paired or traveling-subject data. The patch-wise diffusion design is used to preserve high-resolution anatomical details while remaining computationally feasible. Experiments on both traveling-subject datasets and clinical cohorts demonstrate strong image-level harmonization performance, along with some downstream analyses such as tissue consistency and cognition-related correlations.
reviews.text_strengths:
The unpaired setting is realistic and important. Avoiding reliance on traveling-subject data is a clear practical advantage.
The method is well-motivated. The combination of anatomical conditioning and site embedding is intuitive and makes sense for disentangling structure vs contrast.
Experiments are quite extensive.
Patch-based diffusion is a reasonable design choice here, especially for preserving high-frequency anatomical details.
reviews.text_weaknesses: Anatomical representation: This is unfortunately the biggest concern of this paper. The motivation is clear: suppress site-related characteristics while preserving the anatomical traits. From what I understand (and how the paper presents), the motivation is along the lines of simple gradient-based features. Therefore, there could be many alternatives to this. In that sense, there is little justification behind the proposed anatomical representation approach.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The anatomical representation could use further justification or experimental analyses. Otherwise, the paper clearly has some strengths especially the rigorous clinical analyses.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a 3D patch-based conditional diffusion framework for multi-site T1-weighted MRI harmonization. The method introduces anatomy-guided diffusion by constructing site-invariant anatomical maps derived from gradient and high-frequency features. It integrates these with learnable site embeddings to guide patch-wise synthesis. By operating on overlapping high-resolution patches, the framework reduces memory consumption and mitigates blurring commonly observed in latent diffusion approaches. Additionally, the incorporation of manifold-constrained classifier-free guidance aims to stabilize sampling while preserving subject-specific anatomical structures. The method is validated on both traveling-subject and clinical datasets, demonstrating improved harmonization performance and preservation of clinically relevant associations.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.This paper presents a well-motivated and technically sound framework that combines patch-based processing with conditional diffusion, which is a meaningful extension for high-resolution MRI harmonization tasks. The use of overlapping patches is particularly practical, as it addresses both memory constraints and the loss of fine anatomical detail often observed in full-volume or latent-space methods.
2.The introduction of anatomy-guided diffusion through gradient and high-frequency-derived maps is a novel and interesting design choice. This explicitly enforces structural consistency across sites and provides a principled way to disentangle anatomical information from scanner-specific contrast variations.
3.The incorporation of manifold-constrained classifier-free guidance is a thoughtful addition that improves sampling stability while maintaining subject-specific features. This reflects careful consideration of the trade-off between the strength of harmonization and anatomical fidelity.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.This paper does not sufficiently quantify the contribution of the proposed anatomical map components. While gradient and high-frequency features are claimed to guide harmonization, no ablation studies isolate their individual effects (e.g., removing gamma perturbation, gradient, or frequency components). This makes it difficult to assess whether the performance gains stem from the anatomical guidance or from the diffusion framework itself.
2.Although the method achieves strong global performance, the regional analysis reveals inconsistencies. Specifically, certain clinically important ROIs, such as the posterior cingulate and entorhinal cortex, show slightly worse correlations with MMSE compared to baseline methods, suggesting that the harmonization may not uniformly preserve region-specific information. This raises concerns about its reliability for localized analyses.
3.The novelty of the framework is somewhat incremental relative to recent diffusion-based harmonization approaches. Prior work on conditional diffusion for medical image translation and harmonization (e.g., diffusion-based MRI synthesis and style transfer methods) has already explored conditioning mechanisms and structural guidance, and the current work primarily extends these ideas through patch-based processing and feature engineering rather than introducing a fundamentally new formulation.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper addresses an important problem in multi-site MRI analysis and proposes a technically solid and reasonably well-evaluated framework. The combination of patch-based diffusion and anatomy-guided conditioning is practical and shows clear empirical benefits, particularly in preserving global consistency and clinical associations. However, the lack of detailed ablation studies weakens the ability to attribute performance gains to specific components of the method. In addition, the observed regional inconsistencies in clinically relevant ROIs raise concerns about robustness, particularly for applications that require localized accuracy. Finally, while the method is well-engineered, its conceptual novelty relative to existing diffusion-based harmonization approaches is somewhat limited. Overall, this paper is promising but would benefit from deeper analysis and clearer validation of its key design choices, which leads to a weak reject recommendation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper proposes a 3D patch-based conditional diffusion framework for multi-site MRI harmonization conditioned on an anatomical map and site-specific embeddings. Evaluation includes traveling-subject data and a clinical cohort with cognition-related downstream analyses. The reviewers all acknowledge that the problem is practically important, that the combination of anatomical conditioning with site embeddings is a sensible disentanglement strategy, and that the evaluation scope is substantial.
All three reviewers recommend Weak Reject (3), but the AC finds that these rejections are based on somewhat different reasons. R1 provides the most detailed and consistent critique (and the AC weighs it more into the current decision): the MMD-based evidence for site-invariance of the anatomical maps is ambiguously described (which distributions are compared, how results are averaged, and only p-values are reported), and the linear mixed-effects model formula for Task 1 is not stated. More importantly, R1 argues that the proposed method does not clearly outperform STGAN and HACA3 across the reported metrics; STGAN and HACA3 win on matched-subject SSIM/WD/PCC, the baselines can win on mixed-effects tissue volumes, and HACA3 is best for cognitive correlations in more ROIs than the proposed method. This undermines the significance claim. R2 argues that the construction of the anatomical map is under-justified: it amounts to gradient-style feature engineering and the paper does not explain why this particular construction is preferred. R3 notes that there is no component ablation isolating the contributions of the gradient, high-frequency, and gamma-perturbation parts, that certain clinically important ROIs (posterior cingulate, entorhinal cortex) show worse MMSE correlations than baselines, and that the novelty is incremental relative to existing conditional-diffusion harmonization work.
Most of R1 and R2’s concerns can be addressed through clarification and re-analysis of existing results (MMD pair specification, mixed-effects formula, discussion of when to use the proposed method vs. STGAN/HACA3). R3’s request for finer ablations of the anatomical-map components is the one concern that would typically require new experiments, but it is not on its own decisive. Given the uniform but moderate rejection score and the substantial amount of work the paper represents, I recommend inviting the authors to respond in rebuttal before a final decision. While preparing the rebuttal, the authors should carefully read reviewers’ comments and the MICCAI rebuttal guidelines.

All three reviewers opened at weak reject in the initial review but they all gave different reasons. The rebuttal did a good job clarifying the site-invariance (MMD) analysis and the mixed-effects model, and reframing the contribution as the most consistent and balanced method rather than the best on every metric, which moved R1 to accept. The harder concerns, though, are only partly resolved on the submitted manuscript: R2’s point that the anatomical map is under-motivated gradient feature engineering and R3’s point that the paper lacks a component ablation and shows regional inconsistencies are answered mainly by a new ablation run during the rebuttal.
Weighing the one engaged accept (which I weigh the most in the initial review) against two non-response reviewers, and the authors overall effective rebuttal given the 4000 limit, I lean toward accept.

This paper originally received consistent “weak reject” reviews with clear avenues for rebuttal. The extensive work that was put into the methodology and experimentation was recognized by the AC. I believe the authors have adequately addressed the concerns that led to weak rejects, including both novelty and clarification of the contrast-agnostic space. I recommend that this paper be accepted.
The authors have adequately addressed the reviewers’ questions and concerns. The paper is therefore recommended for acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
Dear Reviewers, Area Chairs, and Program Chairs,
We thank you for the careful reading and constructive feedback. We address the main points below.
To preserve anonymity, the GitHub repository is not included in the submission but is already prepared and will be made public after the review process. It contains the full training and inference code, pretrained weights, the exact train/test splits data, and all evaluation scripts used in the paper.
1) Clarification of the anatomical map / site-invariance analysis.
We agree that this is a central step and should be described more explicitly. In Ablation Study 2, MMD was computed between every pair of acquisition sites (si ,sj), not between matched subjects. For each site, we pooled the histogram feature vectors from all scans acquired at that site, and computed the RBF-kernel MMD separately for raw-image histograms and anatomical-map histograms. Thus, each value corresponds to one site-pair comparison. The “per-site” summary is the average of that site’s MMD values against all other sites. The paired t-test compares raw vs. anatomical-map MMD on the same site pairs, so the reduction directly reflects lower inter-site discrepancy for the anatomical map. For brevity, we do not reproduce the full pairwise table here.
Our anatomical map is intended as a simple low-level prior that suppresses scanner contrast while preserving structure, inspired by recent work on anatomical priors (10.1016/j.neuroimage.2025.121297). Gradient magnitude and high-frequency content are chosen because they are less tied to site-specific intensity statistics than raw signal, and random gamma perturbation further reduces leakage of contrast cues into the conditioning map.
2) Mixed-effects model in Task 1.For each method, we fitted a linear mixed-effects model with site as a fixed effect and subject as a random intercept:
tissue_ratio ~ site + (1 | subject)
The dependent variable is the GM or WM tissue ratio. These ratios are normalized by total intracranial volume, defined as GM + WM + CSF, to reduce inter-subject size differences and make comparisons across sites and harmonization methods more comparable.
3) Comparison with STGAN / HACA3 and when our method is most useful.
We agree that no single method dominates every metric. Our claim is not that diffusion is uniformly best, but that it is the most consistent method in our experiments and provides a strong balance between harmonization and preservation of biologically meaningful signals. In the tissue-level analysis, our method is the only one that consistently achieves both low marginal R² and high conditional R² across GM and WM, whereas STGAN and HACA3 are stronger in one tissue but less consistent in the other. In the cognition analysis, our method achieves the highest global mean absolute correlation and improves over the preprocessed baseline. This is also consistent with Fig. 2, where our method shows fewer over- and under-segmentation errors than the Anatomy Target, suggesting more robust anatomical preservation. At the same time, we acknowledge that STGAN and HACA3 can be stronger in specific metrics or regions.
4) Nature of the contributions / ablations.
We appreciate the request for more component-level justification. The manuscript already includes three targeted analyses: guidance ablation (CFG vs. CFG++), the site-invariance test for the anatomical prior, and downstream clinical preservation analyses. Together, these support the full design: patch-based high-resolution synthesis, anatomy-guided conditioning, and manifold-constrained guidance. We also performed an additional internal ablation of the anatomical representation components: removing the gradient component caused a marked SSIM drop (-0.28 drop), indicating that gradient information is the main contributor; removing the high-frequency component did not significantly reduce SSIM, suggesting a smaller contribution. Other components could also merit further investigation.

title: Anatomy-Anchored Self-Supervision: Distilling Vision Foundation Models for Invariant Ultrasound Representation
abstract: Self-supervised pre-training paradigm has gained increasing prominence for learning transferable representations in medical imaging, yet existing methods for ultrasound (US) images operate at the image or frame level, overlooking the anatomical context for clinical-aligned representation learning. In this work, we propose an anatomy-anchored ultrasound Self-Supervision framework (ANAUS) that shifts representation learning from generic visual regions to clinically meaningful anatomical structures. Utilizing a learnable latent prompt engine alongside a one-time domain  adaptation on existing public image-mask pairs, we empower the LP-SAM module to achieve annotation-free anatomy delineation at scale. Building upon this anatomical grounding, we propose a dual-policy self-supervised learning paradigm consisting of inter-view semantics-aware anatomy-separating alignment and contextual core-region prediction to enhance representation learning. Specifically, the former enforces feature invariance within identical anatomical regions while promoting discriminability across distinct structures; the latter compels the model to reconstruct corrupted regions, thereby capturing fine-grained structural details. Extensive evaluations on diverse public benchmarks demonstrate that ANAUS consistently outstrips current state-of-the-art methods while maintaining the computational efficiency essential for clinical deployment. Code is available at https://github.com/zhcz328/ANAUS.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The AnaUS framework is introduced to shift representation learning from general visual regions toward clinically meaningful anatomical structures. LP-SAM, incorporating a learnable potential cueing engine, is also introduced.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The motivation of leveraging anatomical structures as anchor points is well-justified and forward-looking. 
2.The experimental results are strong and cover a wide range of settings. 
3.Strong generalization ability: As shown in Figure 4, LP-SAM is able to segment previously unseen anatomical structures during fine-tuning, enabling subsequent comparative learning.
The availability of open-source code supports the reproducibility of the research.

2.There is room for more comprehensive analysis of hyperparameters.

N/A

The article presents well-motivated objectives, a novel approach, and experimental results that demonstrate certain advantages.
