reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes A2ONet for laparoscopic liver landmark detection, addressing two challenges: (1) illumination attenuation in underexposed surgical regions and (2) the structural mismatch between pixel-wise segmentation and continuous curvilinear landmark geometry. The architecture integrates three modules: an illumination field compensation (IFC) block based on reflectance-illumination decomposition with a learnable temperature parameter; a frequency–orientation selective filter (FOSF) using Haar wavelet decomposition and Gabor filtering to suppress texture interference and enhance curvilinear structures; and an alternating seg–curve optimization (ASCO) decoder that iteratively couples dense segmentation with Bezier curve modeling through cross-attention-based curve-to-mask fusion. The model uses ResNet-34 for RGB encoding and a frozen SAM-b encoder for depth features from Depth Anything V2.Evaluated on L3D-2K (2,000 images), L3D (1,152 images), and P2ILF (183 images), A2ONet reports DSC of 53.51% / 65.31% / 43.02% respectively, improving over the previous best (D2GPLand+) by 1.85% / 0.69% / 0.87% DSC.
reviews.text_strengths:
S1.Well-motivated and clearly structured problem formulation. The paper identifies two concrete, practically relevant failure modes — illumination attenuation and the localization-continuity tradeoff — and designs dedicated modules for each. The introduction provides clear visual examples (Fig. 1) of blue-circle attenuation errors, yellow-circle segmentation false positives, and pink-circle endpoint localization failures that motivate the approach.
S2.Technically sound module design with principled foundations. Each component is technically well-motivated and clearly described: the IFC block builds on a reflectance-illumination decomposition assumption (akin to Retinex, though the paper does not use that term) with a learnable intensity collapse (Eq. 1); the FOSF module combines Haar wavelet frequency analysis with Gabor orientation filtering; and the ASCO decoder models landmarks as Bezier curves with soft rasterization (Eq. 4) and differentiable control-point updates (Eq. 5). The interplay is well-articulated: IFC addresses appearance, FOSF addresses feature-level texture suppression, and ASCO addresses the output-level geometry gap.
S3.Thorough ablation study demonstrating component complementarity. Table 2 systematically isolates the contribution of each module (IFC, L_illum, FOSF, ASCO, L_curve) through six progressive variants, showing that each addition yields measurable improvement. Adding L_illum to IFC (V1→V2) yields the largest single-step DSC gain (+2.22%), and further combining with FOSF (V2→V4: +2.03%) produces a substantial cumulative improvement, validating the complementarity of illumination compensation and frequency filtering.
S4.Comprehensive baseline comparison. The paper benchmarks against 16 methods across three categories (general segmentation, SAM-based adaptation, task-specific detection), providing a well-contextualised evaluation landscape. The consistent improvement across all three datasets and all three metrics (DSC, IoU, ASSD) lends credibility to the approach.
S5.Clean mathematical exposition. The equations are well-defined and the notation is consistent throughout. The paper makes the training pipeline clear (end-to-end with joint supervision, Eq. 6) and specifies all key hyperparameters.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
W1.No uncertainty estimates or statistical significance tests. (General Review Consideration §5, §6) The paper reports single-point performance numbers throughout Tables 1 and 2 with no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. Given that the improvements over D2GPLand+ are modest — 1.85% DSC on L3D-2K, 0.69% DSC on L3D, and 0.87% DSC on P2ILF — it is not possible to assess whether these gains are statistically meaningful. The number of training runs, random seed policy, and variance across seeds are not disclosed. Without at least a paired test or multi-seed standard deviation, the evidence for superiority over D2GPLand+ is incomplete.
W2.Notable validation–test performance gap unexplained. The ablation study (Table 2) is conducted on the L3D-2K validation set, where the full A2ONet achieves DSC 45.16% / IoU 33.76%. However, Table 1 reports DSC 53.51% / IoU 38.32% on the L3D-2K test set — an 8.35% DSC gap favouring the test set. This is unusual (typically validation and test performance are comparable or test is slightly lower) and warrants explanation. Possible causes include different data characteristics between splits or overfitting to validation-set early stopping, but the paper does not discuss this discrepancy.
W3.No inference time or model complexity analysis. (Clinical significance — General Review Consideration §1) The paper motivates A2ONet for intraoperative anatomy guidance and AR-guided laparoscopic interventions, so reporting runtime, parameter count, or FLOPs would help assess practical deployability. Yet no inference speed (FPS), parameter count, or FLOPs are reported. The architecture includes a ResNet-34 encoder, a frozen SAM-b encoder, Depth Anything V2 for monocular depth estimation, Haar wavelet transforms, Gabor filtering, and a multi-stage ASCO decoder with cross-attention — these components together likely carry a non-trivial computational cost. Without runtime analysis, the practical applicability for the stated clinical use case remains unclear.
W4.Minimal discussion of limitations and failure cases. (General Review Consideration §8) The conclusion mentions no limitations at all. A brief sentence states A2ONet “provides a stable and robust prerequisite for AR-guided navigation,” but no failure case analysis is provided. Given the moderate absolute performance on L3D-2K (53.51% DSC), understanding where and why the method fails — for example across landmark types, illumination conditions, or unusual anatomy — would be valuable.
W5.P2ILF evaluation protocol is non-standard. The paper acknowledges that P2ILF’s official testing set is unavailable, so it subdivides the 167-image training set into 124 train / 43 test. This means (a) results are not directly comparable with future work that uses the official test set, and (b) 43 test images is very small, amplifying variance concerns (further supporting W1). The paper does not discuss this limitation.
W6.Curve-based evaluation absent. The paper acknowledges excluding “curve-only methods” because their evaluation protocol “precludes fair benchmarking against mask-based predictors.” However, since a core contribution is the explicit Bezier curve modeling (ASCO), it would strengthen the paper to report curve-specific metrics (e.g., endpoint localization error, Frechet distance between predicted and ground-truth curves) that directly validate this contribution. Relying solely on mask-based metrics (DSC, IoU, ASSD) may not fully capture the benefit of curve modeling.
W7.Data diversity and label quality not discussed. (General Review Considerations §3, §4) The three datasets are from the same clinical domain (laparoscopic liver surgery), but the paper does not discuss patient demographics, inter-annotator agreement for landmark labeling, or how annotation noise might affect the thin curvilinear structures being detected. Given that the paper does not report inter-rater agreement, annotation protocol details, or label uncertainty for thin curvilinear landmarks, this omission is notable.
W8.Depth estimation dependency not ablated. The paper uses Depth Anything V2 for monocular depth estimation as input to the frozen SAM encoder. This is a significant design choice, yet no ablation examines A2ONet’s sensitivity to depth quality or compares against using no depth input. The absence of such analysis leaves the depth modality’s contribution and the method’s robustness to depth estimation errors unclear.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
C1.The absence of multi-seed results (mean ± std) and statistical tests (e.g., Wilcoxon signed-rank or paired t-test on per-image DSC) limits confidence in the reported improvements over D2GPLand+, which I weight in my recommendation.
C2.The validation–test DSC gap on L3D-2K (45.16% vs. 53.51%) is notable. An analysis of the composition of the val/test splits (e.g., per-landmark-type breakdown, illumination distribution) would help explain this discrepancy and increase confidence in the results.
C3.The absence of runtime analysis (FPS, parameter count, FLOPs) limits assessment of the claimed intraoperative applicability, particularly given the multi-encoder architecture. Without these figures — ideally also for the D2GPLand+ baseline — readers cannot judge whether A2ONet meets a practical latency budget.
C4.Consider reporting curve-specific evaluation metrics (endpoint error, Frechet distance) to directly validate the ASCO contribution. The current evaluation via mask-based metrics alone may understate the benefit of explicit curve modeling.
C5.The values of λ_curve and λ_illum in Eq. 6 and the top-K value for the curve proposer are not specified, which hinders reproducibility. The sensitivity of performance to these weights is also unclear.
C6.The paper omits a limitations discussion entirely. Notable unaddressed gaps include: (a) dependence on Depth Anything V2 quality for laparoscopic images, (b) absolute performance levels (DSC ~ 53% on L3D-2K suggests substantial room for improvement), and (c) computational cost considerations for real-time surgical guidance. This omission limits the reader’s ability to contextualise the contribution.
C7.Without a depth-ablation (e.g., using only RGB features), the contribution of the depth modality and robustness to depth estimation errors remain unclear, which limits the strength of the depth-integration claim.

The paper presents a well-designed architecture that addresses genuine challenges in laparoscopic liver landmark detection. The three proposed modules (IFC, FOSF, ASCO) are technically principled and their complementarity is convincingly demonstrated through systematic ablation. The consistent improvement across three benchmarks and all metrics supports the method’s effectiveness.
However, the absence of uncertainty estimates and statistical tests (W1) is a significant weakness given the modest improvement margins (0.69–1.85% DSC over D2GPLand+). Without statistical validation, the claimed SOTA status is not firmly established. The unexplained validation–test gap (W2), missing computational analysis for the claimed intraoperative application (W3), and lack of limitations discussion (W4) are further notable omissions.
I lean toward accept because: (a) the problem is clinically relevant and well-motivated, (b) the architectural design is sound with clear ablation support, (c) improvements are consistent across all three datasets and metrics (not cherry-picked), and (d) the ASSD improvements (3.65–7.79 pixels across the three datasets) are more substantial in relative terms than the DSC gains, suggesting real improvement in boundary quality. However, this rating is contingent on the authors addressing W1 (statistical tests) and W3 (runtime) in the rebuttal.

meta_reviews.text: All three reviewers rated this paper positively. The reviewers acknowledged the methodological soundness, improved results, and clear presentation. Authors are encouraged to incorporate the reviewers’ suggestions into their final manuscript to the fullest extent possible.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for recognizing the clinical relevance and motivation (R1, R3), clear presentation (R2), and consistent multi-dataset improvements (R1, R3) of our work. We address the remaining concerns below:
Q1.Statistical significance (R1, R3): We have performed significance tests against D2GPLand+ on all three datasets, confirming our statistically significant improvements. We will report the mean±std results. Beyond DSC and IoU, A2ONet also substantially reduces ASSD, supporting improved boundary localization.
Q2.Model complexity and efficiency (R1, R3): Although A2ONet integrates multiple modules, its trainable components are lightweight, relying mainly on convolutions and gating operations. The computational cost and inference speed are comparable to other SAM-based methods, reaching real-time inference.
Q3.Curve-based evaluation (R1, R3): Our current comparison focuses on mask-based metrics to ensure consistency with existing segmentation benchmarks, but we agree that they may not fully reflect the benefit of explicit curve modeling. In future work, we will develop more comprehensive landmark evaluation metrics, including curve-specific metrics, to enable fairer comparison between mask- and curve-based methods.
Q4.Design of IFC block and visualization (R1, R2): Unlike general low-light enhancement, our setting mainly suffers from spatially non-uniform laparoscopic illumination, with central saturation and peripheral attenuation. IFC is therefore designed as a lightweight task-oriented module to compensate this specific attenuation pattern without introducing heavy enhancement networks, preserving clinical efficiency. We sincerely thank R2 for this suggestion. The illumination-perturbation ablation would be helpful to assess prediction stability under different illumination settings.
Q5.Depth-modality justification (R3): Our encoder design follows D2GPLand+, whose depth-modality ablation (Table 10) demonstrates that adding depth features clearly improves performance over RGB-only input, and using a stronger depth estimator further improves the results. This supports that depth provides useful geometric cues for landmark detection.
Q6.Parameter clarification and convergence (R2, R3): We will clarify that the logit function is: logit(x)=log(x/1−x), where x is clamped to [10^−6, 1–10^−6] for numerical stability. We will also specify all hyperparameters, including λcurve=0.2, λillum=0.1, and the top-K=16.Ablations on key parameters and curve-update convergence will be included in future extended work.
Q7.Dataset protocol and characteristics (R3): The validation-test gap on L3D-2K is mainly due to the distribution difference between the patient-level validation and test set. Similar gap are also observed in D2GPLand+ under the same dataset setting, as reflected in Table 2 (test set) and Table 4 (validation set). For P2ILF, we will release our code to facilitate future comparison. Despite the small test set, our improvements remain statistically significant. We will also discuss data diversity, annotation quality, and label uncertainty in journal version.
Q8.Limitations and clinical validation (R1-R3): Due to the inherent difficulty of curvilinear structure segmentation in laparoscopic liver images, the absolute segmentation metrics leave room for improvement, especially in failure cases such as ambiguous junctions between silhouettes/ridges and ligaments, and false predictions under tissue or instrument occlusion. Our method is robust against reflections and there are few bleeding incidents in current datasets. We will further validate the detected landmarks in downstream pre-to-intraoperative 2D-3D liver registration to assess their clinical utility for AR guidance in the future.

title: Attribute-Aware Federated Learning with Pseudo-Bag Augmentation for Multi-Center WSI Classification
abstract:
Federated learning (FL) on gigapixel whole slide images (WSIs) remains challenged by severe cross-center heterogeneity arising from inconsistent staining protocols, scanning optics, and slide digitization settings. Existing FL approaches typically rely on coarse feature statistics or require iterative transmission of synthetic images, making it difficult to capture domain-specific pathology priors while preserving privacy. To solve these problems, we propose FedGMM-Bag, a generative federated learning framework that performs cross-center distribution alignment through attribute-aware pseudo-bag generation without sharing raw WSIs. Each center constructs a compact multi-attribute Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) group of its local data, which is communicated once and used to synthesize cross-domain pseudo-bags for augmenting local MIL training. FedGMM-Bag introduces two complementary mechanisms: distribution replay to introduce external morphological diversity and covariance-aligned feature mapping to achieve fine-grained cross-domain alignment.
Comprehensive experiments on three heterogeneous multi-center datasets demonstrate that FedGMM-Bag consistently outperforms existing federated and pseudo-bag methods on both seen and unseen centers. These results demonstrate its strong cross-domain generalization and its suitability for privacy-preserving federated pathology under real-world heterogeneity.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This study introduces a generative federated learning (FL) framework for whole slide image classification that synthesizes pseudo-bag across institutions based on attribute aware gaussian mixture model (GMM) summaries coined FedGMM. As opposed to prior works focused on stain-style transfer and harmonization, including synthetic slide distillation; here, the authors posit that GMMs can capture key statistical descriptors for effective transfer across institutions. This includes modeling the variability in patch counts across slides, class wise densities, intra-bag compositions and top-class wise patches, coupled together each local model can sample from the other center’s distributions for augmentation in what is termed distribution replay, and features are further aligned with covariance-based mappings. To validate this approach, an inhouse pancreatic cohorts was used, including public TCGA renal cell carcinoma subtype cohort, and the Camelyon17 dataset. Experiments reveal that FedGMM improves over existing approaches with notable gains, and lower entropy discrepancy across institutions.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper is well written with a lot of details on the proposed attribute aware GMM construction. The motivations are equally reasonable as FL is a timely and practical framework to address the challenge of privacy in medical AI.
The idea of using a generative approach to sampling is intuitive and interesting. The different level of attributes modeled in this work seem reasonable and capture the core of sources of heterogeneity across institutions.
The authors perform several experiments to validate their approach i. e. , a private cohort and two public datasets. This supports the possibility of reproducibility. In addition, several recent state of the art approaches were compared, which clearly shows the benefits of FedGMM.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
While I appreciate the use of GMMs as presented in this work. It is not entirely clear why this is a more principled approach compared to other generative approaches. The authors do not sufficiently motivate this choice.
This framework has several moving parts and the selection of components in the GMM is not quantitatively validated or discussed. For instance, for each GMM group 4 components for patch count, 8 for class specific modeling, and so on without any justification. Thus, it is unclear to the reader if there was hyperparameter search or some heuristic for balancing these components.
The authors leverage ImageNet pretrained ResNet50 to obtain features from the datasets. While this is reasonable, it is unclear if the results presented are a result of the backbone limited feature representation. Ideally, including recent pathology foundation specific models can clearly contextualize the FL task since these models have been trained on diverse data and less sensitive to the existing FL challenges. This should have been validated.
It is unclear if only using pseudo bags-only would provide reasonable gains. This evaluation is missing from the study, as the authors only augment the same number of pseudo bags as the initial training set. Thus, it is unclear how effective sensitive the approach is to the number of bags generated.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
In Introduction, L4.”analisys” – > “analysis”
The methodological design of this work is similar to Fedbip [3][Chen et al. CVPR25], a discussion on the differences would help clarify differences if any. Including [17] Pettersson et al. Federated Gaussian Mixture Models.
In Methods 2.2 Class-Specific Attribute Modeling subsection: [last sentence] Why do the authors describe ‘class specific attribute modeling’ as capturing ‘multi-modal morphological patterns’ ? I do not see how this is multi-modal.
In Methods 2.2 Bag-Composition Attribute Modeling subsection: [Last sentence] the authors state that ‘synthetic bags preserve realistic intra-bag composition’; was this validated quantitatively?
In implementation details, How did the authors arrive at the number of components 4/8/4/4, no justification about this.
There is a discrepancy on the reported scores of HistoFS in Table 1 [RCC] from that of the original paper, this is unclear especially if the same splits were used.
The discussion on Fig2.(d,e) is unclear. From a reader perspective, it is hard to understand how to interpret this particular analysis since we do not know which Institutes are annotated and how discrepancy and cross domain heteregeinty is resolved from one cohort to the other.

Overall, this is an interesting study that address a timely challenge in FL for computational pathology. There are merits to the presented methodology, but some of the claims in the paper are not supported by the results and lack some clear discussions on choice of hyperparameters and positioning of their work in the literature. One of the larger issues is the lack of ablations on the existing pathology foundation models. This is important, because if the main concern is heterogeneity and cross cohort variability, it’s only natural to base all evaluations on a strong foundation model rather than a ResNet50.In turn, this will ultimately inform readers whether this problem is still largely unsolved despite having models trained on millions of data points from diverse cohorts. The current score is a reflection of the aforementioned issues and would benefit from further clarifications.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
I thank the authors for the detailed rebuttal and for running the foundation model experiment I requested.
However, the new CONCH results actually reinforce my concerns rather than resolve it. This makes the overall story weaker in my view. On RCC the gap is essentially saturated; this suggests much of the reported gain in the main paper is tied to using ResNet50 features, and the cross-center heterogeneity problem is largely already addressed by a modern foundation model backbone. The GMM grid search and pseudo-bag ratio sweep are useful additions, and the HistoFS discrepancy clarification is appreciated.

reviews.text_contribution:
This paper addresses the problem of federated learning for multi-center whole slide image (WSI) classification under strong data heterogeneity and privacy constraints. The authors propose a framework termed FedGMM-Bag, which models each center’s data distribution using an attribute-aware Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) and leverages these compact statistical representations to generate cross-domain pseudo-bags for augmenting local multiple instance learning (MIL) training.
Specifically, each center constructs a multi-attribute GMM capturing patch-level distributions, class-conditional features, intra-bag composition, and top-K discriminative regions. These GMMs are shared across centers instead of raw data. Two pseudo-bag generation strategies are introduced: (1) distribution replay via GMM sampling to inject external domain diversity, and (2) covariance-aligned feature mapping to explicitly align feature statistics across centers. The generated pseudo-bags are then used to enhance federated MIL training under a standard FedAvg paradigm.
The method is evaluated on multiple multi-center WSI datasets, demonstrating improved cross-center generalization compared to several existing federated and pseudo-bag-based methods.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper tackles federated learning under cross-center heterogeneity for WSI classification, which is a highly relevant and realistic problem. Variations in staining, scanning, and acquisition protocols are well-known challenges in pathology AI, and the inability to share raw WSIs further complicates model training. The problem setting is therefore well-motivated and of clear clinical relevance.
Proposes a privacy-preserving and communication-efficient framework: Instead of sharing raw data or high-dimensional features, the method communicates compact GMM-based statistical summaries. This is an interesting design choice, as it reduces communication overhead while preserving privacy to a certain extent. Compared to approaches that rely on synthetic image sharing or repeated feature exchange, this formulation is relatively lightweight and potentially more practical.
Introduces a structured way to model cross-center distribution via multiple attributes: The use of an attribute-aware GMM group (patch count, class distribution, composition, top-K features) is a structured attempt to capture different aspects of WSI variability. This multi-level modeling of distribution (instance-level and bag-level) is conceptually reasonable and aligns with the hierarchical nature of WSI data.
Combines two complementary pseudo-bag generation strategies: The combination of distribution replay (sampling-based augmentation) and covariance-aligned mapping (feature-level alignment) is a sensible design. The former increases diversity, while the latter attempts to explicitly reduce domain gaps. This dual strategy is a strength compared to methods that rely solely on one type of augmentation.
Relatively comprehensive experimental validation: The method is evaluated on multiple multi-center datasets, including unseen centers, which is important for demonstrating generalization. Reporting both AUC and entropy (for cross-center consistency) is also a positive aspect, as it reflects robustness rather than only accuracy.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Major Comments
1.Weak Methodological Innovation; More Like a Combination of Existing Ideas
Structurally, this work mainly integrates several existing directions: federated learning (FedAvg), the MIL framework (CLAM), GMM distribution modeling, and pseudo-bag data augmentation. These components themselves are not new; the authors’ main contribution lies in combining them and designing an attribute-aware GMM system and two pseudo-bag generation strategies. This combination is more of a “reasonable engineering design” than a clear methodological breakthrough. For example, GMM is used to model feature distribution, pseudo-bags for enhancement, and covariance alignment for alignment—similar approaches exist in different fields. It is suggested that the authors further clarify: what is the truly new core idea compared to existing federated WSI methods, rather than just improvements on modules?
2.The rationale and necessity of GMM modeling are not adequately explained.
The paper’s key assumption is to use a multi-attribute GMM to characterize the central feature distribution of WSI and to perform cross-domain generation based on this. However, several questions remain:
Is GMM sufficient to represent the complex distribution of high-dimensional WSI features?
Why choose GMM instead of a stronger generative model (such as VAE, diffusion, etc.)?
Is there redundancy or repetitive modeling among multiple attributes (patch count, class, composition, top-K)?
3.Performance Improvement Exists, but Its Persuasiveness is Limited
Experimental results show that the method does outperform the baseline on multiple datasets, but the overall improvement is small, mostly around 1%. Considering the additional modeling, generation, and alignment steps introduced by the model, this gain is somewhat limited. More importantly, there is a lack of in-depth analysis of the “source of improvement.” For example, which part (GMM modeling, replay, mapping) truly brings about the improvement? Under which data distributions or centrality differences is the effect more significant? It is recommended to add more granular analysis, rather than just reporting overall metrics.
4.Insufficient Statistical Analysis
Although the paper reports the mean and standard deviation of multiple experiments, it does not perform significance testing. This is crucial given the current small performance improvement. If the difference is not statistically significant, then the method’s advantage needs to be stated more cautiously. It is recommended to supplement with statistical significance analysis, or at least to discuss the reliability of the results more objectively in the paper.
5.Comparison Methods Still Have Room for Improvement
The current baseline includes some classic MIL methods and existing federated learning methods, but overall it is still biased towards traditional methods. Given that this work emphasizes cross-center generalization and distribution modeling, it is recommended to add some more recent and stronger comparative methods, especially those from the last two years in the areas of federated pathology or self-supervised methods. Otherwise, while the current comparison is reasonable, it is insufficient to fully demonstrate the advantages of the method.
6.The authors demonstrated the alignment effect of pseudo-bag on distributions using t-SNE, but this is more qualitative. Several questions remain:
Does pseudo-bag introduce noise or misdistribution?
Could it lead to overfitting the model to a “synthetic distribution”?
Are the benefits of replay and mapping stable?

reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes FedGMM-Bag, a federated learning framework for multi-center whole slide image (WSI) classification under strong data heterogeneity. The key idea is to represent each center’s data distribution using an attribute-aware Gaussian Mixture Model. These compact GMM representations are shared across centers and used to generate cross-domain pseudo-bags to augment local MIL training and improve cross-center generalization without sharing raw data. Experiments on multiple datasets show improved performance over existing federated and pseudo-bag methods
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Representing each center’s data distribution with an attribute-aware GMM is a neat and conceptually sound idea.
2.The paper clearly addresses a realistic challenge in federated pathology: cross-center heterogeneity under strict privacy constraints.
3.The integration of GMM-based distribution modeling with pseudo-bag augmentation is reasonably novel and technically meaningful.
4.The method is evaluated on multiple datasets (PANC, RCC, CAMELYON17), and shows consistent improvements over strong baselines
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The number of GMM components is a critical hyperparameter that directly affects distribution modeling quality. However, the paper does not provide ablation or analysis on this factor, making it unclear how robust or sensitive the method is to this choice.
2.Although communication cost is low, the cost of fitting multiple GMMs and generating pseudo-bags across centers is not thoroughly analyzed.
3.The experimental evaluation is conducted on datasets with relatively few centers (typically 2–3 centers) . While the results are promising, this setup may not fully reflect the level of heterogeneity encountered in real-world federated pathology settings.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I lean towards a weak accept for this paper. The work addresses an important and practical challenge in federated computational pathology and introduces an interesting and intuitive GMM-based framework for modeling cross-center heterogeneity. However, the paper has several limitations. The novelty is moderate, and key design choices, particularly the number of GMM components, are not sufficiently analyzed. In addition, the evaluation is conducted on datasets with relatively few centers, which limits the strength of claims regarding scalability and robustness under real-world heterogeneity. Some modeling assumptions (e.g., Gaussian mixtures) may also restrict expressiveness. Finally, the code is not publicly available, which limits reproducibility and makes it harder to verify the reported results and adopt the method in practice.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I want to thank the author for their effort in preparing the response, i think most of my concerns were alleviated.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper addresses an important and practical problem in federated learning for computational pathology, and the proposed GMM-based framework is conceptually interesting with promising empirical results across multiple datasets. However, the main issue is the unclear methodological novelty and justification, as the approach appears to combine existing components (FL, MIL, GMM, pseudo-bag augmentation) without sufficiently clarifying the core innovation or why GMM is the most appropriate modeling choice compared to alternative generative approaches. In addition, the experimental validation is not fully convincing, due to limited analysis of key design choices (e.g., GMM components), lack of statistical significance testing, and insufficient investigation into the source of performance gains. There are also concerns regarding baseline comparisons and evaluation settings, including the absence of stronger or more recent methods (e.g., foundation models), and limited validation under realistic multi-center heterogeneity. The final decision will depend on how convincingly these concerns are addressed.

The paper addresses an important and practically relevant problem in federated computational pathology: robust WSI classification under severe cross-center heterogeneity and privacy constraints. Reviewers appreciated the clear motivation, communication-efficient framework, and the integration of attribute-aware GMM modeling with pseudo-bag augmentation. The extensive evaluation across multiple datasets, including unseen-center settings, further supports the practical value of the proposed approach. While concerns were raised regarding the degree of methodological novelty, the reliance on an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 backbone, and the lack of evaluation with recent pathology foundation models, I do not believe these issues outweigh the overall strengths of the work. The proposed framework provides a practical and effective solution to a challenging real-world problem and demonstrates consistent improvements under heterogeneous federated settings. The authors should nevertheless address the reviewers’ comments in the final version, particularly by clarifying the methodological novelty, discussing the relationship to recent pathology foundation models, and better highlighting the limitations and scope of the proposed approach. Overall, I believe the paper makes a meaningful contribution and merits acceptance.

The paper got two accepts and one reject after rebuttal, and I tend to reject this paper. The main reason is that as the fast development of pathology models, a new and powerful foundation model should be used for patch feature extraction. Many problems that exist when using traditional feature extractors (such as ResNet50) no longer exist when using foundation model feature extractors. The results in the rebutal also support this point. When a foundation model is used for the CAMELYON dataset, the genalization performance whill be much higher than the results listed in this paper.

The paper proposes FedGMM-Bag, a federated learning framework for multi-center whole slide image classification.
Based on the reviewers’ feedback and the authors’ rebuttal, I recommend accepting this manuscript. Two out of three reviewers moved to accept post-rebuttal, agree that the major concerns have been addressed, recognizing the method design and evaluation.

author_feedback_text:
We thank reviewers and the AC for constructive feedback. We address the concerns below.
1@R1R2 Novelty: We respectfully clarify that our contribution is not the isolated use of FL, MIL and GMM, but a WSI-specific federated formulation for hierarchical, bag-structured pathology data. Each center is summarized by an attribute-aware GMM group modeling patch-count variability, class-conditional feature density, intra-bag composition, and top-K discriminative patterns, which enables DR for diversity injection and CM for second-order alignment. Thus, the novelty lies in turning cross-center WSI heterogeneity into a controllable generative representation for privacy-preserving federated MIL.
2@R1R2 GMM: We do not claim GMM is universally stronger than VAE/GAN/diffusion; it better fits our federated WSI-MIL objective: feature-space, class-conditional pseudo-bag synthesis/alignment rather than pixel-level generation. GMM compactly estimates local bag-level feature distributions via mixture weights, means, and covariances, enabling closed-form density estimation, interpretable components, low communication, and component-wise sampling. VAE/GAN/diffusion would require heavier training and extra conditioning to control structured bag attributes. Thus, GMM is a principled choice for efficient bag-level modeling.
R2-2 The attributes are sequentially dependent rather than redundant, GMM groups preserve multi-level WSI heterogeneity and naturally support DR/CM.
R2-3 Tab.3 already shows progressive gains. Since GMM and DR CM are sequentially coupled in the generation pipeline, they cannot be fully separated into independent ablations.
R1-2R4-1 GMM component: 4/8/4/4 was selected by grid search. On RCC, it gives the best average AUC/entropy 0.9821/0.0765, outperforming 2/4/2/2 0.9564/0.1139, 4/8/8/8 0.9812/0.0867, and 4/12/8/8 0.9807/0.0862.These results were omitted due to space limits.
3@R1R2R4 Experimental evidence:
R1-3 Foundation model: With CONCH features, FedGMM-Bag still improves over HistoFS (PANC 0.9532 vs. 0.9485; RCC 0.9981 vs. 0.9978), showing the gain is not tied to a weak backbone. We used ResNet50 in the main paper to better isolate the contribution of federated distribution modeling.
R1-4 PseMix in Tab1 already serves as a pseudo-bag-only baseline.
We also evaluated different pseudo-bag ratios 0.5x/1x/1.5x/2x/2.5x. On RCC, average AUCs are 0.9673/0.9821/0.9818/0.9782/0.9756; on PANC, the best result is 0.8516 at 1.5x. Since larger ratios do not consistently improve performance, we use 1x as the best performance-overhead trade-off.
R1-minor: We will clarify these points in the revision. The discrepancy mainly arises from different feature extractors (HistoFS: ViT; ours: ResNet50).
R2-3 Gains are consistent across 3 datasets, with lower entropy and one-shot GMM transmission (~0.28 MB/center in RCC), indicating a favorable robustness-efficiency trade-off compared with HistoFS.
R2-4 Paired testing against HistoFS gives p=0.04782, indicating significance.
R2-5 We already include recent strong FL WSI baselines, especially FedWSIDD(MICCAI 2025) and HistoFS(CVPR 2025), together with representative general FL and MIL pseudo-bag methods. To the best of our knowledge, there are very limited additional recent federated WSI pathology methods that are both directly comparable to our setting and reproducible under the same protocol.
R2-6 We agree that t-SNE is only qualitative. Tab3 already shows that DR-only improves robustness quantitatively, CM-only is weaker alone, and the full model performs best, indicating that replay/mapping are stable and complementary rather than causing harmful drift to a synthetic distribution.
R3-2 The extra cost mainly comes from one-time GMM fitting and lightweight pseudo-bag sampling on pre-extracted features, rather than a heavy per-round burden.
R3-3 We follows standard Fed WSI benchmarks, which are limited in center number; we will clarify this scope and note larger-scale validation as future work.

title: AutoLand: A Data-Efficient Automated Agentic Workflow for Universal Medical Landmark Detection
abstract: Medical landmark detection varies significantly across modalities and clinical protocols, posing unique challenges for developing universally applicable models. Conventional approaches typically entail training bespoke architectures per dataset or relying on general-purpose heuristics with fixed rules. However, these methods suffer from limited scalability and lack the semantic reasoning required to adapt to complex anatomical variations. To address these limitations, we propose AutoLand, a data-efficient autonomous workflow for landmark detection in medical images, leveraging a Vision Language Model (VLM) as a medical analysis agent. Specifically, AutoLand integrates a Physics Fingerprint Extraction module to extract precise physical characteristics, ensuring the agent aligns with modality-specific data properties. Subsequently, a Medical Deep Learning Library is queried during reasoning to retrieve specialized network architectures and optimization protocols, enabling the formulation of expert-level training strategies with only a few samples. This workflow enhances robustness and adaptability while reducing manual intervention. Experiments on three datasets show that AutoLand significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, ablation studies confirm that our agentic paradigm effectively overcomes the limitations of fixed baselines through semantic reasoning. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChiZai123456/AutoLand.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution is an agent-guided workflow that formulates dataset-specific training pipelines for medical landmark detection from limited annotations, by combining modality-aware physics fingerprints with a constrained medical deep learning library.
reviews.text_strengths:
(1) The paper proposes an interesting and well-motivated direction. 
(2) Automating per-dataset configuration for landmark detection could reduce manual tuning effort and expert dependence, which is relevant for real medical settings where datasets are limited and heterogeneous. 
(3) The physics fingerprint is a simple but practical idea. It provides the agent with compact modality- and acquisition-related information that may help guide more dataset-specific strategy selection. 
(4) The cross-dataset evaluation is reasonably broad. Validation on cephalometric X-ray, chest X-ray, and cardiac MRI helps support the claim that the framework is not tied to a single anatomy or modality. 
(5) The paper is clearly motivated and generally easy to follow.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(1) The agentic framework is not described in enough detail, especially the prompt design, constraint mechanism, and strategy parsing. 
(2) The bridge from generic architecture selection to landmark detection is unclear, including the prediction head and task-specific design details. 
(3) Baseline fairness is unclear, as tuning budgets, hyperparameters, augmentations, and model settings are not standardized or sufficiently described. 
(4) The comparison does not isolate the value of the agent itself, since no non-agent AutoML baseline is included. 
(5) The data-efficiency claim is not fully validated, because performance is only reported under a fixed 1:1:8 split. 
(6) Potential patient-level leakage is not clearly ruled out, particularly for the cardiac MRI dataset. 
(7) Practical feasibility remains unclear, including compute cost, latency, and the reliability of the agent-generated strategies.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The idea is relevant, timely, and potentially impactful, and the ablation studies suggest that both the physics fingerprint and the curated medical DL library contribute meaningfully to performance. However, my overall score is limited by several weaknesses in the current manuscript, including unclear dataset and experimental pipeline details, baseline comparisons that are not yet fully convincing, and reproducibility gaps in the description of the framework. Clarifying these aspects would substantially improve the quality and credibility of the work.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes AutoLand, a data-efficient automated agentic workflow for universal medical landmark detection. It takes a large vision-language model (VLM) as a medical analysis agent to automatically synthesize dataset-specific training strategies, integrating a Physics Fingerprint module to extract modality-acquisition related data properties and a curated Medical Deep Learning Library for executable pipeline construction. Evaluations on cephalometric X-rays, chest X-rays, and cardiac MRI show superior performance over mainstream baselines, and ablation studies verify the effectiveness of the two core components. The work provides a new agentic paradigm for reducing manual tuning in universal medical landmark detection.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Technical novelty: Using VLM as a medical analysis agent to generate executable training strategies from a constrained DL library is an innovative system-level attempt for automated universal medical landmark detection. The Physics Fingerprint effectively provides modality-aware cues to alleviate agent hallucinations.
2.Experimental validation: Evaluated on three typical medical imaging modalities with comprehensive baselines and solid ablation studies; both quantitative metrics and qualitative visualizations are provided to support the effectiveness.
3.Practical value: The workflow targets the pain point of manual dataset-specific tuning in few-sample scenarios, which has high application potential for clinical deployment of landmark detection models.
4.Presentation clarity: The pipeline is clearly decomposed into three modules with formalized equations, making the core design easy to follow.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The Physics Fingerprint only covers basic statistics and can be extended with more clinical metadata
2.The reliance on Qwen3-VL-235B lacks computational overhead quantification.
3.The landmark detection formulation and agent guardrail mechanism need more detailed description.
4.Multi-seed experiments and statistical significance tests are suggested to enhance rigor.
5.Insufficient discussion and comparison with representative universal landmark detection works, such as (UOD: universal one-shot landmark detection).
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
This paper puts forward a novel agentic automation paradigm for universal medical landmark detection with solid experimental results and high clinical application potential. To further improve the paper, it is recommended to: 1) Add multi-seed experiments and statistical tests; 2) Supplement detailed engineering details of the agent and DL library; 3) Cite and compare with the following representative works on (universal) (one-shot) landmark detection: 
Uod: Universal one-shot detection of anatomical landmarks
Pele scores: pelvic x-ray landmark detection with pelvis extraction and enhancement
Learning to Localize Cross-Anatomy Landmarks in X-Ray Images with a Universal Model

AutoLand proposes an innovative agentic automation workflow for universal medical landmark detection, which combines VLM reasoning, Physics Fingerprint and Medical DL Library to solve the problem of manual tuning in few-sample scenarios. The core idea is novel, the experimental results on three modalities are promising, and the work has clear clinical value. Although the paper has imperfections in experimental details, related work completeness and technical description, these issues can be well addressed through minor revisions. The core contribution is solid and meets the basic acceptance standard of MICCAI, so a weak accept is recommended.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of this paper is the proposal of an automated workflow for general medical landmark detection. It leverages a VLM as an agent to guide the selection of components and training strategies, effectively automating the workflow to handle different modalities and anatomical structures.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper provides an interesting and original solution to general keypoint detection. Instead of relying on fixed architectures or general-purpose heuristics, it creatively uses a VLM agent to adaptively formulate strategies.
It effectively addresses key challenges in the current field of general keypoint detection, such as sensitivity to data modality and anatomical variations.
The method has been validated across different datasets, demonstrating its initial capability, and the overall execution of the paper is quite solid.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
General keypoint detection methods are highly sensitive to data modality and anatomical structures. While validated on several datasets, the evaluation lacks sufficient diversity. Datasets from different anatomical regions (e.g., publicly available hand X-ray, spine X-ray, and abdominal ultrasound datasets) should be included to fully prove the method’s universality.
Lack of Transparency in Agent Strategy: It remains unclear how one can verify that the strategy selected by the VLM agent is indeed the optimal one. Additionally, the paper lacks discussion on failure cases, such as whether the method falls back to baseline models like U-Net under certain conditions.
For the Cardiac dataset split, the authors state that 5,293 LAX and 15,024 SAX slices are obtained from 144 patients. Adjacent slices from the same patient share highly similar anatomical structures. There is no confirmation that the split was performed strictly at the patient level. Splitting these slices randomly across training, validation, and test sets will lead to severe data leakage.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Overall, this paper presents a solid and interesting VLM-guided solution that addresses real challenges in general landmark detection. The major factors leading to my current score are the promising novelty of the workflow, offset by significant concerns regarding the evaluation. Specifically, the risk of data leakage in the Cardiac dataset is a critical issue that must be clarified. Furthermore, the lack of anatomical diversity in the evaluation datasets and the missing verification of the agent’s optimality prevent a higher score. If the data leakage concern is resolved and the evaluation is broadened, I would be willing to give a higher evaluation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

meta_reviews.text: AutoLand introduces a novel agentic paradigm that uses a VLM together with a Physics Fingerprint and a curated medical DL library to automatically synthesize dataset-specific training strategies for universal medical landmark detection — a timely, well-motivated direction with clear clinical value. All three reviewers consistently affirm the originality of the workflow, the effectiveness of both core modules in ablations, and solid cross-modality validation on cephalometric X-ray, chest X-ray, and cardiac MRI; remaining concerns (cardiac patient-level split, broader baselines, agent reliability) are addressable in camera-ready.

title: Automated Disentangling Analysis of Skin Colour for Lesion Images
abstract:
Machine-learning models applied to skin images often have degraded performance when the skin colour captured in images (SCCI) differs between training and deployment. These discrepancies arise from a combination of entangled environmental factors (e.g., illumination, camera settings) and intrinsic factors (e.g., skin tone) that cannot be accurately described by a single “skin tone” scalar – a simplification commonly adopted by prior work. To mitigate such colour mismatches, we propose a skin-colour disentangling framework that adapts disentanglement-by-compression to learn a structured, manipulable latent space for SCCI from unlabelled dermatology images. To prevent information leakage
that hinders proper learning of dark colour features, we introduce a randomized, mostly monotonic decolourization mapping. To suppress unintended colour shifts of localized patterns (e.g., ink marks, scars) during colour manipulation, we further propose a geometry-aligned post-processing step. Together, these components enable faithful counterfactual editing and answering an essential question: “What would this skin condition look like under a different SCCI?”, as well as direct colour transfer between images and controlled traversal along physically meaningful directions (e.g., blood perfusion, camera white balance), enabling educational visualization of skin conditions under varying SCCI. We demonstrate that dataset-level augmentation and colour normalization based on our framework achieve competitive lesion classification performance. Ultimately, our work promotes equitable diagnosis through creating diverse training datasets that include different skin tones and image-capturing conditions.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a method for generating modified versions of an existing skin lesion by altering its color features (e. g. , luminance, skin tone, camera settings).
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper is well written.
Illumination and color differences can heavily affect the performance of skin lesion analysis models, and finding ways to deal with such variation can be impactful.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The main weakness is the paper validation, which is notably hard when generating counterfactuals, as there are no ground truths. But because validation is not straightforward, it also requires more effort to provide evidence that the proposed method works. 
For example, the paper’s first results are qualitative (subsection 3.1). To support the authors’ claim that “The figure confirms that the model produces diverse yet realistic skin colour variations,” we would ideally need an assessment from a dermatologist, as it is hard to say that just from one image, and without really knowing the potential variations an image can exhibit in the wild.
Moreover, as skin lesions exhibit different visual characteristics across skin tones [1,2], simply modifying healthy skin color might produce unrealistic skin lesions and provide incorrect priors (regarding the frequency of dermoscopic attributes or their appearance) when training dermatologists or machine learning models. I believe this is very important as it can perpetuate biases in skin lesion diagnosis models. I would suggest that the authors explicitly limit the scope of their solution to environmental factors (e. g. , illumination, camera settings) while preserving skin tone intact.
Finally, it would help to have more comparisons to similar methods. The only comparison happens with citation [16], but only in one of the experiments performed (Table 1).
[1] Gloster Jr, Hugh M. , and Kenneth Neal. “Skin cancer in skin of color. “ Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology 55.5 (2006): 741-760.
[2] Karampinis, Emmanouil, et al. “Race-specific and skin of color dermatoscopic characteristics of skin cancer: a literature review. “ Dermatology Practical & Conceptual 13.4 Suppl 1 (2023): e2023311S.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I believe the paper should be rejected due to the lack of validation and comparison with other methods. Also, there are potential problems of using the proposed method to simulate skin lesions in underserved populations without proper evaluation, which could perpetuate biases.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Using a diagnostic model as a proxy for evaluating another diagnostic model has important limitations, as models do not necessarily rely on clinical features to make predictions. To partially mitigate this, subgroup analysis could help increase trust that the proposed method is not detrimental to underrepresented skin tones, and clarify which groups benefit most from the procedure. Such analysis would also provide evidence on whether the potential generation of unrealistic or biologically implausible lesions for specific demographics affects downstream performance. Given these methodological concerns, along with the risk of uncontrolled color manipulation in skin lesion analysis, I recommend rejection.
