reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper addresses depression severity estimation from audiovisual clinical interview recordings. The authors identify a granularity mismatch in existing approaches: standard regression methods predict continuous severity scores but ignore clinically meaningful categorical boundaries (e.g., none/mild/moderate/severe), treating errors that cross these boundaries the same as within-category errors.
To address this, the paper proposes Multi-Granularity Supervision, combining three complementary loss functions: (1) standard MSE regression for continuous score prediction, (2) Ordinal Consistency Regularization (OCR), which amplifies learning at clinical severity thresholds, and (3) Prototype-based Severity Contrastive Learning (PSCL), which organises the feature space to reflect ordinal severity structure. The authors provide a theoretical proof that OCR induces boundary-aware gradient amplification, with gradient magnitude peaking at clinical thresholds.
The method is evaluated on four standard depression benchmarks (AVEC 2013, AVEC 2014, DAIC-WOZ, E-DAIC) across visual, audio, and multimodal settings, achieving state-of-the-art results on all datasets. Ablation studies with statistical significance tests confirm that each component contributes independently.
reviews.text_strengths:
S1.Novel and well-motivated methodology: The multi-granularity supervision framework addresses a real clinical problem - that standard regression treats all prediction errors equally, regardless of whether they cross clinically meaningful severity boundaries. The combination of MSE, OCR, and PSCL is, to the best of this reviewer’s knowledge, novel for depression severity estimation.
S2.Comprehensive comparison: The paper compares against 20 methods across four standard benchmarks (AVEC 2013, AVEC 2014, DAIC-WOZ, E-DAIC), covering visual-only, audio-only, and multimodal settings. State-of-the-art performance is achieved across virtually all configurations.
S3.Rigorous ablation and statistical testing: The ablation study systematically removes each component and includes Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, paired t-tests, and bootstrap confidence intervals - exceeding the statistical rigour normally provided.
S4.Theory-to-practice validation: Theorem 1 is empirically validated in Figure 4, where OCR loss peaks at the clinical thresholds as predicted. This connection between theoretical motivation and experimental evidence strengthens the paper’s narrative.
S5.Additional analyses: The paper includes hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, Grad-CAM interpretability visualisations showing clinically relevant facial regions, and detailed component analysis of the contrastive learning module, providing a thorough understanding of the method’s behaviour.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
W1.Insufficient related work and baseline descriptions: The related work section discusses only two prior depression estimation methods, yet Tables 1 and 2 compare against 20 methods. The paper would benefit from briefly describing the key baselines, particularly the closest competitors (e.g., DepMGNN, FC-AEN, SIMMA), so the reader can understand what approaches the proposed method improves upon and why. Additionally, CORAL and SORD are discussed as motivation but not included as explicit experimental baselines. Given that the competing methods are not described, it is unclear whether any of them already employ ordinal regression approaches, making it difficult to assess whether the proposed method’s advantage comes specifically from the multi-granularity formulation.
W2.Clarity and accessibility: The paper is difficult to follow for readers outside the area. The paper would benefit from a clearer description of the overall pipeline beyond the architecture diagrams. The input modality, preprocessing steps, and model architecture are largely left to be inferred from figures rather than described explicitly in the text. The four evaluation datasets are named but not described (number of subjects, recording conditions, label distributions). The evaluation protocol (e.g., whether the standard challenge partitions were used) is not explicitly stated. Readers unfamiliar with these benchmarks would need to check the original challenge papers to verify that comparisons are conducted under identical conditions. A few sentences describing the end-to-end pipeline, datasets, and evaluation protocol would significantly improve accessibility for the broader MICCAI audience.
W3.No limitations discussion: The paper does not discuss any limitations of the proposed approach. A brief limitations paragraph in the conclusion would strengthen the paper.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The paper includes helpful illustrations and tables that support the reader’s understanding. If additional space is needed (e.g., for expanding the related work), Figure 2 could be reduced in size, since Figure 3 represents the main contribution. Minor note: Figure 1 explains the two motivating problems effectively, but is visually crowded. For example, the MSE loss box in Figure 1a is placed inside the graph, which is initially confusing - this information could be incorporated into the Case A and Case B boxes instead. The emoji icons next to Challenge 1 and 2 are redundant and add visual clutter.

The paper presents a novel and well-motivated approach to depression severity estimation, combining continuous regression with boundary-aware ordinal regularization and contrastive feature learning. The core idea - that prediction errors crossing clinical severity boundaries should be penalized more than within-category errors - is clinically meaningful and elegantly addressed through the multi-granularity supervision framework.
The experimental evidence is strong: state-of-the-art results across four benchmarks, thorough ablation studies with proper statistical testing, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, and empirical validation of the theoretical claims. The level of experimental rigour exceeds what is typically seen.
The main weaknesses are presentational. The related work section is too brief, leaving the reader unable to understand what the 20 baseline methods do or how they relate to the proposed approach (W1). The paper assumes significant familiarity with the depression detection benchmarks, making it difficult to follow for the broader MICCAI audience (W2). These issues do not undermine the contribution but should be addressed in the camera-ready version.
Overall, the strengths - particularly the novelty of the approach, the comprehensive evaluation, and the rigorous statistical analysis - clearly outweigh the presentational weaknesses.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper addresses the challenging domain of severity predictions, where ground truth is often both continuous (e.g., between 0 and 5) and ordinal (e.g., low, moderate, high severity). The authors introduce additional regularization guided by the ordinal class labels and also use continuous values for regression loss, such as MSE.
reviews.text_strengths:
The theoretical justifications for the methodologies presented strengthen the contribution.
The authors also establish state-of-the-art results on several benchmark datasets for depression severity.
The paper was well written, with key contributions made clearer using diagrams.
Overall, the methods could be valuable for automated severity assessment, beyond the domain of depression.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
My main feedback concerns the decoupling of the model from the optimization process. It is not clear which one is the primary contributor to SOTA performance. Is it achieved via task-specific modeling, such as using carefully curated audio and video feature extractors and Mamba encoders? Or is it because of the loss functions and regularizations introduced by the authors?
It would further strengthen the study if the authors could examine what happens if the same (or similar) architecture is trained with
simply MSE loss
MSE loss + multi-class classification loss
or other ordinal classification losses used in the literature
The authors mention comparing against several baselines. But ideally, one would want to show and separate the effects of the introduced loss function.
Some minor feedback:
In Abstract: “This granularity mismatch leads to boundary-agnostic optimization and unstructured representations.” – unstructured representations sound a bit vague, especially when, in the abstract, the readers do not know what type of structure you are talking about.
Figure 2: Raw Input -> Are both top and bottom labels “Video”, or one should be “Video” and another should be “Audio”?
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Please see the strengths and weaknesses above.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_ethics:
In Fig. 2, the data appear to be videos. Please discuss whether these are patient videos and whether they are subject to HIPAA compliance.
Also, do the authors have the subject’s consent to publish their photo (simply blurring the eyes does not make the data de-identifiable)?

meta_reviews.text: All three reviewers recommend acceptance, with strong consensus on the paper’s merits: a novel and clinically meaningful multi‑granularity supervision framework, state‑of‑the‑art results across four benchmarks, and exceptional experimental rigor including thorough ablations and statistical testing. Minor concerns, such as the need for clearer baseline descriptions, disentangling the contribution of the loss functions from the architecture, are addressed in a revision. Overall, the paper makes a solid and valuable contribution. Conclusion: Early Accept.

author_feedback_text:
Dear Area Chair and Reviewers,
We sincerely thank the reviewers for their careful reading, thoughtful evaluation, and highly constructive comments. We are truly encouraged by the positive feedback and deeply appreciate the time and expertise dedicated to improving our work. We will faithfully address all concerns in the camera-ready version. Our detailed responses follow.
Q1.Architecture vs. loss contribution and ordinal-classification objectives [R3, R2-W1].
We sincerely thank R3 for this insightful question, which goes to the heart of our contribution. The ablation in Table 3 directly addresses the relative contribution of architecture and optimization. With the Mamba backbone fixed, moving from MSE-only to PSCL, OCR, and the full objective consistently reduces MAE on AVEC2013 and AVEC2014, validated by Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, paired t-tests, and bootstrap CIs. This confirms measurable gains from the proposed losses without changing the backbone. We fully agree with R3 that head-to-head comparisons against alternative ordinal losses under the same backbone would further isolate our objective’s contribution, and we gratefully take this excellent suggestion as a valuable direction for future work. Regarding CORAL and SORD, we will clarify their conceptual difference: they reformulate regression as ordinal classification, whereas our method preserves continuous regression and introduces ordinal information only as regularization, without altering the task formulation.
Q2.Input modalities, pipeline, datasets, and evaluation protocol [R1, R2-W2].
We deeply appreciate R1 and R2 for this perceptive suggestion, which will substantially enhance the readability and reproducibility of our paper. In the Datasets and Implementation paragraph, we will clarify that experiments cover visual, audio, and audio-visual settings: visual inputs use HOG+SVM face features and audio inputs use STFT-based log-Mel features. We will also describe the four benchmarks, namely AVEC2013/2014 (BDI-II, 0–63) and DAIC-WOZ/E-DAIC (PHQ-8, 0–24), with severity thresholds and official splits.
Q3.Related work and baselines [R2-W1].
We are very grateful to R2 for this constructive suggestion, which will strengthen the positioning of our work. We will explicitly position the closest competitors, including DepMGNN, FC-AEN, SIMMA, PointTransform, and AVA-DepressNet, as point-wise regression methods without explicit ordinal supervision, which is the gap our method addresses. CORAL and SORD will be described as ordinal-classification approaches that discard continuous scores. As they produce discrete grades rather than continuous BDI-II/PHQ-8 outputs, they are not directly comparable under our regression metrics (MAE/RMSE); we will make this explicit in §2.All revisions will remain within §2.Q4.Limitations [R2-W3].
We sincerely thank R2 for this valuable suggestion, which will further improve the rigor of our paper. We will add a concise statement in the conclusion noting that our evaluation relies on public benchmarks with limited scale and diversity, and that broader validation across larger and more diverse cohorts remains future work.
Q5.Figures and wording [R1, R2, R3].
We greatly appreciate the reviewers’ meticulous attention to figures and wording. In the camera-ready version, we will: (i) correct Figure 2 by labeling the lower “Raw Input” branch as “Audio”; (ii) replace “unstructured representations” with “ordinally unstructured representations”; and (iii) following R1’s suggestion, streamline Fig. 3 by reducing internal Mamba details to highlight the overall flow, and trim redundant descriptions of loss terms.
We again sincerely thank the reviewers for their careful reading and constructive suggestions. These targeted revisions will improve the clarity, rigor, and value of the paper for the MICCAI community.

title: BRAIN: Bi-directional Motion Reasoning with Dynamic Memory Pruning for Surgical Video Segmentation
abstract: Accurate instrument tracking and segmentation is essential for robot-assisted surgery, where failures pose direct threats to patient safety. Current methods focus on dealing with the large intra-class variations of different instruments, neglecting the critical process of instrument’s abrupt disappearance and reappearance, which significantly misleads the predictions of advanced models. We identify two critical challenges hinders the addressing of these issues: instrument misidentification due to abrupt positional shifts and redundant memory caused by long-term instrument absence. To address these two challenges, we present bi-directional motion reasoning with dynamic memory pruning for surgical video segmentation (BRAIN). The bi-directional motion reasoning module first detects abrupt positional shifts from forward and backward trajectories and corrects errors via a mask reselection mechanism. Then, a dynamic memory pruning module maintains a compact yet diverse memory bank by filtering out redundant frames captured during instrument absence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods by 5.27% and 7.28% on EndoVis 2018 and 2017 benchmarks, respectively.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses two important challenges in surgical video segmentation: abrupt positional shifts and long-term instrument absence. By explicitly modeling these issues, it offers a meaningful and practically relevant perspective on improving robustness in real-world surgical scenarios.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper is motivated by realistic challenges in surgical videos, which are indeed common in clinical surgical navigation settings. Addressing these issues enhances the practical relevance of the work.
2.The proposed framework is clearly organised, with complementary modules (BMR and DM) that target different aspects of the problem. The overall design is coherent and easy to follow.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The paper does not engage sufficiently with recent related work in surgical video segmentation using large foundation models, such as EndoMamba: An Efficient Foundation Model for Endoscopic Videos via Hierarchical Pre-training, Memory-Augmented SAM2 for Training-Free Surgical Video Segmentation, and ReSurgSAM2: Referring Segment Anything in Surgical Video via Credible Long-term Tracking (all MICCAI 2025). This weak positioning makes the claimed novelty less convincing. Also, the limited experimental comparison (in Table 1) with recent related methods further reduces confidence in the paper’s contribution relative to the current state of the art.
2.The method involves several key hyperparameters (e. g. , thresholds for motion consistency, weighting factors, and memory pruning criteria), but the paper does not provide systematic ablation or sensitivity analysis. This makes it difficult to assess the robustness and reproducibility of the design choices.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Although the work addresses a relevant problem and shows promising results, the novelty would need to be better established through stronger engagement with recent related work, especially foundation-model-based methods in surgical video segmentation. The current work also lacks a systematic sensitivity analysis for several key hyperparameters, which makes the robustness of the proposed design harder to assess.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The response is not substantial enough to change my assessment. I still think the paper does not engage sufficiently with recent work. Therefore, I will maintain my score.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a framework (BRAIN) to address abrupt positional shifts and long-term instrument absence in surgical video segmentation. It introduces a Bidirectional Motion Reasoning (BMR) module for motion consistency modelling and a Dynamic Memory (DM) pruning module to maintain representative memory entries.
reviews.text_strengths: The use of bidirectional tracking (Kalman filtering combined with RTS smoothing) and memory diversity-based pruning provides a reasonable and interpretable design. The method demonstrates consistent and significant improvements over SAM2 and related baselines on EndoVis benchmarks.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The method involves multiple critical hyperparameters, including τ, γ, k, λ, L, and β. However, only β is studied in the ablation (Fig. 4), while all other parameters are fixed without sensitivity analysis. The lack of systematic analysis raises concerns about robustness and reproducibility.
2.The appearance score used in Motion-Guided Mask Reselection is not clearly compared to standard feature matching approaches in ReID literature. Its differences and potential advantages are not sufficiently explained.
3.When motion inconsistency is detected, especially under abrupt shifts or long-term absence, the memory bank itself may contain corrupted, occluded, or misidentified entries. In such cases, relying on appearance-based reselection may reinforce existing errors rather than correct them. This critical dependency is not analyzed or validated.
4.It is unclear which prompting strategy (among those described in Table 1) is used for the results reported in Table 2.5.In the BMR module, the contribution of bidirectional reasoning is not isolated. In particular, the effect of RTS backward smoothing is not independently evaluated, making it unclear whether the gains come from forward Kalman tracking or backward smoothing.
6.Although BRAIN introduces the BMR module on top of SAM2, the paper does not analyze the additional computational cost or complexity, which is important for practical deployment.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a framework with improvements over SAM2.However, the method involves multiple hyperparameters without sensitivity analysis, and key components are not clearly justified. The contribution of forward and backward components not evaluated separately. In addition, some experimental details and computational cost are not clearly reported.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have adequately addressed most of the concerns raised and improved the explanation of several technical components. Therefore, I support acceptance.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper targets a specific failure mode in surgical video segmentation: instrument disappearance and reappearance. The authors identify two concrete problems: (1) motion inertia where models keep tracking the last known location and latch onto wrong instruments after abrupt shifts, and (2) redundant memory where memory banks fill with empty or occluded frames during long absences, degrading re-identification.
Their solution, BRAIN (Bidirectional motion Reasoning with dynAmic memory prunIng for surgical video segmentatioN), combines:
Bidirectional Motion Reasoning (BMR): Forward Kalman filtering plus backward RTS smoothing to detect motion inconsistencies (abrupt shifts), with a mask reselection mechanism that switches to appearance-based matching when motion is unreliable
Dynamic Memory Pruning (DM): Dissimilarity-based pruning of redundant memory frames to maintain a compact, diverse memory bank instead of SAM2’s fixed recent-frame buffer
They evaluate on EndoVis17/18, showing improvements over SAM2 and SurgSAM2 baselines, particularly for instruments with high absence rates. This is a surgical-specific adaptation of SAM2’s video segmentation framework, adding classical tracking (Kalman filter) and memory management to handle occlusion and reappearance better than generic video segmentation.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The problem formulation is precise and clinically grounded. Unlike vague claims about “surgical challenges,” the authors define concrete phenomena: motion inertia (Fig. 1) and instrument absence quantified via IAR (Instrument Absence Ratio). The safety argument—that misidentification could cause unintended robotic manipulation—is specific and credible. Fig. 2 showing baseline collapse at IAR > 60% is compelling evidence that current methods fail exactly where they matter most.
2.The bidirectional motion reasoning is elegant and well-motivated. Using RTS backward smoothing to detect inconsistencies with forward predictions is a classic signal processing technique [19], but the application to surgical instrument tracking is thoughtful. The Mahalanobis distance-based consistency score (J_t) provides a principled way to detect “teleports” or abrupt re-entries. The dynamic weighting scheme, which decays motion trust as a function of absence duration, is intuitively motivated: an instrument unseen for 50 frames should not be trusted for motion predictions.
3.The memory pruning mechanism addresses a real SAM2 limitation. SAM2’s fixed-length memory bank (initial frame + 6 recent frames) is known to struggle with long occlusions. The dissimilarity-based pruning with minimum retention policy (always keep reference frame, max 6 additional frames) is simple but effective. Fig. 6’s visualization showing memory bank composition under different settings is genuinely helpful for understanding why this matters.
4.Strong empirical results on challenging classes. Table 2 shows massive improvements on historically difficult categories: Clip Applier (+20.62%: 45.29% → 65.91%) and Ultrasound Probe (+35.63%: 25.62% → 61.25%). These are instruments that frequently disappear and reappear, so the gains directly validate the method’s design intent. The ablation in Fig. 7 showing BMR and DM are complementary.
5.Honest about building on SAM2 rather than claiming novelty from scratch. The paper clearly positions itself as extending SAM2 and SurgSAM2, not replacing them.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The core components are largely classical, not novel. Kalman filtering for object tracking dates to the 1960s, RTS smoothing is from 1965, and memory management in visual tracking has been extensively studied (e.g., SAMURAI uses motion-aware memory, MoSAM does spatial-temporal memory selection). The specific combination is new, but the individual pieces are well-established. The paper cites some related work but doesn’t clearly articulate what BRAIN does differently from these concurrent SAM2 adaptations.
2.The “dynamic” memory pruning is less dynamic than claimed. The dissimilarity-based selection (Sec. 2.2) uses a fixed threshold β=6 and fixed maximum memory size (6 frames). This is essentially static pruning with a dissimilarity heuristic, not truly adaptive to scene complexity. A more dynamic approach might adjust memory capacity based on estimated occlusion duration or instrument motion predictability. The ablation in Fig. 4 shows performance vs. β but doesn’t explain why β=6 is optimal or how to set it without validation data.
3.Missing comparison to non-SAM2 surgical trackers. Table 2 compares BRAIN to task-specific methods (ISINet, TraSeTR, S3Net, MATIS, LACOSTE) and SAM-based approaches, but these are mostly single-frame or category-level methods. There’s no comparison to modern surgical video tracking methods that explicitly handle occlusion, such as TraSeTR’s temporal consistency or LACOSTE’s stereo-temporal fusion. The claim that BRAIN “surpasses strong task-specific models” is partially true but conflates different problem settings (instance-level vs. category-level, video vs. single-frame).
4.The appearance score during reselection is underspecified. When J_t ≥ τ (motion inconsistent), BRAIN switches to appearance matching using “cosine similarity between the embedding vector extracted from M_{t,i} and that of the most confident mask in the memory bank.” But if the instrument has been absent for 100 frames, the memory bank contains only old embeddings. How does appearance matching work when the instrument reappears with different orientation, lighting, or occlusion? The paper doesn’t analyze failure modes where appearance changes drastically during absence.
5.Limited analysis of IAR-specific performance. The paper defines IAR and shows baseline collapse (Fig. 2), but doesn’t report BRAIN’s performance stratified by IAR bins. Does BRAIN maintain 80%+ accuracy at IAR > 60%? The abstract claims “significant outperformance” but without IAR-stratified results, we can’t verify that the gains come specifically from handling high-absence cases versus general improvement.
6.The evaluation protocol has gaps. They “exclude the first and last frames of each sequence” following standard protocol, but surgical videos often have the most instrument entry/exit at boundaries. This exclusion might artificially inflate performance. Also, using SurgSAM2’s instance-level annotation protocol for evaluation is fine, but the comparison to category-level methods in Table 2 is unfair—these methods weren’t designed for instance tracking.
7.No discussion of computational cost. Adding Kalman filtering, RTS smoothing, and dissimilarity computation to SAM2’s per-frame inference adds overhead. Is BRAIN real-time? SAM2 is already computationally heavy; the extra modules might push it beyond practical deployment limits for robotic surgery. Given the safety framing, latency analysis is relevant.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The architectural novelty is thin. Kalman filtering, RTS smoothing, and memory pruning are established techniques. The contribution is primarily in applying them to SAM2 for surgical video, with sensible design choices. This is valuable engineering but not a conceptual breakthrough. The paper cites SAMURAI and MoSAM but doesn’t clearly differentiate from these concurrent works, I’d like to see a direct comparison or clearer articulation of the unique aspects.
I’m also concerned about generalization beyond EndoVis. These datasets are relatively controlled (short sequences, limited instruments, static camera). Real surgical videos have smoke, blood, lens cleaning, and camera movement that might break the Kalman motion model. The paper doesn’t test robustness to these perturbations or discuss failure modes beyond the clean ablation scenarios.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses two critical failure modes in surgical video segmentation: abrupt positional shifts after instrument reappearance and memory pollution from prolonged instrument absence. The proposed BRAIN framework features two core modules: BMR module combining Kalman filtering and RTS smoothing to detect motion inconsistencies, and DM pruning module that removes redundant frames based on embedding dissimilarity. Experiments on EndoVis17 and EndoVis18 demonstrate significant improvements over SAM2-style methods, with ablations confirming the complementary roles of BMR and DM.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Accurately identifies and quantifies critical real-world challenges (abrupt positional shifts and high Instrument Absence Ratio) with compelling visual data.
2.The bidirectional modeling using Kalman filtering and RTS smoothing is mathematically sound. The dynamic fusion strategy linking motion weights to absence duration is highly practical.
3.The DM module’s redundancy-aware filtering is a simple, and effective solution to prevent empty or incorrect frames from dominating the memory bank, which can be applied to other domains with BMR module.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The exact nature of the “embedding vector” used in Eq. 10 and the appearance score is unclear. The authors must clarify if this relies on fragile binary mask shapes or robust image-level semantic features (e.g., SAM2 Mask Tokens), and specify the distance metrics and normalization used.
2.Introducing RTS smoothing and pairwise memory dissimilarity inherently adds computational overhead. The total absence of runtime analysis (FPS, GPU memory) makes it impossible to compare against “real-time” baselines, which is a critical omission for latency-sensitive surgical applications.
3.The paper mixes results copied from original papers (some using category-level or prompt-free settings) with the fine-tuned, instance-augmented BRAIN. The fairness of the experimental setup should be emphasized more.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper proposes a logically sound and practically valuable framework to address critical surgical tracking failures. The reported performance gains are impressive. However, the manuscript suffers from ambiguous technical details regarding feature extraction, a critical lack of runtime efficiency analysis, and potentially uncontrolled baseline comparisons. If the authors can clarify the embedding implementation, provide hardware-specific runtime metrics, and ensure fair baseline comparisons during the rebuttal, this work will be a very strong contribution to the field.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The paper addresses a meaningful and practically important failure mode in surgical video segmentation, and the reported gains on challenging re-entry and long-absence cases are compelling. I agree that the main limitations are real, especially the somewhat incremental novelty relative to recent SAM2-style surgical adaptations and the limited evaluation scope beyond EndoVis benchmarks.
That said, the rebuttal satisfactorily addressed several decision-critical concerns, e.g., runtime and memory overhead, providing additional sensitivity analysis, isolating the contributions of Kalman filtering and RTS smoothing, specifying the embedding/similarity design, and reporting IAR-stratified results. These responses do not remove all concerns, but they increase my confidence that the method is technically sound, targeted to a real problem, and supported by meaningful empirical improvements. On balance, I support acceptance.

meta_reviews.text:
The rebuttal should address four decision-affecting concerns. First, runtime, FPS, and GPU-memory analysis, which is critical given the safety framing and is currently absent. Second, a systematic sensitivity analysis of the multiple hyperparameters τ, γ, k, λ, L, β—of which only β is currently studied—and an isolated ablation that disentangles forward Kalman tracking from backward RTS smoothing within the BMR module. Third, an explicit specification of the embedding vector and similarity metric used in the motion-guided mask reselection, together with a discussion of long-absence re-entry behaviour, raised by R3: how appearance matching works when the instrument reappears after long absences with corrupted or stale memory entries. Fourth, IAR-stratified performance to substantiate the central claim that the method specifically improves the high-absence regime, and clearer positioning with respect to concurrent SAM2 adaptations such as SAMURAI and MoSAM, and to recent surgical-video foundation models such as EndoMamba, Memory-Augmented SAM2, and ReSurgSAM2.

The paper proposes bidirectional motion reasoning combined with dynamic memory pruning for surgical video segmentation on the EndoVis benchmarks. The reviewers raised four decision-affecting concerns: missing runtime and memory analysis given the safety framing; insufficient sensitivity analysis of multiple hyperparameters and a lack of an isolated ablation that separates forward tracking from backward smoothing; the unspecified embedding vector and similarity metric used in the motion-guided mask reselection, along with a question about behavior under long-absence re-entry; and positioning relative to concurrent SAM2 adaptations and recent surgical-video foundation models. The rebuttal substantively addresses the first three concerns, providing efficiency numbers, a hyperparameter sweep with reported sensitivities, isolating the contributions of the forward and backward components, explicitly specifying the embedding and similarity, and providing a stratified analysis under high-absence regimes. Two reviewers explicitly endorsed acceptance after the rebuttal. The remaining Reject concerns the positioning of related work, which the camera-ready version must improve.

After rebuttal, there are two Accept and one Reject. The other reviewer did not update. After reading the paper as well as the reviews and author rebuttal, I think the paper is a good work with good performance and method design. Major concerns include limited engagement with recent related work and incremental novelty. Pros outweigh cons and therefore the recommendation is Accept.
The authors managed to provide satisfactory answers.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for the constructive comments. We are encouraged that BRAIN is recognized as “well-motivated” (R3), “easy to follow” (R1), and “clearly organised” (R1,2), with “significant improvements” (R2,3) and “quantifying critical real-world challenges” (R4). We will release code upon acceptance. 
1 Computational cost (R2,3,4). BRAIN (46.75 FPS, 0.02 s/frame, 3.23 GB) adds negligible overhead over SAM2 (52.18 FPS, 0.02 s/frame, 3.14 GB) on A800, since extra modules use simple matrix computation, RTS uses a short temporal window (L=15), and DM prunes redundant frames to further speed up the process. 
2.1 Hyperparameter sensitivity (R1,2,3). BRAIN is insensitive to γ, k, L; τ and β are interpretable. λ=e^-n adjusts dynamically with n, not manually tuned. We evaluated τ/γ/k∈{0.1,…,0.9}, L∈{10,12,15,17,20}, and β∈{3,…,7}. BRAIN is stable to score fusion (γ), tracker-update gating (k), RTS window (L) with 0.06/0.05/0.09% IoU variation. τ and β are more influential, with 1.26/1.32% variation. τ controls motion-inconsistency detection: small τ over-triggers appearance reselection and large τ misses abrupt shifts. β controls memory pruning: small β over-prunes context, large β keeps redundant memories. Thus,τ=0.5,β=6 balance best. “Dynamic” means dynamic memory-frame selection, not capacity adjustment; dynamic capacity yields comparable Dice (86.48%) but lower efficiency (29.07 FPS). Failures mainly occur when both cues vanish, e.g., severe lens occlusion/blur, or strong camera shake, a shared open challenge. 
2.2 BMR ablation (R2). We isolate BMR: Kalman improves Dice from 83.44% to 85.13%, and RTS further improves it to 86.51%, confirming both contributions.
3.1 Reselection (R2,3). Appearance reselection uses the most confident memory embedding (0.13% high-confidence errors), so corrupted, occluded, or misidentified frames do not dominate the appearance score. As analyzed in Fig. 6, DM suppresses empty, low-confidence, and redundant absent frames, enabling robust appearance matching after many absent frames. BMR improves current-frame mask quality and reduces drift; together, BMR and DM reduce repeated use of erroneous memories. When re-entry involves orientation, lighting, or occlusion but no abrupt positional shift, BRAIN selects mask using both motion and appearance cues. With IAR > 60%, including occluded re-entries, appearance matching localizes the target in 91.2% of cases.
3.2 Embedding/ReID (R4,2). Embedding is a SAM2 feature-pooled mask-level semantic vector. Appearance score is L2-normalized cosine similarity to the most confident memory embedding. BMR considers both motion and appearance scores, differing from ReID methods that recognize identities by simply fusing all frames. 
4.1 Novelty (R1,3). Although SAMURAI, MoSAM, EndoMamba, Memory-Augmented SAM2, and ReSurgSAM2 improve surgical video representation or tracking, they ignore long instrument absence with abrupt positional shifts, a critical cause of performance reduction. Instead of simply combining Kalman and RTS like previous methods (SAMURAI), we innovatively propose BMR to correct mask selection under abrupt positional shifts and DM to remove redundant long absent frames, jointly enabling SOTA performance (e.g., SAMURAI, 79.69% Dice).
4.2 IAR-stratified (R3). For low/mid/high IAR (<30%, 30–60%, >60%), BRAIN obtains 87.43/81.85/93.30% IoU, compared with SAM2’s 83.23/79.85/52.15% and SurgSAM2’s 85.17/81.47/65.06%. The largest gain at high IAR confirms that BRAIN targets long-absence/re-entry failures. 
5 Prompt/ Fairness (R2,3,4). Table 2 uses the full-mask prompt. 
Table 1 is the fair comparison, where SAM2, SurgSAM2, and BRAIN use the same instance-level protocol and prompt setting. The standard VOS first/last-frame exclusion changes performance by only 0.03%. Table 2 is a broad reference covering category-level, prompt-free setting. In the same instance-level setting, BRAIN beats occlusion-aware trackers e.g., LACOSTE/TraSeTR (85.6/81.0% Dice)

title: BrainACU: Asynchronous Coordination Unit Modeling for Dynamic Brain Network Analysis
abstract:
Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) provides crucial insights into dynamic brain network mechanisms underlying psychiatric disorders. While deep learning methods have advanced rs-fMRI-based disease recognition and dynamic brain network modeling, existing approaches are often limited by two key assumptions: (1) fixed subnetwork partitioning, where predefined functional templates or partition rules impose a fixed region-subnetwork mapping that, although interpretable, restricts the discovery of complex coordination patterns; and (2) synchronization assumption, where inter-subnetwork interactions are modeled as strictly time-aligned, overlooking physiologically plausible delays and weakening diagnostic signals.
To address these limitations, we propose BrainACU, an asynchronous coordination unit modeling framework for dynamic brain network analysis. BrainACU removes fixed partitioning by learning coordination units (CUs) directly from data, capturing both synchronous and asynchronous coordination. Using conventional sliding windows, we segment BOLD sequences into temporally consistent patches for subsequent CU learning and interaction modeling. BrainACU then learns stable ROI-to-CU mappings via data-driven clustering with cross-sample consensus, and projects variable-size CU signals into a unified latent space for dimensional alignment. Finally, an asynchronous interaction module models both time-aligned and time-lagged unit-level dependencies to form dynamic brain network representations. Experiments on ASD, MDD, and BD demonstrate that BrainACU outperforms existing methods and provides more discriminative and interpretable dynamic brain network evidence. Our code: https://github.com/guoguiliang111/BrainACU.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes BrainACU, a framework that addresses two limitations in dynamic brain network analysis: fixed subnetwork partitioning and the assumption of strict temporal synchronization. Its key contributions include: (1) Data-driven CU Discovery: Learning Coordination Units directly from BOLD signals via consensus clustering; (2) Asynchronous Interaction Module: Using directed attention and lag-promoting regularization to capture time-shifted dependencies between brain units; and (3) Improved Performance and Interpretability: Achieving state-of-the-art results across three disorders and providing “lag-step statistics” to visualize disease-related temporal delays.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Relaxing the “zero-lag” synchrony assumption is physiologically well-motivated, as neural propagation involves inherent delays. 
2.The consensus clustering approach for CU discovery allows the model to adapt to different disorders where canonical templates might be suboptimal. 
3.The model was tested on multiple disorders (ASD, MDD, BD) and outperformed dynamic baselines like BrainDGT and ST-GCN.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The proposed “Coordination Units” are essentially derived from k-means clustering over ROIs. This is conceptually similar to many existing parcellation or clustering-based approaches and does not fundamentally differ from prior functional grouping methods. 
2.The authors fix the number of Coordination Units at K=3.While the paper argues that fixed templates restrict the discovery of complex patterns, the proposed data-driven CU discovery via consensus clustering essentially functions as a clustering-based parcellation. Setting K=3 is biologically oversimplified, as the human brain is typically organized into more granular networks (e. g. , Yeo 7 or 17 networks). The authors have not demonstrated how these learned CUs correspond to known functional systems. Additionally, without visualizing these ROI-to-CU mappings or providing a biological mapping, it is difficult to determine if the “asynchronous delays” learned between these units are neuroscientifically meaningful or merely data artifacts. 
3.The framework maps variable-sized CU signals to a shared latent dimension d using CU-specific linear projections. However, if the number of ROIs within each CU varies significantly, projecting them into the same low-dimensional space (d=36) may lead to severe information bottlenecks for large CUs or representation bias for smaller ones. A more detailed justification or sensitivity analysis regarding this dimension alignment is required. 
4.Regarding Equation 8, the L_lag penalty successfully forces the model to capture time-shifted dependencies. However, since the brain is partitioned into only three broad units, the granularity of the “dynamics” being modeled is quite coarse. If a single CU aggregates regions with distinct functions, the resulting time-lagged signals might represent an uninterpretable average of multiple competing processes. The authors should clarify what these units represent to justify the analysis of their temporal delays. 
5.The evaluation on ABIDE is restricted to the NYU site. While this reduces multi-center variability, it limits the assessment of the model’s robustness and generalization. Please clarify if this selection was due to sample size constraints at other sites or concerns regarding overfitting, and discuss the model’s potential performance in a multi-site transfer learning setting. 
6.The asynchronous interaction module models directed cross-CU attention across a token timeline. The authors should provide a quantitative discussion on the computational overhead (FLOPS, inference time) compared to standard self-attention or static GNN baselines to justify the added architectural complexity.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses an important problem and proposes a conceptually interesting framework. However, the core idea of coordination units is not sufficiently novel and is implemented using a relatively simple clustering approach. The biological interpretability is weak, and the experimental design has limitations (e.g., dataset selection, lack of cross-site validation). The performance improvements are also modest. Overall, the paper is below the acceptance threshold.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
While the authors provided detailed clarifications for several concerns in their rebuttal, their response to Concern 3 (Data Inconsistency between Table 1 and Table 2) has exposed a fatal flaw in both the methodological robustness of the proposed framework and the rigor of their experimental evaluation. Consequently, I am downgrading my rating and recommending a Reject. 
1.The admission that a simple change in the cross-validation random seed caused a massive 4.2% performance drop (81.0% vs. 76.8%) on the MDD task (N=397) proves that the proposed framework is highly volatile and overfitted, as the diagnostic outcomes of 16–17 patients flip purely based on how the data is split. 
2.Furthermore, utilizing unaligned random seeds across Table 1 and Table 2 violates standard benchmarking protocols and raises serious concerns regarding selective reporting (cherry-picking) to showcase optimized numbers in the main ablation table. 
3.This extreme seed-dependency strongly implies that the learned coarse-grained (K=3) coordination units and asynchronous delays are merely overfitting to localized data noise rather than capturing reproducible, clinically reliable neuroscientific signatures, making the manuscript unsuitable for publication at MICCAI.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: BrainACU proposes a data-driven coordination unit framework that jointly models synchronous and asynchronous inter-unit dependencies in rs-fMRI, demonstrating consistent diagnostic improvements over fixed-partitioning and zero-lag baselines across multiple psychiatric disorders.
reviews.text_strengths:
The two core limitations addressed — fixed subnetwork partitioning and the synchronization assumption — are both well-motivated by neuroscientific evidence and clearly distinguished from prior work. The use of directed cross-CU attention to jointly model time-aligned and time-lagged coordination is a principled and elegant design that directly addresses the synchrony bias in existing dynamic connectivity methods.
The ablation study systematically removes each component and reports consistent performance drops across all three diagnostic tasks, providing clear evidence for the contribution of CU discovery, latent alignment, asynchronous interaction, and each regularization term. The lag-step statistics further offer mechanistically interpretable evidence that disease groups exhibit larger temporal delays in cross-CU coordination, connecting the model’s behavior to known neurophysiology.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
A critical inconsistency exists between Table 1 and Table 2.The methodology states that K=3 is used throughout, yet the performance reported for K=3 in Table 2 (e.g., 81.0%/80.1% ACC/AUC for HC vs. MDD) is substantially higher than the full model reported in Table 1 (76.8%/77.9%). These two tables appear to report results under different experimental conditions without explanation, raising serious concerns about the reliability of the reported numbers.
The model is constrained to K=3 coordination units across all tasks and disorders, which is a very coarse granularity relative to established brain network parcellations. The rationale for fixing K=3 is based solely on a grid search showing K=3 outperforms K=2, 4, and 5, but a broader range and task-specific sensitivity analysis would be needed to justify this as a general choice.
The primary dataset (MDD and BD cohort) is private, with institution and ethics details anonymized. Combined with a relatively small sample size (246 HC, 151 MDD, 126 BD), this limits both reproducibility and the generalizability of the reported performance. The public evaluation is restricted to a single ABIDE site (NYU, 172 subjects), which is insufficient to establish broad applicability across datasets.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The inconsistency between Table 1 and Table 2 undermines the reliability of the reported results, and while the core idea of asynchronous coordination unit modeling is well-motivated, the limited public evaluation and small private dataset prevent a confident assessment of generalizability.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I appreciate the authors’ thorough responses to my comments. They have provided reasonable explanations regarding the inconsistencies between tables, the dataset limitations, and the choice of K=3.Overall, I believe this work would be of interest to the MICCAI community.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces a Transformer-based framework (BrainACU) for dynamic fMRI diagnosis. BrainACU learns data-driven Coordination Units (CUs) that eliminate the need for fixed subnetwork parcellations and predefined functional templates. Additionally, it integrates both synchronous and asynchronous coordination modeling within a unified attention-based architecture. Two method-aligned regularizers encourages different CUs to encode complementary coordination patterns and lag-aware cross-CU coupling. The framework demonstrates superior performance on one public dataset (ABIDE) and a private cohort for three diagnoses (MDD, BD, ASD), outperforming multiple state-of-the-art baselines.
reviews.text_strengths: It is interesting and novel to model both time-aligned and time-lagged dependencies across data-driven coordination units via directed cross-CU attention, it enables the architecture to integrate dynamic brain network information more effectively by modeling asynchronous interactions among subnetworks.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
a) For the Asynchronous Interaction Module, the lagged interactions are modeled at the CU level, where CUs are obtained via data-driven clustering (with K=3 in experiments), raising concerns regarding interpretability. Since these CUs represent abstract groupings rather than predefined neurobiological units, and because interactions are primarily learned at this coarse level, the model’s biological interpretability remains inherently constrained. A deeper exploration of the learned interactions (e.g., attention patterns) align with established neurobiological principles would strengthen the paper. 
b) The paper states that hyperparameters were tuned on an internal validation set using a five-fold cross-validation scheme. However, the results reported in Table 1 (e.g., NYU: ACC =72.3%, AUC=74.1%) exceed those those in Table 2 for K=3 (ACC =71.0%, AUC =71.8%), which is quite counterintuitive. To ensure reproducibility and methodological transparency, the authors should explicitly clarify whether these results are obtained under identical data splits, train/validation/test boundaries, and evaluation protocols. Moreover, due to the limited sample size, performance variance across splits may be significant. Independent validation on larger datasets would strengthen the robustness and generalizability of the reported conclusions.
Minor points:
a) The notation in Equation 3 lacks sufficient definition; please explicitly define all symbols.
b) The architectural logic depicted in Figure 1 is unclear. The relationships between the modules are not clearly defined, leading to confusion.
c) In the “Interpretability Analysis of Asynchronous Coordination” section, the disease cohort used for lag-step statistics is not specified.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Although the proposed framework is innovative, its empirical validation is constrained by limited sample size and several methodological inconsistencies, which collectively undermine the reliability and persuasiveness of the reported findings.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: After reviewing the rebuttal, I find that the authors have convincingly addressed most of my concerns. The core methodological innovation of modeling both time-aligned and time-lagged functional dependencies across data-driven coordination units (CUs) via directed cross-CU attention, is conceptually sound and substantively novel. Importantly, the rebuttal strengthens the paper’s scientific grounding by clarifying the design rationale and elaborating on the biological interpretability of the learned CUs. Overall, I consider the rebuttal sufficient. The paper is reasonably motivated and presents a novel framework for modeling asynchronous brain interactions. My final decision is Accept.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper presents BrainACU, a data-driven framework for dynamic brain network analysis through the discovery of data-driven coordination units and an asynchronous interaction module. While aligning asynchrony in the latent space has novelty, all reviewers noted that the small, fixed clustering parameter for the coordination unit and its influence on the projection. Several critiques were raised about the limited evaluations.

This paper presents BrainACU, a data-driven framework for dynamic brain network analysis through the discovery of data-driven coordination units and an asynchronous interaction module. While aligning asynchrony in the latent space has novelty, all reviewers noted that the small, fixed clustering parameter for the coordination unit and limited evaluations. The rebuttal mostly addressed reviewers’ questions regarding the novelty of the paper over existing clustering-based parcellation methods, and the discussion on data and experimental results.

The authors seem to have addressed the concerns raised in the original reviews and have resolved the discrepancy in reported results across tables. If accepted, I would urge the authors to maintain consistent experimental protocols as is standard practice in cross validation and make sure the biological interpretability and justification for parameter selection choice features into the explanation in the paper.

This paper’s contribution is an asynchronous coordination framework for dynamic brain network analysis, and the idea is interesting because it aims to model temporal coordination in a less rigid way than synchronous alternatives. Although the rebuttal helped clarify parts of the coordination-unit design, the post-rebuttal signal still appears divided rather than convincingly positive, suggesting that the response improved presentation more than core confidence. On balance, the conceptual interest is not enough to overcome the remaining uncertainty about methodological necessity and validation strength.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for constructive feedback.
1.CLARIFICATION ON THE METHODOLOGICAL CONTRIBUTION OF CU DISCOVERY (R1)
(a) Our contribution is not k-means itself, but the complete pipeline integrating data-driven CU discovery with asynchronous modeling. Three distinctions from standard parcellation: (i) per-subject clustering of brain regions, aggregated via a co-association matrix, reflecting population coherence while accommodating individual variability; (ii) CUs serve as the organizational basis for lag-aware directed attention, and no prior work combines data-driven macro-unit discovery with explicit time-lagged interaction modeling; (iii) ablation (Table 1, “w/o CU Discovery”) shows fixed partitions degrade all tasks. We acknowledge k-means is standard; the novelty lies in how and why it is deployed, not the algorithm itself. (R1-Q1)
2.JUSTIFICATION FOR K=3 & BIOLOGICAL INTERPRETABILITY (R1, R2, R4)
(a) We mapped CU assignments against functional networks (BD cohort). The learned CUs capture functionally coherent circuits: CU0 aggregates subcortical/limbic structures (caudate, putamen, thalamus; 55.6%) with temporal regions, consistent with cortico-subcortical loops for emotion regulation and reward processing [32]; CU1 combines prefrontal DMN (37.2%), CEN (25.6%), and visual areas (18.6%), mirroring the self-referential/executive control axis [17]; CU2 groups sensorimotor cortex (41.4%) with limbic structures (hippocampus, amygdala; 20.7%), reflecting sensory-limbic integration pathways disrupted in affective disorders [5]. No CU maps to a single canonical network, which is by design, consistent with Mitra et al. [20] who showed lag structure is orthogonal to canonical RSNs. Regarding lag interpretability (R1-Q4): if lag signals were within-CU averaging artifacts, they would affect disease and control groups equally; Fig. 2 shows disease groups exhibit systematically larger lag steps [20, 19], and this consistent disease-control divergence serves as functional validation. (R1-Q2/R1-Q4/R4-Q1)
(b) K=3 is empirically optimal (Table 2) and consistent with the Triple Network Model [17], which posits three macro-level functional systems underlying psychopathology. Our data-driven CUs recover a compatible three-way granularity without imposing network priors, supporting K=3 as biologically plausible. (R1-Q2/R2-Q2/R4-Q1)
3.DATA INCONSISTENCY BETWEEN TABLE 1 & TABLE 2 (R2, R4)
(a) We thank the reviewers for identifying this issue. The inconsistency arose from different random seeds for CV fold partitions between Table 1 and Table 2, which with moderate sample size (N=397) can shift CV means by several percentage points (e.g., K=3 MDD: 81.0% vs. 76.8%). Crucially, K=3 ranks first in all tasks; the relative ordering is unchanged. After unifying fold partitions, the ranking remains identical with K=3 matching Table 1.We will update the camera-ready and open-source all configurations. (R2-Q1/R4-Q2)
4.DIMENSION ALIGNMENT BOTTLENECK (R1)
(a) This concern is mitigated by design: our balanced k-means variant (Sec. 2.2) constrains CU sizes to be approximately equal, and each CU has a dedicated projection W_k in R^{d x |V_k|} whose capacity scales with CU size. Sensitivity over d∈{16–64} further confirms stable performance (variance < 0.6%). (R1-Q3)
5.GENERALIZATION & DATASET LIMITATIONS (R1, R2)
(a) Evaluated on full multi-site ABIDE (871 subjects, 17 sites): BrainACU achieves 69.7% ACC, outperforming BrainDGT (66.8%) and ST-GCN (57.2%), demonstrating cross-site transferability. (R1-Q5/R2-Q3)
6.COMPUTATIONAL OVERHEAD (R1)
(a) Async module adds ~2.5ms inference and ~4.2% FLOPs over a static GNN baseline, operating on M patches with K=3 units. (R1-Q6)
7.NOTATION & FIGURES (R4)
(a) Eq.3: A_ij=co-clustering frequency, N=training subjects, z_i^(n)=ROI i cluster label for subject n, C=total ROIs. Will redraw Fig.1 and annotate Fig.2 with cohort details. (R4-Q3/Q4/Q5)
Ref: [32] Haber & Knutson, Neuropsychopharmacology 35(1), 4-26 (2010)

title: Brain-Adapter: A Dual-Stream Vision-Language MIL Framework for Comprehensive 3D CT Diagnosis of Acute Intracranial Pathologies
abstract: Automated diagnosis of 3D brain CT scans is essential for critical care, yet it remains challenging due to the heavy reliance on manual annotations and the limited semantic understanding of conventional models. While 2D foundation vision-language models (VLMs) have shown strong generalization, adapting their slice-level representations for 3D volumetric analysis remains challenging. In this paper, we propose Brain-Adapter, a novel dual-stream multiple instance learning (MIL) framework that leverages pre-trained 2D biomedical VLMs and raw diagnostic reports for robust scan-level multi-label classification. Specifically, we introduce a Text-Conditioned Attention (TCA) mechanism, utilizing raw diagnostic sentences as semantic queries to dynamically align visual cues with specific disease concepts. Concurrently, a parallel visual MIL stream captures global scan characteristics, supervised by structured labels extracted via a Large Language Model (LLM). To ensure representation coherence, a consistency constraint enforces synergy between the two streams. During inference, an Uncertainty-Aware Refinement (UAR) module dynamically calibrates and fuses these dual-stream predictions to resolve ambiguous cases. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art 3D models and standard MIL approaches. By eliminating the reliance on dense annotations, Brain-Adapter offers an annotation-efficient framework for 3D acute intracranial pathology analysis. Code is available at https://github.com/Scatteredrain/Brain-Adapter.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: Adapting the 2D biomedical visual language model BiomedCLIP to 3D NCCT volumetric data; the approach does not rely on dense annotations but instead uses raw radiology reports as the supervision source.
reviews.text_strengths: First, the problem is significant and clinically relevant; CT triage for acute intracranial lesions is inherently a high-value task. Second, the methodology flows logically, with a coherent connection between TCA, ABMIL, consistency constraints, and UAR. Third, the use of raw reports rather than densely annotated data ensures practical scalability.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The structured labels are extracted by an LLM, but their quality is not validated. The method section explicitly states that the structured supervision labels come from LLM-driven logic-set extraction and serve as the ground truth for the supervised branch. If the LLM misses labels, introduces incorrect labels, or over-standardizes the free-text impressions when extracting the 21 classes, then the supervision itself becomes unreliable. 
2.The report text is used both for training supervision and semantic alignment, creating a potential shortcut through the text modality. TCA uses the raw report and its fine-grained sentences as text features, while the logic-set supervision is also derived from the same report. If the model relies too heavily on the explicit diagnostic semantics contained in the report rather than on the image itself, this may create a weak form of leakage in which the report is effectively supervising itself. 
3.The comparison against stronger 3D medical classification baselines is insufficient. The only 3D models in Table 1 are ViT-B and Swin-B, which may not represent the strongest current baselines for 3D medical classification. 
4.In addition, the performance gap between the trained-from-scratch and pre-trained models needs further explanation. Why do some pre-trained models not outperform their from-scratch counterparts after initialization with pre-trained weights?
5.The explanation of the ablation results is not fully consistent with the actual numbers. In Table 2, adding the consistency constraint worsens the Hamming Loss, yet the paper states that the “sequential integration of components consistently drives performance upward. ” This is not true for all metrics. 
6.Attention heatmaps do not automatically imply reliable interpretability. Without quantitative localization evaluation or expert assessment from clinicians, the interpretability claim remains weak. 
7.The label definition mixes pathological findings with etiological context, making the task boundary less clean. If the label set contains both imaging findings and etiological context, the task formulation becomes semantically mixed, and some labels may not be reliably inferable from the image alone.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

In summary, the paper is promising, but several key issues remain insufficiently addressed, including the reliability of LLM-extracted labels, potential text-driven leakage, limited 3D baseline comparisons, and overclaimed conclusions from the ablation and interpretability analyses. Overall, the current evidence is not yet strong enough to fully support the paper’s claims.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
1.The proposed “Open-set Alignment” module appears conceptually closer to a combination of cross-attention and contrastive learning, rather than a genuine open-set recognition framework. While the design is reasonable and empirically motivated, the terminology may somewhat overstate the methodological novelty of this component.
2.The paper lacks sufficient implementation and engineering details to ensure reproducibility. In particular, the construction process of the fine-grained pathological descriptions is not clearly specified, and several important training settings (e.g., prompt formulation, LoRA configuration, optimization details, and logic-set extraction pipeline) remain unclear. In addition, the manuscript does not mention whether the source code will be publicly released, which further limits reproducibility and practical verification of the proposed method.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces Brain-Adapter, a dual-stream multiple instance learning (MIL) framework designed to adapt pre-trained 2D biomedical vision-language models (VLMs) for the 3D diagnosis of acute intracranial pathologies. The framework consists of a Text-Conditioned Attention (TCA) mechanism for open-set alignment and a parallel visual MIL stream for logic-set supervision. Furthermore, the authors propose an Uncertainty-Aware Refinement (UAR) strategy to dynamically fuse dual-stream predictions during inference. The method is evaluated on an in-house clinical dataset of 852 non-contrast head CT scans and an external CQ500 dataset for zero-shot transferability.
reviews.text_strengths:
Intuitive and Promising Methodology: The overall design of the Brain-Adapter framework is highly intuitive and demonstrates significant potential. The dual-stream architecture elegantly balances explicit semantic guidance with implicit visual evidence.
Strong Interpretability: The method provides excellent interpretability. The Text-Conditioned Attention (TCA) mechanism can effectively localize the specific slices manifesting the lesions. Even in cases of misclassification, the ability to pinpoint the abnormal slices holds substantial clinical value.
Innovative Inference Strategy: The Uncertainty-Aware Refinement (UAR) mechanism is a clever design that dynamically calibrates visual predictions with text-guided evidence only when the visual discriminative logic is ambiguous.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Asymmetry Between Claims and Experimental Validation: The paper’s title and introduction position it as both a “MIL framework” and an “Adapter” for 2D VLMs to 3D tasks. However, the experimental design only validates the former. While comparing against other MIL aggregation methods (e.g., ABMIL, TransMIL) is necessary and sufficient for the “MIL framework” claim, the paper lacks specific architectural designs tailored for efficient fine-tuning (aside from simply applying LoRA). The framework essentially functions as a novel training paradigm rather than a dedicated adapter.
Insufficient Baselines for VLM Adaptation Claims: Because the authors claim to solve the “open problem” of “effectively transferring their [2D VLMs] representational power to 3D volumes,” the experimental baselines are incomplete.
To support the “Adapter” claim, the authors should compare Brain-Adapter with other parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods based on the same pre-trained model (e.g., CLIP-Adapter, CoOp, VPT).
More importantly, the effectiveness of the adaptation should be validated on more pre-trained models, rather than solely relying on BiomedCLIP. Crucially, there are already several foundation models specifically trained for the CT modality (e.g., recent 3D Head CT and CTA foundation models). Failing to conduct experiments on these domain-specific foundation models significantly weakens the claim that this framework is a generalized solution for 3D CT diagnosis.
Incomplete Quantitative Evaluation for Interpretability: In Figure 3, presenting only the slice aggregation weights and qualitative visualizations is insufficient. The authors should provide quantitative results regarding the accuracy of slice-level localization to substantiate the interpretability claims.
Unsupported Claims on Scalability: Both the abstract and conclusion highlight the method’s “scalability.” However, there are no experiments in the paper to support this claim (e.g., performance comparisons under 1%, 10%, and 100% data regimes).
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I personally appreciate the proposed methodology; it is intuitive, interpretable, and holds clinical potential. However, the current manuscript suffers from a critical asymmetry between its stated contributions and its experimental validation. While it successfully demonstrates superiority over traditional MIL frameworks, it fails to provide sufficient evidence for its claims as a generalized VLM adaptation method. The lack of comparisons with other PEFT methods and the failure to validate the framework on CT-specific foundation models make the core “Adapter” contributions unconvincing. Additionally, unsupported claims regarding scalability and missing quantitative evaluations for slice localization further weaken the paper.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I thank the authors for the detailed rebuttal. The clarification of the “adapter” scope, together with the added PEFT/FM comparisons and LLM-label validation, satisfactorily addresses my main concerns. Some limitations remain, especially on localization and broader generalization, but these are understandable given the MICCAI format and rebuttal constraints. I recommend acceptance, provided that the final version carefully qualifies claims on generalization, scalability, and interpretability.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
1.Innovatively proposes a case-level multi-label diagnostic approach that leverages a pretrained vision–language model (VLM), addressing the issue that knowledge learned from 2D pretraining cannot effectively support 3D tasks.
2.Adopts a weakly supervised training strategy that relies only on paired radiology reports, and reduces the dependence on dense manual annotations through contrastive learning.
3.Achieves alignment between image slices and the corresponding report text via contrastive learning and the proposed Text-Conditioned Attention (TCA) module.
4.Proposes UAR, an uncertainty-based inference enhancement method, which improves the model’s prediction accuracy.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Author converts free-text impressions into usable weak supervision (via LLM-based structuring) and also leverages report sentences for alignment training, reducing reliance on dense or expensive manual annotations
2.By jointly training a text-alignment stream and a visual MIL stream (with a consistency constraint), author combines open-vocabulary semantic grounding with stable discriminative learning, improving robustness compared to using either one alone
3.Author introduces text-conditioned attention to retrieve disease-relevant slice evidence and uses it to regularize training and calibrate uncertain predictions, rather than relying solely on unguided visual pooling
4.Author provides additional zero-shot experiments
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The paper does not specify which LLM is used for label extraction, and the lack of prompt details reduces reproducibility.
2.It would be helpful to report the accuracy of the LLM-extracted labels (e.g., via a small-scale manual verification).
3.The authors are encouraged to provide inference-time statistics, such as runtime/latency (and related efficiency metrics).
4.The paper does not explicitly commit to open-sourcing the code or models
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

1.The authors successfully adapt a pretrained 2D vision–language model (VLM) to a 3D medical imaging task, demonstrating methodological novelty.
2.The paper provides extensive comparative experiments, including comparisons against both 2D-based approaches and native 3D models.
3.The additional zero-shot evaluation experiments are appreciated and satisfactory.
4.Unfortunately, the paper does not specify the exact LLM used or the prompting details, and it also does not make an explicit commitment to open-source the code/models
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: It solved my problem very well

meta_reviews.text:
I recommend Invite for Rebuttal. Reviewer 1 was positive overall, but questioned the quality of the LLM-extracted supervision labels and the possibility of text-driven leakage. Reviewer 2 was negative and argued that the paper’s transfer and adapter claims are broader than what the experiments actually validate. Reviewer 3 was supportive, while still noting missing implementation details and the need to verify the extracted labels more carefully. I also share these concerns, as many important details remain insufficiently described, particularly the LLM-based label extraction process, label validation, and implementation details.

The rebuttal substantially improves confidence, the authors report manual validation of extracted labels, clarify that inference is CT only, provide additional PEFT and foundation-model comparisons, and add quantitative slice-localization evidence.

Reviewers #3 and #4 agreed to accept this manuscript given its merit and rebuttal, while reviewer #2 found several overclaimed points in the paper. The authors are strongly encouraged to revise their claims as per reviewer #3’s suggestions.

The remaining concerns are about novelty framing and reproducibility. The first issue is valid, but not invalidating in my opinion. For the second concern, the authors promised to share implementation details in the project repository. I recommend acceptance, given that the authors release the code and all processing details.

title: BrainAnytime: Anatomy-Aware Cross-Modal Pretraining for Brain Image Analysis with Arbitrary Modality Availability
abstract: Clinical diagnostic workups typically follow a modality escalation pathway: after initial clinical evaluation, clinicians begin with routine structural imaging (e.g., MRI), selectively add sequences such as FLAIR or T2 to refine the differential, and reserve molecular imaging (e.g., amyloid-PET) for cases that remain uncertain after standard evaluation. Consequently, patients are observed with heterogeneous and often incomplete modality subsets. However, most current AI models assume fixed data modalities as the model inputs. In this paper, we present BrainAnytime, a unified pretraining framework pretrained on 34,899 3D brain scans from five datasets that support brain image analysis under arbitrary modality availability spanning multi-sequence MRI and amyloid-PET. A single model accepts whatever imaging is available, from a lone T1 scan to a full multimodal workup. Pretraining learns structural-molecular correspondences between MRI and PET via cross-modal distillation (RCMD) and prioritizes disease-vulnerable anatomy via atlas-guided curriculum masking (PACM), all within a shared 3D masked autoencoder (Multi-MAE3D). Across four downstream tasks and five clinically motivated modality settings, BrainAnytime largely outperforms modality-specific models, missing-modality baselines, and large-scale brain MRI pretrained foundation models on most modality settings. Notably, it surpasses the strongest missing-modality baselines with relative improvements of 6.2% and 7.0% in average accuracy on CN vs. AD and CN vs. MCI classification, respectively. Code is available at https://github.com/SDH-Lab/BrainAnytime.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs
