The response reasonably clarifies my main concerns regarding the role of SWA, the contribution of the DINO-guided module, and the computational cost of the proposed memory scheme. While broader ablations would still strengthen the paper, I find the main concerns sufficiently addressed. I maintain my positive recommendation.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper proposes a coherent framework for improving spatial localization in CLIP-based few-shot medical anomaly detection and demonstrates consistent empirical gains across multiple datasets and settings. Reviewers agree that the problem is important and the overall approach is well motivated, with strengths in experimental performance and clarity of presentation. At the same time, several substantive concerns are consistently raised across reviews, including the need to better clarify novelty relative to prior CLIP+DINO and sliding-window approaches, more clearly isolate the contribution of individual components (particularly the dominant effect of sliding-window aggregation), provide deeper analysis of key design choices (e.g., DINO priors and prototype design), and discuss computational cost and fairness of comparison .
Given these points, the paper is forwarded to rebuttal. Authors are encouraged to address these concerns through careful clarification, additional analysis based on existing results, and improved positioning. In accordance with conference policy, no new major experiments should be introduced; instead, rebuttal should focus on explanation, analysis, and justification. Reviewers are requested to re-evaluate the paper in light of the rebuttal.

The paper proposes a coherent framework for improving spatial localization in CLIP-based few-shot medical anomaly detection by combining vision foundation model priors with CLIP-based anomaly scoring. Reviewers recognized the importance of the problem, the practical relevance of spatial-aware anomaly detection, the generally clear presentation, and the consistent empirical performance across multiple datasets and shot settings. The initial concerns mainly related to attribution of gains, novelty relative to prior CLIP+DINO and sliding-window approaches, the role of the DINO-guided module and prototype memory design, and computational cost. The rebuttal clarified these points in a generally satisfactory manner and helped position the contribution more clearly. While the novelty remains moderate and some analyses could be strengthened in the final version, the paper presents a well-motivated and practically useful contribution. I therefore recommend acceptance. The authors should incorporate the rebuttal clarifications, more carefully discuss the contribution of each component, and explicitly acknowledge remaining limitations in the camera-ready version.
All three reviewers recommend acceptance post-rebuttal.

The authors have provided solid and comprehensive responses in the rebuttal, satisfactorily clarifying the key technical and methodological queries raised during the review phase. Specifically, the authors have successfully articulated the core innovations of their framework over existing CLIP+DINO baseline. Crucially, they have provided compelling empirical evidence to quantify the independent contributions of individual modules; specifically, the authors demonstrated that incorporating the DINO-guided module into the baseline alone yields a 15.85% improvement in Dice similarity without relying on sliding-window aggregation, effectively proving that the performance gain is inherently driven by their core methodological design rather than the sliding-window mechanism. Furthermore, the deeper analyses regarding the DINO prior, prototype design, computational overhead, and baseline fairness have successfully resolved the remaining technical doubts.
By rigorously untangling the driving forces behind the performance gains and justifying the theoretical depth of their foundation model integration, the paper delivers validated, high-impact insights to the community.
In light of MICCAI policy that no new results can be added in the rebuttal phase, I have re-evaluated this paper based on its original content. The design works effectively (bringing large performance gains, as evidenced in the original manuscript), is technically sound, and the paper is easy to follow. Therefore, I recommend acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We are glad and encouraged that reviewers find our work “well-motivated” (All), “addresses an important limitation” (All), “strong empirical gains” (All), “solid” (R1), “comprehensive evaluation” (R2), and “supportive qualitative results” (R3). All the reviewers expressed positive ratings. Thanks for the constructive comments. Responses to the remaining concerns are as follows.
Q1 (R1): Difference from SSR.
A1: Our method differs from SSR in two main aspects: (i) the role of DINO and (ii) whether CLIP features are directly enhanced. SSR uses DINO only as a post-hoc auxiliary cue by combining DINO affinity with CLIP affinity to suppress CAM noise, without improving CLIP features themselves. In contrast, we use DINO as a structural prior during feature learning to directly enhance CLIP representations, leading to stronger spatial localization for anomaly detection.
Q2 (All): Concerns on sliding-window aggregation (SWA).
A2: (1) Despite SWA’s gains, the other two modules (DINO-guided fusion & PSM) constitute the core scientific contribution in this work, aiming at addressing two fundamental problems of few-shot anomaly detection: the lack of fine-grained local structural information for precise spatial localization and inefficient use of limited support data. These modules and SWA are highly complementary, as our core modules build robust and discriminative features that provide the foundation for SWA to further enhance spatial resolution and improve the final localization quality.
(2) Notably, even without SWA, adding only the DINO-guided module to the baseline still brings a +15.85% Dice gain, showing that the improvement is not mainly driven by SWA.
(3) For fair comparison, we also apply SWA to competing methods. With SWA, MVFA and MadCLIP achieve 48.19 and 50.61 Dice, respectively, still clearly below our 56.33, demonstrating the effectiveness and complementarity of our core modules.
Q3 (R1, R3): Efficiency and scalability of our method.
A3: (1) For SWA, as stated in our manuscript, we concatenate all cropped sub-images along the batch dimension, obtaining whole-image embeddings in a single forward pass. This utilizes GPU parallelism and incurs only a marginal increase in inference time: < 0.025s on an NVIDIA A40 GPU. (2) For our memory scheme, the main overhead comes from storing the memory bank and computing patch-prototype similarities. Let d be the feature dimension, m^2/n^2 the patch number per image for MVFA/ours, and n_n/n_a the normal/abnormal prototype number in our memory scheme. Under the k-shot setting, memory size comparison: MVFA:kd
m^2 vs Ours:(n_n+n_a)d. Similarity FLOPs per image: MVFA:2kd
m^4 vs Ours:2d(n_n+n_a)*n^2.With k=4, n_n=50, n_a=4, m=17, n=37 (typical for MVFA and ours), our memory and FLOPs are < 5% and <23% of MVFA, respectively. Also, our design is independent of the shot number k, yielding better scalability.
Q4 (R2): More ablation studies on PSM.
A4: Although adding abnormal images to a dense memory bank improves Dice from 53.65 to 55.38, it remains below our PSM (56.33) and incurs higher computation (See Q3). This confirms that the gain also benefits from the prototype design rather than merely adding abnormal data. For fusion weights, the fixed average already yields consistent gains, indicating our robustness without complex coefficient tuning. Additional optimization may further improve performance.
Q5 (R2): Evaluation of DINOv3 as a standalone anomaly detector.
A5: When frozen DINOv3 is used alone for anomaly detection via support–query patch matching, it yields only 12.43% Dice on LiverCT (4-shot). This suggests that, in the medical domain, DINOv3 may not reliably establish cross-image patch correspondences without task-specific adaptation. In contrast, within-image affinities are more reliable and can be effectively exploited by our method to improve spatial localization.
Minor concerns like the Fig. 3 caption and careful claim of classification results will be carefully revised.

title: B-spline Activations as Intrinsic Uncertainty Estimators in Medical Image Segmentation
abstract:
A fundamental tension underlies uncertainty estimation for
clinical segmentation: Bayesian methods—MC Dropout, Deep Ensembles, TTA—demand repeated inference incompatible with real-time workflows, while single-pass alternatives either alter the training objective(EDL) or impose global architectural constraints that risk distorting learned representations (DUQ, SNGP, DDU). The core scientific question is whether prediction uncertainty can be read directly from the activation geometry of a learned function in a single forward pass, without auxiliary losses, repeated sampling, or global architectural change. We identify a principled answer in the local-support property of B-spline basis functions within Kolmogorov–Arnold Network (KAN) layers: because each basis function has compact support, activation concentration directly proxies training-data density—well-covered inputs produce winner-take-all activation while distribution boundaries and misclassified sites produce dispersed patterns. We verify this statistically (Mann Whitney p<0.001, Cohen’s d up to 1.61 across colonoscopy, ultrasound,and dermoscopy) and operationalize it via the Residual KAN Head, a plug-and-play classifier adding <0.01M parameters that preserves segmentation accuracy (Dice change <0.3%). On four medical imaging benchmarks, our single-pass method achieves the best selective prediction per formance in 4 of 12 backbone×dataset settings at 6.9× faster inference than multi-pass alternatives.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: Authors propose to use a KAN residual network to estimate uncertainty in semantic segmentation. They show that learned B-spline functions activate in a way that reflects a deterministic coverage signal, and this signal can be uncovered in a single pass, in contrast to multi-pass uncertainty estimation methods. By designing a residual head around KAN they also estimate this uncertainty without changing the loss function and with minimum impact on performance (measured as DICE). Authors validate the method by first showing there’s no significant decrease in DICE on four medical imaging databases and compare to other uncertainty methods in a ranking task (using E-AURC), showing comparable performance to SOTA.
reviews.text_strengths:
Novelty - The application of KAN activations as a signal of support is novel, to the best of my knowledge. 
Applicable method - Authors claim the FPS supports real-time deployment.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Statistical evaluation - the E-AURC table would benefit from std values and a statistical support for claims and comparisons should be added. 
Unclear scope - While the authors show that the uncertainty signal carried by B-spline activation reflects distributional coverage, they do not explain if there is a relation between distributional coverage and model confidence, and in particular whether pixel, segment, or boundary reliability capture the true confidence that can be useful in practice. For example, it is not clear if the per-pixel uncertainty represented by entropy in B-spline activations can be calibrated to inform decisions beyond the ranking task that is demoed in the paper.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
My suggestion is, first, to clarify the relation between distributional coverage and model confidence. Some SOTA methods estimate only model confidence and do not explicitly account for distributional coverage or distribution shift, and it is not clear whether the present manuscript addresses both or only uncertainty related to distributional coverage. Second, the manuscript would benefit from a discussion of how the derived uncertainty signal can be used in practice; that is, whether the uncertainty can be calibrated and whether the model supports calibration. Although no existing approach provides universally reliable uncertainty estimates, some perform better than others in terms of calibration, and it would be helpful to give some intuition for where the presented model falls. Third, confidence intervals and statistical testing should be added to support the claims made in the paper.

Poor statistical evaluation.
Unclear scope: The usefulness of uncertainty estimation is demonstrated through per-frame averaging, and it is not clear whether uncertainty at the pixel or region level also translates downstream. It is also unclear whether model uncertainty is captured, in addition to uncertainty arising from distributional coverage. The authors show that the uncertainty signal carried by the B-spline activation reflects distributional coverage, but the relation between distributional coverage and model confidence is not obvious. It is also not clear how the approach could be used in practice: the authors only demonstrate the use of averaged uncertainty to rank segmented frames, whereas broader practical use would likely benefit from some discussion of whether the uncertainty can be calibrated.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors will update the submission with statistical testing and a clearer explanation of the scope and applicability of their method. The promised additions answered my concerns.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper addresses uncertainty estimation in clinical image segmentation, where existing approaches either rely on computationally expensive multi-pass inference (e.g., test-time augmentation, MC Dropout) or introduce modified training objectives and architectural constraints (e.g., evidential learning). The authors propose a single-pass uncertainty estimation method based on the activation geometry of Kolmogorov–Arnold Network (KAN) layers. Leveraging the local-support property of B-spline basis functions, they interpret activation dispersion as a proxy for prediction uncertainty, where concentrated activations indicate well-supported regions and dispersed activations indicate uncertain predictions.
To operationalize this idea, a lightweight Residual KAN Head is introduced and integrated into existing segmentation architectures. The method derives pixel-wise uncertainty directly from activation patterns without requiring repeated inference, modified loss functions, or changes to the backbone.
Experiments on four medical imaging datasets across multiple backbones show that the proposed approach achieves competitive or superior uncertainty estimation performance compared to both multi-pass and single-pass baselines, while maintaining segmentation accuracy and significantly reducing computational cost.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper proposes a novel perspective on uncertainty estimation by linking activation dispersion in KAN layers to prediction uncertainty. The interpretation of local B-spline support as a proxy for data density is intuitive and provides a clear conceptual foundation.
The proposed Residual KAN Head is lightweight and can be incorporated into existing segmentation architectures with minimal overhead, without requiring repeated inference or modifications to the training objective.
Efficient single-pass uncertainty estimation: The method enables uncertainty estimation in a single forward pass and is substantially faster than multi-pass approaches such as MC Dropout and test-time augmentation, making it attractive for real-time applications.
The approach achieves competitive or superior uncertainty estimation performance across multiple datasets and backbones, while preserving segmentation accuracy.
No degradation of primary task performance: In contrast to some alternative single-pass methods, the proposed approach maintains segmentation accuracy across all evaluated settings.
The method is validated on several medical imaging benchmarks and backbone models, supporting its general applicability.
Initial ablation analysis: The paper includes an ablation study investigating architectural components (e.g., the role of the KAN head and grid size), providing initial insight into the behavior of the method.
The figures are very well designed and help to illustrate the core ideas of the paper effectively.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
While an ablation study is provided, it is relatively narrow in scope and does not sufficiently disentangle the contribution of key design choices (e.g., spline order). The current analysis (e.g., Table 4) remains limited and could be better structured to provide clearer insights.
While the method is significantly faster than multi-pass approaches, it is slightly slower than other single-pass methods. This trade-off is not clearly discussed, which somewhat weakens the efficiency argument.
Certain aspects of the training procedure and integration of the Residual KAN Head (e.g., whether training is fully end-to-end or partially frozen) are not explicitly described, which makes the method harder to fully assess.
Some sections lack sufficient explanation (e.g., the “Inference Efficiency” section contains little to no descriptive text), and certain tables or formatting choices (e.g., Table 4 structure) reduce clarity.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The paper presents an interesting and conceptually appealing approach to single-pass uncertainty estimation. In particular, the use of activation dispersion in KAN layers as a proxy for uncertainty is a novel and well-motivated idea, and the overall framework is simple and practical to integrate.
For further improvement, a more detailed and structured ablation study (e.g., including additional hyperparameters such as spline order) and a clearer discussion of efficiency trade-offs compared to other single-pass methods would strengthen the paper.
Minor comments:
Table 4: The “Factor” column contains only a single entry (“Head Design”) and could be simplified or removed to improve clarity.
Section 3.3: Minor formatting issue (“strongest” extends into the margin).
Section 3.4 (“Inference Efficiency”) lacks explanatory text and would benefit from additional discussion.
Some references point to arXiv preprints instead of final published versions (e.g., KAN paper).

The paper presents a conceptually interesting and well-motivated approach to single-pass uncertainty estimation based on activation geometry in KAN layers. The proposed method is simple, practical, and demonstrates competitive performance across multiple datasets and backbones, while preserving segmentation accuracy and offering a clear efficiency advantage over multi-pass methods.
However, the overall contribution is somewhat limited by a relatively narrow ablation study, minor inconsistencies in the reported results, and aspects of the presentation that could be improved for clarity.
Overall, the paper provides a solid and relevant contribution with clear practical potential, although it would benefit from a more thorough experimental analysis and improved presentation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The original submission already presented a conceptually interesting and practically relevant approach to single-pass uncertainty estimation with competitive empirical performance. In their rebuttal, the authors directly addressed several of my main concerns, particularly regarding computational efficiency, training details, ablation scope, and reproducibility.
The clarification that the method is trained fully end-to-end, the more nuanced discussion of efficiency trade-offs relative to other single-pass approaches, and the planned release of code and experimental configurations significantly improved my confidence in the work. The authors also provided reasonable justification for the chosen ablation scope and acknowledged remaining limitations transparently.
Overall, the rebuttal strengthened the paper considerably, and I believe the work constitutes a solid and practically relevant contribution suitable for acceptance.

meta_reviews.text:
This submission proposes an uncertainty estimation method for image segmentation using b-spline activation functions. The reviews diverge in appreciation, note potential relevance to the field, but also converge on major concerns: unclear scope of uncertainty and motivation of application, limitations in the experimental evaluation, concerns on computational performance. A rebuttal should clarify these points with realistically minor changes to the manuscript. For these reasons, the recommendation is to request a rebuttal.

The rebuttal was helpful in addressing the reviewer concerns on a statistical validation, computational efficiency, and methodological scope. A consensus has been reached to recommended for acceptance due to the practical value and novelty of its single-pass uncertainty estimation approach.

I recommend rejection. The paper studies an interesting direction—using B-spline/KAN activation patterns as a single-pass uncertainty signal for medical image segmentation—but the current evidence is not sufficiently convincing for acceptance. The central claim that B-spline activation dispersion serves as an intrinsic uncertainty estimator remains largely heuristic and empirically under-validated; the pixel-level statistics show correlation with errors/boundaries, but do not establish reliable uncertainty estimation, calibration, or density-awareness.
Experimentally, the results are mixed. The proposed method achieves the best E-AURC in only 4 of 12 settings, while multi-pass baselines often outperform it despite higher cost. The advantage over single-pass alternatives is also not decisive, as EDL is competitive or better in several cases. Important uncertainty baselines discussed in the paper, such as DUQ, SNGP, DDU, or deep ensembles, are not evaluated. The validation sets are also small for some datasets, and the paper lacks stronger statistical testing, calibration analysis, OOD/domain-shift evaluation, and broader ablations.
Overall, while the idea is potentially useful, the novelty and empirical support are currently insufficient. The claims about intrinsic uncertainty estimation and clinical real-time applicability are stronger than what the presented results justify.

The paper presents a useful single-pass uncertainty quantification method with competitive performance. The authors have properly addressed reviewers’ concerns, including outlying the scope and significance of their results.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and AC for the feedback. We address the AC’s convergent themes below.
1.SCOPE OF UNCERTAINTY [R1, R3, AC]. Our signal captures an epistemic component of predictive reliability arising from limited training-data coverage, not a full Bayesian decomposition. Local-support B-spline bases concentrate activation where inputs are well-covered during training and disperse it where coverage is sparse. Fig. 3 supports this: misclassified pixels show significantly higher activation entropy than correct ones (Cohen’s d up to 1.61, all p<0.001), and boundary pixels exceed interior ones (d up to 1.43)—confirming coverage-to-reliability and pixel-level discriminability. We will clarify in Sec. 2.1.2.STATISTICAL EVALUATION [R1, AC]. Per-cell ±std (3 seeds) computed; std on best cells is small (e.g., ISIC/UNet 18.7±1.2). Wilcoxon signed-rank across 12 backbone×dataset settings: Ours significantly outperforms Softmax (11/12, p=0.0015) and achieves statistical parity with the strongest multi-pass baselines (TTA×8 p=0.42, MC Dropout×10 p=0.79) as well as EDL (p=0.79), while running 6.9–8.9× faster than multi-pass methods and preserving Dice unlike EDL. Full results will be added to Table 2.3.APPLIED FRAMING [R1, AC]. Our framework targets selective prediction (Sec. 2.3): uncertainty ranks images so unreliable cases can be deferred for clinician review. Ranking and calibration address distinct clinical needs—ranking supports triage prioritization (our focus); calibration supports threshold-based automation. Fig. 4 demonstrates the practical sufficiency of ranking: at 50% coverage, our curve approaches the oracle on ISIC/UNet and clearly outperforms TTA/MC Dropout, confirming frame-level uncertainty supports the “defer top-k uncertain cases” workflow without absolute confidence thresholds. Because activation entropy is a continuous scalar, it remains compatible with post-hoc calibration (e.g., temperature scaling) if threshold decisions are needed.
4.LOCAL SUPPORT VISUALIZATION [R3]. Fig. 2 shows per-basis activation intensity but not Bk(x) themselves. We will add a compact-support Bk(x) inset and a brief B-spline definition in Sec. 2.1.The one-pass mechanism: during a standard forward pass, the KAN layer evaluates B-spline bases for each input feature; we read the distribution of these already-computed values as uncertainty, no additional computation needed.
5.COMPUTATIONAL PERFORMANCE [R2, R3, AC]. Our claim concerns sequential repeated inference in latency-sensitive workflows (not all multi-pass methods). Table 3: TTA 100.69 ms; MC Dropout 129.48 ms; ours 14.60 ms. Among single-pass methods, our 1.1× overhead (14.60 vs. 12.79 ms) is slightly above Softmax (13.12) and EDL (13.5). However, Softmax ranks significantly worse (p=0.0015); EDL requires loss modification and degrades Dice up to 2.5%. Ours maintains Dice (<0.3%) without altering training, matching EDL in win count (6/12 each) while preserving accuracy across all settings.
6.ABLATION SCOPE AND TRAINING [R2]. Table 4 isolates grid size G and residual structure, the two largest empirical factors. We fix S=2 and acknowledge spline-order sensitivity is not experimentally disentangled. Mechanistically, G directly controls the resolution of the basis decomposition (K=G+S) and is the dominant factor, as the G=5→3 effect (E-AURC 82.1→50.8) confirms. Training is fully end-to-end with no frozen components.
7.REPRODUCIBILITY AND MINOR ISSUES [R1, R2, R3]. Upon acceptance we will release code, checkpoints, and config files with a reproducibility checklist; we will also expand Sec. 3.4, update arXiv refs, simplify Table 4, and fix Sec. 3.3 formatting.
We hope these clarifications address the reviewers’ and AC’s concerns; all promised revisions will be incorporated in the camera-ready.

title: C²RM-Seg: Causal Counterfactual Reasoning with Structural-Semantic Priors for Weakly Supervised Histopathological Tissue Segmentation
abstract: Histopathological image segmentation is critical for computer-aided pathological diagnosis and prognosis analysis. Although weakly supervised methods reduce the reliance on pixel-level annotations, they are often limited by low-quality pseudo-masks and accumulated label noise. In particular, existing Class Activation Mapping (CAM) approaches are vulnerable to spurious correlations, and conventional networks struggle to jointly preserve fine-grained tissue morphology and global semantic consistency. To address these issues, we propose C\textsuperscript{2}RM-Seg, a unified framework that tightly integrates causal inference with foundation model priors. In the classification stage for pseudo-label generation, we introduce a Causal Counterfactual Reasoning Module (C\textsuperscript{2}RM), which projects features into latent causal factors and learns a causal structure matrix to enable counterfactual interventions. By attenuating confounding contextual effects, C\textsuperscript{2}RM refines CAM activations and yi
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

This dual-path architecture combines traditional ResNeSt structural features with semantic priors from DINOv3 using a gating mechanism to balance global semantics and morphological details. To manage the inherent noise in weak supervision, a margin loss guided by prediction uncertainty is introduced to dynamically balance margin enforcement and confidence penalties.

C2RM-Seg addresses an important weakly supervised histopathology segmentation problem and presents a complete pipeline: CAM refinement, structure–semantic segmentation, and uncertainty-aware training. The submitted experiments compare against relevant WSSS and foundation-model baselines on two public datasets, report variance, boundary metrics, efficiency, and include meaningful ablations. While R1 raises valid concerns that the causal interpretation of Z^{cf} = Z − AZ is stronger than what is rigorously proven, the rebuttal clarifies the intended SCM-inspired approximation, and the original manuscript already provides component ablations and feature visualization supporting its practical effect. I do not consider the additional rebuttal-only stress tests or encoder comparisons, but the submitted evidence is still sufficient. The method should revise claims to “SCM-inspired/counterfactual feature correction” rather than fully verified causal deconfounding, and better explain the assumptions behind the latent factor graph.

I recommend rejection. While the paper addresses an important problem in weakly supervised histopathological tissue segmentation, the main technical claims are not sufficiently convincing. In particular, the proposed causal counterfactual reasoning module is presented as causal deconfounding, but the learned factor matrix and subtraction-based intervention do not provide a rigorous or empirically validated causal model. As a result, the central motivation of removing staining-driven confounders remains largely asserted rather than demonstrated.
The method also appears to combine several existing ideas—CAM refinement, foundation-model features, dual-branch fusion, gating, and uncertainty-aware loss—without clearly establishing which component is truly novel or necessary. The experimental validation is limited to two datasets, and the improvements over strong recent WSSS baselines are relatively modest given the added complexity. More importantly, the paper lacks targeted evidence on stain/domain robustness, pseudo-label quality, causal validity, and generalization across centers or scanners, which are essential for supporting its main claims.
Overall, although the direction is relevant, the current submission overstates its causal contribution and does not provide sufficiently strong methodological or experimental evidence to justify acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the reviewers for their insightful feedback. 
1.Mathematical Foundation and Empirical Evidence of Z^{cf} = Z - AZ (R1,R2,R3): 
This is not a heuristic, but strictly derived from Structural Causal Models (SCMs). In SCM, features are modeled as Z = AZ + \epsilon, where AZ quantifies confounding effects (e.g.,staining bias) via dependency matrix A, and the exogenous variable $\epsilon$ represents the pure, unconfounded causal signal (e.g.,intrinsic morphology). Performing counterfactual intervention to block causal paths from confounders mathematically equates to isolating \epsilon. By simple rearrangement, \epsilon = Z - AZ. Thus, Z^{cf} = Z - AZ is the exact algebraic implementation of extracting deconfounded features by stripping away learned spurious correlations. While this establishes the theoretical soundness, the empirical evidence confirming that AZ genuinely captures confounding noise rather than useful foreground features in practice is detailed in Point 3 (Weight Analysis of Matrix A) and Point 4 (Staining Stress Test) below. To address R1’s concern regarding evaluation, we emphasize that the methods compared in our experiments are highly representative and top-performing mainstream in WSSS.
2.Latent Factor Meaning & Anti-Collapse (R2):
Multi-class CAM optimization inherently forces channel groups to learn distinct patterns. Although previously omitted due to space limits, our analysis shows C2RM reduces inter-factor cosine similarity from 0.68 to 0.21.Alongside t-SNE (Fig. 3), this proves decoupling without collapse.
3.Why Subtract Noise, Not Foreground? (R2, R3):
Global staining acts as a network “shortcut”, whereas foreground morphology is localized. Although omitted previously due to space limits, our analysis of matrix A shows its high-weight connections are sparse and strictly directed from background to foreground factors. Thus, subtracting AZ strips away spurious shortcuts rather than the foreground.
4.Proof of Causal Deconfounding (R1, R3):
Although omitted previously due to space limits, we conducted a staining robustness stress test (extreme color jittering and Macenko normalization) to prove our mechanism. Under severe confounding, the baseline mIoU collapsed by 5.24%, whereas C2RM-Seg showed a mere 1.57% drop. This verifies that causal deconfounding is the core driver of our performance gains.
5.Architectural Novelty & Cross-Path Gating (R1):
Our dual-branch design is not mere concatenation. The major bottleneck in WSSS for pathology is pseudo-label boundary. Our Cross-path Gating addresses this by using spatial confidences derived from high-frequency local structures (ResNeSt) to dynamically “throttle” the injection of DINOv3’s global semantics. This prevents smooth global features from blurring fine-grained tissue boundaries.
6.Why DINOv3 Instead of UNI or CONCH? (R2):
We conducted comparative experiments using UNI and CONCH as the semantic branch. Under identical settings, UNI and CONCH achieved mIoUs of 78.41% and 78.75%, respectively, both lower than DINOv3 (79.62%). While UNI/CONCH excel at image-level classification, DINOv3’s self-supervised objectives (mask prediction) make it far superior for pixel-level dense prediction.
7.Proof of “Structure vs. Semantic” Roles (R2):
Though omitted earlier due to space limits, our Fourier spectrum and bIoU analyses on single branches show ResNeSt features are rich in high frequencies. Conversely, DINOv3 exhibits strong low-frequency semantics but blurry boundaries (bIoU drops by 4.2%). Their complementarity under our gating mechanism validates our design.
8.Comprehensive Ablations & Sensitivity (R3):
Omitted from the original submission due to strict space constraints, we conducted sensitivity analyses for the number of latent factors K in {4, 8, 16, 32}. The model achieves optimal performance at K=8 (mIoU 79.62%). Capacity is limited at K=4 (77.2%), but performance remains highly stable at K=16, 32 (79.12%).

title: CAG-WM: A Synthetic-Data-Driven Coronary World Model for Autonomous Guidewire Navigation
abstract: Automated guidewire navigation in percutaneous coronary intervention can reduce radiation exposure and clinician workload. However, existing methods suffer from low sample efficiency and struggle with long-horizon guidewire navigation. World models offer a promising solution, but scarce paired angiographic-3D data leaves end-to-end world model approaches unexplored. To address these challenges, we propose CAG-WM, the first synthetic-data-driven world model for autonomous coronary guidewire navigation. Specifically, we construct dynamic synthetic coronary angiography–3D data and train a world model within a SOFA-based simulation environment to learn vessel–guidewire dynamics and perform internal multi-step rollouts for long-horizon navigation. CAG-WM is trained on 100 synthetic cases with full-view angiographic renderings and corresponding 3D voxelized coronary models, and evaluated on 20 multi-center clinical cases and 10 public datasets. Experimental results show that CAG-WM achieves a success rate exceeding 80% in clinical cases, significantly outperforming competing methods. Even in unsuccessful cases, the guidewire remains close to target lesion. Despite slightly longer per-step inference time, CAG-WM achieves the shortest total navigation time (about 2 min) thanks to its higher success rate, which reduces premature termination at the maximum step limit. Code and data is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CAG-WM-FEA0.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of this paper is the proposal of CAG-WM, a comprehensive world model framework for autonomous coronary guidewire navigation, which systematically integrates synthetic coronary angiography 3D data construction, a SOFA-based physics simulation environment, and a TD-MPC2-based world model to enable long horizon planning from angiographic observations to control actions. The key innovation lies in leveraging synthetic data to address the scarcity of real paired data, while explicitly modeling guidewire vessel dynamics to support multi step imagination based reasoning, ultimately leading to significantly improved navigation success rate and efficiency on real clinical data, and demonstrating the feasibility of applying world models to complex endovascular intervention tasks.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Well motivated problem with clear clinical relevance:The paper tackles autonomous coronary guidewire navigation, a high impact and technically challenging task in PCI that involves long horizon planning under partial observability. 
2.Novel integration of synthetic data, physics simulation, and world models:A key contribution is the coherent integration of synthetic angiography 3D data generation, SOFA-based physical simulation, and a TD-MPC2-based world model into a unified training pipeline. While each component exists individually, combining them to form a closed loop system for learning guidewire vessel dynamics is original and practically valuable, especially for data scarce medical robotics tasks. 
3.Demonstrated effectiveness on real clinical data despite synthetic training:The method is trained entirely on synthetic data yet shows clear performance gains over RL and existing world model baselines on multi center clinical datasets. This suggests that the approach has promising generalization ability and provides an encouraging step toward real world deployment in endovascular intervention tasks.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Limited analysis of synthetic-to-real generalization:While the method is trained on synthetic data and evaluated on real clinical cases, the paper provides limited analysis of the domain gap between synthetic and real angiography. For instance, it would strengthen the work to include additional studies on how differences in imaging characteristics or anatomical variability affect performance. Prior sim-to-real studies often include such analyses or adaptation strategies, and incorporating similar evaluations here could further support the claimed generalization ability. 
2.Methodological novelty is primarily at the system level:The proposed approach builds upon existing world model frameworks, particularly TD-MPC2 , with task specific adaptations in observation design and reward formulation. While this integration is well-motivated and effective for the application, the methodological contribution is mainly at the system and application level rather than introducing a fundamentally new world model formulation. Clarifying this positioning could help better align expectations regarding novelty. 
3.Clarity and fairness of baseline comparisons could be improved:The proposed method leverages structured inputs such as guidewire points, vessel centerlines, and target locations (Sec. 2.3) . It is not entirely clear whether all baselines are provided with the same input representations, or whether some operate on different modalities. Providing additional clarification or controlled comparisons with consistent observation spaces would make the performance gains more directly attributable to the proposed modeling approach.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
No

This paper tackles an important and clinically relevant problem and presents a well engineered integration of synthetic data, physics-based simulation, and world models, with empirical results showing clear improvements over existing baselines. However, the strength of the contribution is somewhat limited by the lack of thorough analysis of synthetic-to-real generalization, the primarily system level novelty, and some ambiguity in baseline fairness. Overall, the work is promising and potentially impactful.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_strengths:
(1) Technical novelty and innovation: Applying a world model to coronary guidewire navigation is a relevant and reasonably novel direction. The integration of synthetic full-view CAG, reconstructed 3D anatomy, and SOFA-based physical simulation is a meaningful systems contribution. Figures 1 and 2 present the high-level workflow clearly.
(2) Experimental rigor and validation: The paper evaluates against three classes of baselines: model-free RL, planning-based methods, and world-model-based methods. It reports three metrics on two test sources (InCAG and VMR), and includes a reward ablation study. At a minimum, the experimental surface is broader than many papers in this area. Tables 1 and 2 attempt to characterize performance, failure quality, and runtime.
(3) Clarity of presentation: The manuscript is generally well organized. The problem setup, framework overview, experimental protocol, and result sections are easy to follow. Figure 1 provides a useful system overview, and Figure 3 offers qualitative visualizations of navigation trajectories and training-space coverage.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(1) The main concern is that the algorithmic novelty appears limited. The core seems closer to “TD-MPC2 + task-specific observation engineering + reward design + synthetic simulation environment” than to a substantially new world-model formulation. The paper claims “the first synthetic-data-driven world model,” but the actual methodological advance over TD-MPC2 is not sharply defined. For a top-tier venue, the manuscript needs to separate system integration novelty from algorithmic novelty much more clearly.
(2) The manuscript repeatedly claims the method is end-to-end from angiographic observations to actions, but Sec. 2.3 explicitly states that it first detects the stenosis target, tracks guidewire points, and extracts vessel centerlines before encoding them with TCNs and an MLP. Sec. 3.1 further states that all perceptual information required by the observation is pre-extracted prior to training. This is not a standard end-to-end setup; it is a staged pipeline with substantial structured intermediate supervision. The wording is therefore misleading.
(3) The mathematical and physical descriptions are under-specified. Eq. (2) is not explained in enough detail for reproducibility, and the dynamic vessel-wall deformation model is especially unclear. The manuscript claims dynamic vascular properties, but it does not establish whether the displacement field reflects realistic cardiac/respiratory motion or merely synthetic perturbations. At present, the dynamic environment seems plausible as a simulation device, but not yet clinically validated.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The coronary artery at the top center of Figure 1 seems to have been artificially created? The branching of the small blood vessels doesn’t look very realistic.

The major factors behind my recommendation are the mismatch between the paper’s claims and the supporting evidence, the limited isolation of its true methodological contribution, and the lack of sufficient experimental rigor. In particular, the claimed novelty beyond existing TD-MPC2-style world models is not clearly established, and the “end-to-end” characterization is overstated given the method’s reliance on pre-extracted structured inputs.

reviews.text_contribution:
The authors propose CAG-WM, a framework for autonomous coronary guidewire navigation in PCI. The framework consists of 2 parts: (i) an EG3D-based[1,2] training data generation strategy; (ii) a TD-MPC2[3] backbone with modifications on input encoder and reward design. The experiments are conducted on a private dataset (InCAG, 20 cases) and a public dataset (10 cases), with customized evaluation/benchmark procedure. Compared to the top-3 most similar works [4,5,6], the novelty and contribution of this work lies in its data generation strategy and the open codebase.
[1] Chan et al., EG3D, arXiv 2021.
Multi-view consistent 3D GAN:
proposed for natural images e.g. faces.
[2] Cao et al., ATC-CAG, AAAI 2026.
Translational correction for PCI camera calibration:
via an EG3D[1]-based synthetic coronary angiography generation pipeline.
[3] Hansen et al., TD-MPC2, 2024.
Model-based (MPC) RL algorithm:
proposed for general robotic continuous control tasks.
[4] Robertshaw et al., MICCAI 2025.
TD-MPC2 world model for mechanical thrombectomy:
applies the same backbone [3] to guidewire navigation from aortic arch to carotid/cerebral vessels in SOFA.
[5] Scarponi et al., IROS 2024.
SAC-based coronary guidewire navigation with dynamic vessel wall:
explicitly models cardiac-motion-induced vessel deformation in SOFA.
[6] Schegg et al., RoboSoft 2022.
Planning-based coronary guidewire navigation:
MPC-based path planning for coronary bifurcation traversal in SOFA.
reviews.text_strengths:
Practical data generation strategy:
[2] produces what I consider the most realistic synthetic coronary angiography (XA/DSA) images to date, built upon EG3D[1], though [2] only applies this capability to translational correction for PCI camera calibration. The present work directly inherits this generation pipeline from [2] and repurposes it for supporting simulation environments for guidewire navigation training. While the generation module itself is not new, I view this as a valuable contribution: the gap between synthetic training data and transferable navigation policies has been repeatedly identified as a bottleneck in prior literature [7,8], yet no prior work has offered a convincing solution. That said, I note with some puzzlement that although the pipeline produces highly realistic 2D angiographic images, the method does not directly consume these images. Instead, it extracts intermediate representations (point coordinates, centerlines) and discards the visual realism. This appears to leave the most distinctive advantage of the generation pipeline underutilized, and I would appreciate the authors’ clarification on this design choice or correct my misunderstanding
(I have to say the method and experiment part is too confusing, and some parts seem to be blurred. :-) )
.
Open codebase:
I carefully went through the codebase, and confirmed that the codebase contains the full SOFA-based CAG-EVE environment plus the TD-MPC2 training/evaluation scripts, but the perception/data-generation pieces described in the paper (EG3D angiography synthesis, guidewire/centerline detectors, and the 20-case clinical geometry set) are missing, which prevents end-to-end reproduction of the reported “from angiography” results.
Graphical content:
Figures are high quality and well designed. Videos are informative and attractive.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.
On task setup, experimental description, and missing information.
Even as a reviewer familiar with this domain, I was unable to determine the following key information from the paper alone, prior to inspecting the released codebase.
1.
Source of 3D models for clinical cases.
How are the 3D vessel models for the 20 multi-center clinical cases obtained? Via the same multi-view angiographic reconstruction pipeline in Sec 2.1? Or from CTA? If from angiographic reconstruction, how many views are used? What reconstruction method is applied? What are the spatial resolution and reconstruction error?
2.
Multi-view temporal synchronization.
If multi-view angiographic reconstruction is used, clinical views are typically acquired in different cardiac cycles (weak async), meaning vessel morphology differs across views due to cardiac motion. Is ECG-gating used to select images from the same cardiac phase? How is this handled? [8] (AutoCAR) specifically addresses this dynamic sparse-view reconstruction problem.
3.
Coordinate dimensionality.
Are the input coordinates g_i, c_j in R^2 or R^3? This is never explicitly stated. SOFA is a 3D simulator; rotation actions degenerate under 2D projection; nearest-neighbor matching between guidewire and centerline requires the same dimensionality, all suggesting 3D. But this directly bears on the claim of “from angiographic observations” (2D angiography only provides 2D information).
4.
Dynamic modeling and simulation.
[5] (Scarponi, IROS 2024) explicitly models cardiac-motion-induced vessel wall deformation as a core contribution. What level of dynamic modeling does CAG-WM provide in comparison? If cardiac motion is not modeled, what exactly is the “real” data experiment? Is it direct XA observation, or a static rendering?
THESE INFORMATION MATTERS BECAUSE
they prevent reader from assessing several key claims made in the paper, including “the first,” “real world/data,” and the purported differences from [3,4,5]. More specially, some related works I list below(I am not asking author to compare these methods bacuase they may not release thier code or data, but the thing is you should at least EITHER clarify the difference compared with them, in terms of method, task setup, eval way; OR report what is conducted in the exp and method in a clear and more descriptive language). In fact there are many and I can’t list them all, e.g. CathSim.
```
[4] Robertshaw, MICCAI 2025
Anatomy: Aortic arch → carotid/cerebral (MT)
Core algorithm: TD-MPC2
Simulator: SOFA
Vessel model: 10 real patient CTA
Observation input: Guidewire tip coords (3D)
Dynamic vessel: No
Test environment: SOFA simulation
Open-source code: No
Comments: Same backbone as CAG-WM; 65% SR on aortic arch
[5] Scarponi, IROS 2024
Anatomy: Coronary
Core algorithm: SAC
Simulator: SOFA
Vessel model: Real CTA
Observation input: Guidewire tip coords (3D)
Dynamic vessel: Yes (cardiac motion)
Test environment: SOFA simulation
Open-source code: No
Comments: Directly comparable anatomy; explicit cardiac dynamics
[6] Schegg, RoboSoft 2022
Anatomy: Coronary
Core algorithm: Planning-based (MPC)
Simulator: SOFA
Vessel model: Real CTA
Observation input: Guidewire + vessel geometry
Dynamic vessel: No
Test environment: SOFA simulation
Open-source code: No
Comments: Directly comparable anatomy; planning approach
CAG-WM (this paper)
Anatomy: Coronary
Core algorithm: TD-MPC2 + TCN encoder
Simulator: SOFA
Vessel model: 100 synthetic (EG3D) + 20 clinical (source ?) + 10 VMR
Observation input: Guidewire coords + centerline coords + target (2D or 3D ?)
Dynamic vessel: “Diffeomorphic displacement field” (source and physical meaning ?)
Test environment: SOFA simulation (described as “real clinical cases”)
Open-source code: Yes
Comments: SR 84.7% — but is the difference due to anatomy, encoder,reward, or data volume? No discussion provided.
```
2.
On overclaiming.
Below I identify several instances where the paper’s claims appear to exceed what the experiments actually demonstrate. Due to the missing details above, some of these assessments are based on my inference rather than certainty.
“End-to-end from angiographic observations” vs. what appears to be an image to point extraction to RL agent pipeline.
Evidence from the paper: The Abstract states the method “learns…from angiographic observations in an end-to-end manner.” The Introduction criticizes [4] for “lack[ing] an end-to-end mapping from angiographic images to navigation actions,” implying CAG-WM achieves this. Section 2.3 writes: “given a synthesized angiography image I_t, we detect the stenosis target p*, track the guidewire to obtain N points {g_i} [12], and extract vessel centerline C [26].” Yet the same paper states: “All perceptual information required by observation is pre-extracted prior to training.”
Analysis by training/testing phase: During
training
, all information is directly available from the SOFA simulator, guidewire node positions {g_i} are internal simulator state (no detection network [12] needed); centerlines {c_j} are pre-extracted from the 3D model in Sec 2.1; target p* is manually specified on the centerline. The paper acknowledges this. During
testing
, clinical vessel geometries are imported into SOFA (see below), so testing also occurs within the simulator. Guidewire coordinates, centerlines, and targets can therefore be directly read from the simulator at test time as well.
On the citation of [12] and [26]: The references to a guidewire detection CNN [12] and a centerline extraction method [26] in Sec 2.3 create the impression that these features are extracted from angiographic images. However, within a simulation environment, this information is directly accessible from the simulator and these vision algorithms would not need to be (and likely are not) executed. These citations appear to gesture at a future deployment pipeline rather than describe the current system’s actual data flow.
I ask the authors to clarify explicitly: are [12] and [26] actually run during training or testing? Is the image encoder jointly trained? Does the angiographic image enter the network at all?
Perception error propagation: If the method were truly deployed clinically on live angiographic images, it would require a complete perception front-end (guidewire detection + centerline extraction + target localization), and errors in each module would propagate to navigation performance. This gap is not discussed.
I suggest the authors discuss this at least qualitatively, even without new experiments.
Dependency: The missing coordinate dimensionality from W1 exacerbates this issue, if inputs are confirmed to be 3D, the contradiction with “from 2D angiographic observations” becomes even sharper.
“Real clinical cases.”
Independent evidence: Fig 3.A displays navigation results for clinical cases, showing
both a CAG modality row and a SOFA modality row
for each case. This directly confirms that testing is performed within the SOFA simulator, the guidewire is virtual, physical interactions are simulated, and observations are obtained from the simulator. Regardless of how the 3D vessel model is obtained, the operating environment itself is not “real.”
A more accurate description would be: “evaluated on simulated environments constructed from 20 clinical coronary geometries,” rather than “evaluated on 20 multi-center clinical cases.”
<space is limited, I can not write them all>
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
- **"Real clinical cases."**
- Independent evidence: Fig 3.A displays navigation results for clinical cases, showing **both a CAG modality row and a SOFA modality row** for each case. This directly confirms that testing is performed within the SOFA simulator, the guidewire is virtual, physical interactions are simulated, and observations are obtained from the simulator. Regardless of how the 3D vessel model is obtained, the operating environment itself is not "real."
- A more accurate description would be: "evaluated on simulated environments constructed from 20 clinical coronary geometries," rather than "evaluated on 20 multi-center clinical cases."
- Since the source of the 3D models is not disclosed, I cannot even assess how faithful these "clinical geometries" are to the actual patient anatomy, if they are coarsely reconstructed from a small number of angiographic views, the distance from "real" is even greater. **I ask the authors to clearly define the scope of "real" and disclose the 3D model source.**
- **"Dynamic."**
- Since the source and physical meaning of the displacement field are not disclosed (see W1.4), I cannot determine whether "dynamic" refers to physiologically meaningful cardiac-motion-induced vessel deformation (as explicitly modeled in [5]), or merely to the general contact mechanics inherent in any SOFA simulation (which would not constitute an additional contribution). If the latter, the use of "Dynamic" in the Sec 2.2 title and "incorporating dynamic vascular properties" in the Abstract would be overstatements. Furthermore, the equation presented in this section appears to be standard SOFA constraint mechanics; the symbols defined therein are not referenced elsewhere in the paper. **I ask the authors to clarify the source of the displacement field: is it derived from a cardiac motion model? What are its frequency and amplitude?**
- **Baseline selection and argumentation logic.**
- Context: In the autonomous guidewire navigation literature, existing benchmarks and open-source platforms (CathSim, stEVE [10]) predominantly focus on aortic arch to supra-aortic navigation, where datasets and standardized evaluation protocols are relatively mature. Coronary-specific benchmarks are comparatively scarce. If the paper's primary technical contribution is world-model-based guidewire navigation, one would expect the method to first be validated on existing benchmarks with established baselines, or alternatively, to port existing domain-specific methods to the coronary setting and analyze what makes coronary navigation specifically harder and how the proposed modifications address those challenges.
- Current state: Table 1 compares against six generic RL/planning methods (SAC, TD3, CEM-MPC, DreamerV3, TD-MPC, TD-MPC2). None of the domain-specific methods that the paper itself cites, [4] (same TD-MPC2 backbone), [5] (coronary-specific with dynamic modeling), [6] (coronary planning), appear in the experimental comparison or are even qualitatively discussed in terms of performance differences. I do not require the authors to add experiments with these methods (simulator setups and anatomies may differ), **but I do expect a discussion section that qualitatively analyzes the relationship to and differences from [4,5,6], and that articulates what specific challenges coronary anatomy poses over the aortic arch.**
- **Other minor overclaiming.**
1.Equation (2): Sec 2.2 devotes a full paragraph to the constrained dynamics formulation (Timoshenko beam + contact constraints + Gauss-Seidel solver). The presentation reads as if this is a contribution of the paper, but it is standard SOFA simulation machinery. Moreover, the symbols defined in Eq. (2) are not referenced again in subsequent sections, making this passage serve no functional role in the paper.
2."Coronary-Specific Observation Modeling": The Sec 2.3 subsection title suggests a modeling paradigm tailored to coronary anatomy. In practice, the content describes two TCN encoders applied to coordinate sequences followed by MLP fusion, a generic sequence encoding scheme equally applicable to any tubular vascular anatomy with no coronary specificity.
3.Suggestion: I recommend the authors explicitly acknowledge the scope of experimental validation in a dedicated limitations section, and frame clinical aspirations as future work rather than realized contributions. The Conclusion already mentions "Future work will expand validation cohorts and advance evaluation on physical vascular phantoms and in vivo experiments", **I suggest extending this honest framing to the rest of the paper.**
3.**Minor issues.**
1.Self-reference error in Sec 2.2: "The 3D coronary models from Sec. 2.2 are imported into SOFA", but Sec 2.2 is the SOFA simulation section itself. This should reference Sec 2.1 (Synthetic Data Construction).
2.Likely typo in Table 2: The entry "83.3+-0.082" for CAG-WM on VMR likely should read "83.3+-8.2."

\#\#\#\# Some notes after reading the codebase

- Environment & agent code are complete, but no EG3D synthesis(this may be partially available), perception front-end, or 20-case clinical data(is the mesh refers to the clinical data?) are included, so "from angiography" claims remain untestable.
- Observations are purely SOFA 3D states (Tracking3D, Target3D, etc.), confirming inputs are R^3 despite the paper's 2D phrasing.
- Both training and evaluation run fully inside SOFA with TrackingOnly; there is no interface to live fluoroscopy, so "real clinical cases" are actually simulated on imported meshes.
- The simulator is static (SofaBeamAdapter with fixed vessel meshes); no cardiac-motion or displacement-field model is present despite the "dynamic" narrative.
- No implementations of domain baselines ([4-6]) or perception references [12, 26] exist, so comparisons and pipeline diagrams in the paper cannot be reproduced.

I would recommend acceptance of this paper
IF
the authors can address the significant issues of
overclaiming
and omission/misleading of critical experimental details. That said, the underlying technical/resources contributions, upon these issues resolved, are appreciated.

meta_reviews.text: The submission is well written. However, reviewers note that some claims are too strong (e.g., “the first world model”), as key components like TD-MPC are largely based on prior work. The contribution appears to be mainly at the application level. Further comments can be found in the reviewers’ feedback.

title: CalCErt: Bin-wise Certification of Confidence Calibration in Medical Image Classification
abstract: Deep neural networks remain vulnerable to adversarial perturbations, which can distort not only predictions but also confidence scores, undermining uncertainty calibration. While existing certification methods focus on preserving the predicted category, providing guarantees on how calibration behaves under adversarial attacks remains overlooked. In this work, we introduce CalCErt, a simple and efficient post‑hoc strategy that certifies bin‑wise confidence calibration for any pretrained differentiable classifier. Our approach combines empirical calibration estimates, statistical concentration bounds, and local Lipschitz estimates of the confidence function to derive data‑dependent upper bounds on worst‑case miscalibration within an l2-ball of radius R. We evaluate CalCErt across 11 medical image classification tasks and multiple adversarial perturbations, demonstrating substantially higher certified coverage than baseline strategies while maintaining competitive tightness.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose a novel post-hoc method to estimate an upper bound on calibration error under bounded adversarial perturbations. Their estimate relies on a local approximation of the confidence constants, using the gradient of the confidence function. Authors conduct extensive experiments using well-established datasets in the medical image classification domain.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper is generally well written and easy to follow. 
2.Authors verify trustworthiness and usability of the proposed upper bound on calibration error under various bounded perturbations.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
I have concerns regarding evaluation metrics:
1.It seems like those high coverage rates come at the expense of tightness. Authors should use a principled metric that reflects the trade-off between tightness and coverage in the main table. 
2.The problem with the “overshoot” metric is as follows: if your bounds are not tight, then naturally the overshoot will be small because the bounds are close to the rare bins where the bounds are violated. Thus, the “overshoot” metric is actually misleading: it will be lower for bounds with inferior tightness.
I also have remarks concerning notation and readability:
1.It would be beneficial if you had explained how these notions of uncertainty (statistical, empirical, and noise-based) relate to well-established uncertainty decomposition into aleatoric and epistemic parts
2.Notation would benefit from polishing. In your definition, Ak(δ) is a function of δ, but at the same time, you treat it as a scalar.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Table 1 is hard to interpret because it presents a trade-off between coverage and tightness, and the main table does not reflect how well the method balances coverage and tightness. The proposed “overshoot” metric is highly misleading because it is lower for methods with worse tightness. Based on this unreliable and unjustified metric, the paper tries to prove that CalCErt’s tightness is actually good.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: After authors’ response, I still have concerns with the metrics presented and how impactfull the paper would be.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a method for providing bin-wise bounds for calibration errors under adversarial attacks. The method is based on local Lipschitz bounds and can be applied to any differentiable model. The result is an upper bound of the calibration error per confidence bin, under perturbations. To my knowledge, this is the first work on calibration certification. Alongside the proposed method, the authors propose a simple baseline and evaluate their method on MedMNIST, where the proposed method consistently outperforms the baseline.
reviews.text_strengths:
This seems to be the first work on calibration certification. The authors compellingly motivated the problem and I agree this is a problem well worth solving.
The paper (especially the introduction and methods section) are very well written, easy to follow, concise and clear – well done.
The proposed method seems theoretically sound and elegant.
The proposed method is posthoc and does not rely on any (computantionally heavy) adversarially robust training.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
I suspect that the evaluation is slightly biased. The proposed method is evaluated only on samples in robust bins (i.e. narrower bins), so it seems natural that the coverage is better. Would it make sense to evaluate the coverage on the same data (robust bins only) for fair comparison?
Along similar lines: Since the proposed method uses robust bins, what happens to the samples that are not in any robust bins because they are close to the bin boundaries? Are there any calibration bounds for them, and if not, could the authors justify this?
I believe an analysis of lambda, the Lipschitz constant R and the proportion of certified samples would be relevant and interesting, but this is currently missing from the manuscript.
Detailed comments:
In Sec. 4.2, the authors day “CalCErt certifies substantially more samples”. What is meant by this? Is this shown in the results anywhere?
“Bin-wise Certification of Confidence Calibration certification methods [11, 7, 11, 17, 36]”: Ref 11 is listed twice

N/A

Certification of calibration is a completely novel but clinically meaningful contribution
The proposed method is solid and seems to work well

reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I keep my accept recommendation as I still think it’s an innovative and timely idea, also after reading the other reviewer comments.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes CalCErt, a post-hoc framework that bounds worst-case calibration error under L2 perturbations using empirical calibration, concentration bounds, and local Lipschitz estimates.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper studies adversarial robustness from an underexplored problem which is certifying calibration robustness, not only prediction robustness.
2.The training-free nature of the method makes it post-hoc, furthermore it is architecture independent so it can be readily deployed on pretrained models
3.The number and extent of explorations are good in terms of architectures and datasets
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The guarantee relies on an approximate local Lipschitz estimate which is based on the gradient norm of the confidence function - the the certificate is not fully exact.
2.If I understand correctly, the method is calibration only, and does consider the robust accuracy, so a model may still be confidently wrong under perturbation.
3.The adversarial evaluation is somewhat limited, relying mainly on FGSM, BIM, PGD, and RFGSM, which weakens the empirical stress test - AutoAttach or the optimization based CW-L2 would be good additions
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
