meta_reviews.text:
The paper proposes a novel post-hoc method to estimate an upper bound on calibration error under adversarial perturbations. The paper is a useful contribution to responsible AI direction; however, there are some concerns raised by the reviewers that must be addressed, e.g., evaluation of the trade-off between tightness and coverage, a fairer comparison, and experiments with advanced adversarial attacks.

This paper is an early attempt in the direction of certification of calibration by proposing bin-wise bounds for calibration errors under adversarial attacks. The paper received mixed reviews. The reviewers’ concerns are genuine, especially the trade-off between coverage and tightness, and limited immediate impact. However, I feel that the paper should be of interest to the community working towards responsible AI and motivate future research in this direction.

While the authors have provided a reasonable rebuttal, two of the reviewers remain unconvinced about the key metrics and tradeoffs involved. Given the theoretical nature of the contributions, the paper would benefit from a longer version with stronger proofs and justifications. Hence, the paper cannot be recommended for acceptance despite its technical contributions,

The paper presents an interesting and underexplored study on adversarial robustness, focusing on certifying calibration robustness rather than only prediction robustness. This is a valuable direction, especially for medical imaging, where reliable confidence estimates are critical. The post-hoc nature of the proposed method further increases its practical relevance, as it can potentially improve robustness without requiring major changes to existing models. The empirical results appear strong enough to justify the benefits of the approach, and the concerns raised during review were addressed in an acceptable manner. Overall, the paper offers a unique and meaningful contribution, and I recommended for acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
R1.Coverage/tightness tradeoff. We agree that both metrics should be read jointly. We could look at a tradeoff in the form of C=coverage-Ⲗ*tightness. We can report C in Tab. 1 for Ⲗ=1, and also add a Pareto plot for varying values of Ⲗ. The average value of C (Ⲗ=1) for 0.11 for L2-CAL, 0.24 for ASC, and 0.53 for CalCErt.
R1.Overshoot is misleading. This is a fair point, a method which predicts very high bounds, will have a high tightness, but no overshoot. However, we still believe that the fact in the cases where the bounds are violated, it is not violated as much as other methods is interesting. We argue that it is preferable to have a method which predicts looser bounds, but which rarely fails, and fails at a small margin, rather than a method which tries to get tight bounds, but get large errors when it fails.
R1.Aleatoric/epistemic link and notation. We will clarify in the refined version that the statistical deviation corresponds to epistemic uncertainty because it corresponds to a finite-sample estimation of \hat{A_k}, which would vanish with sufficiently large data. Similarly, the Lipschitz deviation reflects epistemic uncertainty, as it is model-induced. The empirical miscalibration corresponds to the residual epistemic uncertainty and the aleatoric uncertainty.
R2.Robust bins only. We agree that this is a fair point raised by the reviewer. However, we would like to specify that all methods are evaluated on the same dataset, and that the sub-bins do not impact the samples on which CalCErt is applied. We will make sure to modify the manuscript so that it is clear to the reader.
R2.Ablation for values of R. We agree with R2 that this analysis would be interesting for the reader. We propose to include an ablation sweeping for multiple values of R, and to report the mean Lipschitz value L_k, width of the sub-bin γ_k, coverage, and tightness. Due to lack of space, we could remove other results such as the ResNet 18 table.
R4.Approximate Lipschitz estimate. This is correct, we use a gradient-based estimation, which yields a first-order certificate. This allows to make the computation tractable. We will make sure to emphasize this point in the refined manuscript.
R4.Calibration vs accuracy. The method is indeed focused on certifying calibration and not accuracy. The model may then be confident about a wrong prediction, but if it is calibrated, marginally over the dataset, it should be confident on a wrong prediction only on a fraction of the samples.
R4.Other attacks. Our objective with CalCErt is not to defend against any specific attack, but rather to provide a post-hoc, model agnostic approach to calibration certification. The bound in equation (4) holds for any value of δ<R, so it covers any l2-bounded attack. CalCErt requires no retraining, or attack-specific finetuning. We will clarify this framing further in the refined version of the manuscript, and emphasize that this work is a first step towards calibration certification.

title: CalcSeg: Confidence-aware 3D Latent Context Curriculum Learning For Myocardial Scar Segmentation From Single-Stack LGE-CMRs
abstract: Myocardial scar segmentation from single-stack late gadolinium–enhanced cardiac magnetic resonance (LGE-CMR) imaging has been a longstanding and clinically important challenge, particularly in the presence of low tissue contrast, diffuse, and small scar regions. These challenges are further intensified by the limited availability of 3D spatial context. This paper presents CalcSeg, a Confidence-aware latent context curriculum learning framework that leverages fused 3D feature representations from single-stack 2D LGE-CMR images for robust scar segmentation. Specifically, we introduce a dynamic semi-supervised curriculum learning strategy that progressively expands training from easier to more challenging scar cases using a learned confidence-aware scoring function. Such a function integrates errors in the predicted scar maps with quantified epistemic uncertainty and scar burden estimation to automatically assess sample difficulty without requiring manual labels. To compensate for the limited spatial context in single-stack acquisitions, we then develop a latent slice-wise self-attention to capture inter-slice dependencies and infer 3D spatial representations from sparse 2D inputs. We evaluate CalcSeg on multi-center clinical LGE-CMR datasets and benchmark against existing scar segmentation networks. Experimental results show that CalcSeg consistently outperforms all competing methods, particularly with substantial improvements on clinically challenging cases. Our code is released at https://github.com/vfb8zv/CalcSeg.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors present CaucSeg, a segmentation technique for scar in LGE CMR images. The approach includes an uncertainty-based curriculum learning (“UCL”) approach and a cross-slice attention mechanism. Results on a combination of private and public dataset suggest that the proposed technique outperforms other recent SOTA methods.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper is quite well written and overall easy to follow.
Whilst the parts of the pipeline are not new, the specific combination proposed is interesting, suitable to the task at hand and sound.
The results are believable and the improvement over SOTA seems substantial.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Limited validation. Despite having access to different datasets (some public, some private), the authors merged them when performing their validation. This reduces the chances of independent inter-paper comparisons, which are one of the limiting factors for research in LGE segmentation.
Questionable experimental setting. The authors state “We quantify the segmentation performance using Dice Similarity Coefficient computed over the myocardium for the complete dataset and 6 known difficult cases, and the percentage error in scar volume. ” This is very problematic to me: what was the training/validation/test split? Was there one? The paper doesn’t mention this very crucial piece of information.
Issues with uncertainty estimation. The paper claims that epistemic uncertainty “progressively decreases with the stages” of UCL, and uses this as evidence that the curriculum is working as intended. However, in Fig. 3 the y-axis is labelled “mean uncertainty”, and the mean across the whole test set (left panel) appears approximately stable across stages while only the std shrinks. This would indicate that UCL homogenises uncertainty across samples, not that it reduces it. The authors should (i) discuss this finding thoroughly and (ii) clarify exactly how the plotted “mean uncertainty” and its spread computed (per-sample MC-Dropout std aggregated how, over what?).
Misuse of the term “unsupervised”. The paper repeatedly describes the proposed curriculum as “unsupervised”, but the difficulty score relies on the per-sample errors against the ground-truth segmentation. This requires labels and is therefore not unsupervised in the sense the term is normally used in the curriculum learning literature, where “unsupervised CL” refers to difficulty estimation without access to labels.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Page 6: “6 known difficult cases”. Known how? Aren’t 6 too few to draw meaningful conclusions and numerical estimates?

The results seem somewhat solid, despite a rather limited (and possibly very questionable) validation. More information from the authors is needed during rebuttal to clarify possible flaws with their work.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors’ provided some needed clarifications over the experimental set-up and data split that are most reassuring. While the work is still limited on the evaluation side, it now seems solid enough for publication at MICCAI.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper addresses the problem of myocardial scar segmentation with CaucSeg, introducing an unsupervised curriculum learning strategy that leverages predictive uncertainty to estimate sample difficulty. Additionally, it proposes a 3D latent context modeling approach to improve consistency across 2D slices within a stack.
reviews.text_strengths:
Myocardial scar segmentation is a challenging and important problem for the medical imaging community.
The presented method shows improved performance against the baselines, both quantitatively and qualitatively. The idea of using curriculum learning for the myocardial scar segmentation is promising.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
I find the paper to be written in a very confusing way. Particularly the section on “3D Latent Context Modeling” is very hard to understand, while being one of the contributions of the paper. It is unclear whether the latent representation z represents 2D or 3D features, it’s also not represented anywhere in Fig. 1 to aid understanding. Some variables are never defined, such as C in the softmax formula, B, and F. The “disentangled slice-wise self-attention” is never clearly described. The description of this module is dense and lacks clarity regarding the data flow, with the naming not exactly matching between text and figure. This makes the architectural novelty difficult to verify or reproduce. The “custom residual decoder” used is also never described. The loss function and curriculum scoring are introduced abruptly and are not explained with sufficient clarity. Several terms are defined mathematically, but the paper does not provide enough intuition for why these components are combined, how the weights were chosen, or how the resulting optimization behaves during training.
The experimental results section provides very little analysis of the results. The ablation study is limited. It shows that each component helps, yet it does not disentangle whether the curriculum or the attention module is responsible for most of the gain on the hard cases, missing a combination where only UCL is used. Further, there is no discussion on why CaucSeg outperforms the baselines. The paper reports improvements over ScarNet, the myocardial scar segmentation SOTA method, but the experimental section does not sufficiently explain
why
the proposed method is better. In particular, it is unclear whether the gains come from the confidence-aware curriculum, the 3D latent context module, or simpler training effects.
The empirical evaluation is incomplete with respect to recent literature. In particular, the paper does not compare against or cite a recent relevant method, ScarElastic [1], which appears closely related and has reported strong performance on myocardial scar segmentation. Additionally, the manuscript includes a baseline denoted as “ScarNet (Sup. CL),” but does not provide a citation or sufficient detail to clearly identify this method. Clarifying the identity of this baseline and including relevant recent methods such as [1] would strengthen the empirical evaluation.
In Fig. 1 the images only show the myocardium with all the other tissues being masked. Is this a preprocessing step in the pipeline? No description of such masking is present in the dataset dataset section, which makes it confusing as to what is the actual input to the model.
[1] Zou, R., Li, Y., Zhou, N., Guan, X., Li, G., Xie, D., … & Luo, C. (2025). ScarElastic: continuous elasticity field modeling for myocardial scar delineation in LGE-CMR.
npj Digital Medicine
.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

While the method is promising and tackles an important problem, the presentation requires revisions before it becomes a meaningful contribution to the MICCAI community. In the current state, the writing of the methodology section precludes reproducibility and makes it difficult for the reader to verify the claimed technical novelty. These issues are not minor wording problems and are unlikely to be resolved in a short rebuttal. For these reasons, I recommend rejection.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: While the paper addresses the important problem of myocardial scar segmentation, there are major issues that lead me to recommend a rejection. Namely, it is unclear what the exact input to the method is and how it is obtained. In the dataset section, the authors state, “All slices were cropped and masked to the left ventricle and resized to 224^2.” However, what is presented in Fig. 1 does not reflect a left ventricle mask; only the myocardium is shown on the images, while the left ventricular blood pool cavity has been completely zeroed out. How these highly precise myocardial masks are obtained remains unexplained, and the authors failed to clarify this in their rebuttal beyond making circular references back to the dataset section. It remains unknown whether clinicians must first manually delineate the myocardial area at test time, or if the masks are generated by an external automated method. If the inputs rely on a secondary segmentation method, the authors fail to address how often epicardial and endocardial scars are inadvertently excluded from the input images due to prior segmentation errors. Because these critical preprocessing details are absent from the manuscript, the pipeline is non-reproducible. Furthermore, such a restrictive masking step is not standard practice in prior works, where the concurrent segmentation of healthy myocardium, blood pool, and scar is typically part of the multi-class objective. Ultimately, it is unclear how isolating the input domain in this manner affects the performance of the baseline methods, which significantly downgrades the reliability of the presented comparative results.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces CaucSeg, a framework designed for myocardial scar segmentation from single-stack LGE-CMR images, which are notoriously difficult due to sparse slice sampling and low tissue contrast. The main contributions are twofold: (1) A 3D latent context module that utilizes slice-wise self-attention and sinusoidal positional embeddings to model longitudinal anatomical consistency across 2D slices. (2) An unsupervised, confidence-aware curriculum learning strategy that dynamically adjusts the training complexity. Unlike traditional curriculum learning that relies on predefined difficulty levels, CaucSeg uses a model-adaptive difficulty score combining predictive inaccuracy (Dice and scar burden) with epistemic uncertainty (via Monte Carlo Dropout). The method is validated on a large-scale, multi-center dataset of 976 patients, significantly outperforming existing CNN and Transformer-based baselines.
reviews.text_strengths: he slice-wise self-attention module is an intelligent solution to the “anisotropy problem” in CMR. By performing latent fusion on 2D features rather than using full 3D convolutions, the authors effectively capture out-of-plane context without the computational overhead or sensitivity to breath-hold displacements common in 3D-UNet architectures. The shift from supervised to model-adaptive curriculum learning is a timely contribution. The integration of epistemic uncertainty into the difficulty score allows the model to prioritize samples where the “ground truth” might be ambiguous (e.g., the gray zone of fibrosis), which is a common clinical reality in LGE-CMR.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Terminology Ambiguity: The authors refer to the curriculum as “unsupervised.” While the difficulty scoring is automated, the segmentation task is supervised. This distinction should be clearer to avoid confusion with self-supervised or unsupervised segmentation methods.
Parameter Sensitivity: The difficulty score D_i depends on three weighting parameters \gamma_j. The manuscript lacks a sensitivity analysis or a clear heuristic for selecting these weights. Given that curriculum learning can be sensitive to the order of sample introduction, this is a significant omission.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The manuscript provides a robust and technically sound solution to myocardial scar segmentation, one of the most challenging tasks in cardiac AI. The dual innovation of 3D latent context for sparse stacks and the uncertainty-guided curriculum is highly relevant to the MICCAI community. The scale of the validation (976 patients) is exceptional for a conference submission and provides high confidence in the results. While there are minor concerns regarding terminology and parameter sensitivity, the overall performance gains, particularly on clinically challenging, low-contrast cases, demonstrate a clear advancement over established SOTA models like ScarNet and UNETR.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper proposes a myocardial scar segmentation framework that combines confidence‑aware curriculum learning with slice‑wise latent self‑attention to better handle sparse stacks, low contrast, and highly heterogeneous scar patterns.
While all reviewers recognise the importance of the results and the interesting combination of uncertainty‑guided training progression and cross‑slice context modelling, in a rebuttal, it would be important for the authors to (i) clearly specify the data splits and evaluation protocol, (ii) correct or clarify the terminology around “unsupervised” curriculum learning, (iii) provide a more careful interpretation of the uncertainty experiments, and (iv) substantially improve the clarity of the method description, especially for the slice‑wise attention and decoder design. Overall, the paper tackles an important problem with promising ideas and encouraging results, but clearer presentation and experimental clarification are needed to fully establish its contribution.

The paper addresses an important clinical problem with an interesting combination of uncertainty-guided curriculum learning and slice-wise latent self-attention. The rebuttal successfully clarifies several presentation issues and also explains the uncertainty analysis more carefully, and therefore, it can be accepted. 
R2 maintains it is unclear whether manual myocardial delineation is required at test time and whether this masking disadvantages multi-class baselines. I would really like this answered.

This paper proposes CaucSeg, a new framework for myocardial scar segmentation from single-stack late gadolinium-enhanced cardiac magnetic resonance (LGE-CMR) images. The core innovation lies in introducing a “confidence-aware unsupervised curriculum learning” strategy combined with a slice-wise self-attention-based 3D latent context modeling module. The main concerns include clarification for experiment settings , results analysis, interpretation of uncertainty results, and performance comparison. The author’s response address most of them. The input of the method needs further clarification. Figure 1 shows the input of the SAX images with only the myocardium region kept, which is not consistent with the descriptions in the text.

The paper addresses an important clinical problem and reports promising results, and the rebuttal clarified several issues including the data split, uncertainty analysis, and terminology around the curriculum. However, a central concern remains unresolved: the manuscript does not clearly explain how the LV/myocardial mask used as preprocessing is obtained at inference time, nor how this affects reproducibility and fairness of the baseline comparisons. This ambiguity affects the exact task being solved and the clinical interpretation of the results.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for all valuable feedback and constructive suggestions. Our responses to the major questions are summarized below.
[M,R1,R3] Clarification on “Unsupervised” Curriculum Learning (UCL)
Our intent was to distinguish our approach from manually annotated difficulty ratings, i.e., scores are computed automatically using Dice, uncertainty and scar burden error rather than clinician-assigned labels. Although uncertainty provides an unsupervised signal, we agree that it may be confused with typical unsupervised training methods that do not use ground-truth label supervision. We will update the terminology with semi/weakly-supervised.
[M,R1] Data Splits & Evaluation Protocol
All metrics are computed on the independent test set, including 6 clinically challenging cases from a site, explicitly flagged by experts. The train-val-test split was 7:1:2.
The uncertainty is computed as the mean standard deviation across 100 MC-Dropout samples per subject, yielding one scalar per subject. Fig.3 shows mean and standard deviation of these uncertainty values. The overall mean (left, Fig.3) appears relatively stable since high-confidence cases dominate the test set (ratio 22:6). In contrast, when stratified by difficulty (right, Fig.3), uncertainty decreases substantially across stages for the clinically challenging subgroup. We will clarify this in the revised paper.
[M,R2] Please note that z is a 2D per-slice latent representation produced independently for each slice, with ‘F’ total slices, yielding a 3D tensor prior to self-attention (SA). The disentangled slice-wise SA is a standard transformer operation [7,22] applied across slices “performing explicit 2D-to-3D latent feature fusion on the encoded latent representation z.” The term “disentangled” describes SA alternating between spatial and slice-wise attention, following the space-time attention in Arnab et al., 2021.
All notations (B=batch size, F=total slices, C=projection dimension), and the “custom residual decoder” referring to an employed ResNet-based decoder instead of the standard MedSAM decoder will be clarified.
[R1] We appreciate the suggestion to keep validation separated between public and in-house datasets wherever dataset sizes allow. However, current public LGE datasets are relatively small, particularly for difficult cases, motivating us to incorporate private institutes’ data. Fully separated validation remains valuable for future work as larger public datasets become available.
[R2] The improved performance of our method over the baselines stems from combining the two proposed modules: slice-wise SA & UCL. Tab.1 includes results from ScarNet with CL, which uses a 2D transformer backbone and is analogous to the UCL-only ablation. Tab.2 shows that our SA improves overall segmentation performance, UCL particularly improves difficult cases, and their combination yields the best overall performance. These findings suggest SOTA methods underperform since they lack richer 3D context, operating on isolated 2D slices and random batch selection.
Thanks for referring to ScarElastic. Our framework could be easily incorporated on top of ScarElastic by using it as an alternative backbone. We will include this reference in our revised manuscript, and will clarify that “ScarNet (Sup.CL)” denotes ScarNet[30] trained with CL.
Masking is a preprocessing step applied prior to training and inference, as stated in the dataset section. The loss function and curriculum scoring are independent from the architectural design, as described in the method section. The focal loss parameters followed [Lin et al., 2018] with related values provided in the parameter setting section.
[R3] Based on our empirical findings, the parameters are stable as they are automatically derived from each metric’s scale via the inverse of its order of magnitude. This ensures all metrics are in the same numerical range and no single metric dominates. We will clarify this in the revised paper.

title: CALHippo: Cell Segmentation for Neuronal Density Inference in the Human Hippocampus
abstract: Reliable estimates of cellular composition and anatomical distribution in the human brain are essential for biologically plausible circuit models. In the hippocampus, existing reconstructions rely on low-resolution (LR) data without explicit cell-type-resolved annotations, limiting quantitative maps of excitatory neurons, inhibitory interneurons, and glial cells. Using newly released 1 um/px BigBrain sections of the right hippocampus, we present CALHippo, Cellular Annotation Library for the Hippocampus, a multiscale resource for cell-type-resolved reconstruction of the human CA complex. CALHippo includes the first expert-validated, cell-level annotated dataset spanning all Cornu Ammonis (CA1-CA4) subfields with explicit three-class labels, together with a lower-resolution mesoscale cellular point-cloud map. High-resolution (HR) cell instances are obtained through a human-in-the-loop pipeline combining foundation-model-based segmentation, iterative expert correction, and model ensembling, and are classified as excitatory neurons, inhibitory interneurons, or glial cells. To extend sparse HR annotations to the full volume, we project them into the 20 um/px LR BigBrain space and use the resulting class-specific supervision maps to train a UNet-based density estimation model. The predicted density maps enable slice-by-slice inference across the full CA complex and are sampled to generate a class-resolved mesoscale cellular point cloud. Code (https://github.com/AImageLab-zip/CALHippo-Framework) and dataset (https://ditto.ing.unimore.it/calhippo) are publicly released to support reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper presents a multiscale pipeline for reconstructing cell-type-resolved hippocampal organization from histological BigBrain data. Its main contributions are as follows. 
(i) an expert-validated three-class cell annotation dataset for human hippocampal CA1-CA4 at 1 µm resolution. 
(ii) a human-in-the-loop annotation/segmentation pipeline built on existing cell segmentation models for this challenging domain. 
(iii) a compact U-Net-based density estimation model in the 20 µm BigBrain space. 
(iv) a 3D point-cloud reconstruction of excitatory, inhibitory, and glial cell distributions across the CA complex.
reviews.text_strengths: A major strength of the paper is the creation of an expert-validated three-class hippocampal cell dataset at 1 µm resolution, which is both difficult and valuable. Another strength is the end-to-end multiscale pipeline that uses this dataset to produce a cell-type-resolved 3D point-cloud reconstruction across the CA regions. Overall, the paper provides a potentially useful resource for the community.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Contribution (ii) is less convincing as a methodological novelty. From the current presentation, it appears closer to a careful application of existing HITL segmentation workflows based on models such as Cellpose, rather than a genuinely new hippocampus-specific technical framework. If there are domain-specific annotation difficulties and corresponding technical solutions, these should be made much more explicit.
Although the Otsu-based baseline is recent in terms of publication date, it still seems to represent a relatively simple intensity-thresholding strategy. The paper would benefit from clarifying whether this baseline is included because it reflects the current standard practice in BigBrain hippocampal reconstruction, or merely as a lightweight reference method.
Table 4 is interesting as a potential biological output of the pipeline, but in its current form, it feels somewhat disconnected from the main validation. I fully appreciate that biological validation at this scale is extremely challenging; however, without stronger grounding or discussion, the CA-wise cell counts read more like an auxiliary result than a firmly supported conclusion.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
I provide the following minor comments in the hope of improving this paper. 
・I wasn’t sure whether the “ppm” (e. g. , @1 ppm) in Fig. 1 refers to “parts per million”, μm, or something else. Maybe μm. 
・Contribution (iv) is better understood as a sampled 3D cellular distribution derived from predicted density maps, rather than a direct geometric reconstruction. 
・Since this is presented as an instance segmentation pipeline, the evaluation would benefit from clearer instance-level overlap analysis, e. g. , IoU-threshold-based AP/PQ or class-wise overlap statistics, beyond centroid-based matching alone. 
・Fig. 1 would be more informative if it included representative zoomed-in examples of inhibitory and glial cells, not only the dominant excitatory population. Such examples would help readers better understand why these classes are more difficult for Cellpose-SAM and why human-in-the-loop correction and model merging are needed.

I view this paper positively in terms of its potential value to the community, especially as a resource contribution. However, I would like to point out several aspects that currently seem insufficient for a MICCAI paper.
First, the originality of the proposed pipeline is not yet sufficiently clear. At present, the paper mainly reads as a substantial expert-driven annotation effort on a difficult dataset. I acknowledge that this effort is valuable in itself, but I do not clearly see methodological novelty in the pipeline shown in Fig. 1.If there are dataset-specific technical innovations, design choices, or annotation strategies that are particular to hippocampal histology, these should be described much more explicitly.
Second, the comparison in Table 3 feels relatively weak, making the paper’s main contribution appear to be the effort of constructing supervised training data rather than the modeling approach itself. This is not necessarily a problem if the paper is framed primarily as a dataset/application contribution, but the current presentation should better align with that emphasis.
Third, I found Table 4 difficult to interpret. It is not yet clear how the reported CA-wise cell counts should be understood biologically. I appreciate that biological validation at this scale is very challenging. Still, the paper would benefit from stronger contextualization of these numbers, for example, through discussion of consistency with known hippocampal trends, limitations of the estimate, or, if feasible, comparison with external biological reference data. In other histology settings, one possible strategy is to compare adjacent sections stained with alternative protocols for specific cell populations, though I understand this may not be practical for the present dataset.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal substantially addresses my main concerns. In particular, the authors clarified the primary contribution as a dataset/resource and mesoscale atlas rather than a purely methodological advance, provided additional annotation-quality evidence, including inter-/intra-expert AER and final AER within expert variability, and added useful dataset construction/statistical details. The biological interpretation of Table 4 is also better grounded by comparing neuron-like counts with prior estimates. Some details still need to be clearly incorporated in the final manuscript, especially class-wise annotation reliability and consistency of the reported matched HR/LR data, but I think the concerns are fixable and mostly addressed by the rebuttal.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper’s main contribution is a practical pipeline for deriving 3D, cell-type-specific density maps of the human hippocampus from BigBrain histology.
The approach combines human-in-the-loop cell segmentation on 1 µm sections, cell-type classification based on foundation-model embeddings and morphological descriptors, and supervised transfer to 20 µm data via a U-Net for dense prediction.
This design is meant to make cell-level information available at the scale of the full hippocampus, thereby supporting large-scale anatomical reconstruction and enabling comparison with established neuroanatomical cell-count estimates.
reviews.text_strengths:
The main strengths of the paper are the novelty of the resulting resource, the relevance of the problem, and the care taken in the methodological design.
Most notably, the work appears to provide a novel 3D cell-density map of the human hippocampus with cell-type-specific information and coverage across CA1–CA4 of the right hemisphere, extending beyond what has previously been available in the literature.
The technical pipeline is carefully constructed, especially the segmentation stage, which combines expert labels, comparison of multiple models, an ensemble strategy, and analysis of annotator variability.
The evaluation is also reasonably thorough, including sensible data splits, cross-validation, ablations for newly introduced loss terms, and comparison of the resulting maps against prior neuroanatomical estimates.
In addition, the explicit classification of excitatory, inhibitory, and glial cells increases the biological relevance of the final atlas.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
A major concern is that several important preprocessing and dataset-construction steps are not described clearly enough to make the work fully reproducible.
For example, the manuscript states that registration was used to align the 1 µm and 20 µm data, but my understanding is that the BigBrain data already include 1 µm images aligned to the 20 µm reconstruction.
It is therefore unclear why an additional registration step was necessary, which data exactly were used, and whether the authors relied on existing aligned data or performed their own alignment.
This should be clarified.
Related to this, the creation of the training datasets is insufficiently documented.
Section 2.1 does not clearly state how many 1 µm sections were used, how the relevant regions of interest were selected, how patches were extracted, how many patches were generated, or how training, validation, and test splits were defined.
While patching details are mentioned later in the density-estimation section, it is not clear whether the same settings also apply to the 1 µm segmentation and classification stages.
Likewise, the training parameters for the instance-segmentation models are not provided.
If default settings from prior work were used, this should be stated explicitly, and the dataset statistics should still be reported in full.
Another major weakness is that several parts of the method are introduced only at a high level and remain too vague in their actual implementation.
The projection of cell densities from 1 µm to 20 µm space is one example: the role of variables such as d and beta is not sufficiently explained, making it difficult to follow how the target density maps are generated.
Similarly, a custom Adaptive Thresholding Method (ATM) is introduced but neither properly described nor referenced.
If ATM is a novel component, it requires a clear methodological explanation.
If it is adapted from prior work, the relevant citation should be provided.
The manuscript is also unclear about the anatomical definition of the training and prediction regions.
It is not sufficiently explained how the CA1–CA4 regions of interest were identified, which anatomical reference or annotation source was used, and how whole-slide images were cropped to the corresponding regions for training and inference.
Because the final claims concern subfield-specific hippocampal density mapping, the precise derivation of these ROIs is an important part of the method and should be documented more carefully.
The cell-type-classification component is interesting, but several methodological choices are not justified well enough.
The authors reduce the embedding dimensionality using PCA, but they do not report the explained variance or justify why n = 20 components were selected.
It would also be important to understand the relative contribution of the handcrafted morphological features versus the foundation-model embeddings.
In addition, the manuscript does not state whether feature normalization was performed before concatenation, which can materially affect downstream classification performance.
The density-estimation stage is also under-specified.
The authors state that nnU-Net is used, but configuration details are missing.
Given that nnU-Net is highly configuration-dependent, key settings should be reported so that the model setup can be interpreted and, ideally, reproduced.
More generally, several notation issues further reduce clarity.
For example, alpha is introduced in the text as the weighting factor for the pixel-wise loss term, but it does not appear in the corresponding equation.
The notation should be made consistent throughout.
A further weakness is the limited presentation of qualitative results.
The paper contains only a single overview figure, which is useful conceptually but does not allow the reader to assess the quality of the segmentation results, cell-type classification, or the resulting density maps in sufficient detail.
Representative close-up examples would be important here, especially given the complexity of the pipeline.
In addition, the figure lacks scale bars, which makes it difficult to interpret the spatial extent of the shown fields of view.
I also have concerns about the stability of the reported cell counts.
According to the manuscript, centroids are obtained using a sampling-based procedure, specifically multinomial sampling with N trials, but N is not specified.
Since final cell counts are derived from sampling, the paper should report variability across repeated sampling runs, for example in the form of standard deviations or confidence intervals, to demonstrate the robustness of the estimates.
I appreciate that the authors made their code available in a well organized structure.
Nevertheless, I think the above details regarding the methodology and experimental design should also be addressed in the manuscript, as they fundamentally contribute the the understanding of the results.
Finally, the discussion section remains relatively limited and reads largely as a summary of the paper rather than a broader reflection on the implications and limitations of the approach.
For example, it would be valuable to discuss to what extent the proposed pipeline could generalize beyond the hippocampus to other brain regions or even to whole-brain mapping.
Related to this, the paper would benefit from a clearer discussion of the annotation effort required for the human-in-the-loop stages, since this is directly relevant for assessing scalability.

The main reasons are that the paper addresses a relevant problem, presents a novel result, and appears methodologically sound overall.
In particular, the 3D cell-type-specific density mapping of the hippocampus seems to be a meaningful contribution that goes beyond prior literature.
My score is moderated by the fact that several technical details are currently insufficiently explained, which makes parts of the pipeline hard to assess and limits reproducibility.
This includes dataset curation, ROI definition, some methodological components, and the sampling-based cell counting procedure.

To my knowledge, this is one of the first works to provide a cell-level annotated dataset covering the full CA1–CA4 regions, which could be a valuable resource for the community
The paper proposes a density-estimation model for three cell types, including glial cells. This could be useful for more comprehensive cellular analysis.

reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Annotation reliability. 
How many expert annotators were involved? The inter-annotator agreement is reported using AER = (FP+FN)/(TP+FN), with values >0.35 between annotator A and B. I understand this task can be difficult even for experts, but this still seems like a fairly high disagreement.
2.Glial annotation and density estimation.
The global SQ is around 0.55, and glia recall is <0.8.This makes me wonder how reliable the glial annotations and density estimates are. Could you comment on how these performance levels affect the glia results, and whether any validation or uncertainty analysis was done?
3.CA4 cell count.
In Table 4, CA4 (hilus) seems to have a much higher total cell count than CA2 and CA3, which may be inconsistent with previous studies. For example, West and Gundersen (1990) [1] report mean neuron counts of approximately 16×10⁶ in CA1, 2.7×10⁶ in CA3–CA2, and 2.0×10⁶ in the hilus per hippocampus. I understand those are neuron counts, not total cells, but could you explain this difference?
4.Evaluation metric.
Can you explain why you chose NAE for density estimation? Metrics like MSE or RMSE are more commonly used, so it would be helpful to know if your results are consistent under those as well.
5.Table 3 clarity.
Table 3 is a bit confusing. “Ours CA1” and “Ours All CA” seem to be evaluated on different datasets, so comparing them directly (with bold/underline) may not be appropriate. It might be clearer to separate them.
[1] West MJ, Gundersen HJ. Unbiased stereological estimation of the number of neurons in the human hippocampus. J Comp Neurol. 1990 Jun 1;296(1):1-22.doi: 10.1002/cne.902960102.PMID: 2358525.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
My main concern is the reliability of the dataset annotations. Given the relatively high inter-annotator disagreement (AER > 0.35), I am unsure how reliable the labels are for training and evaluation. Could the authors provide additional analysis to better characterize annotation quality?

While the paper presents potentially valuable contributions, my main concern is the reliability of the dataset annotations. The relatively high inter-annotator disagreement raises questions about label quality, which directly affects both the segmentation results and the downstream biological conclusions.

reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
I thank the authors for their rebuttal. My major concern regarding annotation quality is partially addressed by their explanation of expert variability, the reported final AER of 0.25, and the statement that all annotations were expert-reviewed. I also appreciate the motivation for ATM.
However, my remaining concern is that the submitted results do not clearly isolate the specific contribution of ATM to the final annotation quality. The rebuttal states that adding ATM improves glial recall measurably, but Table 1 appears to show ATM alone and the final merged result, rather than a direct comparison of the merged pipeline with versus without ATM. Therefore, from the existing results, I cannot fully assess whether the reported improvement is due to ATM, the merging procedure, the other segmentation models, or their combination.
Since the rest of the work appears solid, and this is my only remaining concern, I am inclined to support acceptance. I strongly recommend that the camera-ready version clarify the role and implementation details of ATM, the definition of “Merged-models,” and the interpretation of Table 1.Providing a quantitative ablation study on the contribution of ATM to the merged pipeline would further strengthen the paper.

meta_reviews.text:
The review is mixed: one week accept and two week reject. The concerns are serious but fixable.
Points to address:
Annotation quality
dataset/statistics details
dataset vs method contribution

The paper is strong as a dataset, atlas, and application/resource paper rather than as a novel segmentation-method paper. The methodological pipeline appears to rely largely on existing components, but the expert annotation effort, multiscale integration, and cell-type-specific hippocampal density mapping are potentially useful to the community.

The final revised recommendations are two Accepts (R1, R3) and one Reject (R2). However, it is worth noting that R2 changed their recommendation from Weak Accept to Reject after seeing the earlier recommendations from the other reviewers, both of whom later changed their recommendations to Accept. All reviewers believe that the paper can be further improved for the camera-ready version without significant additional work.

The paper presents a multiscale pipeline for reconstructing cell-type-resolved neuronal density maps in the human hippocampus from BigBrain histology. Its main contributions are an expert-validated three-class hippocampal cell annotation dataset, a human-in-the-loop annotation/segmentation pipeline, a compact density estimation model in the 20 µm BigBrain space, and a 3D point-cloud reconstruction of excitatory, inhibitory, and glial cell distributions across the CA complex.
The initial reviews were mixed and overall borderline, with scores of 3 / 4 / 3.Reviewers appreciated the potential value of the work as a resource contribution, especially the expert-validated hippocampal cell dataset and the possibility of producing cell-type-specific density maps at scale. However, the reviewers raised several concerns: limited methodological novelty, unclear positioning of the contribution as a dataset/resource versus a new method, insufficient details on dataset construction and registration, uncertainty about annotation quality and inter-annotator variability, limited instance-level segmentation analysis, and questions about the biological interpretation of the reported CA-wise cell counts.
The rebuttal addressed several of these concerns. The authors clarified that the main contribution should be understood primarily as an expert-validated dataset/resource and mesoscopic atlas, rather than as a purely methodological advance. They provided additional information on annotation quality, including inter- and intra-expert AER, the final AER being within expert variability, and the fact that annotations were expert-reviewed. They also clarified the motivation for the adaptive thresholding module, the HR-to-LR transfer strategy, the construction of matched HR/LR data, and the biological interpretation of the CA-wise counts by comparing neuron-like counts with prior estimates.
Some concerns remain. In particular, the final manuscript should more clearly describe the implementation and contribution of the ATM component, class-wise annotation reliability, the role of merged models, registration details, and the consistency of the matched HR/LR data. The ablation of ATM versus the full merged pipeline remains incomplete, and the biological interpretation should still be carefully framed as an atlas/resource contribution rather than a fully validated biological conclusion.
After rebuttal, the reviewer opinions are A / R / A. Reviewers 1 and 3 moved from weak reject to accept, mainly because the rebuttal clarified the contribution, provided annotation-quality evidence, and better grounded the biological interpretation. Reviewer 2 moved to reject, emphasizing that some methodological details and design choices remain insufficiently justified. I place greater weight on the two positive post-rebuttal assessments and on the value of the dataset/resource contribution, while acknowledging that the methodology itself is not the primary strength.
I recommend Accept. The paper is not a strong methodological contribution, but it provides a useful and difficult-to-obtain resource for the community, and the rebuttal sufficiently mitigated the most serious concerns regarding annotation quality and contribution framing. The remaining issues should be addressed in the camera-ready version, especially the clarification of ATM, merged-model details, annotation reliability, and the interpretation of the density maps.

author_feedback_text:
The reviewers recognized our work as a valuable resource for the community (R1,R3), highlighting the expert-validated cell-level hippocampal dataset spanning CA1-4 (All), appreciating its potential for comprehensive cellular analysis (R2,R3), as well as the careful multiscale pipeline, sound evaluation, released code, and biologically relevant atlas (R1,R2).
Contribution and scope [R1,R2]
This paper’s primary contribution is the first expert-validated three-class cellular dataset for human CA1-4 in Merker-stained BigBrain tissue, together with a class-resolved mesoscale atlas of the CA complex. Methodologically, the key contribution is the HR-to-LR transfer strategy: a few annotated HR images are used to supervise cell prediction across complete LR image sets. Together with HR segmentation ensemble and instance classification, this pipeline is reusable for cell-resolved mapping in other brain regions.
Annotation quality and ATM [All].
Two experts independently annotated two WSIs, yielding an inter-AER of 0.35; re-annotation by the same experts gave an intra-AER of ~0.3, supporting intrinsic tissue variability. Both values and the low prediction SQ are driven primarily by glial cells, which exhibit poorly defined boundaries in Merker silver-stained tissue and are frequently misidentified as tissue artifacts. This ambiguity motivated ATM, which combines adaptive thresholding with filters grounded in glial cytoarchitectonic properties (color, eccentricity, and area) to better capture glial instances. Adding ATM to the ensemble improves glial recall measurably, with the final pipeline achieving AER 0.25, within the range of expert variability. All annotations were expert-reviewed.
Biological interpretation [R1,R3]
The concern about CA4 comes from comparing our total-cell estimates with neuron-only stereology. Restricting Table 4 to neuron-like classes (excitatory+inhibitory), our counts closely match prior estimates cited by R3 [1
]: CA1 15.2M vs 16M, CA2+CA3 2.8M vs 2.7M, and CA4 2.3M vs 2.0M, supporting biological plausibility. We also observed a ~1:1 glia/neuron-like ratio, consistent with [2
] findings. We will revise Table 4, cite these works, and clarify that Gandolfi et al. [2] is included as the only available domain baseline on BigBrain hippocampus data.
Dataset construction and registration [R1,R2]
CA1-4 ROIs were taken from the BigBrain hippocampal subfield reference [3*]. To build the LR training data, we first mapped HR coordinates with the provided affine transforms to crop the corresponding LR regions, then applied deformable alignment to correct residual HR-LR tissue mismatch to prevent misaligned density targets. From the available 24 matched HR/LR pairs, we extracted 505 patches and split them 80/20 by WSI ID to avoid leakage.
Method and minor fixes
[R1] Instance evaluation is not centroid-only: centroid matching defines TP/FP/FN, but Dice, HD95, and SQ, also reported class-wise, assess overlap and boundary quality; we will additionally report IoU-threshold-based PQ. [R2] PCA with n=20 was chosen empirically to reduce embeddings so they do not dominate morphology/context cues, and both feature groups are normalized. For density-map generation, each cell centroid is projected to LR, then replaced by a Gaussian kernel whose variance is scaled by other local cell distances, controlled by d and fixed beta as in [18]; this smooths sparse regions while preserving cell counts. For the sampled point cloud, N is the predicted region density count; repeated sampling changes only the coordinates, not the expected counts. [R3] NAE was chosen to compare relative count errors across imbalanced classes, while SSIM measures spatial agreement. 
We will clarify the contribution focus, add missing segmentation/nnU-Net settings, ATM details, and improve tables, figures, notation, and cell visualizations.

title: Calibrated Confidence Expression for Radiology Report Generation
abstract: Safe deployment of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) in radiology report generation requires not only accurate predictions but also clinically interpretable indicators of when outputs should be thoroughly reviewed, enabling selective radiologist verification and reducing the risk of hallucinated findings influencing clinical decisions. One intuitive approach to this is verbalized confidence, where the model explicitly states its certainty. However, current state-of-the-art language models are often overconfident, and research on calibration in multimodal settings such as radiology report generation is limited. To address this gap, we introduce ConRad (Confidence Calibration for Radiology Reports), a reinforcement learning framework for fine-tuning medical LVLMs to produce calibrated verbalized confidence estimates alongside radiology reports. We study two settings: a single report-level confidence score and a sentence-level variant assigning a confidence to each claim. Both are trained using the GRPO algorithm with reward functions based on the logarithmic scoring rule, which incentivizes truthful self-assessment by penalizing miscalibration and guarantees optimal calibration under reward maximization. Experimentally, ConRad substantially improves calibration and outperforms competing methods. In a clinical evaluation we show that ConRad’s report level scores are well aligned with clinicians’ judgment. By highlighting full reports or low-confidence statements for targeted review, ConRad can support safer clinical integration of AI-assistance for report generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/ChantalMP/Conrad.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes ConRad, a reinforcement-learning framework for calibrating verbalized confidence in radiology report generation. Instead of only generating a report, the model is trained to output either a report-level or sentence-level confidence score jointly with the report text. The key idea is to optimize confidence expression with GRPO using a logarithmic scoring-rule reward, so that the model is encouraged to align its stated confidence with an external report-quality signal. The work is clinically motivated because calibrated confidence could support selective human verification and targeted review of uncertain findings. Overall, the main contribution is to bring confidence calibration from general language modeling into multimodal radiology report generation in a practically interpretable form.
reviews.text_strengths: First, the paper addresses an important and timely problem, since safe deployment of radiology LVLMs requires not only good reports but also reliable uncertainty signals. Second, the proposed formulation is interesting because it moves beyond post-hoc uncertainty estimation and directly trains the model to produce interpretable verbalized confidence alongside the report. Third, the paper studies both report-level and sentence-level confidence, which is clinically meaningful because the latter can support targeted review of specific findings rather than only whole-report triage. Fourth, the experimental evaluation is fairly solid, including calibration metrics, OOD evaluation on IU-Xray, and a small clinician study showing better alignment with expert judgment. Finally, the paper presents consistent empirical gains over several baseline confidence estimation methods while largely preserving report-generation quality.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The main weakness is that the novelty is somewhat incremental rather than fully groundbreaking, because the paper extends existing lines of work on confidence calibration and uncertainty-aware radiology report generation rather than introducing a completely new paradigm. In addition, the clinical evaluation is still relatively limited, as it only involves 50 reports and 3 raters, which is useful but not yet strong enough to fully establish clinical utility. Some methodological choices also need clearer justification, such as the dependence on GREEN / Precision GREEN as the external correctness signal and whether calibration quality transfers robustly beyond that metric. Moreover, the paper focuses on calibration while intentionally not improving report quality itself, which is reasonable, but this also limits the broader practical impact of the method. Overall, these issues prevent me from rating the paper more strongly, but they do not outweigh the paper’s clear motivation, sound design, and promising empirical results.

reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes ConRad, a reinforcement learning framework designed to address the overconfidence and insufficient calibration of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) in radiology report generation. The main contribution is the introduction of a scoring-rule-based RL approach that fine-tunes medical LVLMs to jointly generate radiology reports and calibrated confidence estimates, supporting both report-level and sentence-level confidence expression. Additionally, the framework integrates the GRPO algorithm with logarithmic scoring rule rewards, and a continuous correctness signal provided by an automated report-quality metric, enabling calibration without manual confidence supervision. Extensive experiments on MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray datasets verify its effectiveness, showing that ConRad substantially improves calibration performance compared to competing methods.
reviews.text_strengths:
Firstly, this paper addresses the challenge of uncalibrated confidence in radiology report generation, where LVLMs often produce overconfident outputs with hallucinations, and proposes a novel RL-based framework that models confidence expression as a policy optimization problem. This approach effectively addresses the gap in multimodal calibration research.
Secondly, the framework supports both report-level and sentence-level confidence expression, enabling confidence-guided triage of complete radiology reports and targeted review of uncertain statements to facilitate selective radiologist verification in clinical workflows.
Thirdly, the experimental validation is comprehensive and rigorous, covering multiple datasets, various baseline comparisons, and a small-scale clinical evaluation with radiologists, fully demonstrating the method’s calibration effectiveness, generalization ability, and clinical alignment.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Firstly, the paper states that the continuous correctness score s is derived from the GREEN metric but provides no detailed explanation of how GREEN quantifies radiology report quality to generate a continuous value in the range of [0,1], nor does it verify whether the s obtained by this metric can accurately reflect the actual clinical quality of radiology reports.
Secondly, the reward scaling factor λ is set to 100 without a systematic parameter sensitivity analysis, and the paper provides no explanation for this specific choice or guidance on adapting λ across different LVLMs or radiology datasets.
Thirdly, the clinical evaluation is limited to 50 reports with three raters, and the sample size is too small to draw definitive conclusions about the alignment between ConRad’s confidence scores and clinical judgment.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper addresses the critical issue of overconfidence in Large Vision-Language Models by introducing a reinforcement learning framework for calibrated verbalized confidence. Using the Group Relative Policy Optimization algorithm, the model is trained to express its certainty, either at the report or sentence level, alongside the generated findings. The framework utilizes a logarithmic scoring rule as a reward function, which mathematically incentivizes the model to align its stated confidence with the actual clinical correctness of the report (as measured by the GREEN metric), ensuring that the expressed certainty is a reliable indicator for radiologist verification.
While the paper presents significant contributions, its recommendation for acceptance is contingent upon the authors clarifying the following points during the rebuttal phase:
1.Reviewers noted that the work extends existing uncertainty-aware paradigms rather than introducing a fundamentally new one. Specifically, since the method intentionally focuses on calibration without seeking to improve the underlying report quality (BLEU/CIDEr), its broader clinical impact is somewhat constrained compared to models that improve both accuracy and reliability.
2.The human evaluation is limited to only 50 reports and 3 raters. This sample size is statistically insufficient to definitively conclude that the model’s “verbalized confidence” aligns with expert clinical judgment or to establish widespread clinical utility.
3.The framework’s “correctness signal” relies entirely on the GREEN (or Precision GREEN) metric. Reviewers pointed out a lack of justification for why GREEN is an appropriate proxy for clinical truth in this RL loop, nor is there evidence that the calibration remains robust if evaluated against different factual correctness benchmarks (e.g., RadGraph or CheXbert).
4.A significant reward scaling factor (lambda = 100) is used without a sensitivity analysis or systematic justification. It remains unclear how this parameter should be adapted for different LVLMs or datasets, which raises concerns about the framework’s generalizability and the stability of the RL training.
5.Include a high-level summary of the GRPO algorithm and why it was chosen over other RL methods (like PPO) for this specific calibration task.

The authors have addressed the reviewers’ comments well. Two reviewers acknowledged the significance of the work. Therefore acceptance of the paper is concluded.

the reviewers agree the paper is clinically motivated, but share concerns that the authors need to better justify and validate the correctness signal used for calibration due to GREEN being an automated proxy. The authors addressed the issue well by human evaulation (3 radiologists, 50 repors), as well as showing calibration improvements transfer beyond GREEN to CheXbert and RadGraph metrics.

The paper is accepted, as the reviewers agree that it addresses an important safety problem in radiology report generation by improving uncertainty estimation and confidence calibration for VLMs. Although the novelty is somewhat incremental and the clinical validation remains limited, the method shows consistent gains in clinically interpretable calibration. The remaining issues mainly concern clarity and presentation, which can be addressed in the final revision.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and the AC for their valuable feedback and for recognizing the clinical motivation and importance of our work (R1,R2,R3) as well as our thorough (R2), rigorous (R3) and fairly solid (R1) experimental evaluation. In the following, we address all comments:
Novelty (R1)
ConRad introduces confidence estimation for the multimodal setting of radiology reporting by teaching LVLMs an internal understanding of calibrated confidence. Unlike prior work, which is mainly based on sampling, external probes, or report-extracted uncertainty phrasing [24-27,29], ConRad directly trains the LVLM to express calibrated confidence jointly with the generated report on both report and sentence level.
Report stability (R1)
Our method is intentionally designed to keep the task performance of the trained model unchanged, as this prevents unintended or accidental changes of reporting behavior. We propose ConRad as a post-training method that can perform targeted training of confidence calibration alone.
Human evaluation (R1,R3)
Our goal here was to provide an initial indication of alignment between model confidence predictions and clinician judgement and help contextualize the main results. This was achieved by considerable effort of 3 expert radiologists who agreed to rate 50 reports on sentence level. We of course agree that a larger number of readers would further strengthen the study.
GREEN (R1,R2)
We agree that GREEN is only a proxy for clinical correctness. We chose it as it is currently among the most clinically meaningful radiology report metrics. It explicitly targets clinically significant factual errors and was shown to align better with expert evaluation than prior metrics [17]. Additionally, the reward only requires a scalar correctness signal, so the same framework could be optimized against any metric. 
If it is of interest to the reviewers, we can report calibration of the same GREEN-trained model using alternative correctness metrics. Compared with Verbalize Base, ConRad also clearly reduces ECE when correctness is measured by CheXbert (0.52→0.20) or RadGraph (0.72→0.19), indicating that the learned calibration transfers beyond the training metric.
Lambda (R3)
The choice of λ was inherited from initial PPO experiments, where it led to faster convergence. However, in GRPO rewards are normalized within each sampled group before computing advantages, so the λ only influences the trade-off between format and task reward, which led to similar convergence in initial experiments.
Clarifications (R2)
We will add these clarifications to the final manuscript:
GRPO is the standard RL algorithm for LLM finetuning. It samples multiple candidate outputs for the same input, normalizes and compares their rewards within this output group, and updates the model to increase the likelihood of the comparatively higher-reward outputs.
Confidence ordinality: In SFT, textual confidence tokens are treated as independent labels. In contrast, our reward varies continuously with the distance between predicted confidence and correctness, so near-misses are preferred over large miscalibration. This better reflects that confidence is ordinal, i.e., discrete but meaningfully ordered, rather than categorical.
Baselines: Verbalize Supervised mimics GREEN labels token-wise via cross-entropy; Trained Probe predicts correctness from hidden states rather than verbalizing it; Sequence Probability, P(True), and Self-Consistency are post-hoc; Verbalize Base is zero-shot prompting.
GREEN is a common report generation metric evaluating a candidate report against the reference report using an LLM as a judge, evaluating the ratio of matched findings and clinically significant errors.
Markov Decision Process (MDP): RL is usually formulated as MDP modeling sequential decision processes. For our problem, the confidence-token predictions are the actions, the prompt and report form the state, and the log-score provides the per-rollout reward.

title: CalibSleep: Cross-Modal Calibration and Rule-Aware Learning for Automatic Sleep Stage Classification
abstract: Automatic sleep staging is a fundamental task in sleep health assessment and clinical diagnosis, yet it remains challenging due to insufficient exploitation of multimodal complementarity, heterogeneous physiological signals, and complex sleep stage transition patterns. This paper proposes CalibSleep, a dual-stream sleep stage classification framework that jointly models time-domain EEG/EOG signals and their corresponding time–frequency representations. CalibSleep employs modality-specific encoders to capture complementary temporal and spectral features, and introduces a cross-modal calibration module to explicitly align heterogeneous representations and adaptively balance modality contributions. Furthermore, physiological prior knowledge of sleep stage transitions is incorporated through a rule-aware classification strategy, improving prediction stability and clinical consistency without relying on complex long-range temporal modeling. Experiments on an in-house clinical dataset from Shanghai Jiao Tong University Affiliated Sixth People’s Hospital and the public SHHS1 dataset demonstrate that CalibSleep achieves accuracies of 89.6% and 88.3%, respectively, outperforming existing methods. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of each proposed component. These results indicate that CalibSleep provides an effective and well-generalizable solution for automatic sleep stage classification. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Cx3300903/CalibSleep.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs
Modalities -> EEG / MEG / ECG / Physiological Signals
Modalities -> Mobile / Wearable / Point-of-Care Imaging & Sensors

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper focuses on automatic sleep staging and proposes the CalibSleep framework, a dual-branch cross-modal calibration fusion model. 
It employs bidirectional attention alignment and adaptive calibration fusion for heterogeneous features in time and time-frequency domains, combined with rule-aware stage transition regularization. 
The proposed method achieves superior performance over state-of-the-art approaches on both an in-house dataset and the public SHHS1 dataset, with a design that conforms to sleep physiological rules.
reviews.text_strengths: This paper proposes the CalibSleep, a dual-branch cross-modal calibration fusion framework, for the automatic sleep staging task. By leveraging bidirectional cross-attention to achieve semantic alignment of heterogeneous features in the time and time-frequency domains, combined with adaptive calibration and AASM rule-aware phase transition regularization, it effectively improves the physiological consistency and classification performance of sleep staging. Extensive experiments on both the in-house dataset and the public SHHS1 dataset demonstrate that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The CMC module proposed in this paper achieves semantic alignment through bidirectional cross-attention and uses an adaptive weight α to balance time-domain and time-frequency-domain features. 
However, only the overall effectiveness of the CMC module is verified via ablation experiments; the individual contributions of bidirectional attention and adaptive calibration are not decomposed, making it impossible to clarify their independent effects on performance improvement. 
2.The comparative experiments in this paper only cover several unimodal and time-frequency multimodal baselines, without including high-performance sleep staging methods based on Transformer and graph neural networks in recent years. 
3.The specific design of the AASM transition matrix and the sensitivity of the hyperparameter λtrans are not elaborated, nor is the improvement of regularization on each sleep stage quantitatively analyzed.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Core Factors Leading to the Total Score
1.Strong Advantages Supporting Acceptance
a. The framework is designed to align heterogeneous features while incorporating AASM rule-aware phase transition regularization, which strictly conforms to the physiological rules of sleep staging. This ensures the model’s decisions are interpretable and clinically meaningful, a key highlight of the work.
b.Extensive experiments on both an in-house dataset and the public SHHS1 dataset validate that CalibSleep outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. The competitive results confirm the framework’s effectiveness and robustness.
c.The paper provides sufficient visualization and analysis of model decisions, such as attention weights and feature alignment results, which helps readers understand how the model processes sleep data and enhances the credibility of the method.
2.Minor Deficiencies Leading to “Weak Acceptance”
a.The CMC module’s overall effectiveness is verified via ablation, but the individual contributions of bidirectional attention and adaptive calibration are not decomposed. This fails to clarify the specific role of each sub-component, reducing the transparency of the technical design.
b. Comparative experiments only include traditional unimodal and time-frequency multimodal baselines, lacking direct comparisons with recent high-performance methods based on Transformer and graph neural networks (GNN). This makes it difficult to fully demonstrate the superiority of CalibSleep in the current research landscape.
c.The AASM transition matrix’s specific design and hyperparameter λtrans sensitivity analysis are not elaborated. Additionally, the quantitative improvement of phase transition regularization for each sleep stage is missing, weakening the rigor of the physiological prior integration.

reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes CalibSleep as a dual-stream framework for automatic sleep stage classification that jointly models time-domain EEG/EOG signals and their time-frequency representations. The method introduces a Cross-Modal Calibration module to dynamically align and balance heterogeneous features alongside a rule-aware classification strategy that incorporates physiological sleep transition priors to improve prediction stability.
reviews.text_strengths: The integration of physiological priors via a rule-aware transition loss provides a biologically meaningful constraint to the classification process without relying on complex long-range sequence modeling. The dual-stream architecture effectively captures both temporal and spectral dynamics making good use of modal complementarity. Furthermore the experimental results on both an in-house clinical dataset and the public SHHS1 dataset demonstrate strong empirical performance and reliable generalization capabilities.
reviews.text_weaknesses: While the CalibSleep framework demonstrates solid empirical performance, its architectural novelty is somewhat limited. The model primarily relies on a combination of established neural network components, such as the standard stack of CNN, SENet, and BiGRU for the time-domain encoder, and the existing TimesNet for the time-frequency branch. The cross-modal calibration module also utilizes standard cross-attention and a gating mechanism. Although this combination is effective, it represents more of an engineering integration rather than a fundamental methodological innovation in multi-modal deep learning. Additionally, integrating these multiple modules may introduce extra computational overhead, but the paper lacks a detailed analysis of parameter counts and inference latency which are important for clinical deployment. Finally, including comparisons with more recent transformer-based or graph-based state-of-the-art models would further strengthen the demonstration of the proposed method’s absolute superiority.

N/A

While CalibSleep achieves strong empirical results, its architectural contribution leans more towards an engineering integration of existing components rather than a fundamental methodological innovation in multi-modal deep learning. Furthermore, the absence of a detailed computational efficiency analysis (e.g., parameter count, inference latency) makes it difficult to assess the model’s practical viability for clinical deployment. Given the somewhat limited novelty and the missing comparisons with more recent transformer-based or graph-based baselines, my initial recommendation is a Weak Reject. I would be willing to raise my score if the authors can provide the necessary computational profiling and stronger baseline comparisons during the rebuttal phase.
