reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes CalibSleep, a dual-stream deep learning framework designed for automatic sleep stage classification using EEG and EOG signals. The main contributions are twofold: First, it introduces a cross-modal calibration module (CMC) that explicitly aligns and dynamically balances features from both the time domain and time-frequency representations. Second, it proposes a novel “rule-aware classification” strategy that integrates AASM physiological guidelines into the loss function. This acts as a soft regularization term to penalize physiologically implausible sleep stage transitions between adjacent epochs, achieving high accuracy (89.6% on an in-house dataset, 88.3% on SHHS1) without relying on complex, heavy long-sequence temporal modeling.
reviews.text_strengths: The most striking strength of this paper is the elegant design of the rule-aware transition loss. Instead of employing computationally expensive long-range temporal models (such as large Transformers or deep RNNs) to implicitly learn transition probabilities, the authors ingeniously inject clinical rules directly into the objective function. By calculating the transition matrix of adjacent single-epoch predictions and penalizing unlikely shifts, the model captures essential temporal context and clinical consistency in a highly lightweight and effective manner.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Robustness of Rule-Aware Loss Against Label Noise: While theoretically appealing, the practical utility of the rule-aware loss requires further justification, specifically regarding the inherent ambiguity of sleep stage transitions. Sleep transitions are notoriously fuzzy, and even highly experienced clinicians often disagree when annotating these boundary epochs. For instance, as detailed in the dataset paper “ISRUC-Sleep: A comprehensive public dataset for sleep researchers”, inter-rater disagreement between expert scorers can be as high as 20%. Given that the ground-truth labels themselves contain significant noise during transitions, enforcing a rigid physiological prior matrix might over-penalize the model or force it to learn hard boundaries that do not reflect the continuous nature of human sleep. The authors need to discuss whether this explicit signal remains effective in the presence of such high inter-rater variability.
Lack of Statistical Significance Testing: The quantitative results presented in Tables 1 and 2 report absolute metrics (ACC, MF1, Kappa) but completely omit standard deviations or confidence intervals. Because the performance margins between the proposed method and some baselines (or among ablation variants) are relatively narrow, it is impossible to determine whether these improvements are statistically significant or merely the result of favorable random seeds. To convincingly prove the method’s effectiveness, the authors must conduct multiple runs to report standard deviations and perform appropriate statistical significance tests (e.g., t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests).
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

My recommendation leans towards Borderline Accept / Weak Accept.The paper presents a logically sound architecture. The introduction of the rule-aware loss is a clever, computationally efficient way to integrate clinical priors into a single-epoch classifier, and the cross-modal calibration is well-executed.However, the empirical evaluation currently lacks the rigor expected for publication due to the missing variance measures and statistical significance tests. Furthermore, the core mechanism (the rule-aware loss) rests on an assumption of clear-cut transitions that fails to account for well-documented inter-rater ambiguity in clinical practice.I am willing to raise my score if the authors can provide the necessary statistical significance analyses (mean $\pm$ std across multiple runs) and offer a nuanced discussion/experiment regarding how their transition regularization handles the inherent label noise during sleep stage shifts in their rebuttal.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper proposes a dual-stream framework for automatic sleep stage classification. The reviewers acknowledged the model design, extensive experiments, improved performance, and clinically meaningful interpretability. This paper’s significant would be better highlighted if the authors address several important points raised by the reviewers, such as clarifying the methodological novelty, positioning the work relative to stronger recent baselines (through proper background review), disentangling the contributions of the proposed calibration components, reporting variance and statistical significance, discussing computational cost, deployment practicality, and robustness.

The rebuttal seems to have clarified the intended role of the calibration and rule-aware components and to have preserved a positive overall stance after rebuttal, even though some requests for stronger contextualization and significance analysis remained. Because the core contribution is useful and the main concerns appear manageable rather than fatal, I support acceptance.

The rebuttal addressed the major reviewer concerns satisfactorily, particularly regarding the positioning of the contribution, the role of the calibration components, the interpretation of the rule-aware transition regularization, and the practical deployment considerations. The authors also clarified the rationale behind the architectural design and acknowledged the limitations regarding additional statistical analysis and computational profiling.
The paper presents a technically sound and clinically meaningful framework for automatic sleep stage classification. The integration of cross-modal calibration with physiologically guided transition regularization is well motivated and supported by strong empirical performance on both in-house and public datasets. The rule-aware transition loss provides an elegant and lightweight mechanism for incorporating clinical sleep transition priors without requiring heavy long-sequence modeling.
I recommend acceptance.

The reviewers found the paper clinically motivated and empirically strong. After rebuttal, the main concerns on novelty, baselines, efficiency, and statistical validation were sufficiently addressed, supporting acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and AC for the constructive comments and for recognizing CalibSleep’s design, evaluation, performance, and clinical interpretability. Following MICCAI rebuttal policy, we do not introduce new/additional results, but clarify the submitted evidence and acknowledge limitations where new experiments would be required.
Novelty and positioning. We agree that several low-level encoders use established components. Our contribution is not the isolated use of CNN/BiGRU/TimesNet/cross-attention, but the formulation of sleep staging as calibrated integration of temporal and time-frequency evidence under physiological transition constraints. Unlike simple concatenation or one-way attention, CMC performs bidirectional semantic querying between domains and learns an epoch-adaptive calibration gate alpha to balance temporal and spectral reliability. Fig. 3(a) supports this design: alpha shows meaningful stage-dependent behavior, emphasizing time-domain EOG-related evidence in Wake/REM and spectral evidence in N1-N3.
Component contribution and transition prior. Table 2 evaluates the proposed components: compared with dual-stream concatenation (0.836/0.833/0.828 ACC/MF1/Kappa), adding CMC improves performance to 0.872/0.846/0.841, and further adding rule-aware regularization yields 0.896/0.877/0.874.We agree that the manuscript should better disentangle sub-component roles: bidirectional attention handles cross-domain alignment and feature conflict; adaptive calibration performs sample-wise evidence weighting; Lcalib stabilizes feature consistency during training; and Ltrans penalizes physiologically implausible adjacent-epoch predictions. M encodes adjacent-stage rationality according to AASM-guided sleep evolution knowledge. Ltrans is a probability-weighted soft regularizer, not a hard constrained decoder. lambda_trans=0.1 balances this prior with cross-entropy: lambda_trans=0 degenerates to ordinary classification, while an overly large value may over-constrain ambiguous transitions.
Baselines, computation, and deployment. We apologize that the baseline positioning was not sufficiently clear. Table 1 includes representative unimodal, time-frequency, multimodal, and Transformer-related methods, including SFormer/SleepTransformer and MultichannelSleepNet variants, as well as XSleepNet, SleepBoost, CoReSleep, and CrossFusionSleepNet. We acknowledge that additional GNN comparisons and parameter/latency profiling would further strengthen the paper. Qualitatively, the physiological priors are deployment-friendly: the contrastive calibration loss and transition loss are used only during training and introduce no extra inference-time decoder. CalibSleep operates on 30-s EEG/EOG epochs and does not require whole-night self-attention or graph construction.
Statistical rigor and robustness. We agree that reporting mean/std and significance tests would improve empirical rigor, and we will explicitly discuss this limitation. Nevertheless, the submitted evidence is not limited to one narrow setting: CalibSleep shows consistent gains on the in-house No.6 dataset and external SHHS1 dataset, across ACC/MF1/Kappa, ablation variants, and interpretability analyses.
Robustness to label ambiguity. We fully agree that boundary epochs are ambiguous and inter-rater disagreement exists. Our rule-aware loss does not assume deterministic transitions or override expert labels. It acts on the predicted transition probability p_{t-1}p_t^T and softly discourages implausible transitions, while cross-entropy from manual annotations remains the primary supervision. Thus, ambiguous epochs can still be determined by signal evidence. Fig. 3(b,c) suggests that the regularizer mainly suppresses physiologically unlikely confusion, such as N3-REM, rather than blindly smoothing predictions.
We hope these clarifications address the concerns on novelty, component roles, baselines, practicality, statistical rigor, and robustness.

title: CALM: Interpretable Cross-Modal Alignment for Biomarker Discovery from Unpaired Data
abstract: The interaction between brain structure and genetic influences is key to understanding neuropsychiatric disorders. However, most large-scale datasets are unimodal, providing either neuroimaging or genetics data. We propose CALM, a framework that learns interpretable associations between brain ROIs and genetic pathways from \textit{completely disjoint} populations. CALM aligns the two modalities in a shared latent space via linear projections that simultaneously match the class-conditional latent distributions and ensure group separability. These projections provide interpretable pathway–ROI associations. When trained on unimodal imaging and genetics datasets, CALM generalizes to an unseen paired dataset, outperforming several state-of-the-art methods and ablation baselines. We also demonstrate stability of the learned associations against a paired baseline. Our experiments on autism spectrum disorder reveal immune and metabolic pathways linked to specific cortical regions and are consistent with established literature. Thus, CALM opens the door to leveraging large unimodal repositories for studying cross-modal interactions in brain disorders across disparate datasets.
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This work introduces a multimodal learning framework CALM that can be trained on entirely non-overlapping cohorts, enabling the modeling of associations between neuroimaging features and gene pathways without requiring paired multimodal data from the same subjects.
A shared latent space is constructed via linear projections to align imaging and gene pathway modalities. In addition, a class-conditional distribution alignment strategy is employed to enforce consistent discriminative structures across modalities, facilitating effective cross-modal integration.
The proposed projection mechanism is inherently interpretable.
Even when trained solely on unimodal datasets (imaging or genetic) drawn from completely disjoint subject groups, the model generalizes well to unseen paired datasets and outperforms several existing approaches as well as ablation baselines.
The empirical findings highlight immune- and metabolism-related pathways associated with specific cortical regions, providing meaningful evidence toward understanding the molecular basis of brain disorders.
reviews.text_strengths:
Unlike conventional approaches that rely on paired multimodal data from the same individuals, the proposed method learns cross-modal relationships from disjoint cohorts, improving its applicability in scenarios where paired data are scarce.
By leveraging a shared latent space together with class-conditional distribution alignment, the model is able to establish meaningful inter-modal relationships even in the absence of explicit pairing.
The use of linear projections allows for direct interpretation of region–pathway associations, which is advantageous over black-box models for biomarker discovery and mechanistic insights.
The model trained on fully disjoint unimodal datasets can be transferred to unseen paired datasets, demonstrating strong generalization capability.
The identified associations between immune/metabolic pathways and specific brain regions offer cross-scale (brain–gene) insights relevant to the study of brain disorders.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper does not clearly specify the form of the final classifier (e. g. , whether a linear classifier or another architecture is used). This omission makes the overall pipeline less transparent and may affect both reproducibility and interpretability.
The biological validation of the findings remains limited. It would be beneficial to incorporate external resources (e. g. , the Allen Brain Atlas) to further corroborate the reported brain region–gene pathway associations, thereby strengthening the reliability and biological relevance of the conclusions.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper addresses a central challenge, the scarcity of paired data, in multimodal neuroimaging and genetic data integrationby proposing a framework that can be trained on disjoint cohorts. This design choice is practically relevant and well-motivated. By learning a shared latent space and incorporating class-conditional distribution alignment, the model achieves cross-modal integration while preserving discriminative structure. Moreover, the use of linear projections contributes to interpretability, enabling explicit characterization of associations between brain regions and gene pathways.
A notable strength is the model’s ability to generalize to unseen paired datasets despite being trained only on unimodal data from non-overlapping subjects. This property is both novel and potentially impactful for real-world applications. In addition, the reported associations between brain regions and immune/metabolic pathways provide biologically meaningful insights.
While there is room for improvement in terms of clearer specification of model components and more comprehensive biological validation, the paper presents a well-motivated approach with solid methodological contributions, good interpretability, and promising cross-modal generalization performance.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper proposes CALM, an interpretable framework for learning cross-modal associations between neuroimaging and genetics from completely unpaired and disjoint datasets.
The key contribution is a class-conditional alignment strategy that combines modality-specific encoders with linear projection matrices, enabling the model to align the two modalities in a shared latent space while preserving a direct correspondence between brain ROIs and genetic pathways. This design allows the extraction of an interpretable ROI-pathway association matrix rather than relying on black-box latent fusion.
Experimentally, the method is trained on independent unimodal datasets and evaluated on an external paired dataset, where it achieves the best classification performance among the compared baselines. The paper further validates the learned associations by showing strong agreement with a paired-data baseline and by linking the identified pathway-ROI patterns to established ASD-related findings in the literature.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Novel and practically relevant problem setting.
The paper addresses the important and underexplored problem of learning imaging-genetics associations from completely unpaired datasets. This is practically meaningful because many large public datasets are unimodal and disjoint, making paired multimodal analysis difficult in real-world settings.
2.Interpretable model design.
A major strength of the work is that interpretability is built into the architecture itself. By using per-entity encoders and linear projections, the method preserves explicit correspondence between brain ROIs and genetic pathways, allowing direct extraction of an association matrix. This is more meaningful than typical latent fusion approaches where feature interactions become difficult to interpret.
3.Well-motivated objective formulation.
The combination of class-conditional distribution alignment, supervised contrastive learning, and orthogonality regularization is conceptually coherent. The objective is designed not only to align the two modalities, but also to maintain class discrimination and avoid degenerate solutions in the projection matrices.
Reasonable experimental validation.
The paper includes comparisons against several relevant baselines as well as ablation studies that isolate the contribution of the key loss terms. In addition, the method is evaluated on an independent paired external dataset, which strengthens the empirical validation.
5.Validation of biological consistency.
The learned association matrix shows high correlation with a paired-data baseline (r = 0.87), and the identified pathway-ROI relationships are discussed in the context of established ASD literature. This gives additional support that the learned cross-modal associations are not purely algorithmic artifacts.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Important hyperparameter choices are under-justified.
The method depends on several potentially sensitive hyperparameters, including the weights of the CMMD, contrastive, and orthogonality losses, as well as the contrastive temperature. Although these values are reported, the paper does not clearly explain how they were selected, nor does it provide a sensitivity analysis. This makes it difficult to assess how robust the reported performance is to these design choices.
2.The performance gain over the ablations is relatively modest.
CALM achieves the best overall results, but the margin over the strongest ablation variants is small in Table 1.While the method is conceptually appealing, the empirical advantage of using the full objective over simpler variants is not yet entirely convincing. A stronger discussion of when each component materially helps would improve the paper.
3.Reproducibility is limited by insufficient architectural detail.
The paper states that pretrained autoencoders and classifiers are used, but the exact architecture and pretraining protocol of these encoders are not described in sufficient detail in the main text. Since the encoder design is important for preserving interpretability and for the second-stage alignment, clearer implementation details would improve reproducibility.
4.Biological interpretation remains largely qualitative.
The discussion of the discovered pathway-ROI associations is interesting, but the biological interpretation is mostly narrative and literature-supported rather than quantitatively validated. Additional statistical or biological validation would make the interpretability claim stronger.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Overall, I found the paper interesting and technically well motivated. The problem setting is relevant, and the effort to build interpretability directly into the alignment framework is commendable. I encourage the authors to improve the paper by clarifying the encoder architecture and pretraining details, providing more justification for hyperparameter selection, and strengthening the empirical discussion around the relatively small gains over some ablations. These additions would make the paper easier to reproduce and would further support the practical value of the proposed method.

I recommend Weak Accept. The paper addresses a meaningful and challenging problem—learning interpretable imaging-genetics associations from fully unpaired datasets—and proposes a method that is both conceptually coherent and practically relevant. The interpretability-oriented design, the external paired-data evaluation, and the comparison with a paired baseline are all positive aspects. At the same time, I do not view the paper as a clear accept because some important implementation details are under-specified, the hyperparameter choices are insufficiently justified, and the empirical gains over the strongest ablations are relatively modest. Overall, I think the paper is above the acceptance threshold due to the novelty of the problem setting and the quality of the methodological idea, but I would expect the authors to address the concerns above in the rebuttal and revision.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The rebuttal addresses several of my technical concerns in a serious and constructive way. In particular, the authors provide substantially clearer detail on the encoder/classifier architecture and pretraining protocol, and they clarify that hyperparameters were selected by grid search with 5-fold CV on the unpaired training cohorts without using the ACE dataset. The rebuttal also offers a more explicit explanation of why the association matrix can be interpreted as reflecting ROI-pathway relationships in the aligned latent space.
However, after reading the rebuttal, I remain unconvinced on several points that are central to the paper’s overall strength. First, the empirical advantage of the full model over the strongest ablations is still relatively modest, and the rebuttal explains the intended role of each loss term more clearly than it demonstrates a strong practical necessity of the full objective. Second, the biological validation remains largely qualitative. The authors point to future validation against external resources such as SFARI and the Allen Brain Atlas, but this does not resolve the current limitation of the submitted manuscript. Third, while the baseline and ablation rationale is better explained, I still find the experimental evidence somewhat limited relative to the strength of the interpretability claims.
Overall, I appreciate the novelty of the problem setting and the authors’ thoughtful rebuttal, but I do not think the rebuttal fully resolves the remaining concerns about the strength of empirical support and biological validation. For that reason, I would not change my final opinion to acceptance.

reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes CALM, a framework for learning interpretable cross-modal associations between brain region morphometry and genetic pathways from entirely unpaired and disjoint populations. CALM employs a class-conditional linear transport model to align group-wise distributions across modalities in a shared latent space. Validated against a paired baseline and on an unseen external dataset, it yields stable associations and outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
The main strengths of the paper are:
(1) The paper tackles a clinically relevant and practical problem by learning cross-modal associations from completely unpaired imaging and genetics data.
(2) The method is conceptually simple and well-structured, combining distribution alignment and contrastive learning in a clear and reasonable way.
(3) The experimental evaluation is relatively comprehensive, including external validation on a paired dataset and analysis of association stability.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The main weaknesses of the paper are:
(1) The paper has many formatting issues. For example, the reference formats are inconsistent; the citation of Fig. 3(b) is problematic; the subsection ‘Regularization (L_{orth})’ is missing a colon; the font styles around symbols S(i) and P(j) are inconsistent, etc. The authors need to thoroughly check the manuscript themselves.
(2) There’s a lot of unnecessary italic styling throughout the paper. Italics should really be used only when you want to emphasize a key point.
(3) There are too few baseline comparisons, only three. And the performance gain of CALM over its own ablations is very limited. Also, why is the Ablation L_{OT} using the loss from Ref [3]? What’s the reason?
(4) The association matrix A = W_I^T W_G is just the product of two parameter matrices. Why does that directly quantify pairwise relationships between brain regions and genetic pathways? What’s the interpretability there? Also, why set the latent dimension d = 6? There’s no justification for this choice, and no parameter analysis for this value.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Although the CALM tackles a clinically relevant and practical problem by learning cross-modal associations from completely unpaired imaging and genetics data, I would recommend a weak reject due to the technical concerns highlighted above. A strong rebuttal addressing these issues could be highly beneficial.

meta_reviews.text:
I recommend an Invite for Rebuttal based on the mixed reviewer scores. All reviewers commended the paper for tackling a highly practical and novel problem setting by learning cross-modal associations from completely unpaired imaging and genetics datasets. The proposed method was praised for its conceptually coherent design, its strong generalization to unseen external paired datasets, and its built-in interpretability achieved through linear projections. However, several technical and presentation concerns must be rigorously addressed in the rebuttal. First, the authors need to provide comprehensive implementation details regarding the exact architecture and pretraining protocols of the autoencoders and classifiers used in the pipeline. Second, critical design choices and hyperparameters, particularly the chosen latent dimension size and the various loss weights, require thorough justification and a sensitivity analysis. Reviewers also questioned the modest performance gains of the full model over its ablation variants and requested justification for the limited number of baseline comparisons. Furthermore, the rebuttal must explicitly clarify the mathematical rationale behind using the product of the parameter matrices to directly quantify pairwise relationships and defend its interpretability. Finally, the authors must commit to resolving the manuscript’s formatting inconsistencies and excessive italicization, and they should discuss potential avenues for stronger quantitative biological validation, such as incorporating external resources like the Allen Brain Atlas.

Although the proposed framework addresses the highly practical problem of learning cross-modal associations from completely unpaired imaging and genetics datasets , reviewers remain unconvinced due to the modest empirical gains over ablation baselines. While the authors provided helpful architectural details and hyperparameter justifications during the rebuttal, the biological validation of the discovered associations remains largely qualitative rather than quantitative. Consequently, given these lingering concerns regarding the strength of the experimental evidence and the lack of robust biological validation, the paper ultimately falls below the acceptance threshold.

This manuscript presented a method to align unpaired cross modal data for biomarker discovery. Reviewers found this method to be a practical solution to a novel problem set with a conceptually coherent design.
The weaknesses were missing implementation details, some design choices not being justified, and there being only a few baseline comparison methods.
Overall the reviewers found the rebuttal addressed most points except for the modest gains in the full model over ablation studies which lead to questions about if the full model is really necessary. Additionally the biological validation of the method was qualitative only.
I recommend for acceptance because on balance the negatives (modest gains in ablation experiment, limitations on comparisons) are outweighted by the strength of the novel design which is conceptually interesting.

The rebuttal addresses the reviewer’s concerns well. The work addresses a core challenge by learning cross-modal associations from completely unpaired imaging and genetics data. Overall, the reviewers are positive and I recommend acceptation.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback and for recognizing the important problem of learning cross-modal associations from unpaired imaging and genetic data. We address the major critiques below.
1.Construction of the Association Matrix (Rev 3): Each column of W_I (resp. W_G) defines how a brain ROI (resp. genetic pathway) contributes to each shared latent dimension. L_orth keeps these rows near-orthonormal to maximize the variance captured by these dimensions. L_cmmd and L_con align the two modalities along these shared dimensions. A large entry A_{r,p} implies that ROI “r” and pathway “p” load similarly onto the latent dimensions, indicating that they co-vary in the aligned space. This is analogous to CCA but without paired samples. Columns of W_I / W_G correspond one-to-one to ROIs / pathways, so A can be viewed as an ROI-pathway association matrix.
2.Hyperparameter Selection (Revs 2 & 3): Hyperparameters were tuned via grid search with 5-fold CV on the unpaired ABIDE and SSC datasets, covering latent dimension d, batch size, learning rate, loss weights (λ_cmmd, λ_con, λ_orth), and contrastive temperature. The ACE dataset was never seen during hyperparameter selection, and Table 1 confirms CALM’s generalizability to it. Latent dimension d had the largest impact on performance: larger values tend to overfit the modest training set. Loss weights and contrastive temperature were robust across reasonable ranges and can serve as defaults in future studies.
3.Clarity of Model Architecture (Revs 1 & 2): Both the imaging and genetics branches use the same autoencoder design. Each brain ROI (n_I = 246, 4 morphometric values) and genetic pathway (n_G = 177, 6 phenotypic traits) is encoded independently (preserving a one-to-one correspondence) by a 3-layer per-entity MLP into a 6-dim embedding. A mirrored decoder reconstructs the input. Each encoder also has a 2-layer MLP classifier. Encoders are pretrained with MSE reconstruction and BCE losses. Code will be released upon acceptance.
4.Comparison and Ablation (Revs 1 & 3): Our baselines span key alternative approaches: SUE (NeurIPS 2025) for unpaired cross-modal alignment, UNSEEN (NeurIPS 2023) for missing-modality settings, and G-MIND as an imaging-genetics-specific baseline. SUE requires paired data for fine-tuning, yet CALM still achieves statistically better accuracy and AUC than all three. None of the baselines outputs interpretable ROI/pathway associations, the central deliverable of CALM. Although classification performance is similar across CALM and its ablations, each loss imposes a specific constraint on A. L_cmmd aligns intra-class imaging and genetic distributions, giving A biological relevance. L_con pulls the intra-class samples together across modalities while pushing the inter-class samples apart, anchoring the alignment to the diagnostic axis. Together, they “organize” the latent space, making the associations stable and reproducible across CV folds and consistent with paired results. We note that AUC only evaluates single-modality classification and does not reflect the cross-modal alignment achieved by ‭L_cmmd‬ and ‭L_con‬. L_OT in Table 1 replaces L_cmmd with the Sinkhorn OT loss as a separate ablation.
5.Biological Validation (Revs 1 & 2): As our paper introduces a new framework to link unpaired datasets, we focus on methodology and provide a preliminary demonstration in autism, using single-modality cohorts (ABIDE, SSC) and a matched cohort with both modalities (ACE). Results show (1) high concordance between associations in unpaired and paired scenarios (Fig. 2a) and (2) stability and reproducibility across CV folds (Fig. 2b). As suggested, we are pursuing quantitative validation against the SFARI gene database and the Allen Brain Atlas.
6.Formatting (Rev 3): We will fix inconsistent superscript fonts, a missing colon in the regularization subheading, broken Fig. 3(b) citation, extra italic emphasis, and reference list format.

title: Can Agents Distinguish Visually Hard-to-Separate Diseases in a Zero-Shot Setting? A Pilot Study
abstract:
The rapid progress of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) has led to increasing interest in agent-based systems. While most prior work in medical imaging concentrates on automating routine
clinical workflows, we study an underexplored yet clinically significant setting: distinguishing visually hard-to-separate diseases in a zero-shot setting. We benchmark representative agents on two imaging-only proxy diagnostic tasks, (1) melanoma vs. atypical nevus and (2) pulmonary edema vs. pneumonia, where visual features are highly confounded despite substantial differences in clinical management. We introduce a multi-agent framework based on contrastive adjudication. Experimental results show improved diagnostic performance (an 11-percentage-point gain in accuracy on dermoscopy data) and reduced unsupported claims on qualitative samples, although overall performance remains insufficient
for clinical deployment. We acknowledge the inherent uncertainty in human annotations, conservative binary setting, and the absence of clinical context, which further limit the translation to real-world settings.
Within this controlled setting, this pilot study provides preliminary insights into zero-shot agent performance in visually confounded scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/TruhnLab/Contrastive-
Agent-Reasoning.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors identify the under-explored yet clinically significant problem of distinguishing visually hard-to-separate diseases in a zero-shot setting, propose the novel contrastive multi-agent framework CARE without extra training, conduct extensive benchmarking on two medical imaging tasks to validate that CARE effectively boosts diagnostic performance and reduces unsupported claims, and offer preliminary insights into zero-shot agent performance for visually confounded medical cases.
reviews.text_strengths: The authors address a clinically meaningful and under-investigated task: zero-shot discrimination of visually confusable diseases. They propose a simple yet effective CARE framework that requires no additional training or fine-tuning. Extensive benchmarking and well-designed ablation experiments are conducted on two representative medical imaging tasks, demonstrating clear performance gains over baseline methods. The framework also helps reduce unsupported visual claims, providing interpretable and verifiable diagnostic reasoning.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The novelty of the proposed CARE framework is limited, as it mainly adopts prompt engineering and lacks conceptual and methodological innovation.
2.The task difficulty is overstated. Some disease samples can be visually distinguished by simple features such as color in Mel vs APN Fig1(a).
3.The baseline selection is inappropriate and unfair, mixing models with large performance gaps and different capabilities. Gemini3 > GLM> Qwen3
4.The multi-agent system is not a genuine agent architecture but only uses the same MLLM with different role‑specific prompts, and the agent concept is overstated.
5.The experimental setting is oversimplified and clinically unrealistic, with strict binary classification and no clinical context.
6.The overall performance is still insufficient for clinical use, and the generalization ability is not fully verified.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Although the paper addresses a clinically meaningful task and presents the CARE framework with observable performance improvements, it suffers from limited novelty, overstated task difficulty, inappropriate baseline comparisons, overclaimed multi-agent design, unrealistic experimental settings, and insufficient clinical performance. These critical shortcomings lead to my recommendation of Weak Reject.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper studies a meaningful and relatively underexplored setting: zero-shot differentiation of visually confounded disease pairs from images alone. It proposes CARE, a training-free three-agent framework in which two disease-specific agents generate opposing evidence and a judge performs image-grounded adjudication. The experiments show consistent gains over the Gemini-3-Flash baseline and over matched self-check / majority-vote variants, although the overall performance remains well below clinical-use level.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper’s focus on visually hard-to-separate disease pairs with different management implications is well motivated.
2.For methods, the role split between two specialist agents and an image-grounded judge is intuitive, and the qualitative examples help illustrate what the adjudication step is doing.
3.The empirical section is reasonably solid for a pilot study. The paper evaluates two modalities, compares against several single-agent baselines, and includes compute-matched ablations.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The evaluation setting is controlled, which is reasonable for a pilot study, but it is still somewhat artificial. The XOR formulation simplifies the task and does not reflect real co-occurrence, especially for edema and pneumonia. The paper acknowledges this limitation, but it still weakens the clinical interpretation of the results.
2.The idea is promising, but the current “among the first” wording feels a bit too broad. I think the paper would benefit from a clearer discussion of nearby work on medical agentic reasoning and robustness, especially recent work such as ‘PASS’ (AAAI-26 oral) [1], which studies interpretable and adaptive chest X-ray reasoning through probabilistic agentic workflows, and the MICCAI’25 paper ‘Knowing or Guessing’ [2]. These works do not invalidate the paper’s exact setting, but they do make the novelty boundary look narrower than currently stated. A more precise claim around training-free, zero-shot, image-only contrastive adjudication for visually confounded differential diagnosis would read as stronger and more credible.
3.Reproducibility is fair but not yet strong. The overall framework is understandable, but for a prompting-based method I would still like clearer reporting of prompts, inference settings, and some of the curation details.
4.The chest X-ray result is encouraging, but not fully convincing yet. CARE improves over Gemini-3-Flash, but still remains below Gemini-3-Pro on that task, so the practical benefit of the additional multi-agent overhead is not yet fully clear.
[1] Feng et al., PASS: Probabilistic Agentic Supernet Sampling for Interpretable and Adaptive Chest X-Ray Reasoning, AAAI 2026 Oral. 
[2] Jiang et al., Knowing or Guessing? Robust Medical Visual Question Answering via Joint Consistency and Contrastive Learning, MICCAI 2025.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Overall, I found the paper thoughtful and reasonably careful in its claims. I suggest authors to tighten the related-work positioning and narrow the novelty claim a bit. I think the paper would read better if it explicitly acknowledged adjacent work on agentic medical reasoning and robustness, then emphasized more clearly what is specific here: the training-free, image-only, zero-shot contrastive adjudication setup for visually confounded disease pairs.

This is a weak accept for me. Although the novelty is not yet positioned sharply enough relative to nearby work, and the current evidence is still limited to controlled proxy tasks. However, the paper addresses a good problem, the method is neat and promising, and the empirical gains are real.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: After the rebuttal, I am satisfied that the authors have addressed my main concerns, especially regarding the novelty boundary, data curation, and the practical value of CARE. Some limitations remain, particularly the simplified binary setting and the need for clearer reproducibility details, but I view them as acceptable for a pilot study and support acceptance.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces CARE, a training-free multi-agent framework designed to address the clinical challenge of distinguishing between visually similar diseases, such as melanoma and atypical nevi, in a zero-shot setting. By structuring a “contrastive adjudication” process where two specialized agents argue for opposing diagnoses while a third judge agent verifies their claims against the original image, the study demonstrates an 11-percentage-point accuracy gain on dermoscopy data compared to single-agent baselines. Beyond the methodological contribution, the authors provide a rigorous benchmark across two imaging modalities, revealing that while such structured reasoning significantly reduces unsupported “hallucinated” claims, the overall performance of current multimodal LLMs remains below the threshold required for safe clinical deployment.
reviews.text_strengths:
The CARE system introduces a structured disagreement mechanism that effectively mimics the diagnostic process of human experts. Unlike standard self-reflection or majority-voting methods, CARE forces agents into mutually exclusive roles (one arguing for Disease A, another for Disease B), which successfully surfaces inconsistencies and reduces overconfident “hallucinated” claims.
The study specifically focuses on two clinically significant proxy tasks: melanoma vs. atypical nevus and pulmonary edema vs. pneumonia. These pairs represent a “hard-to-separate” frontier where visual features are highly overlapped, making them an ideal and rigorous testbed for evaluating the reasoning limits of multimodal LLMs.
The method is entirely prompt-based and requires no task-specific fine-tuning or additional annotated data. This makes the framework highly scalable and applicable to other medical imaging domains where high-quality labeled data for training might be scarce.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The authors note the exclusion of congenital and recurrent nevi because these subtypes are “often very difficult without clinical context”. However, as the paper’s title explicitly asks if agents can distinguish “visually hard-to-separate” diseases, manually removing the most challenging cases effectively defines a “simplified difficulty.” The authors should clarify if this exclusion intentionally shielded the zero-shot agents from the most difficult edge cases and whether the 11-percentage-point gain would significantly diminish if these cases were included.
To mitigate class imbalance, atypical nevi were subsampled to match the melanoma count (from 399 original cases to 257). The authors must clarify the specific methodology used for this subsampling (e.g., was it purely random?). Given the “visually confounded” nature of the task, it is critical to discuss whether this selection process introduced any bias or altered the prevalence of hard-to-distinguish cases compared to the original distribution.
The study employs a forced exclusive-or (XOR) setting for diagnosis. In real-world clinical practice, conditions like pulmonary edema and pneumonia frequently co-occur. By forcing a binary choice, the evaluation may artificially inflate accuracy and mask potential conflicts or “hallucinations” the model might encounter when dealing with comorbidities. The authors should discuss whether the Judge Agent should be granted the option of “both” or “neither” to better reflect clinical truth.
While “Blind-CARE” and “Self-Check” variants were tested , the current results do not fully isolate whether the performance gain stems from “contrastive reasoning” or simply the inherent capabilities of a superior judge. A more direct baseline (e.g. a single Gemini-3-Flash model performing a direct diagnosis without any debate assistance) should be emphasized for comparison. If the marginal gain of CARE over a standard single-call model is small, the added computational cost of a three-agent architecture may not be justified.
The qualitative analysis focuses on successful error corrections by the Judge Agent. To provide a balanced view of the system’s limitations, the authors should present cases where “reverse interference” occurred: situations where the two disease-specific agents provided such “persuasive” yet incorrect arguments that they successfully misled the judge.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I recommend a 4 for this submission. The paper presents a timely and well-structured pilot study on using multi-agent MLLMs to distinguish visually confounded medical images, such as melanoma versus atypical nevi. The primary strengths lie in the CARE framework’s novel use of contrastive adjudication, which mimics expert reasoning to mitigate single-agent overconfidence and reduces “hallucinated” evidence, yielding a significant 11-percentage-point accuracy gain on dermoscopy data. However, the score is tempered by methodological concerns regarding the exclusion of the most challenging disease subtypes (congenital and recurrent nevi) and the use of a forced-choice XOR setting. These choices may simplify the problem space and artificially inflate the perceived effectiveness of zero-shot reasoning compared to real-world clinical complexity, where comorbidities frequently co-occur.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have adequately addressed my comments. I recommend acceptance.

meta_reviews.text:
After reviewing this manuscript together with the reviewers’ evaluations, I note that the paper received mixed but generally constructive feedback. The reviewers recognize the clinical relevance of distinguishing visually confounded diseases in a zero-shot setting, as well as the potential value of the CARE framework for contrastive adjudication and reducing unsupported claims. At the same time, several important concerns remain, including limited methodological novelty, possible overstatement of the multi-agent formulation, simplified binary/XOR experimental settings, baseline fairness, and insufficient evidence of clinical realism and generalization. Based on my assessment, these issues would benefit from clarification and targeted response by the authors. I therefore recommend that the paper proceed to the rebuttal phase for further consideration.

The paper is recommended for acceptance based on its solid contribution as a timely pilot study and the thoroughness of the post-rebuttal clarifications. The authors successfully addressed initial concerns regarding baseline fairness and task framing.

the reviewers acknowledges the method is clinical meaningful, timely, with well established empirical gains. the authors addresses the points raised by reviewers well; baseline comparison, the novelty boundary, data curation, and the intended scope as an imaging-only pilot.

This paper proposes CARE, a training-free three-agent framework for zero-shot differentiation of visually confounded disease pairs. The setting is meaningful and underexplored, and the core idea of constructing explicit disagreement for contrastive adjudication is well motivated.
After rebuttal, both Reviewer #2 and Reviewer #3 are satisfied and explicitly recommend acceptance. The main criticisms raised by Reviewer #1 concern limited novelty, baseline fairness, oversimplified experimental settings, and below-clinical performance. The authors have provided substantive responses: they clarified that CARE is a methodology of constructing disagreement rather than mere prompt engineering, which is a valid conceptual contribution; they explained that the baseline comparison is conducted under identical backbone models, thus the gains are fairly attributed; they acknowledged the simplified binary setting and the imaging-only nature as limitations of this pilot study, while noting that the framework can naturally incorporate clinical context in future work; and they were transparent that the current performance is not clinical-ready but aims to expose an unsolved problem to the community. The clarification on the definition of agent is also reasonable.
The remaining concerns, including the binary task formulation and the absence of clinical context, are acknowledged as limitations and are acceptable for a pilot study that opens a new direction. I recommend accept. For the camera-ready version, the authors should: (1) clearly state the limitations regarding binary classification and imaging-only evaluation in the abstract and conclusion; (2) provide the exact definition of agent adopted in this work early in the manuscript; (3) ensure full reproducibility details, including prompts and inference configurations, are documented; and (4) incorporate the newly cited related work as promised in the rebuttal.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for constructive comments and for recognizing the forward-looking nature of this study. We address main concerns below:
1.Limited novelty (R1). CARE is not merely a prompt design, but a methodology of explicitly constructing disagreement. By doing this in a binary diagnosis setting, the system can comprehensively consider both sides before making a final decision. Importantly, it doesn’t require post-training or fine-tuning, with acceptable inference overhead.
2.Below-clinical performance (R1,R2). This study is not meant to claim clinical readiness, but to expose this important yet unsolved problem to the community. We have highlighted this point in Sec 3.2 and Sec 4.
3.Overstated task difficulty and agent concept (R1). We disagree with R1’s claim that melanoma (MEL) and atypical nevus (ANV) can be distinguished “simply by color.” In dermoscopic imaging, color is well known to be an unreliable and highly variable feature due to camera white balance, illumination temperature, etc. MEL vs. ANV remains challenging [15], and reducing it to color greatly oversimplifies the task. Moreover, we have clearly defined “agent” as “systems that can receive observations and perform goal-directed actions” based on [2]. Agent does not necessitate tool-use and RAG, it is the observation-action that really matters.
4.Baseline choice (R1, R3). We believe R1 has misinterpreted Table 1.The models listed there are not direct baselines for CARE, but rather as a benchmark survey to evaluate how current MLLM-based agents perform in this setting. For both R1 and R3, the actual comparison validating CARE is between Gemini-3-Flash (Baseline) and Gemini-3-Flash (CARE), where the underlying MLLM remains identical and only the inference framework changes. Therefore, the reported gains are not derived from comparing against weaker models, but from controlled comparisons under the same backbone model.
5.Oversimplified setting (R1/R2/R3). (1) absence of clinical context. Currently no publicly dataset provides paired imaging and clinical context. Therefore, as stated in the Discussion, our experiments should be viewed as imaging-only proxy tasks. Note that MLLM-based agents can naturally incorporate additional clinical context as textual input, allowing seamless extension to richer multimodal settings. (2) Simplified binary edema vs. pneumonia formulation. This pilot study is to establish that distinguishing visually confounded diseases remains unsolved for MLLM-based agents. As agents already struggle under this binary setting, more realistic non-exclusive formulations would likely be even more challenging. It doesn’t undermine our conclusion.
6.Practical benefit (R2). CARE is designed as a plug-and-play framework rather than a model-specific architecture. Applying CARE to Qwen3-VL-32B improved MEL vs. ANV F1 by 3.8 percentage points and increased the Youden index from 0.347 to 0.426.In principle, CARE could also be applied to Gemini-3-Pro. However, Gemini-3-Pro is limited to 250 API calls per day. An entire CARE inference would require 8 days for dermoscopy and 26 days for chest X-ray evaluation. Due to these constraints, we treated Gemini-3-Pro as a single-agent upper-bound reference rather than another CARE backbone.
7.Related work (R2). We thank R2 for pointing out these works and will cite them. Our work differs from these studies in focus. PASS investigates agents with tool-use mechanisms, while “Knowing or Guessing” proposes training recipes. In contrast, CARE focuses on training-free inference-time contrastive adjudication.
8.Data curation (R3). For ANV, we performed controlled subgroup-aware random sampling. We also apologize for the ambiguity in the manuscript regarding congenital and recurrent nevi. These subtypes were excluded because they are often considered theoretically indistinguishable from melanoma based on dermoscopy alone. The exclusion was to improve rigor rather than simplify the benchmark.

title: Can Experts Adapt Without Training? On Test-Time Modality Generalization in MVLMs
abstract:
Medical vision-language models (MVLMs) promise broad zero-shot generalization, yet their reliability collapses when confronted with unseen modalities and domains, precisely where clinical robustness matters most. To address this gap, we revisit test-time modality generalization from the perspective of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) and ask: can experts route-and-adapt without any optimization during inference? We identify a fundamental specialization-generalization dilemma at test time, where blindly aggregating modality experts dilutes modality-specific knowledge, while selecting one highly confident expert risks mismatch under shift. To address this, we propose MoBE: a fully optimization-free framework that performs dynamic expert selection and adaptation at test time. MoBE combines entropy-guided dynamic routing in MoE settings with expert-wise Bayesian adaptation, enabling experts to update their confidence and adapt online without gradient updates. 
Without parametric updates, MoBE augments a static MVLM with test-time routing and online statistics, achieving average accuracy gains of +4.72, +7.17, and +4.3 over state-of-the-art TTA methods across seen, unseen, and heterogeneous medical benchmarks, highlighting the effectiveness of training-free expert adaptation for robust modality generalization.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs
Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
Medical vision-language models (MVLMs) like BiomedCLIP achieve strong zero-shot performance, but fail under distribution shift from unseen or unknown modalities at test time. The paper identifies a specialization-generalization dilemma: blindly aggregating all modality experts dilutes specialized knowledge, while committing to a single expert risks catastrophic mismatch when the test modality is unknown. To address this, the paper proposes MoBE (Mixture of Bayesian Experts), an optimization-free test-time adaptation framework that dynamically selects and adapts modality experts at inference without any gradient updates or source data access. The main contributions of the paper are as follows:
1- The paper identifies the specialization-generalization dilemma in test-time modality adaptation for MVLMs, where blindly aggregating all modality experts dilutes modality-specific knowledge while committing to a single expert risks catastrophic mismatch when the test modality is unknown. 
2- Rather than using a fixed number of experts which requires manual tuning and performs inconsistently across modalities, MoBE proposes dynamic-k entropy-guided routing that selects a variable number of experts per test sample based on relative entropy differences between experts. Experts within an entropy gap \tau of the most confident expert are included and weighted by inverse-exponential entropy, automatically excluding mismatched experts while emphasizing the most modality-aligned ones. 
3- To address the centroid misalignment between pretrained class prototypes and test feature distributions, the paper proposes Expert Bayesian Adaptation (EBA), where each selected expert maintains two persistent memory variables updated online across the test stream without any gradient updates — class prototypes capturing evolving feature representations and class priors capturing the expert’s historical prediction tendencies. Both are jointly updated through confidence-gated running averages, enabling experts to continuously refine their predictions as more test samples are observed while remaining stable against noisy low-confidence updates.
reviews.text_strengths:
1- MoBE requires no gradient updates, no backpropagation, no source data access, and no modality labels at test time. This is a practically important property — it makes the method deployable in clinical settings where computational resources are limited and labeled data is unavailable.
2- Replacing fixed top-k selection with relative entropy thresholding removes the need to manually tune k per dataset. Figure 3b demonstrates that fixed top-k is sensitive to k — too many experts hurts performance — while dynamic-k automatically matches the best fixed-k performance across modalities. This is a practically meaningful contribution for deployment in diverse clinical settings.
3- The ablation experiments presented in Figure 3a clearly demonstrate the contribution of each component of the method. It is important to see that each component has meaningful contribution.
4- The method is evaluated across three distinct benchmark types (seen modalities, unseen modalities, and heterogeneous datasets) and two backbone families (BiomedCLIP and PubmedCLIP). The consistency of gains across all settings demonstrate the potential of the proposed method.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1- The paper never includes an experiment where the ground truth modality label is used to directly route to the correct expert. For seen modalities in Table 1 this is trivially available — ChestMNIST is X-ray, so simply using the X-ray expert directly would give a natural upper bound. Without this comparison it is impossible to know how much performance is lost due to routing errors, whether EBA adaptation improves over the correct expert alone, or whether dynamic-k routing successfully recovers modality-correct behavior. This is the single most important missing experiment in the paper.
2- The paper is clearly written but it may still be difficult to reproduce the results based on the description in the paper. The details such as the MLP expert architecture, training hyperparameters, the confidence thresholds, the blending parameter \lambda and the entropy gap threshold \tau
are all unreported or underspecified to fully reproduce the results. Furthermore, no source code is provided nor is there any promise to release it upon acceptance. Taken together, these omissions make it effectively impossible for other researchers to independently verify or build upon the reported results.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses a well-motivated and clearly articulated problem — test-time modality generalization in MVLMs — with an elegant optimization-free framework that combines dynamic expert routing and Bayesian adaptation. The empirical results are consistent and convincing, and the ablation studies provide reasonable validation of the key components. However, the paper falls short of a confident accept primarily due to reproducibility concerns as no code is provided or promised. I recommend weak accept, acknowledging that the core idea is sound and the results are promising, but encourage the authors to release code. I would be happy to increase my rating to accept if other reviewers do not identify stronger concerns and authors promise sharing their code.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of this paper is the proposal of an optimization-free method for test-time modality generalization in medical vision-language models. By combining entropy-guided dynamic expert selection with expert-level Bayesian online adaptation, the method enables test-time adaptation to distribution shifts without backpropagation, and its effectiveness is validated on multiple medical imaging benchmarks.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The proposed framework is attractive from a deployment perspective because it is optimization-free at test time. Instead of relying on backpropagation, it combines entropy-based dynamic expert selection with Bayesian online adaptation.
2.The paper explains its method design through the specialization–generalization tradeoff in MoE settings, providing an intuitive framework for why dynamic expert selection is needed.
3.The experimental evaluation includes unseen modalities and heterogeneous medical datasets, which allows the paper to assess the generalization ability of the method from multiple perspectives.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The authors investigate how medical vision-language models can perform test-time adaptation. They propose a fully optimization-free framework that performs dynamic expert selection and adaptation at test time. By augmenting a static MVLM with test-time routing and online statistics, the method improves performance over current state-of-the-art test-time adaptation (TTA) methods on seen, unseen, and heterogeneous medical benchmarks. However, the work still has the following limitations:
(1). The authors’ method is built upon five modality-specialized experts, which are derived from MLP branches fine-tuned on ROCOV2 after partitioning the data by modality. While this design is reasonable in itself, it also means that, compared with single-model baselines, the method introduces additional modality-specialized structure and parameters. The current experiments are still insufficient to fully disentangle whether the observed improvements come primarily from the test-time adaptation mechanism itself, or to a significant extent from the added expert structure and modality-specific priors.
(2). The method involves several key hyperparameters and design choices, such as the threshold for dynamic-k routing, the confidence thresholds in EBA, the fusion coefficient, and the way the test stream order is defined. Test-time adaptation methods are typically quite sensitive to sample order, threshold settings, and initialization strategy.
(3). There is an inconsistency between Table 3 and the main text regarding the average accuracy on the heterogeneous benchmark.
(4). Although the authors emphasize that the method does not require backpropagation, the multiple expert forward passes themselves still impose a nontrivial deployment overhead.
(5). Are some classical CTTA methods developed for conventional models, such as CoTTA, also effective for medical VLMs?
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

It addresses an important problem for the real-world deployment of medical vision-language models and proposes a practically appealing optimization-free test-time adaptation framework centered on dynamic expert routing and Bayesian online adaptation. The experimental evaluation is also relatively broad, covering seen, unseen, and heterogeneous benchmarks, and the ablation studies provide some support for the proposed design. If the authors release anonymized code and a README to improve reproducibility, I would consider raising my score later.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of this paper is the proposal of MoBE (Mixture of Bayesian Experts), a fully optimization-free test-time adaptation framework designed to improve the modality generalization of Medical Vision-Language Models.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The shift from gradient-based test-time adaptation (like TENT or MoME) to a Bayesian, memory-based updating mechanism is highly original and practical. By updating statistical variables (prototypes and priors) rather than network weights, the method avoids catastrophic forgetting and significantly reduces the computational overhead typically associated with continuous learning at test time.
2.The dynamic-$k$ routing with inverse-entropy weighting is a highly elegant solution to the MoE routing problem. Using a relative gap threshold ($\tau$) rather than a hard cutoff ensures that the model can dynamically fall back on multiple experts when uncertainty is high, or rely on a single expert when confidence is absolute.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The framework’s success relies heavily on the semantic foundation provided by the 5 pre-trained ROCOv2 modality experts (CT, MRI, X-ray, Ultrasound, Angiogram). As seen in the BloodMNIST (microscopy) results, when a target modality is entirely disjoint from the source experts’ knowledge base, the entropy-based routing loses discriminability, and performance gains are marginal.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper offers an elegant, optimization-free solution to test-time modality shifts in medical VLMs by combining dynamic expert routing with Bayesian updates. Its strong empirical validation and clinical feasibility make it a highly compelling contribution despite a minor increase in inference overhead.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
The reviewers provided scores of accept, weak accept, and weak reject.
The main reason for the weak reject, according to the justification section, is that the authors do not share the code. This issue was also raised by Reviewer 1.However, MICCAI guidelines do not require code release for acceptance. Although I encourage the authors to share the code, this should not be considered an acceptance criterion.
All reviewers are generally positive about the work, including the methodology, broad experimentation, clinical feasibility, efficiency, and performance gains. The remaining concerns are minor and can be addressed with small changes in the final version of the manuscript. Therefore, I recommend acceptance and encourage the authors to incorporate the reviewers’ comments into the final version.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback. We are encouraged that Reviewer_1 valued MoBE’s training-free deployment, dynamic-k routing, clear ablations, and consistent gains; Reviewer_2 highlighted the optimization-free design, intuitive specialization-generalization motivation, and broad seen/unseen/heterogeneous evaluation; and Reviewer_4 recognized the originality and practicality of Bayesian memory adaptation with dynamic-k routing. We address the concerns below and will incorporate the clarifications, and will release our GitHub codebase with camera-ready submission.
Reviewer_1–
1.1 [Routing with Ground Truth Labels]: We thank the reviewer for this important suggestion. Fig. 1(b) compares expert routing using self-entropy versus cross-entropy. The latter uses ground-truth labels and therefore serves as an oracle comparison. Although this is a compact figure, it shows that self-entropy-based routing can be a practical alternative when labels are unavailable at inference. We agree that an additional modality-wise ablation comparing oracle versus self-entropy routing would be valuable; however, due to space constraints and the inclusion of several other ablations, we summarized this comparison through Fig. 1(b).
1.2 [Reproducibility]: We agree that some implementation details should be stated more explicitly. Sec. 3.1 already specifies the backbone, frozen encoders, (E=5) ROCOv2-derived experts, modality partitioning, preprocessing, batch size, GPU, and evaluation metric. We will add the missing values for the MLP architecture, tau, theta_1, theta_2, and stream ordering in a few additional lines in the camera-ready version. The algorithm itself is defined by Eqs. (1)-(5). Overall, we will release the code publicly with camera-ready submission.
Reviewer_2–
2.1 [Component-wise effect]: We agree that MoBE benefits from both modality-specialized experts and test-time adaptation. Fig. 3(a) disentangles these effects by comparing frozen BiomedCLIP, fixed top-(k) MoE, dynamic-(k), EBA, and full MoBE. This ablation shows that expert structure helps, dynamic routing improves expert selection, and EBA adds further gains through online posterior refinement.
2.2 [Reproducibility]: We will clarify the selected hyperparameter values and test-stream ordering to make the method reproducible. We will also release the code.
2.3 [Typo]: Correct. The heterogeneous benchmark average is 46.49%, as reported in Table 3.The main text value 46.69% is a typo and will be corrected to 46.49%. This does not change the conclusion that MoBE achieves the best average performance.
2.4 [Additional forward passes]: We agree. MoBE avoids backpropagation but still requires multiple expert forward passes. Table 5 already reports this trade-off: MoBE is slower than frozen BiomedCLIP but faster than optimization-based MoME while achieving higher accuracy. We will state this limitation explicitly in the paper.
2.5 [CoTTA baseline]: We compare against representative TTA/VLM adaptation baselines, including TENT, EATA, TPT, WATT, TDA, CoOp/CoCoOp, and MoME. CoTTA is designed for teacher-student updates and augmentation consistency in conventional classifiers, which does not directly match our frozen zero-shot MVLM setting.
Reviewer_4–
4.1 [Available experts’ dependency]: We agree. MoBE relies on the semantic coverage of the available expert bank. BloodMNIST illustrates this limitation: microscopy is weakly covered by the five ROCOv2 experts, making entropy less discriminative and reducing gains. This defines the operating regime of MoBE rather than contradicting the method: routing and EBA are most effective when the expert bank partially covers the test modality. A sentence around this will be added in the main paper, that future work should expand expert coverage or add fallback/rejection mechanisms for poorly covered modalities.

title: Cancer-Type-Agnostic Pan-Cancer Gene Expression Prediction from Histopathological Images
abstract: Gene expression profiles play a crucial role in understanding cancer pathogenesis, guiding personalized treatment, and predicting clinical outcomes. However, traditional gene expression detection relies on invasive tissue sequencing, which is time-consuming and costly. Existing image-based gene prediction methods are often limited to specific cancer types and fail to adapt to the pan-cancer scenario with diverse histological features. To address these challenges, we propose a novel pan-cancer image-based gene expression prediction method (PIGP) that enables gene expression prediction without the need for prior acquisition of cancer type information. Specifically, the model directly extracts discriminative features from pan-cancer histopathological images to preliminarily determine the cancer type, and further combines pan-cancer networks and corresponding cancer-type-specific networks to predict the corresponding gene expression levels. Extensive experiments on the pan-cancer dataset (HEST) have shown that the Pearson correlation coefficient for specific genes reaches up to 0.743. Moreover, heatmaps and distribution maps confirm the biological rationality and interpretability of the predicted results. This approach provides a cancer-type-agnostic computational framework for pan-cancer gene expression prediction and may support future translational studies. Our code is available at https://github.com/oceanflyfly/PIGP
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers
Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of the paper is the formulation of pan-cancer gene expression prediction from histopathological images without prior knowledge of cancer type, framed as an open-set generalization problem.
reviews.text_strengths: A major strength of the paper is the extensive experimental evaluation. The authors validate their approach across a large number of datasets (10) and compare different embedding strategies using as many as 13 models, which is a substantial effort. This breadth of experimentation provides a solid and comprehensive assessment of the proposed method and strengthens the credibility of the reported results.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
A main weakness of the paper concerns clarity and presentation rather than the overall approach. In particular, some claims appear overstated, such as describing the method as a “universal solution” with strong clinical translation potential, which should be moderated given the current level of validation.
Additionally, the manuscript would benefit from clearer positioning of the data modality. It should explicitly state early on that the approach is based on spatial transcriptomics, rather than generically referring to histopathological images, to avoid confusion with standard WSI-only settings.
Finally, some methodological details are not sufficiently specified. For instance, the selection and role of the genes used in the experiments are not clearly described, which limits interpretability and reproducibility.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I recommend acceptance as the methodological approach is well-grounded and clearly structured. The experimental setup is comprehensive and up-to-date, and the extent of the evaluation is particularly strong, involving a large number of datasets and embedding models. These aspects collectively support the overall quality and relevance of the work.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have significantly improved the manuscript during the rebuttal phase, further strengthening a work that was already of high quality in its original submission. The revised version provides clearer explanations and a more polished presentation of the methodology and results, making the overall contribution more solid and convincing. Overall, I believe the revisions positively enhanced both the clarity and the impact of the paper.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper’s main contribution is a novel method (PIGP) to infer gene expression from H&E-stained histological slides. The method aims to address two major limitations in existing gene expression prediction methods: lack of spatial context and cross-cancer heterogeneity. It does so by using 2 specific modules, each designed to deal with one of the drawbacks: a graph convolutional layer is tasked to bring spatial awareness in each spot’s representation while a duplicated branch deals with the cross-cancer generalization (with one branch being cancer specific and the other global).
Extensive experiments on an adapted HEST-1k benchmark demonstrate superior performance compared to the approach introduced in the benchmark paper, across both tasks and foundation models.
reviews.text_strengths:
While spatial context modelling is not novel itself in gene expression prediction (HisToGene, Hist2ST, iSTAR, MISO), to the best of our knowledge, this is the first cancer-aware architecture proposed for this specific task within the digital pathology community.
Beyond the novelty, the major strength of the paper lies in the scale of its experiments: the benchmark covers 13 foundation models and 10 indications, with the paper’s method demonstrating shared improvements across tasks and extractors. This outlines the broad generalization capability of the method.
Another strong point is the ablation study. It effectively highlights the importance of the dual-branch component; compared to using a GCN alone, this addition almost systematically increases performance (in 125 out of 130 task x model pairs).
reviews.text_weaknesses:
We noted several weaknesses:
Regarding methodology, gene expression prediction from H&E images is not a new task, and several methods have tried to tackle the issue (e.g. ST-Net, HisToGene, Hist2ST, iSTAR, MISO, in addition to those cited by the authors). There is no comparison with any existing methods beyond the simple ridge regression used in the HEST-1k paper. If none of the existing methods are applicable to the setting chosen by the authors, it would be interesting to state it explicitly and detail why.
The paper would also benefit from several clarifications, regarding missing information and inconsistencies:
The authors state that 13 highly variable genes were selected for the tasks, whereas the original HEST-1k paper uses 50 genes.
