2) The caption of fig. 2 refers to the synthesis phase (“VQ-VAE decoding”) but this is not illustrated. In fact, the inference process is not clearly described in the manuscript and should be explicitly detailed.
3) What does “label y” (Fig. 1) represent in your present scenario/task?
4) What is the reason behind the distinct number of slices used when resampling the volumes in the public and private datasets? Is the median number of slices indeed 6 for both public datasets? This seems low for clinical CMR acquisitions.
5) What is the embedding dimension of CardioDiT (variable e in section 2.2)? Is it the same as the autoencoder?
6) Please clarify the meaning of “physiologically uninterpretable” EF values for the factorized 2D+t LDM. If this refers to inconsistencies in temporal dynamics (due to independent slice synthesis), this should be explicitly stated. As written, the statement could be interpreted as referring to spatial discontinuities (as also observed in Fig. 2), which may occur in practice (due to breath-hold acquisition) and do not necessarily invalidate EF estimation.
7) Please justify the decision to merge the results of the two public datasets, and clarify how this was performed (e.g., averaging metrics across datasets vs. computing metrics jointly over all samples).
8) Please comment on the W2 results. CardioDiT appears closer to the training distribution than the real test set is, which may suggest potential overfitting or memorization effects.
9) Similarly, the reduced variability in volume curves (as suggested by the narrower IQR in Fig. 3) may indicate limited sample diversity. It would be helpful to discuss this aspect. Future work may consider complementing the analysis with diversity or coverage metrics.
Minor remarks:
Some abbreviations (e.g., VQ, VAE, GAN) are not defined at first use.
VQ-VAE is referred to as “VQ-GAN” in Fig. 1; please standardize the terminology.

While the manuscript presents a well-executed study with strong experimental validation and compelling results, the novelty and positioning of the methodological contribution are not sufficiently clear, particularly in relation to closely related prior and concurrent work. A more explicit and careful framing would strengthen the manuscript and better delineate its contribution. That said, the overall quality of the analysis and experimental evaluation is solid and supports acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I update my recommendation from weak accept to accept. The manuscript presents a strong experimental study with compelling results, and the rebuttal somewhat clarifies the positioning of the contribution with respect to prior and concurrent work (one would expect the camera-ready version to follow accordingly). I also appreciate the additional methodological clarifications regarding implementation details, temporal processing, inference, and metric computation. While I still believe some concerns, particularly regarding memorization/diversity assessment and the interpretation of unreliable EF estimation, were perhaps dismissed somewhat too readily in the rebuttal, they do not detract significantly from the overall quality and validity of the work. Considering the strength of the experimental validation, the relevance of the task, and the overall impact of the results, I believe the manuscript is worthy of acceptance.
reviews.text_ethics: The authors make use of a private dataset (page 3), but no explicit statement is provided regarding ethical approval or IRB compliance.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces CardioDiT, a latent diffusion framework for unconditional synthesis of short-axis cine cardiac MRI that operates on full 4D (3D spatial + temporal) volumes rather than factorized 2D+t or channel-merged 3D+t representations. A spatiotemporal VQ-GAN first encodes 2D+t slices into a compact latent space; the resulting per-slice latents are then stacked and processed jointly by a Diffusion Transformer with 4D positional encodings and FlashAttention. The paper evaluates this approach against progressively stronger baselines on public (ACDC + M&Ms-2) and private multi-scanner datasets using a clinically grounded metric suite that includes CineMA-based FID, through-plane structural similarity (d-SSIM), inter-slice alignment (ARED), and ejection-fraction distribution matching.
reviews.text_strengths:
The controlled experimental ladder from 2D+t factorized to 3D+t channel-merged to fully 4D diffusion provides a clear and well-motivated comparison structure. Few papers in cardiac generative modeling attempt this kind of progressive ablation across spatiotemporal coupling strategies, and the design itself should be useful as a template for future work in this area.
The evaluation metric suite goes meaningfully beyond FID-only assessment. The inclusion of ejection-fraction distribution matching via Wasserstein distance, through-plane alignment (ARED), and domain-specific FID computed with CineMA foundation model features rather than ImageNet-pretrained Inception reflects careful thinking about what matters for cardiac MRI synthesis.
CardioDiT-L achieves better distributional quality than the 3D+t U-Net baseline at roughly one-third the parameter count (177M vs. 578M) and less than half the VRAM, with the full pipeline fitting within 24 GB. This practical accessibility lowers the barrier for academic labs working with consumer-grade GPUs.
The scalability ablation across three model sizes (S/B/L) with explicit reporting of parameter counts, inference times, and VRAM requirements provides useful engineering guidance and demonstrates that the framework has room to grow with additional compute.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The baseline comparison simultaneously changes the architecture class (U-Net to transformer) and the spatiotemporal coupling strategy (factorized to joint 4D), making it impossible to attribute improvements to 4D coupling specifically. A factorized DiT baseline (using separate spatial and temporal attention within the same transformer framework) would have isolated the variable the paper claims to study. Without this control, the central thesis that joint 4D modeling is the key driver of improvement remains plausible but not conclusively supported, and the evidence is equally consistent with transformers simply being more efficient than U-Nets for this task.
All quantitative comparisons use only N=50 synthetic samples with no confidence intervals, bootstrap estimates, or significance tests. At this sample size, FID and precision/recall can exhibit substantial variance, and because all metrics are computed on the same 50 generated samples they are not statistically independent. The quantitative differences in Table 1 should therefore be treated as preliminary rather than established. The paper does not explain why N=50 was chosen or whether it reflects a computational constraint.
The model achieves recall of 0.70 on the public dataset and 0.54 on the private dataset, meaning it fails to cover 30-46% of the real data distribution. For the paper’s stated applications of data augmentation and privacy-preserving sharing, systematically excluding nearly half the anatomical and pathological diversity is a serious limitation. The paper does not analyse which phenotypes or modes are missing, nor does it discuss the downstream consequences of this coverage gap.
Despite the “fully 4D” framing used throughout the abstract and introduction, the VQ-GAN encodes 2D+t slices independently along the depth axis, meaning inter-slice spatial information is discarded before the transformer stage. The 4D coupling is introduced only at the diffusion model level. The paper does not test whether a 3D-aware autoencoder would improve results or analyze how much inter-slice information the current factorized encoding loses.
The core transformer block architecture is specified only in supplementary material of a concurrent, unpublished submission that was not available for review. This means the reviewable novelty reduces to the 4D extension (positional encodings and patchification), and independent reimplementation from the main text alone is not possible. Additionally, the temporal standardization to 32 frames via cyclic repetition could inflate temporal consistency metrics by imposing artificial periodicity, yet no analysis of this effect is provided.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses a genuinely important question and introduces a clinically grounded evaluation framework that the field should adopt. However, the experimental evidence does not adequately support the central claim. The most critical issue is that the baseline comparison confounds architecture class with coupling strategy: the observed improvements may reflect the advantage of transformers over U-Nets rather than the benefit of 4D joint modeling. A factorized DiT baseline would have resolved this ambiguity and was feasible within the scope of the work. The evaluation, while thoughtfully designed in its choice of metrics, is statistically underpowered at N=50 with no uncertainty quantification, and the substantial recall gap (covering only 54-70% of the real distribution) goes unanalyzed despite being directly relevant to the paper’s stated applications. The dependence on an unpublished concurrent submission for the core architecture specification further limits what can be assessed from the manuscript alone. A revision addressing the factorized transformer baseline, larger-sample evaluation with confidence intervals, and analysis of the recall gap and cyclic repetition confound would substantially strengthen the contribution.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The rebuttal addressed the cyclic-repetition concern by clarifying that temporal metrics are computed over one detected cardiac cycle rather than the padded 32 frame window, so the artificial periodicity cannot inflate temporal consistency scores. The recall discussion is also correctly reframed and the relative ordering across baselines (with CardioDiT best) still remains. The N=50 choice is now reasonably justified by sample-size matching with the validation set, and the authors explicitly commits to editing Table 1 to soften the claims.
On the central methodological critique (comparison confounds architecture class with coupling strategy) the authors do not run the factorized-DiT control but narrow the claim from “4D coupling causes the gains” to “a joint 4D transformer is an effective realization of spatiotemporal coupling”, which is what the experiments actually support.

meta_reviews.text:
Reviewers agree the paper tackles an important problem in 4D cardiac MRI synthesis and includes a strong empirical evaluation across datasets with clinically relevant metrics. Two reviewers rated it Weak Accept, while one raised concerns about novelty and experimental attribution. The rebuttal should clearly position the contribution relative to closely related prior/concurrent work, justify whether gains stem from full 4D modeling rather than architecture changes, and clarify statistical robustness and implementation details.

The paper presents a well-motivated framework for 4D cardiac MRI synthesis. Reviewer opinions diverged after rebuttal: R1 moved to reject; R2 and R3 moved to accept. The central confound, that gains may reflect the transformer-over-U-Net advantage rather than 4D joint modeling per se, was not resolved experimentally, and the authors narrowed their claim accordingly. The authors are expected to incorporate the reframed novelty positioning, and add the clarified implementation and temporal processing details in the final version.

The rebuttal narrows the claim appropriately and two reviewers moved to Accept. R1 remains Reject, but the main remaining concern is attribution of gains rather than fatal unsoundness. Camera-ready should explicitly soften “fully 4D proves superiority” claims and state that the factorized-transformer control is future work.

This paper proposes CardioDiT, a full 4D implicit diffusion framework designed to address spatiotemporal consistency in cardiac MRI generation. However, the main conclusion that highlighting the role of full 4D modeling for improvement of anatomical and temporal consistency, is not well supported according to the current experiments. This is a non negligible issue that was not resolved in the rebuttal, leading the paper unacceptable for publication.

author_feedback_text: Novelty & baselines(R1/Q1,Q2,Q5;R2/Q1;R3/Q1). We agree related work should be clearer, will add [15] to the introduction and adjust novelty framing. [17] models only ED/ES phases; [15] uses the same latent encoding but a channel-merged LDM with a 3D U-Net denoiser, i.e. our 3D+t baseline. CardioDiT instead models the latent cine volume as spatiotemporal patches with global self-attention. This offers direct long-range slice-time coupling instead of indirect receptive-field growth, improving consistency and fidelity. 4D coupling & architecture(R3/Q1;R1/Q2). Do gains stem from 4D modelling or architecture? Our comparisons increase coupling progressively: 2D+t via inter-slice conditioning, 3D+t within the U-Net class, and CardioDiT via global attention over latent spatiotemporal patches. We do not claim that every gain isolates “4D coupling” independently of architecture; rather, a joint 4D transformer is an effective realization of such coupling. Moving from 2D+t to 3D+t improves consistency but reduces fidelity. Concurrent work (supplement) suggests that replacing U-Nets with transformers improves diffusion fidelity, here translated to 4D. An in-depth analysis of factorized transformer modules [11] is future work. Implementation & temporal processing(R1/Q4,Q8;R2;R3/Q5). Clarification on implementation and temporal metrics: We will revise Fig. 1/caption and Sec. 2.1-2.2 to explain inference/VQ decoding. The supplement details DiT architecture; code/configs will be public. The label y is zero as no labels were available; embedding dimension e matches the autoencoder. Temporal metrics used one cardiac cycle with detected key frames, so temporal consistency is not a metric artifact. Statistical Robustness(R3/Q2). We agree uncertainty estimates would strengthen interpretation and will temper claims. N=50 per model matches the 50 validation cases, ensuring equal real/synthetic sample sizes. Notably, feature metrics use 50 × 32 time-point vectors, not only 50 volume-level vectors. This improves stability relative to one feature vector per volume, and trends are consistent across data pools/ablations. Using the same 50 samples per model supports comparable metrics. We acknowledge that Tab. 1 differences are preliminary. Future work will synthesize larger cohorts and report significance where applicable. Scope. Several suggestions concern further analysis. We emphasize that the manuscript already provides a broad evaluation within the 8-page limit: multiple distributional and functional metrics, diverse private/public data pools, visual analysis, and ablations. We will expand the discussion on augmentation/privacy and on extension to other dynamic modalities. 4D modelling(R1/Q3;R3/Q4). Concerns regarding the “fully 4D” claim and the absence of end-to-end latent representation: “Fully 4D” refers to the DiT operating on the latent 3D+t volume. The 2D+t VQ-GAN follows cine CMR acquisition: anisotropic slices with coarse through-plane resolution but fine in-plane temporal detail. To our knowledge, no established 3D+t/4D VQ-GAN exists for this setting. Systematically comparing latent encoders is beyond scope. Diversity(R2;R3/Q3). Recall indicates imperfect coverage: Recall is a limited feature-space estimate, not direct phenotype diversity and should not be read as exactly 30% absent phenotypes. Within this limitation, CardioDiT has the best recall among compared methods. W2 was computed on validation samples, so it does not imply memorization and may reflect EF differences between splits. Clarifications(R1/Q1,Q6,Q7;R2). Public datasets were merged before training and evaluated jointly over all validation samples. Volumes were cropped to preserve cardiac content. Charts use public samples or samples generated from models trained on them. The 2D+t baseline shows discontinuities from independent slice synthesis, not breath-hold artifacts; hence, EF estimation is unreliable. All clarifications will be added in the camera-ready upon acceptance.

title: CardioGS: Deformation-Driven 4D Gaussian Splatting with Self-supervised Cardiac Clock Learning for Rotational DSA Reconstruction
abstract: Rotational digital subtraction angiography (DSA) captures sparse C-arm projections of beating coronary vasculature over a 5–8 s sweep, where each frame conflates two temporally distinct processes: quasi-periodic cardiac motion deforming vessel geometry and monotonic contrast-agent transport modulating opacity. Under sparse views, parameterizing both with a single acquisition timestamp is highly ambiguous. We present CardioGS, a deformation-driven 4D Gaussian Splatting framework that reduces this ambiguity through dual temporal coordinates. A self-supervised ClockNet learns a monotonic cardiac clock u(τ)∈[0,1] via Gauss–Legendre quadrature of a bounded instantaneous frequency, adapting to heart-rate variability without ECG gating. Since u(τ) is monotonic, quasi-periodicity is imposed through cycle-consistency regularization on sparse deformation control nodes. Geometry is conditioned on the learned clock while appearance is conditioned on acquisition time in canonical space. On porcine rotational cardiac DSA with 15–60 views, CardioGS outperforms recent baselines in both 2D synthesis and 3D vessel geometry. The code is available at: https://github.com/131366/cardiogs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents CardioGS, a deformation-driven 4D Gaussian Splatting framework for reconstructing coronary vasculature from sparse rotational digital subtraction angiography (DSA). The key challenge addressed is the non-identifiability caused by cardiac motion under sparse acquisition. The method uses temporal modeling: a self-supervised ClockNet learns a monotonic cardiac clock, after which geometry and appearance are conditioned on temporal variables. This allows improved reconstruction on porcine DSA data.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper addresses a challenging and clinically relevant imaging scenario of rotational DSA, operating under sparse-view acquisition conditions. The proposed method demonstrates improvements over baselines. In addition, the inclusion of ablation studies helps clarify the contribution. Finally, the public release of the code is a strong positive aspect.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The framework combines multiple sophisticated components, which makes the overall method difficult to interpret. Most of mathematical formulations would benefit from additional intuition to improve accessibility. For example, the curriculum design with the parameter beta seems heuristic, and its impact is not evaluated. Furthermore, several limitations could be more explicitly discussed: for example, since the deformation model depends on the learned cardiac clock, inaccuracies in ClockNet negatively affect geometry reconstruction.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Overall, I lean toward a weak accept, as the paper addresses a clinically relevant and challenging problem with improved performance, despite a complex and somewhat heuristic design.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Some claims are not formally justified.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose a method to decouple opacity changes caused by contrast agent transport from vessel geometry deformations induced by cardiac motion. The paper comes with the design of the architecture that uses three separate modules for three separate tasks to build the time dependent 3D Guassian Splatting representation. The first module’s goal is to predict the patient’s heart rate that is then used by the second module to model vessel geometry changes caused by cardiac motion. The last module is used to estimate gaussian opacity parameters with respect to the time, which gives the model a chance to take into account contrast agent transportation flow between reference frames. The information flow is designed in a way that blocks responsible for opacity never know about geometry deformations and geometry blocks know nothing about the opacity changes, which makes cardiac motion and contrast agent transport influences separated. Authors provide experimental evidence demonstrating that the proposed architecture outperforms prior approaches in terms of 3D reconstruction quality.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper is well written and concise. The architecture figure is particularly informative, making the overall approach clear and easy to understand.
2.The idea of splitting time conditioning into two separate factors, cardiac motion and contrast agent transport, rather than using a single temporal input, is both novel and well-motivated. The experimental results indicate that this design choice leads to noticeable improvements in 3D reconstruction quality. More broadly, the findings suggest that modeling different sources of temporal inconsistency separately is beneficial not only for reconstruction performance but also for improving model interpretability.
3.The proposed approach appears adaptable to other 3D reconstruction tasks, such as lung imaging, suggesting broad applicability.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Regarding the cardiac clock, while the rationale for avoiding direct modeling of the modular phase is well explained, it is not entirely clear why the model predicts heart rate (frequency) instead of directly estimating the final conditioning u(tau). Additional clarification on this design choice would strengthen the methodological justification.
2.The discussion of limitations and future work could be expanded. A slightly more detailed analysis would help readers better understand the broader implications of the proposed approach and its potential impact on the field.
The authors adopt a control-node-based approach to manipulate
3.Gaussian geometries. It would be valuable to understand whether this design choice is driven purely by computational efficiency or also by domain-specific considerations related to vessel structures. Additionally, it raises the question of whether directly manipulating Gaussian parameters could further improve reconstruction quality, even at the cost of increased computational complexity.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Overall, I find this paper to be solid, well-executed, and meaningful. The proposed architectural design is clear, well-motivated, and supported by experimental results demonstrating improvements in 3D reconstruction quality. In particular, the explicit disentanglement of cardiac motion and contrast agent transport is an interesting and promising idea that contributes to both performance and interpretability, and may have relevance beyond the specific application studied.
That said, I do have several questions, particularly regarding certain design choices, and some aspects of the method could benefit from further clarification or justification. While these concerns are not fundamental flaws, they slightly limit my confidence in the overall strength and generality of the contribution. Addressing these points would strengthen the paper and improve its clarity.
Overall, I lean toward a Weak Accept.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I would like to thank the authors for their detailed and highly convincing rebuttal. They provided an excellent, mathematically elegant explanation for why the model predicts instantaneous frequency rather than directly regressing the cardiac clock. Integrating this frequency naturally guarantees monotonicity while allowing the extraction of the total cycle count, which is critical for defining the cycle-consistency loss. Furthermore, the authors successfully clarified that the control-node graph is much more than a computationally driven design choice. It actually serves as a vital spatial regularizer that enforces coherent vessel motion and prevents isolated local deformations under highly sparse projections. I also appreciate their willingness to adjust the manuscript’s claims regarding identifiability and their honest discussion concerning dataset limitations. The proposed method for decoupling quasi-periodic cardiac motion from monotonic contrast agent transport is highly innovative and yields strong experimental results. Because the rebuttal thoroughly addressed my main concerns and strengthened my confidence in the paper, I am upgrading my recommendation to Accept.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors have developed a Gaussian Splatter method, CardioGS. CardioGS is a deformation driven 4D Gaussian Splatting framework that reconstructs 3D vessel geometry. THe are doing so by utilizing i) ClockNet, ii) Curriculum learning, and iii) Sparse control node deformation graph with cycle consistency.
reviews.text_strengths:
Major Strengths:
1.Monotonic cardiac clock controls the continuous positional encoding and provides cycle consistency regularization. Instead of using raw timestamp conditioning alone, the model learns a monotonic reparameterization of time through an instantaneous frequency integrated by Gauss–Legendre quadrature.
2.Well discussed theory and components needed for the moving pieces of this work. 
3.The deformation module is not an unconstrained per-point warp. It is a sparse control-node graph with KNN-RBF interpolation, plus cycle-consistency regularization. That is a good compromise between flexibility and stability.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Major Weakness:
1.Even though the field is queried in canonical space, the 4D hash grid still allows, (i) temporal variation that mimics motion and (ii) especially along projection rays. This is apparent when I looked at the shared repository. 
2.ClockNet enforces monotonicity (this is good), but there is a high chance it will learn neal-linear mapping from the data due to KNN based graph formation.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

There are several inconsistencies. A core reason is the limitation itself. the proposed framework is the inherent ambiguity in disentangling deformation, appearance, and temporal dynamics from projection-only supervision. Despite the use of canonical-space modeling and cycle-consistency regularization, multiple latent configurations can produce similar rendered projections, potentially leading to non-unique or biased solutions.
If the authors can defend this position, I am willing to change my score.
Another issue that I request the authors to fix is their reference section. The formatting and information for some of the reference needs attention.

reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents CardioGS, a deformation-driven 4D Gaussian Splatting framework that restores identifiability through dual temporal coordinates. The results show its promising performance compared to the SOTA models in both 2D synthesis and 3D vessel geometry.
