meta_reviews.text:
This submission proposes coronary reconstruction using 4d gaussian splats. The reviews are found constructive and feedback converges on: appreciation of the disentanglement of cardiac motion and contrast agent propagation, but also on lacking clarity of the method (difficult interpretation of combination of multiple components) and design choices. High suspicion of AI generated text including likely hallucinated references (e.g., 13). Serious clarifications to these major concerns may improve the quality, and better highlight the relevance of the submission. For these reasons, and with respect to the other submissions, the recommendation is towards requesting a rebuttal for serious clarification on methodological inconsistencies, and design choices.

The authors successfully addressed most major methodological concerns regarding the cardiac clock, and spatial regularization in their rebuttal. Although concerns still remains due to lingering doubts about formal disentanglement guarantees, the overall agreement is that there are no major flaws preventing publication of this preliminary work. Recommendation is towards Borderline Acceptance.

The concerns were mainly on overstated claims while rebuttal is mainly to clarify and explain without adding new experiments or results. On an engaged count of two accepts and a deferring reject, with a third standing weak accept, the paper clears the bar. A worry about AI-style text and one likely fake reference is identified, so this MUST be handled in the camera-ready submission. What need to be handled too is “the lack of guarantees for disentanglement” pointed by R1 who vote for accept but still not convinced. I stand with R1 too. I recommend accept but not top of the batch.

The authors have largely clarified the previously unclear points in their rebuttal, and most of the reviewers appear satisfied with the responses, with agreeing on acceptance. The AC therefore recommends acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for constructive comments that help improve the manuscript’s clarity and rigor.
Reference reliability [Meta,R3]. Ref. 13 has an erroneous/incomplete entry due to a verification oversight. It served only as broad DSA background, not to support any method assumption, loss term, comparison, or conclusion. We apologize; it will be corrected or removed, and references re-checked for accuracy and relevance.
Projection ambiguity [Meta,R3]. We agree projection-only supervision cannot guarantee unique disentanglement of appearance, deformation, and temporal dynamics. Similar projections may arise from true displacement or opacity changes that alter apparent vessel location and perceived motion along projection rays. CardioGS does not prove uniqueness; its separated opacity-at-τ and clock-conditioned geometry pathways make the ambiguity more constrained, improving conditioning relative to generic time-conditioned fields. Opacity is queried at canonical undeformed Gaussian positions and acquisition time τ, so it cannot directly move centers/covariances. Geometry uses a spatially coherent, clock-conditioned sparse control-node graph with cycle consistency. We will use “reduces ambiguity” or “improves conditioning,” not “restores identifiability.”
Method design and reliability [R2,R3,R1]. [R2: frequency vs. u(τ)] The learned frequency is the positive cardiac-clock progression rate; integrating gives cumulative progress w(τ)=∫_0^τ f_θ(s)ds, so u(τ) is monotonic while allowing nonuniform progression. With a smooth unwrapped clock rather than a wrapped phase, cycle consistency needs the scale of one cardiac cycle in normalized u-space. The integral gives C=w(1); after normalization, one cycle corresponds to Δu=1/(C+ε). Direct u(τ) regression is possible, but would need extra monotonicity constraints and a separate cycle-scale estimate.
[R3: near-linear clock] A clock close to acquisition time is valid when cardiac progression is regular. ClockNet does not force nonlinearity; it is adaptive, near-linear for regular motion and nonlinear when progression is irregular. Graph topology/RBF weights are built from canonical 3D positions, while node transforms are time-conditioned; thus KNN formation enforces spatial coherence, not temporal linearity.
[R2/R1: deformation prior, beta, clock sensitivity] The graph is not merely computational; it encodes coherent vessel motion. CardioGS remains per-Gaussian, but shared control nodes/KNN-RBF couple deformations, avoiding isolated local geometry explanations under sparse projections; node-number ablation and the graph gain support this expressiveness-regularization trade-off. Beta is a stability curriculum: start with reliable acquisition-time conditioning, then introduce learned-clock conditioning. It was set by stability tuning; fuller hyperparameter study remains future work. If clock prediction is inaccurate, geometry may degrade, especially with irregular motion/poor projections. Yet even in the hardest 15-view case, experiments show no systematic degradation.
Data scope and metric/visual gap [R4]. [R4: private data] Evaluation is on one private in-vivo porcine rotational cardiac DSA dataset; we acknowledge this limitation. To our knowledge, no comparable public cardiac benchmark provides dynamic projections, calibrated geometry, and dense-view 3D reference. Once new public/internal in-vivo DSA data become available, we will expand evaluation for fair comparison.
[R4: metrics vs. visualization] R2-Gaussian is t-independent; 4DRGS models time-dependent rendering. For quality metrics, R2-Gaussian outperforms 4DRGS only on CD/HD at 15 views; its lower GauN is expected for a static model. Its worse PSNR/SSIM and visualization indicate weaker temporal rendering. CD/HD after ICP favor phase-averaged 3D alignment under extreme sparsity, whereas visualization and PSNR/SSIM reflect dynamic 2D synthesis; this is not a contradiction to dynamic modeling.

title: CARE: Clinically Aligned Retrieval Evidence for Consistent Radiology Report Generation
abstract: Automatic radiology report generation has the potential to assist radiologists by providing preliminary clinical descriptions. Despite recent progress in medical vision-language models, generated reports often contain factual inconsistencies and repetitive templated findings, indicating weak grounding to image evidence. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves grounding by conditioning on prior reports; however, existing end-to-end optimization suffers from representation inconsistency, as actively updated query representations diverge from stale historical keys. This mismatch destabilizes the retrieval space and disrupts supervision. We propose CARE (Clinically Aligned Retrieval Evidence), a multimodal framework introducing temporally coherent retrieval supervision. CARE maintains a shared memory queue populated by a slowly evolving momentum key encoder to ensure a stable representation space. We further introduce a disease-aware alignment objective that enforces diagnostic agreement between input images and retrieved reports to guide generation. Trained on IU-Xray and evaluated on the unseen MIMIC-CXR-RRG dataset, CARE significantly improves report quality. It nearly doubles clinical entity extraction performance in training-free adaptation settings and substantially reduces repetitive report collapse across multiple backbones. The source code is available at: https://github.com/Levii-zhu/CARE
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose CARE (Clinically Aligned Retrieval Evidence), a multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework designed to improve the factual consistency of radiology reports. To solve the representation inconsistency caused by actively updated queries diverging from stale historical keys during end-to-end training, CARE implements a slowly evolving momentum key encoder coupled with a shared memory queue. Additionally, it introduces a disease-aware alignment objective to ensure that the retrieved evidence is diagnostically compatible with the input visual features.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) Elegant Theoretical Motivation: The paper identifies a fundamental bottleneck in end-to-end RAG optimization—the destabilization of the retrieval space. Adapting the momentum update mechanism (inspired by contrastive learning paradigms like MoCo) to manage cross-modal retrieval queues is a technically sound and elegant solution. 
2) Exceptional Zero-Shot Domain Adaptation: The framework exhibits remarkable out-of-domain generalization. On the unseen MIMIC-CXR benchmark, simply populating the external memory queue with target-domain text (without any image or label fine-tuning) nearly doubled the clinical entity extraction performance (RG-F1), highlighting its flexibility for real-world deployment. 
3) Effective Mitigation of Mode Collapse: The N-gram diversity analysis effectively proves that CARE successfully breaks the “shortcut learning” loop. By anchoring generation to stabilized retrieved evidence, the model avoids regurgitating rigid, repetitive templates (e. g. , defaulting to “clear lungs”), resulting in richer and more clinically detailed reports.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) Frozen LLM Limits Deep Adaptation: The framework freezes the core LLM parameters during training to save compute, optimizing only the query encoder and projection layers. While efficient, this approach may bottleneck the model’s ability to deeply internalize complex, institution-specific reasoning logic or highly specialized syntactic styles for longer reports. 
2) Unverified Robustness to Noisy Retrievals: The system assumes the retrieval queue will return highly relevant and accurate evidence. However, real-world Electronic Health Records (EHR) are notoriously noisy. The paper lacks an ablation study or stress test demonstrating the generator’s robustness and self-correction capability when forced to condition on erroneous or contradictory retrieved reports. 
3) Absence of Human Expert Evaluation: Although the automated clinical metrics (e. g. , RadGraph F1) show significant improvement, these metrics cannot fully capture clinical fluency, coherence, and clinical utility. The lack of qualitative assessment by expert radiologists slightly weakens the clinical impact claims.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

CARE provides a highly effective, theoretically grounded solution to a known problem in RAG-based report generation. The stabilization of the retrieval space via momentum encoders yields undeniable empirical benefits, particularly in zero-shot cross-dataset generalization. My score is slightly conservative (Weak Accept) because of the reliance on the rigid CheXbert labeler for alignment and the lack of an anonymized code repository for review. I look forward to the authors’ rebuttal regarding the ablation study on the unseen dataset and their plans for reproducibility.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have addressed the majority of my concerns.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: Addresses a Real and Underexplored Problem (RAG Instability) and Identifies a subtle but important issue: representation inconsistency in end-to-end RAG training. Proposes a momentum memory queue to stabilise the retrieval space. This is a meaningful systems-level contribution, not just performance tuning.
reviews.text_strengths:
Well-Motivated Retrieval Design (MoCo-style for Multimodal RAG)
Adapts momentum encoder + memory queue (from contrastive learning) to both multimodal retrieval and report generation.
Clinically Meaningful Alignment Objective
Introduces disease-aware alignment loss and enforces diagnostic consistency between input image and retrieved reports.
Improves Generalization
Demonstrates training-free adaptation to unseen dataset (MIMIC-CXR) with nearly 2× improvement in entity extraction (RG-F1).
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Method is well-engineered but lacks strong conceptual novelty. Core components are known: MoCo-style momentum encoder RAG, contrastive learning, label alignment.
Still Relies on Retrieval Quality (Upper Bound Issue), no mechanism to verify or filter incorrect retrieved evidence.
No Fine-Grained Alignment: Alignment happens at report level (retrieval) not at entity-level grounding or region-level correspondence.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N.A.

Please see strength and weakness above. Overall, it’s an useful application in the clinical domain and improvements are clearly illustrated throughout the manuscript.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: concerns well addressed. recommend for acceptance.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents a method for improving radiology report quality via a framework that alters the RAG of a VLM. A momentum encoder and a shared memory queue are added to the model, which smooths the retrieval representation space during optimization. Additionally, a disease-aware alignment objective is employed to encourage retrieval of cases with similar pathologies. This is implemented as a softmax relaxation in the label space and is paired with the query encoder to couple the retrieval with visual representation. The retrieved evidence is combined with image features and fed into an LLM to produce the output radiology report. The method is fine-tuned on the IU-Xray dataset and evaluated on both the IU-Xray dataset and the unseen MIMIC-CXR-RRG dataset. Nine metrics are employed for comparison: Mi-F1, Ma-F1, RG-F1, RG_ER, and CliQ0 for the clinical metrics, and B-1, B-4, MTR, and R-L for the lexical metrics.
reviews.text_strengths:
The generalization study of training on IU-Xray and assessing on MIMIC-CXR-RRG is appreciated to assess the ubiquity of the method
Multiple models are employed for testing the method (LLaVA-Med and LLaVA-Rad), which further helps to give generalized performance measures, as LLMs are known to produce wildly varying results depending on the system prompt and employed model.
The provided ablation study justifies the inclusion of the various proposed components.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Of all the employed metrics, the ones that are most relevant to clinical utility appear to be RG-F1 and CliQ0.However, the model consistently underperforms in these categories compared to other methods. Thus, the claims by the authors for the utility of the method are dubious. It is unclear to this reviewer how any of the other proposed benefits of the model, such as the N-grams in Figure 2 or the lexigraphical metrics, can outweigh the impact of superior clinical accuracy metrics.
An opportunity is missed to compare the proposed method fine-tuned on the MIMIC-CXR dataset to compare with state-of-the-art performance models. The provided method demonstrates highly substandard performance to the fine-tuned methods. While this is somewhat expected, it could have been counterbalanced with a fine-tuned example.
The CheXbert F1 score is mentioned on page 5, but does not appear to be reported in any of the tables.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The labels in figure 2 are too small and should be increased for readability.
The image in Figure 3 is formatted poorly and should be larger for visibility.
The paper uses the term “hallucinations” twice. The term is highly ambiguous can refer to several different items; see https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41811081/ for a overview of some of the definitions (although the work unfortunately lacks citations for many of the employed definitions). Various definitions have been posed by entities such as OpenAI (https://storage.prod.researchhub.com/uploads/papers/2020/06/01/language-models.pdf) and (very recently) the FDA (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ailsci.2025.100145). To promote scientific clarity and preciseness, I suggest that the term hallucination be changed to a more precise phrasing for the two occurrences in the paper, or an explicit definition of the term with a relevant citation provided in the introduction.

My impression of this paper is that it fails to improve performance compared to other approaches on the most relevant metric for clinical tasks. Compared to RG-F1 and CliQ0, every other metric appears to be a distraction. Furthermore, overall performance is substantially substandard compared to fine-tuned models, which further restricts the applicability of the method.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
I thank the authors for their response to the provided feedback, particularly the clarifications about the CheXbert F1-score. However, this new information only leaves me with a sense that the results are muddled and inconclusive.
After reading the other reviewer’s comments, the impression I am left with of this paper at the end of the review process is that it is an incremental advancement with limited novelty aimed at a functional application. However, the desired function (training-free cross-domain adaptation in the medical domain) retains astoundingly low performance. It is unclear if the proposed method will be of any utility when such a solution becomes practical, as it is likely that the underlying technology must change a substantial amount before reaching usability.
Since the authors mention that they are targeting practical clinical deployment in their work from the second line in their rebuttal, I lean towards rejection as I believe that they have failed to make meaningful steps towards that goal. Sufficient novelty would persuade me that progress is being toward a more permanent solution, but the current contribution, to me, appears transient in nature.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper addresses the instability of retrieval-augmented generation in radiology. Existing RAG frameworks often suffer from “representation drift,” where updated query encoders diverge from static historical keys in the retrieval database. CARE introduces a momentum-based retrieval supervision mechanism to maintain a stable representation space. This is paired with a disease-aware alignment objective to ensure that retrieved reports provide a consistent diagnostic prior for the language model decoder.
While the paper presents good contributions, its recommendation for acceptance is contingent upon the authors clarifying the following points during the rebuttal phase:
1.A significant concern is the model’s reliance on the quality of retrieved evidence. Reviewers noted that the framework lacks a mechanism to filter or “self-correct” when the retrieval queue returns erroneous, noisy, or contradictory reports from the EHR.
2.While the paper highlights improvements in linguistic metrics, reviewers pointed out that the model underperforms in categories most relevant to clinical utility, such as RadGraph F1 and RadCliQ. The reviewer argued that lexical diversity or N-gram improvements cannot outweigh the impact of superior clinical accuracy, making the authors’ claims regarding clinical utility questionable.
3.The framework is seen as well-engineered but conceptually incremental. It relies on established components like MoCo-style momentum encoders and standard contrastive learning. Furthermore, alignment occurs only at the report level. The model lacks entity-level grounding or region-to-text correspondence, which limits its ability to pinpoint specific visual findings.

The authors have addressed the reviewers’ comments well. Two reviewers acknowledged significance of the work. Therefore acceptance of the paper is concluded.

The scores are still mixed after the rebuttal. Although CARE is well motivated, I recommend rejection. The contribution is incremental, adapting known momentum-queue and contrastive ideas to RAG, while lacking entity- or region-level grounding and robust filtering of noisy retrieved evidence. Most importantly, the method underperforms on key clinical utility metrics such as RG-F1 and CliQ0, and the rebuttal does not convincingly establish practical clinical value or meaningful progress toward deployment.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their highly constructive feedback and recognition of CARE’s theoretical motivation. Our work resolves systems-level retrieval instability to enable robust, training-free cross-domain adaptation for practical clinical deployment. Primary concerns are addressed below.
Q1: (R1, R2) Robustness to noisy retrieved evidence.
Although CheXbert pseudo-labels are standard in prior work, CARE mitigates their rigidity through soft retrieval-guided conditioning rather than hard retrieval supervision. Retrieved candidates receive adaptive soft weights (α) based on continuous visual-textual similarity, naturally suppressing noisy or incompatible evidence during alignment. Generation is jointly conditioned on visual features and weighted retrieval evidence, while supervision still comes from the ground-truth report, reducing over-reliance on noisy retrievals. We will note the lack of adversarial stress-testing as a limitation.
Q2: (R3) Concerns regarding slightly lower RG-F1 and CliQ0 performance.
We agree that RG-F1 and CliQ0 are important clinically grounded metrics. However, these global overlap metrics may not fully capture sensitivity to less frequent pathological findings. Because normal cases dominate the training distribution, standard SFT models often converge toward repetitive “normal” templates, maintaining strong report-level scores while underdetecting abnormalities. This behavior is evident in LLaVA-Rad (SFT), which achieves high RG-F1 (38.0) but lower pathology-sensitive performance (5Mi/5Ma-F1: 34.4/23.2), and is even more severe in LLaVA-Med (1.0/0.3). In contrast, CARE stabilizes retrieval grounding and consistently improves abnormality sensitivity across both backbones (35.1/26.9 and 20.4/15.4). Our diversity analysis is intended as complementary evidence that CARE mitigates repetitive template collapse rather than memorizing dominant normal patterns. We will clarify this distinction more explicitly in the revised paper.
Q3: (R3) Missing comparison to MIMIC-CXR-fine-tuned version.
We would like to clarify that while supervised models naturally achieve higher MIMIC-CXR scores, CARE targets a fundamentally different setting: training-free cross-domain adaptation. In clinical environments, institutions often lack the computational resources or annotated data required for repeated retraining. Under this zero-shot constraint, adapting the retrieval memory via CARE demonstrates significant effectiveness, improving RG-F1 from 7.0 to 13.0 without any target-domain training. We will clarify this in the revised paper.
Q4: (R2) Conceptual novelty.
While the core components (e.g., MoCo) are established, our novelty is functional rather than strictly architectural: resolving an underexplored systems-level instability in multimodal RAG. Beyond expanding the negative pool, CARE leverages the momentum queue to maintain a temporally stable retrieval space. Prior systems assume a static space; updated queries drift from stale queue keys, destabilizing LLM retrieval supervision. CARE stabilizes this process, ensuring reliable supervision under distribution shifts. We will clarify this stabilization perspective more explicitly in the revised manuscript.
Q5: (R1) Frozen LLM.
We froze the LLM to isolate our retrieval stabilization module and maintain a minimal training footprint. This bottlenecks internalizing institution-specific syntactic styles; integrating PEFT (e.g., LoRA) will be outlined as a next step.
Q6: (R3) Missing definition of “CheXbert F1 score”.
We apologize for the missing definition of “CheXbert F1 score”, which we refer as 5Mi-F1 and 5Ma-F1 metrics in tables 1 and 2.We will clarify this in the dataset and evaluation metrics section.
Other comments:
We will improve figures qualities with more enlarged labels and clearer format (R3). We will also rephrase “hallucination” to “factual inconsistency” for a more precise expression (R3). Our code will be released upon acceptance (R1, R2).

title: CARE: Confidence-Aware Reasoning for Reliable Medical VQA
abstract: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) has enabled medical Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to produce Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning for visual question answering, yet these models suffer from confidence miscalibration—a systematic gap between expressed certainty and actual diagnostic accuracy that undermines clinical trust. We propose CARE, a Confidence-Aware medical REasoning framework that jointly optimizes accuracy and calibration through a dual-stage pipeline. First, a scalable Medical-CoT synthesis provides structured cold-start data for Supervised Fine-Tuning. Second, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a novel Confidence-Aware Reward (CAR) mechanism ties the model’s confidence to diagnostic correctness within the reward signal. Across three Medical VQA benchmarks, CARE achieves the highest diagnostic accuracy while obtaining the lowest Expected Calibration Error and Hallucination Rate, establishing a foundation for trustworthy clinical decision support.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs
Machine Learning -> Reinforcement Learning / Control / Decision-Making

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents CARE, a two-stage post-training framework for medical VQA that targets both diagnostic performance and confidence calibration. The method first constructs label-consistent medical chain-of-thought trajectories and then trains a Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone via SFT followed by GRPO using a Confidence-Aware Reward (CAR). CAR defines confidence from the model’s own token probabilities and rewards high confidence on correct outputs while penalizing high confidence on incorrect ones. Experiments on VQA-RAD, SLAKE, and PathVQA evaluate accuracy/recall, ECE, and hallucination rate against several recent medical reasoning MLLM baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper addresses a clinically meaningful problem that is more specific than simply improving Med-VQA accuracy. Focusing on whether model confidence tracks diagnostic correctness is important for triage, escalation, and safe downstream use, and this is a well-motivated target for medical reasoning models.
The proposed training recipe is simple and practically implementable. CAR is integrated directly into GRPO without introducing a separate uncertainty head or a complicated auxiliary model, which makes the method easy to understand and potentially easy to adopt in related medical MLLM pipelines. 
The empirical results are strong and consistent on the reported benchmarks. In Table 1, CARE is the only method reported to rank first across accuracy, ECE, and hallucination rate on all three datasets, which suggests that the method is not merely trading calibration for accuracy or vice versa.
The training-stage analysis is useful. The separation of Training-Free, SFT, RL, and SFT+RL provides a more informative picture than a single end-point comparison, and the open-ended versus closed-ended discussion offers practical insight into when structured CoT initialization appears most helpful.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The central contribution of CAR is not cleanly isolated by the current ablations.
Table 2 varies training stages, but there is no same-backbone comparison between RL with a standard accuracy/form reward and RL with CAR.
The evaluation metrics could be removed to set aside more room for ablation studies.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper is well organized, the practical motivation is clear, and the headline empirical numbers are strong across three benchmarks. It could be better if the ablation studies provides more evidence of the performance gain brought by CAR.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The author response can address my concerns.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes CARE, a confidence-aware reinforcement learning framework for medical VQA. It introduces a confidence-based reward to align model confidence with diagnostic correctness. The method combines CoT data synthesis, SFT initialization, and RL optimization. Experiments show improvements in accuracy, calibration, and hallucination across multiple benchmarks.
reviews.text_strengths:
Strengths
1.The paper studies confidence miscalibration in medical VQA. This is an important and practical problem for clinical deployment.
2.The pipeline is clear and well structured. The combination of CoT data synthesis, SFT initialization, and RL optimization is easy to follow.
3.The experiments cover multiple datasets. The evaluation includes accuracy, calibration, and hallucination metrics. Results are consistently strong across benchmarks.
4.The overall presentation is good and easy to follow
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Weaknesses
Method
1.The paper defines confidence as the average token probability of the generated output. This definition is explicit, but is it a valid proxy for answer-level confidence? It seems closer to generation likelihood than epistemic uncertainty. How sensitive is this measure to output length or decoding settings such as temperature?
2.The method may lack sufficient insight. Several recent works [1,2,3] have explored confidence-aware or confidence-driven optimization. What is the key methodological difference between CAR and these approaches?
3.The reward design may not guarantee true calibration. It encourages higher confidence scores derived from token-level probabilities on correct outputs and penalizes them on incorrect ones. But does this ensure alignment with empirical accuracy, or only reshape token-level likelihood?
Experiments
1.The hallucination metric relies on a VLM judge (Lingshu-32B), but the inference setup is unclear. How are temperature, prompting, and evaluation consistency controlled?
2.The contribution of the proposed reward is not isolated. In Table 2, the ablation only compares training stages, without isolating CAR. It may be helpful to include comparisons with RL without CAR to better understand its impact.
3.It may also be important to report statistical significance. In Table 1, results on small datasets such as VQA-RAD are presented without variance. How stable are these improvements across different runs?
[1] Gu, Bowen, et al. “Probabilistic medical predictions of large language models.” npj Digital Medicine 7.1 (2024): 367.[2] Li, Pengyi, et al. “Confidence is all you need: Few-shot rl fine-tuning of language models.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2506.06395 (2025).
[3] Prabhudesai, Mihir, et al. “Maximizing confidence alone improves reasoning.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2505.22660 (2025).
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper studies an important problem and presents a clear pipeline with strong empirical results across multiple benchmarks. However, the method is not fully convincing. The confidence definition based on token-level probabilities is not well justified, and the contribution of the proposed reward is not clearly isolated.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Thank you for the clarification on the confidence computation, the role of CAR, and the evaluation settings. These responses address most of my concerns. The hallucination evaluation setup is clearer, though the reliability of the judge could still be better validated in future work (e.g., consistency across multiple evaluation rounds). Overall, I find the rebuttal convincing and will support acceptance.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces an automated pipeline for constructing reasoning trajectories from visual content, questions, and answers, along with a novel reward mechanism designed to calibrate the output token confidence of the reasoning model, which encourages high confidence for reasoning paths that lead to correct answers and low confidence for those that do not.
reviews.text_strengths: The research problem addressed in this paper, calibrating the output confidence of MLLMs, is both practical and significant. Well-calibrated confidence scores can serve as a critical indicator for clinicians, enabling them to better assess the reliability of model outputs and make more informed decisions.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The connection between the two proposed contributions needs to be clarified. Specifically, it remains unclear how the constructed CoT data benefits the confidence-calibrative RL training, or conversely, how the proposed RL reward leverages the constructed CoT data to achieve better calibration. Further elaboration on the interplay between these two components would help readers understand how they jointly strengthen the overall framework.
2.The novelty of the proposed CoT curation process warrants further clarification. Several existing methods already construct CoT data from visual content, questions, and final conclusions [1], making the distinction of the proposed approach less apparent. Including a discussion of related multi-modal medical CoT construction methods (e.g., [1][2]) would provide important context and help readers better appreciate the specific contributions of this work.
3.The rationale behind the confidence calibration reward requires more justification. The reward is computed by averaging the confidence scores across all output tokens; however, not all tokens are equally informative with respect to the final conclusion — for instance, tokens such as
or punctuation marks carry little semantic relevance. Whether the inclusion of such tokens distorts the reward signal is not discussed. Additionally, the claim that "a white-box signal derived from the model's own output distribution can be directly tied to diagnostic correctness within the reward function" lacks sufficient supporting evidence and should be substantiated more rigorously.
4.Additional experiments are needed to more convincingly support the paper’s claims. The rationale for benchmarking compact-scale models (≤3B parameters) against the trained 7B model should be clarified, as this comparison may not be entirely fair. More importantly, ablative studies that individually quantify the contributions of the proposed CoT construction and the new reward to overall performance improvement are necessary. The current ablation focuses on different training schemes, which does not directly validate the two core contributions. Furthermore, the confidence shift shown in Figure 3 is somewhat expected given that the reward directly supervises this behavior. A more informative analysis would present the confidence shift conditioned separately on correct and incorrect conclusions, which would provide stronger evidence that the model genuinely learns to re-calibrate its confidence during the reasoning process rather than simply responding to the reward signal.
[1] Niu, Shuai, et al. “Multimodal clinical reasoning through knowledge-augmented rationale generation.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2411.07611 (2024).
[2] Sun, Haoran, et al. “Chiron-o1: Igniting multimodal large language models towards generalizable medical reasoning via mentor-intern collaborative search.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2506.16962 (2025).
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1.Figure 2 contains display errors in the Confidence-Aware Reward section that should be corrected before publication.
2.The confidence allocation depicted for the “Wrong Diagnosis” case in Figure 1 may be misleading to readers. The model appears to exhibit a low confidence distribution when producing an incorrect answer, which could actually be interpreted as a desirable behavior, since outputting a wrong answer with low confidence is generally preferable to doing so with high confidence. Clarifying the intended message of this illustration, and distinguishing between what the current model does versus what the proposed method aims to achieve, would help avoid confusion.

The unclear connection between the two proposed contributions, the insufficient justification for the confidence calibration reward, the limited novelty of the CoT data curation pipeline, and the lack of ablative experiments that directly validate the core claims, collectively prevent me from recommending acceptance at this stage. Substantial revisions addressing these issues would be necessary before the paper is ready for submission to another venue.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I thank the authors for their efforts. The rebuttal adequately addressed my concerns regarding the confidence calibration reward design, which should be reflected in the revision. However, my concerns about the CoT construction method remain unresolved. In the rebuttal, the authors stated that “the Medical-CoT synthesis is not claimed as a standalone novelty over prior medical rationale construction.” Yet in the original manuscript, the CoT construction method is listed as a main contribution, occupies roughly half of the main figure, and is described in a dedicated subsection. This inconsistency leaves the concerns raised in Points 1 and 2 of my original review unaddressed. Additionally, the authors introduced new experimental results directly in the rebuttal, and it is unclear whether these can be fully incorporated and discussed in the revision within the page limit. For these reasons, I am moving my rating to Weak Reject, but still leaning towards rejection.

meta_reviews.text:
As the AC, personally I like this paper and I believe my judgement is also aligned with the reviewers. The strength of this work is clear, e.g. topic relevance, well-structured story and the comprehensive evaluation.
I invite the authors to rebuttal and would like to see if the following potential weaknesses can be addressed:
1.Explanation about the validity of the answer-level confidence proxy 
2.The methodology differentation to the similar works as mentioned by R2 and R4
3.The persuasiveness of the evaluation, e.g. statistics analysis, the contribution of the proposed CoT construction and reward design
Good luck!

The authors offered a detailed rebuttal and several concerns are well addressed. I recommend the acceptance of the paper, but the authors shall not view this work as the final product of the project. If you want to publish at a higher platform, you may also want to address the weaknesses of using generated CoT supervision and judge-based hallucination scoring. Best luck and looking forward to seeing your future work.

As noted by the reviewers, many raised concerns have been properly addressed in the rebuttal. A remaining point of dispute concerns the curation of SFT cold-start data. The meta-reviewer partly agrees with R3’s argument that, as CoT synthesis for cold start is a common practice, the authors should not overclaim their contribution in this regard in the camera-ready version.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the AC and reviewers for recognizing the clinical relevance, clear story, and comprehensive evaluation of CARE. The major concerns are whether CoT/CAR contributions are isolated, confidence validity, and how CARE differs from related work. We address them below.
Ablation for CoT and CAR (R1Q1/R1Q2/R2Q5/R4Q4). We conducted an ablation study under different GRPO settings on SLAKE:
Setting / ACC / ECE / HR
Base GRPO: 71.25 / 25.92 / 16.37
with CoT: 77.94 / 18.89 / 14.88
with CAR: 82.47 / 14.83 / 12.38
CARE: 87.30 / 11.50 / 7.01
This confirms their complementarity: CoT strengthens reasoning initialization, while CAR improves calibration beyond standard GRPO.
Validity of confidence proxy (R2Q1/R4Q3/R2Q3). Prior work defines calibration as confidence-performance alignment [1]. Accordingly, we use ECE to directly evaluate whether our answer-level confidence proxy aligns with actual accuracy. The consistent ECE reductions in Table 1 and our new ablation support the validity of this proxy, showing that CAR improves confidence-accuracy alignment rather than merely increasing likelihood.
Differentiation from confidence-driven works (R2Q2). Mentioned rencent work ask the model to report confidence, or reward high confidence alone. Instead, CAR use confidence in GRPO as a correctness-conditioned calibration term.
Does CAR really recalibrate? (R2Q3/R4Q4). We further added conditioned confidence analysis on VQA-RAD. After CAR, confidence increases on correct predictions and decreases on incorrect predictions:
OPEN Question: correct +0.84, incorrect -0.59
CLOSED Question: correct +0.07, incorrect -0.16
This shows CARE shifts confidence according to correctness.
Statistics (R2Q6/R4Q4). We added statistical analysis on VQA-RAD (4-times):
Model / ACC / ECE
MedVLThinker-7B: 65.44±0.68 / 45.95±0.53
Lingshu-7B: 65.99±2.21 / 40.51±1.33
CARE: 76.32±0.95 / 20.31±1.28
CARE remains clearly better than strong 7B baselines in both accuracy and calibration, supporting the stability of the improvement on this small dataset.
Differentiation from medical CoT works (R4Q1/R4Q2). The Medical-CoT synthesis is not claimed as a standalone novelty over prior medical rationale construction. Its role is to provide a cold start for confidence-aware RL. CoT stabilizes the reasoning format and answer span, reduces noisy exploration in open-ended medical reasoning, and supplies structured trajectories whose final answers can be verified. Thus, CoT improves reasoning structure, then CAR aligns answer confidence with correctness.
Confidence computation in CARE (R4Q3). We compute confidence only within the
span, excluding reasoning, formatting, and special tokens (like
). The claim mentioned in your question can be support by ECE metrics in our experiment, detailed explanation please refer to the second response question. This is also consistent with recent confidence-based reasoning studies [2].
Evaluation details and fairness (R1Q3/R2Q4/R4Q4/R4Q5/R4Q6). We will add the full hallucination-judge protocol: Lingshu-32B uses deterministic decoding, a fixed prompt/rubric, identical inputs for all methods, so random seeds do not affect the judge outputs. Compact models are included only for completeness; the primary comparison is with 7B-8B models, where CARE still leads. We will also fix the Fig. 2 rendering issue, revise Fig. 1 to distinguish existing miscalibration from CARE’s target behavior, and remove metric details to save space for ablations.
We believe these new ablations, conditioned confidence analysis, and statistical results directly address the main concerns and substantially strengthen the evidence for CARE.
[1] Taming Overconfidence in LLMs: Reward Calibration in RLHF, ICLR 2025.[2] Confidence as a Reward: Transforming LLMs into Reward Models, ICLR 2025.

title: CARformer: Class-Aware Representation Learning for Small-Cohort, Imbalanced Psychiatric Disorder Classification in Brain MRI
abstract: Structural MRI (sMRI) has revealed morphological correlates associated with psychiatric disorders, motivating neuroimaging-based diagnostic support tools. However, multi-class classification from sMRI remains chal-lenging in small-cohort psychiatric settings, where site-level datasets often contain only a few hundred subjects and exhibit class imbalance, and where subtle inter-class differences further complicate discrimination. We propose a class-aware representation learning framework (CARformer) that adapts domain-pretrained encoders for 3D sMRI multi-class psychiatric classifica-tion. The framework includes (1) a class-aware Bag-of-Queries (CA-BoQ) module that learns class-aligned query representations to aggregate class-specific dis-criminative evidence under inter-class differences, and (2) a Class-Aware Contrastive (CAC) learning strategy that strengthens class separation under imbalance. We evaluated the framework across two sites from a public brain MRI dataset to assess robustness under differences in diagnostic composition, class imbalance, and imaging acquisition proto-cols. Our results demonstrate consistent improvements in macro AUC and AUPRC over existing standard 3D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) backbones and domain-pretrained fine-tuning frameworks across both sites, supporting the practical utility of class-aware adaptation of domain pre-training in small-cohort, imbalanced psychiatric imaging tasks. Source code is available at: https://github.com/xyfu33/CARformer.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose a novel framework, termed CARformer, to address the challenges of small-sample, class-imbalanced, and multi-class classification in psychiatric sMRI analysis. Specifically, the method introduces two novel class-aware components: the CA-BoQ module for class-specific feature aggregation and the CAC strategy for confusion-aware contrastive learning. Through evaluation on two independent clinical sites, the paper shows that the proposed approach outperforms several baseline methods and substantially improves the recognition of minority classes.
reviews.text_strengths:
Well-motivated problem setting: The study targets a highly relevant and practically important clinical challenge, namely small-sample, imbalanced, and multi-disease classification in psychiatric neuroimaging.
Methodological novelty: The “class-aware” design is conceptually interesting and appears well tailored to the problem setting.
Rigorous experimental evaluation: The method is assessed on two independent and heterogeneous clinical sites, which strengthens the robustness of the findings and suggests good generalization potential.
Promising empirical performance: The reported improvements are clear, especially for minority classes, with particularly notable gains on metrics such as AUPRC.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a meaningful methodological idea and promising empirical results, particularly for minority-class recognition. However, the current manuscript requires substantial revision before it can meet the standard for publication, mainly because the description of the method lacks essential details, which raises concerns regarding rigor and reproducibility.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors’ response is comprehensive and substantive. They have directly provided the key methodological details that were previously missing, making the overall rationale, implementation, and reproducibility of the CARformer framework much clearer. Regarding the control of potential confounding factors, the authors also offered a reasonable explanation that is consistent with common practices in clinical neuroimaging research. Based on these revisions and responses, I believe that the manuscript has now reached an acceptable level for publication.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors build on a domain-pretrained 3D Uniformer encoder and propose CARformer, which combines a Class-Aware Bag-of-Queries module for aggregating class-specific discriminative representations for classification and a Class-Aware Contrastive learning strategy for transfer learning. Overall, the paper presents a relatively complete class-aware representation learning framework and explores its potential for more objective diagnostic support in psychiatric disorders.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The motivation is well grounded. The paper tackles the problem under realistic clinical constraints, including small sample size, class imbalance, and limited single-site data, which makes the problem itself practically meaningful.
2.The dual-branch design is reasonable. The combination of global average pooling and CA-BoQ helps balance training stability and discriminability, which is a sensible design choice for this task.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The evidence for generalizability is insufficient. The experiments are conducted only on two sites from a single dataset, both from Japanese cohorts. There is no cross-dataset or cross-ethnicity validation, which limits the evidence for broader generalization. In addition, the set of baseline methods is relatively limited and somewhat outdated.
2.Important implementation details are missing. In particular, the paper does not clearly explain how the confusion matrix W is updated or how the corresponding weights are computed, which affects reproducibility and makes the CAC component harder to assess.
3.The interpretability claim is not sufficiently supported. The attention maps in Figure 2 do not appear to indicate stable and reproducible disease-related biomarkers across sites. This weakens the authors’ claims regarding spatial interpretability and biological consistency.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper does not yet demonstrate sufficient practical utility, and the experimental evidence is not strong enough to support its broader claims. In particular, the evaluation is limited to two sites from a single dataset, without cross-dataset or cross-ethnicity validation, and the set of baselines is relatively limited. As a result, the current study is insufficient to establish the method’s robustness and real-world applicability.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: After reading the rebuttal, I am satisfied with the authors’ clarification. My initial concern was partly due to my limited familiarity with this specific dataset and task setting. The authors’ response helped clarify the data usage and the motivation behind their experimental design. I now find their explanation reasonable and believe that the main concern I raised has been adequately addressed. Therefore, I am willing to revise my assessment in a more positive direction.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose a class-aware representation learning framework for multi-class psychiatric disorder classification from brain sMRI under small-cohort, imbalanced data distributions.
reviews.text_strengths: The authors propose a novel CARformer framework that integrates two complementary class-aware components to address multi-disorder discrimination under small-cohort, imbalanced psychiatric sMRI settings, which improves inter-class separability through class aware supervised contrastive supervision with confusion-informed negative re-weighting.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The introduction mentions co-morbidities and suggests that the methodology would be beneficial in determining overlap. However, the rest of the paper follows a traditional 3 group differential diagnosis path, all-be-it with the capability of handling different group sizes.
There is no real explanation as to why the accuracy for HC or MDD is significantly different between hospitals. Given the proposed method is only better in 50% of the measures in the KUT dataset it suggests that CARFormer is not so much better than the other methods tested.

N/A

The methodology does not seem to provide a significant improvement in accuracy compared to previous methods and there is no clear pathway to clinical application. Multimorbidity of psychiatric and neurodevelopmental disorders is an important area for research and this method may provide a useful tool in the future, but at present that has not been proven.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
This decision is grounded in the work’s clinically well-motivated research target on small-cohort imbalanced psychiatric disorder classification, the methodological novelty of the proposed CARformer framework, and valid dual-site experiments showing clear improvements for minority classes, alongside mixed but marginally competitive overall reviewer scores. To facilitate fair further evaluation, the authors must primarily address these key points: complete missing implementation details of CA-BoQ, GAP fusion and the confusion matrix update strategy, clarify unregulated clinical confounders like age and sex, respond to limited cross-dataset generalization and outdated baseline settings, justify unstable attention map interpretability and explain inconsistent model performance across experimental sites.

All three reviewers updated their final recommendations to Accept after reading the authors’ comprehensive rebuttal, which clarified key methodological details and improved the rationale and reproducibility of the CARformer framework. They found the authors’ explanation of confounding factor control aligned with common practices in clinical neuroimaging research and acknowledged that their initial concerns were partly due to a lack of familiarity with the dataset and task setting. Overall, they believe the authors’ responses have adequately addressed their comments.
Authors have adequately addressed all reviewers’ concerns. There is a consensus toward acceptance, which I agree with.

Based on the three post-rebuttal reviews, all reviewers are satisfied with the authors’ responses. Reviewer #1 finds the response comprehensive and substantive, noting that the manuscript has reached an acceptable level for publication. Reviewer #2 acknowledges that their initial concern has been adequately addressed and revises their assessment positively. Reviewer #3 confirms that the authors have adequately responded. Therefore, I recommend acceptance of this paper.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the Reviewers(Rs) and AC for their constructive feedback and for recognizing CARformer’s clinical motivation, class-aware methodological novelty, minority-class performance gains, and dual‑site evaluation in real‑world data conditions. We address the key concerns below and will add these clarifications and code-release information in the revised manuscript.
Methodology Clarification: (R1 Q7.1a) CA-BoQ and GAP logits are fused by weighted additive logit blending, z=z_GAP+ α*z_BoQ, with fixed α=0.3.GAP provides a stable global classifier from the pretrained encoder, while CA-BoQ uses K learnable class-aligned queries and a diagonal per-query head to produce class-specific logits. (R1 Q7.1b; R2 Q7.2) We clarify that the CAC confusion matrix W is updated only from validation predictions. Before the first validation pass, CAC uses uniform negative-pair weighting with W_ij=1.After each validation epoch, W is computed from the row-normalized validation confusion matrix, clipped to [1,2], with diagonal entries reset to 1; subsequent epochs use exponential smoothing with decay = 0.5.In CAC, W_ij reweights only negative pairs between classes, while positive pairs remain as weight = 1.(R1 Q7.1c) Class-query stability is supported by both architectural and regularization designs: (i) class-aligned query slots with LayerNorm before/after cross-attention and a shared diagonal class-query head; (ii) a query-diversity penalty (λ_div = 10^-3) to reduce query collapse. CAC operates GAP-pooled features rather than query embeddings. 
Confounder handling (R1 Q7.2): Table 1 reports diagnostic-group demographics and scanner protocols for each SRPBS site (Tanaka et al., 2021). Although the cohort is not fully matched across diagnostic groups at baseline, potential confounding was mitigated through site-specific evaluations and subject-level stratified train/validation/test splits, preserving diagnostic distributions and balancing age and sex across subsets.
Generalizability & baselines (R2 Q7.1) a) As a primarily methodological contribution, our experimental design was necessarily scoped by the availability of data. We note that the dataset we used is currently the only publicly available resource for the research community to study this clinically important problem. We will better justify this scope and explicitly discuss cross-dataset and cross-ethnicity limitations. b) Our baselines include 3D CNNs used for psychiatric sMRI classification (Zhang et al., 2023), BrainMVP (Rui et al., CVPR 2025) – a brain MRI pretraining model evaluated on brain MRI classification tasks and benchmarked against training-from-scratch and general/medical-domain SSL methods; and PCRLv2 (Zhou et al., TPAMI 2023), a strong medical-domain SSL framework. These represent task-relevant 3D sMRI classifiers and pretrained medical/brain MRI fine-tuning comparators, rather than only generic CNNs.
Attention map (R2 Q7.3) UTO and KUT involve different disease contrasts, HC/MDD/BD versus HC/MDD/SZ, Fig. 2 visualizes CA-BoQ’s class-specific attention within each differential-diagnosis task, rather than testing invariant disease biomarkers across sites. Because competing diagnoses differ, discriminative evidence for the same class, such as MDD, may also differ across sites. 
Site performance differences (R3 Q7.2) We like to respectfully suggest that HC/MDD metrics should not be interpreted as the same binary task repeated across hospitals; MDD is contrasted with BD in UTO but with SZ in KUT, and sites differ in class distributions and acquisition protocols. CARformer is designed to improve class separation, in highly imbalanced KUT setting, it achieved best macro AUC/AUPRC and substantially improving minority-class MDD AUPRC from 0.196 with ResNet18 (the second-best macro baseline) to 0.700.Comorbidity/overlap clarification (R3 Q7.1) We clarify that comorbidity/symptom overlap is used as clinical motivation for the difficulty of 3-class psychiatric differential diagnosis.

title: Case-Specific Priors-Guided Multimodal Fusion for Prognosis Prediction in Head and Neck Cancer
abstract: Accurate prognosis prediction for head and neck cancer typically necessitates integrating highly heterogeneous clinical and pathological evidence by sophisticated multimodal fusion. However, existing fusion techniques are usually grounded in case-generic clinical rationales about complementary synergies across modalities, underestimating case-specific variance. In this study, we propose a prognosis prediction framework that explicitly incorporates Case-specific Priors to guide Multimodal fusion (named CPM). It leverages broad medical knowledge of LLMs to characterize each case’s (case-specific) intra-modal contexts and inter-modal relations, as well as case-generic multimodal rationale, as priors, enabling three-stage priors-guided multimodal fusion: (i) Intra-modal Context-guided Calibration (IntraCC) that leverages case-specific intra-modal priors to guide feature calibration within each modality; (ii) Inter-modal Relation-guided Interaction (InterRI) that leverages case-specific inter-modal priors to guide pair-wise feature interaction in modality pairs; and (iii) Multimodal Rationale-guided Aggregation (MultiRA) that leverages case-generic multimodal priors to guide final feature aggregation over all modalities. On the well-established HANCOCK challenge dataset involving four distinct medical modalities, our CPM achieved a mean AUC of 83.98% for predicting 5-year overall survival and 2-year recurrence-free survival, improving upon the baseline by 7.58%, pioneeringly demonstrating the effectiveness of LLM-derived medical priors in guiding multimodal fusion for prognosis prediction.
subject_areas: Applications -> Outcome Prediction / Prognosis / Longitudinal Modeling
Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes CPM, a case-specific priors-guided multimodal fusion framework for head and neck cancer prognosis prediction. The key idea is to use an LLM to derive three types of clinically grounded priors for each case—intra-modal contexts, inter-modal relations, and a multimodal rationale—and then use these priors to guide fusion in three stages: IntraCC for modality-wise calibration, InterRI for relation-guided pairwise interaction, and MultiRA for final rationale-guided aggregation. The method is evaluated on the four-modality HANCOCK dataset and shows improved AUC over the selected baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The problem is meaningful and well motivated. The paper addresses an important limitation of existing multimodal prognosis models, namely that most fusion strategies are case-generic and do not explicitly account for case-specific cross-modal correspondence. This is a reasonable and clinically relevant motivation in heterogeneous oncology settings. 
2.The empirical results are promising. On the HANCOCK dataset, CPM achieves the best reported performance among the compared methods, and the ablation study suggests that each of the three stages contributes to the final result.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The whole framework depends on the quality of the LLM-generated priors, especially the inferred inter-modal relations. However, the paper does not provide direct validation of these priors, such as expert comparison, consistency analysis, prompt sensitivity, or error propagation analysis. This makes it unclear how trustworthy the priors are. 
2.The paper does not provide stronger evidence that the final system offers faithful, reliable, or clinically actionable interpretability beyond improved predictive performance.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

1.The paper addresses a meaningful problem and proposes a well-designed framework for case-specific priors-guided multimodal fusion. The idea of using LLM-derived priors to guide different stages of the fusion process is interesting, and the empirical improvements are encouraging. 
2.However, the approach depends heavily on the LLM’s ability to correctly interpret modalities and infer reliable relations, while the paper does not sufficiently analyze the trustworthiness or faithfulness of these priors. 
3.Although the method incorporates rich prior information, the final predictions lack case-level reasoning and do not provide sufficient interpretability.

By using the recently published large language models, it became feasible to analyse patients per cases and generate multimodal evidence,

N/A
