author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers (R1, R2, R3) and the Meta-Reviewer for recognizing the novelty and clinical relevance of the proposed ClinLoop framework. We are encouraged that R1 and R2 recommended acceptance, while R3’s weak-reject recommendation mainly concerns clearer experimental details and additional analysis. We are committed to releasing the code upon acceptance and reporting statistical analysis, including p-values, in the final paper.
R1: Clinician expertise and reviewer variability. The clinician-in-the-loop stage involved three breast imaging/oncology clinicians with 12, 8, and 5 years of experience, respectively. Disagreements were resolved by consensus; unresolved cases were assigned lower confidence tags rather than treated as high-confidence gold labels. As described in Sec. 3.4, all deferred cases and a budgeted subset of high-impact samples are reviewed, and confidence-tagged labels are fed back for iterative updates. Together with the ensemble disagreement check in Sec. 3.2, model-level uncertainty pre-filters ambiguous predictions for prioritized review, while confidence-weighted retraining down-weights uncertain judgments. This design mitigates both model uncertainty and inter-reader variability across different expertise levels.
R1/R2/R3: Code and reproducibility. We will release the training/evaluation code, configuration files, split-generation scripts, preprocessing instructions, and trained model recipes upon acceptance. The clinical images cannot be publicly released due to institutional governance, but we will provide sufficient implementation details to reproduce the method on comparable data.
R2: Statistical analysis. We agree that statistical testing should be reported. The manuscript uses 5-fold patient-level cross-validation with a held-out calibration split and reports discrimination, calibration, and selective-prediction metrics. We have now performed paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests across the five folds comparing ClinLoop with the strongest non-ClinLoop baseline. The main improvements are statistically significant (p<0.01). We will add mean±std and p-values for Macro-F1/Joint-Acc, ECE, and selective risk.
R3: Baselines and methodological details. We agree that the baseline descriptions were too compressed. We will expand Secs. 4.1–4.3 to clarify that all deep baselines use the same patient-level folds, preprocessing, augmentation, optimizer, and training schedule. Single-modality baselines use 3D ResNet-50/MedicalNet for CT/MRI and EfficientNet-B4/ImageNet for DM. Missing-modality baselines include late fusion, MoE-style fusion, and modality dropout, all re-implemented under the same protocol. Radiomics baselines use an IBSI-compliant PyRadiomics pipeline with first-order, shape, and texture features (GLCM/GLRLM/GLSZM), ICC-based reproducibility filtering, LASSO selection, and 5-fold CV-tuned LR/SVM. LLM baselines use the same case inputs described in Sec. 4.3 and map outputs to TNM labels. For ClinLoop, CT/MRI use slice-based attention aggregation, DM uses a 2D CNN backbone, and multimodal fusion is conditioned on a modality mask to support arbitrary input subsets.
R3: Ablation and component contribution. We agree that a dedicated ablation should be made explicit. We will add component-wise ablations for mask-conditioned fusion, ensemble/TTA uncertainty, conformal QA, modality-consistency checking, calibrated pseudo-labeling, and closed-loop clinician feedback. Tables 2 and 3 already show the benefit of the full loop; the added ablation will make the source of the gains clearer.

title: ClinRAG-GRAPH: Clinical-Prior Retrieval-Augmented Graph Model with Domain Adversarial Learning for Breast pCR Prediction
abstract: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) response prediction is clinically important for treatment stratification in breast cancer. However, robust pre-treatment pathological complete response (pCR) prediction remains challenging due to insufficient cross-modal modeling, multicenter imaging heterogeneity, and weak evidence-grounded interpretability. We propose ClinRAG-GRAPH, a Clinically informed Retrieval-Augmented Generation Graph framework, for pre-treatment pCR prediction from DCE-MRI, structured clinical variables, and biopsy-derived pathological biomarkers. ClinRAG-GRAPH constructs an intra-patient clinical-prior graph and applies a prior-guided relation-aware graph convolutional network for structured multimodal representation learning. To improve cross-center robustness, we introduce a dual-branch domain-adversarial learning strategy to suppress protocol-related MRI bias while preserving pCR-relevant features. To enhance interpretability, we further incorporate large language model (LLM)-driven subgraph RAG module that retrieves clinically analogous historical cases and integrates retrieved evidence for pCR inference. We assemble a large-scale multicenter NAC breast cancer cohort for extensive validation, drawing from two public sources and three in-house centers.Results show that ClinRAG-GRAPH achieves AUCs of 0.815 on the internal test set and 0.774/0.712 on two external test sets, demonstrating robust pre-treatment pCR prediction across centers. The code is available at the anonymized https://github.com/miccai26-1181/ClinRAG-GRAPH.
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers
Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper addresses the clinically significant task of pretreatment pathological complete response (pCR) prediction for breast cancer patients undergoing neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC). The authors propose a novel multimodal framework (ClinRAG-GRAPH), with the following primary contributions:
1.Clinically Informed Multimodal Graph Modeling: The authors introduce a prior-guided, relation-aware graph convolutional network (PRAttn-RGCN). Moving beyond conventional feature concatenation across MRI, clinical, and pathological data, the method constructs an intra-patient directed graph. By encoding clinical practice guidelines into hierarchical edge priors, it enables more clinically grounded cross-modal fusion.
2.Domain Adversarial Learning for Multicenter Generalization: To mitigate heterogeneity arising from scanner variability and imaging protocols in multicenter DCE-MRI data, the paper implements a dual-branch domain-adversarial learning strategy. This approach effectively disentangles domain-invariant representations from site-specific noise, substantially improving robustness on independent external cohorts.
3.LLM-RAG Mechanism for Enhanced Interpretability: The framework integrates an LLM-driven subgraph retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) module. During inference, rather than outputting a scalar probability alone, the model retrieves historical cases with analogous graph attention patterns and multimodal signatures. This evidence-grounded reasoning significantly improves the clinical interpretability and trustworthiness of the predictions.
4.Extensive Multicenter Validation: The method is evaluated on a large-scale, multicenter breast cancer cohort comprising two public datasets and three institutional datasets. Comprehensive internal comparisons and rigorous external testing robustly demonstrate the model’s performance and translational potential under realistic distribution shifts.
reviews.text_strengths:
The strongest aspect of this work lies in its rigorous, clinically grounded experimental design and thorough evaluation framework. Specific strengths include:
1.Large-Scale Multicenter Cohort and Rigorous External Validation: Cross-institutional generalization remains a critical challenge in medical AI. The authors assembled a substantial cohort across five institutions (two public, three internal). Rather than relying exclusively on internal cross-validation, they reserved two fully independent external centers (Ycenter and Qcenter) for unbiased out-of-distribution testing. This validation strategy provides robust empirical evidence of the model’s resilience to real-world distributional shifts.
2.Clinically Aligned Evaluation Metrics: Beyond relying on AUC alone, the authors report balanced accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. This multi-metric approach appropriately accounts for the class imbalance inherent in clinical datasets and directly reflects diagnostic utility, particularly in balancing false-positive rates with the reliable identification of true pCRs.
3.Comprehensive Ablation Analysis: Despite the methodological complexity—integrating graph-based modeling, adversarial domain adaptation, and retrieval-augmented generation—the ablation experiments (Table 3) are methodically designed. By isolating the clinical prior (CP), graph attention mechanism (PR), domain adversarial component (ADV), and the RAG framework, the authors demonstrate that each element yields measurable performance gains, particularly on external cohorts. This systematic validation confirms that the architectural choices are substantively motivated and functionally integrated rather than arbitrarily combined.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
While the overall methodology is sound, the presentation of the proposed framework (particularly Figure 1) and the lack of critical implementation details require significant improvement:
1.Poor presentation clarity and severe text-figure mismatch in Figure 1:
(a) Figure 1 lacks self-explanatory elements, leaving several visual components unexplained:
1) Unexplained abbreviations: Abbreviations such as Emb. and Tab. Enc. appear in the figure, but their full terms are not provided in the figure itself or the caption.
2) Unexplained symbols: The
tag next to the nodes and the “scissors” symbol in Part C are not explained regarding their specific operations or states in either the figure or the caption.
(b) There is a noticeable disconnect between the figure and the Methodology section, lacking terminology consistency:
1) Figure 1B uses descriptive module names like Self-Transformation, Linear Transformation, and Message Weighting, whereas Section 2.2 describes the process entirely using rigorous mathematical symbols. The visual elements lack a direct mapping to the equations, making it difficult to follow.
2) The figure introduces concepts not explained in the text: For example, the
tag is shown in Figure 1A, but Section 2.1 (which introduces the prior graph construction) never mentions the concept of a “mask” or its specific implementation mechanism.
2.Missing implementation details of the MRI feature extractor:
In Section 2.3, the imaging node initialization is defined as f-img(·). However, in the implementation details (Section 3.1), the authors only mention the cropping and concatenation sizes of the DCE-MRI images (192, 256, 256), omitting the specific architecture of the Imaging Backbone . This critical omission significantly hinders the reproducibility of the paper.
3.Privacy and compliance risks regarding LLM clinical deployment:
The paper utilizes an LLM for retrieval and explanation but fails to specify whether it relies on calling an external API or local deployment. In real-world clinical Medical Image Computing (MIC) scenarios, transmitting sensitive data—including patient graph embeddings and multimodal features—to external LLM APIs (e.g., DeepSeek) poses significant privacy and compliance risks. Conversely, locally deploying a large-parameter LLM requires massive computational resources. The authors should clarify their deployment strategy. Furthermore, to truly demonstrate the clinical viability of the LLM framework, it is highly recommended to conduct validation experiments using a locally deployable, small-parameter LLM to assess whether the performance drop remains within an acceptable range.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a well-motivated, clinically relevant multimodal framework with rigorous multicenter validation and thorough ablation studies. The methodological novelty, particularly the integration of clinical priors with graph attention and domain-adversarial learning, is clearly demonstrated. However, the manuscript requires minor revisions to improve figure-text consistency, clarify key implementation details (especially the imaging backbone), and address LLM deployment privacy considerations. Addressing these points would strengthen both reproducibility and clinical readiness, warranting a weak accept

They clarified the specific architecture of the MRI encoder, explained that the LLM used in the paper is API-based, and stated that during inference the LLM only receives de-identified embeddings and attention features rather than raw patient data, which helps mitigate privacy concerns. They also committed to adding explanations for the abbreviations and symbols in Figure 1.Overall, this paper addresses a clinically important problem, presents a method with a certain degree of novelty, and provides relatively comprehensive experimental validation. Taking into account the clarifications provided in the rebuttal, I am inclined to maintain my final decision of Weak Accept.

Third, the paper integrates a large language model into the inference process to further enhance prediction performance and interpretability.

reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The proposed GCN largely follows standard design paradigms; therefore, its technical contribution mainly credits to clinical priors. However, the formulation and utilization of these priors require further clarification and experimental validation. For instance, why are the strong priors fixed? Are soft priors learnable? How does the initialization of these priors affect performance? What if use the R-GCN without priors, in addition to Table3? Additionally, it would be helpful to report the statistical properties (e.g., mean and standard deviation) of the learned priors after training.
2.The generalization capability of the proposed method is not fully convincing. Although it significantly outperforms competing methods on the internal dataset and the external Ycenter, its performance drops substantially on the external Qcenter, where it only achieves marginal improvements, while other methods remain relatively stable across datasets. The proposed framework integrates clinical-prior-guided graph networks with LLM-based RAG for interpretable breast pCR prediction. Its strengths lie in the rigorous validation on extensive multicenter cohorts and a sound architecture that balances domain-adversarial robustness with evidence-grounded reasoning. Through the review scores as 4 or higher, there are several concerns that should be addressed via a thorough rebuttal: 1) More details on formulation and utilization of clinical priors, 2) Explanation regarding performance drop in external cohort, 3) LLM concerns raised by the three reviewers

Congratulations!

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers (R) for their feedback. We have clarified the concerns and will improve the writing accordingly.
Q1.Lack description for image encoder. (R1,R2)
Thank you for pointing this out. We omitted details of the MRI encoder in the manuscript. The MRI encoder is DenseNet-121, as specified in encoder.py of the anonymized code. We will add this clarification to manuscript.
Q2.LLM mechanism and decision rule. (R1, R3)
We thank the reviewers for the opportunity to clarify. PRAttn-RGCN is the diagnostic backbone, while the LLM-guided retrieval branch only provides auxiliary evidence by generating a schema-constrained retrieval plan over fixed similarity routes. Thus, the framework is not DeepSeek-specific, and any schema-compliant LLM can be substituted. 
For each query, the LLM receives the prompt together with patient’s sub-graph embedding, MRI/clinical/pathological embeddings, and edge-level attention weights. 
Finally, the LLM cannot “disagree” with PRAttn-RGCN because it does not produce a prediction. Any difference arises only between the PRAttn-RGCN output and the neighbor-derived estimate, which are combined deterministically: 
p_final = b·p_R-GCN + (1-b)·p_neighbors), b=0.7.
PRAttn-RGCN remains the dominant decision source. Retrieval can adjust borderline cases but cannot override a confident backbone prediction.
Q3.Clarification of clinical priors. (R3)
Thank you for this insightful comment. Strong-prior edges are derived from breast cancer guidelines and expert consensus, representing clinically validated and stable medical facts. We keep them fixed to preserve such knowledge and reduce the risk of learning dataset-specific shortcuts under limited sample size or center bias. For less deterministic relations, soft priors are learnable but initialized with larger weights, while uncertain relations are weakly initialized and mainly learned from data. Priors are injected only as a first-layer log-bias to calibrate early R-GCN message passing, leaving deeper layers fully learnable. As shown in Table 3, adding clinical-prior improves AUC over vanilla R-GCN.
Q4.Qcenter generalization and adversarial learning. (R3)
Thank you for raising this point. We agree that Qcenter is a more challenging external domain, where our method still achieves the best at AUC, bACC and SEN. 
The adversarial branch is applied only to MRI to reduce protocol-related imaging bias, not all sources of external distribution shift. Its impact on pCR prediction is therefore limited, especially because prior studies and our analysis suggest that pathological factors dominate pCR prediction. This is also supported by Fig. 4, where few highly ranked edges are image-related. We will clarify that adversarial branch improves robustness when MRI bias is a major domain-shift source.
Q5.Privacy risks regarding LLM. (R2)
We used API-based LLM for three reasons. First, privacy risks are mitigated, as stated in Sec. 2.4, the LLM only receives de-identified embeddings and attention features, not raw patient data. Second, API-based use of properly de-identified medical data is already an established practice in healthcare AI workflows when privacy and governance requirements are met. Third, local deployment is limited by computational resources.
Q6.Fig. 3 clustering and selection bias. (R1)
Thank you for this observation. Fig.3 aims to visualize binary class separation across internal and external cohorts, not to claim that external sub-clusters are free from selection bias. We will clarify this interpretation.
Q7.Writing details. (R2,R3)
We will correct all typos related to Table 2; revise notation errors and ambiguities, such as clarifying that τ denotes the temperature coefficient and replacing it with t; and explain undefined abbreviations (Emb. as Embedding, Tab. as Table, and Enc. as Encoder). We will clarify
as edge-prior mask and the scissors symbol denotes the gradient-reversal-based adversarial decoupling branch.

title: CMD-AD: Cross-Modality Distillation from fMRI-EEG for Single-Modality Alzheimer’s Disease Diagnosis
abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) disrupts both the spatial organization and temporal dynamics of brain functional connectivity, which can be jointly characterized by fMRI and EEG. fMRI-derived functional connectivity networks (FCNs) encode multiscale spatial topology, and EEG-derived FCNs capture multiband temporal coupling patterns, providing complementary information for AD diagnosis. However, paired fMRI-EEG acquisitions are rarely available in clinical practice, and existing fusion methods require both modalities at inference, limiting real-world deployment. To address this challenge, we propose CMD-AD (Cross-Modality Distillation for AD diagnosis), a three-stage framework that distills fused spatiotemporal knowledge into single-modality encoders to improve their performance. In Stage 1, hierarchical graph attention aggregation (HGAA) encoders are independently pretrained on each modality to extract multiscale fMRI spatial features and multiband EEG temporal features. In Stage 2, scale-wise bidirectional cross-modality fusion (BCMF) integrates fMRI and EEG representations at each parcellation scale, producing fused spatiotemporal targets. In Stage 3, teacher-student distillation transfers the fused spatiotemporal targets back to each modality-specific encoder, enabling accurate single-modality diagnostic performance without paired inputs. Evaluated on 8 multicenter datasets, CMD-AD improves fMRI-only accuracy from 73.51% to 75.50% and EEG-only accuracy from 63.52% to 65.02%, with AUC increasing from 80.88% to 83.70% and from 71.63% to 73.77%, respectively. These results demonstrate that cross-modality training can effectively enhance single-modality deployment for AD diagnosis. Our code is available at: https://github.com/yizhixiaolinya/Code-MICCAI2026_fMRI-EEG.git.
subject_areas: Modalities -> EEG / MEG / ECG / Physiological Signals

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper focuses on the clinical necessity of multi-modal brain imaging (fMRI-EEG) diagnosis for Alzheimer’s disease (AD), and proposes an innovative three-stage framework named CMD-AD. The methodological framework is well-designed and the experimental data are relatively sufficient to support the innovation.
reviews.text_strengths:
This paper designs a three-stage framework for cross-modal fusion and knowledge distillation to meet the demand for multi-modal diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease. 
It achieves efficient complementation between fMRI spatial structures and EEG temporal features, and transfers the capability of the fusion model to the single-modal encoder via distillation. 
The effectiveness of the proposed method is validated on eight multi-center datasets.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Table 2 shows that performance drops significantly when the multi-scale hierarchical structure is removed, yet the correlation between the multi-scale hierarchy and pathological brain region characteristics in AD is not explained.
2.Experimental comparisons mainly focus on several traditional methods and unimodal models, lacking direct comparisons with representative multimodal state-of-the-art methods in recent years.
3.It is suggested to add modal weight analysis and interpretable visualization to improve the scientificity and credibility of the proposed method.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Main Factors Leading to the Total Score
1.Strong Strengths Supporting Strong Acceptance
a.The paper targets AD diagnosis, a global public health challenge with urgent clinical demands. By effectively fusing fMRI (spatial structure) and EEG (temporal features), the work directly addresses the complexity of AD pathology, demonstrating substantial academic value and potential for clinical translation.
b.The proposed three-stage cross-modal fusion and knowledge distillation architecture is logically coherent and technically novel. The integration of multi-modal fusion and knowledge distillation ensures both high performance and practical deployability in real-world clinical scenarios, showing clear innovation over single-modal or conventional fusion approaches.
c.Extensive experiments on eight multi-center datasets provide strong evidence of the framework’s effectiveness and generalization capability. The results sufficiently validate the core contributions of the work, with adequate ablation studies and experimental controls supporting the reliability of the conclusions.
d.The paper is well-organized, with clear explanations of the model architecture, implementation details, and experimental settings. Most key hyperparameters and procedures are well-documented, ensuring good reproducibility of the research.
2.Minor Deficiencies, Not Barring Acceptance
a.While the performance drop with the removal of the multi-scale hierarchical structure is observed, the underlying connection to AD pathological brain regions is not fully explained. This is a minor point and can be easily addressed with additional analysis in the revision.
b.The comparative experiments focus on traditional and single-modal methods, lacking direct head-to-head comparisons with recent state-of-the-art multi-modal models. However, the existing results already demonstrate clear superiority on the evaluated benchmarks, and this gap can be closed in the rebuttal.
c.The paper would benefit from modal weight analysis and visualization of feature fusion to enhance clinical interpretability. However, the core claims of the paper are already well-supported by the experimental data, and this addition would further strengthen the work without changing its overall conclusion.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes CMD-AD, a cross-modality distillation framework that leverages complementary spatiotemporal information from fMRI and EEG to improve Alzheimer’s disease diagnosis under single-modality settings. Specifically, it introduces a three-stage pipeline—modality-specific hierarchical encoding, scale-wise bidirectional fusion, and teacher–student distillation—that transfers fused multimodal knowledge into individual modality encoders, enabling accurate inference without requiring paired data at test time.
reviews.text_strengths:
Addresses a clinically realistic and important problem: This work enables single-modality deployment while leveraging multimodal information during training, improving clinical feasibility.
Comprehensive and convincing evaluation: The method is validated on eight multicenter datasets, including both single-modality and paired cohorts, which is relatively extensive for this domain.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The baseline selection is limited and not up-to-date. The comparisons are restricted to conventional single-modality brain network models (e.g., BrainNetCNN, BrainGNN), while more recent and stronger methods such as BrainNetTF [1], Alter [2], as well as multimodal or incomplete-modality learning approaches specifically designed for brain networks, are not included [3, 4, 5]. This raises concerns about the fairness and competitiveness of the reported performance gains.
[1] Kan, Xuan, et al. “Brain network transformer.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (2022): 25586-25599.[2] Yu, Shuo, et al. “Long-range brain graph transformer.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37 (2024): 24472-24495.[3] Wang, Hu, et al. “Learnable cross-modal knowledge distillation for multi-modal learning with missing modality.” International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland, 2023.[4] Yang, Yanwu, et al. “Incomplete learning of multi-modal connectome for brain disorder diagnosis via modal-mixup and deep supervision.” Medical Imaging With Deep Learning. PMLR, 2024.[5] Sun, Kaicong, et al. “Achieving multi-modal brain disease diagnosis performance using only single-modal images through generative AI.” Communications Engineering 3.1 (2024): 96.2.The paper addresses a problem that has been extensively studied in prior work (e.g., incomplete multimodal learning and cross-modal distillation for brain networks). However, the manuscript fails to adequately review these closely related studies, and more importantly, does not clearly articulate what distinguishes the proposed method from existing approaches. As a result, it is difficult to assess the actual novelty and incremental contribution of the work.
3.Several key hyperparameters are introduced but not clearly specified or discussed, including the distillation weights (η, κ), the temperature parameter τ. The paper does not describe how these parameters are selected, nor does it provide their tuning range, step size, or selection criteria, making the method insufficiently transparent and difficult to reproduce.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The baseline selection is limited and not up-to-date, and several relevant methods are missing. Moreover, although the problem has been widely studied, the paper does not clearly position its contribution against prior work, making the novelty unclear.
Overall, I recommend weak reject.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal addresses several missing baselines and implementation details. However, many of these comparisons and discussions were absent from the original manuscript, and the positioning against closely related multimodal/incomplete-modality methods remains insufficiently clear.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes CMD-AD, a three-stage cross-modality distillation framework designed for Alzheimer’s disease (AD) diagnosis. It addresses the clinical challenge where paired fMRI-EEG data is rarely available during inference. The method pretrains hierarchical encoders on single modalities (Stage 1) , learns fused representations from paired subjects via scale-wise bidirectional cross-modality fusion (BCMF) (Stage 2) , and distills this fused knowledge back into single-modality encoders (Stage 3). This enables robust single-modality deployment while benefiting from cross-modality training.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The method directly targets a highly practical constraint in clinical neuroimaging: training with paired multi-modalities (fMRI-EEG) but deploying with only one.
2.The three-stage design is logically sound. The scale-wise bidirectional cross-attention (BCMF) ensures structured alignment between multiscale fMRI parcellations and EEG band-informed representations.
3.The authors evaluated the framework across eight multicenter datasets. It shows clear quantitative gains against representative single-modality baselines. For instance, after distillation, fMRI-only accuracy improves from 65.25% to 69.75%, and EEG-only accuracy improves from 59.67% to 64.33%.
4.The Grad-CAM saliency maps demonstrate consistent biologically plausible emphasis on association systems across multiple parcellation scales.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Stage 2 and 3 training rely on paired fMRI-EEG cohorts, which have a severe lack of AD-positive subjects. Specifically, PEARL-Neuro provides 78 NC pairs with zero AD pairs, while BrainLat provides only 15 AD pairs against 17 NC pairs. This raises concerns about the teacher model’s ability to reliably learn disease-specific spatiotemporal interactions.
2.The submission only compares against standard single-modality FCN classifiers. It lacks comparisons with alternative missing-modality strategies, such as cross-modal synthesis, latent space imputation, or existing KD frameworks tailored for incomplete modalities. Several highly relevant cross-modal knowledge distillation papers are missing from the references.
3.The evaluation involves 8 multicenter datasets with heterogeneous ages and demographics. However, there is no explicit harmonization (e.g., ComBat) or covariate adjustment mentioned.
4.There are minor theoretical/notation inconsistencies. In Eq. (2) and Eq. (4), the text defines channel-aggregated features by averaging over channels, yet the equations utilize both per-channel and aggregated symbols in ways that make the residual injection unclear.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The recommendation of a Weak Accept balances the method’s strong practical motivation and measured empirical gains against several evaluation gaps. The framework addresses a highly relevant clinical problem—deploying robust models when complementary paired data is unavailable at inference. The ablation studies clearly demonstrate the utility of each component, and overall metrics improve significantly over baselines (e.g., fMRI-only AUC improves from 72.38 to 78.64). However, the paper is held back by the severe lack of AD-positive pairs in the fusion/distillation training split , lack of multi-site harmonization, and the omission of relevant missing-modality baselines. If these evaluation robustness concerns are addressed in the rebuttal, the paper is a solid contribution.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

meta_reviews.text:
While the motivation of exploiting multimodal complementarity is meaningful, the current submission has limitations that need to be addressed in the rebuttal including missing related works, evaluations, notations.

The paper addresses a clinically relevant problem and proposes a reasonable cross-modality distillation framework for single-modality AD diagnosis. However, the main concerns remain insufficiently resolved after rebuttal, particularly regarding limited novelty relative to existing incomplete-modality and cross-modal distillation methods, inadequate positioning against related work, missing or post-hoc baseline comparisons, and uncertainty about the reliability of the paired fMRI-EEG training data given the severe scarcity of AD-positive paired subjects. Although the rebuttal clarified several implementation details, these issues affect the strength and trustworthiness of the claimed contribution. Rejection is recommended.

This manuscript is rejected due to multiple critical issues raised by all reviewers. First, the work only compares against traditional single-modality models and standard classifiers, while missing state-of-the-art multimodal, incomplete-modality learning and advanced brain network methods published in recent years, which undermines the fairness and persuasiveness of performance results. Second, the correlation between the core multi-scale hierarchical structure and pathological characteristics of Alzheimer’s disease is not elaborated, and modal weight analysis and reliable visual interpretation are absent. Third, closely related prior studies on incomplete multimodal learning and cross-modal distillation are not thoroughly discussed, and the unique advantages and incremental contributions of the proposed method are not clearly stated. Fourth, key hyperparameters lack detailed specifications, tuning strategies and selection criteria. Additionally, the training datasets suffer from severe imbalance with extremely limited AD-positive samples, raising doubts about the model’s capability to capture disease-related patterns. No effective harmonization or covariate adjustment is conducted for heterogeneous multicenter data, and minor inconsistencies exist in theoretical notations and formula definitions.

This paper proposes a unified feature distillation from fMRI-EEG for Single-Modality using their multi-site datasets. The reviewers’ critiques were mainly related to performance evaluation with state-of-the-art methods, discussion on experimental setting, and clarification on data harmonization. While those are important aspects, the paper demonstrates its novelty and incorporates intensive data harmization, which maintain its value.

author_feedback_text:
We appreciate all reviewers’ recognition of our technical novelty and practical value. Below, we concisely address the reviewers’ main concerns:
1) R1/R2/R4: clinical motivation and novelty. In clinical practice, paired fMRI-EEG provides complementary spatial-temporal information, but inference often has only fMRI or EEG. CMD-AD targets this bottleneck by leveraging paired fMRI-EEG during training while requiring only one modality at inference. Its main innovation is scale-wise cross-modality distillation: BCMF aligns fMRI and EEG at each scale to construct fused multiscale spatial-temporal features, which are distilled into each single-modality encoder. Compared with HC-GNN/MCSP, CMD-AD discards the fusion branch after training and requires only one modality at inference. It also avoids missing-modality synthesis as in R2-[5]. More importantly, instead of transferring only global latent knowledge (R2-[3,4]), CMD-AD distills per-scale fused features to capture hierarchical brain-network alterations induced by AD.
2) R2/R4: stronger and missing-modality baselines. Under the same subject-level splits and preprocessing, we additionally report R2-[1,2] and R2-[3-5]. R2-[1,2] are competitive at Base (Stage 1), yet CMD-AD exceeds them by 1.7/2.5 and 1.51.0 fMRI ACC/AUC points, and 3.0/5.0 and 2.0/3.0 EEG points. With CMD-AD distillation, R2-[1,2] further gain 4.5/5.2 and 4.7/5.7 fMRI points, and 7.0/8.5 and 6.3/7.5 EEG points. CMD-AD (Distill) also exceeds R2-[3-5] by 3.7/4.3, 2.7/3.7, and 3.7/5.0 fMRI points, and 2.0/3.0, 1.6/2.5, and 3.6/6.0 EEG points. These results show gains also come from scale-wise fusion and distillation, not backbone choice only.
3) R4: paired AD scarcity and Stage-2 sampling. We agree that paired AD subjects are limited, but CMD-AD does not learn the AD/NC boundary from paired data alone. Stage 1 trains disease-aware encoders on all labeled single-modality data. Stage 2 builds on these encoders to learn fMRI-EEG correspondence via BCMF and produce fused representations for Stage 3 distillation. Thus, paired data mainly support cross-modal alignment rather than for classification alone. Class balancing is applied only within the paired training split after subject-level splits are fixed, leaving validation/test distributions unchanged.
4) R2: hyperparameters and reproducibility. We apologize for omit hyperparameter search details. In Stage 3, η and κ weight feature- and logit-level distillation, while τ controls teacher-logit softness. We select them on held-out validation splits using AUC, searching η,κ∈{0.1,0.2,…,1.0} and τ∈{1,2,3,4}. The selected setting, η=0.5, κ=0.5, and τ=2, is fixed for all folds and modalities. We will add these details to Sec. 4.1.5) R1/R4: R1/R4: multiscale pathology and interpretability. We thank the reviewers for requesting clearer pathological interpretation and modal-weight analysis. AD-related FC alterations can occur at both system and regional levels, so coarse parcellations capture system-level disruption while finer parcellations preserve local ROI interactions. This explains why removing the multiscale hierarchy causes the largest performance drop. Fig. 2 supports this interpretation, as Grad-CAM consistently highlights association systems more strongly than primary sensory systems across scales. The learned scale-wise modality weights show greater reliance on fMRI at intermediate ROI scales, reflecting its spatial specificity, while EEG maintains complementary temporal contributions. Additional BCMF feature visualization shows tighter same-class fMRI-EEG alignment and larger AD-NC separation after fusion.
6) R4: harmonization and notation. We apologize for omit harmonization details due to space. FCNs are ComBat-harmonized before training, and all methods use the same harmonized inputs. For Eqs. (2) and (4), H^bar denotes the channel-aggregated feature used to compute attention context, which is then injected into each per-channel feature via the residual connection.

title: CMSA-Net: Causal Multi-scale Aggregation with Adaptive Multi-source Reference for Video Polyp Segmentation
abstract:
Video polyp segmentation (VPS) is an important task in computer-aided colonoscopy, as it helps doctors accurately locate and track polyps during examinations. However, VPS remains challenging because polyps often look similar to surrounding mucosa, leading to weak semantic discrimination. In addition, large changes in polyp position and scale across video frames make stable and accurate segmentation difficult.
To address these challenges, we propose a robust VPS framework named CMSA-Net. The proposed network introduces a Causal Multi-scale Aggregation (CMA) module to effectively gather semantic information from multiple historical frames at different scales. By using causal attention, CMA ensures that temporal feature propagation follows strict time order, which helps reduce noise and improve feature reliability. Furthermore, we design a Dynamic Multi-source Reference (DMR) strategy that adaptively selects informative and reliable reference frames based on semantic separability and prediction confidence. This strategy provides strong multi-frame guidance while keeping the model efficient for real-time inference.
Extensive experiments on the SUN-SEG dataset demonstrate that CMSA-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance, offering a favorable balance between segmentation accuracy and real-time clinical applicability. The code is available at https://github.com/wangtong627/CMSA-Net.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper’s main contribution is a real-time video polyp segmentation framework (CMSA-Net) that improves robustness under low contrast and large inter-frame motion/scale changes by combining two key ideas:
1.Causal Multi-scale Aggregation (CMA): a spatio-temporal attention module that lets the current frame aggregate information from multiple spatial scales of reference and past adjacent frames under a causal (time-ordered) attention constraint, aiming to reduce feature contamination and improve discriminability.
2.Dynamic Multi-source Reference (DMR): an efficient online reference-frame maintenance strategy that keeps a compact set of reference frames and updates them adaptively based on (i) foreground–background semantic separability (via prototype similarity) and (ii) prediction confidence (entropy), providing stronger and more reliable guidance than a fixed single reference without the overhead of large memory banks.
Together, CMA+DMR deliver SOTA accuracy on SUN-SEG while maintaining real-time inference speed, supported by ablations showing the two components are complementary.
reviews.text_strengths:
Well-motivated problem framing: Directly targets key VPS pain points—low contrast (weak semantics) and large inter-frame motion/scale changes.
CMA is a solid technical contribution: Multi-scale feature aggregation with a causal (time-ordered) attention constraint to reduce cross-frame feature contamination.
DMR is practical and efficient: Dynamically maintains multiple reference frames using separability + confidence cues, avoiding brittle fixed references and heavy memory banks.
Convincing empirical support: Comprehensive SUN-SEG evaluation (Easy/Hard, Seen/Unseen) with clear ablations validating each design choice.
Real-time orientation: Reports complexity/speed and designs for clinical feasibility rather than purely offline accuracy.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
DMR can be brittle because it is self-scored from the model’s own predictions. Both “semantic separability” (prototype distance via masked pooling) and “confidence” (entropy) are derived from p_t. This risks selecting wrong-but-confident frames as references and amplifying errors over time; the paper lacks drift/stability analysis.
The “causal / real-time” story is not fully pinned down by the evaluation protocol. The method is presented as causal and suitable for real-time use, but experiments are described on fixed clips (e. g. , 6 frames). The paper should explicitly define a strict streaming inference setup (no future access under any sliding window) and report latency/long-sequence behavior.
Insufficient implementation detail for reproducibility. CMA’s attention tokenization and tensor shapes (how multi-scale features are concatenated/flattened, exact masks, Q/K/V formation) and DMR’s update mechanics are not specified to the level needed for easy reimplementation.
Writing/typos and notation issues reduce clarity. “Casual” appears where “Causal” is intended, and there are minor formula/notation inconsistencies (e. g. , the attention scaling term is written in a nonstandard way). These don’t change the idea, but they hurt readability and confidence in exact implementation.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Pros: The CMA (multi-scale + causal temporal attention) and DMR (dynamic multi-source reference updating) are well-motivated for VPS under low contrast and large inter-frame variation. Results on SUN-SEG are strong across Easy/Hard and Seen/Unseen, and ablations show CMA and DMR are both important. Efficiency reporting (GFLOPs/FPS) supports the real-time angle.
Cons (why not higher): DMR is scored from the model’s own predictions (prototypes/entropy), which may create a feedback loop (e.g., “wrong-but-confident” references); the paper lacks stability/drift analysis. The “causal/real-time” evaluation protocol is not fully specified as strict streaming with per-frame latency/long-sequence behavior. Minor writing/notation issues (e.g., “Casual” vs “Causal”) reduce clarity/reproducibility.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes CMSA-Net for video polyp segmentation, which combines a Causal Multi-scale Aggregation (CMA) module with a Dynamic Multi-source Reference (DMR) strategy. The main contribution is a temporally causal and multi-scale feature aggregation mechanism that improves current-frame segmentation using reference and adjacent frames, together with an adaptive reference update strategy based on semantic separability and prediction confidence. The method is validated on the SUN-SEG benchmark and shows consistent performance gains with competitive real-time inference efficiency.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper addresses an important and clinically relevant problem, namely video polyp segmentation under weak semantic contrast, large spatio-temporal variation, and real-time constraints.
2.The proposed method is technically coherent: CMA and DMR are complementary, with CMA enhancing temporally causal multi-scale aggregation and DMR improving the quality of reference information.
3.The experimental evaluation is relatively solid, including comparisons with multiple prior methods, ablation studies, and efficiency analysis on different SUN-SEG subsets (easy/hard, seen/unseen).
4.The paper demonstrates a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off, which is valuable for practical deployment in colonoscopy scenarios.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The novelty appears moderate rather than highly significant. While the method is effective, it can be viewed as a structured extension of existing VPS designs that already exploit temporal aggregation, reference frames, or long-/short-term interaction, such as PNS/PNS+, SALI, MAST, and STDDNet.
2.The empirical evidence is mainly based on a single benchmark (SUN-SEG). Therefore, claims regarding robustness and generalization should be stated more cautiously.
3.Some methodological details remain unclear and affect reproducibility, including the exact handling and number of references in DMR, whether dynamic updates are applied during training and/or inference, and several notation inconsistencies in the paper.
4.Although the method consistently improves over prior baselines, some gains over the strongest same-backbone baselines are relatively modest on certain subsets, so the empirical advantage is solid but not overwhelmingly large.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I recommend a weak accept. The paper tackles an important and clinically relevant task, and the proposed CMA + DMR design is technically coherent and supported by reasonably solid experiments, including comparisons, ablations, and efficiency analysis on SUN-SEG. The method appears effective and practically relevant due to its favorable real-time performance. My reservation is that the novelty is moderate rather than highly significant, and the empirical support for robustness/generalization is still limited by evaluation on a single benchmark. In addition, some methodological details and notation inconsistencies reduce clarity and reproducibility. Overall, I believe the paper is above the acceptance threshold, but mainly as a solid and useful contribution rather than a highly impactful one.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents CMSA-Net, a neural network architecture designed for video-based polyp segmentation in colonoscopy sequences. The authors introduce dedicated modules for multi-frame and multi-scale feature fusion, aiming to address challenges such as weak semantic discrimination and significant spatio-temporal variation in endoscopic videos. The proposed method is evaluated on two datasets and compared against 14 existing approaches. Experimental results indicate consistent improvements across all reported metrics relative to competing methods.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper provides a clear and detailed description of the proposed network architecture, including its individual modules and the rationale for their design. This level of transparency makes the method easy to follow and reproducible, and helps the reader understand how the different components contribute to addressing spatio-temporal challenges in video-based polyp segmentation.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Limited Novelty in Multi-Scale Feature Fusion
The proposed multi-scale feature fusion module offers limited novelty, as similar approaches have been extensively studied in prior work. Moreover, the design appears relatively simple compared to more recent and advanced fusion strategies, some of which have demonstrated superior performance.
2.Marginal Performance Gains over Recent Methods
Despite extensive comparisons with existing approaches, the reported improvements are incremental, particularly when compared to recent methods such as STDDNet (ICCV 2025). Additionally, results in Table 3 indicate that GELOP achieves higher performance than the proposed method (R) on certain metrics, which weakens the claim of consistent superiority.
3.Missing Ablation on Loss Components
While the paper includes ablation studies on architectural modules, it lacks a detailed analysis of the loss design. There is no ablation isolating the contribution of individual loss components, either for the segmentation loss or for the overall objective, making it difficult to assess their effectiveness.
4.Inconsistency Between Quantitative and Qualitative Results
The qualitative results do not convincingly reflect the quantitative improvements reported in the paper, particularly compared with STDDNet. The visual examples fail to clearly demonstrate the claimed performance gains, raising concerns about the consistency of the evaluation.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

An important missing component is a detailed ablation study on the loss design. In particular, the paper would benefit from an analysis isolating the contribution of each loss component, both within the segmentation loss and the overall training objective. This would help clarify the role of the optimization strategy in the reported performance gains.
I encourage the authors to include such an ablation study in the rebuttal to strengthen the paper and improve the clarity of their contributions.
