meta_reviews.text: This submission proposes CMSA-Net, a video polyp segmentation framework that leverages causal multi-scale aggregation to model temporal dependencies and improve semantic discrimination across frames. Three reviewers (R1, R2, R3) vote for weak accept. The work is above the acceptance threshold and is suitable for acceptance. That said, several important issues should be addressed in the final manuscript to strengthen clarity, rigor, and reproducibility: R1 raises a meaningful concern that DMR relies on model predictions, which may introduce a feedback loop where incorrect but confident predictions are reinforced. R2 notes that evaluation is limited to a single dataset and novelty is moderate. R3 highlights the lack of detailed ablation studies on the loss function.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank all reviewers for their constructive comments and for recognizing the importance of video polyp segmentation, the coherence of CMA+DMR, and the solid SUN-SEG evaluation. We address the main concerns below.
Novelty (R2,R3). We agree that temporal aggregation, reference frames, and multi-scale features have been explored in VPS. Our novelty lies in their causal and role-aware integration. Existing methods often rely on fixed/single references or aggregate frames without explicitly modeling the causal relations among reference, adjacent, and current frames, which may cause feature contamination or unreliable guidance under large variations (Fig. 1). CMSA-Net addresses this via (1) CMA, which performs multi-scale aggregation under a time-ordered attention constraint, and (2) DMR, which maintains compact multi-source references using complementary separability and confidence cues. Table 4 shows that removing CMA or DMR leads to clear degradation, especially on Hard-Unseen, supporting their complementary roles.
DMR stability (R1). We appreciate the concern about self-reinforcement. DMR includes several safeguards. First, it uses two complementary cues (separability and confidence) rather than a single score. Second, both scores incorporate temporal consistency, preventing selection based solely on entropy or prototype distance. Third, cooldown intervals limit frequent updates. Finally, DMR maintains a compact reference set instead of accumulating all historical frames, which constrains error propagation. The strong Hard-Unseen results and the “w/o DMR” ablation in Table 4 indicate that DMR improves robustness in the submitted evaluation.
Causal/real-time setting (R1). CMSA-Net is causal by design. In Sec. 2.1, an adjacent frame at time t only attends to reference frames and past frames up to t; the current frame uses only reference and past adjacent frames within the window. No future information beyond the prediction target is used. The 6-frame clip is the implementation of this causal window rather than an offline setting. Table 3 reports 38/47 FPS with PVTv2-B2/Res2Net-50, supporting real-time feasibility.
Single benchmark (R2). We agree that more datasets would strengthen generalization claims. Nevertheless, SUN-SEG is the largest and most widely used VPS benchmark, with 49,136 annotated frames and diverse clinical conditions (low contrast, fast motion, illumination changes, instruments, etc.). It is also the standard benchmark used by representative works such as PNS+, SALI, MAST, and STDDNet. Thus, we believe SUN-SEG provides a rigorous basis for evaluation.
Magnitude of gains (R2,R3). We agree that gains over strong baselines (e.g., STDDNet) are sometimes moderate. However, consistent improvements across subsets and metrics remain meaningful. More importantly, CMSA-Net shows clearer advantages in difficult settings (Hard-Seen/Hard-Unseen and challenging qualitative cases), which directly correspond to the targeted clinical challenges.
Loss ablation (R3). Our contribution focuses on architecture rather than loss design. We adopt standard segmentation losses (Dice, weighted IoU, weighted BCE), consistent with prior VPS works. Thus, improvements mainly reflect the effect of CMA and DMR, and Table 4 already isolates the main architectural components.
Reproducibility and notation (R1,R2). We acknowledge that some details and notation could be clearer. The manuscript specifies multi-scale features, Q/K/V construction, attention heads, clip length, and DMR cooldown intervals. We will correct typos (e.g., “Casual” → “Causal”) in the camera-ready version and release code and models upon acceptance.
We thank the reviewers again for their valuable feedback.

title: Coarse-to-Fine Meta-Reweighting with Dynamic Retrieval for Adult-to-Pediatric Domain Adaptation in Tumor Segmentation
abstract: Deep learning models face challenges in medical image segmentation under limited annotations, particularly in pediatric brain tumor cases. Simply augmenting pediatric datasets with adult cases is suboptimal due to anatomical and developmental differences. We propose a two-stage meta-reweighting framework: a coarse stage that performs cross-domain binary segmentation for stable localization, and a fine stage that refines pediatric-specific subregions with gradient-alignment-based reweighting. To further improve pediatric relevance,  we introduce a gradient-similarity–driven retrieval mechanism that selects representative pediatric meta-cases as a stable reference set for weight computation, avoiding reliance on noisy online samples. This design enables effective loss reweighting while maintaining computational efficiency. Experiments on BraTS-PEDs demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art reweighting approaches, achieving a 6.1% improvement in Dice score and a 20.84 mm reduction in HD95, highlighting its robustness for pediatric brain tumor segmentation in low-data settings. Code is available at https://github.com/abod-alfakih/MDR2.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper presents a method for pediatric glioma segmentation that leverages both adult and pediatric glioma images during training. The approach is trained in two stages: the first performs binary tumor segmentation, while the second focuses on pediatric tumor parsing. In the second stage, a set of representative pediatric cases is identified every five epochs to reweight the influence of training samples based on their similarity to these cases. The results demonstrate that, compared with the selected methods, the proposed approach achieves improved performance.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper is well motivated. Pediatric glioma is underrepresented while adult glioma is a highly study task. This contrast highlights the potential impact of leveraging knowledge from adult data to improve pediatric applications.
The proposed method is interesting. Finding the more representative samples could lead to improve optimization and help mitigate overfitting to the adult cohort.
The method description and the figures are clear, and the paper is easy to follow
The ablation results show that the independent elements of the proposed approach improve the performance and complement each other
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Comparison with state-of-the-art. The method shows improved results compared with several methods for training with noisy data, data scarcity, or domain adaptation. However, there are no comparisons against methods specifically developed for pediatric glioma segmentation, such as those proposed in the BraTS-PED 2023 challenge [a], which uses the same dataset as this work. Including such comparisons would provide a more task-relevant benchmark and better contextualize the contribution.
Missing baseline with only pediatric images. The introduction explains how training with both populations will affect the performance on the underrepresented pediatric cohort. However, it is unclear how the method performs when it is only trained on pediatric data. The first row in Table 1 may correspond to this setting, but it could also be trained only on adult images. Clarifying this point is important for understanding the benefit of incorporating adult data. Moreover, when compared to the BraTS-PED 2023 challenge results, the reported performance looks substantially lower, even though those methods were trained using only pediatric data. While the results are not directly comparable since its different evaluation sets (official test vs. selected test subset), the difference with several of those methods, mainly in ET, is large enough to raise questions about the method’s performance against approaches designed for this task.
The paper claims that the proposed approach has “lower computational and memory overhead” but does not include quantitative comparisons to support this statement
The introduction says that there are only 99 labeled cases for pediatric glioma analysis suggesting that that is the total number of samples available, but that is only the number of cases in the version of the dataset used. The more recent BraTS-PET 2024 has 261 [b]. Also, section 2 says that BraTS 2024 is used but the number of patients match those of 2023.
The order of sections 2.3, 2.4 and 3 is strange. The explanations of the baselines experiments are before the experimental setup. Also, section 2.3 should be closer to or merged with section 3.2 since they are highly related.
[a] Fathi Kazerooni, Anahita, et al. “BraTS-PEDs: Results of the Multi-Consortium International Pediatric Brain Tumor Segmentation Challenge 2023.” Machine Learning for Biomedical Imaging 3.June 2025 issue (2025): 72-87.
[b] Kazerooni, Anahita Fathi, et al. “The brain tumor segmentation in pediatrics (BraTS-PEDs) challenge: focus on pediatrics (CBTN-CONNECT-DIPGR-ASNR-MICCAI BraTS-PEDs). “ arXiv preprint arXiv:2404.15009 (2024).
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses an important problem and presents an interesting approach. The method is easy to follow, and the results suggest improvements over several baselines. However, key aspects of the evaluation are missing. In particular, there are no comparisons with methods specifically designed for the same task and dataset. Also, without a clearly defined pediatric-only baseline, it is difficult to assess the benefit of adding adult data. This particular clarification is necessary considering the motivation of how training with both cohorts tend to overfit to adult populations.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The provided clarifications and the new comparison with state-of-the-art methods in BraTS-PED improve the paper’s readability and contextualize the results better in the pediatric glioma segmentation task.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a two-stage framework for adult-to-pediatric brain tumor segmentation under limited pediatric labels. In the first stage, the model performs binary tumor localization on mixed adult and pediatric data to learn coarse tumor extent. In the second stage, it refines pediatric tumor subregions using meta-reweighting, where a dynamically updated set of pediatric “meta-cases” is selected by gradient similarity and used to reweight training samples according to alignment with pediatric gradients.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper addresses an important and clinically relevant problem. Pediatric brain tumor segmentation is clearly a low-data regime, and the manuscript is well motivated around the difficulty of leveraging adult data without simply inheriting adult-specific biases.
The proposed formulation is intuitive and reasonably well matched to the problem. The idea of separating coarse tumor localization from fine pediatric-specific subregion refinement is sensible, and the use of the coarse mask as an auxiliary channel in the fine stage is clearly described.
The dynamic retrieval mechanism is a potentially useful extension over fixed or arbitrary meta-sample selection. The method computes a mean pediatric gradient, scores pediatric cases by cosine similarity, and uses the top 10 as meta-cases for reweighting.
The empirical section includes more than a single benchmark comparison. The paper provides an ablation study, comparisons against several reweighting/domain adaptation baselines, four-fold results, and backbone sensitivity experiments.
Within the paper’s own experiments, the full method consistently improves over its internal baselines.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper has multiple reference-integrity problems. The manuscript states that it uses “BraTS 2021 (1,251 adult cases) [11],” but reference [11] in the bibliography is actually the 2024 BraTS post-treatment glioma challenge paper, not the standard BraTS 2021 adult pre-operative dataset. The baseline section also describes DA [6] as “supervised Domain Adaptation,” while the cited reference is explicitly titled Unsupervised domain adaptation for pediatric brain tumor segmentation. In addition, “L2RW [7]” is cited as a skin-lesion segmentation paper, whereas the standard L2RW reference is Ren et al., Learning to Reweight Examples for Robust Deep Learning (ICML 2018). I also note that MGR-DAS is described as [9] in the baseline section but appears as [10] in Table 2.Reference [1] is relevant, but poorly placed. It is a prior pediatric transfer-learning MICCAI paper, so it fits better as prior work on adult-to-pediatric adaptation than as support for the claim about tumor incidence.
Several of the strongest claims are overstated relative to the actual evidence. In particular, the abstract states that the method “significantly outperforms state-of-the-art reweighting approaches, achieving a 10.7% improvement in Dice score and a 24.6 mm reduction in HD95.” Those numbers correspond to the gain over naive mixed training in Table 1, not the strongest competing reweighting baseline in Table 2, so the abstract wording is stronger than the evidence clearly supports.
Likewise, the paper claims “state-of-the-art pediatric segmentation performance,” but it does not compare against the leading methods summarized in the BraTS-PEDs challenge results paper, where top pediatric approaches included nnU-Net/Swin UNETR ensembles, Auto3DSeg, and self-supervised nnU-Net variants.
The evaluation protocol is ambiguous. Section 2.1 states that BraTS-PEDs is randomly divided into 70 training and 29 testing cases, but in the same paragraph it says the experiments are repeated under a 4-fold cross-validation scheme. Section 2.4 again refers to robustness evaluation using four-fold cross-validation. It is therefore unclear whether the main reported results are based on a fixed 70/29 split, cross-validation averages, or a mixture of both. In a 99-case pediatric dataset, this ambiguity is a major issue.
Reproducibility is limited by missing implementation detail. The paper gives the high-level equations and some training settings, but several important details are absent: how sample-level gradients are computed in practice for 3D segmentation, whether gradients are computed over all parameters or a subset, how patch-level gradients are aggregated, how checkpoints are selected, and how hyperparameters such as retrieving 10 meta-cases every 5 epochs were chosen.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Thank you for addressing an important pediatric imaging problem. The paper’s central idea is reasonable and the component ablations are helpful. My main recommendation is to improve the paper’s precision: audit the references carefully, clarify the exact evaluation protocol, and provide a more complete description of the implementation details needed for reproducibility. I also encourage the authors to calibrate a few of the strongest claims more conservatively to better match the presented evidence.

I rate this paper as 3 (Weak Reject) because it presents a reasonable and potentially useful idea, but the current submission falls slightly below the acceptance threshold due to concerns about reference accuracy, evaluation clarity, and reproducibility. The core method is a two-stage adult-to-pediatric segmentation framework combining coarse binary localization, fine pediatric subregion refinement, and dynamic gradient-similarity retrieval for selecting pediatric meta-cases. This is a coherent approach, and the paper shows consistent improvements over its internal baselines.
The main factors lowering my score are as follows. First, several references are misused or misdescribed, which reduces confidence in the technical framing and literature review. Second, the evaluation protocol is not clearly specified, making it unclear which setup underlies the main reported results and how model selection was performed. Third, some claims are stronger than the evidence supports, especially the statement of “state-of-the-art pediatric segmentation performance,” given the limited comparison set and the lack of comparison to stronger pediatric or challenge-leading methods. Finally, reproducibility is only moderate in the current draft: while the high-level method is understandable, important implementation details are missing, particularly regarding sample-level gradient computation in 3D segmentation, the practical implementation of dynamic retrieval, and the basis for the efficiency claims. The statement that code will be released upon acceptance is positive, but the manuscript alone is not yet detailed enough for confident reproduction.
Overall, I view this as a promising but not yet fully convincing submission. The problem is important, the method is plausible, and the empirical trend is encouraging, but the paper would need more careful citation handling, a clearer and unambiguous evaluation protocol, and more precise reporting of implementation details and training procedure to reach the acceptance bar.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
This remains a relatively close decision for me, but the rebuttal addresses enough of my concerns that I am willing to support Accept, provided that the authors follow through on their stated commitment to release the code and to correct the citation/reference issues in the final version.
The clarification of the evaluation protocol resolves my main ambiguity about how to interpret the results, and the added runtime/implementation details and stronger-pipeline experiment improve both the reproducibility and the empirical positioning of the work. While I still see some weaknesses, I think the paper is now just above the acceptance threshold, especially if the promised code release and reference corrections are carried through in the camera-ready version.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses the critical problem of pediatric brain tumor segmentation under limited annotated data by leveraging abundant adult data. The authors propose a two-stage coarse-to-fine meta-reweighting framework with dynamic gradient-similarity retrieval to mitigate the adult–pediatric domain gap. The coarse stage performs cross-domain binary tumor localization, while the fine stage refines pediatric-specific subregions using gradient-aligned sample reweighting. Experiments on BraTS-PEDs show clear improvements over state-of-the-art reweighting and domain adaptation methods in both DSC and HD95.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Well-designed two-stage strategy: Separates cross-domain consistent localization and pediatric-specific refinement, which is intuitive and effective.
2.Efficient reweighting: Avoids costly bi-level optimization and maintains low computation overhead, suitable for clinical deployment.
3.Clear writing and logical structure: The paper is well organized, with clear figures and formulas.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.How were the meta-cases selected, what is the clinical rationale, do they include rare cases?
2.Lack of generalization analysis in other pedritric datasets
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The method is technically sound, well-motivated, and clearly presented.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper presents an interesting two-stage meta-reweighting method for adult-to-pediatric domain adaptation under limited pediatric segmentation annotations. However, the paper is unclear and not rigorously written, leaving several parts difficult to interpret. The major issues are: (1) the evaluation protocol is unclear (R1R2), it is uncertain whether the main results are from cross-validation or a separate test set. (2) The paper also lacks comparison with BraTS-PED challenge-specific SOTA baselines, making it difficult to assess the actual contribution of the proposed domain adaptation (R1R2). More importantly, (3) the paper contains multiple citation errors, including issues with cited baselines and datasets (R1R2). (4) overstated claims without sufficient numerical evidence, such as “lower computational and memory overhead” (R1) and “state-of-the-art pediatric segmentation performance” (R2). Overall, the method is interesting, but the paper is not sufficiently rigorous and the rebuttal should address these concerns from the reviewers.

The rebuttal addressed the reviewers’ major concerns, and all reviewers now recommend acceptance. To further improve the paper, the authors are encouraged to thoroughly correct inconsistencies in references and tables, including those not mentioned, and to commit to releasing the code upon acceptance. In addition, the BraTS-PED dataset has evolved over time, and updated versions with much more subjects are now available.

After considering the rebuttal and updated reviews, I recommend acceptance. All three reviewers support accepting the paper, and the rebuttal has sufficiently addressed the main concerns. Although some weaknesses remain, the paper is above the acceptance threshold, provided that the authors follow through on the promised code release and corrections in the final version.

Following the rebuttal period, all reviewers recommended acceptance. Most acknowledged that the paper addresses an important problem using a reasonably novel approach. The authors should pay close attention to writing quality and formatting in the camera-ready version.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their insightful feedback and positive assessment of our coarse-to-fine meta-reweighting framework. We address the concerns below:
(1) Comparison with BraTS-PED Challenge Winners (R1, R2):
The top-performing methods in the BraTS-PED 2023 challenge, such as CNMCPMI2023 and Auto3DSeg, rely on ensemble pipelines that combine U-Net, Swin-UNETR, and ResNet architectures with larger model capacities and patch sizes. In contrast, our experiments use single U-Net or Swin-UNETR models with a smaller 64³ patch size and lower-parameter models due to limited computational resources, which may particularly affect ET performance in pediatric-only training. Nevertheless, as shown in Table 3(B), the proposed method consistently improves both backbones, indicating that it functions as a plug-and-play, backbone-agnostic learning framework. To directly address the reviewers’ concerns, we integrated the proposed method into the challenge-winning CNMCPMI2023 pipeline ( U-Net and Swin-UNETR with additional post-processing) on our split. This improved the average Dice score of the CNMCPMI2023 pipeline from 0.763 to 0.822, further demonstrating compatibility with SOTA ensemble pipelines.
(2) Baseline Clarification (R1):
The first row in Table 1 is indeed the pediatric-only baseline. We will clarify this explicitly in Table 1 caption. 
(3) Cross-Validation Ambiguity (R2):
We would like to clarify that all main results are based on a fixed 70/29 pediatric train/test split for fair comparison with prior work. The additional 4-fold cross-validation experiments (25, 25, 25, and 24 testing cases) were conducted separately as a robustness analysis (only Table 3(A)). We agree Sec. 2.4 could be clearer, and we will revise it to avoid ambiguity.
(4) Reference Inconsistencies (R2):
We sincerely thank R2 for the meticulous audit. DA [6] is primarily an unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) study; however, the paper also reports all supervised DA results as an upper-bound reference. In our comparison, we selected the best-performing supervised DA from this paper. For L2RW [7], we cited the medical-image implementation paper (skin lesion) that applied L2RW, but we agree that the original ICML 2018 L2RW paper should also be cited. References [9] and [10] are conference/journal versions of the same work, and we will fix the numbering inconsistency, and the BraTS 2021 [11] citation will be corrected accordingly.
(5) Reproducibility, Implementation Details, and Computational Efficiency (R1, R2, R3):
Parameter-Efficiency: To minimize overhead, our method avoids bi-level optimization and restricts gradient computation to only over the encoder and decoder (∼4.45M parameters), excluding the ViT layers (∼100M parameters). As a result, our method requires 3.26 min/epoch, compared to 26.42 (MWN), 28.32 (L2RW), and 6.82 (MGR-DAS). We will add it to Table 2 
Gradient Computation: We use micro-batching to compute sample-level gradients within 3D patches.
Full implementation details will be available on GitHub upon acceptance, per MICCAI’s double-blind policy.
(6) Meta-case Selection & Generalization (R3):
Meta-cases are selected based on similarity to the average pediatric gradient G_ref (section 2.2 (i)), which prioritizes representative pediatric tumor patterns (e.g., missing/small edema regions) while reducing the influence of rare cases (e.g., large ED regions). Clinically, this helps the model focus on consistent pediatric characteristics rather than adult-dominant patterns. For testing on another dataset, we tested our method on pediatric brain tissue segmentation, and due to space limits, included only pediatric tumor segmentation. 
(7) Paper Organization (R1,R2):
We agree that the organization of Secs. 2.3, 2.4, and 3 can be improved for readability. In addition, the reported 10.7% Dice improvement is relative to naive mixed training rather than the strongest competing (MGR-DAS), which is 8.5%. We will revise them in the revised version.

title: COAST: Context-Aware Differential Learning for Gene Expression Prediction in Spatial Transcriptomics
abstract:
Spatial transcriptomics enables profiling of spatial gene expression but is limited by high cost and low throughput, motivating prediction from H&E histopathology images. Existing context-aware methods mainly supervise absolute expression, while relative expression relationships between spots are rarely used explicitly.
We propose COAST, a context-aware differential learning framework for spatial gene expression prediction. 
COAST conditions the local and global context features with type-specific modulation and aggregates the target and context spot tokens using a Transformer encoder to capture both fine-grained local patterns and slide-level structure.
It is trained with a joint objective that combines absolute expression regression with signed differential regression between the target and context spots.
Experiments on multiple spatial transcriptomics datasets show consistent improvements in correlation- and distribution-based metrics, demonstrating the effectiveness of context-aware differential learning for histology-based spatial gene expression prediction.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes COAST, a framework for predicting spatial gene expression from H&E images. The method combines type-specific feature modulation for target and context spots, a Transformer encoder for joint context modeling, and an auxiliary differential regression loss that supervises expression differences between spots in addition to absolute prediction. Experiments are conducted on seven SpaRED datasets, along with a downstream survival analysis on TCGA-LUAD.
reviews.text_strengths:
(1) The idea of explicitly modeling relative expression differences between nearby spots is biologically well motivated. The differential regression objective is a reasonable way to encode this prior, and the ablation results support its contribution. 
(2) The experimental evaluation is reasonably comprehensive, with results on seven datasets, multiple metrics, qualitative visualizations, and ablations of the main design choices. 
(3) The downstream survival analysis, while limited in scope, is a useful addition and suggests that the predicted expression profiles retain clinically relevant information.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(1) The overall framework is reasonable, but the methodological novelty appears somewhat limited. The main components, feature modulation, Transformer-based aggregation, and auxiliary differential supervision, are all established ideas, and the paper could better clarify what is uniquely enabled by their combination. 
(2) The survival prediction experiment is a useful addition, but the results are fairly modest and somewhat inconsistent across folds. As presented, this evidence only provides limited support for the claim that the learned representations capture clinically meaningful prognostic information. Reporting statistical testing or stronger downstream validation would make this part more convincing. 
(3) The baseline comparison could be strengthened by including more recent context-aware methods, such as TRIPLEX (CVPR 2024), M2OST (AAAI 2025), and MERGE (CVPR 2025), to better position the contribution relative to the current SOTAs.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper studies a relevant problem and presents a method that is generally well motivated, with reasonably broad experimental evaluation across multiple datasets. I also found the differential supervision idea intuitively sensible, and the results suggest that it contributes to performance. However, my overall score is limited by the relatively modest methodological novelty, the lack of comparison with several recent context-aware baselines, and the fact that some of the supporting evidence, especially the downstream survival analysis, is not yet strong enough to fully substantiate the broader claims. Overall, I think the paper has merit, but in its current form, I place it slightly below the acceptance threshold.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
Thank you for the detailed rebuttal. I appreciate the clarification that the contribution is a task-specific and biologically motivated adaptation of signed target-context differential supervision for H&E-to-ST prediction, rather than a claim of a generic new differential objective. The additional discussion on biological relevance and fairness of implementation is also helpful.
My main concern, however, remains only partially resolved. In particular, I still find the lack of direct comparison with several recent and highly relevant context-aware methods (e.g., TRIPLEX, M2OST, and MERGE) to be a notable weakness. Because the paper is also positioned around context-aware modeling of target-context relationships, these comparisons would be important for more convincingly establishing the contribution relative to the current state of the art. The conceptual distinctions raised in the rebuttal are reasonable, but in my view they do not fully replace direct empirical comparison.
I also appreciate the authors’ clarification regarding the survival analysis. This experiment is a useful additional evaluation, but as currently presented it still offers only limited support for stronger claims about prognostic relevance.
Overall, I think this is a relevant and promising paper, but under the final binary decision, I lean slightly toward rejection.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes COAST, a context-aware differential learning framework for predicting spatial gene expression from H&E histopathology images. The primary innovation is a joint learning objective that combines absolute expression regression with a signed differential regression between target spots and surrounding context spots, explicitly supervising relative spatial relationships. The framework also introduces a type-specific feature modulation mechanism to adaptively integrate heterogeneous local and global contextual information. The method is validated on seven spatial transcriptomics datasets and demonstrates clinical utility through downstream survival prediction on the TCGA-LUAD cohort.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The proposed signed differential learning objective represents a conceptually elegant approach that captures stable spatial gradients and relative biological relationships, effectively addressing the sensitivity of traditional absolute regression to slide-level batch effects.
2.The framework utilizes a sophisticated type-specific contextual feature modulation mechanism that adaptively conditions local and global features through learnable parameters, successfully resolving signal conflation in multi-scale spatial data.
3.The evaluation is exceptionally rigorous, spanning seven diverse datasets and demonstrating consistent, substantial performance improvements over strong state-of-the-art baselines across multiple metrics.
4.The inclusion of thorough ablation studies systematically validates each component of the architecture, such as context sampling sizes and the differential loss weight, demonstrating that the performance gains result from the full integrated configuration.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The baseline comparisons may be influenced by the choice of feature extractor. Since the proposed framework utilizes a modern foundation model (UNI), it might possess an inherent representational advantage over older baselines. Clarifying whether baseline hyperparameters were optimally tuned for these specific datasets, along with providing deeper implementation specifics (e.g., target gene selection criteria, inference-time global context grid), would enhance the fairness and reproducibility of the evaluation.
2.While the downstream survival prediction results are promising, the clinical validation is currently limited in scale to a single dataset cohort (TCGA-LUAD). Exploring the framework’s performance across additional clinical cohorts or broader clinical tasks would more comprehensively establish the translational robustness of the predicted representations. Additionally, there is a minor presentation oversight in Table 3 regarding this experiment: the “Avg.” row for the number of patients and slides incorrectly displays the total sum (e.g., 162 and 294) rather than the actual average, which should be corrected for clarity.
3.The paper lacks a deeper biological interpretability and theoretical analysis regarding the properties of the differential learning objective. Specifically, it is currently unclear how this supervision affects different gene categories (e.g., housekeeping vs. tissue-specific genes), nor does it provide attention map visualizations to verify if the model focuses on biologically relevant morphological regions rather than random areas.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses a genuine limitation in histology-based spatial transcriptomics prediction with an elegant and effective differential learning objective. The methodological design is technically sound, and the experimental validation is highly rigorous, demonstrating consistent state-of-the-art performance across a wide variety of datasets. The inclusion of the downstream survival prediction task is a strong addition that fits perfectly with MICCAI’s translational goals. The weaknesses identified primarily relate to the scale of the clinical validation and nuances in baseline comparisons, neither of which fundamentally undermine the strong core contributions of this work.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have satisfactorily addressed the primary concerns raised in my initial review. Regarding baseline fairness, their justification for evaluating original architectures rather than forcing the UNI extractor is methodologically sound, especially since COAST still outperforms PEKA. Furthermore, the authors effectively resolved my critique regarding biological interpretability by providing a detailed breakdown of performance across specific gene categories (tumor-associated, immune/TME, and stromal/ECM). While clinical validation remains limited to a single cohort, acknowledging this limitation is acceptable.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces COAST, a context-aware differential learning framework for spatial transcriptomics gene expression prediction. Unlike existing methods that solely regress absolute expression values, COAST explicitly models relative expression differences between target and context spots. By integrating both local and global contexts via a Transformer encoder, it effectively captures spatial gradients and structural variations.The reconstructed expression representations demonstrate strong prognostic value in predicting overall survival for TCGA-LUAD, highlighting their practical biological and clinical significance.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Instead of solely relying on absolute expression regression, the paper introduces “signed differential regression.” By explicitly modeling relative expression differences and spatial gradients between regions, the method is more robust against batch shifts and better captures true biological structures, such as tissue boundaries and tumor-stroma transitions.
2.The framework doesn’t just blindly aggregate neighborhood data. It explicitly distinguishes between local and global contexts using type-specific feature modulation (learning specific scale and shift parameters). This ensures heterogeneous spatial signals are processed appropriately before being fed into the Transformer.
3.Beyond standard predictive metrics, the paper validates the method’s downstream utility. The reconstructed spatial expressions successfully predict overall survival in TCGA-LUAD cohorts (achieving a higher C-index than image-only baselines), proving the model captures clinically meaningful biological information rather than just statistical correlations.
4.COAST consistently outperforms multiple representative baselines (e.g., STNet, Hist2ST, PEKA) across seven datasets and diverse metrics (PCC, MI, AUC, NRMSE). This cross-dataset, cross-metric success proves the method’s robustness.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
First, the methodological novelty is somewhat limited. While the proposed method works, it acts more as a task-specific integration of existing technical modules rather than a strong paradigm shift. The authors claim that this direction is “largely unexplored” in histology-based ST; however, Differential Ordinal Regression has clear precedents in pathology image analysis. For instance, the authors themselves cite DIOR-ViT, which explicitly models ordinal relationships between samples using a differential objective. COAST essentially migrates this concept from classification/ranking to regression. The underlying mathematical logic of predicting differences between sample pairs, rather than absolute values, is a mature concept in computer vision and metric learning.
Second, the study lacks biological granularity in its performance evaluation. The paper reports the average prediction performance across 128 genes but fails to discuss or analyze which specific categories of genes (e.g., tumor markers vs. basal metabolic genes) are predicted more effectively. This omission limits the biological insights and interpretability of the proposed framework.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1.I suggest slightly tempering the novelty claims regarding the “signed differential regression” mechanism in the final version. Given the maturity of this mathematical logic in metric learning and computer vision, accurately framing it as a “clever adaptation and integration” for the heterogeneous context of spatial transcriptomics—rather than a ground-up exploration—will elevate the academic rigor of the paper and better align with the expectations of top-tier medical imaging venues.
2.Although the paper demonstrates the potential for overall survival (OS) prediction on the TCGA-LUAD cohort, for spatial transcriptomics research, supplementing the analysis of specific biological processes in the appendix or future work (e.g., evaluating the model’s performance in predicting genes related to the tumor microenvironment or tumor-stroma boundary gradients) would greatly broaden the interdisciplinary impact of this work. Understanding exactly which specific biomarkers correspond to the “structural consistency” captured by the model is key to bridging the gap between AI and clinical medicine.

1.Comprehensive Benchmarking and Robust Empirical Performance
The authors conducted extensive evaluations across seven distinct SpaRED datasets encompassing diverse tissues and species (e.g., AHSCC, EHPCP1, MMBO). The proposed COAST framework consistently outperformed six competitive baseline models across five independent evaluation metrics, showing notable improvements in both correlation (e.g., PCC, MI) and distribution-based metrics (e.g., NRMSE). This rigorous benchmarking provides strong confidence in the framework’s generalizability and robustness against tissue-specific variations.2.Practical Clinical Translation via Downstream Task Validation
A significant strength of this work is its demonstration of clinical feasibility. The authors did not stop at expression prediction but validated the prognostic value of the reconstructed gene expression representations on the TCGA-LUAD cohort for overall survival (OS) prediction. Achieving an average C-index of 0.6029—which is highly comparable to the actual bulk RNA sequencing baseline (0.6042) —is a compelling empirical result. This underscores the practical value of the proposed method in utilizing cost-effective H&E imaging for clinical prognostication.3.Sensible Architectural Design and Solid Ablation
Although differential regression is an established concept in metric learning, its specific integration into the spatial transcriptomics domain is well-executed here. The architecture seamlessly handles heterogeneous contexts by applying type-specific scale and shift parameters to modulate local and global features prior to Transformer aggregation. Furthermore, the joint optimization of absolute and differential regression objectives forms a coherent engineering solution. The provided ablation studies adequately validate these structural choices.Summary Statement: Overall, despite the limitations regarding deep biological interpretability (e.g., gene-specific performance analysis) and the derivative nature of the core learning objective, the paper presents a highly effective, well-engineered solution. The solid experimental design and the demonstration of clinically relevant outcomes make this a valuable contribution to the computational pathology community, warranting acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The clarification on baseline fairness is reasonable. Using original implementations and settings while matching target genes, splits, and metrics is an acceptable evaluation protocol, and I agree that forcing all baselines to use the same foundation-model features could distort their intended designs. The inclusion of recent methods such as PEKA and NH2ST also helps address the concern about missing context-aware or foundation-model-based baselines.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper covers an important problem and the reported results indicate that the empirical performance is promising. However, concerns are raised on the methodological novelty, the positioning with respect to recent context-aware state-of-the-art methods, the validity of baseline comparison with the use of the modern foundation-model feature extractor, and the strength of the clinical and biological validation. In particular, the authors are encouraged to make clear why the proposed differential learning framework is unique, to justify the baseline comparison in term of the implementation and tuning fairness, to justify the missing/baseline and possibly the recent baseline in the comparison, to interpret the survival analysis result with more rigorous statistical evidence, and to add more biological interpretation such as the gene-category level performance or qualitative interpretability of the model. Please make a careful and focused rebuttal to the reviewers since it will be important for the final decision.

After rebuttal, R2 and R3 vote acceptance, finding the clarifications on baseline fairness, biological interpretation, and the role of recent baselines sufficient, while R1 remains a borderline Reject mainly due to missing direct comparisons with TRIPLEX/M2OST/MERGE and limited survival evidence. Given the relative strong results and that most post-rebuttal concerns were reasonably addressed, I vote acceptance of this paper.

The reviewers agreed that COAST addresses an important H&E-to-ST prediction problem, with a sound context-aware differential learning framework and consistently strong results across seven SpaRED datasets. The rebuttal clarified the intended novelty as a task-specific integration of signed target-context differential supervision rather than a generic new differential objective, and it reasonably addressed concerns on baseline fairness, biological interpretation, and limitations of the survival analysis. While the lack of direct comparison to some recent context-aware methods and the modest clinical validation remain weaknesses, the overall empirical evidence, ablations, and two post-rebuttal accept recommendations support acceptance.

Two reviewers recommended accept. The third however had concerns on the lack of direct empirical comparisons with highly relevant context-aware methods (TRIPLEX, M2OST, and MERGE). Additionally, the survival analysis in the paper offers insufficient empirical evidence to fully substantiate the paper’s claims regarding prognostic relevance. These are valid concerns and I’m inclined to reject the paper in its current form.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for the comments. In revision, we will clarify novelty, baseline fairness, recent baselines, survival statistics, and biological interpretation.
A1.(R1, R3) Uniqueness and novelty.
COAST does not claim a new generic differential objective. Its contribution is a tailored spatial context-aware differential supervision for H&E-to-ST prediction. 
Existing ordinal/differential objectives are used for class ordering or relative differences among samples within the same class, whereas COAST defines intra-slide target-context expression differences as signed gene-wise values. This explicitly models biological spatial changes in ST (e.g., tumor-stroma boundaries and glandular regions).
COAST also differs from existing context-aware H&E-to-ST models. TRIPLEX and M2OST learn the multi-scale image context centered around the the target, while COAST directly incorporates both proximal and distal context patches as separate spatial references. Although MERGE can utilize patches within the same slide, it aggregates them via GNNs. In contrast, COAST learns signed relative differences. Thus, the novelty of COAST lies not in differential learning alone, but in adpating singed gene-wise differential supervision to spatially related proximal and distal tissue contexts for ST prediction. We will revise the manuscript to present COAST as a task-specific and biologically motivated integration of context modeling and differential regression.
A2.(R2) Fairness of baseline implementation.
To ensure fairness, we evaluated all baselines using their original implementations and settings while matching target genes, splits, and metrics. Target genes were the dataset-specific Moran’s I-based HVGs provided by SpaRED benchmark. Since several baselines include the image encoder itself, forcing all methods to use the same foundation-model features could distort their intended architecture rather than improving fairness. To compare against a recent foundation-model-based method, we included PEKA, which uses two powerful foundation models (H-optimus-0 and scFoundation). COAST outperforms PEKA. We will clarify these in the final version.
A3.(R1, R3) Missing or recent context-aware baselines.
While the comparison does not exhaustively cover all recent context-aware methods, it includes representative strong baselines from the most relevant directions.
NH2ST (MICCAI 2025) is a graph-based context-aware method, while PEKA (MICCAI 2025) is a recent foundation-model-based method. NH2ST also reported higher PCC than TRIPLEX on several benchmarks, supporting its role as a strong context-aware reference.
Thus, our comparison includes context-aware and foundation model based methods, not only classical baselines. For relationship to context-aware methods, please see A1.
A4.(R1) Statistical interpretation of survival analysis.
We agree that fold-wise performance shows some variance and stronger downstream tasks would further validate our method. Fold-wise variation may be ascribable to the limited sample size and disproportionate distribution of survival events. Moreover, k-fold cross-validation is designed to be evaluated holistically, as the aggregated performance provides a more stable assessment. The MICCAI rebuttal guideline strictly prohibits the inclusion of additional experiments. We will acknowledge the fold-wise variance and a single downstream task as limitations of our study.
A5.(R3) Biological interpretation and qualitative interpretability.
We agree that the 128-gene average limits biological interpretation. Using existing test predictions, we computed gene-category PCC. COAST outperformed PEKA/NH2ST for tumor associated genes (0.4100 vs. 0.3959/0.3096), housekeeping/basal genes (0.4100 vs. 0.3896/0.3261), immune/TME genes (0.3436 vs. 0.3239/0.2581), and stromal/ECM or tumor-stroma boundary genes (0.3630 vs. 0.3153/0.2490), indicating gains across biologically meaningful groups.

title: CoGaze: Closed-Loop Eye-Face Alignment for Multi-center Mobile Gaze-Based Cognitive Screening in Older Adults
abstract: Mobile screening is increasingly needed for frequent, low-burden assessment of cognitive impairment in communities and households, and eye tracking offers scalable oculomotor signatures for this purpose. However, mobile gaze estimation is fragile under coupled shifts from aging-related appearance changes, uncontrolled capture noise, and fluctuating engagement, which can corrupt downstream oculomotor features. We propose CoGaze, a closed-loop gaze reasoning framework for mobile videos of older adults. CoGaze formulates gaze estimation as structured alignment between ocular appearance and facial geometric context. It stabilizes ocular representations with a prototype–anchor dictionary retrieved by normalized cosine attention, refines eye–face evidence via reciprocal cross-attention, and enforces temporal alignment using differential spatiotemporal attention with a segment-level consistency objective to reduce jitter and drift without blurring true saccades. We collect a deployment-oriented multi-center dataset from 7 sites (July–December 2025) with 119 gaze-task subjects and 114 clinically labeled assessments. CoGaze achieves mean error 1.29 cm/2.03 cm on phone/tablet and improves screening to 85.1% accuracy (5-fold CV). The code is available at: https://github.com/xiangxuebei/CoGaze

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes CoGaze, a closed-loop eye–face alignment framework for robust mobile gaze estimation in older adults. The method integrates an ocular prototype–anchor dictionary, reciprocal cross-attention between eye and facial features, and differential spatiotemporal attention to reduce jitter and drift in gaze trajectories. The authors also introduce a multi-center mobile dataset and demonstrate that improved gaze estimation leads to modest gains in downstream cognitive screening performance based on derived oculomotor features.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper presents a technically strong and well-motivated contribution to mobile gaze estimation under challenging real-world conditions. The proposed closed-loop eye–face alignment mechanism is novel and addresses practical issues such as aging-related appearance variation, motion noise, and temporal instability. The method demonstrates consistent improvements over strong baselines across multiple devices and tasks, with clear gains in both localization error and robustness metrics. The collection of a multi-center dataset is also a valuable contribution, and the focus on deployment-oriented settings (mobile devices, older populations) is timely and relevant. Overall, the work is well-executed from a machine learning and systems perspective.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The main limitation of the paper is that the clinical contribution is relatively limited compared to the methodological focus. While the work is framed as cognitive screening, the primary advances lie in gaze estimation, and the downstream clinical analysis remains shallow. The paper does not provide detailed insight into which oculomotor features are most informative, how they relate to cognitive domains, or how the model could support clinical decision-making.
The evaluation of cognitive screening performance is also limited. The reported accuracy (85.1%) is obtained via 5-fold cross-validation on a relatively small dataset (114 subjects), without external validation. This raises concerns about generalizability, especially given class imbalance and potential site-specific biases. Furthermore, the improvement in screening performance appears modest relative to the substantial gains in gaze estimation, and it is not clearly demonstrated whether these gains translate into meaningful clinical benefit.
In addition, the paper lacks a discussion of limitations. Important aspects such as dataset size, cohort composition, potential biases, and deployment constraints are not critically examined. A more balanced discussion would strengthen the paper.
Finally, while the method is technically sophisticated, it remains unclear how much of the downstream improvement is attributable to the proposed alignment mechanism versus general improvements in gaze accuracy or feature extraction.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a strong and well-executed methodological contribution to mobile gaze estimation, with clear improvements over existing approaches. However, the clinical relevance is limited, and the cognitive screening component is not sufficiently developed or validated to support strong translational claims. In particular, the lack of external validation, limited analysis of clinical features, and absence of a discussion of limitations weaken the overall impact. While the work is promising, it would benefit from stronger clinical grounding and more rigorous evaluation of the screening task.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The rebuttal usefully clarifies several methodological points, especially that downstream classification used subject-level stratified 5-fold cross-validation and that all compared methods shared the same folds, features, and classifier. This addresses possible concerns about within-subject leakage and helps explain the source of the reported downstream gains.
However, my main concern regarding clinical validation and generalizability remains only partially addressed. The current submission still lacks external validation, held-out-site/device evaluation, or leave-one-center-out analysis, despite being framed as a multi-center, deployment-oriented study. The cognitive-screening results are based on internal cross-validation on a relatively small cohort of 114 subjects, with limited dementia cases, which weakens the strength of the translational claims.
Overall, I still view the paper as a technically strong and promising methodological contribution with practical relevance, but not one that is sufficiently validated clinically to merit stronger enthusiasm. I therefore remain on the accept side, but only as a weak accept.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses a meaningful and timely problem by connecting mobile gaze estimation with downstream cognitive screening in older adults, and the multi-center dataset is a notable strength. However, while the results are promising, the current manuscript does not yet provide enough clarity and depth in the evaluation protocol, downstream classification setting, and ablation study to fully support the strength of its claims.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper studies a meaningful problem and has clear practical relevance, especially for mobile cognitive screening in older adults. A clear strength is the multi-center dataset collected from seven sites, which makes the work more valuable than papers evaluated only on small or single-site data. I also think it is a plus that the paper connects gaze estimation with downstream cognitive screening, rather than stopping at the intermediate task. Overall, the motivation is strong, the application setting is realistic, and the reported results are promising.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The paper is framed as a multi-center, deployment-oriented study, but the evaluation setup is still not clear enough. I was not fully sure how the subject splits were done, whether the cross-validation was strictly subject-independent, or how much the results reflect true cross-center robustness. For this kind of application, those details matter a lot.
2.The cognitive-screening part also needs more explanation. The paper shows that screening accuracy improves when using gaze features from CoGaze, but the downstream pipeline is only described at a fairly high level. It is therefore hard to tell whether the gain really comes from better gaze estimation, from the classifier itself, or from the particular split of a relatively small and imbalanced cohort.
3.The ablation study feels too thin for a method with this many components. The model includes the ocular prior dictionary, the multi-scale face branch, the eye-face interaction module, and the temporal alignment design, but only part of these are actually examined in the ablation table. Because of that, it is still not very clear which pieces are doing the heavy lifting.
4.I also felt that some of the presentation is a bit stronger than the evidence currently supports. The overall idea is interesting, but terms like “closed-loop reasoning” and the broader claims about robust mobile screening would be more convincing with stronger generalization tests and more detailed analysis across centers, devices, or subject groups.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper addresses a meaningful and timely problem by connecting mobile gaze estimation with downstream cognitive screening in older adults, and the multi-center dataset is a notable strength.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I recommend acceptance, as the rebuttal sufficiently clarified the main concerns regarding the evaluation protocol and downstream screening setup, although some limitations remain in the depth of robustness analysis and the ablation study.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose a closed-loop eye-face alignment framework for gaze inference tailored to mobile cognitive screening in older adults, and construct a mobile gaze prediction dataset comprising 119 participants.
reviews.text_strengths:
(1) The study constructs a relatively comprehensive dataset involving seven scenarios, dual mobile devices (smartphones and tablets), gaze data from 119 participants, and clinical cognitive labels from 114 participants, which strengthens the empirical basis of the work.
(2) The task focuses on older adults, which distinguishes it from previous gaze estimation models developed for more general populations or settings.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(1) The method mainly relies on a basic TSM for temporal modeling, without exploring stronger video modeling architectures such as Transformers. Moreover, since the main difference from conventional gaze estimation methods lies in the face-eye cross-attention design, the manuscript should better explain why this design is sufficient to handle pose jitter, illumination changes, occlusion, age-related appearance variations, and attention fluctuations.
(2) The experimental section lacks comparisons with several classical gaze estimation methods.
(3) It would be helpful to evaluate the model on standard datasets such as GazeCapture to further verify its generalizability. In addition, since the method targets older adults, the manuscript should more clearly define the age range of the intended population.

This assessment is mainly based on prior gaze estimation studies, the method proposed in this work, its experimental results, and the released code.
