meta_reviews.text:
The reviewers commonly raise concerns that the dataset contribution and scale are overstated, since Colon-Bench is derived from REAL-COLON and appears to consist of curated clips/windows rather than full-procedure videos, with unclear and inconsistent reporting of dataset units and counts. They also emphasize that the annotation and VQA generation pipeline lacks sufficient methodological detail, human-expert verification, reproducibility information, and error analysis, while the relatively low reported annotation quality and heavy reliance on Gemini may introduce noise and bias into the benchmark.

Most of the concerns raised by the reviewers (human expert confirmation, Bias on Gemini, …) were addressed in the author’s feedback.
Dataset, code, prompts, SKILL.md, and Jsons will be released on Hugging Face and GitHub on acceptance.
Furthermore, the authors will make their dataset and codes publicly available. It will contribute to the community’s progress.
This manuscript is worthy of acceptance.

This paper received Reject, Reject, and Accept.
The paper makes a real contribution in dataset curation and annotation: 528 lesion windows extracted from REAL-COLON’s 60 full-procedure videos, spanning 14 lesion categories (vs prior single-polyp datasets) with 300k bounding boxes, 213k segmentation masks, and 133k words of clinical descriptions, and the dataset is publicly released; however, the two post-rebuttal Rejects raised structural concerns that the rebuttal did not fully resolve: the pipeline-evaluation circularity (Gemini models generate the lesion proposals, bounding boxes, lesion descriptions, and VQA questions, and Gemini 3 Pro/Flash then top all four benchmark tasks), the dataset-size misrepresentation in Table 1 (528 lesion windows compared against REAL-COLON’s 60 full-procedure videos), and the limited human verification of the AI-generated VQA pairs (10% sample by the authors themselves).
My decision to accept rests on the dataset’s tangible value to the community (14 lesion categories vs prior single-polyp datasets, dense multi-modal annotations, and confirmed public availability), and is conditional on the authors severely addressing the remaining concerns in the camera-ready.
The authors must (1) explicitly disclose the Gemini-dependence throughout the annotation and VQA-generation pipeline and discuss the resulting benchmark bias as a known limitation; (2) correct Table 1 to compare like with like (lesion windows vs lesion windows, full-procedure videos vs full-procedure videos) and add duration statistics for the 528 windows; (3) acknowledge the limited human verification (10% sample by the authors) as a known limitation rather than a quality endorsement; (4) add EndoBench (NeurIPS 2025) to the related work and discuss the disjoint scope (static images vs video); and (5) reframe the 55.4/48.6 precision/recall in Table 2 to make the cross-taxonomy mismatch with REAL-COLON’s polyp-only labels explicit.

The reviewer points out that EndoBench is suitable for VQA but inadequate for segmentation and detection due to the need for full-length procedure testing and unverified AI filtering, while also noting that the rebuttal failed to address evaluation bias towards Gemini models and that the paper requires major revisions to improve methodological clarity and explain low precision/recall results.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers; each section first quotes the criticism.
(1) “Gemini-3 wins, so the benchmark is biased toward Gemini” [R1, R2].
To refute the bias hypothesis, we tested a recently released non-Gemini control: open-source Gemma 4 31B achieves 63.8 / 59.9 / 85.1 / 47.2 on Prompted-VQA / Unprompted-VQA / Classification-Acc / Seg-mIoU, almost matching Gemini 3 Pro (top of Table 3) .
(2) “How are adversarial VQA distractors generated for debias?” [R1].
Distractors come from a Gemini-3 call seeing only the question and correct answer (not the video), emitting 4 length, style, and specificity-matched alternatives; positions are re-randomized. Blind text-only LLM accuracy drops from ~70% (naive distractors) to ~20% (random), confirming text cues are not exploitable.
(3) “Human-expert verification and VQA content are under-specified” [R1, R2].
All windows were reviewed by the authors with Dr. J.H., a surgeon with over 30 years of GI/colonoscopy practice (11.6% expert-rejection, Fig.1). Lesion descriptions are AI-generated by the verification agent; the expert accepts/rejects the window+annotations+description package. Two tiers: Prompted (bbox, no time refs) and Unprompted (no bbox, time-referenced queries); questions cover lesion type, size, location, interventions, and process descriptions. Up to 10% of VQA pairs were manually checked by the authors with 98% correctness (supp. mp4).
(4) “Table 2 Precision/recall 55.4 / 48.6 indicate a noisy benchmark” [R1, R2, R3].
Specificity 94.4% is the relevant reliability indicator. The 55.4 / 48.6 figures compare our 14-category annotations against REAL-COLON’s polyp-only labels from a commercial detector flagging ~12% of REAL-COLON’s frames; most of our categories (ulcers, bleeding, angiectasia, etc.) are absent from this reference, so the labels mismatch by definition. Table 2 will be reframed for R3’s false-negative concern; we target representative lesion-spectrum coverage, not exhaustive frame-level recall.
(5) “No release commitment” [R1, R2].
Dataset, code, prompts, SKILL.md, and Jsons will be released on Hugging Face and GitHub on acceptance. Detailed methodology was in a supplementary PDF disallowed by MICCAI 2026 this year and will fold into the camera-ready.
(6) “Missing EndoBench (NeurIPS 2025)” [R1].
EndoBench (Dec 2025) is concurrent with our Feb 2026 submission and will be cited. It evaluates static-image VQA on general endoscopy. Colon-Bench is the first video colonoscopy benchmark: dense video segmentation, binary lesion classification (over a 14-category lesion spectrum), and prompted/unprompted video VQA. Disjoint scope.
(7) “Inconsistent units: 60 vs 528 vs 1,597 in Table 1 & Sec. 2.2 “ [R1, R2, R3].
60 source recordings are full-procedure videos scanned end-to-end; 528 = annotated lesion windows extracted from them (duration: median 59.9 s, mean 87.9 s, std 83.2 s); 264 clips in segmentation benchmark. 1,597 = VQA clip pool: Prompted (bbox) + Unprompted (no bbox) renderings of accepted windows + confirmed non-lesion distractors. Table 1 will add duration stats; Sec.2.2 will spell out the 528/264/1,597 relation; “full-procedure” softened to “representative full-procedure coverage”.
(8) “Pipeline and Colon-Skill are under-specified” [R1, R2].
Each agent uses a JSON-templated prompt; t_p = window duration (s) for temporal grounding. The AI-cued confirmation agent ingests the clip with bbox+description overlay and outputs accept/reject + rationale. Colon-Skill aggregates up to 20 common errors per lesion category (a design choice) into anti-error rules (e.g., “a flat lesion on a haustral fold without a fibrous tether is Sessile”). +9.7% gain across model families.
In sum: bias is refuted (Gemma 4 control + debiasing Q/A); verification was by a 30+ year senior surgeon, including the VQA check; reproducibility committed; precision/recall are cross-taxonomy. We respectfully ask R1 to reconsider, citing their own “potential to be highly impactful” assessment.

title: Community-Aware Dynamic Graph Learning for Brain Disorder Diagnosis
abstract: Functional MRI (fMRI)-derived dynamic brain functional connectivity (dBFC) holds signiﬁcant potential for characterizing brain disorder-speciﬁc abnormalities in macroscopic neural activity patterns underlying cognition and behavior. Yet, standard approaches usually estimate connectivity via zero-lag correlations. This simpliﬁcation ignores temporal lags among diﬀerent brain regions, which are biologically meaningful markers of directed neural propagation and diverse pathological brain states. Furthermore, existing graph learning models often underexploit the brain‘s hierarchical modular architecture and struggle to capture disorder-induced community switching of brain regions between functional modules. In this work, we propose the Community-aware Dynamic Graph Neural Network (CaDGNN) framework to learn the spatiotemporal interaction patterns in lag-aware dBFC networks for brain disorder diagnosis. First, CaDGNN incorporates a lag-aware dBFC network construction module to encode spatiotemporal propagation patterns of brain activation by explicitly incorporating inter-regional time delays. Then, a temporal community co-occurrence encoder is introduced to extract temporal community structures and model dynamic inter-regional interactions. Based on this, a dual-level dynamic learning module models the switching behavior of graph nodes between communities and the temporal evolution of community structures simultaneously for ﬁnal diagnosis. Evaluations on four independent datasets demonstrate that CaDGNN outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Our ﬁndings highlight the diagnostic value of incorporating both lag-aware dynamics and modular structure into graph learning. The codes of CaDGNN are available at https://github.com/Alyrrraa/CaDGNN.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This work proposes a Community-aware Dynamic Graph Neural Network which constructs lag-aware dynamic functional connectivity networks to explicitly model inter-regional time delays. It further integrates community structure into graph learning to capture modular brain organization. The proposed method is validated on multiple datasets for brain disorder diagnosis.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper presents a framework for brain disorder diagnosis by integrating lag-aware dynamic functional connectivity with community-aware graph learning. 
2.The proposed dual-level modeling provides a multi-scale perspective for capturing both local and global brain dynamics. 
3.The method is evaluated on multiple datasets, and includes basic interpretability analyses.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The claimed novelty is limited. The overall framework is conceptually similar to dFCExperts(Chen, Tingting, et al. “dfcexpert: Learning dynamic functional connectivity patterns with modularity and state experts. “ IEEE transactions on medical imaging (2025). ), with differences mainly in specific implementations. In addition, lag-based functional connectivity is not new. The method appears as a combination of existing techniques rather than being driven by a unified and well-justified research motivation. 
2.The concatenation of zero-lagged matrices in Fig. 1(d) lacks clear explanation and justification. 
3.The performance on ADNI is unusually high, especially for the CN vs. EMCI task, and is significantly higher than competing methods, raising concerns about fairness and possible data leakage. 
4.The performance of baseline methods is generally low. Important related methods, particularly those based on dynamic FC and community detection, are missing from the comparison. 
5.Fig. 3(a) lacks explanation. 
6.The methodology behind the Visualization Analysis in Section 3.3 is not clearly described. 
7.In Fig. 2, grouping the same metrics together would improve readability and comparison.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Limited novelty, and the experimental results are difficult to interpret.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The author appropriately addressed the concerns.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces CaDGNN, a community-aware dynamic graph neural network designed for brain disorder diagnosis using rs-fMRI data. The authors move beyond standard zero-lag connectivity by proposing a lag-aware network construction that explicitly models inter-regional time delays in neural propagation. To capture the brain’s evolving modular structure, they design a temporal community co-occurrence encoder. Finally, the method integrates a dual-level graph learning module to simultaneously capture intra-community node switching and inter-community temporal evolution.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The shift from instantaneous (zero-lag) functional connectivity to lag-aware dynamic connectivity is well-motivated and better reflects the actual neurophysiological propagation of brain signals.
2.The experimental setup is very thorough. The authors validated their framework on four distinct datasets (ADNI, a local dataset, ABIDE, and ADHD-200) covering three different disorders. This demonstrates generalizability.
3.CaDGNN consistently outperforms a solid range of recent baselines (e.g., STA-GIN, BMR, BISTFormer) across multiple evaluation metrics, showing notable improvements in ACC and AUC.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.While the overall lag-aware framework and hierarchical design are novel, the downstream learning modules heavily rely on off-the-shelf components, such as standard Transformer encoders and Graph Attention Networks (GAT). The algorithmic contribution lies more in how the data is pre-processed and structured rather than in the neural network operators themselves.
2.The lag-aware network construction relies on a three-point parabolic interpolation of the cross-covariance function to estimate delays. The authors do not adequately discuss or ablate how robust this heuristic is against the typical noise and artifacts found in rs-fMRI data.
3.The title of Section 2.2 contains a clear typo: “Grpah Learning” should be corrected to “Graph Learning”.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
It would be beneficial to include a brief discussion on the computational overhead introduced by the lag-aware dBFC construction and the multilayer network analysis, especially when compared to simpler zero-lag methods.

The authors propose a biologically sound approach to graph learning for brain networks by incorporating temporal delays and dynamic community structures. The extensive validation across four datasets provides good evidence of the method’s effectiveness. However, the core neural network architectures lack significant novelty, as they largely rely on existing Transformer and GAT modules. Additionally, the lack of robustness analysis for the lag estimation and the missing details for the local dataset are concerns that limit the overall impact. If the authors can address the robustness of the pre-processing and provide more context for the local dataset in their rebuttal, it would strengthen the case for acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a new framework for brain disorder diagnosis, called CaDGNN. Its main contribution has three parts. First, it introduces lag-aware dynamic functional connectivity into the model, instead of using only zero-lag correlations. Second, it adds temporal community detection to capture how brain regions change their community membership over time. Third, it uses a dual-level graph learning design to model both ROI-level dynamics and community-level temporal evolution. Overall, the paper aims to combine delay information, modular organization, and temporal dynamics in one diagnostic framework.
reviews.text_strengths: The main strength of this paper is that its method is relatively complete. It does not only use static functional connectivity. It also does not rely on a simple temporal model. Instead, it combines lag information, community structure, and temporal learning in one framework. This gives the method some novelty. The experiments are also carried out on multiple datasets and tasks, including ADNI, ABIDE, ADHD-200, and a local MCI dataset. The results show that the method outperforms several baselines on some tasks. Another strength is that the paper includes an interpretation analysis of discriminative ROIs and connections, which makes the model more informative.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1 The lag values are estimated at the individual level. However, the manuscript does not show whether the learned lag patterns are robust to inter-site heterogeneity. Since multiple datasets and different preprocessing pipelines are involved, the reported lag effects may be influenced by site-specific acquisition or preprocessing differences.
2 The merging of clusters across different time points relies on the assumption that the same community label is directly comparable over time. This assumption is important, but it is not sufficiently validated in the current manuscript. The authors should provide evidence for cross-temporal label consistency, examine the effect of the temporal coupling parameter ω, and clarify how the method avoids artificial merging caused by label switching.
3 The study uses the Schaefer-500 atlas, which is a very high-resolution parcellation. This choice increases feature dimensionality and model complexity, and may also increase the risk of overfitting. The manuscript does not show whether the performance gain is robust across different atlas resolutions. Repeating the experiments with lower-resolution parcellations, such as Schaefer-100 or Schaefer-200, would strengthen the methodological validity.
4 The community-level graph is constructed with an all-ones adjacency matrix, so each time point is fully connected to all others. This design weakens the explicit modeling of temporal order and may bias the model toward global similarity rather than local temporal evolution. The authors should evaluate more constrained temporal connections, such as local time windows neighborhoods, to justify the current design and clarify the contribution of temporal structure.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The method combines lag-aware dynamic connectivity, temporal community modeling, and dual-level graph learning in a unified way. This gives the paper some methodological novelty. The paper proposes lag-aware dynamic functional connectivity network construction and community-based temporal clustering. The rebuttal should address reviewers’ critical questions, including the novelty of the proposed method, robustness, and a clear explanation of the lag pattern.

The rebuttal addressed reviewers’ major questions, including the novelty of the proposed method, robustness, and a clear explanation of the lag pattern.

This is a borderline paper. While the rebuttal is responsive to many of the critiques, I remain unconvinced about the importance of this method. The experimental results focus almost exclusively on diagnostic prediction and do not evaluate the novelty or robustness of the learned brain networks. I am also suspicious of the ADNI results. The proposed method achieves substantially higher classification performance than the baseline methods and the current literature based on rs-fMRI. This points towards information leakage, perhaps in the selection of hyperparameters. Ultimately, this is yet another “brain network extraction” paper that uses classification as a proxy for impact, and I lean towards rejection.

The reviewers found the paper methodologically relevant and empirically well supported, with validation across multiple datasets. After rebuttal, the main concerns on novelty, robustness, lag modeling, and experimental fairness were addressed, and the reviewers did not raise further major objections. Acceptance is recommended.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback. Below we address the concerns.
Q1(R1-1, R2-1): Novelty. CaDGNN and dFCExperts follow fundamentally different paradigms. dFCExperts decouples spatial state from temporal state aggregation on zero-lag dBFC; CaDGNN jointly models spatiotemporal coupling in lag-aware dBFC networks. The key distinction is the CCE module, which couples the spatiotemporal features by tracking each node’s switching history across communities over time, a mechanism absent in dFCExperts. Ablation (Fig.2) confirms removing CCE causes larger performance drop than removing Transformer encoder, validating that improvements stem from spatiotemporal community modeling rather than standard operators. We acknowledge Transformer/GAT are established components; our contribution is their principled composition for spatiotemporal brain network modeling.
Q2(R2-2, R3-1): Lag Robustness. Three-point parabolic interpolation mitigates the discrete TR sampling limitation for lag estimation. It refines the CCF peak using only its two neighbors, avoiding noise-prone broader CCF regions while requiring no extra hyperparameters. ADNI, ABIDE, and * are processed with the same DPARSF pipeline. Results on the single-site * dataset further indicate lag effects are not solely driven by multi-site acquisition. Following prior work, we discount delays >4s and convert to TR-specific shifts, reducing artifact-prone long delays while keeping lag estimation comparable across datasets.
Q3(R3-2,4): Temporal Community. CaDGNN does not detect communities per segment and artificially merge them. Instead, Temporal Community Detection (TCD) treats time windows as layers and links the same node across adjacent layers via coupling parameter ω. Community assignments are inferred through a single joint optimization, inherently encouraging temporal consistency while allowing network-driven switching. This design reduces the risk of artificial merging due to label switching. For the community-level graph, the all-ones adjacency enables flexible cross-window information exchange; GAT then learns nonuniform temporal attention, so windows are not equally aggregated. Ablation (w/o CG, Fig.2) validates this design’s contribution.
Q4(R1-3,4): Fairness & Baselines. Two types of baselines are included, spanning dynamic brain activity models (ST2GCN, BISTFormer) and modularity-prior GNNs (BMR, similar to dFCExperts in its decoupled modeling way). We use strict subject-wise 5-fold cross-validation, ensuring that all samples from the same subject are assigned to the same fold to prevent subject-level leakage across train/test splits. No demographic or clinical variables are used as input features. As shown in Table 1, most compared methods achieve relatively high performance on ADNI, especially for CN vs. EMCI, indicating intrinsic separability of the diagnostic tasks rather than an artifact of our method.
Q5(R3-3): Atlas Resolution. Schaefer-500 is widely adopted in brain network studies. Its finer parcellation captures functional boundaries coarser atlases may miss, important for detecting subtle disorder alterations. CaDGNN’s consistent performance across four datasets with varying acquisition suggests results are not driven by atlas resolution alone. Moreover, TCD naturally groups ROIs into communities, providing built-in regularization against overfitting at higher resolutions.
Q6(R1-2,5,6): Clarifications. For Fig.1(d), the concatenation combines complementary information: X_{fc}^t preserves current synchrony, H^t encodes lag-aware community dynamics. Fig.3(a) shows sensitivity of k (KNN neighbors) and w (window length), color denoting ACC. For Sec.3.3, Grad-CAM is applied to ROI-level embeddings from intra-level graph learning; importance scores are computed from class-score gradients and averaged across subjects.
Q7(R1-7, R2-3): Paper Readability. We apologize for the ‘Grpah’ typo. We will regroup Fig.2 by metrics and correct the typos.

title: Co-MoCo: Collaborative Learning Enabled Motion Compensation for Weight-Bearing CBCT
abstract: Weight-bearing cone-beam computed tomography (WB-CBCT) enables physiological load-bearing imaging but suffers from motion artifacts caused by involuntary patient tremors. Existing software-based approaches typically address image-domain restoration and motion estimation as separate problems, often leading to over-smoothed reconstructions or suboptimal convergence. To address these problems, we propose Co-MoCo, a collaborative motion compensation framework that integrates image-domain priors with physical consistency through an end-to-end differentiable pipeline. The framework employs a two-stage optimization: Stage I utilizes a Motion-Aware Dual-Decoder Network (MADN), trained via Optimal Transport Conditional Flow Matching (OT-CFM), to generate an artifact-free prior. In Stage II, this prior is integrated into an end-to-end differentiable correction loop to iteratively refine 6-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) rigid motion trajectories. This synergistic design enables image restoration and motion estimation to mutually regularize each other. Extensive experiments on simulated datasets demonstrate that Co-MoCo significantly outperforms competing methods, achieving SSIM of 0.9849 under mild motion and 0.9152 under severe motion, with performance gains of up to 0.0528. Real-world validation on human and porcine hind limbs further confirms its superior robustness in artifact suppression and detail preservation for high-quality WB-CBCT imaging. Code is available at https://github.com/TomSHINING/CoMoCo.

2.Comprehensive experiments and evaluation:

reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.While the paper presents a real-world validation on human volunteers and porcine hind limbs , the evaluation is purely qualitative. 
2.The proposed Co-MoCo framework relies on an iterative optimization pipeline (Stage II) that updates motion parameters over 100 iterations using a differentiable cone-beam backprojector and a neural network. However, the authors do not report the memory footprint or the time required to reconstruct a single 3D volume on their NVIDIA RTX 4090 setup
3.In Section 2.2, the authors describe the Motion-Aware Dual-Decoder Network (MADN) and state that it takes a motion intensity map ($\sigma_{jit}$) as input. N/A

Major factors supporting the acceptance:
Clinical Relevance & Motivation: The paper tackles a highly relevant and challenging problem in musculoskeletal imaging—motion artifacts in Weight-bearing CBCT caused by involuntary tremors. Solving this has direct clinical utility.
Methodological Novelty
Major factors limiting a higher score:
Missing Computational/Runtime Analysis: The iterative nature of the differentiable backprojection (Stage II requires 100 iterations) raises significant concerns regarding computational efficiency and memory overhead. The authors completely omit runtime metrics. For a method targeting clinical application, assessing the time required to reconstruct a single 3D volume is critical.
Lack of Quantitative Real-World Metrics: While the visual results on human and porcine data (Figure 4) are encouraging, the evaluation of the real-world porcine data—which explicitly had a stationary reference—is entirely qualitative. The absence of quantitative metrics (like SSIM, PSNR, or MSE) on this real data makes it difficult to objectively verify the method’s effectiveness outside of simulated environments.Incomplete
Technical Details: Crucial details regarding the architecture and training of the “pre-trained discriminator” (used to extract the motion intensity map $\sigma_{jit}$) are omitted, which hinders reproducibility. Furthermore, the reliance on a purely rigid 6-DoF assumption ignores the reality of non-rigid soft tissue deformations during patient tremors.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents Co-MoCo, a collaborative motion compensation framework for weight-bearing CBCT. The method targets motion artifacts in WB-CBCT caused by unstable standing posture, tremor, or fatigue, and attempts to address the limitation that image-domain restoration and motion parameter estimation are often treated separately. Specifically, the proposed framework first employs a Motion-Aware Dual-Decoder Network to learn an artifact-free image prior, and then embeds this prior into an end-to-end differentiable motion correction loop to iteratively optimize a 6-DoF rigid motion trajectory. Experimental results show that the method outperforms multiple image restoration and motion compensation baselines under both mild-motion and severe-motion settings, while also demonstrating promising artifact suppression and detail recovery on real human volunteer and porcine hind-limb data. Overall, the manuscript is clearly written, the methodological logic is complete, and the figures are intuitive and easy to follow.
reviews.text_strengths:
(1) The topic is highly practical and addresses a current clinical pain point. The paper focuses on motion artifacts in weight-bearing CBCT, which is a clinically relevant problem in orthopedic and musculoskeletal rehabilitation scenarios. The introduction clearly explains the clinical value of WB-CBCT for weight-bearing imaging of the knee, foot/ankle, and lower extremities, as well as its susceptibility to involuntary patient motion due to the relatively long scanning time. Therefore, the work is well motivated and has a clear application background.
(2) The method is well designed and demonstrates a meaningful degree of innovation, with a clear collaborative relationship between its components. The paper attempts to let image restoration and motion parameter estimation mutually reinforce each other within a unified framework, which is more valuable than using restoration-only or motion-estimation-only strategies. In particular, under severe motion, single-module methods are clearly limited, whereas the joint framework is still able to maintain high image quality, suggesting that the proposed design brings real synergistic benefits.
(3) The quantitative experiments are comprehensive. The study includes both mild-motion and severe-motion settings and compares the proposed method against multiple image restoration and motion compensation approaches, making the results readable and convincing.
(4) The real-data examples enhance the credibility of the method. In addition to simulation experiments, the authors also validate the framework on a real WB-CBCT system using human volunteer data and porcine hind-limb data. Although this part is still mainly qualitative, it nevertheless shows that the method is not limited to a purely simulated environment and has a certain degree of practical feasibility.
(5) The proposed method not only achieves better numerical results than the competing methods, but also shows more intuitive improvements in residual blur reduction, streak artifact suppression, and preservation of high-frequency details. For motion artifact correction tasks, metric improvements alone are sometimes insufficient to demonstrate practical value, and the visual improvements shown in this paper make the conclusions more convincing.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(1) The real-data validation remains largely qualitative and lacks further quantitative analysis. Although the human volunteer and porcine hind-limb results strengthen the practical relevance of the paper, this part currently relies mainly on visual inspection and lacks a more systematic quantitative evaluation. As such, the generalization ability and stability of the method in real clinical scenarios have not yet been fully established.
(2) The assumption on the motion model is somewhat idealized. The paper mainly models patient motion as a 6-DoF rigid trajectory. While this assumption may be reasonable for some motion patterns in lower-limb WB-CBCT, in real scenarios, especially when soft tissue or local limb posture changes are more pronounced, more complex local non-rigid deformations may still occur. The paper does not yet discuss the applicability boundary of this assumption in sufficient depth, and therefore the robustness of the method under more complex motion patterns remains to be demonstrated.
(3) The discussion of runtime efficiency and deployment cost is insufficient. The manuscript does not explicitly report the inference time or optimization time per case. Given that the proposed framework may require iterative optimization of motion parameters within a differentiable reconstruction loop, runtime and computational cost will be important considerations for future clinical deployment. The current version is somewhat limited in this respect.
(4) Some baselines perform relatively poorly under severe motion, but the paper does not further analyze the reasons for this. Several image-domain baselines show substantial performance degradation in the severe-motion setting, yet the manuscript does not discuss why these baseline results are poor. This weakens the completeness of the comparative study to some extent.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Overall, I am inclined toward weak accept, because I believe this paper addresses a clinically meaningful and practically valuable problem, and the proposed framework is also technically well motivated. In addition, the manuscript is generally clear and easy to follow, and the qualitative and quantitative results together make the work convincing as a promising solution for motion artifact suppression in WB-CBCT.However, I do not give a full accept for two main reasons. First, the validation on real data still relies primarily on qualitative analysis, and the evidence for robustness and generalization in realistic clinical settings remains limited. Second, the method appears difficult to reproduce in practice, since the framework is relatively complex and the paper does not indicate that the implementation code will be publicly available. As a result, reproducing the full pipeline may require substantial effort.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I appreciate the authors’ efforts in providing additional clarification and supplementary quantitative results in the rebuttal. However, I still feel that several issues have not been fully addressed. The quantitative validation on real data appears to remain limited and may not be sufficient to establish the generalization and stability of the method in practical clinical scenarios. The discussion of the 6-DOF rigid body motion assumption is reasonable, but it also shows that it is not applicable to more complex local or non-rigid body motion. In addition, although the authors now report computational cost, the reported runtime suggests that clinical deployment may still be challenging.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes Co-MoCo, a motion compensation framework for Weight-bearing CBCT (WB-CBCT). It addresses motion artifacts through a two-stage process: first, training a Motion-Aware Dual-Decoder Network (MADN) using Optimal Transport Conditional Flow Matching (OT-CFM) to serve as an artifact-free prior; second, utilizing this frozen prior within a differentiable correction loop to iteratively optimize the 6-DoF rigid motion parameters (P-Matrix) based on physical consistency. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance across both simulated motion datasets and real-world clinical scans.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper innovatively couples an image-domain generative prior with a physical forward model, solving the motion-corrupted inverse problem by iteratively optimizing 6-DoF rigid motion parameters to overcome the over-smoothing limitations of pure image-domain methods.
2.The paper introduces Optimal Transport Conditional Flow Matching (OT-CFM) to train a dual-decoder network (MADN), which serves as a high-quality, artifact-free manifold regularization constraint for the subsequent joint optimization of physical parameters.
3.The paper demonstrates the clinical feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed framework through comprehensive validation on both simulated motion datasets and real-world clinical scans.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The motivation for selecting Optimal Transport Conditional Flow Matching (OT-CFM) as the artifact-free prior, rather than other generative models, is insufficiently justified. Additionally, the authors need to clarify whether the identical flow matching setup is applied across different motion parameters, and rigorously explain how a completely frozen MADN can consistently guarantee reliable prior guidance during the iterative optimization process.
2.The strategy of alternating optimization between image domains and motion parameters has been extensively explored in previous literature. The authors should properly cite these prior works and explicitly discuss the methodological differences and specific advantages of the proposed framework over existing alternating optimization schemes.
3.To convincingly demonstrate its effectiveness, the experimental section must include a quantitative comparison with at least one state-of-the-art baseline method that jointly optimizes image and motion parameters.
4.The authors are strongly encouraged to open-source their codebase and release the real-world clinical dataset to facilitate reproducibility and benefit related research within the medical imaging community.
5.The manuscript lacks structural cohesion in the methodology section. The logical flow and transitions between Sections 2.1, 2.2, and 2.3 are somewhat disjointed and require further elaboration to present a unified narrative.
6.The paper omits critical computational efficiency metrics. The authors should report and compare the network parameter counts and running times against the baseline methods to verify the real-time clinical feasibility of the proposed pipeline.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Although the proposed physics-guided framework demonstrates strong clinical feasibility and innovative design, the manuscript still requires crucial clarifications regarding its theoretical motivation, joint-optimization baseline comparisons, and computational efficiency metrics.

meta_reviews.text:
The authors proposed Co-MoCo, a collaborative motion compensation framework that integrates image-domain priors with physical consistency through an end-to-end differentiable pipeline. Stage 1 contains a Motion-Aware Dual-Decoder Network (MADN) trained via Optimal Transport Conditional Flow Matching (OT-CFM) to generate an artifact-free prior. In Stage 2 this prior is integrated into a correction loop to iteratively refine 6-DoF rigid motion trajectories.
Reviewers all gave weak acceptance/borderline scores. The motivation behind image-domain priors with physical consistency is widely acknowledged, and the experiments are comprehensive with real-patient data. However, it’s noted that common concerns include (1) qualitative evaluation on real-patient data, which might be reasonable since there is no motion GT, but the authors might need to further discuss this and include potential future directions with motion-tracking devices to get GT; (2) lacking computational cost information since there are iterative optimization loops; (3) the validity of the 6-DOF motion trajectory assumption; (4) the intuition behind artifact-free prior selection and (5) concerns regarding baseline comparisons. The authors are encouraged to address these concerns and provide other missing details as required by the reviewers.

Thank the authors for providing this detailed response. Most of the concerns were sufficiently addressed, including real data quantitative analysis and runtime report. The authors are encouraged to discuss the potential of non-rigid motion modeling in the camera-ready version.

After rebuttal, the paper leans toward acceptance. The reviewers agreed that the problem is clinically important and that the proposed Co-MoCo framework offers an interesting integration of learned image priors with physics-based motion correction for WB-CBCT. The rebuttal addressed several major concerns by providing runtime and memory estimates, clarification of the 6-DOF assumption, additional details on the motion-intensity discriminator, and discussion of prior alternating-optimization methods. Two reviewers were satisfied by the rebuttal and now recommend accept. Reviewer 2 maintains a reject recommendation, citing limited real-data validation, long runtime, and the remaining limitations of the rigid-motion model. These are valid concerns and should be acknowledged, particularly the high computational cost and limited quantitative real-data evidence. However, given the novelty and clinical relevance of the framework, the improved clarification after rebuttal, and the overall positive reviewer balance, I recommend acceptance.

The authors have responded to most of the reviewers’ comments. While one reviewer still has concerns about the evaluation and feasibility of clinical deployment, I think the authors should expand their discussion on the limitations in the final version.

author_feedback_text:
We thank AC for the insightful summary. We thank R2 and R3 for accepting our paper as “tackles a highly relevant and challenging problem”, “addresses a clinically meaningful and practically valuable problem”, and thank R4 for appreciating our work as “strong clinical feasibility and innovative design”. Below, we provide point-by-point responses.
AC-Q1&R2-Q1&R3-Q1: Lack of quantitative analysis on real data
Acquiring GT in WB-CBCT scans is hard due to inevitable patient motion, though motion-tracking devices [1] could provide reliable references in future work. To provide a quantitative analysis on real data, we report results on the porcine case in Fig. 4.Our approach achieves lower MSE (6691.25 vs. 7412.84/8688.25/10147.37), higher SSIM (0.8411 vs. 0.8132/0.7881/0.7171), and higher PSNR (35.49 vs. 34.55/33.08/31.44) than Thies’s, Uformer, and FDK.
[1] Maier J, et al. Inertial measurements for motion compensation in weight-bearing cone-beam CT of the knee.
AC-Q2&R2-Q2&R3-Q3&R4-Q6: Lack of computational cost information
Our method, run for 100 iterations with 40 control points on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 (projection size 400×1024×1536; volume 80×512×512/80×256×256), requires 9055/2256 sec and 14.0/12.9 GB GPU memory, while Thies’s [25] takes 8840/2203 sec and 15.3/13.7 GB GPU memory.
AC-Q3&R2-Q4&R3-Q2: Validity of the 6-DOF assumption
The 6-DOF rigid motion assumption is widely adopted for bone-dominant motion. However, lower-limb motion can be influenced by joint articulation and soft-tissue deformation. On real data, performing separate optimizations for thigh, knee, and leg can mitigate this issue, as shown in Fig. 4.Above limitations and potential of non-rigid modeling will be discussed in revision.
AC-Q4&R4-Q1: Intuition behind artifact-free prior
1)OT-CFM enables stable and continuous trajectory learning by leveraging few-step transport estimation, providing faster inference than diffusion-based models. As shown in Tables 1 and 2, it also outperforms competing NN methods. 2) The MADN maintains a unified flow framework and uses varying degrees of motion information through a pre-trained discriminator, thereby performs effectively across different motion intensities. Additional ablation studies were omitted due to constraints.
AC-Q5&R3-Q4: Concerns about baseline comparisons
Under severe motion, image quality is highly degraded. Purely image-domain NN provides multiple plausible solutions for a single voxel, leading to excessive blurring. The proposed framework utilizes real projections and scan geometry as strong physical constraints through a differentiable P-Matrix back-projector, thus iteratively narrowing solution space toward a physically consistent state.
R2-Q4&R3-Q4&R4-Q4: Concerns about reproducibility
We promise to release code once acceptance. Clinical datasets cannot be shared due to hospital privacy.
R2-Q3: Lack of implementation details of pre-trained discriminator
Motion maps are generated by a lightweight U-Net trained on simulated motion dataset (vary degrees of motion) to provide motion intensity information for the MADN. More details will be found in our released code.
R4-Q2&Q3: Discussion and comparison with existing alternating optimization schemes
Previous alternating schemes primarily rely on costly, view-constrained forward-projector, suboptimal regularizers such as TV and VIF and on scarce high-quality CAD (on head data). In contrast, we utilize a differentiable P-Matrix back-projector to enable strong physical constraints and high-quality OT-CFM guidance. As noted in Table 1, we have included a comparison with the state-of-the-art alternating optimization scheme by Thies [25]. More comprehensive comparisons will be conducted in future work.
R4-Q5: Lack of structural cohesion in methodology
Our methodology is organized as: Problem Formulation (Sec. 2.1), Prior Generation (Sec. 2.2), Physical Modeling (Sec. 2.3), Overall Architecture (Sec. 2.4). We will improve structural coherence in revision.

title: Comparative Analysis of Automated Frame Selection Methods for Glaucoma Detection in Smartphone-Based Low-Quality Fundus Video
abstract: Ultra-low-cost smartphone-based fundus imaging offers a scalable glaucoma screening solution in resource-limited settings, yet deployment is challenged by severe acquisition noise. While short video is preferred over single-image capture in such settings, selecting diagnostically relevant frames from degraded recording remains an open problem, as existing quality assessment methods often fail under these extreme noise conditions of low-cost imaging. This work presents a domain-informed frame selection framework tailored to ultra-low-cost fundus video. The method integrates optic disc localization as a spatial quality gate with complementary spectral and structural quality metrics (retinal saturation, red-channel dominance, vessel density, and sharpness). These metrics are combined via a multiplicative fusion strategy, penalizing frames that fail in any single modality. Evaluation on a multi-center dataset of 284 smartphone-acquired videos using a MobileNetV3-based classifier shows this holistic fusion (mainly S_total) significantly stabilizes sensitivity and F1-Score compared to single-metric approaches. Fusion-based frame selection achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.95 ± 0.04, closely approaching a semi-automated expert baseline (0.98 ± 0.01). These findings demonstrate that robust frame selection bridges the gap between automated and expert intervention, enabling reliable glaucoma screening on ultra-low-cost imaging platforms.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
1.This paper proposes an automated frame selection framework for ultra-low-cost fundus videos, which includes localization of the optic disc region and multiplicative fusion of four frame selection indicators.
2.This paper conducts corresponding experiments on the proposed automated frame selection framework, validating the feasibility of the method on a multi-center private dataset of smartphone-based fundus videos. Under the proposed framework, the classification performance for glaucoma achieves an AUC of 0.95, an accuracy of 0.89, a sensitivity of 0.87, a specificity of 0.90, and an F1-score of 0.86, which is very close to semi-manual methods. Statistical calculations show no significant difference between them, indicating that the proposed framework can effectively bridge the gap between automatic selection and expert intervention.
3.At the clinical application level, the automated frame selection framework proposed in this paper can assist in the deployment of ultra-low-cost smartphone-based fundus imaging. Even under challenging conditions with severe imaging noise, this framework can relatively accurately select diagnosis-relevant frames from degraded footage, addressing the shortcomings in this application domain.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The automated frame selection framework proposed in this paper integrates the optic disc localization task into the frame selection task, using the pre-trained YOLOv8n from reference [2] to detect the optic disc and form the region of interest (ROI). Meanwhile, a comparative analysis based on the optic disc detection results shows that this ROI strategy offers certain advantages.
2.The automated frame selection framework proposed in this paper performs multiplicative fusion of four frame selection indicators, accompanied by detailed visualization analysis and ablation experiments, verifying the algorithmic robustness brought by multiplicative fusion.
3.The construction and use of the dataset in this paper are relatively standardized. This private dataset was collected from two clinical centers, comprising 284 fundus videos (114 glaucoma patients, 170 healthy patients). Each video (10–17 seconds) was recorded by trained staff under mydriatic conditions. Glaucoma cases were clinically confirmed, while healthy subjects were validated through comprehensive ophthalmic examinations (visual field testing, intraocular pressure measurement, slit-lamp examination) and adjudicated by senior ophthalmologists.
4.The automated frame selection framework proposed in this paper holds value for clinical deployment and can assist ultra-low-cost smartphone‑based fundus imaging. Even under challenging conditions with severe imaging noise, this framework can relatively accurately select diagnosis‑relevant frames from degraded footage.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The algorithmic novelty of this paper is somewhat insufficient. In the proposed automated frame selection framework, the main innovations lie in the ROI strategy and the multiplicative fusion strategy. Regarding the ROI strategy, which localizes the optic disc region in fundus images, this is already a common technique in glaucoma research and is not highly innovative. Moreover, the paper employs the results of others’ work, namely the pre-trained YOLOv8n from reference [2], which further diminishes the novelty of the ROI strategy. As for the multiplicative fusion strategy—multiplying four existing frame selection indicators—this fusion method is too straightforward and simplistic, lacking algorithmic depth.
2.The text of this paper contains some minor errors. In Table 1, the metric name “Red Score” is used, which is inconsistent with the earlier “Red-Channel Intensity Score (RSC)”.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The algorithmic novelty of the automated frame selection framework proposed in this paper is limited, and the experimental completeness is slightly lacking. However, the overall experimental results of this framework are quite impressive, as its classification performance for glaucoma is very close to that of semi-manual methods. Therefore, it holds certain value for practical application and deployment.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The core technical contribution is a multiplicative fusion of four existing image quality metrics (retinal saturation, red‑channel dominance, vessel density, Laplacian‑based sharpness), combined with an optic disc detector to gate the analysis to the region of interest. Each of these components is well established in the literature and is used here in a straightforward, plug‑and‑play manner. The fusion itself (multiplication of normalized scores) is a simple heuristic without theoretical grounding or learned adaptation. No new algorithm, model architecture, or learning paradigm is introduced.
While the application domain (ultra‑low‑cost video) is challenging, the paper does not demonstrate that its approach substantially advances the state of the art beyond careful engineering of existing tools. A comparison against even basic deep learning‑based quality assessment models (e.g., a lightweight CNN trained on the same data) is missing, making it impossible to assess whether the proposed hand‑crafted metrics offer any advantage over data‑driven alternatives.
It does not meet the bar for novelty expected at a top conference.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses an important and clinically relevant problem: automatically selecting the optimal frame from short smartphone-captured fundus videos to enable accurate glaucoma diagnosis.
reviews.text_strengths: The key strength of the paper lies in the methodological novelty proposed for frame selection, along with an attempt to evaluate the approach by comparing it with a semi-automated baseline.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The key weakness of this work is the limited reliability of the semi-automated baseline. In the baseline, the final frame is selected manually by the first author from the top-20 ranked candidates. This introduces two concerns: (1) the proposed method may fail to include the truly optimal frame within the top-20 candidates, and (2) the first author does not appear to be a clinical expert (e.g., an ophthalmologist), which raises questions about the validity of the final frame selection.
A more appropriate evaluation would involve an independent expert (such as a trained ophthalmologist) selecting the optimal frame, followed by a direct comparison with the frame selected by the proposed algorithm.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Additional concerns include missing or unclear experimental details. For example, the average length of the input videos is not clearly specified (the paper only mentions “several hundred frames”), which makes it difficult to assess the practical setting.
Finally, the proposed method does not outperform the semi-automated baseline, which raises questions about its effectiveness and practical utility.
