In contrast, we avoid classifier gradients and instead learn salient and common features at the distribution level to perform controlled edits, such as swapping and interpolation. Although our approach is classifier-free, we evaluate the generated (swapped) images with a pre-trained classifier, following prior VCE work, to verify whether the counterfactual edits induce the expected class changes. The fact that swapped images are mostly classified as the target class (Table 4) suggests that the learned salient factors capture meaningful discriminative patterns 
As stated in the conclusion, our method does not enable causal discovery, similarly to recent VCE approaches
Novelty (R2): The methodological novelty does not lie in using StyleGAN2 as a backbone, but in the formulation of counterfactual generation. Unlike prior methods that search for directions in the W+ space maximizing classifier prediction changes, we decompose the W+ space into common and salient factors, generating counterfactual (swap) from distributional differences between classes rather than classifier objectives, as noted by R1 and R3
Datasets resolution (R2,R3): Datasets from MedMNIST+ are provided at 224×224 resolution and were resized to 256×256 to match the input requirements of StyleGAN2.We will clarify this in the revised manuscript
Classifier failure modes (R1): We acknowledge that we did not include experiments on bias reproduction in classifier-guided VCE methods, as this has already been shown in prior work (e.g., [35]). We leave evaluation of our method on controlled bias datasets for future work
Clinical relevance (R2): Qualitative results were assessed by expert medical doctors and biologists, but no formal multi-expert reader study was conducted. The focus was methodological development on MedMNIST+, with a future journal extension planned to include a full reader study
Training stochasticity (R2, R3): We will update Table 4 to report mean and std over 5 training. Rankings and performance differences between methods remain very similar. For example, FR values are 0.955 (±0.02) for our method and 0.976 (±0.02) for ACE
Clarifications (R3): We will clarify that we follow a two-stage training similar to [5], learning first common and salient factors in the W+ space, which is more regularized and editable, and refining details in the F space (layer 8 as in [5]) without changing the semantic edit direction learnt in the W+ space. We only use W+ and F space, with StyleGAN2 generators trained per dataset and then kept frozen. Hyperparameters are selected on validation sets (and not tuned on the test sets) and are the same for all datasets. Inference time is reported in Table 4.Similarly to previous CA works [1,7,10,22,34], we use summation instead of concatenation to avoid extra parameters (to map back to the W+ dimension)
Tables (R1,R3): Tables will be reorganized with clearer, self-contained captions. Table 1 compares our method with contrastive baselines, while Table 4 evaluates counterfactuals against VCE-specific methods. We will clarify that the swap operation in Table 1 is equivalent to the counterfactual generation in Table 4.FID differences arise because Table 1 uses random X,Y pairs, whereas Table 4 fixes either Y or X using the images of Fig. 3

title: Counterfactual Stress-Testing for Fixing Lung Cancer Segmentation Models
abstract:
Segmentation models for lung cancer on CT can achieve strong performance yet remain brittle to clinically relevant morphological and textural variations, with failures more prevalent in certain phenotypes. We introduce a counterfactual stress-testing framework that makes this brittleness measurable and actionable. We learn a conditional 3D tumour generator that produces identity-preserving counterfactual CT crops and corresponding pseudo-label masks by intervening on a compact set of radiomic “parent” features. Sweeping each feature across its empirical quantiles produces Counterfactual Robustness Curves (CRCs) for a baseline segmentation model, highlighting the feature regimes in which performance collapses.
We define hard regimes as CRC regions where performance falls below a user-defined threshold and use them to select counterfactuals for targeted fine-tuning. On a publicly available CT cohort, CRCs expose consistent failure regions for small volumes, low sphericity, and high fractal dimension. Counterfactual fidelity analysis confirms that interventions achieve the intended feature changes with limited drift in non-target features. Targeted counterfactual fine-tuning guided by CRCs improves test segmentation performance compared with classical data augmentation and unconditional generative sampling.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Causal Inference / Counterfactual Reasoning

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents a Counterfactual Stress-Testing framework for lung cancer segmentation on CT. The core idea is to generate identity-preserving counterfactual tumor crops by intervening on interpretable radiomics attributes, then using these counterfactuals to measure phenotype-specific robustness through Counterfactual Robustness Curves (CRCs), and then perform targeted fine-tuning on the hardest counterfactual regimes. The paper shows that this framework not only reveals clinically meaningful failure modes, but also improves segmentation performance more effectively than standard augmentation or untargeted generative sampling.
reviews.text_strengths:
This paper addresses an important and clinically meaningful robustness problem in lung tumor segmentation tasks. It operates beyond average test-set performance and generic augmentation, and instead asks which specific tumor phenotypes can lead to segmentation failure.
The paper proposes a practical way to intervene on interpretable tumor-specific radiomics factors, generate corresponding counterfactual image-mask pairs, and visualize how segmentation performance changes across controlled phenotype shifts. This is visualized well in the shown images as well. This approach is further compared against strong augmentations and generative models.
The experimental section is very brief and thoroughly explanative for a 9 page paper.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
There are only two points this reviewer would like to point out:
1.The counterfactual interventions are defined mainly through tumor-intrinsic radiomics descriptors extracted from the tumor segmented regions themselves. Small question: what are the statistics of the segmentations? is the approach viable across the entire corpus of tumor sizes or is it susceptible to big/small clear/unclear tumors? The current framing makes the interventions interpretable, but it also narrows the stress-testing space. Failure modes driven by tumor-context interactions may not be fully captured by the current set of intervention variables, which rely on the the radiomics features that capture the tumor characteristics itself but not of the composite scan (which is imperative to a proper nnU-Net segmentation). 
2.The framework depends on pseudo-label masks from the generator, so generator bias may propagate into both stress testing and repair. This is partly similar to recent self-supervised learning frameworks that leak their position bias into the learning.
Not so important, but this reviewer also found the presentation of the flow-based generator and OT machinery somewhat dense relative to the main paper contribution, and some of the causal or identifiability language may be stronger than necessary in practice. A significant portion of the time was spent on analyzing and drawing the paper flow graphs on OT and flow matching than the overall holistic approach at hand.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The paper is very well written, just a small pinch. Its nnU-Net everywhere in the paper, except one place where it is written nnUNet: “We evaluate the nnUNet on each counterfactual image and compute Dice against the corresponding generator mask pseudo-label. “

This paper proposes a well-motivated and practically useful framework for understanding and improving segmentation robustness in a way that is more interpretable than standard augmentation-based approaches. It focuses on what kinds of tumors can cause a problem and on less of scanner/acquisition parameter variations or other noise sources (a more common setting studied across the board). The methodology is thoughtful, the empirical comparisons are strong, and the paper tells a compelling end-to-end story from diagnosis to targeted model improvement. Overall, a well-written paper except for the two weaknesses that can be very well accounted for in the revised discussion.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal satisfactorily addresses my concerns, clarifying the SCM/abduction formulation and its approximate implementation while providing solid evidence of identity preservation outside the tumor. The added HD95 analysis further strengthens confidence by confirming boundary robustness alongside Dice improvements. This reviewer also appreciates the clearer positioning as a practical framework for counterfactual robustness.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a counterfactual stress-testing and repair framework for lung tumor segmentation, which leverages flow-matching generative networks conditioned on radiomics parents to inpaint tumors on patient-specific exogenous factors. The idea itself is oif certain novelty and the flow of the paper is easy to understand.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper presents extensive analysis of the generated counterfactual examples including their effect on downstream segmentation, their fidelity wrt. an in-house validation set and the evolution of segmentation performance over intervention deciles.
The idea of leveraging hard counterfactual example is a popular way of enhancing downstream segmentation performance and the authors’ implementaton is of novelty.
The paper is generally well-written and easy to understand.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
– The result of this paper is only tested on one dataset (NSCLC Radiogenomics), while there exists more datasets on lung cancer segmentation in general (MSD-Lung, etc). The author should provide reasons why they choose not to test their method on them. Also, the results are only evaluated on dice, evaluating them with other widely used metrics such as HD95 can be better.
While complementing segmentation dataset with counterfactual samples is of significance intuitively, there exists a line of work that does tumor inpainting that also boosts downstream tumor segmentation performance, some even utilize textual prompts to be of more versatility (LesionDiffusion, GuideGen, DiffTumor, FreeTumor, etc). Discussing the differences or comparing with them can make the proposed counterfactual method more convincing.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The method itself is acceptable, but it is only tested on one dataset with only one metric, and the reported performance gain is not that significant (+0.03 dice). I also would like the author to discuss the advantages (if any) of their counterfactual design with other tumor inpainting/genesis pipelines.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: the authors’ rebuttal solves most of my problems, i recommmend the authors add the analysis they provided in their rebuttal in the final version.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a counterfactual stress-testing framework for CT lung tumour segmentation. The core is a conditional 3D flow-matching generator trained with minibatch OT coupling, conditioned on six radiomic parents. The authors use reverse-time ODE integration to abduct the exogenous factors from a factual crop, then swap one parent to a value at a chosen decile and regenerate the counterfactual. Sweeping across deciles gives Counterfactual Robustness Curves for a baseline nnU-Net. Counterfactuals where the baseline scores below Dice 0.7 are mined and used to fine-tune the segmenter (CF-hard). On an independent NSCLC test cohort, CF-hard reports the best mean Dice (0.84) among BigAug, GAN-Aug, Rad-OS, and a CF-rand ablation, compared to a baseline of 0.77.
reviews.text_strengths:
The motivation is clinically relevant. The paper correctly points out that current robustness work measures sensitivity to corruptions like noise or motion, but rarely isolates which tumour attributes drive failure. Framing robustness as sensitivity to interpretable radiomic attributes is a reasonable response to this gap.
Individual-level CRCs are a distinctive angle. Most prior robustness analyses operate at the cohort level. Asking, within a single patient, how the prediction would change if the tumour were larger or more spherical is a different kind of question, and one that could be useful for deployment auditing.
The ablation study demonstrates the importance of the fine-tuning sample selection strategy. Comparing CF-hard to CF-rand with the same number of added samples makes it clear that the gain comes from targeting failure regimes rather than from more training data.
The experimental setup uses an in-house cohort for generator training and two public NSCLC datasets for segmentation training and independent testing, which is a reasonable and diverse data arrangement.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The SCM assumption that an intervention on one parent changes only that parent is not met in practice. Markovian abduction–intervention–prediction requires the parents to be mutually independent and independent of U. Table 1’s non-target drift (0.11 to 0.26 z-score, highest for fractal dimension) is direct evidence that, on this data, interventions on one parent move the others. Section 4.3 acknowledges this but does not resolve it. Without clean target isolation, the framework sits closer to conditional regeneration than to a causal intervention.
2.The identity-preservation claim is never empirically validated. The whole framework relies on abduction recovering a non-tumour latent so that intervening on r leaves the surrounding anatomy intact. Table 1 only measures radiomic drift inside the tumour mask, which says nothing about what happens outside it. Basic checks are absent: background SSIM or difference maps, cycle consistency of abduction then regeneration, or cross-patient swap tests. Without these, CRC drops at extreme deciles cannot be separated from unintended background drift.
3.The chosen parents do not represent the failure modes the intro emphasises. The introduction frames the problem around small lesions, poorly defined boundaries, GGO, and adjacent anatomy with similar attenuation. Of the six parents, only volume directly targets small lesions. Fractal dimension captures geometric complexity but not partial-volume or GGO-induced fuzziness, mean HU partially reflects GGO but not its spatial pattern, and attenuation similarity with adjacent tissue (a contrast property rather than a tumour-internal one) is not covered at all.
4.Dice is the sole evaluation metric despite the paper’s own warning. The opening notes that mean Dice can hide brittle behaviour, yet CRC construction, hard-sample selection at τ = 0.7, and the final test-set comparison all use Dice alone. HD95 or surface Dice would directly probe the boundary-complexity failures the method claims to address, and could plausibly change which counterfactuals get labelled hard.
5.Figure 4’s method comparison is reported for only one feature, and that feature is the most favourable to the narrative. The left and middle panels show baseline-only CRCs for wavelet entropy and volume; only the right panel compares all methods, and only under fractal-dimension intervention. Fractal dimension is the feature where the baseline collapses most sharply in Table 2 and where generator image fidelity is lowest among shape-related parents (ρ = 0.85, drift = 0.26). Its extracted value also depends on the exact mask used, which makes it particularly hard to separate true segmentation brittleness from generator-mask artefacts at extreme deciles. A method-comparison grid across all six features, or test-set Dice stratified by quintile, would be needed to show the gain generalises.
6.The dataset description is internally inconsistent and does not match the cited sources. Reference [1] (Aerts et al.) is NSCLC-Radiomics (Lung1, 422 subjects with manual GTV), and [2] (Bakr et al., Sci. Data 5:180202, 2018) is NSCLC-Radiogenomics (211 subjects, masks released for only 144). Section 4.1 assigns the names in reverse. Even after correcting the swap, the 207-case test split does not align with 144 available Radiogenomics masks, and the provenance of the test masks is not stated. Table 1 and Figure 4 also report results on an “in-house validation set” that is never defined: the 100 public validation cases from Section 4.1, a slice of the 1,472 generator-training crops, or a third cohort. Since the headline rests on a test-set Dice improvement, these need to be stated precisely.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1.”Two A100 GPUs (48 GB)” does not match any real A100 variant. The A100 ships as 40 GB or 80 GB.
2.Figure 4’s y-axis is labelled “CRC response” but the term is never defined. Figure 2 uses “Dice” on the same type of plot.
3.Figures and tables sit far from where they are first referenced.
4.The hardness threshold τ = 0.7 is applied uniformly across features, but Table 2 shows baseline Dice differs substantially between them (volume Q1 at 0.62 vs fractal Q1 at 0.84). A uniform threshold will pull in very different fractions of counterfactuals per feature and may bias CF-hard toward features with the weakest baseline.

The motivation and the shape of the contribution (patient-level CRCs, hard-mining failure regimes) are appealing. The main concern is that the SCM framing the whole framework rests on is not backed up by the evidence in the paper. The independence assumptions are hard to accept for this feature set, Table 1’s drift shows directly that interventions leak across parents, and identity preservation outside the tumour mask, the whole reason abduction is invoked, is never tested. The overall impression is less a new causal method than an analysis pipeline built on a conditional generator, dressed in SCM language. The dataset description also does not match the citations and leaves the test-set provenance unclear, which weakens the reported Dice improvement.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The central issue is unchanged. The rebuttal confirms that the theoretical conditions for counterfactual identifiability (exact dynamic-OT coupling) are not met in practice, yet continues to invoke Ribeiro et al. (2025) as justification. This does not close the gap between the SCM framing and the experimental evidence.
Several other concerns raised in the review were acknowledged but not resolved. The mismatch between the failure modes motivating the work (poorly defined boundaries, similar-attenuation adjacent structures) and the chosen radiomic parents was conceded as a limitation. Non-target drift in Table 1 was attributed to finite-sample error, but this explanation does not resolve the concern. I do not believe the current manuscript meets the acceptance threshold for MICCAI and would benefit from revision and resubmission.

meta_reviews.text:
A counterfactual stress testing framework to identify the failure modes in tumor segmentation is presented, which then is used to improve segmentation performance. The counterfactual generation using the 3D flow matching with minibatch coupling and radiomic features conditioning is seen as novel. The paper is well-written and experimental evaluation are reasonable to establish downstream utility. Concerns were raised regarding certain claims including identity preservation as well as several minor concerns that should be addressed carefully in the rebuttal.

The authors addressed most of the reviewers’ concerns and the updated results satisfied reviewers’ concerns. However, as pointed out by reviewer 2, please acknowledge the limitations and position the work clearly taking in to account its limitations and what it can address.

This paper targets a sharp angle in lung cancer segmentation through counterfactual stress testing and is sufficiently validated. Essentially, it asks: for the same patient, and also at the population level, which tumor attributes (among selected radiomic features) would cause the segmentation model to fail? An additional practical outcome is that the generated failure-mode samples can be used to augment training and improve the original segmentation network.
The remaining concerns are: (1) identity preservation is a key component and is partially validated, but changing one radiomic feature may also affect other features, which needs further exploration; (2) the generated masks may introduce additional pseudo-label errors; (3) validation on additional datasets with broader comparisons would further strengthen the paper.

All reviewers agree that the paper has merits on how it presents an interpretable robustness check allowing to identify difficult tumors. The rebuttal touches on most concerns, and two out of three reviewers believe their points have been sufficiently addressed.

author_feedback_text:
1.Identity preservation and SCM framing [R1, R4]. The SCM/abduction angle is central to the method. Our goal is not to generate another plausible tumour, but to answer an individual-level counterfactual question: what would this same case look like if one radiomic parent were changed? This requires abduction–intervention–prediction: without this step, generative augmentation changes both tumour phenotype and patient-specific anatomy. This is motivated by the identifiability theory in [1], which shows that, under dynamic-OT/flow-matching assumptions, the monotonic transport map supports unique abduction for high-dimensional counterfactual prediction. Thus, the Markovian SCM formulation is important because it separates patient-specific exogenous variation from the intervened radiomic parent and makes the CRC an individual-level counterfactual robustness curve rather than an unconditional synthesis curve. This is precisely the property needed for clinically meaningful stress testing of the same patient. We agree that our implementation is approximate. The non-target drift in Table 1 reflects finite-sample/finite-capacity error rather than perfect parent isolation. In particular, minibatch OT with a batch size of only 100 due to memory requirements cannot exactly recover the population dynamic-OT coupling required, so leakage between correlated radiomic features is expected and will be explained in the paper. We also agree that identity preservation should be checked outside the tumour. We have now computed background preservation on the overlapping non-tumour region after removing both factual and counterfactual masks: background MSE is 0.03 ± 0.01 and SSIM is 0.89.These new results support the claim that the patient-specific context is largely preserved.
2.Radiomics scope [R2, R4]. We agree that the current parents are tumour-intrinsic and do not capture all context-driven failures. We will state this limitation and add validation-set ranges showing that CRCs span the tumour distribution in the validation set: volume 46–129 cm³, sphericity 0.33–0.80, fractal dimension 2.38–2.78, mean HU −20 to 118, HU SD 35–199, and wavelet entropy 2.1–6.9.Table 2 already shows failures across multiple parents/quintiles. Fig. 4 shows one method-comparison CRC for illustration. Generalisation is assessed on the independent test set in Table 3, where CF-hard outperforms all baselines.
3.Boundary metrics [R2, R4]: Dice was used for CRCs and τ=0.7 mining because it is the standard nnU-Net selection metric and gives a stable failure criterion across parents. We now add HD95: baseline 8.7±5.5 mm, BigAug 7.2±4.6, GAN-Aug 7.5±4.8, Rad-OS 8.1±5.1, CF-rand 6.9±4.7, and CF-hard 5.6±3.8.Thus, CF-hard improves boundary accuracy as well as overlap. We will also explore HD95/ASD-based mining as future work.
4.Pseudo-labels, related work and minor errors [R1, R2, R4]. We agree pseudo-label bias is possible; we do not treat generator masks as perfect, and support them with fidelity, drift, and added background-preservation checks. Since CF-hard and CF-rand use the same generator, pseudo-labels, and sample budget, the gain isolates CRC-guided failure selection. MSD-Lung is valuable future validation. We do not use LesionDiffusion, GuideGen, DiffTumor, and FreeTumor as direct baselines as we already control for augmentation benefit with BigAug and GAN-Aug under the same sample budget but will include them in our related work. Our distinct contribution compared to these methods is to diagnosing and repairing named radiomic failure regimes. We will correct the swapped NSCLC-Radiomics/Radiogenomics citations, state cohort provenance, exclusions, splits, and mask sources, and define the in-house validation set. We will also fix the A100 typo, relabel Fig. 4’s y-axis as Dice, and improve figure placement.
[1] Ribeiro, F.D.S., Santhirasekaram, A., Glocker, B.: Counterfactual identifiability via dynamic optimal transport. arXiv preprint arXiv:2510.08294 (2025)

title: CPAgents: Agentic Composite Phenotype Generation for Cardiac Disease Association
abstract: Identifying robust associations between cardiac imaging phenotypes and clinical diseases is fundamental to population-scale cardiovascular research and reliable risk stratification. However, current phenome-wide association studies rely on pre-defined, single-variable phenotypes or expert-crafted features, which limits their ability to capture clinically meaningful non-linear effects and cross-phenotype interactions. To address this, we propose CPAgent, an iterative phenotype-Composition framework for cardiovascular Phenome-wide association study (PheWAS) that automatically constructs and validates interpretable composite phenotypes (e.g., polynomial, ratio, and interaction forms) from base imaging features. Specifically, our system coordinates three agents: (i) an Analyst that identifies statistical pathologies and nominates candidate transformations; (ii) a Proposer that generates constrained, medically and statistically motivated expressions under numerical safety rules; and (iii) a Verifier that evaluates candidates using multi-stage criteria and produces transparent evidence trails for accepted phenotypes. Evaluated on a population-scale cardiac imaging cohort, the discovered composite phenotypes markedly improve disease discrimination: across 72 classifier–disease–metric combinations, our variants achieve the top rank in 56 cases versus 18 for baselines, with gains observed across all nine clinical disease categories. Our framework yields compact, clinically interpretable phenotype formulas with transparent evidence trails, enabling scalable discovery of stronger phenotype-disease associations beyond expert-driven feature selection.
subject_areas: Applications -> Outcome Prediction / Prognosis / Longitudinal Modeling
Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces CPAgents, an agentic framework for automatically constructing interpretable composite phenotypes from cardiac imaging data. By integrating statistical profiling, LLM-guided feature generation, and multi-stage validation, it discovers clinically meaningful feature combinations that improve disease association analysis and classification performance compared to expert-defined and prior automated approaches in large-scale cohorts.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper’s key strengths are its structured agentic framework for feature discovery, combining statistical analysis with LLM-guided generation, and its focus on interpretable, closed-form phenotypes. It includes a robust multi-stage validation process and a comprehensive evaluation across diseases and models, demonstrating consistent performance gains and practical relevance on large-scale clinical data.
reviews.text_weaknesses: A key weakness is limited conceptual novelty. The overall pipeline closely resembles prior work on LLM-driven feature engineering and symbolic composition, such as LLM-FE (Abhyankar et al. , 2025) and agent-based systems like MESHAgents (Zhang et al. , 2025). The Analyst–Proposer–Verifier loop is intuitive but not clearly differentiated from existing multi-agent or symbolic regression frameworks.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
CPAgents presents a compelling agentic framework for cardiac phenotype discovery with strong empirical results. The three-agent design is well-motivated, though broader dataset validation and computational cost analysis would strengthen the contribution.

CPAgents uses three AI agents to automatically discover interpretable composite cardiac phenotypes, outperforming expert-defined features across nine diseases.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes CPAgents, a three-agent LLM framework for automated composite phenotype discovery in cardiovascular PheWAS. An Analyst profiles statistical properties of base features, a Proposer generates closed-form candidate transformations over a constrained AST operator set, and a Verifier filters them via ΔAUC, ElasticNet stability, and SHAP ranking. Candidates are accepted through a cross-classifier ensemble rule with early stopping.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The analyse–propose–verify decomposition is clean and better scoped than most LLM-FE work. Grounding the Proposer with Analyst statistics (ΔAIC, MI, ICC) is a meaningful design choice.
2.The evaluation is large-scale and leakage-aware. A 6:2:2 split with discovery restricted to train+val, five seeds, and bootstrap stability selection show care.
3.The 72-configuration ranking analysis avoids cherry-picking. The silhouette score, association heatmap, and agent-level ablation triangulate the core claim well. Which deserves credit.
4.The sex-stratified allometric LVM Z-score example is a convincing demonstration that LLM medical priors can surface genuinely clinical constants. This is really intuitive.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
I would like to have few clarifications from the authors regarding-
1.Gains are small and often within overlapping standard deviations. SVM Hypertension is 0.759±0.006 vs 0.755±0.007.No paired significance tests (DeLong, bootstrap, Wilcoxon) are reported to back the 56 vs 18 ranking claim. Can you do the paired-significance tests and report the results in your rebuttal?
2.I think a compariosn with non-LLM AutoFE methods (OpenFE, AutoFeat, featuretools) or a random search over the same operator set O could be really intuitive to observe. Without these, the LLM’s contribution cannot be isolated from the AST pipeline itself. The ablation already removes agents but never the LLM.
3.LLM reproducibility is unclear. Results use DeepSeek-V3.2 and GPT-5.1 at default temperature. The five-seed averaging does not isolate LLM stochasticity from classifier seed variance. A temperature-0 run would help. While working on LLMs, I think this is necessary to report in the results table.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Method is strong and well written but the absolute gains are often within one standard deviation, the baseline set omits standard non-LLM AutoFE methods needed to credit the LLM specifically, and no paired significance tests back the ranking claim. The iterative accept rule is a multiple-testing procedure that is not characterized. If authors resolve the queries mentioned in the weakness section, I will be happy to make this an ‘accept’. Good luck.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal satisfactorily addresses my main concern on statistical validation and partially addresses the AutoFE baseline gap through an OpenFE comparison. However, the LLM-specific contribution and reproducibility are still not fully isolated, so I lean toward a weak accept rather than a strong accept.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a novel agent‑based framework for cardiovascular phenome‑wide analysis that automatically constructs and validates interpretable composite phenotypes from base cardiac imaging features. The key contribution lies in decomposing phenome construction into three interacting agents—an Analyst that identifies statistical pathologies, a generator of statistically motivated phenotype expressions, and a Verifier that evaluates candidates and provides transparent evidence trails. Together, these components aim to produce robust, interpretable, and reproducible phenotypes suitable for large‑scale cardiovascular studies and downstream association analyses.
reviews.text_strengths: A major strength of the paper is its emphasis on interpretable composite phenotypes, moving beyond single imaging measurements toward higher‑level constructs that better reflect cardiovascular disease complexity. This aligns well with clinical reasoning and phenome‑wide study objectives. A second strength is the agent‑based formulation, where analysis, synthesis, and verification are explicitly separated, providing built‑in quality control and reducing manual, ad‑hoc feature engineering.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The is the use of the term “phenome‑wide association study” without performing any actual association analysis, particularly genetic associations, which may lead to conceptual ambiguity under traditional PheWAS definitions. Second, the framework operates exclusively on pre‑extracted imaging features, inheriting any biases or limitations of upstream steps. Third, while statistically well motivated, the proposed criteria for phenotype construction are not explicitly grounded in pathophysiological or clinical priors, leaving the clinical meaningfulness of some composite phenotypes to be inferred rather than demonstrated.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The work reflects a solid and novel methodological contribution with clear strengths in interpretability. While the paper does not fully realize a traditional PheWAS and has limitations related to scope, these issues are largely clarifications rather than fundamental flaws.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper received a mixed review. The key strengths of the paper include a well-structured agentic framework, strong clinical interpretability and translational potential, rigorous and large-scale evaluation design, as well as clinical relevance to cardiac imaging. At the same time, following weakness has been identified by the reviewers, including limited conceptual novelty relative to existing pipeline, insufficient statistical validation of performance gain, and missing critical baseline comparisons. I would recommend an invite for rebuttal such that the authors can address concerns raised by reviewers.

The authors have satisfactorily addressed All Reviewers’ criticisms, suggestions and observations. It is recommended, however, that the authors incorporate the statistical analysis performed, in the final version of the paper, as well as the clarifications needed, which authors acknowledged.

The rebuttal addressed the non-LLM AutoFE baseline difference and speculated about the stat significance testing. This addresses some of the serious critiques from the review round. I think the actuality of this paper and the sota agentic methods place this one above the threshold and recommend accept.

The authors have satisfactorily addressed the concerns raised in the original reviews. Though some of the comments could have used additional justification (as raised by R2), the contributions are strong, and the paper deserves to be published in the current form.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback. We are pleased that the reviewers recognised CPAgents as a compelling framework for clinical reasoning, highlighting its “clean analyse-propose-verify decomposition” (R1, R2), “interpretable composite phenotypes” (R1, R3), “robust leakage-aware validation” (R1, R2), and “comprehensive evaluation” (R1, R2).
< Statistical validation of performance gains (R2-W1, Meta) >
To statistically validate the reported gains, we performed paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for the overall matched AUC comparisons and paired DeLong tests for disease-level AUC comparisons against MESHAgents under matched evaluation settings. Both our DeepSeek-V3.2-based and GPT-5.1-based agents show significant improvements over MESHAgents, with p less than 0.05 in all tests. We will explicitly clarify the statistical significance of these comparisons in the revised version.
< Additional baselines against AutoFE and novelty (R1, R2-W2, Meta) >
We agree AutoFE methods such as OpenFE [Zhang et al., 2023] are useful references. However, CPAgents are designed with a different objective from conventional AutoFE pipelines, which typically search shallow algebraic combinations to maximize predictive accuracy on a fixed target. CPAgents are motivated by the construction of clinically interpretable composite phenotypes under explicit validity constraints. Candidate phenotypes are generated within a constrained closed-form operator space and are then filtered through verifier-based checks for physiological plausibility, statistical stability, and cross-classifier consistency. In our evaluation, OpenFE underperformed both baselines, indicating that unconstrained feature generation alone is insufficient for this setting. Directly applying unconstrained algebraic feature search may require additional filtering to ensure unit consistency and valid value ranges for downstream classification. We will make this distinction clearer in the revised version and position AutoFE methods as useful comparative references.
< LLM reproducibility (R2-W3)>
We agree that unconstrained LLM generation can raise reproducibility concerns. In our framework, however, the LLM is not used as a raw stochastic generator whose outputs are directly evaluated. Instead, it proposes candidate features within a predefined feature space, and each candidate must pass deterministic structural, unit-consistency, and value-range checks before downstream evaluation. Under this fixed validation and evaluation protocol, we report results averaged over five independent seeds, covering both LLM-generation stochasticity and classifier seed variance. The non-zero temperature is used only to diversify candidate proposals, while the retained candidates are governed by the fixed constraints and validation protocol. We will emphasize this constrained generation-and-validation design in the revised version.
< Clarification of PheWAS scope, feature dependency, and clinical grounding. (R3-W1/W2/W3) >
First, we agree that “PheWAS study” may be ambiguous under the traditional genetic PheWAS definition. Our work does not perform genetic association analysis but a PheWAS-inspired, disease-wide association analysis between cardiovascular imaging-derived phenotypes and clinical outcomes. To avoid confusion, we will revise the terminology to “phenome-wide imaging phenotype association analysis”. Second, we acknowledge that CPAgents operates on pre-extracted imaging-derived features, which is an intentional design choice to ensure interpretability, unit-level validity and fair comparison under a shared feature space. Third, we agree that clinical grounding should be made more explicit. The LLM component is intended to support exploratory hypothesis generation rather than to serve as a standalone source of clinical evidence. We will clarify the current scope and discuss external evidence grounding through curated biomedical literature or clinical guidelines as a future work.

title: CPR: Chained Perceptual Refinement for Coarse-to-Fine Medical Image Classification
abstract: High-resolution medical images contain fine-grained, spatially sparse cues that are critical for diagnosis, yet preserving full resolution incurs substantial computational and memory costs. Most deep models process images uniformly, leading to redundant computation or loss of diagnostic detail under downsampling. We propose Chained Perceptual Refinement (CPR), a coarse-to-fine framework that formulates medical image analysis as a sequential global-to-local decision process. Starting from a low-resolution global view, CPR dynamically predicts the center and spatial extent of refinement regions, extracts high-resolution evidence from the original image, and incrementally integrates it with global context. By keeping the backbone input size fixed while contracting the perceptual field, CPR preserves diagnostic fidelity with constant peak GPU memory. Extensive experiments on five medical imaging datasets and multiple backbone architectures demonstrate that CPR consistently outperforms both fixed-resolution and multi-scale state-of-the-art baselines, achieving improvements of up to 2.27% over the second-best method. It also achieves up to a 19.6× reduction in GFLOPs at matched accuracy, establishing a superior accuracy–efficiency trade-off for high-resolution medical image analysis.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a CPR framework that reconstructs high-resolution medical image classification as a sequential decision-making process from global to local. By dynamically predicting the center coordinates and spatial range of the refined region at each step, adaptive perceptual field contraction is achieved while keeping the input size of the backbone network fixed, thus achieving a balance between diagnostic accuracy and computational efficiency; This method has achieved advanced performance on multiple publicly available medical imaging datasets of different modalities
reviews.text_strengths: This paper (1) innovatively reconstructs the classification of high-resolution medical images as a sequential decision-making process from global to local. The strategy network simultaneously predicts the center coordinates and spatial range of the refined region, achieving dynamic scale contraction, which is closer to the gradual focus diagnosis process of clinical doctors than the fixed size and unconstrained block sampling in existing methods. (2)The state transition mechanism accumulates evidence in a residual manner without increasing input resolution. (3) At the same time, a reduction in computational complexity was achieved with the same accuracy, and the experimental setup was clear.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Method novelty, experimental adequacy, clarity of charts, and other aspects
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes the Chained Perceptual Refinement (CPR) framework for high-resolution medical image classification. Starting from a low-resolution global view, this method progressively predicts the locations of interest and the scale of the cropped regions, extracting local evidence from the original high-resolution image and fusing it with a continuously updated perceptual state. The authors aim to preserve as much fine-grained information as possible, crucial for diagnosis, as possible while maintaining a relatively fixed backbone network input size and peak memory. Experiments on five public datasets and various backbone networks demonstrate that this method achieves a good trade-off between accuracy and computational efficiency.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper addresses a highly practical problem: how to preserve fine-grained diagnostic information in medical images without performing dense, high-resolution inference.
2.The proposed stepwise refinement approach from global to local is intuitive and reasonable. Furthermore, the predicted location and scale are more suitable for medical images with significant resolution differences than fixed-size cropping.
3.Experiments cover five public datasets, multiple medical imaging modalities, and various backbone networks, providing more convincing validation than single-dataset validation.
4.The paper reports not only accuracy but also memory usage and GFLOPs, consistent with the method’s core efficiency claims.
5.Qualitative visualization and scale-controlled ablation experiments provide strong support for the method’s behavior.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Regarding methodological novelty, the authors need to more clearly define the differences between this paper and existing adaptive vision/coarse-to-fine methods. The current work shares a clear conceptual connection with existing methods such as Adaptive NN, OverLock, and PAMIL in the core idea of “global overview followed by local region focus” or “dynamically driven region selection.” Therefore, based solely on the current manuscript, I cannot fully determine the key innovations of CPR and its irreplaceability compared to these works.
2.Ablation experiments are still incomplete. There is a lack of comparison with simpler alternatives, such as fixed coarse-to-fine scheduling, non-reinforcement learning pruning strategies, and deterministic attention mechanisms. Therefore, the necessity of PPO and the chained design cannot be fully confirmed at present.
3.There are some inconsistencies in the wording. For example, the abstract emphasizes predicting the crop center, while the method section defines (x_t, y_t) as the top-left coordinate; the descriptions of the state variables z_t and H_t are also inconsistent.
Wang, Yulin, et al. “Emulating human-like adaptive vision for efficient and flexible machine visual perception.” Nature Machine Intelligence (2025): 1-19.
Lou, Meng, and Yizhou Yu. “Overlock: An overview-first-look-closely-next convnet with context-mixing dynamic kernels.” Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2025.
Zheng, Tingting, Kui Jiang, and Hongxun Yao. “Dynamic policy-driven adaptive multi-instance learning for whole slide image classification.” Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF conference on computer vision and pattern recognition. 2024.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
This work is promising overall, but I suggest the authors further enhance the transparency of the experiments and the details of the methodologies. In particular, I recommend clarifying the data partitioning protocol (whether it is patient-level partitioning in the applicable context), reporting the variance or statistical test results of multiple replicate experiments, adding clinically relevant metrics other than accuracy for class-imbalanced tasks, and adding control experiments against simpler non-reinforcement learning refinement strategies. Furthermore, adding a discussion of failure cases and methodological limitations would make the paper more complete.

I believe this is a borderline, slightly positive submission. The paper addresses an important problem, its methodology is well-designed, and it demonstrates an attractive accuracy/efficiency tradeoff across multiple datasets. However, the current version is insufficiently novel compared to existing adaptive vision methods, lacking adequate implementation details, variance of repeated experiments, and stronger ablation studies. Therefore, the strength of the evidence is weaker than some of the paper’s claims. I currently lean towards a positive recommendation, primarily because the approach has practical value and broad experimental coverage, but I hope the authors will clarify issues regarding reproducibility and comparative fairness in their rebuttal.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal addresses my main concerns. The authors clarified the relationship to prior adaptive/coarse-to-fine methods, provided additional stability evidence with multiple random seeds, discussed concrete failure cases and limitations, and added stronger ablation/comparison results that better support the contribution of the chained policy design. While some implementation details could still be clearer, the paper’s practical significance and overall empirical support are now sufficient for acceptance.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces an image classification framework evaluated on high-resolution medical datasets. The core of the approach is an iterative, multi-pass inference strategy. In the initial pass, the full-resolution image is downsampled to a canonical resolution to extract global contextual features. Subsequently, a learned policy network predicts a bounding box to localize a salient region from the original high-resolution input. This region is then cropped, rescaled, and forwarded through the network to capture fine-grained local details. This process is repeated iteratively to progressively aggregate discriminative information. By maintaining a fixed canonical resolution throughout the passes, the model facilitates the processing of high-resolution imagery with a constant memory footprint. Experimental results across five datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior accuracy with lower computational overhead compared to existing baselines.
reviews.text_strengths: The proposed method is supported by a thorough evaluation across five diverse datasets. The results consistently demonstrate that the framework achieves superior classification performance while maintaining significantly lower computational and memory overhead compared to traditional high-resolution processing techniques.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The core concept of utilizing iterative local crops to extract fine-grained information is well-established in the literature, yet the manuscript lacks a comprehensive discussion of, and comparison with, relevant prior art. While the authors compare their work to AdaptiveNN, they overlook several foundational and contemporary models with similar architectural parallels:
RA-CNN [a]: This model similarly employs a recurrent, iterative approach to propose variable-sized crops with intermediate supervision.
SSPS/M2Former [b]: Recent work that also utilizes variable-sized patches for fine-grained recognition.
Feature Accumulation Strategies: The proposed formulation closely resembles a recurrent network with a linear gate. Similar strategies using LSTMs for feature refinement have been proposed by Shroff et al. [c], and alternative aggregation methods, such as positional aggregation in TNet [d], already exist.
Therefore, the authors should contextualize their contribution relative to these and other similar methods and ideally provide quantitative comparisons to justify the necessity of the new formulation.
Evaluating against only one specialized model (AdaptiveNN) is insufficient for a paper claiming a superior “low-cost” approach. The authors should include standard iterative or hard-attention baselines to substantiate their claims of achieving a better accuracy-to-cost trade-off.
To validate the efficacy of the policy network, the ablation study should include a configuration where crop boxes are randomly sampled rather than predicted. This is a critical baseline to demonstrate that the learned policy network is identifying salient regions and that the performance gains are not merely a byproduct of processing higher-resolution patches, regardless of their location.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The motivation behind this work, addressing the challenge of high-resolution image processing under strict resource constraints, is highly relevant to the medical imaging community. Furthermore, the empirical results demonstrate consistent performance gains across several benchmarks. However, the manuscript’s primary weakness is the lack of a thorough contextualization within the existing literature on coarse-to-fine iterative mechanisms. This paradigm has been extensively explored, and without a comprehensive comparison against both classical and modern “hard-attention” baselines, the technical novelty and comparative effectiveness of the proposed architecture remain unproven. Consequently, I am leaning toward a rejection at this stage. I would be open to revising my assessment only if the authors can provide a substantive rebuttal that demonstrates clear, unique contributions relative to some closely related methods.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The proposed method is relevant, and it has been tested on multiple datasets to demonstrate its generalization capabilities. My main initial concern was the lack of discussion of previous similar methods, which has been addressed in the rebuttal. If the authors can include those in the final version of the paper, then I would like to increase my recommendation.

meta_reviews.text:
This manuscript has received mixed reviews (scores: 4, 4, 3), with major concerns centered on insufficient novelty differentiation from existing adaptive vision methods, incomplete ablation studies, and lack of comparison with relevant coarse-to-fine baselines. The authors are suggest to address these limitations in the rebuttal phase.

After rebuttal, all reviewers decide to accept the paper, the author successfully adderss the problems , and I recommend the acceptance of the paper.

The paper addresses an important and practical problem in high-resolution medical image classification, aiming to improve the balance between diagnostic performance and computational efficiency. The initial reviews raised concerns about novelty, comparison with related adaptive/coarse-to-fine methods, and the completeness of ablation studies. The authors’ rebuttal provides reasonable clarification addressing these main concerns. Importantly, the reviewer opinions converged toward acceptance after the rebuttal, indicating agreement that the major concerns were sufficiently addressed. While the method remains somewhat incremental and some implementation details could still be improved, the overall empirical results across multiple datasets are positive. I therefore recommend acceptance.

After considering the reviews and rebuttal discussion, I recommend acceptance. The paper addresses an important and practical challenge in medical imaging: preserving fine-grained diagnostic information in high-resolution images under limited computational budgets.
The proposed coarse-to-fine refinement framework is well motivated and demonstrates a strong balance between accuracy, memory efficiency, and computational cost across multiple datasets, modalities, and backbone architectures. In particular, the chained refinement mechanism and adaptive scale-aware region selection provide a clinically meaningful alternative to fixed-resolution or fixed-crop strategies.
While some concerns regarding novelty relative to prior adaptive vision and coarse-to-fine methods were initially raised, the rebuttal satisfactorily clarified the distinctions from related work and strengthened the empirical support through additional analyses, ablations, and discussions of stability and failure cases. Overall, the paper presents a technically sound and practically valuable contribution with sufficiently broad experimental validation for acceptance at MICCAI.

author_feedback_text:
We use W to denote Weakness and R to denote Reviewer.
(Joint Reply: R1-W1, R2-W1) Novelty and relation to adaptive/coarse-to-fine methods. We thank the reviewers for raising this point. CPR differs from prior adaptive, hard-attention, and coarse-to-fine methods in three key aspects: (1) it predicts both crop location and scale, rather than using fixed-size crops, predefined multi-scale inputs, or only location proposals; (2) it performs chained perceptual refinement, where each step updates a residual perceptual state instead of independently aggregating local crops; and (3) it targets high-resolution medical classification with fixed backbone input size and bounded memory. Compared with AdaptiveNN, CPR adds adaptive scale refinement; compared with OverLock, CPR revisits the original high-resolution image via adaptive crop-and-refine actions rather than context-mixing kernels; compared with PAMIL, CPR addresses image-level classification rather than WSI MIL.
(R1-W2) Stability, variance, and statistical reliability. We repeated CPR with three random seeds on COVID and BUSI datasets. CPR obtains 98.64 ± 0.17% on COVID and 95.16 ± 0.30% on BUSI, consistently outperforming the compared baselines. The small standard deviations indicate that CPR is robust across different runs, suggesting that the policy-gradient-based learning component does not introduce noticeable performance instability.
(R1-W3) Failure cases, clinical reliability, and limitations. We thank the reviewer for this important suggestion. Our qualitative inspection identifies two main failure modes. First, CPR may over-contract the crop when lesions are subtle, diffuse, or spread over a large region, which can lead to the loss of useful contextual information. Second, when visually salient non-lesion structures are present, the policy may attend to irrelevant regions and accumulate misleading evidence. These observations suggest that CPR is most effective when discriminative evidence is spatially localized, while diffuse, ambiguous, or weakly contrasted lesion patterns remain challenging. We will add this failure-case analysis to the revised manuscript.
(R2-W1) Novelty. Please see R1-W1.
(R2-W2) Ablation completeness. To address the reviewer’s concern, we include additional ablation baselines on the BUSI dataset using the ViT-S model: Random Crop, Fixed Coarse-to-Fine, Deterministic Attention, and No-Chain CPR. These variants achieve 93.29%, 93.61%, 94.25%, and 94.25%, respectively, while the full CPR achieves the best performance of 94.89%. These results further validate the effectiveness of CPR.
(R2-W3) inconsistencies in wording. We will thoroughly check the manuscript revise the inconsistent wording to ensure clarity and consistency in the revised version.
(R3-W1) Similar Architectural Baselines. We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. To address this concern, we additionally compare CPR with four related architectural baselines: (1) RA-CNN, (2) M2Former, (3) Focus Longer to See Better, and (4) TNet. On BUSI, these methods achieve 88.82%, 93.61%, 90.10%, and 94.25%, respectively, while CPR achieves the best performance of 94.89%. On COVID, they achieve 98.25%, 95.71%, 95.59%, and 98.37%, respectively, while CPR further improves the performance to 98.67%. These results demonstrate that CPR consistently outperforms these baselines, further validating the effectiveness of our proposed method.
(R3-W2) Policy network ablation. We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. To address this concern, we report two additional baselines on the BUSI dataset using the ViT-S model: CPR with Random Crop and CPR with Deterministic Attention. These baselines achieve 93.29% and 94.25%, respectively, while the full CPR achieves 94.89%. These results indicate that the learned policy network provides more effective region selection than random cropping or deterministic attention, thereby contributing to the overall performance improvement.

title: CPS4: Class Prompt Driven Semi-supervised Spine Segmentation with Class-Specific Consistency Constraint
abstract: Vision-Language Model (VLM) has great potential to enhance the quality of pseudo labels in semi-supervised spine segmentation by leveraging textual class prompts to generate segmentation map, but no one has studied it yet. Although promising, it lacks explicit constraints to ensure consistency between spine class prompts and spine unit region, resulting in unsatisfactory performance in multi-class segmentation map generation. In this paper, we propose CPS4, the first text-guided semi-supervised spine segmentation network using class prompts to enhance the quality of spine pseudo labels. Specifically, CPS4 is implemented through two training stages. (i) Class-specific consistency constrained VLM pretraining stage: we propose token- and pixel-level attention loss to optimize the consistency between class prompts and spine units, forcing the textual class prompt to be closely coupled with the target spine unit in the semantic space. (ii) Class Prompt driven semi-supervised spine segmentation stage: using the pretrained vision–text encoder, we derive each class-specific binary segmentation map for the unlabeled spine image and integrate them into an unified multi-class segmentation map, improving the quality of the spine pseudo label generated by the semi-supervised spine segmentation network. Experimental results show that our CPS4 achieves superior spine segmentation performance with Dice of 80.44%, only using 5% labeled data on the public spine segmentation dataset, surpassing popular semi-supervised learning and VLM methods. Our code will be available.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This manuscript proposes CPS4, a novel framework for semi-supervised spine segmentation that leverages Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to enhance pseudo-label quality. Addressing the limitation of existing VLMs which lack explicit constraints between textual class prompts and specific anatomical regions, the authors introduce a two-stage training strategy.
Stage 1 (Pretraining): A class-specific consistency constrained VLM pretraining stage is introduced, utilizing proposed token-level and pixel-level attention losses to enforce tight semantic coupling between class prompts (e. g. , “Lumbar Vertebra 1”) and their corresponding spine units in the feature space.
Stage 2 (Segmentation): In the semi-supervised segmentation stage, the pretrained vision-text encoder generates class-specific binary segmentation maps for unlabeled images. These maps are aggregated into a unified multi-class pseudo-label to guide the training of a Mean Teacher-based method.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The integration of textual class prompts into semi-supervised spine segmentation is a significant and timely contribution. While VLMs have been explored in medical imaging, this work is the first to explicitly address the “cross-class interference” problem in multi-class spine segmentation by designing class-specific consistency constraints (token- and pixel-level attention losses). This moves beyond simple image-text alignment to fine-grained region-prompt binding. 
2.The methodological design is logical and well-grounded. The two-stage approach effectively decouples the challenging task of learning robust vision-language alignment from the segmentation optimization. 
3.Spine segmentation is critical for clinical applications but suffers from high annotation costs due to the multi-class nature (vertebrae + discs). By demonstrating superior performance with only 5% labeled data (achieving ~80.44% Dice), this work offers a practical solution to reduce the reliance on expensive expert annotations.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The method relies heavily on the quality and specificity of the textual class prompts (e. g. , “A magnetic resonance image of a {class name}”). The paper does not discuss the sensitivity of the model to prompt engineering variations (e. g. , synonyms, different sentence structures). In clinical settings, terminology can vary; the robustness of the method to such linguistic shifts is not evaluated. 
2.The proposed framework requires a dedicated pretraining stage (Stage 1) before the actual semi-supervised segmentation training (Stage 2). The paper lacks a detailed analysis of the total computational cost (GPU hours) compared to end-to-end SSL methods. For practical deployment, the efficiency of generating 20 separate attention maps (for 20 classes) per unlabeled image during Stage 2 inference/training needs to be quantified. 
3.The experiments are conducted solely on the MRSpineSeg dataset. While the results are impressive, the method’s generalizability to other modalities (e. g. , CT spine scans) or other multi-class anatomical structures (e. g. , abdominal organs) remains unproven. A cross-modality experiment or a discussion on potential domain shifts would strengthen the claims. 
4.The dataset description notes that “Not all images contain 19 spinal structures. “ The method generates attention maps for all 20 classes for every unlabeled image. The paper does not explicitly explain how the framework handles cases where a specific vertebra is absent in the field of view. Does the VLM generate false positive attention maps for missing classes, and if so, how does the aggregation step mitigate this noise in the pseudo-labels?
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper is well-organized and clearly written. The motivation for addressing cross-class interference in VLM-based pseudo-labeling is compelling and addresses a genuine gap in the literature. The experimental results are robust, showing consistent improvements across different labeling ratios. While the computational cost and modality generalization are minor concerns, the core contribution of class-specific consistency constraints for multi-class SSL is significant and well-executed
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes CPS4, a novel semi-supervised spine segmentation framework that leverages textual class prompts to generate high-quality pseudo labels. Methodologically, it introduces a class-specific consistency constraint using token- and pixel-level attention losses during VLM pre-training to ensure strict semantic alignment and prevent cross-class interference. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CPS4 achieves state-of-the-art performance on spine MRI datasets across various labeled ratios.
reviews.text_strengths: Overall, the motivation for this work is clear, the authors have well articulated their methodology, and the proposed approach has achieved promising experimental results.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The method heavily relies on class prompts, and the paper explicitly treats prompt-object consistency as the central issue. However, the prompt design is hard-coded to a single template, namely “A magnetic resonance image of a {class name},” without any prompt sensitivity analysis. As a result, it remains unclear whether the reported gains are robust to different textual formulations or are partially tied to this specific handcrafted prompt.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Please refer to the strengths and weaknesses above.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors address the challenge of label scarcity in multi-class spine segmentation (Vertebral Bodies and Intervertebral Discs) by utilizing textual class prompts to guide a semi-supervised learning (SSL) process. The CPS4 framework operates in two stages. In the first stage, a vision-text encoder is trained using proposed token-level and pixel-level attention losses to ensure tight semantic coupling between specific spine class prompts and their corresponding image regions. In the second stage, the pretrained VLM generates class-specific binary maps for unlabeled data, which are aggregated into unified multi-class pseudo-labels to supervise a student-teacher segmentation network.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.This appears to be the first work to explicitly introduce textual class prompts into the semi-supervised spine segmentation domain.
2.The introduction of specific consistency constraints, namely the token-level and pixel-level losses, directly addresses the known issue of VLMs failing to focus on small or specific anatomical objects. The token-level loss aggregates attention activations toward the predicted spine unit, and the pixel-level loss prevents over-aggregation into subregions, ensuring the VLM covers the entire target unit.
3.The model achieves a Dice score of 80.44% using only 5% labeled data. It consistently outperforms established baselines like Mean Teacher (MT), MedCLIP, and MGCA across various labeling ratios (5%, 10%, 25%, 50%).
4.The ablation study clearly demonstrates that both token-level and pixel-level losses provide complementary gains, with the full model significantly outperforming the baseline.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The authors acknowledge that the MRSpineSeg dataset consists of volumetric (3D) images. However, the proposed architecture uses a 2D ResUNet. Spine anatomy is inherently 3D, and spatial consistency between adjacent slices is critical for identifying specific vertebrae (e.g., distinguishing T12 from L1). By treating slices as independent 2D inputs, the model ignores the rich volumetric context provided by the MRI. This is a step backward from the current state-of-the-art medical image segmentation, which typically employs 3D U-Net variants or Transformers to maintain anatomical continuity. The authors should justify why a 3D baseline (like nnU-Net) or a 2.5D contextual approach was not employed, and provide a comparison to prove that their text-guided pseudo-labels compensate for the lack of 3D spatial information.
2.The method generates pseudo-labels by “stacking” binary maps from the VLM and adding them to teacher predictions. However, the authors do not explain how they handle label conflicts. What happens if a pixel is predicted as both “L1” and “L1/L2 disc” by different class-specific maps? A simple summation of two potentially misaligned probability maps (in the loss function) does not seem mathematically sound - if both models are confident, the resulting “label” could exceed valid probability ranges or create highly noisy gradients. A more robust approach, such as Bayesian fusion or confidence-weighted averaging, is missing.
3.The method for aggregating 19+ class-specific attention maps into a single pseudo-label lacks a robust mechanism for handling overlapping predictions or false positives in slices where certain structures are absent. If the VLM is forced to produce a “T10” segmentation map for a slice that only contains “L5,” it will likely pick up noisy, similar-looking features. Stacking these “hallucinated” structures into the final pseudo-label could introduce significant systematic errors that the student network will then memorize.
4.The method relies on OTSU automatic thresholding to binarize attention maps into pseudo-labels. However, the paper lacks a sensitivity analysis or discussion on whether OTSU remains robust across different MRI qualities or if it tends to “over-segment” in noisy images.
5.Statement like “but no one has studied it yet.” (abstract). Such absolute statements can be risky; it is often safer and more professional for authors to claim to be “among the first” or “to the best of our knowledge.”
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

CPS4 offers a novel VLM-based approach to semi-supervised spine segmentation with impressive low-label performance (80.44% Dice at 5% labels), yet it faces significant technical hurdles. The use of a 2D architecture for volumetric data ignores essential 3D spatial context and lacks comparison with standard 3D baselines like nnU-Net. Additionally, the pseudo-label aggregation process is mathematically vague, providing no clear strategy for resolving label conflicts or preventing hallucinations in slices where specific anatomical structures are missing. Without a robustness analysis for its thresholding methods and a justification for its 2D/3D trade-offs, the paper’s current methodological rigor does not fully meet the standard for acceptance at this stage.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have successfully addressed my previous concerns regarding the model architecture and experimental validation during the rebuttal. The proposed method is sound and outperforms the baseline models. I am happy to recommend acceptance.

meta_reviews.text:
All reviewers are inclined to finalize their decisions following the rebuttal. The authors are advised to address the concerns raised by Reviewers 3.

All reviewers have reached a consensus in favor of accepting the paper.

R1 changed their recommendation from Weak Accept to Accept, while R3 changed from Weak Reject to Accept. Both reviewers were satisfied that the rebuttal addressed their concerns with the initial version of the paper.
After the rebuttal, all reviewers agreed that the paper should be accepted. The Area Chair supports this consensus and recommends acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
Thanks to all reviewers for your careful reviews and appreciation of our work, such as novel framework (R1R2R3), significant contribution (R1), compelling motivation (R1R2), superior experiment (R1R2R3), and well writing (R1R2).
Q1: Prompt Robustness (R1R2). A1: CPS4 is robust to synonyms and different sentence structures. For sentence structures, the prompts “A magnetic resonance image of a {class name}”, “A spine MR image containing {class name}”, and “The anatomical structure of {class name} in MRI” achieved mDice of 80.44, 80.35, 80.47.For synonyms, removing “Vertebra” or replacing it with “Spine”, e.g., “Lumbar Vertebra 1”, “Lumbar 1”, and “Lumbar Spine 1”, achieved mDice of 80.44, 80.32, 80.39.These small fluctuations demonstrate the robustness of CPS4.
Q2: Efficiency Analysis (R1). A2: CPS4 requires no extra inference cost, since attention maps are generated only during training. On an NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU, both CPS4 and baseline take 18 ms/image during inference. For training, CPS4 takes 13h34min in total, while the baseline takes 9h31min. The additional cost includes 2h31min for stage 1, 1h19min for attention map generation in stage 2, and 13min for the loss backpropagation.​ Despite additional cost, CPS4 brings a 6.19 mDice improvement under 5% labeled data.
Q3: Generalizability (R1R3). A3: This work focuses on 2D spine segmentation. In our another work, we extended CPS4 and evaluated it on 3D semi-supervised spine segmentation, including 3D organ and 3D spine tasks. Using 3D nnUNet as the backbone, under 10% labeled data, CPS4 achieves 82.63 mDice on MACT organ dataset, outperforming MT and CLIP by 10.93 and 3.69; on MRSpineSeg dataset, CPS4 achieves 73.44 mDice, outperforming MT and CLIP by 7.07 and 3.81.Using 3D ResUNet as the backbone, under 10% labeled data, CPS4 achieves 82.06 mDice on MACT organ dataset, outperforming MT and CLIP by 8.95 and 2.33; on MRSpineSeg dataset, CPS4 achieves 72.64 mDice, outperforming MT and CLIP by 6.59 and 4.25.These results validate CPS4’s generalizability across different segmentation scenarios.
Q4: Absent-Class Handling (R1R3). A4: After OTSU divides each attention map into foreground and background where each attention map is normalized to [0,1], we compute mean attention score of the foreground region. If this mean score is lower than 0.5, the class is regarded as absent, and its binary map is set to background. This reduces false-positive activations from missing classes. We will clarify this in the revised manuscript.
Q5: Label Conflicts and Probability Maps Summation (R3). A5: For label conflicts, if a pixel is predicted as different classes after OTSU, we select the class with the highest score in attention maps, producing a non-overlapping text-guided label. For example, if both L1 and L1/L2 are activated at one pixel, but their original attention scores are 0.82 and 0.65, this pixel is assigned to L1.For probability maps summation, we add teacher prediction and text-guided label, normalize the added score, and apply argmax to obtain a one-hot pseudo label. For example, if teacher prediction is [0.7,0.2,0.08,0.02] and text-guided label is [1,0,0,0], their summation is [1.7,0.2,0.08,0.02]. After normalization, it becomes [0.85,0.1,0.04,0.01]. The final one-hot label is [1,0,0,0]. We will add these explanations in the revised manuscript and further evaluate Bayesian fusion and confidence-weighted averaging to assess their potential benefits over our fusion strategy.
Q6: Sensitivity Analysis of OTSU (R3). A6: OTSU is robust to different MRI qualities. Gaussian noise is added to unlabeled MRI inputs during the text-guided label generation process in Stage 2.Standard deviations were set to 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, and CPS4 achieves mDice scores of 80.44, 80.31, 80.12, under 5% labeled data. Compared with the original result of 80.44 without noise, performance drops are only 0.00, 0.13, 0.32.These minor decreases indicate that OTSU is robust to different MRI qualities.

title: CRIMSON: A Clinically-Grounded LLM-Based Metric for Generative Radiology Report Evaluation
abstract: We introduce CRIMSON, a clinically grounded evaluation framework for chest X-ray report generation that assesses reports based on diagnostic correctness, contextual relevance, and patient safety.
