meta_reviews.text:
This submission presents a clinically relevant and technically sound study on transferring angiography-derived information to ECG representations for severe coronary stenosis classification.
The main strengths are the clear clinical motivation, the new angiography-ECG cross-modal pretraining setting, the reasonably large internal paired cohort, and the comparative experimental validation. After checking the manuscript, the core contribution is supported: the proposed StenCE framework improves ECG-based severe stenosis classification, with the strongest result reported for the most severe threshold, and the paper also includes baseline comparisons, multi-threshold evaluation, and an ablation supporting the main design choices.
The decisive concerns are the absence of external validation, the selected angiography-referred population that introduces acknowledged selection bias, and the fact that performance declines substantially for less severe stenosis levels. These are real limitations. However, some reviewer criticisms are only partially supported. After checking the manuscript, the concern that evaluation focuses only on the most severe cases is overstated because the paper already evaluates several stenosis thresholds and discusses the resulting drop in performance. Similarly, the criticism that the contribution is too limited methodologically to merit consideration gives insufficient weight to the new modality pairing, the comparative evidence, and the ablation study. Accordingly, I assign limited weight to those criticisms in the overall assessment.

author_feedback_text:
Thank you for the review. We acknowledge the comments regarding the lack of external validation. We currently do not have access to datasets collected at different institutions or from diverse patient populations, which limits our ability to perform such evaluations at this stage. We, however, highlight that we have a large internal data cohort captured using different scanners, providing strong evaluation, and as part of future work, aim to evaluate it on multisituational datasets
We also agree that the dataset is subject to selection bias, which we explicitly acknowledge in the limitations section. Constructing a fully unbiased dataset would require angiograms from asymptomatic individuals. However, acquiring such data is inherently challenging, as it would involve exposing healthy patients to an invasive angiographic procedure without a clinical indication.
Regarding the comments on evaluating different severity thresholds, Table 1 and Figure 3 present both the data distribution and model performance across multiple thresholds. While we do not explicitly adopt the threshold defined by the American College of Cardiology guidelines, the evaluated thresholds closely align with those recommendations.
Lastly, the novelty of our work does not stem from the contrastive pretraining methodology itself, but rather from the adaptation of the CLIP framework to paired angiography and ECG data. Specifically, our contribution lies in extending a multi-view encoder architecture for contrastive learning by introducing separate CLS and CLIP tokens, enabling effective alignment between angiography and ECG modalities within the contrastive framework.

title: Cross-Modal Prediction of DNA Methylation from Histology Images
abstract: DNA methylation is a key epigenetic regulator of gene expression and a well-established hallmark of cancer. However, clinical methylation profiling remains costly and time-consuming, limiting routine use, particularly in low-resource settings. Inferring DNA methylation from routinely acquired histology images may serve as a scalable and cost-effective surrogate approach, providing early indications of methylation patterns prior to molecular profiling. We propose GraphCpG, a graph neural network-based framework for predicting continuous DNA methylation beta values across 10,000 CpG sites from H&E-stained whole slide images (WSIs) of gliomas, a tumour class in which methylation plays a central diagnostic and prognostic role. We evaluate the inferred methylation profiles in clinically relevant downstream tasks, including survival stratification and prediction of mitotic and immune subtypes, which capture tumour proliferative activity and tumour microenvironment states, respectively. Across TCGA glioma cohorts, predicted methylation features support significant survival separation and improved subtype classification performance relative to clinical and histology-only baselines, with AUROC gains of ≈ 17% and 3%, respectively. In some settings, methylation-based models achieve performance comparable to multi-modal approaches, and in certain cases yield improvements of up to ≈ 2% AUROC, highlighting the predictive value of histology-derived methylation signals. Pathway enrichment of well-predicted CpG-associated genes identifies immune and inflammatory processes consistent with glioma biology, providing supportive evidence for the biological relevance of the inferred signals. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to demonstrate that immune and mitotic subtypes can be predicted from DNA methylation profiles inferred directly from WSIs, highlighting the potential of scalable, image-based molecular characterization in glioma.
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The authors have, for the first time, demonstrated GraphCpG, a GNN based network that can predict DNA methylation beta values across 10000 CpG islands directly from H&E stained WSIs. This has led them to faciliatate the process of inferring clinical and molecular parameters like survival analysis, mitotic subtype prediction and immune subtype classification. As per their claim GraphCpG based methylation profiles were 
consistently outperformed both clinical and histology-only baselines, suggesting that immune subtype characteristics are more effectively captured through DNA methylation than through direct image-derived features.
reviews.text_strengths: The authors have demonstrated a novel methodology to capture CpG islands and methylation patterns from WSIs using GraphCpG GNN for DNA methylation pattern prediction. Very few studies have attempted to gauge the deep learning aspect of methylation beta values to predict molecular and clinical parameters. For example, Hoang et al, 2024 in Nature Medicine introduced a deep learning model, DEPLOY, that classifies CNS tumors from WSIs, generates predictions for DNA methylation beta values, and classifies tumor types into ten methylation classes in all CNS tumours using MLP (multilayer perceptron). Whereas in this case, the authors and team have built a novel methodology by using GNN, primarly on gliomas TCGA dataset and succesfully predicted survival analysis, mitotic subtypes and immune checkpoints after regression analysis based on methylation patterns. Now, this manuscript has used tissue segmentation, path embedding using Delaunay triangulation for better histological assesment by using spatial graphs for better geometric alignment. Furthermore, downstream analysis of the immunological aspects using Pathway Enrichment performed using the MSigDB hallmark 2020 library with Enrichr, and then confirmed by GSEA, showed correlation of TNF-α/NF-κB signaling, Coagulation and Apoptosis, NF-κB signaling drives proliferation, inflammation with relevant methylation patterns linked to immune and inflammatory processes in gliomas. The prediction utility was further validated by comparing GraphCpG with a comprehensive experimental framework (uni-modal, multi-modal, and clinical baselines) which proves as an excellent evidence for clinical utility.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
All evaluations rely on internal 3-fold cross-validation within TCGA, given subclass heterogeneity and interobserver variability across institutions, scanners, and staining protocols, external validation cohort is essential. 
One of my primary concerns with the paper is that even though it projects the methodology and the technical aspect very logistically however working on 450k epic array data is redundant, theoritically it is ok otherwise it does not make much sense because we have 935k or 850k Illumina Epic Chip array data available in the datasets now, so for practically imprelemting it, its essential to use the updated CpG island dataset. 
Only on 502 patients’ data isnt a strong sample size but to begin with its not so bad. The main issue is that gliomas have molecular/intratumoral heterogeneity. The analysis is blurred unless predictions are derived from true GBM or LGG cases, hence lack of transparency of sublasses used for methylation pattern prediction will be misleading practically. The authors mention that “Methylation-based models consistently outperformed both clinical and histology-only baselines, suggesting that immune subtype characteristics are more effectively captured through DNA methylation than through direct image-derived features” is a bold claim and therefore needs validation in a larger and external cohort to prove this statement further. 
Median Spearman 0.42, only 42% variance, insufficient for confident clinical deployment without improving regression performance.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper justifies strong computational ground and adheres to CAI aspects but falls short in the clinically translational aspect. The novel approach to predicting methylation pattern if expanded and verified using a robust external cohort while ensuring the accurate inclusion of subclasses of gliomas, will enable better utilization of the GraphCpG model and also validate its robustness as a strong generazible protocol.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Although the study is not yet ready for clinical translation, it presents a technically novel graph-based framework for continuous methylation inference from histology and demonstrates consistent downstream utility across survival and subtype prediction tasks. The rebuttal clarifies the main methodological concerns, including within-fold feature selection and model specification, and the authors now appropriately frame external validation as future work. For these reasons, I consider the paper a solid computational pathology contribution and recommend acceptance, while encouraging a more ambitious external validation study in future work.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes GraphCpG, a graph neural network that predicts continuous DNA methylation beta values from H&E whole slide images in glioma. The predicted profiles are then used for survival analysis and for classifying mitotic and immune subtypes in matched TCGA LGG and GBM cases.
reviews.text_strengths:
The clinical motivation is real. Molecular profiling is slow and uneven in practice, and a histology-based surrogate for methylation-derived signals would matter if it works.
Histology-to-methylation prediction isn’t new, but pushing to continuous CpG-level values at this scale, and then asking whether the inferred profiles are actually useful for glioma-relevant tasks, is the right next step.
The graph formulation is a relatively novel choice in this setting, and the motivation — capturing spatial tissue architecture rather than treating patches as a bag — is sound.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The training objective for the multi-output prediction is the single biggest thing I couldn’t resolve on my own. I spent a while trying to reconcile Equations 2-4 with the 10,000 CpG claim and couldn’t land on a consistent reading. Either z_i is a vector and Equation 4 needs re-expressing, or the task is not what Section 2.1 describes.
The correlation-based CpG filtering and top-1k selection need to be fold-internal. As written, I can’t tell whether they are, and if they aren’t, the downstream numbers are optimistic.
The survival analysis is hard to read without clinical-only and histology-only baselines. On its own, the reported number doesn’t tell me how much the methylation prediction is adding.
The immune subtype result is the one I’d push hardest on. LGG and GBM have very different immune landscapes, and combining them means the classifier may be partly learning tumor type or grade. This needs to be acknowledged directly and reflected in the interpretation of the result.
The sample counts don’t add up: 502 patients in Section 2.1, but 417 cold + 124 hot = 541 in Section 3.1.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1.The dimensionality of z_i^(l), g^(l), and F(G) in Section 2.4 is the first thing I’d fix. From the text, z_i^(l) reads as a patch-level prediction and F(G) as slide-level, but it’s never stated whether these are scalars or 10,000-dim vectors. Equation 4 is written as a scalar pairwise ranking loss, which doesn’t square with a 10,000-output task. If the ranking loss is applied per-CpG and then aggregated, say so; if something else is happening, the equation needs to reflect that.
2.State explicitly that correlation-based filtering and top-k CpG selection are performed on the training fold only. If not, that should be acknowledged clearly and the downstream results interpreted accordingly.
3.The sample count discrepancy in Section 3.1 needs to be resolved — 502 vs. 541 isn’t a rounding issue.
4.The survival claim is stronger than the evidence supports without clinical-only and histology-only baselines. Without those comparisons, the framing should be tempered accordingly.
5.On the immune subtype task: please discuss the LGG/GBM confound directly. At minimum, the paper should acknowledge that tumor type may be driving part of the signal and interpret this result accordingly.
6.Table 1 — the fold variance eats most of the gaps you’re claiming as improvements. Several of these differences read as ties given the reported variability, and the text should reflect that.
7.The enrichment analysis is interesting but post hoc — it’s conditioned on the well-predicted CpGs, so it can support biological plausibility but can’t establish that the model has learned meaningful methylation structure. Framing it as suggestive rather than confirmatory would help.
8.Minor: Figure 2 labels are too small to read.
9.From a reproducibility perspective, please specify whether the CTransPath encoder is frozen or fine-tuned, and clarify the exact implementation of the multi-output loss. Given the number of moving parts in the pipeline, a code release would be materially helpful.

This is a promising paper on a problem I think matters, and I like the direction — the graph formulation and the move toward clinically relevant glioma tasks are both the right instincts. My score is borderline because several methodological things I’d need to interpret the results aren’t resolvable from the text: the multi-output objective, the fold structure of the downstream selection, and the sample-count inconsistency. These are all fixable in rebuttal, and if they are, my concerns would drop substantially.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
I maintain an accept recommendation, but this remains a borderline paper. I do not view the lack of external validation or definitive translational impact as sufficient grounds for rejection in a MICCAI methodological submission, but the final version needs much more careful reporting and interpretation.
The rebuttal directly addressed two of my most important concerns. First, the authors clarified that the patch-level predictions, pooled layer outputs, and slide-level prediction are all C-dimensional vectors over the 10,000 CpG sites, and that the ranking loss is applied per CpG and aggregated across CpG outputs. This resolves the dimensionality ambiguity in the submitted equations, although the manuscript still needs the corrected loss expression. Second, they confirmed that correlation-based CpG filtering and top-k CpG selection were performed within each training fold. This substantially reduces my concern that the downstream classification and survival numbers were inflated by test-fold leakage.
Several concerns remain after the rebuttal. For the survival analysis, clinical-only and histology-only survival baselines are not part of the submitted evidence, so the current result should be framed as showing prognostic association of inferred methylation features rather than added value over simpler clinical or image-only models. I do not expect new survival experiments in rebuttal, but the claim should be narrowed accordingly. The immune subtype experiment remains potentially confounded by LGG/GBM composition; the rebuttal acknowledges this, but because no controlled or stratified analysis is in the submitted evidence, the immune-subtype claim should be interpreted cautiously. The sample-count discrepancy was acknowledged as corrected, but the rebuttal does not state the corrected counts, which leaves a reproducibility issue. The loss clarification also does not fully address calibration: a per-CpG ranking objective can support relative methylation ordering, but the paper should be careful when describing the outputs as continuous beta-value estimates. Finally, some reported gains in Table 1 are small relative to fold variability, and the rebuttal does not substantially change that interpretation.
Overall, I think the paper is promising enough for acceptance because the central methodological direction is useful, the graph-based WSI formulation is reasonable, and the two most serious fixable issues from my review – the multi-output loss ambiguity and possible fold leakage in CpG selection – were answered credibly in the rebuttal. My acceptance is contingent in spirit on the final version explicitly correcting the loss formulation, reporting the corrected sample counts, stating the frozen encoder setting, and tempering the survival, immune-subtype, and enrichment-analysis claims.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: A method based on GNN was proposed to predict methylation values from pathological images, and the performance of downstream tasks was enhanced based on the predicted methylation information.
reviews.text_strengths:
(1) This work try to demonstrate that DNA methylation profiles predicted from WSI images can be used to classify subtypes in gliomas. This goes beyond prior work that only predicted methylation or tumour types, showing that histology-derived epigenetic signals capture clinically meaningful tumour phenotypes.
(2) The authors evaluate predicted methylation on three clinically relevant tasks: survival stratification, mitotic subtype classification, and immune subtype classification. They compare against clinical, histology‑only, methylation‑only, and multi‑modal baselines. The methylation‑only model outperforms histology and clinical baselines, and in some settings matches multi‑modal approaches, demonstrating the practical utility of the inferred profiles.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(1) Limited novelty of predicting methylation from histology. Some previous works already predict continuous DNA methylation values from H&E images, including for LGG and GBM. The proposed GNN offers incremental architectural changes but is not shown to outperform existing methods, as no direct comparison is provided (Section 3.1 Regression Results).
(2) The accuracy of the model is not high, and the selection criteria are not clear. Firstly, for the prediction of methylation values, the correlation coefficient is set at a threshold of 0.4, which itself is not very strong. And in subsequent tasks, sometimes the top 10 are selected, such as survival analysis (Section 3.1), and sometimes the top 1000 are selected, such as classification prediction tasks (Table 1). This highly selective pipeline may overestimate clinical utility.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The innovation of the method is insufficient. It is suggested that this work be further expanded into a clinical application under the framework of two-stage prediction, which will be interesting.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I still have concerns about the methodological innovation of this work. If only GNN is used for modeling, it is equivalent to solving a new task using traditional methods, and this work is not a pioneering work based on HE image prediction of methylation values. I suggest that the author should consider how to better design a specific network architecture to handle methylation prediction tasks, in order to solve the practical dilemma of insufficient prediction performance.

meta_reviews.text:
The reviews are mixed, with one weak-accept, one weak-reject, and one reject recommendation. The paper addresses an important and clinically relevant problem: predicting DNA methylation profiles from routine H&E whole-slide images and using the inferred profiles for glioma-related downstream tasks. The reviewers recognize several strengths, including the graph-based WSI formulation, the attempt to predict continuous CpG-level methylation values, and the evaluation on survival, mitotic subtype, and immune subtype prediction.
However, the reviewers raise substantive concerns. The main issues are: (1) the multi-output methylation prediction objective is not sufficiently clear, especially how the ranking loss and slide-level predictions apply to 10,000 CpG outputs; (2) the CpG filtering and top-k selection procedures must be clearly shown to be fold-internal to avoid optimistic downstream results; (3) the evidence for clinical utility is limited by internal TCGA cross-validation only, lack of external validation, and modest methylation regression performance; and (4) several interpretation issues need clarification, including the LGG/GBM confounding in immune subtype classification, missing clinical/histology baselines for survival analysis, lack of direct comparison with prior histology-to-methylation methods, and the reported sample-count inconsistency.

After considering the reviews and rebuttal, I recommend acceptance. The paper addresses an important computational pathology problem by predicting continuous CpG-level methylation profiles from H&E whole-slide images and evaluating the inferred profiles on glioma-related downstream tasks. The rebuttal resolves two important technical concerns: the authors clarified that the methylation predictions are C-dimensional CpG vectors and that the ranking loss is applied per CpG and aggregated, and they confirmed that CpG filtering and top-k selection were performed within each training fold. These clarifications reduce concerns about objective ambiguity and potential test-fold leakage.

After reviewing the paper in detail, I share the concerns regarding the level of methodological innovation in this work. The paper would be substantially strengthened by a more task-specific network architecture tailored to the unique characteristics of methylation prediction, particularly to better address the practical challenge of limited predictive performance. Given the current level of methodological novelty and the limited empirical support, this was not an easy decision, I regretfully have to recommend rejection.
The work lacks specific architectural design and algorithmic innovation, remaining an application of existing models rather than a methodological contribution.

author_feedback_text:
Rebuttal to the Reviewers’ Comments
General Remarks: First, we thank the reviewers for their insightful comments and careful observations. We note that all three reviewers recognized the importance of our work for predicting continuous CpG methylation profiles from H&E histology images using graph-based WSI formulation and the value of evaluating these inferred methylation signals across downstream glioma-specific clinically relevant tasks. In the remainder of this rebuttal, Rx refers to Reviewer# x and MRx refers to Meta Reviewer’s point# x.
[MR1/R2] Prediction Setup and the Ranking Loss: The multi-output formulation is in Section 2.4.In the revised paper, we will explicitly state that the predictions z_i^(l), g^(l), and F(G) are all C-dimensional vectors corresponding to predictions across all C=10,000 CpG sites. We will also revise Eq.(4) to explicitly define the ranking loss for each CpG site and aggregate the losses across CpG outputs.
[MR2/4/R2] Clarity: We confirm that correlation-based CpG filtering and top-k CpG selection were performed within each training fold. We will revise the discussion surrounding the enrichment and survival analyses to present these findings more cautiously and as supportive rather than confirmatory evidence of biological relevance. We have corrected the discrepancy in the reported sample counts in Section 3.1 and clarify that the CTransPath encoder was frozen during feature extraction.
[MR3] Performance Interpretation and External Validation: The reported median correlation (0.42) should be interpreted in the context of cross-modal histology-to-methylation prediction tasks, where moderate correlations (0.27, 0.33[1], 0.45[2]) have been reported due to substantial biological and technical variability. We agree that external validation would further strengthen the findings. Accordingly, we will revise the paper to add this point to the discussion as part of future work.
[MR4/R3] Positioning Relative to Prior Work: Prior approaches primarily employed MLP-based or conventional ML methods for continuous methylation prediction, while GraphCpG uses a GNN to model spatial relationships between histological regions for predicting methylation profiles across 10,000 CpG sites. Feature Selection: The threshold of 0.4 follows prior methylation prediction studies [1, 2] and was used to identify comparatively well-predicted CpG sites. The downstream feature-selection procedures were task-specific: smaller CpG subsets were used for Cox regression, whereas larger subsets were retained for classification tasks using MLP classifiers. We included evaluations using all CpG sites, correlation-filtered CpGs and top-1,000 CpG subsets for classification tasks to assess the effect of feature selection on downstream performance.
[MR4] Immune Subtype Analysis: We acknowledge that differences between tumor classes may contribute to part of the predictive signal in addition to immune subtype characteristics, and we will interpret the findings accordingly.
[R1] Methylation Platform: Regarding methylation platforms, the TCGA LGG and GBM datasets predominantly use HM450 arrays, although we agree that EPIC/850k arrays are more ubiquitous nowadays. We will explicitly state this as a limitation of our work, if the paper is accepted.
[R3] Novelty Challenge: As the MR has established, the reviewers recognize several strengths, chiefly: (a) the graph-based formulation for prediction of continuous CpG-level methylation values, and (b) the evaluation on clinically relevant downstream tasks in survival analysis and prediction of mitotic subtypes and immune subtypes.
[1] Hoang, Danh-Tai, et al. “Path2Omics Enhances Transcriptomic and Methylation Prediction Accuracy from Tumor Histopathology.” Cancer research 85.24 (2025): 5098-5112.[2] Hoang, Danh-Tai, et al. “Prediction of DNA methylation-based tumor types from histopathology in central nervous system tumors with deep learning.” Nature Medicine 30.7 (2024): 1952-1961.

title: Cross-Surface Representation Learning for Accurate Gingiva Prediction in CBCT
abstract: Accurate gingival segmentation from Cone-Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) is critical for periodontitis management and implantology, yet remains challenging due to low soft tissue contrast and the adhesion of adjacent tissues such as the cheeks and the tongue. In standard CBCT, the gingival margin is essentially indistinguishable from the surrounding mucosa, so existing methods either rely on additional intra-oral scan (IOS) data or apply voxel-based deep-learning methods that struggle with boundary precision. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a protocol-and-method co-design. First, we introduce a chair-side scanning protocol that uses a mouth retractor and an impression tray to physically isolate the gingiva from buccal and lingual tissues during acquisition, creating a continuous high-contrast air interface that makes the gingival margin imageable in CBCT in the first place; the protocol requires no scanner modification and adds less than one minute to the standard CBCT workflow. Second, building on this controlled input, we propose a cross-surface representation (CSR) that recasts the 3D volumetric segmentation as 1D radiodensity profile regression along tooth surface vertex normals, together with a band-aware Gaussian regression (BGR) module that produces a continuous, topologically consistent confidence field on the tooth manifold. Experiments demonstrate that the method outperforms strong 3D voxel baselines, achieving expert-level accuracy without auxiliary IOS data.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses CBCT-based gingival margin prediction, a clinically important task for periodontal assessment and implantology that is severely limited by low soft-tissue contrast in standard CBCT acquisitions. The paper makes a dual contribution: first, a standardised physical scanning protocol using a mouth retractor and impression tray to create a continuous high-contrast air interface between the gingiva and surrounding oral tissues; second, a cross-surface representation (CSR) that transforms the inherently 3D volumetric segmentation problem into structured 1D radiodensity profile regression along tooth surface vertex normals, combined with band-aware Gaussian regression (BGR) to produce a smooth continuous confidence field for the gingival margin. Evaluated on 28 clinical cases (684 teeth), the method substantially outperforms voxel-based baselines including nnU-Net across all four tooth categories.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Physical protocol co-design is the defining innovation. 
2.Cross-surface representation is anatomically motivated and principled
3.Band-aware Gaussian regression avoids discrete classification
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Applicability to standard (non-protocol) CBCT scans is uncharacterised. 
2.Per-fold breakdown is absent
3.Normal direction limitations for multi-rooted teeth are not discussed
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper makes a compelling Clinical Translation contribution by co-designing a physical scanning protocol and a surface-normal-anchored algorithmic pipeline that together enable CBCT-based gingival margin prediction at near-expert accuracy, without auxiliary IOS data. The hardware-software integration, the cross-surface representation, and the consistent multi-tooth-category results are all strengths. The main weakness, lack of characterisation on non-protocol scans, is an important limitation for clinical translation and should be addressed in discussion, but it does not diminish the contribution of demonstrating that the method works well under the proposed protocol.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of this paper is that it does not directly segment the ambiguous gingival boundary in CBCT using a conventional voxel-based formulation, but instead reformulates the task on a tooth-surface geometric prior through a cross-surface representation based on surface-normal intensity profiles. Combined with Gaussian soft-band regression, the method is designed to more stably predict a thin and ambiguous boundary. The standardized physical scanning protocol, which improves the separability of the input itself, is also a practical contribution.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The CSR idea is anatomically well motivated and, to the best of my knowledge, is a novel and well-matched formulation for this task, making it more convincing than simply applying a larger segmentation model.
2.The performance gains are non-trivial. In particular, the improvements over nnU-Net in both MAE and IoU suggest that the proposed representation provides a meaningful practical advantage.
3.Figs. 1–3 effectively connect the clinical problem, the methodological design, and the resulting performance, making the overall message easy to follow.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The main weakness is the limited evidence for generalizability. Since all data were acquired using the authors’ specialized physical scanning protocol, it remains unclear whether the method would perform similarly on routine clinical CBCT scans. As presented, the reported gains appear to reflect a combination of algorithmic improvement and acquisition-specific advantages.
2.The evaluation scale is limited. Although 684 teeth may appear substantial, the study includes only 28 patients, and it is not clearly stated whether the data split was performed at the patient level.
3.The experimental comparisons are somewhat limited, as the baselines are mainly older voxel-based models. The evaluation would be more convincing if it also included relatively recent and stronger 3D segmentation baselines, such as 3D UXNet or SwinUNETR, to better position the proposed method against the current state of the art.
4.Reproducibility and ethical reporting are insufficiently documented. Important details such as data acquisition approval, IRB/consent, the split protocol, and the training/evaluation setup for tooth segmentation are not described clearly enough.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper addresses an important clinical problem, and the CSR+BGR framework built on a tooth-surface prior is well aligned with the structure of the task. The quantitative results also show clear improvements over the baselines. However, by MICCAI standards, the evidence for generalizability and the overall evaluation design are not yet fully convincing. In particular, all data were collected under a specialized acquisition protocol, the comparisons remain mostly limited to voxel-based baselines, and the dataset scale and split protocol are only sparsely described. Overall, the idea is interesting and has clear potential, but in its current form it is difficult to strongly support acceptance, and the paper feels more like a borderline submission that would benefit from additional validation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The rebuttal adequately addresses most of my major concerns. In particular, the authors clarify that the physical scanning protocol is a necessary prerequisite for making the gingival margin visible in CBCT, rather than merely an acquisition advantage. They also explain that all baseline methods were evaluated on the same protocol-acquired data and patient-level five-fold split, which helps isolate the algorithmic contribution of the proposed CSR+BGR framework. The additional results with stronger recent baselines such as SwinUNETR and 3D UXNet further strengthen the experimental validation.
Although some concerns remain regarding the dependence on the specialized acquisition protocol, and further validation across broader clinical settings would still be valuable, the rebuttal makes the necessity and scope of the protocol sufficiently clear. The authors also address the concerns about patient-level splitting, ethics approval, anonymization, and reproducibility details. Overall, I find that the rebuttal resolves the main issues that led to my original weak reject recommendation. Therefore, I am willing to change my recommendation to accept.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This work presents a novel framework that combines specialized physical scanning protocols with geometry-prior-driven deep learning to achieve accurate gingival margin prediction in cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT). The main contributions are as follows: (1) the introduction of a standardized physical scanning protocol that uses a mouth opener and impression tray to physically isolate the gingiva from the buccal and lingual tissues during scanning, creating a high-contrast air interface; (2) the proposal of a Cross-surface Representation (CSR) that transforms the 3D voxel segmentation task into a 1D intensity distribution analysis along the surface normals of teeth; and (3) the design of a Band-aware Gaussian Regression (BGR) module that predicts a continuous confidence field on the point cloud manifold, providing an alternative to traditional discrete voxel classification.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Pragmatic clinical insight: Instead of solely relying on algorithmic solutions to address the low soft-tissue contrast in CBCT, this study innovatively introduces clinical physical aids—a mouth opener and impression tray—to reshape the imaging boundaries. This front-end approach to improving data quality demonstrates practical thinking and strong clinical awareness.
2.Novel task formulation: The unconstrained 3D voxel segmentation problem is elegantly reformulated as a scalar field regression task constrained by geometric priors derived from the tooth surface mesh. Through CSR, the method extracts features along the tooth-surface normal direction corresponding to the “bone–gingiva–air” transition, effectively reducing background anatomical noise. This formulation offers theoretical advantages in handling adherent soft-tissue edges.
3.Empirical validation: Experiments show that the proposed approach achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.38 mm without requiring auxiliary intraoral scan (IOS) data for registration. This has the potential to simplify clinical periodontal assessment workflows and reduce cumulative errors from multi-modal registration.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The method’s strong reliance on upstream geometric priors renders it potentially sensitive to error propagation. Both the CSR and BGR modules are fully dependent on the accuracy of the tooth surface meshes extracted by nnU-Net. However, in real-world CBCT clinical data, metal artifacts—such as those from crowns or implants—can lead to failed tooth segmentation or severely distorted surface meshes. The manuscript lacks an analysis of how such upstream mesh extraction errors may impact the robustness of downstream gingival predictions.
2.The manuscript compares the BGR network, which leverages point cloud and surface normal features, with conventional 3D CNNs (e.g., 3D U-Net, DeepLabV3+) that operate directly on raw CBCT voxels. While this comparison demonstrates that “surface-constrained” approaches outperform “unconstrained voxel classification,” it does not sufficiently establish the inherent advantage of the Gaussian regression (BGR) itself. To make the evaluation more rigorous, I suggest the authors to include a baseline model that also operates on the tooth surface manifold—e.g., a PointNet++ or graph neural network performing direct binary classification on the point cloud.
3.Although the physical scanning protocol effectively enhances image contrast, the manuscript does not discuss its applicability boundaries in extreme clinical scenarios. For instance, in patients with severe gag reflex, limited mouth opening, or partial tooth loss, the placement of the physical tools may be constrained, which could limit the generalizability of the proposed method.
4.The introduction quickly jumps to the limitations of voxel-based CNNs but overlooks a deeper discussion of the methodological context. Given that the core of this work is the transformation of the 3D volumetric gingiva segmentation problem into a tooth-surface-based manifold problem, I recommend that the authors supplement the Introduction or Related Work sections with a discussion of existing methods for tooth, gingiva, and alveolar bone segmentation in medical image analysis, as well as recent literature on surface-, mesh-, or graph-based learning (e.g., [1][2]). Currently, the manuscript cites only 16 references; adding relevant studies would provide a more comprehensive background.
5.I recommend that the authors supplement the manuscript with figures showing the actual 1D intensity profile curves extracted from the three regions. Additionally, visualizations of the continuous Gaussian confidence fields predicted along the tooth surfaces could be included. Providing these visualizations would greatly enhance the interpretability of the method and increase readers’ confidence in its effectiveness.
[1] Wang C, He Z, Chen L, et al. ITMatch: Arch-Guided Semi-supervised Tooth Arrangement via Iterative Confidence Evaluation[C]//International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025: 268-277.[2] Zhou, Z., Chen, Y., He, A., Que, X., Wang, K., Yao, R., & Li, T. (2024). NKUT: dataset and benchmark for pediatric mandibular wisdom teeth segmentation. IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics, 28(6), 3523-3533.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Please see weakness above.

Addressing key challenges in medical image analysis does not always require stacking increasingly complex network architectures. The authors of this work precisely identify the core difficulty in CBCT gingival segmentation and propose an elegant solution that combines physical pre-scanning isolation with algorithmic post-processing constraints. This geometry-driven representation learning aligns naturally with periodontal anatomical features. Overall, the approach is methodologically sound and represents a compelling and meaningful exploration.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I appreciate the author’s response to my comments, which to some extent resolved my confusion. Although this paper still has some shortcomings, I believe it is a meaningful work. The author should complete all the promised revisions in the final manuscript, and I recommend accepting this paper.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper addresses an important clinical problem and introduces a thoughtful combination of a physical scanning protocol and a geometry-prior-based formulation. Reviewers generally find the method promising, but also note concerns about generalizability beyond the specialized protocol, limited baseline comparisons, and incomplete reporting. The authors are encouraged to address these points in rebuttal.

This paper addresses an important clinical problem and proposes a thoughtful protocol-plus-method co-design for gingiva prediction in CBCT. The cross-surface representation and band-aware Gaussian regression are well motivated and align naturally with the anatomy of the task. Although one reviewer raised concerns about generalizability, I am more persuaded by the reviewers who saw the protocol as an enabling prerequisite rather than a confounder, and the rebuttal further clarified the split protocol and baseline fairness. Overall, I believe the methodology is convincing, and the reported gains are meaningful, so I am inclined to accept this paper.

Although some limitations remain regarding the dependence on a specialized acquisition protocol and the need for broader clinical validation, the rebuttal adequately addresses the main concerns by clarifying the necessity and scope of the protocol, confirming patient-level evaluation and reproducibility details. Therefore, the AC recommends acceptance.

Two reviewers explicitly upgraded to Accept (R2=3→Accept, R4=4→Accept). Rebuttal effectively addressed main concerns: confirmed patient-level splits and ethics approval. Innovation is outstanding: physical scanning protocol + cross-surface representation + Gaussian regression.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the Meta-AE and reviewers for recognizing the clinical motivation, the protocol and method co-design, and the consistent gains over voxe-based methods. We address the major concerns below.
(1) Protocol scope and isolation of algorithmic gain [Meta reviewer, R1.1, R2.1]. The protocol is a prerequisite that makes CBCT gingival margin imaging tractable. In routine CBCT, buccal and lingual soft tissues adhere to the arch with nearly identical intensity to gingiva, leaving the margin invisible even to experienced clinicians, and no algorithm can recover information that is not encoded. Our lip retractor and impression tray protocol introduces this air interface as a simple chair side add on to the existing CBCT workflow, using routine clinical aids with no scanner modification. All comparison methods in Table 1 use the same CBCT data acquired under this protocol and the same patient level five fold split. The gains over nnU-Net (0.38 vs 0.50 mm MAE, 56.2% vs 34.6% IoU@0.3mm) therefore reflect the algorithmic contribution rather than any acquisition advantage.
(2) Baseline comparisons [Meta reviewer, R2.3, R4.2]. We appreciate the suggestion of stronger voxel baselines. Our method still outperforms recent architectures. SwinUNETR yields 0.48 ± 0.16 mm MAE and 37.1 ± 17.6% IoU@0.3mm, and 3D UXNet yields 0.46 ± 0.15 mm MAE and 38.8 ± 17.4% IoU@0.3mm. These will be added to Table 1.R4.2 also requested a surface manifold baseline. This is already present in Table 2 as “w/o Cross surface (K=1)”, which uses the same PointMLP encoder on the same tooth point cloud with coordinates and normals only, i.e. direct surface classification. Its IoU is 35.7% vs 56.2% for the full model, isolating CSR. “w/o Gaussian Band” reaches 53.2%, isolating BGR.
(3) Reporting, ethics, and reproducibility [R1.2, R2.2, R2.4, R4.4, R4.5]. The five fold cross validation is patient level with no patient overlap, on 28 patients and 684 teeth spanning gingivitis to Stage IV periodontitis. The study was approved under SH9H-2026-T98-1, with anonymized data and informed consent. We will state the split protocol, IRB approval, and anonymization explicitly. We will expand the Introduction and Related Work to cover tooth, gingiva, and alveolar bone segmentation together with surface, mesh, and graph based learning, including the suggested ITMatch and NKUT references. We will also report training and evaluation details for the upstream nnU-Net tooth instance segmentation that precedes Marching Cubes and Laplacian smoothing, and provide a per fold MAE and IoU breakdown.
(4) Clinical boundaries, robustness, and interpretability [R1.3, R4.1, R4.3, R4.5]. For multi rooted teeth the gingival margin lies at the CEJ on the crown above the furcation, so root multiplicity does not affect surface normals in the sampled −0.3 to 1.7 mm band. Molars achieve 0.39 mm MAE and 55.6% IoU, consistent with single rooted teeth. On error propagation, we excluded target teeth with full crowns or in tooth implants while retaining minor restorations. On this cohort the upstream nnU-Net reaches 96% Dice on teeth, sufficient to support stable downstream prediction. Stratified evaluation on severe metal artifact cases is left as future work. The protocol uses standard intraoral aids and is well tolerated, though severe gag reflex, restricted mouth opening, or extensive tooth loss can constrain placement, and we will state these boundaries in the Discussion. For interpretability we will add figures showing the 1D intensity profiles from the three anatomical regions and the predicted Gaussian confidence field rendered on the tooth surface.
We believe these clarifications and additions address the central concerns and respectfully hope the reviewers will consider raising their recommendation

title: CrownFusion: 3D Dental Crown Generation Using Geometry Images and Latent Diffusion
abstract: We introduce CrownFusion, a latent diffusion model to generate 3D dental crown designs from geometry images, a 2D-grid encoding of surface coordinates. Departing from traditional approaches that use point clouds, our “CrownImage” representation not only unlocks the full power of image-based generative architectures, but also preserves fine geometric detail by operating at far higher spatial resolutions than point clouds to alleviate smoothing artifacts in the 3D generation. Conditioned on jointly learned embeddings of the surrounding dentition, our probabilistic diffusion model produces anatomically plausible crowns with morphological variations tailored to individual patient cases. To accommodate multiple valid designs, we propose an occlusal fit metric based on proximity to the antagonist teeth. We evaluate our method through quantitative experiments and qualitative studies involving expert testimonials. We also release the FDI 16 Crown Dataset, comprising 11,513 annotated intra-oral scans, to support future research in dental CAD.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of this paper is the introduction of CrownFusion, a methodological framework for 3D dental crown generation. This approach relies on the use of geometry images (CrownImages), which represent tooth surfaces as high-resolution 2D grids encoding full 3D coordinates. This representation enables the application of latent diffusion models for generating complex shapes with a VAE uses for latent space encoding. By combining this formalism with a conditional diffusion transformer that integrates embeddings of adjacent and antagonist teeth, the method can produce multiple anatomically plausible crown designs tailored to individual patients. It thus overcomes the limitations of previous approaches based on point clouds or depth map representations, particularly in terms of geometric quality and anatomical consistency. Furthermore, the paper introduces a clinically relevant occlusal fit metric based on the proximity between the generated crown and the antagonist teeth, providing an objective criterion to evaluate the functional quality of the proposed designs. Finally, the authors release a large annotated dataset of intraoral scans, helping to support and stimulate future research in digital dentistry and anatomical shape generation.
reviews.text_strengths:
This paper introduces a formulation of 3D dental crown generation based on the use of geometry images. This approach transforms a complex 3D surface modeling problem into a 2D image generation task while preserving the full geometric information. This is particularly interesting because it allows the direct use of powerful diffusion architectures originally designed for images, without suffering from the smoothing artifacts commonly associated with point cloud-based methods.
Moreover, the paper proposes a conditioning strategy, in which representations of neighboring and antagonist teeth are integrated into the model through cross-attention mechanisms. This design enables the generation of crowns that are anatomically realistic and functionally consistent with each patient’s specific anatomy.
Furthermore, the method is fully generative and models a distribution of plausible crowns rather than producing a single deterministic solution, aligning with the variability observed in clinical practice, where multiple designs can be acceptable for a given patient. It also demonstrates strong clinical relevance. Expert evaluations as well as a reduction in the need for manual corrections and intersection artifacts compared to existing methods.
Finally, the experimental evaluation by introducing a domain-specific occlusal fit metric. This metric better reflects the functional performance of the crowns than standard geometric distances. The release of a large, realistic, and annotated dataset of intraoral scans further strengthens the impact of the paper and the reproducibility of its results.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The use of geometry images, while effective, is not entirely novel. Prior works already explored geometry images, including in diffusion-based generative settings. As a result, the contribution lies more in adapting this representation to the dental domain rather than introducing a fundamentally new formulation.
Moreover, the overall generative framework combining a VAE, a latent diffusion model, and transformer-based conditioning closely follows established pipelines such as Latent Diffusion Models and SiT architectures. This reduces the degree of architectural novelty, even though the integration is well executed.
In addition, the reliance on a variational autoencoder for latent space encoding introduces well-known limitations, including reconstruction blur, loss of high-frequency details, and a delicate trade-off between compression and fidelity. These limitations are particularly critical in this setting, as even small latent errors can lead to noticeable geometric distortions in the reconstructed meshes. Alternative approaches such as diffusion models operating directly in pixel could potentially better preserve fine structures.
Furthermore, the geometry image parameterization assumes a simple, disk-like topology. This restricts the method’s ability to generalize beyond individual teeth and limits its applicability to more complex anatomical structures.
Finally, the generation time is relatively high, around five minutes per case, which may hinder practical deployment in clinical settings. This is significantly slower than deterministic approaches could be a limiting factor in time-sensitive environments. But it remains valuable if it is use for planning where timing is not so sensitive.

Regarding Reviewer 2’s comment #3 under weaknesses: we would like to clarify that the crown generation is primarily conditioned on the surrounding/adjacent teeth, which serve as the main geometric context for determining crown morphology. The only information derived from the tooth preparation is the margin line, which defines the crown-gingiva border and ensures a proper fit at the preparation boundary. We agree that the adjacent teeth are the dominant signal for crown shape, and our model reflects this. We will make the conditioning inputs more explicit in the camera-ready version.

title: CSAM-HQ: A Multi-stage Refinement Framework for Surgical Instrument Segmentation based on SAM and Probabilistic Graphical Models
abstract: Accurate surgical instrument segmentation is essential for navigation and safety in minimally invasive surgery. However, existing vision-based approaches remain susceptible to boundary ambiguity, topological fragmentation, and inter-class interference in complex surgical scenes, leading to compromised geometric precision and false positives. To address these challenges, we propose CSAM-HQ, a hierarchical refinement framework built upon the prototype-based Segment Anything Model. CSAM-HQ adopts a coarse-to-fine paradigm, where prototype-driven semantic localization first produces reliable global predictions, followed by a learnable HQ-Token with residual correction to refine boundaries and recover high-frequency geometric details, particularly for thin structures. To further mitigate inter-class conflicts, we design an IoU-aware mask quality calibration head that adaptively suppresses ambiguous predictions. In addition, a fully connected conditional random field is incorporated to enforce pixel-level spatial and appearance consistency, improving structural coherence. This dual refinement strategy enhances geometric fidelity while maintaining parameter efficiency. Extensive experiments on EndoVis2017, EndoVis2018, and CATARACTS demonstrate consistent improvements over prior methods. The proposed framework substantially improves thin instrument segmentation and reduces inter-class ambiguity across diverse surgical environments. Code is available at https://github.com/shixueyi/CSAM-HQ.

The first is to have the HQ-Token block that is based on the HQ-SAM paper, which performs residual correction on the mark generated by SurgicalSAM. The second is a post-processing step using conditional random fields (CRFs). In this work, the prompt encoder, mask decoder and the HQ-Token block are trained while the SAM ViT-H encoder is frozen. Results are evaluated on EndoVis2017, EndoVis2018 and CATARACTS datasets.

meta_reviews.text:
The rebuttal should address four decision-affecting concerns. First, the apparent numerical inconsistencies on EndoVis2017: the reported mean IoU does not match the average of the per-class column, and Challenge IoU and standard IoU values appear identical for SAM-based competitors; both need to be checked and corrected. Second, missing technical details that prevent reproduction: how the HQ-token is generated, what the two-way transformer is, the meaning of variables in Equations 1 and 2, and how the IoU-aware mask quality calibration head referenced in the abstract relates to the methodology section. Third, evaluation against a boundary-aware metric such as Hausdorff distance, which is more aligned with thin-instrument segmentation than IoU alone. Fourth, an explicit limitations and failure-mode analysis, particularly for the classes where the model underperforms.

The paper proposes a coarse-to-fine refinement framework built on a prototype-based Surgical SAM with an HQ-Token and a CRF spatial regularizer, and evaluates it on EndoVis2017, EndoVis2018, and CATARACTS. The reviewers identified four decision-affecting concerns: a numerical inconsistency in the reported mean class IoU on EndoVis2017; missing technical details for the HQ-Token, the two-way transformer, and the IoU-aware mask quality calibration head; the absence of a boundary-aware metric; and the absence of a limitations and failure-mode analysis. The rebuttal acknowledges and corrects the reporting inconsistency, clarifies the protocol explaining the equality between Challenge IoU and standard IoU for the SAM-family competitors, defines previously underspecified components, and commits to a limitations section. Two reviewers moved to Accept after the rebuttal; one maintained Reject, arguing that the integration does not constitute a significant technical contribution. The integration is clean, and after the corrections, the empirical results remain competitive. The camera-ready must implement the table correction, the methodology clarifications, and the protocol footnote.

The rebuttal has been evaluated by 3/4 reviewers with 2 increasing their score to accept and 1 lowering to reject. My opinion is that the aspect of comparison to recent SOTA is a very important one and the validation and metrics used as noted is not comprehensive. My opinion is that the paper is rejected.

This paper introduces CSAM-HQ, a SAM-based surgical tool segmentation framework that combines a learnable high-quality token for boundary refinement with a CRF-based structure-aware optimization stage. The application is clinically relevant and the focus on reducing boundary ambiguity for thin instruments is well motivated.
After rebuttal, three of the four reviewers support acceptance. The authors have corrected the numerical inconsistency in the reported IoU (revised to 62.51% mcIoU), clarified the evaluation protocol, and provided detailed explanations of the HQ-token, the two-way transformer, and the IoU-aware head. The role of the CRF has been reframed as a synergistic spatial regularizer that bridges foundation model semantics with low-level structural consistency, which addresses part of the novelty concern. A limitations section discussing performance trade-offs on large homogeneous surfaces and the CRF latency will be added.
Reviewer #4 continues to recommend rejection, citing limited technical novelty and outdated baselines. While the concern about incremental contribution has some merit, the consistent improvements on a challenging surgical benchmark, the practical integration of coarse-to-fine refinement with CRF post-processing, and the positive assessment by the majority of reviewers justify acceptance.
I recommend accept. For the camera-ready version, the authors must: (1) correct all numerical errors and clearly distinguish standard IoU from Challenge IoU in the evaluation protocol; (2) include the promised limitations discussion on class-specific trade-offs and CRF inference cost; (3) add HD95 or a comparable boundary-sensitive metric if feasible, or explicitly note its absence as a limitation; (4) update Fig. 1 with clear module boundaries and tensor flows; and (5) expand the related work discussion with the suggested recent baselines as committed in the rebuttal.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback. We are encouraged that they recognized the value of adapting foundation models to surgical scenes and our HQ refinement strategy. Below we address the main concerns point by point.
G1: Performance trade-offs and limitations (R1-Q4, R2-Q2, R3-Q1)
Regarding the performance drop on classes such as Ultrasound Probe and the possible prototype bias, this reflects a structural trade-off in our design. Our coarse-to-fine HQ-Token strategy focuses on high-frequency details to recover thin structures and sharp boundaries. However, for large homogeneous surfaces or complex articulated joints, such sensitivity may cause internal fragmentation compared with SurgicalSAM’s prototype-driven smoothing. We will add a “Limitations” section to discuss these trade-offs and the inference latency introduced by CRF.
G2: Evaluation metrics and protocols (R1-Q3/Q5, R2-Q1)
The reported 66.554% mcIoU was a clerical error during result compilation. Our evaluation script, adapted from ISINet, outputs both the arithmetic “Mean Class IoU” and dataset-level “Mean IoU” ((∑I/∑U)). We inadvertently reported the latter and will correct it to 62.51%, matching the arithmetic mean of the reported classes. For fair comparison, we followed SurgicalSAM’s official codebase, which skips false positives for absent classes, resulting in identical standard IoU and Challenge IoU. We will add a footnote to clarify this protocol dependency. We also agree that HD95 can complement overlap scores and will evaluate it in future work.
G3: Methodology details and contributions (R1-Q1/Q2, R4-Q2/Q3/Q4)
Regarding the novelty of the CRF (R4-Q2/Q4), our contribution is not to invent classic dense CRF, but to build a synergistic framework bridging foundation model semantics and low-level structural consistency. In complex surgical scenes with specular reflections, SAM-based models often produce topologically fragmented masks. The learnable HQ-Token improves high-frequency boundary refinement, while CRF serves as a spatial regularizer to reduce internal fragmentation and repair broken thin structures or voids. We will emphasize this integration and rename Sec. 2.3 to “CRF-based Structure-Aware Optimization.” We will also clarify that E_y is minimized only during inference. The “two-way transformer” refers to SAM’s standard cross-attention block, and we will add the appropriate citation. T_HQ is a learnable tensor. In Eq. 2, σ is the sigmoid function, and Φ_upsampled denotes upscaled features. The IoU-aware head is used through the T_iou token to evaluate mask confidence and suppress in-frame noise; the omitted description will be added to Sec. 2.2.G4: Baselines and computational complexity (R1-Q6/Q7, R4-Q5)
Comparisons with recent models S3Net and PartSAM are valuable suggestions. Following the conference policy, we reserve these comparisons for future extensions. However, we will expand Related Work to discuss these methods, including HQ-SAM, while clarifying that HQ-SAM is interactive and prompt-dependent, whereas our framework is automated. Regarding complexity, our parameter efficiency claim refers strictly to learnable parameters (4.65M to 4.99M). We acknowledge the CRF introduces an inference latency, which will be distinguished from training complexity in the revision.
Specific clarifications
a. We will redesign Fig. 1 with clear visual boundaries and colored arrows to indicate the input/output tensors of each module (R4-Q1).
b. We apologize for the manual pasting error in the “Ours” column of Fig. 3 (rows 2/3) and have corrected the alignment (R2-Q3). we will also add the missing textual reference to Fig. 2 in Section 2.3 (R4-Q2).
c. We will correct “Surgical Anything Model” to “Segment Anything Model” (R1-Q1), and list all missing CRF hyperparameters in the Implementation Details (R1-Q8).
We hope this addresses your concerns and clarifies our design, evaluation protocol, and empirical results.

title: CSGE: Break the SSL Bottleneck in Medical Image Segmentation via Collaborative Semantic-Geometric Experts
abstract: Semi-supervised learning for medical image segmentation, particularly within the prevalent Teacher-Student architecture, is frequently hindered by recursive error accumulation and the inherent rigidity of hard-threshold pseudo-labeling. These limitations lead to three critical bottlenecks: semantic-geometric misalignment, chronic confirmation bias, and significant loss of boundary information. To address these, we propose CSGE, a novel paradigm shifting from pseudo-label filtering to collaborative semantic-geometric refinement. CSGE synergistically leverages multimodal medical knowledge and geometric priors. By exploiting semantic cues from the textual modality, BiomedCLIP provides robust semantic anchoring, while SAM serves as a geometric refinement expert. We introduce a Conflict-aware Iterative Co-evolution module that detects discrepancies via XOR operations to drive iterative pseudo-label refinement. Furthermore, we replace hard thresholds with a spatial trust-aware soft-weighted consistency loss to maintain gradient flow within uncertain regions. Evaluated across three modalities (1%–30% labels), CSGE outperforms state-of-the-art methods, notably achieving a 4.9% average Dice improvement under the extreme 1% setting to demonstrate its robustness. Our code is available at https://github.com/yufei050201/CSGE.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs
Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a semi supervised learning framework CSGE that integrates BiomedCLIP for semantic anchoring and SAM for geometric refinement, and introduces conflict aware iterative co evolution and spatial trust awareness to overcome semantic geometric misalignment, confirmation bias, and boundary loss.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper synergizes BiomedCLIP’s semantic anchoring with SAM’s geometric refinement. 
2.It introduces a conflict aware iterative co evolution module that uses XOR based discrepancy detection and iterative prompt resampling to correct boundaries and mitigate confirmation bias in teacher student learning. 
3.The spatial trust awareness optimization replaces hard threshold pseudo label filtering with a soft weighting consistency loss, preserving gradient flow in uncertain regions and enhancing noise robustness.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The framework heavily relies on two external foundation models (BiomedCLIP and SAM), which may limit its practical applicability in resource constrained clinical settings. 
2.The conflict aware iterative co evolution module and spatial trust map introduce additional hyperparameters (e. g. , Gaussian kernel σ and loss weight λ) that require dataset specific tuning, potentially reducing generalizability across diverse medical imaging modalities. 
3.The experimental validation is limited to standard U Net backbones and three public datasets; the paper lacks thorough analysis of multi class segmentation scenarios, cross domain shifts, or comparisons with more recent teacher student SSL methods.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1.How is the conflict aware iterative co evolution module initialized and terminated? 
2.Does the spatial trust map create circular dependency between the teacher and the pseudo label? 
3.What is the computational overhead of integrating BiomedCLIP and SAM into the teacher student pipeline?

The framework introduces several design choices that raise technical concerns. First, the conflict aware iterative co evolution module detects discrepancies via XOR operation on binarized predictions (teacher pseudo label vs. SAM mask), which discards uncertainty information and may amplify noise in early training stages. Second, the spatial trust map uses the Dice similarity between the teacher’s soft prediction and the final pseudo label as a global trust weight, potentially creating a circular dependency, since the pseudo label itself is partly derived from the teacher, this could reinforce existing biases rather than providing independent reliability quantification. Third, the method relies on pre computed gScoreCAM saliency maps from BiomedCLIP to define regions of interest, but these offline saliency maps are static and do not adapt to the student’s evolving representations, limiting dynamic refinement. Additionally, the loss formulation includes both an L2 consistency loss (L_con ) between student and teacher outputs and a spatially weighted unsupervised loss (L_unlabel ) against the refined pseudo label; the paper does not analyze potential conflicts or redundancy between these two supervisory signals.
The experiments are confined to three 2D binary segmentation datasets (chest X ray, polyp, dermoscopic images) with no evaluation on 3D medical volumes (e.g., CT, MRI) or multi class segmentation tasks, which would better reflect real world clinical complexity. While the authors claim the framework is architecture agnostic, the main results only use a standard U Net backbone; the extension analysis briefly mentions MedSAM and SAM3 but provides no quantitative comparison or ablation on other segmentation networks (e.g., Swin UNETR, nnU Net). The paper reports average Dice/IoU over three random seeds but omits standard deviations or statistical significance tests, making it difficult to assess the robustness of the claimed 4.9% average improvement. Furthermore, the comparison with state of the art methods is incomplete, Table 1 is referenced but not shown in the provided excerpt, and no implementation details or hyperparameter tuning for competing methods are disclosed. Finally, despite claiming lightweight inference, the paper provides no runtime, memory footprint, or parameter count analysis for integrating two large foundation models (BiomedCLIP and SAM) into a teacher student pipeline, which is critical for assessing clinical deployability.
