reviews.text_contribution: Anomaly detection of brain lesions is critical for supporting neurological disease diagnosis and surgical planning. This study proposes DDecomp, which is based on masked autoencoders trained on healthy data and decomposes predictive uncertainty into the epistemic component for unsupervised anomaly detection. The method was validated on different datasets for different lesion types.
reviews.text_strengths:
The decomposition of the epistemic component for unsupervised anomaly detection is interesting
Different lesion types have been included for comprehensive evaluation
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The methods considered for comparison were too limited
The selected evaluation metrics were not sufficient
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The method is not necessarily restricted to diffusion MRI. It can be directly applied to other MRI modalities. Please discuss.
The claim that the epistemic component is more suitable for anomaly detection should be supported with experimental evidence.
The major concern about this work is the lack of comparison with state-of-the-art methods. There are numerous unsupervised anomaly detection methods that can be applied to the tasks in this paper. For example, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.media.2019.01.010, https://proceedings.mlr.press/v172/kascenas22a.html, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-04965-0_43, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-96625-5_1, and many others.
To be clinically useful, the anomaly scores need to be converted to binary lesion masks. However, the proposed method does not address this problem. There are no Dice coefficients or distance measures available to evaluate the accuracy of lesion boundaries. The clinical relevance remains to be justified.
Since MC sampling is used, the computation efficiency should also be evaluated.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The two major factors that led to my original recommendation are not addressed:
1) It is not clear how F3 is computed and what it represents. The selection of \beta=3 is not justified. Also, threshold selection is challenging, yet it is unknown how it was performed for each method. Thus, it is still not convincing that this method can lead to good segmentation accuracy.
2) The two methods selected for comparison were insufficient. They are not the common ones used for comparison by existing literature.
Therefore, the advantage of the proposed method has not been adequately demonstrated by the experiments, and I stick to my original recommendation.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper describes a method for mapping anomalous / out-of-distribution regions in images after learning from a population of images from ostensibly healthy subjects. The paper focusses specifically on diffusion MRI and uses the HCP data set for training. The authors aim to separate aleatoric uncertainty (from noise etc) from epistemic uncertainty (inherent to the data) and map regions of high epistemic uncertainty as indicative of signals that do not arise in the training data and thus likely to represent pathological tissue.
reviews.text_strengths:
The idea has good novelty (at least I haven’t seen normative modelling and abnormality detection done this way)
I particularly like the idea of inferring the posterior on the mask by treating it as a nuisance variable.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
I don’t fully understand why high epistemic uncertainty necessarily corresponds to abnormality. There may be very common signal combinations for which epistemic uncertainty is high (e.g. where many signal combinations map to the same diffusion parameters).
Not necessarily a weakness but a question: the HCP data set is predominantly “healthy” but pathologies certainly exist and are visible in the images (the website provides lists and locations). Are these excluded from training or is the training robust to modest inclusion of “abnormal” signals? If the trained model were then applied to the training data, does it pick up such abnormalities?
The Discussion is thin. No mention or acknowledgement of limitations / further work etc, which should be corrected.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I’m not 100% on this as there are certainly queries, but I like the idea and the work seems to have high novelty.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I still like this work. It does have some limitations but some nice ideas in there too so I think worthy of acceptance. I’m leaving my score as it is.

meta_reviews.text:
This manuscript proposes a masked autoencoder based framework for anomaly detection in diffusion MRI that decomposes predictive uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic components. Reviewers thought that this was an interesting and innovative approach to a relevant and challenging problem, and yielded promising qualitative results. However, they also raised a number of concerns that are too serious to directly recommend acceptance. It would be helpful if authors could comment on them in their rebuttal, keeping in mind that no new results are permitted at this point: 1.All reviewers questioned how helpful and reliable the separation between aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty really is for separating lesions from other abnormalities such as image artifacts. They thought that this was not demonstrated clearly enough. 2.The accuracy of the proposed approach as a lesion segmentation tool has not been quantified, and reviewers missed a comparison to multiple plausible baselines for anomaly detection. 3.It is unclear how abnormalities in the HCP training data have been handled. 4.The sources and characteristics of the clinical data used in this work are not sufficiently transparent. 5.Reviewers expressed doubt that, without making source code available, it will be possible to reproduce this work. 6.It is not clear why the authors focus on diffusion MRI, since the method should be more widely applicable.

Some limitations remain after rebuttal and should be clearly stated in the final version of the paper, in particular, assumptions regarding image quality that underlie the proposed separation between aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty, and assumptions regarding effects of training data contamination being negligible. Concerns regarding reproducibility have been addressed by promising the release of code and model weights along with the paper. Authors are encouraged to include additional information about selection of anomaly score threshold and stability of results w.r.t. this choice, which is a major remaining concern. Despite this, I agree with the positive reviewer majority vote after rebuttal.

The uncertainty decomposition idea is genuinely novel and the dMRI application is well-motivated. However, the UAD field offers a substantial number of directly applicable methods and situating the contribution in this context is not optional. Adding baseline comparisons requires only additional rows in a table and deferring this to a journal extension is not an appropriate rebuttal response. The claimed improvements cannot be properly assessed without this context. Additionally, no dataset information is provided beyond lesion type, including sources, demographics, or acquisition protocols. This is feasible even under anonymity and its absence makes it impossible to assess generalizability, site bias, or protocol dependence for a method that explicitly claims robustness across these factors.

I am choosing to accept this paper, but I do agree with one of the points raised by R2, that the experimental baselines are disappointing. Still, it is innovative and interesting, and with 2 vs 1 it becomes editorial choice.

author_feedback_text:
Uncertainty Separation (R1–3, AC): We apologize for confusion over how to separate lesions from image artifacts. Our method first estimates total uncertainty, then decomposes it into epistemic and aleatoric components via variance analysis of MC sampling and heteroscedasticity modeling. Epistemic uncertainty (measured as variance of predictive means across MC-dropout and masked samples) captures OOD from the healthy training distribution, e.g., pathological lesions with rare anatomical patterns. Image artifacts (e.g., protocol shifts, noise, and signal combinations) also shift test data from the training data characteristics, but these commonly exist across visible and masked tokens in MAE during inference, which will be captured by our heteroscedastic likelihood computation. Thus, the two uncertainties can be separated for epistemic lesion identification. Our comparison with MAE-UAD and DDEvENet shows that separating these uncertainties largely improves the identification. But, we acknowledge that our method relies on high-quality processed data and QC to exclude failures. Otherwise, severe imaging artifacts (e.g., reconstruction failures) may be recognized as epistemic OOD.
Segmentation Accuracy & UAD Comparison (R2, AC): (1) We will clarify that Fβ (Tab. 1) quantifies segmentation accuracy by measuring the similarity between binary lesion masks (by thresholding the anomaly scores) and manual segmentation. (2) Due to space limit, our current work compared two most relevant approaches: MAE-UAD (a reconstruction-error method from the same MAE family as ours) and DDEvENet (an uncertainty estimation method designed for dMRI on the same task and data as ours). We agree that including more UAD methods will strengthen our evaluation, and will expand to discuss these work and include comparisons in future journal extension.
Abnormalities in Training (R3, AC): We confirm that no cases were excluded due to pathologies during training, and acknowledge that incidental abnormalities may be present when learning the healthy population normative model. As such cases are rare and spatially sparse relative to normal whole‑brain tissue, they will cause limited contamination rather than deviating the learned normative model. Moreover, our random masking design further prevents such contamination because abnormal regions form a small fraction of visible token targets. The heteroscedastic likelihood will also assign higher variance to such isolated high-residual observations, reducing their effects on the learned mean. Identifying such cases in the training set would require further investigation into abnormal data characteristics, which is beyond the scope of this work. But we believe these abnormalities would be detected as they lie outside the learned normative distribution.
Data Transparency and Code (R1, AC): Due to the anonymous policy, we did not include source of our in‑house clinical data. Upon acceptance, we will add data details, including demographics and clinical characteristics. Further, we confirm that the code and trained weights will be released.
Beyond dMRI (R2, AC): AC and R2 are correct that our method can be generally applied to other modalities. We will clarify that it is a general uncertainty-decomposition framework, not task-specific. This work focuses on dMRI as it’s a natural application for separating aleatoric variability from epistemic OOD response due to its inherent variation from acquisitions, scanner differences, and microstructural pathology.
Computation Efficiency (R2): Our method requires K (# of random masks, 100) x T (# of MC-dropout samples, 10) forward passes for inference, which takes ~2 min per subject.
Expanded Discussion (R3): As suggested, we will expand Discussion to include limitations regarding severe artifact effects, reliance on high-quality processed data, potential abnormalities in the training data, and future work on testing beyond dMRI as well as comparisons with more UAD methods.

title: DD-INR: Dynamics-Driven Implicit Neural Representation for Accelerated Whole-Brain Functional MRI Reconstruction
abstract: Accelerated acquisition of fMRI enables enhanced detection of neurovascular (BOLD) activity in the brain, but image reconstruction becomes challenging with high k-space undersampling: Task-evoked BOLD signals are small in magnitude, which traditional anatomical MRI reconstruction methods fail to recover, as they favor spatial accuracy over temporal fidelity. We present DD-INR, a \emph{D}ynamics-\emph{D}riven \emph{I}mplicit \emph{N}eural \emph{R}epresentation framework tailored for accelerated fMRI that benefits from incoherent time-varying sampling and a tailored spatio-temporal prior, outperforming traditional methods, demonstrated in simulation and in-vivo acquisition, both in terms of image quality and retrieval of activation patterns.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes an INR-based reconstruction method for accelerated task fMRI. The signal is decomposed into a static background, estimated from temporally aggregated measurements, and a dynamic component represented by an INR with spatial or spatiotemporal regularization. The goal is to focus the reconstruction on the weak task-related BOLD fluctuations rather than the time-invariant anatomical background.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in accelerated fMRI. The basic modeling choice is appropriate for this setting: the dominant signal is largely static, whereas the quantity of interest is a much smaller dynamic component. Estimating the background separately and reserving the INR for the dynamic residual is therefore a reasonable design. The method is organized clearly at a high level, and the regularization imposed on the dynamic term is appropriate for task fMRI. The simulation results are encouraging, and within the comparison set included in the paper, the proposed method improves the reported activation maps and time-series metrics.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper gives the impression of introducing a new reconstruction framework for accelerated fMRI, but the underlying ideas are closer to existing work than the manuscript acknowledges. The separation of slowly varying background structure from a smaller dynamic component is already established in accelerated fMRI and dynamic MRI reconstruction. Petrov et al. used a low-rank plus sparse model for accelerated fMRI, including prospective experiments, and Chiew et al. incorporated task-related temporal information directly into highly accelerated fMRI reconstruction through a constrained low-rank model. More broadly, INR-based reconstruction for dynamic MRI is already an active direction. I would therefore encourage the authors to position the paper more narrowly, as an INR-based implementation of a background-plus-dynamic strategy for accelerated fMRI.
Several key quantities are introduced with less precision than one would expect in a methodological paper. The notation around (f_\theta) is not defined carefully enough when first introduced, and the construction of the background estimate (\hat{x}
{bg}) through (A
{1:T}^{\dagger}y_{1:T}) remains largely intuitive. The idea itself is acceptable, but the operator, the temporal aggregation step, and the underlying assumptions should be stated more explicitly.
The numerical results are favorable, but the qualitative evidence is more limited than the wording suggests. In Fig. 3, the recovered curves are improved relative to the noisier baselines, but they still do not follow the expected response especially closely in an absolute sense. I would therefore encourage the authors to moderate the stronger claims about the accurate recovery of amplitude and phase.
The paper would benefit from a more direct discussion of downstream fMRI inference. In this area, image quality alone is not the decisive criterion. Prior work has already noted that nonlinear reconstruction can affect temporal correlations, effective degrees of freedom, and statistical sensitivity. That point deserves more careful treatment here.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
I think the paper is built around a relevant idea, and I agree with the decision to distinguish the dominant background from the much weaker dynamic signal. My main recommendation is to sharpen how the work is presented. In my view, the contribution is best described as an INR-based implementation of a background-plus-dynamic reconstruction strategy for accelerated fMRI, rather than as a fundamentally new reconstruction framework. The paper would be stronger with a more precise formulation of the method, especially the notation around (f_\theta), the definition of (\hat{x}_{bg}), and the optimization problem being solved. I would also encourage a more direct discussion of the closest fMRI-specific prior work and a more careful treatment of how the reconstruction may affect downstream statistical analysis.

The paper addresses a worthwhile problem and is based on a coherent modeling idea. However, I do not think the current version makes a sufficiently strong case for acceptance as a methodological contribution. The main reason is that the conceptual ingredients of the method are closer to existing fMRI and dynamic MRI reconstruction work than the manuscript presently indicates. In addition, the formulation needs to be stated with greater precision, some of the claims are stronger than the qualitative evidence supports, and the in vivo validation is limited.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper introduces an INR-based framework for fMRI reconstruction from accelerated acquisition. There are two main contributions. First, the paper introduces an additive model for fMRI data, which consists of the static background component plus a temporally varying dynamic component. By explicitly modeling the background as static, i.e., constant across dynamics, INR only need to focus on modeling the temporally varying component. Second, two regularization methods are proposed. The authors demonstrate that the two regularization methods results in improved agreement of the ROI-averaged time series with ground truth despite the fact that little or no temporal model/prior is imposed.
little model/prior is imposed in the temporal domain
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Heuristically, modeling fMRI data as a static background component plus a temporally varying dynamic component makes a lot of sense, similar to residual learning, or the low-rank plus sparse (L+S) reconstruction approach. The authors argue that such a decomposition allows the INR to focus its capacity on modeling the dynamic component as opposed to repeatedly learning the static background component. 
2.The authors provide a strong justification for their choice to do Fourier feature embedding separately in space and time. Specifically, their justification for this is two-fold, i.e., reducing number of total parameters and the ability to allocate different bandwidths for spatial versus temporal features.
3.The authors perform extensive evaluation on both simulated data where a ground truth is available, and on data acquired in vivo. This includes quantitative (Table 1) and qualitative (Figs. 2 and 3) evaluations against ground truth when using the simulated data, and also qualitative evaluation when using in vivo data. 
4.Finally, it is non-trivial that the proposed regularization works well. The proposed regularization does NOT explicitly assume a hand-crafted model for the temporal signals across dynamics. It only encourages neighboring voxels to have similar temporal patterns.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper is already very clear and well-written although additional details can be incorporated during revision to further improve the clarity and highlight the contribution of this work.
1.For readers not familiar with INR, it might be unclear (until later in the paper) that the method does not require training on a carefully curated dataset but instead works on a single subject. Consider clarifying or maybe briefly highlighting this in the abstract and introduction so that the readers can better appreciate this work.
2.At the bottom of page 3, it is unclear how \hat{x}
{bg} is estimated. Later in the paper, the authors explain that \hat{x}
{bg} is obtained from temporally aggregated measurement. Is the (k, t)-space data temporally aggregated first into 3D k-space without the temporal dimension? Or is it the case that a least-squares problem is solved assuming the underlying image to be reconstructed is temporally static?
3.At the top of page 4, the authors presents two regularizers in (3) but only introduces the latter one, i.e., “spatially regularize the temporal derivative”. It might be helpful to at least briefly describe the former one as well. 
4.Why does the image contrast differ across different methods in Fig. 2? Is it because of scaling during visualization?
5.In Table 1, it might be helpful to also compute and report tSNR. It helps to make the claim that the proposed method improves temporal stability.
6.In Fig. 4, the reconstructed image for PnP looks over regularized in the spatial domain. Is the regularization parameter for PnP properly tuned?
7.In the discussion, the authors attempt to explain the different behaviors of spatiotemporal vs spatial regularizations. However, the discussion does NOT explain why R_{xyz} results in more temporal smoothing whereas R_{xyz, t} results in less temporal smoothing in Fig. 3.It might be helpful to include more in-depth discussion about this behavior in the discussion section.
There is one technical question though. When using INR for 3D+t MRI reconstruction, it is reasonable (and in fact common) to assume that the underlying 3D+t data satisfies certain regularity condition in both space and time, e.g., spatiotemporally continuous. In the current formulation (static background + dynamic), does the regularity condition still holds after removing the static background. There is no issue with regularity in the temporal domain because temporally a constant is removed and adding/subtracting a constant doesn’t change the regularity of the underlying function. However, there might be an issue in the spatial domain. Say the static background reconstruction is not perfect and there are artifact in the estimated static background \hat{x}
{bg} which introduces spatial discontinuities. In this case, even if it is assumed that the 3D+t fMRI data is continuous, the dynamic component to be modeled using INR is NOT spatially continuous because of the spatial discontinuity in \hat{x}
{bg}.
One small limitation of the work is that joint reconstruction is performed across all dynamics, making it hard to apply this method for real time fMRI applications.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
There are some typos and aesthetic issues that should be addressed during revision.
1.At the bottom of page 3, there is a \hat missing from \hat{x}_{bg}.
2.At the bottom of page 5, there is a subscript missing (F_2 instead of F2).
3.Fig. 2.The color bar is hard to see. The black background of the text box is aesthetically unpleasing. I am also have trouble finding where the blue arrows are.

The method is sound and the evaluation is extensive with both simulation and in vivo experiments. The contribution of decomposing fMRI data into a static background component plus a temporally varying dynamic component makes sense and is novel. The proposed regularization methods are also sound. A score of 5 is given instead of 6 because both contributions are quite standard.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: DD-INR is an INR framework for accelerated 3D+time fMRI reconstruction. The key design is a signal factorization into a static background (reconstructed via conjugate gradient from temporally aggregated k-space) and a dynamic component modeled by a SIREN with decoupled spatial/temporal Fourier feature embeddings. The dynamic component is regularized using TV on the spatial gradient of the temporal derivative, computed via autodifferentiation. Evaluated on simulated (SNAKE) and in vivo (single subject, visual block design) data against NUFFT, CG, CS, PnP, and a generic INR baseline.
reviews.text_strengths: The problem framing is sharp and well-motivated: BOLD signals are 2–5% intensity fluctuations superimposed on a strong static background, and dedicating INR capacity exclusively to the dynamic residual is a principled design choice. The use of autodifferentiation to compute the temporal derivative for regularization is elegant and technically clean. The comparison against PnP-fMRI (a strong domain-specific baseline) strengthens the evaluation. Both simulation with ground-truth activation maps and in vivo results are provided, with appropriate fMRI-specific metrics (F2-score, GLM z-score maps, BOLD time-series correlation). The performance gap over baselines is large and consistent — Corr of 0.909 vs. 0.84 for PnP and 0.40 for generic INR is a meaningful improvement.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Single subject in vivo evaluation.
The in vivo experiment involves one healthy volunteer with a single task paradigm (visual block design). This is insufficient to assess generalizability across subjects, tasks, motion levels, or scanner variability. The simulation compensates partially but uses a simplified phantom (white/gray matter/CSF only), which may not capture the full complexity of real fMRI noise.
2.Static background assumption is fragile.
The background is estimated once from temporally aggregated measurements and frozen throughout reconstruction. This is violated by head motion, physiological noise (cardiac/respiratory fluctuations), and slow scanner drifts — all common in fMRI. The discussion acknowledges motion but dismisses it without quantitative analysis. No experiment tests robustness under varying motion levels.
3.Reconstruction time is prohibitive for practical use.
~2 hours per scan on an RTX 6000 GPU is noted as “comparable to traditional methods” — but this is not accurate for clinical or large-scale research use. Standard CS fMRI reconstruction is typically minutes, not hours. This severely limits the practical appeal of the method, and no analysis of the computational bottleneck or potential speedups is provided beyond attributing cost to NUFFT.
4.Hyperparameter sensitivity is uncharacterized.
The regularization weights (λ = 10⁻² and 2×10⁻³), warm-up schedule, Fourier embedding dimensions (Bxyz ∈ R²⁵⁶ˣ³, Bt ∈ R⁶⁴), and network width (512) are all fixed without ablation. Given the sensitivity of SIREN-based methods to initialization and frequency parameters, and the critical role of λ in balancing data fidelity vs. regularization for weak BOLD signals, this is a significant gap.
5.No resting-state fMRI evaluation.
The method is evaluated only on task-based fMRI with a simple block design — the easiest possible activation pattern to recover. Resting-state fMRI (functional connectivity, default mode network) involves weaker, less structured temporal fluctuations and represents the majority of clinical and research fMRI use. No discussion of applicability to this setting is provided.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The problem formulation is well-motivated and technically sound. The performance gains over all baselines — including a domain-specific PnP method — are substantial and consistent across simulation and in vivo settings. The core idea of dynamics-centric INR factorization is a genuine contribution to accelerated fMRI reconstruction. The main weaknesses are limited in vivo evaluation scope, uncharacterized hyperparameter sensitivity, and the 2-hour reconstruction time which limits practical utility. These are addressable in a revision but would benefit from author response on the robustness and scalability points.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text:
The reviewers see the paper as a well-motivated idea: separating static background from weak dynamic BOLD signals lets the INR focus on what matters, and this yields strong, consistent gains with convincing fMRI-specific evaluation.
There were concerns about validation (single subject, simple task), assumptions like static background may break under motion, reconstruction is slow, and downstream statistical reliability and robustness remain underexplored.
The paper would raise good discussion in MICCAI. The authors should discuss and address them in the final version.

title: DEC-Net: A Multi-Task Distillation Expert Collaboration Network for Glioma Grading and Molecular Subtyping Using Multimodal MRI
abstract: Glioma grading and molecular subtyping are challenging due to significant intratumoral heterogeneity and inter-task interference in multi-task learning settings. Existing multi-task learning approaches often fail to effectively disentangle shared and task-specific representations, limiting their ability to capture complex biological patterns. To address these issues, we propose the Distillation Expert Collaboration Network (DEC-Net), which comprises two key modules. First, a Distillation ResModule utilizes a knowledge distillation mechanism to guide a ResNet backbone in learning discriminative multimodal representations from tumor-relevant regions. Second, a Progressive Mixture-of-Experts module hierarchically integrates shared and task-specific experts, enabling layer-wise adaptation of representation spaces to mitigate inter-task interference. Furthermore, a multi-task dependency loss is introduced to explicitly model the biological correlation between glioma grades and subtypes, thereby improving prediction consistency. Extensive experiments conducted on a large hybrid cohort comprising UCSF-PDGM and EGD datasets, along with external validation on the TCGA dataset, demonstrate that DEC-Net achieves superior performance and robust generalization compared with state-of-the-art methods for non-invasive glioma diagnosis.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper proposes DEC‑Net, a Distillation Expert Collaboration Network for joint glioma grading and molecular subtyping from multimodal MRI. The framework integrates three complementary components: (1) a Distillation ResModule (DRModule) that employs an anomaly‑guided teacher-student mechanism to focus learning on tumor‑relevant regions; (2) a Progressive Mixture‑of‑Experts (PMoE) module that balances shared and task‑specific representation learning to mitigate inter‑task interference; and (3) a Dependency Loss (D‑Loss) that explicitly models biological correlations between grade, IDH mutation, and 1p/19q status. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets (UCSF‑PDGM, EGD, and TCGA) show improved AUCs and accuracy over previous CNN‑based multi‑task baselines, with consistent external‑test performance demonstrating good generalizability.
The integration of anomaly‑guided distillation and biologically informed dependency modeling is interesting and moderately novel. While the DRModule and PMoE build on existing ideas, the D‑Loss provides a distinctive, biologically meaningful regularization contribution.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper is clearly written, logically organized, and experimentally thorough. The authors evaluate on both internal and external cohorts and provide ablation studies confirming the contribution of each module. The method’s performance remains strong under domain shift, suggesting good robustness.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Some methodological details could be clarified, for example, the rationale for center cropping (which may exclude boundary information) and whether inference used patch aggregation or whole‑volume prediction. 
The paper does not discuss its own limitations, and recent transformer‑ and foundation‑based multimodal approaches are omitted from comparison.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This is a technically solid and well‑motivated study that advances multi‑task glioma classification through thoughtful module design and strong validation. The paper is sufficiently novel, clearly presented, and experimentally convincing.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I maintained my acceptance recommendation because the paper’s strengths outweigh its limitations, and the concerns raised in the initial review were sufficiently clarified in the rebuttal or left as reasonable directions for future work.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes DEC-Net, a unified multi-task framework for jointly predicting glioma grading and molecular subtypes from multimodal MRI, aiming to address inter-task interference while leveraging shared representations. It introduces a progressive mixture-of-experts module to balance shared and task-specific feature learning, enabling more effective multi-task optimization. In addition, the method incorporates a dependency-aware loss to explicitly model the biological correlations among tasks, encouraging more consistent and clinically plausible predictions.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Strong Empirical Performance
The proposed method demonstrates consistent performance improvements over existing approaches on both internal and external datasets. Notably, the model maintains its advantage even under domain shift, suggesting a certain level of robustness and generalization capability.
2.Public Availability of Code
The authors provide publicly available code, which enhances the reproducibility of the work and facilitates future research building upon this method.
3.Comprehensive Ablation Study
The paper includes a thorough ablation study evaluating the contribution of each proposed component. This analysis helps demonstrate that the individual modules are complementary and collectively contribute to the overall performance improvement.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Insufficient Analysis of Expert Routing Dynamics 
While the model successfully separates shared and task-specific experts, an in-depth analysis of their individual contributions is lacking. Providing a more granular investigation into how these experts are utilized across different tasks, along with an interpretability analysis of the routing mechanism, would significantly strengthen the justification for this architectural design.
2.Architectural Complexity and Presentation Clarity 
The proposed framework integrates multiple intricate modules, resulting in a relatively complex architecture that can be challenging to follow. While space limitations are acknowledged, a more streamlined explanation or supplementary visualizations detailing the data flow through these key components would greatly improve the paper’s readability and reproducibility.
3.Limited Scope of Baseline Comparisons 
The current experimental comparisons are primarily restricted to multi-task learning (MTL) methods. To comprehensively evaluate the proposed approach, the authors should include strong single-task baselines or more recent state-of-the-art architectures. This would rigorously demonstrate whether the performance gains stem from the multi-task synergy itself rather than merely the overall model capacity.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper tackles a crucial clinical challenge with a well-designed multi-task framework (DEC-Net). The major factors driving my positive score are the model’s strong, consistent empirical performance across both internal and external datasets (demonstrating impressive robustness to domain shift), the thorough ablation study, and the provision of public code for reproducibility.
However, I am leaning toward a Weak Accept rather than a Strong Accept due to a few analytical and structural limitations:
1.Lack of deep analysis: The paper needs a more granular, interpretability-focused analysis of how the PMoE routing dynamically allocates shared and task-specific experts.
2.Presentation clarity: The architecture is quite complex, and the manuscript would benefit from a more streamlined explanation or clearer visual flow of the components.
3.Missing single-task baselines: Comparing only against other multi-task methods leaves it unclear whether the performance gains stem from true multi-task synergy or simply an increase in overall model capacity.
Overall, despite these gaps in baseline comparisons and interpretability, the robust experimental results, public availability, and significant clinical potential make this paper a valuable contribution to the field.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I appreciate the authors’ clear and concise rebuttal. My previous concerns regarding the limited baseline comparisons and the lack of expert routing dynamics have been sufficiently addressed with the newly provided single-task performance results and the specific shared/task-specific routing ratios. I am satisfied with these clarifications and happily confirm my final decision to Accept this paper.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose DEC-Net, a multi-task deep learning framework for joint glioma grading and molecular subtyping from multimodal preoperative MRI (T1, T1ce, T2, FLAIR). The framework comprises three components: (i) a Distillation ResModule (DRModule) in which an EMA-updated teacher branch, gated by a spatial discrepancy map obtained from an unsupervised anomaly-detection pre-training stage, distils multi-scale features into a student ResNet; (ii) a Progressive Mixture-of-Experts (PMoE) module with shared and task-specific experts and per-task softmax gating under dense routing, stacked across L layers; and (iii) a Dependency Loss (D-Loss) derived from an empirical class-conditional co-occurrence matrix P computed on the training set, intended to encode biological correlations among the three tasks. Training uses focal loss combined with D-Loss and the distillation loss, with fixed balancing coefficients. Evaluation is performed via 5-fold cross-validation on a combined UCSF-PDGM + EGD internal cohort and held-out external testing on TCGA-GBM/LGG, benchmarked against nine multi-task glioma methods using AUC and accuracy. Anonymised source code is provided.
reviews.text_strengths:
Clinically meaningful joint formulation. Non-invasive preoperative prediction of glioma grade together with IDH mutation and 1p/19q co-deletion is of genuine clinical value, and jointly modelling the three tasks respects the biological coupling among the canonical diagnostic categories.
Substantial multi-centre cohort with a genuinely held-out external test set. Training and cross-validation span two institutions (UCSF-PDGM and EGD, total n=1,214), and TCGA-GBM/LGG (n=167) is used exclusively as an external cohort. Many prior works report single-centre results only, and it enables a meaningful assessment of domain shift.
External-test generalisation. On TCGA, DEC-Net leads the best competing baseline. Several baselines (e.g., MTAFNet, MFEFNet, MLNet) experience substantial AUC drops under domain shift, whereas DEC-Net degrades more gracefully. The relative ranking of methods also changes between internal and external evaluation, which is consistent with a genuine test of generalisation.
Complete module ablation. Table 3 enumerates all eight on/off combinations of DRModule, PMoE, and D-Loss rather than the more common single-leave-one-out design.
Reproducibility. Preprocessing is specified (SRI24 co-registration, 1 mm isotropic resampling, skull-stripping, z-score normalisation), optimiser (AdamW), learning rate (1e-4), batch size (8), epoch count (100), and loss weights (alpha=0.3, beta=0.1) are all reported. An anonymised code repository is linked.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.No statistical significance testing. Table 2 reports mean and standard deviation across cross-validation folds, but no paired statistical test (DeLong for AUC, McNemar for accuracy, or paired Wilcoxon on fold-level scores) is provided. Several internal-test “wins” fall within one standard deviation of the runner-up. Without paired testing, the claim of “consistently outperforms SOTA” on the internal cohort is not empirically supported.
2.Handling of a large fraction of Unknown labels is not stated, with a plausible confound in the D-Loss. Table 1 shows that IDH status is Unknown for 42% of EGD and 11% of TCGA, and 1p/19q status is Unknown for 68% of EGD and 18% of UCSF-PDGM. The paper does not state how these cases are handled during training and evaluation. This matters on two fronts. First, the effective per-task labelled sample sizes are materially smaller than the headline n=1,214; for 1p/19q in particular the labelled pool may be well below 700.Second, if P is estimated only from fully-labelled patients, it is computed on a biased subsample.
3.Unspecified fold stratification. UCSF-PDGM and EGD are acquired on different scanners and protocols. A random patient-level split mixes sites across train and validation folds, which allows the model to exploit site-specific cues (residual intensity distributions, etc.) and can inflate internal-test metrics. The paper does not state whether folds are patient-level only, site-stratified, or class-stratified, nor does it report per-fold site composition.
4.Unverified fairness of the nine SOTA baselines is unverified. The paper does not state whether the baselines were re-implemented in-house, whether they were trained under the same preprocessing pipeline, input size (128×128×128), modality set, and augmentation, whether they received the same hyperparameter-tuning budget, or how they handle Unknown labels. Several baselines (MTTU-Net, MDLNet, CMTLNet, MTAFNet, MLNet) are multi-task glioma methods whose original publications use different cohorts and label subsets. Simple re-implementation could systematically disadvantage them.
5.Methodological novelty is incremental. The EMA teacher-student mechanism is the Mean Teacher scheme of Tarvainen and Valpola (NeurIPS 2017) not the cited reference [27] which is a 2025 application paper. Progressive Layered Extraction (PLE) is not cited or contrasted. The D-Loss is a label-correlation regulariser from the multi-label classification literature. The paper’s contribution is therefore the combination applied to joint glioma profiling, which is a legitimate application-style contribution, but the current framing presents each component as novel without acknowledging the closest prior art.
6.Unexplained interactions in the ablation. In Table 3, the “PMoE + D-Loss” configuration underperforms “D-Loss only” on Grade AUC (91.68 vs 92.63) and 1p/19q AUC (82.37 vs 84.77), while the full three-module model then jumps to 95.11 and 85.45 respectively. This is a super-additive effect that is not discussed.
7.No calibration or operating-point analysis. For a method positioned to “support precise clinical decision-making”, calibration and a sensitivity-at-fixed-specificity table would strengthen the clinical framing.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Table 2 header: “Interal Test” should read “Internal Test”.
Preprocessing omits N4 bias-field correction, which is standard for harmonising multi-site brain MRI. Worth commenting on whether this was tested and found not to help, or simply omitted.
Reference [27] (EMA) cites a 2025 self-distillation paper rather than Tarvainen, Antti, and Harri Valpola. “Mean teachers are better role models: Weight-averaged consistency targets improve semi-supervised deep learning results.” Advances in neural information processing systems 30 (2017)., which is the canonical reference. Consider adding the original source.
The claim that DRModule “preserves deployment efficiency” would be strengthened by a FLOPs and parameter-count comparison against the plain student backbone, since the teacher is used only at training time.
Rebuttal questions (to focus the authors’ response):
Q1.How are Unknown IDH (EGD 42%, TCGA 11%) and Unknown 1p/19q (EGD 68%, UCSF 18%) cases treated during training, during evaluation, and importantly during estimation of the conditional matrix P in Eq. 8? What are the effective per-task labelled sample sizes?
Q2.CV stratification: are the five folds patient-stratified only, or also site-stratified across UCSF-PDGM and EGD? Please provide per-fold site composition.

The paper addresses a clinically meaningful problem (non-invasive joint prediction of glioma grade, IDH mutation, and 1p/19q co-deletion) on a larger-than-typical multi-centre cohort with a genuinely held-out external test set. The external-test margins over strong multi-task baselines are the most convincing part of the empirical case, and the ablation design is above the typical standard.
The paper falls short of the acceptance threshold on four grounds.
First, no statistical significance testing is provided despite several internal-test wins that fall within one standard deviation of the runner-up. Paired DeLong and McNemar tests on existing fold-level scores would substantially strengthen the case and are answerable in the rebuttal.
Second, handling of the large Unknown-label fractions is not stated. This affects both the effective training sample size and more seriously the estimation of the conditional probability matrix P in Eq. 8, which is the core of the proposed D-Loss. If Unknowns are dropped from P estimation, the prior is computed on a biased subsample and this bias propagates into every gradient update.
Third, the 5-fold CV stratification on the combined UCSF-PDGM + EGD cohort is not specified. Multi-site MRI with random patient-level splits carries non-negligible site-leakage risk, and without site-stratified or leave-one-site-out evidence the internal-test margins cannot be cleanly interpreted as generalisation rather than site exploitation.
Fourth, methodological novelty is incremental: the EMA teacher-student scheme is Mean Teacher, PMoE closely tracks Progressive Layered Extraction (PLE which was not cited), and D-Loss is a standard label-correlation regulariser. The combination applied to joint glioma profiling is a legitimate application-style contribution, but the current framing presents each component as novel.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The two most structurally serious concerns raised in my initial review have been addressed to a satisfactory degree. The authors confirmed that samples with Unknown labels were excluded from training, evaluation, and P-matrix estimation, and provided the effective per-task labelled sample sizes (Grade n=1,166; IDH n=910; 1p/19q n=632). The confirmation that 5-fold cross-validation is site-stratified across UCSF-PDGM and EGD substantially mitigates the site-leakage concern I had raised. Combined with the genuinely held-out TCGA external test set, the validation design is now sufficiently credible.
The authors also report that DeLong and McNemar tests were conducted, with p < 0.05 for several AUC comparisons and all ACC comparisons against baselines. While these figures are not present in the submitted manuscript, the directional claim is plausible given the fold-level standard deviations in Table 2.
Concerns that remain unresolved: the super-additive ablation interaction between PMoE and D-Loss is not discussed; the EMA/Mean Teacher and PLE citations were promised but are not in the submitted manuscript; and calibration figures on the external cohort are absent. These are appropriate targets for the camera-ready revision.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper proposes a multi-sequence MRI-based framework for glioma grading and molecular subtyping. However, the overall architecture appears overly complex, while only marginal improvements are observed compared with existing methods. To capture tumor-relevant regions, it is unclear why existing well-established tumor segmentation methods are not adopted, as many of them can already achieve highly accurate tumor delineation (e.g., Dice score > 0.9). In addition, class imbalance (e.g., IDH status) is a well-known challenge in glioma. Although focal loss is employed, it would be helpful to further report accuracy and recall for IDH mutation and 1p/19q co-deletion, to better assess model performance.

The concerns regarding the paper have been addressed, and all reviewers agree to accept the paper.

The paper proposes DEC-Net, a multi-task framework for joint glioma grading, IDH prediction, and 1p/19q prediction from multimodal MRI. All reviewers accepted the paper after rebuttal, which appears to have addressed the main concerns sufficiently.
However, the authors should more carefully address class imbalance by including additional metrics, such as per-class performance, sen/spe, in the camera-ready version. They should also include statistical analyses for the comparisons and more clearly position their technical contributions relative to the existing literature. In addition, rows 4, 5, 6 of the ablation study show that the roles of DRModule and PMoE are not fully evident, and this should be better discussed.

This paper proposes DEC-Net, a multi-task framework for glioma grading and molecular subtyping from multimodal MRI. Reviewers appreciated the clinical relevance, strong performance on both internal and external cohorts, and the comprehensive ablation studies. I agree with the reviewers that the method is technically sound and well validated. The rebuttal satisfactorily addressed concerns regarding unknown-label handling, cross-validation design, statistical significance testing, and baseline fairness. While some components build upon existing methods, the overall framework demonstrates clear practical value and strong generalization ability. Therefore, I recommend acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer (MR) for their constructive comments. We address their concerns below.
1.Model Complexity and Performance(MR, R2Q2, R3Q1):
The pre-trained network extracts tumor-relevant regions, the distillation framework enhances feature representation, the expert network mitigates inter-task interference, and the biologically guided D-Loss optimizes multi-task prediction. Together, these components improve glioma grading and molecular subtyping. Statistical tests on internal data show significant improvements: for AUC, significant differences are observed compared with several baseline methods (DeLong test, p < 0.05); for ACC, improvements are significant compared with all baseline methods (McNemar test, p < 0.05).
2.Rationale for Not Adopting Existing Tumor Segmentation Methods（MR）：
Gliomas affect the whole brain environment. Focusing only on tumor segmentation masks is insufficient to capture the complete affected regions. Our approach captures comprehensive tumor-relevant areas without relying solely on existing segmentation methods.
3.Sensitivity (SEN) and Specificity (SPE) for Our Task (MR,R3Q7):
Internal test SEN/SPE: Grade 88.14 ± 1.83 / 91.55 ± 2.47; IDH 84.99 ± 5.57 / 85.47 ± 2.79; 1p/19q 79.48 ± 5.25 / 79.89 ± 4.28.Due to space limits, these metrics were omitted from main tables but demonstrate superior performance over other methods.
4.Implementation and Inference Details (R1Q1):
The center cropping effectively captures the core brain area while removing boundaries. During inference, we perform whole-volume prediction rather than patch-based aggregation.
5.Baseline Comparisons and Limitations (R1Q2, R2Q3):
Our core contribution lies in multi-task learning , and our experiments mainly compare with recent SOTA multi-task methods. In our experiments, single-task results were evaluated. For ACC, multi-task synergy outperforms single-task baselines (Grade ACC 85–87% , IDH ACC 80–82%, and 1p/19q ACC 72–74%). We will add a brief discussion of limitations in the revised version. 
6.Expert Routing Analysis (R2Q1):
Full visualization of expert contributions is omitted due to page limits. We instead report the ratio of shared/task-specific expert selection: Grade (86/14), IDH (74/26), and 1p/19q (68/32). These results indicate that each task leverages different experts while showing task-related patterns, supporting the effectiveness of our routing mechanism.
7.Handling of Missing Labels (R3Q2):
Samples with missing labels were excluded from model training, P-matrix estimation, and evaluation. We did not adopt pseudo-labeling, as unreliable pseudo-labels may introduce noisy prior knowledge and lead to model hallucination or error accumulation. As shown in Table 1, the valid annotated sample sizes are 1,166 for Grade, 910 for IDH, and 632 for 1p/19q. These counts are used for P-matrix estimation. 
8.Cross-Validation Stratification (R3Q3):
Our five-fold cross-validation is site-stratified. Each fold contains one-fifth of samples from both UCSF-PDGM and EGD, ensuring that data from different scanners and protocols are represented in every fold. Additionally, (1) bias-field correction was applied during preprocessing, (2) there are no strong site-specific correlations that could inflate metrics, and (3) external validation confirms the model’s robustness.
9.Fairness of Baseline Comparisons (R3Q4):
To ensure a fair comparison, all nine SOTA baseline methods were evaluated under identical experimental settings, including the same preprocessing pipeline, fixed input size, consistent modality combination.
10.Citation and Methodology (R3Q5):
We will add proper citations for EMA teacher-student and PLE. In our work, these components are adapted for glioma tasks, considering task correlations. Specifically, we introduce a shared-and-specific structure and a D-Loss guided by biological priors, which together constitute a novel application-oriented contribution for multimodal glioma analysis.

title: Decoding the Alzheimer’s Continuum: Interpretable Multi-gate Routing for Diagnosis and Transition Prediction
abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) manifests as a continuous progres-sion from normal cognition (NC) through mild cognitive impairment (MCI) to dementia. However, most deep learning approaches reduce this continuum to disjointed classification tasks, largely ignoring dynamic stage transitions. To decode this complex progression, we propose M3AD, a unified framework that jointly addresses three-class diagnosis classifi-cation and diagnosis stage transition prediction using only T1-weighted sMRI. M3AD leverages an interpretable multi-gate mixture of experts architecture, employing specialized routing mechanisms to dynamically capture both diagnosis-specific pathological patterns and shared struc-tural features across the continuum. It further integrates clinical priors (age, sex, eTIV) via adaptive attention fusion to enhance generaliza-tion. M3AD achieves 95.13% accuracy, compared to 90.44% reported by MCLNC under its original experimental setting, and 94.87% for transi-tion prediction. Crucially, analyzing the multi-gate routing reveals dis-tinct expert activation signatures distinguishing stable from progressive MCI, providing a mechanistic basis for individual-level progression risk stratification.
subject_areas: Applications -> Outcome Prediction / Prognosis / Longitudinal Modeling

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a unified multi-task learning framework named M3AD to address diagnosis classification and stage transition prediction within the Alzheimer’s disease continuum. The framework employs a Multi-gate Mixture of Experts (MMOE) architecture, which not only captures diagnosis-specific pathological patterns but also shares structural features. Furthermore, the model innovatively integrates clinical priors (age, sex, eTIV) via adaptive attention fusion technology to enhance its generalization capabilities. The framework achieved outstanding performance on a large cohort comprising 12,037 sMRI scans across six datasets.
reviews.text_strengths:
Figure 1 clearly illustrates that the proposed multi-task unified architecture effectively avoids the diagnostic probability conflicts caused by independent OVO classifiers.
The analysis of the dual-gate routing mechanism reveals distinct expert activations for stable vs. progressive MCI, providing a basis for individual risk assessment.
Integrating features like age, sex, and eTIV at Stage 2 has strong clinical relevance and significantly improves diagnostic accuracy.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The “2D slice + majority voting” strategy lacks justification. The authors must explain why a native 3D network was not used and address the potential loss of 3D spatial context.
It is unclear whether the baselines in Table 1 benefit from the same SimMIM pre-training as the proposed model. The authors should unify these conditions or provide ablation studies to prove the architecture’s inherent superiority.
The methods compared in Table 1 are relatively old. Quantitative comparisons with recent state-of-the-art models (e. g. , from 2024 or 2025) are needed to validate the paper’s novelty.
Despite mentioning a long-tail distribution, the paper lacks specific strategies for handling imbalanced categories. A detailed per-class performance analysis should be added.
The quantitative discussion on cross-cohort validation (Section 3.2) is inadequate. The paper needs to analyze how differing distributions of clinical priors across cohorts impact model generalization.
Figure 2 fails to clearly highlight the core innovations (like the Adaptive Attention Fusion module). Visual cues such as borders or shading are needed to help readers quickly identify structural novelties.
Equations (2) and (3) use code-style terminology (e. g. , Tokenize, Shift_W, DWConv). These must be replaced with standard, formal mathematical symbols.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The clinical question is sound, the manuscript is complete, and the novelty is good.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have responded to my related concerns.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper proposes M3AD, a multi-task multi-gate mixture-of-experts framework that jointly performs three-class Alzheimer’s
diagnosis (NC/MCI/AD) and diagnosis stage transition prediction (Stability/Progression/Reversion) from T1-weighted structural MRI alone. The key contributions are a unified architecture replacing independent classifiers integration of clinical priors through an adaptive attention fusion, a two-stage training strategy with SimMIM pretraining to initialize expert specialization followed by multitask fine-tuning; and interpretability analysis. The framework is validated on 12,037 scans across six cohorts.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper makes a compelling argument that diagnosis classification and stage transition prediction are complementary
tasks that should be jointly modeled rather than treated independently. The ablation in Table 2 confirms that multi-task
learning consistently outperforms single-task variants, lending empirical support to this design choice.
Table 2 systematically dissects the contribution of multi-task learning, SimMIM pretraining, Tok-MLP, clinical priors
(individually and combined), and fusion stage placement. Each component is shown to contribute meaningfully, and the
ablations are well-structured. The finding that eTIV is the most impactful single clinical prior and that Stage 2 is optimal
for fusion are informative design insights.
The interpretability analysis is compelling. The expert-gate activation shift for AD-aligned experts when comparing stable
vs. progressive MCI is a clear, interpretable signal.
Good scale and multi-cohort validation. Using 12,037 scans across six cohorts with proper subject-level fold isolation and
cross-cohort generalization testing strengthens the claims considerably. The preprocessing is thorough and welldocumented.
Code availability.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The comparisons in Table 1 are not fair. Results for prior methods are cited from their original papers, which used
different datasets, splits, and preprocessing.
Why 2D slices? AD atrophy is inherently volumetric. Extracting sagittal slices and doing majority voting throws away 3D
spatial information. This choice is never justified, and no 3D baseline is compared.
Transition prediction metrics are incomplete: despite severe class imbalance (dominance of “Stability”), only aggregate
accuracy and F1 are reported. The paper should report per-class metrics (precision, recall, F1) for each of the three
diagnosis classes and each transition class. Aggregate metrics hide performance on the clinically most important
subgroups.
The cross-cohort experiment (Table 1, right) only tests NC vs. AD binary classification, which is the easiest
discrimination task. Cross-cohort evaluation for the three-class and transition tasks would be far more informative.
Several design choices are unjustified. Why 8 experts with this specific shared/aligned split? What’s the temperature τ?
What’s the λ in Eq. 5? Was task loss weighting explored? Masking ratio 0.6, why?
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses a clinically relevant problem with a technically reasonable approach. The multi-task formulation is well motivated, the ablation study is thorough, and the interpretability analysis offers genuinely interesting insights into expert routing behavior.
However, several issues push it below the acceptance threshold.
The most critical is the unfair comparison in Table 1: mixing
results from different experimental protocols while claiming SOTA improvement is misleading and undermines the paper’s central performance claim. The 2D slice-based approach is a significant unexplained limitation for a volumetric neuroimaging task.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have consistently responded all reviewers’ questions. Although I still find the 2D approach a limitation of the proposal, I think this work could raise interest to the attendants to MICCAI 2026.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of this paper is the proposal of M3AD, a unified multi-task Vision Transformer that leverages a Multi-gate Mixture-of-Experts and adaptive clinical fusion to simultaneously diagnose Alzheimer’s disease and predict its future progression, validated on over 12,000 multi-center MRI scans.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper proposes M³AD, a unified multi-task framework that jointly models the current Diagnosis Stage (DS) and the future DS Transition (e.g., Stability, Progression, Reversion) within a single architecture, rather than treating them as isolated classification problems.
2.The authors evaluate their method on a massive scale for neuroimaging, utilizing 12,037 T1-weighted MRI scans across six independent cohorts. This large-scale, multi-cohort approach, combined with a rigorous 5-fold cross-validation setup that explicitly confines all longitudinal scans of the same subject to a single fold to prevent data leakage, makes the empirical evaluation credible and robust.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The authors extract 2D sagittal slices from 3D MRI volumes and assign the subject-level diagnosis and progression labels to every single slice during training. However, Brain atrophy in early-stage Alzheimer’s (MCI) is highly localized (e.g., in the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex). Therefore, many lateral or extreme medial sagittal slices contain absolutely no pathological information. Assigning a “Progressive MCI” label to a healthy-looking slice introduces massive label noise during training, which degrades feature learning.
2.The authors claim the superiority of their multi-task framework, but fail to compare it with a vanilla multi-task learning baseline (e.g., a standard ViT with Hard Parameter Sharing using two task-specific linear heads). In Table 1, prior baselines are only evaluated on the diagnosis task, ignoring the transition task. In Table 2, the ‘Multiple Tasks’ setting only validates that training two tasks is better than one within the proposed architecture, but it does not justify the necessity of the complex components (like the multi-gate routing) over a simple multi-task approach.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The overall score is mainly driven by the strong clinical motivation and large‑scale, multi‑cohort evaluation, which demonstrate that the proposed unified framework is empirically robust and potentially impactful for modeling the AD continuum.
However, the paper is limited by methodological concerns regarding the absence of a fair comparison against a simple vanilla multi‑task baseline and the noisy 2D slice‑level labeling strategy, so I lean toward a weak accept (borderline) recommendation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper jointly models current AD diagnosis and future stage transition in a unified multi-task framework. The large-scale evaluation across six cohorts, the subject-level fold isolation, the detailed ablations, and the expert-routing analysis are clear strengths.
The comparison in Table 1 is potentially unfair because prior results appear to come from different datasets, splits, and preprocessing pipelines, which weakens the claimed SOTA performance. In addition, the paper does not compare against a simple vanilla multi-task baseline, making it hard to tell whether the complex multi-gate MoE design is necessary.
The 2D slice-based strategy needs strong justification. Assigning subject-level diagnosis and transition labels to all sagittal slices may introduce substantial label noise, especially for localized early AD pathology.
The comparison is incomplete due to the absence of a 3D baseline and recent 2024/2025 baselines.
The authors should further report per-class transition metrics and clarify key hyperparameters and cross-cohort results for the harder multi-class/transition tasks.

The authors have responded all reviewers’ questions.

The overall recommendation from the three reviewers, after rebuttal, leans toward acceptance, with R1 and R2 made their final recommendations to Accept and R3 maintaining a borderline Weak Accept. The reviewers acknowledged the strengths of the unified multi-task framework, the large-scale multi-cohort evaluation with rigorous subject-level isolation, and the interpretable expert-routing analysis for distinguishing stable versus progressive MCI.

The paper presents a well-motivated work for joint AD diagnosis and status transition prediction, evaluated on a relatively large multi-cohort datasets. Implementations in terms of 2D slices hamper the significance of the proposed method.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for recognizing M3AD’s unified multi-task design that resolves NC/MCI/AD exclusivity (R1, R3), the component-wise ablations and interpretable expert-routing for stable vs. progressive MCI (R2), the clinical motivation (R3), and the multi-cohort subject-level evaluation (R2, R3). We respond by theme.
[T1] 2D sagittal slices vs. 3D networks (R1.Q1, R2.Q2, R3.Q1)
We agree early AD/MCI atrophy is spatially localized and some sagittal slices may carry limited pathological evidence. Our 2D sagittal design is not a claim of 2D superiority, but a resolution-preserving scalability trade-off. As noted in Raptor [1], 3D volumetric modeling incurs cubic-order computational costs and demands datasets orders of magnitude larger than 2D counterparts, motivating 2D-based alternatives. Under comparable memory, 3D training often requires heavy downsampling (e.g., ~80×96×80 in [2]), weakening subtle medial-temporal cues (hippocampal/entorhinal atrophy). Raptor’s Tab. 7 reports that sagittal-only embeddings already achieve competitive performance, while tri-axis (A+C+S) fusion yields further gains. This supports our sagittal-only design as a reasonable single-view choice under our memory and preprocessing constraints, and we acknowledge multi-view fusion as a clear future direction. Regarding label reliability, slice labels are weak supervision derived from subject-level diagnosis/transition labels. All slices and longitudinal scans of one subject stay within 1 fold; predictions use subject-level majority voting, mitigating isolated unreliable slices at inference though not training-time label noise. We will note this limitation in the revision.
[T2] Table 1 and comparison fairness (R1.Q2/Q3, R2.Q1, R3.Q2)
Table 1 is a reference comparison (see footnote); the controlled comparison is Table 2, where all variants share identical ADNI splits, preprocessing, and SimMIM pretraining. We will avoid overstating cross-study superiority and distinguish reference from controlled ablation. The Multiple Tasks rows in Table 2 report full M3AD under joint supervision, not a hard-sharing MTL baseline; they isolate the gain of joint over single-task training under the same routing. Hard-sharing MTL removes diagnosis-aligned experts and task gates, so cannot evaluate our routing. [2] has a different objective/protocol; [3] targets histopathology MIL. Neither addresses NC/MCI/AD exclusivity jointly with transition prediction; unified-protocol comparison remains future work.
[T3] Class imbalance and cross-cohort scope (R1.Q4/Q5, R2.Q3/Q4)
Class imbalance is handled via weighted cross-entropy (weight 1.0 for majority, higher for rare transitions: NC-to-AD progression, MCI-to-NC reversion). We will add this detail and report per-class precision/recall/F1 for both tasks. For external validation, transition prediction is limited by the lack of standardized longitudinal MCI follow-up labels, and 3-class cross-cohort diagnosis is complicated by heterogeneous MCI definitions. ADNI has more than 50 sites in its cohort study protocol, which provides intrinsic multi-center evaluation for both diagnosis and transition tasks. Extending external validation beyond NC/AD binary diagnosis remains future work.
[T4] Hyperparameters (R2.Q5)
τ=1.0/0.5 (pretrain/finetune); λ=0.5 in Eq.(5); 8 experts = 2 shared + 2 NC + 2 MCI + 2 AD; SimMIM mask 0.6; AdamW lr 1e-4/5e-5, wd 0.05, cosine + 10-ep warmup; task-loss 1:1.A full hyperparameter table will be included in the revision.
[Minors] Figure and notation (R1.Q6/Q7)
We will revise Fig. 2 to emphasize dual-gate MMoE routing and Stage-2 clinical prior integration, and replace the code-style Tok-MLP/UNeXt notation [4] with formal mathematical notation.
We hope our responses address the reviewers’ concerns and thank them for their constructive feedback.
Refs: [1] An et al., Raptor, ICML 2025.[2] Ding et al., Denseformer-MoE, IEEE TMI 2025.[3] Li et al., M4, MedIA 2025.[4] Valanarasu & Patel, UNeXt, MICCAI 2022.

title: Decouple and Reason: Anatomically Guided Two-Stage Grounding of Lung Lesions in 3D Chest CT from Free-Text Reports
abstract:
Automatic voxel-level grounding of lung lesions from free-text reports in 3D chest Computed Tomography (CT) is critical for clinical interpretability. 
However, this task remains highly challenging due to the intricate spatial complexity of large 3D volumes and the heterogeneity of free-text findings. 
Existing end-to-end approaches often struggle to simultaneously learn the localized feature representations required for accurate 3D segmentation and the complex semantic understanding needed for text alignment, leading to suboptimal grounding performance. To overcome this fundamental limitation, we propose a novel decoupled framework that disentangles the problem into two specialized stages: (1) class-agnostic lesion segmentation and (2) text-volume reasoning. 
This structural separation allows the model to first extract candidate sub-volumes by localizing potential abnormalities.
Subsequently, intensive cross-modal reasoning is performed to align these localized sub-volumes with free-text medical findings. 
To resolve the spatial ambiguities inherent in local regions, the reasoning module is augmented with explicit anatomical guidance, utilizing relative spatial coordinates and lung lobe priors. Evaluated on the ReXGroundingCT benchmark, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in instance-level metrics on the official leaderboard.
These results demonstrate that decoupling detection from reasoning is a highly effective paradigm for handling the complexity of 3D medical visual grounding. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/khuhm/DAGG.
