meta_reviews.text:
This paper proposes HierEM, a hierarchical expectation–maximization framework that treats each site’s annotation as a noisy observation of an underlying clean mask and decomposes label variability into global, site-, and case-level components. The reviewers agree that the problem is clinically important, the hierarchical generative formulation is theoretically coherent, and the leave-one-site-out evaluation is a clever design choice.
Scores split 4/3/6.R1 and R2 raise concerns that are specific and grounded. R1 notes the paper lacks ablations isolating the contributions of the hierarchical structure, the site-specific noise model, and soft-label aggregation, and that no hyperparameter sensitivity or PIRADS-stratified analysis is reported. R2 identifies several discrepancies between the text and the tables (including wrong units and conflicting Dice numbers), flags an unexplained large standard deviation on Site 1, and raises a more substantive concern that extending STAPLE to a setting where each case has a single annotation implicitly assumes uniform annotator behavior within a site. R3 gives a Strong Accept, but the review is short and does not engage with the concrete details of the paper nor it justifies why the paper is outstanding, so I gave it less weight. R1’s review is also superficial and raised concerns that are somewhat generic.
Given the split scores and somewhat unconvincing reviews (which is unfortunate for the authors and the community), I went through the paper myself and found R2’s point on the uniform-within-site assumption the most significant one; it touches the validity of the estimation that the whole framework rests on, and the authors should engage with it carefully, including possible clarification, implications, and any conditions under which the assumption is reasonable. The reporting discrepancies (units, conflicting Dice numbers, unexplained Site 1 standard deviation) are smaller in scope but should also be addressed, since they affect how the results are read. The ablation and sensitivity requests are harder to resolve in a rebuttal but are worth acknowledging. I invite the authors to respond before a final decision. Please refer to MICCAI rebuttal guidelines. Good luck.

I thank the authors and all three reviewers for their active participation in the rebuttal phase. Following the rebuttal, the authors effectively addressed the significant concerns raised during the initial review round, including inconsistencies in results, underlying assumptions of the method, and potential limitations. All three reviewers agreed that the paper should be accepted. Considering the merits in the paper, authors’ effective rebuttal, and the unanimous agreement from the reviewers, I recommend acceptance.
Congratulations! Well done
Reviewer consensus achieved.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the comments from the reviewers and the clear guidance from the AC.
Reviewer 2: single annotation per case / STAPLE assumption
We agree that annotators within the same site should not be identical, even under the same protocol, as suggested by R2.But we clarify that we do NOT assume uniform behaviour within sites.
First, algorithmically, HierEM includes case-specific latent variables, u_k and v_k, in addition to the site-level variables (a_s, b_s) in Eq. 2, modelling the hierarchy of global, site-level, case-level variabilities. During training, the model specifies probabilities of observed labels given unknow latent clean label(Eq.1), and allows each case to move away from global and site averages by case variables (u_k, v_k) (eq.2). For reporting, site-level statistics can be estimated by pooled sensitivity and specificity over within-site annotators, but these do NOT assume all annotators at a given site perform identically. 
Second, from the data point of view, HierEM also addresses a different problem from classical STAPLE. STAPLE experiments used multiple annotations for every case, allowing individual-reader sensitivity and specificity to be estimated directly. Our HierEM is designed for multi-site data with single annotation for each case. It is noteworthy that, a site may involve multiple annotators, but each case is annotated only once. In practice, such single-annotation-per-case multi-site datasets are much more commonly available than datasets requiring multiple annotators to annotate every case. These within site annotators are expected to follow the same site-level annotation protocol, for example PI-RADS in dataset1 and Likert in dataset2, but their actual labelling behaviour may still differ due to individual judgement, experience. In HierEM, such residual case-wise discrepancies are not forced into a single site-level α/β. Instead, the case-level latent variables (u_k, v_k) allow the effective sensitivity and specificity, \alpha_{s,k} and \beta_{s,k}, to vary from case to case.
Reporting results
We sincerely thank R2 for identifying several typos and formatting issues. We are grateful for the careful reading and humbled by the attention to detail. Among these, we clarify that 1) the current value for Dice in Site3 is 31.20% both in table and text; and 2) the correct standard deviation for Site 1 should be 11.88 instead of 21.88.We will correct these. Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we also added AURC to Fig. 2, with smaller area indicates lower risk.
Ablation concerns of contribution of the hierarchical structure
We use the same strong and efficient U-Net backbone across all methods to ensure a fair and controlled comparison. Since our method is agnostic to the segmentation backbone, this controlled setting reduces architectural differences as a potential factor. The experimental design is progressive and aims to demonstrate the contribution of site- and case-level modelling: we start with U-Net baseline, then add soft-label bootstrapping, flat EM modelling without case-level variables, and finally the proposed HierEM. The experiments serve not only as comparisons against relevant baselines, but also as an ablation of the main methodological components. We agree that a more systematic comparison study could further strengthen the work and will consider in future work.
PIRADS-stratified analysis by reviewer1
This study included cases contain PI-RADS/Likert ≥3 lesions. We focus on comparing methods within this clinically meaningful lesion-positive population. We agree that PI-RADS/Likert-stratified evaluation would be clinically valuable, may potentially expand clinical applicability, although due to the fixed diagnostic patient cohort used in our test set, such stratification needs be carefully designed to reflect any intended real-world patient cohorts. Following the AC suggestion, we will acknowledge these.

title: Deep Probabilistic Cerebrovascular Atlas
abstract: Cerebrovascular modeling remains a foundational challenge in medical image analysis due to the intricate, multi-scale topology and extreme anatomical variability of the brain’s vascular tree. Traditional discrete representations, such as voxel grids, face challenges in capturing the continuous nature of these highly variable structures, often leading to spatial wash-out during population averaging. In this study, we introduce VITAL, an implicit neural atlas framework for brain vessel modeling. To address the multi-scale nature of the cerebrovasculature, spanning from major arteries to distal branches, VITAL utilizes a dynamically routed Mixture-of-Experts architecture that decouples multi-scale features, enabling effective and continuous vascular reconstruction. To our knowledge, we present the first continuous conditioned probabilistic neural atlas of the human cerebrovasculature, enabling cross-sectional modeling of age-related morphological changes and sex-stratified vascular differences across the adult lifespan. Furthermore, we evaluate VITAL on subjects with stroke-related neurological disorders, demonstrating its potential as a exploratory normative reference for anomaly analysis.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes VITAL, a continuous implicit neural representation (INR) framework aimed at constructing a probabilistic cerebrovascular atlas. To address the multi-scale nature of the brain’s vascular tree and the spectral bias inherent in standard INRs, the authors integrate a dynamically routed Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture combined with FiLM modulation. The method is evaluated on the healthy IXI dataset for atlas construction and on the TopCoW stroke dataset to demonstrate its potential for anomaly detection via test-time adaptation.
reviews.text_strengths:
1, Methodological Exploration: The application of INR to overcome the partial volume effects and aliasing inherent in discrete voxel grids for highly variable vascular structures is an interesting engineering exploration.
2, Architectural Design: Introducing an MoE mechanism to theoretically decouple multi-scale spatial frequencies (e. g. , low-frequency global geometry of major arteries vs. high-frequency local details of distal branches) is a conceptually appealing approach to mitigating the spectral bias of standard MLPs (like SIREN).
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Summary:
It appears the authors lack a practical understanding of real-world cerebrovascular challenges, which undermines the claimed clinical meaning of the work.
1.Insufficient Performance for Clinical Cerebrovascular Applications
The results have severe vascular discontinuity and alignment errors, which limits the framework’s clinical applicability. 
1.1 Dataset Limitations vs. Classic Methods: The model relies on the IXI MRA dataset resampled to a $256 \times 256$ in-plane resolution. At this resolution and field strength, the primarily visible structures are the macro-vasculature (large to medium arteries like the CoW). For these macro-structures, standard discrete processing methods (e. g. , Frangi-based vessel tracking, graph-cut methods, or conventional 3D CNNs) already achieve reliable performance. The necessity of a complex MoE-INR architecture is not fully justified given that the dataset does not clearly capture the micro-vascular details that INRs are theoretically designed to preserve.
1.2 Unclear Deviation Maps: The visual results presented in Figures 1, 2, and 3 are ambiguous, overly smoothed. Thus, it cannot provide sufficient evidence for reviewers to validate the method’s efficacy. Based solely on the visual performance in these figures, it appears the authors lack a practical understanding of real-world cerebrovascular challenges, which fundamentally undermines the claimed clinical significance of the work.
This visual ambiguity is validated by the results in Table 1.An SSIM of 0.84 (reflecting an approximate 20% intensity reconstruction error), a Dice score of merely 0.71, and an Average Surface Distance (ASD) of 4.18 mm are highly problematic. Crucially, cerebrovascular imaging data is volumetrically dominated by macro-vasculature (large arteries). 
Because these large vessels constitute the vast majority of the target signal, baseline metrics are naturally inflated if the main arterial trunks are even partially captured. The fact that the proposed method still yields such subpar overall metrics. Despite the inherent statistical advantage provided by macro-vessel dominance, the method exposes severe algorithmic deficiencies. Consequently, the framework lacks the precision and reliability required for meaningful clinical tasks such as stroke localization or surgical planning. 
1.3 Quantitative Discontinuities: The quantitative results in Table 1 show a whole-brain Connectivity Error of 183.69 ± 130.67, indicating notable vascular fragmentation. Furthermore, the framework yields a PSNR of 24.98 dB, an SSIM of 0.84, and an Average Surface Distance (ASD) of 4.18 mm. In cerebrovascular anatomy, where many medium vessels are 1-3 mm in diameter, an average error of 4.18 mm exceeds the size of the anatomical structures themselves, limiting the model’s ability to precisely quantify pathological deviations.
2.Limitations in Modeling Discrete Topological Mutations
The framework relies on MoE and FiLM modulation to capture anatomical variability. However, it is limited to handle discrete topological changes.
2.1 On page 4, the modulation mechanism is described: “Following [10], the concatenated conditioning vector $\tilde{z}
{i}=[z
{i},c_{i}]$ is mapped to layer-specific scale ($\gamma$) and shift ($\beta$) parameters via a linear projection. “
2.2 FiLM modulation applies global affine transformations (scaling and shifting) to the intermediate feature maps of the SIREN network. While modifying the frequency and phase of a continuous sine wave is effective for modeling global continuous morphing (e. g. , generalized widening or tortuosity due to aging), it is less suited for discrete local topological mutations. For example, the congenital absence of an A1 segment in the Circle of Willis is a binary (1-to-0) structural break. A global linear projection of a latent code cannot easily execute localized topological erasure without introducing artifacts (e. g. , semi-transparent vessels). The paper lacks theoretical or visual demonstration showing how FiLM and MoE accurately enforce these discrete topological graph changes. 
3.Incomplete Baseline Comparisons
The quantitative evaluation of the atlas reconstruction (Table 1) omits comparisons against standard clinical registration methods. 
3.1 The Evidence: On page 5, the authors explain their baseline selection: “We compare VITAL against a state-of-the-art INR-based brain modeling baseline CiNeMA [9]. Traditional voxel-based registration methods are excluded as they do not employ a generative latent space for subject-specific reconstruction. “
3.2 The Evidence: On page 5 (Preprocessing), the authors state: “For anatomical context, T1 images were segmented using FastSurfer [12] and rigidly registered to the MRA space via ANTs [4]. “
3.3 The Critique: The authors use traditional registration tools (ANTs) for foundational data alignment but exclude state-of-the-art deformable registration methods (such as ANTs SyN) in their performance benchmarks. Since the primary metrics evaluated in Table 1 (e. g. , ASD and Connectivity Error) assess geometric alignment accuracy, the lack of a generative latent space in traditional methods does not justify excluding them from an alignment comparison. 
4.Methodological Circularity in Clinical Anomaly Detection
The experimental design for the TopCoW stroke dataset (Section 3) involves a circular dependency during the inference phase, which affects its clinical utility. 
4.1 The Evidence: On page 7, the authors state: “Given the inherent imaging protocol variations between datasets and the severe morphological deviations in stroke subjects, relying solely on intensity reconstruction is prone to misalignment. Therefore, we employed supervised test-time adaptation using $\mathcal{L}
{rec}+\mathcal{L}
{seg}$ to investigate vascular anomalies, with the segmentation mask serving as a topological anchor. “
4.2 The Critique: A primary objective of an anomaly detection system is to discover and segment abnormal vascular regions. By requiring the patient’s ground-truth segmentation mask ($\mathcal{L}_{seg}$) during the test-time adaptation phase to achieve alignment, the algorithm relies on the intended output to process the input. A model that requires a pre-existing mask of the anomaly to perform localization cannot be directly applied to a real-world diagnostic workflow. 
5.Terminology Mismatch: “Spatio-Temporal Evolution” vs. Cross-Sectional Interpolation
The manuscript uses longitudinal terminology to describe cross-sectional data manipulations. 
5.1 The Claim: In the Abstract, the authors declare: “. . . we construct the first continuous spatio-temporal neural atlas of the human cerebrovascular system. . . “ and on page 7: “Fig. 4 presents the spatiotemporal evolution of VITAL atlas spanning the adult lifespan from 20 to 80 years. “
5.2 The Reality: The dataset description on page 5 states: “In this study, we used MRA scans and corresponding T1 images from healthy adults (19-87 years old) in the IXI dataset [6]. “ The methodology relies on computing target latent codes via “Gaussian kernel regression over the trained population” (page 5).
5.3 The Critique: The IXI dataset is strictly cross-sectional, containing single-timepoint scans of different individuals at various ages. Modeling true “spatio-temporal evolution” generally requires longitudinal data (repeated scans of the same subjects over time). Interpolating a latent code between subjects of different ages mathematically generates a cross-sectional age-related morphological mean, rather than a longitudinal aging trajectory. 
6.Inconsistencies Regarding Discretization and Partial Volume Effects
The motivation for utilizing an Implicit Neural Representation is to bypass the limitations of discrete grids; however, the preprocessing pipeline partially conflicts with this objective.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

My recommendation for this manuscript is Reject.
It appears the authors lack a practical understanding of real-world cerebrovascular challenges. While the integration of Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) for cerebrovascular modeling is an interesting engineering exploration, the paper suffers from several flaws across its clinical logic, experimental design, and conceptual claims.
The major factors driving this decision are:
1.Methodological Circularity in Clinical Evaluation: The most fatal flaw is the logical tautology in the anomaly detection experiment (Section 3). By requiring the ground-truth segmentation mask of the stroke anomaly during the test-time adaptation phase to achieve anatomical alignment, the framework relies on the intended diagnostic output to process the input. This circular dependency completely invalidates the model’s utility in any realistic clinical triage workflow.
2.Insufficient Empirical Performance and Unfair Baselines: The quantitative results demonstrate severe topological fragmentation and alignment errors (e.g., an Average Surface Distance of 4.18 mm and a Connectivity Error of 183.69). For cerebrovascular anatomy, an error margin of >4 mm often exceeds the diameter of the vessels themselves, rendering the atlas clinically unreliable. Furthermore, the authors deliberately excluded standard, state-of-the-art deformable registration methods from their baseline comparisons, making it impossible to objectively assess their claims of superior topological alignment.
3.Mathematical and Conceptual Inadequacies: The framework’s reliance on global affine transformations (FiLM) is mathematically ill-equipped to model discrete, localized topological mutations (e.g., congenital vessel absences), leading to ambiguous probabilistic outputs rather than deterministic structures. Additionally, the manuscript makes severe scientific overclaims by repeatedly characterizing the latent interpolation of static, cross-sectional data (the IXI dataset) as longitudinal “spatio-temporal evolution.”
Thus, the combination of a flawed clinical validation paradigm, subpar quantitative performance, and significant conceptual misrepresentations indicates that this work requires profound restructuring in both its mathematical priors and experimental design. It does not meet the scientific and clinical standards expected for MICCAI.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
1.Regarding “Circularity in TopCoW analysis”
The authors argue that the mask used for test-time adaptation (TTA) “contains only observed vessel… labels,” “doesn’t supervise the deviation map,” and merely “anchors alignment.”
This defense reveals a critical misunderstanding of cerebrovascular pathology (specifically in stroke datasets like TopCoW) and the mechanics of image registration/alignment.
The Logical Flaw:
In clinical, a stroke patient with occlusion, a major vessel (e.g., the MCA) is missing from the scan.
If the VITAL framework uses this topologically incomplete pathological mask as the explicit target to optimize the latent code ($Z_t$) and spatial alignment parameters of a healthy atlas, the optimization process will inevitably be pathologically biased.
The network will forcefully warp the healthy atlas to minimize the loss against an empty space where the vessel should be.
Conclusion: 
You cannot align a healthy topological prior to a pathologically broken target by using the broken target’s mask as the primary geometric anchor.
This will distort the latent space alignment, making the subsequent deviation map a meaningless product of misregistration rather than a true reflection of the anomaly.
2.Regarding “Metric interpretation”
The authors argue that high Dice indicates “memorization” and that the metrics should be read merely as an ablation showing MoE is better than CiNeMA. They state VITAL is a “normative reference.”
The Physical Flaw: 
While a probabilistic atlas should not memorize individual topology, it must provide a baseline accurate enough to be clinically meaningful.
The authors ignore the absolute scale of their error. According to Table 1, the Average Surface Distance (ASD) is 4.18 mm. 
In human cerebrovascular anatomy, the diameter of major arteries (e.g., ACA, MCA, PCA) is typically between 1.5 mm and 3.5 mm.
Conclusion: 
If the reference has an intrinsic geometric uncertainty/error larger far than the physical diameter of the vessels, it cannot reliably compute a deviation map for anomalies (such as a 2mm occlusion or a 3mm aneurysm).
The margin of error dwarfs the physiological signal and the results is meaningless for clinical.
3.Regarding “Topology Mutation”
The authors state that congenital absences appear as “regions of low vessel probability and high uncertainty rather than hard topology deletions.”
Acknowledgment：
This is a fair mathematical admission.
Limitation:
However, it confirms my initial critique: the framework blurs across distinct discrete topological states (e.g., presence vs. absence of the A1 segment) by outputting a muddy average probability.
4.Regarding “Age-conditioned vs. longitudinal terminology”
I acknowledge and appreciate the authors’ concession to revise the terminology from “spatio-temporal evolution” to “cross-sectional lifespan morphological modeling.”
This resolves the scientific overclaiming issue regarding the dataset’s nature.

The paper presents a well-motivated and technically sound approach to modeling vascular structures, addressing a relevant and challenging problem. The methodology is clearly described and generally well organized, making the contributions easy to follow. In addition, the experimental results are strong and convincingly demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors present the first spatiotemporal atlas of the human cerebrovascular system constructed using implicit neural representation with an MoE architecture.
reviews.text_strengths:
This is a very well-written and comprehensive piece of work.
The main novelty lies in the application. The overall framework based on which this method is developed, i.e., CINA/CINeMA, has already been around for a while and is popular for atlas construction but has never been applied to cerebrovascular atlas construction.
In terms of the framework, the authors further incorporate an MoE architecture beyond the original CINeMA, and demonstrate its effectiveness in improving the overall performance of the proposed method. The motivation for the MoE architecture is well-explained. For an 8-page short paper, the authors provide a lot of experimental results to support the usefulness of the MoE architecture (Table 1), characterization of how the proposed MoE architecture work indeed result in different experts specializing in different areas of the vasculature (Fig. 2(c)), and usefulness for downstream tasks (clear separation of Normative vs. Pathological in Fig. 3(c)).
Key design choices are well-justified. For example, the authors employ a label-stratified coordinate sampling approach to ensure sufficient sampling of the foreground coordinates, which are relatively sparse.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Although the application of INR to cerebrovascular atlas construction is quite new and, in fact, first of its kind, the novelty of the method itself is somewhat limited. From a method stand point, the authors are aware and acknowledge previous works, e.g., CINeMA [9] and MoE for INR [5], which greatly influenced this work. The proposed method does not introduce much new stuff beyond a combination of [9] and [5].
There are also some ambiguities in the description of the method.
1.In Section 2.1, what is vessel intensity value I(x) referring to? Is it the intensity values of the MRA images?
2.Also in section 2.1, the author claim that affine transformation is used. However, the formulation of the transformation is rotation plus translation makes it sounds like a rigid transformation is used? It would be helpful to clarify.
3.Fig. 2(b) and the discussion thereof are hard to follow. There are a lot of information in Fig. 2(b) and I believe it would be helpful to provide more explanation. Specifically, it would be helpful to mention that, e.g., VITAL tend to assign larger probability than competing methods, which demonstrates that less smoothing occurs spatially.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
There are some places where additional discussions/explanations would be appreciated.
1.On page 2, the authors mention that “… SIREN … difficult to simultaneously encode the low-frequency … and the high-frequency …”. Isn’t the sinusoidal activation patterns of SIREN designed specifically to mitigate this very issue?

Despite the limited novelty, I believe the work is still of interest to the MICCAI community for a couple of reasons. 1.The application of INR to modeling vasculature of the brain is novel. 2.Having a spatiotemporal cerebrovascular atlas is not only cool in its own right but of great importance to research and clinical applications.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The clarifications provided by the authors address the ambiguities. Although the novelty is somewhat limited, I still believe this work is highly relevant to the MICCAI community. In particular, using INR for the task of cerebrovascular atlas construction is not only interesting but also relevant for clinical applications.
Authors’ responses to R1 is very informative and highlights some of R1’s misunderstand of the scope and clarifies the intended use case of this work. The responses are well-written and convincing.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper proposes VITAL, an implicit neural atlas with a Mixture-of-Experts architecture for cerebrovascular modeling, applied to anomaly analysis on stroke subjects. Several substantive concerns are raised across the reviews. The methodological novelty appears limited as the approach largely combines CINeMA and MoE-for-INR, and warrants stronger articulation. More fundamentally, the anomaly analysis exhibits a circular dependency where the test-time adaptation relies on the patient’s segmentation mask through L_seg, and the validity of the resulting deviation maps as a clinical signal needs to be defended. The reported metrics, including an average surface distance exceeding the diameter of medium cerebral vessels, are also difficult to contextualize given the omission of standard deformable registration baselines. Further concerns include the characterization of cross-sectional latent interpolation as “spatio-temporal evolution,” and ambiguities in population-level versus subject-level conditioning and in the transformation formulation. The rebuttal should address the major reviewers’ concerns including these points.

This paper proposes VITAL, an implicit neural atlas with a Mixture-of-Experts architecture for continuous probabilistic modeling of the cerebrovascular system, applied to atlas-to-subject deviation analysis on stroke data. The reviewers acknowledge that applying INR to cerebrovascular atlas construction is the first of its kind and clinically relevant, and that the MoE design is well motivated and supported by ablations. The rebuttal clarified the intended scope as a probabilistic population atlas and normative reference rather than a standalone diagnostic system; under this scope, the masks in test-time adaptation function as alignment anchors and the metrics are appropriately read as an ablation against the closest generative atlas baseline. The authors are encouraged to revise the “spatio-temporal evolution” terminology and to soften wording suggesting surgical-grade precision, as committed. The novelty lies primarily in adapting existing components, but the application is genuinely new for this anatomy and the empirical support is convincing.

Reviewers summarized strengths of your work, novel aspects and noted that your solution to the specific application area may be of potential interest. The rebuttal helped to clarify open issues and misunderstandings. Would the paper be accepted, authors are strongly encouraged to improve the final write-up by including recommendations by reviewers, in particular to improve clarity in order to avoid misunderstandings.

Based on the reviewers’ evaluations, the authors’ rebuttal, and the initial meta-review, the paper is recommended for acceptance. While Reviewer #1 raised serious concerns about clinical utility, insufficient performance, and terminology, two other expert reviewers (R2 and R4) found the work well-motivated, technically sound, and of clear interest to the MICCAI community. The rebuttal convincingly clarified the scope as a probabilistic population atlas and normative reference, not a standalone diagnostic or segmentation tool, and addressed the major points by revising the “spatio-temporal” terminology to cross-sectional age-conditioned modeling, explaining the role of the mask in test-time adaptation, and contextualizing the metrics as an ablation of the MoE architecture relative to the closest INR baseline. The accepting reviewers’ post-rebuttal assessments reaffirmed their support, noting that the responses resolved ambiguities and underscored the novelty and relevance of applying implicit neural representations to cerebrovascular atlas construction.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank all experts for their constructive comments [R1,R2,R4]. We are encouraged that R2 and R4 found our work well-motivated, technically sound, and of clear interest to MICCAI. We clarify all key concerns below.
Scope [R1]. Several concerns appear to arise from interpreting VITAL as a segmentation, diagnostic, or surgical-planning system. This is not our intended claim. VITAL is a continuous probabilistic population atlas and normative reference: it models healthy population variability and enables atlas-to-subject comparison, not a standalone diagnostic, segmentation, or navigation tool.
Circularity in TopCoW analysis [R1]. This concern follows from the same scope misinterpretation. The masks used in test-time adaptation contain only observed vessel and brain-region labels, which can be obtained from existing segmentation tools. They don’t contain anomaly labels, lesion masks, stroke labels, or ground truth about pathology. The deviation map is computed after atlas projection as the mismatch between the healthy population prior and observed anatomy (Figs. 1 and 3). So the mask anchors alignment; it doesn’t supervise the deviation map. We will clarify this more.
Metric interpretation [R1]. The metrics measure atlas-to-subject reconstruction quality of a probabilistic population prior, not supervised segmentation accuracy. Extremely high Dice might indicate memorization of individual topology rather than a meaningful population prior, the opposite of what a normative atlas should achieve. Table 1 should be read mainly as an ablation: MoE (K=4)+Lmoe improves over CiNeMA across most metrics, including PSNR (+3.2 dB), SSIM (+0.05), ASD (-0.98 mm whole-brain, -0.52 mm CoW), conn. error (-112), and center. distance (-0.95 mm). We will revise the wording to avoid implying surgical-grade precision, which is not claimed.
Baseline comparisons [R1]. Table 1 evaluates conditional reconstruction within generative atlas frameworks; CiNeMA is the closest comparable baseline. Fig. 2 includes NLR/MultiMorph to illustrate population-level wash-out in discrete atlases, not to claim superiority over deformable registration in a geometric alignment benchmark. ANTs was used solely for intra-subject (T1 to MRA) rigid preprocessing to align anatomy labels, which is a standard procedure, and not as an atlasing baseline.
Age-conditioned vs. longitudinal terminology [R1]. We agree that IXI is cross-sectional and that spatio-temporal evolution overstates the design. We will use age-conditioned atlas and cross-sectional lifespan morphological modeling instead. The intended contribution, a continuous implicit function conditioned on age modeling population-level morphological variation across the adult lifespan, is a standard approach in normative brain atlasing.
Topology Mutation [R1]. FiLM alone does not guarantee deterministic binary graph edits, but VITAL uses spatial latent codes rather than a single global latent code for local variation without global compensation, with MoE partitioning cross-scale capacity. Anatomical variants are represented probabilistically: congenital absences appear as regions of low vessel probability and high uncertainty rather than hard topology deletions.
Clarifications [R2,R4].
1) VITAL conditions at two levels: z encodes subject-specific variation; c encodes population-level covariates.
2) K=4 was selected as a capacity-cost trade-off supported by the ablation in Table 1 (K=2 vs. K=4); Fig. 2c is qualitative and representative, not a comprehensive evaluation.
3) Yes, it should be ‘vascular’.
4) I(x) denotes MRA intensity. The transformation is rigid to avoid over-warping sparse vascular branch.
5) Fig. 2b shows VITAL assigns more mass to high vessel probability than voxel-based atlas methods, indicating less spatial wash-out.
6) SIREN mitigates spectral bias, but a monolithic SIREN shares one parameter set across scales, causing capacity competition; MoE explicitly partitions this capacity (Fig. 2c).

title: Deep-IMMA: an Interpretable Immune-Aware Multimodal Deep Representation Learning for Cancer Prognosis and Recurrence Prediction
abstract: Cancer prognosis and recurrence prediction from histopathology images has relied on morphology focused models or genomic data. However, these approaches insufficiently capture the spatial organization and interactions between epithelial, stromal, and immune cell populations, increasingly recognized as important contributors to disease progression. We propose Deep-IMMA (Deep Immune-Aware Multimodal Multi-task Alignment), a general multimodal learning framework that derives biologically grounded prognostic representations directly from histopathology images. Deep-IMMA introduces a two-stage architecture that encodes the tumor–immune microenvironment via structured multimodal supervision. In Stage 1, tile-level visual embeddings are learned via joint multi-task multimodal supervision from structured textual captions and spatial cell-type maps, with an auxiliary cross-modal consistency objective, yielding semantically enriched and immune-aware representations. This joint training integrates vision, text, and spatial priors while requiring only histology image at inference time. In Stage 2, these representations are aggregated using a spatially aware Multiple Instance Learning module that explicitly preserves neighborhood relationships and immune topology, improving slide-level risk discrimination. Using prostate cancer as a case study, we evaluate Deep-IMMA on a tri-modal prostate cancer histology dataset (Prostate-TriMod), comprising 717 prostate tissue microarray (TMA) core images from 212 patients. Deep-IMMA achieves a test AUROC of 0.761 (95% CI: 0.666–0.847), outperforming prognostic models based on only morphology and clinical data for recurrence prediction. Importantly, Deep-IMMA generates interpretable spatial–textual outputs, including tile-level semantic descriptions, immune-infiltration and attention heatmaps, enabling spatially grounded risk interpretation. These results demonstrate that immune-aware multimodal supervision can establish a robust, transparent and cost-effective baseline for cancer prognosis, bypassing expensive auxiliary data.

Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a 2 stage framework for predicting prostate cancer biochemical recurrence from histopathology slides by learning immune-aware representations. In the first stage, it trains a vision backbone using tissue maps with structured cell/immune annotations, and text captions to build biologically grounded tile-level embeddings. In the second stage, these embeddings are aggregated with a spatially aware multiple instance learning model that preserves spatial relationships and highlights prognostic regions. Their method is designed to improve prediction performance and interpretability by modeling tumor and immune interactions. They used a 212-patient cohort, and their reports improved recurrence prediction over standard baselines
reviews.text_strengths:
1) They have a strong biological motivation focused on tumor–immune microenvironment which is evident through explicit modeling of tissue compartments. 
2) They have rich multi-task supervision (segmentation, counts, immune labels, captions) to enrich representations. 
3) Their model produces interpretability attention maps of immune infiltration between recurrence and non-recurrence phenotypes. 
4) They also combine vision, language, and spatial signals in a unified framework.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) There’s a heavy reliance on expensive supervision, including pixel-level (on tiles) tissue segmentation maps. Additionally, the dice score is very low ~0.22.They argue segmentation is not meant to be precise but “interaction-centric,” but this is not fully convincing. If segmentation is inaccurate, it is unclear how reliable downstream biological supervision is. 
2) it is unclear what the role of the Q-former is. 
While the attention maps are good, have they been evaluated by a pathologist?
3) No external validation: it would be great if this were validated. 
It is unclear whether the claimed tumor–immune interaction is actually modeled or if the model only learns co-occurrence patterns through shared supervision and spatial proximity. 
4) It is unclear what staining or slide type was used. Is it H&E primarily? Why does it say virtual H&E from DAPI? The images seem to be TMA and not biopsy slides. 
5) Usually prognostic models are evaluated in terms of C-index, hazard ratio, survival curves. 
6) Also unclear where is the structured text from captions coming from?

reviews.text_contribution: Deep-IMMA is a two-stage foundation model adaptation framework that learns biologically grounded prognostic representations from histopathology by explicitly encoding tumor–immune microenvironment (TIME) structure through structured multi-task supervision. Stage 1 adapts a frozen UNI backbone with a Q‑Former bottleneck using uncertainty‑weighted multi‑task learning to jointly model tissue architecture, immune infiltration phenotypes, cellular composition, and vision–text alignment with BioMedBERT, producing immune‑aware tile embeddings. Stage 2 aggregates spatially encoded tiles with a Top‑K gated MIL model to predict biochemical recurrence with auxiliary Gleason grading and attention sparsity. Extensive ablations confirm each component’s necessity, and on a tri‑modal prostate cancer cohort the full model achieves AUROC 0.761, outperforming ABMIL and logistic baselines while yielding interpretable tissue, immune, and attention maps.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Biologically grounded supervision is a compelling idea. Instead of purely morphological features, the framework explicitly encodes immune-tumor spatial interactions (6 immune infiltration phenotypes) as structured supervision signals. This is well-motivated by pathology literature showing immune contexture predicts outcomes.
2.Unified multi-task framework is elegant. Jointly training segmentation, captioning, classification, and regression within a single Stage 1 pipeline with uncertainty-weighted losses is a clean design that avoids training separate models.
3.Thorough ablation study. The paper systematically ablates Stage 1 components (backbone, alignment loss) and Stage 2 components (spatial encoding, Top-K, auxiliary grade, sparsity regularization), with CIs for all results.
5.Practical clinical value. The model works from histology alone (no MRI/genomics), making it more clinically accessible.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.very small dataset and single-site evaluation. Only 212 patients / 711 slides from a single institution. The 95% CI for AUROC is wide (0.666-0.847), and with only 44 test patients, results could be unstable. No external validation on any public prostate cancer dataset (e.g., TCGA-PRAD) is provided. For clinical prognosis claims, multi-site validation is essential.
2.Limited baselines — no comparison with modern pathology VLMs or survival models. The baselines are only Logistic Regression and ABMIL. No comparison with CONCH, PathChat, CLAM, TransMIL, or any recent WSI-level prognosis methods. The claim of outperforming “morphology-only” models lacks comparison with current SOTA slide-level prognosis methods that also use foundation model features.
3.Virtual H&E images (from DAPI/autofluorescence) limit generalizability. The entire pipeline uses virtual H&E converted from fluorescence imaging, not standard H&E. This is a significant limitation for clinical deployment since most pathology labs use conventional H&E staining. The paper does not discuss or validate whether the learned representations transfer to real H&E.
4.U-net decoder architecture is underspecified. Critically, the paper does not specify which intermediate ViT layers from the frozen UNI backbone provide skip connections to the U-net decoder, how many skip connections are used, or the decoder architecture details (layers, channels). Or do you directly use Qformer semantic ebmeddings for segmentation? how do you do that? Since standard ViTs lack the natural multi-scale feature hierarchies of CNNs, how skip connections are constructed for a U-net decoder from a ViT is a non-trivial design choice that directly impacts segmentation quality — and this is entirely undocumented, hindering reproducibility.
5.No survival analysis or time-to-event modeling — binary BCR classification discards censored data. BCR prediction is framed as binary classification rather than survival analysis (Cox regression, C-index), which is the standard approach for recurrence prediction in oncology. This is a significant methodological limitation: the paper mentions excluding slides that “lacked BCR labels,” but in clinical practice many patients are censored (lost to follow-up or have not yet recurred at the time of data collection). Binary classification forces exclusion of censored patients, wasting valuable data and potentially introducing selection bias. Survival analysis methods (e.g., Cox proportional hazards, discrete-time survival models) naturally handle censoring and provide time-to-event predictions that are more clinically actionable than binary yes/no recurrence labels.
6.Batch size for Stage 1 multi-task training is not reported — a critical omission for the InfoNCE alignment loss. The paper does not report the training batch size for Stage 1.While the segmentation, classification, and regression losses work well with small batches, the InfoNCE contrastive alignment loss (L_align) is known to be highly sensitive to batch size. Without knowing the batch size, it is impossible to assess whether the contrastive alignment is properly trained or undertrained, and the result cannot be reproduced.

meta_reviews.text:
This work proposes a multimodal, immune-aware framework for prostate cancer recurrence prediction that combines structured supervision signals, vision-language alignment, and spatial MIL aggregation to learn biologically informed representations from histopathology. Reviewers consistently acknowledge that the problem is clinically meaningful and that the attempt to explicitly model tumor–immune microenvironment interactions is a strong and relevant motivation. The overall pipeline is well-structured and demonstrates thoughtful integration of multiple supervision sources, with the potential to support more interpretable prognostic modeling. The use of histology-only inputs for inference is also noted as a practical advantage.
At the same time, there is a shared concern that the methodological novelty of the work is limited. The proposed approach largely integrates existing components, including multitask learning, vision-language feature alignment, and MIL-based aggregation, into a unified pipeline. While this combination is reasonable and well-engineered, it is not yet fully clear what fundamentally new learning principle or architectural contribution is introduced beyond this integration.
There are also concerns regarding the strength and clarity of the experimental validation. The study is conducted on a relatively small, single-institution cohort, which limits confidence in generalization. Several reviewers also note that the evaluation would benefit from stronger comparison against more recent pathology foundation models and more clinically standard prognostic frameworks. In addition, the use of a binary recurrence formulation instead of time-to-event survival modeling raises questions about clinical completeness, as it discards censoring information that is typically important in oncological prognosis.
Another recurring point is the limited clarity around certain components of the framework. In particular, the role and construction of structured textual supervision, the reliability and interpretation of immune-related annotations, and the relative contribution of each supervision signal are not fully disentangled. This makes it difficult to assess how much of the reported performance gain is driven by biologically meaningful learning versus correlated supervision or model scaling effects. Interpretability claims based on attention maps are also viewed as promising but would benefit from more rigorous validation.
Overall, the submission addresses an important clinical problem and presents a well-motivated multimodal learning framework with clear practical relevance. Despite limitations in novelty and validation breadth, the work is solid, clinically grounded, and of interest to the community. With improved clarity and stronger experimental support, it could represent a meaningful contribution.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and Area Chair for the constructive feedback. Below, we clarify points that may have led to ambiguity in the manuscript.
1.Implementation Details and Architecture (R1, R2, R3):
Stage 1 of our model uses the UNI vision transformer backbone. For segmentation, visual tokens from blocks 3, 6, and 9 are reshaped into spatial maps and projected to 256, 128, and 64 channels, respectively, before being used as decoder skip features. The Q-Former is a compact semantic bottleneck for vision-text alignment: 64 learnable queries attend over image tokens, and the query features are used for auxiliary prediction, image-text alignment, and downstream aggregation. Batch sizes were 32 (Stage 1) and 4 (Stage 2).
2.Data Representation, Captions, and Domain Gap (R1, R2, MR):
The image data consist of prostate tissue microarray (TMA) cores rather than whole biopsy-slide WSIs. Each core includes virtual H&E/histology images generated from DAPI/autofluorescence imaging, paired single-cell-derived tissue maps, immune phenotypes, and structured captions. Captions are rule-based summaries from the single-cell table, including cell counts, cell-type abundance levels, and immune-infiltration phenotypes; they are not free-form manual annotations or generated text. Regarding the virtual H&E domain gap, Deep-IMMA builds on UNI, pretrained on large-scale real H&E WSIs, including prostate pathology data. We agree that real H&E validation would further strengthen generalizability.
3.Survival Analysis and Risk Stratification (R1, R2, MR):
We acknowledge that time-to-event modeling and C-index evaluation are clinically important for predicting recurrence, especially in the presence of censoring. In this study, recurrence prediction was formulated as binary BCR classification to evaluate immune-aware representation learning under a controlled patient-level split. Stage 2 MIL model outputs a continuous recurrence probability, interpretable as a risk score for stratifying recurrence phenotypes. Thus, current results demonstrate risk-discrimination capability, while survival modeling with censoring is outside the scope of the current project.
4.Segmentation Dice and Biological Supervision Reliability (R1, R2):
We agree that the segmentation branch should not be interpreted as a high-accuracy standalone segmentation model. Its role is an auxiliary spatial/semantic anchor for tissue composition and tumor–immune topology, not pixel-perfect boundaries. Structured captions and immune-phenotype labels are derived from single-cell/tissue annotations rather than from predicted segmentation maps. Thus, low boundary-level DICE values do not directly imply that immune supervision itself is unreliable. Ablations in Table 2 suggest that spatially structured supervision and aggregation contribute to discrimination of recurrence risk.
5.Interpretability (R3, MR):
We present attention and immune-pattern maps as evidence. The maps highlight regions with immune-infiltration patterns consistent with known tumor–immune dynamics and help examine which tissue regions contribute to recurrence prediction. Pathologist assessment would further strengthen this interpretation.
6.Baselines Comparison and Contribution (R2, R3, MR)
Broader benchmarking would further strengthen the study. The submitted experiments compare pathology foundation backbones, including UNI, Prov-GigaPath, and H-optimus-0, and evaluate recurrence prediction against logistic regression and ABMIL with targeted ablations (Table 1,2). These analyses were designed to isolate the effects of immune-structured supervision and spatial aggregation within the same patient-level split, rather than to provide exhaustive benchmarking. The main contribution is injecting tumor-relative immune topology into foundation-model adaptation, enabling H&E-only risk discrimination and spatial interpretation.

title: DEER: A Foundation Model with Dual-Branch CT-Enhanced Embeddings for Thoracoabdominal Radiographs
abstract: The chest and abdomen are critical, anatomically complex regions with diverse pathologies, with digital radiography (DR) serving as the primary modality for screening and diagnosis. Developing an effective DR foundation model with strong disease discrimination through self-supervised learning remains a significant challenge. Moreover, prior research has largely overlooked abdominal DR and the potential of computed tomography (CT) localizers as a bridge to fine-grained CT knowledge. In this work, we pioneer the incorporation of large-scale, previously neglected CT localizers and CT reports to train a unified DR foundation model on both chest and abdominal regions. We propose a dual-branch contrastive pretraining approach using 1.1 million DR and 1 million CT localizers, each paired with radiologist reports. By integrating comprehensive knowledge from CT reports, we substantially enhance the model’s capability in DR interpretation. Extensive evaluations on 10 downstream tasks demonstrate the superiority of our model. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first foundational pretraining framework that jointly leverages DR, CT localizers, and reports, scaling to an unprecedented 2.1 million image-report pairs. It offers valuable insights into CT-enhanced intelligent DR diagnosis and scalable multimodal medical foundation models, with demonstrated robustness across diverse clinical tasks. The model is available at https://github.com/sunyh1/DEER.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs
Special Topic -> AI for Neglected Diseases & Limited-Resource Settings
Special Topic -> AI for Population Health, Public Health & Epidemiology

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes DEER, a foundation model for thoracoabdominal digital radiograph (DR) interpretation. The key idea is to use CT localizers as a bridge to incorporate richer diagnostic information from CT reports into DR representation learning. The authors design a dual-branch contrastive learning framework where one branch aligns DR images with DR reports and another aligns CT localizers with CT reports, sharing a ViT backbone. The model is pretrained on 2.1 million image-report pairs (1.1M DR + 1M CT localizers) and evaluated on 10 downstream classification tasks spanning chest, abdomen, pelvis, and spine.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The idea of leveraging CT localizers as a previously overlooked data source is novel and clinically well-motivated. Localizers are routinely acquired during CT scanning but rarely utilized for model training. Pairing them with diagnostically rich CT reports to enhance DR representations is a creative use of existing clinical data. 
2.The scope of evaluation is broad, covering 10 downstream tasks across multiple anatomical regions (chest, abdomen, pelvis, spine) and diverse pathologies (pulmonary diseases, congenital heart diseases, COVID-19, fractures, developmental dysplasia, spondylolisthesis).
The paper addresses the underexplored area of abdominal DR interpretation, which has practical clinical value. Most existing DR foundation models focus exclusively on chest X-rays. 
4.The paper is generally well-written and the figures (especially Fig. 1) effectively communicate the overall framework and data composition.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The dual-branch design is essentially standard CLIP contrastive learning with two separate CLS tokens and projection heads sharing a ViT backbone. The contribution is primarily data-driven (scale and data source) rather than method-driven.
2.The ablation in Fig. 3e only compares “with vs. without localizer,” but adding localizers also adds 1 million extra training samples.
3.Since DR and CT localizer images are not paired (they come from different patients and examinations), the transfer of CT diagnostic knowledge to DR representations relies entirely on implicit sharing through the backbone weights. However, no analysis is provided to verify that this transfer actually occurs. The authors could provide: (a) probing experiments testing whether DR-branch features can predict CT-report entities, (b) attention map comparisons across branches, or (c) feature similarity analysis between the two branches. Without such evidence, the “CT-enhanced” claim remains unsubstantiated.
4.All 10 tasks are classification tasks. For a foundation model built on a CLIP framework, the absence of zero-shot classification and linear probing experiments is a significant gap. These are the standard protocols for evaluating the quality of pretrained representations and would more directly reflect the benefit of pretraining than fine-tuning, which can mask representation quality differences.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents an interesting idea, using CT localizers to enhance DR representations. However, I have several concerns as detailed in the weaknesses section, most notably the limited methodological novelty, the failure to disentangle localizer-specific contributions from data scale effects and the lack of evidence for the claimed cross-branch knowledge transfer.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The manuscript proposes DEER, a foundation model for digital radiography image understanding. DEER adopts a dual-branch cross-modal pretraining strategy, incorporating CT localizers and their corresponding textual reports to enhance DR image representation. The model is pretrained on the largest dataset to date comprising 2.1 million image–report pairs, and its effectiveness is validated across a wide range of downstream tasks covering diverse anatomical regions.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The manuscript leverages CT localizers as a bridge to incorporate the richer information contained in 3D CT reports into the training process, thereby facilitating the understanding of 2D digital radiography images. The resulting dataset constructed under this paradigm is valuable in both modality diversity and scale.
2.A shared encoder is used for DR and CT localizer images, coupled with separate projectors to refine their respective representations, constitutes a reasonable and meaningful dual-branch design.
3.The downstream experiments and evaluation protocols are comprehensive.
4.The manuscript is well-written and generally easy to follow.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The motivation of the manuscript appears to stem from two aspects: (1) the underexplored potential of CT localizers, and (2) the neglect of abdominal DR. In addition, the authors state in the abstract that “Developing an effective DR foundation model with strong disease discrimination through self-supervised learning remains a significant challenge.” While these claims are reasonable, they would benefit from a more detailed discussion and stronger grounding in related work. In particular, it would be helpful to specify which existing models have adopted what types of pretraining strategies, as well as the modality and scale of the datasets used, so that these high-level assertions can be better contextualized and more convincingly supported.
2.The experimental implementation details require more thorough description. For instance, it is unclear whether all models are evaluated under a unified experimental setting or with their individually optimized configurations (e.g., input image resolution), and which datasets lack predefined train–test splits and therefore require cross-validation.
3.The statistical significance analysis presented in this work requires further clarification. For example, how the comparison pairs for the t-test are defined and selected.
4.It can be observed that some downstream tasks exhibit relatively large standard deviations (e.g., COVIDGR and PelviXNet), which in turn lead to higher p-values in the t-test. The underlying reasons for this phenomenon should be further analyzed and explained.
5.Section 3.5 can be regarded as an ablation study evaluating the effect of incorporating LOC into the pretraining process. However, the experimental setup requires more detailed description. In particular, a more rigorous design would control for the scale of pretraining data to ensure that the observed performance gains arise from the additional modality rather than simply from increased data scale. In addition, as I understand that the y-axis in Fig. 3(e) represents percentages, which should be explicitly labeled or clarified to avoid potential confusion.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The manuscript presents a clear motivation, with a well-designed and effective methodology. The downstream experiments cover a broad range of tasks, and the evaluation is comprehensive, with results presented in a clear and objective manner. The paper is well-structured, logically organized, and easy to follow. In addition, the authors’ commitment to releasing the proposed foundation model would constitute a valuable contribution to the community. Although certain aspects require more detailed explanation, likely due to space limitations, the overall coherence and completeness of the pipeline meet the standard for acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The concept of incorporating CT localizers and their corresponding textual reports to enhance DR image representation in this paper is novel, and the proposed method is well-designed and effective.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper’s main contribution is the introduction of DEER, a large-scale thoracoabdominal radiograph foundation model that uses dual-branch contrastive pretraining with DR, CT localizers, and reports to learn more disease-discriminative radiograph representations.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The problem setting is important and clinically meaningful. The paper goes beyond chest-only radiograph foundation models and expands the scope to thoracoabdominal radiographs, with additional transfer evaluation on pelvic and spinal tasks.
2.The use of CT localizers as a bridge is an interesting idea. Leveraging CT localizers and CT reports to enhance DR representations is a novel and intuitively motivated design choice.
3.The scale of pretraining and the breadth of evaluation are strong. The model is pretrained on 2.1 million image-report pairs and evaluated across 10 downstream tasks covering chest, abdomen, pelvis, and lumbar spine.
4.The empirical results are strong. DEER shows competitive or superior performance across multiple datasets, and the paper presents consistent gains from image-report pretraining and additional LOC incorporation.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The source of the performance gain is not sufficiently disentangled. Although the paper emphasizes the architectural advantages of DEER, the proposed method also benefits from substantially larger-scale data and strong pretrained initialization, making it unclear how much of the improvement is truly attributable to the CT-enhanced dual-branch design itself. As a result, the current results do not fully isolate the methodological contribution of the proposed framework.
2.The paper does not fully establish whether LOC and DR are sufficiently distinct to justify separate branch-specific modeling. Since both are fundamentally 2D projection-based radiographic images, it remains unclear whether the observed gains from incorporating LOC reflect true modality complementarity or are instead driven by confounding factors such as increased data scale, richer CT-report supervision, or broader anatomical coverage.
3.A further concern is the potential misalignment between CT localizers and CT reports. Because CT localizers are typically acquired before the actual CT scan for scan planning and field-of-view determination, the final CT coverage may differ from that of the localizer. Consequently, some findings described in the CT report may correspond to regions that are only partially covered, or not visible at all, in the localizer image, which could weaken the assumption that localizers provide well-aligned supervision for report-guided representation learning.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Please refer to the weaknesses.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I have carefully read the authors’ rebuttal and appreciate their effort in providing detailed and thoughtful responses. The rebuttal clarified several aspects that were previously unclear to me. While some concerns remain, to the best of my knowledge, this is the first work to leverage CT line-of-consistency (LOC) in this context. I believe that the proposed formulation may serve as a useful foundation for future studies building on this direction. Therefore, I am willing to raise my score to the acceptable range.

reviewers agree the paper is well motivated, and the main concerns are methodological rather than presentational, reviewers’ concerns should be addressed in rebuttal before acceptance

the reviewers acknowledges the idea is novel, clinically meaningful, and empirically promising, the authors have also addressed reviewers’ concerns well with evidence.
The authors have addressed most of the concerns raised by reviewers. I recommend Accept.

The paper leverages CT localizers and CT reports to enhance thoracoabdominal DR foundation-model pretraining. Although the reviewers raised valid concerns about whether the gains come from LOC-specific knowledge transfer versus added data scale, the rebuttal provided useful clarifications and additional evidence that LOC contributes more effectively than simply adding other modalities or more data. Overall, the work is well motivated and broadly evaluated.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the reviewers for their valuable suggestions and for recognizing the novelty of using LOC and the clinical significance toward thoracoabdominal DR. The final version will be revised accordingly and will include the following information.
Q(R1): Contribution is data-driven rather than method-driven.
A: LOC are visually similar to DR while naturally paired with CT reports, yet they have been largely overlooked in prior research. Our novelty and methodological contribution are identifying LOC as an effective bridge for enhancing DR learning, which may provide useful insights for future foundation model development.
Q(R1, R2, R3): In Fig. 3e, is the improvement brought by LOC due to additional 1M data samples, broader anatomical coverage, or the modality itself?
A: During this work, we conduct exploratory experiments. We did not observe consistent improvements in DR tasks when adding modalities other than LOC. Specifically, we sampled 1M non-DR image-text pairs from MedTrinity-25M, including modalities such as CT and MR across anatomical regions like chest and abdomen. When adding these additional 1M samples to the DR training data, performance decreases (CHD-CXR -0.5%, PelviXNet -0.9%, compared to DEER). On BUU-LSPINE, it decreases -12.4% from DEER, even substantially worse than training without additional data. In contrast, using LOC and CT reports led to improvements, suggesting that the gain mainly comes from LOC and CT reports rather than simply from increasing the data scale. LOC can serve as an additional modality, further boosting DR foundation models beyond large-scale DR datasets.
Q(R1): Zero-shot and linear-probing.
A: We did not include zero-shot evaluation because most of the compared methods are not directly applicable in a zero-shot setting. Since baseline models are not pretrained on abdominal data, we focus on the fine-tuning setting to ensure a fair comparison under MICCAI’s page limit. In fact, as a CLIP framework, DEER has advantages under linear-probing (CHD-CXR +1.4%, PelviXNet +0.6%, over the best baseline).
Q(R3): Justify separate branch-specific modeling.
A: Even though both DR and LOC are 2D projection images, LOC has a lower dose and poorer image quality compared to DR (Fig. 1), resulting in a domain gap. Before full evaluation, we conducted ablation studies on a subset of the data. The results show that directly mixing DR and LOC for joint training without a dual-branch design leads to degraded performance (CHD-CXR -0.5%, PelviXNet -1.2%).
Q(R3): Pretrained initialization.
A: Using pretrained initialization is a standard practice. RAD-DINO & MedGemma are both initialized from large-scale pretrained DINOv2 & Gemma. DEER still outperforms.
Q(R3): LOC and CT reports may not align well.
A: LOC are used for CT scan planning, and in most cases their coverage is broader than the final CT, thereby encompassing anatomy described in the CT report. Even providing only weak supervision, our novelty is introducing largely overlooked LOC into DR model training and boosting performance, as in “Q(R1, R2, R3)”.
Q(R1): Further evidence for knowledge transfer from CT to DR.
A: We appreciate this insightful suggestion. While DEER potentially enables predicting CT report entities, evaluating this would require a DR-CT paired dataset, which is very rare and beyond the scope of this work. Due to page limits, data source limits, and restrictions on supplementary material, we focus the main paper on primary results and key insights. In the future we will explore CT entity prediction (Sec 4), and detailed feature-level analyses.
Q(R2): Implementation details.
A: We use each model’s native pretraining resolution and apply unified settings for fine-tuning. The t-test is performed across runs of different models. For datasets without an official test split, we adopt 5-fold cross-validation and report the mean and std across folds (Sec 3.1). The relatively large std is due to inter-fold variability.

title: Defining Robust Ultrasound Quality Metrics via an Ultrasound Foundation Model
abstract:
Clinicians lack a principled framework to quantify diagnostic utility in ultrasound reconstructions.
Existing standards like PSNR and VGG-LPIPS are inadequate, failing to account for modality-specific physics or the structural nuances of acoustic imaging.
We close this gap with a TinyUSFM-based evaluation framework featuring two distinct metrics: TinyUSFM-uLPIPS, a full-reference perceptual distance based on multi-layer token relations, and TinyUSFM-NRQ, a deployable no-reference quality score utilizing clean-manifold modeling and worst-region aggregation to detect localized harmful artifacts. 
We demonstrate that the presented metrics have four unique advantages: 1) Task-linked quality, where TinyUSFM-uLPIPS achieves superior calibration with semantic task damage, accurately reflecting Dice-score drops in segmentation where VGG-based metrics fail; 2) Cross-organ comparability, maintaining stable scoring scales and consistent severity rankings across diverse anatomical sites and domain-shifted data; 3) PSNR-consistent sensitivity, with TinyUSFM-NRQ providing a reliable quality score without ground-truth images that remains consistent with traditional fidelity benchmarks (i.e. PSNR); and 4) Clinical utility, improving the prediction of expert preference from 47.2% to 72.8% accuracy and producing super-resolution reconstructions preferred by sonographers. By integrating these advantages into a unified assessment and optimization loop, this work establishes a modality-aligned standard that finally bridges the gap between algorithmic performance and diagnostic utility. Our code is available at https://github.com/sextant-fable/US-Metrics.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a TinyUSFM-based framework with full- and no-reference metrics that better capture clinically relevant degradation than standard perceptual measures. It demonstrates improved alignment with task performance and clinician preference.
reviews.text_strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear clinical relevance. Strong use of domain-specific foundation model features, comprehensive evaluation (task-based, cross-organ, clinician study), and practical no-reference metric.
reviews.text_weaknesses: Limited comparison with recent learned IQA methods and reliance on a specific foundation model. Insufficient ablations and limited detail on clinical study and computational cost. The tests were done at very low quality values (PSNR range 20-25).
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
This is globally a good and timely contribution. 
A few clarifications could further strengthen the paper:
Could the authors clarify how their approach compares to more recent learned IQA methods in medical imaging or ultrasound specifically?
To what extent do the gains come from the metric design versus the TinyUSFM backbone? 
Have alternative feature extractors been considered?
Could the authors provide more details on the clinician study (e. g. , number of clinicians, inter-rater agreement, case diversity)?
Additional ablations (e. g. , layer contributions in uLPIPS or aggregation in NRQ) would help better understand key design choices. 
Tests at higher PSNR values would help showing the validity of the metric at different quality ranges.

The paper addresses an important problem in ultrasound imaging and proposes a technically sound and well-motivated solution using foundation model features. The introduction of both full-reference and no-reference metrics, along with strong validation through task-based evaluation and clinician studies, represents a meaningful contribution.
While there are some limitations (e.g., limited comparison with recent methods, lack of ablations, and dependence on a specific model), the work is considered valuable and relevant to the MICCAI community.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces two novel ultrasound metrics: (1) TinyUSFM-uLPIPS: A full-reference perceptual distance metric; (2) TinyUSFM-NRQ: A no-reference quality score. The author systematically validates four key advantages of the framework: task-linked quality, cross-organ comparability, PSNR-consistent sensitivity, and clinical utility. And utilizes the TinyUSFM feature space as a perceptual loss for image super-resolution, producing reconstructions preferred by clinicians.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Methodological Novelty: The core innovation lies in leveraging the feature space of an ultrasound-specific foundation model (as opposed to natural-image models) to define quality metrics. This directly addresses the fundamental issue of domain mismatch. 
2.Comprehensive and Convincing Evaluation: The validation is exceptionally thorough, demonstrating value from multiple complementary angles.
Task-Linked Quality: Using the drop in segmentation Dice score as a “ground truth” to prove the proposed metrics better reflect semantic damage than VGG-LPIPS.
Cross-Organ Generalizability: Testing on a large-scale dataset covering multi-organs demonstrates the stability and comparability of the metrics.
Clinical Alignment: The blinded clinician study increases the accuracy of predicting expert preference from 47.2% to 72.8%.
Optimization Application: Serving as a perceptual loss, it guides the generation of super-resolution images superior in both fidelity and clinical acceptability.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Major concerns:
1.Dependence on the Foundation Model: The framework’s performance and generality heavily rely on the quality and training data of the TinyUSFM model. The paper does not deeply discuss how potential biases in the foundation model itself (e.g., on rare pathologies or images from novel devices) might affect the reliability of the metrics. While inherent to foundation model-based approaches, this should be acknowledged as a limitation.
2.Limitation in Evaluation Scope: Experiments focus primarily on static images. Ultrasound is often used dynamically (e.g., echocardiography, fetal screening). The paper does not explore the metric’s capability to assess dynamic quality factors like temporal consistency or motion artifacts. This is an important future direction but can be noted as a current limitation.
3.Comparison with a Broader Range of NR Methods: While compared with NIQE, BRISQUE, and KDE-UQA, other learning-based methods in medical IQA exist. A more detailed discussion on the distinction and potential advantages of the proposed approach compared to these methods would be beneficial.
Minor concerns:
The presentation of the figures can be more visually appealing, for instance, by reducing the overlap between text and legends (Figures 2 and 3).
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper addresses the critical disconnect between algorithmic metrics and clinical utility in ultrasound imaging, holding high clinical and practical value. And presents the first unified quality assessment framework leveraging an ultrasound foundation model. The design of the two novel metrics is ingenious and tailored to ultrasound physics. The evaluation process is excellently designed, providing a complete evidence chain from numerical simulation, downstream tasks, and cross-domain generalization to blinded clinician studies, making the claims highly convincing.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
