N/A

This paper addresses an impoortant problem - quality analysis in medical imaging. It also shows solutions, which are based on leveraging existing models. Unlike most IQA papers, provisions are made for both the full reference and no reference cases. Experimentally, many uses of the metrics have been shown.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

meta_reviews.text: All three reviewers recommend Acceptance. The consensus is on the significance and novelty of this work, which addresses the critical disconnect between algorithmic metrics and clinical utility in ultrasound imaging. The paper presents the first unified quality assessment framework built upon an ultrasound foundation model, introducing two well-motivated metrics tailored to ultrasound physics that cover both full-reference and no-reference scenarios. The evaluation is comprehensive and convincing, spanning numerical simulations, downstream task performance, cross-domain generalization, and blinded clinician studies, forming a complete evidence chain that strongly supports the claims. For all these reasons, recommendation is towards Acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the reviewers, Area Chairs, and Program Chairs for their careful reading, constructive comments, and positive assessment of our work. We are grateful that the reviewers recognized the significance of addressing the disconnect between conventional algorithmic image-quality metrics and clinical utility in ultrasound imaging, as well as the novelty of using an ultrasound foundation model to define both full-reference and no-reference quality metrics.
The reviewers’ comments provided useful guidance on how to make the paper clearer and more balanced. In the camera-ready version, we will more explicitly discuss the limitations of relying on a TinyUSFM backbone, including potential issues related to foundation-model bias, rare pathologies, unseen devices, and domain shift. We will also sharpen the discussion of related work by comparing our framework more clearly with recent learned IQA methods in medical imaging and ultrasound, and by distinguishing the contributions of the metric design from those of the ultrasound-specific representation.
We will revise the camera-ready manuscript to improve clarity and readability without changing the fundamental content of the work. Specifically, we will add a more explicit limitation discussion on the reliance on TinyUSFM and on the current focus on static ultrasound images, noting dynamic quality factors such as temporal consistency and motion artifacts as important future directions. We will also clarify the clinical study protocol, including reader evaluation details and case diversity, where space permits. In addition, we will improve the presentation quality of the figures and reduce visual clutter, as suggested by the reviewers.
We also appreciate the comments regarding ablations, higher-PSNR settings, and alternative feature extractors. While the final manuscript must remain within the scope of the submitted work, we will make the existing design choices and evaluation scope more transparent, and we will discuss these points as useful directions for future work. Overall, the feedback has helped us better understand how to present the contribution as a clinically motivated, modality-aligned framework for ultrasound image quality assessment, and we thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer again for their constructive evaluation.

title: DeformTTA: Morphology-Aware Controllable Deformation for Test-Time Adaptation in Fetal Cardiac Ultrasound Image Segmentation
abstract: Fetal cardiac segmentation frequently suffers from performance degradation under domain shifts induced by heterogeneous scanners and rapid physiological motion. Standard test-time adaptation (TTA) methods typically rely on generic consistency or entropy minimization, which lack explicit anatomical constraints and fail to preserve biological plausibility under complex cardiac deformations. We propose  DeformTTA, a physiology-driven TTA framework that bolsters segmentation robustness by explicitly modeling cardiac dynamics. Unlike domain-agnostic augmentations,  DeformTTA leverages a deformation network to simulate realistic fetal heart movements, integrated with a generative model for authentic texture synthesis. Furthermore, a morphology-aware shape prior is introduced to regularize the adaptation process, ensuring the structural integrity of the predicted segmentations. By optimizing for motion-conditioned consistency and morphological alignment,  DeformTTA effectively generalizes to target domains during inference. Multi-center experiments demonstrate that  DeformTTA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, particularly in segmenting complex pathological cases. Code is available at https://github.com/SplinterLi/DeformTTA.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Synthetic Data / Data-centric AI

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
(1) Proposes DeformTTA, a physiology-driven TTA framework for fetal cardiac ultrasound segmentation. It integrates explicit anatomical constraints with generative models to address cross-center domain shifts and pathological variations. 
(2) Introduces a morphology-aware regularization mechanism using a BR coefficient. This serves as a mathematical prior to penalize biologically implausible topological deformations during unsupervised inference. 
(3) Develops a structure-centric, controllable morphological deformation module. By operating on Gaussian-smoothed distance fields and utilizing an anatomical gating network, it simulates non-rigid physiological movements for data augmentation. 
(4) Integrates a ControlNet-based conditional generative model into the TTA pipeline. It uses the generated deformation masks to synthesize target-domain style images, reducing interpolation artifacts from standard spatial warping and allowing optimization on consistent cross-view pseudo-samples.
reviews.text_strengths:
(1) Utilizes the BR coefficient as a morphological constraint to maintain the topological integrity of the ventricles and atria, mitigating the boundary collapse issues often observed in standard entropy minimization methods. 
(2) Isolates high-frequency speckle noise from deformation calculations by employing one-hot Gaussian-smoothed fields to guide displacement field generation. 
(3) Implements an effective “deform-then-generate” strategy. By using a fine-tuned ControlNet, it converts geometric deformations into realistic ultrasound images for adaptive optimization. 
(4) Demonstrates strong quantitative performance on a 650-case multi-center dataset. The method performs favorably against established domain generalization algorithms and recent TTA frameworks (including TEGDA), achieving a Mean Dice of 76.38% and reducing HD95 to 4.888 mm.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(1) High Inference Latency: The generative diffusion pipeline (which generates 4 augmented samples and performs 2 gradient steps per test image) adds approximately 3 to 5 seconds of processing time per case. This limits its feasibility for real-time intraoperative clinical applications, restricting its use primarily to offline analysis.
(2) Cold-Start Dependency: The TTA process relies heavily on the accuracy of the initial segmentation prediction from the pre-trained baseline model (nnU-Net). In scenarios with severe domain shifts (drastic probe angle changes or heavy acoustic shadowing), the initial mask may fail entirely. The framework currently lacks an explicit rejection sampling or self-correction mechanism to prevent subsequent error propagation.
(3) Underutilization of Temporal Dynamics: The current approach performs independent adaptation based on 2D static images, treating end-diastolic and end-systolic frames as isolated instances. Despite having a deformation module that simulates motion, the framework does not leverage the inherent temporal consistency present in continuous ultrasound video frames.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

(1) Methodological Justification: The paper presents a logically sound TTA pipeline by combining anatomical priors (BR coefficient) with conditional generative models (ControlNet). Estimating displacement via Gaussian distance fields effectively bypasses speckle noise and models physiological myocardial scaling.
(2) Empirical Justification: The method demonstrates measurable robustness against pathological domain shifts, notably reducing the HD95 metric and performing well on complex congenital heart disease samples (HLHS) compared to recent baselines.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: After reading the authors’ rebuttal, I believe they have adequately addressed my main concerns. Overall, I remain positive about the work and support acceptance.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The author proposed a new framework to tackle the problem of data distribution shift for the problem of fetal echocardiography segmentation. The core idea is to make test-time adaptation anatomy-aware by combining a morphology prior, controllable deformation, and ControlNet-based image synthesis before per-test optimization. The proposed method enables performance gain for segmentation models.
reviews.text_strengths:
THe problem is important and well motivated, where the different aspect of fetal cardiac ultrasound may affect the i.i.d assumption.
The method is domain-informed rather than generic. Using a boundary-regularity shape descriptor, Gaussian-smoothed structural fields, controllable deformation, and motion-conditioned synthesis is more tailored to fetal heart dynamics than plain entropy minimization
The ablation is directionally useful and suggests the deformation module is important, the qualitative figure on page 7 is focused on clinically relevant abnormal cases rather than only easy examples.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
I find the dataset is a bit confusing, the dataset contains scans from two hospitals and also with normal/pathological. THis makes it really hard to tell where the performance gain actually come from.
The ablation text states ControlNet removal changes HD95 from 24.31 to 59.61 mm, but Table 2 reports 4.888 to 11.92 mm. Those cannot both be correct.
“MedSAM [7]” is mentioned, but reference [7] is the LoRA paper, not MedSAM. That is a concrete reference error.
The table 2 shows w/o shape prior regularization, but the objective function doesn’t have any term for this one.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper has a good application, a sensible domain-specific idea, and strong-looking reported gains. But at the current state, I do not think it clears the rigor bar for a top-tier acceptance because too many important pieces are either under-specified or internally inconsistent. With a cleaner and fully specified method section, a disentangled experimental design, corrected tables/references, and stronger statistical evaluation, this could become a competitive MICCAI paper.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
1.The paper proposes DeformTTA, a novel physiology-driven test-time adaptation (TTA) framework designed for fetal cardiac ultrasound segmentation under domain shifts. 
2.It introduces a Boundary Regularity (BR) coefficient to explicitly quantify anatomical morphology, which serves as a standardized shape prior to regularize the adaptation process. 
3.It develops a Controllable Morphological Deformation module that operates on structure-centric Gaussian-smoothed fields. This simulates realistic fetal heart movements while avoiding texture-based overfitting.
4.It integrates a ControlNet-based generative model to synthesize high-fidelity, target-style imagery conditioned on the deformed masks, allowing the model to optimize for motion-conditioned consistency and morphological alignment.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The integration of explicit physiological cardiac dynamics into the TTA process is innovative. Moving away from traditional domain-agnostic generic augmentations or purely entropy-based TTA methods, this work elegantly uses biological priors to prevent catastrophic failure under complex deformations.
2.The introduction of the Boundary Regularity coefficient provides a specific, quantifiable morphological constraint. Formulated as a radial coefficient of variation, it establishes a standardized shape prior that explicitly prevents the adaptation process from yielding biologically implausible shapes.
3.The framework integrates a ControlNet-based generative model into the TTA pipeline to resolve interpolation artifacts common in traditional geometric warping. Conditioned on the deformed masks, the generative model synthesizes artifact-free, target-style images.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.As acknowledged by the authors in the conclusion, the generative TTA process is computationally expensive, adding 3-5 seconds of processing time per case. In the context of ultrasound, which is inherently a real-time imaging modality, this computational bottleneck severely limits immediate clinical deployment.
2.The framework relies on an initial mask to generate structural fields. If the initial model prediction is flawed, the morphology-aware shape prior and the subsequent deformations will be misguided. The paper lacks a fallback or self-correction mechanism to recover from catastrophic initial failures.
3.The methodology does not provide sufficient detail on the pre-training or fine-tuning process of the ControlNet and the Deformation Network.
4.The comparison method is somewhat outdated, with only one from 2025.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The proposed DeformTTA framework introduces a valuable conceptual shift by explicitly incorporating physiology-driven constraints for fetal cardiac ultrasound segmentation under domain shifts. Furthermore, empirical results on a multi-center dataset demonstrate solid improvements over state-of-the-art test-time adaptation baselines. However, there are unaddressed practical limitations: the significant computational overhead restricts its deployment for real-time ultrasound, and the strict dependency on initial prediction quality poses unresolved robustness concerns.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper proposes a physiology-driven test-time adaptation framework for fetal cardiac ultrasound segmentation. Reviewers find the problem clinically important and appreciate the domain-informed design and strong multi-center results. However, they raise concerns about high inference latency that limits real-time use and the strong dependence on initial mask quality. They also note inconsistencies between the tables and text, a misattributed reference, and missing training details. Given these mixed assessments, the paper is invited to rebuttal for the authors to address the concerns.

Two reviewers initially accepting and one weakly rejecting due to internal inconsistencies, missing training details, and a reference error. The rebuttal effectively clarified these issues, including the HD95 inconsistency, citation error, and cold-start robustness, leading all three reviewers to accept post-rebuttal.

This paper proposes a test-time adaptation framework for fetal cardiac ultrasound segmentation. All reviewers agree that the method has merit and that the authors addressed all raised concerns in the rebuttal. I agree with them and recommend acceptance.

The rebuttal was effective: the authors satisfyingly answered most concerns and addressed a few points that needed clarifications. I therefore recommend acceptance.
However, although reducing generation time from 1 to 0.5s is better, it’s not going to permit intra-operative or real time applications, where the time threshold is usually around 200ms for perceptual visual continuum. Moreover, it’s a bit cheap to say “we have run a new baseline but cannot show the results”. This type of claim should be banned because they are not supported by evidence. Nonetheless, as said above, I still find the rebuttal convincing, and the general framework is appealing and well evaluated. I will thus recommend highlighted poster.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback, and address the concerns below.
1.[R1-W1/R3-W1] Inference latency
The computational overhead of our TTA process comes from two parts: 1) Image generation, which is the most time-consuming part. In practice, we can optimize this part by using xFormers + DDIM 2-step + fp16 + torch.compile, reducing time from 1172.7 ms to 451.8 ms per image (2.60x). For 4 representative frames, the runtime drops from about 4.8 s to 1.8 s, with negligible accuracy change (Delta = -0.01%). 2) Model parameter updating, which requires 142 ms for our 2 optimization steps. Furthermore, we can also adapt our method to new domain under per-domain TTA setting. Precisely, we can collect a set of images from the new domain without annotation, and adopt our DeformTTA once offline before online usage on the new domain. This helps to improve the performance on new domain without extra online cost.
2.[R1-W2/R3-W2] Cold-Start Dependency
We further statistically analyze the results by stratifying the initial masks into three categories based on Dice score: Low (<50%), Medium (50%-75%), High (>75%). Our DeformTTA improves the performance for all tiers, even with more gains on the Low tier. This is probably because of two reasons about the generation part in our DeformTTA: 1) The deformation network has chance to make the pseudo-labels closer to optimal segmentation; 2) The diffusion model with ControlNet can generate samples with similar intensity distribution with the new domain, improving the generalization ability of the segmentation network. This explains why our DeformTTA is also effective when initial pseudo-labels are relatively poor.
3.[R1-W3] Temporal dynamics
We agree video-level temporal consistency is important. The current 2D design is constrained by available labels (annotated ED/ES frames without dense temporal correspondence). We will explicitly state this limitation and discuss optical-flow-guided video adaptation as future work.
4.[R2-W1] Dataset design clarity
Our split is intentionally challenging clinical and two-axis shifted: source training set = 200 normal 4CH scans from Hospital-1 (screening center); test set = 450 CHD 4CH scans from Hospital-2 (referral center). Shift comes from both center (scanner/protocol) and pathology (unseen structural abnormality).
5.[R2-W2] HD95 inconsistency: 24.31->59.61 vs 4.888->11.92
We apologize for this mistake. The in-text values were pixel-space HD95 before physical calibration; Table 2 reports clinical HD95 in mm. We will correct this inconsistency and report HD95 consistently in mm.
6.[R2-W3] Citation error (MedSAM vs LoRA)
You are correct. The citation for “fine-tuned MedSAM” should be MedSAM (Ma et al., 2024); LoRA should be cited separately for the fine-tuning strategy. We will correct this into “fine-tuned MedSAM [Ma et al., 2024] with LoRA [7]”, and review the remaining references.
7.[R2-W4] Table 2 vs method naming mismatch
The row “w/o Shape Prior Regularization” actually means removing the smooth loss in Eq. (3) that implements the BR-coefficient-based shape prior. We will rename it to “w/o Smooth Loss (Shape Prior Reg.)” and align wording in the method section for better clarity.
8.[R3-W3] Missing training details
The details of pre-training the deformation network and fine-tuning ControlNet are as follows:
Deformation network: lightweight U-Net (3 encoder/decoder stages, 32 base channels), predicts displacement (u_x, u_y) from Gaussian-smoothed one-hot distance fields, 100 epochs, Adam lr=3e-4, weight decay 1e-4.- ControlNet: SD1.5 initialization, 5,000 steps, source-domain image-mask pairs (200 cases), batch 4, AdamW lr=1e-5, 256x256, RGB-encoded 7-class mask condition.
We will incorporate these details in the revision.
9.[R3-W4] Comparison with more methods
Excellent suggestion. We have compared to the most related TEGDA [31]. Per rebuttal policy, we cannot provide more comparative results in this response.

title: DeGenseGS: Geometrically and Semantically Decoupled Surgical Scene Understanding in 4D Gaussian Splatting
abstract: Real-time, text-promptable 4D reconstruction is indispensable for autonomous surgical interaction. Severe misalignment between semantic meaning and physical anatomy still persists, largely because existing solutions integrate Vision–Language Models into deformable fields via a rigid coupling scheme that tightly binds semantic features to geometric warping. In this paper, we propose DeGenseGS, Geometrically and Semantically Decoupled Surgical Scene Understanding in 4D Gaussian Splatting, a novel framework that independently models semantic evolution and geometric deformation. Specifically, we propose a HexPlane-based spatiotemporal entanglement module that uses shared kinematic latents to synchronize semantic mutations with scene dynamics, while explicitly disentangling semantic updates from geometric deformation. To further ensure robustness against reconstruction artifacts, we devise a Rasterization-Native Semantic Extraction mechanism that infers semantics from topologically continuous feature maps. Additionally, we incorporate an angular-aligned optimization strategy that conforms to the native hyperspherical latent space, thereby preventing semantic distortion. Extensive evaluations on the CholecSeg8k and EndoVis18 datasets demonstrate that DeGenseGS achieves state-of-the-art performance. Our framework yields enhanced geometric completeness and robust semantic-anatomic alignment, enabling spatially continuous segmentation despite drastic tissue deformation and topological transitions.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents DeGenseGS, a text-promptable 4D Gaussian Splatting framework that explicitly decouples geometric deformation and semantic evolution for dynamic surgical scene understanding. Specifically, it introduces a Kinematics-Conditioned Latent Disentanglement module built on HexPlane, which leverages shared kinematic latents to separate geometric and semantic optimization branches, thereby eliminating spurious geometric warping caused by dominant semantic gradients. In addition, the paper proposes a Rasterization-Native Semantic Extraction mechanism that directly extracts semantics from 2D rasterized feature maps with topological continuity and under the structural guidance of RGB images, generating robust and hole-free segmentation masks. To enhance semantic stability in highly deformable scenes, it also introduces Angular-Aligned Semantic Distillation to regularize the vision-language model latent space in the hypersphere domain, effectively mitigating feature collapse. Experiments demonstrate that DeGenseGS achieves state-of-the-art performance on the CholecSeg8k and EndoVis18 datasets, with clear advantages in handling severe tissue deformation and topological changes such as surgical cauterization.
reviews.text_strengths:
Strengths:
(1) Existing 4DGS methods tightly couple semantics and geometry in a single deformation branch, leading to severe gradient interference and false geometric warping during semantic mutation. DeGenseGS explicitly disentangle these two processes in 4DGS for surgery. It uses shared kinematic latents to enable independent geometric and semantic decoding, which is a novel paradigm that fundamentally solves the misalignment problem. 
(2) Instead of extracting semantics from 3D Gaussians directly, this work proposes to infer semantics from topologically continuous 2D rasterized feature maps, combining superpixel aggregation and edge-preserving filtering. This design is original for 4DGS and effectively improves boundary accuracy and robustness against reconstruction artifacts, which is critical for clinical applications. 
(3) The paper formulates semantic distillation as angular similarity learning in the native hyperspherical latent space, rather than simple L2 loss. This is a novel optimization strategy for open-vocabulary 4D reconstruction, which effectively prevents semantic distortion and feature collapse in dynamic scenes. 
(4) Extensive comparisons against SOTA methods (LangSplat, OpenGaussian, SurgTPGS, etc. ). Validated on two standard surgical benchmarks: CholecSeg8k and EndoVis18.Clear ablation studies verifying each core component. Quantitative gains are substantial: +14.74% mIoU over the best baseline on CholecSeg8k. Qualitative results show consistent improvement in deformed and topological-changing regions.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Weaknesses:
(1) The abstract claims “real-time” reconstruction, but the paper does not report FPS, inference time, or rendering speed. Readers cannot verify whether the method meets the real-time requirement for intraoperative usage. 
(2) The paper only qualitatively explains that decoupling reduces gradient interference, but lacks quantitative gradient analysis, e. g. , gradient norm comparison between coupled and decoupled modes. The theoretical justification for why semantic gradients no longer distort geometry is not fully supported. 
(3) The paper mentions “Open-Vocabulary” and “Text-Promptable” capabilities. However, the evaluation (Tables 1 and 2) focuses on standard segmentation classes (Gallbladder, Instruments, etc. ). There is a lack of qualitative results showing the system’s performance on truly unseen or arbitrary text prompts. If the evaluation is restricted to pre-defined classes present in the dataset, the “Open-Vocabulary” aspect is not fully demonstrated beyond standard semantic segmentation. 
(4) The authors have not released the source code. For the better development of the community, the authors are encouraged to make their code publicly available, which will also facilitate the reproduction of the proposed method and fair comparisons among peers.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper proposes DeGenseGS for 4D surgical scene understanding, which novely decouples geometry and semantics to avoid false warping. It has solid technical designs including a HexPlane-based disentanglement module, rasterization-native extraction, and angular-aligned distillation. Experiments show significant performance gains over SOTA methods on standard surgical benchmarks with convincing ablation studies. However, it overclaims open-vocabulary ability, lacks real-time speed verification, has insufficient theoretical analysis, and does not release code. Overall, the work is innovative and effective with clear clinical value, so I give weakly accept.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Based on the authors’ rebuttal, the concerns have been addressed. Acceptance is recommended. However, it is still suggested that the authors consider open-sourcing their work.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces DeGenseGS, a 4D Gaussian Splatting framework designed for surgical scene understanding, with the central methodology stemming from decoupling geometric deformation from semantic evolution. For this aim, the work introduces the Rasterization-Native Semantic Extraction mechanism and the Manifold-Aligned Optimization strategy, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method.
reviews.text_strengths:
-Interesting point of view: The work identifies a meaningful issue in dynamic surgical scenes: semantic changes do not necessarily imply geometric deformation. The example illustrated in Fig. 1 clearly demonstrates this mismatch and provides an intuitive motivation.
-Clear empirical improvements over the strongest baseline:
On the CholecSeg8k/EndoVis18 datasets, the method consistently demonstrates meaningful improvement.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
-The central “decoupling” claim is intuitively reasonable but insufficiently validated. Specifically, in Table 3, the authors define S-G Decoupling as the combination of Section 2.2 (the actual ‘decoupling’ idea) and Section 2.4 (RNSE post-processing, if I understand properly), and ablate both jointly — not sure how much improvement can be attributed to the core decoupling idea.
-The method description is unclear and a bit incomplete at the implementation level, especially for the textural/semantic feature parts, and the total losses to train the Gaussian (the pipeline shows rendered RGB and depth, but does not refer to how they are specifically used). If i understand correctly, the semantic attribute per gaussian is dynamically predicted at each timestep? and the loss for training the gaussian attributes contains rgb rendering err and depth rendering err or? A revision of the methodology presentation can help the readers to better understand the method.
-A bit overclaim(?): 
1)The title identifies the work to address ‘surgical scene understanding’, while from the content, only prompt-instructed-segmentation is considered as the downstream task for the Gaussians.
2) The performance of OpenGaussian is insanely low—would be good to include some discussion or more background regarding how these baselines are set up.
-Others: obvious mistakes in Tab 1 and Tab 2 of the best bolded values. Reference 23 is wrongly placed for SurgTPGS. Pipeline figure quality should be improved(e.g., the way to plot a Gaussian in the attributes ).
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

As mentioned in the weakness:
1)The ablation combines the actual decoupling module with RNSE, making it unclear how much of the improvement truly comes from the proposed disentanglement. 
2)The methodology description is somewhat incomplete—particularly regarding the semantic feature representation and the training losses—making it difficult to clearly understand the optimization pipeline.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The reviewers’ concerns have been largely addressed. While the reviewer still highly suggests revising the framing as a segmentation method rather than the much broader ‘scene understanding’ at its current state.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes DeGenseGS, a 4D Gaussian Splatting framework that introduces semantic understanding into a dynamic surgical scene reconstruction pipeline and ultimately enables semantic segmentation.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Problem to solve is meaningful in surgical scenes, where semantic change and geometric deformation are often not well aligned.
2.The reported results are promising, with clear improvements over prior baselines, and the ablation supports the effectiveness of the main design.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The contribution is presented somewhat diffusely. The paper discusses dynamic reconstruction, 3D semantics, and text-promptable understanding, while the final evaluation is still mainly based on 2D segmentation results. The authors should better highlight the paper’s own core contribution and, in particular, clarify the actual difference from SurgTPGS.
2.The paper claims that the method can avoid spurious geometric displacement, but does not provide basic reconstruction comparisons to directly support this point. If improved geometric stability is part of the contribution, it should be evaluated more explicitly.
3.Important practical statistics are missing: runtime-related results such as FPS should be reported since the authors mentioned ‘real-time’ is important.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1.The current 2D datasets are not sufficient to fully evaluate 3D semantics, and they also limit the demonstration of the method’s full capability. It would be better to include dedicated 3D evaluation in the future, for example using simulated or ex vivo data.
2.The “first” claim could be worded more carefully. My concern is not necessarily overclaiming, but that the statement is qualified by too many conditions, making the novelty positioning less clear.

This paper addresses a meaningful problem in dynamic surgical scene understanding and presents a reasonably method that gains over strong baselines. Although I still have some concerns about the novelty positioning and the lack of more direct reconstruction/runtime evaluation, I think the overall contribution is solid and relevant for acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Thank you for the response. The response addresses my main concerns. The clarification of the difference from SurgTPGS and the reported runtime numbers make the contribution and practicality clearer. I still think direct 3D/4D geometric evaluation would better support the claim of improved geometric stability, but this does not change my overall assessment. I am satisfied with the rebuttal and maintain my recommendation.

meta_reviews.text:
While reviewers agree on the overall contribution, they question on ablation performed, lack of direct reconstruction comparison in 4D/3D sense and runtime evaluation.

Authors addressed the reviewers concerns and all reviewers suggested for acceptance. It is suggested that authors maintain reproducibility through open source code and datasets. Also, R2 suggestion on revising the framing as a segmentation method rather than scene understanding.
All reviewers suggest the acceptance of this paper as the rebuttal addressed their main concerns.

After reviewing the rebuttal letter and reviewers’ post-rebuttal comments, I recommend the paper for acceptance. The authors are suggested to open-sourcing thier work and perform the 3D/4D geometric evaluation before the camera-ready submission.

author_feedback_text:
We thank reviewers and are encouraged by your positive comments on novel paradigm, meaningful motivation, and substantial gains. Below we address main concerns. Code will be released upon acceptance.
1.Running time. (R1, R3) DeGenseGS renders at 70 FPS; full text-prompted querying with VLM matching and RNSE takes ~0.56s/frame, on par with SurgTPGS[15] at 67 FPS and 0.6s/frame. Will be reported.
2.Task definition. (R1) We agree that Open-Vocabulary is inappropriate and will rephrase it to Text-Promptable throughout. Following SurgTPGS, all baselines use the same CLIP-style prompts on standard surgical classes for fair comparison. Unseen prompts will be evaluated in the extension.
3.Theoretical justification of decoupling. (R1) Eq. 2 decodes ΔG and Δf_sem via independent branches. By the chain rule, the two gradients do not interfere, resolving the gradient-interference issue of PCGrad[21] architecturally. It preserves only motion-consistent components as a shared inductive bias. Formal proof will be added in Sec. 2.2.4.Ablation of KCLD and RNSE. (R2) Following the reviewer, we report the individual effect of each module. KCLD alone gives 64.19/41.02 on CholecSeg8k/EndoVis18 and RNSE alone gives 56.84/40.54, both over the baseline in Tab. 3 row 1.KCLD contributes a larger gain via gradient-level decoupling, while RNSE corrects 2D readout artifacts. They are complementary and the full model (row 4) is best. This will be added to Tab. 3.5.Method description. (R2) The semantic attribute is dynamically predicted per timestep: each Gaussian stores a base semantic feature, and the semantic branch predicts a per-timestamp residual that is alpha-blended into the rendered semantic map. For training, the rendered RGB and stereo depth errors supervise the geometry branch, while semantic alignment and smoothness losses supervise the semantic branch only, acting on disjoint parameters and realizing decoupling at the loss level. We will clarify the methodology accordingly.
6.Scene understanding framing. (R2) Our method is essentially an interactive segmentation framework: beyond text prompts, it can also segment the scene without any prompt and output masks with corresponding instances, which is itself a form of scene understanding. We will adjust the claim accordingly.
7.OpenGaussian baseline. (R2) Designed for static 3D scenes, its instance-level semantic association is fragile under deformation, occlusion, and topology change, causing unstable labels and near-zero masks. We followed official settings and tuned key hyperparameters; similar low results are reported in SurgTPGS on dynamic data. Setup details will be added.
8.Minor fixes. (R2) All noted issues, including bolded values in Tab. 1/2, the misplaced Ref. 23, and pipeline figure quality, will be fixed.
9.Difference from SurgTPGS. (R3) Our core contribution is geometry-semantic decoupling in dynamic 4DGS. SurgTPGS tracks semantic features with deformation, so semantic change may still be coupled with geometric motion. We instead share kinematic conditioning but use separate geometry and semantic branches, so appearance changes like cauterization do not cause false deformation. Theoretical analysis: see #3.10.Reconstruction comparison. (R3) DeGenseGS gains +1.06 PSNR, +0.030 SSIM, −0.0010 LPIPS over SurgTPGS, while segmentation improves much more, +14.74 mIoU. With ablation and qualitative results, the gain mainly comes from geometry-semantic decoupling rather than RGB reconstruction.
11.Segmentation evaluation. (R3) We follow the task setting of SurgTPGS and related work for fair comparison. The 2D segmentation is performed on views rendered from 4DGS, and is the prerequisite for downstream tasks such as instrument tracking and VQA. Currently, semantics for dynamic 3D reconstruction are mainly evaluated on 2D datasets, as no 3D semantic ground truth is available. Dedicated 3D evaluation on simulated or ex vivo data will be added in the extension.

title: Demographic-Conditioned State Space Models for ECG-Based Age Estimation
abstract: This study introduces a novel demographic-conditioned architecture that leverages Mamba2 State Space Models (SSMs) and a dual Attention Aggregation mechanism to integrate 12-lead ECGs with patient sex metadata for biological age estimation (ECG-age). The architecture efficiently captures long-range physiological dependencies, while an attention-based aggregation mechanism renders the model invariant to lead availability and signal duration. Trained on the full CODE cohort (N=1.3 million) and validated on the CODE-15% test set (N=233k), the model achieves a mean absolute error of 6.72±5.81 years (R^2=0.80) in chronological age prediction. This performance surpasses a common used 1D-ResNet baseline (8.44±7.12 years, R^2=0.69). This improved precision strengthens ECG-age as a prognostic biomarker: patient hearts predicted to be over 8 years older than their chronological age exhibited a higher Hazard Ratio (HR) for all-cause mortality (HR 2.06, 95% CI 1.92-2.21) compared to the 1D-ResNet baseline (HR 1.80, 95% CI 1.68-1.92) on the CODE-15% test set. These results demonstrate that the SSM-based architecture yields an ECG-age marker that is prognostically superior to current baseline models. Code is available at: https://github.com/B-Bracke/demographic-ssm-ecg-age
subject_areas: Applications -> Outcome Prediction / Prognosis / Longitudinal Modeling
Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs
Modalities -> EEG / MEG / ECG / Physiological Signals

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a multimodal state space model for predicting biological (ECG-derived) age from electrocardiograms. The model employs a convolutional stem followed by a bidirectional Mamba2-based backbone with adaptive layer normalization and dual-axis attention aggregation. The framework incorporates biological sex metadata for conditioning and is evaluated on a large-scale ECG dataset (CODE, N≈1.3M), with external validation on SaMi-Trop. The study compares sex-conditioned and sex-agnostic variants and evaluates downstream associations with mortality risk using hazard ratios.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper leverages a very large-scale dataset (CODE), which is a significant strength and provides strong statistical power.
The proposed architecture adopts modern sequence modeling techniques (state space models and attention-based aggregation), which are relevant for long ECG signals.
The inclusion of external validation (SaMi-Trop) and survival analysis (hazard ratios based on ECG-age deviation) goes beyond simple regression metrics and connects the task to clinical outcomes.
The comparison between sex-conditioned and sex-agnostic modeling provides an interesting and practically relevant perspective.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Limited comparison with more recent approaches
While there is no clearly established state-of-the-art benchmark for ECG-age prediction, comparisons are primarily limited to an earlier baseline (i. e. , the 2021 1D-ResNet-based model). As a result, it is difficult to assess how the proposed method relates to more recent advances in ECG representation learning.
2.Generalization limitations on external data
Although the proposed model shows improved performance and stronger risk stratification on the CODE dataset, the generalization to external data (SaMi-Trop) is limited, with relatively low R² values (0.35–0.38) and lack of statistically significant hazard ratio results. This weakens the overall robustness of the findings.
3.Limited strength of clinical impact
The paper includes discussion on prognostic value and demonstrates improved risk stratification compared to the baseline. However, the overall impact remains somewhat limited, as the improvements are not consistently supported across datasets, particularly in external validation.
4.Incremental problem formulation
The work follows the established paradigm of ECG-based biological age estimation. While the proposed architecture incorporates modern modeling techniques, the overall problem formulation remains similar to prior work, limiting the novelty of the contribution.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a well-executed study with a modern modeling approach and leverages a very large dataset, which is a significant strength. The problem is relevant, and the inclusion of survival analysis adds clinical context. 
However, the overall contribution is somewhat incremental, and it remains unclear whether the observed improvements in ECG-age prediction translate into meaningful clinical benefits. The limited comparison with recent methods and reduced generalization on external data further weaken the claims. 
Despite these limitations, the scale of the study and the engineering contribution make it a valuable addition, and it falls slightly above the acceptance threshold.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: After reading the rebuttal, I maintain my original Weak Accept-level recommendation. The authors reasonably clarified the rationale for the baseline and dataset choices, but the lack of comparisons with recent Transformer/SSM-based ECG models and the weaker external validation results remain limitations of the submitted paper. Overall, the paper is still slightly above the acceptance threshold due to its large-scale evaluation, modern modeling approach, external validation, and survival analysis.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of the paper is the development of an ECG-based age prediction model built on a State Space Model (Mamba) backbone with a dual attention aggregation mechanism. The goal is to estimate ECG-based (biological) age from 12-lead ECGs, optionally together with patient sex metadata. The model is trained on a big cohort of ECGs and shows improvement over baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper is written in clear language and is easy to follow.
2.The motivation and idea are clear and well-explained. Predicting biological age from ECG is, in my view, a strong and interesting idea with potential clinical relevance.
3.The use of a large dataset makes the results more reliable and increases confidence in the overall findings.
4.The observation that sex-agnostic prediction performs similarly to, or comparably to, sex-conditioned prediction is valuable.
5.All implementation details are provided, making this work reproducible.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The claim of methodological novelty is not fully convincing, as related ECG works using Mamba/SSMs (e.g., ECGMamba, S2M2ECG) exist and are not discussed. Even if recent, they should at least be referenced.
2.The choice of baselines is limited. In particular, a Transformer/ViT-style baseline (e.g., convolutional stem + transformer backbone), which is now common in ECG modelling, is missing.
3.The choice of 400 Hz sampling rate is not justified, especially since 100 Hz and 500 Hz are more standard in the literature.
4.While the paper mentions interpretability via temporal and lead attention, no qualitative analysis is shown. In my view, once it is included in the figure and mentioned in the text, it is important to demonstrate which patterns the model attends to and whether they are clinically meaningful.
5.Regarding the reported improvements: while the model reduces MAE (e.g., from ~8.4 to ~6.7 years), it is unclear whether this difference is clinically meaningful. For me, it is questionable whether distinguishing between, for example, a 9-year vs. 7-year age gap would materially affect clinical decision-making.
6.The use of the term “multimodal” may be somewhat overstated, as the model incorporates only a single scalar metadata variable (sex) alongside the ECG signal, rather than multiple high-dimensional or semantically distinct modalities.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Mentioned references:
1.ECGMamba: Towards Efficient ECG Classification with BiSSM - https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10098
2.S2M2ECG: Spatio-temporal bi-directional State Space Model Enabled Multi-branch Mamba for ECG - https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.03066
3.MSECG: Incorporating Mamba for Robust and Efficient ECG Super-Resolution - https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.04861

Thanks to the authors for the work.
I believe the work is well motivated and built around a strong idea. The paper is easy to follow and clearly written. The results appear reliable, supported by training on a large-scale cohort. I found the observation that the raw ECG signal may already capture sex-related physiological differences both interesting and potentially clinically relevant.
The main weaknesses are the limited set of baselines and the related work discussion. In particular, the lack of comparison with a ViT/Transformer-based approach is a notable omission, given its current relevance in ECG modelling. Additionally, similar recent works using Mamba/SSM architectures are not referenced or discussed, which weakens the novelty claim.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The author’s feedback partially addresses my concerns, and I would keep a positive recommendation.
The authors clarify the choice of baseline, the 400 Hz sampling rate, and the use of the term “multimodal,” which I find reasonable.
However, I still think the clinical utility of the MAE improvement is not fully resolved. The rebuttal states that MAE decreases from 8.44 to 6.72 years, with reduced variance and improved hazard ratios. This supports better statistical performance, but it still does not fully explain how clinical decision-making would change in practice. For example, it remains unclear whether distinguishing between a predicted ECG-age gap of approximately 7 years versus 8–9 years would lead to different clinical actions. I therefore think the paper should frame ECG-age mainly as an adjunctive prognostic or screening signal, rather than implying direct clinical actionability.
The authors state that the main difference from prior ECG SSM models is the dual attention aggregation mechanism. However, this is not analyzed in the paper. Without isolating the contribution of the attention module, it is difficult to know whether the performance gain comes from this component specifically, from the backbone, from dataset scale, or from other implementation choices.
Overall, despite these limitations, the work is well executed, uses a large-scale dataset, and presents useful results. I would maintain my Weak Accept recommendation.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
o Proposes a novel multimodal architecture for ECG-based biological age estimation that combines convolutional feature extraction with bidirectional Mamba 2 state space models to capture long-range temporal dependencies in 12 lead ECG signals (fusing ECG features with biological sex)
o Integrates patient metadata (sex) via adaptive layer normalisation, and evaluates both sex-conditioned and sex-agnostic inference strategies
o Trains and evaluates the model at scale on the large (1.3M recordings) CODE cohort, with internal validation on CODE 15 and external validation on the SaMi Trop cohort
o Demonstrates improved age estimation over a 1D ResNet baseline
reviews.text_strengths:
o Well written and well structured
o Proposes a novel and well-articulated architecture combining bidirectional state space models with attention-based aggregation for long ECG sequences
o Strong technical motivation for architectural choices, which are all clearly explained step by step
o Trained and evaluated on a very large-scale dataset with additional external validation, which strengthens the empirical credibility
o Demonstrates consistent improvements over a commonly used 1D‑ResNet baseline for age prediction and prognostic stratification
reviews.text_weaknesses:
o Clinical utility is insufficiently justified. The model’s MAE (~7 years) is close to the 8‑year ECG‑age threshold used for prognostic stratification. This raises concerns about misclassification across the ±8 year boundary, and potential overinterpretation in clinical settings, purely due to prediction noise. In practice, this high error may over- or under-alarm clinicians/patients
o The term “multimodal” appears overstated, as the only non‑ECG input is biological sex, which provides limited additional information and appears redundant in some experiments
o While conceptually interesting, the high prediction error limits near-term clinical applicability, reducing the relevance of the contributions for MICCAI’s translational focus
o The discussion does not sufficiently address how ECG‑age predictions should be used responsibly in practice, given the observed uncertainty
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Molecular profiling (e.g., proteomics) is limited currently, but it may well become more widely available as evidence builds supporting its use in organ age profiling, e.g., work by Tony Wyss-Coray’s team!
The experimental design is sound and includes large-scale training and external validation.

This is a technically strong and thoughtfully designed study with a clear methodological contribution. However, the clinical value proposition is not yet convincing: the prediction error remains high relative to the prognostic threshold, the multimodal aspect is limited, and the practical implications of ECG‑age estimates are insufficiently discussed. As a result, the work appears promising but premature for acceptance at MICCAI in its current form.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text:
The reviews are mixed, with two weak-accept recommendations and one weak-reject recommendation. The paper presents a SSM/Mamba-based architecture for ECG-based age estimation, trained on a large CODE cohort and evaluated with both internal and external validation. The reviewers recognize several strengths, including the scale of the study, clear architecture, improved regression performance over a 1D-ResNet baseline, sex-conditioned versus sex-agnostic analysis, and the inclusion of survival analysis for prognostic relevance.
However, the reviewers raise several important concerns. The main issues are: (1) the methodological novelty is incremental, and related recent ECG Mamba/SSM and Transformer-style baselines are not sufficiently discussed or compared; (2) the external validation results are weaker than the internal results, with limited R2 and less consistent prognostic significance on SaMi-Trop; (3) the clinical utility of the ECG-age gap remains insufficiently justified, especially given that the MAE is close to the 8-year prognostic threshold; and (4) the term “multimodal” may be overstated because the only non-ECG input is biological sex, and the interpretability claims based on attention are not yet supported by qualitative analysis.

After considering the reviews and rebuttal, I recommend acceptance.
The rebuttal reasonably clarifies the baseline choice, the use of the CODE-standard 400 Hz sampling rate, the expected domain gap on SaMi-Trop, and the intended role of ECG-age as an adjunctive prognostic or screening signal rather than a standalone clinical decision tool. The authors also agree to tone down the “multimodal” framing. Important limitations remain, including incremental novelty, lack of recent Transformer/SSM ECG baselines, weaker external validation, and limited evidence for clinical actionability. Nevertheless, given the scale, reproducibility, external evaluation, and generally positive reviewer opinions, the paper is above the acceptance threshold.

Although evaluation with newer methods is mentioned, the reviewers concur that this is a paper with a comprehensive evaluation. The survival analysis is relevant for a clinical application of age estimation. My assessment is that the positive aspects outweigh the weaknesses, so I suggest acceptance.

This is an interesting and clinically relevant study, particularly in using ECG-age for mortality risk stratification and testing generalization in a severe-pathology cohort. Although the “multimodal” claim should be toned down and broader SSM/Transformer baselines would strengthen the work, the rebuttal reasonably addresses the main concerns, and the reported improvements in MAE, variance reduction, and hazard ratio suggest meaningful potential clinical value.

author_feedback_text:
General Response to All Reviewers:
We sincerely thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback. We agree that further evaluations are vital. However, due to MICCAI’s strict 8-page limit, we carefully scoped this submission as a foundational proof-of-concept. What separates our approach from prior ECG SSM models is our unique dual attention aggregation mechanism, which ensures robustness against varying signal durations and missing leads, coupled with a flexible integration mechanism for tabular metadata. Specific concerns are addressed below.
——-
1.Baselines, Dataset Selection, and Future Cohorts (Reviewers 1 & 2)
Critique: Missing comparisons to Transformers and SSM-based models, and limited external generalization.
Response: We acknowledge the omission of recent parallel SSM works and will add references to ECGMamba, S2M2ECG, and MSECG in the revision. We selected the 1D-ResNet as our primary baseline because it is the seminal architecture published alongside the CODE and SaMi-Trop datasets, enabling a direct and rigorous comparison on the exact same data splits. Furthermore, validating the prognostic value of ECG-age requires large-scale datasets linked with long-term mortality data, which exclude public sets like PTB-XL. Because SaMi-Trop is a severe-pathology cohort (Chagas cardiomyopathy) with double the mortality rate of the training data, a domain gap and performance drop are expected. To address this and conduct broader validations, we are applying for data access to the Harvard-Emory ECG Database (10M ECGs), the SHIP and HNR cohorts (Germany), and MIMIC-IV. Extensive benchmarking against recent Transformers and SSMs on these diverse cohorts is underway for a journal extension.
2.Clinical Utility vs. MAE (Reviewers 2 & 3)
Critique: Is a drop in MAE clinically meaningful given the 8-year threshold? Could this cause misclassification?
Response: We understand the concern regarding prediction noise near the 8-year threshold. However, the MAE reduction (8.44 to 6.72) is coupled with a substantial variance reduction (SD dropped from 7.12 to 5.81). This tighter error distribution means fewer patients are misclassified across the ±8-year boundary due to random noise. This precision drives our statistical improvement in risk stratification (HRs for all-cause mortality improved from 1.80 to 2.06). We will clarify that ECG-age is intended as an adjunctive screening flag in routine exams, not a standalone diagnostic, mitigating false alarm risks
3.The “Multimodal” Label (Reviewers 2 & 3)
Critique: “Multimodal” is overstated since the only non-ECG input is biological sex.
Response: We agree that utilizing only biological sex limits the traditional scope of “multimodal.” Our intention was to propose a foundational architecture capable of deep metadata fusion that can scale with high-dimensional metadata (e.g., extensive comorbidities) in future work. We will tone down the “multimodal” claims in the text and are open to adjusting the title (e.g., “Demographic-Conditioned”).
4.Technical Specifics: 400 Hz and Explainability (Reviewer 2)
Critique: Why a 400 Hz sampling rate, and where are the attention visualizations?
Response:
400 Hz Sampling Rate: While 500 Hz is standard clinically, 400 Hz is the native preprocessing standard established by the CODE dataset authors. To maintain strict comparability with the 1D-ResNet baseline, we adhered to the same dataset-specific sampling rate.
Explainability: We agree visual explainability is crucial. However, merely overlaying attention weights onto ECG signals without rigorous clinical context can be misleading. Proper analysis requires carefully linking scores to established physiological ECG features. Due to the 8-page limit, we lacked the necessary space for this evaluation. A comprehensive interpretability analysis is a core component of our planned extended journal submission

title: DenseTRF: Texture-Aware Unsupervised Representation Adaptation for Surgical Scene Dense Prediction
abstract: Dense prediction tasks in surgical computer vision, such as segmentation and surgical zone prediction, can provide valuable guidance for laparoscopic and robotic surgery. However, these models often suffer from distribution shifts, as training datasets rarely cover the variability encountered during deployment, leading to poor generalization. We propose Dense TRF, a self-supervised representation adaptation framework based on texture-centric attention. Our method leverages slot attention to learn texture-aware representations that capture invariant visual structures. By adapting these representations to the target distribution without supervision, DenseTRF significantly improves robustness to domain shifts. The framework is implemented through conditioning dense prediction on slot attention and model merging strategies. Experiments across multiple surgical procedures demonstrate improved cross-distribution generalization in comparison to state of art segmentation models and test distribution adaptation method for dense prediction tasks.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This work presents a pixel-wise prediction framework for surgical image segmentation based on transformer-derived visual features combined with slot-based object-centric representations to capture invariant visual structures. Additionally, it incorporates a domain adaptation mechanism that combines representations learned from multi-domain data with target-specific adaptation, enabling improved robustness to domain variability across different surgical settings.
reviews.text_strengths:
This work addresses the important challenge of domain-specific adaptation in surgical imaging, proposing a framework that adapts representations to center- or domain-specific variability.
Additionally, the experimental evaluation is exhaustive. The method is compared against a wide range of baselines, including both conventional segmentation architectures and foundation models, and is evaluated across multiple datasets, varying data regimes, and a abblation study.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Although the proposed method demonstrates improved performance over the evaluated baselines, the analysis is limited to frame-wise metrics and does not consider temporal consistency. In surgical video applications, temporal stability is an important factor, as predictions should be coherent across consecutive frames. The paper would benefit from an evaluation of temporal consistency and potentially from incorporating mechanisms to enforce temporal coherence. But it could be for a next version of the method.
Additionally, the performance (IoU, DICE) remains relatively modest. The paper lacks a discussion explaining the underlying reasons for these limitations and does not provide insights into potential improvements for both segmentation accuracy and temporal stability in future work.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The work addresses an important challenge in surgical image analysis, namely domain-specific adaptation, and proposes a well-motivated framework based on slot representations. The experimental evaluation is comprehensive, including comparisons with both conventional methods and foundation models across multiple datasets and data regimes.
However, the paper would benefit from a clearer discussion of the moderate performance (e.g., IoU and DICE) and from outlining future directions, particularly regarding improvements in segmentation accuracy and temporal consistency.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper describes a general framework based on Slot Attention to adapt the dense features from a pre-trained encoder such that downstream dense predictions improve robustness to domain shifts.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper describes an interesting adaptation framework, that clearly shows significant improvement on robustness to domain-shifts.
Conceptually the method is sound and make sense.
The results certainly are convincing. At low data regime, this adaptation framework seems to significantly bump performance on target domains.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The framework remains complex and the figure and text lack some clarity. Some learning curriculum details remain unclear.
During the continual learning phase, it is quite unclear from the text and figure (Sec. 2.2) which modules are frozen (encoder? dense head?), how the branches are initialised (from the base branch? both branches training at same speed?)
The other big question is: after each adaptation round, parameters are averaged between branch. The resulting parameters are applied to what? the target branch? both branches? I would assume only the target branch. But then why not applying a exponential moving average? these abrupt parameter changes will throw the stochastic gradient descent all over the place I would assume
The term texture centric is only justified by the patch permutation during continual training phase.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
improvements on figures would benefit the camera-ready: make it clear what is learnt at what stage etc
Another unclear point: at comparison with foundation model adaptations, how are these trained? on base distribution only? at low data regime? 
In other words: you are comparing (1) a foundation model that has never seen the target domain images to (2) your adapted framework that was trained on (un-labelled) target domain?

The factors leading to that score are:
the method and goals are clear
some learning curriculum details are unclear
the framework remains complex
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes DenseTRF, a framework for unsupervised test-distribution adaptation in surgical dense prediction tasks. The core idea is to use slot attention to learn texture-aware, object-centric representations via reconstruction, then adapt these representations to target deployment distributions using only unlabeled data. Experiments on three surgical datasets under extreme low-data regimes show improvements over segmentation architectures and foundation model baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Well-identified problem. The paper targets a good point in surgical AI: models trained on limited annotated data from one set of procedures degrade under distribution shift at deployment. The insight that texture-based representations may be more stable than geometry-based ones in surgery is intuitive and grounded in domain knowledge.
2.Principled integration of object-centric learning with adaptation. The combination of slot attention with a periodic model-merging strategy is a coherent design. The merging mechanism addresses the tension between target specialization and catastrophic forgetting, and the paper provides evidence (the “w SA w/o ada” ablation) that naive slot attention without adaptation can actually hurt performance, validating the need for the proposed strategy.
3.Thorough experimental design. The evaluation includes five independent runs with different seeds, statistical significance testing, three complementary metrics, performance curves across varying annotation ratios, and comparisons against both task-specific architectures and foundation model baselines. The ablation study is well-structured with clearly defined variants that isolate each component’s contribution.
4.Clinically relevant evaluation regime. Testing under 1–5% annotation availability is a realistic scenario for surgical applications, where dense annotation is prohibitively ex pensive. The demonstration that DenseTRF maintains stable performance even at 1% is practically significant.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The “texture-aware” claim lacks direct evidence. This is the paper’s central conceptual claim, yet it is not directly validated. The paper asserts that patch-order permutation (borrowed from SPOT [10]) encourages texture-centric slot grouping, but provides no visualization or analysis showing that the learned slots actually capture texture properties rather than other visual cues. Without more visual and quantitative evidence, “texture-aware” remains an aspirational label rather than a demonstrated property.
2.Limited novelty of individual components. Each component of DenseTRF is drawn from existing work: slot attention from Locatello et al. [13], the DINOSAUR reconstruction framework from Seitzer et al. [20], patch-order permutation from SPOT [10], and model merging from continual learning [27]. The paper’s contribution lies in their combination and application to surgical adaptation, which is reasonable, but the paper could more explicitly discuss what is genuinely new versus assembled.
3.Incomplete ablation of the merging strategy. The periodic merging is presented with a fixed 50/50 weight (Eq. 4), but several design choices are left unexplored: How many merging rounds are performed? How sensitive is performance to the merging frequency? What happens with asymmetric weights ? The current ablation tests whether adaptation helps at all (“w SA w/o ada”) but does not dissect the merging mechanism itself. 
4.Efficiency discussion. Table 1 shows DenseTRF has 388 MB parameters — larger than most baselines except Mask2Former. For a method motivated by deployment in real settings, there is no discussion of inference speed, latency, or computational cost. A comparison of FLOPs or inference FPS would contextualize the deployment claim.
5.Missing qualitative results. For a dense-prediction paper, there are no segmentation visualizations showing predicted masks against ground truth. Such visualizations would help readers understand where DenseTRF improves. The slot attention masks are shown in Fig. 2(b), but not analyzed in detail.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a well-motivated approach to unsupervised adaptation for surgical dense prediction, with a rigorous experiments featuring multiple runs, statistical testing, and consistent improvements across three surgical domains. However, several factors above prevent a stronger recommendation. I lean toward acceptance, but would encourage the authors to strengthen the work.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper has received 3 positive reviews with all reviewers acknowledging its methodological novelty, well-thought method design, problem importance and extensive validation. However all reviewers agree on the need for more details on the method development (all) and make key remarks on the need for additional results discussions to highlight the model’s contribution (ablations - Rev3), explain limitations and modest gains ( Rev #1), perform a computational complexity analysis (Rev #3). The authors should take care of these concerns.
My recommendation is for the paper to be accepted

title: DentalPSAM: Lifting SAM to Dental Plaque Segmentation with Hybrid 2D-3D Knowledge Fusion
abstract:
Accurate segmentation of dental plaque from intraoral scan (IOS) is crucial for assessing oral hygiene practices. However, the scarcity of 3D dental plaque datasets and the limitations of relying solely on either 3D geometric or 2D appearance information
present significant obstacles. To address this, we introduce DentalPSAM, a hybrid 2D-3D model for 3D dental plaque segmentation. DentalPSAM features an interleaved dual-branch architecture with an appearance-enhanced 3D mesh branch and a geometry-enhanced 2D SAM branch, built upon the zero-shot learning capabilities of the Segment Anything Model (SAM). These branches process 3D IOS and its 2D rendered images in parallel, integrating both geometric and appearance information. To achieve better alignment between 2D and 3D features, we employ model stitching to connect SAM encoder with both branches through lightweight adaptation. Moreover, we present the first open-source 3D intraoral scan dataset for dental plaque segmentation. The code is available at https://github.com/HKU-HealthAI/DentalPSAM.
