meta_reviews.text:
The motivation is sound and the ablation credibly supports each component. The authors should address the most important points raised by the reviewers, especially with regard to the theoretical consistency of the orthogonality regularization, the clarity of the experimental setup and dataset definitions, and the reliability of the baseline comparisons.

All three reviewers moved to accept post-rebuttal. The theoretical inconsistency in the orthogonality regularization was resolved convincingly, dataset definitions and hyperparameters were clarified, and computational overhead was shown to be manageable. The rebuttal addressed the most critical concerns raised in the original reviews. As AC, I note one important limitation that should be acknowledged in the final version. The contribution is evaluated exclusively within the RD paradigm, and no comparison against diffusion-based UAD methods is provided despite these methods addressing the same task under the same normal-only training assumption. Establishing where DDP Loss stands relative to the broader UAD landscape, not just within RD, would substantially strengthen the clinical relevance claim and help readers contextualize the contribution appropriately.

This paper presents a well-motivated and effective methodological refinement for medical image anomaly detection. The authors’ comprehensive rebuttal successfully resolved initial reviewer concerns regarding theoretical consistency, experimental clarity, and baseline evaluation. The proposed approach offers a practical, efficient solution that demonstrates strong clinical relevance and clear performance improvements. Following the rebuttal, all reviewers unanimously recommend acceptance.
The reviewers are satisfied with the rebuttal.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and the meta-reviewer for their constructive comments. Following the meta-review, we organize our response around theoretical consistency, experimental clarity, baseline reliability, and other remaining points.
1.For the theoretical consistency of the orthogonality regularization, (R3.4) we agree that when K>C, the Gram matrix of normalized directions has rank at most C, and therefore it cannot exactly approximate a full-rank K×K identity matrix. The phrase approach the identity in Eq. (6) was imprecise and may incorrectly suggest an unrealizable strict orthogonality constraint. In fact, because each direction vector is L2-normalized, the diagonal entries of the Gram matrix are already fixed to one. Thus, Eq. (6) mainly penalizes the off-diagonal correlations between projection directions, making R_orth a soft inter-direction decorrelation constraint that reduces redundancy and alleviates direction collapse, rather than enforcing K strictly orthogonal directions. The rank limitation only implies that this regularizer cannot reach zero when K>C, but it does not invalidate its role in promoting directional diversity. (R3.1) K controls the number of candidate projection directions explored during hard-direction mining, rather than the dimension of an orthogonal basis. We use K=4096 to provide denser directional coverage for discovering discriminative teacher-student (TS) discrepancies, reflecting a trade-off between coverage and computational cost. We will clarify this design choice in the revision. (R3.3) The Gaussian noise is only the input to a learnable sampler, rather than fixed random directions. The final directions are learned through hard-direction mining, so the method is not designed to rely on lucky initialization. Moreover, using a large candidate direction set reduces dependence on any single initialized direction.
2.For the clarity of the experimental setup and dataset definitions, (R2.1) in our setting, normal breast ultrasound images are treated as the normal class, while all lesion-containing images, including benign and malignant cases, are treated as anomalies. We will explicitly report the class mapping, sample counts, and train/test splits. (R2.3) We used λ_orth=0.1 and an alternating schedule of 10 student updates followed by 1 sampler update. We will add these omitted implementation details in the revision. (R3.2) Projection-based scoring adds computation, but profiling under our test-time setting shows manageable overhead: the sampler has only 4.1M parameters, about 2.5% of the 165M full model, while full inference requires 108G FLOPs and 1.1 GB peak CUDA memory.
3.For the reliability of the baseline comparisons, (R2.2) AUC evaluates score ranking across thresholds, whereas ACC and F1 reflect threshold-based classification, so they need not vary consistently. We followed the evaluation protocol of prior UAD works and rechecked the code and data splits. Skip-TS and SCRD4AD show consistent trends on both datasets, suggesting that these differences arise from their score distributions rather than evaluation errors.
4.For other remaining issues, (R1.1/R1.3/R1.5) we agree that broader validation across anatomical regions, modalities, datasets, and more challenging qualitative cases would strengthen the evidence of generalizability. However, MICCAI rebuttal guidelines do not allow additional experiments or substantial experimental changes. Our current study therefore focuses on breast ultrasound anomaly detection, a clinically meaningful and annotation-scarce setting, to examine whether DDP Loss improves the RD paradigm. (R1.2/R1.4) Diffusion-based methods are valuable, but they belong to a different generative paradigm. Since our contribution is a loss-level improvement for RD, we compare mainly with representative RD-based methods. RD is suitable here because normal-only TS distillation matches scarce abnormal annotations and yields interpretable multi-scale discrepancy cues.

title: Discriminative Synergistic Temporal Diffusion for Ultrasound Video Thyroid Nodule Segmentation
abstract: Automatic ultrasound video object segmentation (VOS) is crucial for thyroid nodule diagnosis and treatment, which still remains challenging due to small nodules and blurred, noisy boundaries induced by tissue deformation and probe motion. Although recent diffusion VOS methods have shown superior performance by gradually reconstructing tumor structures from noise features, they typically treat heterogeneous lesion cues equally throughout the segmentation process, neglecting the fact that their contribution varies across different denoising stages. Motivated by the coarse-to-fine annotation logic of clinicians, we propose a Discriminative Synergistic Temporal Diffusion (DSTD) framework that can explicitly assess the step-wise contribution of motion and texture guidance during each denoising timestep. Specifically, a Retentive Motion Perception module is designed to capture temporally consistent motion patterns while suppressing irrelevant tissue noise, and a Discriminative Texture Perception module evaluates the confidence of different texture representations to enhance ambiguous boundaries. Furthermore, a Synergistic Controller is introduced to adaptively balance these complementary guidance cues in a timestep-dependent manner. Moreover, we construct a large-scale ultrasound thyroid nodule dataset with 374 pixel-level annotated videos. Extensive experiments on 3 medical video datasets demonstrate that DSTD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, involving small nodules and blurred boundaries. We shall release our dataset, code, and results upon publication.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a Discriminative Synergistic Temporal Diffusion (DSTD) framework for ultrasound video thyroid nodule segmentation, which dynamically integrates motion and texture guidance cues during the diffusion denoising process. In addition, the authors construct a large-scale ultrasound thyroid nodule dataset containing 374 pixel-level annotated videos, and evaluate the proposed method on multiple medical video segmentation benchmarks.
reviews.text_strengths: The proposed method introduces a Retentive Motion Perception (RMP) module to capture temporally consistent lesion motion patterns, a Discriminative Texture Perception (DTP) module to enhance boundary representation using wavelet-based texture features, and a Synergistic Controller (SC) to adaptively balance these cues at different diffusion timesteps.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.While the paper introduces a new dataset consisting of 374 annotated ultrasound videos, more details regarding the annotation protocol, inter-observer agreement, and dataset diversity would improve the clarity and reproducibility of the work. 
2.The paper focuses mainly on architectural design and quantitative results, but provides limited analysis of why the proposed method works. Additional visualization or interpretability analysis would help better understand the contribution of the motion and texture guidance modules. 
3.The experimental analysis could be further strengthened. In particular, more comparisons with recent diffusion-based or transformer-based medical video segmentation methods would make the evaluation more convincing. 
4.More visulizations can be added to show the learned representations of the propsoed model.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A.

I recommend Weak Accept because the paper addresses an important clinical task and proposes a reasonable diffusion-based framework that integrates motion and texture cues, and the method achieves improvements over several recent methods. The introduction of a dataset with 374 annotated ultrasound videos is also a valuable contribution. However, the paper would benefit from clearer dataset details, deeper analysis of the proposed modules, and broader comparisons with recent methods.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a well-motivated approach that explicitly considers the heterogeneous effects of motion and texture cues over time to address complex medical video scenarios. Combined with a large-scale, pixel-level annotated thyroid nodule video dataset, this approach promises to make a valuable contribution to the field. Extensive experiments on multiple medical video datasets demonstrate that this method offers significant and sustained improvements over existing approaches, particularly in handling complex scenarios such as small lesions and poorly defined boundaries.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.DSTD explicitly considers the contribution of heterogeneous cues over time. Compared to previous structures that directly and uniformly handle all guiding features, DSTD achieves higher segmentation accuracy across a variety of challenging clinical segmentation scenarios.
2.The proposed dataset containing 374 pixel-level annotated ultrasound videos is a valuable contribution and may contribute to future research.
3.This paper demonstrates sustained improvements over various existing techniques on multiple datasets, including complex cases with micronodules and irregular boundary shapes.
4.This coarse-to-fine diffusion structure enhances practical relevance and is well-suited for handling ultrasound-specific challenges such as micronodules and blurred boundaries.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Although the dataset appears to be a high-quality, large-scale video dataset, the statistical analysis and diversity description of this ultrasound thyroid nodule video dataset in Section 1 of this paper are limited.
2.Some implementation details (e.g., hyperparameters or module settings) could be further clarified to improve reproducibility.
3.While the method is effective and well-motivated, this work would be more valuable if further analysis were conducted, such as analyzing the respective roles of different wavelet bases in the DTP module.
4.The collaborative controller sounds interesting, but could be further clarified, for example, by more explicitly comparing it with existing fusion methods based on gating or attention mechanisms.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper provide a clear motivation, a rigorously designed methodology, and comprehensive performance testing on multiple medical datasets. The proposed stage-adaptive diffusion framework effectively simulates the effects of motion and texture cues over time, aligning closely with clinical practice and improving performance in complex scenarios. The proposed large-scale labeled dataset makes a valuable contribution to the research community. This method demonstrates sustained advantages over various existing approaches and is supported by extensive ablation experiments.
However, several limitations were noted: limited statistical/diversity analysis of the dataset, missing implementation details affecting reproducibility, insufficient analysis of wavelet bases in the DTP module, and lack of explicit comparison with existing gating/attention fusion methods for the collaborative controller.
Despite these shortcomings, the core technical novelty, clinical relevance, and the valuable public dataset outweigh the issues. The weaknesses are addressable in a revision and do not undermine the paper’s overall impact.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have solved all my questions. Given the method novlety and the contribution of high-quality dataset to related research, I recommend for acceptance.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: It proposes a video segmentation framework, DSTD, that attempts to adaptively weight motion and texture cues across diffusion timesteps for ultrasound thyroid nodule segmentation.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper tackles a highly pertinent and notoriously difficult challenge in medical image analysis: segmenting small thyroid nodules with blurred boundaries in ultrasound videos. The problem statement is well-defined and practically significant.
The authors demonstrate consistent and solid quantitative improvements (Dice, Jaccard, etc.) across multiple datasets, including their private dataset and two public medical video benchmarks (DPSTT and SUN-SEG). The results indicate a robust generalization capability.
Compiling and pixel-level annotating 374 ultrasound videos is a highly labor-intensive process. Even pending clarification on its relationship to prior releases, this represents a valuable resource for the medical AI community.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The paper introduces two major modules: Retentive Motion Perception (RMP) and Discriminative Texture Perception (DTP). However, in ultrasound video, consistent motion patterns and texture representations are often inextricably linked. The paper fails to prove that these are truly heterogeneous cues rather than two different mathematical ways of looking at the same pixel intensity changes. The SC is essentially an additional attention/weighting layer. The paper argues it mimics clinical logic, but provides no proof that the model actually focuses on motion first and texture later. It might simply be learning to ignore noisy features regardless of their types. 
2.KANs are a recent trend, but the authors do not justify why a standard MLP or attention mechanism wouldn’t suffice. Without a specific ablation comparing them to standard components, it is not clear whether the insertion of this layer is necessary or a complexity bloat. 
3.The paper uses Haar, DB3, and Dmey wavelets, but does not provide any explanation as to why these specific kernels were chosen or why three is the optimal number. If the model is truly “adaptive,” it should theoretically work with any bank of filters; without this proof, the choice feels like manual hyperparameter tuning disguised as discriminative perception. 
4.The authors highlight the release of a 374-video thyroid ultrasound dataset as a primary contribution. However, a highly relevant existing dataset for this specific task, VTUS (100 videos), was recently introduced alongside the ViVim framework (Yang et al., TCSVT 2025).
First, it is crucial to clarify the relationship between this newly proposed dataset and VTUS. Does the 374-video dataset include the 100 videos from VTUS? If so, the claim of releasing a ‘new’ 374-video dataset needs to be appropriately contextualized to accurately reflect the incremental contribution.
Alternatively, if the two datasets are indeed entirely distinct with no overlap, then the authors have omitted a critical external validation. Since this submission focuses specifically on thyroid nodule segmentation, relying solely on general medical video datasets (breast BUV2022 and polyp SUN-SEG) for external validation—while ignoring the most relevant domain-specific public dataset—leaves a significant gap in demonstrating the model’s true generalizability. 
5.The paper claims real-time performance for a diffusion-based framework. However, diffusion models are typically characterized by high iterative latency compared to linear-time models like Mamba-based models (e.g., Vivim). The authors must report the exact Frames Per Second (FPS) and Inference Memory usage to demonstrate a significant speed advantage or comparable efficiency to existing works likes Vivim.
6.The Baseline removes all memory-related enhancements. This sets an artificially low bar.8.Please rate the clarity and organization of the paper.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This submission addresses a highly relevant clinical problem and proposes a logically sound framework (DSTD) that intuitively mirrors the clinical diagnostic workflow. The reported quantitative segmentation results are also promising.
However, the current manuscript contains critical gaps in experimental validation and clarity that prevent me from recommending acceptance at this stage. First, the lack of inference efficiency metrics (FPS and memory consumption) is a significant omission, especially considering the known latency challenges of diffusion models compared to baseline architectures like ViVim. Second, the architectural introduction of KAN layers and specific wavelet kernels lacks proper ablation to prove their necessity over simpler, standard components. Finally, the relationship between the newly proposed dataset and the existing VTUS dataset remains unclarified, and the model lacks validation on the public VTUS benchmark.
Therefore, my initial recommendation is a Weak Reject. However, I consider this a borderline paper and I am open to raising my score to an Accept if the authors can satisfactorily address these key issues in their rebuttal.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text:
The reviewers generally agree that this work addresses a clinically important and challenging problem in ultrasound video segmentation. The proposed diffusion-based framework is considered well motivated, and the reported quantitative improvements across multiple datasets are viewed positively. In addition, the introduction of a large pixel-level annotated ultrasound video dataset is regarded as a potentially valuable contribution to the community.
However, there are still several points that need to be clarified, including but not limited to:
1.The authors should provide clearer details on the newly introduced 374-video dataset, including annotation protocol, inter-observer agreement, diversity/statistics, and clarify its relationship (if any) to existing datasets such as VTUS.
2.Several architectural choices require stronger support, such as KAN layers and wavelet kernels. Additional ablation or clearer justification will help to make this convincing.
3.Given the diffusion-based design, inference efficiency should be reported more explicitly (e.g., FPS, memory usage), particularly in comparison with existing efficient video segmentation models.
4.Implementation details remain insufficiently specified and should be clarified to improve reproducibility.

Reviewers are overall positive and support acceptance. The rebuttal addressed the main concerns about the method design and clarified the contribution of the dataset, and the post-rebuttal reviewers who updated their opinions are supportive. One reviewer did not submit a post-rebuttal update, so this conclusion partly relies on the original recommendation, but the overall direction remains positive.

I have read the manuscript, review comments, rebuttal letter. All three reviewers recommend acceptance (after rebuttal). The responses addressed the concerns about dataset details, ablation of architectural, and inference costs.
The author’s response addresses the reviewers’ concerns.

Using 4 and 5 kernels achieves 69.04/79.21/84.72/79.88 and 69.75/79.55/86.19/78.75 in Jac/Dice/Pre/Rec, respectively, showing improved adaptability to varied thyroid nodule morphologies.

RMP inputs adjacent memory frames to extract temporally consistent motion features, while DTP only selects top-K similar frames (Eq3,Sec2.2) to extract wavelet-domain texture features. We added visualizations of RMP, DTP, and SC maps, showing that RMP focuses on temporally consistent candidate regions, DTP highlights tumor-related boundaries, and SC assigns higher motion weights at early timesteps but higher texture weights at later timesteps. title: Disease-Consistent Visual-Text Alignment and Fusion for Reliable Radiology Report Generation
abstract: Automatic medical report generation (MRG) has significant clinical value, as it can alleviate the heavy workload of report writing for radiologists. Recent studies adopt retrieval-based strategies to inject external diagnostic knowledge into report generation. However, reliable MRG remains challenging because existing methods often retrieve diagnostically inconsistent reports and lack mechanisms for selective visual-text integration. In this work, we propose DCAF, a Disease-Consistent Visual-Text Alignment and Fusion framework for reliable radiology report generation. DCAF incorporates a Disease-Consistent Retrieval Enhancer that integrates disease priors via multi-positive contrastive learning and a disease-matching constraint to improve diagnostic consistency during retrieval. To better mimic the selective diagnostic reasoning process of radiologists, we further design an Optimal Transport-Enhanced Cross-Modal Fusion module that selectively integrates clinically relevant textual knowledge. In addition, an auxiliary disease-aware feature extraction mechanism encodes predicted diagnostic hypotheses into visual representations, enabling hypothesis-driven visual reasoning. Extensive experiments on IU X-Ray and MIMIC-CXR demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both language generation quality and clinical efficacy.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes DCAF, a retrieval-augmented radiology report generation framework designed to improve diagnostic reliability. The method combines (i) a Disease-Consistent Retrieval Enhancer with disease-prior multi-positive contrastive learning and a disease-matching constrained retrieval objective, (ii) an Optimal Transport-Enhanced Cross-Modal Fusion module for selective use of retrieved textual knowledge, and (iii) a Disease Classifier for disease-aware feature extraction. On MIMIC-CXR and IU X-Ray, the method reports improved natural language generation metrics and CheXbert-based clinical efficacy metrics relative to the compared baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The problem setting is clinically meaningful and well motivated. The manuscript identifies a concrete limitation of retrieval-augmented medical report generation: semantically similar reference reports may still be diagnostically inconsistent, which can reduce the reliability of the generated report. 
2.The proposed framework is coherent and aligned with the stated objective. The Disease-Consistent Retrieval Enhancer explicitly incorporates disease priors into image-text alignment and retrieval; the Optimal Transport-Enhanced Cross-Modal Fusion module is intended to selectively use clinically relevant retrieved text rather than treating all retrieved tokens equally; and the auxiliary Disease Classifier provides an explicit disease-aware learning signal for the visual representation. 
3.The empirical results are consistently strong on the reported benchmarks. On MIMIC-CXR, the method improves BLEU-4 from 0.137 (STREAM) / 0.136 (KIA) to 0.146 and clinical efficacy F1 from 0.499 (EKAGen) to 0.552.On IU X-Ray, BLEU-4 improves from 0.098 (PromptMRG) to 0.105 and F1 from 0.211 to 0.256.These gains are meaningful for this task and are observed on both language and clinical proxy metrics. 
4.The experimental section includes useful supporting analyses. The ablation study on MIMIC-CXR shows incremental gains when DMCL, DCR, OTCF, and DFE are added, the top-k study provides some sensitivity analysis for retrieval, and the qualitative example is consistent with the paper’s claim that the proposed framework reduces clinically inconsistent statements.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The methodological novelty appears moderate rather than substantial. DCL [12] already uses contrastive learning for chest X-ray report generation; PromptMRG [10], EKAGen [2], STREAM [25], and KIA [27] already incorporate diagnosis, knowledge, or retrieval signals into report generation; and the OT-based attention mechanism is adapted from MPSA / OT-Seg [26]. The current contribution is therefore best characterized as a task-specific integration of several reasonable ideas, and the paper would benefit from a clearer positioning of what is fundamentally new beyond the combination. 
2.The central claim of reliability is supported mainly by automatic proxy metrics. Clinical efficacy is evaluated only through CheXbert-based precision, recall, and F1 on 14 labels. No radiologist study, factual error taxonomy, or patient-level safety analysis is provided. For a paper emphasizing ‘reliable’ report generation, stronger clinical validation would materially strengthen the claim. 
3.The paper uses CheXbert-derived disease labels both to supervise disease-consistent retrieval and to evaluate the generated reports. Because both the retrieval supervision and the downstream clinical efficacy metric depend on the same report-derived automatic labeler, there is a risk that proxy alignment and label noise partially drive the reported gains. This limitation should be discussed more explicitly. 
4.Reproducibility is only partial in the current version. The manuscript does not provide an anonymized code link, and several implementation details are insufficiently specified, including the loss weights (lambda_match, lambda_cls, lambda_gen), retrieval queue size and update policy, the exact top-k setting used on each dataset during training and inference, the handling of uncertain labels from CheXbert, and the precise integration point of MPSA within the generation architecture. 
5.Some experimental and presentation choices need clarification. The IU X-Ray evaluation follows PromptMRG [10] by directly transferring a model trained on MIMIC-CXR to the entire IU X-Ray dataset, which is useful for transfer evaluation but is not equivalent to a standard in-domain benchmark. In addition, Eq. (2) and Eq. (4) would benefit from clearer dimensional and probabilistic explanations, and Table 1 contains minor presentation issues such as the ‘Precison’ typo.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem in radiology report generation and presents a technically coherent framework. The empirical improvements on MIMIC-CXR and IU X-Ray are consistent across both language generation metrics and clinical proxy metrics, and the ablation study supports the usefulness of the main components. These are positive aspects. At the same time, the methodological novelty is moderate, the reliability claim is supported mainly by automatic report-derived proxies, and the reproducibility section should be strengthened with additional implementation details. Overall, I view the paper as marginally above the acceptance threshold for MICCAI, with the final assessment benefiting from clarification during rebuttal.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The rebuttal resolves some clarification issues, especially regarding the IU X-Ray zero-shot protocol and reproducibility details. 
However, the core contribution still appears to be an integration of existing ideas. The reliability claim remains mainly supported by CheXbert-based automatic metrics, while no radiologist study, factual-error analysis, or independent clinical evaluation is provided. Since CheXbert-derived labels are also used in the method, the proxy-coupling concern remains. Therefore, I do not think the paper is above the acceptance threshold.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a retrieval-augmented radiology report generation framework (DCAF) to address disease-level inconsistencies in retrieval and cross-modal fusion. The three core contributions are: (1) a Disease-Consistent Retrieval Enhancer (DRE) combining multi-positive contrastive learning—supervised by CheXbert-derived labels—with a disease-matching constraint to enforce diagnostic consistency; (2) an Optimal Transport-Enhanced Cross-Modal Fusion (OTCF) module using Multi-Prompt Sinkhorn Attention (MPSA) to selectively weight textual evidence; and (3) an auxiliary disease classifier that injects predicted disease probabilities back into the visual representation space. The authors claim that their framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on MIMIC-CXR and IU X-Ray datasets.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Well-identified and clinically grounded problem. The paper targets three concrete failure modes of existing retrieval-augmented methods: inconsistent retrieval, uniform cross-modal fusion, and the absence of disease semantics. The modular design makes the contribution highly decomposable and ablation-friendly.
2.Multi-positive contrastive learning with disease-label supervision. As the authors claimed, using CheXbert-extracted labels to define positive sets in the contrastive objective (Eq. 1) is a principled improvement over standard single-positive CLIP-style learning. This directly addresses retrieval consistency and provides the largest single-module gain (+0.034 F1) in the ablation.
3.Optimal Transport for selective cross-modal fusion. Applying MPSA to enforce globally constrained attention weighting is a methodologically sound approach that better models radiologists’ selective integration of reference reports.
4.Comprehensive ablation. Table 2 provides a clean incremental ablation over all components, with consistent monotonic gains, lending credibility to each module’s individual contribution.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Reliance on CheXbert labels introduces systematic bias. The DRE module relies entirely on CheXbert pseudo-labels for training supervision. Furthermore, the CE metrics are evaluated using the
same
CheXbert tool. This introduces a severe circular dependency; the high CE scores may reflect overfitting to CheXbert’s inherent biases rather than genuine clinical correctness.
2.IU X-Ray evaluation protocol is methodologically weak. The model is trained on MIMIC-CXR and evaluated directly on the
entire
IU X-Ray dataset (Section 3), including training samples. This is non-standard and potentially introduces data leakage. Standard practice (e.g., R2Gen, M2KT) is to train and test within IU X-Ray using its own splits. The paper should either follow standard IU X-Ray splits or clearly justify the cross-dataset zero-shot evaluation protocol, as the current setup makes results on IU X-Ray difficult to interpret.
3.Limited Methodological Novelty: The core components are essentially direct applications of existing techniques. The multi-positive contrastive learning is a direct adaptation of
SupCon
(Khosla et al., NeurIPS 2020 [1]), which has already been explored in similar contexts (e.g.,
PromptMRG
(Jin et al., AAAI 2024 [2]),
DCL(Li et al., CVPR 2023 [3])
). The MPSA module is explicitly imported from
OtSeg
(Kim et al., ECCV 2024 [4]). The disease-aware feature injection (DFE) is conceptually very similar to the knowledge-adaptive mechanism in M2KT(Yang et al., MedIA 2023 [5]).
4.Absence of LLM-Based Baselines: The baseline pool consists largely of pre-2024 encoder-decoder models. Modern methods leveraging Large Language Models (e.g., LLaVA-Med, MedGemma) demonstrate substantially higher performance, making the absolute “SOTA” claim overstated.
5.Computational Overhead of k=18: Table 3 shows the model peaks at $k=18$ retrieved reports. Retrieving 18 references and attending over them with iterative Sinkhorn algorithms is computationally expensive. No inference cost or latency analysis is provided.

medical report generation. In: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial

[3] Li, M., Lin, B., Chen, Z., Lin, H., Liang, X., Chang, X.: Dynamic graph en-

[4] Kim, K., Oh, Y., Ye, J. C.: OtSeg: Multi-prompt Sinkhorn attention for zero-shot
semantic segmentation. In: European Conference on Computer Vision, pp. 200–
