reviews.recommendation_label: Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
reviews.text_contribution: This paper studies continual test-time adaptation (CTA) for 3D vessel segmentation under domain shift, a setting that is both practically important and technically challenging because 3D vascular structures are highly topology-sensitive. The authors propose DyCo-CTA, which departs from the conventional fixed teacher-student paradigm by dynamically switching the two roles according to relative prediction reliability. In addition, the paper introduces a pseudo-break transformation to simulate topology-breaking perturbations during adaptation and a topological regularization objective to preserve global vessel connectivity beyond pixel-level consistency. To the best of my knowledge, this is the first work to explicitly formulate and evaluate CTA in the context of 3D vessel segmentation, and the paper demonstrates clear gains on both cerebrovascular and cardiovascular benchmarks.
reviews.text_strengths:
Important and timely problem setting. The paper addresses continual test-time adaptation for 3D vessel segmentation, which is highly relevant for real-world medical deployment under cross-center and cross-device distribution shifts. This is a meaningful extension of CTA to a clinically relevant structured segmentation problem.
Clear technical novelty. The proposed method is not a minor variant of existing CTA pipelines. The dynamic collaborative mechanism challenges the common assumption that the teacher is always more reliable than the student, which is particularly reasonable in complex 3D vascular segmentation. This is a well-motivated and interesting design choice.
Topology-aware formulation is well aligned with the task. The pseudo-break transformation and the topological regularization are both tailored to the structural characteristics of vessels. Rather than relying only on generic entropy minimization or pixel-level consistency, the method explicitly targets connectivity preservation and the reduction of topology-breaking artifacts such as disconnections and spurious branches.
Strong empirical evaluation. The paper provides experiments on both cerebrovascular and cardiovascular datasets and reports consistent improvements over a broad range of CTA baselines. The long-term adaptation experiment is also valuable, as it directly addresses error accumulation and catastrophic forgetting, which are central concerns in CTA.
Good overall paper quality. The method is conceptually coherent, the ablation study supports the contribution of each component, and the submission also provides an anonymized code link, which further strengthens reproducibility.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper is strong overall, and my concerns are relatively minor. First, the computational overhead and memory/runtime cost of DyCo-CTA are not analyzed in sufficient depth. Since CTA is an online adaptation setting, efficiency is important for practical deployment, especially in 3D medical imaging.
Second, although the paper argues that this is the first CTA work for 3D vessel segmentation, the final version could better position itself with respect to prior topology-aware tubular segmentation and topology-enhanced adaptation literature, for example recent topology-preserving tubular segmentation and topology-aware TTA works. A sharper discussion of what is fundamentally new here beyond extending teacher-student CTA to 3D vessel data would make the contribution even clearer.
Third, some implementation details could be explained more thoroughly, such as the sensitivity to the pseudo-break construction strength, the choice of the persistence threshold, and the robustness of the dynamic switching criterion. These points mainly affect completeness and reproducibility, rather than the validity of the core idea.
Overall, these weaknesses do not undermine the main contribution or the empirical strength of the paper.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I recommend a strong accept because the paper addresses an important and underexplored problem, proposes a technically coherent and clearly motivated solution, and demonstrates consistent gains across multiple challenging 3D vessel segmentation benchmarks. The combination of dynamic teacher-student role switching, pseudo-break transformation, and topology-aware regularization is well matched to the structural properties of vascular segmentation and goes beyond a routine application of existing CTA ideas. I also appreciate the inclusion of long-term adaptation experiments, which directly evaluate robustness to error accumulation over time. While I would welcome a stronger analysis of computational cost and a more explicit discussion of the relationship to prior topology-aware work, these issues are secondary and do not detract from the main contribution. Overall, I view this paper as a high-quality and impactful contribution that should be accepted.

meta_reviews.text: This paper addresses an important and underexplored problem, proposes a technically coherent and clearly motivated solution, and demonstrates consistent gains across multiple challenging 3D vessel segmentation benchmarks. The work is technically solid and likely to attract interest from researchers working on test-time adaptation, domain shift, and structure-preserving medical image segmentation.

The comments on terminology, method clarification, implementation details, sensitivity analysis, computational cost, and relation to prior topology-aware work are very useful. We will revise the final version carefully to address these points and make the paper clearer and more complete.
Thank you again for the constructive feedback and for supporting our work.

title: Dynamic Spatial-Temporal Mapping for EEG-to-fMRI Synthesis via Gaussian-Guided Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network
abstract: EEG-to-fMRI synthesis aims to generate high spatial-temporal resolution fMRI, pivotal for diagnosing brain diseases, using accessible EEG signals. However, current static regression methods fail to account for regional variations in EEG-fMRI time delays and cannot disentangle spatially mixed EEG signals. To address this, we propose DSTP, a framework that explicitly parameterizes this dynamic spatial-temporal mapping. We introduce a Dynamic Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network (DHGNN) to model the evolving mapping between scalp electrodes and brain regions of interest (ROIs). Moreover, we embed a learnable Gaussian Mask into the message-passing mechanism. This acts as an adaptive temporal gate, effectively filtering the EEG history to identify the specific time window that aligns with each ROI’s hemodynamic response. Additionally, a Transformer module integrates the historical evolution of these states, while a multi-objective loss preserves temporal dynamics and brain topological consistency alongside reconstruction accuracy. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that DSTP achieves state-of-the-art performance. Notably, the model exhibits superior zero-shot generalization across tasks and spatial resolutions, proving its ability to learn intrinsic physiological mapping rules rather than overfitting to specific distributions.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Synthetic Data / Data-centric AI
Modalities -> EEG / MEG / ECG / Physiological Signals

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes DSTP, a dynamic spatiotemporal mapping framework for EEG-to-fMRI synthesis. The method introduces a dynamic heterogeneous graph neural network to model the time-varying relationships between EEG electrodes and fMRI ROIs. The authors further propose a learnable Gaussian mask to model ROI-specific hemodynamic delays. Transformer-based temporal modules and a multi-objective loss are further used to improve reconstruction fidelity and preserve functional connectivity. Experimental results on resting-state and auditory-task datasets show that the proposed method outperforms several baselines and demonstrates promising cross-task and cross-resolution generalization ability.
reviews.text_strengths:
-The method has a certain degree of novelty. The authors propose using a Gaussian function with mean and variance parameters to model ROI-specific hemodynamic functions, and apply this function as a temporal mask in the message-passing mechanism, reflecting the authors’ unique insights into neural signal analysis and deep learning. 
-The method description is relatively clear, and the correspondence between formulae and symbols is good. 
-The experimental design is relatively complete, including comparisons with baseline methods, ablation experiments covering the basic modules, and additional validation on an independent dataset. 
-The dataset split is handled reasonably, and comparisons are made under both intra-subject and inter-subject settings.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
-The authors mention two main challenges in the Introduction, among which 2) Spatial Ambiguity is not addressed in a particularly unique way in the paper. 
-The authors emphasize the subject specificity of the HRF in the cited literature, but the Gaussian mask modeled in the paper seems to have only region specificity. 
-The HRF usually does not follow a unimodal Gaussian distribution, and a single pair of $\mu$ and $\sigma$ parameters may not fully capture the region specificity of the HRF. Moreover, this modeling choice is not well supported by the experiments. 
-In Section 2.1, the authors mention that the constructed heterogeneous graph has directed Electrode-to-ROI edges $\epsilon_{ER}$ and undirected Functional edges $\epsilon_{FC}$. The definitions of these two variables should be explained there; otherwise, they may confuse readers. 
-The authors state that the constructed heterogeneous graph is dynamic, but this dynamic property seems to depend only on the time-varying attention parameters in message passing. Therefore, the dynamic graph structure should be more clearly distinguished from dynamic message passing. 
-The third term in Equation (5) refers to the neighborhood of node $k$. If FC is not sparsified, this almost means that the neighborhood of $k$ contains all other nodes. The expression of the formula could be simplified here to reduce symbolic redundancy. 
-Why is the edge weight in Equation (3) obtained by using the fMRI ROI node state at the previous time step $(t-1)$ and the electrode features at the current time step (after hemodynamic Gaussian masking)? What is the physiological basis for this design? How does the formula behave at $t=0$?
-Some references do not follow the required format. 
-The main acquisition parameters for EEG and fMRI are not provided. 
-Some important information is missing, which reduces the reproducibility of the paper, such as the atlas used for fMRI ROI signal extraction, the time window length $L$, the feature dimension $d$, and the latent dimension. 
-This citation is inappropriate: Unlike methods relying on static network structure [2], our graph structure dynamically evolves [20, 19, 4, 13], allowing the model to capture time-varying dependencies between the electrodes and ROIs. 
-There is inappropriate bolding in Table 2: for the intra-subject setting and ConnMSE, DSTP (Ours) is not the best result.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Although some issues still remain, the paper may still be suitable for publication at MICCAI as a preliminary study, given its methodological novelty and relatively sufficient experimental design, provided that the above weaknesses are adequately addressed and revised, especially by adding the missing information to improve reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes the DSTP framework to address the core challenges in EEG-to-fMRI synthesis and validates the model’s performance and generalization ability through relatively comprehensive experiments. The authors construct a dynamic heterogeneous graph, using EEG electrodes and fMRI ROIs as graph nodes, and model the spatiotemporal mapping relationship through dynamically evolving edges between the electrodes and ROIs. The paper further uses Gaussian functions to model region-specific hemodynamic response functions (HRFs) and introduces them into the message-passing process of the graph neural network. In addition, the authors design a multi-objective optimization function that includes reconstruction loss, correlation loss, and functional connectivity loss. Experimental results on multiple EEG-fMRI datasets show that DSTP achieves strong performance on temporal correlation, functional connectivity correlation, and other metrics under both intra-subject and inter-subject settings.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The method has a certain degree of novelty, especially the combination of a dynamic heterogeneous graph and Gaussian-guided message passing, which is broadly consistent with the underlying physiological mechanism. The learnable Gaussian mask is used to simulate region-specific hemodynamic responses and serves as a weighting factor in message passing, helping the model identify the EEG history segments most relevant to fMRI generation.
2.A multi-objective optimization strategy is adopted, taking into account temporal correlation loss and FC matrix reconstruction loss in addition to reconstruction accuracy. This design is well aligned with the main application scenarios of fMRI.
3.The overall experimental results are strong. From the reported results, DSTP achieves the best overall performance relative to the baselines under both intra-subject and inter-subject settings.
4.The ablation study is relatively complete and covers the effectiveness of the main modules.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.There is a lack of direct validation of physiological plausibility. At present, the effectiveness of the Gaussian mask design for simulating ROI-specific HRFs is only validated through fMRI reconstruction performance, without directly examining whether the learned \mu and \sigma are physiologically interpretable.
2.Some experimental results are not fully consistent with the description in the paper. In Table 2, the proposed method does not achieve the best Conn MSE under the intra-subject setting, and this trade-off is not discussed in the manuscript.
3.Some important details are missing. The specific dimensionalities of parameters in the model structure, as well as the time-window length L and feature dimension d, are not reported explicitly, which limits the reproducibility of the paper.
4.The manuscript does not clearly define the reported mean and variance values. It is unclear whether these statistics are computed across time points or across cross-validation results.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Although the paper still has some issues, its overall level of innovation and experimental support is sufficient for publication as preliminary work at MICCAI.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses the challenges of spatial ambiguity arising from volume conduction and the individual/regional variability of the hemodynamic response function (HRF) in EEG-to-fMRI synthesis. The authors propose DSTP, a dynamic spatial-temporal mapping framework comprising two core components: (1) a Dynamic Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network (DHGNN) that explicitly models the evolving mapping between scalp electrodes and brain regions, and (2) a learnable Gaussian mask-guided message passing mechanism that serves as an adaptive temporal gate to capture ROI-specific HRF delays and dispersions. Experiments on resting-state and task-based datasets are reported, demonstrating performance improvements over existing methods.
reviews.text_strengths:
Strengths and Contributions
Physiologically Grounded Problem Formulation: The manuscript correctly frames EEG-fMRI synthesis as a dynamic spatial-temporal mapping problem rather than a static regression task. This perspective directly addresses the core challenges of volume conduction and regional HRF heterogeneity, reflecting sound theoretical insight.
Interpretable and Rational Methodological Design: The learnable Gaussian mask elegantly incorporates HRF priors as a soft constraint, balancing data-driven flexibility with physiological interpretability. The DHGNN, with its heterogeneous nodes and dynamic edges, effectively models the non-stationary cross-modal spatial correspondence. The multi-objective loss function is appropriately designed to preserve functional connectivity topology.
Promising Direction for Generalizability Assessment: The paper presents preliminary evidence of zero-shot generalization across tasks (resting-state to auditory task) and spatial resolutions (DiFuMo 64 to 512), suggesting that the model may capture intrinsic physiological mapping principles rather than merely overfitting to dataset-specific distributions.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Lack of Statistical Rigor in Experimental Evaluation: The performance comparisons presented in Tables 1 and 2 entirely omit statistical significance testing (e.g., paired t-test, Wilcoxon signed-rank test). Given the reported standard deviations (e.g., Intra-subject Tcorr: 0.458±0.173 vs. 0.416±0.166), superiority based solely on mean rank ordering cannot be confidently distinguished from random variation. This omission substantially undermines the credibility of the reported empirical gains for a MICCAI submission.
Internal Inconsistency in Methodological Design: The functional connectivity weights in Equation (5) are pre-computed from the training set and remain fixed during both training and inference. This design choice appears at odds with the central premise of “dynamic evolution” and may introduce systematic bias in the presence of domain shifts (e.g., inter-subject evaluation). The authors do not provide sufficient justification for this static prior.
Insufficient Detail in Generalization Experiments: The description of the zero-shot generalization experiments in Section 3.4 is overly cursory. Critical details regarding the source-domain training and target-domain testing protocols, as well as whether baseline methods (e.g., UnEBOLT) received equivalent pre-training and data splits, are absent. This lack of detail prevents independent assessment of the reported findings.
Relatively Limited Sample Size: The primary experiments rely on resting-state data from 22 subjects (29 scans) and task-based data from 10 subjects (16 scans). For a model architecture incorporating Transformer-based temporal modules and dynamic graph structures, this sample size poses a non-trivial risk of overfitting and limits the generalizability of the conclusions.
Incomplete Writing and Compliance Statements: The manuscript lacks an Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval statement concerning data usage, as well as any indication of data availability or code release intent. Furthermore, a dedicated Limitations section is absent.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

First, the problem investigated in this manuscript holds clear clinical and neuroscientific significance. EEG-to-fMRI cross-modal synthesis is an important direction in brain imaging research, and the two core challenges addressed—spatial ambiguity due to volume conduction and regional heterogeneity of the hemodynamic response function—are well identified. Framing the task as dynamic spatial-temporal mapping rather than static regression reflects an understanding of the underlying physiology, and the problem formulation is valid.
Second, the methodological design is purposeful and exhibits a degree of novelty. The Dynamic Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network explicitly distinguishes electrode and ROI nodes to model time-varying spatial correspondences, while the learnable Gaussian mask introduces HRF priors as soft constraints, balancing data-driven flexibility with physiological interpretability. The multi-objective loss function, which jointly constrains reconstruction accuracy, temporal correlation, and functional connectivity topology, is thoughtfully constructed.
Third, the experimental results demonstrate performance improvements over existing methods, and the preliminary zero-shot generalization experiments across tasks and spatial resolutions suggest that the model may capture intrinsic physiological mapping principles rather than merely fitting dataset-specific distributions.
Nevertheless, the current manuscript contains a critical shortcoming: the complete absence of statistical significance testing. The performance comparisons presented in Tables 1 and 2 report only means and standard deviations, without any p-values or inferential statistics. Given the substantial standard deviations and modest differences in mean values for several metrics, it is not possible to reliably determine whether the observed gains of DSTP reflect genuine performance advantages or random variation. For a MICCAI submission, this omission materially undermines the credibility of the empirical conclusions.
Additional concerns include a logical inconsistency between the static functional connectivity weights and the central premise of dynamic evolution, insufficient detail in the description of the generalization experiments, a relatively limited sample size, and missing statements regarding ethics approval and limitations.
In summary, this reviewer acknowledges the contributions of the manuscript in terms of problem formulation and methodological design. However, the notable deficiencies in experimental rigor prevent an unconditional recommendation for acceptance in its current form.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text: All three reviewers generally support acceptance (two accept, one weak accept) and recognize the paper’s novel dynamic heterogeneous graph neural network with a learnable Gaussian mask to model region‑specific hemodynamic delays for EEG‑to‑fMRI synthesis. They appreciate the physiologically motivated design and the multi‑objective loss. However, they consistently point to insufficient experimental rigor, including a complete absence of statistical significance tests, missing reproducibility details (model dimensions, time window, atlas), and incomplete validation of the Gaussian mask’s physiological plausibility. It is strongly suggested that the authors thoroughly address the reviewers’ concerns to raise confidence in the reported advantages.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the meta-reviewer and reviewers for their constructive feedback and for recognizing the novelty of our dynamic heterogeneous graph framework and Gaussian-guided temporal modeling for EEG-to-fMRI synthesis, as well as the physiologically motivated design and the multi-objective loss. We have carefully considered the major concerns and grouped them into the following categories for clarification
Physiological interpretation and scope (R1-C1/R1-C2/R1-C3/R1-C7, R2-C1, Meta-C3).
Our goal is not to suggest that a single Gaussian can fully characterize the complete HRF or all subject-specific hemodynamic variability. Instead, the Gaussian mask is intended as a compact ROI-conditioned temporal gating mechanism that highlights the most relevant EEG history during message passing, while broader temporal dependencies are further modeled by the downstream temporal module. We also recognize that the current evidence for the Gaussian mask remains primarily empirical and reconstruction-based, while a more direct physiological interpretation of the learned μ and σ parameters remains an important direction for future investigation.
Dynamic graph clarification and methodological consistency (R1-C4/R1-C5/R1-C6/R1-C11, R3-C2).
We appreciate the reviewers’ comments on the distinction between dynamic graph construction and dynamic message passing. In the current model, the main time-varying component lies in the Gaussian-guided electrode-to-ROI interaction together with the evolving ROI states, whereas the functional-connectivity term in Eq. (5) is used as a fixed prior estimated from the training data. We recognize that the present wording may leave room for ambiguity, and the role of dynamic cross-modal interaction versus fixed structural prior could be more clearly articulated
Experimental rigor and result interpretation (R1-C12, R2-C2/R2-C4, R3-C1/R3-C3/R3-C4, Meta-C1).
We appreciate the reviewers’ thoughtful comments regarding statistical rigor, protocol clarity, and the calibration of the reported conclusions. Regarding Table 2, we recognize that under the intra-subject setting the full model does not achieve the lowest ConnMSE in the ablation study, and this trade-off could have been described more carefully in the manuscript. At the current stage, we view the results as showing the strongest overall empirical trade-off across major metrics and settings, rather than uniform superiority on every ablation entry. We also acknowledge that formal statistical significance testing is not included in the present manuscript, such analysis could provide additional perspective on the reported comparisons, and we appreciate this as a valuable consideration for subsequent refinement. As for the data sample issues, given that paired EEG-fMRI is extremely rare, we have to follow the existing works’ usage of the available dataset with a limited sample size.
Reproducibility, reporting, and compliance (R1-C8/R1-C9/R1-C10, R2-C3, R3-C5, Meta-C2).
We appreciate the reviewers’ concerns regarding reproducibility and reporting completeness. The manuscript already specifies several parts of the training setup, including the optimizer, training epochs, batch size, learning rate schedule, Gaussian-mask initialization, loss weights, but we recognize that some implementation and dataset details are not stated as explicitly as they could be, including certain acquisition and dimensional settings. We also recognize that the present submission does not include an explicit code-availability or limitations statement, and we are positively considering making implementation details and configuration settings publicly available in the future.

title: Dynamic Sub-domain Modeling for Robust Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Intra-domain distribution shifts are common in medical image segmentation due to variations in acquisition protocols, reconstruction settings, and anatomical morphology, even when data originate from the same nominal domain. We propose a fully automatic segmentation framework that explicitly models latent sub-domains without gradient-based adaptation at inference. Our method dynamically discovers sub-domains via a nonparametric prototype mechanism, expanding only when novel distributional modes are detected. Each prototype conditions a specialized expert via a hypernetwork, forming a prototype-conditioned expert field over the latent manifold. Soft routing with uncertainty-based temperature scaling enables parameter-free test-time adaptation by calibrating sub-domain posteriors without updating model weights. Experiments on 2D medical benchmarks demonstrate improved robustness and granular segmentation accuracy under intra-domain shifts.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a sub domain modeling framework for robust medical image segmentation under intra domain distributional heterogeneity. The key contributions are a formal problem reformulation that treats single domain segmentation as inference over a latent sub domain mixture variable. Merging a hypernetwork that maps each prototype to lightweight adapter deltas for a shared SAM-style decoder. Uses an implicit expert field over the sub domain manifold an uncertainty tempered soft routing that modulates expert mixing through disagreement based temperature scaling enabling fully parameter free test time inference. The framework is evaluated across 20 public segmentation benchmarks spanning CT, MRI, endoscopy, dermoscopy, ultrasound, fundus, histopathology and PET and CT outperforming strong baselines including nnU-Net, MedNeXt, Mamba-based models.
reviews.text_strengths:
Strengths
– Framing intra domain heterogeneity as a latent mixture is underexplored in medical image segmentation. 
– The ability to determine K from data with bounded growth, merging, and pruning is a good technical advance over standard MoE approaches. It avoids the need for prior knowledge about the number of sub domains. 
– The strict constraint of no test-time gradient updates is clinically important for deployment. 
– 20 datasets across 6+ imaging modalities under a unified 2D protocol, with worst case sub domain Dice and Boundary F1 alongside standard metrics is comprehensive 
– All four main components dynamic vs. fixed-K discovery, hypernetwork vs. static adapters, uncertainty tempered vs standard routing, ROI vs global only descriptor are individually ablated and shown to contribute to the design choices. 
– The UMAP visualization and uncertainty and routing analysis in Fig 2 and 3 provide genuine insight into what the model has learned going.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Weaknesses
– Fig. 2(b) appears uniformly positive across all 20 datasets and all 13 baselines, with no losses shown. The authors must provide per dataset breakdowns and appropriate statistical significance testing for example Wilcoxon signed rank. 
– For datasets lacking metadata, sub domains are constructed by clustering training image descriptors. Since the same descriptor network contributes to both sub domain definition and model behavior, this risks circular evaluation of robustness. 
– The paper explicitly claims to report runtime and peak GPU memory, but these figures are absent from all tables and figures. 
– UMAP visualization is underspecified. Fig. 2(a) shows only Dataset A and Dataset B without identifying which of the 20 datasets these correspond to. 
– The paper does not discuss scenarios where the framework may underperform
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses an important problem of intra-domain heterogeneity as a structural ceiling in medical image segmentation with a technically sound and novel framework. The evaluation scope across 20 datasets is impressive, and the focus on worst case sub domain Dice is clinically well motivated. However, several concerns prevent a stronger recommendation, please refer to weaknesses section.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
1.This paper addresses an important and underexplored problem, which is intra-domain heterogeneity in medical image segmentation. 
2.Evaluation results on 20 datasets surpass other competitors.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Well-motivated problem framing. The paper points out a common but under-addressed failure mode, even within one dataset, shifts from scanner/protocol/patient morphology can create a mixture of sub-distributions that a single model averages over.
2.The proposed architecture is technically sound. For example, modulating the routing temperature based on expert disagreement is a clever mechanism to prevent overconfident predictions on ambiguous boundary cases.
3.The evaluation includes 20 distinct public datasets spanning multiple modalities (MRI, CT, Ultrasound, Endoscopy, Dermoscopy, etc.). providing evidence of the method’s generalizability.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.In Section 4 (Settings), the authors state: “runtime and peak GPU memory are reported.” However, this data is completely missing from the provided text.
2.Since the network relies on automatic prompts to generate local descriptors, the paper lacks details on how robust the system is to poor-quality automatic prompts. If the initial prompt generation fails or is highly inaccurate, does the sub-domain descriptor “r” collapse, leading to incorrect expert routing? An ablation or discussion on prompt sensitivity would strengthen the paper.
3.Considering the substantial heterogeneity across the 20 datasets, particularly in modality and degree of intra-domain variation, it is important to clarify whether the key hyperparameters τ, ρ, and α were kept fixed across all datasets or tuned separately for each one. If a single hyperparameter setting works well across 20 highly diverse datasets, that would be a major strength and should be explicitly highlighted. If, instead, these parameters were tuned per dataset, the paper should clearly describe the tuning protocol and discuss the associated overhead when transferring the method to a new dataset, especially relative to methods such as SAM2/MedSAM2 that do not appear to require this level of dataset-specific tuning.
4.The notation around the temperature scaling is currently under-specified. the paper does not clearly define either T_0 or the subscript r in T_r.
5.A key concern is how the method behaves when a genuinely new sub-domain appears at test time. Because the prototypes are fixed during inference, the model can only reweight known experts and cannot explicitly instantiate a new prototype for an unseen mode.
6.Figure 2(a) does not convincingly support the paper’s core claim of meaningful sub-domain discovery. While Dataset A shows some clustered structure, Dataset B appears largely as a homogeneous blob with no clear sub-domain separation. Thus, it remains unclear whether the reported gains come from explicit sub-domain modeling or simply from the increased capacity introduced by the hypernetwork, multiple experts, and routing mechanism. The current results and ablations do not sufficiently disentangle semantic expert specialization from a generic MoE/ensemble effect.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Although this paper is well-motivated and focuses on an interesting and practical problem in medical image analysis. The key concern is that the paper does not convincingly show that the performance gains come specifically from latent sub-domain discovery, rather than simply from the increased capacity and flexibility of the prototype-conditioned multi-expert architecture. The evidence for meaningful sub-domain structure is indirect, with no sufficiently direct visualization or analysis of learned sub-domains, routing behavior, or expert specialization. In addition, the paper lacks important implementation details needed for reproducibility and fair assessment.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a Dynamic Sub-domain Modeling framework that treats single-dataset medical image segmentation as inference over latent sub-domains, using a frozen SAM encoder, task-specific descriptors, and nonparametric dynamic prototypes to handle intra-dataset heterogeneity. A hypernetwork-generated expert field with an uncertainty tempered soft routing mechanism enables gradient free inference, and the method achieves strong performance across 20 public datasets, with average Dice improvements of about +3.9 over strong baselines and overall Dice 87.9 / HD95 11.8.
reviews.text_strengths:
Conceptual novelty and perspective: The work reframes intra-domain variability (scanner, protocol, anatomy differences) as meaningful structure rather than noise, dynamically assigning specialized experts to discovered sub-domains and improving boundary delineation (e.g., Boundary F1).
Dynamic, nonparametric sub-domain discovery: Nonparametric prototypes allow the number of sub-domains to grow as new modes appear during training, avoiding the need to predefine sub-domain counts and enhancing adaptability.
Inference-time practicality: The framework is fully gradient free at test time, relying on the learned prototypes and routing mechanism without parameter updates, which is attractive for stable and efficient clinical deployment.
Broad and convincing validation: The method is evaluated on 20 datasets across multiple imaging modalities and consistently outperforms strong baselines such as nnU Net 2D, SegMamba, and MedSAM2+APG, with supporting analyses (e.g., UMAP) to illustrate generalization.
Robust performance under domain shifts: The dynamic combination of experts yields high Dice (87.9) and competitive HD95 (11.8) across heterogeneous domains, including previously unseen distributions.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Limited architectural/detail transparency: Key components such as the prototype memory bank, the structure of expert models, and the mechanism by which experts expand remain under-specified, which hinders reproducibility and makes it hard to reimplement the method faithfully.
Sensitivity to thresholding and noise: Prototype creation hinges on a threshold parameter τ; despite pruning/merging, real world noisy clinical data may require careful tuning, weakening claims of full automation.
Dependence on SAM-based descriptor space: Sub-domain descriptors are derived from a frozen SAM encoder, so if this backbone fails to capture highly specialized medical textures, sub-domain discovery and expert specialization may be suboptimal.
Lack of explicit 3D modeling: The approach operates slice wise in 2D and does not explicitly enforce inter-slice or volumetric consistency, which is important for many 3D medical segmentation tasks.
Incomplete statistical analysis: While mean values and 95% confidence intervals are reported, there are no formal significance tests (e.g., paired t tests or Wilcoxon tests), so the strength of claims over baselines is not rigorously quantified.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I recommend a weak accept because the paper offers a fresh and practically meaningful approach to robust medical image segmentation under intra-dataset heterogeneity, with clear empirical gains, but also has notable gaps in technical detail and analysis. The idea of dynamic sub-domain modeling with nonparametric prototypes, coupled with a hypernetwork-generated expert field and uncertainty tempered routing, is conceptually strong, leads to gradient free inference, and yields consistent improvements over well-established baselines on 20 diverse datasets. At the same time, the reproducibility concerns (insufficient description of the prototype memory and expert expansion), sensitivity to the threshold τ, lack of explicit 3D consistency, and missing statistical significance tests prevent a full, unreserved acceptance. Overall, the contribution is novel and promising, and the experimental results are compelling enough that, despite these limitations, the work is suitable for publication with revisions that clarify the architecture, better analyze prototype behavior and scaling, and strengthen statistical validation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text: This work received overall positive comments (with two reviewers recommending weak accept and one reviewer suggesting weak reject). Reviewers acknowledge the novelty of the proposed framework, and the comprehensive evaluation on 20 public segmentation benchmarks, as well as the importance/relevance of the addressed problem. On the other hand, the lack of important details for its reproducibility, sensitivity analysis to several hyperparameters, and the absence of evidence that the reported gains genuinely stem from latent sub‑domain discovery undermine its overall impact. Given the limited space in the MICCAI format, and the overall positive comments, I recommend the acceptance of this work. Nevertheless, I strongly suggest the authors to address these comments in the revised version (or even in a GitHub public repository for the reproducibility concerns).

title: DynFS-MoE: Dynamic Functional-Structural Mixture-of-Experts for Post-Traumatic Epilepsy Diagnosis
abstract: Post-traumatic epilepsy (PTE) is a severe complication of traumatic brain injury (TBI). Yet, early identification remains challenging due to the complex structural and functional alterations it induces in the brain. To address this, we propose a dynamic multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) framework that integrates functional and structural connectivity through time-aware functional-structural encoding and class-conditioned expert routing. Within this framework, modality-specific and cross-modal experts learn complementary representations, while a Modality-Class MoE (MCoE) module dynamically adjusts expert weights according to each classification objective. Experimental results across three binary classification tasks demonstrate that the framework consistently outperforms static fusion baselines, and interpretability analyses further reveal meaningful interactions among regions of interest (ROIs). This dynamic multimodal expert framework effectively captures class-dependent brain interaction patterns and provides an interpretable approach for PTE diagnosis and risk stratification.
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: In this work, the authors propose a dynamic multimodal Mixture-of-Experts framework that integrates functional and structural MRI through time-aware functional-structural encoding and class-conditioned expert routing. By combining time-aware functional-structural encoding with class-conditioned expert routing, the model adaptively integrates fMRI and sMRI information and captures class-specific brain patterns.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.sMRI can leverage a temporal MoE mechanism to select the most informative patches within fMRI segments for cross-modal fusion and routing. 
2.Modality-specific experts are employed to extract individual feature representations from each modality, producing dedicated embeddings that preserve modality-unique information. 
3.A class-based MoE module adaptively selects the most class-relevant modality patches to facilitate more discriminative classification.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The number of subjects in the dataset is relatively small, with only around 20 samples for each type. Will this affect the validity of the results? Should a larger dataset be used to validate the findings? 
2.More state-of-the-art methods should be included in the comparative experiments for model performance evaluation. 
3.In addition to discussing binary classification problems, is it feasible to apply the model to a three-class classification task that distinguishes among HC, TBI and PTE? 
4.The text in Figure 2 is too small and should be optimized for better readability. 
5.A more comprehensive ablation study is recommended.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

While the paper presents a novel DynFS-MoE framework, a dynamic multimodal Mixture-of-Experts approach for PTE diagnosis post-TBI, the associated experimental data, result analysis, and other key components remain to be further optimized and improved.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper aims to address a highly challenging clinical task: diagnosing the risk of progression to post-traumatic epilepsy (PTE) following traumatic brain injury (TBI) using structural MRI (sMRI) and functional MRI (fMRI). To tackle the issues of information loss and modality competition present in traditional fusion strategies, the authors propose a dynamic multimodal Mixture-of-Experts framework, DynFS-MoE. This method includes a time-aware encoder, Modality-Specific Experts (MSoE), and a core Modality-Class MoE (MCoE) module, which dynamically allocates feature patches using a 3D class-conditioned routing mechanism. Additionally, the paper introduces a brain interpretability regularizer based on Conditional Mutual Information (CMI) to prevent routing collapse. Evaluated on a cohort of 69 subjects, DynFS-MoE significantly outperforms existing static graph network baselines across three binary classification tasks and provides highly compelling spatial-temporal interpretability for epileptogenesis.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The MCoE module is a significant innovation in this paper. Unlike standard MoEs that route solely based on input features, MCoE constructs the routing logits as a 3D tensor, explicitly introducing the conditional constraint of “disease class”. This allows the model to dynamically adjust its reliance on different modalities according to different disease phenotypes.
2.The interpretability analysis is exceptionally well-executed and aligns perfectly with clinical logic. The derived routing weights compellingly demonstrate that TBI diagnosis heavily relies on static structural connectivity (sMRI), whereas PTE diagnosis cleverly down-weights the reliance on sMRI and shifts focus to dynamic functional abnormal discharges in early/mid-temporal segments (S2-S4). Furthermore, the ROI interaction heatmaps reveal progressive “frontal-occipital” abnormal connectivity unique to PTE, which is highly consistent with existing neuropathological literature.
3.Utilizing scaled dot-product attention to inject global sMRI structural priors into local fMRI temporal patches via residual connections is a lightweight yet highly effective strategy. This cleverly mitigates modality competition prior to entering the MoE routing layer.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Critically Small Dataset and High Overfitting Risk: The entire study is based on only 69 subjects (26 HC, 24 TBI, 19 PTE). Training an MoE architecture containing complex routing mechanisms and regularizations on such a tiny dataset is highly susceptible to severe overfitting.
2.Severe Disconnect Between Figures and Text: There is a confusing disconnect between the framework diagram and the textual description. For instance, Section 2.4 specifies that the input to MCoE incorporates both cross-modal fusion and modality-specific processing from prior layers, but in Figure 1, the input to MCoE appears to solely come from the cross-modal fusion path, demonstrating a clear inconsistency.
3.Lack of Explicit Mathematical Constraints for “Modality-Specific” MSoE: In Section 2.3, the authors claim that MSoE extracts “modality-specific features”. However, structurally, MSoE is merely a standard MoE layer. The paper lacks any explicit loss function or physical isolation to force a certain expert to “only process fMRI” or “only process sMRI”; it relies entirely on data-driven learning.
4.Missing Unimodal Baselines and Key Ablation Details: Since one of the paper’s claimed innovations is that “dynamic multimodal fusion is superior to unimodal methods,” comparisons with unimodal baseline models must be included. Moreover, the current ablation study only verifies the routing strategy, lacking a systematic component-wise ablation of the core modules.

N/A

reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces a DynFS-MoE framework that utilizes a class-conditioned joint distribution to dynamically route modality patches to specialized experts. This is a significant step beyond static fusion methods.
reviews.text_strengths: Develops a time-aware functional-structural encoder that partitions fMRI into temporal segments and uses scaled dot-product attention to integrate structural connectivity features; MoE-based dynamic modality fusion; strong performance on a clinical dataset; A Brain Interpretability Regularizer based on conditional mutual information is used to reveal disease-specific brain interaction patterns.

The paper lacks a comparison against a standard multimodal fusion baseline, such as simple feature concatenation, to isolate the specific benefit of the MoE routing; he paper does not report $p$-values or formal statistical significance tests to confirm that the improvements over baselines are statistically robust.

meta_reviews.text:
The three reviewers offer a mixed overall recommendation, with two weak accepts and one weak reject. They confirmed the novel DynFS-MoE framework for its dynamic, class-conditioned routing and clinically meaningful interpretability, but unanimously raise serious concerns about the extremely small cohort (only 69 subjects) that heightens overfitting risk and limits generalizability.
Further shared weaknesses include the absence of unimodal and simple fusion baselines, a lack of statistical significance testing, inconsistencies between text and figures, and insufficient ablation studies. The authors should prepare the rebuttal to address those concerns.

After considering the initial reviews, the authors’ rebuttal, and the updated reviewer assessments, the paper is recommended for acceptance. The reviewers acknowledged the novelty of the DynFS-MoE framework and its clinically meaningful interpretability. The authors also addressed the reviewers’ concerns in the rebuttal by providing statistical tests that confirmed significant improvements over baselines, clarifying the framework’s design and correcting the figure inconsistency, and justifying the dataset size by the clinical rarity of post-traumatic epilepsy. The work’s dynamic class-conditioned routing and multimodal fusion, despite the data limitations, are seen as sufficiently valuable for publication.

Two reviewers (Weak Reject, Weak Accept) did not submit post-rebuttal assessments. The third reviewer recommends to accept this paper. I share this assessment.
Reviewers appreciated particularly the methodological contribution of this work paired with the conducted (interpretability) analyses. A shared main criticism centred around the small sample size of the dataset. However, I agree with the authors that acquiring a suitable, large dataset is challenging, given the application. I consider the provided evidence as sufficient and would down-weight this critique.

This paper contributes a clinically motivated dynamic functional-structural mixture-of-experts framework for post-traumatic epilepsy diagnosis, with a sensible attempt to combine heterogeneous signals in a difficult small-sample setting. The rebuttal seems to have clarified the design motivation and the overfitting-mitigation perspective, which keeps the paper acceptable after rebuttal.

author_feedback_text:
General Response[R1,R2,R3]:
We sincerely thank the AC and reviewers for their constructive comments.
Sample Size Issue:We spent 4 years collecting this dataset because PTE is a relatively rare neurological disorder requiring long-term follow-up for definitive diagnosis. Acquiring both fMRI and DTI data is also costly, while preprocessing and manual curation are highly time-consuming. Existing studies used similarly limited cohorts: [1] included 24 HC and 22 TBI subjects [2] included HC: n=13, TBI: n=16, and TBI converters/seizure group: n=17.To our paper survey, no prior study has simultaneously included larger TBI and PTE cohorts with both fMRI and DTI modalities. Moreover, our work is the first to jointly investigate fMRI and DTI for TBI/PTE-related epilepsy using a deep learning framework. 
[1] Kang et al. (2025), Relationship Between Structural and Functional Network Connectivity Changes for Patients With Traumatic Brain Injury and Chronic Health Symptoms.
[2] Raizman et al. (2020), Traumatic Brain Injury Severity in a Network Perspective: A Diffusion MRI–Based Connectome Study.
Overfitting in Small Samples [R2]:To mitigate overfitting in a relatively small dataset, we adopt a lightweight MoE with class-conditioned dynamic routing instead of a large dense architecture, activating only selected experts per sample to control effective capacity. We further apply conditional mutual information regularization to constrain modality–expert routing, improving stability. DynFS-MoE consistently improved performance, while ablation studies confirmed the importance of class-conditioned routing.
Comparison with Unimodal Methods and Statistical Significance [R2,R3]: 
Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we conducted Welch’s t-test between DynFS-MoE and the best baseline methods. For HC vs. PTE, DynFS-MoE improved ACC, AUC, and F1-score by 5.0%, 7.7%, and 9.5%, respectively. Improvements in AUC and F1-score were highly significant (p<0.001), while ACC also achieved significance (p<0.05). Compared with the best unimodal models (fMRI-FC MLP or sMRI MLP), DynFS-MoE further improved AUC and F1-score by 15.1% and 11.0%. For TBI vs. PTE, DynFS-MoE improved ACC by 6.9% and AUC by 22.4% over the best baseline, both with high significance (p<0.001).
We also compared our approach with recent SOTA models, including MultiViT (2024), IBrainGNN (2025), and AGIIBM (2025). DynFS-MoE consistently outperformed competing methods across all cohorts, achieving ACC gains of 2.7%, 7.7%, and 10.0%, respectively. [R1-2]In addition, DynFS-MoE (AUC=0.67) can flexibly support 3-class classification and achieves an average improvement of 2.41% across 3-class classification tasks.
Figure–Text Inconsistency[R2]:
[R2-2] We thank the reviewer for identifying the inconsistency between Fig. 1 and Section~2.4, and we will revise the arrow connection to MCoE in Fig.1.Section~2.4 states that the input to the MCoE is the refined modality patch embeddings $Z={z_i}
{i=1}^{|P|}$ after cross-modal fusion and modality-specific processing. Each $z_i$ incorporates both the cross-modal fusion outputs from Section~2.2 ($\tilde{f}^{(k)}$, $z
{\text{fused}}^{(k)}$) and the MSoE outputs from Section~2.3.Therefore, MCoE operates on joint representations containing both cross-modal interactions and modality-specific specialization.
[R2-3] In the MSoE module, fMRI (color blocks) and sMRI (red-highlighted blocks) are already represented as modality-specific inputs. Specialization arises from the modality-defined patch space, routing mechanism, and class-conditioned dispatch. Specifically, DynFS-MoE constructs modality patches $P={f^{(1)},\dots,f^{(K)},s}$ and routes them through $P_\theta(E=e_j\mid P=p_i)$, enabling experts to specialize to different modality distributions. In addition, the class-conditioned routing and conditional mutual information regularizer $I(P;E\mid Y)$ encourage modality- and class-dependent expert associations instead of uniform expert sharing.

title: EA-LDM: Explicit Alignment Latent Diffusion Model for Patient-Specific CT Reconstruction from Bi-planar X-Rays
abstract:
Reconstructing 3D CT volumes from bi-planar X-rays offers
a low-dose, efficient alternative to CBCT for Adaptive Radiotherapy.
However, the anatomical overlaps in X-rays and the ill-posed nature of
this task often lead to spatial ambiguity and a loss of patient-specific
details in existing methods. In this paper, we propose EA-LDM, an Explicit
Alignment Latent Diffusion Model framework to address these challenges.
First, we introduce an Explicit Alignment (EA) strategy, where
an alignment network maps 2D X-rays directly into a pre-trained 3D CT
latent space, utilizing volumetric semantic priors to resolve spatial ambiguity.
Second, to recover patient-specific details, we propose Patient-
Specific Optimization (PSO). Formulated through a bi-level optimization,
PSO effectively incorporates priors from the pre-treatment planning
CT while maintaining robustness to temporal anatomical changes.
Experiments on a collected clinical dataset demonstrate that our method
significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in both structural
fidelity and perceptual quality.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper aims to address the limitations of cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) in intraoperative settings by proposing a method for CT reconstruction from biplanar X-ray images. The proposed approach is patient-specific, incorporating individualized optimization to improve reconstruction accuracy. Furthermore, it enables intraoperative registration with preoperative CT data through explicit alignment latnet diffusion model (EA LDM), facilitating better anatomical correspondence during surgery.
reviews.text_strengths:
This paper focuses on the registration of intraoperative X-ray images with preoperative CT by leveraging CT reconstruction from only two biplanar X-ray views (anteroposterior and lateral). The proposed method incorporates patient-specific modeling and optimization, enabling it to account for inter-patient variability as well as temporal anatomical changes that may occur between preoperative imaging and surgery. These features enhance its suitability for real-world clinical applications.
The approach has been extensively validated on standard datasets and demonstrates competitive performance when compared with existing state-of-the-art methods in the literature.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper remains overly generalized, and does not adequately address how the proposed framework can be adapted or customized to different anatomical regions. While the methodology is presented as broadly applicable, there is limited discussion on anatomy-specific constraints, variations, or the need for specialized modeling strategies.
Although the RADCURE dataset (focused on oropharyngeal anatomy) is used for evaluation, the paper does not clearly explain how the algorithm is trained or tailored for this specific anatomical domain. In particular, it is unclear whether the model incorporates anatomy-aware priors or whether it relies purely on generic feature learning.
Furthermore, the use of pretrained CT-based weights for processing X-ray inputs raises concerns. Given the inherent domain gap between CT volumes and X-ray projections, such pretrained representations may not yield meaningful latent features for accurate 2D-to-3D reconstruction. A more detailed justification or domain adaptation strategy is needed.
A central challenge that is insufficiently addressed is the reconstruction of a 3D volume from only two biplanar X-ray images (AP and lateral). This is a highly ill-posed problem, and the paper does not convincingly demonstrate how the proposed method overcomes the associated ambiguities.
Additionally, the availability of preoperative CT scans suggests that the problem could instead be formulated as a 2D–3D registration task. In such a scenario, intraoperative X-rays could be registered to the preoperative CT, allowing surgical planning to proceed directly on the CT data without requiring full 3D reconstruction. The paper does not provide a clear comparison or justification for choosing reconstruction over registration.
In this context, the motivation for employing EA-LDM for 3D reconstruction needs to be more explicitly articulated. Specifically, the advantages of this approach should be clearly contrasted against conventional 2D–3D registration methods in terms of accuracy, robustness, computational efficiency, and clinical utility.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper does not sufficiently justify the choice of 3D reconstruction over conventional 2D–3D registration approaches. In scenarios where preoperative CT is available, 2D–3D registration is a well-established and often more accurate solution compared to reconstructed 3D volumes from sparse X-ray views. The authors should clearly articulate the advantages of their reconstruction-based approach, particularly in terms of accuracy, robustness, and clinical relevance, in comparison to existing registration techniques.
Additionally, the proposed architecture lacks a clear mechanism for adapting to the specific anatomical region of interest. Different anatomical structures exhibit distinct geometric, textural, and pathological characteristics, which typically necessitate customized modeling strategies. The paper does not discuss whether the model incorporates anatomy-specific priors, constraints, or training adaptations, raising concerns about its generalizability and clinical applicability.
The experimental validation is limited to standardized datasets, which may not adequately reflect real intraoperative conditions. The transition from controlled datasets to real surgical environments introduces several challenges, including patient positioning variability, imaging noise, occlusions, and workflow constraints. The paper does not describe any operating room (OT) setup, workflow integration, or practical deployment considerations. For applications such as tumor resection or biopsy, it is essential to outline how intraoperative imaging would be acquired, processed, and utilized within the surgical pipeline.
Furthermore, the comparative analysis is primarily restricted to diffusion-based and GAN-based methods. While these are relevant, the omission of Neural Radiance Field (NeRF)-based approaches is notable. NeRF-based methods have demonstrated strong capabilities in multi-view 3D reconstruction with reduced hallucination artifacts, and their inclusion would provide a more comprehensive and balanced evaluation of the proposed method.
How the weighting parameters for the loss functions lambda 1 to lamda 5 is selected must be mentioned

reviews.text_contribution: This work introduces EA- LDM, a framework for patient-specific 3D CT reconstruction from biplanar X-rays. To address the spatial ambiguity in X-ray images, the work proposes Alignment Networks that map 2D X-rays into a pretrained 3D CT latent space, and a bi-level Patient-Specific Optimization (PSO) strategy that balances population-level generalization with patient-specific refinement. The proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in PSNR and SSIM.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Comprehensive ablations clearly demonstrate the individual contributions of Explicit alignment (EA) and PSO. The downstream segmentation evaluation using reconstructed CTs across anatomies (Section 3.4) is a particularly strong validation.
2.The bi-level PSO strategy is an interesting formulation where the lower-level optimization ensures generalization while the upper-level refines patient-specific details.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Reproducibility is a concern. The weighting hyperparameter in Eq. 3 is undefined, and the variables “x M” and “x N” in Fig. 2(a) are not explained. Combined with the absence of open-source code, replication would be difficult.
2.Evaluation is limited to DRR-based reconstructions, and validation on real biplanar X-ray images would be necessary to better assess the clinical feasibility of the proposed approach.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Although the proposed EA and PSO strategies are well motivated and clearly contribute to the improved performance, the underlying latent diffusion model appears similar to prior works such as DIFR3CT. It would strengthen the paper if the authors more clearly articulate how their latent diffusion model differs from existing approaches. 
In Section 3.4, the cohort size used for this evaluation is not specified, which makes it difficult to assess the robustness of the results. Additionally, the analysis relies primarily on qualitative visualizations so, including quantitative metrics would further strengthen the claims.
Also, to improve reproducibility, the paper would benefit from clearly defining all hyperparameters or providing an open-source implementation of the work.

The paper presents a well-structured and detailed approach to CT reconstruction from biplanar X-rays, leveraging explicit alignment (EA) networks and patient-specific optimization (PSO) as its core contributions. The ablation studies clearly demonstrate the individual impact of EA and PSO, showing the value of each component. However, reproducibility concerns and the lack of evaluation on real X-ray images are notable gaps. These limitations led me to the decision

reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have addressed reproducibility concerns by clarifying hyperparameters and ambiguous symbols. However, the architectural novelty of the Alignment Network (AN) still does not feel sufficiently differentiated. An ablation study specifically isolating the contribution of AN would strengthen the paper and provide more convincing evidence of its actual impact.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper proposes EA-LDM, an explicit-alignment latent diffusion model for patient-specific CT reconstruction from bi-planar X-rays. The reviewers recognized the potential clinical relevance of reconstructing or aligning patient-specific 3D anatomy from sparse intraoperative X-ray views, as well as the technical contributions of explicit alignment networks and patient-specific optimization. Some reviewers also considered the paper well structured, with useful ablation studies and competitive quantitative results against recent reconstruction baselines.
However, the reviews also identified several important concerns. The clinical motivation and problem formulation are not fully clear, especially why full 3D reconstruction from two X-rays is preferable to conventional 2D–3D registration when preoperative CT is available. Reviewers also raised concerns about the ill-posed nature of reconstructing 3D CT from only AP/lateral X-rays, the lack of validation on real biplanar X-ray images, and unclear adaptation to specific anatomical regions. The use of pretrained CT-based latent representations for X-ray inputs also requires stronger justification given the domain gap. There are additional reproducibility concerns, including undefined hyperparameters, unclear variables in figures, and missing details about cohort sizes and loss weighting.
Given the relatively positive scores from two reviewers and the overall quality of the submission, I recommend giving the authors a rebuttal opportunity. The authors should carefully address the reviewers’ concerns during rebuttal.

Despite highly polarized post-rebuttal feedback (Accept, Accept, Reject), the authors’ rebuttal successfully dismantled the negative consensus by resolving core clinical and technical misunderstandings. First, they justified the reconstruction task over traditional 2D-3D registration by explaining that active radiation dose optimization strictly requires updated 3D tissue density volumes rather than mere spatial alignment. Second, they established true clinical utility, showing that pairing instantaneous bi-planar X-rays with historical pCTs accurately captures ongoing temporal anatomical variations (e.g., tumor regression) while entirely bypassing the high radiation dose and minute-long gantry rotations mandated by onboard CBCT or limited-angle scans. Third, they clarified that multi-view rendering baselines were not ignored, as the heavily outperformed baseline INRR3CT is itself a NeRF-based architecture. Backed by a 92-patient clinical cohort demonstrating superior numerical (PSNR/SSIM), visual, and downstream segmentation fidelity, this well-grounded framework satisfies publication standards and is recommended for acceptance.
Authors have adequately addressed comments.

The clinical scenario targeted by this work remains somewhat controversial. In addition, many technical details and design choices are not clearly explained, and the overall organization of the manuscript needs substantial improvement. Given the considerable amount of revision required, I do not believe the paper is suitable for publication in its current form.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their insightful comments.
Adaptation to Specific Anatomical Structures [R1-1/2]
EA-LDM is not limited to a specific anatomy, but a general framework for CT reconstruction. Through Patient-Specific Optimization (PSO) on the patient’s own pCT, the model learns detailed anatomical priors and enables adaptation to temporal anatomical changes. Moreover, region-specific loss can further boost performance. Its robustness has been validated on complex head and neck data.
Domain Gap Problem [R1-3]
We clarify that the Alignment Network (AN, Fig. 2) is designed for X-rays, so CT pretrained weights are not directly applied. We agree that a domain gap does exist. However, a shared latent semantic representation has been validated for reconstruction [1] since both rely on kV X-rays and similar attenuation. We thank Reviewer 1 for pointing out a promising future research direction regarding the domain gap.
Ill-posed Nature [R1-4]
For the ill-posed nature, we emphasize that exact reconstruction is unattainable; our goal is to approximate the ground truth by leveraging priors, e.g., patient-specific priors from pCT. Experiment results showed our method achieved best performance by exploiting these priors.
Why not Registration or Limited-angle CT [R1-5, R3-4]
Adaptive Radiotherapy (ART) requires updated 3D tissue density for dose optimization. 2D-3D registration is insufficient as it estimates only position. Limited-angle CT takes 10–30s to acquire 30–100 projections, causing image degradation from organ motion (e.g., peristalsis) and higher radiation.
Clinical Application [R1-6, R3-1/2]
Radiotherapy is a cancer treatment using radiation to destroy tumors, delivered over multiple fractions across several weeks. In the standard ART workflow, a planning CT (pCT) is first acquired, on which the clinical target and radiation dose are determined. At each fraction, CBCT is acquired from the onboard kV system for patient setup and plan optimization (e.g., dose optimization) before treatment, which is time-consuming, high-dose, and increases complication risks. Therefore, our application directly utilizes the bi-planar X-ray mode of the same kV system to reconstruct CT volumes, offering a faster, lower-dose substitute for CBCT. Moreover, as the anatomy constantly changes over the treatment weeks, it is important to reconstruct CT at each fraction rather than relying on the pCT.
About the Evaluation [R1-7, R2-2/4]
NeRF-based comparison. We clarify that INRR3CT is NeRF-based, which we quantitatively outperform quantitatively (e.g. +2.1 dB PSNR) and qualitatively.
DRRs as synthetic X-rays. While we agree that real X-ray data is ideal, collecting such data is ethically prohibitive due to additional radiation solely for research. Therefore, evaluation with DRRs remains standard in this field [1,2].
Quantitative results and cohort sizes in Sec.3.4.This experiment used data from all 92 patients, and quantitative metrics align with qualitative findings, which surpass the runner-up method by 6.2% in HD95 and 2.3% in IoU.
About Hyperparameters [R1-8, R2-1]
Weighting parameters. Loss weighting was set to balance the scales: λ₃=100, λ₄=0.1, and others=1.Unclear variables in Fig.2.AN in Fig. 2 uses M=4 encoder stages and N=3 decoder stages.
Difference with Previous LDM [R2-3]
Unlike previous work, our training uses EA to suppress 2D ambiguity and PSO to exploit patient-specific priors. Architecturally, we propose AN for cross-reference information from orthogonal views.
All the above discussions will be added to the revision.
[1] Shen, L., Zhao, W., Xing, L.: Patient-specific reconstruction of volumetric computed tomography images from a single projection view via deep learning. Nat. Biomed. Eng 3, 880–888 (2019)
[2] Ying, X., Guo, H., Ma, K., Wu, J., Weng, Z., Zheng, Y.: X2CT-GAN: Reconstructing CT from biplanar x-rays with generative adversarial networks. In: Conf. Comput. Vis. Pattern Recognit. pp. 10619–10628.(2019)

title: ECFR: Entropy-Consistency Flow Rectification in Test-Time Adaptation for Medical Foundation Models
abstract: Deploying medical Foundation Models (FMs) is often severely compromised by continuous clinical distribution shifts. While Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) offers a promising solution, existing paradigms rely on overly simplified, uni-directional optimization that blindly enforces confidence on flawed representations, inevitably precipitating error accumulation and model collapse. To address this critical safety gap, we propose Entropy-Consistency Flow Rectification (ECFR), which fundamentally redefines TTA as a spatial routing problem. Central to our approach are the Entropy-Consistency Quadrants, which explicitly disentangle streaming data into distinct diagnostic states. Guided by this spatial partitioning, ECFR pioneers a quadrant-wise flow rectification strategy: it consolidates potentially correct samples via minimization while actively sequestering high-risk erroneous inputs via maximization, strictly halting the propagation of erroneous gradients. Furthermore, a dynamic memory bank continuously calibrates these quadrant thresholds against distribution drift. Comprehensive evaluations on two state-of-the-art (SOTA) medical FMs across three diverse out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets demonstrate that ECFR successfully prevents model collapse, achieving superior accuracy and confidence calibration for safe clinical deployment. The code is available at https://github.com/EndoluminalSurgicalVision-IMR/ECFR.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a test-time adaptation method that improves medical FMs under distribution shifts. The method utilizes entropy and prediction consistency and applies bidirectional optimization to consolidate reliable predictions or suppress high-risk ones.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The work is well-motivated to address distribution shifts in medical AI deployment. 
2.The entropy–consistency quadrants provide a clear and interpretable diagnostic view. 
3.The results show consistent improvements across multiple datasets using multiple metrics.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Lack of clarity in notation and definitions in metric definition. This makes the method harder to follow.
Streaming with batch size 1 makes the FIFO memory bank (N=128) the only source of distributional context. There are no sensitivity analyses for memory bank size N. 
3.ECFR-0.5 uses q=0.5, is performance stable across other values?
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper is well-motivated. The results show the effectiveness of the proposed method. But the concerns needed to be addressed before acceptance.
