We thank all reviewers once more for their time and constructive engagement. We are confident the camera-ready version will address the raised concerns and further strengthen the paper.

title: EchoVQA: Enabling Conversational Assistance for Point-of-Care Cardiac Ultrasound
abstract: Point-of-care transthoracic echocardiography enables cardiac assessment in virtually any clinical setting, yet its diagnostic utility remains constrained by the expertise required for image acquisition and interpretation. Visual question answering (VQA) offers a promising paradigm for bridging this expertise gap through interactive clinical assistance, but existing echocardiography VQA datasets are limited in scale, restricted to high-quality images, and only cover a few views. We introduce EchoVQA, the first large-scale VQA dataset for echocardiography, comprising 14,299 images and 74,819 question-answer pairs. The dataset integrates public sources (EchoNet-Dynamic, CAMUS) with our own point-of-care acquisitions from two handheld probes (Lumify, Clarius), spanning diverse views and including both high-quality and suboptimal images. Uniquely, EchoVQA includes acquisition guidance questions to help users optimize transducer positioning toward a diagnostic apical 4-chamber view for left ventricular ejection fraction estimation—a challenging task for novice operators in point-of-care settings. We further develop a parameter-efficient method based on multimodal learnable prompts achieving state-of-the-art performance on most benchmarks, including EchoVQA, with significantly fewer trainable parameters than existing state-of-the-art approaches. Data and code: https://huggingface.co/datasets/filbel/echoVQA.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs
Modalities -> Mobile / Wearable / Point-of-Care Imaging & Sensors

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper introduces EchoVQA, a large-scale cardiac ultrasound VQA benchmark with 14,299 images and 74,819 QA pairs, combining public datasets (EchoNet-Dynamic, CAMUS) and newly collected point-of-care data. It features fine-grained stratification by view and quality, and uniquely includes acquisition-guidance questions.
It proposes a parameter-efficient three-level prompting framework on top of LLaMA-2-7B, integrating visual prompts, dataset-level textual prompts, and retrieval-based instance prompts. With only 104M trainable parameters, it achieves performance comparable to LLaVA-Med and LLaVA-Tri.
reviews.text_strengths:
The dataset fills a critical gap, expanding prior echocardiography VQA resources from only hundreds of QA pairs to a large-scale benchmark with real point-of-care data, significantly enhancing clinical relevance.
The inclusion of acquisition-guidance questions is novel, extending VQA from image interpretation to assisting probe operation, directly addressing real-world needs of novice sonographers.
The human-in-the-loop data generation pipeline is well-designed, combining expert-defined templates, LLM-based generation, and multi-expert verification to reduce hallucinations and improve reliability.
The method is parameter-efficient, achieving near-SOTA performance with only 104M trainable parameters compared to much larger models like LLaVA-Med and LLaVA-Tri.
The three-level prompting design is well-validated, with ablations showing complementary contributions from each component rather than redundancy.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The point-of-care data are limited in scale and diversity (≤12 subjects), which weakens claims of generalizability and clinical robustness.
The clinical validity of acquisition-guidance QA is not verified, lacking inter-rater agreement or user studies to confirm real-world usability.
The expert review process is unclear given the dataset size, with no details on full vs. partial validation or quality control statistics.
The methodological contribution is largely compositional, combining existing techniques, and the gains from test-time optimization are marginal relative to its computational cost.
The evaluation lacks domain-specific echocardiography baselines and shows limited generalization beyond radiology-heavy settings.
Potential dataset bias and incomplete ethical disclosure, along with clarity issues in figures and presentation, further limit reliability and transparency.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The dataset clearly fills an important gap (PoC echocardiography VQA with acquisition guidance), and the method provides a reasonable PEFT-based approach with solid SOTA-level results. However, concerns remain: (1) the PoC data involve only 12 subjects, limiting diversity and weakening claims of large-scale generalization; (2) the clinical validity of acquisition-guidance QA is not supported by user studies; and (3) the methodological novelty is largely a cross-domain combination of existing techniques. Clarifying data release plans, providing subject diversity statistics, and reporting the latency of TTO would strengthen the work.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal confirms a data release commitment and provides subject demographics, but the two most critical concerns — clinical validity of acquisition-guidance QA and TTO computational cost — remain unsupported by evidence, and the 12-subject PoC cohort limitation is not resolved.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces a new echocardiography benchmark alongside a parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) strategy. The proposed benchmark consolidates existing public datasets with self-collected point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) images to construct a comprehensive set of echocardiographic question-answering pairs. To improve model performance, the PEFT strategy incorporates three complementary components: visual adaptation prompts, dataset-level prompts, and test-time optimization.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The problem this benchmark aims to address is practically motivated. Despite its clinical importance, visual question answering for POCUS remains a largely underexplored area.
2.The question types curated in the benchmark are closely aligned with real-world POCUS interpretation tasks, reflecting strong potential for clinical applicability.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Some additional clarification on the benchmark construction would help readers better understand the design choices. For instance, it would be helpful to explain the rationale behind combining conventional echocardiography from public datasets (EchoNet-Dynamic and CAMUS) with self-collected POCUS images, as well as the key similarities and differences between these data sources. Additionally, since echocardiography is inherently temporal, it would be worth discussing the motivation for using images rather than video clips as input. Finally, as echocardiographic interpretation typically involves multiple views (e.g., A4C, A2C, PLAX, PSAX), clarifying why the benchmark focuses on A4C images — particularly given that existing benchmarks such as MIMIC-Echo-VQA already cover a broader range of views and conditions — would strengthen the paper’s positioning.
2.Further elaboration on the benchmark construction pipeline would help establish its soundness. Specifically, clarifying the relationships among “expert templates,” “category labels,” and “questions” would be beneficial. It would also be helpful to describe how category labels are assigned to each image, how expert templates and category labels interact in the QA generation process, and to provide examples of the resulting QA pairs at each stage.
3.The use of GPT-4o for fine-grained QA generation raises a few points worth addressing. First, given that GPT-4o’s availability may change over time, it would be helpful to discuss contingency plans for reproducing or extending the benchmark when the same model is unavailable. Second, providing some validation or evidence of GPT-4o’s echocardiographic analysis capability would strengthen confidence in the quality of the generated ground-truth annotations, as this is a specialized domain that may benefit from additional scrutiny.
4.The connection between the proposed PEFT strategy and the Echo-VQA benchmark could be made more explicit. The introduction motivates the benchmark by highlighting the scarcity of echocardiography-specific data, yet the PEFT experiments rely on general-purpose medical VQA datasets for training rather than splits derived from Echo-VQA itself. It would be helpful to clarify two related points: first, how the constructed Echo-VQA dataset contributes to MLLM performance improvement, and second, since echocardiographic content appears to constitute a relatively small fraction of the general-purpose training data, what accounts for the observed performance gains on Echo-VQA specifically.
5.The experimental comparisons could be further strengthened by including more recent medical MLLMs, such as MedGemma, Lingshu, and their LoRA fine-tuned variants, to provide a more up-to-date performance reference. In addition, reporting FLOPs for the compared methods would offer a clearer picture of computational costs, since these reflect the parameters actually involved in the optimization process and are important for fair comparison.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
See weakness above.

A strong benchmark paper should construct a rigorous and well-motivated benchmark that can meaningfully stress-test current methods from important yet underexplored perspectives, while also offering insights into existing limitations and potential future directions. Given that the EchoVQA dataset is the central contribution of this work, meeting these expectations is essential. While the paper addresses a practically relevant problem, the curation process and benchmark constitution would benefit from further clarification and refinement to better establish their soundness. Additionally, incorporating more recent methods and deeper analysis that more fully leverages the proposed benchmark would considerably strengthen the experimental section.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I thank the authors for their efforts. However, several issues remain unresolved. The concern regarding why conventional echocardiography and self-collected point-of-care data are combined, despite the paper’s title explicitly stating “point-of-care cardiac ultrasound,” has not been adequately addressed. Additionally, the concerns surrounding the benchmarking comparisons and implementation details of the proposed PEFT method remain outstanding. Furthermore, the EchoVQA training and validation data configuration and statistics used for stage 2 fine-tuning are not sufficiently explained, particularly given that the benchmark and training data are split from the same source. In light of these unresolved concerns, I have decided to maintain my original score.
reviews.text_ethics: The paper mentioned that they self-collected echocardiography data for constructing the benchmark. This may need ethical approval for data curation.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper presents a twofold contribution. Firstly, it introduces EchoVQA, a dataset of images and VQA pairs combining public and new images collected by the team. All the information was validated by medical experts. Secondly, authors present a method to address the VQA problem which combines simple yet effective techniques such as parameter optimisation, visual adaptation prompts, instance level prompts and fine-tuning using a medical vocabulary. Results show that the method can consistently perform both on benchmarks and in the newlye presented dataset.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper is easy to follow and impacts the reader from the abstract. All justifications are properly made, and it is clear that authors have thoroughly investigated this field. The work integrates effectively public and private datasets, which resonates to the community that has worked with the former. Authors also clearly understand which are the pains in the medical sector (i.e. sonographers/clinicians not being available at certain times) and all the data acquisition and labelling pipeline has been validated by experts. Every method presented in section 1 is there for a reason, as they have compared and benchmarked against all of them. The sunburst diagram presented in Fig1 is noteworthy, and it is a great example of good practices in visualisation.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The weaknesses I found in the paper are minor, yet I think it is important for me to point them out. In Fig 1, authors could have simply used “im” for images and that could have helped them arrange better the text across the circle. The depiction of step 2 in Fig 2 is a bit confusing; I would have liked to see more detail on how the GPT agent pipelines these steps. Also, I would have liked to see some percentages on how much data is needed from step 1 to help the agent complete the task in 2.In Fig 3 step b, you should have depicted how the question looks like after going through the tokenizer coming into this part of the pipeline. In Table 1, it is unclear why the baseline GPT-4V doesn’t have parameters (I assume because it is a fully closed model) and why it cannot be used in PathVQA and your EchoVQA. References could be standardised better (there are some references that have multiple links and on some you don’t show the conference acronym) and I would have liked to see more references to work previously presented in MICCAI (you only have one workshop paper) to show that you are continuing a trend that interests the people that regularly publish in this venue.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper is very interesting and relevant, and presents a major contribution in the field. The reproducibility aspect is a bit of a concern as authors don’t specify if both the data and the method will be released, but the paper itself is very explanatory and will motivate insightful discussions in this field.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I stand by my previous decision and I think the paper is interesting and publishable.

meta_reviews.text:
Reviewers ask for a clearer justification of why conventional echocardiography and self-collected point-of-care data are combined, why the benchmark is image-based rather than video-based, and why the focus is limited to A4C views. They also ask for a much clearer explanation of the QA generation pipeline, including the relationship between expert templates, category labels, GPT-based generation, and expert validation.
The number of subjects appears small, and there is not enough evidence yet that the acquisition-guidance questions are clinically valid or useful in practice. Reviewers specifically ask for more detail on subject diversity, expert review coverage, and whether there is any inter-rater agreement or user-level validation.
The method contribution seems largely compositional, and about whether the experiments fully leverage the proposed benchmark. Stronger positioning against more recent medical multimodal large language models, together with clearer reporting of computational cost and the role of test-time optimization, would strengthen the paper.
These are central enough questions that rebuttal is appropriate before a final decision, and the paper could still move either way depending on how convincingly they are addressed.

Reviewers agree that the clinical problem is important and that the benchmark addresses a meaningful gap in echocardiography-focused VQA. The inclusion of acquisition-guidance questions extends VQA beyond image interpretation toward practical operator assistance. The benchmark itself is the primary contribution of the work, whereas the methodological contribution is generally viewed as incremental and largely compositional.
The main concerns relate to the limited size of the POCUS cohort, the absence of user studies or inter-rater agreement analyses for acquisition-guidance questions, and insufficient initial clarity regarding benchmark construction, QA generation, and the rationale for several design choices. The rebuttal provided reasonable clarification regarding dataset composition, expert validation, IRB approval, benchmark scope, and the QA generation pipeline, addressing many of these concerns.
While limitations remain regarding dataset diversity, clinical validation, and comparisons with more recent medical multimodal models, these do not outweigh the value of the benchmark contribution.
For the camera ready:
Clarify benchmark construction and QA generation workflow in greater detail.
Improve discussion of limitations arising from the small POCUS cohort.
Clearly describe expert review procedures and quality assurance measures.
Expand discussion of image-level versus video-level design choices and A4C-only scope.
Improve positioning relative to recent medical multimodal large language models and echocardiography-specific methods.
Report computational costs and inference overhead associated with test-time optimization.
VERY IMPORTANT: All images, QA pairs, expert templates and QA generation prompts must be released under a permissive license and accessible without barriers, e.g. via huggingface or zenodo. Without this the paper would need to be rejected.

The paper introduces EchoVQA, a clinically motivated benchmark for conversational assistance in point-of-care cardiac ultrasound, together with a parameter-efficient VQA framework. Reviewers found the benchmark timely and clinically relevant, particularly the acquisition-guidance component. Concerns focused on cohort scale, benchmark construction details, and limited evidence for clinical validity and efficiency. The rebuttal clarified the dataset design, QA generation pipeline, and evaluation protocol. While some limitations remain, the overall benchmark contribution and experimental evidence place the paper above the acceptance bar.

I recommend acceptance. Two of the three reviewers support acceptance after the rebuttal. The main contribution, the EchoVQA benchmark with acquisition-guidance questions for point-of-care echocardiography, fills a genuine and underserved gap, and the rebuttal clarified the points the Meta-AC raised. The remaining concerns, including the small 12-subject PoC cohort, the lack of a user study validating acquisition-guidance usefulness, the combination of conventional and PoC data, and the unreported TTO compute cost, are real but reflect requests for additional validation rather than evidence that the results are invalid. I therefore recommend acceptance, with the suggestion that the camera-ready temper generalization claims given the small PoC cohort, clarify the EchoVQA train and test split configuration, and frame the novice-operator user study and FLOPs/latency reporting as necessary follow-up work.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback, and R1/R3 for recognizing EchoVQA as addressing a critical gap. We clarify the dataset pipeline, benchmark scope, and evaluation protocol below.
Dataset scope, combining sources, image vs. video, A4C (R1#1, R2#1). EchoVQA spans 14,299 images and 74,819 QA pairs across EchoNet-Dynamic, CAMUS, Lumify, and Clarius, stratified into view-quality categories. The data sources are complementary: the 12-subject PoC subset (7F/5M, age range 23.52–40.57, 3 White / 9 Asian) supplies deployment-like acquisition variation and guidance signal across the non-diagnostic-to-diagnostic spectrum, largely absent from public data, while the public partition adds demographic/pathology breadth from hospital settings.
EchoVQA is image-level rather than video-level because acquisition guidance is real-time and frame-specific. Per-image QA is more fine-grained: a clip may begin with LV cutoff and end off-axis, requiring different guidance (“slide medially” vs. “rotate counterclockwise”), while a single video-level instruction would be ambiguous. Image-level guidance therefore provides richer supervision and composes with downstream video LVEF models that assume a diagnostic A4C clip. A4C is the canonical PoC view for LVEF — the most clinically actionable PoC measurement — and one of the hardest for novices to acquire [1,16]; multi-view extension is future work.
Expert coverage, IRB, validity (R1#2, R1#3, R1#6). All 74,819 QA pairs were reviewed by 4 experts (Sec. 2.3); given scale, we prioritized full-coverage correctness review over inter-rater agreement on a subset. Guidance was authored or revised by experts following standard acquisition practice [2,16]. A novice-operator user study on guidance efficacy is conducted as separate system-level validation, but was outside this submission. PoC scans collected under IRB (Sec. 2.1). Data/code will be released upon acceptance (R1, R3).
QA pipeline (R2#2-#3,R3). Per Sec. 2.2/Fig. 2: experts (i) categorize each image and (ii) author category-specific template QAs, e.g., for A4C_High_Qual: “Can I use this for EF measurement? Yes”, and for A4C_Low_Qual: “Can I estimate EF? No, the view quality is insufficient.”. GPT-4o turns these into image-specific QA capturing within-category variability (LV cutoff, foreshortening, low contrast). Conditioned on category label, templates, and image (not assigning categories) GPT-4o generates pairs like “Q:Can EF be measured? A:No, the LV apex is cut off,” which experts validate for image-grounded correctness.For replication,GPT-4o is not essential;stronger successor MLLMs could reduce expert corrections.
Method, baselines, compute (R2#4, R2#5, R1#4–5). Stage 1 (Sec. 3.2) aligns vision–LLM on medical image-caption corpora; Stage 2 fine-tunes per VQA dataset, including EchoVQA splits. Thus EchoVQA gains come from EchoVQA fine-tuning plus EchoVQA-adapted text prompts and TTO (R2#4). Comparisons follow prior per-dataset fine-tuning and strict exact-match/recall metrics (LLaVA-Med, LLaVA-Tri [ICLR 2025], PeFoMed). On echo-specific baselines (R1#5): we agree this would further strengthen the evaluation. Existing echo-specific models such as EchoCLIP and EchoPrime are primarily contrastive/retrieval-style, making direct comparison non-trivial. Still, including them as complementary baselines would indeed have been beneficial for completeness. MedGemma and Lingshu (2025) fold benchmark training splits into generalist multi-stage tuning, so they are not apples-to-apples. Even under Lingshu’s MedEvalKit (LLM-as-judge, looser than our recall), our method exceeds Lingshu-7B and MedGemma-4B-IT on aggregate accuracy (Lingshu Table 6). We report trainable parameters as the optimization-cost proxy and will clarify FLOPs/latency if permitted;TTO adds bounded per-query overhead scaling with vocabulary. We claim not per-component novelty but the medical-VQA-specific combination: visual adaptation prompts, text prompt learning, and TTO.

title: ECLIPSE: EHR-Constrained Localized Inference for Pan-Tumor Segmentation
abstract: Accurate tumor segmentation is essential for tumor-centric clinical modeling, yet most existing methods remain organ-specific or rely primarily on imaging and generic semantic prompts, neglecting incorporating patient-specific clinically recorded tumor burden into spatial inference. In routine practice, electronic health record (EHR) systematically record lesion count, longest diameter, and coarse anatomical subregion, providing structured but indirect spatial cues. Mapping structured clinical descriptors to voxel-level tumor delineation is challenging in pan-tumor settings, where cross-organ variability expands the spatial hypothesis space and sparse EHR descriptors alone cannot uniquely determine tumor location. To address this, we propose ECLIPSE (EHR-Constrained Localized Inference for Pan-Tumor Segmentation). Specifically, through a dedicated Clinical-Constrained Hypothesis Generation (CCHG) module, ECLIPSE reformulates pan-tumor segmentation as a feasibility-constrained localization–refinement process. First, a tumor-type prompt–conditioned spatial response map is estimated within the decoder space of a pretrained model to generate dense tumor hypotheses. Second, CCHG injects structured EHR descriptors as soft spatial constraints to enforce lesion count consistency, size plausibility, and regional coherence, producing clinically consistent bounding box prompts. Finally, the inferred bounding boxes are encoded as spatial prompts to refine voxel-wise delineation. Across 14 public and private tumor datasets comprising 5,360 cases for training, evaluation and testing, ECLIPSE achieves a mean DSC of 61.41%, outperforming the strongest baseline by +7.44%. It further improves performance on mixed tumor data (+8.91%), private clinical data (+3.88%), and attains the best DSC (71.23%) on an unseen dataset, demonstrating robust generalization.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes ECLIPSE, a pan-tumor segmentation framework that incorporates structured clinical tumor descriptors into spatial inference rather than treating them as auxiliary multimodal inputs. The key idea is to use a Clinically-Constrained Hypothesis Generator (CCHG) to transform coarse tumor-type-conditioned visual response maps into clinically admissible bounding box hypotheses under anatomical, cardinality, and scale constraints, and then use these automatically generated box prompts to refine segmentation. Overall, the paper contributes a clinically motivated coarse-to-fine formulation that connects image evidence, structured EHR descriptors, and prompt-based refinement in a unified framework.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The problem formulation is clear and clinically meaningful. Instead of vaguely claiming that EHR information may help segmentation, the paper identifies a more specific issue: image-only coarse spatial hypotheses may be clinically implausible, and structured descriptors such as subregion, lesion count, and tumor size can serve as feasibility constraints during hypothesis generation. 
2.The proposed pipeline is logically coherent. The method follows a clear sequence of coarse visual localization, clinically constrained hypothesis selection, and prompt-based refinement. This is much more convincing than a loosely assembled multimodal design. 
3.The role of structured clinical information is better motivated than in many prior multimodal segmentation papers. Here, EHR descriptors are assigned explicit functional roles in spatial inference, rather than being simply concatenated as additional features. 
4.The empirical gains appear substantial across datasets, suggesting that the overall framework is effective and that structured clinical priors may indeed improve pan-tumor segmentation performance.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The main concern relates to pseudo EHR descriptors in experiments. For public datasets without available EHR, the authors generate pseudo descriptors from the ground-truth masks is understandable given the scarcity of public datasets with structured EHR. However, it remains important to clarify whether the private Colon-FD cohort uses real EHR-derived descriptors or similarly generated pseudo descriptors. And it would also be helpful to explain how the pseudo descriptors are generated from the ground-truth masks for the public datasets. If Colon-FD indeed uses real structured clinical information, then this concern is largely alleviated and the paper would have a much stronger clinical grounding. 
2.Several implementation details are not sufficiently specified. In particular, the definition of the parameter α in box generation is unclear, the role of “FC” in the framework figure is not explicitly explained, and in formula 11 may contain a notation inconsistency or requires clarification. These issues do not appear to undermine the overall method, but they reduce clarity and reproducibility. Manuscript only states that a combined Dice and BCE loss is applied, without clearly defining the exact formulation, weighting, or whether both stages follow the same supervision scheme. 
3.The ablation section could also be clearer. In Table 2, the exact configuration of the “Baseline” is not clearly defined. In addition, since CCHG is the core methodological contribution and consists of multiple feasibility constraints, the paper would be strengthened by including internal ablations within CCHG. This is a relatively minor issue compared with the main methodological concern above, but it would still help readers better understand what is being ablated.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
One minor suggestion is to further improve the clarity of the method description. In particular, please clarify whether Eq. (11) should use the original response map S or the clinically constrained response map S-tilde, since the latter appears to be introduced by CCHG for feasibility-aware hypothesis generation. It would also be helpful to clarify how the pseudo EHR descriptors are generated from the ground-truth masks for the public datasets. In addition, please clarify whether the descriptors used for the private Colon-FD cohort are derived from real EHR records or similarly generated pseudo descriptors. These clarifications would further improve the paper’s readability and reproducibility.

I recommend this paper because it presents a clinically meaningful pan-tumor segmentation framework with a coherent methodological pipeline. The motivation is reasonable, and the overall formulation is fairly well developed. In particular, the progression from coarse visual localization, to clinically constrained hypothesis generation, to prompt-based refinement is logically consistent and methodologically sound. The reported improvements across multiple tumor types and datasets also suggest that the framework is effective in practice.
My main concern is pseudo EHR descriptors. In particular, it should be clarified whether the private Colon-FD cohort uses real EHR-derived descriptors or pseudo descriptors generated from the masks. If the Colon-FD evaluation is based on real EHR-derived descriptors, I would assess the paper more positively.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: After reading the rebuttal, my main concern regarding pseudo EHR descriptors has been sufficiently addressed. In particular, the authors clarified that the private Colon-FD cohort uses real clinical EHR-derived descriptors rather than pseudo descriptors generated from ground-truth masks, which substantially strengthens the clinical validity of the framework.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper presents EHR-Constrained Localized Inference for Pan-tumor Segmentation (ECLIPSE), a framework that integrates tumor burden descriptors from electronic health records (EHR) into spatial inference via a Clinical Constrained Hypothesis Generation (CCHG) module. The framework generates localization hypotheses through tumor type prompt-conditioned spatial response maps. The CCHG module encodes structured EHR descriptors as soft spatial feasibility constraints, producing clinically informed bounding box proposals that are automatically generated as prompts and fed back into the decoder for refinement.
reviews.text_strengths:
The method demonstrates consistent and clinically meaningful improvements over four established baselines across all seven tumor types
The ablation study clearly demonstrates the necessity of the CCHG module
The integration of EHR descriptors as soft spatial constraints is a clinically motivated and novel approach
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Major:
The evaluation relies exclusively on DSC. 
The dataset composition is insufficiently described. Are some tumor types severely underrepresented?
No limitations section is present.
Minor: 
Figure 1 requires significant magnification to read and Figure 2 lacks numbers and descriptions that are only introduced later in the text
The CCHG module is introduced and described multiple times throughout the paper unnecessarily.
The DSC gains are ranging from 3.88% to 8.91%, but the authors do not discuss the clinical relevance of these margins or cite supporting literature.
Runtime is not reported, which is relevant for clinical deployment assessment
The bibliography does not conform to MICCAI formatting guidelines.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The evaluation relies exclusively on DSC. Complementary metrics such as HD95 would provide a more complete picture of clinical utility, particularly given the pan-tumor setting where tumor sizes and boundary complexity vary significantly across types.

The paper presents a clinically motivated and technically sound framework for pan-tumor segmentation, with a novel integration of EHR-derived constraints into spatial inference. The method demonstrates consistent and meaningful improvements over four established baselines across all tumor types. The large and diverse dataset of contrast-enhanced CTs further supports the validity of the results. The weaknesses are largely minor and addressable. The most significant being the exclusive use of DSC, insufficient dataset description, missing limitations discussion, and unclear annotation provenance. None of these undermine the core contribution, and most can be addressed through clarification in the rebuttal. A weak accept is recommended.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors addressed my comments in the rebuttal.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes ECLIPSE, an EHR-constrained framework for pan-tumor CT segmentation. Its central contribution is to shift the role of structured clinical records from passive auxiliary metadata to active spatial feasibility constraints during inference. Specifically, the method first produces a tumor-type prompt-conditioned response map, then uses structured descriptors such as anatomical subregion, lesion count, and longest diameter to select clinically admissible tumor hypotheses and convert them into bounding-box prompts for segmentation refinement. This formulation is interesting because it treats segmentation not only as voxel-wise appearance recognition, but also as a constrained localization problem conditioned on how tumors are actually documented in clinical practice. The paper further evaluates this idea across multiple tumor types and datasets, including mixed-tumor, private clinical, and unseen tumor settings.
reviews.text_strengths:
The most appealing aspect of the paper is its attempt to connect clinical reporting logic with spatial segmentation. Many recent universal or prompt-based medical segmentation methods still rely on generic image prompts, while this work asks a more clinically grounded question: if radiologists already record lesion count, approximate size, and anatomical subregion, can these descriptors narrow the spatial search space for tumor segmentation? This is a meaningful perspective, especially for pan-tumor segmentation where purely image-driven models may produce diffuse or anatomically implausible responses.
Another strength is that the proposed CCHG module has an intuitive role in the pipeline. The module does not merely concatenate EHR features with image features; instead, it operationalizes clinical descriptors as constraints on where and how many lesions should be proposed. This makes the method easier to understand than many black-box multimodal fusion strategies. The improvement from the baseline to baseline+CCHG is also large, suggesting that the constraint mechanism is doing something substantial rather than serving as a cosmetic component.
The paper also makes a reasonable effort to evaluate generalization across different tumor sites. The inclusion of an unseen adrenal tumor dataset and a private Colon-FD cohort gives the work more clinical breadth than a single-organ study. The qualitative results are consistent with the stated motivation: ECLIPSE appears to reduce anatomically implausible spillover and produce more localized tumor masks than several universal segmentation baselines. This supports the broader claim that structured clinical priors can help suppress false positives in heterogeneous pan-tumor scenarios.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The chosen baselines are mostly universal or prompt-based segmentation models, but the paper does not compare with strong CT tumor segmentation pipelines trained or adapted for the same organs, such as nnU-Net-style organ-specific or tumor-specific baselines. This matters because the proposed method receives highly informative clinical constraints, whereas some baselines may receive only point or text prompts. The comparison, therefore, mixes two questions: whether ECLIPSE is a better segmentation model, and whether extra localization information helps segmentation. A fairer evaluation would include strong 3D CT tumor baselines, organ-specific expert models, and a setting where the same EHR-derived boxes or constraints are provided to competing promptable models.
The formulation of the tumor-type prompt and class input is underspecified. The method assumes a tumor-type prompt, but the paper does not clearly define where this prompt comes from at inference time, whether it is extracted from EHR, manually selected, or assumed to be known. This is not a small implementation detail, because in pan-tumor CT segmentation, the model must know whether it is searching for a liver tumor, a kidney tumor, a lung tumor, an adrenal tumor, or multiple possible lesions. If the class is externally provided, the task becomes segmentation of known clinical findings rather than open pan-tumor detection. If the class is not externally provided, the paper needs to explain how the organ or tumor type is inferred.
Relatedly, the current CCHG descriptor E = (r, n, d) appears too simplistic for realistic multifocal and multi-organ disease. A patient may have lesions in different organs, with different diameters and different anatomical subregions. The paper evaluates a “mixed tumor” dataset, but it is not clear whether it handles a single CT volume containing simultaneous heterogeneous tumor types, such as liver and kidney tumors in the same scan. The current description suggests a single tumor-type prompt, a single subregion descriptor, and a single longest-diameter parameter for box expansion. This may not generalize to multi-lesion cases where each lesion has its own organ, size, and location descriptor.
The evaluation is also too narrow. Reporting only DSC does not sufficiently characterize tumor segmentation performance. Tumor segmentation is highly sensitive to small lesions, lesion-level detection, false positives outside plausible organs, and boundary accuracy. Metrics such as HD95, NSD, lesion-wise recall/precision, false-positive volume, count consistency, and small-lesion stratified performance would provide a much clearer picture. This is particularly important here because the method explicitly claims improvements in localization, count consistency, and anatomically constrained prediction, but the evaluation does not directly measure these properties.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
I encourage the authors to more explicitly position the task. At present, the manuscript sometimes reads like a general pan-tumor segmentation method, but the actual setup appears closer to segmentation of known clinical findings under structured report-derived constraints. This distinction is important and should be stated clearly. A clinically useful version of this framework should be tested under realistic EHR uncertainty: missing subregion, approximate or wrong diameter, incorrect lesion count, multiple lesion descriptors, and contradictory image–EHR evidence. The method should also have a mechanism to express uncertainty or reject infeasible constraints rather than always forcing the top-n peaks into tumor boxes.

I assign a weak reject because the paper presents a promising, clinically motivated idea, but the current evidence does not yet convincingly demonstrate that the proposed method works under realistic clinical conditions. The major factor behind my score is the potential oracle nature of the pseudo-EHR protocol, in which key descriptors are generated from ground-truth masks of public datasets. Since these descriptors directly constrain localization and bounding-box generation, the reported improvement may not reflect the model’s ability to infer tumors from CT and real EHR, but rather its ability to exploit annotation-derived spatial priors. In addition, the baseline comparison does not include strong dedicated CT tumor segmentation models; the evaluation relies only on DSC, and the handling of tumor-type prompts, multi-organ multifocal disease, and upstream anatomical segmentation errors remains unclear. I would be much more positive if the authors provided a stronger evaluation under noisy/real EHR descriptors, added lesion-wise and boundary metrics, compared with organ-specific 3D tumor baselines, and clarified the clinical inference protocol.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
I appreciate the authors’ rebuttal and clarifications. The response partially addresses my concerns, especially by clarifying that the tumor-type prompt and descriptors are derived from EHR findings, and that multi-lesion cases are processed finding-by-finding and then merged. This makes the task setting clearer: ECLIPSE is best understood as EHR-constrained segmentation of known/suspected clinical findings, rather than fully open pan-tumor detection.
However, several concerns remain only partially resolved. First, the baseline comparison is still not fully convincing. The authors explain why universal and prompt-based models were selected, but the absence of strong organ-specific or tumor-specific 3D CT baselines remains a limitation, especially because ECLIPSE receives clinically informative constraints. Second, the handling of heterogeneous multi-organ disease is clarified conceptually, but the manuscript should explicitly describe how multiple EHR findings are represented, processed, and merged, rather than leaving this implicit. Third, the evaluation remains narrow. I understand that new metrics may not be allowed during rebuttal, but the lack of lesion-level detection, boundary, false-positive, count-consistency, and small-lesion analyses weakens the empirical support for the claimed localization and clinical-plausibility advantages.
Overall, the rebuttal improves my understanding of the method and addresses some ambiguity in the task formulation. While the paper still has important limitations in evaluation breadth and baseline fairness, the clinical motivation is meaningful, and the EHR-constrained formulation is potentially useful. Therefore, I am willing to raise my recommendation to a weak accept, provided that the final version clearly states the task setting, clarifies the multi-finding inference pipeline, expands the implementation details, and explicitly acknowledges the limitations regarding baselines and evaluation metrics.

meta_reviews.text:
The reviewers overall appreciate the motivation and formulation of the problem with the EHR-constrained pan-tumor CT segmentation. However, the reviewers also raised concerns regarding pseudo EHR descriptors, a single DSC-only metric for evaluation, insufficient dataset/implementation descriptions, unclear annotation process, unclear clinical inference protocol, and a lack of evaluation under noisy/real EHR descriptors. Authors are suggested to address these comments carefully.

Authors’ rebuttal addressed the main concerns. There are some remaining concerns regarding evaluation. However, there is clear merit in the work and all three reviewers recommend acceptance. I strongly suggest the authors utilize the extra space in the camera-ready to discuss the limitations of this work.

Important concerns raised by the reviewers, especially regarding the setup of specific datasets and prompt descriptors, have been answered in the rebuttal, leading to a positive rating from the reviewers, which I support. I strongly support the request to include at least a contour-based evaluation metric as recommended by the reviewers in a camera-ready version, which is also allowed under the rebuttal guidelines: “It is, however, allowed to amend the presentation of existing results.”, which includes additional metrics on same datasets/experiments already presented in the paper.

The paper proposes a clinically meaningful and technically sound pan-tumor segmentation framework that integrates EHR-derived constraints into spatial inference. Its clear progression from coarse localization to refined segmentation is methodologically logical and supported by consistent improvements across multiple datasets.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the AC and reviewers for their constructive feedback and for recognizing the clinical motivation (R2, R3, R5), methodological novelty (R2, R3, R5), and potential practical value (R3, R5) of our work. Below, we address the reviewers’ comments point by point.
1) Pseudo-EHR descriptors and Colon-FD clinical grounding (R2-Q1, R5): ECLIPSE targets EHR-constrained pan-tumor segmentation of suspected clinical findings. Colon-FD uses real clinical EHR, where tumor type, lesion count, maximal diameter, and coarse anatomical location are extracted from clinical records. For public datasets without released EHR, pseudo descriptors only simulate such clinical EHR information: lesion count is obtained by connected-component analysis, maximal diameter by the largest physical lesion extent, and anatomical subregion by the overlap with predefined organ subregions. 
2) Baselines and fair comparisons (R5-Q1): For strong CT tumor baselines, we selected recent SOTA universal/prompt-based models because they are most relevant to ECLIPSE and have been benchmarked against nnU-Net-style pipelines in several prior studies, such as Universal Model or MA-SAM. Unlike point prompts that directly mark tumor locations, ECLIPSE infers feasible tumor regions from clinically available EHR descriptors without manually specified tumor points. Due to page limits and rebuttal policy, we will clarify this choice and provide more detailed comparisons in an extended version.
3) Tumor-type prompt and multi-organ disease (R5-Q2/Q3): The tumor-type prompt is obtained from the EHR, where tumor type and subregion have already been preliminarily identified, as described in Sec. Introduction and Fig. 1(b). Importantly, MSWAL is a public mixed-tumor dataset, with many scans containing multiple tumor types or lesions from different organs. For such cases, ECLIPSE processes each tumor finding separately with its own prompt and EHR descriptor, and then merges the masks. The MSWAL results support this strategy. 
4) Evaluation beyond DSC (R3-Q1, R5-Q4): We agree that additional metrics may provide complementary perspectives. In the submitted manuscript, we used DSC as the primary metric because it is widely adopted in tumor segmentation benchmarks and enables consistent comparison across all baselines and datasets. The qualitative results in Fig. 3 provide complementary visual evidence. Following the rebuttal policy, we do not introduce new metrics here. A more comprehensive evaluation will be provided in the journal version.
5) Implementation details (R1-Q2): We clarify that α is a safety-margin coefficient for expanding the EHR-reported tumor size d into a loose segmentation box. “FC” denotes a Fully Connected layer, and S in Eq. 11 is the spatial response map from Eq. 5.The training loss is Dice+BCE with 1:1 weighting for both stages. 
6) Ablation study (R2-Q3): The “Baseline” in Table 2 denotes the model before CCHG, namely the ViT and CLIP encoders with multimodal fusion followed by the decoder, as described in Sec. 2.1 and Fig. 2.CCHG further introduces three feasibility constraints: anatomical subregion for regional coherence, lesion count for cardinality consistency, and tumor size for scale plausibility. As these complementary constraints are methodological necessities for generating clinically plausible tumor masks, we omitted internal ablations due to page limits; but we will clarify the baseline configuration and the role of each CCHG component.
7) Dataset, limitations, and presentation (R3-Q2/Q3): The dataset composition is summarized in Fig. 1 with corresponding references; we did not include an additional dataset table due to page limits. We will add a concise limitations paragraph discussing pseudo-EHR simulation and reliance on anatomical priors. We will also enlarge Fig. 1, add clearer annotations in Fig. 2, remove repeated CCHG descriptions, and correct the bibliography.
All revisions mentioned above will be updated in the final paper.

title: EdgeCVS: Democratization of surgical AI with a Distilled Edge-Deployable Critical View of Safety (CVS) model
abstract: Critical View of Safety (CVS) assessment has become a central safeguard against bile duct injury during laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC). Current deep learning-based solutions achieve strong performance but rely on massive backbone architectures (up to >1B parameters) that hinder real-world deployment, specifically in resource-constrained operating rooms. We challenge the assumption that such scale is necessary. Because CVS assessment is confined to a specific surgical phase and anatomical region, its visual representation occupies a compact, low-dimensional manifold. Guided by the hypothesis that this reduced semantic dispersion enables substantial model compression without sacrificing accuracy, we introduce EdgeCVS, a phase-gated distillation framework that compresses a high-capacity teacher into a 5M-parameter edge-efficient student. By incorporating anatomical spatial priors and phase-gated pseudo-labels, the compact model recovers complex decision boundaries. EdgeCVS achieves mAP close to the most recent state-of-the-art models while reducing the parameter count to 1.5%, enabling real-time inference (40 FPS) on standard CPUs.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors studied the feasibility of a real-time CPU-based surgical AI for automated CVS assessment. The method is distillation from big to small models.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The clinical motivation is clear 
2.The paper is well written and easy to understand.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.For such an application focused paper on tiny ML, the authors should compare with all the relevant state-of-the-art. Since, the primary problem of CVS is segmentation, comparing the performance with the Neural Cellular Automata (NCA) that typically has only thousands of paprameters, is a must. A bit of search in Scholar revealed this paper where a foundation model is distilled into the NCA: https://link. springer. com/article/10.1007/s11548-025-03425-x
2.Figure 2 and 3 contains too much information that is not very easy to comprehend. Consider re-designing those.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Missing comparison with state-of-the-art.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: My concerns are not addressed properly. Either the authors sidestepped (specific point about a paper example rather than the general NCA as a method for segmentation/ classification) or used flowery language to convolute the triviality of the method. As such, I do not see any reason for this paper to be accepted.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a lightweight model for CVS assessment that can run in real time on CPU hardware. The main idea is to compress a large teacher model into a 5M-parameter student by combining segmentation-based supervision, soft predictions from the teacher, and pseudo-labels from additional unlabeled data. The practical contribution is strong: the final model is much smaller (reducing the parameter count to 1.5%) while staying close to teacher performance and being much faster for deployment.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper addresses an important and practical problem. Real-time CPU deployment is very relevant for surgical AI. The experiments are structured around clear ablations. In particular, Figure 4 shows the effect of the proposed components on models of different sizes, and Table 1 shows that the final 5M model remains competitive while being far more efficient in terms of inference speed.
Concretely, for the proposed 5M model, performance increases from 58.8 to 63.7 with segmentation supervision, then to 65.2 with distillation, and finally to 68.9 with additional pseudo-labeled data in mAP (teacher at 71.4).
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The methodological novelty is more limited than the paper presentation sometimes suggests. The final gain comes from combining known ingredients: segmentation-based auxiliary supervision, teacher-student learning, and pseudo-labeling. Among these, the gain from distillation itself seems modest (1.5%) compared with the gains from segmentation supervision and adding more pseudo-labeled data.
I also found the framing of RQ1 weaker than RQ2 and RQ3.The question of whether the CVS task has lower variability seems partly expected from the fact that the task is already restricted to a specific surgical phase and anatomical region. In addition, the “manifold” analysis is done in the embedding space of a specific pretrained encoder, so this is not an intrinsic property of the raw data itself, but a property of that chosen representation.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I recommend weak accept because the paper has clear practical value and strong relevance for deployable surgical AI. The authors show that a 5M-parameter model can remain competitive for CVS assessment while running in real time on CPU hardware, which is an important result. The experiments are solid and include meaningful ablations.
My concerns are mainly about novelty and positioning: the method is a combination of known ideas, and the effect of distillation alone is fairly small. I also found RQ1 weaker than the rest of the paper.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
Among all the reviews, the main concern appears to have been raised by Reviewer 1 regarding the missing comparison with an NCA segmentation model. However, the problem addressed in this paper is a multilabel classification problem, while segmentation is used only as an auxiliary task. Therefore, I do not consider this concern to be grounds for rejection.
My other concerns, namely the limited novelty and the limited effect of distillation, cannot be addressed in the rebuttal. Nevertheless, in my opinion, the work remains solid enough from the perspective of practical deployment, both in terms of accuracy and inference time.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper’s main contribution is EdgeCVS, a practical framework for compressing a very large surgical AI model into a tiny edge-deployable model for Critical View of Safety (CVS) assessment during laparoscopic cholecystectomy, without losing much accuracy. The paper shows that accurate surgical AI for CVS can be made small, fast, and deployable on ordinary hardware by exploiting the task’s low visual complexity and using targeted distillation plus pseudo-labeling.
reviews.text_strengths:
A particularly strong aspect is the claim that CVS assessment lies on a compact, low-diversity visual manifold because it is restricted to a specific surgical phase and anatomy. This is interesting because it gives a principled reason why aggressive compression should work here, rather than treating model shrinking as just an engineering trick.
The paper makes especially good use of unlabeled videos by restricting pseudo-label generation to the Calot’s triangle dissection phase, where the signal is most relevant. This is a strong data-centric idea: instead of adding arbitrary more data, the method adds task-aligned data density, which is more meaningful for a compact model.
Compressing from a 305M-parameter teacher to a 5M-parameter student while staying close to SOTA performance is a major strength. The paper does not just show a smaller model works; it shows that a model with about 1.5% of the teacher’s size can still recover much of the teacher’s decision quality.
The deployment story is unusually strong. The paper reports real-time CPU inference above 40 FPS, which directly supports the claim that the method could run on ordinary hospital hardware rather than requiring specialized GPUs.
The method is compared against recent CVS challenge teams and prior Endoscapes baselines, and remains competitive despite using vastly fewer parameters. This strengthens the claim that the contribution is not just efficiency in isolation, but an efficiency–accuracy frontier improvement.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper’s strongest practical result is real-time CPU inference, which is important. But there is no prospective study, no user study with surgeons, no analysis of whether the system changes decisions in the OR, and no evidence that it improves safety outcomes. So, the “democratization of surgical AI” claim is only partially demonstrated.
A big part of the gain comes from densifying the training manifold using teacher-generated classification and segmentation pseudo-labels. However, the paper does not provide much calibration, confidence filtering, or error analysis of those pseudo-labels. That matters because a compact student can also inherit systematic teacher mistakes.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Although the paper does not yet demonstrate prospective clinical utility and lacks a thorough analysis of pseudo-label quality, it presents a technically sound and practically meaningful step toward deployable surgical AI by showing that phase-gated, task-aligned distillation can produce a CPU-real-time CVS model with competitive accuracy. For that reason, I judged as weak accept.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The author’s rebuttal is reasonable, and they have made revisions in response to the comments. There is no change to the initial decision of “weak accept.”

meta_reviews.text:
This paper studies the feasibility of a real‑time CPU‑based surgical AI for automated CVS assessment, with a clear clinical motivation and a strong emphasis on deployability. Reviewers acknowledge that demonstrating a 5M‑parameter model that remains competitive while being far more efficient, achieving real‑time CPU inference, is practically relevant. However, there is consensus that the methodological novelty is limited, as the approach largely combines known components; segmentation‑based supervision, teacher–student learning, and pseudo‑labeling, and that the gain from distillation itself appears modest relative to other components. For an application‑focused paper on tiny ML, a key concern is the missing comparison with relevant lightweight state‑of‑the‑art models, which weakens the positioning of the contribution. Additional concerns include that the manifold analysis is representation‑dependent, that analysis of pseudo‑label quality is limited, and that claims regarding broader impact are only partially demonstrated. Authors should address each concern raised by the reviewers, clarify their positioning, justify methodological choices, and appropriately contextualize claims.

The rebuttal convincingly addresses one major concern by clarifying that the task is classification (not segmentation), making some suggested comparisons less relevant. However, other key issues remain: limited novelty (combining known components like distillation, segmentation supervision, and pseudo-labeling), lack of comparison to lightweight baselines, and limited analysis of pseudo-label quality and broader impact. These points cannot be fully resolved by clarification alone. Despite this, the reviewers lean towards Acceptance.

While there is clear motivation for the work, the paper still lacks technical novelty and clinical validation. The rebuttal addresses some of the raised concerns but not adequately to clear the major issues. Therefore, I recommend a rejection.

After reading the paper and reviews post-rebuttal my opinion is for the paper to be accepted. I believe the work deals with an important and open problem of (edge deployment) with a method that presents interesting novelty. The validation is comprehensive.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback. We address the major concerns below.
Task definition (R1): R1 states “the primary problem of CVS is segmentation” and suggests missing benchmarking against tiny ML segmentation models. We respectfully clarify: the benchmarked task is CVS multi-label classification - predicting whether each Critical View of Safety (CVS) criterion is met, evaluated on SAGES-CVS and Endoscapes benchmarks, which define our SOTA scope. Segmentation is used exclusively as an auxiliary training signal; the segmentation head is discarded at inference and no segmentation metrics are reported. The NCA method (eNCApsulate) suggested by R1, addresses segmentation and depth estimation on capsule endoscopy - a different task, anatomy, modality, and benchmark - with no published results on any CVS dataset, making the comparison infeasible.
Missing tiny ML SOTA comparison (R1): EdgeCVS is not a tinyML models benchmarking study, it is a data-centric, dual-modality distillation framework that exploits task-specific manifold structure to enable extreme compression. The framework is backbone-agnostic; EdgeNeXT-Small was selected as a strong representative within the established 2.5-10M parameter edge deployment range. The correct evaluation is therefore vertical: how close does the student get to the teacher and SOTA on CVS benchmarks (Table 1 & Figure 4). To the best of our knowledge, no lightweight method has published results on SAGES-CVS or Endoscapes.
Manifold analysis (R3): We acknowledge that measuring dispersion in a pretrained embedding space is representation-dependent and falls short of intrinsic dimensionality (ID) metrics. However, classical ID analysis is not directly applicable to video data, as estimates are dominated by temporal autocorrelation between neighboring frames, violating the i.i.d. assumption these metrics require. Using the EVA02-Large embedding space, the source of the distillation signal itself, was our most principled available proxy. We will acknowledge this representation dependency as a limitation in the final manuscript.
Methodological novelty (R3): While individual components are established, their contribution lies in unification: MTL, KD, and phase-gated semi-SL are not independent modules but three expressions of a single data-centric dual-modality distillation process, coupling soft classification and segmentation predictions across seen and unseen phase-gated data to probe edge model compression limits. This unification produces a non-trivial result: in general vision tasks, compressing a large model to a small one keeps a significant gap, EdgeCVS substantially closes it on the CVS task. The modest +KD gain in isolation is precisely what reveals this: the bottleneck is not signal quality on existing annotated data but manifold coverage on unseen data, distinguishing EdgeCVS from standard distillation. The contribution is both a deployable surgical AI solution and a transferable hypothesis: task-specific manifold structure determines compression potential, a principle we demonstrate on CVS and propose for similar phase-gated tasks.
Pseudo-label quality (R4): To mitigate teacher noise, pseudo-label generation averaged logits across multiple training epochs to reduce variance. Both classification and segmentation pseudo-labels were generated as soft labels encoding the teacher’s probabilities, propagating the teacher’s uncertainty rather than noisy hard pseudo-labels. The consistent gains from +MTL and +SemiSL across all four model sizes in Figures 3 & 4 suggest soft pseudo-labels encode reliable signals. We will update the manuscript accordingly.
Prospective clinical validation (R4): The current work establishes the technical foundation, a deployable model retaining large teacher performance, that we hope will enable and inspire such clinical studies. We will revise the manuscript to frame clinical validation as future work enabled by this contribution.

title: EEGRFusion: Uncertainty-Aware EEG-to-Image Evidence for Adjunct Bedside Assessment of CMD in Disorders of Consciousness
abstract: Assessments for disorders of consciousness are frequently confounded by absent or inconsistent behavioral output, particularly in cognitive motor dissociation, motivating objective and interpretable EEG-based visual-semantic evidence as an adjunct to bedside evaluation. We present EEGRFusion, an EEG-to-image framework that projects EEG into a visual-semantic space and enables (i) zero-shot image retrieval and (ii) EEG-conditioned image generation, together providing clinician-reviewable cues of stimulus-evoked processing. For robust EEG representation, we introduce MAMD, a montage-aware temporal dual-path encoder with a Mamba backbone. For generation, to address the CLIP semantic bottleneck, EEG variability and related issues, we learn an EEG-to-CLIP conditional prior using Rectified Flow and decode it with a frozen diffusion backbone equipped with an IP-Control Fusion Adapter to mitigate semantic and structural drifts. Experiments on THINGS-EEG demonstrate improvements in retrieval accuracy and reconstruction quality over baselines. We further provide uncertainty heatmaps demonstrating multi-sample variability to facilitate risk-aware interpretation. The code is available at https://github.com/hcy1026/EEGRFusion.
subject_areas: Modalities -> EEG / MEG / ECG / Physiological Signals

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents a method for generating images from EEG signals to support clinical behavioral assessment in patients with Cognitive Motor Dissociation (CMD). The key contributions are: (1) a novel EEG encoder that produces stable EEG representations; (2) a Rectified Flow-based prior that enables sampling of a CLIP image embedding conditioned on an EEG representation; (3) a Control Adapter module appended after the IP-Adapter and SDXL-turbo pipeline to address structural drift inherent in images generated based on an CLIP image embedding, and to produce uncertainty heatmaps that enhance clinical interpretability. Together, these additions improve the fidelity of EEG-conditioned image synthesis.
reviews.text_strengths:
Clarity and justification of design choices: The paper is well-written and easy to follow. Each design choice is clearly motivated and the training procedure is described in sufficient detail to support reproducibility.
Novel EEG encoder with strong empirical justification: The proposed EEG encoder is compared against multiple baseline EEG encoders using retrieval accuracy as a generator-independent proxy metric. The results justify the architectural choices for the EEG encoder before the generation pipeline is introduced.
Well-motivated use of the Control Adapter: The Control Adapter addresses the structural drift inherent in CLIP-conditioned generation. This is a known limitation of CLIP embeddings, which encode high-level semantic information at the expense of low-level spatial and structural information. Moreover, the curriculum training strategy for training the Control Adapter is a clever solution to the cold-start problem: by using blurred ground-truth images as control images and gradually transitioning to SDXL-Turbo outputs, the Control Adapter learns reliable structural conditioning before being exposed to noisier, model-generated control images.
Limitations are acknowledged.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The clinical motivation requires stronger justification: The model is trained and evaluated on THINGS-EEG2, which consists of healthy subjects viewing naturalistic images under an RSVP paradigm. CMD patients represent a fundamentally different population. The authors should justify why a model trained on healthy-subject data can be expected to transfer to this clinical population.
The authors should clarify whether the model is trained and tested on data from the same subject (within-subject evaluation) or evaluated on held-out subjects (cross-subject evaluation).
Tables 3 and 4 (reconstruction quality and ablation study) report results only for Subject 8.The authors should justify why the results are not averaged across all subjects to give a fairer picture of the method’s performance.

N/A

The proposed method is methodologically interesting, and the paper is clearly presented.
