reviews.recommendation_label: Strong Reject — must be rejected due to major flaws
reviews.text_contribution: The reviewer did not understand the paper sufficiently well to point out contributions.
reviews.text_strengths: The reviewer did not understand the paper sufficiently well to point out any strength.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The literal presentation of the paper is very poor, and large parts appear to be AI generated:
a) The abstract and introduction are particularly poor, and appear to be 100% AI generated. After reading both, the reviewer still has no idea on what is the exact task to be solved in this paper. What is EEG-to-image? What exactly is visualized from the EEG in the image? How does this relate to CLIP? How does Diffusion come into play here? How is any of these related to DoC? What is assessed at “bedside”, and why is this important?
b) Some kind of “representation boundaries” are mentioned several times without explaining what this would be.
c) It remains mysterious what the “noise endpoint” and the “data endpoint” (section 2.2) should be. Can the authors provide these in their own terms? Is one of these related to images, or to EEG embeddings?
d) What would be a “structural drift”, “layout”, “semantics”, “IP-Control” (section 2.3)? At which location do the authors extract “UNet features”, from which kind of data, and what is the dimensionality of such features? What is SDXL-Turbo?
2.The description of the dual-path model, and other parts of the pipeline are insufficient and partially wrong:
a) For their temporal path, the authors indicate that the batch dimension (B) is changed. This is clearly wrong. The input needs to be shaped as BxTxC and not TxBxC.
b) The authors mention “fourier feature electrode coordinate encoding” and “coarse region priors” without providing any hint on what this is or how they have applied this.
c) Since Bi-Mamba blocks build the main blocks in their module, a brief introduction on these blocks would be required.
d) It is mentioned that temporal path and spatial path are fused, but not how. There is no final overview of the model topology.
e) The authors mention a “CLIP loss”, but it is not clear what the “CLIP loss” is. Do they mean unsupervised contrastive loss? Similarly, it is not clear what the “MSE loss” is, and on which elements it is computed.
3.The experimental setup, and evaluation metrics are unclear:
a) The authors mention “training image conditions” and “test image conditions”, without describing what such conditions would be. Again, the task to be solved (RSVP) is unclear.
b) Section 3.2 discusses zero-shot identification, but it is unclear what should be identified, and how.
c) Other evaluation metrics are just named (2-way z-score, 2-way-acc) without telling what are the two ways.
d) The reviewer does not understand how the uncertainty heatmaps in figure 2 are computed, or what they are showing. Why is a pixel-wise uncertainty important, and not a global, image-wise uncertainty?
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The license of the “anonymized” source code includes a copyright for Chenyuan Hong, indicating an author and infringing anonymization. The code repeatedly reference directories in /home/diaoyueqin, indicating another author name.
Graphics are stored and imported as pixel graphics (.jpg/.png). Better options would be vector graphics (.eps/.pdf).

For a non-expert, this paper is illegible. Many concepts are assumed to be known. While claimed several times, the application of the method as bedtime assessment tool is unclear. The exact task to be solved remains mysterious throughout the entire paper, and it is unclear what the evaluation metrics evaluate. Anonymization of the code is not done properly.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The provided code clearly failed to pass the anonymization test. Why were the authors invited to write a rebuttal?
Many of my questions were not answered by the authors. I would not trust that the paper improves to a reasonable state where it could be publishable, without additional review.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper needs some improvement in writing for readability when there are too many abbreviations used. Also need more justification on how a model trained on healthy subjects will be translated to patient populations.

The concerns raised have been addressed.

The paper explores an interesting and clinically motivated direction by investigating EEG-to-image generation as adjunct evidence for bedside assessment in disorders of consciousness. Reviewer 2 appreciated several aspects of the work, including the motivation, the proposed EEG encoder, and the integration of a Rectified-Flow prior with a Control Adapter framework.
However, after carefully reviewing the paper, the reviews, and the rebuttal, I do not believe the current submission reaches the level required for acceptance. In particular, I found Reviewer 3’s concerns regarding the paper’s clarity, methodological presentation, and overall readability to be substantial and difficult to dismiss. A major issue is that the core task formulation, model pipeline, and evaluation methodology are often insufficiently explained, making it difficult. While Reviewer 1 provided a positive recommendation, the review itself was relatively limited in technical depth and did not substantially engage with many of the concerns later raised by the other reviewers. Overall, although the topic is interesting and the proposed direction has potential, I do not recommend acceptance in its current form.
Reviewer 3 noted a potential anonymization issue, citing a copyright notice containing an author name and directory paths revealing another individual’s identity. I was unable to locate these identifiers in the currently available materials and therefore could not independently verify the concern. However, it is possible that such information was present in an earlier version accessible during the review process and later removed. If so, the anonymization concern would be legitimate.

The reviewers raised concerns regarding the clinical translation of a model trained on healthy-subject EEG data, the clarity of the experimental protocol, and the readability of the manuscript. The rebuttal addressed these concerns satisfactorily by clarifying that the work is intended as an algorithmic validation of EEG-to-image decoding rather than a clinically validated DoC/CMD deployment system. The authors also clarified the evaluation protocol, the use of Subject 8 for consistency with prior work, the interpretation of uncertainty heatmaps, and several methodological details that were insufficiently explained in the original submission.
While the clinical applicability to DoC/CMD patients remains a limitation, the paper appropriately positions this as future translational work rather than a demonstrated clinical claim. The methodological contribution is technically sound, supported by comprehensive experiments, and reproducible through the provided code and implementation details. Overall, I believe the major concerns were sufficiently addressed and the paper is above the acceptance threshold.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for your constructive comments. We appreciate the recognition of our “motivated contribution”(R1&2), “methodologically novel design”(R1&2), and “reproducibility”(R1-3). Below we address general concerns followed by specific points. 
1.Dataset representativeness and clinical translation(R1-3, AC). THINGS-EEG is a large-scale
82,160 trials
and representative benchmark released by the THINGS initiative and leading institutions, and is widely used in EEG-to-image studies (ATM, UBP etc.). Healthy-subject data are not directly deployable to patients, so our work is claimed as algorithmic validation of stimulus-evoked EEG-to-visual-evidence decoding, as a first translation step before patient-specific calibration. Although DoC/CMD EEG introduces differences, healthy EEG also has large inter-subject variability; our results support robustness to variability, making the model promising for clinical transfer. CMD patients may retain stimulus processing without overt behavior, making behavioral assessment insufficient[1-4]. Decoded visual evidence from EEG signals can provide adjunct, clinician-reviewable support. We will add references and perform DoC/CMD validation in the future. 
2.Experimental details(R2&R3). Retrieval is within-subject. Following published baselines, we report generation results on Subject 8 for fairness. Image conditions and RSVP are from THINGS-EEG acquisition protocol, not our task. We will clarify these points and further explain zero-shot N-way retrieval identification: N candidates include a true image and N-1 distractors, ranked by EEG-image embedding similarity. The 2-way metric is the N=2 case. Pixel-wise uncertainty is computed from 10 stochastic generations and can reflect both object reliability and structural stability. Unstable/failed generations make the object uncertain; structural drift affects background regions. From another perspective, the heatmap shows that Control Adapter reduces layout instability and thus better helps clinicians identify regions requiring caution.
To R3, due to page limits, some details common in EEG-to-image studies are not fully restated. Gaining more related knowledge from [7] may be helpful for better understanding.
3.Task definition, readability and AI use(AC). Due to page limits, many abbreviations are used, we will remove them except MAMD and RFFA. EEG-to-image is not to visualize raw EEG traces, but to infer visual evidence from stimulus-evoked EEG: retrieval of the viewed image and reconstruction of a stimulus-consistent image. CLIP provides the visual embedding; diffusion synthesizes the image. AI was not used to generate or write the content but only for grammar/language polishing. 
4.MAMD details. The batch dimension B is not changed. The permutation only follows PyTorch Transformer’s sequence-first convention. We will clarify notation and expand Fourier electrode encoding, region priors, and Bi-Mamba. Dual-path representations are fused by addition as shown in Fig.1(overview). Our paper defines CLIP loss and MSE loss and states paired EEG-image embeddings. Rectified Flow separately uses MSE between predicted and target velocities. We will add formulas for clarity.
5.Generation details. “Representation boundaries” means the ability of EEG embedding to represent visual information. In Rectified Flow, the noise endpoint is a Gaussian noise vector, the data endpoint is the target CLIP image embedding, EEG embedding as condition. Semantics denotes object/category content; layout denotes edges/background. Structural drift means alteration of original layout. SDXL-Turbo is a pretrained latent diffusion image generator with a denoising U-Net; U-Net features are its multi-scale intermediate maps. “IP-Control” is our module combining IP- and Control-Adapter.
6.Code and figures. I appreciate your note. This is my first submission and I lack experience. I will carefully remove personal paths and license metadata and use vector graphics.

title: Efficient Conformal Volumetry for Template-Based Segmentation
abstract: Template-based segmentation, a widely used paradigm in medical imaging, propagates anatomical labels via deformable registration from a labeled atlas to a target image, and is often used to compute volumetric biomarkers for downstream decision-making. While conformal prediction (CP) provides finite-sample valid intervals for scalar metrics, existing segmentation-based uncertainty quantification (UQ) approaches either rely on learned model features, often unavailable in classic template-based pipelines, or treat the registration process as a black box, resulting in overly conservative intervals when applied directly in output space. We introduce ConVOLT, a CP framework that achieves efficient volumetric UQ by conditioning calibration on properties of the estimated deformation field from template-based segmentation. ConVOLT calibrates a learned volumetric scaling factor from deformation space features. We evaluate ConVOLT on template-based segmentation tasks involving global, regional, and label volumetry across multiple datasets and registration methods. ConVOLT achieves target coverage while producing substantially tighter intervals than output-space conformal baselines. Our work paves way to exploit the registration process for efficient UQ in medical imaging pipelines.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: Structure volumes from an individual’s MRI were once estimated by warping the scan to an atlas so that volumes can be estimated by summing the Jacobians of the deformation over the labels in the atlas. This work uses a ridge regression with various features derived from the deformations to predict how to rescale these volume estimates so they are more accurate. Confidence intervals are estimated from a separate calibration set.
reviews.text_strengths: The proposed method mostly gives tighter confidence intervals on test data than the other methods investigated.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The manuscript presents a simple idea in a difficult way, with a information missing about how the ridge regression was done in practice. How were hyper-parameter(s) derived?
More recent approaches don’t try to segment structures using pure image registration. There is usually some form of machine learning involved as well, which will limit the usefulness of the proposed approach. There is a large literature on multi-atlas label propagation for refining segmentations, and there are other hybrid methods for combining deep earning segmentation with the outputs from nonlinear registration.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The problem setup should say which way the warping is done: atlas to individual or individual to atlas?
As few people at MICCAI will be familiar with the concepts, I think the introduction should say what conformal prediction actually does (rather than use impenetrable text like “finite-sample valid coverage guarantees for scalar metrics”).
The use of $x$ to denote a spatial location (as in $J_i(x)$), as well as a set of features (as in Eq. 1) makes the manuscript harder to follow than it needed to be.
Does $X_{\mathrm{test}}$ refer to the same thing as $X_{n+1}$?
Don’t display brain images pointing face down (Figure 1). Is the “deformation field” shown in Figure 1 a map of Jacobians?

The proposed method has limited applicability given that relatively few people use purely registration-based methods for structure segmentation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: Improves uncertainty quantification of volumetric measurements from template-based segmentation by predicting the multiplicative regression coefficient from deformation features.
reviews.text_strengths: The method seems to be novel, although based on known techniques.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The approach is demonstrated only on volumetric biomarkers.
Some aspects of the method are mentioned only in the experimental part and without much detail, namely the regressor, the similarity function and the features used for the regression.
The effect of the different features should be studied more, beyond just showing the graph in Figure 3 with hard to interpret labels.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
In References, citing preprints should be avoided if possible.

The work is reasonably novel and experimentally validated.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper proposes a conformal prediction (CP)-based uncertainty quantification (UQ) method for template-based segmentation, termed ConVOLT. The method aims to address two limitations in existing CP-based UQ approaches: their reliance on learned model features and the tendency to produce wide intervals when CP is applied directly in the output space.
ConVOLT conditions CP on statistics derived from the deformation field by training a regressor that predicts the scaling factor between ground-truth volumes and predicted volumes. CP is then applied using the absolute error of this scaling factor regressor as the nonconformity score, yielding prediction intervals for the predicted volumes.
The authors evaluate ConVOLT on three datasets using two types of registration methods and compare it against three CP baselines. The results show that ConVOLT achieves the desired coverage while producing narrower prediction intervals on most datasets.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Novelty: The proposed solution is well suited to the application domain. The authors incorporate deformation field statistics into the conformal prediction (CP) framework, addressing a gap that, to my knowledge, has not been explored in existing methods. The manner of incorporation is also meaningful rather than superficial. In particular, the choice of nonconformity score, based on the absolute error of the volume scaling factor, is domain-specific and differs from standard residual- or quantile-based approaches. This design is supported by a clear rationale, namely that multiplicative errors in the deformation propagate multiplicatively to the scalar target.
2.Rigorous Analysis: The authors provide a comprehensive evaluation by analyzing both coverage and interval size across global, regional, and label-wise volumetry. In addition, they examine the regression model to provide interpretability, with results that support the usefulness of deformation field statistics in datasets where ConVOLT shows improved performance. The paper also offers a reasonable explanation for the comparatively weaker performance on the NLST dataset when using the Demons registration method.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Formulation: The proposed method relies on an intermediate regressor to predict the volume scaling factor from deformation field statistics, and then applies conformal prediction to the residuals of this regressor. It is not clear why this two-step approach is necessary. An alternative formulation could directly condition the conformal prediction procedure on the deformation-derived features. For example, by using quantile regression with these features to predict intervals for the volumes. This would eliminate the need for the intermediate regression step. The authors could clarify why the current design provides advantages over a more direct conditioning approach.
2.Data Split: The data split (10/15/5) for ThoraxCBCT raises concerns as it results in a test set of only 5 samples. This makes it difficult to draw reliable conclusions about coverage and interval efficiency. With 5 samples, coverage can only be evaluated in increments of 20%, and this is reflected in a relatively large standard deviation of coverage (0.14), indicating high variability. Additionally, the calibration sets is unusually large relative to the dataset size (0.4/0.4/0.2, 10/15/5), raising questions about why such a large calibration set is needed and whether the method requires it to achieve stable coverage. 
3.Baselines: The authors mention CQR (conditional quantile regression) as a baseline but cite Conformalized Quantile Regression. Can the authors clarify whether Conformalized Quantile Regression was actually used? Additionally, it is unclear what features were used for CQR — the only indication provided is that “residual volumetric variability is largely explained by volume magnitude itself.”
4.Ablation: Which features are considered localized and which are global? Additionally, can the authors explain the reduction in prediction interval size for VoxelMorph on ThoraxCBCT?
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The major factors that led to my overall score are the novelty and domain relevance of the proposed method, as well as the rigorous evaluation provided. The paper makes a meaningful contribution by incorporating deformation field statistics into the conformal prediction framework, addressing a gap in existing methods. The choice of nonconformity score, based on the volume scaling factor, is well-justified for the application domain. The authors provide thorough analyses across global, regional, and label-wise volumetry, and they examine model interpretability, which strengthens the evidence for their approach.
While some aspects could be clarified. For instance, the necessity of the intermediate regressor, the small test set for ThoraxCBCT, and details of the CQR baseline. These do not outweigh the contribution of introducing a domain-specific conformal prediction method that demonstrates improved coverage and narrower prediction intervals.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have adequately addressed my comments on the important aspects of the paper (Formulation, Baselines, Features Used); therefore, I stand by my previous decision to accept it.

meta_reviews.text:
The goal of this work is to provide an atlas-based segmentation approach combined with conformal prediction to predict the volumes of structures of interest. Features from the deformation field between the atlas image with segmentation and the image to be segmented are used to regress the volumes of interest and the conformal approach provides confidence intervals.
Major strengths of the paper:
Reasonable regression approach to predict volumes and their confidence interval for an atlas-based segmentation approach.
Evaluation shower tighter confidence intervals than competing approaches.
Major weaknesses of the paper:
While the approach might be relevant for atlas/template-based segmentation, modern segmentation approaches have lately been dominated by deep-learning segmentation approaches (as by and large direct segmentation is empirically easier than accurate registration). This raises concerns about the timeliness of / need for the proposed approach.
Features that are being used for regression have not been clearly described; also with respect to the competing approaches.
There are some concerns regarding sample sizes for the experiments.
Suggestions for rebuttal:
Discuss the timeliness / need of the approach in context of modern deep-learning based segmentation approaches. In what settings would one still want to use this approach? Could it be used (in a modified form) for deep learning segmentation methods?
Address sample size concerns.
Clarify what features were used and how they were chosen (for your own method as well as for competing approaches).
What is the rationale in performing regressions exclusively based on deformation features?
Address remaining reviewer concerns as space permits.

The authors have addresses these concerns satisfactorily in the rebuttal. Specifically,

After the rebuttal, this paper received overall positive recommendations. Reviewer 3 explicitly stated that all three previously raised concerns had been addressed, and Reviewer 2 maintained an Accept recommendation. Reviewer 1 did not resubmit an updated review. After revisiting the paper in light of the reviews and rebuttal, I find that the proposed method offers a novel contribution in the context of conformal prediction. Although the limited size of the ThoraxCBCT dataset remains a weakness, it does not outweigh the overall merit of the work.
In light of the post-rebuttal discussion and the overall reviewer consensus, I recommend Accept. For the camera-ready version, the authors are encouraged to further improve the clarity of the presentation and to incorporate the reviewers’ constructive suggestions where appropriate.

The paper is interesting, particularly because it moves beyond output-space conformal prediction and instead explores learned model features as more appropriate signals for uncertainty estimation. This direction is important for medical imaging, where directly applying CP in the output space can often lead to overly wide and less useful prediction intervals. The reviewers raised some questions regarding the timing and positioning of the work, but the paper appears timely and relevant to the medical imaging community. The empirical results are also strong and support the effectiveness of the proposed approach. Overall, this is a solid contribution, and I recommend acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the reviewers and AC for the constructive feedback. We are glad that reviewers found our work novel and well evaluated (R2, R3). We focus on the top concerns.
Applicability/timeliness (R1,M): We respectfully clarify that registration/template-based volumetry remains relevant despite modern direct segmentation. ConVOLT targets settings where registration remains central: atlas-defined anatomical consistency and atlas/template deployment (OASIS), and longitudinal/respiratory analyses requiring dense correspondence or regional volume change (ThoraxCBCT, NLST). Such settings remain actively studied in volumetric deformable registration (e.g., VoxelMorph/TransMorph/HyperMorph/SynthMorph, Learn2Reg). Moreover, ConVOLT is not restricted to classical “non-ML” registration: we evaluate using VoxelMorph, a learning-based registration method. R1’s point about multi-atlas and hybrid deep-registration methods is therefore complementary rather than disqualifying — any pipeline that estimates deformation fields exposes the geometric quantities that ConVOLT leverages for efficient volumetric UQ. For direct segmenters, an analogous extension would use logits, embeddings, feature maps, or probabilities.
Sample size for ThoraxCBCT (R3,M): We agree ThoraxCBCT is small. With 5 test cases, split-level coverage is coarse and variable; under a simple binomial approximation with marginal coverage near 0.9, test noise alone gives sqrt(0.9*0.1/5)=0.13, close to the observed SD=0.14.We included it because it is a clinically relevant low-sample registration benchmark from Learn2Reg. The 15-case calibration split was chosen because split CP at alpha=0.1 estimates an upper conformal quantile; fewer calibration cases would make this more discrete/conservative. This applies to all split-CP methods, not only to ConVOLT.
ConVOLT features (R1-R3,M): We clarify that ConVOLT features are listed in the “Experimental Protocol” with notation from the problem setup. ConVOLT features were chosen a priori to summarize quantities expected to reflect registration difficulty: Jacobian statistics for expansion/contraction, Jacobian quantiles and folding fractions for extreme local volume changes, displacement and grad log-J/divergence/curl summaries for deformation magnitude and spatial irregularity, and fixed-warped similarity residuals for residual mismatch. Global experiments compute features over the full mask; regional/label experiments compute the same feature types restricted to the region/boundary.
ConVOLT versus CQR (R3,M): We agree that CQR conditioned on deformation features is a reasonable alternative, but it lacks ConVOLT’s structural constraints. Mapping a conformal interval in beta-space back to volume preserves non-negativity and scales interval width with the predicted volume. It separates point correction from uncertainty calibration: one ridge regressor estimates an interpretable multiplicative correction, while split CP supplies the finite-sample-valid radius. It also reduces the estimation burden in small-data and label-wise settings by using a single regressor rather than two conditional quantile regressors per target. Finally, coefficients directly indicate deformation features associated with multiplicative volumetric bias, whereas CQR has separate lower- and upper-quantile models whose effects on interval size are less transparent.
Baselines (R3,M): SCP uses no conditioning features; LCP conditions on |Yhat^0| using local calibration; CQR is conformalized quantile regression and conditions on baseline volume/change. These output-space baselines intentionally do not use registration internals, because the central comparison is whether deformation-aware calibration improves over black-box/output-space calibration.
Minor clarifications (R1,R2): We used closed-form ridge regression with an unpenalized intercept and fixed lambda=1e-2.We used NCC similarity, a standard VoxelMorph-style objective.

title: Efficient Flow Matching for Sparse-View CT Reconstruction
abstract: Generative models, particularly Diffusion Models (DM), have shown strong potential for Computed Tomography (CT) reconstruction serving as expressive priors for solving ill-posed inverse problems. However, diffusion-based reconstruction relies on Stochastic Differential Equations (SDEs) for forward diffusion and reverse denoising, where such stochasticity can interfere with repeated data consistency corrections in CT reconstruction. Since CT reconstruction is often time-critical in clinical and interventional scenarios, improving reconstruction efficiency is essential. In contrast, Flow Matching (FM) models sampling as a deterministic Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE), yielding smooth trajectories without stochastic noise injection. This deterministic formulation is naturally compatible with repeated data consistency operations. Furthermore, we observe that FM-predicted velocity fields exhibit strong correlations across adjacent steps. Motivated by this, we propose an FM-based CT reconstruction framework (FMCT) and an efficient variant (EFMCT) that reuses previously predicted velocity fields over consecutive steps to substantially reduce the number of Neural network Function Evaluations (NFEs), thereby improving inference efficiency. We provide theoretical analysis showing that the error introduced by velocity reuse is bounded when combined with data consistency operations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FMCT/EFMCT achieve competitive reconstruction quality while significantly improving computational efficiency compared with diffusion-based methods. The codebase is open-sourced at https://github.com/EFMCT/EFMCT.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The proposed paper presents an accelerated flow matching framework with an application to sparse-view CT reconstruction. Flow-matching for CT (FMCT) uses a trained velocity v (a neural network) to sample an image from pure noise by iteratively solving an ODE with the trained velocity v. This framework can be used to solve an inverse problem by adding a data consistency (DC) update at each iteration. The problem is that this approach requires many evaluations of v, which is computationally expensive. The authors noticed experimentally that the velocity v does not change much after each iteration and therefore propose to reuse the same v for M iterations. Under basic regularity conditions on v, the approximate trajectory obtained by recycling the same velocity is expected not to deviate significantly from the trajectory obtained by reevaluating v at each iteration.
The authors demonstrate that their method Efficient FMCT (EFMCT) achieves similar image quality with much fewer neural network function evaluations (NFE).
reviews.text_strengths:
This is a novel and well-motivated approach that could become an important direction for flow-matching-based CT reconstruction, especially in the case of large volumes where computational cost is critical.
The idea of reusing the velocity field is simple yet effective, and the empirical observation that consecutive velocities are similar is convincing. The method has strong practical relevance and the experimental results support the claimed efficiency gains.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
It seems to me that there is a problem in the proof. The current proof is based on an update of the form
x_{k+1} = DC(x_k - Delta t v_tk (x_tk))
and
xhat_{k+1} = DC(x_k - Delta t v_tk0 (x_tk0))
with DC kappa-non-expansive.
However, the update defined in (6) and (7) is
x_{k+1} = x’_k+1 + DC(x_tk - tk v_tk(x_tk))
with
x’_k+1 = x_k - Delta t v_tk (x_tk).
With this model, the error |delta_k+1| is bounded by
(kappa + 1) |delta_k| + (tk*kappa + Delta t) | v_tk - v_tk0 |.
With this upper bound, I find that |delta_k0+M| is O(Delta t) and not O(Delta t^2).
The authors should carefully re-examine the proof and modify the statement if necessary.
Minor
There is a notation clash between xhat_0 (the expected non-noisy image E(x0 | x1)) and xhat_k (the alternative algorithm).
The Euler scheme in the single step error part corresponds to the image-to-noise ODE, while the rest of the paper considers sampling from noise to image. This should be clarified.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The method seems to work and can potentially drastically speed up FM reconstruction in CT, especially for large volumes.
However, there might be an issue in the proof. The authors should check it carefully, make the relevant modifications, and adjust their claims if necessary.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I was already satisfied with this paper, and my only concern was the issue in the proof (cf. Q7). I have no more concern regarding the paper now that the authors have promised they will amend the proof in the final version of the paper.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a novel CT reconstruction method based on flow matching. Unlike conventional diffusion models, flow matching enables deterministic sampling through an ODE-based formulation. Building on this property, the paper aims to reduce the NFEs by reusing gradients across adjacent sampling steps. The experimental results show that gradient reuse can effectively reduce NFEs while achieving better performance than the baseline methods.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.This paper proposes a diffusion-based solver for CT reconstruction based on the flow matching method.
2.By leveraging the deterministic nature of flow matching, the paper demonstrates the similarity of velocities between adjacent steps and proposes reusing gradients across neighboring steps to reduce the NFEs, thereby accelerating CT reconstruction.
3.The paper further proposes an adaptive and efficient flow matching sampling strategy based on the data-fidelity error across adjacent iterative steps, in order to further reduce the NFEs.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
I particularly like the paper’s proposed strategy for reducing NFEs, as it is both intuitive and well motivated. However, I believe the manuscript still has the following issues:
1.In the left panel of Fig. 1, why does the similarity exhibit a noticeable drop near 50 steps? The paper does not seem to provide an explanation for this phenomenon.
2.Does the central assumption of the proposed method still hold when Poisson noise is introduced?
3.From a clinical perspective, fan-beam geometry is more realistic than parallel-beam geometry. In addition, the visualization results do not indicate the HU window settings. I recommend that the authors present the images with appropriate windowing so that finer structural differences can be more clearly revealed.
4.The baselines selected by the authors are relatively old and were not specifically designed for CT reconstruction. The manuscript does not include more recent diffusion-based sampling or reconstruction methods developed specifically for CT reconstruction. I encourage the authors to refer to relevant studies published in recent years in venues such as MICCAI and journals such as TMI.
5.The paper does not provide sufficient training details for the flow matching model. Moreover, some of the compared methods, such as DPS and MCG, are originally built upon diffusion models rather than flow matching models. This raises a potential concern about the fairness of the comparison.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1.Why do the authors use the conjugate gradient method to enforce data consistency? Why not directly adopt an (L_2) or (L_1) norm formulation?
2.Have the authors attempted to apply gradient reuse to diffusion models as well? In diffusion models, the gradients in the middle and late stages are also relatively stable.
3.The authors may consider including perceptual metrics, such as LPIPS, which could better reflect the ability of different methods to preserve fine details, for example when comparing ADMM-TV and EFMCT.
If the authors can adequately address these weaknesses and concerns, I would be willing to raise my score.

The method proposed in this paper is interesting; however, the experimental evaluation is not sufficiently rigorous.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have addressed my concerns.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces a method for sparse-view CT reconstruction using flow matching models. First, flow matching is used to learn a velocity field that transforms Gaussian noise into CT images. Then, the sampling process is incorporated with data consistency operators to sample CT images conditioned on the observed measurements. A velocity reuse technique is proposed to accelerate inference, with theoretical analysis showing that the error remains first-order under the reuse. Results show competitive accuracy and improved speed of the proposed method.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The motivation of accelerating CT reconstruction is convincing and potentially useful for clinical practice.
2.The authors attempted to provide theoretical guarantees for their proposed method, which is essential for its reliable use and often neglected in the field.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The theoretical statement is relatively unclear. Some notations are not consistently defined, and the proof appears to omit important steps. Specifically, it is unclear why the bounds on $| \delta_{k+1}|$ and $| \delta_{k_0 + M}|$ hold. The update rule for $\hat{x}_k$ lacks a formal definition, and it is unclear whether the refinement step in (9) is used. Similarly, $x_k$ is defined without the DC operator, but later seemed to denote iterates that include it. The bounded velocity is used but not stated as an assumption. Overall, the proposition and its proof appear too compressed and hard to follow in the current form.
2.Additionally, a formal description of the DC operator is missing, except that it uses conjugate gradient. What problem does it solve? How does it enforce or enhance data consistency? The authors may want to clarify on this in more details.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The proposed method is well-motivated and empirically validated. Although the theoretical results appear reasonable, the clarity of assumptions, notations, and the proof can be significantly improved.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The issues with the proof remain:
1.\hat{x}_k lacks a formal definition.
2.x_k is defined without the DC step (ie for unconditional sampling), but its seems to represent the iterates involving DC. This may have contributed to the confusion on how DC is applied.
The authors’ rebuttal attempts to explain in words how the proof will be fixed, but the explanation itself is somewhat unclear and lacks the precision and rigor of mathematical terms. Unfortunately, it’s not fully convincing to me.
Although it’s very valuable to see a formal guarantee on the method, the way it’s currently presented falls short of the standard for publication.

meta_reviews.text:
Reviewers are in principle in favor of this work but there are a number of concerns that need clarification. I agree with the work being of interest to the community in principle, as the efficiency of CT reconstruction is a major and important clinical concern. Please organize and rank the mentioned criticisms and address them in a rebuttal. A very important clarification is regarding the theory and the proof, which was mentioned by more than one reviewer. Another aspect that is crucial is to clarify if there are more recent state of the art works on CT reconstruction that were not discussed or compared to, and if so why these were omitted from the experimental setup.

Majority of reviewers agree that this work is a good contribution for the MICCAI community. Concerns regarding the proof and the comparison to other methods have been convincingly addressed in the rebuttal. Minor remaining issues should be considered by the authors in case of acceptance. I agree with the majority assessment to accept this work.

After carefully reviewing the rebuttal letter, I agree with Reviewer #3 that the authors have the potential to further improve the clarity and presentation of the manuscript. Nevertheless, I still find the work interesting and believe it contains sufficient novelty and practical value. Therefore, I lean toward accepting this paper.

This paper proposes EFMCT, an efficient flow matching framework for sparse-view CT reconstruction that reduces NFE by reusing velocity fields across adjacent sampling steps.
Reviewers broadly agree that the core contribution is novel, well-motivated, and practically meaningful. The most important contribution is achieving comparable quality with significantly fewer NFE, which is empirically well-supported.
The shared remaining concern is the proof. The rebuttal acknowledges a mathematical error, corrects the bound from O(M²Δt²) to O(M²Δt), and describes the fix verbally, with the authors promising to release the corrected proof in the public repository. R3 remains unconvinced without the corrected mathematics. However, since the core contribution lies in efficiency rather than the theoretical bound, and the empirical results directly demonstrate the efficiency gain, the proof issue is a presentation concern rather than a fundamental validity concern.
The strength outweighs the weaknesses and I recommend acceptance. That said, the authors should fix the proof in the final version to guarantee the correctness of the overall manuscript.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their positive assessment (novelty, motivation, practical relevance) and constructive feedback. We address the concerns below.
Issues in proof(R1R3)
We carefully re-examined the proof and agree there was a discrepancy between the theoretical formulation and the actual update rule. The previous proof modeled the DC step on the current state, while the actual algorithm applies DC to the estimated clean image. We revised the proof by: 1)unifying notation (x̃) for the reuse trajectory, 2)consistently using the reverse noise-to-image ODE, and 3)explicitly modeling DC on the estimated clean image.
The single-step bound remains O(Δt²), matching Euler local truncation error, while the accumulated deviation over one reuse block becomes O(M²Δt), rather than O(M²Δt²). We corrected the proposition and adjusted the claims accordingly. The complete proof will be released in the public repository.
DC operation(R2R3)
We use conjugate gradient [Fletcher 1964] as the DC operation because it efficiently solves the least-squares problem (AᵀA+γI)x=x̂₀+Aᵀy. Compared with directly injecting L1/L2 gradients into the generative process, the decoupled optimization is less sensitive to delicate guidance-step tuning since DC refinement is separated from generative transport dynamics.
Choice of baselines/lack of CT-specific methods(R2)
Our goal is not to outperform every recent CT-specific diffusion variant, but to investigate whether flow matching can serve as an efficient alternative to diffusion-based solvers. We therefore selected representative baselines covering different DC strategies: DPS (posterior sampling), MCG (manifold guidance), PGDM (pseudo-inverse guidance), and DDS (decoupled CG refinement).
Recent benchmark (DM4CT, ICLR2026) suggests many diffusion-based CT methods (including more recent ones) achieve comparable reconstruction quality while differing substantially in computational cost. Motivated by this, our focus is introducing flow matching for sparse-view CT reconstruction and improving efficiency through velocity reuse, rather than incremental PSNR gains over every recent diffusion variant. We agree that adding more recent CT-specific baselines would further strengthen the evaluation and will clarify this limitation in updated version.
Perceptual metrics LPIPS(R2)
We computed LPIPS and will include it in the revised version. Although ADMM-TV achieves slightly higher PSNR/SSIM than FMCT on AAPM 40-view reconstruction, its LPIPS is substantially worse (ADMM 0.272 vs FMCT 0.101/EFMCT 0.129), indicating weaker perceptual detail preservation.
Reuse strategy for diffusion/Poisson noise(R2)
Due to the stochastic SDE nature of diffusion models, we empirically observe that score reuse is less stable for diffusion than for flow matching, often requiring more iterations and producing worse reconstructions. Under noisy measurements, DC corrections become less stable and interrupt reuse steps more frequently, although the strategy remains effective under moderate noise levels. We will include this in the discussion.
Training details and fairness(R2)
The diffusion and flow models use identical architectures, datasets, optimizers, and training settings. The primary difference is the learning target: diffusion learns score, while flow matching learns the velocity field. We will add training details into the paper.
Velocity similarity drop near final steps(R2)
We empirically observe that final sampling stages perform the most detailed refinement, leading to larger velocity deviations and lower cosine similarity. Accordingly, our initial implementation disables reuse in the final stages(flow_recon.py, line 88).
Geometry choice(R2)
We use parallel-beam geometry to provide a controlled setting isolating reconstruction methodology from geometry-specific acquisition factors. Nevertheless, (E)FMCT remains geometry-agnostic. Preliminary fan-beam experiments show similar trends in reconstruction quality and acceleration.

title: Eigen-Directed Random Projection for Medical Image Class Incremental Learning
abstract: Class-incremental learning (CIL) is essential for medical imaging systems that incorporate new diseases over time, as it avoids sacrificing performance on previously learned conditions. We first revisit a broad range of CIL methods on medical benchmarks and find, unexpectedly, that a previously proposed classifier-based analytic paradigm can outperform many widely used state-of-the-art alternatives. Motivated by this observation, we examine this paradigm more closely and observe that existing classifier-based methods fail to adequately separate features of similar examples and leave them too close in the representation space, resulting in insufficient margins and reducing separability as new classes arrive. To address these limitations, we specifically propose a training-free analytic margin-expansion framework that builds the classifier using an eigen-directed design, enlarging discriminative margins along principal data directions while preserving complementary detail. Across many commonly used medical benchmarks, our method consistently improves over a wide range of CIL baselines, and extensive ablations and theoretical analysis further support the proposed design. Code will be released at https://github.com/hmep313/EDRP_MICCAI.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes EDRP (Eigen-Directed Random Projection), a replay-free class-incremental learning method for medical image classification that replaces purely random analytic feature expansion with a partially data-aligned projection derived from the principal eigenspace of buffered features. The key idea is if medical classes are fine-grained and easily entangled, then standard random projections may not expand margins sufficiently, so the classifier should emphasize principal directions while retaining a random complement.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The proposed method is conceptually clean and lightweight, it is essentially a structured modification of the analytic projection/classifier pipeline rather than a heavy continual-training framework. 
2.The authors provide reasonable ablations and some analysis of the role of eigen-directed projection, including the effect of the number of principal components and a storage comparison. 
3.The storage-efficiency claim is potentially useful, since the paper reports substantially lower storage than RanPAC while preserving the appeal of a training-free analytic classifier.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The core change is replacing part of RanPAC’s random projection with a principal-direction-aligned projection, which is intuitive but not especially deep, and the theoretical margin argument is fairly basic. 
2.Fig. 1 discusses different pretraining regimes (IN1K/BioMed/UniMed), but the main experiments are conducted with a single frozen ViT-B/16-IN1K backbone, limiting the strength of claims about medical foundation models more broadly. 
3.The evaluation protocol raises questions about clinical realism, especially the constructed “MedMNIST-Sub” benchmark formed by shuffling classes across four datasets/modalities, which may not reflect how diseases are introduced incrementally in practice.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I would lean reject. The paper is technically sound. However, I do not find the contribution strong enough for acceptance because the core idea is a fairly modest extension of the RanPAC-style analytic classifier paradigm, the theoretical insight is limited, and the empirical gains over the strongest baselines are generally small. More importantly, the evaluation does not fully establish that the method is a meaningful advance for medical continual learning specifically, the benchmarks are somewhat synthetic, the backbone setting is narrow, and the paper does not convincingly demonstrate superiority over the strongest emerging medical CIL directions beyond a selected set of baselines. Overall, this feels more like a careful incremental improvement than a sufficiently compelling new step for MICCAI.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal does clarify most of my concerns, so I’m happy to change my rating to a more positive one.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper addresses class-incremental learning (CIL) for medical imaging. The authors first conduct a systematic benchmark of existing CIL methods on medical datasets and find that classifier-based analytic methods (e.g., RanPAC) unexpectedly outperform more recent CLIP-based and prompt-based alternatives. They then identify a key limitation of RanPAC’s random projection: it is agnostic to the anisotropic structure of medical feature embeddings, leaving similar classes poorly separated. To address this, they propose EDRP (Eigen-Directed Random Projection), a training-free method that constructs a data-aware projection by aligning with the principal eigenvectors of the feature covariance. Experiments on four medical benchmarks (Skin8, MedMNIST-Sub, PBC, ChestX) show consistent improvements over baselines with reduced memory overhead.
reviews.text_strengths:
The initial finding that simpler classifier-based analytic methods outperform more sophisticated CLIP-based and prompt-tuning CIL methods on medical benchmarks is a useful contribution as it challenges the assumption that newer, more complex methods are always better in domain-specific settings.l.
The motivation behind the propsoed approach (separate in a better way the features) makes sense and motivates EDRP
The method is training-free and buffer free (even if there is a buffer of features) and reduces memory consumption substantially compared to RanPAC (e.g., from ~411 MB to ~40 MB on Skin8)
Results validate the hypotesis and the proposed method. Additionally the paper is well written and easy to follow- weak baselines on ChestX: while four datasets are used, the absolute performance on ChestX is very low (29.76% Last Accuracy), and the joint training upper bound is only 55.51%, raising questions about whether the task setup or feature extractor is appropriate for this dataset.
the method requires maintaining a feature buffer and performing eigendecomposition on its correlation matrix. The paper does not provide runtime comparisons or discuss how the buffer size B affects computational cost and scalability
Common CIL metrics such as Forgetting, forward transfer and backward transfer are not reported
reviews.text_weaknesses:
weak baselines on ChestX: while four datasets are used, the absolute performance on ChestX is very low (29.76% Last Accuracy), and the joint training upper bound is only 55.51%, raising questions about whether the task setup or feature extractor is appropriate for this dataset.
the method requires maintaining a feature buffer and performing eigendecomposition on its correlation matrix. The paper does not provide runtime comparisons or discuss how the buffer size B affects computational cost and scalability
Common CIL metrics such as Forgetting, forward transfer and backward transfer are not reported
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

From a scientific point of view, the paper and the research are well conducted, and I find that the main message can be useful for the research community working on CIL in the medical domain. The results confirm their claims.

reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal adequately addresses my three main concerns. The improvements over the strongest analytic baselines remain modest, but the contribution is methodologically coherent and the message is useful for the medical CIL community.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper proposes Eigen-Directed Random Projection, a training-free class-incremental learning method designed to improve fine-grained separability in medical image classification. The key idea is to augment random projection with eigen-directed projections that are better aligned with the principal directions of pretrained medical image features. This is motivated by the observation that medical image features, particularly from ViT-based encoders, can be anisotropic, with discriminative information concentrated along specific feature directions.
Compared with RanPAC, which uses Gaussian random projection, the proposed method combines random projections with eigen-directed components that target feature directions associated with class confusion. The classifier is then learned analytically using ridge regression. The paper evaluates the method across several medical imaging benchmarks and compares it with a broad set of class-incremental learning methods, including analytic classifier-based methods, CLIP-based methods, prompt-based methods, and LoRA-based methods. The results suggest that EDRP improves average and final accuracy, especially in challenging medical class-incremental settings where visually similar classes are difficult to separate.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem in medical image analysis: class-incremental learning in settings where new disease or cell categories may be introduced over time without full retraining. This is clinically relevant because medical datasets are often expanded gradually, and models need to preserve prior knowledge while learning new categories.
A major strength is the clear methodological motivation. The authors identify a mismatch between standard random projection and the geometry of medical image features. Random projection treats all feature directions equally, whereas medical image features may have an anisotropic spectrum in which only some directions are highly discriminative. The proposed eigen-directed projection is a reasonable and technically interesting way to exploit this structure.
The experimental evaluation is broad. The paper compares 14 class-incremental learning methods across 4 medical datasets, which makes the empirical contribution useful even beyond the proposed method itself. The finding that analytic classifier-based methods outperform several recent CLIP-based, prompt-based, and LoRA-based methods in this setting is valuable and worth reporting.
The ablation study is also a strength. The results suggest that eigen-directed projection and random projection provide complementary benefits. In particular, the ablation showing that EDP alone improves performance over the baseline, and that adding RP further improves performance, supports the claim that the two components are not redundant.
The ChestX results are particularly notable. EDRP appears to substantially outperform several competitors on this difficult benchmark, with relatively low variance. This suggests potential robustness in a challenging medical imaging setting where many methods perform poorly.
The method is computationally attractive because it is training-free and uses analytic classifier learning. This makes it potentially practical for medical imaging scenarios where repeated retraining may be expensive or difficult.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
A key weakness is that some implementation details are underspecified. The feature buffer is central to the proposed method, but the paper does not clearly explain how it is constructed, how many samples it stores, whether it remains fixed or grows as new tasks arrive, and how memory scales with the number of tasks. Since the paper claims memory efficiency, this point needs to be clarified. If the buffer grows with the number of tasks, the memory advantage over RanPAC or related methods may be less convincing in longer class-incremental sequences.
The ChestX comparison table appears incomplete. Table 2 includes RanPAC, InfLoRA, PROOF, and joint training, but it does not include some of the closest competitors from Table 1, such as SLDA and LoRanPAC. Since the ChestX results are one of the strongest empirical claims in the paper, the comparison should include the most relevant competing methods, or the authors should explain why they were omitted.
The dual-view mapping algorithm needs more detail. The authors do not clearly specify how the projection dimension is split between the random projection branch and the eigen-directed branch. This is important for reproducibility and for understanding how sensitive the method is to this design choice.
The paper would benefit from a clearer analysis of forgetting over time. A plot showing accuracy after each new task is introduced would help readers understand whether the method preserves old knowledge better than competitors, rather than only improving final or average accuracy.
The experiments appear to rely on a ViT-B/16 backbone. The anisotropic spectrum argument is plausible for ViT features, but it may not generalize to CNN-based encoders or other pretrained feature extractors. Testing the method with an additional backbone, or explicitly acknowledging this as a limitation, would strengthen the paper.
There are also minor presentation issues. Figure 5 could be improved by making the class mean markers more visible. There are small writing issues, including the typo “dirven” on page 5.Some explanatory sentences, such as the statement about discriminative cues lying outside the dominant subspace, should be rewritten for clarity.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I recommend weak accept. The paper presents a genuine empirical and methodological contribution, and the proposed eigen-directed projection is a reasonable and interesting extension of random projection for medical class-incremental learning. The experimental evaluation is broad, and the ablation studies support the main design choices. The ChestX results are particularly promising and suggest that the method may be useful in difficult medical imaging settings.
However, I view the contribution as incremental rather than landmark. The method builds on existing analytic classifier-based class-incremental learning approaches, especially RanPAC, and the novelty lies primarily in the eigen-directed projection component. The paper also has some reproducibility limitations due to missing implementation details about the feature buffer and projection dimension split. The incomplete ChestX comparison and lack of a task-by-task forgetting analysis weaken the empirical case. Overall, the paper is marginally above the acceptance threshold, but the rebuttal should address these concerns.
Furthermore, the improvements with the proposed method are still marginal compared to the other methods.

Reviewers think that the paper has clear methodological motivation, broad experimental validation, and promising results. However, there is some concern regarding single frozen ViT backbone and evaluation clinical realism that authors are encouraged to address.

The reviewers unanimously agreed that the proposed method offers a solid methodological advancement for continual learning in medical imaging by addressing the anisotropic structure of feature embeddings. During the rebuttal phase, the authors successfully resolved the primary concerns regarding evaluation realism, memory buffer scalability, and missing baseline comparisons.

Most of the major concerns have been addressed by the rebuttal. The authors are encouraged to carefully follow the reviews and revise the draft accordingly, if it is eventually accepted by this round of MICCAI.
The authors have addressed most of the concerns raised by reviewers. I recommend Accept.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank all reviewers. We’re glad to receive three posititve scores of 5/4/4.We carefully address concerns below and code will be released in revision.
Q1: Modest extension of RanPAC (R1). A1: We respectfully clarify that EDRP is not a drop-in replacement. Our work follows a complete pipeline: (1)benchmarking that reveals classifier-based methods unexpectedly outperform alternatives in medical CIL; (2)margin-theoretic analysis showing separability is bottlenecked by the weakest projection directions; (3)diagnosing the mismatch between isotropic projection and anisotropic medical spectra; (4)a dual-view design where each component contributes non-redundantly, with a memory reduction.
Q2: More backbones (R1, R3). A2: We first want to kindly clarify that our framework is backbone-agnostic, and the benefit of eigen-directed projection is orthogonal to backbone choice, since Fig. 2b is a general property of ViT embeddings regardless of pretraining data. We have conducted the evaluation on medical-domain backbones on Skin8, EDRP consistently outperforms RanPAC and LoRanPAC (e.g., +2.56% and +2.30% Last Acc on BioMed, +1.51% and +1.75% Last Acc on UniMed).
Q3: Non-shuffled setting on MedMNIST-Sub (R1). A3: The shuffling protocol we initially designed was intended to simulate a complicated multidisciplinary consultation scenario. In the non-shuffled configuration, our EDRP still maintains its advantage over both RanPAC and LoRanPAC (e.g., +1.08% and +14.98% Acc), further indicating the generality of our method.
Q4: Low performance of most methods on ChestX (R2). A4: Prior work Star-Prompt reports joint training with only 48.92% Acc on ChestX, consistent with our Table 2.The reason for such low performance lies in intrinsic dataset difficulty. Even so, our EDRP still achieves the highest accuracy.
Q5: Buffer scalability (R2, R3). A5: Unlike prior medical CIL methods that store raw images for replay (e.g., ACL), our feature buffer stores only compact ViT embeddings (768-dim per sample), which is approximately 196 times more compact than a single image (224×224×3). This efficiency allows us to buffer 80% of per-class samples’ embeddings for more accurate eigenspace estimation. Although RanPAC’ buffer size does not change with the number of tasks, it needs to store a full M²-dimensional covariance matrix (e.g., M=10^4), which ovbiously exceeds our total storage as shown in Table 5.Q6: Missing forgetting metrics (R2, R3). A6: EDRP achieves a BWT of −12.50% vs. RanPAC’s −13.84% on Skin8, indicating less forgetting. We will include forgetting metrics in revision. Thanks.
Q7: Incomplete comparison on ChestX (R3). A7: In our original experiments, EDRP consistently outperformed SLDA by +11.62%, RanPAC by +17.47%, and LoRanPAC by +3.70%. However, SLDA and LoRanPAC were omitted from Table 2 as they were unstable across seeds and showed no obvious advantage. We’ll clarify in revision. Thanks.
Q8: Projection dimension split (R3). A8: M is evenly split: M_f = M_a = M/2; we’ll clarify this point in revision.
Q9: Algorithm classification in Fig.1 (R4). A9: Thanks for carefully reading our work. The Classifier-based category refers to methods keeping the backbone frozen with only classifier updates. While these methods do use pre-trained ViTs, they differ from the Pre-trained ViT-based category, which adapts the backbone via prompts/LoRA. We will clarify this distinction.
Q10: Buffer contents and privacy (R4). A10: The buffer stores compact ViT embeddings that cannot be inverted to reconstruct original images, offering privacy advantages.
Q11: Shuffling and first-session adaptation (FSA) (R4). A11: Category shuffling means we randomly reorder the 36 classes from MedMNIST’s four sub-datasets across tasks. The FSA strategy, originally proposed in RanPAC, applies a lightweight adapter on task 1 before freezing the backbone to improve downstream feature quality.
Q12: Presentation issues (R3, R4). A12: We’ll fix all these minor issues. Thanks.

title: EmERGE: A Multimodal LLM-Based Evidence-Mediated ECG Report Generation and Evaluation Approach
abstract:
Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have significantly advanced the automatic generation of electrocardiogram (ECG) reports. However, current approaches handle diagnosis as a simple signal-to-text mapping task, overlook clinical reasoning, and thus suffer from hallucination and poor interpretability.
We propose an evidence-mediated ECG report generation and evaluation (EmERGE) approach that reframes the task as structured causal reasoning. It incorporates six clinically validated ECG features, such as rhythms and rates, P waves, and P-R intervals. These features act as explicit mediators, enabling MLLMs to perform diagnostic conditional reasoning using interpretable electrophysiological evidence.
Experiments demonstrate that EmERGE substantially improves ECG report quality, outperforming state-of-the-art grounded report generation methods by 13\% in clinical efficacy and 9\% in interpretability.
To verify whether diagnostic conclusions rely on causal evidence, we developed a rule-guided counterfactual evaluation protocol. The protocol applies signal-level interventions to clinically relevant leads and waveform segments to validate the link between selective evidence and diagnostic outcomes. EmERGE establishes an evidence-driven, causality-focused approach, providing a viable solution for real-world clinical applications.
The source code and prompts are available at .

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The manuscript proposes EmERGE, an evidence-mediated ECG report generation framework that reformulates ECG interpretation as a two-step reasoning process rather than a direct signal-to-text mapping task. The central idea is to introduce structured electrophysiological evidence as an explicit intermediate representation between multimodal ECG input and the final report. 
Its main contributions are:
1) Evidence-mediated report generation: six clinically defined ECG evidence dimensions (e. g. , rhythm/rate, P wave, PR interval, QRS complex, ST segment, T wave/QT interval) are extracted first and then used to condition diagnostic report generation. 
2) Clinically motivated causal formulation: the method explicitly models diagnosis as being mediated by interpretable ECG evidence, which improves transparency relative to prior end-to-end MLLM approaches. 
3) Rule-guided counterfactual evaluation: the paper introduces signal-level perturbation tests designed to assess whether diagnostic outputs change selectively when evidence-relevant waveform regions are modified. 
4) Evaluation with two strong backbones: the framework is instantiated with PULSE and GEM backbones (EmERGE(P), EmERGE(G)) and shows improved performance on both in-domain (MIMIC-IV) and out-of-domain (PTB-XL) settings.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) Clinically meaningful problem formulation: The paper addresses an important weakness of existing ECG report generation systems: they may produce fluent reports without demonstrating that the conclusions are grounded in electrophysiological evidence. Reframing the task around explicit evidence extraction is well motivated and clinically sensible. 
2) Interpretable intermediate representation: The use of six structured ECG evidence dimensions is a strong design choice. It aligns with how cardiologists reason about ECGs and provides a more auditable interface than direct end-to-end text generation. 
3) Interesting evaluation beyond surface-level text metrics: The rule-guided counterfactual protocol is a meaningful addition. In particular, evaluating Targeted Sensitivity, Non-target Invariance, and Diagnosis Response Consistency goes beyond standard report-generation metrics and attempts to probe whether the model’s diagnostic behavior is causally aligned with waveform evidence. 
4) Consistent empirical gains across multiple protocols: The method improves over strong baselines not only on LLM-based clinical metrics (e. g. , AccD, Rel, Fid), but also on classification-oriented metrics (macro/micro F1) and counterfactual consistency measures. This makes the overall empirical case stronger than if only one metric family had improved. 
5) Cross-backbone applicability within the tested setting: The framework is evaluated with two representative backbones, PULSE and GEM, and yields gains in both cases. This suggests that the approach is not narrowly tied to one specific model implementation. 
6) Clinical relevance: Improving evidence grounding and interpretability is highly relevant for eventual real-world deployment of ECG reporting systems, where unsupported but plausible-sounding conclusions are particularly problematic.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) Methodological novelty is stronger in formulation than in implementation: While the use of structured ECG evidence as an intermediate representation is novel and meaningful in this application domain, the underlying machinery—multi-round prompting, staged generation, and conditioning on intermediate text—is still relatively close to existing multi-step LLM reasoning patterns. The manuscript would be stronger if it more clearly distinguished what is conceptually new from what is inherited from general LLM prompting practice. 
2) Dependence on LLM-generated supervision: The structured evidence annotations are partially constructed using GPT-4o together with machine measurements. This is practical, but the paper does not sufficiently analyse how noisy or biased these pseudo-labels may be, nor how sensitive the final system is to errors in this supervision. 
3) Counterfactual perturbation realism is not fully established: The counterfactual evaluation is one of the most interesting parts of the paper, but also one of the least fully validated. It is not entirely clear whether the proposed signal-level interventions always correspond to physiologically realistic ECG changes, and therefore how strongly one can interpret these results as evidence of true causal validity. 
4) Evaluation emphasis remains skewed toward LLM-derived scores: Although the paper reports classification and counterfactual metrics in addition to LLM-based clinical evaluation, the headline improvements are primarily emphasized through LLM-derived scores. A more balanced presentation of the non-LLM evaluation results would strengthen the empirical claims. 
5) Limited failure-mode analysis: The qualitative examples are helpful, but the manuscript does not provide a sufficiently systematic breakdown of where the method still fails. For example, it would be useful to disentangle errors caused by incorrect evidence extraction from those caused by evidence-to-diagnosis reasoning. 
6) Reproducibility details are incomplete at the current stage: Although the authors state that code will be released after acceptance, the manuscript does not disclose important implementation details such as the exact prompt templates, evidence-extraction criteria, or thresholding decisions used in constructing the six-dimensional evidence space. These omissions make exact replication difficult. 
7) Reference formatting is inconsistent and should be carefully audited: Several citations appear to correspond to recent preprints, but they are not consistently identified as such, and some entries lack clear bibliographic details such as venue information or arXiv identifiers. This does not affect the core technical contribution, but it reduces clarity and makes it harder to assess the status and maturity of the cited prior work. The authors should carefully revise the bibliography and clearly distinguish peer-reviewed publications from preprints.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The paper tackles an important and timely problem in medical report generation, and the evidence-mediated perspective is a promising direction. 
A few suggestions that could further strengthen the work:
1) Clarify more explicitly what part of the method is genuinely novel relative to existing multi-step LLM prompting frameworks, as opposed to being a careful domain adaptation of those ideas. 
2) Provide a more detailed justification of the signal-level counterfactual intervention design, ideally including discussion of physiological plausibility and boundary cases where such perturbations may not correspond to realistic pathology changes. 
3) Expand the analysis of failure modes, for example by separately reporting cases where the evidence extraction is correct but the final reasoning is wrong, versus the reverse. 
4) Improve the bibliography by ensuring that all preprints are properly labeled and that all references contain complete and accurate publication information.

The manuscript presents a well-motivated and clinically relevant approach to ECG report generation. Its main strength lies in introducing explicit structured evidence as an intermediate reasoning layer, which improves interpretability and leads to consistent gains across multiple evaluation settings. The counterfactual evaluation framework is also a valuable contribution, as it moves beyond standard report-generation metrics and attempts to assess whether diagnostic behavior is selectively responsive to waveform evidence.
At the same time, the work has several limitations. The implementation is somewhat incremental from a general LLM-reasoning perspective, the supervision pipeline depends partly on LLM-generated evidence annotations, and the realism of the counterfactual perturbations is not yet fully established. In addition, while the empirical results are strong, many of the most prominent gains are reported through LLM-derived clinical metrics, and the manuscript would benefit from broader objective or expert-based validation.
Overall, I place the paper marginally above the acceptance threshold. The clinical motivation is strong, the empirical evidence is consistently positive, and the counterfactual analysis introduces an interesting discussion point for the community. However, the paper would benefit from clarification in rebuttal regarding reproducibility details, evaluation balance, and the validity of the proposed counterfactual design.
