reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper tries to solve a real problem that I think has been ignored for too long. Most pathology VLMs only look at one magnification level at a time, but real pathologists dont work that way. They zoom in and out and connect what they see at different scales. So the authors built Scale-VQA, a benchmark with 4685 questions from 177 TCGA whole slide images, annotated at three magnification levels by experienced pathologists. They also made a pipeline to prevent models from guessing the right answer just from the text without looking at the images. And finally they trained ScaleReasoner-R1 using reinforcement learning which beats other models on both their new benchmark and the existing PathMMU benchmark.
reviews.text_strengths: I think the motivation of this paper is one of the strongest parts. It is clinically very logical. Pathologists do not just stare at one zoom level, they move between low and high magnification to build their diagnosis. I have not seen many papers that actually try to teach a model to do the same thing in a structured way, so this feels like a genuine gap being filled.The leakage-aware curation pipeline is what I found most interesting technically. The idea of using other strong models like Gemini and Qwen as adversaries to test whether a question can be answered without the images is clever. It is a simple but effective quality control step and I think other benchmark papers should adopt something similar.I also appreciated that pathologists were involved from the very beginning of annotation, not just at the end for validation. This is not always done and it makes the dataset more trustworthy from a clinical standpoint.The result showing that training on cross-scale data also improves single-scale performance on PathMMU is interesting and a bit surprising. It suggests the model is learning something more general about pathology reasoning, not just memorizing cross-scale patterns.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
My biggest concern is the size of the dataset. 177 whole slide images across 15 organ types is quite small. Some organs have around 20 slides which is really not enough to draw strong conclusions. I understand it is hard to get expert annotations at scale but the authors should at least discuss this limitation more honestly instead of making broad generalization claims.
I have noticed that ScaleReasoner-R1 actually performs worse than Patho-R1 on the PathCLS subset, both on tiny and full test sets. This is a clear regression and the authors never mention it anywhere in the paper. This bothers me because it suggests the model may be forgetting something specific to that subset and the reader deserves an explanation.
Another thing that I think is a problem is that GPT-5.2 was used to generate the benchmark questions and it is also one of the compared models in the evaluation table. This creates a circular dependency. It is hard to know if GPT-5.2 is being evaluated fairly here or if it has some kind of advantage or disadvantage because of its role in creating the data. The authors should at least acknowledge this openly.
The reward weighting lambda equals 0.2 is just stated without any ablation or explanation. I would like to know if the results change meaningfully with different values. It seems like an important choice that was made without justification.
There are also no statistical significance tests anywhere. With 380 samples per reasoning dimension some of the differences between models might not be meaningful and we cannot tell from the paper as written.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
I think separating the benchmark contribution from the model contribution more clearly in the writing would help readers evaluate each part independently. Right now they are mixed together which makes it a bit harder to follow. Also I would find per-organ accuracy breakdowns useful because averaging across 15 very different organ types can hide a lot of variation. One small thing I noticed is that the GPT-5.2 reference seems unusual and the arXiv identifier should be double checked for accuracy.

I think this paper has a genuinely good idea at its core and the leakage-aware pipeline is a real contribution that the community can benefit from. The transfer from cross-scale to single-scale performance is also a nice finding. But the dataset is small, the PathCLS regression is unexplained, the GPT-5.2 circularity is unaddressed, and there are no significance tests. These are not minor issues. I am willing to accept this paper if the authors respond clearly to these points in the rebuttal, especially the PathCLS drop and the GPT-5.2 overlap between data construction and evaluation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper presents a clinically motivated cross-scale pathology VQA benchmark and training paradigm that addresses an important limitation of current pathology VLMs, which typically operate on isolated single-scale images despite pathologists routinely integrating evidence across magnifications. The Scale-VQA benchmark, pathologist-guided annotation process, and leakage-aware curation pipeline are meaningful contributions, and the reported performance of ScaleReasoner-R1 on the proposed benchmark is strong. The finding that cross-scale supervision transfers to overall PathMMU performance is also interesting.
The main concerns are about interpretation and scope. The benchmark is built from a relatively small number of WSIs, so the generalization claims should be framed carefully. The authors should clarify in rebuttal how WSI-level separation was maintained, how GPT-5.2 was used during data/question construction relative to its role as an evaluated baseline, and how to interpret the observed regression on the PathCLS subset compared with Patho-R1.The rebuttal should also clarify the choice of the RL reward weighting and the extent to which leakage-aware screening was independent of the final evaluated models.

I recommend acceptance. The rebuttal addressed the main concerns by clarifying that multi-scale views and QA from the same WSI are kept in the same split to avoid leakage, that GPT-5.2 was used only to draft candidate MCQs from text captions before leakage screening and pathologist verification with its final Scale-VQA accuracy of 58.51% well below ScaleReasoner-R1 at 82.89%, that the PathCLS regression reflects a trade-off between cross-scale evidence integration and label-centric priors, and that the reward weighting is 0.8 for correctness and 0.2 for format with a notation error acknowledged. Additional clarifications on leakage-screening independence (text-only adversary accuracy near chance), multi-scale dependency, and McNemar significance testing (p<0.001) addressed R2 and R3’s points, leading R1 and R3 to maintain their positive recommendations. R2 lowered the score to Reject, citing evaluation and model-comparison concerns, and the small dataset size of 177 WSIs remains a limitation. Still, these are framing-level issues that cannot be expanded under the MICCAI rebuttal policy. The leakage-aware curation pipeline and cross-scale reasoning formulation are recognized as meaningful contributions to the community.

The paper introduces a cross-scale training and evaluation paradigm for pathology vision-language models. The main contributions are SCALE-VQA, a curated benchmark of multiple-choice questions grounded in pathology images across different magnifications, and SCALEREASONER-R1, a reinforcement-learning-trained model intended to improve cross-scale pathological reasoning by linking global tissue patterns with fine cellular details.
The initial reviews were uniformly but weakly positive, with scores of 4 / 4 / 4.Reviewers appreciated the importance of cross-scale reasoning in pathology, the attempt to mimic pathologists’ diagnostic workflow, the leakage-aware curation strategy, and the potential value of SCALE-VQA as a community benchmark. The main concerns were the limited dataset size, possible data leakage or circularity in the data construction and evaluation pipeline, the small number of WSIs, insufficient validation of whether the benchmark truly requires visual cross-scale reasoning rather than exploiting textual or linguistic shortcuts, unclear PathCLS regression, limited statistical testing, and limited comparison to broader VLM baselines.
The rebuttal addressed several key concerns. The authors acknowledged the limited dataset scale and agreed to avoid broad generalization claims. They clarified the leakage-aware curation pipeline, stating that QA pairs from the same WSI remain in the same split to avoid leakage. They also explained the PathCLS regression as a trade-off caused by shifting the model toward cross-scale evidence integration rather than single-image category recognition. In response to concerns about GPT-based circularity, they stated that GPT outputs were used as draft candidate MCQs but not directly accepted as final QA, and that the benchmark was finalized through leakage-aware screening and pathologist verification. The rebuttal also clarified the reward-weight notation and summarized ablation and comparison evidence supporting multi-scale dependency.
Some concerns remain. The dataset is still relatively small, and the evaluation remains limited compared with the breadth of claims about pathology VLM reasoning. Some reviewers remained concerned about the benchmark construction process, possible residual leakage/circularity, and whether the task fully distinguishes visual reasoning from language priors. The final version should clearly describe the dataset construction pipeline, leakage-control steps, GPT-assisted generation and human verification process, statistical testing, and the limitations of the benchmark scale.
After rebuttal, the reviewer opinions are A / R / A. Reviewer 1 recommended accept, stating that the major concerns regarding dataset leakage and evaluation bias were partially resolved. Reviewer 2 moved to reject, remaining dissatisfied with the evaluation methods and model comparisons. Reviewer 3 recommended accept and viewed the leakage-aware curation and cross-scale reasoning framing as valuable enough to create useful discussion.
I recommend Accept. The paper is not without limitations, especially regarding dataset scale and the need for more rigorous evaluation of visual reasoning versus language priors. However, the problem is timely and important, the cross-scale pathology VLM framing is relevant to clinical diagnostic workflows, and the rebuttal addressed the most serious concerns about leakage and benchmark construction sufficiently for acceptance. The work should be accepted with clear limitations, and the camera-ready version should carefully document the curation pipeline, leakage prevention, model-comparison setting, and residual benchmark limitations, but the authors should avoid adding new experiments or new baseline comparisons beyond what is permitted by the MICCAI guidelines.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for the insightful feedback and will address main concerns below
[1] Dataset scale (R1, R3): We acknowledge the limited scale and will avoid broad generalization claims. We’re actively scaling to include more WSIs, organs, and pathological patterns. Beyond the dataset, our contribution includes a reproducible, leakage-aware curation pipeline for visually grounded cross-scale patho VQA, which was appreciated as a “rigorous” strategy (R1) that “other benchmark papers should adopt” (R3). We’ll open-source Scale-VQA and the curation pipeline to benefit the community to build larger datasets. Also, our results suggest that a small but high-quality, outcome-verifiable cross-scale data can provide effective RL signals for patho VLM, consistent with recent evidence [a]. For WSI-level separation, multi-scale views and QA derived from the same WSI stay in the same split to avoid leakage
[2] PathCLS regression (R3): PathCLS is converted from classification datasets into MCQs, whereas other PathMMU subsets are built from image-text sources with morphology-focused descriptions. Thus, PathCLS is closer to single-image category recognition, while the others more align w/ descriptive, evidence-grounded reasoning. Since our RL objective emphasizes cross-scale evidence integration, fine-tuning may shift the model away from some label-centric priors learned by Patho-R1, causing a trade-off on this subset, while improving other evidence-oriented subsets and overall PathMMU
[3] GPT5.2 circularity (R3): We acknowledge the concern. To clarify, GPT-5.2 was used in text-based construction stage to draft candidate MCQs from cross-scale captions; its outputs weren’t directly accepted as final QA. The benchmark was finalized through leakage-aware screening and pathologist verification of visual support, answer correctness, and distractor plausibility. While GPT-5.2 may have advantages in text-based analysis, eval on our final pathologist-verified questions requires cross-scale visual evidence integration and image-text alignment ability. As shown in Tab.1, GPT has 58.51% ACC on Scale-VQA, far below ScaleReasoner-R1(82.89), suggesting that the commercial VLMs may rely on textual priors in med-VQA, and hence struggle with the cross-scale grounded visual reasoning required by our bench. This is also consistent with existing literature [b] 
[4] Reward weight (R3): We apologize for a notation error: answer correctness weight is 0.8, format is 0.2.As Patho-R1 already exhibits instruction-following ability, the format reward regularizes malformed outputs, while the dominant acc reward drives cross-scale reasoning improvement. We’ll correct the formula and add justification
[5] Ablation&Comparisons&Stats(R2): Ablations on key pipeline components: (i)after leakage screening, text-only adversary ACC (%) drops to 32.8 (Qwen3Max) and 29.5 (Gemini3Pro), close to chance (25%), confirming shortcut suppression; (ii) Avg across 4 models and 5 dimensions, dropping 1 view reduces ACC (%) by 3.8, dropping 2 by 8.5, text-only by 17.8, confirming multi-scale dependency. Our experiments already include representative 7B medical VLMs for a fair same-param comparison in Tab.1-2.For stats significance, ScaleReasoner-R1 achieves 82.89 ACC, CI [80.43, 85.09], vs. Gemini (2nd best) at 60.90, CI [57.84, 63.87]. McNemar’s test confirms significance (χ² = 141.11, p < 0.001) across all dimensions
[6] Clinical feasibility & novelty (R1): We agree that MCQ eval doesn’t fully demonstrate real-world feasibility. Our clinical involvement lies in expert annotation/validation, and Scale-VQA is positioned as a controlled benchmark for cross-scale visual integration. We also clarify that our novelty is not GRPO, but the clinically grounded cross-scale reasoning formulation&curation pipeline that makes outcome-based RL meaningful for patho VLMs. 
[a] Wang et al.RL for Reasoning in LLMs with One Training Example [b] Asadi et al. Mirage the illusion of visual understanding

title: Equity-Aware Self-supervised Multi-domain Connectome Representation Learning for Major Depressive Disorder Diagnosis
abstract: Graph-based models have shown promise in neuroimaging by identifying abnormal functional brain connectivity in psychiatric disorders. However, current approaches for functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging analysis have several limitations. Most methods estimate connectivity only from time-domain correlations, ignoring frequency dependent phase synchronization that provides complementary information about neural communication. In addition, existing models typically learn representations using diagnostic labels. For disorders such as Major Depressive Disorder, these labels are heterogeneous and site-dependent, which limits generalization across institutions and populations when labeled data are scarce. Finally, reliability and equity are rarely considered during representation learning, leading to demographic bias and inconsistent subgroup performance. To address these challenges, we propose RESOLVE (Robust and Equitable Self supervised learning for functiOnaL connectiVity modEling), a self-supervised multi-domain connectome representation learning framework. RESOLVE employs dual graph encoders to learn from correlation- and coherence-based connectivity and promotes consistency across the two domains. We further introduce a topology-preserving reconstruction objective that maintains the intrinsic organization of the brain network. To improve reliability, we learn demographically invariant representations by aligning subgroup distributions in the latent space using an Optimal Transport objective. Experiments on the REST-meta-MDD dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in balancing diagnostic performance and demographic bias compared to existing methods. Source code is available at: https://github.com/shashivipul/RESOLVE_2026.git.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Algorithmic Fairness / Safety / Regulation

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents RESOLVE, a self-supervised graph representation learning framework that leverages functional connectivity in both the time and frequency domains. To ensure reliability and equity, it incorporates a topology-preserving reconstruction objective to maintain brain network organization and an Optimal Transport-based alignment module to produce demographically invariant representations, thereby reducing bias across subgroups. Experiments on the REST-meta-MDD dataset show the superiority of the proposed method.
reviews.text_strengths: This method incorporates frequency-domain coherence and time-domain correlations, which may capture a more comprehensive representation of neural communication compared to single-domain approaches.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1）Most of the comparison models chosen by the authors were published in/before 2022.The article lacks comparisons with more recent technologies. Furthermore, the lack of comparisons with cross-domain (or domain-adaptive/generalization) methods raises concerns about the robustness and reliability of the reported results, especially when distributions shift. It is recommended to enhance this aspect of the paper by incorporating comparisons with state-of-the-art techniques to improve the overall innovativeness of the study. 
2) The authors compute coherence between ROIs only within the 0.01–0.1 Hz frequency band. It is unclear whether the same band-pass filtering (0.01–0.1 Hz) was already applied during preprocessing. If so, the subsequent analysis is essentially conducted within the same frequency range, meaning that the frequency setting is consistent and does not introduce any additional information filtering step. This raises the question of whether potentially informative higher-frequency fluctuations are unintentionally excluded. A discussion or ablation analysis on different frequency bands would strengthen the paper. 
3) Experiments are conducted only on REST-meta-MDD, which may limit generalizability to other disorders, such as ASD and ADHD. 
4) Hyperparameters, such as the k-nearest-neighbor value (k=10) and the coherence threshold (0.3), are selected empirically without a detailed sensitivity analysis. 
5) How can the data be split within a 5-fold cross-validation to obtain 70% training, 10% validation, and 20% testing sets?

meta_reviews.text:
Based on the three reviews, the paper has notable strengths. However, R1 raises substantial concerns about outdated baseline comparisons (mostly pre‑2022), lack of comparison with domain adaptation/generalization methods, limited frequency‑band analysis, evaluation on only one dataset (REST‑meta‑MDD), and missing hyperparameter sensitivity analysis. R2 suggests improving the fusion strategy and presentation clarity. R3 is generally positive but recommends testing on additional datasets and polishing the writing.
Besides, novelty is limited. The proposed framework combines existing techniques—dual‑domain (time/frequency) connectivity, contrastive learning, reconstruction loss. More important, the paper asserts that minimizing the optimal transport loss LDP aligns subgroup representations and promotes demographic‑invariant embeddings, thereby reducing disparities. However, no solid evidence is provided to support this claim.

The rebuttal does a good job in clarifying the comparison baselines and model novelty in the paper. Post rebuttal, all reviewers lean towards accepting the paper and I am in agreement as well. All major concerns seem to be addressed.

This paper contributes an equity-aware self-supervised representation learning framework for connectome-based MDD diagnosis, and its attempt to treat fairness as a central design objective is a meaningful strength. The rebuttal appears to have responded effectively by clarifying why fairness is not merely an auxiliary analysis and by better grounding the method in the observed utility-fairness behavior, which helped maintain this paper qualified for acceptance.

The paper addresses a clinically relevant and timely problem in fairness-aware self-supervised connectome learning. The rebuttal adequately addresses the main concerns about recent baselines, the demographic alignment loss, frequency-band choice, hyperparameter selection, fusion design, and cross-validation split. All active reviewers support acceptance after rebuttal, and the remaining issues are mainly presentation and clarification rather than core validity.

author_feedback_text:
We thank reviewers for constructive comments. We are encouraged that they recognized strong motivation(R4,R5), clarity(R1), novelty(R4), thorough evaluation/ablations(R4,R5) & clinical relevance of equity-aware diagnosis with biologically meaningful results(R5).
Q1:Baseline. GCDA[24] & CoRE-BOLD[22] are both 2025 SOTA. GCDA is an SOTA SSL benchmark designed for cross-site generalization. RESOLVE outperforms both in utility & FATE under cross-site distribution shift & Gaussian noise. Prior generalization-based approaches don’t explicitly address fairness.
Q2:L_DP loss. Section 3.1 provides 3 quantitative validations of L_DP: (i)Table 1 shows RESOLVE is the only method achieving positive FATE on both cross-site protocols, reducing demographic parity difference more effectively than baselines.(ii)In Fig.2(c),RESOLVE w/o L_DP shows a clear rise in ΔDP, showing its contribution to reducing subgroup disparity.(iii)Fig.2(b) shows RESOLVE preserves best utility-fairness tradeoff across labeled-data fractions.
Q3:Dataset. MDD is used as a proof-of-concept due to established gender bias. However, RESOLVE is disease/cohort agnostic. Our cross-site validation (S20→S14 & S20→S21) already evaluates realistic distribution shifts & demographic composition, where RESOLVE achieves SOTA performance. The OT alignment performs non-parametric matching between two subgroup distributions, making it applicable to arbitrary binary subgroup populations. We also validated RESOLVE on ABIDE dataset with consistent improvement. Due to rebuttal policy,results will be detailed in GitHub repo upon acceptance.
Q4:Novelty. RESOLVE is, to our knowledge, 1st equity-aware multi-domain SSL framework for connectomes without task labels, a setting previously unaddressed in neuroimaging. It delivers 3 connectome specific contributions: (a)Representation-level fairness in SSL: since diagnostic labels are unavailable during pretraining, RESOLVE enforces demographic invariance in fused latent space via OT alignment, unlike prior methods that mainly operate in supervised prediction space (b)Joint multi-domain reconstruction: RESOLVE reconstructs both correlation & coherence based connectomes from a fused embedding, rather than a single connectivity view, introducing a novel SSL pretext (c)Graph-level cross-domain SSL: Jointly modeling time & frequency domain connectivity while preserving ROI interactions. No prior method unifies SSL pretraining, multi-domain connectome learning, & equity-aware latent representation learning.
Q5:Frequency. The 0.01–0.1 Hz range is widely established as Low-Frequency Fluctuation(LFF) band in seminal rsfMRI literature, capturing dominant spontaneous BOLD fluctuations while attenuating low frequency drift(<0.01Hz) & physiological noise(>0.1Hz)[C1,C2]. The same filter is applied during preprocessing to isolate this signal. RESOLVE’s frequency encoder captures phase synchronization within this band, which a time-domain encoder doesn’t explicitly model. This will be clarified in camera ready.
Q6:k & threshold. Following prior literature, we tuned k∈[5,15] & threshold∈[0.1,0.6] via grid search on validation data. Due to page limit we didn’t provide the analysis.
Q7:READOUT. READOUT (Global mean pooling,in Sec.3) aggregates ROI(node)-level embeddings into a subject(graph)-level vector.
Q8:CV split. We use standard 5-fold CV where each fold holds 20% for testing; rest 80% is split as 90:10 into training and validation, yielding a 72/8/20 split. We will correct it in camera ready.
Q9:Fusion. RESOLVE aim to derive its gains from objectives in Eq. 9 rather than fusion complexity, yet outperforms SOTA baselines including transformer-based architectures. Exploring attention-based fusion is a promising future direction.
Q10:Presentation. RESOLVE acronym is expanded in Introduction; we will additionally include it in Abstract. We will rename Problem 1 to Problem Statement.
C1: Cordes et al.,AJNR, 2001
C2: Biswal et al.,Magn Reson Med. 1995

title: ESRT: Endoscopic Stereo Reconstruction Transformer
abstract: Accurate endoscopic stereo reconstruction is essential for disease diagnosis and 3D visualizations in surgery. To achieve endoscopic stereo reconstruction from endoscopic stereo images under specular reflections, illumination variations, and smooth texture conditions, we propose the endoscopic stereo reconstruction transformer (ESRT). ESRT captures fine-grained textures by introducing a row-wise cross-attention mechanism that explicitly constrains correspondence search along the horizontal direction and prevents attention from being computed over geometrically invalid regions. Furthermore, we present a distillation-based training strategy that transfers geometric knowledge from a pretrained model without requiring endoscopic 3D annotations. The proposed method achieves the best performance on the SCARED dataset while maintaining real-time efficiency.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes ESRT, a transformer-based method for endoscopic stereo reconstruction. The main idea is to use row-wise cross-attention to restrict stereo matching along the horizontal direction, together with a distillation strategy that learns from a pretrained 3D reconstruction model without using endoscopic 3D annotations. The method is tested on the SCARED dataset and reports better depth metrics than several existing endoscopic reconstruction methods.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper addresses an important problem, as depth estimation and 3D reconstruction in endoscopy are clinically useful but technically difficult due to specular reflection, weak texture, and unstable correspondence. The row-wise attention design is reasonable for stereo endoscopy, since disparity mainly occurs along the horizontal direction and this constraint can reduce unnecessary matching and computation. The reported efficiency is also a positive point, with fewer parameters, lower GFLOPs, and about 44 FPS compared with DUSt3R. The experiments cover several recent endoscopic reconstruction methods, and the visual examples look better than some baselines in selected cases.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The paper mainly combines a transformer reconstruction framework, epipolar/row-wise matching, and teacher-student distillation. These ideas have already appeared in related forms in stereo matching, transformer-based 3D reconstruction, and model distillation. DUSt3R already performs dense 3D reconstruction with cross-view matching, while Endo-FASt3r and EndoSfM3D have explored foundation-model-based endoscopic reconstruction. The paper does not make the difference from these works sufficiently clear. 
2.The distillation strategy is also rather standard. Using DUSt3R as a teacher and training a smaller student model is useful, but the formulation itself does not seem very new. More analysis is needed to show why this distillation is specifically suited to endoscopic stereo reconstruction, rather than being a straightforward compression/adaptation of an existing teacher model. 
3.The comparison is not fully convincing. Many baseline results are directly taken from previous papers, but the training and evaluation settings may not be exactly the same. It would be better to rerun key baselines under the same protocol, especially DUSt3R, Endo-FASt3r, and EndoSfM3D. 
4.The clinical claim is overstated. The paper mentions real-time clinical applicability, but the experiments are only on SCARED, which is based on porcine cadaver data. There is no validation on real clinical gastroscopy cases, no lesion measurement task, and no user study with clinicians.

N/A

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents a transformer-based feedforward 3D reconstruction method for endoscopy. The model takes in a stereo pair of images and outputs the point cloud. The authors utilize epipolar constraints and teacher-student distillation.
reviews.text_strengths:
Strong results. Out of the comparisons provided by the authors, their approach (ESRT-Row) achieves best performance in depth estimation
Effective ideas. student outperforms teacher despite the latter being frozen, demonstrating that the epipolar constraint and multiscale encoder are helpful
Practicality. The authors demonstrate that their model is efficient compared to some baselines. Furthermore, their method seems like it does not require ground truth and is trained only with pseudolabels.
Good writing. The method is clearly described and the paper flows well
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Limited method novelty. Row-wise (or epipolar constrained) transformer-based 3D reconstruction/depth estimation/stereo matching is fairly dated, and the first work of its kind also includes SCARED in their experiments (STTR Stereo Transformer, Li et al). The method is DUSt3R pointmap prediction + distillation + epipolar constraints, which has limited novelty
Lack of ablation. For this type of study, the lack of thorough ablation is concerning, even though there are many components that raise several questions. How does distillation compare with train-from-scratch and full supervision from SCARED GT? How do the different loss term ideas contribute? How does DiNAT compare with other backbones like plain ViT (DINOv2-pretrained for instance) or Swin?
Limited evaluation. Since this is stereo depth estimation, I am curious how the proposed model compares against methods like FoundationStereo, RAFT-Stereo, CREO-stereo, etc. Furthermore, DUSt3R is a originally a two-view reconstruction model. Would using FoundationStereo or another stereo model as a teacher be better since it’s more well-suited for this task?
I am unsure if the entire training pipeline requires any ground truth data for training, or if the training only comes from pseudolabels from the teacher. Was any SCARED ground truth data used for training? Please clarify.
Writing. I am unsure if the paper does indeed propose a “reconstruction transformer”. The proposed model seems to be more of a stereo depth estimator. Perhaps this claim can be made if other non-stereo datasets were also used to evaluate the model (e.g., C3VD). There are also other writing concerns, like the paper being motivated in the Introduction section with gastroscopy, but the method is only evaluated with ex-vivo porcine data.

N/A

Please clarify the above concerns. The paper is well-scoped and demonstrates good ideas. Ultimately, my biggest concerns are in the lack of novelty, lack of ablation studies, and the framing of a reconstruction work rather than depth estimation.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper addresses the clinical task of endoscopic 3D reconstruction, targeting critical challenges in endoscopic imaging including specular reflections, illumination variations, smooth textures, and unstable depth estimation. It presents the Endoscopic Stereo Reconstruction Transformer (ESRT). Its main contributions are summarized as follows:
1) It introduces a row-wise cross-attention mechanism that enforces horizontal epipolar constraints to reduce geometric ambiguity and invalid correspondences.
2) It employs a distillation-based training strategy that leverages a generic pre-trained model as the teacher network, enabling the transfer of geometric priors without requiring endoscopic 3D annotations.
3) It constructs a lightweight multi-scale encoder-decoder architecture based on DiNAT, which achieves state-of-the-art performance on the SCARED dataset while realizing real-time inference at 44 FPS.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) Precise problem formulation: The work accurately targets real-world clinical challenges in endoscopy. The three key objectives enforcing epipolar constraints, alleviating annotation scarcity, and achieving real-time performance are highly consistent with the clinical translation-oriented goals of MICCAI medical imaging research.
2) Effective core innovation: The proposed row-wise cross-attention is simple and physically meaningful, which directly conforms to the horizontal disparity property of stereo endoscopy. The motivation is solid and the design is reasonable.
3) Practical training strategy: The knowledge distillation scheme successfully addresses the shortage of endoscopic 3D annotations, aligns with the mainstream trend of self-supervised/weakly-supervised learning in medical imaging, and exhibits strong extensibility.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) Over-reliance on the distillation strategy: The paper does not thoroughly discuss or analyze the quality of the “pseudo ground truth” provided by the teacher model under domain differences, nor the potential systematic biases. It remains unclear whether the method is overly dependent on the teacher model.
2) Insufficient ablation studies: The paper lacks complete and independent ablation studies for the three core components: row-wise cross-attention, knowledge distillation, and multi-scale fusion. As a result, the actual quantitative gains of each module cannot be verified.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

1) The research topic is highly consistent with clinical demands, as endoscopic 3D reconstruction is a key technology for surgical navigation and disease diagnosis.
2) The core innovation, row-wise cross-attention, features clear motivation, original design, and remarkable effectiveness, resolving critical limitations of Transformers in endoscopic stereo matching.
3) The method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while enabling real-time inference, demonstrating high clinical translation value.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: My decision is to accept this paper, because there is a high likelihood that the proposed row-wise cross-attention will produce strong effects in endoscopy or other stereo matching scenarios. However, due to space limitations or other reasons, the ablation study section is relatively limited.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a Transformer-based framework (ESRT) for 3D reconstruction from endoscopic stereo images. Based on the assumption that stereo correspondences exist mainly in the horizontal direction, the correspondence search is restricted to the horizontal direction by introducing row-wise cross-attention, thereby suppressing attention computation to geometrically invalid regions. In addition, a distillation-based learning strategy using a pre-trained model (DUSt3R) as a teacher allows learning without 3D annotation; the best performance is reported at AbsRel 0.048 compared to existing methods on the SCARED dataset.
reviews.text_strengths:
(1) Endoscopic stereo reconstruction is an important issue in clinical applications and the significance of addressing it is clear.
(2) )The design of restricting the correspondence search to the horizontal direction by row-wise cross-attention is a reasonable architectural choice that reflects the stereo geometry and contributes to the reduction of computational cost.
(3) The distillation-based learning strategy is practical in that it allows learning without 3D annotation, which is difficult to obtain in the endoscopic domain.
The design to weight the training signal according to the confidence of the teacher by confidence-aware loss is also reasonable.
(4) The proposed method achieves an inference speed of 44fps with 154.45M parameters, about 29% of DUSt3R (532.34M) and 20% of GFLOPs, showing a significant improvement in terms of efficiency.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(1) There is a fundamental discrepancy between the claims of the paper and the validation domain.
This thesis is positioned throughout as a method for gastroscopy and gastric mucosa. Specifically, the Abstract and Section 1 as a whole are motivated in the context of gastric cancer and precancerous lesion diagnosis, while Section 2.3 states that the proposed decoder “better represents the gastric mucosa during correspondence matching‘ and the Conclusion states that ’we plan to apply the method for gastric cancer and precancerous lesion diagnosis”.
However, the experiments are based only on the SCARED dataset (‘acquired from fresh porcine cadaver abdominal anatomy’), which is intraperitoneal data from porcine cadavers, and both the target tissue and imaging conditions are different from the gastric SCARED is different from the gastric mucosa in both target tissues and imaging conditions. Therefore, the gastric mucosa-specific nature repeatedly claimed in the paper is not supported at all experimentally. The architecture of the proposed method itself also consists of a general multi-scale feature extraction and attention mechanism, with no explicit gastric mucosa-specific design elements. Thus, the basis for claims such as ‘better represent the gastric mucosa’ is unclear.
To resolve this discrepancy, either (i) the entire article needs to be reorganised into a general stereoendoscopic reconstruction and the gastric mucosa-specific claims removed, or (ii) an evaluation with data closer to the target domain, such as ex-vivo gastric tissue, should be presented. Both directions are beyond the scope of what can be addressed in the REBUTTAL and require essential revisions.
(2) The paper reports only AbsRel, SqRel, RMSE and RMSELog and lacks threshold-based accuracy measures (δ < 1.25, δ < 1.25², δ < 1.25³), which are standard in the endoscopic depth estimation field. The group of endoscopic depth estimation-based methods listed for comparison (AF-SfMLearner, DARES, EndoDAC, Endo-FASt3r, EndoSfM3D) all report these δ indicators and are more than comparable with these methods in the same table, It is desirable to have the same indicators; the lack of δ indicators undermines the completeness of the comparison and makes it difficult for the reader to relate the present method to existing endoscopic depth estimation benchmark results.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1) row-wise cross-attention is designed on the assumption that the corresponding points are in the same image row, which is strictly a geometric relation that is only valid for rectified stereo inputs. Although the paper describes ‘stereo endoscopes produce disparity mainly along the horizontal direction’, the presence or absence of rectification for SCARED data and the details of pre-processing are not explicitly stated. In order to clarify the conditions for application of the method, it would be desirable to add a sentence about the input image being rectified and the pre-processing for this purpose.
2))) Section 3 states that ‘The inference FPS of ESRT is around 44.Such results show the efficiency of our method compared with SOTA transformer-based methods.’ The hardware used for the comparison, the input resolution and the batch size are not given (‘The training is performed on a computer with two 4090 GPUs~’ is not an accurate hardware description). This is not an accurate description of the hardware). Also, while a comparison of the number of parameters and GFLOPs with DUSt3R is useful, the results for fps under comparable conditions need to be stated side by side.

The paper contains interesting technical elements: efficient stereo correspondence estimation with row-wise cross-attention and a distillation-based learning strategy. However, despite the fact that the entire paper claims to target gastroscopy and gastric mucosa, the experiments are based only on SCARED, which is laparoscopic data, and there is a fundamental discrepancy between the claimed target domain and the validation data. No gastric mucosa-specific design elements can be found in the method itself, and claims such as ‘better represent the gastric mucosa’ are not supported experimentally or theoretically. This discrepancy cannot be resolved without reconstructing the entire paper or additional validation in the target domain, which is beyond the scope of what can be addressed in the rebuttal.
In addition, no standard δ-threshold indicators have been reported in the field of endoscopic depth estimation, and the comparison with existing methods lacks completeness.
For these reasons, we consider that the claims of the proposed method are not sufficiently validated and that it cannot be adopted.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
We commend the authors for reconstructing the clinical framing and stating that they are repositioning this study as a general stereo endoscopic reconstruction framework. On the other hand, this modification requires essential reorganisation across Abstract, Introduction, Methods and Conclusion, and is beyond the scope of what can be addressed at the camera-ready stage. Although the rebuttal may clarify the position of the paper, the initial clinical problem importance will be relatively weakened and, as a result, the importance of validation of the methodological contribution itself will increase.
On this basis, the main concerns raised by Meta-Reviewers and multiple reviewers regarding methodological novelty and experimental validation (comprehensive ablation, teacher pseudo-labelling dependence, differentiation from existing methods, inadequate evaluation, etc.) are considered to be more important. The main concerns regarding methodological novelty and experimental validation (comprehensive ablation, teacher pseudo-labelling dependency, differentiation from existing methods, sufficiency of evaluation, etc.) remain unresolved.
The main concerns have therefore not been sufficiently resolved by the rebuttal, and the original decision to reject is retained.

meta_reviews.text:
The reviewers commonly question the novelty and evidence behind the method, noting that it largely combines existing ideas—DUSt3R-style pointmap prediction, epipolar/row-wise matching, and standard teacher–student distillation—without clearly distinguishing itself from related stereo or endoscopic reconstruction methods, and without sufficient ablations to isolate the effects of distillation, row-wise attention, multi-scale fusion, losses, or backbone choices. They also raise concerns that the evaluation is incomplete and misaligned with the paper’s clinical claims, since experiments are limited to SCARED porcine cadaver data despite repeated gastroscopy/gastric-mucosa motivation, key baselines may not be evaluated under the same protocol, standard depth metrics are missing, and the dependence on teacher-generated pseudo labels is not adequately analyzed.

This paper has limitations on the experiments and evaluation:
-Discrepancy between the clinical motivation (gastroscopy) and the validation (SCARED porcine abdominal anatomy).
-Ablation study is limited.
However, the methodology has good novelty, and it is effective for the applications:
-Row-wise cross-attention
-Multi-scale backbone
This paper is expected to contribute to future advances in stereo reconstruction from endoscopic images, and I think it is acceptable.
The authors managed to provide convincing answers to the comments raised by the reviewers. The method is potentially impactful in the field of 3D reconstruction.

The paper addresses an important problem and reports promising efficiency and SCARED performance. The row-wise attention is reasonable, and the rebuttal clarifies the rectified-stereo setting and training without SCARED GT pointmaps.
However, the main concerns remain. The novelty is limited, as the method combines DUSt3R-style pointmap prediction, epipolar/row-wise matching, multi-scale features, and standard distillation. The experiments lack key ablations, matched baseline comparisons, teacher-dependence analysis, and standard depth metrics. The original gastroscopy/gastric-mucosa framing is also not supported by the SCARED-only validation and would require substantial reframing.
Overall, the work is promising but not sufficiently novel or validated for acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the Meta-Reviewer (MR) and Reviewers (R1–R4) for their time and expertise, and address the primary concerns below.
1.Methodological Contribution and Novelty [MR, R1, R2]
Novel Synergy: Unlike existing transformer-based reconstruction methods, our framework jointly integrates a multi-scale backbone and row-wise attention to explicitly enforce horizontal epipolar constraints across different feature scales. This design enables effective feature alignment and direct 3D reconstruction under strong specular reflections and visually similar textures in endoscopic images, without explicitly estimating camera intrinsic parameters or poses. By suppressing attention in geometrically invalid regions, the proposed architecture provides a physically meaningful solution for robust stereo matching in challenging endoscopic scenarios.
Beyond Compression: Our distillation-based strategy uses sparse but reliable teacher correspondences, enabling the student model through multi-scale interaction and row-wise attention to effectively learn geometry-aware stereo matching. Thus, the student model surpasses the teacher model and achieves more robust performance under challenging endoscopic conditions. 
2.Clinical Framing and Validation Domain [MR, R4]
We appreciate R4 and the MR’s concern regarding the discrepancy between our clinical motivation (gastroscopy) and validation (SCARED porcine abdominal anatomy).
Gold-Standard Validation: The SCARED dataset is the gold-standard MICCAI challenge benchmark for “stereo correspondence and reconstruction of endoscopic data”. Validating on SCARED is a necessary step to demonstrate technical merit within the surgical vision community.
Refinement of Claims: We acknowledge that our “gastric mucosa-specific” phrasing may be overly focused. Following R4’s suggestion, we will reframe the final manuscript as a general endoscopic stereo reconstruction framework, positioning “gastric diagnosis” as a primary future clinical application. 
3.Experimental Setup and Training Pipeline [R1, R2, R4]
Experimental Settings: In Table 1, for experimental fairness, the results for Endo-FASt3R and EndoSfM3D were directly adopted from their original papers, as both methods are designed for monocular temporal reconstruction rather than stereo-pair matching. Therefore, their evaluation results were only based on the left-view split of the SCARED dataset, and our comparisons follow the same protocol. Their performance would further degrade with stereo-pair training, because they rely on temporal reprojection optimization rather than stereo correspondence learning.
Training Strategy: For DUSt3R and ESRT, both methods use the rectified stereo pairs officially provided by SCARED under the same train/test split, making the row-wise cross-attention assumption valid. DUSt3R requires GT pointmap supervision, while ESRT does not use any SCARED GT pointmap for training. Instead, ESRT uses a DUSt3R teacher pretrained on large-scale stereo datasets without exposure to SCARED, and only utilizes sparse reliable pseudo correspondences for distillation. The proposed multi-scale and geometric-constrained design then learns robust stereo matching for challenging endoscopic features without dense annotations.
4.Ablations and Efficiency Evaluation [R2, R3, R4]
Ablation Studies: Table 1 provides an explicit ablation: ESRT-Full vs. ESRT-Row. The improvement in AbsRel from 0.053 to 0.048 directly quantifies the “remarkable effectiveness” of our row-wise constraint.
Hardware and FPS: The 44 FPS were measured on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU with batch size 1 and input resolution 320x256, consistent with the SCARED dataset setting used by the SOTA methods.
5.Quantitative Completeness: $\delta$ Metrics [R4]
Prior Studies: As shown in the experiments in EndoSfM3D, which is superior to other SOTA methods, $\delta$ is also omitted due to limited space. We appreciate reviewers’ understanding.

title: Estimated Age-Guided Cerebral Microbleed Segmentation
abstract: Cerebral microbleed (CMB) segmentation is complicated by extreme class imbalance and data scarcity due to low prevalence. Given the positive correlation between the prevalence of CMBs and aging, integrating age-related biomarkers offers a promising strategy to improve segmentation performance. In this study, we propose AgeCMBNet, a framework that leverages estimated chronological age derived from anatomical T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging. A pre-trained Meta-matching model was used to estimate each subject’s chronological age. Based on the median age of the training cohort, we implement a two-branch decoder architecture where younger and older adults are processed through different decoders while sharing a common image encoder. Experiments on an in-house dataset and the public MICCAI VALDO 2021 Challenge dataset demonstrate that our approach outperforms conventional segmentation models and existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, our model shows robust generalizability on the ATLAS v2.0 stroke dataset, which has a weaker correlation between estimated age and lesion volume. Our code is available at https://github.com/junmokwon/AgeCMBNet
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers

title: Evidential Fusion Network for Multimodal Survival Prediction Under Missing Modalities
abstract: Recent multimodal survival prediction models have demonstrated strong predictive performance by leveraging complementary information across modalities. However, such models generally assume data completeness and exhibit limited robustness toward missing modalities, which are frequently encountered in real-world clinical settings. We propose the Evidential Missing Modality Survival Fusion model for multimodal survival prediction under missing modalities. EMMS offers a straightforward, computationally effective approach to survival analysis without requiring a generative phase for missing data. By employing Dempster–Shafer theory and the newly introduced Gaussian Random Fuzzy Numbers for multimodal decision fusion, it considers both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty alongside modality reliability for fusion. Moreover, the model treats missing modalities as vacuous evidence, preventing interference with available inputs and naturally reflecting increased uncertainty and calibrated predictions. Extensive experiments on four cancer datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance while providing calibrated and interpretable uncertainty estimates under incomplete multimodal observations, without extra computational overhead. Code is available at https://github.com/YuchengXing99/EMMS.
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers
Applications -> Outcome Prediction / Prognosis / Longitudinal Modeling
Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes an Evidential Missing Modality Survival Fusion (EMMS) framework to address the common issue of missing modalities in multimodal cancer survival analysis. The method leverages Dempster–Shafer theory and Gaussian Random Fuzzy Numbers (GRFN) to model uncertainty and treats missing modalities as vacuous evidence, enabling an imputation-free fusion strategy. Demonstrating the method on multiple TCGA cancer datasets under different missing-modality scenarios.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Addressing missing modalities in multimodal survival analysis is important for real-world deployment. 
2.The paper evaluates different missing rates, which improves the practical relevance of the study. 
3.Experiments are conducted on four TCGA cancer cohorts, which provides a relatively diverse validation setting.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) and GRFN-based survival modeling are not new (see [17, 18]). The main contribution of this work is applying these existing techniques to the missing modality setting, which is incremental and does not constitute a substantial methodological advance. 
2.Some abbreviations such as ERFS are not defined at first use, naming is inconsistent (e. g. , Dispro vs. DisPro), and inconsistent bold formatting applied to both full sentences and individual words. 
3.The symmetric KL divergence-based Alignment Loss (Eq. 11) for aligning pathology and genomics predictions is problematic, given that forcing distributional similarity between inherently heterogeneous modalities risks compromising complementary information, particularly in cases of modality conflict. The Prototype Learning component (Eq. 4) lacks specification of the prototype number K and initialization strategy, which severely hinders reproducibility and prevents a rigorous evaluation of the method’s robustness. 
4.The experimental comparison is limited. The paper does not include several important missing-modality methods such as SMIL [20], M3Care [28], and Flex-MoE [27]. Using only DisPro and MUSE as baselines is insufficient to support claims of strong or state-of-the-art performance.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

1.Methodologically, it lacks substantial novelty, as it only incrementally applies existing EDL and GRFN techniques to the missing modality setting. 
2.The proposed Alignment Loss is problematic, risking loss of complementary information between heterogeneous modalities, and critical details of Prototype Learning are unspecified, undermining reproducibility.
3.The experimental evaluation is incomplete: key missing-modality baselines are excluded, and only two baselines are insufficient to support state-of-the-art performance claims.
4.Persistent presentation issues (undefined abbreviations, inconsistent naming/formatting) further reduce the manuscript’s professionalism and readability.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Although the rebuttal provides some clarifications, I still find the methodological novelty insufficient, the method comparison inadequate to support the SOTA claim, and several key implementation details insufficiently specified.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces the EMMS model for multimodal survival prediction with missing modalities. It uses Dempster-Shafer theory and GRFN to fuse two modalities. It treat missing modalities as vacuous evidence with zero epistemic strength. Experiments on four TCGA datasets show satisfying performance under different modality missing settings.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.It is a novel idea to use the Dempster–Shaferevidential theory and GRFNs to handle the modality missing problem, bypass the imputation hallucination and imputation-free’s information loss.
2.The paper is clearly written, well-structured and easy to follow.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.How many prototypes are used in each branch? It is also unclear whether these prototypes are semantically meaningful, for example, whether they correspond to distinct risk patterns. In addition, how are the prototypes initialized? Since there appears to be no explicit mechanism to encourage diversity or separation among them, what prevents the prototypes from becoming redundant or collapsing during training?
2.The interaction between modalities appears to be rather weak, as it is introduced only at the final Gaussian-distribution level. Since the WSI and genomic features are encoded independently and no explicit cross-modal feature interaction is modeled, could this lead to inconsistent or divergent modality-specific predictions before fusion?
3.Why are the epistemic strengths produced by the two unimodal branches directly comparable? Since the pathology and genomics branches are trained separately and may have different scaling behaviors, it is unclear what guarantees that their epistemic strengths are calibrated onto a common scale and can therefore be reliably used for cross-modal weighting in fusion.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Despite some weaknesses that still need to be clarified, this paper proposes a novel strategy for handling missing modalities in survival modeling that is both efficient and effective. Overall, I recommend accepting this paper.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper presents a well-motivated, uncertainty-aware method for cancer survival prediction under missing-data situations. The reviewers raised critical concerns regarding technical details, experimental justifications, and methodological novelty.

The authors’ rebuttal and clarifications addressed most concerns.

The paper proposes EMMS, an Evidential Missing Modality Survival Fusion framework for addressing missing modalities in multimodal cancer survival analysis. Its focus on missing modalities is both practical and clinically important. The reviewers raised several important concerns, but the authors addressed them comprehensively in the rebuttal, including adding baselines such as Flex-MOE and further demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method. Overall, the work is solid and relevant, and I recommend acceptance.

Two out of three reviewers recommend acceptance after the rebuttal. The application of Dempster-Shafer theory and Gaussian Random Fuzzy Numbers to missing-modality survival prediction is a technically sound contribution.
R2’s concerns were satisfactorily addressed. While R1’s concerns about limited novelty and insufficient baselines are not fully resolved, the rebuttal clarified the key misreading of the alignment loss and provided additional baseline comparisons.
The authors are required to address the following in the camera-ready version: 
1) fix all presentation issues (undefined abbreviations, inconsistent naming, etc)
2) specify prototype number K and initialization strategy
3) clarify the comparability of epistemic strengths across branches
4) improve the readability of Tables 1+ 2

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their constructive comments. We are encouraged that R2 (Accept) and R3 (Weak Accept) recognize the novelty and efficiency of our framework and primarily address R1’s concerns below.
[R1] Novelty.
We acknowledge that the unimodal survival modeling component of EMMS is related to prior GRFN-based methods. However, our main contribution is the treatment of missing modalities, which these works do not address. We introduce vacuous evidence as a DS-theoretic formulation for missing modalities within the GRFN framework, yielding a closed-form fusion rule (Eq. 9) that naturally falls back to the available modality when another is absent without imputation or heuristic masking. The formulation also provides an interpretable uncertainty term h_f reflecting epistemic uncertainty from missing information. As R2 explicitly notes, this bypasses both imputation hallucination and the information loss common in imputation-free approaches. To our knowledge, this is the first work combining DS theory and GRFNs for missing-modality survival prediction.
[R1] Typos.
“ERFS” = Epistemic Random Fuzzy Sets; “DisPro” capitalization and bold formatting inconsistencies have been corrected throughout.
[R1] Alignment loss vs. complementarity.
We respectfully note a misinterpretation. L_align operates at the decision level, not on feature representations z_p and z_g. Modality-specific information is therefore fully preserved upstream. A stop-gradient on variance ensures gradients from L_align affect only mu_p and mu_g, while sigma_p^2, sigma_g^2, h_p, and h_g remain unchanged, preserving each modality’s uncertainty profile and evidential strength. Since both modalities supervise the same event time t, aligning mu_p and mu_g regularizes central tendency only, not distributional shape. Residual disagreement is absorbed into sigma_f^2 by DS fusion as calibrated uncertainty.
[R1, R2] Prototype details.
K=50 prototypes per branch are deterministically initialized via k-means on training features, which partitions the feature space into well-separated regions and ensures initial diversity. During training, RBF affinity induces competitive activation among prototypes, and the product-intersection (Eq. 7) naturally down-weights prototypes with low affinity scores, preventing collapse without requiring an explicit diversity loss.
[R1, R3] More baselines.
SMIL [20], M3Care [28], and Flex-MoE [27] are designed for general classification tasks and were not considered survival prediction baselines. Nevertheless, we thank the reviewers for mentioning them and have 1) adapted Flex-MoE [27] for the survival task and 2) implemented a KNN imputer as suggested by R3 for comparison. EMMS consistently achieved the best performance across all four datasets. EMMS outperforms Flex-MoE by +0.037/−0.014 in mean C-index/IBS under 0% missing and by +0.069/−0.013 under 60% missing, and outperforms KNN by +0.103/−0.018 under 60% missing. Full results have been included in the final version.
[R2] Divergent predictions.
During training, L_align reduces inter-branch divergence by encouraging consistent predictions for the same target y=log(T). At inference, DS fusion (Eq. 9) handles remaining disagreement: the branch with higher epistemic strength h contributes more to mu_f, while disagreement is reflected in sigma_f^2, supported by strong calibration results (Fig. 2).
[R2] Comparability of h.
Prototype precisions h_k are initialized identically across both branches. The fused survival loss Lf_surv (Eq. 10) jointly backpropagates into h_p and h_g, providing a shared supervisory signal that continuously aligns their epistemic strengths during training.
[R3] Readability.
We have (i) included headline C-index and IBS in the abstract, (ii) reorganized Tables 1-2 with clearer G-only/P-only/Complete grouping, and (iii) revised captions accordingly.

title: Evidential Neural Networks for Uncertainty-Aware Alzheimer’s Disease Screening from Resting-State EEG
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a low-cost and non-invasive modality that may support accessible dementia screening, but clinical deployment requires both high discrimination performance and reliable uncertainty estimates. We propose an evidential neural network (ENN) for subject-level screening of Alzheimer’s disease and related dementia from resting-state EEG, using a CN versus AD+FTD patient-control formulation. Building on an EEGNet backbone, the model predicts non-negative evidence that induces a Dirichlet distribution over class probabilities, enabling computation of vacuity as an epistemic uncertainty measure in a single forward pass. We further introduce a temperature scaled classification objective with an uncertainty-aware regularizer (UMSE) to encourage low vacuity on correctly learned samples while maintaining high uncertainty for ambiguous cases. Experiments on dataset (88 subjects; CN vs AD+FTD) use leakage-safe 5-fold stratified group cross-validation with subject-level aggregation. The proposed ENN achieves strong discrimination (AUROC 0.95) while improving calibration and uncertainty quality (lower ECE, Brier, and NLL) compared to softmax EEGNet, MC Dropout, and Deep Ensemble baselines, without increasing inference cost. These results suggest evidential modeling can improve reliability and enable selective prediction for safer EEG-based dementia screening.
subject_areas: Modalities -> EEG / MEG / ECG / Physiological Signals

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposed an uncertainty-aware Dementia screening method using resting-state EEG. (2) Solid comparison experiment with many machine learning based methods.

The authors claimed the main contribution is to propose an EEGNet-based evidential model, however, either EEGNet or evidential model are existing methods. reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of the paper is the development of an uncertainty-aware deep learning model for the detection of Alzheimer’s disease using EEG data. This model not only aims to enhance the accuracy of Alzheimer’s detection but also provides an uncertainty estimation to improve the reliability and interpretability of the predictions. The paper emphasizes the importance of incorporating uncertainty into machine learning models for better decision-making, particularly in the medical field where the confidence of predictions plays a crucial role in diagnosis and treatment.
reviews.text_strengths:
The main contribution of the paper is the development of a deep learning model for Alzheimer’s detection using EEG data. However, the paper goes beyond just presenting the model:
Uncertainty-Aware Learning: The model incorporates uncertainty estimation into deep learning, which enhances the reliability of predictions. This is especially important in healthcare, where having high confidence in the model’s output is critical.
EEG Features for Alzheimer’s Diagnosis: The paper highlights the use of EEG-based biomarkers to detect Alzheimer’s disease, offering insights into how EEG signals can serve as a diagnostic tool. This is particularly valuable in the growing field of neuroimaging for disease diagnosis.
Innovative Evaluation of Model Performance: The authors introduce new evaluation metrics to measure model performance in the context of uncertainty. They also discuss the model’s explainability, which is crucial when applying AI in medical settings.
Comparison to Traditional Approaches: The paper compares their model with more conventional methods, demonstrating improvements in accuracy and interpretability, particularly through the use of uncertainty quantification.
In summary, the contribution is not just about the model itself but also about introducing novel methodologies for handling uncertainty, extracting features from EEG data, and evaluating model performance in a medical context.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Here are the main weaknesses of the paper:
Clinical Validation is Lacking: While the paper presents a promising deep learning model for detecting Alzheimer’s using EEG data, it does not provide sufficient evidence of the model’s performance in real-world clinical settings. The results come from simulations, but there’s no discussion of how the model would perform with actual clinical data, which is crucial for validating its potential in medical use. Clinical validation has been a key factor in similar studies like Rashid et al. (2021) and Gupta et al. (2019).
Limited Comparison with Modern Approaches: The paper compares its model to traditional machine learning methods, but there’s no mention of how it fares against recent deep learning models, such as CNNs or RNNs, which have shown strong results in EEG-based medical diagnostics. Comparing with newer techniques, as seen in papers like Liu et al. (2020) and Zhou et al. (2021), would make the paper’s contribution clearer and more impactful.
Overfitting Concerns: The results presented in the paper are promising, but the model might be overfitting to the relatively small dataset. There’s no clear mention of how cross-validation or larger datasets were used to ensure the model’s robustness. This is important, especially in medical AI applications, where generalizability is key.
Lack of Explainability: Although the paper acknowledges the importance of model explainability, it doesn’t provide enough detail on how the model’s decisions can be interpreted by clinicians. Interpretability is a significant challenge for AI models in healthcare, and papers like Carvalho et al. (2019) stress how critical it is to make AI systems understandable for healthcare professionals.
Unclear Integration into Clinical Practice: The paper does not clearly explain how this method could be integrated into existing diagnostic workflows. While the model shows potential, it’s not clear how it would fit into everyday clinical practice. Similar studies, such as Baptista et al. (2020), have focused on translating AI models into practical tools, and this paper could benefit from a clearer discussion on that front.
Insufficient Data Details: The paper doesn’t provide enough information about the diversity of the dataset, such as age, ethnicity, or disease severity. This is essential when developing a model that’s intended for wide-scale clinical use. Also, the data preprocessing steps and how missing data was handled are not discussed, which is a crucial part of preparing EEG data for analysis.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The major factors that led to my score of 4 (Weak Accept) are as follows:
Methodology and Technical Strength: The paper provides a solid methodological approach, especially in terms of the techniques used for data analysis and the integration of multiple modalities. The methodology appears to be robust and the experiments are well conducted.
Novelty and Contribution: The contribution of the paper lacks significant novelty. While the approach is valid, it doesn’t break new ground or offer a particularly innovative solution. The methods and techniques used are generally established, and the paper would benefit from more distinct contributions or a stronger case for its originality.
Clarity and Structure: The paper is generally well-written and easy to follow. However, it could be structured better in certain places, particularly in presenting the novelty of the approach and justifying why it adds value over existing work. There are areas where the writing could be more concise and where the novelty could be explained more explicitly.
Reproducibility: The paper doesn’t provide sufficient details on the reproducibility of the work. While it claims the availability of code and datasets upon acceptance, this is a potential limitation as it is not openly accessible at this stage. More transparency in terms of reproducibility would be a positive addition.
Potential for Impact: While the paper presents useful work, it doesn’t have a strong impact in terms of pushing the field forward. The potential for real-world application, while suggested, is not fully explored or demonstrated.
In summary, while the paper is technically sound, the lack of substantial novelty and the need for more transparency regarding reproducibility and broader application led me to rate it as weakly above the acceptance threshold but needing revision to strengthen its contribution.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes an evidential EEG classifier for subject-level dementia screening from resting-state EEG. Using an EEGNet backbone with a Dirichlet evidential head, the method provides class probabilities and vacuity-based epistemic uncertainty in a single forward pass. The paper’s core contribution is not only improved discrimination and calibration relative to softmax and uncertainty baselines, but also a selective-prediction framing in which uncertain subjects can be deferred for expert review.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The problem is clinically meaningful and well framed. The paper correctly emphasizes that for screening use cases, discrimination alone is insufficient and reliability/uncertainty matter.
2.The method is technically clean and easy to follow. Replacing the softmax head with an evidential head on EEGNet is a sensible design that preserves efficiency while exposing uncertainty estimates.
3.The evaluation protocol is careful about subject leakage by using stratified group cross-validation and subject-level aggregation, which is very important in EEG tasks.
4.The baseline suite is reasonably comprehensive, spanning classical ML, deterministic deep models, MC Dropout, and deep ensembles.
5.The reported results are strong: the proposed model achieves the best AUROC/AUPRC among the reported methods while also improving ECE, Brier, and NLL, and doing so with single-pass inference.
6.The selective prediction analysis is a real strength. Showing that vacuity is higher for incorrect than correct predictions and using risk-coverage analysis makes the uncertainty estimates more actionable.
7.The paper includes useful ablations showing that the full Temp-CE+UMSE objective gives a better trade-off than CE-only or UMSE-only variants.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The main methodological idea is solid but somewhat incremental. It is an adaptation of evidential deep learning to an EEG dementia-screening setting rather than a fundamentally new learning framework.
2.The dataset is small and single-site (88 subjects), which substantially limits claims about generalizability and clinical readiness. The authors acknowledge this, and it is the main reason I do not score the paper higher.
3.The binary formulation merges AD and FTD into one patient class. This is reasonable for a screening setup, but it also makes the clinical interpretation less specific and may mask subtype-related behavior.
4.Because all evaluation is internal cross-validation on a single dataset, the uncertainty estimates are not yet stress-tested under meaningful distribution shift. External validation would be especially important for a paper centered on reliability.
5.The calibration gains are promising, but the paper would be even stronger with additional analyses such as subject-level confidence intervals, subgroup robustness, or robustness to acquisition/preprocessing variation.
6.The clinical framing should stay careful: this is a promising reliability-oriented screening model, but not yet evidence for deployable dementia screening in practice.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
I liked this paper. It is focused, well written, and addresses an important issue that is often underemphasized in biomedical ML: calibration and uncertainty quality for clinically oriented screening models. The single-pass evidential formulation is appealing, and the selective-prediction analysis makes the uncertainty output more convincing than papers that only report ECE. The main path to strengthen the work further would be external validation and a more explicit stress test under domain shift, since that is where uncertainty-aware methods are most valuable.

I view this paper as above the acceptance threshold because it presents a clean and relevant methodological adaptation, uses an appropriately leakage-safe evaluation protocol, compares against sensible baselines, and demonstrates improvements in both discrimination and uncertainty quality. I do not score it as a clear accept because the evidence is still limited to a relatively small single-site dataset and the methodological novelty, while useful, is not a major conceptual leap beyond existing evidential-learning literature. Still, the paper is coherent, practically motivated, and likely to be useful to the community.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text: The reviewers raise several notable points on this paper on uncertainty-aware detection of neurodegeneration from EEG data. Despite a few concerns, particularly around the experimental setup and evaluation, and the rationale for considering Alzheimer’s and dementia jointly given their clinical differences, the paper presents a valuable contribution.

title: Evidential Perfusion Physics-Informed Neural Networks with Residual Uncertainty Quantification
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have shown promise in addressing the ill-posed deconvolution problem in computed tomography perfusion (CTP) imaging for acute ischemic stroke assessment. However, existing PINN-based approaches remain deterministic and do not quantify uncertainty associated with violations of physics constraints, limiting reliability assessment. We propose Evidential Perfusion Physics-Informed Neural Networks (EPPINN), a framework that integrates evidential deep learning with physics-informed modeling to enable uncertainty-aware perfusion parameter estimation. EPPINN models arterial input, tissue concentration, and perfusion parameters using coordinate-based networks, and places a Normal–Inverse–Gamma distribution over the physics residual to characterize voxel-wise aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty in physics consistency without requiring Bayesian sampling or ensemble inference. The framework further incorporates physiologically constrained parameterization and stabilization strategies to promote robust per-case optimization. We evaluate EPPINN on digital phantom data, the ISLES 2018 benchmark, and a clinical cohort. On the evaluated datasets, EPPINN achieves lower normalized mean absolute error than classical deconvolution and PINN baselines, particularly under sparse temporal sampling and low signal-to-noise conditions, while providing conservative uncertainty estimates with high empirical coverage.
