Overall, I believe the paper’s motivation, method design, and experimental evidence are sufficiently sound, and I am inclined to accept it.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank all reviewers (Rn) for their comments and for recognizing the strengths of our work, including its strong quantitative and qualitative performance across multiple datasets (R1,R2,R3), the original formulation combining flow matching with DMTet (R1,R2,R3), and its excellent generalization capability (R2,R3). The reviewers (Rn) raised a few questions and sought clarifications(Rn.m) , which we address below.
【Unclear presentation (R1.1)】. The missing details were unfortunately omitted due to page limits and narrative compression, but they do not reflect fundamental methodological flaws. The resolution of DMTet is 128^3, and N = 277410 tetrahedral vertices. Each vertex stores a 4D attribute consisting of a 3D displacement vector and one SDF value.
【DMTet Parameterization (R1.2)】.We clarify that the DMTet representation is not predicted by a preprocessing network. Instead, each training mesh is converted into a fixed DMTet parameter space through a deterministic fitting procedure. The fitting minimizes the Chamfer distance between the DMTet-extracted mesh and the target, combined with SDF regularization and Laplacian terms. 
【Projection-Correction (R1.4)】. L_cond measures the SDF consistency exclusively within a narrow band around the defect boundary, preventing the generated implant from drifting away from the observed conditional defect. L_lap is a local Laplacian smoothing term in Eq. (3). We will explicitly define L_cond, L_lap, the complete optimization objective, and add the omitted hyperparameters as $lambda_i=0.1$ for all ODE steps and step size $\eta = 1 \times 10^{-3} $ in Sec. 3.【CAD Integration (R3.2)】. Since FDMMBone outputs an explicit continuous triangular mesh, it circumvents complex post-processing. The result can be directly exported as an STL/OBJ file and imported into standard medical CAD software (e.g., 3D Slicer, 3-matic) for non-manifold checking, Boolean validation, and rapid manufacturing preparation.
【Network Architecture (R1.3)】. We apologize for the misleading schematic in Fig. 1.The refinement network is indeed a U-Net architecture, not an MLP. We will update Fig. 1.【Baseline (R1.4,R2.1,R3.1,R2.2)】.We guarantee that all competing baselines were strictly retrained on our datasets using the identical train/test splits, preprocessing pipeline, and evaluation metrics. Regarding the suggested skull-specific baselines, they were not presented in the submitted manuscript due to the page limit. Since our evaluation covers multiple anatomical structures, in the previous version, we prioritized generally applicable 3D completion methods. We highly respect the suggested strong skull-specific baselines ([A] Wodzinski 25, [B] Wodzinski 24). In our preliminary comparison, [A] achieved DSC/bDSC/HD95/MMD of 0.916/0.924/1.80/0.201 on MedShapeNet, 0.919/0.922/1.77/0.207 on Mandibular, and 0.923/0.927/1.72/0.191 on SkullBreak. [B] achieved 0.922/0.920/1.74/0.193 on MedShapeNet, 0.918/0.924/1.79/0.210 on Mandibular, and 0.926/0.931/1.68/0.169 on SkullBreak. We will cite and compare these two methods in the revised (R1.4). Our model was trained for 33 hours on two NVIDIA A800 GPUs. During inference, generating a single implant takes approximately 2.9 seconds in total (R2.1). Among this runtime, the 200-step ODE solver takes the majority of the computation (approx. 2.1s), while the projection-correction and the subdivision-based refinement stage add a very lightweight overhead (approx. 0.8s combined) (R3.1). There is the ablation typo. Removing the conditional injection (A6) leads to the most significant performance drop (Table 2) (R2.2). 
We will incorporate the above clarifications and fix minor errors in the final version. We will add the missing citation (Lipman, 22), clarify assigning fixed $±1$ SDF values to avoid numerical artifacts. The ablations and robustness to noisy input will be discussed in the final version. We will provide a GitHub repository containing all our code.

title: FDRAS: Failure Diagnosis and Repair for Airway Segmentation
abstract:
Airway segmentation from chest CT is essential for safe navigation of the bronchoscopy and the targeting of distal lesions. However, segmentation models frequently exhibit structural failures under domain shift, including disconnected distal branches and boundary leakage. Existing post-hoc refinement methods either apply heuristic topology operations or directly predict corrected masks, implicitly coupling error localization and correction, and limiting controllability. 
We propose FDRAS (Failure Diagnosis and Repair for Airway Segmentation), a two-stage reliability framework that explicitly decouples failure localization from conservative correction.
Given a CT volume and an initial segmentation, FDRAS performs hypothesis verification by predicting two complementary error maps: (1) a Signed Distance Function (SDF)-based geometric error map capturing boundary discrepancies, and (2) a tree-level connectivity error map localizing disconnected branches via skeleton analysis. These error maps condition a mask-only refinement network through cross-attention, enabling targeted updates while preventing topology drift.
By externalizing structural inconsistencies and anchoring correction to predicted failure fields, FDRAS enables topology-aware repair rather than direct mask transformation. Under strict zero-shot evaluation across two external datasets and multiple backbones, FDRAS improves branch-level detection and connectivity by up to +4.8 percentage points (pp) compared to the strongest competing refinement, while maintaining competitive voxel-level accuracy, demonstrating its effectiveness as a post-hoc structural reliability layer for deployment.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: FDRAS is a backbone-agnostic post-hoc framework for airway segmentation refinement under domain shift. Given an initial segmentation mask and a CT volume, a diagnosis network predicts two structural error maps: an SDF-based boundary discrepancy field and a skeleton-derived tree connectivity map localizing disconnected branches. A refinement network then applies residual correction to the mask using cross-attention conditioned on these maps. The framework is trained on ATM dataset (240 cases, nnUNet-generated initial segmentations) and evaluated zero-shot on AirRC (254 cases) and AeroPath (27 cases) datasets with two backbone configurations (nnUNet and TfeNet). A single ex-vivo lung specimen provides qualitative validation under an in-vivo-to-ex-vivo distribution shift.
reviews.text_strengths:
The explicit decoupling of failure localization from correction is the central methodological distinction from prior work. Existing methods either stop at error detection without correction (quality-control methods) or perform correction without prior explicit localization (PTR, UTR, ATRNet). FDRAS places supervised error prediction as a distinct, interpretable stage, giving the refinement network conditioned access to spatially localized failure information rather than operating from global features alone.
The complementary error representation covers the two main failure modes in airway segmentation under domain shift. The SDF error map is dense and continuous, capturing geometric boundary discrepancies throughout the volume. The tree error map is sparse and binary, localizing branch-level connectivity failures. Together they form a structured representation of structural failure that neither metric alone would capture.
The evaluation setup is appropriately strict. Training is on ATM; evaluation is zero-shot on two external datasets with different population characteristics (AirRC: pulmonary nodules; AeroPath: airway pathologies). Testing across two backbones with different architectures and performance levels tests the backbone-agnostic claim under realistic conditions.
The ablation in Table 2 isolates both critical design choices (cross-attention conditioning and error-map conditioning). Removing cross-attention produces the largest structural degradation (TD drop >7 pp on both datasets); removing error conditioning produces a large DSC drop on AirRC (–7.7 pp). Both components are shown to be necessary.
The ex-vivo validation tests a severe distribution shift. The backbone is a 3D U-Net trained on separate private ex-vivo data. The acquisition context shifts from in-vivo CT to ex-vivo CT. FDRAS receives no additional training, yet the predicted SDF error map highlights geometric inconsistencies at distal branches, and the refinement restores branch continuity toward the nodule region. As a single case it is only qualitative evidence, but under conditions where failure would be easy to justify.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
With TfeNet on AeroPath, FDRAS reduces DSC by 3.5 pp (87.2 vs 83.7) and precision by 6.6 pp (85.4 vs 78.8). The paper attributes the precision drop to distal branch recovery, not spurious over-segmentation. But a simultaneous DSC drop contradicts this: if the added segments were anatomically correct branches, DSC would be stable or improve. TfeNet already achieves 90.5% TD and 87.4% BD on AeroPath before refinement, suggesting the backbone performs well on this pathological set. FDRAS may be diagnosing structural failures that are not present and introducing incorrect corrections. No per-case analysis or stratification is provided to explain this behavior.
The training configuration for the TfeNet experiments is not stated. The methods section describes FDRAS as trained on nnUNet-generated initial segmentations. If FDRAS was retrained with TfeNet as the source backbone, this must be stated, as it would mean backbone-agnostic operation requires retraining per backbone, a different claim than backbone-agnostic inference.
The diagnosis network is the paper’s most novel component, yet no evaluation of error map prediction quality is provided. The SDF and tree error maps during training are derived from GT. The diagnosis network must learn to predict these from (M, I) at inference without GT. No comparison between predicted and GT-derived error maps is shown. The ablation demonstrates that removing error conditioning hurts performance (Table 2, w/o EM), but this does not confirm the predicted maps accurately localize failures. The corrective benefit may arise from the conditioning mechanism or from generic spatial features of (M, I) rather than from precise error localization.
No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for either dataset. This could be particularly useful in the case of AeroPath, which contains only 27 cases.
The ablation evaluates error-map conditioning as a whole (w/o EM) but does not separate SDF-only from tree-only configurations. The two maps capture distinct failure modes. Knowing their individual contributions would validate the two-map design and guide future work.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The decoupled two-stage design is a methodological contribution and the zero-shot evaluation is rigorous. The ex-vivo case is a strong evidence of generalization. The primary uncertainty is the TfeNet-AeroPath regression and the unresolved training configuration for TfeNet experiments, which limit confidence in the backbone-agnostic claim. Rebuttal should address: (a) case-level analysis of the TfeNet-AeroPath regression; (b) an explicit statement of whether FDRAS was retrained for TfeNet. Secondary concerns should be addressed in revision.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
My initial review raised five concerns: the TfeNet-AeroPath DSC and precision regression, the unstated TfeNet training configuration, the missing standalone diagnosis-stage evaluation, the absence of confidence intervals on the small AeroPath cohort (n=27), and the missing SDF-only versus tree-only ablation. The rebuttal addresses the main ones. The TfeNet training configuration is now explicit (single FDRAS checkpoint trained on ATM with frozen nnUNet predictions, no TfeNet retraining), the TfeNet-AeroPath regression is given a per-case re-aggregation consistent with distal-branch recovery (TD up in 25/27 cases, BD in 19/27), and FDRAS is honestly reframed as a bounded topology-aware reliability layer rather than a re-segmenter.
The meta-reviewer’s three asks (TfeNet-AeroPath trade-off, diagnosis-stage depth, nnUNet-vs-TfeNet gap) are addressed in the same passes. The standalone diagnosis evaluation and the SDF-only versus tree-only ablation are deferred to the supplement, but the rebuttal’s core answers hold.
I recommend accepting it.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents FDRAS, a two-stage post-hoc framework for airway segmentation refinement under domain shift. Rather than directly predicting a corrected mask, the method separates failure diagnosis from repair. Given a CT volume and an initial airway segmentation, the diagnosis stage predicts two complementary error maps – an SDF-based geometric discrepancy map and a tree-level connectivity error map derived from skeleton analysis. These predicted failure maps then condition a refinement network through cross-attention, with the aim of making conservative, localised corrections while preserving already-correct regions. The model is trained on ATM and evaluated in a strict zero-shot setting on AirRC and AeroPath, using both nnUNet and TfeNet backbones. The paper reports improvements in structural metrics, including tree detection and branch detection, over prior post-processing baselines, alongside additional qualitative ex-vivo validation.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper addresses a clinically relevant and practically important problem. In airway segmentation, structural continuity and distal branch completeness are often more important than voxel-wise overlap alone, particularly for applications such as bronchoscopy navigation and lesion targeting. Framing the problem as post-hoc refinement under domain shift is therefore well motivated.
The central idea of decoupling error localisation from correction is appealing and reasonably original in this setting. The manuscript makes a convincing case that existing approaches tend either to diagnose failures without repairing them, or to repair masks without explicitly modelling the underlying errors. Introducing an intermediate error-representation layer is a sensible and useful contribution.
The structural error representation is also well designed. Combining a dense SDF discrepancy field with a sparse tree-connectivity map aligns well with the failure modes described in the introduction, namely both boundary errors and disconnected distal branches. This is a stronger formulation than relying on connectivity cues alone.
Training on ATM and testing zero-shot on two external datasets is appropriate for the paper’s domain-shift claims, and the use of two different backbones supports the claim that the framework is not tied to a single upstream segmenter. The reported gains on structural metrics appear meaningful, and the ablation results support the contribution of both explicit error conditioning and cross-attention. Overall, the paper is clearly written and easy to follow.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The main weakness is that the empirical validation remains somewhat narrow relative to the broader framing around deployment reliability. Although the zero-shot evaluation is valuable, the experiments are confined to airway segmentation alone. As a result, the paper is convincing as a task-specific airway refinement study, but somewhat less so as a more general reliability-layer contribution.
A further limitation is that the diagnosis stage, which is conceptually central to the method, is not evaluated in sufficient depth on its own. The paper supervises training using ground-truth discrepancy maps, including the skeleton-derived tree error map, but provides limited analysis of how accurately these maps are predicted at inference or how diagnosis quality relates to final repair quality. Stronger standalone evaluation of this stage would materially strengthen the paper.
Some of the performance trade-offs also warrant more cautious discussion. In Table 1, precision drops noticeably in some settings, particularly with TfeNet on AeroPath. The authors suggest this reflects recovery of distal branches rather than implausible over-segmentation, which is plausible, but the support provided is largely qualitative. A clearer discussion of when such added branches are beneficial versus potentially false positive would improve the paper.
Finally, the ex-vivo validation is interesting but remains qualitative, which limits the strength of any conclusions drawn from it. The paper would also benefit from more explicit analysis of failure cases and limits, particularly since the conclusion notes that severely collapsed segmentations cannot be fully recovered. For a post-hoc repair framework, understanding where the method stops helping is central to its practical value.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The paper would be strengthened by explicit evaluation of the diagnosis stage itself, for example by quantifying how well the predicted SDF and tree-error maps match their supervised targets, and whether improved diagnosis translates into improved repair.
More detail on the retraining protocol for PTR, UTR, and ATRNet would also be helpful, given the importance of these comparisons. The precision drop observed in some settings deserves fuller discussion, ideally with examples distinguishing acceptable branch recovery from clear false positives.
The ex-vivo section is promising, but should be framed more explicitly as qualitative external validation to avoid overstatement. Since the paper emphasises conservative correction, it would also be valuable to quantify how much of the mask is altered during refinement, or how consistently the method preserves already-correct regions.

This is a solid and clinically relevant paper with a clear motivation, a sensible and reasonably novel method, and convincing zero-shot improvements on structural airway metrics across two external datasets and two backbones. The main contribution is not merely incremental performance improvement, but a useful reformulation of segmentation repair as diagnosis-conditioned correction. The weaknesses relate primarily to depth of analysis rather than to a fundamental flaw: the diagnosis stage is not evaluated as thoroughly as it could be, the ex-vivo evidence is qualitative, and some precision trade-offs deserve more careful discussion. Overall, however, the paper makes a meaningful contribution to airway segmentation reliability and is likely to be of interest to the MICCAI community.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
After reading the authors’ rebuttal, I remain supportive of acceptance. The response does not fully resolve every concern raised in my original review, but it addresses the main points in a thoughtful and credible manner and improves confidence in both the framing and the empirical interpretation of the work. In particular, the additional clarification regarding the TfeNet-AeroPath setting is helpful, as the reported per-case branch-level improvements suggest that the method is consistently recovering structural completeness rather than producing only unstable average gains.
Overall, the rebuttal strengthens the paper sufficiently for me to retain an accept recommendation, while still recognising that some of the claims should be framed carefully in the final version.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: Incomplete airway segmentations render them not very useful in clinical applications. This work contributes an airway segmentation refinement method that uses two steps to identify and fix these problematic segmentations. The work presents a failure diagnosis and repair (FDRAS) framework that shows competitive performance on zero-shot applications, and outperforms other refinement methods on two datasets when starting with initial segmentations from two backbone networks.
reviews.text_strengths:
Improving reliability of airway segmentation using a diagnostic method that also repairs errors in distal branches/discontinuities, instead of
another
segmentation framework is a useful contribution in this work. Many airway segmentation methods need refinement steps to obtain fully useful airway networks.
Decoupling the errors into boundary discrepancies (measured using signed distance function (SDF)) and branch connectivity using skeleton analysis, is an interesting way to improve the reliability of airway segmentation quality.
Strong zero shot performance is reported in Table 1, and thorough evaluations (including ablations) are reported.
Additional validation on ex-vivo human lung specimen is a valuable contribution that is seldom seen in airway segmentation works. I hope the authors will make this specimen data available along with the code.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Method is not described in detail. For example, the authors say “feature embeddings extracted by lightweight 3D convolutional blocks” or “employ a spatially reduced cross-attention operator”. The specific choice for these modules is not defined anywhere. So, would any “lightweight 3D convolution” block work? And the specific value for the reduction factor s is not mentioned.
The initial segmentations analysed are shown using two backbone networks (nnUnet and TFeNet). Why are the refinement approaches, including FDRAS unable to improve nnUnet to the level of TFeNet? Is this because there are large gaps in performance already with the backbones (about 12 pp DSC)? This points to the limitations of refinement approaches as they are heavily dependent on the initial segmentation. What is the prescribed approach then to obtain useful segmentations?
The qualitative comparison shown in Fig 2 is not actually showing a problem with distal airways. The zoom inset is for the main bronchi, and I am quite surprised that already the input segmentation has the “hole” which is not rectified by other methods. Why is this so challenging? Perhaps focusing on loss of connectivity in smaller airways might make this qualitative example more compelling.
Justification for chosen hyperparameters (five lambda terms). How were these parameters chosen? And how sensitive is the performance of the method to these choices? Also, curious to see many of these parameters are simply set to 1? Is it fixed across different datasets?
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I have a few concerns about the choice of hyperparameters, model design, and usefulness of refinement approaches. These can be clarified in the rebuttal.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: My concerns raised about the improvement on initial segmentation were partially addressed; the authors also commit to including more method details in the revised version.

meta_reviews.text:
Although three reviewers give weak accept score, they raise several major concerns, which need to be further evaluated in the rebuttal. These major concerns include:
1) Potential ineffective of FDRAS module: “With TfeNet on AeroPath, FDRAS reduces DSC by 3.5 pp (87.2 vs 83.7) and precision by 6.6 pp (85.4 vs 78.8). The paper attributes the precision drop to distal branch recovery, not spurious over-segmentation. But a simultaneous DSC drop contradicts this: if the added segments were anatomically correct branches, DSC would be stable or improve. TfeNet already achieves 90.5% TD and 87.4% BD on AeroPath before refinement, suggesting the backbone performs well on this pathological set. FDRAS may be diagnosing structural failures that are not present and introducing incorrect corrections.”
2) The diagnosis stage, which is central to the method, is not evaluated in sufficient depth. “The paper provides limited analysis of how accurately these (discrepancy/error) maps are predicted at inference or how diagnosis quality relates to final repair quality.”
3) Limited performance improvement of the refinement method: “The initial segmentations are shown using two backbone networks (nnUnet and TFeNet). Why are the refinement approaches, including FDRAS unable to improve nnUnet to the level of TFeNet? Is this because there are large gaps in performance already with the backbones (about 12 pp DSC)? This points to the limitations of refinement approaches as they are heavily dependent on the initial segmentation.”
Hence, rebuttal is required for this paper.

After the rebuttal, all reviewers keep their initial positive score, although one reviewer’s concern is partially addressed (regarding the improvement on initial segmentation). Recommend acceptance of this work.

All three reviewers recommend acceptance after rebuttal. Reviewers generally agreed that the diagnosis-conditioned repair framework is well motivated, clinically relevant, and demonstrates consistent improvements in structural airway metrics under domain shift.
The rebuttal successfully clarified the TfeNet-AeroPath trade-off, the backbone-agnostic evaluation protocol, and the intended role of FDRAS as a topology-aware reliability layer rather than a full re-segmentation method. While a more detailed standalone evaluation of the diagnosis stage would further strengthen the work, the main concerns have been adequately addressed. The presentation could also be improved, including figures, tables, and some implementation details. I recommend acceptance.

The rebuttal addressed the most decision-critical issues. It clarified that a single FDRAS checkpoint trained on ATM with frozen nnUNet predictions was used for both nnUNet and TFeNet evaluations, with no TFeNet-specific retraining. Overall, the reviews and rebuttal support acceptance. The paper makes a meaningful contribution to airway segmentation reliability and is likely to be of interest to the MICCAI community.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the AC and reviewers for their feedback and address the main concerns: TfeNet-AeroPath trade-off, diagnosis, backbone, and protocol clarity.
1.TfeNet-AeroPath Regression and Precision Drop (AC, R1 & R2)
We agree that the TfeNet-AeroPath results require careful interpretation. Reorganizing the existing case-level outputs (without new experiments, per MICCAI rules) shows that FDRAS consistently improves branch-level metrics: TD rises in 25/27 cases and BD in 19/27, while Dice improves in roughly half of the cases. Voxel-wise DSC and precision may decrease slightly relative to the ground truth, as FDRAS occasionally alters voxels outside annotated branches. While this enhances distal connectivity, these modifications are not explicitly validated and are noted as a limitation and a potential direction for future research. Branch-level gains indicate that FDRAS effectively restores distal structures without introducing grossly implausible anatomy. If permitted, we will include this per-case summary with relevant statistical reporting in the supplement.
2.Diagnosis-Stage Evaluation (AC, R1 & R2)
In the submitted manuscript, diagnosis is evaluated through its functional role in repair: it is supervised with GT-derived SDF and skeleton/tree error targets, and removing error-map conditioning reduces DSC by 7.7 pp on AirRC and 6.5 pp on AeroPath. This supports the usefulness of predicted error maps for repair, but we agree it is not a complete standalone diagnosis benchmark. If permitted, we will add map-level diagnosis assessment from the existing predictions and GT-derived targets in the supplement, along with SDF-only/tree-only ablations.
3.Dependence on Initial Segmentation Quality (AC & R3)
The gap between nnUNet and TFeNet arises from initial segmentation quality: FDRAS improves structural completeness but cannot create branches entirely missing in the initial mask. Nevertheless, applying FDRAS to nnUNet narrows the gap with TFeNet: DSC on AirRC differences decreases from 12.6 pp to 4.1 pp, while TD/BD differences also decrease, indicating meaningful structural recovery. On AeroPath, similar trends are observed. By targeting errors without full re-segmentation, FDRAS can improve the structural completeness of the backbones evaluated. We will clarify this in the Conclusion and present FDRAS as a bounded, topology-aware reliability layer for targeted correction, designed to enhance existing segmentations rather than replace them.
4.Backbone Protocol and Implementation Clarity (R1 & R3)
R1 asked about backbone handling: the same FDRAS checkpoint trained on ATM with frozen nnUNet predictions was used for all nnUNet and TFeNet evaluations; no TFeNet-specific retraining was performed.
R3 asked for architectural details: lightweight 3D blocks use two 3×3×3 convolutions with instance normalization and ReLU, with up-sampling via ConvTranspose3d and skip connections. Cross-attention uses spatial reduction s=4 with residual addition. Loss weights were set to default values to avoid scenario-specific tuning. These details clarify model design and hyperparameters. Code and weights will be released upon acceptance; architectural details will be added to Methods, and sensitivity analysis noted as future work.
5.Ex-Vivo Validation and Qualitative Claims (R1, R2 & R3)
R3 asked why standard methods fail and whether Fig. 2 shows distal airway failure. We will revise the figure/caption to highlight a clearer distal case. The zoom inset shows a “hole” in the main bronchi not corrected by other methods, which assume common in-vivo shapes and do not model structural errors, limiting recovery of ex-vivo cases. We agree the validation is qualitative: FDRAS can operate on extreme cases, while main evidence remains zero-shot evaluation on AirRC and AeroPath.
We thank the AC and reviewers again and will revise the manuscript accordingly.

title: Feature Space Guidance for Breast Cancer Classification in DCE-MRI
abstract: Dynamic contrast enhanced breast MRI (DCE-MRI) is a powerful clinical tool for breast cancer detection, providing high resolution anatomical detail together with rich temporal contrast information. However, high dimensional 4D inputs, small lesions, and heterogeneous acquisition protocols across clinical sites hinder robust automated classification of healthy, benign, and malignant cases. To address these challenges, we propose a framework that dynamically analyzes latent representations to adapt to protocol-specific characteristics. Spatial variability is mitigated by reducing confounding background uptake and compensating for misalignment caused by deformable soft tissue. Additionally, relationships in the latent space across phases are leveraged to select the most informative temporal features, improving robustness to protocol-specific temporal variability. Finally, task specific discriminative features are promoted through large scale supervised lesion segmentation pretraining, which substantially enhances downstream finetuning. Evaluated under leave-one-center-out validation on the ODELIA dataset and the held-out AMBL cohort, the proposed framework substantially outperforms finetuned radiology foundation models and prior methods, improving mean AUROC by nearly 8 points and balanced accuracy by 4 points over the strongest baseline. Additionally, our method achieved first place in the MICCAI ODELIA Breast MRI Challenge 2025, further demonstrating its effectiveness for robust breast cancer classification. We publicly release our codebase under https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/CURIAtor.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper tackles the challenge of protocol variability and high-dimensionality in dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI (DCE-MRI) for breast cancer classification. The authors propose a three stage hierarchical framework consisting of a 3D segmentation model for spatial bounding, an adaptive temporal phase selector (CURIAtor) that uses foundation model embeddings to identify the most informative contrast phases, and an anatomically pretrained model fine-tuned for classification. Evaluated using rigorous leave-one-center-out cross-validation on the ODELIA dataset and a held-out AMBL cohort, the method significantly outperforms fixed phase selection, static maximum intensity projection (MIP) approaches, and direct finetuning of standard foundation models.
reviews.text_strengths:
The CURIAtor module introduces a solution to temporal sampling variability by dynamically selecting the most informative post-contrast phase based on feature-space dissimilarity, it bypasses the limitations and biases of static phase selection rules.
The validation pipeline is strong through utilizing leave-one-center-out cross-validation across five distinct clinical centers, alongside an entirely unseen multi-site dataset (AMBL), and provides a highly realistic assessment of out-of-distribution generalizability.
By specifically addressing the heterogeneity of acquisition protocols (varying temporal resolution, number of phases, and contrast timing) across different clinical sites, the method targets a major barrier to the deployment of automated DCE-MRI screening tools.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
While the reported performance gains are substantial (e. g. , an 8 AUROC point improvement over MIP baselines), the paper currently lacks statistical significance testing for the results presented in Table 1.Could the authors incorporate more statistical tests to validate the robustness of these multi-center improvements?
The ablation study in Table 2 effectively demonstrates the value of the adaptive CURIAtor module compared to fixed temporal combinations (e. g. , Pre + Post1 + Post2). However, how does this 3-phase selection approach compare against standard sequence modeling baselines (such as recurrent networks, 3D+t convolutions, or temporal transformers) designed to natively process the entirety of the 4D sequence?
While the paper excellently evaluates center-level protocol shifts, there is no breakdown of model performance across different tumor characteristics. Can the authors discuss whether the proposed adaptive temporal sampling maintains consistent sensitivity across varying lesion sizes, morphological types (e. g. , mass vs. non-mass enhancement), or molecular subtypes?
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper presents an effective, clinically motivated, and well-engineered solution to handling 4D protocol variability in DCE-MRI. Its primary strength is the novel adaptive phase selection mechanism (CURIAtor), which, when combined with rigorous multi-center evaluation, clearly establishes state-of-the-art performance. Although the inclusion of statistical significance tests and a broader comparison against native 4D sequence models would strengthen the technical validation, the current results already demonstrate a clear and substantial improvement over standard clinical AI approaches, making this a strong contribution to the field.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a DCE-MRI based framework for breast cancer classification, aiming to distinguish healthy, benign, and malignant cases. The method consists of three major stages. First, a breast segmentation model is used to localize the breast region, which reduces computational burden and helps suppress irrelevant background noise outside the anatomically relevant area. Second, the method uses latent features extracted from a radiology foundation model to adaptively select the most informative post-contrast phase based on feature dissimilarity. Third, the model is pretrained on a tumor segmentation task so that the encoder can learn lesion-relevant features before being finetuned for the downstream classification task. Overall, the proposed multi-staged design is reasonable and well-motivated, and the reported results suggest that it outperforms other methods in cross center evaluation.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.One major strength of this work is its clinical relevance. Robust classification on multi-center breast DCE MRI is an important and challenging task, and this study directly addresses highly practical issues, especially protocol heterogeneity across centers and the sparsity of small lesions relative to the full image volume.
2.The paper is generally clearly written and well organized. The proposed framework is conceptually coherent, with a clear internal structure: it first reduces irrelevant background through anatomically informed ROI extraction, then addresses temporal heterogeneity through adaptive phase selection, and finally improves downstream classification through large-scale lesion-aware pretraining. This multi-stage design is well motivated and easy to follow.
3.The reported experimental results are promising and support the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The model shows performance advantages over several compared baselines. In addition, the paper states that the method achieved first place in the corresponding MICCAI challenge, which further suggests the competitiveness and potential practical value of the approach.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The dataset description is insufficient. The manuscript does not clearly describe the class distribution of the three categories, and in particular, it lacks detailed statistics on scanner vendors, acquisition protocols, and center-specific differences. For a paper whose main objective is cross-center generalization, these details are essential. Requiring readers to search for this information elsewhere is not helpful and weakens the clarity and completeness of the study.
2.The core rationale behind the adaptive temporal selection module has not been fully validated. The method selects the post-contrast phase that is most dissimilar to the first post-contrast phase in latent feature space. Still, the paper does not sufficiently demonstrate that this phase is truly the most clinically informative. Although Figure 2 provides three examples, it would be much more intuitive if these examples were directly matched with the actual MR images from the corresponding time points. I assume a large distance in feature space may reflect meaningful delayed washout information, but it could also arise from noise, motion artifacts, registration error, or scanner induced domain shift. In particular, Figure 2 raises a question: for the three illustrated cases, why is the final time point not the most dissimilar one? In DCE MRI, contrast enhancement typically evolves over time, so one might expect the difference to increase gradually. Additional explanation and more intuitive visualization with real DCE MRI images would strengthen the argument.
3.The implementation details of the foundation model baselines remain unclear. The paper compares against Merlin, VISTA3D, CT FM, and Curia as finetuned FM baselines, but it is not clear how these models were finetuned, whether any layers were frozen, and whether they used the same input setting as the proposed method. In addition, several of these models were originally developed for CT rather than breast MRI. Furthermore, Table 2 appears questionable. It reports mean values across datasets, but the reported mean AUROC of 74.89 is identical to the AMBL AUROC in Table 1, rather than the overall mean, maybe an error/typo? Please check this carefully. It would also be more informative if Table 2, like Table 1, reported center-specific results rather than only aggregated values.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Overall, this study addresses a clinically meaningful problem, and the reported results suggest that the proposed framework is effective for cross center breast cancer classification on DCE MRI. 
However, the dataset description is missing and lacks important information needed to assess the validity of the cross center evaluation. Moreover, the core principle of the adaptive temporal selection module would be clearer with stronger justification and a more intuitive explanation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: After reading the rebuttal, I think the authors have sufficiently addressed my main concerns. In particular, the explanation regarding DCE-MRI kinetics is convincing, as enhancement patterns may show wash-in, plateau, or washout, and the final phase is not necessarily the most informative or most dissimilar phase. The authors also provided additional details regarding the foundation-model baselines and acknowledged the issue in Table 2.Moreover, they indicated that they will revise the manuscript to improve the dataset description and extend the figure with corresponding MRI examples. Overall, I consider the rebuttal satisfactory and will maintain my original recommendation of Accept.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The authors propose a focus on breast MRI classification in the scenario of heterogeneous protocols. That is, the authors introduce a method selecting the appropriate sequences maximizing the performances.
The method is evaluated on the recent multi-centric ODELIA dataset.
Some ablation is performed to straighten the advantages of the proposed method.
reviews.text_strengths:
The choice of the adequate MRI sequences is not obvious, especially when the protocols vary. An automated selection of the sequences may be relevant not only in breast, but in other modalities as well.
The paper is generally clear and the ablations illustrate the advantages of the proposed method.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The paper seems to lack the context of the state of the art. Not much is said about the Odelia Challenge and the winners (https://odelia2025.grand-challenge.org/odelia-breast-mri-challenge-2025-winners/). This makes it difficult to position the method. With that, it seems to have limited contribution with regard to the performances increase. For instance, other works (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.27326) allow to achieve higher scores.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
State of the art
I wonder whether the authors could discuss the ODELIA challenge and the most performant methods? And how the proposed situates in this context.
Results 
It appears that the most of the performances is gained by
not using the whole volume
using post_1 sequence 
Could the authors put some light on it?

While being quite well written, and clearly presented, the manuscript lacks state of the art. Relying on the ODELIA challenge involves the comparison to the main challengers so the proposed method is easier to situate.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The answers provided by the authors are structured and comprehensive. That is, the authors provide some reasonable arguments with regard to some questions raised in the review, specifically about comparison to the ODELIA challenge competitors. 
The adaptive selection of temporal points appears clearer now.
I would expect these responses to appear in the final manuscript. 
Yet, I change my opinion to “accept”.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper addresses an important clinical problem in breast DCE-MRI classification under heterogeneous acquisition protocols. Reviewers generally found the proposed framework clear and clinically motivated, especially the adaptive phase selection strategy and the strong multi-center validation design.
The main concerns are related to positioning and evidence rather than fundamental flaws. The paper should better situate itself against the ODELIA challenge winners and other recent state-of-the-art methods. The rationale behind the adaptive temporal selection module also needs clearer validation, including whether feature-space dissimilarity truly identifies clinically informative phases rather than noise or protocol effects. Reviewers also requested more dataset details, clearer baseline implementation details, and statistical testing or subgroup analysis.

The paper addresses an important and clinically relevant problem, and reviewers generally agreed that the framework is well designed and supported by strong multi-center evaluation. The main concerns were related to positioning, statistical reporting, and clarification of the adaptive phase selection strategy rather than fundamental methodological issues. The rebuttal addressed these points clearly and satisfactorily, and the reviewers who initially raised concerns updated or maintained their final recommendation as accept
Congratulations!
The authors delivered structured and comprehensive responses addressing reviewer concerns, particularly regarding comparisons with ODELIA challenge methods and adaptive temporal point selection.

title: FedAgree: Label-Free Performance Estimation Under Distribution Shift for Federated Medical Imaging Analysis
abstract: Federated Learning (FL) has recently emerged as a popular paradigm in healthcare, enabling collaborative model training across hospitals while preserving patient privacy. However, distribution shifts arising from different acquisition devices, patient populations, or clinical protocols can lead to substantial performance degradation when models are deployed at new sites. Out-of-distribution (OOD) performance estimation is thus critical to assess this degradation, but labelled OOD data from target hospitals is scarce or expensive to obtain. Agreement-on-the-Line (AotL) (Baek et al., 2022) addresses this by predicting OOD accuracy without labelled data via agreement between pairs of model checkpoints, though obtaining multiple models for this purpose is computationally expensive. We observe that FL naturally resolves this: diverse client checkpoints are already produced during training at no additional cost. We propose FedAgree, a method to facilitate agreement-based OOD evaluation in federated settings by leveraging both local and cross-client checkpoints. We introduce five checkpoint strategies that progressively expand the use of cross-client information and evaluate them on diverse medical imaging modalities (dermoscopy, retinopathy, histopathology), under both IID and non-IID settings. Our empirical results demonstrate that federated healthcare settings offer an ideal environment for practical, label-free OOD evaluation.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes FedAgree, a method to facilitate agreement-based OOD evaluation in federated settings by leveraging both local and cross-client checkpoints. It introduces five distinct checkpoints strategy (local anchor, anchor peer, history, peer and full) that expand the use of cross-client information evaluating them on different medical imaging modalities under both IID and non-IID settings. The empirical results demonstrate that federated healthcare networks provide an ideal enviroment for practical, label-free OOD evaluation.
reviews.text_strengths:
The core observation is practically valuable: FL training naturally produces diverse model checkpoints at no additional cost, and exploiting them for OOD performance estimation is a well-motivated and non-obvious insight. The connection to AotL is principled and clearly formalized.
The non-IID evaluation on Camelyon17-WILDS is convincing and clinically relevant: each client maps to a different hospital, which directly reflects realistic FL deployment. The improvements over all baselines are substantial (e. g. , FedAgree-Full achieves MAE of 14.80 vs 34.67 for AotL-Local).
The R² coefficient is proposed as a practical reliability check for the linear fit, which is a useful operational tool for practitioners to decide when to trust the OOD estimate.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
In the IID setting with FedAvg, all clients receive the identical global model at the start of each round and train on data drawn from the same distribution. Client checkpoints within the same round therefore differ only due to local mini-batch stochasticity, resulting in nearly identical models across clients. This undermines the core motivation for cross-client checkpoint diversity in Table 2, and the observed gains may not reflect genuine multi-client benefit. The paper does not discuss this confound.
HAM10000 was collected from multiple clinical sites with different acquisition modalities. The paper treats it as an IID dataset with uniform partitioning, ignoring the site metadata. A non-IID split based on acquisition source would have been a clinically motivated setup directly analogous to Camelyon17, and would have produced a more meaningful evaluation. This is a missed opportunity that weakens the medical FL claim.
K=4 clients is too small to support general conclusions. With only 4 clients, checkpoint diversity is limited even in non-IID settings. It is unclear how FedAgree scales in larger federations (K=10, 20, 50) where diversity may increase but variance may also grow. This is not discussed in the paper nor in limitations.
Low R² in non-IID settings is not operationally addressed. The paper reports R² values of 0.30–0.72 on Camelyon17 and notes that estimates should be treated with caution, but provides no guidance on what practitioners should do when R² is low in a real clinical deployment. For a paper claiming clinical utility, this is a significant gap.
Density estimation baselines are excluded without justification. Methods based on density estimation share the same objective as FedAgree (estimating OOD performance without labels) and are cited in the related work. Their exclusion from the comparison is not explained. While they may require access to raw target data — which conflicts with FL privacy constraints — this should be stated explicitly as the reason for exclusion.
Fig. 1 is not self-explanatory. It uses four overlapping symbol types representing different quantities in the same plot. Understanding what each symbol means requires simultaneously reading the caption and Section 3.2.For the only figure in the paper, which should communicate the central intuition, this is a clarity issue.
Privacy implications of checkpoint sharing are not discussed. The paper assumes trusted partners under institutional agreements, but sharing all checkpoints from all rounds exposes the full training trajectory of each client. This is a non-trivial privacy concern in medical FL that deserves at least a brief discussion.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The authors provide a link to an anonymized repository, but most files in the repository are empty. This effectively prevents reproducibility of the reported results. The authors are strongly encouraged to ensure the repository is complete before final submission.

FedAgree addresses a practically relevant problem and the idea of exploiting FL checkpoints for OOD performance estimation is well-motivated. The non-IID results on Camelyon17 are genuinely convincing and demonstrate a clear benefit. However, the IID experiments — which constitute the majority of Table 2 — are methodologically confounded by the use of FedAvg with IID partitioning, where cross-client checkpoints are nearly identical and provide no meaningful diversity. Furthermore, HAM10000’s multi-source structure is ignored in favor of an artificial IID split, missing an obvious and clinically motivated non-IID evaluation opportunity. Combined with the small federation size (K=4), the lack of operational guidance for low-R² scenarios, and the absence of justification for excluding density estimation baselines, the experimental evidence is insufficient to support the generality of the claims.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This article aims to address the challenge of OOD generalization in federated learning frameworks based on agreement-on-the-line. While AotL is typically computationally expensive, the core claim states that federated learning naturally addresses this issue, simplifying the process of OOD generalization via model agreement.
reviews.text_strengths:
The proposed method, FedAgree, is a very simple and natural extension of Agreement-on-the-Line for the FL framework. The intuition that federated learning naturally produces diverse checkpoints across clients at no extra training cost is clear and convincing.
This article includes an exhaustive analysis of the impact of 6 different checkpoint strategies, which strengthens the empirical soundness of the evaluation.
The authors provide anonymized code.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Storing all model checkpoints for each client at each round is inefficient with respect to space. In low-resource environments, it may not be feasible to save so much data for evaluation. Have the authors considered any techniques to mitigate the space requirement? I would appreciate a discussion of the space complexity in the final manuscript.
Figure 1 is not referenced, nor discussed in the article
The experiments lack ablation. While the analysis of various checkpoint strategies can, in a sense, be considered an ablation on its own, the article would be strengthened by further analysis. For example, how does the performance change as the number of clients increases/decreases? How does it change as more training rounds are conducted? Do checkpoints from early rounds (when the models are not yet well trained) carry useful information relative to ones collected from later rounds? I am also curious if aggregation strategies other than FedAvg have a significant impact on the performance. What about varying levels of heterogeneity in data volume/class-balancing across clients? I understand that rebuttal space is limited and the authors may not be able to touch on all of these points, but I would certainly appreciate a bit more insight into some of these topics.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I appreciate the simplicity of the approach, and that the results sufficiently demonstrate the effectiveness of FedAgree across multiple checkpoint strategies. However, I have concerns about the overall space complexity of the approach, particularly in lower resource environments. I also find it the experimental analysis somewhat underwhelming. The lack of ablation of number of clients, training time, etc raise some additional concerns for me. That said, I would be willing to increase my score given a strong rebuttal on these points as I do find the method to be overall interesting and relevant to the MICCAI community.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors adequately address my concerns about space complexity and certain aspects of ablation analysis. I am happy to accept this paper.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The authors evaluate the OOD (‘out of distribution’) of datasets trained at different ‘sites’, a method to evaluate different training distributions. The authors perform this with training data from various datasets, such as CIFAR and HAM1000.
The method is solid for evaluating federated learning distributions between sites. The sites have similar enough distributions that it’s difficult to state how far this could be pushed; however the concept is demonstrated and it makes sense as an evaluation during FL training.
reviews.text_strengths: This was performed on a variety of datasets and demonstrated a clear bias between sites, which was able to be quantitated.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The agreements of the OOD distributions were very similar distributions, which is a good metric. It would be useful to know how far the metrics could have been pushed for OOD datasets.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This is a solid method and the authors demonstrated it clearly. It may not be a game changer in terms of FL methods, but is useful to characterise.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Similar to above, the results are fine, just not very exciting. The authors justified their work, addressing reviewer comments within the limitations provided.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper proposes a label-free method for estimating OOD performance by leveraging model checkpoints from both local and cross-client training. The method builds on Agreement-on-the-Line and introduces five checkpoint selection strategies. The framework is evaluated on multiple datasets under both IID and non-IID settings.
The reviews are mixed. This paper addresses an important and practical problem, the idea is clear and well-motivated, and empirical evaluation is sound. However, there are also several concerns need to be carefully addressed:
1.The IID FedAvg experiments may be confounded and may not support the claimed benefit.
2.The experimental analysis lacks certain aspects.
3.Storage and privacy costs of checkpoint sharing are not adequately discussed.
4.Baseline selection and exclusions need further justification.

The paper proposes FedAgree, a method that adapts Agreement-on-the-Line to federated learning for label-free out-of-distribution performance estimation.
Based on the post-rebuttal positions, I recommend Accept. The rebuttal evidently resolved R2’s concerns about space complexity and ablation analysis, and R3 found the authors’ clarifications are adequate.

The paper proposes an interesting methodology for OOD accuracy estimation based on agreement on the line (AotL) concept. It appears to be a sufficiently novel application of the AotL concept and the results are fairly convincing. Most of the concerns raised by the reviewers have been clarified in the rebuttal. Hence, the paper can be accepted.

Two reviewers recommend to accept this paper post-rebuttal. One reviewer did not submit a post-rebuttal assessment (pre-rebuttal: WR).
The authors submitted an effective rebuttal clarifying raised concerns such as choice of clients K, stochasticity of IID sample draws, time/storage complexity.
The idea and approach to evaluate OOD performance in an federated learning environment is well motivated and, even though methodologically rather simple, pretty effective.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback. Reviewers consistently acknowledged that FedAgree addresses a practically relevant problem, that exploiting FL checkpoints for OOD estimation is a well-motivated and non-obvious idea, and that the method is simple, effective across multiple checkpoint strategies, and relevant to the MICCAI community. We address the main concerns below.
Nr of clients: K=4 represents a lower-bound for FedAgree: being the regression fit based on pairwise agreement points, fewer clients = fewer regression points = noisier line fit; K=10/20/50 would strictly increase the pool of variance-reduced agreement pairs. Consistent with this, History/Peer/Full, which enlarge the checkpoint pool temporally, outperform Local Anchor in Table 2, confirming that more checkpoints lead to lower MAE. Similarly, larger values of T could increase the reliability of the method.
IID diversity: We respectfully disagree with R1’s statement that cross-client diversity in the IID setting reduces to mini-batch stochasticity. Two independent sources of randomness shape each client’s model: SGD stochasticity, and the variance from the local dataset itself being a finite IID draw of the shared distribution. The latter makes FedAgree’s pairwise agreements more informative due to the induced variance. The non-trivial gaps between AotL (which uses models differing only by mini-batch stochasticity) and FedAgree variants in Table 2 empirically confirm this.
HAM10000 Non-IID experiments: HAM10000 contains images from only two clinical sites (Vienna and Melbourne). A non-IID split by acquisition source would therefore yield K=2, which we believe does not reflect a realistic federated setting and has been therefore not considered.
Missing baselines: Density estimation methods target OOD detection rather than OOD accuracy estimation, and require access to raw target data features, making them inapplicable under FL privacy constraints. We will clarify this in the related work.
Storage complexity: For K=4, T=10, and a ResNet18 (~42.7 MB), total storage per client is ~427 MB — feasible in clinical federated infrastructures and advantageous compared to storing high-resolution medical imaging data. In extreme resource-constrained edge devices, FedAgree can operate via streaming peer checkpoint pairs on demand within the secured partner network, discarding them immediately — reducing working memory to 2x ~42.7 MB at any time.
Time complexity: The (regression + prediction) phase adds minimal overhead. On Camelyon (the largest dataset), intermediate strategies require only ~0.8s on average (~1.5× AotL); the Full strategy ~2.3s (~4.0× AotL), which remains a negligible overhead anyway.
Early- vs late-round checkpoints: Early-round checkpoints, although coming from not well-trained models, are valuable because they help ‘draw’ the agreement line. Using only very similar checkpoints produce clustered agreement points that provide little information about the line’s slope and intercept. Early checkpoints introduce models from distinct regions of the loss landscape, which contribute to a better-spread set of points and a more robust linear fit.
Low-R^2 scenarios: FedAgree provides an uncertainty-aware performance estimation approach with R^2 being a practical reliability check. As a practical rule, if R^2 is low in safety-critical scenarios, we recommend falling back to manual performance estimation by labeling a representative set of images as a secure alternative.
Client heterogeneity: Our experiment on Camelyon17 already provides a setting with heterogeneous data volumes across clients (H1: ~59K, H2: ~35K, H3: ~85K, H4: ~130K, H5: ~147K). We acknowledge that further exploring client heterogeneity is an interesting aspect left for future work.
Code: The anonymized repository linked in the paper is complete and visualisation of empty files may have been a temporary issue with the anonymized repository service.

title: FedCHDP: Federated Concept-Guided Dual-Modal Prompting for CHD Diagnosis
abstract: Early detection of Congenital Heart Disease (CHD) relies heavily on subjective ultrasound interpretation. While AI offers automation, privacy regulations and data fragmentation remain major barriers. Federated Learning (FL) enables privacy-preserving collaboration, yet deploying pre-trained vision-language models like CLIP in non-IID settings is challenged by inter-hospital heterogeneity and semantic overfitting to site-specific biases. To address these issues, we propose FedCHDP, a novel federated concept-guided dual-modal prompting framework. On the textual side, we construct a federated medical concept library that decomposes diagnostic queries into fine-grained clinical descriptors (i.e., chamber numbers, flow numbers and flow patterns), enforcing semantic consensus across clients. An uncertainty-aware gating mechanism further adaptively fuses dynamic concept cues with global priors to rectify ambiguous predictions. On the visual side, we introduce a global-guided contrastive alignment that calibrates visual prompts using disease prototypes, aligning local embeddings with global semantic centers to mitigate distribution shifts. Experiments show that FedCHDP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods for multi-center CHD identification.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes FedCHDP, a federated vision–language framework for first-trimester CHD diagnosis from fetal cardiac ultrasound. On text side, it introduces a federated medical concept library that decomposes class prompts into fine-grained descriptors and fuses a concept-conditioned prompt with an unconditional disease prompt via an uncertainty-aware gate. On the visual side, it aggregates visual prototypes into global disease prototypes and uses a contrastive alignment to mitigate cross-site distribution shifts. Experiments on a 4-center dataset show gains over recent baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The concept-guided textual prompting, which explicitly encodes clinically interpretable dimensions, is well motivated for CHD subtyping. 
2.The uncertainty-aware gating between unconditional disease priors and instance-conditioned concepts is a simple yet practical mechanism that is well aligned with clinical reasoning. 
3.The figure is clear and lovely.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The writing needs further refinement, particularly in the method section, where the notation is difficult to follow. For example, in Section 2.1, $C$ denotes the class and $c_i$ denotes a concept, but the meaning of $K_m$ is unclear. It is also unclear what $c_{i,m}$ represents and whether it is a one-hot indicator. 
2.The figures do not clearly annotate the variables, which further limits readability. 
3.The prototype aggregation strategy is relatively naive, relying on sample-size-weighted averaging, which may introduce prototype bias under severe class imbalance or in the presence of low-quality clients. 
4.The dependence on manually annotated concept labels may limit the applicability and scalability of the method.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Q1.How are the semantic anchors instantiated for each concept value? Are they defined using fixed templates or curated from clinical guidelines?
Q2.What is the visual prompt in Section 2.3? Its definition is currently unclear.
Q3.Could the authors report leave-one-center-out results to better assess cross-site generalization? If this is not feasible, please at least provide per-center test performance and cross-site confusion matrices.
Q4.Would ultrasound-specific pretraining for the vision encoder change the comparative landscape versus CLIP-based approaches?

My recommendation is mainly based on concerns about clarity and methodological strength. The writing is not sufficiently clear, and several key concepts and notations are inadequately defined, which makes the method difficult to follow. In addition, the prototype aggregation strategy is relatively weak, as it relies on a simple averaging scheme that may be vulnerable to bias under class imbalance or low-quality client updates.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors have addressed most of my concerns. Their rebuttal and the newly reported results help clarify the model design and support its effectiveness.
If the paper is accepted, I would strongly encourage the authors to further improve the presentation and organization of the manuscript, as the current writing appears somewhat rushed and is occasionally difficult to follow. In addition, since the study relies on private data, making the dataset publicly available in the future, if possible, would be highly valuable to the community and would also enhance reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a novel federated dual-modal prompt tuning framework based on CLIP for congenital heart disease prediction. To ensure semantic consistency across clients, the authors construct a federated medical concept library utilizing fine-grained clinical descriptors. For the textual prompt, an uncertainty-aware gating mechanism is introduced to guarantee prediction stability in ambiguous cases. Meanwhile, for the visual prompt, the method aligns local class prototypes with global ones via contrastive learning to effectively mitigate data distribution shifts.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The proposed method systematically addresses the challenges of using CLIP for clinical CHD prediction in a federated learning setting from both textual and visual modalities. Specifically, it identifies the semantic gap in the text modality and the distribution gap in the image modality, and provides tailored strategies for each. For the textual modality, it constructs a global concept library with fine-grained clinical descriptors; for the visual modality, it introduces a contrastive learning mechanism to mitigate distribution shifts.
2.The proposed uncertainty-aware gating mechanism effectively fuses the prediction of conditional predicted concepts with unconditional generic knowledge to mitigate prediction uncertainty in ambiguous cases. This mechanism is not only methodologically novel but also holds substantial clinical significance.
3.The empirical evaluation is comprehensive, showing significant improvements over baselines. The effectiveness of the proposed textual and visual components is well-supported by ablation studies. Additionally, the inclusion of t-SNE visualizations (demonstrating category-wise clustering and distinct decision boundaries), along with hyperparameter sensitivity and model convergence analyses, makes the experimental claims highly convincing.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The overall description of the method’s pipeline is not entirely clear, and several details, particularly in Figure 2, require further optimization. For instance, the figure does not explicitly denote which components (e.g., the authors can use a sign on the visual prompt) are trainable during the process. Furthermore, for classification loss, $L_{cls}$ , it remains ambiguous whether this loss measures the similarity between the text embedding and the image prototype, or the text embedding and the image embedding. Although the figure appears to illustrate similarity with the prototype, using the image embedding seems more reasonable. Finally, the methodology section fails to formally formulate the model aggregation process, especially regarding the visual prompt and the textual concept library. The variables $V$ and $T$, denoting the visual and textual encoders respectively, are defined in the text but are never formally utilized in the subsequent equations or methodological formulations.
The proposed method is a dual-modal prompt tuning framework. However, many of the compared baselines—such as CoCoOp, KgCoCoOp, FedTPG, PromptFL, and FedVPT—are strictly single-modal (either textual or visual). This asymmetric comparison raises concerns regarding experimental fairness. It remains ambiguous whether the reported performance gains stem from the proposed methodological innovations or simply from the additional information provided by the second modality.
Addressing non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data is a fundamental challenge in federated learning, particularly for classification tasks. However, the authors fail to evaluate their method under severe label skew scenarios. Specifically, they do not employ standard techniques, such as the Dirichlet distribution, to simulate non-IID label distributions across different clients. This significant omission leaves the robustness and generalizability of the proposed framework in highly class-heterogeneous environments highly questionable.
The proposed method involves multiple types of information exchange between clients and the server, such as visual prompts, a medical concept library, and prototypes. In addition, the server is required to compute global prototypes, and each client needs to optimize multiple loss functions. However, the paper does not provide a thorough analysis or comparison of the resulting communication and computational overhead. This lack of evaluation may limit the practical applicability of the method in real-world clinical scenarios.
The experimental results lack the reporting of variance or standard deviations across multiple runs. This omission makes it difficult to assess the true robustness and stability of the proposed model, as the reported performance improvements could be attributed to random seed variations.
Please correct minor typographical errors throughout the paper to improve its rigor. Examples include “fused text enbedding” in Figure 2 and “boundaries..” in the Figure 3 caption.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a meaningful and fairly well-validated federated dual-modal prompt tuning framework for clinical CHD prediction. The method is motivated and empirically strong, and the uncertainty-aware fusion mechanism is particularly interesting. However, concerns remain regarding methodological clarity, fairness of baseline comparisons, robustness under stronger non-IID settings, and the lack of communication/computation overhead analysis. Overall, I view the paper as slightly above the acceptance threshold for MICCAI.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
After reading the rebuttal, I believe the authors have addressed most of the major concerns raised by the reviewers. In particular, they clarified the notation and methodological pipeline, explained the roles of semantic anchors and visual prompts, and provided additional experimental evidence, including variance over multiple seeds, stronger baseline comparisons, leave-one-site-out evaluation, and communication/computation cost analysis. These responses substantially improve the clarity, completeness, and credibility of the work.
Some concerns still remain. The technical novelty is somewhat incremental, as the method mainly integrates concept-guided prompting, uncertainty-aware fusion, and prototype-based alignment. The reliance on fine-grained clinician-annotated concepts may also limit scalability, and the sample-size-weighted prototype aggregation may still be suboptimal under extreme client imbalance. Nevertheless, given the clinically meaningful problem setting, the coherent framework design, the strong empirical results, and the fact that the rebuttal has resolved most reviewers’ concerns, I believe the paper is marginally above the acceptance threshold.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper proposes FedCHDP, a federated dual-modal prompting framework for CHD diagnosis based on vision-language models. The key idea is to address semantic ambiguity and cross-site distribution shift in federated settings via:
1.A concept-guided textual prompting mechanism, which decomposes disease semantics into fine-grained clinical concepts. 
2.An uncertainty-aware gating module to fuse global and instance-specific predictions. 
3.A global-guided contrastive alignment strategy to calibrate visual prompts using aggregated disease prototypes. 
The method is evaluated on a multi-center fetal echocardiography dataset and shows consistent improvements over several prompt-learning and federated baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.This paper has clear motivation and a well-defined problem. The paper clearly identifies two key challenges in federated VLM: semantic ambiguity in prompt learning and distribution shift across clients. The problem setting is clinically meaningful. 
2.This paper has technically well-structured framework. The dual-modal design (text + vision) is logically consistent. Concept-guided prompting is intuitive and clinically interpretable. Also, the uncertainty-aware gating is a nice touch and mimics clinical reasoning. 
3.This paper has strong experimental results. It has significant improvement over baselines. It also has done comprehensive experiments include multi-class evaluation, ablation study, t-SNE visualization and hyperparameter analysis.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.It limits novelty in core components. Many components are incremental combinations of existing ideas such as prompt learning, prototype alignment and uncertainty gating which has been widely used. Also, the novelty mainly lies in integration rather than fundamentally new methodology. 
2.There are several weaknesses in the assumption of concept annotation. The method relies on fine-grained concept labels, however; in practice such annotations are expensive and not always available. Also, the paper does not discuss the robustness to noisy annotations. 
3.The experimental comparison raises some fairness issues. Specifically, several baselines (e.g., ZS-CLIP) are relatively weak and may not provide a sufficiently strong reference point. In addition, the paper lacks comparisons with more recent federated vision-language learning methods, as well as non-prompt-based federated baselines (e.g., FedAvg with a strong backbone). More importantly, it remains unclear whether the reported performance gains primarily stem from the proposed methodological design or from the additional supervision introduced by fine-grained concept labels.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses an important and clinically relevant problem and presents a well-designed framework that integrates concept-guided prompting and prototype-based alignment in a federated setting. The experimental results are strong and demonstrate consistent improvements over existing methods. However, the overall novelty is somewhat limited, as the method mainly combines existing techniques rather than introducing fundamentally new ideas. Additionally, the reliance on fine-grained concept annotations and limited discussion of reproducibility weakens the impact. Overall, the paper is solid and practically meaningful, but could be strengthened in terms of novelty justification and experimental completeness.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
