However, they also raised serious concerns about the paper’s novelty, empirical significance, and methodological clarity: (1)​the performance gains over strong baselines are modest and the core components (frequency enhancement, prototype learning, text guidance) build largely on existing ideas, with limited demonstration of fundamentally new insights; (2) the reliance on an inaccessible in-house dataset undermines reproducibility, and the contribution of textual guidance is not convincingly isolated or analyzed; and (3) the manuscript lacks statistical validation, clarity in architectural illustrations, and discussion of computational efficiency and clinical usability. The rebuttal has successfully addressed most concerns, notably adding statistical testing, improving figure clarity, and committing to code and test-set release. Since the review scores are all positive after rebuttal, I recommend accepting this manuscript.

author_feedback_text:
Thank you for the constructive feedback and positive remarks. We appreciate the reviewers’ recognition of our work as a “methodological contribution” (R1–R3), with a clinically important HR-VWI segmentation setting (R1/R3), a valuable HiRA dataset (R1/R2), comprehensive evaluation (R1/R2), and a modality-aligned design that performs well against strong baselines (R1/R3). Below, we address the specific concerns raised.
Common Questions:
Code: We will release our code upon acceptance.
Dataset: First, we have to clarify HiRA has the local IRB/EC approval, and we will add the corresponding ethics statement in the revised manuscript. To support test, we will release our test dataset and plan to share an expanded dataset in future extension work.
(R1 W1) Due to the difficulty of HR-VWI aneurysm annotation, the current size of HiRA is limited, which restricts the observed performance gains. We are continuously expanding HiRA for more comprehensive validation. Regarding the statistical significance of the proposed modules, case-level paired Wilcoxon tests with Holm-Bonferroni correction show that our method outperforms the no-module Baseline and the best single-module variant on all datasets/metrics (corrected p<0.05), demonstrating the effectiveness of TFEM and DPBM. TFEM with Text also outperforms TFEM w/o Text on most metrics (corrected p<0.05), confirming the benefit of text guidance.
(R1 W2) Please refer to the common questions.
(R1 W3) Text guidance is designed for the specific challenges of HR-VWI aneurysm segmentation, rather than serving as a simple class prompt. In HR-VWI, aneurysms are often small with weak boundaries, sparse foregrounds, and confusing high-frequency responses from artifacts, parent-vessel edges, or background textures. To address this, we use aneurysm-specific text as a semantic prior for feature selection: TFEM filters frequency-enhanced tokens toward aneurysm/wall-relevant boundary cues, while DPBM ranks prototypes to build more discriminative foreground/context banks. We performed an ablation study to verify this design. Compared with prior text-guided methods that mainly use text for general conditioning, our aneurysm-specific HR-VWI text improves Dice by +1.3, +1.1, and +1.5 points for TFEM, DPBM, and the full model, respectively, with corrected p<0.05.(R1 W4) Please see (R1 W3)
(R1 W5) Our model has 215M parameters and 1.236 TFLOPs, compared with 182.16M parameters and 3.29 TFLOPs for CausalCLIPSeg, making it feasible for practical HR-VWI aneurysm analysis.
(R1 W6) We will provide more clear explanations for the existing figures. For Fig. 2, we will clarify the symbols and their relationships: in DPBM, Q is the segmentation query and K/V are text-ranked foreground/context prototype banks; in TFEM, Q is the segmentation query and K/V are text-filtered frequency features. We will also specify that MHCA denotes multi-head cross-attention and replace “cos” with cosine alignment. For Fig. 3, since HiRA is designed for aneurysm analysis, we visualize prediction errors on aneurysm and vessel-wall surfaces to show the spatial relationship between aneurysm segmentation and wall assessment. This demonstrates that our method provides more reliable wall/aneurysm delineation for practical HR-VWI analysis.
(R2 W1) Please see (R1 W3)
(R2 W2) As discussed in (R1 W3), TFEM relies on text-guided feature selection. Without text, added frequency features become unconstrained and may introduce redundant cues from artifacts, parent-vessel edges, or background textures, thereby impacting segmentation.
(R3 W1) Please see (R1 W6)
(R3 W2) Please see (R1 W1) and (R1 W3)
(R3 W3) Please see (R1 W1) and (R1 W3) for the significance analysis and text-guidance explanation. We will revise the description as suggested.

title: From Baseline to Future CT: Large-Scale Diffusion Pretraining for Single-Scan IPF Progression Prediction
abstract:
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) exhibits variable CT progression, from subtle interstitial changes to overt architectural distortion. Longitudinal imaging data is often sparse and confounded by non-rigid deformation, making accurate delineation of disease progression from single timepoint data a fundamental clinical imperative. We investigate single-scan IPF progression in thoracic CT by synthesising a future scan conditioned on the baseline scan, time horizon and patient covariates. To preserve fine lung structure under limited disease-specific longitudinal data, we decouple a transferable thoracic generative/longitudinal prior from disease-specific adaptation. We first learn a detail-preserving latent representation using patch-based autoencoding with overlap-average stitching. 
We then pretrain a covariate-conditioned latent diffusion model and longitudinal ControlNet on a large-scale thoracic CT screening dataset (>30,000 scans; >12,000 patients), and finally adapt the model to IPF progression synthesis with lung-focused patch-decoded supervision. Across internal IPF cohorts and a fully held-out external cohort, the screening-pretrained configuration achieves the strongest in-lung fidelity and lowest feature-space distance, and significantly outperforms training the progression adaptor without longitudinal pretraining. These results support thoracic diffusion pretraining as a reusable generative foundation for data-limited longitudinal disease modelling.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper proposes a four-stage generative framework for predicting disease progression in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) from a single baseline thoracic CT scan. The central design decision is to separate a transferable thoracic generative and longitudinal prior, learned from a large-scale lung cancer screening dataset (31.110 scans, 12.443 patients), from IPF-specific fine-tuning on a much smaller cohort (629 training patients, 986 scan pairs).
Stage 1 trains a patch-based 3D convolutional autoencoder on screening data, mapping 256³ volumes to 4-channel 64³ latents using lung-biased patch supervision and an autoencoder loss combining pixel fidelity, SSIM, gradient, KL regularization, and a 3D PatchGAN adversarial term. Stage 2 pretrains a covariate-conditioned latent diffusion model on full-volume screening latents, conditioning on age, sex, height, BMI, pack-years, and lung volume. Stage 3 pretrains a ControlNet adaptor on longitudinal screening pairs, injecting the baseline latent and time interval as control signal. Stage 4 fine-tunes this adaptor on IPF pairs with additional change-consistency regularizers and patch-decoded voxel-level supervision to enforce local parenchymal fidelity. At inference, DDIM sampling is combined with latent-average stabilization and overlap-average stitching for full-resolution 256³ output.
The central claim is that longitudinal pretraining on screening data is the dominant factor in enabling stable high-capacity 3D diffusion progression modelling, which would otherwise be intractable on cohort-scale IPF data alone.
reviews.text_strengths:
The pretraining strategy is the most clearly supported contribution. The decision to learn a thoracic prior from a large-scale screening dataset, where repeat imaging is available and acquisition variability is broad, and then adapt to a data-limited disease cohort, is a reasonable approach to a real bottleneck. The Scratch ablation, which retains the screening-pretrained autoencoder and diffusion backbone but trains the ControlNet exclusively on IPF data, degrades consistently across all reported metrics on both the internal and external test sets. The primary comparison is statistically significant after Holm correction on both sets, which makes the benefit of longitudinal pretraining the most credibly established result in the paper.
The evaluation design is a further strength. The paper reports both an internal test set and a fully held-out external site, giving at least a preliminary view of behavior under site shift. Statistical testing uses paired one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction, which is appropriate given the directional hypothesis and the multiple metrics being tested. The AE ceiling (deterministic reconstruction of the ground-truth follow-up through the frozen autoencoder) contextualizes the headroom remaining in the progression modelling component: the ceiling is at 0.981 SSIM versus the proposed model at 0.947, indicating that the compression step itself is not the bottleneck.
Supplementing pixel-level metrics with a perceptual distance based on an open-source thoracic CT foundation model encoder is also appropriate. For IPF, where the clinically relevant features are local and spatially subtle, perceptual alignment in an encoded feature space is a more meaningful quality measure than global SSIM alone.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The evaluation is restricted to image fidelity metrics, with no assessment of clinical utility. SSIM, MSE, PSNR, and ViT feature distance measure how closely a synthesized scan resembles a ground-truth follow-up, but they do not address whether the predicted progression is clinically informative. For IPF, the clinically relevant question is whether the model can predict the trajectory of functional decline with any accuracy. The paper acknowledges the absence of expert-annotation-free voxel-level progression measures as an active area of research, but that acknowledgment does not substitute for a downstream evaluation, even a surrogate one. Without some correlation between synthesized image changes and functional endpoints, the clinical value of the approach remains asserted rather than demonstrated.
The external test set contains 17 pairs. This is too small to draw reliable conclusions about generalization under site shift. The results show the same metric ordering as internal testing, which is encouraging, but with this sample size the standard deviations dominate and the evaluation cannot support strong generalization claims. The paper itself flags this as a limitation, but it is worth noting that “transfer feasibility” is the most that can be responsibly claimed, not stability across sites.
The comparison with prior work is narrow. The most directly comparable published method for single-scan IPF follow-up synthesis is Jiang et al. (2025) [6], published in Medical Image Analysis. The paper excludes it on the grounds that it uses text-based lung-function conditioning and 2.5D slice-based synthesis, which differ from the proposed setting. The exclusion is not unreasonable on technical grounds, but the clinical task is identical, and the paper would benefit from a more explicit discussion of what the input difference implies for the comparison. As it stands, the only comparison methods are an in-house latent U-Net and latent cVAE, both matched to the same latent resolution, which is a weaker competitive baseline than the published literature.
No ethics statement appears in the paper. The study uses multi-center patient imaging data collected across several countries. IRB approval or equivalent ethics review is not mentioned anywhere in the text. This is likely a consequence of anonymization requirements, but it should be added to the camera-ready version.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses a real and practically constrained problem: large-capacity 3D generative modelling for a disease with limited longitudinal imaging data. The proposed pretraining-to-adaptation strategy is principled, the ablation evidence directly supports the main claim, and the results hold on an external test set. The reported weaknesses are real, but they do not undermine the core technical finding. A weak accept reflects a solid contribution to the generative modelling for medical imaging literature, with the expectation that clinical grounding and broader benchmarking would strengthen the work in a follow-up.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
My initial review raised four concerns: limited clinical-utility assessment, the small external cohort (n=17), the omitted comparison with Jiang et al. [6], and the missing ethics statement. The rebuttal addresses all four. Clinical scope is honestly bounded as a methodological CT-synthesis study, the external cohort is reframed as supporting transfer feasibility, the Jiang et al. exclusion is defended on input-modality and conditioning differences I find reasonable, and ethics is confirmed.
The meta-reviewer’s additional asks on patch-wise justification and missing implementation and cohort details are also addressed, the latter with a full hyperparameter and architecture dump.
I recommend accepting it.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents pre-training and fine-tuning strategies for 3D patch-wise generative models to predict future CT scans from baseline images. The large-scale pre-training improves future CT prediction, suggesting that the model serves as an effective predictor for IPF progression. Furthermore, the patch-wise training approach effectively preserves lung details. The evaluation, which includes external validation and appropriate metrics, is a notable strength.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The assumption that generative pre-training can enhance longitudinal prediction performance is compelling.
2.Given that PSNR, SSIM, and MSE have inherent limitations in evaluating generative models, the inclusion of ViT distance and Airway error is a significant addition.
3.The study benefits significantly from a substantial pre-training dataset and rigorous external validation, which enhance the generalizability of the proposed model.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Lack of Evidence for Patch-wise Training Benefits
The rationale behind using patch-wise training to preserve details is not sufficiently justified. The authors did not provide comparative results between whole-image training and patch-size ablations. Since other architectures like U-Net and CVAE can also be implemented in a patch-wise manner but may not show similar detail preservation, the authors should clarify if whole-image experiments were conducted for comparison.
2.Insufficient Qualitative Evidence and Performance Issues
The qualitative evaluation is limited, with only two results provided. It is difficult to assess a generative model’s performance based on such a small sample. Specifically:In Fig. 2A, the Ground Truth (GT) at t=1 shows honeycombing patterns, which the proposed model fails to predict accurately.In Fig. 2B, the GT at t=2 exhibits ground-glass opacities, yet the model does not reflect these features well.Additionally, the authors should provide results for the ‘from-scratch’ training setup to demonstrate the actual gain from pre-training.
3.Limited Ablation of Baseline Models
The ablation study is relatively weak. Given the recent advancements in generative modeling, why did the authors limit their comparison to only two models (U-Net and CVAE)? A broader range of diffusion-based baselines should be considered.
4.Missing Experimental Details
The manuscript lacks essential experimental details such as batch size, learning rate, GPU specifications, and Hounsfield Unit (HU) windowing used in pre-processing. Furthermore, the absence of source code makes the figures and results difficult to reproduce.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The authors claim contributions in three areas: pre-training, longitudinal synthesis, and the preservation of lung details.
While the first contribution is interesting, it is a well-established fact that larger datasets improve generative performance. Although the quantitative results are promising, it remains unclear whether these results stem from general high-fidelity generation (typical of diffusion models) or a genuine capability to model follow-up progression.
There are insufficient qualitative examples to support the model’s efficacy.
While patch-wise encoding can preserve details, the compared latent U-Net and CVAE models also operate under patch-wise settings. Without a direct comparison between patch-wise and full-image experiments, the third contribution is not convincingly validated.
Although this study has potential, it is not yet ready for publication in its current form.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
First, regarding the classification of this paper as a methodological work: the MICCAI Call for Papers explicitly states that “manuscripts should clearly demonstrate innovations and contributions over state-of-the-art methodologies.” However, the ablation studies for your proposed method remain insufficient to justify this. Even if closely related prior works are scarce, simply comparing your model against basic architectures like a U-Net or VAE does not constitute a plausible ablation study to verify its superior performance over existing methods.
Second, although the authors state that the patch-wise approach is not a contribution, Section 2.1 is dedicated to it, suggesting it is a component of the proposed methodology. I remain skeptical about the “frequency-preserving” claims attributed to your model, especially since the ablation models utilizing the same patch-based framework do not seem to exhibit or address this property.
Lastly, the qualitative evidence remains weak. The specific details and outcomes of the senior thoracic radiologist’s review are not sufficiently clarified or demonstrated in the text.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a four-stage 3D generative framework for synthesizing future thoracic CT scans from a single baseline scan in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). The core idea is to decouple a transferable thoracic generative prior from disease-specific adaptation to overcome the limited size of longitudinal IPF cohorts. The authors propose a multistage approach, leveraging a pretrained ControlNet adaptor on longitudinal screening pairs that is then finetuned on IPF-specific pairs. At inference, follow-up latents are sampled via DDIM, averaged across m independent samples for variance reduction, and decoded with overlap-average stitching. The model is evaluated against a latent U-Net regressor and latent conditional VAE on internal IPF cohorts and a held-out external site, with ablations systematically isolating the contribution of longitudinal pretraining.
reviews.text_strengths:
(i) Authors attempt to addresses a genuine and difficult clinical problem, predicting IPF progression from a single baseline CT. Furthermore, their methodoly attempt to do this by decoupling strategy (large-scale thoracic pretraining followed by limited-data IPF adaptation) is well-motivated and addresses a real bottleneck in longitudinal disease modelling.
(ii) Operating in a 256³ latent space rather than 2.5D slice-based synthesis better captures volumetric fibrotic structures (traction bronchiectasis, honeycombing) that are clinically meaningful in IPF. The patch-based autoencoding with overlap-average stitching is a practical and technically sound solution for making high-resolution 3D synthesis tractable.
(iii) The paper includes internal and external held-out cohort evaluation (site-shift), a systematic ablation study isolating the contribution of longitudinal pretraining (Proposed vs. Scratch), and appropriate statistical testing (paired one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction). The AE ceiling also provides a useful upper bound for contextualizing the progression modelling gap.
(iv) Training the ControlNet adaptor from scratch on cohort-scale IPF data alone is insufficient for stable high-capacity 3D diffusion modelling. This is consistently demonstrated across all metrics on both the internal and external test sets (all Holm-corrected p < 0.001 internally; p < 0.05 externally).
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(i) Reported metrics (SSIM, MSE, PSNR, ViT feature distance, airway volume error) are generic image fidelity measurements. There is no radiologist assessment of whether the synthesized progression patterns (e.g., extent of honeycombing, ground-glass opacity change, reticulation) are clinically plausible or directionally accurate relative to ground truth. This limits the ability to assess whether the model is learning meaningful IPF-specific progression rather than generic texture fidelity. [Minor]
(ii) The external cohort comprises only 17 baseline–follow-up pairs. While the site-shift result is encouraging, this sample size does not provide sufficient statistical power to draw robust conclusions about deployment generalization. The authors acknowledge this, but it remains a meaningful limitation for a key claim of the paper. [Minor]
(iii) Jiang et al. [6] is the most directly comparable single-scan IPF progression prediction method. The authors cite differences in input assumptions and generation regime to justify omitting a quantitative comparison, but at minimum a qualitative comparison or discussion of performance relative to reported numbers in [6] would substantially strengthen the experimental positioning.
(iv) Key details necessary to reproduce the work are absent. For example, the depth and width of the 3D U-Net denoiser and ControlNet, the number of training steps/epochs for each stage, and the optimizer choice and learning rate schedule. Furthermore, the value of m (number of latent samples averaged at inference for stabilization) is missing. [Major]
(v) The results tables report aggregate means and standard deviations across all test pairs without stratifying by disease severity or progression phenotype (e.g., stable vs. rapidly progressive IPF trajectories, baseline fibrosis extent, FVC decline category). Without this information, it is unclear whether the reported performance is driven primarily by stable IPF cases, where the follow-up scan closely resembles the baseline, or whether the model generalizes to the more clinically challenging rapidly progressive phenotype. This is particularly relevant for the external cohort, where patient demographics and disease stage distributions relative to the internal cohort are unreported. Stratified results or at minimum a table of cohort characteristics (age, sex, baseline FVC % predicted, median follow-up interval) would allow readers to contextualize the clinical scope and potential bias of the reported metrics
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
(i) Authors need to include hyperparameter values for training and fine-tuning of the ControlNet on both the large-scale screening dataset (Stage 3) and the IPF-specific dataset (Stage 4). Although certain values such as loss weights (λ) would be released with the code, either a table or one-line description of evaluated ranges would be beneficial. Learning rates, batch sizes, and number of training steps per stage should also be included in the methodology as either a short sentence or table.
(ii) The paper claims to outperform related methods but does not include a direct quantitative or qualitative comparison with Jiang et al. [6], which is the most relevant prior work for single-scan IPF progression prediction. Authors should clarify why this comparison is infeasible and ideally provide at least an indirect performance contextualization.
(iii) Authors should provide a cohort characteristics table (age, sex, baseline FVC % predicted, median follow-up interval, distribution of stable vs. progressive trajectories) for both the internal and external test sets. Without this, it is difficult to assess whether reported metrics are inflated by an over-representation of stable IPF cases or whether the model generalizes to rapidly progressive phenotypes, which are more clinically consequential.

Lack of hyperparameter description in methodology, along with missing demographic information regarding the datasets makes the results difficult to interpret alone. Methodologically, ablation experiment alongside comparison to a model trained from scratch and U-Net comparison are satisfactory and paper is relatively interesting.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The methodology proposed in this work is innovative and addresses a current critical problem in medical imaging regarding generating synthetic future for 3D volumes when follow-ups are limited. Authors address the limited comparison provided in the original manuscript and provide a rational for it, although this should still be included in discussion section.
Authors have addressed missing experimental parameters to ensure reproducibility for the given methodology, which was a major limitation of the original manuscript.

meta_reviews.text:
The reviewers acknowledge a four-stage generative framework with strong evidence supporting the benefit of large-scale longitudinal pretraining and generally sound evaluation design. However, concerns remain regarding limited clinical validation, small external cohort, insufficient qualitative evidence, and incomplete experimental details. For rebuttal, authors should clarify clinical relevance, justify patch-wise design, expand comparisons to prior work, and provide missing implementation and cohort details to strengthen credibility.

The rebuttal satisfactorily addressed the major concerns, and the paper now presents a solid and well-supported contribution to longitudinal 3D medical image generation.

Reviewers appreciated the generative diffusion based approach for pretraining to longitudinally predict IPF. However, limited baselines and ablations is still considered a weakness. Authors must clearly explain the limitations of the study and rationale for the specific set of experiments performed.

After rebuttal, the post-rebuttal opinions lean positive, with two reviewers recommending acceptance and one maintaining rejection. Reviewer #2 found that the rebuttal adequately addressed concerns about clinical scope, the small external cohort, comparison with Jiang et al., and the ethics statement. Reviewer #3 also recommends acceptance, noting that the method is innovative for future 3D CT synthesis under limited follow-up data and that missing experimental details were clarified. However, Reviewer #4 remains negative due to insufficient comparison with stronger state-of-the-art methods, limited ablation support for the patch-wise design and frequency-preserving claims, and weak qualitative/radiologist evidence.
Overall, the final version should clearly discuss the remaining limitations regarding clinical validation, small external cohort size, qualitative evidence, and incomplete comparison to stronger generative baselines. The authors should provide the full open-source implementation to improve the reproducibility.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the Reviewers and Chairs.
Clinical scope/metrics (R2-R4). We agree that radiologist scoring and downstream endpoints are important for assessing clinical utility. This is a methodological study of longitudinal CT synthesis: generated follow-up CT is evaluated against observed follow-up in-lung, structurally and in thoracic feature space. We do not claim deployment-level utility. The Discussion confirms our focus on in-lung similarity rather than an IPF-specific endpoint, for which annotation-free CT-based standards remain underdeveloped. CT foundation-model distance and airway error assess thoracic feature alignment and airway structure, complementing SSIM/MSE/PSNR.
Progression vs generic generation (R3). R3 questioned whether gains reflect progression modelling or generic high-fidelity generation typical of diffusion. Proposed vs Scratch ablation isolates this: both use the same screening-pretrained autoencoder (AE) and diffusion (LDM) backbone, differing only in ControlNet (CN) longitudinal pretraining; thus latent image quality and diffusion capacity are controlled. Scratch degrades across all metrics, including airway error (Tables 1-2), while Proposed significantly improves pre-specified fidelity/perceptual metrics. This suggests gains arise from a transferable longitudinal adaptor, not merely a high-capacity diffusion backbone.
Patch-wise design (R3). We agree that patch/full-volume ablations would characterise this design. However, the main isolated claim is longitudinal pretraining, not universal superiority of patch-wise training. Patch-wise autoencoding and overlap-average stitching make 256^3 synthesis tractable while preserving a 64^3 latent grid. Direct 256^3 AE training at comparable capacity exceeded A6000 memory, while reducing capacity would confound comparison; stronger compression attenuated high-frequency detail in senior board-certified radiologist review. The high AE ceiling in Tables 1-2 indicates that the representation preserves follow-up detail, so the remaining gap is progression modelling rather than decoding. All comparison models use the same latent representation.
Qualitative evidence (R3,R4). We agree that Fig. 2 cannot exhaustively establish clinical plausibility. The cases are illustrative, and evidence rests primarily on aggregate paired evaluation across all test pairs. In these examples, senior thoracic radiologist review identified local fibrotic progression patterns, including traction bronchiectasis in zoomed regions, which were absent or over-smoothed in baseline outputs. Predicting exact emergence/extent of subtle patterns from one scan remains challenging; definitive assessment requires clinical endpoint validation.
Prior work (R2,R4). Jiang et al. is the closest clinical-task prior, but direct comparison is not straightforward because inputs, datasets, and generation regimes differ. Jiang et al. use OSIC data, lung-function-test guidance via CLIP text encoding, and 2.5D slice generation; our framework uses baseline CT, time horizon, and covariates for full-volume 3D synthesis in a 64^3 latent space. Reported numbers are not directly comparable. Without identical conditioning, data, and implementation, comparison would conflate formulation with performance. We therefore used baselines with identical inputs/conditioning (latent U-Net/cVAE), providing a controlled evaluation.
Reproducibility/cohort/ethics (R2-R4). Scans were clipped to [-1200,800]; AdamW; initial LRs AE/LDM/CN/IPF-finetune=1e-4/3e-5/6e-5/4e-6; effective-batch =6/16/4/4; epochs=120/100/50/30.AE channels=(64,128,256); LDM/CN channels=(128,256,512), 2 ResBlocks, condition channels=5.
Diffusion used T=1000, DDIM=300, m=5 on Nvidia A6000.Configs/code will be released upon acceptance. 
Scans were de-identified and used under relevant data-governance/ethics approvals. Details were omitted for anonymisation. 
The external cohort is modest, supporting transfer feasibility, not deployment generalisation.

title: From Exams to Trajectories: Neural Controlled Differential Equations for Longitudinal Mammography Vision-Language Pretraining
abstract: Longitudinal analysis of a patient’s screening history is fundamental to mammography interpretation. Yet existing deep learning models struggle with the irregular, continuous-time nature of screening data, where patient histories involve unevenly timed multi-view exams paired with evolving textual reports. To address this gap, we introduce \textbf{Dynamo}, a novel multi-modal pretraining \underline{\textbf{dyna}}mic framework for longitudinal \underline{\textbf{m}}amm\underline{\textbf{o}}graphy with two key innovations to model exam timelines as latent trajectories, i.e., a coarse-fine grained exam-level temporal encoder based on Neural Controlled Differential Equations (Neural CDEs) and a Temporal Visual Question Answering (TVQA) loss for query-driven masked token prediction conditioned on temporal context. We perform comprehensive evaluations on downstream tasks including risk prediction using large-scale datasets (EMBED and CSAW-CC), BI-RADS assessment, and breast density classification. Across all benchmarks, Dynamo achieves overall gains over state-of-the-art vision-only and CLIP-style models, improving both calibration and temporal reasoning. On the EMBED dataset, representative gains include   relative reduction in Risk Prediction’s Brier Score,  relative improvement in BI-RADS , and  relative improvement in BI-RADS AUC in zero-shot settings. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/Mortal-Suen/Dynamo}{this URL}.
subject_areas: Applications -> Outcome Prediction / Prognosis / Longitudinal Modeling
Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a multi-modal approach to mammography using a “continuous-time longitudinal encoder” and a temporal VQA as main novelties.
reviews.text_strengths:
The problem solves a difficult problem and reports improvements to an important application.
The idea of using continuous-time encoder is new in this setting.
There is an ablation study on the different components (Table 3)
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper is impossible to read when printed. I suspect it violates guidelines by making font sizes too small in tables. As a further example, Fig 2(a) is very hard to see even in the pdf when zoomed-up and the different models are hard to compare.
The intuition behind the continuous-time advantage is not well described/motivated. The source data is inherently at discrete time events so the natural choice is to model it as such. Right now this is disregarded due to “heuristic”. The new approach is in my opinion also heuristic. Then, on the other hand, there is nothing wrong with heuristics! However, one would like to understand why it works better and what priors it brings.
Given that there is not any new technical novelty, the evaluation becomes more important. First, it is not clear whether the numbers come from previous work or if it is re-implemented. Then, I have tried to compare to previous work, for instance, Mirai [32], which the authors claim to follow, but the experiments in the present paper do not seem to be conducted in the same manner even though it is using the same data. Training and test sets are not described.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper deals with an important problem and shows promising empirical results. However, the current presentation raises concerns regarding clarity and evaluation. In particular, key experimental details are missing, making it difficult to assess the fairness of comparisons and the relation to prior work (e.g. Mirai).
Additionally, the methodological contribution is somewhat incremental, and the motivation for the continuous-time formulation is not sufficiently convincing.
Overall, while the work has potential, the current version does not yet meet the bar for acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I am fine with accepting this paper. The authors wrote a good rebuttal, particularly regarding the motivation of a continuous model.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents a novel framework for longitudinal breast cancer prediction using mammograms and associated text reports. The proposed framework extracts image embeddings through a pretrained image encoder (Mirai) and generates temporal-informed embeddings for each patient using a neural controlled differential equations block. Masked text reports are encoded using Bio-Clinical BERT and used for temporal visual question answering (TVQA). Predictions are made using a gated fusion approach of both modalities. For training, besides the standard cross-entropy loss, the authors propose adding auxiliary contrastive loss functions to reinforce patient-specific embeddings, breast-view asymmetry, and image-text alignment. The framework is tested with one main dataset and compared with other works and methodologies, in both risk ranking, calibration and time dependent AUCs. This work improves upon current approaches and provides useful insights into best practices and design choices for longitudinal breast cancer prediction.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper is well written and structured
The proposed multimodal framework effectively combines mammographic images with masked text reports for risk prediction
The design of the auxiliary losses has clinical relevance (asymmetry aware loss)
The experimental evaluation is comprehensive, including comparisons with multiple baselines across several metrics (e.g., WMAE, Brier score, c index, and time dependent AUCs)
The ablation study is comprehensive and offers insights into the contribution of each component
The reported results are promising and competitive compared with existing methods
reviews.text_weaknesses:
There is no formal statistical comparison with competing methods (e.g., confidence intervals or significance tests), which limits the robustness of the performance claims
The paper provides limited information about the dataset distribution and follow-up times, which makes it harder to assess generalizability
Only one dataset is used to report metrics. The results obtained with another dataset are summarized in a figure with no numerical information
Computational aspects are not reported, such as training and inference times, or the number of trainable parameters, which are important for real world deployment considerations
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Figure 1 contains typos (e.g., “Maskd”, “Hideen”) that should be corrected for clarity
In Table 1 the reported Brier scores appear to be in percent, but it’s not indicated
Section 3.3 does not mention Table 2 (second paragraph)
The dataset splitting and any temporal or patient wise partitioning are not described
Figure 2a is visually dense and could benefit from simplification to improve readability or replacement with another form of reporting

The paper presents a strong, well motivated, and experimentally validated multimodal framework for longitudinal breast cancer risk prediction. The combination of image embeddings, temporal modeling, and text based TVQA is innovative and clinically relevant. The ablation and comparison studies are convincing, and the overall presentation is clear. The main weaknesses are mostly related to missing details, which could be addressed in a minor revision, without affecting the main contribution.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: interesting methodology and rather complete evaluation

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces Dynamo, a multimodal pretraining framework for longitudinal mammography that models patient screening histories as continuous-time latent trajectories using Neural Controlled Differential Equations . The approach combines a coarse-to-fine Neural CDE temporal encoder to handle irregular exam intervals and a Temporal Visual Question Answering (TVQA) objective to align imaging with report text over time. The method is evaluated on large-scale datasets across multiple downstream tasks including risk prediction, showing improvements over vision-only and vision-language modeling.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper clearly identifies two important gaps: discrete-time modeling limitations for irregular screening intervals and lack of temporal grounding in vision-language mammography models.
2.The TVQA objective is an interesting contribution: It allows temporal reasoning in language and provides a more structured supervision signal.
3.There is a complete experimental validation that includes multiple datasets, diverse tasks, ablations and robustness analysis to irregular sampling.
4.There is a use of clinically relevant evaluation metrics like the use of Risk Prediction’s Brier Score, C-index, and long-horizon AUC.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The EMBED dataset only uses synthetic reports. This may limit the realism of language supervision like having a potential bias toward structured patterns. This limitation is acknowledged but not deeply analyzed.
2.There is little discussion of efficiency, training cost or inference speed, which is important for clinical adoption.
3.The robustness analysis is a strong point, but could include more realistic missing-data scenarios. How does Dynamo perform with real radiology reports instead of pseudo-reports?
4.Can the authors provide qualitative examples demonstrating temporal reasoning (e.g., report changes over time)? How sensitive is the model to irregular sampling density in extremely sparse histories?
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper presents a well-motivated and technically solid approach to longitudinal multimodal modeling in mammography. There is a meaningful clinical relevance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I am happy with the explanation on sensitivity to irregular sampling computational. The proposed changes talking about the challenges of not finding real datasets, to revise figure 1 and to mention the computational aspects will improve the final paper.

meta_reviews.text: Two of the reviewers recommended accept, while one reviewer recommended reject. The positive reviewers found the problem to be important and relevant, and the novelty of the contributions sufficient in this domain. The concerns from the negative reviewer include issues with legibility and motivation for continuous time modeling. The reliance on pseudo-reports is another concern. I recommend this paper is invited for a rebuttal to resolve these concerns.
The authors provided a strong rebuttal, the paper is well-written, has interesting methodological contributions, and offers a strong evaluation.

This paper proposes Dynamo, a framework for longitudinal analysis of mammography images with modeling of patient records (screening history) as continuous-time latent trajectories using Neural Controlled Differential Equations. Before the rebuttal, the reviewers asked for more details on the motivation for the continuous-time formulation, implementation, and computational aspects, as well as sensitivity to irregular sampling. The authors addressed these points in the rebuttal, providing clear explanations of the benefits of continuous modeling, especially for irregular screening intervals. Given the completeness of the experimental validation, the high interest of the gaps addressed in the paper to the community, and the originality of the methodological contribution, I recommand acceptance of this paper.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for the feedback and will add clarifications. We are glad they appreciate the difficulty and importance of the problem(R1,R3), the novelty of leveraging a continuous-time encoder(R1), our clinical relevant losses(R2), and comprehensive empirical studies(R1,R2,R3).
*Intuition behind continuous-time advantage (R1)
While exams are discrete, the underlying disease evolution is continuous and sampled at irregular intervals. Our approach explicitly captures this by integrating a latent state over real elapsed time, imposing a smooth-in-time prior that improves robustness to irregular sampling and missing visits, versus discrete models with ad-hoc positional encoding. Empirically, replacing NCDE with a Transformer degrades i.e. C-index from 82.79 to 75.38 (Table 3), and NCDE is markedly more stable under visit-dropout/irregular regimes (Fig. 2b). We will improve this description.
*Novelty (R1)
Clinically, disease progresses continuously while exams are irregular, and interpretation combines stable phenotypes with subtle, view-specific asymmetries. We encode these priors by introducing the first exam-level Neural CDE for longitudinal mammography, using coarse (phenotype) and fine (asymmetry/view-local) streams, augmented with trajectory‑conditioned TVQA and explicit asymmetry regularization.
*Evaluation and dataset distribution (R1,R2)
To ensure a fair comparison, we adopt a common protocol instead of reusing prior numbers. All baselines are trained and/or evaluated on the same EMBED/CSAW-CC patient wise 70/10/20 train/val/test splits as Dynamo. Multiple follow up visits are available for approx. 64% (EMBED) and 75% (CSAW-CC) of patients. Differences from published Mirai style results can arise from cohort construction, horizons, and preprocessing. Mirai and AsymmMirai were directly evaluated using public final checkpoints. CLIP, DINOv2, Random-ViT, ALBEF, MedGemma, and Mammo-CLIP used public pretrained encoders, with downstream heads/finetuning on patient wise splits. OncoNet, VMRA-MaR, and MaMA were retrained as public final checkpoints matching the task were unavailable.
*Computational aspects (R2,R3)
The final model has 121M parameters. Training used PyTorch FP16 DDP on 8 NVIDIA H200 GPUs for 30 epochs, batch size 256, requiring 132 GPU+CPU hours. Inference on 115,810 test samples required 0.3 h, or 0.0024 h per 1000 instances. We will add the computational aspects in the revision.
*Synthetic reports (R3)
We follow prior work in synthesizing reports, due to the lack of available datasets. However, we agree that we could further elaborate the potential challenges with this approach and will do so in the future work section.
*Qualitative examples of report changes (R3)
Fig.1 contains a concrete TVQA instance: the model is asked to recover a masked dynamic term describing a BI-RADS category change at a 1 year follow up, with candidate terms encoding opposite temporal directions. The prediction is conditioned on the NCDE state z_i, which summarizes the patient history up to exam i. We will revise Fig. 1 to highlight this example more clearly.
*Sensitivity to irregular sampling (R3)
While we can see a noticeable drop when comparing the performance for the patients with the most regular screening intervals to the most irregular ones (Fig. 2b), this drop is considerably smaller for the proposed method compared to the common transformer-based approach. NCDE natively treats missing exams as longer integration intervals, which stabilizes performance in extremely sparse settings.
*Formal statistical comparison (R2)
This is a fair comment and formal statistical comparisons were not reported due to the considerable computation requirements of these models.
*Typos, presentation, visually dense (R1,R2)
Thank you for pointing out the typos. The choice of summarizing the CSAW-CC results in a figure was motivated by space constraints. We understand that this was sub-optimal and will revise it in the final version.

title: From Geometry to Clinic: A Physics-Aware Evaluation Framework and Benchmark for Automated Dental Crown Design
abstract: Recent advances in deep learning have demonstrated remarkable potential in automating dental crown design. However, existing evaluation protocols predominantly rely on geometric similarity metrics (e.g., Chamfer Distance), which are clinically agnostic and fail to capture functional failures such as occlusal interference or open contacts. To bridge this gap, we present CrownBench, a physics-aware evaluation framework and benchmark that shifts the paradigm from geometric approximation to clinical validity. We propose a set of clinically-interpretable digital metrics, mathematically formulating implicit clinical experiences into explicit constraints: Feasibility Metrics (e.g., Occlusal/Proximal Feasibility Rates) for survival validation, and Quality Metrics (e.g., Occlusal Contact Distribution) for personalized quality assessment. Benchmarking state-of-the-art methods on CrownBench reveals a severe “Geometric Trap,” where geometrically accurate models still suffer from low clinical success rates. Furthermore, a rigorous blind user study confirms that our framework aligns significantly better with human expert judgments than traditional metrics. Our code and dataset are released at https://github.com/JiaminWoo/CrownBench.
subject_areas: Applications -> Digital Twins / Simulation / Synthetic Data

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces CrownBench, a clinically grounded benchmark for evaluating automated dental crown design beyond geometric similarity. It shows that the proposed physics-aware metrics better reflect clinical validity and expert judgment than conventional geometric metrics.
reviews.text_strengths: Major strengths of the paper include its attempt to move beyond conventional geometry-based evaluation and to discuss clinically oriented evaluation metrics for dental crown design, which is a relevant and potentially useful direction for the field.
reviews.text_weaknesses: Major weaknesses of the paper include its limited novelty, as the proposed metrics mainly repackage clinically intuitive criteria into an evaluation framework rather than introducing a fundamentally new methodology. More importantly, these metrics seem to offer limited practical guidance for improving crown design algorithms themselves, whereas the central challenge in this area is still methodological advancement in generation and optimization. In addition, the paper may overstate the distinctiveness of its evaluation setting. Recent studies have already begun to adopt multiple evaluation perspectives beyond simple geometric similarity, making the claimed gap less compelling than presented.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper contains several noticeable inconsistencies and presentation errors, including mismatched dataset/test-set sizes, unclear metric definitions, and inconsistent numerical scales in Table 1.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors focus on automated crown design and propose a multi-dimensional evaluation framework that extends assessment from geometric similarity to clinical usability. The paper also includes extensive experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness and practical value of the proposed evaluation framework.
reviews.text_strengths: The authors introduce a set of clinically oriented evaluation metrics for automated crown design and validate, through extensive experiments, their effectiveness compared with traditional metrics such as Chamfer Distance.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.In Table 1, the ADF score of Human Design is reported as 100, which appears questionable and should be checked carefully.
2.In the Human-AI Alignment Validation section, the authors state that three senior dentists participated in the experiments, but the paper does not clearly describe how the dentists’ subjective ratings were collected, nor does it report inter-rater agreement. Providing such details and results would further strengthen the robustness of the experimental validation.
3.Although the proposed metrics can all be computed directly, this type of evaluation criterion may lack flexibility and may be difficult to adapt to real-world scenarios. Moreover, in Figure 2, the Spearman correlation for the overall dimension is only 0.52.The authors should further discuss: (1) whether these metrics could be better integrated in practice, for example through weighting schemes or other aggregation strategies; and (2) what advantages this metric-based approach has over methods based on model-encoded similarity.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper addresses an important problem in automated crown design and proposes a clinically motivated evaluation framework beyond conventional geometric similarity metrics. The idea is meaningful and supported by extensive experiments, making the work potentially valuable. However, important concerns remain, including unclear details in the human evaluation, limited discussion of metric integration and practical robustness, and a possible error in Table 1.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
A set of quantitative metrics designed to evaluate quality of dental crown.
A rigorous blind user study on a subset of the 500 paired molar crown cases confirms that the proposed metrics aligns significantly better with human expert judgments than traditional metrics.
reviews.text_strengths:
Solid framing of the problem space: existing
evaluation protocols predominantly rely on geometric similarity metrics(e.g., Chamfer Distance), which are clinically agnostic and fail to capture functional failures such as occlusal interference or open contacts. Thus need better evaluation method.
The design of the metrics set is clinically-motivated and embeds domain knowledge into the feasibility metrics and quality metrics.
Comprehensive benchmarking of multiple generative models which in itself is a good resource for the research field, and meanwhile along with the correlation study from blind user study, also shows the capability of the proposed metrics to distinguish different methods which aligns with human expert judgement.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The main contributions are metric design and benchmarking, lacking in solid modeling or algorithmic advances
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The major strengths of the paper (see answer to question 6) are equally battling with the major weakness of the paper (see answer to question 7). Considering this paper is very well organized(solid motivation, clear mathematical formulas, well-designed experiments including benchmarking and blind user study, and nice listing of limitations and potentials), my overall feedback is a weak accept
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of this paper is the introduction of CrownBench, a physics-aware evaluation framework and benchmark tailored for automated dental crown design. The authors aim to shift the evaluation paradigm from clinically agnostic geometric approximation (e.g., Chamfer Distance) to clinical validity. They propose a novel set of Digital Clinical Metrics that mathematically formulate implicit clinical constraints into explicit feasibility (e.g., Occlusal/Proximal Feasibility Rates) and quality metrics. Through benchmarking, they expose a “Geometric Trap” in current state-of-the-art methods and demonstrate via a user study that their metrics align better with human expert judgments.
reviews.text_strengths:
High Clinical Relevance & Paradigm Shift: The paper addresses a critical bottleneck in the MICCAI community regarding dental restoration: the disconnect between standard CV metrics (e.g., Chamfer Distance) and actual clinical viability. Exposing the “Geometric Trap” is a highly valuable contribution that urges the community to rethink how generative models are evaluated.
Novel Formulation of Clinical Knowledge: Translating qualitative clinical procedures, like the Virtual Articulating Paper and Digital Dental Floss, into explicit, computable mathematical formulations (OFR, PFR) is an elegant methodological innovation.
Valuable Community Resource: The introduction of CrownBench and the promise to release a paired clinical dataset of real-world cases with expert human designs is a significant contribution that will facilitate future research.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Critical Data Discrepancy and Limited Scale: There is a major contradiction regarding the dataset size that severely undermines the credibility of the experimental results. Section 3.1 states the dataset comprises 500 cases partitioned with an 8:1:1 ratio, which implies a test set of only 50 cases. However, Section 3.2 claims that Table 1 presents comparisons “across 1,000 test cases”. If the test set is indeed only 50 cases, this scale is far too small to establish a robust and reliable benchmark for the community.
Lack of Sensitivity Analysis for Clinical Metrics: The proposed feasibility metrics heavily rely on hard-coded empirical thresholds (e.g., [-0.2mm,0.5mm] and [-0.3mm,0mm]). The authors fail to provide a sensitivity analysis. It is crucial for a benchmark to demonstrate whether slight variations in these predefined tolerance thresholds would drastically alter the ranking of the benchmarked methods.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
While the paper astutely attempts to avoid the fallacy of ‘more contact area is better’ by introducing COC and OCD, these metrics may still introduce new failure modes. For instance, if the adjacent reference tooth suffers from pathological severe wear (excessive flat contact), the COC metric would penalize a healthy, point-contact crown design. Furthermore, the OCD metric is highly sensitive to the DBSCAN hyperparameters (e.g., radius); without rigorous justification, a singular, massive, and clinically unacceptable contact area could be erroneously clustered into ‘multiple valid points’, masking functional failures.

I am recommending a Weak Accept for this paper. The motivation is outstanding: translating clinical constraints into computable metrics perfectly aligns with MICCAI’s focus on clinical translation. The mathematical formalization of the “Geometric Trap” is insightful. However, a benchmark paper lives and dies by its experimental rigor, which is currently lacking. The critical contradiction regarding the number of test cases (50 vs. 1000) raises significant concerns about the validity of Table 1.I am highly open to raising my score to an Accept if the authors can convincingly resolve the data discrepancy and provide the missing robustness checks in their rebuttal.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: After considering the manuscript and rebuttal together, I would update my score from Weak Reject to Weak Accept. The authors clarify the major reporting errors regarding the test-set size and Human Design ADF, provide missing details and inter-rater agreement for the blinded dentist study, and report threshold sensitivity analysis showing stable method rankings. These points directly address my main concerns. Some reservations remain, including the relatively small 50-case held-out test set, the serious presentation errors in the original manuscript, and the empirical nature of several thresholds/parameters. Overall, however, the paper addresses an important evaluation gap in automated crown design, and the rebuttal improves my confidence enough to support an acceptance.

meta_reviews.text:
I would recommend to address the weaknesses raised by Reviewers, especially:
1.Noticeable inconsistencies and presentation errors
2.Unclear details in the human evaluation, limited discussion of metric integration and practical robustness, and a possible error in Table 1.

While reviewers before and post-rebuttal raised several key concerns, the authors addressed several concerns of two reviewers. I would recommend to include it in camera-ready.
The reviewers showed some enthusiasm for this work being presented at the conference. Several concerns remain but the overall contributions are strong enough to justify acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
Contributions (R1, R3) & Advantages over similarity-based evaluation (R2). CrownBench is not intended as another crown-generation architecture, but as a clinically grounded evaluation methodology and benchmark. Defining the correct clinical target is essential: stronger models optimized toward clinically agnostic objectives may still move the field in the wrong direction. Prior works mainly report CD/HD or distance-thresholded accuracy/F1, which remain similarity to a single reference design. Occlusion/proximal analyses are usually case-level visualizations rather than scalable test-set quantification. Our study exposes this “geometric trap”: low CD can suffer from clinical failures. CrownBench translates implicit chairside criteria into explicit, interpretable, and auditable metrics. This matters because crown design is a one-to-many task: the human reference crown is not uniquely optimal and may itself require clinical adjustment. Moreover, these metrics provide the foundation for differentiable losses or reward terms for diffusion guidance or reinforcement learning.
Reporting errors in test-set size and Table 1 (R1, R2, R4). We thank reviewers for pointing out two typos: “1,000 test cases” should be “50 held-out test cases”, and Human Design ADF should be 1.00, not 100.00.We will correct both and they do not affect the experimental conclusions. Regarding scale, each case is a complete clinical molar-restoration instance with preparation jaw, opposing jaw, adjacent teeth, margin, and expert design, which is costly to collect and comparable to or larger than many prior crown-design study. The full dataset (500 cases) and evaluation code will be public as the first benchmark in automated dental restoration.
Human rating collection and agreement (R2). Our manuscript reported the blinded study, dentist experience, Likert scale, and four dimensions, but omitted collection/agreement details. We will clarify that dentists reviewed anonymized 3D visualizations including the generated crown and context, with method identity hidden and sample order randomized. For each case/dimension, the mean rating from three dentists was used as the human reference for Spearman analysis. Inter-rater agreement was high: ICC=0.868/0.874/0.884/0.844 for occlusion/proximal/margin/overall.
Metric integration and flexibility (R2). We will clarify that the overall automated score was computed by averaging the dimension-specific metrics with equal weights. For deployment, CrownBench also supports hierarchical aggregation: feasibility metrics (OFR/PFR/MSI) first serve as safety gates, since good morphology should not compensate for occlusal interference, open contact, or poor margin; quality metrics (COC/OCD/ADF) then rank feasible designs. If a single scalar is required, task-specific weights can be calibrated from expert ratings or manufacturing standards while keeping individual metrics visible. This also explains why overall correlation is lower than dimension-specific correlations: overall acceptability is multi-factorial.
Robustness, thresholds, and parameters (R2, R4). We added a compact sensitivity analysis: OFR with occlusal lower bound -0.15/-0.20/-0.25 mm and upper bound 0.45/0.50/0.55 mm, and PFR with proximal lower bound -0.25/-0.30/-0.35 mm. Absolute pass rates changed as expected, but method rankings remained unchanged, supporting that the main conclusion does not depend on one hard-coded threshold. For COC, we agree that pathological wear or unusual occlusal schemes are boundary cases where this context assumption may be less reliable. We will state this limitation and recommend condition-specific thresholds or upstream pathology screening. For DBSCAN, parameters were empirically validated on human-designed references to match clinically meaningful contact separation and avoid splitting one broad contact patch into multiple valid contacts. We will add this justification and a supplementary check.

title: From Patches to Patients: A Study of the Tile-to-Slide Performance Transferability in Digital Pathology
abstract: Foundation Models (FMs) have recently redefined the stateof-the-art in histopathology by providing robust representations for wholeslide image (WSI) analysis. However, selecting the optimal foundation model (FM) for a specific clinical cohort currently requires multiple preprocessing steps, followed by computationally expensive feature extraction and the training of a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) aggregator for every model. In this work, we investigate whether efficient tile-level linear probing can serve as a reliable proxy for slide-level performance, reducing the need to run full slide-level pipelines for every candidate encoder. We benchmark 19 state-of-the-art FMs on 42 slide-level and 16 tile-level tasks, comparing tile probing metrics against slide-level outcomes using ABMIL and Mean Pooling aggregations. We observe a high correlation between tile and slide performance across varying task difficulties, indicating that encoder representation quality is the primary determinant of WSI success. Sensitivity analyses show that transferability is stable across models and is more influenced by cohort sizes and numbers of tiles per slide than by average task difficulty. We also measure the agreement in best performing models between tile and slide-level tasks, showing tile benchmarks reliably shortlist strong candidates. Overall, our study indicates that tile-level benchmarking provides an efficient and practical first step for narrowing down candidate models, while slide-level evaluation remains essential for final validation on clinical tasks.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper presents a large-scale benchmarking study investigating whether tile-level performance correlates with slide-level performance in digital pathology. It evaluates 19 state-of-the-art foundation models across 42 slide-level tasks and 16 tile-level tasks, demonstrating that tile-level benchmarking serves as a strong proxy for slide-level model selection.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper provides the first large-scale tile-to-slide benchmarking study and quantifies the overall tile-to-slide transferability. 
2.The experimental evaluation is thorough. The authors benchmark 19 open-source pathology foundation models, covering 16 tile-level tasks and 42 slide-level tasks. 
3.The paper shows that tile-level benchmarking is a strong proxy for slide-level model selection in digital pathology, reducing the need to run full slide-level pipelines and providing an effective way to select candidate models.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.While the paper presents extensive statistical analyses demonstrating consistency between tile-level and slide-level tasks, it does not provide sufficient insight into the underlying causes of this consistency, such as the relationships between features. 
2.The slide-level evaluation uses two aggregation strategies: mean pooling with linear probing and attention-based MIL (ABMIL). Potential aggregation-specific bias should be discussed.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The work is interesting and the results are promising. However, the issues raised in the weaknesses need to be discussed.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper asks whether tile-level linear probing can reliably predict slide-level model rankings, benchmarking 19 pathology foundation models across 16 tile tasks and 42 slide tasks. The main finding is that rankings correlate strongly (ρS ≈ 0.92 for mean pooling, ρS ≈ 0.81 for ABMIL).
reviews.text_strengths:
The scale of the study is genuinely impressive (15,000+ V100 GPU-hours) and the result is reproducible on public datasets.
The leave-one-model-out analysis is a good robustness check.
The practical motivation is real — FM selection is a genuine bottleneck.
The finding that top/bottom of the leaderboard is stable while mid-ranks scramble under ABMIL is a concrete and useful observation.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Limited novelty and somewhat expected findings
The central result — that models with better tile representations also produce better slide features — is fairly intuitive, since slide-level predictions are directly computed from aggregated tile embeddings. The contribution would be stronger if the paper explained when and why the correlation breaks down, rather than primarily confirming that it holds. The ABMIL gap (ρS drops from 0.92 to 0.81) is the most interesting finding but is underexplored.
2.Weak practical payoff given the stated conclusion
The paper concludes that tile benchmarks are useful for “shortlisting” but that “slide-level validation remains essential.” If practitioners still need to run full slide pipelines for final selection, the actual computational savings are unclear. The paper doesn’t quantify how many models can be pruned by tile-level screening, or what the expected error rate of that pruning is in practice.
3.Missing random baseline for top-5 overlap (Fig. 4)
The micro-level analysis reports top-5 overlaps but never compares against a random baseline. With 19 models and top-5 selection, the expected random overlap is non-trivial. Without this, it is impossible to assess whether the reported 82–100% “at least one shared model” probability is meaningfully above chance.
4.Tile tasks may not be representative
All 16 tile-level tasks come from a single benchmark (THUNDER). The slide tasks span 10 anatomical sites and 4 clinical categories. The tile tasks are skewed toward local morphology (tumor detection, histologic pattern recognition), which may structurally favor models that also do well on aggregated slide tasks. The transferability claim rests heavily on this benchmark design choice, which isn’t critically examined.
5.ABMIL — the more clinically relevant aggregator — shows weaker transferability, and this deserves deeper analysis
ABMIL is generally preferred in practice over mean pooling because it learns task-specific attention. Yet this is precisely where tile-level correlation is weakest. The paper attributes this to “additional variability introduced by learning,” but doesn’t investigate which types of tasks or which models are most affected, which would be the actionable insight.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

See the above major weaknesses
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: While multiple pathology foundation models have been developed, it is computationally expensive to test all of them on a specific cohort and slide-level task to select the optimal foundation model. The authors of the paper ask a question on whether tile-level performance can be transferred to slide-level performance, because a tile-level task would be computationally more efficient than a slide-level task. The authors comprehensively benchmark 19 foundation models on 42 tasks and show that there is a strong correlation between tile-level and slide-level predictions. Since comparing foundation models for a slide-level task would require lots of storage and compute resource, it would offer an efficient way to select a few foundation model candidates by conducting a tile-level task which is generally lighter.
reviews.text_strengths: The major strength of the paper is the comprehensiveness of the study design and analysis. The study is conducted on 42 clinical tasks using 19 foundation models. Rank correlation between slide-level and tile-level benchmarks in Figure 2 clearly shows that tile-level tasks can potentially replace slide-level tasks for selecting potential foundation models. Additional sensitivity analysis indicates that the transferability can be influenced by cohort sizes and number of tiles per slide which is important to understand when using the proposed method.
reviews.text_weaknesses: I wonder if tile-level analysis is really more efficient. One reason why MIL is powerful is because MIL only requires slide-level labels without tile-level labels where tile-level labels can be extremely tedious and laborious. However, if tile-level analysis is needed to select foundation models, one has to additionally label tiles in a cohort. While the proposed method can be computationally efficient, by considering laborious effort of labeling tiles, the authors must comment whether it is really efficient overall.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I like the thorough analysis and the proposal to alternatively use tile-level performance to determine which foundation models to test for a specific cohort and task. One doubt I have is whether it is really efficient overall after considering an additional tile-level annotation process.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper presents an in-depth study on the transferability of pathology foundation models from tile-level modeling to slide-level modeling. The overall motivation and the observation of a high correlation between tile-level and slide-level performance are interesting. All three reviewers recognize the contribution and potential impact of the work.
On the other hand, I also agree with Reviewer #3 that this observation does not necessarily imply that tile-level tasks can be effectively used to select the best foundation models for WSI-level tasks, as it still higly relies on manual annotations. Nevertheless, the current observation itself, supported by large-scale evaluations across 42 tasks and 19 foundation models, is impactful enogh for discussion at MICCAI. I therefore rate this paper as an early accept.
The theoretical value of the paper would be further strengthened if the authors could provide a more thorough discussion of why ABMIL shows a weaker correlation than mean pooling.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback and for recognizing the scale, comprehensiveness, and practical motivation of our study (15,000+ GPU hours, 19 foundation models, 16 tile-level tasks, 42 slide-level tasks). We are glad that they found the evaluation robust and the findings highly relevant for addressing the bottleneck of Foundation Model (FM) selection in digital pathology. Below, we address your concerns by sections. All discussions in this rebuttal will be incorporated into the final manuscript.
I) Underlying causes of tile-to-slide transferability & the impact of aggregation (ABMIL vs mean-pooling)
To explain the showcased tile-to-slide consistency, one should note that slide-level predictions are generally performed by aggregating tile representations. As a result, informative tile-level features from a powerful encoder will likely lead to high slide-level performance, although other factors such as spatial contextualization or slide-level aggregation strategies may play a role depending on the task. Mean pooling acts as a direct evaluation of the frozen FM’s representation spaces, which is why it correlates so highly (Spearman r=0.92) with tile-level linear probing. Conversely, ABMIL introduces learned task-specific parameters that reshape this feature space to optimize for the slide-level label prediction. This added flexibility shifts the evaluation further away from the FM’s initial representation space, introducing aggregation-specific variability. However, we emphasize that, despite this variability, the Spermann correlation remains strong (r=0.81, with permutation p-values=0.0004). We included ABMIL as a slide-level aggregation strategy in our evaluation because it is a commonly-used and robust method that often matches the performance of more complex MIL architectures, as shown by Shao et al. (“Do Multiple Instance Learning Models Transfer?”, ICML 2025).
II) Practical payoff: computational vs. annotation efficiency
Reviewers raised valid questions regarding the true efficiency of tile-level benchmarks, as they require laborious manual annotations, and that slide-level validation is still ultimately required. We agree that human annotation is expensive, but it is a one-time, fixed cost (which is already absorbed by leveraging public benchmarks like THUNDER). In contrast, evaluating new FMs or conducting hyperparameter searches represents a recurring, iterative hardware cost. Our results demonstrate that running a fast tile-level evaluation is an effective proxy for quantifying the incremental improvement of a newly pre-trained FM before committing vast compute resources to full slide-level MIL evaluation. While fine-grained final selection still benefits from slide-level validation, tile-level benchmarking effectively filters underperforming models, saving large amounts of computational resources in the development cycle, making it complementary to the slide-level benchmark.
III) Dataset representativeness and potential bias
We acknowledge that our 16 tile-level tasks (derived from THUNDER) may be skewed toward local morphology. In fact, our micro-level transferability analysis (Fig. 4) reflects this limitation: overlap is lower for immune profiling compared to molecular or mutation tasks, likely because immune profiling relies on an understanding of more complex spatial tissue architecture. To maintain objectivity, we utilized a broad set of publicly available tile-level datasets.
