To verify that our findings are not driven by the specific set of tile-level datasets used in the study, we performed a leave-one-out sensitivity analysis, finding that the slide-tile Spearman correlation remained stable regardless of which tile dataset was excluded. We hope this highlights the community’s need for more diverse, context-aware tile-level datasets, which we believe will only strengthen these transferability correlations in the future and thus lead to more accessible and faster benchmarks.

title: From Perception to Anticipation: Forecasting Vessel–Instrument Interactions in Endoscopic Surgery under Unreliable Observations
abstract: Vessel safety in endoscopic surgery, particularly in Endoscopic Submucosal Dissection (ESD), is currently supported by segmentation-based visual guidance, which provides spatial awareness but cannot anticipate dangerous vessel–instrument interactions before they occur. To address this limitation, we formulate vessel–instrument interaction anticipation as a new task that predicts the upcoming interaction state from a short observation window of frames and predicted segmentation masks. This task presents a fundamental tension between observation reliability and temporal sufficiency, as both visual and segmentation-derived inputs are inherently noisy, yet the brief observation window offers no margin to absorb such noise, with different interaction categories further exhibiting heterogeneous temporal evidence patterns.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper introduces a novel task of vessel–instrument interaction anticipation in endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD), aiming to predict future interaction states (no interaction, approaching, touching) from short observation windows. This shifts the focus from retrospective recognition to proactive anticipation, which is clinically meaningful. 
To support this task, the authors present a new annotated multi-case dataset consisting of 30 real ESD procedures with clip-level annotations. Methodologically, the paper proposes a framework that explicitly addresses noisy and unreliable observations, a common issue in endoscopic vision.
The approach combines three key ideas:
(1) a cross-modal latent recovery (CLR) mechanism to enforce consistency between visual and geometric features,
(2) an explicit separation of reliability estimation and temporal modeling, and
(3) a dual asynchronous memory module that captures both short-term dynamics and long-term trends, guided by a reliability score.
Extensive experiments suggest improved robustness to segmentation noise and demonstrate the feasibility of real-time inference.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper addresses a clinically relevant and well-motivated problem. Anticipating vessel–instrument interactions has clear implications for preventing complications such as vessel injury during ESD, making the shift from perception to anticipation highly meaningful.
A major strength is the introduction of a new task and dataset, which provides a foundation for future research. The task is clearly defined and distinct from existing work on phase detection or segmentation.
The work also stands out by explicitly modeling observation uncertainty, rather than relying on end-to-end learning to implicitly handle noise. The separation between reliability estimation and temporal modeling is conceptually clean and well motivated. 
Methodologically, the combination of cross-modal consistency and dual memory mechanisms is interesting and reasonably well aligned with the problem structure. The empirical results are convincing, with consistent improvements over baselines, particularly under unstable or noisy conditions.
Finally, the demonstrated real-time performance strengthens the practical relevance of the approach.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
A key limitation is the insufficient description of the annotation process, which is particularly critical given that a new task is introduced. Important details such as annotator expertise, annotation protocol, handling of temporal transitions, and inter-annotator agreement are missing. This raises concerns about the reliability and reproducibility of the dataset.
Related to this, the paper lacks transparency and reproducibility in several aspects. Core components such as the CLR module, reliability score computation, and gating mechanisms are described at a high level but not specified in sufficient algorithmic detail. Additionally, the main methodological figure 2 is very hard to understand and visually overloaded. The temporal and/or logical path remains intransparent. Having this complexity in mind, it is a major weakness that there is no statement regarding code and/or data availability.
Another concern is the reliance on automatically generated vessel segmentations (SAM2) as a core input to the proposed framework. While the paper explicitly aims to be robust to segmentation noise, no quantitative evaluation of segmentation quality is provided. Such a validation would provide an important reference for contextualizing the reliability of the input signal. 
Without this information, it is difficult to disentangle whether the reported robustness primarily arises from the proposed cross‑modal and memory mechanisms, or whether it benefits from already sufficiently accurate upstream segmentation. A quantitative assessment or at least a discussion of expected segmentation quality would strengthen the methodological clarity and interpretability of the results.
Finally, the evaluation is restricted to a single, internally collected dataset, with no external validation. This makes it difficult to assess robustness across different clinical settings, devices, or institutions.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a strong conceptual contribution with clear clinical motivation and introduces a novel and relevant task. The idea of explicitly modeling reliability and combining it with temporal reasoning is promising, and the empirical results are encouraging.
However, several critical issues limit the current contribution. In particular, the lack of a detailed annotation protocol, the absence of reproducibility information, and the lack of validation of the underlying segmentation quality weaken the overall reliability of the work.
With improved transparency, stronger validation (especially of the segmentation backbone), and clearer methodological specification, the paper could become a solid contribution.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The rebuttal substantially addresses the main concerns raised in my initial review. Specifically:
(1) The annotation process is now clearly specified, including annotator expertise, a concrete labeling rule based on the 4th-s target frame, dataset splits at case level, and quantitative inter-annotator agreement (94.4% / Cohen’s κ=0.90). This resolves my central concern regarding dataset reliability and reproducibility.
(2) The methodological clarifications provide the missing algorithmic detail: the formulation of the alignment reliability term, the distinct roles of the three gating signals (ψ_t, r_t, λ_t), the composition of the 10-D geometric descriptor, the layer-selection ablation for f_t^(8), and the sensitivity of key hyperparameters. Together with the explicit commitment to release code, weights, and the annotation protocol, the reproducibility concern is largely mitigated.
(3) The segmentation quality is now quantified (Dice/IoU = 84.64/73.37), and the differential F1 drop under visually unstable clips (8.17 for the proposed model vs. 32.84 for the baseline) provides convincing evidence that the reported robustness stems from the proposed reliability-aware mechanisms rather than from clean upstream input. This directly addresses my methodological concern about disentangling segmentation quality from model contribution.
A remaining limitation is the absence of external validation across institutions or devices, which the rebuttal does not address. Given the scope of a conference paper and the strength of the conceptual contribution, the clear clinical motivation, the introduction of a novel and well-defined task, and the now-clarified methodology, I consider this an acceptable limitation to be discussed in the final version.
Overall, the paper makes a meaningful contribution by shifting from retrospective recognition to proactive anticipation of vessel–instrument interactions, and the rebuttal has adequately resolved the main issues raised. I therefore recommend acceptance, conditional on the authors incorporating the clarifications and the committed code/data release into the camera-ready version.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper introduces the task of vessel–instrument interaction anticipation in ESD procedures, aiming to predict future interaction states from short video clips with noisy segmentation masks. To achieve this aim, it proposes a framework combining:
A cross-modal latent recovery (CLR) module to enforce consistency between visual and geometric features; A dual asynchronous memory module that separates short-term and long-term temporal features, with reliability-aware updates.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Clinically relevant, Anticipating instrument–vessel interactions before contact is a meaningful step toward proactive surgical safety systems.
2.The emphasis on robustness to noisy inputs is well-motivated and practically relevant.
3.The combination of cross-modal learning and temporal modeling is logically structured.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper is difficult to follow, with many concepts, variables, and modules introduced without sufficient explanation:
1.The core prediction task is not clearly specified early on. It is not immediately clear whether this is a standard classification problem, a sequence prediction task, or a forecasting problem.
2.Several terms, equations and components are introduced with insufficient intuition or justification, making it hard to understand how they contribute to the final prediction. For example, (a) the intermediate feature f(8) was selected for feature fusion, was other selections and impacts well studied? (b)The cosine similarity computation is inconsistent between the image and the text.(c) It is not clear how a_vis and a_align are derived. (d) Not all the components of the 10D geometry descriptor listed. (e), what is anticipation signal, and how it was computed (the classification results or computed on top of it?) (f) Hyperparameters such as memory sizes, thresholds, and fusion weights are not well analyzed. It is unclear how sensitive the method is to these choices.
2.The dataset is not well explained. what is the statistics of each class, how the dataset is split (randomly or clips from the same videos in the same set etc).
3.How noisy was the segmentation result, and how was cases with long periods lacking a reliable reference handled?
4.How was the instrument tip extracted?
Overall, the lack of clarity significantly hinders understanding and weakens the paper’s impact.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper tackles a relevant and potentially impactful problem: anticipating vessel–instrument interactions for surgical safety, and proposes a reasonably structured framework combining cross-modal learning and temporal modeling. 
However, I recommend weak rejection due to poor clarity and insufficient explanation. The paper does not clearly define the learning problem formulation early on. Important concepts are not rigorously explained. Many components are introduced in a dense and abstract manner, with limited intuition or concrete examples.
As a result, it is difficult to fully understand or reproduce the method.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
While the rebuttal provides additional implementation details and clarifies several definitions, my primary concerns regarding clarity, rigor, and reproducibility remain insufficiently addressed.
First, many essential methodological components are still described only at a high level without enough formalization or justification. The clarification of the 10-D geometry descriptor is also still incomplete, as the exact descriptor formulation and normalization procedures are not fully specified.
Second, the rebuttal confirms that several critical experimental details were absent from the original submission rather than demonstrating that the paper itself is sufficiently self-contained.
Third, the robustness claims remain only partially convincing. While the authors report segmentation Dice/IoU scores and relative degradation comparisons, there is still limited analysis of failure cases involving prolonged unreliable segmentation, severe occlusion, or unstable instrument visibility. In particular, manually annotating the instrument tip weakens the practical realism of the setup and leaves uncertainty regarding how the full pipeline would perform under fully automated conditions.
Overall, although the rebuttal improves understanding of the method, I do not believe it sufficiently resolves the underlying concerns about clarity, completeness, and experimental rigor. Therefore, my recommendation remains rejection.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
Formulation of a Novel Anticipation Task:
The paper effectively shifts the paradigm from reactive perception to proactive safety by formalizing the Vessel-Instrument Interaction Anticipation task. Unlike conventional segmentation-based methods that provide only instantaneous spatial awareness, this new task focuses on forecasting potential risks within a short temporal window. This transition is highly relevant for clinical settings where early warning systems are critical for preventing intraoperative complications.
Robust Hierarchical Framework:
To address the challenge of noisy surgical data, the authors propose a well-structured hierarchical architecture. The Cross-modal Latent Recovery (CMLR) module is particularly noteworthy for its use of an information bottleneck to filter out segmentation noise, ensuring that only reliable features are used for reasoning. Furthermore, the Dual Asynchronous Memory (DAM) module cleverly decouples transient instrument dynamics from stable interaction prototypes, enabling robust and accurate temporal forecasting even under unreliable observation conditions.
reviews.text_strengths:
The most significant strength of this paper is the formalization of the Vessel-Instrument Interaction Anticipation task. While existing research in surgical AI has largely focused on real-time segmentation and perception, this work proactively addresses surgical safety by forecasting potential risks before they occur. Shifting the focus from reactive detection to predictive anticipation is a highly meaningful contribution that directly addresses the need for early warning systems in complex procedures like Endoscopic Submucosal Dissection (ESD).
The proposed hierarchical architecture is also technically impressive, particularly in its ability to handle noisy and unreliable surgical data. The Cross-modal Latent Recovery (CMLR) module effectively utilizes an information bottleneck to filter out noise from segmentation masks, ensuring that the temporal reasoning process is based on reliable features. Furthermore, the Dual Asynchronous Memory (DAM) module is a clever solution for modeling the heterogeneous nature of surgical interactions. By decoupling transient instrument dynamics from stable interaction prototypes, the framework maintains high predictive accuracy even when frame-level observations are limited or degraded.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
While the task of anticipation is novel, the reported Macro F1 score of 70.80% suggests that the system may still produce a significant number of false alarms or missed detections. In a high-stakes surgical environment like Endoscopic Submucosal Dissection (ESD), a 30% error margin could lead to alarm fatigue for surgeons or, more critically, a failure to prevent actual vessel damage. The authors should have provided a more detailed failure case analysis to discuss how these errors would be managed in a real clinical setting.
The dataset composition also raises concerns regarding the generalizability of the proposed framework. The study utilizes a newly constructed multi-case ESD dataset, but the paper does not specify the diversity of the surgical equipment or the variations in anatomical conditions across different patients. Since the appearance of vessels and the handling of instruments can vary significantly between surgeons and hospital settings, the lack of cross-center validation or a more diverse testing set limits the proof of the model’s robustness.
Another weakness lies in the definition of the anticipation window. The paper mentions predicting upcoming states from a short observation window, yet it does not clearly define the exact lead time or the prediction horizon. Without a rigorous analysis of the trade-off between the prediction horizon and accuracy, it is difficult to evaluate whether the system provides enough reaction time for a surgeon to actually alter their movement and avoid an accident.
Finally, although the dual asynchronous memory module is designed to handle temporal reasoning, its superiority over simpler temporal models like Transformers or LSTMs with attention mechanisms is not sufficiently justified through extensive ablation studies. The authors should have compared their memory module against a wider range of state-of-the-art temporal architectures to clearly demonstrate that the added complexity of dual asynchronous processing is necessary for achieving the reported performance.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper proposes a practical and original framework for real-time risk anticipation that goes beyond simple perception by utilizing an information bottleneck and dual asynchronous memory to overcome noise and temporal uncertainty in surgical videos.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
The authors present an interesting method for endoscopy. The reproducibility of the methodology should be better guaranteed in the manuscript. More details on the dataset should be provided.

The authors managed to opportunely improve the methods and the dataset description.

The responses addressed the concerns about description of the annotation process and reproducibility, missing algorithmic detail. Need to address the issues of robustness claims, descriptions of essential methodological components in final revision.

This paper introduces a novel and clinically meaningful task: vessel–instrument interaction anticipation in endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD), shifting from retrospective recognition to proactive forecasting, supported by a new annotated multi-case dataset and a reliability-aware framework combining cross-modal latent recovery and dual asynchronous memory. R3 regarded the task formulation as a highly meaningful contribution and the architecture as technically impressive. R1 moved from Weak Reject to Accept post-rebuttal, finding the main concerns — annotation protocol and inter-annotator agreement, dataset splits, segmentation quality, and evidence that robustness stems from the proposed mechanisms — substantially addressed. R2 maintained reject on clarity grounds, which the authors should take seriously.
On balance, the novel task, clear clinical motivation, dataset contribution, and a convincing rebuttal support acceptance. For camera-ready, authors should fold in the rebuttal clarifications, deliver the committed code/data release, and discuss the lack of external validation.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback. R1 appreciated the “conceptually clean” decoupling and “convincing” results; R2 valued a “meaningful step” toward proactive surgical safety; R3 recognized the “highly meaningful contribution” and “technically impressive” architecture.
Responses below:
1.Dataset construction & annotation (Meta, R1, R2, R3):
(i) Dataset. The dataset contains 3330 clips from 30 cases across four sites (esophagus/stomach/colon/rectum: 310/400/2200/420 clips) and three classes (no_interaction/approaching/touching: 1650/960/720 clips). All cases were split at the case level into 22 training and 8 testing cases (2430/900 clips), avoiding within-video leakage while preserving label/site distributions.
(ii) Annotation. Two trained annotators with 4+ years of endoscopic research experience independently labeled all clips, using the visible vessel–instrument relation at the target frame. For state-changing clips, the label follows the state at the 4th-s target frame. Initial agreement was 94.4% with Cohen’s kappa=0.90, and disagreements were resolved by consensus.
2.Task formulation & lead-time (R2, R3):
The task is a forecasting problem formulated as 3-class classification of the future interaction state. The model takes 16 frames from a 3-s observation window and predicts the state at the 4th-s target frame, yielding Δt=1s lead time. The anticipation signal in Fig.4 is the class-wise softmax probability on f^m (Eq.1), and its touching curve rises 0.5–1s before contact, supporting timely preventive response.
3.Method clarifications (Meta, R1, R2):
(i) CLR.
f_t^(8) is an intermediate ViT-B layer preserving spatial detail before semantic abstraction. Layer ablation over {6, 8, 10, 12} confirms layer 8 is optimal, outperforming the second-best setting, f_t^(10), by 1.73 Macro-F1.- 10-D geometry descriptor encodes spatial proximity (tip-vessel distance), motion (1st-/2nd-order changes, moving average), position (tip x, y), visibility (vessel area ratio, tip and vessel visibility), and topology (tip-inside-vessel).
(ii) Reliability terms. Two reliability signals are estimated before fusion: a_t^vis measures geometric observation stability and visibility from g_t, while a_t^align=[1+cos(h_t^f,h_t^g)]/2 measures consistency between the visual and geometric latent representations. (Fig.2 notation will be aligned with the text formula.)
(iii) Gating. ψ_t weights transient-memory readout, r_t (Eq.3) controls prototypal admission/compensation, and λ_t (Eq.5) balances transient and prototypal fusion.
(iv) Hyperparameters. Transient/prototypal memory sizes (8,20) perform best among 2–40, with nearby settings within 0.79 Macro-F1.Threshold τ=0.50 performs best over 0.3–0.7, and fusion weight λ_t (Eq.5) is learned end-to-end, with category-adaptive values shown in Fig.3(b).
4.Segmentation performance, impact & instrument tip (R1, R2):
Segmentation noise has limited impact due to our reliability-aware mechanisms. Vessel segmentation achieves Dice/IoU=84.64/73.37, and the visible active-tip center is manually annotated to isolate vessel-mask noise from tip-localization errors. Fig.3(a) analyzes visually unstable clips with inconsistent masks: F1 drops by 8.17 for our model vs. 32.84 for the baseline, showing that robustness arises from the proposed mechanisms rather than clean input. For prolonged unreliable spans, r_t blocks prototypal admission, preserving accumulated prototypes.
5.Failure analysis & clinical interpretation (R3):
Errors mainly arise in non-routine motion patterns and concentrate more on the ambiguous approaching class than on the safety-critical touching class, as shown in Tab.1 (F1=64.3 vs. 73.7). For clinical use, r_t filters low-reliability evidence, while sustained high-risk predictions support surgeon verification.
6.Code & data release (Meta, R1, R2):
We will open-source code, weights, and annotation protocol. The dataset will be released under a data-use agreement.

title: From Point Estimates to Distributions: GMM Pooling for MIL in Preterm Birth Prediction
abstract: Preterm birth (PTB) prediction can enable targeted surveillance and timely intervention, yet most ultrasound-based models use a single selected transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) frame per patient despite routine exams acquiring multiple cervical images. We formulate PTB prediction as a multiple instance learning (MIL) problem, representing each patient as a variable-sized bag of TVUS images with a single outcome label. To move beyond standard MIL aggregators that collapse a bag into a point estimate, we propose a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) pooling, which summarizes all images in a bag into a fixed-length representation by modeling their feature distribution. This design captures intra-patient variability. We evaluate the method on a private clinical cohort and on a public lymph node metastasis benchmark. For PTB prediction, GMM pooling improves over the instance-based model PR-AUC from 0.44  to 0.56. On the lymph node benchmark, it achieves state-of-the-art performance with 0.91 F1-score and 0.89 ROC-AUC for classification and 0.18 MAE for regression. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/HussainAlasmawi/GMM_Pooling.
subject_areas: Applications -> Outcome Prediction / Prognosis / Longitudinal Modeling
Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose a new method for using a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) to pool features from a variable number of instances (images) to create a fix-sized representation to feed into a classifier. Unlike previous approaches to this problem, the GMM approach has the advantage that it is able to capture inter-relationships between features. The method is validated on two tasks: pre-term birth prediction on a private trans-vaginal ultrasound and a public histopathology dataset.
reviews.text_strengths: The proposed pooling mechanism is well motivated and addresses an important theoretical limitation of other pooling methods. Min/mean/max pooling reduce instances to a single point estimate, which lacks expressiveness. Other attempts at representing a distribution over instances usually consider only marginals for each feature dimension. To my knowledge, this is the first attempt to explicitly formulate a trainable neural network architecture that captures a multidimensional distribution over instances. It seems reasonable to suppose that this would be important in solving certain types of pooling tasks.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Despite its potential theoretical advantages, the results are not especially compelling. On the preterm birth task, the task used to motivate the paper, the GMM pooling performs worse than much simpler baselines (max pooling, attention pooling), depending on the metric. Slight improvements are seen on the lymph node dataset classification task (but not the more challenging regression task), though this dataset is treated like an afterthought in the paper. 
Though I appreciate the general technical motivation for more advanced pooling mechanisms, it is not really clear to me why this is important in the PTB application. My understanding is that in clinical practice, cervical measurements are taken and this is used to predict the risk of pre-term birth. The authors do not adequately justify why automating the cervical measurement process would be insufficient and a more sophisticated (but less interpretable) classifier is necessary, and the vital comparison to using cervical measurements to predict risk (current practice) is not evaluated experimentally. 
The paper is also muddied by the inclusion of the segmentation part of the model, which is quite tangential to the main methodological contribution. The use of the features from the center of a UNet is rather unconventional, and is not the natural choice for evaluating the pooling methodology. I don’t understand why the choice of pooling mechanism for the intermediate features would have any effect on the segmentation branch, so it’s not clear to me what I can draw from the “Segmentation Dice” column of Table 1.Generally, the segmentation part of the paper is discussed little and does not add much to the paper.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
This may be a little tangential, but I am not convinced that it is correct or useful to describe this problem as multiple instance learning. It shares similarities with MIL in that it involves learning from a variably-sized bag in a permutation invariant way using a bag-level label. However, my understanding is that MIL has further assumptions: that each individual instance has a label and the label of the bag is that “ANY” operator over instance labels. Clearly when you need to model a full multidimensional distribution over feature vectors, the problem does not have these characteristics of MIL because all instances contribute to the label. This is not a critique of the formulation or the approach, merely a comment on terminology. I am also aware that others have stretched the definition of MIL (including reference [16] and going right back to ABMIL), so maybe it is too late. But I would suggest the authors consider whether this is the best terminology.
Is “K” in Figure 3 meant to be “P”?

Major factors are lack of performance benefit of the method over simpler baselines, and innapprorpriate matching of method to the clinical applications.
Nevertheless, I would encourage the authors to pursue their interesting methodological developments.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have understood the feedback from the reviewers, but their response does not change my opinion of the paper, which is that this is a technically interesting direction that I think will make a strong paper with further work, but that this particular presentation is muddled as it conflates application with method and involves extraneous components (the segmentation part), and does not convince me of the value of the approach empirically.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper formulates PTB prediction as a multiple instance learning (MIL) problem to address the limitation of insufficient information from a single image.
The authors propose a GMM pooling module to overcome the drawbacks of conventional point-estimate pooling methods.
Experiments on a private PTB dataset and a public lymph node dataset demonstrate that the proposed model achieves competitive performance.
reviews.text_strengths:
This paper formulates PTB as a MIL problem, which better conforms to clinical practice and has strong clinical utility.
The study is conducted on a cohort of clinically defined high-risk pregnant women, making the task more challenging and better reflecting the potential value of the model in real clinical settings.
Experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate the generality and robustness of the proposed distribution-based pooling strategy.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(1) This paper clarifies that density-based pooling does not explicitly model cross-dimensional dependencies in the feature space. Given that the authors propose GMM pooling to address this issue, how exactly does GMM pooling explicitly capture such dependencies?
(2) The study uses a small PTB dataset and therefore applies 5-fold cross-validation. However, it is unclear whether the data splitting was performed randomly and whether an independent test set was used.
(3) The differences in PR-AUC between GMM pooling, max pooling, and attention pooling are very small (below 0.01). Although the authors claim that GMM pooling is more stable, the paired t-test yields a p-value of 0.873, indicating no statistically significant difference. Thus, the observed lower standard deviation might merely reflect random fluctuation. Furthermore, GMM pooling involves two sets of attention weights: instance importance weights and soft instance-to-component responsibilities. Without clear performance gains, is attention pooling not simpler to implement and more suitable for real-world deployment?
(4) This paper lacks comprehensive ablation studies to verify the contribution of key components, such as the instance importance weights, soft instance-to-component responsibilities, and learnable probes.
(5) This study employs U-Net to segmentation, but what is the role of segmentation in the PTB task?
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper addresses a meaningful clinical task and presents a reasonable density-based MIL approach. However, experimental validation, and motivation of the proposed method need improvement.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The author have made efforts to address the concerns, and I maintain my original decision.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper attempt to improve how instance aggregation is performed in multiple instance learning (MIL) problem. Instead of collapsing the embedded features of each instance in a bag into a single-point with simple aggregator (max, mean, etc), the author proposed estimating their joint distribution with Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) prior to that.
reviews.text_strengths: The proposal of aggregating MIL features with GMM pooling is interesting. Conventional approaches aggregate feature of the instances in a bag into a single point. According to the author, this “create an information bottleneck by collapsing within-bag variability that may be informative for bag-level prediction”, to which I agree. Distribution-based MIL pooling aims at resolving this issue, but doesn’t capture inter-feature dependencies, which is addressed by the author in this work.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
the author noted that “all patients were prospectively classified as high-risk for PTB by the treating clinicians”, even though only 44 out of the 182 cases were eventually PTB. It would be nice to evaluate the method also on the low-risk cases, and I am concerned about whether there’s a sample selection bias here.
the author noted that “the comparison between GMM and max pooling showed no significant difference” on the preterm birth dataset, and did not report similar comparison on the lymph node dataset. i am curious about the advantage of using GMM pooling over the simpler methods.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

While there are minor weaknesses about the paper, the proposed method remains interesting, and may find wider applications across different MIL problems within the community.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors had addressed my concerns sufficiently, with a minor suggestion to rephrase the notion “all patients were prospectively classified as high-risk for PTB by the treating clinicians” to something along the line of “all patients were identified as high-risk for PTB following
by the treating clinicians".
I am keeping my opinion that GMM pooling is an interesting approach and may find broader applications within our community. Therefore I would recommend accepting the paper.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper received mixed reviews, including two weak accepts and one weak reject. The authors are invited to submit a rebuttal. The paper proposes a GMM-based pooling strategy for MIL, which reviewers considered an interesting attempt to address a limitation of conventional pooling methods: collapsing instance embeddings into a single point estimate. By modeling the distribution of instance embeddings, the method has potential value for capturing richer within-bag information. However, the reviewers raised several important concerns, including the lack of clear improvement over simpler baselines, insufficient clinical motivation for the preterm birth application, small dataset size, missing ablation studies, unclear role of the segmentation branch, and limited evidence of statistical significance. Overall, the method is potentially useful, but its practical advantage and empirical support require further clarification; therefore, the authors are invited to submit a rebuttal before a final decision is made.

After rebuttal, this paper receives three accept recommendations and one rejection. The AC acknowledges that the proposed GMM pooling strategy addresses an important limitation of conventional MIL pooling by modeling within-bag instance distributions rather than collapsing them into a single point estimate. Although the empirical gains on the preterm birth task are modest and the segmentation branch remains somewhat tangential, the rebuttal reasonably clarifies the methodological motivation, the role of segmentation as an auxiliary inductive bias, the patient-level cross-validation protocol, and how GMM pooling captures feature dependencies through mixture covariance. The majority of reviewers view the approach as technically interesting, generally well motivated, and potentially applicable beyond the presented tasks. Therefore, despite remaining concerns about limited clinical comparison, small dataset size, and marginal performance improvement over simpler baselines, the AC believes that the paper makes a useful methodological contribution to MIL and recommends acceptance.

This paper received two accept and one reject after rebuttal. I recommend rejection of this paper. The main reason is that this paper formulate a MIL problem, without comparing to sota instance aggretators in the MIL field. The MIL techniques, especially the instance feature aggregators, have developed very fast in recent years. These techniques are mostly used for pathology image analysis, which is also a task used for evaluation in this paper. There are too many aggregators that are more powerful than the simple baselines used in this paper.
GMM Pooling sounds technically interesting regardless of its limitations.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank reviewers for their comments and suggestions. We appreciate that R1 highlighted the novelty and strong theoretical motivation of GMM pooling, particularly its ability to capture feature distributions and inter-feature relationships compared with standard pooling approaches. We also appreciate that R2 noted the methodological contribution and clinical relevance, highlighting that the formulation aligns with practice and shows consistent behavior across datasets.
We also note that R4 found the approach interesting and valuable, especially for mitigating information loss in conventional MIL pooling and its potential applicability to broader problems.
Lack of performance advantage R1,R2,R4: We agree that GMM’s performance gains are marginal. However, GMM pooling addresses a representation limitation rather than optimizing only for predictive performance. Standard pooling collapses a bag to a single point, discarding intra-bag heterogeneity, while GMM models the instance distribution via multiple components. This is important in medical imaging, where variability is intrinsic. We observe consistently lower variance across runs, which may indicate improved robustness despite similar average performance. Weak clinical motivation R1: Yes, cervical length is a standard metric in clinical practice, but it is a rudimentary, subjective, and has limited predictive power [AJOG 2015, PMCID: PMC4675685]. Our goal is to assess whether full-image information can improve risk prediction by capturing clinically relevant imaging patterns beyond a single measure (e.g., cervical funneling and shape variations). Our model implicitly learns cervix characteristics through segmentation, resulting in a more comprehensive and consistent PTB risk assessment. Segmentation motivation unclear R1,R2: The segmentation branch is not a primary contribution; rather, it serves as an auxiliary task that encourages the model to learn anatomically meaningful features. This acts as an inductive bias, guiding the feature representation used for pooling and classification. The reported Dice scores are included for completeness, but the paper’s main focus is the pooling mechanism. We will revise the manuscript to better clarify the role of the segmentation branch as an auxiliary inductive bias. Dataset & evaluation R2,R4: The dataset size is limited, but the fetal application is unique. To ensure a rigorous evaluation, we perform 5-fold cross-validation with patient-level splits to prevent data leakage, repeated across 3 random seeds (15 runs), and report aggregated results. Given the cohort size, an independent held-out test set is not available, and cross-validation is standard practice in this setting. Regarding cohort composition, all patients were prospectively identified as high risk, reflecting the real-world clinical use of transvaginal ultrasound, where screening is not performed in the general population. This also makes the prediction task more challenging due to reduced class separability. We agree that evaluating on a broader population, including low-risk cases, would be valuable, and consider this an important direction for future work. We will clarify patient-level splitting in the revision. How GMM captures feature dependencies R2: GMM pooling represents a bag as a mixture of Gaussian components, where each component models feature relationships through its covariance structure. This allows dependencies between features to be captured. In contrast, density-based pooling treats each feature dimension independently, ignoring such relationships. Ablation analysis R2: While additional ablations could add detail, we emphasize that the paper already includes the most critical analyses (e.g., temperature and probes), which capture the core behavior of the method. Further ablations will be included in future work. Typo R1: Fig3: “K” → “P” thanks. We will revise the manuscript to clarify these points and incorporate the suggested improvements.

title: From Scanning Guidelines to Action: A Robotic Ultrasound Agent with LLM-Based Reasoning
abstract: Robotic ultrasound offers advantages over free-hand scanning, including improved reproducibility and reduced operator dependency. In clinical practice, US acquisition relies heavily on the sonographer’s experience and situational judgment. When transferring this process to robotic systems, such expertise is often encoded explicitly through fixed procedures and task-specific models, yielding pipelines that can be difficult to adapt to new scanning tasks. In this work, we propose a unified framework for autonomous robotic US scanning that leverages a large language model (LLM)–based agent to interpret US scanning guidelines and execute scans by dynamically invoking a set of provided software tools. Instead of encoding fixed scanning procedures, the LLM agent retrieves and reasons over guideline steps from scanning handbooks and adapts its planning decisions based on observations and the current scanning state. This enables the system to handle variable and decision-dependent workflows, such as adjusting scanning strategies, repeating steps, or selecting the appropriate next tool call in response to image quality or anatomical findings. Because the reasoning underlying tool selection is also critical for transparent and trustworthy planning, we further fine tune the LLM agent using a RL based strategy to improve both its reasoning quality and the correctness of tool selection and parameterization, while maintaining robust generalization to unseen guidelines and related tasks. We first validate the approach via verbal execution on 10 ultrasound scanning guidelines, assessing reasoning as well as tool selection and parameterization, and showing the benefit of RL fine tuning. We then demonstrate real world feasibility on robotic scanning of the gallbladder, spine, and kidney. Overall, the framework follows diverse guidelines and enables reliable autonomous scanning across multiple anatomical targets within a unified system.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper presents a unified and timely framework for autonomous robotic ultrasound scanning using an LLM-based agent. It translates scanning guidelines into dynamic tool use, integrating reasoning, planning, perception, and robot execution in a clinically relevant setting. Importantly, it achieves this without relying on heavily hand-crafted, task-specific pipelines, marking a meaningful step toward more general robotic ultrasound systems.
reviews.text_strengths:
Novel and Compelling Framework: The idea of translating scanning guidelines into dynamic tool use via an LLM-based agent is highly compelling and timely. 
Unified System: The framework successfully integrates reasoning, planning, perception, and robot execution within a single agentic pipeline. 
Generalizability: The contribution is highly meaningful because it does not rely on heavily hand-crafted, task-specific pipelines, which is an important step toward more general robotic ultrasound systems. 
Clinical Feasibility: The real-world demonstrations on multiple anatomical targets (gallbladder, spine, and kidney) significantly strengthen the practical value and clinical relevance of the work.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Guideline Construction & Retrieval: It would be helpful to clarify how the scanning guidelines are constructed, formatted, and retrieved in practice. Since the guideline database is an important part of the framework, more detail on how these instructions are written and organized would improve reproducibility. 
RL Fine-tuning Details: The RL fine-tuning component is interesting, but the design choices in the reward function could be discussed in more depth. For example, what motivated the specific weighting terms in Eq. 1–4, and how sensitive is the final performance to these choices?
Experimental Setup Clarity: For the verbal interaction experiments, it may be useful to further explain how the 20 guidelines were designed, how diverse they are, and to what extent the held-out guidelines differ from the training ones. 
Failure Mode Analysis: A brief discussion of failure modes—especially for the gallbladder case mentioned in the real-world experiments—would make the paper even stronger.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
There is also potential for more development in future directions. In particular, it would be interesting to know whether the proposed guideline-driven agent could be extended to additional anatomies, more complex interventional ultrasound settings, or broader human-robot collaborative imaging scenarios.

Overall, I find this to be a strong systems paper, and potentially among the first works to formulate robotic ultrasound in this guideline-driven agentic manner. The overall paper is written clearly and the main idea is easy to follow. The real-world experiments effectively demonstrate the system’s capabilities. While there are places where the writing could be polished slightly for conciseness and clarity, and some methodological details (e.g., guideline construction, RL reward design) need further elaboration, the core contribution is solid and well-presented. Therefore, I lean towards acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes an agentic framework designed to achieve autonomous robotic ultrasound (US) scanning. The primary contribution over existing work is the reasoning capability that interprets system states and observations to guide robotic actions.
reviews.text_strengths:
The introduction effectively contextualizes the problem, making the paper’s objectives and intended contributions easy to follow. The figures are well-designed, presenting the framework and pipeline clearly.
The methodology pragmatically leverages existing software tools, suggesting a framework that could be highly effective in practice.
The bridge between high-level LLM reasoning and low-level robotic control for specialized medical tasks like US scanning is highly relevant.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The authors claim “reasoning capability over state and observations” as a core contribution, yet the core method is unclear:
(1) There is no formal definition of what constitutes a “state” or an “observation” within this framework.
(2) It is unclear how raw sensory data and US images are converted into text-based tokens or descriptors that an LLM can process. Without this detail, the “reasoning” remains a “black box.”
2.The workflow for path generation and refinement lacks sufficient detail:
(1) Localization of organs: While skeletal atlas registration is mentioned, the paper does not explain how soft-tissue organs (e.g., kidneys) are localized relative to the skeletal landmarks.
(2) Path Definition: It is unclear if the scanning path is a simple linear interpolation between landmarks or another form that more sufficiently covers the anatomy.
(3) Refinement & Segmentation: The trajectory refinement section lacks citations and technical specifics. Crucially, the authors do not specify which algorithm or model is utilized for the 3D US segmentation.
3.Experimental Validation:
(1) While gallbladder scans include visual evidence, the results for spinal and kidney scans are presented only as text. Additional visual proof (e.g., reconstructed volumes or overlayed trajectories) or numerical results (e.g., success rates/reconstruction accuracy) will convince the reader better.
(2) The paper does not report results from repeated trials. Without metrics on success rates or variance of trajectories across multiple runs, it is hard to assess the system’s robustness or statistical significance.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The integration of LLMs into medical robotics is a timely and promising direction. The methodology is also sound and can be effective in practice. 
However, the technical depth and experimental rigor of the manuscript can be improved. Specifically, the “reasoning” mechanism based on states and observations requires further description, and the real experimental validation can be more solid. Therefore, the final decision depends on the rebuttal.

1.Developed a unified agentic system that uses LLMs to interpret clinical scanning handbooks via RAG, transforming static protocols into dynamic, decision-dependent robotic actions.

reviews.text_strengths: I appreciate the direction of this research, despite its imperfections. It effectively unleashes the reasoning potential of LLMs and provides a distinct advantage over other autonomous control schemes , even though its drawbacks are also clearly evident.

While this approach ensures the agent produces well-formatted and executable commands, it fails to bridge the gap between logical correctness and actual medical efficacy. Consequently, the model is incentivized to mimic reference traces rather than optimize for the best possible clinical outcome in a real-world setting.
The architecture reduces complex, high-stakes medical maneuvers into a simplified sequence of textual reasoning and discrete tool calls. This paradigm may work for rigid, standardized protocols, but it lacks the high-frequency haptic feedback and sub-millisecond responsiveness required for safe physical interaction, making its true clinical utility in doubt.

N/A

meta_reviews.text:
All the reviewers recognize the proposed LLM-based agentic framework as both novel and timely, specifically the unified pipeline and the clinical feasibility demonstrated through real-world anatomical scans, including the gallbladder, spine, and kidney.
In summary, the proposed work presents a significant and meaningful step in medical ultrasound robotics, and I lean towards early acceptance, However, authors should address the limitations raised by the reviewers, e.g. clarity of state/observation definition and sensor data to text conversion. author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank all reviewers for their thoughtful and constructive feedback. We are encouraged that the reviewers recognized the timeliness and relevance of our work, with R1 describing the idea of translating scanning guidelines into adaptive robotic scanning decisions via an LLM-based agent as “highly compelling and timely,” and R3 noting that the agentic approach offers a “compelling solution” with a “distinct advantage over other autonomous control schemes.” We also appreciate that R1 acknowledged the unified integration of reasoning, planning, perception, and robot execution, while R2 positively highlighted the clear problem contextualization, well-designed figures, and practical use of existing software tools. Importantly, R1 recognized the generalizability of our framework beyond hand-crafted, task-specific pipelines, and both R1 and R2 emphasized the relevance of bridging high-level LLM reasoning with low-level robotic control for robotic ultrasound. Finally, we thank R1 for recognizing that our real-world demonstrations on multiple anatomical targets strengthen the practical and clinical value of the work.
Our work proposes a guideline-driven agentic framework for autonomous robotic ultrasound, where the LLM serves as the high-level “brain” that retrieves scanning steps, reasons over the current state, and selects appropriate perception, planning, patient-guidance, and robot-execution tools. In contrast, the tools and low-level robot controllers act as the execution and reflex layers, handling real-time contact, force regulation, and robot motion. Therefore, the key contribution of this work is a unified hierarchical system that enables non-linear, decision-dependent scanning workflows beyond fixed rule-based pipelines, supported by RL fine-tuning and validated on held-out guidelines as well as real-world gallbladder, spine, and kidney scans
In this context, we would like to clarify the role of the LLM in our system (R3Q2 and R3Q4). The LLM is not intended for high-frequency physical control; instead, similar to human motor control, it performs high-level reasoning while dedicated low-level modules handle real-time contact, force regulation, and safety-critical interaction. Similarly, our RL fine-tuning is not designed to learn an unconstrained clinically optimal policy (R3Q1), but to make the LLM a reliable guideline-grounded planner. Given the dependence of robotic ultrasound on scanning guidelines and the risk of LLM hallucination, we intentionally prioritize faithful guideline following, correct tool selection, and valid parameterization, while recognizing patient-specific clinical optimization as an important future direction.
We also want to further clarify some minor implementation details regarding state representation (R2Q1) and path generation/refinement (R2Q2). Raw ultrasound and camera inputs are processed by the corresponding perception tools, whose outputs are returned to the LLM as structured text for high-level reasoning and tool selection. The current path generation is implemented as a simple trajectory connecting anatomical feature points. While more advanced path planning could be incorporated, this is not the main focus of the paper, and we will clarify this in the revision.
To further improve clarity and reproducibility, we will make several minor revisions following the reviewers’ suggestions. Specifically, we will briefly clarify guideline construction and the design of training/held-out guidelines, with code and guideline examples released for further details (R1Q1, R1Q3). We will also clarify the RL reward design (R1Q2), add a short failure-mode discussion for the gallbladder case (R1Q4), and strengthen experimental validation by adding repeated-trial numerical results and releasing an online video with additional visual evidence (R2Q3).

title: From Sparsity to Geometry: Spatial Modeling for 3D Reconstruction from Biplanar Bone X-rays
abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction from biplanar X-rays has high clinical values and remains technically challenging. Existing methods emphasize larger datasets and stronger networks, with less focus on spatial modeling. This usually works well for X-ray inputs with dense structural cues (e.g., chest). However, for inputs with sparse foreground  (e.g., long-bone), the impact of geometry unawareness might be significant and introducing such constraints may be helpful. Here, we introduce ExpGS (Explicit Gaussian Splatting), a spatial modeling framework that uses a fixed virtual biplanar geometry to eliminate per-case camera metadata at inference. By preserving non-degenerate anteroposterior/lateral ray constraints within a consistent frustum-intersection volume, it reduces background interference and stabilizes reconstruction. ExpGS reduces to canonical and implicit modeling as geometric constraints relax. Experiments were performed on two CT datasets with distinct content-sparsities, Femur (long bones) and LIDC (chest), whereby synthetic X-rays and matched virtual geometry were obtained from CT projections for training and testing. Results show that spatial modeling  confers only minor benefits to information-dense LIDC but substantially improves reconstruction stability (SSIM 86.13%) on the sparse Femur dataset, comparing both with other methods and with the two ablated forms of ExpGS. Our work establishes the importance of geometric constraints for content-sparse planar inputs such as long bones. Implementation is available at: https://github.com/HKUSZH/ExpGS.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposed to incorporate spatial modeling in 3D reconstruction from biplanar bone X-rays which had sparse contents.
reviews.text_strengths:
The idea is novel and motivated by an empirical observation of x-rays with sparse contents
The spatial modeling approach is intuitive and achieved by sampling multiple points along the 3D ray
The idea was validated using fermur bone x-ray dataset with significant performance gain achieved
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Effectiveness of the spatial modeling techniques was only verified in x-rays with sparse contents, not in more general setting such as lung x-rays.
Not much details were provided for implementation
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
More implementations are expected so that the reproducibility can be facilitated. Open-source codes or demons will be helpful.

Very interested and effective idea which is validated with sufficient experimental evidence.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes ExpGS, a spatial modeling framework for 3D reconstruction from biplanar X-rays based on explicit geometric constraints. The key idea is to impose a fixed virtual AP/LAT camera geometry and perform reconstruction via Gaussian splatting, enforcing non-degenerate ray intersections in a predefined frustum. The work compares three regimes: explicit, canonical, and implicit spatial modeling, under a controlled setup and shows that explicit geometry improves reconstruction stability, particularly in sparse anatomical settings such as long bones. Training is performed using multi-view 2D projection consistency loss, without direct 3D supervision.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Clear motivation and well-defined hypothesis
The paper isolates a specific factor: spatial/geometric modeling and studies its role in reconstruction quality under varying input sparsity. This is a focused and well-motivated research question.
2.Controlled experimental design (architectural side)
The comparison between explicit, canonical, and implicit modeling under the same backbone and training protocol is methodologically sound and allows attribution of performance differences to spatial assumptions rather than confounding factors.
3.Insight on sparsity vs geometry
The observation that explicit geometry matters more in low-information regimes (e.g., femur) than in dense settings (e.g., chest) is interesting and potentially valuable for the community.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Unclear and potentially flawed evaluation protocol:
The most serious concern is the evaluation setup, which is both unclear and potentially misleading: The model is trained and evaluated entirely on projections simulated from CT volumes.
The loss is defined only in projection space (2D), with no direct supervision on 3D geometry
Evaluation is performed on “held-out AP/LAT projections generated from the corresponding CT volumes”
However, the paper does not clearly specify:
how these “held-out” projections differ from the input AP/LAT views. Whether they correspond to different camera parameters, perturbations, or simply re-renderings under identical geometry.
This creates a fundamental ambiguity: It is unclear whether the model is evaluated on truly unseen projections or simply on projections generated under the same synthetic setup and geometry as the inputs.
This raises a concerns about evaluation circularity. If held-out AP/LAT projections are not meaningfully different from the conditioning inputs, the task risks becoming partially redundant.
2.No direct evaluation of 3D reconstruction quality
All metrics (SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS) are computed in projection space (2D), however, the method is framed as a 3D reconstruction approach, but it is not validated in 3D.
3.Synthetic-only setup
Both training and testing rely entirely on synthetic projections from CT. No validation on: real radiographs, mismatched geometry or noisy acquisition conditions.
4.Dataset limitations
Femur dataset is very small (34 volumes)
Results on LIDC show only marginal gains, suggesting limited impact in realistic dense scenarios
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The paper would significantly benefit from explicit clarification of:
how held-out projections are generated
how they differ from input views
Inclusion of true 3D evaluation metrics
Validation on real X-ray data
Comparison under geometry mismatch scenarios

While the paper addresses an interesting question regarding the role of spatial modeling in biplanar reconstruction and presents a controlled architectural comparison, the evaluation methodology is insufficient to support the main claims.
The most critical issue is that both training and evaluation are conducted entirely in projection space using synthetic data,
the notion of “held-out” projections is not clearly defined and
no 3D reconstruction accuracy is measured.
As a result, it is unclear whether the method truly improves 3D reconstruction or simply optimizes 2D projection consistency under a closed simulation setup.
Given these concerns, the paper does not meet the standards expected for a MICCAI contribution in its current form.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
After reading the rebuttal, I revise my assessment toward acceptance.
The rebuttal successfully clarifies the most important concern regarding the evaluation protocol and the interpretation of the “held-out projections.” In particular, the authors explain that the task is not AP/LAT-to-AP/LAT reprojection, but rather AP/LAT-conditioned reconstruction of a 3D Gaussian representation that is subsequently rendered across a full 72-view orbit. The evaluation therefore measures multi-view consistency on unseen test CT volumes, with the reported metrics dominated by novel-view renderings rather than the conditioning projections themselves. This clarification substantially resolves the concern about potential evaluation circularity.
I also appreciate the clarification that the work intentionally follows a projection-supervised 3DGS/NeRF-style reconstruction paradigm rather than direct voxel-supervised reconstruction. Within this formulation, the use of rendered-view metrics is consistent with related recent literature. While the lack of direct 3D evaluation remains a limitation, I no longer consider it a fatal methodological issue.
The rebuttal also adequately contextualizes the synthetic-only setup. The authors correctly position the work as a controlled methodological study designed to isolate the role of spatial modeling under known geometry and sparse anatomical conditions, rather than as a clinically deployable reconstruction system. The discussion regarding why explicit geometry provides larger benefits in sparse settings than in dense chest anatomy is coherent and aligns with the reported experimental observations.
The paper still has limitations. Validation on real radiographs, robustness to geometry mismatch and acquisition noise, and direct 3D geometric evaluation would strengthen the claims further. In addition, the femur dataset remains relatively small. However, these limitations are now clearly acknowledged and do not invalidate the core methodological contribution.
I believe the rebuttal resolved the main ambiguity underlying my initial concerns. The paper presents a focused and well-controlled study on the role of explicit spatial modeling for sparse biplanar reconstruction, and I support acceptance.

The proposed method combines a transformer/MLP-based model with explicit spatial constraints, to improve performance on sparse datasets. The method is evaluated on two X-ray datasets.
