I am not an expert in this topic, but this seems a nicely presented method for the sparse reconstruction problem, with a method that improves on prior work.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The paper presents a fairly systematic approach to an interesting problem. I agree with the other reviewers that sharing the code would be helpful, and I am happy to see that the rebuttal includes a promise to publish the code on acceptance.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper presents a novel and well-motivated approach to incorporating explicit geometric constraints for biplanar 3D reconstruction, with promising results, particularly in sparse settings. While reviewers appreciate the methodological clarity and controlled experimental design, there are notable concerns regarding the evaluation protocol (e.g., reliance on synthetic data and projection-space metrics), limited validation of true 3D reconstruction quality, and reproducibility details. Given the mixed assessments, I invite the authors to provide a rebuttal addressing these issues, particularly clarifying the evaluation setup and strengthening evidence for 3D reconstruction performance.

The authors have addressed the reviewers’ comments. Discussion on the evaluation should be expanded, especially regarding why 3D evaluation was not conducted.

The decision is to accept the paper. The authors propose an effective method incorporating explicit geometric constraints for biplanar 3D reconstruction which performs particularly well in sparse anatomical settings. During the rebuttal phase they successfully clarified critical misunderstandings regarding the evaluation protocol by explaining that the performance metrics reflect novel view renderings across a full orbit.

I recommend acceptance. The paper presents a focused and well-motivated study of explicit spatial modeling for 3D reconstruction from biplanar X-rays, with particular benefit in sparse anatomical settings. The core idea is intuitive, technically clear, and supported by controlled comparisons between explicit, canonical, and implicit spatial modeling strategies.
The rebuttal substantially addressed the main concern about the evaluation protocol. In particular, the authors clarified that AP/LAT views are used as conditioning inputs, while the predicted 3D Gaussian representation is evaluated through rendering over a 72-view orbit on unseen test CT volumes. This resolves the earlier concern that the method may only be performing redundant AP/LAT reprojection. The authors also clarified implementation details and committed to code release.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their helpful, thoughtful feedback. Our responses are as below:
Q1 Verification of spatial modeling effectiveness (R1)
A1: We also validated on LIDC chest/lung data, representing dense anatomy. While LIDC lacks the same controlled ablation as femur, the compared methods cover explicit (ExpGS), canonical (DIF-Gaussian, PerX2CT), and implicit (DiT, X2CT-GAN) paradigms, providing complementary evidence in dense anatomy.
Q2 Implementation details and reproducibility (R1, R3)
A2: Implementation details: ResNet-50 encoder; 8-layer Transformer (8 heads, d=512); N=64 depth samples; 256^2 resolution; Adam (lr=1e-4, batch=4). Supervision: 72 views/CT, 4 sampled views/iteration. Code will be released upon acceptance.
Q3 Evaluation protocol, held-out projections, and potential circularity (R2)
A3: We apologize for the imprecise wording. We confirm that Table 1 reports metrics averaged over all 72 rendered views per test CT, not just AP/LAT. The actual protocol: 72 DRRs per CT (5° intervals); AP/LAT are inputs; 4 random views sampled as supervision during training; at evaluation, the predicted Gaussian field is rendered to all 72 views and compared to ground truth. Thus, the task is AP/LAT –> 3D representation –> multiview rendering, not 2D-to-2D copying. To clarify, the 72-view evaluation spans the full angular orbit; two re-rendered views at the AP/LAT angles are kept to ensure full orbit coverage, and the reported metrics are dominated by novel-view renderings (70/72).
Here, “held-out” refers to unseen test CT volumes (e.g. 8 testing CTs in Femur, and 100 LIDC test cases), where AP/LAT views are given as inputs and the predicted 3D field is rendered around the orbit. We will correct the misleading phrase “held-out AP/LAT projections” in the manuscript.
Q4 Projection-space loss and no direct 3D supervision (R2)
A4: Although CT volumes are available for DRR generation in this controlled study, our training objective intentionally follows projection-supervised 3DGS/NeRF-style reconstruction rather than voxel regression. We agree direct 3D evaluation would further strengthen the claim.
Q5 3D quality evaluation (R2)
A5: We acknowledge the lack of direct 3D metrics is a limitation. Our focus is a geometry-consistent multi-view Gaussian representation; rendered-view metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) are commonly used for 3DGS-based medical reconstruction (3DGR-CAR by Fu et al. 2024; Gaussian Pancakes by Bonilla et al. 2024). Direct voxel-level evaluation requires converting 3DGS into voxels with a standardized protocol, which may introduce extra variables. We will clarify this limitation and evaluation scope.
Q6 Synthetic-only setup (R2)
A6: We acknowledge that synthetic projections cannot prove generalization to real clinical X-rays. We use CT-derived projections as a controlled setting to compare spatial modeling under known geometry, consistent views, and clear supervision. This setting is admittedly idealized, but avoids ethical (dosage) and physical challenges, and is commonly used in recent related methodological works, such as VolumeNeRF (MICCAI 2024) and DCT-Net (MICCAI 2025). Thus, our experiments are controlled projection-supervised validation, not clinical-deployment validation; real X-ray generalization, geometry mismatch, noise, and domain adaptation remain future work.
Q7 Small femur dataset and marginal gains on LIDC (R2, R3)
A7: We agree that the Femur set is relatively small (n=34), reflecting the scarcity of long-bone CT data. Our LIDC scale ablation (Fig. 4) shows that even at 5% training data (45 cases, comparable to Femur scale), all methods remain stable, confirming that the conclusion is driven by spatial modeling rather than data scale. Marginal LIDC gains are expected: explicit geometry benefits sparse inputs (femur) more than dense anatomy (chest), consistent with the main findings of our work.

title: From Trajectories to Phenotypes: Disease Progression as Structural Priors for Multi-organ Imaging Representation Learning
abstract:
Imaging-derived phenotypes (IDPs) summarize multi-organ physiology but provide only static snapshots of diseases that evolve over time. In contrast, longitudinal electronic health records encode disease trajectories through temporal dependencies among past diagnosis events and comorbidity structure. We hypothesize that IDPs and disease trajectories contain partially shared disease-relevant structure.
We propose a trajectory-aware distillation framework that transfers structural knowledge from a generative disease trajectory Transformer into an organ-wise IDP encoder. A population-scale trajectory model trained on longitudinal diagnosis sequences produces subject-level embeddings that supervise IDP representation learning via geometry-preserving alignment. During downstream prediction, trajectory and imaging representations can also be fused via cross-attention.
Across 159 diseases in the UK Biobank cohort, trajectory-aware pretraining consistently improves both discrimination (AUC) and time-to-onset prediction (MAE), with the largest gains for low-prevalence diseases. Similarity relationships in IDP embedding space also align with those in trajectory space, providing supportive evidence for partially aligned representation geometry.
These results suggest that population-scale generative disease models can serve as structural priors for data-limited imaging modalities, improving robustness under realistic cohort constraints.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs
Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning
Special Topic -> AI for Neglected Diseases & Limited-Resource Settings
Special Topic -> AI for Population Health, Public Health & Epidemiology

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a distillation framework that transfers disease progression knowledge from a EHR-based trajectory transformer into a multi-organ imaging phenotype encoder. The pre-trained imaging transformer demonstrated improved classification performance across diseases. The overall idea of leveraging population-scale longitudinal EHR data to enrich imaging-based disease prediction is interesting and practically motivated.
reviews.text_strengths: The core idea of borrowing structural knowledge from large-scale longitudinal EHR data to guide imaging predictors is well-motivated and practically useful. The framework is evaluated across a large number of diseases with a carefully partitioned cohort design that attempts to prevent information leakage. The comparison of different alignment objectives provides useful insight into how distillation loss choice affects downstream performance for classification versus time-to-onset prediction tasks.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The major concern is a potential information leakage issue that undermines the fairness of the comparison, particularly for the fusion model. Since the fusion model directly uses each evaluation subject’s own pre-imaging trajectory embedding, the model may already have direct access to prior diagnosis of the disease being predicted or closely related comorbidities. A fair evaluation would require predicting only diseases with first onset strictly after the imaging visit. In addition, I have some concerns regarding the disagreement of IDP similarity and trajectory similarity (Fig. 3). Despite the positive correlation, the IDP similarity is very low while the trajectory similarity is generally above 0.8.Also, the confidence interval in fig 3b is not consistent with Fig. 3a, where IDP similarity spans a much wider range at any given trajectory similarity. This result to some extent challenges the claim that imaging and trajectory representations share a common latent disease manifold. 
Finally, several methodological details including the specific imaging modalities, organ systems, and IDP selection criteria are never clearly stated.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The major concern is a potential information leakage issue in the fusion model, which directly uses each evaluation subject’s own pre-imaging trajectory embedding at inference time. For chronic and recurring diseases this gives the model direct access to prior diagnosis information, making the comparison against the scratch imaging model unfair. The paper’s central claim of a shared latent disease manifold is also not convincingly supported in Fig 3.The major positive point is in the improved performance pre-trained IDP encoder, which only leveraged the knowledge from population-wide longitudinal EHR.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: Addressing the broad challenge of disease progression modelling, the authors present a method that a) uses ICD-codes based patient trajectories as priors to guide pretraining of an encoder that produces predictive embeddings from Image-Derived Phenotypes (IDP) [which they call their trajectory-distillation framework], and b) fuses information from temporal disease trajectories with static IDPs to show improved predictive performance on disease occurrence and time-to-event (disease) prediction.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Novel Method: Using ICD trajectory embeddings as structural priors is an interesting formulation, and the authors show that it helps learn embeddings from IDPs which boost prediction performance on disease forecasting, especially in low-prevalence disease. This could be a useful paradigm even outside of this context, in the larger scope of learning with asynchronous modalities recorded at different time resolutions. 
2.Experimental designs are sound and rigorous, with the baselines of IDPs and trajectory embeddings providing meaningful context to interpret their results. 
3.Post-hoc analysis of disease-wise gains in AUC is further informative.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The “shared latent manifold” hypothesis for IDP and disease trajectories is hard to digest. While I understand the intuition, I am not convinced that the experiments and results support the claim. The spearman of 0.166 on the permutation test on pairwise IDP and trajectory embeddings is significant, however the following could be confounders:
a. Age, BMI, Sex: Controlling for these in the experiment would give a stronger support for the shared latent manifold theory, since these could be potential confounders that cause similar embeddings in both spaces. This is because, as I understand it, the claim is that the disease progression trajectory and IDP share a common latent manifold (independent of demographics). If this is not the claim, then could the authors please clarify? 
b. The InfoNCE Alignment objective: The embeddings are learned by aligning projections of the embeddings using contrastive learning. This alignment might be driving the pairwise similarity, in which case the effect is a result of the training strategy not a natural phenomenon. It would be more meaningful to do the same experiment but on the non-pretrained embeddings [as a suggestion for future work]. 
2.Unclear Writing: Some parts of the paper could be rewritten for clarity. [See Comments below] 
3.Missing Discussion of Limitations, Related Work and Future Work: I understand that the authors show extensive experiments, and there is an 8-page limit, but there is no discussion of related work on predicting disease progression on IDPs, or disease trajectories, or even mention of related technical works [Contrastive Representation Distillation, ICLR 2020]. Most importantly, there is no discussion of limitations or implications for use in future research, which is important for any reader trying to interpret these results.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1.Writing and Experimental Details:
a. The abstract and introduction mention “temporal dependencies and comorbidity structures” : For example, “Disease progression is governed by temporal dependencies and comorbidity relationships that cannot be fully captured by static imaging measurements alone.” It is unclear to the reader (who hasn’t read ahead) what temporal dependencies are being referred to. I think the authors might mean to say “temporal dependencies in past disease diagnosis.” 
b. The Methods Section mentions: “Training objective. The model is trained with a joint objective consisting of next-event cross entropy and a time-to-next-event likelihood term that models the distribution of inter-event time gaps” – Could the authors please clarify how they modelled the time-to-next-event term (the distribution on the inter-event time gaps).
2.I would be interested in the authors’ comments about the issues mentioned with the Shared Latent Manifold Hypothesis. I understand that this is a conference paper, so extensive experimentation could be out of scope, and I think this paper should be presented at MICCAI either ways, but it is important to discuss the interpretation and limitations of their results. 
3.In a related sense, the missing discussion of limitations, related works should be addressed by the authors.

I think this work should be accepted and discussed at MICCAI but the paper could be improved (preferably addressing the points in the comments section) before publication.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a trajectory-aware distillation framework that transfers disease progression knowledge from a generative EHR-based trajectory model to an imaging-derived phenotype (IDP) encoder via representation alignment. It shows that incorporating trajectory-informed structure improves disease prediction, especially for low-prevalence conditions, and enables effective fusion of longitudinal and imaging data.
reviews.text_strengths:
Clean experimental design to prevent subject and temporal leakage
Intuitive and interesting motivation for using temporal trajectories to enrich static IDPs
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Some central claims are only supported by weak correlations, making the evidence less convincing.
Experiments are conducted on a single dataset (UK Biobank) and mainly compare internal variants.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
I have concerns about the strength of evidence supporting some key claims. In particular, the prevalence-dependent trend in Fig. 2b appears weak (low correlation and marginal significance), and the representation alignment results in Fig. 3 are based on relatively small effect sizes. I suggest either moderating these claims or providing stronger supporting analyses.
I think the experimental evaluation could be strengthened. Table 1 mainly presents internal comparisons (e.g., scratch vs. pretrained, different fusion strategies), but lacks comparison to strong prior baselines such as EHR-based models (e.g., BEHRT, Med-BERT) or multimodal methods without distillation. This makes it difficult to assess how the proposed method compares to existing approaches.
The model descriptions are somewhat unclear, particularly in Table 1.The differences between “IDP Baseline,” “IDP Organ (Transformer),” and the fusion models are not fully specified. Providing a clearer taxonomy or summary table of model variants would improve readability and reproducibility.
All experiments are conducted on a single dataset (UK Biobank). I think evaluating additional cohorts, if feasible, would strengthen the claims about generalizability.

The contribution appears somewhat incremental, building on existing distillation and contrastive alignment frameworks. In addition, the evaluation lacks rigorous comparison to strong prior work, making it difficult to assess the true advantage of the proposed method.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text: Overall all reviewers found this manuscript presents a useful and interesting algorithm for MICCAI. I am recommending this manuscript for acceptance. Authors in the final version of the manuscript, I recommend addressing the information leakage (R1) and limitations of the comparison methods (R3).

author_feedback_text:
Dear Area Chair and Reviewers,
We sincerely thank all reviewers for the constructive feedback and positive assessment of our work. We are encouraged that the reviewers found the proposed trajectory-aware distillation framework interesting and potentially useful for MICCAI. Our primary goal is to evaluate whether longitudinal disease trajectories can provide useful structural priors for multi-organ IDP representation learning under realistic imaging-cohort constraints, rather than to claim definitive evidence for a universal disease manifold.
Leakage and Prediction Setting (R1, Meta-review)
We agree that the evaluation protocol should be clarified more explicitly. Our downstream prediction setting follows an incident-only risk-set design with imaging as baseline. For each target disease, subjects with diagnosis onset at or before imaging are excluded as prevalent cases, and positives therefore correspond only to incident post-imaging cases. Controls are sampled from subjects who had already undergone imaging and remained event-free at the corresponding case time. Thus, the task is future-onset prediction after imaging rather than current-state classification.
To further prevent temporal leakage, trajectory embeddings used for distillation and downstream fusion are computed only from diagnosis records strictly prior to imaging acquisition. In addition, the downstream IDP-only and fusion pipelines explicitly exclude target-derived variables such as
label
and
delta_time
from the feature set, with runtime leakage checks. We will revise the manuscript to make this protocol explicit and easier to follow.
Shared Structure Claim (R1, R2, R3)
We agree that our current evidence should not be framed as definitive proof of a shared latent disease manifold. The observed alignment between IDP and trajectory similarity is statistically significant but modest, and should be interpreted as preliminary empirical evidence consistent with partially aligned disease-relevant structure. We will moderate the relevant wording accordingly.
Baselines and Scope (R3, Meta-review)
Our design isolates the effect of trajectory-informed priors through controlled comparisons across IDP-only, trajectory-only, and fusion settings, rather than through an exhaustive benchmark. We agree that the absence of broader comparisons to EHR and multimodal methods is a limitation of the current study. In our formulation, models such as BEHRT and Med-BERT can also be viewed as alternative trajectory encoders/teachers rather than only downstream baselines, and exploring such alternatives is an important direction for future work.
Methods (R1, R2, R3)
We will clarify the problem formulation, the Delphi trajectory-teacher objective, and the role of trajectory-aware distillation in the Methods more clearly. We will also expand the IDP description: the 301 quantitative phenotypes cover five system-level groups, namely brain MRI grey-matter volumes, skeleton/body-composition measures, cardiac MRI traits, abdominal MRI traits, and pulmonary measures including spirometry and lung volume. The IDP baseline operates on concatenated IDPs, whereas the organ-aware variants group features by organ and aggregate them by concat, weighted pooling, or a transformer.
Overall, we will revise the manuscript to (1) make the leakage-prevention and evaluation protocol fully explicit, (2) reduce overclaiming regarding manifold-sharing interpretations, (3) improve methodological clarity and model taxonomy, and (4) strengthen discussion of limitations, external validation, alternative trajectory models, and future directions.
We thank the reviewers again for their thoughtful comments and suggestions.

title: FSE-Reg: Enhancing 3D Deformable Registration with Frozen Large-Scale Pre-trained Segmentation Encoders
abstract: Learning-based deformable registration enables fast feed-forward inference, yet robustness to limited training data and domain shifts remains challenging. We propose FSE-Reg, which reuses a shared frozen backbone from large-scale pre-trained 3D segmentation encoders as an anatomy-aware feature space for correspondence learning. Built on this fixed representation, FSE-Reg uses a standard coarse-to-fine residual pyramid decoder and a multi-scale feature-level similarity constraint in the frozen feature space, providing anatomy-aware matching cues without segmentation outputs or labels. We further design a lightweight Difference-Product Interaction Fusion module (DPI-Fuse) to explicitly model mismatch and agreement signals for flow refinement. Experiments on abdominal CT and brain MRI benchmarks demonstrate improved accuracy with plausible deformations and strong external generalization without fine-tuning, compared with intensity-driven networks, joint segmentation–registration pipelines, and foundation-feature-based matching approaches. Code will be made publicly available in a future release.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes FSE-Reg, a 3D deformable registration framework that reuses a shared and frozen 3D segmentation encoder as an anatomically aware feature backbone. The proposed model leverages a large-scale pretrained 3D segmentation encoder backbone in a frozen manner and learns a coarse-to-fine residual decoder for deformation estimation. In addition, by incorporating multi-scale feature-space similarity constraints and DPI-Fuse-based interaction refinement, the method improves registration accuracy by encouraging more natural deformations and achieving meaningful generalization performance without additional fine-tuning of the backbone.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The overall framework and motivation of the proposed method are described in a clear and accessible manner, and the importance of the method as well as its key contributions are generally well explained.
2.In conventional segmentation-assisted deformable registration approaches, output-level cues such as masks or pseudo-labels may be directly affected by registration errors or be vulnerable to domain shift. In this regard, it is interesting that the present work addresses this issue from the perspective of multi-scale feature-level similarity constraints, and proposes a structure that progressively refines the registration field at the feature-representation level rather than directly transferring output-level cues.
3.Compared with joint segmentation-registration learning-based deformable registration methods, which often suffer from high computational cost and complex multi-stage training procedures, this paper presents a comparatively efficient learning pipeline by employing a frozen 3D backbone and introducing decoder designs such as the DPI-Fuse module.
4.The experiments are designed in a sufficiently diverse manner to support the validity of the proposed framework, and the overall performance improvements achieved by the method make the paper reasonably convincing.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Although the proposed framework provides detailed analyses and meaningful results, the claim of meaningful generalization without fine-tuning on unseen datasets could be better supported by additional experiments with a wider variety of 3D backbones. Such analyses would provide stronger evidence for the authors’ claim.
2.The main novelty of the paper appears to lie in the overall framework design, and among its components, the DPI-Fuse module seems to be one of the key novel elements. However, based on the ablation study, the contribution of DPI-Fuse to performance improvement does not appear sufficiently prominent, which leaves some room for doubt regarding the independent effectiveness of this module.
3.Although the overall results are well presented, Fig. 2 is less effective in illustrating registration quality. The small image size and boxed regions make local differences difficult to compare, and a more direct comparison with the fixed images would improve the qualitative presentation.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

As there are many strengths in the proposed method, I have rated as weak accept.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes FSE-Reg, a deformable registration framework that reuses a shared frozen large-scale pre-trained 3D segmentation encoder as the backbone, avoiding the need to train a registration encoder from scratch. On top of this frozen feature space, the method introduces a multi-scale feature-level similarity constraint to provide anatomy-aware matching cues, together with a lightweight Difference-Product Interaction Fusion (DPI-Fuse) module for flow refinement. Although the methodological novelty is incremental, the framework is technically sound and demonstrates strong empirical performance.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The proposed framework is cleanly structured: the frozen encoder provides stable multi-scale anatomical features, while the trainable decoder performs deformation estimation on top. The DPI-Fuse module, although lightweight, is a reasonable interaction design that explicitly models both mismatch and agreement cues between fixed and moving features, which is intuitive and well integrated into coarse-to-fine flow refinement.
2.The experimental results are convincing and represent the strongest aspect of the paper. FSE-Reg consistently outperforms competitive baselines across multiple datasets, with particularly clear gains on external datasets (AMOS and DIR-QA) without fine-tuning. 
3.The paper includes extensive comparisons across multiple backbones, multiple datasets, qualitative visualizations, early-stage convergence analysis, and ablation studies. The ablation experiments clearly demonstrate the contribution of each component.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The paper emphasizes that only a lightweight deformation decoder is trained on top of the frozen encoder, but the actual computational complexity is not clearly quantified. The paper does not report decoder parameter counts, total trainable parameters, FLOPs, runtime, or memory usage compared with baseline registration methods. Including such analysis would better substantiate the claimed efficiency advantage.
2.Although DPI-Fuse is shown to be effective in the ablation study, its evaluation is limited to removal-based comparisons. The paper does not compare DPI-Fuse against stronger alternative interaction mechanisms such as correlation-based fusion, attention-based fusion, or simpler competitive baselines like concat-only fusion. As a result, it is difficult to determine whether the proposed fusion design is uniquely advantageous.
3.While the framework is technically sound and practically effective, the main contributions are largely based on integrating existing ideas in a well-engineered manner rather than introducing a fundamentally new registration paradigm. The paper’s value lies more in strong empirical validation than in conceptual novelty.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I recommend Weak Accept because the paper presents a technically sound and practically useful registration framework with strong empirical results. The proposed method is well designed, and the experiments are convincing, with consistent improvements over strong baselines across multiple datasets, including robust performance in no-fine-tuning external evaluation settings. The ablation studies are also comprehensive and clearly support the contribution of each component.
The main weaknesses are that the methodological novelty is somewhat incremental, the claimed lightweight design lacks quantitative complexity analysis, and DPI-Fuse is not compared against stronger alternative fusion baselines. Despite these limitations, the paper demonstrates clear practical value and solid experimental validation, which justifies acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces a novel image registration framework with three main contributions: using a pre-trained and frozen 3D segmentation encoder as the encoder of the registration network, deep supervision through encouraging warped feature maps to be close to the fixed feature maps, and DPI-Fuse.
reviews.text_strengths:
There are quite a few interesting ideas/results in this work.
1.The authors demonstrate in Fig. 3 that by using a frozen encoder, there is less parameter to train, which results in faster convergence during training. The faster convergence can also be attributed to the fact that using a frozen pre-trained encoder disentangles representation learning (encoder) from learning deformation fields (decoder). Therefore, the decoder only need to focus on predicting deformation fields from already information-rich features.
2.The idea that one can use a pre-trained 3D segmentation encoder as the encoder for the registration network is quite interesting and the motivation is for this idea is strong. The pre-trained 3D segmentation encoder is trained on a segmentation task, and is thus able to extract richer features with anatomy-related information, which is potentially helpful for image registration task. Furthermore, the authors argue that doing so also allow them to perform what they call feature-space anatomical consistency.
3.The motivation for DPI-Fuse makes sense and results in improvement in performance. Specifically, the authors claim that difference captures mismatch and product captures agreement, both of which are important for image registration task.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The novelty of the work is somewhat limited. 
1.The idea of using an pre-trained and frozen feature extractor (contribution 1) instead of relying on intensity information is not new. A somewhat related but old idea was introduced in HAMMER by Shen D, et al., IEEE TMI, 2002 (https://doi.org/10.1109/tmi.2002.803111). There was no pre-trained networks back then but the idea is similar, i.e., relying on higher dimensional features instead of intensity information alone.
2.As far as I know, not a lot of work explore deep supervision in the context of image registration. However, the idea of enforcing consistency in the feature-space is still somewhat standard and simple. This essentially boils down to introducing an additional loss term that computes dissimilarity between warped and fixed feature maps at different resolutions.
The clarity of the paper can be greatly improved. 
1.At the end of section 1, the authors introduce DPI-Fuse and claim that it is used for “explicit difference/product interactions”. However, it is unclear at this point what difference/product interaction mean and how this interaction is potentially helpful for image registration.
2.Section 2.2 is quite verbose. The entire section can be summarized as follows. Intensity-based dissimilarity is ambiguous while feature-based dissimilarity is more informative. Therefore, an additional loss term based on cosine-similarity is included that quantifies dissimilarity between warped and fixed feature maps at different resolution levels. Consider making this section more concise. 
3.The line right after equation (1). What does (\cdot)(p) mean? This notation is not standard and is hard for the readers to understand.
4.In Section 2.3, the “difference term” makes sense. However, it is unclear why the “product term” quantifies agreement. It might be helpful to elaborate on this.
The results are not convincing. 
1.In Table 1, it is somewhat strange that VoxelMorph and TransMorph have very poor performance. Are they fully and properly trained to convergence? It would also be helpful to include a baseline using conventional methods (e.g., ANTs’ SyN). 
2.The authors claim at the bottom of page 6 that scaling SAT backbone from Nano to Pro improves performance. However, the authors then claim that stronger pre-trained encoder yields stronger performance. This is indeed the case for SAT Nano vs. Pro but is not the case for STU-Net-S/B/L/H. A similar trend is not observed. The authors might wish to provide some explanation for why a similar pattern is not seen with STU-Net.
3.Since the percentage of non-positive Jacobian determinant is relatively large, the authors might wish to include visualization of the deformation fields so that the readers can better understand whether the model is able to produce great performance in terms of Dice/TRE while maintaining smoothness/regularity of the deformation field.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This work is very borderline. The three main contributions are not trivial, but they are not substantial either, especially the first two contributions. However, the work presents an interesting idea, i.e., one can directly use (and freeze) the encoder of a pre-trained segmentation network as the encoder of a registration network, which I believe is worth sharing with the rest of the community doing image registration.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text: This paper proposes FSE-Reg, a 3D deformable registration framework that utilizes a frozen, pre-trained segmentation encoder as an anatomically aware feature backbone. The reviewers consistently highlight the framework’s efficient design, which simplifies training by disentangling representation learning from deformation estimation, and acknowledge the effectiveness of the multi-scale feature-space similarity constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the method achieves competitive performance and strong generalization across various datasets without additional fine-tuning. However, concerns were raised regarding the incremental nature of the methodological novelty, the lack of quantitative complexity analysis for the decoder, and the need for more rigorous comparisons of the DPI-Fuse module against alternative fusion mechanisms. Despite these limitations, the reviewers reached a consensus that the work is technically sound and practically valuable, providing scores of 4 (Weak Accept), 4 (Weak Accept), and 4 (Weak Accept).

title: FunPiQ: A New Benchmark for Pixel-Level Quality Assessment in Fundus Images
abstract: Color fundus photography (CFP) is the most common ophthalmic imaging modality for large-scale screening. However, it is highly susceptible to degradations, making robust fundus image quality assessment (FIQA) crucial. The criteria for what constitutes high-quality at the image level vary across clinical tasks, making FIQA dependent on expert knowledge. This motivated the development of automated methods and datasets. While existing datasets aim to standardize image-level quality, their criteria often differ. Furthermore, image-level labels preclude the quantitative evaluation of localized degradations, which is essential for trustworthy FIQA. We argue that pixel-level FIQA based on anatomical visibility represents a more task-agnostic, explainable approach. In this work, we introduce FunPiQ, the first FIQA benchmark to provide pixel-level quality annotations. In addition, we propose EFIQA-CP, an explainable-by-design (EBD) method that uses quality pseudo-labels based on anatomical visibility to train a CNN via Non-Negative Positive-Unlabeled learning. Extensive evaluations of classification methods with post-hoc explanations, anomaly detection methods, and EBD methods demonstrate the superior performance of the last and, particularly, of EFIQA-CP. Our code, weights, and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/penway/FunPiQ

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces FunPiQ, the first benchmark dataset for fundus image quality assessment (FIQA) that provides pixel-level quality annotations based on anatomical visibility. Additionally, it proposes EFIQA-CP, an “Explainable-by-Design” (EBD) framework. This model improves upon the existing EFIQA by incorporating a shallow CNN adapter for better global context and utilizing Non-Negative Positive-Unlabeled (nnPU) learning to mitigate the noise in anatomical pseudo-labels.
reviews.text_strengths:
Novel Dataset: The introduction of pixel-level annotations is a significant step forward from traditional image-level labels, addressing the need for fine-grained, task-agnostic quality assessment.
Methodological Soundness: Transitioning from post-hoc explanations to an “Explainable-by-Design” approach enhances the clinical trustworthiness of the AI system.
Addressing Label Noise: The use of nnPU learning is a clever and scientifically justified way to handle the inherent noise in pseudo-labels derived from anatomical segmentations.
Comprehensive Evaluation: The paper compares the proposed method against a wide range of baselines, including anomaly detection and post-hoc explanation methods.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Incomplete Technical Specifications: The manuscript lacks critical training details. There is no mention of the optimizer used, specific learning rates, batch sizes, or data augmentation strategies, which hinders reproducibility.
Ambiguous Clinical Translation: While the pixel-level Dice and QWK scores show improvement, the paper does not sufficiently discuss how these metrics translate into actual clinical utility or diagnostic reliability.
Visual Communication Issues: Figure 1, which describes the pipeline and dataset, is visually congested and lacks a clear logical flow. The distinction between data selection, manual annotation, and the supervision process is difficult to follow.
Unjustified Architecture Choices: The choice of the “shallow CNN adapter” is mentioned as a solution for global context, but there is limited ablation or theoretical justification comparing it to other potential bridging architectures (like ViT-based adapters).
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The introduction of the FunPiQ dataset is a highly valuable contribution to the ophthalmic imaging community. However, the paper in its current form feels unpolished in its technical reporting. The absence of hyperparameter details and the cluttered nature of the primary system figure (Fig 1) make it difficult to fully validate the experimental results. If the authors provide a more rigorous technical appendix and improve the visual clarity of their methodology, this could easily move to an “Accept.”
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces a pixel-level FIQA benchmark dataset with expert annotations FunPiQ, the first dataset specifically designed for pixel-wise quality assessment in fundus images, addressing a significant gap in the field.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.FIQA is a valuable benchmark dataset. The expert-annotated labels and clinically meaningful categorization (good / usable / bad) make this dataset particularly relevant for real-world applications.
2.The experiments include multiple baselines (supervised, explainable, and anomaly detection methods), diverse datasets, and multiple evaluation metrics.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Dataset limitation. The FunPiQ dataset contains only 300 images. While pixel-level annotation is costly, this limited size may compromise the statistical reliability and representativeness of the benchmark.
2.Unfair comparison. The proposed method is trained on a proprietary internal dataset, whereas other methods are trained on public datasets or use pretrained weights. Given that this paper establishes a new benchmark, this setup raises concerns about fairness.
3.Insufficient ablation. In Table 2, the proposed EFIQA-CP and the baseline EFIQA show comparable performance. It remains unclear whether the improvement stems from architectural changes or training data. At a minimum, both models should be trained on the same dataset to fairly demonstrate the superiority of the proposed architecture.
4.Missing quantitative evaluation. One advantage of pixel-level annotation is the ability to quantitatively measure the accuracy of attention maps, rather than relying solely on qualitative visualization. Therefore, in addition to Fig 2, quantitative results should be reported for comparing quality maps.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The tiny FunPiQ dataset compromising benchmark reliability; unfair comparisons; insufficient ablation; and lack of quantitative evaluation for attention maps.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have addressed all my concerns. I recommend acceptance.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper introduces FunPiQ, the first public benchmark providing pixel-level quality annotations for fundus image quality assessment. The dataset comprises 300 images sourced from three existing datasets (EyeQ, BRSET, mBRSET) across two countries, annotated by expert readers under ophthalmologist supervision into the same three classes in pixel-level quality based on anatomical visibility.
Besides, the authors propose EFIQA-CP, an improvement over the existing EFIQA method, which replaces the original linear adapter with a wide-yet-shallow CNN featuring a larger receptive field, and substitutes BCE loss with nnPU learning to handle noisy vessel-based pseudo-labels.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Addresses a genuine gap in previous datasets:
Pixel-level quality annotation is a meaningful step beyond entire image labels, as degradations in CFP are inherently local. The decision to base quality criteria on anatomical visibility rather than task-specific clinical requirements is a principled design choice that improves cross-task generalizability, and the multi-source, multi-device, multi-ethnicity sampling adds practical relevance.
2.Comprehensive and fair benchmark:
The paper evaluates seven methods spanning three distinct paradigms on the same held-out benchmark, with consistent statistical testing (large bootstrapping). The use of multiple complementary metrics covering both ordinal agreement and binary rejection tasks provides a thorough and well-rounded comparison.
3.Targeted and well-justified method improvements:
The two modifications in EFIQA-CP (wider receptive field and nnPU) are both directly motivated by identified failure modes of EFIQA (foveal false positives and pseudo-label overfitting). The ablation study confirms the contribution of each component, lending credibility to the design choices.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Limited Dataset Size and Questionable Sampling Strategy:
The dataset contains only 300 images, and while this scale is arguably acceptable given that FunPiQ is intended solely as an evaluation benchmark with costly pixel-level annotation, the sampling strategy requires stronger justification. All images are pre-selected from existing datasets based on having been labeled as “bad” at the image level, meaning the benchmark entirely excludes images of acceptable or good overall quality. This creates a distribution that is unrepresentative of real clinical screening scenarios, where the majority of images are of sufficient quality. The authors do not justify why this selection strategy was chosen over a quality-stratified sampling across all quality levels, nor do they discuss how this distributional bias might affect the conclusions drawn from benchmark comparisons.
2.Subjective Annotations Without Agreement Reporting, and Unclear Clinical Utility:
Pixel-level quality annotation is substantially more subjective than image-level labeling, particularly at the boundaries between Good/Usable regions, which are very ambiguous. Despite this, the paper reports no inter-annotator agreement metric (e.g., Cohen’s kappa or Fleiss’ kappa), which is a significant omission for a benchmark whose primary contribution is the quality of its annotations.
More fundamentally, the practical utility of pixel-level quality maps for real-world CFP workflows remains unclear. While the localization of degradations is conceptually appealing, the paper does not provide any quantitative evidence that pixel-level quality information leads to measurable improvements in downstream clinical tasks (e.g., disease grading, screening accuracy) compared to image-level quality assessment. Without such evidence, the added burden of pixel-level annotation is difficult to justify from a clinical applicability standpoint.
3.Limited Methodological Contribution and Training Conditions:
EFIQA-CP’s contributions are relatively modest, consisting of two incremental modifications to the existing EFIQA: replacing a linear adapter with a wider CNN and substituting loss functions. Neither modification introduces conceptual novelty, and the ablation study reports only a single mDice value on the merged dataset, which is insufficient to fully characterize each component’s contribution. More critically, EFIQA-CP is trained on a private single-center dataset captured with a single device (Topcon Maestro 2), whereas the competing baselines are trained on different public datasets. This inconsistency in training data makes it impossible to attribute EFIQA-CP’s performance advantage to its architectural design rather than to a more favorable training distribution. A fair comparison would require either training all methods under identical conditions or explicitly analyzing the impact of training data choice.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

As discussed above, the paper is generally good as a small size testing CFP benchmark, however, it suffers from some major concerns.
So I will wait for the rebuttal and give 3-weak reject in this stage.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors response to many concerns and state clear some of my questions. I have to say that I am statisfied but not enough (especially for size and Clinical utility).
I will raise my score to accept but it is still weak accept.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper introduces FunPiQ, a pixel-level fundus image quality assessment benchmark, and reviewers recognized its potential value for ophthalmic imaging and fine-grained quality localization. They also appreciated the inclusion of multiple baselines and the motivation to move beyond image-level quality assessment. However, several substantive concerns should be addressed in rebuttal. Reviewers questioned whether the 300-image benchmark is sufficiently representative, especially given the sampling strategy from images already labeled as poor quality. They also raised concerns about missing inter-annotator agreement, unclear clinical utility of pixel-level quality maps, limited evidence that the proposed method improves over EFIQA rather than benefiting from different/private training data, and incomplete implementation details. A focused rebuttal on these and other points raised by reviewers would help reassess the contribution.

The paper presents FunPiQ, a timely and useful benchmark for pixel-level fundus image quality assessment, together with EFIQA-CP as an explainable-by-design baseline. The reviewers recognized the value of moving beyond image-level FIQA toward localized quality assessment, and the rebuttal satisfactorily addressed the main concerns regarding dataset size, sampling rationale, quantitative evaluation, implementation details, and the comparison between EFIQA and EFIQA-CP. In particular, the authors clarified that the EFIQA/EFIQA-CP ablation used the same training data, reducing concerns that the improvement was mainly due to different training conditions, and provided missing implementation details to improve reproducibility. The paper’s clinical relevance is plausible, especially for localized quality control and image reacquisition, although reviewers noted that the clinical utility of pixel-level maps should be discussed more clearly. Overall, the rebuttal sufficiently mitigates the main concerns, and post-rebuttal reviewer opinions support acceptance. The final paper should clarify the benchmark’s intended use, annotation protocol/limitations, clinical utility discussion, and reproducibility details.

Reviewers are broadly supportive of the paper and agree that the benchmark contribution is valuable. The rebuttal addressed the main concerns, especially around presentation and technical clarification, and the updated reviewer opinions remain positive. One reviewer did not provide a post-rebuttal update, but the available evidence still supports a positive overall assessment.

author_feedback_text:
We thank reviewers for noting the relevance of FunPiQ as first pixel-level (PL) fundus image quality assessment (IQA) benchmark (R1,R2,R4); the comprehensive evaluation (R1,R2,R4); the failure-mode-driven design of EFIQA-CP (R1,R4); the use of multi-source, multi-device data (R4); and the principled visibility criteria (R4). We address reviewers’ concerns as prioritized by AC.
FunPiQ size (R2,R4)
FunPiQ is a test-only benchmark, so all 300 images are used for evaluation. The size is consistent with or larger than established CFP datasets with expert PL labels: vessels (DRIVE:40, Leuven-Haifa:240), lesions (IDRiD:81, DDR:757), and optic disc (OD)/cup (Drishti-GS:101, RIM-ONE-r3:159). Annotation is challenging due to the expertise required to distinguish quality degradations from disease signs. Statistical robustness benefits from the paired comparison design, which controls for image-level variation.
Sampling strategy (R4)
FunPiQ is designed to evaluate the localization of degradations by IQA methods (i.e. their explainability) task-agnostically (not mirroring specific prevalences), complementing image-level IQA benchmarks. Selecting image-level Bad images produces a rich mix of Good, Usable, and Bad regions (Fig.1B), so that each image tests the model’s ability to differentiate regions. This is common for PL tasks, where only images with objects of interest (in our case, degradations) are evaluated (e.g. IDRiD). We will add this rationale.
Clinical utility of quality maps (R2,R4)
Quality maps offer advantages over global scores. Combined with anatomical localization, they enable dynamic, task-specific IQA without retraining—e.g. detecting periphery and OD visibility for DR screening and glaucoma. Maps also support deployment-time quality assurance, especially for non-experts, as they show where quality is insufficient rather than an opaque global score, aiding reacquisition.
Inter-annotator agreement (R4)
We followed a consensus protocol: readers produced initial annotations on separate subsets under standardized criteria, which were then refined by a board-certified ophthalmologist. While this setup is common (e.g. IDRiD, DDR), it produces a single gold standard. We will report this as a limitation and planned extension.
EFIQA vs EFIQA-CP (R1,R2,R4)
For ablation, EFIQA was trained on the same data as EFIQA-CP, so each component’s effect is isolated: EFIQA|+our CNN adapter|+nnPU (EFIQA-CP): mDice 62.67|63.36|65.10; QWK 63.26|67.00|68.41.Thus, the gain is due to architecture and loss, not data. The CNN adds the global context absent in EFIQA’s per-patch linear adapter, while remaining shallow to avoid overfitting. We chose CNN as CNN decoders (features→pixels) are standard for PL medical tasks (e.g. nnU-Net, SwinUNETR, TransUNet). ViT adapters are an interesting future direction. We will clarify these points, while adding an ablation table with all metrics.
SOTA comparison (R2,R4)
Due to the different nature of the methods (end-to-end, explainable-by-design, anomaly detection [AD]), using the same training dataset would not be fair. Thus, we follow common benchmarking practices (e.g. KiTS and Learn2Reg MICCAI challenges) and use official weights or code when available or reimplement otherwise. AD methods, originally for industrial imaging, were tuned on high-quality CFPs (as required by their formulation) with broad disease diversity.
Implementation details and Fig.1 (R1)
EFIQA-CP uses AdamW, LR=1e-3, 20 epochs, batch 16, input size 1024×1024, no augmentation, and nnPU (π=0.05). These details will be added. Code and weights are now at the anonymized repo. We substantially improved Fig.1, unifying the flow of data, stages, and examples.
Quantitative evaluation (R2)
All metrics were computed by PL comparison against FunPiQ manual maps. This enables the quantitative paired evaluation in Tab.2.Fig.2 is complementary. We will make this explicit, and add mDice values to Fig.2 maps to show quantitative–qualitative alignment.

title: Fusion-E2Pulse: A Multimodal Event-RGB Fusion Network for Non-contact Pulse Wave Reconstruction
abstract: Non-contact pulse wave reconstruction hinges on the precise recovery of waveform morphology, including the dicrotic notch. Conventional RGB-based methods, which extract physiological signals from recorded facial videos, are constrained by the integral imaging mechanism of standard cameras, where the exposure process induces a smoothing effect that attenuates subtle vascular pulsation details. Conversely, neuromorphic event cameras, while offering exceptional sensitivity to intensity fluctuations, are inherently susceptible to noise and artifacts induced by minor motion. To exploit the synergy between frame-based integration and event-based differential sensing, we propose a novel multimodal network named Fusion-E2Pulse. This framework utilizes filtered RGB signals as structural priors to suppress motion artifacts, while leveraging the high-sensitivity of event streams to recover fine-grained morphological details. Experimental results demonstrate that Fusion-E2Pulse achieves compelling performance, effectively balancing noise suppression and morphological fidelity; under the subject-independent split (w/ ICA prior), it achieves a mean absolute error of 0.73 bpm for heart rate estimation, a waveform correlation of up to 0.919, and a diastolic phase duration error of 22.18 ms, supporting its ability to preserve fine-grained physiological waveform morphology.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
Propose a novel event-RGB multimodal fusion paradigm for non-contact pulse wave reconstruction, which complementary solves the inherent limitations of single-modal methods (RGB over-smoothing, event noise vulnerability).
Design an attentional fusion bottleneck (Squeeze-and-Excitation + Self-Attention) to adaptively calibrate the weights of dual-modal features, avoiding early fusion interference.
Construct a time-frequency adversarial supervision framework integrating WGAN-GP, Soft-DTW morphological loss, and STFT spectral loss to guarantee periodic consistency and waveform fidelity.
Achieve new SOTA results on the EMPD dataset, enabling precise recovery of pathological biomarkers (e. g. , dicrotic notch) with low heart rate error and high waveform correlation.
reviews.text_strengths:
Well-motivated fusion logic
The work accurately exploits the physical complementarity between event cameras (high sensitivity to subtle pulsations) and RGB cameras (stable structural periodicity). The design directly targets the core bottlenecks of single-modal non-contact pulse monitoring, with clear clinical and technical value.
Sound network architecture
The dual-stream encoder avoids premature modal interference; the attentional fusion bottleneck adaptively balances noise suppression and detail preservation, which is well-suited for physiological signal characteristics.
Innovative time-frequency adversarial supervision
Different from conventional time-domain GANs, the frequency-domain discriminator focuses on physiological periodicity, and the composite loss effectively optimizes both heart rate accuracy and waveform morphology. Ablation studies verify the necessity of each loss component.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Unresolved cross-site timing bias
RGB is captured from the face while event streams are from the wrist, introducing Pulse Transit Time (PTT) error. The paper does not model or calibrate this systematic bias, which affects morphological accuracy.
Insufficient generalization validation
Experiments are only conducted on the EMPD dataset. No cross-dataset testing, no evaluation under challenging conditions (large motion, varying illumination, different camera hardware), so the clinical robustness is unproven.
Lack of real-time deployment analysis
Inference speed, computational complexity (FLOPs/Params), and edge-device feasibility are not reported, which is critical for clinical real-time monitoring applications.
Missing comparison with SOTA baselines
The paper only conducts comparisons with traditional rPPG algorithms (CHROM, ICA, POS) and a simple event-only network, but does not compare with any advanced deep learning-based methods for rPPG or pulse wave reconstruction (e. g. , PhysNet, RhythmFormer, PulseGAN).
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Expand related work and discuss recent SOTA works on event camera-based physiological measurement and rPPG waveform reconstruction.

The fusion paradigm is well-motivated and technically sound; the time-frequency adversarial supervision is innovative; experiments are comprehensive. 
This is a solid, well-executed work with clear novelty and practical value. It meets the acceptance criteria of MICCAI. Minor revisions are recommended to address the weaknesses above.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes Fusion-E2Pulse, a multimodal framework for non-contact pulse wave reconstruction that combines RGB video and event-camera signals to recover physiologically meaningful waveform morphology. The method is motivated by the complementary sensing properties of the two modalities: RGB signals provide smoother and more stable low-frequency structural information, while event streams are more sensitive to subtle intensity fluctuations and therefore potentially preserve fine-grained pulse morphology, but are also more vulnerable to motion-induced noise. To exploit this complementarity, the paper introduces a two-stage pipeline consisting of multimodal data preparation and adversarial pulse reconstruction. The reconstruction model uses dual encoders for RGB and event inputs, an attentional fusion bottleneck with SE and self-attention modules, a decoder with skip connections, and a discriminator operating in the frequency domain. Training combines adversarial, morphological, and spectral objectives. Experiments on the EMPD dataset evaluate both heart-rate estimation and waveform morphology under time-split and record-split protocols, with comparisons against event-only and RGB-derived baselines. The main contribution is a multimodal fusion framework aimed not only at HR estimation but also at reconstruction of fine-grained pulse waveform landmarks such as the dicrotic notch.
reviews.text_strengths:
Well-motivated multimodal formulation: The paper addresses a meaningful limitation of standard camera-based pulse reconstruction by arguing that RGB sensing smooths subtle pulsatile dynamics, while event cameras can capture finer changes but are more fragile to noise and motion. The proposed fusion of RGB structural priors with event micro-dynamics is intuitive and clinically relevant for waveform reconstruction, especially when the goal goes beyond scalar HR estimation toward morphology recovery.
Clear architecture and pipeline design: The overall method is easy to follow. Figure 1 on page 3 clearly presents the two-stage design, including preprocessing for both modalities, dual encoders, attentional fusion, decoder, and the frequency-domain discriminator. The roles of the main modules are well separated, and the description of event preprocessing and RGB signal extraction is sufficiently concrete to understand how the final inputs are constructed.
Good emphasis on waveform morphology rather than HR alone: A notable strength is that the paper does not reduce the task to heart-rate estimation only. In addition to MAE, RMSE, MAPE, and HR correlation, the authors evaluate waveform correlation, SNR, systolic and diastolic phase duration, and pulse width. This is appropriate for a pulse reconstruction paper whose stated aim is to preserve subtle landmarks such as the dicrotic notch. The waveform examples in Figure 3 and the morphology metrics in Tables 1 and 2 strengthen this aspect of the work.
Useful ablation over losses and fusion variants: Table 2 provides a reasonably informative ablation over adversarial, spectral, and morphological losses, and also compares different RGB priors, namely CHROM, ICA, and POS. This helps support two central claims: first, that adversarial training alone is insufficient, and second, that multimodal fusion improves over event-only reconstruction.
Strong empirical performance within the presented setup: Within the EMPD benchmark and the baselines considered, Fusion-E2Pulse appears consistently strong. The best fusion variant achieves lower HR error than the event-only model and far better results than the RGB-only priors, while also improving waveform-level measures. The record-split evaluation is especially useful because it attempts to test generalization across samples rather than only within-record continuity.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The main limitation is that the experimental comparison is too restricted for the scope of the claims. The paper compares against event-only and classical RGB-derived signals such as CHROM, ICA, and POS, but it does not compare against stronger learned rPPG or waveform-reconstruction approaches such as PhysNet, RhythmFormer, PulseGAN, or other recent deep models discussed in the paper itself. Since the manuscript claims state-of-the-art performance, the absence of direct comparison to modern learning-based baselines makes that claim difficult to assess.
The RGB branch is not learning directly from raw video in the same way as many modern RGB-based baselines. Instead, it uses pre-extracted signals from CHROM, ICA, and POS as structural priors. This is a reasonable design choice, but it also means the comparison against RGB-only methods is somewhat asymmetric. The fusion system benefits from a learned reconstruction model on top of both modalities, whereas the RGB-only baselines are classical signal-processing outputs rather than comparably expressive learned models. This weakens the strength of the empirical conclusion that the proposed approach is broadly superior.
All experiments are conducted on EMPD, which is valuable and multimodal, but still represents a single benchmark with a specific acquisition setup. Given that the method depends on coordinated RGB, event, and contact-PPG data, external validation is understandably difficult, but the lack of evaluation on another dataset or under clearly distinct conditions makes it hard to judge robustness across devices, skin tones, motion patterns, or illumination regimes.
The paper combines several familiar ingredients: dual-stream encoding, attention-based fusion, adversarial learning, Soft-DTW, STFT-based loss, and classical rPPG priors. The overall combination is sensible and appears effective, but the architectural novelty at the module level is limited. The main contribution is better characterized as a careful multimodal integration of existing ideas for a less-explored sensing setup than as a fundamentally new modeling framework.
Important implementation and protocol details could be clearer.
The paper gives the main optimizer settings and loss weights, but several details remain underspecified for full assessment and reproducibility. For example, the exact event aggregation strategy, ROI localization robustness, preprocessing sensitivity, sequence lengths used during training, and details of how the discriminator input is normalized or parameterized are not fully elaborated. Since the method relies heavily on preprocessing and modality synchronization, more detail would improve confidence in reproducibility.
The paper is motivated by cardiovascular screening and waveform morphology, but the experiments stop at signal-level reconstruction metrics. There is no downstream validation showing that the reconstructed waveforms improve clinically meaningful tasks such as disease stratification, arterial stiffness assessment, or reliable dicrotic-notch localization under realistic deployment conditions. This does not invalidate the work, but it does mean the clinical relevance remains indirect.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
This is a well-motivated and technically coherent paper on an interesting sensing setup. I particularly appreciate that the work focuses on waveform morphology rather than only HR estimation, and that the evaluation includes both temporal and record-level split protocols. The main way to strengthen the paper would be to broaden the baseline suite. In particular, the manuscript would benefit from comparison against stronger learned RGB-based and pulse-reconstruction methods, not only classical CHROM, ICA, and POS priors. It would also help to clarify the fairness of comparison, since the proposed system uses a learned fusion and reconstruction model while the RGB-only counterparts are classical extracted signals rather than end-to-end learned models. Finally, a more detailed discussion of robustness to motion, illumination, and sensor variation would strengthen the practical impact of the work.

My recommendation is based on the fact that the paper presents a meaningful and well-executed multimodal approach to a relevant problem, namely high-fidelity non-contact pulse reconstruction from complementary event and RGB sensing. The motivation is sound, the system design is clear, and the experiments show consistent gains over the baselines that are included. I also view the emphasis on waveform morphology as a positive aspect, since this better matches the medical value of pulse-wave analysis than HR estimation alone.
At the same time, I do not consider the current empirical evidence fully sufficient for a stronger acceptance recommendation. The baseline suite is too narrow, especially given the state-of-the-art claim, and the novelty lies more in thoughtful multimodal integration than in a clearly new modeling principle. The reliance on a single dataset also limits how strongly one can assess robustness and generalizability. Overall, I think the paper is solid and potentially useful, but it would be notably stronger with broader learned baselines and clearer positioning relative to recent deep rPPG and waveform-generation methods.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.text_contribution: This work proposes Fusion-E2Pulse, a multimodal deep learning approach that fuses signals from an RGB and an event camera for remote photoplethysmography (rPPG). The approach consists of two major stages conducted in series. First, multimodal data preparation, which involves extracting pulsatile waveforms from the RGB and event cameras independently using classical techniques. Second, adversarial pulse reconstruction, which amounts to generating a denoised pulsatile signal by combining the two extracted signals using a deep fusion network-style architecture. The proposed method is evaluated on the EMPD dataset, demonstrating minor improvements over the event-only baseline.
reviews.text_strengths:
Novelty: the proposed Fusion-E2Pulse architecture is novel, as the literature contains no other works that specifically fuse RGB and event camera information for rPPG. This is only possible because of the EMPD dataset, which this work utilizes, and whose architecture the proposed method is largely based upon [1].
Strong evaluation protocol: the work uses a comprehensive suite of evaluation metrics for both HR estimation and pulsatile signal morphology and provides useful baseline comparisons, enabling rigorous comparison with related work.
Thorough ablation study: the authors conduct a strong ablation study (sec 3.3) that helps understand the impact of the different loss components in the final proposed training objective. 
References: 
[1] Feng, Q., Li, P., Gao, R., Jiale, X., Gong, R., Li, Y.: Empd: An event-based multimodal physiological dataset for remote pulse wave detection (part 1 of 9) (Feb
2026). https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18765701
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Incremental novelty: while the proposed method is novel, it is largely identical to the architecture proposed by the original work that developed the EMPD dataset [1]. In particular, the proposed event preprocessing is identical to the event aggregation module of the original work, and the adversarial pulse reconstruction stage largely resembles the waveform reconstruction module of the original work.
Incremental/insignificant results: the experimental results suggest that the proposed fusion method offers minor gains in performance in comparison to the already very strong event-only baseline, which resembles the method proposed in the original EMPD dataset work [1]. Table 1: HR MAE is improved by 0.1-0.2bpm and SNR is improved by <0.5db, which are clinically insignificant. Figure 3: Bland-Altman analysis reveals that fusion methods do shrink 95% limits of agreement by ~1-1.5bpm

2026). https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18765701
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Could there be data leakage in the record split experiments? In particular, can the authors please clarify how many subjects in the test set were not seen in the training or validation set? I believe a stronger evaluation protocol would be to partition the dataset at the subject level, i.e., assign each of the 83 subjects to the train, validation, or test set.

The paper’s methodology is largely similar to the very strong event-only baseline proposed in the original EMPD work, with minor modifications to incorporate RGB signal fusion. Nevertheless, the experimental results suggest that introducing this RGB fusion only improves rPPG performance incrementally (HR MAE by ~1 bpm and SNR by ~0.5 dB). Therefore, my initial score for this work is a “weak reject”.
