reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents a classification model for ultrasound standard plane view localization. The authors design and cascade multiple modules to meet the requirements of real-time performance and high accuracy in ultrasound applications. They validate their approach and its differences from prior methods on both a public and a private dataset.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.From a real clinical perspective, focusing on ultrasound standard plane classification is timely.
2.GCM-Net achieves both high accuracy and meets the real-time requirements of ultrasound scanning.
3.The authors provide a realistic scenario simulation test, which strengthens the paper.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Although the authors focus on the recognition of ultrasound standard planes, the task is narrowly formulated as a classification problem, which limits the practical applicability of the method in real clinical settings.
2.Table 1 introduces the private dataset AbdoSP-9.I note that the authors define 9 categories; however, to my knowledge, this categorization does not follow a complete clinical standard [1], and no corresponding medical justification is provided for this design. According to prior work [1], the liver alone includes 13 standard planes, suggesting that the proposed AbdoSP-9 has limited coverage. This significantly undermines the credibility of the problem setting. In addition, treating N-SP as an independent category introduces a very broad semantic space, and the manuscript does not clarify how these negative samples are constructed. These issues indicate substantial dataset-related limitations, raising concerns about the reliability of the reported metrics and their potential clinical applicability.
3.Although Table 2 reports performance on FPU23, the improvement in accuracy is marginal, and an accuracy of 99.53% may indicate severe overfitting.
4.The evaluation in Section 3.4 appears superficial. The authors should provide a more detailed description of the implementation process corresponding to Figure 2.5.The comparative analysis is insufficient. While foundation models may offer advantages during training, the authors should also report the performance of conventional frame-by-frame models on the proposed dataset to justify the necessity of GCM-Net. Furthermore, although Section 3.4 claims that GCM-Net achieves good real-time performance, quantitative metrics such as FPS are not provided for precise comparison.
[1] Zhang, J., Chen, Y., Zeng, P., Liu, Y., Diao, Y., & Liu, P. (2023). Ultra-attention: automatic recognition of liver ultrasound standard sections based on visual attention perception structures. Ultrasound in Medicine & Biology, 49(4), 1007–1017.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Although this paper timely addresses the important problem of ultrasound standard plane recognition, the dataset construction lacks support from established clinical standards, and the comparative experiments are not sufficiently transparent. Therefore, I believe the current version of the paper is not suitable for publication at MICCAI.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal addresses several implementation-level concerns, including TCR details, latency, memory bank size, training iterations, and additional hyperparameter analysis. However, my major concern remains largely unresolved. The clinical definition and coverage of AbdoSP-9 are still not sufficiently justified as a standard abdominal ultrasound plane recognition protocol, and the NSP category remains broad and weakly specified. The validation is still limited to a single-center private dataset without external multi-device or pathological testing. Moreover, the methodological contribution mainly integrates existing components rather than introducing a substantially novel formulation.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The authors present GCM-Net, an anatomy-aware framework designed for the robust classification of standard planes in abdominal ultrasound. The main contributions of paper are;
a weighted fusion module that uses learnable scalar weights to dynamically integrate hierarchical spatial details with high-level semantic features.
To handle inherent speckle noise and background artifacts, the paper introduces the AAGR module, which filters out the background/surrounding noise from features before feeding into classification head.
the authors employed a supervised contrastive loss branch alongside a first-in-first-out memory bank to increase the discriminability of morphologically similar anatomical planes.
To validate clinical utility, the authors also performed a readers study on six continuous scanning videos.
reviews.text_strengths:
The authors proposed a system which can adapt its focus to irregular or elongated organ shapes, which is much more flexible and allows the model to be easily adapted to different types of ultrasound scans.
The proposed LMFF module that uses adjustable scalar weights to adaptively balance fine-grained spatial details with high level semantic information. Along with physical geometric constraints, such as a trapezoidal probe mask, which is effective way to filter out background noise and speckle artifacts.
The use of memory-bank-based supervised contrastive learning strategy (though not new but) allows the model to better distinguish between morphologically similar anatomical planes.
The system was validated using real-time clinical video streams and a readers study was also done to validate the key frames selected by the model which makes the claims of paper solid and clinically grounded.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The model lacks manual ground truth for the anatomical centroids (c_x, c_y); instead, it relies on implicit supervision from the classification task, which means the attention center is optimized for prediction accuracy rather than being strictly validated against anatomical landmarks.
The size of memory bank M for contrastive loss is not provided.
TCR is credited with achieving the expert-validated clinical accuracy of 81.25%, but the authors do not provide a dedicated mathematical breakdown or a TCR subsection in the Methodology section.
Authors mention that the AbdoSP-9 dataset was curated by “chief physicians” , but the paper does not specify if multiple experts cross-verified the labels or provide a Kappa coefficient to measure agreement.
The model is described as capable of real-time processing (~15fps), yet the paper never specifies the actual processing speed (latency) of the entire pipeline on the NVIDIA RTX 4080 hardware.
For the dynamic scanning evaluation, the success rate is reported as 70.83% , but the paper does not explicitly define the mathematical threshold (e.g., a specific confidence score or time window) used to categorize a detection as a “success” vs a “failure”.
Minor:
There is no mention of the number of training epochs or total iterations.
The authors also didn’t mention how many trainable parameter did their trainable (peft) adapters added on top of frozen encoder.
The figure 1(b) should have separate boxes/outlines separating LMFF and AARG modules.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper does solve an actual problem in clinical field. The AAGR)is a clever, task-specific alternative to standard attention.
The inclusion of clinical reader study shows the authors are thinking about real-world deployment, not just curated benchmarks. But the lack of explanation for TCR module and lack of anatomical ground truths for centroid regression, raises reproducibility concerns.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
Thanks to the authors for the detailed rebuttal. Most of my specific concerns were directly addressed with concrete answers:
1.annotation reliability is now supported by a Fleiss’ Kappa of 0.7114 from cross-verification across one chief physician and two physicians on 30 subjects substantial agreement.
2.the TCR formulation is now fully specified (30-frame moving average, 3.0s warmup, validation-derived threshold, 60-frame patience window), which resolves the methodology gap I flagged.
3.End-to-end latency of 65.25 ms/frame on RTX 4080 (FP16/TF32), including pre- and post-processing, gives the concrete real-time figure that was missing.
4.The memory bank size (M=512), training iterations (10,000), and trainable parameter counts (~7.10M adapters, ~9.72M total) are now provided.
Two of my concerns remain unresolved:
1.The “success” vs “failure” threshold for the 70.83% dynamic scanning success rate is still not explicitly defined. This needs a one-line mathematical definition in the camera-ready.
2.The anatomical centroid claim is defended qualitatively rather than quantitatively. The authors mentioned heatmap visualizations in the appendix will help illustrate the behaviour, but MICCAI don’t allow appendix and the model still relies on implicit supervision rather than any validation against anatomical landmarks. I’d accept this as a known limitation, but it should be stated as such.
Must be included in the camera-ready:
1.full TCR formulation as described in the rebuttal.
2.kappa value and annotation cross-verification protocol in Section 3.1.3.end-to-end latency figure (65.25 ms/frame).
4./tau and /lambda ablations.
5 mathematical definition of the dynamic scanning success criterion.
6 AAGR heatmap visualizations (adjusting in Figure 2 or as separate figure) AND/OR explicit acknowledgement that anatomical centroid supervision is implicit rather than landmark-validated.

meta_reviews.text:
Some reviewers show the interesting of this work. However, there are some concerns shown by the reviewers, including but not limited to:
1.Limited methodological novelty
2.Insufficient justification of task setting of classification and the private dataset.
3.The ablation study is incomplete。
4.Details are missing (e.g., TCR module, training details)

While concerns regarding methodological novelty remain and the contribution is best characterized as an incremental system-level innovation rather than a fundamentally new method, the reviewers generally agreed on the clinical importance of the problem, the soundness of the technical approach, and the value of the experimental validation. The work demonstrates clear practical relevance and consistent performance gains on a clinically meaningful task. Taking into account both the methodological contribution and the clinical/application impact, the paper provides sufficient merit for acceptance in my view. I therefore support acceptance. In the camera-ready version, the authors should incorporate the key clarifications from the rebuttal.

The clinical definition and coverage of the private AbdoSP-9 protocol lack rigorous justification; combining multiple distinct organ systems (liver, gallbladder, pancreas) into a arbitrary 9-class paradigm without following accepted radiological standards compromises its utility as a reliable clinical benchmark. Methodologically, the network represents an incremental assembly of established components (medical foundation model adaptation, basic scalar multi-layer feature fusion, and memory-bank supervised contrastive learning) rather than a novel paradigm. Furthermore, the validation is entirely constrained to a single-center private dataset without multi-center, multi-device, or pathological variability testing, which fails to support the claims of real-world clinical translatability or robustness against genuine patient anomalies.
The paper is interesting, proposing a strong method to solve an important task. The rebuttal addressed the major reviewer concerns.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for recognizing our method’s novelty, clinical relevance and realistic applicability. Below, we address the key concerns.
1.Dataset Validity(@R1,R2,R3)：
Generalization(R1): GCM-Net demonstrates generalizability across two dimensions: (1) multi-domain applicability, evidenced by 99.53% accuracy on the public fetal dataset FPUS23, in addition to the AbdoSP-9 dataset (2) temporal robustness, confirmed by video testing (Sec 3.4) on unseen clinical ultrasound scan with real-world patient motion.
Clinical protocol(R2): AbdoSP-9 aims to provide fine-grained subxiphoid screening of multiple organs (liver, gallbladder, pancreas), including essential pancreatic planes (PB, PT) often omitted in single-organ studies, rather than expanding coverage through intercostal views as in [1]. Our 8 SPs were curated by chief physicians based on established clinical standards [2] to balance diagnostic depth with robotic navigation utility. For comparison, contemporary work like Cai et al. [3] utilizes only 6 SPs. The N-SP category includes transitional/blurred frames, specifically designed to enhance deployment robustness.
Annotation verification(R3): A subset (30 subjects) was cross-verified by one chief physician and two physicians, yielding a Fleiss’ Kappa of 0.7114.Discrepancies were resolved via consensus. We will add these details to Sec 3.1.[1] Zhang J, et al. (2023). Ultra-attention: recognition of liver ultrasound standard sections. Ultrasound Med Biol, 49(4), 1007-17.[2] Zhang M (Ed). (2018). Atlas of Humman Body Ultrasound Scanning (Rev. ed.). Science Press.
[3] Cai Q, et al. SEMC: Structure-Enhanced MoE Contrastive Learning. Proc. AAAI, 2026.2.TCR & Real-time Processing(@R2, R3):
We will add the complete TCR formulation to the revision. The TCR applies a 30-frame moving average for temporal smoothing. Following a 3.0-second warmup, exceeding a validation-derived threshold triggers peak-tracking. To mitigate transient noise, the task locks if no new maximum is reached within a 60-frame (2.0 seconds) patience window. End-to-end latency is 65.25 ms/frame on an RTX 4080 (FP16/TF32), including pre-processing (1024x1024 resizing, normalization), inference, and post-processing, making it fully suitable for real-time clinical use.
3.AAGR & Visualizations (@R3, R1)：
The anatomical centroid supervision does not rely on manual annotation. Nevertheless, the regressed coordinates consistently converge to meaningful anatomical structures during optimization, demonstrating that the model can reliably localize relevant landmarks without explicit ground truth. 
To further support the claimed anatomy awareness, we will add qualitative visualizations in the revised appendix, including Gaussian attention heatmaps overlaid on ultrasound frames, which show that the AAGR module consistently focuses on the relevant anatomical regions.
4.Implementation Details & Ablations (@R1, R3):
We will add the following implementation details in the revised manuscript. Specifically, the SAM ViT encoder is frozen. The bottleneck adapters add ~7.10M trainable parameters to the backbone. Total trainable parameters (adapters, neck, classification head) are ~9.72M.
We evaluate τ and λ on AbdoSP-9.Optimal performance (81.37%) occurs at τ=0.1, where low temperature facilitates hard negative mining to distinguish subtle anatomical variances. Higher τ (e.g., 76.03% at 0.5) over-smoothes the distribution. λ=0.6 yields the peak accuracy (81.37%), balancing contrastive regularization with classification (76.49% at 0.2; 78.47% at 1.0). Notably, AAGR σ_w, σ_h is adaptively predicted, not fixed. The memory bank size M is set to 512, trained for 10000 iterations. We will expand the implementation details accordingly.
The bare MED-SA backbone (72.37%) underperforms MedViTv2 (73.44%), while our GCM-Net achieves 81.37% (+9%), proving the proposed LMFF, AAGR, and SupCon drive the improvement rather than the backbone.
We hope these address your concerns.

title: GeneRAG: A Retrieval-Augmented Framework for Spatially Resolved Gene Expression Prediction
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) is pivotal for deciphering molecular organization, yet cross-modal variability challenges accurate H&E based profiling. Existing models struggle to generalize to unseen genes and lack clinical interpretability. We propose GeneRAG, a model-agnostic Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework with a Dual-Constrained Retrieval module. Unlike conventional black-box networks that rely solely on fixed parameters, GeneRAG explicitly decouples knowledge storage from model training. By optimizing an Elastic Net-based sparse sampling matrix, GeneRAG integrates morphological and biological constraints to fetch relevant samples from a pre-constructed bank. Leveraging conserved gene correlations, this enables accurate reconstruction of comprehensive profiles, including entirely unseen genes. On the HEST-1k dataset, GeneRAG seamlessly enhances state-of-the-art models in a plug-and-play manner, improving Stem’s PCC-10 from 0.8322 to 0.8711(Breast dataset). For zero-shot generalization (5,000 genes), Stem+GeneRAG achieves a PCC-5000 of 0.5188, vastly outperforming DeepSpot (0.0748). GeneRAG provides robust, transparent predictions, highlighting its potential for clinical deployment.
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose GeneRAG, a retrieval-augmented approach for spatial transcriptomics prediction from histology images. The method combines morphological similarity and partial gene expression predictions to retrieve relevant samples from a reference bank and reconstruct full gene expression profiles via a sparse optimization framework. The approach is model-agnostic and demonstrates improvements across multiple datasets, including imputing the expression of genes.
reviews.text_strengths:
Interpretability: The retrieval-based formulation provides an intuitive and transparent mechanism for prediction. By explicitly selecting and weighting similar reference patches, the model allows one to trace predictions back to specific morphological patterns and corresponding gene expression profiles. This is a meaningful advantage over black-box deep learning approaches.
The method is conceptually straightforward and avoids heavy architectural complexity. The use of a sparse optimization framework when imputing the expression.
Generalization to unseen genes is a addressing the closed-set limitation
Model-agnostic and can be integrated with different backbone models
Despite its simplicity the method shows improved predictive performance across datasets
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Limited methodological novelty: The core idea of retrieval-based reconstruction and bimodal dictionary-like modelling has been explored in prior multimodal and biomedical settings. The methodological contribution is minimal.
The framework relies on sample-level similarity to approximate gene–gene dependencies. It would be interesting to compare against more direct approaches, such as conditional modelling or latent factor-based methods, which explicitly capture gene relationships.
The multi-stage pipeline (initial prediction -> retrieval -> expression aggregation) may accumulate errors, particularly when the initial gene prediction is inaccurate.
Dependence on reference bank: Performance is likely sensitive to the diversity and coverage of the training dataset, raising questions about generalization to out-of-distribution samples.
The method assigns per-sample weights over a reference bank, which may limit its ability to generalize beyond the training distribution. This design makes the method inherently dependent on dataset coverage and raises concerns about robustness under domain shift as no cross-dataset validation results are reported.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The method is simple, interpretable, and clearly presented, but offers limited methodological novelty. Its reliance on per-sample retrieval raises concerns about generalization under domain shift, especially without cross-dataset evaluation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: fThe rebuttal reframes reference-bank dependency as a strength for domain adaptation, but this does not fully address the OOD concern. Since predictions are reconstructed from retrieved samples, the method still fundamentally depends on the coverage and diversity of the reference bank, making robustness under distribution shift insufficiently validated.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a retrieval-and-reconstruction approach for H&E-to-spatial-transcriptomics prediction. Given an initial prediction from a frozen backbone, the method solves a dual-constrained ElasticNet optimization to find a sparse set of training samples that best reconstruct the query in both morphological and gene expression spaces. The resulting sparse weights are then applied to the full gene bank, enabling prediction of genes unseen during backbone training. This replaces the kNN retrieval used in prior work (e.g., BLEEP) with a more principled optimization-based formulation, and in the authors’ experiments improves prediction performance, particularly for zero-shot gene extrapolation.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The retrieval module introduces no additional trainable parameters. The sparse weight vector α is obtained by solving a convex ElasticNet optimization at test time, which guarantees a global optimum and eliminates the risk of overfitting in the retrieval step. This is a meaningful practical advantage over methods that require training additional neural network components for retrieval or alignment.
2.The decoupling between the optimization target (anchor genes and morphological features) and the reconstruction target (full gene panel) is a well-motivated design choice. By leveraging conserved gene-gene co-expression structure, the method enables prediction of genes that were entirely unseen during backbone training. The zero-shot extrapolation results on 5,000 genes, while requiring more rigorous baselines for proper evaluation, demonstrate a capability that most existing methods cannot offer by design.
3.The framework is genuinely model-agnostic. The authors demonstrate consistent improvements across three architecturally distinct backbones — a pure vision model (UNI), a multimodal foundation model (EXAONE Path 2.5), and a diffusion generative model (Stem). This plug-and-play flexibility lowers the barrier to adoption and allows practitioners to benefit from the retrieval module regardless of their choice of backbone.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The paper claims to be “the first universal retrieval-augmented framework for spatial transcriptomics,” but this is factually incorrect. BLEEP (Xie et al., NeurIPS 2023) already performs retrieval-augmented gene expression prediction from a reference bank of paired image-expression entries. 
2.The zero-shot comparison against DeepSpot in Table 2 is fundamentally asymmetric. DeepSpot must predict 5,000 genes entirely from learned parameters, whereas GeneRAG retrieves ground-truth expression profiles from the training set. This is not a fair evaluation of the retrieval formulation. The appropriate baselines would be alternative retrieval strategies with access to the same reference bank — such as kNN in the image embedding space, kNN in the gene space, or kNN with a weighted dual-modality similarity — which would isolate the contribution of the ElasticNet sparse reconstruction over simpler retrieval mechanisms.
3.Computational cost is never discussed. The method solves an N-dimensional ElasticNet optimization for every test spot individually. A typical Visium slide contains ~5,000 spots, and the reference bank may contain tens of thousands of entries. The scalability of this approach to large cohorts or whole-slide-level prediction is unclear and could be a significant practical limitation that undermines the claimed ease of clinical deployment.
4.The foundation models used as backbones (UNI, CONCH, EXAONE Path 2.5) were pretrained on massive histopathology datasets that may overlap with the HEST-1k evaluation data. The paper does not discuss or rule out this potential contamination. Since the retrieval module relies on the frozen encoder’s feature space, pretraining data overlap would make the morphological retrieval artificially easy, inflating results in a way that is difficult to disentangle from the method’s actual contribution.
5.The “interpretability” claim is overstated. Showing top retrieved patches and their weights is a property shared by any retrieval-based method, including simple kNN. The sparse weights do not provide meaningfully richer explanations than similarity scores for the purpose of clinical reasoning.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1.The paper positions GeneRAG as “the first universal retrieval-augmented framework” for spatial transcriptomics. However, prior methods such as BLEEP and other retrieval-based approaches already explore related ideas in this space. I encourage the authors to soften and better localize this claim. The sparse reconstruction formulation and zero-shot extrapolation results appear sufficiently novel on their own and do not require a broad priority claim.
2.For Table 1, it would be helpful to clarify how predictions are generated for the foundation-model baselines (UNI, CONCH, EXAONE Path 2.5) in the without-GeneRAG setting. Since these models are primarily encoders, more detail on the decoder/prediction head, training strategy, and whether the encoder is frozen or fine-tuned would help readers assess baseline strength and reproducibility.
3.The manuscript would be strengthened by clarifying whether any overlap exists, or can be ruled out, between the pretraining corpora of the foundation-model backbones and the HEST-1k evaluation data. At present, this is difficult to assess from the paper. If overlap cannot be ruled out, that limitation should be discussed explicitly.
4.The comparison against DeepSpot is informative, but the two approaches have different information access at inference time: DeepSpot performs purely parametric prediction, whereas GeneRAG retrieves and recombines training-set reference profiles. Acknowledging this asymmetry would help readers interpret the reported margins more appropriately.
5.Since the method solves an ElasticNet-style retrieval optimization for each test spot, runtime and scaling analysis would be valuable. Reporting average inference time per spot or slide, and how performance/runtime vary with reference bank size, would improve the paper’s practical relevance.
The core idea is interesting, and my concerns are mostly about positioning and evaluation clarity rather than a fatal flaw in the method itself. If the authors address these issues convincingly in rebuttal, I would be open to revising my score upward.

I assigned a score of 3 because, while the paper presents an interesting idea and reports promising empirical results, I do not yet find the current presentation strong enough for a higher score. In particular, the novelty claim appears overstated: positioning GeneRAG as “the first universal retrieval-augmented framework” for spatial transcriptomics is difficult to reconcile with prior retrieval-based methods already cited or closely related in the literature. In addition, several important experimental details remain unclear, especially how the foundation-model baselines without GeneRAG (e.g., UNI, CONCH, EXAONE Path 2.5) are converted into gene-expression predictors, which makes it hard to fully assess baseline strength and reproducibility. The comparison to DeepSpot is also not entirely like-for-like, since GeneRAG has access to a training-set reference bank with ground-truth profiles at inference time, whereas DeepSpot performs purely parametric prediction. Finally, the paper would benefit from a clearer discussion of possible pretraining/evaluation overlap for the pathology foundation models and from runtime/scalability analysis, given that the proposed method solves an ElasticNet optimization for each test spot. Overall, I view these as meaningful weaknesses in novelty positioning, evaluation clarity, and practical reporting rather than fatal flaws in the core idea, which is why I settled on a 3 rather than a lower score.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The response and promised changes address most of my concerns, I would like to raise the score to 5.actually I think the largest concern is the overclaim of the first RAG system, but since they promise to change the wording, I am good with the paper, I think the novelty of the method is good despite some minor weaknesses.

reviews.text_contribution:
This work introduces GeneRAG, a retrieval-augmented framework for spatial transcriptomics that aims to mitigate cross-modal variability.
The proposed approach improves interpretability by addressing the black-box nature of deep learning models, providing visual and transcriptomic rationales based on retrieved reference samples.
The method demonstrates zero-shot generalization to unseen genes and exhibits a model-agnostic design, allowing integration with a variety of existing state-of-the-art architectures in a plug-and-play manner.
reviews.text_strengths: The concept of performing retrieval using both image features and gene expression features appears to be a well-founded and reasonable design choice.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper does not provide details on how the dataset is split; could the authors clarify what experimental setting is assumed? In recent work, it has become common to evaluate under both intra-patient and inter-patient settings. However, when generalizing across patients, gene expression profiles can differ substantially due to batch effects. Does the proposed method still operate effectively under such conditions? It seems likely that certain assumptions are made, and therefore clearly specifying the scope of applicability and underlying assumptions of the method is very important.
The definitions of each component in Equation (1) appear to be unclear and somewhat inconsistent. It seems that $D_{\text{img}}$ and $D_{\text{anchor}}$ are defined as a set, yet the output appears to have the same dimensionality as $f_{\text{img}}$. My understanding is that D is matrix $D_{\text{img}} = ( f_{\text{img}}^(1) … )$, and that a weighted aggregation over samples in the dataset is performed using $\alpha$, resulting in a single feature representation.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

As noted in the weaknesses section, I am concerned that retrieval-based approaches are often evaluated with insufficiently validated or inaccurately specified data pool requirements. However, this issue is common across other retrieval-based methods as well. I agree with the overall concept of the approach, and since it has the potential to advance the exploration of retrieval-based methods, I believe it is acceptable to accept it.

reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The reviewers were convinced by the rebuttal. They thought that using both genetic features and image features makes sense and is a good design choice.

meta_reviews.text:
Paper Summary
The paper proposes GeneRAG, a retrieval-augmented framework for predicting spatial transcriptomics from histology images. It aims to address limitations of existing approaches, particularly lack of interpretability and inability to generalize to unseen genes. The method first generates initial gene expression predictions and morphological features using a pretrained backbone, then formulates a dual-constrained retrieval process that leverages both image similarity and partial gene predictions to retrieve relevant samples from a reference bank. A sparse ElasticNet optimization is used to weight retrieved samples, and the final full gene expression profile is reconstructed as a weighted combination of these references, enabling prediction of unseen genes and improving performance across multiple backbones .
Key Strengths
The paper presents a conceptually simple and interpretable framework that provides transparent predictions through explicit retrieval and weighting of reference samples. The approach is flexible and model-agnostic, allowing integration with different backbone architectures without additional training. It demonstrates consistent empirical improvements and introduces a principled optimization-based retrieval mechanism that avoids additional trainable parameters. The ability to generalize to unseen genes through leveraging gene correlations is viewed as a meaningful capability, and the combination of morphological and gene-based retrieval is considered a reasonable and well-motivated design.
Key Weaknesses
The novelty is considered limited due to similarities with prior retrieval-based approaches, and some claims about being the first of its kind are seen as overstated. Concerns are raised about fairness and clarity of experimental comparisons, particularly in zero-shot settings where the method benefits from access to a reference bank. The evaluation lacks sufficient detail regarding dataset splits, baseline implementation, and potential data overlap from pretrained models. There are also concerns about scalability due to per-sample optimization, as well as robustness and generalization under distribution shifts given reliance on a reference bank. Some methodological descriptions and formulations are unclear, and reproducibility details are insufficient.
Review Summary
All reviewers agree that the paper addresses an important problem and proposes an interpretable and flexible retrieval-based framework with promising empirical performance and zero-shot capabilities. There is consensus that the design is intuitive and that combining morphological and gene information for retrieval is reasonable. However, reviewers also consistently raise concerns about limited methodological novelty and insufficient clarity in positioning relative to prior work. There is further agreement that evaluation details and experimental fairness need improvement, particularly regarding baseline comparisons, dataset assumptions, and potential data leakage. Given these mixed perspectives, the paper would benefit from clarification and stronger justification before a final decision.
Decision
Invite to rebuttal. The paper shows promise but has unresolved concerns regarding novelty, evaluation fairness, and clarity.
Rebuttal Focus
The rebuttal should focus on addressing concerns, particularly by clarifying the novelty and positioning relative to prior retrieval-based methods, including correcting or moderating claims. The authors should justify the fairness of experimental comparisons, especially in zero-shot settings, and provide clearer descriptions of baseline implementations and dataset splits, including assumptions about intra- and inter-patient generalization. It is also important to address potential data leakage from pretrained models, discuss computational cost and scalability of the optimization process, and clarify unclear methodological formulations.

The rebuttal successfully addressed most of the key concerns raised in the initial reviews, particularly regarding novelty positioning, experimental protocol, baseline implementation, and scalability. These clarifications convinced two reviewers to raise their assessments to acceptance. While concerns about reference-bank dependence and OOD robustness remain, they are not sufficient to outweigh the method’s demonstrated effectiveness and practical value. Therefore, I recommend acceptance.

The paper addresses the limitations and black-box nature of deep-learning regression models in histopathology-based spatial transcriptomics prediction. The approach implements a dual-constrained sparse optimization method that explicitly selects and weights paired reference tissue patches to predict high-dimensional expression panels. Its key strengths include an interpretable inference trail, and a plug-and-play design. The rebuttal deflated original overstatements regarding priority, clarified the FISTA matrix operations and the dataset splits. The technical soundness supports acceptance.

This paper proposes GeneRAG, a retrieval-augmented framework for spatial transcriptomics prediction with the ability to generalize to unseen genes. Reviewers appreciated the model-agnostic design, the retrieval-and-reconstruction formulation, and the strong performance across multiple datasets and backbone models. I agree with Reviewers #2 and #3 that the proposed framework addresses an important limitation of existing methods and provides a practical and interpretable solution.
The main concerns were related to novelty positioning, scalability, and dependence on the reference bank. The rebuttal satisfactorily clarified the novelty claims, experimental protocol, and computational considerations. While the dependence on the reference bank remains a limitation, this is a common challenge for retrieval-based approaches and does not undermine the main contribution. Overall, I find the work technically sound, well evaluated, and worthy of acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely appreciate the Area Chairs for managing the review process, and the reviewers for their constructive feedback recognizing our framework’s zero-shot scalability and ability to address closed-set limits. Following MICCAI policy prohibiting new experimental results, we address the major concerns grouped by topic below.
1.Phrasing, Notation & Claims
[R1,R2,M] “First universal retrieval”: To prevent misinterpretation, as in our intro, we don’t claim priority over the retrieval paradigm. By “first universal,” we specifically meant the first model-agnostic framework—a plug-and-play module integrating with any backbone. We will refine positioning to a “model-agnostic retrieval-augmented framework.”
[R2] Interpretability: We do not assert superior clinical reasoning, but simply emphasize our approach’s transparency compared to SOTA black-box models (e.g., Stem, TRIPLEX, Foundation-only). We will precisely articulate this as the “inherent transparency of reference-based models.”
[R3] Eq.(1) Notation: For mathematical rigor, we will explicitly redefine D_img∈R^{dxN} and D_anchor∈R^{kxN} as matrices.
2.Scalability & Bank Dependency
[R2,R3,M] Cost & Scalability: Test-spot optimization concerns are resolved by our joint structure. Eq.(1) is algebraically equivalent to a multi-output ElasticNet problem. Using FISTA solvers, it processes via batched matrix operations for fast convergence, completing inference within minutes per slide. Since large-scale ST profiling is typically run as offline batches clinically, we expect this to be highly practical.
[R1,M] Bank Dependency & OOD: While OOD vulnerability is a universal challenge, we expect our bank dependency to turn it into a core strength. Just as traditional RAG dynamically adapts by updating reference documents, GeneRAG enables instant domain adaptation simply by replacing the bank with target data, without weight updates. This parallel inspired our naming.
3.Baselines & Experimental Setup
[R2,M] Asymmetric baseline (DeepSpot) & ElasticNet Rationale: Comparing against DeepSpot was inevitable. No prior retrieval work attempted prediction on such a massive scale (5,000 genes). To our knowledge, DeepSpot is the most recent baseline attempting 5,000-gene prediction, making it the necessary benchmark to show how our zero-shot framework breaks their parametric “closed-set limits.” Furthermore, a direct comparison against the existing kNN-based SOTA model (BLEEP) is already provided in Table 1.Therefore, replacing ElasticNet with kNN here is an internal ablation, not a SOTA comparison. Simple kNN is inherently limited by heuristic constraints (e.g., fixed k) and redundancy. Adopting ElasticNet was a fundamental evolution; its L1 penalty actively penalizes redundancy, dynamically determining a sparse, complementary reference set that kNN cannot achieve.
[R2,R3,M] Foundation models set up & Contamination: We strictly applied linear probing (frozen encoder) to assess pure representational power. While image-level overlap with HEST-1k is possible during pretraining, models were blind to ST labels (0% contamination). Low standalone backbone performance vs. the massive leap upon integrating GeneRAG confirms our pure contribution.
[R3,M] Dataset Split & Batch Effects: We did not employ arbitrary splits, strictly adhering to the SOTA Stem (ICLR 2025) Leave-One-Slide-Out (LOSO) protocol (p.6, ‘~strictly following the experimental design [21]’). The datasets’ diverse compositions naturally subjected our framework to both scenarios:
(Intra-patient): In Prostate and HER2ST, LOSO inherently tests intra-patient generalization.
(Inter-patient & Batch Effects): In the Kidney dataset (23 slides, 22 patients), LOSO naturally forms a strict inter-patient test; test slides (e.g., ‘20-0038’) belong to completely unseen patients.
To ensure the evaluation context is entirely transparent, we will explicitly clarify these setups in the text and release all codes via our GitHub upon publication.

title: Generative Anchor-Guided Federated Domain Generalization for Heterogeneous Pan Cancer Image Analysis
abstract: Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a key paradigm for collaborative cancer subtyping classification, which enables the development of diagnostic models across distributed institutions while preserving data privacy. Despite the emergence of federated approaches, their performance is often constrained by the assumption of a unified label space, which fails to account for the heterogeneous diagnostic criteria encountered in real-world multi-center collaborations. To address this, we propose FedGMA, a framework designed for federated domain generalization under disjoint semantics. Our method introduces generative anchor-based semantic decoupling (GASD), which projects latent prompts into task-specific geometric coordinates to decouple feature learning from local label definitions. We further propose geometric consistency regularization (GCR) to regularize the latent space using a memory bank, ensuring representational compactness and separability under limited batch sizes. To evaluate our approach under heterogeneous label spaces, We construct a large-scale benchmark with 4,796 whole slide images across 8 cancer types. FedGMA achieves 76.42% average AUC, outperforming the state-of-the-art by 4.96% on unseen target domains.
subject_areas: Special Topic -> AI for Neglected Diseases & Limited-Resource Settings

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper studies federated domain generalization for computational pathology under heterogeneous, disjoint label spaces. It proposes FedGMA, which uses generated geometric anchors and a consistency regularizer to learn a shared representation across pan-cancer clients. The problem setting is meaningful and the benchmark construction is valuable. However, the method is closely related to recent geometry-based classifier design in federated learning, and the current positioning and experimental comparison are not yet sufficient to clearly establish the novelty and advantage of the proposed formulation.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper addresses a relevant and practically motivated FedDG setting with heterogeneous local semantics, which is more realistic than the standard shared-label assumption. 
2.The benchmark is a useful contribution, spanning 4,796 WSIs across 8 cancer types under disjoint label spaces. 
3.The method is reasonably organized, and the ablation suggests that both the anchor generation module and the regularization term contribute to performance.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The related-work positioning is incomplete. Although the proposed method is not identical to ETF-based methods, it is clearly related to the broader family of geometry-based classifier design in federated learning. In that sense, the paper would benefit from a more complete discussion of recent geometry-driven approaches and stronger comparison to this line of work. 
2.Fig. 1 does not explain the method clearly enough. The overall pipeline is shown, but the interaction among orthogonal prompts, generated anchors, local supervision, and geometric regularization is still difficult to follow from the figure itself. 
3.The empirical results are promising, but the current comparison set is not strong enough to fully support the claimed methodological advantage. Since more directly related geometry-based baselines are missing, the reported gains are not yet sufficient to demonstrate that the proposed formulation is clearly preferable to other structured classifier designs.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

1.Expand the related-work discussion and add more direct comparison to recent geometry-based federated methods, especially those using structured classifier geometry.
2.Revise Fig. 1 and the method presentation to more clearly illustrate how the generated anchors are constructed and how they interact with local training and federated aggregation. 
3.Clarify more explicitly what distinguishes generated anchors from other geometry-based classifier formulations, and why this specific design is preferable in the heterogeneous-label FedDG setting.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
1.This work tackles the highly realistic yet under-explored challenge of completely disjoint label spaces across institutions. While such label heterogeneity is inherent in multi-center pathology collaborations, it remains largely unaddressed in the current federated learning literature.
2.The authors introduces GASD, which reframes classification as a geometric registration problem. By synthesizing consistent anchors via a shared hypernetwork, it effectively bypasses gradient conflicts caused by label heterogeneity.
3.They Proposes GCR, leveraging a memory bank to retrieve historical negatives. This ensures feature compactness and stable alignment between image features and generative anchors under limited batch constraints.
4.The authors construct a comprehensive pan-cancer benchmark of 4,796 WSIs, providing a reusable and substantial resource for future research in generalizable pathology analysis.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper targets a highly practical yet challenging scenario in federated learning where different medical institutions possess completely non-overlapping label sets. 
2.The conceptual shift of redefining traditional classification as a geometric registration problem on a hypersphere is both innovative and mathematically sound. By utilizing a shared hypernetwork to map semantic-free latent prompts into generative anchors, the proposed framework effectively mitigates gradient conflicts typically caused by heterogeneous label spaces, ensuring stable knowledge aggregation across diverse clients.
3.The effectiveness of the proposed model is rigorously demonstrated through extensive experiments on a large-scale pan-cancer dataset.
4.The study provides profound insights into the model’s internal behavior using anchor similarity heatmaps and KDE-based feature distribution analyses. The empirical observation that adenocarcinoma subtypes from different organs converge in the latent space strongly suggests that the hypernetwork successfully captures organ-invariant histomorphological primitives. This finding provides compelling evidence for the model’s ability to learn biologically meaningful representations beyond mere label matching.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Alignment with Meta-Learning Paradigm and Missing Baselines
While this paper claims to address Federated Domain Generalization, the proposed framework mandates fine-tuning with labeled support sets from unseen target domains. This “global pre-training followed by rapid local adaptation” pipeline is fundamentally aligned with the meta-learning paradigm established by Per-FedAvg [Fallah et al., NeurIPS 2020] and further explored by test-time adaptation approaches such as FedICON [Tan et al., NeurIPS 2023] or TTA-FedDG [Liang et al., AAAI 2025]. The absence of comparisons with these adaptation oriented baselines makes it difficult to assess whether the proposed approach offers tangible advantages over established adaptation strategies in federated settings.
2.Insufficient Coverage of Contemporary Baselines
The selected baselines predominantly span 2021 to 2023 and do not adequately represent the current state of the art. Recent advances in federated domain generalization have introduced diverse strategies including domain adversarial generation (FedDAG [Che et al., TMI 2025]), test-time adaptation for federated settings (TTA-FedDG [Liang et al., AAAI 2025]), and non-IID histopathology-specific federated style transfer (HistoFS [Raswa et al., CVPR 2025]). Benchmarking the proposed geometric framework against such contemporary methods is necessary to substantiate its claimed superiority within the evolving research landscape.
3.Insufficient Justification for Architectural Design
Reframing classification as geometric registration on a hypersphere is a compelling concept, yet several core design decisions lack empirical justification. First, the orthogonality constraint imposed on task prompts is presented as essential for maximal separability, but no comparison with random initialization is provided to validate this claim. Second, the choice to generate anchors via a shared hypernetwork, rather than learning them directly as trainable vectors per client, introduces additional architectural complexity. Since learnable anchors can realize an equivalent hypersphere classification structure without a generator, this design choice requires explicit experimental evidence demonstrating its necessity.
4.Incomplete Ablation and Sensitivity Analysis
The reported ablation leaves critical hyperparameters such as memory bank size, temperature, and hypernetwork depth unexamined. Moreover, the support set ratio is fixed at 10% throughout all experiments, which constitutes a non-trivial amount of labeled data in the pathology domain. A sensitivity analysis across varying ratios (e.g., 1%, 5%) is essential to disentangle whether the performance gains originate from the quality of the pre-trained representation or from the GASD+GCR loss structure favoring the fine-tuning process.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

While the fundamental concept is quite compelling, the experimental validation is insufficient. The ablation study lacks key analyses to justify the proposed design choices, and comparisons with recent state-of-the-art methods are missing.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The core idea proposed in this paper, reframing classification as a geometric registration problem through the generative anchor based semantic decoupling module and geometric consistency regularization, is conceptually sound. The anchor similarity heatmaps and KDE distribution analyses convincingly support the claim that the model learns organ invariant representations. Furthermore, through the rebuttal, the authors substantially strengthened the previously insufficient experimental validation and the justification for their core techniques. Taking these factors together, I have revised my score for this paper to Borderline Accept (4).

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces FedGMA, a federated learning framework designed to address the challenge of federated domain generalization for pan-cancer subtyping classification in heterogeneous label spaces within pathological image analysis.​ FedGMA integrates Generative Anchor-based Semantic Decoupling (GASD) to separate feature learning from local label definitions, and Geometric Consistency Regularization (GCR) to ensure the compactness and separability of the latent space. Evaluated on a large-scale benchmark comprising 4,796 whole slide images across 8 cancer types, FedGMA achieves an average AUC of 76.42%, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art methods.
reviews.text_strengths: This paper makes timely contributions to the fields of federated learning and computational pathology. Its strength lies in innovatively addressing the long-standing “heterogeneous label space” problem in pan-cancer image analysis within federated learning. By introducing the Generative Anchor-based Semantic Decoupling (GASD) mechanism, the authors cleverly disentangle feature learning from local, diverse diagnostic criteria, which is crucial for achieving truly generalizable pan-cancer diagnostic models. This approach not only solves a technical challenge but also aligns with pathological observations of shared invariant histomorphological features across cancer types. The inclusion of Geometric Consistency Regularization (GCR) further enhances the model’s robustness and the quality of feature representation, especially under limited batch sizes, by ensuring the compactness and separability of the learned latent space. Furthermore, the construction of a large-scale multi-cancer benchmark dataset is a valuable contribution in itself, providing a standardized evaluation platform for future research in this domain. The significant performance improvements and the in-depth interpretation of the model’s internal mechanisms (e.g., through anchor similarity heatmaps) strengthen the paper’s persuasiveness and credibility.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
While FedGMA demonstrates excellent performance, several aspects of the paper could be further refined.
Firstly, as the paper states that a strictly orthogonal static latent prompt matrix is used in Generative Anchor-based Semantic Decoupling (GASD) to ensure maximal separability of the initial latent space, a more detailed mathematical derivation or theoretical analysis regarding the profound theoretical basis for choosing “orthogonality” as a specific constraint, and its unique advantages in fostering the learning of a “consistent geometric lexicon,” could be provided. Furthermore, the paper could elaborate on the intrinsic mechanisms and design choices of the Hypernetwork in transforming semantic-agnostic latent prompts into task-specific geometric anchors.
Secondly, the Geometric Consistency Regularization (GCR) module plays a crucial role in ensuring the compactness and separability of the latent space. However, the paper lacks sufficient sensitivity analysis for key parameters within the GCR module, such as memory bank size and negative sampling strategies. The absence of systematic ablation studies demonstrating how these parameters impact model performance, stability, and generalization ability (e.g., comparison across different memory bank sizes) limits a comprehensive understanding of the module’s robustness.
Additionally, although the paper indicates that fine-tuning and evaluation were performed on unseen target domains, it does not elaborate on the “costs” associated with this fine-tuning process, including the required amount of fine-tuning data, the number of iterations, and the actual contribution of fine-tuning to the final performance. If FedGMA can perform well without fine-tuning or with minimal fine-tuning data, it would further highlight its domain generalization capabilities; thus, a more transparent presentation of fine-tuning inputs and outputs would be highly beneficial.
Finally, despite significant performance gains, the absolute AUC values for certain cancer types like BLCA and UCEC remain relatively low (e.g., BLCA 59.74%, UCEC 64.61%). This might suggest higher heterogeneity or diagnostic difficulty for these specific cancer types, warranting further discussion on the model’s limitations or future improvement directions in addressing such particular challenges. What’s more, as the paper has demonstrated statistically significant differences between FedGMA and other methods using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, the AUC result table does not report 95% confidence intervals. Including 95% CIs would more intuitively display the credible range and stability of AUC estimates, providing readers with more comprehensive performance evaluation information, especially when comparing different methods.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper writing, organization, and comprehensive experiments and analysis are major factors of my score.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I think the authors’ response partly addressed my questions. I prefer to give a boderlined acceptance.

meta_reviews.text:
Based on the three reviews (two “Weak Reject” and one “Weak Accept”), the paper is clearly borderline. The reviewers raise substantial concerns that can potentially be addressed. In the rebuttal, the authors must: (1) add missing geometry‑based and meta‑learning baselines (e.g., Per‑FedAvg, TTA‑FedDG, FedDAG); (2) provide ablation on key hyperparameters (memory bank size, support set ratio); (3) clarify the orthogonality choice and the hypernetwork design; and (4) improve Fig. 1 to clearly explain anchor generation and interactions.

Two of the three reviewers raised their scores to accept after the rebuttal, acknowledging the paper’s conceptual strength (geometric registration for federated domain generalization with disjoint label spaces) and its valuable benchmark. Hence, I recommend Accept.

The paper addresses a federated domain generalization under completely disjoint label spaces. Reviewers appreciated the practical motivation, the large-scale pan-cancer benchmark, and the consistent performance improvements across unseen target domains. The proposed FedGMA framework introduces an interesting geometric formulation that decouples feature learning from local label semantics using generative anchors and geometric consistency regularization. The experimental results and visualization analyses support the effectiveness of the approach. Although the reviewers raised concerns regarding the theoretical justification, baseline coverage, and positioning relative to prior geometry-based methods, the rebuttal addressed these issues reasonably well. Therefore, I recommend acceptance.

The paper has initially received mixed reviews and it was invited for rebuttal. The authors submitted a rebuttal to address the comments of the reviewers. After the rebuttal, two reviewers updated their scores indicating that their comments had been properly addressed in the rebuttal and even if they highlight that the paper is borderline, they propose its acceptance. The AC read the paper, reviews, rebuttal and justification of rating and they agree that the paper is borderline, but it could be interesting for the community.

author_feedback_text:
We thank AC and reviewers for the constructive feedback. 
Q1: Comparisons with meta-learning and geometry-based methods (R1Q1, R1Q3, R2Q1)
A1: Our FedGMA achieves an average AUC of 76.42%, outperforming Per-FedAvg (49.07%, meta-learning, 2020), FedCCFA (56.69%, geometry-based, 2024), and TTA-FedDG (72.40%, test-time adaptation, 2025). Regarding meta-learning-based methods, Per-FedAvg struggles with extreme label heterogeneity because gradients from conflicting local semantics lead to severe interference in the shared encoder. Standard geometry-based methods inherently assume a predefined and shared global label space, making them mathematically inapplicable to our completely disjoint label space setting. We will discuss these contemporary methods in the revised related work section.
Q2: Contemporary baselines selection (R2Q2)
A2: Most FedDG methods assume a shared global label space, making them inapplicable to our disjoint setting. Our benchmark prioritized compatibility with extreme label heterogeneity, focusing on strategies like the prototype-based family. Specifically, we included FedAdapterProto[17] (2025) to represent the state of the art. We acknowledge that recent works such as FedDAG provide valuable insights and will incorporate these comparisons in our journal extension.
Q3: Missing hyperparameter ablations (R2Q4, R3Q2)
A3: We conducted extensive ablations in our preliminary experiment. They were omitted due to space limitation. For the support set ratio, zero-shot evaluation yields 67.42% AUC. Fine-tuning with 1%, 5%, and 10% data yields 72.85%, 75.10%, and 76.42%. For memory bank size, the performance is robust (76.31% for M=16 vs 76.42% for M=32). Other parameters such as temperature and hypernetwork depth were selected based on standard empirical practices to balance representative capacity and training stability. Full sensitivity analyses will be provided in our anonymized repository upon acceptance.
Q4: Fine-tuning cost and implementation details (R3Q3)
A4: The training and fine-tuning frameworks maintain consistency. We utilize SGD optimization with a learning rate of 1e-3.The fine-tuning process is performed on a 10% support set and lasts for 10 epochs.
Q5: Justification for orthogonality over random initialization (R2Q3, R3Q1)
A5: Mathematically, orthogonal initialization ensures maximum and uniform inter-class margins, a principle consistent with Neural Collapse (Papyan et al., 2020). Empirically, random initialization fails to maintain this margin, causing severe feature collapse. Our preliminary experiments showed that random initialization drops the average AUC by approximately 9%. 
Q6: Rationale for shared hypernetwork (R1Q3, R2Q3, R3Q1)
A6: Our hypernetwork acts as a universal geometric dictionary designed to transform semantic-agnostic latent prompts into task specific anchors. If clients learned these anchors directly as local trainable vectors, the vectors would severely overfit to their highly heterogeneous and disjoint local label spaces. This would re-introduce exact semantic conflicts during server aggregation. 
Q7: Clarity of Figure 1 (R1Q2)
A7: We will revise Figure 1 based on the reviewer’s suggestions to enhance clarity.
Q8: Low performance on certain classes and absence of confidence intervals (R3Q4)
A8: The lower performance on BLCA and UCEC is caused by their inherent and notoriously high intra class morphological heterogeneity. However, FedGMA still outperforms baselines on these difficult classes by a significant gap of 2-8%. Addressing extreme intrinsic heterogeneity remains a future direction. Regarding the confidence intervals, we completely agree that they improve rigorousness. Due to strict space limits, they were initially omitted, but we will add them for all metrics in the revised version.

title: Gene-Selective Morphological Conditioning with Heteroscedastic Flow Matching for Spatial Transcriptomics
abstract: Predicting spatially resolved gene expression from histology images requires capturing how tissue morphology relates to each gene, but the strength of this coupling differs across genes. Current methods assign every gene the same morphological representation, overlooking this heterogeneity. We introduce gene binding modules that decompose morphological features into functional sub-spaces, letting each gene attend selectively to relevant programs rather than a shared global representation. To capture inter-gene dependencies, compact regulator tokens compress and redistribute information across gene groups, modeling coordinated transcriptional programs. The framework further learns per-gene heteroscedastic uncertainty that focuses model capacity on morphologically predictable genes during training, and modulates stochastic sampling at inference: tightly coupled genes receive near-deterministic generation while loosely coupled genes are sampled more broadly. Experiments on four spatial transcriptomics datasets show consistent improvements over both deterministic and generative baselines. The learned modules recover biologically coherent gene groupings without supervision, validated through pathway enrichment analysis, demonstrating that the framework provides interpretable biological insights beyond prediction accuracy.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The authors propose a gene-selective generative framework for predicting spatial gene expression from histology images. The key idea is to model heterogeneous coupling between morphology and gene expression, where some genes are assumed to be tightly coupled (predictable from morphology) and others loosely coupled (less predictable). The method incorporates gene-wise attention, regulator tokens to capture gene–gene dependencies, and heteroscedastic uncertainty to adapt prediction confidence per gene. 
The main contribution is moving beyond direct black-box regression and attempt to model gene-specific relationships to morphology, and inter-gene dependencies via gene-selective conditioning and uncertainty-aware flow matching. Second, the idea of strongly and weakly morphology-coupled genes in modelling.
reviews.text_strengths:
Moves beyond standard regression which is a meaningful step forward.
Structured modelling of gene–gene interactions using regulator tokens
Gene-specific morphological subgrouping instead of a single shared feature, allowing each gene to attend to different morphological programs, which aligns better with biological intuition.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Limited generalizability / risk of dataset bias: The notion of “tight” vs “loose” coupling is learned implicitly from the dataset and may reflect dataset-specific correlations rather than true biology. For example, ERBB2 appears tightly coupled in Fig. 1, but this could be driven by the dataset being enriched for HER2+ cases. It is unclear how well this would transfer to a different cohort.
The paper does not perform cross cohort validation, train on one and test on another. Which is critical given that we know these models are capturing dataset-specific correlation patterns and the notion of tight and loose coupling is likely to make the domain shift even worse [see Dawood et al 2026 nature biomedical engineering]
From Table 2, performance appears sensitive to the number of regulator tokens. This raise concerns that the model may be learning dataset-specific configurations, which could limit generalization.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This is an interesting and well-motivated step toward more structured modelling of spatial transcriptomics. However, the current formulation appears to rely heavily on dataset-specific correlations, and lacks evidence of robustness under distribution shift. Addressing generalization and improving biological interpretability would significantly strengthen the work.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a mean flow matching based framework for spatial transcriptomics prediction and achieves the best overall performance among the compared methods on multiple datasets. On top of the conditional generative formulation, it introduces Regulator Attention to model gene dependencies, Gene Binding Module Attention to capture the associations between tissue morphology and different genes, and Uncertainty-Aware Flow Matching to account for the intrinsic variability in morphology to gene expression mapping. These designs are reasonable and work together well.
reviews.text_strengths: 1.The overall idea is meaningful and reasonably novel. The authors cast spatial gene expression prediction as a conditional generative problem with flow matching, which is a natural way to model the one-to-many relationship between tissue morphology and gene expression. 2.The proposed modules are well motivated. 3.The empirical results are solid. The method achieves the best overall correlation performance on multiple datasets, especially on harder settings with more genes, which supports the value of the proposed design.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper also has some weaknesses. 
First, the assumption that the image feature can be decomposed into 6 morphological programs is not fully convincing. This design is reasonable, but the paper does not give strong enough evidence that such a fixed decomposition is biologically meaningful or consistently valid across datasets. The ablation only shows that K=6 works better empirically, but it does not fully justify the modeling assumption itself.
Second, the method does not achieve the best MSE or MAE on the four datasets, and this point needs a clearer explanation. The paper argues that deterministic methods are naturally better on pointwise error because they predict the conditional mean, while the proposed method focuses more on modeling uncertainty and diversity. This is reasonable, but it still leaves some concern about absolute prediction accuracy.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I gave this paper a weak accept because the overall idea is meaningful, the proposed modules are well motivated, and the method shows solid experimental performance across multiple datasets. In particular, the paper addresses an important problem and achieves strong correlation results with a reasonable generative framework. At the same time, some parts of the method are not fully justified, and the gains are less clear on MSE and MAE, so I do not see it as a strong accept. Overall, I think the paper has enough novelty and practical value to merit acceptance, but it still has some limitations.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a flow-matching framework for histology-to-spatial-transcriptomics prediction that addresses three biological observations: (1) genes differ in how tightly their expression couples to tissue morphology, (2) genes are organized into coordinated transcriptional programs, and (3) a well-calibrated generative model should modulate per-gene stochasticity.
reviews.text_strengths:
Clear, biologically-grounded motivation. Fig. 1 is excellent: panel (a) shows that among morphologically similar spots, gene expression heterogeneity varies widely (ERBB2 tightly coupled, COL1A1 broadly variable — quantified via coefficient of variation over 10 regions); panel (b) shows the block-diagonal co-expression structure; panel (c) illustrates the adaptive-stochasticity intuition. This is the kind of motivation figure that turns three components into a coherent story.
Each component is tied to a specific biological observation. Gene binding modules ↔ heterogeneous morphology–expression coupling; regulator tokens ↔ coordinated transcriptional programs; heteroscedastic flow matching ↔ gene-specific stochasticity. This is a well-constructed narrative.
Strong empirical results. Wins or ties best on ρ10/ρ50/ρ200\rho_{10}/\rho_{50}/\rho_{200}
ρ10​/ρ50​/ρ200​ across all four datasets; the pattern of growing margins with broader gene panels (42% relative gain on ρ200 BC-I vs. smaller gains on ρ10) is exactly what the gene-selective story predicts.
Comprehensive baseline comparison. 10 methods spanning deterministic regression (ST-Net, HisToGene, TRIPLEX), graph-based (Hist2ST), retrieval (BLEEP, EGN), multi-scale (M2OST, THItoGene), diffusion (Stem), and flow matching (STFlow). This is the most thorough baseline coverage in this field.
Clean ablations. Table 3 isolates each component (B → B+M → B+P → Ours); Table 2 does hyperparameter analysis for MM
M and KK
K; the ρ200 gains from M and P individually are comparable and combine to give the full method — convincing that both components contribute.
Interpretability analysis is exceptional. Fig. 4 shows gene binding modules recovering block-diagonal structure (Mod1 = secretory/adhesion, Mod3 = cytoskeletal/metabolic, Mod4 = ECM/signaling, Mod5 = stromal/immune, Mod0 = immunoglobulins), validated against Enrichr-detected pathways including EMT, antigen processing, and neutrophil degranulation. Regulator tokens show the expected complementary pattern (broad, cross-module attention). This is unsupervised emergence of biologically sensible structure and is a significant result beyond prediction accuracy.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(W1) Heteroscedastic flow matching vs. UA-Flow / Kendall–Gal positioning
The heteroscedastic-NLL loss (Eq. 5) is exactly Kendall & Gal’s classical formulation, applied to the velocity regression of flow matching. The paper cites Kendall & Gal [8] but frames “heteroscedastic flow matching” as if it were a new generative-modeling paradigm (“introduces heteroscedastic flow matching” is implicit in the framing). In reality:
The loss is Kendall–Gal.
Using σθ\sigma_\theta
σθ​ as the SDE diffusion coefficient (Eq. 6) for per-gene adaptive sampling is the actual novel technical move in this paper.
UA-Flow (arXiv 2602.10326, Feb 2026) concurrently proposes heteroscedastic velocity-field modeling for image generation; the paper may or may not have been aware of this depending on its submission date.
The paper’s actual contribution — Kendall–Gal-style heteroscedastic output combined with per-gene SDE coefficient for uncertainty-aware generation — is novel in the ST context but should be positioned more precisely. Please distinguish the output-space per-gene formulation from UA-Flow’s velocity-space formulation in the revision.
(W2) Uncertainty calibration is not directly evaluated
The paper motivates heteroscedastic modeling with “well-calibrated” per-gene uncertainty (Fig. 1c).
