meta_reviews.text: Reviewers agree the paper proposes a well-motivated self-supervised pretraining framework for sulcal labeling, with strengths in leveraging large unlabeled data, effective transfer learning design, and strong performance under extreme label scarcity. However, they note limitations including potentially unfair baseline comparisons, incomplete ablation/validation of key components, and insufficient analysis of data factors (e.g., age, noise sensitivity). Overall, the work is considered novel but needing more rigorous and fair evaluation.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank all the reviewers and the Area Chair for their insightful comments and for recommending our paper for acceptance.
Reviewer #1
R1.W1 ( Comparison with DINOv3 )
We completely agree that this comparison is inherently asymmetric. As stated in the manuscript, DINOv3’s performance ‘highlights a structural domain gap between natural RGB images and distorted cortical topologies’. The cubemap projection used is the state-of-the-art for spherical-to-planar mapping, as it mitigates the polar singularities inherent to equirectangular projections while maintaining geometric consistency suitable for 2D convolutional kernels (even though it is not a conformal map). Our goal was not to claim absolute superiority, but to show that 2D projections create a structural bottleneck and a powerful foundation model fine-tuned on this projection still fails to match a surface-native approach. DINOv3 was used strictly due to lacking spherical foundation models. Spherical feature maps (curvature and sulcal depth) also differ drastically from the volumetric T1 MRI data on which some medical foundation models are trained. 
R1.W2 (TPI Ablation)
Replacing soft initialization with random initialization yields Dice 0.74 ± 0.03 / ESI 0.17 ± 0.03, confirming the benefit of our strategy. This result was omitted from the original submission due to space constraints, as properly discussing the TPI’s contribution (which is most salient in the very low-data regime (5 subjects)) would have required an additional table and an extended analysis. We also note that monitoring TPI weights during training reveals an increase in the importance assigned to the sulcal lines channel. This confirms that soft initialization enables a progressive integration of semantic information into the pre-trained backbone.
R1.W3 ( Age Distribution )
UK Biobank subjects are older adults (40–69 years), whereas the labeled cohort consists mostly of young adults (20–35 years). However, our self-supervised objective targets intrinsic topological features (local curvature and depth variations) rather than age-dependent traits like cortical thickness or sulcal width. Since sulcal topology, as defined by fundi lines, remains highly stable throughout adulthood, and our task is labeling rather than morphometry, this age gap does not hinder the transferability of the geometric priors.
R1.W4 (Figure 3 vs. 1D definition)
Figure 3 is a population-level visualization on a template brain: the Elocal metric is computed on the 1D sulcal lines and then aggregated across all test subjects, accompanied by statistical tests. We chose this representation over individual prediction overlays to provide a more globally informative picture of systematic gains and failures of the method across the full test set.
Reviewer #2
We sincerely thank Reviewer #2 for the positive assessment. Exploring Transformer-based architectures and masked autoencoder pre-training paradigms is indeed a natural and promising next step.
Reviewer #3
R3.W1 (Sensitivity to mis-traced sulcal lines)
First, TRACE parameters were carefully calibrated through expert quality control, and the extracted lines were further refined via graph-based morphological operations (erosion and dilation) specifically designed to suppress false traces and fill small gaps. Second, the TPI is a learned module optimized end-to-end on lines that already carry inherent variability, meaning the network implicitly learns tolerance to imperfect inputs rather than relying on perfectly traced fundi. A formal robustness analysis under synthetic perturbations of the input lines would be a valuable extension and will be noted as future work.
R3.W2 (Comparison with BrainVISA) 
Borne et al. [1] is the BrainVISA-based automatic labeling pipeline, already included as the volumetric baseline in Figure 2A and evaluated on the exact same dataset. The comparison therefore exists, and we will make this connection more explicit in the final version.

title: Geometry-Aware Manifold Trajectory Modeling for Task fMRI Activation Mapping
abstract: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) measures task-evoked neural activity through blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signals and enables activation mapping to localize task-related brain responses. Conventional activation mapping typically relies on the general linear model (GLM), which assumes linearity and a predefined hemodynamic response function (HRF). However, mounting evidence indicates that BOLD responses are nonlinear and state-dependent. Meanwhile, the high dimensionality and low signal-to-noise ratio of fMRI further challenge the linear assumption. These limitations motivate a neural-manifold view, in which high dimensional task dynamics evolve on a low-dimensional state space. We propose a geometry-aware manifold trajectory modeling framework that represents task-related activity as structured trajectories. The framework identifies a central baseline cluster, computes geodesic distances from each embedded frame to this cluster along the manifold trajectory graph, and converts them into vertex-wise activation maps via the proposed Manifold Geodesic-based Similarity (MGS) without HRF fitting. Using the Human Connectome Project (HCP) motor-task fMRI dataset, we uncover a petal-like looped trajectory, indicating a reproducible low-dimensional organization of task-evoked dynamics. At the individual-level, MGS robustly recovers canonical motor activations despite substantial single-subject fMRI noise. At the group-level, compared with HRF-based GLM, MGS yields more discriminative activation patterns and highlights task-related effects less emphasized by GLM, demonstrating the advantage of geometry-aware manifold trajectories for task fMRI activation mapping. Code is available at https://github.com/PCMLYR/ManifoldTraj_MGS

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a data-driven method to model temporal dynamics of task fMRI data using manifold clustering and trajectories, which, unlike the commonly-used GLM approach, does not depend on the assumption of linearity and selection of the hemodynamic response function, which varies across brain regions and subjects. The method averages the time series of 100 scans to produce a smoother and stronger response to the motor task, which makes the manifold projection and clustering more robust. The temporal clustering of the manifold projects clearly show that the different conditions can be clustered correctly when accounting for the delay of the hemodynamic response, which motivates the study in the first place. The condition-level group analysis shows activation maps that are comparable to the GLM baseline.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The geodesic distance to the baseline cluster is an interesting way of representing the group-level response to the different conditions in the task. 
2.The proposed approach does not assume linearity in the BOLD response and doesn’t depend on defining a hemodynamic response to retrieve task-related activation maps.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The advantage provided by the Manifold Geodesic-based Similarity over averaging over the BOLD signal on the same folds (MGS without the weight vector w) is not shown. 
2.No quantitative analysis was described. 
3.The proposed approach uses the group-level geodesic distance to weight the importance of individual-level responses, which can bias the individual-level activation maps towards the group response.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Major concerns:
1.My main major concern is that the benefit of using UMAP projections, clustering in the manifold space and geodesic distances is not shown over a simple averaging over the BOLD frames within the condition blocks. The MGS equation only uses the geodesic distance in the weight vector w. The manuscript would highly benefit from showing a comparison with an “MGS” activation map that is calculated without the weight w. This would completely remove the group-level bias and would show how much the MGS activation maps depend on the process of projecting, clustering and calculating the distance at the group level. This “weightless” MGS could still take the resting-state blocks just like the proposed MGS does, and would make the comparison direct. 
2.The manuscript is limited to a qualitative analysis. It would benefit from a quantitative analysis that, for instance, calculates the sensitivity, specificity and Dice of the MGS-recovered maps using the GLM activation maps as the ground truth. 
3.The manuscript also lacks an individual-level trial study to see if the proposed MGS approach can recover trial-level maps better than the GLM or hemodynamic deconvolution methods such as Paradigm Free Mapping and Total Activation.
Minor comments:
1.Figure 2 would highly benefit from being consistent with the colours across UMAP plotting and clustering plotting. 
2.It is not clear whether the resting state pseudo-blocks were picked randomly or in the same order as with the task data. 
3.It is not clear if each frame (time point) is projected along the geodesic path. I think they are but authors should make that clearer. 
4.I believe that Figure 3 shows $\Delta \text{MGS}$ and not MGS.

The decisive factor in this recommendation is the novelty of representing group-level task responses as manifold trajectories without assuming a specific hemodynamic response function or linearity in the BOLD signal. There is clear potential in using the proposed UMAP embedding space to study individual- and group-level responses to different types of stimuli, and the geodesic distance to the baseline cluster is an interesting and principled way of encoding task-evoked dynamics.
That said, the contribution is weakened by the absence of a quantitative analysis and by a missing ablation that is critical for interpreting the results. The activation maps shown are qualitatively compelling, but the manuscript would need to report sensitivity, specificity and Dice against a GLM reference to substantiate the claims more rigorously. More importantly, the benefit of the manifold projection and geodesic weighting over a simpler averaging of the BOLD frames within condition blocks is not demonstrated. Without a comparison against a weightless version of MGS, it is difficult to assess how much of the observed performance comes from the manifold geometry itself rather than from the block-averaging procedure. These are addressable weaknesses, but they do keep this submission at the borderline.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors addressed all three of my major concerns and my four minor clarifications in their response. On the weightless-MGS ablation (Q1), they argued that the geodesic weighting is, by construction, the component that separates MGS from a normalized block-averaged BOLD summary. The argument is internally consistent but does not constitute the empirical evidence I requested, and the question of whether the manifold geometry adds information beyond block averaging therefore remains open in the submitted manuscript. On the quantitative comparison with GLM (Q2), the authors reported Dice and sensitivity values in the rebuttal, but per the MICCAI guidelines these cannot enter the camera-ready and I do not weight them in this assessment. On the individual-level trial study (Q3), the authors acknowledged the value of a comparison against single-trial GLM or hemodynamic deconvolution methods but did not offer it. The four minor clarifications were addressed correctly, and the authors committed to releasing the code through an anonymous repository.
In line with the AC guidance that meta-reviewers should not penalize papers for failing to provide new experimental results in the rebuttal, I do not downgrade my recommendation on those grounds. My initial Weak Accept was based on the manuscript as submitted, and the rebuttal did not surface anything that materially changes that assessment. The novelty of the manifold-trajectory framing and the principled use of geodesic distance to baseline as a data-driven, HRF-free signature of task engagement outweigh the rigor gap, and I maintain my positive recommendation.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: A task fMRI activation mapping framework based on low-dimensional manifold trajectory and geodesic distance modeling is proposed; the MGS index is designed to achieve the transformation from geometric dynamics to vertex-level activation maps; and the potential of this method in restoring classical motion activation patterns and improving the compactness of population activation maps is verified on HCP motor-task data.
reviews.text_strengths: The topic is novel, attempting to introduce low-dimensional manifold trajectory geometry into task fMRI activation mapping; the methodological framework is relatively complete, and the MGS index has a certain degree of interpretability; on HCP motor-task data, it can recover the topology of motor body parts with neurophysiological rationality and shows a more compact group activation pattern compared to traditional GLM.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The paper points out that compared to GLM, MGS yields “more compact and discriminative” group activation maps. However, the current support for this point in the paper mainly relies on qualitative visualization comparisons, lacking sufficient quantitative results for comparison. For example, methods such as IOU comparison of activation regions lack quantitative comparison results.
2.When comparing different modules, the paper lacks comparisons of their effectiveness. For example, is the performance derived from manifold modeling itself, shared templates, or geodesic distance?
3.Some parameter settings in the paper are based on empirical values, lacking sensitivity analysis of these parameters, such as sensitivity analysis of different n_neighbors, min_dist, and distance metrics.
4.The paper uses a fixed 6-frame delay alignment, calling it coarse latency alignment rather than HRF fitting. The authors should provide the rationale for using this parameter, whether it is based on experience or experimental conclusions.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The method presented in this paper is novel, but it lacks sufficient experimental evidence to demonstrate its effectiveness.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The rebuttal partially addresses my concerns. In particular, the authors provide additional quantitative comparison with GLM using Dice and sensitivity, and they give a more reasonable explanation for the fixed 6-frame delay based on the HCP TR and plausible BOLD timing.
However, my main concerns are not fully resolved. The response still does not provide ablation studies that separate the contributions of manifold modeling, shared templates, and geodesic distance. The explanation of replacing the geodesic weight with an all-one vector is useful, but it remains conceptual rather than experimental. Similarly, the authors acknowledge that broader sensitivity analysis would be useful, but they do not provide actual sensitivity results for n_neighbors, min_dist, or distance metrics.
Therefore, while the rebuttal improves the clarity of some points, I do not think it fully resolves the methodological validation concerns.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This manuscript proposed a geometry-aware manifold trajectory modeling framework that characterizes task-fMRI activation as structured trajectories. The main idea is to calculate the geodesic distances to a baseline cluster on the manifold trajectory, and convert them into vertex-wise activation maps via the proposed Manifold Geodesic-based Similarity (MGS) without requiring HRF fitting. The HCP motor-task dataset was used to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed method and showed superior performance compared to conventional HRF-based GLM methods.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The background and motivation is well justified.
2.The formation of brain task activation mapping using manifold geodesics is novel.
3.Both qualitative and quantitative evaluations are performed to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Lacking independent reproducibility data. Although the authors used HCP motor task data, it is unclear whether the identified pattern and mapping characteristics is reproducible in other motor-related data, even in other task fMRI data.
2.Lacking details for subject selection. They merely used a subset of 100 subjects from the HCP dataset. However, it is unclear why not using all subjects (~1000) in this dataset.
3.Lacking comprehensive comparisons. The authors should perform comprehensive comparisons between the proposed method with conventional GLM-based methods to show its superiority in identifying meaningful activation patterns. Moreover, the authors should compared the proposed method with other manifold-based methods.
4.Lacking justification of parameter-setting. Some of the parameter selection is unclear. For example, different embeddings and different latency shifts.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The formation of brain task activation mapping using manifold geodesics is novel.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have addressed my concerns about data inclusion, etc. I appreciate the novelty of this study in fMRI analysis.

meta_reviews.text:
Perhaps the most pervasive approach to perform segregational analysis in neuroimaging, inc. fMRI, is by using a characterization of the response function as a factor in the general linear model. Although less popular due to their inherent complexity, topological and geometrical approaches can also carry out such analysis with some collateral benefits over the plain statistical counterparts (although of course, strictly speaking the GLM is a manifold, but we hardly think of it as such). This paper is one good example of topological and/or geometrical approaches. The manuscript presents a framework to characterize brain activation at group level that exploit the geometry of the underlying manifold, where the actual modelling occurs, to make statements about task-related effects that would otherwise be missed by the GLM.
All reviewers coincide in highlightin the novelty of the approach, and whilst perhaps for me this is less so (I happen to work very closely to this field), but I do coincide that there is novelty here.
Among the weaknesses, the lack of quantitative evidence (R1/R2/R3) and the arbitrary decisions over the parameterization (R2/R3) have dominated the reviews. Coupled with the lack of direct access to the code (R1/R3), hence limiting the reproducibility, these shortcomings have somewhat limit the potential that the drat could have had.
Nevertheless, given the two more senior reviewers, and I concurr, in supporting acceptance, but the split decision, I recommend inviting a rebuttal. Specifically, the rebutall must address:
Affording quantitative evidence inc. comprehensive comparison (R3) e.g. vs classical GLM, and about the effectiveness of the individual components (R2).
Provide rationale and/or empirical evidence to justify parameter setting.
Disclose code details

The pre-rebuttal meta-review identified three major issues: (1) lack of quantitative evidence and comparison against classical methods such as the GLM; (2) unjustified parameter choices; (3) unavailability of source code. The rebuttal only partially addressed these points with Reviewer #2 explicitly maintaining the Reject score after the rebuttal. Quantitative benchmarking and ablation studies remain absent, and advantage over the gold standard (GLM) has been attempted but not clearly evidenced. Despite genuine novelty, the evidentiary basis for acceptance is insufficient at this time.

Despite some lingering concerns, the authors have done a good job addressing the main critiques to extent allowed by MICCAI (i.e., no new experiments). This work would be of interest to the community.

All reviewers are satisfied with the quality of the rebuttal responses and have voted to accept the paper. I think the authors have done a good job addressing all concerns raised during the review and plan to address the comment on reproducibility upon acceptance by releasing their Github repository.

author_feedback_text:
Thank all reviewers for valuable comments. Our responses are presented as follows.
1.Quantitative comparison vs GLM (MR-Q1, R1-Q2, R2-Q1, R3-Q3)
We thank the reviewers for requesting quantitative evidence. We had computed Dice and sensitivity between MGS and GLM group maps for the five motor conditions (Dice: 0.61, 0.66, 0.82, 0.72, and 0.79 for l/r hand, l/r foot, and tongue; sensitivity: 1 for all). Still, we think using GLM as absolute ground truth is not fully appropriate, since our goal is to examine whether task-activation information encoded in looped manifold trajectories can be translated into vertex-wise activation statistics under possible HRF mismatch. Thus, the experiment is not merely a qualitative comparison with GLM, but an evaluation of the activation information carried by the looped manifold trajectory. The GLM comparison further confirms that MGS recovers canonical motor activation patterns.
2.Effectiveness of individual components (MR-Q1, R1-Q1, R2-Q2)
We agree that a weightless-MGS control is a meaningful ablation. In Eq. (2), w(dG) transfers manifold-trajectory information into the vertex-wise activation statistic. Replacing it with an all-one vector would reduce MGS to a normalized block-average BOLD summary and discard the baseline-departure/return profile learned through UMAP, DBM clustering, and geodesic distance estimation. Thus, the geodesic weighting is the component that separates MGS from simple block averaging. Task condition blocks were used to provide the same design basis as GLM, where condition blocks are convolved with an HRF, enabling direct comparison while avoiding HRF fitting in MGS. Future work can further reduce task-label dependence by defining task-related segments from the unsupervised loop trajectory.
3.Parameter setting (MR-Q2, R2-Q3&4, R3-Q4)
The 6-frame shift equals 4.32 s at the HCP TR of 0.72 s and falls within a physiologically plausible range for motor/sensorimotor BOLD timing. Chen et al. (2023), “BOLD Response is more than just magnitude: Improving detection sensitivity through capturing hemodynamic profiles”, reported motor-cortex HRF peaks around 3–4 s, while canonical HRF models peak around 5 s. Fig. 2A also supports this choice, as the 6-frame shift gives clearer condition-coherent petals than 0-frame labels. The shift was fixed before MGS computation. For UMAP, n_neighbors=40, 2D embedding, and standardized Euclidean distance were fixed before activation inference as moderate settings to preserve the smooth group-level trajectory and reduce vertex-wise scale effects. We agree that broader sensitivity analysis would be useful, but these parameters were not tuned to optimize the final activation maps.
4.Dataset scope and selection (R1-Q3, R3-Q1&2)
Fig. 3 reports individual-level ΔMGS maps, showing subject-level motor patterns. We agree that direct individual-level comparisons with GLM or deconvolution methods would further strengthen the evaluation. We also tested HCP Emotion and Relational tasks and observed consistent MGS behavior, but omitted them due to the MICCAI page limit. For subject selection, we used the official HCP 100-unrelated subset to reduce family-structure dependence and evaluate the method on a diverse independent cohort. We expect the same conclusion to hold on the full HCP-YA 1113-subject dataset.
5.Code availability (MR-Q3)
We apologize for not preparing open-source code at submission. We have prepared an Anonymous GitHub repository named /r/MGS-0B07/. If accepted, the repository will be moved to GitHub and linked in the final paper.
6.Minor clarifications (R1)
We thank R1 for the careful reading and detailed suggestions. We agree on Fig. 2 color consistency. Rest pseudo-blocks followed the same order as task blocks. Each frame was projected along the estimated geodesic path. Fig. 3 indeed shows ΔMGS. We will clarify these points if accepted.
We hope these responses clarify key points. Thanks again for all the thoughtful evaluations.

title: Geometry-Aware Point-to-Voxel Fusion via Gaussian Splatting for Intracranial Aneurysm Segmentation
abstract: Intracranial aneurysms (IAs) carry high mortality upon rupture, and their accurate segmentation from CTA is essential for clinical intervention. However, many IAs are small and morphologically resemble normal vascular bends, rendering them difficult to distinguish by intensity alone. Voxel-only networks frequently misclassify these subtle protrusions as tortuous healthy vessels, while point-based architectures capture geometry but lack dense semantic context. To bridge this gap, we propose GeoP2VNet, a geometry-aware method that injects explicit surface geometry into a voxel backbone via three modules: Geometric Feature Extraction (GFE) computes rotation-invariant point descriptors; a differentiable Point-to-Voxel (P2V) Gaussian splatting layer projects sparse geometric cues onto aligned voxel features; and Dual-Gated Residual Fusion (DGRF) selectively amplifies geometric priors at anatomically significant regions while suppressing them in normal segments. On 205 CTA cases (266 lesions) with 5-fold cross-validation, GeoP2VNet achieves a Dice of 0.770, outperforming nnU-Net (0.663) and SwinUNETR (0.578), while reducing false positives by 92%, from 0.317 to 0.024 per case. Code is available at https://github.com/somtiannes/GeoP2VNet.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose extracting explicit geometric features from the vessel surface and combining them with intensity- or voxel-based features. This is done via three modules: a geometric feature extraction (GFE) module to extract geometric features, a Gaussian splatting layer to project these features into voxel features, and a dual-gated residual fusion to combine both feature types for intracranial aneurysm segmentation.
reviews.text_strengths: Combining geometric and intensity features will address the limitations of each in aneurysm segmentation. Also, the fact that the geometric features are not learned may provide an interpretable way to assess their impact on the model.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The ablation may have provided a way to assess geometric features in more detail, for instance, by making some changes or alterations to the cloud points.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The term CTA (Computed Tomography Angiography) is not defined in the paper. 
The method for reproducing the geometric feature is somewhat unclear, while a handcrafted guide on how to design such features would improve the paper.

The feature discrimination analysis supports the authors’ claims and highlights the contribution of each component in the method.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper follows a recent trend of combining CT radiology scans with vessel segmentations to guide model attention to the areas that are most relevant for aneurysm detection. Unlike previous work, which uses vessel information either as a binary mask or as a distance map, the authors extract geometric features from point clouds representing the vessels and use differentiable Gaussian splatting to generate features. Then, a dual-gated residual fusion mechanism is used to enable the model to “decide” which parts of this information to use, leading to a significant boost in detection performance. The geometric feature extraction pipeline is lightweight and depends only on the availability of 3D vessel segmentations.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper contributes to bridging the gap between medical imaging and general 3D computer vision by applying 3D feature extraction and Gaussian splatting in a way that enables DL architectures to leverage vessel information in a principled way, which itself is critical for aneurysm detection. I believe this is a very clever way to integrate vessel information.
The proposed gating mechanism, while simple, has a positive impact and highlights the need to modulate geometric information for effective aneurysm detection.
The authors propose using a nnDetection model to generate candidate ROIs, simplifying the computational cost of running the model on entire scans. With more training data, this could lead to close-to-perfect filtering of relevant areas.
The architecture achieves a very high recall with few to no false positives, albeit this has serious caveats that I will discuss in the weaknesses section.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
There is limited clarity about how the vessel segmentation labels were obtained. The authors claim “Vessel masks are predicted solely from CTA volumes without accessing aneurysm annotations.”, which implies the authors labelled the training data not only for aneurysm detection but for vessel segmentation too. While the authors claim that they also trained the segmentation model using 5-fold cross validation, it is not clear whether the folds were a 1:1 match (ideally, each model should use vessel segmentations from a segmentation model that only had seen the exact same training data, without any access to the evaluation data for that fold). This raises concerns about data leakage as there is a non-zero chance that the areas where aneurysms occur have morphological differences present in the vessel segmentations that the downstream model could leverage to predict the existence of an aneurysm. Furthermore, there is no indication about what extent of the brain vasculature is covered in these annotations. The authors should clarify on this point.
The need to train a new vessel segmentation model on newly annotated data seems questionable considering there are several publicly available models dating as far back as 2023 that can segment vessels, ranging from just the Circle of Willis to almost the entire arterial network. Likewise, datasets such as TopCoW, TopBrain, and VesselVerse could have been used to train a segmentation network. In all fairness, this is not a weakness per se, but using existing data or models could have helped solve the critical concerns listed above.
The evaluation does not provide insight on whether the proposed method generalizes well outside of the training data, which per the authors’ own claims only contains aneurysms from a few arterial regions. The authors describe using five-fold cross-validation on a single data set with no held-out data. Essentially, this means that the models are evaluated in-domain. As of today, there exist over 400 CTA evaluation scans with dense aneurysm annotations from datasets such as the Large IA Dataset (https://zenodo.org/records/6801398) or CMHA (https://springernature.figshare.com/articles/dataset/CMHA_Intracranial_Aneurysm_CTA_Image_3D_Model_Dataset_with_Clinical_Morphological_Hemodynamic_Data/26965450), plus the RSNA dataset with over 800 aneurysms annotated as coordinates. The Large IA Dataset also contains a sizeable training partition with over 1,000 scans. Even if the authors were compute-limited, they could have used a subset of the available training and evaluation data to better evaluate their approach. I’m sharing these links in hopes you can use them to resubmit the paper if it’s rejected, but please take into account that no new results can be reported in the rebuttal.
No evaluation is provided to ablate the impact of the candidate ROIs. While this is a clever way to save compute, a sliding window approach could have been implemented to have a better idea of how this model would perform in a real life scenario, particularly since results are reported based on an oracle fallback for the aneurysms where the ROI detection model failed. Likewise, there is no ablation for the use of the vessel segmentation masks as-is without Gaussian splatting, meaning there is no way to tell if the contribution comes from the features or the vasculature itself.
There are no comparisons with respect to methods in the literature that use vessel information to enhance aneurysm detection and the only two baselines are fairly simple methods that use only voxel information.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The authors make a strong methodological contribution to aneurysm detection but the study has serious flaws that make it difficult to evaluate its potential as a tool that the clinical community could benefit from. In particular, the possibility of data leakage from training the vessel segmentation model on the same data used for aneurysm detection could make the results meaningless. Even if the authors confirm that data leakage was avoided, the evaluations made are lacking, with no acknowledgement of the large amount of available annotated data that could be used to validate the model and no comparisons with respect to existing models that tackle aneurysm detection in CTA scans. I encourage the authors to explore the datasets that were shared in the review if they want to make a more compelling argument for the relevance of their work in case the paper gets rejected.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The author response addresses the most critical issue and confirms that cross-validation does avoid data leakage. I’m also satisfied with the justification of training the vessel segmentation model fully in-domain.
I still feel that the authors ignore very relevant baselines proposed over the last few years. They argue that their approach is “not comparable to end-to-end vessel-aware pipelines bundled with skull stripping/TTA/component filtering and partially non-public preprocessing”. As long as these baselines can be run with the materials that are available online the comparisons remain relevant and it’s up to the authors to discuss the impact of the “non-comparable” design choices.
In any case, I find the response regarding the external validation data wholly insufficient. While it is true that some of these public datasets are not a 1:1 match for the authors’ setup, the Large Intracranial Aneurysm dataset can be accessed quite easily through a form in Zenodo, and includes dense segmentation masks for 1,000+ aneurysms across 1,000+ scans. Moreover, the CMHA dataset provides aneurysm detection masks as 3D STL surfaces that can be converted into dense masks using 3D Slicer or even Python scripts.
I’m switching my review to an accept due to the methodological contribution of the paper, but I’d strongly encourage the authors to use the additional space to add results on the Large IA dataset if the meta-reviewers deem it acceptable or at the very least to include such results in their GitHub repository (to clarify, my choice to accept is
not
conditioned on the authors doing this)

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a framework to address the limitations of voxel-only segmentation in CTA, where ambiguous vessel intensities make small aneurysms difficult to distinguish from normal vessels. The main contribution is the integration of point-cloud-based geometric features into a voxel backbone, allowing explicit surface geometry to be used as a prior for aneurysm segmentation.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper addresses a clearly motivated problem: small aneurysms often resemble normal vascular bends, making intensity-only segmentation difficult.
2.The use of Gaussian splatting as a fixed-kernel point-to-voxel projection is effective, as it enables smoother and more natural embedding of geometric features than simple nearest-neighbor assignment.
3.The overall design is coherent and well motivated, with geometric feature extraction, point-to-voxel projection, and gated fusion combined in a consistent manner.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Although the use of Gaussian splatting for modality fusion is a reasonable and technically sound design choice, the underlying idea of using point-cloud geometry as a prior is already quite common, which limits the overall methodological novelty.
2.The range of comparative baselines is limited. Since the paper emphasizes geometry-aware fusion, comparisons with more geometry-aware or vascular-structure-aware methods would strengthen the claims. In particular, because SwinUNETR is included as part of the ablation study, the comparison in Table 2 is effectively reduced to nnU-Net, which makes the empirical scope appear rather narrow.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper presents a clinically meaningful problem with a clear motivation, a well-structured method, and a reasonable ablation study. The integration of geometric and voxel-based information is technically sound, and the paper is generally well presented. However, the overall methodological novelty remains limited, as the key idea of using point-cloud geometry as a prior is not particularly new despite the reasonable use of Gaussian splatting for modality fusion. Moreover, the comparative evaluation is somewhat narrow; since SwinUNETR is included in the ablation study, the effective comparison in Table 2 is largely limited to nnU-Net. Overall, while the work is solid and clinically relevant, I find it slightly below the acceptance threshold.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The concern regarding novelty has been addressed by clarifying the contribution of voxel re-projection using Gaussian splatting. However, the lack of sufficient comparison with existing models remains unresolved. As a result, it is still difficult to fully assess whether the proposed methodology, whose main contribution lies in integrating Gaussian splatting, is sufficiently strong.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper fuses point cloud geometric features with voxel features via Gaussian splatting and dual-gated residual fusion for intracranial aneurysm segmentation. The approach makes sense and the non-learned geometric features are a nice touch for interpretability. R1 was positive and recommended an oral, while R2 and R3 provided more detailed technical critiques.
R2 raised what I consider the central issue: the vessel segmentation model was trained on the same dataset as the aneurysm detection model, and it is not clear whether the cross-validation folds were aligned between the two. If not, morphological cues in the vessel segmentations could leak information about aneurysm presence, which would undermine the results. This may have a reasonable explanation that the authors simply did not describe clearly enough, so I want to give them the opportunity to address it.
R2 also noted that some results rely on oracle fallback where the ROI detector failed, which makes reported performance hard to interpret at face value. R2 and R3 both noted that baselines are too narrow, with no vessel-aware aneurysm detection methods compared and Table 2 effectively reducing to nnU-Net alone.
For the rebuttal, please try to address all reviewers’ concerns, epecially the following four: 
1.confirm that vessel segmentation folds exactly match detection folds with no data overlap;
2.justify the absence of vessel-based detection baselines; 
3.discuss why available external datasets were not used;
4.clarify what Gaussian splatting adds over using vessel masks directly.
Point 1 is the one that matters most for my final recommendation.

This is a borderline accept and I agree with all reviewers’ comments on the original submission.
The round one review turned on one question above all others: whether the vessel-segmentation model and the aneurysm model shared cross-validation folds, since a leak there would have made the reported gains meaningless. The rebuttal settles it. The authors use a single patient-level 5-fold split for both stages, train each fold’s vessel model only on that fold’s training patients, and note that the vessel labels are binary lumen masks carrying no aneurysm information, so there is no aneurysm signal to memorize. R2, who is Very confident and who had raised this exact concern at a Weak Reject, accepted the explanation and moved to Accept. R1 had already recommended acceptance independent of rebuttal. MICCAI rebuttal rules do not allow the authors to add new experiments, but R3’s concern is correct and clearly more baseline comparisons are needed although partly answered by the existing “w/o Gating” ablation. This is the major issue should be solved in the future work.

Although the rebuttal somehow addresses the data-leakage concern and clarifies the novelty of voxel re-projection using Gaussian splatting, important concerns remain regarding insufficient comparisons with recent relevant baselines and inadequate external validation, making it difficult to fully assess the strength and impact of the proposed methodology. Therefore, the AC recommends rejection.

Overall, there is consensus that the paper addresses a relevant clinical problem and proposes a technically sound geometry-aware fusion approach for aneurysm segmentation. The main concerns have been adequately clarified in the rebuttal, and I therefore recommend acceptance.
At the same time, there remain valid concerns about the limited comparison to vessel-aware baselines, the lack of external validation. I encourage the authors to address these points as much as possible in the camera-ready version. I also strongly encourage the authors to make the code and model weights publicly available for the benefit of the community.

author_feedback_text:
We thank R1–R3, who affirm both the methodological (“strong methodological contribution,” “clever vessel integration”) and clinical (“coherent and well motivated”) value of our work. We address each concern below.
(1) R2 — Fold alignment and absence of leakage.
No data leakage. We used one fixed patient-level 5-fold split for both vessel segmentation and IA segmentation. In each fold, both models train only on the training cases and are evaluated only on the held-out cases. Vessel masks for held-out cases come from the vessel model trained only on the training cases. No held-out case enters vessel-model training, validation, hyperparameter tuning, model selection, or IA-segmentation training. Vessel labels are binary lumen annotations with no aneurysm masks. Therefore, any morphology in the predicted vessel mask is inferred from the held-out CTA itself, not memorised from training exposure. We agree §3.2 was not explicit enough and will revise accordingly.
(2) R2&R3 — What Gaussian splatting adds over direct vessel masks.
A binary mask encodes only vessel location, not the surface properties (curvature, density, normals) driving discrimination (Fig. 3b: aneurysm/vessel ratios 1.23–1.27×). Our 10-D descriptors are splatted onto the voxel grid via differentiable, sub-voxel-continuous projection—smoother than nearest-neighbour voxelization, and more directly aligned with fixed geometric descriptors than generic learnable rendering [11].
(3) R2 — External validation.
Public IA resources each differ in access/modality/annotation/task: Large IA is access-restricted, CMHA has CTA + 3D models but no voxel-wise IA masks, RSNA has coordinates only, CADA uses 3DRA not CTA (closed), and IntraA is hemodynamic. Our 266-lesion multi-vendor cohort, dual-expert annotation, 5-fold CV + 95% CIs supports an in-domain study. External validation is future work.
(4) R2&R3 — Vessel-aware baselines.
Our method is not comparable to end-to-end vessel-aware pipelines bundled with skull stripping/TTA/component filtering and partially non-public preprocessing. We will release code, preprocessing, and hyperparameters. In Table 3, the “w/o Gating” variant is itself a vessel-aware geometric variant: being vessel-derived, the 10 descriptors inherently mix vessel-location information with surface geometry (curvature, density, normals). It already beats the Baseline (Recall 75.0→84.6, FPs halved), though this inherent mix is necessarily noisy across channels. We agree mask-as-channel is the cleanest ablation for disentangling descriptor content from vasculature presence. That said, simply re-weighting these geometric feature channels yields a substantial leap (DSC 0.591→0.770; DGRF learns heterogeneous weights—Fig. 3c: Density 13.8%, NV 13.0%, Curvature 12.1% vs ~7–9%), supporting that surface geometric content contributes beyond vessel-awareness alone. We will add this control in the camera-ready if permitted.
(5) R2 — Why train a new vessel model?
With matched folds (see (1)), our in-house vessel model introduces no leakage. We prioritized internal rigour for this submission, and external vessel models are future work. Meanwhile, our framework already tolerates moderate-quality vessel masks (Dice 77.35%).
(6) R2 — Oracle fallback.
All methods receive identical ROI inputs under the same 5-fold protocol. 84.6% come from the detector, with oracle covering the remaining detector misses. The evaluation is therefore fair for matched-patch segmentation comparison.
(7) R3 — Novelty.
We acknowledge that using point-cloud geometry as a prior is not new in itself. Our key novelty lies in modality alignment: to our knowledge, we are the first to re-project sparse point-cloud surface features back into the dense CTA voxel grid via Gaussian splatting and jointly train this voxel-aligned geometric stream with the voxel backbone for IA segmentation.
(8) R1 — CTA + GFE design guide.
CTA = Computed Tomography Angiography. Per-channel GFE formulas accompany our code.

title: Geometry-Aware Self-supervised Learning for Whole-Heart 3D+t Representation
abstract: Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) is a clinical reference standard for assessing cardiac morphology and function. Whole-heart assessment relies on sparse multi-plane cine acquisitions from complementary short-axis (SAX) and 2/3/4-chamber long-axis (LAX) views across the cardiac cycle. Although large-scale cohorts such as UK Biobank provide tens of thousands of such studies, most scans remain unlabeled, and learning compact whole-heart representations from the resulting high-dimensional 3D+t data is still challenging under practical memory constraints. To address this, we introduce a geometry-aware self-supervised learning framework for whole-heart representation learning from sparse multi-plane cine CMR. First, we inject patient-space coordinates into spatio-temporal tubelet tokens, which preserves explicit spatial identity and enables shared per-plane encoding. Next, we explicitly model cross-plane structure by aggregating multi-plane features into a latent 3D volume via voxel-query cross-attention. To ensure geometric consistency while keeping supervision efficient, we reconstruct masked tubelets by coordinate-constrained trilinear reprojection from the latent volume. Finally, we adopt hierarchical masking that combines intra-plane tubelet masking with inter-plane plane dropping, turning reconstruction into cross-plane completion and strengthening global 3D reasoning. Experiments show that coherent 3D anatomy can be decoded from the learned latent volume using a lightweight linear probe, and that masked-plane reconstruction recovers missing views from remaining planes. Moreover, our method improves downstream multi-plane segmentation over state-of-the-art methods, while maintaining favorable efficiency under the same input setting. Code is available at this \href{https://github.com/Liwei-Hu1/Geometry_Aware_CMR_Pretraining.git}{URL}.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a geometry-aware SSL framework designed to learn 3D+t representations from sparse, multi-plane cine CMR. The authors introduce patient-space information to encode sparse and unordered multi-plane cine CMR. The authors also adopted a volume modelling module to enforce geometry-consistency. The authors introduce hierarchical masking, intra-plane tubelet masking and inter-plane plane dropping, to force the model to perform cross-plane anatomical reasoning.
reviews.text_strengths:
The integration of physical patient-space coordinates (multi-modality information) into the transformer architecture is a principled approach to handling sparse, intersecting medical imaging planes.
The plane-to-volume and volume-to-plane projection enforces a strong geometric prior. The plane-to-volume module also seems a good translational adaptation of VoxFormer.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Motivation and Efficiency: The authors state that the primary motivation is to utilise the unlabeled data in datasets via SSL. However, it remains unclear whether the ultimate goal is to propose a “Cardiac Foundation Model” for various downstream tasks or simply to achieve label-efficiency for standard segmentation. If the goal is strictly segmentation performance, the architectural complexity, which involves patient-space coordinate injection, voxel-query cross-attention, and trilinear reprojection. It appears high for the incremental gains shown in Table 1.To claim the “favourable efficiency,” the authors should report total training FLOPs or total parameter sizes, comparing to compared methods. Specifically, it is necessary to demonstrate that SSL pre-training +”lighthead” fine-tuning offers a genuine advantage over training a strong, established baseline like nnU-Net from scratch.
2.Experimental Validation and Representation Analysis: In the Representation Analysis subsection, the authors show that the model performs cross-plane completion rather than simple 2D inpainting. While this proves the model has learned a spatial prior, there is a risk that the model is simply generating an “average” heart shape that is anatomically plausible but not patient-specific. The potential clinical application of this “cross-view inpainting” is not sufficiently discussed. The authors should demonstrate how this capability benefits specific clinical workflows, such as maintaining diagnostic accuracy in the event of missing clinical views or improving the robustness of automated pipelines faced with sparse acquisitions.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
in Eq (4), e_{vis} refers to shared encoder right? the notation of it wasn’t explained.
in Fig 1, as you described the input to recon decoder is c_{i,j} and V, which means the inputs in Phase I to the decoder should ve illustrated as (darker blue + lighter blue), respectively? You illustrated as (colour + dark grey = V + masked tokens)? Also, dark grey appears in the previous column too.

The preliminary recommendation of Weak Accept is justified by the following major factors: The proposed framework is methodologically innovative and well described in the paper. However, as mentioned in the major weakness, I believe the authors need to justify the motivation and application of the proposed work.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a geometry-aware self-supervised framework for learning whole-heart 3D+t representations from sparse multi-plane cine CMR. The method injects patient-space coordinates into tubelet tokens, aggregates multi-plane features into a latent 3D volume via voxel-query cross-attention, and reconstructs masked regions through coordinate-constrained trilinear sampling. A hierarchical masking strategy encourages cross-plane reasoning, and the learned representation is evaluated via reconstruction, probing, and downstream segmentation.
reviews.text_strengths: The motivation is well grounded, and leveraging DICOM geometric information to enable cross-plane reasoning is natural and intuitive. The overall framework is conceptually clean, and the experimental evaluation is relatively comprehensive.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The plane-to-volume aggregation is still largely implemented via generic cross-attention, although the spatial relationship between voxel queries and tubelet tokens is explicitly available through patient-space coordinates. It may be beneficial to explore more geometry-constrained aggregation strategies, such as distance-aware attention or coordinate-based deterministic lifting, which could better preserve spatial consistency in the latent volume and make the subsequent trilinear interpolation assumption more justified.
2.The method appears to assume that anatomical structures are roughly aligned across subjects in patient-space coordinates. It would be helpful to discuss whether any preprocessing is required to ensure that corresponding chambers fall into similar regions of the latent grid, especially when handling heterogeneous acquisition protocols.
3.Since the method models spatiotemporal information, it would be helpful to include additional experiments evaluating temporal consistency, cross-phase reconstruction, or missing-frame completion to better demonstrate the learned temporal dynamics.
4.Some details in Fig. 1 are unclear. For example, the meaning of the colored border around “Geometry-injected visible tokens” is not explained, and it is ambiguous whether masked tokens are also fed into the Volume Modelling Module or only used during reconstruction. Clarifying these visual elements would improve readability and make the pipeline easier to follow.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Although some details of the method still need further clarification, this paper proposes a well-motivated and practical geometry-aware self-supervised framework and provides relatively reliable experimental verification, making an overall significant contribution.

meta_reviews.text:
A further rebuttal is required for the reviewers to reach a consensus.

Good work.

The paper presents a insightful approach by incorporating explicit geometric priors into multi-plane CMR self-supervised learning. Its strength lies in addressing the alignment of orthogonal planes using physical coordinates. The main concerns include motivation clarification, results explanation, performance comparison, and ablation study. The author’s response address most of them and all reviewers agree to accept the paper.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for recognizing that our motivation is “well grounded”(R3), and that our geometry-aware design uses patient-space/DICOM coordinates to replace implicit view embeddings(R2), providing a principled geometric prior for cross-plane reasoning under sparse intersecting cine planes(R1,R3).
Q1: Clarifying the primary motivation(R1)
A1: The motivation is to learn an effective geometry-aware whole-heart 3D+t representation for downstream tasks such as segmentation, motion tracking, image enhancement. It is not for segmentation alone, although we use it as a proxy test. We don’t consider it a foundation model either, since it is very specific to geometry/motion, and uses limited samples.
Q2: Regarding “favourable efficiency”(R1)
A2: The efficiency advantage is relative to global fusion over all multi-plane tokens. Sec.2.2 shows that such global fusion has O(S^2n^2) attention complexity, whereas our shared per-plane encoding reduces this to O(Sn^2), with cross-plane interaction deferred to a compact latent volume. Thus, the explicit geometry prior is used to improve fusion efficiency, not to add complexity.
Q3: Is the representation analysis just generating an “average heart”(R1)? 
A3: It’s not because it is difficult for an average heart encoding to be decoded accurately into very different images of many individuals. We further observed substantial diversity in the 3D encoding space across subjects, suggesting that the network learns subject-conditioned rather than average-heart representations.
Q4: Clinical relevance of the representation analysis(R1)
A4: Relevant applications include correcting MRI breath-hold slice-misalignment artefacts, improving 3D shape/motion quantification by using LAX/SAX input, and sparse-view 3D reconstruction to reduce the number of acquired slices and scanning time.
Q5: Regarding ablation studies(R2)
A5: Our components jointly address one central problem: learning coherent 3D+t representations from sparse multi-plane cine CMR. DICOM coordinates provide the shared spatial frame, plane-to-volume modelling forms the latent 3D representation, and hierarchical masking forces cross-plane completion rather than 2D inpainting shortcuts. Existing results support them: 1)Fig.2(a) shows coherent 3D anatomy decoded from the latent volume, 2)Fig.2(b) shows missing-plane reconstruction from remaining views, and 3)Table 1 shows consistent gains over WholeNet under the same input setting. Since these components define the proposed geometry-aware formulation, removing any of them would change the intended representation setting rather than provide a meaningful ablation.
Q6: Requests for comparison with MAE-style methods and CineMA(R2)
A6: We selected WholeNet as the closest baseline because it also uses multi-plane SAX/LAX inputs and learns a 3D+t representation. In contrast, plain MAE-style methods are designed for single-image/video inputs and do not model multi-plane inputs or 3D geometry. CineMA is an impressive CMR foundation model for 2D+t cine images, but lacks an explicit 3D representation. Table 1 shows that our explicit 3D representation improves performance while avoiding computationally expensive global attention across planes.
Q7: Additional methodological clarifications(R2,R3)
A7: Temporal consistency evaluation is useful but remains future work. For distance-aware constraints, our voxel-query cross-attention learns geometry-conditioned correspondences from patient-space coordinates, while hard distance matching is suboptimal for sparse SAX/LAX cine CMR due to partial-volume effects, slice thickness, and view-dependent boundary offsets. For cross-subject alignment, our method does not assume identical chamber locations, but uses each subject’s DICOM metadata as input. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on the reported Dice scores in Tables 1–2 show statistical significance and support our conclusions.
Minor modifications: We will clarify Eq. (4) notation and improve Fig.1 readability.

title: Geometry-Aware Superpixel Graph Transformer with Metadata for Skin Lesion Classification
abstract: Automated skin cancer classification from dermoscopic images remains challenging due to heterogeneous lesion structure, strong intra-class variability, and subtle visual differences between benign and malignant cases. Existing CNN/ViT pipelines typically rely on global or patch-level features and often combine patient metadata via late fusion, which limits spatially grounded multimodal reasoning. We present a novel region-based graph learning framework that explicitly models lesions as graphs of spatially coherent superpixel regions represented as frozen CNN features. To capture fine-grained lesion arrangements, we encode inter-regional geometry as edge attributes and introduce a dedicated metadata context node connected to all regions, providing structured integration of demographic/clinical variables within the same relational space. Node representations are updated using our edge-aware graph transformer followed by attention-driven propagation, and a final graph-level embedding for benign–malignant classification. Experiments on four public benchmarks demonstrate that explicit region-level relational modeling and graph-native multimodal fusion yield consistent gains over the state-of-the-art. Consequently, we establish a new graph-centric perspective in which CNN features are modeled as relational nodes and improved through contextual integration, yielding more expressive and robust classifications.
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers
Applications -> Outcome Prediction / Prognosis / Longitudinal Modeling
Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper proposes a new graph-based approach, GeoMeta-GT, to combine both image features and metadata. The graph is built from nodes corresponding to superpixels (SLIC) in the image, with features given by a frozen CNN, as well as an additional node with metadata features. Then, edges are based on spatial proximity (neighbors) with their features given by geometric attributes, based on distances and orientation. The authors propose a transformer-based message passing strategy that takes into account edge features in the computation of the attention weights, thereby promoting locally adaptive aggregation. The final classification is given by a classification head based on a final feature refinement and graph pooling operations. 
GeoMeta-GT is applied to skin cancer classification, in a binary normal vs melanoma setup. Results show substantial improvements against other state of the art approaches on multiple benchmark datasets.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper proposes several contributions: 1) a novel geometry-aware message passing algorithm that allows information flow to be conditioned on spatial relationship between nodes, unlike most graph-based approach which often assume that the adjacency matrix itself is representative of the graph geometry; 2) a graph-based approach to fuse superpixel features with metadata. Extensive evaluation on four public datasets validates the proposed approach and shows substantial improvements on the binary classification of dermoscopy images as either benign or malignant.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The validation appears to be done on a single backbone, although the authors do provide an ablation study showing the impact of different backbones in performance. Additionally, most dermoscopy datasets are multiclass, including multiple subtypes of benign and malignant lesions, and part of the real-world clinical challenge differentiating between these subtypes (differential diagnosis). In this work, the evaluation is done only on a binary problem defined as benign vs malignant, therefore simplifying the task.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Below is a list of major comments and questions:
In eq (2), the numerator Qi . Kj + êij suggests that the dot product between Qi and Kj is performed first and then the êij features are added to the result. However, in the text, the authors say that the edge embedding is injected into the key before the dot-product. If the text is correct, putting (Kj + êij) in parenthesis would help clarify.
In eq (3), why are Dj and eij multiplied by new matrices W4 and W5, instead of the previously used W2 and W3?
In structural refinement, the authors suggest that the refined embedding Zi is obtained through similarity-based propagation, claiming it allows visually or semantically similar superpixels to exchange information even if they are spatially distant. However, in eq (4), Zi appears to be a combination of neighbors j in N(i), where N(i) is previously defined as the spatial neighbors of node I (based on the Euclidean distance between superpixel centroids), which would contradict the previous claim.
In the training details, the authors mention a frozen “CNN backbone” without explicitly identifying it. Then, in the ablation studies, they show a comparison between several backbones, but never clarify which backbone ended up being used for the remaining results. Additionally, this opens up questions about whether different backbones would show similar improvements with the proposed GeoMeta-GT.
In the ablation studies, the authors start with the impact of geometric edge encoding, which is actually shown in Fig 2 (b), while the following section on model variations is shown in Fig 2 (a). I suggest switching the order.
Fig 2 would also benefit from improved legend, clarifying what the symbols mean - if they actually have any meaning or if color is the only discriminator needed.
The F1 scores are very similar to the accuracy ones. For clarity and space, consider removing F1 results from the text on the ablation studies without tables or figures. I would also remove it from Fig 2, to simplify my previous comment.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I stand by my original assessment that the paper proposes an interesting approach to fuse image information with metadata using a graph-based strategy and that the proposal is supported by strong experimental validation. The author’s rebuttal addresses most of my concerns and is convincing.

reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a Geometry-Aware Superpixel Graph Transformer with Metadata for skin lesion classification, named GeoMeta-GT. GeoMeta-GT designs a geometry-attributed superpixel graph representation and a fusion mechanism that incorporates metadata as graph nodes, and develops an edge-aware graph Transformer to achieve spatially aware aggregation of diagnostically relevant regions. It further introduces a similarity-weighted refinement module to coordinate semantically consistent regional features. Experimental results on multiple public benchmarks show that GeoMeta-GT achieves state-of-the-art performance.
reviews.text_strengths: 1.The paper proposes a dedicated solution for the skin lesion classification task, which is highly meaningful in clinical practice. 2.GeoMeta-GT represents lesion subregions as superpixel nodes, explicitly encodes geometric information on the edges, and integrates metadata as graph nodes. This structured design is more effective than standard feature fusion pipelines. 3.The experimental study is comprehensive, and the ablation experiments provide a detailed analysis of the contribution of each module. 4.The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
reviews.text_weaknesses: 1.The paper only reports some of the main hyperparameters of the proposed model in the Training Details section, while lacking a description of the implementation details for the baselines. This may lead to inconsistencies in the reported performance of different baseline methods. 2.The paper mainly reports statistical metrics such as accuracy, but lacks sufficient clinical analysis. 3.The paper repeatedly claims that the proposed method is robust and generalizable under heterogeneous settings, yet the experiments only include four random train/test splits and do not provide an external validation protocol.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I find the main idea interesting: superpixel-based region graphs with geometry-aware attention and metadata-as-node fusion is a plausible and potentially useful contribution for skin lesion analysis. The paper is also reasonably clear and includes detailed experiments. The paper is clearly positioned against patch methods and argues for more spatially grounded multimodal reasoning, which is a sensible direction for dermoscopic analysis.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The author’s rebuttal resolved my doubts. Overall, the experiment was thorough, and I tend to accept it.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a GeoMeta-GT framework that models lesions as superpixel graphs and integrates patient metadata as a dedicated context node.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper is well-organized and easy to understand. GeoMeta-GT achieved SOTA results across ISIC2024, HAM10000, PAD-UFES-20, and HIBA benchmarks. GeoMeta-GT demonstrated superior robustness on challenging, heterogeneous datasets.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Superpixel-based graphs for skin lesion diagnosis are well-established in prior researches like SLED [1] and “Seeing the Skin Deeper” [2]. The authors should explicitly clarify their unique technical distinction compared to these existing frameworks.
The proposed designs (Edge-aware Graph Transformer, Structural Refinement and Global Readout) act as general-purpose feature enhancers, lacks a clear link to the unique challenges of Skin Lesion Classification.
The “orientation” attribute versus “distance” remains unclear. An ablation study isolating “distance-only” vs. “full GEE” is required.
The model relies on frozen backbones(e.g.,VGG,EfficientNet) pre-trained on natural images (ImageNet). The authors should address the potential domain gap when applying these frozen features to dermoscopic images and whether domain-specific fine-tuning would significantly alter the performance.
Critical parameters in graph construction(the number of superpixels ($K$) and neighbors ($n$)) lack sensitivity analysis.
The framework’s performance is tethered to the SLIC-based decomposition. The authors should evaluate robustness against different superpixel algorithms.
Minor Weaknesses
The ablation analysis in Fig.2 is difficult to interpret for precise quantitative comparisons. It is recommended to present these results in a tabular format to clearly show the performance delta between model variants.
“Evaluating Backbone Efficiency” section evaluates performance rather than computational efficiency. Notably, the 4% gap between backbones (e.g., on ISIC2024) exceeds the gains from the proposed modules. The authors must ensure that comparisons with SOTA methods used consistent backbones to maintain a fair evaluation.

Unsupervised skin lesion segmentation via structural entropy minimization on multi-scale superpixel graphs[C]//2023 IEEE international conference on data mining (ICDM). IEEE, 2023: 768-777.[2] Jerlshin J G, Pal A R, Datta R, et al. Seeing the Skin Deeper: Interpretable Multi-Task Framework for Skin Lesion Diagnosis using Superpixel Graphs[J]. IEEE Access, 2026.
