meta_reviews.text:
The paper proposes a superpixel-based graph Transformer with geometry-aware edge encoding and metadata-as-node fusion for skin lesion classification. The reviews are close to the acceptance boundary, with one Accept, one Weak Accept, and one Weak Reject. The reviewers generally acknowledge the clinical relevance, clear presentation, and strong results across multiple dermoscopy datasets. However, several points require clarification before a final decision, especially the technical distinction from prior superpixel-graph methods, the necessity of the geometry-aware edge encoding and structural refinement modules, and the sensitivity to SLIC decomposition, number of superpixels, and graph-neighbor settings. The authors should also clarify backbone usage, baseline implementation fairness, and whether the claimed robustness is supported beyond random train/test splits. The rebuttal should focus on novelty over existing superpixel graph frameworks, key ablations, graph-construction sensitivity, and fair comparison protocols.

The rebuttal clarifies the technical distinction from prior superpixel-graph methods, provides additional evidence for geometry encoding, and addresses the main concerns about SLIC sensitivity, graph construction, backbone usage, and baseline fairness. Although the contribution remains somewhat incremental and the evaluation is limited to binary classification without prospective external validation, the method is technically coherent and the post-rebuttal reviewer balance supports acceptance.
The rebuttal addresses most of reviewers’ concerns.

This paper proposes GeoMeta-GT, a geometry-aware superpixel graph Transformer with metadata fusion for skin lesion classification. The problem is clinically relevant, and the paper presents strong empirical results across multiple public datasets. After considering the reviews and rebuttal, I find that the authors have adequately addressed the reviewers’ main concerns. The overall methodological contribution, strong experimental performance, and comprehensive evaluation are sufficient to support acceptance. Therefore, I recommend Accept.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewers for their constructive feedback and address the main concerns: novelty, module necessity, graph sensitivity, and evaluation protocol.
Novelty over prior superpixel graphs [Meta, R3].
Superpixel graphs are established in dermoscopy; GeoMeta-GT does not claim novelty from SLIC, but from the reasoning formulation on these regions. SLED is segmentation-oriented, whereas our model performs multimodal benign/malignant classification. Relative to diagnosis-oriented superpixel graph frameworks, GeoMeta-GT: (i) encodes distance/orientation as edge attributes used in transformer attention, so geometry directly conditions message passing rather than appearing only as adjacency; (ii) represents metadata as a context node connected to all regions, allowing patient context to modulate regional evidence via message passing instead of late concatenation; and (iii) CNN for stable descriptors while the graph module for lesion-level relational adaptation. Hence, the contribution is an edge-attributed, metadata-aware graph transformer, not a generic superpixel graph.
Why are geometry and refinement lesion-specific [Meta, R1, R3]?
In dermoscopy, malignancy cues are spatial: asymmetry, border irregularity, heterogeneous pigmentation, and repeated suspicious patterns depend on the arrangement of lesion subregions. Geometric edge encoding captures these layouts, and the transformer uses them to weight neighboring evidence. Regarding refinement, as R1 notes, Eq. (4) acts only on the constructed graph neighborhood. It re-weights candidate messages by feature similarity, reinforcing consistent lesion evidence and suppressing noisy superpixels, without creating new long-range edges. This is a clarification of wording/notation, not of the method.
Ablation evidence and orientation [Meta, R3].
R3 concerns about orientation and distance. Distance-only results support the mechanism: full distance+orientation encoding outperforms distance-only on all datasets (ISIC: 98.61 vs 96.17; HAM10000: 98.23 vs 95.23; PAD-UFES-20: 97.17 vs 94.18; HIBA: 95.41 vs 91.13), showing that orientation contributes complementary layout information, particularly for asymmetry and directional border variation.
Graph construction and SLIC sensitivity [Meta, R3].
The concern is dependence on a single SLIC/K/n setting. K controls lesion granularity and n the local context: too small K merges heterogeneous regions, too large K fragments coherent patterns, and too sparse/dense neighborhoods under/over-smooth. Sensitivity over K={15,25,35,50,65,75} and n={4,6,8,10} identifies K=50, n=6 as the best trade-off, with stable mid-range performance. Replacing SLIC with SEEDS (Berg et al., ECCV 2012) or Felzenszwalb (Felzenszwalb et al., IJCV 2004) gives similar results (e.g., 96.17/96.07 on ISIC), showing the transformer is partition-agnostic, though SLIC is preferred for boundary adherence and efficiency.
Backbone, baselines, and robustness [Meta, R1-R3].
The main experiments use ResNet152; the backbone study is a sensitivity analysis, not a protocol change. All ablations share the same preprocessing, splits, input size, optimizer, and backbone, so performance gains reflect graph reasoning, not backbone choice. We use the same binary benign/malignant setting and train/test protocols as the baselines, ensuring comparable evaluation conditions. Results taken directly from prior papers. We concur with R2/R3 that “robust” or “generalizable” does not imply prospective external validation. Our claim is narrower: GeoMeta-GT shows consistent performance across four public dermoscopy datasets and fixed repeated splits. Prospective validation and multiclass differential diagnosis remain future work.
Minor clarifications.
Parenthesize edge injection into the key in Eq. (2); in Eq. (3), use separate projections for attention and message update; “Backbone Efficiency” should be “backbone sensitivity”; clarify Fig. 2 to a table and remove redundant F1 plots.

title: GES-Net: A Gesture, Error, and Smoothness Aware Network for Surgical Skill Assessment
abstract: With robotic-assisted surgery (RAS) increasingly adopted into clinical practice, automated skill assessment becomes essential for its transformative potential in surgical analytics and education. Existing RAS skill assessment methods are limited to black-box models that purely predict skill scores from input videos. This design offers no assessment transparency and only a crude, uninterpretable numerical score as feedback to users. Moreover, the majority of relevant studies are developed and validated in controlled simulation settings, with unproven generalization to real-world clinical contexts. This work introduces GES-Net, a multi-task learning framework integrating surgical gesture recognition, error detection, and skill assessment. GES-Net comprises two core components: semantic alignment and multi-dimensional evaluation. For semantic alignment, the model fuses visual features with gesture semantics through gated cross-attention and scheduled masked guidance, while a multi-stage temporal reasoning module captures complex gesture transitions. For multi-dimensional evaluation, GES-Net employs soft error weighting to dynamically emphasize error segments and uses jitter features to quantify operational smoothness. This design enables both accurate RAS skill assessment and transparent diagnostic feedback. Validated on two publicly available datasets JIGSAWS and RARP-skill, our approach outperforms recent baselines with SCC improvements of 0.05 in LOSO, 0.07 in LOUO on the JIGSAWS suturing task, and 0.05 on RARP-skill.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs
Surgery -> Surgical Skills, Workflow & Team Dynamics

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a pipeline for surgical skills assessment from video using a multi-task approach, with auxiliary tasks on gesture and error. The method is evaluated on the JIGSAWS and RARP datasets, and seems to outperform prior work.
reviews.text_strengths:
Model represents an improvement over prior work on two distinct datasets for surgical skills assessment.
Paper explores the interplay between skill, gestures, and errors.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Some of the comparisons in the results are biased by differing amounts of information used by each model.
Justification on the interpretability of the feedback provided by the model is missing.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The model nicely leverages auxiliary information about gesture, errors, and jitter to improve performance.
Comparison against alternative baselines is biased because the proposed method uses more annotation. The proposed method uses gesture and error annotations, while many of the baseline methods do not. By providing the model access to this further information, it will bias the comparison. Of course, the other models are not designed to use this information, but it means the comparisons should be considered with this context in mind.
The ablation study does not seem to measure the value of the gesture head.
More justification or discussion on how the gesture-error analysis, smoothness metrics, and soft error distribution can be used for interpretable feedback would be helpful.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes GES-Net, a multi-task robotic surgical skill assessment framework that jointly models multiple factors. Its central contribution is to move beyond a black-box score predictor by introducing a semantically informed architecture that uses gesture-text alignment and error-aware temporal aggregation to improve both accuracy and interpretability. The method is evaluated on JIGSAWS and RARP-skill, with reported gains over recent baselines, especially on suturing tasks and on the clinical RARP-skill dataset.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper targets an important weakness in current robotic surgical skill assessment methods: many output only a single score, with limited diagnostic value. The proposed decomposition into gesture, error, and smoothness is well motivated and closer to how human evaluators think about performance.
2.Rather than attaching auxiliary heads in a superficial way, the paper uses the auxiliary tasks in structurally meaningful places. This is a good example of using domain knowledge to shape the architecture, not just to add extra losses.
3.Among the proposed modules, SMG is interesting. It uses gesture labels for guidance early on, then partially masks them to encourage the model to infer semantics from visual cues rather than overfitting to dense labels. That is a thoughtful design choice for balancing supervision and autonomy.
4.The performance on RARP-skill is a notable strength. The paper reports SCC 0.76 and MAE 1.38, outperforming listed baselines by a meaningful margin. Since one of the paper’s messages is improved generalization to real clinical settings, this result matters.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The paper’s distinctive contribution is mainly the particular combination of gesture alignment, error weighting, and jitter modeling for skill assessment. That is valuable, but it is not a major methodological leap. This is especially relevant given prior work already cited by the authors on interpretable or gesture-aware skill assessment, such as Wang et al. 2020, ViSA 2022, Contra-Sformer 2023, and step-by-step prompting for error detection in robotic videos by Shao et al. 2024.
2.GES-Net is more interpretable than a plain regression network, but the paper occasionally suggests stronger transparency than it actually demonstrates. For example, gesture-feature similarity and error-weight profiles are useful diagnostics, but they do not yet amount to fully validated interpretability; there is no case study showing that surgeons or educators find these outputs actionable; the model still depends on learned latent features whose semantics are not fully disentangled.
3.A major practical limitation is that the method relies on gesture labels and binary error annotations during training. That is substantially more annotation than pure score-prediction methods require. The paper motivates this by saying single-score supervision is sparse, but it does not fully discuss the annotation burden or whether the accuracy gains justify that additional supervision. Since dense error labels are expensive in clinical videos, this matters for real-world scalability.
4.The paper evaluates only needle passing and suturing because these contain binary error annotations, excluding knot tying. That narrows comparability with broader JIGSAWS skill-assessment literature. It also means the method is demonstrated mainly on tasks where the extra supervision is available, rather than across the full benchmark.
5.The comparison table mixes methods with missing MAE values and methods that may not use the same supervision or auxiliary labels. The paper says some methods were reimplemented using official code for fairness, especially on RARP-skill, but the exact reproduction protocol is not described in enough details. It is therefore hard to know how directly comparable all reported gains are.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper tackles an important and practical problem, and it realizes that with a model design that is technically coherent tied to surgical assessment concepts. The combination of gesture semantics, error-focused aggregation, and smoothness modeling is well motivated, and the empirical results are compelling. The ablations also show that the proposed components actually contribute.
My main concerns are that the paper’s novelty is more system-level than foundational, its interpretability claims are somewhat stronger than the validation supports, and its reliance on dense auxiliary labels may limit scalability.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
reviews.text_contribution: The manuscript addresses an important and timely problem in computer-assisted surgical education: automated assessment of surgical skill in robotic surgery. The proposed framework is technically well motivated, combining semantic information, temporal modeling, and an attention-based mechanism in a coherent way. The paper is clearly written, the methodological pipeline is easy to follow, and the release of code is a significant strength that enhances reproducibility. The empirical results are strong, and I particularly appreciated that the evaluation goes beyond aggregate performance and also includes analysis of errors and failure cases. Overall, I found this to be a solid and well-executed contribution.
reviews.text_strengths: The manuscript has several major strengths. First, the proposed framework appears technically well designed and well motivated, combining semantic information, temporal modeling, and attention gating in a coherent and complementary way rather than as an ad-hoc combination of modules. Second, the paper is clearly written and easy to follow, with a strong methodological presentation that makes the overall pipeline understandable and reproducible. In addition, the empirical results are strong, with high performance metrics that suggest the proposed approach is effective for the task. I also particularly appreciated that the evaluation goes beyond aggregate performance and includes analysis of errors and failure cases, which provides more insight into the behavior and limitations of the model than standard reporting alone. Finally, the availability of code is a significant strength, as it greatly improves reproducibility, transparency, and the potential impact of the work within the community.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The main weaknesses of the paper are not in the core technical contribution, which is strong, but rather in aspects that could further strengthen its broader impact and interpretation. In particular, it would be useful to discuss how to deploy realistically and assessm the validity in real training settings.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
My comments are mostly intended to strengthen the paper further rather than to challenge its main contribution, which I think it is indeed valuable.
1.Since the paper is positioned in the context of surgical skill assessment, it would be valuable to discuss more explicitly how the model outputs could be used in real training or assessment settings. 
2.The paper would be further strengthened by a brief discussion of deployment considerations, including inference efficiency, robustness in real-world training environments, and whether the method is intended for offline benchmarking or real-time formative feedback.

I assigned this paper the highest score because, in my opinion, it combines the qualities one would expect from a very strong contribution: it tackles an important and practically relevant problem, proposes a technically sound and well-motivated method, presents the work clearly, and supports its claims with strong empirical evidence. In addition, the paper demonstrates good scientific maturity through careful evaluation and reproducibility practices, including code availability and analysis beyond headline metrics. While there are still aspects that could be expanded in future versions—particularly around practical deployment—these do not detract from the overall quality of the work. Overall, I found this to be a well-executed, convincing, and impactful contribution that stands out positively among typical submissions.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text: This paper proposes GES‑Net, a multi‑task framework for robotic surgical skill assessment that jointly models gesture semantics, error awareness, and motion smoothness, evaluated on JIGSAWS and RARP‑skill. Reviewers agree the problem is timely and important, the architecture is well motivated by domain knowledge, and the use of auxiliary tasks is structurally meaningful rather than superficial. Results are strong across the datasets, particularly on the clinical RARP‑skill benchmark, and the analysis extends to failure‑case insights. Key concerns focus on fairness of comparisons (due to additional supervision from gesture/error labels), interpretability claims that exceed current validation, and scalability given the reliance on dense auxiliary annotations; some ablations (e.g., isolating the value of the gesture head) could be clearer. Overall, this is a technically sound and well‑executed contribution.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the AC and reviewers for their feedback. We are encouraged that reviewers recognize the significance of the topic explored (R1, R2, R3), the soundness of the method design (R2, R3), strong empirical results (R1, R2, R3), and good writing quality (R1, R2, R3). We provide clarifications on the received comments:
Fairness of comparisons (R1): 
Our method utilizes additional annotation types (gesture and error labels) beyond the skill score labels used by most baselines. This is indeed a design premise of our framework: the core contribution is to demonstrate how jointly leveraging multiple types of readily available surgical annotations can improve skill assessment performance and feedback. The comparison with single-task baselines is intended to quantify the benefit of this multi-task paradigm. Comparisons with other multi-task frameworks, which also leverage auxiliary annotations beyond skill scores, are included in Table 1.
Scope of verification for interpretability (R1, R2, R3): 
A qualitative analysis of the jitter features and soft error weighting on the RARP-skill dataset is provided in Figure 3.The jitter curves capture operation smoothness differences across surgeons and reveal surgical steps with frequent pauses, offering targeted feedback for skill improvement. Similarly, the soft error weighting indicates which steps involve errors critical to skill improvement, providing insights beyond simple skill score prediction. In future work, we plan to include quantitative analysis and a user study based on surgeon feedback to further explore the impact of smoothness metrics and soft error distributions on surgical workflow optimization.
Application scalability (R2):
We appreciate the reviewer raising this point. Surgical gesture recognition and error detection are well-established tasks in the surgical AI community, and the gesture and error labels used in our framework are sourced from publicly available datasets, requiring no additional annotation effort beyond what is already available. Nevertheless, we acknowledge that the reliance on auxiliary annotations may limit scalability in settings where such labels are unavailable. Future work will explore weakly supervised approaches for the auxiliary tasks to reduce this dependency.
Deployment considerations (R3):
The current framework is designed for offline skill assessment, where videos are processed post-procedure to provide structured feedback to trainees. This is standard in surgical training; thus, real-time inference is not required. We acknowledge that inference efficiency and robustness in real-world environments are important considerations for broader deployment, and we plan to include a dedicated discussion of these aspects in future extended versions of this work.

title: GFR-MIL: Glance–Focus–Reflect Based Multiple Instance Learning for Multi-Scale Whole Slide Image Analysis
abstract: Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) has emerged as the dominant paradigm for computational Whole Slide Images (WSIs) analysis. To capture richer diag-nostic cues while maintaining computational efficiency, recent MIL methods have adopted coarse-to-fine sampling strategies that use low-magnification overviews to guide high-resolution patch selection. However, the unidirection-al nature of such strategies prevents the model from correcting suboptimal re-gion selection, leading to irreversible loss of critical diagnostic information. To address these challenges, we propose GFR-MIL, a novel Glance-Focus-Reflect framework where the Reflect module provides top-down feedback from high-resolution fine-grained features to recalibrate low-resolution global representations, establishing bidirectional cross-scale interaction for MIL-based WSI analysis. This iterative closed-loop mechanism emulates the cogni-tive workflow of experienced pathologists, who rapidly glance at the global tissue context, focus on suspicious regions, and reflectively revise initial judgments. To further address information loss from unsampled regions, we in-troduce a Recycling Mechanism and a memory masking strategy, ensuring comprehensive slide-level supervision throughout training. Extensive experi-ments across 7 public cohorts demonstrate that GFR-MIL consistently outper-forms state-of-the-art methods on both cancer subtyping and prognosis predic-tion tasks, with thorough ablation studies validating the contribution of each proposed component.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes GFR-MIL, a model that mimics the image-reading patterns of experts and is designed according to the Glance-Focus-Reflect cognitive paradigm. It achieves patch aggregation and WSI analysis through bidirectional closed-loop interaction between low-resolution global context and high-resolution local fine-grained features. The paper evaluates the model’s performance on six public datasets and presents interpretability heatmaps.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) The authors have modeled the image-reviewing process of pathologists, with a meticulously designed framework that provides a counterintuitive discussion of the necessity of each component. 
2) The authors conducted a comprehensive evaluation of their method against nine other approaches across six datasets, covering cancer prognosis prediction and cancer subtyping tasks; overall, their method is competitive.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) Although the authors conducted extensive comparisons of model performance, the improvement in subtype prediction performance on TCGA-NSCLC relative to the baseline appears to be minimal, and the authors did not report on statistical significance. 
2) Unlike other datasets, confidence intervals were not reported when comparing with BRCAS. 
3) During the sampling phase of the Glance Module, the authors claim to select the top-k% instances, but they do not report the value of k nor analyze the impact of varying k on model sensitivity. 
4)While the paper repeatedly emphasizes computational efficiency through coarse-to-fine selection and claims that GFR-MIL achieves strong performance while attending to only 30% of slide regions, the actual end-to-end efficiency remains insufficiently substantiated. In particular, the framework still requires dual-resolution preprocessing and feature extraction, iterative stacked GFRBlocks, cross-scale feedback through the Reflect module, recycling of unselected regions, and multi-round feature aggregation, all of which may introduce non-trivial computational and memory overhead.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The proposed method exhibits a certain degree of novelty, but the key parameters of the model have not been explained. The authors have provided a targeted and largely satisfactory response to my four concerns:
NSCLC improvement (Q1): They acknowledge that TCGA‑NSCLC subtyping is a near‑saturated task relying on few discriminative patches, and redirect attention to the prognosis tasks (five datasets) where GFR‑MIL achieves consistent and notable C‑index gains. They also report a 44% reduction in preprocessing cost (27.5s vs 48.9s for ABMIL‑Gated). This is an acceptable clarification — the method’s value is clearer on harder tasks, while remaining efficient on saturated ones.
BRACS confidence intervals (Q2): They correctly note that BRACS provides official fixed train/val/test splits, and they followed this standard protocol. Under such fixed splits, reporting standard deviations is not standard practice. This resolves my concern.
Top‑k% sampling ratio (Q3): The authors explicitly state that the two GFRBlocks use k = 20% and 10% (total ~30% of patches), referencing [28]. They also argue that the closed‑loop Reflect module recovers missed regions in round 2, making the framework architecturally robust to k, supported by SOTA performance across 7 datasets. This is a reasonable justification, though an ablation on k would have been stronger. I accept the explanation.
Computational efficiency (Q4): This is addressed convincingly. The authors now provide concrete numbers (to be added to the final paper)
The rebuttal has successfully resolved my major concerns, particularly the critical issue of computational efficiency. The method remains novel and well motivated, and the empirical evaluation is solid. I maintain my original score of Weak Accept.

reviews.text_contribution:
The main contribution of this work lies in the formulation of an iterative cross-scale MIL framework for WSIs, where global and local information are not simply fused once, but are progressively coordinated through repeated rounds of selection, local modeling, and feedback refinement. 
Compared with conventional MIL pipelines that rely on one-shot instance selection or flat aggregation, the proposed method introduces a more structured diagnostic reasoning process and provides several task-specific designs, including gated regional sampling, recycling of unselected information, feedback-based low-resolution updating, and history-aware region suppression.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The proposed GFR-MIL framework is well motivated by the diagnostic workflow of pathologists and provides a clear and intuitive coarse-to-fine reasoning paradigm. 
2.The proposed gated sampling, entropy regularization, and recycling mechanism together form a relatively complete sparse selection pipeline that is both practical and technically sound.
3.The iterative Reflect module with memory constraint introduces a meaningful multi-round refinement strategy, which is conceptually appealing for WSI analysis and has the potential to improve representation completeness.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.In Fig. 1, the number of stacked GFRBlocks is denoted as N, but the manuscript does not clearly specify its value. It is also unclear whether the parameter D introduced later refers to the number of GFRBlocks. This point should be clarified, as it appears to be a key architectural hyperparameter.
2.The paper does not provide any analysis of the computational cost, such as FLOPs, inference time, or GPU memory consumption. Since the proposed GFRBlocks appear to introduce nontrivial overhead, and the dual-resolution design may further increase both computational complexity and inference latency in practical deployment, it would be important to analyze the trade-off between performance and efficiency.
3.The visualization in Fig. 2 is currently not sufficiently clear. In particular, the semantic meaning of different colors (e.g., red vs. blue) is not well explained, making it difficult to understand what exactly the figure is intended to demonstrate. More interpretable visualizations and clearer figure captions would strengthen the paper.
4.Since the method is based on multi-round Glance–Focus–Reflect reasoning, it would be helpful to analyze whether different blocks attend to different types of regions. For example, do earlier blocks focus on the most salient lesions, while later blocks identify complementary or previously overlooked regions? Such analysis is currently missing.

This paper proposes a novel GFR-MIL framework that models iterative cross-scale interaction for WSI analysis. The Glance–Focus–Reflect paradigm is conceptually appealing and the experimental results show consistent improvements over strong baselines.

Overall, despite these limitations, the idea is novel and promising. I lean towards a weak accept, while encouraging stronger computational cost analysis.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper has a coherent and potentially useful idea for WSI MIL, and two reviewers lean toward acceptance. However, the acceptance case depends on whether the authors can substantiate the experimental claims. The method is presented as efficient and more complete than previous coarse-to-fine MIL approaches, but the current evidence does not sufficiently support this. In particular, the lack of runtime, memory, FLOPs, patch ratio, and end-to-end preprocessing cost weakens the central efficiency claim. The experimental comparison is also not fully convincing unless the authors include or clearly justify the absence of relevant hierarchical/coarse-to-fine baselines. The reported improvements appear modest in some settings, and missing confidence intervals or statistical significance further limits confidence.

The proposed Glance–Focus–Reflect paradigm is conceptually appealing to me, and the empirical results demonstrate consistent improvements over robust baselines.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for the constructive feedback, and code will be released upon acceptance.
Q1 for R2&Meta: NSCLC Improvement.
Subtyping on TCGA-NSCLC is a near-saturated task as it depends on a few discriminative patches[26]. GFR-MIL matches top performance while reducing preprocessing cost by 44% (27.5s vs 48.9s for ABMIL-Gated, median 15,135 patches @20x). On prognosis tasks requiring global WSI context [27], GFR-MIL consistently outperforms all competitors across five datasets with notable C-index gains (Table 1). GFR-MIL thus offers efficiency on saturated tasks and accuracy on challenging ones.
[26] IEEE TMI, vol. 44, no. 9, pp. 3756-3769.[27] CVPR, 2025, pp. 5144-5153.Q2 for R2, 8&Meta: BRACS Confidence Intervals.
BRACS provides official fixed train/val/test splits (Sec 3.1), we follow this standard protocol for direct comparison with prior work.
Q3 for R2: Top-k% Sampling Ratio.
The two GFRBlocks use k = 20% and 10% (Sec 3.2), selecting ~30% of patches in total, consistent with [28]. Notably, the closed-loop Reflect module recovers regions missed in round 1 during round 2, making GFR-MIL architecturally robust to k. This is supported by SOTA performance across 7 datasets with widely varying patch counts (Tables 1, 2).
[28] arXiv:2603.00667 
Q4 for R2, 3, 8&Meta : Computational Efficiency and Trade-Off
Recycling Mechanism is training-only to ensure gradient flow (Sec 2.2). At inference, GFR-MIL processes only the 2.5× WSI and ~30% of 20× patches. On TCGA-KIRC (median 19,187 patches @ 20×), preprocessing (dual-resolution feature extraction) drops from 51.3s (full 20×) to 30.4s per slide, and the full pipeline (stacked GFRBlocks, Reflect feedback, and multi-round aggregation) costs 85.7G FLOPs, 0.55GB memory, and 11.3ms inference, versus 189.5G/0.93GB/14.5ms (TransMIL) and 571.7G/2.0GB/29.8ms (RRT). Similar trends hold across all 7 datasets. These omitted details will be added.
Q5 for R3: Parameters N and D. 
N in Fig. 1 denotes the number of stacked GFRBlocks, equivalent to D in Sec 3.2, with a value of 2.We will unify this notation in the final version.
Q6 for R3: Fig. 2 Visualization Clarity.
The red highlighted areas denote the high-attention regions identified by GFR-MIL, while the blue areas indicate the low-attention regions. We will clarify this in the caption.
Q7 for R3: Multi-Round Attention Behavior.
The two GFRBlocks are functionally complementary by design. The first selects salient top-ranked regions, and the memory mask (Sec 2.4) then suppresses them, forcing the second to find overlooked yet discriminative ones (0% spatial overlap). Ablation confirms each contributes (Table 3). We will color-code Fig.2 by round, with the first round in black boxes and the second in green. Per-round histological profiling is left for future interpretability work.
Q8 for R8&Meta: Coarse-to-Fine Baselines.
We addresse coarse-to-fine baselines from two angles. (1) RLogist [13], a representative coarse-to-fine method, reports in its own paper that it underperforms high-resolution MIL baselines. We therefore prioritized comparisons with the latest and strongest high-resolution methods [19, 20], where GFR-MIL achieves SOTA across all 7 cohorts. (2) In Table 3, replacing our bidirectional Reflect with a unidirectional Gumbel-Softmax reduces GFR-MIL to a standard coarse-to-fine pipeline, and the resulting drop confirms our design’s advantage.
Q9 for R8: Survival Evaluation Metrics.
C-index is a standard metric in computational pathology survival analysis, widely adopted in recent works [20, 27]. GFR-MIL ranks first across all 5 distinct cancer cohorts, validating its superiority. Further KM analyses will be conducted in future.
Q10 for R8: Qualitative Baseline Comparison.
GFR-MIL achieves unique interpretability. Unlike conventional MIL with diffuse whole-slide attention heatmaps [2], it outputs discrete localized boxes for per-round selected regions (Fig. 2). Qualitative baseline heatmap comparison is left for future work.

title: GG-AE: Genetically-Guided Autoencoder for Disentangling Structural Networks of Brain Atrophy
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases exhibit substantial phenotypic heterogeneity arising from the interplay of genetic risk and non-genetic factors, which is often obscured in standard neuroimaging analyses. Although structural MRI captures brain atrophy, it reflects a final overlapping pathway of diverse etiological processes, making it difficult to disentangle genetically driven degeneration from environmental or lifestyle-related effects. We propose a Genetically Guided Autoencoder (GG-AE), a self-supervised framework that leverages disease-associated genetic variation as a biological anchor to constrain the representation learning of brain atrophy. The framework first learns a compact genetic latent representation using a variational autoencoder, and subsequently decomposes voxel-wise imaging data into a genetically aligned subspace and a residual subspace using a dual-latent imaging autoencoder with non-negative, part-based decoding. On semi-synthetic data with known ground truth, GG-AE achieves improved recovery of genetically driven atrophy patterns compared to unguided and correlation-based baselines. When applied to real ADNI data, the model identifies spatially interpretable atrophy patterns and genetic associations that are consistent with established Alzheimer’s disease findings, while isolating non-genetic variation in a residual component. These results demonstrate the potential of genetically guided representation learning for disentangling disease heterogeneity and enabling mechanistically grounded imaging–genetics analysis. Our code is available at https://github.com/marilenadp/GG-AE.

reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a genetically guided autoencoder (GG‑AE), a self‑supervised framework for disentangling brain atrophy patterns into genetically driven components and non‑genetic residual components from structural MRI and SNP data.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.It adopts a genetically guided paradigm instead of simple multimodal fusion, making the modeling strategy more consistent with the biological direction from genotype to phenotype. 
2.It introduces non-negativity and soft orthogonality constraints to derive additive, localized brain structural patterns, leading to strong interpretability.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The abstract and introduction overstate the contributions by claiming to be “the first to disentangle genetically driven versus non-genetic brain atrophy”, despite the existence of prior work addressing similar problems. 
2.The model demonstrates insufficient novelty and is merely a trivial combination of existing mature techniques. It integrates VAE, dual-latent autoencoder, NMF-style decoder, and InfoNCE alignment, none of which are new. No novel network architecture, loss function, or disentanglement theory is proposed. The so-called “genetic guidance” is essentially contrastive alignment plus orthogonality regularization, which has been extensively explored in multimodal disentanglement research, leading to no theoretical contribution. 
4.The paper does not compare against state-of-the-art multimodal disentanglement methods such as disentangled VAE, MoCo, DIP, and other modern contrastive disentanglement frameworks. It only evaluates against conventional baselines including NMF, vanilla autoencoder, and Deep CCA. 
Ablation analyses are seriously incomplete. While the paper includes permutation tests and a Deep CCA variant, it lacks systematic ablation on critical components: non-negativity constraints, soft orthogonality constraints, dual-latent structure, and two-stage genetic pre-training. It remains unclear whether each design choice is independently essential or only provides marginal improvement via simple component stacking.

reviews.text_contribution:
The authors propose a staged autoencoder framework (GG-AE) that first leverages a variational autoencoder (VAE) to learn a representation of genetic risk from SNPs and an imaging autoencoder with a Non-Negative Matrix Factorization (NMF)-inspired decoder for interpretability through additive, part-based spatial maps. The imaging autoencoder’s latent space is split into a subspace aligned with genetic representation from the frozen vae and the residual subspace is for non-genetic variation.
They evaluate on semi-synthetic data that’s derived from the UK BioBank (UKB) and then also on real Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) data.
reviews.text_strengths:
The NMF-inspired decoder is well-motivated and practical. This is because this approach produces addtive, spatially interpretable components.
Their overall approach of explicitly partitioning genetic and then non-genetic into a residual subspace is well-motivated/novel as most fusion approaches tend to treat them symmetrically. This is good because the authors thus allow their method to respect real-world directionality (genotype goes to some intermediate molecular proces which then results in the phenotype). A symmetric version would blend genetic/non-genetic and make it unclear which modality is actually contributing.
Their ADNI results look biologically meaningful/relevant. This is because the genetic patterns found line up with known AD neuroanatomy and known SNP associations, also I like that their residual part shows no significant genetic association.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
My primary concern is in regard to using 54 pre-selected AD-associated SNPs as input to the real-data evaluation. With all input SNPs already curated for AD relevance, the VAE’s representation learning task is pretty simplified, since it’s compressing 54 AD signals into K dimensions rather than distinguishing AD-relevant from AD-irrelevant genetic variation. This means the downstream imaging model is constrained to align with an already AD-enriched latent space, which, in my opinion, stacks the deck in favor of recovering AD-relevant spatial patterns. To be clear, I’d say this does not predetermine the spatial maps or the partitioning across K=3 components, but it does make one wonder how dependent the framework’s performance is on this curated input. Since this paper presents GG-AE as a general framework, but the real-data evaluation relies on a highly curated SNP set that eliminates the challenge of distinguishing disease-relevant from irrelevant genetic variation, a task the VAE would need to handle for less well-characterized diseases or in discovery-oriented settings. I’d say it remains unclear how sensitive the framework is to the composition and purity of the input SNP set.
QUESTION: Can the authors report/comment on the expected sensitivity of the framework to SNP set composition?
I do note that the semi-synthetic experiments partially address this concern with the ADNI pre-selected SNPs, and I appreciate that it’s grounded in actual/real UKB data. However, the genetic simulation lacks features that would make it a convincing test. Specifically, the 95 non-risk SNPs are drawn independently from baseline MAFs with no correlation structure, making the 5 causal variants per pattern trivially identifiable. In real genotype data, risk SNPs are embedded in haplotype blocks where neighboring variants carry partial signal through LD, and polygenic background contributes correlated noise across many loci. Additionally, there is no pleiotropy (each SNP maps to exactly one pattern) and no population stratification. Thus, I’m still unsure regarding input sensitivity to realistic/real-world SNP input/set composition.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I think the authors core proposed approach (asymmetry for genetic guidance with NMF-inspired decoding for interpretability) is well-founded. ADNI results themselves look solid biologically. Overall methodological design is generally robust, I appreciated the Perm GG-AE experiment for architectural bias as an example.
As outlined in the weakness section, I find the SNPs input to the real-world ADNI test data experiment to be potentially biased, thus making it unclear how much of this is actually the GG-AE itself learning meaningful structure in real data. While I appreciate the semi-synthetic grounded in UKB, I note my weakness section comment regarding the simulation setup.
As such, I’m giving a weak accept because the core approach is well-motivated with reasonable results, but I’d like greater clarification regarding SNP input set impact/sensitivity to the GG-AE.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
I vouch for the paper to be accepted. The authors clarify in their rebuttal that GG-AE is meant to take in some already curated SNP set to guide the learned imaging representation/spatial patterns.
For example, this could be from existing biological knowledge or other data-driven methods explicitly developed for SNP-disease association discovery (where there are numerous methods already developed).
As such, the core novelty that asymmetry in their design allows for voxel-imaging dimensionality to not drive the learned imaging-genetic representations, but instead allow underlying genetic information to be the driver is a useful methodological contribution that could be applied to other disease with well characterized SNP sets and varying structural/spatial patterns in imaging data.

The reviews were mixed, with R2 and R3 recommending weak accept but R1 recommending reject. All reviewers raised concerns about the paper that should be addressed in the rebuttal. Besides the other mentioned fixable and addressable points answer the novelty and contribution concerns of R1 should be part of the rebuttal.

Following the rebuttal, two of the three reviewers recommended acceptance. R2 and R3 found the clarifications regarding the paper’s positioning as a biologically motivated imaging-genetics framework rather than a general-purpose disentanglement contribution convincing. R1’s concerns about missing comparisons and incomplete ablations reflect a different evaluation perspective rather than fundamental technical issues and are offset to a reasonable extent by the controlled, semi-synthetic validation and the biological plausibility of the ADNI findings. After considering the reviews and rebuttal, I recommend acceptance. The paper proposes a genetically guided autoencoder for interpretable imaging-genetics analysis of brain atrophy, combining genetic guidance with an NMF-inspired decoder to separate genetically associated structural patterns from residual variation.
The rebuttal clarifies that the contribution is not intended as a general disentanglement theory, but as a biologically motivated framework for interpretable imaging-genetics discovery using curated SNP sets. This addresses the main concern about task positioning. The semi-synthetic validation and ADNI results provide reasonable evidence that the learned patterns are biologically meaningful. Some limitations remain, including incremental use of existing components, limited ablation against broader disentanglement methods, and sensitivity to SNP-set selection.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their valuable feedback. R1 appears to interpret our paper as a general-purpose disentanglement framework, leading to critiques regarding limited novelty in disentanglement theory, lack of comparisons with broad multimodal disentanglement models, and reliance on existing components. However, as also noted by R2/R3, this work is primarily a biologically motivated model for interpretable imaging-genetics discovery rather than a general disentanglement theory contribution. Specifically:
1.Interpretable structural pattern discovery remains underexplored in recent deep imaging-genetics work, which has focused largely on classification. Unlike most prior approaches, GG-AE is an unlabeled, data-driven framework for mechanistic representation learning without disease labels.
2.A key contribution is integrating an NMF-inspired decoder within a deep autoencoder. Although widely used for interpretable neuroimaging decomposition, NMF is inherently linear with dedicated optimization procedures. GG-AE preserves NMF-style interpretability while enabling scalable self-supervised learning with more expressive encoders. So, we integrated contrastive alignment and orthogonality regularization within an interpretable NMF-based imaging-genetics framework to disentangle NMF components, which to our knowledge has not been explored previously.
3.Voxel-level imaging creates severe dimensional imbalance that can dominate genetic signals. GG-AE, instead of symmetric fusion, directly models the biological direction from genotype->phenotype by using genetic variation to guide imaging representations, as also recognized by R2.
Thus, while GG-AE combines existing methodological components, our contribution lies in their biologically motivated integration for interpretable self-supervised imaging-genetics analysis.
Regarding baselines/ablations (R1), we focused on methods commonly used in unsupervised imaging-genetics analysis, since the goal was mechanistic representation learning rather than benchmarking all multimodal disentanglement models. Existing disentanglement methods are rarely evaluated for self-supervised imaging-genetics settings with voxel-wise neuroimaging and severe modality imbalance, and implementing them was beyond this study’s scope. We therefore used representative baselines including Deep CCA, imaging-only decomposition methods, and permutation controls. While additional ablations could further isolate individual design choices, the 8-page limit led us to prioritize controlled semi-synthetic validation with known ground truth and application to real data, as appreciated by R2/R3.
Regarding SNP selection (R2) and genetic VAE modeling (R3), GG-AE is intentionally guided by the selected SNPs relevant to the biological question, and the current real-data experiment therefore focused on AD-related variants. Our goal was not to distinguish AD- from non-AD-related SNPs or learn a fully disentangled genetic factorization, but rather to learn a compact representation that guides separation of heterogeneous structural atrophy patterns within the AD spectrum. SNP selection can be adapted to different objectives, including disease-specific, multi-disease, or LD-pruned variant sets. Because SNP inputs are sparse we used a VAE to capture latent genetic distributions rather than deterministic embeddings alone, while progressively increasing β-weighted KL regularization and sigmoid-transformed latent sampling encouraged stable distributed representations. The genotype simulation was designed as a controlled proof-of-concept to evaluate if GG-AE can recover genetically associated structural components while separating residual variation, rather than model full genetic architecture, including LD and polygenic effects. Nevertheless, the observed SNP-latent associations, imaging alignment behavior, and permutation-control experiments support the biological relevance of the learned representations.
Code will be released.

title: GGFI-Net: Genomics-Guided Cross-Modal Imputation for Multimodal Survival Analysis with Missing Modality
abstract: Survival prediction modeling has shown promise in capturing diverse tumor phenotypes from multimodal data, such as radiomics and genomics. However, its clinical application is often hampered by two major constraints: missing modalities in fragmented datasets, and severe overfitting caused by high-dimensional features in small-sample regimes. To address these challenges, we propose a Genomics-Guided Cross-Modal Feature Imputation Framework (GGFI-Net) for survival analysis. Specifically, we introduce a Lightweight Cross-Modal Mapper (LCM) that learns a structured mapping from genomic to radiomic latent spaces, enabling the imputation of missing modalities without the computational overhead of heavy generative models. Furthermore, we design a Genomics-Driven Survival Distillation (GDSD) module. This teacher-student architecture transfers survival-relevant discriminative knowledge from complete genomic profiles to supervise the latent radiomic representations, effectively mitigating overfitting and ensuring the prognostic fidelity of the imputed features. Unlike prior fusion or generative imputation methods, GGFI-Net explicitly models cross-modal survival-consistent feature alignment. Experiments on public pancreatic cancer cohorts demonstrate its superiority. Notably, on the modality-deficient TCGA-PAAD dataset, GGFI-Net significantly outperforms genomics-only baselines, improving the C-index from 0.645 to 0.679. It also maintains robust performance on the modality-complete CPTAC-PDA dataset (C-index: 0.709). These results confirm that GGFI-Net provides a highly robust and clinically feasible solution for incomplete multimodal survival modeling under data scarcity.
