First, it clearly identifies the key limitation of existing CLIP-style global vision–language alignment for LGE MRI report generation: insufficient modeling of region-level scar patterns and cross-slice structural continuity, making the work clinically well-motivated. It proposes a novel Global–Local Structure-Aware Alignment framework (GLSA-RG) with unified structural graph representations, including intra-slice, cross-slice, and AHA 17-segment textual graphs, enabling fine-grained structure-aware visual-text alignment beyond coarse global matching. The authors build a multi-center LGE MRI dataset with paired reports to alleviate data scarcity. Extensive experiments and ablations show the model outperforms state-of-the-art methods on both internal and external validation, with improved clinical accuracy and structural consistency. The global–local alignment paradigm advances 3D medical vision-language modeling for structured cardiac report generation.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper offers a strong technical contribution with real potential for clinical translation in automated LGE MRI report generation. The proposed GLSA-RG framework, with its global-local structure-aware alignment and unified structural graph representation, addresses a critical, often-overlooked limitation of existing CLIP-style vision-language methods: the failure to model fine-grained regional scar patterns, cross-slice continuity, and AHA 17-segment anatomical dependencies. This paradigm is generalizable and could benefit other 3D medical vision-language and structured reporting tasks, and the authors’ multi-center paired dataset is a valuable contribution to the field. However, there are several key issues that require clarification, including insufficient methodological details for reproducibility, incomplete clinical validation with missing segment-level performance metrics, lack of interpretability visualizations, and unaddressed real-world clinical applicability.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
Automated LGE MRI reporting is a challenging clinical task and an interesting technical problem. Weaknesses are the incremental methodological novelty, limited dataset characterization, and reliance on automatic or GPT-based metrics. In the rebuttal, the authors should strengthen the evidence for clinical reporting quality, and better position the contribution in currently existing report-generation methods.

The rebuttal addressed the main concerns: the expert clinical evaluation by two cardiologists provides human-assessed evidence beyond automatic metrics, the dataset heterogeneity is clarified, and the task-specific design choices are justified. R1 and R4 did not change the rating and R3 moved to accept. Overall the paper meet the threshold of acceptance.

After considering the reviews and rebuttal discussion, I recommend acceptance. The paper addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem in automated LGE MRI report generation, with clear clinical motivation and meaningful technical contributions.
The proposed GLSA-RG framework is well designed and introduces a coherent global–local structure-aware alignment strategy that explicitly models intra-slice regional interactions, cross-slice continuity, and structured myocardial segment relationships. Compared with prior global-only vision–language alignment approaches, the proposed framework provides a more clinically grounded representation for capturing subtle enhancement patterns and structural consistency in LGE MRI.
The experimental evaluation is reasonably comprehensive, including multi-center paired MRI-report data, external validation, comparisons with recent baselines, and multiple ablation studies. The reported improvements are consistent across both standard report-generation metrics and clinical evaluation metrics, supporting the effectiveness of the proposed alignment and graph modeling strategies.
While some concerns remain regarding the depth of human clinical evaluation, dataset description, and reproducibility details, the rebuttal adequately addressed the main reviewer concerns and clarified the intended scope and contribution of the work. Overall, I believe the paper provides a valuable and practically relevant contribution to 3D medical vision-language modeling and automated structured report generation, and is suitable for acceptance at MICCAI.
All reviewers highlight the contributions of the paper and suggest to accept the submission.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their valuable feedback and address their concerns below.
AC, R1W1: Novelty 
(1) Task novelty: We address automated LGE MRI report generation, a clinically important, challenging, and underexplored task, as acknowledged by R1, R3, and R4.(2) Framework novelty: Although some components draw on existing ideas, our main contribution is a unified, task-specific framework for cardiac MR and structured report generation that does not rely on segmentation. R4 recognizes it as a “novel global-local structure-aware alignment framework.”
(3) Component novelty: We introduce intra-slice and cross-slice graph modules to model regional interactions and cross-slice continuity, enabling precise characterization of subtle myocardial enhancement patterns.
AC, R1W2: Limited human assessment, error analysis, and ethics
Regarding Point 1, two cardiologists with over 10 years of clinical experience were invited to evaluate existing results. They independently reviewed 20 randomly selected reports using a 5-point Likert scale to assess enhancement detection accuracy and report usability. Their analyses were consistent with existing results and further supported our superiority over the baseline Med3DVLM. These analyses will be included.
Regarding Point 2, Table 1 already characterizes model errors and demonstrates consistent improvements over prior state-of-the-art methods. We will further include additional qualitative error analysis on existing results.
Regarding Point 3, All data were properly anonymized in accordance with institutional and data governance guidelines.
R3W1: Dataset description
The development cohort includes normal, myocardial infarction, and DCM cases, while the external cohort primarily comprises DCM cases. Variations in report terminology, granularity, and imaging systems (Siemens vs. Philips) introduce substantial heterogeneity, increasing task difficulty and enabling a more rigorous evaluation of robustness and generalizability.
R3W2: Deeper experimental analysis including case studies and error analysis 
The manuscript already included a representative qualitative case study (Fig. 3) to support interpretability. Our method identified subtler enhancement patterns (e.g., apical inferior wall enhancement), produced fewer localization errors, better captured continuous inferior wall enhancement across adjacent slices, and reduced anatomically inconsistent segment assignments.
Existing experiments in Table 1 characterize model errors and demonstrate consistent improvements over prior state-of-the-art methods. We will include additional qualitative error analysis on existing results.
R3W3: Stronger baselines
Our experiments already include representative state-of-the-art report generation methods under identical settings (Table 1). Some additional structure-aware approaches were excluded due to differing settings, limiting fair comparison. We will add citations and discussion for a more comprehensive overview.
R3W4: Generalization ability
The proposed global–local structure alignment paradigm is modality-agnostic. The short-axis continuity modeling and AHA 17-segment graph are cardiac-specific anatomical priors and would need to be replaced with organ-specific structural priors when extending our method to other anatomies.
R4W1: Reproducibility
We will open-source our code to provide full details for reproducibility.
R4W2: Missing segment-level metrics
Our task focuses on report generation, so conventional segment-level metrics are less applicable. Our case analysis already covers lesion location and extent accuracy. We will explore finer-grained localization metrics in future work.
R4W3: Lack of interpretability visualizations
See our reply to R3-W2.
R4W4: Clinical applicability
While our work focuses on methodological advancement, its promising results, together with the unanimous recognition of its clinical significance by all reviewers, suggest its potential for clinical applicability.

title: Good Enough? An Investigation on the Impact of Label Quality in Large-Scale Medical Datasets
abstract: Manually refining radiological segmentation masks is highly resource-intensive. To determine when this expert commitment is truly justified for the training of segmentation models, we investigate the relationship between label quality and model performance. Expanding beyond models trained directly for inference, we conduct the first study isolating the impact of label quality in pre-training datasets. While high-quality labels remain essential for models proceeding directly to deployment, we find no evidence that strict label quality is crucial for pre-training efficacy. These results question the necessity of exhaustive human-in-the-loop refinement for massive corpora intended for pretraining and suggest that expert effort is more effectively invested in well-curated downstream target datasets.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper makes a data-centric contribution by systematically investigating how label quality affects medical image segmentation, particularly distinguishing between direct training (in-domain use) and pre-training + fine-tuning scenarios. Instead of proposing a new model, it introduces a large-scale, controlled experimental framework where high-quality annotations are replaced with realistic pseudo-labels generated by different models (e. g. , nnU-Net, MedSAM, TotalSegmentator), thereby simulating varying levels of annotation noise. Using this setup across multiple datasets and segmentation models, the paper reveals a key finding: while label quality is crucial for models trained and deployed directly, it is surprisingly less important for pre-training, as fine-tuning on clean data largely compensates for noisy pre-training labels. Model performance strongly correlates with label quality in the in-domain setting, but this dependency largely disappears after fine-tuning. Based on these findings, the paper provides actionable insights for dataset construction—suggesting that expensive expert refinement may not be necessary for large-scale pre-training datasets, and that effort should instead focus on high-quality downstream annotations.
reviews.text_strengths:
First, it addresses a highly relevant and practical problem in medical imaging: the trade-off between annotation quality and scalability. Given that large datasets such as DAP-Atlas or AbdomenAtlas require thousands of hours of expert effort, the paper tackles an important question—whether such costly refinement is necessary—making the work highly impactful for both dataset construction and model development. 
Second, the paper proposes a novel and well-designed experimental framework to study label quality. Instead of relying on synthetic noise (as commonly done in prior works using perturbations or morphological operations), it generates realistic pseudo-label noise using a diverse set of models (nnU-Net, TotalSegmentator, STU-Net variants, MedSAM). This setup closely mimics modern dataset curation pipelines and avoids unrealistic assumptions about noise distributions, which is a clear methodological improvement over prior studies
reviews.text_weaknesses:
First, the study relies entirely on pseudo-labels generated by models as a proxy for annotation noise, which may not fully capture real-world annotation errors. Although this is more realistic than synthetic perturbations, it still differs from genuine human annotation variability. As a result, the conclusions may not fully generalize to real clinical annotation settings. 
Second, the experimental setup, while controlled, is somewhat limited in model diversity. The study fixes a single segmentation architecture (DynUNet / nnU-Net style training) to isolate data effects. While this improves internal validity, it raises concerns about external validity: it is unclear whether the conclusions hold for other architectures, especially newer foundation models or transformer-based segmentation approaches.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I recommend a Weak Accept (4/6).
The main factor supporting this score is the paper’s strong problem formulation and practical relevance. It addresses an important and timely question in medical imaging—whether high-quality annotations are necessary at scale—which has clear implications for dataset construction and resource allocation. The study is particularly valuable because it reflects realistic modern data pipelines based on pseudo-labeling, rather than relying on artificial noise.
Another key strength is the novel experimental perspective, especially the explicit separation between in-domain training and pre-training + fine-tuning. The finding that label quality is critical for direct deployment but largely irrelevant for pre-training is both non-trivial and impactful, and could influence how large-scale medical datasets are built. The experimental design is also carefully controlled and comprehensive, covering multiple datasets, label generators, and evaluation settings, which makes the conclusions convincing.
However, the score is limited to weak accept due to several factors. The novelty is moderate, as the general topic of label noise and annotation quality has been studied before, and the paper mainly extends prior work to a larger-scale and pre-training setting. In addition, the study relies on pseudo-labels as a proxy for annotation noise, which may not fully reflect real-world clinical annotation variability. The work is also largely empirical, with limited theoretical or mechanistic analysis of why the observed phenomena occur.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This study provides a pragmatic framework for optimizing annotation efforts in medical image segmentation by revealing a fundamental asymmetry between pre-training and finetuning stages. The authors demonstrate that while downstream performance is highly sensitive to the precision of fine-tuning segmentation labels, large-scale pre-training on cohorts such as Word, Amos, and CT1K-Abd is remarkably robust to noise. By utilizing a diverse range of label generators including nnU-Net, MedSAM, and the STU-Net family to produce masks with varying Dice scores (70-90%), the research proves that suboptimal pseudo-labels can facilitate feature transfer nearly as effectively as expert-curated ones. Given the high cost and limited availability of medical experts, the paper suggests developers prioritize expert labor for refining small-scale fine-tuning sets while leveraging automated, high-throughput labeling for massive pre-training collections.
reviews.text_strengths:
Extensive and diverse 3D datasets: The study is grounded in a robust experimental framework, utilizing a wide array of large-scale 3D medical segmentation datasets that accurately reflect the complexities of clinical volumetric imaging across various anatomical regions.
Comprehensive simulation of label noise: A significant merit of the work is the inclusion of diverse label-generation models, such as nnU-Net, MedSAM, and the STU-Net family. By leveraging these varied architectures to produce a spectrum of pseudo-label qualities, the authors successfully simulate real-world annotation noise and its impact on model training.
Clear and coherent presentation: The manuscript is well-structured and the results are presented with a high degree of transparency. The figures and tables are clearly plotted, making the core findings regarding the relationship between pre-training and fine-tuning easy to understand at a glance.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Lack of self-supervised learning baselines: A critical methodological gap is the absence of comparisons with self-supervised learning (SSL) paradigms (e.g., DINO). Without an SSL baseline, it remains unclear whether the pre-training gains stem from the “noisy labels” or simply from the model’s exposure to a larger data volume.
Undefined boundary of label noise: While the study shows pre-training is robust to label quality (Dice 70-90%), it fails to explore the “break-down point” of this robustness. It remains unknown whether a noise threshold exists or if even completely randomly generated masks would yield similar results, which leaves the actual necessity of using “pseudo-labels” for pre-training unproven.
Technical error in visualization: There is a noticeable technical oversight in Figure 3.c, where the bar representing the STU-Net Large results for the AbdomenAtlas dataset is missing. It is unclear whether this is a plotting error or if the performance value is lower than the visible y-axis limit.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper delivers a large scale empirical study on the role of annotation quality in 3D medical image segmentation. The authors convincingly show that pre training is robust to noisy labels, while fine tuning remains highly sensitive to precision. This insight offers practical guidance for resource allocation, suggesting that automated labeling can be used effectively for pre training, with expert annotation reserved for fine tuning where accuracy is most critical.
Despite its strong experimental scale and clear engineering value, the work leaves methodological gaps. The absence of self supervised learning baselines limits the ability to disentangle the effects of label guidance from data volume, and the robustness limits for label quality are not fully explored. Overall, the study provides valuable clarity on label quality requirements in medical pre training, and I recommend a Weak Accept.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper systematically studies the relationship between label quality and model performance in medical image segmentation. The authors construct pseudo labels using seven segmentation models and quantify pseudo-label quality on four base datasets using Dice and Surface Dice. Based on these, the paper conducts in-domain experiments with DynUNet, and further performs pre-training and fine-tuning experiments on two additional datasets. The results suggest that, in the in-domain setting, model performance is overall positively correlated with dataset quality. In the pre-training experiments, even when relatively low-quality pseudo labels are used for pre-training, the fine-tuned models on the additional datasets still outperform models trained from scratch.
reviews.text_strengths:
1 The paper addresses an interesting and practically relevant problem, and the use of model-generated pseudo labels to mimic modern dataset construction pipelines is a meaningful and moderately novel experimental setting.
2 The overall logic of the paper is clear, and the experimental setup is described in sufficient detail, supporting reproducibility.
3 The experiments are fairly comprehensive, covering seven pseudo-label generation models and four base datasets, with additional evaluation on one extra model and two extra datasets.
4 The empirical analysis is relatively thorough, and the figures and tables are well organized and easy to follow.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1 I remain unconvinced by the second conclusion in 3.1.The reported performance trend is obtained by fitting a quadratic polynomial to only seven discrete data points, yet several actual nnUNet points deviate noticeably from the fitted curve. From the figure, the performance of Orig does not appear to exceed nnUNet and even drops substantially in some cases. Therefore, the statement “As the dataset quality approaches 100, the performance curves begin to plateau” does not seem to be fully supported by the raw plotted results, and may be overly influenced by the fitted trend rather than directly supported by the discrete experimental observations.
2 In 2.2, the second finding states that “nnUNet outperforms on most datasets, achieving Dice scores from 82.8% to 95.2%.” However, I could not find any value corresponding to “82.8” in the table. This indicates that there is an issue in either the main text or the table, and the reported numbers should be carefully checked and made consistent.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper studies a practically meaningful question, namely how label quality affects model training and transfer performance. Overall, the experiments are fairly comprehensive and the results are clearly presented. However, the current version still contains inconsistencies between the main text and the reported tables/figures, and some conclusions do not fully align with the raw plotted results. This suggests that the interpretation may rely too heavily on the fitted trends while underemphasizing the actual discrete observations.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text: This work investigates how label quality affects medical image segmentation. All reviewers tend to accept it. However, there are also several concerns raised, eg. limited theoretical analysis etc. Please try to fix them if possible.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback and their general positive assessment. We address the main concerns below.
Pseudo-labels as a noise proxy (R1). Our pseudo-label setup is intentionally faithful to current large-scale practice, where datasets [8, 20, 27] are themselves constructed from model-generated masks with sparse expert verification, rather than via the synthetic perturbations used in prior work [1, 3, 24]. We acknowledge that for smaller, manually annotated cohorts, inter-rater variability may be the more realistic noise source. For this study, we deliberately keep the noise model consistent across our four datasets, which span 100 to 5,200 cases, to enable a controlled comparison of how the same noise type interacts with dataset scale. 
Architectural diversity (R1). With well over 100 full 3D segmentation training runs already required to span our 8 label variants, 4 base datasets, and 2 fine-tuning targets, adding an architecture family scales this beyond our available hardware resources. We deliberately fixed DynUnet to isolate the data effect; DynUnet/nnU-Net remains the most consistently competitive 3D backbone in the recent literature, so we believe studying this architecture is the most beneficial to the community. Extending the architecture selection is a natural and interesting follow-up.
SSL baselines and breakdown point (R2). We restricted ourselves to supervised pre-training to avoid a task shift between pre-training and fine-tuning, and because Li et al. [13] (ICLR 2024) report supervised pre-training to be much more sample-efficient than SSL on 3D medical data, so the question for us became how important data quality is under the more efficient supervised pre-training regime. Regarding the breakdown point: MedSAM on AbdomenAtlas reaches only 39.4% Dice and 24.8% Surface Dice (Table 1),  well below any plausible expert-curation threshold, yet models pretrained on it still play in the same league with models pretrained on higher quality datasets (Fig.3c). This datapoint already probes the low-quality regime, though a fully randomized-mask control would push it further, and we agree it is an interesting follow-up.
Missing STU-Net Large bar in Fig. 3c (R2). This is not a plotting oversight: STU-Net Large pre-training on AbdomenAtlas did not converge under our fixed, deterministic training schedule. We will mark this explicitly in the camera-ready version and thank R2 for catching it.
Plateau claim and quadratic fit (R3). R3 is right that the 2nd-degree fit smooths the discrete observations. The intended claim that marginal gains shrink at high label quality is most clearly carried by AbdomenAtlas (Fig. 2, right), where the four STU-Net variants span ~4 Dice points in label quality but yield largely overlapping model performance and even perform similarly to the model trained on the original labels.
82.8% inconsistency (R3). Correct: 82.8% is a leftover from BTCV experiments that were removed for spatial reasons from the final manuscript; the actual lower bound in Table 1 is now 83.7% (Word). We thank R3 for catching this and will fix it.

title: Graph Neural Networks for Morphometric Characterization of the Aortic Valve
abstract: Clinically significant geometrical measurements of the aortic valve, such as the intercommissural distances and angles, are enabled by aortic valve morphometry. While morphometry typically relies on detecting key anatomical landmarks of the aortic valve (nadirs and commissures), the accuracy of morphometric measurements derived from these landmarks remains under-investigated. In this study, we devise a graph-based representation, where morphometric measurements of the aortic valve are represented as graph nodes, and their anatomical relationships are represented as graph edges that encode the dependencies of the underlying landmarks. Such representations, which therefore encapsulate the geometric variability of landmark detection, are optimized through a graph neural network (GNN) that integrates geometric features and structural context to compute anatomically consistent morphometric measurements. The proposed GNN approach was evaluated on 280 cardiac computed tomography images consisting of three cohorts from two different institutions with both healthy and pathological aortic valve cases. By computing 29 different morphometric measurements (18 linear and 11 angular) with the proposed GNN approach and comparing them to those obtained from direct landmark detection, we observed a reduction in the mean absolute error by around 15-25% on average. The results demonstrate an improved anatomical consistency of the proposed GNN approach in extracting morphometric measurements, and its robustness to landmark detection uncertainty.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper suggests a graph-based approach for the geometric representation and assessment of the aortic valve via a connected landmarks.
reviews.text_strengths: The authors address a relevant clinical problem. The idea of the consideration of the spatial relations between relevant landmarks via graph representations is well motivated. The approach is well described.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper seems to be work-in-progress. There are several mistakes (e. g. surgerical, landmarks of the aortic,. . . ) in the text and references, which do not support the statements in the text ([7]). 
There is no assessment of the of inter- or intraobserver variability of the reference annotations or an ablation study.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a well motivated approach for improving the extraction of relevant geometrical parameters to TAVI planning CTs. The method strongly depends on a preprocessing step, which is implemented with a standard method. In the evaluation the assessment of the reproducibility of the reference method is missing. The authors do not present an ablation study.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper presents a GNN-based method for optimizing aortic valve morphometric measurements derived from pre-segmented landmarks. Landmarks are first created from nnU-Net, producing N=10 candidate points per landmark. The method then constructs a graph-based representation where each node corresponds a measurement, and edges are weighted by the similarity of shared landmark subsets between measurements. Each node holds K=1000 randomly sampled candidate landmark-point combinations, described by geometric descriptors (distances, angles, anisotropy). A GNN with graph convolutional layers shares context across interdependent measurements, then produces softmax weights over candidates. The final measurement is a weighted sum over the candidate measurement values — the GNN selects among candidates rather than regressing measurements directly.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The problem is clinically relevant. Accurate aortic valve measurements are important for surgical planning, and automating robust measurement from detected landmarks addresses a real clinical need.
2.The graph-based representation is well-motivated and clearly formalized. Defining edges via similarity of landmark subsets is an intuitive and principled way to encode anatomical dependencies between measurements.
3.The GNN architecture — from row-wise MLP embedding, through mean-pooled context, GCN message passing, context re-injection via residual MLP, to softmax-weighted candidate selection — is described in detail with clear notation and equations. The design choice to select among anatomically plausible candidates rather than directly regressing measurements is a sensible inductive bias.
4.The evaluation covers a comprehensive set of 29 measurements (18 linear, 11 angular), and results show consistent improvement over the baseline.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Reference [6] is cited in the context of deriving measurements from landmarks, but it is a general anatomy review that describes aortic root structure — it does not define a measurement protocol. The 29 evaluated measurements remain undefined: which landmark subsets are used and what geometric operations are applied for each measurement are not specified in the paper or in the cited reference.
2.The geometric descriptor for larger set of landmarks is described with “e.g.” and “etc.”, leaving the exact feature set and dimensionality D unspecified. Since the descriptor is the foundational input to the entire pipeline, the complete feature list should be explicitly stated.
3.The baseline comparison is insufficient to isolate the GNN’s contribution. The baseline uses a single Center-of-Mass point per landmark, while the proposed method uses a GNN-weighted average over K=1000 candidate combinations. The observed improvement could arise from three distinct sources: (a) the inherent robustness of ensembling over multiple candidates, (b) the GNN’s learned weighting, or (c) diversity among candidate points. Without an ablation comparing uniform (equal-weight) averaging over the same K=1000 combinations against the GNN-weighted result, the reader cannot determine how much of the improvement is attributable to the GNN architecture versus the trivial benefit of multi-candidate averaging.
4.No training loss function is specified anywhere in the paper. The architecture is described in full detail, but the optimization objective — what the GNN is trained to minimize — is absent. This raises several unanswered questions: whether MSE or MAE is used, how losses across linear (mm-scale) and angular (degree-scale) measurements are balanced, whether any regularization is applied to the softmax weights, and what serves as the ground truth reference for supervision.
5.The ground truth was provided by “an experienced cardiovascular surgeon” but no inter-observer variability analysis is reported. For clinical measurements, a single annotator’s measurements are insufficient to establish a reliable reference standard. Without inter-observer analysis, it is unclear whether the GNN’s improvement is within the noise floor of human measurement variability.
6.The authors acknowledge dependence on landmark detection accuracy as a limitation but provide no quantification. No landmark localization error is reported, and no sensitivity analysis examines how upstream detection noise affects downstream measurements. Without this, it is impossible to assess whether the GNN is learning genuinely optimal geometric weighting or compensating for detection noise.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Questions for the authors:
1.Could you provide the complete landmark-to-measurement assignments for all 29 measurements, including the geometric operation used to compute each measurement from its landmarks? Are these based on an established clinical protocol?
2.What is the training loss function? How are linear and angular measurement losses scaled or balanced?
3.What is the performance of uniform (equal-weight) averaging over K=1000 candidate combinations compared to CoM and compared to GNN-weighted averaging? This ablation is essential to separate the ensembling benefit from the GNN’s learned contribution.
4.What is the landmark detection accuracy (e.g., mean localization error in mm)? How does downstream measurement accuracy vary across cases with good vs. poor landmark detection?
5.K=1000 random combinations are sampled, but the total combinatorial space is N^L per measurement where L is the number of landmarks. For measurements with many landmarks, is K=1000 sufficient to cover the space? Does this vary by measurement, and was any analysis performed on the sensitivity to K?
Minor Issues:
There’s a typo in Page 6, results section: “resuls” should be “results”
There’s a type in Page 3, method section, Landmarks and Landmark Candidate Points: “Ket” should be “Let”

The paper addresses a clinically relevant problem and proposes an interesting graph-based formulation connecting interdependent aortic valve measurements through shared landmarks. The GNN architecture is clearly described at the equation level.
However, the paper has several significant methodological gaps that collectively prevent reproducibility and undermine the evaluation. The landmark-to-measurement assignments — which define the graph structure, the input features, and the measurement computations — are never specified or cited. The geometric descriptor features are incompletely described. No training loss function is provided. These are not minor implementation details but core components of the method: the reader cannot determine what is being measured, what features describe it, or what the network optimizes.
The experimental evaluation is weakened by an insufficient baseline. Comparing a single-point estimate (CoM) against a learned ensemble of 1000 candidates conflates ensembling benefits with the GNN’s learned contribution. Key ablations — uniform averaging baseline, graph vs. no-graph comparison — are missing. The ground truth relies on a single expert without inter-observer analysis, and the acknowledged limitation regarding landmark detection accuracy is stated without any quantification.
While the core idea has merit, the current manuscript does not provide sufficient methodological detail for reproducibility or sufficient experimental evidence to support its claims. Addressing the missing specification (landmark assignments, full feature set, loss function) and adding the ablation studies described above would substantially strengthen the paper.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
I thank the authors for the thorough rebuttal, which substantively addresses my main concerns. The clarified loss function (unweighted MSE), geometric descriptor set, inter-observer variability analysis, and uniform averaging ablation are all reassuring and demonstrate that the GNN’s contribution is genuine and clinically meaningful. I am updating my recommendation to Accept.
I strongly encourage the authors to incorporate the following in the camera-ready version:
The landmark-to-measurement assignment table as promised, ideally accompanied by a figure illustrating landmark positions and measurement geometry, with citations to the measurement protocol followed.
The training loss function — even a single sentence suffices.
The complete geometric descriptor list and dimensionality.
The inter-observer variability and landmark localization accuracy results, which were available but unreported and are essential for interpreting the method’s clinical significance.
The uniform averaging ablation result, which isolates the GNN’s contribution from ensembling.
These details would transform the paper from a promising method with insufficient specification to a strong, reproducible contribution.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The primary objective of this article is to obtain precise three-dimensional landmarks of the aortic valve in order to derive more accurate morphometric measurements. The study focuses on the development of a refinement mechanism based on graph neural networks (GNNs). This mechanism takes as input the anatomical landmarks detected using “conventional” methods (nnU-Net) and produces morphometric measurements of the subjects under study as output. The challenge arises from the fact that the nnU-Net framework produces a point cloud for each detected anatomical landmark rather than a single representative point. Consequently, an additional processing step is required to determine a unique and reliable landmark position from this point cloud. In this study, two strategies are investigated: (i) the point cloud is approximated by a sphere, and its center of mass (CoM) is taken as the landmark location from which morphometric measurements are derived (conventional approach); and (ii) the point cloud is directly introduce to a graph neural network (GNN), which infers the morphometric measurements without explicitly estimating a single landmark point (proposed approach).
reviews.text_strengths: Although the proposed methodology has been applied in other domains for extracting anatomical measurements, to the best of our knowledge, it has not previously been used to derive measurements related to the aortic valve. Additionally, the method has been trained and evaluated using three different cohorts from two independent institutions, which supports its robustness and generalizability.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The main limitation of the proposed approach, as acknowledged by the authors, is that it functions primarily as a refinement tool. Consequently, if the initial landmark detection results are highly inaccurate, the method cannot effectively correct them. Nevertheless, in practical terms, current landmark detection techniques are generally robust, and in cases of failure, it is reasonable to assume that inconsistent results would be readily identified by a specialist. Furthermore, the non-public nature of the datasets used in this study limits the ability to fully assess the generalizability and external validity of the proposed method.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Overall, this is a comprehensive and original study that presents promising results. However, from a reproducibility standpoint, neither the datasets nor the source code are made publicly available through platforms such as GitHub, which restricts independent validation and broader adoption of the method.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
It is clear that this article exhibits certain limitations in terms of technical detail and the reporting of results, as noted by several reviewers. Perhaps the most significant limitation is the absence of an ablation study that would explicitly demonstrate the contribution of GNNs to model performance.
Nevertheless, the manuscript presents a novel and well-motivated approach, whose primary strengths lie in its originality and potential clinical applicability. The idea of refining landmark-derived measurements using GNNs is conceptually appealing and potentially impactful, and the reported results provide some support for this premise. 
In summary, while a more comprehensive ablation study would strengthen the work, this limitation does not, in my view, substantially detract from its overall quality.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This work proposes a graph neural network (GNN)-based approach for automated morphometric analysis of the aortic valve. Landmark detection outputs are used to construct a graph where nodes represent measurements (with uncertainty modeled via multiple candidate points per landmark) and edges encode interdependencies between measurements. The method is evaluated on CT data from two institutions (including healthy and pathological cases), showing improved accuracy (15–25%) over measurements derived directly from automatically detected landmarks, using manual measurements as reference.
reviews.text_strengths:
Novelty: The work explores an original hypothesis by shifting the focus from landmark detection to the refinement of landmark-derived morphometric measurements using a GNN. This is relevant, as many pipelines directly compute measurements from detected landmarks without modeling anatomical constraints or interdependencies. The proposed approach explicitly incorporates these relationships, which is conceptually appealing and, according to the results, impactful. Given the prevalence of landmark-based pipelines in medical imaging, this idea may generalize to other clinical applications and be of broader interest to the community.
Mathematical formalism and illustration: The methodology is clearly described, well thought out, and mathematically well formulated. The authors are also commended for Fig. 1, which effectively illustrates the proposed pipeline and aids understanding.
Adequate experimental design: The evaluation is well designed, using CT data from two institutions with both healthy and pathological cases. Comparison against landmark-based measurements, using manual measurements as reference, is appropriate, and implementation details are sufficient to support reproducibility. A limitation is the absence of a dedicated generalization assessment, as data from both institutions appear to be used in both training and testing.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Limited interpretability: The approach lacks interpretability in the final measurements. Since the GNN aggregates multiple candidate landmark configurations, each measurement is derived from a weighted combination rather than a single consistent landmark set. Even in the theoretical case where a single configuration dominates, different measurements may rely on different candidates of the same anatomical landmark. This prevents identifying or visualizing the exact landmark positions underlying the results, limiting verification and reuse in downstream tasks. In practice, one would need to revert to the original landmark outputs (e.g., center-of-mass), despite their lower accuracy.
Lack of ablation study: The manuscript lacks analysis of key design choices in the GNN. The impact of the number of candidate points per landmark (Nᵢ), the number of candidate geometric descriptors per measurement (K), the contribution of specific feature groups in these descriptor vectors (e.g., is compactness relevant?), the embedding dimension (E), and other architectural components (e.g., edge weighting mechanism) is not analyzed. Such ablations would be important to assess the method’s robustness.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1) In the related work section, please clarify the distinction between the strategies described in the first and third groups. Both appear to rely on segmentation-based pipelines. Is the difference primarily related to the downstream task (morphometry vs. other applications), or is there a methodological distinction?
2) It is not explicit from the Introduction, (and to a minor extent the abstract) that the proposed method explicitly leverages detected landmarks and their associated uncertainty, rather than solely optimizing measurements based on anatomical relationships. This is a key aspect of the methodology (as it anchors the solution to the input image) and should be more clearly reflected in the contribution description. Its importance only becomes evident in the Methods section.
3) Contribution 3 appears to follow directly from Contribution 2 (i.e., the GNN formulation modeling landmark uncertainty and interdependencies), rather than constituting an independent contribution. Please clarify or reconsider this distinction.
4) Are there measurements that depend on more than three landmarks? An example descriptor is provided (anisotropy), but the wording (“can compute”) introduces ambiguity. Please clarify whether such cases are effectively used in the method.
5) Consider discussing the interpretability limitation (see above) in the discussion or limitations sections.
6) Please clarify the rationale for including the compactness feature. If C_f is a candidate set of landmarks for a given measurement f, the centroid is a physical location in the input volume. Why is compactness needed? If used as just another geometric descriptor, why was compactness chosen over alternatives?
7) Please provide further details about the dataset, particularly regarding the types of pathologies included in the cohorts.
8) Was nnU-Net trained using the default configuration (automated hyperparameter selection), with the only particularity being how the GT masks were created? If so, please state this explicitly for transparency and reproducibility.
9) Consider highlighting the best-performing method for each measurement in Table 1 (e.g., use bold font) to improve readability and emphasize the results.
Minor remarks:
Please proofread the manuscript for grammatical errors or unclear phrasing. A non-exhaustive list includes:
First sentence of Related Work: (p.2) the aortic root and valve are complex anatomies, not their 3D representation.
“key anatomical landmarks of the aortic, where” (p.2): a word appears to be missing.
“where architectures both CNN architectures” (p. 2): duplicated wording.
“Ket the key” should read “Let the key” (p.3)
“probability that are at least for distance d apart from the” (p.3): unclear phrasing.
Variable N is not defined in the landmark set notation, nor its relationship to index i.
Consider removing “with shared landmarks” from the initial edge definition (p.4). In practice, edges exist between all measurement pairs (as reflected in the square symmetric adjacency matrix), hence the need to define the zeroed connection strength where no actual shared landmarks exist.

The manuscript presents a novel and well-motivated approach, with strengths in its originality and the adequacy of its experimental design. The idea of refining landmark-derived measurements through a GNN framework is both conceptually interesting and potentially impactful, and the evaluation convincingly supports it. While the lack of an ablation study is a notable limitation, it does not detract from the overall validity of the work.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
I maintain my original accept recommendation. The manuscript presents a valid, interesting, and potentially impactful contribution, particularly given the originality of refining landmark-derived morphometric measurements through a GNN framework and its possible applicability to other landmark-based problems in medical imaging.
I further commend the authors for the additional methodological clarifications, particularly regarding the valve measurements, descriptors, and loss formulation. The inclusion of previously unreported landmark detection baseline performance and inter-/intra-observer variability analyses further strengthen and contextualize the results. Finally, although ablation and noise robustness studies cannot be added, the discussion provided increases confidence in the robustness and validity of the proposed approach.
reviews.text_ethics: The authors make use of private datasets (pages 5-6), but no explicit statement is provided regarding ethical approval or IRB compliance.

meta_reviews.text:
While reviewers agreed that the paper addresses a clinically relevant problem with a well-motivated, detailed graph-based GNN architecture and validation across multiple cohorts, they also raised serious concerns about the paper’s methodological clarity, evaluation rigor, and reproducibility: First, critical methodological details are missing, including undefined aortic valve measurements, unspecified geometric descriptors, and no stated training loss function, hindering reproducibility. Second, the evaluation is insufficient—baseline comparisons fail to isolate the GNN’s contribution, there is no inter-observer variability analysis for ground truth annotations, and no quantification of how landmark detection errors affect downstream measurements. Third, the paper contains text/referencing errors and uses non-public datasets, limiting external validity and trustworthiness.
Since the reviews are mixed, we would like to invite the authors to provide a rebuttal. In addition to clarify other concerns, please try to address the following points during rebuttal: provide more details about the aortic valve measurements and their landmark subsets, specify the full geometric descriptor set and training loss function; conduct an ablation to isolate the GNN’s contribution (vs. multi-candidate averaging), report inter-observer variability for annotations, and quantify how landmark detection noise impacts measurements; correct text/referencing errors and provide details to enhance external validity (e.g., dataset access or more cohort details).

Reviewers agreed that the paper addresses a clinically relevant problem with a well-motivated graph-based approach for refining aortic valve measurements, and that the method is comprehensively evaluated across multiple institutions, demonstrating potential robustness and generalizability. However, they also raised serious concerns about the paper’s technical completeness and scientific rigor: (1)​critical methodological details were missing or underspecified, including the measurement protocol linking landmarks to clinical metrics, the complete geometric descriptor set, and the training loss function; (2) the contribution of the GNN was not convincingly isolated, as the improvement could stem from multi-candidate ensembling rather than learned relational modeling, and no ablation with uniform averaging was provided; and (3)​the reliability of the reference standard was unclear, with no inter-observer variability analysis, no quantification of landmark localization accuracy, and limited discussion of clinical interpretability and robustness. The rebuttal has successfully addressed most concerns by supplying the missing specifications, reporting inter-observer variability and landmark detection performance, and clarifying the loss formulation and descriptor design. Since the review scores are all positive after rebuttal, I recommend accepting this manuscript.
Though with some limited novelty and short in ablation study, in general it is a quite interesting and novel study

The paper presents a clinically relevant and well motivated method for refining aortic valve morphometric measurements using graph-based modeling of landmark dependencies. The rebuttal addressed several important concerns, including measurement definitions, descriptor details, loss function, observer variability, landmark localization performance, and ethical approval. While the ablation analysis and external generalization remain limited, the contribution is sufficiently novel and the reported results support acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for providing valuable feedback. Several comments are pointing to new/additional experimental results, which are however not allowed in the rebuttal. Nevertheless, we indicate on our framework performance that will be considered in our eventual future work. We therefore focused on the following comments:
Measurement details (MR, R#2, R#6):
The evaluated morphometric measurements are computed from anatomically defined landmark subsets using deterministic geometric operations. Depending on the measurement, these operations include Euclidean distances, angles between vectors or plane normals, centroid-based angular calculations, and ellipse fitting using SVD and Powell optimization. We will provide a list of landmark-to-measurement assignment for each morphometric measurement in Table 1.
Geometric descriptors, loss function and compactness (MR, R#2, R#6):
Candidate descriptors consist of: 1) Euclidean distances between landmarks, 2) angular relationships encoded as cosine similarities, 3) PCA descriptors using the two largest eigenvalues, and 4) compactness as the mean distance of participating landmarks to their centroid (describes spatial dispersion and overall scale of landmark configuration, complementing pairwise distances with a rotation-invariant global descriptor). The model is trained using a standard MSE regression objective applied jointly across all predicted measurements (with no weighting of linear and angular measurements, auxiliary losses or softmax regularization terms).
Ablation study (MR, R#1, R#2, R#6):
We differentiated the contribution of graph-based weighting from candidate-based averaging, and evaluated a uniform averaging baseline using the same candidate sets and the same number of candidate combinations, but without GNN. Compared to CoM, the reduction in MAE was the greatest for GNN, whereas uniform averaging achieved smaller improvements, indicating that the observed gains are not solely explained by ensemble averaging, but additionally benefit from GNN. We acknowledge this experimental suggestion, and will consider it in our future work.
Observer variability (MR, R#1, R#2):
In terms of normalized MAE, the proposed GNN achieved an error of 2.5±0.9% for linear and 9.6±10.2% for angular measurements. For a subset of 25 cases, the inter-observer variability was 3.0±1.6% and 15.4±15.8%, while the intra-observer variability was 1.6±1.0% and 8.4±9.5%, respectively, confirming that the proposed framework operates within the inter-observer variability. Note that no new experiments were performed, as these results were already available but not reported.
Noise (MR, R#5):
We evaluated the effect of perturbations applied to candidate landmark coordinates using different Gaussian noise levels, and GNN showed substantially greater robustness compared to the CoM baseline. The relative advantage of GNN over CoM increased with noise, indicating that graph-based aggregation improves robustness by leveraging anatomical contextual information. We acknowledge this experimental suggestion, and will consider it in our future work.
Landmark localization (R#1, R#2, R#6):
This was performed by nnU-Net with the default configuration and automatic hyperparameter selection. The only task-specific modification was ground truth mask generation (spherical landmark-centered regions with a radius of 3.6 mm). Based on the predicted heatmaps, the landmark localization error was below 0.95 mm for 99.4% of landmarks (only two exceeded 3.6 mm). Note that no new experiments were performed, as these results were already available but not reported.
Code and Data (All):
We are evaluating the possibility of publicly releasing the source code. For data, we will allow sharing upon reasonable request. Ethical approval for data acquisition and usage exist and will be reported.
Text/referencing errors (MR, R#2, R#6):
Thank you, we will correct the typos and referencing errors.

title: Graph-of-Differences: Anatomy-Structured Difference Alignment for Medical Image Re-identification
abstract: Medical image re-identification (MedReID) supports longitudinal patient linkage but is prone to shortcut learning and often produces decisions that clinicians cannot interpret in terms of named anatomy. We propose Graph-of-Differences (GoD), a framework that grounds identity comparison in explicit anatomical structure. Each image is represented as an anatomy graph with nodes corresponding to named anatomical regions. For an image pair, soft node correspondence is established and differences are computed over matched regions. A graph-level difference alignment objective links these anatomy-matched differences to the global backbone difference, ensuring retrieval signals are anchored in homologous structures rather than arbitrary spatial tokens. Explanations are defined over named graph nodes and evaluated using node insertion and deletion tests, providing verifiable structure-level evidence instead of unstable pixel heatmaps. On internal benchmarks, GoD improves Rank-1 accuracy by +7.1 percentage points on fundus and +3.1 percentage points on chest X-ray over a strong frozen-backbone baseline, with additional gains in zero-shot external transfer demonstrating improved accuracy and generalization through anatomy grounding.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes Graph-of-Differences (GoD) for medical image re-identification. The method represents each image as an anatomy graph whose nodes correspond to named anatomical regions, establishes soft correspondence between nodes across image pairs, computes differences over matched anatomy, and aligns those graph-level differences with the global backbone difference. The model is built on top of a frozen MaMI encoder, with training limited to the graph encoder, fusion module, and projection head. The paper also proposes node-level explanations over anatomical structures and evaluates them using insertion/deletion-style faithfulness analysis. Experiments are reported on fundus and chest X-ray datasets in both internal and zero-shot external settings, with gains over the frozen-backbone baseline.
reviews.text_strengths:
This is a well-motivated paper on an important problem. In medical image re-identification, retrieval performance alone is not enough; it also matters whether the model’s decision can be related to anatomical structures that a human can inspect. The paper tackles that issue directly by enforcing comparison over named anatomy rather than unconstrained token-space differences. That is a sensible and potentially useful design choice. 
The technical story is coherent. The anatomy graph construction, soft correspondence, and difference-alignment objective fit together naturally. The ablation study is one of the strongest parts of the paper: simply adding a graph branch is not enough, while correspondence plus alignment produces the main gains. That makes the proposed mechanism more convincing. 
The explanation analysis is also better than what is often seen in similar papers. Rather than relying only on qualitative saliency maps, the paper includes node insertion/deletion-style faithfulness evaluation with confidence intervals. That gives some evidence that the highlighted nodes are actually used by the model. 
Finally, the external zero-shot results are encouraging. The fact that gains are still observed on CheXpert and Messidor-2 suggests that the method may be learning somewhat more stable anatomical cues rather than only dataset-specific shortcuts.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
My main concern is the paper’s positioning with respect to prior work. The key claim is that GoD improves on token-space comparison by enforcing anatomical correspondence, but the related-work discussion feels incomplete. In particular, there is a directly relevant prior paper, “Graph Feature Embeddings for Patient Re-Identification from Chest X-Ray Images” (SIBGRAPI 2024), which proposes a graph-based approach for chest X-ray patient re-identification. Even if the proposed formulation here is different, this prior work should be cited and discussed explicitly, since it is close in spirit and problem setting. Without that discussion, the novelty claim feels weaker than it should. 
A second issue is that the evaluation is somewhat narrow relative to the strength of the claims. The experiments compare mainly against a frozen-backbone baseline and internal ablations. That is a clean design for isolating the effect of the proposed graph-based alignment, and I do appreciate that. However, for a strong methodological paper, I would also want to see comparison against stronger practical baselines, especially end-to-end MedReID systems. This is particularly relevant because the backbone here is MaMI-based, and the original MaMI paper reports stronger results after end-to-end tuning. As written, the paper shows that GoD improves a controlled frozen baseline, but not yet that it is the strongest or most competitive approach overall. 
The paper’s interpretability claim is promising, but in my view slightly overstated. The node-level explanations are clearly more structured than generic pixel saliency maps, and the insertion/deletion analysis is a meaningful step beyond purely qualitative explanation. Still, “clinically auditable” is a strong claim. The paper does not include clinician studies, expert agreement, or any user-grounded evaluation showing that these explanations actually help humans verify or challenge model decisions. I would therefore frame this more cautiously as improved structure-level interpretability with preliminary faithfulness evidence. 
Another important limitation is parser dependence. The method relies on modality-specific anatomical parsing to build the graphs, but robustness to noisy or missing masks is not evaluated. Since the practical usefulness of the method depends directly on graph quality, this is not a minor omission. A simple robustness experiment with degraded or partial masks would have strengthened the paper considerably. 
There are also some presentation issues. The manuscript still contains unresolved cross-references such as “Table ??” and “Tables ??–??,” including in places that matter for the experimental section. This makes the submission feel unfinished. 
Finally, some of the external improvements, especially on fundus, are fairly small. I would have liked to see confidence intervals or significance testing for those results before drawing a strong conclusion about generalization.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
I think this paper has a genuinely interesting core idea, and the ablations are carefully designed. My main suggestion is to sharpen the novelty claim and make the validation story more complete. In particular, the paper would benefit from a clearer discussion of related graph-based MedReID work, comparison to a stronger end-to-end baseline, and at least one robustness experiment for imperfect anatomical parsing. I would also encourage the authors to tone down the “clinical auditability” claim slightly unless they can provide more direct human-centered evidence.

This paper presents a thoughtful and technically coherent idea: enforcing anatomical correspondence before computing cross-image differences is a sensible way to structure the MedReID problem, and the ablation study supports the importance of the proposed components. The explanation analysis is also stronger than average for this area. However, I do not think the current version makes a complete enough case for acceptance as a methodological contribution. The novelty position is weakened by incomplete engagement with closely related graph-based re-identification work, the empirical comparison is mainly against a frozen baseline rather than stronger practical baselines, parser robustness is not evaluated, and parts of the manuscript remain incomplete at the presentation level. Overall, I see this as a promising paper that would benefit from revision and a stronger validation story.

reviews.text_contribution:
The main contributions includes the following:
1.Anatomy-Structured Difference Alignment: A graph-level objective that establishes soft node correspondence across image pairs and aligns these structured differences with the global backbone signal.
2.Clinically Auditable Explanations: A shift from unstable pixel-level heatmaps to node-level attributions over named structures, which are quantitatively audited via node insertion and deletion tests.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Novel Methodology: The Graph-of-Differences framework introduces a structured way to ground identity comparisons in named anatomical regions rather than arbitrary spatial tokens. This directly addresses shortcut learning, where models rely on scanner artifacts rather than biology.
2.Verifiable Explainability: Unlike unstable pixel-level heatmaps, GoD provides node-level attributions over named structures. The authors quantitatively validate this using node insertion/deletion tests, proving that the attributed nodes are causally linked to the model’s decisions.
3.Strong Empirical Performance: The model demonstrates consistent improvements across multiple modalities. Specifically, it improves Rank-1 by +7.1 pp on fundus and +3.1 pp on CXR over a state-of-the-art frozen-backbone baseline.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Scope Limitations: Currently, the method is limited to 2D images. Extending this to 3D volumetric data (CT/MRI) would require significantly more complex graph correspondence and higher node counts, which the authors acknowledge as future work.
2.Dependency on Parsers: The framework relies heavily on modality-specific anatomical parsers (like CheXmask). Failure or inaccuracies in these masks can degrade the quality of the anatomy graph, which remains a bottleneck for deployment in new modalities.
3.Highly Technical: The paper presents a significant barrier to entry, as the core methodology is difficult to understand without high-level technical knowledge in both graph machine learning and medical imaging.

reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper addresses an important issue: lack of interpretability and shortcut learning in medical re-identification. To my perspective, using anatomy to guide comparison is intuitive and meaningful for clinical use.
2.The paper provides a more structured form of explainability by offering node-level explanations tied to specific anatomical regions. This makes the interpretations more meaningful and clinically relevant compared to traditional pixel-based heatmaps, which are often unstable. In addition, the authors include quantitative evaluation through insertion and deletion tests to support the faithfulness of these explanations.
4.The result demonstrates gains across multiple datasets and zero-shot settings and Includes ablation studies and explainability evaluation, supporting the effectiveness of the method.

For example: The experiments section says “All hyperparameters are reported in Table ??” and the explainability section refers to “Fig. 4, Tables ??–??.” There are also potential typo in the paper. For example: ““Interna(ODIR)l”. The author needs to get them fixed. Also, parts of the writing need further polishing to improve readability for a general audience. reviews.text_strengths: The paper has several clear strengths. (1) The motivation is well presented and easy to follow. The authors identify an important limitation of existing MedReID methods that identity matching may rely on shortcut features, while the resulting decisions are difficult to verify against named anatomical structures. The proposed solution is also logically connected to this motivation, moving from anatomy graphs to node correspondence, difference alignment, and node-level explanation. (2) The method is interesting and reasonably convincing. Rather than simply adding a stronger backbone or relying on post-hoc heatmaps, the paper introduces an anatomy-structured comparison mechanism, which makes the identity-matching process more interpretable. (3) The experiments are relatively complete. The evaluation covers both fundus and chest X-ray datasets, includes internal and external settings, and provides ablation studies. The insertion/deletion analysis is also useful because it gives quantitative support for the claimed node-level explanations.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The paper could be further improved in several aspects. (1) The clinical feasibility could be strengthened by including clinician evaluation or reader studies to verify whether the proposed node-level explanations are truly useful in practice. (2) The robustness of the method to anatomy parsers or segmentation quality could be further analyzed, as inaccurate masks or landmarks may affect graph construction and downstream performance. (3) The current evaluation is limited to 2D imaging (fundus and chest X-ray), and it would be valuable to explore the applicability of the framework to 3D modalities such as CT, MRI, or PET/CT. (4) The explanation validation could be further strengthened, as insertion/deletion tests, while useful, do not fully demonstrate that the model relies on clinically meaningful anatomical cues rather than dataset-specific correlations.
