meta_reviews.text:
This is promising and well-motivated work with a strong empirical element. All reviewers agree that the work addresses an important limitation in MedReID and appreciate the explainability contribution and relatively comprehensive experimental validation.
However, some concerns remain regarding dependence on parsers, robustness, baseline comparisons and interpretability claims. There are also some minor presentation issues to rectify.
If results exist, the fine-tuned model should be reported; otherwise, the authors must justify the frozen backbone. The authors should also demonstrate some evidence of robustness of the parser and review the claims of interpretability. It is also important to clarify the distinction from existing work.

This submission proposes a graph-based framework for anatomy-based re-identification, R3 and R5 liked the explainability approach. R2 and R4 has concerns on missing fine-tuned baselines, reproducibility details, and dependence on parser. R2 and R4 did not provide feedback on rebuttal. The rebuttal addressed most of the concerns (showing orthogonal performance from requested baselines). For all these reasons, and with respect to the other submissions, the recommendation is towards Acceptance.

The rebuttal directly addresses the key concerns by adding fine-tuned MaMI results, parser-robustness stress tests, external confidence intervals, reproducibility details, a clearer distinction from prior graph-based MedReID work, and a more cautious interpretability framing; therefore, despite remaining limitations on clinician validation and 3D extension, I support acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We thank reviewers for recognizing GoD’s motivation, the strong ablation (graph alone is inert; correspondence+alignment drive gains), the faithfulness audit, and zero-shot gains.
[R2.1] Prior graph-based MedReID. The SIBGRAPI 2024 paper “Graph Feature Embeddings for Patient Re-Identification from Chest X-Ray Images” uses graph features as a single-image embedding; it does not establish per-pair correspondence between named anatomy, compute differences over matched nodes, or provide faithfulness-audited node-level explanations. GoD’s novelty is the per-pair Graph-of-Differences—a structured difference objective enforcing identity comparison over homologous anatomy. We will cite and contrast in Sec.1.[R2.2 / R4.3] Fine-tuned baseline. The frozen backbone in Tab.2 isolated GoD’s contribution from MaMI tuning. We now also report end-to-end fine-tuned MaMI:
Method CXR R1 Fundus R1
Backbone frozen : 0.8659 / 0.6396
Backbone fine-tuned (MaMI) : 0.8841 / 0.6712
GoD (frozen backbone) : 0.9033 / 0.7111
GoD (fine-tuned backbone) : 0.9089 / 0.7253
GoD’s gain is orthogonal to backbone tuning: on fine-tuned MaMI it still adds +2.5 pp CXR/+5.4 pp fundus, and the best absolute result is GoD+fine-tuned.
[R2.3] Interpretability framing. We agree “clinically auditable” overstates current evidence. We will revise throughout to “structure-level interpretability with quantitative faithfulness evidence”—what insertion/deletion tests show — and note full auditability requires radiologist user studies (future work).
[R2.4/R3.2/R4.4/R5.2] Parser robustness. Soft correspondence (Eq.5) absorbs parser errors via row-softmax down-weighting mismatched/missing nodes. Stress test (CXR R1/Fundus R1):
Perturbation CXR Fundus
Clean (default) : 0.9033 / 0.7111
10% nodes dropped randomly : 0.8987 / 0.7044
30% nodes dropped : 0.8821 / 0.6852
50% nodes dropped : 0.8543 / 0.6517
5-px mask dilation : 0.8951 / 0.7038
10-px mask dilation : 0.8782 / 0.6859
No graph (frozen backbone) : 0.8659 / 0.6396
GoD stays above the no-graph baseline through 50% node dropout and 10-px mask noise. Added to Sec-4.[R2.5/R4.1] Presentation. We will fix unresolved cross-references (Table??), the “Interna(ODIR)l” typo, and define R@1 at first use.
[R2.6] External CIs. Messidor-2 external gain will carry bootstrap 95% CIs: GoD R1 = 0.6579 [0.6491,0.6664] vs. backbone 0.6499 [0.6398,0.6604].
[R4.2] Reproducibility. We will add: batch 64, BatchHard sampler, 224x224 input, ImageNet normalization, label smoothing 0.1, plus the external-eval protocol.
[R4.5] Per-node attribution propagation. Per-node delta_i are read from the graph branch where the alignment loss directly operates, so the insertion/deletion audit targets exactly the component the attributions describe—tight by construction. Propagating through the fused embedding z(x) requires learned credit assignment, which we defer rather than approximate: an approximate propagation would conflate graph-branch faithfulness with fusion gating and weaken the current guarantee.
[R4.6] Tab.2/Tab.3 inconsistency. 0.8659 (Tab.2) is a single seed; 0.8723+-0.0005 (Tab.3) is the three-seed mean. We will report the seed-averaged value in both.
[R3.1/R5.3] 3D extension. GoD transfers directly to 3D: replace 2D parsers with volumetric segmentors (TotalSegmentator) and the node encoder with a coord-aware GNN for denser graphs and 3D correspondence. We list this as immediate future work.
[R3.3] Accessibility. We will add a short intuition paragraph in Sec.2 introducing the graph-of-differences idea before the formal definitions.
[R5.1/R5.4] Reader study and explanation depth. Insertion/deletion tests establish faithfulness; clinician studies establish utility. A forced-choice reader study with collaborating clinicians (GoD node-level vs. pixel-saliency baselines on agreement and verification time) planned in post-camera-ready.

title: Group Equivariant Diffusion for Anomaly Detection in Computational Cytology
abstract:
Computational cytology on whole-slide images is challenging
because malignant cells are rare, heterogeneous, and annotated slides are scarce. Anomaly detection frameworks can be trained on normal slide-negative patches and then applied at test time to flag abnormal patches in held-out slides. Most unsupervised anomaly detection approaches including generative ones (GAN-based and diffusion-based), are tuned to organ-level imaging and require large curated datasets. In cytology the signal is cell-centric: rotating or flipping a single-cell patch does not change its diagnostic class, yet standard diffusion models treat transformed views as distinct inputs, leading to transformation-dependent reconstructions and unstable anomaly scores. We propose a D4-equivariant diffusion framework that enforces rotation and reflection symmetry both architecturally, via a D4-equivariant U-Net, and at inference, via equivariant noise coupling and (optionally) frame averaging. This alignment with biological invariance yields transformation-consistent pseudo-healthy reconstructions and more stable anomaly ranking under symmetry. On two publicly available cytology datasets of bone marrow and peripheral blood smears, our D4-equivariant diffusion models achieve higher AUC and retrieve more abnormal cells in the top K
predictions than non-equivariant generative baselines, a deep one-class, and a multiple instance learning based method, while substantially reducing score variance across rotations and flips. Code is available at https://swchmida.github.io/D4diffCyto/.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a diffusion-based anomaly detection framework for computational cytology that explicitly enforces equivariance for cell images. In particular, the method incorporates a D4-equivariant U-Net architecture, equivariant noise coupling and frame averaging. The author further provides both theoretical arguments and empirical evidence demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
reviews.text_strengths:
Strong logical grounding: The author provides theoretical guarantees in Section 2.3 to address potential concerns regarding the proposed framework. Specifically, they show that symmetrizing the denoiser does not increase the DDPM training risk, and that symmetry-respecting averaging preserves the false positive rate without degrading the detection trade-off.
Clarity and coherence: The paper clearly presents its core objective and maintains a focused narrative throughout. Most components of the proposed framework appear well-motivated (e. g. , the introduction of equivariant noise coupling to enforce symmetry in the diffusion process). The experimental results provide convincing empirical support for the claims. In addition, the inclusion of pseudo code (Algorithm 1) improves the reproducibility of the method.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The overall methodological novelty appears somewhat limited, as most components are adaptations of existing techniques. The main contribution lies primarily in their integration rather than the introduction of fundamentally new methodological ideas.
The theoretical guarantees rely on strong symmetry assumptions that may not strictly hold for real cytology data, where cell morphology and acquisition conditions are not perfectly D4-invariant.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Overall, the paper is well structured and clearly written. I particularly appreciated that many of the questions that arise while reading are addressed within the paper itself. One minor suggestion is that the framework illustration in Fig. 1 could be made more detailed, which would help readers better understand the overall pipeline at an early stage of the paper.

The proposed method presents a well-motivated problem and a corresponding solution that fits well within the MIC category. Specifically, the paper addresses the problem of enforcing equivariance in diffusion-based anomaly detection, which is an interesting and relevant direction. Although the solution may appear relatively simple, it is clearly formulated and well justified. Furthermore, the authors provide both solid theoretical explanations and extensive experimental results, which together strongly support the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Although I raised concerns regarding limited methodological novelty and the assumptions related to D4-invariance, I believe that the paper’s well-motivated problem definition and the academic value of the proposed framework outweigh these weakness.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a D4-equivariant diffusion framework for anomaly detection in computational cytology. Since in cytology the signal is cell-centric, standard diffusion models may produce transformation dependent reconstructions and unstable anomaly scores. To address this, the paper introduce a dihedral-equivariant diffusion framework that enforces D4 symmetry throughout partial-diffusion reconstruction via a U-Net denoiser with D4-equivariant architecture, together with inference time equivariant noise coupling (EN) and frame averaging (FA). Experiments on two public cytology datasets achieve higher AUC and retrieve more abnormal cells in the top K predictions.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The observation that diagnostic class should not change under rotations and flips for single-cell patches is reasonable, while standard generative detectors treat rotated views as distinct inputs, inducing orientation-dependent score variation. The paper is well motivated from a computational cytology perspective. 
2.The method is clearly presented and the algorithmic is easy to follow. 
3.The ablation study includes the comparison between FA-only, FA+EN, together with the reported reduction in anomaly-score variance across rotations and flips, which provides evidence that the proposed method improve transformation consistency.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The novelty is limited. Based on Section 2, the main components are U-Net denoiser with a D4-equivariant architecture [9,16], diffusion anomaly detection via partial reconstruction [22,35], and inference-time symmetry enforcement through equivariant noise coupling (EN) and frame averaging (FA) [22,35], all of them are individually known. Consequently, the proposed approach seems more like a combination of known components than a substantially new diffusion framework.
2.The experiment results are inconsistent across two datasets and often small against the strongest baselines, which weakens the central claim and raises concerns about the generalization of the proposed method.
The paper on Page 8 shows that the D4 model is statistically inconclusive on AML LMU. So the positive result is mainly on MLL. Does this suggest that the effectiveness of the method may depend on the specific dataset rather than reflecting a robust improvement? As a result, it remains unclear whether the proposed method generalizes reliably across different cytology dataset, or whether its effectiveness is sensitive to the underlying data distribution.
3.There are some inconsistent ablation study results across two datasets. Section 3.4 states FA-only slightly degrades AUC on MLL, while FA+EN improves it, why FA+EN performs worse than FA-only in terms of AUC on AML LMU? Besides, the D4 convolutional U-Net slightly outperforms the attention-augmented variant in MLL but not on AML LMU. This suggests that the performance gains may be sensitive to implementation details and dataset properties .
4.The theoretical section is supportive, but some claims are insufficiently justified and therefore not fully convincing. Section 2.3 gives intuitive statements about D_4 averaging can not increase DDPM risk and invariant detection under class-conditional symmetry, but no proof is provided in the paper. Besides, the analysis relies on strong symmetry assumptions that may not hold in real cytology patches.
5.The qualitative results in Figure 2 raise concerns about the practical localization ability of the method. The displayed MSE values are very small and the anomaly maps appear weak and poorly localized. This suggests that the method may be capturing patch-level differences without producing sufficiently clear or clinically meaningful pixel-level abnormality maps.
6.In section 2.1, the notation is somewhat inconsistent: x_0 is introduced as coming from the normal training distribution , but is also used to denote a test sample.
7.Some typos: in section 2.3, “Invariant detection under class-conditional symmetry:Let Y…”

reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The following issues remain material and prevent me from raising my score.
1.Generalization claim is not supported on AML-LMU. Reframing the endpoint as TP@K is reasonable, but the underlying fact is unchanged: on AML-LMU, as the authors themselves acknowledge, the results are “statistically inconclusive”, which suggests that the performance gains may be sensitive to implementation details and dataset properties. These results do not justify the claim of a robust, generalizable improvement.
2.Theoretical results remain unproven. The sketch that Jensen’s inequality applies to the group-averaged denoiser, and that the detection result follows from class-conditional label symmetry, is helpful as intuition, but the rebuttal does not actually contain the derivation. 
Combined with the limited methodological novelty, I do not intend to raise my score.

reviews.text_contribution:
This paper proposes a D4-equivariant diffusion framework for anomaly detection in computational cytology, targeting the key issue that cell-level morphology is invariant to rotations and reflections, while standard diffusion models are not.
The method introduces:
1.D4-equivariant U-Net architectures to enforce symmetry at the model level.
2.Equivariant Noise (EN) and Frame Averaging (FA) at inference to ensure transformation-consistent sampling trajectories.
3.A partial diffusion reconstruction framework (AnoDDPM-style) to compute anomaly scores.
Results show consistent improvements over multiple baselines, including diffusion and GAN-based anomaly detectors.
reviews.text_strengths:
The application of dihedral group equivariance (D4) to diffusion models specifically to address the biological invariance of single-cell cytology is well-motivated.
The authors evaluate the method using a highly realistic metric for budgeted clinical review workflows: the number of true positives in the top-K retrieved anomalous predictions (e.g., TP100/200/400).
Section 2.3 provides risk bound via Jensen’s inequality and justification of invariant scoring under group symmetry. This significantly strengthens the contribution beyond empirical work.
The study benchmarks against a wide array of relevant methods, including multiple instance learning (ItS2CLR), deep one-class models (Deep SVDD), and several generative detectors like f-AnoGAN, THOR, and BerDiff. AUC improves from 0.63 → 0.68, TP400 improves from 57 → 78 (large practical gain).
reviews.text_weaknesses:
While the performance gains on the MLL dataset are clinically and statistically significant, the improvements on the AML LMU dataset are statistically inconclusive. This limits the strength of the generalizability claims across different cytology modalities.
The ablation studies reveal that the $D_{4}$ convolutional U-Net without attention performs best on the MLL dataset, whereas the attention-augmented variant achieves the strongest performance on the AML LMU dataset. The paper lacks a deeper investigation or hypothesis regarding why this architectural discrepancy exists between the two datasets.
Only two cytology datasets, where both are similar modalities (single-cell patches). Missing whole-slide validation and cross-domain generalization
Assumes perfect D4 invariance, which may not fully hold for staining artifacts or slide preparation biases, Need analysis of symmetry violations.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

While the methodological novelty is somewhat incremental, the combination of theory, domain insight, and practical impact makes this work above the acceptance threshold.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
Two reviewers gave rather positive evaluations of the paper with high confidence. However, regarding the negtive evaluation and other mentioned issues, the authors should should meticulously address reviewers’ concerns. Especially, the concerns about the limited novelty, inconsistent data reported and insufficient justification. Other concerns about experiment result analysis are also needed to response.

Reviewers noted clear motivation and generally positive evaluations. The rebuttal addressed several clarifications and mitigated part of these issues. Overall, though several concerns remain, the rebuttal supports the final acceptance with two rather positive recommendation.

This work develops a method for anomaly detection in cytology images using a diffusion model. In particular, the approach develops a D_4 equivariant diffusion model to ensure that the quasi-normal reconstructions which are used for abnormality assessment do not change based on rotations by 90, 180, 270 degrees or flips.
The approach is tested on two different datasets with statistically significant improvements with respect to competing methods on one of the two datasets.
In general, the reviewers (and this meta reviewer) appreciated the goal of using this approach for more efficient screening of cytological abnormalities by experts and the combination of theory, domain insight, and practical utility.
While concerns were raised (and somewhat remained after the rebuttal) with respect to novelty and the statistically inconclusive results for one of the experimental datasets, the approach itself is sufficiently interesting in my opinion to be presented at MICCAI.
The rebuttal doesn’t fully address reviewers’ concerns.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and AC for recognizing the motivation of our work, its clear formulation, theoretical grounding, strong evaluation, top-K gains, and practical relevance.
A. Novelty (R2,R3,R4): Our contribution is the first systematic study of dihedral equivariance for diffusion-based unsupervised anomaly detection in cytology, with a unified algorithm treating architectural and inference-time equivariance as complementary routes to the same invariance property. This is a non-trivial adaptation to partial-diffusion anomaly scoring, where the goal is not generation/translation but stable top-K ranking under budgeted cytologist review. Prior cytology or diffusion-based medical anomaly-detection work has not enforced D4 structure or measured score variance under symmetry. We agree that equivariant convolutions, partial diffusion, and test-time averaging have precedents; our novelty lies in their task-specific integration and validation for cytology anomaly detection.
B. Statistical significance (R3,R4): Our primary clinical endpoint is budgeted top-K retrieval: reducing thousands of candidate cells to a few hundred suspicious patches for cytologist review. AUC summarizes global ranking, while TP@K measures this operational goal. On MLL, the gains are clear: FA+EN improves AnoDDPM from TP400/200/100 = 57/30/18 to 78/53/34, with significant AUC and TP400 gains (p<0.001 and p=0.006). On AML-LMU, the margin is statistically inconclusive (AUC p≈0.125, TP400 p≈0.275), but D4 variants still give the best or tied-best top-K results: TP400=325, TP200=162, TP100=86.Thus, AML-LMU shows favorable but not statistically conclusive gains, not a contradiction of the method.
C. Architectural ablation differences (R3,R4): Our claim is not that one D4 backbone is universally optimal, but that D4 structure improves transformation-consistent scoring. The attention variant mainly adds capacity/context modeling. Thus, D4-conv may suffice for MLL’s smaller 250x250 bone-marrow patches, while attention can help on AML-LMU’s larger 400x400 peripheral-blood patches with greater visual diversity. Both support the trend: D4-conv improves MLL over AnoDDPM (AUC/TP400 0.675/74 vs 0.633/57), and D4-conv+attn improves AML-LMU (0.720/325 vs 0.694/311). We clarify that attention is dataset-dependent, not the core contribution.
D. D4 assumptions and proof clarification (R2,R3,R4): We agree real cytology data are not perfectly D4-invariant due to staining/acquisition effects. Our assumption is instead class invariance: rotating/flipping a centered square single-cell patch should not change its normal/abnormal label. Sec. 2.3 is an idealized justification for symmetry-respecting scoring; the empirical question is whether this reduces orientation-induced score variation, which our D4 variants do while improving top-K retrieval. For R3, the DDPM-risk result follows from Jensen’s inequality applied to the group-averaged denoiser, and the detection result from class-conditional label symmetry. We will clarify the assumption in the proof sketch.
E. Qualitative anomaly maps (R3): Fig. 2 is only a qualitative visualization; the method and metrics use scalar patch-level anomaly scores. Unlike MRI, OCT or X-ray lesions, cytology abnormalities are often not sharply localized, but expressed through nuclear size/shape, chromatin texture, nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, cytoplasm, staining, and overall atypia. Thus, maps show reconstruction-deviation patterns within suspicious cells, not pixel-level segmentation. Since our goal is to reduce thousands of patches to a few hundred for cytologist review, patch-level top-K retrieval is the endpoint. We have revised the caption accordingly.
We will address other comments (x0 notation, Sec. 2.3 typos, Fig. 1/2 captions). For R4’s whole-slide/cross-domain point, we agree this is important future work; this study focuses on controlled single-cell patch evaluation for rare-cell retrieval before slide-level deployment.

title: Group-Conditioned Representation Modulation for Fair Skin Disease Diagnosis
abstract: Training models on heterogeneous medical data often results in performance disparities across demographic groups. In skin disease diagnosis, these disparities are particularly challenging since sensitive attributes can correlate with clinically relevant factors, making traditional suppression-based fairness interventions potentially harmful to diagnostic accuracy. This limitation motivates us to revisit this problem through a multi-objective optimization perspective, where each group defines a performance objective within a shared backbone. When aggregate performance is optimized under shared parameterization, the learned representations may under-express group-specific characteristics due to shared capacity allocation. To mitigate such effect, we propose a group-specific interference masking framework that enables conditional parameter utilization without altering the backbone architecture. The method identifies representation components that lack stable alignment with a given group and selectively modulates them without introducing additional trainable parameters. Experiment results demonstrate that the proposed approach consistently reduces inter-group performance gaps while maintaining competitive overall accuracy. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/GIM-FAC9/.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of this article is the introduction of a multi-objective optimization perspective on fairness in skin disease diagnosis, diverging from traditional methods that suppress sensitive attributes which often contain clinically crucial diagnostic signals. The authors propose Group-specific Interference Masking, a framework that addresses the suboptimal representation of under-expressed demographic groups caused by shared capacity allocation in standard joint training
reviews.text_strengths: The major strength is Group-specific Interference Masking (GIM). GIM calculates a group-specificity score to identify and selectively mask convolutional channels that lack stable alignment with a given demographic group during fine-tuning. This method is highly parameter-efficient, as it operates entirely on a pretrained backbone, keeps all weights shared across groups, and introduces absolutely no additional trainable parameters or inference overhead. Through comprehensive experiments on the Fitzpatrick-17k and ISIC 2019 datasets, the authors demonstrate that GIM successfully reduces inter-group performance disparities while maintaining highly competitive overall diagnostic accuracy, thereby achieving a significantly improved accuracy-fairness trade-off compared to existing bias-mitigation baselines
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The core concept of conditional representation modulation via channel masking is not a groundbreaking paradigm shift. The authors themselves compare their work to existing baselines like SCP, which also performs channel pruning to remove disparity inducing channels, and FairPrune, which prunes parameters whose importance differs across groups. The primary technical novelty here is limited to the specific calculation of a “group-specificity score” using prototype cosine similarity
to generate the binary masks. The framework’s experimental validation is entirely restricted to VGG-11 and ResNet-18, so evaluating a new computer vision mechanism exclusively on older, low-capacity models is a major limitation for a top-tier modern conference. The method exhibits severe sensitivity to the mask ratio (r). The methodology is formulated and tested strictly around binary demographic groups (g∈{0,1}). To achieve this, the authors artificially binarize complex variables, compressing the Fitzpatrick 17k dataset into just “light skin” (types 1-3) and “dark skin” (types 4-6), and limiting the ISIC 2019 dataset to binary sex
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

While the proposed GIM framework presents a parameter efficient approach to addressing shared capacity allocation in fair skin disease diagnosis, its contributions are ultimately too incremental. The core mechanism of channel masking heavily overlaps with existing baselines like SCP and FairPrune
, with the primary technical novelty restricted to the prototype cosine-similarity scoring. Furthermore, the experimental validation is severely limited by modern standards, as the authors rely exclusively on outdated, low-capacity architectures like VGG-11 and ResNet-18, leaving the method’s scalability to contemporary models unproven. The framework also demonstrates extreme hyperparameter brittleness, achieving its optimal accuracy-fairness balance at a very narrow mask ratio of r=2% before predictive performance begins to degrade at just r=4%. Finally, the evaluation oversimplifies complex demographic variables into binary attributes and completely lacks an intersectional fairness analysis, which undermines its practical clinical relevance and the authors’ unsupported claims of multi-group extensibility
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The main contribution of this paper is the introduction of Group-specific Interference Masking (GIM), a novel framework designed to reduce performance disparities in skin disease diagnosis across demographic groups without sacrificing overall diagnostic accuracy.
The core components of this contribution include:
A Multi-Objective Optimization Perspective: The authors shift away from traditional “suppression-based” fairness interventions, which often attempt to hide sensitive attributes like skin type. Instead, they reframe fairness as a multi-objective optimization problem where each demographic group represents a distinct performance objective within a shared model backbone.
Group-specific Interference Masking (GIM): This framework enables conditional parameter utilization. It identifies specific convolutional channels that lack stable alignment with a particular demographic group and selectively suppresses them using binary masks during fine-tuning.
Channel Utility Scoring: The paper proposes a method to quantify “group-conditional utility” for individual channels by calculating group-specificity scores. These scores determine which channels are consistently useful for a group and which ones create representational interference.
High Parameter Efficiency: A significant technical contribution is that GIM achieves group-conditioned adaptation without altering the backbone architecture or introducing any additional trainable parameters. The intervention operates entirely through fixed binary masks applied to activations and gradients.
Empirical Validation on Clinical Benchmarks: The authors demonstrate that their approach consistently reduces inter-group performance gaps on the Fitzpatrick-17k and ISIC 2019 datasets. Notably, the method maintains competitive overall accuracy and provides the most substantial benefits to groups that originally exhibited the lowest baseline performance
reviews.text_strengths:
The major strengths of the paper “Group-Conditioned Representation Modulation for Fair Skin Disease Diagnosis” include its innovative framing of fairness, its parameter-efficient technical approach, and its strong empirical results that prioritize clinical accuracy.
1.Novel Problem Formulation: Fairness as Multi-Objective Optimization
A core strength is the authors’ departure from traditional fairness methods that aim to suppress sensitive attributes. They argue that in dermatology, attributes like skin type are clinically relevant because they encode vital diagnostic signals, such as UV susceptibility. Instead of “attribute blindness,” they frame fairness as a multi-objective optimization problem where each demographic group is a separate performance objective within a shared backbone. This allows the model to capture group-specific characteristics rather than forcing a “compromise representation” that may degrade performance for all.
2.Original Technical Framework: Group-specific Interference Masking (GIM)
The GIM framework introduces a highly original way to manage model capacity without altering the underlying architecture.
Channel Utility Scoring: The authors developed a method to identify which convolutional channels provide stable, group-aligned behavior. By calculating group-specificity scores based on prototypes, they can quantify a channel’s utility for a specific demographic.
Conditional Modulation: Rather than removing channels globally, GIM uses these scores to create binary masks that selectively suppress low-utility channels for a given group during fine-tuning. This enables group-conditioned expressiveness while allowing groups to still share high-utility parameters.
3.Exceptional Parameter Efficiency
A significant practical strength is that the method requires no additional trainable parameters and does not change the backbone architecture. The entire intervention operates through fixed binary masks applied to intermediate activations and gradients. This makes it a lightweight and “practical direction” for improving fairness in existing clinical models with fixed capacity.
4.Strong Demonstration of Clinical Feasibility
The paper directly addresses “the cost of fairness”—the tendency for fairness interventions to reduce overall diagnostic accuracy.
Maintaining Accuracy: Experimental results on the Fitzpatrick-17k and ISIC 2019 datasets show that GIM consistently reduces inter-group performance gaps while maintaining or even improving competitive overall accuracy.
Targeted Improvement: The method is particularly effective for groups that originally showed lower baseline accuracy, suggesting it successfully helps those groups better express their statistical structures.
5.Rigorous Evaluation and Insightful Ablations
The work is supported by a comprehensive evaluation against numerous state-of-the-art baselines (e.g., FairPrune, SCP, HSIC) and uses robust metrics like Equal Opportunity (EOpp), Equalized Odds (EOdds), and the FATE score to measure the accuracy-fairness trade-off. Furthermore, their ablation studies provide deep insight into the mechanism:
Mask Ratio: They demonstrated a clear trade-off where a small degree of masking (e.g., 2%) optimizes both accuracy and fairness.
Swap Masking: By showing that applying one group’s mask to another leads to performance degradation, they provide empirical evidence that the learned masks truly encode group-dependent information rather than arbitrary channel selections.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
While the paper presents a novel and efficient approach to fairness in skin disease diagnosis, several weaknesses or limitations can be identified from the sources:
Sensitivity to the Mask Ratio Hyperparameter: The effectiveness of the GIM framework is highly dependent on the selection of the mask ratio (r). The authors acknowledge a clear trade-off where a small amount of masking improves fairness and accuracy, but “excessive masking can restrict shared representational capacity and reduce overall accuracy”. This requires careful manual selection using validation data for each specific task.
Primary Focus on Binary Groupings: Although the authors state that their formulation is extensible to multi-group settings, the methodology and all reported experiments focus exclusively on binary cases (e.g., light vs. dark skin, male vs. female). The performance and complexity of the method in more granular, multi-group demographic scenarios are not demonstrated.
Heuristic Selection of Target Layers: The method applies modulation at specific points, such as the “final convolutional layer” for VGG-11 or the “layer4 block” for ResNet-18.The paper does not provide a generalized rule for selecting these layers across different or more modern architectures, suggesting the selection may be heuristic or require trial and error.
Dependency on the Initial Backbone: The channel utility scores are calculated based on a frozen pretrained model. This implies that if the initial model is severely biased or has failed to learn relevant features for a specific group during pretraining, the resulting prototypes and masks may be suboptimal.
Limited Diversity in Evaluation: The empirical validation is restricted to two datasets (Fitzpatrick-17k and ISIC 2019) and uses relatively older backbones like VGG-11 and ResNet-18.It is unclear how the method translates to more complex architectures (e.g., Transformers) or a wider variety of medical imaging tasks.
Fixed Model Capacity Constraints: The framework is intentionally designed for fixed model capacity. While this is a strength for efficiency, it could be a limitation in cases where a model lacks the fundamental representational power to handle diverse demographic groups, where adding parameters might be necessary for a truly fair solution.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Key Strengths
Novel Conceptual Framing
Original and Efficient Methodology:
The Group-specific Interference Masking (GIM) high parameter efficiency
Superior Empirical Performance
High Reproducibility
Overall, the paper provides a compelling and innovative approach to fairness that is particularly well-suited for the unique constraints of dermatological diagnosis. It is a high-quality contribution that should be accepted.
