meta_reviews.text:
All three reviewers acknowledged that this paper does have merits. It proposes an interested and well justified idea. The experimental designs are also reasonable and, in principle, support the proposed idea. The paper is well written.
However, the reviewers also raised some major concerns.
All three reviewers consider the current evaluation is not sufficient to demonstrate the clinical effectiveness and usefulness of the proposed model. Some reviewers argued that while the idea is interesting, the methodological novelty is somehow limited. The reviewers also suggested comparisons with some recently proposed/released models. Many implementation and experiment details should be further clarified.
In the rebuttal, please carefully study the comments raised by the reviewers, and provide responses to them particularly to the major concerns mentioned above.

After rebuttal, all reviewers suggest accepting this paper. Please further revise the manuscript bases on the comments in the final version.

The paper presents a well-motivated and novel approach for pathology report generation by modeling the inherent local-to-global hierarchy of whole slide images within a hyperbolic Lorentz space. In their rebuttal, the authors successfully resolved the reviewers’ primary concerns by detailing the text decomposition pipeline and providing clinically meaningful evaluation metrics, such as diagnostic accuracy and factual completeness. Because all three reviewers found these additions compelling and upgraded their final opinions to “Accept,” the paper is recommended for the conference.

The reviewers appreciate the novelty of incorporating hyperbolic geometry for hierarchical modeling in pathology report generation and acknowledge the coherent framework. However, key concerns include the incremental nature of the technical contribution, limited evaluation scope, insufficient demonstration of clinical reliability, and missing methodological details. Based on the authors’ rebuttal addressing these issues satisfactorily, the general consensus is to recommend acceptance, with suggestions for further strengthening the clinical significance in the final version.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their insightful comments, and especially the positive recognition of our motivation (noted as ‘clear and well justified’).
[Report Decomposition (R1,R2,R3)]
Reports are decomposed using a “low-level priority” regex matching principle designed by our pathologists: individual sentences are categorized via lexicons (Global: diagnosis/carcinoma/stage/grade/subtype/conclusion/overall/status/malignant/benign; Region: size/diameter/infiltration/invasion/margin/boundary/multifocal/location/gross finding/lymphovascular invasion; Local: atypia/differentiation/mitosis/necrosis/calcification/stroma/pleomorphism/papilloma/proliferative/in situ), with unmatched sentences defaulting to Global. Empty levels are backfilled with the full report. During training, the supervision of the Global level is nested, encompassing both the global report and all sub-level reports.This design ensures semantic consistency, preventing error propagation even if minor matching deviations occur.
The following comparison (TCGA-B6-A0IP) validates our approach: unlike Bi-Gen, which misidentifies cancer type and size, our method ensures an accurate Global diagnosis while precisely capturing Region (size) and Local (morphology) details.
GT (Decomposed): [Global] The pathological diagnosis is infiltrating carcinoma, lobular type… [Region] The gross examination revealed a 1.7 cm tumor with no lymphatic/vascular invasion. [Local] The non-neoplastic breast tissue showed proliferative fibrocystic changes.
Ours: [Global] The findings are consistent with invasive lobular carcinoma of the breast… [Region] Gross examination identifies a 1.7 cm solitary lesion; no macroscopic evidence of multifocality. [Local] The presence of intraductal papilloma and fibrocystic changes.
Bi-Gen: The pathological slide indicates that the patient underwent a modified radical mastectomy on the right breast. The mass was found to be a poorly differentiated invasive ductal carcinoma with a tumor size of 2.0 cm.
[Evaluation Metrics (R1,R2,R3)]
We report BLEU and METEOR to maintain consistency with prior MICCAI works like HistGen. To address medical validation requirements, we provide the following supplementary evaluations:
Diagnostic Accuracy: Subtype identification accuracy on the BRCA dataset reached 0.613, significantly outperforming Bi-Gen (0.525).
Clinical Semantics: Our model achieved a $Fact_{ent}$ score [1] of 0.483, surpassing Bi-Gen (0.479) and MI-Gen (0.467). Furthermore, balanced scores across the Local (0.535), Region (0.510), and Global (0.483) levels confirm the model’s diagnostic reliability across all granularities.
[About Novelty (R1)]
1.We emphasize that this work is the first to introduce hyperbolic geometry to pathology report generation. WSIs and reports naturally possess hierarchical structures; leveraging this hierarchy effectively mitigates logical inconsistencies during report generation. Accordingly, we utilize Hyperbolic Space to unify both modalities.
2.The radial position constraint explicitly regulates the hierarchical mapping by embedding global features near the hyperbolic origin while pushing local details toward the boundary. 
3.Unlike traditional single-modality hierarchical WSI modeling, we propose a cross-modal hierarchical framework. By using a Memory Bank to fuse historical semantic priors with current visual features, our model simulates a pathologist’s global-to-local reasoning, ensuring strict logical consistency across diagnostic granularities.
[Other questions (R1)]
Implementation Details: Image embedding dimension is 1024, text is 512, and initial curvature $\kappa = 1.5$. Weights for $L_{ent}$ and $L_{pos}$ are set to 0.1.Code will be open-sourced.
References: The duplicate citations resulted from different BibTeX sources(GitHub vs. Google Scholar) and will be corrected in the revised version.
[1] Improving factual completeness and consistency of image-to-text radiology report generation.

title: HadBalance: A Plug-and-Play Unified Global Geometric Prior Framework for Generalizable Biomedical Segmentation
abstract:
Precise biomedical image segmentation is crucial for clini-
cal diagnosis. Geometric cues (e.g., boundary, shape, and topology) can improve structural consistency, yet most are task-specific and lack a unified geometric foundation that generalizes across organs and modalities. We are motivated by the observation that many medical segmentation targets exhibit globally near-convex shapes. A convex region is one in which any two interior points can be connected by a line segment entirely contained within the region. In practice, medical targets may exhibit small local concavities or boundary irregularities; we refer to such globally convex-like shapes as near-convex. Motivated by this, we derive Hadwiger Shape Priors from Hadwiger’s theorem as an interpretable global regularizer using three 2D measures: area A, perimeter P , and Euler characteristic χ, enabling transfer across organs and modalities. However, because medical datasets are shape-heterogeneous, enforcing near-convex priors uniformly can over-regularize non-convex anatomy (with significant concavities), washing out concavities and fine
details and degrading segmentation accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose Conflict-Aware Objective Balancing (CAOB), which integrates shape priors with segmentation in a gradient-aware manner. For each prior, CAOB removes only the gradient component that conflicts with segmentation while preserving the remaining aligned component, and adaptively regulates objective influences to prevent prior dominance. This enables stable use of shape priors on shape-heterogeneous data without erasing genuine concavities or fine structural details. We call this plug-and-play framework HadBalance.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Algorithmic Fairness / Safety / Regulation

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces a Hadwiger-based prior for training segmentation models in medical imaging. Based on the observation that most anatomical structures are approximately convex, the authors use geometric properties (area, perimeter, and Euler characteristic) which, according to Hadwiger’s theorem, characterize convex bodies. To prevent the prior from over-regularizing the model during training, they propose a COAB module. This module suppresses gradients from the prior when they conflict with the segmentation loss, ensuring that the prior does not dominate the learning process.
reviews.text_strengths:
The manuscript is generally well-structured and clearly written. It provides a detailed explanation of the Hadwiger prior and the underlying theorem, making the work accessible and understandable for readers
The proposed method is well-formalized and presented in a way that is straightforward for the reader to follow
The use of real-world datasets, although limited to three, is a positive aspect, as it allows readers to evaluate the applicability of the method in practical scenarios
The authors have made the source code publicly available. While the training and inference scripts are not included, the provided code still enables readers to implement the method with minimal effort
The figures are carefully curated and, when viewed on a PC with the ability to zoom, are clear and easy to interpret
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Major weaknesses:
The authors state that they “observe that most medical segmentation targets are globally near-convex”. I think this is a very strong claim which is not supported by any evidence in the paper. It is also informal, how is it measured or quantified in this context? It is also unclear which types of medical structures were considered when making this statement. Even if it was an assumption, this is quite strong and should be better justified, either through empirical analysis or references to prior work
The authors said in the manuscript “Incorporating geometric cues [. . . ] is a common way to improve structural consistency; however geometric priors are largely task-specific [. . . ] and lack a unified foundation that generalizes across most organs and modalities and supports transferable geometric constraints”; the term “foundation” in this sentence feels somewhat vague and could be replaced with a more precise description of what is lacking. Also, the statement appears to frame task-specific geometric priors as a limitation due to their lack of generalizability, but, in medical imaging it is often both reasonable and expected for priors to be tailored to specific anatomical structures, as different organs exhibit distinct shapes and variability. The sentence needs to be rephrased for clarity and precision
The AGB module, as much as it is well formalised and if I understood correctly, computes alpha(t) for each optimisation step, using the non-linear least-squares solver from scipy. This introduces a number of significant practical issues that are not discussed anywhere in the paper (except for a brief two word mention in the conclusion). First of all, the complexity of the scipy solver scales with the number of network parameters at least linearly, and more importantly it is embedded within another optimization process, so it adds a lot of computational overhead. Moreover, scipy does not support GPU computation; therefore, if the authors indeed used the scipy solver, it implies that either data must be transferred between GPU and CPU during each optimization step or the model training is being done on CPU, both of which are highly inefficient. The drawback of the training time is not discussed, and comparison of training costs are not reported in the experiment and result section
The authors do not compare their method with other state-of-the-art approaches on each dataset. As a result, it is not possible to assess whether their work achieves comparable performance to existing methods on the datasets they use
Standard deviations and COnfidence intervals are missing in every table of quantitative results. Given also the fact that train/validation/test set sizes are not reported, it is difficult to assess whether their method provide statistically significant results from the other methods, given that performance differences are very low for the most part (e. g. 86,19 vs 86,35)
In the conclusions, the authors state: “In this paper, we observe that many medical segmentation targets exhibit globally near-convex geometry”. This claim is too strong and not supported by the evidence presented. The manuscript only includes a few examples from three medical targets, which is insufficient to generalize broadly. Additionally, the statement is informal and should be either supported with empirical analysis, clarified as an assumption, or softened to reflect the limited scope of the evidence
Minor weaknesses:
The images in the manuscript are quite small, making it difficult for readers, especially in printed format, to distinguish details such as text and formulas.
In the introduction, where the authors outline their key contributions, colons are overused: “Our key contributions are as follows: 1: [. . . ]”. I recommend using a closing parenthesis after the item number instead, like “1) […]”, to improve readability
The datasets used in the experiments are barely described, consisting of just a three-sentence paragraph with only citations. There is no discussion of what the datasets contain, the number of observations, or how the data were collected
In the experimental setting, the authors train several backbones, they measure their performance, and perform a new training from scratch using the strongest backbone with their COAB module (for each dataset). While this comparison between backbone A + COAB versus backbone A alone is reasonable, it is unclear why only the strongest backbone was selected for this experiment. The manuscript does not provide any justification for this choice, why not add COAB to all the backbones for a more complete comparison?
DRIONS-DB dataset is missing in the ablation study, with no justification in the text; also the Module / Loss columns are repeated in the table
“HadBalance outperforms NASH and Fairgrad” is very strong, given the fact that only in few comparisons there is a clear separation between the methods (3 out of 9). The claim needs to be softened
The authors perform a comparison of their method against two gradient-optimisation methods (NASH and FairGrad), however they do not explain in a few words what they are and how they operate, for more clarity they should be explained briefly

N/A

The manuscript does not include comparisons with state-of-the-art methods on the datasets used, making it difficult to assess the relative performance of the proposed approach. Additionally, the quantitative results lack standard deviations or confidence intervals, and the reported differences in performance are very small, which limits confidence in the findings. The manuscript also does not discuss any limitations of the study,

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a plug-and-play biomedical segmentation framework called HadBalance, which employs a unified global geometric prior and conflict-aware optimization algorithm. It introduces Hadwiger shape priors for near-convex shape regularization and designs the CAOB algorithm to adaptively resolve gradient conflicts. Experimental results show that the framework achieves consistent performance improvements across different organs and modalities.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.This method uses area, perimeter, and Euler characteristic as a theoretically sound, interpretable, and transferable global shape prior for medical segmentation. Unlike task-specific geometric constraints, this prior generalizes to different organs and modalities, representing a significant conceptual advancement.
2.This method addresses a key practical problem: shape priors often over-regularize non-convex anatomy. CAOB automatically removes conflicting gradient components (PGPs) and adaptively balances the loss (AGB) without requiring manual weight adjustments, making it stable and easily integrated into existing models.
3.The framework was validated on three different datasets (carotid artery, polyp, optic disc) using six mainstream backbone networks. Its performance outperforms strong baselines including nnUNet, TransUNet, and state-of-the-art multi-task optimizers (Nash-MTL, FairGrad), particularly showing consistent gains in boundary accuracy.
4.HadBalance is model-agnostic and can be directly integrated into existing segmentation pipelines, demonstrating strong clinical and engineering potential.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.CAOB requires separate backpropagation for each loss term, which increases training time and GPU memory usage compared to standard single backpropagation methods. This paper does not provide efficiency analysis or optimization strategies.
2.Experiments were conducted only on three near-convex-dominated 2D datasets. Its performance on highly non-convex organs (e.g., liver, lung, heart) and 3D volume data has not been tested, limiting its generalization potential.
3.This paper does not compare with state-of-the-art learnable shape priors or topology-aware segmentation methods, making it difficult to determine the relative advantages of Hadwiger constraint-based methods.
4.Convergence of fixed-point iteration in AGB is not analyzed. Stability and sensitivity to hyperparameters (e.g., pooling size, ρ) have not been thoroughly discussed.

N/A

This paper proposes a novel and effective segmentation framework, which is well-motivated and yields significant experimental results. However, the framework has limitations in terms of computational cost, validation scope, and theoretical analysis. Despite its solid core idea and well-functioning method, I recommend a weak acceptance.

meta_reviews.text:
The idea is not completely obvious, and the theoretical foundation is interesting, but whether it will have real impact in medical AI is still unclear because the evidence is limited. The three reviewers gave recommendations of reject, accept, and weak accept; I’d like the authors to partake in rebuttal (issues: the near convex assumption, the missing benchmarks, the efficiency analysis, etc.).

Despite a split from reviewers, I recommend acceptance. I think the CAOB mechanism addresses the practical over-regularization problem in a mathematically sound way. The rebuttal adequately resolved the two sharpest concerns: the near-convex assumption was conceded and softened with prior-work support, and the SciPy efficiency objection was clarified. Missing benchmarks against architecture-level shape-prior methods and modest performance margins remain a limitation, but are defensible given the plug-and-play framing and the meaningful boundary-level predictions. I encourage authors to amend their camera-ready with proper discussions.

I recommend rejection. The paper addresses an interesting direction—using global geometric priors for biomedical segmentation—but the current submission does not sufficiently support its claims of being unified, generalizable, and plug-and-play.
The main concern is that the core assumption, namely that many biomedical targets are globally near-convex, is not rigorously justified. The connection between Hadwiger’s theorem and the proposed practical losses is also overstated: area, perimeter, and Euler characteristic do not uniquely encode near-convexity and may be inadequate for complex or highly non-convex anatomy.
The methodological novelty is limited. The proposed regularizers resemble existing shape/topology losses, and the conflict-aware optimization component is not clearly distinguished from prior multi-objective gradient-balancing methods. The derivation and practical stability of the adaptive weighting strategy are also insufficiently analyzed.
The experiments are too narrow for the paper’s broad claims. Evaluation is limited to three relatively small 2D datasets, with no strong evidence on more challenging non-convex, thin-structure, multi-component, 3D, or cross-domain settings. The reported gains are mostly modest, and statistical validation, runtime analysis, and stronger comparisons to recent shape/topology-aware segmentation methods are missing.
After reviewing the authors’ rebuttal and the post-rebuttal recommendations from reviewers, I recommend Accept. The rebuttal effectively addresses the key concerns.

author_feedback_text: We thank the reviewers and ACs. Responses are as follows (R: Reviewer, Q: Question): The near-convex assumption: We agree that “most medical segmentation targets are globally near-convex” was too strong; our intent was to use near-convexity as a qualitative motivation, not to make a universal empirical claim over all medical structures. We will revise “most” to “many”, soften “we observe that”, and add convex/star-convex prior references (Liu et al., 2020; Liu et al., JMIV 2025; Royer et al., CVPR 2016; StarDist, MICCAI 2018) with examples such as optic disc, nuclei, and cardiac structures. HadBalance does not pre-classify samples as near-/non-convex; instead, it applies A/P/χ priors to all samples and uses CAOB to suppress conflicting prior-gradient components when these priors would over-regularize genuine non-convex structures [R1Q1Q5, R2Q3]. The missing benchmarks: Dataset-specific SOTA methods such as Polyp-PVT (Dong et al., 2023) and Meng et al. (MICCAI 2022) are useful per-dataset baselines, but our experiments test HadBalance as a plug-and-play global geometric-prior framework rather than a separately tuned SOTA pipeline for each dataset [R1Q4]. Shape-prior methods such as You et al. (TMI 2025) and Song et al. (IJCAI 2024) introduce architecture-level modules/statistical shape models, so a direct comparison would mix architectural and training effects with our Hadwiger-prior and CAOB contributions. Topology-aware methods such as Hu et al. (NeurIPS 2019) and Li et al. (TMI 2025) mainly target topology preservation for topology-critical structures, such as vessels, and address a different objective from our work [R4Q3]. For [R1Q9], we selected the strongest backbone on each dataset as a stricter setting to test whether HadBalance can further improve an already strong baseline. The efficiency analysis: CAOB follows the per-objective-gradient paradigm: separate gradients are needed to estimate conflicts and balance objectives. The A/P/χ regularizers are lightweight pooling/convolution/gradient-magnitude operations; the main overhead is multiple backward passes, which is shared by methods such as FairGrad and Nash-MTL. The SciPy solver is not applied to the full gradients or network parameters. After per-objective gradients, we compute pairwise inner products on GPU to form a small K×K Gram matrix (K=4), and SciPy only solves the resulting 4-dimensional α problem. Thus, the CPU transfer is limited to this small Gram matrix, not full gradients or parameters, and training remains GPU-based [R1Q3, R2Q4, R4Q1Q4]. Regarding convergence, AGB does not perform high-dimensional fixed-point iteration; it solves a low-dimensional constrained least-squares problem for K=4 weights, and stability is empirically supported by CAOB ablations and gradient-alignment analysis. Sensitivity was under-discussed: D = {7,15,31} was fixed across experiments for multi-scale A/P/χ maps, while ρ is a scale-control term whose absolute effect is mitigated by the subsequent α normalization rather than acting as a dataset-specific loss weight [R4Q4]. Generalization analysis: 3D extension is feasible, but not by directly reusing the 2D A/P/χ formulation; it would require 3D intrinsic volumes and a redesigned differentiable 3D χ computation [R2Q2, R4Q2]. Highly non-convex organs are outside the validated scope of this submission, since Hadwiger priors are primarily motivated by near-convex geometry, and we therefore do not claim generalization to such organs here [R4Q2]. Results Analysis: We agree that the CUBS DSC margin is small and should not be judged from a single Dice value alone. Full HadBalance improves the strongest CUBS backbone by +1.21 BFScore, and on the more shape-heterogeneous CVC-ClinicDB, it improves over LS by +1.04 DSC, +1.50 IoU, and +1.64 BFScore, indicating that CAOB more robustly integrates Hadwiger priors without manual loss-weight tuning [R1Q4]. We will add confidence intervals to better reflect statistical uncertainty [R1Q4, R2Q1].

title: Hallucination Detection and Correction in Medical VLMs via Counter-Evidence Verification
abstract:
Vision-Language models (VLMs) reliability in medical diagnosis is challenged by trust-undermining hallucinations.
Existing hallucination detection approaches mainly focus on identifying factual inconsistencies between generated text and reference data. While some studies analyze where models attend in images, they seldom verify whether such attention truly reflects the visual evidence supporting the generated text. To address this gap, we propose Counter-Evidence Verification (CoEV), a training-free plug-and-play framework that detects and corrects hallucinations through evidence-based factual consistency verification. CoEV performs bidirectional verification between textual assertions and visual evidence, testing whether each statement is supported by its corresponding evidence region, and assigns each statement into a four-quadrant diagnostic map capturing combinations of text factuality and visual grounding.
CoEV detects hallucinated content and serves as a post hoc refinement tool, correcting hallucinations without retraining. Extensive experiments on four medical datasets show that CoEV combats hallucinations in VLMs.For hallucination detection, CoEV consistently outperforms existing methods, improving average PR-AUC and ROC-AUC by 3.0% and 3.9% absolute points respectively, with notable gains of up to 18.5% in specific VQA scenarios. For hallucination correction, it improves Micro-F1 by up to 12.5%, reduces hallucination rates by over 11.9% on medical report generation, and also boosts medical VQA accuracy. These results show that CoEV enables reliable detection and correction of hallucinations, providing clinicians with dependable, evidence-based cues for diagnosis. Code is avaliable at https://github.com/Zhounan1222/CoEV.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces Counter-Evidence Verification (CoEV), a training-free, plug-and-play framework for both detecting and correcting hallucinations in medical Vision-Language Models (VLMs). The core innovation is a counterfactual intervention approach: for each clinical claim extracted from VLM output (via a semantic parser, CheXbert), CoEV localizes the corresponding visual evidence region (via a grounding model, Maira-2), then masks that region and re-queries the VLM. If a claim persists despite masking its supporting visual evidence, it is deemed linguistically driven rather than visually grounded. Claims are mapped onto a Four-Quadrant Diagnostic Map combining textual factual correctness (f) and visual grounding attribution (z) into four interpretable categories: Q1 (correct + grounded), Q2 (incorrect + grounded), Q3 (incorrect + ungrounded), Q4 (correct + ungrounded). Only Q1 claims are considered non-hallucinated. CoEV further enables hallucination correction by prompting the VLM to rewrite flagged sentences using validated visual evidence. Evaluation on four datasets (MIMIC-CXR, IU-Xray, VQA-RAD, MIMIC-VQA) across four VLM backbones demonstrates improvements in both detection (PR-AUC +3.0%, ROC-AUC +3.9%) and correction (F1-5 +7.01%, VQA accuracy +13.04%) over existing baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
1- Novel counterfactual intervention mechanism : The idea of masking visual evidence regions and re-querying the VLM to test the causal dependency of claims on visual input is genuinely creative and conceptually appealing. Unlike purely similarity-based or uncertainty-based approaches (RadFlag, SE), CoEV provides a causal lens on hallucination testing whether removing visual evidence changes the model’s output. This goes beyond correlation to probe actual visual grounding.
2- Interpretable four-quadrant diagnostic taxonomy : The Q1-Q4 mapping along the factual correctness x visual grounding axes (Eq. 6) is a valuable conceptual contribution. It distinguishes between language-driven bias (Q2), visual misinterpretation (Q3), and total failure (Q4), which is clinically meaningful. Clinicians can understand why a claim was flagged, not just that it was flagged a significant advantage for trust and adoption.
3- Unified detection and correction framework : Unlike detection-only methods, CoEV provides actionable correction for both closed-ended Med-VQA (via verification, Eq. 7) and open-ended report generation (via sentence-level refinement, Eq. 8). The correction results are compelling, particularly the +27.16% accuracy gain for Qwen2-3B on MIMIC-VQA (Table 3).
4- Comprehensive experimental evaluation : The paper evaluates across 4 datasets spanning two task types (MRG and VQA), 4 VLM backbones of varying scales and training paradigms (general-purpose: InternVL3-2B, Qwen2-3B; medical-tuned: Lingshu-7B, LLaVA-Med), with multiple complementary metrics. This breadth provides solid evidence of generalizability across architectures.
5- Training-free, plug-and-play design : CoEV requires no fine-tuning or additional labeled data, making it practically deployable as a post-hoc layer on any existing VLM pipeline. This is a major practical advantage for clinical adoption.
6- Well-structured ablation study : Table 4 cleanly demonstrates that both diagnostic axes (textual and visual) contribute complementary signal, with the combined model achieving the best F1-Score (0.6112). The progressive improvement pattern is convincing.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1- Simplistic masking strategy may introduce artifacts : The Evidence Intervention Module (Eq. 4) masks regions with black pixels. This is a crude intervention that could introduce distribution shift: VLMs may react to the unnatural black patch itself (as an out-of-distribution artifact) rather than to the genuine absence of visual evidence. More principled interventions (e. g. , inpainting with plausible tissue textures, Gaussian blurring, or learned perturbations) should be discussed. The authors should at minimum analyze whether the black mask itself triggers false behavioral changes in the VLM, potentially inflating the false positive rate for hallucination detection.
2- Under-specified claim persistence function : The function phi(c_i, T’_i) in Eq. 5, which determines whether a claim persists in the re-generated output after masking, is critically under-defined. Is this exact string matching? Semantic similarity? CheXbert re-extraction? This is the linchpin of the entire CECE module, and different implementations would yield vastly different results. Without this specification, the method cannot be reproduced.
3- Self-correction circularity concern : The correction mechanism (Eq. 8) relies on the same VLM that generated the hallucination to rewrite the flagged sentence. If the VLM has a systematic bias (e. g. , always reporting cardiomegaly), re-prompting it with “corrected” evidence may not overcome this bias. The paper does not discuss when self-correction fails or analyze the correction failure modes. A control experiment using a different VLM for correction would strengthen the claim.
4- Insufficient statistical rigor : No confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests are reported for any result across Tables 1-4.Given that the method involves stochastic components (VLM generation variability, grounding model uncertainty), the reported improvements may not be statistically meaningful. For instance, the gains on IU-Xray for LLaVA-Med detection (Table 1) are modest, and without uncertainty estimates, it is impossible to assess reliability.
5- Ablation study limited to a single dataset : Table 4 presents ablation results only on MIMIC-CXR. The relative contribution of textual vs. visual axes may differ on datasets with different characteristics (e. g. , VQA-RAD with shorter answers vs. MIMIC-CXR with full reports). Extending the ablation to at least one VQA dataset would strengthen the analysis.
6- Ground-truth dependency on GREEN model : The entire evaluation relies on the GREEN model [18] to generate hallucination ground-truth labels. GREEN’s own accuracy and potential systematic biases are not discussed. If GREEN shares biases with the VLMs being evaluated, the ground-truth labels may systematically undercount or overcount certain hallucination types. No validation against human radiologist annotations is provided.
7- Limited to chest X-ray domain : All four evaluation datasets involve chest radiography. The method’s reliance on CheXbert (chest X-ray specific) and Maira-2 (radiology grounding) raises questions about generalizability to other modalities (CT, MRI, pathology, dermatology). The paper does not discuss what adaptations would be needed.
8- Computational overhead not reported : CoEV requires running the VLM at least twice per claim (original + masked), plus CheXbert extraction and Maira-2 grounding for each claim. For a report with multiple claims, this could multiply inference cost significantly. No runtime analysis or GPU memory requirements are provided.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

CoEV addresses the clinically important problem of hallucination detection and correction in medical VLMs with a genuinely creative approach: counterfactual visual evidence intervention. The core idea masking evidence regions and re-querying the VLM to test causal visual dependency – is more principled than existing similarity-based or uncertainty-based methods, providing a causal rather than correlational assessment of hallucination. The four-quadrant diagnostic taxonomy (Q1-Q4) adds interpretability that is valuable for clinical deployment. The unified detection + correction framework is practically useful, and the experimental evaluation is comprehensive (4 datasets, 4 backbones, both detection and correction tasks).
The main factors supporting acceptance are:
Conceptual novelty: The counterfactual masking approach is a distinct and well-motivated mechanism that clearly differentiates CoEV from prior work.
Strong correction results : The VQA accuracy gains (avg. +13.04%) and report quality improvements are substantial and clinically meaningful.
Breadth of evaluation : The cross-dataset and cross-architecture evaluation demonstrates robustness.
The main concerns are:
Masking artifact risk : Black-pixel masking is a crude intervention that could confound the causal interpretation.
Under-specification of phi : The claim persistence function is critically under-defined, hindering reproducibility.
Statistical rigor : No confidence intervals or significance tests.
Self-correction circularity : Using the same VLM for correction is methodologically questionable.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper proposes Counter-Evidence Verification (CoEV), a training-free and plug-and-play framework for detecting and correcting hallucinations in medical vision–language models (VLMs). The key idea is to perform claim-level counterfactual verification by masking the visual regions associated with each generated clinical claim and testing whether the claim persists. This enables a direct assessment of whether a claim is grounded in visual evidence.
The method further integrates a four-quadrant diagnostic mapping that jointly considers factual correctness and visual grounding, providing an interpretable taxonomy of hallucination types. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets (e.g., MIMIC-CXR, IU-Xray, VQA-RAD, MIMIC-VQA) and tasks (report generation and Med-VQA) demonstrate that CoEV improves both hallucination detection and downstream task performance.
Additionally, the framework supports post-hoc correction, including answer verification for VQA and sentence-level rewriting for reports, highlighting its practical utility in clinical AI systems.
reviews.text_strengths:
(1) Novel and intuitive formulation of claim-level counterfactual verification
The paper introduces a simple yet effective idea: verifying each claim by masking its associated visual evidence and observing whether the claim persists. Compared to prior global perturbation approaches, this localized, per-claim intervention better captures causal dependence between visual input and generated text.
(2) Interpretable diagnostic framework
The proposed four-quadrant taxonomy (factuality × grounding) provides a clear and clinically meaningful decomposition of hallucination types, enabling fine-grained analysis rather than binary detection. This improves interpretability and aligns well with clinical needs.
(3) Training-free and model-agnostic design
The method operates at inference time without retraining the base VLM, making it practical for real-world deployment where retraining large medical models is often infeasible.
(4) Strong empirical coverage
The evaluation spans multiple datasets, tasks, and model types (general and medical VLMs), demonstrating robustness and general applicability. Improvements in detection metrics (AUC) and downstream performance are generally consistent.
(5) Practical correction mechanisms
Beyond detection, the framework supports post-hoc correction (verification and rewriting), which is valuable for clinical workflows where actionable outputs are required.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(1) Key components are under-specified, affecting reproducibility
Several critical modules are not described in sufficient detail, including claim extraction, evidence localization, factuality assessment, and persistence estimation.
In particular, the paper suggests that evidence regions are localized by a “radiology expert,” which is not scalable in practice. If an external grounding model is used instead, this introduces hidden dependencies that weaken the claim of being training-free and may lead to error propagation. Clear disclosure of these components is necessary for reproducibility.
(2) Potential evaluator–label leakage and circularity
The use of the same or closely related tools for both label construction and factuality evaluation raises concerns about evaluation bias and circular reasoning. This setup may inflate the reported performance improvements and should be carefully justified or mitigated.
(3) Limitations of masking-based counterfactuals
The masking strategy may introduce distribution shifts or artifacts, and may not adequately handle cases where visual evidence is global, diffuse, or distributed across multiple regions (e.g., cardiomegaly or interstitial patterns).
The paper does not provide a sensitivity analysis on mask size, shape, or alternative masking strategies (such as blur or inpainting), making it unclear how robust the method is.
(4) Lack of computational efficiency analysis
The approach requires multiple additional model inferences for each claim, which could result in significant computational overhead. The paper does not report runtime or scalability, especially for long reports containing many claims, making it difficult to assess practical feasibility.
(5) Limited statistical rigor
The paper does not report confidence intervals, statistical significance tests, or variability across runs. Some reported improvements are unusually large and would benefit from stronger statistical validation.
(6) Incomplete comparison with related work
The method is closely related to prior work on visual counterfactual testing and verification, but these connections are not sufficiently discussed. Additional comparisons with relevant approaches would help better position the contribution and clarify its advantages.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
This work addresses an important problem in medical AI, and the idea of claim-level counterfactual verification is both intuitive and promising. To further strengthen the paper, I encourage the authors to:
Provide detailed descriptions of all key components (claim extraction, grounding, factuality scoring, persistence computation), including model choices and hyperparameters.
Clarify the role of external models and annotations, and refine the “training-free” claim accordingly.
Add statistical analysis (confidence intervals, significance testing) to support the reported improvements.
Report runtime and computational cost, especially in comparison to existing baselines.
Include robustness studies on masking strategies and challenging cases (e.g., diffuse findings).
Expand comparisons to include related verification and counterfactual methods.
Overall, the work is promising and has strong potential impact if these issues are addressed.

The paper proposes a novel and intuitive framework for hallucination detection based on claim-level counterfactual verification, with strong interpretability and practical relevance to clinical AI. The empirical evaluation is broad and demonstrates consistent improvements across tasks and datasets.
However, the work has several limitations that prevent it from being a clear accept. In particular, key components are under-specified, raising concerns about reproducibility and hidden dependencies. The use of external evaluators may introduce bias, and the lack of statistical rigor and runtime analysis weakens the empirical claims. Additionally, robustness to masking strategies and comparisons with closely related methods are insufficient.
Overall, the paper presents a promising and potentially impactful idea, but requires additional methodological transparency and stronger evaluation to fully meet top-tier standards.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text:
[Note from PCs: review submitted by Reviewer #1 has now been removed from the system]
I recommend inviting a rebuttal. I note that Reviewer #1 appears to have reviewed a different paper, as the review repeatedly refers to “GLoVe” and global-local verification rather than the submitted CoEV counter-evidence verification method. I therefore do not rely on Reviewer #1’s assessment in forming this recommendation.
Based on the substantive reviews from Reviewers #2 and #3, the paper addresses an important clinical safety problem: detecting and correcting hallucinated claims in medical VLM outputs. The proposed claim-level counter-evidence verification strategy is promising, since masking visual evidence and re-querying the VLM provides an intuitive way to test whether a generated clinical statement is visually grounded. The four-quadrant diagnostic map and the extension from detection to correction are also useful and interpretable.
However, several issues need clarification before a final decision. The rebuttal should specify key components, especially claim extraction, evidence localization, factuality scoring, and the claim-persistence function after masking. The authors should also address whether black-pixel masking introduces artifacts, discuss possible circularity in label construction and factuality evaluation, report statistical significance or confidence intervals, and provide runtime analysis. A convincing rebuttal on these points would substantially strengthen confidence in the contribution.

I recommend acceptance. Reviewer #1’s review has been removed and was not considered in the final assessment. Based on the substantive reviews from Reviewers #2 and #3, the paper presents a promising and clinically relevant framework for hallucination detection and correction in medical VLMs.
The main contribution, claim-level counter-evidence verification by masking visual evidence and checking whether the claim persists, is intuitive, novel, and practically meaningful. The four-quadrant diagnostic map also provides useful interpretability, and the evaluation covers multiple datasets, tasks, and VLM backbones.

Most of the clarity issues raised by the reviewers have been addressed in the rebuttal. The problem is timely, and the baselines are up to date. The authors should commit to releasing the data splits upon acceptance for reproducibility. Based on the content of this paper itself, I consider it sufficient for acceptance.
However, my major concern remains the concurrent submission “GloVe”. The two papers do share a common motivation: detecting hallucinations in medical VLMs by checking whether generated claims are supported by visual evidence. The tasks also overlap, including report generation and medical VQA. The baselines and datasets overlap a lot as well (MIMIC-CXR). The methods are not identical for sure, CoEV uses visual region masking as a counter-evidence intervention, while GLoVe combines global semantic assessment with local grounding verification. But there is still methodological overlap, as both rely on the same claim extraction and visual grounding/localization.

I recommend acceptance. The paper proposes CoEV, a training free framework that detects and corrects hallucinations in medical VLMs through claim level counterfactual visual masking, organized via an interpretable four quadrant taxonomy of factuality and visual grounding. Both reviewers scored the paper 4 and recognized its conceptual novelty, clinical relevance, and broad evaluation across four datasets and four VLM backbones. The rebuttal concretely resolves the major concerns by specifying the previously under defined components (CheXbert for claim extraction and persistence, MAIRA-2 for grounding, CheXbert based factuality scoring), clarifying that correction uses Qwen rather than the original VLM, decoupling ground truth labels (GREEN) from factuality scoring (CheXbert), and reporting significance testing at p < 0.05 along with runtime numbers (3.47s vs 1.78s for VASE).

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback and recognition of CoEV as a novel, training-free framework for medical hallucination detection and correction. Reviewer #1’s comments reference “GLoVe” and “global-local verification,” which are unrelated to our submission; therefore, we do not provide a response to Reviewer#1.We provide point-to-point responses to the other comments, which will be integrated into the final version of the paper.
[Q] Key Components (R#2, R#3).
[A] To ensure reproducibility, we clarify the implementation details as follows:
(1) Claim Extraction: CheXbert as the semantic parser P(·) extracts positive disease labels (Cpos) from text.
(2) Evidence Localization: The pretrained radiology grounding model MAIRA-2 generates bounding boxes using images and disease descriptions as input.
(3) Persistence Estimation (ϕ): ϕ(c_i, T’i) is implemented by feeding the report T’i into the semantic parser P(·) to verify if the claim (c_i) persists as a positive finding despite the absence of visual evidence.
(4) Factuality Assessment: factual correctness is determined based on CheXbert disease labels extracted from the generated report and the reference report. claims are considered factual if their labels are semantically consistent.
[Q] Intervention Strategy & Artifacts (R#2, R#3).
[A] (1) Masking Strategy: Black-pixel masking ensures rigorous “information zeroing”, which ensures visual evidence is genuinely inaccessible. We leave the exploration of alternative interventions for future work and add a corresponding discussion in the limitations section.
(2) As illustrated in Fig. 2 in our paper, masking Region A primarily suppresses Claim A while leaving unrelated findings largely unaffected. This localized behavioral change suggests that the VLM response is mainly influenced by evidence removal rather than by a global OOD artifact effect.
[Q] Statistical Rigor (R#2, R#3).
[A] We acknowledge this omission. We have conducted repeated-run analysis and statistical significance testing, and the improvements over the strongest baselines remain statistically significant across datasets (p < 0.05). Furthermore, the consistent gains across 4 datasets and 4 VLM backbones suggest the improvements are robust rather than due to random variance.
[Q] Computational Efficiency (R#2).
[A] CoEV is a training-free, plug-and-play solution, avoiding the high costs of fine-tuning. CoEV averages 3.47s per image (vs. 1.78s for VASE) on a NVIDIA L20 (48GB). Given the clinical importance of hallucination detection, we believe this additional latency is a reasonable trade-off for improved reliability and interpretability.
[Q] Clarification on Circularity (R#2).
[A] We clarify that the correction mechanism is model-agnostic and does not rely on the original VLM. In our implementation, Qwen is used as the correction model, taking only textual evidence and flagged claims as input without reusing the original image.
[Q] Generalizability Beyond Chest X-ray (R#2).
[A] CoEV is currently developed and evaluated on chest X-ray data. It is modality-agnostic in principle, relying on claim-level counterfactual verification rather than chest X-ray-specific modeling. Extending CoEV to other modalities is part of our future work and would require adapting parsing and grounding modules to modality-specific tools.
[Q] Evaluator-Label Independence (R#3).
[A] We clarify that CoEV uses CheXbert for factuality assessment, while hallucination ground-truth labels are constructed using GREEN. Although these are different tools, some domain bias may still exist, which will be discussed in the revised manuscript.
[Q] Comparison with related works (R#3).
[A] Unlike VCD/SID’s global perturbations, we use evidence-guided local counterfactual interventions to explicitly test visual grounding. We will incorporate a more detailed discussion of these methodological distinctions in our updated manuscript.

title: HAM-BGT: Harmonic-Aware Multimodal Brain Graph Transformer for Brain Disease Diagnosis
abstract: Functional and structural brain networks characterize inter-regional functional coordination and anatomical connectivity, respectively, supporting brain disorder diagnosis and mechanistic studies. However, most existing multimodal brain network methods rely on simple feature concatenation, or treat functional and structural networks as independent graphs during fusion, overlooking their inherent coupling as revealed by connectome harmonics and thus failing to adequately capture cross-modal interactions for diagnosis. Specifically, eigenmodes of the structural connectome form a Fourier-like basis, and functional patterns can be described as energy distributed across these modes. To address these issues, we propose a Harmonic-Aware Multimodal Brain Graph Transformer (HAM-BGT) for deep joint modeling of multimodal brain networks. HAM-BGT introduces a Spectral Graph Filtering-Based Harmonic Encoding module to inject structural topological priors into functional connectivity representations. It then stacks multimodal brain graph Transformer layers to capture local-to-global dependencies. Each layer is followed by a Harmonic-Aware Filter that adaptively reorganizes regional features across frequency bands, enabling efficient extraction of harmonic-driven structure-function coupling patterns. Across multiple diagnostic tasks, HAM-BGT achieves state-of-the-art performance and identifies disease-relevant biomarkers, offering a harmonic-informed computational perspective to understand structure-function coupling in brain disorders.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes the Harmonic-Aware Multimodal Brain Graph Transformer (HAM-BGT), a novel framework for brain disease diagnosis that explicitly models the inherent structure-function coupling in multimodal brain networks via connectome harmonics.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The approach is highly interesting, introducing a novel method to explicitly combine DTI-derived structural harmonics with functional features. 
2.The experimental validation is thorough, demonstrating the framework’s effectiveness across multiple public datasets (ADNI and ABIDE) against strong baselines. 
3.The manuscript is clearly written and logically structured, making the complex connectome-harmonic concepts and the proposed architecture easy to follow.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.he proposed framework introduces several crucial hyperparameters, yet there is no comprehensive sensitivity analysis. 
2.The ABIDE dataset subset utilized in the experiments contains only 95 subjects. Given that Transformer-based architectures are inherently data-hungry and prone to overfitting on small datasets, evaluating such a highly parameterized model on a small cohort raises concerns regarding the robustness and true generalizability of the reported results. 
3.In Section 3.4, the authors identify the top 10 most discriminative ROIs for each diagnostic task using a t-test. However, the specific implementation details of this statistical analysis are currently insufficient.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
While the proposed SGFBHE module effectively fuses structural harmonic priors with functional representations at the node level, the subsequent multimodal brain graph Transformer treats the network as a fully connected graph. This design choice might dilute explicit topological information during long-range message passing. A highly valuable enhancement (or a direction for future work) would be to incorporate the structural connectivity matrix or harmonic-derived structural topologies directly into the self-attention mechanism. The authors could consider drawing inspiration from advanced Graph Transformers that simultaneously learn both node and edge features (e. g. , using structural connectivity as spatial attention biases). This would further deepen the structure-function coupling throughout the entire deep learning process.

The proposed HAM-BGT framework elegantly integrates connectome harmonics to explicitly model structure-function coupling within a multimodal Transformer, yielding strong empirical performance on both the ADNI and ABIDE datasets.
However, I hold back from a strong accept due to the lack of hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (e.g., the number of retained eigencomponents) and concerns regarding potential overfitting on the small ABIDE cohort.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes HAM-BGT, the first framework to explicitly model structure-function coupling in multimodal brain networks via connectome harmonics. The key idea is that functional brain activity can be decomposed as energy distributed across structural connectivity eigenmodes (connectome harmonics), providing a principled basis for fusing fMRI-derived functional connectivity and DTI-derived structural connectivity. The framework introduces three synergistic components: (1) Spectral Graph Filtering-Based Harmonic Encoding (SGFBHE), which uses radial basis filters at each structural eigenfrequency to extract harmonic-specific spatial patterns, masked by binarized structural connectivity to suppress spectral leakage; (2) multimodal brain graph Transformer layers for capturing both short- and long-range ROI dependencies; and (3) Harmonic-Aware Filters after each Transformer layer, which apply GFT→spectral filtering→IGFT with learnable Gaussian-smeared filters and Tukey windowing to enforce connectome-harmonic constraints during message passing. Evaluated on ABIDE (ASD vs. NC, N=95) and ADNI (AD vs. NC, AD vs. MCI, MCI vs. NC, N=468).
reviews.text_strengths:
Genuinely novel and theoretically grounded perspective that advances the field. Connectome harmonics theory [Atasoy et al., Nature Neuroscience 2016] — where structural connectivity eigenmodes form a Fourier-like basis constraining functional dynamics — is a well-established neuroscience framework that has not been computationally exploited in the deep learning community for brain disease diagnosis. This paper offers the first systematic bridge between this theoretical framework and practical disease classification. Unlike the other papers in this batch that combine known components, HAM-BGT introduces a fundamentally new computational lens for multimodal brain network modeling. This represents a genuine contribution to the MICCAI community.
Technically sound and physically interpretable module design. (a) SGFBHE (Eq. 1-4): The radial basis filters h_i(λ) (Eq. 2) at each eigenvalue λ_i function as band-pass filters isolating harmonic-specific structural patterns. The binarized anatomical mask Ã_s (Eq. 3) suppresses spectral leakage along verified pathways — this is more physically principled than standard Laplacian positional encoding because it explicitly constrains information flow to anatomically verified connections. (b) Harmonic-Aware Filter (Eq. 6-8): The GFT→spectral filtering→IGFT pipeline is a well-defined signal processing operation applied in the connectome-harmonic domain. The combination of Gaussian smearing for smooth filter response and Tukey windowing for spectral truncation artifact suppression is technically well-motivated. (c) The gating mechanism f_{θ1} before GFT provides node-wise adaptivity, allowing different ROIs to have different spectral responses — this is important as different brain regions may contribute differently to different harmonic modes.
The most comprehensive and convincing experimental evaluation among the reviewed papers. (a) Four diagnostic tasks spanning two datasets (ABIDE: ASD vs. NC; ADNI: AD vs. NC, AD vs. MCI, MCI vs. NC). (b) Nine baseline methods including recent strong baselines from top venues: ALTER (NeurIPS 2024), BrainNetTF (NeurIPS 2022), Cross-GNN (TMI 2023), MME-GCN (MedIA 2022). (c) Table 1 results show consistent and substantial margins: ASD vs. NC: 78.9% ACC (+5.1% over best multimodal baseline MME-GCN 73.8%); AD vs. NC: 84.7% (+5.1% over MME-GCN 79.6%); MCI vs. NC: 70.9% (+3.8% over Cross-GNN 67.1%). These margins are substantial and consistent across all four tasks, providing strong evidence of the method’s effectiveness. (d) The evaluation includes four metrics (ACC, SPE, SEN, AUC), more comprehensive than Papers #659 and #1496.
Rich and clinically plausible interpretability analysis. Fig. 3 provides both discriminative ROI and discriminative connection analyses across all four tasks. ASD: precuneus (PCUN) and rectus gyrus (REC), consistent with social cognition and self-referential processing deficits; AD: angular gyrus (ANG) and hippocampus (HIP), reflecting memory and semantic processing impairments. The discriminative connections analysis (frontal lobe connections SFG/MFG for ASD; SFG connections for AD) adds value beyond node-level analysis and is supported by cited neuroscience literature.
The ablation study (Fig. 2) effectively validates each component. Removing SGFBHE drops performance >5%; replacing SGFBHE with standard Laplacian encoding also degrades significantly, specifically validating the harmonic filtering approach over generic spectral methods; removing the Harmonic-Aware Filter consistently hurts performance. These ablation results cleanly demonstrate that performance gains stem from the proposed harmonic-specific modules rather than the Transformer backbone alone.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Core assumption limitations are not discussed. (a) Connectome harmonics assume the structural connectome is a stable substrate on which functional patterns fluctuate. In brain diseases, structural connectivity itself degenerates (e.g., white matter lesions in MS, amyloid-related disconnection in AD). Using a patient’s degraded structural connectome to define the harmonic basis may introduce systematic bias — the “Fourier basis” is itself corrupted. The paper should discuss whether harmonic modes derived from diseased structural networks remain meaningful. (b) Only the first k=40 eigenmodes are retained and high-frequency components are suppressed by the Tukey window. However, localized connectivity disruptions (e.g., focal lesions) may produce high-frequency signatures that are systematically suppressed. This design choice could miss important disease patterns.
Computational complexity analysis and scalability discussion are missing. (a) Eigendecomposition (Eq. 1) is O(N³) per sample. For N=90 (AAL atlas), this is manageable, but scalability to finer parcellations (Schaefer-400, Schaefer-1000) is unclear. (b) The Harmonic-Aware Filter requires two matrix multiplications with V (N×k) per layer — GFT and IGFT. With L layers, this adds O(L·N·k·d) per sample. (c) No training/inference time comparison with baseline methods is provided. Given that several baselines (BrainGNN, BrainIB) are simpler architectures, the practical computational overhead should be quantified.
Hyperparameter sensitivity analyses are incomplete. The following are set without justification or sensitivity study: (a) k=40 eigencomponents — this determines spectral resolution and is arguably the most important hyperparameter. How does performance vary for k ∈ {10, 20, 40, 60, 80}? (b) σ in Eq. (2) and Eq. (8) — controls bandwidth of radial basis filters and Gaussian smearing. (c) Tukey window parameters — controls spectral truncation behavior. (d) J=50 Gaussian basis functions — large relative to k=40 eigencomponents. (e) λ_cut = 1.1·λ_k — the cutoff frequency. These are all free parameters in the spectral filtering design, and their combined sensitivity should be analyzed.
The ABIDE subset is very small (95 subjects) — the same small subset used by Paper #659.While results are strong, the 5-fold CV with ~19 test samples per fold limits generalizability claims. A cross-site generalization analysis (using ABIDE’s multi-site structure) would strengthen the paper significantly.
OCREAD readout is introduced without justification for its selection over simpler alternatives (mean/sum pooling, attention pooling). The readout strategy can significantly affect graph-level classification performance, and this choice should be analyzed.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
A brief accessible introduction to connectome harmonics in Section 1 would help readers unfamiliar with this neuroscience concept. Currently, the paper assumes familiarity.
Fig. 1(a) is information-dense; step numbers or clearer flow annotations would improve readability.
A comparison with Paper #659 (BrainCMCA) — which uses the same ABIDE subset and similar ADNI data — would be informative and should be encouraged in the camera-ready.
The paper would benefit from a spectral energy analysis: how does the energy distribution across harmonic modes differ between patients and controls? This could provide novel neuroscientific insight beyond classification accuracy.

HAM-BGT presents the strongest contribution among the papers reviewed in this batch, warranting acceptance based on: (1) Genuine novelty: the connectome harmonics perspective is theoretically grounded in established neuroscience and has not been computationally exploited for disease diagnosis — this is a new lens, not an incremental combination of existing modules. (2) Technical depth: SGFBHE and Harmonic-Aware Filter are well-designed modules with clear physical interpretations (band-pass harmonic filtering, spectral leakage suppression, Tukey windowing) that go beyond standard graph learning operations. (3) Convincing experiments: four diagnostic tasks, nine baselines including recent strong methods (ALTER, BrainNetTF), and consistent substantial improvements (+3.8-5.1% ACC over best baselines). (4) Rich interpretability with clinically plausible biomarkers. The main weaknesses — missing computational complexity analysis, incomplete hyperparameter sensitivity, and undiscussed assumption limitations — are addressable in revision and do not undermine the fundamental contribution. The paper opens a new research direction connecting neuroscience theory to practical clinical tools.

reviews.text_contribution: This study proposes the Harmonic-Aware Multimodal Brain Graph Transformer (HAM-BGT) to address the limitations of existing multimodal brain network methods, which often rely on simple feature concatenation or treat functional and structural networks as independent graphs, thus ignoring their inherent coupling revealed by connectome harmonics. HAM-BGT integrates a Spectral Graph Filtering-Based Harmonic Encoding module to infuse structural topological priors into functional connectivity representations, and stacks multimodal brain graph Transformer layers to capture local-to-global dependencies. Each layer is paired with a Harmonic-Aware Filter that adaptively reorganizes regional features across frequency bands, enabling efficient extraction of harmonic-driven structure-function coupling patterns. Across multiple diagnostic tasks, HAM-BGT achieves state-of-the-art performance, identifies disease-relevant biomarkers, and provides a harmonic-informed computational framework to deepen the understanding of structure-function coupling in brain disorders.

title: Harmless Copyright Protection for CT Dataset
abstract: Dataset is essential for advancing deep learning in healthcare, yet its unauthorized use raises serious concerns regarding patient privacy leakage and intellectual property infringement. Existing copyright protection methods typically rely on backdoor-triggered verification mechanisms, but these methods inherently introduce security vulnerabilities by embedding malicious backdoor behaviors that can lead to abnormal outputs. To address this issue, we propose a novel harmless copyright verification threat model. Unlike traditional methods that depend on trigger-activated abnormal outputs as verification signals, our approach instead uses prediction accuracy on watermarked samples as the verification criterion. The core idea is to enforce improved performance on trigger-injected samples, enabling reliable ownership verification without inducing malicious behaviors. Specifically, we propose a Learnable Measurement-Domain Harmless Backdoor Watermark (LMHBW) method. Unlike traditional image-domain watermarking techniques, which operate on reconstructed images that are easily accessible and thus vulnerable to tampering, we shift the protection to the measurement domain prior to image reconstruction. Motivated by the fact that raw measurement data are typically confined within imaging devices (e.g., scanners) and are rarely exposed externally, this design enhances the stealthiness and robustness of the embedded watermark against detection and removal. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed threat model enables effective and reliable watermark verification while remaining behaviorally harmless, and further validate the feasibility and advantages of measurement-domain watermarking for medical imaging copyright protection.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of this paper is proposing a novel “harmless” copyright protection method for medical CT datasets. Traditional backdoor watermark methods prove dataset ownership by forcing the AI model to make incorrect or abnormal predictions when a trigger is present, which creates severe security risks in healthcare applications. To fix this, the authors introduce a new verification approach that checks if a suspicious model has a higher prediction accuracy on watermarked samples, rather than making it fail. Furthermore, to keep the watermark robust and prevent it from ruining the visual quality of the medical images, their method (LMHBW) embeds a learnable watermark directly into the raw, pre-imaging “measurement data”. This ensures the final reconstructed images remain completely safe for clinical diagnosis while successfully proving data ownership.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.It improves security by using prediction accuracy for verification instead of causing the model to make dangerous mistakes
2.It embeds the watermark in the raw measurement data, making the protection much harder to detect and remove compared to traditional image-level methods. 
3.It uses a learnable mask that successfully proves data ownership without ruining the visual quality of the reconstructed medical images.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The experiments are conducted on a very small subset of the COVID-19 Low-Dose CT dataset, using only 15 COVID and 15 normal cases for training, and 5 of each for testing. Furthermore, it appears to treat the data as 2D slices rather than continuous 3D volumes. This limited scale fails to demonstrate clinical feasibility or prove that the learnable mask can maintain both visual fidelity and verification accuracy across massive, highly diverse, real-world 3D medical datasets. 
2.The methodology relies solely on standard Filtered Back-Projection (FBP) to reconstruct the images from the watermarked measurement data. In modern clinical practice, advanced Iterative Reconstruction (IR) or Deep Learning-based Reconstruction (DLR) techniques are heavily used for noise reduction. These non-linear, aggressive denoising algorithms could easily filter out or distort the subtle measurement-domain watermark (LMHBW), potentially breaking the downstream prediction-accuracy verification entirely.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The authors introduce a compelling approach to medical dataset copyright protection by shifting the verification signal from harmful, abnormal predictions to benign prediction accuracy gains, thereby mitigating critical security risks associated with traditional backdoor watermarks. Furthermore, embedding the learnable watermark (LMHBW) within the pre-imaging measurement domain is a clever strategy that inherently enhances stealthiness against post-imaging tampering while preserving visual fidelity. However, my enthusiasm is dampened by the limited scope of the experiments. The validation relies on a very small-scale dataset evaluated as 2D slices rather than complete 3D volumes, which fails to fully demonstrate clinical feasibility. More importantly, the current framework solely utilizes standard Filtered Back-Projection (FBP); it remains unclear whether the subtle measurement-domain watermark would survive the non-linear, aggressive denoising of modern Iterative Reconstruction (IR) or Deep Learning-based Reconstruction (DLR) algorithms standard in current clinical practice.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal has adequately addressed my main concerns, so I am satisfied with the authors’ response and recommend acceptance.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: They address the important problem of copyright protection for CT datasets and propose a Learnable Measurement-Domain Harmless Backdoor Watermark (LMHBW). Compared with prior watermarking methods, LMHBW enables ownership verification while preserving prediction accuracy, whereas earlier approaches often introduced malicious output behavior and increased adversarial vulnerability. The paper further demonstrates superior verification performance over existing methods.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.A key strength of the paper is the novelty of its loss design: it combines multiple loss terms to preserve reconstruction quality, ensure that the watermark remains verifiable, and maintain high predictive accuracy on watermarked samples.
2.Another strength is that the paper defines the problem very clearly. The introduction is well written and accessible even to readers outside the specific field, and the topic itself is timely and important, with broad relevance to researchers and practitioners concerned with AI privacy and data protection.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.A major weakness of the paper is the choice of baselines. The compared methods are from 2019 and 2022, which are relatively old for a rapidly evolving field. Although the paper cites the more recent work by Sun et al. (2025) on EntropyMark, it neither includes a direct comparison with that method nor explains why such a comparison was omitted. This makes it harder to assess the true novelty and competitiveness of the proposed approach against the current state of the art.
2.There is also some ambiguity in the presentation of the results. For example, in Table 1, it is unclear what backbone model is being used and what watermarking ratio is assumed. In Table 2, only the proposed method is evaluated across different architectures, whereas it would be more informative to include the same architectural comparison for the baselines as well. That would allow for a fairer and more complete evaluation.
3.In addition, the paper lacks clarity in several technical details and contains a few minor writing issues. For instance, in Equation 5, (m_c) is not defined, and the abbreviation “FBP” appears before its full form is introduced. Some model details are also missing, such as which version of CLIP was used, whether it was pretrained on medical data, and which ResNet variant was adopted. The absence of citations for these architectures further reduces clarity.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

My main concern regarding the paper is the lack of comparison with current state-of-the-art methods.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: One of my main concerns was the comparison with recent methods. The authors have addressed the concerns I raised, and I believe the research topic is timely and important for the field.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose a novel backdoor watermarking method for CT datasets aimed at protecting the intellectual property of medical imaging data. The key innovation lies in embedding a learnable mask within the measurement domain rather than the image domain, which increases robustness against adversarial replication. To support this approach, the authors design three custom loss functions that jointly preserve reconstruction fidelity while ensuring reliable watermark verification. A pre-trained CLIP model is leveraged as part of the feature consistency objective, and experimental results are reported to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Overall, the paper addresses a timely and relevant problem in the intersection of medical imaging and data copyright protection, offering a fresh perspective through its measurement-domain formulation.
reviews.text_strengths: The central idea is novel, with contributions that are twofold. First, the watermark is implemented as a learnable mask inserted in the measurement domain rather than the image domain, which makes it more difficult for an adversary to replicate through adversarial watermarking. Second, the authors introduce three custom loss functions that jointly ensure images are reconstructed without loss of fidelity while preserving the effectiveness of copyright protection.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Major Comments
The authors refer to CLIP as the pre-trained model but do not clarify whether they employ the original CLIP model or a custom variant pre-trained on domain-specific data. Since the features generated by CLIP are highly dependent on the pre-training data, this ambiguity raises concerns regarding the validity of the feature consistency loss.
An ablation study is strongly needed, particularly given the use of three distinct loss functions. Although page constraints may limit the scope, a thorough ablation study would provide empirical evidence that each of the three losses contributes meaningfully to the overall performance.
The introduction of the learnable mask is described in vague terms, and additional details would strengthen the presentation. A brief background on the measurement domain, along with some intuition regarding what the data represents in this domain, would provide valuable context for the reader.
An important open question is the practical adoption of measurement-domain watermarking in physical devices such as CT scanners. While the proposed approach is novel, its feasibility for real-world deployment warrants further discussion.
Minor Comments
The abstract would benefit from including specific numerical results rather than the current general statement that “experimental results demonstrate that the proposed threat model enables effective watermark verification while remaining harmless.”
There is a typo on Page 2, paragraph 2: “embeddedinto” should be corrected.
The acronym “FBP” is used prior to its formal introduction (Page 5, following Equation 1).
The organization of Section 2.2 could be improved. The authors introduce two objectives but, rather than proceeding directly to the loss functions, first describe a masking strategy before returning to the loss formulation. Restructuring this section would enhance readability.
The authors should justify the selection of SSIM as the image-fidelity loss metric. A citation to prior work establishing SSIM as a standard choice for this purpose would be sufficient.
Figure 3 would benefit from explicit annotations to clearly highlight the issues present in the images.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The proposed approach of embedding a learnable watermark in the measurement domain is novel and makes this a strong contribution to MICCAI.
