meta_reviews.text:
The paper addresses an important problem in medical image segmentation: balancing long-range context modeling with fine boundary preservation. The proposed HEDS-Net is technically coherent, and the reported results across four datasets are promising. In particular, the HVST block is a reasonable hybridization of global state-space modeling and local enhancement, and the training-side deep supervision strategy is practically useful.
The main strengths of the paper are:
1, The paper addresses the important challenge of balancing long-range context modeling with fine boundary preservation in medical image segmentation.
2, HEDS-Net integrates global SSM modeling, local multi-scale enhancement, refined skip fusion, and progressively weighted deep supervision into a unified U-shaped framework.
3, The method reports consistent improvements across four datasets and representative CNN, Transformer, and SSM baselines.
4, The ablation and qualitative results indicate that the proposed components contribute to the final performance.
The main remaining concerns are:
The novelty is partly incremental, as the method builds on known ideas such as global-local hybrid modeling, skip refinement, and deep supervision.
Comparisons with closely related hybrid architectures and recent Mamba/SSM-based segmentation methods could be more complete.
Efficiency analysis would be stronger with parameters, FLOPs, latency, and memory statistics.
Overall, these concerns mainly concern positioning, completeness of analysis, and presentation/reproducibility clarification. They do not undermine the main technical idea or the empirical conclusions. Given the positive reviewer consensus, the consistent results across datasets, and the practical relevance of the proposed framework, I recommend Early Accept. The authors should address the above issues in the camera-ready version. These revisions would improve the presentation and reproducibility, but they are not severe enough to delay the paper to rebuttal given its overall strength and positive reviewer consensus.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the Area Chair and all reviewers for their careful evaluation and constructive suggestions. We have carefully considered each concern and will revise the final version accordingly.
1.Novelty and Positioning (AC, R1, R2)
We acknowledge the concern that global-local modeling, skip refinement, and deep supervision have been previously explored. However, HEDS-Net is not presented as three isolated conceptual breakthroughs, nor is it merely a loose engineering assembly. Its contribution lies in a task-oriented SSM segmentation design: HVST integrates VSS global modeling with ADCA local enhancement through a scheduled local-to-global fusion; AXIS-Bridge employs decoder-conditioned gating prior to horizontal and vertical descriptor refinement; and DS-Head utilizes epoch-decayed supervision and is removed during inference. Collectively, these components address a common practical challenge in SSM-based segmentation—preserving fine anatomical details while maintaining global semantic coherence. We will clarify this scope and avoid overstating isolated novelty.
2.Comparisons, Analysis, and Related Work (AC, R1, R2, R3)
We agree that related hybrid and Mamba/SSM methods should be discussed more clearly and acknowledge that some citations are outdated. Direct comparisons are already included: Table 1 reports TransFuse, TransUNet, VM-UNet, and HC-Mamba where applicable, and Table 2 includes TransUNet, Swin U-Net, TransDeepLab, UCTransNet, MEW-UNet, and VM-UNet on Synapse. Therefore, the main issue is not the absence of relevant baselines but rather that the discussion does not clearly organize them by method family. In the revision, we will relate TransFuse and TransUNet to CNN-Transformer hybrids, MEW-UNet to multi-axis modeling, and VM-UNet and HC-Mamba to SSM/Mamba segmentation, while incorporating recent medical Mamba/SSM literature without overclaiming superiority over unevaluated methods.
3.Efficiency and Additional Ablations (AC, R1, R2)
We appreciate the requests for detailed parameters, FLOPs, latency, memory usage, and targeted variants, including progressive versus fixed fusion, AXIS-Bridge versus simpler skip attention, and progressive versus fixed deep supervision. We agree that computational efficiency is crucial for practical deployment and will include a discussion of this aspect in the final version. Rather than claiming a lightweight architecture, we provide the following statistics to transparently present the accuracy-complexity trade-off (input size: 256×256, single RTX 3090): HEDS-Net contains 44.61M parameters and 6.06G FLOPs; FP32 inference takes 19.85 ms per image (batch size = 1, averaged over 100 runs) with a peak memory usage of 329.7 MB. Regarding progressive fusion, we examined fixed-alpha behavior during method development to compare static fusion weights with scheduled local-to-global fusion. The observed trend supported the motivation for progressive fusion; however, this analysis was omitted due to page limitations and because Table 3 prioritized module-level effects of HVST, AXIS-Bridge, and DS-Head. We will refine the discussion of the existing ablation study and consider these more fine-grained analyses in future follow-up work where appropriate.
4.Reproducibility and Code Consistency (R2)
We take this concern seriously. The publicly available code should correspond exactly to the manuscript: the HVST block must be complete and executable, and the loss functions should follow BCE+Dice for binary segmentation and CE+Dice for multi-class segmentation. We will review and correct the implementation to ensure consistency among the code, method description, and conclusions.
We believe these revisions substantially strengthen the paper and respectfully ask the Area Chair and reviewers for Camera-ready.

title: HemoPIC: A Physics-Informed Cerebral Hemodynamics Digital Twin for Brain Perfusion
abstract: Perfusion imaging guides clinical evaluation of stroke and brain tumors by characterizing tissue-level hemodynamics. Routine quantification relies on manual arterial input function (AIF) selection followed by deconvolution, producing summary maps without an executable temporal model for simulation or mechanistic insight. Tracer-dynamics-based models infer transport or compartmental parameters from perfusion time series, but do not yield clinically actionable perfusion indices (e.g., CBF, CBV, MTT) that inform diagnosis and treatment decisions. In this work, we propose HemoPIC, a physics-informed cerebral hemodynamics digital twin that explains perfusion time series through tracer mass conservation and a lumped parameter hemodynamic model. Specifically, HemoPIC solves a constrained inverse problem that jointly estimates digital twin parameters and latent states from perfusion imaging, eliminating manual AIF selection and deconvolution from routine perfusion quantification while directly producing clinically actionable perfusion summary maps. Experiments demonstrate that HemoPIC reconstructs tracer dynamics, generates physiologically consistent perfusion maps with lesion hypoperfusion patterns, satisfies central volume consistency, and yields a mechanistic hemodynamic digital twin. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/jhuldr/HemoPIC.
subject_areas: Applications -> Digital Twins / Simulation / Synthetic Data

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This work introduces a new, physics-informed learning approach for perfusion imaging via lumped parameter hemodynamics modelling.
reviews.text_strengths:
The introduction of a Lumped Windkessel model proves successful in capturing patient-specific hemodynamics.
This is the first work, according to the authors, in capturing both inflow/outflow perfusion phases.
Results are in line with a conventional perfusion (deconvolution) model.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Lack of Comparative Baseline Analysis
The current manuscript lacks a comprehensive comparative evaluation, which makes it difficult to properly contextualize the reported findings. While the authors acknowledge previous efforts in this domain, the following points must be addressed to demonstrate the state-of-the-art positioning of this work:
Direct Comparisons: No quantitative comparisons are provided against relevant prior art, specifically references [15] and [16] already cited in the text.
Physics-Informed Benchmarks: The evaluation should include comparisons with alternative modelling approaches like PINN-based ones, such as those proposed by de Vries et al. (MIDL 2024, MedIA 2023), which are highly relevant to the methodology described.
Methodological Transparency: The “single baseline” deconvolution model requires further detail. Please specify the exact approach used (e. g. , is this a block-circulant SVD approach?) to ensure the comparison is fair and reproducible.
2.Clarification of Clinical Context
There is a recurring overstatement throughout the narrative suggesting that current perfusion models “do not yield clinically actionable perfusion indices (e. g. , CBF, CBV, MTT) that inform diagnosis and treatment decisions. “ This statement contradicts the extensive clinical evidence regarding EVT decision-making via perfusion mismatch, which is a standard of care in clinical routine [NEJM 2018]. I recommend the authors temper these claims and adjust the messaging to accurately reflect the established role of current perfusion software in stroke routine.
3.Impact of Diffusion Terms
The authors adopt an advection-diffusion framework but opt to disregard the diffusion terms. However, prior research (e. g. , [14-16]) has demonstrated that these terms are essential for capturing physiologically relevant tracer propagation dynamics in the brain. To justify this modeling choice, the authors should provide ablation studies comparing the model’s performance with and without the inclusion of diffusion processes.
4.Evaluation of Tmax and Clinical Actionability
In clinical practice, both Tmax and CBF maps are vital for defining penumbra regions and identifying perfusion mismatch. By omitting Tmax from the comparative analysis, the manuscript misses a crucial metric for determining the clinical utility of the proposed method. Including Tmax is necessary to support the authors’ claims regarding clinical actionability, especially when positioned against established clinical software.
5.Performance Metrics and Lesion Identification
To better evaluate the proposed model’s efficacy in lesion identification compared to the baselines, the authors should report ROC or Precision-Recall (PR) curves. Such analysis is necessary to provide a clearer understanding of the method’s capability in lesion detection and, consequently, its potential for treatment-decision support.
de Vries, Lucas, et al. “Accelerating physics-informed neural fields for fast CT perfusion analysis in acute ischemic stroke. “ Medical Imaging with Deep Learning. 2024.
De Vries, Lucas, et al. “Spatio-temporal physics-informed learning: A novel approach to CT perfusion analysis in acute ischemic stroke. “ Medical image analysis 90 (2023): 102971.
Albers, Gregory W. , et al. “Thrombectomy for stroke at 6 to 16 hours with selection by perfusion imaging. “ New England Journal of Medicine 378.8 (2018): 708-718.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
-

While the work incorporates a novel lumped parameter modeling strategy, the lack of proper baseline comparisons precludes a transparent assessment against state-of-the-art approaches. Without benchmarking against established approaches, the relative performance and actual clinical utility of the proposed model cannot be objectively assessed. Providing these comparisons is essential to contextualize the findings within this field.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes HemoPIC, a physics-informed cerebral hemodynamics digital twin for brain perfusion imaging that aims to infer clinically actionable perfusion summary maps directly from routine perfusion data without requiring manual arterial input function (AIF) selection or deconvolution. The core idea is to couple tracer mass conservation with a regionally aggregated lumped Windkessel model, and to estimate latent inflow, outflow, volume, and resistance/compliance parameters through a constrained inverse problem. In addition to producing standard perfusion quantities such as CBF, CBV, and MTT, the method is designed to reconstruct the full tracer inflow-outflow passage and expose mechanistic latent dynamics that can support forward simulation and counterfactual analysis. This makes the paper more than a map-estimation method; it is framed as a patient-specific, physics-grounded digital twin for cerebral perfusion.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper’s strongest aspect is the quality of the methodological formulation. The proposed model is mathematically well grounded, clearly motivated, and very coherent for a medical imaging paper submitted to MICCAI. Rather than introducing another loosely constrained learning pipeline, the authors derive the method from tracer transport, regional inflow-outflow balance, and a lumped Windkessel closure, then formulate estimation as a constrained inverse problem with interpretable parameters and regularization. The writing is also strong: the methods section is clear and thoughtful, and the paper does a good job of explaining how the inferred latent states relate to clinically familiar perfusion concepts. On the experimental side, the paper shows several encouraging results: the produced maps appear physiologically plausible, lesion hypoperfusion patterns are visible, regional central volume consistency is reasonably preserved, and the model offers capabilities beyond standard deconvolution, including full tracer passage reconstruction and interpretable time-scale parameters. The paper is conceptually original and I love the fact that the authors have provided anonymized code implementation.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The main weakness is that the empirical validation is still somewhat indirect relative to the ambition of the paper. Much of the evaluation compares HemoPIC to conventional deconvolution-derived perfusion maps on ISLES 2017 and emphasizes similarity of scale, lesion contrast, regional ratios, and central volume theorem consistency. These are useful sanity checks, but they do not fully establish that HemoPIC is clinically superior, more accurate with respect to ground-truth physiology, or more robust across acquisition settings. In several places, the paper demonstrates consistency with conventional outputs rather than a clearly stronger downstream endpoint. Specifically, the study is limited to a 44-patient ISLES 2017 cohort, which is a reasonable starting point but still small for a method making broad claims about routine perfusion quantification and digital-twin-based assessment. Another concern is that some practical parts of the pipeline remain dependent on design choices that may affect the inferred quantities, such as the construction of the shared arterial proxy curve, anatomical partitioning via segmentation and clustering, and voxelwise modulation of regional means using existing data maps. These choices are sensible, but they introduce modeling assumptions that could influence the resulting maps and deserve more discussion. While the method is presented as enabling simulation and counterfactual analysis, the paper only offers limited demonstration of these twin-specific advantages beyond reconstructed tracer curves and inferred Windkessel time scales.

I assigned this paper a Weak Accept. The strongest factor in its favor is the quality of the methodological contribution. The paper is mathematically grounded, clearly written, and proposes a genuinely interesting formulation that goes beyond standard perfusion post-processing. In particular, the coupling of tracer mass conservation with a regional lumped Windkessel model, and the estimation of latent inflow/outflow dynamics through a constrained inverse problem, is a thoughtful and well-structured contribution. I also found the framing compelling: the method is not only intended to produce clinically familiar perfusion maps such as CBF, CBV, and MTT, but also to reconstruct the full tracer passage and expose latent hemodynamic states for simulation-oriented analysis. This gives the paper conceptual originality and distinguishes it from purely deconvolution-based approaches. I did not score the paper higher because the empirical validation, while encouraging, remains somewhat indirect relative to the paper’s ambition. The experiments are mainly performed on the 44-patient ISLES 2017 cohort, and much of the evaluation emphasizes agreement with deconvolution-derived maps, physiological plausibility, lesion contrast, and central volume consistency. These analyses are useful, but they do not fully demonstrate that the method yields clearly superior clinical utility, stronger generalization, or more accurate physiological estimation beyond consistency with conventional outputs. In addition, several practical modeling choices, such as the construction of the global arterial proxy curve, the anatomical partitioning strategy, and the way regional estimates are distributed voxelwise, could meaningfully influence the final maps and deserve more discussion. I found the paper technically strong and above threshold, but the validation is not yet comprehensive enough for a stronger accept.

reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I recommend acceptance because this paper makes a genuinely novel and well-founded methodological contribution. HemoPIC introduces a physics-informed cerebral hemodynamics digital twin that reconstructs full tracer inflow–outflow dynamics and directly produces clinically relevant perfusion maps without manual AIF selection or deconvolution. The formulation is mathematically strong, clearly presented, and substantially more original than many incremental submissions. My main reservation was that the experimental validation was somewhat indirect relative to the ambition of the work. The rebuttal addressed this reasonably well by tempering the clinical claims and adding lesion-identification analysis showing that HemoPIC preserves lesion-relevant perfusion contrast. Although further validation would still strengthen the paper, I view it as clearly above threshold overall and recommend Accept. Kudos to the authors!

This is one of the strongest papers in this batch. Reviewer #3 assigned the maximum score (6, independent of rebuttal) and Reviewer #2 upgraded to Accept post-rebuttal. The paper presents a genuinely innovative physics-informed digital twin framework for cerebral hemodynamics, and Reviewer #3’s endorsement reflects the technical depth of coupling computational fluid dynamics with neural inference. author_feedback_text:
We are encouraged that all reviewers recognized HemoPIC as a conceptually original, well-motivated, and mathematically grounded formulation for perfusion modeling.
We especially appreciate R2 and R3 for noting that HemoPIC is “not another loosely constrained learning pipeline”, and offers “a clear operational benefit to clinical users”.
Our central goal is to establish HemoPIC as a new foundation that simultaneously reconstructs and links observed tracer dynamics, latent hemodynamics, and clinically familiar perfusion maps — without relying on the AIF or deconvolution used in existing models.
First, we address comments on evaluation and related work.
1.Clinical claims (R1, R2)
We agree that the current manuscript demonstrates methodological feasibility, physiological consistency, and perfusion-map recovery, rather than definitive clinical superiority or treatment-decision support.
We will temper our clinical wording accordingly, and present HemoPIC as a
foundation
for larger-scale validation of its generalizability and clinical actionability.
2.Downstream lesion identification (R1, R2)
We agree that, beyond the direct map-consistency analyses in Figs. 2-4, downstream lesion identification provides additional evidence of clinical relevance.
We performed ROC analysis on ISLES2017 and HemoPIC-derived maps. HemoPIC matched or exceeded ISLES2017 maps in ROC AUC: 0.76 vs 0.75 for CBF, 0.58 vs 0.58 for CBV, and 0.72 vs 0.69 for MTT. These results further support that HemoPIC preserves lesion-relevant perfusion contrast.
3.Clarifications on related work (R1)
We will strengthen these in the Introduction:
(a) PIANO [15,16] is not a direct comparison: as an advection-diffusion model, its estimates are velocity (V) and diffusion (D) fields from tracer outflow, which are
not standard
in clinical practice. In contrast, HemoPIC is designed to
connect
full inflow-outflow tracer dynamics to clinical perfusion maps.
(b) ISLES2017 maps: we clarify that our deconvolution baselines were
not
independently tuned, but taken directly from ISLES2017, with processing details described in [21]. They serve as fixed, silver-standard clinical references, rather than hand-selected baselines.
(c) Other benchmarks, including PINN variants, are relevant but target a
parallel
objective: improving the speed, robustness, and accuracy of conventional
AIF-based
computation, whereas HemoPIC derives these maps by reconstructing the underlying hemodynamics. As also noted by R2, this makes HemoPIC fundamentally different and “more than a map-estimation method”.
Further, we clarify other points on model formulation.
4.Diffusion (R1)
The diffusion term in PIANO is
not
actual molecular motion as in DWI/DTI (Sec. VI-C in [15]).
Instead, it: 
(a) represents macroscopic intra-voxel-level tracer
advection
, to compensate for unresolved fine-scale flow effects at coarse perfusion-imaging voxel resolution (Sec. II-A in [15]);
(b) contributes much less than advection (Sec. V-D in [15]).
In contrast, HemoPIC’s regional integration converts the diffusion term into a net boundary-flux residual rather than a voxel-wise field. We set this residual to zero as a lumped approximation, since effective inflow, outflow, and storage
capture
regional tracer exchange.
5.Tmax (R1)
Since HemoPIC reconstructs the full tracer passage and arterial proxy through latent hemodynamics, Tmax is
naturally recoverable
as a downstream measure of tracer arrival delay. Briefly, we define HemoPIC-derived Tmax as the nonnegative peak delay between the reconstructed tissue tracer curve and the inferred arterial proxy.
6.Compressed physics model (R3)
We agree that HemoPIC shows clinical consistency as a compact model, and more complex formulations may improve expressivity. These formulations may also raise
identifiability
challenges: we are studying when latent physiology is reliably recoverable from observations, and when more complex setups may fail.

title: Hepato-LLaVA: An Expert MLLM with Sparse Topo-Pack Attention for Hepatocellular Pathology Analysis on Whole Slide Images
abstract:
Hepatocellular Carcinoma diagnosis relies heavily on the interpretation of gigapixel Whole Slide Images. However, current computational approaches are constrained by fixed-resolution processing mechanisms and inefficient feature aggregation, which inevitably lead to either severe information loss or high feature redundancy. To address these challenges, we propose Hepato-LLaVA, a specialized Multi-modal Large Language Model designed for fine-grained hepatocellular pathology analysis. We introduce a novel Sparse Topo-Pack Attention mechanism that explicitly models 2D tissue topology. This mechanism effectively aggregates local diagnostic evidence into semantic summary tokens while preserving global context. Furthermore, to overcome the lack of multi-scale data, we present HepatoPathoVQA, a clinically grounded dataset comprising 33K hierarchically structured question-answer pairs validated by expert pathologists.
Our experiments demonstrate that Hepato-LLaVA achieves state-of-the-art performance on HCC diagnosis and captioning tasks, significantly outperforming existing methods. Our code and implementation details are available at Hepato-LLaVA-23DC.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents Hepato-LLaVA, a multimodal large language model tailored for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) analysis on whole slide images. The work has three primary contributions. First, the authors introduce HepatoPathoVQA, a multi-scale VQA dataset comprising 33K QA pairs spanning WSI, ROI, and patch levels, constructed via a hierarchical reasoning pipeline using Gemini and validated by expert pathologists. Second, they propose a Sparse Topo-Pack Attention mechanism that organizes patch tokens into local packs with summary tokens, enforcing structured sparse interactions that reflect 2D tissue topology rather than treating the slide as a flat 1D sequence. Third, a three-stage training pipeline (MAE pretraining, MoCo pretraining, and LoRA-based instruction tuning with a Q-Former connector) is designed to progressively align visual and language representations for diagnostic tasks.
reviews.text_strengths:
The clinical motivation is well-grounded. The paper identifies a real limitation in existing WSI-MLLMs — the mismatch between 1D sequence modeling and the inherently 2D spatial structure of pathological tissue — and proposes a concrete architectural response. The hierarchical diagnostic reasoning embedded in the dataset pipeline (coarse-to-fine, macroscopic to microscopic) aligns with actual pathologist workflows.
The Sparse Topo-Pack Attention is a reasonable design. The local-pack / summary-token structure is intuitive, and the paper makes a plausible case that it reduces redundancy compared with dense slide modeling.
HepatoPathoVQA is a meaningful dataset contribution. Covering three spatial scales with both VQA pairs and caption data for pre-training, and validated by three pathologists under blind evaluation (Pearson r=0.96, <2% rejection rate), it addresses a genuine data gap in HCC-specific computational pathology.
The quantitative results are strong and the ablation studies are reasonably comprehensive. The comparison across connector types, token counts, and training strategies in Tables 2 and 3 provides clear support for the main design choices. The gap between Hepato-LLaVA (Avg 0.83) and the next best method (0.66) is substantial.
Code is made available via an anonymized link, which supports reproducibility.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The main weakness is that the evaluation is largely self-contained. The training data and benchmark are both derived from the same Gemini-assisted pipeline on the same pool of 200 WSIs, so it is hard to judge how much of the gain would transfer to an external cohort with independently curated labels.
I also think the paper could do a better job isolating where the gains actually come from. The method combines a new sparse encoder, a new multi-scale dataset, and a multi-stage training recipe, but the ablations do not fully separate these factors. In particular, the contribution of the MoCo stage is not shown directly.
Another missing piece is efficiency evidence. The paper motivates the method partly in terms of redundancy and computational cost, but does not report runtime, memory, or inference cost.
Finally, the open-ended evaluation relies partly on LLM-based scoring, and I would have liked to see either stronger human evaluation or at least more detail on how reliable that metric is in this setting.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses a legitimate problem in WSI-based pathology MLLMs and proposes technically reasonable solutions backed by solid experimental results. The dataset contribution alone has value for the community. That said, the absence of any external validation is the main factor holding back a stronger recommendation — the benchmark used for evaluation was constructed by the same pipeline used to generate training data, which makes the performance numbers difficult to fully trust at face value. The missing MoCo ablation and lack of runtime analysis are secondary concerns. If the authors can provide even preliminary results on an external HCC cohort and clarify the MoCo contribution in the rebuttal, I would be willing to revise upward.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have adequately addressed my main concerns. The additional MoCo ablation (w/o MoCo: 0.75 vs full model: 0.83) confirms that each training stage contributes meaningfully. The cross-dataset evaluation on WSI-Bench, while showing a modest gap from SOTA (0.502 vs 0.566), provides at least preliminary evidence of generalizability beyond the self-constructed benchmark. The reported inference time (4.3 mins/slide) also substantiates the efficiency claims. I am raising my score to 5.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper proposes Hepato-LLaVA, a Multi-modal Large Language Model (MLLM) tailored for Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC). To effectively and efficiently capture and summarize information from gigapixel whole slide images (WSIs), a Sparse Topo-Pack Attention mechanism is introduced to preserve the 2D tissue topology of WSIs.
In addition, the authors construct HepatoPathoVQA, a multi-scale WSI dataset for HCC diagnosis via visual question answering (VQA). Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves around a 20% improvement in HCC diagnosis, outperforming existing approaches.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper proposes a WSI topology-aware attention mechanism. Most recent WSI models treat patch tokens as a flattened 1D sequence during processing, which overlooks the inherent 2D structure of WSIs and breaks the underlying tissue topology. In addition, tissues or lesions often span multiple neighboring patches while exhibiting weaker correlations with distant patches; thus, tokens from neighboring patches should be more important than distant tokens in the local view at the lowest scale. The proposed Sparse Topo-Pack Attention organizes patch tokens into several 2D hierarchical views and processes them hierarchically, effectively preserving the 2D tissue topology while efficiently aggregating global WSI information across patches.
2.The paper constructs a multi-scale WSI VQA dataset with three different scales of HCC samples. The authors claim that this is the first multi-scale WSI dataset for HCC, which helps bridge the gap between research datasets and real-world clinical practice, and provides a valuable resource for future studies.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The ablation study is incomplete. The paper conducts experiments on different design choices of the connector; however, the connector is only a part of the proposed MLLM. A more comprehensive ablation, with different proposed modules enabled or disabled, is suggested to better evaluate the effectiveness and individual contributions of the proposed components.
2.The proposed method is compared with six state-of-the-art methods on the constructed HCC dataset. However, although the models are trained on an HCC dataset, the proposed method may have the potential to generalize to other diseases. 
It would strengthen the paper, especially for a journal extension, to include comparisons on additional HCC datasets or datasets from other diseases.
3.A minor issue: the full name of VQA should be defined before introducing the abbreviation.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

In addition to developing the HCC-specialized MLLM, the paper introduces a novel topology-aware attention mechanism that effectively preserves WSI topology while efficiently extracting global WSI information. The paper also constructs a multi-scale WSI VQA dataset for HCC diagnosis, providing a valuable resource for future research.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The reviewer considers the paper to have sufficient contributions, and the authors adequately addressed the reviewer’s concerns in the rebuttal.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: For hepatocellular carcinoma analysis on whole-slide pathology images, the authors propose Hepato-LLaVA, a domain-specific multimodal model with a Sparse Topo-Pack Attention design that explicitly uses tissue topology to compress gigapixel slides more efficiently while retaining diagnostically important local details. They also introduce HepatoPathoVQA, a clinically grounded multi-scale dataset that supports coarse-to-fine reasoning across whole-slide, ROI, and patch views, enabling the model to learn more clinically useful visual-language understanding for diagnosis.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The motivation is well grounded, and the proposed Hepato-LLaVA surpasses previous pathology-specific multimodal large models on hepatocellular carcinoma analysis. 
2.The authors also construct HepatoPathoVQA, a large-scale multi-scale dataset that provides a strong foundation for subsequent hepatocellular pathology analysis on whole-slide images. 
3.In addition, they introduce HepatoPathoBench, which facilitates a more systematic evaluation of existing multimodal large models in hepatocellular pathology analysis.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The proposed Sparse Topo-Pack Attention (STPA) appears to be applied in the slide encoder, whereas the ablation results in Table 3 focus on the connector. This discrepancy makes it hard to determine whether STPA itself improves token efficiency.
2.The paper also introduces additional MAE pretraining and MoCo pretraining stages, both of which may bring independent performance gains. Since existing models such as SlideChat and WSI-LLaVA do not adopt these training stages, it remains unclear whether the performance improvement truly comes from STPA.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The main reason is that the current manuscript does not provide clear evidence that the proposed Sparse Topo-Pack Attention strategy is truly effective for hepatocellular pathology analysis on whole-slide images.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper introduces a multi-modal large language model for fine-grained analysis of hepatocellular pathology which utilizes a “sparse Topo-pack” attention mechanism to integrate local and global information. Additionally, they introduce a multi-scale visual-question-answering dataset, HepatoPathoVQA.
Reviewers agree that the dataset with its multi-scale setup addresses an important task and gap in digital pathology. They further appreciate the overall design of the attention mechanism and the model from coarse to fine.
They criticize, however, that the evaluation is largely self-contained (see comments below) and that the ablation studies do not sufficiently disentangle all components. Additionally, no information about runtime or computational complexity is provided.
In the rebuttal, the authors should address how reliable/independent a benchmark is on a dataset that shares substantial parts of the pipeline with the pipeline for generating training data, and why performance improvements can be expected to translate to independent tasks or datasets. Furthermore, please address the comment on how well the ablation studies demonstrate the utility of the proposed method and to what extent changing (pre-)training steps may bias the results.
Please note there should be no new results added in the rebuttal phase.

Reviewers agree that the authors adequately addressed concerns in their rebuttal and univocally vote for acceptance. The overall assessment however may be seen as borderline as the authors added new ablation studies in their rebuttal.

The paper presents a meaningful methodological contribution, supported by a valuable dataset resource and strong experimental results. Overall, the paper is considered to make a solid contribution and meets the acceptance threshold for MICCAI.

The main concerns raised by reviewers are the lack of external validation, reliance on a self-constructed benchmark, and insufficient evidence supporting the effectiveness of the Sparse Topo-Pack Attention strategy for HCC pathology. The authors have addressed most of the concerns in the rebuttal.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all the reviewers and the Area Chair for their insightful comments and recognition of our work. Below, we address the main concerns regarding Ablation, Data, and Inference.
Q1.Ablation (Component Disentanglement & STPA Effectiveness)
Dear reviewer #2, #3, #4,
Our proposed modules act as an integrated whole to solve redundancy and information deficiency issues in existing slide encoders when processing WSIs. Both the MoCo training and the Q-Former connector depend on the summary tokens produced by the STPA slide encoder. Due to this tight coupling and strict page limits, our paper only included the connector ablation. 
We now provide additional results on HepatoPathoBench. First, Hepto-LLaVA w/o MoCo scored 0.75, validating the effectiveness of our two-stage pre-training strategy. Although lower than our full Hepto-LLaVA (0.83), it still higher than SlideChat (0.66) and WSI-LLaVA (0.65), which is also consistent with the findings of Prov-GigaPath[1]. Second, fine-tuned WSI-LLaVA scored 0.70, which uses LongNet as the slide encoder and trains on the same dataset. This is higher than WSI-LLaVA (0.65) but lower than Hepto-LLaVA (0.83), directly validating the effectiveness of our designed STPA architecture.
Together with the additional ablation results, these findings further demonstrate that the performance gains mainly originate from our designed STPA architecture, and that each proposed component consistently contributes to the overall improvement.
Q2.Data (Quality, Evaluation Fairness, and Generalization)
Dear reviewer #2, #3,
We strictly separate the training and validation sets at the patient level with no WSI overlap. All samples are generated through the same unified pipeline rather than curated as dataset-specific groups. To guarantee high quality and avoid homogenization, the pipeline integrates 3 different resolutions and 8 sub-categories, and all annotations were subjected to strict quality control. Three professional pathologists conducted blind evaluations of the generated data, achieving high consistency (Pearson r=0.96) and a rejection rate of <2\%. Furthermore, the LLM-based open-ended evaluation results strongly align with our human expert judgments.
We also note that the currently available HCC subset in WSI-Bench contains only 27 WSIs and 103 QA pairs, while our HepatoPathoBench further introduces multi-resolution evaluation, making the benchmark more comprehensive and challenging. To further validate cross-dataset generalization, we directly evaluated our model on the HCC subset of WSI-Bench without additional adaptation. Our Hepto-LLaVA scored 0.502, remaining competitive with the current SOTA result of 0.566.
Q3.Efficiency and Computational Complexity
Dear reviewer #2, #4
By restricting patch-level interactions within local packs and utilizing summary tokens for inter-pack global context, STPA reduces the theoretical attention overhead to roughly 1%. Coupled with a lightweight backbone and blank-patch filtering, our end-to-end feature extraction (from SVS to PT tensors) averages 4.3 mins/slide, a significant acceleration compared to the 19.3 mins/slide required by Prov-GigaPath [1]. Furthermore, our slide encoder and connector condense the final visual input for the LLM to just 32 tokens, whereas Prov-GigaPath requires 576 tokens, yielding substantial efficiency advantages during downstream LLM processing.
Q4.The Minor Issue
Dear reviewer #3
We will add the full definition of Visual Question Answering (VQA) before its first occurrence in the revised manuscript.
[1] Xu et al., “A whole-slide foundation model for digital pathology from real-world data”, Nature 2024.

title: HERO: Hypothesis-Driven Evidence Retrieval from Omics for Multi-task Breast Cancer Analysis
abstract: Matched multi-omics can improve WSI-based biomarker and prognosis prediction, but most existing pipelines use omics as a parallel feature stream or textual context rather than as an explicit retrieval constraint. HERO asks whether observed omics can be a testable morphology hypothesis: a sparse pathway-to-morphology prior maps DNA methylation and miRNA into a K-dimensional intent vector m (K=16), TF-IDF retrieval over structured 10× captions selects endpoint-relevant regions, and a cosine gate c=cos(m,v) triggers deterministic deficit-driven repair when c<τc. This closed-loop design bounds VLM calls, reduces reliance on embedding-based semantic matching, and makes every retrieval and verification step lexically auditable. On TCGA-BRCA (930 WSIs, patient-level 5-fold CV), HERO sets new state-of-the-art across ER, PR, HER2, subtype, and risk prediction, outperforming both multimodal fusion and VLM-based baselines.
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers
Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs
Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper presents an interesting and potentially impactful idea: rather than treating omics as a conventional parallel feature stream, it uses omics as both a retrieval prior and a consistency constraint for pathology evidence selection. In particular, DNA methylation and miRNA are first transformed into an intent vector $m$ and a keyword set $Q$, which guide patch retrieval through caption-based lexical matching. The retrieved evidence is then verified against the molecular hypothesis via a consistency score $c=\cos(m,v)$, with an additional deficit-driven repair step when the alignment is insufficient. This closed-loop design is conceptually novel and distinguishes the work from standard multimodal fusion or post-hoc interpretability approaches.
At the same time, I am not yet fully convinced by the current presentation and experimental support. While the overall framework is well motivated and the reported results are promising, several important aspects remain insufficiently specified or insufficiently validated. In particular, the method relies heavily on text-mediated intermediate representations, yet the prompts, structured outputs, and captioning details are not described in enough detail for reproducibility. More importantly, the paper does not fully rule out alternative explanations for the observed gains, especially given the strong correlation between the omics input and the prediction targets. Additional clarification on label provenance, stronger shortcut-control ablations, and more rigorous validation of the caption-based intermediate pipeline would substantially strengthen the paper. Overall, I view this work as promising, but I believe the current manuscript still leaves several key methodological and experimental questions unresolved.
reviews.text_strengths:
This paper presents an interesting and well-motivated framework for multi-task breast cancer analysis from whole-slide images and matched multi-omics. The main strength of the work is its clear methodological position. Instead of treating omics as a standard parallel feature stream, the proposed method uses omics to guide two key parts of the pipeline: where to look in the slide and whether the retrieved visual evidence is sufficient to support the molecular hypothesis. This is an important distinction from prior approaches, which mainly rely on post-hoc MIL localization, VLM-based reading without specific priors, or conventional multimodal fusion. In this sense, the paper offers a clear and recognizable contribution. 
Another strong point is the coherence of the overall design. The pipeline forms a closed loop from the omics-derived intent vector m, to the keyword set Q, to Top-64 patch retrieval, to the visual evidence vector v, the consistency score c, the deficit term d=m−v, and finally the repair step. This information flow is logically connected and easy to follow. I also appreciate that the method uses checklist matching and TF-IDF retrieval instead of relying only on embedding-based retrieval. This makes the retrieval and verification process more transparent and easier to inspect.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Insufficient methodological detail limits reproducibility. 
The paper presents a clear four-stage framework, but many details that are important for reproduction are still missing. For example, the prompts, output formats, decoding settings, and keyword extraction rules are not fully described. These are not minor implementation choices, because they directly affect retrieval quality and evidence verification.
2.Eq. (1) and several Stage 1 definitions remain unclear. 
The formulation of Eq. (1) is not fully precise, especially the normalization term, whose exact meaning is difficult to interpret from the current text. In addition, the paper does not provide the full definitions of the 16 morphology axes, the checklist terms, or the detailed pathway-to-axis assignments in W. As a result, the proposed prior is conceptually appealing, but still difficult to reproduce in practice.
3.The implementation of Stage 3 repair is still under-specified. 
Stage 3 is one of the most important parts of the method, but some key steps are not explained clearly enough. In particular, it is not clear how the final “best 64” patches are selected after the repair patches are added back to the pool. It is also unclear whether the model captions the full 8×8 mosaic, each 20× patch separately, or both.
4.The text-based bridge is interesting, but it may introduce a same-model bias. 
The method uses text as an intermediate bridge between omics and image evidence, which is an interesting design choice. However, the same model family is used both to generate intermediate captions and to make the final prediction. The paper shows that Qwen2.5-VL can generate captions, but it does not yet show strongly enough that these captions are pathologically accurate and stable enough to support the downstream reasoning process. Why not chose medical domian VLMs ?
5.The risk of shortcut learning from omics is not fully excluded. 
The omics input is highly related to several prediction targets, especially HER2, subtype, and possibly risk. This raises the concern that the model may rely heavily on molecular priors instead of truly learning to organize image evidence. Although the paper compares different retrieval strategies under the same diagnosis head, stronger control experiments, such as removing or shuffling omics, would be needed to rule out this alternative explanation more convincingly.
6.The data and label sources are not described clearly enough. 
The experimental section clearly reports the TCGA-BRCA cohort, including 930 WSIs, 878 patients, 14,115 CpGs, and 315 miRNAs, as well as the prediction targets ER, PR, HER2, subtype, and risk. However, the manuscript does not explain in enough detail how these target labels were obtained or defined. For example, it is unclear whether ER/PR/HER2 labels come from IHC/ISH results or from clinical phenotype tables, how subtype is defined, and how the risk labels are constructed. This weakens the interpretation of the results, especially because omics is used as an input while the targets are also strongly related to molecular status.
7.The fairness of the baseline comparison needs to be discussed more carefully. 
The paper states that, for fairness, all multimodal baselines were implemented using the same concatenated DNA methylation and miRNA vectors as the proposed method. While this makes the input setting more uniform, it may also move some baselines away from their original or best-performing configurations. As a result, the comparison may reflect performance under a unified input protocol rather than the true strength of each baseline in its intended setting. This point is particularly important for methods such as MCAT, MOTCat, and SurvPath, which are based on different modeling assumptions.
8.External validation is missing. 
All experiments are conducted on TCGA-BRCA using patient-level 5-fold cross-validation, which is a reasonable internal evaluation setup. However, this is still a single-dataset, single-cohort, and single-cancer study. For a method that depends heavily on caption quality, predefined vocabularies, and omics-to-morphology correspondence, the lack of external validation makes it difficult to assess robustness across scanners, staining conditions, institutions, and population shifts. The proposed consistency gate may improve internal reliability, but it does not by itself demonstrate cross-center generalization.
9.Table 3 provides only limited support for the importance of W. 
The paper uses W-noise, W-drop, and W-shuffle to argue that the prior W captures meaningful biological structure. However, noise and drop lead to only small performance changes, while shuffle causes a more visible drop. This suggests that the coarse structure of W may be useful, but it does not strongly demonstrate that the precise expert-designed mapping is essential. In addition, the paper does not clearly define how noise and drop are implemented or how strong these perturbations are, which makes the robustness claim harder to evaluate. 
10.The ablation study is still incomplete. 
The paper focuses the main ablation study on HER2 and Risk, which is reasonable because these tasks are likely to depend strongly on retrieval quality. However, since the method is presented as a unified multi-task framework, it would also be useful to show whether similar trends hold for ER, PR, and subtype. In addition, while the paper shows that text-based retrieval outperforms visual-only retrieval and that gate+repair is helpful, it does not provide more direct ablations of the final diagnosis stage, such as using only the final 20× mosaic, only the molecular narrative, only the consistency summary, or removing the narrative input altogether. Without these analyses, the contribution of each Stage 4 input remains unclear.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a meaningful shift from treating omics as a parallel feature stream to using omics as a retrieval-controlling hypothesis. However, the current manuscript still leaves several important methodological and experimental questions unanswered, especially regarding reproducibility, shortcut risk, and the reliability of the text-mediated intermediate representations. I therefore view this work as promising but not yet fully convincing in its current form.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of HERO is a novel hypothesis-driven evidence retrieval framework that uses matched multi-omics data (DNA methylation + miRNA) as a testable morphology hypothesis to actively guide region selection and verify molecular-visual consistency in whole-slide images via a cosine consistency gate and deficit-driven repair, enabling more accurate, interpretable, and endpoint-aware multi-task breast cancer analysis.
reviews.text_strengths: One notable aspect is the concept itself. Most papers merely regard biological data as an additional feature or something similar. However, in this case, it is utilized as a hypothesis that directs the entire retrieval process. I appreciate this methodology. The consistency gate mechanism, where the author(s) assess whether the observed image corresponds with the molecular signal, is quite ingenious. If the score falls below a certain threshold, it automatically seeks different patches. This approach is logical. The results are also exceptionally robust. The author(s) conducted tests on the TCGA dataset, which comprises 930 slide images, and they outperformed all other methods. The enhancement in HER2 is 0.050 AUC, which is a significant figure. Additionally, the improvement in risk prediction is 0.030 C-index. These enhancements are particularly noteworthy for challenging prediction tasks. Another commendable aspect is the transparency of the system’s operations. One can observe which regions it focuses on, the features it identifies, and how these contribute to the final outcome. This transparency is crucial for doctors or clinics, as they need to understand the rationale behind the machine’s decisions. The author(s) employ word matching instead of complex embedding techniques, which ensures that interpretations do not deviate into nonsensical territory. Everything can be traced back to the actual text. The ablation study presented in table 2 is informative. When the author(s) compare text-based retrieval with visual-only embedding, the text-based approach significantly outperforms by a margin of 0.077 on HER2 AUC. This finding is intriguing as it indicates that the significance of pathology terminology outweighs the aesthetic appeal or prominence of the images. Furthermore, the robustness aspect concerning the W matrix is commendable. The author(s) manually constructed W based on medical guidelines, and when they shuffled it, the performance decreased by 0.033.In contrast, when they merely added noise, the performance drop was only 0.009.This demonstrates that the author(s) are not merely fitting random elements but are genuinely encoding authentic biological knowledge.
reviews.text_weaknesses: Initially, the author(s) conduct tests using only a single dataset. While TCGA is well-known, it is essential to evaluate other datasets to demonstrate the general applicability of the findings. Furthermore, the 930 slides are relatively small compared to contemporary standards. Regarding the axes defined, specifically the 16 morphological features, are this exclusive to breast cancer? Can this methodology be applied to other types of cancer? This remains uncertain. Additionally, the speed of the process raises concerns. They report a duration of 57 seconds per slide using two powerful GPUs, which is quite substantial. In a real hospital setting, such a wait time per case is impractical. Moreover, the VLM model is invoked multiple times at various stages, and the repair process occurs in 37% of the slides, indicating a significant amount of additional computation. The authors should provide more insight into which components consume the most time. Why was K=16 selected in the first place? As shown in Table 3, K=32 yields nearly identical results (0.867 vs. 0.865). Why not opt for 32 or even 8? Although they perform a sensitivity analysis, this suggests that the author(s) may not have thoroughly optimized this parameter. Which specific 16 axes did the author(s) choose, and what was the rationale behind selecting these particular axes? There is also a lack of discussion regarding potential failures (the sad path). They present one successful case in Figure 3, but what happens when the system identifies incorrect regions? What if the genetic data does not align with the morphological data? Such discrepancies can occur in real cancer cases. While the consistency gate provides some assistance, what about these adverse scenarios? The entire system relies on the Qwen2.5-VL model for generating image captions. If this model inaccurately describes the morphological features, it could lead to failures downstream. They claim that a structured prompt enhances reliability, yet the author(s) do not provide any analysis to support this. For instance, how often does the VLM misdescribe features? What percentage of the captions is genuinely accurate? The construction of the W matrix is also ambiguous. The author(s) mention adherence to WHO guidelines, but the specifics are unclear. What happens when different pathways suggest the same axis? To what extent is human judgment involved in this process? Would different individuals arrive at different W constructions? Finally, for actual deployment in a hospital setting, validation on entirely different datasets is necessary. This includes variations in hospitals, scanners, and staining techniques. Five- Five-Fold CV on single dataset is not enough.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
TECHNICAL CONCERNS
In equation 1 they put negative signs but are not clear enough. High methylation means pathway down? Should be clearer in text.
The TF-IDF on 300 captions seem small. How stable is the IDF weight? If they pick 300 different representatives instead, does retrieval ranking change lot?
The threshold for consistency is 0.5 but why? They show in table 3 it works but they do not really justify why 0.5 is good choice. Seems kind of arbitrary.
Figure 3 is very messy and hard to read. Too much information, text too small.
They generate “molecular narrative” text but then not really use it much afterward? Or maybe use but not explain clearly.

This paper introduces an innovative and promising concept and utilizing matched multi-omics data as a testable morphology hypothesis to actively facilitate evidence retrieval and confirm consistency in whole-slide image (WSI) analysis. The hypothesis-driven retrieval, combined with a consistency gate and deficit-driven repair, is an intelligent approach that addresses a significant limitation in current MIL, VLM-based, and multimodal fusion methodologies. The findings on TCGA-BRCA are robust (new state-of-the-art across various endpoints, with substantial improvements on HER2 (+0.050 AUC) and risk prediction (+0.030 C-index)), and the ablation studies effectively demonstrate the importance of text-based retrieval and the consistency mechanism. The focus on interpretability (lexical matching, auditable evidence chain) represents a distinct advantage for clinical application.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: Authors introduce HERO, a four-stage pipeline designed for retrieval based on omics data. The framework not only retrieves relevant evidence but also evaluates whether the retrieved results align with expected outcomes. If discrepancies are detected, HERO initiates a repair loop to refine the retrieval process and improve consistency.
reviews.text_strengths: Novelty: HERO’s main strength is the introduction of a RAG-like pipeline for whole slide images (WSIs), where retrieval is not treated as a one-shot step but is coupled with a verification and repair loop. This verify-retry mechanism ensures that retrieved omics evidence is actively checked against expectations and refined when necessary, leading to more reliable outputs. The approach also represents a shift from standard practices.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Abstract’s opening claim: The first sentence of the abstract appears somewhat strong, as there is existing literature supporting the claim that predicting biomarkers and prognosis from WSIs benefits from matched multi-omics data. For example: Hu, Jia, et al. “Prediction of clinicopathological features, multi-omics events and prognosis based on digital pathology and deep learning in HR+/HER2− breast cancer.” Journal of thoracic disease 15.5 (2023): 2528.- Terminology and claims in the introduction: The term “evidence drift” could be reconsidered in favor of more established terminology such as “retrieval bias”, which may better convey the underlying issue. Additionally, the statement that VLM-based WSI readers and multi-agent systems explore without endpoint-specific priors appears somewhat strong. In practice, such priors can often be incorporated through prompting, and acknowledging this could provide a more balanced perspective.
Limited clarity in methodology: While the architectural components are presented, the overall description remains quite concise, which may hinder full comprehension. In particular, some variables and acronyms are not explicitly defined. A more structured and detailed exposition of the pipeline, including clearer definitions and intermediate steps, would improve readability and make the method easier to follow.
Training and fine-tuning details: It is not entirely clear why only Stage 4 is fine-tuned with LoRA. Clarification on whether tuning other stages was considered, and how this might affect performance, would be valuable. Moreover, additional details on the training process across all models, especially regarding convergence criteria and fine-tuning protocols for the baselines, would help ensure a fair and transparent comparison.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Formatting issue in Section 2.3: The equation extends beyond the page margins, which affects readability. Adjusting the formatting would improve the presentation.

I thank the Authors for their work and for addressing an important problem. The paper presents an interesting and conceptually meaningful approach with promising results, but would benefit from clearer methodological exposition and more detailed experimental reporting.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text: The authors propose HERO, a novel retrievel framework to integrate omics data in computational pathology analysis. While the paper could benefit from providing more methodological details and experimental reporting, all reviewers agree that the method is novel and promising. The paper can create opportunity for discussion and potentially inspire similar work. Therefore I recommend acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their careful reading and constructive feedback. It is encouraging that the main point of HERO was clear: we use omics not as another feature vector, but as a hypothesis that tells the model where to look and then checks whether the retrieved tissue evidence agrees with it. Several parts of the paper were too compressed, and a few claims should be worded more carefully. We do not add new experiments here; instead, we will use the camera-ready revision to add concise clarifications where space permits.
We will add a compact algorithm/table with the 16 morphology axes, example checklist terms, the Stage-1 output schema, the 10x/20x prompts, decoding settings, and the construction and perturbation of W. Eq. (1) will be rewritten to state that the denominator is pathway-wise averaging over selected features, and that the negative sign converts promoter hypermethylation and miRNA-mediated repression into pathway down-regulation scores. We will also state that W is binary/nonnegative before row normalization, fixed across folds, and not learned from endpoint labels.We will also clarify the repair step. The 10x captions are generated for the 300 representative patches. The selected 20x crops are arranged into a coordinate-labeled 8x8 mosaic and processed by the VLM in one call, which returns structured tile descriptions. If c < tau_c, we compute the deficit from m-v, score unselected representatives by score_10 + w’^T a_i, add the top 32 candidates, and rebuild the final 64-patch mosaic from this repaired pool before one more 20x captioning pass. This final selection step will be described more clearly.
We do not claim that omics alone is uninformative; several targets are molecularly related by definition. Our point is that HERO uses omics to organize visual evidence, not to replace it. We will clarify that endpoint labels come from TCGA clinical/molecular annotations and survival endpoints, not from the input omics vectors used by HERO, and we will spell out the definitions for ER/PR/HER2, subtype, and risk. We will also soften wording such as “prevents shortcut learning”: W, lexical retrieval, and the controlled VLM baselines are safeguards and diagnostic checks, not proof that shortcuts are impossible.For baselines and parameters, we will add the missing caveats. Multimodal baselines were run with the same DNA methylation+miRNA input for a controlled comparison, but this may not be each method’s best original setting. K=16 was chosen as a practical middle point: K=8 is less specific, while K=32 gives little extra gain but requires more vocabulary design. tau_c=0.5 was not tuned per endpoint; the sensitivity results show similar behavior from 0.3 to 0.7.We will also define W-noise, W-drop, W-shuffle, and state that TF-IDF is fit locally on the 300 representative captions of each slide. Only Stage 4 is tuned because Stages 1-3 are kept deterministic and frozen, so the effect of the retrieval and verification mechanism can be isolated.
We used Qwen2.5-VL because it gives an open and reproducible captioning/diagnosis pipeline under one setup. However, structured prompting does not guarantee pathologic correctness. We will revise the text to say that checklist matching and the consistency gate make the evidence chain inspectable, while caption errors and possible same-model bias remain limitations.Finally, we will state the other limitations more directly. TCGA-BRCA 5-fold CV is internal validation. We also acknowledge the computational overhead (57s/WSI) raised by Reviewer #3; optimizing the multi-stage VLM calls and inference speed is a critical next step before real-world clinical deployment. We will replace or qualify “evidence drift” as “retrieval bias”, soften the abstract opening, improve Fig. 3 readability, fix the long equation formatting, and add the missing LoRA/training details.

title: Heterogeneity-Adaptive Diffusion Schrödinger Bridge for PET-Guided Whole-Body MRI Translation
abstract:
While whole-body multimodal medical imaging scanners have
been increasingly recognized for more effective medical applications, the excessive long acquisition time in PET–MR scanning is a major obstacle in more efficient clinical practice. Deep learning–based MRI translation provides a potential solution to reduce scan duration. However, current
models often focus on specific anatomical regions and face challenges for whole-body scans that consists of highly heterogeneous feature distributions mainly due to (1) different anatomical regions across whole-body, and (2) lesions or pathological tissues. This paper tackles the challenges
through a novel Heterogeneity-Adaptive Diffusion Schrödinger Bridge (HA-DSB) framework. By explicitly modeling translation as stochastic transport between source and target distributions, HA-DSB incorporates region context embeddings derived from a vision-language model (VLM) to enable region-specific modeling. To enhance fidelity of the pathological tissue, lesion-aware metabolic prior from PET is integrated directly into the bridge dynamics through a dual-stage guidance mechanism. Specifically, a PET-guided noise modulation module adaptively scales spatial diffusion perturbations during the forward process, while PET features are leveraged during the reverse process to selectively amplify lesion-relevant structures via an attention mechanism. Experiments demonstrate the superiority of our method across all body regions in whole-
body MRI translation and show improved translation quality in lesion areas under PET guidance.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose a Heterogeneity-Adaptive Diffusion Schrödinger Bridge (HA-DSB) framework for PET-guided whole-body MR translation. To handle highly heterogeneous feature distributions across the whole body, the method incorporates region context embeddings derived from a vision-language model (VLM). Furthermore, it integrates a dual-stage PET guidance mechanism, comprising forward process noise modulation and reverse process multi-scale attention, to enhance the structural fidelity of pathological tissues.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Methodological Formulation: Explicitly modeling MR translation as a stochastic transport problem between source and target distributions via DSB is theoretically sound and effectively addresses the over-smoothing issues inherent in standard implicit diffusion alignment for whole-body datasets. 
2.Targeted Adaptive Mechanisms: The dual-stage PET guidance is logically designed. Using PET uptake to spatially modulate the forward diffusion perturbations correctly redistributes the learning difficulty, preventing the model from heavily biasing toward dominant healthy tissues. 
3.Good Intra-Domain and Lesion-Specific Evaluation: Compiling a dataset of 246 whole-body PET/MR subjects is a commendable effort given the prolonged acquisition time and high cost of this modality. More importantly, the explicit isolation and evaluation of a clinically confirmed lesion cohort (21 patients) demonstrates a rigorous experimental design, providing convincing evidence of the method’s superiority in synthesizing pathological regions within the source distribution.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Clinical Assumption Limitations: The noise modulation mechanism assumes that lesions typically manifest as focal high-uptake signals in PET. This design fundamentally neglects hypometabolic or photopenic lesions. The framework’s performance on low-uptake pathological structures remains unverified and theoretically questionable. 
2.Empirical Parameter Sensitivity: The spatial scaling map bounds for the noise modulator \mathcal{M}
\phi are set to s
{min}=0.2 and s_{max}=2.0 without theoretical justification. The paper lacks an ablation study analyzing the model’s sensitivity to these hyperparameters. 
3.VLM Dependency and Reliability: The generation of region context embeddings relies entirely on Google Gemini 3 Pro. While the authors state its reliability has been empirically verified, the paper lacks transparency regarding how hallucinated labels or misalignments in slice-level organ classification were systematically handled or filtered during training. 
4.The risk of distribution shift in single-center data: The dataset, while large, is collected from a single institution using a single scanner model. The framework’s robustness against multi-center distribution shifts and varying acquisition protocols is unverified, which limits its immediate clinical translation potential.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
No.

This submission addresses a highly significant clinical bottleneck (prolonged whole-body PET/MR acquisition) with a highly tailored and mathematically rigorous approach (HA-DSB). The quantitative and qualitative results, especially the improvements in lesion-containing areas, demonstrate clear clinical utility. However, the paper operates on a simplified assumption regarding PET lesion signatures and lacks sensitivity analyses for key hyper-parameters. I am recommending a Weak Accept, contingent upon a satisfactory rebuttal clarifying the robustness of the noise modulator and the framework’s applicability to non-hypermetabolic lesions.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have addressed and responded to the questions I raised. I have no further questions.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a heterogeneity-adaptive diffusion Schrödinger bridge framework for PET-guided whole-body MRI translation. Its main contribution is to explicitly model both anatomical and pathological heterogeneity in whole-body imaging through region-aware conditioning, PET-guided modulation, and PET-aware attention, leading to improved synthesis quality across body regions, especially on lesion-containing slices.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper addresses a clinically meaningful and well-motivated problem. In whole-body PET/MR examinations, multiple MR sequences are often required, resulting in long acquisition time. In this context, PET-assisted whole-body MR-to-MR translation is clinically relevant because it may reduce the need for acquiring additional MR sequences and improve scanning efficiency. The method is technically sound and reasonably novel in adapting a Schrödinger bridge framework to heterogeneous whole-body PET/MR translation, and the experiments show consistent improvements over competitive baselines, with particularly encouraging results on lesion-containing slices. The paper is also clearly written and well presented.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The ablation study could be stronger. Since the method includes several key components, more detailed ablations would be helpful to isolate the contribution of each module. And it seems that the author does not intend to make the project code open source.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Because this paper has clear clinical significance, is written clearly and logically, and has a high degree of innovation in methods. However, since the authors did not express any intention to release the source code, it can only be given a score of four.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposed a heterogeneity-adaptive diffusion Schrödinger bridge framework for whole-body MRI translation in PET/MR imaging. The method incorporates region-context embeddings to model anatomical heterogeneity across body regions and introduces PET-guided lesion-aware mechanisms to improve translation quality in pathological areas.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem, namely whole-body MRI translation in PET/MR, which is more challenging than region-specific translation due to large anatomical variability across the body. The method is designed to account for both regional heterogeneity and lesion-related information, and the overall framework is clearly motivated from the clinical and technical challenges described in the paper.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The reliability of the automatically generated body-location and organ labels is not sufficiently validated. The paper states that Google Gemini 3 Pro is used to generate these labels and that their reliability has been empirically verified, but no supporting experiments or detailed analysis are provided. This is a fundamental issue because the usefulness of the proposed conditioning depends directly on label quality.
It is unclear whether the frozen PubMedBERT encoder is suitable for encoding fine-grained anatomical labels in MRI. The paper does not provide evidence that PubMedBERT can adequately represent subtle organ-level distinctions in this imaging setting.
The rationale for fusing coarse-grained body-location information with fine-grained organ information through multi-head cross-attention is insufficiently justified. The paper does not explain why both are needed or whether this design is more effective than using either source alone. No ablation is provided to support the necessity of this component.
Table 1 reports per-region quantitative results on the test set, but statistical significance is not provided, making it difficult to judge whether the reported improvements are robust.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I recommend rejection because several key design choices are not sufficiently validated or justified. In particular,
the paper does not provide convincing evidence for the reliability of the automatically generated anatomical labels, even though these labels are central to the proposed conditioning strategy.
The use of a frozen PubMedBERT encoder for fine-grained MRI-related anatomical semantics is also not adequately supported.
the motivation and effectiveness of fusing body-location and organ information are not clearly demonstrated.
the lack of statistical significance analysis weakens confidence in the reported quantitative improvements
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

meta_reviews.text:
Mixed reviews 2 weak accept and 1 reject. All reviewers suggested that the paper is well motivated and addresses an important question.
Key issues to address in rebuttal include: (1) assumptions and clinical cases, particularly the reliance on hypermetabolic PET signals and lack of validation on low-uptake lesions (R1); (2) validation of key components, including the reliability of VLM-generated labels and justification of the conditioning design (R1, R3); (3) limited robustness and generalization, due to single-center data and lack of evaluation under distribution shifts (R1); (4) clarity on key modules and hyperparameters (R1, R2, R3).
The authors should carefully address the reviewers’ comments and provide clarification on important methods and results questions.

Reviewers 1 and 2 recommend accept. The work presents a principled, mathematically sound methodological contribution by leveraging a Diffusion Schrödinger Bridge for PET-guided whole-body MRI translation.
While Reviewer 3 suggested reject initially. They have not provided post-rebuttal comments. Based on their initial reviewers, major concerns on design choices whereas it seems to be resovled from other reviewers comments.

The proposed HA-DSB turns PET into whole-body MRI with a Schrodinger-bridge diffusion model, using PET uptake and region labels to keep lesions sharp instead of washed out, which is innovative and reasonable.
Of the four points for reject, two ask for work that MICCAI rules forbid at rebuttal (a label-fusion ablation and a significance test on Table 1, they are important though!), and two are fair (the Gemini-generated anatomy labels are unvalidated, and a frozen PubMedBERT may miss fine organ detail) but are already answered by the design and rebuttal. Specifically, organ labels enter Eq 5 only as a small correction to the more reliable body-location embedding, so label noise does not break the model, and R1 raised the same worry and judged it resolved.
Accept as a plain poster, not a highlight, since it is single-center on one scanner, carries no significance test. PLEASE note leans on a camera-ready promise for the label evidence, otherwise I don’t see it is acceptable to MICCAI.
