meta_reviews.text:
The motivation behind applying low-rank modeling to deeply learned non-linear features should be better justified, along with the assumption that backgrounds lie in a low-rank subspace and lesions are sparse outliers. The authors should clarify the baseline used in the ablation and explain why ablations were performed only on TN3K rather than the main benchmarks. The choice of K in PCA and the empirical thresholds should be better justified. The reliance on GT-derived background features for the memory bank, and how this is handled at inference, should be explained. Finally, the framing of the “Oracle Teacher” as knowledge distillation should be clarified, given that it is a heuristic cosine-similarity formula rather than a learned teacher network.

The rebuttal addressed the major concerns raised during the original review period. Further comparisons with more baselines and plug-and-play modules can be part of future work.

The use of the clinically inspired “Search-by-Subtraction” idea is interesting. Employing reconstruction error from an orthonormal basis also appears reasonable. However, the reviewers raise several concerns regarding the methodological details (e.g., the low-rank background assumption) as well as the experimental evaluation. Additionally, the presentation of the paper needs improvement. The authors’ rebuttal partially addresses some of the reviewers’ concerns. Overall, I consider this paper to be borderline acceptable.

Two reviewers Weak Reject (R1=3, R3=3), with R1 maintaining Reject after rebuttal. Core assumption (low-rank background) lacks rigorous validation. Serious experimental design issues including inconsistent ablation datasets.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers (R1, R2, R3) and meta-reviewer (Meta) for the constructive feedback. We have grouped the major concerns regarding claim calibration, terminology, and experimental framing, and address them below.
Low-rank background prior (R1, R3, Meta). Regarding concerns that applying PCA to non-linear deep features may be mathematically questionable or lacks rigorous validation: we do not claim a theorem that medical backgrounds are globally low-rank in raw image space, nor that lesions are universally sparse outliers. Motivated by search-by-subtraction, LRBP relies on the encoder to model nonlinearity and then uses an explicit linear PCA basis as an efficient, interpretable empirical feature-space prior; kernelized variants can add cost and reduce residual-map interpretability. The operational question is whether scalar residual energy, even without vector direction, is useful for FG/BG separation. The manuscript provides this evidence: a BG-learned basis captures most BG energy with small rank, residual energy separates FG/BG with AUCs of 0.971 (Kvasir-SEG) and 0.890 (BUSI), and median residuals show clear shifts. Thus, our intended claim is an empirical feature-space prior, not a proved intrinsic low-rank structure of medical images.
Memory bank, PCA updates, and inference (R1, R3, Meta). Addressing concerns about reliance on ground-truth (GT) at inference and potential training instability: GT masks are used only during training, specifically for sampling background features, computing the background reconstruction loss, and constructing the GT-guided gate target. At inference, no GT information is used: the memory bank and PCA basis are frozen, and within LRBP, test images are processed by projection onto the learned basis. Furthermore, the PCA basis is a non-trainable buffer updated periodically from the memory bank, not an optimizer-updated parameter. Thus, PCA updates are gradient-free and decoupled from AdamW/backpropagation, mitigating the concern that the basis introduces optimizer-level training instability.
Ablation baseline and TN3K dataset (R2, R3, Meta). Regarding the concern that ablations on TN3K may not be sufficiently controlled or lack a clear baseline: in Table 1(b), the baseline is explicitly the identical ResNet-34 U-Net used in the main study. All LRBP ablation variants use the same TN3K split, host, and training protocol; only the LRBP component changes. The SE block is included only as an additional architectural comparison. TN3K, our largest auxiliary dataset, was used for component analysis to provide a stable setting for rank sweeps and mechanism analysis, while Kvasir-SEG and BUSI were used for the main benchmark evaluation across three host architectures.
Choice of K and empirical thresholds (R2, Meta). Addressing the lack of explanation for PCA K values and heuristics: K=16 was selected empirically and is consistent with Fig. 2(a), where the BG basis reaches 95% cumulative explained variance at around K=10–13 across Kvasir-SEG and BUSI; K=16 is therefore a conservative rank. We also reported a rank sweep in the TN3K ablation (K=4, 16, 64), confirming K=16 offers the best trade-off. The Dice<0.5 criterion is used only for hard-sample mining during training, not as an inference threshold. These are empirical settings, not universal constants.
“Oracle Teacher” terminology and gating (R1, R3, Meta). We agree this is a heuristic, not classical KD. It is GT-guided gate supervision: FG/BG cosine similarity is a separability proxy for when residual injection is reliable. Table 1(b) compares static injection, no teacher guidance, and a heuristic gate. Our intent was privileged supervision, not a separate teacher model.
Overall, these concerns mainly reflect framing issues rather than contradictions in the empirical findings. LRBP remains a decomposition-free inference-time plugin using a learned background basis and adaptive gating to improve boundary accuracy.

title: InSPIRE: Multiparameter Inversion for Ultrasound Computed Tomography via Sequential Position-Based Implicit Representation
abstract: Simultaneous reconstruction of sound speed and acoustic impedance in Ultrasound Computed Tomography (USCT) is essential for quantitative tissue characterization but remains a severely ill-posed inverse problem. Conventional Full Waveform Inversion (FWI) methods often suffer from cycle-skipping and parameter crosstalk due to non-convex optimization landscapes and limited low-frequency data. We propose InSPIRE, a framework for robust, unsupervised multiparameter inversion via sequential position-based implicit representations. Unlike discrete pixel-based approaches, we parameterize physical properties as continuous spatial functions using implicit neural representations. We construct a geometry-aware positional encoding with radially modulated Fourier features, imposing spatially adaptive spectral bias to resolve high-frequency details in the central imaging region where ring-array illumination is restricted. To disentangle parameter crosstalk, we introduce a dual-branch architecture with frequency-adaptive coordinate attention that dynamically adjusts feature importance across frequency stages, enabling independent reconstruction of sound speed and acoustic impedance. We devise a frequency-progressive sequential optimization strategy stabilizing convergence by updating the reference state with implicit noise regularization during bandwidth transitions. Extensive validation on synthetic phantoms and in vivo breast data demonstrates that InSPIRE outperforms conventional multi-scale FWI, yielding high-fidelity parametric maps with minimized crosstalk, superior convergence, and enhanced reconstruction quality.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents an unsupervised INR-based framework for multiparameter ultrasound computed tomography (USCT), aiming to jointly reconstruct sound speed and acoustic impedance. The method combines a geometry-aware positional encoding with radially modulated Fourier features, a dual-branch architecture with frequency-adaptive coordinate attention, and a sequential frequency-progressive optimization strategy. Experiments on synthetic and in vivo breast USCT data show improvements over several FWI- and DIP-based baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Joint reconstruction of sound speed and acoustic impedance is an important extension of quantitative USCT, since the two parameters carry complementary information about tissue properties and interfaces. The paper is also well motivated by two well-known challenges in waveform inversion, namely cycle-skipping and parameter crosstalk. 
2.The geometry-aware encoding is well aligned with the ring-array acquisition setting, and the dual-branch design is a reasonable architectural choice for separating parameters with different spatial characteristics. Likewise, the frequency-progressive strategy is consistent with standard practice in stabilizing FWI optimization.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The current submission appears highly continuous with [1] at the levels of problem formulation, methodological perspective, and empirical presentation. Both works formulate USCT reconstruction as a subject-specific unsupervised INR/FWI problem, both exploit acquisition geometry in the coordinate representation, and both follow a very similar experimental narrative including synthetic studies, in vivo visualization, ablation analysis, and convergence behavior. While the present paper extends the target from single-parameter sound-speed reconstruction to joint sound speed and acoustic impedance estimation, the manuscript does not yet make sufficiently precise which aspects constitute a substantive methodological advance beyond this prior line of work. 
2.Several components are introduced simultaneously: geometry-aware radial modulation, a dual-branch formulation, frequency-adaptive coordinate attention, and sequential optimization. However, the manuscript does not fully clarify which of these should be viewed as the primary scientific contribution, and which are better understood as design choices that support the move to multiparameter inversion. This makes the contribution boundary somewhat diffuse. 
3.Since no in vivo ground truth is available, the validation mainly relies on CNR and qualitative structural consistency. This is understandable in the application setting, but it also means that the practical significance of the impedance estimates is somewhat less firmly established than the framing of the paper may suggest. 
[1] Wang Z, Yan W, Liu Z, et al. P²INR-FWI: An Implicit Neural Representation Method for Speed of Sound Image Reconstruction in Ultrasound Computed Tomography. In: International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025: 420–430.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1.Please clarify more explicitly how this work should be distinguished from Wang et al. [1] in methodological terms. In particular, which parts of the present framework are best viewed as conceptual advances, rather than extensions of an existing INR-based USCT reconstruction paradigm? 
2.Please clarify what the paper considers to be its principal contribution:
the move to multiparameter inversion itself, the dual-branch/FACA design, the geometry-aware radial modulation, the sequential optimization strategy, or the integration of these components. 
3.Please discuss more directly the intended methodological relationship between this paper and prior INR-for-USCT reconstruction work, especially in terms of problem scope, technical inheritance, and claimed novelty. 
[1] Wang Z, Yan W, Liu Z, et al. P²INR-FWI: An Implicit Neural Representation Method for Speed of Sound Image Reconstruction in Ultrasound Computed Tomography. In: International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025: 420–430.

This is a relevant and technically competent paper on an important USCT reconstruction problem. The method is reasonably designed and the experimental section is broadly complete. My main reservation is not about technical quality per se, but about novelty positioning: the current version does not yet distinguish itself sharply enough from the most closely related prior INR-based USCT work, particularly Wang et al. [1].
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes InSPIRE, an unsupervised framework for multiparameter inversion in Ultrasound Computed Tomography (USCT). It introduces three main components: a geometry-aware positional encoding with radially modulated Fourier features to address ring-array illumination constraints; a dual-branch architecture with Frequency-Adaptive Coordinate Attention (FACA) to disentangle sound speed and acoustic impedance crosstalk; and a sequential frequency-progressive optimization strategy with noise regularization to prevent cycle-skipping.
reviews.text_strengths:
6.1 Novel formulation. The adaptation of Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) for USCT is mathematically elegant, specifically the radially modulated Fourier features that cleverly incorporate the physical constraints of ring-array geometry.
6.2 Effective Disentanglement. The proposed dual-branch FACA module successfully mitigates the velocity-density crosstalk, which is a notorious challenge in traditional Full-Waveform Inversion (FWI).
6.3 Clinical Feasibility. The unsupervised nature of the framework means it can operate without paired training data or ground truth labels. It demonstrates superior performance over standard FWI and DIP methods on both synthetic and in vivo data.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
7.1 On page 2, the manuscript states that recent work adapted “DIP” to USCT sound-speed inversion [22,26], but this conflates two rather different ideas: the original Deep Image Prior of
Ulyanov et al. [22], which is a general untrained convolutional image prior for image restoration, and Yan et al. [26], which describes a USCT-specific untrained neural network integrated into an FWI framework for breast sound-speed imaging. The experimental section then refers to “DIP [26]” as a baseline, which makes it unclear whether the comparison is against the original DIP, Yan et al.’s USCT-specific UNN/FWI method, or an in-house variant. This ambiguity matters because baseline identity directly affects the interpretation and fairness of the reported gains. In addition, Wu et al. [25] is cited in the introduction, but the manuscript does not explicitly discuss it as the closest prior on multiparameter USCT FWI, nor explain why it is not included as an experimental baseline. I therefore suggest adding a short paragraph that explicitly distinguishes InSPIRE from (i) Yan et al., which focuses primarily on sound-speed-only untrained inversion within an FWI-style framework, and (ii) Wu et al., which addresses classical multiparameter USCT FWI without the proposed coordinate-based implicit representation, geometry-aware encoding, or dual-branch decoding. If Wu et al. is not used as a baseline, the reason should also be stated clearly.
7.2 A central claim of the paper is reduced multiparameter crosstalk. I think this concern should be evaluated more directly than by image quality metrics alone. A feasible addition would be a controlled synthetic experiment with spatially separated sound-speed and impedance anomalies, together with a simple leakage/contamination metric that quantifies off-target energy mapped into the wrong parameter image. A more advanced sensitivity/Hessian-style analysis would also be valuable, but I would view that as optional rather than mandatory for this paper.
7.3 The manuscript explicitly motivates the sequential frequency-progressive strategy as a way to stabilize convergence in the presence of cycle-skipping, and the current results do suggest
improved convergence behavior. However, the evidence is still obtained under a relatively mild synthetic setup: homogeneous initialization, fixed 40 dB noise, and a single frequency schedule
starting from 400 kHz. I therefore think the cycle-skipping claim would be much more convincing with one targeted stress test, preferably by varying the initial model error and/or the available
low-frequency content. For example, the authors could perturb the homogeneous background model more aggressively, or repeat the experiment with the lowest frequency band removed. An SNR sweep would also be useful as an additional robustness check, but I would view that as secondary.
7.4 An important methodological clarification concerns the chosen parameterization. Eq. (1) is written in terms of sound speed and density, whereas the inversion variables are defined as sound speed and acoustic impedance. This is a valid choice in principle, since acoustic FWI can indeed be formulated in a velocity–impedance parameterization, but the manuscript should
state this explicitly and explain how the forward model and gradients are implemented under (c,z). At present, it is unclear whether Eq. (1) is re-expressed directly in (c,z), or whether density is derived internally from z/cfor the solver. Because parameterization strongly affects sensitivity, trade-off, and crosstalk in multiparameter FWI, a brief justification for choosing (c,z) in this ring-array USCT setting would make the method section substantially clearer [5,11–13].
7.5 The ablation study in Table 3 is currently difficult to interpret because its description appears inconsistent with the reported numbers. The text states that “the baseline uses a DIP network without Geometry-Aware Positional Encoding (GAPE) or attention modules (FACA),” which suggests that the ablation should start from a DIP-based configuration and then incrementally add the proposed components. However,
the first row of Table 3 (“Base ×, GAPE ×, FACA ×, Freq-Progressive ×”) reports exactly the same quantitative results as the FWI baseline in Table 1, whereas the second row (“Base ✓, GAPE ×, FACA ×, Freq-Progressive ×”) matches the DIP results in Table 1.This creates ambiguity about what “Base” actually denotes and how the ablation sequence should be interpreted.
I therefore suggest that the authors clarify whether Table 3 is intended to represent an incremental progression from FWI → DIP-style base network → +GAPE → +FACA →
+frequency-progressive optimization, or instead an ablation entirely within the neural-prior family. As currently written, the table mixes baseline definitions in a way that makes the
contribution of each component harder to assess. Since the ablation study is one of the main pieces of evidence supporting the paper’s claims, this inconsistency should be resolved explicitly.
7.6 The in vivo results are promising, but some of the manuscript’s clinical wording appears stronger than the current evidence supports. In particular, the conclusion states that the method provides information for “clinical diagnosis” and is “particularly suitable for clinical applications,” while the in vivo validation consists of only three volunteer cases evaluated mainly by ROI/background CNR and qualitative structural correspondence. I therefore suggest framing the in vivo study more explicitly as preliminary feasibility evidence, and softening claims of clinical diagnosis, clinical robustness, or clinical utility unless additional lesion-level, pathological, or reader-based validation is provided.
7.7 The manuscript provides enough information to understand the overall framework, but a few implementation details still seem necessary for reproducibility. In particular, it would be helpful to state explicitly either in the paper, the supplement, or released code: (i) the exact frequency-stage schedule used by InSPIRE itself, (ii) the noise scale σ in Eq. (10), (iii) the key
Fourier-feature settings (at least the dimensionality and scaling of B), and (iv) the numerical specification of the shared encoder / dual-decoder architecture, or a clear pointer to an exact
standard implementation if one is used. These items appear important because the reported gains depend on the interaction between architectural bias and staged optimization.
7.8 The geometry-aware radial modulation is intuitively motivated, but the current justification remains largely heuristic. Because the manuscript explicitly attributes the radial weighting to reduced illumination / spectral coverage in the central region of the ring-array setup, I would encourage the authors to provide at least one more direct supporting analysis or experiment.
This does not necessarily require a heavy Hessian-based study; even a simple geometry- or radius-dependent sensitivity/illumination analysis, or an empirical radial ablation showing that central emphasis is specifically beneficial in this acquisition setup, would make the physical motivation more convincing.
[1] Tancik, M., Srinivasan, P., Mildenhall, B., Fridovich-Keil, S., Raghavan, N., Singhal, U.,
Ramamoorthi, R., Barron, J., Ng, R. Fourier Features Let Networks Learn High Frequency
Functions in Low Dimensional Domains. NeurIPS, 2020.[2] Shabtay, N., Schwartz, E., Giryes, R. PIP: Positional-encoding Image Prior. arXiv, 2022.[3] Hou, Q., Zhou, D., Feng, J. Coordinate Attention for Efficient Mobile Network Design. CVPR,
2021.[4] Bunks, C., Saleck, F. M., Zaleski, S., Chavent, G. Multiscale Seismic Waveform Inversion.
Geophysics, 1995.[5] Operto, S., Gholami, Y., Prieux, V., Ribodetti, A., Brossier, R., Métivier, L., Virieux, J. A Guided
Tour of Multiparameter Full-Waveform Inversion with Multicomponent Data: From Theory to
Practice. The Leading Edge, 2013.

N/A

I rated this paper as Weak Accept because it addresses an important and challenging problem in USCT and presents a reasonably well-motivated solution, but the current empirical and
methodological support is not yet strong enough for a firmer recommendation. The main strength is the focus on joint reconstruction of sound speed and acoustic impedance, which is
more clinically meaningful and technically more difficult than sound-speed-only imaging. I also found the overall framework coherent: the geometry-aware positional encoding is tied to the
ring-array setting, the dual-branch decoder with FACA is motivated by reducing multiparameter crosstalk, and the frequency-progressive optimization is designed to improve convergence and mitigate cycle-skipping. The unsupervised, instance-specific formulation is also practically relevant for USCT, where paired ground truth is scarce. Within the reported experiments, the results are promising, with improvements over FWI, mFWI, and the neural-prior baseline on synthetic data, as well as encouraging in vivo results on three breast cases.
My score remains borderline because several issues need clarification. First, the baseline definition is somewhat ambiguous, especially the use of “DIP” versus the USCT-specific untrained method in Ref. [26], which affects the fairness and interpretation of the comparison. Second, the claims regarding reduced crosstalk and improved resistance to cycle-skipping are plausible, but the current evidence is still indirect and would benefit from more targeted controlled experiments. Third, the paper should more clearly explain the chosen parameterization, since Eq. (1) is written in terms of sound speed and density whereas the inversion variables are sound speed and acoustic impedance. Fourth, the ablation study is difficult to interpret because the table and its description are not fully consistent. Finally, the clinical wording is somewhat stronger than warranted by the current evidence, given that the in vivo study includes only three volunteer cases and reproducibility-related implementation details remain limited. Overall, I view
the paper as slightly above threshold, but my support would depend on the rebuttal adequately addressing these points.

meta_reviews.text: As all three reviewers have independently arrived at a positive recommendation, I extend my congratulations to the authors on the acceptance of their paper at this stage.

author_feedback_text:
We are grateful for the acceptance of our paper and the reviewers’ valuable feedback. We address the main concerns as follows:
1.Methodological Novelty (R1 and R2): We clarify how InSPIRE differs from Wang et al. and Yan et al. Wang’s P2INR-FWI uses point-wise MLP processing individual coordinates, while InSPIRE employs field-wise U-Net processing the entire coordinate field. This is critical for multiparameter inversion: our shared encoder captures global spatial context, enabling dual-branch decoders to independently reconstruct sound speed and impedance while mitigating crosstalk. Point-wise processing lacks spatial context to model distinct parameter characteristics. Yan et al. uses DIP mapping noise to images, whereas InSPIRE maps coordinates to physical parameters, providing continuous representation and stronger high-frequency modeling via Fourier features. Wu et al. [25] uses discrete FWI with optimal transport, a different paradigm from our coordinate-based continuous representation, making direct comparison less meaningful. 
2.Experimental Design and Ablation (R2 and R3): We clarify Table 3’s ablation design. Row 1 is classical FWI. Row 2 uses DIP [26] as baseline for comparison with prior untrained neural USCT work. Rows 3-5 incrementally add our components. The transition from Row 2 to Row 3 includes shifting to coordinate-based input and adding GAPE. Coordinate-based formulation is a core design enabling our geometry-aware and frequency-adaptive modules. We note that coordinate-input U-Net without GAPE/FACA/frequency-progressive performs comparably to DIP, confirming coordinate-input provides similar regularization while enabling our proposed modules. This will be clarified in the final version. Regarding R3’s concern about GAPE’s modest gain, in synthetic experiments the ring-array geometry degradation is relatively mild, making radial weighting less pronounced. GAPE’s value is demonstrated through cumulative effects and becomes more critical in real scenarios with stronger illumination inhomogeneity. 
3.Technical Details and Reproducibility (R2 and R3): Regarding the parameterization in c and z, our forward solver internally derives ρ=z/c, then solves Eq.(1) with gradients backpropagating to c and z. We chose this parameterization because impedance directly corresponds to tissue interfaces, facilitating dual-branch disentanglement. We will clarify this and provide complete implementation details in the final version. For computational cost, InSPIRE requires approximately 119 minutes on synthetic data using A100 GPU versus 170 minutes for DIP and 100 minutes for FWI. InSPIRE is faster than DIP and only moderately slower than FWI while delivering substantially improved reconstruction quality.
4.Clinical Validation (R1 and R2): We agree our in vivo study represents preliminary feasibility evidence on healthy volunteers rather than definitive clinical validation. Regarding impedance practical significance, acoustic impedance reveals tissue interfaces complementary to sound speed. While ground truth is unavailable, we validated structural consistency by comparing impedance gradients against USCT reflectivity maps in Fig. 5, demonstrating physically meaningful tissue boundaries. Additionally, quantitative characterization in healthy populations establishes baseline references for early screening protocols critical for preventive healthcare. InSPIRE shows promise for clinical applications, though further validation with patient cohorts and pathological correlation is needed.

title: INST-Align: Implicit Neural Alignment for Spatial Transcriptomics via Canonical Expression Fields
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures mRNA expression while preserving spatial organization, but multi-slice analysis faces two coupled difficulties: large non-rigid deformations across slices and inter-slice batch effects when alignment and integration are treated independently. We present INST-Align, an unsupervised pairwise framework that couples a coordinate-based deformation network with a shared Canonical Expression Field, an implicit neural representation mapping spatial coordinates to expression embeddings, for joint alignment and reconstruction. A two-phase training strategy first establishes a stable canonical embedding space and then jointly optimizes deformation and spatial-feature matching, enabling mutually constrained alignment and representation learning. Cross-slice parameter sharing of the canonical field regularizes ambiguous correspondences and absorbs batch variation. Across nine datasets, INST-Align achieves state-of-the-art mean OT Accuracy (0.702), NN Accuracy (0.719), and Chamfer distance, with Chamfer reductions of up to 94.9% on large-deformation sections relative to the strongest baseline. The framework also yields biologically meaningful spatial embeddings and coherent 3D tissue reconstruction. The implementation is available at https://github.com/BonianHan/INST-Align.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents INST-Align, an unsupervised framework for spatial transcriptomics slice alignment and reconstruction. The main contribution lies in coupling a deformation network with a shared canonical expression field, enabling joint optimization of spatial alignment and expression modeling within a continuous representation. Experimental results show competitive alignment performance across multiple datasets and demonstrate that the learned representations can support downstream biological analysis.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Although INST-Align is optimized for alignment (embedding quality is a byproduct rather than the primary target), it still produces spatial embeddings that are useful for clustering analysis.
2.The Spatial Expression Alignment Loss and Jacobian Regularization are biologically motivated and reasonably designed.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The abstract claims state-of-the-art performance, but the results are not consistently strong across all datasets (e. g. , D1 and D2), where existing methods remain competitive or superior. A more balanced discussion and analysis of these cases would strengthen the paper. 
2.It is not clearly specified whether all baselines use the same preprocessing (e. g. , adaptive ICP) and data splits. In addition, key hyperparameters (e. g. , in Eq. (6) and (8)) are fixed without sensitivity analysis, raising concerns about robustness and reproducibility. 
3.The ablation does not fully disentangle the contributions of individual components, particularly the loss terms in Phase 2 (e. g. , L_recon vs. L_match). Moreover, it is conducted on a single dataset, which limits its generality. 
4.While the method is designed to jointly perform alignment and integration, the results suggest that improvements are uneven. In particular, Phase 1 mainly enhances embedding quality, while its impact on alignment metrics is less evident, weakening the claim of strong mutual benefit. 
5.Although the method achieves favorable average performance, improvements are not consistently dominant across datasets or metrics. For example, gains in Chamfer distance are not always matched by comparable improvements in OT or NN accuracy, making the practical advantage less clear.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper tackles an important problem in spatial transcriptomics and proposes a technically sound framework with biologically motivated components. It achieves competitive performance and produces useful spatial embeddings for downstream analysis. However, the contribution is limited by insufficient evidence: the claimed state-of-the-art performance is not consistently supported, experimental fairness is unclear, hyperparameter sensitivity is not analyzed, and the ablation study is incomplete. The method presentation could also be clearer. Overall, the work is promising but remains borderline due to limited validation and analysis.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I appreciate the authors’ detailed rebuttal and clarification efforts. The responses sufficiently addressed my concerns regarding the motivation of the paired-to-canonical design, component isolation, computational cost, and reproducibility, and the additional explanations are generally consistent with the empirical results presented in the manuscript. While some limitations remain, particularly regarding biological validation and global multi-slice consistency, I believe the work presents a technically solid and interesting framework for joint spatial alignment and integration in spatial transcriptomics. Therefore, I maintain my accept recommendation.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes INST-Align, an unsupervised pairwise framework for spatial transcriptomics (ST) slice alignment, featuring a 2-stage coupled non-rigid deformation network with a shared Canonical Expression Field implemented as implicit neural representation (INR). Slice-specific expression INRs with a shared decoder are first pretrained to establish a common embedding space; the source INR is then removed and the deformation network are jointly optimized with the canonical decoder. Loss includes a geometry-feature matching loss, reconstruction loss, and Jacobian regularization. The paper reports experiments on nine datasets and claims state-of-the-art mean OT Accuracy, NN Accuracy, and Chamfer distance, and unaffected embedding quality.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper is motivated by a real and important problem. Multi-slice spatial transcriptomics alignment remains a challenging. The paper’s motivation for coupling geometric alignment with expression-level information is logical and broadly consistent with recent reviews and benchmarking studies in ST. 
2.The proposed combination of a shared canonical field and coordinate deformation is novel and technically reasonable.
3.The model architecture is clearly presented. The two-stage fitting (pretraining and joint training of deformation and canonical consistency) is well established and logically organized.
4.The method is evaluated on diverse spatial transcriptomics datasets, and the paper reports multiple alignment metrics, including OT Accuracy, NN Accuracy, and Chamfer distance. In addition, the authors provide a downstream evaluation of biological embedding quality.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The experimental gains are somewhat uneven, and the biological validity of the learned embeddings remains under-validated. Some performance variation is expected given the noisy and unsupervised nature of spatial transcriptomics alignment. However, the downstream analysis in Table 2 shows that INST-Align does not achieve SOTA embedding quality, which weakens the strength of the claimed “joint alignment and integration” formulation. This cannot be fully dismissed as a mere “byproduct”, since the paper emphasizes biologically meaningful embeddings, and getting a good embedding is the final touch to a scientific analysis. 
2.The manuscript does not provide clustering visualizations. Although the paper includes a 3D reconstruction example on DLPFC, the visualization is shown only with ground-truth labels, and DLPFC itself exhibits relatively limited slice-wise deformation, making this example less compelling as evidence for the claimed advantages. 
3.The central methodology is not fully analyzed. The manuscript does not provide a direct analysis of how the shared canonical field mitigates batch effects, nor does it isolate the contribution of the proposed Spatial-Expression Alignment Loss in the ablation study. This is important because recent benchmarking work suggests that multi-slice ST performance is highly context dependent and that alignment and integration quality should be dissected carefully.
4.Implementation details and computational cost are insufficiently reported. This is a concern because the full training pipeline requires 700 epochs in total (300 + 400), which is difficult to judge the practical efficiency of the proposed method relative to competing alignment approaches.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1.In Phase 1, two separate ExprINRs are trained for the reference and target slices, respectively, but the target-slice INR is discarded in Phase 2.If the target-slice encoder is no longer used, how does the final “shared” canonical expression field retain target-specific biological information in a principled way? More specifically, what is the conceptual advantage of the proposed design over using only the reference slice to define the ExprINR and then learning deformation from the target slice into that space? 
2.In Fig. 2(a), the two slices appear to have noticeably inconsistent orientation after rigid ICP pre-alignment. Could the authors clarify the precise role and necessity of the initial rigid ICP step? 
3.Could the authors provide implementation details such as training device, wall-clock time per subject, number of optimization steps, and memory usage? Given that the method requires a 700-epoch two-stage optimization schedule, the computational cost may be substantially higher than that of many competing alignment methods, some of which run in seconds to minutes.
I would be open to raising my score to 4 or 5 if the authors can convincingly address the concerns above.

This paper has a good idea, addresses an important problem, and reports promising results, especially in difficult large-deformation cases. The methodological intuition is sound and the technical design is coherent. However, the paper does not yet validate its central assumption with the level of experimental rigor. In particular, it does not convincingly isolate the benefit of the shared canonical field as the main causal factor, and its biological validation remains limited relative to the strength of its claims.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents INST-Align, a novel unsupervised pairwise framework for spatial transcriptomics that couples a coordinate-based deformation network with a shared Canonical Expression Field. The core contribution is the joint optimization of spatial alignment and expression integration, utilizing an implicit neural representation to map spatial coordinates to expression embeddings. The authors emphasize that cross-slice parameter sharing of this canonical field regularizes ambiguous correspondences and absorbs batch variation, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple datasets.
reviews.text_strengths:
Accurate reconstruction of coherent 3D tissue volumes from serial sections is a critical challenge, as slices undergo complex non-rigid distortions such as tearing and folding during sample preparation. However, existing alignment methods often treat alignment and integration as independent steps. Relying on integration-based methods risks over-correcting and diminishing genuine biological diversity, while geometric methods lack expression-level feedback. Furthermore, biological complexity makes ground-truth correspondences largely unattainable, raising the need for a robust unsupervised strategy.
To overcome these limitations, the authors design INST-Align, which employs a two-phase training strategy to establish a stable canonical embedding space before jointly optimizing deformation and spatial-feature matching. Furthermore, the proposed spatial-expression alignment loss combines geometric proximity and canonical-field feature similarity to drive unsupervised non-rigid registration. This design aims to turn alignment into a mutually constrained reconstruction task.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The integration of a deformation network with a shared canonical field represents a highly promising and valuable approach for ST multi-slice alignment. To further elevate the clarity and impact of this strong manuscript, the authors might consider clarifying a few methodological details:
1.The use of an asymmetric weighting scheme in the Jacobian regularization to penalize tissue compression more heavily than expansion is an intuitive and physically plausible design choice. However, since the specific weights chosen directly impact the smoothness of the displacement field, their specific values could benefit from a bit more validation. The paper would be further strengthened if the authors could provide a brief ablation study or visualize the resulting vector fields under different weight settings. This would beautifully illustrate that they indeed preserve biologically plausible cell densities without introducing artifacts.
2.The claim that the spatial-expression alignment loss utilizes an adaptive temperature and EMA scale factors is compelling. While the current two-phase training is a solid baseline, the interpretability of this dynamic matching could be made even more convincing. The authors might consider visualizing the convergence curves of these dynamic scaling factors during the joint optimization phase. Showing that these parameters stabilize naturally over the 400 epochs would wonderfully solidify the paper’s core contribution regarding optimization stability.
3.The model achieves impressive state-of-the-art results across most datasets, particularly in Chamfer distance reduction on large-deformation sections. However, to provide a more comprehensive evaluation, it would be valuable to briefly discuss the potential for error accumulation when performing 3D tissue reconstructions from consecutively aligned slices. Including a short discussion in the conclusion regarding how the current pairwise framework might be extended to include a global multi-slice consistency objective would provide readers with a more objective understanding of the model’s limitations and future scalability.
4.The biologically meaningful embeddings generated by INST-Align are one of its strongest aspects. There is, however, a minor area for expansion regarding the biological validation, which is currently limited to clustering-based metrics like ARI and NMI. Could the authors kindly clarify or evaluate how these embeddings perform on specific spatial trajectory inference tasks or continuous phenotype mappings? Detailing this downstream utility would greatly help readers fully understand the mechanics and ensure the biological relevance of the canonical field.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Novelty and Significance (High)
Methodological Rigor (Medium)
Experimental Validation (Medium)
Reproducibility and Transparency (Low)
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
It is an interesting paper that presents an important problem and proposes a coherent method with a novel coupling between non-rigid deformation and a shared canonical expression field. However, the results do not quite convincingly support the claims. The performance gains are inconsistent across datasets and metrics. It is unclear how much of the gain results from joint alignment and integration, especially from using a shared canonical field and spatial-expression alignment loss. We believe that more experiments are needed to better demonstrate the utility of the learned embeddings. Reproducibility needs more information such as fairness of preprocessing, the sensitivity to hyper-parameters, the run time, and any other relevant information for replicating the experiments. Please carefully address these points with clear evidence and additional ablations/analyses, and make the manuscript more balanced.

After rebuttal, R1 maintains Accept after the clarifications on design, ablations, cost, and reproducibility, while R2 raises the score to Accept after the authors addressed concerns about pre-ICP, canonical space, and experimental interpretation. R3 originally rates weak reject but did not submit final rating. After review, I think the concerns would not block this paper. I vote for acceptance.

This work proposes a registration approach for spatial transcriptomics from different sections. The developed approach makes use of implicit neural representations to model the spatial deformation as well as mRNA expression.
While there was mixed review enthusiasm before the rebuttal, reviewer sentiment was largely positive after the rebuttal. Reviewers appreciated the tackled problem and the average gains obtained by the proposed method compared to competing approaches. There are some remaining concerns regarding the quality of the obtained joint embeddings (as performance is lower than for specialized methods) and the ability of the approach to extend to multi slice alignment (the dreaded banana effect comes to mind for 3D reconstructions from pairwise 2D registration) but overall this paper provides an interesting approach for a challenging task. Hence, in my opinion, it is suitable for presentation at MICCAI.

The reviewers generally agreed that the paper addresses an important problem and introduces a novel framework that jointly models spatial alignment and expression integration through a shared Canonical Expression Field. Although concerns were initially raised regarding the consistency of performance gains, component attribution, biological validation, and reproducibility, the rebuttal provided satisfactory clarifications grounded in the submitted manuscript, leading both initially borderline reviewers to raise their final recommendations to Accept. Given the methodological novelty, strong overall experimental performance, and positive post-rebuttal consensus, I recommend acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and MR. All numbers below are from the submitted manuscript or characterizations of the submitted runs.
1.SOTA claim [R1.1, R1.5, R2.1, MR-1].
The claim is best
mean
across nine datasets. On D1/D2, top methods differ by at most 0.037 OT and 0.031 NN; on D3 we lead OT (.839) and NN (.849). The advantage is decisive under large deformations: Chamfer 12.6/17.1/11.9 on MB2/MB11/ME vs. 166.2/103.3/12.0 (Spateo) and 173.1/51.7/235.5 (PASTE). Mean OT .702, NN .719, Chamfer 22.6 are best across all baselines. The abstract phrase “the strongest baseline” will be replaced with “PASTE”, consistent with §3.2 and Conclusion.
2.Why paired-then-canonical [R2.Q1, MR-2].
A reference-only ExprINR would bake the reference’s batch signature
into
the canonical signal; deformation would then drag the source onto reference-specific artifacts. Phase 1’s two ExprINRs share one decoder (§2.2): the decoder must reconstruct
both
slices from coordinates alone, forcing slice-specific noise into the reconstruction residual and out of the canonical embedding. This is the integration step. The source INR is discardable in Phase 2 because the deformation network maps source coordinates into the canonical frame, where one shared field suffices. The design is the explicit mechanism behind “joint alignment+integration”, not redundant scaffolding.
3.Component isolation [R1.3, R2.3, R3.1, MR-2].
Table 3 dissociates three orthogonal axes: removing Phase 1 collapses embedding (ARI .334->.045) with alignment intact (OT .810->.813); removing Phase 2 degrades alignment (Chamfer .36->.56); removing Jacobian degrades both (Chamfer .49, ARI .287). The Phase-1 ablation pattern reproduces on MouseEmbryo (OT .75->.69, ARI .22->.13), confirming the trend is not dataset-specific.
4.Cost and reproducibility [R1.2, R2.Q3, MR-4].
On MouseEmbryo (~37k cells, single RTX 5080 16GB) INST-Align trains in 95 s – faster than PASTE (232 s) and STalign (435 s), competitive with Spateo. The 300+400-epoch schedule is dataset-agnostic and runs on consumer hardware. All datasets use the identical Dong et al. [11] pipeline; baselines run released code under default init. Core design is fixed across all nine datasets – two-phase training, shared canonical field, spatial-expression matcher, 5:1 Jacobian asymmetry. Only scale/geometry settings vary, and were fixed before final evaluation: robustness in the architecture, not missing sensitivity.
5.Specific items.
R2.Q2 (ICP).
Rigid ICP removes only translation/rotation; the residual in Fig. 2(a) is exactly the tearing/folding the non-rigid step corrects – expected, not failure.
R3.1 (Jacobian).
The 5x compression penalty follows the local-invertibility argument of [29]: near-singular compression destroys the diffeomorphism, expansion does not. Table 3’s “w/o Jacobian” row quantifies the effect.
R3.2 (tau / scales).
In the submitted runs, tau, s_sp, s_ft stabilize within 0-25, 0-10, 12-65 epochs across all datasets – natural early self-calibration.
R3.3 (drift).
Acknowledged as a current limitation in the Conclusion.
R2 / R3.4 (biology).
The canonical field is coordinate-conditioned and differentiable; trajectory inference and continuous phenotype mapping are
downstream uses of the same trained model
, not separate methodology – consistent with Table 2, where our embeddings beat PCA and Seurat despite alignment being primary.
Closing.
Each MR ask – inconsistent gains, isolation of contributions, utility of embeddings, reproducibility – is answered from the submitted Tables 1-3 plus characterizations of the submitted runs, in compliance with rebuttal policy. R1 already recommended Accept (5, very confident). R2’s Q1/Q2/Q3 are addressed in §2/§5/§4 and R3’s asks in §3/§5; on R2’s own terms (“open to raising my score to 4 or 5”), we ask R2 and R3 to update their scores.

title: Interaction-Aware Contrastive Multi-task Learning for Joint Segmentation and Malignancy Classification in Thyroid Ultrasound
abstract: Ultrasound-based thyroid malignancy assessment requires both accurate nodule delineation and discriminative diagnosis. Joint segmentation and classification is therefore a promising solution to reduce error propagation and improve diagnostic consistency. However, existing joint pipelines often couple tasks mainly through shared parameters or prediction-level cues, providing limited feature-level interaction between branches. This weak coupling can lead to attention-boundary mismatch and poorly aligned cross-task representations. We propose IC-MTL, an interaction-aware contrastive multi-task framework that explicitly models bidirectional cross-task interaction and introduces supervised contrastive regularization on the post-interaction representations to jointly encourage lesion-aligned attention and class-separable diagnostic features. IC-MTL is evaluated on the public DDTI benchmark and a real-world clinical dataset. Across both datasets, IC-MTL improves performance over staged baselines and recent state-of-the-art joint models. Qualitative analyses further indicate improved lesion-aligned attention and more separable representations, supporting more reliable clinical risk stratification.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes IC-MTL, a multi-task framework for joint thyroid nodule segmentation and malignancy classification in ultrasound images. It introduces a bidirectional Cross-Task Interaction (CI) module that utilizes source-derived gating to transfer boundary information to the classification branch and malignancy semantics to the segmentation branch. It integrates a Supervised Contrastive Multi-Task Regularizer (SCMR) applied to post-interaction features at both pixel and image levels to align the representation geometry across tasks.
reviews.text_strengths: The framework explicitly addresses the inherent clinical interdependence between anatomical delineation and pathological diagnosis. The CI module formalizes bidirectional message passing as a mathematically clear, gated residual update. Applying supervised contrastive objectives symmetrically on post-interaction features successfully shapes feature separability at multiple granularities.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The CI gating formulation lacks algorithmic novelty and conceptually duplicates established multi-task paradigms like cross-stitch networks, sluice networks, and FiLM-like modulation. The evaluation completely omits mandatory quantitative comparisons against these classic feature-exchange architectures and recent thyroid-specific joint models. The methodology leaves critical technical details undefined, including backbone architecture, SCMR projection head dimensions, and pixel-level subsampling strategies for managing foreground/background imbalance. The dynamic loss reweighting scheme relies on an arbitrary Dice score threshold, introducing unfair training heuristics. The study lacks statistical significance testing and fails to report computational overhead, inference time, or memory consumption constraints.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The framework targets a highly relevant clinical bottleneck and demonstrates consistent empirical gains through logically motivated task coupling. However, the core algorithmic innovation remains marginal compared to existing cross-task feature modulation literature. The empirical validation is fundamentally compromised by the exclusion of direct comparisons with established multi-task baselines and thyroid-specific joint networks. The absence of statistical significance testing makes the modest performance gains unreliable. Missing architectural specifics and memory management details for the pixel-level contrastive loss severely hinder both reproducibility and real-world clinical deployability.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes IC-MTL, an interaction-aware contrastive multi-task learning framework for joint thyroid nodule segmentation and malignancy classification in ultrasound images. The framework introduces two tightly coupled components: (1) a bidirectional Cross-task Interaction (CI) module that explicitly exchanges boundary-sensitive segmentation features into the classification branch (Seg→Cls) and malignancy-discriminative classification semantics into the segmentation branch (Cls→Seg) via a learned gated residual message-passing mechanism; and (2) a Supervised Contrastive Multi-task Regularization (SCMR) component that applies supervised contrastive objectives at both the pixel level (foreground/background separation for segmentation) and image level (benign/malignant separation for classification) on the post-interaction feature representations. The framework is evaluated on the public DDTI benchmark and an independent clinical dataset from a local hospital, demonstrating improvements in malignancy classification AUC and accuracy over staged and joint baselines while maintaining competitive segmentation DSC.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Principled bidirectional cross-task interaction with clearly defined roles for each direction.
The central contribution of IC-MTL is the explicit formalization of information flow between the segmentation and classification branches in both directions. The design is grounded in a clear clinical rationale: boundary and shape cues from segmentation are informative for malignancy assessment (per TI-RADS morphological descriptors), and malignancy-related semantics can sharpen segmentation by refining attention to lesion-relevant regions. This bidirectionality is not merely architectural but is implemented with role-specific message-passing operators and validated through direction-specific ablation. Removing Seg→Cls reduces AUC by 5.53 percentage points (85.92 → 80.39), and removing Cls→Seg reduces DSC by 0.66 points (92.38 → 91.72), confirming that each direction contributes to its intended target task in the expected direction.
2.SCMR applies contrastive regularization at both task-appropriate granularities.
The supervised contrastive regularization is applied at the image level for classification (pulling benign/malignant embeddings together within class and apart between classes) and at the pixel level for segmentation (pulling foreground/background pixel embeddings apart). This dual-granularity contrastive framework is conceptually consistent with the different feature geometries required by each task and is supported by the ablation: removing SCMR (Cls) drops ACC from 90.00 to 84.67, and removing SCMR (Seg) drops DSC from 92.38 to 90.72, suggesting that the two contrastive terms have complementary and largely non-overlapping effects.
3.Thorough ablation study with component-level granularity.
Table 2 includes ten experimental conditions covering: classification-only baseline, staged pipeline baseline, full joint model without proposed components, removal of CI entirely, removal of each CI direction independently, removal of SCMR entirely, and removal of each SCMR term independently. This level of ablation granularity significantly strengthens confidence in the contribution of each proposed component and provides clear evidence for both CI and SCMR as necessary elements.
4.Rich qualitative analysis supporting mechanistic interpretation.
Figure 3 provides t-SNE feature visualization comparing class separability across competing methods (Chowdary et al., Luo et al., He et al., and IC-MTL before and after CI), Grad-CAM attention maps for both DDTI and local datasets, and segmentation feature map comparisons before and after CI. Together, these analyses provide an intuitive and multi-faceted verification that CI improves feature separability, attention-boundary alignment, and lesion-focused segmentation activations in the expected ways, going beyond what tables alone can convey.
5.Evaluation on two datasets with different characteristics.
Testing on both the public DDTI benchmark and an independent clinical dataset collected at a separate hospital provides a reasonable assessment of generalization under scanner and population shift. The two-dataset evaluation is particularly valuable because the local clinical dataset includes ultrasound video sequences rather than static images, adding a degree of real-world complexity.
6.Dynamic loss re-weighting strategy is practically sound.
The two-stage training schedule that prioritizes segmentation until DSC ≥ 0.8, then shifts emphasis to classification, is a pragmatic solution to the common problem of task imbalance in multi-task learning. The rationale — stable spatial representation first, then discriminative semantic learning — is aligned with how clinicians sequentially assess thyroid nodules (first locate, then characterize), and it reduces the risk of classification branch overfitting on unreliable segmentation features early in training.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Both evaluation datasets are relatively small, limiting the generalizability of conclusions.
The DDTI dataset contains 347 images from 299 patients, and the local clinical dataset contains 4,598 images from 116 patients. While five-fold patient-level cross-validation is used to prevent leakage, the effective validation set per fold is approximately 60–70 images for DDTI and approximately 23 patients for the local dataset. The AUC standard deviations of ±6.77 (DDTI) and ±6.95 (local) reflect this limited sample size and indicate that performance estimates are not stable across folds. For a malignancy classification system intended for clinical use, validation on 100+ independent test cases would be a more credible basis for clinical conclusions. Furthermore, neither dataset constitutes a prospective or multi-center cohort.
2.Hyperparameter sensitivity is not analyzed.
The model involves several hyperparameters with non-trivial impact on performance: the DSC threshold (0.8) that triggers the loss re-weighting stage transition, the two sets of loss weights (α, β, γ, γ_seg, γ_cls) for each training phase, and the contrastive temperature τ = 0.5.The paper states these were “chosen empirically on the validation folds,” but no sensitivity analysis is provided. It is not clear whether the reported performance gains are robust to moderate perturbations of these values, or whether they depend critically on the specific configuration. A brief sensitivity sweep over at least the DSC threshold and τ would strengthen the reproducibility and robustness claims.
3.Performance on the local dataset shows non-negligible DSC degradation relative to the best baseline.
On the local clinical dataset, IC-MTL achieves DSC 87.77%, whereas He et al. achieves DSC 88.28%. While the paper characterizes this difference as “marginal,” it is worth noting that the local dataset represents a more challenging real-world setting (acquired from video sequences, different scanner characteristics, independent clinical site), and that the segmentation branch in IC-MTL is jointly optimized with classification, which may introduce trade-offs. A more detailed analysis of the cases where IC-MTL’s segmentation falls behind — e.g., whether these are systematically the difficult malignant nodules with irregular boundaries — would inform the clinical interpretation.
4.No investigation of the interaction between CI and different encoder architectures.
All experiments use the same shared encoder backbone. The generalizability of the CI mechanism across different encoder architectures (e.g., transformer-based vs. CNN-based encoders) is not assessed. As the field moves toward foundation model backbones for ultrasound, it would be valuable to know whether the gated residual CI operator remains effective when features are extracted from, e.g., a pretrained SAM or MedSAM encoder.
5.Code and data release is not planned.
The paper does not mention any plan to release code or dataset. While the local clinical dataset cannot be released for privacy reasons, the code for IC-MTL should be made available for community use and reproducibility. The lack of a code release commitment limits the practical impact of this contribution.
6.The Grad-CAM visualizations in Figure 3b are presented on a small scale.
The qualitative results in Figure 3b are presented at a resolution that makes it difficult to verify the claimed attention-boundary consistency improvements, particularly for the local dataset examples. Enlarged selected examples with clearer visual comparisons would substantially improve the interpretability of these qualitative results.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
IC-MTL is a well-executed and clearly motivated framework. The main recommendation for improvement is to expand the evaluation to a larger cohort, ideally including at least one additional external site, to substantiate the generalization claims with greater statistical confidence. Publishing the code would also significantly increase the community uptake of this work. Adding hyperparameter sensitivity analysis — even as a brief supplementary table — would improve the reproducibility claim. For future work, exploring whether the CI module generalizes to stronger or pretrained encoder backbones (e.g., SAM-based) would be a valuable direction given the current momentum in foundation model adaptation for ultrasound analysis.

IC-MTL presents a methodologically sound and clearly motivated framework for joint thyroid nodule segmentation and malignancy classification. The bidirectional cross-task interaction module addresses a genuine limitation of prior joint models — the asymmetric or implicit coupling between tasks — and the supervised contrastive regularization at dual granularities provides a principled approach to multi-task feature space alignment. The component-level ablation is thorough, the qualitative analyses are rich and informative, and the framework demonstrates consistent improvement over representative baselines on two datasets. The main limitations are the small size of both evaluation datasets, the absence of hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, and the lack of code release. These limitations reduce the confidence with which clinical generalization claims can be made, but do not undermine the methodological contribution. The paper is marginally above the acceptance threshold, and its acceptance would be strengthened by rebuttal clarifications regarding the local dataset size context and any plans for code release or expanded validation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes bidirectional cross-task interaction (CI) and supervised contrastive multi-task regularization (SCMR) for a multi-task framework for joint segmentation and malignancy classification in thyroid ultrasound, thereby strengthening feature-level coupling between the two tasks and improving overall diagnostic performance.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The problem setting is clinically well motivated, as nodule boundary and shape information are closely related to malignancy assessment in thyroid ultrasound, making joint segmentation and classification a reasonable and meaningful direction.
2.The proposed design is conceptually clear: rather than relying only on a shared encoder, it introduces bidirectional cross-task interaction (CI) to explicitly exchange features between the two branches, and SCMR to make the post-interaction representations more discriminative.
3.The paper includes fairly thorough and appropriate ablation studies, including removal of CI, directional interaction terms, and SCMR, which helps support the contribution of each component.
4.The method is evaluated on both a public benchmark (DDTI) and a local clinical dataset, which is a strength compared with studies validated on only a single dataset.
5.The paper provides qualitative analyses such as t-SNE, Grad-CAM, and feature-map comparisons, which help illustrate the intended effect of the proposed interaction mechanism beyond the reported quantitative metrics.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The paper argues that CI improves classification by transferring segmentation-informed morphology, and Fig. 3b is presented as qualitative evidence of improved attention–boundary consistency. However, it is not obvious that the Grad-CAM visualizations clearly support this claim; in some cases, the heatmaps from He et al. appear at least as well aligned with the lesion mask. Could the authors provide stronger, preferably quantitative, evidence that the classification gains are specifically driven by morphology-informed interaction rather than generic multi-task regularization?
2.Although the paper seems to prioritize classification in practice, this is not clearly justified in the framing of the joint task. On DDTI, IC-MTL improves both DSC and classification metrics, whereas on the local dataset it improves classification but not segmentation over He et al. As a result, the claimed advantage of the joint framework is somewhat difficult to interpret. A stronger evaluation would be true cross-dataset external validation rather than separate within-dataset cross-validation.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Please refer to the weaknesses above. If these concerns are adequately addressed, I would be open to raising my score.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

title: Interactive MWA Planning via Probabilistic Inverse Inference
abstract:
Microwave ablation (MWA) is a well-established curative treatment for unresectable tumors. However, current clinical planning strategies rely predominantly on geometric heuristics that neglect patient-specific physiology, often resulting in incomplete tumor ablation or unintended damage to healthy tissues. While physics-based bioheat finite element simulations can model the underlying electromagnetic and thermal interactions, their computational cost renders them impractical for interactive clinical planning. We propose a novel, human-in-the-loop computational framework for interactive, patient-specific preoperative MWA planning. At its core there is a deep learning inverse model that directly infers clinically actionable ablation parameters (generator power, ablation duration, and axial depth) given a target tumor mask. 
The model assesses with sub-second latency the feasibility of insertion paths proposed by the clinician. When viable, it predicts optimal settings to maximize tumor coverage while minimizing collateral damage. Our framework also supports multi-antenna strategies via a sequential optimization scheme. It has been validated against in vivo porcine experiments and tested on patient data. Our solution achieved an overall Technical Success Rate of 97% across 116 clinical cases and generated viable multi-antenna treatment plans with sub-second latency (~300 ms per antenna). This interactive framework bridges the gap between high-fidelity bioheat modeling and interactive clinical decision-making, enabling safe, efficient, and personalized MWA strategies.
subject_areas: Applications -> Digital Twins / Simulation / Synthetic Data

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of this paper is a real-time, patient-specific planning framework for microwave ablation that directly infers optimal treatment parameters (power, duration, and insertion depth) from a target tumor using a probabilistic inverse model. By combining a fast surrogate model with forward-in-the-loop training, the method enables interactive, clinician-in-the-loop planning with sub-second latency while maintaining high tumor coverage and minimizing damage to healthy tissue.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper introduces a direct inverse inference approach that predicts clinically actionable parameters (power, duration, depth) from the target tumor, avoiding iterative optimization. This is particularly novel for MWA, where the parameter space is complex and highly coupled, making traditional search-based methods impractical for real-time use.
2.The combination of a physics-informed forward surrogate model with a forward-in-the-loop training strategy is a strong contribution. Optimizing the inverse model based on predicted ablation outcomes aligns the learning objective with clinical goals, which is both elegant and practically meaningful.
3.The method is validated across synthetic data, in vivo porcine experiments, and a clinical dataset. This multi-tier evaluation strengthens the credibility of the approach, particularly the inclusion of in vivo validation and clinically meaningful metrics such as technical success rate and ablation efficiency.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.While the use of synthetic FEM data is well-motivated, it remains unclear whether the dataset size (2400 samples) and its variability are sufficient to capture the full complexity of patient-specific anatomy and perfusion patterns. Additional analysis or ablation studies on data efficiency and diversity would help better support the robustness of the learned models.
2.The sequential multi-antenna strategy does not appear to account for tissue property changes induced by prior ablations (e. g. , reduced perfusion or altered thermal properties). In the current formulation, only the residual tumor mask is updated, while the underlying perfusion map remains unchanged. This simplification may limit the physical realism and accuracy of multi-antenna planning, and this limitation is not explicitly discussed.
3.the study lacks comparison against meaningful baselines. In particular, it would be valuable to compare the proposed method with standard clinical practice, such as manufacturer-provided power–time charts or heuristic-based planning. Such a comparison would help better quantify the practical benefits and clinical relevance of the proposed framework.
4.The reproducibility of the proposed framework is limited. Key components, such as the FEM-based data generation pipeline and training details, are not described in sufficient detail to enable full reproduction. In the absence of code or additional implementation details, it is challenging to assess whether the method can be reliably replicated.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses an important and clinically relevant problem and proposes a novel inverse planning framework for real-time microwave ablation. The combination of a physics-informed surrogate model with direct inverse inference is well-motivated and enables interactive, clinician-in-the-loop planning with impressive computational efficiency. The work is further strengthened by comprehensive validation, including in vivo experiments and retrospective clinical evaluation, demonstrating promising performance and practical applicability.
While there are some limitations, such as insufficient methodological details, lack of strong baselines, and questions regarding generalization from synthetic data, these do not outweigh the overall novelty, technical soundness, and potential clinical impact of the work.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The authors present a novel, deep-learning-based framework for real-time Microwave Ablation (MWA) planning. The core innovation lies in a dual-model architecture:
1) Forward Surrogate Model: Pre-trained on Finite Element Method (FEM) data to predict necrosis masks. It effectively accounts for heat-sink effects by integrating patient-specific perfusion and vascular maps.
2) Inverse Planning Model: Utilizes the surrogate model within its training loop to optimize antenna parameters and trajectory depth. By penalizing discrepancies between the predicted ablation zone and the target tumor mask, the model learns to derive optimal strategy parameters.
Based on the previous models, they developed an interactive planning where clinicians are able to plan the MWA tumour ablation and the platform suggests and provide the optimal planning parameters and the estimated ablation.
In general, the article is well written and can be easily followed.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) Computational Efficiency: By replacing computationally expensive FEM simulations with deep learning surrogates, the tool achieves the high-speed execution necessary for an interactive clinical interface.
2) Biological Accuracy: The inclusion of perfusion maps ensures that the cooling effects of surrounding vasculature are factored into the plan, without relying only on geometric heuristics.
Validation: The study is well-structured and provides robust evidence through validation on open datasets and an in vivo assessment of the forward surrogate model.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
In the results, the authors presented the Ablation Efficiency score. For single antennas, they reported a smaller value (0.44) with respect to the overall (joint single antenna and multiple antenna plannings). The authors justified these results on sub-centimeters tumours, that are smaller than the minimum physical ablation volume achievable by a MWA device. 
From my point of view, the authors should provide: 1) the minimum achievable ablation volume; 2) the number of sub-centimeters tumours in the validation datasets. In my understanding, the cases where the tumour volume is smaller than the minimum ablation could be presented separately, providing a better understanding on the application.
As a minor weakness, especially in the introduction, the authors states frequently the need of real time during planning. While I understand the importance of a fast and responsive simulation in a planning applications, at first read I was misleaded thinking the clinical application had the need of a real time planning framework (e.g. intraoperative needs). I suggest to review the introduction and better explain that, from a usability point of view of a planning application, having a very fast simulation framework can be very beneficial. I suggest to change the term “real-time” with “high-performance” computing capabilities in this text.

reviews.text_contribution: Real-time (i.e., within clinical time constraints) computational framework for liver tumour microwave ablation planning based on deep learning and probabilistic inverse inference. reviews.text_strengths:
1.The study aims to develop a solution that integrates well into the clinical workflow. Because clinician input is required to initiate the planning process, the proposed system is designed to assist clinicians rather than replace them.
2.The methods are described clearly and in sufficient detail, especially considering the space constraints of MICCAI papers.

5.Physically meaningful accuracy metrics, including the Hausdorff distance, are employed in the validation.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Although both the Dice coefficient and Hausdorff distance are used as validation metrics, it is unclear how the Hausdorff distance is computed in practice. In particular, the manuscript does not explain whether it is calculated on the boundaries (surfaces) of the ablation-induced necrotic regions.
2.Insertion of ablation antennas is likely to cause tissue deformation and potential target (tumour) displacement. While addressing this issue may be beyond the scope of the current study, acknowledging it explicitly as a limitation would strengthen the paper.
3.The Hausdorff distance is reported in millimetres; however, without information about the image resolution, these values are difficult to interpret. The manuscript should include information about image resolution to contextualise the reported distances.
