author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their constructive assessment and for recognizing the novelty and potential clinical relevance of the work. We focus on the main points that require clarification.
1.Baseline comparison with current clinical practice (R1). R1 asked for a comparison with clinical practice. We believe this comparison is already included: the forward model was compared against manufacturer-provided power-time tables, which represent the standard planning reference and do not account for patient-specific anatomy or vascular heat-sink effects. In the in vivo validation, our method achieved a DSC of 0.82, compared with 0.59 for this baseline.
2.Role and size of the synthetic dataset (R1). R1 questioned whether 2400 synthetic samples are sufficient to capture patient-specific variability. These samples are not intended to form a complete atlas of human anatomical variability. Their role is to train the surrogate to reproduce the coupled electromagnetic-thermal response generated by the FEM solver under varying local conditions. The goal is not to memorize specific anatomies, but to approximate the physics of MWA across plausible tissue and vascular scenarios. We increased variability by randomizing vessel-generation parameters within literature-based ranges, perfusion values, and tumor morphology. We acknowledge that no finite synthetic dataset can exhaustively sample all tumor-vessel configurations, but our aim is to expose the model to diverse plausible cases so that it learns the simulated physical process rather than fixed geometries.
3.Ablation Efficiency in single-antenna cases (R2). R2 questioned the lower AE reported for single-antenna treatments. This reflects a physical constraint of MWA: even low settings (30 W, 180 s) create a minimum lesion size, typically on the order of 2 cm in diameter. For sub-centimeter tumors, covering the tumor plus the required oncological margin necessarily produces an ablation volume that is large relative to the target. AE therefore decreases because the minimum achievable lesion overshoots the small target. We will also include the number of sub-centimeters tumors in the validation dataset.
4.Use of “Real-Time” (R2). We agree that “real-time” may be misleading, as it could suggest an intraoperative requirement rather than the intended preoperative planning context. We have therefore removed “Real-Time” from the title. “Interactive” better reflects the intended clinical use: fast feedback allowing the clinician to explore and refine treatment plans during preoperative planning.
5.Sequential ablations, tissue changes, and deformation (R1 and R3). R1 noted that previous ablations modify tissue properties. Updating the tissue map after each virtual ablation would be straightforward within our framework. However, we did not include this step because there is no clear consensus on how tissue properties should be modified after necrosis, especially dielectric and thermal parameters. We therefore avoided introducing an assumption that could not be robustly justified. Currently, sequential planning updates the residual tumor mask while keeping pre-treatment tissue properties unchanged. R3 also noted that antenna insertion may cause deformation and target displacement. This falls outside the paper scope, but we agree that it can introduce prediction errors and will acknowledge it as a limitation.
6.HD95 computation and image resolution (R3). HD95 is computed on the surfaces of the predicted and reference necrotic regions. After thresholding the predicted probability map, we extract the boundary voxels of both masks and compute the 95th percentile of the bidirectional surface-to-surface distances. Distances are converted from voxel units to millimeters using image spacing. All volumes are resampled to an isotropic resolution of 0.6 x 0.6 x 0.6 mm^3 before training and evaluation, so HD95 values correspond to physical discrepancies in the resampled space.

title: Interpretable Local-to-Global Estimation of Brain Aging Speed From Morphological Changes Using Longitudinal Structural MRI Data
abstract: Accurate characterization of brain aging is essential for understanding cognitive decline and assessing the risk of neurodegenerative disease. Brain age estimated from cross-sectional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data provides a snapshot of brain health relative to chronological age, and the derived brain age delta has emerged as a promising biomarker. However, brain age delta reflects cumulative effects at a single time point and fails to capture ongoing aging dynamics. Longitudinal approaches address this limitation by estimating age differences between scan pairs to derive aging speed. Nevertheless, existing methods primarily rely on intensity or texture differences between images, overlook the spatial heterogeneity of aging processes, and provide limited interpretability. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel framework that estimates brain aging speed from longitudinal deformation fields obtained via diffeomorphic image registration. Instead of solely generating a single global estimate, our method produces patch-wise local aging predictions and adaptively integrates them into a unified global prediction, improving both predictive performance and interpretability. Evaluated on large-scale datasets, our approach achieves superior accuracy compared with existing methods and enhances the identification of abnormal aging patterns in diseased populations. Code is available at https://github.com/Kateridge/MorphologyAgingSpeed.
subject_areas: Applications -> Outcome Prediction / Prognosis / Longitudinal Modeling

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper proposes a longitudinal framework to estimate brain aging speed using deformation fields derived from diffeomorphic registration between MRI scan pairs. 
Instead of relying on intensity differences, it models spatially heterogeneous aging by producing patch-wise local aging estimates across the brain. 
These local predictions are then adaptively aggregated into a global aging speed, improving interpretability and capturing regional dynamics. 
Experiments on ADNI, OASIS3 and AIBL datasets show improved accuracy and better detection of abnormal aging patterns compared to prior methods.
reviews.text_strengths:
The approach is novel and interesting to model longitudinal morphological trajectories based on a diffeomorphic registration framework.
The results are strong, especially for cross-site generalization compared to previous state-of-the-art.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The first part of your model (deep learning-based diffeomorphic image registration) follows exactly the VoxelMorph pipeline. Is it trained along with the actual regressor of aging speed based on the Jacobian determinant map? If yes, do you observe a correlation between the registration accuracy and the speed aging prediction accuracy?
(Suggestion) In your model, you only consider time difference (t2-t1) between two scans, implicitly assuming the morphological changes do not depend on the initial timepoint t1 (i. e. original age). According to current brain charts [Bethlehem, Nature 2022], we know this is not true because brain morphology typically evolves non-linearly with time (and is even different across sex). I wonder whether including the original timepoint t1 (and maybe sex) as input to the model (in addition to the two scans) would refine the quality of the brain aging speed estimation.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper proposes an elegant framework to model regional brain aging speed based on diffeomorphic fields. The model is simple and the results are strong compared to prior works. In practice, it allows to accurately distinguish MCI -> AD converters from non-converters using MRI at the group level.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have successfully answered my main concern about age- and sex-dependent modeling of brain atrophy. I believe there is still room for improvement but the results given here are already promising and deserve to be published at MICCAI.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose a method to predict age differences between two longitudinal brain MRI scans by leveraging morphological information derived from diffeomorphic registration, combined with patch-based localized estimation. The experiments suggest that using morphology-based features improves performance compared to relying solely on intensity information, and that localized (patch-level) modeling outperforms global representations.
reviews.text_strengths:
Well-motivated and clearly presented idea: The paper is built on a clear and intuitive premise that longitudinal data can better capture aging dynamics compared to cross-sectional approaches. In addition, the use of localized (patch-level) information is well justified, as it enhances both interpretability and predictive performance.
Meaningful use of morphological information: Leveraging morphology derived from diffeomorphic registration is a strong design choice, as it focuses on biologically relevant changes rather than relying solely on intensity-based features.
Comprehensive experimental validation: The experiments are generally sufficient to support the main claims, including comparisons between morphology vs. intensity features and localized vs. global modeling.
Evaluation on downstream clinical tasks: The inclusion of experiments on diseased populations strengthens the practical relevance of the work and demonstrates potential clinical utility.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Limited methodological novelty: While the combination of morphology-based features and patch-level modeling is well motivated, each component has been explored in prior work (e.g., registration-based morphometry and patch-based learning). The paper would benefit from a clearer articulation of what is fundamentally new beyond this integration, and how it advances the state of the art.
Missing details on hyperparameter weighting: The paper does not specify the hyperparameters that control the relative strength of each loss term.
Unexpected generalization behavior: The model achieves lower error (MAE and RMSE) on the external test set than the internal set, which is counterintuitive.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a well-motivated approach to longitudinal brain age modeling, and the experimental results generally support the main claims. The use of morphology and localized estimation is meaningful and relevant. However, limitations such as modest novelty, missing methodological details (e.g., hyperparameters) weaken the overall contribution. Overall, I find the work promising but with some shortcomings, leading to a weak accept recommendation.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper proposes a framework for estimating brain aging speed from longitudinal structural MRI by leveraging deformation fields obtained via diffeomorphic registration.
Instead of producing a single global prediction, the method:
-computes Jacobian determinant maps to quantify voxel-wise morphological changes,
-partitions these maps into patches,
-predicts local aging speed per patch,
-aggregates local predictions into a global estimate using learned relevance weights.
The framework is trained on cognitively unimpaired subjects and evaluated on longitudinal datasets, with the goal of improving both predictive performance and interpretability compared to existing longitudinal and cross-sectional approaches.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper addresses an important limitation of brain age delta by explicitly modeling aging dynamics through longitudinal data, which is a meaningful and relevant direction.
2.The use of deformation fields and Jacobian determinants as representations of structural change is technically sound and biologically meaningful compared to intensity-based differences.
3.The patch-wise regression framework is an interesting design choice that enables spatial interpretability while maintaining a global prediction.
4.The paper includes:
-comparisons with cross-sectional and longitudinal baselines,
-ablation studies (without morphology / without local prediction),
-evaluation on internal and external datasets.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Figure 3 presents trends of aging speed across different diagnostic progression groups (e.g., CU-to-CU, MCI-to-AD), computed as averages within age bins.
However, the manuscript does not report:
-the number of samples per group
-the number of samples per age bin
-any measure of variability (e.g., standard deviation, confidence intervals, or error bars)
This is a critical limitation, as the observed trends may be strongly influenced by differences in sample size across groups or bins. In particular, progression groups are likely smaller and unevenly distributed across age ranges, which can lead to unstable estimates and misleading trends.
As a result, it is difficult to determine whether the reported differences reflect genuine biological effects or are artifacts of sampling variability.
2.The paper concludes that progression groups exhibit higher aging speed based on the trends in Figure 3.However, no statistical test is reported to compare these groups, and no uncertainty estimates are provided. Given the lack of quantitative support, these conclusions appear overstated.
3.The proposed aging speed metric is central to the contribution, yet its validity is not rigorously demonstrated. In particular, the paper does not show:
-correlation with clinical outcomes or cognitive measures,
-comparison with established biomarkers (e.g., brain age delta) beyond qualitative trends,
-robustness or stability of the metric across subjects.
As a result, it remains unclear whether the proposed measure captures meaningful biological aging dynamics or primarily reflects model-specific behavior.
4.The method relies entirely on deformation fields obtained via diffeomorphic registration. However, no analysis is provided regarding:
-sensitivity to registration errors,
-robustness across different registration approaches,
-potential artifacts introduced by misalignment.
Given that the Jacobian determinant maps are the core input to the model, this is an important missing validation.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper proposes a well-designed framework for estimating brain aging speed from longitudinal MRI data and demonstrates improved predictive performance over existing methods.
However, the evaluation does not provide sufficient statistical support for key claims, particularly regarding differences between diagnostic groups. The absence of information on sample sizes per group and per age bin, as well as the lack of uncertainty estimates, makes it difficult to assess the reliability of the reported trends.
In addition, the proposed aging speed metric is not thoroughly validated, and the method’s dependence on image registration is not analyzed in terms of robustness.
Overall, while the method is promising, the current evidence is not sufficient to fully support the conclusions, placing the paper slightly below the acceptance threshold.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
Thank you for the detailed and well-structured rebuttal. I appreciate the authors’ efforts in directly addressing the main concerns raised in the review.
In particular, the additional clarification regarding Figure 3, including the reporting of sample sizes per group and age bin, as well as the inclusion of statistical testing, significantly strengthens the validity of the group-level analysis. This resolves my primary concern regarding the interpretability of the reported trends.
Furthermore, the additional validation of the proposed aging speed metric through statistically significant correlations with cognitive measures (e.g., MMSE, CDR, ADAS13) provides important evidence supporting its clinical relevance, addressing another key limitation identified in the original review.
While the discussion on registration robustness remains somewhat qualitative, the authors provide reasonable justification given the within-subject setting and the scope of the rebuttal.
Overall, I believe the rebuttal has sufficiently addressed the major concerns raised in my review. I therefore update my recommendation to acceptance.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper got mostly positive feedback. Still, there are important methodological points raised by Rev. 4 that need to be addressed in a rebuttal. An additional point to discuss, raised by Rev. 1, is that the speed is assumed in the paper to be independent of age and sex, which is not true. Thus, the method is expected to fail when applied to younger populations.

The authors addressed the reviewers’ main concerns. Brain aging speed is a useful complement to brain aging estimation, providing additional features to characterize diseased populations.

I think that the idea is interesting. Although some weaknesses still remain, I thought that authors have provided a good discussion on this early-stage but interesting research, and have provided some convincing responses to specific critiques. I strongly encourage authors to include better clarifications and revisions as suggested by reviewers to strengthen the final version. I would argue for accept.

Although pairwise training has been developed for longitudinal brain age analysis (LSSL, LNE, LILAC, etc), the proposed method is novel in terms of local patch treatment and deformation-based pairwise learning. The sample size is acceptable. The results seem to be stronger than LILAC, the SOTA. These strengths outweighs the minor weaknesses.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback. Following meta-review, we first address the methodological and statistical concerns, then respond to additional points.
Q1: Statistical rigor of group comparisons (Fig. 3) [R4-C1,C2; Meta-Review] 
We appreciate this important concern. We have amended Fig. 3 to include 1) sample sizes per group and per age bin, and 2) Wilcoxon rank-sum test results between converter and non-converter groups, overall and within each age bin. 
Brain age delta showed significant differences (p < 0.01) between two non-converter groups of different disease severity (CU->CU vs. MCI->MCI) across all age bins and overall. For aging speed, MCI->AD differed significantly from both non-converter groups across all age bins (p < 0.01), while CN->MCI differed significantly in the 60-64 age bin. Crucially, the non-converter groups (CU->CU vs. MCI->MCI) showed no significant aging speed differences across most age bins, confirming that aging speed captures disease progression rather than severity, unlike brain age delta.
Q2: Age and sex as confounders [R1-C2; Meta-Review]
We agree brain morphology changes nonlinearly with age and differs between sex. In our framework, the Jacobian determinant maps may already implicitly encode age-dependent atrophy patterns. Incorporating t_1 as an input feature at the output layer of regressors yielded comparable performance on CU subjects (MAE :1.15, R2: 0.67 internal test; MAE: 0.72, R2: 0.58 external test), suggesting Jacobian maps already capture substantial age-related information. However, more advanced conditioning methods (e.g., FT-Transformers or FiLM) may further improve predictions, which is a promising future work, and we will discuss this limitation in the revised manuscript.
Q3: Validation of the aging speed metric [R4-C3]
Spearman correlations between the estimated aging speed and longitudinal cognitive change (on ADNI CU test + all ADNI MCI/AD subjects) were statistically significant: MMSE (-0.23), CDR (0.28), FAQ (0.24), ADAS13 (0.23), all p < 0.001.These further confirm aging speed captures clinically meaningful cognitive decline, not merely model-specific behavior.
Q4: Registration robustness [R1-C1, R4-C4]
Our framework is end-to-end and jointly trained; registration and regression errors decrease simultaneously, with registration converging first. 
The registration part is a within-subject registration task, which is inherently easier than cross-subject registration, reducing susceptibility to large misalignment. Also, Table 2 (rows 5–6 vs. 2–3) consistently shows improvements over methods without morphological features, demonstrating the utility and robustness of deformation-based representations. Nevertheless, we agree that a systematic comparison across registration methods is a valuable future work.
Q5: Novelty [R3-C1]
Our contribution addresses two limitations of prior works: 1) intensity-based methods are sensitive to imaging noise and variability, whereas within-subject registration-derived Jacobian determinants provide morphology-driven, noise-robust features reflecting anatomical aging; 2) existing methods predict a single global aging speed, whereas our patch-wise prediction with learned aggregation explicitly models spatial heterogeneity, improving both prediction accuracy (Table 2) and interpretability (Fig. 4). Their integration within a jointly optimized framework is, to our knowledge, novel.
Q6: Hyperparameter details [R3-C2]
Default hyperparameters were used for registration, similar to prior studies [5]. The full loss is: 1.0
L_reg + 0.01
L_smo + 1.0
L_local + 1.0
L_global. These details will be added to the manuscript.
Q7: Lower external test error [R3-C3]
This reflects dataset characteristics: AIBL has a narrower age range and smaller longitudinal intervals (\Delta t) than ADNI/OASIS (Table 1). All comparison methods achieved lower external errors, confirming a dataset-level rather than model-specific effect.

title: Interpretable Longitudinal Disease Forecasting with Graph-Based Multimodal Encoding and Population-Aware Language Generation
abstract: Multimodal longitudinal records provide critical insights into disease evolution and support disease understanding and early intervention. However, existing methods struggle with irregular and incomplete multimodal data, overlook the population-level progressions, and offer limited interpretability for clinical forecasting. To address these challenges, we propose a unified multimodal longitudinal forecasting framework that jointly predicts future disease status while generating explanations. Our approach employs a multimodal language model (MLM) with a novel longitudinal language tuning scheme that learns from generated hierarchical interpretations, enabling forecasting alongside structured explanatory outputs. Furthermore, a multimodal bipartite graph module is proposed to model missing and heterogeneous records, while a dual-memory module retrieves population-level patterns to support report generation. Experimental results on the ADNI dataset demonstrate significant improvement of the proposed method in both disease forecasting and result interpretation compared with state-of-the-art methods.
subject_areas: Applications -> Outcome Prediction / Prognosis / Longitudinal Modeling
Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper proposes ENIGMA (ENable Interpretable multimodal longitudinal modeling with bipartite Graph encoding and population Memory-Augmented generation), a multimodal language model (MLM) framework for interpretable Alzheimer’s disease forecasting. The core innovations include:
1.First MLM-based Longitudinal Forecasting Framework: To the authors’ knowledge, this is the first multimodal language model specifically designed for longitudinal disease forecasting that jointly predicts future disease status while generating hierarchical structured explanations.
2.Bipartite Graph Encoding (BGE): A novel module that handles incomplete and heterogeneous multimodal longitudinal records (MRI images, time-variant clinical variables, time-invariant demographics) using graph neural networks. The bipartite graph structure represents records as nodes with missingness reflected in connectivity, enabling robust handling of missing data.
3.Hierarchical Interpretation Construction: The framework generates structured explanations at four temporal scales:
Visit Impression (VI): Current normative status
Recent Changes (RC): Most recent evolution patterns
Long-term Changes (LC): Historical trajectory from initial visits
Progression Status (PG): Expected evolution toward forecasting target
These hierarchical interpretations are constructed using normative modeling (FreeSurfer volumetric quantiles) and synthesized via GPT-5.2 to create teaching supervision.
4.Dual Population Memory (DPM): Two memory banks (record memory and impression memory) that capture population-level multimodal disease evolution patterns and textual impressions, enabling population-aware forecasting and clinically relevant explanation generation.
5.Longitudinal Language Tuning: A novel training scheme where the MLM learns from generated hierarchical interpretations, enabling forecasting alongside structured explanatory outputs.
The framework addresses key limitations of existing methods: inability to handle irregular/incomplete multimodal data, lack of population-level pattern modeling, and limited clinical interpretability.
reviews.text_strengths:
Strength 1: Novel Integration of MLMs for Interpretable Clinical Forecasting
This is pioneering work bringing multimodal language models to longitudinal disease forecasting with structured interpretability, addressing a critical gap in medical AI where most models are “black boxes. “
The hierarchical explanation structure (VI, RC, LC, PG) is clinically meaningful and mirrors how physicians reason about disease progression - considering current status, recent changes, long-term trends, and expected trajectory.
The dual-task learning (forecasting + explanation generation) is elegant: the model learns better disease representations by being forced to generate clinically grounded explanations, not just predict labels.
Strength 2: Sophisticated Handling of Missing and Heterogeneous Data
The bipartite graph encoding (BGE) is technically sound for handling incomplete multimodal longitudinal records - a ubiquitous challenge in real clinical data.
Graph structure naturally represents variable-time relationships with missingness encoded in connectivity patterns, more principled than simple imputation or loss masking.
The method handles three types of variables (time-variant tabular, time-invariant tabular, imaging patches) in a unified framework using GNN with multi-head attention.
Strength 3: Strong Empirical Results with Comprehensive Evaluation
Impressive improvements over strong baselines: 84.2% accuracy vs. 76.4% for best baseline (UniLM), 89.3% AUC vs. 89.0% for GraFITi.
Outperforms recent LLM/MLM methods (DTGPT, NoteLM, ViT-LM) across all metrics, demonstrating the value of the proposed architectural innovations.
Multi-faceted evaluation: quantitative forecasting metrics (ACC, SEN, SPE, F1, AUC), NLG quality metrics (BLEU, METEOR, ROUGE-L, BERTScore), LLM-based judge evaluation, AND clinician evaluation across 6 dimensions.
Comprehensive comparisons: 9 baselines covering single-modality, multi-modality, and VLM approaches.
Qualitative analysis (Fig. 3) shows the model generates more accurate, structured, and clinically coherent explanations compared to strong baseline (NoteLM).
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Weakness 1: Questionable Quality of GPT-Generated Teaching Labels
Issue: The entire hierarchical interpretation structure (VI, RC, LC, PG) is generated by GPT-5.2 and used as teaching supervision. The paper states “To avoid manual summarization, we provide GPT-5.2 with the complete four-visit longitudinal records. . . “ However, there is no validation mechanism to verify the correctness of these GPT-generated annotations.
This is problematic because: (1) The model is learning from potentially hallucinated or inconsistent explanations, (2) GPT-5.2 may not have medical expertise to accurately interpret normative deviations and generate clinically appropriate explanations, (3) No gold standard from actual clinicians is used for comparison.
The reviewer asks (from focus points): “What are the mechanisms put in place for verifying the annotation given by ChatGPT considered as reference for the teaching for the different annotation VI, RC, LC, PG?” - This critical question is not addressed in the paper.
Specific references: For concerns about LLM-generated medical data: Thirunavukarasu et al. , “Large language models in medicine,” Nature Medicine 2023; Singhal et al. , “Towards Expert-Level Medical Question Answering with Large Language Models,” arXiv 2023.
Weakness 2: Missing Statistical Significance Testing
Issue: No statistical significance tests are reported for the forecasting results in Table 1.While the proposed method shows improvements (e. g. , 84.2% ACC vs. 76.4% for UniLM), there are no p-values, confidence intervals, or significance tests (e. g. , DeLong test for AUC comparisons, McNemar’s test for accuracy).
Given that results are reported on a test set of only 297 clips, statistical testing is crucial to establish whether observed differences are significant or could occur by chance.
Reviewer’s focus note: “Need statistical test DeLong for AUC”
Specific references: DeLong et al. , “Comparing the areas under two or more correlated receiver operating characteristic curves: a nonparametric approach,” Biometrics 1988.
Weakness 3: Inconsistent and Unexplained Baseline Comparisons
Issue: The reviewer notes “Why is LaTIM missing in the Visit missing comparison?” suggesting that some baselines are not consistently evaluated across conditions.
Some baseline methods (DTGPT, NoteLM) are given an unfair advantage by providing ground-truth volumetric measurements directly as input, while other methods must extract this from imaging. The paper acknowledges this (“DTGPT and NoteLM are unable to process MRI images, instead ground-truth volumetric measurements are directly provided”) but doesn’t fully account for this advantage in interpretation of results.
The paper claims improvements over NoteLM on explanation quality, but NoteLM has access to privileged information (ground-truth volumes), making the comparison less meaningful.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Major Comments:
1.CRITICAL: Provide validation mechanism for GPT-generated hierarchical interpretations (VI, RC, LC, PG). Consider having expert clinicians validate a subset of generated explanations against ground truth, or compare GPT-generated vs. human-generated explanations on a validation set. 
2.Add statistical significance testing (DeLong test for AUC, McNemar’s test or bootstrap for accuracy) for all comparisons in Table 1.
3.Clarify why LaTIM is missing from visit missing comparisons and ensure all baselines are evaluated consistently. 
4.Provide more details on clinician evaluation methodology: How many clinicians? What were their qualifications? How were the 10 cases selected? Inter-rater agreement?
Minor Comments:
1.Consider ablation studies isolating the contribution of: (a) bipartite graph encoding vs. simpler missing data handling, (b) dual population memory vs. no memory, (c) hierarchical interpretations vs. single-level explanations. 
2.Provide training time and computational cost comparisons with baselines. 
3.The claim “first MLM-based longitudinal forecasting framework” should be carefully verified - provide explicit comparison with any concurrent work. 
4.Include failure case analysis: When does the model generate incorrect explanations? When does forecasting fail?
For extension:
1.How sensitive is the method to the quality of GPT-generated teaching labels? What happens if GPT-5.2 generates incorrect interpretations?
2.Can the framework handle variable numbers of visits (not just 4)?
3.How does performance degrade with increasing amounts of missing data?

Recommendation: Accept. The paper makes significant methodological contributions with strong empirical validation. Weaknesses can be addressed in camera-ready version (add statistical tests, clarify baselines, provide GPT label validation).
Positive Factors:
Novel and ambitious work bringing multimodal language models to interpretable longitudinal disease forecasting - addresses a critical need for explainable medical AI
Strong technical contributions: bipartite graph encoding for missing data, dual population memory, hierarchical interpretation framework
Comprehensive evaluation with impressive results: 84.2% ACC, 89.3% AUC, outperforming 9 baselines including recent LLM/MLM methods
Multi-faceted evaluation methodology: forecasting metrics, NLG quality, LLM-based judging, AND clinician evaluation
Qualitative results (Fig. 3) demonstrate clinically meaningful, structured explanations that align with normative evidence
Tackles real clinical challenges: missing data, heterogeneous modalities, need for interpretability
Use of public ADNI dataset enables reproducibility
Code release commitment
Concerns:
Primary concern: Lack of validation for GPT-generated teaching labels is a methodological weakness, but doesn’t invalidate the overall contribution since the model still achieves strong empirical results
Missing statistical significance testing (but this can be added)
Some baseline comparison inconsistencies
Missing some implementation details

reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: My concerns were tackle and I was already convinced that the paper should be accepted.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
1.The authors aim to develop a model to explain the disease progression via text generation using LLM.
2.The authors proposed Bipartite graph encoding module to encode incomplete multimodal longitudinal records.
reviews.text_strengths: The authors introduced a graph-based multimodal encoder tailored to irregular, missing longitudinal data by treating time and variables as a bipartite graph with edge embeddings for observed values and a query-time aggregation mechanism.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The authors mentioned that their main contribution is to design Bipartite graph encoding (BGE). However, the authors have not emphasized the good points of this module. What is the novelty of this module? In addition, what is L_da^i loss in equation (1)? How is it computed?

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The authors propose ENIGMA, a framework for forecasting Alzheimer’s disease progression from longitudinal multimodal records (3D MRI + tabular clinical/demographic variables across multiple visits) that produces both a categorical diagnosis at a future visit and a structured natural-language explanation. The system has three main components. First, a Bipartite Graph Encoding (BGE) module represents each subject’s multi-visit records as a graph where variable nodes connect to time nodes, with edges present only where data is observed; this is intended to handle missingness and modality heterogeneity, and is processed with a 4-layer graph neural network using multi-head attention. Second, a Dual Population Memory (DPM) module maintains two memory banks — one over multimodal record embeddings, one over text-derived “impression” embeddings — trained with a SwAV-style swap loss to capture cohort-level progression patterns. Third, a multimodal language model (Qwen3-4B-Instruct with LoRA) consumes the individual embedding, the population memory, and a task instruction, and is trained to generate explanations at multiple temporal scales (Recent Changes, Long-term Changes, Progression) alongside the diagnostic prediction.
The training supervision for the explanation task is itself synthetic: GPT-5.2 is given the structured longitudinal data (cognitive scores, brain volume quantiles, w-scores, slope labels) and asked to write the reference explanations, which then serve as teacher-forcing targets. Evaluation is on 2,342 four-visit clips from 399 ADNI participants, with subjects who converted to AD before visit 4 excluded. Forecasting is scored against the actual visit-4 diagnosis (ACC, SEN, SPE, F1, AUC); explanations are scored with NLG metrics (BLEU, METEOR, ROUGE-L, BERTScore), an LLM-as-judge using GPT-5.2 across six dimensions (Consistency, Historical Fidelity, Prognostic Fidelity, Structural Specificity, Helpfulness, Human-likeness), and a small clinician panel. Reported forecasting accuracy of 0.842 substantially exceeds the strongest baseline at 0.764.
reviews.text_strengths: The forecasting result itself is the cleanest piece of evidence and looks genuinely strong. The visit-4 diagnostic label is an objective ground truth independent of the language modeling, and a jump from 0.764 to 0.842 accuracy over the best baseline is not trivial. The robustness experiments under missing tabular variables and missing visits (Fig. 4c, 4d) are a sensible addition and the model appears to degrade gracefully. The bipartite graph formulation for handling irregular and incomplete longitudinal records is a reasonable design choice and builds on a defensible line of prior work (GraFITi, GRAPE). The motivation — that visualization-based interpretability via image synthesis demands expert reading, while structured language explanations are more directly useful — is well-taken.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Circularity in the explanation evaluation. 
This is my main substantive concern, and it runs through several parts of the evaluation in a way that is not adequately acknowledged.
The reference explanations used as training targets are written by GPT-5.2 from the structured input data. The same GPT-5.2 is then used as the LLM-judge to score candidate explanations across the six clinical-correctness dimensions in Table 2.The model under evaluation is, to a meaningful extent, being trained to imitate the judge’s writing on inputs the judge has already seen in structured form, and is then graded by that judge. The first row of Table 2 makes this concrete: “GPT (GT)” is itself scored and receives 4.04–4.96 across the six dimensions, i.e., the judge rates its own outputs as near-ceiling. The authors do not comment on this, and the implications for the relative ordering of methods in Table 2 are unclear.
The clinician evaluation in Fig. 2 is the right instrument for breaking this loop, but as reported it cannot do that work. Ten explanations, across five methods, scored on six dimensions by two clinicians, with no inter-rater agreement statistics, no confidence intervals, no significance tests, no rubric beyond the one-sentence definitions in the text, no statement on blinding or order randomization, and no information about the clinicians’ subspecialty or experience reading ADNI-style cases. With those gaps, the radar plot in Fig. 2 is suggestive at best.
I would want to see, at minimum: the full prompt and rubric used by the LLM-judge (in supplementary); inter-rater agreement (Cohen’s κ or ICC) for the clinician panel; a substantially larger clinician sample and ideally a blinded pairwise preference protocol rather than absolute Likert scores, which are notoriously poorly calibrated across raters; and explicit discussion of the circularity introduced by using GPT-5.2 as both supervisor and judge.
Asymmetric baselines for explanation quality. 
DTGPT and NoteLM are given ground-truth volumetric measurements as text input, while image-based methods (including ENIGMA) must extract this from MRI. The authors note this and treat it as a handicap they overcome, but it cuts in both directions: the text-only baselines lack feature-extraction noise, which should favor their explanation quality, but they also lack any mechanism to identify imaging findings the volumetrics don’t capture. It is hard to read Table 2 cleanly given this asymmetry, and a more apples-to-apples baseline — say, NoteLM given the same MRI features ENIGMA extracts — would strengthen the case.
Single-cohort evaluation. All results are on ADNI, with one preprocessing pipeline (FreeSurfer + MNI152), one LLM backbone (Qwen3-4B), and an exclusion criterion (no pre-visit-4 converters) that selects for slower progressors. There is no external cohort validation. For a paper whose central claim includes “population-aware” forecasting, the absence of any out-of-distribution test is notable.
Minor / Clarification Questions
The notation nn.Embedding should be spelled out (it’s a learnable lookup table); calling it by its PyTorch class name will not be transparent to all readers. The phrase “L = 4 layers GNN using multi-head attention blocks” deserves a sentence clarifying that the GNN is attention-based message-passing rather than convolutional, since “GNN” is overloaded in the literature. The w-score concept is used heavily but never defined; one sentence (“residual from a covariate-adjusted normative model, divided by residual SD”) would help readers outside the normative-modeling community. The rationale for selecting α_cl = 2.0, α_ca = 1.0, the 25% router sparsity target, and the memory length of 64 (Fig. 4a is shown but the criterion is unstated) should be made explicit. The footnote deferring “detailed implementation documentation” to a post-camera-ready GitHub release is a familiar dodge, and given how much methodological detail is unspecified in the main text, I would want to see at least a methods supplement at review time.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
1) The paper proposes ENIGMA, an interpretable multimodal language model framework for longitudinal disease prediction.
2) It introduces a bipartite graph encoding scheme to handle incomplete, multimodal, and longitudinal records.
3) The paper further proposes a dual population memory to support individual-level interpretation with population-level patterns.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) This paper focuses on predicting future status from historical follow-up records while requiring the model to provide interpretable explanations.
2) The three types of explanations enable the model to distinguish recent changes, long-term trends, and future progression.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) The explanation supervision heavily relies on GPT-generated content. As a result, the model may learn GPT-style explanations rather than explanations that truly reflect clinical expert reasoning.
2) Section 2.1 states that GPT uses complete four-visit longitudinal records and diagnoses to generate explanations, where the progression status describes the change from the most recent record to the target visit. This suggests that the explanation supervision may include the true diagnosis, cognitive scores, or even future imaging statistics from the fourth visit. While using such information as training targets may be acceptable, it raises concerns when evaluating explanation quality. If the reference explanations themselves depend on future ground-truth information, a closer match between the generated and reference explanations does not necessarily indicate that the model has truly inferred these changes from historical data.
3) The paper states that 2342 four-visit clips were constructed from 399 ADNI participants, with a train/validation/test split of 1764/281/297.However, it does not clearly specify whether the split was performed at the participant level. If different clips from the same participant appear in both the training and test sets, the longitudinal prediction task would suffer from serious data leakage, and the reported performance could be overestimated. For multi-visit datasets such as ADNI, this is a critical issue that must be clarified.
4) The method is complex, and its reproducibility is relatively poor.
5) n Table 1, the AUC of the proposed method is 0.893.However, in the modality ablation study in Table 3, the Image + Tabular setting achieves an AUC of 0.932, while the full MLM component in the last row again reports an AUC of 0.893.6) Figure 1 is difficult to read, and the paper introduces too many variables, which substantially reduces the overall readability.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The explanation supervision and evaluation rely excessively on GPT, while the paper suffers from poor readability and limited reproducibility.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors clearly state that the data split was performed at the participant level, which substantially alleviates the main concern about longitudinal data leakage. However, they still do not sufficiently explain whether GPT-generated explanations truly reflect clinical reasoning, whether the reference explanations rely on future ground-truth information, whether text-matching evaluation is fair, how reproducible the method is, why the AUC results are inconsistent, or how the readability of the figures can be improved. In particular, the AUC inconsistency between Table 1 and Table 3, as well as the potential use of future information in explanation supervision, require direct clarification.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper presents an ambitious and potentially impactful multimodal language model framework for interpretable longitudinal AD forecasting, with one reviewer strongly supporting acceptance while others provide mixed assessments (scores: 5 / 4 / 3 / 2) . While reviewers acknowledge strong empirical performance and novelty in combining forecasting with structured explanation generation, several critical concerns remain. In particular, the reliance on GPT-generated supervision without validation, potential data leakage in longitudinal splits, and circularity in explanation evaluation (e.g., using the same LLM for supervision and judging) need to be carefully addressed. Additional issues include unclear methodological details, baseline fairness, and reproducibility; the authors are encouraged to respond to these points in the rebuttal to clarify the validity and robustness of the proposed approach.

After the rebuttal, two reviewers recommended acceptance, one reviewer suggest reject, and one reviewer did not respond (with the original rating 2). Most of the concerns are raised due to clarity and reproducibility, which may not be easy considering the complexity of the method. The authors should try to improve the figures and descriptions, and include the discussions in the rebuttal in the revision.

After carefully reviewing the authors’ rebuttal, I have revised my initial assessment to Accept. The authors have provided a thorough, evidence-based response that directly addresses the core concerns raised by the reviewers, including participant-level split to prevent data leakage, validation of GPT-generated ground truth via clinician assessment, mitigation of evaluation circularity using Sonnet-4.6 as an independent judge, high clinician inter-rater agreement (Cohen’s κ = 0.79), statistical significance testing with McNemar tests, clarification of AUC inconsistencies, and provision of an anonymized code repository for reproducibility.

The rebuttal substantially alleviates the key concerns on participant-level data leakage, GPT-generated supervision reliability, LLM-judge circularity, statistical testing, and reproducibility, and although some issues about future-information-dependent explanations and table consistency remain, the strong empirical performance and positive post-rebuttal assessments support acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We thank reviewers/ACs and clarify key concerns below:
Dataset [R2Q2Q4/R4Q3]: We split dataset in participant level (319 train/41 val/39 test), yielding clips with no participants overlap. Tabular variables include 6 demographics (e.g. Sex/Age/Edu/Ethnicity/Race/Marry), APOE4, and 6 cognitive scores. MRI data are complete for all samples, whereas 22% records exhibit tabular missing values.
GT-reliability [R1/3/4Q1]: We construct GT similarly to how junior doctors are taught to trace evidence given target status. We also invite two senior clinicians to recognize GT’s quality across all 6 dims (CS 4.8 HF 4.9 PF 4.6 SS 4.7 HP 4.5 HL 4.8) together with Fig 2, suggesting GT’s reliability. Notably, similar GT-summary setups have been adopted in recent medical reasoning works, such as GEM(NIPS25) and ClinRaGen(ACL25), which supports our design.
LLM-judge circularity [R3Q1]: Using same LLM in GT-summary and LM-judge is adopted by prior works (GEM) since two stages are independent with different contexts and tasks. LM-judge‘s prompt instructs LM to rate candidate hieratically using given data, stats, rubric and output format, e.g. “You are a clinical reasoning evaluator. Input… Evaluate quality on… Output STRICT JSON…”. Rubric emphasizes objective evidence, e.g. “missing a key V1-V3 trend should score 3” in historical fidelity (full prompt and rubric in anonymized link). We further use Sonnet-4.6 as LM-judge across metrics, GPT-summarized GT achieves avg score of 3.86 as upper bound and ENIGMA ranks best among all methods (3.70 vs. suboptimal ViTB-LM 3.51).
Human evaluation [R3Q1/R4Q2]: Beyond GT text matching, the evaluation also includes historical and prognostic fidelity in both the LM-judge and clinician rubrics. Specifically, we include two clinicians’ blinded ratings for 10 cases, providing them with full records, labels, normative stats and shuffled text candidates. Two clinicians achieved high agreement (Cohen’s κ 0.79).
Fairness [R1Q3/R3Q2]: DTGPT/NoteLM cannot read MRI, we provide volumetric features as a realistic upper-bound proxy, and we also include MLM baselines, e.g. ViTB-LM, with MRI encoders and structured tabular for symmetric comparisons.
BGE novelty [R2Q1/5]: Unlike prior pre-visit fusion or missing completion works, BGE models fine-grained cross-time interactions in a unified graph. It is trained directly with missing value and irregularity thanks to edge disconnection design and learnable time encoding. L_da^i is a cross-entropy loss aligning the representation of visit i with disease status.
Reproducibility [R3Q4]: Full settings/code are online (sent to ACs due to Rebuttal Guide). Some important details are shared below. Experiments use 1 L40S GPU and cost 3.4h pretraining (batch size 16/100 epochs) and 2.0h finetuning (batch size 4/6 epochs) with lr=3e-5 and anneal decay. Checkpoints are selected by validation AUC with early stopping. We empirically search αcl from 1 to 3, αda in 0.5 1.0 1.5, sparsity 1/8 1/4 1/2.
Statistic significance [R1Q2]: McNemar tests (p<0.05) are conducted to assess statistical significance showing ENIGMA significantly improves accuracy.
Modality ablation justification [R4Q5]: First panel in Table 3 presents an ablation study of the multimodal encoder (BGE) under different modality inputs, rather than the full MLM pipeline. which leads to AUC difference.
Tabular data domination [R2Q7]: Experimental results indicate that tabular data contribute more, likely due to their closer relevance to AD diagnosis (e.g., cognitive scores). However, MRI still provides complementary anatomical cues.
Visit missing comparison [R1Q3]: Fig 4 tests extra input missing at inference stage. As LaTiM utilize the single record for inference, it is not directly comparable in this setting.
Related work [R2Q8]: Direct comparison is limited as W1/W2 lack public code. We compared W3 by adjusting into status prediction without PET, obtaining F1=0.652/AUC=0.796.We will discuss W1–3 in Related Work.

title: Interpretable Medical Image Diagnosis via VLM-based Concept Alignment and Graph Reasoning
abstract: Interpretable medical image diagnosis requires predictions grounded in clini-cally meaningful findings that physicians can inspect and correct. While Con-cept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) route predictions through predefined imaging signs, they treat concepts as independent scalar scores and struggle to align fi-ne-grained visual features with clinical semantics. We present ConceptAlignE-G, a framework that integrates vision-language model (VLM) based concept alignment with graph reasoning to bridge this gap. Built on BiomedCLIP, a concept-aware perception module grounds each imaging sign in a dedicated visual-semantic embedding space, enabling fine-grained alignment between sign-specific visual features and expert-defined text embeddings. The predict-ed sign probabilities are then used to construct a dynamic sign-image relation-al graph, where a GCN incorporates broader image context beyond the concept bottleneck for disease classification. On CT-based appendicitis differentiation and ultrasound-based breast cancer diagnosis, ConceptAlignE-G outperforms both black-box classifiers and existing concept-based methods in diagnostic AUC and sign recognition. Beyond accuracy, it provides per-sign prediction probabilities and interpretable decision weights, and supports clinician-driven intervention at inference time.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes ConceptAlignE-G, an interpretable medical image diagnosis framework that combines VLM-based concept alignment with graph reasoning. The method first uses BiomedCLIP to align image features with predefined clinical signs through sign-specific concept-aware perception modules, and then builds a dynamic sign-image graph where predicted sign probabilities serve as edge weights for GCN-based disease classification. The framework is evaluated on two tasks: CT-based appendicitis differentiation and ultrasound-based breast cancer diagnosis. The paper argues that the method improves both diagnostic performance and interpretability by providing sign-level probabilities and allowing clinician intervention at inference time.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper addresses an important and highly relevant problem for MICCAI: moving beyond black-box predictions toward clinically meaningful and editable explanations. The focus on radiological signs is well motivated and better aligned with clinical workflow than standard saliency-based explanations. 
2.The proposed framework is reasonably well designed. In particular, the idea of learning sign-specific visual subspaces via the concept-aware perception module is interesting, and the use of predicted concept probabilities to drive a graph-based diagnostic layer is a sensible extension beyond standard concept bottleneck models. 
3.The paper includes experiments on two different tasks and modalities, including an external test set for the appendicitis task. This is stronger than evaluating only on a single internal dataset. 
4.The interpretability mechanism is more actionable than post-hoc visualization methods. The concept intervention examples are a valuable part of the paper, since they show how correcting concept predictions can directly change the final diagnosis without retraining.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The experimental validation is still somewhat limited. The breast ultrasound dataset is small, and the paper does not provide enough evidence about robustness, such as confidence intervals, variance across folds/runs, or more detailed statistical analysis beyond a limited DeLong test claim. 
2.The baseline comparison is not fully convincing. The proposed method is built on BiomedCLIP, whereas the black-box and concept-based baselines appear to use ResNet50 backbones. This makes it difficult to disentangle the gain from the proposed method itself versus the gain from a stronger pretrained encoder. Stronger foundation-model-based baselines would be needed for a fairer comparison. 
3.The “graph reasoning” component is relatively simple. The graph is essentially a star-shaped structure with one image node and concept nodes, and the aggregation resembles weighted fusion of concept embeddings into the image representation. As a result, the technical novelty of the graph module may be viewed as incremental rather than substantial. 
4.The interpretability evaluation is mostly qualitative. While the case studies are nice, the paper lacks more systematic evidence that the explanations are faithful, clinically useful, or preferred by experts. For example, there is no quantitative evaluation of intervention success rate, concept calibration, or expert assessment of explanation quality.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I find the paper promising and relevant, with a clear motivation, a reasonable methodological design, and encouraging results across two medical imaging tasks. The sign-level interpretability and intervention mechanism are especially appealing. However, I am not fully convinced by the current empirical evidence, mainly due to the fairness of the baseline setup, limited quantitative interpretability evaluation, and the relatively modest technical depth of the graph reasoning component. Overall, I see this as a bweak accept paper: interesting and potentially valuable, but still needing stronger experimental support to justify a higher score.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper introduces ConceptAlignE-G, an interpretable framework for medical image diagnosis that uses clinically meaningful imaging signs as intermediate concepts.
The method relies on a dual-encoder setup based on BiomedCLIP, allowing text descriptions of disease signs and associated image features to be mapped into a shared latent space. A concept-aware perception module extracts sign-specific image representations, which are aligned with concept text embeddings to estimate the probability of each sign.
These sign probabilities are then used to construct a dynamic sign-image relational graph, which is processed by a graph convolution layer to combine image semantics, concept-level evidence, and textual concept knowledge for the final disease prediction. An additional practical aspect is that, because the prediction explicitly depends on intermediate concept scores, a clinician can in principle intervene by correcting concept values at inference time and obtain an updated prediction without retraining.
Overall, the contribution is a concept-based diagnostic framework that combines sign-specific visual extraction, language-grounded concept alignment, and graph-based aggregation to improve interpretability while maintaining competitive diagnostic performance.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper addresses an important and timely problem in medical AI: improving trust and interpretability in diagnostic models. This is clinically relevant, especially as explainability and accountability are becoming increasingly important for deployment and regulation.
2.The framework provides a more meaningful intermediate explanation than standard saliency or heatmap-based methods. Instead of only indicating where the model attends, it predicts clinically meaningful signs that can be directly interpreted by users.
3.The use of a domain-specific vision-language model, BiomedCLIP, is well motivated. Leveraging text descriptions of imaging signs gives the concept layer semantic grounding and is a sensible way to incorporate medical prior knowledge.
4.The paper is generally well organized and easy to follow, and the method description appears sufficiently detailed for understanding the main pipeline.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The experimental comparison is not fully controlled. The proposed method uses a BiomedCLIP image encoder with a ViT backbone, while the all black-box baselines use ResNet50 (+ DenseNet101). This creates a major methodological confound: it is unclear how much of the gain comes from ConceptAlignE-G itself versus the stronger pretrained backbone and multimodal pretraining. A fairer comparison would include a BiomedCLIP-based black-box classifier with the same, and most likely stronger, image encoder and training protocol, as well as for the CBM/CEM/CCBM-style baselines.
2.The claimed advantage over other concept-based and VLM-based approaches is not yet fully convincing. The paper argues that fixed concept sets create representational bottlenecks, but the proposed method still relies on an explicit set of K binary sign concepts and text embeddings for those signs. In practice, it still routes prediction through a predefined concept interface, so the distinction from existing concept bottleneck approaches should be clarified more carefully, or better explained.
3.The graph reasoning component appears relatively simple. The graph is a star graph centered on the image node, and the paper does not clearly establish why a GCN is preferable to simpler fusion strategies such as concatenation, gated weighting, or MLP-based aggregation. The paper includes ConceptAlignE as an ablation, which however does not target my concer.
4.The breast ultrasound experiment is based on a small dataset (252 images with five-fold cross-validation). That makes claims of superiority less convincing, especially when using a strong pretrained encoder. The paper reports AUC/ACC and mentions DeLong testing, but confidence intervals, fold variance, and broader pairwise statistical testing are missing or incomplete. Given the small sample size and modest margins in some comparisons, stronger statistical reporting is needed.
5.Robustness is not sufficiently characterized. In particular, the paper would benefit from analysis of sensitivity to prompt wording for the text concepts and to concept-label noise, since both are central to the proposed multimodal concept alignment approach.
6.Minor typos are present here and there in the manuscript.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
I encourage the authors to strengthen the experimental section with more controlled and targeted ablations. In particular, the paper would be significantly stronger if it included:
(1) a black-box BiomedCLIP classifier with the same image encoder and training protocol;
(2) CBM/CEM/CCBM-style baselines built on the same backbone/features;
(3) an ablation comparing the proposed GCN-based fusion against simpler alternatives; and
(4) robustness experiments for concept-label noise, missing concept labels, and prompt wording.
The paper would also benefit from stronger statistical reporting, especially for the small breast ultrasound dataset. Reporting confidence intervals, fold-wise variance, and significance testing for the key pairwise comparisons would make the conclusions more convincing.

This paper addresses an important problem in medical imaging: how to improve interpretability and trust in AI-based diagnosis using clinically meaningful intermediate concepts. The proposed framework is well motivated, clearly presented, and practically relevant. I also find the combination of sign-specific feature extraction, language-grounded concept alignment, and concept-based intervention at inference time to be useful and potentially impactful for clinical AI.
At the same time, I have reservations about the strength of the empirical evidence supporting the claimed methodological advantages. The comparisons are not fully controlled because the proposed model uses a stronger BiomedCLIP ViT-based encoder while most baselines use ResNet50, making it difficult to isolate the gain from the proposed concept alignment and graph design. In addition, the graph module is relatively simple and the paper does not yet show clearly that it outperforms simpler fusion mechanisms for the right reasons.
The experimental evidence is also somewhat limited by the small size of the breast ultrasound dataset and by incomplete statistical reporting. The method further inherits a reliance on explicit concept annotations, but the practical impact of this limitation is not deeply examined.
Overall, I view this as a solid and relevant methodological contribution with good clarity and an interesting interpretable design, but with limited novelty relative to prior concept-based/VLM-based work and with evaluation issues that keep it closer to the acceptance boundary than to a clear accept.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents ConceptAlignE-G, an interpretable medical image diagnosis framework that combines vision-language model (VLM) based concept alignment with graph convolutional network (GCN) reasoning. The framework aims to address key limitations in existing concept bottleneck models by introducing sign-specific feature extraction through a concept-aware perception module and incorporating broader image context through graph reasoning. The authors validate their approach on two clinical tasks: CT-based appendicitis differentiation and ultrasound-based breast cancer diagnosis.
reviews.text_strengths:
Introduces a concept-aware perception (CAP) module that extracts sign-specific visual features for each imaging finding rather than using a shared global representation, enabling more precise alignment between visual features and clinical text descriptions.
Constructs a dynamic sign-image relational graph where edge weights are determined by predicted concept probabilities, allowing a GCN to aggregate image semantics, concept text knowledge, and sign predictions jointly for disease classification.
The framework naturally supports concept-level intervention at inference time, where clinicians can override incorrect sign predictions and the corrected values immediately propagate through the graph to update the final diagnosis without requiring model retraining.
Testing on both CT and ultrasound modalities with different anatomical targets (appendix and breast) demonstrates some generalizability of the approach.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The appendicitis dataset, while multi-center, contains only 1156 patients, and the breast cancer dataset has merely 252 images. These sample sizes are quite small by modern deep learning standards, particularly for a model with multiple components (text encoder, image encoder, CAP modules, GCN). The risk of overfitting is substantial, and it remains unclear how well the approach would scale to larger, more diverse datasets. The reported improvements over baselines, while consistent, are often modest, raising questions about clinical significance.
While the intervention mechanism is technically sound, its practical value is unclear. In real clinical workflows, would radiologists actually review per-sign probabilities and manually correct them? The paper provides few anecdotal examples where intervention changes the prediction, but no systematic evaluation of how often radiologists would need to intervene, how difficult it is to identify which concepts to correct, or whether the corrected predictions are actually more accurate.
It lacks of sufficient ablation study. Why is a single GCN layer sufficient? Was a deeper graph network explored? The star topology seems restrictive, as it assumes concepts only interact through the central image node rather than allowing direct concept-to-concept relationships that might capture known clinical correlations.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper makes reasonable technical contributions to interpretable medical image analysis and demonstrates consistent, if modest, improvements over baselines. The integration of concept-aware perception with graph reasoning is sensible, and the framework addresses real limitations of existing concept bottleneck models. The validation on two clinical tasks sounds good. However, the work has limited ablation study, poor reproducibility details, smaller dataset experiments for concluding robust generalization and the unvalidated clinical utility of the intervention mechanism.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text: All reviewers acknowledged that the authors are addressing an important problem in medical image analysis. Reviewers also recoganized the contributions in methodology and the use of multiple datasets.

author_feedback_text:
We appreciate the reviewers’ thoughtful comments. A few clarifications on the major points:
On baseline fairness (R1-W2, R2-W1, R2-W2). The concern about backbone mismatch is fair, but BiomedCLIP is not merely a stronger encoder plugged into our pipeline. The CAP module and the graph both depend on the shared vision-language space (Sections 2.2–2.4). Table 1 already shows that stripping the CAP module (BiomedSigLIP) or dropping the GCN for a linear layer (ConceptAlignE) hurts performance within the same BiomedCLIP backbone. This suggests the gains come from the sign-specific perception and graph aggregation, not just the pretrained weights. As for CBM/CEM/CCBM, these methods were built around unimodal CNN encoders; porting them to BiomedCLIP would require redesigning their core feature extractors, which goes beyond a standard baseline comparison. We also want to clarify the distinction from standard CBMs (R2-W2): our CAP module learns sign-specific subspaces instead of projecting one global image feature onto concept vectors, and the GCN fuses image semantics with concept text knowledge and sign probabilities jointly. The text embeddings act as fixed semantic anchors drawn from clinical vocabulary.
On the graph module (R1-W3, R2-W3, R3-W3). The star topology mirrors how radiologists actually reason—evaluating each sign relative to the target lesion (Section 2.4). We use a single GCN layer because deeper propagation tends to over-smooth on such a small graph. The ablation in Table 1 supports this: replacing the GCN with a linear layer drops the appendicitis test AUC from 0.713 to 0.685, so the graph structure does add value over simple aggregation.
On dataset size and statistics (R1-W1, R2-W4, R3-W1). We agree the breast ultrasound dataset is small (252 images). We ran five-fold cross-validation with DeLong testing; the per-fold breakdown was omitted for space. The appendicitis task at least includes an external test set (n=202, unseen centers), which gives a more meaningful generalization signal than internal validation alone.
On interpretability and intervention (R1-W4, R3-W2). The intervention examples in Figure 2c–d are meant to show what the architecture makes possible, not to claim a validated clinical workflow. Real-world utility would need proper human factors studies, and we see that as important follow-up work.
On reproducibility (R1, R3). We will release the source code in the near future.
Thank you for the careful review.

title: Interpretable Probabilistic Medical Image Segmentation via Gaussian Process with Explicit Modelling of Annotation Bias and Variability
abstract: Deep learning-based medical image segmentation models are trained using annotations that exhibit systematic bias and variability across raters. While probabilistic multi-rater approaches can emulate annotator-specific delineations, annotator characteristics are typically encoded implicitly in deep latent feature space, making direct analysis of their influence on predictive distributions less straightforward. We propose a logit-space probabilistic segmentation framework based on stochastic variational Gaussian Process that explicitly decomposes predictions into an image-dependent reference logit distribution and annotator specific perturbations parameterised by bias and variance. This formulation enables more explicit analysis on how intra- and inter-rater variability propagate to predictive distributions. We evaluate the method on a multi-annotator medical image dataset, which shows that explicitly modelling annotator specific perturbations improves uncertainty calibration while maintaining comparable segmentation accuracy, compared with state-of-the-art multi-rater probabilistic segmentation method. The learned bias and variance parameters quantitatively reflect annotator-specific behaviour. Furthermore, controlled perturbation experiments over bias and variance demonstrate how changes in annotator parameters systematically influence predictive performance. The code used in this paper is made publicly available at https://github.com/QiLi111/GPS-Var.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses the multi-rater segmentation problem, where the goal is to recover a latent gold-standard segmentation from multiple annotators who may exhibit different biases and variances in their labeling behavior. The proposed approach uses a Gaussian Process as a generative prior over the latent segmentation, and models each annotator’s output through two scalar parameters: a bias term mu and a variance term sigma. The core contribution of the model is its interpretability — rather than learning implicit, non-linear annotator representations as in PIONONO (ICCV 2023), each rater is described by two clinically meaningful quantities, mu and sigma. Experiments are conducted on a trans-rectal ultrasound dataset, showing Dice performance comparable to PIONONO and improved Expected Calibration Error (ECE).
reviews.text_strengths:
Clarity and presentation. The paper is well-written and easy to follow. The problem is clearly introduced, the relationship to prior work is well articulated, and the notation is consistent throughout.
Principled probabilistic formulation. Framing the problem with latent variables that encode the gold segmentation and the annotator-style segmention is neat and clean. It allows a better and principled understanding of this problem.
Interpretable annotator characterization. Reducing each annotator to a (mu, sigma) pair enables interpretability and makes the model’s assumptions about rater behavior explicit and auditable. These parameters can support downstream tasks like annotator quality assessment or data curation.
Improved calibration. The reported improvement in ECE over PIONONO is a positive point. However, I wonder if this calibration gain came from the annotator modeling or the latent Gaussian Process. Anyway, this kind of results are really useful for trustworthy deployment of AI in the clinic.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Insufficient baselines. The empirical evaluation compares the proposed method against only two baselines: a deterministic U-Net and PIONONO. This is a significant gap. The multi-rater segmentation literature has a number of well-established methods that should be included — most notably reference [30] in the paper’s own bibliography, which is one of the foundational works in this area utilizing confusion matrices for annotator modeling. Additional relevant baselines would include Probabilistic U-Net (Kohl et al. , 2019), which also models annotation uncertainty via a latent variable formulation or STAPLE, which is considered the gold-standard for multi-rater segmentation fusion.
Single-dataset evaluation. All experiments are conducted on a single, highly specific trans-rectal ultrasound dataset. This severely limits the generalizability of any conclusions drawn from the results. The trans-rectal ultrasound setting has particular characteristics — specific image quality, anatomical structure, and annotator pool — that may or may not be representative of multi-rater disagreement in other modalities or tasks. The fact that performance is nearly equivalent to PIONONO on this dataset makes it especially unclear what the proposed method actually contributes. It is entirely possible that the GP prior is beneficial in certain regimes (e. g. , small datasets, high annotator disagreement, specific noise structures) and detrimental in others. Without evaluation across multiple datasets — such as LIDC-IDRI for lung nodule segmentation, QUBIQ for multi-organ uncertainty, or the datasets used in PIONONO and [30] — the paper cannot make general claims about the value of the proposed approach.
Insufficient justification for the GP prior. The choice to use a Gaussian Process as the segmentation model is not adequately motivated. GPs are not a standard choice for pixel-level segmentation: their computational complexity scales cubically with the number of input points in the naive formulation, making them poorly suited for high-resolution medical images without substantial approximation. The paper utilizes 512 inducing points and reports time of processing per image, but a comparative study with PIONONO and baselines at training/inference time would strengthen this design choice.
Annotator model cannot capture structure-dependent disagreement. This is the most fundamental conceptual limitation of the paper. The two-parameter annotator model assumes that each rater has a global, structure-agnostic bias and variance. In other words, if rater A tends to over-segment, the model assumes this is true for all structures in all images. This may be empirically false in most real annotation scenarios. In clinical practice, annotators typically agree on unambiguous structures but disagree specifically on ambiguous boundaries, rare pathologies, or regions where their training or domain expertise differs. A rater might consistently over-segment the prostate but have no systematic bias on the seminal vesicles. The current formulation has no capacity to represent this, because mu and sigma are scalar quantities associated with the rater as a whole, not with specific structures or image regions. The current state of the literature, as the authors themselves acknowledge by citing PIONONO and [30], has moved beyond simple over/under-segmentation models toward representations that capture richer, structure-dependent opinion distributions. Although expressed in the limitations of the paper, I encourage the authors to consider this comment to improve their work.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The authors can improve the paper by expanding the experimental evaluation across multiple datasets and baselines (as the ones commented above), provide a computational analysis of the GP formulation, and design experiments that concretely demonstrate the value of interpretable annotator parameters over deep non-linear mapping produce by deep neural nets.

The paper is well-written and tackles a relevant problem with a coherent probabilistic framework. The improved ECE and the interpretable annotator parameterization are genuine contributions. I personally value and acknowledge the emphasis on interpretability.
