The idea of extracting a per-image style code and using it to condition synthesis is well established in the computer vision literature, e.g. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-58580-8_13 , https://doi.org/10.1109/ICCV48922.2021.01389
The manuscript would benefit from a clearer discussion of what is fundamentally new in the proposed formulation.
The contrastive learning formulation for style extraction appears simplistic and only weakly justified. Positives and negatives are derived from the same target image via spatial cropping and intensity perturbations, which raises questions about what enforces consistency of style representations across different images that share similar acquisition characteristics. Emergent capabilities may arise from such training but this aspect is not well discussed.
The clustering of style embeddings plays a central role in selecting representative styles for downstream segmentation training, yet this step is treated largely as a post hoc procedure. The sensitivity of the results to the clustering method, the number of clusters, or the style selection strategy is not explored, and comparisons against using all target images (thus avoiding clustering entirely) as style references are missing.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The motivation for emphasizing intra-domain variability would benefit from clearer positioning with respect to modern image translation methods, in particular diffusion-based approaches, which are generally less prone to mode collapse and already capable of generating diverse outputs. A brief discussion of why this issue remains relevant in this context would strengthen the introduction.
Several claims regarding generalizability and robustness would benefit from tighter justification or more precise wording, especially where they rely primarily on qualitative observations, e.g. “the learned style embedding space exhibits
meaningful clustering without any supervision” and “the same
source image produces visually distinct outputs across references while preserving anatomy”.
The decision to restrict contrastive learning to target-domain images only is not discussed. It would be useful to explain why source-domain images are excluded and whether their inclusion was considered as these would provide additional diverse styles.
Fig. 4 is informative but could be strengthened with additional contextual information, such as indicating institutional or scanner provenance, to support the interpretation of learned styles.
There are occasional grammatical issues and minor phrasing ambiguities that would benefit from careful proofreading to improve readability, especially regarding the use of references as subjects in sentences.

The manuscript addresses a relevant problem of intra-domain variability in medical image domain adaptation for downstream segmentation training and demonstrates measurable gains on a realistic benchmark. The approach is technically sound and integrates well with an established synthesis pipeline.
However, the methodological novelty is limited, with several core ideas closely related to prior work in style-based image translation. Key design choices, particularly the contrastive style learning setup and the clustering strategy, are only weakly justified.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose IntraStyler, a framework for domain adaptation that does not require site labels to distinguish between imaging sites. The method comprises two components: a contrastive learning module that captures style representations, and a generative framework that synthesizes images in the target domain. Following standard practice, a segmentation network (nnUNet) is then trained on the synthetic images using segmentation labels from the source domain. The authors demonstrate that IntraStyler outperforms existing methods, including the winner of the CrossModa Challenge.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The proposed method is technically sound and novel. By removing the requirement for site codes, which is a limitation of the CrossModa Challenge winner, the approach improves clinical applicability.
2.The use of SLERP is well-motivated, offering finer control over style transfer and reference image generation and is supported by the qualitative figure 3.3.Both quantitative and qualitative results are compelling.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Evaluation is limited to a single dataset (CrossModa), raising questions about generalizability of the method.
2.The comparison is restricted to a small set of baseline methods, and no ablation studies are provided to assess the contribution of individual components.
3.Several terms in the loss function, specifically L_Adv and L_PatchNCE, are left undefined, which undermines reproducibility and clarity.
4.The caption for Figure 3 should be revised. Describing the output as a smooth transition between two reference images is somewhat misleading, as the interpolated image may adopt the style of the second reference image without fully aligning with its structure.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The core idea of unsupervised domain adaptation without site labels is clinically relevant and well-executed, with results that surpass the CrossModa Challenge winner. However, single-dataset evaluation, no ablation studies, and undefined loss terms limit the strength of the contribution. Despite these limitations, the novelty and practical value makes this an interesting contribution.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper proposes a 3D unpaired image translation framework for cross-modality MRI domain adaptation that eliminates the need for predefined site/scanner labels using a contrastively trained style encoder.
Reviewers acknowledge that the paper is addressing a real-world clinical bottleneck: modeling intra-domain variability without relying on coarse sub-domain labels. The contrastive learning strategy is principled, and the method successfully outperforms a highly competitive baseline (the CrossMoDA challenge winner).
To be addressed in final version:
1.Explicitly acknowledge the limitation of evaluating on a single dataset/modality pair (ceT1→T2) and the potential need for modality-specific tuning in other applications.
2.Better position the method relative to prior computer vision literature on style-conditioned synthesis (e.g., StarGANv2, AdaIN) and temper overly broad novelty claims (e.g., “first 3D unpaired…”).
3.Explicitly define all terms in the loss functions (specifically $L_{Adv}$ and $L_{PatchNCE}$).
4.Discuss the impact of the k-means clustering strategy and the uncontrolled number of reference images used (7 vs. 3).
5.Update the captions and context for Figures 3 and 4 as suggested by R3 and R4.

title: InvDetect: Unsupervised Medical Anomaly Detection in the Noise Latent Space of DDIM
abstract: Anomaly detection in medical images is useful for early diagnosis and treatment planning. Unsupervised methods are attractive because they avoid manual annotations and generalize well to unseen anomalies. However, existing unsupervised methods face fundamental limitations: reconstruction-based methods often suffer from pixel-level mismatch of generated pseudo-normal images, and embedding-based methods often fail to separate normal and abnormal images sufficiently in embedding spaces. In this paper, we propose an unsupervised method named InvDetect to address both limitations. InvDetect performs anomaly detection in a noise latent space induced by Denoising Diffusion Implicit Model (DDIM) inversion, which avoids generating pseudo-normal images thus prevents pixel-level mismatch. By training DDIM exclusively on normal image patches, InvDetect constructs a structured noise latent space in which normal patches form a compact cluster and abnormal patches deviate significantly. This yields better separation between normal and abnormal patches to produce a more reliable pixel-wise anomaly map. At last, we refine the anomaly map by enforcing spatial contiguity of abnormal regions, which reduces isolated false positives and false negatives in the final detection result. Experiments on four real-world medical imaging datasets demonstrate that InvDetect consistently outperforms eighteen prior unsupervised anomaly detection methods.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of the paper is a new formulation of unsupervised medical anomaly detection in the noise latent space induced by DDIM inversion, designed to address two major limitations of prior work at once: pixel-level mismatch in reconstruction-based methods and insufficient normal/abnormal separation in embedding-based methods. The authors train DDIM only on normal patches, invert unseen patches into the noise latent space, score them with a lightweight one-class SVM, and then refine the resulting anomaly map using a latent-similarity-based spatial contiguity refinement (SCR) module. This yields a conceptually clean pipeline that avoids pseudo-normal image synthesis while still producing pixel-wise anomaly localization.
reviews.text_strengths:
First, the paper is motivated by a very clear problem formulation. It identifies two concrete failure modes in prior unsupervised anomaly detection pseudo-normal reconstruction mismatch and weak abnormality separation in generic embedding spaces and proposes a method that directly targets both. The idea of avoiding pseudo-normal image generation altogether and instead detecting anomalies directly in an inversion-induced latent space is simple yet compelling.
Second, the empirical evaluation is broad. The method is tested across four very different medical datasets/modalities and compared against 18 prior baselines, including both reconstruction-based and embedding-based approaches. The ablation comparing InvDetect and InvDetect w/o SCR also supports the importance of the proposed refinement step.
Third, the paper includes a useful runtime-versus-Dice analysis rather than reporting accuracy alone. This helps position the method in terms of practical efficiency and shows that the approach remains competitive among stronger but slower methods.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The main weakness of the paper is that its central hypothesis is not validated directly enough. The claim that normal and abnormal patches become better separated in the DDIM noise latent space is intuitive and plausible, but the evidence remains largely indirect, relying mostly on final detection performance rather than explicit latent-space analysis. The paper would be much stronger with more direct support, such as latent distribution visualizations, separation statistics, or calibration-style analyses.
In addition, several components of the pipeline are not novel in isolation: one-class SVM is a classical normality estimator, and patch-based aggregation is also standard, so the main novelty appears to lie primarily in the inversion-induced noise latent space itself. This makes stronger component-level ablations particularly important; comparisons against alternative scoring models or normality estimators would help clarify which parts of the method are truly essential.
The method also depends heavily on a fixed patch-based design, yet no sensitivity analysis is provided for patch size or stride.
Finally, reproducibility and practical applicability would be improved by more detailed reporting of the DDIM inversion settings and clearer analysis of computational scaling, especially since runtime is dominated by DDIM inversion and grows with the number of patches.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Overall, I found this to be a solid and well-motivated paper with strong empirical performance. The idea of avoiding pseudo-normal image generation and instead performing anomaly scoring directly in an inversion-induced noise latent space is both interesting and practically meaningful. The multi-dataset evaluation and the SCR ablation are also convincing strengths. My main reservations are that the central latent-separation claim is not directly analyzed in enough depth, and some additional ablations would strengthen the paper. For these reasons, I place the paper slightly above the acceptance threshold as a Weak Accept.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a novel approach to use the latent space of an inverted DDIM for anomaly detection. Concretely, after training the DDIM on patches extracted from images of healthy patients, the latents corresponding to normal patches should form a Gaussian cluster, to which a one class SVM is fitted to model the normal distribution. Additionally, the authors propose to binarize the anomaly score map using an energy based formulation that aligns the segmentation mask with the anomaly scores while including neighborhood consistency.
reviews.text_strengths:
Although the proposed method is in the mid range in terms of runtime, it runs much faster than the image reconstruction methods with newer generative models and it performs consistently well over all evaluated domains in terms of anomaly segmentation scores.
The spatial contiguity refinement (SCR) is a novel way to threshold the anomaly score map in an unsupervised manner and is a good contribution to the field.
The manuscript empirically demonstrates that the latent space of DDIM is useful for separating between normal and abnormal samples and intuitively explain this with the way the latent space is constructed by DDIM inversion.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Most state of the art methods evaluate the anomaly score maps without thresholding with metrics such as AUROC or AUPR. Reported anomaly segmentation scores are usually obtained by using a fixed threshold, a threshold such that the F1 score on a small labeled set is maximized, or a threshold to reach a predefined false positive rate on a small set of normal images. The manuscript provides only segmentation scores and does not explain how the threshold is set for the state of the art methods and for the proposed method without SCR. Therefore, it is impossible to evaluate if the comparison is fair.
Both Dice score and precision are highly affected by class imbalance, which is usually the case in anomaly detection.
The manuscript does not justify why the additional training of a one class SVM is required instead of using the probability density of the multivariate normal distribution, which should be the distribution of the latents corresponding to normal patches.
It was not evaluated if SCR preserves small anomalies or if they are removed. From the formulation, it is more likely that small anomalies are removed or suppressed, which would also be in line with the smaller performance improvement on the BTCV dataset compared to the proposed method without SCR, as BTCV tends to contain smaller anomalies.
Using only abnormal images in the test set is quite atypical for anomaly detection, which could be beneficial for methods that process the image in a patch-wise fashion as normal regions are much less affected by abnormal regions in the same image. While this is a desirable property, its impact on the scores might be over-amplified in comparison to the typical setup with normal + abnormal samples during testing.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Please add references to the literature for DDIM and particularly DDIM inversion, especially as there is almost no explanation provided.
The statement that the proposed method outperforms embedding-based methods because the latter do not explicitly separate normal and abnormal embeddings is vague, because the proposed method does not separate the two classes explicitly either.
PaDiM would most likely be considered as a method using a probabilistic model instead of a memory bank in the introduction.
License of the datasets should rather be a footnote than a reference.

Despite the above mentioned issues in the evaluation and comparison, the usefulness the latent space of DDIMs for anomaly detection and the unsupervised segmentation with SCR are of great interest to the anomaly detection communities in MICCAI and possibly beyond the medical domain.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes InvDetect, an unsupervised medical anomaly detection method that operates in the DDIM inversion latent space instead of reconstructing pseudo-normal images. A DDIM is trained on normal patches, a one-class SVM scores inverted latents, and a graph-cut spatial refinement yields the final mask. Experiments cover four medical datasets against a broad set of unsupervised baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
Doing UAD in the DDIM inversion latent space is a clean idea that sidesteps the pixel-mismatch issue of reconstruction-based methods.
The pipeline is simple and lightweight (one-class SVM + graph-cut) with practical runtime.
Evaluation spans four modalities and a reasonably broad set of baselines.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The central claim that normal latents concentrate near N(0, I) while abnormal ones drift away is taken largely on faith. Some direct evidence (norm distributions, t-SNE/UMAP, or a latent-space AUROC) would make the motivation much more convincing.
The evaluation leans on Dice/Precision from thresholded binary masks, which are sensitive to post-processing. Since the proposed method has a dedicated graph-cut step and most baselines do not, the comparison may be unfair. Is there any other metric can be used without any post-processing?
Dataset curation is underspecified. BraTS2021 is typically tumor-only so the source of “normal” training data is unclear, and for BTCV the anomaly definition is not obvious — both matter a lot in a normal-only setup.
The choice of a one-class SVM in a high-dimensional latent space is not compared against simpler density estimators (e.g., Mahalanobis), and hyperparameter handling for SCR reads inconsistently between per-dataset tuning and fixed values.
The method is purely 2D, which is a real limitation for volumetric CT/MRI where 3D context would likely help both separability and spatial contiguity. Key implementation details (DDIM steps, noise schedule, patch size/stride sensitivity) are also unclear.
Minor: there is no such thing as ‘train a DDIM’, which is a sampling method applied on a trained denoiser. The authors are recommended to correct the phrasing.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The idea is nice and the results look promising, but the experimental rigor is not quite there: the central latent-space claim lacks direct evidence, the evaluation protocol can bias comparisons, and dataset definitions need tightening. These are fixable, so I lean towards weak accept.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text: All three reviewers recommend acceptance. The core idea of performing UAD directly in the DDIM inversion noise latent space, bypassing pseudo-normal image synthesis, is clean and well-motivated, and the SCR module is a genuine contribution to unsupervised anomaly localization. Reviewers share one common concern worth addressing in the final version: the central claim that normal latents concentrate near N(0,I) while abnormal ones drift away lacks direct empirical support. Please revise these claims. Latent distribution visualizations or a latent-space AUROC would substantially strengthen the paper.

author_feedback_text: We thank all the reviewers for their valuable comments. We will carefully address the raised comments in the camera-ready version, following the camera-ready submission guidelines.

title: Inverse Protocol Prediction from Spheroid Microscopy Imaging via Morphology-Aware Structured Learning
abstract: We introduce Inverse Protocol Prediction (IPP) as the task of inferring experimental culture conditions directly from a single bright-field spheroid image. We formulate IPP as a structured multi-label prediction problem and propose a protocol-aware learning framework that integrates morphology extraction, multimodal representation learning, and dependency-aware inference. Morphometric descriptors derived from automated spheroid segmentation are fused with deep visual embeddings via a morphometry vision fusion module. To capture biological and procedural dependencies, we incorporate a Hierarchical Multi-Task Transformer (HMTT) that is conditioned to predict across protocol attributes. The framework is trained with domain-adversarial supervision and morphology-preserving augmentation and tested for cross-dataset generalisation. Hybrid convolution attention encoders achieve the best performance, reaching 95.7% multi-attribute accuracy. Results demonstrate that structured, dependency-aware modeling enables reliable reconstruction of experimental protocols from imaging alone, supporting reproducibility auditing and protocol validation in 3D cell culture systems.
subject_areas: Applications -> Outcome Prediction / Prognosis / Longitudinal Modeling

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces the task of Inverse Protocol Prediction (IPP), formulated as a structured multi-label learning problem aimed at reconstructing experimental conditions (cell line, culture medium, seeding density, and imaging setup) directly from microscopy images. Extensive experiments are conducted on the SLiMIA dataset, along with cross-dataset evaluation on RxRx1, benchmarking multiple deep learning architectures.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) The paper introduces a novel problem formulation and new research direction for spheroid image analysis. Additionally, the paper demonstrates the feasibility of this direction through a comprehensive empirical study.
2) The paper introduces a custom deep learning (DL) network for mitigating acquisition bias.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) The motivation for the proposed task is not adequately established in the introduction. The paper argues that protocol or metadata inconsistencies may remain undetected and affect reproducibility; however, in curated experimental datasets, metadata (cell line, media, seeding density, imaging setup) are explicitly recorded.
2) The paper lacks a dedicated methodology section, with the proposed framework primarily described through a high-level figure (Fig. 1) and scattered implementation details. Critical components such as the morphometry–vision fusion mechanism and the hierarchical multi-task transformer (HMTT) are not formally defined (no mathematical formulation, or architectural specification).
3) The paper addresses acquisition bias through a custom DL framework. However, the effectiveness of this strategy is evaluated using only a single model configuration, without comparison to alternative architectures or bias-mitigation techniques.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper introduces an interesting and novel research direction by formulating Inverse Protocol Prediction (IPP) for spheroid image analysis. However, the paper has several critical shortcomings that limit its suitability for acceptance (see Weaknesses). Taken together, while the paper presents a promising idea, the current formulation lacks sufficient methodological rigor, clarity, and experimental validation. Strengthening the problem motivation, providing a clear and formal methodological description, and conducting more comprehensive evaluations would be necessary for the work to be competitive.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
=> The central premise that “metadata inconsistencies undermine reproducibility in large-scale microscopy studies” is unsubstantiated. The submission neither cites a documented reproducibility failure attributable to undetected protocol inconsistencies, nor validates the workflow against a realistic auditing scenario involving synthetically or naturally mislabeled metadata. As a result, the practical utility of IPP as an auditing framework is not demonstrated.
=> The paper reports morphometry-vision fusion and dependency-aware inference as one of its primary contributions. However, the ablation shows the full model achieves Macro-F1=0.8681 versus image-only at 0.8662 (\Delta=0.0019). Consequently, the proposed components do not produce any verifiable empirical improvement over a plain image encoder.
=> Finally, the HMTT and fusion module lack formal specification; the rebuttal supplies formulations that should have appeared in the paper itself. Moreover, Figure 1, which constitutes the sole high-level description of the proposed framework, is never referenced in the text.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors present a deep learning based pipeline for predicting experiment/imaging protocol based on microscopy images of cell spheroids.
reviews.text_strengths:
The approach is novel and addresses an existing need - there is limited prior research on the topic of inverse protocol prediction in general. In addition to the listed application areas of reproducibility auditing and protocol validation, the work has potential in data standardization in gathering large biomedical image datasets from different sources.
The methods applied seem appropriate for the aims of the study, and use is generally well justified. The authors have taken steps towards reducing bias in gathering the datasets by performing ablation studies and cross-data set validation, among others.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The impact of the study is limited by focusing on cross-replicate generalization rather than showing the robustness of the method – with timepoints being the only measure with held-out test classes (2 out of 109 classes). For the timepoints, a more modest prediction (F1 score of 0.75) was achieved. To my understanding, the paper does not disclose the accuracy of the model in predicting the held-out classes – this would be of interest due to being both the metric with the lowest accuracy and with held-out classes.
To me, it would be intuitive to consider image intensity and contrast measures to be metrics that could inadvertently point the network to lean towards microscopy images taken in a specific study and introduce bias that way. If I have understood correctly, withholding images with a differing intensity spectrum could reveal how much the network relies on these factors instead of the textures.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The method seems promising and addresses a novel and interesting approach to image data. There are some small shortcomings, which can be clarified without a lot of extra work.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The answers provided by the authors have been sufficient, and with the minor clarifications suggested the by the authors in their rebuttal will further improve the paper regarding the parts where there was room for confusion.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces Inverse Protocol Prediction (IPP) for inferring experimental culture conditions directly from a single bright-field spheroid image. The authors combine automatic spheroid segmentation, morphometric feature extraction, image morphology fusion, and hierarchical multi-task prediction of protocol attributes. The paper reports very strong mean per-attribute performance and further examines biological aspects.
reviews.text_strengths:
Predicting protocol metadata from spheroid morphology is a well-motivated problem for reproducibility auditing and quality control in high-throughput 3D culture experiments.
The experimental split by technical replicate is a strong design choice and is more credible than random image-level splitting for this problem. It reduces the risk of obvious leakage across acquisition sessions.
The empirical study is broad with multiple segmentation models benchmarked and several IPP architectures are compared including convolutional, transformer, hybrid, fusion-based, and hierarchical variants.
The manuscript includes useful per-label analysis showing which protocol variables are strongly versus weakly recoverable from morphology.
The biological-only evaluation is a thoughtful addition because it attempts to separate biologically meaningful prediction from acquisition-driven variables.
The interpretability analysis is relevant and practically useful. The paper does not just chase high accuracy, but also tries to assess whether predictions are based on plausible biological cues versus technical confounders.
The overall practical framing is strong. Even if novelty at the module level is moderate, the task formulation and benchmarking package could be valuable.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
HMTT is positioned as a key contribution but it is not the best-performing model in the main table, and the paper does not clearly show that hierarchical conditioning improves joint protocol consistency over simpler structured baselines.
The paper should clearly explain whether uncertainty is computed across seeds and how confidence intervals were derived.
The paper would be stronger with comparison to simpler structured multi-label baselines or at least with a clearer discussion of why HMTT is preferable.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The task itself is interesting and useful. The practical motivation is strong, and the main evaluation is more careful than average because of the replicate-aware split, biological-only analysis, and per-label reporting. My impression is that the core contribution is real and that most weaknesses are addressable through better specification, clearer analysis, and tighter positioning rather than through a fundamentally different study.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have addressed all the points.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper presents a method for reconstructing experimental conditions from microscopy images. As reviewers commented, it introduces a novel problem formulation. There are however various questions that lead to different ratings from the reviewers. For example, the motivation needs to be more clearly elaborated. Method descriptions should be more formal. The effectiveness for addressing acquisition bias should be more clearly demonstrated. Results on the held-out set should be included. And there are various other comments as well.

After the rebuttal, the ratings contain one reject and two accept. The reviewer giving the reject rating has various good points, such as marginal performance improvement and unclear method formulation. Considering the method contributions of the paper, these weaknesses are relatively minor. Please make sure to improve the writing in the final version.

The paper introduces Inverse Protocol Prediction (IPP) as a novel and potentially useful task for microscopy quality control and reproducibility analysis. Reviewers recognized the originality of the problem formulation, the replicate-aware evaluation design, the broad benchmarking effort, and the biological interpretability analysis. Two reviewers supported acceptance and found the rebuttal sufficient, while one reviewer remained negative mainly due to concerns about motivation, methodological clarity, and the limited empirical gain of the structured components.
In my view, the rebuttal addresses the main concerns reasonably well. The authors clarified that IPP is not meant to replace recorded metadata, but to serve as an auditing and protocol-consistency tool in large microscopy workflows. They also clarified the structured role of HMTT, the morphometry-vision fusion mechanism, confidence interval computation, and the purpose of the biological-only evaluation, which still showed strong performance and supports that the method is not driven only by acquisition artifacts.
The paper still has some weaknesses. The motivation could be framed more sharply, and the methodological description in the manuscript appears thinner than ideal for a MICCAI paper. In addition, the empirical advantage of some structured components over simpler baselines remains modest. However, the core contribution of the work is broader than any single module: it is the introduction and systematic study of a new structured inference task with a careful replicate-aware benchmark. Considering the novelty of the task, the practical relevance, and the generally positive reviewer response after rebuttal, I would lean Accept.

The paper introduces a novel and useful problem formulation, inverse protocol prediction from spheroid microscopy images, and the overall presentation appears to have sufficient value for MICCAI.
For the camera ready version, the authors should temper claims about the proposed HMTT/fusion contribution. The reported gain of the full model over image-only appears very small. Also, the formal definitions supplied in rebuttal should be incorporated along with clearer discussion of uncertainty estimation and why the structured model is preferable to simpler baselines.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for their constructive feedback and for recognizing the novelty of the IPP task, replicate-aware evaluation protocol, and biological interpretability analysis. We address the main concerns below.
Motivation and practical relevance of IPP: IPP is not intended to replace recorded metadata, but rather to serve as a complementary auditing framework for detecting protocol drift, incomplete/non-standardized annotations, acquisition inconsistencies, and cross-site variability in large microscopy workflows. Importantly, the biological-only evaluation (excluding microscope, magnification, and replicate variables) still achieves Biological Macro-F1=0.914, supporting that IPP captures biologically meaningful morphology-protocol associations rather than only acquisition artifacts.
Methodology and HMTT clarification: We agree that additional formalization would improve clarity. Due to space constraints, some implementation details were condensed. The submitted pipeline trains RefineNet for binary segmentation and freezes it before IPP training; morphometrics are computed only from predicted masks, avoiding annotation leakage. For multimodal fusion, the image encoder produces visual embeddings (z_img = f_θ(x)), while normalized morphometric descriptors (m ∈ R^d) are projected as shape tokens and fused through a Transformer encoder before per-attribute prediction heads. HMTT factorizes inference as (P(y₁,…,y_K | x) = ∏ₖ P(yₖ | x, y_<k)), using teacher forcing during training and autoregressive decoding during inference. Domain-adversarial training optimizes (L_total = L_bio+L_domain) using a gradient reversal layer.
Importantly, HMTT is not intended as the sole primary contribution or necessarily the best-performing architecture. Rather, the paper systematically evaluates convolutional, transformer, hybrid, fusion-based, and dependency-aware approaches to study the role of inductive bias, explicit morphometric priors, and label-structure modeling in IPP.
Acquisition bias and robustness: Acquisition confounding is addressed through: (i) replicate-exclusive splitting; (ii) biological-only IPP excluding acquisition/replicate labels; and (iii) domain-adversarial training with replicate identity treated as domain. Grad-CAM further shows that biological predictions focus on spheroid morphology (boundary, compactness, internal organization), whereas replicate-related predictions exhibit diffuse/background attention patterns. We agree that an explicit intensity-spectrum holdout would provide an additional stress test and acknowledge this as a future direction.
Held-out classes and robustness clarification: Results are reported on held-out technical replicates rather than random image splits. For 7/8 attributes, all validation/test classes appear during training; only timepoint includes two unseen test-only classes (000h and 032h), which are included in Table 4 evaluation. The lower timepoint F1 reflects gradual and overlapping morphological transitions rather than framework failure. Robustness is further supported by zero-shot transfer to RxRx1, where Image-Shape Fusion achieves F1=0.768 despite substantial modality/acquisition shift.
Confidence intervals and reproducibility: Table 3 reports mean ± SD across three independent seeds (42,123,999), with 95% confidence intervals computed as (1.96×SD / √3). Segmentation and RxRx1 confidence intervals were computed analogously over evaluation samples. We acknowledge this could have been clearer. Code and implementation details will be released upon publication to support reproducibility.
We thank the reviewers for the thoughtful feedback. We believe the discussion clarifies that the primary contribution is the introduction of IPP as a structured inference problem together with a replicate-aware benchmarking framework for studying biological and acquisition-related morphology signatures. We will address these clarity issues in the permitted minor revision.

title: Inversion from ECG Foundation Model
abstract: Electrocardiogram (ECG) foundation models (FMs) are increasingly deployed as cloud services. For downstream tasks such as disease diagnosis, they return compact embeddings from input ECG signals. In this paper, we find that such embeddings pose significant privacy risks: adversaries can use the exposed embeddings and invert the original ECG, which leads to the inference of sensitive clinical attributes. To assess this vulnerability, we introduce SHINE, a new ECG inversion method that inverts ECG signals from the exposed embeddings. SHINE consists of ECG mapper and ECG inverter. Specifically, SHINE trains ECG mapper to approximate the embedding space of victim ECG FM, which is then used to synthesize the necessary data to train ECG inverter from scratch. Our evaluation against four state-of-the-art ECG FMs shows that SHINE achieves high-fidelity inversion. Importantly, the inverted ECGs retain sensitive clinical attributes, including cardiovascular disease indicators up to 99.6%, almost identical to the original ECG. These results demonstrate that the exposed ECG embeddings preserve substantial physiological information so that when deploying ECG FM, stronger security countermeasures need to be devised. To our knowledge, this paper is the first to report that the exposed embeddings can be inverted to the original ECG signals.
subject_areas: Modalities -> EEG / MEG / ECG / Physiological Signals

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
1.The paper is the first to demonstrate that embeddings from ECG foundation models can be inverted back into clinically meaningful ECG signals.
2.It presents the SHINE method, a query-efficient two-stage attack framework that operates within realistic cloud constraints, comprising an ECG Mapper and an ECG Inverter. It overcomes two key barriers: the absence of pretrained ECG decoders and the limitations imposed by query budget constraints.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper is the first to frame ECG embedding inversion as a privacy attack vector against cloud-deployed foundation models, which is novel. 
2.The paper presents a clever use of pseudo QR pairs, in which rather than requiring massive real-world queries to the victim model (which is infeasible under cloud constraints), SHINE trains a lightweight ECG mapper on a small number of real query-response pairs and then uses it to generate a large synthetic training set. 
3.The evaluation is notably thorough across multiple dimensions, testing against both CNN-based and transformer-based architectures, but also incorporating clinically meaningful interval metrics such as the absolute differences between RR intervals and QT durations extracted from the original and inverted ECGs.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The chosen baseline (adapted DiffuSETS) is acknowledged by the authors themselves to be a poor fit. Stronger baselines should be considered, such as gradient-based optimization in embedding space or nearest-neighbor retrieval, to better demonstrate SHINE’s true advantage. 
2.SHINE is trained and evaluated on PTB-XL and CPSC2018 only. Evaluation on more diverse datasets (e. g. , MIMIC-IV-ECG) would strengthen the generalizability claims. 
3.The paper calls for stronger countermeasures but evaluates none. Even a basic analysis of how SHINE performs under differential privacy noise or embedding perturbation would significantly strengthen the practical impact of the work.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses a genuinely novel and clinically important problem, demonstrating for the first time that ECG foundation model embeddings can be inverted to recover sensitive patient information. The pseudo QR pair synthesis strategy is technically clever and the evaluation is reasonably thorough. These are meaningful contributions that warrant publication.
However, several weaknesses prevent a stronger score:
1.The baseline comparison is too weak to convincingly demonstrate SHINE’s true advantage, and stronger baselines (gradient-based optimization, nearest-neighbor retrieval) are notably absent.
2.The absence of any defense evaluation limits the practical impact of the work.
3.The lack of a discussion section and the indirect clinical evaluation leave important questions unanswered
The paper is marginally above the acceptance threshold primarily because the problem formulation is novel and important for the MICCAI community, and the results are compelling enough to provoke meaningful discussion about privacy in clinical AI deployments. However, the authors should be expected to address the weak baseline comparison and the absence of defense evaluation in their rebuttal.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The contribution of the paper consists of two main models. The first one is an ECG mapper, which aims to approximate and learn the transformation between two spaces, mapping ECG signals into the embedding space of the target model. The second one is an ECG inverter, which is trained using pseudo-synthetic data generated by the mapper, where real ECG signals are paired with embeddings produced by this proxy model. Using these pairs, the inverter learns to reconstruct the original ECG signal from the embedding representation.
reviews.text_strengths:
Query-efficient training strategy: The use of a surrogate mapper to approximate the embedding space reduces the need for extensive query access to the victim model, which can ultimately be related to the optimal subset of data that represents the total variance in a dataset (a data distillation idea).
Clinically meaningful evaluation: The study evaluates not only signal reconstruction but also the preservation of clinical attributes, strengthening the practical relevance of the results, arguably the most important aspect. The authors cite [23], whose core idea suggests that this approach can serve as insight for black-box interpretability during clinical decision-making.
Relevant and timely problem: The paper addresses privacy risks in ECG foundation models, particularly in cloud-based settings. It is a relevant idea; in my opinion, however, it does not fully capture the potential of this work. This aspect of privacy becomes a necessity when most of these foundation models are commercial and potentially used in real clinical decision-making.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The proposed approach mainly consists of combining standard components (CNN/Transformer architectures and MSE loss) within a training pipeline. The novelty lies primarily in the use of a surrogate mapper and pseudo pairs, which may be seen as an incremental contribution rather than a new method base don MIC outlines.
The performance of the inverter is heavily dependent on the quality of the learned mapper. Any approximation error in the mapper may propagate to the pseudo query-response pairs, potentially affecting the fidelity of the inversion.
Although the paper is framed as a privacy attack, the main contribution is methodological (training strategy), raising questions about whether the work truly advances understanding of privacy risks or mainly proposes a reconstruction pipeline. This continue into the lack of discussion on alternative interpretations, which basically, the obtained results could also be interpreted from a representation learning or interpretability perspective (i.e., what information is retained in embeddings), but this angle is not explore
Maybe a crucial idea is the dataset bias and distribution alignment, where the proposed ethod relies on public datasets (e.g., PTB-XL) to approximate the embedding space. But never used other types of dataset like MUSIC or the demo of MIMIC-IV, or what happens the real clinical data were several methods are constructed to digitalize the ECG, where exist a shift-domain that shows when a ECG is digitalized how the leve lof signal (Pixel-mV) affects the reconstruction or diases identificators. This idea affects the robustness of the method under domain shift (e.g., different hospitals, devices, populations) is not evaluated.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
I appreciate the work, and the underlying idea is crucial. However, in my opinion, this moment calls for stronger explainability and interpretability of large black-box models, such as foundation models (FMs).

Based on the MIC evaluation, this paper should be rejected. However, the real potential of this work lies in interpretability, specifically, in how a function can reconstruct an ECG signal capable of identifying disease-related patterns (although this must be validated on real-world datasets, where domain shift may significantly affect performance). Furthermore, extending this approach to define thresholds for each condition represents a promising direction with substantial potential.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This study investigates the privacy vulnerabilities of ECG foundation model embeddings, showing that exposed embeddings can leak sensitive information through inversion attacks. To overcome the challenge of limited query–response (QR) pairs, the authors introduce an ECG mapper that approximates the victim model, allowing the creation of pseudo QR pairs. These pseudo pairs, combined with real QR pairs, are used to train an ECG inverter. Experimental results demonstrate that ECG signals reconstructed from embeddings retain clinical prediction performance similar to the original ECGs, highlighting that the embeddings preserve significant clinically relevant information and present a substantial privacy risk.
reviews.text_strengths:
This paper is one of the first to examine privacy vulnerabilities in ECG foundation model embeddings, presenting a timely and well-justified problem.
Introducing an ECG mapper to generate pseudo QR pairs offers a practical and novel solution to the challenge of limited query access in black-box settings.
The method shows promising performance: inverted ECGs achieve clinical prediction results comparable to those of original ECGs, reinforcing the claim of significant information leakage.
Evaluating the method on an external dataset strengthens the experimental design and further supports its generalizability.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The authors do not clarify why the ECG mapper must use the same CNN-based or transformer-based architecture as the victim foundation model. This rationale should be evaluated, ideally through an ablation study.
Metrics like MAE (e.g., 0.47) lack sufficient context, making it difficult to assess their relevance to meaningful differences in ECG waveform morphology. While RR and QT intervals are more interpretable, the clinical implications of the results are not addressed.
The rationale for comparing against the proposed baseline is unclear, particularly if no strong or established baseline exists. Instead, the authors should focus on thoroughly justifying and evaluating each component of their method, as well as systematically varying model architectures. Demonstrating the performance of each choice under different real QR pair budgets would provide more meaningful insights.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses a timely and important problem with a clear and novel formulation, and proposes a practical solution through the use of pseudo query–response pairs. The empirical results are convincing, particularly the demonstration that inverted ECGs retain clinically relevant information, which highlights a meaningful privacy risk. The use of an external dataset further strengthens the evaluation.
While there are notable weaknesses—particularly in the justification of architectural choices, interpretability of reconstruction metrics, and clarity of baseline comparisons—these issues primarily affect the depth of analysis rather than the core contribution. Overall, the paper makes a valuable contribution and merits acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have clarified my concerns. I do not have any further comments.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper proposes SHINE to invert ECG foundation model (FM) embeddings back to original ECG signals. The approach is novel and valuable from a privacy-attack perspective. However, given the small datasets used, there are several key points the authors should address in a rebuttal:
1.Experiments are limited to PTB-XL and CPSC2018.The authors should discuss SHINE’s robustness across different hospitals, devices, populations, and sampling rates, and clarify the limitations of small datasets for foundation model applications.
Robustness of pseudo QR pairs: SHINE relies on ≤1000 direct QR pairs to generate pseudo QR pairs. The authors should analyze how the quantity and quality of these pseudo pairs affect inversion fidelity, and indicate the minimum number of direct QR pairs required for stable performance.
2.The mapper and inverter are matched to the victim FM’s architecture (CNN or Transformer). The authors should clarify how SHINE performs if the architecture is unknown or misestimated, and how mapper errors propagate to the inverter.
3.More clinically meaningful metrics should be provided (e.g., arrhythmia detection, disease-specific sensitivity/specificity), and evaluation on additional heterogeneous datasets (e.g., MIMIC-IV-ECG) would strengthen claims.
4.SHINE’s performance under embedding perturbations, differential privacy, or other defenses should be discussed or simulated.
5.Authors should clarify the applicability and generalizability of SHINE to larger, more diverse ECG FMs and explain how small dataset experiments translate to foundation model settings.

The paper addresses a novel and clinically important privacy and interpretability question: whether ECG foundation model embeddings can be inverted to recover sensitive signals. Reviewers note meaningful technical ideas and a reasonably thorough evaluation, with remaining concerns about stronger baselines and validation on broader real-world data. The overall assessment is positive.
The authors addressed Reviewer’s concerns. I would recommend to include it in camera-ready paper.

This is probably the most novel and consequential paper in my stack. It identifies a concrete privacy vulnerability of ECG foundation-model embeddings. The experiments are broad for the problem scope, covering four ECG foundation models and showing clinically meaningful leakage. All reviewers like the paper, and I personally like this paper very much.
But the authors shall not view this work as the final product of their project. It would be nice to see the systematic mitigation strategies in their potential journal extension. Best of luck and looking forward to seeing this work carry out the real contribution to the AI medical community!

author_feedback_text:
1.Experiment datasets[MR,R1,2,3]
The main goal of our study is to demonstrate that exposed ECG embeddings can leak sensitive clinical attributes, which makes ECG FM vulnerable to privacy attack. Four FMs we test were trained with many datasets such as Harvard-Emory, MIMIC-IV-ECG, and CODE-15%, but not with PTB-XL dataset. So PTB-XL is a natural choice for us to ensure attacks from unknown data. Then CPSC2018 is used to evaluate our ECG mapper and inverter. Please note that CPSC2018 dataset has different distribution from PTB-XL so that we can confirm that the results are not driven by PTB-XL-specific bias. Furthermore, we tested with other dataset (CSN) and had similar results, but we could not include due to the space limit.
2.Limited defense evaluation[MR,R1]
Yes, our current evaluation does not include defense methods. In privacy-attack perspective, we believe revealing the attack surface itself has merit. Our work follows other leakage analysis studies that revealing and characterizing practical vulnerabilities is treated as a primary contribution [Carlini et al., USENIX Security ’21]. We leave the evaluation of defense mechanisms to future work.
3.Baseline selection rationale—gradient-based optimization, nearest-neighbor retrieval[R1,3]
Because this is the first to reveal ECG inversion, there is no well-established baseline. So we select a baseline from other domains (Vision) that are compatible with our threat model and query budget. We find that gradient-based optimization is impractical because it requires nearly 120k queries for a single inversion, far exceeding our ≤1000 budget. We did not choose nearest-neighbor retrieval as it retrieves the closest existing sample from a predefined candidate pool, rather than reconstructing the target input. Thus, we choose a pretrained decoder-based inversion as our baseline: it uses a decoder to reconstruct the input from exposed embeddings, following [DiffusETS, Patterns ’25].
4.Clinically meaningful evaluation[MR,R1,3]
The CPSC2018 dataset includes 9 diseases: 1st-degree AV block, atrial fibrillation, left bundle branch block, premature atrial contraction, right bundle branch block, sinus rhythm, ST depression, ST elevation, and ventricular ectopics. We ran experiments for all 9 diseases. Averaged over 4 ECG FMs and 2 direct QR pair budgets, SHINE achieves normalized AUROCs of 96.0% for atrial fibrillation and 95.7% for left bundle branch block, with similar results for other diseases. Due to the space limit, however, we present only the average across the nine diseases in Table 2.5.Robustness of direct/pseudo QR pairs[MR,R2,3]
We ran experiments with a number of direct QR pairs between 250 and 8000.We find that SHINE can preserve sensitive attributes with 500 direct QR pairs. Specifically, SHINE achieves normalized AUROCs of 90.3% for age and 95.2% for disease over 4 FMs (§3.2). This indicates that SHINE approximates victim ECG FM’s embedding well enough by using only 500 direct QR pairs. With 500 direct QR pairs, we find that the right number of pseudo QR pairs for fidelity is more than 20000 (21337 in our case).
6.Architecture selection rationale[MR,R3]
We ran various experiments to find out a proper model architecture for ECG mapper and inverter. The results show that the proper architecture depends on FM. In other words, if FM adopts CNN, the mapper and inverter of CNN gives the best approximation. So for the experiments with 4 FMs, we design ECG mapper and inverter, depending on FM. Regarding whether FM architecture can be known, there are some literature that identify the model architecture from their embeddings.
7.Generalization over diverse FM[MR]
Yes, it is a next step. But, please note that ECGFounder has been trained with 10.7M ECGs, which makes it most extensive FM that exists today. So since our attack is feasible with only 500 queries for ECGFounder, we expect that our attack can be effective to other (small) FMs even with less than 500 queries.

title: IOSVLM: A 3D Vision-Language Model for Unified Dental Diagnosis from Intraoral Scans
abstract: 3D intraoral scans (IOS) are increasingly adopted in routine dentistry due to abundant geometric evidence, and unified multi-disease diagnosis is desirable for clinical documentation and communication. While recent works introduce dental vision-language models (VLMs) to enable unified diagnosis and report generation on 2D images or multi-view images rendered from IOS, they do not fully leverage native 3D geometry. Such work is necessary and also challenging, due to: (i) heterogeneous scan forms and the complex IOS topology, (ii) multi-disease co-occurrence with class imbalance and fine-grained morphological ambiguity, (iii) limited paired 3D IOS–text data. Thus, we present IOSVLM, an end-to-end 3D VLM that represents scans as point clouds and follows a 3D encoder-projector-LLM design for unified diagnosis and generative visual question-answering (VQA), together with IOSVQA, a large-scale multi-source IOS diagnosis VQA dataset comprising 19,002 cases and 249,055 VQA pairs over 23 oral diseases and heterogeneous scan types. To address the distribution gap between color-free IOS data and color-dependent 3D pretraining, we propose a geometry-to-chromatic proxy that stabilizes fine-grained geometric perception and cross-modal alignment. A two-stage curriculum training strategy further enhances robustness. IOSVLM consistently outperforms strong baselines, achieving gains of at least +9.58% macro accuracy and +1.46% macro F1, indicating the effectiveness of direct 3D geometry modeling for IOS-based diagnosis.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
IOSVLM makes two separable contributions. First, it introduces IOSVQA, a large-scale multi-source VQA dataset of 19,002 IOS cases and 249,055 QA pairs spanning 23 oral diseases and two scan types (single-arch, occluded-arches). This is the first dataset of this scope designed for multi-disease IOS diagnosis with language generation, and it captures real-world co-occurrence of multiple diseases within a single scan. 
Second, IOSVLM itself is a 3D encoder–projector LLM architecture that processes native IOS point clouds for generative diagnostic VQA.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.IOSVQA dataset is a significant community contribution
2.Geometry-to-Chromatic Proxy (GCP) is an original and well-analysed contribution
3.Performance results are compelling
4.The two-stage design , freeze LLM in Stage 1 to stabilise geometric alignment, fine-tune with LoRA in Stage 2 on high-quality data, is principled and consistent with best practices in VLM training. The ablation comparing training modes (Table 3) provides clear attribution.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Multi-view rendering protocol for 2D baselines is underspecified
2.GCP ablation does not fully isolate the normal-specific contribution
3.LLM selection rationale is not in the main text. 
4.Inference time and memory requirements are not reported
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

IOSVLM makes a solid dual contribution, the IOSVQA benchmark and the GCP proxy , and the experimental results convincingly support the claim that native 3D geometric modelling outperforms multi-view rendering for IOS diagnosis. The paper is appropriate for MICCAI as an application-of-existing-methods-to-new-problem contribution. The main concerns are: (1) the underspecified 2D baseline rendering setup, which is needed to confirm the comparison is fair; and (2) the GCP ablation gap, which limits the interpretability of the GCP contribution. These are genuine weaknesses but not sufficient grounds for rejection on their own. The inference cost omission and LLM selection justification are minor presentation issues. I recommend weak accept, with a suggestion to the authors to add rendering specifications and the LLM selection rationale in their camera-ready version.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper’s primary contribution is IOSVLM, a dentistry-focused vision-language model developed together with a large-scale dental VQA dataset. The main novelty of IOSVLM is that it directly encodes intraoral scan data using a 3D encoder, instead of depending on 2D rendered or captured views of the scans. The paper also introduces a geometry-to-chromatic proxy to compensate for the absence of color information in IOS data. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms existing multimodal large language models from both general and medical domains on this task.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.A major strength of the paper is its direct use of a 3D point cloud encoder together with an LLM for intraoral scan data. This is an important direction for digital dentistry, since IOS is inherently a 3D modality. Compared with approaches based on a small number of 2D photographs or rendered views, operating directly on 3D point cloud data preserves richer geometric information and is therefore better aligned with the underlying clinical data source. This makes the formulation both technically meaningful and practically relevant.
2.Dataset contribution
The paper also makes a strong data contribution by curating a large-scale dental VQA dataset. This is valuable because progress in dentistry-focused multimodal models is often constrained by the lack of domain-specific benchmark data. Although the evaluation has some limitations, the proposed model still demonstrates stronger performance than existing off-the-shelf proprietary LLMs in this setting, which already provides a compelling reason to consider this model over more general alternatives for dental applications.
3.Another strength is the thorough ablation study. The paper also provides empirical justification for key design choices and training decisions. This makes the work more convincing, since the reader can better understand which components contribute to performance and why the proposed setup is effective.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Limited evaluation against relevant dental baselines.
The paper compares IOSVLM against existing multimodal large language models from both general and medical domains, but it does not compare against prior dental vision-language models such as OralGPT [1] and ArchMap [2]. This is a notable limitation because the current superiority over general-purpose MLLMs is not especially surprising, given that those models were not designed for dentistry and were not trained for this specific data setting. To support a stronger claim of state-of-the-art performance, the method should be evaluated against existing dentistry-specific VLMs or MLLMs, even if those methods operate on 2D photographic views rather than direct 3D IOS data. Such a comparison would better isolate the value of the proposed framework.
2.Insufficient clarity on the dataset contribution.
The paper states that the IOSVQA dataset is curated by aggregating data from three sources, but the provenance of each component is not sufficiently clear. In particular, it is unclear whether datasets such as MaloccIOS and DiseaseIOS were newly collected and annotated by the authors or whether they are existing resources that were reorganized into a unified benchmark. This distinction matters because the contribution is substantially stronger if the work involves original data collection, annotation, or expert curation, rather than dataset aggregation alone. The paper would benefit from a more explicit breakdown of which parts are newly created, which parts are reused, and what curation or annotation effort was required.
3.Unclear quality control for GPT-generated rationales.
The paper mentions the use of GPT-4o to generate rationales or chain-of-thought style explanations. While synthetic supervision is increasingly common, it also raises concerns about factual reliability and hallucination. The manuscript does not clearly explain whether the generated rationales were validated, manually reviewed, or filtered through any quality-control procedure. This is important because incorrect or low-quality rationales may affect both training quality and interpretability claims. A discussion of rationale verification, filtering criteria, or human evaluation would make this part of the dataset and training pipeline more convincing.
4.Limited discussion of broader design trade-offs and future directions.
The geometry-to-chromatic proxy appears effective for compensating for the lack of color information in IOS data, but the discussion of this design choice remains somewhat limited. In particular, the paper does not sufficiently address how this proxy compares with settings where true color information is available. Since some IOS formats can include color information, it would be valuable to discuss whether models trained on true colored IOS data might ultimately outperform proxy-based approaches, even if such datasets are currently harder to collect. This would help position the proposed method more clearly within the broader development path of dental multimodal modeling.
5.Minor presentation issue.
In Figures 1(a) and 1(b), the meaning of legend labels 1, 2, 3, and 4 is unclear. These labels should be explicitly defined in the figure caption or main text for readability.
References
[1] OralGPT: A Two-Stage Vision-Language Model for Oral Mucosal Disease Diagnosis and Description
[2] ArchMap: Arch-Flattening and Knowledge-Guided Vision Language Model for Tooth Counting and Structured Dental Understanding
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

My recommendation is based on the paper’s strong technical and clinical motivation but incomplete empirical support. The proposed use of a native 3D point cloud encoder for intraoral scan data is well motivated and represents a meaningful step for dentistry-focused multimodal modeling. The associated dataset contribution also adds value. However, the lack of comparison with prior dental vision-language models significantly weakens the strength of the paper’s claims. As a result, while I view the work as promising and relevant, the current evidence is not yet sufficient to fully support a stronger acceptance recommendation. If the concerns mentioned here are addressed, I am willing to make a stronger recommendation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
1.The paper construct the first large scale multi-source IOS diagnostic VQA dataset.
2.The paper introduce the first end-to-end VLM that takes native 3D IOS geometry as input for unified diagnosis, achieving clear performance advantages.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper constructs a large-scale dataset by integrating three existing datasets. The resulting dataset effectively captures real-world scenarios involving co-existing diseases and heterogeneous inputs, which is crucial for robust model training.
2.Leveraging this large-scale dataset, the paper adopts a two-stage training strategy to develop the first end-to-end vision-language model (VLM) that directly takes native 3D intraoral scans (IOS) as input for unified diagnosis. The proposed model achieves state-of-the-art overall performance, demonstrating both strong clinical applicability and significant value to the research community.
The ablation studies are comprehensive and well-designed. The paper provides thorough experimental evaluations of key model components and offers insightful analyses that help explain the observed performance improvements.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The contributions of the paper are primarily technical, and the overall model design lacks sufficient novelty. The proposed “geometry-to-chromatic proxy” essentially replaces RGB values in the point cloud with surface normals. However, the use of normal information for feature extraction has been widely explored in prior point cloud methods such as PointNet, PointNet++, and DGCNN, which limits the originality of this component.
2.The paper does not provide sufficient details regarding the training procedure, particularly for the two-stage training strategy. For example, it remains unclear whether the loss functions used in the two stages are identical or different, and how they are designed and optimized in each stage.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Although the contributions of the paper are primarily technical and may lack strong novelty, it presents the first vision-language model (VLM) for diagnosis based on native 3D intraoral scans (IOS), effectively addressing an important gap in the field. Therefore, I would be inclined to support acceptance, provided that the authors release the source code and trained model checkpoints to facilitate reproducibility and benefit the broader community.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
All three reviewers consider the paper has strong technical contributions and the experiments can convincingly support the advantages of the proposed methods. In addition, the authors also constructed a new large-scale dataset to facilitate further investigations. All three reviewers suggest accepting this papers.
It is anticipated that the authors can address the following concerns in the final version. (1) Release the codes and data to facilitate further studies. (2) Add rendering specifications and the LLM selection rationale. (3) If possible, see if you can compare the proposed model with more prior dental vision-language models, as suggested by one of the reviewers.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers and AC for their valuable comments!
Reviewer #1
Q1: Rendering protocol
A1: All 2D baselines use the same IOS renderings. Following orthodontic conventions, occluded-arch scans are rendered into five views: frontal in occlusion, left/right buccal in occlusion, maxillary occlusal, and mandibular occlusal. Single-arch scans use four views: frontal, left/right buccal, and occlusal.
Q2: GCP ablation
A2: We will add ablations with constant white, random pseudo-color, raw normals, and GCP to better isolate the normal-specific contribution of GCP in future work.
Q3: LLM selection
A3: Qwen3VL-8B was selected because it is open-source, reproducible, moderately deployable, instruction-following, and designed for multimodal spatial understanding, suiting geometry-grounded IOS diagnosis. Our scale/version ablation supports its accuracy-cost trade-off.
Q4: Inference cost
A4: IOSVLM can run on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 and uses 20765 MB GPU memory. Average inference time is 1.71 s/sample for label-only output and 4.8 s/sample for diagnosis+rationale.
Reviewer #2
Q1: Dental-specific baselines
A1: Existing dental VLM/MLLMs are mostly 2D models or lack executable weights. A fair IOS baseline should support multi-image IOS renderings. The only open-source dental model we found supporting multi-image input is OralGPT-Omni-7B, but checkpoint access needs author approval. We requested access but have not yet been approved, so we cannot report its result now. We will state this limitation and add such baselines once accessible.
Q2: Dataset provenance
A2: IOSVQA is not simple aggregation. MaloccIOS and DiseaseIOS are private datasets collected/curated by our team, while Bits2Bites is public. Our work includes registration, label harmonization, mapping report-derived 2D diagnoses to IOS labels, QA construction, and multi-disease formatting. In MaloccIOS, 557 cases were corrected by 28 orthodontists, yielding 7,628 high-quality samples; DiseaseIOS and Bits2Bites were annotated by experts.
Q3: GPT-generated rationale quality
A3: GPT-4o was not used to generate disease labels. Labels come from clinical reports/expert annotations; rationales are auxiliary supervision for about 50% of high-quality Stage-2 samples. To reduce hallucination, generation was label-conditioned and constrained by disease definitions. We filtered outputs inconsistent with the target label, containing extra labels, or failing format checks. No rationale is used in noisy Stage-1.We will state that full expert validation was not performed and discuss this limitation.
Q4: GCP vs true-color IOS
A4: We do not claim GCP is superior to reliable true color. If large-scale true-color IOS with consistent acquisition becomes available, RGB-based or RGB+geometry models may outperform GCP, especially for appearance-related findings such as caries or mucosal changes. GCP addresses the common setting where IOS color is absent, inconsistent, or unavailable after export, and where many labels are geometry-driven. We will position GCP as a practical proxy and discuss true-color IOS as a complementary direction.
Q5: Fig. 1 labels
A5: Labels 1–4 denote disease-specific category labels for visualization; their meanings are not shared across diseases. We will clarify this in the caption.
Reviewer #4
Q1: GCP novelty
A1: The novelty is not simply using normals as features. GCP uses geometry-derived local separability cues as a chromatic proxy to bridge color-free IOS point clouds and RGB-pretrained 3D encoders. Normals are one instantiation; the idea can extend to other geometry attributes and color-missing 3D domains.
Q2: Training details
A2: Both stages use standard autoregressive next-token cross-entropy loss. Stage 1 trains 1 epoch with the LLM frozen, using LR 5e-6 for the 3D encoder and 3e-5 for projectors. Stage 2 freezes the 3D encoder and trains 15 epochs with LR 1e-5 for projectors and 1e-4 for LoRA parameters, rank 8 and alpha 16.We use Adam and train on NVIDIA H200.

title: IRIS: An Intelligent Vision-Language System for Ocular Surface Diseases via Topic Tree and Scene-Driven VQA Generation
abstract: While Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) demonstrate remarkable generic capabilities, their clinical reasoning in specialized domains like ocular surface diseases (OSDs) is severely hindered by a paucity of high-fidelity, multimodal instruction-tuning data. To dismantle this data bottleneck, we introduce IRIS, an Intelligent Recognition and Interaction System tailored for fine-grained OSD understanding via external eye photography. First, we curate IRIS-120K, the largest and most comprehensive OSD visual question-answering (VQA) dataset to date. Crucially, to overcome the semantic shallowness of conventional image-caption pairs, we propose a synergistic data generation paradigm to explicitly inject clinical priors. Our data engine operates via a dual-branch framework: 1) a Topic Finding Tree (TFT) that hierarchically anchors visual features to precise anatomical and pathological concepts, enforcing rigorous medical deduction logic; and 2) a Scene-driven strategy that synthesizes role-adaptive clinical dialogues to ensure pragmatic generalization. By explicitly aligning a compact 4B-parameter VLM on this structurally enriched corpus, IRIS achieves highly competitive performance and outperforms both generalist and specialized medical VLMs with up to 34B parameters within this dataset. Our findings underscore that structured knowledge injection effectively bridges the domain gap, unlocking the potential for resource-efficient, expert-level AI deployment on mobile edge devices for scalable OSD screening. Code, datasets, and model weights will be publicly released by this \href{https://github.com/hwei-hw/IRIS}{repo}.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs
Machine Learning -> Synthetic Data / Data-centric AI

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents IRIS, a vision-language system for ocular surface disease understanding from external eye photographs. The work proposed a data-centric framework that constructs IRIS-120K, which the authors position as the largest external-eye VQA dataset to date, using a dual-branch data engine: a Topic Finding Tree (TFT) that organizes supervision around ocular anatomy and pathological findings, and a Scene-driven generation strategy that simulates role-specific clinical interactions. A compact Qwen3-VL model fine-tuned with LoRA on this corpus is reported to outperform substantially larger general and medical VLM baselines across several VQA settings.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper addresses an under-served but clinically relevant modality. Most ophthalmic foundation-model work is concentrated on fundus/OCT, whereas this paper focuses on external eye images for ocular surface disease understanding, which is a meaningful and relatively neglected direction.
The empirical gains are strong, especially relative to model size.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The clinical validity of the dataset and test set is not yet sufficiently convincing. A central concern is that much of the pipeline relies on VLM/LLM-based generation and filtering, including the final quality control of the test pool with GPT-5-mini. The paper does not clearly report how much of the final dataset, especially the so-called “gold-standard” test set, was verified by ophthalmologists, nor does it provide inter-rater agreement or systematic error analysis.
