reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
Anomaly detection framework for congenital heart disease (CHD) screening using four-chamber (4CH) fetal echocardiography videos.
There are two stages to the architecture where stage 1 trains a latent motion trajectory (LMT) model on normal fetal cardiac videos to get a 1D scalar signal that tracks the cardiac phase-related signal. During inference, the video is scored using a spectral regularity measure computed from this 1D signal. The spectral regularity measures the proportion of high frequency power in the LMT assuming that normal cases produce smooth and quasi-periodic motion while CHD/anomalous cases have high frequency content.
The LMT model is an autoencoder and the paper evaluates it with two decoder heads - one that uses reconstruction and another that uses registration.
THe method is tested on one in-center and two external datasets and outperforms baselines and performance comparable to clinical experts.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper addresses a clinically significant problem of detecting a rare condition (congenital heart disease). The design premise of the method is that “structural defects and functional irregularities are often interleaved: altered anatomy can induce abnormal contraction patterns, suggesting that motion provides complementary cues for detecting abnormality.” It is intuitive and grounded in physiological mechanisms of the disease. The problem is best formulated as an anomaly detection one given the abundance of normal cases.
The data used in training and evaluation come from multiple centers and captured on a diverse set of ultrasound machines. This is crucial to establishing the robustness of any clinical workflow and addressing issues of domain shift (as seen in the results of this method).
The inference time evaluation of a spectral regularity measure provide an interpretable framework for clinicians to assess the model predictions.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
There is significant performance degradation on external test sites drop from 92.72 to 75.56 (Set 2) and 67.25 (Set 3) AUROC. It is clearly acknowledged. The paper would benefit from a more in depth analysis of this drop.
The test-time protocol uses manual cropping of the heart ROIs while the training uses an automatic tool. This can be a confounding factor as well as is a major practical constraint. THe paper could report test performance with the use of the automatic cropper as well.
The 80th percentile threshold on normal validation data is a reasonable heuristic, but its behavior across sites is not analyzed. Does the score distribution of normals shift across sites? A calibration analysis would be informative and clinically important.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The model is trained and evaluated on fetal echocardiography videos. While fetal ultrasound is a common procedure during pregnancy, fetal echocardiography still remains a specialized modality and the broader clinical problem would be better addressed by having a method that works on the more routine imaging.

The paper addresses a clinically significant problem of detecting a rare condition. The design premise of the method is sound and grounded in physiology. The method is evaluated on multi-center, diverse acquisition protocols. The contribution is meaningful but the experimental analysis needs strengthening to fully support the claims (especially the performance degradation on external sites).
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors present a framework for detecting abnormality in fetal US 4CH clips. The method is based on an auto-encoder model encoding a 1D latent motion trajectory and the definition of an abnormality score based on spectral analysis of that latent.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper is well written, the scope and the problem neatly exposed. The method is clear and addresses a clear clinical need. The evaluation is fair and nicely explained.
The reviewer appreciates the indenpendance of the test set vs. the internal training set. The methodology to evaluate the results is also appreciated, with blinded clinical experts comparison.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The code base is not provided
On the reconstruction head, it looks like the loss used combines an L2 between the output anchor and the input, and an L2 between the output at time t and the input. The authors could have explained more why the first term was needed, as it seems counter intuitive to impose that term. The registration loss makes more sense mathematically.
The poor specificity results (on test set 2 and 3) are somewhat surprising and concerning. The authors could have discussed that a bit further.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Introduction: 
some related methods (TVAE, DISCOVR) are referenced later in the manuscript instead of at first appearance
Methods:
Normalised cross correlation is used as acronym without being defined
The self-supervised AE model imposes the latent feature to be a linear expression of a learnt video-wise fixed latent point (anchor) and a learnt global vector in the latent dimension (trajectory). The coefficient (alpha_t) of this global vector becomes the 1D signal that is later analysed for its spectrum to detect abnormality.
It is quite neat to formulate this as a pure self-supervised auto-encoder reconstruction (or registration) problem. It forces the latent space to artificially focus (1) a static representation of the 4CH view, and (2) on cyclic motion to explain the variability across the US clip.
On the reconstruction head, it looks like the loss used combines an L2 between the output anchor and the input, and an L2 between the output at time t and the input. The authors could have explained more why the first term was needed, as it seems counter intuitive to impose that term. The registration loss makes more sense mathematically.
Results:
The reviewer appreciates the indenpendance of the test set vs. the internal training set. The methodology to evaluate the results is also appreciated, with blinded clinical experts comparison. 
The higher performance of the registration-based reconstruction loss makes sense: it is better posed mathematically.
The poor specificity results (on test set 2 and 3) are somewhat surprising and concerning. The authors could have discussed that a bit further.

The key factor for this score are:
neat and clear method, self-supervised, mathematically sound (with registration loss)
fair evaluation with blinded experts, independent test sets
clear delivery, well wriiiten

meta_reviews.text: This paper proposes an unsupervised anomaly detection framework for congenital heart defect screening in fetal four-chamber echocardiography. All reviewers find the paper well written and the self-supervised, physiologically grounded formulation original, interpretable, and clinically meaningful. They appreciate the multi-center evaluation with independent external test sets and blinded expert comparisons. The main concerns are the specificity drop on external sites and the need for deeper discussion of generalization, calibration, along with clarifications on the loss formulation and missing experimental details. Overall, the reviewers view these as points for refinement rather than fundamental flaws.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for their constructive feedback. We provide the following clarifications regarding the main points raised.
Method rationale (R1)
Our spectral score is not intended to detect rhythm disorders. The hypothesis is instead that a model trained only on normal 4CH videos learns a normal latent motion representation, where frame-wise variation can be compactly described along a shared 1D motion direction. For abnormal hearts, the projection of each frame onto this normal motion axis may be less stable because of altered anatomy, abnormal contraction patterns, or out-of-distribution appearance. These effects can introduce local fluctuations in the extracted latent trajectory, even when the underlying rhythm is regular. The spectral regularity score is therefore used as a compact measure of deviation from learned normal latent dynamics, not as a direct measure of arrhythmia. 
Relation to supervised CHD screening methods (R1)
We agree that supervised image-based methods have reported strong performance in the literature (the paper listed by R1). Our work addresses a different setting: anomaly detection from fetal 4CH videos, without using labelled CHD cases for training or threshold selection. This is motivated by the rarity and heterogeneity of CHD and by the abundance of normal fetal cardiac videos in screening practice. The aim is not to replace fully supervised multi-view diagnostic systems, but to explore whether motion-derived normality modelling can provide a complementary screening cue.
Dataset clarification (R1)
All data included in this study were acquired during the second trimester. We resampled videos to 30 Hz because some retrospective test videos were stored at 30 Hz. Using a common frame rate reduces confounding from different temporal sampling rates. At 30 Hz, fetal heart rates of approximately 120–180 bpm still yield around 10–15 frames per cycle, which is sufficient for the low-dimensional spectral summary used here.
Multi-site evaluation and external-set specificity (R1–R3).
The training and validation data were acquired at the same hospital, using GE Voluson machines, while the external sets include Fujifilm, Canon, and Samsung systems (no machine overlap). We agree that the drop in specificity on external sites is important. A likely explanation is that vendor/site-dependent appearance changes shift the anomaly-score distributions of both normal and CHD videos. Because the operating threshold was fixed using only the normal validation set, external normal cases may receive higher scores, reducing specificity. Future deployment would therefore benefit from site/vendor calibration or additional normal-only training data from the target domain. Importantly, under the same domain gap and thresholding protocol, LMT-Reg remained the strongest deep learning method on both external sets and maintained relatively high sensitivity, which is desirable for screening.
Manual cropping at test time (R2).
For the test sets, we used manual heart ROI cropping to reduce confounding from fetal/probe motion and standardise comparison across vendors. The automatic cropper tool was itself developed mainly on GE data, so applying it to external vendors could introduce an additional, uncontrolled source of domain shift. We agree that end-to-end evaluation using automatic cropping is important for practical deployment and will be included in future work.
Reconstruction loss (R3).
The first L2 term in the reconstruction loss follows the original LMT formulation and encourages the decoded anchor to represent the mean/static appearance of the video. 
Additional analyses and reporting.
We agree that additional analyses would strengthen the work, including comparison of estimated heart-rate frequency with manual measurements, reconstruction/registration errors for normal versus CHD cases, and site-wise calibration. These will be addressed in follow-up work.

title: Latent Pathology–Age Decoupling in Functional Connectivity Graphs for Multi-task Schizophrenia Assessment
abstract:
Accurate prediction of clinical symptoms and cognitive deficits from functional connectivity is essential for advancing precision psychiatry in schizophrenia (SZ).
However, predicting these clinical and cognitive measures from brain functional connectivity remains challenging. A key barrier is that age-related brain changes substantially overlap with SZ pathology, predisposing models to exploit age-correlated variance rather than genuine pathological signals. At the same time, hard removal of age signals degrades performance on cognitive tasks where aging and pathology interact. To this end, we propose a Latent Pathology-Age Decoupling (LPAD) framework that enforces explicit latent constraints to decouple age-related variations from pathological features. The framework introduces a dual-stream architecture with pathology-age orthogonal decoupling and supervised contrastive regularization to suppress age-driven shortcuts, followed by a clinically-informed gated modulation mechanism that reintroduces age as a subordinate contextual reference. Experiments demonstrate that LPAD achieves performance improvements across all eight clinical symptom and cognitive deficit tasks, with external validation suggesting cross-site generalizability, and linear probe analysis and spatially complementary region-of-interest profiles between the two streams corroborating effective pathology-age decoupling. Code is available at https://github.com/SCSE-Biomedical-Computing-Group/LPAD.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a novel Latent Pathology–Age Decoupling (LPAD) framework to improve prediction of clinical symptoms and cognitive deficits in schizophrenia using functional connectivity (FC) data. LPAD explicitly disentangles age-related brain changes from pathological features through a dual-stream graph encoding with orthogonal latent constraints and supervised contrastive regularization. It then selectively reintroduces age as a gated contextual modulator for aging-sensitive tasks. The approach is validated on two datasets, showing consistent performance improvements across eight clinical and cognitive prediction tasks, with external validation demonstrating cross-site generalizability. Interpretability analyses further support effective pathology-age separation.
reviews.text_strengths:
Introduces a novel and principled framework (LPAD) addressing a key challenge in schizophrenia FC analysis: confounding between age and pathology.
Clinically-informed gated modulation (CIGM) thoughtfully reintroduces age as a contextual factor, preserving aging-sensitive cognitive signals.
Extensive experiments across multiple symptom and cognitive domains demonstrate statistically significant improvements over strong baselines.
External validation on an independent clinical dataset supports cross-site generalizability, which is critical for clinical translation.
Comprehensive interpretability analyses, including linear probes and spatial ROI mapping, provide biological plausibility and insight into the pathology-age decoupling.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The impact of preprocessing choices (e. g. , denoising, parcellation scheme) on model performance is not clearly discussed, limiting reproducibility and understanding of robustness.
Sample size is relatively small.
The study design and dataset usage, particularly which dataset serves as external validation, could be described more clearly to improve transparency.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Overall, this work presents a well-motivated and technically rigorous approach to disentangling age and pathology effects in schizophrenia functional connectivity analysis. The LPAD framework’s novel latent decoupling strategy combined with clinically-informed gating demonstrates strong empirical performance and cross-site validation, supported by meaningful interpretability analyses.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a Latent-Pathology-Age Decoupling (LPAD) framework that aims to disentangle age-related features from pathology-related features via an orthogonality constraint. The disentangled age representation is then reintroduced in a controlled manner through a Clinically-Informed Gated Modulation module to predict schizophrenia clinical symptoms.
reviews.text_strengths: Main strength of the paper is the explicit reuse of age-related features after disentanglement, rather than discarding them. Additionally, the overall orchestration of the modules appears coherent, suggesting a well-designed pipeline.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
There are several concerns, mainly related to the clarity and completeness of methodological descriptions:
1 ) The description of the GPSConv-GINE layer is unclear and requires substantial clarification. Unlike widely established models such as GCN or GAT, this combination is not standard and cannot be assumed to be familiar to the reader. The GPS model is essentially a Graph Transformer framework that integrates local message passing with global attention, along with various encoding strategies while GINE model extends GIN by incorporating edge features into the aggregation process.
It is not clear from the paper whether these two models are combined, and if so, how the integration is implemented, which components of the GPS framework are actually used and the motivation for choosing a Graph Transformer-based approach.
2 ) The baseline models lack sufficient explanation. For example, the abbreviation “MT” is introduced without definition. Some relevant prior works on disentangling age as a covariate (e.g., cited in [33]) are mentioned in the text but not included in the main comparison table. This makes it difficult to assess the fairness and completeness of the experimental comparison.
3 ) The paper states that two datasets are used, but it is not clear whether the datasets are merged and if merged, what are differences acquisition protocols etc..
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Overall, while the idea of disentangling and reusing age-related features is promising and well-motivated, the current presentation lacks sufficient clarity in key methodological components and experimental setup. Addressing these issues would significantly improve the paper’s reproducibility and impact.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses the problem that age-related brain changes overlap with SZ pathology, and proposes a framework for clinical and cognitive prediction that enforces explicit latent constraints to decouple age-related variations from pathological features, and reintroduces age as a subordinate contextual reference through a clinically-informed gated modulation.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper tackles the age confounding issue in schizophrenia, which is very relevant. The idea of removing age first and then reintroducing it as context is intuitive and aligns well with clinical reasoning.
2.The ablation study is thorough and shows each part actually helps.
3.The Interpretability analysis is thorough.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The cosine orthogonality penalty only removes linear dependencies, whereas the aging process is inherently nonlinear. It is therefore possible that z^p still encodes age-related information or z^a encodes pathological information in a nonlinear form that this constraint cannot capture.
2.The node-level scalar gate g_i is computed solely from h^p. However, after being constrained by L_ortho, h^p is supposed to be free of age-related information, so how can it reliably decide how much contextual information from v_i should be injected?
3.The linear probe shows that z^p no longer contains age-related information, but there is no corresponding evidence that z^a is free of SZ-related pathological features.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

well-motivated, solid experiments.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text: The reviewers are all positive about the novelty of the proposal and well designed experiments. The authors should explicitly acknowledge limitations raised by the reviewers, e.g., inability to disentangle non-linear aging effects and small sample sizes, and improve clarity on the points raised by reviewer 2.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and AC. We accept the meta-reviewer’s two limitations—no theoretical guarantee of nonlinear age removal, and limited sample size—and will state both in the camera-ready.
Nonlinear decoupling and bidirectionality (R3-1, R3-3). L_ortho enforces only linear orthogonality and cannot guarantee removal of nonlinear age–pathology coupling. The linear probe shows z^p does not predict age (R²=-0.176) but does not symmetrically test whether z^a predicts pathology. Both will be listed as limitations, with bidirectional probing and nonlinear extensions as future work. Existing analyses still jointly support bidirectional separation: (1) Fig. 3(b) shows zero overlap (Jaccard=0.000) between top-10% ROIs; age-stream ROIs concentrate in subcortical/temporal regions consistent with normal aging, while pathology-stream ROIs anchor in SZ-related DMN—if z^a retained pathological information, its ROIs would more likely overlap with SZ-related DMN. (2) z^a is driven by explicit age regression supervision, which with L_ortho exerts directional pressure toward age representation. (3) Fig. 3(a) shows clear t-SNE cluster separation, indicating separation persists in nonlinear spaces.
Gating on h^p (R3-2). The asymmetric gate g_i=σ(w_g^T h_i^p) is intentional. Under L_ortho the pathology branch suppresses age-related shortcuts while retaining pathology-severity information. The gate does not recover age from h^p; it determines, based on pathological representation, whether a node needs age-context modulation. Clinically, age–SZ pathology interactions are more pronounced in pathology-affected regions [20,8], so stronger-pathology nodes need more age modulation. Table 2 confirms this: removing CIGM yields the largest cognitive drop on WM (Δcorr=0.023), the task most sensitive to aging–pathology interactions.
GPSConv-GINE (R2-1). We will clarify in Sec. 2.1.GPSConv [25] is a hybrid graph transformer layer combining local message-passing with global attention. We instantiate the local module with GINE [12,32], which naturally exploits continuous FC edge weights w. GPSConv-GINE is thus a GPSConv layer using GINE as its local MPNN, motivated by GINE preserving continuous FC weights (often weakened in GCN/GAT) and GPSConv’s global attention modeling cross-network long-range dependencies disrupted in SZ.
Dataset usage (R2-3). Datasets are not merged. COBRE (n=135) is used solely for five-fold cross-validation in Table 1; the local dataset (n=35) serves only as independent external validation in Fig. 2.They differ in protocols and cognitive batteries (MCCB T-scores vs. BACS raw scores), so no merged training was performed. We will explicitly label the local set as held-out external validation in Sec. 3.1 and Fig. 2 caption.
Baseline coverage (R2-2). MT denotes Multi-Task; the full term will appear at first occurrence. [33] is built on sMRI-derived structural graphs with explicit covariate disentanglement; its modality, graph construction, and supervision differ from our FC-based subject-wise prediction, making fair reproduction under identical FC inputs infeasible. For comparability, Table 1 includes two directly corresponding FC-based age-deconfounding baselines: MT-SZ_ar (regression residualization [4]) and MT-SZ_adv (adversarial deconfounding [6,1]), reimplemented under identical FC inputs and task setup.
Preprocessing and sample size (R1). We agree preprocessing and parcellation affect FC modeling and that the paper underdiscusses this. Experiments use fMRIPrep [7] with FC on the Power-264 atlas [24]; the camera-ready will discuss denoising, parcellation, and FC construction. We acknowledge sample size as an important limitation; COBRE (n=135) and the external set (n=35) are comparable to recent multi-site SZ studies.

title: Latent-CURE: Interpretable Breast Cancer Diagnosis via Dual-Asymmetric Chain-of-Thought
abstract: Multimodal Large Models have significantly advanced automated breast ultrasound diagnosis. However, most existing frameworks utilize opaque, end-to-end paradigms prioritizing global statistical correlations over structured clinical reasoning. Consequently, these models remain susceptible to shortcut learning amid extreme real-world epidemiological imbalances, often bypassing rare but decisive malignant indicators for dominant benign patterns. To address this disconnect, we propose Latent-CURE, a novel diagnostic framework driven by asymmetric weighted chain-of-thought methodology grounded in latent space reasoning. Unlike traditional approaches, our framework constructs an implicit reasoning trajectory forcing the model to sequentially infer standardized BI-RADS morphological descriptors before converging on a final diagnosis. Furthermore, to combat the extreme scarcity of critical malignant features, we couple this architecture with a dual-asymmetric optimization strategy. By dynamically adjusting margins and weights, this strategy safeguards high-specificity malignant descriptors from being overshadowed by common benign priors. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that our knowledge-injected approach provides transparent clinical evidence while achieving robust, accurate diagnostic performance in imbalanced medical cohorts.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose Latent-CURE, a novel diagnostic framework driven by asymmetric weighted chain-of-thought methodology grounded in latent space reasoning.
reviews.text_strengths:
Unlike traditional approaches, our framework constructs an implicit reasoning trajectory forcing the model to sequentially infer standardized BI-RADS morphological descriptors before converging on a final diagnosis. 
The authors evaluated their framework using an IRB-approved multicenter dataset of 666 breast ultrasound cases,
partitioned 8:2 for training and testing, with all diagnostic labels strictly derived from the surgical histopathology gold standard. 
Table 2 shows quantitative diagnostic performance comparison across different model architectures, such as ResNet18 and various versions of Qwen. Based on the metrics used (accuracy, precision, specificity, and MCC), their proposed Latent-CURE comes out on top.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The content is mostly good. Weaknesses are mostly related to presentation. The text in many of the figures is impossibly small to read. The last section “Discussion and Conclusion” lacks substance; it is too brief and vague. And for some reason the section heading is not appropriately capitalized.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The content is mostly good. There is some concern about the potential reproducibility of the work. While the tables show relevant information clearly, the same cannot be said about some of the figures. I cannot fully judge the content of the figures because there is a lot of information masked by the small print, which becomes too blurry when I try to enlarge it on the screen.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The proposed Latent-CURE framework enhances breast ultrasound diagnosis by shifting away from standard end-to-end prediction toward a transparent, step-wise reasoning process. It aligns the model’s diagnostic trajectory with standard BI-RADS descriptors, sequentially analyzing the margin, calcification, and orientation before concluding. To combat dataset imbalance, the method couples an implicit chain-of-thought in the latent space with a Dual-Asymmetric Loss (Dual-ASL) mechanism. This innovative combination ensures that rare but critical malignant features are actively preserved to inform the final diagnosis.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) I like the overall narrative and structure of the paper; it is easy to follow and well-motivated.
2) While latent CoT has been explored before, combining it with a structured, multi-step feature-based reasoning pipeline is interesting and fits well with the clinical setting.
3) The Dual-ASL formulation is well-motivated for long-tailed clinical distributions and directly addresses the imbalance issue in a principled way.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) Can you expand upon the selection of feature trajectory i.e. margin → Calcification → orientation and then diagnosis? Are these permutations invariant? Also What is the contribution of each feature? Is there any ablation regarding that? 
2) What is the level of annotation regarding the reasoning steps?
3) Many design choices are limited to breast cancer diagnosis. Can authors clarify if this framework is limited to breast cancer diagnosis? Have you conducted any experiment which proves the generalization capability?
4) It is not clear from the paper what exactly is the contribution of individual components—feature-based reasoning or dual asymmetric optimization. What are the numbers without Dual-ASL (is it row 2 from Table 3)? If so, why are they so low even compared to the Qwen baselines? Also from Table 2, does Qwen3-VL-Embed-COT actually have 0 specificity?
5) I like the overall flow of the paper, but there are instances where key details need to be much more clear—for instance, what exactly are these anchors and how they are selected? Or in Sec 3.3, which model is used for direct SFT?
6) How are anchor texts and queries constructed for each step? Please provide the exact phrases, tokenization approach, and whether alternative phrasings were tested.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Although this paper has merit, my current assessment is a weak reject. This decision is based mainly on the limited novelty of the approach and several ambiguities in the writing. I am open to reconsidering after reading the authors’ rebuttal.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I thank the authors for their rebuttal. While the method adds genuine value, I remain unconvinced that all three claimed contributions are independently proven. The latent reasoning conceptually parallels Process Reward Modeling (PRM), making Dual-ASL—which protects minority features—the true core contribution. Furthermore, it is unclear why standard CoT collapses so drastically without Dual-ASL, implying the reasoning module is entirely dependent on it. The paper would be significantly strengthened by adding ablations for the reasoning order and hyperparameters (w,m), alongside generalizable takeaways for other datasets. I lean towards a Weak Reject, but would not mind an Accept (would suggest the authors to integrate the rebuttal clarifications into the final manuscript. There is sufficient space to achieve this with minor restructuring).

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes Latent-CURE, a breast ultrasound diagnosis framework that reformulates multimodal large model (MLM) inference as a deterministic metric learning problem in latent space rather than open-ended text generation. The three core contributions are: (1) an implicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) module that forces sequential alignment with BI-RADS morphological descriptors (margin > calcification > orientation > diagnosis) before producing a final label; (2) a Dual-Asymmetric Loss (Dual-ASL) that applies feature-specific dynamic margins and sample weights to protect rare malignant anchors from gradient starvation under long-tailed class distributions; and (3) empirical validation on a 666-case IRB-approved multicenter BUS dataset, where the method achieves 93.78% accuracy and 87.07% MCC, outperforming both pure vision classifiers and general-purpose MLMs.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) Clinically grounded reasoning structure. Encoding the BI-RADS reasoning sequence directly into the latent trajectory is a meaningful design choice. Rather than treating clinical interpretability as a post-hoc explanation, the CoT pathway is architecturally enforced, which is a genuine departure from most end-to-end approaches.
2) Deterministic output via metric learning. Replacing probabilistic decoding with cosine nearest-neighbor retrieval over predefined semantic anchors is an elegant solution to the hallucination problem in medical MLMs. The theoretical guarantee of zero-hallucination outputs (within a bounded anchor set) is well motivated.
3) Dual-ASL is well-targeted. The combination of dynamic angular margin and asymmetric gradient weighting addresses a real and well-documented failure mode (gradient starvation on minority clinical features). The ablation in Table 3 compellingly demonstrates that the Dual-ASL is indispensable, removing it causes specificity to collapse from 97.16% to 4.26%.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) Small and single-modality dataset. With only 666 cases (approximately 533 training / 133 testing), the dataset is quite limited for a paper claiming state-of-the-art on a general clinical problem. Standard deviations are reported across seeds, but no cross-validation is performed. Generalizability claims are difficult to substantiate, and the potential for overfitting to this specific cohort is real. The paper does not report the benign/malignant split, which is critical context for evaluating MCC and specificity figures.
2) Dual-ASL hyperparameters appear hand-tuned without principled justification. Table 1 lists specific values (e.g., w=6.0, m=0.5 for malignant final diagnosis; w=4.0, m=0.4 for non-parallel orientation) but provides no ablation over these values and no description of how they were selected. It is unclear whether these were derived from held-out data, domain knowledge, or grid search, raising concerns about reproducibility and potential data leakage in hyperparameter selection.
3) The ‘implicit CoT’ framing is somewhat misleading. The latent trajectory is not truly a chain-of-thought in the generative sense, it is a fixed sequence of binary retrieval steps over predefined anchor pairs. This is closer to a cascaded multi-task metric learning setup. The distinction matters for claims of interpretability: the model outputs one of two pre-specified text labels per step, not a free-form rationale. Authors should clarify this distinction more precisely.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Latent-CURE addresses a clinically relevant problem with a technically interesting approach. The reformulation from generative decoding to latent-space metric retrieval is novel and well-motivated, and the Dual-ASL ablation provides convincing evidence of the loss function’s importance. However, several issues prevent a confident acceptance recommendation. The dataset is small (666 cases) with an unreported class split. The Dual-ASL hyperparameters appear hand-tuned without ablation or principled derivation. The comparison with frontier MLMs conflates zero-shot and fine-tuned conditions. The fixed CoT ordering lacks empirical justification.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have addressed most of the concerns and clarifications I asked for - including the dataset split and training setup.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper presents Latent-CURE, a dual-asymmetric chain-of-thought framework for interpretable breast cancer diagnosis using latent space reasoning and BI-RADS-aligned clinical workflows. All three reviewers acknowledge the work’s meaningful methodological contributions, strong quantitative performance on a multicenter breast ultrasound dataset, and the clinical value of its structured, interpretable inference pipeline. Key shared weaknesses include problematic presentation quality, insufficient ablation studies, unclear design rationales, limited dataset scale, and ambiguous generalizability across broader cancer tasks. Reviewers hold mixed recommendations, with two weak accept votes and one weak reject decision heavily contingent on thorough author rebuttal to address technical and writing ambiguities. Overall, the work demonstrates solid technical innovation and clinical motivation but requires targeted revisions to resolve unclear details, improve readability, and validate component-specific contributions for final acceptance.

There are still concerns on the effectiveness of each proposed innovation and potential reproducibility of the work.

Two reviewers support acceptance (R1=4, R3=4→Accept). R2 maintains Reject but states “would not mind an Accept” — a borderline case. The dual-asymmetric chain-of-thought approach for interpretable breast cancer diagnosis addresses a clinically important problem.

This paper introduces Latent-CURE, an interpretable diagnostic framework that reformulates open-ended generative decoding into a deterministic metric retrieval process within a protected continuous latent space to enforce a clinically grounded BI-RADS reasoning trajectory (Margin -> Calcification -> Orientation) for imbalanced breast ultrasound diagnosis. To protect rare but highly specific malignant features from gradient starvation against abundant benign priors, the authors couple this latent pathway with a novel Dual-Asymmetric Loss (Dual-ASL) optimization strategy that dynamically tunes angular margins and sample weights. While a negative recommendation persists due to concerns regarding domain specificity, structural dependencies on Dual-ASL to prevent standard chain-of-thought collapse, and blurry visual resolutions in some figures, these limitations are convincingly mitigated. Backed by an exceptionally solid empirical validation using an IRB-approved multicenter dataset of 666 pathologically verified cases where Latent-CURE achieves a state-of-the-art diagnostic accuracy of 93.78% and protects specificity from class-imbalance collapse.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the chairs and reviewers for their review. We are encouraged that R1/R3 recognize Latent-CURE’s contribution and performance, and that R2 finds it well-motivated and technically interesting. Remaining concerns involve novelty, design clarity, scope, and presentation. We provide detailed responses below. We thank R1 for highlighting presentation issues, and will revise typos, formatting, figure readability, and discussion clarity in the final version.
Contribution/CoT framing (R2 & R3). Latent-CURE is not free-form generative CoT decoding rationales. Sec.2.1 reformulates diagnosis as deterministic cosine retrieval in normalized latent space. The contribution is coupling clinically ordered BI-RADS latent-anchor retrieval with feature-conditioned Dual-ASL: the former gives bounded intermediate evidence, the latter protects high-specificity anchors under imbalance.
Anchors/annotations/phrase robustness (R2). Supervision is descriptor-anchor level, not free-text rationale annotation. Intermediate steps use binary BI-RADS descriptors distilled after physician consultation (Sec.3.1); final labels come from surgical histopathology. Fixed anchor phrases are used in training/testing: “Not circumscribed margin”/”Circumscribed margin”, “No suspicious calcification”/”Suspicious microcalcifications”, “Parallel orientation”/”Non-parallel orientation”, and “Malignant”/”Benign”. In Eq.(3), q_t denotes step-specific retrieval context: implementation uses fixed user text “CoT”, while step identity comes from the active anchor pair and H_{t-1}, not freely varied query wording. Anchors/queries use Qwen3-VL-Embed-8B tokenizer/encoder. Phrase perturbation is valid; prompt-robustness studies test character-, word-, sentence-, and semantic-level variants, but this is not submitted evidence, so we do not claim prompt-invariance. Unlike open-ended prompting, Latent-CURE targets a controlled medical workflow where training/deployment share standardized BI-RADS anchors; phrase mismatch is constrained.
Feature trajectory/components (R2 & R3). The order margin->calcification->orientation->diagnosis is not permutation-invariant. Sec.2.2 defines it as a clinical progression from macro-structural cues to micro-signals and diagnosis. Since each step conditions on previous anchors through H_{t-1}, z_t=f_theta(X_v+q_t+H_{t-1}) changes if the order changes. We do not claim global optimality; the Discussion lists sequence changes and feature contribution as future questions. Table 3 separates modules: Direct SFT gives 91.79% Acc / 96.45% Spec / 83.26% MCC but is opaque; Standard CoT (“without Dual-ASL”) drops to 62.69% / 4.26% / -3.95%; full Latent-CURE gives 93.78% / 97.16% / 87.07%. Thus, Standard-CoT collapse is the failure mode Dual-ASL addresses: descriptor reasoning alone can leave high-specificity anchors under-optimized and biased toward majority-prior collapse. Table 2 reports Qwen3-VL-Embed-COT specificity as 0.00+/-0.00.
Dataset split/metrics/scope (R2 & R3). The claim is confined to the submitted BUS setting: 666 IRB-approved multicenter cases, 8:2 split, and histopathology-derived final labels. The test subset has 87 malignant and 47 benign cases; accuracy alone can mislead, because an all-malignant predictor obtains 64.93% accuracy but 0 specificity, matching Qwen3-VL-Embed-COT in Table 2.Thus we emphasize specificity and MCC. We do not claim external validation or generalization to all cancers; new tasks require task-specific anchors/workflows.
Dual-ASL weights/margins (R3). Sec.2.3 states that w and m are conditioned on epidemiological prior and diagnostic specificity, and Table 1 discloses all values. These values were fixed a priori from physicians’ clinical prior on descriptor rarity/specificity; they were not derived from training-set descriptor prevalence, not selected by grid search, and not fitted on the test set. Thus Table 3 is module ablation rather than hyperparameter ablation; the controlled mechanism evidence is Table 3.

title: Latent-to-Latent Flow for Volumetric Stochastic Segmentation
abstract: Uncertainty arising from inter-observer variability in medical image segmentation plays an important role in developing treatment plans. Research in this area is inhibited by the lack of multiple annotations for large-scale medical datasets, especially for volumetric data, which suffers from additional scaling and computational complexity challenges. Flow matching has emerged as a powerful framework for generative modelling and has also been demonstrated to maintain strong performance when working with latent representations of images. In this work, we introduce a latent-to-latent flow technique for stochastic segmentation of medical volumes via encoded representations of both the image and label space. We evaluate our method on two challenging applications covering delineation uncertainty for radiotherapy planning and multiple organ structure segmentation, improving efficiency up to 14x compared with full resolution models while maintaining clinically relevant performance. Code available at: https://github.com/biomedia-mira/L2L-Flow.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper addresses a real bottleneck in volumetric stochastic segmentation, namely the computational cost of full-resolution generative modeling.
reviews.text_strengths: This is a solid paper on an important problem: making stochastic segmentation practical for 3D volumes. The paper is technically clear, the proposed latent-to-latent formulation is sensible, and the efficiency motivation is well justified. I especially liked that the paper does not oversell the limitations of existing metrics and includes qualitative clinical context. The main caveat is that the performance story is mixed: the method is attractive primarily as an efficiency tradeoff rather than as a clear accuracy improvement over the strongest full-resolution baseline.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The strongest full-resolution baseline still wins on the main quality metric. 
On the radiotherapy dataset, Flow-SSN with the shifted schedule achieves the best GED, while L2L-Flow is presented as competitive but not superior. On CURVAS, the gap is more noticeable, especially for the pancreas, and the paper needs a higher-resolution 2x latent variant to recover part of that gap. The paper should frame the contribution more explicitly in those terms.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

See strength.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper identifies performance degradation of Flow-SSNs on high-resolution volumetric medical data, and introduces a simple time-shifted noise schedule resulting in significantly improved stability and performance at scale.
It also introduces the Latent-to-Latent Flow (L2L-Flow), an efficient and scalable volumetric stochastic segmentation approach that enables up to 14× faster inference compared to Flow-SSNs, whilst retaining competitive performance.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper addresses a real bottleneck: stochastic segmentation in 3D is costly, and uncertainty from inter-observer variability matters clinically. That motivation is well stated and relevant.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
[1] The novelty feels somewhat incremental.
The paper combines known ingredients: flow matching / Flow-SSN, latent generative modeling, label autoencoding, a shifted schedule inspired by prior latent flow work.
The combination is useful, but the conceptual novelty may be viewed as moderate rather than major. The strongest contribution is likely engineering and empirical scaling, not a fundamentally new formulation.
[2] Baseline fairness could be discussed more carefully.
The models are compared at fixed ROI size and similar training setup, but some baselines may not be fully optimized for 3D or for the exact computational budget used here. The paper notes challenges with MoSE and SSN in 3D, but the discussion could better separate “methodological weakness” from “insufficient adaptation/tuning.
[3] Flow matching may increase the trainning time and the trainning time should be reported to analysis the effiency.
[4] How does it compared with diffusion based appraoch? Because diffusion model are also an generative model.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The novelty is a bit limited; more experiments should be compared with more baselines, as well as the diffusion model method. In addition, a abalation study of efficiency should be reported.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The novelty seems quite limited. In addition, this paper lacks a diffusion model baseline.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: Uncertainty arising from inter-observer variability in medical image segmentation plays an important role in treatment planning. In this work, the authors introduce a latent-to-latent flow technique for stochastic segmentation by leveraging encoded representations of both the image and label spaces. The method is evaluated on two applications and demonstrates improved efficiency while maintaining competitive performance.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper proposes a modified shift schedule that significantly improves training stability and performance of Flow-SSNs in volumetric settings.
2.The method builds on Flow-SSNs and introduces a novel approach that learns a flow transport from a latent, volume-conditional prior to a latent label distribution.
3.The results across two applications demonstrate strong clinical potential.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Based on the reported results, L2L-Flow appears to achieve performance similar to Flow-SSNs, aside from improvements in inference time. The paper would benefit from a clearer discussion of why faster inference is clinically important and how it impacts real-world workflows.
2.Uncertainty modeling is presented as a key motivation, but the paper provides limited analysis of uncertainty. More comprehensive evaluation and discussion are needed, particularly in relation to the two clinical application scenarios.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The proposed method builds on Flow-SSNs, but the reported performance gains are limited, which raises some concerns regarding the level of novelty and practical improvement over existing approaches. While efficiency improvements are noted, their clinical impact is not sufficiently discussed. In addition, uncertainty modeling is presented as a key motivation of the work, yet the paper lacks a thorough uncertainty analysis and does not clearly demonstrate how this aspect contributes to the proposed clinical applications.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a latent-to-latent (L2L) flow-based stochastic segmentation framework as an extension of Flow Stochastic Segmentation Networks (SSNs). Instead of modeling stochasticity in pixel space, the authors perform uncertainty modeling in latent space using a dedicated mask encoder–decoder and a latent flow prior. The method aims to address computational and scalability limitations of pixel-space flows, particularly for volumetric medical image segmentation, and is evaluated on multiple datasets including a radiotherapy delineation task.
reviews.text_strengths:
The work addresses a relevant and well-known limitation of flow-based SSNs, namely their reliance on pixel-space transformations, which are computationally expensive for volumetric data.
The proposed latent-to-latent formulation is conceptually sound and well motivated.
The application to uncertainty-aware segmentation in radiotherapy is timely and practically relevant.
Reported inference speed improvements indicate potential for clinical usability.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Insufficient architectural detail
o The paper does not provide sufficient architectural information for the mask encoder–decoder (e.g., number of channels, latent dimensionality, depth).
o Similarly, architectural details of the latent flow/prior model are underspecified.
o This lack of detail makes it difficult to assess the expressive capacity of the latent space, compare with prior SSN implementations, or reproduce the method.
2.Ambiguity in latent prior design
o It is unclear whether the latent flow model is architecturally symmetric for image and label latents or whether different capacities are used.
o Explicit description of the flow architecture would improve clarity and reproducibility.
3.Downsampling factor choices (×2 vs ×4)
o Different downsampling factors are used across datasets, but no explicit justification is provided.
o An ablation study comparing ×2 and ×4 downsampling—especially added to the quantitative results table—would strengthen the analysis and help clarify the trade-offs between accuracy and efficiency.
4.Radiotherapy uncertainty analysis clarity
o In the uncertainty visualization and contour analysis, it is unclear whether the “SSN contours” correspond to pixel-space SSN, flow-based SSN, or the proposed L2L Flow model.
o This ambiguity makes it difficult to interpret the comparative uncertainty results.
5.Inference speed vs. performance trade-off
o The reported ~14× speedup appears to correspond to the ×4 downsampled model, whereas the paper notes that the ×2 model achieves better segmentation performance.
o It would be beneficial to include qualitative results for the ×2 model, as well as a discussion of its runtime trade-offs.
6.Consistency of experimental reporting
o For robustness and transparency, results for both ×2 and ×4 configurations should be reported consistently across tables, quantitative metrics, and qualitative examples.
7.Cross-validation protocol details
o While a 5-fold cross-validation strategy is mentioned, the exact training/validation splits are not clearly described.
o The reference to “16 samples” is ambiguous: it is unclear whether these correspond to validation cases, test cases, or randomly selected samples.
o Clarifying these points would improve experimental rigor.
8.Lack of ablation on latent generation design
o No ablation study is provided to justify the use of a dedicated mask encoder–decoder over simpler latent representations obtained via standard downsampling/upsampling.
o Such an analysis would strengthen the methodological justification of the proposed pipeline.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a promising and meaningful extension of flow-based stochastic segmentation to latent space, with clear motivation and relevance to volumetric medical imaging. However, the lack of architectural clarity, limited ablation studies, and some inconsistencies in experimental reporting currently weaken the paper’s technical transparency and reproducibility. Addressing these concerns would significantly strengthen the submission.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
After considering the authors’ responses, I would like to maintain my weak accept recommendation.
The rebuttal does a good job of clarifying the intended contributions, particularly the positioning of the latent-to-latent (L2L) flow framework and its role in enabling efficient 3D stochastic segmentation. I also appreciate the additional context provided around clinical relevance and uncertainty evaluation, especially the discussion involving inter-observer variation, which I found meaningful.
That said, some of my earlier concerns are still only partially addressed. In particular, important architectural details of the mask encoder–decoder and the latent flow design remain unclear. While the authors mention that code will be released, having these details in the paper is important for assessing the method’s capacity and reproducibility at review time.Similarly, the discussion around downsampling choices (×2 vs ×4) would benefit from more complete and consistent quantitative comparisons. I also still feel that an ablation justifying the use of the dedicated latent generation module would strengthen the paper.
Overall, I believe this work explores a promising and relevant direction, particularly in tackling scalability challenges of flow-based SSNs and improving efficiency for uncertainty-aware segmentation. However, clearer presentation and more complete experimental detail would further strengthen the contribution.

meta_reviews.text:
Mixed reviews, but all reviewers acknowledge the potential of the contributions and established improvements. I would propose to give the authors the opportunity to address the raised concerns in a rebuttal.

Only one out of four reviewers submitted a post-rebuttal score. The original reviews were mixed 5-3-3-4, and in addition to the 3 that remained a reject, I got an email from the 4 that proposed to accept, as her/his concerns were mostly addressed and mentioning that “…this work explores a promising and relevant direction, particularly in tackling scalability challenges of flow-based SSNs and improving efficiency for uncertainty-aware segmentation. However, clearer presentation and more complete experimental detail would further strengthen the contribution.”. Still very much a borderline case.

This work is interesting due to its focus on a stochastic, uncertainty-aware segmentation attempt, which is shown to be made very efficient. Reviewer concerns regarding novelty and failed comparison to diffusion baselines were convincingly discussed. I think this is relevant work that should be discussed at the conference.

After the rebuttal, R2 maintained the Reject recommendation, R5 maintained the Accept recommendation, and R1 and R4 did not provide updated reviews. Based on the authors’ rebuttal and the reviewers’ comments, the paper is not recommended for acceptance. Although the paper demonstrates some strengths, including addressing a practical problem and achieving promising improvements in inference speed, it also exhibits several fundamental limitations, including insufficient clarification of the performance–inference speed trade-off and its clinical utility, as well as insufficient uncertainty analysis. The authors are encouraged to address the reviewers’ comments when revising the paper for submission elsewhere.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their valuable feedback and address the main concerns below
Novelty/Clinical Impact (R2, R4, R1): We politely push back on remarks about limited novelty by reiterating our two main technical contributions. Firstly, we identify a previously unknown issue with Flow SSNs, limiting direct application to 3D. We resolve this by proposing a time-shifted noise schedule tailored to the loss. The resulting method is not just a baseline but sets a new state-of-the-art in 3D stochastic segmentation. Our proposed solution achieves the strongest performance on two challenging segmentation tasks. Secondly, our L2L-Flow addresses efficiency (up to 14x faster inference) and offers a highly competitive alternative to our voxel-space Flow-SSN, with a controllable efficiency/performance trade-off. Importantly, L2L-Flow is tailored for stochastic segmentation, employing a two-sided interpolant between an image prior and a latent label distribution. This differs from standard latent flows where one side is a fixed noise distribution. L2L-Flow is also more easily applicable to different 3D problems compared to Flow-SSN, as noise schedule tuning is no longer required for strong performance. The efficiency benefits of L2L-Flow enable novel applications such as uncertainty-guided adaptive radiotherapy planning. Efficient contour generation allows real-time updates to treatment plans and reduces the likelihood of inter‑fraction anatomical changes between imaging and treatment delivery. As suggested by R1, we will make the framing of our contributions clearer in the final version.
Uncertainty Evaluation (R4): Our quantitative evaluation includes standard metrics such as GED, but also went further by evaluating clinical utility through expert review. This qualitative evaluation revealed key limitations of these metrics, where instances of contours with strong GED performance didn’t show clinically meaningful variation. This was especially true of low-rank SSNs as discussed in Section 4.3.We therefore performed further analysis, adding clinical context to our results (noted as a strength by R1), which is largely missing in other works. Fig. 3 evaluates contour variation of our models in relation to clinically meaningful inter-observer variation (IOV). Alongside GED, this enabled our clinicians to assess the usefulness of predicted contours. Importantly, our proposed flow-based methods exhibited the strongest alignment with expert IOV.
Baseline Comparisons (R2): We did not compare to diffusion models as rectified flows are from the same model family, and Flow-SSN was already shown to perform better than CCDM [28]. All baselines were faithful 3D adaptations of their 2D implementations and training procedure to ensure fairness. Baseline efficiency comparisons focused on inference time due to its importance in downstream clinical use. Training efficiency was similar across models. As demonstrated by our time-shifted 3D Flow-SSN, scaling and optimising 2D methods for 3D is non-trivial. We will make the nuance surrounding these technical challenges clearer in the final version.
Ablations (R2, R5): In the radiotherapy experiments, 4x downsampling was already sufficient to achieve comparable performance to our time-shifted 3D Flow-SSN. An efficiency ablation study was performed on CURVAS in Section 4.4.Due to the small size of the pancreas, we performed a further experiment at 2x downsampling to quantify the speed vs performance tradeoff, as shown in Fig. 4 & 5.A strength of L2L-Flow is its flexibility at adapting the latent capacity depending on data complexity. Scales such as 8x have potential application, and can be explored in future work. We will make the rationale behind our ablation choices clearer in the final version
Architecture Details (R5): We will release the code covering full implementation details with the publication. The implementation for the rectified flow was adapted from the open-source Flow-SSN codebase.

title: Learnable Gaussian Prototype Guided Ordinal Learning for Fine-Grained WSI Grading
abstract:
Advances in digital pathology have enabled large-scale automated grading through deep learning-based analysis of whole slide images (WSIs), which is essential for cancer diagnosis and prognosis. However, existing WSI classification methods typically treat grades as independent categories, ignoring the ordinal and progressive nature of their relationships.
Overlooking this intrinsic relationship leads to unstable boundaries and inconsistent predictions. Although ordinal regression and classification models have been explored to model the label continuity, they primarily enforce output orderings instead of learning continuous feature representations, leading to discrete embeddings that ignore inter-grade similarity. To address these problems, we propose GPO-MIL, an ordinal multiple-instance learning framework that constructs a severity-aligned Gaussian prototype space to model disease progression. A global set of Gaussian prototypes is learned and reordered by their correlation with slide grades, forming an interpretable benign-to-severe axis that guides responsibility-based prototype attention. An ordinal-aware optimization further stabilizes this progression structure and enhances grading consistency. Experiments on our in-house pancreatic cytology dataset and two public histopathology grading datasets, including CAMELYON17 and PANDA, demonstrate consistent gains in grading accuracy and calibration, along with interpretable prototypes that align with pathological progression.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes GPO-MIL, a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) framework for fine-grained histopathological grading that explicitly models the ordinal nature of disease progression. The key contributions are: (1) Severity-Aware Ordered Prototype Space: A Gaussian Mixture Model fitted on training features and reordered by Spearman correlation with slide grades to form a benign-to-severe axis; (2) Responsibility-Guided Instance Aggregation: A two-stage attention mechanism that conditions instance features on the ordered prototype semantics; (3) Ordinal-Aware Optimization: A combination of coarse-to-fine hierarchical grading, Multi-Margin N-Pair loss for monotonic embedding structure, and prototype separation regularization.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper correctly identifies that existing MIL methods treat grading as independent categorical classes, ignoring the progressive nature of pathological changes. The ordinal formulation is well-motivated for cytology (pancreatic LBC) and histopathology grading (PANDA, CAMELYON17), where adjacent grades share morphological similarities. This is a meaningful advance over standard MIL.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
GMM prototypes are similar to prototype-based MIL methods though the ordinal reordering is new. 
Prototype attention are standard self-attention and cross-attention mechanisms; the prototype-conditioned variant is a natural extension. 
The GMM is pre-fitted on training features before MIL optimization begins, then frozen for warm-up epochs. This two-stage process may lead to suboptimal prototypes that don’t adapt to the specific grading task. While prototype means are updated after warm-up, the covariances remain fixed—limiting the model’s ability to refine the prototype shape. 
The visualizations (Figures 3-4) show successful cases, but there is no analysis of whether the model struggles with specific morphological patterns
The LBC dataset (in-house pancreatic cytology) cannot be verified by reviewers. While the results are promising, the community cannot reproduce or build upon this evaluation. The paper should clarify if the LBC dataset will be released or if additional public cytology datasets could validate the method. 
Code needs to be open source.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper addresses a clinically important problem, ordinal grading in computational pathology, with a technically sound and empirically validated solution. The integration of GMM prototypes with severity-aware ordering and prototype-conditioned attention is coherent and effective. Results are strong across three datasets, and ablation studies are thorough. However, the methodological novelty is incremental (combining existing techniques), and the evaluation lacks ordinal-specific metrics that would fully validate the ordinal learning claim.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a prototype-guided ordinal multiple instance learning framework for fine-grained whole-slide image grading. Its main contribution is the construction of an ordered Gaussian-based prototype space that explicitly captures the progression structure of pathological grades, together with an ordinal-aware optimization strategy that preserves label ordering during training.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The proposed method introduces an ordered prototype space, which is a reasonably novel way of injecting grade progression structure into MIL-based pathology models.
2.The combination of prototype-guided representation learning and ordinal-aware optimization is methodologically coherent.
3.The empirical evaluation across multiple datasets provides useful evidence that the proposed design is practically relevant.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The evaluation is not fully aligned with the ordinal nature of the task. Given the paper’s ordinal design, ordinal-aware metrics such as MAE or quadratic weighted kappa would be important to show whether the method reduces the severity of grading errors rather than only improving standard classification scores.
2.The fairness of the empirical comparison is not fully convincing. Using the same epoch and learning-rate settings for all baselines is not necessarily fair, since different methods may require different optimization configurations to achieve their best performance.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses an important problem and proposes an interesting ordinal-aware framework for WSI grading. The overall idea is meaningful and the multi-dataset results are reasonably promising. My main reservations are that the evaluation could better reflect the ordinal nature of the task, and the fairness of the baseline tuning strategy is not fully convincing. Overall, I view this as a borderline but positive submission, hence a weak accept.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This manuscript proposed GPO-MIL, an ordinal multiple-instance learning framework that constructs a severity-aligned Gaussian prototype space to model disease progression for a crucial diagnostic task (grading) in computational pathology. The main technical contribution lies in learning a severity-aligned Gaussian mixture prototype space reordered by Spearman correlation with pathological grades, then integrate responsibility-guided prototype attention and ordinal-aware optimization to model the continuous disease progression.
reviews.text_strengths:
[1] Meaningful motivation. This work addresses the critical limitation of conventional weakly-supervised learning manners that treats grading as independent classes while ignoring the ordinal and progressive nature of pathological grading, which is common in CPath.
[2] Comprehensive experimental validation. Validated on one in-house cytology dataset with two public histology datasets, demonstrating the robustness of the proposed method.
[3] Good organization. The illustration and logic of the description is easy-to-follow.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
[1] Related works. Lacks discussion on recent ordinal regression or prototype-based MIL in pathology grading.
[2] Hyper-parameters. The weight tuning of three losses lacks explanation. The number of prototypes (K=8/16) is set heuristically, have the authors did sensitivity analysis?
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper presents a novel also well-motivated method for ordinal WSI grading. The experimental results are convincing.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text: The paper proposes a prototype-guided ordinal multiple instance learning framework that constructs a severity-aligned Gaussian prototype space and uses ordinal-aware optimization to explicitly model disease progression for fine-grained histopathological grading in whole-slide images. Though there are concerns about incremental novelty and insufficient discussion of related works, all reviewers give positive scores and the motivation and comprehensive experimental validation are recognized by the reviewers.

title: Learnable In-Context Templates for Medical Image Segmentation via In-Context Learning
abstract: In-Context Learning has emerged as a promising paradigm for automated medical image segmentation, enabling foundation models like SegGPT to generalize to new tasks using annotated support examples. However, existing approaches typically rely on retrieving raw images as prompts, which suffer from two critical limitations: the inherent noise in raw medical data often misleads the model, and the repetitive retrieval process incurs severe computational latency. To address these challenges, we propose a novel framework, Learnable In-Context Templates, which shifts the paradigm from sample retrieval to template learning. We introduce an In-Context Distillation strategy to optimize a compact set of learnable templates, condensing the representative lesion patterns of a target dataset. By distilling essential semantic features and filtering out raw image noise, these refined templates provide a cleaner, more concentrated support set. Extensive experiments on six datasets demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art ICL baselines. Notably, our approach shows broad adaptability across diverse medical modalities and achieves a substantial order-of-magnitude reduction in inference latency, offering an efficient solution for clinical deployment. Code will be available at: .
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Synthetic Data / Data-centric AI
