reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper replaces query-time retrieval of raw support examples with a small set of Learnable In-Context Templates. Concretely, it clusters training images in encoder space, initializes one template per cluster from a centroid image-mask pair, and then optimizes each template with a frozen ICL model (In-Context Template Distillation). In inference, the optimized templates are used jointly as the support set, allowing the model to leverage a compact and reusable set of dataset-level semantic priors rather than query-specific retrieved instances. Empirical results from 6 benchmarks have shown that the method consistently and significantly improved SegGPT and UniverSeg.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper presents a clear methodological contribution: it replaces query-time support retrieval with a compact set of learnable image-mask templates, which is a well-defined and practically motivated design choice.
The proposed pipeline is coherent and easy to follow. It is model-agnostic in presentation and is validated on two distinct ICL backbones, SegGPT and UniverSeg.
The empirical results are consistently positive across six datasets, and the efficiency analysis supports a meaningful practical benefit over retrieval-based prompting.
The ablation studies help validate the proposed design.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The main comparison relies on relatively early retrieval-based baselines, while more recent medical ICL methods such as Iris [1], Tyche-IS [2], and ICL-SAM [3] substantially broaden the design space. Empirical evidence showing whether Learnable In-Context Templates improves over these stronger and more recent alternatives, or transfers effectively beyond the two backbones considered here, would be needed to support the paper’s broader claims.
The abstract states that “our approach achieves superior robustness against domain shifts and reduces inference latency by two orders of magnitude,” but the current experimental section does not fully substantiate either claim. In particular, the paper does not present a dedicated domain-shift evaluation, and the latency results appear closer to an order-of-magnitude improvement instead.
The proposed framework likely shifts computation from inference to training, which can be a reasonable trade-off in practice. That said, the paper does not report the overhead cost of clustering and template optimization, so the full computational trade-off remains unclear.
[1] Gao, Y., Liu, D., Li, Z., Li, Y., Chen, D., Zhou, M., & Metaxas, D. N. (2025). Show and segment: Universal medical image segmentation via in-context learning. In Proceedings of the Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Conference (pp. 20830-20840).
[2] Rakic, M., Wong, H. E., Ortiz, J. J. G., Cimini, B. A., Guttag, J. V., & Dalca, A. V. (2024). Tyche: Stochastic in-context learning for medical image segmentation. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (pp. 11159-11173).
[3] Hu, J., Shang, Y., Yang, Y., Guo, X., Peng, H., & Ma, T. (2024, December). ICL-SAM: Synergizing in-context learning model and SAM in medical image segmentation. In Medical Imaging with Deep Learning.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper introduces a clean and practically motivated alternative to retrieval-based in-context learning by replacing query-time example selection with a small set of learnable templates. The approach is conceptually simple, broadly applicable, and demonstrates consistent empirical gains across multiple datasets and two ICL backbones, with added efficiency benefits. However, the evaluation does not fully support some of the stronger claims (e.g., robustness to domain shift, two orders-of-magnitude latency gains), and comparisons to more recent and competitive ICL-based segmentation methods are missing. Additionally, the training-time overhead is not quantified, leaving the overall efficiency trade-off unclear. Despite these limitations, the core idea is sound and potentially impactful, warranting weak acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors addressed my concern about optimization cost and trade-off, and showed that this method works better than Tyche-IS. I believe that this paper should be accepted.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes Learnable In-Context Templates, a framework for in-context medical image segmentation that replaces instance-level retrieval with optimized learnable templates. The framework consists of three stages: semantic clustering-based initialization, in-context distillation-based optimization, and multi-template inference. Evaluated on six benchmarks, LICT consistently improves Dice scores while reducing inference latency by roughly two orders of magnitude compared to retrieval-based counterparts.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper is well motivated and addresses two concrete limitations of retrieval-based ICL segmentation through a conceptually simple template-learning framework.
2.The empirical evaluation is reasonably comprehensive, including six datasets, comparisons with multiple strong baselines, efficiency analysis, and ablations on optimization design, loss terms, and cluster number, which together support the practical value of the method.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.While the method is interesting, the paper does not fully clarify its novelty relative to closely related ideas such as prototype learning, visual prompt tuning, and dataset condensation; at present, the contribution appears somewhat incremental as a combination of existing concepts adapted to ICL segmentation.
2.The analysis remains mostly performance-driven, and the paper lacks deeper interpretability or mechanistic evidence showing what the learned templates actually capture, how they differ from raw cluster-center exemplars, and why they improve robustness under domain shift.
3.The fairness of comparison could be discussed more, since the support size and context construction differ between backbones (e.g., SegGPT vs. UniverSeg), and the proposed method uses all learned templates at inference; a stricter capacity-controlled comparison would strengthen the claims.
4.The efficiency claim is convincing at inference time, but the paper does not sufficiently discuss the optimization cost of learning templates, the overall training/inference trade-off, or how the computational profile changes as the number of templates or dataset scale increases.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The method is simple and reasonably well validated, with ablations that support its design choices. However, the novelty is somewhat moderate, as the approach can be viewed as a combination of prototype-style learning and prompt optimization adapted to in-context segmentation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
I appreciate the authors’ careful and constructive rebuttal. The response addresses my main concerns reasonably well. In particular, the authors clarify the novelty of the proposed learnable in-context templates relative to dataset condensation, prototype learning, and visual prompt tuning by emphasizing the shift from raw instance retrieval to dataset-level template abstraction for ICL segmentation. They also provide a more convincing explanation of why learned templates are preferable to raw cluster-center exemplars, including an additional SNR analysis suggesting that template optimization suppresses modality-specific noise and preserves cleaner lesion morphology.
The rebuttal also partially resolves my concerns about comparison fairness and efficiency. The authors clarify that they follow the official support-size settings for SegGPT and UniverSeg, and they provide additional evidence that the gains persist under smaller support sizes. Moreover, they quantify the offline optimization cost of template learning and explain how this cost can be amortized by the substantial reduction in inference-time retrieval overhead.

meta_reviews.text:
The rebuttal should clarify how the learnable templates differ from related work, and the novelty/superiority against recent medical ICL segmentation methods. Also, the authors should demonstrate the claimed domain-shift robustness and “two orders-of-magnitude” latency improvement. In addition, what the learned templates capture and why they outperform raw cluster-center exemplars need to be explained.

The paper presents a well-motivated approach to in-context medical image segmentation by replacing query-time support retrieval with compact learnable templates. Although the novelty is moderate and some claims on domain shift and latency were initially overstated, the rebuttal clarified the method’s distinction from related work. Overall, the work is sufficiently solid and accepted by all reviewers after rebuttal.

The authors have provided highly convincing and comprehensive responses in their rebuttal, successfully resolving the key technical and methodological concerns. Specifically, the authors have clearly articulated the distinction between their learnable templates and related works. Crucially, they have provided direct empirical comparisons with the recent medical in-context learning method, Tyche-IS; the proposed framework outperforms Tyche-IS, boosting the Dice similarity coefficient from 72.81% to 86.26% on the TNUI dataset, and from 53.93% to 73.06% on the CVC-ColonDB dataset, thereby solidly validating its superior adaptability and efficacy. Furthermore, the authors have properly clarified a conceptual ambiguity regarding “domain shift” in the original text, precisely redefining it as the inherent zero-shot performance degradation in in-context learning; they successfully demonstrated the model’s broad adaptability across multi-modality clinical data (e.g., ultrasound and colonoscopy) rather than explicit cross-dataset adaptation. The authors have also provided a thorough explanation of what information the learned templates capture over original cluster centers.
By successfully decoupling clinical efficacy from high computational overhead, the proposed learnable template framework offers a novel solution that achieves both multi-modality generalization and clinical-grade inference speed for medical in-context learning.
Consequentially, one of the reviewers raised their rating from “Weak Accept” to “Accept” following the post-rebuttal discussion. Given the strong consensus and the paper’s solid technical contribution, the AC recommends the acceptance of this manuscript.

The paper presents a clean, practical idea: replacing runtime support-set retrieval with a small set of learnable in-context templates, which improves both segmentation accuracy and inference efficiency. The method is well-validated across six datasets and two ICL backbones (SegGPT, UniverSeg), with solid ablations. Reviewer #2 turned to Accept after rebuttal, Reviewer #3 gave Weak Accept, and Reviewer #1’s Weak Reject (confidence 2) does not outweigh the overall positive consensus.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank all reviewers for the constructive comments and address concerns below.
1.Optimization Cost and Trade-off (R2, R3)
While template learning incurs an offline cost (e.g., about 50ms/image/epoch; ~50mins for TNUI’s 1K training set over 50 epochs), it eliminates repeated support-set loading and runtime retrieval, saving ~1000ms per inference. This cost is quickly amortized over TNUI’s test set (~300 cases) and becomes even more advantageous under common repeated-evaluation protocols (e.g., >10 runs). It also reduces storage I/O, benefiting clinical deployment. We will explicitly detail this training-inference trade-off in the revision.
2.Key Differences and Novelty (R1, R3)
We respectfully clarify the key differences between our method and related approaches.
1) Dataset Condensation: Trains independent models but remains tied to noisy instance-level samples.
2) Prototype Learning: Extracts latent abstractions, losing the fine-grained spatial information preserved in our pixel-level templates.
3) Visual Prompt Tuning: Adapts parameters but lacks the interpretable pathological semantics captured by our morphology-preserving templates.
None of the above distill dataset-level lesion geometry into explicit contextual priors for ICL segmentation.
In essence, we shift the focus from what to retrieve to what to represent—replacing noisy, redundant exemplars with compact, semantically grounded templates. These distinctions establish our method as a genuine paradigm shift, not an incremental adaptation.
➤ R1
1.DICE not optimal
We thank the reviewer for the observation. While absolute Dice scores vary across datasets, our method delivers consistent, substantial gains across all six benchmarks. For example, on TNUI, it improves SegGPT [22] from 31.76% to 80.34% and outperforms Dual-SC [9] (68.93% → 80.34%). These results firmly validate our empirical effectiveness.
2.Formatting and Reproducibility
We will revise the formatting issues. To ensure reproducibility, we will release all code and weights upon acceptance.
➤ R2
1.Comparison with recent baselines
We sincerely thank the reviewer for these valuable references. Iris [1] unfortunately lacks public code, preventing a direct comparison. Since ICL-SAM [3] builds on UniverSeg—already included in our evaluation—we instead provide comparion with Tyche-IS [2]. Our method improves Dice from 72.81% to 86.26% on TNUI and from 53.93% to 73.06% on CVC-ColonDB, demonstrating effective transfer to newer ICL methods.
2.Domain Shift & Latency
We apologize for the lack of clarity. By “domain shift,” we referred to ICL’s inherent vulnerability under zero-shot settings, not explicit cross-dataset adaptation. Our primary goal is to demonstrate broad adaptability across diverse modalities (e.g., ultrasound, colonoscopy). We will revise the manuscript to replace “domain shift” with more precise phrasing emphasizing multi-modality adaptability. We also agree the latency claim was overstated and will revise it to “a substantial order-of-magnitude reduction”.
➤ R3
1.Why learned templates are preferable
We thank the reviewer for the question. Unlike raw cluster centers that retain artifacts, our templates capture distilled lesion geometry. In-context distillation suppresses modality-specific noise, raising SNR from 18.16 dB (raw training set) to 20.35 dB (learned templates). This denoising provides cleaner priors, forcing the model to focus on intrinsic morphology rather than spurious variations, directly enhancing robustness under domain shift. We will include this SNR analysis in the revision.
2.Capacity-Controlled Comparison
To ensure a fair comparison, we followed the official baseline settings (K=4 for SegGPT, K=64 for UniverSeg), where our method with identical template capacity consistently outperforms. More importantly, even with non-optimal support set size, our gains persist (e.g., on SegGPT/ISIC, K=1 improves from 58.64% to 71.23% and K=2 from 61.38% to 72.74%).

title: Learning Beyond Pixels: Structured Knowledge Topology Consistency for Semi-supervised 2D/3D Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Semi-supervised learning (SSL) has become a pivotal strategy for medical image segmentation by harnessing unlabeled data. However, most consistency-based paradigms focus on aligning pixel-level outputs, failing to capture the high-order structural knowledge and diagnostic logic essential for complex anatomical interpretation. Motivated by the hierarchical reasoning process in clinical diagnosis—where radiologists progressively integrate local cues, global context, and anatomical priors—we propose \textbf{SKTC-Net}, a novel framework centered on \textbf{Structured Knowledge Topology Consistency}. We reformulate the semi-supervised objective by mimicking three critical aspects of clinical diagnosis: (i) \textbf{Where to look}: \textit{Spatial Attention Consistency} aligns saliency maps to ensure consensus on salient anatomical regions; (ii) \textbf{How to compare}: \textit{Relational Structure Consistency} preserves the global topological distribution among learning samples to mimic comparative diagnosis; and (iii) \textbf{How to reason}: \textit{Evolutionary Flow Consistency} constrains the inter-layer feature transitions to maintain a stable diagnostic reasoning path. Evaluations on ACDC (2D) and Pancreas (3D) datasets demonstrate that SKTC-Net consistently performs superior. Notably, SKTC-Net achieves consistent gains in low-label settings (e.g., +3.47\% Dice at 10\% Pancreas), attributed to the complementary supervision from multi-level structural constraints.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a new semi-supervised medical image segmentation method. The authors argue that existing methods mostly focus on output pixel level consistency while ignoring high order structural knowledge. Their method enhances semi-supervised learning by simulating the clinical reasoning process.

The three proposed modules are basically well designed with implementation details and applicability.
The experiments are comprehensive and the performance improvements are notable.
Existing models can directly adopt the proposed modules.

1.The innovation of core components such as SAC may not be as significant as the authors claim. Similar ideas have been widely discussed in the community, for example Attention Transfer (ICLR 2017).
2.The experiments only use MRI data. The performance on other modalities such as ultrasound remains questionable.
3.The paper claims applicability to both 2D and 3D tasks, but the method is introduced from a 2D perspective without clear explanation of how it adapts to 3D data.
4.Some theoretical connections are not clearly explained. For instance, RSC enforces consistency on the inter sample similarity in feature space, but the authors relate it to anatomical structure preservation without sufficient justification.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper is well written, and i find it satisfying to read. However, i have some minor concerns.
1.RSC constrains the similarity between samples in a batch rather than direct anatomical structures. Why can the former be equated to the latter? Does RSC incorporate spatial location information of organs, and is there functional overlap with SAC?
2.The ablation study does not isolate the individual contribution of each loss component. Only sequential addition is shown.
3.The three constraints may contribute differently across different organs and modalities. Could an adaptive weighting mechanism be designed instead of a fixed α?
4.What is the computational overhead of the dual student architecture and the matrix computations? How do the parameter count and inference time compare with existing methods?
5.In Figure 3, the right side only shows conceptual descriptions such as “where to look”. It would be helpful to also indicate how each constraint is implemented, for example “agreement between spatial saliency maps”.
6.In Section 2, it is unclear whether 
F_i^l refers to a single sample or the entire batch.
7.Why are MT and CPS used as baselines in Table 5 but not included in Tables 1 and 2?
8.Minor formatting issue: In Equation (1), the use of \mathcal{D} should be consistent.

Considering the novelty, although questioned by all of us, the authors’ explanation is acceptable to me. The authors also clarified the potential extension to 3D data and the anatomical prior modeling. So, I’ll keep the ‘accept’.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes SKTC-Net, a semi-supervised segmentation framework that extends consistency regularization beyond pixel-level outputs to structured representations, including spatial attention, inter-sample relationships, and inter-layer feature transitions.
reviews.text_strengths: The work is well motivated and extends conventional consistency learning to structured feature spaces through attention, relational, and hierarchical constraints. The method demonstrates consistent improvements across multiple benchmarks and shows good compatibility with existing semi-supervised frameworks.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) The novelty is limited and largely incremental, as the method mainly extends standard consistency regularization (e.g., Mean Teacher, CPS) to different feature representations rather than introducing fundamentally new learning principles.
2) The “clinical reasoning” motivation appears largely conceptual, and the proposed modules (SAC, RSC, EFC) can be interpreted as standard attention alignment, feature similarity matching, and feature correlation constraints, which are common in representation learning.
3) The contribution of each component is relatively modest. As shown in the ablation study, individual modules provide only incremental improvements, suggesting limited standalone impact.
4) The method introduces multiple consistency constraints, increasing model complexity without sufficient analysis of computational overhead or training stability. The evaluation is limited to standard benchmarks, without further validation such as cross-dataset generalization or robustness analysis.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a well-engineered and empirically effective extension of consistency-based semi-supervised segmentation, with consistent improvements across benchmarks. However, the level of novelty is moderate and mainly lies in combining existing ideas rather than introducing fundamentally new concepts, and the experimental validation could be further strengthened.(see weakness)
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
Motivated by the hierarchical reasoning process of radiologists in clinical diagnosis, this paper proposes a structured knowledge topology consistency network (SKTC-Net), a novel framework for semi-supervised medical image segmentation. Unlike existing methods that rely on redundant network branches, SKTC-Net systematically mimics the clinical diagnostic process across three orthogonal dimensions:
(1) Where to look: Spatial attention consistency (SAC) aligns saliency maps to enforce consensus on critical anatomical regions.
(2) How to compare: Relation structure consistency (RSC) preserves global topological relationships among samples in a batch by aligning their similarity matrices, mimicking comparative diagnostic logic.
(3) How to reason: Evolutionary flow consistency (EFC) constrains inter-layer feature transitions to capture the flow of feature abstraction and maintain a stable reasoning path.
The proposed method demonstrates superior performance on both the ACDC and Pancreas datasets.
reviews.text_strengths:
Novel and Well-Motivated Concept: The idea of systematically mimicking the hierarchical clinical reasoning of human experts (local cues, global context, and anatomical priors) without adding redundant network branches is highly novel and logically sound.
Purpose-Driven Architecture: The architectural design is highly cohesive. Each proposed module (SAC, RSC, EFC) aligns perfectly with its intended diagnostic dimension, making the framework intuitively understandable and theoretically robust.
Strong Empirical Performance: The experimental validation is solid. Achieving superior results on recognized benchmarks like ACDC and Pancreas clearly demonstrates the practical effectiveness of the proposed structural consistency constraints.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Poor Readability (Sentence Length): The manuscript suffers from overly long and complex sentences, which significantly hinders readability and makes the core concepts difficult to grasp. The manuscript would greatly benefit from being rewritten with shorter, more concise sentences to improve clarity.
Notation Ambiguity: The variable l is used interchangeably throughout the mathematical formulations to denote both “layer” and “labeled” data. This overlapping notation is highly confusing and poses a significant risk of misunderstanding the equations.
Missing Definitions: The loss term L_con is introduced in the text and equations, but is not explicitly defined, leaving a gap in the methodological explanation.
Insufficient Justification for SAC: While SAC effectively focuses on spatial information, the paper lacks a clear comparative analysis with prior spatial attention methods, such as Park et al. [1]. The authors need to explicitly state the novel aspects and structural advantages of SAC over this existing approach.
Lack of Rationale for Cosine Similarity: In the RSC module, cosine similarity is utilized to align similarity matrices. However, it is not clear why this specific metric is chosen over other distance metrics (e.g., L_1 or L_2 norms) or deep learning-based semantic comparison methods (e.g., attention mechanisms or SAM). The authors should elaborate on the specific advantages of using cosine similarity for topological distribution comparison.
Missing Recent Related Works: Several highly relevant and recent papers in the field of semi-supervised medical image segmentation are missing. Including discussions on the following works would strengthen the literature review:
(1) Zhu et al., “AdvMIM: Adversarial Masked Image Modeling for Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation”, MICCAI, 2025.(2) Wang et al., “GraphCL: Graph-based Clustering for Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation”, ICML, 2025.(3) Liu et al., “Translation Consistent Semi-supervised Segmentation for 3D Medical Images”, TMI, 2025.(4) Peng et al., “DMformer: Difficulty-adapted Masked Transformer for Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation”, BHI, 2025.
[1] Park et al., “Enhancing Intrinsic Features for Debiasing via Investigating Class-Discerning Common Attributes in Bias-Contrastive Pair”, CVPR, 2024.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper presents a highly original and thoughtfully designed framework that successfully translates clinical diagnostic logic into a functional semi-supervised learning architecture. The experimental results are robust and clearly validate the superiority of the proposed method. However, the overall readability is heavily compromised by excessively long sentences, and the ambiguous mathematical notations (e.g., overlapping l) create unnecessary confusion. Given the strong core methodology and empirical success, I recommend a Weak Accept. If the authors revise the manuscript to significantly improve clarity, rectify the notation issues, provide the missing justifications (for SAC and cosine similarity), and update the related works.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors have adequately clarified the distinction between SAC and Park et al., demonstrating that the two methods differ in both purpose and technical formulation. The justification for cosine similarity in RSC, particularly its scale-invariance and suitability for topological alignment, is reasonable and accepted. Regarding readability, notation ambiguity, and missing definitions, the authors have acknowledged all issues and committed to revising accordingly. I trust that these presentation improvements will be properly reflected in the final version.
I encourage the authors to ensure that all promised revisions, including notation fixes, explicit definition of L_con, and incorporation of recent related works, are fully addressed in the camera-ready submission.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper received mixed reviews, with major concerns focusing on comparisons with similar works and the claim of “mimicking clinical reasoning.” Also, the technical contribution is challenged since it combines several existing designs without a clear justification. In addition, the theoretical relevance between the model design and 2D/3D anatomical structures requires further clarification. Therefore, the authors are invited to submit a rebuttal.

After the rebuttal, all reviewers provided positive comments on this work. The main contribution is a “knowledge-level” consistency training beyond the common pixel-level regularization. Experiments demonstrated its effectiveness. The authors should further refine the paper in the camera-ready version, and a final acceptance recommendation is given.

After carefully reviewing the rebuttal and the post-rebuttal reviewer comments, my recommendation is to accept the paper. The paper proposes SKTC-Net, a semi-supervised medical image segmentation framework that extends consistency learning beyond pixel-level predictions to structured representations, including spatial attention, inter-sample relations, and inter-layer feature transitions. Although the novelty is somewhat incremental and the clinical reasoning motivation may be more conceptual than mechanistic, the method is technically sound, clearly motivated, and empirically effective across multiple benchmarks. The rebuttal adequately addressed the main concerns regarding 3D applicability, computational overhead, the distinction between SAC and prior attention methods, the use of cosine similarity in RSC, and presentation issues such as notation ambiguity and missing definitions. Given the consistent performance improvements, compatibility with existing semi-supervised frameworks, and unanimous post-rebuttal support from the reviewers, I recommend acceptance, with the expectation that the authors will fully implement the promised clarifications and readability improvements in the final version.

The proposed structured knowledge topology consistency network (SKTC-Net) is recognized as a well-motivated and empirically effective framework for semi-supervised medical image segmentation. While initial concerns were raised regarding the incremental nature of the modules, 3D generalizability, and presentation ambiguities, consensus among reviewers post-rebuttal highlights that the authors have resolved these concerns through convincing empirical clarifications and committed manuscript revisions.

author_feedback_text:
We appreciate the reviewers’ feedback. Following rebuttal guidelines, we’re unable to add new experiments in the responses.
Novelty and Relation to Prior Work (R1, R2, R3): The core contribution is the systematic unification of three orthogonal diagnostic dimensions into a coherent topology consistency framework. SAC differs from Attention Transfer (ICLR 2017): we operate in a dual-student semi-supervised paradigm for unlabeled data consensus, not supervised model compression. The three modules are mutually reinforcing—SAC enforces intra-sample spatial consensus, RSC preserves inter-sample relational topology, and EFC stabilizes inter-layer reasoning dynamics. Table 3 shows synergistic gains, exceeding the sum of individual contributions. Concerning R3’s fundamental new learning principle, MT and CPS frameworks are both introduced into the field of medical image segmentation in semi-supervised classification. Most of the existing excellent work is based on the innovation and modification of the two frameworks, including UAMT, BCP, AD-MT, and so on.
RSC and Anatomical Structure (R1): RSC aligns batch-wise similarity matrices to preserve the global topological distribution of cases in feature space. Anatomically similar patients naturally cluster closer in latent representation; stabilizing this topology mimics radiologists’ comparative diagnostic reasoning. RSC and SAC are functionally orthogonal: SAC operates on spatial attention maps for intra-image localization, while RSC uses flattened global vectors where spatial information is collapsed, preserving only inter-sample relationships.
3D Adaptability and Dataset Modality (R1): All modules naturally extend to 3D. SAC aggregates channels over 3D spatial dimensions; RSC flattens 4D feature tensors; EFC computes Gram matrices between adjacent 3D layers after adaptive pooling. The Pancreas experiments in Table 2 use VNet on 3D CT volumes, explicitly validating 3D applicability. Benchmarks include ACDC (MRI) and Pancreas (CT).
Ablation Study (R1): Sequential ablation demonstrates progressive complementary effects, as modules interact synergistically. Stepwise gains: CPS baseline (80.04 Dice), plus SAC (+1.69), plus RSC (+0.29), plus EFC (+2.20), reaching 84.22.Due to page limits, isolated ablations will be considered in future extended versions.
Computational Overhead (R1, R2): SKTC adds no parameters or branches. Inference uses a single student at the same speed as standard backbone. Training time on ACDC (5% label, RTX 3090): SS-Net 2.44hr, UA-MT 2.57hr, AD-MT 1.95hr, ALHVR 3.41hr, SKTC-Net 2.94hr. Note that this is not an additional experiment; it is a numerical count of an existing experiment.
Cosine Similarity in RSC (R3): Chosen for scale-invariance across layers/students, angular alignment capturing topological relationships for anatomical clustering, and simplified gradient computation via L2-normalized vectors.
Discussion on SAC (R3): Park et al. addresses debiasing in classification via bias-contrastive pairs and Grad-CAM. SAC serves a fundamentally different purpose in semi-supervised segmentation: it enforces dual-student consensus on spatial saliency maps to localize anatomical regions in unlabeled medical images, without auxiliary samples or bias-negative scoring. The technical forms differ: Park et al. uses dot-product similarity with relative-exploitation scores; SAC uses channel-wise power aggregation with L2 normalization.
Notation, Readability and Missing Related Works (R1, R3): We acknowledge these issues and will fix them: reserve l for layer index and D_L for labeled data; explicitly define L_con as standard semi-supervised consistency loss (Dice between predictions, CPS-style); restructure long sentences. These are presentation improvements. Due to space constraints, the submitted version had only limited space for literature discussion. We will incorporate these recent works in future versions to refine the literature review section.

title: Learning Class Difficulty via Dynamic Focal Attention for Histopathology Segmentation
abstract:
Frequency-based loss reweighting, the standard remedy for imbalanced histopathology segmentation, implicitly assumes that rare classes are difficult. Yet difficulty also arises from morphological variability, boundary ambiguity, and contextual similarity, all largely orthogonal to class frequency. We propose Dynamic Focal Attention (DFA), a simple, efficient mechanism that learns class-specific difficulty directly
within the cross-attention of query-based mask decoders. DFA adds a learnable per-class bias to the attention logits, reweighting representations before prediction rather than gradients after it. Initialised from a
centred log-frequency prior to prevent gradient starvation and then optimised end-to-end, the bias adapts to difficulty signals as they emerge
during training, unifying frequency- and difficulty-aware reweighting in a single attention-bias framework. On three benchmarks (BCSS, BDSA, CRAG), DFA consistently improves Dice and IoU, matching or exceeding
a two-stage difficulty-aware baseline without a separate estimator or extra training stage. This shows that encoding difficulty at the representation
level is a principled alternative to conventional loss reweighting.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes Dynamic Focal Attention, a learnable attention-based mechanism that models class difficulty dynamically and reweights feature aggregation accordingly, going beyond frequency-based or fixed focal loss approaches. They test their approach using Path-SAM on 3 pathology datasets
reviews.text_strengths:
The redefinition of class difficulty beyond frequency is insightful and well-supported
-The proposed Dynamic Focal Attention is a simple yet novel formulation that introduces learnable, difficulty-aware bias directly in attention (representation-level).
Training time reduction is very applealing
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The method is only validated on SAM-Path / query-based transformer segmentation, so its effectiveness beyond this family of architectures remains unproven.
The method is only validated on histopathology datasets, so its generalization to other medical imaging modalities is not demonstrated.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Despite some limitations, the paper presents a novel and well-motivated approach to modeling class difficulty beyond frequency.
The method is simple, effective, and consistently improves performance, making it an interesting and worthwhile contribution.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper addresses the problem of class imbalance in semantic segmentation of histopathology images. Typical methods use approaches that focus on class frequency to modify weights accordingly, assuming that rare classes are the most difficult ones. The authors show that this is not always true, and morphological variability, boundary ambiguity and other factors have a strong impact in class difficulty. They propose a method that, building on SAM-Path semantic segmentation model, introduces class difficulty as a bias scalar term per class in the focal attention calculation. Three approaches for the bias calculation are compared: using pixel frequency of each class, using a Dice coefficient per class obtained with a pre-trained baseline model, and a dynamic alternative that treats the bias as a learnable scalar that is optimized during training, which is the main proposal of the authors. An initialization strategy for the learnable scalar based on class frequency is also proposed as a more robust alternative to the zero-initialisation. It is shown that a higher scalar value corresponds with a badly segmented class, while a lower value corresponds with better segmentation.
The method is evaluated on three public histopathology image databases. The different attention bias proposals are compared on the three benchmarks. Results show that the proposed dynamic focal attention method outperforms the rest for most of the classes in terms of Dice and IoU, especially improving the most difficult classes.
reviews.text_strengths:
It presents a generic histopathology image semantic segmentation model, which is a clinically relevant problem, that shows robust performance on three different databases with multiple classes.
It addresses the class imbalance problem in segmentation of histopathology images with an original approach that adds little computational cost to the baseline method.
It proposes a dynamic focal attention method to improve the segmentation of especially difficult classes, and the authors empirically show that there is a significance improvement in those cases on different classes and databases.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Performance improvement with DFA is consistent but small. In general, there is a bigger improvement from Base w/o FL to CFFA, but very little from CFFA to the proposed DFA. It is true that it does not add a lot of computational complexity with respect to CFFA, but it does not bring a lot of performance improvement either. A similar thing occurs with the proposed warm initialization of the learnable bias (Table 2): there is a big difference in the learned scalars between cold and warm initialization, but this does not reflect so much in a Dice improvement.
There may be classes that are difficult in some of the images but easier in other images, such as tumour or stroma, what would happen with the learnt difficulty score in those cases? Would it affect the attention and thus the final segmentation of the class? Intra-class inhomogeneity is not addressed in any way. 
Training strategy:
The compared methods are trained for few epochs in each database (30, 20 and 60). Why those values? With more epochs, would DFA, CFFA and HCFA performance results be more similar? Would there still be a consistent improvement with the proposed DFA strategy? From my point of view, this is a point of concern.
Experimental setup: how many images are there in each database? A few more details would be helpful. Also, it is not mentioned how train/validation/test are organized in the training strategy. Is one split used? A cross validation scheme?
Minor things:
Section 2.2 should belong to the results section since it is not a methodological description but rather an analysis between class pixel frequency and Dice score on the databases
At the end of the method description, an Lreg term is mentioned but it is not clear where it belongs since it does not appear anywhere in equation 7.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

It presents a novel way of learning class difficulty during training and shows it consistently improves semantic segmentation in three different histopathology image databases with little additional computational cost. However, the improvement is rather small and there are some concerns about the training strategy that would need clarification. Besides, the contribution seems to be incremental over previous works.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors address all my concerns in a satisfactory way. I believe the revised manuscript should be accepted for MICCAI.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This work addresses semantic segmentation in histopathology. Even though the title includes “Imbalanced Histopathology Segmentation”, the authors tackle the difficulty of histopathology segmentation, showing that the frequencies and segmentation difficulties of each class are disconnected. They think difficulties stem from morphological variability, boundary ambiguity and contextual similarity. The authors proposed three variants of the attention mechanism for the SAM-Path decoder: Class Frequency Focal Attention (CFFA), Hard Class Focal Attention (HCFA), and Dynamic Focal Attention (DFA), using a Focal Attention Bias framework. They present experimental results using three publicly available segmentation datasets: BCSS (breast cancer), BDSA (brain tissue) and GRAG (colorectal adenocarcinoma).
reviews.text_strengths:
-Explore the difficulty of medical segmentation
-Proposal of three attention mechanisms under a Focal Attention Bias framework
-Experimental evaluation with three publicly available datasets of different parts: breast, brain and colon.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
-Misleading title
-Insufficient survey of related works
-Incorrect mathematical definitions and unclear derivation
-Unclear explanations
-Incorrect visual explanation of Fig. 1.-Unconvincing experimental evaluations without comparative evaluations
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors’ rebuttal is unconvincing, and the fundamental problems remain.
For example, even though they claim to refine the title to “Learning Class Difficulty via Dynamic Focal Attention for Histopathology Segmentation,” they do not clarify the difficulty of histopathology images for the segmentation task. Instead, they just say “the primary evidence for the difficulty-learning is the learned class-level attention bias \delta_c profile and per-class performance”. It does not make sense. It seems they focus solely on the performance attack rather than exploring the true class difficulty in histopathology segmentation. Where did the segmentation difficulty come from ? I think the image’s characteristics. Since there is no guarantee that Q, K, and V remain unchanged before and after adding a learnable \delta_c during training, comparative evaluations and visualisations should be necessary for a fair presentation that will clarify the segmentation difficulty in an input image for the histopathology segmentation. I think the experimental evaluations and presentations don’t match their titles.
Furthermore, the authors’ claims about Figs. 2 and 3 are irrational. In BCSS, Inflammatory is the hardest class in Fig. 3, and the Dice score is the smallest among the five classes in Fig. 2.However, it might come from the low frequency. On the other hand, “Necrosis” is the second hardest class in Fig. 3, but the Dice score is almost the same as the second highest one (”Stroma”) in Fig. 2.In addition, even though “Other” is 0.158 smaller than “Necrosis” in Fig. 3, that should mean “Other” is easier than “Necrosis”; the Dice score of “Other” is 5.6% smaller than “Necrosis”. From the results, I do not think that \delata_c accurately reflects the true difficulty of pathological segmentation. The authors’ analysis lacks fairness and objectivity.
Moreover, given the current status, I cannot expect satisfactory revisions to definitions, figures, descriptions of related work, the logical flow and readability. Even if they can, the camera-ready manuscript should become a fully different manuscript from the submitted one. NOTE: If the authors think reproducibility is important for the scientific work, the correct derivation of Eq. 5 with appropriate description and explanations should have been presented, even if it was in the Appendix or supplemental material.

meta_reviews.text:
The work proposes a class difficulty learning method for histopathology image segmentation with imbalanced issue by developing a dynamic focal attention mechanism. The recommendation is mixed among reviewers. The main disagreements are on empirical evaluation, methodology effectiveness, lack of sufficient evidences and explanations for some claims, and some writing issues. Based on my reading, I think that the reviewers raised effective concerns. Please try to fix these concerns in the rebuttal.

Two reviewers agree to accept and one reviewer for rejecting. I read the rebuttal and reviewers’ comments after the rebuttal. I think that the rebuttal solves the main concerns, though it does not fully eliminate the concerns. But due to the novelty of the method, I tend to accept.

After rebuttal, this paper receives two accept recommendations and one reject recommendation. The AC acknowledges that the paper addresses an important issue in imbalanced histopathology segmentation and proposes a simple dynamic focal attention mechanism to learn class difficulty beyond frequency, with consistent but modest gains across three public datasets. However, the rebuttal does not sufficiently resolve the major concerns about the clarity and rigor of the method formulation, the correctness and completeness of mathematical definitions, the strength of the evidence supporting the claimed interpretation of learned class difficulty, and the lack of convincing comparative analysis against related boundary-, context-, or difficulty-aware segmentation methods. Several key revisions would substantially change the submitted manuscript rather than merely clarify it. Therefore, despite the interesting motivation and positive reviews, the AC believes that the current paper remains methodologically and experimentally under-supported, and recommends rejection.

The majority of reviewers find this paper insightful. I also consider the idea of integrating class-specific bias into the attention mechanism to be both novel and inspiring. I agree in part with R3’s comments that the paper could be better organized and that some methodological details are missing. The authors are encouraged to include more method details and ablation studies in a future version.

author_feedback_text:
We thank reviewers for constructive feedback. We are encouraged that R1/R2 found the method novel, simple, and consistently effective, and we will revise the paper to improve clarity, reproducibility, and positioning.
R1 — Generalization. Focal Attention Bias requires only cross-attention with class queries, so it is directly applicable to other query-based mask decoders. Cross-architecture and cross-modality validation is planned for a journal extension.
R2 — CFFA→DFA gap. The mean gain is modest because CFFA already captures the frequency-related component of difficulty; DFA targets the non-frequency residual, so gains concentrate on hard classes: Inflammatory +2.7, Other +0.7, Leptomeninges +0.7, Superficial +0.5, Gland +1.7 Dice, with no easy-class tradeoff. We will emphasize these per-class difficulty-sensitive gains.
R2 — Warm-start. Cold initialization can keep $\delta_c$ near zero because rare classes receive weak gradients through the softmax self-gating term. Warm-start avoids this collapse by yielding the intended class-discriminative profile by boosting/lowering $\delta_c$ for hard/easy classes. Thus, warm-start is useful not only for the +0.75 Dice gain, but also for stable learning of the difficulty profile.
R2 — Intra-class inhomogeneity. DFA models class-level expected difficulty, not image-specific difficulty. Local adaptation is still governed by the token-dependent $QK^T$ term, which preserves spatially varying feature matching. We will clarify this scope and discuss region-conditioned difficulty bias as future work.
R2 — Training schedule/splits. The 30/20/60 epoch schedules were selected from validation-loss plateaus and were identical for all compared methods on each dataset; thus, the schedule does not preferentially benefit DFA over CFFA/HCFA. We used one fixed train/val/test split per dataset following the SAM-Path protocol, with 20% of training held out for validation. For BDSA, 10 WSIs produce ~82K 1024^2 patches, with held-out data split at the slide level. We will add these details to Sec. 3.1.R2 — Sec. 2.2 and L_reg. Agreed. Sec. 2.2 is empirical analysis and will move to the Results section; Eq. 7 will explicitly include L_reg.
R3 — Title and related work. We will retitle to “Learning Class Difficulty via Dynamic Focal Attention for Histopathology Segmentation.” We will expand related work positioning DFA as a complementary class-level attention-bias intervention.
R3 — Equations/notation. Eq. 1 uses broadcast addition of a class-wise bias $b$ across $N$ spatial positions; we will denote this by $\oplus$, define all tensor shapes, and remove unnecessary $\cdot$ notation.
Eq. 5 was compressed for space; the full softmax Jacobian is
$\partial \tilde{\alpha}
{i,k} / \partial \delta_c = \tilde{\alpha}
{i,k}(\mathbf{1}
{k=c} - \tilde{\alpha}
{i,c})$,
with on-diagonal self-gating $\tilde{\alpha}
{i,c}(1 - \tilde{\alpha}
{i,c})$ motivating the gradient-starvation argument. We will include the complete derivation.
R3 — Eq. 7 / Fig. 1.We will define L_dice, L_focal, L_mse, f_c, IoU, and iou_c explicitly. Fig. 1 will be redrawn with shape-consistent Q (C x d), K, V (N x d), and logit (C x N) blocks; $\otimes$ defined as matrix multiplication, $\oplus$ as broadcast addition, and x used for size notation.
R3 — Fig. 2 vs Fig. 3.The figures are complementary: Fig. 2 shows frequency and difficulty are not reliably aligned, while Fig. 3 relates learned $\delta_c$ to baseline Dice. For example, in BCSS, Inflammatory and Necrosis have near-identical frequency but learned delta = +0.41 vs. +0.07, matching a 22-point Dice gap. This cannot be produced by a purely frequency-driven scheme.
R3 — Attention visualization. DFA modulates class-level attention bias, while spatial selectivity remains governed by $QK^T$; thus, the primary evidence for the difficulty-learning claim is the learned $\delta_c$ profile and per-class performance gains, rather than attention-map visualization.

title: Learning Directional Semantic Transitions for Longitudinal Chest X-Ray Analysis
abstract: Chest X-ray (CXR) interpretation often requires longitudinal comparison to assess disease progression. Existing approaches typically rely on temporal feature fusion or inter-study discrepancy modeling, yet remain limited in capturing subtle progression semantics and overlook the inherently directional nature of disease trajectories. In this paper, we propose ProTrans, a novel vision-language pretraining framework that formulates disease progression as a directional semantic transition between paired CXR studies. ProTrans leverages radiology reports to anchor individual CXR representations within interpretable disease states, and introduces a learnable progression feature map to explicitly encode semantic shifts between states, aligned with report-derived progression descriptions. To enforce direction-aware perception, ProTrans incorporates a reversed temporal modeling process and imposes bidirectional reconstruction consistency across states and transitions, thereby disentangling directional semantics and promoting coherent trajectory modeling. Extensive experiments on longitudinal downstream tasks, including disease progression classification and progression captioning, demonstrate that ProTrans consistently outperforms existing methods, establishing a unified pretraining framework for longitudinal CXR understanding.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper proposes ProTrans framework that models disease progression as a directional semantic transition using a learnable progression feature map between paired CXR embeddings.
Joint state and transition contrastive alignment that grounds both CXR states and their interval transitions in a shared semantic space using radiology reports
Directional awareness is given via reversed temporal modeling. A backward sequence with a separate learnable reversed progression map is constructed, forcing the model to distinguish direction of change from mere change detection.
reviews.text_strengths:
The problem that this paper is tackling is clinically important and underexplored.
Framing progression as a directional semantic transition is conceptually well motivated.
Evaluation is reasonably broad, covering both classification and captioning, with appropriate clinical metrics.
It is additionally good practice that overlap with MS-CXR-T is excluded from the pretraining set.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Progression encoder design
Figure1 (b) indicates that temporal attention is applied over the reshaped tensor (B-N_I)x3xD, while spatial attention is handled separately over (B-3)xN_IxD. This means cross-time interaction is built around fixed patch indices across visits. For Paired CXRs, where patient positioning, inspiration, and projection can vary, I believe it is a nontrivial assumption.
Captioning details
The manuscript only states that the learned progression representations are fed into a frozen BioMistral-7B. However it does not explain which visual representation are fed to the LLM, how they are projected into the language model input space, how many visual tokens were used, or what parameters are actually optimized. More implementation details are needed.
Irreversible clinical findings
Not all findings are reversible. The framework assumes all disease processes are reversible (‘improve’ -> ‘worsen’) but there are cases such as fibrosis, calcification, scarring, and post-surgical changes. A calcified nodule cannot de-calcify. Training the model on clinically impossible transitions conflates irreversibility with directionality and prevents the model from learning to flag impossible trajectories. Irreversible findings should be supervised only through the reconstruction path, where directionality is enforced geometrically rather than through flipped semantic labels. At minimum, this assumption should be acknowledged and discussed as a limitation.
End-to-end training
The overall objective jointly combines all losses from the start and my intuition is that training all losses simultaneously from the start may make it difficult to learn good progression representations, which is the core contribution since P would be encoding transitions between states that are themselves still being learned. I am curious whether a curriculum approach, establishing stable state representations first before introducing the transition and reconstruction objectives, would improve the quality of the learned progression features.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Do you plan to release the code? I’d particularly like to inspect the temporal attention implementation to better understand how cross-visit spatial correspondence is handled.

Questions
1.Was the visual encoder initialized from the pretrained weights or trained from scratch? Also why did the author train end-to-end instead of staged training?
2.What exact visual representation is passed to BioMistral-7B?
3.How are irreversible findings handled?
The paper addresses a clinically important and underexplored problem, and the evaluation covers appropriate tasks and metrics. However, key technical and clinical concerns, particularly around the progression encoder’s spatial alignment assumption, unexamined reversibility assumption in label flipping, and some of the design and pipeline choices, weakens confidence in the current claims. I am wiling to revise my score based on the author’s rebuttal, especially if the questions above are addressed.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The rebuttal addressed some implementation concerns, including the captioning interface, visual encoder initialization, planned code release. However several limitations remain only partially resolved (spatial alignment, etc.)
My main remaining concern is the handling of clinically invalid reversed supervision. The rebuttal states that invalid reversed labels were not used, but the manuscript does not clearly explain how this was determined. This issue cannot be resolved simply by relying on chest imagenome labels or by assuming that dataset-provided progression labels are clinically reversible. Clinically irreversible or non-regressing findings may require phrase-level filtering, e.g., calcification, scarring, fibrosis, surgical changes,etc. Edema or effusions can still be irreversible. The paper should acknowledge this and discuss this as a clinical limitation.
Despite these concerns, the paper addresses an important and underexplored clinical problem, proposes a reasonable architecture, and includes relevant evaluations across progression classification and captioning. The paper is not fully convincing and the novelty is moderate, but I think it remains slightly above the acceptance threshold.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes ProTrans, a longitudinal chest X-ray pretraining framework that models disease progression as a directional semantic transition between prior and current studies, using joint state-transition contrastive alignment and bidirectional reconstruction. The idea of explicitly learning transitions rather than only fusing features or modeling differences is novel and well motivated, and the paper presents strong experimental results on both progression classification and progression captioning.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The overall technical direction is strong and timely. Modeling longitudinal progression as a semantic transition, together with contrastive supervision and directional constraints, is a fresh idea that goes beyond standard temporal fusion.
2.The experimental section is generally thorough and convincing for a MICCAI submission. The paper evaluates on multiple downstream tasks, compares against several relevant baselines, and includes ablations that support the usefulness of the proposed pretraining framework.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The method combines too many loss terms and training constraints, which makes the source of improvement hard to interpret. Even with the ablation study, it remains difficult to disentangle how much comes from state alignment, transition alignment, bidirectional modeling, or reconstruction, so the mechanism behind the gains is still somewhat unclear.
2.Figure 1 does not communicate the method clearly enough. The overview contains many blocks and arrows but is not modularized well, so it is hard to quickly understand the data flow and identify which component is the main contribution.
3.The encoder choices are not fully justified for the chest X-ray setting. The paper uses ViT-B/16 and BioClinicalBERT, but does not explain why it does not adopt encoders that were specifically pretrained on CXR data, which could be a stronger and more natural choice for this problem.
4.The improvement on MS-CXR-T over Coca-CXR is not consistently strong at the per-category level. Although ProTrans achieves the best average accuracy in the text prototype setting, the gain over Coca-CXR is small overall, and ProTrans is worse on three of the five findings, which weakens the claim of broad superiority on this benchmark.
5.The similarity-map analysis in Figure 2 raises a robustness concern that is not discussed. Since the visualization appears to rely on position-sensitive image features, it is unclear how well the method would work when prior and current CXRs are not well aligned due to pose, cropping, or acquisition differences.
6.The paper could do more to discuss the practical limits of the transition representation. The method assumes that a learnable transition map can reliably capture disease evolution, but the manuscript does not examine failure cases where progression cues are weak, spatially shifted, or confounded by acquisition variation.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The main reason for the positive score is that the paper introduces a genuinely interesting formulation of longitudinal CXR analysis as directional semantic transition learning, and supports it with solid experiments across classification and captioning tasks. The main reservations are about interpretability and presentation: the training objective is quite complex, some design choices are not fully justified, and the empirical advantage over the strongest baseline is not uniformly strong across all categories.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal adequately addresses my main concerns. In particular, the authors clarify that the progression map is intended as an explicit semantic transition representation rather than a simple soft feature fusion, and they provide a reasonable explanation for why semantic transition learning may reduce sensitivity to spatial misalignment compared with direct subtraction or low-level feature differencing. They also clarify the captioning implementation, the use of CXR-pretrained visual initialization, and the handling of clinically invalid reversed labels. While some concerns remain, especially regarding robustness to acquisition variation, the complexity of the training objective, and the limited per-category gains over the strongest baseline on MS-CXR-T, these issues do not outweigh the paper’s strengths. Overall, the paper presents a novel and clinically relevant formulation for longitudinal CXR progression modeling, supported by solid experiments and useful ablations. I therefore maintain a positive recommendation and support acceptance.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper proposes ProTrans, a longitudinal CXR pretraining framework that models disease progression as a directional semantic transition using a learnable progression feature map between paired embeddings, supported by joint state-transition contrastive alignment and bidirectional reconstruction. Reviewers acknowledged that it is a clinically important and underexplored problem, a novel formulation of progression as directional semantic transition, and a broad evaluation covering classification and captioning. Weaknesses are also pointed out: (1) The progression encoder assumes patch‑wise spatial correspondence across visits, which is fragile given variation in patient positioning, inspiration, and acquisition (R2, R3). (2) The complex multi‑loss objective makes the source of improvement unclear; a direct ablation of the progression map itself is missing, and the contribution of the LLM component is not isolated (R3, R4). (3) Empirical gains over Coca‑CXR are not uniform across findings, and the abstract/introduction contains vague jargon (R3, R4).
Issues to be discussed in rebuttal:
Spatial alignment assumption in the progression encoder under realistic CXR variation.
Handling of irreversible clinical findings and their impact on directionality learning.
Disentangling the contribution of the progression map via targeted ablation; clarifying whether the map is actively used or a “soft” addition.
Missing captioning details (visual tokens, projection, trainable parameters).
Justification for not using CXR‑pretrained encoders.

The paper introduces a novel and clinically relevant framework for modeling disease progression as directional semantic transitions in longitudinal chest X-rays. The rebuttal effectively clarified implementation details, encoder choices, and the role of the progression map, addressing the majority of critiques from Reviewers #2 and #3.They clarified that the progression map is an explicit semantic transition representation (not a “soft” addition), explained the captioning interface (projection layer into frozen BioMistral), confirmed CXR-pretrained ViT initialization, and acknowledged that irreversible findings were not subjected to reversed supervision because the Chest ImaGenome labels primarily involve reversible conditions (e.g., edema, effusion). They also proposed a targeted ablation removing the progression map, though this was a promise rather than an existing result. Reviewers #2 and #3 found the rebuttal adequate and changed their scores to accept, while Reviewer #4 remained unconvinced about whether the progression map is actually used and noted that the ablation cannot be added post-submission. Despite these limitations, the problem is underexplored and important, the method is well-motivated, and the evaluation is solid. While the strength outweighs the remaining issues, I believe the paper is above the acceptance threshold.

This paper proposes ProTrans, a longitudinal chest X-ray pretraining framework that models disease progression as directional semantic transitions between prior and current studies through joint state-transition contrastive alignment and bidirectional reconstruction. The work presents a conceptually interesting formulation for progression modeling, supported by evaluations across both progression classification and captioning tasks with clinically meaningful metrics. The main remaining concerns are that the progression encoder may still be sensitive to spatial misalignment across longitudinal CXRs, the contribution of the learnable progression map is not fully isolated due to the lack of a targeted ablation, and the handling of clinically invalid reversed supervision could be more clearly justified and discussed as a limitation. However, the rebuttal adequately clarified several implementation and design choices and two reviewers maintained positive recommendations after rebuttal. Overall, this work presents a technically reasonable and clinically meaningful formulation for longitudinal progression modeling that appears slightly above the acceptance threshold.

The paper addresses an important longitudinal CXR progression modeling problem with a novel directional semantic transition framework and solid experimental validation, despite some remaining limitations.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their constructive comments and for recognizing the clinical importance (R2,3), novelty (R2,3), and comprehensive evaluation (R2,3) of our work. Upon acceptance, we will publicly release the code and model weights to facilitate reproducibility. We clarify concerns below.
1.Progression map and spatial alignment (R2,3,4): We agree that longitudinal CXRs are often not spatially aligned, which motivated the use of semantic transition. Unlike direct subtraction or low-level feature differencing, which can be easily confounded by acquisition variation, ProTrans learns disease progression at the semantic level. Specifically, we use state contrastive alignment to ground prior/current images into corresponding semantic states, and introduce a learnable progression map to explicitly model the shift between them. Similar to CLS token in ViT, this map interacts with prior/current visual maps via the progression encoder and is supervised by report-derived progression descriptions via transition contrastive alignment, encouraging it to capture semantically grounded progression cues. We clarify that the progression encoder first uses temporal attention to capture local cross-time cues, and then uses spatial attention to exchange information globally across all visual tokens. After pretraining, the learned progression map is directly used for downstream tasks. It is an explicit transition representation rather than a soft addition. To further disentangle its role, we will add a targeted ablation that removes the progression map and replaces it with direct prior-current feature fusion. This directly tests whether downstream performance comes from explicit transition learning rather than from generic paired-image fusion. 
Although ProTrans aims to reduce sensitivity to acquisition variation by learning semantic transitions rather than raw visual differences, we agree that this doesn’t fully mitigate robustness concerns. We will add failure-case analysis and explicit registration as future extensions.
2.Captioning implementation (R2): The learned progression map is projected into the LLM embedding dimension via a trainable linear layer and used as visual prompts for frozen BioMistral. Only the projection layer is optimized during downstream adaptation, isolating the contribution of the learned progression features. We will add more details.
3.Irreversible findings (R2): We agree that flipped semantic labels are inappropriate for irreversible findings. In our work, we didn’t apply reversed semantic supervision when the reversed label is clinically invalid. Our current supervision from Chest ImaGenome mainly includes findings such as edema, pleural effusion, etc., where improved/worsened transitions are clinically valid. Reconstruction further provides a label-free visual constraint.
4.Training strategy and components (R2,3): Good point on curriculum training. Our motivation for joint optimization is that state and transition learning are coupled: if the model is first trained only with state alignment, it may learn good single-study semantic features but ignore progression-relevant cues. Combining transition alignment encourages the state space to support directional disease evolution. Ablation study shows that removing state/transition alignment, reconstruction, or bidirectional modeling degrades performance, with transition alignment causing the largest drop. All components contribute to reliable progression learning.
5.Encoder choice (R2,3): We initialized the visual encoder (ViT-B/16) with CXR-pretrained weights. ProTrans is a backbone-agnostic progression pretraining framework, and can be combined with stronger backbones. 
6.Others: q^t is a BxB one-hot alignment matrix, B is the batch size; element indexed by k denoting the k-th sample in the batch (R4). “w/o bidirection” means removing the reversed temporal modeling (R4). We will improve Fig.1 (R3) and abstract, introduction (R4), and add InfoNCE citation (R4).

title: Learning Diverse and Realistic Polyp Data via Style-Fused Diffusion Models
abstract: Polyp segmentation is critical for early colorectal cancer screening, yet its performance is limited by the quantity and diversity of annotated data. Existing synthesis methods typically rely on masks from public datasets, inheriting structural biases and limiting morphological diversity, while often neglecting style realism, producing synthetic images with inconsistent color and texture. To address these issues, we propose SFD-Polyp, a style-fused conditional diffusion framework that conditions generation on ground-truth masks and injects appearance cues via a Style Integration Module (SIM), enhancing texture and style consistency while preserving mask-aligned semantics. We further introduce Morphology-Preserving Mask Synthesis (MPMS) to generate multiple anatomically plausible mask variants at inference, expanding morphological diversity. Experiments on five public polyp datasets demonstrate that training with the synthesized data consistently improves segmentation across multiple baseline models, highlighting the potential of diffusion-based data generation to enhance generalization in data-limited medical imaging scenarios. Our code is avaliable at: https://github.com/zhaiying0925/SFD-polyp.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
