Without this baseline, it is unclear whether the AUC gains in Table 1 stem from the prompt-in-embedding-space design or simply from the additional disease supervision signal, regardless of how it is parameterized.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

RadFinder makes two genuine contributions that justify acceptance: a large-scale proprietary dataset with careful curation, and the snippet localization task which is a well-motivated and well-executed idea. The mining pipeline is rigorously validated and the result (MAE 36.3mm vs. 67.0mm) is convincing.
However, several concerns prevent a stronger recommendation.
The retrieval gains are primarily dataset-driven the RefCT-only ablation already surpasses all baselines before any methodological novelty is added and the comparison table is incomplete: Pillar-0 is cited four times and its RATE protocol is directly reused, yet it is absent from Table 1 despite being open source and trivially evaluable.
The ablation table, read carefully, does not fully support the multi-objective narrative: the localization loss shows no effect on all global metrics (reframed as “no degradation”), and the prompt loss slightly but consistently degrades Merlin retrieval, without discussion. Furthermore, the prompt-based disease supervision is never compared against the natural baseline of a standard classification head trained on the same labels, making it unclear whether the AUC gains stem from the design choice or simply from the additional supervision signal.
Acceptance is contingent on the authors providing Pillar-0 numbers in the rebuttal and more carefully scoping their methodological claims.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper’s main contribution is the introduction of RadFinder, a unified 3D CT vision–language model that combines large scale global report–volume contrastive pretraining with prompt based disease supervision and a new intra scan snippet localization objective. The medical staff often link their reports to specific axial slices and this information is now incorporated to guide towards the most relevant slices. This is enabled by building a large dataset of 98k report–volume pairs and automatically mining 262k snippet–slice references from these radiology reports, allowing the model to learn both global semantic alignment and fine grained axial grounding. As a result, RadFinder achieves state of the art retrieval performance, competitive disease classification, and substantially improved slice level localization, all within a single shared embedding space.
reviews.text_strengths:
Approach incorporating radiologists comments for spotting most relevant slices is nice and pragmatic. The chosen architecture is well structured and explained via Fig. 1. As model strategy processing of 3D volumes is utilized at reduced size of 128x128x32 to allow for resource handling. Here it is questionable, if entire 3D volume processiong for adequate 3D information classification is still the best way to go as redundancy is high and slice information low AND fine grained details might be overseen due to resampling. Thus, recent trends clearly favor full resolution orthogonal slices of selected / chosen quality. But at least in this work slice-level embeddings are incorporated, too
RadFinder achieves R@10 = 31.5 on CT RATE, clearly outperforming prior methods such as BrgSA (22.2) and SPECTRE (18.2) under identical evaluation. This is really a very meaningful jump, especially as CT RATE is a difficult benchmark where even marginal improvements can be seen as substantial.
RadFinder’s AUC of 83.8 on CT‑RATE and 77.0 on Rad‑ChestCT is essentially tied with the best existing models like MPS‑CT (83.8 / 77.3). Due to that, RadFinder does not significantly advance state of the art in disease classification as the improvements largely come from prompt‑based structured label supervision, a technique already used successfully in 2D VLMs. Compared to high‑resolution slice‑based approaches:
Methods like MedVista3D-ViT or BrgSA use full-resolution orthogonal slices and sometimes detailed local features, which naturally benefit classification tasks that depend on small-scale image details. Given that RadFinder processes downsampled 3D volumes (128×128×32 windows), achieving parity with such methods is respectable but not groundbreaking.
RadFinder drops the mean absolute error from 67 mm down to 36 mm, nearly a factor of two improvement over the best baseline (SigLIP2 finetuned). So this is by far the most impressive technical achievement of the paper.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
State-of-the-art presented in the introduction is not very easy to read. Besides, for 3D CT processing, all the approaches that incorporate 2D slices or selected axial/coronal/sagittal slices only are not mentioned, thereby forcing a trade-off between capturing fine-grained details and maintaining the global structural anatomical context, cf. Setio et al. 2016 “Pulmonary nodule detection in ct images: False positive reduction using multi-view convolutional networks”. CLIP-style 2D representation as input for 3D models are recent trends, too (Wang et al. 2022 MedCLIP: Contrastive learning from unpaired medical images and text) or (Lee et al. 2024 “Read like a radiologist: Efficient vision-language model for 3d medical imaging interpretation.”)
Paper rather hard to read regarding the writing style. 
Medical reports/diagnosis could be encoded by international standard such as Snomed-CT instead of the utilized simplified technical binary decisions such as “absence of hepatic lesion”. These could then still be formed as encoding for the classification model but would allow for a standardized taxonomy. 
RadFinder’s potential and superiority is highest in retrieval and localization, but not in disease classification per se, where full-resolution 2D slice models are really competitive.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Incorporation of radiographer findings is quite innovative and boosts the paper. The writing style itself could be improved to increase clarity.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper introduced RadFinder, a 3D CT vision–language model that augments contrastive pretraining with prompt-based disease supervision and a novel snippet-slice localization objective, mined from 98k report–volume pairs (262k snippet–slice pairs).
Reviewers agreed on the strength of the paper, including novel, well-motivated localization task; clever use of radiologist report references; strong retrieval and localization gains; clean shared embedding space; large-scale data curation. though some weaknesses are also shared by the reviewers, including performance appears largely dataset-driven (private data, not released); classification only ties SOTA; localization loss shows null effect on global metrics; clarity issues. Overall, the reviewers (scores 5/4/5) and AC recommend acceptance, citing the innovative localization idea and substantial empirical results despite concerns about dataset bias and incomplete ablations.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and AC for their thoughtful feedback and address their comments below.
“SPECTRE is trained on A+B+C […] A controlled comparison same data, RadFinder method vs. SPECTRE method is missing.” (R2)
To clarify, SPECTRE was trained on B+C+D (CT-RATE, Merlin, INSPECT), not A+B+C. A=RefCT is our internal dataset and was never available to SPECTRE.
The controlled same-data comparison is therefore already in Table 1, row “Public datasets, no loc.”
The method-driven gain is substantial on every metric except MAP@5.
“RefCT only already achieves R@10 26.3, surpassing all published baselines before adding any of the three training novelties” (R2)
To clarify, the “RefCT dataset” row in Table 1 applies all our training novelties, it just removes the public datasets from the training mix.
“core advantage may come largely from the internal RefCT dataset” (R1)
“performance gains seem predominantly dataset-driven” (R2)
Both contribute. The “Public datasets, no loc.” row in Table 1 isolates the method effect, the “RefCT-only” row isolates the data effect. The full model combines both.
“competitors […] fvlm, TotalFM, or Pillar0” (R2)
fVLM is in Table 1 (AUC; the authors do not report CT-RATE retrieval). Pillar-0 and TotalFM publish no comparable retrieval or classification numbers on CT-RATE.
“The implementation reports an effective batch size of 4096 […] which […] implies gradient accumulation” (R2)
The gradient accumulation we use is mathematically equivalent to using a true batch size of 4096: We collect all 4096 embeddings first, then accumulate the gradients with all negatives.
“The prompt loss […] slightly but consistently degrades retrieval on the Merlin benchmark […] This trade-off is not discussed.” (R2)
The prompt loss degrades Merlin results slightly outside the confidence interval while it lifts CT-RATE AUC by 0.27 points and Rad-ChestCT AUC by 0.14 points, a favorable trade-off.
“The prompt-based disease supervision is never compared against a standard classification head trained on the same binary labels. […] Without this baseline, it is unclear whether the AUC gains […] stem from the prompt-in-embedding-space design or simply from the additional disease supervision signal.” (R2)
In Table 1, the “Global loss only” row uses the disease prompts during evaluation, but does not use any of the disease supervision. AUC drops sharply on both CT-RATE and Rad-ChestCT, showing the importance of the supervision signal.
“The added complexity of the prompt approach […] is only justified if it outperforms a simpler linear probe or MLP head on the same encoder” (R2)
A distinct advantage of prompt-based classification over a linear classification head is the potential transferability to new diseases and the possibility to improve the prompts without changing the model.
“All localization evidence appears to be on the authors’ own RefCT test set.” (R1)
We agree. No public CT snippet-slice benchmark exists.
“Medical reports/diagnosis could be encoded by international standard such as Snomed-CT” (R3)
Mapping free-text reports properly to an international standard is a complex topic and out of scope for our paper, where we apply an existing method to structure reports.

title: Learning to Segment Burns with Limited Labels: A Dual-Path Cascaded Network with Uncertainty-Guided Teacher Diffusion Exposure
abstract: Automated burn segmentation from color images remains challenging due to tissue heterogeneity, ambiguous burn boundaries, and limited pixel-level annotations. We propose UADA-MSPCNet, a semi-supervised segmentation framework that improves annotation efficiency and boundary delineation. The method integrates a dual-path cascaded architecture that combines high-resolution spatial encoding with hierarchical atrous contextual aggregation for joint structural and semantic modeling. To leverage unlabeled data, we employ an uncertainty-aware teacher-student module in which predictive uncertainty modulates consistency supervision and cross-scale pseudo-label learning. In addition, diffusion-generated burn images are introduced exclusively through the teacher pathway, enriching feature exposure while avoiding synthetic bias in student optimization. This teacher-side generative exposure improves pseudo-label calibration under limited supervision. Experiments on the EBIS dataset demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art supervised and semi-supervised methods across multiple labeling settings, achieving superior Dice scores and boundary accuracy. These results highlight the effectiveness of integrating cascaded contextual modeling, uncertainty-aware consistency, and controlled generative augmentation for reliable burn segmentation.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper addresses semi-supervised burn segmentation. It uses a dual-path encoder that combines a shallow spatial stream with a ResNet backbone and cascaded atrous convolutions. This is placed inside an uncertainty-aware mean teacher setup with cross-scale pseudo-supervision between the two pathways. The main design choice is to pass diffusion-generated synthetic burn images only through the teacher in a forward-only manner, so synthetic data shapes pseudo-labels through EMA and BatchNorm updates without directly affecting student training.
reviews.text_strengths:
Teacher only diffusion sounds interesting and seems novel, which can further be extended to other, more general problems.
Experimental results support efficacy of the proposed approach.
The application targets an important clinical problem, as burn annotation is expensive and expert-dependent, so a label-efficient method with preserved boundary fidelity is genuinely useful rather than benchmark-driven.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Since the proposed method relies on diffusion, it would have been more informative to include one or two generative-model-augmented SSL baselines in the comparison.
Some technical details are missing - e. g. , the definition of the uncertainty term in the loss or the exact form of the spatial and contextual predictions in CSPS.
Evaluation is restricted to a single dataset, and the clinical generalization claim would be substantially strengthened by including an external cohort.
The comparative SSL methods appear to have been re-implemented by the authors, and UA-MT underperforming MT in their table is unusual, raising the possibility that baselines are not tuned to their typical strength.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Although technical novelty seems to be decent, I am not fully convinced that the efficacy of the proposed method is well demonstrated. Only one small dataset was used, and reproducibility is questionable, especially for the baseline methods. See weaknesses for details.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
Burn injury image segmentation faces challenges such as morphological heterogeneity and requirements for high precision edge detection. Balancing between contextual feature representation and boundary detection remain challenge
in deep learning model design for burn image segmentation especially when labeled data is scarce.
In this paper, a dual-path encoder is proposed that consists of two complementary streams: a high-resolution spatial stream that preserves boundary fidelity through three convolutional blocks, and a dense cascade atrous contextual stream that progressively captures multi-scale contextual information via a ResNet-101 backbone. This architecture enables the model to simultaneously exploit local spatial cues and global semantic dependencies.
reviews.text_strengths: A semi-supervised teacher–student framework is designed based on the proposed dual-path backbone to enhance diffusion-generated samples through the teacher pathway by jointly optimizing representation learning and pseudo label calibration.
reviews.text_weaknesses: Experiments are conducted on the dataset of burn images of 512 *512 resolution including 392 training and 208 test images. There is still a lack of experimental analysis on multicenter data.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Burn injury image segmentation is critical for clinical treatment planning and assessment. However, burn image processing remains challenging due to the high variability in skin texture and precise edge detection requirement. This paper provides a clear and thorough analysis of the challenges in burn image processing, particularly the high variability in texture and the stringent requirements for edge detection accuracy. In response to the specific demands of burn image analysis, the authors design an algorithm that effectively balances texture recognition and boundary delineation performance. The research demonstrates a notable innovation for burn image analysis.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes MSPCNet, a well-justified architecture that effectively decouples high-resolution spatial feature extraction from global contextual reasoning. The use of a regulated cascaded atrous formulation notably improves upon standard parallel pooling as it densifies contextual aggregation for complex tissue morphologies.
reviews.text_strengths:
The teacher-side diffusion exposure provides a novel way to leverage generative data without polluting the student network’s training distribution. Standard data augmentation exposes the student network to synthetic artifacts. By restricting these images to the teacher, authors allow the framework to benefit from a broader feature space without polluting the student’s gradient-based learning.
The architecture is specifically designed to handle the clinical complexity of burn wounds by simultaneously focusing on fine boundary details and broad tissue patterns.
The framework intelligently identifies and ignores uncertain regions in unlabelled data, which prevents the model from reinforcing its own mistakes during training.
The method provided effectively addresses a significant bottleneck, the high cost and difficulty of obtaining expert annotations for complex skin injuries.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The introduction of a diffusion model into the teacher pathway creates a significant computational bottleneck during the training phase. The paper lacks a cost-benefit analysis regarding training time. If the performance gain is marginal compared to the student-teacher model using simpler generative augmentations, the practical utility of a diffusion-based teacher in a clinical pipeline is questionable.
In clinical practice, a model trained primarily on lighter skin tones may fail to accurately delineate burn margins on darker skin, where contrast between healthy and injured tissue is reduced. There is no demographic breakdown of performance.
If the diffusion model is trained only on the same limited labeled set, it is essentially just a complex interpolator of that small sample size. It’s unclear whether the diffusion model is actually providing new semantic information or simply rearranging the same sparse features. The authors should clarify whether the diffusion model was pretrained on a large external dataset.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper demonstrates substantial improvements over the current state-of-the-art medical segmentation model, nnU-Net, particularly in low-label scenarios.
Teacher-side diffusion exposure is a good technical contribution that effectively utilizes diffusion models to enrich feature representation while successfully avoiding the common pitfall of introducing synthetic bias into the student network’s optimization.
The MSPCNet dual-path design is well-reasoned for the specific clinical challenge of burn segmentation, effectively balancing the need for fine boundary delineation with global contextual aggregation of heterogeneous tissue.
The authors conducted a thorough evaluation using five random splits and multiple metrics, proving that the model excels not just in overlap, but in precise boundary localization as well.
The ablation studies clearly validate that each component contributes measurably to the final performance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text: Strong clinical relevance and novel teacher-only diffusion strategy warrant acceptance despite the single-dataset limitation. Authors should clarify diffusion pretraining, add computational cost, and discuss demographic bias.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for their careful evaluation, constructive feedback, and positive assessment of the paper. We are encouraged that the reviewers and meta-reviewer recognized the clinical relevance of the problem, the effectiveness of the proposed MSPCNet framework, and the novelty of the teacher-only diffusion exposure strategy for low-label burn segmentation.
Regarding the diffusion framework, the diffusion model was trained exclusively on the EBIS training split with strict train/test partition separation and without external datasets or additional annotations. Importantly, synthetic samples were introduced only through the teacher pathway rather than as direct supervision for the student network. Teacher parameters remained governed solely through EMA updates from the student, while synthetic exposure influenced only teacher-side feature statistics and pseudo-label formation. The objective was to improve pseudo-label calibration while avoiding synthetic-distribution bias during student optimization. Consistent with this motivation, the ablation study in Table 3 of the submitted manuscript showed that applying diffusion augmentation to both teacher and student reduced both segmentation performance and calibration quality, whereas restricting synthetic exposure to the teacher improved Dice, HD95, and ECE.
Regarding computational cost, the diffusion component was used only during training and was not involved during inference. Final deployment, therefore, requires only a single forward pass through the student network without additional inference overhead. Teacher-side diffusion exposure introduced approximately 18–20% additional training overhead while consistently improving Dice, HD95, and calibration under limited supervision.
We also appreciate the request for additional methodological clarity. The uncertainty-aware consistency formulation and CSPS supervision mechanism are described in Sec. 2.2–2.3 through uncertainty-modulated consistency weighting, temperature-scaled pseudo-label sharpening, and confidence-guided supervision between spatial and contextual pathways. We will further improve the exposition of these components for clarity and reproducibility in the camera-ready version within the permissible revision limits.
Regarding reproducibility and baseline fairness, all comparative SSL methods were evaluated using identical preprocessing, augmentation policies, train/test splits, optimization schedules, and evaluation protocols. The observed UA-MT behavior remained consistent across five random splits under the same experimental settings.
Finally, we agree that broader demographic and multi-center validation remain important future directions. The current EBIS dataset does not provide demographic subgroup annotations for reliable stratified analysis across skin-tone distributions, and this limitation has already been acknowledged in the manuscript.
We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer again for their thoughtful comments and valuable suggestions.

title: Learning to Trim: End-to-End Causal Graph Pruning with Dynamic Anatomical Feature Banks for Medical VQA
abstract: Medical Visual Question Answering (MedVQA) models often exhibit limited generalization due to reliance on dataset-specific correlations, such as recurring anatomical patterns or question-type regularities, rather than genuine diagnostic evidence. Existing causal approaches are typically implemented as static adjustments or post-hoc corrections and do not explicitly refine representations during training. To address this issue, we propose a Learnable Causal Trimming (LCT) framework that integrates causal pruning into end-to-end optimization. We introduce a Dynamic Anatomical Feature Bank (DAFB), updated via a momentum mechanism, to capture global prototypes of frequent anatomical and linguistic patterns, serving as an approximation of dataset-level regularities. We further design a differentiable trimming module that estimates the dependency between instance-level representations and the global feature bank. Features highly correlated with global prototypes are softly suppressed, while instance-specific evidence is emphasized. This learnable mechanism encourages the model to prioritize causal signals over spurious correlations adaptively. Experiments on VQA-RAD, SLAKE, SLAKE-CP and PathVQA demonstrate that LCT consistently improves robustness and generalization over existing debiasing strategies.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Causal Inference / Counterfactual Reasoning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper addresses the problem of spurious correlations and poor out-of-distribution generalization in medical visual question answering (MedVQA). The authors propose a new framework called Learnable Causal Trimming (LCT), which integrates debiasing into end-to-end model training rather than relying on static causal correction or test-time adaptation.
The method has two main technical components. First, the paper introduces a Dynamic Anatomical Feature Bank (DAFB), updated through a momentum mechanism, to capture dataset-level recurring anatomical and multimodal patterns that may act as shortcut cues. Second, it proposes a Causal Trimming (CT) module that measures the similarity between instance-level visual features and the feature-bank prototypes, then applies a differentiable soft mask to suppress features that are highly correlated with these global priors while preserving more instance-specific evidence. An additional orthogonality loss is used to further reduce residual correlation between the trimmed features and the feature bank.
The main contribution of the paper is therefore an end-to-end trainable debiasing framework for MedVQA that is inspired by causal reasoning and designed to improve robustness under both standard and out-of-distribution settings. The method is evaluated on VQA-RAD, SLAKE, PathVQA, and SLAKE-CP, where it shows consistent improvements over prior work.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper addresses an important and clinically relevant problem. Shortcut learning and poor robustness under distribution shift are major limitations of current MedVQA systems. The paper targets this issue directly, which makes the work timely and relevant to the MICCAI community.
2.The proposed framework is coherent and reasonably novel in how it integrates debiasing into training. The combination of a momentum-updated dynamic feature bank and a differentiable trimming mechanism is intuitive and well motivated. A key strength is that the method incorporates debiasing into end-to-end optimization instead of using static adjustment or only test-time adaptation.
3.The experimental evaluation is solid and supports the paper’s main claim. The method is evaluated on multiple MedVQA benchmarks, including the OOD benchmark SLAKE-CP, and shows consistent gains over prior work. The ablation study and qualitative visualizations further strengthen the empirical support.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The causal interpretation is stronger than what is formally justified by the method. While the framework is motivated by causal reasoning, the actual implementation is closer to a confounder-aware feature suppression approach. The paper does not fully justify why the feature bank is a faithful proxy for a latent confounder or under what assumptions the trimming operation corresponds to causal adjustment.
2.The component-level novelty is moderate. Several ingredients of the method, such as momentum-updated prototype/memory-style representations, similarity-based masking, and decorrelation losses, are related to existing ideas. The main novelty lies in their integration for MedVQA debiasing, but the distinction from prior debiasing/causal MedVQA works could be made clearer.
3.Some additional analysis is still missing. The paper would be stronger with more discussion of hyperparameter sensitivity, computational overhead, and the possible risk of suppressing clinically meaningful but common anatomical structures together with shortcut features.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I lean toward weak acceptance because the paper addresses an important problem in MedVQA and presents a coherent method with encouraging empirical results. In particular, the focus on reducing shortcut learning and improving OOD robustness is highly relevant for medical AI, and the proposed framework is a meaningful step beyond static debiasing or test-time-only adjustment. The evaluation is also reasonably comprehensive for this domain, including multiple datasets, an OOD benchmark, ablations, and qualitative analysis.
My main reservations concern the strength of the causal claims and the fact that some method components are built on relatively standard ideas. I also think the paper would benefit from more analysis regarding efficiency and sensitivity to design choices. However, despite these limitations, the paper offers a useful and practically relevant contribution, and the OOD improvements make the work valuable for the MICCAI audience.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses the problem of spurious correlations and poor out-of-distribution generalization in Medical Visual Question Answering (MedVQA). The main contribution is a Learnable Causal Trimming (LCT) framework that incorporates causal-style debiasing directly into end-to-end training, rather than relying on static causal adjustment or test-time adaptation. Specifically, the paper introduces a Dynamic Anatomical Feature Bank (DAFB) to model dataset-level priors and a differentiable Causal Trimming (CT) module to suppress visual features that are highly correlated with such global prototypes, with the goal of encouraging the model to focus on instance-specific diagnostic evidence. The method is evaluated on VQA-RAD, SLAKE, PathVQA, and SLAKE-CP, where it shows consistently improved performance, especially under distribution shift.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper is clearly written and easy to follow.
2.The overall method is conceptually appealing.
3.The experimental results are convincing overall.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The method relies on region-level trimming, but the paper does not clearly explain how regions are defined in practice. It seems likely that patch-level features are used, but the exact setup should be clarified.
2.Since the paper argues that DAFB captures dataset-level confounders, it would be helpful to visualize which regions are most similar to the learned bank after training, and whether they indeed correspond to the expected shortcut-related patterns.
3.The ablation baseline differs from the PMC-CLIP result reported in Table 1.The paper should clarify whether this is due to re-implementation or different training settings.
4.The related work could be expanded. The paper [1] is relevant to representation alignment and robustness in MedVQA.
[1] Bridging the Semantic Gap in Medical Visual Question Answering With Prompt Learning
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper is clearly written, the method is easy to follow, and the experimental results are overall convincing, especially under OOD evaluation. The idea of integrating causal-style trimming into end-to-end MedVQA training is meaningful and appears effective in practice. My concerns are mainly about clarity and additional validation rather than fundamental flaws. In particular, the paper should better explain how regions are defined, provide stronger evidence for what DAFB actually captures, and clarify the baseline inconsistency. Overall, I believe the paper is above the acceptance threshold for the venue.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a spurious shortcut-mitigating MedVQA method centered on a learnable causal trimming framework. It suppresses regions highly correlated with dataset-level priors, while emphasizing instance-specific diagnostic evidence. Experiments validate its effectiveness in boosting both accuracy and out-of-distribution generalization.
reviews.text_strengths:
End-to-end learnable causal trimming is new and beneficial to the literature. The momentum-updated DAFB provides a dynamic, annotation-free proxy for latent confounders, addressing the limitation of static confounder dictionaries in prior causal MedVQA works.
Improved OOD accuracy and Grad-CAM quality.
Compared to competitive prior works.
The proposed trimming module can be packed into the ViT encoder and easily injected to VLM models.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The contribution of L_{orth} remains unknown in the ablation studies.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

End-to-end learnable causal trimming is new and beneficial to the literature.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper proposes a learnable causal trimming framework for Medical VQA, integrating a dynamic anatomical feature bank with a differentiable feature suppression mechanism to improve robustness under distribution shift.
The reviewers agree that the paper tackles an important and clinically relevant problem, and presents a coherent and practically meaningful end-to-end debiasing framework. The method is conceptually appealing, and the experimental results are solid and consistently support the claimed improvements. While modeling the confounder C as dataset-specific priors via the feature bank raises a potential concern of learning dataset-dependent bias that may limit generalization, the improved performance on OOD benchmarks (e.g., SLAKE-CP) partially alleviates this issue. However, validation under more diverse distribution shifts would further strengthen this claim. Meanwhile, the work could also be further strengthened by better justifying the causal interpretation of the framework (particularly the role of the feature bank as a proxy for confounders) and improving the methodological clarity of key components (e.g., region/feature definition and implementation details).

author_feedback_text: We thank the reviewers and the meta-reviewer for their positive feedback and constructive suggestions. We will carefully refine the camera-ready version in light of the reviewers’ valuable comments to further improve the clarity and completeness of the paper.

title: Learning to Unify Deformable Shape and Texture Representations for Cardiac Video Classification
abstract: Deformable shape representations have proven to be robust complements to texture features in cardiac image classification, offering geometric priors that are invariant to imaging artifacts and intensity variations. However, existing deep networks perform simple concatenation to combine these distinct feature representations, which neither fully exploits their complementary nature nor learns cross-modal feature dependencies. Furthermore, this results in uniform attention across all timepoints; hence ignoring the varying diagnostic importance across the cardiac phases. In this paper, we propose a novel cardiac video classification model that, for the first time, learns temporal features in an integrated space of deformable shape and image texture representations. In particular, we design a bi-directional cross-attention in the latent space to fuse latent deformable shape and image features, allowing each modality to adaptively weight the other based on spatio-temporal correspondence. In contrast to current methods that apply uniform weighting across all the cardiac phases, our approach learns to dynamically adjust the contributions of shape and texture representations, derived from images, over time. We demonstrate state-of-the-art classification performance on a cine cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) video dataset, achieving improved interpretability from attention mechanisms that identify diagnostically critical cardiac phases and modality contributions.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents ShapeFuse framework to unify features from both image intensity and deformable shape registration for the classification of cine CMR videos. Several neural network modules are developed for effective feature fusion, including a bidirectional cross-modal temporal attention block, an adaptive gating module, and a diagnostic importance pooling layer. The performance is evaluated on the myocardial wall motion abnormalities classification task.
reviews.text_strengths:
The proposed ShapeFuse framework incorporates features from both image intensity and motion tracking to improve the CMR classification performance.
Novel neural network modules are designed to fuse features from different sources.
The paper is structured well, and the methodology is clearly described.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The classification performance is only evaluated on a simple binary classification task using a single public CMR dataset.
There is no comparison with state-of-the-art CMR video classification approaches.
Transformer-based architectures are not explored as backbone models in the evaluation. EfficientNet [18] and DenseNet [13] are NOT transformer-based models.
An ablation study assessing the individual components of the proposed ShapeFuse framework is not provided.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The performance of the proposed approach is evaluated only on a simple binary CMR classification task. Its effectiveness remains unclear on more complex problems, such as multi-disease classification or CMR segmentation. Additionally, the evaluation is conducted on a single dataset, while commonly used public CMR datasets, such as ACDC and M&Ms, are not considered.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors did not address my concerns during the rebuttal process. There are several factual errors in both the manuscript and the authors’ response.
Both ACDC and M&Ms datasets are widely used public cine CMR datasets similar to [20]. However, in the rebuttal, the authors claimed that “disease classification from cardiac MRI datasets like ACDC typically requires full 3DxT volumetric analysis”. In fact, cardiac diseases such as the DCM and HCM in the ACDC dataset can be identified using the 2DxT mid-ventricular short-axis slides. The ACDC dataset also includes patients with previous myocardial infarction and abnormal LV contraction, which has similar setting as the dataset [20] used in this paper.
In the manuscript, the authors claimed that “we validate our model on classification tasks, adopting convolutional architectures (ResNet [10]) and transformer-based models (EfficientNet [18] and DenseNet [13]) as image encoder backbones”. However, both EfficientNet [18] and DenseNet [13] are convolutional neural networks and are NOT transformers. The authors did not response to my comment to correct this error.
For ablation study, the authors argued that “ShapeFuse’s bidirectional attention and adaptive gating are tightly coupled”. Actually, the inputs of the Adaptive Gating block can be replaced by the features extracted by both image and shape encoders without BCTA. The Adaptive Gating can also be simply replaced by the concatenation operation. In addition, the proposed Diagnostic Importance Pooling module was not evaluated.
In the rebuttal, the authors stated that “due to the space constraints, we could only show experiments on three image encoder backbones”. However, the submitted manuscript did not fully utilize the 8 pages allowed by MICCAI. Without additional ablation experiments, the current results in this paper cannot fully validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
Overall, this paper lacks sufficient empirical validation, particularly in terms of evaluations on multiple public datasets and comprehensive ablation studies. Since additional experiments are not allowed during the rebuttal phase, the current form of the paper does not meet the standards expected for acceptance at MICCAI.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes ShapeFuse, which introduces a bidirectional cross-modal temporal attention and adaptive fusion mechanism to effectively combine deformable shape and texture features over time for cardiac video classification, improving both performance and interpretability.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper’s main strengths are a novel cross-modal temporal attention mechanism that explicitly models interactions between shape and texture features, and an adaptive fusion strategy that dynamically weights modalities and cardiac phases. It is also clinically meaningful by leveraging motion information and shows consistent improvements across multiple settings with good interpretability.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Improvements are not clearly attributable to the proposed fusion module.
The model heavily relies on deformation features from a pretrained registration network, but the paper does not isolate whether the performance gains come from the fusion design or simply from introducing motion information. This makes the main contribution difficult to validate.
2.Not truly a joint learning framework despite the claim.
The paper claims to “jointly learn the fusion of shape and texture representations.” However, in practice, the shape (deformation) features are extracted from a pretrained registration network and kept frozen during training. This means the shape representation is not jointly optimized with the classification objective, and the model only learns to fuse fixed features rather than learning shape and texture representations together. This creates a mismatch between the claimed formulation and the actual implementation.
3.Fusion strategy is a direct application of existing techniques.
The proposed fusion mechanism mainly combines standard cross-attention and gating, which are widely used in prior multimodal learning. The paper does not introduce a new formulation tailored to cardiac video data, but rather applies existing modules in a relatively straightforward way.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper tackles a meaningful problem and presents a sensible way to combine deformation and texture features for cardiac video classification. The idea is well motivated and the results are consistently strong across different settings, with some useful interpretability. There are still concerns about where the improvements really come from, the lack of true joint learning, but overall the paper is solid enough to be slightly above the acceptance threshold.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The author’s reponse answered my question.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: It used a bidirectional cross-modal temporal attention module for frame fusion and an adaptive fusion gate to dynamically control the modality weights.
reviews.text_strengths: The network is well designed. The use of a bidirectional cross-modal temporal attention module for frame fusion is novel, and the adaptive gating mechanism for improving model performance is also interesting.
reviews.text_weaknesses: For the table one, please bold the best value. For example, for the last column, the best values are 0.977 for the VM and 0.968 for the LRN. The method you mark values is misleading.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper is well organized and easy to follow. The method is interesting and well designed. The experiments (ablation studies) are complete, and the results are promising. The authors also evaluated several backbone models and included some interpretability analysis, which strengthens the paper. Overall, the paper provides reasonable support for the proposed method.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal resolves my main concerns. Providing code is important for reproducibility, and I encourage the authors to release their code in the final version.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper proposes a framework for combining deformable shape and texture representations for cardiac video classification. Reviewers agree that the problem is meaningful and that incorporating motion information is important for this task. The proposed design, including cross-modal temporal attention and adaptive fusion, is considered reasonable, and the experimental results show consistent improvements.
At the same time, several concerns were raised. The evaluation is limited to a relatively simple binary classification task on a single dataset, and stronger validation on additional datasets or more complex settings would improve confidence. It is also not fully clear whether the performance gains come from the proposed fusion design itself or from the inclusion of deformation features. In addition, the method does not strictly perform joint learning, since the shape representation is extracted from a pretrained model and kept fixed.

The paper addresses a meaningful problem in cardiac video analysis and proposes a coherent framework for integrating deformable shape and texture representations. Reviewers generally agreed that the proposed cross-modal temporal attention and adaptive fusion design are technically sound and consistently improve performance across different backbones and registration models. The rebuttal clarified concerns regarding the contribution of the fusion module and the interpretation of the joint learning framework.
The author’s response addresses the reviewers’ concerns.

The paper proposes “ShapeFuse,” a novel framework for cardiac video classification that integrates deformable shape and image texture features. The core innovation lies in replacing naive feature concatenation with a Bidirectional Cross-Modal Temporal Attention mechanism and an Adaptive Gating strategy. Main concerns focus on experimental aspects, including backbone analysis, performance comparison, and ablation studies. The authors’ response explain them reasonably and clearly.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their encouraging recognition of our novel bidirectional cross-modal temporal attention mechanism, adaptive fusion strategy, and strong interpretability. The main concerns/questions are addressed below.
Experimental Evaluation on Single Dataset [M,R1]. ACDC and M&Ms are commonly used for evaluating 2DxT registration models. In contrast, disease classification from cardiac MRI datasets like ACDC typically requires full 3DxT volumetric analysis, which would require extending our framework to a 4D deformable registration setting to properly capture spatiotemporal deformation dynamics. Given that the publicly available 4D registration models for this setting remain quite limited, as well as the rebuttal phase does not permit additional experiments, we are unable to include this evaluation here. However, we’d be glad to include this in future work.
SOTA comparison and additional ablation study [M,R1]. Please allow us to clarify that our primary contribution is the fusion module, which is backbone-agnostic where any SOTA CMR feature extractor can be used as the image encoder backbones and be combined with shape features through ShapeFuse. Due to the space constraints, we could only show experiments on three image encoder backbones; notably, additional experiments with a transformer-based backbone yielded consistent performance gains across all metrics. We are happy to include these results/comparisons if MICCAI allows us to.
Regarding the ablation study, ShapeFuse’s bidirectional attention and adaptive gating are tightly coupled — the gate operates on cross-modally attended representations from BCTA, so removing one without the other collapses the design. The +Attention baseline in Tab. 1 serves this purpose by replacing bidirectional cross-modal attention with self-attention, and the consistent performance gap across all backbones directly quantifies the contribution of ShapeFuse.
Contribution of ShapeFuse to Overall Performance [M,R2]. Tab. 1 is designed to validate the contribution of each component (image, shape, and image+shape) under different fusion modules. The ‘Image/Shape’ rows show the classifier’s performance trained independently on latent image and shape features. All fusion variants receive these identical features, so performance differences among them solely reflect the contribution of the fusion design. Across all backbones, ShapeFuse consistently outperforms all other fusion alternatives, confirming that the performance gains stem from our fusion module design.
Joint Learning [M,R2]. We thank the reviewer for highlighting this ambiguity and will revise the phrasing in the final version. To clarify, “jointly learn the fusion” refers to jointly training the fusion module and classifier together — not jointly optimizing the feature extraction networks. The deformation features are extracted from a pretrained registration network, whose parameters are intentionally kept fixed throughout training, so that performance differences across fusion strategies purely reflect the fusion module’s contribution. Jointly fine-tuning all components would conflate the fusion module’s contribution with changes in the underlying feature representations.
Contextual Novelty of the Fusion Design [M,R2]. We would like to clarify that while cross-attention and gating are established components, their application to fusing latent deformable shape and image texture representations in cardiac video classification is unique. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has explicitly modeled cross-modal dependencies between these two complementary latent representations in this setting. The consistent performance gains across all image encoder backbones and two registration networks empirically validate the effectiveness of the proposed fusion design over all competing fusion strategies.
[M,R3] Thank you for the suggestion; we will bold the best values across all metric in the revised version.

title: Learning What Can Move: Patient-Specific Motion Subspaces from a Single Scan
abstract: Learning-based registration treats motion as the first citizen, yet motion is inherently \emph{relational}, requiring two time points to define, and entangles learned parameters with both the fixed and moving domains. Any change in modality, dimensionality, or acquisition protocol therefore demands specialized adaptations. We approach this differently: rather than learning motion itself, we learn the \emph{motion subspace}. Unlike motion, the subspace of plausible deformations is an \emph{intrinsic} property of anatomy, potentially inferable from a single scan. This reframing leads to an asymmetric architecture in which only the fixed image couples the network, predicting patient-specific scalar \emph{motion modes} that span the subspace, instantiating motion then reduces to estimating a small set of coefficients from various observations via a closed-form solver. A mode normalization layer resolves the signed-scale ambiguity inherent in mode–coefficient decomposition, making network integration feasible. On 4D-lung CT dataset, the learned modes approach iterative pTVReg in accuracy while the coefficient solver runs in 7.5\,ms. Without retraining, the same modes unify four observation modalities (3D image, 2D image, 2D mask, surface points), all achieving Dice above 0.9, demonstrating that patient-specific motion subspaces can be inferred from static anatomy and serve as unified modes for multi-modality motion reconstruction.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors present a method to predict the motion subspace of a given anatomy. From a dataset of 4D CT images, the method learns a set of modes to explain the motion observed in the images. This enables anatomically-constrained motion prediction from real-time, sparse observations such as 2D images or surface displacements. In the authors’ formulation, the modes are scalars and predicted once, and the coefficients are vectors optimized dynamically to fit each new observation. This contrasts with prior works that required a patient-specific 4D CT image for real-time motion estimation from sparse observations.
reviews.text_strengths:
The method predicts a reusable motion subspace rather than specific deformation instances. This regularizes the predicted motion and ensures it belongs to an anatomically plausible motion subspace.
The method simplifies real-time motion prediction down to coefficient solving, alleviating computing constraints in real-time applications and reducing risks of overfitting to unrealistic deformations to fit the observations.
The use of scalar rather than vector displacement modes brings rotational invariance to network predictions, making the method more robust to non-standard image orientations.
The mode prediction + solver optimization enables 3D motion prediction from arbitrary observations, making the method highly flexible in its potential applications.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Conditions acceptance rating:
The paper should absolutely discuss the RMSim paper (https://iopscience. iop. org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/acb484/pdf) which is extremely close conceptually. Cited from RMSim: “We present a novel 3D Seq2Seq deep learning respiratory motion simulator (RMSim) that learns from 4D-CT images and predicts future breathing phases given a static CT image. “ This is very closely related and highly relevant as prior work, even if the proposed approached, based on a subspace formulation, is genuinely different.
Major:
The main strength of the method, the plausibility of predicted deformation, is also an important weakness. The method is dependent on the availability of motion-specific data to train the subspace prediction method: if the motion to be predicted does not exist in the dataset, predictions will fail. This is particularly relevant in interventions where the anatomy is deformed by the action of the clinician, for example due to the manipulation of the anatomy by surgical tools. These types of deformations are very unlikely to be represented in the training data, and due to the formulation of the method, will fail to be accurately predicted.
The paper does not evaluate the ability of the method to predict out-of-domain deformations. It claims to decouple “what deformations are plausible (modes, predicted once) from which deformation occurs (coefficients, solved per observation)”. This is a somewhat strong affirmation: the space of plausible deformation is vastly greater than the space of deformations observed in the training data, currently restricted to breathing and potentially cardiac motion 4D CTs.
The method was only trained and evaluated on breathing motion prediction from a single dataset. The quality of the validation would have been improved by training on one dataset and evaluating on another, ideally experimentally acquired, to evaluate the robustness of the method to deviations from the breathing patterns observed at train time. It would have been further improved by evaluating its accuracy on other types of motion, such as cardiac motion.
Minor:
Linearity assumption is unexamined. The method assumes anatomical motion is always well-approximated by a low-dimensional linear subspace. This is a strong assumption that is never discussed or justified. Non-linear motion subspaces are a known alternative (see https://arxiv. org/pdf/2404.17620), and the paper does not address under which conditions linearity breaks down.
Choice of K is insufficiently justified. Only K=1 and K=2 modes are evaluated, with no sensitivity analysis on K. It is unclear how to choose K for a new anatomy or motion type.
The 2D gradient approximation lacks justification. When only a 2D slice is available, the method substitutes ∇I_fix for ∇I_mov in the Jacobian definition. The validity of this approximation is non-trivial and unexplained. A more natural formulation — restricting the problem to 2D and computing gradients directly in 2D — is not considered or compared against.
The solver and network details are in “Experiments and Results”, and should be moved to Methods section.
Abstract: “instantiating motion then reduces to estimating a small set of coefficients from various observations via a closed-form solver. “ This is unclear
Introduction: Need to explain the benefit of generating a reusable motion subspace rather than deformation instances.
Introduction: “We introduce a scalar-mode parameterization that naturally admits a closed-form coefficient solver, together with ModeNorm layer that resolves the signed-scale ambiguity in basis–coefficient decomposition” 
The signed-scale ambiguity should be briefly introduced before.
Methods: The “training” part of Fig. 1 could be made a little clearer by replacing the curved arrow with a straight arrow pointing straight down. As it is, it seems L_reg is somehow related to the solver, which it isn’t.
Nevertheless, contributions are novel and the method has great potential to enable anatomically accurate, fast registration from sparse observations
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper addresses a meaningful and underexplored problem: learning a patient-specific motion subspace from a single static scan, enabling anatomically-constrained real-time motion estimation from sparse observations without requiring a patient-specific 4D acquisition. The scalar mode prediction-based solution is original and well justified. The ModeNorm fix to sign ambiguity is clever : in this work, as opposed to traditional registration works, both the modes and coefficients vary: the modes are predicted by the network and the coefficients computed by the solver, and both parts could apply arbitrary scaling, if it were not for the ModeNorm layer.
The practical implications, real-time 3D motion estimation from 2D images or surface signals, without patient-specific 4D CT, and novelty of the method are enough to justify the “accept” recommendation, despite the insufficient validation and lack of proper sensitivity/ablation study in the paper, which should be addressed in a revision, in accordance with MICCAI’s rules.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors’ rebuttal did not fully address all reviewer concerns, notably the lack of clarification regarding the 2D gradient approximation and the motivation for the choice of K. These remain open points that should be addressed in the final version.
More importantly, the authors’ claim that the linear combination limitation is a training data issue independent of their method is not convincing. Methods from the literature trained on unsupervised, cross-patient registration tasks do not exhibit this limitation; it is a structural consequence of the proposed framework, not an artifact of the data. The authors should acknowledge this more honestly.
That said, these weaknesses do not undermine the core contribution. The method is sound and novel, the paper addresses a relevant problem, and the experimental results support the claims. The paper deserves publication, conditional on the authors revising the discussion of limitations to be more transparent about what is a method-intrinsic constraint versus a data-dependent one.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This work propose to train a network to produce subspace of motion vector fields from static images. The papers assumes all possible motions can be derived from static anatomy.
This network provides a pathway for performing downstream tasks such as 2D to 3D DVF estimation without retrainning.
reviews.text_strengths: The strength of the paper lies with its novel application of deriving DVF modes from static anatomy and applying the derived modes for various downstream tasks without requiring required model for each specific task.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The claim that all possible motion can be restricted to a low-dimensional subspace is very questionable. For example, patients with bronchus obstruction on one side of the lung will have drastically different motion from those without such obstructions. This motion difference is unlikely to be distinguishable from a single static image.
In my opinion, the quantitative comparison with baseline methods are not sufficient. For example, the base line is only established with 3D to 3D task. What about baseline comparison with other tasks?
It is true that the pipeline eliminates the need to retrain for other tasks. However, the ultimate real world clinical goal is to make registration more accurate. From the presented results, the proposed method does not outperform one of the baselines and there is lack of comprehensive information on inference speed. Again, without comprehensive baselines for other downstream tasks, the evaluation of the performance is infeasible.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Fonts on your figure 4 is too small.

The study builds on a very questionable assumption. The registration performance is not necessarily better than baselines and there is a lack of comprehensive evaluation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
My previous opinion was that the method cannot generalize to every possible motion such as bronchial obstruction. After reviewing the authors’ response, I agree this might be a limitation of the training data instead of that of the method itself. Given this and combined with the clear advantage in computational speed, I now recommend acceptance.
I still think it would be nice to demonstrate quantitative results beyond 3D to 3D but I’m not sure whether this is allowed during this stage.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This work shifts from learning motion directly to learning a patient-specific motion subspace inherent to anatomy. By predicting scalar motion modes from a single scan and solving for coefficients via closed-form methods, it enables multi-modality motion reconstruction without retraining.
The paper offers an entirely new approach to image registration by limiting the solution space by one image of the image. This approach offeres interesting applications.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper proposes a novel approach to image registration that creatively decouples the estimation of the deformation field from the two images. Instead of relying on pairwise observations alone, they first infer a patient-specific motion subspace from a single static scan, which defines what deformations are anatomically plausible for the subject. This decoupling of deformation plausibility from the registration process itself allows them to model the allowed motion subspace for just one of the images. By pre-defining this constrained subspace, they reduce the problem’s complexity and avoid the need to explore implausible deformations during registration. They then select the appropriate solution from the far fewer remaining degrees of freedom very quickly with the second image.
This approach brings big gains in speed as compared to the classical image registration approaches as thousends of parameters would be have to be optimised in classical DIR where as in thie approach only a handful needs to be optimised resulting in a large speed gain.
reviews.text_weaknesses: What I did not understand is on why is there an arrow in Figure 1 that points from the “Fixed image” to the “2.2 Closed-form solver”. This makes no sense to me as the authors claim to decouple the two images
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper offers a fresh new approach to solving the image registration problem with a creative approach that also offers speed advantages.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper introduces a novel and clinically meaningful approach for learning patient-specific motion from a single scan, enabling real-time estimation without 4D data, with a creative design such as ModeNorm. Despite its originality and practical potential, the work relies on some questionable assumptions and lacks thorough validation and analysis. With two positive and one negative rating, the AC recommends proceeding to rebuttal before making a final decision.

Although some concerns remain regarding the 2D gradient approximation, the choice of (K), and the need for a more transparent discussion of method-intrinsic versus data-dependent limitations, the core contribution is sound and novel. The paper addresses an important problem, and the experimental results demonstrate clear advantages, particularly in computational speed. Therefore, the AC recommends acceptance.
Authors have adequately addressed reviewers concerns in the rebuttal.

I thank the authors and the reviewers for this insightful rebuttal.
Authors satisfyingly addressed concerns about generalisation to new motion (data curation) and clarification of the positioning of the work with existing literature, and successfully defended their choice of baselines.
However, the authors acknowledged a few limitations, namely the lack of sensitivity analysis on K, missing extension to other out-of-domains datasets and organs.
Overall, this paper introduces a highly novel registration framework which is highly promising. The experimental section lags a bit behind, but 1) it is still reasonable, and 2) it is counter-balanced by the strong emphasis on methodological aspect. Given the very interesting framework and high novelty, I recommend this paper not only for acceptance but also for oral.

author_feedback_text:
We thank (meta-)reviewers for constructive feedbacks.
1.R2|(1)“The claim that all possible motion can be restricted to a low-dimensional subspace is very questionable”, obstruction example, (2)”This motion difference is unlikely to be distinguishable from a single static image.”
Before addressing R2’s points, we clarify some concepts: motion subspace refers to a set of a_k(x), patient-specific and predicted by the network; a specific motion D(x,t_i)=sum^K_k(a_k(x)*w_k(t_i)).
We separate two claims R2 conflates: (1)expressiveness of a low-rank subspace vs. (2)predictability of a patient-specific subspace from a static scan.
Expressiveness is not an open question for respiratory DVFs: Li et al. (2011) and follow-ups empirically validated low-dim linear subspaces on 4D-CT. Even higher-DOF regimes (CFD flow fields) use linear subspaces (POD), with larger K. Intuitively, approximating D(x,t) by sum^K_k(a_k(x)*w_k(t)), as K grows, error diminishes.
BO is thus not a counter-example to expressiveness. The last sentence conflates “motion” and “motion subspace”. We assume the reviewer refers to whether the network can predict the patient-specific subspace when such variability is rare in training. As long as BO cases exist in training, the network can learn the subspace. We acknowledge this as a training-data diversity limitation rather than model formulation. Details in p2.
2.R1|Training-set dependence and OOD
Acknowledged; we will add an explicit limitations sentence. Two conditions considered:
(i)Anatomy-conditioned variants present in clinic but rare in current training (e.g., BO in p1): a data-coverage issue rather than model limitation, addressable by curating cohorts with such phenotypes. This is common in supervised learning, not specific to our method, and data curation is a standard solution.
(ii)Tool-induced/interventional deformation (R1’s surgical example): outside our scope, which targets physiologically driven motion (respiratory, with cardiac a natural extension). Will state this explicitly.
3.R1|Benchmarks, datasets, baselines
Agreed, broader benchmarks (more datasets, regions, clinical validation) would strengthen the work. The page budget was spent framing a new problem: predicting a subspace rather than a deformation. Cross-dataset/anatomy evaluation is planned for journal extension.
4.R2|“no improvement”
We target real-time motion recovery: system latency budget (e.g., MR-Linac IGRT) is ~100 ms total, of which we target ≤10 ms for motion recovery, differing from DIR with no apples-to-apples baseline. We use pTVReg as a high-accuracy reference (3–5 min/pair, more dataset-robust than the learning baseline) to bound accuracy sacrificed under ~10 ms. NetADM beats the ResNet-18 baseline (Dice 0.921 vs 0.882) and approaches pTVReg (0.930) at ~24000× speed-up (7.5 ms vs 3–5 min).
6.Others
RMSim and Neural Modes: will cite in related work. RMSim implicitly encodes motion via 3D-ConvLSTM Seq2Seq, while we learn a linear subspace enabling closed-form solving from sparse observations at ~10 ms. Neural Modes target on computer graphics applications with elastic equilibrium(material force model), a regime distinct from ours (we model neither tissue mechanics nor excitation).
Decoupling and Fig 1 arrow: “Decoupling” is at the representation level: f_θ(I_fix)→modes uses only I_fix; the solver ingests whatever real-time observation is available (3D image, 2D slice, 2D mask, surface points), never I_mov as a network input.
2D gradient: Follows the classical Thirion-demons static-force form (small-warp linearization). The “directly 2D” alternative computes gradients on warped images and discards out-of-plane displacements; preliminary tries showed instability.
K: K=2 already approaches pTVReg (diminishing returns).
Writing/reproducibility: We will clarify the abstract on coefficient solving, move solver/network details to Methods, enlarge Fig 4 fonts, release code upon institutional approval.

title: Learning Where to Look: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Robust Micro-ultrasound Prostate Cancer Detection
abstract: Micro-ultrasound (μUS) is a new, emerging, and promising imaging modality for prostate cancer (PCa) detection, but accurate identification of suspicious tissue remains highly dependent on clinical experience, leading to substantial inter-observer variability. Machine-learning assistance can reduce this variability; however, training reliable deep models is challenging because supervision is sparse and noisy—typically limited to core-level histopathology outcomes (e.g., cancer grade and its percentage in a biopsy core) without pixel-level lesion annotations and under severe class imbalance. We introduce Prost-RL, which reframes μUS PCa detection as a spatially aware, policy-driven inference problem by learning where to look before decoding. Prost-RL integrates a lightweight reinforcement-learning policy into a foundation-model encoder–decoder to generate interpretable spatial attention maps that act as soft prompts for both cancer-likelihood heatmap prediction and image-level classification. We further propose Adaptive Policy Optimization (APO) to stabilize hybrid supervised–RL training and a noise-robust objective combining symmetric cross-entropy with negative-entropy regularization to mitigate weak-label noise and encourage sharp localization. On a cohort of 6,607 biopsy cores from 693 patients across five clinical sites, Prost-RL achieves 79.0 ± 3.5 AUROC with 64.6 ± 6.3% sensitivity at 80% specificity for core-level detection (+2.1 AUROC and +4.5 sensitivity points over the strongest baseline), and 79.3 ± 5.8 AUROC for clinically significant cancer classification. The learned policy highlights biopsy-aligned regions, providing transparent, spatially grounded evidence alongside quantitative risk predictions. Code is available at: https://github.com/DeepRCL/Prost-RL.
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers
Machine Learning -> Reinforcement Learning / Control / Decision-Making
Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning
