reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a dual-branch real-time detection framework for fine-grained laryngeal lesion stratification in Narrow-Band Imaging endoscopy. Built upon YOLO11n, the method adds an auxiliary prototypical learning branch to the standard detection head, using multi-scale feature fusion, RoIAlign, and a cosine-similarity-based prototype constraint to explicitly organize lesion representations around three clinically meaningful prototypes: SCC, LEUKO, and LR. The authors further design a two-stage training strategy consisting of a bootstrap stage with detection-only optimization followed by joint optimization of detection and prototype losses, with class prototypes updated via EMA. Experiments on a retrospective RETRO cohort and an independent prospective PROS cohort show that the approach improves macro F1 while preserving competitive detection performance, with the largest benefit observed for the difficult and underrepresented leukoplakia category.
reviews.text_strengths:
The clinical problem is important and well targeted. The paper addresses risk stratification of laryngeal lesions in NBI endoscopy rather than lesion localization alone, which is more directly aligned with real clinical decision-making.
The method is purposefully designed. Instead of simply appending another classifier, the authors use prototypical learning to explicitly structure the embedding space, with the goal of reducing confusion among morphologically similar classes and mitigating background/context bias.
The gain on the difficult LEUKO class is notable. On RETRO, the Proposed (Proto) model reaches an LEUKO F1 of 0.42, clearly above YOLO11nano (0.26) and RT-DETR (0.15); on the prospective PROS cohort, it still achieves 0.40, outperforming competing methods. This is practically meaningful for a minority and clinically challenging class.
The evaluation is relatively comprehensive. The paper includes comparisons with both CNN- and Transformer-based detectors, ablations on bootstrap epochs, backbone adaptation strategies, and the contribution of the prototype head, as well as an external prospective test set.
The framework remains reasonably efficient. The authors state that the model still has only 7.45M parameters after adding the prototype branch, supporting its potential for real-time clinical deployment.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The end-to-end evaluation is not sufficiently clear. In Table 2, Proposed (Yolo) and Proposed (Proto) are reported in separate rows, and the Proto row does not include detection metrics. This makes it unclear whether the final classification results are based on GT boxes, predicted boxes, or some post-processing pipeline. For a framework claiming joint detection and stratification, this point should be explained more explicitly.
The degree of “fine-grained” stratification is still limited. The current task uses only three classes, with all low-risk lesions grouped into a single LR category. This somewhat reduces the granularity of the task and makes the claim of fine-grained stratification slightly overstated.
The external prospective dataset is relatively small. PROS includes only 327 images from 64 patients, with a distribution heavily skewed toward SCC. While having an independent prospective cohort is a strength, the scale still limits the robustness of the conclusions.
Comparison against more direct imbalance-aware or discriminative baselines is limited. The paper mainly compares against different detector families, but it does not fully rule out whether the gain comes primarily from handling minority classes or enforcing a more discriminative embedding space, rather than from the specific prototype-head design itself. Comparisons to metric-learning, center-loss, class-balanced, or focal-style classification enhancements would strengthen the claim.
The statistical testing section could be more rigorous. The authors use image-level bootstrap and describe the comparisons as independent pairwise tests, but the models are evaluated on the same test sets. The assumptions and pairing strategy should be clarified more carefully.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I assign this paper a weak accept. The main reason is that it presents a reasonable and fairly complete framework for a clinically relevant problem, namely fine-grained laryngeal lesion stratification in NBI endoscopy, and shows reasonably consistent classification gains on both retrospective and independent prospective cohorts, especially for the difficult minority LEUKO class. The paper also includes meaningful ablations supporting the role of the bootstrap strategy and the prototype head. At the same time, the weaknesses are also clear: the end-to-end evaluation protocol is not fully transparent, the external test set is limited in size, and the ethics/statistical reporting could be strengthened. Overall, I consider the paper slightly above the acceptance threshold, but not strong enough for a confident accept.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_ethics: I recommend that the authors explicitly add an ethics approval, informed consent, or waiver statement in the manuscript to remove ambiguity regarding compliance for the patient data used.

meta_reviews.text: This paper received positive feedback from all three reviewers. The integration of prototypical learning into YOLO is novel and practical, with classification improvements especially for challenging classes. The use of a prospective testing cohort further strengthens its clinical relevance. Nonetheless, reviewers raised concerns about the lack of clarity in overfitting mitigation, how detection and classification heads integrate during inference, and limited evaluation transparency. The scalability and novelty could also be improved by including more classes and broader comparisons with alternative methods. In addition, one reviewer suggested that authors explicitly add an ethics approval regarding compliance with the patient data used.

title: Leveraging Pathology Co-occurrence for Test-Time Adaptation in Chest X-Ray Diagnosis
abstract: Medical imaging models often degrade when deployed at new clinical sites due to differences in imaging equipment, protocols, and patient populations. Test-time adaptation (TTA) addresses this by updating a pretrained model using only unlabeled target data, without access to source data. However, existing TTA methods were designed for single-label classification on natural image benchmarks, minimizing entropy uniformly across all samples without considering label dependencies. This overlooks a key property of multi-label medical imaging: pathologies do not occur independently but exhibit structured co-occurrence patterns. In this work, we propose Co-occurrence Weighted Adaptation (CoWA), which leverages disease co-occurrence patterns as a reliability signal for adaptation. CoWA estimates label co-occurrence structure from model predictions and downweights samples that deviate from expected patterns, enabling adaptation to rely more on consistent predictions while reducing the impact of noisy ones. We evaluate CoWA on chest X-ray benchmarks under domain shifts and demonstrate consistent improvements over established baselines.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper studies test-time adaptation for multi-label chest X-ray diagnosis by exploiting pathology co-occurrence patterns. The problem is important, and the proposed CoWA framework is clinically motivated: it uses an estimated co-occurrence matrix from target-domain predictions to weight samples during entropy minimization, rather than treating all labels and all samples independently. The idea is intuitive and differs from standard TTA pipelines. The empirical results are generally positive, but the performance gains are overall modest, and the current validation remains limited to chest X-ray classification.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper addresses an important and practical problem. Test-time adaptation for multi-label medical diagnosis is highly relevant, and incorporating disease dependency structure is a meaningful direction for this setting. 
2.The proposed method is simple and well motivated. Using pathology co-occurrence as a reliability signal for sample weighting is intuitive, easy to implement, and compatible with standard entropy-based TTA. 
3.The experimental section is reasonably complete. The paper compares against several established TTA baselines and includes additional analyses on co-occurrence matrix evolution, sample-weight reliability, and norm ablation.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The empirical gains are relatively limited. Although CoWA is often competitive and frequently ranks first or second, the absolute improvement over strong baselines is generally modest, which weakens the overall impact of the method. Table 1 shows that many of the gains are small. 
2.The validation scope is narrow. All experiments are conducted on chest X-ray classification, so it remains unclear whether the proposed idea would generalize to other medical imaging modalities or other multi-label diagnostic tasks. 
3.The method relies on dataset-level co-occurrence structure, which may introduce or amplify bias. The paper itself notes that co-occurrence patterns vary across datasets. In practice, such variation may reflect differences in label definitions, patient populations, or institutional case mix rather than stable disease mechanisms. Since CoWA directly estimates and uses these correlations during adaptation, it may reinforce dataset-specific associations rather than clinically robust relationships. This limitation is important and currently under-discussed.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper should expand the discussion of limitations, especially the risk that co-occurrence-based adaptation may amplify dataset-specific bias caused by annotation differences, population shift, or non-causal correlations. The authors should frame the method more cautiously as exploiting target-domain statistical dependence, rather than implying that it captures a stable clinical structure across domains. The paper would be strengthened by additional analysis showing when co-occurrence-based weighting helps and when it may fail, particularly under stronger shifts in label prevalence, population composition, or labeling criteria.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces a novel idea for unsupervised TTA. The authors argue that most TTA approaches aren’t designed for multi-class tasks. In biomedical scenarios, diseases often co-occur. Maybe that could be used to help with the adaptation part. They calculate an average co-occurrence matrix over the entire target dataset using the pretrained source model. Then they calculate the distance of each data point from this average co-occurrence matrix. The lower this distance, the higher the certainty and thus the higher the loss weight. This helps give more stable gradients for training?
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Good visualizations and well presented results.
2.Interesting analysis in Table2 of the performance of the different L-norms.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.This work seems like an importance sampling (IS) based approach for TTA applications. However, no theoretical connections or formulations were drawn against that. PRIORITIZED EXPERIENCE REPLAY https://arxiv.org/pdf/1511.05952.There are some other things as well like being careful with the distribution of the IS-weights o.w. There are some stability concerns etc, which our paper fixes in a very adhoc way via max(w_min,w_i). Maybe there are some better annealing strategies for this?
2.That leads me to another question: IS helps accelerate the convergence speed, so maybe if the authors showed us the validation curves of the classification performance on the val/test datasets over time, we might see something along the lines that other methods might be coming close to the performance of COWA but taking slightly longer. It will also be interesting to validate that an increase in the convergence speed is indeed in fact happening.
3.No ablation studies: What if we replace max(w_min,w_i) with just w_i? What happens then? 
a. Some numerical metrics or visualizations of the stability of the gradients (measured perhaps by the var(grad) over time ) vs simple L = H, L = wi*H, L = max(w_min,wi) * H would be helpful.
b. The H(.) is the shannon entropy right?
4.Otherwise, marginal improvements over AdaBN and also sometimes AdaBN beats this work. So the results aren’t even showing consistent improvements either.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The idea of the paper is indeed very novel. However, it needs a lot more theoretical and experimental validation and exploration to be good enough for MICCAI standards.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: After reading the reviews and the rebuttal, I feel that this work is promising but not yet ready for publication at this venue. The authors need to incorporate the suggested improvements into the submission for a reevaluation.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces Co-occurrence Weighted Adaptation (CoWA), a novel source-free test-time adaptation method that dynamically estimates a pathology co-occurrence matrix from target domain predictions to serve as a per-sample reliability signal for multi-label medical image classification. Unlike standard approaches that indiscriminately minimize entropy for all predictions regardless of label dependencies, CoWA downweights samples with clinically inconsistent disease combinations and assigns higher weights to structurally coherent ones. By incorporating this underlying clinical dependency structure into the adaptation process, the method improves the diagnostic robustness of medical imaging models against cross-institutional domain shifts without requiring any source data or target annotations.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The proposed question is a important yet hardly studied one, which being solved will greatly imporve the generalization ability of existing multi-label prediction models.
2.The method prevents severe performance degradation on vulnerable or low-prevalence disease classes by explicitly suppressing unreliable gradient updates that standard methods would otherwise reinforce. The overall demonstration of methods is clear and easy to follow.
3.Comprehensive evaluations across multiple chest X-ray domain shift scenarios show that CoWA consistently achieves superior or highly competitive diagnostic accuracy compared to established TTA baselines.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.It seems when adapt to the target domain the threshold hyperparameter is fixed. Although the author did ablation studies to show the effectiveness of the chosen threshold, it could be better if the author could make the threshold also adapt to the domain field.
2.When adapt to the domain field, CoWA heavily relies on the model’s initial predictions on the target domain to dynamically estimate the pathology co-occurrence matrix. If an extreme domain shift causes the pre-trained model to produce highly inaccurate initial predictions, the resulting empirical matrix will be flawed. It would be better if author can discuss the possibility of this kind of situation.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The author has identified an important problem and proposed an effective method to solve it, but there are still some concerns, as noted in the Weakness section.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Thanks authors for their detailed responses which clearly address my concern and I believe it should be accepted given its methodology novelty and good experiment results.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper introduces CoWA, a test-time adaptation framework for multi-label chest X-ray diagnosis that uses pathology co-occurrence patterns to weight samples during entropy minimization. While clinically intuitive, reviewers hold divided opinions due to limited performance gains and theoretical gaps.
-R2’s concern regarding the marginal empirical improvements, particularly instances where baselines like AdaBN outperform CoWA.
-Discuss the risk of the method reinforcing dataset-specific biases rather than capturing stable clinical structures, especially across different populations (R1).
-Connect the formulation to Importance Sampling and provide ablation studies for the weight truncation strategy to prove gradient stability (R2).
-Explain how the framework handles severe initial prediction errors where the estimated co-occurrence matrix might be fundamentally flawed (R3).

This submission proposes an intuitive test-time adaptation framework that incorporates pathology co-occurrence for multi-label medical classification, initially drawing divided reviews regarding empirical gains and theoretical grounding. In the rebuttal, the authors successfully addressed major concerns by providing concrete evidence of gradient stability, clarifying the instance-reweighting formulation, and pledging to reframe the scope to account for dataset-specific bias. Given that the majority of reviewers (2/3) found the clarifications compelling and favor acceptance, the Area Chair recommends a Weak Accept, contingent upon the authors fully integrating these post-rebuttal revisions into the final manuscript.

I recommend reject: R2 (Faculty) maintained Reject independent of rebuttal on marginal empirical gains (AdaBN sometimes outperforming CoWA) and unresolved theoretical gaps (importance-sampling connection, weight-truncation stability), and the two soft “4 — would not mind if rejected” votes from R1 (no post-rebuttal update) and R3 do not outweigh a Faculty Reject to a documented performance concern that the rebuttal could not resolve.

I agree with most reviewers that the paper highlights an important yet currently overlooked problem in test-time adaptation: diseases are co-occurring. Most reviewers find the method novel and the experiments convincing. Although the paper lacks some in-depth performance analysis and ablation studies, it would still spark meaningful discussion at MICCAI.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and AC for the valuable feedback.
[R1w1, R2w4: Performance Gains]
Avoiding severe degradation on vulnerable classes is as clinically important as maximizing mean AUROC, where CoWA’s gains concentrate. As Tab.1 shows, on Pt. under NIH→MIMIC, No-Adapt achieves 57.5 yet TENT drops to 49.1 and AdaBN to 48.3, while CoWA preserves 55.7.As R1 noted, CoWA achieves the best or second-best mean AUROC across all shifts and is the only method without a severe drop, whereas baselines exhibit large regressions relative to No-Adapt on multiple shifts (e.g., AdaBN on NIH→CheX, TENT on CheX→NIH, EATA on NIH→VinDr; Tab.1). We attribute this robustness to CoWA’s modeling of dependency-based inconsistencies during adaptation, which AdaBN cannot capture as it only updates BN statistics.
[R1w3, R3w2: Robustness and Bias]
CoWA’s reliance on target-derived signals raises two concerns: that poor initial predictions could corrupt M (R3w2), and that dataset-specific co-occurrence may reinforce biases rather than reflect stable clinical structure (R1w3). For the first: (i) threshold binarization (Eq. 1) blocks low-confidence activations from entering M; (ii) M accumulates across batches, dampening early-stage noise (Fig. 3). Empirically, NIH→MIMIC already captures this regime (Tab.1): source predictions on rare classes (e.g., Pt.) are unreliable yet CoWA achieves the highest mean AUROC. We agree with R1, and note this is intrinsic to unsupervised TTA: any target-derived signal can reinforce target-domain biases. We will reframe the contribution as exploiting target-domain dependence rather than stable clinical structure.
[R2w1: Relation to IS]
We thank R2 for the IS perspective, which sharpened our framing. CoWA shares IS’s intuition of upweighting reliable samples, but is better framed as confidence-based instance reweighting [1,2]: IS weights are likelihood ratios that make the objective an unbiased estimator under the target distribution, whereas CoWA weights are not likelihood ratios and Eq. 4 is not constructed for unbiased estimation. Their role is instead to suppress unreliable training signals, with weight magnitude reflecting per-sample reliability (Fig. 4). The functional form in Eq. 3 follows a Gibbs (maximum entropy) solution under an expected cost constraint [3], providing principled grounding rather than an arbitrary choice.
[R2w1, R2w3a: Stability]
CoWA addresses R2’s stability concern both structurally and empirically. By construction, CoWA weights are bounded in [w_min, 1] (Eq. 3, 4), precluding the heavy-tail and weight-collapse behavior of unbounded IS weights. Empirically, we measured BN-affine gradient L2-norm variance over adaptation on CheX→MIMIC under three losses, where H(·) is the (Shannon) binary entropy per class, summed over pathologies (R2w3b):
(A) L=H: 2.38e-5
(B) L=w_i·H: 1.05e-5
(C) L=max(w_min,w_i)·H: 1.02e-5
(A)’s 2.3× higher variance is consistent with TENT’s instability on rare classes (Tab.1). The near-identical variance of (B) and (C) addresses R2w3a: consistency-based reweighting accounts for most of the stabilization, while w_min serves as an early-stage safeguard before M stabilizes (Fig. 3); Fig. 4 further shows the weight distribution lies well above w_min after adaptation. More elaborate annealing strategies are left for future work.
[R2w2: Convergence]
To test R2’s hypothesis that baselines may approach CoWA with more iterations, we measured AUROC validation curves across adaptation steps. The gap widens rather than narrows: CoWA exceeds TENT at every iteration, and after both methods peak at iter 30, TENT’s post-peak AUROC declines 1.42× faster.
[Future Work]
(R1w2) As CoWA is modality-agnostic, extending it to other modalities would be a valuable next step. (R3w1) We also agree that a principled adaptive threshold for M estimation is a worthwhile direction.
Ref. [1] Kumar et al. NIPS 2010, Self-Paced [2] Ren et al. ICML 2018, Reweight [3] Jaynes, 1957, Info Theory

title: LinGuinE: Longitudinal Guidance Estimation for Volumetric Tumour Segmentation
abstract: Longitudinal volumetric tumour segmentation is critical for radiotherapy planning and response assessment, yet this problem is underexplored and most methods produce single-timepoint semantic masks, lack lesion correspondence, and offer limited radiologist control. We introduce LinGuinE (Longitudinal Guidance Estimation), a PyTorch framework that combines image registration and guided segmentation to deliver lesion-level tracking and volumetric masks across all scans in a longitudinal study from a single radiologist prompt. LinGuinE is temporally direction agnostic, requires no training on longitudinal data, and allows any registration and semi-automatic segmentation algorithm to be repurposed for the task. We evaluate various combinations of registration and segmentation algorithms within the framework. LinGuinE achieves state-of-the-art segmentation and tracking performance across four datasets with a total of 456 longitudinal studies. Tumour segmentation performance shows minimal degradation with increasing temporal separation.We conduct ablation studies to determine the impact of autoregression, pathology specific finetuning, and the use of real radiologist prompts. We release our code (https://github.com/n-e-garibli/LinGuinE) and substantial public benchmarking for longitudinal segmentation, facilitating future research.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces LinGuinE, a framework for longitudinal guided segmentation, which can be used with any combination of registration and promptable segmentation algorithms.
reviews.text_strengths:
The authors generalize the idea of earlier works like Hering et. al. and LesionLocator, building a plug and play framework, which works with any combination of registration and guided segmentation algorithm to track a tumor through the whole image sequence. By separating the temporal component in the form of simple registration, it enables training on single-timepoint data alone.
The authors introduce an initial boosting method, which can make the model more resilient to slight registration errors.
The authors use 4 datasets with multiple pathologies, showing the generalizability of the proposed framework.
The authors demonstrate the capabilities of LinGuinE using the state-of-the-art in registration and promptable registration methods.
The authors show additional improvements in performance by in-distribution finetuning of the promptable segmentation method used in the framework.
The authors show the robustness to elapsed time between scans for their LinGuinE framework, compared to the baseline methods.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
As also noted by the authors, ED is suboptimal as a metric, when many lesions don’t have associated predictions. Therefore, it would have been interesting to see something like a detection rate as an additional metric to Dice.
Minor: The authors claim that their framework is “the first temporally direction agnostic framework, allowing radiologists to provide prompts at any timepoint, facilitating retrospective analysis”. While this is true by design, e. g. LesionLocator can also be applied per timepoint in a non-autoregressive fashion.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The proposed framework shows strong performance, outperforming all evaluated baselines. While the paper doesn’t introduce major methodological novelty, the provided framework and insights are highly relevant in the context of tracking and longitudinal segmentation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: A Longitudinal segmentation method to track tumour growth and treatment response based on interactive segmentation approaches.
reviews.text_strengths:
Proposes an innovative solution to a relevant clinical problem
Validates on multiple datasets
Compares the performance of multiple backbones and compares the proposed approach to relevant baselines.
Achieves state-of-the-art results.
Performs relevant ablation studies
reviews.text_weaknesses: A significant limitation, as noted by the authors, is the potential for disappearing lesions. In a fully automated context, this scenario could lead the model to segment an unrelated structure, resulting in an inaccurate response assessment. However, this issue is a candidate for mitigation in future research.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Interesting paper to read, creative idea, and innovative approach to a very relevant clinical problem, making use of novel interactive segmentation methods.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses longitudinal tumor segmentation and tracking from minimal radiologist input. The main contribution is LinGuinE, a flexible framework that combines image registration, prompt propagation, and guided volumetric segmentation to produce lesion-level segmentations across all scans in a longitudinal study from a single source-timepoint prompt. A key aspect of the work is that the framework is temporally direction agnostic, does not require training on longitudinal data, and can reuse existing registration and promptable segmentation algorithms. In addition to the framework itself, the paper provides a relatively broad benchmark across four datasets and analyzes practical aspects such as temporal degradation, autoregression, boosting, and the use of real radiologist prompts.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper addresses a clinically meaningful and underexplored problem. Longitudinal lesion tracking with segmentation is more relevant to treatment monitoring and response assessment than standard single-timepoint semantic segmentation.
The proposed workflow is practical. Allowing a radiologist to provide guidance at one timepoint and propagate it across a longitudinal study is a reasonable and potentially useful clinical interaction model.
Even though the method is conceptually simple, the results are strong, and the benchmarking itself is a valuable contribution to this task
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The algorithmic novelty is moderate. At its core, the method is a combination of existing ingredients, image registration, propagated prompts, guided segmentation, and optional boosting. The main contribution is therefore more of a practical framework and benchmarking effort than a fundamentally new algorithm.
While temporal direction agnosticism is useful in practice, it is partly a natural property of a registration-based prompt propagation pipeline, so I would not view it as a major conceptual novelty.
A key practical dependency of the framework is the quality of the underlying registration. If registration is inaccurate, the propagated prompt may fall outside the target lesion or even near a different lesion, which can lead the guided segmentation stage to fail or segment the wrong object. The paper partially acknowledges this issue and introduces boosting as a mitigation, but it does not provide a systematic analysis of failure cases or robustness to registration inaccuracies. Given that real longitudinal scans often involve anatomical changes and imperfect alignment, this deserves more explicit discussion.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The main factors behind my score are the strong practical value of the problem setting, the clinically meaningful workflow, and the breadth of the empirical evaluation. I think the paper makes a useful contribution by addressing longitudinal lesion tracking and segmentation from minimal radiologist input, which is more relevant to real follow-up analysis than standard single-timepoint segmentation
My main reservations are that the algorithmic novelty is moderate, since the framework mainly combines existing components, and that the method depends on registration quality without a deeper robustness analysis.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text: The reviewers have a clear view on the paper as it provides a low-input solution for tracking lesions over time an area that has a clear clinical benefit. Moreover the presentation of the work and the evaluation and later discussion seem solid and were celebrated by the reviewers. While I am giving the paper a provisional accept following the reviewer’s recommendations, I do think it is more of an integration work with a good evaluation. I strongly recommend the authors to comment on the criticisms of reviewer 6.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all the reviewers for their feedback and careful consideration of our manuscript. We are grateful for the positive remarks and appreciate the thoughtful criticisms raised.
To R1 and R6: We agree that the key value of our contribution lies in the practicality and clinical relevance of the framework, along with the benchmarking efforts and new insights into an under-explored problem, rather than major algorithmic novelty. At the same time, we believe there is novelty in repurposing algorithms trained on single time-point data for longitudinal use, the boosting mechanism, and the plug-and-play nature of LinGuinE, which distinguishes it from prior work.
To R6: Regarding reproducibility, we would like to kindly point out that most of our results on UniToChest, 4DCBCT, and APLCT should be reproducible by the community since the data and many algorithms are public. We also pledged to release our code package and our ground truth masks for UniToChest (https://github.com/n-e-garibli/LinGuinE). We had not included links to the assets at the time of review to preserve anonymity.
To R6: Regarding the concern on the dependence of our framework on underlying registration quality. We considered this issue during development and explored robustness to out-of-tumour point propagation, including experiments with rigid registration. However, we prioritised including other analyses in the manuscript, such as experiments on time-direction agnosticism, the use of real radiologist prompts, and temporal degradation, because we felt these were both more novel and more clinically relevant. We also hope that the effect of registration quality is partially reflected in Table 1, where performance on the lung cancer datasets improves when LGI is used instead of UGI. More broadly, many modern guided segmentation methods are trained such that exact guidance location is not critical, and some closed-set algorithms can perform well as long as the guidance point is sufficiently close to the target object. In our experience, this means that even relatively simple registration can be effective in the LinGuinE setting, making the choice of segmentation algorithm more important than the choice of registration. Whilst we would like to support that claim empirically, unfortunately our understanding is that editing the manuscript to include additional results is not permitted.

title: LiSAD: A Label-Efficient Implicit Model with Spatially Adaptive Directional Total Variation for Spatial Transcriptomics
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) provides unprecedented opportunities to understand tissue structures. Spatial domain identification serves as a core task to partition tissue regions. Current methods achieve initial success on such task, however struggle to identify accurate domain boundaries and rarely attempts supervised paradigm.  To address these challenges, we propose a Label-efficient implicit model with Spatially Adaptive Directional total variation (LiSAD).  LiSAD adopts implicit neural representations (INRs) with a hypergraph learning framework to transform discrete ST data into continuous representations while modeling high-order topological relationships for spots.  We propose a spatially adaptive directional total variation (SADTV) regularization for accurate boundary identification. Furthermore, we propose a label-efficient optimization strategy that leverages minimal expert prior knowledge to learn refined biological representations.  Experimental results on multiple datasets show that LiSAD outperforms current methods by 3-7% in adjusted rand index (ARI), validating its effectiveness. We propose a practical label-efficient paradigm for ST analysis. LiSAD achieves a superior trade-off between annotation economy and diagnostic accuracy, enabling accurate domain identification with minimal expert priors. Code is available at https://github.com/BioMedIA-repo/LiSAD.
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers
Applications -> Outcome Prediction / Prognosis / Longitudinal Modeling
Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper addresses the spatial domain identification in spatial transcriptomics (ST) by transforming ST data into a continuous representation using implicit neural representation (INR) and a hypergraph learning framework with a label-efficient (supervised) scheme. It also uses a total variation-based regularizer for boundary identification. 
The paper identifies 1.ST data being sampled on a discrete spatial grid, 2.non-sharp transitions between domains in a tissue sample, 3.failing to use at least a limited number of pathologist annotated spots as the deficiencies in existing graph-based ST domain segmentations. This paper used INR to transit from discreet ST to continuous, a spatially adaptive directional total variation (SADTV) regularizer to preserve boundaries, and some pathologist labeled spots.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper is well-written, and almost all the aspects a reader anticipates have been addressed.
The ARI and NMI results with the datasets DLPFC, HBC, and STARmap have significantly improved.
The ablation shows the contribution of individual interventions.
Visualizations in Fig. 2 show domain segmentations much closer to the ground truth.
Fig. 3 shows the contribution of SADTV to resolve thin boundaries.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The three interventions—neural representation of ST data, a directional total variation regularizer, and some pathologist labeled spots—themselves are not novel.
Does Lipschitz continuity result from the INR itself or is it dependent on the underlying spatial transcriptomics dataset? How essential is this for the overall performance? Also, can SADTV be applied on the reconstructed gene expressions?
As I noticed, M = 30 spots are annotated by pathologists. How should this number depend on the number of domains to be segmented? How are the spots selected for annotation? I have noticed Fig. 2b which shows saturated performance beyond M = 5.
None of the four papers against which the results are compared report numerical results. Therefore, I presume that the results in Table 1 are authors’ replications. This hinders conforming that the results are actually superior. A comparison with papers that report ARI, e. g. , Luo et. al. , STINR: Deciphering Spatial Transcriptomics via Implicit Neural Representation, CVPR 2025, is important.
How would the performance be affected if the a. spatially varying, and b. directional nature in total variation loss formulation are removed?
The first addition in Table 2 is pathologist annotated labels (label efficient). I am curious to know the improvements achievable by INR and SADTV without pathologist annotated labels.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
I SADTV is the no. of nearest neighbors equal to 2k or K?
Consider using a different symbol for the annotation dataset as D has already been used for no. of gene expressions. 
Consider citing the papers in the tables too for easy reference. 
Please give descriptive caption for tables.

Considering the strong results and the justifications, I selected “Weak Accept.” However, I still have concerns regarding novelty and the independent verification of results. I would be willing to upgrade my rating if these concerns are adequately addressed.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal answers almost all the questions. Other reviewers too seem to perceive this work as a valuable contribution.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors introduce a label-efficient implicit model for accurate boundary identification in spatial transcriptomics. The method integrates hypergraph learning and a variation regularization strategy to model topological relationships, while the overall framework is trained under a supervised paradigm.
reviews.text_strengths:
(1) The paper proposes a simple yet effective framework with INR-enhanced hypergraph representation learning to capture high-order topological structures within the tissue microenvironment, and a SADTV regularization strategy to ensures the smoothness within the spatial domain.
(2) The incorporation of supervised learning enables efficient utilization of limited expert annotations and demonstrates clear performance improvements.
(3) The paper is well written and easy to follow, with clear model diagrams and visualizations.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(1) The paper basically aggregates some commonly used components, such as hypergraph learning and supervised objectives, and therefore exhibits limited methodological novelty.
(2) There appears to be an issue in Equation (5): the numerator in the exponent of the denominator should be “pm”.
(3) In Equation (6), the meaning of the “i” preceding ϕi,j is unclear and requires clarification.
(4) The data split strategy is not clearly described; a detailed explanation of how the training and test sets are splitted is needed to improve reproducibility.
(5) The LiSAD (Full) model shows only moderate improvement compared with Label-efficient + INR baseline, and the ablation study is conducted on a single cohort, raising concerns about the effectiveness and generalizability of the SADTV regularization.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a technically sound framework with clear performance improvements. However, the methodological novelty is limited, and several details (e.g., equations and data split strategy) require clarification. In addition, the experimental validation is somewhat limited, particularly in terms of generalizability. Overall, both the methodological novelty and the experimental validation require further clarification to fully substantiate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Thank you for the authors’ feedback. My major concerns have been addressed, and I am inclined to accept this manuscript.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This article introduces a label-efficient implicit model for spatial domain identification in spatial transcriptomics (ST). It integrates implicit neural representation and hypergraph neural network to convert discrete ST data into continuous spatial fields. Modeling high-order cellular topological relationships overcomes the limitations of discrete sampling and fixed pairwise graphs. It introduces a label efficient supervision framework. Using minimal expert annotations to guide representation learning greatly reduces annotation costs while improving accuracy, making it suitable for clinical pathology workflows.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.It combines INR for continuous spatial modeling with hypergraphs for capturing higher-order cell communities. This design better captures subtle spatial changes and complex tissue structures.
2.The proposed SADTV enhances the true domain boundaries while suppressing noise, improving the problem of inaccurate boundaries in conventional total variation and clustering methods.
3.This framework uses extremely sparse expert labels that are consistent with the real pathology annotation workflow. 
4.This paper is well-organized, with intuitive illustrations, clear mathematical formulas, and thorough explanations of motivation, methods, and results.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.SADTV relies on pre-defined K-neighbors, which may still fail in highly irregular or low-quality tissue slices, similar to the fixed neighbor GNN model.
2.The core innovation of this article is not well expressed. On the contrary, they seem to be a loose combination of incremental technology modules, including implicit neural representation (INR), hypergraph modeling, total variation (TV) regularization, and label efficient learning. Further refinement is needed to express innovative points.
3.Some mathematical symbols and expressions lack clear definitions when they first appear, which reduces readability.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The overall evaluation of this article is based on technological novelty, clinical relevance, contribution novelty, limitations, and writing quality.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The author’s explanation and description of the innovation are insufficiently in-depth and fundamental, and fail to reveal the internal mechanisms among the combined modules from fundamental principles. Meanwhile, the illustration of the mechanism of SADTV, one of the core innovations, is rather weak, with limited analysis of its advantages and essential principles. 
Therefore, based on the current statements in the paper and explanations provided in the rebuttal, the overall contributions of the proposed method remain unclear.

meta_reviews.text:
The reviewers generally liked the clear writing style, the promising empirical performance, and the potential clinical relevance of exploiting the fact that only a limited set of expert annotations is required to identify the spatial domains in a clinical dataset. The main concerns, though, are (1) limited methodological novelty, as the authors are just combining pieces of existing works and it is not clear what their unified new contribution is; (2) the limited ablation results which should have made SADTV (and thus the paper) more convincing; and the potential generalizability of SADTV to other similar clinical problems; (3) label-selection and data-splitting procedures are not clear to us and should be clarified to better reflect the label-efficient setting in the paper; (4) the comparison results are not reported fairly by the baseline models. For instance, the comparison between our results and the reported ones of baseline methods is actually comparing with our reproduction of those baseline results, instead of directly comparing to the reported ones of the baseline. Rebuttal should discuss these questions and address those issues with sufficient explanations, justification, and evidences.

After rebuttal, R1 and R2 support acceptance, finding that most concerns were addressed, while R3 remains concerned that the innovation and SADTV mechanism are not sufficiently explained. After careful review, the concerns could not block this paper in my opinion. I vote for acceptance.

The rebuttal addresses several methodological and protocol concerns, including the annotation selection strategy, the absence of a conventional train/test split, baseline reproduction, and additional SADTV ablations across datasets. Although the method remains an integration of existing components and the novelty is moderate, the clarified label-efficient clinical setting and post-rebuttal reviewer balance support acceptance as a borderline/weak accept.

The paper presents a clinically relevant label-efficient framework for spatial transcriptomics domain identification, with consistently strong empirical performance and clear gains over both unsupervised and label-efficient baselines. The rebuttal adequately clarified most concerns regarding label selection, dataset splitting, baseline reproduction, and SADTV ablations; although novelty and mechanistic explanation remain somewhat limited, the overall contribution and evidence support acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and address the concerns below.
1.Novelty of LiSAD (R1Q1, R2Q1, R3Q2)
Application-wise, LiSAD novelly shifts spatial domain identification from unsupervised algorithms to a clinically interactive paradigm guided by expert annotations, which is more suitable for clinical scenarios. Technically, LiSAD introduces INR and hypergraph learning to address discrete sampling and multicellular modeling, respectively, offering a continuous and higher-order topological representation scheme for ST. To address the challenge of boundary identification, LiSAD further designs SADTV as a regularizer tailored for ST data, providing a new formulation for boundary-sensitive modeling in ST. Thus, we believe LiSAD demonstrates sufficient novelty and is not a simple assembly of existing components.
2.SADTV Effectiveness and Ablation Study (R1Q5, R2Q5)
As stated in Sec. 3.3, SADTV shows moderate overall gains because it mainly targets boundary regions, which occupy only a small portion of the tissue section. Fig. 3 shows improved boundary recognition. Moreover, removing the adaptive weighting term and the directional term leads to ARI drops of 0.01 and 0.04 on DLPFC, respectively, validating the proposed design. SADTV also shows consistent effectiveness across datasets: removing it decreases ARI by 0.05 on HBC and 0.03 on STARmap, suggesting its potential generalizability to similar clinical problems with ambiguous tissue boundaries.
3.Strategy for selecting expert-annotated spots (R1Q3)
Based on clinical practice, expert labels are selected from high confidence spots inside domains rather than ambiguous boundary regions. To simulate this process, we compute each spot’s KNN neighborhood label purity as q_i = (1/K) * sum_{p_j ∈ N_i} 1(y_j = y_i) for each spot p_i, and randomly select M annotated spots from high purity candidates in each domain. Only these selected labels are used for optimization.
4.Dataset split (R2Q4)
As stated in Sec. 2.3, only expert annotated spots are used for optimization, while all remaining labels are used only for whole slice evaluation. This follows the common spatial domain identification protocol, rather than a conventional train/test split.
5.Fairness of baseline reproduction and comparison with STINR (R1Q4)
Table 1 baselines are reproduced with official code and recommended settings under a unified environment. Our reproduced results are in the same range as those reported in the STAIG supplement, supporting the reliability of reproduction and the fairness of the comparison. For reference, STINR reports an ARI of 0.63 on DLPFC, while LiSAD achieves 0.76.LiSAD still clearly outperforms STINR, confirming its effectiveness.
6.Target of SADTV and Neighborhood Design (R1Q2, R3Q1)
We clarify that SADTV is applied to the reconstructed gene expression, as shown in Eq. 6.For predefined neighborhoods, SADTV uses 2K-nearest neighbors to enlarge the local receptive field and adaptive weights to adjust neighbor contributions, mitigating fixed-neighborhood rigidity.
7.Performance without expert annotations (R1Q6)
Without expert priors, the label-free variant HAE+INR+SADTV with embedding clustering achieves an ARI of 0.63, higher than STAIG’s 0.61 in Table 1, indicating that the proposed components still improve representation quality without expert supervision.
8.Source and role of Lipschitz continuity in INR (R1Q2)
Lipschitz continuity arises from INR-based modeling, as supported by [10]. It smooths and stabilizes the reconstructed data, providing a noise-robust basis for SADTV. The ablation results about INR in Table 2 verify its effectiveness.
9.Definition of M and total annotation number M×S (R1Q3)
There may be a misunderstanding about the definition of M. As stated in Sec. 2.3, S is the number of domains, and M is the number of labeled spots per domain. Thus, the total annotation number is M×S, linear in the number of domains.
10.Writing Issues
We will correct all issues in notation.

title: LLM-Bootstrapped Targeted Finding Guidance for Factual MLLM-based Medical Report Generation
abstract: The automatic generation of medical reports utilizing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) frequently encounters challenges related to factual instability, which may manifest as the omission of findings or the incorporation of inaccurate information, thereby constraining their applicability in clinical settings. Current methodologies typically produce reports based directly on image features, which inherently lack a definitive factual basis. In response to this limitation, we introduce Fact-Flow, an innovative framework that separates the process of visual fact identification from the generation of reports. This is achieved by initially predicting clinical findings from the image, which subsequently directs the MLLM to produce a report that is factually precise. A pivotal advancement of our approach is a pipeline that leverages a Large Language Model (LLM) to autonomously create a dataset of labeled medical findings, effectively eliminating the need for expensive manual annotation. Extensive experimental evaluations conducted on two disease-focused medical datasets validate the efficacy of our method, demonstrating improved tuberculosis clinical efficacy and most NLG metrics over state-of-the-art models. The code is available at https://github.com/UCPRER/Fact-Flow.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes Fact-Flow, a framework for reducing factual errors in medical report generation. The key idea is to first extract clinical findings from medical images and then generate reports conditioned on these structured intermediate representations. In addition, the authors leverage large language models (LLMs) to automatically generate labeled clinical finding data, aiming to reduce the cost of manual annotation. Experimental results demonstrate improved factual correctness compared to existing methods while maintaining high linguistic quality.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper tackles an important problem in medical report generation, namely factual errors (hallucinations). Introducing clinical findings as an explicit intermediate representation is intuitive and aligns well with real-world clinical workflows, effectively decoupling visual understanding from language generation. 
2.The use of LLMs to automatically construct a label taxonomy is a practical and meaningful contribution, addressing the high cost of annotation in medical datasets. 
3.The method shows consistent performance improvements across multiple MLLMs and datasets, providing reasonable evidence for its generalizability and effectiveness.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.While the MLLM is prompted with both vision tokens and classification labels, the paper does not provide a comparison with a setup where only prompts (without vision tokens) are used. This makes it difficult to isolate the contribution of visual features to report generation performance. 
2.The discussion of related work is somewhat limited. Although the paper covers the general progression from CNN-RNN to Transformer and MLLM-based approaches, it lacks a comprehensive review of closely related work on fact-guided or structured report generation, which is directly relevant to the proposed method. 
3.The constructed label set is not sufficiently described in terms of concrete examples and granularity. Without a clear understanding of how concepts are organized (e. g. , handling of similar findings, distinction between general findings and severity levels), it is difficult to assess the clinical validity and appropriateness of the taxonomy. 
4.The proposed framework consists of multiple components (label taxonomy construction, multi-label classification, and fact-guided generation), but the current experiments do not sufficiently disentangle their individual contributions. As a result, it is unclear which component is primarily responsible for the observed performance gains. 
5.Although comparisons with an oracle (ground-truth labels) are provided, there is limited analysis of the gap between predicted and ground-truth labels. This makes it difficult to identify bottlenecks in the pipeline. Furthermore, the interpretation of evaluation metrics, including clinical efficacy, is not sufficiently explained, making it harder to judge the practical clinical significance of the improvements.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
To strengthen the paper and clarify the effectiveness of the proposed method, the following points should be addressed:
1.Include an ablation study evaluating report generation without vision tokens (i. e. , using only fact-flow prompts) to better isolate the contribution of visual inputs. 
Expand the related work section to more clearly position the method with respect to fact-guided and structured report generation approaches, improving clarity on novelty and contribution. 
2.Provide a more detailed description of the constructed label taxonomy, including representative examples, granularity, and design principles (e. g. , handling of diseases, findings, anatomical locations, and severity levels), to enhance understanding of its clinical validity and reproducibility. 
3.Conduct a more thorough analysis of the individual contributions of each component (label generation, classification model, and fact-guided generation) to clarify which parts drive performance improvements. 
4.Further analyze the gap between predicted labels and oracle (ground-truth) labels, discussing its impact on final report quality and identifying potential bottlenecks. 
5.Provide clearer explanations of evaluation metrics such as clinical efficacy, including their definitions and clinical implications, to better contextualize the reported improvements.

The paper addresses an important and practical problem with a well-motivated framework and demonstrates consistent empirical improvements. However, several aspects—particularly component-wise analysis, taxonomy transparency, and evaluation clarity—require further clarification to fully establish the contribution and clinical significance of the work.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal adequately addressed several of my concerns, particularly regarding the role of visual information, pseudo-label interpretation, and limitations of the sequential pipeline design. While some concerns regarding methodological novelty and component-level analysis remain, I believe the work is technically sound and suitable for acceptance.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper proposes Fact-Flow, a three-stage plug-and-play framework that improves factual accuracy in MLLM-based medical report generation by explicitly decoupling visual recognition from language generation.
Stage 1 uses an LLM (GPT-5-mini) to automatically bootstrap a multi-label clinical finding taxonomy from unstructured training reports, thereby eliminating expensive manual annotation via batch extraction, iterative hierarchical merging, and frequency-based filtering.
Stage 2 trains a multi-label image classifier (DINOv3-ConvNeXt) with logit adjustment for long-tail class imbalance, predicting finding presence/absence from medical images.
Stage 3 fine-tunes an MLLM (Qwen2.5-VL, MedGemma, or LLaVA-Med via LoRA) conditioned on the predicted label set serialised as a structured natural-language prompt, grounding generation in explicitly identified clinical facts.
Evaluated on a public TB chest X-ray dataset and a private multimodal Chinese ophthalmology dataset, Fact-Flow demonstrates consistent improvements in RadFact clinical efficacy and NLG metrics over directly fine-tuned MLLM baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
S1: Clinically well-motivated problem framing. Factual hallucination and finding omission are the primary barriers to clinical deployment of MLLM-based reporting. The cognitive decoupling hypothesis (recognition is not narration) is principled and supported by the literature.
S2: Novel automated annotation pipeline. The LLM-bootstrapped taxonomy construction (batch extraction, hierarchical synonym merging, frequency filtering) eliminates the need for manual labelling in new clinical domains. As per my understanding, no prior MRG method uses an LLM to generate the multi-label training supervision from existing reports. This is the paper’s most original contribution.
S3: Architecture-agnostic, plug-and-play design. The framework is validated across three architecturally distinct MLLMs (Qwen2.5-VL 7B, MedGemma 4B, LLaVA-Med 7B), consistently improving all three. This breadth strengthens the generalisability claim substantially.
S4: Strong diagnostic of baseline failure. The mode-collapse pathology of vanilla MLLMs: Qwen2.5-VL with precision=1.0 and recall=0.0145, LLaVA-Med with all-zero clinical efficacy is clearly and quantitatively demonstrated, making a compelling case for factual grounding.
S5: Use of RadFact for clinical efficacy evaluation. Adopting LLM-based entailment scoring rather than n-gram metrics for the TB task is methodologically appropriate and ahead of much of the field in MRG evaluation practice.
S6: Oracle ablation (Table 4). The predicted vs. ground-truth label oracle experiment cleanly identifies label quality as the pipeline bottleneck, guiding future research priorities.
I also appreciate the authors for providing code in an anonymised format for reproducibility.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
W1: Logical contradiction: long-tail filtering (Stage 1) vs. long-tail optimisation (Stage 2). Frequency-based filtering at θ=15 preemptively removes rare findings from the taxonomy. Logit adjustment in Stage 2 then attempts to re-balance rare labels, but it cannot recover classes that were deleted in Stage 1.The paper simultaneously claims to protect rare labels (Stage 2) and eliminates them as a design choice (Stage 1). I would request the authors to address this logical inconsistency in the pipeline’s stated goals.
W2: No clinical efficacy metric for the larger ophthalmology dataset. The ophthalmology dataset is the larger and more complex of the two. Reporting only NLG metrics (BLEU, CIDEr) for a Chinese-language clinical dataset is insufficient. Could the same GPT-5-mini used in Stage 1 for Chinese report annotation could, in principle, be repurposed for a RadFact-style clinical entailment evaluation? The absence of any factual correctness metric for the primary multimodal dataset is an evaluation gap that could be addressed.
W3: TB dataset seems small for reliable claims without statistical testing. 561 training / 160 test images. No confidence intervals, no significance tests, no multi-seed variance. At this scale, single-image shifts move accuracy by ~0.6%. Wilcoxon tests or bootstrapped confidence intervals are the minimum expected standard.
W4: No sensitivity analysis on key hyperparameters (θ, b, κ, τ). The entire Stage 1 taxonomy depends on θ=15 (yielding 7 labels for TB, 42 for ophthalmology). No experiment varies θ or examines how the downstream clinical efficacy changes with taxonomy size. This is a missing ablation.
W5: Classifier error propagation not analysed. Macro-F1 of 0.52 on TB means substantial per-class errors. These are injected into Stage 3 via a declarative, authoritative prompt (“The image shows the following findings…”), giving the MLLM no mechanism to express uncertainty or reject erroneous inputs. The large gap between predicted-label (F1=0.28) and oracle-label (F1=0.44) performance is reported but not decomposed. Requesting the authors to clarify which finding categories are most commonly misclassified, and how do those errors manifest in generated reports.
W6: Stage 1 validation sample of n=50 is statistically inadequate. 50 reports represent 2.7% of the ophthalmology training set. Perfect 100/100 coverage and matching accuracy on 50 samples from a 1,854-case dataset with 42 labels, including many rare ones, cannot be reliably extrapolated. Inter-rater agreement (Cohen’s Kappa) between the LLM and a second clinical reviewer is not reported.
W7: Please cite the GPTs models used.
Once again, I congratulate the authors for their hard work in addressing an important challenge in Medical LLMs.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper addresses an important and clinically relevant problem of factual inaccuracies in MLLM-based medical report generation. The work proposes a well-motivated three-stage framework that decouples visual recognition from language generation. The idea of using LLM-bootstrapped multi-label supervision is interesting and potentially impactful, particularly as a scalable alternative to manual annotation. The method is clearly presented and shows consistent improvements across multiple MLLMs and datasets, with appropriate use of clinical evaluation (RadFact) on the TB task. The oracle ablation further provides useful insight into the role of label quality.
However, several weaknesses limit confidence in the results and must be addressed. There is a conceptual tension between Stage 1 filtering (removing rare labels) and Stage 2 long-tail optimisation that needs clarification. The evaluation is incomplete: the larger ophthalmology dataset lacks any clinical efficacy metric, and the TB dataset is small with no statistical significance testing or variance analysis. Key design choices (e.g., threshold θ and other hyperparameters) are not studied, and error propagation from the classifier to the generator is not analysed. Additionally, Stage 1 validation is based on only 50 samples, which is insufficient to support strong claims about annotation quality. Finally, the LLM used for label bootstrapping is not properly specified or cited, raising reproducibility concerns.
The paper has promising ideas and solid initial results, but the above issues must be addressed. Hence, my recommendation is to invite the authors to rebuttal to justify stronger acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
After reading the rebuttal, I maintain a weak accept. The authors provide reasonable and transparent clarifications for several major concerns. In particular, their explanation of frequency filtering versus logit adjustment resolves the apparent contradiction: filtering is used as a minimum-support/noise-control step, while logit adjustment only mitigates imbalance among retained labels. They also adequately address the visual-token concern by pointing to the label-only versus image+label ablation, where visual information provides additional gains. I also appreciate that they agree to rename LLM-generated annotations as pseudo-labels and to treat the oracle rows as upper bounds within the bootstrapped label space rather than true expert ground truth.
Important limitations remain. The lack of confidence intervals, statistical testing, or multi-seed variance still limits confidence in the reported gains, especially on the small TB test set. The larger ophthalmology dataset still lacks a factual/clinical efficacy metric, so factual correctness claims should be restricted to the TB dataset. Error propagation from the classifier to the generator is acknowledged but not decomposed by category, and the system has no uncertainty/rejection mechanism for incorrect predicted labels. Stage-1 validation remains limited at the report level, and no sensitivity analysis is provided for key hyperparameters.
Hence, the rebuttal satisfactorily clarifies the main conceptual issues and appropriately softens several claims, but it does not fully resolve the empirical robustness concerns. I therefore recommend acceptance, but only as a borderline accept rather than a strong accept.
I once again would like to congratulate the authors for their efforts to help grow the MICCAI community with relevant contribution towards improving the factual reliability of MLLM-based medical report generation.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper is well written, clearly structured, and easy to follow. It addresses a well-defined problem and situates itself appropriately within the literature on medical report generation. The proposed decomposition into visual recognition and language generation is well motivated and represents an interesting and potentially impactful contribution.
The design choices are generally sound, and the experimental evaluation covers the key components of the framework, providing a reasonably comprehensive assessment of its effectiveness.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
My main concern is the absence of any statistical significance analysis supporting the claim that the proposed method outperforms prior work. Reporting higher metric values alone is not sufficient to establish superiority, especially when improvements are relatively small.
This is particularly important for metrics such as BLEU-4, ROUGE-L, CIDEr, and METEOR, where absolute differences (e.g., +0.2) are difficult to interpret in terms of practical significance.
I strongly recommend performing a paired bootstrap resampling test to compare the proposed method against baselines. This would allow the authors to:
Report confidence intervals for each metric
Assess whether improvements are statistically significant
Strengthen the claims made in Table 1
Including such analysis would substantially improve the rigor of the evaluation.
Then, the paper refers to the LLM-generated label vectors (the Y annotations) as “ground truth.” This terminology is somewhat misleading.
Typically, “ground truth” implies human-verified, highly reliable annotations, whereas in this case the labels are automatically generated and therefore inherently noisy. A more appropriate term would be “pseudo-labels” or “weak labels.”
This is not merely a terminological issue as it also affects how results should be interpreted. For instance, in Table 4, the oracle model using both labels and images outperforms the one using labels alone. While this result is valid, it raises an important question: would performance further improve if the labels were truly accurate (e.g., expert-annotated)? Clarifying this distinction would lead to a more precise discussion of the results.
Also, as this is a machine learning paper, it is important to clearly specify how data is used at each stage of the pipeline.
While it appears that all components are trained using only the training split, this is not stated explicitly. The authors should clarify:
Which data is used to derive the taxonomy
Which data is used to train the classifier
Which data is used to fine-tune the multimodal model
Making this explicit would help rule out any potential data leakage or bias and improve reproducibility.
Finally, the paper would benefit from a brief discussion of some potential limitations of the proposed framework. In particular:
The reliance on LLMs both for label generation (Stage 1) and, indirectly, for evaluation (e.g., via RadFact) may introduce a degree of circularity, where the system is partially aligned with the same type of model used for supervision and assessment.
The multi-stage nature of the pipeline (label extraction -> classification -> report generation) may lead to error propagation, where inaccuracies in intermediate predictions affect the final output.
These aspects do not undermine the validity of the approach, but acknowledging and discussing them would provide a more complete picture of the method and its practical implications.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This is a solid and well-presented paper with a promising idea and encouraging empirical results. However, the evaluation would benefit from additional rigor, particularly through statistical significance analysis and clearer reporting of experimental details.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors acknowledged the concern regarding the use of the term “significant” and proposed replacing it with “consistently.” I agree that this change is more appropriate in the absence of formal statistical testing.
However, my main concern still remains. Such results are a core part of the paper, and therefore I believe this aspect should be supported more rigorously.
Importantly, I do not view this as requiring a fundamentally new experiment. Statistical analyses such as paired bootstrap resampling are typically performed on already available model predictions over the test set and therefore generally do not require retraining models or collecting additional data. For this reason, I believe it would be reasonable for the authors to include such analysis in the final version of the paper, even if it cannot be fully incorporated during rebuttal.
Regardless of whether this is formally considered a “new experiment” or not, I consider this analysis necessary to properly support the paper’s main empirical claim. Without stronger evidence that the reported improvements are robust and meaningful, I do not believe the current evaluation is sufficient for acceptance.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper proposes a three-stage framework designed to improve the factual groundedness of Multimodal Large Language Models in radiology. It utilizes a “bootstrapping” approach where an LLM automatically extracts a structured label taxonomy and pseudo-labels from existing free-text reports, bypassing the need for manual annotation. A dedicated classifier is then trained to predict these findings from images, providing a declarative “factual stream” that prompts the MLLM to generate reports aligned with specific clinical findings.
While the paper presents good contributions, its recommendation for acceptance is contingent upon the authors clarifying the following points during the rebuttal phase:
1.The pipeline preemptively filters out rare findings in stage 1, effectively deleting them from the taxonomy. However, Stage 2 later attempts “long-tail optimization” via logit adjustment. As reviewers noted, the model cannot optimize for classes it has already discarded, undermining the claim that the framework protects rare clinical findings. Clarify the contradiction between frequency-based filtering and long-tail optimization.
2.The TB dataset is extremely small (160 test images), and the paper lacks confidence intervals, significance tests (e.g., Wilcoxon or paired bootstrap), or multi-seed variance reporting. Without these, the marginal gains in BLEU or CIDEr scores cannot be distinguished from random noise.
3.The framework is highly susceptible to cascading errors. Since the MLLM is given an authoritative prompt (“The image shows the following findings…”), it has no mechanism to reject or question incorrect labels from the Stage 2 classifier. The significant performance gap between “predicted-label” and “oracle-label” setups highlights this bottleneck, yet the paper lacks a detailed analysis of which finding categories are failing most frequently. Reclassify “ground truth”, and discuss the impact of label noise on the final MLLM output.
4.The “ground truth” labels are actually LLM-generated pseudo-labels. Validating this extraction process on only n=50 samples (less than 3% of the dataset) is statistically inadequate to prove the reliability of a 42-label taxonomy. Furthermore, using LLMs for both supervision (Stage 1) and evaluation (RadFact) introduces a risk of circularity that is not addressed.
5.The paper treats several key hyperparameters as fixed without sensitivity analysis. It is unclear how the size of the taxonomy or the aggressiveness of the logit adjustment impacts clinical efficacy, making it difficult to assess the framework’s robustness across different medical domains.

The authors have addressed the reviewers’ comments well. Two reviewers acknowledged the significance of the work. Therefore acceptance of the paper is concluded. It is strongly recommended to include statistical test results in the final version.

The paper is proposing using automated ground truth labeling for a finding classifier followed by a language model to generate text containing those findings. The evaluation of such generated text is also through mostly lexically-based metrics suitable for evaluation. While one can understand the benefits of automation in annotation, it cannot be taken seriously unless there is a formal comparison with ground truthed datasets when they do exist. Besides, LLM currently mix multiple findings into single concepts, cannot easily respect laterality and location constraints, etc. so the resulting report produced is likely to mismatch ground truth report on such fine-grained aspects of what is a finding and its description. The BLEU, ROUGe and other lexical scores will continue to score high. Since the Radgraph F1 is low (0.3) this indicates that any clinical significance may still be low by this method.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for recognizing Fact-Flow’s motivation, automated annotation pipeline, and gains across MLLMs/datasets.
[R2W1: filtering vs. long-tail optimization] We agree the wording was unclear. Filtering and logit adjustment address different problems. Filtering is a minimum-support/noise-control step: labels in <θ reports are too weak for reliable pseudo-label supervision or stable MLC training. Logit adjustment is applied only within the retained taxonomy to mitigate imbalance among supported labels. We do not recover discarded labels, and will revise “protect rare findings” to “improve retained low-frequency findings.”
[R3/R2W3: statistical reliability] We agree CIs, paired bootstrap tests, or multi-seed variance would strengthen evaluation. Since rebuttal rules disallow new results, we will avoid statistical claims and change “significant” to “consistent.” Submitted TB results show clinical-F1 gains for all MLLMs: Qwen2.5-VL 0.0286→0.2831, MedGemma 0.2266→0.3055, and LLaVA-Med 0→0.2016.Ophthalmology results are limited to NLG metrics, where Fact-Flow improves most metrics.
[R1Q1: visual tokens] Table 4 includes Label Only (Pred), which uses predicted labels without image tokens. Adding images improves clinical F1 from 0.2115 to 0.2831; with oracle labels, from 0.3750 to 0.4421.Thus, visual evidence and factual prompts are complementary.
[R1Q4/R1Q5/R2W5/R3: components, metrics, and error propagation] Because Fact-Flow is a sequential pipeline, removing an upstream stage makes downstream stages undefined. We therefore combine intrinsic validation with end-to-end ablations. Table 5 evaluates Stage-1 taxonomy quality and Stage-2 MLC performance; Table 4 identifies Stage-2 label quality as the main bottleneck: oracle labels raise Image+Label clinical F1 from 0.2831 to 0.4421.We cannot add per-category decomposition in rebuttal, but will clarify failure modes: false positives may induce unsupported findings, false negatives may cause omissions, and coarse labels may reduce laterality/location/severity specificity.
