The current system has no uncertainty/rejection mechanism for incorrect Stage-2 labels. To clarify the metric interpretation, RadFact precision/recall reflect unsupported generated and omitted reference entities, respectively, and F1 balances both.
[R3: pseudo-label terminology] We agree “ground truth” is imprecise. We will rename LLM-generated annotations as “pseudo-labels.” The Table 4 oracle rows are upper bounds within the bootstrapped label space, not expert-verified ground truth.
[R2W6/R3: Stage-1 validation and circularity] The n=50 report-level check is a sanity check of report-to-label matching, not proof of noiseless supervision. It is complemented by full-taxonomy ophthalmologist validation: 80% valid/decidable, 15% context-dependent, 5% overly generic, and 0% invalid/pseudo-concepts. We will avoid overclaiming reliability. RadFact does not use our taxonomy and is not a closed loop over our labels, but is still LLM-based, so we also report NLG metrics, and we will discuss this limitation.
[R2W2: ophthalmology factual evaluation] We agree a validated clinical-efficacy metric for Chinese ophthalmology reports would strengthen the work. Building a RadFact-style evaluator would require a new evaluator/experiment; we will restrict factual-efficacy claims to TB.
[R2W4/R1Q2/R1Q3/R2W7/R3: robustness and reproducibility] b and κ are context-budget parameters, θ controls minimum support, and τ=1 follows logit-adjustment practice; all were fixed before test evaluation. Submitted experiments cover different taxonomy sizes (7 TB vs. 42 ophthalmology labels), but not a full sensitivity study, which we will state as a limitation. We will also add taxonomy examples/design principles, position fact-guided/structured MRG, specify/cite LLMs, and clarify data usage: taxonomy/classifier/MLLM training use only training data; validation is for model selection; test only for final evaluation.

title: LLM-Steered Clinical Knowledge Discovery for CVD Outcome Modeling
abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) modeling has become highly accurate, yet most models remain “black boxes” that prioritize predictive scores over reliable and reusable clinical knowledge. We propose Evidence-Grounded Learning (EGL), which repeatedly tests candidate variable sets under a fixed evaluation budget and records auditable evidence about which factors and pairwise relationships are consistently supported. EGL–LLM adds an interpretable large language model (LLM) control plane that uses a semantic agenda to decide what to test next, while keeping the evidence definitions and budget unchanged. On the COPDGene cohort, EGL shows reliable convergence of core evidence and recovers clinically plausible dominant factors and cohort-relevant interaction patterns. Semantic steering broadens the exploration path while preserving stable dominant factors and redirecting evidence acquisition toward alternative interaction neighborhoods, supporting evidence-grounded discovery that yields auditable cohort-level insights. Code is available at https://github.com/liangyuxuan1/EGL.
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers
Special Topic -> AI for Population Health, Public Health & Epidemiology

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper addresses the problem of explainable knowledge discovery in cardiovascular disease (CVD) modeling, moving beyond conventional black-box prediction toward clinically reusable insights. The main contributions are as follows,
1.The authors propose an EGL framework that reformulates clinical modeling as a process of evidence accumulation rather than single-model optimization. It constructs a graph-structured representation of knowledge, where nodes and edges encode feature importance and interactions derived from repeated empirical validation. 
2.The method models feature subset distributions using an Ising-based formulation and performs optimization via Gibbs sampling combined with REINFORCE, enabling structured exploration of high-order feature combinations. 
3.A paired probing strategy is introduced to quantify both individual feature contributions (∆f) and pairwise interaction effects (Γ_uv) through a difference-in-differences scheme, resulting in an auditable evidence ledger. 
4.The framework incorporates a large language model (LLM) as a semantic controller to guide feature subset exploration under a constrained budget. Through structured prompts (e. g. , must_include, prefer_exclude, frontier_edges), the LLM aims to improve the efficiency of interaction discovery.
reviews.text_strengths:
Major Strengths
1.The paper shifts the focus from predictive performance to reusable clinical knowledge discovery, aligning well with current demands for interpretability and reliability in medical AI. 
2.The proposed method integrates feature subset search, statistical validation (paired probing), reinforcement learning, and graph-based representation into a unified pipeline, demonstrating strong internal logical consistency. 
3.Unlike traditional feature importance methods that focus on marginal effects, the work quantifies interaction effects via a difference-in-differences formulation, offering a more expressive and informative representation of feature relationships.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Major Weaknesses
1.Experimental results suggest that the LLM primarily alters the search trajectory without significantly improving the final discovered features. In some cases, it even slows convergence. Moreover, the paper lacks thorough ablation studies (e. g. , different prompts, alternative LLMs, or removal of semantic guidance) to justify its inclusion. 
2.The evaluation is restricted to a single dataset (COPDGene), with no cross-dataset or cross-population validation, limiting confidence in the generalizability of the proposed approach. 
3.The paper does not include comprehensive comparisons with established feature selection and knowledge discovery methods (e. g. , LASSO, Boruta, SHAP-based selection, or causal discovery approaches), weakening the empirical support for its claimed advantages. 
4.Several key design choices are insufficiently motivated, including the use of the Ising model for feature subset modeling, the adoption of REINFORCE instead of more stable alternatives, and the specific design of the LLM agenda and model selection. 
5.The method involves extensive subset sampling, K-fold evaluation, and paired probing, leading to substantial computational cost. However, the paper does not provide a detailed analysis of efficiency or scalability. 
6.The method section is dense, with heavy notation and limited intuitive explanation. Important components such as the reward design and evidence ledger are not sufficiently clarified, affecting accessibility. 
7.There are concerns regarding reference formatting and overall writing redundancy, which detract from the paper’s presentation quality.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper addresses an important and timely problem—moving from black-box prediction toward interpretable and reusable clinical knowledge discovery in CVD modeling. The proposed Evidence-Grounded Learning (EGL) framework is conceptually novel, particularly in its formulation of knowledge as an evidence accumulation process and its integration of feature subset search, statistical probing, reinforcement learning, and graph-based representation. The explicit modeling of feature interactions via paired probing is also a meaningful contribution beyond standard feature attribution methods.
However, several limitations prevent a stronger recommendation. The empirical validation is limited to a single dataset, and comparisons with established feature selection or causal discovery baselines are insufficient. The contribution of the LLM module is not fully convincing, as it mainly alters the search trajectory without clear gains in final outcomes. In addition, some design choices lack sufficient justification, and the overall method introduces notable computational complexity.
Despite these weaknesses, the paper presents a novel perspective with potential clinical impact, and its core framework could inspire future work on interpretable knowledge discovery. Therefore, I recommend a weak accept.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper introduces a novel framework for clinical knowledge discovery in cardiovascular disease (CVD) modeling by combining Evidence-Grounded Learning (EGL) with LLM-driven semantic control (EGL–LLM). The key contributions are: 
EGL: A method that learns a distribution over feature subsets to identify reproducible node and edge effects (marginal and interaction evidence) via an Ising-form policy and paired probing. 
EGL–LLM: An extension that integrates a large language model (LLM) to generate interpretable, semantically guided agendas (e.g.,
must_include
,
frontier_edges
) for subset sampling and probing, prioritizing clinically meaningful exploration. 
Auditable Evidence Ledger: A graph-based ledger that accumulates reproducible evidence (node/edge effects) through repeated cross-validation, enabling transparent and reusable clinical insights.
reviews.text_strengths:
Novel Integration of LLMs in Clinical Discovery.
EGL–LLM is the first to use an LLM for semantic steering of feature exploration in CVD modeling. The LLM generates agendas based on real-time evidence (e.g., uncertainty, stability) rather than purely statistical criteria, addressing the “black-box” problem in predictive models.
Structured Methodology for Interaction Discovery
The Ising-form distribution over feature subsets, combined with counterfactual probing (e.g., comparing subsets with/without a feature), provides a principled way to test marginal and interaction effects.
Empirical Validation of Clinical Plausibility 
Both EGL and EGL–LLM recover clinically plausible dominant factors (e.g., Agatston score, hypercholesterolemia) and interactions (e.g., Agatston score with comorbidities). 
Negative interactions (sub-additive effects) highlight redundancy in overlapping CAC-related markers, aligning with known clinical mechanisms
Efficiency in Interaction Evidence Consolidation 
EGL–LLM achieves faster convergence of interaction evidence in later iterations, demonstrating the value of semantic steering in prioritizing meaningful neighborhoods.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Limited Generalizability:
The framework is evaluated only on the COPDGene cohort (smokers/COPD patients). No analysis is provided for non-COPD populations or other diseases, limiting the applicability of the findings.
No comparisons are made to existing feature selection/interaction discovery methods (e.g., SHAP, Bayesian networks), making it unclear whether EGL–LLM offers unique advantages.
Ambiguity in Clinical Plausibility:
While factors like Agatston score are labeled as “clinically plausible,” the paper lacks references to prior studies or statistical validation of these associations in COPDGene. 
The LLM’s role in avoiding domain-specific biases is not addressed; there is no evidence that generated agendas align with validated clinical knowledge (e.g., clinician review).
Methodological Limitations
Fixed Evaluation Budget: The identical budget for EGL and EGL–LLM ensures fair comparison but may not reflect real-world scenarios where resources vary. 
Reward Function Design: The scalar reward R(S) combines confirmation and acquisition terms, but the weighting of AUC/AuPRC in the metric summary m(.) is not explicitly defined, leaving room for arbitrary tuning.
CT Pipeline Sensitivity: The CT-derived biomarkers are processed via a specific pipeline, but no comparison is made to alternative methods, risking overfit to this pipeline.
Risk of Missing Data Bias: 
Clinical variables are filtered by a 70% missingness threshold, but the paper does not address how missing data in the remaining 30% might bias the evidence ledger.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The current evaluation is limited to the COPDGene cohort, which makes it difficult to assess how well the proposed framework would generalize to other populations, datasets, or disease settings.
Several discovered factors and interactions are described as clinically plausible, but this plausibility is not clearly validated against prior literature, external evidence, or clinician review.
The manuscript would benefit from a clearer discussion of the LLM component, particularly regarding possible bias inherited from pretraining data and whether any domain-specific tuning, adaptation, or validation of the generated agendas was performed.
The paper does not compare EGL–LLM with existing feature selection or interaction discovery methods, which makes it difficult to evaluate the specific added value of the proposed approach.
It would also be helpful to clarify whether the absence of external validation and baseline comparisons is due to scope limitations or is left for future work.

The paper introduces a novel framework (EGL–LLM) that addresses critical gaps in clinical knowledge discovery for CVD modeling. The empirical results are promising, and the evidence ledger concept is innovative. 
The lack of external validation, clinical plausibility checks, and methodological comparisons limits the confidence in the framework’s broad utility. However, the work provides a strong foundation for future research and has the potential to advance interpretable CVD risk modeling.

reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have satisfactorily addressed my comments and questions.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper proposes an evidence-grounded learning (EGL) framework for clinical knowledge discovery in cardiovascular disease (CVD) outcome modeling. Instead of focusing on a single predictive model, the paper aims to identify reproducible and interpretable feature level and interaction level evidence by learning a distribution over feature subsets.
The framework combines an Ising-form probabilistic sampling policy with a paired probing strategy to estimate marginal and interaction effects, which are accumulated in an evidence ledger. A key contribution is the integration of a large language model (LLM) as a semantic control plane that guides subset sampling and probe selection through structured agendas, with the final goal of improving exploration efficiency and clinical plausibility of discovered relationships in CVD modelling.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) Interesting and timely research direction: The paper shifts the focus from pure predictive performance to clinical knowledge discovery, which is highly relevant for medical AI where interpretability and reproducibility are critical, minimizing the black box label associated with AI-driven diagnosis in medicine.
2) Novel integration of LLMs for semantic guidance: The use of an LLM as a control mechanism to guide feature exploration based on clinical semantics is a creative idea. Rather than using LLMs for prediction, the work leverages them to evaluate and steer the discovery of clinically meaningful feature subsets and interactions.
3) Effort toward interpretability and transparency: The concept of an evidence ledger that accumulates marginal and interaction effects provides a more interpretable alternative to black-box models, potentially helping mitigate the black-box nature of standard ML approaches.
4) Methodological coherence: The framework (sampling, probing, evidence accumulation, and control) is logically structured and consistent, even if complex.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) Limited theoretical grounding of the LLM control component: While the idea of semantic steering is interesting, the role of the LLM remains heuristic. There is no formal objective or theoretical justification explaining why or how the LLM-guided agenda improves convergence or guarantees better discovery of clinically relevant interactions.
2) Insufficient analysis of the LLM contribution: The paper would benefit from deeper analysis or ablation of the LLM component. For example, isolating the effects of agenda shaping versus probe prioritization, or comparing against simpler heuristic strategies, would strengthen the claims.
3) Clarity issues in method description: The paper is conceptually dense and sometimes difficult to follow, especially in the description of the sampling policy, reward formulation, and interaction between EGL and the LLM control plane. Several components (e.g., “semantic agenda”, “control paths”) are introduced at a high level without sufficient intuitive explanation.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
This is an interesting and promising direction toward bridging machine learning and clinical knowledge discovery. The idea of combining probabilistic exploration with LLM-based semantic guidance is compelling and could inspire future work.
To further strengthen the contribution, the authors are encouraged to improve the clarity of the methodological description, and to provide a more rigorous analysis of the role and impact of the LLM component. In particular, clearer justification and more detailed evaluation of the semantic control mechanism would significantly enhance the paper.

The paper offers an interesting and relevant research direction with the focus on evidence-grounded clinical knowledge discovery rather than predictive modeling. Moreover, the introduction of the LLM as a semantic control mechanism is interesting and demonstrates good results in the exploration of feature interaction.
However, the research has some limitations in terms of the absence of theoretical foundations and analysis of the LLM component mentioned in the paper , which is the core of the research. Moreover, the clarity of the methodology can be improved in the paper.
Overall, the conference paper is above the acceptance threshold in terms of originality and potential impact.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The rebuttal clarified several important aspects of the proposed framework, particularly the intended role of the LLM component as a semantic scheduler rather than a direct predictive or optimization module. The authors provided a clearer explanation of how the LLM influences exploration of interaction neighborhoods while leaving the evidence estimation process unchanged.
The response also clarified the rationale behind the Ising-form distribution, Gibbs sampling, and REINFORCE-style optimization, which improved the overall interpretability of the framework.
While concerns regarding the lack of strong theoretical grounding and limited experimental isolation of the LLM contribution remain partially unresolved, the rebuttal sufficiently addressed the main conceptual misunderstandings and strengthened the overall coherence of the work.
Overall, I maintain my positive assessment of the paper. The work presents an interesting and timely direction for interpretable and evidence-grounded clinical knowledge discovery, with meaningful potential impact for medical AI.

meta_reviews.text:
Although three positive scores, several critical concerns have been raised by all the reviewers about the limited ablation studies, the lack of cross-dataset validation, insufficient comparison, and insufficient justification. The authors are invited to submit a rebuttal to carefully respond and clarify all the concerns raised by the reviewers.

This paper was initially invited for rebuttal following the primary review period, where reviewers raised several concerns. After carefully evaluating the authors’ rebuttal, the reviewers’ revised feedback, and re-examining the paper, I conclude that the authors have effectively addressed the key concerns raised, and the work now meets MICCAI’s publication standards.

The work was rated positively by the three reviewers, recognizing the novelty and the contribution of the work. The possiblity of address technical concerns in the rebuttal was taken and appreciated by 1+ reviewer(s).

Although there are initial concerns regarding limited ablation, cross-dataset validation, and comparison to baselines, authors have adequately addressed reviewers’ concerns in their rebuttal. R2 and R3 now recommend acceptance, acknowledging the novelty and potential impact of the work. The rebuttal clarified the role of the LLM as a semantic scheduler, justified key design choices, and explained the scope of the current study regarding dataset limitations. While the paper would benefit from further quantitative validation, it already presents a valuable contribution to interpretable clinical knowledge discovery. Hence, AC recommends acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for recognizing the novelty of evidence-grounded clinical knowledge discovery. Reviewers raised several related comments regarding the role of LLM, comparison with existing methods, cross-dataset validation, and the justification of key design choices. We therefore provide a unified response organized around these shared themes. 
1.Role of LLM. Our proposed Evidence-Grounded Learning (EGL) follows numerical scores and can over-test locally good but clinically redundant regions. LLM in our enhanced EGL-LLM serves as a semantic scheduler to explore clinically meaningful features and consolidate interaction evidence. For example, vanilla EGL may stick to interaction between one strong node (like Agaston score) and others, but LLM can explore edges between other variables. Thus, LLM only suggests what features to test, while EGL still verifies them. As shown in Fig.2a, EGL quickly settles on the main nodes, while EGL-LLM keeps small substitutions around it, which helps avoid repeatedly testing the same locally strong variables and keeps the search open to nearby clinically related alternatives. The wider MDS footprint in Fig.2c shows expanded exploration without reducing edge acquisition (Fig.2b); identical top nodes confirm stable individual-variable effects (Fig.2d). The main difference between EGL and EGL-LLM is in the interaction set (Fig.2e), which is the intended effect: semantic scheduling redirects tests toward different neighborhoods of interaction.
2.Comparison with other methods. We agree that LASSO, Boruta, SHAP-based selection, Bayesian networks, and causal inference methods are important. However, their objectives and outputs are not the same as those of EGL. Feature selection methods mainly return selected or ranked predictive variables, while knowledge discovery methods often estimate model-specific interactions, dependencies, or causal structures. EGL instead evaluates the reproducibility of marginal and pairwise evidence through repeated matched subset comparisons and outputs a stable evidence graph. Thus, a fair comparison would require a unified protocol to translate different outputs into comparable node- and edge-level evidence and to assess stability and biological plausibility consistently. We will clarify this limitation, construct fair baselines and perform a comparative study in the future.
3.Cross-dataset validation. COPDGene is a strong primary testbed rather than a narrow single-site dataset: it is a large multi-site cohort and combines CT-derived cardiac/CAC phenotypes with risk factors, comorbidities, medications, and CVD labels. Its scale, site diversity, and multimodal coverage provide a meaningful setting for evaluating stable evidence discovery. We agree that external validation across multiple cohorts would further strengthen the findings, but such validation requires careful harmonization of imaging pipelines, clinical variables, and outcome definitions. We therefore regard this as an important direction for future work beyond the scope of the current study.
4.Justification of key design choices. The Ising-form distribution models correlated feature subsets in binary states (sampled vs not sampled), allowing candidate variables to be sampled jointly when interactions exist. Gibbs sampling was used as a standard sampler for Ising-type distributions. We used a REINFORCE-style algorithm because the search involves stochastic sampling, making it infeasible to backpropagate gradients through the full sampling–evaluation process. The reward captures two types of evidence: the marginal gain from adding an individual variable and the excess joint gain from adding a pair of variables beyond their separate contributions. Practical hyperparameters, including the missing-rate filter, reward weights, and the magnitude of the LLM-induced bias, were tuned empirically but omitted due to space limits.

title: Localization-Grounded Supervision: Revisiting Vanilla SFT of Large Vision-Language Models for Medical Image Analysis
abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) achieve strong performance on general-domain tasks. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is commonly used for domain adaptation. However, unlike traditional pretrain-finetune paradigms, the benefits of large-scale pretraining do not reliably transfer to LVLMs in medical image analysis. Using the proposed DePass-VL framework, we quantitatively analyze the failure of LVLMs. Together with attention-based qualitative analysis, we find that LVLMs struggle to effectively focus on task-relevant regions, indicating a lack of fine-grained vision-language semantic alignment. Although pretrained LVLMs exhibit strong 2D spatial alignment, this capability is not effectively activated during SFT. To address this gap, we propose Localization-Grounded Supervision (LGS), which introduces explicit localization signals to accelerate semantic alignment and improve both performance and interpretability. For 3D medical imaging tasks, pretrained LVLMs lack intrinsic 3D spatial alignment due to limited volumetric exposure. We therefore incorporate 3D anatomical localization data through multi-task learning to jointly build spatial and semantic alignment in 3D space. Experiments across anatomical regions, imaging modalities, model architectures, and parameter scales demonstrate that LGS is a simple yet effective paradigm for LVLM adaptation in medical image analysis. The code is available at: https://github.com/MSIIP/LGS
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper studies why vanilla supervised fine-tuning of LVLMs often fails to fully transfer pretrained capabilities to medical image analysis, and proposes Localization-Grounded Supervision (LGS), which incorporates explicit localization signals to improve spatial grounding, semantic alignment, and downstream performance in both 2D and 3D medical imaging tasks.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper addresses an important question for medical LVLM adaptation, namely why vanilla SFT often does not fully translate pretrained capabilities into downstream medical performance. 
2.The proposed method is simple and easy to integrate, and the overall motivation is clear. 
3.The paper includes qualitative and quantitative analyses, including attention visualization and DePass-VL, to support its central claim about insufficient semantic alignment under vanilla SFT. 
4.Experiments cover both 2D diagnosis and 3D report generation, as well as multiple architectures and parameter scales.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The proposed method is conceptually simple, and the methodological novelty is limited. The core idea is to augment the supervision target with localization signals, and extend this to 3D through an additional localization task with multi-task learning. While practical, this is more a supervision design than a substantially new modeling contribution. 
2.Some of the reported gains, especially on the 2D diagnosis tasks, are extremely large. For example, the improvement on CrossMoDA2021 is surprisingly large for such a lightweight change, which raises concerns about benchmark difficulty, possible shortcut signals, or whether the vanilla SFT baseline is sufficiently strong. 
3.The 2D diagnosis benchmarks are derived from segmentation datasets by treating slices with lesion masks as positive and slices without masks as negative, with a balanced 1:1 setting. This construction is convenient, but it may oversimplify the task and may not fully reflect realistic fine-grained medical diagnosis scenarios. 
4.The paper makes broad claims about the limitations of vanilla SFT and attributes them mainly to insufficient semantic alignment. Although the attention analysis and DePass-VL results are suggestive, the current experiments may not be sufficient to support such general conclusions across medical LVLM settings.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper studies an important problem in medical LVLM adaptation and proposes a simple localization-grounded supervision strategy to improve spatial grounding during SFT. The motivation is clear, and I appreciate the effort to combine analysis with experiments across both 2D and 3D settings. While the method is conceptually simple and some of the reported gains raise questions about benchmark difficulty, I still find the overall message meaningful and the empirical results promising. Overall, I view the paper as slightly above the acceptance threshold.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
After reading the rebuttal, I would keep my recommendation as Accept. The authors provided useful clarifications on several of my main concerns. In particular, they clarified that the CrossMoDA2021 experiment is a derived 2D slice-level binary lesion-presence classification task rather than the original 3D segmentation challenge, and that vanilla SFT and LGS are compared under the same split, training setup, and prompt setting. They also clarified the LUNA16 dataset construction, where positive samples are selected from the middle slice of the nodule mask and negative samples are selected from adjacent slices outside the mask boundary, which partially alleviates my concern about overly coarse shortcut signals.
The rebuttal also improves the methodological clarity of LGS. The authors clarify that LGS does not introduce a new detection head or regression loss, but simply changes the autoregressive target sequence from answer-only prediction to answer plus textual localization coordinates. This makes the method’s simplicity and practical value clearer. I also appreciate that the authors acknowledge the need to reposition the contribution relative to prior grounded medical VLMs, moderate the broad claims about vanilla SFT, and present DePass-VL mainly as a region-level application/adaptation of DePass rather than an entirely new attribution method.
That said, some limitations remain. The method is still conceptually simple, the novelty is moderate, and several important experimental details, including split sizes, patient-level split protocol, variance across seeds, and more complete comparisons with related grounded medical VLM work, still need to be clearly included in the final version. Overall, however, the rebuttal addresses my main concerns sufficiently, and I continue to view the paper as a useful and practically meaningful contribution slightly above the acceptance threshold.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper makes two related claims. First, through attention visualization and a VLM-adapted version of DePass (called DePass-VL), the authors argue that vanilla supervised fine-tuning of large vision-language models on medical tasks fails to produce strong fine-grained vision-language semantic alignment because attention is diffuse and the ratio of contribution from task-relevant image regions to non-relevant ones is close to 1.Second, they propose Localization-Grounded Supervision (LGS), in which the model is trained to predict bounding-box coordinates alongside the answer, to exploit the pretrained 2D spatial grounding of LVLMs. For 3D tasks, where pretrained LVLMs lack volumetric grounding, an auxiliary 3D anatomical localization task is added via multi-task learning. Experiments cover 2D disease diagnosis on LUNA16 and CrossMoDA2021, 3D report generation on RadGenome-Chest CT, and scaling across 2B/4B/8B variants of Qwen3-VL and InternVL3.5.
reviews.text_strengths:
The central empirical observation that vanilla SFT on small-lesion medical tasks produces diffuse attention and doesn’t push the LVLM to attend to the lesion, is an interesting and useful finding. Also quantifying it with a region-level attribution score is a nice contribution.
The idea of attaching bounding-box outputs to the answer to push grounding during SFT is simple and the kind of thing that’s easy for others to adopt. I like simple interventions, and the paper presents this one cleanly.
The scaling robustness in Figure 5 that shows the effect across two architecture families and three model sizes is a good presentation of the paper’s contribution, and the consistency of the gains across scales is a useful piece of evidence.
The attention visualization pairs in Figure 2 are informative. The diffuse-vs-concentrated contrast is visually persuasive, and the accompanying DePass-VL contribution ratio in Figure 3 implements what the pictures suggest.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Direct prior art on grounded medical report generation is not cited. MAIRA-2 (Bannur et al., “MAIRA-2: Grounded Radiology Report Generation”, Microsoft Research 2024) does essentially the same thing the paper proposes: train an LVLM to predict bounding boxes interleaved with report text as tokenized outputs, using standard cross-entropy on the combined sequence. No special grounding loss; no regression head; grounding is handled autoregressively. VividMed extends this with anatomical segmentation grounding. RadVLM (Deperrois et al. 2025) similarly includes grounding with bounding-box supervision as an instruction type. MedGround frames the “image–text–box triplet” as the key to closing the cognitive-perceptual gap. None of these are cited. The “localization coordinates as a complementary output format” is not a new idea in medical LVLMs. It has a two-year history. The paper’s contribution needs to be repositioned relative to that literature: is the insight that it works with standard Qwen3-VL/InternVL3.5 out of the box without custom detection heads (that is a reasonable, if narrower, contribution), or is it the attention analysis that motivates the choice? Reframing the work as such would be more novel.
The CrossMoDA2021 result is implausibly high. Table 1 reports Qwen3-VL (LGS) at ACC=0.9844 / F1=0.9846 on CrossMoDA2021.CrossMoDA2021 is a cross-modality domain adaptation challenge (ceT1 to hrT2) for vestibular schwannoma and cochlea segmentation; it is not easy. The paper converts it to 2D slice classification by presence of segmentation mask. A jump from 0.5938 (vanilla SFT) to 0.9844 with the same backbone and the only difference being that bounding-box coordinates are now in the output is not a small effect. It’s 40 accuracy points on an allegedly balanced 1:1 positive/negative split. The obvious hypotheses are (i) the test split shares patients with the training split (no patient-level split is mentioned), allowing anatomical shortcut learning; (ii) the test set is small and fortuitously easy; (iii) the slice-level “positive = slice has a mask” task is largely solvable by looking at the anatomy visible in the slice, and the bounding-box supervision effectively teaches the model “output a box whenever the relevant anatomy is on screen.” None of these are ruled out by the text. Please provide: cohort sizes, train/val/test split protocol (especially patient-level), class balance per split, and variances.
The LUNA16 benchmark construction is nonstandard and underspecified. LUNA16 is a nodule-detection challenge (888 scans, LIDC-IDRI); the paper converts it to 2D slice classification. Again, no split protocol, no patient-level separation is noted, no dataset size, no discussion of how slice-level labels are derived (a slice can contain a nodule partially or have a nodule a few slices away so how are borderline slices handled?). These details matter because the whole argument rests on Table 1’s numbers.
DePass-VL is a thin extension. The paper presents DePass-VL as a “regional contribution analysis framework tailored for LVLMs” and one of its two quantitative contributions. DePass-VL partitions input tokens into three groups (task-relevant image regions, non-relevant image regions, other) and runs the standard DePass decomposition. Given a bounding box, doing this is straightforward as it’s an application of DePass, not a methodological extension of it. I would tone down the “we propose DePass-VL” claim to at most, “we apply DePass to LVLMs under a region-level partition.”
The attention analysis conflates two different things. Section 2.1 focuses on self-attention weights from answer tokens to image tokens. But in modern decoder-only LVLMs, the signal that propagates to the output logit is not the attention weight alone rather it’s the attention-weighted value vectors run through downstream MLPs and residual streams. DePass itself exists precisely because attention weights are not faithful attributions. The paper acknowledges this at the start of Section 2.2 (“attention-based analysis captures interactions within MHSA but does not account for other components such as the MLP”), which is correct but then the narrative continues to lean on the attention visualisation in Figure 2 as the primary qualitative evidence, and Section 4.5 re-emphasises it. I would recommend making DePass-VL the main evidence and the attention maps the illustrative companion, not the other way round.
Table 1 reports point estimates. Figures 4 and 5 likewise. With the kind of tiny derived datasets being used (slices from LUNA16 / CrossMoDA2021), seed-to-seed variance on VLM SFT can be substantial. Please report at least three seeds and include standard deviations; without them the 4-5 accuracy point gains are not convincingly separated from noise, and the 40-point CrossMoDA jump, while too large to be noise, still wants verification that it isn’t a single-seed artefact.
The “RL-based methods don’t replace SFT” claim is over-strong from the evidence. The paper runs GRPO on both datasets with apparently one configuration and reports it underperforming SFT. Fine, but GRPO notoriously needs careful reward design and base-model initialisation. Concluding that “RL-based methods such as GRPO do not currently replace SFT as a practical training paradigm for LVLMs in medical image analysis” from two datapoints with a single hyperparameter setting is not warranted. This can be softened.
Vanilla SFT accuracies in Figure 5 look unlike seen in practice. The Qwen3-VL 2B/4B/8B vanilla SFT curves seem to plateau around 0.5 accuracy on a 1:1 balanced LUNA16 slice task i.e. essentially chance. A modern 8B LVLM should be able to memorise or at least noisily fit a small balanced classification task, even with suboptimal prompting. To explain these given numbers in the submission, the paper should explain what’s going wrong (learning-rate issue, answer-format mismatch, prompt-ending whitespace, LLM-head-frozen-vs-not, etc.); if they are seed-selected or early-training snapshots, the figure needs caveats. At face value, the vanilla-SFT baseline looks under-tuned.
Qwen3-VL (ref [3]) is trained on a very large multimodal corpus that almost certainly includes LIDC-IDRI and LUNA16 derivatives in some form. The paper acknowledges this concern in Sec4.2 (“potential overlap with pretraining data may bias evaluation”) but the only mitigation is “derive 2D from 3D segmentation data.” That doesn’t actually address the data overlap concern. If the pretraining corpus contained LUNA16 images with or without captions mentioning nodules, slice-level labels derived from the same volumes can still be overlapping. A held-out set, or at minimum a de-identified subset with noise applied, would be more convincing. In the 3D setting (RadGenome-Chest CT / CT-RATE), this concern increases as CT-RATE is heavily circulated in the VLM community.
Quantitative comparison to MAIRA-2 or similar grounded-VLM baselines is absent. The 3D report generation numbers on RadGenome-Chest CT (F1 0.263, IoU 0.673) are presented without reference to MAIRA-2, VividMed, RadVLM, or any of the other grounded-VLM papers. These are not all directly comparable (MAIRA-2 is chest X-ray, not 3D CT), but the paper’s main empirical claim is that LGS is the right paradigm for grounded medical VLM training, and that claim is not tested against the closest existing paradigm.
Minor citation issues.
-Ref [9]: the citation should ideally point to both the challenge and the paper if the authors used the challenge framework.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The central observation (vanilla SFT attention is diffuse and adding bounding-box outputs concentrates it) is reasonable and strong, and the empirical scaling evidence is useful. But the paper overstates its novelty relative to MAIRA-2 and related grounded-VLM work, which it does not cite. One of its main results (CrossMoDA2021 at 98% accuracy) is not adequately defended against shortcut-learning concerns; dataset splits and protocol details are not enough; there are no error bars; and the GRPO narrative is not based on evidence seen in practice. With better positioning against prior art, a properly defended CrossMoDA result, patient-level splits, and some seed-averaged numbers, this would be a good paper. As submitted it’s below my bar for the venue.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper investigates why vanilla supervised fine-tuning (SFT) underperforms for LVLMs in medical imaging and propose 3 fold contribution in this direction: by extending DePass framework to LVLM which they call ‘DePass-VL’, introduce a technique Localization-Grounded Supervision (LGS) that uses localization signals to improve spatial alignment during SFT and lastly also show the improvement not just for 2D dataset but 3D dataset.
reviews.text_strengths:
The abstract and introduction dig into the core problem of pretrained models to understand why vanilla SFT fails and authors claim to introduce an interpretability with DePass-VL to understand this better.
The idea of incorporating explicit localization signals (LGS) is simple and practically useful - specially for small lesions which they show in Figure 2
The authors attempt to mitigate data leakage concerns which I really like and appreciate. They identified that large pretrained models may have seen common datasets like LUNA16 and for a fair comparison they went further by constructing datasets from 3D segmentation sources, which is a thoughtful design choice.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The paper lacks essential details about dataset construction. Specifically, the number of samples for training/validation/test splits. In Table 1 - even though the datasets used to derive the images is 3D segmentation dataset - with the metrics reported it seems like authors did a classification task - lesion or no-lesion. Task is not explicitly clarified in the paper. These omissions make it difficult to assess statistical significance, lower bound and reproducibility.
2.Figure 5 reports results for InternVL3.5, but these results are not included in Table 1.A unified presentation would improve clarity and allow easier comparison across models. It would benefit the authors to include these results in Table 1.
3.The comparison with GRPO is underexplained. In particular, the paper does not clearly describe the training setup (reward design, policy definition, hyperparameters, etc). And why use GRPO and not other methods. Overall, comparison with RL is ill-motivated.
4.Contribution of DePass-VL is not justified. To understand the novelty and requirement, it would benefit the paper if there is a description of what is lacking is DePass and how authors resolve it. Moreover, compare how this interpretability contribution helps understanding vanilla SFT better.
5.In case of LGS which is the most significant contribution of the paper, key details are missing from the text on how is it implemented. This include mainly how are localization signals incorporated into training (and loss formulation)
6.Minor comments
a. Overall the writing feels a bit disintegrated in the paper. I like the effort put in for the experiments and the idea but I struggled to find key details and map them to the figures.
b. Section 4.5 largely reiterates observations already presented in Figures 2 and 3, and thus can be avoided.
c. Fig 3(b): x-axis says Vanilla SFT/LGS and I assume pink violin plot is SFT and blobs are LGS. If this is the case, the interpretation ‘value smaller than 1 indicates that LGS enhances the LVLM’s focus on task-relevant regions‘ is also valid for Vanilla SFT.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The authors have good instincts and present an idea specifically LGS and qualitative analysis of why vanilla SFt on LVLM fails. However, despite these strengths, the paper suffers from a lack of methodological clarity, incomplete experimental details, and several presentation inconsistencies. In particular, key aspects of the proposed method and evaluation setup are insufficiently described as mentioned above, making it difficult to fully assess and reproduce the reported results. 
While the overall direction is compelling, these gaps have led me to recommend a weak accept.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
I thank the authors for their response and for addressing several of my concerns.
Regarding dataset construction, the authors indicate that the relevant details will be added to the paper. While this is appreciated, it would have been more informative had at least a summary of the construction procedure been provided directly in the rebuttal. Furthermore, if the dataset is non-standard, additional baseline comparisons would be necessary to disentangle whether the reported improvements stem from the data itself or from the proposed algorithmic contributions. This remains an open concern.
Regarding GRPO, the authors state that they will reduce the emphasis on this component. I would like to clarify that the level of emphasis was not the issue I raised; my concern was directed at the rationale for its necessity in the first place, which has not been adequately addressed.
On the positive side, I appreciate that the authors have agreed to provide clarification on LGS and DePass-VL, and that they commit to including the InternVL3.5 results in the main table. These are meaningful improvements to the manuscript.
Taking all of the above into account, I will maintain my score at weak accept.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper proposes a simple LGS method to address the diffuse attention problem after the vanilla SFT on various tasks of MLLMs. However, there exist certain concerns on the novelty (e.g., comparison with prior work like MAIRA-A), unexpectedly high performance gains on CrossModaby LGS, and insufficient explanations on implementations and datasets. Therefore, the authors are encouraged to clarify these points for rebuttal.

The rebuttal addresses the reviewers’ concerns and therefore I lean towards acceptance. The authors are encouraged to justify the method choice (e.g., GRPO) and provide in-depth discussions on expperiments in the final version.
All reviewers highlight the contributions of the paper and suggest to accept the submission.
The reviewers appreciate the motivation and extensive experimental results, and the initial concerns have been mostly addressed during the rebuttal. I recommend accepting this submission.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback. We are encouraged that the reviewers recognize the importance of revisiting vanilla SFT for medical LVLM adaptation, the practical value of LGS, and the usefulness of our analyses. We address the key concerns below.
1.Novelty and prior grounded medical VLMs (R1&R2)
We thank R2 for pointing out related works such as MAIRA-2.We agree that predicting localization coordinates with text has been explored. Our contribution is not claiming coordinate prediction itself as new. Instead, we use localization output as a supervision interface to analyze and improve vanilla SFT for off-the-shelf LVLMs. The key contribution is the combination of simple supervision design, mechanistic analysis of vanilla SFT failure, and extension to 3D medical imaging. We will revise Introduction to clarify this positioning.
2.CrossMoDA result and baseline fairness (R1&R2)
Our CrossMoDA experiment is not the original 3D cross-modality segmentation challenge, but a derived 2D slice-level binary lesion-presence classification task. Thus, the high accuracy should not be interpreted as solving the original CrossMoDA task. Comparisons in all experiments are controlled (no patient-level data leakage): vanilla SFT and LGS use the same base model, split, learning rate, batch size, optimizer, epochs, parameter-freezing strategy, and prompt setting. The only intended difference is that LGS adds localization coordinates to the answer target. The substantial improvement over baseline precisely demonstrates the simplicity and effectiveness of LGS. We will add training details in the revised version, and release the split for reproducibility.
3.Dataset construction and benchmark purpose (R1&R2&R3)
We agree that dataset construction needs more detail. The 2D benchmarks are controlled fine-grained spatial diagnosis tasks, not full clinical diagnosis simulations. Take LUNA16 as the example, we select CT scans with a single lung nodule, use the middle slice of the nodule mask as the positive sample, and use the adjacent slice just outside the mask boundary as the negative sample. This creates lesion-near negatives and reduces coarse anatomical shortcuts. We will report train/validation sizes, patient/scan-level split, label rules, and more details in the revised version.
4.LGS implementation (R3)
LGS does not add a detection head or regression loss. Training still uses standard autoregressive next-token cross-entropy. The only change is the target sequence: vanilla SFT predicts only the answer, while LGS predicts the answer plus textual coordinates, e.g., “Yes, [x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max].” For 3D tasks, report-generation samples are mixed with anatomical localization. We will add target examples and loss formulation in the revised version.
5.DePass-VL and attention analysis (R2&R3)
We will revise to clarify that DePass-VL is the first adaptation of DePass to LVLMs with region-level token partitions: task-relevant image regions, non-relevant image regions, and other tokens. As correctly pointed out (R2), attention weights alone are not faithful attributions. Thus, DePass-based contribution analysis will be the main quantitative evidence, while attention maps will be presented as qualitative illustrations in the revised version.
6.Claim scope, GRPO, variance, and presentation (R1&R2&R3)
We will moderate claims: insufficient fine-grained semantic alignment is an important factor in fine-grained medical tasks, not a only universal cause. We will also soften the GRPO conclusion and present it only as a preliminary comparison, with added reward and hyperparameter details. If permitted by the rebuttal and revision policy, we will report mean±std for the main results in Tab.1, Fig.4&5.Finally, we will add InternVL3.5 results in Fig.5 to Tab.1, improve Fig.3(b) caption, clarify that the plotted value is the per-sample relative ratio, and shorten the repetitive Section 4.5.

title: LoFi: Location-Aware Fine-Grained Representation Learning for Chest X-Ray
abstract: Fine-grained representation learning is crucial for retrieval and phrase grounding in chest X-rays, where clinically relevant findings are often spatially confined. However, existing methods remain limited on these tasks, as contrastive models lack explicit region-level supervision and large vision language models often fail to generalize fine-grained representations under external validation. To address these limitations, we propose Location-aware Fine-grained representation learning (LoFi), which jointly optimizes sigmoid, captioning, and location-aware captioning losses using a lightweight large language model. The location-aware captioning loss enables region-level supervision through grounding and dense captioning objectives, thereby facilitating fine-grained representation learning. Building upon these representations, we integrate a fine-grained encoder into retrieval-based in-context learning to enhance chest X-ray grounding across diverse settings. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves superior retrieval and phrase grounding performance on MIMIC-CXR and PadChest-GR.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces Location-aware Fine-grained representation learning with the purpose of training a vision-language model able to localize and describe fine-grained features of medical images better than previous approaches. Following previous work, the authors trained their model on MIMIC-CXR and additionally evaluated it on PadChest-GR. Results for retrieval-based in-context learning on both datasets show performance superior to prior work.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper merges findings from two papers (SigLip and LoCa) to propose one unified training framework and applies it to radiology. Comparison with previous methods is thorough and results are convincing.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited to the combining of two previously introduced methods and its application to two radiology datasets.
