meta_reviews.text:
The authors presented a multi-anchor guided diffusion framework to utilize intermediate-dose scans as anchors to supervise the reverse diffusion process and create a dose-aligned denoising path. All three reviewers acknowledged the novelty of the approach and its performance gain. However, several key concerns might still warrant a rebuttal.
Statistical Modeling (Poisson vs. Gaussian). As pointed out by Reviewer 2, the paper models the Gaussian diffusion chain as a surrogate for PET’s inherent Poisson statistics. While this is a common approximation, it might be concerning at ultra-low dose levels (e.g., 1/20 or 1/50 dose) when the low photon count makes the Gaussian approximation significantly less accurate.
Validity of the Trajectory Alignment. The Boundary Calibration was introduced to statistically align the intermediate diffusion outputs with intermediate dose levels. However, it remains unclear if this statistical alignment truly captures the physical dose characteristics or if it simply performs a sophisticated interpolation. Specifically, the mapping between the early trajectory and the starting dosage 1/10 might need a clearer physical justification.
Generalizability and Fixed Anchors: Reviewer 1 and the AC are concerned that the denoising trajectory is overly dependent on the specific anchors (1/2, 1/4, 1/10) used during training, given the 1/20 dose as the conditioning. The cross-vendor evaluation was limited to the same 1/20 dose level, which might not sufficiently demonstrate the model’s generalization.
The authors are encouraged to clarify these concerns along with other minor points given by the reviewers during the rebuttal phase.

The authors clarified that their trajectory does not model the exact physical model in low-dose imaging, but rather a stochastic parameterisation of progressive image degradation. This made the foundation of their work more solid. However, they didn’t further discuss the limitation in the generalization to different dose levels, especially when the conditioning has a different dose level rather than 1/20 dose, and for the ultra low dose 1/50 level pointed out by R2. A remaining concern of mine is whether the denoising trajectory modeling in training is limited to a specific low dose input and for all other intermediate dose levels. Considering these, I am giving a weak acceptance.
All reviewers are positive about this paper. After reviewing the feedback from both the reviewers and the authors, I believe the paper meets the acceptance criteria and recommend acceptance.
The authors have addressed the reviewers questions.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and AC for the valuable feedback. We are encouraged that the reviewers recognized the effectiveness of the trajectory-level supervision design, particularly the timestep-dependent anchor guidance and dose-consistent denoising behavior of MAP-Diff. We address the main concerns below.
Q1 (R2, Meta-R1): Gaussian diffusion vs. Poisson PET statistics.
MAP-Diff does not require the diffusion forward process to be a physically exact model of PET photon-counting noise. Instead, the Gaussian forward process serves as a stochastic parameterisation of progressive image degradation. The key requirement is preservation of an ordered degradation structure across diffusion timesteps rather than exact equivalence between Gaussian and Poisson noise. Boundary calibration (Sec. 2.3) aligns diffusion states with real intermediate-dose PET images by matching degradation signatures (NMAE and SSIM within the body mask) relative to the clean full-dose image. Thus, the calibration targets statistically comparable degradation levels rather than identical noise distributions. Crucially, MAP-Diff supervises the clean prediction hat{x}_0(x_t,t) rather than the injected noise itself. Fig. 3 and Table 2 show that this trajectory-level supervision consistently improves both intermediate and final reconstruction quality over standard 3D DDPM using the same Gaussian diffusion formulation. Therefore, the observed gains arise from the proposed anchor-guided trajectory regularisation rather than the specific corruption model.
Q2 (Meta-R1): Validity of trajectory alignment and whether it is interpolation.
MAP-Diff is not an interpolation framework. The stochastic reverse diffusion process remains conditioned only on the 1/20-dose input, while anchors supervise only the predicted clean estimates during training and do not replace the reverse diffusion updates. The standard noise prediction objective (L_{noise}) also remains unchanged. If the model collapsed to deterministic interpolation, accurate noise pred across diffusion timesteps would be impossible. Instead, the anchor loss acts as a trajectory-level regulariser that guides clean predictions toward dose-consistent intermediate states while preserving stochastic generative behaviour. Table 2 further supports this interpretation: constant weighting (S8), which over-constrains all timesteps equally, significantly degrades performance compared with timestep-adaptive weighting. This indicates that MAP-Diff improves dose consistency through stage-wise trajectory regularisation rather than deterministic interpolation.
Q3 (R1, Meta-R1): Generalizability and dependence on fixed anchors.
MAP-Diff demonstrates cross-scanner generalisation on the external United Imaging uEXPLORER cohort under the clinically relevant 1/20-to-full-dose setting. The selected 1/10, 1/4, and 1/2 anchors are real intermediate-dose PET images available in the multi-dose dataset. Table 2 shows that one- or two-anchor variants still outperform the no-anchor baseline, indicating that MAP-Diff is not strictly dependent on any exact anchor combination, although full coverage provides the strongest guidance. Moreover, anchors are training-only; inference requires only the 1/20-dose input. MAP-Diff shows consistent improvements across both internal and external cohorts.
Q4 (R1, R2, R3): Minor clarifications.
The denoiser uses a 3D U-Net DDPM backbone. Timestep zones are calibrated rather than uniformly divided. The body mask is obtained by thresholding the non-background PET region. The loss weighting coefficient in Eq. (7) is fixed to lambda=0.2 across all experiments. MAP-Diff uses the same backbone and sampling procedure as 3D DDPM; anchors are training-only targets, so inference memory usage and runtime remain unchanged. We appreciate R2’s suggestions on additional diffusion baselines and 1/50-dose evaluation, which are complementary to the current study and do not affect the proposed trajectory-supervision formulation.

title: MARBLE: Lightweight EEG-to-fMRI Translation via Mamba-Attention and ROI-Conditioned Decoding
abstract: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) provides high-resolution whole-brain activity measurements but is constrained by high cost, limited accessibility, and restrictive acquisition conditions. Recent advances in cross-modal synthesis have enabled the inference of fMRI signals from electroencephalography (EEG), facilitating estimation of whole-brain activity from portable, low-cost recordings in naturalistic settings. Despite promising results, existing approaches rely on Transformer-based encoders that lack inductive biases for the causal, delayed nature of hemodynamic responses, and provide limited insight into how region-specific predictions are formed. In this paper, we propose MARBLE (Mamba-Attention for ROI-conditioned BOLD Estimation), an end-to-end framework for whole-brain EEG-to-fMRI translation. MARBLE employs a hybrid Mamba-Transformer encoder, where selective state-space modeling provides an inductive bias for HRF-related temporal structure while maintaining linear-time complexity. ROI-conditioned decoding heads operating on a shared latent representation generate region-specific BOLD time series. Our approach provides a favorable trade-off between reconstruction performance and computational efficiency, using 3.2x fewer model parameters and 2.3x less peak memory. Reconstructed functional connectivity matrices demonstrate preserved temporal dynamics and inter-regional structure, and cross-attention topographies reveal network-specific electrode contributions without explicit spatial supervision.
subject_areas: Modalities -> EEG / MEG / ECG / Physiological Signals

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors present a novel deep learning model that can translate EEG signals into fMRI signals by employing a temporal Mamba plus Transformer encoder and a ROI-wise decoder, while maintaining region specificity and needing fewer parameters than state-of-the-art models (due to the linearity offered by Mamba). In addition, the decoders’s cross-attention mechanism allows the direct mapping of attention weights to the brain, making the model interpretable ad-hoc. The proposed approach performs comparably or better than the state-of-the-art models used as baseline and can faithfully reconstruct functional connectivity matrices.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The architecture proposed here is novel in the incorporation of temporal Mamba and ROI-wise cross-attention, which reduces the number of parameters of the model and makes projecting attention weights to the brain possible, respectively. 
2.The proposed model performs better than state-of-the-art models that it was compared with across most of the metrics presented here.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.There are implementation details missing (data split and sizes of model inputs and outputs). 
2.The authors do not discuss any limitations of the model. 
3.FC can have negative values too. Authors should either include negative correlations in to the FC matrix, or justify the use of connections that are positive only. 
4.Authors do not report statistical significance of their proposed model being better than the state-of-the-art approaches. 
5.The authors do not describe how they adapt the LaBraM model (EEG-specific foundation model) to perform the EEG-to-fMRI task, which undermines the validity of using it as a baseline. The authors should better motivate its use. 
6.The sample size is limited to 22 subjects, which warrants a generalizability study of the proposed model to out of distribution data.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Major concerns:
1.Statistical significance of the performance differences between MARBLE and the baselines is not reported. Given the small sample size of 22 subjects, it is not clear whether the improvements shown in Table 1 are meaningful or within the range of expected variability. 
2.The functional connectivity matrices shown only include positive correlations. FC matrices can have negative values, and restricting to positive connections only either discards meaningful anti-correlations or implies a specific analytical choice that is not justified anywhere in the manuscript. 
3.The sample size of 22 subjects is limited. The manuscript would benefit from a generalizability analysis, or at least a discussion of how the model is expected to perform on out-of-distribution data. 
4.The use of LaBraM as a baseline is not well motivated. LaBraM is an EEG-specific foundation model pre-trained for EEG classification tasks, and it is not clear how the authors adapted it to perform the EEG-to-fMRI translation task. The other baselines are sufficient for comparison, but the authors should at minimum clarify how LaBraM was used.
Minor comments:
1.The data split is not described with enough clarity. While a 3:1:1 subject-specific split is mentioned, it is not clear how many subjects fall into each set or how many time points each split contains. 
2.The input and output sizes of the model are not explicitly stated. It appears that the model takes 16-second EEG windows as input and predicts one fMRI time point at a time, but this should be stated clearly. 
3.The model was trained for only 20 epochs. The authors should justify that this is sufficient for convergence, or report training and validation loss curves to support this. 
4.Limitations are not discussed.

The architecture proposed here is genuinely interesting: the combination of temporal Mamba and ROI-wise cross-attention is a principled design choice that addresses known limitations of purely Transformer-based EEG encoders, reduces the parameter count, and enables direct projection of attention weights to the brain. The reported performance is also competitive with, and in most cases better than, the baselines.
However, the evaluation has enough gaps to tip the balance toward a weak reject. The most important concern is the absence of significance testing on a 22-subject dataset, which makes it difficult to assess whether the reported improvements over the state of the art are meaningful or within the range of expected variability. The treatment of functional connectivity is also incomplete, as restricting to positive-only connections without justification leaves an important part of the analysis in question.
None of these weaknesses are fundamental. Adding significance tests and justifying or correcting the FC analysis would substantially strengthen the manuscript. With these revisions, this work would be above the bar for acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors addressed all four of my major concerns and my four minor clarifications in their response. On the positive-only functional connectivity matrices (Q2), the authors clarified that FC-Corr is computed on the full signed upper-triangular correlation matrix and that the 25% top-edge threshold is applied only to the rightmost panels of Fig. 4 for visualization, not to any quantitative metric. On reread this is consistent with Sec. 3.2, and my original concern reflected a misreading of the figure rather than a substantive analytical issue. On the LaBraM baseline (Q4), the authors clarified that LaBraM is included as a foundation-model-only control, initialized from the LaBraM-base checkpoint with the classification head replaced by the same multi-ROI regression head used across baselines and trained under identical conditions. This is a principled use of LaBraM as a control for the value of EEG-to-fMRI specific design, and resolves my concern. On statistical significance (Q1), the authors did not provide formal significance tests, but argued that mean and standard deviation across 6 held-out scans under a subject-independent protocol consistent with prior work captures the dominant source of variability, and tempered the “superior performance” framing to a “balanced trade-off”. On sample size and generalization (Q3), the authors acknowledged the 22-subject, single-site, eyes-closed cohort as a limitation and committed to stating it explicitly in Sec. 4.The minor clarifications were addressed correctly, with sufficient implementation detail to support reproduction.
In line with the AC guidance that meta-reviewers should not penalize papers for failing to provide new experimental results in the rebuttal, I do not weigh the absence of formal significance testing or an expanded cohort against the paper at this stage. Two of my four major concerns turned out to be misreadings of the manuscript that the rebuttal correctly clarified, and the remaining two are acknowledged as valid limitations that the authors will discuss explicitly in the camera-ready. The novelty of the temporal Mamba plus ROI-conditioned cross-attention design, the competitive performance against state-of-the-art baselines, and the interpretability afforded by ROI-attention topographies outweigh the remaining rigor concerns. I upgrade my recommendation from Weak Reject to Accept.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes MARBLE, a lightweight whole-brain EEG-to-fMRI translation framework. The method combines a Mamba-Transformer encoder with an ROI-conditioned cross-attention decoder to predict ROI-level BOLD time series more efficiently while improving reconstruction performance and preserving functional connectivity structure.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The method improves synthesis performance while reducing the number of parameters and memory usage, which enhances its practical value.
2.The evaluation simultaneously demonstrates signal reconstruction quality and functional connectivity preservation.
3.The ablation study highlights the effectiveness of two key modules, namely the ROI-CA decoder and tMamba.
4.The paper provides an attention-based interpretability analysis, revealing corresponding relationships between brain functional networks and EEG electrodes.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The evidence supporting the main innovation claims is insufficient. The authors argue that tMamba is better suited than a Transformer for modeling HRF-driven delays and unidirectional dependencies, but they do not provide direct evidence for this claim, such as further analysis of whether the temporal dependencies learned by Mamba are consistent with the physiological characteristics of the hemodynamic response.
2.Some results do not support a blanket claim that the proposed method outperforms the baselines. For example, FC-Corr is slightly lower than that of NeuroBOLT and UnEBOLT, so the use of the term “superior performance” in the main text is not fully appropriate.
3.Some implementation details are still missing, such as the specific structures of the encoder and decoder.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I recommend acceptance because this paper proposes a well-motivated and practical approach that achieves a good balance among performance, efficiency, and interpretability. Although some claims should be stated more cautiously and some implementation details need clarification, the overall technical contribution and experimental evidence are sufficient for acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors’ response has addressed my concerns well, particularly through the additional implementation details and the more carefully calibrated conclusions based on the experimental results. These revisions will significantly improve the quality of the paper, and therefore I support its acceptance.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a lightweight architecture for cross-modal synthesis of fMRI signals from EEG. Specifically, a Mamba-based transformer encoder with state-space modeling to capture HRF dynamics and an ROI-conditioned decoder for generating region-specific BOLD time series.
reviews.text_strengths: The proposed solution—with the choice of architecture, along domain-specific enhancements (encoder with state-space model and decoder with ROI-conditioning)—provides improvement in performance as a reduction in model size. The model also includes interpretability as an inherent feature.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Several conceptual and methodological aspects need more clarification:
(a) Resting state fMRI corresponds to spontaneous BOLD fluctuations that are slow, continuous oscillations that reflect intrinsic network activity. So, the use of state-space model for capturing HRF-driven temporal dynamics seems like a conceptual mismatch.
(b) EEG has poor sensitivity to deep subcortical structures (hippocampus, thalamus, basal ganglia). Performance comparison of the ROI-conditioned heads on subcortical vs. cortical ROIs would have given more credit to “whole-brain” activity estimation from EEG.
(c) Several works have already proposed combining Mamba with Transformers. So major contribuitions are ROI-conditioned decoding heads and the cross-modal EEG-to-fMRI translation objective specifically.
(d) An ablation study to observe the contribution of Transformer blocks in addition to the tMamba would have been more insightful.
(e) Cross-attention topographies revealing network-specific electrode contributions in Figure 5 would have been more meaning when compared with topographies generated without ROI-CA module.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Lack of major novelty factor as well as clinical utility of the proposed method.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
The reviews are mixed, with two reviewers leaning toward weak accept and one toward weak reject. The reviewers highlight critical evaluation gaps that undermine the claims from the authors: the lack of statistical significance testing on the small 22-subject dataset, the unjustified restriction to only positive functional connectivity values, and insufficient evidence that the Mamba component genuinely captures hemodynamic response dynamics. 
Additional concerns include missing implementation details, an unmotivated and unclear LaBraM baseline, limited novelty due to prior Mamba-Transformer hybrids, and the need for analysis of subcortical ROI performance and model limitations. The authors should prepare the rebuttal to address those concerns.

In the rebuttal, the authors clarified that the functional connectivity analysis already used signed correlations and that the LaBraM baseline was appropriately adapted as a foundation-model control, resolving two major concerns raised by Reviewer 1.The remaining issues such as small sample size, softened superiority claims, and missing implementation specifics were either addressed through textual clarifications or acknowledged as limitations for the camera-ready version. Two reviewers confirmed their recommendations to Accept after the rebuttal. Based on the final reviewer assessments and the authors’ responsive revisions, the paper can be recommended for acceptance.

Despite some lingering concerns, the authors have done a good job addressing the main critiques to extent allowed by MICCAI (i.e., no new experiments). This work would be of interest to the community.

The draft proposes a lightweight EEG-to-fMRI translation framework combining a Mamba-Transformer encoder with an ROI-conditioned cross-attention decoder.
The rebuttal provided missing implementation details requested by R1 and R2 (embedding dimensions, ROI query count, training split, input/output dimensions), substantially improving reproducibility.
Consequently, R2 upgraded to accept post-rebuttal. However, R1 maintain the weak reject score.
Despite this hiccup, I think the paper’s core contributions - extreme parameter efficiency and inherent interpretability via ROI-conditioned cross-attention - are well evidenced.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and the Area Chair for their constructive feedback. We are encouraged that the reviewers recognize the practical value, efficiency, and interpretability of MARBLE, and we address the main concerns below.
(1) Statistical significance (R1-1), superiority claims (R2-2). Table 1 reports mean ± std across 6 held-out scans under a subject-independent protocol consistent with prior studies [16,18]. The standard deviation reflects inter-subject variability, the main source of variation in this setting. MARBLE showed consistent improvements across metrics and Yeo networks (Fig. 2), indicating stable rather than isolated gains. Ablations further support component-specific contributions (ROI-CA: FC-Corr −0.061, tMamba: Corr −0.010). While formal statistical testing could further strengthen the evaluation, we believe the reported trends are meaningful within the benchmark setting used in prior work. Regarding claims, we agree that “superior performance” is too strong given that FC-Corr is slightly lower than [16,18]. We instead claim a balanced trade-off between reconstruction quality, efficiency, and interpretability.
(2) Positive-only FC matrices (R1-2). FC was computed using Pearson correlation without thresholding or sign filtering. FC values are predominantly positive in our data. As stated in Sec. 3.2, FC-Corr is computed on the full signed correlation matrix (upper-triangular); the 25% top-edge threshold is applied only to the rightmost panels of Fig. 4 for visualization and does not affect any quantitative metric.
(3) Generalization concerns (R1-3). We acknowledge the 22-subject cohort is limited, constraining generalization. The subject-independent protocol follows standard practice [16,18], and we used cross-subject splits to evaluate generalization within available data. We will state the single-site n=22 cohort and eyes-closed-only condition as explicit limitations in Sec. 4.(4) HRF interpretation (R2-1, R3-a), novelty (R3-c), additional ablations (R3-d, R3-e). tMamba was not intended to model hemodynamic responses, but to capture temporally extended EEG dependencies from 16-second EEG windows for regression to slow-varying BOLD signals. The contribution of tMamba is supported by ablation. We will soften “captures HRF dynamics” to “provides inductive bias for HRF-relevant structure” in the revision. The Mamba–Transformer encoder is a deliberate efficiency choice for this domain-specific application. Our central novelty is ROI-CA, which is the largest contributor in our ablation, enabling ad-hoc interpretability via attention topographies (Fig. 5), absent in adapter-based decoders. ROI-specific topography (Fig. 5) is intrinsically defined by the ROI-CA mechanism: without ROI queries, no ROI-conditioned attention map exists to compare against.
(5) Missing implementation details (R1, R2). MARBLE uses embedding dim 64, depth 4, Mamba state size 16, conv width 4, dropout 0.2.The ROI-CA employs 64 ROI queries with the same embedding dim. The 3:1:1 split is over subjects, with no subject in multiple splits. Each input is a 16-s, 26-channel EEG window at 200 Hz; the target is the BOLD signal across 64 ROIs at the corresponding fMRI time point. Training for 20 epochs was selected based on monitored validation loss, which plateaued well before termination.
(6) LaBraM motivation (R1-4). LaBraM [13] is included as a foundation-model-only control. We initialize from LaBraM-base and replace its classification head with the same multi-ROI regression head used across baselines, under identical training conditions. This isolates the contribution of EEG-to-fMRI specific design over a generic large-scale EEG foundation model.
(7) Subcortical sensitivity (R3-b). We acknowledge EEG limitations in subcortical regions. The DiFuMo atlas includes cortical and subcortical ROIs, and results are reported across all regions. A separate cortical-versus-subcortical evaluation is an interesting direction for future work.

title: Marginal Constrained Morphological Prototype Learning for Patch Search in Whole Slide Images
abstract: Digital histopathology images are fundamental to modern oncology, enabling precise cancer diagnosis and the identification of clinically relevant morphological features. Due to the gigapixel scale of Whole Slide Images (WSIs), the dominant paradigm remains a two-step pipeline that encodes patches with a pre-trained backbone and aggregates features via Multi Instance Learning (MIL). However, this paradigm inherently limits optimization; encoders are often kept fixed, and prototype-based approaches are not always tightly coupled with the slide-level discriminative objective. Here, we propose Marginal-Constrained Morphological Prototype Learning (MMPL), a framework that formulates WSI diagnosis as the selective retrieval of informative patches. MMPL introduces two core innovations: (1) global prototype learning optimized via Sinkhorn-Knopp assignment against a momentum-stabilized feature queue (2) prototype-guided top-k patch selection. By focusing only on the top-k most informative patches, MMPL reduces the number of processed instances up to 99.3%, substantially lowering computational requirements. Experimental results on three WSI benchmarks demonstrate that MMPL outperforms the previous best baseline by up to 4.2% in weighted F1 for metastasis detection and 1.8% for tumor subtyping. Crucially, this breakthrough efficiency enables the vision encoder to learn discriminative morphological features, further rendering end-to-end training practical. The code will be available at https://github.com/dmis-lab/MMPL.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes MMPL, a prototype-based WSI framework to improve patch selection and computational efficiency in slide-level prediction. The method learns global morphological prototypes using a queue and Sinkhorn-Knopp-based balanced assignment, and then uses these prototypes to retrieve top-k informative patches for slide classification. Evaluation results on three WSI benchmarks are presented to demonstrate the advantages of the proposed method.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper addresses an important problem in WSI analysis: how to make patch selection more targeted rather than typical all-patch MILs. 
2.The paper includes several useful analyses, including low-tumor-prevalence robustness, prototype assignment visualization, and ablations on the queue, prototypes, and clustering strategy. 
3.Some of the results look strong, such as the performance gain on CAMELYON16 and TCGA-NSCLC with the ResNet50 backbone.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The method description is too short and hard to understand. The paper states that prototypes retrieve top-k relevant patches, but it does not clearly explain the exact rules. How many patches are selected per prototype, whether duplicates are allowed across prototypes, and how the final subset is assembled before aggregation?
2.The efficiency argument also feels incomplete. The paper emphasizes processing fewer instances, but it still seems that all patches need to be encoded at least once to populate the queue and compute prototype similarities. Without runtime or memory measurements, it is hard to know what the practical gain really is. 
3.The UNI-backbone results look inconsistent. On CAMELYON16, the gain is very large, whereas on TCGA-NSCLC, MMPL actually underperforms PANTHER on AUC. The results need more explanation.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper has a solid underlying idea and some encouraging results, but the current presentation and validations are not very clear and not totally convincing, as stated in the Weaknesses above.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal clears up some of the confusion, especially on the retrieval rule, the UNI result, and where the efficiency gain is supposed to come from. Still, I do not think it is enough to support acceptance. The method still feels only moderately novel, and the current validation is not sufficient to clearly separate the method from related work. I keep my score at Weak Reject and my final recommendation is Reject.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes MMPL, a prototype-driven MIL framework for WSI analysis that integrates dynamic global prototype learning and optimal-transport-based assignment to guide top-k patch selection. The key idea is to align prototype learning with slide-level supervision and enable efficient end-to-end training by focusing only on informative patches.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The combination of momentum-based prototype updates and OT-based assignment is reasonable and well integrated. Compared to prior prototype methods (e.g., PANTHER), the idea of aligning prototypes with task objectives is meaningful.
2.The top-k selection strategy significantly reduces computation while maintaining or improving accuracy, which is important for real-world WSI deployment.
3.The method shows consistent improvements across multiple WSI benchmarks, with clear gains in WF1 and AUC. Ablation studies are also reasonably thorough.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The proposed prototype-based top-k patch retrieval is quite similar in spirit to recent MoE-style routing methods that also select a subset of informative patches [1]. However, the paper does not clearly explain how this approach differs from or improves over these methods. In particular, it is unclear whether the benefit comes from the prototype design itself or simply from sparse patch selection. This makes the positioning of the method less clear.
2.Some parts of the method (e.g., interaction between queue, momentum encoder, and OT assignment) are not explained as clearly as they could be, making the framework slightly harder to follow.
3.While some qualitative results are shown (Fig. 3), there is still limited quantitative analysis of how prototypes evolve, how stable they are, and how they relate to pathological semantics across datasets.
[1] Wu, Junxian, et al. “Learning heterogeneous tissues with mixture of experts for gigapixel whole slide images.” Proceedings of the Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Conference. 2025.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Overall, the paper is technically solid and shows promising results, but there are still some important issues that need to be addressed. In particular, the positioning with respect to recent MoE-based patch selection methods is unclear, and several key design choices (e.g., prototype learning mechanism) are not sufficiently analyzed or explained. These make it harder to fully understand where the performance gains come from. That said, I think the idea is interesting and relevant to the field. If the authors can better clarify the differences from MoE-style methods and provide a deeper analysis of the prototype behavior, I would be happy to raise my score.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: My main concerns were resolved during the rebuttal phase, so I recommend acceptance after the rebuttal.

reviews.recommendation_label: Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a prototype-driven framework for WSI analysis that formulates slide-level prediction as a selective patch retrieval problem. Its main contributions include dynamically learning global morphological prototypes via a momentum-updated feature queue, introducing an optimal transport–based assignment (via Sinkhorn-Knopp) to enable balanced and task-aware prototype matching, and performing BoVW-style weighted aggregation over top-k selected patches to improve both computational efficiency and representation quality. Together, these designs allow more effective identification of informative regions while supporting end-to-end training of the encoder.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper has several notable strengths: it presents a well-motivated and coherent framework that integrates prototype learning, optimal transport, and top-k patch selection into a unified pipeline; the use of Sinkhorn-based assignment provides a principled way to enforce balanced and task-aware prototype utilization; and the dynamic prototype learning with a momentum queue is technically sound and helps capture global morphological patterns. In addition, the method demonstrates strong empirical performance across multiple benchmarks, while significantly improving computational efficiency by focusing only on informative patches, making the approach both effective and practical.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The main limitation of the paper lies in its relatively incremental novelty, as the overall framework shares notable similarities with prior prototype-based and selective aggregation methods for WSI analysis. Although the use of optimal transport and top-k retrieval introduces some technical differences, the conceptual advancement over existing approaches is not entirely clear. More importantly, the paper does not include direct comparisons with closely related work (e.g., methods based on dynamic encoding or prototype-driven representation learning [1]), making it difficult to fairly assess the actual performance gains. Additionally, some design choices (such as the specific benefits of OT assignment over simpler alternatives) are not sufficiently justified through ablation or analysis.
[1] Dynamic Residual Encoding with Slide-Level Contrastive Learning for End-to-End Whole Slide Image Representation.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I lean toward accepting this paper due to its solid technical design and practical effectiveness. While the overall idea is somewhat related to existing prototype-based and selective aggregation methods, the integration of momentum-based global prototype learning with optimal transport assignment is well-executed and provides a principled way to improve prototype utilization. The framework is coherent, and the top-k retrieval strategy offers clear computational benefits without sacrificing performance. In addition, the experimental results are strong and consistently demonstrate improvements across multiple benchmarks. Despite some missing comparisons with closely related work, the paper still provides a meaningful and practically valuable contribution to WSI analysis.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I maintain my recommendation for acceptance.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper proposes a prototype-driven MIL framework for WSI analysis that integrates dynamic global prototype learning with top‑k patch selection to improve both computational efficiency and slide‑level classification performance. The reviewers agree that the method shows solid and consistent improvements on several WSI datasets. The weaknesses include insufficiently clear method description and lack of comparison with closely related work. Please respond to the major concerns of the reviewers, including the following points: clarify the exact patch selection rules,explain the inconsistent UNI‑backbone results,clarify the difference from MoE‑style routing methods,explain the interaction between the queue, momentum encoder, and OT assignment.

This paper received two rejects and one accept after rebuttal. I recommend rejection of this paper and the main reason is the insufficient evaluation. The major results are reported with ResNet50 as the backbone, but its performance is much lower than using UNI as the backbone, which makes the Resnet50 results useless in practice. As a pathology foundation model (such as UNI) can result in higher performance, only improvement over this strong baseline is practically meaningful.

The paper presents a well-motivated and practically relevant framework for efficient WSI analysis through prototype-driven patch selection. Reviewers appreciated the integration of dynamic prototype learning, optimal-transport-based assignment, and top-k patch retrieval within a unified framework, as well as the strong empirical performance across multiple benchmarks. The method also demonstrates meaningful computational advantages by focusing on informative patches while maintaining competitive accuracy. Although concerns were raised regarding novelty and additional comparisons with related prototype-based methods, the rebuttal addressed many of these issues satisfactorily. Overall, the paper provides a solid contribution to efficient and scalable WSI analysis, and I support acceptance.
This is an interesting piece of work, and the authors have satisfactorily addressed the majority of the reviewers’ concerns during the rebuttal.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank all reviewers for their thoughtful and constructive feedback. Below, we provide point-by-point responses.
(Reviewer 1)
Patch selection rules: We compute the cosine similarity between the patch features of the input WSI and the learned prototypes. The total retrieval budget of k patches is then dynamically partitioned among prototypes in proportion to their slide-level attention weights, which are learned via a gated attention layer trained on the downstream task. Each prototype retrieves its assigned share of the most similar patches, and the retrieved instances are concatenated into the final informative subset capped at k. Since the OT formulation via Sinkhorn-knopp promotes uniform assignments, the retrieved patches are encouraged to align with a single prototype, although minor overlaps may occur as this is not enforced explicitly.
Inconsistent UNI‑backbone results: The WF1 and AUC results for MMPL with UNI on the TCGA-NSCLC dataset were incorrectly reported. The correct performance is WF1: 0.950 ± 0.03 and AUC: 0.980 ± 0.003 (originally misreported as WF1: 0.984 and AUC: 0.907). We apologize for any confusion. 
Upon careful re-examination of all logs and result tables, we confirmed that this was the only reporting error. Importantly, despite this correction, the main conclusions remain unchanged. With the UNI backbone, MMPL still outperforms PANTHER on most metrics, while showing competitive AUC on TCGA-NSCLC.
Efficiency: While all patches are encoded during the forward pass, the primary memory bottleneck lies in storing intermediate activations for backpropagation during training. Our efficiency gain stems from selective backpropagation. In fact, training ABMIL with 10,000 patches using a ResNet50 is infeasible (1.06TB of memory). In contrast, MMPL restricts gradient updates to only the top-100 patches (only 22.26GB), enabling end-to-end optimization even with a single NVIDIA RTX 3090.(Reviewer 2)
Distinctions from MoE-style routing (PAMoE): While MMPL and PAMoE share identifying informative patches, a key difference is reliance on external priors for expert specialization. MoE-based models typically learn gating via a weighted sum of diverse expert outputs through downstream loss. However, in the WSI-MIL setting, expert specialization is often difficult to achieve due to data scarcity and low label complexity, which can lead to unstable routing. PAMoE also acknowledges this challenge in their paper (see Section 4.2). In contrast, MMPL formulates self-supervised learning via an OT-based framework. Using a shared MLP across all patches and Sinkhorn-knopp, our prototypes capture diverse morphological patterns without requiring external knowledge. Thus, the improvements stem from prototype design rather than simple patch selection.
“Interaction between the queue …”: By employing an EMA-updated encoder for stable representation shifts, we populate the feature queue to mitigate the local bias inherent in individual slides. Within this stabilized global context, we formulate prototype assignment as an OT problem with Sinkhorn-Knopp. This enables robust prototype evolution from scratch during training, which then guides a dynamic top-k retrieval process.
Quantitative Prototype analysis: While we agree that a more comprehensive quantitative analysis would further strengthen the paper, additional experiments are difficult to include due to the rebuttal guidelines regarding new results.
Importantly, the current results in Table 2 and Fig 3c provide quantitative evidence that the prototypes avoid collapse and capture relevant pathological semantics on CAMELYON16 with high quantitative consistency. 
(Reviewer 3)
Novelty over prior work (DRE-SLCL): While DRE-SLCL relies on random sampling and external reports, MMPL learns global prototypes in a self-supervised manner during training. This enables the vision encoder to be optimized on informative patches retrieved through prototype guidance.

title: MaRS: Robust Out-of-Distribution Detection via Mahalanobis Residual Scoring
abstract: Foundation models provide highly descriptive representations for medical images, yet their reliability degrades under distribution shifts arising from changes in patients, devices, or acquisition conditions. Reliable out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is therefore essential for safe deployment. Recent post-hoc detectors efficiently exploit frozen embeddings (e.g., kNN), whereas reconstruction-based OOD detection in latent feature space has seen limited adoption due to inconsistent performance. In this work, we show that the limitation of reconstruction-based methods in latent space does not stem from poor reconstruction quality, but from how reconstruction errors are scored. Standard L2 residual norms collapse the anisotropic residual structure, thereby suppressing informative deviations. To address this limitation, we introduce MaRS (Mahalanobis Residual Scoring), a label-free OOD detector that learns an in-distribution manifold using a lightweight autoencoder and measures deviation via a Mahalanobis distance on reconstruction residuals, yielding variance-aware OOD scores. Across three imaging modalities, multiple types of distribution shift, and different model families and scales, MaRS outperforms established confidence-, distance-, and reconstruction-based baselines, while remaining fully post-hoc and lightweight. The code is available at github.com/francescodisalvo05/mars.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
MaRS is an unsupervised method to detect out-of-distribution (OOD) samples. It starts by training a lightweight undercomplete autoencoder for reconstruction on frozen features extracted with a deep-learning model. The difference between reconstructed and original features is then computed and modelled as a multivariate Gaussian distribution by estimating the covariance matrix. The Mahalanobis distance is then used as an OOD score, with the intuition that points that are off the normal-data manifold break correlations in the residual space.
MaRS is evaluated against strong baselines on MIDOG from OpenMIBOOD, covariate shift on X-ray images, and semantic shift on dermatoscopy images. Its performance in terms of AUROC and FPR@95 is found to be very competitive. Ablation studies investigate the effect of the feature extractor backbone (ViT vs DINOv3) and the role of normalization.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper addresses an important problem in medical image analysis with an approach that is built logically. The intuition that anisotropies in the (reconstructed) feature manifold may be helpful for OOD detection is very reasonable and nicely exploited. An analysis of the different eigenvalues is presented as evidence of the underlying hypothesis. 
Results are formulated in terms of AUROC over multiple runs, which is the right direction to assess consistency in this case. Several types of distribution shifts are analyzed in the different datasets, thus helping to understand performance across application scenarios. 
Claims are formulated appropriately to the study by stating that “MaRS consistently outperforms latent-space and reconstruction-based baselines”, leaving the judgement on the state of the art to future systematic evaluations or community experience.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The selection of datasets used for experiments leaves several open questions and is not fully aligned with the goals stated in the introduction. In fact, despite the mention of OpenMIBOOD, MaRS is benchmarked on MIDOG only, leaving out PhaKIR and OASIS-3 without justification. Instead, the authors choose to report results on two datasets from the MedMNIST+ collection with OOD tasks engineered by separating a label subset. This is also somewhat incomplete, as MedMNIST+ has many more datasets, and is described in a rather confused way towards the end of the “Datasets” paragraph of section 3.1.On the one hand, results on incomplete subsets raise the question of whether they hold for the missing entries. This question persists in the ablation studies which are restricted to one of the three benchmarks and the other two respectively. On the other hand, the stated goal is detecting “changes in patient populations, imaging devices, acquisition protocols, and artefacts”. X-ray results address population and part of MIDOG addresses target scanners, but the rest of MIDOG and dermatoscopy address semantic shifts. 
2.While running experiments with three different seeds goes in the right direction, the statistical analysis needs better reporting. For a start, runs are not reported individually (e. g. with median [min, max]). Most critically, the details of the Wilcoxon signed-rank test are not specified. Since 3 metric pairs at the dataset-split level would be insufficient for statistical significance, it seems that the test has been performed at the image or pixel level, but the specification is missing. It would also be helpful to report the type of averaging for the metrics in general. Finally, the comment on Mahalanobis++ being deterministic was insufficient for me to understand how the comparison is performed in that case. 
3.The comparison between confidence-based and reconstruction-based methods could be considered unfair, since reconstruction trains small multilayer models while confidence-based methods are limited to a linear head. A small ablation would have been helpful to reduce this confounder. 
4.While the authors comment on the stability of the estimation of the covariance matrix in the case of Mahalanobis++ in section 3.3 Backbone size / Results, the justification that follows does not state clearly why the same estimation is expected not to be an issue in the case of MaRS. Because of the many parameters that are being estimated, it would be helpful to relate “high-dimensional variability” and “preserving directions most sensitive to distributional shifts” to quantitative measures.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Please be consistent with the usage of the name “MaRS” or “MahRS” across the paper. I refrain from quoting exact positions as I believe a “find and replace” will yield the best results.
Consider rewriting parts of the introduction to make the interplay between reconstruction and latent spaces or foundation models crystal clear early on, by stating explicitly and at the beginning that the reconstruction considered in this work is performed on extracted features. I found it quite confusing in my first read; luckily figure 1 considerably helped to understand the basic approach. Likewise, the comment “all operating directly in latent feature space” in section 3.1 “Methods” could be interpreted as applying only on distance-based baselines, hiding that confidence-based methods are also based on frozen representations.
The description of the normalization ablation could be easily improved by specifying if the backbone’s final LayerNorm was included or removed for the prior experiments, and if it is reintroduced with trained mean and variance or a simple normalization of features to zero mean and unit variance is applied.
It would be nice to verify explicitly if the reconstruction residuals are actually centered around zero on in-distribution held-out data, since that might impact the interpretation of the multivariate Gaussian distribution.
In the last paragraph of section 2.3 it is claimed that subtracting the learned projection makes a single covariance matrix sufficient. This is shown only indirectly and for the data at hand, while it might not hold for datasets with more complicated topologies. I recommend a minor adjustment to a more precise formulation.
The second paragraph of the discussion section 4 should be probably called “conclusions” instead of “discussion” again. Also, the meaning of “data sparsity” at the very end is not clear from the context.

The method presented in the submission addresses an important problem, is logically built, and is interesting for discussion as it is simple but competitive, although the observed performance is not revolutionary.
The concerns about the choice of datasets and the statistical analysis need to be addressed in the rebuttal to ensure results are solid, and the discussion of the types of OOD shifts addressed should be aligned with results.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The rebuttal has limited space to answer a wide range of concerns, and it is successful in addressing a few to different degrees.
For example, difficulties in accessing OASIS-3 are well noted, and the description of the Wilcoxon test is provided and acceptable, although pairing random seeds in runs with different methods is not perfectly clean. On the other hand, the justification of excluding endoscopy images compared to pathology or X-rays could be subject to debate, and the discussion on Maha++ does not address the different comparison because of its deterministic nature.
Overall, the rebuttal sheds some light on a few of the open questions, which confirms my initial assessment. The paper could be accepted, but still has several minor weaknesses that are outweighed by its merits only by a small margin.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces MaRS, a post-hoc out-of-distribution detection method for medical imaging that operates on reconstruction residuals from a lightweight autoencoder trained on in-distribution representations. The central contribution is the identification that standard L2-based reconstruction error scoring collapses the anisotropic residual structure, thereby discarding information relevant to OOD detection. To address this, the authors propose replacing L2 scoring with Mahalanobis distance on residuals, yielding a variance-aware OOD score. The method is evaluated across three imaging modalities including histopathology, dermatoscopy, and X-ray, with ablation studies on different design choices.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper is well written and easy to follow. The problem of OOD detection in medical imaging is well motivated, and the core argument that the failure of reconstruction-based methods stems from scoring rather than reconstruction quality is presented clearly.
2.Evaluation spans three imaging modalities
3.The paper includes ablation studies on key design choices, which helps isolate the contribution of individual components.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.While the paper reports mean FPR, this aggregation may obscure clinically relevant variability across datasets. In safety-critical medical imaging applications, per-dataset FPR values would allow readers to assess whether the aggregate gains of MaRS reflect consistent improvements or are driven by strong performance on a subset of datasets. Given the importance of FPR in deployment contexts, reporting per-dataset FPR alongside the existing mean would substantially strengthen the empirical evaluation.
2.The performance gain by MaRS over other approaches like Mahalanobis++ and Residual (Table 1) is modest. However, MaRS introduces two sources of additional computational cost: the training and inference overhead of the autoencoder, and the estimation of the full covariance matrix over residuals required for Mahalanobis scoring. It is therefore unclear whether this marginal gain justifies adoption over computationally cheaper alternatives.
3.The authors justify using pre-normalization features for MaRS by arguing that LayerNorm suppresses variance anisotropy, and that preserving this structure benefits Mahalanobis-based scoring. However this argument applies equally to Mahalanobis++ which also relies on a covariance matrix to capture anisotropic structure. Figure 3 shows that Mahalanobis++ performance decreases under pre-normalization, while MaRS improves. If anisotropy preservation were the primary explanatory factor, both methods should benefit from pre-norm features given their shared reliance on covariance estimation. The authors do not account for this asymmetry, leaving their justification incomplete.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The method is referred to as MahRS in the experimental table while rest of the paper uses MaRS. This inconsistency should be resolved for clarity and consistency throughout the manuscript.

While this is an interesting read, the paper only introduces incremental upgrades to existing methods. See the weakness section for further details.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
1) The authors claim that covariance estimation on reconstruction residuals is more informative for OOD detection than on raw embeddings. However, the gains for MIDOG –CS/Near-OOD/far-OOD/X-Ray/Derma are 0.87, -0.37, -0.01, 1.09, 2.Additionally, in the reported FPR, the method only shows clear performance gain on MIDOG-CS/X-ray (2/4). As the performance gain is marginal, to show the method’s competitive advantage, a more rigorous analysis is required.
2) The claim that anisotropy of variance in raw embeddings is not necessarily aligned with OOD-relevant direction needs more concrete evidence.
Though the application of Mahalanobis in reconstruction residuals is novel, the paper fails to show clear competitive advantage, and contributions are clearly incremental. Therefore, my overall recommendation is reject.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a label-free OOD detection method based on Mahalanobis distance. The approach is post hoc and operates on frozen model features. The focus on the paper is primarilty in detection ood samples in medical domain which could arise either due to chnage in machine, population etc..
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper is mathematically sound and based on simple PCA and Mahalanobis metric concepts
The paper is evaluated across multiple datasets
reviews.text_weaknesses:
While the paper does compare with different OOD methods, none of the compared methods are state-of-the-art in the medical domain, which makes it challenging to establish the merit of the proposed method in the context of medical data. For example, the OpenMIBOOD (2025) dataset while mentioned, is not evaluated.
It is not clear how part 1 of Figure 1 is related to the proposed approach in the paper. The experimental section in the paper talks about DinoV2 and other unsupervised models. Where does the decoder component come in these cases? The setup should be more clearly defined.
There are some minute writing. Unnecessary dashes at the end of words such as “reconstructions” and “residual” are present in the Introduction section. Similar dashes appear at several other places in the paper.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

While the paper is well written, the method’s efficacy is not well established. The improvements are not significant, and comparisons with strong baselines are lacking, making the claim weaker.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
Please prioritize addressing the key issues raised by the reviewers, including justifying the dataset choices and missing benchmarks (e.g., OpenMIBOOD), reporting per-dataset metrics (especially FPR) with clearer statistical details, and clarifying whether the observed gains justify the additional computational cost, including the pre-normalization versus Mahalanobis++ discrepancy.

This paper introduces MaRS, a post-hoc out-of-distribution detection method for medical imaging that operates on reconstruction residuals from a lightweight autoencoder trained on in-distribution representations. The use of Mahalanobis distance in the reconstruction-residual space is a novel and well-motivated contribution, and the method is practically appealing as a lightweight post-hoc approach. While some reviewers raised concerns that the empirical gains are marginal, the authors’ rebuttal provides acceptable clarifications regarding the dataset choices and includes corresponding t-tests to support the statistical validity of the reported improvements. Overall, the rebuttal addresses most of the crucial concerns, and the remaining issues do not appear severe enough to outweigh the paper’s novelty and practical relevance. Therefore, the paper is recommended for acceptance.

After rebuttal, a single reviewer is in favor of the paper. Even that reviewer finds the rebuttal only partly convincing and sees the paper as being acceptable only by a small margin. It is my impression that the paper would benefit greatly from a larger scale and more careful revision that provides stronger evidence for the benefit over state of the art alternatives, possibly on a broader choice of datasets. Authors attribute the relatively modest advantages in their experiments to the fact that they do not use class information - maybe they could achieve even stronger results by modifying their approach so that it can account for that information as well, when available?

As stated by reviewer 1, the authors addressed some of the key concerns in the limited space available in the rebuttal. The paper presents a valuable modification to a popular OOD detection method which could be interesting to a big part of the community.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their thoughtful feedback. We are encouraged that they recognized the importance of OOD detection (R1,R2), the soundness of our formulation (R1,R3), the usefulness of anisotropic residual structure for this task (R1), and the clarity of our work (R1,R2,R3). We also appreciate the positive assessment of extensive evaluation (R1,R2,R3), strong baselines (R1), and ablations on backbone choice and normalization (R1,R2). We address major concerns below.
[R2] What is novel beyond standard Mahalanobis scoring?
We respectfully clarify that MaRS is not a simple re-use of Mahalanobis scoring. Our work shows that covariance estimation on
reconstruction residuals
is more informative for OOD detection than on raw embeddings. Specifically, Sec. 3.2 quantitatively demonstrates that after subtracting the learned ID projection, the OOD signal concentrates in anisotropic low-variance residual directions, making Mahalanobis scoring effective. This leads to a label-free method that replaces class-conditional statistics with global ID residual covariance and significantly outperforms the class-dependent Mahalanobis++ (Maha++).
[R1,R2] Why does pre-LayerNorm help MaRS but not Maha++?
Because MaRS and Maha++ estimate covariance in fundamentally different spaces. Maha++ estimates covariance directly on embeddings, where variance mixes semantic and class variation. In raw embeddings, this anisotropy is not necessarily aligned with OOD-relevant directions. MaRS instead subtracts the learned ID manifold projection and estimates covariance on reconstruction residuals. There, low-variance directions reflect stable ID reconstruction behavior, so deviations along them are informative OOD signals (Fig. 2). LayerNorm suppresses this residual variance structure, explaining why MaRS benefits from pre-normalization whereas Maha++ does not. We thank the reviewers for allowing us to clarify this important distinction.
[R1,R3] Could you clarify the dataset choice?
Yes, we did not categorically exclude OpenMIBOOD, but limited our evaluation to MIDOG (from OpenMIBOOD) due to access and scope constraints. OASIS-3 is access-restricted and approval was not available in time. PhaKIR focuses on surgical endoscopy, whereas our evaluation targets broad, established 2D imaging modalities where off-the-shelf foundation-model embeddings are commonly utilized. We therefore focused on histopathology, chest X-ray, and dermatoscopy, including diverse distribution shifts.
[R1,R2] Are the FPR95 gains consistent, and how was significance tested?
MaRS consistently outperforms the strongest unsupervised reference method (Residual), while also improving over Maha++ on several settings. Following Table 1, FPR95 (lower is better) for MaRS/Maha++/Residual is: MIDOG-CS 30/32/35, nearOOD 53/52/57, farOOD 0/0/0, X-Ray 36/40/40, Derma 94/94/95.The Wilcoxon test was computed on the 15 paired aggregate results from 5 dataset splits and 3 runs, yielding p=0.018.We reiterate that MaRS is fully unsupervised and does, in contrast to Maha++, not rely on the availability of class labels.
[R2] Does MaRS justify its computational cost over Mahalanobis++?
Yes, MaRS is computationally lightweight. AE training is one-time and takes only a few minutes on cached embeddings using our small two-layer MLP encoder-decoder. At inference, MaRS adds only minimal overhead from one embedding-level AE forward pass. It then computes a single Mahalanobis score in residual space using one global ID residual covariance. In contrast, Maha++ computes Mahalanobis distances to all class-specific means using a shared embedding covariance. Thus, MaRS is label-free and avoids class-dependent computation, thereby scaling more favorably as the number of classes increases.
[R3] What does decoder mean in Fig. 1?
The decoder in Fig. 1 is part of our proposed autoencoder module and reconstructs feature embeddings, not images, as detailed in the caption.

title: Mask to Concept: Auto-Promptable SAM3 via Efficient Test-Time Concept Embedding Search for Few-Shot Annotation
abstract: Transforming foundation segmentation models from human-prompted tools into auto-promptable annotators is critical for scalable medical data annotation. Current methods commonly depend on external feature matchers or auxiliary networks to automate geometric prompting, but introducing architectural overhead and limiting performance scalability. Although SAM3 natively supports concept segmentation via reusable text prompts, its direct use in medical imaging is hindered by a lack of fine-grained clinical knowledge and the ambiguity of human-written descriptions. In this work, we propose Mask to Concept (M2C), an efficient framework that adapts SAM3 for medical few-shot annotation without external modules, parameter retraining, or manual text engineering. Using only a few labeled images, M2C enables SAM3 to automatically search for transferable visual concepts entirely within its frozen architecture: it initializes a learnable concept embedding, uses it to prompt segmentation, and updates the embedding by gradients of minimizing the concept segmentation error. We further introduce a Hybrid Uncertainty Estimation (HUE) module that calculates the prediction entropy and maps concept predictions back to the box prompts, measuring concept-geometry prompting inconsistency. Highly uncertain samples are flagged actively for human correction, and the corrected masks are then fed back to M2C to continuously search for more precise concept embeddings, forming a self-enhancing annotation loop with minimal expert effort. Experiments on medical segmentation benchmarks show that our method achieves SOTA few-shot segmentation performance and outstanding annotation efficiency, offering a practical and efficient pathway toward scalable medical image labeling. Codes are at https://github.com/Huster-Hq/M2C.

reviews.recommendation_label: Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper introduces Mask to Concept (M2C), a training free framework that turns SAM3 into an auto promptable annotation system for medical image segmentation. The core idea is to learn a concept embedding from only a few labeled images by optimizing it through segmentation feedback, enabling the model to automatically discover transferable visual concepts within a frozen SAM3 backbone. This removes the need for external prompt generators or additional trainable modules, and instead relies on iterative refinement of the concept embedding guided by segmentation error. The method is further extended with a Hybrid Uncertainty Estimation module that identifies uncertain predictions by measuring entropy and concept geometry inconsistency, and uses these cases to trigger human correction. Corrected annotations are then fed back into the system, forming an active, self improving annotation loop aimed at reducing expert labeling effort.
Overall, the experimental results suggest strong few shot segmentation performance and improved annotation efficiency across medical benchmarks, supporting the practical value of the approach. However, some of the performance and generalization claims may be somewhat overstated, and the strength of the improvements likely depends on the specific benchmarks and baselines used.
reviews.text_strengths:
The main strengths of the paper are the strong and convincing experimental results, supported by excellent ablation studies and insightful analysis. The empirical evaluation is particularly thorough, with carefully designed experiments that clearly demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed M2C framework. The annotation efficiency analysis is a highlight of the work: the results show that the hybrid uncertainty estimation not only improves active selection of hard samples but also enables a meaningful early exit strategy for easy samples, which are confidently segmented via concept aligned embeddings before further updates. This design leads to consistently better performance under fixed annotation budgets and clearly outperforms random sampling baselines, while the full system achieves the best annotation quality with minimal human effort. The ablation studies further strengthen the paper by showing that both uncertainty components contribute complementarily, and that combining them is essential for efficiently distinguishing easy and hard samples to reduce annotation cost. 
In addition, the paper is very well written with a clear and compelling storyline that guides the reader through motivation, method, and results in a coherent way. The qualitative and quantitative results are well aligned and reinforce each other, and the comparisons on annotation efficiency provide a strong practical argument for the system’s usefulness in real medical labeling workflows. Overall, the presentation is strong and contributes significantly to readability and impact.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The main weakness of the paper lies in the limited mathematical grounding and interpretability of the proposed uncertainty formulation. While entropy is a well established and theoretically sound uncertainty measure, the concept geometry prompting inconsistency term is less rigorously motivated, making the final hybrid uncertainty score feel somewhat heuristic despite strong empirical performance. 
Closely related to this, it remains unclear whether the resulting uncertainty estimates are well calibrated. The paper does not provide a thorough analysis of calibration quality or position the proposed uncertainty formulation within the broader landscape of uncertainty estimation methods in medical imaging. This makes it difficult to assess how the method relates to established probabilistic or Bayesian approaches. 
In addition, the overall algorithm resembles iterative refinement strategies similar in spirit to expectation maximization, but this connection is not explicitly discussed or formalized. A clearer theoretical framing could improve interpretability and strengthen the methodological contribution. 
Finally, the dataset selection is somewhat limited, relying on relatively standard and potentially dated benchmarks, with limited diversity in modalities and task settings. Broader evaluation would improve confidence in the generality of the findings. Overall, while the engineering design is strong and the empirical results are convincing, the main limitation is the lack of deeper mathematical rigor, calibration analysis, and broader validation.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper presents a strong and well executed contribution to training free few shot medical image segmentation and annotation using SAM3.The experimental results are particularly convincing, with a carefully designed evaluation protocol, strong ablation studies, and clear gains in annotation efficiency under limited human labeling budgets. The proposed hybrid uncertainty estimation and early exit mechanism are shown to be highly effective in practice, and the empirical evidence is consistent across settings. In addition, the paper is very well written with a clear storyline that makes both the motivation and technical approach easy to follow.
The main limitations are relatively minor compared to these strengths. The hybrid uncertainty formulation is only partially theoretically grounded, as the concept geometry prompting inconsistency term is heuristic in nature and its connection to established uncertainty theory is not fully developed. It also remains unclear whether the resulting uncertainty estimates are well calibrated, and a deeper comparison to standard uncertainty estimation frameworks in medical imaging would strengthen the positioning of the method. Finally, the dataset selection is somewhat limited in diversity, which slightly restricts conclusions about broad generalization.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: While I may have emphasized the strengths in my initial review, the rebuttal did not change my overall assessment. The paper presents a solid and well-executed contribution.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: In this paper, the authors introduce a new approach to adapt pretrained segmentation models for medical images in order to solve the medical few-shot labeling challenge. SAM-3 pretrained model is extended with learned concept embeddings. A hybrid uncertainty estimation is introduced as well to be able to carry out active learning. The authors demonstrate the superiority of this approach by achieving SOTA results in Kvasir-SEG and ISIC-2017.
reviews.text_strengths:
(*) The considered task is practically relevant. With the emergence of strong text promptable feature extractors like SAM3, the idea of repurposing those model for domain specific medical applications is timely. The authors identify the SAM3 text prompting shortcomings for fine-grained medical concepts.
(*) The training is very efficient computationally since it solely requires learning the concept embedding. This is a major advantage compared to methods requiring auxiliary networks or feature matchers.
(*) The combination of prediction entropy and concept-geometry inconsistency is well-motivated and also technically sound. Empirically, it shows complementary benefits for the overall quality.
(*) strong empirical results: regardless of any other consideration, the combination shows a superior performance to any other active learning approach. it is very likely that this approach also generalizes to other domains. Given the publicly available code, testing this approach would be a low-hanging fruit.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(*) The concept embedding search is per se not new. It is functionally identical to prompt tuning or textual inversion (Gal et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2022), both cited by the authors. Extending pretrained SAM3 with this concept remains limited in novelty.
(*) Claiming a training free method is not correct. The authors still have to train the concept encoding. it is definitely a minor fraction with very low computational implications but the authors are deliberately overselling their method.
(*) Setting the threshold arbitrarily to 0.6 without an appropriate sensitivity analysis raises concerns about stability.
(*) Critical evaluation: It is important to have a baseline using SAM3 with optimized text prompts. either manually or automatically. As of now it’s unclear whether the learnable embedding E is actually superior to simply finding better text descriptions.
(*) Unfair comparison: SAM3 vs. SAM-H baselines. SAM3 is a larger and stronger than the original SAM model. As of now the contribution of the M2C is questionable since the performance gains may reflect just the stronger base model.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Based on the limited novelty and evaluation concerns explained in the weaknesses, I tend to no accept this paper.

reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
Strengths of the rebuttal include:
1-fixing some of the missing ablations/baselines,
2-clarity in explaining the annotation process,
