Weaknesses of the rebuttal include:
1-Theory supporting the notion of uncertainty,
2-Calibration issues,
3-Originality compared to prompt tuning/textual inversion,
It is important that the “training-free” claim be addressed, as it is included in the title of the paper.
In general, the paper is extremely practical while theoretically vulnerable.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper describes an approach to reduce the dependency of the Segment Anything Model on geometric or textual priors/inputs.
The proposed approach relies on segmentation based on concepts derived from text prompts, as introduced in SAM3.The method aims to reduce the annotation burden.
reviews.text_strengths:
The proposed approach requires only a few parameters to be trained.
The evaluation is well conducted, and the ablation study is useful.
The performance of the proposed approach is strong, requiring only a small number of annotations.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper claims that no external modules or additional parameters are required, which is somewhat misleading. In practice, the proposed approach relies on training concept embeddings. Even if this approach requires only a few examples, as suggested by the results, some training is still necessary.
The approach is evaluated on relatively simple segmentation tasks. For a fair comparison, it would be interesting to compare it with a baseline model such as nnU-Net, or a similar method, under the same data conditions. In addition, Figure 3 is unclear. Why do human annotations start at 250 and 180, respectively? These values correspond to around 30% of the ISIC dataset, and basic active learning approaches might achieve similar performance with the same amount of data.
The paper does not clearly explain how human annotation is simulated. For images with low confidence, are the annotations applied to the entire image (based on ground truth), or only to the low-confidence regions? Evaluating the number of corrected pixels could be an interesting additional metric.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper constructs Mask to Concept, a framework designed to adapt SAM2/3 for few-shot medical image segmentation by optimizing concept embeddings to automate the prompting process. The strengths of the work lie in its high computational efficiency, strong empirical performance across multiple benchmarks, and a well-motivated hybrid uncertainty estimation module that effectively reduces manual annotation effort. However, reviewers have raised concerns regarding the “training-free” claim given the optimization of embeddings, the lack of rigorous mathematical grounding for the uncertainty formulation, and the need for fairer comparisons against optimized text prompts or stronger baselines like nnU-Net. Additionally, further clarification is required regarding the simulation of human corrections and the sensitivity of the chosen hyperparameters. With average scores (6, 3, 4) leaning toward a rebuttal to address these methodological clarifications and validation concerns.

Based on the outcome of the rebuttal process, two reviewers assigned an “Accept” score, while one reviewer assigned a “Reject.” Notably, although Reviewer 2 recommended rejection, he also emphasized that “the paper is extremely practical”. The authors should clearly clarify the “training-free” claim in the camera-ready version. Given that the overall sentiment is positive, the inclination is to “Accept” this paper.

The paper proposes to adapt SAM3 for few-shot medical annotation by optimizing a concept embedding from a few labeled masks and using a hybrid uncertainty score for human-in-the-loop sample selection. While the idea is potentially useful, the current evidence is not sufficient for acceptance.
My main concern is that the claimed contribution is not convincingly isolated. The method is described as “training-free,” but it still performs gradient-based optimization of a learnable embedding using labeled masks, which is closer to test-time prompt/embedding tuning than a truly training-free method. The novelty over existing prompt tuning, textual inversion, and few-shot SAM personalization methods is not clearly established.
The experimental comparison is also problematic. M2C uses SAM3, whereas the SAM-based baselines use SAM-H, so the reported gains may largely reflect the stronger backbone rather than the proposed concept-search mechanism. The paper lacks essential controls, such as direct SAM3 text prompting, SAM3 with box/point prompts, SAM3 with naive learned prompts, and variants that isolate the effect of concept embedding optimization from the effect of the backbone.
The annotation-efficiency evaluation is not fully convincing. Human corrections are simulated with ground-truth masks, and the overall quality metric includes human-labeled samples, which can inflate the apparent efficiency. The uncertainty module uses heuristic components and a fixed threshold, but there is no calibration analysis or robust validation that HUE reliably identifies truly difficult or low-quality cases across datasets.

The paper presents a framework for few-shot medical image annotation with SAM3 by optimizing concept embeddings and using hybrid uncertainty estimation to reduce manual annotation effort. Although concerns remain about the “training-free” wording and theoretical grounding of uncertainty, the rebuttal clarified these issues. Overall, the work is empirically strong and sufficiently valuable for acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank all reviewers for constructive comments and for recognizing the ‘practical relevance’(R2), ‘efficient computation’ (R2,R3), ‘superior performance’ (R1,R2,R3), ‘thorough/well evaluation’ (R1,R3). Below we address the specific concerns:
R2(Q2)&R3(Q1): We agree that “training-free” may be interpreted too broadly. Our intended meaning is that M2C requires neither conventional few-shot segmentation (FSS) training nor fine-tuning SAM3.Thus, it is more precisely described as FSS-pretraining-free or SAM3-retraining-free, rather than strictly “training-free”. We appreciate the reviewers’ comments and will revise the wording to avoid misleading.
R1:
Q1&Q2: U_CGPI is indeed not derived as a formal Bayesian uncertainty estimator. However, we would like to clarify that many effective uncertainty criteria in practical annotation and active learning systems are heuristic or task-driven not strictly probabilistic. We evaluated calibration quality through an uncertainty-error correlation analysis using 1−Dice as the real error. Spearman correlations for U_ENT,U_CGPI,and U_HU are 0.76,0.73,and 0.81,respectively.The results show that U_CGPI is well calibrated with real errors, while the hybrid score provides the most reliable uncertainty ranking.
Q3: Thanks for this insightful observation. Our system indeed shares a conceptual connection with EM. The “E-step” infers latent variables (predicting pseudo-masks) using the current concept embedding, while the “M-step” optimizes it. We agree that EM perspective enhances our theoretical foundation and will include it in the revision.
Q4: Due to space constraints, this work evaluates two representative datasets with different modalities and lesions. We acknowledge this limitation and will verify on broader datasets in future work.
R2:
Q1: Although concept embedding search plays a similar role to prior works, our novelty lies in bridging SAM3’s text-centric design and the lack of fine-grained medical textual priors using few-shot samples. This simple pipeline achieves strong performance and generalization compared with more complex methods, suggesting a promising direction. More importantly, M2C is not an isolated embedding search algorithm; its core contribution is coupling this mechanism with HUE to form an efficient closed-loop annotation system.
Q3: The 0.6 threshold was empirically selected, not arbitrary. On Kvasir-SEG, lowering it to 0.5 increases 0.26× manual cost for only a 0.5% Dice gain, whereas raising it to 0.7 reduces 0.34× cost but drops Dice by 5.3%. Thus, 0.6 is a cost-effective trade-off, and the system is relatively insensitive to moderate variations around this threshold. SOTA results on two datasets with different modalities and lesion types further support generalizability.
Q4: We further tested 10 manual and LLM-generated text prompts.The best Dices were only 0.24(Kvasir-SEG) and 0.38(ISIC-2017),confirming SAM3’s limited medical text understanding, aligning with recent work [1].
[1]MedSAM3:Delving into Segment Anything with Medical Concepts
Q5: Existing methods mainly rely on SAM’s geometric prompting capability, and this improvement from SAM to SAM3 is limited. After replacing their backbones with SAM3, M2C remains superior: Kvasir 1-shot: ProtoSAM(73.7), Matcher(71.5), SPFS-SAM(71.1), MAUP(48.2), Ours(76.3); ISIC 1-shot: ProtoSAM(68.6), Matcher(57.9), SPFS-SAM(56.3), MAUP(56.5), Ours(75.9).
R3:
Q2: On Kvasir-SEG, nnU-Net trained with 1/5/10 annotations obtains Dice of 25.8/34.6/42.6, respectively, significantly lower than M2C. Detailed annotation-efficiency curves are provided in the code link.
It is noted that the human annotation starts from x=0, not x=250 or 180 in Fig.3.The bottom region without model-performance curves is cropped only for space efficiency.
Q3: For reliability, we use the provided GT masks to simulate human-corrected annotations. The total corrected pixels for each method in Fig.3(a): M2C(15.2M), SPFS-SAM(22.4M), Multiverseg(51.1M).

title: Mask-Guided Attention Regulation for Anatomically Consistent Counterfactual CXR Synthesis
abstract: Counterfactual generation for chest X-rays (CXR) aims to simulate plausible pathological changes while preserving patient-specific anatomy. However, diffusion-based editing methods often suffer from structural drift, where stable anatomical semantics propagate globally through attention and distort non-target regions, and unstable pathology expression, since subtle and localized lesions induce weak and noisy conditioning signals. We present an inference-time attention regulation framework for reliable counterfactual CXR synthesis. An anatomy-aware attention regularization module gates self-attention with organ masks, confining structural interactions to anatomical ROIs and reducing unintended distortions. A pathology-guided module enhances pathology-token cross-attention within target anatomical regions during early denoising and performs lightweight latent corrections driven by an attention-concentration energy, enabling controllable lesion localization and extent. Extensive evaluations on CXR datasets show improved anatomical consistency and more precise, controllable pathological edits compared with standard diffusion editing, supporting localized counterfactual analysis and data augmentation for downstream tasks.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes an inference-time attention regulation framework for counterfactual CXR synthesis, aiming to improve anatomical consistency and localization of pathological edits in diffusion-based image editing. Instead of modifying the model architecture or training procedure, the method introduces a set of test-time interventions during diffusion sampling, including anatomy-aware self-attention gating based on organ masks, pathology-guided cross-attention reweighting, and a lightweight latent correction step
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Well-motivated problem formulation
The paper addresses a known issue in diffusion-based medical image editing, namely structural drift during generation, and clearly articulates the challenges of maintaining anatomical consistency while introducing localized pathological changes.
2.Training-free and flexible design
A key strength of the method is that it operates entirely at inference time without requiring retraining or additional learnable modules. This makes the approach flexible and potentially easier to apply across datasets or domains compared to methods that rely on task-specific training.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Unclear applicability to high-resolution medical imaging
Chest X-rays are typically high-resolution images (e. g. , 1024×1024 or higher), which are important for detecting subtle pathological patterns. However, the paper does not clearly specify the resolution at which the method operates or evaluate its performance at clinically relevant resolutions. If the method is limited to lower resolutions, it may only capture coarse changes, significantly limiting its clinical usefulness.
2.Limited clinical relevance of the constrained editing setup
The method constrains generation within lung regions using segmentation masks. While this may improve quantitative metrics by restricting modifications to a smaller area, most clinically relevant findings in CXR are already concentrated in the lung region. Therefore, preserving or improving non-target regions (outside the lungs) may have limited clinical value, and the reported gains may not fully reflect meaningful improvements for diagnosis.
3.Questionable clinical utility of counterfactual CXR generation
The clinical motivation for counterfactual generation in CXR is not sufficiently clarified. While counterfactual analysis is often valuable in complex diseases with multiple interacting factors or unclear mechanisms (e. g. , neurodegenerative disorders), its role in CXR—where many findings are more directly observable—remains unclear. The paper does not convincingly demonstrate what specific clinical questions or workflows this approach would support.
4.Lack of clear clinical application scenario
Although the paper claims potential benefits such as data augmentation and interpretability, it does not provide concrete clinical use cases or evaluations (e. g. , reader studies or downstream clinical tasks) to support these claims. As a result, the practical impact of the generated counterfactual images remains uncertain.

reviews.text_contribution: The proposed method utilizes two attention control mechanisms to ensure structural consistency and precise lesion editing in chest X-rays. First, Anatomy-aware Attention Regularization prevents structural drift that may occur during lesion correction by suppressing self-attention regions using organ masks. Simultaneously, Pathology-guided Attention Regulation amplifies cross-attention of pathology tokens within the target region and performs attention energy-based latent spatial correction to precisely control the location and extent of minute lesions. Through these complementary approaches, it generates counterfactual images that reflect accurate pathological changes while preserving the patient’s intrinsic structure.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Operating solely at inference time, which provides computational efficiency.
2.The lung masks utilized in this study are automatically segmented based on high image contrast, facilitating the acquisition of large-scale data and ensuring high accuracy without the need for manual annotation by medical specialists. Furthermore, the characteristics of the lungs, which possess stability in position and shape, contribute to the model learning consistent spatial reference points.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Table 1 shows only marginal performance gains over prior work. The proposed method fails to outperform ‘ProgEmu’ on both LPIPS and FID (bold formatting appears to be incorrectly applied in the table).
2.The paper cites InstructX2X[18] in the introduction ‘Structural instability’. Given that InstructX2X adopts a similar mask-and-prompt-based editing strategy, it is recommend to be included as a baseline in the SOTA comparison of Table 1.
3.In Figure 2, cardiomegaly represents pathological enlargement of the heart, and thus the pathology token’s attention should be concentrated on the cardiac region. However, since Omega is derived from the lung segmentation mask (M_anat), the cardiac region either falls entirely outside the mask or is only indirectly captured at the boundary where the lung and heart overlap. As a result, the cross-attention amplification (Eq. 6) cannot accurately target the cardiac region, and the self-attention gating (Eq. 5) may even suppress information flow toward the heart. It would be worth clarifying which specific design choice accounts for the visually plausible ‘mild cardiomegaly’ result shown in Figure 2.
4.The qualitative results for ‘mild pleural effusion’ and ‘mild cardiomegaly’ in Figure 2, much like Table 1, make it difficult to clearly identify the advantages of the proposed method over prior work. Given that attention modulation is the central methodological contribution targeting localized pathology, it is recommended to include attention map visualizations. (Specifically to verify whether attention is indeed concentrated on the target region and whether leakage into non-editing regions is effectively suppressed.)
5.The first contribution stated in the Introduction claims “~reduce repeated training and maintenance costs under cross-device and cross-domain shifts, improving generality and controllability”. It is unclear which aspect of the proposed method substantiates this claim of improved generalization, and no supporting experiments across different devices or domains appear to be provided.

reviews.text_ethics:
1.The results in Table 1 raise concerns about whether the proposed method offers meaningful gains over SOTA, and whether the core contributions are being adequately captured by the evaluation metrics.
2.M_anat is limited to lung segmentation masks, effectively constraining the spatial prior Omega to only three conditions (left, right, and bilateral lung). More fundamentally, these conditions are fixed prior to inference through simple text keyword parsing, meaning Omega is assigned independently of where the diffusion model actually responds to the given instruction. This implicitly assumes that the model’s editing intent aligns with the predefined organ mask, an assumption that does not always hold. As mentioned earlier, cardiomegaly is a representative counterexample, and based on the dataset used, pleural effusion and others could be further considered.

This paper was reviewed by three experts in the field. The initial recommendations were one Weak Accept and two Weak Rejects. After the rebuttal, two reviewers recommended acceptance, while one reviewer maintained a Reject recommendation. While the paper has some limitations regarding clinical utility and application, it also demonstrates several strengths, including well-motivated problem formulation and training-free attention regulation design. Therefore, the paper is recommended for acceptance to MICCAI 2026.The authors are encouraged to incorporate the necessary changes discussed during the rebuttal process into the final camera-ready version.
The authors addressed some of the reviewers’ major concerns. However, the paper presentation requires improvement in organization and clarity.

author_feedback_text:
We appreciate reviewers’ comments and grouped the responses below.
Reply@R1/R3-Clinical utility:
We do not position counterfactual CXR generation as replacing radiological diagnosis, and will clarify this scope in the final version. Its value is to create controlled “what-if” pairs that preserve patient anatomy while selectively changing a target pathology. These pairs support shortcut-bias inspection and audit whether diagnostic AI relies on the intended lesion rather than background, acquisition style, or unrelated anatomy, and can support augmentation for underrepresented findings. Thus, preserving non-target regions is central to counterfactual validity. We agree expert studies would further validate clinical usefulness, while this work focuses on anatomy-consistent and pathology-controllable generation.
Reply@R1/R2/R3-Resolution and generality:
Our experiments use 512×512 images, as stated in the implementation details. This is a practical setting for latent-diffusion editing and enables fair comparison with diffusion baselines under feasible memory cost. We agree this should not be interpreted as diagnostic-resolution clinical deployment, especially for subtle findings, and will make this limitation clearer in the final version. Also, our “generality” claim refers to regulating attention at inference time without retraining new control branches for each setting, not to an empirically proven cross-device or domain performance gain. The submitted evidence mainly supports inference-time controllability in CXR; high-resolution and broader cross-domain validation remain important future directions.
Reply@R2-ROI prior and cardiomegaly:
We clarify that M_anat/Ω is not lung-only. Sec. 2.3 states that organ masks include “left/right lung and heart,” and M_ROI is selected or combined from them using anatomical cues in the text. Thus, Ω is not restricted to left/right/bilateral lung: lung or pleura findings use lung ROIs, while cardiomegaly uses the heart/cardiac-silhouette ROI. Ω is not designed to automatically discover lesion locations from the model response; it is an interpretable anatomical prior for constraining where a specified counterfactual edit should occur. For shape-changing findings such as cardiomegaly, the ROI is a soft prior and can include the cardiac boundary/margin rather than a rigid original mask, allowing plausible enlargement of the cardiac silhouette. The model response is still involved through pathology-token cross-attention: Eq. 7 measures how token attention aligns with Ω, and Eq. 9 corrects the latent trajectory according to this concentration rather than blindly forcing pixels to change. If the selected ROI mismatches the target pathology, regulation may be less effective; this is a limitation of ROI-based regulation rather than a contradiction of the method.
Reply@R2-Metrics and baselines:
We thank R2 for catching a clerical bolding error in Table 1: ProgEmu is better on LPIPS and FID, and the boldface should be corrected; this does not affect the reported values. Our claim is a trade-off among pathology alignment, structural preservation, realism, and inference-time flexibility: our method achieves the best Conf and CLIP-I while remaining competitive on LPIPS/FID without training extra control branches. For counterfactual editing, lower LPIPS/FID may reflect conservative editing or realism, but not necessarily successful target-pathology realization. The ablation also supports this: removing pathology cross-attention reduces Conf/CLIP-I, while removing anatomy regularization reduces SSIM. Attention-map visualization would clarify the mechanism and, if space permits, can be included in the final version. Our baselines cover major paradigms including inpainting, progressive editing, instruction-based generation, and multimodal autoregressive counterfactual generation; InstructX2X trains a local editing model, whereas our method performs training-free inference-time attention regulation.

title: MASurv: Risk-Conditional Martingale Adversarial Training for Calibrated Multi-slide Survival Prediction in Whole-Slide Histopathology Images
abstract: Survival prediction from whole slide images (WSIs) is central to computational pathology, yet existing multiple instance learning (MIL) methods optimise exclusively for discrimination, with no explicit calibration objective. Miscalibration is especially harmful in clinical deployment, where systematic prediction errors across patient subgroups lead to inequitable risk estimates. We present MASurv, which augments discrete-time survival training with an Adversarial Conditional Moment Test (ACMT) on counting-process residual increments, directly encoding the calibration condition as a moment-orthogonality restriction decomposed locally in time within matched risk strata. A second ACMT task regularises within-patient prediction inconsistency for multi-slide patients. On our internal institutional cohort (662 patients, 5-fold cross-validation (CV)), MASurv achieves the best ICI = 0.096 and WG-ICI = 0.188, a 25% subgroup-calibration reduction over the NLL-only baseline (Cohen’s d = −1.54, very large effect). More critically, on zero-shot internal→TCGA-LUAD transfer (509 patients), MASurv is the only method retaining both discrimination (C-index = 0.680 ± 0.044) and calibration (D-cal p = 0.143, ICI = 0.079 ± 0.002); all baselines collapse (ICI > 0.36, D-cal p ≈ 0).
subject_areas: Applications -> Outcome Prediction / Prognosis / Longitudinal Modeling

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes MASurv, a calibration-oriented survival prediction framework for whole-slide histopathology. The key idea is to enforce conditional calibration through adversarial conditional moment testing on counting-process residual increments, together with an auxiliary multi-slide consistency objective. Results on an internal SUNY cohort and zero-shot transfer to TCGA-LUAD suggest improved calibration, especially in terms of ICI, WG-ICI, and D-calibration, while maintaining competitive discrimination.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in WSI survival modeling: calibration rather than pure ranking performance. The method is theoretically motivated by counting-process martingale residuals and evaluates both internal and external generalization. The inclusion of subgroup calibration analysis and ablations is appreciated.

1.The paper lacks comparisons with methods that explicitly optimize prediction calibration, such as SCMIL[1] and X-CAL[2] (the latter is also mentioned in the limitations section). 
2.The writing and presentation of the paper would benefit from further improvement to enhance overall readability.

Scmil: Sparse context-aware multiple instance learning for predicting cancer survival probability distribution in whole slide images[C]//International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland, 2024: 448-458.
[2] Goldstein M, Han X, Puli A, et al. X-cal: Explicit calibration for survival analysis[J]. Advances in neural information processing systems, 2020, 33: 18296-18307.

reviews.text_strengths:
(1) The problem is important and timely: moving beyond C-index to calibrated risk prediction, especially subgroup calibration, is clinically meaningful.
(2) The method is well motivated: using martingale residuals for calibration is principled, and residual-level adversarial training is better justified than feature-level approaches.
(3) The experimental protocol is strong: patient-level splits, 5-fold CV, zero-shot external evaluation, multiple calibration metrics, and informative ablations.
(4) The external results are compelling: MASurv is the only method that maintains both discrimination and calibration under zero-shot transfer, which is highly relevant for deployment.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(1) Missing calibration-specific baselines: the lack of comparison with methods such as X-CAL or post-hoc recalibration makes it unclear whether gains come from ACMT specifically or from optimizing calibration in general.
(2) Missing matched baseline on external data: the identical NLL-only baseline is not reported on TCGA, which weakens the claim that ACMT improves cross-institution calibration.
(3) Limited generalization evidence: results are based on a single disease, dataset pair, and encoder, which is insufficient to fully support broad claims of cross-institution calibration transfer.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes MASurv, a calibration-oriented survival MIL method for WSIs. The key idea is to use adversarial conditional moment testing (ACMT) on martingale residual increments to improve subgroup calibration and multi-slide consistency. The topic is important and the problem setting is interesting.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful gap. Most prior WSI survival work optimizes NLL and reports C-index, whereas this paper explicitly targets calibration and worst-group calibration. That is a worthwhile direction and clinically relevant. The external zero-shot TCGA results further underscore the importance, as MASurv achieves much better ICI/WG-ICI and is the only method with non-rejected D-calibration in the external setting.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The paper omits important details, which hurts clarity and makes the method harder to follow. The related work section feels incomplete and lacks a clear logical flow, especially in motivating the adversarial design. The experiments miss the relevant calibration baseline, which weakens the empirical support for the main claims.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Here are some questions:
1.Eq. (1) is introduced without notation explanation, which hurts readability; moreover, the claim that systematic non-zero correlation is “equivalent” to subgroup miscalibration appears too strong and would need a more careful justification.
2.The motivation for the adversarial formulation is insufficiently explained. The paper states that calibration is enforced adversarially, but does not clarify why an adversarial critic is necessary or preferable to simpler moment-matching penalties.
3.The related-work section is not well connected, especially the adversarial-training paragraph, which distinguishes the method from domain-adversarial learning but does not clearly motivate the proposed adversarial design.
4.Fig. 1 is hard to parse and appears inconsistent with the main text (“stage” in the figure vs. “slide count” in Sec. 3.3).
5.The method uses sex, ECOG, and slide count as nuisances, and the evaluation also emphasizes groups based on sex / ECOG / slide-count. But the data section says the cohort includes other covariates such as age and Charlson Comorbidity Index. Why were these three chosen, and why were others excluded? Or did I miss something?
6.The optimization objective is not written rigorously: Eq. (7) suggests a single minimization, while Sec. 3.3 states that the critic maximizes the ACMT objective. The roles of the last two terms are not clearly explained. In particular, the paper does not make it sufficiently clear how L_consist and L_ent are defined, why they are needed, and how they interact with the main ACMT objective.
7.X-CAL is discussed as a relevant prior calibration method, yet the empirical comparison is deferred without sufficient justification.

My score is mainly driven by three concerns: an unclear motivation for the adversarial training design, limited clarity and rigor in the method presentation, and the lack of direct comparison with other relevant calibration methods. Although the problem is important and the results are promising, these issues make the current version less convincing than it could be.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I lean toward borderline accept. The rebuttal addresses most of my concerns, especially regarding notation, adversarial motivation, covariate choice, and the optimization objective. However, my support depends on whether the camera-ready version actually incorporates the promised clarifications, as several technical details remain insufficiently clear in the current submission.
reviews.text_ethics: The manuscript explicitly names the source institution for the internal cohort. In the paper, it shows as “SUNY (internal cohort). 662 lung cancer patients, SUNY Upstate Medical University” on Page 5.If this dataset is not publicly available (I’m not sure if it is a public dataset), could this potentially raise a double-blind anonymization concern under MICCAI policy? This may be worth checking.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper proposes an approach for multi-slide survival prediction for histopathology image analysis with improved calibration.
Reviewers highlight the importance of model calibration and the overall motivation within the paper. Ablation studies are seen as valuable, and external results for zero-shot transfer as seen as strong.
Reviewers are missing comparisons with explicit prediction calibration methods such as X-CAL or SCMIL, including for zero-shot prediction on the external cohort. Additionally, the motivation of the adversarial method is not fully clear.
In their rebuttal, authors should more clearly explain why no comparison was conducted with methods such as X-CAL or with post-hoc recalibration. They should further explain the motivation for the adversarial formulation more clearly.
Of note, the goal of the rebuttal should not be to add additional comparison methods or similar, as these results cannot be sufficiently assessed by the reviewers within the rebuttal process.

The rebuttal addressed important questions regarding methodological details and comparison methods, with a reasonable reply also to reviewer #1 who did not update their assessment. I therefore lean towards accept.
Reasonable reviewer comments have been addressed.

Thank you the authors for the detailed rebuttal and clarifications. The rebuttal addressed many concerns effectively, particularly around the motivation for adversarial calibration, positioning relative to X-CAL and SCMIL, methodological clarity, and the distinction between feature invariance and residual calibration. The experimental evaluation was generally viewed as comprehensive, and the proposed objective is supported by consistent ablation evidence.
Reviewers acknowledged improved clarity and stronger positioning after rebuttal. Remaining concerns are largely about presentation and completeness of technical explanations rather than fundamental validity of the approach, and I recommend the authors to address these appear in the camera-ready version.
Overall, the paper presents a technically sound and well-motivated contribution with convincing empirical evidence for robust calibration under cross-institutional transfer. I recommend Accept.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the Reviewers and Area Chair. We address AC’s two priorities first.
1.(AC-1, R1-W1, R2-W1, R4-Q7) X-CAL, SCMIL, post-hoc recalibration.
Post-hoc recalibration is not designed for subgroup-conditional calibration under censoring and typically requires held-out calibration data from the deployment distribution, unavailable in zero-shot transfer (§4.3). X-CAL [15]: Goldstein et al. ([15] §6) state conditional calibration is “in general infeasible even to measure (let alone optimize) … without strong assumptions”; X-CAL is a marginal D-calibration proxy with no time-local moment and is not formulated for multi-slide MIL; adapting it would test adaptation choices, not the calibration principle. ACMT targets a different statistical object: conditional residual-moment orthogonality at risk-stratum level. SCMIL [Yang MICCAI’24] trains censored NLL on a Gaussian-mixture head (Eq. 9) with no calibration objective in its training loss; its contributions are architectural (SoftFilter, SCSA sparse attention, RegisterMDN), not a residual-calibration objective comparable to ACMT.
2.(AC-2, R4-Q2) Adversarial motivation.
Conditional calibration requires E[ΔM̂|f(W)]=0 for every measurable f, an infinite family of moment constraints (GMM/conditional-moment view, §3.3, [8]). A scalar fixed-direction penalty enforces only one such f and misses non-linear and interaction violations; the critic D_ψ implements a worst-case test over its parametric class. Fig. 5 (§4.4) corroborates: ACMT→BCE raises ICI; Feature-adversary on z_i (closest DAT analogue) gives the worst WG-ICI; Global-moment and No-conditioning degrade ICI; No-adversary raises ICI. The form of the objective, not its mere presence, drives the gain.
3.(R2-W2) Matched NLL-only baseline on TCGA.
Table 1 isolates mechanism on SUNY: NLL Baseline ICI=0.117, WG-ICI=0.249 vs. MASurv 0.096/0.188.On TCGA, three NLL-trained MIL baselines span architecture at constant loss (ABMIL ICI=0.392, DTFD-MIL 0.366, DeepAttnMISL 0.382; D-cal p≈0); MASurv (ICI=0.079, D-cal p=0.143) remains calibrated. With SUNY↔TCGA Spearman ρ=−0.70, the gap supports lack-of-calibration-objective over architecture-specific failure as the explanation. We agree the exact λ_ACMT=0 row on TCGA would be informative.
4.(R2-W3) Generalization scope.
SUNY (n=662) and TCGA-LUAD (n=509) span institution, scanner, population, and label process: the principal calibration-relevant shift axes. We acknowledge a single disease (LUAD) and single encoder; cross-encoder (UNI, GigaPath) and cross-cancer extensions are future directions (§5).
5.(R4-Ethics) Anonymization.
The cohort is de-identified under institutional protocols; the institution name was data provenance only and will be relabeled as an internal institutional cohort in camera-ready. No author names, grant IDs, or identifying acknowledgments are present.
6.(R4-Q1, Q3, Q4, Q5, Q6 and R1-W2) Method clarity and presentation.
L_consist enforces stop-gradient consistency between patient hazards λ̂

The min-max in §3.3 applies to the ACMT terms (Eqs. 5–6) within the summed loss (Eq. 7): critics D_ψA, D_ψB maximise; the model minimises Eq. 7.Sex, ECOG, and slide count cover demographic, clinical, and multi-slide axes; age and CCI overlap with legitimate hazard signal and were excluded to avoid orthogonalizing against true risk.
