title: Maximizing Domain Generalization in Automated Fetal Brain Biometry
abstract: Reliable fetal brain biometry is important for prenatal neurodevelopmental evaluation and disease diagnosis, yet current clinical practice relies largely on manual annotation, which is time-consuming and susceptible to inter-observer variability. While deep learning has been applied to automated biometry, pre-trained models tend to underperform when deployed in unseen clinical environments due to domain shifts. Motivated by the lack of domain adaptation methods specifically tailored to biometry tasks, we propose BioTTA, a backbone-agnostic, source-free unsupervised test-time adaptation (TTA) framework that leverages geometric consistency between landmark heatmaps and regressed biometric scalars as a powerful self-supervisory signal for online adaptation. Specifically, BioTTA jointly optimizes three complementary self-supervised objectives at test time, namely length consistency loss, entropy minimization loss, and boundary-gradient loss, all further constrained by atlas-guided anatomical priors, to enable robust adaptation without target labels or access to source data. Extensive experiments on multi-center datasets demonstrate that BioTTA achieves measurement errors on target domains comparable to or lower than those of supervised fine-tuning, while maintaining expert-level diagnostic performance. Code: https://github.com/birthlab/BioTTA.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses an important topic, namely the reduced performance of AI-based methods for fetal brain biometry analysis in cross-domain settings, due to variations in image characteristics across different sources, as well as intrinsic changes in the fetal brain related to gestational age and pathological conditions. To solve this problem, the authors propose the BioTTA framework, an unsupervised test-time adaptation pipeline that adapts pre-trained models to data from other sources during inference, without the need for manual annotations. Particularly, a backbone is first trained for predicting biometric measurements and landmark heatmaps. Afterwards, the pre-trained backbone is adapted through self-supervised optimization, where the model adapts to unlabeled test samples by minimizing entropy, length consistency, and boundary-gradient losses, incorporating also atlas-informed anatomical priors for landmark heatmap prediction. The authors also developed an automated web-based system that reads a 3D image, extracts the biometric measurements, and generates standardized reports for clinical analysis/evaluation.
reviews.text_strengths: This paper presents several strengths. First, the methodological design is well developed and carefully thought out, resulting in a novel framework for test-time adaptation. In particular, the approach combines different self-supervised objectives that not only leverage landmark heatmap predictions but also incorporate their relationships with biometric lengths and their expected positions along structural edges. Additionally, a structural prior based on an atlas is used to enforce anatomical plausibility. Another strength is the comprehensive evaluation. The authors train the backbone model(s) on a single dataset and perform two types of evaluations, each across two different datasets: a quantitative evaluation (analyzing biometric measurement errors) and a diagnostic evaluation (assessing the final diagnostic performance of the method in conditions such as ventriculomegaly and germinal matrix hemorrhage). They also compare their method with state-of-the-art approaches for the quantitative evaluation and with observer variability for the clinical assessment. Finally, another strength is the application of the proposed method in a web-based system, demonstrating the authors’ intention to translate the approach into clinical practice.
reviews.text_weaknesses: Concerning the weaknesses, despite the strong evaluation presented by the authors, where two out-of-domain datasets were used for quantitative assessment, in one of the datasets only three measurements were evaluated (LFC), whereas 11 measurements were considered in the other (FeTA). Although this still allows the assessment of the method across different datasets, this lack of uniformity in the analysis may raise questions about how the method would perform across a broader set of measurements on the LFC dataset. Another weakness is the modest discussion of the results. While the authors present the results and their main conclusions, the discussion lacks depth and could be improved by adding comprehensive insights.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The authors state that the WCT and FeTA datasets were annotated for all measurements, whereas this was not the case for the LFC dataset, where only landmark annotations for three measurements were used. The authors should clarify why the same level of annotation was not performed for the LFC dataset.
The authors present Figure 3 to illustrate results on example images with different gestational ages (GA). However, no specific discussion is provided in the manuscript regarding this figure. Including such a discussion could strengthen the paper, particularly by highlighting what conclusions can be drawn about the performance of the method across different GA, as well as its advantages compared to other methods under varying GA conditions.
The results section would benefit from more in-depth analysis and interpretation. For example, Table 2 shows that BioTTA does not outperform the senior radiologist (although it is comparable) on the OoD-GMH dataset, while it does outperform on FeTA. This difference in performance should be discussed. Is one dataset more challenging than the other for the method or for the radiologist?

This paper presents a complete and well-structured study addressing an important and timely problem. The proposed methodology is clearly described and introduces an innovative test-time adaptation framework that effectively integrates multiple self-supervised objectives with anatomical priors, resulting in a coherent and well-motivated pipeline. The recommendation is further supported by the strength of the experimental validation and the inclusion of a web-based application, which highlights the potential for clinical translation. While the discussion of the results could be more in-depth (which can be addressed in the rebuttal), and some aspects of the evaluation could benefit from greater uniformity, these limitations do not significantly detract from the overall quality, completeness, and contribution of the paper.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors have responded reasonably well to some of the concerns raised in the initial review, particularly the more direct questions regarding the dataset and the insights obtained from the comparison with the radiologist. These clarifications addressed part of the reviewers’ concerns.
However, the authors did not sufficiently address (or justify) the previously mentioned lack of depth in the discussion section. In particular, the manuscript would still benefit from a more critical analysis of the results and limitations, as highlighted in the first review.
Nevertheless, as also stated in the initial evaluation, the topic addressed by the paper is highly relevant, and the methodological design is well developed and carefully thought out, resulting in a strong framework for test-time adaptation. Considering the overall quality, relevance, and potential impact of the work, the reviewer maintains the recommendation for acceptance.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses an important problem in fetal brain biometry, namely cross-domain generalization, and attempts to solve it under a source-free unsupervised test-time adaptation setting. The authors propose BioTTA, which is intended as a biometry-aware TTA framework. Concretely, the method uses several self-supervised objectives, including a length consistency loss, to adapt the model at test time without target labels. The paper also goes beyond reporting technical metrics and attempts to demonstrate clinical usefulness through comparison with clinical experts.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper tackles an important problem in FeTA biometry and adopts a reasonable constraint setting, namely source-free unsupervised test-time adaptation. The use of a length consistency loss to design a biometry-aware TTA framework is a clear methodological contribution. In addition, the authors attempt to move beyond laboratory-style AI evaluation by comparing BioTTA with clinical experts, which reflects an interest in practical clinical utility. Finally, the ablation study is well designed and clearly shows the contribution of the main components of the proposed method.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The main weakness of this paper is that the comparison framework is not sufficiently fair. In domain adaptation, different paradigms allow access to different kinds of information, and comparison methods should therefore be matched under the same information constraints. For clarity, one can distinguish four settings: (A) OOD detection, which aims to identify whether an input is outside the source distribution; (B) UDA, which uses target data during training; (C) TTA, which uses target input during inference; and (D) SDG, which assumes no access to target information at all. This paper clearly belongs to (C), namely source-free unsupervised test-time adaptation, so the core evaluation should be organized within that setting.
Major weakness 1.Essential baselines for source-free unsupervised TTA are missing
In this setting, I believe the following comparisons are necessary for a fair evaluation.
(i) Source Model
This is the basic baseline and is required to show how the source-pretrained model performs on the target domain without adaptation.
(ii) A generic source-free TTA baseline
TENT is the most direct example. The authors are clearly aware of it and mention it in the paper, yet it is omitted from the reported comparisons. I would be interested in hearing the authors’ reasoning here. For a paper proposing a source-free test-time adaptation method, comparison against a generic baseline such as TENT appears highly relevant unless there is a clear reason why such a comparison would not be appropriate in this setting.
(iii) Common source-free TTA methods used for medical brain image inputs
Although this paper uses dense spatial prediction through heatmaps and landmark localization rather than segmentation, it would still be strongly desirable, or at least worth discussing explicitly, to compare against source-free TTA methods that are commonly used in medical brain imaging. Examples include Karani et al., “Test-time adaptable neural networks for robust medical image segmentation,” atlas-guided TTA for 3D medical segmentation, and one-pass or plug-and-play medical TTA methods such as TestFit. Even if the authors believe that these methods cannot be applied directly to FeTA biometry, the paper should explain why they were not considered appropriate. At present, such an explanation is not provided.
(iv) A source-free TTA method with a similar key idea or with the same target domain, i.e., FeTA
This point is particularly important. Through reference [10], the authors are already aware of a TTA study that is directly related to FeTA or fetal brain MRI morphometry. That study shares substantial overlap with the present paper: fetal brain MRI morphometry, target domain = FeTA, TTA, and the use of anatomy or atlas priors. It is therefore a strong comparable method and should be included experimentally. Differences in backbone, annotation protocol, or exact label setting may exist, but such differences are usually not sufficient to justify complete exclusion. At minimum, the paper should explain why this comparison was not performed.
(v) Ablation over the proposed components
I mention this only to complete the evaluation framework. This is not a weakness. On the contrary, the authors handled this part well.
By contrast, the methods that are actually reported do not match the proposed paradigm.
FetalSynthGen [24] is based on synthetic data augmentation to improve robustness during training. It is not an inference-time online adaptation method(C), and therefore it does not belong to the same source-free TTA setting as the proposed approach. (maybe this is B or D)
DGMLD [8] uses 10 labeled target samples and is therefore target-supervised. It may serve as an upper-bound reference, but it is not an appropriate core baseline for source-free unsupervised TTA. (this is B)
In other words, the key baselines in (ii), (iii), and (iv) are missing, while the reported comparisons mostly involve methods that do not share the same information constraints as the proposed method. As a result, the current experiments do not convincingly show how competitive BioTTA is as a source-free TTA method. Instead, they read more like a list of methods from different paradigms placed in the same table.
Major weakness 2.Table 2 is interesting, but it does not directly validate the claimed advantage of the TTA method
Table 2 is clinically interesting. In our field, it is important not only to compare technical metrics, but also to demonstrate actual clinical usefulness. If designed rigorously and fairly, this kind of evaluation could add substantial value even if the purely technical comparisons were somewhat limited. For that reason, I view Table 2 as potentially very meaningful. However, as currently described, it is not fully clear to me what exactly this table is validating, and I would be interested in the authors’ clarification.
From the paper, my understanding is the following:
BioTTA predicts landmarks and biometric measurements.
Those biometrics are then converted into VM diagnosis, VM grading, and GMH grading using rule-based clinical criteria.
The radiologists, in contrast, directly interpret the MRI scans.
If this interpretation is correct, then Table 2 may not directly test the advantage of BioTTA as a TTA method. Rather, it would compare a full TTA-based biometry pipeline against human readers. That is a different question. In that case, the table would read more as an AI-pipeline-versus-human-reader experiment than as a controlled validation of the proposed TTA method itself. This would not make the evaluation unimportant, but it would make its role in the paper different from what I initially expected.
A fair TTA-oriented evaluation would require at least the following comparisons:
source model biometry → rule-based diagnosis
generic TTA biometry → rule-based diagnosis
BioTTA biometry → rule-based diagnosis
This would allow the reader to assess whether the proposed TTA actually improves downstream diagnostic usefulness relative to other TTA methods or to the source model alone. From a clinical workflow perspective, an even better comparison would be radiologist alone versus radiologist + model measurement assistance. As it stands, Table 2 appears potentially interesting and important, but I am not yet certain how it should be interpreted in relation to the central TTA claim. I would therefore welcome clarification from the authors.
Minor weakness
The authors partially explain why they chose setting (C), but they do not fully answer why this setting is more appropriate than (A), (B), or (D) for the actual clinical deployment scenario. Questions remain, such as: how many optimization steps are acceptable per patient at test time; whether this conflicts with real-time or near-real-time workflow; whether per-patient online updating is operationally acceptable; and whether the setting assumes a continuous target stream or independent one-shot patients. That said, I do not regard this as a major weakness in a short paper, and this point alone would not lead me to reject the submission.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

What matters most to me is not whether the method looks technically fancy, but whether the paper addresses an important problem and evaluates it in a fair and convincing way. This paper clearly addresses an important problem, and I do not think the chosen constraint setting is fundamentally misguided. However, I do feel that several core elements of a fair comparison framework are currently missing or insufficiently explained, especially for a paper that positions itself as a source-free TTA method.
I do not believe that a conference paper must compare against every baseline that a reviewer can imagine. It would be excessive to reject a paper simply because it did not include every recent study under the same constraint setting. However, I do care a great deal about whether the authors selected fair comparison methods within the framework they themselves claim to operate in. If the comparison framework is substantially ambiguous, or if several of its key components are missing, acceptance becomes difficult.
If the authors can convincingly explain why the important comparison groups in (ii)–(iv) were not included, and if they can clarify that Table 2 is indeed meaningful for evaluating BioTTA in a way that differs from my current interpretation, then I believe the paper could still have publishable value. At this stage, my judgment is weak reject, and I would welcome the authors’ rebuttal.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
After reading the rebuttal and the other reviews, I would like to clarify why I maintain my Reject. My concern is not that the paper lacks merit. On the contrary, I agree that the clinical problem is important, that the source-free test-time adaptation setting is well aligned with clinical deployment, and that the proposed method is task-specific and technically meaningful. In particular, the length-consistency idea, differentiable landmark extraction, and the overall biometry-aware adaptation design are reasonable contributions, and the ablation study supports the importance of the proposed components.
However, precisely because the paper is positioned as a source-free unsupervised TTA method, I believe the central evidence should show whether BioTTA is better than appropriate methods under the same information constraints. My concern is not that the authors failed to include every possible baseline or every recent TTA paper. That would be an unreasonable expectation for a MICCAI short paper. Rather, my concern is that the comparison framework does not clearly define a minimal set of comparable methods within the same source-free, unlabeled-target, test-time adaptation regime, nor does it clearly explain why the selected methods are the appropriate ones for this regime.
For example, I would have expected a comparison framework with a logic such as: “among generic TTA methods, we compare against methods whose information constraints and task form are reasonably compatible, such as TENT and possibly other applicable entropy- or stability-based TTA baselines(EATA and SAR); methods requiring a different training protocol, such as auxiliary-task training(eg, TTT), or methods assuming a continual target stream(eg, CoTTA), are excluded for these specific reasons; segmentation-specific medical TTA methods are discussed but not used as direct baselines because their output structure is incompatible with landmark heatmap biometry.” I am not saying that these exact methods must all be included. The key point is that the paper should provide a principled comparable-method selection under the claimed TTA setting.
Regarding TENT specifically, I still do not fully understand the rebuttal explanation, as detailed in the additional comment below. I separated that point as an additional comment because it is not the central basis for my final recommendation. I am willing to accept the authors’ clarification that a TENT-like entropy-minimization baseline was intended to be represented in the ablation study. My main concern is broader: even if TENT is treated as present, the manuscript still does not provide a clear and principled comparator-selection logic for the central source-free TTA claim.
Instead, even after considering the rebuttal, the main comparison remains difficult to interpret from this perspective. The reported methods mix different information regimes: the Source Model is a no-adaptation lower reference; FetalSynthGen is a training-time domain randomization / domain generalization method; DGMLD is presented in a target-supervised or fine-tuned form; supervised fine-tuning uses target labels and is therefore an upper/reference setting; and BioTTA is the only clearly source-free unsupervised TTA method in the main comparison. These methods are useful references, but they do not by themselves establish whether BioTTA is a better TTA method than appropriate alternatives under the same source-free test-time information constraint. In particular, FetalSynthGen and DGMLD may be relevant neighboring methods, but the manuscript does not sufficiently justify why they form the main comparator set for the central source-free TTA claim.
This is why I still cannot conclude that BioTTA is well validated as a TTA method, even though I agree that it is well motivated and task-specific. The strongest statement I can make from the current evidence is that the authors propose a plausible method for an important clinical problem and show strong improvements over a mixture of no-adaptation, domain-randomization, and target-supervised reference settings. However, I do not think the current comparison framework is sufficient to establish that BioTTA is superior as a source-free unsupervised TTA method.
The same issue also applies to the radiologist comparison. I agree that Table 2 is clinically interesting and valuable. It supports the claim that an AI-based biometry-to-rule pipeline can reach diagnostic performance comparable to clinical readers. This is useful evidence for clinical usability. However, as clarified in the rebuttal, Table 2 is not evidence of the specific gain from BioTTA as a TTA method. It does not compare source-model biometry followed by the same rule-based diagnosis, generic-TTA biometry followed by the same rule-based diagnosis, and BioTTA biometry followed by the same rule-based diagnosis. Therefore, Table 2 helps bridge the clinical motivation, but it cannot show that BioTTA improves downstream diagnosis relative to no TTA or to another comparable TTA method. The manuscript language, including statements that BioTTA is benchmarked against radiologists and provides diagnostic reliability comparable to senior radiologists, risks blurring the distinction between the clinical usability of the full pipeline and the TTA-specific contribution.
I have considered the more positive interpretations from the other reviews and the meta-review. I agree with them that the paper addresses an important problem and contains meaningful technical contributions. My recommendation remains Reject not because I require a larger number of baselines, nor because I require one specific method that happens to be missing. Rather, it is because the paper does not yet provide the essential comparison logic needed to support its own central claim: that BioTTA is an effective source-free unsupervised TTA method for this clinical biometry problem.
[Additional comment: TENT clarification]
I have carefully reviewed your response regarding the inclusion of the TENT baseline. Even under these favorable interpretations, I still encounter inconsistencies that make the comparison framework difficult to understand. The rebuttal states that “the ablation setting with only entropy minimization is equivalent to TENT, which alone actually increases error.” I considered several possible interpretations of this statement.
First, if the authors refer to the
Lent
-only row in Table 3, then this does appear to be the natural entropy-only setting, since
Lent
is defined as the entropy minimization loss. However, this row does not increase error. It improves the average error from 2.761 mm for the source model to 1.995 mm, corresponding to a -27.74% relative change. Under this interpretation, the rebuttal’s claim that entropy minimization alone increases error contradicts Table 3.Second, if the authors instead refer to the row that increases error to 3.016 mm (+9.240%), that row includes both Atlas Guide and
Lent
. Therefore, it is not an entropy-only setting and cannot be directly equated with canonical TENT. Under this interpretation, the statement “increases error” is consistent with the number, but the identification with an entropy-only/TENT setting is not.
Third, if the intended TENT-equivalent result is neither of these rows, then I cannot identify where the TENT-equivalent baseline is reported in the submitted manuscript. In that case, the concern about the absence of an explicitly reported generic source-free TTA baseline remains.
Finally, even if the
Lent
-only row is accepted as the TENT-equivalent baseline, it was not reported as an explicitly named TENT baseline in the main comparison table. This matters because TENT is not a minor ablation component but the canonical generic comparator for source-free TTA. Presenting it only as an unnamed ablation row makes it difficult to assess the relative gain of BioTTA over a standard TTA method.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper studies the domain-shift problem in automated fetal brain MRI biometry. The authors note that current clinical practice still relies on manual annotation, which is time-consuming and subject to inter-observer variability, while deep learning models often suffer substantial performance degradation when deployed across centers due to differences in scanners, imaging protocols, field strengths, SVR reconstruction methods, gestational age ranges, and pathology diversity. To address this gap, the paper proposes BioTTA, a backbone-agnostic, source-free unsupervised test-time adaptation framework. The method consists of supervised pretraining on a labeled source domain followed by sample-wise adaptation on unlabeled target data, without access to source data or target labels. Its key insight is that the regression branch, which integrates global features, is more robust to domain shift than the spatially sensitive heatmap branch. Based on this, the framework jointly optimizes three self-supervised losses at test time: a length consistency loss enabled by a sparse weighted differentiable landmark detector to overcome the non-differentiability of argmax and distill geometric knowledge from the regression branch to the heatmap branch; an entropy minimization loss to suppress background noise and sharpen confidence at anatomical landmarks; and a boundary gradient loss to anchor predictions to high-contrast anatomical boundaries. The framework further incorporates atlas-guided anatomical priors by registering gestational-age-matched atlases to the target image space and using the resulting anatomical masks to constrain predicted heatmaps. Experiments on 259 fetal brain MRI scans from five centers show substantial improvements on FeTA and LFC, with performance comparable to or even better than supervised fine-tuning using 10 labeled target samples, and additional diagnostic evaluation is reported on ventriculomegaly and germinal matrix hemorrhage. Overall, the paper presents BioTTA as the first TTA framework for fetal brain biometry, with the differentiable landmark detector and regression-to-heatmap distillation as its main methodological innovations, supported by multi-center validation on both CNN and Transformer backbones.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) The methodological innovation is substantial and task-specific. The sparse weighted differentiable landmark detector resolves the gradient-blocking issue in converting heatmaps to coordinates, and the length consistency loss leverages the task-specific geometric structure of biometry by enforcing consistency between inter-landmark distance and regression output. This regression-to-heatmap distillation is the core algorithmic contribution rather than a simple combination of existing losses. The integration of atlas priors is also reasonable, as the gestational-age-matched fetal brain atlas provides structural constraints to keep landmarks within anatomically plausible regions.
2) The experimental validation is extensive and forms a relatively complete evidence chain. The method is evaluated on 259 images from five centers using two target-domain datasets, FeTA and LFC. It is validated on both a CNN backbone (BioCNN) and a Transformer backbone (BioFormer), suggesting that the approach is not dependent on a specific architecture. The ablation study supports the central claims, with the full framework achieving a 47.12% error reduction over the source-model baseline. Moreover, without target annotations, the method reaches performance comparable to or even better than supervised fine-tuning with 10 labeled target samples.
3) The paper has clear clinical deployment value. The problem definition targets a real bottleneck in fetal brain biometry, namely domain shift in practical cross-center deployment, rather than a purely academic setting. The source-free formulation is well aligned with clinical requirements because it avoids access to source data and target labels, thereby reducing privacy-compliance and annotation-cost barriers. In addition, the paper goes beyond reporting measurement errors and evaluates diagnostic performance on ventriculomegaly diagnosis and germinal matrix hemorrhage grading against three radiologists with different levels of experience, which supports its clinical relevance.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) The core assumption is insufficiently validated, and the potential impact of registration on individualized structural characteristics is not analyzed. The paper assumes that the regression branch is more robust to domain shift than the heatmap branch, but does not provide direct experimental evidence for this claim. More importantly, the atlas registration process may alter individualized brain structural characteristics through nonlinear deformation, potentially distorting morphological measures such as gray matter volume or cortical thickness. The paper does not analyze the effect of registration error on biometry accuracy, nor does it discuss whether degraded registration quality in pathological brains, such as ventriculomegaly or germinal matrix hemorrhage, may introduce systematic bias.
2) The technical boundary with related work is not sufficiently clear, and the novelty requires further clarification. Li et al. (MIDL 2025) has already presented a highly similar anatomy-guided test-time adaptation method for automated fetal brain MRI morphometry that also uses atlas registration to constrain heatmap prediction. Although BioTTA differs in its TTA mechanism and self-supervised loss design, the use of atlas priors is highly overlapping, and the paper does not adequately clarify the technical distinction and contribution difference. In addition, the entropy minimization loss and boundary gradient loss are largely direct applications of the TENT paradigm and common edge-based constraints, respectively, which limits their novelty.
3) The diagnostic evaluation remains limited in scope, and the potential for normative reference construction is not explored. The paper validates only ventriculomegaly diagnosis and germinal matrix hemorrhage grading, without evaluation on other common fetal brain abnormalities such as agenesis of the corpus callosum, cerebellar maldevelopment, or neural tube defects. More importantly, although the adapted model could in principle support automated biometry on unlabeled data from new centers and potentially enable gestational-age-specific normative reference construction, the paper does not discuss this direction or evaluate sensitivity for abnormality detection.
4) The experimental validation and statistical rigor are still limited. The ablation study is conducted only on BioCNN, without corresponding ablations on BioFormer or analysis of interactions among the loss terms. The reported improvements are not accompanied by statistical significance testing, so some smaller gains may not be significant. The fairness of some comparisons is also unclear, for example when DGMLD is used outside its intended metric scope. In addition, the target-domain sample size is limited, with only 50 cases each in FeTA and LFC.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper addresses an important and clinically meaningful problem in fetal brain MRI biometry, namely the degradation caused by domain shift in cross-center deployment. The motivation is strong, as current manual biometry is time-consuming and variable across observers, while existing adaptation methods for this task remain largely unexplored. The main contribution is a source-free test-time adaptation framework that is well matched to realistic clinical deployment. In particular, the sparse weighted differentiable landmark detector and the length consistency loss constitute the central methodological contribution by using task-specific geometric structure to transfer robust information from the regression branch to the heatmap branch. The experimental evidence is also relatively strong, with multi-center validation, two target datasets, two backbone families, ablation analysis, and diagnostic evaluation against radiologists, and the reported performance is comparable to or better than supervised fine-tuning with a small number of target labels. At the same time, there are nontrivial limitations, including insufficient validation of the core robustness assumption, unclear novelty boundaries relative to closely related prior work, limited disease coverage, and incomplete experimental and statistical analysis. Overall, I find the problem important, the core methodological idea meaningful, and the empirical results convincing enough to support a weak accept recommendation despite these concerns.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

meta_reviews.text:
The reviewers find merit in this paper - particularly regarding the importance of the application and novelty (sparse weighted differentiable landmark detector and length consistency loss, task-specific geometric structure) as well as the cross-center aspect and general performed validation. The source-free test time framework is adapted well to clinical need.
There are however major weaknesses / points to be addressed:
more in-depth discussion of the results (incomplete experimental and statistical analysis), insufficient validation of the core robustness assumption, unclear novelty boundaries relative to closely related prior work (BioTTA, missing groups in table 2)

The authors have addressed some of the concerns and there was feedback and discussion with the reviewers. While one reviewer continues to recommend acceptance and mentioned that some concerns have been addressed, they specify themselves that the criticism re lack of depth, more critical analysis were not appropriately addressed and that the acceptance recommendation is mainly based on the topic being highly relevant and the methodology being interesting.
The other reviewer engaged intensively with the rebuttal and maintained (even stronger then before) the recommendation reject arguing similarly that the main concern about methodological clarity and a lack of proof about the main contribution, supervision free TTA.
In summary, significant strengths remain
important application with possible future impact
interesting methodological contribution,
Identified WEAKNESSES remain
lack of proper comparison to the state of the art
insufficient methodological clarity with regard to the exact contributions
lack of critical evaluation/discussion of the results

The reviews are mixed, with two reviewers recommending acceptance and one reviewer maintaining rejection after rebuttal. I agree that Reviewer 2 raises a substantive concern: for a paper positioned as source-free unsupervised test-time adaptation, the comparison framework should more clearly separate no-adaptation, domain generalization, supervised adaptation, and true source-free TTA baselines. The rebuttal only partially resolves this, and the authors should explicitly clarify the TENT-equivalent ablation, the relationship to the atlas-only prior, and the role of Table 2 as clinical-usability evidence rather than direct evidence for the TTA component.
However, I do not consider this issue sufficient for rejection. The paper addresses an important clinical deployment problem in fetal brain biometry, proposes a task-specific and technically meaningful framework, including differentiable landmark extraction and length-consistency-based adaptation, and provides multi-center validation with two backbones, ablations, and clinically oriented diagnostic evaluation. Reviewers 1 and 3 judge the work to be relevant and above the acceptance threshold, and Reviewer 2 also acknowledges the merit, clinical relevance, and meaningful technical design, despite disagreeing on the sufficiency of the validation.

After rebuttal, R2 remains a reject, finding the TENT explanation inconsistent with the reported ablation numbers and the radiologist comparison incapable of isolating the TTA-specific gain. Because of these unresolved fundamental issues, the recommendation is therefore Reject.

author_feedback_text:
# R1:
LFC metrics: Only 3 cerebellar measurement labels are available in the LFC public dataset, which limits our evaluation scope.
BioTTA on OoD-GMH: The OoD-GMH dataset (SS/TSE sequences, NesVoR recon) exhibits a larger domain gap from the source domain in acquisition parameters and reconstruction methods, resulting in more pronounced distribution shift. Nevertheless, BioTTA’s diagnostic results remain comparable to senior radiologists, validating its cross-domain generalization and clinical utility.
# R2:
Regarding the comparison framework:
(ii) TENT is a source-free TTA baseline that updates BN parameters by minimizing entropy. Our method adopts the same update strategy while designing three self-supervised losses: length consistency, entropy minimization, and boundary gradient. Consequently, the ablation setting with only entropy minimization is equivalent to TENT, which alone actually increases error. The next revision will explicitly note that TENT is already included in the ablation framework.
(iii)The method of Karani et al. targets segmentation tasks and is not applicable to landmark heatmap regression-based biometric measurement. Unsupervised TTA methods for brain biometry are extremely scarce. We tested DGMLD [8], a TTA method specifically designed for fetal cerebellar measurement that exploits the cerebellum’s regular geometric contour for boundary pre-training. However, DGMLD’s direct TTA version performed much worse than the source model, likely due to large imaging parameter differences, so we adopted its supervised fine-tuned version.
(iv) To comply with the double-blind policy, we cannot discuss the relationship with the reference [10]. Technically, [10] is equivalent to our atlas-constraint only ablation setting, and our results confirm that the proposed additional losses yield significant improvements over this baseline, which will be explicitly clarified in the next revision.
Regarding Table 2:
(1) BioTTA’s quantitative advantage over other methods is demonstrated in Table 1; (2) Table 2 validates clinical usability by comparing with radiologists; (3) We appreciate this suggestion and will supplement other methods’ diagnostic performance in the next revision. “Preliminary experiments confirm that the source model achieves an accuracy of 0.921 and F1 of 0.924 for VM Diagnosis, and an accuracy of 0.908 and F1 of 0.912 for GMH Grading on the OoD-GMH dataset, both inferior to BioTTA (Acc 0.932, F1 0.934 and Acc 0.919, F1 0.922, respectively).
# R3:
Regression branch robustness: In segmentation domain adaptation, auxiliary prediction of global quantities such as region proportions has been shown to be effective and domain-invariant (Bateson et al., 2020). Inspired by this, we introduce a length regression branch to model more global structural relationships among landmarks (Song et al., 2024). Empirically, this branch provides stable structural guidance for the heatmap branch and improves robustness under domain shift.
Atlas registration constraint: We warp atlas landmarks to the test image space with a 4 mm radius soft constraint to prevent outlier heatmap maxima, which only provides a search region without strictly confining predictions or relying on fine structural details.
MIDL short paper: To comply with the double-blind policy, we cannot discuss the relationship with that paper. Our ablation study demonstrates that the additional losses significantly improve performance over using the atlas alone.
Space limitations: (1) Standard developmental curves with gestational-age-specific percentiles have been constructed but omitted due to space; they will be publicly released with the codebase. (2) Larger-scale validation with broader pathological coverage and more rigorous ablation experiments is planned for future work. (3) OoD annotation is highly time-intensive, requiring experts to manually label anatomical landmarks; we currently annotated 50 cases and will expand in subsequent studies.

title: MBFAD: Benchmarking Balance Function Assessment with Environmental Perturbation and Synergistic Tasks
abstract: Balance function assessment is vital for proactive health monitoring and fall prevention. However, conventional clinical methods are heavily influenced by subjective judgment, leading to potential inconsistencies in evaluation. While the rapid development of wearable technology has provided a significant research hotspot for objective monitoring, current methods rarely identify stability states through activity semantics. Furthermore, the lack of publicly available datasets containing true imbalance states severely hinders the development of robust assessment models. To address these challenges, we introduce MBFAD, a multi-modal benchmark encompassing a ternary paradigm of static, dynamic, and reactive balance activities. MBFAD collects synchronized whole-body kinematics and plantar pressure data from 29 subjects and induces true imbalance states using an environmental perturbation scheme. Based on this, we propose the M^2-Balance Framework, a synergistic multi-task architecture for joint activity recognition and stability analysis. Within M^2-Balance, the HSConv module captures multi-scale features through recursive convolution to provide semantic priors, while the CSConv module utilizes an expected channel damage matrix to mitigate high-dimensional redundancy and identify stability-sensitive channels. Experimental results on SisFall, PDS and MBFAD datasets demonstrate that M^2-Balance outperforms existing models, establishing a fundamental paradigm for modeling synergistic activities and stability in the Balance function assessment domain. The code and dataset will be released at https://github.com/huaingyingqin/MBFAD.
subject_areas: Modalities -> Mobile / Wearable / Point-of-Care Imaging & Sensors

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This manuscript addresses balance function assessment using wearable multimodal sensing, motivated by limitations of subjective clinical evaluation and by the lack of public datasets with authentic instability events. The dataset and problem formulation are distinctive, while the model is a competent integration of existing ideas with moderate methodological novelty.
The strongest contribution is the benchmarking and data-collection design. The authors introduce MBFAD, a multimodal benchmark comprising synchronized whole-body kinematics and plantar pressure data from 29 subjects across 14 activities under both normal and perturbation conditions. This stands as a new dataset production, an original way to use data.
Also, the authors propose the M2-Balance, a framework that uses human activity recognition as a prior for balance assessment. Prior work treats activity recognition, fall detection, and balance analysis as separate pipelines, whereas the authors fuse this information.
reviews.text_strengths:
MBFAD combines whole-body kinematics, plantar pressure, reactive tasks, and perturbation-based acquisition in a single dataset. Table 1 compares MBFAD with prior datasets and shows that MBFAD uniquely includes kinematics, pressure, reactive activities, and perturbation together. The acquisition setup is also clearly illustrated in Figure 1.
Using activity recognition as a prior for balance assessment is sensible because stability risk is context-dependent across activities. The paper explicitly formulates this distinction in Section 3.1.It operationalizes it through parallel HAR and BFA streams in Section 3.2, along with an architecture diagram, making the design easy to follow (although some details are missing).
The comparison against multiple baselines on SisFall and PDS includes modality and task ablations on MBFAD in Tables 2 to 4.This is good experimental practice and strengthens the argument that both multimodality and joint learning matter.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The most substantial contribution to the field is the MBFAD, which contains 29 subjects, all young adults around 20 to 22 years old. The motivation of the paper is about fall prevention and balance health. The absence of older adults or clinical populations is a serious limitation for translational claims. The data may still be useful as a technical benchmark, but the current cohort is not representative of the target populations most at risk.
The paper presents only in Figure 2, the necessary data preprocessing steps (coordinate alignment, timestamp, sliding window, etc). None of these steps is explicitly presented. The details needed to reproduce the results are not provided, so the explanation of data collection and processing is limited. Also, no description of the training and inference details (optimizer, epochs, learning rate, etc. ). There are no details in the data or the splits (are they the same as in [22]?)
It is not clearly explained how the balance function labels, especially the high/ low risk labels, were assigned. The authors mentioned that, with two rehabilitation experts and without a precise label-generation protocol, it is difficult to fully assess whether the labels are strong enough to support future clinical claims.
The conclusion discusses the broader implications of moving toward context-aware stability analysis and suggests future value in this direction. However, the paper does not address key limitations, including a young, small cohort, a lack of clinical validation, and insufficient evidence for generalization to real patient populations.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Explicitley clarify how the BFA labels were defined. What determines high risk versus low risk for each window or sample, especially under perturbation?
Clarify the split protocol. Was the evaluation subject-independent?
Please report the preprocessing settings explicitly. Figure 2 shows these stages conceptually, but not enough detail for replication.
Report the full training details, including the optimizer, batch size, learning rate, number of epochs, early stopping policy, and the values of alpha and beta in the joint loss.
Explain how p-values were computed in Tables 2 to 4.
Please The paper should evaluate older adults or clinical populations, or at least discuss why results from young adults should transfer.
H ∈ R S×L -> L is never explicitly defined (the interpretation is that each modality feature h(s) is an L-dimensional vector, where L is the feature length).
Similar comment to F ∈ RH×W ×C;
Minor typos/inconsistencies: 
Introduction: “quality of life [14] . the primary”; “enter of Pressure data , while Wu et al. [24]”; “3.2 Overview The M2-Balance Framework pipeline (Fig. 2)”

The recommendation is justified by the enumerated points, both in the major strengths and limitations.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper’s main contribution is the introduction of the MBFAD benchmark, a multimodal dataset for balance and fall assessment structured around static, dynamic, and reactive activities, along with a novel sensory perturbation setup (air cushion) to simulate balance disturbances. In addition, the authors propose the M²-Balance Framework, a multitask model that jointly learns human activity recognition and balance assessment, and demonstrate its effectiveness on both the proposed dataset and existing public datasets.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper presents several notable strengths. First, it introduces a novel multimodal benchmark (MBFAD) for balance and fall assessment that explicitly models static, dynamic, and reactive activity paradigms, which is more comprehensive than many existing datasets. Second, the incorporation of sensory perturbation via an air cushion is an original idea that enables controlled simulation of balance disturbances, providing a more realistic experimental setup compared to standard recordings. Third, the proposed M²-Balance Framework leverages a shared encoder for jointly learning human activity recognition (HAR) and balance/fall assessment (BFA), which is a meaningful multitask formulation that can improve representation learning. Finally, the authors validate their approach on both the collected dataset and public benchmarks, demonstrating consistent improvements over baseline methods, which supports the generalizability of the approach.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The paper has several important weaknesses. First, the evaluation protocol is insufficiently described and potentially flawed, as it is unclear whether subject-independent validation (e.g., leave-one-subject-out or subject-wise splits) is used, raising concerns about possible data leakage. Second, the reported results appear to rely mainly on sliding window-level metrics, without providing sequence-, trial-, or subject-level evaluation, which limits practical relevance. Third, although the paper reports p-values, the statistical analysis is not properly described. The authors do not specify which statistical tests were used, whether assumptions were checked, or how multiple comparisons were handled, making it difficult to assess the validity of the claimed significance. Finally, the clinical applicability is limited, as the dataset appears to be collected primarily from younger adults, while fall risk assessment is most relevant for geriatric populations. The lack of validation on elderly or clinical cohorts reduces the translational impact of the work.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents an interesting idea with a novel benchmark and the use of sensory perturbation for balance assessment. However, the decision is mainly driven by concerns regarding evaluation rigor and clinical relevance. The evaluation protocol is unclear, particularly with respect to subject-independent validation, raising potential data leakage issues. Results are primarily reported at the sliding window level, without sequence- or subject-level analysis, which limits their real-world applicability. In addition, although p-values are reported, the statistical methodology is not sufficiently described, making it difficult to assess the validity of the findings. Finally, the lack of validation on geriatric or clinical populations weakens the clinical impact, which is critical for a MICCAI submission. Overall, while promising, the work requires stronger experimental design and validation to meet MICCAI standards.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.text_contribution: Authors collect a new dataset (29 subjects, 14 activities) for balance function assessment and for human activity recognition. Also, authors propose a new AI model, called M^2-balance for (presumeably) 14-class classification for activity recognition, and binary classification for balance function assessment.
reviews.text_strengths: The newly acquired dataset MBFAD that consists of data of 29 subjects for 14 activities, using 16 IMU sensors on the body and 32 in-sole sensors for each shoe, is a good contribution. In addition, authors also implement and evaluate a new AI model, called M^2-balance for (presumably) 14-class classification for activity recognition, and binary classification for balance function assessment.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
This reviewer has the following comments:
Consider additional age groups, of middle age people and possibly elderly
Authors may want to define/describe all 14 activities done by each of the 29 subjects, under berg or brunel scale methods. They should especially explain the sensory perturbation-based motions and reactive motion.
In section I, authors state that they have collected kinematics data from 59 body locations, while in section II, they state that they have used 16 9-axis IMU sensors for kinematics data collection. Is each IMU sensor at a given location measuring more than one body organ/element? Please reconcile both statements.
The variables L, H,W,C represent the dimensions of the feature maps, but are not defined in Eqs. 1,2.- In section 3.3, authors make mention of G groups? Is G=14, corresponding to 14 different activities that subjects do? Or, does it mean something else?
Authors may want to explain the rationale/reasoning behind Eq. 2.In order words, why did they decide to split the intermediate feature map into two maps and then to concatenate the first half O_1^1 with the next group F^{i+1}?
Is F^i from Eq. 2 and F_n from Eq. 3 the same? If so, then better to use a consistent notation. Or, are they different?
What is N in Eq. 3? What is the motivation for Eq. 3 that shows us the absolute difference of two convolutions (of the feature map with the kernel), that is then averaged over N?
Eq. 6: Authors may want to do an ablation on parameters alpha and beta, to learn more about their individual contributions. Also, authors may want to define the two loss functions.
Overall, the mathematical description of the proposed AI model (M^2-balance) needs improvement in terms of rigor.
Authors seem to have fully omitted the key data pre-processing details which is something very important to better understand the contribution of this work, and for the reproducibility of this work. They show a glimpse of their pre-processing pipeline in Fig. 2, but do not talk about it in the paper at all.
Similarly, authors make mention of the 2 feature extractors MotionNet and PressureNet in Fig. 2, but again, they don’t mention important details such as backbone architecture of these 2 encoders in the paper at all.
Authors present their results in results section, but without specifying the precise details of the problem being solved. That is, for activity recognition problem, they probably have solved a 14-class classification problem (as hinted in Fig. 2). If that is the case, they need to mention it in the results section (Table 2) with clarity.
Table 2: Authors do not describe their data splitting methodology, and of the related works. Thus, it is not possible to infer something meaningful out of these results unless and until we get to know the data splitting methodology for all the works (related works, and authors’ work). And as authors may already know, the leave some subjects out cross validation methodology is the preferred data splitting method, as otherwise there will be data leakage between train and test sets.
For the BFA task, authors report the results in table 3, 4.However, I would like to know how authors have computed the accuracy values for this task. I mean, Fig. 2 tells me that authors solve a binary classification problem here (low risk, high risk). How do authors compute the fall risk to be high or low, for a given subject? I would also like to know the data splitting methodology for this task as well.
What is the fate of the collected MBFAD dataset? Will it be made public for the benefit of fellow researchers?
Overall, the paper presents an interesting idea, i.e., a new MBFAD dataset and M^2-balance AI model. However, there is an ambiguity regarding the results reported in the results section, because authors have not mentioned the data splitting methodology, as well as the key data pre-processing details. Also, the mathematical explanation of proposed M^2-balance framework requires polishing and improvement. Finally, it is not clear whether authors plan to release their collected dataset to the public.

meta_reviews.text:
I recommend an Accept based on the consensus of the reviewers, who all provided positive evaluations. The reviewers unanimously praised the introduction of the MBFAD benchmark, noting its novel integration of synchronized whole-body kinematics, plantar pressure, and reactive activities, along with the original use of sensory perturbation via an air cushion to simulate authentic balance disturbances. Furthermore, the proposed M²-Balance framework was commended for its synergistic, multi-task approach that jointly learns human activity recognition and balance assessment to improve representation learning.
While the core contributions are strong, the reviewers raised several methodological and clinical points that must be addressed in the camera-ready version. The authors must clarify the evaluation protocol, specifically detailing whether subject-independent data splitting was employed to prevent data leakage between the training and testing sets. They also need to enhance reproducibility by including thorough descriptions of the data preprocessing steps, training hyperparameters, and the specific backbone architectures of the feature extractors. Additionally, the mathematical descriptions require refinement to explicitly define all variables, such as L, H, W, C, G, and N , and clearly explain the rationale behind the feature map splitting and the joint loss function parameters. From a clinical perspective, the authors must acknowledge the dataset’s limitation of comprising primarily young adults and discuss the generalizability and translational applicability of these results to older, at-risk geriatric cohorts. Finally, the manuscript must explicitly clarify the protocol used by the rehabilitation experts to assign the high-risk and low-risk balance function labels and detail the specific statistical tests utilized to compute the reported p-values. Addressing these clarifications will significantly strengthen the final manuscript.

We will revise the manuscript to clarify this rationale and discuss subject level assessment as an important direction for future clinical validation. title: MDL-DA Track: Self-supervised Sperm Motility Direction Learning and Density-Adaptive Association for Sperm Tracking
abstract: Existing multi-object tracking methods typically rely on motion models or appearance features for target association. However, in sperm multi-target tracking tasks, the appearance of the targets is highly similar and the motion patterns are complex. It is difficult for both appearance and motion features to exhibit stable tracking performance in targets with different distribution densities simultaneously. Additionally, it is difficult to obtain the motility direction label of sperm targets. This paper proposes Self-supervised Sperm Motility Direction Learning and Density-Adaptive Association for Sperm Tracking (MDL-DA Track). In the sperm detection module, a multi-task learning framework combining self-supervised Sperm Motility Direction Learning (SMDL) and object detection is constructed. Through self-supervised learning of temporal bounding boxes, motion direction information is captured. YOLOX is jointly employed to model both sperm target locations and motion directions. In the sperm tracking module, a motion direction-enhanced Density-adaptive Object Association (DOA) strategy is proposed to handle differences between sparse and dense target distributions. The DOA strategy adaptively selects association rules according to local target density. For targets with sparse distributions, matching is dominated by motion information. For targets with dense distributions, association is achieved by combining motion, appearance, and direction features, thereby enhancing tracking robustness in complex scenarios. Experimental results on the public VISEM-Tracking dataset and Electron Microscopy Sperm dataset show that MDL-DA Track outperforms several state-of-the-art methods in multi-object tracking. On the public dataset, higher order tracking accuracy and multiple object tracking accuracy are improved by 2.5%-3%. Ablation studies further demonstrate that SMDL and DOA effectively reduce erroneous associations in dense scenarios and enhance robustness in sparse scenarios.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper draws inspiration from the biological insight that “the direction of sperm movement is consistent with its head-tail orientation” to improve upon traditional tracking algorithms. The authors gained a deep understanding of the clinical challenges faced by conventional tracking methods in sperm tracking—namely, that approaches relying solely on motion and appearance are prone to identity switches—and made targeted improvements accordingly, achieving favorable results compared to baselines. They construct self-supervised signals using short-term frame displacements, thereby avoiding the cost of manual annotation. Furthermore, by integrating local density with feature weights, the method alleviates the problem of trajectory overlap in dense regions.
reviews.text_strengths:
The strengths of the paper are as follows:
(1) Proposed a self-supervised sperm motility direction learning approach based on inter-frame displacement of the sperm, which provides geometry-aware orientation cues that remain stable under dense interactions and abrupt motion, improving
association reliability. 
(2) Proposed a two-stage sperm target association for sparse-region sperm matching and dense-region sperm matching, which further, which enhances density adaptive.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(1) The algorithm performance in static sperm scenario is not described clearly. The author only mentioned it in the conclusion section. Additional experiments are needed to evaluate its performance on static sperm scenario. 
(2) It should be clearly explained why the branch weight λ=0 still improves the performance.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
(1) Fig. 1 should be briefly introduced in the context so readers know its purpose. 
(2) Paragraph 3 in the Methodology section should be moved after equation (1) to explain the parameters in the formula.

The paper proposed a self-supervised approach to learning sperm motility direction and density-adaptive association for sperm tracking, which significantly improved tracking performance compared to other SOTA algorithms. Ablation study confirmed the contribution of each module of the approach.
However, the paper has some weaknesses, such as the lack of a static sperm scenario and a detailed explanation of the parameters in the equations.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes MDL-DA Track, a two-stage multi-object tracking framework tailored for sperm tracking that augments a YOLOX detector with a self-supervised direction branch (SMDL) and introduces a density-adaptive association (DOA) strategy. SMDL predicts per-detection orientation (sinθ, cosθ) using pseudo-labels from short-term displacement, while DOA switches between motion-dominant sparse matching and a parallel motion/appearance association in dense regions, both enhanced by the learned direction cue. On VISEM-Tracking and an Electron Microscopy Sperm dataset, the method reports consistent improvements over strong baselines (e.g., TOPICTrack, OCSort), with 2.5–3% gains in HOTA/MOTA and stronger identity preservation metrics.
reviews.text_strengths:
A. Technical novelty and innovation
The addition of a lightweight, geometry-aware direction head within YOLOX trained via displacement-derived pseudo-labels is a novel approach, where a domain-informed extension that decouples orientation from displacement magnitude.
The density-adaptive association strategy is practical and aligns with the unique sparsity/density variability of sperm videos. In which authors integrate learned direction consistently into both sparse and dense association costs is a coherent design.
B. Experimental validation
Fair comparisons are conducted by using the same detector across methods; ablations isolate the impact of DOA and SMDL, and a hyperparameter sweep for \lambda is provided.
Results are reported as mean +- standard deviation across splits, improving statistical credibility relative to single-split reporting.
C. Clarity of presentation
The methodological flow is clear: detector with SMDL -> density estimation -> two-stage association with well-specified cost terms and components.
The choice to represent direction via (sinθ, cosθ) and the constraint to positive samples with sufficient displacement are well-motivated.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
It’s still unclear to reviewers the following:
First, “Self-supervised” direction learning indeed relies on ground-truth inter-frame associations (to compute displacement labels), which are weak/self-labeled rather than unsupervised; the dependence on annotated tracks thus should be clarified.
Several elements referenced in the method, e.g., “motion reliability,” trajectory-level direction aggregation, are not formally defined, leaving ambiguity in implementation details critical for reproducibility.
More ablation studies are required to provide (to the appendix should be fine). They include: (i) breakdown of performance across sparse vs. dense; (ii) comparisons to segmentation-based or microscopy-specific trackers (e.g., classical cell/sperm tracking pipelines), which are currently absent.
Other points:
The current figure method needs to be polished for further highlight adaptations to the sperm tracking. For instance, the “displacement computation” should be replaced by the optical flow vectors demonstrating displacement, etc.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Both the method contributions and experiments are significant and well-motivated. The paper can be further improved by enhancing the visualization of the method figure and by providing details, including additional ablation studies on parameter sensitivity.
