reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper presents MDL-DA Track, a sperm multi-object tracking framework for microscopic videos. The authors claim two main contributions:
1- Self-supervised Sperm Motility Direction Learning (SMDL), which uses a YOLOX-based detector with an additional direction prediction branch trained using pseudo-labels made from temporal bounding box movement
2- Density-Adaptive Object Association (DOA), which changes the association strategy based on local target density, relying more on motion movements in sparse regions and combining motion, appearance, and direction vector in dense regions.
The reported experiments on VISEM-Tracking and the Electron Microscopy Sperm dataset show improvements over several existing trackers in HOTA, MOTA, IDF1, and AssA.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper is generally well structured and easy to follow. The motivation, method, and experiments are presented in a coherent way, and the two main components of the approach, SMDL and DOA, are described clearly enough that the overall pipeline is understandable.
Another strength is that the paper addresses a clearly defined problem. The authors identify that, in sperm tracking, appearance cues are weak because the targets are highly visually similar, while motion cues become less reliable in dense and crowded regions. The proposed method is at least well aligned with these stated challenges, with SMDL intended to provide an additional direction cue and DOA intended to adapt association behavior to local density.
The paper also has practical application relevance. Accurate sperm tracking is an important component of computer-aided sperm analysis systems, and improvements in association-related tracking metrics may be useful for downstream motility analysis. While the paper does not demonstrate clinical translation directly, the application itself is meaningful.
A further positive aspect is that the paper includes ablation and sensitivity analyses rather than only a single comparison table. This makes the experimental section more complete and helps show the individual effect of the proposed components.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The novelty appears limited. The two core ideas are direction-aware association and adaptive use of different association cues depending on the tracking situation, but both themes already exist in prior MOT literature. OC-SORT explicitly incorporates direction consistency into association to improve robustness under non-linear motion and occlusion, while TOPIC/TOPICTrack already proposes a parallel motion/appearance association framework with conflict resolution and adaptive cue selection. In that context, the paper is more of an adaptation of existing MOT ideas to sperm tracking than a new tracking formulation.
The experimental comparison is a notable weakness of the paper. Although the paper includes a few newer baselines, the comparison in Table 1 remains dominated by older generic MOT methods, even though the paper’s main claims focus on sperm tracking and robustness in dense, crowded scenes. In particular, the paper does not compare against relevant papers such as Sperm YOLOv8E-TrackEVD (https://www.proquest.com/docview/3067437403), YOLOv4 with improved DeepSORT for sperm detection and tracking (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-26465-4), and an IMM-based multi-sperm dynamic tracking algorithm (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1746809425006834). Also, the dense-scene claim would be more convincing if the paper were compared against stronger crowded MOT baselines such as ConfTrack (https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/WACV2024/html/Jung_ConfTrack_Kalman_Filter-Based_Multi-Person_Tracking_by_Utilizing_Confidence_Score_of_WACV_2024_paper.html), TrackTrack (https://cvpr.thecvf.com/virtual/2025/poster/35174), and Hybrid-SORT (https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/28471), all of which address occlusion, identity preservation, or association in crowded settings. Even if not all of these methods are directly optimized for microscopy, the absence of stronger recent sperm-specific and dense-scene comparators makes the empirical case less convincing.
Finally, some of the most important choices in DOA are not analyzed. The paper includes an ablation study and a sensitivity analysis of the direction-loss weight, which are useful, but it provides much less evidence on sensitivity to the density threshold, adaptive neighborhood radius, and association weights.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper is clearly written, and the overall idea is easy to follow. The problem is well motivated, and the reported results show consistent gains over the baselines. However, my main concern is that the methodological novelty appears limited relative to prior MOT literature, since the core ideas of direction-aware association and adaptive use of different matching cues are already present in prior works such as OC-SORT and TOPIC/TOPICTrack. As a result, the method feels more like a task-specific adaptation to sperm tracking than a substantially new tracking formulation. In addition, the experimental case is not fully convincing. Most of the compared methods are either generic MOT trackers or older baselines, and I would have liked to see comparisons against more recent general MOT and sperm-specific tracking methods. I would also like to see more ablation of the DOA design choices, especially the density-related parameters and the association weighting.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: After reading the reviews and the rebuttal, I acknowledge the effort by the authors to differentiate their contribution from the previous. I think it should be made even clearer this differentiation in the camera-ready, and assuming that the authors will do a good job with that, I am willing to accept the paper.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper proposes a self-supervised framework for sperm tracking with direction learning and density-adaptive association.
The reviewers’ scores are 5, 4, and 3, indicating mixed opinions.
The reviewers agree that the method is well motivated and demonstrates promising improvements over existing approaches.
However, concerns remain regarding the level of methodological novelty, the clarity of certain design choices, and the completeness of experimental validation.
In particular, the novelty should also be clarified with respect to prior cell tracking studies that jointly model detection and motion estimation.
The AC therefore recommends inviting the paper for rebuttal.
The authors are encouraged to carefully address the reviewers’ comments in the rebuttal, particularly regarding the novelty with respect to existing tracking methods, additional analysis of the proposed components, and the completeness of experimental evaluation and comparisons.

The paper proposes MDL-DA Track, a sperm multi-object tracking framework for microscopy videos. It combines a sperm motility direction learning branch trained from inter-frame displacement pseudo-labels with a density-adaptive association strategy that changes the use of motion, appearance, and direction cues between sparse and dense regions. The problem is practically relevant, and the method reports consistent improvements on VISEM-Tracking and an Electron Microscopy Sperm dataset.
The initial reviews were mixed but overall close to positive, with scores of 5 / 4 / 3.Reviewers appreciated the clear motivation, domain-informed use of direction cues, density-adaptive association design, and consistent empirical gains. The main concerns were limited novelty relative to prior MOT methods such as OC-SORT and TOPIC/TOPICTrack, incomplete comparison with recent sperm-specific or crowded-scene trackers, insufficient analysis of static sperm cases and DOA design choices, ambiguity in the term “self-supervised,” and missing implementation or notation details.
The rebuttal addressed several of these concerns. The authors clarified how their direction learning differs from trajectory-history-based direction modeling in OC-SORT, and how their density-adaptive association differs from the cue-selection strategy in TOPICTrack. They also clarified that “self-supervised” means no additional manual orientation labels rather than fully unsupervised learning, explained the lambda=0 ablation, and committed to clearer notation, definitions, additional ablations where space allows, more domain-specific comparisons, and code release. These responses were sufficient for the reviewers to converge to a positive recommendation.
Some limitations remain. The contribution is still best viewed as a well-designed, domain-specific adaptation and integration of existing MOT ideas rather than a fundamentally new tracking formulation. The comparison to recent sperm-specific and dense-scene trackers remains incomplete, and the sensitivity of DOA parameters such as density thresholds, neighborhood radius, and association weights should be better clarified. The camera-ready version should also clearly define the self-supervised setting and provide the missing implementation details.
After rebuttal, the final recommendation is A / A / A. Reviewer 2 kept a positive assessment after finding that the rebuttal addressed the main concerns, and Reviewer 3 moved from Weak Reject to Accept based on the authors’ effort to better differentiate the contribution from prior work. The score improvement mainly reflects improved confidence in the novelty framing, domain-specific motivation, and planned clarification of reproducibility details.
I recommend acceptance. The post-rebuttal reviewer consensus is positive, and the paper addresses a meaningful microscopy tracking problem with a coherent domain-informed method and consistent empirical evidence. While the remaining concerns on novelty, comparator coverage, and DOA parameter analysis should be noted, they are not sufficient reasons for rejection and can be addressed in the final version.

After rebuttal two reviewers are happy with the response. And the other reviewer did not provide post-rebuttal decision. But his pre-rebuttal recommendation is Accept. So all three reviewers are positive. Overall this is a well-written paper with good novelty and experimental verification. So the final recommendation is Accept.

Reviewers’ concerns were solved after the rebuttal. After reading the paper, rebuttal and the reviews after the rebuttal, the AC recommends accepting this paper which should be revised based on the three reviewers’ feedback.

author_feedback_text:
We thank reviewers for recognizing novel (R2), meaningful, easy to follow, clearly written, experimental section complete (R3), well-motivated (R2, R3), clearly defined problem (R1, R3), significant improvement (R1, R2).
Innovation (@R3)
Sperm tracking suffers from uneven distribution, target overlap in dense scenes, and illumination interference in sparse scenes, making motion direction information indispensable.
Given that sperm head and tail orientation generally align with its moving direction, we propose MDL-DA Track. Its core innovations are: 1) SMDL module generates pseudo motion direction labels from target positions to supervise the lightweight direction branch, enabling the detector to learn motion direction cues from image features. 2) DOA strategy estimates local target density and adaptively adjusts the association weights of IoU, appearance and motion direction features.
Ours Vs. OC-SORT
Although both methods use directional information, they differ fundamentally in motivation and information source. OC-SORT infers trajectory direction from historical trajectories and inter-frame position changes. Therefore, it relies on trajectory continuity and motion estimation quality, which may be affected in dense sperm scenes with frequent occlusion, interaction, and irregular motion.
In contrast, our SMDL module learns morphologically aware directional representations from appearance. It uses inter-frame displacement as supervision and directly infers motion-related direction cues from current frame features without relying on accumulated trajectory history. Our method further integrates directional learning into both detection and association via joint optimization, forming a specialized framework for sperm tracking.
Ours Vs. TOPICTrack
Our innovation lies not in redeveloping parallel association, but in designing a density-adaptive mechanism. TOPICTrack employs a unified association strategy for all targets, selecting IoU or appearance cues based on the degree of motion change. Sperm tracking features uneven in-frame density, where association cues vary substantially between sparse and dense regions — a scenario ignored by TOPICTrack.
Our DOA adopts different strategies for different density regions: motion matching is mainly used in sparse regions, while fusion of motion, appearance and direction is used in dense regions. In addition, the mechanism is structurally independent and compatible with other MOT frameworks.
Meaning of Self-Supervision (@R2)
The term “self-supervised” here means that our direction learning does not require additional manual orientation annotations, such as sperm head-tail orientation or motion direction labels. We acknowledge that this is not strict self-supervision and will clarify this definition in the revised manuscript.
Ablation on branch weight λ (@R1): Table 1 first row denotes the baseline without our DOA. In contrast, when λ=0, the model still retains the full DOA workflow, and the direction branch remains active during forward propagation and modulates shared features. This enables the backbone to capture richer geometric structural information via structural inductive bias. We will add these explanations to the revised manuscript.
Other ablation experiments (@R1, R2, R3): We have already conducted more detailed ablation experiments, but they were not included in the original manuscript due to page limits. We will add more ablation results in the revised version if space allows.
Comparison Experiments (@R2, R3): We compare with representative MOT methods including ByteTrack and BoT-SORT, which address dense tracking challenges via detection confidence, appearance modeling, motion estimation and temporal memory. We agree to add more domain-specific methods.
Other details (@R1, R2): We will revise the descriptions of key concepts, unify and standardize notations, and provide clearer definitions for core symbols.
Code: We will release the source code publicly upon paper acceptance.

title: MDPNet: A Multi-Scale Deformable Prototype Network for Accurate and Interpretable Medical Image Classification
abstract:
There is an increasing demand for medical image classifiers that deliver both high diagnostic accuracy and clinically actionable interpretability. Existing post-hoc explanation methods, such as saliency maps and Grad-CAM, can highlight discriminative regions but often provide limited insight into the underlying decision logic, which can reduce clinical confidence. Prototype learning offers a promising case-based alternative; however, conventional prototype-based models are often limited by single-scale feature representations and sensitivity to class imbalance, which can degrade accuracy and yield less stable explanations.
To address these limitations, we propose MDPNet, a Multi-Scale Deformable Prototype Network that improves classification performance while providing prototype-grounded interpretability. MDPNet integrates a multi-scale feature extraction module to capture both fine-grained morphological patterns and global contextual semantics, and introduces a deformable prototype learning mechanism that adaptively aligns prototypes with spatial variability in clinical images. In addition, we adopt a logit-adjusted loss to mitigate the impact of class imbalance during training. Extensive experiments show that MDPNet achieves 93.28±1.54% accuracy on a private premature ventricular contraction (PVC) dataset, 97.90±0.37% accuracy on the public OCT dataset, and 87.65±2.54% accuracy on the public CT dataset, consistently outperforming strong CNN/Transformer baselines and recent prototype-learning approaches.
subject_areas: Modalities -> EEG / MEG / ECG / Physiological Signals

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors introduce an interpretable framework for medical image and time-series classification that consists of multi-scale feature extraction and a deformable prototype learning strategy.
reviews.text_strengths:
-The method is evaluated on three different datasets representing diverse data modalities (ECG, OCT, and CT) in terms of classification performance. 
-An ablation study is provided (again focused on classification performance). 
-Some qualitative exploration of learned prototypes is included for the ECG case (Figure 3)
reviews.text_weaknesses:
My main concern is that the authors claim interpretability as their primary contribution; however, this aspect is only indirectly evaluated through classification performance. The study would be significantly stronger if it included a quantitative evaluation of the robustness and quality of the explanations. Even more compelling would be an assessment involving clinicians, who are the intended end users of the model.
Minor:
-There is repetition between the last paragraph of the introduction and the listed key contributions.
The manuscript claims the framework is designed for image classification, but Figure 1 illustrates a time-series signal. It may be more accurate to state that the framework is generalizable to data with spatial or temporal relationships.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes MDPNet, a prototype-based framework for medical image classification that combines multi-scale feature extraction with a deformable prototype learning mechanism. The authors argue that this framework is higher performance compared to the baselines while being more interpretable.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper addresses an important problem of combining performance and interpretability in medical imaging and presents a conceptually coherent method that integrates multi-scale features with deformable prototype learning.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The paper has several notable weaknesses. First, the overall novelty is limited, as the method primarily combines existing components such as multi-scale feature extraction, deformable prototypes, and logit adjustment without introducing a fundamentally new idea. Second, the interpretability claims are not convincingly validated; the evaluation relies mainly on qualitative visualizations without quantitative metrics or user studies to demonstrate clinical usefulness. Third, the empirical improvements over strong baselines are relatively modest, especially on public datasets, which weakens the impact of the contribution. In addition, the choice of benchmarks is not particularly strong, with one dataset being saturated (OCT) and another being small and potentially unreliable (COVID-CT), raising concerns about generalizability. Finally, the paper lacks deeper analysis, including limited discussion of failure cases, when the method is most effective, and the computational overhead introduced by the proposed components.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses the need for both accuracy and interpretability in medical image classification by proposing MDPNet, an interpretable classification framework that integrates a Multi-Scale Feature Extraction Module (MSFEM), a Deformable Prototype Learning Module (DPLM), and a logit-adjusted loss. Specifically, MSFEM incorporates a multi-scale spatial pyramid attention mechanism into the DenseNet bottleneck layers, while DPLM adopts the deformable prototype-matching strategy of Deformable ProtoPNet. The method is evaluated using five-fold cross-validation on a private premature ventricular contraction (PVC) dataset, as well as the NEH OCT dataset and COVID-CT-Dataset.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Clear motivation. The paper identifies two key limitations of existing prototype-learning methods in medical image classification, namely spatial rigidity and single-scale representation.
2.Relatively comprehensive experimental design. The method is evaluated on three datasets from different imaging modalities, and the ablation studies provide reasonable support for the effectiveness of the individual components.
3.The discussion of failure cases is informative. Section 3.4 provides an honest analysis of two representative failure modes: prototype–feature mismatch under ambiguous morphology, and confusion caused by subtle inter-class differences. This discussion is valuable for future research.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The novelty is incremental and primarily lies in combining existing methods for a medical imaging task. MSFEM is directly derived from the multi-scale spatial pyramid attention mechanism in [22] (Yu et al., 2024), with the main adaptation being its insertion into DenseNet bottleneck layers rather than the introduction of a new multi-scale mechanism. DPLM directly adopts the deformable prototype strategy of Deformable ProtoPNet [7] (Donnelly et al., CVPR 2022), and the logit adjustment is taken directly from Menon et al. [15]. The authors should further clarify why this combination is non-trivial and what benefits it provides beyond a straightforward aggregation of existing components.
2.The evaluation of interpretability is too limited. I encourage the authors to include prototype visualizations on the OCT and CT datasets.
3.The writing and figure presentation could be further improved. Figure 3 is difficult to follow, and I suggest adding more detailed annotations, legends, or textual explanations.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1.The authors should clarify what the fundamental innovation is beyond assembling existing techniques.
2.The authors should explain why DenseNet was chosen as the backbone for MSFEM, instead of alternatives such as ResNet or ViT.
3.It is also worth discussing whether using 100 prototypes per class for PVC, or 50 per class for OCT/CT, is excessive. Have the authors analyzed the impact of the number of prototypes on both classification performance and interpretability?

The paper addresses a clinically meaningful problem, and the proposed method consistently outperforms the baselines across three datasets. The ablation studies are reasonably designed, and the discussion of failure cases is candid and useful. However, the central weakness of the paper lies in its limited technical novelty: all three major components are directly adopted from, or only slightly adapted from, existing methods, and their combination does not yet demonstrate sufficiently deep technical insight.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper addresses a clinically meaningful problem and presents a conceptually coherent framework. However, the limited novelty and insufficient interpretability validation prevent a stronger recommendation. I recommend acceptance with the expectation that the authors will substantially improve the interpretability evaluation (e.g., quantitative faithfulness metrics, expert assessment) and clarify the novelty contribution in the final version. If the authors cannot address these concerns in rebuttal, the paper may need to be rejected.

The rebuttal successfully address the concerns raised by reviewers.

The paper addresses a clinically meaningful problem and presents a coherent prototype-based framework for medical image classification. The reviewers raised valid concerns regarding incremental novelty, limited interpretability validation, modest gains on some public datasets, and insufficient analysis of failure cases and efficiency. The rebuttal responds to these concerns in a generally reasonable manner by clarifying the motivation, promising additional interpretability analysis, failure-case discussion, efficiency reporting, and prototype/backbone analysis. While some concerns, especially regarding novelty and clinical interpretability, are not completely eliminated, the reviewer consensus after rebuttal is positive. I therefore recommend acceptance. The authors should clearly incorporate the relevant clarifications, interpretability discussion, failure-case analysis, efficiency details, and prototype/backbone analysis in the final version.
The rebuttal has adequately addressed the main concerns from all reviewers and is sufficient to support acceptance. Therefore, I recommend Accept.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the reviewers for their constructive comments. We have revised the manuscript to better clarify the interpretability, novelty, dataset-specific results, efficiency, backbone choice, and prototype settings.
Common Q1: Interpretability validation.
We agree that interpretability should be supported by both visual and quantitative evidence. In the revision, we added a prototype-removal analysis, where top-ranked matched prototypes are removed or masked during inference to evaluate their contribution to prediction. The performance drop shows that the prototypes are not only visual explanations but also decision-relevant evidence. Moreover, we expanded the clinical discussion. For PVC classification, subtype-specific cues may appear across different ECG leads and local waveform segments. Our prototype matching helps trace predictions back to representative diagnostic patterns, improving case-level interpretability over black-box classifiers.
Common Q2: Incremental novelty.
Our contribution is not a simple combination of existing modules, but a clinically motivated evidence-matching framework. Medical diagnostic cues are often subtle, distributed, and non-contiguous. In PVC classification, discriminative evidence may appear across multiple ECG leads and waveform segments. Conventional prototype methods usually rely on fixed or local matching, which may be insufficient for such evidence. We therefore integrate multi-scale representation with deformable prototype matching to capture flexible evidence correspondence while preserving prototype-level interpretability. We revised the Introduction and Method sections to clarify this motivation.
R1 Q1: Repetition and inconsistent task description.
We have checked the manuscript and revised repeated or inconsistent descriptions in the Abstract, Introduction, and Method sections. 
R3 Q1: Limited baseline gains and dataset representativeness.
We agree that gains on OCT and CT are smaller than on PVC due to differences in task difficulty and diagnostic patterns. PVC is a five-class fine-grained task with subtle inter-class differences and distributed cues across ECG leads, where deformable prototype matching is particularly useful. OCT and CT contain more visually salient or localized patterns, leaving less room for improvement over strong baselines. Still, our method achieves competitive results on these datasets while providing additional prototype-level interpretability. We clarified this in the revision.
R3 Q2: Failure cases and efficiency.
We strengthened the failure-case and efficiency analysis. Two failure types were discussed: weak/incomplete discriminative cues and highly similar classes such as LVOT vs. RVOT. These cases show the remaining difficulty in fine-grained inter-class discrimination. For efficiency, we added parameters, FLOPs, and inference time. The extra cost mainly comes from multi-scale feature extraction and deformable prototype matching. We clarified that our method aims to balance performance, interpretability, and computational cost.
R3 Q3: Too many concepts.
We reorganized the method by clarifying the roles of multi-scale representation, deformable prototype matching, prototype-based interpretability, and logit adjustment, while removing redundant terminology.
R4 Q1: Writing and Fig. 3.We revised the writing and improved Fig. 3 by enlarging key regions, adding clearer labels, and rewriting the caption to better explain the visualization pipeline.
R4 Q2: DenseNet choice.
DenseNet was selected because it provided better feature reuse and stability than ResNet, and was more suitable than ViT for limited medical data.
R4 Q3: Prototype number.
We added prototype number sensitivity analysis. Too few prototypes may miss diagnostic variations, while too many introduce redundancy. The final setting balances performance, interpretability, and efficiency. More prototypes were used for PVC due to its more challenging five-class classification task.

title: MEASURE: Multi-Task Slice Selection and Regression for Neonatal Brain Biometry
abstract: Quantitative brain biometry from MRI is essential for evaluating brain growth in preterm-born neonates, yet manual measurement is time-consuming and suffers from inter-rater variability. Existing automation approaches require dense voxel-wise annotations that are costly to obtain and sensitive to domain shifts. We present MEASURE (Measurement Estimation via Anatomical Slice Understanding and REgression), the first annotation-efficient deep learning framework for Kidokoro-protocol neonatal brain biometry. Our two-stage approach mirrors the clinical workflow: a ViT-based multi-task slice selector identifies optimal measurement planes, followed by a multi-task regression network with measurement-specific spatial attention that jointly predicts all biometrics without voxel-level supervision. Experiments on 470 developing Human Connectome Project subjects demonstrate that explicit plane selection consistently outperforms end-to-end 3D volumetric baselines, and our proposed predictor outperforms multi-task regression approaches on simulated thick-slice data.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Synthetic Data / Data-centric AI

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a two-stage framework for predicting neonatal brain biometry measurements. In the first stage, a Vit model is used for slice selection, identifying the optimal measurement planes by selecting the most appropriate slice for each measurement. However, rather than formulating the problem as a binary classification task, it was defined as a three-class classification problem, distinguishing between the optimal slice, its neighbouring slices, and all remaining slices, under the assumption that neighbouring slices also represent near-optimal measurement planes. In the second stage, a regression network is employed to estimate the biometric measurements, where mechanisms such as spatially adaptive routing, measurement-specific attention pooling, and anatomical attention regularization are used to improve the prediction. Although fetal brain biometry estimation has been extensively studied in the literature, neonatal biometry estimation has received comparatively less attention. Therefore, this work addresses an important gap and has the potential for significant impact.
reviews.text_strengths: Although the motivation and clinical importance of the proposed method are clear, and the methodology is well formulated through a two-stage approach, first detecting the optimal measurement slice and subsequently estimating the measurements on those slices (thus avoiding the more challenging task of directly estimating 2D measurements from 3D data), while also incorporating different components in the network to improve estimation accuracy, the main strength of the paper lies in its strong end-to-end evaluation. The authors present a comprehensive evaluation, including the required statistical analysis for biometric measurement assessment (Pearson correlation, MAE, ICC, Bland-Altman), intra-rater analysis, ablation studies on different parts of the model, and comparisons with state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, the method is also applied to the FeTA dataset to demonstrate its generalization performance.
reviews.text_weaknesses: Since the Kidokoro scoring system for assessing brain abnormalities is highly mentioned throughout the manuscript, being used to present the clinical motivation of the work, a more explicit connection between the results of the paper and this scoring system should have been provided. The Kidokoro scoring system does not necessarily rely on the specific biometric measurements extracted in this work, while also considering additional MRI findings. In fact, the Kidokoro score relies on a combination of MRI findings, such as signal abnormalities, structural alterations, and developmental features, where some of them can be inferred from the biometric measurements. Therefore, the paper could be more explicit about how the retrieved measurements can be used, or how the proposed methodology could be extended, to support the computation of a Kidokoro score.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The scheme in Figure 1, particularly part (b), could be improved by explicitly including the lightweight CNN that encodes inter-slice difference maps. As currently presented, it appears that the through-plane augmentation is applied to the features F extracted by the ResNet, rather than being applied to the input channels and subsequently fused with F.
Additionally, Figure 1 would benefit from the inclusion of input/output nomenclature (e. g. , F, F’, F_out) to better guide the reader through the mathematical description of the method.
Although the mathematical formulation is well presented, the inputs to the ResNet are not entirely clear. How are the inputs for each plane combined before being fed into the ResNet? Moreover, for each plane, is the input a six-channel representation composed of the central slice, neighbouring slices, and coordinate channels? How are these coordinate channels defined (e. g. , Cartesian, radial, etc. )? Please clarify.
The authors state on page 7 that “the predictor consumes top-2 candidates. ” However, the methodology section seems to indicate that the predictor takes only the top-1 candidate as input, represented by a six-channel input (2.5D input plus coordinate channels). Is this correct? Please clarify.
In Table 1, within the ablation study, does the “base” model correspond to the version without attention pooling, SAFA, and AAR? This could be stated explicitly in the paper.
Although it is presented as an additional experiment, the evaluation on the FeTA dataset would benefit from further clarification, particularly regarding the use of “GA only. ” How was the pipeline adapted to operate using only gestational age information? Please clarify.

The paper addresses a clinically relevant problem and proposes a well-structured framework. A key strength is the comprehensive end-to-end evaluation. Overall, the completeness of the manuscript (clinical relevance, well-designed framework, and strong validation) put the manuscript above the acceptance threshold from the reviewers’ perspective.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
Regarding the reviewer’s concerns related to the Kidokoro assessment, the authors clarified that MEASURE automates only the quantitative biometric component, which represents just one part of the Kidokoro framework, instead of leading the reader to assume that the proposed methodology automatically estimates or extracts the full score. This clarification makes the manuscript more accurate and fair in the way the contribution is presented.
In addition, the authors addressed several points that were previously unclear to the reviewer, even if some of the responses were relatively brief.
Overall, considering that the topic is relevant, the methodology is well formulated through a two-stage approach, and the authors present a comprehensive evaluation, the reviewer considers that this work is above the acceptance threshold.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper presents MEASURE, a two-stage deep learning framework for neonatal brain biometry that mimics the clinical workflow. It first performs multi-task slice selection using a ViT-based model, then predicts multiple biometric measurements via a regression network with measurement-specific attention. The approach is annotation-efficient, avoiding dense voxel-level supervision, and demonstrates strong performance on the dHCP dataset with comprehensive evaluation.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper addresses a clinically important problem with strong alignment to real-world measurement workflows and eliminates the need for dense annotations, improving practical applicability. The proposed two-stage architecture is well motivated and thoughtfully designed. The work is supported by comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation, including cross-validation, multi-metric analysis, ablations, and comparison against human variability, with clear and reproducible presentation. In addition, Fig. 2 demonstrates high interpretability, where attention maps reflect the underlying biometry of interest.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The evaluation of thick-slice conditions relies on simulated data rather than real clinical acquisitions, limiting practical validation. The study depends on single-expert annotations without inter-rater analysis, and comparisons with 3D methods may be biased due to explicit slice supervision. Furthermore, interpretability claims are only qualitatively supported, cross-domain generalization evidence is limited, and some architectural components (e.g., SAFA, AAR) show inconsistent gains.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a well-motivated and technically sound approach with strong experimental validation and clear clinical relevance. Although there are limitations in real-world validation and annotation diversity, the work is solid and demonstrates meaningful improvements.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents MEASURE, a two-stage deep learning framework for automated neonatal brain biometry. The method decomposes the task into (1) slice selection using a ViT-based multi-task classifier and (2) measurement prediction via a ResNet-based regression model with additional modules (SAFA and measurement-specific attention pooling). Stage 2 uses a ResNet-34 backbone augmented with the proposed SAFA module — which combines through-plane difference maps with spatially adaptive fine/coarse routing — and measurement-specific attention pooling with AAR. A key motivation is to avoid voxel-level annotations by relying only on slice indices and scalar measurement labels.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Clinically well-motivated and annotation-efficient design.
The proposed framework requires only slice indices and scalar measurements as supervision, avoiding voxel-level annotations entirely. This is a practically meaningful advantage for neonatal brain MRI, where expert annotation is costly and time-consuming.
2.Rigorous and transparent evaluation protocol.
The paper presents a strong and well-structured evaluation, including 5-fold cross-validation, multiple complementary metrics (ICC, Pearson r, MAE), and statistical testing with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction. Notably, the authors explicitly mark ablation cases where variants outperform the full model but are not statistically significant (◦), demonstrating a commendable level of transparency that is often lacking in similar works.
3.Inclusion of clinically relevant evaluation (Bland–Altman analysis).
The use of Bland–Altman analysis provides additional clinical context beyond standard ML metrics, which is often missing in similar work. While not novel, this analysis helps interpret model performance relative to intra-rater variability and improves the practical relevance of the evaluation.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Cross-domain experiment does not support — and in fact weakens — the generalization claim.
The FeTA evaluation is presented as evidence of architectural transferability, but the results are not convincing. The image-only configuration fails to converge, and even when combined with GA, image features provide only limited and inconsistent improvements, with no gains for some structures (e.g., HV, LCC). While the authors attribute this to limited data, the results more strongly indicate sensitivity to domain shift and data scale. As such, this experiment reads less as supporting evidence and more as a demonstration of the method’s limitations, weakening the overall claim of generalizability.
2.Single-site, single-protocol dataset severely limits generalizability.
All experiments are conducted on a single dataset (dHCP) acquired under controlled conditions. This does not reflect real clinical variability, where neonatal MRI often involves lower resolution, thick slices, and motion artifacts. 
3.Limited empirical contribution of SAFA and AAR.
Although the authors explicitly mark non-significant results (◦) and provide partial explanations (e.g., interpretability trade-offs for AAR), the empirical evidence supporting these modules remains weak. In particular, SAFA shows statistically significant improvement only in a small subset of metrics, while AAR does not yield significant gains. The provided explanations are largely qualitative and do not sufficiently justify their inclusion as key components of the method.
4.The fine/coarse routing mechanism relies on under-justified heuristic gating.
The mixing weight 𝑟 is defined using a Sobel-derived edge complexity map, a fixed threshold 𝜏, and a learnable temperature, but the paper does not adequately explain how the fixed threshold is chosen or how sensitive performance is to this design. This makes the routing mechanism appear heuristic rather than well-validated, especially given the low contrast and noise characteristics of neonatal MRI.
5.The proposed “attention” mechanism is closer to spatial weighting than relational attention.
The measurement-specific attention operates as a spatial weighting (i.e., weighted pooling) over feature maps, rather than modeling interactions between spatial locations (e.g., via query-key-value attention). While effective in practice, this limits its ability to capture global dependencies and reduces the conceptual novelty of the module.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The primary factor behind my weak reject recommendation is that the experimental evidence does not sufficiently support the paper’s claims of generalizability and methodological contribution.
Most importantly, the cross-domain (FeTA) experiment is not convincing and in fact weakens the generalization claim. The image-only configuration fails to converge, and even with GA, image features provide only limited and inconsistent improvements, with no gains for some structures (e.g., HV, LCC). While the authors attribute this to limited data, the results more strongly suggest sensitivity to domain shift and data scale rather than architectural robustness.
This concern is further compounded by the fact that all main experiments are conducted on a single dataset with homogeneous acquisition conditions, which does not reflect real-world clinical variability. As such, the paper does not provide sufficient evidence that the method would generalize beyond the specific setting considered.
In addition, the empirical contribution of the proposed modules is limited. The ablation results show that SAFA yields statistically significant improvements only in a small subset of metrics, while AAR does not demonstrate significant gains. Although the authors provide qualitative explanations (e.g., interpretability trade-offs), these do not sufficiently justify presenting these components as key contributions.
Finally, some design choices appear heuristic and insufficiently validated. In particular, the fine/coarse routing relies on a Sobel-based complexity map and a fixed threshold without justification or sensitivity analysis, and the proposed “attention” mechanism functions primarily as spatial reweighting rather than modeling meaningful spatial relationships. These factors further limit the novelty and robustness of the approach.
Overall, while the problem and overall framework are well-motivated, the current evidence is not strong enough to fully support the paper’s broader claims, leading to a weak reject recommendation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The rebuttal addresses several concerns in a reasonable and professional manner, particularly by clarifying terminology, acknowledging dataset limitations, and reframing the FeTA experiment as a limited transfer study rather than definitive evidence of broad generalization. However, my overall assessment remains unchanged.
The main reason is that the empirical support for some of the paper’s key methodological components remains weak. In particular, AAR is presented throughout the paper as an important methodological contribution, yet the ablation results show no statistically significant performance gains and in several cases slightly worse results. In the rebuttal, the authors clarify that AAR is intended primarily as an interpretability-oriented regularizer rather than a component designed to improve predictive accuracy. While this clarification is helpful, the paper does not provide sufficient evidence that the resulting attention maps offer clinically meaningful interpretability benefits that justify the observed performance trade-off. As a result, the practical necessity and impact of AAR remain unclear.
Overall, I appreciate the authors’ thoughtful responses and believe the work is promising, but I still find the current evidence insufficient to fully support the paper’s broader methodological and clinical claims.

meta_reviews.text:
Given contraversary comments, it would be good to clarify those key concerns from the reviewers.

I agree with the majority of the reviewers.

After rebuttal, R1 maintained Accept and R2 remained Weak Accept, while R3 maintained Reject, citing insufficient empirical support for key components such as AAR and limited evidence for the claimed interpretability benefits. While the work addresses an important clinical problem, the current evidence is insufficient to fully support its broader methodological and clinical claims, leading to my recommendation of Reject.

The authors see merit in the provided rebuttal answers for this paper.
The strengths of a highly relevant topic, well formulated methodology through a two-stage approach, and comprehensive evaluation, are met with remaining concerns of no significant performance gains (with however attention maps provided as a new benefit) for example. All in all, the methodology could result in interesting discussions.

author_feedback_text:
##### We apprecia all reviewers for recognizing the overall framework, clinical relevance, comprehensive evaluation, and transparent reporting. ####
[R1] Kidokoro scoring connection. Full Kidokoro scoring also requires signal abnormalities, structural alterations, and qualitative findings beyond biometry. We will clarify that MEASURE automates the quantitative biometric component, is a module that can be integrated with quantitative detectors toward comprehensive automated scoring.
[R1] Clarifications. (a) Input: 6ch = 3 slices (2.5D) + 3 coordinate channels (x,y,radial). (b) Selector returns top-2; predictor randomly samples one as center slice. (c) Base = ResNet-34 + GAP + prediction heads. (d) GA-only is a univariate linear regression baseline per FeTA challenge protocol, not an input to our pipeline.
[R2] 3D comparison framing. This comparison tests clinical workflow-based decomposition benefits and plane-aware supervision, not intrinsic 2D-vs-3D superiority. We will revise wording.
[R2] Interpretability. Measurement-wise pooling maps directly determine predictions via measurement-specific weighted pooling, providing spatial explanations of which regions contribute to each biometric. We agree this is demonstrated qualitatively (Fig. 2) rather than via quantitative localization.
[R2] Single-expert annotations. Table 2 compares model–expert with intra-rater variability (>3-month re-measurement) via Bland–Altman LoA ratios. We acknowledge inter-rater analysis will strengthen the validation.
[R2&R3] Simulated thick-slice. Our simulation provides preliminary robustness evidence, not a substitute for real clinical MRI. We will make this limitation explicit.
[R2&R3] FeTA cross-domain. This was not intended as proof of broad generalizability, but as a transparent transfer test under substantial domain shift (term neonatal to younger fetal, N=470 to N=70). In context, most FeTA challenge methods did not outperform GA-only regression, our Image+GA improves MAE for 3/5 targets with clear gains for sBIP and TCD. We will clarify this as limited but non-trivial evidence of architectural adaptability.
[R2&R3] Role of SAFA and AAR. We will clarify the component hierarchy: measurement-specific pooling is the main performance driver (Table 1, largest ablation gap). SAFA provides selective, statistically supported benefits (FDR-corrected for BPW and IHD, p=0.036), consistent with its through-plane context role. AAR only works with the presence of measurement-specific pooling (Table 1, w/o pooling ablation is also excluding AAR), and is not intended as an independent component to improve regression accuracy, Rather, it regularizes pooling maps via symmetry/smoothness/distinctiveness, consistent with the structured behavior qualitatively illustrated in Fig. 2.We will revise framing accordingly.
[R3] Attention terminology. We agree that our module is not relational query–key–value attention, but measurement-specific spatial attention pooling. We will clarify this terminology and emphasize that its contribution is target-specific spatial aggregation for constructing distinct biometric representations in multi-measurement neonatal biometry.
[R3] Fine/coarse routing threshold. We want to clarify that Sobel complexity map c is normalized per-sample to [0, 1], τ is fixed as the midpoint of [0,1] complexity range. Setting τ = 0.5 intuitively means that locations with normalized edge complexity above 0.5 are preferentially routed toward the fine branch. Routing sharpness is controlled by temperature t, learned end-to-end, allowing the model to adapt how aggressively it differentiates regions. We will clarify the Sobel complexity map normalization, τ justification explicit in Section 2.3.
[R3] Dataset limitation. dHCP is the largest publicly available standardized neonatal MRI cohort for controlled method development. We will state explicitly that multi-site validation remains future work.
We appreciate all reviewers for their efforts.

title: Measuring Prediction Uncertainty in Neural Cellular Automata
abstract:
Neural cellular automata (NCA) provide a lightweight alternative to encoder–decoder segmentation networks.
However, it can be difficult to decide when a prediction should be trusted. 
Here, we study uncertainty estimation for NCA-based medical image segmentation without modifying the underlying architecture or retraining the model. Our approach is motivated by viewing the NCA as a dynamical system where convergent attractors correspond to confident predictions.
Concretely, we propose resilience, a simple measure that leverages the intrinsic iterative structure of NCAs by probing the stability of the final prediction under small perturbations of the automaton state. Predictions that return to the same solution are deemed confident, while those that change substantially are flagged as uncertain.
We evaluate uncertainty by its ability to predict segmentation quality using selective prediction metrics (∆Dice@9 and AURC) and ranking metrics (AUROC and AUPRC). Across multiple medical segmentation benchmarks, resilience identifies failure cases more reliably than baselines, improving trust and safety in NCA-based models.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a training-free uncertainty estimation method tailored to Neural Cellular Automata (NCA) for medical image segmentation. The central idea exploits NCA’s iterative dynamical-system structure: after running the NCA for T steps to obtain the final state S_T and prediction m, Gaussian noise is injected into the latent state, the automaton is allowed to relax for an additional T’ steps to produce a new prediction m’, and uncertainty is defined as u_res = 1 − IoU(m, m’).
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Conceptually clean and NCA-native. Framing the NCA as a dynamical system and probing the basin of attraction around the final state is a natural fit, more so than transplanting feed-forward uncertainty methods (MC dropout, deep ensembles) onto NCA. The intuition is well-explained. 
2.Truly training-free and architecture-agnostic. No dropout layers, no retraining, no modification of the readout — the method can be dropped onto an existing NCA segmentation pipeline at zero cost. This is genuinely valuable for practitioners.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Missing the most relevant baselines. The paper compares only against NCA-internal uncertainty signals, but does not include any of the standard uncertainty methods adapted to NCA: MC dropout (which can be applied to NCA by adding dropout to the local update network and retraining — this is not “architecture-changing” in any prohibitive sense), deep ensembles (training multiple NCAs with different seeds), or input-perturbation TTA with stronger augmentations. Without at least one of these as a reference, it’s unclear whether the dynamical-system framing actually buys anything over more conventional baselines. 
2.The noise magnitude σ and the relaxation length T’ are the two parameters that fully determine the behavior of the method, yet neither value nor sensitivity is reported. A simple sweep would let readers calibrate the method and would address the obvious concern that the results are tuned per-dataset. 
3.Resilience uses one noise sample per image. A natural extension is to compute mean and variance over multiple perturbations, which would likely be both more informative and more stable. The paper does not justify why a single sample is preferred or report results for multiple samples. 
4.The NCA baseline is intentionally weak. The paper states that no dataset-specific tuning is performed, leading to mIoU as low as 0.43 on Kvasir-SEG. Uncertainty methods are easier to evaluate when models make many errors, so the strong gains may not transfer to a well-tuned NCA. At least one experiment with a competitively trained NCA would address this concern. 
5.Computational cost is not reported. “Highly efficient” is claimed in the conclusion but never quantified. Resilience requires T’ additional NCA iterations beyond the standard T, which is a substantial overhead (potentially 50–100% more compute per image), and this should be made explicit and compared against the cost of TTA. 
6.Distribution shift evaluation is mentioned but underreported. Section 3.1 mentions augmenting the test sets of ClinicDB and Kvasir-SEG with geometric/photometric perturbations, but Table 2 does not separate clean vs. perturbed results, so the reader cannot tell whether resilience holds up under shift specifically.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The proposed method is conceptually clean and the empirical results across five datasets are encouraging, but the paper has two structural weaknesses that I find hard to overlook for a methods contribution: the absence of any conventional uncertainty baseline (notably MC dropout, which is the standard reference in the field), and the lack of sensitivity analysis for the two hyperparameters that fully control the method’s behavior. The weak NCA baseline also makes it difficult to know whether the gains generalize to a competitively trained model. The idea is good and worth pursuing, but in its current form the experimental case is incomplete. I would consider raising my score if the rebuttal adds at least an MC-dropout-on-NCA comparison and σ/T’ sweeps.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces a method to estimate uncertainty in Neural Cellular Automata (NCA) by perturbing NCA states. Stable segmentation generation with perturbations is correlated with low uncertainty, while instability or variability in the segmentation output resulting from perturbed states is associated with higher uncertainty. This was confirmed quantitatively by estimating the Dice gain using the 90% most confident samples, where the proposed method shows the highest gains overall in both Dice and failure detection compared to competing methods for estimating uncertainty in NCA. An important contribution of the paper is providing a single uncertainty score per image, which assists in evaluating the segmentation’s reliability and in flagging samples for additional human review (failure detection/deferral).
reviews.text_strengths: First to introduce uncertainty estimation method within NCA segmentation approaches, therefore providing a method of assessing the risk associated with NCA-based segmentation with quantitative measures for detecting segmentation failures as presented in this paper.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Introduction: As NCAs are not well-known within the community, a more detailed explanation into the mechanism in which NCAs produce segmentations from input images would have been useful. This can be added in the third paragraph in the introduction. What advantages do NCAs provide over standard encoder-decoder-based architectures.
Table 1 summarizes the results for the NCA baseline performance on the different datasets. It would have been useful to also have a standard UNet performance to compare it to, or at least discuss why it would not be useful within the scope of the paper.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Questions:
Section 2.2: 
○ Is the perturbation done only twice? Or is the explanation in section 2.2 only for demonstrative purposes? If it is only twice why? And if it were done several times, how would the u_res score be computed?
Section 3.4: For failure detection how was the u_res thresholded in order to determine the threshold for failure (not accepting a segmentation from the model) What criteria was used to determine this threshold.
What is the computational cost of introducing perturbations to the states to estimate uncertainty?
Minor Comments:
Page two: “…sharp final mask can still be unreliable if it has not truly settled,…” settled is not the correct or appropriate term to use here.
The method “resilience” was italicized in some places and not in others (like in the abstract/introduction). The authors should be consistent by italicizing the method’s name everywhere for ease of legibility.
Section 2.1: “Given a 3 color input image” reword to “..RGB input image”
Tta (test time augmentation) should be capitalized

Introduction of uncertainty for NCA-based segmentation is a valuable contribution for improving the safety of deployment of segmentation models.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces “resilience,” a novel, training-free method for estimating uncertainty in Neural Cellular Automata (NCA) based medical image segmentation models. The core idea is to treat the NCA as a dynamical system and probe the stability of its final prediction. This is achieved by taking the final state of the NCA, adding a small Gaussian perturbation, and allowing the model to run for a few more iterations. The uncertainty is then quantified as one minus the Intersection-over-Union (IoU) between the original and the “relaxed” segmentation masks. The authors evaluate their method on five medical segmentation benchmarks, comparing it against other NCA-native uncertainty baselines. They show that resilience consistently improves selective prediction (∆Dice@90) and is competitive in failure detection (AUROC/AUPRC).
reviews.text_strengths: This paper addresses the important and timely topic of uncertainty quantification. The core idea of “resilience” as a proxy for stability in a dynamical system is elegant and intuitive.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Inadequate Contextualization and Baseline Comparison:
The paper positions NCAs as a “lightweight alternative” to standard encoder-decoder architectures like U-Net but fails to provide any comparison to them. This is a critical omission. The reported Dice scores in Table 1 are quite low for several datasets (e.g., 0.60 for Kvasir-SEG, 0.74 for ClinicDB). It is highly likely that a standard U-Net would achieve significantly better segmentation performance. If the primary claim is that NCAs are a viable alternative, the authors must demonstrate this through direct comparison.
More importantly, for an uncertainty paper, there is no comparison to established uncertainty methods on U-Net architectures (e.g., MC-Dropout, Test-Time Augmentation, or Ensembling). The central question is not just whether resilience is the best uncertainty method for NCAs, but whether NCA with resilience is a competitive combination for uncertainty-aware segmentation in general. Without this broader context, the practical relevance of the proposed method is unclear. If a U-Net is more accurate and its uncertainty estimates are more reliable, the motivation for using the proposed NCA-based approach dissolves. The authors must provide a compelling justification (e.g., computational efficiency, specific robustness properties) for their method in the context of the wider literature.
2.Insufficient and Unsound Evaluation of Uncertainty:
The evaluation of uncertainty is superficial and misses key aspects that are standard in the field. My primary concern is the complete lack of analysis regarding the spatial correspondence between uncertainty and segmentation error. A good uncertainty method should produce high uncertainty in regions where the model is incorrect (e.g., at object boundaries or in mis-segmented areas). The paper only reports image-level uncertainty metrics, which obscure this crucial spatial information. The authors should have included analyses that are common for segmentation uncertainty, such as:
Visualizing the pixel-wise uncertainty maps and comparing them to error maps.
Reporting metrics that measure spatial overlap, such as the Generalized Energy Distance or pixel-wise correlation between uncertainty and error.
Analyzing uncertainty calibration (e.g., using Expected Calibration Error).
Furthermore, Figure 2 is a missed opportunity. It shows images with high and low uncertainty but does not show the corresponding resilience maps (i.e., a visualization of the difference between the original mask m and the relaxed mask m’). This would have provided at least some qualitative insight into the spatial properties of the proposed uncertainty measure. As it stands, the evaluation does not convincingly demonstrate that the proposed u_res is a spatially meaningful or well-calibrated measure of uncertainty.
Minor Weaknesses:
Lack of Ablation Studies: The method relies on several key hyperparameters, yet their influence is not studied. What is the role of the noise magnitude sigma? How sensitive is the method to the number of initial iterations T and relaxation iterations T’? A thorough ablation study is necessary to understand the method’s robustness and provide guidance for practitioners.
Practicality and Generalizability: The paper does not discuss how one would set a threshold on u_res to flag “bad” predictions in a real-world application. Is this threshold dataset-dependent? Moreover, the proposed method is defined for binary segmentation via IoU. It is unclear how it would be extended to multi-class segmentation problems, which are common in medical imaging. The authors should discuss these limitations.
Missed Baseline Opportunity: An ensemble of NCAs seems like a natural and powerful baseline for uncertainty estimation. Given that ensembling is a gold standard, its absence is conspicuous. Comparing resilience to an NCA ensemble would provide a much stronger benchmark for its performance.
Clarity and Presentation:
The citation formatting on page 2 ([5,10,11,12]) is unconventional; citations should typically appear at the end of a clause or sentence.
One can see an over-use of em-dashes, which can make sentences convoluted and feel “LLM-esque.”
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

While the paper presents a clever idea for NCA-based uncertainty, it fails to meet the standards for publication at MICCAI due to two fundamental flaws. First, it lacks a comparison to the most dominant and relevant baselines (i.e., U-Net based methods), making it impossible to judge the practical value of the work. Second, its evaluation of uncertainty is incomplete and lacks the standard spatial analysis required to validate an uncertainty method for segmentation. Combined with the missing ablation studies and issues with referencing, the paper feels premature. The authors should be encouraged to perform the necessary experiments and analyses to properly situate their work and validate their claims before resubmission.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text: The paper introduces a training-free uncertainty estimation method for NCAs for medical image segmentation. The reviewers see clear methodological value in this contribution, in particular its architecture-agnostic nature and the fact that the methodological choices are well argued. Despite some concerns on the lack of comparisons against relevant baselines, the work is a solid contribution to the field.

title: Measuring What VLMs Don’t Say: Validation Metrics Hide Clinical Terminology Erasure in Radiology Report Generation
abstract: Reliable deployment of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in radiology requires validation metrics that go beyond surface-level text similarity to ensure clinical fidelity and demographic fairness. This paper investigates a critical blind spot in current model evaluation: the use of decoding strategies that lead to high aggregate token-overlap scores despite succumbing to template collapse, in which models generate only repetitive, safe generic text and omit clinical terminology. Unaddressed, this blind spot can lead to metric gaming, where models that perform well on benchmarks prove clinically uninformative. Instead, we advocate for lexical diversity measures to check model generations for clinical specificity. We introduce Clinical Association Displacement (CAD), a vocabulary-level framework that quantifies shifts in demographic-based word associations in generated reports. Weighted Association Erasure (WAE) aggregates these shifts to measure the clinical signal loss across demographic groups. We show that deterministic decoding produces high levels of semantic erasure, while stochastic sampling generates diverse outputs but risks introducing new bias, motivating a fundamental rethink of how “optimal” reporting is defined.
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers
Machine Learning -> Algorithmic Fairness / Safety / Regulation
Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of this paper is formalizing a vocabulary-level diagnostic framework to evaluate radiology report generation. Specifically, it introduces Clinical Association Displacement (CAD) and Weighted Association Erasure (WAE) to quantify how standard decoding strategies can lead to template collapse. This framework helps reveal how the erasure of critical clinical terminology is often hidden behind high aggregate text similarity scores.
reviews.text_strengths: A major strength of this work is its empirical identification of a genuine and often overlooked evaluation blind spot. The authors astutely point out that models can game traditional metrics like BERTScore by producing safe and generic templates. Furthermore, treating the decoding strategy itself as a primary confounding variable is a very insightful experimental design. The sensitivity analysis clearly illustrates the fundamental trade-off between semantic erasure under deterministic decoding and emergent bias under stochastic sampling, providing a strong empirical foundation for their observational claims.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The primary weakness of the paper is its conceptual and methodological incrementalism. While the identified problem is significant, the proposed solution relies on standard statistical techniques. The CAD framework is essentially a direct application of the log ratio of unigram probabilities with Dirichlet smoothing, which is a well-established method in text analysis. Applying this to generated text is a natural extension rather than a fundamentally new methodology. Secondly, the paper lacks direct clinical validation. It remains unproven whether the reference-aligned demographic association shifts measured by CAD and WAE actually correspond to clinically meaningful diagnostic errors or patient harm. Finally, critical reproducibility details are missing, such as the exact patient and site-level data splits and the specific prompts used for the GPT-4.1 baseline.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I recommend a weak reject because there is a notable gap between the importance of the problem identified and the depth of the proposed solution. The paper does an excellent job of highlighting how conventional metrics fail to penalize template collapse. However, the proposed CAD and WAE metrics are conceptually incremental and lack the rigorous clinical validation necessary to justify their adoption as definitive fairness or diagnostic metrics in medical AI. Without reader studies or validation against true clinical outcomes, it is difficult to accept these surrogate metrics as a robust standard, making the overall contribution somewhat limited for a top-tier venue.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
After reading the rebuttal, I appreciate the authors’ clarifications, especially that CAD/WAE are intended as complementary, system-level diagnostics rather than per-sample clinical metrics. However, the rebuttal does not substantially change my assessment.
My main concerns remain. First, the proposed method is still conceptually incremental: it formalizes a useful intuition—checking whether clinically relevant terminology is preserved—but does not convincingly show why CAD/WAE are methodologically necessary beyond simpler clinical term/entity coverage or omission analyses. Second, the clinical validity of the proposed metrics remains insufficiently established. The rebuttal gives intuitive examples, but still does not show that CAD/WAE correlate with diagnostic correctness, radiologist judgment, patient-level errors, or clinical utility. Third, reproducibility remains only partially addressed, since code, prompts, and model weights are promised post-acceptance, while several protocol details remain unclear in the submitted manuscript.
Overall, I agree that the paper identifies an important evaluation blind spot in radiology report generation. However, the rebuttal mainly reiterates the motivation and intended use of the metrics rather than resolving the concerns about novelty, clinical validation, and reproducibility. I therefore maintain my recommendation to reject.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper examines a limitation of current evaluation practices in radiology report generation, where standard text similarity metrics (e.g., BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore) can assign high scores to outputs that rely on repetitive, generic templates while omitting clinically specific terminology.
To analyze this issue, the authors propose Clinical Association Displacement (CAD), a vocabulary-level framework that measures how the demographic associations of clinical terms (e.g., between male and female reports) shift between reference and generated corpora. They further introduce Weighted Association Erasure (WAE), which aggregates these term-level shifts into a global measure of lexical displacement.
Using these metrics, the paper studies the effect of different decoding strategies and shows that deterministic decoding tends to produce high-scoring but lexically collapsed outputs, while stochastic decoding increases diversity but can introduce new demographic associations. The authors suggest using CAD and WAE as complementary evaluation tools to detect such failure modes and to better distinguish models that produce clinically informative reports from those that achieve high scores through generic generation.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper is well-motivated. Direct NLP metrics are not clinically representative, and high overlap scores can mask clinically uninformative outputs. This is a valid and important issue in medical report generation.
2.The proposed idea to detect such cases of collapsing through analyzing what the model does not say is interesting and novel.
3.The results are informative and align well with intuitive expectations. They show that deterministic decoding yields high evaluation scores but leads to severe template collapse and loss of clinical terminology, while stochastic decoding improves diversity at the cost of increased bias and instability. This trade-off is consistently demonstrated and can provide useful insights into model behavior for future work.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Corpus-level analysis only: CAD/WAE operate at the dataset level and do not provide per-sample insight. In contrast to standard metrics (e.g., BERTScore, BLEU), which can be evaluated per sample, the proposed metrics are not directly applicable at the individual report level. This limits their usefulness for analyzing specific model errors or for practical clinical validation.
2.Unclear link to clinical correctness: While the paper reports text-based metrics (e.g., BERTScore, RateScore) as indicators of clinical performance, it does not establish whether CAD/WAE correlate with true diagnostic accuracy or clinical utility. It remains unclear whether improvements in these metrics correspond to better medical outcomes.
3.Overemphasis on inference: The paper attributes the observed effects primarily to decoding strategy. However, similar phenomena (e.g., template collapse or loss of terminology) may also originate from training dynamics, such as data imbalance or reliance on language priors. This aspect is not sufficiently discussed.
4.Minor presentation issue: Figure 2 layout (subfigure labeling) could be improved for clarity.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

My recommendation is to accept. The paper addresses an important and underexplored issue in evaluating radiology report generation with VLMs and provides a diagnostic framework. The findings are clear and informative. However, I encourage the authors to address the points above.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
Regarding the corpus-level nature of CAD/WAE, my concern was not that corpus-level analysis is inappropriate. I agree that bias, terminology erasure, and template collapse are naturally system-level phenomena. My concern was rather that, unlike standard metrics such as BLEU, ROUGE, or BERTScore, which can be computed both at the corpus level and at the individual-report level, the proposed metrics operate only at the corpus level. This limits their usefulness for identifying specific erroneous reports or supporting granular clinical validation. However, the authors clarify that CAD/WAE are intended as supplementary system-level auditing tools rather than replacements for standard metrics. This framing is reasonable and largely satisfies my concern.
Regarding clinical validation, I still think the paper should be careful not to overstate the clinical meaning of CAD/WAE. The authors provide plausible examples of clinically relevant terminology erasure, and I agree that a full clinical trial is not necessary for this paper. However, the proposed metrics remain indirect text-level indicators rather than validated measures of diagnostic correctness or patient impact. Therefore, they should be presented as tools for flagging potential clinical risks, not as direct evidence of clinical harm or clinical utility.
Overall, the rebuttal clarifies the intended role of the proposed metrics and addresses my main concern sufficiently. I would maintain my positive recommendation.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper identifies a research gap in current radiology report generation evaluation: models that achieve high surface-level similarity scores (e.g., BLEU, BERTScore) often suffer from template collapse, where they produce safe, generic text while erasing specific clinical terminology. To quantify this, the authors introduce Clinical Association Displacement and Weighted Association Erasure. These metrics measure demographic-based word association shifts and clinical signal loss, specifically highlighting how deterministic decoding strategies can lead to the erasure of critical diagnostic details across different patient populations.
