reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Authors addressed some of my questions.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents MERIT, which is a hierarchical multi-scale Mamba framework for whole-slide image analysis, specifically for predicting treatment responses. Its main contributions include a dual-branch hierarchical snake scanning strategy for preserving 2D spatial locality in 1D sequences, and a mechanism for retaining information transmission that utilizes learnable message marking and residual propagation to alleviate the inherent long-distance forgetting problem in the Mamba model.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The dual-branch snake-shaped scanning is a clever and intuitive physical adjustment method, which can maintain the local two-dimensional topological structure during the process of converting a sequence of billion-pixel holographic images into a one-dimensional sequence for use in the state space model.
2.By using a learnable short-term memory unit and a bidirectional scanning method, the one-way forgetting problem of the mamba model was solved, which is an excellent design with a simple structure and reasonable method.
3.The authors provided an anonymized code repository, which greatly improved the reproducibility.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The “message tagging” and bidirectional sequence scanning method used to solve the “Mamba forgetting” problem are highly derivative. They are conceptually identical to the standard category tags ([CLS]) used in the visual transformer and the bidirectional processing strategy widely adopted in existing visual Mamba architectures. The proposed framework is more of an empirical combination of existing engineering techniques rather than a completely new paradigm.
2.The state space model is mainly designed to handle extremely long sequences with linear complexity. However, MERIT uses a grid-based spatial extraction/pooling strategy, significantly shortening the overall sequence length before the sequence reaches the serial Mamba blocks. Applying a complex bidirectional Mamba model on this already shortened sequence and adding additional tags weakens the main theoretical advantages of the state space model. This raises a question: Can the standard Transformer also exhibit equally excellent performance at these grid-level tags? This makes choosing the Mamba model seem somewhat forced, merely to take advantage of a popular architecture.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The authors should conduct a more in-depth discussion on the reason why “Mamba” is absolutely necessary for this specific architecture. Given that the grid division has reduced the sequence length, conducting direct comparative experiments and comparing your “message tagging + Mamba” module with the standard “transformer encoder” running on the same grid markers will clearly demonstrate whether the performance improvement is due to the Mamba architecture itself or merely to your effective feature extraction and tagging strategies.

My recommendation is “weak accept”. This paper addresses an important clinical issue, achieves outstanding empirical results, and demonstrates a very solid engineering design, including a complete evaluation process. I must point out that the innovation in the method is relatively limited; the core components - the snake scan, global message marking, and bidirectional scan - are direct applications of mature technologies rather than fundamental innovations. However, despite relying on the gradual combination of known architectural techniques, its robust execution, strong predictive performance, and obvious clinical relevance have enabled this work to exceed the acceptance criteria. It provides sufficient empirical value and offers a solid foundation for the MICCAI community.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The author’s rebuttal answered my questions. I think this is a solid piece of work with complete experiments and a closed theoretical framework. However, I still believe there are certain flaws in the innovation of this article, but such flaws can be accepted, so I think it can be accepted.

meta_reviews.text:
The reviews are mixed but generally recognize the clinical relevance, solid engineering, reproducibility, and promising empirical performance of MERIT. During rebuttal, please specifically address: 1) the methodological novelty over existing visual Mamba/Transformer designs, especially message tokens, bidirectional scanning, and topology-preserving scanning; 2) whether Mamba is necessary given the shortened grid-level sequence, ideally with a direct comparison to a Transformer encoder under the same setting; 3) more complete ablations isolating each proposed component; and 4) interpretability and clinical robustness, including heatmap generation/validation and discussion or evidence of external, few-shot, or zero-shot generalization. These points will be important for the final decision.

The post-rebuttal consensus is positive. Reviewers found the paper clinically relevant, empirically strong, and technically well executed, with useful designs for multi-scale WSI modeling and Mamba-based information retention. Although methodological novelty and external clinical validation remain somewhat limited, the rebuttal addressed the main concerns sufficiently. I therefore recommend acceptance.

The paper proposes MERIT, a hierarchical Multi-scale Mamba framework with Enhanced Retention of Information, specifically designed for treatment response prediction from whole slide images (WSIs). The work addresses an important and clinically relevant problem in computational pathology, and the proposed architecture is well-motivated. Most reviewers recognized the technical contribution of the paper and found the authors’ rebuttal satisfactory. Therefore, I support acceptance of this paper at MICCAI.

All reviewers agree accept.
The rebuttal addressed the reviewers comments.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their constructive comments. We will clarify these descriptions in the final version and address the main concerns below.
1.Mamba necessity and ablation (R3).
We clarify that the grid is not pooling and does not shorten the Mamba input. The overall design aims to largely preserve low-/high-resolution patch sequences, while the grid organizes spatial topology and aligns low-/high-res patches. Thus, the Mamba input remains a full multi-scale sequence with shape (L,d), where L=l+h+m often exceeds 20k; l/h/m count low-/high-res patch features and MSG tokens. A vanilla Transformer on the same sequence would incur quadratic attention cost and exceed GPU memory. Hence, Mamba is necessary for efficient long-sequence modeling, while its compact parameters also help reduce overfitting risk in small cohorts.
The sequence becomes compact only after Mamba extracts grid-wise MSG memories; using this derived MSG sequence for Transformer comparison would change the input representation and would not be a fair same-setting comparison. Nevertheless, Table 1 compares MERIT with multi-scale, Transformer-based, and SSM baselines using the same feature extractors. Table 2 ablates the claimed modules; removing each part degrades performance, supporting that the gain comes from the proposed components.
2.Methodological distinction (R1, R3).
MERIT’s novelty lies in a WSI-specific retentive information-transfer paradigm that preserves and exchanges grid-wise multi-scale information while mitigating Mamba’s degradation on long WSI sequences. The topology-preserving scan maps multi-scale WSI structures into a spatially aligned sequence, where each grid contributes one MSG memory carrier between low- and high-resolution patch segments. Forward Mamba first writes multi-scale context into MSG memories. Residual propagation then consolidates these memories through global calibration and channel mixing for inter-grid exchange; the updated memories are reinserted before backward refinement, where the reverse scan redistributes them to mitigate long-range forgetting. The final prediction aggregates a grid-wise sequence of forward/backward MSG memories rather than a single global token. Thus, MERIT is not a simple use of tokens or bidirectional scanning, but an aggregation–exchange–reinject–redistribute mechanism for WSI information retention. This differs from ViT/CLS readout tokens and Vision Mamba scans mainly used for image-sequence adaptation. Table 2 shows performance drops after removing MSG or residual propagation, while Fig.3 and sequence-contribution analysis verify MSG as a high-contribution information hub and show reduced information decay.
3.Interpretability (R2).
Fig.3/Sec.3.5 provide clinical visual examples. Grad-CAM heatmaps are generated by back-propagating the prediction score to patch feature activations, computing gradient-weighted importance scores, and mapping them to WSI coordinates using stored patch positions. The highlighted model-attended regions were reviewed by pathologists and correspond to clinically meaningful tissue patterns, including tumor-rich regions as shown in Fig.3.
4.Clinical robustness (R2).
Strict zero-/few-shot testing is valuable, but it is a different transfer-learning protocol from the setting targeted in this submission. Our work focuses on the clinically realistic limited-sample supervised setting: treatment-response cohorts are inherently small, and each training fold contains only limited labeled WSIs. Under this practical constraint, MERIT uses fixed foundation-model features and a compact 0.45M-parameter design, enabling it to learn predictive WSI representations from limited training samples while reducing overfitting risk. The consistent results across multiple cohorts, cancer types, and treatment settings support its generalization and a degree of robustness under small-sample clinical conditions. We will extend MERIT to strict zero-/few-shot protocols in future studies.

title: Merlin Plus: A Large-Scale, Multi-cancer, Image-Mask-Report Dataset
abstract: Multi-cancer segmentation in computed tomography (CT) is fundamentally limited by the scarcity of tumor masks across different organs. We present Merlin Plus, the first large-scale CT dataset with radiologist-created tumor masks across 9 organs. Merlin Plus extends the Merlin dataset by adding 1,153 per-voxel tumor masks and longitudinal metadata. To create these tumor masks, we developed a report-based active-learning framework in which radiology reports identify tumor cases for annotation and support training of a tumor segmentation model. The model generates initial masks, which radiologists review and correct to produce the final masks, reducing annotation burden while maintaining high-quality annotations. Besides tumor masks, the longitudinal metadata in Merlin Plus enables temporal modeling of cancer progression. By directly addressing the major bottleneck of limited multi-cancer segmentation masks, Merlin Plus supports scalable multi-organ cancer detection, segmentation, and longitudinal analysis in CT. Dataset is available at: https://github.com/MrGiovanni/MerlinPlus

reviews.recommendation_label: Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper introduces a large dataset of abdominal CT from multiple cancers with refined segmentation masks obtained via active learning under guidance of radiologists. The dataset adds to existing public CT datasets of tumors with new additional tumor types including spleen, adrenal glands, bladder, gallbladder, esophagus, stomach, duodenum, prostate, and uterus. 
It also includes longitudinal metadata enabling temporal modeling of cancer progression. Radiologist refined AI-generated masks in an active learning fashion obtains high quality masks with reduced human burden.
reviews.text_strengths:
Large-scale CT (25,494) dataset with radiologist validated lesion-level masks spanning 9 organs
This dataset complements existing tumor datasets with additional organs and more detailed masks compared to previous datasets, eg. ULS.
The proposed active learning for segmentation from reports is novel and can be generalized to other applications
reviews.text_weaknesses: The quality of final refined masks is not discussed. For example, a limited study on reproducibility, and inter-observer variably could assist in gaining confidence about the quality of final masks.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Paper described release of a large dataset of CT and tumor mask pairs that can greatly assist the community in developing relevant AI models. To create reliable high quality mask, they introduce an active learning refinement process, making mask creation under often busy radiologist schedules feasible. This methodology alone is highly valuable tool for similar tasks and is justifiably submitted as another paper.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper presents Merlin Plus, a large-scale CT dataset of 25K scans with voxel-wise lesion masks covering nine tumor types mostly absent from existing public segmentation datasets. It addresses a bottleneck that publicly available annotated data is largely restricted to liver/kidney/pancreatic/lung tumors. The dataset is derived from the original Merlin cohort (Stanford Hospital) and is enriched with lesion masks and malignant/benign labels derived from cross-referencing ICD codes with radiology reports.
The second contribution is a report-based active learning annotation pipeline that allegedly substantially reduces annotation time. The pipeline bootstraps from the R-Super report supervision framework (Bassi et al., MICCAI 2025) to address the “cold-start problem” when no existing segmentation model covers the target tumor types. Subsequent active learning cycles combine automatic mask refinement using report-extracted tumor attributes (location, size, count) with a “report-confidence score” (Dice between the soft model output and the report-refined binary mask) to identify and prioritize uncertain cases for radiologist correction.
Finally, Merlin Plus provides longitudinal metadata, enabling temporal modeling of cancer progression. This is claimed by the authors as a contribution but no further details are given and the (longitudinal) CT images and IDC codes fully stem from the original Merlin dataset.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Clinically relevant gap addressed with meaningful scale.
The focus on 9 tumor types absent from public segmentation datasets addresses a genuine and important gap. Although there partially exist datasets with some of the annotated lesion subtypes, having ONE comprehensive dataset is a major advancement.
2.Clever use of existing reports to initialize the annotation pipeline.
The approach of leveraging existing radiology reports as weak supervision (i.e. starting from R-Super to produce reasonable initial proposals) rather than only requiring fully manual masks from scratch is elegant.
3.Intuitive active learning criterion. The report-confidence score (Dice between the soft model output and the report-refined binary mask) is a cheap and sensible proxy for uncertainty: poor model predictions require large corrections in Step 3, resulting in low Dice and flagging the case for radiologist review.
4.Longitudinal metadata and multi-modal annotations.
The inclusion of anonymized CT dates and patient IDs enabling longitudinal tracking, combined with ICD-coded malignancy labels, makes Merlin Plus significantly richer than a standard segmentation benchmark. If the authors’ claims hold and this is indeed novel, this opens doors for temporal modeling and survival analysis that most datasets in this space do not support.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.(Critical) Baseline comparison is insufficient and potentially flawed
The only public baseline is ULS23 (de Grauw et al., Medical Image Analysis 2025). ULS is a prompt-based universal lesion segmentation model trained with center-cropped patches, assuming a lesion is ALWAYS present in the patch center. Running it as a fully automatic sliding-window model would introduce a fundamental evaluation mismatch. The paper does not clarify whether the evaluation was prompt-based or automatic.
If prompt-based: comparison should include e.g. LesionLocator (Rokuss et al., CVPR 2025), a zero-shot universal tumor segmentation and tracking model or a general-purpose prompt-based segmentation model e.g. MedSAM2 (Ma et al., arXiv 2025).
If fully automatic: relevant baselines would include GF-Screen (Wu et al., ICLR 2026), a reinforcement-based pan-cancer segmentation model covering many lesion types, or general-purpose models such as VISTA3D (He et al., CVPR 2025) and SegVol (Du et al., NeurIPS 2024),VoxTell (arXiv 2025) or TotalSegmentator (Wassertal et. al.) for lesions.
I acknowledge that running all of these may not be feasible, but at minimum the ULS evaluation mode should be clarified and at least one stronger baseline must be included for proper evaluation.
2.(Critical) Evaluation metrics are insufficient
The primary metric in Table 1 is detection F1-score (organ-level, volume-thresholded) with sensitivity and specificity. While detection performance is relevant and consistent with the R-Super protocol, DSC is the standard metric for segmentation and is almost entirely absent from the main results. DSC values are only buried in the table caption for a subset of models (“Average DSC: 17 for MedFormer, 25 for R-Super with masks, 10 for R-Super reports only”) without a proper per-organ breakdown.
This raises two concerns:
The reported DSC values are very low. Averages of ~17–25 are far below what lesion segmentation methods typically achieve on established benchmarks (e.g., LiTS, KiTS, PanTS: DSC 40–70+). Values in this range warrant explicit discussion: are they driven by small/early-stage lesions, annotation quality, or model underfitting? The paper is silent on this.
A dataset paper validated through segmentation models must report segmentation quality. Detection F1 alone does not demonstrate the value of voxel-wise masks, which are the primary contribution. Without per-organ DSC, downstream users cannot meaningfully assess model quality.
Finally, no standard deviation is reported anywhere in Table 1, making it difficult to assess result reliability across runs.
3.Authors claim “For per-voxel annotations, we focused on malignant tumors for 9 organs missing masks in public datasets.” however several public datasets actually encompass large parts of these lesion types e.g. “Q. Chen et. al. Scaling Tumor Segmentation: Best Lessons from Real and Synthetic Data”.
4.Figure 1 issues
The caption for panel (a) describes an organ-wise distribution reporting “the number of CT scans with lesions and the number of small lesions (< 2 cm)”, but the actual panel (a) appears to show qualitative CT/mask examples of an adrenal lesion, i.e. caption and figure content do not match.
Only one number per organ appears in the distribution plot, not the two numbers (# CTs and # small lesions) described in the caption.
Panel (b) shows longitudinal time point distribution but is missing a Y-axis, making it impossible to assess what fraction of patients actually have more than one scan. Or how many patients had 3+ examinations. Is this longitudinal data novel or already existent in the original Merlin dataset?
5.(Minor) Pipeline novelty is slightly overstated
Steps 1–3 (including sub-steps 3A–3D: report attribute extraction, organ-constrained masking, ball convolution-based tumor localization, and volume-matched binarization) closely follow the R-Super framework (Bassi et al., MICCAI 2025), which is also the primary baseline in the paper. The genuine novelty seems to be the report-confidence score (Step 4) and the active learning loop around it. The authors should clearly delineate what is directly adapted from R-Super vs. what is new, rather than presenting the full pipeline as their contribution.
6.No ablation on the active learning selection criterion
The report-confidence score is presented as a key design choice, but there is no experiment showing it actually outperforms alternative selection strategies (e.g., random selection, entropy-based uncertainty). While I am generally convinced of the idea, even a simple annotation efficiency curve would substantially strengthen this claim.
7.Missing annotation statistics
Step 5 mentions “e.g., the 50 masks with the lowest score per tumor type” leaving the actual number ambiguous.
The total number of active learning cycles is not reported.
It is unclear how many masks were radiologist-refined vs. automatically accepted as high-quality. Were in the end all masks at least visually inspected?
8.(clarity and organization) Manuscript appears incomplete
Several issues suggest the paper was submitted prematurely:
Keywords section still reads “First keyword · Second keyword · Another keyword”
Section 2.1 contains an unfilled placeholder: “we create # multi-tumor masks in just 5 months”. Howerver, the total mask count is arguably the most important statistic for a tumor lesion dataset paper and is missing
The sentence “R-Super teacher segmentation models to segment tumors” is syntactically broken
The paper does not fill the allotted page limit; space could have been used for additional dataset statistics or a qualitative figure
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The dataset motivation is generally strong, i.e. bootstrapping multi-cancer segmentation from existing radiology reports, an is well-motivated in the paper. The 9 tumor types covered are genuinely underserved in public benchmarks. However, the submission has issues that go beyond minor revisions: (1) The Dice score, the standard metric for segmentation, is almost entirely absent from the results table, and the reported average values (~17–25) are very low without any discussion or explanation; (2) the sole external baseline (ULS) is used in a potentially inappropriate evaluation mode, and the comparison set is narrow given recent work such as GF-Screen (ICLR 2026), LesionLocator (CVPR 2025), and VISTA3D (CVPR 2025), (3) the manuscript is incomplete, with a critical placeholder for the total mask count in Section 2.1 and multiple figure errors; (4) the novelty of the annotation pipeline is partially overstated given its close overlap with R-Super. For the rebuttal, I would particularly like to see: the total mask count (manually revised by radiologists), a clarification of the ULS evaluation setup, a clearer scoping of what is novel beyond R-Super, and a proper per-organ DSC table with discussion of the low absolute values. With these addressed, this work could be competitive for acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
After considering the rebuttal, I lean slightly toward weak reject but acknowledge that the authors have made a serious effort to address the core concerns raised by all three reviewers. The rebuttal provides the missing inter-rater reliability numbers (mean DSC ~52 across 9 tumor types), the previously-absent total mask count (1,153, all radiologist-revised), clarifies the ULS evaluation setup, adds 5 stronger baselines including an external evaluation, and offers a reasonable explanation for the low absolute DSC values via the inter-reader ceiling argument. The report-confidence score is also validated with concrete precision numbers.
Residual concerns: per-organ DSC remains low for several organs (duodenum, prostate, stomach), the dataset scale (1,153 masks) is more modest than the “large-scale” (25K) framing suggests, the manuscript was clearly rushed (multiple placeholders, broken sentences, inconsistent counts), the single-site Stanford-only limitation, and substantial methodological overlap with the concurrent TR-Distillation submission. However, the dataset addresses a genuine, clinically important gap in public CT segmentation resources (9 underserved tumor types), and the report-based active learning framework is a legitimate methodological contribution. On balance, the community value of the released resource outweighs the remaining evidentiary gaps, provided the camera-ready incorporates the rebuttal’s added analyses and fixes the manuscript issues.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper presents Merlin Plus, a dataset extension of the existing Merlin cohort (Stanford Hospital, 25,494 CT–report pairs), augmenting it with radiologist-validated voxel-wise tumor masks for 9 abdominal tumor types currently absent from public segmentation datasets: spleen, adrenal glands, bladder, gallbladder, esophagus, stomach, duodenum, prostate, and uterus. The contribution has three components:(1) The dataset itself i.e voxel-wise masks for ~8,000+ lesion occurrences across 9 organs (with per-organ counts ranging from 108 for esophagus to 2,085 for spleen), augmented with clinical metadata (age, sex, race, scanner type, anonymized IDs, scan dates), malignant/benign labels derived from ICD-10 cross-referenced with reports, and longitudinal structure (multiple time points per patient).(2) A report-based active learning pipeline that addresses the cold-start problem by initializing the annotation loop with R-Super-trained segmentation (no masks required), followed by a six-step cycle: R-Super inference -> report-constrained mask refinement (organ dilation, Ball-Convolution-based tumor localization, volume matching) -> report-confidence scoring (Dice between soft mask and report-refined mask) -> radiologist review of lowest-confidence cases → fine-tuning on accumulated masks and reports. Claimed ~5× speedup (30 min -> 5 min per scan).(3) Empirical demonstration that models trained on Merlin Plus (MedFormer, R-Super with masks+reports) substantially outperform both public multi-tumor models (ULS) and models trained on the original Merlin (report-only supervision) across the 9 tumor types, with +10% F1-Score improvement on average.
reviews.text_strengths: Major Strengths1.This is a genuinely impactful dataset for an under-served clinical problem. The motivation is compelling and accurate: public CT tumor segmentation datasets are dominated by liver, kidney, pancreas, colon, adrenal, and lung tumors, while cancers in the other organs collectively account for roughly half of global cancer mortality. Releasing voxel-wise masks for spleen, adrenal, bladder, gallbladder, esophagus, stomach, duodenum, prostate, and uterus tumors (particularly rare types like esophagus (n=108) and duodenum (n=249)) represents substantial community value. If released as promised, this fills a real gap that cannot be addressed by methodological improvements alone.2.Report-based active learning genuinely solves the cold-start problem. The core insight i.e that traditional active learning fails when no adequate seed model exists for the target tumor types, and that R-Super can bootstrap reasonable initial masks from report supervision alone, is well-motivated and non-obvious. The design choice to couple Ball-Convolution-based tumor localization with report-derived counts and diameters is a clever way to inject weak structural priors that reduce radiologist correction burden. This is a legitimately novel workflow contribution, not just “LLM + active learning.”3.The report-confidence score is a principled triage mechanism. Using the Dice between the soft (pre-refinement) mask and the report-refined mask as a proxy for “how much did the refinement have to do” is a sensible signal for flagging unreliable cases. Low Dice implies that the model’s confidence was misaligned with the report description, which is precisely the condition under which radiologist review adds the most value. The intuition that refinement magnitude correlates with unreliability is well-argued.4.Comprehensive multimodal integration. Beyond masks, the dataset ties together CT, radiology reports, ICD-9/ICD-10 codes (2.9M+ assigned codes, 16,553 unique values), patient demographics, scanner metadata, and longitudinal timestamps. This richness enables research beyond segmentation (longitudinal progression modeling, demographic fairness studies, scanner-invariance analysis) that narrower datasets cannot support.5.Evaluation against both public models and within-dataset baselines. Table 1 compares against ULS (the strongest public multi-tumor baseline), a classification baseline, and R-Super trained on reports alone. The within-dataset comparison (Merlin vs. Merlin Plus) isolates the value of the masks themselves, while the ULS comparison isolates the value versus the state of the public art. Both comparisons are meaningful and the gap (+10% F1 on average) is substantial.6.Small-lesion coverage. Explicit reporting of lesions under 2 cm is important for the early-detection use case the paper motivates. Early-stage tumors are precisely the small-diameter cases that most benefit from mask-level supervision.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Major Weaknesses
Four radiologists created/corrected the masks, yet there is no reported measure of inter-rater agreement (Dice, Hausdorff, surface distance), no double-reading subset, and no analysis of which tumor types showed high versus low annotator concordance. For small lesions (<2 cm) across rare tumor types (esophagus n=108, duodenum n=249), inter-rater variability is typically substantial and directly affects downstream model ceiling performance. Without this, the claim of “high-quality segmentations” is an assertion rather than a demonstration. This is a critical omission for a dataset paper.
2.A quantitative validation of the active learning pipeline is missing. The paper claims a 5× speedup (30 min -> 5 min per scan) but provides no data supporting this: no time-motion study, no breakdown by tumor type or lesion size, no comparison against a from-scratch annotation arm on a matched subset, no reporting of how many cases required full redrawing versus minor correction. Similarly, the number of active learning cycles run, the number of masks corrected at each cycle, and the per-cycle performance improvement are absent. For a paper whose second core contribution is the annotation pipeline, these metrics are essential.
3.The Dice scores are surprisingly low and under-discussed. Table 1’s caption reports average Dice of 17 (MedFormer), 25 (R-Super with reports+masks), and 10 (R-Super reports only). A DSC of 25 for a “state-of-the-art” segmentation model trained on “radiologist-validated” masks is remarkably poor and it implies that the masks are either too inconsistent to learn from, the tumors are genuinely too hard (likely in some organs), or both. This deserves substantial discussion and per-organ breakdown, but the number appears only in the caption and is never addressed in the text. A dataset paper claiming segmentation value cannot leave a DSC of 17–25 unexplained.
4.The report-confidence score has an unexamined failure mode. The scoring mechanism (Dice between soft and report-refined mask) flags cases where the refinement did substantial work. But this conflates two distinct failure modes: (a) the soft mask was wrong and the refinement correctly fixed it (flagged as unreliable, appropriately), and (b) the soft mask was right but the refinement mechanically moved it (e.g., due to imprecise organ mask dilation or a tumor slightly outside the reported slice), also flagged as unreliable, but incorrectly. There is no validation that radiologist-flagged masks actually had errors versus cases where the score fired spuriously. Without a precision/recall analysis of the flagging mechanism, we don’t know whether the radiologist time is well-spent.
5.The single-site bias is unaddressed. All CT scans are from Stanford Hospital. Scanner distribution, patient demographics, and imaging protocols are not compared to other healthcare systems. Models trained on Merlin Plus may exhibit substantial performance degradation on data from hospitals with different scanner vendors, contrast protocols, or patient populations. The paper does not evaluate on an external test set, does not report scanner or demographic confounders in performance, and does not discuss this limitation. For a dataset paper intended to serve the community, external validation is a reasonable expectation.
6.There is a methodological ambiguity in Step 3(D) volume matching. The report-derived volume estimation uses “sphere/ellipsoid volume approximations” from 1D diameters, with a 30% agreement tolerance. The choice of sphere vs. ellipsoid is not specified per tumor type, and the 30% threshold is unjustified; tumors are rarely spherical, and report diameters often capture only the long axis. This procedural step materially affects ground-truth quality and warrants more scrutiny.
7.Overlap with concurrent submission is not disclosed in-paper. The companion paper (TR-Distillation, 4063 concurrent submission) shares substantial machinery (R-Super, Ball Convolutions, the same LLM extraction pipeline, the same tumor-type focus). While the program chairs’ note handles the formal disclosure, from a reviewer’s standpoint the two papers read as two angles on the same research program. This paper would benefit from clearer articulation of what is novel in Merlin Plus beyond applying the (previously published) R-Super framework to a new cohort.
8.Ethics, consent, and release mechanism are completely absent. The paper claims Merlin Plus will be “publicly available” but does not describe the data use agreement, IRB approval, de-identification protocol beyond the phrase “anonymized patient IDs,” or the license under which masks will be released. Given that this is a Stanford Hospital dataset with demographic metadata including race, the paper must address these points. Stanford’s Merlin dataset itself has specific access controls that Merlin Plus inherits, and this should be explicit. This is particularly important because Section 2.2 describes ICD code integration from the same patient encounter — additional PHI that needs explicit disclosure of de-identification.
9.”ICD-10 codes identify malignancy” claim is clinically imprecise. ICD-10 codes record encounter-level diagnoses but do not reliably identify whether a specific imaging finding on a specific scan is malignant. A patient may have a historical cancer diagnosis (recorded in ICD-10) but the lesion visible on the current scan may be benign, treated, or unrelated. The paper states malignancy is “cross-checked with reports,” but the cross-checking procedure is not described. Mislabeling of benign lesions as malignant (or vice versa) at scale would materially compromise the dataset.
10.THere are many inconsistencies and errors in the text. The abstract states 25,494 scans; Section 2.3 states 25,528 scans. The keywords are placeholders (“First keyword · Second keyword · Another keyword”). Section 2.1 contains the unfilled token “create # multi-tumor masks.” Reference [13] cites arXiv:2601.22134 with year 2026 — this appears to be a non-existent/future arXiv ID. Footnote 2 refers to “these 8 tumor types” while the main text consistently claims 9 tumor types. These errors in a submission suggest rushed preparation and reduce confidence in the numerical precision throughout.
11.The ULS is a weak comparator that the paper over-attributes meaning to. ULS is a universal lesion segmentation model, it was designed for lesion agnosticism, not organ-specific cancer segmentation. Showing that a model trained on in-distribution tumor-specific data outperforms an out-of-distribution universal lesion model at F1 score is expected. The more meaningful comparison ( against organ-specific segmenters fine-tuned on ULS subsets or on related cohorts ) is not conducted.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
I encourage the authors to consider the following for the camera-ready / a revision:
(a) Most important: Report inter-rater reliability on a double-read subset (e.g., 50 cases per tumor type, dual-read by two of the four radiologists), and report Dice/surface distance/Hausdorff agreement. This substantially strengthens the “high-quality” claim.
(b) Quantify the annotation-time claim. A small time-motion study (even n=20 scans timed with and without the pipeline) would turn “5× faster” from an assertion into evidence.
(c) Add a per-organ Dice table (not just F1) to the main text. The surprisingly low average Dice of 17–25 (caption of Table 1) deserves explanation and per-organ breakdown in the main body.
(d) Validate the report-confidence score as a flagging mechanism: on a held-out subset, measure the precision/recall of “flagged masks actually needed correction” vs. “flagged masks were acceptable.”
(e) Fix textual errors: placeholder keywords, the “# multi-tumor masks” token in Section 2.1, inconsistent scan counts (25,494 vs. 25,528), and the possibly-invalid arXiv ID in reference [13].
(f) Add an external validation experiment (even a small one on a public dataset containing one of the 9 tumor types (e.g., stomach or esophagus from the Medical Segmentation Decathlon)) would substantially strengthen generalization claims.
(g) Provide explicit statements on IRB approval, HIPAA de-identification of dates and demographics, and the intended data use agreement.
(h) Clarify the relationship to the companion TR-Distillation submission and what, specifically, is the contribution of this paper versus that one.
(i) Consider a failure-case figure: for which tumor types did the active learning loop struggle most? Where did radiologist correction patterns suggest systematic model failure?

This is a submission with high potential community value but meaningful evidentiary gaps. Dataset papers live or die on two axes: (1) does this dataset fill a real gap, and (2) is the annotation quality credible enough that the community should trust it?
On axis (1), the answer is clearly yes. Tumor types representing roughly half of global cancer mortality are under-served by public CT segmentation datasets, and Merlin Plus directly addresses this. If released as promised, it fills a gap that no methodological contribution could substitute for, and the companion experiments demonstrate that models trained on it outperform public alternatives by substantial margins.
On axis (2), the paper is weaker. The claim of “radiologist-validated” masks rests on no reported inter-rater analysis, no time-motion validation of the efficiency claim, no validation of the report-confidence triage mechanism, and average Dice scores (17–25) that are surprisingly low and unexplained in the main text. The active learning pipeline is cleverly designed but the paper does not quantify how much each component contributes or where the remaining errors concentrate. Combined with textual issues (placeholder keywords, unfilled tokens, inconsistent scan counts, a likely-invalid reference), the paper reads as valuable work in a somewhat rushed state.
The report-based active learning framework itself (particularly the cold-start solution via R-Super and the report-confidence scoring) is a genuine methodological contribution worth disseminating, independently of the dataset release. The Ball-Convolution–based tumor localization within reported organs is a neat concrete use of weak supervision priors.
On balance, the dataset’s community value and the novelty of the report-first active learning framework outweigh the evidentiary gaps, which are fixable in rebuttal/camera-ready. A convincing rebuttal providing (i) inter-rater reliability numbers, (ii) an explanation or fix for the low Dice, and (iii) explicit IRB/ethics statements would move this to a clear accept. Failure to address these points would move it to a weak reject, particularly the inter-rater question, which is foundational for any dataset paper claiming “radiologist-validated” annotations.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
My pre-rebuttal recommendation was Weak Accept (4), with the explicit condition: “A convincing rebuttal providing (i) inter-rater reliability numbers, (ii) an explanation or fix for the low Dice, and (iii) explicit IRB/ethics statements would move this to a clear accept. 
The rebuttal directly addresses all three of these conditional requirements with concrete data.
My personal recommendation is Accept for two reasons:
1.The community benefits substantially from this dataset, and rejecting on policy technicalities (rather than scientific merit) when the evidence exists is the wrong tradeoff for an under-served clinical problem
2.The submitted manuscript’s failures were preparation issues, not scientific ones . the work itself appears solid and the rebuttal demonstrates the team has the data to support their claims
I therefore move to Accept.
reviews.text_ethics: The paper introduces voxel-wise masks, ICD-9/ICD-10 codes, patient demographics (age, sex, race), scanner metadata, and dated longitudinal imaging timestamps to an existing dataset. While the original Merlin cohort presumably has appropriate IRB approval and de-identification, Merlin Plus adds categories (race, scan dates, demographic metadata) that require explicit statements about: (a) HIPAA-compliant de-identification (in particular, dates require shifting, not just removal of year); (b) IRB approval extending to the augmented dataset and mask release; (c) the data use agreement and access controls under which the dataset will be released. The authors should address these explicitly in rebuttal and in the camera-ready.

meta_reviews.text:
The reviewers’ opinions on this paper diverged considerably: One Strong Accept and one Reject. The other reviewer who recommended Weak Accept also raised quite a few questions. Thus, I would like to see the authors’ clarification on points such as the Dice score (R2 and R3), baseline comparison (R2), incomplete paper (R2 R3), inter-rater reliability (R3), etc.

The authors have made considerable efforts in the rebuttal to address concerns from reviewers such as Dice score, baseline comparison, inter-rater reliability, etc. Since the released dataset is of great community values, I recommend acceptance, in line with all reviewers.
The paper is warranted acceptance even without the new results. It has received strong and weak accept pre-rebuttal. The presented large dataset of CT and tumor mask pairs can greatly assist the community, if released. The new comparison and reader study is a plus but the existing contribution is already sufficient.
The reviewers like the dataset contribution and found the authors’ rebuttal satisfactory including the approach for “cold start problem” when encountering unseen tumors by leveraging clinical text.

The authors have adequately addressed all of the reviewers’ concerns. Accordingly, I recommend acceptance of the paper. Several details clarified in the rebuttal should be included in the final version.

title: MetaFormer: Efficient Metadata-Guided Transformer for Patient-Aware 12-Lead Electrocardiogram Reconstruction
abstract: Reconstructing 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) signals from single-lead wearable recordings bridges the gap between long-term monitoring for critical paroxysmal events and the clinical gold standard required for accurate diagnosis. However, existing methods treat this ill-posed inverse problem as a generic regression task, failing to resolve physiological ambiguities and consequently reconstructing toward population averages. To address these problems, we propose MetaFormer, an efficient reconstruction network that utilizes demographic characteristics to enforce patient-aware physical consistency. We introduce a meta tokenizer to parse heterogeneous clinical metadata into a unified semantic manifold, which establishes patient-specific physiological context to guide the reconstruction. To resolve the cross-lead spatial ambiguity, a metadata-guided Transformer aligns latent representations of the reconstructed signal with individual physiological baselines. Experimental results on two large-scale benchmarks demonstrate that MetaFormer outperforms other state-of-the-art methods while reducing computational cost by ~73%, and closely approaches the performance of original 12-lead ECG signals on downstream arrhythmia classification. The code is available at: https://github.com/xych3/MetaFormer.
subject_areas: Applications -> Digital Twins / Simulation / Synthetic Data
Modalities -> Mobile / Wearable / Point-of-Care Imaging & Sensors

By addressing the physiological ambiguity inherent in this ill-posed inverse problem, the method improves reconstruction accuracy and avoids the tendency of existing approaches to regress toward population averages. Experimental results demonstrate that MetaFormer outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both reconstruction quality and computational efficiency, while achieving performance on downstream arrhythmia classification tasks that is close to that of real 12-lead ECG signals.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes MetaFormer, a metadata-guided Transformer for reconstructing full 12-lead ECG from a single reference lead (Lead I), aiming to mitigate the inherent physiological ambiguity of the inverse problem. The core ideas are a meta tokenizer that embeds heterogeneous demographic attributes (age, sex, height, weight) into robust meta tokens (with sinusoidal encodings for continuous variables, type embeddings, and learnable null tokens for missingness), and a metadata-guided Transformer that injects these tokens via cross-attention to align latent ECG representations with patient-specific priors. On PTB‑XL and CSN, MetaFormer improves reconstruction quality and efficiency over recent methods (EKGAN, mEcgNet, ECGrecover) and yields reconstructions that approach the original 12‑lead signals on downstream arrhythmia classification.
reviews.text_strengths: This work has several strengths in methodology, validation, presentation, and potential relevance. It introduces a metadata tokenizer that can model heterogeneous patient attributes, preserve ordinal structure in continuous variables, and handle missing information through learnable null tokens and simulated dropout. It also designs a metadata-guided cross-attention mechanism that uses patient-specific priors to alleviate cross-lead ambiguity in ECG reconstruction. The overall model is relatively compact and efficient, combining MorphResBlocks with a lightweight Transformer bottleneck to maintain favorable parameter and FLOP cost compared with baseline methods. The experiments cover two large-scale benchmarks, PTB-XL and CSN, and show consistent improvements across multiple reconstruction metrics, including RMSE, PSNR, and CosSim. The ablation studies further examine both metadata injection strategies and tokenizer variants, while the downstream arrhythmia classification results show relatively small gaps compared with original ECGs, supporting the usefulness of the reconstructed signals. The paper is also generally clearly presented: the motivation is easy to follow, the connection between the problem setting and the model design is reasonable, and the method is described with sufficient detail. Overall, the results suggest that metadata conditioning can be a useful way to improve single-lead-to-12-lead reconstruction while keeping the model efficient, and the framework may also be informative for other metadata-informed biosignal or medical inverse problems.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
What are the exact splitting protocols for PTB‑XL and CSN (patient-level vs record-level), and are there any repeated patients across train/val/test? Can you report results with strict patient-level splits to rule out leakage?
Which metadata fields are actually available per dataset (e.g., do PTB‑XL/CSN include height/weight), and what is the missingness pattern? What p_drop was used, and how sensitive are results to higher missingness and to incorrect metadata?
How is the “resample to a fixed length of 512” implemented relative to the original sampling frequencies and 10 s durations? Are you cropping, downsampling, or segmenting beats? Please clarify the temporal resolution seen by the model and its impact on morphology fidelity.
Can you provide per-lead reconstruction metrics and error distributions (e.g., limb vs precordial leads), and per-diagnosis performance deltas in the downstream classifier to identify where metadata helps most?
How was the classifier based on [8] adapted to 12‑lead inputs, and what were the training details (architecture, optimizer, epochs, splits)? Are the reported AUC/F1 averaged over multiple runs with confidence intervals?
Have you tested cross-dataset generalization (e.g., train on PTB‑XL, test on CSN) and robustness to noise or motion artifacts on the input lead? If so, how does metadata guidance affect robustness?
Did you consider adding simple physiological constraints (e.g., Einthoven’s law, Goldberger relations) or vectorcardiographic priors as auxiliary losses? If attempted, how did these interact with the metadata-guided attention?
What is the contribution of each metadata attribute individually (age, sex, height, weight)? An ablation per attribute would clarify which priors are most informative for reconstruction.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This is a relevant and generally well-motivated paper that addresses an important limitation of single-lead wearables by incorporating patient-aware priors into 12-lead reconstruction. The metadata tokenizer and cross-attention design are reasonable and efficient, and the method shows consistent improvements over baseline approaches on two benchmarks, with downstream diagnostic results that also support its practical value. To further strengthen the work, it would be helpful to improve methodological rigor, including clearer patient-level split protocols, statistical significance testing, and per-lead analysis. The paper could also benefit from more robustness and cross-dataset generalization experiments, as well as additional discussion of physiological constraints and time–frequency objectives. Clarifying several experimental details, such as resampling and classifier setup, and adding subgroup or fairness analyses would further improve the overall reliability of the study. Overall, MetaFormer provides a useful step toward patient-aware ECG reconstruction and shows reasonable practical relevance, though several aspects could be strengthened to make the contribution more convincing.

title: MetaVFM: Meta-Learned Efficient Adaptation of Vision Foundation Models for Medical Imaging
abstract: Adapting vision foundation models (VFMs) to medical and other domain-shifted tasks involves trade-offs among target-task accuracy, the number of trainable parameters, and the number of optimization steps required for convergence, considerations that are particularly pronounced in medical imaging. While parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods substantially reduce trainable parameters, they typically do not reduce the number of optimization steps, leaving the training step budget a dominant computational cost. Moreover, PEFT performance is highly sensitive to adapter placement, rank allocation, and initialization. These design choices are often set through per-dataset hyperparameter search, making adaptation both configuration-sensitive and training-intensive. To address these challenges, we propose MetaVFM, a meta-learning framework that predicts adapter placement, rank, and initialization for unseen datasets with no per-task search. MetaVFM learns a meta-space from a shared-weight Super-Adapter trained on 90+ datasets, enabling fast retrieval of a configuration and initialization that speeds fine-tuning convergence. We evaluate MetaVFM on 17 datasets, including multiple medical imaging benchmarks. MetaVFM attains the highest average accuracy, ranking top-1 or top-2 on nearly all datasets, while other methods are often strong on some datasets but weak on others, reflecting sensitivity to configuration and initialization. Under a fixed epoch budget, MetaVFM converges 2–3× faster than strong PEFT baselines, with particularly pronounced improvements on medical datasets, highlighting its effectiveness and robustness in the medical domain. The code and experimental setup are available in the Meta-VFM repository (https://github.com/meclotfi/Meta-VFM.git).

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
Adapting Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) like DINO to new tasks requires careful choices about adapter placement, rank, and initialization — three tightly coupled design decisions that are typically set through expensive per-dataset hyperparameter search. While PEFT methods reduce trainable parameters, they do not reduce the number of training steps needed for convergence, leaving step budget as a dominant computational cost. MetaVFM addresses both problems simultaneously by learning a meta-space that enables retrieval-based adapter configuration and initialization for new unseen datasets with no per-task search. 
The framework operates in three stages. First, a shared-weight Super-Adapter is trained on each of 90+ datasets, using a nested prefix parameterization where lower-rank adapters are prefixes of higher-rank ones, allowing thousands of rank/placement configurations to be evaluated from a single trained module per dataset. This builds an adapter zoo — a large collection of dataset-configuration-performance triples. Second, dataset and adapter embeddings are aligned by training two encoders jointly. These embeddings are trained with a composite loss enforcing performance alignment, ranking consistency, and inter-dataset geometry preservation via FID-weighted similarity. During inference on a new unseen dataset, its embedding is computed from a small sample of images and the best adapter configuration is retrieved via cosine similarity under a parameter budget, followed by lightweight fine-tuning with the meta-learned initialization. 
Evaluated on 17 unseen datasets spanning fine-grained, general, scene, and medical domains, the results demonstrate that the methods performs on par with many of the methods when trained 100 epochs (Table 1) and it outperforms baselines such as Linear Probing, MLP, Lora with limited training budged (Table 2) by matching their epoch 10 accuracies at epoch 5 in some cases.
reviews.text_strengths:
1- The problem is well-motivated with clear empirical justification. Figure 1 demonstrates that LoRA performance varies non-monotonically across module-rank combinations and that optimal configurations differ across datasets.
2- The design of the Super-Adapter is technically elegant. The nested prefix parametrization where lower-rank adapters prefixes of higher ones and share a common core is an interesting idea. Training a single super adapter per dataset to generate an entire adapter zoo is significantly more efficient than training independent adapters for each config.
3- The retrieval-based inference mechanism eliminates the need for any hyperparameter search on new datasets — a single cosine similarity lookup replaces multiple training runs.
4- Evaluating on 17 datasets spanning fine-grained, general, scene, and medical domains provides broad coverage. The fact that all evaluation datasets are held out from meta-space training makes the retrieval genuinely zero-shot and the evaluation honest.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Accuracy gains over the methods in Table 1 at 100 epochs is marginal. Table 1 shows MetaVFM achieves only 0.2 points average improvement over APLA. It is also unclear whether the difference between the other methods is significant, e. g. , 91.0 AdaptFormer vs 91.9 MetaVFM. Without statistical significance testing or standard deviations reported in Table 1, this difference is essentially within noise range and cannot be considered a meaningful accuracy improvement over the strongest parameter selection methods.
2.Table 2 only compares convergence speed against basic methods — Linear Probing, MLP, Full Fine-tuning, and LoRA. The strongest methods from Table 1 — APLA, ARC, GPS, SPT-Adapter — are entirely absent from the convergence analysis. Since these methods also use sophisticated initialization and configuration selection strategies, they may converge just as quickly as MetaVFM. Without this comparison the 2–3× faster convergence claim is only demonstrated against weak baselines and cannot be generalized to the full set of competitors.
3.The meta-space is trained on 90+ datasets but the paper never lists which datasets were used. Without this information it is impossible to verify whether the evaluation datasets represent genuinely novel visual types or whether similar dataset types — for example other bird classification or retinal imaging datasets — were present during training. This is a fundamental evaluation transparency issue that undermines the “truly unseen” claim.
4.Training one Super-Adapter per dataset across 90+ datasets is the most computationally expensive part of the framework, yet the paper never reports the total wall-clock time, GPU hours, or computational cost of building the adapter zoo. Without this the practical feasibility of the approach for other researchers is unclear, and the claimed efficiency advantage over per-task search is only partially substantiated.
5.In the ablation results presented in Table 3, mean +- std results show significant overlap between different components of the method. It is unclear whether these results are statistically significant.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

While MetaVFM addresses a well-motivated problem and introduces technically interesting components — particularly the Super-Adapter’s nested prefix parameterization and the dataset–adapter meta-space — the experimental validation falls short of supporting the paper’s central claims. The accuracy gains over the strongest baselines in Table 1 are marginal and not statistically validated. The paper’s convergence efficiency claim — 2–3× faster than PEFT baselines — is only demonstrated against weak methods such as LoRA and Full Fine-tuning in Table 2, while the strongest competitors from Table 1 are entirely absent from the convergence analysis. Given that these weaknesses are significant and not easily addressed through revision, I would recommend rejection
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I appreciate the authors’ detailed rebuttal, which addresses several of my main concerns. I recommend acceptance, with the expectation that the promised dataset catalog, standard deviations, and additional analyses of the predicted adapter configurations, such as layer placement, rank allocation, and domain-specific structural patterns, will be included in the final version or released with the code.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The manuscript introduces MetaVFM, a meta-learning architecture designed to optimize the deployment of Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) in medical contexts. The primary innovation lies in the elimination of traditional, resource-heavy hyperparameter searches for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT). By utilizing a shared-weight Super-Adapter trained across a vast array of datasets, the framework establishes a “Meta-Adapter Space.” This space enables the system to predict optimal adapter placement, rank distribution, and weight initialization for novel medical tasks instantaneously. The approach seeks to drastically lower the computational barrier for adapting large-scale models to specialized clinical domains where data and compute may be constrained.
reviews.text_strengths:
Computational Efficiency via Meta-knowledge: The transition from iterative per-task searching to a predictive meta-learning paradigm is highly significant. By bypassing the traditional training step budget overhead, the work addresses a major practical bottleneck in applying foundation models to diverse medical imaging modalities.
Extensive Empirical Validation: The authors demonstrate the robustness of their approach by evaluating MetaVFM across 17 distinct datasets. The reported 2-3x speedup in convergence while maintaining or exceeding the accuracy of established PEFT methods like LoRA and AdaptFormer provides a compelling case for the utility of the Meta-Adapter Space.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
W1: Ambiguity in Meta-Feature Extraction for Medical Tasks. A critical technical omission is the detailed explanation of how the system extracts “meta-features” from a previously unseen medical dataset to query the Meta-Adapter Space. If the meta-features rely on generic ImageNet-based descriptors, the framework might struggle with highly specialized medical textures (e.g., OCT or histopathology) that differ fundamentally from natural images. A formal analysis or visualization of the meta-space distribution for medical vs. non-medical tasks is necessary.
W2: Over-reliance on Super-Adapter Convergence Stability. The entire framework hinges on the quality of the Super-Adapter. However, the paper lacks a theoretical or empirical proof regarding the stability of training a single shared-weight structure on over 90 heterogeneous datasets. There is a risk of “inter-task interference” where the weights favor dominant natural image features over subtle medical ones, yet the authors do not provide an ablation study on how the composition of the meta-training set influences downstream medical performance.
W3: Lack of Domain-Specific Baseline Comparisons. While the paper compares MetaVFM against general-purpose PEFT methods, it fails to include recent medical-specific adaptation techniques, such as those incorporating clinical knowledge graphs or domain-specific self-supervised pre-training. Comparing MetaVFM against a foundation model already pre-trained on medical data (e.g., RadImageNet) would clarify if the meta-learning gains are complementary to domain-specific pre-training.
W4: Missing Structural Sensitivity Analysis. The manuscript asserts that MetaVFM predicts the best “rank” and “location” for adapters. However, there is no visualization or table showing what these predicted configurations actually look like for medical tasks compared to natural ones. For instance, do medical tasks consistently require deeper adapter placement or higher rank allocation? Providing these insights would validate the “intelligence” of the meta-learner beyond simple accuracy metrics.
W5: Implementation Complexity and Reproducibility Concerns. The complexity of the Meta-Adapter Space and the dual-stage training process (Super-Adapter training followed by Meta-learner optimization) presents a high barrier for clinical researchers. Without more granular details on the hyper-network architecture or the specific loss functions used to align the meta-space, reproducing the results on private clinical datasets remains a significant challenge. w6.Lack of latest paper citations. [1] Meta-learning for few-shot open task recognition[2] Transductive few-shot adapters for medical image segmentation [3] SubQuad: Near-Quadratic-Free Structure Inference with Distribution-Balanced Objectives in Adaptive Receptor framework [4] Meta-Learning Guided Pruning for Few-Shot Plant Pathology on Edge Devices [5] NeuroSymb-MRG: Differentiable Abductive Reasoning with Active Uncertainty Minimization for Radiology Report Generation [6] LLaMA32-Med: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Multimodal LLMs for Medical Visual Question Answering [7] FedCA: Federated Domain Generalization for Medical Image Segmentation via Cross-Client Feature Style Transfer and Adaptive Style Alignment [8] FALCON: Few-Shot Adversarial Learning for Cross-Domain Medical Image Segmentation [9] Meta-XPFL: An explainable and personalized federated meta-learning framework for privacy-aware IoMT [10] Ida-net: Individual difference aware medical image segmentation with meta-learning
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The decision to award a Weak Accept is based on the undeniable merit of reducing the search cost for model adaptation, which is a vital step toward democratizing foundation models in healthcare. The technical implementation of the Meta-Adapter Space is innovative and shows clear performance benefits. However, the “black-box” nature of the meta-feature extraction and the lack of a deep dive into why certain adapter configurations are chosen for medical data limit the paper’s theoretical contribution. Strengthening the explanation of the meta-feature mapping and providing qualitative analysis of the predicted architectures would make this a much stronger submission.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper received mixed scores of accept, weak accept, and reject. I would be interested in clarifications from the authors on the following points:
(1) Please comment on whether the improvements over “Parameter Selection / Search / Composition” methods, for example, in the average results in Table 1 and Medical-Average, are statistically significant.
(2) Elaborate on how the convergence speed compares to “Parameter Selection / Search / Composition” methods. In particular, does the claim that “these results correspond to an effective 2–3× reduction in steps-to-target under a fixed short training budget” hold?
(3) Describe the pre-training dataset zoo, and clarify whether medical tasks are included and how test-data leakage is prevented.

After rebuttal, the paper received positive scores, with 1 “Reject” shifting to “Accept”. Reviewers originally recommending “Accept” remained positive. The clarifications provided by the authors are convincing. I endorse acceptance and expect the authors to incorporate the promised additional dataset details in the project’s repository.

The manuscript is recommended for acceptance as the post-rebuttal consensus shifted positively, with reviewers commending the technical novelty of the meta-learned adapter space and the efficiency of the Super-Adapter design. Nevertheless, the decision notes significant reservations raised during the discussion phase regarding the marginal practical effect size, borderline statistical significance, and potential test-data leakage from the undisclosed meta-training zoo. The authors are strictly required to fulfill their rebuttal commitments—specifically integrating the full 91-dataset catalog, reporting all standard deviations, and providing the structural sensitivity analysis—in the final camera-ready version to guarantee transparency and reproducibility.

The paper addresses an important and practical problem in adapting Vision Foundation Models without expensive per-task hyperparameter search. Reviewers generally agreed that the motivation is strong, the proposed meta-adapter framework is technically interesting, and the evaluation across diverse unseen datasets is comprehensive. The rebuttal also addressed several major concerns regarding dataset transparency and additional analysis. While some performance gains are modest in the fully converged setting, the practical benefit of reducing search cost and improving convergence efficiency was considered valuable. Overall, the paper provides a meaningful contribution and I support acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We thank R1, R3, and R5 for their feedback. We are encouraged that they recognized MetaVFM’s strengths: R1 highlighted the motivation, Super-Adapter design, zero-shot retrieval, and held-out evaluation; R3 found the method novel/inspiring and experiments comprehensive; and R5 recognized the value of replacing per-task search with predictive meta-learning. We clarify the concerns below.
[R1] Accuracy gains. The key result in Tab.1 is consistency: MetaVFM remains top-1/2 across heterogeneous datasets, while others perform well on some datasets but drop on others. This matters because the target dataset is unknown in advance. A paired Wilcoxon test gives: MetaVFM-T5 vs. APLA: 11 wins/2 ties/4 losses, p≈0.035, and vs. AdaptFormer: 16 wins/1 loss, p≈0.0016.Tab 1 std± were omitted due to space and will be added on GitHub. MetaVFM jointly selects rank, placement, and initialization without per-task search, using <3M trainable params vs. ~7M for APLA. Thus, the contribution is an accuracy, convergence-speed, and parameter-efficiency trade-off, not only an accuracy gain.
[R1, R5] Zoo transparency, cost, and reproducibility. The 91-dataset catalog can’t fit in the paper, and MICCAI disallows textual/PDF supplementary. We will release the full catalog on GitHub and add the held-out protocol in the paper to verify the “unseen” setting. Zoo construction is a one-time offline cost: it took only 5 days on 8 GPUs for all 91 datasets (~2 GPU-hours per dataset-backbone). Compared with per-task search, a single adapter costs ~1 GPU-hour, so heuristic search over a few rank/placement candidates already exceeds the Super-Adapter cost. Meta-space training takes ~1h on an M3 laptop. For a new dataset, MetaVFM only needs millisecond retrieval + short fine-tuning, not zoo rebuilding. The repo will include scripts, configs, checkpoints, and embeddings.
[R1] Convergence and ablation. Tab.2 targets MetaVFM’s specific claim: reducing steps-to-accuracy via dataset-aware initialization. APLA/ARC/GPS/SPT-Adapter are strong structure/search baselines, but do not provide such initialization nor claim faster convergence. Tab.3 further supports this claim: it evaluates the full 1/5/10-epoch trajectory, not only epoch-10 overlap. Removing meta-initialization drops epoch-1 average by 4.8%, showing that the learned initialization drives faster early adaptation. Rank/FID/PCA losses mainly refine retrieval geometry, so their gains are smaller but consistent.
[R5] Medical Meta-features. Dataset embeddings are computed from sampled images using self-supervised DINO features with PCA/FID geometry, not ImageNet classifier outputs. The meta-space visualization (Fig.3) supports this: medical datasets occupy nearby regions, suggesting meaningful medical-domain structure rather than generic natural-image semantics.
[R3] Other PEFTs. R3’s suggestion is insightful. We use LoRA because rank/placement gives a flexible parameter–performance trade-off, but the current space inherits LoRA’s limits. Extending the zoo to other PEFTs is a promising direction to select the best adapter family per dataset.
[R5] Super-Adapter. We do not train one Super-Adapter across all 90+ datasets. Each dataset–backbone pair has its own Super-Adapter, sharing weights only across ranks/placements within that dataset and not across tasks. Task transfer occurs later through the meta-space.
[R5] Structural sensitivity and citations. We agree this is a useful interpretability analysis. We, indeed, did it and found that active sites vary across datasets, from sparse layouts (few layers are adapted) to dense ones. We also observe domain-specific trends: medical tasks often favor attention-heavy placements, while texture datasets use lighter, low-rank patterns. Due to space, we omitted it, but we will release the meta-space/zoo for further study of rank allocation and structure/accuracy trade-offs. We will cite the most relevant suggested works and clarify how they differ from ours in objectives.

title: Microglia-RTS: Instance Segmentation of Microglia in Hypoxic Ischemic Fetal Sheep Brain Histology
abstract: Hypoxic–ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) is a major cause of neonatal death and lifelong neuro-disability, with limited treatment options beyond therapeutic hypothermia within 6 hours of birth. In translational fetal sheep models, microglia are central to inflammatory injury cascades and are a key immunohistochemical readout for evaluating therapeutic efficacy. Still, their quantification and morphological grading in histological images remains largely manual, limiting throughput, reproducibility, and mechanistic insights.  We propose Microglia-RTS, a two-stage pipeline for microglia instance segmentation in high-resolution histology for preclinical drug screening. The first detection stage adapts a modified RT-DETR with a pretrained DINOv3 ConvNeXt backbone that incorporates a novel adaptive query selection module to tune the number of object queries per image based on local cell density. The second segmentation stage fine-tunes the Segment Anything Model (SAM2) to produce cell masks from detector proposals. Patch-based inference with overlap-aware stitching enables high-resolution processing of images, preserving intricate cellular details. We evaluate Microglia-RTS on a new fully annotated dataset comprising ~7,000 cell instances, classified into ameboid, intermediate or ramified, across 45-Iba1 stained hypoxic–ischemic fetal sheep brain images from three white matter regions (IGWM1, IGWM2 and PVWM). The modified detector achieved an F1-Detection score of 0.55±0.01 during validation, considerably surpassing the baseline model, and the fine-tuned SAM2 achieved an average Dice-score of 0.86±0.01. Across 5-fold cross-validation on whole images, Microglia-RTS achieved a mean panoptic quality of 0.48±0.02, supporting scalable microglia analysis for pre-clinical HIE drug discovery by reducing observer bias and accelerating quantitative endpoint extraction.

reviews.text_contribution:
1.The authors have created a new, annotated dataset of Iba1-stained microglia over three morphological classes (i.e. ameboid, intermediate, and ramified) in three white-matter regions (i.e. IGWM1, IGWM2, and PVWM) in hypoxic-ischemic sheep brains. The dataset comprises of approximately 7000 images, and uses the three morphological classes instead of four to six alike in other studies in order to preserve biological interpretability and simplify annotation.
2.An instance-segmentation framework was proposed, whereby two models (RT-DETR and SAM2) are combined, along with adapted pretraining, novel modifications to the SAM2 architecture, and an optimised training methodology. The modified RT-DETR surpassed the baseline model with regards to F1-detection score.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper presents a new, annotated dataset of Iba1-stained microglia whereby there are three morphological classes instead of four to six. This is to preserve biological interpretability, making it less complex and simplifying annotation.
2.The authors combine an RT-DETR and SAM2, in which the RT-DETR contains a novel adaptive query branch which predicts the query count at runtime using an MLP. 
3.Overall, the framework produces fast detection of HI in fetal sheep which is beneficial in such a time crucial medical assessment.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Some metrics have not been referenced, i.e. Dice and Dice loss.
2.Some details are missing from the paper, for example, P and G in Equation 3 should be defined to guide the reader through the workings of the equations.
3.F1 detection scores are seemingly low, leaving room for improvement, however, this could possibly be the nicheness of the dataset.
4.An older version of RT-DETR (version 2) is being used, when there is a more SOTA version (version 3) that has been out for over a year.
5.There is no conclusion.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1.Please provide references for metrics. I.e. Dice: Dice (1945) Measures of the Amount of Ecologic Association Between Species. Dice loss: Milletari et al. (2016) V-Net: Fully Convolutional Neural Networks for Volumetric Medical Image Segmentation.
2.Please define P and G in Equation 3 to guide the reader through the workings of the equations.
3.Consider using a more SOTA version of RT-DETR (version 3).
4.Please provide a conclusion or rename the discussion to “Discussion & Conclusion”.
5.Ensure you include your Acknowledgements if accepted.
6.Ideally provide links to code and data for reproducibility.

The paper is well written and the authors have created a new, annotated dataset of Iba1-stained microglia whereby there are three morphological classes instead of four to six. This is to preserve biological interpretability, making it less complex and simplifying annotation. The authors combine two models (RT-DETRv2 and SAM2), whereby RT-DETRv2 isn’t the most SOTA model. The dataset itself is innovative and somewhat should be published as a MICCAI paper, however, the model itself and the slight change to the RT-DETR model for novelty purposes is not quite innovative enough. The figures are very well presented and the models have been very well evaluated. However, there is limited reproducibility as the code nor the dataset have been linked by the authors.
