author_feedback_text:
We would like to thank the meta-reviewer and the reviewers for their thorough and constructive feedback. In revising the paper, we have strengthened the scientific and structural aspects of the work, and we believe the camera-ready version meets the standards and expectations set out in the reviews. Relevant changes are addressed individually below:
Meta-Reviewer Comments: We would like to thank the meta-reviewer for their positive recommendation and for clearly identifying the two camera-ready conditions, which we have addressed.
A new “Data Availability” paragraph has been added to the manuscript confirming our data policy as follows: “The dataset is not publicly available due to ethical restrictions; data and code may be shared upon reasonable request, subject to formal agreements.”. While we must limit the data at this point, there is intention to possibly release a full extended dataset alongside a forthcoming peer-reviewed journal article, subject to ethical updates.
The version of RT-DETR is now explicitly justified in the Methods section: RT-DETRv2 was chosen over the newer RT-DETRv3 for reproducibility and portability, as it had official support in the HuggingFace Transformers Library at project inception, while RT-DETRv3 was only available through a standalone research repository. The Future Directions paragraph notes that since detection remains the main performance bottleneck, RT-DETRv3 is a natural candidate for further investigation.
The detection values are now contextualised in the Discussion in terms of task-intrinsic difficulty: the relatively low F1 of 0.55 likely reflects the combined challenge of instance detection in clustered microglial environments and three-way morphological classification along a biologically continuous ramified-to-ameboid spectrum.
Reviewer #1
We thank the reviewer for the positive assessment and recognition of the paper’s structure and reproducibility. We hope the revisions made through the review process have brought the paper to the standard required for MICCAI.
Reviewer #2
We sincerely thank Reviewer 2 for their thorough and constructive review, which has substantively improved the camera-ready manuscript.
We have added references for both dice score and dice loss in the methods section, and the variables in Eq. 3 are now defined explicitly in the surrounding text. The discussion section has also been renamed to “Discussion and Conclusions”.
We agree that there is room for improvement with the F1 detection score, likely due to the fact that the dataset is intrinsically challenging. The Discussion has been extended to make this explicit, and we further note in the Discussion that overall performance is currently “detection-limited rather than segmentation-limited”.
As mentioned in the response to the Meta-Review, we have now justified the use of the RT-DETRv2 over RT-DETRv3 in the methods section, and provided a new “Data Availability” paragraph has been added, which outlines our data sharing policy, and encourages readers to contact us if they would like to collaborate
Reviewer #3
We thank Reviewer 3 for their generous and encouraging assessment of the manuscript, and especially for the thoughtful methodological observations.
We fully agree that a runtime comparison would be informative. As the MICCAI 2026 camera-ready guidelines do not permit the addition of new results or experiments, this comparison has been retained as something we will include for the extended journal version of this work that is currently in preparation.
A short justification has also been added to the Methods, noting why a learned MLP was preferred over alternatives for object count estimation.
We thank the meta-reviewer for the time and care they invested in evaluating this work, and for the constructive feedback that shaped our revisions. We hope the changes described above have meaningfully improved the clarity and reproducibility of the camera-ready manuscript in a satisfactory way.

title: MicroscopyCLIP: A Domain-Specific Vision-Language Model for Optical Microscopy
abstract: Microscopy images provide fine-grained visual evidence of cellular morphology and are fundamental to biomedical research and clinical diagnosis. However, existing vision-language models, including CLIP and its medical variants, are primarily trained on natural images, radiology data, or medical literature, and therefore lack effective semantic alignment for microscopy imagery, limiting their performance in microscopy zero-shot recognition and cross-dataset transfer capability. In this paper, we propose MicroscopyCLIP, a domain-specific vision-language model tailored for microscopy image understanding. We construct a large-scale microscopy image-text dataset consisting of approximately 210K fluorescence microscopy images paired with textual descriptions, followed by systematic expert verification to ensure semantic consistency. Based on this dataset, we perform full-parameter fine-tuning of a pretrained CLIP model to realign the vision-language embedding space for microscopy data. Experiments demonstrate that MicroscopyCLIP substantially improves the zero-shot classification performance for microscopy images. On a held-out 8-class kidney cell benchmark, it achieves 66.17% Top-1 accuracy under prompt-based zero-shot inference without task-specific training on the target dataset. Across six external microscopy benchmarks, MicroscopyCLIP consistently outperforms existing vision-language models in both zero-shot and linear probing settings, indicating robust cross-dataset generalization. Code: https://github.com/SeriYann/MicroscopyCLIP
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs
Machine Learning -> Synthetic Data / Data-centric AI

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper presents a microscopy-specific adaptation of CLIP for optical microscopy image understanding. Its main contribution is the combination of
a large curated microscopy image-text corpus with 207,988 kidney cell images paired with expert-reviewed captions, and
a two-stage progressive full-parameter fine-tuning strategy that adapts a pretrained CLIP model to microscopy semantics.
Empirically, the resulting model substantially improves zero-shot recognition on a held-out 8-class kidney benchmark (66.17% Top-1) compared with CLIP, MedCLIP, BioMedCLIP, and PMC-CLIP, and also shows strong transfer across six external microscopy classification datasets in both zero-shot and linear-probe settings.
In my view, the strongest contribution is not a new vision-language architecture, but rather a useful domain resource plus a practical adaptation recipe that appears effective for microscopy
reviews.text_strengths:
The motivation is clear and timely. The paper identifies a real gap: existing CLIP-style medical models are largely aligned to natural images, radiology, or biomedical literature, but not to fine-grained microscopy morphology.
The dataset construction effort is meaningful. The authors do more than generate captions automatically; they describe a hierarchical expert-review protocol and even report revision statistics for morphology, spatial relations, and identity expressions. This adds credibility to the data curation pipeline.
The empirical gains are strong, especially for zero-shot recognition. The jump on the held-out kidney benchmark is very large (66.17% versus 10.68%/14.94%/7.04%/9.78% for the compared baselines), and the model remains competitive across six external datasets.
The paper includes a useful ablation on training strategy. The two-stage progressive fine-tuning performs better than single-stage full fine-tuning and much better than LoRA under the reported setting, which supports the authors’ adaptation choice.
The manuscript is generally well organized. Figures 1 and 2 communicate the pipeline clearly, and the narrative is easy to follow
reviews.text_weaknesses:
-The methodological novelty is limited. The model keeps the standard CLIP objective and mainly contributes data curation plus a progressive fine-tuning schedule. This makes the work more of a domain adaptation/resource paper than a clearly novel vision-language method.
-The scope of the paper is broader than what the evidence supports. 
The paper title and some claims suggest a general solution for optical microscopy. However, the training data appear to be concentrated on kidney cell fluorescence microscopy with only eight cell types. I would encourage the authors either to narrow the scope of the claims or to add broader pretraining data and evidence across microscopy modalities.
A key claimed contribution is expert verification of LLM-generated captions, but there is no direct ablation comparing raw LLM captions versus expert-verified captions. Without this, it is difficult to quantify how much of the gain comes from human verification rather than from domain-matched fine-tuning alone.
Although the paper positions MicroscopyCLIP as a vision-language model, evaluation is restricted to classification and linear probing. There is no retrieval or caption-alignment evaluation, even on a held-out subset of the constructed paired corpus. This weakens the evidence that the paper improves cross-modal alignment, as opposed to primarily improving visual features for classification.
The claim of “zero-shot” evaluation is conceptually misleading, especially for the in-domain kidney experiment. 
The model is trained on a kidney dataset with eight predefined cell types, and the text supervision explicitly contains class-level semantic information. It is then evaluated on a held-out split of the same 8-class kidney problem using prompts such as “A microscopy image of {class}. ” This is not zero-shot in the strict sense of recognizing previously unseen classes; rather, it is closer to label-aligned recognition without training an additional classifier head. Therefore, the statement that the model achieves “66.17% Top-1 zero-shot accuracy” is overstated and potentially misleading.
-The captioning pipeline suffers from severe label leakage. 
The caption-generation prompt explicitly inserts the variable “{cell_type}” and instructs the LLM to identify the cell type, justify the classification, and explain its physiological role. This means the textual supervision is not an independently observed description derived from the image alone; instead, it is conditioned on the ground-truth label from the beginning. As a result, the model may mainly learn to align images with class names and associated prior knowledge, rather than learning genuine image-text grounding. This is a major methodological flaw.
-There is a serious risk of data leakage in the claimed cross-dataset generalization experiments. 
The paper states that the training corpus of 207,988 microscopy images is selected from public datasets including references [22] and [9]. Later, one of the downstream external benchmarks used for evaluation is MCF7 / A549 Cytoplasm [9]. If dataset [9] contributes to both training and downstream testing, then the claim of “cross-dataset generalization” is questionable unless the authors provide a strict proof of no overlap at the image, sample, or source level. As currently written, the experimental protocol raises a serious concern about data leakage
-The main paper does not provide enough implementation detail for full reproducibility. For example, the exact CLIP backbone, precise stage-wise freezing policy, learning-rate values, batch size, augmentation strategy, stage split, dataset split sizes, and leakage-control protocol are not clearly specified in the manuscript.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
This is a promising submission, and I believe it could become significantly stronger with a more careful experimental decomposition of the claimed contributions. 
In particular, I strongly encourage the authors to add: 
(i) an ablation of raw LLM captions versus expert-verified captions, 
(ii) an image-only domain-adaptation baseline trained on the same microscopy corpus, and 
(iii) a held-out retrieval or image-text matching evaluation on the constructed paired dataset.
I also recommend tempering the scope of the claims. As written, the paper reads as if it solves optical microscopy broadly, whereas the evidence is centered on kidney-cell microscopy and transfer to a handful of classification datasets.
Finally, please add complete implementation details and multi-seed statistics.

My recommendation is a weak reject. 
I see clear merit in the work: the problem is relevant, the selected dataset is potentially valuable, and the empirical results are strong enough to show that the approach is useful in practice.
However, I do not think the current version is yet strong enough for acceptance as a MICCAI methodological contribution. The main reason is that the paper does not convincingly disentangle what actually drives the gains. The current evidence cannot tell whether the improvement comes primarily from (a) expert verification, (b) the mere presence of domain-matched image-text data, (c) progressive fine-tuning, or simply (d) domain adaptation of the visual encoder on kidney data.
In addition, the paper’s scope is broader than the evidence currently supports, and the cross-modal nature of the claimed contribution is under-evaluated because no retrieval or text-alignment benchmark is reported.
Overall, I find the work promising and potentially publishable after strengthening the experiments and narrowing or better substantiating the claims, but I would currently place it slightly below the acceptance threshold
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
After reading the rebuttal, I move my recommendation from Weak Reject to Weak Accept. The authors addressed several key concerns by clarifying the expert verification process, revision ratios, LLM used, implementation details, dataset split/checkpoint selection, lack of sample-level overlap, and by agreeing to narrow the scope and use the more precise term “prompt-based zero-shot inference.”
However, one important concern remains: the caption-generation pipeline is still label-conditioned. Expert verification improves caption quality but does not fully remove the risk that the model learns class-name alignment rather than genuinely image-grounded vision-language correspondence. The raw-versus-verified caption ablation and new retrieval results are useful, but they should be clearly reported and interpreted cautiously.
Overall, I view the paper as a valuable microscopy-domain resource and practical CLIP adaptation study, rather than a strong methodological contribution. With the clarified scope, implementation details, no-overlap documentation, retrieval results, and caption ablation included in the camera-ready version, the paper is acceptable for MICCAI.
reviews.text_ethics:
I do not see an obvious ethics concern from the manuscript. The paper appears to use publicly available datasets and does not raise an immediate red flag regarding human-subject privacy or research integrity in the main text.
That said, the final camera-ready version should clearly document dataset licenses/usage terms and any relevant access restrictions for the released corpus.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents MicroscopyCLIP, a domain-specific vision-language model for optical microscopy. The main contribution is the construction of a microscopy image-text pair of about 208K kidney cell images. Text captions are generated by an LLM but revised by experts. A ViT based model was trained using two-stage domain adaptive fine-tuning. The model is evaluated on an in-domain held-out kidney dataset and six external microscopy benchmarks under zero-shot and linear-probe settings. The main contribution of the paper is creating a large dataset and the empirical gains of domain specific training over CLIP, MedCLIP, BioMedCLIP, and PMC-CLIP for zero-shot microscopy classification.
reviews.text_strengths:
Large microscopy dataset
The paper identifies a very important gap in the field. Existing vision-language models in biomedicine are indeed dominated by radiology, pathology, and general biomedical image-text pairs, while fine-grained optical microscopy remains underrepresented. Authors collected 208k cell images from kidney tissue spanning 8 different cell types.
Expert revised captioning
The captions were first generated by an LLM in a structured way. Then the hierarchical expert revisions were conducted. Junior researchers did the first revision, followed by the senior expert revision.
Training strategy
The benefit of two-stage training strategy is well demonstrated by ablations. Two-stage alignment shows better performance than one-stage full-layer training.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Lack of novelty
The paper does not present a methodological contribution. However, I would not consider this a major concern, as the primary motivation of the work is to develop a model that produces better embeddings for microscopy images.
Dataset splits are not defined
Although the training dataset (208k images) is described in detail in Figure 1, the held-out test set is not clearly defined. It would be helpful to report the number of cells in each class in the test set.
Scope of the dataset
Although the image-text pairs fill a very important gap, the dataset consists only of human kidney tissue spanning eight different cell types. In future studies, it could be improved by including additional tissues in the training dataset.
LLM generated captions are (too) structured
Because the captions appear to follow a highly consistent structure, the model may partially rely on this fixed textual format during alignment. Introducing greater variation in phrasing or in the ordering of descriptive components could encourage the model to learn more robust image-text associations rather than patterns tied to caption structure alone. Such variation could also function as a form of text augmentation.
Evaluations are narrow
Evaluations are limited to zero-shot classification and linear probing. As acknowledged in the manuscript, “Since the downstream microscopy benchmarks do not provide paired image-text annotations, cross-modal retrieval evaluation is not applicable in this study.” However, additional analyses such as image-image retrieval, UMAP visualizations, or other embedding-quality metrics, including kNN-based evaluation, could still be included. A strong visualization would be showing the embeddings before the alignment and after the alignment in one of the external cohorts.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Which LLM was used to generate reports?
How many generated captions were reviewed by experts? Was all of the data manually reviewed by experts, or did you perform expert review only on a randomly sampled subset, followed by further refinement or correction using the LLM?
Could you clarify this section:
“The revision rates exhibit a hierarchical gradient: 47.5% at the morphological level (D2), largely involving refinement of nuclear morphology descriptions and removal of imprecise or overly generalized visual statements; 66.3% at the spatial level (D3), clarifying structural localization or eliminating unsupported spatial inferences; and 17.6% at the identity level (D4), mostly consisting of terminology normalization rather than category changes.”
What do these ratios represent? Fraction of generated reports needed to be corrected in each category? Fraction of generated reports reviewed by the experts?
How was the best checkpoint selected? Was it watched over the internal held-out dataset?

The paper contributes an image-text paired dataset to the microscopy field.
The model achieves better performance compared with other biomedical CLIP models.
The evaluation includes only zero-shot classification and linear probing, and could be further enriched.
It is unclear how many generated reports were reviewed by experts, which raises questions about the quality of the dataset.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Although novelty and the scope of the paper is limited, the effort for cell-caption pairs are significant. My concern was validity of captions created for images as they were initially created with an LLM. Authors now clarify that all captions went under review by experts. Authors also acknowledge that the scope of the paper is limited to kidney and they will tune down the claims for all microscopy.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper presents MicroscopyCLIP, a microscopy-domain adaptation of CLIP for optical microscopy image understanding. Its main contribution is the construction of a microscopy image-text corpus of roughly 208K kidney cell images with LLM-generated captions that are subsequently manually revised and expert-verified, followed by domain-adaptive fine-tuning of a pretrained CLIP model using the standard symmetric contrastive objective. The paper further studies a two-stage progressive fine-tuning strategy, in which later layers are adapted first before full end-to-end tuning, and demonstrates improved zero-shot recognition and cross-dataset transfer on multiple microscopy benchmarks.
reviews.text_strengths: A main strength of the paper is its experimental evaluation. The authors test on many datasets, covering both in-domain and cross-dataset settings, compare against several relevant baselines, and include ablation studies on the fine-tuning strategy and prompt design. Overall, the empirical section is fairly comprehensive.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The paper has several weaknesses. First, although the authors emphasize the construction of a large-scale microscopy image-text dataset, the paper does not provide enough detail about how the captions are actually generated, including the specific prompt design principles, the generation rules, and the rationale behind the final caption formulation. The expert verification process is also insufficiently documented: the paper does not clearly explain how the review was conducted in practice, how many samples were examined, or provide concrete examples of revision cases, which makes the reliability of the caption quality control less convincing. Second, the technical depth of the paper appears limited. The overall framework mainly combines LLM-based caption generation, standard CLIP-style contrastive training, and a simple two-stage fine-tuning strategy, without demonstrating a clearly novel model design or training objective tailored to microscopy. Finally, the paper lacks important implementation and reproducibility details, such as batch size, learning rate, and other training settings, making it difficult to fully assess or reproduce the reported results.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The main reason for my recommendation is that the paper lacks sufficient technical depth and novelty. The overall method largely consists of LLM-based caption generation, standard CLIP-style contrastive training, and a simple two-stage fine-tuning strategy, without a clearly distinctive modeling or optimization contribution tailored to microscopy. In addition, the paper does not provide enough experimental and implementation details to support reproducibility, such as batch size, learning rate, and other key training settings. The dataset construction and caption verification pipeline are also insufficiently described, especially with respect to prompt design, expert review procedure, and quality control details. Although the experimental section is relatively broad, the limited technical contribution and the lack of reproducibility details make the overall paper unconvincing in its current form.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: After reading the authors’ rebuttal, my concerns were not sufficiently addressed. In particular, the authors did not fully respond to my questions. The method still appears to lack fundamental technical novelty, as it mainly combines LLM-based caption generation, standard CLIP-style contrastive training, and a relatively simple fine-tuning strategy without a clearly microscopy-specific model design or objective. In addition, the paper still does not provide enough detail about intermediate data processing, caption construction, expert verification, or data augmentation procedures. These missing implementation details make the work difficult to reproduce and weaken confidence in the reported results. Therefore, I maintain my decision to reject the paper.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper presents a new image-text dataset on kidney cell images which is used to fine tune a pretrained CLIP model. Reviewers agree with the two contributions of the paper: the dataset and fine-tuning strategy. There are a list of comments and concerns, leading to mixed review scores (Weak Reject, Weak Accept, and Reject). Some major weakness items include: the methodology is lack of novelties; the scope is over-claimed, the expert verification on image captions is unclear, labeling and experiment setting are questionable, and the technical implementation is missing.

After the rebuttal, all reviewers still have a long list of concerns in addition to the previous critical concerns such as the lack of novelties and limited scope. After reading the paper, rebuttals and reviews after the rebuttal, the AC recommends rejecting this draft this time.

This paper contributes a fluorescence microscopy image-text dataset on human kidney tissue and a domain-adaptive CLIP fine-tuning framework. 
The rebuttal addressed the main concerns well—adding image-text retrieval results, quantifying the gain from expert-verified captions, ruling out data leakage, and providing implementation details. The authors also appropriately narrowed their claims and the “zero-shot” terminology. The remaining concern about limited technical novelty is valid, but the contribution is reasonably positioned as a domain-specific resource and adaptation framework, which fits MICCAI’s scope.

This masnucript introduces a large image-text kidney cell image dataset and a practical fine-tuning strategy for CLIP-style model training. Although this work may not exhibit strong technical novelty, the proposed dataset and the CLIP adaptation method are valuable to the biomedical image analysis community. In addition, the rebuttal addresses several key concerns from reviewers, such as clarification of image caption verification, potential data leakage, implementation details, and scope of claims.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback. We address the major concerns below.
[R1] Label leakage in the captioning pipeline
We agree that the caption generation process is label-conditioned. However, the label is not used as the sole supervision target, but as contextual guidance for generating structured biological descriptions. Importantly, expert reviewers subsequently verified and revised captions against the underlying microscopy image content, particularly for morphological and spatial descriptions. Therefore, the final supervision signal is not limited to class identity alone, but also contains image-grounded biological information.
[R1] Data leakage
There is no sample-level overlap. Reference [9] is a paper aggregating multiple independent image collections. Our training data draws exclusively from the kidney cortex fluorescence microscopy subset. MCF7/A549 Cytoplasm is a completely separate subset with different cell types.
[R1, R2, R3] Methodological novelty
We agree that the primary contribution of MicroscopyCLIP is not a fundamentally new VL architecture, but rather a microscopy-specific VL resource and domain-adaptive alignment framework. Existing biomedical CLIP-style models mainly focus on radiology, pathology, or biomedical literature, while microscopy-specific vision-language alignment remains largely underexplored. To our knowledge, MicroscopyCLIP is among the first large-scale VL alignment efforts specifically targeting this underexplored gap.
[R1] “Zero-shot” terminology
We acknowledge that “zero-shot” may be interpreted differently in the broader ML literature. Our usage follows the original CLIP definition. We will also revise the manuscript to use the more precise term “prompt-based zero-shot inference”.
[R1, R2] Raw LLM captions vs. expert-verified captions
Initial captions were generated using GPT-4o, and all captions underwent manual expert verification. The revision ratios (e.g., D2: 47.5%) represent the percentage of captions requiring manual correction in the corresponding category. To further evaluate the impact of expert verification, we compared raw and verified captions. Raw generated captions achieve 55.89% (Kidney) and 25.23% (Jurkat), while expert-verified captions achieve 66.17% and 32.26%, confirming consistent gains from expert verification.
[R1, R2] Retrieval evaluation
We agree retrieval evaluation strengthens the paper. We therefore generated paired text descriptions for the held-out test set using the same captioning pipeline and conducted image-text retrieval evaluation. Specifically, image-to-text retrieval improves from 3.1%/6.1% (CLIP) and 1.8%/4.5% (MedCLIP) to 12.4%/22.5% at R@5/R@10, while text-to-image retrieval improves from 2.7%/5.5% (CLIP) and 2.4%/5.1% (MedCLIP) to 9.4%/18.9%. MicroscopyCLIP consistently improves retrieval performance over both baselines. Additional retrieval metrics and UMAP visualizations will be included in the camera-ready version.
[R1, R2, R3] Implementation details
Here we provide the implementation details and will include a complete table in the camera-ready version. Backbone: ViT-B/32 initialized from OpenAI CLIP. Effective batch size: 1024 across 4 GPUs with mixed-precision training. Stage I: lr = 1e-4 for 5 epochs. Stage II: lr = 1e-5 for 25 epochs. Training and validation subsets were created using stratified 85%/15% splitting within each class. The held-out kidney test set consists of a separately predefined subset containing 47,280 images. Exact split statistics and per-class sample counts will be included in the camera-ready version. The best checkpoint was selected based on validation loss.
[R1, R2] Scope of claims
We accept this criticism and will narrow the title and abstract to more precisely reflect the current scope: fluorescence microscopy of human kidney tissue, with demonstrated transfer to 6 external datasets. Broader microscopy modalities will be explored in future work.

title: MiGAD: Gut Microbiota-informed Genetic Surrogates for Multimodal Alzheimer’s Disease Diagnosis
abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) pathology begins years before clinical symptoms, making early and reliable diagnosis from a single modality inherently uncertain. Growing evidence links the gut microbiota to early AD through the gut-brain axis, but direct microbiome profiling is highly heterogeneous and temporally unstable, limiting its utility as a deployable screening biomarker. To bridge this gap, we propose a gut microbiota-informed genetic surrogate-driven multimodal framework for AD diagnosis (MiGAD), which incorporates gut-brain axis related genetic evidence and distills multimodal knowledge into an MRI-only model for deployable screening. Our framework comprises three stages. First, we perform microbiota-informed candidate variant selection by integrating multi-cohort microbiome genetic evidence and derive transferable subject-level genetic representations. Second, we perform aligned cross-modal token fusion with a hierarchical Transformer to integrate MRI, clinical tabular features, and genetic tokens for AD classification. Third, to handle missing peripheral modalities in real-world screening, we distill the multimodal teacher into an MRI-only student model. We evaluate our approach on 6,500 participants from UK Biobank and ADNI. The multimodal model achieves ACC=0.878 and AUC=0.963, while the distilled MRI-only student improves AUC from 0.825 to 0.910 over an MRI-only baseline. These results demonstrate that microbiota-informed genetic surrogates provide stable complementary signals for AD staging while preserving real-world usability.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper proposes MiGAD, a novel framework for Gut Microbiota-informed Genetic Surrogates for Multimodal Alzheimer’s Disease Diagnosis, which integrates gut-brain axis mechanisms into AD diagnosis using stable genetic proxies instead of volatile direct microbiome data. The main contributions are threefold:
(1)Microbiota-informed Genetic Surrogates: It introduces a pipeline using Mendelian Randomization and colocalization on GWAS data to identify 12,634 genetic variants that serve as stable, transferable proxies for gut microbiome status, overcoming the heterogeneity of direct microbiome profiling. 
(2)Aligned Cross-Modal Fusion: It develops a hierarchical Transformer with explicit InfoNCE contrastive alignment to robustly fuse MRI, clinical, and genetic surrogate tokens, achieving state-of-the-art performance (AUC 0.963) on 6,500 participants from UK Biobank and ADNI. 
(3)Deployable Knowledge Distillation: It proposes a multimodal-to-MRI distillation strategy that transfers gut-brain axis knowledge into an MRI-only student model. This significantly improves screening accuracy in resource-limited settings (AUC from 0.825 to 0.910), enhancing real-world clinical usability.
reviews.text_strengths:
(1) Novel Methodological Formulation: The paper innovatively proposes “Microbiota-informed Genetic Surrogates” to capture gut-brain axis signals. By leveraging Mendelian Randomization on GWAS data, it bypasses the instability of direct microbiome profiling, using stable host genetic variants as reliable proxies for AD diagnosis. 
(2) Clinical Deployability via Distillation: The proposed Multimodal-to-MRI knowledge distillation strategy effectively addresses data scarcity in real-world screening. The distilled MRI-only student model significantly outperforms baseline imaging models (AUC 0.825 vs. 0.910), demonstrating strong practical utility where peripheral data is unavailable. 
(3) Robust Cross-Modal Alignment: The integration of an explicit InfoNCE contrastive learning objective ensures semantic consistency across heterogeneous modalities. Ablation studies confirm that this alignment mechanism is critical for maximizing the performance of the hierarchical Transformer fusion architecture. 
(4) Rigorous Large-Scale Validation: The method is evaluated on 6,500 participants from two distinct cohorts (UK Biobank and ADNI). This large-scale, cross-cohort validation demonstrates the model’s robustness and generalizability across diverse demographic and clinical populations.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(1) Fundamental Flaw in Causal Logic and Surrogate Validity: The core premise relies on the unproven assumption that selected genetic variants effectively proxy for gut microbiome composition. However, reverse causality is a significant confounder: AD pathology may influence microbiome composition via changes in diet, medication, or behavior. The paper fails to empirically validate that these variants predict actual microbial profiles in the study cohort. If this link is weak, the “microbiota-informed surrogates” are merely standard AD-risk loci, rendering the proposed mechanistic innovation illusory. 
(2) Modality Gap in Knowledge Distillation: Stage III forces an MRI-only student to mimic multimodal teacher representations (h_T). However, MRI captures structural changes, whereas genetic/clinical data reflect systemic states. It is questionable whether structural imaging alone can truly reconstruct these peripheral signals. The performance gain may stem from fitting the teacher’s output distribution rather than learning genuine gut-brain mechanisms, a claim unsupported by interpretability analysis linking student attention to biologically relevant regions. 
(3) Unfair Comparison with Multimodal Baselines: The evaluation in Table 3 is methodologically inconsistent. Only MADDi integrates three modalities (imaging, tabular, genetics), while HyperFusion and DAFT use only imaging and tabular data. Comparing MiGAD—which leverages genetic surrogates—against baselines lacking genetic input fails to isolate the specific benefit of the proposed selection strategy. A fairer assessment would require baselines that also incorporate genetic data (e. g. , PRS-enhanced models). 
(4) Insufficient Experimental Details: Key reproducibility details are omitted, including the dataset splitting strategy (e. g. , random or site-based) and specific MRI data augmentation techniques. 
(5) Poor Readability and Undefined Notations: The manuscript lacks clarity in its mathematical formulation. Several notations are introduced without explicit definitions, such as the classification loss L_cls(Eq. 6), the projection function fm(*) (Eq. 4), etc.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper proposes MiGAD, a novel framework that integrates gut-brain axis mechanisms into AD diagnosis using stable genetic proxies. Its main strengths are the innovative use of microbiota-informed genetic surrogates to bypass microbiome instability, robust performance on large cohorts (UKB/ADNI), and a practical knowledge distillation strategy that enables deployable MRI-only screening.
However, the score is limited by several weaknesses: the biological validity of the genetic surrogates is not empirically validated against actual microbiome data; the comparison with multimodal baselines is inconsistent regarding modality usage; and the manuscript lacks key experimental details (e.g., data splitting) and clear mathematical definitions. Despite these issues, the methodological novelty and clinical applicability warrant acceptance.

title: MIL-PF: Multiple Instance Learning on Precomputed Features for Mammography Classification
abstract: Modern foundation models provide highly expressive visual representations, yet adapting them to high-resolution medical imaging remains challenging due to limited annotations and weak supervision. Mammography, in particular, is characterized by large images, variable multi-view studies, and predominantly breast-level labels, making end-to-end fine-tuning computationally expensive and often impractical. We propose Multiple Instance Learning on Precomputed Features (MIL-PF), a scalable framework that combines frozen foundation encoders with a lightweight MIL head for mammography classification. By precomputing the semantic representations and training only a small task-specific aggregation module (40k parameters), the method enables efficient experimentation and adaptation without retraining large backbones. The architecture explicitly models the global tissue context and the sparse local lesion signals through attention-based aggregation. MIL-PF achieves state-of-the-art classification performance at a clinical scale while substantially reducing training complexity. We release the code for full reproducibility on https://nikolajovisic.github.io/mil-pf/.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper proposes taking advantage of modern foundation models to overcome the challenges related to high resolution images and limited annotations in medical imaging. The authors claim that frozen pretrained encoders provide useful and discriminative features that generalize well for mammography, even if originally trained in other domains (eg, DINOv2). As such, these pre-computed features can be plugged into a smaller, computationally less demanding model to perform the final classification task. 
Their proposed framework is called Multiple Instance Learning on Precomputed Features (MIL-PF) and is designed to be lightweight and easy to adopt in clinical scenarios, since it involves training very few parameters and requires only image level labels. Evaluation of this framework is done on mammography breast-level classification with complementary lesion detection (trained in weakly supervised). Experimental validation is extensive, using three popular benchmarks in the field - EMBED, VinDr, and RSNA, and the proposed approach is compared against few but meaningful state of the art alternatives. Results suggest that the proposed framework achieves comparable or better classification results than other approaches specific of mammography image analysis.
reviews.text_strengths: This paper provides a simple yet effective approach to leverage pretrained foundation models for the downstream task of classifying multiview mammography images. This approach requires little training and only needs image level annotations. The paper provides extensive and solid evidence that the proposed MIL-PF approach often outperforms alternative state of the art approaches. The authors perform several runs for each experiment, provide sufficient ablation studies and validation to give support to their claims. Overall, it offers a simple yet effective approach to train models on downstream tasks while relying on pre-computed features obtained from frozen foundation models. The authors also show that multiple foundation models can be plugged in with similar performances, regardless of being previously trained on this type of data, thereby opening new possibilities based on generic foundation models, ie, models not necessarily trained on mammographies or even medical images).
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The major weakness of the paper is its novelty. On one hand, using frozen foundation models for downstream tasks has been extensively explored in the last few years. The paper’s reference [8] is one such example, which already uses features extracted with a frozen MammoCLIP to perform the classification of mammography images. Another work that compares multiple foundation models for this specific task, including a non-medical DINOv2, is [A], also published in MICCAI 2025.Additionally, there are plenty of other works based on this type of approach for other applications. 
The proposed MIL framework is also not novel, as the described Perceiver-style cross attention is identical to recent approaches based on prompt learning or context optimization (see, eg [B]). While this paper provides additional evidence that this line of work is relevant and effective, it is not proposing a novel approach. 
Nonetheless, I conceive that it may be the first to combine the using pre-computed features from foundation models with a cross attention mechanism to aggregate patch level information for a MIL framework. 
The results are also not always convincing, in the sense that some of the alternative approaches achieve equally good or better results in some of the tests. This is particularly evident in the classification results for VinDr and also for the (weakly supervised) detection metrics, considering the results obtained with [8]. The latter could be indicative that modality-specific encoders can be better at capturing medically relevant features than generic ones.
[A] Germani, E. , Selin-Türk, I. , Zeineddine, F. , Mourad, C. , & Albarqouni, S. (2025, September). Bias and generalizability of foundation models across datasets in breast mammography. In International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention (pp. 24-34). Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. 
[B] Chen, H. , & Martel, A. L. (2025, September). Breast Cancer Detection from Multi-view Screening Mammograms with Visual Prompt Tuning. In Deep Breast Workshop on AI and Imaging for Diagnostic and Treatment Challenges in Breast Care (pp. 91-100). Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The MIL-PF approach proposed in this paper provides a simple and effective way of exploiting existing foundation models for the classification of breast cancer. Despite its merit, the core contributions of the paper are in line with other previous works, limiting its novelty, as explained in the major weaknesses part of the review.
Below is a list of additional comments, questions, and suggestions.
In the Introduction, the authors claim that training of CLIP-like models is challenging due to the lack of enough textual data. However, there are multiple approach that counter this argument, including eg MammoCLIP, MedCLIP, MedSigLIP.
In the Experimental Setup, the authors state that “Lesions, defined as tissue changes that could be related to breast cancer, represent our R_i”. What do they mean? R_i is mentioned a couple of pages before referring to the sparse regions of interest in an image. It is not clear, in the context of the paragraph, what is implied in this sentence.
The authors address a binary problem where BI-RADS 1 is the negative class, and BI-RADS 4, 5 and 6 are all associated with the positive class. What do they do for image with BI-RADS 2 and 3? Are they discarded?
And what about the state of the art approaches to which they compare against? Are they all trained on same labels? For instance, [8] originally tackles the binary problem of classifying the presence of a lesion: BI-RADS 1 means no lesion, 2-5 means there are suspicious lesions.
What is the original embedding size (possibly different for each encoder)? Why are they reduced to 16 then 8 before the fusion? Did the authors try other sizes?
“MIL-PF being the first in the literature to discover generalization properties of the general encoders to the mammography domain” – The work in [A] seems to suggest similar properties, although DINOv2 is not the best performing encoder.
It is also arguable that MedSigLIP may be considered a generic foundation model, especially because its training data included some types of x-ray images and CT’s, which are similar to mammograms.
The results do not show the standard deviation or the p-values assessing the statistical significance of the improvements compared to the alternative approaches.
It does not mention on which dataset the Explainability Analysis (detection capability analysis) was performed. Can you clarify?
The ablation study comparing the performance with different combinations of attention paths (global or local attn only VS both), in Table 4 (right), shows very similar performances between the single attention and both. It is not clear if there is any benefit to the dual stream – p-value could help.
Minor comments
“Mutliple runs” – typo
Table 4 is the first table to be referenced in the text.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Overall, this paper presents a valuable contribution to the specific application of breast cancer and mammography image analysis. They show that a simpler and more accessible framework achieves state of the art results, requiring training less parameters than the alternatives. Despite its limit methodological novelty, application-wise it is a good contribution.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper demonstrates that general-purpose vision foundation models, such as DINOv2 and MedSigLIP, exhibit outstanding generalization performance in the mammography domain even without task-specific fine-tuning. To address the input resolution constraints of these base models, we propose the Multiple Instance Learning on Precomputed Features (MIL-PF) framework, which extracts features through a dual-stream approach: a global stream for general tissue context and a local tile stream for capturing fine-grained lesion signals.
Also, the paper incorporated a Perceiver-style cross-attention mechanism as the aggregation module to effectively focus on sparse, task-relevant local signals among a vast number of unannotated tiles. The proposed architecture achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on large-scale clinical benchmarks, such as the EMBED dataset, while requiring only a lightweight task-specific module.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper demonstrates that general-purpose vision foundation models (e.g., DINOv2, MedSigLIP) can achieve state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in mammography classification without the need for task-specific fine-tuning of the backbones. This is achieved through global-local dual-stream architecture that effectively balances overall tissue context with fine-grained lesion signals
While maintaining a highly efficient and lightweight structure (~40k parameters and 2M FLOPS per forward pass), the framework provides interpretable attention maps. This visual feedback demonstrates strong potential for xAI.
Overall, the manuscript is well-written and follows a clear, logical structure that effectively communicates the technical framework and clinical motivations. The method section is theoretically sound, and the experimental setup is robust, characterized by large-scale evaluations and a rigorous validation process.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
While the empirical findings regarding the generalization of foundation models to mammography are valuable, the proposed architecture lacks significant technical novelty. The framework primarily relies on a combination of existing components—specifically, a frozen backbone with a standard Perceiver-style cross-attention mechanism and a late-fusion strategy
Despite the competitive classification performance, the model exhibits notably low detection accuracy (mAP) for small lesions, though the authors correctly identify this as a limitation tied to the large input tile sizes and mark it for future work
Given the 11% variance in Spec@Sens=0.9, the authors should provide p-values and confidence intervals to establish statistical significance over baselines. Reporting the mean and standard deviation across all 36 runs, rather than only the best-performing validation model, is essential to confirm the framework’s true clinical stability and sensitivity.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
While maintaining frozen encoders is more efficient , the paper would be more compelling if it explored the trade-off between performance gains and efficiency when applying Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning such as LoRA. Furthermore, it would be beneficial to include experiments with additional vision encoders known for strong generalization, such as I-JEPA.

Although the work does not propose a fundamentally new architectural paradigm, it successfully demonstrates that state-of-the-art performance can be achieved by leveraging pretrained vision foundation models coupled with a Perceiver-based aggregation head. This study is a solid contribution that shows a possibility of using frozen encoders for high-resolution medical imaging tasks.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: My main concern in the initial review was the lack of architectural novelty, as the proposed models are built upon existing architectures. After reading the authors’ rebuttal and the other reviews, I believe the empirical finding — that strong performance can be achieved with pretrained backbones under a parameter-efficient setting — is itself a meaningful contribution relevant to the MICCAI community. Given the practical value of this finding, I update my recommendation to accept.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposed an MIL pipeline for mammography classification. The pipeline extract features from foundation model and train a lightweight MIL head on top of the extracted features.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper tackles relevant and important clinical problems. The writing is clear and easy to follow. The pipeline is computationally efficient.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The methodological novelty is very limited, as the approach mainly combines existing components, including frozen foundation encoders, standard MIL formulations. The claimed contribution “We formalize a class of mammography-motivated MIL problems and propose an architecture designed to address them.” is also very weak. Similar problem formulations have already been explored in prior work across various medical imaging domains, such as cardiology and retinopathy screening, and these prior literature are not explicitly discussed in the current manuscript.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

While the paper presents a practical and efficient framework for mammogram classification, the overall contribution is primarily an integration of existing techniques with limited methodological novelty.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I have read the authors rebuttal as well as reviewers from other reviewers. Overall i am ok with the paper being accepted, but i think the novelty should not be over-claimed and related works should be more carefully discussed.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper received mixed reviews, including two weak accepts and one reject. The work addresses a practically relevant problem in mammography classification and presents a simple, efficient, and clearly organized framework based on frozen foundation-model features and lightweight MIL aggregation; the positive reviews highlight its empirical strength, including evaluation on multiple mammography benchmarks and evidence that precomputed features from general or medical foundation models can achieve competitive, and in some cases state-of-the-art, performance. However, the main concern is limited methodological novelty, as the framework largely builds on established ideas such as frozen feature extraction, MIL aggregation, and Perceiver-style cross-attention, making its distinction from prior work insufficiently clear. The paper would benefit from stronger positioning against related studies, including MammoCLIP-based feature extraction, foundation-model comparisons in mammography, and visual-prompt or Perceiver-style aggregation methods. Several experimental and methodological details also require clarification, including label definitions, dataset handling, embedding-size choices, detection-analysis settings, and the statistical significance of the reported improvements. Overall, the paper is practically meaningful and empirically promising, but its contribution relative to existing work remains somewhat unclear; therefore, the authors are invited to submit a rebuttal before a final decision is made.

After rebuttal, this paper receives three accept recommendations, including two reviewers who maintained weak acceptance and one reviewer who changed from rejection to acceptance. The AC acknowledges that the paper addresses a clinically important problem in mammography classification and proposes a simple, efficient, and practically attractive MIL framework built on precomputed frozen foundation-model features. The reviewers consistently recognize the paper’s strengths in clear presentation, computational efficiency, use of only image-level labels, and extensive evaluation across multiple mammography benchmarks.

The paper presents MIL-PF, a simple and efficient framework using frozen foundation-model features with a lightweight MIL head for mammography classification. Reviewers agree that the methodological novelty is limited, as the work combines existing components, but the rebuttal clarified the positioning and practical contribution. The empirical results are strong, especially on large-scale mammography benchmarks, and the framework is computationally attractive with very few trainable parameters. Overall, the paper makes a valuable application-oriented contribution and is recommended for acceptance, provided the final version avoids overclaiming novelty and better situates the work relative to prior methods.
The authors have addressed the concerns regarding novelty, ablation study, and p-values, and discussed related works. All reviewers are convinced to accept this manuscript after the rebuttal.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for the valuable feedback. They note that MIL-PF is simple yet effective [R1], tackles relevant clinical tasks [R3] and demonstrates valuable and extensively evaluated performance [R1, R2]. All found the method highly efficient and clearly presented.
[R1, R2, R3] Novelty: We agree that MIL-PF relies on existing parts and, in the paper, we never claim any of the fundamentals (frozen encoders, Perceiver, dual-stream, etc.) as novel. Rather, we demonstrate the mammography benefits of our particular component arrangement (end of Sec. 3.3). Known parts and ~30x less trainable parameters (single encoder forward pass in training) are preferred when constrained clinically or in hardware, and, since we achieve state-of-the-art results this way, we find MIL-PF valuable for MICCAI; especially since no significantly similar mammography setting is present in the literature. Finally, we will adapt the final wording to emphasize these specifics in the light of reviewers’ comments.
[R3] Novelty: R3 raises novelty versus cardiac/retinal, but doesn’t point to specific work. Closest analogs we found are Shad et. al (Nature 2026, arXiv:2312.00357) for frozen foundation models, Huang et al. (ISBI 2025, arXiv:2403.06024) for MIL, and MVCINN (Luo et. al., AAAI 2023) for multi-view/attention. Crucially, none combine all, and none target MIL-PF’s regime: ~5k×5k images, variable number of views, sparse ROIs, bag-labels without text reports.
[R1] Novelty: We consider [A] (Germani et al.), [B] (Chen & Martel) and [8] valuable, but none comprehensively covers MIL-PF’s goal. [A] focuses on the foundation model biases, not classification, and not important domain architectural specifics like MIL-PF, and, even in this context, the DINOv2’s value is not recognized (as R1 notices), which is an important MIL-PF’s insight, thanks to the large clinical benchmark (EMBED). We respectfully disagree that [B] is identical to Perceiver-style attention used in our paper. In [B], the prompts are injected in the backbone’s internals; MIL-PF’s latent sits entirely outside the encoder, querying over precomputed embeddings - precisely enabling efficiency. We acknowledge similarities with [8], but demonstrate superior classification performance, precomputing importance, simpler architecture and general encoders’ potential over MammoCLIP. 
[R1] Results not convincing: On the largest (most diverse) dataset, MIL-PF improves AUC by 4% and Spec. by 20% over the strongest baseline, remaining best or almost the best on the other classification tasks, while massively decreasing trainable parameters over the baselines.
[R1, R2] p-values: would strengthen the claims. However, MIL-PF’s EMBED gains are large and reproduce well across 2 encoders, 3 datasets, and 3 metrics, while the 36 runs’ val/test near-perfect alignment indicates stability.
[R1] Dual-stream ablation: While p-values would be useful, we consider the 36 runs’ increase of >1% in AUC and especially increase of up to 10% in Spec. significant enough for our dual-stream claims.
[R1] CLIP: No scaled text-image mammography corpus exists; MammoCLIP relies on templated/synthetic captions as a workaround; requires sacrifice of arbitrary input resolution and native multi-view support, important specifics MIL-PF handles by design. MedCLIP and MedSigLip are not trained on mammography.
[R2] LoRA/JEPA: We consider these very promising, but the limitation of MIL is the encoder backprop, as the signal is sparse. They would, moreover, reintroduce expensive encoder forward passes per epoch; precomputing avoids this.
[R1] Embedding size: is encoder-specific, as R1 expects. 16/8 ablation is missing due to space limit, but we see no gains increasing them; decreasing degrades the results.
[R1] Will clarify: lesion regions are sparse and of clinical interest (R_i phrasing); baselines are trained on the exact splits as MIL-PF (Sec 3.3); XAI is shown on VinDr; BI-RADS 2,3 cases are discarded; formatting issues will be fixed.

title: MINT: Molecularly Informed Training with Spatial Transcriptomics Supervision for Pathology Foundation Models
abstract: Pathology foundation models learn morphological representations through self-supervised pretraining on large-scale whole-slide images, yet they do not explicitly capture the molecular state of the tissue. Spatial transcriptomics technologies bridge this gap by measuring gene expression in situ, offering a natural cross-modal supervisory signal. We propose MINT (Molecularly Informed Training), a fine-tuning framework that uses spatial transcriptomics as molecular supervision for pretrained pathology Vision Transformers. MINT appends a learnable ST token to the ViT input to encode transcriptomic information separately from the morphological CLS token, preventing catastrophic forgetting through DINO self-distillation and explicit feature anchoring to the frozen pretrained encoder. Gene expression regression at both spot-level (Visium) and patch-level (Xenium) resolutions provides complementary supervision across spatial scales. Trained on 577 publicly available HEST samples, MINT achieves the best overall performance on both HEST-Bench for gene expression prediction (mean Pearson r = 0.440) and EVA for general pathology tasks (0.803), demonstrating that spatial transcriptomics supervision complements morphology-centric self-supervised pretraining.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper proposed MINT (Molecularly Informed Training with Spatial Transcriptomics Supervision)
the ST and CLS tokens capture complementary information—
the ST token specializes for molecular signals while the CLS token retains morphological transferability—and that combining both yields consistent improvements in a backbone-agnostic manner.
Under the official HEST-Bench and EVA evaluation framework, MINT achieves the best overall performance on both benchmarks (mean Pearson r=0.440 and EVA average 0.803).
reviews.text_strengths:
The establishment of a method for fine-tuning on spatial transcriptomics datasets is highly commendable.
The validity of introducing ST tokens and the overall framework is demonstrated through thorough evaluation.
The motivation is clear, and efforts toward fine-tuning foundation models are highly important.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
To what extent does learning ST signals contribute to performance? I am interested in the performance when using only $L_{DINO}$, as well as when combining $L_{DINO} + L_{distill}.
How effective is the positive-only supervision that ignores zeros? For observed genes, zero values can still represent an important signal of low expression, so discarding them may result in a loss of useful information.
How does the performance compare to models trained from scratch for gene expression prediction?

N/A

As noted in the major strengths, I agree with the concept of the study and believe it is a valuable contribution to the community.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I found the rebuttal convincing. Methods for tuning foundation models with ST are still underexplored. I believe this work will serve as a useful baseline for the community.
reviews.text_ethics: As noted in the major strengths, I agree with the concept of the study and believe it is a valuable contribution to the community.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
1) This paper proposes a fine-tuning framework for spatial-transcriptomics (ST) prediction using only HE patches. It augments the traditional DINO framework with two additional supervision losses.
2) The paper further shows the morphological transferability of the pretrained backbone through the authors’ reported experiments through both HEST-Bench and EVA.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) The paper studies a meaningful problem with clear practical relevance.
2) The proposed framework is technically coherent and clearly presented. Its method is easy to follow, and the overall design is internally consistent. The paper is generally well organized, and the training objectives are described in a relatively clear way.
3) The design of the ablation study well supports the authors’ claim that the ST token and distillation strategy play complementary roles.
4) The distillation-based design for mitigating catastrophic forgetting is interesting and may provide useful guidance to the community for incorporating new supervisory signals into pretrained pathology foundation models.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) The most serious issue is the lack of direct comparison with prior spatial transcriptomics-based models. Although the paper cites several prior works ([11-14]) on histology-based gene expression prediction and related ST-supervised learning, these methods are not included as direct experimental baselines.
2) The HEST-Bench improvements are not entirely surprising because in-domain data with labels were used during training. This makes the benchmark more favorable to the proposed model than to other foundation models. An additional ST-prediction benchmark would be needed for a fairer comparison.
3) The core idea, namely adding an extra supervision loss and using distillation to stabilize fine-tuning, is somewhat trivial and seems more like a careful combination of existing techniques in the pathology-ST setting.
4) The paper’s central claim of avoiding catastrophic forgetting is interesting, but it is supported only indirectly. While the reported results are suggestive, the paper does not provide sufficiently strong mechanistic evidence that the pretrained morphological feature space is truly preserved during ST-guided fine-tuning. A feature-space visualization would be helpful.

N/A
