meta_reviews.text:
The paper addresses an important and practical problem in multimodal medical image segmentation under missing modalities, and the reviewers generally find the proposed framework meaningful with promising results across multiple datasets. At the same time, the submission is currently borderline due to concerns about methodological clarity and justification, particularly regarding the use of Mamba as backbone, the role and contribution of the DFA module, and the explanation of key design choices in the method and Figure 1.I recommend moving the paper to the rebuttal phase, where the authors should focus on clearly addressing these points and clarifying the current evidence without the need for additional experiments.

Although concerns remain regarding clarity and validation, the rebuttal addressed most reviewers’ concerns about implementation and motivation, and the overall balance of reviews supports acceptance, with the required revisions to better justify error propagation and improve methodological clarity.

The rebuttal addresses the main concerns with additional backbone comparisons, clearer missing-modality formulation, modality-specific DFA clarification, and planned complexity/visualization analyses. Although some components remain incremental, the method appears well motivated, competitive across arbitrary missing-modality settings, and sufficiently validated for acceptance.

After considering the rebuttal and updated reviews, I recommend acceptance. The overall reviewer feedback is sufficiently positive, although some concerns remain. The rebuttal clarifies several important issues, and the authors should incorporate these clarifications and further discuss the remaining concerns in the final version.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the Area Chair and Reviewers for their constructive feedback. We will revise the manuscript to improve method clarity, Fig. 1, related work, visualization, and proofreading.
1.Mamba & non-Mamba backbone comparison (R1W2&R2W1&R3W3):
We use Mamba because 3D missing-modality segmentation requires long-range volumetric context with manageable cost. 3D CNNs have limited effective receptive fields, while 3D Transformers require quadratic token complexity. Mamba provides global modeling of large anatomical context to infer missing latent semantics, with linear complexity. We have additionally conducted comparisons with ResNet3D-18 (CNN) and Swin3D (Transformer), which achieved Avg Dice of 0.7155 and 0.7284, respectively, both below MoCaf-Mamba. We will add these results and Params/FLOPs/throughput comparisons.
2.Arbitrary missing modalities & MCFS formulation (R2W2&R3W2/R3W3&R4W1):
MoCaf-Mamba can handle any number of missing modalities. Tables 1–3 include all missing subsets; e.g., three modalities are missing for single-modality BraTS inputs. In implementation, all K modality slots are fixed and ordered; unavailable slots are zero-filled, and modality dropout challenge the model with arbitrary patterns. Thus, Φ_fuse receives a fixed-dimensional ordered input and doesn’t need to be permutation-invariant. We will rewrite Eq. (1) with an availability mask and correct the notation. The Style Token is a modality-level prior, while patient-specific information comes from fused spatial features, inter-individual differences are preserved. Unlike placeholder or pixel-level reconstruction methods, MCFS performs supervised feature-space completion conditioned on available modality context.
3.Completion-before-alignment and DFA clarification(R1W1&R2W3&R3W4/W5&R4W2):
Completion is placed before alignment because aligning absent/zero features is ill-posed. MCFS first reconstructs segmentation-relevant latent anchors under feature reconstruction loss, after which DFA refines residual geometric discrepancies. We will add t-SNE/feature-map visualizations before/after MCFS and DFA to better show that completion stabilizes representations and DFA reduces mismatch. We will also clarify Eq. (3): DFA does not use one shared field for all modalities. The offset predictor outputs modality-specific 3D fields Δ_i, and each feature F_i is warped by its own bounded field λ · tanh(Δ_i). DFA is applied hierarchically because residual mismatch may occur at different semantic scales, requiring scale-specific correction. Although DFA gives a moderate gain (+0.5 Avg Dice), it improves the thin alignment-sensitive PZ from 65.0 to 65.8.
STM Clarity and Complexity (R2Min2&R4W3):
E_spatial denotes the output of the local 3D convolutional branch. STM forms K modality tokens plus one hybrid token at each voxel and applies self-attention only along this modality-token dimension, not over spatial voxels. Thus, the attention length is K + 1 (≤5), making the overhead small. We will clarify token construction and report Params/FLOPs/throughput.
5.Performance and Comparisons (R2Min4&R3W5):
Under extreme cases, i.e. only one modality is available, MoCaf-Mamba remains competitive; e.g., T1c-only TC on BraTS2023 is 89.5 vs. 89.6 (mmFormer). More importantly, our goal is robustness under arbitrary missing patterns, where MoCaf-Mamba achieves the best average Dice across BraTS2023, Prostate158, and MM-WHS. We will compare with DRIFA-Net when available for 3D missing modality, and otherwise discuss it in related work/limitations
Presentation fixes and visualization (R1W3&R2W4/W5/Min1/Min3&R3W1/W4&R4):
We will redesign Fig. 1 with clearer arrows/fonts and an illustration of residual inter-modality misalignment; reorganize “Multimodal Fusion and Alignment”; add feature-space visualizations; and fix the undefined F_k, duplicate “Results on BraTS2023”, abstract formatting, and non-English code comments.

title: Modality-Agnostic Domain Generalizable Medical Image Segmentation via Self-Coordinated Focusing
abstract: The domain gap caused by variations in image appearance is a primary obstacle to transferring medical image segmentation models from laboratory research to clinical practice. To address this issue, domain generalization techniques have been introduced to enhance the transferability of the model. However, due to the static nature of existing perception and feature extraction mechanisms, current methods still lack sufficient adaptability in practical generalization scenarios. Inspired by the highly generalizable dynamic information focusing and fusion capabilities of the human visual system, this paper proposes the Self-Coordinated Focusing Network (SCFNet), a novel model designed for modality-agnostic medical image segmentation with domain generalization ability. The model comprises two core components: Dynamic Focusing Convolution (DFC) and the Interactive Attention Fusion Decoding (IAFD) module. DFC dynamically adjusts convolutional aggregation weights and receptive-field scales by pre-perceiving target types and their spatial scale distributions, enabling input-adaptive, target-aware feature perception. Furthermore, IAFD enhances feature fusion efficiency and information interaction during decoding by decomposing semantic information and introducing interactive attention across semantic hierarchies. We evaluate SCFNet on ten datasets spanning four imaging modalities. Experimental results demonstrate that SCFNet consistently outperforms multiple state-of-the-art methods in multi-modal settings, exhibiting superior segmentation accuracy and stronger generalization capability.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a modality-agnostic network for medical image segmentation with the ability to generalize across different domains. The model includes a Dynamic Focusing Convolution (DFC) component and an Interactive Attention Fusion Decoding (IAFD) component to achieve this goal.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes SCFNet, a modality-agnostic medical image segmentation model aimed at improving domain generalization across different clinical datasets and imaging modalities. The main contribution is a U-shaped segmentation architecture built around two proposed modules: Dynamic Focusing Convolution (DFC), which adaptively adjusts convolutional aggregation weights and receptive-field scales based on the input, and Interactive Attention Fusion Decoding (IAFD), which uses wavelet-based decomposition and cross-level interactive attention to improve decoder-side feature fusion. The paper evaluates the method on 10 datasets across dermoscopy, radiology, ultrasound, and colonoscopy, and reports improved performance in both seen and unseen clinical settings.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) The paper addresses an important and practical problem.
Domain shift is a major barrier to deploying segmentation models in real clinical settings, and the paper directly targets this issue by evaluating on unseen datasets across multiple modalities. This is a meaningful and clinically relevant problem formulation.
2) The method is reasonably well motivated and architecturally coherent.
The paper presents a clear intuition inspired by dynamic visual focusing and translates it into two concrete modules, DFC and IAFD. The framework diagram on page 3 helps explain how adaptive perception and decoder fusion are integrated within the overall network.
3) The empirical evaluation is broad.
The experiments cover four imaging modalities and ten datasets, with both seen-domain and unseen-domain testing. This is broader than many medical segmentation papers that focus on only one modality or one dataset pair. The quantitative results in Tables 1 and 2 show consistent gains over several strong baselines.
4) The reported results on unseen datasets are strong.
The paper’s most convincing evidence is the improvement under unseen clinical settings, where the gains over prior methods become larger in some cases. This supports the claim that the method is aimed at generalization rather than only in-domain optimization.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) The methodological novelty is only moderate, especially for DFC.
The paper explicitly states that the feature-focusing part of DFC. In other words, an important component of the proposed method is already built on top of CondConv-style dynamic convolution, which reduces the novelty of this module. The paper would be stronger if it more clearly articulated what is fundamentally new beyond extending dynamic kernel weighting and adding scale attention.
2) The paper is not sufficiently differentiated from very closely related prior DG work.
The most relevant prior work appears to be MADGNet [22], titled “Modality-agnostic domain generalizable medical image segmentation by multi-frequency in multi-scale attention.” This prior work is extremely close in both problem setting and high-level design language. Although the paper compares against MADGNet in Tables 1 and 2, the method section does not sharply explain what conceptual gap remains after[A], and why SCFNet should be seen as a substantial advance rather than another dynamic/frequency-attention variant. Similarly, the paper itself cites domain and content adaptive convolution based multi-source domain generalization [3], which also suggests that adaptive convolution for medical DG is already an active direction.
3) The evaluation protocol is broad, but the exact training setup is somewhat unclear.
It is not fully clear whether the model is trained jointly across modalities, separately per modality, or with some shared protocol across datasets. The paper presents itself as “modality-agnostic,” but the experiments are organized by modality-specific datasets and tasks. This ambiguity makes it hard to judge how strong the claimed modality-agnostic generalization really is.
4) Important ablation studies are missing.
Given that the main claim rests on two new modules, I would expect ablations such as:
baseline U-Net vs +DFC vs +IAFD vs full model,
effect of the feature-focusing and scale-focusing branches separately,
effect of the wavelet decomposition in IAFD,
computational cost and parameter overhead.
These analyses are important for understanding where the performance gain comes from, but they are not presented in the current manuscript.
5) Baseline selection is somewhat mixed for a domain-generalization paper.
While the paper compares against several strong segmentation models, many baselines are generic segmentation architectures rather than specialized DG methods. Since the central claim is about domain generalization, stronger comparison to more dedicated DG segmentation methods would make the evidence more convincing.
[A] Nam J H, Syazwany N S, Kim S J, et al. Modality-agnostic domain generalizable medical image segmentation by multi-frequency in multi-scale attention[C]//Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF conference on computer vision and pattern recognition. 2024: 11480-11491.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper studies an important problem and reports strong empirical results across multiple datasets and modalities. The breadth of the evaluation is a real strength, and the unseen-domain performance is encouraging. I also think the proposed architecture is sensible and the paper is generally well presented.
My main hesitation is that the paper does not yet make a sufficiently strong case for novelty and methodological distinctiveness. The DFC module is explicitly built as an extension of existing dynamic convolution ideas, and the closest prior work, especially MADGNet [22], is highly similar in both problem framing and design philosophy. In addition, the lack of ablations makes it difficult to understand how much each proposed component really contributes, and the exact training setup for the modality-agnostic claim is not as clear as it should be. For these reasons, I currently place the paper slightly below the acceptance threshold, though a strong rebuttal clarifying novelty and protocol could improve my assessment.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper addresses an important problem with a broad, well-executed evaluation and demonstrates strong generalization performance. However, the moderate novelty, insufficient differentiation from MADGNet, missing ablations, and lack of efficiency analysis keep it from being a strong accept. A rebuttal that clarifies novelty relative to prior work and provides missing ablation/efficiency results could strengthen the case.

After reading the rebuttal, I recommend ‘Accept’ to this paper.

The rebuttal clarifies the experimental protocol and better differentiates SCFNet from CondConv, MADGNet, and DADC. However, the central concerns remain unresolved. The paper provides no concrete efficiency analysis despite added architectural complexity, and the clarified protocol shows intra-modality cross-center testing rather than stronger modality-agnostic generalization. The reported results are promising, but without evidence isolating the proposed components and their computational cost, the methodological claims are insufficiently supported.

While the proposed modality-agnostic segmentation framework shows broad empirical results across multiple datasets, consensus post-rebuttal highlights that the manuscript lacks indispensable component-level ablation studies, which cannot be excused by page limits. Furthermore, critical concerns remain unresolved regarding the limited methodological novelty relative to closely related prior work, the lack of clinical efficiency profiling, and ambiguous training details.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank all Reviewers and the Meta-reviewer for your time and constructive comments. Below, we clarify the issues raised by Reviewers.
Novelty and differences from prior DG (Domain generalization) works. (Reviewers 3, Meta-Reviewer1)
Thanks for your valuable comments. Compared with CondaConv [4], DFC is not a simple addition of scale attention, but an innovative optimization of the dynamic mechanism for lesion-characteristic domain shifts. The novelty and differences lie in the following 3 aspects: In the dynamic coding stage, DFC introduces spatial-distribution awareness to preserve region-level spatial information. In the dynamic operating range, it not only generates dynamic convolutional weights but also dynamically adjusts the aggregation range. In the dynamic granularity, it extends image-level dynamics to region-level dynamic perception. These designs enable more adaptive and effective feature extraction under domain shifts. Compared with MADGNet [22] and DADC [3], SCFNet handles domain shifts in a different way. MADGNet mainly relies on multi-scale convolutional branches and frequency attention, which apply the same operations to all inputs and thus remain essentially static. Although DADC introduces dynamic feature extraction, its dynamicity is mainly limited to image-level convolutional weight generation based on global pooling. In contrast, SCFNet performs spatial-distribution-guided region-level dynamic perception by dynamically adjusting both weights and aggregation ranges. Together with advantage-information interaction fusion, SCFNet can better handle characteristic shifts across images and among different regions within an image, leading to more accurate and generalizable segmentation.
Experimental setting and baseline selection. (Reviewer 3)
SCFNet is trained separately for each modality with the corresponding seen data: two merged seen datasets for colonoscopy and one seen dataset for each other modality. The trained model is then tested separately on each seen and unseen dataset of the same modality without additional adaptation, to evaluate segmentation performance and cross-center generalization. Here, “modality-agnostic” means that SCFNet is a unified segmentation framework without requiring modality-specific priors or designs. We will optimize the description in the paper to avoid ambiguity. The baselines were selected by considering both method-level perception characteristics and the task-level need for generalization. We highly appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion to strengthen comparisons with dedicated DG segmentation methods, and will conduct more systematic evaluations in future work.
Ablation and efficiency. (Reviewers 2, 3, and 4, Meta-Reviewer1)
We apologize that these analyses are not fully presented due to space limitations. During preparation of the paper, we conducted ablation and efficiency analyses on DFC, IAFD, the overall architecture, the balance among parameters, computation consumption and performance, and so on. These analyses demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed modules, architecture, and hyperparameters. We sincerely hope to share them in more detail during the conference discussion.
Hyperparameter and cross-domain validation. (Reviewers 1 and 2)
We agree that these analyses are important for evaluating stability and applicability. Current experiments focus on intra-modality cross-center generalization, with hyperparameters set based on preliminary analyses. We will conduct sensitivity analysis and explore cross-imaging-domain validation in future work.
DFC scaling, distinctiveness, experimental description, and Fig. 2.(Reviewers 1, 2 and 3)
We sincerely thank the reviewers for their valuable suggestions regarding the method description, implementation details, and figure readability. We will optimize the descriptions of the scaling implementation of DFC, method distinctiveness, and experimental settings, and adjust the layout of Fig. 2 to improve readability.

title: Modeling Clinical Workflow for SYNTAX Scoring from Coronary Angiography Videos
abstract: The SYNTAX score is a clinically established tool for assessing anatomical lesion complexity in coronary artery disease and guiding subsequent treatment. However, automated SYNTAX scoring is commonly formulated as a direct regression problem from coronary angiography videos to patient-level scores. In this work, we reformulate SYNTAX scoring as a vessel segment identity-preserving anatomical reasoning problem and propose a hierarchical modeling framework that explicitly aligns learning with the clinical workflow. Our approach maintains vessel segment identity across frames and views, estimates stenosis severity at the segment level, and aggregates evidence hierarchically according to coronary anatomy. Simultaneously, to address the scarcity of domain-specific data, we integrate and complete multiple public coronary angiography datasets, constructing a large-scale resource featuring completed vessel segmentation and derived structural annotations. Experiments demonstrate that vessel segment-level stenosis embedding enhances explanatory power and reduces prediction variability compared to baseline models, with the R^2 score improving by 0.201 and dev STD decreasing by 18.4%. These results highlight the necessity of structure-aligned modeling for reliable and stable automated SYNTAX scoring from multi-view coronary angiography videos. The GitHub link is https://github.com/VersaceSu7/SYNTAX_score_777.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper reformulates automated SYNTAX scoring as a vessel segment identity‑preserving anatomical reasoning task and proposes a hierarchical modeling framework aligned with clinical workflow. It integrates multiple public coronary angiography datasets to build a large‑scale annotated resource and achieves better prediction performance and stability than baseline methods
reviews.text_strengths:
1.It proposes a vessel segment identity-preserving hierarchical framework that aligns with clinical workflow for SYNTAX scoring. 
2.It designs a coronary artery representation network using stenosis attention heatmaps and multi-view videos for accurate score prediction. 
3.It integrates and completes multiple public coronary angiography datasets to provide large-scale structured annotations. 
4.It enables more stable and interpretable SYNTAX predictions across heterogeneous multi-view data with improved performance.
reviews.text_weaknesses: Insufficient experimental details are provided, which hinders result reproducibility
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I recommend to accept this paper, as it successfully addresses the automated SYNTAX score prediction task with a clinically aligned hierarchical framework, delivers clear innovation and reliable performance, and provides a valuable dataset for the community.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper at hand describes a multi-stage pipeline to perform syntax scoring. First, a frame attention step selects frames of interest, then a vessel segmentation segments the coronary arteries, subsequently, the vessels are split into their subsegments, and bounding boxes are created for each vessel subsegment. Then for each subsegment the degree of stenosis is estimated and a stenosis attention heatmap is aggregated over all segments, this heatmap is then leveraged to filter the original image and fed into a vision encoder and some aggregation modules to end up with the final syntax score.
reviews.text_strengths:
The whole pipeline is a smart way to capture the across view segment scores and is well motivated by the clinical workflow of the scoring. 
Moreover, the proposed workflow outperforms the previously reported SYNTAX scoring performance on the Cardiosyntax dataset.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The segmentation step does not look very robust looking at the videos provided, hence the value of the automatically generated segmentation masks is not that great.
In general, with such a exhaustive multi-step pipeline it would be good to also evaluate the individual steps to capture potential butterfly effects and minimize potential failure cases. 
Moreover, I highly disagree with the choice of performance metric. For a regression task with clear clinically relevant thresholds it better captures the performance with respect to the clinical task at hand if the individual risk class-wise metrics are reported as well. However, I’ve seen that the original publication on the Cardiosyntax also uses this - in my opinion - not task-optimal metric.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a novel approach with the currently best reported performance on SYNTAX scoring. There are some major weaknesses, which however do not outweigh the positive sides for a conference paper.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Still an accept from my side

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
1.The article presents a hierarchical modeling approach that preserves the identity of vessel segments. This framework mimics the thought process of cardiologists when interpreting images, first examining local vessel segments and then summarizing them hierarchically into the left and right coronary artery systems.
2.Methodologically, this approach combines discrete vascular segments with continuous spatial features by generating narrow attention heatmaps. This ensures the consistency of the identity of the same anatomical vascular segment across different viewpoints and motion frames, reducing ambiguity during multi-view feature fusion.
3.Currently available multi-view coronary angiography datasets suffer from fragmented annotation. The authors integrated multiple public datasets and supplemented the vessel segmentation labels for approximately 1.2 million images, providing a valuable resource for subsequent research.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.This paper proposes a hierarchical modeling framework that preserves vessel segment identity. By extracting the vessel centerline and constructing a connected graph, this method decomposes the vessel tree topology into structurally stable linear vessel segments, allowing vessel identity to be anchored to the topological structure rather than to the pixel appearance, which is highly susceptible to changes in multiple viewpoints, cardiac motion, or contrast agents.
2.The study introduces a “segment-aware decision field” and a hierarchical feature aggregation mechanism, which aligns with the actual clinical workflow of cardiologists. Simultaneously, the model strictly groups and hierarchically summarizes multi-view video features according to the physical anatomical structure of the left and right coronary arteries, effectively preventing erroneous entanglement and confusion of features between different anatomical systems.
3.Regarding data utilization and domain resource development: Addressing the long-standing pain points in the field of coronary angiography multi-view video, such as the scarcity and fragmentation of high-quality labeled data, the authors innovatively integrated multiple publicly available datasets. They completed complete vessel segmentation labels for up to 1.2 million images, constructing and committing to open-sourcing this imaging dataset with extremely high clinical translational potential.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The experimental section of this paper only compares the proposed framework with the single baseline model CarS and its variants. If this study claims that its hierarchical aggregation and spatiotemporal processing are superior to traditional “black box” models, it should introduce more representative spatiotemporal video analysis baselines for comparison. For example, models such as CathAI’s automated coronary interpretation could be introduced, with slight modifications to their feature extraction backend to adapt them to the SYNTAX regression task, thus more convincingly demonstrating the superiority of this strategy.
2.When transforming discrete segment-level narrowing assessments into continuous spatial representations, the paper states that the Gaussian form is not optimal. Therefore, comparative experiments with different spatial kernel functions or continuous distribution strategies based on accurate lumen profiles should be added to the experimental section. Otherwise, the design of this core module will lack solid theoretical support and sufficient experimental verification.
3.When non-intersecting blood vessels overlap in a specific two-dimensional viewpoint, the algorithm inevitably generates “pseudo-bidding nodes.” This pseudo-topological structure incorrectly truncates what should be complete blood vessel segments, fundamentally altering the connected graph structure from that viewpoint. Furthermore, the segmentation diagrams shown in Figure 2 from different viewpoints are positioned relatively close together, failing to adequately illustrate the effect. Therefore, it is necessary to clearly explain how the current method identifies and eliminates “pseudo-bidding points,” and supplement this with relevant robustness analysis or ablation experiments, specifically demonstrating how it effectively avoids entanglement of erroneous anatomical features.
4.The mechanism for obtaining the key parameter $s_k$ appears to be a black box, as the paper doesn’t explain in detail how this crucial parameter is derived. If it’s automatically estimated by an algorithm, then specific implementation details and the accuracy of this step must be provided, as it directly determines the quality of the subsequent heatmap generation.
5.The keyframe extraction method is opaque. In Figure 2, the feature information for the entire framework comes from selecting keyframes from the case sequence. In real coronary angiography videos, many frames are invalid due to factors such as incomplete or dissipated contrast agent and angiography deviation caused by heartbeat. The paper does not explain how these frames were selected. It is recommended to supplement the specific algorithmic logic for keyframe selection.
6.The current evaluation is based solely on cross-validation using a mixture of these publicly available datasets. Given that the annotation and completion strategies for these datasets are designed by the researchers themselves, this introduces certain risks. The model must be rigorously validated on an independent external clinical cohort completely uninvolved in the training and label completion pipeline. Otherwise, the model may simply overfit to the self-designed pseudo-label completion logic and may not truly generalize to the complex and ever-changing real-world clinical environment.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

While this research demonstrates significant value in modeling clinical workflows and integrating large-scale open-source datasets, its core methodologies and clinical validation still suffer from significant shortcomings. First, the model fails to account for the unavoidable vessel overlap issue in real-world 2D angiography. Second, the experimental section only compares the model with a single CarS baseline and its variants, failing to adequately demonstrate its superiority over other advanced spatiotemporal video analysis frameworks; furthermore, the core “segment-aware decision field” directly employs a Gaussian distribution without sufficient ablation experimental support. Finally, regarding clinical validation, it lacks completely independent external clinical cohort testing without label completion. Overall, the paper’s current status is slightly below the direct acceptance standard, but if the authors can provide compelling robust experiments, rich baseline comparisons, and clarify the aforementioned issues during the defense phase, this work still has the potential for acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors’ rebuttal has addressed the remaining concerns raised during the initial review. Specifically, the authors clarified the frame-selection mechanism, explaining that while full sequences are shown in the supplementary video, adnd high-quality clips were used for training via a ResNet-34 classifier. They also justified the choice of evaluation metrics based on clinical guidelines and provided a clear distinction between their work and CathAI (which relies on 2D images rather than temporal video data).
The promising performance on CardioSyntax, along with their commitment to open-sourcing the dataset (120 patients, 800+ videos), code, and trained weights upon acceptance, makes this a complete paper. I recommend accepting this paper.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper addresses the important problem of automatic SYNTAX scoring for coronary arteries. The approach taken is interpretable breaking down the problem into artery segmentation and stenosis calculations. All reviewers have seen the merit but there are some concerns raised. Authors are invited to submit a strong rebuttal addressing these concerns.

All three reviewers are on board for acceptance for this paper addressing an important problem of SYNTAX scoring. Many aspects of a good paper are present in this one.

There is consensus among the reviewers that the paper addresses an important clinical problem and proposes a clinically aligned framework. The rebuttal clarified the main concerns. I therefore recommend acceptance.

The initial reviews were generally positive but raised several substantive concerns. R1 supported acceptance and emphasized the clinical alignment, structured annotations, and performance gains, while noting that some experimental details were insufficient for reproducibility. R2 also recommended acceptance but raised concerns about segmentation robustness, error propagation in a multi-stage pipeline, and the lack of clinically risk-stratified metrics. R3 initially recommended weak rejection, mainly due to limited comparison with other spatiotemporal or angiography models, insufficient analysis of the Gaussian decision-field design, possible failure modes caused by vessel overlap or pseudo-bifurcation points, unclear frame selection, and the lack of an independent external clinical cohort.
The rebuttal was useful in clarifying several points. It explained that the supplementary videos showed complete sequences, whereas training used selected high-quality clips identified with a ResNet-34 classifier; it also clarified the frame-selection procedure, the origin of the segment parameter through the VesSAM skeleton-graph splitting procedure, and the distinction between the proposed video-based SYNTAX scoring pipeline and CathAI-like stenosis-estimation systems. The rebuttal also explained the rationale for using the reported regression metrics for comparability with CardioSyntax and described measures intended to reduce error accumulation, including iterative segmentation refinement, segment tracking, and overlap removal during vessel cropping. These clarifications were sufficient for R3 to move from weak reject to accept, and R2 maintained an accept recommendation.
Some limitations remain. The submitted paper still does not provide an independent external clinical validation cohort, and the absence of risk-class-wise clinical metrics limits assessment of clinical decision impact. The Gaussian form used for the decision field is acknowledged as a practical continuous representation rather than an optimized or fully validated design, and there is limited ablation of alternative kernels or lumen-profile-based spatial representations. The comparison set is also relatively narrow, relying mainly on CarS and variants rather than a broader set of adapted video or angiography baselines. These issues should be considered when interpreting the clinical readiness of the method.
Overall, the strengths outweigh the remaining limitations for a MICCAI conference paper.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the meta-reviewer and reviewers for their constructive comments. We are encouraged that R1 recognized our segment identity-preserving hierarchical framework, structured annotations, and improved performance, while R2 noted that our pipeline is clinically well motivated and achieves the best reported CardioSyntax performance. We address the main concerns below.
R2Q1: The videos provided in the supplementary material show the segmentation results of the complete videos. We did not remove low-quality frames, especially the first few frames where no vessels are visible, because we wanted to present the full video sequence. During training, however, we only used high-quality video clips.
R1Q1, R3Q5: We annotated high-quality video segments from all video-frame data of 120 patients. We then trained a binary classifier to distinguish high-quality frames from other frames. The training set contains more than 800 videos from 120 patients. Specifically, we trained a ResNet-34 model for this task. If the paper is accepted, we will release this dataset, the code, and the trained weights.
R2Q2: We strongly agree with this concern. However, public datasets currently lack full-pipeline annotations, which is also one of the main challenges in this field. Nevertheless, our method already includes several strategies to reduce error accumulation. These include iterative training of the segmentation model for better mask generation, a more stable frame-level segment tracking algorithm, and avoiding overlap when cropping vessel videos.
R2Q3: According to clinical guidelines, the SYNTAX score can indeed be divided into several risk levels. One major reason we used the metrics in the paper is that they reflect prediction reliability while also allowing a fair comparison with CardioSyntax. In future work, we will further promote and explore more suitable evaluation metrics.
R3Q1: To the best of our knowledge, CathAI is not a full-pipeline automatic coronary angiography interpretation model. It uses 2D images rather than temporal video data, and its final goal is stenosis detection and severity estimation. In addition, its code, weights, and dataset have not been publicly released, making it difficult to reproduce. Among current works on temporal coronary angiography analysis, a representative example is STQD-Det published in TPAMI, but it also does not release any files that would allow reproduction.
R3Q2: What we intended to express is that we do not claim the Gaussian distribution used in our method is the optimal choice. We used it mainly because it provides a continuous representation. This is a good research direction and problem. In future work, we will continue to explore more suitable representation methods.
R3Q3: In fact, the purpose of using bifurcation points for vessel segmentation and tracking is to generate stable video crops for each vessel segment. We remove video crops with high overlap. DeepCoro then outputs the stenosis severity for each input video crop. We map the stenosis severity of all cropped videos into heatmaps using Gaussian distributions. The heatmap represents all suspicious stenosis regions in the image. In our view, incorrect bifurcation points do not significantly affect the actual meaning of the heatmap. This is because, regardless of whether a vessel is mistakenly divided into multiple segments, if stenosis exists, it will still be reflected in the heatmap.
R3Q4: The extraction process of $s_k$ is not a black box. We follow Algorithm 1 in VesSAM, which performs vessel segments splitting based on the skeleton graph and bifurcation points.
R3Q6: We fully agree that external validation is very important. However, to the best of our knowledge, there is currently no other publicly available large-scale multi-view video coronary angiography dataset. This limitation is also one of the key motivations for our research in this field.

title: MORI-Seg: Learning Morphological Geometry for Instance Segmentation Without Instance Annotations
abstract: Instance-level quantification of kidney functional units is essential for morphometric analysis, yet most publicly available pathology datasets provide only semantic segmentation annotations, where adjacent structures of the same class are merged into single regions. This prevents reliable instance-level analysis and limits downstream quantitative studies. Existing heuristic post-processing methods often yield suboptimal instance separation, particularly in crowded and adherent regions, while deep learning-based instance segmentation approaches typically require intensive instance-level annotations that are costly and labor-intensive to obtain. We propose MORI-Seg, a deep learning framework that enables instance segmentation without requiring instance-level annotations. Instead of heuristic splitting or instance supervision, MORI-Seg learns morphology-aware geometric representations directly from semantic masks by jointly modeling object-centric distance fields and boundary-band representations to encode interior structure and contact interfaces. A class-conditioned feature disentanglement module further promotes intra-instance coherence and inter-instance separation. Under semantic-only supervision, MORI-Seg decomposes connected semantic regions into distinct instance masks in an end-to-end manner. Experiments demonstrate improved instance separation accuracy and more reliable morphometric quantification compared with classical post-processing pipelines and representative semantic-to-instance learning approaches. The official implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/ddrrnn123/MORI-Seg.

reviews.recommendation_label: Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes MORI-Seg, a new deep learning framework, for the segmentation of renal pathology instances using only semantic-level supervision. Its core contribution lies in learning morphologically aware geometric representations directly from semantic masks, eliminating the need for time-consuming instantiation-level annotations.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Unlike heuristic methods or general seman-to-instance methods, MORI-Seg explicitly combines kidney-specific morphological priors. 
2.This method provides a new idea for the instance annotation of pathological images and does not require a lot of time to annotate the images. 
3.The model was trained and tested on different datasets, verifying its generalization ability on different stained images. 
4.A detailed comparative experiment was conducted, and the selected comparative methods included different frameworks and were compared with multiple latest methods from 2026.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.This work employs a specific category of magnification strategies, which can further discuss the sensitivity of the morphologically aware branch to changes in image resolution, or whether fixed-size patches would limit the capture of extremely large or slender structures. 
2.The provided network framework diagram is not conducive to reading. A clear version needs to be provided.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This method can perform reliable instance segmentation without instance-level labels. The introduced boundary band mapping and distance field provide a multi-faceted geometric signal, logically resolving the failure mode of the previous embedding method. Furthermore, the design choice of removing auxiliary branches during reasoning ensures that the increased morphological intelligence does not come at the cost of computational speed, making it suitable for large-scale clinical full-slice imaging.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper proposes MORI-Seg, a framework for instance segmentation in pathology images under semantic-only supervision, aiming to address the practical limitation that most public datasets provide only semantic masks without instance-level annotations.
The key idea is to bridge the gap between semantic segmentation and instance segmentation by explicitly incorporating morphology-aware geometric priors into the learning process. Specifically, the method introduces a morphological geometry branch that jointly models:
1、object-centric distance fields, capturing interior structure of instances
2、boundary-band representations, encoding contact interfaces between adjacent objects
In addition, a feature-level instance disentanglement module is designed to promote intra-instance compactness and inter-instance separability. The framework is trained end-to-end using only semantic masks, and all auxiliary branches are removed during inference, preserving the original instance segmentation pipeline.
The method is evaluated on renal pathology datasets and compared with heuristic post-processing methods, fully supervised instance segmentation models, and semantic-to-instance approaches, demonstrating improved instance separation and morphometric reliability.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper tackles a very important and realistic problem in computational pathology: the lack of instance-level annotations. Most prior works either rely on heuristic post-processing (e.g., watershed, morphology) or require expensive instance masks. This work directly targets this gap and proposes a solution that operates under semantic-only supervision, which is highly valuable for large-scale clinical deployment.
The introduction of morphology-aware geometric modeling is a strong and well-justified idea. In particular:
The distance field modeling captures object interior structure in a continuous manner.The boundary-band representation explicitly models contact regions, which are critical for separating touching structures
This combination is both intuitive and tailored to pathology images, where structures are often irregular and densely packed. Compared to prior semantic-to-instance approaches (e.g., pixel embedding [Chen et al., MICCAI 2019], boundary-aware methods such as DCAN [Chen et al., MedIA 2017]), this formulation explicitly incorporates domain-specific morphology priors, which is a meaningful advancement.
An important practical advantage is that all auxiliary branches are used only during training and removed at inference, preserving the original RTMDet-Ins pipeline.
This makes the method attractive for real-world deployment, as it improves performance without increasing inference complexity.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1、Although the overall framework is well designed, its components are related to existing lines of work:
Distance map supervision has been used in boundary-aware or regression-based segmentation (e.g., InstaBound, distance regression methods)
Boundary modeling is a common strategy (e.g., DCAN, boundary-aware segmentation)
Instance embedding and feature disentanglement are also well studied (e.g., pixel embedding methods)
The novelty lies mainly in how these components are combined and adapted to pathology morphology, rather than introducing a fundamentally new formulation. While this is acceptable, the paper could better emphasize what is truly new compared to recent works such as InstaBound (MedIA 2026) or SIM (CVPR 2023).
2、Limited comparison with the most recent semantic-to-instance methods
Although several baselines are included, comparison with very recent methods (2024–2025) is still somewhat limited. For example:
Recent morphology-guided or binary-to-instance methods (e.g., DyMorph-B2I, 2025)
More advanced foundation-model-based segmentation pipelines
Including such comparisons would further strengthen the empirical claims.
3、Ablation analysis could be deeper
While the ablation study shows the contribution of distance and boundary priors, the analysis remains somewhat limited:
The interaction between feature disentanglement and geometry modeling is not deeply explored
Sensitivity to hyperparameters (e.g., λ weights, boundary width) is not analyzed
It is unclear how robust the method is to different semantic mask qualities
More detailed analysis would help better understand the behavior of the model.
4、Generalization beyond renal pathology is not fully demonstrated
The method is designed with renal morphology in mind, which is reasonable, but:
It is unclear how well the approach generalizes to other organs or tissue types
The morphology priors may be domain-specific
A brief discussion or additional experiment would strengthen the generality of the method.
5、Interpretability and error analysis could be improved
Although qualitative results are provided, the paper lacks:
quantitative evaluation of instance separation quality (e.g., split/merge errors)
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Overall innovations and improvements in experimental results
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes MORI]Seg, a deep learning framework for instance segmentation in renal pathology images that operates under semantic-only supervision. Its main contributions are: L1) enabling instance segmentation without any instance-level annotations; L2) incorporating explicit morphological priors of renal structures by jointly modeling object-centric distance fields and boundary-band representations to guide instance separation; and L3) demonstrating through cross-dataset evaluation that this approach consistently outperforms heuristic post-processing and existing semantic-to-instance methods in terms of instance separation accuracy and morphometric reliability.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.It addresses the critical and common challenge in medical imaging where only semantic annotations are available, bridging the gap between annotation cost and analysis need.
2.The integration of morphology-aware geometric priors (distance fields and boundary bands) with feature disentanglement provides a principled and effective way to decompose connected semantic regions into instances.
3.The method demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on a challenging renal pathology dataset under semantic-only supervision, significantly outperforming both classical heuristics and recent learning-based baselines.
4.The auxiliary geometric branches are only used during training and removed at inference, ensuring no extra computational overhead in deployment.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The experiments are exclusively conducted on renal pathology datasets LKI for training, KPMP for evaluation). The generalizability of the proposed morphology-aware priors to other medical image domains (e.g., cell nuclei, neurons, or organs in radiology) is not demonstrated.
2.The framework is built upon the RTMDet-Ins architecture. The paper does not sufficiently explore how the choice of the base model affects the final performance or the relative gain from the proposed components.
3.While the inference cost is the same as the base model, the paper lacks a discussion on the increased training complexity and time due to the additional geometric branches and loss terms.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper presents a well-motivated, technically sound, and empirically validated solution to a significant problem in medical image analysis. The core idea of leveraging explicit morphological geometry for instance separation under weak supervision is novel and effectively executed. The results are compelling and clearly demonstrate the method’s superiority over relevant baselines. Despite the limited scope of validation, the work is solid, clearly presented, and offers a valuable contribution to the field of weakly-supervised instance segmentation in medical imaging.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text: This paper received two weak accepts and one strong accept, and all reviewers recommended acceptance. The final recommendation is to accept the paper. The paper addresses a clear practical need in biomedical image segmentation evaluation, where instance-wise assessment is often more clinically meaningful than global semantic metrics, while existing tools remain fragmented, limited, or inconvenient for 2D/3D biomedical use cases. The proposed panoptica package provides a modular and extensible pipeline covering instance approximation, instance matching, and instance-level metric computation, enabling unified evaluation of semantic and instance segmentation outputs. Its open-source implementation, support for multiple metrics, applicability to both semantic and instance maps, and demonstrations on two biomedical tasks make it a useful contribution to the community. Although the experimental comparison with existing tools and runtime analysis could be strengthened, these limitations do not outweigh the practical value of the framework. Overall, the paper provides a reusable and timely evaluation tool for instance-based segmentation assessment; therefore, the final recommendation is acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and AC for the positive and insightful feedback and summarize the comments into three major and two minor concerns. 
[Major concerns]
C1.Clarification of novelty beyond existing semantic-to-instance methods (R2):
We thank the reviewer for pointing out similarities to prior distance-map, boundary-aware, and embedding-based methods. We would like to clarify that the novelty of MORI-Seg lies in introducing a morphology-aware geometric learning framework specifically designed for renal pathology under semantic-only supervision.
(1) MORI-Seg enables reliable instance segmentation without any instance-level annotations, without requiring instance-level annotations.
(2) MORI-Seg jointly models object-centric distance fields and boundary-band representations to explicitly capture renal pathological morphology in densely packed regions.
(3) We introduce geometry-guided feature disentanglement to improve intra-instance compactness and inter-instance separability.
We will further clarify the differences from DCAN, InstaBound, SIM, and embedding-based methods in the revised manuscript.
C2.Generalization, backbone dependency, and magnification strategy (R1, R2, R3):
We thank the reviewer for raising the concern regarding the additional training complexity introduced by the geometric branches. Compared with the baseline model (57.309M parameters), MORI-Seg introduces only a marginal parameter increase of 0.024M. The training time increases from 10:02:08 to 12:53:32 due to the additional geometric supervision and optimization objectives. The auxiliary branches introduce minimal memory overhead and no additional inference cost since all geometry branches are removed during deployment.
Multi-scale sampling is necessary because renal pathological structures vary significantly in size, with some categories containing very small or thin structures while others are much larger. Our multi-scale sampling strategy follows OmniSeg.
RTMDet-Ins was selected because it achieved the best overall performance in our preliminary experiments. In future work, we plan to further investigate the generalizability of MORI-Seg by integrating the proposed morphology-aware modules into other segmentation frameworks and backbones.
C3.Comparison with recent methods and foundation model (R2, R3, AC):
We will include more comprehensive discussion. Some recent approaches such as DyMorph-B2I still rely on heuristic post-processing and manually designed morphology rules, which differs from our end-to-end learning-based framework. 
Regarding foundation-model-based methods, we have included a DINOv3-style feature extractor combined with Mask2Former as a strong baseline, and MORI-Seg still achieved superior performance under semantic-only supervision.
[Minor concerns]
C4.Limited validation on additional datasets and organs (R2, R3):
We agree that broader validation would strengthen the paper. Due to current dataset limitations, experiments focused mainly on renal pathology. We agree broader validation would strengthen the paper and will clarify this limitation in the manuscript.
C5.Additional metrics and deeper ablation analysis (R2):
We additionally performed statistical significance analysis on all existing results to validate the observed improvements. The p-values from the Wilcoxon signed-rank test show statistically significant improvements, with all p-values between the proposed methods with other methods less than 0.001, including both the baseline comparison and the ablation study settings. More detailed split/merge statistics and sensitivity analyses will be included in future work.

title: MoSE: Mixture-of-Scale-Experts for Medical Image Restoration
abstract: Medical image restoration (MedIR) is crucial for obtaining high-quality medical images and enabling accurate diagnosis. Existing unified restoration models often suffer from parameter redundancy and high computational cost due to their shared architecture design. While Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) introduces sparse computation, the homogeneous design of experts struggles to handle diverse degradation patterns, resulting in texture distortions and anatomical structure loss. To address these challenges, we propose Mixture-of-Scale-Experts (MoSE) framework, which employs scale-heterogeneous experts operating with different anatomical context ranges, and dynamically selects the most suitable expert for each input. A scale-aware load-balancing loss further promotes balanced expert utilization. Furthermore, we develop an Orientation-Contrast Guided (OCG) filter, combining Haar wavelet–based directional sensing with local contrast enhancement to guide high-frequency reconstruction of fine-grained structures. Finally, we propose a novel Anatomical Texture-Level Similarity (ATLS) metric to better evaluate the structural fidelity of restored anatomical textures. Extensive experiments on a private endoscopic super-resolution dataset and a public all-in-one MedIR benchmark (CT, PET, and MRI) demonstrate that MoSE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative metrics and visual quality while maintaining high inference efficiency.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a “Mixture-of-Scale-Experts (MoSE) “ network for medical image restoration. It introduces scale-heterogeneous experts with progressive receptive fields, dynamically routing inputs to shallow-wide experts for local high-frequency details or deep-narrow experts for global contextual priors. scale-heterogeneous experts with progressive receptive fields, dynamically routing inputs to shallow-wide experts for local high-frequency details or deep-narrow experts for global contextual priors. It also proposes a novel Anatomical Texture-Level Similarity (ATLS) metric, which leverages a pre-trained visual-language embedding model to assess patch-wise structural and semantic fidelity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that this framework achieves state-of-the-art performance and high inference efficiency across multiple medical imaging modalities.
reviews.text_strengths:
(1) The authors conducted extensive testing on highly challenging multimodal benchmarks. Experiments covered not only the public, comprehensive MedIR dataset, which includes CT denoising, MRI super-resolution, and PET synthesis, but also a private high-resolution endoscopic super-resolution (ESR) dataset obtained through clinical collaboration, fully validating the model’s robustness across different imaging mechanisms.
(2) While maintaining a high PSNR, the inference time was significantly lower than mainstream methods such as TAT ​​and SwinIR, demonstrating the superiority of sparse activation architectures in real-time clinical processing.
(3) A scale-aware load balancing loss was introduced, minimizing the coefficient of variation between importance and load to ensure that experts at different scales are fully utilized during training.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(1) The design of heterogeneous experts has been extensively explored in the literature of deep learning and MoE. While this paper emphasizes its specificity and progressive receptive field design in medical image degradation and describes its architectural flexibility in handling diverse medical image degradation compared to traditional MoE, it does not adequately discuss or compare existing heterogeneous architectures in the MoE field.
(2) The authors propose a new evaluation metric, ATLS, and demonstrate its superiority over other methods in experiments. However, the ATLS metric relies on a general vision-language pre-trained model, Qwen3-VL-Embedding, for feature extraction. Although the authors claim its sensitivity to minute textures, medical images (such as endoscopic microvessels and MRI tissue structures) have highly specialized and unique noise distributions. The authors do not provide any evidence that the model’s embedding similarity is highly correlated with the visual evaluation (MOS) of professional radiologists.
(3) The model simultaneously uses shared experts to provide geometric priors and dynamically selected heterogeneous scale experts, which are fused through channel cross-attention (C-XCA). When the local features of the scale expert conflict with the global prior of the shared expert, the authors lack a deep theoretical explanation for whether a simple attention mechanism will lead to the distortion of the anatomical structure.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper has some shortcomings in terms of innovation. The design of heterogeneous expert models has been extensively studied in the fields of deep learning and multimodal (MoE). Although this paper emphasizes its specificity and progressive receptive field design in medical image degradation and describes its architectural flexibility compared to traditional multimodal models when dealing with various medical image degradation problems, it does not fully discuss or compare existing heterogeneous architectures in the field of multimodal models.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I feel that the author has earnestly addressed the issues I raised. I find the author’s rebuttal to be highly reasonable; in particular, the explanation regarding “scale-heterogeneous experts” was convincing and, in my view, demonstrates a certain degree of innovation.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper presents a heterogeneous mixture-of-experts framework for medical image restoration in which experts are differentiated rather than sharing a uniform architecture. The design combines shallow wide experts for local detail recovery with deep narrow experts for broader anatomical context. A routing mechanism selects one scale specific expert per input, while a shared expert operates in parallel to provide stable geometric priors. The method also introduces an OCG module to enhance fine detail reconstruction and proposes ATLS as a texture sensitive evaluation metric that complements PSNR and SSIM.
reviews.text_strengths:
The motivation for the study is reasonable. Conventional all-in-one models can be computationally inefficient, while homogeneous mixture-of-experts frameworks may not capture the diversity of anatomical structures and degradation patterns. The heterogeneous expert design sounds appropriate.
The experimental design includes ablations and the reported results show consistent incremental improvements, across multiple tasks including endoscopic super resolution, MRI super resolution, CT denoising, and PET synthesis.
The paper emphasizes both performance and efficiency. It achieves competitive PSNR with reduced inference time and parameter count supports the practical value.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
In Figure 4, highlighting specific regions with arrows and briefly explaining the observed improvements across different methods would improve interpretability.
It is unclear whether Figure 5a reports inference time and PSNR jointly across all tasks or if the results are separated by modality. This should be clarified.
For Figure 5b, the interpretation “As the number increases, the deviation decreases, and the curves stabilize at around 100 patches. Considering both stability and efficiency, we adopt 100 patches as the default setting.” of patch count in ATLS evaluation appears ambiguous. As far as I understand the ATLS correctly, ATLS is an evaluation metric that the paper proposed to measure the output of the model to the ground truth target for more local, fine details, and patch is randomly sampled from each case to evaluate the similarity. In that frame, I believe the increasing patch number would always increase the reliability of the evaluation.
The rationale for selecting a subset of patches instead of evaluating over the full image is not clearly justified.
From table 2, three single expert baselines did not achieve the best results compared to the author’s methods. It would be useful to better understand why the combined expert setting outperforms single expert baselines.
The OCG module is introduced as a key contribution, but its effect is not clearly visualized.
The routing mechanism is described as adaptive, yet there is limited empirical analysis of its behavior. It would be valuable to examine expert utilization patterns, relationships between input characteristics and routing decisions, and whether meaningful specialization emerges across experts.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper is well motivated and addresses a relevant problem in medical image restoration. The idea of using heterogeneous experts with different receptive field characteristics is sensible, and the experimental section is fairly broad, covering multiple tasks with ablations and efficiency comparisons. These are meaningful strengths, and I do see practical value in the proposed framework.
However, several aspects of the paper would benefit from clearer analysis and presentation. In particular, the proposed ATLS metric needs better justification and interpretation, the role and visible effect of the OCG module are not sufficiently demonstrated, and the routing mechanism is not analyzed in enough depth to show that meaningful expert specialization is actually being learned.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Authors appropriately addressed to the concerns.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces a Mixture-of-Scale Expert to achieve scale-aware routing and an Orientation–Contrast Guided filter for detail reconstruction.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The introduction of MoSE is novel.
2.The use of multimodal LLM for quality evaluation is novel.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The introduction of different expert E_k is unclear. Do they differ in the number of downsampling stages or in the number of blocks?
2.Does MoSE use top-k gating or top-1 gating?
3.What is the difference between the Scale-Aware Load-Balancing Loss and the standard load-balancing loss? The paper does not provide clear evidence or explanation of what makes it “scale-aware.”
4.Additional experiments are needed to demonstrate that different anatomical regions indeed select different experts.
5.The authors compare their method with many approaches from natural image processing. However, there is a growing number of open-source, general-purpose MedIR methods, such as Restore-RWKV [1], RAT [2], DASMamba [3], and DaPT [4]. The authors should include more comparisons with MedIR methods and discuss them in the Introduction and Related Work sections.
[1] Yang Z, Li J, Zhang H, et al. Restore-rwkv: Efficient and effective medical image restoration with rwkv[J]. IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics, 2026.
[2] Yang Z, Chen H, Qian Z, et al. Region attention transformer for medical image restoration[C]//International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland, 2024: 603-613.
[3] Chan S C K, Shi L, Huang B, et al. Directional Adaptive Shuffle-Based Visual State-Space Models for Medical Image Restoration[C]//International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025: 160-170.
[4] Wei J, Yang G, Wang Z, et al. Degradation-Aware Prompted Transformer for Unified Medical Image Restoration[J]. IEEE Transactions on Image Processing, 2025, 34: 8583-8598.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
I encourage the authors to release their code publicly. At present, I am inclined to accept this paper; however, my final assessment will depend on the authors’ response, and the score may be raised or lowered accordingly.

The paper is well organized and has good motivation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The author has addressed my concerns.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper proposes a Mixture-of-Scale-Experts framework for medical image restoration with promising empirical performance across multiple modalities. Reviewers appreciate the motivation, efficiency gains, and broad experimental validation. However, there are notable concerns regarding the level of methodological novelty, justification of the proposed ATLS metric, and insufficient analysis of the expert routing mechanism and architectural design choices. Given these mixed evaluations, I invite the authors to provide a rebuttal addressing the concerns on novelty, metric validation, and deeper analysis of the model behavior.

The authors have addressed most of the reviewer comments. In the final version, the authors should down tone the claim of SOTA performance as there is no comparison with task-specific image restoration methods, and should include this as a primary limitation of the experiments.
The authors’ responses effectively address the reviewers’ concerns. I recommend acceptance, while encouraging the authors to consider the reviewers’ suggestions in the final revision.

After reading the rebuttal, I recommend Accept. The paper proposes a mixture-of-scale expert design for medical image restoration. The method has a concrete structure: the experts use different receptive fields, the router selects a scale-specific branch for each input, and a shared branch is kept in parallel to provide stable geometric context. The experiments cover several restoration settings, including endoscopic super-resolution, MRI super-resolution, CT denoising, and PET synthesis. The reported results show gains in restoration quality while keeping inference cost lower than several transformer-based baselines.
My initial concerns were mainly about evidence and presentation. The heterogeneous expert design is related to existing MoE work, so the paper needs to explain what is specific to medical restoration rather than presenting heterogeneity itself as new. The rebuttal clarifies this point and gives a more convincing account of the scale-specialized design. It also addresses the routing mechanism, the scale-aware loss, and the role of the OCG module. These additions make the method easier to judge as a medical restoration model rather than only as a generic MoE variant.
Some issues should still be fixed in the final version. ATLS should be presented carefully, since an embedding-based metric is not a substitute for reader studies or clinical visual assessment. The paper should also make the expert routing behavior visible, clarify the patch sampling used by ATLS, and include the missing MedIR comparisons or at least discuss them directly. I do not think these points change the decision, because the core method and the empirical results are sound enough for acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely appreciate the valuable comments on the motivation, efficiency, and strong experimental evaluation of our method. Our feedback is as follows. 
Q1(R1&R2&R3): Novelty clarification of scale-heterogeneous experts. 
MoSE is designed for the diverse anatomical texture complexities in medical image restoration. MoSE uses three experts with different downsampling depths for dynamic scale selection, avoiding reliance on a fixed single-scale expert that may over-smooth details or lack context. Unlike natural-image heterogeneous expert methods such as MoCE-IR and AdaptIR, MoSE designs experts according to the scale of anatomical structures in medical images, with the shared expert and OCG providing structural and high-frequency guidance. MoSE outperforms MoCE-IR on MedIR tasks.
Q2(R1&R2): Medical validity and patch sampling of ATLS. 
ATLS uses patch-level rather than full-image comparison because subtle but important differences may be averaged out by large similar background regions in full-image evaluation. We adopt 100 patches as more patches improve reliability but increase computational cost and may reduce sensitivity to local; ATLS empirically stabilizes around 100 patches, with only minor changes at 150/200.To validate its medical relevance, we evaluate 20 paired restoration results where PSNR/SSIM and ATLS give inconsistent rankings. Method names and metric values are hidden; two junior clinicians independently select the image more suitable for diagnosis, and a senior clinician reviews the results. Clinicians tend to prefer images with higher ATLS even when PSNR/SSIM are lower, indicating ATLS better aligns with clinical perception and complements pixel-level.
Q3 (R1): Fusion between shared and scale experts. 
The shared expert and selected scale expert provide complementary information. The scale expert remains the main restoration path, while the shared expert provides auxiliary global basic feature guidance through residual and learnable C-XCA fusion. Since C-XCA mainly performs channel-wise feature reweighting rather than spatial geometric rearrangement, it reduces the risk of distortion.
Q4(R2&R3): Expert routing, utilization, and specialization. 
MoSE uses top-1 gating. On the ESR test set, the router assigns 40%, 33%, and 27% of images to Experts 1–3, showing balanced usage without expert collapse. To verify routing effectiveness, we group images by their router-selected expert and randomly sample 50 images from each group. For each image, we keep the input unchanged and separately perform inference using each non-selected expert. The router-selected expert consistently achieves better PSNR/SSIM than the two non-selected experts, with gains of 0.045–0.612 dB in PSNR and 0.003–0.023 in SSIM. This confirms that MoSE learns meaningful scale-specific specialization.
Q5(R2): Figure clarification and visualization. 
For Fig. 4, we will add arrows to highlight and briefly explain the observed improvements. For Fig. 5a, we clarify that it reports the test results on the Endoscopic SR (ESR) dataset. For OCG, visualization results show that it better preserves micro-vessel contours and mucosal textures in endoscopic images, while producing clearer low-contrast tissue boundaries in MRI/CT images.
Q6 (R3): Scale-aware load balancing. 
In practice, instead of enforcing a uniform distribution as in the standard loss, we weight routing probabilities I_e with a depth-based bias, enabling adaptive routing of images to scale experts according to their frequency characteristics.
Q7(R3): Additional Method Comparisons. 
We add comparisons with the suggested MedIR methods. Restore-RWKV, RAT, DASMamba-MedIR, and DaPT achieve average PSNR/ATLS of 36.02/0.83, 37.57/0.86, 36.15/0.84, and 37.21/0.85 on AMIR, and 31.49/0.72, 32.23/0.77, 31.74/0.74, and 32.01/0.76 on ESR. MoSE performs better (AMIR: 38.21/0.88, ESR: 33.88/0.83).
We will incorporate all revisions into the final version, and release our code and ESR dataset.

title: Motion-Conditioned Multi-view Fusion for Myocardial Infarction Localization from Echocardiography
abstract: Myocardial infarction (MI) remains a leading cause of mortality worldwide. Echocardiography (Echo) is a widely available modality for MI assessment, where regional wall motion abnormality is a key indicator. Prior learning based methods for myocardial motion analysis often use handcrafted descriptors or densely supervised estimation, but the need for extensive annotation limits applicability. Foundation models have recently improved vision-based Echo analysis; however, most methods operate on single views and segment-level localization remains unreliable under view-dependent ambiguity, especially in apical views. To address this, we propose MCF-Net, a novel motion-guided multi-view fusion framework that fuses myocardial motion cues with foundation model representations to localize infarction. Visual features are extracted using EchoPrime, a pretrained Echo foundation model shared across dual views. Cardiac motion is modeled with extremely sparse supervision: a single annotated template frame is transferred across videos to initialize point tracking, avoiding dense labels. Motion-derived segment-aware soft masks provide coarse spatial priors that selectively enhance features for challenging myocardial segments. A motion-conditioned fusion mechanism then integrates motion and vision across views, refining predictions without overriding strong appearance cues. On segment-level MI localization, MCF-Net achieves 72.4% F1 and 84.9% accuracy, outperforming state-of-the-art motion-only, vision-only, and fusion baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/GYang1619/MCF-Net-MICCAI2026.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses a clinically relevant task and presents a fairly complete methodological framework. The proposed framework utilizes a pretrained foundation model to extract rich visual representations and introduces Motion Guided Soft Refinement to focus feature extraction on infarction-relevant regions. Motion Conditioned Fusion further modulates appearance features using view-specific motion and enables cross-view interaction between motion dynamics and visual semantics, thereby improving fine-grained localization.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Unlike methods that only determine whether MI is present, this work tackles segment-level localization, which is more consistent with the clinical logic and is also more challenging than coarse-grained classification.
