The problem setting is meaningful and clinically relevant, as it goes beyond simple classification to a finer-grained task. 
2.The authors emphasize that the entire dataset requires only a single manually annotated template frame, which is then transferred to all videos through template matching and point tracking. This design indeed reduces the burden of dense annotation.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The sparse motion initialization relies on a single annotated template, NCC-based matching, and a fallback-to-prior strategy. This may introduce structural bias or propagate initialization errors, especially when transferring across A4C and A2C views. 
2.According to the sensitivity curves on page 8, the soft refinement strength λ has a narrow effective range, and performance drops when masking becomes too strong. This suggests that the refinement mechanism may be heuristic and not inherently robust. 
3.The dataset is relatively small, no external validation is provided, and no subgroup analysis is conducted. For a localization task, this is a substantial limitation. 
4.The paper verifies that MCF and MSR help, but does not sufficiently dissect why they help, under what conditions they fail, or how robust the sparse motion pipeline is.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

1.The motivation is clear, but the innovation is limited.
2.The model design is reasonable, but the experiment is not enough.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors introduce MCF-Net, a framework for localizing myocardial infarction in echocardiography using two different cardiac views. It combines pretrained visual features from EchoPrime with motion information obtained from tracking a small number of points. A key idea is to rely on very minimal motion supervision—starting from just a single manually annotated frame for the entire dataset—to estimate motion patterns of the heart. These motion cues are used to generate soft masks that help refine the visual input and fuse information across the two views (A2C and A4C).
reviews.text_strengths: The topic is very interesting, and the paper is well written. It also presents a clear methodological contribution, with two key components: motion-guided soft refinement and motion-conditioned cross-view fusion.
reviews.text_weaknesses: Although using only a single annotated template frame for the entire dataset is an interesting idea, the approach relies on transferring one A4C template to all videos—including A2C views—using patch matching, with a fallback to atlas coordinates when the matching confidence is low. This raises concerns about how robust the method is, especially in cases with severe pathology or poor image quality. In addition, the paper does not explain whether the method can handle cases where only one view is available. There is also no statistical significance analysis for the quantitative results, and the authors do not discuss the limitations of their approach or potential failure cases.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper is well written, technically novel, and the topic is clinically important and interesting; however, it lacks statistical significance analysis and discussion of failure cases.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: Within the context of myocardial infarction localization in A2C/A4C multi-view echocardiography, authors propose (action) co-leveraging existing motion tracking and EchoPrime echo/text foundation model embedding for improved 12-segment MI classification. CoTracker3 with limited supervision informs both a localized video-brightening (MSR) before the foundation model and modulation of the foundation model output after (MCF) before multi-head attention. Experimental results show improved MI localization over baseline and competing methods, and an ablation study provide additional evidence.
reviews.text_strengths: Their model shows improved (and sota) results over the baseline EchoPrime-only model, including repeated performance testing against several baselines and competing methods, and ablation study on the specific MSR/MCF additions. An informed approach to injecting prior knowledge (specific motion tracking of the myo wall) into the otherwise fixed cross-purpose foundation model for MI detection.
reviews.text_weaknesses: the improvement is modest (though persistent), unclear whether MSR (and all of 2.1) adds anything that some simpler contrast enhancement would not.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
how different are naive fusion and EchoPrime+MCF to have such different performance, is it just the FiLM conditioning?|| The MSR colormap in Fig. 1 begs the question whether simply brightening the LV (which can be localized blindly on such curated datasets) produces better EchoPrime output, and if so by how much; it seems likely that MCF with its additional model complexity is still worth doing, but it would be disturbing if the foundation model output could be so vastly improved with simple image processing. (Not impugning the validity of Fig 3 and discussion)|| The method seems to require temporal and spatial correspondence across views; is temporal provided implicitly by the ED-ES videos? And when the initial manual fiducials are propagated to the other view through NCC, are you assuming a point correspondence, because A2C/A4C are intended to be on orthogonal planes? Also, the fiducials appear scattered in inner and outer walls, but the paper does not mention a particular protocol. Lastly, patch matching through NCC has plenty of priors to cite in registration, leaving space for discussion on more advanced concepts.|| Though [6] is cited, it should be again in the first mention of CoTracker in text, at the end of 2.1.|| Good non-EchoPrime models are tested, but Gomez 10.1016/j.medengphy.2025.104400 (lesser journal than [5]) reports excellent results and it is more recent.

Improved SOTA results with reasonable testing against baseline and competing methods, some novelty of application to MI detection of the MCF main concept (modulate FM output with complementary info, cross attention).
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: This reader appreciates the authors’ responses to the issues raised.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper presents a technically sound approach to a challenging clinical problem, with a smart integration of motion cues into a strong visual backbone. However, it is held back by a lack of robustness analysis for its core motion pipeline and a validation strategy that is not deep or rigorous enough.

This paper presents MCF-Net, a sparse motion-guided multi-view fusion framework for myocardial infarction (MI) localization in echocardiography, integrating pre-trained visual models with cardiac motion cues. The main concerns include the motion robustness, the effectiveness of the MSR and MCF, and statistical significance of the results. The authors clarified these concerns well and acknowledged the limitation of the single dataset. Given the clinical importance, the whole methodology design, and the promising results, I would like to recommend the work to be accepted.

The authors proposed MCF-Net, a Motion Conditioned Fusion Network for segment-level myocardial infarction localization from dual-view echocardiography. MCF-Net utilizes a pretrained foundation model to extract rich visual representations and introduces Motion Guided Soft Refinement to focus feature extraction on infarction-relevant regions. Motion Conditioned Fusion modulates appearance features using view-specific motion and enables cross-view interaction between motion dynamics and visual semantics, improving fine-grained localization.
The method is technically solid. Though the novelty might be limited as an integration to the current FM, the motion vector feature injection is clearly motivated. The validation is further strengthened through the authors’ response, though the rigorousness is still somewhat limited due to the restriction of rebuttal. I am giving a weak acceptance considering all these.

The motion-guided fusion with sparse tracking is a reasonable and clinically motivated contribution, and the rebuttal adequately addressed the main concerns arouns robustness and the transfer strategy

author_feedback_text:
We thank reviewers/AC for the assessment. We are encouraged that the paper was recognized as clinically relevant MI localization (R1), well written and technically novel (R2), and supported by SOTA results and baselines (R3). The AC noted a technically sound approach with smart motion integration. Our key clarification is that sparse motion is not a fragile pipeline, but a low-supervision physiological prior, quality controlled and injected softly into EchoPrime.
1) Motion robustness and A4C/A2C transfer (R1,R2,R3,AC). The concern is whether one-template NCC initialization propagates errors; our response is that A4C was chosen to target an identified failure mode. Per-view analysis showed EchoPrime is stronger on A2C than A4C: AUROC/PR-AUC 0.880/0.745 vs. 0.796/0.644, with SEG3/SEG6 near-random (AUROC 0.683/0.635). These results, omitted due to space, identify A4C as the main failure mode. Thus, single annotation in A4C makes within-view transfer anatomically consistent while targeting the harder view. For A2C, robustness comes from localized NCC in a 41x41 window (<=20 px drift), fallback to atlas prior (Eq.2), and simpler anatomy. Each view is initialized/tracked independently; no physical A2C-A4C correspondence is assumed. QC removes unreliable trajectories, and substantial visual inspection suggested retained points are mostly on/near the LV wall. We will clarify this protocol and failure modes.
2) MSR is not heuristic and not simple brightening (R1,R3). The concern is whether MSR is generic LV enhancement; our clarification is that it is a dynamic, trajectory-derived guidance for A4C attention failure. EchoPrime can be distracted by non-LV chamber structures in difficult A4C cases, so MSR uses a per-frame Gaussian mask from tracked myocardial points and boundedly modulates the clip as in Eq.3.Thus MSR is trajectory-dependent, time-varying, wall-localized and bounded, while preserving raw Echo context. This also explains Fig.3: EchoPrime is trained on natural Echo clips, so strong masking/augmentation or excessive lambda distorts its expected input distribution; moderate lambda provides a weak anatomical cue.
3) MCF is beyond naive fusion/FiLM (R1,R3). The concern is how naive fusion and MCF differ. Naive fusion mixes heterogeneous spaces: 512-d EchoPrime embeddings and 128-d CoTracker descriptors. Direct fusion becomes EchoPrime-dominated or harmful, as EchoPrimeNF drops to F1 59.3 vs. EchoPrime 64.3 (Table 1). MCF maps motion to view-specific conditioning, reweights visual embeddings by scale/shift, then uses joint motion as query Q against visual tokens as K,V in cross-view attention (Eq.4/Sec.2.3). Motion neither replaces vision nor merely concatenates; it asks which visual features, for this patient/view, are relevant. This explains Table 2: MCF alone reaches F1 70.3 and full model 72.4.
4) Validation, statistics and single-view use (R1,R2,AC). We agree external validation and subgroup/failure analysis would strengthen generalization. We are limited by available public data: to our knowledge, HMC-QU is the only public benchmark with paired A2C/A4C Echo and segment-wise MI labels. Its size supports methodological validation, but clinical deployment requires larger external validation. We repeated experiments over 3 seeds with mean+/-std and observed consistent gains over motion-only, vision-only and fusion baselines (Table 1), with coherent ablations (Table 2). Paired patient-level bootstrap confirms F1 improvement over EchoPrime: Delta=0.08, 95% CI=[0.01,0.15], p<0.05.For single-view use, Fig.1 has self-contained branches; given 1 view, the corresponding branch produces its 6 AHA-segment predictions. The main contribution remains dual-view localization covering 12/17 AHA segments.
5) Minor points/ethics. We will cite CoTracker at first mention, add NCC/registration discussion, and cite Gomez et al. as related cascaded LV-segmentation/feature-classification work. We will clarify use of public de-identified data.

title: MPFlow: Multi-modal Posterior-Guided Flow Matching for Zero-Shot MRI Reconstruction
abstract:
Zero-shot MRI reconstruction relies on generative priors, but single-modality unconditional priors produce hallucinations under severe ill-posedness. 
In many clinical workflows, complementary MRI acquisitions (e.g. high-quality structural scans) are routinely available, yet existing reconstruction methods lack mechanisms to leverage this additional information.
We propose MPFlow, a zero-shot multi-modal reconstruction framework built on rectified flow that incorporates auxiliary MRI modalities at inference time without retraining the generative prior to improve anatomical fidelity.
Cross-modal guidance is enabled by our proposed self-supervised pretraining strategy, Patch-level Multi-modal MR Image Pretraining (PAMRI), which learns shared representations across modalities.
Sampling is jointly guided by data consistency and cross-modal feature alignment using pre-trained PAMRI, systematically suppressing intrinsic and extrinsic hallucinations.
Extensive experiments on HCP and BraTS show that MPFlow matches diffusion baselines on image quality using only 20% of sampling steps while reducing tumor hallucinations by more than 15% (segmentation dice score). This demonstrates that cross-modal guidance enables more reliable and efficient zero-shot MRI reconstruction. Code is available at https://github.com/edshkim98/MPFlow.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposed a flow matching-based posterior sampling method that leverages multi-modal information learned from contrastive learning. Experiments demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed component.
reviews.text_strengths: 1.The idea of introducing a multi-modal feature-level constraint to reduce extrinsic hallucination is interesting.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The compared baselines are limited to diffusion models. Recent work on flow-based inverse problems solving is missing. For example, “PnP-ﬂow: Plug-and-play image restoration with ﬂow matching”, ICLR 2025.Also, for diffusion-based baselines, the paper only includes DPS related approaches. Better performing solutions like DDNM (Zero-Shot Image Restoration Using Denoising Diffusion Null-Space Model, ICLR 2023) were omitted. 
2.The evaluation on MRI reconstruction is limited to simulated magnitude data from the BraTS dataset. Real-world complex-value multi-coil raw data were not evaluated. 
3.The initial noise optimization module did not lead to significant improvement according to the ablation study, which however increases computational cost.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The weaknesses outweigh the strengths significantly. I would lean to reject the submission.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The strongest unresolved issue is the MRI realism/generalizability concern. The paper frames the method as MRI reconstruction and defines the forward model broadly enough to include complex-valued k-space tasks, but the actual evaluation is on HCP super-resolution and BraTS simulated accelerated reconstruction using magnitude-style image data, with no real complex-valued multi-coil raw MRI experiment. The paper’s own experimental setup lists HCP T2 super-resolution and BraTS FLAIR k-space reconstruction with T1 auxiliary images, rather than fastMRI-like raw multi-coil reconstruction. This limits the strength of the clinical reconstruction claim. This is a major limitation, not a minor extension. Since the method is presented as an MRI reconstruction framework, the absence of real multi-coil raw-data experiments substantially weakens the empirical validation.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper makes a strong and well-motivated contribution to zero-shot MRI reconstruction. Its central idea—integrating auxiliary anatomical information into a posterior-guided generative reconstruction framework—is both elegant and conceptually insightful. In particular, the proposed method leverages auxiliary MR images at inference time, without requiring retraining or modification of the generative prior itself.
The patch-level multimodal representation learning framework(PAMRI) is practical and technically well aligned with the nature of MRI reconstruction. By operating in a learned latent space rather than enforcing direct pixel-level consistency between different MR contrasts, the method offers an effective way to handle the intensity and contrast mismatch across modalities. The use of mutual-information-based adaptive weighting in the patch alignment objective is particularly thoughtful and strengthens the multimodal formulation.
The authors validate the method across two distinct reconstruction tasks and datasets, covering both super-resolution and k-space reconstruction settings. In addition to standard image-quality metrics, they evaluate hallucination-related behavior and downstream task performance, which makes the empirical validation substantially more convincing. Overall, the paper presents a clear methodological contribution supported by comprehensive experiments.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Rather than retraining or redesigning the generative prior to incorporate auxiliary inputs, the method uses the auxiliary modality to guide posterior sampling, which is a clean and flexible design.
2.The proposed PAMRI module is a particularly strong technical component. The use of patch-level multimodal representation learning is well motivated for MRI reconstruction, where preserving local anatomical structure is essential. Moreover, aligning modalities in a learned latent space, instead of imposing pixel-level(may be TV/Sobel) consistency, is especially suitable for multi-contrast MRI. In this regard, the adaptive mutual-information-based weighting is also a thoughtful addition: it provides a practical mechanism to account for cross-contrast mismatch while still extracting shared anatomical information. This is an original and technically meaningful way to exploit auxiliary MR images.
3.The paper is very clearly written.
4.The evaluation is comprehensive and convincing. The method is validated on two distinct MRI reconstruction settings, which strengthens the claim that the framework is general. In addition, the authors also assess hallucination-related behavior and downstream clinical relevance through segmentation-based analysis. It demonstrates that the method improves not only reconstruction fidelity in a numerical sense, but also structural and semantic reliability in ways that are meaningful for medical imaging applications.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper is overall strong, and I did not identify major conceptual flaws that substantially weaken the main claims.
One minor concern is the behavior of the DIP baseline, which appears visibly noisy and may be operating in an overfitting regime. Since DIP is known to be sensitive to stopping criteria, it would be preferable to clarify whether early stopping or a tuned stopping protocol was used for this baseline. A better-controlled DIP comparison would improve the fairness of the experimental presentation.
That said, this issue does not materially affect my confidence in the proposed method or the main conclusions of the paper, since the gains over the stronger generative baselines remain convincing.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

My recommendation is primarily based on the clarity of the paper, the originality and elegance of the core idea, and the strength of the experimental validation. The method is conceptually well designed, and the writing makes the technical motivation and implementation easy to follow.
In addition, the proposed latent-space multimodal alignment strategy is well suited to MRI, where direct intensity correspondence across contrasts is often unreliable. The experiments are comprehensive, spanning multiple datasets, tasks, and evaluation protocols, including both conventional reconstruction metrics and downstream assessments related to hallucination and clinical relevance. Taken together, these factors make the work a high-quality and compelling contribution.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The primary idea of this paper, auxiliary mri data informed reconstruction is compelling, and the authors have effectively implemented it using the modern deep learning concept of latent space alignment. I believe this paper could have a positive impact on future research in MRI reconstruction, considering that clinical acquisitions typically do not rely on single-modality data.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes MPFlow, a framework for zero-shot MRI reconstruction that introduces an auxiliary MRI modality as inference-time posterior guidance without retraining the unconditional generative prior. The method consists of two components: (1) PAMRI, a self-supervised patch-level cross-modal pretraining module that learns shared representations between target and auxiliary modalities; and (2) a multi-modal posterior-guided flow matching procedure that injects both data-consistency and PAMRI feature-alignment gradients into a rectified flow sampler, together with an initial noise selection mechanism. Experiments are conducted on HCP T2 super-resolution and BraTS FLAIR accelerated reconstruction, using fully-sampled T1 as the auxiliary modality. The authors report improvements in image quality metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) and in hallucination-related indicators (SHAFE and tumor segmentation Dice).
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Meaningful and moderately novel problem formulation. Most zero-shot reconstruction methods rely on a unimodal unconditional prior. Framing inference-time multimodal guidance as a way to reduce hallucination—without retraining the prior—is a practically motivated and reasonably original angle.
2.Coherent end-to-end design. The pipeline from cross-modal representation learning (PAMRI) to posterior guidance and initial noise selection tells a consistent story; the components are not arbitrarily concatenated.
3.Evaluation beyond PSNR/SSIM. Including SHAFE and tumor segmentation Dice as proxy hallucination metrics is a meaningful step toward clinically relevant evaluation, going beyond standard pixel-level distortion measures.
4.Efficiency argument is concretely demonstrated. The authors show that fewer sampling steps can still match or exceed diffusion-based baselines, which is a substantive efficiency claim rather than a theoretical one.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.FlowDPS comparison is missing. All main comparisons are against diffusion or DIP methods, despite the prior being a rectified flow. The paper cites FlowDPS [13] but provides no experimental comparison. Since FlowDPS is a directly comparable flow-based posterior sampling method, a comparison would calibrate how much gain comes from the multimodal guidance over a competitive unimodal flow baseline, rather than only over the paper’s own base model in Table 3a.
2.PAMRI necessity is not sufficiently justified. The ablation only compares w/ PAMRI vs. w/o PAMRI, without testing simpler auxiliary guidance alternatives. It therefore remains unclear whether the full patch-level contrastive design is necessary over a simpler baseline.
3.Hidden computational overhead makes Table 1 comparisons unfair. The initial noise selection (S=8, t_noise=0.2T) incurs 8x20+80=240 NFE at the nominal T=100 setting—2.4× the baseline cost. Efficiency comparisons must be re-reported at matched NFE.
4.Patch operator P(⋅) undefined; background handling unspecified. The sampling strategy for P(⋅) is never stated. More critically, without background masking on skull-stripped BraTS data, all-zero patches will cause NMI to be undefined and contrastive representation collapse. Both issues must be addressed for reproducibility.
5.Symbol clash in Eq. (6). z is used both for the initial noise z ~ N(0, I) in Eq. (4) and for the contrastive features z_i ∈ {u_i, w_i} in Eq. (6). Additionally, the definition of z_j in a positive pair is never stated explicitly. The notation should be disambiguated.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1.The abstract and contribution list should explicitly state that PAMRI requires pretraining on paired, registered multi-modal data from the target domain; the system is not a plug-and-play extension of any off-the-shelf prior.
2.Clarify whether PAMRI and the generative prior share the same training split and dataset.
3.Multi-auxiliary scalability is unaddressed. Eq. (2) naturally extends to multiple auxiliary modalities, yet PAMRI’s single ψ(⋅) encoder and the guidance term in Eq. (8) are designed for one auxiliary input only. The authors should discuss how the framework would extend and how overlapping information across modalities would be handled.
4.Clinical applicability boundary. Both datasets use pre-registered data, so the registration assumption is never stress-tested. It would be worth discussing how the method is expected to behave under imperfect registration (e.g., differing slice thickness, inter-session motion), and whether registering a low-quality target to a high-quality auxiliary is a practical prerequisite in real workflows.

The core idea is genuinely interesting and the method design is coherent. The hallucination evaluation via SHAFE and Dice is reasonable for a venue like MICCAI, though the paper would benefit from a brief acknowledgment of their limitations as proxy metrics. The main concerns driving the score are: (W1) FlowDPS baseline is absent, leaving the source of gains unattributed; and (W3) the true NFE at T=100 is 240, making Table 1 comparisons materially unfair—this requires re-running at matched NFE, not just clarification. A satisfactory rebuttal on these two points would increase confidence in the score.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The submitted paper was already close to acceptance based on a coherent multimodal posterior-guided reconstruction framework and solid hallucination-related and downstream-task evaluation. The rebuttal clarifies my main concerns about the FlowDPS-style comparison and NFE accounting, but much of the supporting evidence is rebuttal-only and should be treated as confidence-increasing rather than equivalent to submitted experiments. Overall, the concerns are sufficiently reduced for an Accept recommendation, but not for highlight consideration.

meta_reviews.text:
The reviewers are mixed but see clear promise in the work, with scores of 3, 5, and 4.The paper proposes an interesting multimodal posterior-guided flow matching framework for zero-shot MRI reconstruction, using auxiliary MR images to guide sampling without retraining the generative prior. The PAMRI representation learning component and the use of hallucination-related/downstream metrics are viewed as meaningful strengths.
However, several issues need clarification before a final decision. The rebuttal should address the lack of direct comparison with flow-based posterior sampling baselines such as FlowDPS or other recent flow/inverse-problem methods, since this is important for attributing gains to the proposed multimodal guidance. The authors should also correct the efficiency comparison by reporting matched-NFE results, as the initial noise selection appears to add substantial hidden sampling cost.

I recommend acceptance. The paper proposes a coherent and interesting multimodal posterior-guided flow matching framework for zero-shot MRI reconstruction, using an auxiliary MR modality to guide sampling without retraining the generative prior. The core idea is well motivated, and the use of PAMRI for latent-space cross-modal alignment is a meaningful way to exploit shared anatomy while avoiding direct pixel-level matching across contrasts.
The rebuttal addressed the main concerns raised during review. In particular, the authors clarified the FlowDPS/DDNM comparisons, matched-NFE accounting, the patch operator and masking strategy, the necessity of PAMRI compared with simpler guidance alternatives, and the role of the noise-optimization module. Reviewers #2 and #3 both support acceptance after rebuttal. Reviewer #1 remains concerned about the lack of real complex-valued multi-coil raw-data validation, which is a valid limitation, but I view it as a scope limitation rather than a fatal flaw for the current contribution.

The authors present an interesting methodology for performing posterior-guided image refinement using an auxiliary image. This wording is specific, as this is not an MRI reconstruction paper, contrary to what the title implies (pointed out by Reviewer 1). However, the authors do define “reconstruction” more broadly as the recreation of high-quality data from limited data. This, however, highlights an issue that is called out in the initial reviews and not addressed. This is the limitation of registered (and seemingly skull-stripped) images in an auxiliary-assisted challenge. This is a strong limitation that is commonly validated in other auxiliary-assisted refinement methods. Further, it takes the method further from the purpose of “reconstruction”, where the assumptions about data preprocessing are necessarily minimal. This is especially true for the two tasks presented here, where registration and skull-stripping would drastically affect the resolution and k-space components.
Additionally, the authors included new experiments conducted in the rebuttal and presented the results as responses to the reviewers’ concerns. This is not allowed under the rebuttal guidelines and cannot carry weight in the acceptance decision at this stage. Unfortunately, most of what the authors present as responses to the author’s concerns fall under this category and must be excluded.
Based on the lack of clarification for some concerns after removing additional experiments, I can only recommend rejection for this paper.

This paper proposes MPFlow, a zero-shot MRI reconstruction framework that introduces an auxiliary MR modality as inference-time posterior guidance without retraining the unconditional generative prior, combining a patch-level cross-modal representation module (PAMRI) with a multi-modal posterior-guided flow matching sampler. The reviewers agree that the core idea of inference-time multimodal guidance to reduce hallucination is original and practically motivated, that the PAMRI latent-space alignment is well suited to multi-contrast MRI where pixel-level correspondence is unreliable, and that the evaluation is convincing in going beyond fidelity metrics to include hallucination-related and downstream segmentation measures, all of which are established within the submitted manuscript. The rebuttal clarified the effective sampling cost and the efficiency comparison, the positioning relative to flow-based posterior-sampling methods, the patch operator and background handling, and the notation, which together resolved the principal points of concern. The main remaining limitation is that the evaluation rests on magnitude-domain super-resolution and simulated accelerated reconstruction, which the authors note follows standard practice in recent reconstruction work; they frame validation on complex-valued multi-coil data as future work and observe that the framework extends to that setting by replacing the forward operator. The authors are encouraged to state the PAMRI pretraining requirement and the registration assumption explicitly, to qualify the reconstruction claim in line with the magnitude-domain evaluation, and to incorporate the noted clarifications in the camera-ready version.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback and for recognizing the importance of mitigating hallucinations in MRI reconstruction. We are pleased that the reviewers found our motivation strong (R2, R3), our method well-designed (R1-R3), and our experiments thorough (R2, R3).
Missing baselines [R1.7.1, R3.7.1]: We evaluated FlowDPS (ICCV’25) and DDNM (ICLR’23) on HCP at T=100 using our pretrained rectified flow and diffusion priors. FlowDPS: SSIM 0.624±0.049, SHAFE 0.216±0.043; DDNM: SSIM 0.764±0.123, SHAFE 0.221±0.107.Both underperform MPFlow. Adding PAMRI guidance to FlowDPS yields SSIM 0.650±0.047, SHAFE 0.204±0.039, confirming PAMRI’s contribution is sampler-agnostic and complementary to recent posterior sampling methods.
Matched-NFE evaluation [R3.7.3]: We agree noise optimization adds NFEs. For fair comparison, we re-ran DPS and DynamicDPS at T=240 (matched to MPFlow’s effective NFE). DPS: SSIM 0.713, SHAFE 0.220; DynamicDPS: SSIM 0.702, SHAFE 0.269.Both remain inferior to MPFlow (SSIM 0.78, SHAFE 0.20), demonstrating that MPFlow’s efficiency advantage is not an artifact of NFE accounting. Removing noise optimization from MPFlow (NFE=100) still yields substantial improvements over Tab. 1 baselines, as shown in Tab. 3.Patch operator [R3.7.4]: P(·) constructs a binary brain mask from the auxiliary image, partitions the image into non-overlapping patches, and selects only patches with sufficient brain content. We will clarify this in the revised manuscript.
PAMRI necessity [R3.7.2]: We compared PAMRI against three intensity-based alternatives: Normalized Mutual Information (NMI), Canny edge loss, and pixel-MSE. NMI: SSIM 0.762±0.036, SHAFE 0.210±0.059; edge loss: SSIM 0.745±0.044, SHAFE 0.255±0.155; pixel-MSE: SSIM 0.748±0.037, SHAFE 0.215±0.053.PAMRI outperforms all three. While NMI is the strongest classical baseline, it still operates at the pixel level and cannot capture the fine-grained structural correspondence that PAMRI’s learned latent space provides. We also observed worsening in SHAFE score across all variants compared to using PAMRI (Tab. 3a), indicating that naive intensity-based guidance cannot suppress hallucinations as effectively.
Noise optimization [R1.7.3]: While the ablation gain in Tab. 3a appears modest, isolating noise optimization against the vanilla baseline yields SSIM 0.754, SHAFE 0.218, a consistent ~2% improvement.
Multi-coil data [R1.7.2]: Our evaluation on magnitude images follows standard practice in recent MRI reconstruction work (DynamicDPS, DiffDeuR); all baselines operate on magnitude data for direct comparability. PAMRI’s cross-modal guidance is orthogonal to magnitude vs. complex domain, the framework extends naturally to complex-valued reconstruction by replacing the forward operator. We agree validation on multi-coil raw data (e.g., fastMRI) is valuable future work.
DIP baseline [R2.7.1]: We used measurement-loss-based early stopping for DIP. We tried multiple stopping points and observed minimal change in noise level, likely because measurement loss correlates poorly with image quality on heavily ill-posed problems, making the optimal window narrow and difficult to tune reliably.
Notation [R3.7.5]: We will disambiguate the overloaded use of z in Eq. 4 vs. Eq. 6 and clarify positive pair definitions in the revised manuscript.
Contribution list [R3.12.1]: We will revise the abstract and contribution list to explicitly state PAMRI’s pretraining requirements.
Training data [R3.12.2]: PAMRI and the generative prior use the same training split and dataset, disjoint from the test set.
Multi-auxiliary and registration [R3.12.3-4]: We agree multi-auxiliary scalability and stress-testing under imperfect registration are important next steps for clinical deployment.

title: MRI2Rep: Autoregressive Structured Report Generation for 3D Liver MRI
abstract:
Manual reporting of 3D MRI studies is time-consuming, yet end-to-end, structured report generation for 3D liver MRI remains underexplored due to volumetric complexity and scarce paired data. We propose MRI2Rep, an autoregressive framework for liver MRI report generation. From 3{,}929 real-world MRI–report pairs acquired over a 10-year single-institution cohort, a Report-to-Label Canonicalization (RLC) module converts the free-text reports into structured, closed-vocabulary diagnostic sequences without lesion-level annotations. On a held-out test set, MRI2Rep achieves 76.0\% case-level sensitivity, 29.4\% lesion-level F1 (vs.\ 8.3\% for adapted medical vision–language baselines), and 82.4\% liver-level accuracy. In a blinded reader study, two radiologists rated 75\%/70\% of AI-generated reports clinically acceptable (vs.\ 95\%/100\% for originals), while our automated LLM-based judge (LLM-Eval, 61.8\%) applies a stricter standard, validating it as a conservative proxy. To our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end LI-RADS-structured reporting system for 3D liver MRI. The
code is available at https://github.com/Alena-Xinran/MRI2Rep.git
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose an autoregressive framework, MRI2Rep, that generates structured radiology reports based on 3D MRI volumes of a liver tumors. The contribution is three-fold: 1) a report-to-label canonicalization (RLC) module is proposed to first convert free-text reports to a standard vocabulary to be used for training; 2) an encoder-decoder model is trained to predict these sequences from the MRI sequences; and 3) a hand-crafted sentence template module is used to convert the output sequence back into a report with full sequences. The method is evaluated on a datasets of 3,929 report-image pairs of liver MRI, and compared to four VLMs.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Use of domain-knowledge through LI-RADS and structuring of free-text data: mapping both the free text reports and the outputs of the model therefore on LI-RADS appears a strong choice, as this is a main instrument used by radiologists for accessing liver lesions. 
2.Clinical reader study: letting two radiologists score the generated reports is a good way of accessing whether the reports meet clinical criteria. 
3.Systematic error analysis on test set to discover patterns: gives insight in the methods and direction for future improvements.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The dataset is not described, we only now the number of samples. This makes it very difficult to assess the results: we have no idea where this dataset originates from, how reports where generated, how the scans were acquired, etc. The evaluation setup is also poorly described. A held-out test set is mentioned, but its not mentioned what the size is, how this dataset was created from the main dataset, etc. A cross-validation setup would also have been much stronger, as this could have been a lucky or unlucky split, which we also cant estimate the risk of as we dont know the dataset. No statistical testing is used as well. 
2.Comparison with other methods. Related work on VLMs includes only a few models, four (M3D, CT2Rep, Merlin, RadFM) are used in the comparison experiments. Other models that seem more suitable as these are either newer, trained / evaluated on more similar data (liver MRI) or more data are for example: https://doi. org/10.1016/j. media. 2026.103992, https://doi. org/10.48550/arXiv. 2509.21249.Highly related are also these VLMs specifically made for Liver MRI: https://doi. org/10.3390/app152312578, https://doi. org/10.1016/j. ebiom. 2025.106060, 
3.No clear problem is introduced in the introduction. The authors claim that “automated report generation for 3D
MRI remains largely unexplored”, which seems to be the problem that is being addressed, but that is incorrect, see above. Hence its unclear what technical or clinical problem the proposed methods are exactly addressing. 
3.The organization of the paper can be improved. The abstract misses essential components (see below), the introduction does not include a clear problem statement (see above), results are reported in the introduction which seems to be a repetition of the abstract, the related work section just bullet points some methods without a clear explanation of them, results section does include methods / statistics, 
4.It would be good to perform ablation experiments for both the RLC and the model. Would the other VLMs achieve a similar performance if the RLC setup and vocabulary would already be used?
5.Performance for liver tumor phenotyping, the most important task, is poor across all models including the proposed method (F1 score of 29.4). Hence none of the methods seem to achieve satisfactory results. 
6.Poor reproducibility: no code or data published. 
7.No motivation is provided for using the specific selected sequences (arterial and portal venous phase). Why not use complete MRI exams, mimicking clinical practice? Routinely used other sequences such as a T2-weighted MRI, T1 in-out phase, DWI / ADC are now a crucial missing component in the analysis. 
8.No motivation is provided for the encoder-decoder architecture. How does this compare to the literature?
9.The RLC module is poorly described. Section 3.1 explains what the model does, but not how it performs this task. Besides that is methodologically unclear, its also not reproducible. In the results it seems that LLMs are used based on this module, but thats not explicitly described. 
10.It should be acknowledged that LI-RADS is only applicable for cirrhotic patients. 
11.Abstract: The abstract appears incomplete, there is no discussion / conclusion. Generally the abstract could be improved, the performance of the baselines is not mentioned, and its unclear how this blinded reader study was performed and what “cilinical acceptability” means or what LLM-Eval is.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The two major factors leading to my decision where the absent description of the dataset and poor evaluation setup, which makes it difficult to assess the results, and that many related work was missed making the novelty of the paper unclear and some of the claims unjustified.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
While I appreciate the rebuttal which addresses some of my concerns, unfortunately there are simply too many aspects missing in the paper for me to accept it in its current form.
Specifically w.r.t. the author feedback:
[C1] The dataset and evaluation should have been better described in the paper. k-fold CV may be not the most practical method due to computational resources, but would be much stronger.
[C2] Related work should have been better reported in the paper. See also other comments: none of the methods indeed solve this exact problem, but a better comparison / combination could have been made.
[C3] Indeed the proposed method triples the performance of baselines, but an F1 of 29.4 is still very poor and thus not a satisfactory result.
[C4] It’s clear what the goal of the RLC is and the idea is strong, but the description of the method remians poor and not reproducible, and no code is provided. 
[C6] Agreed that the choice for ART/PV is clinically well-motivated, but technically it would have been stronger to include all standard sequences, even those that are not used for LI-RADS classification. But this is a minor concern.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This work proposes the MRI2Rep framework for templated liver MRI report generation. The framework consists of three components: the Report-to-Label Canonicalization (RLC) module which converts reports into structured diagnostic sequences, an encoder-decoder model which uses uses the input MRI volume to produce the diagnostic sequence, and a sequence-to-report rendering module to deterministically map the diagnostic sequence to output report using hand-crafted sentence templates.
RLC consistently improves the radiologist retention rate of extracted lesion labels across three LLM backends, and various ablation studies were conducted to demonstrate the accuracy of predicted lesions. Radiologists accepted 70-75% of AI-generated reports, compared with automated LLM-Eval which was stricter with an acceptance rate of 61.8%.
reviews.text_strengths:
The authors have included extensive ablation study results in table 2 to justify modelling choices such as the inclusion of of a visual encoder and ART-to-PV pre-training.
Succinct justifications were given in various places which adds to credibility, e.g. inter-rater agreement for the clinical reader study.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The related work section is fairly limited. For instance, recent works in chest X-ray report generation have used structured label extraction as an auxiliary task [1] or basis for generating the full report [2]. Additionally, LLM-based label extraction from radiology reports could benefit from citing more directly relevant works such as [3].
The motivation for introducing stylistic variation in the sequence-to-report rendering stage isn’t clear. Was it to prevent radiologists from identifying AI-generated reports in the reader study? It would be useful to add a sentence to clarify the link if this is the case.
[1] Jianguo Liang. ‘Multi-Task Learning for Radiology Report Generation with Structured Findings Consistency’. Computer Science Bulletin 8, no. 01 (2025): 477–89.https://doi.org/10.71465/csb178.[2] Hou, Wenjun, Kaishuai Xu, Yi Cheng, Wenjie Li, and Jiang Liu. ORGAN: Observation-Guided Radiology Report Generation via Tree Reasoning. Version 1.2023.https://doi.org/10.48550/ARXIV.2306.06466
[3] Castro, Daniel C., Aurelia Bustos, Shruthi Bannur, et al. ‘PadChest-GR: A Bilingual Chest X-Ray Dataset for Grounded Radiology Report Generation’. arXiv:2411.05085.Preprint, arXiv, 7 November 2024.https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2411.05085.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Section 4.1 RLC Validation: Is there a reason for phrasing the metric as retention rate rather than e.g. precision? If I understand correctly, an AI-produced label is retained if it is supported by the original report, i.e. retention rate measures the proportion of true positives to all predicted positives.

The presented framework is well-supported by extensive experiments. From what I understand (first point in the main contributions) the authors intend to make the dataset available, which would be a useful resource.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have clarified the novelty compared to prior works in the literature, though it would be useful to mention these in the paper itself. The work itself appears scientifically sound.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This article focuses on the task of automatic report generation for 3D liver MRI, and proposes the MRI2Rep framework to address the difficulties of “high volume data dimension, large report supervision noise, and lack of lesion level annotation”. The core idea is to first convert free text radiation reports into closed set, auditable structured sequence labels through Report to Label Canonical (RLC), then train a 3D CNN+Transformer encoder decoder model to generate structured diagnostic sequences from multi-phase MRI volume data through autoregression, and finally render them into natural language reports using templates.
reviews.text_strengths: The most impressive aspect of the paper is “end-to-end generation of structured reports”. One of the biggest innovations of this article is RLC, which transforms free text reports into standardized label sequences and achieves a retention rate of around 98% in radiologists’ tests, demonstrating the high quality of label extraction itself.
reviews.text_weaknesses: 1.The structured report generation appears complete, but the core lesion level performance is still not high. 2.RLC is strong, but the entire system heavily relies on the quality of front-end text normalization. 3.”No need for lesion level spatial annotation” is an advantage, but it also limits the accuracy of lesion localization. 4.The model is fragile in scenarios of “post-treatment changes” and “complex medical history”.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The experiment was based on 3929 pairs of MRI report samples, of which 3830 had complete multi-phase sequences. The final model achieved 76.0% case level sensitivity, 29.4% lesion level Lesion-F1, 82.4% liver background classification accuracy on the test set, and achieved a clinical acceptance rate of 75%/70% in the blind evaluation of dual radiologists.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
1.Regarding Lesion-F1, it is only 29.4%
The author’s explanation carries a certain degree of plausibility: 29.4% is not a standard binary classification F1 score, but rather a strict match of type + pos, meaning both lesion type and Couinaud segment location must be accurately determined simultaneously. Moreover, it is a set-F1 score across 5 LI-RADS categories × 9 anatomical regions, making it significantly more challenging than simply determining “presence or absence of lesions.” The author further emphasizes that other 3D-VLM baselines achieve a maximum of only 8.3%, while MRI2Rep has improved to 29.4%, clearly demonstrating its notable advantage in similar tasks.
However, our original skepticism still holds some validity: significant relative improvement does not equate to absolute performance being sufficiently high. For clinical report generation, lesion type, location, and quantity are core facts. The Lesion-F1 score of 29.4% and Triplet-F1 score of 28.1% still indicate instability in the model’s precise structured diagnosis. The original paper’s Table 2 indeed shows MRI2Rep’s Lesion-F1 at 29.4% and Triplet-F1 at 28.1%.
Overall, we agree with the author’s explanation regarding task difficulty and relative improvement, but from an absolute performance perspective, the 29.4% lesion-level F1 score still indicates that the model has a certain gap in generating reliable lesion-level structured reports.
2.Regarding the RLC dependency issue
The author emphasizes that RLC is not merely a simple black-box LLM call, but rather a LI-RADS-guided prompting approach combined with deterministic triplet assembly and per-token evidence sentences. Moreover, it maintains a retention rate of at least 91% across three LLM backends, demonstrating the strong stability of RLC.
The issue does not lie in “RLC being inaccurate,” but rather in the model primarily learning the closed-set label space defined by RLC, rather than the full semantics of complete free-text reports.
Therefore, the high quality of RLC demonstrates its effective semantic normalization at the front end, but it does not mean the system is entirely free from the expressive constraints imposed by a closed-set label space. Complex medical histories, post-treatment changes, follow-up comparisons, ambiguous expressions, and cross-sentence references—once inadequately encoded by the RLC system—become difficult for subsequent models to learn. The original paper also acknowledges that its output is a closed-set structured sequence, rendered into reports via templates.
Overall, the author demonstrates that RLC achieves high-quality label extraction and mitigates concerns about “front-end label noise.” However, this does not eliminate the system’s reliance on the RLC design space. Thus, RLC serves as both a key contribution to improving label quality and auditability in this paper, while also defining the scope of learnable and expressive diagnostic semantics to some extent.
3.3.Advantages and Disadvantages of “No Need for Lesion-Level Spatial Annotation”
The author emphasizes that the “lack of lesion-level spatial annotations” stems from considerations of clinical applicability, as retrospective real-world data typically lacks bounding boxes or segmentations. This claim is valid, and the original paper explicitly highlights “no need for lesion-level spatial annotations” as a core advantage.
However, the experimental results also suggest that this weakly supervised approach may limit the lesion localization capability. The model’s performance on multi-lesion cases significantly declined in the paper, and the authors acknowledged in their rebuttal that the remaining gap is related to the lack of lesion-level spatial annotations.
Overall, the absence of lesion-level spatial annotation is a practical advantage of MRI2Rep, but it may also be a significant factor limiting its lesion localization performance. The authors’ explanation justifies this design, yet its limitations in complex, multi-lesion scenarios remain to be acknowledged. Therefore, this is more of a trade-off between practical usability and fine-grained localization capability, rather than a mere methodological flaw.
4.Regarding post-treatment changes and complex medical history
The author’s response states that post treatment/complex history fragility has been acknowledged and they are ‘lies outside the LI-RADS major feature scope’.
This explanation makes sense at the method boundary, but from the perspective of generating real clinical reports, it is still a limitation that needs to be taken seriously. Because real radiology reports do not only assess the major features of LI-RADS, but often require a combination of past treatments, postoperative changes, follow-up comparisons, and medical history background. The error analysis in the original paper also mentioned that 34.1% of false positives occurred in previous ablation cases, indicating that this issue is not an occasional error, but rather an important source of model false positives.
Overall, the author categorizes post-treatment changes as outside the scope of LI-RADS major feature, which helps to clarify the boundaries of the method presented in this article; But for the task of “automatic report generation”, treatment history and follow-up information are not optional additional information, but important components of the real diagnostic context. Therefore, this issue should not be simply regarded as an out of boundary problem, but rather as an important limitation for subsequent clinical generalization and safety evaluation.
5.Regarding datasets and generalization
The author added that the data comes from a 10-year retrospective cohort of a single tertiary hospital, which enhances the transparency of the data source description; However, from the perspective of model generalization, this also suggests that there is still a lack of external multi center validation. Set over split can improve the coverage of test set categories and enhance the representativeness of internal testing, but it still cannot replace external validation across centers, devices, and scanning protocols. Therefore, the current results better demonstrate the effectiveness of the model on the internal test set, but cannot fully prove its cross center generalization ability.

meta_reviews.text:
I recommend Invite for Rebuttal. Reviewer 1 was clearly negative and argued that the dataset description and evaluation setup are too incomplete to assess the work reliably. I share Reviewer 1’s concern that the dataset description is insufficient. Reviewer 2 was positive and found the framework promising, but still pointed out limited related-work coverage. Reviewer 3 also supported moving forward, while noting that lesion-level performance is still not strong and that the full system depends heavily on front-end normalization quality.

The paper proposes a structured report generation framework for 3D liver MRI, with Report-to-Label Canonicalization as a central contribution. The initial concerns focused on insufficient dataset and evaluation description, limited related-work coverage, low lesion-level F1, dependence on RLC quality, and limited reproducibility. The rebuttal clarified the dataset source, split, MRI sequences, RLC design, baseline mapping protocol, and the interpretation of the strict lesion-level F1 metric. Reviewers 2 and 3 support acceptance after rebuttal and consider the framework scientifically sound and valuable.
The authors have addressed the reviewers’ comments well. 2 reviewers acknowledged the significance of the work with detailed justifications. Therefore acceptance of the paper is concluded.
The authors have adequately addressed most of the reviewers’ concerns. However, the dataset description mentioned in the rebuttal should be detailed further and included in the final version.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the AC and Reviewers (R1-R3). We address six AC-priority points.
[C1] Dataset & evaluation setup (AC; R1.W1).
Dataset: 3,929 multi-phase liver-MRI report-image pairs from a 10-year retrospective cohort at one tertiary academic hospital, on Siemens scanners (predominantly 3T, with earlier 1.5T) using extracellular GBCA (e.g., gadoterate); reports by board-certified abdominal radiologists; IRB-approved (consent waiver). RLC maps free-text reports to closed-vocabulary labels; 3,830 with complete ART and PV are retained (Sec.3.1). Stratified 80/10/10 set-cover split on (type,pos) yields 383 test cases covering rare LI-RADS categories. k-fold CV is impractical for our 3D autoregressive pipeline; set-cover mitigates split variance, and the 21-point Lesion-F1 margin over the best baseline (8.3 to 29.4) is well outside any plausible bootstrap CI at n=383.Code released upon publication (R1.W6).
[C2] Problem statement, related work & novelty (AC; R1.W2/W3; R2.W1).
Sec.1 names two challenges: noisy report-level supervision on small 3D cohorts and volumetric/multi-phase complexity. Our novelty is closed-vocabulary, LI-RADS-structured 3D-MRI report generation, not 3D-MRI reporting in general. Of R1’s 4 cited works, the liver-MRI papers (Appl Sci 2025; eBioMedicine 2025) target classification/VQA, and Media 2026 + arXiv:2509.21249 are general 3D-MRI representation learning; none does end-to-end LI-RADS-structured reporting. CXR structured-finding works (ORGAN, PadChest-GR; R2.refs) are 2D and do not enforce LI-RADS reasoning.
[C3] Lesion-level F1 = 29.4 (AC; R1.W5; R3.W1/W4).
29.4 is strict set-F1 over (type,pos) across 5 LI-RADS by 9 Couinaud sectors - far harder than binary detection. Under the identical protocol (Sec.4.2), all four 3D-VLM baselines score Lesion-F1 at most 8.3 (Tab.2); MRI2Rep more than triples this. Case-level sensitivity 76.0%; blinded radiologists accept 70-75% of reports (k=0.97). The remaining gap reflects the deliberate absence of lesion-level spatial annotations, a framework choice for clinical applicability. Post-treatment / complex-history fragility is acknowledged and lies outside LI-RADS major-feature scope.
[C4] Dependence on RLC / front-end quality (AC; R3.W2; R1.W9).
RLC is an LI-RADS-guided LLM prompting protocol (Sec.3.1) with deterministic triplet assembly and per-token evidence sentences - not a black-box call. Retention at least 91% across three independent LLM backends (Tab.1); the 98.1% headline averages two annotators. Small backend variability shows the structured logic, not any single LLM, drives quality.
[C5] Ablation comparability with VLMs (R1.W4).
Tab.2 evaluates baselines under matched output taxonomy: their free-text outputs are mapped to the same closed (type,pos,qty) labels via identical Claude-3.5 extraction (Sec.4.2). The gap (Lesion-F1 8.3 or lower vs. 29.4) reflects model capability under matched vocabulary, not taxonomy mismatch.
[C6] Sequence choice & architecture (R1.W7/W8).
Our standard extracellular GBCA protocol has no hepatobiliary phase: LI-RADS major features (APHE, washout) are by definition assessed on ART/PV and mandatory for HCC categorisation, a clinically appropriate, not arbitrary, choice. T2 HASTE and T1 Dixon are acquired but ancillary, not major-feature inputs. The without-PV ablation (29.4 to 13.5; Tab.2) supports this. Encoder-decoder follows 3D-captioning practice (CT2Rep, Merlin); the no-visual-encoder ablation (to 10.4) justifies the design.
[Minor] R1.W10: LR-1 to LR-5 apply to at-risk patients; non-HCC tokens (cyst, hemangioma, targetoid) and a cirrhosis liver-background token extend coverage. R1.W11: “clinical acceptability”=radiologist accept/reject of the rendered report (Sec.4.3); “LLM-Eval”=Claude-3.5 LLM-judge over rendered vs reference reports, stricter (61.8%) than radiologists (70-75%). R2: “retention” equals precision numerically but stresses auditability vs. source. Stylistic variation prevents lexical artefacts unblinding readers.

title: MRSeg3D: A Perturbation-Resilient Model for 3D Medical Reasoning Segmentation
abstract: Reasoning-based medical image segmentation has recently gained prominence by enabling complex target identification through natural language instructions. However, current research in 3D Reasoning Segmentation often prioritizes performance on curated benchmarks, leaving models vulnerable to realistic variations in instructions. To enable a systematic analysis of this fragility, we introduce a novel progressive perturbation benchmark spanning three difficulty levels. On this benchmark, state-of-the-art models show unstable performance and semantic drift, where reasoning becomes misaligned with visual evidence under perturbed instructions. We trace this issue to a critical bottleneck: insufficient visual information flow during the reasoning and mask decoding stages, which leads to cascading errors and significant performance degradation under perturbed inputs. To address these challenges, we propose MRSeg3D, a single-encoder architecture designed to facilitate tighter visual-semantic coupling. The core innovation lies in a suite of cascaded vision injectors that enforce persistent visual grounding by anchoring the model to invariant features at key decision points, thereby mitigating reasoning drift. We further introduce a Seg-Local Projector that collaborates with the mask prompt encoder to refine text-visual cues and improve the precision of [SEG] token execution. Experimental results demonstrate significant and consistent performance improvements in the Dice coefficient and text generation quality. This work provides actionable insights for next-generation intelligent clinical systems. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/lihaoqin168/MRSeg3D.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper makes two main contributions. First, it addresses the fragility of 3D reasoning segmentation models when facing perturbed instructions. To measure this, the authors introduce a three-tier benchmark evaluating both instruction robustness and reasoning-segmentation alignment. Second, it proposes MRSeg3D. This single-encoder architecture uses cascaded vision injectors and a Seg-Local Projector to keep visual information grounded during reasoning and decoding. This helps reduce the semantic drift that often happens with complex clinical text.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper’s strengths are its clear problem formulation and targeted design. Instead of treating medical image segmentation just as a standard prompt task, the authors break down consistency into instruction robustness and reasoning-segmentation alignment. This is a very useful perspective for clinical translation. Methodologically, MRSeg3D avoids simply scaling up the language model. The authors noticed that baseline models lose visual evidence as reasoning progresses, so they addressed this directly by re-injecting intermediate visual features. This proves the value of targeted architectural tweaks. Additionally, the experimental evaluation is extensive. Testing on 25 datasets is solid work, and the model clearly outperforms a strong baseline, especially in the most challenging free-text scenarios.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The main weaknesses are the clinical realism of the benchmark and the lack of statistical rigor. The authors describe the Level III test as real-world clinical discourse, but these texts were actually generated by DeepSeek. There is no mention of clinician validation or human quality control. Therefore, the demonstrated robustness really only shows generalization to synthetic prompts, which isn’t the same as clinical readiness. Furthermore, for a paper focused on stability, it lacks multiple-run variance, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests. This makes the performance gains less convincing. Additionally, the data protocols for the 25 datasets are not transparent enough regarding patient-level splits and deduplication. Finally, the mechanistic claim about semantic drift is slightly overstated; it currently reads more like a reasonable hypothesis than a strictly proven mechanism.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

My recommendation of a weak accept reflects the balance between a highly relevant methodological contribution and some noticeable gaps in validation. The paper addresses a genuinely critical and often overlooked bottleneck in 3D reasoning segmentation—linguistic robustness—and provides a structurally sound and empirically effective solution that convincingly outperforms a strong baseline. However, the score is held back from a higher tier because the core narrative heavily relies on the assumption that the synthetic perturbation benchmark equates to real clinical text, a leap made without clinical validation. If the authors can address the dataset transparency issues and provide proper statistical uncertainty bounds during the rebuttal, I would be very open to raising my overall score.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper focuses on improving the robustness of 3D medical reasoning segmentation when input instructions are reformulated or made more ambiguous. Its main contribution is a perturbation-based evaluation protocol together with MRSeg3D, an extension of the single-encoder reasoning-segmentation framework that introduces persistent visual grounding during language reasoning and a dedicated local projection path for segmentation execution. Experiments across multiple datasets and LLM backbones show improved robustness and segmentation accuracy compared with prior single-encoder baselines, especially under more challenging free-text perturbations.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem: robustness of 3D medical reasoning segmentation under perturbed natural-language instructions. Rather than only reporting performance under a fixed prompting setup, the paper explicitly studies instruction-level fragility and reasoning and segmentation consistency, which is an important perspective for clinically relevant multimodal systems.
1.Benchmark contribution
The tiered perturbation benchmark with multiple instruction templates enables a finer-grained robustness analysis as linguistic ambiguity increases, compared with conventional label-style prompting. This evaluation design is a concrete strength because it connects prompt variability to measurable degradation modes.
2.Diagnostic decomposition 
Separately evaluating reasoning quality vs segmentation fidelity is well motivated and can reveal decoupled failures (e.g., stable language understanding with degraded masks), which strengthens interpretability of multimodal errors.
3.Targeted architectural refinement 
As a targeted refinement of a strong single-encoder reasoning-segmentation framework. The vision injectors and the Seg-Local projection path are both tied to specific hypothesized failure modes, namely loss of visual grounding during reasoning and imperfect transformation from [SEG] token representations to final masks. This makes the method design more convincing than a purely heuristic module addition.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The degree of novelty is somewhat limited.
While the paper is well motivated and the architectural design is coherent, MRSeg3D is best understood as a targeted refinement of strong single-encoder reasoning-segmentation baselines, especially R1Seg-3D, rather than a fundamentally new formulation. In particular, the main changes are the addition of intermediate visual injection during reasoning and a local projection path for segmentation execution. These components are reasonable and potentially effective, but they may still be viewed as incremental extensions on top of prior designs.
2.The central mechanism claim is plausible, but not fully established causally.
The authors argue that robustness degradation mainly comes from insufficient visual grounding and semantic drift during reasoning / decoding. While Table 5 and Fig. 6 are consistent with this interpretation, the paper does not include a more explicit mechanism study that separately tests this claim, for example by isolating the effect of visual injection during reasoning versus the effect of the segmentation-side local projection under matched conditions. Therefore, the results support the effectiveness of the proposed design, but they do not fully establish that the claimed mechanism is the primary cause.
3.The perturbation benchmark is useful, but its connection to real clinical language remains limited.
The tiered perturbation protocol is a valuable part of the paper and enables more fine-grained robustness analysis. At the same time, it remains a template-based benchmark designed by the authors. Therefore, the results should be interpreted as robustness under the proposed perturbation setting, rather than robustness to the full diversity, ambiguity, and messiness of genuine clinical language in practice.
4.There is a noticeable gap between the training setup and the evaluation scope.
The paper states that training uses only instruction templates 1 and 5, while evaluation covers a much broader range of perturbation types. This makes the reported robustness results interesting, but it also raises questions about how much of the gain comes from architectural robustness versus generalization under a particular train/test protocol. More discussion of this point would strengthen the paper.
5.Some implementation and reproducibility details remain relatively high level in the main paper.
The paper gives the overall architecture and staged training procedure, but many details that would matter for full reproducibility appear brief in the main text. This is a practical weakness, although it is partially mitigated by the authors’ statement that code and models will be made publicly available.
6.Some claims are framed a bit more strongly than the evidence strictly supports.
The experiments support improved robustness and performance under the proposed benchmark, but broader claims about handling realistic clinical discourse should be stated more cautiously, especially since the paper itself acknowledges that pathology-specific and open-ended clinical scenarios remain challenging.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I am slightly positive on this paper because it studies a meaningful and timely problem, proposes a useful perturbation-based evaluation protocol, and presents a coherent robustness-oriented extension of a strong single-encoder baseline. The experiments are fairly broad and generally support improved robustness under the proposed benchmark. My recommendation is only Weak Accept, however, because the methodological novelty is somewhat limited, the semantic-drift explanation is plausible but not fully isolated experimentally, and the benchmark remains template-based rather than fully representative of real clinical language. Overall, I believe the work is above the acceptance threshold, but only marginally.
