title: MS-GDUN: Multi-scale Graph Deep Unfolding Network with Gradient-Threshold Learning for FMT Reconstruction
abstract: Fluorescence Molecular Tomography (FMT) enables noninvasive quantification of early-stage tumors, but its clinical utility is hampered by the severe ill-posedness of its inverse reconstruction problem. Traditional iterative methods rely on proximal gradient descent and soft-thresholding for non-convex sparse optimization, yet suffer from poor stability under strong noise and tissue scattering—attributed to their sensitivity to hand-crafted parameters, gradient approximation errors, and rigid fixed global sparsity thresholds.To address these limitations, we propose the Multi-Scale Graph Deep Unfolding Network with Gradient-Threshold Learning (MS-GDUN), a physics-guided deep unfolding framework that synergizes iterative reconstruction logic with graph neural networks. MS-GDUN unfolds classical iterative pipelines into a layered learnable architecture, enabling end-to-end joint learning of iteration-specific gradient update directions and node-adaptive sparsity thresholds in place of manual parameter tuning. We construct physics-constrained graphs via finite-element mesh photon transport distances, use Graph Convolutional Blocks (GCB) to model multi-hop photon diffusion correlations, and introduce a Multi-Scale Graph Cross-Attention (MSGC) mechanism to fuse local-global features across four scales, mitigating single-scale limitations and enhancing reconstruction structural consistency.Extensive experiments on simulated and clinical datasets validate that MS-GDUN outperforms state-of-the-art conventional iterative and learning-based methods in tumor localization accuracy and morphological fidelity. This work establishes MS-GDUN as a robust, reliable FMT reconstruction paradigm with great potential for early tumor detection.Code is available at https://github.com/LeTeddy/MS-GDUN.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The proposed MS-GDUN represents a significant advancement in Fluorescence Molecular Tomography (FMT) reconstruction. The framework integrates adaptive multi-scale graph convolution and a node-adaptive sparse update strategy, enhancing both performance and robustness. This novel approach not only preserves physical interpretability but also ensures scalability, while improving the model’s resilience to noise and sparsity, which are common challenges in FMT reconstruction.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Clear and Well-Written: The paper is well-organized and clearly presents both the methodology and experimental results, making the technical aspects easy to understand for readers. 
2.Innovative Methodology: The introduction of a physics-guided deep unfolding framework for FMT reconstruction is highly innovative. By incorporating multi-scale graph convolutional blocks and adaptive sparse updates, MS-GDUN improves the accuracy and robustness of FMT reconstruction, making it a notable contribution to the field. 
3.Strong Experimental Evaluation: The authors provide extensive experimental validation on both simulated and clinical datasets. MS-GDUN significantly outperforms existing methods in key metrics, such as localization accuracy and shape fidelity, underscoring its potential for real-world applications, especially in early tumor detection. 
4.Practical Clinical Relevance: The model exhibits strong potential for clinical translation. Its ability to handle high-resolution meshes and its improved localization accuracy are critical for real-world FMT applications, making it highly relevant for preclinical and clinical use in early tumor detection.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Model Complexity and Computational Cost: While the proposed method offers substantial improvements in reconstruction accuracy, the computational complexity of multi-scale graph convolutions and the node-adaptive sparse update strategy may limit its scalability for large-scale clinical datasets. Exploring optimizations or alternative approaches to reduce computational overhead would strengthen the practical applicability of the method. 
2.Experimental Validation and Dataset Diversity: Although the experimental results are promising, further validation on a broader set of clinical datasets, particularly from different tumor types and imaging modalities, would better demonstrate the generalizability and robustness of the proposed method. Additionally, a more detailed comparison with clinical benchmarks would enhance the claims regarding its clinical applicability.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
In Section 2, especially in the subsections related to the multi-scale graph feature extraction (2.1) and the adaptive sparse update strategy (2.3), a bit more explanation regarding the architecture and the relationships between different stages of the unfolding process would be valuable. Additionally, I would recommend including further details on the computational efficiency of the proposed method, particularly in terms of the required memory and time complexity when dealing with high-resolution meshes.

This paper makes a substantial contribution to the field of FMT by combining deep learning with physics-based models, leading to significant improvements in reconstruction accuracy. The methodology is novel, well-executed, and the experimental validation is comprehensive. The technical innovations and the potential for clinical applications make this work highly impactful.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The author has addressed all my questions, and I am inclined to accept this paper.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: A physics-guided deep unfolding framework is introduced for FMT reconstruction, with three main contributions. First, it incorporates physics-informed global context modeling. Second, it develops a node-adaptive sparsity mechanism with gradient threshold learning to alleviate gradient vanishing and maintain high resolution in multi-source scenarios. Third, it presents a multi-scale graph feature aggregation strategy with cross-attention to address the limitations of single-scale approaches, enabling robust representation of structural details.
reviews.text_strengths: The problem is interesting. Formulation is rigorous. Experiments conducted for simulation and in-vivo.
reviews.text_weaknesses: Although the performance of the method is evaluated through comparisons, the computational complexity is not discussed. Additionally, there are several instances where the readability could be improved for better clarity.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The study is interesting and addresses an important problem. However, I feel that the computational complexity of the proposed approach is not sufficiently discussed. It would be helpful to include details such as training time per epoch, inference time, and memory requirements to better assess the practical feasibility of the method.
Additionally, the presentation of results could be improved for clarity. For instance, in Table 1, the title for MS-GDUN is highlighted in bold, and all corresponding values (except one) are also in bold. It is not clear whether bold formatting is intended to indicate the best-performing values, as this is not explicitly stated and does not appear to be consistent across all entries. Kindly clarify the rationale for this formatting.
Minor Comments
The abbreviation “MS-GDUN” is not defined in the abstract. It would be helpful to introduce it in the abstract.
On Page 3, the full stop is placed before the references [22], [23] in the first sentence; it should be placed after the references.
In Equation (10), the Softplus function is used but not defined. A brief definition would improve clarity for readers unfamiliar with it.
Page 6: The sentence
“To quantitatively evaluate the accuracy of MS-GDUN in source localization and shape reconstruction, we compared it with deep unfolding methods (ISTA-Net and FISTA-Net), a network based on GCN approach (ResGCN), and a based on deep learning reconstruction method (IPS).”
is difficult to follow and appears to be missing a word (e.g., “network”). It may benefit from rephrasing for clarity.
Page 6, Section 3.2: The sentence
“Similarly, ResGCN performed unsatisfactorily when the source separation was small, which can be attributed to its lack of based on deep unfolding generalization capability in graph convolution, leading to training overfitting.”
is unclear and would benefit from revision for readability.
Page 6, Section 3.2: In the sentence
“As indicated by the quantitative metrics in Table 1, MS-GDUN achieved superior performance in terms of Dice,”
it would be helpful to include the corresponding Dice score for completeness.

While the manuscript presents comparative performance evaluations, it does not address the computational complexity of the proposed method, which is important for assessing its practical applicability. Additionally, there are several instances where the clarity and readability of the text could be improved.

reviews.text_contribution: The paper addresses the ill-posedness of Fluorescence reconstruction by introducing MS-GDUN, which is a physics-guided deep unfolding network. The authors transition the traditional sparse graph manifold learning iterative solver into an end-to-end learnable architecture. The Multi-scale graph cross-attention module fuses local and global topological features from the finite-element mesh to dictate the gradient update direction. They also propose a node-adaptive gradient-threshold learning mechanism.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.By mapping the SGML-IRSTA optimization steps directly into the network’s forward pass, the model retains the mathematical interpretability of classical inverse solvers while leveraging the representational power of GNNS.
2.Predict node-level adaptive shrinkage thresholds is a good insight for FMT since tissue scattering severity varies drastically with depth, a global threshold is inherently flawd, the learned spatial adaptivity addresses this physical reality.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.For Deep Unrolling network, the number of unfolding stages is vital hyperparameter as it states the trade-off between reconstruction accuracy, memory footprint and gradient propagation stability. A sensitivity analysis evaluating N versus reconstruction performance and inference time is important for a method of this nature.
2.The study restrict attention to a local neighborhood to control costs, while the actual computational burden is ambiguous. Given the mesh scale (6674 nodes, 33357 elements) and the parallel execution of multi-scale laplacian graph convolutions the memory overhead could be substantial. A quantitaitve comparison of parameter counts, training time per epoch and single-sample inference time aginst the baseline could be helpful.
3.In table 1, the deep learning baseline performs poorly (Dice=39.9%), The authors didn’t clarify if this baseline was tuned to a comparable model capacity and trained to convergence. The comparison lacks of fairness.
4.A code link is provided while in the main text, the training details such as initial learning rate, optimizer choice, and specific numerical values of the neighborhood radii used to construct the multi-scale Laplacian matrices didn’t mentioned, it would be better if these details can be provided.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The method design of MS-GDUN is relevant to the MICCAI community, which bridges the gap between interpretable physics-based inverse solvers and topological graph representation learning. The proposed MSGC and adaptive thresholding mechanisms are well-motivated by the underlying physics of photon scattering. However, the omissions regarding model complexity and hyperparameters (the undefined number of unfolding stages and the hidden computational footprint of executing multi-scale graph cross-attention on dense 3D meshes) are concerns.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors provided a clear rebuttal that addressed few concerns. The quantitative breakdown (linear complexity, 8-10 GB peak memory, and only 7,218 parameters) explained the model’s scalability on dense meshes. The authors also defined the missing hyperparameters such as the 6 unfolding stages and the specific neighborhood radii (0.5/1.0/1.5 mm) which improves the transparency of the methodology. The clarification that the IPS baseline was tuned to convergence on identical data splits, confirming that the comparison is unbiased. Since methodological and computational ambiguities have been resolved, I recommend accepting this manuscript.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper proposes MS-GDUN, a physics-guided deep unfolding network combining graph convolutional blocks, multi-scale graph cross-attention, and node-adaptive sparsity thresholding for FMT reconstruction, validated on simulated and in-vivo data. Several substantive concerns are raised across the reviews. The practical applicability of the framework is difficult to assess given the absence of any characterization of computational cost relative to baselines, which is particularly relevant for a method built on multi-scale graph operations over dense 3D meshes. The role of the number of unfolding stages, a defining hyperparameter for deep unrolling networks, is also not addressed. The fairness of the baseline comparison requires clarification, particularly whether the deep learning baseline was set up under comparable conditions given its notably low Dice. Several training and architectural details, including learning rate, optimizer, and the neighborhood radii used to construct the multi-scale Laplacian matrices, are missing from the main text. Readability also requires improvement, with several unclear or grammatically broken passages and ambiguous formatting in Table 1.The rebuttal should address the major reviewers’ concerns including these points.

This paper proposes MS-GDUN, a physics-guided deep unfolding network for fluorescence molecular tomography reconstruction that combines graph convolutional blocks, multi-scale graph cross-attention, and a node-adaptive sparsity thresholding mechanism, validated on simulated and in-vivo data. The reviewers agree that the method is well motivated by the physics of photon scattering, that mapping the iterative solver into a learnable architecture preserves interpretability, and that the comparative results show clear gains in localization accuracy and shape fidelity. The principal concerns across the reviews and the meta-review were the absence of any characterization of computational cost, the unspecified number of unfolding stages, the fairness of the baseline comparison, and missing training details, together with several readability issues. The rebuttal addressed these concretely, specifying the complexity and memory footprint, parameter count, unfolding stages and neighborhood radii, and the conditions under which the baseline was tuned, and the two reviewers who had placed the paper at or below the threshold confirmed these resolved their concerns. The authors are encouraged to fold the complexity analysis, hyperparameter specification, and the noted formatting and language corrections into the camera-ready version, as committed.

Following Reviewer #2 upgrading to accept after the rebuttal, all three submitted opinions favor acceptance. Strengths include the principled deep unfolding framework, multi-scale graph modelling, the gradient-threshold mechanism for adaptive sparse recovery, and competitive performance against comparison baselines. The primary weaknesses raised by R1 (implementation details) and R4 (comparison depth) were partially addressed in the rebuttal.
All the reviewers are satisfied with the rebuttal.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their valuable comments. We have thoroughly addressed all concerns with detailed explanations and quantitative results to improve the work’s rigor and reproducibility.
1.Computational Complexity & Scalability (R1, R2, R4)
(1) Complexity analysis: Multi-scale Laplacians (L0–L3) are precomputed, fixed, and shared across stages with no learnable parameters. They are sparse by design—each node connects to a small local neighborhood, yielding O(N) non-zeros. Sparse multiplication eliminates O(N2) dense costs, reducing graph operations to O(N). KNN cross-attention is local, and adaptive sparse updates run node-wise. Overall complexity is linear in N, ensuring scalability. On 6,674-node meshes, costs are lower than FISTA-Net/IPS and comparable to ResGCN.
(2) Parameter efficiency: MS-GDUN has only 7,218 learnable parameters from 6 lightweight blocks (~1.2K each). No parameters scale with mesh nodes (N=6,674), and Laplacians are fixed. This N-independent design avoids memory explosion for large meshes.
(3) Quantitative runtime/memory: Training: ~1.2 h/epoch (RTX A6000, batch=8). Inference: 80-150 ms/sample. Peak GPU memory: 8-10 GB. Sparse Laplacians and local attention limit overhead, confirming clinical scalability.
2.Methodology & Architectural Design (R1, R4) 
We clarify unfolding dynamics, hyperparameter sensitivity, and training details.
(1) Unfolding stages: Ablation over L=4–10 confirms L=6 optimizes accuracy-efficiency. Stages run sequentially: each takes Xk−1, computes physics-consistent features, extracts multi-scale graph representations via GCB-L, predicts gradients via MSGC, and updates Xk via ASUS. Stages share Laplacians; gradients and thresholds evolve progressively, with early stages correcting global structure and later stages refining local details, forming clear inter-stage dependencies.
(2) Training detail: PyTorch (3.11), 100 epochs, batch=8, RTX A6000, AdamW (1×10−3 LR). Laplacian radii: 0.5/1.0/1.5 mm. All hyperparameters are documented for reproducibility.
(3) Module interactions: GCB-L extracts local (L0–L2)/global (L3) features. MSGC fuses multi-scale features via local KNN attention with sensitivity-weighted keys/values. ASUS applies Softplus-predicted node-adaptive thresholds to suppress noise. Modules form a unified pipeline enhancing structural consistency.
3.Experimental Comparison & Fairness (R1, R4)
(1) Baseline fairness (R4.3): All methods are standard FMT benchmarks, strictly reimplemented and tuned to convergence with identical 8:2 splits and settings. IPS, the pioneering deep learning method, serves as quantitative/qualitative reference. It has competitive localization but inherent sparse-source artifacts (Dice=39.9%, EED=4mm). Including IPS enables comprehensive comparison, highlighting our artifact suppression and structural fidelity. IPS limitations are known; comparisons are unbiased.
(2) Generalization (R1.2): Experiments use simulated dual-source (EED=4/6 mm) and in vivo mouse glioma models—standard FMT setups. Conference scope limits large multi-center experiments; public multi-center FMT data is scarce. Our deep unfolding algorithm is grounded in 3D reconstruction theory, not dataset-specific features, supporting generalization to diverse tumors/modalities. We analyze cross‑tumor and cross‑modality generalization, and benchmark against published results, verifying the method’s robustness and clinical applicability.
4.Manuscript Format Revision (R2)
All formatting and presentation issues have been revised.
(1) Standardized bold formatting for optimal/suboptimal values in Table 1.(2) Defined Softplus: Softplus(x)=ln(1+e^x).
(3) Minor revisions include defining MS-GDUN in the abstract, standardizing reference punctuation, refining sentences, and supplementing exact Dice scores (81.1%/87.7%/54%).
All reviewer concerns are fully resolved with rigorous explanations, quantitative evidence, and clear mechanism interpretations.

title: MSHF-Net: Multimodal Breast Cancer Molecular Subtype Prediction via Segmentation-Guided Hierarchical Fusion Network
abstract: Breast cancer treatment and prognosis depend strongly on molecular subtype. However, conventional invasive biopsy and postoperative pathology can be affected by tumor heterogeneity and sampling bias, which motivates non-invasive, preoperative subtype prediction. While recent deep learning approaches have enabled imaging-based subtype prediction, relying on a single imaging modality often provides incomplete information. Current multimodal fusion methods also struggle to capture differences in information scale and the complementary relationships among Mammography (MG), Ultrasound (US), and clinical data. In addition, because breast lesions often occupy only a small region of the image, weakly supervised classification can be distracted by surrounding background tissue, reducing reliability. To address these limitations, we propose a Multimodal Segmentation-Guided Hierarchical Fusion Network (MSHF-Net) to classify breast cancer into Luminal and Non-luminal subtypes. The model uses Hierarchical Tri-modal Fusion (H-TMF) to better integrate complementary signals from MG, US, and clinical features. It also introduces a Segmentation-Guided Aggregation (SGA) module to strengthen discrimination by combining global context with localized lesion information. Finally, a Class-Balanced Focal (CBF) Loss improves recognition of minority subtypes and mitigates the Luminal/Non-luminal class imbalance. Experiments on the self-collected LGCH-Breast dataset show that MSHF-Net outperforms existing methods across multiple metrics, indicating strong potential for non-invasive multimodal subtype prediction. Code is available at https://github.com/knot41/MSHF-Net.
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers
Applications -> Outcome Prediction / Prognosis / Longitudinal Modeling
Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents MSHF-Net for the preoperative, non-invasive prediction of breast cancer molecular subtype (Luminal vs. Non-luminal) by integrating mammography (CC/MLO), ultrasound, and clinical data. The framework includes three main components: (1) an SGA module that uses tumor masks to guide lesion-focused feature extraction, (2) an H-TMF module for hierarchical multimodal fusion, and (3) a class-balanced focal loss to address label imbalance. Experiments on a single-center in-house dataset of 401 cases show that the proposed method outperforms several baseline approaches.
reviews.text_strengths:
This study addresses an important and highly practical clinical problem rather than a purely technical task. Preoperative, non-invasive prediction of breast cancer molecular subtype has clear potential value for treatment planning and clinical decision-making, and it directly responds to a real unmet need in breast cancer management. In this sense, the work is clinically meaningful and well motivated.
A notable strength of the paper is that it appears to be among the first attempts in this area to jointly integrate mammography, ultrasound, and clinical information for this specific prediction task. This is especially valuable because multimodal clinical datasets of this kind are difficult to collect, often limited in scale, and highly valuable in practice. From this perspective, the contribution of the paper should not be judged only by technical novelty, but also by its effort to address a genuine clinical pain point using scarce and precious real-world data.
Methodologically, the multimodal design is reasonable, and the hierarchical fusion strategy is more structured than simple feature concatenation. The experimental section is also fairly comprehensive, including backbone comparisons, fusion comparisons, modality ablation, and component ablation. Overall, the manuscript is generally well organized and easy to follow.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The main limitation is that the SGA module depends on tumor masks at inference time, yet the paper does not provide an automatic segmentation pipeline or evaluate performance under mask-free, noisy-mask, or automatically generated mask conditions. This reduces the current readiness of the framework for routine clinical deployment. In addition, the fairness of the baseline comparisons is not entirely clear, particularly because the proposed method appears to benefit from additional lesion-mask supervision. Important details regarding the representation and preprocessing of clinical variables are also insufficiently described.
These concerns are meaningful, but in my view they do not outweigh the overall value of the study. Given the clinical relevance of the task, the rarity of the multimodal dataset, and the fact that this work represents an early and important attempt in this direction, these issues seem more like limitations to be addressed in revision or future work than reasons for rejection.
The authors should clarify how tumor masks are obtained during testing and, ideally, provide either a complete segmentation-to-classification pipeline or experiments examining the model’s sensitivity to mask quality. The manuscript would also benefit from stronger statistical analysis, clearer reporting of baseline training settings, and a more detailed description of the design and preprocessing of clinical features. If possible, the authors should also discuss the practical clinical workflow more explicitly, including how the proposed model might be used in real-world settings and what steps are needed to improve deployment feasibility. External validation would further strengthen the paper, although I understand that such multimodal clinical data are difficult to obtain and that this may be beyond the scope of the current study.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Overall, I view this paper positively. It tackles a clinically important and underexplored problem, and it does so with a rare and valuable multimodal dataset collected from real clinical practice. Although some methodological and reporting issues remain, this study should be appreciated as an early and meaningful attempt to address a genuine clinical need rather than as a purely technical exercise. In my opinion, the paper has sufficient merit and practical relevance to merit acceptance, or at least a revision with a positive recommendation, provided that the authors clarify the mask-related issue and improve the reporting of experimental details.

reviews.text_contribution:
This paper proposes MSHF-Net, a multimodal deep learning framework designed for the non-invasive preoperative prediction of breast cancer molecular subtypes (Luminal vs. Non-luminal). The architecture integrates Mammography (MG), Ultrasound (US), and clinical data. The authors introduce two primary modules: (1) Hierarchical Tri-modal Fusion (H-TMF) to capture complementary relationships across different information scales, and (2) Segmentation-Guided Aggregation (SGA) to focus the model’s attention on the lesion area using ROI masks. The method is validated on a private dataset of 400 cases.
there are three main contribution:
1.Scale-Aware Fusion: Develops a hierarchical strategy to merge image-level features with low-dimensional clinical metadata, addressing the “scale gap” in multimodal learning.
2.Attention Refinement: Implements a segmentation-guided mechanism (SGA) that leverages spatial priors to suppress background noise in weakly supervised classification.
3.Multimodal Integration: Demonstrates the value of combining MG and US, which provides a more holistic view of tumor morphology and vascularity than single-modality approaches.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Clinical Relevance: Predicting molecular subtypes via imaging is a high-impact task that could reduce the need for invasive biopsies.
2.Architectural Design: The dual-branch approach (SGA) is logically sound, as pathology-related features are often localized within small regions of a full mammogram or ultrasound frame.
3.Clear Methodology: The paper provides a detailed technical description of the H-TMF and SGA modules, making the approach theoretically reproducible.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
three main weaknesses:
1.Critical Statistical Inconsistency (Accuracy vs. Sample Size): The authors state in Section 4.1 that the test set consists of 40 samples (N=40). Mathematically, for a sample size of 40, any metric derived from a simple count (Accuracy, Precision, Recall) must be a multiple of 1/40 = 2.5%. However, Table 1 reports values such as 80.5%, 80.2%, and 78.3%. These results are mathematically impossible for a 40-sample cohort unless the authors are reporting the average of multiple cross-validation folds without clearly stating so. This lack of transparency regarding the denominator of the performance metrics raises significant concerns about the technical rigor of the evaluation.
2.Limited Clinical Evidence (Single-Center Validation):The study relies entirely on a single private dataset. In medical imaging, models often overfit to the specific hardware (e.g., GE vs. Siemens machines) or scanning protocols of a single institution. Without External Validation on an independent dataset (e.g., public datasets like CBIS-DDSM or a separate hospital cohort), the generalizability and clinical reliability of MSHF-Net remain unproven.
3.Missing Statistical Significance Analysis:The performance gains (e.g., an improvement from 80.0% to 82.5%) are marginal given the small test size. The authors fail to provide P-values or 95% Confidence Intervals (CI). Without these, it is impossible to determine if the proposed H-TMF module offers a statistically significant improvement or if the gain is due to random variance in the small test set.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

While the proposed hierarchical fusion is interesting, the paper suffers from a critical lack of clarity in its experimental results. The mismatch between the test sample size (N=40) and the reported accuracy percentages (e.g., 80.2%) is a major red flag that must be addressed. Furthermore, the reliance on a single-center dataset without statistical significance testing limits the contribution to a “preliminary study” rather than a robust clinical tool suitable for MICCAI.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: While the authors have made efforts to address the raised concerns, I find their rebuttal insufficient to overcome the fundamental limitations of this work. The proposed solutions are either incremental, not adequately demonstrated, or fail to address the core scientific and clinical issues. Therefore, I maintain my recommendation for rejection.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces MSHF-Net, a multimodal framework designed for non-invasive, preoperative breast cancer molecular subtype classification (Luminal vs. Non-luminal). The work addresses the limitations of single-modality imaging and the distraction caused by background tissue. The primary contributions include a Hierarchical Tri-modal Fusion (H-TMF) to integrate Mammography (MG), Ultrasound (US), and clinical features, a Segmentation-Guided Aggregation (SGA) module to combine global context with localized lesion information, and a Class-Balanced Focal (CBF) Loss to mitigate class imbalance. The model was evaluated on the LGCH-Breast dataset, showing strong potential for radiomics-based subtype prediction without the need for histopathology or genomic data about the tumor molecular profile.
reviews.text_strengths:
Major Strengths:
The manuscript is well-written, and the proposed framework is explained with sufficient technical detail and can be easily extend to different medical application setting beyond the considered task of the paper.
The experimentation is comprehensive, featuring an in-depth ablation study that effectively probes the contribution of each individual component within the framework.
The authors provide a wide comparison against state-of-the-art methods, as well as early, late, and attention-based fusion strategies.
The model achieves strong results (82% Accuracy and 85% AUC) on a difficult task, particularly as it relies solely on non-invasive radiomic features and clinical characteristics
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Major Weaknesses:
The paper does not sufficiently elaborate on the rationale behind the specific hierarchical integration design. It is unclear why cross-attention was not applied uniformly across all stages—from the dual MG views to the clinical data integration.
There is a lack of discussion regarding why dynamic integration was utilized for the MG views but not extended to the integration of US and MG.
While results include standard deviation, the manuscript does not specify if these represent a K-fold cross-validation or repetitions over multiple random seeds, which is critical for assessing reproducibility.
While the performance gains of MSHF-Net over the state-of-the-art appear notable, the manuscript does not provide statistical significance tests (Paired t-test, Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test) to confirm that these improvements are consistent and mathematically significant.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Please state the validation protocol used to calculate the reported standard deviations to ensure full reproducibility.

The paper is a solid contribution that addresses a significant clinical need in breast cancer subtype prediction. The methodological design, while raising interesting questions regarding the specific hierarchical fusion choices and dynamic integration, is well-supported by a very thorough ablation study that proves the efficacy of each component. The performance (82% Acc and 85% AUC) is particularly impressive given the reliance on non-invasive modalities. While some minor details regarding the statistical protocol (K-fold vs. random seeds) could be clarified, the overall quality of the framework and the depth of the experimentation make this a strong candidate for the conference independent of a rebuttal.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The author’s responses address my comments very well and clarify the unclear points I’ve raised, including the lack of a statistical test, the validation strategy used to compute the std, and the explanation for choosing different fusion strategies at different levels. I was convinced. Therefore, I recommend the paper for acceptance without hesitation.

meta_reviews.text:
Although two reviewers accepted this paper, one reviewer pointed out that the paper suffers from a critical lack of clarity in its experimental results. The mismatch between the test sample size (N=40) and the reported accuracy percentages is a major red flag that must be addressed. Furthermore, the reliance on a single-center dataset without statistical significance testing limits the impact of this work. The authors should clarify any misunderstandings raised by the reviewer.

The authors have adequately addressed most of the reviewers’ concerns. However, the cross-validation details and other validation aspects mentioned in the rebuttal should be incorporated into the final version.
Though one of the reviewers in not convinced by the rebiutal, I believe the concerns raised by them have been adequately addressed. Thus I recommend accepting the paper

The rebuttal satisfactorily addressed the main concern raised by the weak-reject review. In particular, the authors clarified that the reported results come from three repetitions of five-fold cross-validation, not from a single 40-case test set, which resolves the apparent inconsistency in the reported percentages. They also clarified the use of confidence intervals, described the clinical variables and preprocessing, explained the hierarchical fusion design more clearly, and stated that significance testing was performed and will be reported in the revision.
Some limitations remain, especially the dependence on lesion masks at inference time and the lack of external validation. However, these are better understood as deployment and generalization limitations rather than fatal flaws for the current submission.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their support of our paper, including its “clinically valuable questions” (R1&2&3), “targeted method design” (R1&2&3), “comprehensive experiments” (R1&3), and “clear overall writing” (R1&3). Below, we address two general concerns, then respond to each reviewer.
G1: Experimental Protocols and Statistical Analyses (R1&2&3)
We performed three repetitions of five-fold cross-validation (using three different random seeds), where four subsets were used for training and one subset for evaluation in each run, with the evaluation subset rotated across folds. All results are reported as the mean and 95% confidence interval half-width for each metric. Details will be added to the revision.
G2: Lack of Statistical Significance Tests (R2&3)
We have provided the P-values for the optimal and suboptimal models based on AUC in the anonymous code link. This was omitted from the manuscript due to space constraints but will be added in the revision.
R1Q1: Mask-Related Issue
In Sec 3.1, lesion masks were annotated by two experienced breast radiologists to ensure high-quality supervision. During evaluation, annotated masks were also used as input. This work is not a comprehensive segmentation-classification system; instead, it investigates if concentrating on lesion patches with high-quality masks enhances molecular subtyping.
R1Q2: Clinical Features
Sec 2.2 outlines the clinical modalities, with implementation details in the anonymous code link. We use five clinical features: age, maximal tumor diameter, menopausal state, tumor location, and breast fiber type. The first two are z-score normalized; the others are one-hot encoded.
R1Q3: Comparison Fairness
In Sec 3.1, all experiments used the identical deployment parameters. And each experiment used identical lesion masks for ROI cropping, restricting inputs to lesion regions. Additionally, MSHF-Net’s SGA module uses the mask to generate spatial weight maps, ensuring fair comparison.
R2Q1: Experimental Data
We sincerely apologize for the lack of clarity in experimental results. In Sec 3.1, we mentioned that the test dataset had only 40 samples. However, in subsequent experiments, we performed three repetitions of five-fold cross-validation by partitioning the dataset into training and evaluation subsets. Statistical analysis was conducted using these three repetitions of five-fold cross-validation together with 95% confidence intervals. Accordingly, each reported metric was calculated based on the evaluation results obtained from four folds containing 80 samples and one fold containing 81 samples. Therefore, the results reported in our tables are reasonable and statistically reliable. We will further clarify the description in Sec 3.1 in the revision.
R2Q2: Single-center Dataset
Given that the input modalities for this work include mammography (CC and MLO) images, ultrasound images, corresponding mammography and ultrasound masks, and clinical information, it is quite challenging to obtain such comprehensive multimodal data. However, the model’s generalization ability has been validated to some extent through five-fold cross-validation and the 95% confidence intervals obtained from statistical analyses based on existing datasets.
R3Q1: Hierarchical Fusion
Hierarchical fusion models different levels of multimodal integration. Table 3 shows it outperforms uniform attention fusion, as it better adapts to modality heterogeneity and avoids dominance by a single modality. In contrast, uniform fusion may suffer from suboptimal feature representation due to distribution and semantic gaps, reducing multimodal complementarity.
R3Q2: Dynamic Integration
Fusion strategies are adapted based on modality relationships. Dynamic weighting models the view consistency between CC and MLO, which share anatomy but differ in projection. For heterogeneous modalities such as MG and US, Cross-Attention better captures inter-modal interactions and enhances pathology-relevant complementarity.

title: mSpecFusion-Net: Intelligent Multimodal Smartphone Imaging for Mobile Differential Diagnosis of Psoriasis and Dermatitis and Deep Learning
abstract: Psoriasis and seborrheic dermatitis (SD) often present with highly similar clinical features such as erythema and scaling, leading to frequent diagnostic ambiguity, particularly in primary care and teledermatology. Existing AI approaches based on mobile RGB imaging have shown limited discrimination performance because the two conditions can exhibit overlapping visual manifestations. To address this challenge, we propose a smartphone-based portable multimodal optical imaging and analysis framework that acquires co- and cross-polarized multispectral reflectance images and ultraviolet (UV)-excited autofluorescence, together with a modality-aware deep learning model, mSpecFusion-Net, designed for robust cross-modality integration. The proposed model encodes each modality in parallel and employs an iterative fusion Transformer that repeatedly aggregates complementary information across modalities to form a unified representation for differential diagnosis. Across patient-wise splits, mSpecFusion-Net (PCA + iterative fusion) delivers the strongest overall performance (F1 = 0.9057, ROC-AUC = 0.9461), surpassing RGB-only baselines and widely used backbones. This demonstrates that explicitly reducing inter-wavelength redundancy and progressively refining cross-modality evidence is critical for separating clinically similar conditions. The proposed smartphone multimodal pipeline is readily deployable for teledermatology and scalable to other multimodal mobile diagnostics.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs
Modalities -> Mobile / Wearable / Point-of-Care Imaging & Sensors
Special Topic -> Telemedicine & Mobile Health Imaging

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper presents a hardware-software co-design framework for differentiating between two visually similar skin conditions: Psoriasis and Seborrheic Dermatitis (SD). The authors propose a custom smartphone-based multimodal dermascope (capturing co-polarized multispectral, cross-polarized multispectral, and UV-excited autofluorescence images) paired with a novel deep learning architecture (mSpecFusion-Net). The model utilizes PCA for spectral compression and an iterative-fusion Transformer to aggregate cross-modal features.
The integration of custom mobile optical hardware with a tailored multimodal deep learning pipeline is quite compelling and addresses a real clinical need in teledermatology, even though the sample size is slightly on the lower side (32)? The systematic ablation studies (Tables 2 and 4) are well-structured and clearly justify the architectural choices. However, crucial methodological details regarding data processing and evaluation metrics are missing (especially in Tables 3 and 5), which must be addressed before publication. Also, crucial comparisons with recent work on missing, which should demonstrate how mSpecFusion-Net improves over SOTA architectures and how iterative fusion improves specifically over modern fusion methods.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Innovative Hardware-Software Integration: The combination of an 8-band LED multiplexer with polarization filters and UV autofluorescence on a mobile device seems highly innovative. It provides a unique solution to the limitations of standard RGB imaging.
2.Rigorous Validation Strategy: The use of patient-wise 5-fold cross-validation is excellent. In dermatology AI, random splitting often leads to severe data leakage (where the model learns the patient’s background skin rather than the disease). The authors correctly avoided this pitfall.
3.Strong Ablation Studies: The paper does an excellent job of justifying its complexity. Table 2 proves the utility of PCA, Table 3 validates the iterative fusion module over standard early/late fusion (even though there are concerns regarding this table), and Table 4 confirms the necessity of the multimodal hardware setup.
4.Clinical Relevance: Targeting Psoriasis vs. Seborrheic Dermatitis is a highly practical objective, as these are notoriously difficult to distinguish in primary care and RGB teledermatology.
5.Architectural Innovation: The use of PCA, the concept of iterative fusion, and the overall design seem sufficiently novel and well motivated.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The major weakness of this paper is the lack of clarity and incompleteness when it comes to the evaluations against SOTA architectures and fusion methods. I am listing them below:
1.Ambiguity in Evaluation Metrics (Patch vs. Patient Level): Section 2.4 states that images are “partitioned into a fixed grid of nonoverlapping patches” and that these patches are used as training instances. However, the evaluation tables (Tables 2-5) do not clarify if the reported F1, Accuracy, and AUC metrics are evaluated at the patch-level, image-level, or patient-level.
Why this matters: If a model predicts 100 patches from a single patient’s image and gets 90 right, patch-level metrics will look fantastic, but clinically, we only care about the single image/patient diagnosis. The authors must report patient-level or image-level aggregated metrics (e. g. , via majority voting across patches).
2.Missing PCA Parameters: The paper mentions applying PCA to the multispectral stacks to reduce inter-wavelength redundancy, but omits critical reproducibility details. How many principal components were retained? What percentage of variance was explained by the retained components?
3.Unfair Baseline Comparisons: In Table 5, the proposed model is compared to standard backbones. It is unclear how these baselines processed the multimodal data. Did they receive a concatenated tensor of all modalities (early fusion)? If these baselines were only given RGB images, or if they were not adapted to handle the high-dimensional multispectral stacks properly, the comparison to mSpecFusion-Net is an apples-to-oranges comparison. It doesn’t add any value at all. How these baselines were attained needs critical attention.
4.Fusion Methods: Similarly, Table 3 mentions fusion methods, but fails to provide any detail whatsoever on the specifics (late fusion, how? Concatenation? Attention? Gated?)
5.Lack of comparison to recent works: The authors fail to compare their work against recent multimodal, multispectral, and fusion-based studies. For example, the following papers could be discussed to outline the improvements:
i) https://doi. org/10.1016/j. ibmed. 2025.100271
ii) https://doi. org/10.1109/JBHI. 2026.3682634
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I am leaning towards accepting because the authors addressed a relevant clinical problem, and the proposed framework and architecture are quite innovative. Weak confidence because of the lack of clarity in the evaluation, as mentioned. However, if the authors can discuss/compare some fusion-based models and clarify the details for Tables 3 and 5 properly, I believe this paper should be accepted.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents a smartphone-based multimodal imaging and artificial intelligence framework for the differential diagnosis of psoriasis and seborrheic dermatitis in mobile and remote dermatology settings. The authors combine a portable multimodal dermoscope with a modality-aware deep learning model that performs parallel modality encoding and iterative cross-modality fusion. In addition, the study introduces a PCA-based spectral compression strategy to reduce redundancy across wavelengths before fusion. The results show that the proposed framework outperforms RGB-only, single-modality, conventional fusion, and several generic deep learning architectures, suggesting that clinically grounded multimodal acquisition and progressive cross-modality reasoning can improve the discrimination of visually similar inflammatory skin diseases.
reviews.text_strengths:
Psoriasis and seborrheic dermatitis often present with similar visual appearances, making research on mobile screening and remote dermatological diagnosis highly clinically relevant. This paper proposes a coherent end-to-end framework that includes a smartphone-based multimodal dermoscope, acquisition and calibration procedures, and a dedicated multimodal analysis model. As a result, its contribution is more practically meaningful than that of a purely retrospective classification study.
The proposed iterative fusion design is a meaningful innovation. It allows the model to progressively exchange and refine cross-modal evidence. The results suggest that this strategy outperforms conventional fusion approaches.
The full multimodal iterative fusion model performs clearly better than the RGB-only input setting, demonstrating that explicitly modeling multimodal complementarity is more effective than simply extending generic architectures.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The method used in this paper integrates parallel modality encoders, Transformer-based fusion, PCA-based spectral compression, and iterative multimodal fusion. While the use of these components is reasonable, the work does not demonstrate a strongly novel algorithmic advance. In my view, the most distinctive contribution of this paper lies in the multimodal mobile diagnostic workflow rather than in a fundamentally new core algorithmic design.
During training, the authors divide the images into non-overlapping patches and assign patient-level diagnostic labels to each patch. I am concerned that this strategy may reduce lesion-level contextual information and may not fully reflect how dermatologists integrate the overall morphology of a lesion in clinical practice. I would encourage the authors to provide more discussion to justify this design choice.
Given that the goal of this work is mobile-device-based diagnosis, the paper should report more information on acquisition time, inference time, computational cost, and operational complexity. I encourage the authors to more fully quantify the practical burden of the entire multimodal workflow in order to demonstrate the deployability of the proposed framework.
The presentation of symbols and formulas in the manuscript is not sufficiently clear. For example, the meaning of F in Figure 1 is not explained in the text. I encourage the authors to improve these aspects to enhance the overall quality of the manuscript.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper addresses a clinically relevant and practically important diagnostic problem, and proposes a coherent system-level solution. The combination of smartphone-based multimodal acquisition, PCA-based spectral compression, and iterative modality-aware fusion is well motivated, and the experimental design is generally sound. The results show clear improvements over RGB-only input, single-modality settings, standard fusion strategies, and several generic deep learning architectures, which supports the value of the proposed application framework. That said, the work is still limited by relatively modest methodological novelty at the core algorithmic level and by the lack of details regarding practical deployment. Overall, I believe this study has strong application potential and, in its current form, is above the acceptance threshold.

meta_reviews.text:
Given the overall positive reviews, I recommend acceptance.
Please address the following concerns in the final version: (1) clarify evaluation protocols, particularly whether metrics are reported at patch-, image-, or patient-level; (2) include missing methodological details; and (3) discuss practical deployment aspects such as computational cost and workflow feasibility. Addressing these points will be important to confirm the strength of the contribution.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers and the meta-reviewer. We address the main concerns below; minor points will be addressed in the camera-ready revision.
Evaluation and cross-validation (R1, R2, Meta). All metrics in Tables 2–5 are at the patch level under strict patient-wise 5-fold CV: 32 patients are split into 10 disjoint patient-level groups; per round, 2 groups (~20%) form the test set, 1 validation, 7 training. The test partitions are disjoint and cover all patients, so each appears in exactly one test set, with no identity leakage. Patch predictions can be aggregated by averaging or voting at the lesion/patient level for deployment.
PCA (R1, Meta). PCA is used as discrete band selection on calibrated multispectral stacks, not as a learned feature projection. We rank the 8 bands by cumulative absolute PCA loading and retain the top K=4 per polarization stream. Since this is discrete index selection rather than data-dependent transformation, it is performed once on the calibrated dataset and fixed across folds; parameter learning remains strictly fold-independent, so the leakage pattern typically associated with global preprocessing does not apply.
Statistical reporting (R3). Across 5 folds, the model achieves F1 = 0.9057 ± 0.0612, Acc = 0.9068 ± 0.0576, ROC-AUC = 0.9461 ± 0.0540, PRC-AUC = 0.9358 ± 0.0666 (mean ± SD, micro). One fold yields F1 = 0.8174, reflecting the modest cohort; larger multi-site validation is future work.
Computational cost (R3, Meta). Acquisition takes ~20 s/patient. The model has 4.18 M parameters (16.0 MB, fp32) and 44.7 GFLOPs/image (bs=1), with GPU latency 17.3 ms/image (median, 100 runs). Inference is negligible vs. acquisition, so point-of-care latency is dominated by acquisition.
Ethics (R3). The study was approved by the IRB of Seoul National University Hospital (No. 1908-161-1059), with informed consent from all participants. We will add this to the clinical dataset section.
Baseline fairness (R1). All baselines in Table 5 receive the same multimodal input (Co-P + Cross-P MSI with PCA + UV-AF) under the same split and protocol; RGB-only is in Table 4.We will clarify this in the Table 5 caption.
Comparison with related work (R1, R2). Yang et al. and Siddiqui et al. (S3F-Net) maximize information from single-modality images via anatomical metadata and Fourier features. Our work fuses modalities from distinct physical principles, requires no metadata, and enables acquisition by non-specialists. Wang et al. uses dermoscopic and clinical images, both RGB; our multi-physical-modality approach is fundamentally different. We will add this to the Introduction.
Use of recent baselines (R1, R2). We additionally tested ConvNeXt V2-Base and ConvNeXt V2-Large using the same training protocol and input setting. Both models underperformed our proposed method: ConvNeXt V2-Base achieved an F1 score of 0.736 ± 0.187, and ConvNeXt V2-Large achieved 0.567 ± 0.171, whereas our method achieved 0.906 ± 0.061.Moreover, their per-fold standard deviations (~0.17–0.19) were approximately three times higher than that of our method (0.061).
Novelty (R1, R2). The key contribution is the development of an intelligent mobile multimodal framework for robust smartphone-based skin lesion assessment. Rather than relying on simple multimodal concatenation, conventional early/late fusion, or generic backbone scaling, our framework combines PCA-based spectral compression with iterative cross-modal fusion to progressively refine complementary optical evidence from co-polarized, cross-polarized, multispectral reflectance, and UV autofluorescence modalities. This model-level integration enables compact spectral representation, effective use of modality-specific and cross-modal cues, and more stable learning in a modest-sized clinical cohort. Code will be released upon publication.
Typos and notation (R3). We will correct typos (e.g., “deelp learing”), clarify notation, and refine the technical descriptions throughout.

title: MSQG-3DNet: Multi-scale Token Selection with Query-Decoder and Gated Fusion for 3D Breast Tumor Classification
abstract: Benign–malignant classification in automated breast ultrasound (ABUS) is challenging due to heterogeneous voxel spacing, anisotropic artifacts, and weakly localized malignancy cues distributed across 3D volumes. We propose MSQG-3DNet, a standardized-lattice CNN–Transformer hybrid for lesion-level ROI-based 3D ABUS classification, coupling multi-scale volumetric representation learning with query-guided global evidence aggregation. To reduce inter-case intensity and input-size variability, lesion-centered ROI volumes are intensity-normalized and standardized to a fixed 48 × 48 × 48 lattice. The network employs an SE-enhanced dilated 3D residual encoder to capture multi-scale morphology, followed by dual-scale tokenization with hybrid 3D positional encoding, including coordinate-based encoding, sinusoidal encoding, and scale embedding, to preserve spatial and scale awareness under lattice standardization. LayerScale-stabilized Transformer blocks model long-range dependencies, and a lightweight cross-attention Query-Decoder extracts task-relevant evidence. Finally, a gated fusion integrates complementary global descriptors for malignancy prediction. On an in-house ABUS dataset (8,627 training and 859 test volumes), MSQG-3DNet achieves a test AUC of 96.23%. External evaluation on the public TDSC-ABUS benchmark yields the highest threshold-independent AUC of 71.55% among compared methods, indicating improved benign–malignant discrimination under domain shift, while highlighting the need for operating threshold calibration in clinical use. Code available at: https://github.com/Ferry-Rain-Way/MSQG-3DNet.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes MSQG-3DNet, a 3D ABUS benign-versus-malignant classifier that combines a residual 3D encoder, multi-scale tokenization with hybrid 3D positional encoding, informative token selection, a query-guided decoder, and gated fusion of global descriptors. The submission also reports both a large internal hold-out evaluation and an external evaluation on TDSC-ABUS.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper addresses a clinically relevant 3D ABUS classification problem where weak malignancy cues can be spatially diffuse and difficult to capture with purely local models. 
The proposed architecture is reasonably coherent: token pruning, the query decoder, and gated fusion are not presented as isolated tricks, but as a linked pipeline for reducing redundancy and aggregating sparse global evidence. 
The internal study is fairly substantial for this application area, with 9,486 annotated volumes, a dedicated 859-case test split, progressive ablations, and comparison against prior ABUS-oriented baselines. 
I also view the external TDSC-ABUS experiment as a positive aspect, because the authors at least attempt to test cross-dataset behavior rather than reporting only single-center results.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The main concern is generalization. The external TDSC-ABUS test set contains only 49 cases, and on that set the paper reports the best AUC but only 44.83% sensitivity, so the current evidence is not strong enough to support a broad robustness claim under domain shift. A second issue is the aggressive preprocessing: every volume is normalized and standardized to 48x48x48, yet the paper is motivated by subtle and weakly localized malignancy cues, so the effect of this resampling choice on fine morphology should be analyzed rather than treated as neutral. The comparison set is also limited to two re-implemented competing methods, which makes it difficult to judge how much of the gain comes from the proposed architectural contributions versus the authors’ overall training recipe. Finally, the operating-point story needs more discussion. On the internal set, the final model attains 100% specificity but lower sensitivity than one ablation; on the external set, it again improves specificity at the cost of markedly lower sensitivity. That trade-off is clinically meaningful and should be discussed explicitly, not only through AUC.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
For rebuttal, the most useful additions would be: (1) clarify how thresholds were selected and whether the method can recover a higher-sensitivity operating point without collapsing specificity; (2) quantify how sensitive the results are to the fixed 48x48x48 resampling choice; and (3) explain the external performance drop more carefully, including whether it is mainly due to acquisition differences, annotation differences, or class-composition mismatch. I would also recommend softening the domain-robustness language unless stronger multi-center evidence is available.

I place this paper slightly above the acceptance threshold. The method is technically coherent, the internal evaluation is stronger than average for this application area, and the external test - although limited - is still more informative than having no cross-dataset evaluation at all. My enthusiasm is moderated by the small external cohort, the large internal-to-external performance gap, and the limited breadth of comparisons. Overall, I see this as a credible borderline accept rather than a clearly strong paper.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
After reading the authors’ rebuttal, I appreciate the detailed clarifications and the generally constructive responses to the reviewers’ concerns. The authors adequately clarified the intended clinical scope of the method as a lesion-level characterization framework rather than a complete CAD system, which makes the experimental setting more reasonable. The rebuttal also improved the explanation of the multi-scale token interaction mechanism and clarified that the proposed framework is not merely based on naive token concatenation.
I also appreciate the additional discussion regarding threshold selection and the SEN/SPE trade-off. The authors explained the use of Youden’s index and acknowledged the clinical importance of balancing sensitivity and specificity. In addition, the discussion on the external TDSC-ABUS evaluation and the challenges caused by missing voxel spacing information helps contextualize the observed performance drop under domain shift.
That said, some limitations remain only partially resolved. In particular, the external validation cohort is still relatively small, and the robustness claims should remain conservative. The concern regarding the potential impact of aggressive 48×48×48 resampling on subtle morphological cues was not fully addressed through additional analysis. The comparison breadth also remains somewhat limited. However, I acknowledge that these limitations are partly related to the scarcity of publicly available and standardized 3D ABUS benchmarks.
Overall, despite these remaining weaknesses, I still find the work technically coherent and experimentally stronger. The internal evaluation is substantial, the ablation study is reasonably comprehensive, and the authors made a meaningful effort to evaluate cross-dataset behavior. Therefore, I maintain my borderline positive acceptance.

reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a CNN–Transformer hybrid framework for 3D ABUS benign–malignant classification, combining multi-scale feature extraction with token-based global modeling. It introduces a token selection mechanism, a query-based aggregation module, and a gated fusion strategy to integrate multiple global representations for final prediction.
reviews.text_strengths:
Addresses an important problem in 3D breast ultrasound (ABUS) classification.
Proposes a coherent CNN–Transformer hybrid framework combining multi-scale feature extraction with global modeling.
Introduces a structured pipeline (token selection, query-based aggregation, and fusion) for feature integration.
Provides ablation studies to analyze the contribution of different components.
The paper is clearly written and well-organized, making the methodology easy to follow.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The task is formulated as lesion-centered classification, where the input volumes are already cropped around annotated lesions. While this setting is valid for diagnostic support, it significantly simplifies the problem by removing the need for lesion detection. As a result, the practical applicability of the proposed method in a fully automated clinical pipeline (e.g., screening) may be limited.
2.The multi-scale tokens are simply concatenated and processed with full self-attention, which is a rather brute-force design. This introduces unnecessary interactions across all tokens and is not an efficient or well-structured way to model cross-scale relationships.
3.The model consistently exhibits low sensitivity and high specificity across both datasets, indicating a strong bias toward predicting the benign class. This behavior can be attributed to two factors. First, the in-house dataset is highly imbalanced, with significantly more benign than malignant cases, which may encourage the model to favor the majority class. Notably, this issue becomes even more pronounced on the smaller external dataset, which is relatively balanced, where the sensitivity drops substantially, suggesting poor generalization to malignant cases. Second, the model primarily relies on global representation learning, while malignancy classification often depends on subtle and localized features. This suggests that the proposed architecture may be insufficient in capturing fine-grained local cues critical for detecting malignant lesions.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I lean toward a weak reject. While the paper presents a well-structured CNN–Transformer hybrid framework and provides clear experimental analysis with ablation studies, the overall novelty is limited, as the method mainly combines existing components rather than introducing a fundamentally new design. In addition, the experimental evaluation is not sufficiently comprehensive, with only a small number of baselines and limited comparison to recent relevant methods. More importantly, the model consistently shows low sensitivity and high specificity, indicating a bias toward benign predictions, which is problematic for clinical applications. This issue appears to be related to both dataset imbalance and the model’s reliance on global representations, which may be insufficient for capturing subtle local malignant cues. Overall, while the work is technically sound, stronger justification of its design choices and more convincing empirical validation are needed.

reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes MSQG-3DNet, a CNN-Transformer hybrid architecture for benign-malignant tumor classification in 3D Automated Breast Ultrasound (ABUS). The core methodology addresses the challenges of heterogeneous voxel spacing and weak, dispersed malignancy cues. The authors introduce a pipeline consisting of a residual 3D CNN with Multi-Scale Attention Fusion (MSAF) for local feature extraction, followed by a Transformer encoder. To handle the computational complexity of 3D tokens, the authors incorporate an Informative Token Pruning module, a Query-Decoder for task-focused global evidence aggregation, and a Gated Fusion mechanism to adaptively combine multiple global descriptors (class token, CNN features, pooled tokens, and query tokens). The model is evaluated on a notably large in-house dataset (9,486 volumes) and tested for domain shift on the public TDSC-ABUS dataset.
reviews.text_strengths:
Extensive In-house Dataset: The use of an in-house dataset comprising 9,486 3D ABUS volumes is highly commendable. Annotating and utilizing 3D medical datasets of this scale is rare and provides a strong foundation for the in-house evaluation.
Logical Architectural Design: The integration of CNNs and Transformers is well-motivated. The specific combination of Multi-Scale Attention Fusion, Token Pruning, and Query-Decoder effectively addresses the balance between local textural feature extraction and computational efficiency for 3D volumes.
Thorough Ablation Study: Table 2 and Figure 2 provide a clear, progressive validation of the proposed components. The training dynamics demonstrate that the token pruning and query-guided aggregation successfully stabilize the optimization process.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Unacceptable Clinical Sensitivity on External Data: While the model achieves the highest AUC on the external TDSC-ABUS dataset, its Sensitivity drops drastically to 44.83% (Table 4). In the context of breast cancer screening and diagnosis, missing more than half of the malignant tumors (false negatives) is a critical failure. The model becomes overly conservative (heavily favoring the benign class) under domain shift, rendering the “improved robustness” claim highly questionable from a clinical perspective.
Unrealistic Inference Assumptions (Cropping): The paper states that “lesion-centered 3D bounding-box crops were generated programmatically” based on radiologist annotations. It is entirely unclear how the model operates during real-world inference. Does it require a radiologist or a separate detection network to provide a perfect 3D bounding box first? If so, this limits the method’s fully automated CAD utility and makes the pipeline incomplete.
Limited Methodological Novelty: The individual components—multi-scale CNN backbones, token pruning, query-based cross-attention, and gated fusion—are directly adapted from existing standard computer vision literature without significant domain-specific algorithmic innovation.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I recommend a “Weak Reject.” While the scale of the in-house dataset is highly impressive and the network architecture is logically constructed, several fundamental flaws prevent acceptance in its current form. First and foremost, the severe drop in Sensitivity (44.83%) on the external dataset indicates the model is highly biased toward predicting benign cases under domain shift, making the proposed algorithm clinically unviable in its current state. Second, the assumption of having pre-existing lesion-centered 3D crops for classification is unrealistic for an end-to-end automated system, and the paper fails to explain how this is handled during inference. Finally, the aggressive downsampling to a 48x48x48 grid risks destroying the exact morphological cues the network is supposed to detect. Unless the authors can provide compelling clarifications regarding the inference pipeline and a solution (or at least a rigorous analysis) for the catastrophic drop in external sensitivity in their rebuttal, the paper falls short of the MICCAI acceptance threshold.
