meta_reviews.text: This paper presents a weakly-supervised framework for 3D medical image segmentation by adapting the SAM2 to volumetric data using point-based annotations and multi-axis consistency regularization. The reviewers highlight the practical clinical utility of the approach, the effectiveness of leveraging SAM2’s sequential processing for 3D volumes, and the promising performance gains achieved with limited labels. However, concerns were raised regarding the conceptual novelty of the method, the potential for information leakage during the ROI cropping process, and the lack of comprehensive comparisons with existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the clarity of the multi-round training procedure and the reproducibility of the results require further justification. Given the divergent scores (6, 4, 3), the authors are encouraged to provide a detailed rebuttal addressing the fairness of the experimental setup, the specifics of the point-annotation simulation, and the methodological distinctions from prior work.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and the meta-reviewer for the thoughtful and constructive comments.
(1) Regarding ROI cropping, our task is point-prompted 3D tumor segmentation, not fully automatic tumor localization. At inference, the only test-time prompt is a single foreground point. The 256×256×128 ROI is a fixed-size crop centered on this point and resized to 128×128×128 for computational feasibility. No ground-truth mask, boundary, or tumor-size information is used. The same crop is applied to all compared methods; thus, it does not introduce dense-label leakage or favor our framework.
(2) Regarding point annotations, the WSL setting assumes center-point labels for weakly labeled volumes. For TDSC-ABUS, where dense masks are available, point prompts are simulated from tumor centers of training masks. Dense masks are used only for the fully labeled subset and final evaluation. This protocol directly tests whether most dense 3D masks can be replaced by point-level prompts, and it is consistently applied to all WSL baselines.
(3) Regarding novelty, while pseudo-labeling, consistency regularization, and SAM adaptation have precedents, our contribution is not a generic combination of them. We formulate the first weakly supervised adaptation of SAM2 for 3D medical segmentation by exploiting SAM2’s sequential propagation across orthogonal 2D slice sequences. Three axis-specific SAM2 adapters generate complementary 3D predictions from the same point prompt, while a slice-level detection token estimates tumor presence and weights cross-axis pseudo-label fusion. This design is specific to SAM2-based 3D volumetric adaptation and differs from dense-mask SAM adaptation, SAM-Med3D-style supervised 3D adaptation, and conventional SSL methods that do not exploit multi-axis SAM2 propagation.
(4) The ablation study supports the design. Naïvely reusing same-axis pseudo-labels degrades performance, whereas using predictions from other axes improves DSC. Detection-score-weighted fusion further improves performance, and multi-round cross-axis training provides additional gains before saturation. These results show that the improvement comes not merely from extra weak labels, but from complementary multi-axis guidance and detection-aware pseudo-label construction.
(5) Regarding SOTA comparison, the paper evaluates supervised, semi-supervised, weakly supervised, SAM-based, and SAM2-based baselines under the same split, crop size, prompt setting, and label-budget protocol. Baselines include 3D U-Net with SSL methods, SAM-Med3D, CPC-SAM, MedSAM, SAM2 zero-shot, and SAM2-Adapter variants. Across TDSC-ABUS and the in-house dataset, our method consistently achieves the best DSC; notably, using only 20 fully labeled volumes, it outperforms several baselines trained with all 80 fully labeled TDSC-ABUS volumes, supporting the label-efficiency claim.
(6) Regarding reproducibility and multi-round training, the paper specifies the SAM2 hiera-large backbone, trainable adapters and mask decoder, AdamW optimizer, learning rate, cosine decay, epochs, pseudo-label threshold, focal-loss parameters, and three WSL rounds. The training order is: axis-specific models are first trained with the fully labeled subset; in each WSL round, predictions and detection scores from the two non-target axes are fused to supervise the target-axis model; updated models are then used in the next round. The final model uses the best-performing single axis rather than an ensemble, so the multi-axis design improves WSL training without increasing inference-time complexity.

title: Mutual Distillation of Dual-Foundation Models for Semi-supervised PET/CT Segmentation
abstract:
Organ segmentation from PET/CT is critical for quantitative analysis and radiotherapy planning in oncology.
To ease the high annotation cost for PET/CT annotation, semi-supervised learning provides a practical and effective solution for developing deep models with limited labeled data.
Recent developments in visual foundation models have demonstrated remarkable adaptability with improved efficiency.
In this work, we propose a mutual distillation framework to seamlessly exploit both structural and functional foundation models, which act as modality-specific generalists for distillation of knowledge from structural CT and metabolic PET imaging.
By bridging the gap between the task-specific precision of specialist models and the segmentation priors of different generalist foundation models, we propose a mutual distillation framework MuDuo that synergistically exploits structural and functional foundation models SAM-Med3D for CT and SegAnyPET for PET to mutually distill knowledge to a lightweight student network. Our approach eliminates the need for manual prompts while maximizing the utility of unlabeled data for automatic segmentation, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the AutoPET dataset with only 5 labeled cases.Our source code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MuDuo/
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a mutual distillation framework (MuDuo) that synergistically distill both structural and functional knowledge from structural CT and metabolic PET images via two different foundation models to a lightweight student network for PET/CT organ segmentation. In addition, an IoU-based consensus filtering mechanism was introduced to exclude unreliable predictions and ensure high-quality pseudo supervision.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper is well-organized and easy to follow. The research problem of the anatomical-functional mismatch and cross-modal information fusion in semi-supervised segmentation is well-motivated. The mutual distillation framework that synergistically exploits structural and functional foundation models is somewhat innovative. Segmentation experiments contained the proposed MuDuo and several existing semi-supervised methods in three different data configurations. Ablation studies were implemented to validate the effectiveness of multiple components in the proposed MuDuo.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
It is natural that the combination of multiple foundation models yields superior segmentation performance, as demonstated by previous semi-supervised learning studies. Therefore, the paper has limited technical novelty. However, demonstrating that the combination of structural and functional foundation models leads to a better model, as shown in their experiments, provides valuable insights to the community. 
Segmentation experiments are conducted solely on an outdated U-Net backbone, leaving it unclear whether the observed improvements would hold for other architectures, such as transformers. 
The majority of the semi-supervised methods adopted are relatively dated, and only one is derived from the foundation model SAM.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper addresses the organ segmentation in whole-body PET/CT leveraging both structural and functional foundation model priors to guide learning of a lightweight student network. However, given that both the U-Net backbone and the comparative semi-supervised methods are outdated, the demonstrated effectiveness of the proposed method remains unconvincing. The paper could significantly benefit from experiments showcasing the effectiveness of the technique across different segmentation models, particularly in comparison to more recent foundation model-based methods.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I believe the authors’ rebuttal is acceptable, and the paper can be published in the MICCAI conference.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes MuDuo, a mutual distillation framework for semi-supervised PET/CT organ segmentation. Two frozen foundation models, SAM-Med3D for CT and SegAnyPET for PET, serve as modality-specific teachers that distill knowledge into a lightweight student U-Net. The student’s predictions serve as prompts to generate pseudo-labels, which are filtered by IoU-based consensus and fused via dynamic mixing for consistency regularization. Extensive evaluation on AutoPET with 5/10/20 labeled cases.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Strong motivation for dual-modality foundation models. Exploiting modality-specific foundation models (SAM-Med3D for structural CT, SegAnyPET for functional PET) is a natural and well-justified design for PET/CT segmentation. This goes beyond single-modality SAM-guided SSL.
2.The cross-modality IoU filtering is a principled quality control mechanism. The ablation confirms its importance.
3.The method outperforms all baselines across all label settings. The anonymous code link is provided, supporting reproducibility.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The title should be condensed to “PET/CT Organ Segmentation”, given that this article focuses on organ segmentation rather than the original tumor segmentation task of AutoPET. The corresponding statement of the article should also be clarified
2.Even the best result (49.56% Dice with 20 labels) is relatively low for organ segmentation. The paper should discuss why PET organ segmentation is so challenging.
3.The author state that “We allocate N cases for the training set and the remaining100 - N cases for the test set.” It is not reasonable to put the experiments on these three different sets of data in the table together. Besides, the results are reported as averages across all organs. Per-organ performance would reveal whether the method benefits uniformly or is biased toward certain organs.
4.Ablation study is not comprehensive. How about K=2 or more than 3? It is suggested to make a supplement to reflect the trade-off between performance and prompting efficiency.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

A well-structured framework that naturally extends foundation model-guided SSL to dual-modality PET/CT. The cross-modality consensus mechanism is effective. Despite there are still some limitations refer to weakness, they could be strengthened through rebuttal revision.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper targets semi-supervised 3D organ segmentation on PET/CT, a clinically important task with high annotation cost. The authors propose MuDuo, a mutual distillation framework that uses two frozen modality-specialized foundation models: SAM-Med3D for structural CT (mask prompts) and SegAnyPET for functional PET (multi-point prompts). The method generates high-quality pseudo-labels via cross-modality IoU consensus filtering and fuses them to supervise a lightweight student U-Net. Experiments on AutoPET show state-of-the-art performance under extremely low-label regimes (5/10/20 labeled cases), outperforming SemiSAM+, MT, CPS, and fully-supervised baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The task of PET/CT segmentation is clinically meaningful and important.
2.The method is built upon existing state-of-the-art foundation models.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The main contribution lies in extending foundation-model-assisted semi-supervised segmentation from a single-modality to a dual-modality PET/CT setting, incorporating dual teachers, IoU-based filtering, and pseudo-label fusion. However, the methodological novelty remains moderate.
2.The paper lacks a clear description of how the prompt generator is trained. Specifically, what data and supervision signals are used, and whether the generator is frozen or jointly optimized during training. As this module is central to pseudo-label generation for both teachers, this omission undermines reproducibility.
3.Several hyper-parameters are introduced, such as the IoU threshold for pseudo-label filtering and the number of point prompts. The manuscript does not clearly explain how these values were determined, which limits the practical applicability of the method.
4.The experimental validation is not thorough. Additional analyses (e.g., sensitivity studies, ablation on key components, or evaluation on more datasets) would be needed to support the claims.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Overall, the methodological contribution is limited. The experimental results are promising but not comprehensive.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have made detailed responses to my raised comments. I believe they have done their best to improve the work.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper is borderline (scores 3–5), with reviewers agreeing the idea is solid and results are promising, but pointing to a few fixable issues. The rebuttal should clarify the true novelty beyond combining two foundation models, strengthen the experimental evidence (e.g., generalization beyond U-Net and comparison to stronger baselines), address evaluation gaps (limited ablations, missing per-organ results, dataset setup), and improve method clarity (prompt generator, hyperparameters, training details). Overall, the feedback is constructive, and since at least one reviewer conditions their decision on the rebuttal, a focused response could tip the paper toward acceptance.

Following the rebuttal, all reviewers support acceptance of the paper. The Area Chair concurs with this recommendation and supports the paper’s acceptance.

All reviewers recommended a clear acceptance of this work after the rebuttal. The major contribution lies in the integration of both structural and functional foundation models. Experiments have demonstrated the effectiveness of model designs, and the rebuttal response clarifies some issues. The authors are encouraged to address all reviewer comments in the camera-ready version.

The proposed dual-modality mutual distillation framework (MuDuo) is recognized as a clinically meaningful and technically sound approach to semi-supervised PET/CT organ segmentation. While initial concerns were raised regarding the moderate technical novelty, backbone generalization, and specific parameter settings, consensus among reviewers post-rebuttal highlights that the authors have successfully resolved these queries through detailed empirical clarifications.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank all reviewers for their constructive comments. We especially appreciate R3’s concerns on novelty, reproducibility, hyper-parameter justification, and validation scope. We agree that several key designs should be clarified and will revise the manuscript accordingly.
Regarding novelty, MuDuo should not be positioned as a new generic SSL paradigm. Its precise contribution is a PET/CT-specific dual-teacher semi-supervised framework for organ segmentation. Rather than simply combining two foundation models, MuDuo queries modality-specialized teachers in complementary ways: SAM-Med3D uses CT-side mask prompts to exploit anatomical priors, while SegAnyPET uses PET-side point prompts to exploit metabolic uptake priors. Their outputs are selected by cross-modal IoU consensus and fused as pseudo labels for consistency learning. We will delimit this contribution and avoid over-generalized claims.
We apologize for the unclear description of the prompt generator. In our implementation, it is a lightweight U-Net trained on the labeled subset with organ annotations before the semi-supervised stage. During mutual distillation, the prompt generator, SAM-Med3D, and SegAnyPET are frozen, and only the student model is optimized. For CT, it produces class probability maps as mask prompts for SAM-Med3D. For PET, it produces coarse logits; each predicted organ region is smoothed, and the top-K foreground locations are sampled as point prompts for SegAnyPET. We will add details on its supervision, freezing strategy, and calling order.
Regarding hyper-parameters, MuDuo does not rely on a manually tuned absolute IoU threshold. The fixed tau=0.5 is only an ablation baseline. Our final strategy is adaptive top-50% IoU filtering, where CT/PET predictions are ranked by cross-modal agreement and only the most reliable half is retained. This is more robust to organ size and case difficulty. Table 2 supports this design: adaptive top-50% improves Dice and reduces HD95 over both no filtering and fixed tau=0.5.K=3 is motivated by heterogeneous PET uptake, where one point may cover only the high-uptake core. Table 2 also shows that multi-point prompting improves both Dice and HD95 over K=1.
Regarding validation, we agree that broader evaluation would further strengthen the work. Still, the manuscript includes 5/10/20 low-label settings, PET-only and PET/CT baselines, four metrics, qualitative comparisons, and ablations on teacher configuration, IoU filtering, and prompting. We will clarify that these ablations verify structural-functional complementarity, improved pseudo-label reliability, and better PET-teacher guidance. We will also state the evidence scope: the experiments are based on an organ-annotated AutoPET subset and a 3D U-Net student. Although MuDuo is conceptually compatible with other backbones, we will not claim empirical generalization beyond the reported experiments.
We thank R2 for the comments on title, task description, data split, and absolute Dice. We will revise the title and task description to focus on PET/CT organ segmentation rather than the original AutoPET lesion segmentation task. We will clarify that methods are compared under the same protocol within each label setting, and avoid implying identical test sets across 5/10/20 settings if this is not the case. We will also discuss why the absolute Dice is modest: whole-body PET organ segmentation is challenging due to low PET resolution, blurred boundaries, heterogeneous uptake, uneven organ visibility, and PET/CT spatial mismatch. Thus, our main evidence lies in consistent relative improvements and boundary-metric gains under low-label regimes.
Finally, we accept R1’s concern regarding backbone and baseline scope. We will moderate the related claims: MuDuo shows that cross-modal foundation-model consensus improves semi-supervised PET/CT organ segmentation under the current U-Net student setting, but we will not overstate gains across all architectures.

title: Mutually Promoted Medical Image Segmentation and Classification via Prompt-Driven Interaction
abstract:
The fine-tuned Segment Anything Model has shown strong potential for medical image segmentation, yet it remains class agnostic and cannot provide reliable categorical information alongside the predicted mask. This limits interpretability and increases the risk of selecting anatomically implausible regions when boundaries are ambiguous. Meanwhile, existing medical frameworks often treat segmentation and classification as separate processes, which weakens feature interaction and reduces robustness across diverse organs, lesions, and imaging modalities.
We present BiMI, a mutually promoted framework that integrates a fine-tuned Segment Anything Model with a hierarchical classification branch. To regularize fine-grained recognition under data scarcity, BiMI introduces a Coarse2Fine Matrix that models hierarchical dependencies and enforces semantic consistency between coarse and fine predictions. To strengthen feature interaction between recognition and segmentation, BiMI further adopts a Global2local Feature Enhancement module that aligns global context with local spatial cues. In addition, BiMI incorporates a Text Guidance module that expands the predicted coarse and fine labels into a compact structured description using a frozen language model, and encodes it into a semantic embedding with a frozen text encoder. The embedding conditions structure-aware candidate selection to rank multi-mask hypotheses within the box prompt, improving anatomical plausibility and segmentation stability.
Experiments on six public medical datasets covering CT, MRI, dermoscopy, and endoscopy demonstrate that BiMI consistently improves hierarchical classification and achieves competitive segmentation performance against strong U-Net and SAM-based baselines, with clear gains on several challenging benchmarks.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents a framework integrating a fine-tuned Segment Anything Model (SAM) with hierarchical classification, bridging the gap between image segmentation and fine grained medical recognition. It addresses SAM’s class-agnostic limitations, achieving excellent classification and segmentation performance against U-Net and SAM-based baselines.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper provides a novel integrated SAM-classification framework (C2FM, GFE, SACS modules) with well structured methodology and ablation. It demonstrates strong validation with benchmark methods on 6 datasets, and shows competitive performance results. Overall, there is clinical potential as the method potentially improves interpretability.
reviews.text_weaknesses: Limitations include the reliance on manual box prompts, rather than a fully automated and scalable clinical workflow. There is incomplete evaluation (eg metrics limited to DSC/IOU), and the classification results are somewhat weak on key datasets (such as AbdomenCT1K). SACS is presented as one of the major contributions but not isolated in the ablation (bundled within TG). There are also some missing elements for reproducibility, e. g. the LLM is never identified or cited.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The idea is well-motivated and relevant. The evaluation is broad, covering six public datasets across different imaging modalities (CT, MRI, dermoscopy, endoscopy). Performance results are competitive. There are some weaknesses and aspects requiring clarification but do not overall undermine the core contribution.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal clarifies some but not entirely all of the concerns.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a mutually reinforcing framework called BiMI, which integrates a prompt-based segmentation model built on the Segment Anything Model (SAM) with a hierarchical classification branch for medical image analysis. BiMI introduces three core components: (1) a Coarse-to-Fine Matrix (C2FM) to model hierarchical dependencies and regularize fine-grained recognition under data-scarce conditions; (2) a Global-to-Local Feature Enhancement (GFE) module to align the global context from the SAM encoder with local spatial cues; and (3) a Structure-Aware Candidate Selection (SACS) module, which leverages a frozen language model and text encoder to generate semantic embeddings, and then uses these embeddings to rank multiple mask hypotheses within bounding-box prompts. Extensive experiments on six public medical datasets, demonstrate that, compared with strong baseline models, BiMI achieves competitive segmentation performance while substantially improving the accuracy of hierarchical classification.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Innovative mutually reinforcing framework:
By explicitly modeling the bidirectional interaction between segmentation and hierarchical classification, the proposed
BiMI
framework effectively addresses the issue of semantic inconsistency and improves the anatomical plausibility of medical image segmentation.
2.Technical contributions:
The Coarse-to-Fine Matrix (C2FM) provides a soft regularization mechanism to alleviate data scarcity in fine-grained classification. The Global-to-Local Feature Enhancement (GFE) module successfully aligns global and local features. In addition, the Structure-Aware Candidate Selection (SACS) module cleverly leverages text-guided semantic priors to resolve the inherent multi-mask ambiguity of SAM.
3.Comprehensive experimental validation:
The authors conduct extensive experiments on six diverse public datasets covering multiple imaging modalities (CT, MRI, dermoscopy, and endoscopy) and targets (organs and lesions). The results demonstrate that BiMI outperforms both U-Net-based baselines and recent SAM-based baselines on both segmentation and classification tasks.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Dependence on manual bounding-box prompts:
The current framework relies on manually provided bounding-box prompts for localization, which limits its feasibility in fully automatic clinical applications. Although the authors mention adaptive bounding-box refinement as a direction for future work, they should more carefully discuss the practical clinical relevance of manual prompting compared with fully automatic segmentation pipelines, and possibly consider a user study to justify this design choice.
2.Computational overhead and complexity:
Integrating a frozen large language model (LLM), a text encoder (CLIP), and the SAM architecture introduces substantial computational complexity. The paper lacks a detailed analysis of inference time, memory consumption, and overall computational cost in comparison with simpler baseline models such as nnU-Net or standard SAM.
3.Lack of discussion of failure cases:
Although the quantitative results are strong, the paper would benefit from a more in-depth qualitative analysis of failure cases.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Please refer to the summary and the weakness sections.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: My concerns are mostly addressed, and I am still positive with this work after rebuttal. I am happy to recommend an acceptance.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes BiMI, which is a medical imaging framework that integrates cue-based segmentation with hierarchical classification. The authors construct the C2FM to establish a transition matrix between coarse and fine classes, and use KL divergence to constrain fine class predictions to conform to the coarse class distribution. The GFE contains several designs: (a) SA, (b) FA, (c) Auxiliary Binary Classifier, (d) Cross-Attention Fusion. The SACS uses text to guide the mask selection.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.This method achieves a unified framework for multi-task collaborative optimization and cross-modal knowledge fusion through an innovative bidirectional mutually reinforcing architecture of segmentation and classification, a hierarchical semantic constraint C2FM module, and text-guided anatomical rationality verification. 
2.The proposed feature alignment mechanism retains global discriminative power, avoiding over-alignment. Cross-attention enables dynamic information interaction.
3.The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The manuscript does not follow the MICCAI26 format.
2.The major limitation of this methos is the requirement of manual provision of bounding boxes to locate the target region. The paper acknowledges this in the Conclusion but does not provide a solution.
3.Insufficient validation of the necessity of the two-stage training strategy. Why freeze C2FM training for 50 epochs before joint training in the second stage? Has end-to-end training been attempted? What is the performance difference?
4.The compared SAM-based methods (MedSAM, SAM-Med2D, etc.) are all from 2023-2024.Lack of comparison with stronger baselines like SAM2 and MedSAM2.5.Insufficient interpretability of the SACS module. Definitions of descriptors (compactness, solidity, connectivity, gradient entropy) are not given in the text.
6.As can be seen from Table 3, all performance aspects decreased after adding GFE. So what is the point of adding this module?
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

As described in the weakness.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
Thank you for the authors’ rebuttal. However, my main concerns remain insufficiently addressed.
The rebuttal states that the same box-prompt protocol is used as SAM-style baselines, but this does not resolve the limitation of requiring manual localization.
The explanation of the two-stage training strategy is still largely empirical. The authors state that end-to-end coupling may lead to unstable training, but no quantitative evidence or ablation is provided to support this claim.
The rebuttal regarding SAM2/MedSAM2 is not fully convincing. Even if these models are designed for video or 3D propagation settings, they represent stronger and more recent SAM-family baselines. Without comparison to them, it is difficult to assess the actual competitiveness of the proposed framework.
Although the authors clarify that GFE without FA causes degradation, the ablation still shows that the gain of the full design over SA+TG+C2FM is marginal. Moreover, since GFE is presented as an individual innovation module, the fact that it substantially degrades performance unless coupled with another alignment module raises concerns about its intrinsic reliability and robustness.
Overall, while the rebuttal clarifies some implementation details, it does not adequately address the core concerns. Therefore, I maintain my negative recommendation.

meta_reviews.text:
Scores are 4/4/2, with two reviewers recommending weak accept and one PhD-student reviewer recommending reject “independent of rebuttal” on the basis of format non-compliance, the GFE-hurts-performance ablation, missing modern baselines, and insufficient training-strategy validation. The paper is borderline-leaning-positive, but several of R3’s concerns — particularly the GFE ablation contradiction and the format compliance — are concrete enough that a credible rebuttal is required to retain the weak accepts. The paper is invited for rebuttal; authors should prioritize (a) a direct, principled explanation of the GFE ablation result that shows performance decreasing when GFE is added, (b) at least one comparison against SAM 2 / MedSAM 2 or a clear justification for omitting them, (c) a properly isolated SACS ablation and an end-to-end vs. two-stage training comparison, (d) computational-cost analysis and identification of the LLM used in SACS, and (e) clarification of the ethics concern flagged by R1.

Reviewers agreed that the bidirectional segmentation-classification framework is novel and well-motivated, the three modules (C2FM, GFE, SACS) are clean, the multi-modality evaluation across six datasets is comprehensive, and the clinical potential for interpretability is meaningful. They raised several concerns: (1) reliance on manual bounding-box prompts limits clinical deployment in fully automatic workflows; (2) computational overhead from integrating LLM + CLIP + SAM is not analyzed; (3) recent stronger SAM-family baselines (SAM2, MedSAM2) are missing; (4) the two-stage training strategy is not validated against end-to-end coupling; (5) SACS is bundled with TG in ablation, making its individual contribution unclear; (6) GFE alone (without FA) degrades performance, raising intrinsic-reliability concerns; (7) manuscript format issues (running header, references vs. bibliography); (8) the LLM is not explicitly identified or cited; and (9) failure case analysis is missing.After rebuttal, the authors clarified that GFE’s degradation occurs only without the FA alignment component (the full design achieves the best 79.1/87.7 IoU/DSC), justified the two-stage training based on instability of direct C2FM end-to-end coupling, argued SAM2/MedSAM2 target different protocols (video/3D propagation) orthogonal to BiMI’s contribution, renamed TG to TG/SACS to clarify the ablation, explained that the LLM/CLIP pipeline is offline (no per-image LLM call, no patient data exposure), and confirmed the box-prompt protocol matches SAM baselines. However, the most critical reviewer maintained that the manual-prompt limitation remains, the two-stage training justification is empirical without quantitative ablation, the SAM2/MedSAM2 absence remains a real comparison gap, and GFE’s dependence on FA raises intrinsic-reliability concerns. Final scores are split (Accept, Accept, Reject). Overall, the AC believes that the merits outweigh the drawbacks and recommend accept.

After rebuttal the reviews stand at two leaning accept and one reject.
The rebuttal does clarify the format and SACS/TG notation issues and gives a self-consistent account of the GFE+FA design, and the two positive reviewers are satisfied.
However, the concerns that bear on the paper’s contribution remain. The method is one of many incremental SAM box-prompt adaptations, and the ablation shows the full design improves only marginally over SA+TG+C2FM, with GFE actually degrading performance unless paired with FA — which weakens the case for it as a standalone contribution. 
Given the limited novelty and marginal gains relative to existing SAM-prompt methods, I lean toward rejection despite the rebuttal’s clarifications, as a borderline case.

Two reviewers recommended acceptance after rebuttal, recognizing the innovative framework and comprehensive validation. The authors’ rebuttal partially addressed R3’s concerns. Although some minor concerns such as relying on manual box prompts and comparison with SAM2 remain, I believe they don’t overweigh the contribution.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the AC and reviewers for their time and constructive feedback. We are encouraged by their acknowledgement of the novelty and the superior results of our work. Below we do our best to resolve the key concerns raised by them.
1.Format. We apologize for the confusing running header. We used the official MICCAI 2026 template without modifying margins, font, spacing, or page limit. We will correct the missing short title.
2.GFE. The performance drop in Table 3 occurs only for GFE without FA (i.e., unaligned global feature injection), not the complete design. This verifies our hypothesis in Sec. 2.2: direct global-local fusion may cause semantic misalignment. SA+TG+C2FM gives 78.8/87.3 IoU/DSC; unaligned GFE drops to 73.9/85.3; adding FA gives the best 79.1/87.7.These results do prove the effectiveness of our method.
3.Training. C2FM is not a trainable branch. It serves as a coarse-to-fine prior for the classifier. According to our experience, direct end-to-end coupling of C2FM and other modules would result in unstable training behavior. We believe this is because early inaccurate class predictions can mislead mask selection, while early coarse predictions also introduce noisy priors for fine classification. Thus, we first stabilize the segmentation-related components and classifier, and then integrate them via C2FM, GFE/FA, and SACS.
4.SAM2/MedSAM2.Our comparison focuses on representative U-Net-based and medical SAM-based baselines under the same 2D slice-wise box-prompt protocol. SAM2/MedSAM2 are mainly designed for image-video or 3D propagation settings; while their native protocol defines different tasks, forcing single-slice inference would not reflect their intended design. As for BiMI, its contribution is the segmentation-classification interaction mechanism, which is orthogonal to the SAM backbone.
5.SACS/TG. Sorry for the unclear notation. In Table 3, TG is actually TG with SACS (or TG/SACS) rather than an independent text-only module: it denotes the text-guided candidate-selection path implemented by SACS. Text embeddings are mapped to structural weights. SACS combines them with mask descriptors and SAM’s IoU prediction to rank candidates and select the final mask. Because text is not injected into the decoder, TG without SACS is undefined in our architecture. Our early trial shows that direct text-feature concatenation did not work in practice, which motivates SACS. In Table 3, the TG on/off comparison corresponds to the SACS-path on/off ablation, improving IoU/DSC from 78.0/86.1 to 78.5/86.9.We will rename TG as TG/SACS.
6.Cost, LLM, and ethics. Our BiMI’s online overhead mainly comes from the classifier, GFE/FA, and SACS candidate-mask scoring. The language step is offline: GPT-4 generates coarse/fine label-pair descriptions once, and CLIP encodes them into a precomputed embedding bank. At inference, BiMI only retrieves the embedding for the predicted label pair and applies descriptor-based ranking to SAM candidates, with no per-image LLM call. Apart from SAM and the classifier, the language-guided SACS overhead is limited to embedding lookup, mask-descriptor computation, and score fusion. The LLM receives no patient images, masks, metadata, or clinical notes, and is not used for diagnosis or treatment decisions. Therefore, its use does not incur patient-data privacy or LLM-driven clinical-decision risks.
7.Prompting and evaluation. We acknowledge that BiMI is not fully automatic. We use the same box-prompt interface as SAM-style baselines, adding no extra localization burden. DSC/IoU were used because they are consistently reported across the six datasets for fair comparison. AbdomenCT1K is difficult for all classifiers due to similar slice-level CT appearances, but BiMI remains best under the same protocol.

title: MUX-USCT: A Noise-Robust Neural Network for Ultrasound Computed Tomography
abstract:
Deep neural networks (DNNs) have shown strong potential
for ultrasound computed tomography (USCT) reconstruction in ideal
noise-free environments, yet existing DNNs are vulnerable to the noisy
conditions in clinical practice, as they equally treat inputs that suffer
mild, moderate, or severe noise. More challenging, the distributions of
noise shift along with the environment, indicating the less effectiveness of
noise-aware training, which injects a specific noise distribution into the
training data. We rethink these challenges and observe that the DNN
models can become more robust to noise if we know the noise sources
and filter them out. This filtering operation is very alike the Multiplexers
(or MUX), a fundamental combinational circuit in digital logic design.
However, the challenge here is that noise can happen randomly during
inference; as a result, the manually predefined MUX cannot work. To ad-
dress these challenges, we propose MUX-USCT, a novel encoder-decoder
DNN architecture that encodes the known acoustic acquisition geometry
with an “adaptive MUX” that can automatically identify and filter noise,
where the attention mechanism is applied in reconstructing the speed-of-
sound map. On the OpenPros benchmark, MUX-USCT reaches 6.88 m/s
MAE with 17% fewer parameters than the leading baseline with 7.65 m/s
of MAE. Under simulated clinical noise, it remains stable across diverse
degradation types that cause geometry-agnostic baselines to fail. Results
show that the attention distributions in MUX-USCT reveal patterns that
shift in response to transducer signal degradation.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes MUX-USCT, a geometry-aware deep neural network for robust ultrasound computed tomography (USCT) reconstruction. The key idea is to mimic a hardware multiplexer (MUX) in a learned manner: a path-aware encoder uses transducer attention to assess the information of structured acquisition channels, while a position-aware decoder uses per-pixel cross-attention to route path-region tokens back to spatial locations. Within the scope of the paper’s experiments, the method demonstrates strong robustness under several simulated clinical degradation scenarios, despite being trained only on clean data, and it achieves better clean-data accuracy with fewer parameters than the main baselines reported in the manuscript.
reviews.text_strengths:
6.1 A major strength of the paper is that it does not treat USCT inputs as a generic flattened feature tensor. Instead, it explicitly preserves path identity and transducer identity, and builds the
network around the known acquisition geometry. This is a meaningful architectural contribution, because it aligns the model design with the physics of the sensing system rather than relying purely on generic image-network priors. The MUX analogy is conceptually clear and helps motivate why selective routing may improve robustness. 
6.2 The quantitative and qualitative results are convincing within the simulated benchmark used in the paper. Table 2 shows that MUX-USCT outperforms InversionNet, ViT-Inversion, and Inv-FT on both clean data and the combined S4 degradation scenario, while using fewer parameters. Figures 4 and 5 further show that the method remains substantially more stable than the
baselines across source noise, receiver noise, coupling loss, and combined degradation. This is an important empirical result, especially because Inv-FT is trained with noise augmentation whereas MUX-USCT is not. 
6.3 The attention analysis in Figure 6 is one of the most interesting parts of the paper. The encoder attention maps suggest that corrupted transducers tend to receive lower weights, while the decoder visualizations indicate tissue- or location-dependent routing behavior. Even if these analyses are not yet sufficient to establish clinical diagnostics, they do provide useful insight into what the model may be learning and how the geometry-aware design differs from geometry-agnostic baselines. 
6.4 Table 3 shows a meaningful separation of roles between the encoder and decoder attention modules. Removing encoder attention causes a modest clean-data drop but a large robustness loss under source corruption, while removing decoder cross-attention significantly harms clean reconstruction quality. This supports the claim that the encoder mainly contributes to channel selection robustness and the decoder mainly contributes to spatial reconstruction fidelity.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
7.1 Although the manuscript does not present real-world clinical validation, it makes several application-facing claims, including assisting specialists “in the field” and using attention weights for “clinical monitoring” and transducer health indication. Since all experiments are conducted on OpenPros FDTD simulations with simulated degradations, the current evidence more directly supports robustness on a realistic in-silico benchmark than validated phantom, exvivo, or in vivo clinical utility. I therefore recommend tempering the clinical-use wording, or alternatively adding at least phantom / ex vivo / in vivo validation to better support these application-oriented claims. 
7.2 The choice M=5 is currently fixed without sensitivity analysis, even though MMM directly controls the number of path tokens and therefore affects both representational capacity and
computational cost. I therefore believe the paper would be stronger if it at least included a sensitivity study over MMM. In addition, because the method is presented as being
parameterized by acquisition geometry and the conclusion suggests broader applicability to synthetic-aperture USCT systems, a brief scaling discussion — or, if feasible, a small pilot
experiment—on changed array density / field of view would better support that broader claim. 
7.3 The simulated degradation scenarios are clinically motivated and reasonable as a first step, but some are still simplified. In particular, S3 models coupling loss only as 10–50% amplitude
attenuation, whereas real ultrasound propagation and coupling conditions can also involve phase aberration, frequency-dependent attenuation, and more complex wavefront distortion. In addition, the current study does not examine geometry perturbation, calibration drift, or slight probe deformation. These omissions do not undermine the main contribution, but they do mean that the present evidence is strongest for the four simulated scenarios in Table 1 rather than for a broader range of real-world perturbations. 
7.4 The current comparison mainly shows that a baseline fine-tuned on S1-style source corruption transfers poorly to mismatched degradations such as S2–S4.This is a meaningful finding, but it is somewhat narrower than a general statement about the limits of noise-aware training as a whole. I therefore suggest either adding a stronger multi-noise-trained baseline, or tempering the claim to emphasize the limitation of single-distribution noise-aware fine-tuning under distribution shift. 
7.5 The explanation in Section 2—that corrupted elements produce keys that fall outside the learned clean-signal subspace and therefore receive lower softmax weights—is intuitive and
consistent with the empirical results, but it is still best understood as a heuristic interpretation rather than a formal guarantee. I therefore suggest presenting this mechanism a bit more
cautiously. If feasible, the paper would be further strengthened by adding one stronger stress test, such as a more challenging out-of-distribution corruption setting or a case where a larger fraction of channels are jointly degraded, to better probe the boundary of this explanation. 
7.6 The reported results are mostly point estimates. The paper would be stronger if it included standard deviations, confidence intervals, multiple random seeds, or statistical significance
testing, especially for Table 2 and the ablation results in Table 3.This would help clarify whether the observed improvements are consistently reproducible. 
7.7 A notable missing comparison is against simpler geometry-aware or rule-based channel-selection baselines. This omission is particularly important because the paper’s own motivation experiment in Fig. 2 shows that manual MUX-inspired reweighting already yields large gains under corrupted inputs. Given that result, the current evaluation does not fully disentangle how much of the improvement comes from the general idea of structured channel/path reweighting, and how much specifically comes from the proposed learned encoder-decoder attention design. The paper would therefore be stronger if it compared against at least one simple heuristic baseline, such as signal-quality-based channel masking/reweighting, path-level gating, or another lightweight structured routing method.

Computed Tomography. arXiv, 2025.
[R2] Wu, Y. , Lin, Y. InversionNet: An Efficient and Accurate Data-Driven Full Waveform Inversion. 
IEEE Transactions on Computational Imaging, 2020.
[R3] Virieux, J. , Operto, S. An Overview of Full-Waveform Inversion in Exploration Geophysics. 
Geophysics, 2009.
[R4] Jain, S. , Wallace, B. C. Attention is not Explanation. NAACL, 2019.

I rated this paper as Weak Accept because I found the core idea both meaningful and reasonably well supported within the paper’s experimental scope, but not yet strong enough for a clear accept. The main positive factor is the geometry-aware architectural design: instead of flattening USCT measurements into a generic tensor, the method explicitly preserves path and transducer identity and uses a path-aware encoder plus a position-aware decoder to perform learned selective routing. This is a well-motivated contribution for USCT, where acquisition geometry is physically meaningful rather than incidental. Empirically, the paper is also strong on its chosen benchmark: Table 2 shows that MUX-USCT improves over InversionNet, ViT-Inversion, and Inv-FT on both clean data and the combined degradation scenario S4, while also using fewer parameters;
Fig. 4 and Fig. 5 further suggest substantially better robustness across source noise, receiver noise, coupling loss, and combined degradation. I also found the attention analysis and ablation study useful: Fig. 6 provides some insight into how the model may be downweighting corrupted channels and routing information spatially, while Table 3 supports a meaningful division of labor between encoder attention for robustness and decoder cross-attention for reconstruction fidelity. At the same time, several limitations kept my score at the borderline level. Most importantly, the evidence is still entirely based on OpenPros FDTD simulations with simulated degradations, so I
do not think the current results fully justify some of the more application-facing claims about clinical monitoring, troubleshooting in the field, or broader practical utility. In addition, the robustness evidence is strongest only for the four simulated scenarios studied in Table 1, some degradation models remain simplified, and the comparison against noise-aware training is somewhat narrow because Inv-FT is fine-tuned only on S1-style source corruption. I also think the paper would be stronger with a sensitivity analysis for the fixed choice of M=5, some discussion or experiment on changed acquisition geometry, statistical reporting beyond single point estimates, and at least one simpler geometry-aware or rule-based channel-selection baseline, especially given the strong manual reweighting result already shown in Fig. 2.Overall, I think the
paper is marginally above threshold because the method is well aligned with the sensing physics and the simulation results are promising, but my support would depend on the rebuttal appropriately narrowing the claims and clarifying these missing validations.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: Inspired by multiplexers in digital logic, the paper starts from the observation that, under signal degradation, manually filtering out noisy acquisition paths can substantially improve prostate USCT speed-of-sound (SoS) reconstruction. Building on this intuition, the authors propose MUX-USCT, an encoder-decoder framework that explicitly encodes the physical acquisition geometry and learns to identify and suppress noisy channels. Unlike conventional networks that treat all input channels equally, MUX-USCT uses a path-aware encoder in which attention over transducer elements acts like learned MUX select signals, and compresses each path into regional tokens that capture different acoustic subregions. A position-aware decoder then allows each spatial location to attend to all path-region tokens according to its geometry. Trained on paired clean USCT signals and corresponding ground-truth SoS maps, the model shows stronger robustness across several simulated noise scenarios while also providing interpretable attention maps.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper proposes a well-motivated architecture that explicitly incorporates physical acquisition geometry into the reconstruction framework, together with a position-aware decoder for spatially selective path routing. This is a meaningful departure from geometry-agnostic designs and improves both interpretability and reconstruction quality.
2.The model is trained on paired clean USCT signals and ground-truth SoS maps, and uses the gap between intact-signal statistics and corrupted channels to naturally suppress noisy features at inference time. This gives it stronger robustness across several simulated noise settings without requiring noise-augmented training.
3.The attention visualizations are a notable strength, as they reveal transducer quality estimates and tissue-dependent spatial routing, which could help USCT specialists troubleshoot acquisition issues in practice.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The clinical relevance remains limited because the open dataset is collected and used for training only on phantoms. Although several clinically motivated noise types are simulated, real in vivo conditions are much more complex, involving multiple scattering, reflection, diffraction, and other effects. Even without in vivo ground truth, the paper should at least show in vivo reconstructions and compare them with a classical method such as FWI.
2.The claim of training on “clean” data is somewhat overstated. Since the data are acquired on a real system, they inevitably contain some native noise; the main difference is that the simulated degradations are stronger than the usual system noise. More importantly, it is unclear whether this training strategy would transfer well to realistic settings where the acquisition itself is already highly noisy. The paper does not show that the method can be trained on noisy data while retaining denoising ability.
3.In Table 1, the phrase “10–50% amplitude attenuation” is not precise enough. It should be clarified whether this attenuation is defined through path, transducer, or by some other rule.
4.In Fig. 4, for S1 and S2, the proposed method sometimes appears to perform better as the noise level increases, which is counterintuitive. This raises the possibility that the model is better at detecting severe corruption than moderate corruption. The paper should provide a clearer explanation for this behavior and discuss it explicitly as a limitation of the method.
5.The paper does not provide sufficient visualization or discussion of the bone-related results, and the corresponding training strategy is also unclear.

meta_reviews.text: Given that all three reviewers have recommended acceptance, I am pleased to congratulate the authors on the acceptance of their paper at this phase. Despite a consensus among three positive reviews, two of the reviewers have explicitly stated that their decisions of weak acceptance are conditional. As such, the authors are invited to response after provisional acceptance to clarify the missing details in the experimental validations raised by R1 and R2.Given the limited space, the authors are advised to prioritize the most critical points and allocate their response strategically to maximize the effectiveness of their reply.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers. All three recognized the core contribution: a geometry-aware architecture aligned with USCT sensing physics (R1-6.1, R2-S1), strong robustness without noise augmentation (R1-6.2, R2-S2), interpretable attention (R1-6.3, R2-S3), and a well-supported encoder-decoder division of labor (R1-6.4). We address the major concerns below.
[1] Scope of Claims (R1-7.1, R1-7.5, R2-W1)
R1 and R2 note that clinical-facing language exceeds the simulation-only evidence. We agree. In the camera-ready, we will reframe “clinical monitoring” and “troubleshooting in the field” as potential future applications, and clarify that the attention filtering is an empirical observation, not a guarantee.
On in vivo validation (R2-W1): in vivo USCT data with ground-truth SoS maps is extremely scarce; OpenPros [17] is the largest publicly available prostate USCT benchmark. In vivo validation is an important next step.
[2] Clarifications on Data and Experimental Details (R2-W2, W3, W4, W5)
R2-W2 (“clean data” overstated): While OpenPros [17] phantoms are derived from real clinical MRI/CT and ex vivo specimens, the waveform data (network input) is generated via FDTD simulation and contains no sensor or system noise. “Clean-data training” accurately describes our setup. R2 also asks whether the method transfers when training data itself is noisy. MUX-USCT’s robustness comes from structural design (attention learns to weight channels by informativeness) rather than from specific properties of the training noise distribution. Training on noisy data is a relevant direction, but clean-data training is the standard protocol on this benchmark.
R2-W3 (S3 definition): Coupling loss is applied per-source element. Each degraded source’s waveform amplitude is scaled by a random factor in [0.5, 0.9] (i.e., 10-50% attenuation as stated in Table 1).
R2-W4 (Fig. 4, counterintuitive behavior): This occurs in S1/S2 where the x-axis is noise intensity, not the count of corrupted channels. Stronger noise on a fixed set of channels makes them easier to detect and suppress (Eq. 1), while the pool of clean channels remains unchanged. S3’s x-axis is the number of degraded sources, so increasing it reduces usable information regardless of detection. Moderate corruption remains harder to detect, which we acknowledge as a limitation.
R2-W5 (bone): Fig. 6b directly shows tissue-dependent routing: bone relies more on cross-probe paths (TA->TR, TR->TA) while prostate draws from same-probe reflection (TR->TR). Fig. 5 confirms bone boundary preservation across all scenarios. No tissue-specific training strategy is used.
[3] Baseline Comparisons (R1-7.4, R1-7.7)
R1-7.4 (Inv-FT): We agree that Inv-FT’s S1-only fine-tuning makes its poor S2-S4 transfer partly expected, and we will narrow the claim accordingly. More broadly, real-world noise types and distributions are unpredictable, so exhaustive noise-augmented fine-tuning is not a scalable solution. This motivates MUX-USCT’s design: the model should be structurally adaptive rather than reliant on anticipating every degradation at training time.
R1-7.7 (simpler baselines): The manual reweighting in Fig. 2 requires oracle knowledge of corrupted transducers, which is unavailable in practice. It motivates the approach but is not deployable; MUX-USCT’s contribution is making this selection learned and adaptive.
[4] Additional Analyses (R1-7.2, R1-7.6, R1-7.3, R3)
We appreciate these suggestions. On M (R1-7.2): M=5 already achieves SOTA on both clean and noisy data with 17% fewer parameters (Table 2); a sensitivity study would be a useful follow-up. On statistics (R1-7.6): we will extend evaluation to the full test set and report standard deviations in the camera-ready. On degradation complexity (R1-7.3) and additional ablations (R3): these are natural extensions we intend to pursue. Finally, we intend to release our code upon acceptance to support reproducibility.

title: MVDA-Net: Multi-View Dual-Alignment Network for 3D Carotid Artery Segmentation
abstract: Accurate segmentation of the carotid artery from computed tomography angiography (CTA) images is essential to manage atherosclerotic vascular disease. However, studies specifically targeting carotid artery segmentation in CTA imaging remain relatively limited, and existing 3D segmentation methods face significant challenges when applied to this task, including discontinuous lesion distribution, extreme foreground scarcity, inadequate capture of the vessel wall’s low-contrast subtle double-edge boundaries and irregular calcification contours. Moreover, these methods suffer from insufficient spatial and semantic complementarity modeling in encoder-decoder feature alignment. To address these limitations, we propose a novel Multi-View Dual-Alignment Network (MVDA-Net) that integrates three key innovations: (1) a Spatially-Aware Orthogonal Projection (SAOP) module that enhances global context modeling and representation of small vascular structures through multi-view projection across orthogonal anatomical planes with spatial attention; (2) a Hierarchical Inverted Attention Refinement (HIAR) module that propagates boundary-enhancing inverted attention from deep features to shallow layers for progressive boundary refinement; and (3) a Synergistic Feature Alignment (SFA) module that suppresses redundancy and enhances complementarity through feature differences while modeling semantic relationships via summation for effective spatial-semantic alignment. Comprehensive experiments on one in-house carotid artery CTA dataset (named CA) and three public benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed MVDA-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance. The code for MVDA-Net is publicly available at: https://github.com/Vi-cai/MVDA-Net.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes the Multi-View Dual-Alignment Network (MVDA-Net) for 3D carotid artery segmentation in CTA images, achieving state-of-the-art performance via three modules: SAOP for multi-view projection, HIAR for inverted attention-based boundary refinement, and SFA for spatial–semantic feature alignment.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper proposes MVDA-Net for 3D carotid artery segmentation in CTA, addressing challenges such as discontinuous lesions and severe foreground scarcity.
It introduces three complementary modules: SAOP for multi-view contextual modeling, HIAR for boundary refinement via inverted attention, and SFA for spatial–semantic feature alignment.
The method is evaluated on a newly curated clinical dataset and multiple public benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The use of multi-view pooling and axis projection for handling foreground–background imbalance and capturing global context is not new, as similar ideas appear in prior works (e. g. , APAUNet, LW-CTrans). Likewise, attention mechanisms for boundary refinement have already been explored (e. g. , BMANet), reducing the originality of the proposed design.
2.It is not clearly specified how feature maps (e. g. , F_i and F_(i+1)) are defined and selected. In particular, the indexing iis not justified, and the distinction between low-level and high-level features remains ambiguous.
3.There is a task–evaluation mismatch. Although the modules (SAOP, HIAR, SFA) are claimed to be designed for carotid artery segmentation, it is unclear how well they generalize to other organs or lesions. Moreover, the evaluation on datasets such as MSD Lung, MSD Spleen, and BraTS is not fully aligned with the primary task of 3D carotid artery segmentation stated in the paper.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Several core components extend existing techniques, such as multi-view pooling and attention-based boundary refinement. Although the method is well-motivated and achieves good empirical results, concerns remain regarding the clarity of the architecture and the consistency between the targeted task and the chosen evaluation datasets.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: While the authors provide some clarifications, the rebuttal does not sufficiently address the main concerns. The claimed novelty remains limited, as the core ideas remain close to well-established strategies, and the rebuttal does not sufficiently demonstrate a new mechanism or substantial methodological advance over existing approaches. Moreover, the clarification that F_i and F_i+1 are adjacent encoder features does not fully resolve the methodological ambiguity, as the choice of feature levels and the low-/high-level distinction remain insufficiently justified. The paper should clearly justify why these specific adjacent feature levels are chosen, how the low-level/high-level distinction is operationally defined, and whether the indexing strategy is essential to the performance. The rebuttal indicates that this will be clarified in revision, but it does not provide enough evidence that the current formulation is technically well justified.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose MVDA-Net, a novel U-shaped architecture designed to address the inherent challenges of 3D carotid artery segmentation in CTA imaging. The primary contribution of this work lies in the integration of three specialized modules: the Spatially-Aware Orthogonal Projection (SAOP) module, which enhances global context modeling and small vascular structure representation through multi-view anatomical plane projections ; the Hierarchical Inverted Attention Refinement (HIAR) module, which propagates boundary-enhancing inverted attention from deep to shallow layers to achieve progressive boundary refinement ; and the Synergistic Feature Alignment (SFA) module, designed to optimize encoder-decoder integration through difference-based spatial alignment and summation-based semantic balancing.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper is well-organized and follows a logical structure that enhances technical readability. The authors provide a comprehensive overview of the MVDA-Net architecture, effectively utilizing clear diagrams to illustrate the system workflow and individual module configurations. Each primary component, including the SAOPFormer, HIAR, and SFA, is clearly defined with its own dedicated subsection and mathematical formulation, ensuring the proposed framework is easy to follow.
A notable strength of this work is the explicit alignment between identified challenges in 3D carotid arterial segmentation and the proposed solutions. The authors specifically design the Spatially-Aware Orthogonal Projection (SAOP) module to address discontinuous lesion distribution and extreme foreground scarcity. Simultaneously, the Hierarchical Inverted Attention Refinement (HIAR) and Synergistic Feature Alignment (SFA) modules are purposefully engineered to overcome low-contrast boundary delineation and insufficient spatial-semantic complementarity, respectively.
-The model is evaluated by validating the MVDA-Net across a diverse range of datasets. Beyond testing on a specialized in-house carotid artery dataset, the authors perform extensive experiments on three distinct public benchmarks: MSD Lung, MSD Spleen, and BraTS. Achieving the highest performance across these various anatomical structures and imaging modalities (CT and MRI) provides evidence of the model’s robustness and generalization capabilities.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Although the paper emphasizes boundary refinement via the HIAR module, the evaluation relies solely on the Dice score. To adequately validate the claimed improvements in boundary precision, surface-based metrics such as Hausdorff Distance (HD95) should be included.
While 5-fold cross-validation is mentioned for the in-house dataset, the experimental setup for the three public benchmarks is unclear. The absence of standard deviations (std), confidence intervals, and p-values makes it difficult to assess whether the performance gains over baselines are statistically significant.
There is a lack of clarity in Equations (4) and (5) relative to the architecture shown in Figure 3b. The mathematical formulation of the SFA module is not sufficiently detailed to ensure reproducibility, which is particularly concerning given that the source code is not provided.
The reported input size of 192×192×32 for the MSD Lung dataset appears unusually shallow for the Z-axis. The authors should verify this configuration, as such a significant reduction in spatial resolution could lead to substantial information loss.
The assertion that this is the “first model specifically designed for 3D carotid arterial segmentation in CTA” is an overclaim. Previous studies have already addressed this specific clinical task.
Huang, X., Wang, J., & Li, Z. (2023). 3D carotid artery segmentation using shape-constrained active contours. Computers in Biology and Medicine, 153, 106530.
Xie, H., Gu, H., Li, M., Zhu, L., Wang, T., Li, Z., & Wu, H. (2025). Carotid artery segmentation in computed tomography angiography (CTA) using multi-scale deep supervision with Swin-UNet and advanced data augmentation. Quantitative imaging in medicine and surgery, 15(4), 3161–3175.
Therefore, the authors should revise their positioning relative to these existing works.

However, the novelty is limited and mostly incremental. The evaluation is not fully convincing due to missing boundary metrics and statistical analysis. There are also reproducibility concerns, such as unclear formulations and no code, along with some overstated claims about being the first work in this area.

reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors cleared up their design choices, fixed the overclaim about being the first, and added all the missing details on evaluation and reproducibility. More importantly, the method delivers solid gains across their private dataset and three public benchmarks, and the ablation study proves all three modules actually work.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces the Multi-View Dual-Alignment Network (MVDA-Net), a novel architecture designed specifically for 3D carotid artery segmentation in CTA imaging. MVDA-Net addresses critical challenges in vascular segmentation, including the discontinuous distribution of lesions, foreground scarcity, and boundary refinement. The model incorporates three key modules: the Spatially-Aware Orthogonal Projection (SAOP) module, the Hierarchical Inverted Attention Refinement (HIAR) module, and the Synergistic Feature Alignment (SFA) module. The SAOP module improves small target representation and spatial context modeling by leveraging multi-view projections across anatomical planes, enhancing feature propagation across discontinuous regions. The HIAR module focuses on boundary delineation by refining low-contrast vessel walls and calcification contours through inverted attention mechanisms. The SFA module enhances encoder-decoder feature alignment by capturing both spatial and semantic complementarity. The paper demonstrates the superiority of MVDA-Net through extensive experimental validation on an in-house dataset and public benchmarks, showing its superior performance in segmentation accuracy and boundary delineation.
reviews.text_strengths:
A key strength of this paper is the introduction of the MVDA-Net architecture, which addresses specific challenges in carotid artery segmentation using three innovative modules: SAOP, HIAR, and SFA. The SAOP module enhances small target representation and addresses foreground scarcity by incorporating multi-view projections across anatomical planes. The HIAR module refines boundary delineation by propagating attention from deep to shallow features, improving the delineation of vessel walls and calcifications. The SFA module efficiently aligns encoder-decoder features, improving spatial-semantic complementarity, which is crucial for accurate segmentation of complex vascular structures.
The method is thoroughly validated using both an in-house carotid artery dataset and public benchmark datasets, demonstrating its state-of-the-art performance. The experiments highlight MVDA-Net’s superiority in segmentation accuracy, particularly for challenging structures like vessel walls and calcifications. Carotid artery segmentation is critical for the diagnosis and treatment of atherosclerotic vascular diseases, and the model’s potential to improve segmentation accuracy could have significant implications in clinical decision-making.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper presents a strong methodology for carotid artery segmentation, but there are several areas that could be further strengthened or clarified.
1.While the method is validated on three public datasets (Lung, Spleen, and BraTS), the segmentation tasks on these datasets differ significantly from the task of carotid artery segmentation in terms of morphology, texture, and pathological features. The excellent performance on non-vascular organs and tumors demonstrates the model’s strong feature learning ability, but it does not directly prove the model’s effectiveness in addressing carotid artery-specific challenges, such as the subtle double-edge boundaries of the vessel wall or irregular calcification contours. The results on these non-vascular datasets do not fully validate the model’s ability to handle the unique complexities associated with carotid artery segmentation.
2.The paper primarily uses Dice as the performance evaluation metric, which, while commonly used in segmentation tasks, is not comprehensive enough to assess boundary precision. For a task like carotid artery segmentation, where boundary accuracy is crucial, additional metrics such as Hausdorff distance, average surface distance, or other boundary-specific metrics would provide a more thorough evaluation of the model’s performance. These metrics would particularly help validate the effectiveness of the HIAR module in boundary refinement.
3.The ablation study in Table 2 shows the performance improvements from combining different modules. However, the paper does not delve deeply into the impact of specific design choices within each module.
4.The paper does not mention important efficiency metrics such as model parameter count, FLOPs, training/inference time, or memory usage. These metrics are critical for assessing the feasibility of deploying MVDA-Net in clinical settings, where resource constraints may play a significant role. A discussion on these aspects would help determine whether the model is suitable for real-time clinical applications or large-scale clinical deployment.

Based on the paper’s contributions and thorough evaluation, I would rate it a 5 (Accept), as the proposed model presents solid innovation and strong validation results.
