reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
After reading the authors’ rebuttal, I lean toward acceptance.
The rebuttal addressed most of the concerns raised in my original review, including clarification of the module motivations, additional discussion on the evaluation strategy, and supplementary efficiency-related information. The authors also acknowledged several overstated claims and agreed to revise them in the final version.
Although some concerns remain, particularly regarding the lack of boundary-specific metrics and more comprehensive statistical analysis in the main manuscript, I believe these issues are relatively minor and do not fundamentally affect the overall technical soundness of the work.
Overall, the paper is borderline but slightly above the acceptance threshold due to its solid engineering design, clinically relevant application, and consistent empirical improvements across datasets.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper proposes MVDA-Net for 3D carotid artery segmentation in CTA and introduces three dedicated components, SAOP, HIAR, and SFA, to address foreground scarcity, discontinuous lesions, and boundary refinement. Reviewers appreciated the clear organization of the paper, the generally well-structured method presentation, and the extensive empirical evaluation on both an in-house carotid dataset and multiple public benchmarks. The clinical relevance of carotid artery segmentation was also recognized, and the reported performance is promising.
At the same time, the reviewers raised several important concerns that require clarification. A central issue is the degree of methodological novelty, as some of the core design elements appear related to existing multi-view context modeling, attention-based refinement, and feature alignment approaches. The authors should better position the contribution relative to prior work and moderate claims such as being the first model specifically designed for 3D carotid artery segmentation. Reviewers also noted that some technical details remain unclear, particularly the definition of intermediate feature maps and the mathematical formulation of the SFA module, which affects reproducibility.
On the experimental side, the current evaluation does not fully support all claims. In particular, boundary refinement is emphasized, but only Dice is reported; additional boundary-sensitive metrics such as HD95 or ASD would be important. Reviewers also asked for clearer reporting of the experimental setup on the public datasets, inclusion of uncertainty or significance analysis, and discussion of efficiency metrics. Finally, while the public benchmark results are useful, their connection to the carotid-specific challenges of the target task should be more carefully justified.
Overall, the paper addresses an important application and shows promising results, but the current reviews indicate that several issues regarding novelty, reproducibility, and evaluation remain unresolved. I encourage the authors to use the rebuttal to clarify these points.

This paper presents MVDA-Net for 3D carotid artery segmentation in CTA, combining slice-aware, hierarchical, and boundary-oriented modules. The application is clinically relevant, the technical design is clearly motivated, and the empirical results are consistently strong across multiple datasets.
After rebuttal, two reviewers (R2 and R3) are clearly positive, noting that the authors addressed the main concerns on overclaims, reproducibility, and evaluation details. R1 remains cautious about novelty and the justification of feature-level choices, but these reservations do not override the overall technical soundness and demonstrated practical value. The work is recognized as incremental rather than breakthrough, yet the integrated design delivers solid gains validated by thorough ablation and cross-dataset experiments.
I recommend accept. For the camera-ready version, the authors must: (1) include boundary-sensitive metrics (HD95 or ASD) to substantiate the boundary refinement claims; (2) provide a clear justification for the selection of adjacent encoder feature levels and the operational definition of low-level vs. high-level features; and (3) moderate all remaining overclaims, particularly regarding novelty and task-specificity, in line with the rebuttal commitments.

This paper proposes MVDA-Net, a U-shaped architecture for 3D carotid artery segmentation in CTA imaging, built from three modules (SAOP, HIAR, and SFA) targeting global context, boundary refinement, and encoder-decoder feature alignment.
The majority opinion is positive, though all three reviewers flag limited methodological novelty: the core ideas stay close to well-established strategies, and the contribution is largely one of combining existing components. R1 remains the most critical, noting that the rebuttal did not adequately justify the design choices or clarify operational definitions. R2 and R3 lean toward acceptance, with R2 reversing an initial negative assessment based on the rebuttal. All acknowledge that the method is technically sound and shows consistent gains across a private dataset and three public benchmarks, with an ablation supporting each module.
On balance, the concerns over limited methodological novelty and the somewhat composite nature of the architecture do not outweigh the consistent results and the clinical value of the application. Assuming the authors sufficiently address the requested revisions—R1’s concerns on methodological ambiguity, removal of overstated claims, and stronger statistical and evaluation rigor—I lean toward acceptance.

The reviewers have a consensus on the potential merit and good quality. But in terms of a large volume of medical image segmentation model papers, this paper only justified one task with an existing method with modification. The good quality of this paper still maintains its competitiveness.

author_feedback_text:
We appreciate the comments and respond below.
Reviewer#1
Q1: Originality of the proposed design.
Our method specifically targets key challenges in carotid artery CTA segmentation: discontinuous lesion distribution, extreme foreground scarcity, inadequate capture of low-contrast subtle double-edge boundaries of the vessel wall, and irregular calcification contours.
Different from APAUNet and LW-CTrans, our SAOP addresses the challenge of discontinuous lesions through spatial-aware feature recalibration, improving the spatial distinguishability of multiple lesion regions. Different from BMANet, our HIAR applies an inverted attention mechanism to deep encoder features to suppress high-confidence region responses, guiding shallow features to focus on uncertain regions such as boundaries. To further enhance shallow feature representation, we design 3D SimAM to selectively enhance fine-grained details while suppressing redundancy.
Q2: Unclear definition of feature maps.
In HIAR, F_i and F_(i+1) (1≤i≤4) denote feature maps from adjacent encoder stages. F_i from a shallower stage provides richer spatial details (low-level), while F_(i+1) from a deeper stage provides stronger semantic information (high-level). These definitions will be clarified in the revised manuscript.
Q3: Task-evaluation mismatch and cross-dataset validation.
Except for our self-constructed dataset, no publicly available carotid artery test set provides dense voxel-wise annotations. We further tested on the MSD Lung, MSD Spleen, and BraTS datasets due to their shared challenges with carotid artery segmentation, including extremely low foreground proportions (0.04%, 0.47%, and 1.16%, respectively) and irregular boundaries. Evaluation on these datasets validates the generalization of our method under similarly challenging segmentation scenarios.
Reviewer#2
Q1: Lack of boundary-specific evaluation metrics.
In the HIAR ablation study on CA, the model with HIAR yielded a better HD95 compared to the baseline. This confirms the effectiveness of HIAR in boundary refinement. Due to page limits, these results will be released with the code upon acceptance.
Q2: Experimental setup and statistical significance analysis.
For MSD Lung and BraTS, we followed the official splits of UNETR++ and nnFormer, respectively. These details will be added in the revised manuscript. Statistical significance analysis will be released with the code upon acceptance.
Q3: Unclear descriptions in Eq.(4)-(5) and SFA.
We will clarify Eq.(4)-(5) and SFA with detailed symbols and interactions in the revised manuscript and release the code upon acceptance.
Q4: Input size for MSD Lung dataset.
For MSD Lung, we adopt the same nnUNet-based preprocessing and patch planning strategy as UNETR++. The 192×192×32 is the training patch size; nnUNet’s sampling strategy (33% foreground-centered, 67% random) is applied, ensuring no information loss.
Q5: Overclaim regarding first 3D carotid artery model.
We acknowledge the overclaim and will remove the “first” claim and clarify our positioning relative to prior works. Existing studies only focus on anatomical carotid segmentation, whereas our work targets multi-structure segmentation of vessel wall, lumen, and calcification in carotid CTA.
Reviewer#3
Q1: Please refer to our response to R1Q3.Q2: Please refer to our response to R2Q1.Q3: Ablation analysis.
As shown in Tab.3, ablation on SAOPBlock verifies the effectiveness of adaptive fusion weights. For SFA, the difference-based branch models spatial complementarity, while the summation-based branch balances semantic information. Ablating them individually and jointly confirms that their combination is superior, validating the necessity of both. Due to page limits, detailed results will be released with the code upon acceptance.
Q4: Computational efficiency.
On CA, our method achieves 50.02M parameters, 357.69 GFLOPs, 16.82 GB memory, and 0.068 s inference time, with comparable computational efficiency to baselines.

title: N6-TreeMamba: Radiology Knowledge-Guided 6-Neighborhood Tree Scanning for 3D MRI-Based Stroke Complication Prediction
abstract:
Acute ischemic stroke patients are at high risk of stroke-associated pneumonia (SAP) and hemorrhagic transformation (HT), where early prediction from brain MRI can enable timely interventions. However, when modeling long-range dependencies in MRI sequences, most existing CNN- or Transformer-based models either over-emphasize local patterns or incur high computational cost. Therefore, we propose N6-TreeMamba, a Mamba-based framework that combines a 6-neighborhood tree scanning (N6-TS) strategy to efficiently capture hierarchical long-range interactions. To further align the model with clinical reasoning, we design a radiology knowledge-guided anchoring (RKA) module that leverages white matter hyperintensity (WMH) segmentation to select scanning anchors, 
guiding the model to attend to clinically relevant regions while maintaining global coverage. Experiments on an in-house stroke MRI dataset demonstrate that N6-TreeMamba consistently improves performance while achieving lower computational complexity.
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper studies 3D multi-sequence MRI-based prediction of post-stroke complications (SAP and HT) and proposes N6-TreeMamba, a TreeMamba-based framework for volumetric stroke prognosis. Its key technical components are N6-TS, a 3D 6-neighborhood tree scanning strategy for more locality-preserving token ordering, and RKA, a WMH-guided anchoring module that biases scanning toward clinically relevant regions.
The contribution is therefore best viewed as a task-specific 3D adaptation of tree-scanning Mamba for stroke MRI, rather than a fundamentally new backbone. The evaluation on an in-house clinical dataset strengthens the paper’s practical relevance, although this should be considered an empirical strength rather than a core methodological novelty.
reviews.text_strengths:
1: The paper addresses a clinically meaningful problem. Predicting SAP and HT from brain MRI is relevant to early post-stroke management, so the task itself has potential clinical value. 
2: The experimental section includes relevant Mamba-based comparisons and ablations. The paper compares against several scan-strategy baselines, including GrootVL, and provides ablations for N6-TS, RKA, and anchor composition, which helps isolate where the reported gains come from. 
3: The method is reasonably adapted to 3D MRI. The proposed N6-TS replaces naive linearization with a 3D tree-based scan order, which is a sensible way to better preserve volumetric neighborhood structure during selective scanning. 
4: The evaluation is conducted on an in-house clinical dataset. Although this is not a methodological novelty, it does make the study more practically grounded than a purely benchmark-driven evaluation.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1: The methodological novelty appears limited relative to prior tree-scanning Mamba work. The main technical idea is a task-specific adaptation of TreeMamba-style scanning to 3D MRI, with WMH-guided anchor selection, rather than a fundamentally new sequence modeling framework. 
2: The empirical validation is too limited for the strength of the claims. The study is conducted on only one in-house dataset with 188 patients in total, including only 41 SAP cases and 25 HT cases, and evaluation is based on a single 8:2 train/test split. This is a very limited experimental setting for a clinical prediction paper, especially for HT where the number of positive cases is particularly small. There is no cross-validation, repeated runs, confidence interval, significance testing, or external validation, so it is difficult to determine whether the reported gains are robust or split-specific. 
3: The experimental reporting is somewhat inconsistent. The table caption mentions F1, but the table reports only Acc and AUC. This reduces confidence in the completeness and rigor of the presentation
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I assign a 4 (Weak Accept). The paper is overall of good quality, with a coherent technical narrative, strong visual presentation, and a method that is reasonably well motivated for 3D MRI-based stroke complication prediction. In particular, the use of a 3D tree-based scan design together with WMH-guided anchoring is a sensible and clinically motivated adaptation for volumetric MRI, and the inclusion of evaluation on an in-house clinical dataset makes the study more practically grounded than a purely benchmark-driven paper.
That said, my recommendation is only marginally above the acceptance threshold. The main concerns are that the methodological novelty is somewhat incremental relative to prior tree-scanning Mamba-style work, and the empirical validation remains limited to a single in-house cohort with one train/test split and no external validation or robustness analysis. Still, I find the paper promising, technically meaningful, and potentially impactful if the limitations in validation are better addressed.

reviews.text_contribution:
This paper proposes N6-TreeMamba, a radiology knowledge-guided framework for 3D MRI-based stroke complication prediction. The main contribution lies in integrating clinically meaningful priors into long-range sequence modeling, rather than relying solely on generic architectural improvements.
Specifically, the paper introduces (1) a radiology knowledge-guided anchoring (RKA) module that leverages WMH as clinically relevant cues to guide model attention, and (2) a 6-neighborhood tree scanning strategy (N6-TS) that preserves 3D spatial locality while enabling efficient long-range dependency modeling within a Mamba-based framework.
Overall, the work is well-motivated and grounded in clinical reasoning, addressing the challenge of capturing both global context and localized pathological signals in 3D MRI. Importantly, the contribution goes beyond incremental architectural modification by explicitly incorporating domain knowledge into the modeling process, which enhances both interpretability and practical relevance. In particular, the proposed tree-based scanning strategy provides an effective solution for adapting Mamba’s inherently 1D sequential modeling to 3D volumetric data, compensating for the loss of spatial structure during sequence linearization.
reviews.text_strengths:

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback. We address the main concerns below.
[R1-W2, R2-W2, R3-W1] Experimental validation, dataset scale, and external validation. We fully agree that broader validation strengthens clinical claims. To our knowledge, there is currently no publicly available 3D MRI-based dataset for stroke-associated pneumonia (SAP) or hemorrhagic transformation (HT) prediction, which constrains external benchmarking at this stage. We are actively collecting multi-center private data from collaborating hospitals, and we have committed to a journal extension in which N6-TreeMamba will be validated across multiple centers with larger cohorts and richer subgroup analyses.
[R1-W1] Methodological novelty relative to TreeMamba/GrootVL. We respectfully clarify that N6-TreeMamba is not a straightforward adaptation. GrootVL constructs trees over 2D tokens with attention-based roots and is not applicable to volumetric data without modification. Our contributions are: (i) the N6-TS strategy, which builds an input-dependent minimum spanning tree on a 6-neighborhood 3D graph to preserve volumetric locality. This is a non-trivial extension since naive 3D tree construction over dense tokens is expensive and structure-agnostic; (ii) the RKA module, which replaces attention-based root selection with radiology-prior-driven anchors derived from WMH connected components, farthest-point sampling, and a dilated ring for background; and (iii) a clinical formulation linking WMH priors to SAP/HT prediction. Table 1 shows N6-TreeMamba outperforms GrootVL by +2.50% AUC (SAP task) and +1.98% AUC (HT task) with fewer parameters, indicating the design changes are substantive rather than cosmetic. We will sharpen this framing in the revised Introduction.
[R1-W3] F1 inconsistency in Table 1 caption. We apologize for this oversight. The caption incorrectly mentions F1; the intended metrics are Acc and AUC, as reported in the table. We will correct the caption in the camera-ready.
[R2-W1] Motivation for Mamba over CNN/Transformer and extensibility. We thank the reviewer for the helpful suggestion. We will revise the second paragraph of the Introduction to make the rationale more coherent: CNNs struggle with long-range dependencies in 3D volumes; Transformers capture global context but scale quadratically with token length, which is prohibitive for 3D MRI; Mamba offers linear-time selective scanning, making it well-suited for long-context volumetric modeling. However, Mamba’s effectiveness hinges on the 1D scan order, which motivates our tree-based scanning over naive linearization. Regarding extensibility, the RKA module is architecture-agnostic, where WMH anchors could in principle guide Transformer attention masks or CNN region-of-interest pooling. We will add a brief discussion of this in the Conclusion as a future direction.
We thank the reviewers again for their thoughtful comments, which will substantially improve our work.

title: NASD-Diff: A Noise-Assisted Structural Difference Diffusion Model for CT Angiography Generation from NCCT
abstract: Generating CT Angiography (CTA) from the latent vascular structural information in Non-Contrast CT (NCCT) has significant clinical value and remains highly challenging. With the successful application of diffusion models in medical image modality conversion tasks, research on NCCT-to-CTA generation has been promoted. However, most diffusion-based methods still use random noise to model the entire CTA image, lacking explicit modeling of vascular enhancement changes caused by contrast agent injection, which limits the quality of vascular visualization in generated images. To address this limitation, we propose a Noise-Assisted Structural Difference Diffusion Model (NASD-Diff) for NCCT-to-CTA generation. In the forward process, a noise-assisted structural difference degradation operator explicitly models the attenuation of contrast-enhanced vascular signals while incorporating controllable noise for high-frequency texture modeling. In the reverse process, a dual-decoder network decouples the prediction of vascular structural differences and noise components. Furthermore, a cross-slice conditional embedding module leverages contextual information to enhance the quality of image generation, and a global perception refinement module improves the overall visual perception of the generated images. Experiments on a real clinical dataset demonstrate that NASD-Diff significantly outperforms existing methods in PSNR, SSIM, RMSE, and multiple perceptual metrics, highlighting its effectiveness and clinical potential for high-quality CTA synthesis without contrast agents.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes NASD-Diff, a diffusion-based framework for NCCT-to-CTA synthesis that explicitly models contrast-induced vascular enhancement as a structural difference term in the forward degradation process, while using controlled noise to capture high-frequency texture details. The reverse process is implemented with a decoupled structural-texture network, supplemented by cross-slice conditional embedding and a perceptual refinement module. Overall, the paper’s main contribution is to make the diffusion process more task-aligned for CTA synthesis by replacing purely noise-driven degradation with a vascular-difference-aware formulation.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper addresses a clinically meaningful problem and presents a method whose core design is well aligned with that problem formulation. The overall story is coherent from Abstract to Experiments: the paper identifies the limitation of globally noise-driven diffusion for NCCT-to-CTA synthesis, proposes a structural-difference-aware degradation process, and then validates the design with both baseline comparisons and ablations. The experimental section is reasonably comprehensive for internal benchmarking, including multiple strong baselines, full-metric comparison, component ablation, and analysis of the noise coefficient. The visual results and ablation trends are also consistent with the claimed role of NASD in improving vascular clarity and texture fidelity.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The evidence for clinical utility is still limited. The evaluation is based on a single carotid dataset with 10 test patients and mainly generic image-quality metrics, without reader study, downstream vascular analysis, or external validation. 
2.The core novelty is concentrated in the NASD degradation idea; CSCEM, GPRM, and perceptual refinement feel more incremental, and listing “experimental validation” as a contribution weakens the novelty framing. 
3.The method section leaves several implementation choices underexplained, especially the optimization/training behavior of GPRM, the exact conditioning/prediction interface of the decoupled branches, and the practical role of cross-slice inputs in a still largely 2D pipeline. 
4.The claims are somewhat stronger than the evidence. Statements about “clinical potential” and “clinically acceptable limits” are not yet fully supported by the current experimental protocol. 
5.For a vascular synthesis task, the evaluation lacks anatomy-aware or vessel-specific fidelity measures, which makes it difficult to judge whether the observed metric gains translate into better vascular depiction in a clinically meaningful sense.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I find the paper technically coherent and reasonably well executed, with a task-aware core idea that is more thoughtful than a standard “plug diffusion into translation” approach. However, the current evidence is not yet strong enough for me to be fully convinced at the level implied by the paper’s claims. In particular, the evaluation remains mostly internal and image-metric-driven, while the task itself is vascular and clinically motivated. If the rebuttal can better clarify the methodological details and, ideally, strengthen the case for vessel-level fidelity or clinical relevance, I could see this moving upward. In its current form, though, I place it slightly above the acceptance threshold.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose a framework termed NASD-Diff for generating CT Angiography (CTA) images from Non-Contrast CT (NCCT) without requiring contrast agent injection. The method aims to directly infer CTA images from the implicit vascular information contained in NCCT scans. Compared to conventional diffusion-based approaches, which typically rely on random noise to model the entire CTA image and often lack explicit modeling of vascular enhancement induced by contrast agents, the proposed framework introduces a noise-assisted structural difference degradation operator to explicitly simulate the attenuation process of contrast-enhanced vascular signals. In addition, a dual-decoder architecture is designed to decouple the prediction of vascular structural differences and noise components, thereby improving the fidelity of vascular reconstruction. The framework also incorporates a cross-slice conditional embedding module to leverage contextual information across slices, and a global perception optimization module to enhance overall visual quality. The proposed method is evaluated on a real-world dataset consisting of 492 carotid artery cases. Experimental results demonstrate that NASD-Diff outperforms nine baseline methods across multiple quantitative metrics, including PSNR, SSIM, RMSE, VIF, and GMSD. The main contributions of this work can be summarized as follows: (1) the introduction of a noise-assisted structural difference degradation operator for modeling vascular contrast attenuation; (2) a dual-decoder framework for disentangling vascular structure and noise prediction; and (3) a cross-slice conditional embedding mechanism to exploit contextual information for improved image generation quality.
reviews.text_strengths:
ajor Strengths
Clinically important problem. A software-based strategy to directly generate CT Angiography (CTA) from Non-Contrast CT (NCCT) scans without contrast agent injection could reduce the risk for patients with iodine allergy, renal insufficiency, or multiple myeloma, aligning with MICCAI’s clinical translation priorities.
Noise-assisted structural difference modeling strategy. The changes in vascular structure caused by contrast agent between NCCT and CTA were explicitly captured. Combining this strategy in the forward propagation process of the diffusion model improved the generation of vascular structure and overall texture details.
Decoupling structural difference prediction and noise prediction. Optimizing vascular structure and texture details improves the structural accuracy and detail clarity of the generated CTA images.
Open-source commitment. If the collected carotid artery dataset containing 492 patients and the related code from the paper could be open-sourced, it would be of great significance to the community.
Clean degradation ablation. The results of ablation experiments a and b in Table 2 clearly demonstrate that each contribution proposed by the authors contributes to the overall CTA image generation.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Most issues below are reporting gaps, not technical errors, and can be addressed in the rebuttal without new experiments.
W1.A complete description of perceptual loss [Major]. In the Training and Sampling section, the authors propose using Llpips to perceive similarity from deep features, measuring the visual consistency between the generated CTA image and the real CTA image. It’s important to clarify here whether this involves overlaying the number of image channels to match the natural image, or if some other operation is performed.
W2.Implementation Details [Major]. The authors do not explicitly specify in the Implementation Details whether data augmentation strategies were employed to enhance the model’s robustness and generalization capability.
W3.Diffusion model coefficients [Major]. The full text does not explicitly explain the details of the diffusion model correlation coefficients used in the entire framework, including but not limited to: the number of forward and backward samples, the sampling method, etc.
W4.Model parameters and running efficiency [Major]. The discussion of model parameters and computational efficiency remains insufficient. In particular, sampling time—an inherent bottleneck in diffusion-based models—is not adequately analyzed. Furthermore, the report lacks a comprehensive comparison of runtime performance with competing methods, leaving the efficiency advantages or trade-offs of the proposed approach unclear.
W5.The formula details are insufficient [Moderate]. In formula 3, || ||2 represents the L2 norm or the square term, which needs to be clarified.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Completeness of Figure 4: Figure 4 only shows the visual effect of the noise control factor 1.The comprehensive display of qualitative and quantitative results of components such as NASD and CSCEM in the framework can better illustrate the effectiveness of the framework.

This paper addresses an important and clinically meaningful topic, with investigations on the training parameters of diffusion models, well-designed degradation ablation experiments, and a valuable promise of open-source release.
However, five key issues (W1, W2, W3, W4, W5) require clarification rather than additional experiments.
Although the authors have explored a meaningful research direction, the innovation and advantages of the proposed method are not sufficiently highlighted in the design and description of the method architecture diagram.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes NASD-Diff, a diffusion-based framework for generating CT angiography (CTA) from non-contrast CT (NCCT). It introduces a noise-assisted structural difference (NASD) degradation operator that explicitly models contrast-induced vascular enhancement via a structural difference term, and predicts this structural component and texture noise with a decoupled dual-branch network, augmented by cross-slice conditioning and a perceptual refinement module. On a private carotid dataset, the method outperforms GAN- and diffusion-based baselines on PSNR, SSIM, RMSE, VIF, and GMSD, with ablations supporting the contributions of each component.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.A key strength is the noise-assisted structural difference degradation operator, which reformulates the forward process using the NCCT–CTA structural difference instead of relying only on global random noise. This is interesting because it explicitly targets the vascular enhancement changes that are central to NCCT-to-CTA generation.
2.The reverse model is reasonably well designed for the problem. The Decoupled Structural-Texture Network (DeST-Net) separates structural-difference prediction from noise prediction, while the cross-slice conditional embedding module leverages adjacent-slice context and the refinement module improves perceptual quality. These components are task-motivated rather than generic additions.
3.Empirical study is fairly comprehensive.The paper compares against a broad set of GAN-, translation-, and diffusion-based baselines, reports multiple distortion and perceptual metrics, and includes both component ablations and a study of the noise control coefficient λ. The study is based on paired NCCT–CTA data from 492 patients, with explicit training/validation/test splits and registered image pairs, which strengthens the practical relevance of the experiments.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The forward operator relies on m = x_CTA − x_NCCT computed from registered pairs; m will absorb misregistration and non-vascular differences, potentially biasing the learned “structural difference” away from pure vascular enhancement.
2.The use of LPIPS is clear at a high level, but the manuscript does not specify which pretrained feature backbone is used to compute the perceptual loss.
3.Although the task is clinically motivated, the evaluation is restricted to image-quality metrics and qualitative visual comparisons on a single paired carotid dataset. Stronger claims such as “clinically acceptable limits” and broader “clinical potential” are therefore somewhat ahead of the evidence currently presented, since no reader study or downstream vascular-assessment analysis is included.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Single-center dataset with 10-patient test set may overestimate performance; No discussion of clinically motivated constraints (e.g., HU calibration, injectate timing priors) that may stabilize vascular enhancement realism.

The paper tackles a clinically important problem with a task-specific formulation that is better aligned with NCCT-to-CTA generation than standard noise-only diffusion, and it shows consistent gains on a real paired clinical dataset. My support is not stronger because some aspects of the degradation/restoration formulation remain under-explained.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text: This manuscript received three positive reviews, showing the superior novelty, comprehensive evaluation and well-organized structure. Therefore, a provisional accept is given based on the reviews.

title: NEARL: Interacted Query Adaptation with Orthogonal Regularization for Medical Vision-Language Understanding
abstract: Computer-aided medical image analysis is crucial for disease diagnosis and treatment planning. While vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP exhibit strong generalization ability, their direct application to medical imaging remains hindered by a substantial domain gap. Existing methods for bridging this gap, including prompt learning and unidirectional modality interaction, typically introduce domain knowledge into only one modality. However, such approaches fail to fully exploit CLIP’s inherent dual-modality structure and overlook the synergistic effect of bidirectional cross-modal interaction, resulting in persistent modality misalignment. In this paper, we propose NEARL (iNteracted quEry Adaptation with oRthogonaL Regularization), a novel parameter-efficient VLM framework for bidirectional cross-modal interaction. NEARL consists of two key components: (1) the Unified Synergy Embedding Transformer (USEformer), which dynamically generates compact cross-modal queries to facilitate interaction; and (2) the Orthogonal Cross-Attention Adapter (OCA), which decouples new knowledge into truly novel and incremental components through orthogonal regularization. This design reduces interference from incremental components, enabling more focused learning of novel information and improving modality interaction in VLMs. Notably, NEARL introduces only 1.46M learnable parameters. Extensive experiments on three medical imaging modalities demonstrate state-of-the-art performance (e.g., a 2.3% relative improvement on the pneumonia dataset), along with fast inference and low memory overhead, highlighting its effectiveness for real-world medical vision-language understanding.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a bidirectional cross-modal interaction framework based on VLMs, named NERARL, aiming to address the domain gap when VLMs are directly applied to medical image analysis. The main contributions of this paper are “USEformer”, which is used to generate cross-modal queries, and “Orthogonal Cross-Attention Adapter”, which employs orthogonal techniques to decompose new knowledge and achieve the goal of accurately acquiring new information, with the aim of enhancing the modal interaction within VLMs.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) The comparison with the CLIP backbone in terms of parameter count is interesting and suggests that NEARL achieves competitive inference throughput with limited parameter overhead. While this points toward potential resource efficiency, additional discussion on real-world deployment constraints would further strengthen the claim of clinical applicability. 
2) The proposed adapter module appears to mitigate interference during incremental learning, as indicated by the ablation results. The design rationale is plausible, and the observed improvements in cross-modal interaction are encouraging. However, a deeper analysis of why orthogonality helps, via feature-space visualization or gradient dynamics, would provide more convincing mechanistic insight. 
3) The evaluation spans multiple diseases and imaging modalities, which is a notable strength. Performance gains over prior methods are consistently reported, suggesting reasonable generalization. That said, dataset-specific performance variations and potential biases are not thoroughly examined; addressing these would improve confidence in the method’s robustness across heterogeneous clinical settings.
reviews.text_weaknesses: 1） The baseline methods used in the comparative experiments are relatively outdated. It is recommended to include comparisons with more recent state-of-the-art approaches to better demonstrate the competitiveness of the proposed method. Alternatively, if incorporating newer baselines is not feasible, please provide a thorough discussion explaining why certain recent methods underperform compared to the classical baselines in this specific setting, thereby strengthening the validity and rigor of the experimental evaluation.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Overall, the paper is well-structured and clearly presents its experimental design and results, making the overall argument highly convincing. While there are minor shortcomings in the supporting evidence and the comparative experiments, these do not significantly detract from the core contributions. Given the methodological soundness, clear presentation, and strong empirical results, I recommend a Weak Accept, pending minor revisions to address the points raised above.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: After reading the rebuttal, I maintain my Weak Accept rating. The authors have reasonably addressed several concerns, especially regarding deployment efficiency, backbone choice, additional dataset results, and comparisons with recent baselines. The clarification of the orthogonality constraint also makes the motivation more convincing.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose NEARL, a novel bidirectional cross-modality interaction framework based on vision-language models, comprising USEformer and OCA. USEformer generates learnable queries to enable bidirectional cross-modal enrichment, improving alignment between visual and textual features. OCA decouples truly novel knowledge from incremental updates, preventing interference with pre-trained features. Evaluations across three imaging modalities demonstrate that NEARL achieves superior performance.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.NEARL introduces a bidirectional framework that fully leverages the duality of vision-language models, improving alignment between visual and textual features, which addresses the limitations of prior unidirectional approaches.
2.The OCA module decouples truly novel knowledge from incremental updates using orthogonal regularization, preventing interference with pre-trained features and enabling focused acquisition of new domain-specific information.
3.NEARL achieves superior performance across multiple medical imaging modalities.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Questionable Motivation: While NEARL introduces USEformer and OCA to improve medical vision-language alignment, the overall novelty and practical significance are limited. The framework primarily relies on adapting a frozen CLIP model pretrained on natural image-text pairs with lightweight modules. Given the availability of numerous general-purpose and domain-specific medical foundation models, it is unclear why starting from a frozen natural-image CLIP is preferable to leveraging these pretrained medical models, which may already encode relevant medical visual-language representations.
2.Limited Evaluation Scope: Although NEARL is evaluated across three imaging modalities, experiments are limited to only three datasets, raising concerns about the generalizability to broader medical imaging datasets. Additional evaluation on more datasets could strengthen the evidence.
3.Unclear Task Definition: It is not explicitly stated whether the reported results correspond to zero-shot or other evaluation settings. Expanding the experiment to include multiple evaluation settings (e.g., few-shot, retrieval) would clarify the model’s applicability and robustness.
4.Visualization Comparisons: In Figure 2, the visualizations should be compared against representative bidirectional/unidirectional modality interaction baselines to better illustrate the contribution of the proposed modules to cross-modal alignment.
5.Parameter and Efficiency Analysis: While the authors claim that NEARL introduces only 1.46M additional parameters and achieves fast inference, it is unclear how this compares quantitatively to other baselines. More detailed analysis of parameter efficiency and runtime gains relative to existing methods is needed to support the claimed advantages.

N/A

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contributions of this paper are twofold. First, it proposes the Unified Synergy Embedding Transformer (USEformer), a lightweight module that enables fully bidirectional cross-modal interaction between visual and textual modalities by dynamically generating compact cross-modality queries to extract and fuse complementary information from both sides, achieving deep mutual alignment instead of the unidirectional interaction used in previous works. Second, it introduces the Orthogonal Cross-Attention Adapter (OCA), which applies Gram-Schmidt orthogonal regularization to decouple newly learned medical domain knowledge into truly novel domain-specific components and incremental components relative to the frozen pre-trained CLIP weights, preventing feature interference and helping the model focus on acquiring new medical knowledge efficiently. Besides these two core modules, the whole NEARL framework is designed to be parameter-efficient, only introducing 1.46M learnable parameters while achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple medical imaging modalities, and it also provides strong empirical validation on three representative medical datasets covering X-ray, MRI, and OCT.
reviews.text_strengths: One major strength is the novel bidirectional cross-modal interaction design, which differs from existing prompt learning or unidirectional modality adaptation methods that only optimize one modality or pass information in a single direction; USEformer builds real two-way communication between image and text branches, which better exploits the dual structure of CLIP and alleviates modality misalignment in the medical domain, making the cross-modal alignment more thorough and suitable for medical vision-language tasks. Another strength is the orthogonal regularization mechanism in OCA, which uses a simple yet effective Gram-Schmidt process to strictly separate adaptive features from pre-trained features, avoiding interference with the original generalization ability of CLIP and making the domain adaptation more focused and stable, and this orthogonal design is computationally efficient compared with other orthogonalization methods like Householder transformation, fitting clinical real-time needs. The paper also shows strong evaluation completeness: it tests NEARL on three distinct medical datasets with different imaging modalities and disease types, compares with a wide range of state-of-the-art methods including prompt learning, unidirectional adaptation, and even unimodal medical models, and achieves clear performance gains, such as a 2.3% relative accuracy increase on the pneumonia dataset. Additionally, the framework is highly parameter-efficient with only 1.46M extra parameters, delivers fast inference speed (500 fps on RTX 3090) and low memory overhead, which demonstrates practical clinical feasibility for real-time diagnostic screening. Comprehensive ablation studies and visual feature analysis further verify the effectiveness of each core module and explain the limitations of prior unimodal adaptation strategies, making the work solid and convincing.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The main weakness is that the core ideas of cross-modal interaction via learnable queries and adapter-based fine-tuning with regularization are not completely new in the vision-language field. Learnable query tokens for cross-modal fusion have been explored in many prior VLM adaptation works such as MaPLe and CoCoOp, and orthogonal regularization has also been used in some parameter-efficient adaptation methods to reduce feature conflict, so the overall paradigm of combining query-based interaction and orthogonal adapter follows existing technical routines without a radically new methodological foundation. Also, the experiments are limited to standard medical image classification tasks on three public datasets, without testing on more challenging medical vision-language tasks like image captioning, visual question answering, or lesion segmentation, which limits the demonstration of the framework’s generalization to broader medical VL understanding scenarios. Furthermore, the paper does not provide in-depth analysis on the sensitivity of key hyperparameters such as the number of query tokens, query dimension, and the number of USEformer layers, and there is no comparison with other recent orthogonal or bidirectional adaptation methods specifically designed for medical VLMs, making the novelty and superiority of the design less distinctive in the medical domain literature.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

My overall recommendation is mainly based on several key positive factors that outweigh the minor weaknesses. First, the paper addresses an important practical problem—the domain gap between general VLMs and medical imaging—and provides a clear, effective, and clinically applicable solution with two well-designed complementary modules. Second, the technical design is reasonable and targeted: bidirectional interaction fixes the flaw of unidirectional adaptation, and orthogonal regularization solves feature interference during domain adaptation, both of which are well-motivated and clearly validated. Third, the empirical results are strong and consistent across multiple datasets and modalities, outperforming a large set of competitive baselines with very low parameter overhead and high inference efficiency, showing real practical value for computer-aided medical diagnosis. Fourth, the paper is well-organized, with complete experiments, ablation studies, and visual analysis to support every claim, making it technically solid and easy to follow. Although the core paradigm is not completely revolutionary, the concrete combination and optimization for medical vision-language understanding are innovative enough, and the performance and efficiency gains are significant for real clinical use. Therefore, the work makes a meaningful contribution to medical VLM adaptation and deserves acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

meta_reviews.text:
The principal concerns the authors must address in rebuttal are:
Motivation for using a frozen natural-image CLIP rather than existing medical foundation models (MedCLIP, BiomedCLIP, PubMedCLIP) as the backbone (R2). This is the most consequential critique and directly affects the claimed contribution.
Novelty positioning relative to learnable-query (MaPLe, CoCoOp) and orthogonal-adapter prior work (R3); the combination is reasonable but the delta needs sharper articulation.
Baseline recency — comparisons skew toward older methods (R1); authors should justify selection or add recent medical VLM adapters.
Evaluation scope and task setting — only three datasets, and zero-shot vs. few-shot vs. fine-tuned protocol is ambiguous (R2). Clarification is essential for interpreting the gains.
Quantitative parameter/efficiency comparison against baselines, not just absolute numbers (R2).
Mechanistic evidence for orthogonality — feature-space or gradient-level analysis would substantiate the design claim (R1).

All of the 3 reviewers agreed to accept this paper after rebuttal.
All the reviewers agree the acceptance.
All reviewers provided final acceptance scores.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their comments.
R1-Real-world constraints: NEARL is deployment-friendly with low inference memory (~1 GB) and exceptional data efficiency (only ~4k images for pneumonia adaptation).
R1-Evidence of orthogonality: Prior works (e.g., Cogswell et al., ICLR 2016) suggest that reducing feature redundancy improves generalization. If adapter updates are not orthogonal to frozen features, they introduce overlap and conflict. Baselines show nontrivial angles (>5°), while OCA enforces near-perfect orthogonality (90° ± 0.02°), enabling non-redundant adaptation and generalization.
R1-Performance variations: Improvement margins vary across datasets due to differences in imaging modality, disease characteristics, and task difficulty. For instance, the visual overlap between normal and pathological patterns in X-rays makes adaptation inherently harder. Despite this, NEARL consistently delivers positive gains, highlighting its robustness.
R1- Baseline recency: When tested against recent methods, e.g., HiCroPL (ICCV 2025) and Spotlighter (EMNLP 2025), NEARL consistently performs best, achieving 94.7% v.s. 89.7% and 82.9%, respectively, further demonstrating its effectiveness.
R2-Backbone choice: NEARL is backbone-agnostic and plug-and-play. We adopt natural-domain CLIP because prior medical adaptation works (e.g., ViP) use the same backbone for fair comparison. With a medical backbone (PubMedCLIP), NEARL reaches 94.0%, up from 62.5% (zero-shot), and surpasses baselines e.g., FATE (86.8%) and MaPLe (92.3%).
R2-Evaluation scope: Our evaluation spans three widely used medical imaging modalities: X-ray, OCT, and MRI. On ISIC dermoscopy dataset, NEARL achieves 89.1% acc, outperforming previous methods e.g., FATE (84.5%) and MaPLe (85.8%), further supporting its effectiveness across diverse datasets.
R2-Unclear task definition: Our experiments follow the standard PEFT setting used in prior medical adaptation works (e.g., ViP, XCoOp): all methods are tuned on the full training split with a frozen backbone, rather than zero-/few-shot evaluation, ensuring fair comparison. Few-shot or retrieval-based evaluation is beyond our current scope and left for future study. Thanks!
R2-Visualization comparisons: Most baselines freeze the image encoder. While methods like MaPLe introduce trainable tokens, it does not enforce compatibility with the frozen space. T-SNE shows MaPLe features exhibit weaker separability. Due to the text-only rebuttal format, we cannot include visualization here.
R2-Parameter/efficiency comparison: Existing methods use 8.19K–26.11M parameters at 470–540 fps. NEARL uses 1.46M parameters at a comparable 500 fps, yet achieves the best overall performance.
R3-Differences from recent general and medical adaptation methods: First, NEARL uses learnable vectors as compact cross-modal queries, rather than prompt-based adaptation methods as in CoCoOp, MaPLe, or HiCroPL, enabling layer-wise retrieval of complementary information from the opposite modality. Second, the orthogonality constraint in NEARL is imposed directly in feature space, rather than in weight or gradient space as in O-LoRA and BOFA, thereby effectively reducing feature redundancy and improving representation generalization. Third, unlike bidirectional methods like BiPVL-Seg that merely rely on self-/cross-attention interaction, NEARL performs lightweight CLIP adaptation with compact queries, lightweight adapters, and explicit feature-space decoupling.
R3-Limited to classification: We focus on medical image classification because it is the standard evaluation setting adopted by prior medical CLIP-based methods, e.g., ViP and XCoOp, enabling a fair comparison. Since NEARL is task-agnostic, we will explore it on other tasks in future work. Thanks!
R3-Ablation: Sensitivity analysis on key hyperparameters shows minor performance changes across settings, generally within 2%, indicating that NEARL is robust and not highly sensitive to hyperparameter choices.

title: NeRD: Neuro-Symbolic Rule Distillation for Efficient Ontology-Grounded Chain-of-Thought in Medical Image Diagnosis
abstract: Interpretability is essential for trustworthy medical image diagnosis. However, existing concept-driven interpretable methods have key limitations: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) require scoring all predefined concepts during both inference and manual intervention, imposing a substantial burden on clinicians, while rationale-based generative approaches often select concepts by class discriminability, which can drift from diagnostic ontologies. To address these issues, we propose Neuro-Symbolic Rule Distillation (NeRD), a framework that produces efficient, ontology-grounded reasoning chains that are sufficient yet non-redundant, without manually crafting diagnostic rules. Experiments on three datasets demonstrate strong diagnostic performance and interpretability, and blinded expert evaluation confirms the clinical plausibility of NeRD rationales. Our method further enables a first intervention study for Multimodal Chain-of-Thought-based diagnosis, achieving efficient and effective concept-level intervention. Our code is available at: https://github.com/HongxiY/NeRD.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes NeRD, a neuro-symbolic framework that distills logical rules into compact, ontology-grounded MCoT reasoning chains for medical image diagnosis. The method avoids exhaustive concept scoring (as in CBMs) and class-discriminability drift (as in WISE). The main contributions include automatic rule induction via LogicCBM, a three-step distillation process (activation, simplification, grounding) to generate non-redundant case-specific rationales, a blinded expert evaluation of clinical plausibility, and a simulated concept-intervention study.
reviews.text_strengths:
The method is novel and well motivated, bridging rule‑based interpretability and generative MCoT reasoning.
Generated MCoTs are compact (≈6 concepts per case) and shown to be clinically plausible by expert assessment.
Experiments cover diagnostic accuracy, concept fidelity, expert evaluation, and intervention efficiency. Code is provided.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The abstract and introduction claim “first expert‑in‑the‑loop study”. However, Experiment 3 uses ground‑truth annotations to automatically replace concepts – no real clinician is involved. This is an oracle simulation, not a human‑in‑the‑loop study. Can the authors clarify or correct this claim?
In Experiment 1, the 8 cases per evaluator are sampled from the training set. Because rule induction already fits the training distribution, this may bias the results. Would the findings hold on the test set?
The paper does not compare with some recent concept bottleneck works, such as Evidential Concept Embedding Models (MICCAI 2024) and Concept Rule Learner (MICCAI 2025) by Gao et al. Would the authors add a discussion or experimental comparison?
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The method currently uses ground‑truth concepts for rule grounding. An end‑to‑end evaluation with predicted concepts would strengthen the practical relevance. Also, the “ontology‑grounded” claim could be better supported by incorporating ontological priors earlier in the rule induction process. 
Minor issues: the zero‑shot prompt is not provided; there is a grammar error in Sec. 2.2 (“an selected rule” should be “a selected rule”).

The paper presents a novel method, but two major flaws prevent acceptance in its current form: (1) the claimed “expert‑in‑the‑loop” study is not what the authors actually did (no real clinician); (2) expert evaluation uses training cases, which may bias the results.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes NeRD, a neuro-symbolic framework for generating compact, ontology-grounded multimodal chain-of-thought rationales for medical image diagnosis. Instead of selecting concepts mainly by discriminability, the method first induces explicit logical diagnostic rules over clinical concepts, then distills activated rules into case-specific reasoning chains through rule selection, concept grounding, and finally structures these into MCoTs. The key contribution is to bridge rule-based concept interpretability with generative multimodal reasoning in a way that is intended to be more clinically aligned, non-redundant, and intervention-friendly.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper has several strengths. First, it tackles a clinically meaningful interpretability problem. Second, the proposed pipeline is technically interesting: it combines induced rule activation, logical simplification, and concept grounding to build more structured rationales rather than relying purely on class-discriminative concept selection. Third, a strong blinded human expert plausibility study, and a clinician-intervention experiment. Fourth, the empirical results are solid: NeRD is competitive diagnostically and improves over baselines on both datasets.
reviews.text_weaknesses: My main concern is that the evaluation is not strong enough for the paper’s central claims about interpretability and clinical usefulness. The main quantitative evaluation uses only diagnostic accuracy/F1 and a fairly weak interpretability metric: “concept accuracy” is computed only over the concepts that the model explicitly mentions in its generated chain-of-thought, rather than evaluating completeness, or alignment against the full clinically relevant concept set. A second concern is that the experimental scope is narrow. This makes it difficult to judge how well the framework would transfer to broader medical imaging settings, especially tasks with richer label spaces, more complex ontologies, or longer-form outputs. A third concern is that the framework depends on a fairly strong problem setup (concept-annotated datasets, relies on an explicit concept ontology and concept group structure) that may be non-trivial to reproduce.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Although the paper is well motivated and the proposed rule-distillation framework is interesting, I do not think the empirical validation is strong enough to support the paper’s broader claims about interpretability. Overall, I see this as a promising paper with good ideas, but in its current form I would place it slightly below the bar; it feels closer to an interesting workshop-style paper unless the authors can substantially strengthen the generalization case.

meta_reviews.text:
All reviewers recognize the merits of the paper, while they also have consistent concerns regarding the empirical evaluations and generalizability of the proposed method.

The authors rebuttal addressed most key concerns, e.g., those regarding generalizability and experimental evaluations.

The paper presents a novel and well-motivated neuro-symbolic framework for compact, ontology-grounded MCoT rationales, and the reviews consistently recognize its methodological contribution, clinical relevance, reproducibility through released code, and promising empirical evidence, including expert plausibility and intervention-oriented evaluation. Since concerns remain about the breadth of validation, reliance on concept annotations/ontologies, and the need to temper some clinical-usefulness claims, the work is placed marginally above the MICCAI acceptance bar.

Two reviewers reject (R2=3, R3=4→Reject). R3 downgraded from 4 to Reject after rebuttal because ‘authors didn’t provide details on how to make their paper stronger.’ The ‘expert-in-the-loop’ claim is misleading (actually oracle simulation).

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank all reviewers for recognizing the novelty and motivation of our work. We have addressed their valuable comments below:
1.R1Q1 Expert-in-the-loop Claim
We agree that Exp.3 did not involve live clinical interaction and therefore will revise our claim to reduce ambiguity. However, we would like to emphasise that intervention is indeed driven by human annotated input, as Exp.3 has evaluated how efficiently expert verified concept corrections rectify model errors. NeRD therefore retains strong potential for efficient and effective human-guided concept-level intervention, and this refinement does not affect our core claims/conclusions.
2.R1Q2 Human Eval in Exp.1
Our evaluation has two goals: (1) verify the clinical faithfulness of constructed MCoTs used for training (Exp.1); (2) assess if MLLMs can learn from them (Exp.2). Since induced rules on the training set but not the test set are used for subsequent MLLM training, Exp.1 primarily reports training-set results. We additionally evaluated sampled test cases as a sanity check and observed consistent trends (e.g. Derm7pt: All-Concepts/WISE/NeRD/NeRD-RD 0.75/1.25/1.50/1.00), which will be added to the final version.
3.R1Q3 Comparison with Evi-CEM & CRL
Due to page constraints, we have only included a subset of CBM baselines in the paper. Comparisons of NeRD with Evi-CEM (MICCAI24) and CRL (MICCAI25) on two datasets are as follows (ACC/Intp.,%): Derm7pt: Evi-CEM 78.99/78.31, CRL 77.97/73.99, NeRD 80.76/76.76; F17k: Evi-CEM 88.04/92.66, CRL 88.51/92.55, NeRD 88.66/94.10.NeRD consistently achieves superior performance across almost all evaluation dimensions, which demonstrates its effectiveness. Results will be added in the final version.
4.R2Q1 Interpretability Metric
Consistent with standard concept-based evaluation(e.g. CBM&WISE), we report concept accuracy against human annotations. We further assess MCoT clinical plausibility through a blinded expert study (Exp.1) using only MCoT without images. For completeness of concepts, NeRD outperforms the full concept set, suggesting that NeRD retains diagnostically relevant information while avoiding noise that may dilute salient evidence and reduce diagnostic confidence. Whereas for non-redundancy, NeRD-RD (randomly removing 1–2 concepts) degrades performance, confirming our selected concepts are necessary for correct diagnosis.
5.R2Q2 & R3Q2 Experimental Scope
We extended the evaluation to the WBCAtt dataset (NeurIPS23) for white blood cell classification, a new medical imaging domain with richer labels (5 classes) and complex ontologies (24 morphological attributes). To simulate a challenging scenario, the model is trained using 30% training samples (n=1030) and evaluated on the official test set (n=3099). Main results (ACC/Intp., %): JointCBM 96.10/86.33, SequentialCBM 95.39/86.26, Zero-shot 35.43/36.91, WISE 96.13/85.87, NeRD (Ours) 96.64/92.81.Our NeRD surpasses all competing methods on WBCAtt, demonstrating strong generalization across diverse modalities, rich label spaces, and complex ontologies.
6.R2Q3 Generalizability
We would like to emphasise the broad applicability of NeRD with these following reasons: (1) NeRD can operate in annotation-free settings where concepts can be generated by LLMs and pseudo labeled by CLIP. (2) NeRD does not consume any external ontology/knowledge base as input. The diagnostic logic is induced automatically, which is one of our key contributions. (3) Concept group structure is not required. Derm7pt has concept groups whereas F17k does not, and our pipeline operates on flat, ungrouped concepts in both datasets.
7.R3Q1 Difference from WISE
WISE (Fig. 1b) uses decision trees to pick class-discriminative concepts, which may favor shortcuts that drift from diagnostic ontologies; NeRD (Fig. 1c) induces explicit logic rules and distills the activated ones per case, yielding ontology-grounded, sufficient, non-redundant rationales. We will improve readability in the final version.

title: NetCorr: A Resection-Induced Network Perturbation Framework for Predicting Seizure Freedom in Drug-Resistant Epilepsy
abstract: Drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) is often treated with resective surgery, yet a central clinical challenge remains: given a planned (or completed) resection, what is the likelihood the patient will achieve seizure freedom? Answering this is difficult because the optimal surgical target—the epileptogenic zone (EZ), the brain tissue that generates seizures—is latent and must be inferred from biomarkers derived from intracranial EEG (iEEG). Biomarkers at both channel and network level have been developed and evaluated as independent sources of data stream and thus have shown limited promise in predicting surgical outcomes. We hypothesize that the channel and network level biomarkers are mechanistically connected, and introduce NetCorr, a platform that makes use of this underlying correlation to better predict seizure freedom. Towards this end, we first introduce a regression framework that predicts a channel’s smoothed high-frequency-oscillation with spike (spkHFO) rate from its participation properties in a ripple-band synchronization network, quantifying network-spkHFO coupling via R^2. Secondly, we model resection as a perturbation of the preserved channel coupling scores and construct a 2-dimensional patient signature that summarizes resection-induced shifts in coupling statistics. In a multi-institutional retrospective cohort of 159 pediatric-onset focal DRE patients, this 2-dimensional signature predicts post-surgical outcome with a cross-validated mean F1 score of 95%, significantly outperforming ratio-based baselines using SOZ resection (F1 = 78%) and spkHFO resection (F1 = 79%).
subject_areas: Applications -> Outcome Prediction / Prognosis / Longitudinal Modeling
Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning
Modalities -> EEG / MEG / ECG / Physiological Signals

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents a framework to predict seizure freedom in DREs. It is clinically relevant, well-motivated and also effective.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper targets on a clinically relevant challenge: how to predict the surgical outcome in DRES. 
2.The framework is neat and effective. It first uses a regression framework to model synchronization network–spkHFO coupling based on iEEG data, where a stable, interpretable statistics could be predicted to compare across channels and patients, based on which network perturbation features could be obtained to predict surgical outcome. 
3.The paper is easy to follow, although several details are missing.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The signal length seems variable across patients. It is not clear how, and to what extent, signal length affects the calculation of R2 and the network perturbation features. Is there any instruction of choose IEEG length when applied this method clinically?
2.In section 2.1, it says artifact-free interictal epochs were used for analysis. How robust the method is to noise remain to be explored.

N/A

The framework is novel and effective. But noise robustness should be explored to strengthen its soundness.

reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces NetCorr, a framework that predicts epilepsy surgery outcomes by modeling surgery as a network perturbation and measuring how removing brain regions changes the relationship between network dynamics and pathological signals (spkHFOs), showing improved prediction of seizure freedom compared to existing methods.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper proposes a novel formulation that models surgery as a network perturbation, offering a principled way to link pre- and post-resection brain dynamics.
It introduces an original integration of channel-level (spkHFO) and network-level features, which are typically studied separately in prior work.
The approach demonstrates strong empirical performance, significantly outperforming standard baselines
The evaluation is conducted on a relatively large multi-institutional cohort, supporting the robustness of the findings.
reviews.text_weaknesses: Several methodological choices, such as retaining only the top 10% of network edges and using specific network features (degree and centrality), appear heuristic

N/A

I am not an expert in this specific domain, so my evaluation is based primarily on the clarity of the paper and the evidence presented rather than deep domain-specific judgment. From my reading, the method appears to offer a substantial improvement over existing approaches, with a clear and intuitive formulation and strong reported performance. However, given my limited expertise and some concerns about validation and generalizability, I am not fully confident in assessing the broader impact and robustness of the method. For these reasons, I lean toward a weak accept, acknowledging both the promising results and my uncertainty in fully evaluating the work.
