meta_reviews.text: All three reviewers recognize NeuroAlign as a well-motivated plug-and-play enhancement framework for multimodal brain decoding, with comprehensive experiments across multiple baselines on both visual and linguistic tasks demonstrating consistent improvements. The main concerns include: cumulative-only ablation design without single-module analysis, absence of comparison with simpler alignment methods, insufficient technical detail on the CAF module and computational overhead, non-functional code link, and limited neuroscience interpretability. The authors are encouraged to address these points in the camera-ready version.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the AC and reviewers for your constructive assessment. Following the MICCAI rebuttal rules, we do not report new experiments or data; we clarify the submitted manuscript and specify presentation/discussion revisions.
(1) Ablation design and simpler alignment alternatives (R1/AC). We agree that Table 2 is an incremental ablation, not a full factorial study. Our intention was to verify the designed pipeline order, not to claim that every standalone or two-module variant has been exhaustively isolated. The order is architectural: HDT first regularizes fine-token geometry; CMI then calibrates pooled coarse tokens with semantic prototypes; CAF finally propagates calibrated coarse semantics back to fine tokens. Thus, CAF alone or CMI+CAF without HDT would partly change the intended module interface rather than simply remove a block. We will revise the wording around Table 2 to avoid over-claiming “necessity” from cumulative ablation alone. We also agree that adversarial alignment, plain contrastive projection, and standard cross-attention are valuable simpler controls; since new results are not allowed in rebuttal, we will discuss them as future controlled comparisons. 
(2) CAF details, hyperparameters, and scalability (R2/AC). We will clarify CAF in text. CAF uses fine-resolution tokens as queries and CMI-rectified coarse tokens as keys/values. The decoded semantic signal is injected through a learned sigmoid gate, so coarse semantics are strengthened only when compatible with the fine geometric stream. This differs from plain cross-attention because it is residual and conflict-aware rather than a direct overwrite. We will explicitly list the fixed settings used across experiments, including fine/coarse token resolutions, concept-bank size/top-k retrieval, and loss weights, and clarify that they were kept fixed across baselines rather than tuned per framework. Regarding cost, NeuroAlign is inserted before the frozen generator and does not require additional diffusion or LLM sampling passes. Its overhead is limited to token transport, sparse concept retrieval, and one fine-to-coarse attention block; scalability is mainly governed by token resolution, Sinkhorn iterations, and concept-bank size, not by the parameter count of the downstream foundation model. 
(3) Code link and reproducibility (R1/R3/AC). We apologize for the placeholder code statement. We will remove or correct the non-functional anonymous code claim and, after acceptance, release runnable code, configurations, and preprocessing instructions. We will not include any external link in the rebuttal, consistent with MICCAI policy. This correction does not alter the submitted experimental content. 
(4) Generalization beyond NSD (R1/AC). We acknowledge that current validation is limited to 7T NSD. NSD was chosen because it provides standardized high-quality fMRI, shared test images, and direct comparability with MindEye, MindBridge, UMBRAE, and BrainCaptioning. The method itself is not tied to NSD: it requires only fMRI tokens and a target visual/textual latent space. We will add this limitation and discuss future evaluation on lower-field MRI, additional ROIs, clinical cohorts, and non-fMRI neural signals. 
(5) Neuroscience interpretability and presentation (R3/AC). We agree that the manuscript emphasizes decoding performance more than neuroscientific interpretation. We will add a discussion explaining that HDT transport maps can be inspected as proxies for token-level visual topography, CMI prototypes as semantic anchors rather than neural labels, and CAF gates as indicators of the geometry–semantics trade-off. We will keep these claims descriptive and avoid causal neuroscientific over-interpretation. We will also correct the HDF/HDT typo in Fig. 1 and unify all abbreviations and notation.

title: NeuroFlow: Manifold-Aware Topological Flow Matching for EEG Decoding
abstract: Decoding visual content from non-invasive EEG is fundamentally challenged by representation collapse, semantic ambiguity, and stochastic generation drift. In this work, we propose NeuroFlow, a structured EEG–vision alignment framework that addresses these issues from both representation learning and generation perspectives. To capture transient functional connectivity without inducing dimensional collapse, we introduce a Manifold-Aware Dynamic Graph Encoder regularized by an orthogonality constraint. To further resolve the inherent semantic ambiguity of these encoded features, a Prototype-Guided Semantic Rectification layer is employed to anchor loose EEG representations to the compact support of the visual manifold. Furthermore, we reformulate the generation process using Deterministic Flow Matching, constructing an optimal transport path that ensures stable semantic transport by mitigating the stochastic drift of diffusion models.   Experiments on the THINGS-EEG dataset demonstrate that NeuroFlow outperforms state-of-the-art methods in zero-shot retrieval (Top-1 Acc: 32.4\%, +4.6\% gain) and achieves superior generation fidelity with 5 fewer inference steps. Codes are available at  https://github.com/happyeverymoment/NeuroFlow
subject_areas: Modalities -> EEG / MEG / ECG / Physiological Signals

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The main contribution of this paper is the proposal of NeuroFlow, a novel framework designed to accurately reconstruct visual images from EEG signals. It tackles three major bottlenecks in existing methods: a) Instead of treating brain channels independently, it uses a dynamic graph (DRG) to capture how different brain regions connect, and a special rule is designed to prevent the extracted features from collapsing into useless noise. 
b) Since EEG signals are noisy and hard to read, the model uses a “memory bank” of clear visual prototypes. c) Instead of using slow, random diffusion models, it uses Conditional Flow Matching to create a fast, straight-line path from the brain signal directly to the image, making the generation process stable and faster.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The model achieves state-of-the-art accuracy in zero-shot tasks, successfully matching brain signals to the correct images significantly better than existing methods. 
2.It drastically speeds up the image generation process, requiring fewer steps than traditional diffusion models while still producing higher-quality and more accurate pictures. 
3.The system’s unique design cleverly prevents the common problem of “dimensional collapse” (where data features blur together), making the feature extraction process much more stable and reliable
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The model’s performance is currently only validated on a single benchmark dataset (THINGS-EEG) under a specific zero-shot protocol. The authors acknowledge that they have not yet tested the framework across diverse EEG recording conditions or varying equipment, which is critical for proving real-world reliability in Brain-Computer Interface applications. 
2.Because the model prioritizes aligning the overall semantic meaning rather than fitting high-frequency noise, the generated images may lack exact fine-grained, pixel-level textures compared to the original visual stimuli.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

It introduces an innovative framework that effectively solves critical bottlenecks in EEG decoding, specifically dimensional collapse and semantic ambiguity. The methodology is well-designed, and the results are highly compelling.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal has adequately addressed my main concerns, so I am satisfied with the authors’ response and recommend acceptance.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes NeuroFlow, a two-stage EEG-to-image decoding framework built on: 1) a dynamic graph EEG encoder with Barlow-Twins-style decorrelation, 2) a prototype-guided semantic rectification module, and 3) conditional flow matching for image-embedding generation followed by frozen SDXL + IP-Adapter decoding. On THINGS-EEG, the paper reports improved zero-shot retrieval and competitive generation quality with substantially fewer sampling steps than diffusion-based baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper addresses a real bottleneck in EEG-based visual decoding: unstable conditioning and expensive diffusion sampling.
2.The use of flow matching is a meaningful technical contribution in this domain and is a reasonable alternative to diffusion for faster inference.
3.The retrieval gains in Table 1 are nontrivial.
The paper includes ablation and interpretability analyses rather than only headline results.
The method is modular and the overall pipeline is easy to follow.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The full evaluation is conducted on only THINGS-EEG (Sec. 3.1). For a MICCAI paper, this is a weak validation base, especially for a method claiming broad robustness to semantic ambiguity and stochastic drift. There is no external dataset, no cross-dataset test, and no serious analysis of robustness across acquisition conditions.
In Table 2, ATM is shown at 50 steps and NeuroFlow at 10/20/50 steps, but CoCapturer has no inference time reported, and the comparison mixes methods with different sampling regimes and likely different back-end decoders. It is therefore difficult to determine how much of the gain comes from the proposed transport model versus implementation choices around the frozen generative backbone.
3.Table 1 reports mean ± std across subjects, but there are no significance tests, confidence intervals on method differences, or paired comparisons. Given only 10 subjects, the claim of clear superiority should be supported more rigorously.
4.EEG methods are highly sensitive to inter-subject variability. The paper reports aggregate subject-wise performance, but does not deeply examine cross-subject transfer, leave-one-subject-out settings, or calibration sensitivity. This is a major omission for practical relevance.
5.Ablation evidence is still incomplete. Table 3 supports that the full combination helps, but it does not isolate whether gains mainly come from SigLIP, the prototype memory, the BT regularizer, or the dynamic graph itself under matched backbones and parameter counts. In particular, the paper argues strongly for topology modeling, but the ablation also shows the graph module alone hurts.
6.The paper emphasizes better “high-fidelity” generation, but the reported image metrics are mixed, and some are not especially strong evidence of semantic correctness in EEG-conditioned generation. More semantically grounded evaluation would be needed.
7.The work is closer to brain-computer interface / multimodal generative modeling than to core medical image computing. It may still interest MICCAI readers, but the paper should make the medical or neuroimaging relevance more explicit.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper has a good central idea, and the flow-matching component is the most convincing novelty. But for MICCAI, the current evidence base is too narrow and the evaluation is not yet rigorous enough to fully support the strength of the claims.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
1.A decorrelated dynamic graph encoder that captures transient functional connectivity while mitigating over-smoothing and dimensional collapse.
2.A prototype-guided semantic rectification module that anchors noisy EEG embeddings to visual prototypes for better cross-modal alignment.
3.A flow matching-based generation framework that replaces stochastic diffusion trajectories with deterministic transport, improving generation stability and inference efficiency.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper presents the method as a set of modules, each designed to address a different challenge in EEG visual decoding.
2.The paper goes beyond overall performance and provides extensive ablation and analysis experiments.
3.The proposed method shows consistent performance gains over the compared baselines.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The paper frames representation collapse, semantic ambiguity, and stochastic generation drift as key bottlenecks, but their existence and practical impact in EEG visual decoding are not rigorously established. In addition, many of the cited references are prior visual decoding papers, and it is unclear whether they directly support these claims as the main causes of performance degradation. More direct evidence or more appropriate references would strengthen the motivation.
2.Although each module is intuitively motivated, the overall framework appears largely as a combination of existing components, such as dynamic graph modeling, prototype-based refinement, and flow matching. As a result, the originality of the method and the necessity of each individual component are not fully convincing.
3.While the paper presents flow matching as an important alternative to stochastic diffusion-based generation, in practice it mainly operates as an embedding-space transport module before a frozen SDXL/IP-Adapter backbone. As such, its contribution appears closer to replacing the diffusion prior at the embedding level than to fundamentally changing the overall generative pipeline.
4.The overall flow of the paper is difficult to follow, and the connection between the overview and the method section is not sufficiently clear. In addition, the terminology, notation, and module descriptions are not explained in a sufficiently coherent manner, making the proposed framework feel more like a loose combination of modules than a well-integrated design.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
I encourage the authors to clarify the above concerns in the rebuttal, as my final assessment will depend on how convincingly these issues are addressed.

While the paper is reasonably polished and supported by experimental effort, I find its central motivation and technical claims too ambiguous to be fully convincing. The claimed bottlenecks are not rigorously validated in the EEG decoding setting, the method appears largely as a combination of existing components, and the efficiency advantage is not established through a fully fair comparison. The paper is also difficult to follow at times, as the connection between the overview and the method section is not always clear, and the framework does not read as a fully well-integrated design. Overall, the paper is promising, but in its current form it remains marginally below the acceptance threshold.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal provides additional claims and results, but it does not convincingly address my fundamental concerns about the paper’s motivation, originality, and methodological coherence, which would require substantial revision beyond rebuttal-stage clarification.

meta_reviews.text:
The reviewers agree that the paper addresses an interesting problem and proposes a promising framework, particularly with the use of flow matching for efficient EEG-to-image decoding. The overall approach is well-structured and shows competitive performance. However, several key concerns remain. The main limitation is the weak empirical validation, as experiments are conducted only on a single dataset without analysis of cross-subject variability or robustness. In addition, the statistical significance of the reported improvements is unclear. There are also concerns regarding the clarity of the technical contribution, as it is not sufficiently demonstrated how much each component contributes to the final performance. Furthermore, the fairness of comparisons (e.g., differences in sampling steps and missing baseline details) needs clarification. Finally, the novelty and motivation should be more clearly justified. The final decision will depend on how convincingly these points are addressed.

The paper presents a well-structured framework for EEG-to-image reconstruction and addresses several practical challenges in EEG visual decoding. The proposed NeuroFlow combines dynamic graph modeling, prototype-guided semantic rectification, and flow matching in a coherent manner, and demonstrates consistent improvements in both retrieval and generation tasks. In addition, the paper provides extensive ablation studies and analysis experiments that help support the effectiveness of the individual components. The reviewers raised valid concerns regarding validation on a single dataset, limited robustness analysis across acquisition conditions and subjects, and the degree of novelty of individual modules. However, I think these limitations primarily concern the scope of validation rather than the soundness of the proposed methodology. The experimental results are consistently strong, the technical contributions are well motivated, and the analysis goes beyond simple performance reporting. Overall, while additional validation on diverse EEG datasets would further strengthen the work, I believe the paper makes a meaningful contribution to EEG-based visual decoding and provides sufficient technical and empirical evidence to merit acceptance.

After carefully reviewing the authors’ rebuttal, I have revised my initial assessment to Accept. The authors have provided a thorough, evidence-based response that directly addresses the core concerns raised by all three reviewers.
The rebuttal provides several clarifications however the concerns related to motivation and novelty still exist.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for acknowledging our retrieval performance, computational efficiency, and interpretability, particularly R1 for validating our methodological novelty. We address the core concerns below:
1.Generation Efficiency & Fair Comparison (R1, R2, R3): We clarify that “high-fidelity” primarily denotes semantic (CLIP, Inception) and structural (SSIM) alignment (our semantic scores are superior, as shown in Tab. 2 and Fig. 2). We acknowledge a trade-off in exact pixel-level similarity (PixCorr), as Flow Matching prioritizes semantic manifold alignment rather than fitting high-frequency stochastic details. For a fair comparison, we re-evaluated CoCapturer using the identical frozen backbone in our revision. NeuroFlow achieves better semantic scores in just 20 steps with a >5x speedup, confirming its intrinsic advantage.
2.Cross-Dataset Validation (R1, R2): Evaluated on an MEG dataset under identical protocols, NeuroFlow (Top-1: 14.8%, Top-5: 37.2%) significantly outperforms SOTA methods NICE (10.8%, 32.1%) and CoCapturer (11.3%, 35.0%), demonstrating robust cross-dataset generalization.
3.Component Synergy & Ablation (R2, R3): Ablation shows strong synergy, not mere combination. DRG alone causes topological over-smoothing and performance drops (Fig. 3). Conversely, BT loss alone yields limited improvement lacking dynamic topological guidance. Only their integration mitigates dimensional collapse and preserves features, boosting performance to 30.2%. SigLIP mainly accelerates training with marginal gains (Top-1: 31.9% to 32.4%), thus omitted due to space.
4.Statistical Significance & Cross-Subject (R2): Paired t-tests across 10 subjects confirm NeuroFlow’s improvements are statistically significant (vs. CoCapturer: Top-1 p=0.02, Top-5 p=0.009). Under the stringent Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) setting, our model achieved 12.9% (Top-1) and 31.4% (Top-5) accuracy, significantly outperforming CoCapturer (9.3%, 25.4%), proving robustness to inter-subject variability.
5.Clinical Value & MICCAI Scope (R2): By decoding neural-visual mappings, our research provides a crucial prognostic evaluation tool for populations with cognitive or visual impairments. This aligns perfectly with MICCAI’s core mission of advancing clinical translation and neuro-engineering.
6.Sensitivity & Robustness (R2): Analyses indicate that performance fluctuations from adjusting key hyperparameters lack statistical significance, showing high parameter robustness. We will explore multi-center data for further validation.
7.Theoretical Motivation & References (R3): EEG “semantic ambiguity” intrinsically originates from skull attenuation and volume conduction, while GNN “representation collapse” is a mathematically proven phenomenon. Specifically, dimensional collapse is evidenced by feature redundancy in Fig. 3(d), and semantic ambiguity by the scattered latent distribution before PRL (Fig. 3(b)). Regarding stochastic drift, deterministic transport yields more stable semantic trajectories under weak EEG conditions. We replaced generic visual decoding citations with specific neuroscience and graph theory literature to strengthen our premise.
8.Methodological Novelty (R3): Our framework is a customized, causally-linked design for EEG, not a loose combination. DRG introduces dynamic topology but causes over-smoothing, prompting the decorrelation (BT) constraint; PRL then corrects the noisy geometry; finally, Flow Matching ensures stable transport to the visual space (showing excellent stability across 16.5k paired samples). We do not aim to replace the entire SDXL framework; our core contribution lies in replacing stochastic diffusion with deterministic transport in the embedding space under weak EEG conditions, significantly enhancing generation stability and reducing inference costs.
9.Clarity of Presentation (R3): We will rewrite the methodology section to unify mathematical notations and logical flow, improving overall readability.

title: NeuroSonic: Conditional Flow Matching for EEG-to-Speech Reconstruction
abstract:
Reconstructing continuous speech from scalp electroencephalography (EEG) remains fundamentally challenging. EEG provides a weak, spatially diffuse, and highly variable measurement of distributed cortical activity, whereas speech is organized as a coherent acoustic trajectory with strong harmonic and temporal structure. The resulting mismatch makes waveform regression unstable and causes stochastic multi-step generation to be sensitive to artifact-dependent conditioning and subject variability.
We introduce \textbf{NeuroSonic}, a conditional flow-matching framework for EEG-to-speech reconstruction. Instead of predicting waveforms directly or refining them through stochastic denoising, NeuroSonic learns a deterministic probability-flow velocity field that transports a noise-corrupted acoustic state toward clean speech under EEG conditioning. EEG and audio are embedded into a shared token space and processed by a time-conditioned gated Transformer that parameterizes the transport ordinary differential equation. This formulation models trajectory evolution explicitly while avoiding iterative stochastic sampling.
We evaluate NeuroSonic on the CineBrain and EAV benchmarks under cross-subject evaluation. Across both datasets, the proposed method improves distributional realism, spectral fidelity, and perceptual quality over representative GAN-, diffusion-, and mean-flow baselines, with up to a 26.3\% gain in overall perceptual quality.
The performance gap is most evident in artifact-heavy segments, where conditioning variability is strongest. These findings indicate that deterministic conditional transport provides a stable and effective formulation for EEG-driven speech reconstruction.
subject_areas: Modalities -> EEG / MEG / ECG / Physiological Signals

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This work presents a novel technique for EEG-based speech reconstruction, which is based on conditional flow matching. The authors claim this reduces artifact driven noise and instabilities compared to direct waveform rejection. The results show that this method outperforms other generative techniques such as GANs or Diffusion models.
reviews.text_strengths: The idea of using conditional flow matching for this problem has been justified well and is a significant novel contribution. They evaluate the model in a cross subject task, which is vital to ensure robustness. The authors provide spectrogram, waveform and PSD plots for qualitative comparisons in addition to quantitative evaluations. They even provide supplementary files with reconstructed audio.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) The authors claim this in the introduction “speech evolves along a highly organized acoustic trajectory characterized by harmonic structure and temporal coherence” and “ This perspective is well suited to speech reconstruction, where temporal coherence is intrinsic to the signal structure. “. However, I feel the authors have confused the acoustic temporal dynamics and the time variable used in the flow matching process, the latter having nothing to do with actual EEG/speech time. As I understand it, the t variable (called continuous time by the authors) is just a parameter in the conditional flow matching algorithm used to map the noisy sample (t=0) to the clean sample (t=1). It has no relation to actual temporal characteristics of the waveform as far as I know. Even the time-conditioned transformer works with this t variable and not actual speech/EEG time. The authors should carefully explain how the flow method leads to better temporal coherence, or else remove such claims in the introduction.
2) A related issue is that the explanation of conditional flow matching is not provided in enough detail in this paper. The explanations could be better structured with clear inputs and outputs for each component of the model and corresponding objectives. For example, it is not clear exactly where zt enters the model. It is not clear how the output Z of equation 10 is used in the next line Xpred = net(zt, t, E). If E is used for Xpred, where is Z used? The audio decoder that is used is also not specifically mentioned.
3) The baselines for comparison seem to be constructed and implemented by the authors. Perhaps it would have been better to also compare with existing models that were specifically built for EEG-speech reconstruction. This would allow direct comparison with published work.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I think the paper provides a novel contribution in terms of applying conditional flow matching to this application. However, it could benefit from clearer explanations and structure especially in the methods.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_ethics:
It would be better to add some numerical results to the abstract
In Fig 1, what is zt, epsilon? Since these terms are defined much later on, it would be better to give a short description in the caption. Also, the first part of the caption for (c) actually describes (b) when talking about the decoder. Instead make it specific to the figure (c)
There is an unnecessary repetition of the definitions of E and X.
Define AdaLN in eq 7 and 8
Fig 3 seems to show that DM is almost as good or even better than NeuroSonic. The authors should note this and discuss it.
The authors should cite recent work on flow-based EEG-speech reconstruction. For example: Xiang, Shu, Haobo Ling, and Meihong Wu. “Cross-Modal Alignment and Rectified Flow-Based Latent Representation Synthesis for Enhanced Speech-Driven Alzheimer’s Disease Detection. “ Bioengineering 13.3 (2026): 370.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose NeuroSonic, a conditional flow matching framework that reconstructs continuous speech from scalp EEG. The method reformulates EEG-to-speech reconstruction as conditional acoustic transport: a time-conditioned gated Transformer parameterizes a probability-flow ODE that maps a noise-corrupted acoustic state toward clean speech under EEG conditioning. EEG and audio are patchified and embedded into a shared token space, and the learned ODE is integrated with a fixed-step Heun solver at inference. The authors evaluate NeuroSonic on two public EEG-audio benchmarks, CineBrain and EAV, against GAN, diffusion, and mean-flow baselines under cross-subject splits.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper offers a coherent formulation of EEG-conditioned speech reconstruction as deterministic acoustic transport. Compared with stochastic diffusion, a single-pass ODE integration avoids artifact-dependent noise schedules that can degrade reconstruction across sampling steps. The motivation is well aligned with the statistical properties of scalp EEG described in the introduction.
The use of RMS-normalized attention on queries and keys is a well-motivated design choice. Flow matching with time-dependent interpolation is known to induce feature-scale drift across interpolation times, and the authors explicitly address this source of instability.
The evaluation compares NeuroSonic against GAN, diffusion, and mean-flow baselines on two public datasets under consistent cross-subject splits. The inference-time advantage of flow matching over stochastic diffusion is clearly substantiated by the reported numbers.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
-The evaluation does not validate cross-stimulus generalization. All CineBrain participants are exposed to the same audiovisual stimuli, so a cross-subject split leaves the test audio already present in the training set, paired with other subjects’ EEG. Under this setup, the model can learn to associate an EEG pattern with an already-seen audio segment, rather than decode speech from neural activity. A held-out-episode protocol or cross-dataset generalization from CineBrain to EAV is necessary to support the central claim of EEG-to-speech reconstruction.
The reported metrics measure distributional realism and reference-free perceptual quality, but none assess sample-wise correspondence between the generated waveform and the specific stimulus the subject was listening to. Correspondence-level metrics such as ASR-based WER or stimulus identification accuracy are missing. In particular, NeuroSonic exceeding the ground-truth recording on EAV OVRL is more consistent with a prior-dominant generator sampling from a narrow acoustic manifold than with faithful decoding.
The ablation study is confined to the internal loss formulation, namely clean-state velocity versus endpoint x-loss regression. There is no ablation that isolates the causal contribution of EEG conditioning itself. A shuffled-EEG baseline with mismatched pairs and a null-EEG baseline with zero or Gaussian input are the most direct way to establish that the reported improvements arise from neural decoding rather than from flow matching fitting a narrow audio prior.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
EAV consists of spontaneous conversational recordings, which may implicitly provide cross-stimulus structure since different subjects likely produced different utterances. If the authors clarify this and report, for instance, that there is no overlap between train and test subjects’ speech content, the main concern on stimulus leakage becomes substantially weaker on EAV. This would be a low-cost but high-impact rebuttal addition.

The paper presents a technically sound application of conditional flow matching to EEG-to-speech reconstruction, with stable training, cross-subject generalization, and consistent improvements over GAN, diffusion, and mean-flow baselines. However, the current evaluation cannot distinguish EEG-driven decoding from class-conditional speech generation over a narrow audio manifold, since CineBrain is shared-stimulus across subjects and all reported metrics measure marginal distribution quality rather than sample-wise correspondence with the target stimulus. I recommend weak accept conditional on the rebuttal addressing stimulus overlap between train and test splits, providing at least one correspondence-level metric such as ASR-based WER, and reporting a null or shuffled EEG baseline.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The rebuttal partially addresses my main concerns. The added ASR-WER results are useful because they assess content correspondence beyond FAD/LSD/SC and DNSMOS, and the clarification on EAV reduces the stimulus-overlap concern for that dataset.
However, I do not think the Null-EEG result fully establishes EEG-driven decoding. Since the control uses Gaussian EEG, the degradation can mainly reflect an out-of-distribution conditioning input. A stronger control would be to shuffle real EEG segments within the split and test whether the reconstruction follows the mismatched EEG-paired speech or remains driven by the acoustic prior/corrupted audio state.
Overall, the paper remains technically sound and the rebuttal improves the evidence, but the central EEG-to-speech claim is still not fully separated from speech-prior-driven reconstruction. I therefore keep a marginal positive recommendation.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a method for reconstructing speech from EEG signals using a generative modeling framework based on conditional flow matching. The approach uses a Transformer-based architecture to model a deterministic process that transforms noise into speech while being conditioned on EEG. However, the formulation and overall objective are not clearly articulated, making it difficult to understand whether the method performs true EEG-to-speech reconstruction or a form of EEG-guided speech generation.
reviews.text_strengths:
EEG-to-speech reconstruction, which is an important direction for brain-computer interfaces and assistive communication.
The use of modern generative modeling techniques, particularly conditional flow matching, is timely and aligns with recent advances in speech generation and multimodal learning.
The overall idea of leveraging generative models for neural decoding is interesting and could be promising if supported by stronger evaluation and analysis.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The overall objective is unclear: it is difficult to determine whether the method targets speech reconstruction, generation, or denoising.
The paper does not clearly justify why EEG should be used within a generative denoising/transport framework, nor what specific information (e.g., phonetic, temporal, or semantic cues) is expected to guide reconstruction. Prior work in neural speech decoding (e.g., Willett, 2023; Anumanchipalli, 2019) explicitly models linguistic or articulatory representations, which is not clearly defined here.
The methodological novelty is unclear, and the paper does not demonstrate why this formulation is particularly suited to EEG-to-speech reconstruction compared to existing approaches.
The evaluation relies on audio-quality metrics (FAD, LSD, SC, DNSMOS), which do not assess whether the reconstructed speech preserves correct linguistic content. In contrast, prior work evaluates intelligibility using ASR-based metrics (WER/CER), phoneme accuracy, or human transcription.
The paper lacks standard control experiments (e.g., EEG shuffling, temporal misalignment, or no-EEG baselines), making it unclear to what extent the model actually leverages EEG rather than learned audio priors.
The ablation study is limited and does not isolate key components; comparisons with GAN and diffusion models are not controlled for architecture or capacity, making it difficult to attribute improvements to the proposed method.
No comparison is provided against simpler baselines (e.g., regression-based decoding, CCA, or speech denoising/enhancement), leaving unclear whether the proposed approach offers a meaningful advantage.
Qualitative results (e.g., spectrograms) suggest possible hallucinated harmonic structures, raising concerns about faithful reconstruction.
The datasets include complex audio (speech, music, environmental sounds), but no analysis is provided to separate these components or assess their impact.
Key implementation details (preprocessing, EEG–audio alignment, segmentation, inference) are insufficiently described, limiting reproducibility.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses an interesting problem, but the current submission does not provide sufficient evidence to support its claims. In particular, the lack of clear motivation, limited ablation analysis, and absence of appropriate evaluation for speech reconstruction (e.g., intelligibility metrics and EEG-specific controls) make it difficult to assess the actual contribution of the proposed method. Additionally, the experimental comparisons are not sufficiently controlled to isolate the effect of the proposed approach. As a result, the work does not yet meet the standard expected for acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
Thank you for the response. The added WER results and Null-EEG control are useful.
The WER values remain a bit high, suggesting limited linguistic-content preservation. Please clarify how WER was computed, which ASR system was used, and where the method fails.
Regarding harmonic fidelity, my concern was not that harmonics are unexpected in speech. Rather, it is unclear whether the observed harmonic/formant structures are faithfully reconstructed from the paired reference, driven by EEG conditioning, or produced by the synthesis/transport prior. This concern is consistent with the high WER values, which suggest substantial reconstruction or synthesis errors, even if WER does not directly measure harmonic fidelity.
Finally, the lack of ablations remains a major concern. The Null-EEG control is helpful but insufficient to isolate the roles of EEG conditioning, the acoustic prior, flow matching, model capacity, and learned synthesis priors. Therefore, the main concerns remain unresolved.

meta_reviews.text:
Please provide justifications and clarifications for the concerns raised by the reviewers.

This paper proposes NeuroSonic, a conditional flow matching framework for EEG-to-speech reconstruction. Reviewer scores are 5/4/2, with R1 accepting unconditionally, R2 accepting marginally post-rebuttal, and R4 rejecting.
Reviewers broadly agree that the targeted application is clinically relevant, the formulation is well-motivated, and the method consistently outperforms baselines across two datasets.
The shared concerns fall in the evaluation protocols, such as how the train/test sets are split, the absence of correspondence-level metrics, lack of EEG-specific controls, and limited ablation. The rebuttal partially addresses these by adding WER results, a Null-EEG control showing substantial degradation without valid EEG, and clarifying that test subject EEG is always unseen. The shuffled real-EEG control remains unresolved after the rebuttal.
Considering that the proposed method is genuinely interesting and the evaluations, though not ideal, sufficiently support the claims, the strength outweighs the weaknesses and I recommend acceptance.

R4’s reject rests on concerns (unclear EEG usage, hallucinated harmonics) that despite worth taking into account, but that R1 and R2 -both more senior reviewers- do not share. 
In order to understand this discrepancy I think it is worth noting that R4 categorized this as an “application study” while R1 and R2 both categorized it as a methodological contribution.
In their rebuttal, the authors credibly attribute R4 concerns to a misunderstanding of scalp-EEG constraints and basic speech acoustics. The null-EEG control demonstrates meaningful EEG conditioning, and R2’s post-rebuttal framing as “EEG-conditioned acoustic reconstruction” I believe appropriately scopes the contribution - the framing mismatch likely contributed to R4’s harsh assessment. Moreover, R2 upgraded his score to accept post-rebuttal after the authors provided ASR-WER metrics and clarified the EAV stimulus-overlap concern.

The rebuttal address the reviewers’ concerns but not in full. The work is better packaged as EEG-conditioned acoustic reconstruction, and it should be clarified what the source of the performance gain is.

author_feedback_text:
[R1.1/R1.2] Flow notation: 
t is a flow-path coordinate, not physical EEG/speech time; we will revise the Intro/Sec. 2.2.In training, the audio encoder takes z_t, a corrupted full speech segment, not clean X. EEG/corrupted-audio tokens form Z, which is processed by the t-conditioned Transformer; acoustic tokens are then MLP-decoded to X_pred. Temporal coherence arises indirectly from EEG-conditioned deterministic transport of the spectro-temporal structure of z_t toward X.
[R1.3/R3.6/R3.7] Baselines:
All learned baselines use the same preprocessing and comparable parameter budgets. We will add FESDE (2406.08644), and a denoising baseline. NeuroSonic improves FESDE on Cine: FAD/LSD/SC/DNSMOS(SIG/BAK/OVRL)/WER 62.78/29.69/1.07/1.61-1.62-1.32/1.01 → 39.06/14.24/0.64/1.95-1.64-1.44/0.49, and on EAV: LSD/SC/DNSMOS/WER 24.07/1.08/2.94-2.77-2.24/0.99 → 12.98/0.28/3.31-3.07-2.59/0.46.It also outperforms denoising: Cine FAD/LSD/SC 231.73/120.27/1.13 vs. 39.06/14.24/0.64; EAV 103.66/52.31/0.98 vs. 11.64/12.98/0.28.
[R1.4–R1.7] Text fixes:
We will add representative numbers to the abstract; define z_t, ε, and t in Fig. 1; correct panels (b)(c); define E and X only once; and add the AdaLN definition near Eqs. 7–8.
[R1.8] Spectral trade-off:
Fig. 3 shows a trade-off: DM is closer to GT in some high-frequency regions, while NeuroSonic better matches speech-relevant low/mid bands. Metrics support this: WER on Cine/EAV drops 0.97/0.97 → 0.49/0.46.
[R1.9] Related work:
We will cite Xiang et al. as recent flow-based EEG-speech work.
[R2.1] Generalization:
EAV is conversational rather than a shared fixed-stimulus set; with our cross-subject split, both test subjects and utterances are unseen. For CineBrain, stimuli are shared, but the split is subject-disjoint.
[R2.2/R3.4] Content correspondence:
We add ASR-WER as a sample-correspondence metric. NeuroSonic reduces WER vs. DM from 0.97 to 0.49 on Cine and 0.97 to 0.46 on EAV, showing better paired-content alignment. DNSMOS is reference-free: EAV OVRL above GT reflects cleanness/noise suppression, not content fidelity; WER checks content.
[R2.3/R3.5] EEG control:
We add Null-EEG: trained NeuroSonic with fixed weights, but Gaussian-noise EEG; WER only on dialogue-speech. Performance drops: Cine FAD/LSD/SC/WER 39.06/14.24/0.64/0.49 → 155.64/92.28/0.99/1.02; EAV 11.64/12.98/0.28/0.46 → 17.84/19.44/1.00/0.97.With the acoustic prior fixed, valid EEG adds reconstruction constraints.
[R3.1] Objective:
NeuroSonic performs EEG-conditioned acoustic reconstruction, given aligned EEG, it reconstructs paired speech using EEG conditioning and an acoustic transport prior.
[R3.2] Motivation:
EEG contains speech-evoked responses containing timing, rhythmic/prosodic, and coarse phonetic/semantic cues. Its non-invasiveness makes EEG-guided reconstruction relevant to assistive speech generation for severe speech impairment, while transport supplies coherent acoustics. Unlike Willett/Anumanchipalli, which use invasive recordings and explicit phoneme representations, we use scalp EEG as coarse transport conditioning.
[R3.3] Method novelty:
We formulate EEG-to-speech as conditional flow matching, enabling weak neural cues to guide acoustic reconstruction without stochastic denoising chains. This makes the approach well suited to low-SNR, cross-subject EEG.
[R3.8] Harmonic fidelity:
Spectrograms do not indicate hallucinated harmonics: harmonic/formant patterns are intrinsic to speech, and reconstructions follow reference temporal modulation, not arbitrary templates.
[R3.9] Audio composition:
Cine composition analysis shows speech-dominant vs. non-speech/background-dominant FAD/LSD/SC = 37.31/11.19/0.62 vs. 40.72/16.34/0.65 and OVRL = 1.47 vs. 1.40.
[R3.10] Reproducibility:
Secs. 3.1/3.2 already describe preprocessing/inference. Original datasets synchronize EEG-audio pairs; each EEG segment is recorded during its paired audio stimulus. We use 4-s CineBrain and 5-s EAV windows.

title: NeuroSymb-MRG: Differentiable Abductive Reasoning with Active Uncertainty Minimization for Radiology Report Generation
abstract: Automatic generation of radiology reports seeks to reduce clinician workload while improving documentation consistency. Existing methods that adopt encoder-decoder or retrieval-augmented pipelines achieve progress in fluency but remain vulnerable to visual-linguistic biases, structural misalignment, and lack of explicit multi-hop clinical reasoning. We present NeuroSymb-MRG, a unified framework that integrates NeuroSymbolic abductive reasoning with active uncertainty minimization to produce structured, interpretable reports. The system maps image features to probabilistic clinical concepts, composes differentiable logic-based reasoning chains, decodes those chains into templated clauses, and refines the textual output via retrieval and constrained language-model editing. An active sampling loop driven by rule-level uncertainty and diversity guides targeted training optimization and promptbook refinement. Experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements in structural coherence and interpretability and standard language metrics compared to representative baselines.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes the NeuroSymb-MRG framework to address key challenges in radiology report generation, including visual-linguistic biases, factual inconsistency, and the lack of explicit multi-hop reasoning. The method maps visual features into probabilistic clinical concepts, then generates structured intermediate representations through differentiable neuro-symbolic reasoning chains. It further employs multi-agent orchestration to coordinate visual evidence, knowledge constraints, generation modules, and conflict verification, and produces structured reports through rule decoding, retrieval-augmented draft generation, and constrained language model refinement. In addition, the paper introduces an active sampling and clinical feedback mechanism based on rule-level uncertainty. Experiments on MIMIC-CXR and IU X-ray show higher language-generation metrics than a range of baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.This paper tackles several common limitations of existing methods, including visual-linguistic biases, factual inconsistency, and the lack of explicit multi-hop reasoning, and proposes a unified framework centered on neuro-symbolic reasoning. The problem is meaningful and well motivated in the context of clinical report generation. 
2.The most notable strength of the paper is its attempt to move beyond the conventional end-to-end paradigm for radiology report generation by introducing an explicit neuro-symbolic reasoning stage. Through the pipeline of “clinical concept prediction -> rule composition -> clause generation”,the paper incorporates a structured reasoning process into report generation. 
3.Another task-specific highlight is the active uncertainty minimization mechanism based on rule-level uncertainty. This design combines uncertainty estimation with clinician-in-the-loop refinement, which is well aligned with the practical needs of medical generation tasks. 
4.The paper also provides relatively comprehensive component-level ablation studies. In particular, the authors analyze the roles of core modules such as the differentiable logic layer, rule-guided decoder, active uncertainty minimization, retrieval, and verifier.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The core claims of the paper are improved factual consistency and clinically grounded generation. However, the main experiments still rely primarily on surface-level text overlap metrics such as BLEU, ROUGE-L, and METEOR, while lacking more direct evidence from factual consistency metrics, clinical correctness evaluation, or expert human assessment. As a result, the current experimental results are still insufficient to fully support the paper’s central claims, especially stronger claims such as reducing contradictions and improving clinical grounding. 
2.The paper integrates many components into a single system, including the visual backbone, concept predictor, differentiable logic, rule-guided decoding, retrieval augmentation, LLM refinement, verifier, knowledge agent, and active uncertainty minimization. While this makes the framework comprehensive, the methodological storyline remains somewhat unfocused, and it is difficult to quickly identify what the paper’s single most important methodological contribution is. At its current stage, the work reads more like a carefully designed pipeline than a sharply focused method paper. The novelty boundary and contribution hierarchy would benefit from further clarification. 
3.The specific mechanism of multi-agent orchestration is still not sufficiently clear. Although the paper introduces multiple specialized agents and presents a conflict resolution mechanism based on confidence aggregation, it does not adequately explain the input/output of each agent, their invocation order, or how they actually interact throughout the reasoning and report generation process. Based on the current methodological description, this part appears closer to coordination and packaging of multiple functional modules than to a strict agent-based learning framework. It is therefore difficult to judge whether multi-agent orchestration constitutes a core algorithmic contribution or mainly serves as a high-level system organization strategy. 
4.The connection between active uncertainty minimization and promptbook refinement still requires further clarification. The abstract, contribution summary, and framework figure state that rule-level uncertainty can drive clinician-in-the-loop adjudication and promptbook refinement. However, the paper mainly elaborates on the definitions of uncertainty estimation and active sampling, while providing only limited explanation of the representation of the promptbook, how it is updated, and how it concretely operates in Module 2.Therefore, this part currently reads more like an appealing high-level design idea, while its operational details and actual contribution still need to be made more specific.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
This paper presents a unified neuro-symbolic framework for radiology report generation, aiming to alleviate the problems of factual inconsistency and insufficient reasoning in traditional end-to-end methods through explicit concept prediction, rule composition, and uncertainty-aware refinement. The overall direction is meaningful, the method is fairly well designed, and the ablation study is relatively thorough. 
In my view, there are three main aspects that need to be strengthened. First, the current experiments still do not provide sufficiently direct support for factual consistency, clinical grounding, and contradiction mitigation, because the main evaluation still relies largely on surface-level metrics such as BLEU, ROUGE-L, and METEOR. Second, the method integrates many modules, which makes the contribution hierarchy not yet sufficiently clear; I would encourage the authors to more explicitly highlight the single most central methodological contribution in the revision. Third, the specific operational mechanism of multi-agent orchestration and promptbook refinement still needs to be elaborated further, especially the input-output relationships among modules, their invocation order, and their concrete impact on the final generated reports. If these issues can be addressed more clearly in the rebuttal or in a revised version, the paper would be more convincing.

I give a Weak Accept because the paper proposes a relatively complete neuro-symbolic framework to address factual inconsistency and the lack of explicit reasoning in radiology report generation, and it attempts to move beyond the traditional end-to-end generation paradigm through a structured pipeline of “clinical concept prediction -> rule composition -> clause generation”.In addition, the active uncertainty minimization mechanism driven by rule-level uncertainty, together with the relatively comprehensive ablation study, are also strengths of the paper.
At the same time, however, the paper’s central claims—especially improved factual consistency, reduced contradictions, and clinically grounded generation—still lack sufficiently direct experimental support, since the main evaluation remains focused on text-overlap metrics such as BLEU, ROUGE-L, and METEOR.Moreover, the method contains many components, which makes the overall contribution hierarchy and novelty boundary somewhat unclear.The specific mechanisms of multi-agent orchestration and promptbook refinement also need to be explained more clearly.Therefore, I believe this work has certain potential and is slightly above the acceptance threshold, but it still depends considerably on the rebuttal to clarify these key issues.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper describes a novel approach to apply differential abductive reasoning in the task of radiology report generation. A framework, NeuroSymb-MRG, is proposed to realise abductive reasoning and uncertainty minimisation.
reviews.text_strengths:
The main strengths include:
the application of differential abductive reasoning in radiology report generation.
a sophisticated framework to combine the above with uncertainty minimisation
a comprehensive set of experiments which show consistent improvements from the proposed model
reviews.text_weaknesses: The main weakness is the use of evaluation metrics. For radiology report evaluations, it is well known that Rouge/METEOR scores are limited as they do not deal with semantics and contexts (eg negations) well. It would be important to see the use of other more clinically relevant scores like RATE score, GREEN or similar.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The proposed approach is novel and experiments confirm the efficiency. I believe presenting this work at MICCAI would be beneficial to the community and stimulate good discussions along the methodology and applications.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper tackles the well-known issue of hallucinations and lack of interpretability in automated radiology report generation. The authors propose NeuroSymb-MRG, a framework that moves away from pure black-box text generation. Instead, it extracts visual features, maps them to clinical concepts, and then passes them through a differentiable “neuro-symbolic” logic layer that applies soft logical rules (AND, OR, NOT). The output of this logic layer is then used to retrieve relevant text fragments and fill in report templates. To make training more efficient and reliable, they also introduce an active learning loop that uses Monte Carlo dropout to estimate uncertainty, focusing the model’s learning on the most ambiguous cases.
reviews.text_strengths: Combining differentiable logic with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and active learning is a really fresh take on report generation. It directly addresses the “black box” nature of current LLM-based approaches, which is a huge barrier to clinical adoption. By forcing the model to route its decisions through explicit, soft logical rules before generating text, the system provides a clear audit trail for why a specific sentence was generated. The model achieves very competitive scores on both MIMIC-CXR and IU X-ray, outperforming several recent and strong baselines like MRG-LLM.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The paper relies entirely on standard NLP metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR). In the medical domain, these metrics are notoriously misleading. A generated report that says “There is a pneumothorax” and a ground truth that says “There is no pneumothorax” will have a very high BLEU score, but a catastrophic clinical error. You really need to include clinical efficacy metrics like CheXbert (F1-score for clinical observations) or RadGraph to prove the logic layer is actually improving factual correctness.
2.In the introduction and the ablations (Table 3), you mention a “learned feedback simulator to accelerate clinician-in-the-loop refinement.” However, looking through Section 3, I can’t find a clear explanation of how this simulator actually works. How is the clinician’s feedback simulated during the training loop? What data is it trained on? This needs a dedicated paragraph.
3.How are the diagnostic rules (the soft trees mentioned in Section 3.5) initialized? Do clinicians have to manually define the skeleton of these rules for every possible disease beforehand, or does the network learn the tree structures entirely from scratch? If it’s manual, I worry about how scalable this is to hundreds of rare findings.
4.Running 5 Monte Carlo dropout passes for active sampling during training sounds quite computationally heavy. It would be helpful to include a brief discussion on the training time/memory overhead compared to a standard end-to-end baseline.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The integration of neuro-symbolic logic into radiology report generation is highly relevant to the MICCAI community, as it directly addresses the critical need for interpretability and hallucination reduction in medical AI. The architecture is well-thought-out, and the ablation studies are incredibly thorough, proving the value of the proposed components. The main factors holding it back from a perfect score are the reliance on purely lexical metrics (BLEU/ROUGE) instead of clinical accuracy metrics, and some missing methodological details regarding the feedback simulator and rule initialization. However, the core idea is strong enough, and the empirical results are solid enough, that I believe it should be accepted.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

meta_reviews.text:
The core problem addressed is the lack of interpretability and factual reliability in automated medical report generation. Current “black-box” models often hallucinate or fail to follow logical clinical reasoning. The proposed NeuroSymb-MRG framework attempts to solve this by forcing the model to follow structured, logical steps before producing text.
The reviewers agree that the shift from end-to-end learning to a neuro-symbolic approach (logic-based reasoning) is a significant and “fresh” contribution. It creates a clearer audit trail for clinical decisions.
While the framework includes an “uncertainty” mechanism meant for clinician interaction, the actual utility is questioned because the evaluation relies on word-matching rather than clinical accuracy.
The paper presents a strong, technically sound framework that is highly relevant to the MICCAI community. However, the disconnect between the “factual consistency” claims and the “text-matching” evaluation must be addressed.

title: NoiBox: Safeguard Frontier via Reverse Adversarial Diffusion for Noisy-Box-Supervised 3D Tumor Segmentation
abstract: Voxel-wise 3D tumor segmentation is clinically essential yet prohibitively expensive to annotate at scale. In clinical workflows, radiologists can instead provide a single coarse 3D bounding box as a fast region-of-interest cue. However, such boxes are typically noisy, introducing background contamination near the inner boundary and tumor leakage beyond the box. Naive approaches that enforce hard box-as-mask constraints or use rigid pseudo-labels in self-training amplify confirmation bias and degrade boundary accuracy. To overcome this, we propose a safeguard frontier paradigm that learns 3D tumor segmentation from a noisy box by constructing a soft frontier supervision target. Specifically, we partitions 3D space into a far-field safe background and an inner/outer uncertainty band around the box. Within such band, we mine reliable foreground-core and safe-background seeds via entropy-based reliability, then generates a detached soft frontier target through reverse adversarial diffusion integrating the affinity-driven diffusion evolution with annealed prediction gate to jointly build the safeguard frontier between outward-diffusing foreground evidence and inward-diffusing background evidence. The model training combines a distance-decayed safe-background constraint with a adversarial diffusion consistency constraint. Importantly, the approach is plug-and-play with any 3D backbones. Experiments on MSD-Lung and MSD-Pancreas demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) box-supervised approaches by at least 8.0% in Dice score and exhibits strong robustness to controlled looseness and leakage perturbations, highlighting the practical value of scalable single-box annotation. Codes are at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Noibox-0xAEE499A7.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a 3D tumor segmentation framework named NoiBox, addressing the widespread noisy bounding box supervision problem in medical imaging. To overcome the confirmation bias and boundary deterioration issues arising from directly treating bounding boxes as hard masks or using pseudo-labels, the authors introduce a safeguard frontier paradigm. This method first partitions the 3D space through a Box-induced Uncertainty Field Partition (BUFP) module, extracting high-confidence foreground and background seed points. Subsequently, a Reverse Adversarial Diffusion (RAD) module is employed to solve the Dirichlet minimization problem driven by affinity, generating a soft boundary target. This soft target effectively preserves the uncertainty of the boundary during training, avoiding irreversible error accumulation.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The method proposed in this paper avoids the cost of dense voxel-level annotation, making it possible to train models using large-scale single-box annotation data. 
2.Utilizing the RAD module to handle uncertainty bands represents a novel perspective. The adversarial mechanism, where foreground evidence diffuses outwardly and background evidence diffuses inwardly, ingeniously replaces traditional pseudo-label self-training, effectively mitigating the lack of global consistency in patch-based training.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The experimental section only selected two datasets, making it difficult to verify the generalization of the method proposed in the paper. It is suggested to conduct experiments using additional datasets such as LIDC-IDRI and KiTS19, as in Reference 16.Meanwhile, the analysis of the experimental part is relatively simple and lacks reasonable explanations. 
2.Figure 1 introduces the pipeline of the proposed method, but the process is difficult to understand. It is recommended to provide a detailed introduction in the method section. 
3.The meanings of some formula variables and symbols in the article are not explained, such as formulas (3), (5), (7), and (8). Additionally, there is a lack of logical explanation and analysis for why formula (8) is expressed in the form of CspCse multiplication. 
4.In Fig. 4, we can find that background evidence propagates inward, and can not find foreground evidence propagates outward. It is recommended to select instances where only part of the foreground is covered within the bounding box.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper proposes a practical and high-performance solution for the 3D bounding box supervision problem with noise, which holds great potential for clinical translation. The idea of using bidirectional adversarial diffusion to generate soft labels is ingenious. However, the paper only selects two datasets for validation in the experimental section, making it difficult to verify the generalization performance of the model. Additionally, the paper does not provide a clear description of the methodological process. Based on its excellent experimental results, it is given Weak Accept.
However, I am open to raising my score if the authors can thoroughly address these issues during the rebuttal phase.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: the authors are proposing a novel way of performing box-supervised 3D tumor segmentation. They propose using a safeguard frontier to construct soft targets of both foreground and background voxels that then propagate towards on another to enable soft boundary aware learning.
reviews.text_strengths:
great concise summary of prior work in box-supervised segmentation
great figure 1 - explains the two portions clearly
Compared against a good number of other methods in the box segmentation space
figure 3 is a good visualization of the process
reviews.text_weaknesses:
I’m not sure that the evaluation on public datasets is necessarily a major contribution. The contribution is the methodology, and it’s great that you are using public data for evaluation but it is also expected that to support a contribution, one would evaluate it.
Thorough comparisons were indeed made to other 3D box-supervised methods, but there are a lot of other 3D segmentation methods out there that are reporting / trying to achieve the same goal of tumor segmentation. Did you compare it at all to one of the point prompt based methods like Vista3D ? They are not box-supervised but have similar goals of getting fast low annotation segmentations.
There is limited discussion in terms of impact / how it compares across the domain of tumor segmentation as a whole and no mention or discussion of limitations
Smaller comments:
In the introduction, the first time you use “safeguard frontier” it would be great to explain what you mean by that. It is a term used repeatedly throughout the work, so it would be good to be clear on what exactly you mean by that.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

In a space that is developing so quickly I think it’s important to discuss / address the proposed contributions in context of where 3D segmentation will be going. Much of the work seems to be moving towards point or noun style prompts. 3D Tumor segmentation remains a difficult task and this work aims to improve low annotation segmentation as well as makes interesting contributions to computer vision work. Therefore it could still be a good contribution to the literature. However, without any comparison to state of the art methods that attempt to produce one or few shot segmentations it is difficult to see how relevant the work will be.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The authors present a 3D tumor segmentation framework that takes coarse, noisy bounding boxes as input and learns a soft, probabilistic boundary, avoiding expensive voxel-wise annotation. The framework consists of two modules:
(a) BUFP partitions the image into confident background, confident foreground, and an uncertainty band near the box edges. Each voxel is assigned a confidence score based on geometry and model-consistency, yielding trustworthy seed voxels (“anchors”) for foreground and background.
(b) Starting from the seed voxels, RAD assigns each voxel a value between 0.0 (“background”) and 1.0 (“foreground”) via affinity-guided Dirichlet diffusion. Where both evidence streams meet, voxel value ~ 0.5, is considered the frontier. By avoiding hard class assignments, this yields a soft supervision target that preserves boundary ambiguity during training.
Segmentation results on two Medical Segmentation Decathlon tasks (MSD-Lung and MSD-Pancreas) consistently outperform state-of-the-art box-supervised methods.
reviews.text_strengths:
Strong clinical motivation. Bounding box annotation is genuinely fast and scalable, and the paper’s focus on noisy boxes reflects real clinical practice.
Conceptually elegant and well-motivated. The core idea of letting foreground and background evidence compete and meet at a natural boundary, rather than imposing hard constraints from a noisy box, is intuitive and well-grounded. It directly addresses the confirmation bias problem of pseudo-label self-training methods. Their soft frontier target is a principled way to avoid premature label commitment near uncertain regions.
Works across different backbones. Demonstrating consistent performance gains across two different 3D backbones (SwinUNETR and UNETR) is a meaningful strength. It suggests the method is not tailored to a specific architecture and can be adopted broadly.
Good ablations. The ablation in Table 2 clearly isolates the contribution of each component, and the qualitative visualization in Figure 3 effectively illustrates how the frontier evolves and tightens over training epochs.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Questionable generalizability of the affinity-based boundary mechanism. The affinity graph implicitly assumes tumor boundaries coincide with regions of high feature dissimilarity. This holds for the compact, circumscribed tumors in MSD-Lung and MSD-Pancreas, but is a meaningful limitation for infiltrative tumors (e.g., glioblastoma, peritoneal carcinomatosis) that spread gradually across tissue boundaries. The paper neither discusses this limitation nor evaluates on datasets with more infiltrative morphologies.
Clarity of presentation. The ideas are communicated almost entirely through dense formalism. Key intuitions, particularly what the Dirichlet minimization computes and why it produces 0.5 at the frontier, are absent from the main text. A single intuitive paragraph per key equation would substantially improve readability without sacrificing rigor. Figure 1 is dense and hard to parse on first reading.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The motivation of the paper is easing radiologist annotation burden. This is valid, but arguably too narrow. Any existing tumor segmentation model producing a rough prediction could serve as the noisy input, which means the method does not require a human-drawn box at all. This reframes their method as a refinement layer on top of existing segmentation pipelines, potentially enabling fully automatic iterative self-improvement.

The core idea is novel and well-motivated, the results are consistent, and the clinical relevance is clear. The two main concerns, limited generalizability discussion and presentation quality, are addressable and do not undermine the contribution.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

meta_reviews.text: The reviewers provide consistently positive evaluations (all scores: 4, 4, 5), highlighting the strong methodological contribution, clear clinical motivation, and solid empirical performance of the proposed approach . In particular, the safeguard frontier paradigm and reverse adversarial diffusion mechanism are regarded as novel and well-motivated solutions to noisy box supervision, with consistent improvements demonstrated across datasets and backbones. While some concerns are raised regarding generalization, clarity of presentation, and broader contextual comparisons, these issues are relatively minor and can be addressed in revision. Based on the overall positive feedback and my own assessment, I recommend acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
1.Generalization and experimental analysis. (R#1)
We have conducted additional experiments on LIDC-IDRI. Across two methods, our method improves the average Dice by 2.39 over the second-best baseline and reduces HD95 by 0.17, showing generalization beyond original datasets. Future updates will include dataset-specific observations, failure cases, and discussions on tumor size/boundary ambiguity. Results will be released on our anonymous GitHub.
2.Pipeline clarity. (R#1)
We have added a clearer overview in the method section before introducing the formal equations to improve readability.
3.Formula variables and symbols. (R#1)
We have re-examined and defined all variables and symbols upon first use. As for Eq. (8), (C_{sp}) and (C_{se}) are complementary constraints. Their multiplication acts as a conservative gate, where propagation is encouraged only when both spatial and semantic/evidence consistency are high. This reduces erroneous diffusion across ambiguous boundaries.
4.Foreground evidence propagation. (R#1)
The evolution of the RAD in Figure 3 is used to verify the effectiveness of strategy selection. Foreground evidence indeed expands outward from reliable seeds toward the frontier. Due to MICCAI space limits, we will put the case with partial foreground coverage by the bounding box on our anonymous GitHub.
5.Contribution statement. (R#2)
We agree that public-dataset evaluation should be viewed as validation. Our method demonstrates superior quantitative and qualitative performance against mainstream methods across different datasets. We have revised the contribution statement to focus on our methodological contributions including noisy 3D box-induced uncertainty field partition and safeguard frontier generation via reverse adversarial diffusion.
6.Comparison with Vista3D. (R#2)
We have tested Vista3D with different backbone (SegResNetDS2 and Swin-UNETR). They achieve Dice scores 4.83 and 5.66 lower than our method. As our work focuses on box supervision, we plan to extend comparisons to more prompt-based methods in the future work.
7.Impact and limitations. (R#2)
Compared to fully-supervised methods, our approach targets weakly-supervised tumor segmentation where only bounding boxes are available. It is not intended to outperform strong fully-supervised baselines, but offers a practical alternative when voxel masks are costly. Limitations (boundary ambiguity, infiltrative tumors, clinical verification) were omitted due to space limits, and will be evaluated in future work.
8.Definition of safeguard frontier. (R#2)
We have defined “safeguard frontier” at its first occurrence in the introduction. Specifically, it refers to an estimated conservative boundary between reliable background evidence and uncertain tumor regions, designed to prevent background evidence from incorrectly propagating into tumor areas.
9.Infiltrative tumor limitation. (R#3)
We agree that infiltrative tumors may violate the compact-boundary assumption. However, this limitation primarily affects local boundary smoothness, not overall segmentation accuracy. Reliable seeds affect the tumor segmentation. Our case analysis shows that Dice/HD95 remain robust to minor local deviations. We will explicitly discuss it with representative examples and update results on our anonymous GitHub.
10.Presentation and Dirichlet intuition. (R#3)
We have added intuitive explanations after key equations, clarifying that Dirichlet minimization computes a smooth evidence field on the affinity graph with foreground/background seeds fixed to high/low values. The 0.5 level set marks the balance point between the two, motivating it as the safeguard frontier. Moreover, we have added a clearer overview in the method section to improve readability.

title: Noise-Aware Importance–Uncertainty Disentangled Multimodal Learning for Robust Cancer Survival Prediction
abstract: Accurate cancer prognosis prediction from multimodal data is critical for personalized treatment planning, yet remains challenging due to modality-specific technical noise and heterogeneous prognostic characteristics. In particular, whole slide images (WSIs) and mRNA expression profiles exhibit an overlooked asymmetry: WSIs provide stable but weak prognostic cues, whereas mRNA data offer strong prognostic relevance at the cost of high technical variability. This discrepancy between technical uncertainty and prognostic importance is not explicitly modeled by existing multimodal survival models, leading to fragile cross-modal fusion. We introduce the Noise-Aware Disentangled Multimodal Survival Network (NADMSurv), a framework that formalizes importance–uncertainty asymmetry as a guiding principle for multimodal representation learning. An importance–uncertainty dual-track module jointly performs feature preselection and patient-level noise quantification to encode heterogeneous prognostic patterns. A noise-aware disentanglement mechanism then separates multimodal representations into shared representations and modality-specific representations. To model high-order patient correlations, hypergraph neural networks are employed, and subjective logic is introduced to generate opinions with uncertainty quantification, ultimately achieving evidence-level fusion through cross-attention and consensus operators. Multi-cohort evaluation on TCGA datasets demonstrates consistent improvements in C-index over state-of-the-art methods. By analyzing modality-specific technical noise characteristics and disentangling the importance-uncertainty asymmetry, NADMSurv establishes a principled paradigm for robust multimodal survival prediction. Code and sufficient information are available at: https://github.com/imicjs/NADMSurv.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper addresses an important multimodal survival prediction problem and reports encouraging results on five TCGA cohorts. However, several core methodological claims remain insufficiently supported, especially the assumed importance–uncertainty asymmetry between WSI and mRNA. The rationale for retaining both lowest-SE and highest-SE genes, the Poisson-binomial model for mRNA noise, and the noise pseudo-label construction should be clarified in the rebuttal. The current ablation is also too coarse to isolate the contribution of each major component.
