To justify these additions, the authors should analyze computational trade-offs or evaluate the method on challenging scenarios where the baseline struggles.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
14.The current structure of the paper consists of Introduction, Methods, and Conclusion. However, the standard and highly recommended structure for MICCAI submissions is Introduction, Material and Methods, Experiments, and Conclusion. The experimental setups and results appear to be embedded within the Methods section. To improve readability and align with the community standards, I recommend separating the experimental content from the methodology and organizing the paper into the aforementioned four distinct sections.
15.In the description of NS^3 Block, a module named “VSSM” is introduced without any prior explanation. Assuming this refers to the “Vision Mamba-based state-space module,” it must be defined and explained at its first occurrence to ensure clarity.
16.In the Abstract, the abbreviated name “NS^3Net” is used. Please ensure that the full name of the proposed method is spelled out upon its first appearance in the text.
17.In Eq. (12), the function stopgrad() is used without an explicit mathematical definition or explanation. While the text mentions “stopping gradients through $P$”, the authors should clearly state that the stopgrad() notation in the equation corresponds exactly to this operation to avoid any ambiguity.
18.The font sizes in the figures and tables are too small, making them difficult to read. Please enlarge the text in all visual elements to improve legibility.
19 There are widespread formatting issues and outdated citations throughout the bibliography. The reference list requires meticulous proofreading and updating. Specifically, please address the following types of errors across all references:
Capitalization: Many proper nouns and acronyms are incorrectly lowercased. Please ensure correct capitalization (e.g., “Swin-UNet”, “TransUNet”, “AI”, “X-ray”, “2D & 3D”). Note: If you are using LaTeX/BibTeX, you may need to enclose these terms in curly braces (e.g., {TransUNet}) to preserve capitalization.
Missing Information: Some published conference papers lack necessary details like page numbers (e.g., [2] should include pp. 205-218).
Outdated arXiv Preprints: Several papers cited as arXiv preprints have already been published in peer-reviewed venues and should be updated. For example, [6] (Gu et al.) was published at ICLR 2022, and [7] (Hao et al.) was published in IEEE TMI.
Please thoroughly check and correct the entire reference list before submitting the camera-ready version.

I recommend a Weak Reject for this paper. Although the authors achieve strong results by adopting a modern VSSM baseline, the manuscript suffers from several critical flaws. First, the methodological explanation lacks mathematical rigor, relying heavily on code-based, implementation-specific terminology instead of proper mathematical formulations. Second, there are significant inconsistencies between the architectural diagrams and the textual descriptions, raising reproducibility concerns. Third, the empirical validation is insufficient; the authors fail to compare their proposed modules against alternative standard approaches. Finally, the actual contribution of the proposed novelties appears incremental, as the performance improvements are marginal and heavily reliant on the highly competitive baseline. To reach the acceptance bar, the authors must formalize their method and conduct more comprehensive evaluations.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
I would like to thank the authors for their detailed and comprehensive rebuttal.
Conceptually and empirically, you have adequately addressed my concerns. The explanation regarding the HD95 improvements justifies the seemingly marginal DSC gains, and the clarification that Routing Consistency (RC) operates as a latent routing regularizer rather than a standard semi-supervised prediction-level consistency is well-taken. I recognize that the core idea (NS^3MoE) is novel and the empirical results are sufficiently strong.
However, my final decision must be based on the presentation quality, mathematical rigor, and reproducibility of the initial submission. While you have promised to fix all these issues, a manuscript submitted to a top-tier conference like MICCAI should be structurally and mathematically sound upon initial submission. My overall assessment is borderline now, but since the post-rebuttal system requires a binary choice, I must reluctantly select “Reject”.

meta_reviews.text:
The reviewers recognized the clinical importance of addressing domain shift in retinal vessel segmentation and commended your proposed NS³Net. The integration of frequency-domain expert routing with a Vision Mamba (VSSM) baseline was well-received, particularly given the model’s lightweight profile and strong in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance. While the reviews are generally positive, there is a consensus that the manuscript requires tighter mathematical formalization, structural consistency, and stronger analytical justification for its design choices.
Please ensure your rebuttal addresses the following critical issues:
1) As highlighted by Reviewer 2, please explicitly explain the dimensionality and shape of the high-frequency feature maps as they flow through the Router, and clarify practically how these regions are defined and processed by the experts.
2) Reviewers noted that the performance improvements over the baseline VSSM are relatively marginal. Please provide a justification. Highlight specific computational trade-offs, theoretical advantages, or challenging edge cases (e.g., capturing thin capillaries) where your architecture definitively outperforms the baseline.
Please respond to the other points raised if space allows in the rebuttal.

The reviewers generally recognized the clinical relevance of improving retinal vessel and artery/vein segmentation under domain shift, as well as the strong accuracy-efficiency trade-off of the proposed lightweight model. After considering the reviews and rebuttal, I recommend acceptance.
The main strengths are the frequency-routed NS3MoE design, its integration with a state-space backbone, and the routing-consistency regularization for stabilizing expert selection under photometric variation. The evaluation is also convincing, covering six public datasets, both binary vessel segmentation and A/V separation, and both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings. Although the DSC gains over the VSSM baseline are modest, the reviewers noted that the improvements in boundary-sensitive metrics such as HD95 and the consistent OOD gains provide a more meaningful indication of the method’s benefit.
Some concerns remain around presentation and reproducibility rather than the core technical idea. The camera-ready version should incorporate the rebuttal clarifications on NS3MoE tensor flow, frequency-region routing, routing probabilities, the role of RC as a latent routing regularizer, and the DFT/rFFT formulation. The authors should also fix the architectural diagram inconsistencies, clarify the exact segmentation loss, improve figure/table readability, and moderate claims where the gains are incremental.

The paper presents NS³Net, a lightweight UNet-style architecture for retinal vessel and A/V segmentation built around the NS³MoE block, which combines FFT-based frequency partitioning with region-wise mixture-of-experts routing over high-frequency components, complemented by a Mamba SSM and a two-view routing-consistency loss. After rebuttal, R1 remains weakly positive, R2 moves to accept, and R3 maintains reject. 
Although the field has seen many proposed architectures for retinal vessel segmentation and the absolute DSC gains over baselines such as nnUNet remain modest, the proposed method offers a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off — 4.68M parameters and 10.03 GFLOPs, alongside consistent OOD performance. Notably, R3 states that the remaining reservations are primarily of presentational nature and would be resolved by the promised revisions. On this basis, I recommend acceptance, with the expectation that the authors honor the methodological and presentational commitments made in the rebuttal.
After considering the rebuttal and reviewers’ comments, the paper can be recommended for acceptance. The rebuttal provides convincing clarifications on the performance, efficiency, and method.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the meta-reviewer and reviewers for the constructive comments. 
[Meta, R2, R3] NS3MoE tensor flow, frequency-region definition, and expert processing: Given E_i in R^{B x C_i x H_i x W_i}, NS3MoE uses a channel-wise 2D DFT to obtain amplitude A_i and phase Phi_i; for real-valued features, these are stored in non-redundant rFFT form in R^{B x C_i x H_i x W_i’}, where W_i’=floor(W_i/2)+1.A smooth radial mask M_lp decomposes A_i into A_i^lf = A_i * M_lp and A_i^hf = A_i * (1-M_lp), both in R^{B x C_i x H_i x W_i’}. The router pools A_i^hf to an 8x8 frequency-plane region grid, where each region is a coarse neighborhood of high-frequency Fourier bins, not a spatial patch. It predicts J=4 expert logits per cell, followed by top-k masking and softmax over experts, yielding P_i in R^{BxJx8x8}. For expert processing, raised-cosine radial band-pass masks are applied to A_i^hf to obtain 4 band-isolated responses, each refined by its corresponding expert. The upsampled region-wise probabilities P_i fuse the expert-refined band responses. The fused high-frequency response is recombined with A_i^lf and Phi_i before inverse DFT reconstruction. Thus, routing is region-wise on the frequency grid, whereas expert specialization is radial-band-wise. This enables region-adaptive refinement of diverse vessel-edge and capillary evidence.
[Meta, R2, R3] Marginal DSC gain and accuracy-efficiency trade-off: We agree that the absolute DSC gain over VSSM is modest. However, NS3MoE’s benefit is reflected in improved OOD robustness and boundary-sensitive behavior. By design, NS3MoE targets high-frequency vessel-edge/capillary cues while preserving low-frequency appearance and phase; this aligns with the stronger gains in HD95.In the ablation, replacing the MLP FFN with NS3MoE reduces HD95 on CHASEDB1 from 35.07 to 33.34 and on DRIVE from 38.54 to 36.81; adding RC further reduces HD95 to 30.29 and 33.51, respectively. For retinal vessels, small DSC gains can still reflect meaningful boundary/fine-structure improvements because thin vessels occupy few pixels. These gains are achieved without increasing complexity: VSSM uses 4.76M parameters and 11.12G FLOPs, whereas NS3Net uses 4.68M parameters and 10.03G FLOPs. Thus, NS3Net improves the robustness-efficiency trade-off under domain shift.
[R1] Fixed spectral design and perturbation strategy: The low-pass cutoff, band division, and router grid were fixed to keep NS3MoE lightweight/reproducible and avoid dataset-specific tuning in the low-data setting. The same settings were used across ID/OOD datasets, while the router/experts remain learnable. RC focuses on photometric shifts because they are common in fundus imaging and preserve high-frequency vessel cues. We now discuss blur, FOV, resolution/geometric shifts, adaptive frequency partitioning, and router resolution as future work.
[R2, R3] RC clarification and comparison with UniMatch-style consistency: RC differs from UniMatch-style consistency in setting, target, and mechanism. RC uses only labeled images, without unlabeled data, pseudo-labels, weak/strong matching, or target-domain adaptation. Unlike prediction-level consistency, RC regularizes the latent expert-routing distribution. Specifically, P={P_{s,b}} denotes routing tensors from all NS3MoE blocks, where s indexes stage and b indexes block, and L_RC averages KL(P_{s,b}^{aug} || stopgrad(P_{s,b}^{ori})) over them. Thus, RC is a supervised routing-level regularizer, not a semi-supervised method. In the ablation, all variants use the same base augmentation; the improvement from no-RC to RC isolates the benefit attributable to RC beyond standard data augmentation.
[R3] Formalization: To improve rigor/reproducibility, we revised Eqs. (1), (6)-(8), and (10)-(13); used a DFT formulation; specified rFFT/irFFT as implementation details; defined P, L_seg, and stopgrad; and unified high-frequency/routing notation. We also corrected terminology, Fig. 1/2, structure, fonts, typos, and references.

title: NR-Align: Non-rigid Alignment for Non-simultaneous Two-View 3D Coronary Reconstruction in Complex Cardiac Interventions
abstract: Accurate 3D coronary artery reconstruction from two non-simultaneous Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA) projections is important for guidance in complex cardiac interventions, yet remains unreliable in practice. Cardiac pulsation and respiration introduce non-rigid motion between views, breaking rigid-geometry assumptions and causing cross-view misregistration, which often leads to vessel discontinuities, ghosting artifacts, and topology errors in reconstructed volumes. We propose NR-Align, a motion-aware non-rigid alignment module that reduces cross-view mismatch on dual-view backprojected volumes before downstream 3D reconstruction. To enable controlled training and analysis, we further build a physiology-driven simulation pipeline that synthesizes realistic cardiopulmonary deformations and provides paired 3D vascular ground truth from Coronary Computed Tomography Angiography (CCTA) volumes. Experiments on a synthesized dual-async benchmark constructed from the ImageCAS dataset and on unseen real clinical DSA cases show that NR-Align improves 3D Dice and reprojection agreement, and consistently reduces motion-induced artifacts, yielding more coherent coronary reconstructions. Code will be made publicly available.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Synthetic Data / Data-centric AI

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses the challenge of 3D coronary reconstruction from non-simultaneous DSA views by introducing NR-Align, a 3D dual-head network (Union & Overlap) that corrects non-rigid motion mismatch in backprojected volumes. A key contribution is a physiology-driven SVF simulation pipeline that models respiratory and cardiac motion to bridge the sim-to-real gap. Validated on simulation from ImageCAS and real clinical cases, the method significantly improves 3D Dice and topological consistency over uncorrected baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
High Clinical Relevance: Addresses the critical but under explored issue of non-rigid misregistration in asynchronous single-plane DSA, moving beyond the unrealistic synchronous assumptions of prior works.
Physiology-Grounded Synthesis (questionable): The SVF-based simulation for respiratory and cardiac motion is technically interesting (to be verified). Ablation studies (Table 4) convincingly demonstrate that physiological constraints are essential for clinical generalization.
Novel Dual-Head Architecture: The NR-Align design elegantly separates union and overlap predictions. This structural constraint is well-justified and yields a significant performance gain (+0.10 Dice) over single-head baselines. 
Robust Sim-to-Real Validation: Evaluation on real clinical cases with manual 2D masks provides strong evidence of practical utility and successful domain transfer despite the lack of 3D ground truth.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The cardiac phase and respiration phase are used to model the deformation. But what is the evidence / reference to support such a deformation? (Eq (1) and Eq (2))
What are the parameters in the 2 equations: v_resp, v_card, T_r, T_c?
It is not clear how this is used in the synthesis, which is critical to understand if the synthesis obtained is reasonable.
Insufficient Baseline Comparison (most important): The module is only compared against uncorrected “Raw” inputs. The absence of comparisons with rigid/affine registration, established SoTA deformable models, or DeepCA’s [3] own motion handling makes it difficult to assess the relative contribution.
Limited Anatomical Scope: Evaluation is restricted to the RCA. Given the distinct motion patterns and complexity of the left coronary system (LAD/LCX), the lack of evidence for generalization narrows the claimed clinical impact.
Small Clinical Cohort: The test set is limited to 10 cases from a single site. Large confidence intervals in Table 2 raise concerns regarding statistical significance and robust sim-to-real transfer.
Significant Residual Error Gap: A large performance gap (~0.1 Dice) persists between NR-Align and the upper bound. The paper lacks a decomposition of whether this stems from the alignment module or the downstream reconstructor.
Lack of Computational Benchmarking: The paper does not provide the inference time for the NR-Align module. In complex cardiac interventions, near real-time feedback is essential, and the latency of 3D U-Net-based processing should be quantified.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Minor comments: 1.The lambda_o and lambda_c weighting coefficients in the final loss (Eq. 6) are not specified in the paper. 2.Fig. 1 is informative but the color scheme and label font size are difficult to parse in print. A higher-contrast version may improve readability. 3.The clinical dataset (10 cases, single hospital) could be described with more detail, which is important context for assessing clinical generalizability. (protocol, views, how to establish the ground truth, used in training?)

Refer to the strength and weakness part. The paper addresses a real, underserved clinical problem and presents two technically sound contributions: a physiology-grounded deformation synthesis pipeline and a dual-head non-rigid alignment network. The ablation results are convincing, and preliminary clinical results are encouraging. These factors merit a weak accept. However, the absence of comparison against any existing alignment or registration baseline and other minor weakness make it difficult to contextualize the method’s contribution. Physiology-Grounded Synthesis is also need to be verified. The paper would benefit from a stronger comparative evaluation and broader experimental scope.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Most concerns are addressed. However the experiments are lacking of comparison with more other works such as [5] (it has code public available), and demonstrating the result on LCA.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper at hand proposes a 3D coronary artery reconstruction from two DSA views using a novel “non-rigid mismatch compensation module” to address inconsistencies across the two views. It proposes a simulation pipeline with realistic cardiopulmonary deformations to train the approach and evaluate the task at hand.
reviews.text_strengths:
Interesting method to enable a course segmentation of the vasculature.
A lot of effort went into making the simulated data as realistic as possible.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Really small test data size.
The approach depends on a prior segmentation algorithm and is highly dependent on the cross-view consistency of such a segmentation.
The impact of the parameterization/design of the simulation pipeline itself was not really evaluated.
The results on the clinical test data look quite poor. For me it is not obvious why one view has such a good alignment while the other one is completely off. Maybe it is due to different heart/pulmonary phases between the two views. This fact, however, questions the overall validity of the second view metrics on the clinical data.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The approach looks interesting and there was substantial effort spend on creating a realisticly simulated dataset for training. However, the results on the clinical data look very far from being applicable in practice and the evaluation metrics there do not seem reasonable to me.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I stand with my reject as the authors basically confirmed that the second view metrics are not valid as there was no phase matching applied. Sure somehow the metric improved compared to raw, but given the small data set size this is not necessarily conclusive and the visual impression of the second view projection this is till very far from clinical application as stated before.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper under review addresses a significant challenge in interventional cardiology, namely reconstructing a 3D model of coronary arteries from two 2D DSA projections acquired at different times. The authors propose a method for 3D reconstruction that includes a model for cardio-pulmonary movement. The method is then validated extensively on both simulated and clinical data.
reviews.text_strengths:
The authors developed a simulation pipeline that models heart (torsion) and lung (translation) motions. This allows them to create a large dataset of “mismatched” views with known 3D ground truths for training.
NR-Align Module: A deep learning module that takes a mismatched back projected volume and “rectifies” it. 
The model, though trained on synthetic data, was successfully tested on real clinical DSA cases, showing it can generalize to actual hospital settings.
Unlike many previous methods that assume rigid motion or simultaneous acquisition, this paper directly tackles the non-simultaneous nature of single-plane clinical systems. 
Quantitative results show a huge improvement over raw reconstruction, particularly as deformation increases
reviews.text_weaknesses:
How would the model perform on the LCA that has a more complex 3D shape?
How realistic is the respiration model? As is, it combines a translation and a rotation component. 
What are the inference times for the proposed method?
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper proposes a novel framework for 3D artery reconstruction, the authors include a simulation framework as well as a novel alignment module. The results show the benefits of the proposed method and a successful sim to real deployment is demonstrated.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors responded to concerns related to the deformantion pattern choice. Still think it would be interesting to validate on other arteries as well. The paper is an interesting one and shows that sim to real translation results are promissing in a clinically relevant problem.

meta_reviews.text:
This work tackles non-rigid motion mismatch in 3D coronary reconstruction from non-simultaneous DSA views, with a physiology-driven SVF simulation pipeline and a dual-head alignment network. The problem is clinically important and underexplored, and the sim-to-real transfer is encouraging.
R2 observed that the clinical test results show one view well-aligned but the other completely off, and found the overall clinical performance unconvincing for practical use. This is a concrete observation that the authors need to explain.
R1 noted that the method is only compared against uncorrected raw input with no rigid, affine, or deformable registration baselines, making the contribution hard to contextualize. R1 also questioned the evidence supporting the SVF deformation model in Eq. 1 and Eq. 2, noting that the parameters are not explained. Both R1 and R3 asked about generalization to the left coronary system, which has more complex geometry than the RCA tested here.
For the rebuttal, the authors should mainly focus on address the following issues:
1.explain the asymmetric view performance on clinical data that R2 flagged; 
2.justify the SVF deformation model with references or evidence, 3.discuss why no registration baselines were included, 
4.comment on LCA generalization and inference time. The clinical results question from R2 is most important since it speaks directly to whether the method works in practice.

Please understand this is a difficult decision as the study is valuable, innovative and clinically important, and I understand the challenges behind the data collection and evaluation processes. However, after a careful read of the manuscript, reviews and rebuttal, I believe The paper still falls below the bar, for the reasons below:
1.For a paper whose whole contribution is non-rigid alignment, it is never compared against any real deformable registration, classical or learned. Relabeling Raw as the rigid floor does not fill that gap, so the reported gain cannot be attributed to the proposed design rather than to adding any deformation. That was a standard experiment for the submitted paper, not barred new data, and R1 named it the most important weakness.
2.The clinical evidence is too thin to carry the claim: 10 cases (really too small cohort for meaningful significance analysis and solid conclusion), single site, large confidence intervals, and the second of only two views stays near 0.35 to 0.43 overlap after correction. The reconstruction collapses toward one view, so the two-view premise is only half demonstrated. This is the soundness objection R2 defended at score-2 after rebuttal.
3.Even on simulation ground truth the absolute reconstructi on quality is low, at 3D Dice 0.53.
The problem is genuinely underexplored and the idea is sensible, but the submitted record does not show the method works. I really hope can see a more completed work done and published in a high impact conf or journal.

Although some concerns remain regarding limited comparisons with additional public-code baselines, insufficient validation on LCA or other arteries, and the reliability of second-view metrics without phase matching, the rebuttal addresses most major issues and the paper presents a promising sim-to-real translation approach for a clinically relevant problem. Therefore, the AC recommends acceptance.

The paper proposes a method to reconstruct 3D coronary images from 2D DSA views. The reviewers agree that the paper is interesting. There are some remaining issues after the rebuttal but 2 out of 3 reviewers are satisfied with the responses and recommend acceptance. I feel too that the authors addressed the main concerns.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the AC and reviewers for the constructive feedback. We clarify the main concerns below.
[AC1, R2] Clinical performance and asymmetric view alignment. In real-world clinical practice, this remains an extremely challenging clinical task. In non-simultaneous single-plane DSA, two views are acquired at different time points while the coronary tree undergoes cardiac/respiratory motion, especially during C-arm switching. Thus, the projections may correspond to different physiological states, explaining the asymmetry noted by R2.A single reconstructed 3D vessel state cannot perfectly satisfy two projections acquired under different cardiopulmonary phases. Our goal is to reduce this insufficiently addressed non-rigid mismatch, rather than assume synchronized views; we therefore did not manually select phase-matched frames. Experimentally, NR-Align improves all clinical metrics over Raw: View-1 Dice 0.7638 to 0.8151, View-2 Ot(1) 0.2944 to 0.3526, and View-2 Ot(2) 0.3920 to 0.4322.
[AC2, R1, R2, R3] Physiological validity of the SVF synthesis model. The deformation model is physiologically motivated, not unconstrained random deformation. Prior coronary imaging studies identify cardiac and respiratory motion as major motion factors, motivating our decomposition into cardiac and respiratory phases. In Eq. (1)-(2), T_r/T_c denote respiratory/cardiac periods; v_resp models respiration-dominant displacement, while v_card models localized cardiac-induced non-rigid torsion. The SVF exponential map follows established diffeomorphic modeling [16,19,20], enabling smooth, topology-preserving motion synthesis. Compared with unconstrained SVF, the physiology-aware model transfers better to real clinical data (View-1 Dice 0.7412 to 0.8151), showing that the gain comes from physiologically constrained cardiopulmonary modeling.
[AC3, R1] Baseline comparison. We understand R1’s concern as whether NR-Align improves over simpler motion assumptions such as rigid, affine, or generic deformable modeling. The experiments address this at two levels. First, Raw applies the existing DeepCA pipeline directly to the same non-simultaneous input. Since DeepCA’s motion modeling mainly relies on rigid approximations, Raw provides the relevant rigid-approximation comparison. With only NR-Align added, overall 3D Dice improves from 0.3872 to 0.5295 (+36.8%). Second, our synthesis ablation compares unconstrained SVF, i.e., random non-rigid deformation without cardiac/respiratory phase constraints, with physiology-aware SVF. The physiology-aware model improves clinical View-1 Dice from 0.7412 to 0.8151, showing that the gain comes from physiologically parameterized modeling.
[AC4, R1, R3] LCA generalization and runtime. RCA was selected because it is more affected by cardiac/respiratory motion and is therefore a strict target for non-rigid mismatch correction, not because NR-Align is RCA-specific. NR-Align uses generic backprojected union/overlap cues and does not depend on RCA-specific labels or fixed topology templates; thus, its mechanism can extend to LCA. The inference pipeline is feed-forward without case-specific optimization and the average inference time from loading the input to producing the 3D reconstruction is about 87.8 ms/case.
[R1, R2] Additional concerns. The 10 clinical cases are only an independent real-world evaluation set for sim-to-real transfer, not the training scale of the method; training and quantitative evaluation use the large-scale ImageCAS dataset (1000 cases). Clinical evaluation uses manual vessel masks, so the conclusions do not depend on a specific segmenter. The Upper Bound represents ideal synchronization and serves as a reference; the Raw-to-NR-Align improvement isolates the alignment gain, while the remaining gap reflects residual mismatch and downstream limits.

title: NutriDiff: Phenotype-Consistent Diffusion Augmentation for Malnutrition Screening
abstract: Deep learning for facial-based elderly malnutrition screening shows preliminary feasibility, but clinical data scarcity limits diagnostic performance.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Synthetic Data / Data-centric AI
Special Topic -> AI for Population Health, Public Health & Epidemiology

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces a diffusion-based data augmentation framework tailored for facial malnutrition screening in elderly patients. The method combines view-conditioned LoRA fine-tuning of Stable Diffusion with a novel post-generation filtering step based on handcrafted facial morphological descriptors (temporal, periorbital, malar, jawline regions) and Mahalanobis distance to remove clinically inconsistent samples. This pipeline is integrated into a downstream classifier (CLIP-based), and the authors demonstrate that phenotype-aware filtering of synthetic data significantly improves generalization in a few-shot clinical setting.
reviews.text_strengths:
The subject of elderly malnutrition screening via facial images is clinically relevant and underexplored.
The paper introduces a clinically grounded filtering mechanism that enforces phenotype consistency in diffusion-generated samples, addressing label noise which is a known limitation in medical image synthesis.
The authors propose a multi-view, view-conditioned LoRA adaptation strategy, enabling fine-grained control of facial pose and nutritional state without full model fine-tuning.
The paper combines generative modeling with domain-specific feature engineering (ROI-based descriptors), which is relatively uncommon and well-motivated clinically.
The method introduced demonstrates strong performance gains (e. g. , AUC 0.984, MCC 0.854) over both classical methods and diffusion-based baselines.
The authors provide a systematic ablation study, clearly showing the impact of synthetic data and the necessity of phenotype filtering.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The evaluation suffers from a limited dataset size and single-center cohort (n=92) which reduces reliability and generalizability.
There is no external validation dataset which is critical especially given domain shift (lighting, ethnicity, acquisition device).
Lack of comparison with more recent controllable diffusion methods (e. g. , MedDiff-FT [Xie et al. , MICCAI 2025], VicTr [Susladkar et al. , ICCV 2025]) that explicitly address structural and clinical consistency.
The phenotype descriptors are relatively simplistic (intensity ratios, Laplacian variance, gradients) and may not capture complex anatomical variations compared to learned feature-based approaches.
The binary classification setting collapses malnutrition severity levels, limiting clinical usefulness compared to prior works considering richer stratification (e. g. , GLIM-based grading).
Evaluation of synthetic image quality relies heavily on FID/AFFID, which are known to correlate poorly with clinical realism in medical imaging (as discussed in diffusion literature [Kazerouni et al. , 2023 survey]).
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses an important and underexplored clinical problem and proposes a reasonably novel and well-motivated solution that combines diffusion-based augmentation with clinically informed phenotype filtering. The idea of enforcing phenotype consistency via ROI-based descriptors and Mahalanobis filtering is intuitive and empirically effective, leading to strong performance gains in a challenging few-shot setting. However, the overall contribution remains somewhat incremental relative to recent advances in controllable medical diffusion models, and the validation is limited by a very small, single-center dataset without external testing. Additionally, the handcrafted nature of the phenotype features and the binary problem formulation constrain the clinical and methodological impact. As a result, while the approach is promising and shows potential, stronger validation and positioning against more recent methods would be needed for a higher confidence acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes NutriDiff, a diffusion-based data augmentation framework for facial malnutrition screening in elderly populations. The method fine-tunes Stable Diffusion using view-conditioned LoRA adapters to generate synthetic facial images and applies a phenotype-consistency filtering step based on handcrafted facial region descriptors. The generated data is then used to improve a downstream classifier (CLIP-based) for malnutrition prediction. Experiments on a small private dataset show improvements in classification performance when synthetic data is incorporated. While the approach combines diffusion models with feature-based filtering, the overall contribution primarily lies in data augmentation and computer vision modeling rather than advancing medical image computing methodologies.
reviews.text_strengths:
The use of diffusion models with phenotype-based filtering is a reasonable attempt to improve synthetic data quality.
The integration with a downstream classifier shows empirical performance gains.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Misalignment with MICCAI Scope (Major Concern).
The primary limitation of this work is that it is not well aligned with the core focus of MICCAI. The paper mainly focuses on facial image-based classification and diffusion-based data augmentation, which are more typical of the computer vision community (e.g., CVPR, ICCV, ECCV). The methodological contributions are centered around generative modeling and feature filtering rather than advancing medical imaging techniques, clinical workflows, or image-based diagnosis grounded in medical imaging modalities such as MRI, CT, or ultrasound.
2.Limited Medical Imaging Contribution.
Although the application is related to healthcare (malnutrition screening), the method operates entirely on 2D facial photographs, which are closer to natural image processing rather than medical imaging. The paper does not leverage domain-specific medical imaging knowledge, physics, or clinically grounded modeling, which are central to MICCAI contributions.
3.Incremental Methodological Novelty.
The technical contributions are largely incremental:
Fine-tuning Stable Diffusion with LoRA is now standard practice.
The phenotype filtering step is based on handcrafted features and Mahalanobis distance, which is relatively simple.
4.Weak Clinical Validation.
The experiments are solely done with a private in-house dataset. 
5.Limited Innovation in Diffusion Modeling.
The paper does not propose a novel diffusion formulation but rather adapts existing Stable Diffusion models with conditioning and filtering. Compared to recent advances in medical diffusion models (e.g., structure-aware, physics-informed, or uncertainty-aware diffusion), the contribution is relatively limited.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The main reason for rejection is that the paper is better suited for a computer vision venue (e.g., CVPR, ICCV, ECCV) rather than MICCAI. The contributions are primarily focused on diffusion-based image generation and data augmentation for facial images, with limited advancement in medical imaging methodology or clinical relevance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: paper proposes NutriDiff, a multi-view diffusion augmentation framework for facial-based elderly malnutrition screening
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The four facial ROIs (temporal, periorbital, malar, jawline) are grounded in established nutritional physiology and their use in the paper gives it strong clinical motivation.
2.The ablation study in Table 2 convincingly demonstrates that naive synthetic augmentation can degrade performance and their phenotypic filtering consistently improves all metrics
3.The multi-view design with subject-level score averaging is practical for bedside screening
4.Using separate LoRA adapters per view-class pair is a parameter-efficient strategy that avoids overfitting on the small dataset while capturing view-dependent morphological differences.
5.The paper is clearly written with a logical flow
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The dataset is extremely small and from a single center. this limits generalisability
2.No Cross Validation results
3.No statistical significance tests 
4.There is domain shift between train (ambulatory patients) and test(bedridden ). This has not been analysed or discussed properly
5.No sensitivity analysis of key hyperparameters such as 95th percentile Mahalanobis threshold, the generation multiplier β=8, and the synthetic loss weight γ=0.3.6.No standard augmentation baselines (geometric transforms, color jitter, CutMix, mixup) or non-diffusion generative methods (GANs, VAEs) are included
7.Individual components have limited novelty
8.Reproducibility : The dataset is private. No code release is mentioned
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Go to the weakness section to address the comments.
A t-SNE or UMAP visualization of real vs. synthetic feature distributions before and after filtering would strengthen the qualitative evidence for the filtering mechanism.
What is the landmark detection failure rate on the synthetic images? This affects the practical yield of the generation pipeline.

The paper addresses a clinically relevant and underexplored problem. The problem statement is very important with scant literature so the lack of baselines or diverse datasets is understandable. There is lack of some analysis and tests that weaken the paper contribution along with an already weak novelty.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
The reviews are generally positive, with two reviewers recommending weak acceptance and one reviewer recommending weak rejection. The paper addresses an underexplored and clinically relevant problem: facial-image-based malnutrition screening in elderly patients. I do not agree with the concern that the work is out of scope for MICCAI. Facial image diagnosis can be considered an important part of medical image analysis, with relevance to healthcare screening, geriatric assessment, and related areas such as AI-assisted facial analysis in healthcare and Traditional Chinese Medicine. The proposed diffusion-based augmentation framework, especially the phenotype-consistency filtering using clinically motivated facial regions, is well motivated and supported by ablation results.
Given the positive overall assessment, clear clinical motivation, and empirical gains, I recommend early acceptance. However, several concerns raised by multiple reviewers should be addressed carefully in the final version, including the small single-center dataset, limited statistical rigor, absence of cross-validation or significance testing, lack of external validation, insufficient comparison with standard augmentation and recent generative baselines, and limited analysis of domain shift and hyperparameter sensitivity. The authors are strongly encouraged to clarify these issues, strengthen the discussion, and include recommended analyses where feasible so that the published work can have stronger impact.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the Area Chair and reviewers for their constructive comments and encouraging assessment of our manuscript. We appreciate their recognition of the clinical relevance and underexplored setting of elderly malnutrition screening (R1/R3), the phenotypic consistency filtering based on facial regions associated with nutritional status (R1/R3), the practical multi-view design (R3), and the empirical gains shown in the ablation study (R1/R3).
To clarify the relevance to MICCAI and the work’s medical contribution (R2), our goal is not generic face generation. The paper investigates phenotype-consistent diffusion augmentation for elderly malnutrition screening. Facial images may capture phenotypic cues linked to nutritional status. This potential relevance to healthcare screening and geriatric assessment motivated our MICCAI submission. The filtering step uses facial ROIs tied to nutritional status to reduce mismatch in synthetic samples and to support an image-based clinical screening task.
We agree with the reviewers that the small single-center cohort and the absence of external validation are important limitations (R1/R3). These limitations are partly due to the scarcity of data and prior work on facial image analysis for screening elderly malnutrition. To the best of our knowledge, no public dataset currently targets this task for individuals aged 65 years or older. We also clarify that the submitted test set includes bedridden patients and those receiving enteral nutrition, thereby providing an initial evaluation under more complex clinical conditions.
For cross-validation and statistical rigor (R3), Table 2 in the submitted manuscript reports subject-level 5-fold cross-validation on the training set for ablation and stability analysis. These experiments compare real data, unfiltered synthetic augmentation, and phenotype-filtered synthetic augmentation across two backbones, with the mean and standard deviation reported.
We agree that additional comparisons with traditional augmentation, GAN/VAE-based generation, and recent controllable diffusion methods would further strengthen the evaluation (R1/R3). Given the page limit and the focus of the study, the submitted experiments prioritize diffusion-based augmentation. The main objective is to assess whether phenotypic consistency filtering improves the clinical consistency and downstream screening utility of diffusion-generated samples. Broader comparisons across augmentation families will be an important direction for future work.
We also appreciate the suggestions on hyperparameter sensitivity, landmark detection failure analysis, and t-SNE/UMAP visualization of real and synthetic feature distributions (R3). These analyses would provide useful evidence for understanding the generation and filtering process. Larger multi-center validation, more rigorous statistical and hyperparameter analyses, broader baseline comparisons, and external validation will be important extensions of this work.
We again thank the Area Chair and reviewers for their thoughtful feedback. Their comments will guide our future validation, broader comparisons, and continued clinical extension of this work.

title: Occlusion-aware Disparity Estimation via Depth Prior Embedded Cost Volume for Stereo Endoscopic Images
abstract: Accurate disparity estimation from stereo laparoscopic images is essential for 3D surgical navigation but remains difficult in occlusion regions, where conventional cost volumes produce unreliable matching costs. To address this, we propose Depth Prior Embedded Disparity Estimation Network that leverages monocular depth cues—inherently less affected by occlusion—to refine disparity predictions. Our framework consists of two key components: a Coarse Disparity Estimation (CDE) module that generates an initial disparity prior from an affine-transformed depth map, and a novel Depth Prior Embedded Cost Volume (DPCV). The DPCV encodes this prior into a probability distribution over disparity levels and iteratively fuses it with the traditional correlation volume via a cross-attention mechanism, thereby improving matching robustness in occluded/unmatched regions. reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes an iterative refinement process for the cost volume. This process includes converting a coarse depth estimate into a probability distribution and utilizing a cross-attention mechanism to refine the previous cost volume using the generated distribution. The evaluation results in Table 1 show that the proposed method achieves a strong balance between estimation error and inference time.
reviews.text_strengths: The idea of converting a coarse depth map into a probability distribution (Eq. 2) and using this distribution to iteratively refine the cost volume (Algorithm 1) is both interesting and well-motivated.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Methodology:
Parameter Settings: The procedure for defining or tuning $\sigma$ in Eq. 2 is currently unclear and requires further explanation. 
Unsubstantiated Claims: The authors state that refining the cost volume helps resolve occluded regions in stereo matching. However, the evaluation section lacks specific experiments or ablation studies designed to validate this claim.
Writing & Presentation:
Incomplete List: In the final paragraph of the Introduction, the authors state that their contributions are “fourfold,” but they only enumerate three points (“First. . . “, “Second. . . “, “Third. . . “).
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The core contribution iterative refinement for the cost volume is interesting.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper focuses on disparity estimation for endoscopic images. It particularly pays attention to occluded or unmatched regions. It proposes a depth-prior embedded framework, DEDENet. The model incorporates monocular depth cues into stereo matching. The method mainly includes two parts: a coarse disparity estimation module that generates an initial disparity prior from inverse depth, and a depth prior embedded cost volume that encodes this prior as a probability distribution and fuses it with the original cost volume through cross-attention and iterative refinement. Experiments on the SCARED dataset show generally improved performance, with clearer gains on the keyframe evaluation subset and in challenging occlusion regions.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Clinical and technical relevance: The paper studies stereo disparity estimation for endoscopic images, which is an important problem for 3D reconstruction and surgical navigation. The focus on occluded or unmatched regions is practically meaningful, since these areas are a common source of failure in laparoscopic stereo matching.
2.Reasonable methodological design: The proposed framework introduces monocular depth priors into stereo matching through a coarse disparity estimation module and a depth prior embedded cost volume. Encoding the depth prior as a disparity probability distribution and fusing it with the original cost volume via cross-attention is a sensible design, especially for improving robustness in occluded regions.
3.Solid empirical validation: The paper includes quantitative comparison against several recent baselines on the SCARED dataset, together with ablation studies on the main components such as DPCV, occlusion masking, auxiliary loss, and iterative refinement. These experiments help support that the proposed modules contribute to the final performance.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper is of generally good quality, but several aspects would benefit from further clarification and discussion.
1.Novelty: The overall idea of incorporating monocular depth priors into stereo matching is reasonable, but the methodological novelty appears somewhat limited. The framework mainly combines a coarse depth-to-disparity prior, probability-based prior encoding, cross-attention fusion, and occlusion-aware refinement, all of which are built on top of an existing stereo backbone. The paper would benefit from a clearer explanation of what is fundamentally new relative to prior cost-volume refinement and fusion-based stereo methods.
2.Occlusion-specific evidence: The paper is motivated by improving disparity estimation in occluded or unmatched regions, but the experimental evidence for this claim is still somewhat indirect. Most results are reported on overall metrics, while more dedicated quantitative analysis specifically within occlusion regions would make the central claim better supported.
3.Clarity and technical details: Some parts of the presentation could be improved. For example, the naming of the proposed module is not fully consistent in the method section (DPCV vs DECV in section 2.2, maybe they are the same thing?), and several implementation choices, such as the design of the probability distribution prior and the effect of iteration number, could be explained more clearly. This would make the method easier to follow and assess.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I think the paper is relevant and technically reasonable, especially in its attempt to improve stereo disparity estimation in occluded regions for endoscopic images by incorporating monocular depth priors. The whole framework is well motivated, and the results on the SCARED dataset, particularly on the keyframe subset, are promising. However, my overall score is mainly limited by concerns regarding the clarity of the novelty claim and the lack of more direct quantitative evidence specifically demonstrating improvement in occluded regions. I would like to higher the score after the authors’ feedback and explanation. Anyway, it is a good work.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I am willing to support acceptance. The response clarifies several points, and the method is technically reasonable. I still have some concerns about the occlusion-specific evidence, but I think these can be handled by making the claim more modest and discussing the limitation more clearly in the final version.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper addresses the critical challenge of disparity estimation in stereo laparoscopic images for 3D surgical navigation. The core contribution is a framework that utilizes monocular depth cues to regularize and refine disparity in regions where traditional stereo matching fails, particularly in occluded areas. The authors propose a Depth Prior Embedding Cost Volume (DECV), a Coarse Disparity Estimation (CDE) loss, and an iterative refinement process using occlusion masking to improve the accuracy and robustness of depth perception in surgical environments.
reviews.text_strengths:
Well-Structured Methodology: The integration of DECV, CDE loss, and iterative refinement forms a cohesive and logical pipeline. The architectural choices directly target the identified problem of occlusion in endoscopic scenes.
Ablation Validation: The effectiveness of each proposed module (DECV, CDE loss, masking) is clearly demonstrated through a systematic ablation study, proving their individual contributions to the overall performance.
Efficiency: The model appears to balance the trade-off between inference speed and accuracy effectively, which is vital for real-time surgical navigation.
Clear Motivation: The use of monocular cues as a prior to “fill in” the gaps where stereo correspondence is physically impossible (occlusions) is a sound and intuitive approach for the surgical domain.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Missing State-of-the-Art (SOTA) Baselines: The review of current stereo matching literature is incomplete. The paper lacks a performance comparison with modern high-performance architectures like RAFT-Stereo and IGEV-Stereo, which currently define the SOTA for iterative refinement and cost volume construction.
Specific Impact on Occlusions: While the paper claims to solve occlusion-related issues, there is no isolated quantitative analysis for these regions. Can the authors provide error metrics (e.g., EPE or D1-all) specifically measured inside the occlusion masks? This would verify if the performance gain is truly coming from the proposed occlusion-handling mechanism.
Monocular Uncertainty: Monocular depth estimation is generally less accurate than stereo matching in non-occluded areas. How does the system prevent the lower-fidelity monocular priors from degrading the high-precision stereo-matched regions? A discussion or experiment on the “noise” introduced by the monocular prior is needed.
Domain Specificity: The proposed modules seem generally applicable to natural images. Does the design include specific considerations for the unique properties of endoscopic images (e.g., specular reflections, textureless tissue, or fluid presence) compared to standard outdoor/driving datasets?
Discrepancy in Latency Reporting: In Table 1, the inference speed is reported as 25.65ms, yet Section 4.1 mentions 45.23ms.
Does the 25.65ms figure only account for the proposed refinement modules, excluding the backbone?
For a fair assessment of real-time viability, the total end-to-end processing time (45.23ms) should be the primary metric reported.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

See the weakness part.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The reviewers address some of my concerns in the rebuttal. Based on my initial rating (weak accept) and the authors’ response, I lean on accept for this paper rather than the reject.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper has received 3 bordeline positive reviews. All reviewers agree on the interest of the approach to iterative refine the cost volume via a prior depth estimate. However all 3 identify key limitations in terms of:
1) Limited compairson to SOTA disparity methods. It is crucial for the selected comparison baselind to be fully justified - Rev #3 
2) Validation on occlusions which is the main selling point - all
3) Clarity on introduced novelty of utilizing prior depth information - all
4) Key information on method’s development details - Rev #2, #3 
5) Unclear reproducability without a commitment for public release of code and models. This diminishes the paper contributions- all
The recommendation is for the paper to be invited for rebuttal.

All 3 reviewers are overall satisfied with the rebuttal and recommend acceptance. However the main criticism (SOTA comparison, validation under occlusions) is not addressed or explained and is only left as extension work. Without these points fully addressed the paper should follow the suggestion from R2 and make their claims more modest and discussing the limitation more clearly in the final version.
I recommend acceptance

The rebuttal effectively addressed the reviewers’ concerns, providing sufficient clarification and additional evidence where requested. Following the rebuttal, all reviewers expressed support for acceptance, indicating a clear consensus that the paper meets the standard for acceptance at MICCAI.

After reading the paper and the comments, I felt that the reviewers have identified the major weakness of the paper. 1) using depth prior for stereo matching is not new, which can been seen from recent foundation models in computer vision, such as foundation stereo. Therefore the technical novelty is limited. This work did not compare with the method. 2) Following this comments, this paper failed to catch the sota in the domain, such as foundation stereo, Monster, etc. 3) One of the main selling point about occlusion, but the reviewers are not convinced to this point, but suggest to “making the claim more modest and discussing the limitation more clearly in the final version”. Overall, I suggest to reject the paper.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the Area Chair and all reviewers for the constructive comments. 
1.SOTA Comparison Rationale (R#2, R#3):
We agree with the reviewers that the selection of SOTA baselines in the current experiments is relatively limited,a comprehensive comparison with RAFT-Stereo, IGEV-Stereo, and other SOTA methods related to CV construction​is planned for the extension paper. Regarding the chosen baselines, HSM, DeepPruner, and MSDESIS represent the state-of-the-art for surgical scenarios, while ACVNet​represents the SOTA in CV construction, which is the primary focus of our improvement; further ablation studies will be conducted. GMStereo​is a multi-task framework that incorporates monocular depth estimation, but it does not explicitly use the monocular prior to guide the stereo matching process. 
2.Occlusion Validation (R#1, R#2, R#3):
We acknowledge the reviewers’ concern that the occlusion validation in the current manuscript is insufficient. A quantitative analysis (EPE, D1-all, Bad3)focused on occlusion will be presented in the extension paper. In the current version, qualitative analysis (Fig. 3n) demonstrates that our method yields lower error in the left-image occlusion regions (caused by camera baseline disparity) compared to the backbone (Fig. 3m). This visually proves the efficiency of our approach in occluded areas.
3.Novelty (R#2, R#3):
Our fundamental novelty lies in addressing the precision degradation of CV-based methods at disparity discontinuities. Monocular depth estimation does not suffer from these specific failure modes. Thus, we probabilize the monocular depth prior​to enhance the CV, providing geometric guidance where traditional matching fails. This differs from prior hard features or directly connection concatenation based works.
4.Technical Details and Implementation (R#1, R#2):
R#1:The standard deviation σ in Eq.2 controls the spread of the PDF; we empirically selected σ=0.2.Ablation study is planned for the extension paper.
R#2: a) We have standardized the module naming to DPCV​throughout the manuscript. b)The normal distribution（σ=0.2） for the probability prior was empirically selected; we plan to explore adaptive parameter selection in future work. c)Regarding the iteration number, our ablation study tested various values, and the results indicate that 1 iteration​ currently offers the most balanced trade-off between performance and efficiency.
5.Reproducibility and Resources (R#1, R#2, R#3):
We confirm our commitment to releasing all code upon acceptance. 
6.Monocular Uncertainty(R#3):​We acknowledge that monocular depth estimation is generally less accurate than stereo matching in non-occluded areas. Thus, we restrict CV updates only to masked regions to safely leverage the monocular prior（Alg.1）.
Regarding noise, the CDE implicitly suppresses noise by leveraging the intrinsic geometric relationship between stereo pairs to output robust coarse inverse depth. Notably, although LeRes-ResNet50（applied in this work） and LeRes-ResNeXt101​exhibit different noise characteristics, we observed similar disparity estimation results during training. This result empirically demonstrates that our method is robust to noise in the depth prior.
7.Domain Specificity(R#3): The proposed modules demonstrate effectiveness on the FlyingThings3D dataset during pre-training. This confirms that our method generalizes beyond surgical scenarios to other domains. DPCV targets stereo-occluded regions​where the monocular depth prior is assumed to be more accurate than stereo matching. Consequently, the network’s performance in specular highlight regions depends on whether the underlying monocular depth estimator can effectively handle such artifacts.
8.Latency(R#3):​ The 25.65ms refers to the added overhead of our modules. In the revised manuscript, we report the end-to-end time (45.23ms) as the speed metric .
9.Typo Corrections (R#1):
R#1:We have corrected the “fourfold” to “threefold”.

title: OCS-MAMBA: Object-Centric, Logic-Guided Approach for Surgical Action Understanding
abstract: NA
subject_areas: Surgery -> Surgical Skills, Workflow & Team Dynamics

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors presented OCS-Mamba, a neuro-symbolic architecture for surgical video understanding targeting triplet recognition (instrument, verb, target) and action anticipation.
reviews.text_strengths: The greatest strength of this paper is the integration of individual existing components in the creation of a solid systems. The factored Graph-Mamba design is particularly well-motivated and effective. Additionally, the RAG safety head is a meaningful step toward possible deployment making the work even more interesting. Ablation clearly show the contribution of the losses and how mamba improves long-horizon prediction, strengthening claims.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The manuscript could benefit by considering the following aspects:
The is no formal analysis about Mamba working better than Transformers here. You should be doing a clear evaluation evaluating attention against Mamba and demonstrate how result are better or worse. This is something already shown in the field of animal action recognition (e. g, https://www. sciencedirect. com/science/article/pii/S1574954124004977) where authors shown that Mamba is indeed better than using Transformer (linear attention/transformer) and at the same time requiring less FLOPs and computational resources. You should do something similar, that would strengthen the method.
The manuscript would benefit in a more extensive description of the RAG safety, I believe that is a very important component, especially in the surgery field. However, there is no well evaluation/description. Does it improve accuracy or only interpretability? Can you show real failure cases prevented?
The limitations are described in a very short line in the conclusion section “Current constraints are tailored to cholecystectomy and require adaptation for other procedures, and the fixed slot budget may not generalise to scenes with more entity types. ”. The authors should try to understand what are possible limitations of the method and its usability and write a deeper analysis. This would improve the paper’s clarity and credibility.
Finally, I feel like you give the spotlight to Mamba in your title, however DinoV2+slot attention does a huge amount of work in our framework. I would consider to reconsider the name for publication, like this is somewhat misleading and not completely honest. I would recommend to also test some other image backbone based on Mamba if you want to keep that title.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Although the manuscript could benefit from some deeper analysis, I believe that this is a very good contribution to the field and should be accepted.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
1.The manuscript provides a mixture of object-centric features along with long-term interaction semantics modeling using Mamba based state space model (SSM) for the task of triplet recognition together with the anticipation task at short temporal horizons. 
2.In order to train the model, the manuscript exploits segmentation dataset CholecSeg8k along with CholecT50 and SSG-VQA datasets for triplets and scene graph connectivity.
3.The reported results show improvement on CholecT50 cross validation and on the triplet anticipation task over SOTA triplet models augmented with simple LSTMs.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper is well organized and easy to follow.
2.The concept of utilizing object-centric knowledge has been proven beneficial for surgical workflow tasks but it is more helpful for fine-grained classification tasks. 
3.The idea of using slots for tool-target together inherently allows to model interactions in the slot attention followed by factorized processing of spatial and temporal features aptly utilizing the long-term context. 
4.The ontology loss idea used as a negative constraint acts as a regularizer and forces the model to adhere to allowed constraints. 
5.The use of anticipation tasks together with triplet recognition mutually benefits both as reported in the results.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Slot Attention, famous in the unsupervised object discovery, generates slots that are unordered so the slots can bind to any object in the scene. How are the 21 queries handled to make sure that each query (e.g. grasper or gallbladder) correspond to the object segmentation mask of the same grasper or gallbladder. There is a mention of Presence predictor but does it mean each query is hardcoded to a specific class? Within the same paragraph Ot = ot,k is unclear and should have proper format.
2.The slots that are generated when visualized helps the readers to understand how the slot attention have captured the true object semantics - even though it is not perfect but it should roughly capture the parts of the instrument or anatomical structure to make more sense later in the graph message passing and the ontology constraints part. The lack of this information makes the manuscript a bit incomplete.
3.Overall, the manuscript should make it clear what it means by temporal. Is it short context e.g. 32/64 frames or is it all the frames of a video?
4.In the “Anticipation via State-Rollout” section, there seems to be a disconnect in the phrasing. First the future slots are mean pooled to get a single feature and then I, V, T are separately classified - does it mean no triplet head is present here? Then the manuscript mentions last-frame slots - last frame with reference to which group of frames? Is it a video clip with fewer frames? The manuscript will greatly benefit if these clarifications are properly provided. 
5.The use of RAG guardrail - is it connected to the model training and/or evaluation pipeline? Because it is mentioned once before section 3, but not discussed later. The manuscript should provide clarification on this.
6.The implementation details regarding the value of feature dimension D, Mamba parameters, number of epochs or iterations, batch size, GPUs, etc. are missing which renders a big question on the reproducibility of the said experiments. 
7.Minor weakness - Is there a rationale for choosing LSTM over autoregressive transformer for anticipation baselines?
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The manuscript proposed a method that jointly performs triplet recognition and anticipation by leveraging object-centric features with ontology based constraints and shows good improvement over baselines on both tasks. However, there are some key issues with the components proposed or it is not straightforward from the manuscript such as the slot attention module and the anticipation rollout to task head. On top of these, the lack of implementation details even though the OCS-Mamba contains a lot of important building blocks - Slot Attention, feature dimension, and Mamba, makes the reproducibility aspect of this work challenging.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces OCS-Mamba, a novel object-centric, logic-guided framework for surgical action understanding from video. The method specifically targets the challenges of long procedural durations and complex instrument-verb-target(IVT) interactions in robotic surgery. The proposed approach called Neuro Symbolic Surgical Graph Mamba (OCS-Mama), integrates spatial, structural, and temporal reasoning through a 3 stage pipeline: (1) semantic entity extraction using hybrid DINOv2 and Slot Attention backbone, (2) efficient modeling of long-range temporal dependencies via a linear-complexity Mamba State Space Model, and (3) enforcement of valid surgical relationships using a semantic grammar and logic-constrained loss, complemented by a RAG safety for procedural guideline validation. Empirical results demonstrate that OCS-Mamba outperforms ensemble baselines on public datasets, with notable improvements in short-horizon action anticipation and robust performance in complex surgical scenarios. The work is relevant in the field of robotic surgery and surgical training.
reviews.text_strengths:
The three stage framework moves away from pixel-centric approach and decomposes video frames into discrete semantic entities and focuses on object-centric slots to explicitly track interactions between instruments and targets. The model is hence less prone to hallucinations and can reason about physical and procedural validity of actions
The model enforces surgical safety through a semantic grammar and logic-constrained loss, directly penalizing physically impossible or unsafe instrument interactions. The addition of a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) safety head provides interpretable guidance aligned with procedural guidelines, which is a significant step toward clinical feasibility and real-world deployment
Evaluation on multiple public datasets supports the generalizability of the approach. The ablation studies further validates the effectiveness of each module, supporting claims of improved memory efficiency and safer predictions.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Overall the paper is well-written and very clear. Some comments on weaknesses:
The current approach in terms of logic constraints and ontological matrices for indicating mechanically invalid predictions are tailored to cholecystectomy. The authors acknowledges these constraints require adaptation for other surgical procedure. This thus limits the immediate applicability of the OCS-Mamba method to broader surgical domains
The evaluation is conducted on public datasets such as CholecT50 and CholecSeg8k, thus it is not real how well the demonstration of clinical feasibility or deployment in real surgical environments.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a novel framework for surgical action understanding that enforces clinical safety constraints, resulting in more anatomically plausible and interpretable predictions. Experimental results show that the method outperforms SOTA on public dataset. The work is supported by strong experimental and validation results, and it is overall relevant to the conference in terms of surgical AI.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text: While two reviewers are strongly in favor of acceptance due to the framework’s impressive systems-level integration and innovative logic-guided constraints, R2 explicitly disagrees with a recommendation to reject. All reviewers recognize the paper’s strengths, specifically the effectiveness of the factored Graph-Mamba design for long-horizon prediction, the well-motivated use of object-centric slots, and the clinical potential of the RAG safety head for interpretable surgical guidance. However, there are concerns regarding a critical lack of implementation details—such as Mamba hyperparameters and feature dimensions—which severely hinders reproducibility. Furthermore, the authors must clarify the mechanics of the Slot Attention module regarding how unordered slots bind to specific semantic entities, provide a formal comparative analysis justifying the choice of Mamba over Transformer baselines, and offer a more robust evaluation of the RAG safety head’s ability to prevent real failure cases while discussing the limitations of generalizing these logic constraints beyond cholecystectomy.

author_feedback_text:
We are delighted that our paper has been provisionally accepted and would like to sincerely thank the reviewers and the Meta-Reviewer for their thoughtful, relevant, and constructive feedback. We are especially pleased that the reviewers recognised the novelty and practical relevance of our object-centric methods.
Reproducibility and Implementation Details (R2, Meta-Reviewer):
We agree with the reviewers that some of the implementation details were missing. In the camera-ready version, we will clarify the key architectural and training settings. We also intend to make the source code and full configuration details available upon acceptance.
Slot Attention Clarification (R2, Meta-Reviewer):
We thank the reviewers for pointing out that the slot semantics require clearer explanation. 
The 21 slots are not manually hard-coded to specific classes. Rather, they are object-centric proposals whose semantics are learned through segmentation supervision, presence prediction, and IVT recognition losses. The presence predictor does not impose a fixed slot-to-class assignment, but encourages the slot set to represent relevant instruments and anatomical targets. We use Slot Attention as a structural inductive bias (object-like decomposition into K competing representations), but replace its unsupervised reconstruction objective entirely with task-specific surgical supervision. We will refine the description in the revision and also clarify the notation around $O_t$.
Mamba Temporal Modelling (R1, Meta-Reviewer): Our motivation for adopting Mamba stemmed from the long procedural durations and dense temporal dependencies in surgical videos. Mamba offers linear complexity, efficient state propagation, and improved long-context scalability. The submitted experiments already include relevant Transformer/attention-based baselines, including FUTR, MT4MTL, TERL, and CurConMix. We clarify that OCS-Mamba does not simply replace Transformers with Mamba; DINOv2 remains the visual backbone, while Mamba is used within the factored Graph-Mamba stage for efficient temporal-state propagation over object-centric slot features. We will make this design motivation clearer in the camera-ready version. The title reflects the role of Mamba-based temporal reasoning within the broader object-centric and logic-guided framework.
Anticipation Rollout and RAG Safety Module (R1, R2): Temporal modelling is performed over sequential frame groups rather than full videos simultaneously, where future slot states are recursively propagated before IVT decoding. We acknowledge that this section currently lacks sufficient clarity and will revise it accordingly.
The RAG safety module is used only as an inference-time interpretability and procedural verification component. It is not used during training or optimisation and does not contribute to the reported performance metrics. Its role is to provide post-hoc safety-oriented feedback for predicted actions. A more extensive evaluation of RAG-guided safety verification, including clinical validation and failure-case analysis, remains important future work.
Generalisability and Limitations (R1, R3):
We acknowledge that the ontology constraints are currently tailored to cholecystectomy, the slot budget is fixed, and the evaluation is based on public datasets. These points, together with the need for prospective clinical validation before deployment, will be briefly emphasised in the discussion of future work and limitations.

title: Oculo: A Multilabel Dataset for the Identification of Ocular Abnormalities from Ultrasound Images
abstract: Ocular ultrasound is a critical imaging modality for assessing vitreoretinal pathologies, such as retinal detachment, vitreous hemorrhage, and intraocular tumors. However, interpretation requires specialized expertise and exhibits substantial inter-rater variability, limiting access in resource-constrained settings. Although prior studies have applied deep learning (DL) to ocular ultrasound analysis, progress has been constrained by the lack of public datasets and standardized benchmarks. In this work, we introduce Oculo, a publicly available multi-label dataset comprising 1,630 B-scan images from 1,242 patients, annotated for five ophthalmic abnormalities. We systematically benchmark the performance of four DL backbones and three domain-specific foundation models, across two task settings and three training strategies.
