reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: After reading author’s rebuttal, I am happy to raise to accept.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces Endo-C6, a benchmark for robustness evaluation of endoscopic TVLMs under realistic corruptions; it systematically benchmarks three recent surgical TVLMs on this setting; and it proposes RobustEndoCLIP, a few-shot parameter-efficient adaptation method that improves robustness under corrupted conditions.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper addresses a clinically meaningful and underexplored problem: the robustness of surgical TVLMs under realistic endoscopic corruptions. It introduces a well-motivated corruption benchmark spanning six clinically relevant perturbations. The proposed RobustEndoCLIP is practically interesting because it shows that lightweight few-shot parameter-efficient tuning can substantially improve robustness without changing the prompt-based deployment interface.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The technical novelty of the proposed method appears limited. RobustEndoCLIP is essentially built on top of an existing temporal CLIP-style model and adapts it using VeRA, which is itself an existing parameter-efficient tuning method rather than a new methodological contribution of this paper.
2.The baseline comparison is somewhat narrow. Although the paper evaluates three recent TVLMs, these baselines all come from a closely related line of surgical video-language pretraining work, rather than representing a broader spectrum of temporal vision-language models. As a result, it is still unclear whether the observed conclusions would generalize to a wider set of architectures, including stronger general-domain video-language models or additional medical/surgical multimodal models.
3.The evaluation is still limited in scope, being centered on prompt-based classification with a fixed corruption setting, which makes the robustness claims less comprehensive than they could be.
4.Additional weaknesses are that the “few-shot” setting still uses 16% labeled training data, the corruptions are synthetic rather than real clinical degradation, and the paper provides limited analysis of why VeRA improves robustness beyond reporting the gains.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The main contribution is a clinically motivated robustness benchmark and analysis, while the proposed method is technically incremental.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: In this work, the authors attempt to answer four scientific questions about the robustness of endoscopic visual language models. A Corruption Benchmark–Endo-C6 was defined, and 3 temporal vision-language models (TVLM) were tested. In addition, a few-shot adaptation method, RobustEndoCLIP, was presented to improve the performance of TVLM under various corruptions.
reviews.text_strengths: This study sought to assess the robustness of Temporal Vision-Language Models in the surgical endoscopic setting. The authors compiled three open-source endoscope datasets and conducted a taxonomic study on different types of endoscopic video corruptions. This work conducted empirical studies on three start-of-the-art TVLM models and two PEFT fine-tuning methods.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
My main concern is the lack of methodological innovation. 
The corruption taxonomy is more like common sense rather than the author’s insight/contribution. The dataset is from other open-source works without any re-annotation. Meanwhile, I am not confident that the benchmark experiment is comprehensive or solid. There is no innovation regarding parameter-efficient fine-tuning. In addition, this paper does not specify what task these TVLMs are intended for.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This work is more like an empirical study/benchmark of the existing TVLM model for endoscopic videos. I think this type of work needs to meet higher standards to be accepted by MICCAI. I suggest Weak Rejection.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The author’s feedback emphasizes clinical motivation and clarifies details. However, I am not convinced that this benchmark is comprehensive enough to be accepted.
1) Dataset: There are many endoscopic datasets. As a benchmark study, experiments on only 3 datasets are not sufficient. In https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.27460, the survey includes 76 endoscopic datasets. I recommend adding more datasets/tasks/methods and submitting to a journal.
2) Taxonomy: I still do not think this can be counted as the author’s main contribution… Everyone working in surgical computer vision is quite familiar with these corruptions and mentions these in almost every paper…
3) Baselines: Similar to datasets, please consider including more models to give a comprehensive benchmark. I personally do not accept a benchmark paper that only tests 3 baseline models.
4) Concept: What is the definition of VLM robustness? This study does not provide concrete quantitative metrics to reflect this term. At the beginning, there are 4 questions, but it is really hard to follow them while reading the last parts of the paper. The presentation of this paper can be improved from my perspective.

meta_reviews.text:
Borderline case, where the biggest concern is the lack of novelty. However, the reviewers do mention the merit of an application-based benchmark style paper such as this one, hence I would suggest a rebuttal to break ties.

All three reviewers acknowledged a strong rebuttal, one reviewer indicating that she/he is even more confident about proposing to accept the paper. Some issues remain, as pointed out by reviewer 3 (who propose to reject): Number of data sets used, number of baselines, and limited scope of corruptions (R2). However, there’s only so much you can fit into a MICCAI paper and suggest the authors still extend the work and submit to a journal, as reviewer 3 suggests, but also present the current results at MICCAI, also supported by 2 of 3 reviewers propose an accept, compared to a Weak Reject by the other reviewer.
The idea presented in the paper is interesting, and robustness evaluation is critical in our field. The rebuttal addressed the major points raised by the reviewers.
The answers provided by the authors in the rebuttal letter are complete.

author_feedback_text:
We appreciate the reviewers’ effort and constructive comments. We are glad that R1 recognized the clear motivation, worst-case focus, and large-scale evaluation; R2 highlighted the clinically meaningful Endo-C6 setting and practical robustness gains; and R3 noted the empirical study of TVLM robustness, taxonomy, datasets, and TVLM/PEFT evaluation. Below, we address the concerns point-by-point and will incorporate clarifications in the revision.
R1.1/R2.1 Contribution scope relative to prior work.
We appreciate R1/R2’s framing and will emphasize the paper’s central contribution: a clinically driven Endo-C6 robustness study for temporal surgical TVLMs, with RobustEndoCLIP as the limited-supervision adaptation setting. Prior work addresses natural corruptions, medical VLM robustness, or endoscopic depth estimation, but not prompt-based surgical TVLMs under GI/laparoscopic acquision artifacts. To our knowledge, Endo-C6 is the first benchmark for this setting, combining paired label-preserving corruptions on real clips, domain/temporal artifact structure, limited-supervision analysis, and mean/worst-case reporting. It reveals artifact-specific failures: smoke dominates laparoscopy, GI sensitivity is model-dependent, and clean accuracy poorly predicts corrupted robustness.
R1.2 Prompt-based vs. open-vocabulary scope.
We agree experiments use fixed dataset vocabularies, not held-out-label transfer. Here, “prompt-based” means CLIP-style class-name prompts matched with video embeddings. Claims concern label-preserving corruptions under this interface, not unseen-label adaptation after tuning. We will clarify the task as CholecT50 phase, Kvasir GI landmark/pathology, and TEMSET-24K action classification.
R2.2 Baseline selection.
SurgVLP, HecVLP, and PeskaVLP are recent public surgical TVLMs with comparable CLIP-style interfaces and no Endo-C6 exposure. Identical prompts, sampling, splits, corruptions, and temporal coverage enable controlled comparison; broader VLMs/surgical multimodal models are valuable future works.
R2.3/R3.3 Task scope and benchmark strength.
Endo-C6 evaluates prompt-based temporal clip classification: CholecT50 phases, Kvasir GI landmark/pathology classes, and TEMSET-24K actions. Within this scope, it is comprehensive and solid: full public GI/laparoscopic test splits, 3 datasets, 3untuned TVLM baselines plus RobustEndoCLIP configurations, clean+6 corruptions, 2 temporal coverages, and 294 dataset-level/593,488 clip-level evaluations under identical prompts, sampling, splits, severity, and aggregation. This controlled design isolates video-text alignment failures under label-preserving shifts and avoids broader claims. We will further clarify the task/scope and make it explicit in the final, and extend the scope in future work.
R2.4 Few-shot, corruptions, and VeRA.
The 16% setting is the largest limited clean-label budget; Fig. 4 reports 0/4/8/16%. Synthetic corruptions are deliberate: applied to real test clips, they keep labels/test composition fixed while varying only artifact type/severity, simulating routine endoscopic acquisition artifacts for reproducible paired stress tests. Table 2 shows LoRA can improve clean accuracy, but VeRA gives stronger corrupted performance with far fewer params (1,024 vs. 720,896; 29.13 vs. 16.92 average Mean-C), suggesting better regularization under corruption.
R3.1 Methodological scope and taxonomy.
The core contribution is a clinically motivated robustness benchmark and analysis for temporal surgical VLMs, not a new adaptation algorithm. Endo-C6 is not a generic corruption list: organizing clinically familiar artifacts by domain salience and temporal behavior enables interpretable smoke/laparoscopy and motion/defocus/GI findings.
R3.2 Public datasets and re-annotation. 
We use public datasets to ensure reproducibility and isolate artifact-driven robustness failures. Since Endo-C6 applies label-preserving corruptions to existing test clips, re-annotation is not required.

title: One Sequence to Segment Them All: Efficient Data Augmentation for CT and MRI Cross-Domain 3D Spine Segmentation
abstract:
Deep learning–based medical image segmentation is increasingly used to support clinical diagnosis and develop new treatment strategies. However, model performance remains limited by the scarcity of high-quality annotated data and insufficient generalization across imaging protocols. This limitation is particularly evident in MRI and CT, where models are typically trained on a single acquisition sequence and exhibit reduced robustness when applied to unseen sequences or contrasts. Although data augmentation is widely used to improve general robustness on medical images, its impact on cross-modality generalization has not been quantitatively explored.
In this work, we study a targeted set of data augmentation techniques designed to improve cross-modality transfer. We train three spine segmentation models, each on a single-modality/sequence dataset, and evaluate them across seven out-of-distribution datasets (spanning CT and MRI), reflecting a realistic single-sequence training and multi-sequence/contrast/modality deployment scenario. Our results demonstrate substantial performance gains on unseen domains (average Dice gain of 155%) while preserving in-domain accuracy (average Dice decrease of 0.008%), including effective transfer between CT and MRI.
To mitigate the computational cost typically associated with strong data augmentation, we implement GPU-optimized augmentations that maintain, and even improve, training efficiency by approximately 10%. We release our approach as an open-source toolbox, enabling seamless integration into commonly used frameworks such as nnUNet and MONAI. These augmentations significantly enhance robustness to heterogeneous clinical imaging scenarios without compromising training speed.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors of this paper develop an open-source toolbox for GPU-optimized data augmentations that are designed to improve cross-modality transfer. They train three separate models for spine segmentation and perform an evaluation on seven out-of-distribution datasets. They demonstrate that their method has substantial improvement for unseen domains, and minimal reduction in Dice scores on in-domain data. The authors also conducted extensive ablation studies to assess the effect of each augmentation.
reviews.text_strengths:
The authors perform a significant analysis of their model. This includes comparing models trained on three different datasets, and evaluation on the baseline, nnUNetTrainerDA5, and their proposed method (Table 3). They additionally compare the vertebral, IVD, and canal segmentations using models trained on these three datasets. The reviewer appreciates that the evaluation was performed per scan sequence type.
The authors perform a significant number of ablation studies using their approach (Table 5). They add in each ablation separately to the baseline model to test the effect, and do so for all the models trained on SG in-phase and SG CT.
The authors provided clear qualitative examples comparing the models trained on the three datasets for the nnUNet baseline vs their method.
The manuscript includes a statistical analysis to compare methods.
The authors provide a good discussion.
They make their code open source.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Though the authors commented on the field of domain randomization and other synthetic data generation methods, the manuscript would be improved with a quantitative comparison.
The authors include in their limitations that the generalizability of their method is unknown to other anatomical regions. However, more information should be included about additional problems they may encounter with other datasets.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
It would be useful to include the standard deviation in Tables 3,4, and 5.

Though the authors use novel transforms, perform significant evaluation of their models, and use multiple datasets, the paper could be slightly improved by a comparison to other data augmentation and domain randomization approaches.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Thank you for the rebuttal. However, I believe that due to evaluations of one task, a lack of comparison to other synthetic data-based methods/diffusion methods, the manuscript is not ready for acceptance at this moment.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces a training-free, model-agnostic data augmentation (DA) strategy that is shown to improve generalization on a 3D spine segmentation task. The proposed strategy involves the extension of classic approaches with a list of data augmentation transforms that mostly operate on the intensities or texture of the image (i.e. no additional morphological or geometric deformations). The inevitable additional computation cost is mitigated by an optimized re-implementation of the full DA pipeline, which is shown to significantly reduce the application runtime.
reviews.text_strengths: The manuscript presents several notable strengths. Its focus on usability is commendable, as the proposed approach is model-agnostic and benefits from an optimized GPU implementation. The optimized GPU implementaiton is a very valuable contribution in its own right. The comparison with the nnUNet baseline is rigorous, spanning multiple modalities and supported by statistical significance testing. The work is further strengthened by extensive ablation studies, and the authors provide a balanced discussion of both results and limitations.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The manuscript also presents several weaknesses. On the major side, the experimental validation is limited to a single type of task, and the comparison with the state of the art is insufficient — notably absent are comparisons with diffusion-based approaches for cross-modal generation [1] and SynthSeg [2]. Furthermore, the ablation studies suggest that RedistributeSeg alone accounts for a large share of the generalization improvement in most settings, which weakens the case for the full proposed transformation pipeline. Since RedistributeSeg is not a contribution of this work, this observation somewhat diminishes the overall impact of the paper.
On the minor side, the evaluation on canals raises a methodological concern: given that these structures may not be visible in the CT image, it is unclear whether such evaluation is meaningful, and how the ground truth was defined is not discussed. Finally, the authors do not adequately address a noteworthy ablation result, namely the surprisingly poor performance of single transformations on the SG-CT to SG-water generalization task, which stands in stark contrast to the strong boost observed when all new transformations are compounded. The nature of the interaction between transformations that could explain this behaviour, and why it appears to be specific to this particular setting, warrants further discussion.
[1] Ma, Ji, Jinjin Chen, and Aoxiang Liang. “CT-to-MRI translation of medical volume data based on an enhanced diffusion model.” Scientific Reports (2026).
[2] Billot, Benjamin, et al. “SynthSeg: Segmentation of brain MRI scans of any contrast and resolution without retraining.” Medical image analysis 86 (2023): 102789.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
I thank the authors for their effort in producing a reusable and reproducible scientific contribution. As a minor remark, in Table 3 the brown color is indicated to denote in-domain settings; however, it is unclear why MM CT is not highlighted in brown for the SG CT training example, as both are CT domain.

The paper is well written, with a clear objective and a well-defined scientific question. However, the lack of evaluation across a wider range of tasks substantially limits the generality of the conclusions and reduces the overall impact of the work. Moreover, given that RedistributeSeg consistently dominates the generalization gains across most experimental settings, the paper reads less as a demonstration of the utility of the full proposed data augmentation pipeline, and more as an assessment of the effectiveness of RedistributeSeg alone.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
the concern about the impact and relevance for the MICCAI community has been significantly reduced by the meta review 1
the concern about the utility of the full pipeline, given that RedistributeSeg often provides the major contribution, has been addressed by the authors’ rebuttal. I agree with them that discovering this fact is interesting in its own right and would have been impossible without their extensive ablation studies. Their comment about “there is no single best augmentation for MRI or CT” is also valid.
the lack of comparison with SynthSeg remains a weakness of the paper, although overall the rebuttal is sufficient (in my opinion) to tip the scales towards acceptance. The authors mention SynthSeg’s higher computational and setup requirements: I am not aware of any particularly strong requirements in this sense (especially compared to other state of the art methods), but if the authors feel strongly about this they could introduce a sentence justifying the lack of comparison.
as an additional comment that does not influence my suggestion for a decision on the rebuttal: please include a few sentences explaining how the annotations for canals on CT were defined by the radiologists, given that canals are invisible on CT. Did they use some proxy anatomical landmarks? Or just their own experience? Or some other strategy?

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of this paper is demonstrating that well‑designed, appearance‑based data augmentation is sufficient to achieve strong cross‑domain generalization for 3D spine segmentation, even when training is limited to a single CT or MRI sequence. The proposed augmentation pipeline is implemented efficiently on the GPU within the nnUNet framework. While individual augmentations lead to only modest performance improvements, the results show that the largest gains arise from combining all augmentations together, with the specific order of their application having little impact on performance.
reviews.text_strengths: A major strength of this paper is the thorough and well‑designed ablation study, which systematically evaluates a set of carefully chosen data augmentation techniques targeting contrast and texture appearance variations. These augmentations are explicitly motivated by the challenges posed by multi‑contrast, multi‑parametric MRI as well as cross‑modal differences between MRI and CT, and the study clearly demonstrates how they contribute to improved robustness.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper does not introduce a fundamentally novel methodology. The use of data augmentation to improve contrast‑agnostic segmentation performance has been explored in prior work; for example, Bédard et al. (2025) demonstrate robust spinal cord segmentation across MRI contrasts using aggressive augmentation and contrast‑aware training strategies. As a result, the contribution of this work is primarily empirical rather than conceptual.
Another limitation is that the evaluation is restricted to a single anatomical structure and task, namely semantic spine segmentation. Given the paper’s emphasis on carefully designed augmentations, it would strengthen the contribution to provide guidance on how these augmentation choices generalize to other anatomies or tasks, or to discuss strategies for automating augmentation selection rather than relying on task‑specific manual design.
Ref : Bédard, S., Naga Karthik, E., Tsagkas, C., Pravatà, E., Granziera, C., Smith, A., Weber II, K. A., & Cohen-Adad, J. (2025). Towards contrast-agnostic soft segmentation of the spinal cord. Medical Image Analysis, 101, 103473.https://doi.org/10.1016/j.media.2025.103473
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I recommended a Weak Reject primarily because, while the paper presents a strong and carefully executed empirical study, its core contributions are incremental rather than clearly novel. The use of appearance‑focused data augmentation to achieve contrast‑agnostic or cross‑modality segmentation has been demonstrated in prior work, and the paper does not introduce a new formulation, learning paradigm, or theoretical insight beyond this existing direction. Another factor influencing my score is that the evaluation is limited to a single anatomical structure and task, making it difficult to assess how broadly the proposed augmentation strategy generalizes. I would not strongly oppose acceptance, particularly if the rebuttal can better clarify the paper’s positioning relative to prior work or better articulate the generality and broader impact of the proposed approach.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper introduces a GPU-optimized, model-agnostic data augmentation toolbox aimed at improving cross-modality generalization for 3D spine segmentation. The approach focuses on appearance-based transformations and demonstrates improved robustness on multiple out-of-distribution datasets, while maintaining strong in-domain performance. The authors also provide extensive ablation studies and release their implementation as open source.
All reviewers agree that the paper addresses a relevant and practical problem, and highlight the thorough experimental evaluation as a key strength. In particular, the study includes multiple training settings, evaluation across several datasets and modalities, detailed ablations, and statistical analysis. The practical utility of the method—being training-free, easily integrable, and GPU-efficient—is also appreciated.
However, there is a general consensus that the methodological novelty is limited. I personally do not see this as a limitation because I see this paper as an empirical study, which are welcome at MICCAI. I think that the combination of the GPU-based nnUNet implementation and the thorough evaluation make this paper a good contribution.
Nevertheless, I would like the authors to address several points in their rebuttal. First, I would like them to better position themselves with the literature and to comment on potentially missing baselines: SynthSeg (which is very close in concept and implementation), other augmentation strategies for spinal cord, and cross-modal generation. Additionally, one reviewer notes that a significant portion of the observed gains may be attributed to a single component (RedistributeSeg), which weakens the case for the full pipeline. I would also like the authors to comment on the generalisation to other anatomies and tasks, although I think that the current setup is enough for MICCAI, especially given the depth of the conducted experiments. Finally, small concerns are also to be addressed, such as missing standard deviations, result clarifications, and dataset constructions.
Overall, the paper presents a solid and well-executed empirical study with clear practical value. However, concerns about positioning, clarification of contributions, and discussion of generality, should be addressed in rebuttal.

The authors successfully answered a number of concerns raised in the initial reviews about: 1) including a discussion of the RedistributeSeg augmentation step, 2) clarifying the difference with existing existing works (Bédard et al.), 3) clarifying spinal cord annotations, 4) adding the missing standard deviations. As said earlier, I also think that empirical studies are welcome at MICCAI, especially when they address widespread subjects such as data augmentation (like in this study). Moreover, given the depth of the conducted analysis, I think that the author’s position of keeping the extension to other organs for future work is reasonable.
However, not including a SynthSeg-like method for cross-modal segmentation is a clear flaw for this paper. As pointed out by reviewer 2, it is not true that SynthSeg requires special computational resources, and can be trained on a normal GPU. This flaw is amplified by the fact that abdominal SynthSeg methods [a] have already been trained and are clearly missing here.
Overall, this paper is borderline accept/reject. However, I lean towards acceptance given the broad interest for a thorough empirical study of data augmentation, which goes way beyond the domain randomisation (SynthSeg) community.
[a] Benchmarking of deep learning methods for generic MRI multi-organ abdominal segmentation, Krishnaswamy et al, Journal of Medical imaging, 2025.

R1 changed from Weak Accept to Reject, R2 changed from Weak Reject to Accept, while R3 did not change their initial recommendation of Weak Reject. Although the paper is promising, with two reviewers ultimately recommending Reject, I would also recommend rejection.

My decision relies in large part to the original Area Chair comments, although it takes into account the reviewer’s concerns and the rebuttal answers to them.
For starters, I agree with the original Area Chair, that the framing for the paper is key and as provided by the authors in their rebuttal, I would consider this work an empirical study and not a methodological contribution. In that sense, methodological novelty should not be the main reason for rejection or acceptance.
Based on the empirical study, I also agree that contextualisation is key to make a decision. The authors provided with their rebuttal a reason for why domain randomisation techniques were not included. While I am sympathetic with not including them due to the additional training cost (not viable during rebuttal), I am not entirely sure I can agree with the methods being that different, considering RedistributeSeg as one of the augmentations and the combination of all augmentations if applied to a case. To clarify, I think part of the reasoning is overall sound and adding a few sentences to highlight that would be beneficial, but I would emphasise that there are similarities and that comparison should be performed in a future work (perhaps a journal publication).
I am also not entirely convinced by the argument about a couple of specific cases where RedistributeSeg is not the best augmentation. From the whole ablation table, these are only 2 experiments and in both cases, RedistributeSeg is the second best augmentation not that far behind. Nonetheless, I do agree with the authors that the thorough ablation test is commendable and leads to a deeper and richer analysis.
Apart from that, I believe the authors did a good job of addressing all the minor and major concerns raised by the reviewers and original Area Chair.

author_feedback_text:
The reviewers note the lack of comparisons with SynthSeg and diffusion-based cross-modal generation methods, and that the contribution appears empirical rather than novel, citing a paper by Bédard et al. The validation is limited to a single anatomy, leaving the method’s generalizability unclear. They request a broader discussion of how the augmentation design may transfer to other anatomies.
The primary goal of this work was to perform a detailed empirical study across three datasets, seven sequences, and three segmentation structures to evaluate whether a simple plug-and-play augmentation strategy could generalize without requiring complex pipelines or fine-tuning. We prioritized depth of analysis over broader comparisons.
We agree that extending the study to non-spinal tasks would strengthen it; However, evaluating our pipeline on three distinct structures, each exhibiting different behaviors with respect to contrast and modality, represented a reasonable trade-off for assessing how well the performance generalizes across different anatomical structures, given the 8-page limit. Future work will investigate additional anatomical structures.
We acknowledge that including additional comparative methods, such as SynthSeg, would further strengthen the study. However, given the trade-off imposed by our exhaustive benchmark, we chose to prioritize the inclusion of multiple plug-and-play data augmentation over more complex methods. When designing the study, SynthSeg was not considered a valid competitor due to its higher computational and setup requirements.
Regarding comparisons with Bédard et al.: They simultaneously train on six image contrasts, whereas our problem statement is to demonstrate improved cross-domain transferability when training on a single contrast. In addition, they did not investigate appearance-altering augmentations for improving cross-domain transferability. We will add these details to the literature review section.
The reviewers correctly noted that the RedistributeSeg augmentation alone contributes most to the domain-transfer capabilities. They argue that this weakens the motivation for using the proposed combination of augmentations, especially since RedistributeSeg is not the main contribution of this work.
Our ablation study revealed the strong contribution of RedistributeSeg, which would likely have remained unnoticed without such extensive analysis. We agree that this aspect is mostly true across contrasts. However, the example of training on SG-CT and evaluation on SG-water, also mentioned by the reviewers, provides a counterexample to this statement. Table 5 demonstrates that while RedistributeSeg is the best-performing across most sequences, this is not the case for SG in-phase and SG water when trained on SG CT. This shows that there is no single best augmentation for MRI or CT, underscoring the importance of such extensive ablation. In addition, our study shows that our proposed combination often significantly outperforms RedistributeSeg alone. The discussion will be extended to better explain our results.
The reviewers questioned the ability to evaluate structures such as the spinal canal on CT images, as they are not visible. They also requested the standard deviation in Tables 3, 4, and 5 and noted that labeling a CT as out-of-domain for another CT dataset is confusing.
We agree and mention in the discussion that the CT canal annotations are probabilistic. The fact that the model trained on CT with our augmentation achieves great values on MRI still validates our approach. Moreover, Figure 3 shows that differences in CT predictions compared to the default nnunet are due to real performance issues: the default nnunet does not segment the canal. We will clarify this in the revised manuscript.
We removed the standard deviations to improve readability, but we agree with the reviewers and will add them back in. We will also clarify the color scheme regarding the definition of “in-domain”.

title: Oneclass4ASD: Autism Spectrum Disorder Screening via One-class Classifier
abstract: Eye tracking technology as a non-contact method has become an innovative solution to Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) diagnosis by comparing the fixation data of healthy individuals and those suffering from ASD. Though this strategy seems promising, challenges remain in ASD data collection stage while the collected data often exhibit large intra-variances that seriously disrupt the diagnostic process. From these two problems, it is evident that binary classification methods which rely on data from both the healthy and ASD groups will encounter difficulties during the deployment stage. Therefore, in this paper, we propose a novel perspective that treats ASD as an abnormality detection through the introduction of one-class classification approach, which only requires healthy individuals’ data during training. Moreover, to address the large intra-variance among individuals, we design a novel uncertainty-aware weighting scheme that assigns images different contribution weights based on their effectiveness in distinguishing between ASD and healthy individuals. Additionally, from uncertainty weighting we are able to conduct an image selection process that selects the best-preforming subset of image stimuli for the training process. In comparison to previous research that adopts the binary classification method, our approach achieves comparable results while only using healthy individuals’ data for the training process.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors describe a method for classifying Autistic Spectrum Disorder (ASD) for use as a diagnostic marker, by treating it as an anomaly detection task using a One-Class classification approach on fixation patterns produced by healthy individuals during eye-tracking. The clinical motivation for this is that ASD individuals have uncommon, more erratic gaze patterns than healthy individuals who tend to be more consistent in their response (i. e. what they tend to focus on given a particular image). Rather than restrict themselves to a comparison over a known and fixed diagnostic set of images, they treat this as a general problem for arbitrary input images. Additionally, they introduce a weighting scheme which describes the extent to which each image is likely to produce consistent gaze patterns even among healthy individuals, which is used in two ways; one, as a weighting factor within the classification pipeline itself, and two, as a means of ranking the images so as to then only use the more ‘reliable’ ones for training. They show that this approach achieves better results than more traditional approaches treating healthy and ASD as distinct classes in a binary classification setting.
reviews.text_strengths: While there is no new core methodology introduced as such, this represents a good, novel pipeline consisting of existing components, solving a useful interesting problem in a straightforward manner.
reviews.text_weaknesses: While the broader nature of the pipeline as a whole is mostly clear, the explanations provided can be a bit hand-wavy or lacking in detail at times, making the work harder to follow or be able to replicate the work fully (which is particularly important since no code is provided alongside the paper). Additionally, while they provide ablation studies showing the impact of some components compared to benchmarks, they do not provide much personal insight as to why one approach works and the other does not; they simply use these as evidence that “they happened to make good choices” somehow.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Please provide clarifying definitions for all technical terms used in the manuscript, e. g. fixation diagrams, gaze patterns, fixation sequence, etc
A (very) brief introduction of what one-class classification methods are would be useful early in the manuscript, to orient the reader who has not come across such methods in the past. Given the broad audience of the conference it’s best not to present advanced concepts under the assumption of full prior knowledge.
Please go through your methodology section and clarify all parts and concepts that are ambiguous. E. g. how is the VGG used / set up exactly (e. g. exact nature and dimensionality of inputs, preprocessing involved, and exact nature of outputs); how concatenation is performed (i. e. along what axis), what the 1x1 convolution operation is acting on precisely (i. e. the exact dimensionality of the kernel, otherwise someone unfamiliar with the abuse of terminology common to the field might be confused that this is a 2D operation, effectively a multiplication by a scalar); the exact nature of the “ground-truth fixation map” (is this binary? probabilistic? isolated points? lines? blobs?); what is the exact nature of the “feature vector” (what does 1024-d refer to? are we saying the output of the VGG is 32x32 images expressed as a 1D vector? are the different fixation locations equivalent across images? what is the actual nature of the 1024 vector, is it a one-hot encoding / probabilistic, or does it encode locations in some other manner? what does it mean exactly “to extract a feature from a fixation location”? how are individual fixation locations isolated / differentiated from the probabilistic map?)
Can you clarify why is the softmax operation needed after S_i is obtained, why not use the S_i directly (which is already in the [0,1] range).
Can you provide some more insight as to why you think Resnet-34 / cosine distance do not work as well as your original choices for this particular problem?

This is a useful clinical contribution, providing good rationale and motivation for the work and appropriate methodological approach for attacking the problem. They demonstrate good results and potential for meaningful use in the relevant clinical domain.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
I was happy to recommend acceptance of the manuscript before, and this is still my opinion. Additionally, the authors now state clearly that they are happy to release the source code upon acceptance which was my main concern in terms of reproducibility.
Regarding the author’s rebuttal, I think they address all points adequately. However, I clearly I think all the points they have addressed to the reviewers would have been worth actually addressing in the manuscript, rather than only in the rebuttal, but I see no changes in the manuscript itself. I note the authors say they will make changes post-acceptance? It was my impression that the changes should have been made at this stage so that the reviewers could review these changes, so this is causing me some confusion as to what the actual process is. Nevertheless, I am still of the opinion, as before, that the paper merited acceptance even in its original form.
I agree with the authors’ comments to some of the other reviewers who expressed concerns of clinical usefulness, that the contribution does not need to be an all-or-nothing clinical solution, and that the ability to quickly screen someone is still clinically useful, since these tools do not operate in a vacuum, but typically they are employed in the context of an existing clinical suspicion and a pre-test probability for a diagnosis. Even if it is not highly specific as a test for ASD, if highly sensitive, it can be very useful to quickly rule out an ASD differential (similar to how a d-dimer blood test is used in the emergency department during suspected pulmonary emboli and deep vein thrombosis, for example).

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper tests the idea that ASD (Austism Spectrum Disorder) is an example of “not neurotypical” eye tracking data.
They propose to use the similarity of fixation patterns among different neurotypical individuals to improve classification - which produces an improvement.
reviews.text_strengths: Oneclass approach may reduce reliance on difficult to measure cases, and shows better performance than baseline.
reviews.text_weaknesses: THere are no major weaknesses to this paper.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
I would suggest using the term neurotypical instead of healthy, given that healthy can mean many things. Furthermore it seems that the paper casts ASD as abnormal - which can be stigmatising.
I also found the description of the choice of fixation and features were vague

This appears to be a novel contribution that improves upon a baseline measure across most measures
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a two-stage one-class classification framework, termed Oneclass4ASD, for ASD screening by modeling it as an anomaly detection problem using only healthy subjects’ data. In the first stage, a dual-scale VGG-16 network is used to predict fixation maps of healthy individuals. In the second stage, fixation points are selected from gaze sequences to extract and concatenate visual features, which are further fused using an uncertainty-aware weighting scheme based on fixation map similarity. Finally, the aggregated features are fed into a Deep SVDD module to learn a hypersphere representing normal patterns and detect abnormal deviations.
reviews.text_strengths: The visualizations, together with the proposed framework, provide some evidence that the method is feasible and can effectively capture discriminative gaze-related patterns for ASD screening under the one-class setting.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Concern 1: Potential inconsistency in the two-stage design.
The proposed two-stage framework raises questions regarding the actual interaction between its components. While the first stage is designed to predict fixation maps for healthy individuals, it is not clearly explained how these predictions are utilized in the second stage. In particular, the selection strategy for a fixed number of fixation points (e.g., 12) is not specified, and its connection to the predicted fixation maps remains unclear. Moreover, the extracted “1024-dimensional visual features” appear to be derived directly from the backbone network applied to the original images, rather than from the predicted fixation maps. This suggests that the first-stage model may not play a significant role during inference. Therefore, it would be helpful for the authors to clarify the dependency between the two stages and justify the necessity of this design.
Concern 2: Practical limitations in testing flexibility.
The proposed method appears to rely on aggregating features over a relatively large set of observed images (e.g., hundreds of stimuli) for each subject to compute uncertainty-aware weights. This raises questions about its practicality in real-world or clinical scenarios, where collecting such extensive observations for each new subject may not always be feasible. It would be helpful for the authors to clarify whether the method can generalize to settings with fewer observations or more flexible testing conditions.
Concern 3: While the use of Deep SVDD enables modeling deviations from healthy patterns, it may be inherently limited in distinguishing the underlying causes of such deviations. For instance, individuals with other neurodevelopmental conditions (e.g., ADHD or intellectual disabilities) may also exhibit atypical gaze patterns. It is therefore unclear how the model would differentiate ASD-specific patterns from other forms of deviation, and whether this could lead to potential misclassification. Further discussion or empirical evaluation on this aspect would strengthen the work.
Concern 4: Questionable extent of data efficiency gains. The paper emphasizes alleviating the difficulty of collecting ASD data by adopting a one-class learning paradigm. While this may reduce the need for ASD samples during training, it is less clear whether the overall data collection burden is substantially reduced. For example, the testing phase and the construction of subject-level representations still seem to require a considerable amount of eye-tracking data. It would be valuable for the authors to more carefully discuss the trade-offs and practical implications in terms of data efficiency compared to traditional binary classification approaches.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The recommendation is based on four main concerns: (1) the two-stage framework lacks clear internal consistency, and the dependency between stages appears insufficiently justified; (2) the testing procedure may require extensive per-subject data aggregation, which could limit practical clinical applicability; (3) although the method claims to alleviate ASD data scarcity, it appears that substantial data collection is still required in both feature construction and testing phases, which may weaken the claimed advantage.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The concerns and criticisms raised in my review should be adequately addressed in the final version.

reviews.text_contribution:
1) ASD detection by using anomaly detection formulation. Overcomes the challenges of insufficient and inconsistent ASD fixations.
2) Uncertainty-aware strategy to measure the similarity of fixation pattern from different healthy people, identifying high discriminating stimuli and contribution.
3) The proposed method has reasonable results on the considered dataset without ASD cases.

2) Robust intra-class variations because of uncertainty-aware weighting. This improves the robustness without introducing extra sample points
3) Good performance without complex system design and modulation.

2) One-class assumption may oversimplify all disorder issues to just anomaly detection. Feature learned may lead to false positive issue with other diseases but not ASD.

N/A

Hard to judge the generalization and stability on large-scale practical implementation, where multiple similar disorders are existing in the population.
