meta_reviews.text:
The reviewers see the paper as a timely contribution.
The main concerns are about rigor rather than direction: reviewers ask for clearer human verification and ambiguity handling, stronger decontamination against data leakage, better workflow-stage analysis, stronger open-ended evaluation beyond ROUGE-L, fuller ophthalmology/medical MLLM baselines, and more ablation of the GRPO design.

The main concerns were about how reliable the benchmark is. In particular, the reviewers asked for clearer details on human checking, how ambiguous cases were handled, whether there was any overlap between training and test data, and whether open-ended answers were evaluated well enough. Some reviewers also felt that more ophthalmology-specific baselines and better workflow-level analysis would strengthen the paper.
After rebuttal, all reviewers moved to Accept. Some issues remain, but they can be addressed in the final version.

This paper introduces OphthFlowBench, a comprehensive ophthalmology benchmark that structures clinical assessment into four stages (visual perception, clinical interpretation, disease diagnosis, and clinical management), along with the Oph-RL model that achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple SoA MLLMs. 
Reviewers acknowledged the strong contributions and that the authors addressed most concerns during rebuttal, though some noted remaining issues. Although the initial reviewer scores diverged, all reviewers now agree on acceptance after rebuttal, and I recommend acceptance.

Reviewers agreed that most raised questions were addressed in the rebuttal and consistently recommended acceptance. They acknowledged the contributions of the work, including a very relevant benchmark for ophthalmology and strong empirical results. R2 suggested further refinements for the camera-ready version.

author_feedback_text:
We appreciate valuable comments from reviewers and will consider them carefully in the final manuscript.
Meta concerns on verification and ambiguity handling (R1Q2, R2Q1Q2), leakage (R3Q1), workflow analysis (R2Q4), open-ended evaluation (R3Q2), baselines (R2Q6, R3Q4), and GRPO ablation (R3Q3) are addressed below.
R1Q1: Lower management-stage performance
As an 8B model, Oph-RL is much smaller than proprietary MLLMs. In addition, we made relevant analysis in Sec. 3.2.
R1Q2: Benchmark quality
GPT-4o-mini/GPT-5 were used only for preprocessing and standardization. As stated in Sec. 2.1, all retained samples were further verified by four ophthalmologists.
R2Q1Q2: Handling in refinement
GPT-5 refinement was rule-constrained rather than unrestricted rewriting, following the protocol in “Adaptive Reinforcement for Open-ended Medical Reasoning via Semantic-Guided Reward Collapse Mitigation (CVPR 2026-Findings)”. It only ensured questions were complete, unambiguous, and semantically sufficient, while keeping their form, scope, detail level, and structure aligned with the answers. Ambiguous cases were corrected under these rules, unresolved cases were discarded, and ophthalmologists verified both pre- and post-refinement results.
R2Q3: Clinical-stage definitions
Stages were defined by the dominant cognitive operation: visual perception identifies visible findings; clinical interpretation explains their meaning; disease diagnosis determines disease category; clinical management selects diagnostic or treatment actions. All labels were assigned accordingly and verified by ophthalmologists.
R2Q4: Workflow-level analysis
Table 1 reports stage-wise results. It reveals clear stage-specific bottlenecks: strong perception/diagnosis does not always imply strong management. The workflow design also captures cascading dependency, where errors in perception or interpretation may propagate to diagnosis and management.
R2Q5: Real-world validation
Multi-center real-world validation is important future work but requires substantial expert effort across workflow stages.
R2Q6: Ophthalmology-specific MLLMs
We thank the reviewers for the suggestion. We have included representative ophthalmology-specific MLLMs such as Med-R1-Fundus, and evaluated VisionUnite and FundusExpert, as suggested by the reviewers (The results will be shown in the final version). The result is consistent with our existing findings: current ophthalmology-specific MLLMs still show only moderate performance on workflow-level tasks.
R2Q7: OphthaWeChat baselines
OphthaWeChat is supplementary, not our main evidence. Since it mainly contains classification-oriented questions, it tests generalization to simpler ophthalmic VQA settings.
R2Q8: Common-setting performance
Glaucoma is not underperformance: Oph-RL ranks first, 0.549 vs. 0.547 second-best. Remaining common-modality gaps mainly reflect scale/data coverage, as Oph-RL is 8B while strong baselines such as Qwen2.5-VL-72B are much larger.
R3Q1: Data leakage
SHA-256 hashing found no duplicate sample content.
R3Q2: Open-ended evaluation
ROUGE-L provides a reproducible metric but is not the sole evidence. As shown in Sec. 3.3, OphthaWeChat also uses DeepSeek-V3 as an LLM judge for factual correctness, where Oph-RL achieves the best Open-ended-CN/EN results (language subsets), supporting its open-ended ability.
R3Q3: GRPO ablation
The manuscript compares the SFT with Oph-RL, showing GRPO gains. Our design follows the standard GRPO paradigm using answer and format rewards. Difficulty-aware selection does not change the RL objective. It only filters medium-difficulty samples, since extremely easy/hard cases provide weak learning signals, as also motivated by OralGPT-Omni (CVPR 2026).
R3Q4: Baselines
We evaluated 23 representative MLLMs, covering proprietary, open-source, medical-specific, and ophthalmology-related models such as Lingshu and Med-R1-OCT. More baselines will be considered in future work.

title: Opportunistic Cardiac Health Assessment: Estimating Phenotypes from Localizer MRI Through Multi-modal Representations
abstract:
Cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of death. Cardiac phenotypes (CPs), e.g., ejection fraction, are the gold standard for assessing cardiac health, but they’re derived from cine cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR), which is costly and requires high spatio-temporal resolution. Every magnetic resonance (MR) examination begins with rapid and coarse localizers for scan planning, which are discarded thereafter. Despite non-diagnostic image quality and lack of temporal information, localizers can provide valuable structural information rapidly. In addition to imaging, patient-level information, including demographics and lifestyle, influence the cardiac health assessment. Electrocardiograms (ECGs) are inexpensive, routinely ordered in clinical practice, and capture the temporal activity of the heart. Here, we introduce C-TRIP (Cardiac Tri-modal Representations for Imaging Phenotypes), a multi-modal framework that aligns localizer MRI, ECG signals, and tabular metadata to learn a robust latent space and predict CPs using localizer images as an opportunistic alternative to CMR. By combining these three modalities, we leverage cheap spatial and temporal information from localizers, and ECG, respectively while benefiting from patient-specific context provided by tabular data. Our pipeline consists of three stages. First, encoders are trained independently to learn uni-modal representations. The second stage fuses the pre-trained encoders to unify the latent space. The final stage uses the enriched representation space for CP prediction, with inference performed exclusively on localizer MRI.
Proposed C-TRIP yields accurate functional CPs, and high correlations for structural CPs. Since localizers are inherently rapid and low-cost, our C-TRIP framework could enable better accessibility for CP estimation.
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers
Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning
Modalities -> EEG / MEG / ECG / Physiological Signals

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The author proposes a three-stage model for generating cardiac phenotypes from MRI localiser scans using contrained from ECG and tabular data. The pipeline includes separate encoders for imaging, ECG, and tabular data. 
The authors introduce a localiser-centric contrastive learning framework in which the localiser latent space is aligned with ECG and tabular representations, encouraging embeddings from the same patient to be closer in the shared latent space. The localiser embedding is then used to predict cardiac phenotypes, and only the localiser images is required at inference. 
The model was trained and validated on UK Biobank data, but the specific image inputs are not clearly described despite the dataset’s range of available cardiac scans. Overall, phenotype prediction using the localiser appears comparable to the baseline supervised model based on dynamic CMR sequences.
reviews.text_strengths:
The network architecture and optimisation method are clearly described.
The proposed method could be of considerable clinical interest for public health and patient management.
The proposed multimodal contrastive learning approach appears flexible and extensible, and may be of interest for other applications.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
There is no discussion of model performance for patient diagnosis. The proposed method does not appear to perform well for lower-range LVEF and RVEF prediction, which are among the most important biomarkers. Performance analysis and discussion within the diagnostic range should be provided to improve transparency and strengthen the clinical relevance of the method, particularly given its intended use for opportunistic screening.
The evaluation metrics do not provide sufficient insight for clinical application. The mean difference and limits of agreement provide some insight into prediction stability for models comparison, but they may also be misleading. The absolute differences between the predicted CPs and the ground truth should also be reported for a more robust evaluation.
The description of the input localiser images is ambiguous. The author should clearly state which data were used as localiser images and whether scouting images were included. If so, the specific scouting sequences should be identified. Since the UK Biobank dataset follows a defined imaging protocol, specifying the exact image sequence used as input would remove any ambiguity regarding the data used for each model.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The author proposed interesting approach for combining patient multimodal data as contrained in the model optimisation.
However, the author did not show sufficient proof/analysis/discussion supporting its main utilisation in opportunistic screening.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The author has adequately justified the limitations of the proposed method. Although the method still requires further development in its current form, it can serve as a foundation for future work aimed at achieving the clinical goal the author set out to address. With revised wording to clarify the method’s limitations, the proposed method provides a solid basis for future work in opportunistic screening.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes C-TRIP, a localizer-centric multimodal contrastive learning framework for estimating cardiac phenotypes from routine MRI localizers. The method first pretrains modality-specific encoders for localizer MRI, ECG, and tabular data using masked data modeling, then aligns the localizer representation with ECG and tabular embeddings through a contrastive objective, and finally predicts cardiac phenotypes using localizer MRI only at inference time.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper addresses a clinically relevant and original problem: estimating imaging-derived cardiac phenotypes from routinely acquired, non-diagnostic localizer MRI.
The localizer-centric tri-modal alignment is an interesting methodological contribution, and the multimodal training with single-modality inference is well motivated.
The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, and the figures support the narrative well, particularly the attention maps and latent-space visualization.
The evaluation is thoughtful. First, the authors evaluate their method against Cine MR (CMR), which is the standard technique for cardiac structure and function measurements. Second, the evaluation goes beyond a single regression metric by reporting mean difference (MD), limits of agreement (LoA), and Pearson correlation.
The results support the main claim that the proposed method is particularly promising for structural phenotypes, while CMR remains strongest for functional phenotypes, which is an important and appropriately nuanced conclusion.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Choice of auxiliary modalities in contrastive alignment: The method aligns localizer MRI with ECG and tabular data, but not with CMR, even though CMR is available in the dataset and is the reference modality for phenotype extraction. Please clarify the rationale for excluding CMR as an auxiliary alignment modality. Since the paper aims to enrich localizer representations, it would be helpful to understand whether this was a deliberate conceptual choice, a fairness consideration, or a practical design decision.
Missing explicit details about technical choices:
Please clarify whether the modality-specific encoders are frozen or fine-tuned during Stage II contrastive alignment. The manuscript says the three pre-trained encoders are fused and optimized with a contrastive loss, but does not clearly specify which components remain trainable.
Please clarify the exact input to the Stage III regression head during training. The manuscript states that phenotype prediction is performed solely from localizers during inference, but no details about its training are provided.
Please provide the architectural details of the supervised baselines used for comparison. The current description of the baselines is too brief to assess whether comparisons are fully controlled.
Potential unfairness in the CMR baseline design: The CMR supervised baseline uses only three short-axis time frames from the middle baso-apical slice. This seems sufficient to provide some functional information, but it may be suboptimal for structural phenotype estimation compared with the localizer input, which includes three consecutive oblique-transverse slices and may provide richer spatial cues despite lower image quality. Please comment on the rationale for this restricted CMR representation and whether it may disadvantage the CMR baseline, especially for structural phenotypes.
Table 2 presentation: Please verify that the boldface and shading in Table 2 consistently correspond to the best absolute MD and tightest LoA, as stated in the caption.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I support a Weak Accept for this paper because it addresses a clinically relevant and original problem: estimating cardiac phenotypes from routinely acquired localizer MRI. The paper proposes an interesting methodology, using localizer-centric multimodal contrastive learning to align localizer, ECG, and tabular representations while keeping localizer-only inference at test time, which is both methodologically meaningful and practically relevant as an opportunistic low-cost screening strategy. The paper is generally clear, well organized, and supported by informative figures and a thoughtful evaluation. The results support the authors’ main claim in a balanced way: the method appears especially promising for structural phenotypes, while cine CMR remains stronger for functional phenotypes, which I find credible. My score is not higher because some important implementation details remain unclear. Additionally, I believe the rationale for excluding CMR as an auxiliary modality in the contrastive learning stage should be clarified, since incorporating the reference imaging modality might plausibly further strengthen the learned representation and improve performance. More importantly, I believe that the restrictive preprocessing of the CMR data for baseline evaluation may make the comparison less convincing for structural phenotype estimation. Overall, I believe the paper makes a worthwhile contribution that would interest the MICCAI audience, but it still has enough methodological ambiguity that Weak Accept is the most appropriate recommendation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal successfully addressed my questions and comments. While some limitations remain, the authors acknowledge them appropriately and provide reasonable clarifications. Overall, the paper remains novel, relevant, and of interest to the MICCAI community, and I support acceptance.
reviews.text_ethics:
Please briefly clarify what is meant by “demographically balanced” train/validation/test splits. A one-sentence explanation would be sufficient.
Please add one sentence describing how the UMAPs were computed, including the source embeddings and any key settings if relevant.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper proposes C-TRIP, a tri-modal contrastive learning framework that aligns 1) localizer MRI (cheap, structural), 2) ECG (temporal), 3) tabular metadata (context) to generate an embedding space that enables predicting cardiac phenotypes (CPs). At inference only localizer MRI are used.
The core idea, that routinely discarded localizer scans should be used for opportunistic screening is potentially clinically meaningful.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper is motivated by a clear and clinically relevant problem, namely the cost and complexity of CMR, and proposes a novel and practical idea of repurposing routinely acquired localizer scans within an opportunistic screening framework during MRI scans. The experimental design is comprehensive, including a range of unimodal and multimodal baselines, targeted ablations such as the tabular leakage setting, and a valuable analysis of performance in low-data regimes, which is often missing in similar work. Additionally, the authors make a meaningful effort toward interpretability, with attention maps demonstrating improved anatomical focus over baselines and UMAP visualizations providing insight into the learned representation space.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Functional Estimation Without Temporal Information is Fundamentally Underdetermined
The proposed method seeks to estimate functional cardiac phenotypes (e.g., EF), which are defined by temporal dynamics between end-diastolic and end-systolic states, from static localizer images that lack phase information. This renders the problem fundamentally underdetermined, as the underlying physiological signal is not directly observable. Consequently, the model must rely on indirect structural correlates and population-level priors, rather than true functional measurement. This limitation is reflected in Fig. 3, where predictions exhibit regression-to-the-mean behavior, particularly for functional metrics. While the approach aims to approximate cine-derived biomarkers, these quantities are intrinsically temporal and cannot be recovered from static inputs. Moreover, even volumetric measures such as EDV and ESV are not directly observable from localizers and are instead inferred via proxy signals, making them fundamentally distinct from cine-derived measurements.
Limited Evaluation on a Healthy-Skewed Cohort Masks Model Limitations
The use of the UK Biobank cohort likely obscures the extent of the method’s limitations. This dataset is predominantly composed of healthy individuals, resulting in a relatively narrow distribution of functional metrics such as EF and a low prevalence of severe pathology. In this setting, regression-to-the-mean behavior is not strongly penalized, as predicting values within the typical range (55–65% EF) yields superficially reasonable performance. Consequently, the reported correlations may overstate the model’s practical utility. Crucially, the model is not evaluated under conditions that reflect clinically relevant variability, and its ability to detect pathological states remains unclear. It is therefore unknown whether the method can reliably identify heart failure or distinguish between preserved and reduced EF, which are central requirements for any screening or diagnostic application.
Excluding ECG at Inference is Poorly Justified
The decision to exclude ECG at inference is not well justified. ECG is a low-cost and widely available modality that directly captures cardiac temporal dynamics, which are essential for functional assessment. By discarding ECG at test time, the model is forced to infer functional phenotypes from static structural images, an inherently limited and ill-posed setting reflected in the regression-to-the-mean behavior observed in Fig. 3.Incorporating ECG at inference would likely improve both performance and clinical relevance; at minimum, this setting should be evaluated.
Recommendations on Overstated Clinical Claims Relative to Evidence
“Enable reliable CP estimation when comprehensive CMR cannot be performed.” This implies clinically actionable, patient-level accuracy, which is not supported given the regression-to-the-mean behavior and limited functional performance; revise to state that the method provides approximate, population-level estimates rather than reliable clinical measurements.
“Accurate functional CPs” and “cardiac health assessment.” These claims overstate capability because functional metrics require temporal information absent at inference, meaning the model estimates proxies rather than true function; reframe explicitly as indirect or proxy estimation of functional phenotypes.
“Opportunistic low-cost screening tool.” This is not substantiated, as no evaluation is performed on diseased populations or using diagnostic metrics such as sensitivity or specificity; limit the claim to exploratory or preliminary assessment and avoid positioning as a screening tool without appropriate validation.
“Not a replacement for CMR.” While cautious in wording, the comparison is made against a reduced CMR baseline (single slice, limited frames), understating the true performance gap to full cine MRI; clarify this limitation and avoid implying proximity to the clinical gold standard.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a novel and interesting embedding-based approach, clearly motivated by addressing a relevant clinical problem, namely the use of routinely acquired localizer MRI for opportunistic cardiac assessment. The experimental design is strong, with well-structured and informative ablation studies, and analysis in low-data regimes, all of which support the technical contribution and make the work of interest to the community.
However, the central claims regarding clinical applicability and reliability (particularly for functional cardiac phenotype estimation and screening) are not fully supported by the presented evidence. The absence of temporal information at inference and the observed regression-to-the-mean behavior raise concerns about the validity of functional predictions, and the exclusion of ECG at test time is not well justified. These limitations do not invalidate the contribution but suggest that the clinical claims should be more carefully framed and substantiated during rebuttal, supporting a weak accept recommendation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper proposes C‑TRIP, a multimodal contrastive learning framework that aligns localizer MRI with ECG and tabular metadata during training to enable cardiac phenotype estimation using localizer MRI alone at inference.
The idea is that localizer scans are routinely acquired but discarded, and could therefore be repurposed for opportunistic cardiac assessment. The method is evaluated on the UK Biobank dataset with extensive baselines, ablations, interpretability analyses, and low-data regime experiments.
A major concern raised is that the estimation of functional cardiac phenotypes from static localizer images is limited due to the absence of temporal information, with observed performance likely driven by regression to population priors on a predominantly healthy UK Biobank cohort. Additionally, there are ambiguities in methodological details pointed out by the reviewers that need to be addressed.
I also struggle to see a real-world clinical scenario in which the proposed method would be used. In routine clinical practice, cardiac MRI examinations are explicitly performed to obtain cine imaging, and cine sequences are acquired in essentially all patients undergoing CMR. Situations in which localizer MRI is available but cine data is not and cardiac phenotyping is required are rare. Can the authors further explain their vision for potential use cases?

All reviewers agree on recommending acceptance after the rebuttal. The limitations and framing should be updated in the final version.

This study proposes a promising and interesting network C-TRIP to predict cardiac phenotypes (CPs) using localizer MRI images, ECG signals, and clinical data. The method consists of three stages: pre-training single-modality encoders, multi-modal contrastive learning, and prediction inference. Main concerns raised by reviewers include the evaluation metrics, application in clinical practice, rational of the techniques used, and some overstated claims. The authors’ response acknowledged them and explained properly.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all the reviewers for valuable feedback.
Major comments (R1, R2, R3)
“Limitations on functional CP estimation & healthy volunteer bias”
-We acknowledge the reduced performance of estimating functional CPs from localizers. Although localizers are static, the model still learns phenotype-relevant temporal relations implicitly through multimodal training with ECG. We’ll state this more clearly
-We agree; including ECG at inference could improve functional CP estimation due to explicit temporal information, and remains a future work as new results are not allowed. Yet, ECG is not temporally aligned or jointly acquired with MRI in UK Biobank, which may limit the benefit of joint inference
-We decided to include only localizers at inference to mimic clinically realistic/limited scenarios with readily-available imaging and to push the limits of the localizer’s capability to estimate CPs. Each localizer acquisition spans ~1.1 seconds, exceeding a typical cardiac cycle (~0.8–1s), and may thus preserve weak phase-averaged cues related to cardiac function. When combined with ECG during training, the cardiac phase information is implicitly learnt by C-TRIP, as shown by increased performance w.r.t. localizer baseline
-Despite the UKBiobank’s healthy volunteer bias (Fry et al., 2017), its scale helps capture robust correlations with ~30% of our dataset exhibiting reduced/mildly reduced LVEF (<55%). Crucially, ablation studies show C-TRIP improves regression-to-the-mean behavior seen in tabular baseline, suggesting it does not rely solely on population averages. Besides, our aim is opportunistic assessment from routine readily-available data, which involves scanning healthy populations to extract any incidental findings
“Clinical claims, real-world use cases, patient diagnosis”
-We will frame our contribution as an opportunistic assessment of cardiac function and structure rather than comprehensive opportunistic screening (OS). While we did not evaluate disease classification tasks, estimating CPs from routinely acquired localizers is still relevant for the initial steps of OS, especially to detect potential signs of cardiac dysfunction. The next steps will include diagnosis with risk classification according to EF and disease detection. Our high accuracy in LVM estimation could especially be useful in detecting LV hypertrophy, a result of coronary artery disease. Other real-world applications may include preliminary assessment in resource-limited settings, more importantly a scenario where the model enables real-time decision-making on the necessity of a full CMR protocol
Minor comments
R1 Metrics
Following the Bland–Altman analysis, we report MD & LoA, which are prioritized in clinical applications (Obuchowski et al., 2015). If allowed, we’ll add MAE, which showed similar trends, to our results
R1 Localizers
The localizers are 3 mid-slices from the 18-slice “AA_Heart_Scout” scan
R2 CMR as auxiliary modality
Excluding CMR was a deliberate choice to test whether low-cost and non-imaging modalities (ECG/tabular) could enrich localizers. We’ll state that incorporating CMR during pre-training is future work, as previous work proved that CMR-enriched ECG representations can predict CPs (Turgut et al., 2025)
R2 Implementation
Stage II: Encoders are fully fine-tuned end-to-end
Stage III: the regression head is trained using only localizer embeddings extracted via the Stage II aligned encoder
Baselines use the same regression head as C-TRIP, but are trained from scratch without contrastive learning
R2 CMR baseline
The CMR baseline uses three neighboring SA time frames from the same slice while keeping the number of input channels identical across all models for architectural fairness & computational simplicity
R2 Formatting
We’ll fix Table 2
Demographically balanced: train/val/test splits have statistically similar distributions of age, sex, LVEF
UMAPs used L2-normalized joint embeddings, cosine dist., 15 neighbors, min_dist=0.1

title: OPS: One-Shot Point Prompted Semantics-Aware Learning for Medical Image Registration
abstract: Unsupervised learning is the dominant paradigm in medical image registration, primarily due to its straightforward deployment and independence from labor-intensive manual annotations. However, its optimization objective fails to differentiate between semantically distinct anatomical structures and background regions, resulting in suboptimal registration performance. To introduce semantic priors into unsupervised registration with minimal annotation cost, we propose OPS, a One-shot Point prompt-driven Semantics-aware registration framework. Leveraging the powerful semantic clustering capabilities of the pre-trained vision foundation model DINOv3, OPS requires only extremely sparse point prompts (i.e., one point per organ) on a single reference image slice to extract global semantic anchors. These anchors are then propagated across the entire unlabeled dataset to compute feature similarities with the DINOv3 embeddings of each image volume, thereby localizing semantically consistent regions. This process enables the offline generation of dense semantic similarity maps, which serve as nearly annotation-free anatomical localization priors. Subsequently, we integrate these anatomical localization priors into the registration learning through a dual mechanism: (1) semantic feature embedding to modulate the feature representations, and (2) semantics-aware loss optimization to spatially re-weight the similarity loss, enabling semantic guidance for the registration learning. Comprehensive experiments on two datasets demonstrate that the proposed method enhances the registration performance of state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at https://github.com/xiehousheng/OPS.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes OPS, a one-shot point prompt-driven framework for incorporating semantic priors into unsupervised medical image registration. Specifically, it leverages a pre-trained vision foundation model (DINOv3) to propagate extremely sparse point prompts (one point per organ on a single reference slice) into dense semantic similarity maps across the entire dataset. These maps serve as anatomical localization priors and are integrated into the registration process through both semantic feature embedding and a semantics-aware loss re-weighting mechanism. This design enables the introduction of semantic guidance into unsupervised registration with minimal annotation cost.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The proposed approach introduces semantic awareness by leveraging extremely sparse annotations (one point per organ) on a single reference slice. This is particularly interesting because it significantly reduces annotation cost while still enabling the model to capture anatomically meaningful correspondences, effectively bridging the gap between unsupervised and weakly-supervised registration. 
2.Use of a pre-trained foundation model (DINOv3) to propagate sparse point prompts into dense semantic similarity maps across the dataset. This effectively leverages the semantic clustering capability of foundation models for registration, avoiding the need for dense supervision.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The proposed method relies on extremely sparse point prompts (one point per organ) to construct semantic priors. Could the authors clarify the strategy for selecting these points (e. g. , anatomical center, boundary, or random selection)? In addition, how sensitive is the method to the spatial location and number of selected points? While a basic robustness analysis is provided, a more systematic evaluation (e. g. , varying point locations or using multiple points per structure) would help better understand the stability and generalizability of the proposed approach. 
2.The method assumes that semantic anchors extracted from a single reference slice can generalize across the entire dataset. Could the authors provide further analysis or visualization to demonstrate how well these anchors transfer across subjects with anatomical variability?
3.Additional visualization of the generated semantic similarity maps would help to better assess their quality and interpretability, particularly in challenging cases.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper proposes a novel and practical approach to incorporate semantic priors into unsupervised registration using sparse point prompts and a pre-trained foundation model. Compared to prior work, such as DINO-Reg, which directly uses DINO features for registration, the proposed method introduces an explicit semantic prior construction mechanism by propagating one-shot point prompts into dense semantic similarity maps. This design enables more targeted and interpretable semantic guidance with minimal annotation cost.
The method is well-motivated and shows consistent improvements across datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness and generalizability. Although the sensitivity to point selection could be further analyzed, this does not significantly affect the overall contribution.
Overall, the work provides a meaningful extension over existing foundation model-based registration approaches and supports a positive recommendation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a semantics-aware framework for unsupervised medical image registration. Its main contribution is to use extremely sparse point prompts on a single reference slice to extract DINOv3-based semantic anchors, propagate them across the dataset to generate dense semantic similarity maps, and incorporate these priors into registration through semantic feature embedding and semantics-aware loss re-weighting.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper addresses a clearly motivated problem, namely the semantic blindness of conventional unsupervised registration methods that rely only on global image similarity.
2.The proposed one-shot prompting setup is practically appealing, as it attempts to introduce semantic priors with very limited manual annotation cost.
3.The overall framework is coherent and well organized. The generation of semantic similarity maps and their integration through semantic feature embedding and semantics-aware loss optimization form a consistent pipeline.
4.The empirical results are reasonably strong. The method improves both DSC and HD95 over the compared backbones, and the ablation study supports the contribution of each component.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The workflow is practically appealing, but the technical novelty is somewhat less convincing than the framing suggests. In particular, the method does not introduce a fundamentally new registration formulation; rather, it builds a dataset-wide semantic prior from sparse prompts using frozen DINOv3 features, and then incorporates this prior through relatively standard feature embedding and loss re-weighting steps. As a result, the main novelty seems to lie more in the prompt-to-prior workflow than in a clearly new registration mechanism.1
2.This concern is also reflected in the ablation study. On the abdominal dataset, adding SFE alone improves DSC only from 58.52 to 59.39, whereas SLO alone raises it to 65.42, which is already close to the full model at 66.54.A similar pattern is observed on the hippocampus dataset. This suggests that much of the gain may come from semantic loss weighting itself, while the additional benefit of the prompt-derived feature embedding is comparatively modest.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I gave this paper a Weak Reject because, although the problem is meaningful and the workflow is practically appealing, I was not fully convinced that the technical contribution is strong enough for acceptance. The proposed one-shot prompting setup is interesting, but the main novelty seems to lie more in generating a dataset-wide semantic prior from sparse prompts than in a clearly new registration formulation. In addition, the ablation results suggest that most of the empirical gain comes from the semantics-aware loss re-weighting, while the additional contribution of semantic feature embedding is comparatively modest. Overall, the method is technically sound and reasonably effective, but I felt that the paper would be stronger with a clearer demonstration of what is uniquely enabled by the prompt-derived prior beyond semantic loss weighting.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Most of the concerns have been adequately addressed, and the practicality of the proposed workflow, in particular, represents a significant contribution. Although the efficient point-prompting methodology could be further strengthened by more detailed technical analysis of the SFE and SLO components and a more comprehensive experimental design, these remaining limitations do not substantially weaken the paper’s overall contribution.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper proposes OPS, a framework that introduces semantic guidance into unsupervised medical image registration with minimal annotation. Its main contributions are:
One-Shot Point Prompting: Leveraging DINOv3, it generates dense semantic similarity maps for an entire dataset using only one point per organ on a single reference slice, avoiding costly full segmentation masks.
Dual Integration Mechanism: It incorporates these maps via Semantic Feature Embedding and Semantics-aware Loss Optimization to explicitly guide feature learning and spatial alignment.
Experiments show OPS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised methods on abdominal CT and hippocampus MRI datasets.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper introduces a highly efficient data usage strategy, generating dense semantic priors for an entire dataset from just one point per organ on a single reference slice. This drastically reduces annotation costs compared to traditional weakly-supervised methods requiring full 3D masks, enabling semantic-aware registration on vast unlabeled clinical datasets.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The core reliance on DINOv3 feature similarity assumes consistent feature distributions across images. This breaks down in multi-modal registration (e.g., CT-to-MRI), where intensity and texture differences cause the same organ to have vastly different feature embeddings. The method lacks a mechanism for modality-invariant alignment, severely limiting its clinical scope.
In mono-modal settings, the advantage over existing pseudo-labeling strategies (e.g., using pre-trained segmentation models like nnU-Net to generate coarse masks without any user input) is unclear. The complexity of integrating a massive foundation model may not justify the marginal gain over simply running an off-the-shelf segmenter to get richer spatial priors.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

While the proposed method is technically sound, its practical value needs further clarification.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper received mixed recommendations from the reviewers, including one Weak Reject and two Weak Accepts.
The paper addresses deformable registration using point prompts and a pre-trained vision foundation model, and demonstrates promising results on two datasets. At the same time, the reviewers identified several substantive concerns, including an unclear point selection strategy (R1), unconvincing support for the claimed semantic anchors and the reliance on DINOv3 feature similarity (R1, R3), limited qualitative results (R1), the incremental nature of the methodological contribution (R2), marginal gains from the prompt-derived feature embeddings (R2), and an unclear advantage over a nnU-Net-plus-registration pipeline (R3).
Overall, the paper shows merit in its methodology and in its use of vision foundation models for image registration, and the meta-reviewer therefore recommends that it proceed to rebuttal. The authors are encouraged to focus their response on the major concerns outlined above.

The paper proposes a method that combines DINOv3-based semantic clustering with a single-slice, single-point prompting scheme to construct a dataset-wide dense semantic similarity map, which is subsequently integrated into an unsupervised registration framework through SFE and SLO.
Following the rebuttal, all reviewers expressed overall positive assessments. In particular, Reviewer 2 explicitly recognized that the practicality of the annotation-efficient workflow itself represents a meaningful contribution and accordingly revised the recommendation to Accept; Reviewer 3 also upgraded the rating to Accept. While the lack of a comparison with nnU-Net remains a minor weakness, it does not substantially undermine the core technical contribution or the empirical validity of the paper.
Based on the post-rebuttal discussion and the overall reviewer consensus, I recommend Accept.

This paper proposes to use sparse point prompts to create feature similarity maps using Dinov3 and to incorporate those maps in an unsupervised registration algorithm. After rebuttal, all reviewers agree that the method is technically sound and that the main concerns have been addressed in the rebuttal. There are some remaining concerns about the experimental design and analysis, but the strengths of the paper outweigh its weakness.

Following the rebuttal phase, two of the three reviewers issued a final decision of “Accept,” while the third reviewer did not respond. However, this reviewer’s initial score was “Weak Accept.” Consequently, the overall assessment of the paper is positive (Accept), and it is therefore recommended for acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback and for recognizing that our method enables more targeted and interpretable semantic guidance with minimal annotation cost.
[R2] Clarification on Technical Novelty:
We thank the reviewer for acknowledging the practicality of our workflow. While we do not introduce a new registration architecture, our novelty lies in establishing a point prompted semantics-aware learning that advances unsupervised registration learning at minimal annotation cost. This is done by using extremely sparse point prompts to derive feature similarity maps, and then integrate these maps into the registration learning process via a dual mechanism comprising SFE and SLO. Leveraging the strong generalization capability of DINOv3, our method improves performance on unsupervised registration, which is a clear advantage, and the experimental results substantiate its efficacy. Moreover, our method is plug-and-play and offers users explicit controllability over the registration learning process: by simply altering the point prompts, clinicians can dynamically modulate the network’s attention toward specific anatomical targets during training, thereby enabling customized registration.
[R2] Ablation Study on SFE and SLO:
The ablation results in Table 2 are consistent with our design, and the two components are complementary to each other. SLO directly reshapes the supervision signal, explicitly forcing the optimizer at the training stage to focus on aligning semantically relevant regions, thereby contributing more substantially to performance gains. SFE injects semantic awareness into feature representations at both training and inference stages. This explains why SFE continues to enhance registration performance even beyond SLO.
[R3] Advantage Over Fully Supervised Pseudo-labeling: 
We would like to clarify the difference between OPS and pseudo-labeling schemes. OPS targets unsupervised registration learning, where the segmentation annotations required by model nnU-Net is hard to obtain and OPS needs only a one-shot interaction. Second, segmentation models are strictly constrained by the organ categories and image domains seen during training, often failing on unseen domains or structures. In contrast, OPS builds on DINOv3’s general-purpose visual representations, requires no organ-specific or modality-specific pre-training.
[R1] Prompt Selection Strategy:
For each target organ, we randomly pick a single point prompt within the organ, without requiring precise localization. Table 3 quantitatively demonstrates robust performance under varying random point locations. While multi-point prompting is a good idea, it would enable additional annotation cost, which may be not optimal in a clinical environment.
[R3] Adaptation to Multi-modal Registration:
In fact, OPS naturally accommodates cross-modal scenarios. For example, in CT-MRI registration, only one point prompt targeting the same anatomical structure needs to be provided on each of the CT and MRI reference slices. The CT anchor is then propagated exclusively within CT dataset, while the MRI anchor is propagated exclusively within MRI dataset, thereby generating semantic similarity maps for the same anatomical structure in CT and MRI data to ensure compatibility with OPS.
[R1] Cross-subject Robustness and Additional Visualization:
The cross-subject generalization is quantitatively validated by our existing experiments. Substantial anatomical variability (organ size, shape, position) exists among the 54 abdominal and 260 hippocampus subjects in the datasets. Supported by DINOv3’s strong cross-image semantic consistency, anchors propagate stably across subjects via feature similarity, producing reliable similarity maps under large anatomical variation. In the upper-right corner of Fig. 2, we provide examples of similarity maps, where it can be observed that similarity maps from different samples capture consistent organ-level semantic information.

title: Optimal Steps for Fast Diffeomorphic Shape Registration
abstract:
This paper presents a fast, learning-free registration method tailored to clinical constraints. While shape registration is fundamental to medical imaging, existing techniques often force a trade-off between computational scalability and strict topology preservation. Current diffeomorphic methods are either computationally expensive or demand extensive pre-processing, such as training neural networks on large datasets. This renders them impractical for clinical studies, which often rely on limited cohorts. Image-based methods also require large memory banks to process high-resolution data, while surface-based approaches have received less attention in the deep learning era. In this context, we propose a principled registration algorithm that alternates between a feature-aware matching scheme, a conjugate gradient solver and a diffeomorphic shooting step.
Our pipeline can handle point clouds, curves and surface meshes. It is compatible with clinical workflows and can register a pair of shapes sampled with 10k points each in less than a second, without landmarks or supervision. We demonstrate consistent results on several anatomical structures and showcase the efficiency of our method by computing an atlas from hundreds of complex vertebra scans in a few minutes. Upon publication, our code will be released under the permissive MIT license at: scikit-shapes.github.io.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents a fast, learning-free method for diffeomorphic registration of point clouds, curves, and surface meshes. The method combines feature-aware matching, regularized displacement estimation with a conjugate-gradient solver, and an LDDMM-like diffeomorphic shooting step. The stated goal is to achieve topology-preserving registration at a speed compatible with clinical workflows.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper addresses a highly practical problem: fast, robust, topology-preserving shape registration without requiring large training datasets. This is very relevant to clinical shape modeling workflows, especially for anatomical surfaces where volumetric deep-learning registration may be memory-intensive or require substantial training data.
The method is technically motivated. It combines ideas from non-rigid ICP, coherent point drift, and LDDMM . The regularization step is described clearly, including the kernel normalization, local loss matrices, conjugate-gradient formulation, and preconditioning. 
The empirical results are strong. On the VerSe vertebra experiments, the method achieves better Chamfer distance and HD95 than both VoxelMorph and Deformetrica while being around 40× faster than Deformetrica.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The baseline comparison is limited. VoxelMorph is a volumetric learning-based method and may not be the strongest competitor for surface/point-cloud registration. Deformetrica is a relevant diffeomorphic baseline, but the paper would be stronger with comparisons against CPD, robust optimal transport point-cloud registration, functional maps, non-rigid ICP variants, and recent neural or geometric surface-registration methods.
The paper claims strict topological consistency, but the evidence is not fully sufficient. LDDMM-style shooting can define diffeomorphic flows in continuous settings, but the implementation is on sampled point clouds/meshes, and the paper does not provide a formal proof or a direct measurement of self-intersections, triangle inversions, or Jacobian positivity. The reported log-Jacobian variance is useful but does not by itself establish topology preservation. 
There is a slight inconsistency in the presentation: the abstract says the method works “without landmarks, pre-alignment, or supervision,” yet the method section includes a RANSAC-ICP affine pre-alignment and anisotropic bounding-box scaling. This is not necessarily a problem, but the claim should be revised. 
The experiments are largely focused on vertebrae. Vertebrae are challenging and clinically relevant, but additional anatomical structures with different topology and partial-overlap conditions would strengthen the generality claim. The authors acknowledge partial overlap as future work, which is important because many clinical surfaces are truncated or contain segmentation defects. 
The computational complexity remains quadratic due to kernel matrix-vector products. The paper reports good runtimes for 10k and 40k points, but it is unclear how the method scales to hundreds of thousands of points or to dense multi-organ atlases.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This is a practical, and well-written contribution. The speed and accuracy results are very good, and the method is attractive for clinical shape analysis. The main concerns are the limited baseline set and the need for stronger evidence supporting the topology-preservation claim.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper proposes a new algorithm for shape registration, where the points are represented as point clouds.
First point correspondences are found by creating high-dimensional features followed by nearest-neighbors.
Then an optimization problem is solved to smooth out the map
reviews.text_strengths:
Excellent speed up compared to the state of the art and slightly better accuracy
Elegant algorithm, robust
No neural networks, a big plus for robustness and efficiency.
reviews.text_weaknesses: None
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Excellent paper. Well written, nice algorithms, GPU implementation, good results, smart ideas. 
A breath of fresh air.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a learning-free registration method for anatomical structures, addressing a key gap in the literature: the need for computationally efficient approaches that do not require large training datasets, a constraint that aligns well with clinical settings. Rather than operating on image-based representations, which tend to be memory-intensive, the method works with point cloud and mesh representations of anatomical shapes. Registration is achieved through an iterative pipeline consisting of a matching step, a linear solver, and a diffeomorphic shooting step, which progressively aligns a source shape to a target. Experiments on two datasets demonstrate that the method achieves registration performance comparable to classical LDDMM while matching the speed typically associated with deep learning approaches. The authors further validate the method’s versatility by demonstrating its applicability to atlas estimation.
reviews.text_strengths:
The most notable strength of the paper is its demonstrated combination of high registration accuracy and computational speed, which is particularly valuable in clinical settings where data is scarce, annotation is expensive, and precision is critical. Unlike deep learning methods that require large training datasets, rarely available in medical imaging, this learning-free approach sidesteps that requirement entirely while still matching the speed advantages typically associated with learned methods. 
Beyond raw performance, the paper makes a compelling case that thoughtfully assembling well-established techniques from the shape optimisation literature, such as normalized kernel matrix from diffusion operators and the LDDMM-like diffeomorphic shooting, an close the speed gap with learned methods without sacrificing rigour or interpretability. 
The paper is also well-written and the method is easy to follow, which makes it straightforward to understand and build upon.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The most significant weakness of the paper is its reliance on spatial pre-alignment, which surfaces in two places: the affine initialisation that depends on extrinsic FPFH features, and the exclusive use of 3D coordinates in the two finest scales of the multiscale scheme.
This raises concerns about the method’s sensitivity to the initial alignment and scale of the input shapes, even when anisotropic normalisation is applied. An ablation study removing the pre-alignment step would have strengthened the paper considerably, as it would clarify how much of the registration performance is attributable to the core method versus the initialisation.
Related to this, the reliance on 3D coordinates as features implicitly assumes that the source and target shapes share similar topology — an assumption that does not always hold in clinical practice. A straightforward counterexample is a vascular tree where one branch is absent in the source but present in the target.
The authors do acknowledge partial overlaps as a limitation, but given how frequently topological mismatches arise in anatomical shape analysis, this deserves more explicit treatment.
Finally, a more minor but noteworthy issue concerns the atlas estimation experiment: since the constructed atlas inherits the topology of the chosen template, the result is inherently biased by that choice. This is not discussed in the paper and would be worth at least acknowledging in the limitations section.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Despite some sensitivity to spatial pre-alignment, this paper addresses a genuine and practically important gap in the literature, a registration method that is both fast and accurate without requiring training data, making it well-suited to the realities of clinical practice. It would be a valuable contribution to the MICCAI community.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text:
The three reviewers accepted the paper with ratings ranging from Strong Accept to Weak Accept. The confidence from two of the accept reviewers is “Confident but not absolutely certain (3) “ while the Weak Accept reviewer is “Very Confident (4)”.
While the reviewers are overall very positive, I have some reservations regarding the level of methodological novelty. The proposed approach appears to combine previously published components rather than introducing fundamentally new techniques. In addition, the empirical comparison, particularly against VoxelMorph, may not be entirely appropriate due to the need to convert point sets into segmentations, which may result into the shown low accuracy.
That said, reviewers highlight the solid experimental validation and competitive performance with respect to state-of-the-art methods such as Deformetrica, and find the contribution valuable for the community. I lean towards acceptance, considering the overall positive evaluations and the soundness of the approach, although I agree more with Rv1 comments and Rv3 concerns.
I would suggest the authors to improve the camera ready reflecting in the manuscript responses to the main comments provided in this review.

author_feedback_text:
We want to thank the reviewers and AC for their reviews. We address the main points below, the camera-ready will reflect these clarifications.
Topology preservation (R1). Our shooting Eq. (8) is the LDDMM Hamiltonian flow of Beg-Miller-Trouvé-Younes [4]. With our exponential kernel k(x,y) = exp(-||x−y||/r), the function k(·, q_i) is globally Lipschitz on R^3 with constant 1/r, so the velocity field v_t(x) = Σ_i k(x, q_i(t)) p_i(t) is Lipschitz uniformly in t ∈ [0,1]. By Cauchy-Lipschitz, the flow ODE has unique solutions and φ_t : R^3 → R^3 is a topology-preserving homeomorphism. The kernel normalization Eq. (4) plays an essential role: the spectrum of the normalized kernel matrix is bounded in [0,1] (Kessler-Magnet-Feydy [18, Thm 4.4]), so the kinetic energy is controlled, ||v||² = p^⊤K p ≤ ||p||². At the discrete level, our adaptive Euler step constrains dt so that ||q_i(t+dt) − q_i(t)|| ≤ ℓ, where ℓ is the local sampling length: each step is too small to invert a triangle.
Pre-alignment (R1). The RANSAC-ICP + anisotropic bounding-box scaling is fully automatic and requires no landmarks, supervision, or template-specific tuning, which is what the abstract claims. It is standard procedure in image registration and LDDMM literature where the data can come from different scanners and be aligned differently. This step is applied identically to every baseline. Deformetrica gives very poor results without it. We will modify the abstract wording regarding this aspect.
Baselines (R1, Meta). VoxelMorph is the canonical learning-based reference for medical image registration and Deformetrica is the canonical LDDMM reference. A primary objective of our paper is to demonstrate the massive computational speedup our method offers over classical LDDMM approaches. As shown in our experiments, our approach achieves approximately a 40x speedup over Deformetrica. Furthermore, it accomplishes this while delivering strictly better surface alignment metrics (Chamfer and Hausdorff distances) and preserving better topological integrity, as evidenced by a lower log-Jacobian variance. Comparisons with CPD, robust OT, and non-rigid ICP variants are highly relevant and are intended for extensions of this work.
Anatomical scope (R1, R3). The paper already evaluates two topologically distinct and complex families: 757 vertebrae and 54 lung vascular trees. We are currently partnering with clinicians on ongoing experiments on different datasets to extend the applications of our work.
FPFH and 3D-coordinate matching (R3). The coarse scales (r_1, r_2) use 3D coordinates and FPFH features for robust long-range matching, and the fine scales (r_3, r_4) turn off FPFH and keep 3D coordinates only because by that stage the source already lies within the local convergence basin of the target. This is a multiscale schedule, not a structural assumption of similar topology.
Partial overlap (R1, R3). We identified this limitation in the relevant section of the article and are currently working on it.
Atlas template bias (R3). We will add this to the limitations.
Quadratic complexity (R1). The O(N^2) bottleneck is the kernel mat-vec inside CG and the Hamiltonian shooting. FGT-like schemes and the Giga-scale Kernel Matrix-Vector Multiplication on GPU of Hu et al. are potential lines of inquiry but lack well maintained GPU implementations to date.
Novelty (Meta). A ~40x speedup over Deformetrica at strictly better CD/HD95 is the main claim of our paper. The enabling ingredients are, to our knowledge, new in point-based LDDMM: (i) a Gauss-Newton formulation on a normalized kernel, instead of the quasi-Newton iteration of Deformetrica [5], (ii) the analytic 3x3 Block-Jacobi preconditioner Eq. (7), with closed-form eigenvectors, (iii) CG early termination at tolerance r/10.Combined, these reduce the inner CG loop from 20-30 iterations to 1-5.

title: OPVD: On-Policy Chain-of-Visual-Thought Distillation for Medical Reasoning
abstract:
Recent advancements in enhancing the medical reasoning capabilities of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have predominantly relied on rule-based reinforcement learning (RL) paradigms. However, such approaches are often constrained by their dependence on \textit{sparse answer-level rewards}, which fail to provide dense supervisory signals for intermediate reasoning steps, and by the \textit{computational inefficiency inherent} in requiring extensive sampling for policy exploration. 
To address these limitations, we propose \textit{On-Policy Chain-of-Visual-Thought Distillation} (OPVD) for vision-language medical reasoning, a concise yet efficient framework designed to imbue VLMs with robust medical reasoning abilities. OPVD introduces an interleaved vision-language Chain-of-Visual-Thought (CoVT) mechanism to construct reliable and granular reasoning trajectories. Unlike previous approaches, our OPVD leverages these trajectories to perform token-level dense supervision, effectively distilling multi-modal CoVT knowledge into the model via an on-policy self-distillation strategy where the teacher and student share the same policy model. This eliminates the need for external teachers or costly sampling procedures while maximizing data efficiency. 
Extensive experiments conducted on the public multi-modal medical reasoning dataset demonstrate that OPVD remarkably outperforms existing models trained via standard supervised fine-tuning and RL methods, establishing a new state-of-the-art in efficient and accurate medical visual reasoning.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces On-Policy Visual CoT Distillation (OPVD), a framework for training vision-language models to perform medical reasoning. The method eliminates multi-sampling that is usually required for RL-based methods. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of their method on various medical visual reasoning tasks.
reviews.text_strengths:

2.The method outperforms bigger zero-shot models as well as other models trained using RL, setting a new state-of-the-art.
3.The paper is generally well written and easy to follow.

1.Missing comparison with RL-based approaches: The paper states that OPVD significantly outperforms SFT and RL methods. Including comparisons with RL-optimized Qwen-VL models would help support this claim.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes OPVD, an on-policy self-distillation framework for medical vision-language reasoning. The key idea is to replace sparse reward-based RL supervision with token-level dense supervision derived from Chain-of-Visual-Thought trajectories. The method uses a teacher branch with privileged answer information and an iterative crop-and-zoom mechanism to construct higher-quality reasoning paths, which are then distilled into a student branch under standard inference conditions. The paper shows that this approach can improve both reasoning quality and training efficiency compared with standard supervised fine-tuning and recent RL-based medical reasoning methods
reviews.text_strengths: First, the paper addresses a relevant and timely problem in medical VLM reasoning, namely the inefficiency of RL-based training caused by sparse rewards and repeated sampling. The proposed use of token-level dense supervision through self-distillation is a meaningful conceptual contribution. Second, the method is clearly motivated and reasonably designed: the combination of privileged-answer teacher guidance, interleaved visual-text reasoning, and crop-and-zoom refinement is intuitive and well aligned with medical image understanding. Third, the empirical results are strong for the presented setup. OPVD consistently outperforms SFT baselines and also surpasses recent RL-based methods while requiring fewer sampling steps, which suggests a favorable efficiency-performance tradeoff. Finally, the paper includes ablations on the visual reasoning component and the answer-weighting term, which helps support the importance of the proposed design choices.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The main weakness is that the experimental validation is still relatively limited. The model is trained on only 2,000 MRI samples and evaluated on 900 samples across MRI, CT, and X-ray, which may not be sufficient to establish broad generalizability for medical reasoning. In addition, the comparison setting may not be fully controlled, since the paper states that the exact training splits of MedVLM-R1 were unavailable and the authors constructed their own subsets, making fairness of comparison somewhat uncertain. Another concern is that the teacher branch uses privileged ground-truth answers during trajectory construction, which is effective for training but also raises questions about how much of the improvement comes from richer supervision rather than improved reasoning alone. The paper would also benefit from more extensive analysis, such as additional benchmarks, more diverse modalities/tasks, stronger ablations, and evaluation beyond multiple-choice accuracy.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

My overall assessment is based on a positive view of the paper’s core idea and empirical performance, tempered by some concerns about evaluation breadth. I think the proposed OPVD framework is interesting because it offers a practical alternative to RL-based medical reasoning by using dense token-level supervision and an intuitive visual refinement mechanism.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text:
Although the three reviewers are rather positive about this paper, they raised some concerns about the experiment and evaluation design. As the meta-reviewer, I would like to see their responses to the following concerns:
1.Some of the reviewers have concerns about exps and results: the fairness of the comparison (different training split), the marginal improvement (1-2%), failure analysis, the ablation of richer supervision vas reasoning alone etc.
2.The evaluation pipeline seems to borrow a lot from the paper MedVLM-R1.It is acceptable for MedVLM-R1 to only evaluate on the final answer accuracy since it is one of the first works to carry out VLM reasoning. But since the field of reasoning has advanced significantly and the paper’s highlight is its CoVT, it is now also necessary to verify the intermediate process, i.e., whether the reasoning chain is plausible.

This paper has a clear motivation, while concerns of the comparison fairness and the evaluation pipeline are not well addressed, and the performance is still a bit too marginal. This paper is on the borderline.
All reviewers were satistfied with the rebuttal. The authors should address the remaining concerns in the camera-ready version.

The reviewers are consistently supportive of the paper. OPVD offers a practical alternative to RL-based medical reasoning through on-policy visual-thought distillation, and the empirical results are viewed positively. Some concerns about evaluation breadth and novelty remain, but they do not undermine the main contribution.

author_feedback_text:
Rebuttal
R1Q1 & R3Q1: Generalizability.
We extended evaluation to the large-scale PMC-VQA dataset, including 227k samples, using Qwen2-VL-2B backbone. OPVD achieves a score of 48.7, consistently outperforming other competitors like Med-R1-2B (47.4) and MedVLM-R1-2B (47.5). Crucially, our main experiments train exclusively on MRI data while testing on CT and X-ray, demonstrating robust OOD generalization. This cross-modality and cross-benchmark consistency confirms that OPVD learns transferable, domain-agnostic reasoning patterns rather than overfitting to dataset-specific biases.
R1Q2 & R2Q4: Computation and sampling num.
Toward Qwen2-VL-2B as the base model, OPVD totally requires only ~0.5 EFLOPs during training, which is approximately 6× lower than the ~3.3 EFLOPs consumed by rule-based RL baselines.
The ‘‘sampling num.’’ in Table 1 denotes forward times per training iteration. OPVD requires only 2 forward passes, whereas RL baselines need 4-16 rollouts.
AC-Q1 & AC-Q2 & R1Q3 & R2Q3: Teacher quality and failure analysis.
Teacher trajectories are validated via clinical priors, and Fig. 2 show the cases of the reliable reasoning process of OPVD. Failures mainly occur in complex OOD X-rays where pathologies are obscured, highlighting a need for future omni-modality training recipe.
AC-Q1 & R2Q1: RL-based Qwen comparison.
To ensure a strictly fair comparison, we fine-tuned Qwen2-VL-2B with GRPO under identical training budgets, data splits, learning rates, and batch configurations. Despite matched computational resources, the GRPO baseline achieves an average accuracy of 76.41, falling significantly short of OPVD’s 80.96.This gap stems from fundamental optimization differences: GRPO relies on sparse, answer-level rewards that provide weak gradient signals for intermediate steps, often leading to reward hacking. In contrast, OPVD’s token-level distillation directly aligns the student’s generative distribution with a clinically validated teacher trajectory at each decoding step, enabling precise, dense correction that is substantially more data-efficient and stable for medical reasoning.
AC-Q1 & R2Q2: Conservative framing of gains.
We will revise the claims to conservatively frame the 1-2% improvement in the manuscript. To rigorously validate reliability, we conducted paired statistical tests across multiple random seeds, yielding a p-value of 0.004, smaller than 0.01, when comparing OPVD against the strongest baseline (ViTAR), confirming the improvement is statistically significant rather than due to random variance.
AC-Q1 & R3Q2: Fair comparison.
To guarantee comparison fairness, we re-implemented and re-evaluated all cited baselines using a standardized protocol: identical train/validation/test splits, consistent image preprocessing, unified hyperparameter search spaces, and the same evaluation metrics and random seeds. Under these strictly controlled conditions, OPVD consistently maintains a performance advantage, reinforcing the reproducibility of our findings.
AC-Q1 & R3Q3: Analysis on privileged prior.
To isolate the impact of privileged priors, upon Qwen2-VL-2B, we trained standard SFT and RL baselines directly on the high-quality teacher-generated CoVT trajectories (i.e., using the same privileged reasoning paths as OPVD’s distillation targets). Despite access to identical prior knowledge, both baselines underperform significantly, achieving 64.29 (SFT) and 73.83 (RL) versus OPVD’s 80.96.This clear gap demonstrates that OPVD’s advantage does not stem merely from richer supervision, but from its dynamic on-policy distillation mechanism.
R3Q4: Beyond MC accuracy and benchmarks.
We plan to extend our research on report generation and more diverse benchmarks in future work. The interleaved CoVT architecture is inherently well-suited for these extensions, as it already produces structured, interpretable reasoning chains that can be seamlessly adapted to free-text generation.

title: OR-Action: Multi-Role Video Understanding with Fine-Grained Actions
abstract: Fine-grained understanding of operating room (OR) activity could enable workflow-aware assistance, yet remains difficult due to clutter, occlusions, and limited sensing. The prevailing approach to model this environment is scene graphs as an interpretable representation of OR interactions. Converting their frame-wise relational predictions into temporally extended, fine-grained actions however, is challenging without explicit temporal modeling. To enable a principled temporal evaluation of current OR understanding methods, we introduce the first action-centric benchmark built on a publicly available ego-exocentric OR dataset by defining a fine-grained, multi-role action taxonomy and generating dense action segments via distillation from ground-truth scene graph state changes. Experiments on this benchmark show that current scene graph prediction methods struggle to model temporal structure, even when adding explicit modeling through Graph Neural Networks. We therefore introduce a vision-only temporal model that outperforms graph-based methods significantly when using all available egocentric video as input. Building on this model we also introduce a novel multi- to single-view feature alignment strategy that improves single-view performance on multi-role action recognition, mitigating the need for extensive egocentric video capture. Benchmark and code will be released upon acceptance.
subject_areas: Surgery -> Surgical Skills, Workflow & Team Dynamics

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces OR-Action, a fine-grained, multi-role temporal action benchmark for operating room (OR) understanding, constructed by mapping scene graph annotations from EgoExOR into dense action segments using rule-based heuristics. In addition, the authors propose a vision-only multi-role temporal model based on a video foundation encoder and a multi-view-to-single-view feature alignment strategy. Experiments show that vision-based temporal modelling outperforms scene-graph-based pipelines on this benchmark.
reviews.text_strengths: External OR understanding is highly relevant and challenging due to occlusions, multi-actor interactions, and temporal complexity. OR-Action provides a new evaluation setting for fine-grained, multi-role temporal actions, which is valuable for the community. The paper highlights a significant gap between scene graph prediction and temporal action understanding. The vision-only model is simple, scalable, and benefits from strong pretrained video representations. The teacher–student alignment is relevant for real-world deployment where multi-view data is limited.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Evaluation unfairly disadvantages scene-graph approaches: The benchmark assesses scene-graph models using predicted graphs fed through a rule-mapping pipeline, which can lead to error propagation and misrepresent the limitations of the scene-graph paradigm. 
Comparisons with graph-based baselines are imbalanced: the vision model benefits from strong pretraining, whereas the graph-temporal baselines are simpler. The omission of stronger or hybrid alternatives weakens any comparative claims. 
Short temporal windows limit reasoning: Modelling only ≈16s fails to capture long-term procedural dependencies, restricting the ability to analyse complex OR actions. 
Errors and generalisation remain unexplored: The paper lacks per-class breakdown, detailed failure analysis, and robustness checks across roles or viewpoints.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper introduces an important benchmark but lacks methodological novelty. Heuristic label generation and imbalanced evaluation weaken claims against scene-graph approaches. Conclusions require caution; the benchmark contribution adn reported result justifies weak acceptance despite these flaws.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper presents a new benchmark for ego-centric activity recognition in the OR by extending the public EgoExOR with 78 action classes. Additionally, a vision-only method is provided that outperforms graph-scene-based methods.
