reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: After carefully reading the authors’ rebuttal, I am maintaining my score of a Weak Reject. In their response, the authors presented a substantial amount of new quantitative data, which is promising but against the rule. Evaluating the paper strictly on the contents of the original manuscript, my core concerns remain unresolved. The original submission lacks the necessary multi-cohort validation and contemporary baselines to substantiate its claims of superior spatial alignment and clinical safety. Therefore, while the underlying architecture is elegant, the paper is not ready for acceptance in its current form.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper proposes a novel virtual staining framework from H&E and IHC images for digital pathology. All reviewers acknowledge that the paper is well motivated and appropriately modeled, with clear presentation and organization. However, the evaluation is limited to a single dataset without cross-validation or confidence interval reporting, and the lack of comparison with recent methods significantly weakens the paper’s claims.
The authors should address these concerns in the rebuttal, with particular focus on the experimental setting, as well as the technical concerns regarding potential information loss caused by aggressive resizing and the resulting resolution mismatch with foundation models.

This paper proposes a novel virtual staining framework based on H&E and IHC images for digital pathology. The introduction of the VAR model into the virtual staining task provides a new generative perspective compared with prior GAN-based and conditional diffusion-based approaches. The methodology is technically interesting and demonstrates the potential of autoregressive visual generation paradigms in computational pathology applications.
However, the paper also has several notable limitations. In particular, the lack of sufficiently strong baseline comparisons and the reliance on a single evaluation dataset considerably weaken the overall experimental validation. At present, much of the paper’s contribution is primarily supported through ablation studies rather than comprehensive benchmarking against state-of-the-art methods.
Overall, after balancing the strengths and weaknesses, I consider the merits of the paper to slightly outweigh its limitations. The work introduces a potentially valuable new direction for virtual staining research. Therefore, I support acceptance of this paper.

Post-rebuttal, the majority of reviewers found this contribution sufficiently novel and practically valuable, and the rebuttal convincingly addressed the earlier novelty and design concerns. The remaining reservation concerns single-cohort validation, which the authors should acknowledge as a limitation and mitigate by folding the supplementary baselines and robustness results into the camera-ready. On balance, I recommend acceptance.

This manuscript introduces an interesting virtual staining method for H&E-to-IHC image generation. It uses a frozen pathology foundation model to extract semantic features from H&E images and then feeds them into a conditional visual autoregressive (VAR) framework for IHC token prediction, which is used to generate synthetic IHC images. This study explores a new generative paradigm for virtual staining, and it also includes clinically meaningful evaluation. The rebuttal addresses the reviewers’ concerns about technical novelty, aggressive resizing, statistical robustness, and reproducibility.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback and for recognizing PALETTE’s motivation, clinical relevance, clarity, and scale-aligned formulation. We address the main concerns using only evidence from the submitted manuscript.
R2Q1: Motivation and Novelty.
PALETTE is not merely applying VAR to virtual staining. Its key contribution is a representation-decoupled formulation: frozen pathology foundation-model features provide continuous H&E semantics, while VQGAN/Cond-VAR models discrete IHC texture tokens. Table 3 supports this design: replacing PathFM with a trainable VQ encoder reduces SSIM/PSNR from 0.7589/29.5958 to 0.7279/27.1018; removing conditioning gives 0.6571/18.5512; replacing VAR with a U-Net baseline degrades to 0.6668/13.9647.Pathology-specific FMs also outperform DINOv2.Thus, although feature visualization would be complementary, the submitted ablations provide direct functional evidence for the representation-decoupling claim.
R2Q3, R3Q1: Resizing and Multi-scale Fidelity.
We apologize for not discussing this trade-off more clearly. All methods use the same 256×256 registered-patch preprocessing, so it does not favor PALETTE. Interpolated PathFM features are not independent semantic predictions at each scale; they are scale-aligned conditioning priors. The coarsest feature modulates global context via AdaLN, while finer spatial features guide next-scale IHC token prediction under the scale-causal mask (Sec. 2.1–2.3). Final IHC reconstruction uses the highest-resolution VQ token map, not interpolated H&E features. Table 2 further suggests that diagnostically relevant HER2 and ER patterns are preserved.
R3Q2, R4Q1: Dataset Scope and Robustness.
The submitted evaluation is not a narrow single-task test: IHC4BC contains four biomarkers, 214 patients, and over 92k paired patches, evaluated with a strict patient-level 75/25 split balanced by clinical labels (Sec. 3.1), avoiding patch-level leakage. PALETTE achieves the best SSIM/PSNR on ER, HER2, and PR and the best PSNR on Ki67 (Table 1). Downstream evaluation shows the best HER2 ACC/AUC and ER H-score/Allred-score performance (Table 2), supporting diagnostic relevance beyond perceptual similarity. Furthermore, On BCI, PALETTE obtains 0.5097 SSIM / 22.76 PSNR, outperforming the reported BCI SOTA of 0.477 / 21.16; On HER2match, PALETTE obtains 0.522 SSIM / 22.7 PSNR / 48.5 FID / 0.035 KID, improving over the reported SOTA of approximately 0.510 / 22.5 / 65.2 / 0.050.
R3Q3, R4Q2: Baselines and PAINT.
PAINT is closely related, but it has not been open-sourced. Unlike PAINT, PALETTE decouples frozen PathFM semantic encoding from molecular token generation, instead of relying solely on task-specific latent alignment. To address concerns on modern generative baselines, we also evaluated Star-Diff, PASB, and HistDist under the same setting. For ER/HER2/PR/Ki67, PALETTE achieves SSIM/PSNR of 0.7589/29.59, 0.3422/16.52, 0.8142/32.45, 0.6741/29.94.Star-Diff obtains 0.6851/27.13, 0.2473/15.22, 0.7434/28.65, 0.6735/28.85; PASB 0.6238/23.77, 0.2223/12.88, 0.6680/27.81, 0.4781/22.72; HistDist 0.5824/21.41, 0.2403/14.58, 0.6491/20.59, 0.6006/22.65.
R3Q2, R4Q3: Statistical robustness.
Multiple independent runs show low variance. ER achieves 0.7427 ± 0.0119 SSIM and 28.7836 ± 0.5757 PSNR; HER2 achieves 0.3374 ± 0.0043 SSIM and 16.1274 ± 0.3185 PSNR, indicating stable improvements rather than a favorable random seed.
R4Q4: Ki67 Performance. We agree PALETTE is not best on every metric: Ki67 SSIM is slightly below SynDiff, while PALETTE has the best Ki67 PSNR of 29.9472 (Table 1). Overall, PALETTE is best on seven of eight SSIM/PSNR entries and all downstream clinical metrics (Table 2); we will state this precisely. Sec. 2–3 specify components, losses, scales, training epochs, and implementation details.
R2Q2: Reproducibility. Upon acceptance, we intend to release code, preprocessing scripts, permitted weights, and splits.

title: PancCADx: A Multimodal Framework for Pancreatic Cancer Diagnosis
abstract:
Abstract:
Endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS) interpretation for pancreatic cancer is highly operator-dependent, leading to significant diagnostic variability and limited reasoning transparency. We present PancCADx, an interpretable multimodal framework leveraging Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking with a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) mechanism to align model reasoning with expert clinical logic. To ensure clinical alignment and minimize hallucinations, we utilized a two-stage alignment strategy: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) followed by Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Developed on an internal cohort (n=438) and validated on multi-center external cohorts (n=191), PancCADx achieved 95.74% external sensitivity, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art benchmarks (92.55%) with superior cross-institutional generalizability. In a prospective sequential validation involving 12 clinicians, AI assistance significantly enhanced diagnostic accuracy (+7.7%, p < 0.001) and decision confidence (p < 0.001). Notably, PancCADx effectively bridged the novice-expert gap and improved specificity for senior clinicians (up to 76%). By harmonizing high diagnostic performance with transparent, evidence-based reasoning, PancCADx provides a robust, clinically-aligned solution for objective and trustworthy pancreatic cancer diagnosis.
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: Authors proposes PancCADx, a multimodal reasoning framework for pancreatic cancer diagnosis on endoscopic ultrasonography. It employs a two-stage alignment strategy: Supervised Fine-Tuning to inject expert-level Chain-of-Thought reasoning, followed by Direct Preference Optimization to correct hallucinations without a separate reward model. Validated on multi-center external cohorts and a prospective study with 12 clinicians.
reviews.text_strengths: The SFT-DPO alignment strategy, reminiscent of RLHF which typically demands large-scale preference data, is effectively adapted to a low-resource medical setting through careful pipeline design — including expert-verified CoT distillation and targeted preference pair construction (n=386). The use of Low-Rank Adaptation further enables this data-efficient implementation on a single GPU. Moreover, the validation design is rigorous, incorporating multi-center external cohorts and a prospective clinical study with 12 stratified endoscopists, lending credibility to the reported performance gains.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The paper does not include a Limitations section, which is a notable omission.
2.All p-values for the expert group and most of the senior groups are non-significant, yet the paper does not discuss whether this reflects genuinely limited room for improvement at high baselines or simply insufficient sample size. Explicit acknowledgment of this ambiguity is needed.
3.PancCADx shows notably lower internal accuracy (83.72%) compared to Joint-AI (98.00%), yet the paper frames this solely as Joint-AI overfitting rather than analyzing potential weaknesses of PancCADx on in-distribution data. A more balanced discussion is warranted.
4.Some abbreviations in Table 1 (AIP, CP, NET, SPT) are left undefined. Providing full definitions would make the paper more accessible to early-stage readers who may not be familiar with these clinical terms.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The prospective validation with stratified clinicians is a clear strength over most AI-in-medical-imaging studies that remain purely retrospective. However, the very small expert subgroup (n=2), the unexplored confirmation bias risk in the Conclusion-First protocol, and inconsistencies in metric formatting prevent a stronger recommendation. These issues are addressable in revision — the authors are encouraged to discuss these limitations openly and transparently, which would strengthen the overall credibility of the work.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The rebuttal addresses the main concerns from my review. The authors committed to adding a Limitations section covering the n=2 expert subgroup, Conclusion-First bias risk, and single-organ scope, and to including 95% CIs across all cohorts with unified metric formatting. They explicitly acknowledged that the non-significant p-values for the expert group reflect both small sample size and baseline ceiling effects, reframing this as AI reinforcing expert confidence rather than overclaiming improvement. The Conclusion-First bias defense grounded in recognition-primed decision-making, together with DPO-based mitigation, is reasonable though not fully resolving the underlying risk; appropriately deferred to the Limitations.
The response to the internal vs external accuracy gap is partially satisfactory — the statistical instability argument (n=43, wide CI) is valid, but the Joint-AI overfitting framing remains one-sided. Overall, the prospective validation with stratified clinicians, the data-efficient SFT-DPO pipeline, and the authors willingness to incorporate the requested revisions justify an Accept. Remaining concerns are addressable in the camera-ready revision.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a multimodal framework for pancreatic cancer diagnosis that combines EUS images and structured clinical data, and further aligns a reasoning-capable vision-language model, aiming to improve both diagnostic performance and interpretability; the authors validate the model on multicenter cohorts and evaluate its value as an AI assistant for clinicians in a reader study.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper focuses on pancreatic cancer diagnosis from EUS, a high-impact task with substantial inter-operator variability, so improving consistency and decision support is clinically meaningful.
2.The method combines EUS images with 30 structured EMR variables, which better reflects how clinicians make diagnostic decisions than image-only approaches.
3.The model is evaluated not only on an internal cohort but also on data from three independent external centers, which is a stronger validation setting than single-center testing.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The claim of outperforming the SOTA is not fully supported by the reported results. PancCADx achieves higher sensitivity, but lower specificity, slightly lower accuracy, and slightly lower F1 than Joint-AI.
2.The paper does not present a strongly new technical method at the MICCAI level.
3.The paper does not sufficiently isolate the contribution of individual components, such as image-only vs. multimodal, SFT vs. SFT+DPO, or with vs. without CoT supervision, making it hard to determine which part of the pipeline drives performance gains.
4.Evaluation is incomplete and should include threshold-independent metrics such as AUC.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper addresses an important clinical problem, proposes a multimodal framework that combines EUS images with clinical variables, and includes both multi-center validation and a reader study, which increases its practical interest. However, the final score is limited by several important concerns: the claim of outperforming the state of the art is not fully supported by the reported results, key ablation studies are missing, the evidence for interpretability is still limited, and the evaluation would be more convincing if the authors reported threshold-independent metrics such as AUC in addition to fixed-threshold measures. Overall, while the work is promising and clinically relevant, the current experimental evidence is not yet strong enough to fully support its main claims.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper introduces PancCADx, an interpretable multimodal framework for AI-assisted pancreatic cancer diagnosis via endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS). The core contribution is a reasoning-driven clinical decision support system built on Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking with a Chain-of-Thought mechanism, designed to align model reasoning with expert clinical logic rather than functioning as a black-box classifier. The authors employ a two-stage alignment strategy, Supervised Fine-Tuning followed by Direct Preference Optimization, to minimize hallucinations and ensure clinical relevance in model outputs.
The framework is validated on both internal (n=438) and multi-center external (n=191) cohorts, achieving 95.74% sensitivity on single-frame inputs while outperforming multi-frame state-of-the-art baselines, a notable data efficiency advantage. A prospective sequential validation with 12 clinicians further demonstrates that AI assistance meaningfully improved diagnostic accuracy and decision confidence across experience levels, with particular impact in bridging the novice-expert gap and correcting specificity bias in senior endoscopists. Together, these contributions position PancCADx as a clinically grounded and transparent approach to objective pancreatic cancer diagnosis.
reviews.text_strengths:
This paper has several compelling strengths that make it a strong contribution to the MICCAI community.
First, the clinical motivation is sharp and well-executed. EUS interpretation for pancreatic cancer is genuinely operator-dependent, and the authors don’t just acknowledge this, they build their entire framework around solving it. The decision to address both diagnostic variability and reasoning transparency in a single system is thoughtful and clinically grounded.
Second, the two-stage alignment strategy is a standout methodological contribution. The combination of Supervised Fine-Tuning for reasoning injection followed by Direct Preference Optimization for clinical alignment is novel in this context. What makes it particularly interesting is the construction of the preference dataset, capturing discrepancies between SFT outputs and expert consensus to generate 386 high-quality preference pairs is a rigorous and principled approach to minimizing hallucinations in a high-stakes clinical setting.
Third, the Chain-of-Thought distillation pipeline is well-designed and clinically motivated. The Conclusion-First protocol, anchoring reasoning to the diagnosis before retrospective morphological analysis, is a deliberate design choice that mirrors expert recognition-primed decision-making. Having three senior experts with over 15 years of experience refine the reasoning chains adds meaningful credibility to the interpretability claims.
Fourth, the evaluation is genuinely rigorous. The multicenter external validation across three independent institutions (n=191) is a meaningful test of generalizability, and the results hold up well, PancCADx achieves 95.74% pooled sensitivity against a SOTA baseline trained on richer multi-frame inputs, using only single-frame data. The direct comparison against Joint-AI is fair and transparent, and the authors are commendably honest about where PancCADx trails on specificity.
Fifth, the prospective sequential validation study is one of the strongest aspects of the paper. The self-controlled two-phase design with a washout period is methodologically sound, and the results are meaningful across all experience levels. The finding that AI assistance improved senior clinician specificity from 40% to 76% is striking and clinically significant. The dual benefit of CoT reasoning, reinforcing expert confidence while serving as an educational scaffold for novices, is a genuinely interesting finding that extends the contribution beyond pure diagnostic performance.
Finally, the privacy and data handling pipeline is thorough. The de-identification protocol, IRB approval across participating centers, and STARD guideline adherence reflect a level of clinical rigor that is not always present in AI diagnostic papers.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
While this is a strong paper overall, there are a few areas worth addressing that would further solidify the contribution.
The most notable concern is the internal validation performance. On the Center A holdout (n=43), PancCADx reports 83.72% accuracy and 68.75% specificity, a meaningful drop compared to its external validation results. This is somewhat counterintuitive, and the paper does not fully account for it. The authors make a convincing case that Joint-AI’s near-perfect internal performance reflects overfitting, but the inverse pattern in PancCADx warrants its own explanation. Understanding what drives this discrepancy would strengthen confidence in the framework’s consistency across evaluation settings.
Relatedly, the internal validation set of n=43 is quite small. At this sample size, performance estimates are statistically fragile, and the absence of confidence intervals for this cohort makes it difficult to interpret the results with confidence. Reporting confidence intervals across all cohorts, not just the sequential validation study, would add important statistical transparency.
On the human-AI collaboration findings, the results for expert clinicians specifically deserve closer attention. While the overall narrative around bridging the novice-expert gap is well supported, none of the expert-level improvements in Table 3 reach statistical significance, sensitivity (p=.215), specificity (p>.99), and accuracy (p=.154) all fall short. This does not undermine the broader findings, but the paper should be careful not to overstate AI benefit uniformly across experience levels. The story for novices and seniors is compelling; the expert story is more nuanced.
The framework is validated exclusively on pancreatic EUS, which is appropriate for a focused contribution but limits the generalizability claims. The authors gesture toward broader applicability across GI cancers and imaging modalities, but this remains undemonstrated. Framing the scope more precisely, as a validated solution for pancreatic EUS specifically, with potential for broader application, would be more accurate and still compelling.
Finally, the CoT reasoning quality evaluation relies primarily on subjective Likert-scale assessment across five dimensions. While this captures clinician perception well, there is no quantitative measure of reasoning correctness or factual accuracy independent of the diagnostic outcome. A structured evaluation of the reasoning chains themselves, even on a subset, would meaningfully strengthen the interpretability claims that are central to this work.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
This is a well-executed and clinically meaningful paper that makes a genuine contribution to AI-assisted endoscopic diagnosis. The two-stage alignment strategy, the prospective sequential validation design, and the honest benchmarking against a stronger baseline are all commendable. The work is clearly motivated, methodologically sound, and the results are largely convincing. The authors should be encouraged, this is the kind of human-AI collaboration study the MICCAI community needs more of.
A few additional thoughts for the authors to consider:
The internal validation performance dip is the one finding that lingers. Even a brief discussion acknowledging and contextualizing this, whether attributable to the small holdout size, cohort composition, or the training-validation split strategy, would go a long way in preempting reviewer concern and demonstrating full transparency.
On the expert clinician findings, it may be worth reframing the narrative slightly. The AI assistance story is strongest for novices and seniors, and those results are genuinely impressive. Presenting the expert findings as a nuanced outcome, where CoT reasoning reinforced confidence rather than changing decisions, is actually an interesting insight in itself and worth developing rather than grouping under the general improvement narrative.
The CoT reasoning evaluation would benefit from even a small-scale structured audit of reasoning chain accuracy independent of diagnostic outcome. Given that interpretability is a central claim of the framework, grounding it in something more quantitative than clinician perception would make the contribution significantly more defensible.
Finally, the privacy and de-identification pipeline is thorough and well-documented, this is worth highlighting more prominently, as it directly addresses one of the key barriers to real-world clinical deployment of AI diagnostic tools.
Overall, this is a strong submission and a worthy addition to the MICCAI program.

This paper is recommended for acceptance. PancCADx addresses a clinically significant and well-scoped problem, the operator-dependency and reasoning opacity of EUS-based pancreatic cancer diagnosis and does so with a methodologically rigorous and technically innovative framework. The two-stage SFT-DPO alignment strategy is a novel and principled contribution, and the prospective sequential validation study with stratified clinicians elevates this well above a typical diagnostic AI paper.
The major factors driving this recommendation are the strength and fairness of the evaluation, the clinical grounding of the design choices, and the significance of the human-AI collaboration findings. Achieving 95.74% pooled sensitivity on multicenter external data using only single-frame inputs, against a baseline trained on richer multi-frame data, is a compelling demonstration of both diagnostic performance and data efficiency. The finding that AI assistance improved senior clinician specificity from 40% to 76% is clinically striking and independently meaningful.
The weaknesses identified, particularly around the internal validation performance gap, the small holdout size, and the subjectivity of the CoT quality evaluation, are real but do not undermine the core contribution. They are addressable refinements rather than fundamental flaws, and the overall rigor of the work more than compensates. The honest benchmarking approach, IRB compliance across four centers, and STARD adherence further reflect the maturity of this submission.
PancCADx represents a meaningful step toward transparent, clinically aligned AI decision support in gastrointestinal oncology, and it deserves a place in the MICCAI program. A rebuttal is not needed to reach this conclusion.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
My recommendation remains Accept. The authors’ rejoinder was well-structured, targeted, and effectively addressed the primary points mentioned by all three reviewers without going overboard or promising results beyond the published work.Concerning the internal validation performance gap, the authors clarified that the lower accuracy (83.72%, n=43) reflects statistical instability at small sample sizes, with an approximate 95% confidence interval of [72%, 92%], and a higher proportion of diagnostically challenging cases in the Center A holdout. This is a reasonable and honest explanation, and the commitment to publishing confidence intervals across all cohorts in revision represents a significant advance.
Regarding the expert clinician findings, the rebuttal appropriately reframes the null results; n=2 restricts statistical power; and the authors now expressly characterize this as a confidence reinforcement finding rather than a performance increase. This is exactly the nuance the study required, and I appreciate that they dealt with it immediately.
The SOTA comparability concern identified by R#2 is convincingly addressed. The sensitivity-specificity trade-off is clinically grounded; in a cancer with a 5-year survival rate of about 10%, missed diagnoses are far more risky than false positives. The rebuttal’s clarification that AUC does not apply to reasoning-based generative models is technically correct and should be explicitly mentioned in the final version.
The article contains specific and actionable improvements, such as the addition of a Limitations section, confidence intervals across all cohorts, the definition of Table 1 abbreviations, and structured CoT quality auditing. These are the types of adjustments that boost an existing strong contribution without altering its core assertions.
The flaws noted in my previous review remain, but the rebuttal shows that the writers understand them well and have credible replies. Nothing in the response undermines my trust in the fundamental contribution. PancCADx is still a rigorous, clinically informed, and innovative framework that deserves a position in the MICCAI 2026 program.

meta_reviews.text:
The manuscript was reviewed by three expert reviewers. While acknowledging merits in the proposed work, the reviewers also raised some concerns about methodological novelty and validation. Such concerns should be addressed to strengthen the value of the work.

The reviewers’ concerns have been successfully addressed in the rebuttal, making the work a solid contribution especially for what concerns MIC research.

This paper presents a multimodal framework for pancreatic cancer diagnosis from EUS images and structured clinical data, using SFT and DPO to align a reasoning-capable vision-language model with expert clinical logic. Reviewers appreciated the clinical relevance of the task, the multimodal design, the data-efficient alignment strategy, the multicenter external validation, and especially the prospective reader study with stratified clinicians. Concerns were raised regarding limited ablation analysis, overstatement of state-of-the-art claims, the small expert subgroup, non-significant expert-level improvements, the internal validation performance gap, and the need for clearer limitations and confidence intervals. The rebuttal addressed most of these concerns constructively by agreeing to revise the claims, add limitations, provide confidence intervals, define unclear abbreviations, and better contextualize the expert results and internal cohort instability. While some concerns about component-level attribution remain only partially resolved, the overall clinical validation and human-AI study are strong. I therefore recommend acceptance.

This paper has strong clinical translation value. It combines multicenter external validation with a prospective self-controlled clinician study, which is very rare among the submissions. PancCADx achieves a high pooled external sensitivity of 95.74% and shows meaningful human-AI benefit, especially for novices and senior clinicians, where accuracy/specificity improves significantly. Personally I like this paper much and recommend the acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their thorough and constructive feedback.
1.Technical Contributions (R#2)
Our novelty lies in three innovations: (1) Error-driven preference mining: instead of generic RLHF, we mine preference pairs from the SFT model’s failure modes against expert consensus (386 pairs), making DPO data-efficient in low-resource settings; (2) Conclusion-First CoT grounded in dual-process cognitive theory: prior medical CoT deduces forward (findings to diagnosis), whereas we anchor diagnosis first to prevent logic drift; (3) First evidence that single-frame VLM reasoning matches multi-frame CNN ensembles on EUS, suggesting reasoning quality can compensate for data quantity.
2.SOTA Comparison (R#2)
On comparable multi-center external cohorts (3 centers, ~190 patients), PancCADx achieves 95.74% sensitivity with single-frame input, outperforming Joint-AI’s 92.55% with multi-frame voting. The lower specificity (80.41% vs 84.54%) reflects a deliberate trade-off: in pancreatic cancer (5-year survival ~10%), missed diagnosis carries far greater risk than false positives requiring EUS-FNA. We will revise to “superior sensitivity with stronger interpretability and data efficiency” rather than unconditional superiority.
Regarding AUC: PancCADx outputs categorical conclusions with reasoning chains, not continuous probability scores. AUC requires adjustable thresholds, which is inapplicable to reasoning-based generative models. We will state this explicitly.
3.Ablation and Component Contributions (R#2)
CoT contributes interpretability, not classification gain. In Table 3, CoT reasoning improved senior specificity from 40% to 76% (p=0.003) by providing auditable diagnostic logic.
DPO corrects hallucinations. As described in Section 2.2, error-driven discrepancy mining identified 386 cases where SFT outputs diverged from expert consensus. These preference pairs target systematic biases, e.g., over-reliance on “clear boundary = benign” heuristics and anchoring on normal biomarkers while ignoring indirect imaging signs. DPO penalizes these patterns (Eq. 2), aligning reasoning with expert logic.
Ablating generative VLMs differs from modular CNNs: removing CoT transforms the output structure entirely, requiring different optimization. Per rebuttal guidelines, we address this based on existing manuscript content.
4.Conclusion-First Bias (R#1)
This design mirrors expert recognition-primed decision-making (Ref. 22): experts form rapid diagnostic impressions then retrospectively verify morphological evidence. Moreover, our DPO stage partially mitigates this risk: the 386 preference pairs include cases where the model reached correct conclusions but through selective reasoning, and DPO penalizes such incomplete evidence chains. We will further discuss potential bias risks in the Limitations section.
5.Internal Validation (R#1, R#3)
The lower internal accuracy (83.72%, n=43) reflects statistical instability (95% CI approximately [72%, 92%]) and a higher proportion of diagnostically challenging cases in Center A’s holdout. This reflects fragility of point estimates at small sample sizes, not model weakness. We will add CIs across all cohorts.
6.Expert Group Results (R#1, R#3)
We stratify findings: novices 69% to 90% accuracy (p<0.001); seniors 40% to 76% specificity (p=0.003); experts no significant change (n=2, high baseline). We acknowledge n=2 limits statistical power. For experts, AI reinforces confidence rather than changing decisions, a clinically meaningful finding we will emphasize rather than grouping under general improvement.
7.Response to R#3
We appreciate R#3’s insightful evaluation and will incorporate structured CoT quality auditing in the revision.
8.Planned Revisions
Limitations section (n=2, Conclusion-First bias, single-organ scope); Table 1 abbreviations (AIP/CP/NET/SPT); 95% CIs for all metrics; unified metric formatting; code and model weights upon acceptance.

title: PANet: Probability-Anchored Network for Ultrasound Bone Segmentation
abstract: Ultrasound bone surface segmentation is a critical prerequisite for orthopedic applications such as quantitative analysis and intraoperative navigation. However, reliable segmentation remains challenging due to ambiguous bone boundaries, strong appearance variability, and interference from bone-like soft tissues, often resulting in unstable predictions in complex clinical scenarios. Existing approaches often rely on network designs tailored to specific ultrasound physical priors, which may limit their adaptability across different imaging conditions. In this work, we propose a Probability-Anchored Network (PANet) for robust ultrasound bone segmentation. Built upon a U-Net backbone, PANet explicitly introduces a probability space as an intermediate representation between image features and segmentation results, enabling controllable activation, discrimination, and refinement of bone boundaries. Specifically, global linear bias, local probability exchange, and global attention mechanisms are jointly employed to enhance bone-related responses while suppressing globally inconsistent false positives. Moreover, a unified segmentation head provides globally consistent supervision across all network stages, enabling probability-aligned learning and segmentation-guided attention. Experiments on freehand-scanned long-bone ultrasound datasets demonstrate that PANet achieves more accurate and stable segmentation performance compared with state-of-the-art methods.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes PANet (Probability-Anchored Network) for robust ultrasound bone segmentation. The core contribution is an explicit probability space serving as an intermediate representation between image features and segmentation results, which decomposes segmentation into controllable activation, discrimination, and refinement stages. PANet integrates three key modules: Probability Exchange Module (PEM) for local boundary refinement, Probability Bias Module (PBM) for early bone activation, and Probability Reasoning Module (PRM) with global attention to suppress false positives from bone-like soft tissues. A unified multi-level supervision head aligns probability learning across network stages. Experiments on a freehand long-bone ultrasound dataset demonstrate that PANet achieves superior segmentation accuracy, boundary precision, and stability compared with state-of-the-art methods, while maintaining real-time inference speed for clinical usage.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper introduces an explicit probability space as an intermediate representation between visual features and segmentation outputs, which is conceptually original for ultrasound bone segmentation. Unlike prior methods that rely on ultrasound‑specific physical priors or end‑to‑end feature mapping, PANet decomposes segmentation into activation, discrimination, and refinement within a structured probability domain. This design provides better control over false positives from bone‑like soft tissues and improves boundary stability under ambiguous imaging conditions, which is a meaningful and clinically motivated novelty. 
2.The three complementary components—PEM for local boundary refinement, PBM for early structure activation, and PRM for global false‑positive suppression—are tightly coupled and theoretically consistent. The local–global modeling hierarchy effectively addresses weak boundaries and background interference, two long‑standing challenges in ultrasound bone segmentation. The use of rotary positional embedding within probability‑space attention is technically sound and well justified. 
3.The UPE‑Head provides consistent supervision across stages to align probability learning and guide attention. This design not only boosts performance but also improves the interpretability and traceability of the model’s decision process, which is valuable for clinical translation. 
4.The evaluation is thorough: quantitative comparison with a wide range of state‑of‑the‑art models (U‑Net, TransUNet, BCA‑Net, etc. ), complete ablation studies verifying the contribution of each core module, and clinically relevant metrics including IoU, Dice, HD95, recall, precision, and inference speed. PANet achieves top performance with balanced recall and precision, low HD95, and real‑time inference speed (194 FPS), clearly demonstrating clinical practicality.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The entire dataset is collected from one single ultrasound scanner (Mindray Resona 6) at one institution, with no cross-device, cross-probe, or multi-center experiments. Clinical ultrasound systems vary significantly in gain, frequency, resolution, and artifact patterns, so the generalizability of PANet to real clinical scenarios remains unproven. This is a critical limitation for translation to orthopedic navigation. 
2.The idea of using an explicit probabilistic intermediate space and multi-level supervision is conceptually similar to several existing works in medical image segmentation. While the combination for ultrasound bone is new, the core paradigm is not sufficiently innovative from a methodological perspective. 
3.The ablation removes individual components but does not compare against probability space vs. deep supervision alone in a controlled manner. It also lacks ablation of key hyperparameters (e. g. , probability dimension K, block size in PRM, weight of loss terms) to validate robustness. The relative importance of Gaussian initialization is not rigorously quantified. 
4.The paper claims the probability space improves interpretability but provides no quantitative interpretability analysis (e. g. , uncertainty quantification, failure-mode analysis, or visualization of probability evolution across challenging cases). The link between probability anchors and clinical decision-making is underdeveloped. 
5.Ultrasound bone segmentation is a typical thin-structure segmentation task with extreme foreground–background imbalance. The paper does not discuss whether the loss function, sampling strategy, or post-processing is adapted to this challenge. No results are shown on fracture, implant, or pathological cases, which are clinically more important than healthy long bones.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
This paper presents a technically solid, well‑motivated, and clinically relevant contribution to ultrasound bone segmentation for orthopedic applications. The proposed PANet with a probability‑anchored intermediate representation is carefully designed to suppress false positives and stabilize boundary prediction under challenging freehand scanning conditions, and it is thoroughly validated through comprehensive comparisons and ablation studies, achieving superior performance and real‑time inference speed suitable for clinical usage.

The core contributions show clear value for ultrasound bone segmentation and achieve strong quantitative results. However, several critical limitations prevent it from meeting full acceptance criteria: (1)insufficient clinical validation and generalization evidence, as experiments are restricted to a single‑center, single‑device dataset on healthy volunteers with no evaluation on pathological, fracture, or multi‑scanner data; (2) incomplete ablation and interpretability analysis, lacking rigorous hyperparameter studies and concrete evidence to support the claimed clinical interpretability; and (3) reproducibility gaps in preprocessing, annotation quality control, and runtime optimization details.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses the challenging task of ultrasound bone segmentation. The main contribution is the introduction of a parallel probability space to the feature space of the Unet at different resolutions that can better tackle false positives in comparison to surrounding soft structures.
reviews.text_strengths: Novel methodology which introduces a probability space along a unet backbone. The features of the unet are propagated into this space and further updated and propagated based on neighboring probabilities. Finally the attention-based module predicts confidence of bone in one pixel relative to surrounding structures. This is interesting because it models and updates the uncertainty explicitly. The intermediate maps that this representation creates can also be visualized to further understand the output of the method.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The claim that the method outperforms STOA in challenging imaging conditions would benefit from a more precise definition of what constitutes a challenging case, along with a dedicated evaluation in these settings. It is also worth clarifying whether expert sonographers agree on ground truth segmentations for such cases.
Existing works such as UltraBones100k are publicly available and should have been used for benchmarking. Moreover, the therein proposed bone segmentation method would have been a recent stoa baseline to compare to.
Despite the generic title, the paper focuses exclusively on long bones with no discussion of whether the method would extend to other structures such as the spine.
Overview figure is unintuitive and some parts of the methodology are unclear. Here are some notes and suggestions for improvement:
on the upper part of the figure PRM is shown in yellow separate from UPE head, but further below PRM module contains the UPE head, this is rather confusing.
instead of calling the lower left corner PBM & PEM I suggest calling them probability update module. This contains both PBM & PEM modules. PBM should be marked on the arrow from CNN Feature F to PBM Bias B. PEM should be on the arrow from CNN feature F to PEM weight. 
Figure 1 should have an alone standing description with the pipeline steps. Currently it is not understandable without reading the main text.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Would be good to shortly explain “qualitative analysis” you are mentioning in the abstract.
in the main figure it would be more intuitive to keep visual encoder decoder structure
potential title clash with Path Aggregation Network (PANet) from computer vision

I think that the proposed parallel probability space is a novel approach, particularly interesting because of its explainability characteristic. However, the unclarities in the method and main figure require improvement. Moreover, a short discussion on wide-range applicability of the method as well as quantification and explanation of clinically challenging cases to ensure the claim is appropriate would be needed.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces a novel framework named Probability Anchoring Network (PANet), which outperforms baseline models like U-Net on a self-built large-scale ultrasound bone segmentation dataset, while maintaining an inference speed suitable for clinical real-time applications.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper constructs a large-scale free-hand scanning long bone ultrasound dataset containing 246471 images, conducts five-fold cross-validation, and has a rigorous experimental design. The model has a fast inference speed and high potential for clinical application. Compared to mainstream models such as U-Net, Attention U-Net, and TransUNet, PANet achieves stable improvements in both IoU (81.39%) and Dice (89.43%), and performs well with HD95 (0.97mm). Ablation experiments demonstrate that the global inference module effectively suppresses false positives caused by soft tissue similar to bone texture.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The paper claims to have solved the “boundary blurring” problem and uses HD95 as a distance metric. However, HD95 is sensitive to outliers and cannot reflect the overall boundary fit. In bone segmentation tasks, ASSD (Average Symmetric Surface Distance) is the gold standard for measuring boundary accuracy. The absence of this metric in the paper completely undermines the ability to prove whether the segmentation results truly achieve smooth boundary fit at non-outlier points.
2.The interpretability of the method description is relatively poor. The paper proposes a “probability space”, but fails to clearly explain its physical significance.
The definition and explanation of dimension K are missing, and it is unclear what K=64 channels specifically represent.
3.The comparison method is outdated. Although TransUNet and BCA-Net are compared, the current state-of-the-art medical segmentation models (such as SwinUNETR, nnU-Net) are not included in the comparison. Especially, the citation year of BCA-Net is relatively recent (2025).
4.The data solely originates from a single device (Mindray Resona 6) of a single institution, lacking verification from multi-center and multi-vendor devices, thus casting doubt on its generalization ability. The experiment solely targets a private dataset. Currently, there are numerous datasets related to ultrasound bone imaging, yet none of them are cited in this paper.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Despite the flaws in the paper, such as missing indicators and insufficient comparison, it has constructed a massive dataset and the model’s inference speed holds great clinical practical value.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
Despite several significant concerns raised during the initial review phase, this work demonstrates sufficient methodological novelty and practical utility to warrant early acceptance. The primary strengths of the submission lie in its real-time implementation and its consistent performance gains over established baselines. While these improvements are incremental, their feasibility in time-sensitive environments provides clear value to the field.
To strengthen the final camera-ready version, the authors are encouraged to:
Open-Source Contribution: Release the source code and curated datasets to ensure reproducibility and foster community adoption.
Benchmarking: If feasible, include a comparative analysis against nnU-Net. Given its status as a robust benchmark in medical imaging, such a comparison would provide a more comprehensive validation of the proposed method’s efficacy.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the reviewers for their constructive comments. We have revised the manuscript to improve the writing and figures, clarify key points, and expand the discussion of limitations and future work.
Code and Data Availability
The code and trained models will be publicly released, while the dataset will be available upon reasonable request.
Dataset
1.Future work will include multi-center and cross-device ultrasound data, clinically challenging cases such as fractures, implants, and pathological changes, and other anatomical bone structures to further assess the robustness, clinical applicability, and generalizability of PANet.
2.Regarding UltraBones100K, although it is an important public dataset, our inspection showed that its labels are mainly derived from CT-based automatic annotation and registration rather than frame-wise expert-refined annotations. The resulting label shifts and boundary inaccuracies may compromise the reliability of fine-grained bone surface evaluation; therefore, it was not included in the current experiments.
Experimental limitations
We appreciate the reviewers’ comments on the ablation study, evaluation metrics, comparison baselines, and interpretability analysis. We agree that these aspects are important for a more comprehensive evaluation. Due to the constraints of the MICCAI revision stage, extensive new experiments could not be added. Instead, we have explicitly discussed these limitations in the revised manuscript as important future directions. We will continue to evaluate PANet from more perspectives and present more complete results in subsequent work.
Novelty
We acknowledge that probabilistic representations and multi-level supervision have been explored in medical image segmentation. The novelty of PANet lies not in simply using probability maps or deep supervision, but in treating the probability space as a core intermediate state for network reasoning. Around this state, PANet designs dedicated probability initialization, activation, local exchange, global discrimination, and unified supervision mechanisms to address artifacts, bone-like interference, and boundary discontinuities in ultrasound bone segmentation. Future work will include more detailed comparisons and controlled validations with related probability-driven networks.
Writing and Figures
1.We have optimized Fig. 1 and its caption in response to R2.The figure is intended to emphasize the design of probability space, the roles of the submodules, and the visual evolution of probability maps. Therefore, it is not presented as a conventional U-Net-like architecture.
2.In response to R3, we added explanations of the physical meaning of the probability space and the role of dimension K. 
3.In response to R2, we clarified that the “challenging imaging conditions” mainly arise from ultrasound imaging characteristics. With improved soft-tissue imaging, multiple bone-like soft-tissue structures become visible and may be spatially connected with bone tissues, making bone surface segmentation more difficult. This point has been emphasized in the qualitative comparison. We also clarified that the ground-truth annotations were confirmed by consensus between the data labeler and the surgeon. To avoid ambiguity, the last sentence of the Abstract was removed.
4.In response to R1, the ethics information, which was previously hidden for anonymous review, has now been supplemented.
Scope and Naming
We have further clarified the current experimental scope and stated that future work will evaluate PANet on different bone structures. Regarding the naming conflict, PANet in this work explicitly refers to Probability-Anchored Network, which differs from Path Aggregation Network in both task and methodology. We have written the full name at its first appearance to reduce potential confusion.

title: Parameter-Efficient Self-Supervised Adaptation for EEG-FM under Fixed Computational Budgets
abstract: EEG foundation models pretrained via self-supervised learning promise transferable representations, but their generalization remains limited, especially across diverse clinical datasets. Full fine-tuning is impractical for resource-constrained clinical settings due to high computational requirements. In this work, we investigate whether parameter-efficient self-supervised adaptation, updating only 9–29% of parameters suffices to align representations to target tasks. We evaluate our method on two state-of-the-art models with different pretraining objectives: BIOT (contrastive) and CBraMod (masked reconstruction), and evaluate on three clinical EEG datasets for abnormality detection (TUAB), event classification (TUEV), and seizure detection (CHB-MIT) under both in-distribution and out-of-distribution conditions. SSL adaptation yields consistent gains over linear probing, up to 20x AUCPR. Under a fixed compute budget, peak performance requires only 20–50% of available unlabeled data. Critically, when total window count is fixed, performance remains invariant to patient count, suggesting that performance is dependent on overall temporal window diversity only. Our findings demonstrate that parameter-efficient adaptation enables effective deployment of EEG Foundation models (EEG-FM) with minimal computational overhead and data collection burden.  Code available at: https://github.com/c3n-group/efficient-eeg-adapt
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning
Modalities -> EEG / MEG / ECG / Physiological Signals

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a parameter-efficient self-supervised learning (SSL) adaptation strategy for EEG foundation models. Through this approach, the authors demonstrate that significant performance improvements can be achieved by updating less than 10% of the model parameters, supported by comprehensive comparative analysis.
reviews.text_strengths: Two EEG foundation models are selected, and a normalized evaluation scheme is introduced to ensure a fair comparison between them; this scheme measures the computational overhead of the optimizer. By adjusting the parameter ratio, the study analyzes how PRAUC varies under different settings.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The authors propose a parameter-efficient SSL adaptation strategy for EEG foundation models; however, they fail to sufficiently convince the reviewers why this approach must specifically be applied to the EEG domain. While the method may be suitable for a conference like MICCAI due to its use of EEG data, simply analyzing performance with respect to the number of parameters provides little to no novelty. Furthermore, the content in Section 2.1 appears to describe a general evaluation protocol for self-supervised learning rather than a distinct component of the proposed method.
In other words, it is difficult to determine what specific problem in the MICCAI domain is being effectively addressed. The reviewer’s main concern is that the claimed efficiency in data or parameter usage is not inherently tied to the MICCAI domain and could be evaluated in other domains as well.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

see weaknesses
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper evaluates the adaptation of self-supervised learning (SSL) in the context of foundation models applied to EEG data. The main contributions focus on assessing SSL methods in this specific setting under strict experimental conditions. The paper provides insightful information on foundation models and SSL methods when only limited annotated data are available.
reviews.text_strengths:
The experiments are performed under well-controlled conditions.
The experiment on the trade-off between window size and the number of participants is very interesting.
The comparison between in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings is insightful.
The paper is well written and well organized.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Why is this referred to as zero-shot when the final part of the model is still trained? Even if it is a simple model, these parameters still need to be trained. This aspect is therefore a bit misleading. Moreover, in both cases, the final part of the model is trained. The only difference seems to be whether the backbone is retrained using SSL or not.
Do you think the results would be similar with a model trained on more data, such as the mentioned LaBraM model?
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
There are some minor typos:
The short title (“Title Suppressed Due to Excessive Length”)
“FM” is not defined in the abstract or in the title
“CHB-MIT” is sometimes written as “CHBMIT”

The experiments are well conducted, and the results are insightful for the EEG community.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes and evaluates a parameter-efficient self-supervised adaptation (SA) strategy for EEG foundation models, in which only the final encoder layer is updated using the model’s original SSL objective on unlabelled target-domain data, before downstream linear probing. The approach is evaluated on two pretrained EEG foundation models with distinct objectives (BIOT, contrastive; CBraMod, masked reconstruction) across three clinical EEG tasks under both in-distribution and out-of-distribution conditions. The authors report improvements over zero-shot linear probing, with the largest gains on OOD tasks. A layer-unfreezing ablation argues that updating only the final layer Pareto-dominates multi-layer and full-parameter updates.
reviews.text_strengths:
Clinically motivated and well-scoped. Parameter-efficient adaptation of EEG foundation models is a genuine need at clinical sites with limited compute and unlabelled data access.
Patient-disjoint splits correctly implemented. The authors avoid the common and serious failure mode of subject-level leakage in EEG classification. Official splits are used for TUAB and TUEV. ID/OOD status is explicitly labelled per model–dataset pair.
Layer-unfreezing ablation yields a non-obvious finding. Table 2 shows that updating more layers does not improve performance and actively degrades CBraMod. This provides empirical support for the last-layer design choice and is a useful result for the community, contradicting the intuition that more trainable parameters help.
Two pretraining paradigms evaluated. Demonstrating the effect on both contrastive (BIOT) and masked-reconstruction (CBraMod) pretraining supports the generality of the finding beyond a single SSL objective.
Patients-vs-windows decomposition. Under fixed N = P·W and fixed C, varying P is a thoughtful experimental design that speaks directly to clinical data-collection strategy. The question has been largely ignored in the EEG-FM literature.
Reproducibility adequate for a conference paper. Optimiser, learning rates, weight decay, schedule, batch sizes, window lengths, filtering, resampling, channel montage, and splits are all specified. Datasets are public.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
No supervised baseline. The paper’s framing claims value for self-supervised parameter-efficient adaptation specifically, but the only comparison is against zero-shot linear probing on frozen features. A supervised last-layer fine-tuning control at matched |θ_adapt| on the same labelled target data is not reported. Without it, the reported gains cannot be attributed to the SSL objective. They might simply reflect that updating the last layer on target data (by any means) helps. This is particularly problematic on CHBMIT, where the LP baseline is near-random (BIOT AUCPR 1.53% vs. random baseline classifier 1.48%).
The data-efficiency finding is confounded with the fixed-compute design. Under C = N·E held constant, reducing N mechanically increases E (and thus r). The reported conclusion that “20–50% of data is sufficient” is therefore equivalent to “r ≈ 12 is sufficient at this compute level”. This is a repetition-diversity trade-off at one operating point and not a data-efficiency result. In deployment, practitioners would not hold C fixed. They would use the data they have. The finding should either be reframed as a characterisation of the optimal (N, E) trade-off at fixed C, or C should be varied to establish the claim’s robustness.
The layer-unfreezing ablation (Table 2) uses a single seed. This is the key ablation justifying the “last-layer” design choice, yet it is run at n = 1 while all other experiments use 5 seeds. The differences reported in Table 2 between L and L,L−1 for BIOT, and between L and All for CBraMod are plausibly within seed noise. “Optimal parameter efficiency” claim is not statistically supported as presented.
No statistical testing on main results. Paired significance tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank on paired seed differences, or bootstrap confidence intervals on the difference) would directly support the claimed improvements. Several comparisons have overlapping or near-overlapping SEM bands and the magnitude of statistical evidence cannot be assessed without formal tests.
Patient-agnostic claim weakest where it matters clinically. Figure 2 shows that on CHBMIT (the only dataset with a realistically small cohort range) error bars overlap substantially, and no trend test is reported. The authors acknowledge this limitation in the conclusion. The deployment scenario motivating the claim (“longer recordings from smaller cohorts”) is precisely the small-P regime where the evidence is weakest. A formal trend test would materially strengthen this claim.
Inconsistent parameter-count. The conclusion states SA updates “<10% of parameters,” but Section 3.2 reports 0.92M of 3.19M = 28.8% for BIOT. The “<10%” claim holds only for CBraMod (9.0%).
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Consider reporting the repetition factor r explicitly alongside N in Figure 1, so the repetition-diversity trade-off is visually legible rather than implicit.
The patient-agnostic finding is consistent with recent SSL results in vision. A brief discussion of whether this generalises from natural images to medical time-series, would enrich the contribution.
Future work could compare against LoRA, adapters, at matched parameter budgets to place the last-layer SSL adaptation strategy within the broader parameter-efficient fine-tuning landscape.

The paper addresses a clinically relevant question with several sound elements: patient-disjoint splits, explicit ID/OOD labelling, evaluation across two pretraining objectives, and a layer-unfreezing ablation (Table 2) showing the non-obvious result that updating more layers does not help. Reproducibility is adequate.
The paper falls below the acceptance threshold because the central claim, self-supervised parameter-efficient adaptation is valuable, is not isolated by the experimental design. The only baseline is zero-shot linear probing on frozen features. A supervised last-layer fine-tuning control at matched |θ_adapt| on the same target data is absent. This is the one comparison that would establish whether the SSL objective contributes anything beyond “any last-layer update on target data helps.” The deployment motivation (label scarcity) is not instantiated in the experiments (linear probing uses the full labelled training set). The concern is compounded on CHBMIT, where the LP baseline is near-random (AUCPR 1.53% vs. random floor 1.48%).
Two secondary issues reinforce this. The “20–50% of data is sufficient” finding (Section 3.3) is mechanically entailed by the fixed-compute design C = N·E. It is a repetition-diversity trade-off at one compute level, not a data-efficiency result. The layer-unfreezing ablation (Table 2) uses a single seed while the rest of the paper uses five.
Without the supervised baseline, the central attribution remains unsupported. A supervised comparison provided in the rebuttal, if SA still wins, would move my rating upward.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The rebuttal addresses the majority of my pre-rebuttal concerns substantively. On statistical testing, the authors provide BCa bootstrap confidence intervals on paired SA−LP deltas across all 5 seeds and 6 model–dataset configurations, with all intervals above zero and large effect sizes (Hedge’s g > 0.8 on 5/6 comparisons). They commit to re-running the layer-unfreezing ablation at 5 seeds, with preliminary results confirming the original single-seed finding. For the patient-count claim, Spearman correlations and linear regression slopes are all non-significant, supporting the patient-agnostic conclusion. The parameter-count inconsistency is acknowledged and will be corrected. The authors explicitly accept my characterisation of the data-efficiency finding as a repetition-diversity trade-off at fixed compute and agree to reframe accordingly.
My primary pre-rebuttal concern, absence of a supervised last-layer fine-tuning baseline, is not fully resolved. The authors argue that the LP→SA gain is attributable solely to SA because the linear head is trained identically in both conditions, and that supervised FT does not match their deployment scenario (label scarcity). The first point is correct but does not address whether the SSL objective specifically drives the gain versus any form of last-layer update. The second point is legitimate in principle but is not instantiated in their experiments, since the linear probe uses the full labelled training set. I maintain that a supervised control at matched would strengthen the paper.

meta_reviews.text:
There are inconsistencies in reported parameters, also justify the choice for not using a fully supervised model as baseline. Further statistical evaluations if performed should be reported.

The authors have addressed most of the concerns raised in the review.

The paper addresses an important and clinically relevant problem: parameter-efficient adaptation of EEG foundation models under limited labeled data and constrained computational settings. Reviewers appreciated the patient-disjoint evaluation, explicit ID/OOD analysis, comparisons across multiple SSL paradigms, and the generally strong experimental design and reproducibility. Several concerns were raised regarding the absence of a supervised baseline, the interpretation of the fixed-compute experiments, and the statistical support for some ablations. However, the rebuttal clarified a number of these concerns and appropriately reframed several claims and limitations. While some limitations remain, particularly regarding the SSL-specific attribution, the paper still provides meaningful empirical insights and practical value for the EEG foundation model community. Overall, I support acceptance.

This paper provides a nice study on how much data is actually required for adapting current EEG-FM models to achieve reasonable performance when adapted on a new dataset and task. The authors use standard SSL based adaptation and fine-tuning approaches for this and demonstrate their experiments across important benchmarks used in EEG, as well as some ID/OOD settings. There is no particular novelty in their approach, however, it is a systematized study that explores this aspect of EEG-FM.
I think it’s a valuable contribution to the community of EEG processing, as there have been many EEG-FMs being developed in recent times and this could showcase their capabilities. Although the paper could be improved further in several aspects where more recent FMs could be included, other aspects of validation could be considered, etc. I think it’s a good contribution in it’s current form that could really spark some discussions during the conference.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the reviewers and AC. R2 recommends accept; R1 and R3 weak-reject pending rebuttal. R2 and R3 acknowledge the well-controlled design, ID/OOD comparison with different pretraining objectives, patient-disjoint splits, and patient-window decomposition (R3: largely unaddressed in the EEG-FM literature). We address the AC’s three explicit requests: [A] parameter consistency, [B] supervised-baseline justification, [C] statistical evaluation and, [D] R1’s domain-specificity concern.
[A] Parameter consistency. 10% applies only to CBraMod (0.44M/4.44M=10.0%); BIOT updates 0.92M/3.19M=28.8%. We will revise Abstract/Conclusion with no changes in results necessary.
[B] Justification for omitting supervised fine-tuning (SFT, R3). In Linear Probe (LP) baseline, the pretrained EEG-FM encoder is frozen and only a linear head (LH) is trained on labeled target data. In SSL adaptation (SA), the encoder’s final layer is updated via the model’s own SSL objective on unlabeled target data before the LH is trained. Both train the same LH on the same labeled set with the same encoder frozen at probe time. The LP→SA gain (Table 1) is therefore only attributable to SA, SFT control is not needed to isolate this effect. SFT presumes labeled target-domain data, an assumption that does not match our deployment scenario. Importantly, SSL pretext drives gains across contrastive (BIOT) and masked-reconstruction (CBraMod), indicating the effect lies in the SSL objective, not simply updating extra parameters. Thus, it is a specific instantiation (see Sec 2.1) rather than generic SSL protocol (R1).
[C] Statistical evaluation (R3). (i) Table 1 results: on per-seed SA-LP deltas (5 paired seeds x 6 model-dataset configurations) using bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) bootstrap confidence intervals (95% CI, 9,999 resamples, B. Efron (1987)) lie above zero when considered for performance metrics(AUCPR for TUAB/CHB-MIT, F1 for TUEV), establishing significance at alpha=0.05.Effect size is large on 5/6 comparisons (Hedge’s g > 0.8). (ii) We will also rerun the layer-unfreezing ablation (Table 2, R3) at 5 seeds; first results confirm that updating only the last layer performs as well as updating two or all layers, with 2-7x fewer parameters. (iii) Patient-agnostic claim (Figure 2, R3): Spearman rank correlation between P and performance is negative in any of the 6 model-dataset pairs (p-value in range 0.24 - 0.97). Similarly, linear regression fits on raw observations per model-dataset pair show that all slope parameters (Figure 2) are not significantly different from 0, suggesting a absence of patient count effect. Full statistical account will be added to the final conclusion.
[D] EEG-specific contribution under clinical-deployment constraints (R1). Our central question is: can we leverage representations of pretrained EEG-FMs and adapt them to OOD clinical settings using unlabeled data — and if so, how much data is needed? We would argue that parameter-efficiency is the deployment constraint. We make 3 specific contributions: (i) bridging OOD shifts in EEG hardware, montage and sampling-rate differences (ii) characterizing the unlabeled target-domain data required for adaptation — we agree with R3 this is a repetition-diversity trade-off at fixed C and will reframe; (iii) showing that longer recordings from few patients are as effective as brief recordings from many.
[E] We acknowledge R2’s typo suggestions (define FM in abstract; standardize CHB-MIT; fix short title); release code on GitHub for reproducibility (R1); rename zero-shot LP to linear probe (LP) throughout per SimCLR/CLIP convention (R2); report repetition factor (r) alongside N in Figure 1 (R3). We will also update our conclusion and future work (R3) to include: SSL LoRA based comparison at matched parameter budgets; generalization to other medical time-series; discussion of whether the patient-agnostic finding transfers from natural images to medical time-series.

title: Patch-to-Global: Random Patch Diffusion for Globally Consistent Megapixel Artifact Inpainting in Whole Slide Images
abstract: Although deep learning has advanced Whole Slide Image (WSI) Analysis, tissue artifacts like bubbles and folds often cause silent failures by concealing essential morphology. Current pathology image restoration methods are mostly restricted to small patches, struggling to maintain global structural coherence at a megapixel scale. We in troduce RestorePath, a framework for globally consistent megapixel scale inpainting that reconstructs diagnostic structures in histological image to prevent incorrect high-confidence predictions and lower error rates. Our model utilizes a Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) conditioned on Pathology Foundation Model (PFM) embeddings, integrating Large Kernel Attention (LKA) to manage long-range dependencies during random patch diffusion. Enhanced by Distance-Weighted Interpolation (DWI) and an Adaptive Guidance Scale (AGS), RestorePath ensures structural consistency and fidelity by modulating information from surrounding patches. Evaluations across TCGA-BRCA, BACH, and Camelyon16 datasets for images ranging from 512 to 4608 pixels demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in maintaining histological consistency. RestorePath significantly improves downstream Computational Pathology (CP) tasks, outperforming both raw artifact images and the conventional Detect-and-Discard (D&D) approach. The code is available at https://github.com/PathfinderLab/RestorePath.
