N/A

1.The ultimate contribution of this work to the pathology Mutimodal report generation model is not clear. The extendability is weak based on the current narrative.
2.The three main contributions the authors stated are not well supported by evidence.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
This is an elegant approach to include the gaze information from different pathologists, showing how it helps improve report generation. Its a nice study, but I invite the authors to consider using aditional approaches for baseline, and evaluation in other independent datasets, maybe where reports may not be available but ground Grade groups are, like prior pathology grading challanges. The ACC-G to me is on the low side for clinical utility, but maybe with additional evidence, examples and error analysis we can better appreciate the value of the approach.

Congratulations for your submission. Well done.

The reviewers were largely positive following the rebuttal. The most engaged reviewer noted that the authors clarified the paper’s core contribution.
I find the rebuttal addresses the main concerns adequately. Two reviewers lean toward acceptance, and the reviewer inclined to reject did not submit post-rebuttal comments. On balance, the rebuttal is convincing and the contribution is sound, so I recommend acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the Meta-Reviewer (MR) and Reviewers 1, 2, and 3 (R1, R2, R3) for their insightful feedback. 
We organize our responses as (1)–(11), with “<>” indicating the corresponding reviewer(s).
(1) <R1, R2, R3, MR> If accepted, we will release our code and dataset.
(2)
ACC-G for clinical utility: After additional analysis on the performance of the model on gleason score classification (CLS) following HistGen’s CLS protocol, Gleason CLS AUC improves from 0.71 (baseline) to 0.77 (Ours). It is higher than ACC-G since ACC-G is extracted from generated reports, where the model is optimized for free-text generation rather than score prediction. But the gains over baselines and the pathologist-involved analysis in Response (9) support its clinical utility.
(3)
Generalization: Our observation on PathoGaze [1], a breast-cancer attention dataset with classification (CLS) labels, suggests that human-attention alignment can also improve CLS on another domain from 0.833 to 0.989.
(4)
Error Analysis: For small tumor regions where the baseline VLM is strongly mislocalized, alignment provides only partial correction as it remains constrained by the VLM backbone.
(5)
Methodological novelty: While we acknowledge GazeVLM in Sec. 3.2, our primary contribution is the novel end-to-end pipeline for pathology report generation. We define a new research task and provide a proof-of-concept for grounding clinical narratives in pathologist attention.
(6)
Component coverage: We excluded rare components such as seminal vesicle invasion (positive in only 2 slides), that are insufficient for reliable attention supervision and evaluation.
(7)
Influence of personalization: While our six pathologists (2 specialists, 2 generalists, 2 residents) show diverse gaze behaviors, our "positive-component-filtering" distills shared diagnostic evidence from individual attention. For multi-reader slides, this approach increases heatmap similarity from 0.55 to 0.71.
(8)
Regularization effect and uncertainty: Gains in Tab. 2 suggest that improvements stem from visual grounding rather than mere text-side regularization. Manual verification showed 100% agreement with the LLM results due to the structured reports.
(9) <R2, R3> Evaluation of Interpretability: Our goal is not to add a new visual-support output, but to make existing attention maps more clinically useful, as shown in Tab 2.Pathologists’ evaluation confirms that our method provides strong tumor-focused and clinically meaningful visual support, preferred in 80% of cases over baselines on overall quality and component-specific diagnosis.
(10)
“Plug-and-Play”: Our method requires no architectural changes and adds no parameters. The finetuned layers and original loss coefficients follow each backbone’s default design, while the KL-loss coefficient is shared across models. The only model-specific difference is dataset preprocessing, i.e., grid alignment between gaze heatmaps and visual tokens. Using last-layer attention follows standard grounding practices [2,3] and consistently achieves the best.
(11)
Lack of translation: We focus on prostate cancer report generation, which adapts pre-trained pathology VLMs to a clinical domain. While human attention provides efficient, diagnosis-aware supervision (3 min/slide), segmentation masks are 10-times more costly and frequently unavailable for report-level components like surgical margins. Also, synthetic masks add noise due to current Gleason classification limitations, discussed in Response (2). We expect strong transfer properties to novel cancers once attention data is scaled (discussed in Response (3)), with future work focused on broader cross-domain generalization.
References:
[1] Eye-Tracking, Mouse Tracking, Stimulus Tracking,and Decision-Making Datasets in Digital Pathology.
[2] Grounded Language-Image Pre-training.
[3] Pointing and Asking: A Context-and-Task-Aware Framework for Visual Question Answering.

title: PathoMamba: Piecewise-Diffeomorphic Registration via Stiffness-Modulated State Space Dynamics
abstract: Longitudinal glioma registration faces a fundamental Correspondence - Regularity Conflict: healthy parenchyma requires high stiffness to prevent folding, while tumor evolution demands local plasticity to accommodate mass effect. Current deep learning frameworks, treating the brain as a mechanically homogeneous continuum, fail to resolve this paradox. We propose PathoMamba, a stiffness-modulated State Space Model (SSM) that bridges continuum mechanics and deep learning. By reinterpreting the SSM discretization step (∆) as learnable Numerical Inertia, we actively modulate feature dynamics—enforcing rigidity in healthy tissue while enabling rapid updates in the pathology. This is coupled with a Therapy-Aware Biomechanical objective to robustly model heterogeneous growth and shrinkage trends. Validated on the BraTS-Reg benchmark, PathoMamba matches state-of-the-art Transformer accuracy (1.88 mm) while inferring 2× faster and uniquely guaranteeing 0.00% topological folding, offering a safe, physics-informed solution for clinical monitoring.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper introduces PathoMamba, a novel registration framework designed to address the correspondence-regularity conflict: healthy tissue requires high stiffness to prevent folding, whereas gliomas require high plasticity to model mass effects.
The primary contribution of this work is the Stiffness-Modulated Dynamics (SMD) mechanism. By reinterpreting the discretization step of a State Space Model (SSM) as learnable Numerical Inertia, the authors provide a way to spatially vary the network’s “memory” and feature update rate. This allows the model to treat healthy parenchyma as a rigid, high-inertia material and pathological tissue as a plastic, low-inertia material, and by employing the scaling-and-squaring algorithm, it guarantees topological safety.
The authors also propose the Therapy-Aware Biomechanical Loss to handle the heterogeneous nature of glioma evolution (simultaneous cavity collapse and recurrence).
reviews.text_strengths:
The reinterpretation of the Mamba discretization parameter as physical stiffness/numerical inertia is interesting and theoretically grounded. It moves beyond simple “mask-weighting” and embeds biomechanics into the architecture’s latent dynamics.
The use of an omnidirectional 6-way scanning mechanism successfully adapts the 1D nature of SSMs to 3D medical volumes. Integrating this with a Stationary Velocity Field (SVF) ensures diffeomorphic mappings, which is a clinical necessity.
The proposed method can achieve good topological folding performance while providing a 2x speedup over state-of-the-art Transformer-based models like TransMorph, highlighting the efficiency of the linear-complexity SSM backbone.
reviews.text_weaknesses: Heavily relies on an external segmentation model (nnU-Net) to generate the Signed Distance Function (SDF) prior. While the Mamba backbone offers impressive inference speedups, the quantitative performance (1.88 mm mTRE) does not actually exceed existing state-of-the-art results from literature (e. g. , DIRAC-D or BiPyramid). The contribution appears to be purely about efficiency or the folding ratio, rather than a breakthrough in registration precision for the BraTS-Reg benchmark. The paper also lacks a rigorous reproduction of key state-of-the-art methods for the BraTS-reg benchmark, such as NR-IAM or DIRAC.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

(1) A single 80/20 random split is insufficient for the heterogeneous nature of gliomas, necessitating k-fold cross-validation. Furthermore, the authors didn’t stratify landmarks into “near-tumor” versus “far-from-tumor” zones, which is critical for verifying the claimed biomechanical advantages of the model.
(2) The comparison primarily focuses on general baseline models rather than established BraTS-Reg state-of-the-art methods. The lack of reported accuracy improvement makes the contribution’s value unclear.
(3) The work is currently difficult to replicate due to a lack of source code.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a registration network for longitudinal glioma progression analysis. By incorporating a stiffness-modulated State Space Model (SSM) into a U-Net-like Mamba architecture, together with a mask-based Therapy-Aware Biomechanical Loss, the method aims to achieve relatively rigid registration outside the ROI (glioma region) while allowing deformable registration within and around the ROI. The method is well motivated for the specific clinical problem, as it encourages the registration to focus on pathological changes caused by glioma progression. The paper also evaluates the method on a public challenge dataset and reports promising registration accuracy together with diffeomorphic deformation.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper proposes an interesting modification of Mamba by using a Signed Distance Function (SDF) to dynamically control the update behavior of the SSM in different regions. In this way, the healthy tissue can evolve more slowly while the tumour region can respond more quickly, which is well aligned with the characteristics of longitudinal glioma registration.
2.The paper further introduces a mask-based Trend-Aware Biomechanical Loss (TABL), which penalizes the deformation field according to tumour growth or shrinkage trends. This is a meaningful design for handling heterogeneous pathological changes and is more task-specific than a standard uniform regularization strategy.
3.The paper includes comparisons with several state-of-the-art methods on a public challenge dataset, and the ablation study also shows that the proposed components are useful.
4.The proposed method may also extend to other longitudinal studies with tumor-like lesions and mask guidance beyond glioma registration.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The method section is not clearly described, and some important parts are missing or insufficiently explained, as detailed in the comments below. In addition, no source code link or code placeholder is provided. The authors should either describe the method in more detail or release the code to ensure reproducibility.
2.The experimental and results sections are also unclear. For example, important settings such as the LNCC window size and the number of scaling-and-squaring steps are not provided. Please see the comments below for more details.
3.All experiments lack statistical significance testing. For the BraTS-Reg state-of-the-art results collected from the literature, statistical testing may not be feasible, but at least the reproduced baselines should be tested. The same issue also applies to the ablation study.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1.The paper lacks the parameter settings for the scaling-and-squaring step, such as the number of integration/squaring steps. These details should be clearly described, or the authors should provide code for reproduction.
2.It would be better to add a short description of matrices A and B in Equation 1.3.In Equation 2, the variables W_img, W_sdf, and x_p. are not clearly described. Please add a brief explanation for each variable.
4.For L_sim, the authors use LNCC as the similarity loss, but LNCC implementations can vary, for example in box/window size. The authors should either provide a standard reference or release the code for reproduction.
5.The paper seems to mention L_MK, but its definition or introduction is missing. This should be clarified.
6.It is not clear how the OSM block is used within the U-Net-like architecture from both the figure and the text. The connection between the architecture figure and the method description should be made clearer. If space is limited, the authors could add a brief explanation and cite a reference.
7.In the ablation study, does the full method not include L_diff, or is it omitted in the table due to limited space? In addition, the configuration names are not well aligned with the method section. For example, “Input Concat” should be described more clearly so that readers can understand exactly which design it corresponds to.
8.In Fig. 2, the mask overlay seems to have no transparency, so the original warped image can barely be seen. The visualization should be improved to make the qualitative results easier to interpret.
9.Although the proposed pipeline relies on an auxiliary pretrained nnU-Net at inference to generate the pathology prior SDF, the authors have already briefly discussed this aspect. For a short conference paper, this is likely sufficient. It could still be useful for future work to further discuss robustness to segmentation errors and comparison with image-only baselines.

The current manuscript still has substantial clarity issues, especially in the method description and implementation details. However, I find the core idea novel and well motivated, and it directly targets an important difficulty in longitudinal tumor registration. For this reason, I lean toward weak accept. If the authors can carefully address the above comments, particularly by making the method section clearer and improving reproducibility, the paper has the potential to become a good contribution.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors provided appropriate explanations for several formulas and variables and promised to release the code after acceptance, supporting reproducibility. They also provided deeper explanations and reasonable justifications for the ablation study. Given that the proposed SDF-guided Mamba design and trend-aware biomechanical loss are well aligned with longitudinal glioma registration and may also be extended to other mask-guided tumour-like longitudinal studies, I recommend acceptance.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes PathoMamba, a deformable registration framework for longitudinal glioma imaging that explicitly addresses the conflict between enforcing smooth, topology-preserving deformations and capturing tumor-induced mass effects. Its key contribution is the reinterpretation of the State Space Model (SSM) discretization step as a learnable “numerical inertia”, which enables spatially varying stiffness by modulating the internal model dynamics rather than relying solely on loss-based constraints.
reviews.text_strengths:
A major strength is the novel reinterpretation of the SSM discretization step Δ as a learnable numerical inertia, enabling spatially varying stiffness directly in the model dynamics. This provides a principled mechanism to decouple rigid and non-rigid deformation, addressing the correspondence vs. regularity trade-off in longitudinal tumor registration .
The proposed stiffness-modulated dynamics (SMD) go beyond prior mask-conditioned or loss-weighted approaches by actively modulating the evolution operator using anatomical priors (SDF). This shift from passive regularization to dynamics-level conditioning is technically meaningful. The therapy-aware biomechanical loss (TABL) introduces component-wise, physically interpretable constraints on volume change, improving modeling of heterogeneous tumor evolution beyond standard smoothness regularization. The architecture is efficient and well designed, mitigating SSM’s 1D bias via multi-directional scanning while maintaining linear complexity. Finally, the method achieves competitive accuracy with strict topological guarantees (0% folding) and is supported by targeted ablation studies, demonstrating effective integration of the proposed components
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The experimental validation is limited to a single benchmark (BraTS-Reg) with a fixed data split, and lacks evaluation across datasets or imaging conditions. This restricts conclusions about generalizability, especially given the strong dependence on tumor segmentation quality.
2.The method further relies on an auxiliary segmentation model (nnU-Net) at inference time, introducing an additional dependency that is not jointly optimized and may propagate errors. While some robustness analysis is reported, failure modes under inaccurate segmentations are not systematically studied.
3.the paper lacks comparisons to recent SSM-based registration models (e.g., MambaMorph, VMambaMorph) beyond basic baselines, making it difficult to assess whether the proposed stiffness modulation provides a consistent advantage over closely related architectures
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I recommend a weak accept because the paper presents a technically sound and well-motivated approach with a meaningful conceptual contribution, despite limited overall novelty.
The key factor is the reinterpretation of the SSM discretization step as a learnable physical control variable, enabling spatially varying stiffness directly within the model dynamics. This provides a principled mechanism to address the correspondence–regularity trade-off and goes beyond standard loss-based constraint formulations .
The method is coherent and well engineered, achieves competitive performance with strict topological guarantees, and is validated on a relevant benchmark.
The weaknesse: primarily incremental novelty, reliance on segmentation priors, and limited experimental scope, prevent a stronger recommendation but do not outweigh the core contribution.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper proposes an image registration approach for the BRATS-reg dataset. The goal of the proposed approach is to develop a registration approach that can be applied in the context of brain tumors and where one may want to account for different deformation patters within and outside the tumor region.
The proposed approach uses a state-space approach (Mamba) to modulate the behavior of the network when predicting a stationary velocity field (SVF). Specifically, it makes use of a tumor segmentation and its associatd signed distance field to allow for rapid state changes inside the tumor region and for comparatively smaller changes in the surrouding healthy tissues. Beyond this there is a weighted diffusion regularization of the SVF, a trend-aware biomechanical loss, an LNCC similarity measure, and an undefined L_{MK} loss term.
The paper has several strength:
The reviewers appreciated the goal of using an active modulation of the Mamba timestep to model faster and slower changing tissue effects as well as the integration with the tumor segmentation.
The reviewers appreciated the Trend-Aware Biomechanical Loss.
Reviewers appreciated that due to the SVF formulation diffeomorphic transformations could be obtained.
The paper has several shortcomings:
The work is very task-specific and hence is only evaluated on one dataset (BRATS-Reg)
Some of the notation is not well decribed. (L_{MK}, W_{img}, W_{sdf})
There is significant lack of clarity in the model descriptions themselves as well as in the experiments (see the detailed comments by reviewer 2).
No real accuracy improvements over state of the art are achieved.
The method relies on an external segmentation network.
For the rebuttal please focus on the following aspects:
Please clarify how you will fix the notation / descriptions. For example, what is L_{MK}? What are W_{img}, W_{sdf}? (Just learned parameter matrices?)
Provide a discussion on what L_{TABL} and L_{MK} do.
Address reviewer questions regarding comparisons to state of the art approaches on this dataset.
Provide a clearer discussion of what Table 2 shows and how one should interpret these results. For example, are the differences between methods (2) and (3) in this table simply your approach with the dynamic timestep \Delta versus keeping it fixed (as this seems to be the key contribution)? And is the difference between 3 and 4 the addition of L_{TABL}? What happened to L_{diff}?
Please also comment on the achieved regularity of the velocity field / deformation map inside and outside the tumor region. In particular, what is alpha in Eq. (3) set to and how much lower does the weight become in the tumor region? If it drops very fast it seems there will be hardly any regularity constraint (seems potentially bad). If it drops too slow then this would encode less regularity the deeper one is inside a tumor (is this the intended behavior?). Please discuss.
Please address any other reviewer concerns as space permits.

This paper proposes an image registration approach for the BRATS-reg dataset. The goal of the proposed approach is to develop a registration approach that can be applied in the context of brain tumors and where one may want to account for different deformation patters within and outside the tumor region.
The proposed approach uses a state-space approach (Mamba) to modulate the behavior of the network when predicting a stationary velocity field (SVF). Specifically, it makes use of a tumor segmentation and its associatd signed distance field to allow for rapid state changes inside the tumor region and for comparatively smaller changes in the surrouding healthy tissues. Beyond this there is a weighted diffusion regularization of the SVF, a trend-aware biomechanical loss, an LNCC similarity measure, and an undefined L_{MK} loss term.
The paper has several strength:
The reviewers appreciated the goal of using an active modulation of the Mamba timestep to model faster and slower changing tissue effects as well as the integration with the tumor segmentation.
The reviewers appreciated the Trend-Aware Biomechanical Loss.
Reviewers appreciated that due to the SVF formulation diffeomorphic transformations could be obtained.
The paper has several shortcomings / questions:
The work is very task-specific and hence is only evaluated on one dataset (BRATS-Reg)
Some of the notation is not well decribed. (L_{MK}, W_{img}, W_{sdf}) though could be in a revised version (and was addressed in the rebuttal).
There is significant lack of clarity in the model descriptions themselves as well as in the experiments.
No real accuracy improvements over state of the art are achieved. Though the rebuttal argues that the approach has other benefits such as 1) competitive accuracy, 2) no folding, 3) excellent tumor Dice, and 4) sub-second one-shot inference.
The rebuttal clarified some of the questions / shortcomings above and the reviewers are largely positive. This meta reviewer is concerned about clarity of the writing.

After reading the manuscript and following the review and rebuttal process, I believe this is a strong contribution for the MICCAI audience. The problem addressed is highly challenging, and the proposed solution is innovative. I particularly appreciated the Stiffness-Modulated Dynamics (SMD) mechanism and its integration into a state-space framework. I generally agree with the reviewer’s comments, and I believe the manuscript would further benefit from addressing the most relevant questions and concerns they raised. Incorporating these clarifications would strengthen the overall quality of the paper.

The paper received mixed recommendations following the rebuttal. Reviewer 2 upgraded their assessment to Accept after the authors clarified the formulation, committed to releasing the code, and provided additional hyperparameter details. Reviewer 3 maintained a Weak Accept recommendation, while Reviewer 1 did not update their review and remained at Weak Reject.
Although Reviewers 2 and 3 offered generally positive evaluations and acknowledged the novelty of the proposed method, both continued to express substantive concerns regarding the clarity of the presentation and the limited scope of the experimental validation. In addition, the method’s reliance on segmentation priors and the relatively modest gains over prior state-of-the-art methods further weakened the case for acceptance. In light of the post-rebuttal discussion and the overall reviewer feedback, I recommend rejection.

author_feedback_text:
We thank R1–R3 and AC. R2/R3 endorse our core contribution—reinterpreting the SSM step Δ as learnable Numerical Inertia—and all three acknowledge SMD, the SVF diffeomorphic guarantee, and TABL as novel.
[1] Notation (AC, R2).
L_MK is the SECOND term of Eq.(4): (1/|Ω_shell|)·Σ ReLU(|J_φ|−1−δ), a Monro–Kellie peritumoral-shell penalty suppressing unphysical expansion (|J|>1+δ) in the healthy rim around the tumor; combined with L_diff (w≈1 there since D>0) this maintains |J|≈1, realizing intracranial volume conservation. Full objective: L_total = L_sim + λ_reg·L_diff + λ_bio·(L_TABL + L_MK).
L_TABL applies a per-component Jacobian penalty driven by the observed log-volume ratio η_k = log(V_T1^k/V_T0^k): growing components (η_k>0) pushed toward |J|>1, shrinking ones toward |J|<1, robustly handling simultaneous recurrence and cavity collapse.
W_img, W_sdf (Eq.2) are learnable 1×1×1 convs (per-voxel linear projections of x_p, D_p).
A, B (Eq.1) are standard Mamba matrices [9]; A is S4D-real initialized, B input-dependent.
LNCC uses a 9³ window (MONAI default); scaling-and-squaring uses 7 steps.
[2] Regularity and α (AC).
We set α=1.0 with D_p in mm, so w(D)=σ(D): w(+5)=0.993, w(+1)=0.731, w(0)=0.500, w(−1)=0.269, w(−5)=0.007.The transition is smooth across a ~2mm band around the boundary—not a sharp drop. Three deliberate properties: (i) at the boundary w≈0.5 retains substantial smoothness, preventing folding (Tab.1: 0.00%); (ii) in deep healthy tissue (D≥5mm) w→1 enforces full rigidity where folding risk is highest; (iii) in the deep tumor core (D≤−5mm) w→0 admits the plasticity mass effect requires—this is intentional. Stability inside the tumor is additionally enforced by L_TABL and the SVF parameterization, so smoothness is never the sole constraint.
[3] Table 2 (AC, R2).
Each row isolates one component. (1)→(2): adds passive SDF concatenation at the U-Net input (mask-conditioning baseline). (2)→(3): replaces passive concat with ACTIVE modulation of Δ via Eq.(2)—the proposed SMD; the sole architectural change, directly isolating dynamic vs. fixed Δ. (3)→(4): adds L_TABL+L_MK on top. L_diff is retained in EVERY configuration; the row-(4) “L_sim+L_TABL” label is shorthand for the newly added term—the full L_total objective applies to all rows. The (2)→(3) gap (~0.15–0.20mm) directly quantifies dynamic Δ over passive concatenation—our central architectural claim.
[4] SOTA positioning (R1, R3).
The contribution is not raw mTRE but a unique combination: (i) competitive 1.88mm (tied with DIRAC-D; within 0.03mm of VMambaMorph 1.85); (ii) 0.00% folding—a strict topological safety guarantee no listed method matches; (iii) best tumor Dice 0.81; (iv) sub-second one-shot inference, 2× faster than TransMorph. LapIRN (1.82
) and DIRAC-Opt (1.76
) report MEDIAN TRE under instance optimization at 4–60s/case; mean vs. median and instance-opt vs. one-shot are not directly comparable. R3’s request for SSM comparison is already met in Tab.1: MambaMorph [10] (1.95), VMambaMorph [23] (1.85), and locally reproduced RegMamba (2.24) as the physics-blind ablation.
[5] nnU-Net robustness (R1, R3).
§3.2 reports that under ±5mm SDF perturbation mTRE degrades marginally from 1.88 to ~1.94mm (the printed “0.6mm” is a transcription error), while folding remains 0.00%. Δ_p is co-modulated by image features (W_img·x_p in Eq.2), letting the network override mild segmentation errors via local texture. Catastrophic failure remains a known limitation, as stated.
[6] Other points.
k-fold CV / multi-dataset / further reproductions (R1, R3) cannot be added at rebuttal per MICCAI rules; landmarks are strictly held-out and identical across all locally reproduced baselines, ensuring fair comparison on this split. Code will be released upon acceptance.

title: Patient-Conditioned Vision–Language Priors with Stable Mixture-of-Experts for Label-Efficient Alzheimer’s MRI Staging
abstract: Accurate staging of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) from structural MRI is clinically valuable, yet training reliable multi-class models is constrained by limited labels and by the asymmetric risk of diagnostic errors: a two-stage confusion between cognitively normal (CN) and AD is far more harmful than an off-by-one error with mild cognitive impairment (MCI). We present a label-efficient and safety-aware framework that couples (i) a frozen \emph{patient-conditioned} vision–language prior, built by prompting a pretrained CLIP text encoder with demographics and aligning it with CLIP image embeddings from representative MRI slices, (ii) a \emph{scale-preserving} mixture-of-experts (MoE) router that stabilizes expert utilization under small-batch, imbalanced training, and (iii) an EMA teacher for semi-supervised consistency. Across OASIS and ADNI under 10–50\% labeled data, the proposed model consistently achieves the best accuracy and ordinal agreement while reducing mean absolute error and a clinically weighted mis-staging cost. At 10\% labels, we reach QWK 0.806/0.823 on OASIS/ADNI and reduce clinical cost to 0.158/0.143, substantially shifting the clinical-safety frontier. Notably, with only 20\% labels we match the strongest baseline trained with 50\% labels, indicating a (\sim)2.5(\times) reduction in annotation demand.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a label-efficient framework for ordinal CN/MCI/AD staging from structural MRI that combines three ideas: (1) a patient-conditioned vision–language prior built from a frozen CLIP text encoder prompted by age/sex and a frozen CLIP image encoder applied to representative MRI slices, (2) a scale-preserving, norm-stabilized mixture-of-experts (MoE) head intended to avoid unstable expert usage in low-label, imbalanced training, and (3) an EMA teacher–student semi-supervised learning scheme for leveraging unlabeled scans.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper is clinically well framed, which I appreciated. Rather than treating AD staging as a standard flat 3-class classification problem, it emphasizes the ordinal nature of CN/MCI/AD and explicitly evaluates clinically important quantities such as MAE, screening sensitivity/specificity, AD NPV, and a weighted clinical cost.
2.The evaluation is consistently strong across two public cohorts and multiple label-scarce settings. In Table 1, the method improves over all listed baselines on both OASIS and ADNI across 10%, 20%, 30%, and 50% label ratios, and the gains are not confined to a single metric. This makes the empirical result more convincing than a single-dataset or single-split success.
3.The paper’s low-label/data-efficiency story is one of its strongest aspects. The reported result that 20% labeled data matches the strongest baseline at 50% labels is practically meaningful in this domain, where labels are expensive and often noisy. The paper also visualizes the clinical-safety frontier in Figure 2, which is a thoughtful way to communicate the joint benefit in ordinal agreement and lower staging deviation.
4.The proposed architecture is conceptually clean and modular. Figure 1 clearly explains how the frozen VLM prior, demographic encoder, MoE routing, and EMA teacher interact.
5.The paper addresses an increasingly relevant direction in AD imaging: using multimodal priors and label-efficient training rather than only larger image-only backbones.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The claimed “vision–language prior” is weaker than the title suggests. The “text” is not a radiology report or even rich clinical text; it is a templated sentence generated from only age and sex. That may still be useful, but it is much closer to a demographic prompt than to a true clinical language signal.
2.Without a strong baseline that uses simple learned age/sex embeddings or direct concatenation of demographics, it is unclear whether the gain comes from CLIP-based cross-modal semantics or simply from adding demographics in a fancy way.
3.The paper is missing the most important ablations. There is no image-only backbone + SSL baseline inside the same framework, no ablation removing the VLM prior, no ablation replacing the proposed stable MoE with a standard classifier or standard MoE, no study of the ordinal regularizer, and no analysis of whether the gains come from the EMA teacher rather than the proposed architectural components.
4.The baseline set is not fully convincing for a SOTA claim. The paper compares against several semi-supervised baselines, but not against some of the most relevant recent AD MRI methods involving multimodal/VLM or MoE designs, such as ADLIP.
5.Reproducibility from the manuscript alone is not yet strong enough. Several core details are missing or underspecified: the exact 3D MRI backbone, CLIP variant, number of sampled slices K, preprocessing steps, weak/strong augmentations, pseudo-label thresholding, EMA momentum, number of experts, hidden dimensions, and the precise form of the ordinal regularizer.
6.The low-label results are reported on single splits with no variance analysis, which is a weakness for a label-scarce paper. At 10–20% labels, performance can vary substantially with the sampled labeled subset. Repeating experiments across several random subset samplings or reporting standard deviations would make the claims much stronger.
7.There is a potentially important protocol ambiguity: the paper states that train/validation/test splits are subject-wise, which is good, but it does not say whether the labeled/unlabeled partition within the training set is also subject-wise. Since ADNI and OASIS can contain multiple scans per subject, having one scan labeled and another unlabeled from the same subject could artificially make the SSL problem easier. This should be clarified explicitly.
8.Because age and sex are injected directly into the prior, the paper should include at least a brief fairness or subgroup robustness analysis. Otherwise it is difficult to know whether the gains reflect improved disease modeling or increased reliance on demographic shortcuts.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I place this paper slightly above the acceptance threshold. The strongest reasons are the clinically meaningful problem formulation, the consistent low-label gains across two public cohorts, and the fact that the paper evaluates outcomes that matter in practice—ordinal agreement, catastrophic errors, screening behavior, and weighted clinical cost—rather than only top-1 accuracy.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: In this work, the authors propose a deep learning framework for AD prediction (CN, MC, and AD). The framework is label-efficient
reviews.text_strengths:
Content is well organized and figures are neat and legible
The work is well-motivated
The work is sufficiently evaluated against baselines to demonstrate value and superiority
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Despite acknowledging domain-specific encoders such as MedCLIP, CLIP is chosen without justification.
Authors do not indicate if any experiments were performed to compare and evaluate different prompt templates and their impact on performance.
Vision-language prior: if s captures the alignment between u and t, why is it once again concatenated with u and t and fed to an MLP? Also, what are the implementation details of the MLP such as number of features and activation function used? What is the value of alpha? Were different alpha values swept?
Concatenating demographic tokens with text tokens which already include demographic information seems redundant and is not well-motivated or justified.
The work lacks several implementation details such as learning rate, batch size, momentum value, input normalization strategy, and several other such relevant details.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
For slice-to-image CLIP embeddings, the authors state uniformly sampling along the axial axis. Does this include irrelevant peripheral slices?

The work is relevant and valuable. However, in view of the fact that the authors do not make any mention of availability of source code, the lack of major implementation details severely impedes reproducibility. Further more, most design decisions are not explained or justified.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a label-efficient and clinically safe framework for Alzheimer’s disease staging, which mainly consists of (1) a frozen vision-language prior (VLM prior) constructed based on patient demographic information, (2) a mixture-of-experts (MoE) classification head with scale-preserving and norm-stabilized properties, and (3) a semi-supervised learning mechanism incorporating an EMA teacher. On the OASIS and ADNI datasets, this method achieves optimal performance under label ratios of 10%-50%.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The orientation is clear, grasping the core challenges of label scarcity and clinical asymmetry of diagnostic errors, and designing a targeted clinically weighted cost function.
2.Achieving performance comparable to baseline methods with 50% labels using only 20% labels, addressing the issue of high clinical annotation costs.
3.The three components (VLM prior, MoE routing, and EMA semi-supervised learning) form an organic whole and achieve favorable results.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.It is recommended to supplement ablation studies to verify the necessity and synergistic effects of each component.
2.The comparison baselines are primarily methods from before 2023; it is suggested to compare with the latest methods from 2024-2026.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper makes a contribution to MRI-based staging of Alzheimer’s disease. However, the recommended revisions, specifically ablation studies and expanded baseline comparisons, would substantially enhance the manuscript’s completeness and impact.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper addresses an important and timely problem: label-efficient ordinal AD staging from structural MRI.
The empirical evidence is overall convincing. The method shows consistent gains across two public cohorts and multiple label ratios, and the result that 20% labeled data can match strong baselines using 50% labels is practically meaningful for medical imaging scenarios where annotations are costly.
The framework is also conceptually well organized, combining a frozen VLM prior, stabilized MoE head, and EMA teacher-student learning in a coherent way.
The authors should further clarify key implementation details and strengthen ablations on the VLM prior, MoE head, and EMA teacher.

title: PAVL: Enhancing Feature Prototype Alignment with Vision–Language Model for Semi-supervised Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Semi-supervised medical image segmentation (SSMIS) has garnered significant attention for its ability to reduce radiologists’ manual annotation burden. However, inadequate distinction between different categories in the feature space can lead to difficulty in distinguishing visually similar classes. Vision–language models like CLIP excel at disambiguating such categories through rich semantic representations, but their coarse‑grained embeddings struggle to capture fine structural details in complex medical scans. To address these challenges, we propose a CLIP-based SSMIS framework, which comprises three key components: unified representation matching (URM), prototype alignment (PA) and embedding fusion CLIP (EFCLIP). Specifically, URM aligns spatial feature representations between teacher and student networks to mitigate the impact of high-uncertainty voxels and ambiguous boundaries. Building on this, PA selects high-confidence voxels based on voxel-level uncertainty to construct robust class prototypes. Furthermore,  EFCLIP integrates CLIP’s text  embeddings with  voxel-level visual features, fusing global semantic priors with local spatial structure to enhance the discriminative ability for visually similar  voxels categorize. Extensive experiments on one public and one in-house  medical image datasets demonstrate that PAVL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art SSMIS methods.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes PAVL, a CLIP-based semi-supervised medical image segmentation framework comprising three components: Unified Representation Matching (URM), Prototype Alignment, and Embedding Fusion CLIP. The framework is evaluated on BraTS2019 and an in-house lung adenocarcinoma CT dataset under 10% and 20% labeled data settings, reporting consistent improvements over seven SSMIS baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The PA module’s formulation of voxel embeddings as multivariate Gaussian distributions, combined with inverse-variance weighting for prototype construction and Wasserstein-2 distance for alignment, is theoretically well-motivated. 
2.Table 2 offers a well-structured ablation that goes beyond simple add/remove comparisons: EFCLIP is compared against LoRA fine-tuning and CLIP-only guidance; URM is compared against standard KD and SRD distillation; and the PA module’s Wasserstein-2 distance is compared against Euclidean distance. This design allows readers to evaluate the specific contribution of each methodological choice rather than just the module as a whole. 
3.PAVL achieves statistically significant improvements (p < 0.05, two-sided paired t-test) on most metrics across both BraTS2019 and the in-house dataset under both 10% and 20% labeled settings.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The central claim of PAVL is that CLIP’s semantic representations help distinguish visually similar classes in the feature space. However, both evaluation datasets involve binary segmentation tasks (tumor vs. background), where there are no multiple visually similar classes to disambiguate. Neither dataset provides a scenario that meaningfully tests inter-class confusion. The overall DSC improvement observed does not constitute evidence that the method specifically addresses visually similar class confusion. As currently presented, there is a logical gap between the stated motivation and the experimental evidence. 
2.PAVL adds substantial components on top of the baseline. However, the paper provides no comparison of parameter counts, FLOPs, or training/inference time against any baseline. In semi-supervised learning evaluation, where unlabeled data can be better leveraged by larger models, this confound is particularly important to address. 
3.Section 3.3 contains several sentences reporting Pancreas-CT results (“PAVL sets new state-of-the-art performance, achieving DSC scores of 75.79% and 81.62% with only 10% and 20% labeled data”), yet this dataset is neither described in Section 3.1 nor present in Table 1.The omission raises questions about why Pancreas-CT results were removed and whether selective reporting may be involved.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The authors are encouraged to: (1) either replace the binary segmentation benchmarks with a multi-class dataset (e. g. , multi-organ segmentation, lesions with similar appearance) to validate the visually similar class claim, or add targeted analysis of boundary-ambiguous regions using a dedicated metric; (2) provide a parameter count and FLOPs comparison table against all baselines; (3) reconcile the Pancreas-CT experimental results

The paper proposes a methodologically coherent framework with a well-motivated probabilistic treatment of voxel uncertainty and a reasonable integration of CLIP semantics into SSMIS. The ablation study is more thorough than typical in the field. However, the core motivation—distinguishing visually similar classes—is not validated by the experimental setup. Second, the absence of any parameter or efficiency analysis leaves open the alternative explanation that gains stem from model capacity rather than design. And also some minor flaws are in the current form of this paper. These issues are addressable in revision, and the underlying ideas have merit, but the current submission requires substantial revision.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a novel SSMIS framework based on feature prototype alignment with vision–language (PAVL) to address class confusion in the feature space and CLIP’s limited ability to capture fine-grained spatial structures. PAVL employs the URM strategy to align spatial features between teacher and student models, utilizes PA module to construct more accurate class prototype distributions by voxel level uncertainty, and integrates CLIP’s global semantic prior knowledge with voxel-level local spatial structures. Experiments conducted on the public dataset BraTS2019 and internal medical image datasets demonstrate that PAVL outperforms certain SSMIS methods.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper integrates three components (URM, PA, EFCLIP) into a unified SSMIS framework, offering a relatively complete solution.
URM explicitly calibrates spatial features on high-uncertainty voxels and fuzzy boundaries, concentrating model capacity on hard samples more effectively than global consistency regularization.
PA constructs category prototypes by selecting high-confidence voxels based on voxel-level uncertainty, reducing noise and ensuring stable prototype representation.
EFCLIP uses element-wise product to fuse CLIP text embeddings with softmax probability maps, potentially improving discriminability for visually similar voxel classes.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper does not compare with Text-SemiSeg (MICCAI 2025), which shares the exact task (CLIP-enhanced SSMIS) and similar modular design, and reports competitive results on the same datasets.
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-04971-1_57
PA is highly similar to UPCoL (MICCAI 2023), PCCS (2025), and EPL (2024), which also use uncertainty masks to build/refine prototypes. The paper provides no direct comparison or theoretical differentiation.
Links: https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-43901-8_63; https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.06650; https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06181
The article does not clarify the advantages and disadvantages of element-wise product in EFCLIP compared to more commonly used cross-attention and additive fusion methods.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The proposed framework shows acceptable novelty in system integration and the lightweight EFCLIP design. However, the experimental validation is insufficient to support the claimed superiority. The omission of the most relevant baseline (Text-SemiSeg, MICCAI 2025) and the lack of direct comparison with existing uncertainty+prototype methods (UPCoL, PCCS, EPL) critically undermine the credibility of the results.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses two core challenges in semi-supervised medical image segmentation: poor inter-class distinction in feature space and the failure of CLIP’s coarse-grained embeddings to capture fine structural details in medical scans. It proposes PAVL, a CLIP-based framework composed of unified representation matching, prototype alignment and embedding fusion CLIP modules.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper is well-written with clear logical structure. The narrative flows smoothly from problem statement to method design and experimental validation.
2.It targets common challenges in semi-supervised medical image segmentation and proposes a three-module framework with a complete technical route.
3.The experiments are conducted on both public and in-house datasets under 10% and 20% annotation ratios, providing quantitative and qualitative results.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Major Weaknesses
1.Core modules URM and EFCLIP lack substantial novelty. URM is essentially the classic teacher-student feature-level consistency constraint in semi-supervised learning, only adding simple convolutional modules for adaptation, no substantial methodological innovation. EFCLIP’s text-visual fusion is highly consistent with prior text-based methods, only performing basic semantic fusion, no differentiated innovation.
2.PA module has limited novelty, only formal substitutions to classic methods. Its core logic remains selecting high-confidence samples to build class prototypes, only replacing conventional uncertainty measurement with feature variance, without breaking existing prototype learning-based semi-supervised segmentation frameworks, negligible incremental innovation.
3.Comparative experiments. Most methods in Table 1 are traditional semi-supervised methods, excluding latest foundation model-based SOTAs of the same type, failing to fairly verify the proposed method’s real performance advantage.
4.Ablation study. Table 2 lacks the key control group removing EFCLIP and retaining only URM and PA, making it impossible to separate gains from CLIP pre-training priors and the proposed modules’ contributions.
Minor Weaknesses
1.Method is only validated on two binary 3D segmentation tasks, not covering multi-class segmentation.
2.No limitations of the method are discussed, including computational overhead, inference speed, parameter count and stability.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The overall score is mainly determined by the limited novelty of the proposed modules, unfair comparison with recent SOTA methods, and flawed ablation design, which together weaken the methodological contribution and experimental reliability of this work.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text: This work exhibits strong practical value by systematically utilizing CLIP to resolve inter-class ambiguity and refine boundaries in semi-supervised feature spaces. Reviewers commend the mathematical rigor of the Prototype Alignment module, which effectively models voxel-level uncertainty via Wasserstein-2 distance to construct robust class prototypes.

title: PCRP: Progressive Coarse-to-Fine Refinement for Pathology Grounding
abstract: Pathology Visual Grounding aims to precisely localize pathological tissue regions in histopathology images and output bounding boxes based on professional medical language descriptions. However, in histopathology images, background textures are highly similar, while target regions are small, low-contrast, and blurred at the boundaries. In addition, medical descriptions can be difficult to understand accurately, making it challenging to associate the described textual location with a unique target region. Existing pathology visual grounding methods make insufficient use of fine-grained visual cues and rely more on coarse language-vision alignment, which can easily cause misalignment and drift in difficult samples, such as small targets, occlusion, or blurred boundaries. To address these issues, we propose PCRP (Progressive Coarse-to-Fine), a progressive framework for pathology visual grounding that improves grounding accuracy by strengthening reliable visual cues and performing robust boundary refinement. PCRP consists of four modules: Visual Branch, Text Branch, VWF, and C2F-BAR. This design reduces misalignment and drift in samples with small targets and blurred boundaries, thereby improving robustness and grounding quality. PCRP achieves state-of-the-art performance on RefPath and significantly outperforms PKNet by 11.68% Acc and 9.27% mIoU, validating its effectiveness. The source code is available at https://github.com/wuhengliangliang/PCRP.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper studies pathology visual grounding, aiming to localize pathological regions in histopathology images from medical language descriptions. The authors propose PCRP, a progressive coarse-to-fine framework with two main components: Visual-Word Fusion (VWF) for cross-modal alignment and C2F-BAR for boundary-aware box refinement using SAM-based mask priors. The method achieves strong results on the RefPath benchmark, especially on the more challenging 20× setting.
reviews.text_strengths:
Important task setting. 
Pathology visual grounding is a meaningful and relatively underexplored problem in computational pathology, especially because precise region localization from clinical language has practical value.
Strong empirical performance. 
The reported results on RefPath are impressive, with clear gains over prior methods, particularly on low-magnification images where grounding is more difficult.
Reasonable overall framework. 
The coarse-to-fine design is intuitive, and the use of visual cue enhancement plus mask-based refinement is well aligned with the challenges of small targets and blurry boundaries in pathology images.
Clear presentation. 
The paper is generally easy to follow, and the ablation study helps explain the contribution of each module.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Limited methodological novelty. 
In my view, the main weakness is that the proposed method is largely a combination of existing ideas rather than a clearly new technical contribution. Cross-attention-based vision-language fusion, gated residual updates, coarse-to-fine refinement, curriculum-style training, and the use of SAM-generated priors are all familiar design patterns. While the integration is reasonable, the paper does not sufficiently demonstrate what is fundamentally new beyond adapting these components to pathology grounding.
Heavy reliance on external priors weakens the novelty claim. 
A substantial part of the performance gain seems to come from using SAM3 as a teacher to provide mask priors for refinement. This is practically useful, but it makes the improvement feel more like a strong engineering pipeline built on top of an external foundation model, rather than a novel grounding method in itself. The paper should better clarify how much of the gain comes from the proposed architecture versus the external segmentation prior.
Experimental validation is still somewhat limited. 
Although the gains on RefPath are large, evaluation is restricted to a single benchmark. This makes it difficult to judge generalizability. In addition, the paper does not report variance across runs, statistical significance, or deeper analysis of failure cases. Given the surprisingly large improvement over previous work, stronger validation would be important.
Some claims are stronger than the evidence provided. 
The paper repeatedly emphasizes robustness on difficult cases such as tiny targets, blurred boundaries, and low magnification, but the supporting analysis is still relatively limited. More targeted breakdowns or controlled experiments would make these claims more convincing.
Overall, I think this is a well-motivated and practically useful paper, and the empirical results are strong. However, for me the technical novelty is not sufficient, and the current experimental evidence is not yet strong enough to fully support the scale of the claimed advance. Therefore, my current recommendation is weak reject.

reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes PCRP, a pathology visual grounding framework for localizing pathology regions from referring expressions in histopathology images. The method combines: (i) Visual-Word Fusion (VWF) to inject image-conditioned evidence into token-level textual representations, and (ii) C2F-BAR, a two-stage coarse-to-fine box regression scheme that uses SAM3-derived mask priors with reliability weighting and progressive prompt transition to refine boundaries under box-only supervision. reviews.text_strengths:

2.Good picture, the drawing enables easy following of the methodology

reviews.text_weaknesses:
The weakness is obvious in this work.
I list the major weaknesses from the top-priority to the bottom.
1.The refinement design is methodologically questionable because Stage-2 is driven by SAM3 masks obtained from box prompts, and during early training those prompts are ground-truth boxes. This introduces a strong privileged localization prior into the refinement process, making it unclear whether the reported gains come from better pathology grounding or simply from external mask-based correction under privileged supervision.
This means that the authors claimed that this work relies on vision-language interaction to find the object. However, the import of prior mask localization for the SAM3 actually gains from the object area leakage from ground truth.(mask area -> SAM3 -> prior knowledge)
I couldn’t argue that PCRP achieves good performance in this task, at least in their validated dataset. BUT I am afraid that the major improvement is from the attention area leakage via SAM3.
2.When excluding the SAM3 and corresponding enhancement module C2F-BAR. The VWF is essentially text-to-vision cross-attention with gated residual fusion. The novelty is moderate.
3.In real pathology workflows, the key challenge is often to detect tiny or easily overlooked abnormal regions that may not have been pre-localized by a human or an upstream model. However, the main gain of PCRP comes from Stage-2 refinement driven by SAM3 masks obtained from a box prompt. This design mainly improves localization around an already available candidate region, rather than demonstrating the ability to discover missed tiny targets. Therefore, the method seems better characterized as a candidate-refinement framework than a clinically meaningful solution for reducing oversight of subtle pathology findings.
4.All EXPERIMENT is only validated on a SINGLE DATASET.

The paper is relevant to MIC, and the reported gains on RefPath are substantial, which makes it a borderline submission rather than an outright reject. reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes PCRP, a progressive coarse-to-fine framework for pathology visual grounding. The method tackles two main issues in this task: semantic drift in language-image alignment and inaccurate localization under weak or blurry boundaries. To address these, the authors introduce Visual-Word Fusion (VWF) to inject image-conditioned visual evidence into word-level text features, and C2F-BAR, a two-stage regression framework that refines coarse predictions using confidence-weighted mask priors from a frozen SAM3 teacher. reviews.text_strengths:
(i) The paper studies a meaningful and relatively underexplored problem in computational pathology, namely visual grounding from pathology-specific referring expressions. 
(ii) The quantitative results are strong. The qualitative examples are also helpful.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(i) The main limitation is that the evaluation is restricted to RefPath only. The results on this benchmark are strong, but it is still hard to tell how well the method would generalize beyond this dataset or to other pathology grounding settings. 
(ii) The method depends on a frozen SAM3 teacher for mask priors, but the paper does not really analyze how sensitive the final performance is to the quality of these priors. This is particularly relevant because the Stage-2 refinement may be vulnerable when the Stage-1 box is already off-target. 
(iii) The paper would be stronger with a clearer discussion of computational overhead. Since the method introduces a two-stage refinement pipeline and relies on external mask generation, some reporting of runtime or inference cost would help readers judge the practical trade-off. 
(iv) While the ablations are useful, the analysis remains somewhat high level. It would be helpful to see more failure case analysis, especially for cases where the SAM3 prior is noisy or the referring expression is ambiguous. 
(v) There are a few presentation issues that should be cleaned up in the final version. For instance, the reference list appears to contain a duplicated citation for PathVG, and a few parts of the method section could be written more clearly.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
(i) References [18] and [19] seem to be the same PathVG paper, with the same authors, title, venue, and page numbers. The reference list and in-text citations should be cleaned up accordingly.
(ii) The paper would be stronger with more discussion of generalization beyond RefPath, since the current evaluation is limited to a single benchmark.
(iii) A brief analysis of runtime or computational overhead would also be helpful, given the two-stage design and the additional use of SAM3-based priors.
(iv) In the Stage-2 refinement part, the refined prediction should correspond to b1, and the loss function later also explicitly supervises b1 and b0.However, Eq. (8) is written as b0 = VLT(…), which is likely a notation error and should probably be b1
(v) The dependence on the quality of SAM3-generated mask priors deserves more analysis, especially in cases where the Stage-1 proposal is inaccurate.

I am leaning Weak Accept. The main reason is that the paper makes a fairly clear methodological contribution to pathology visual grounding and backs it up with strong empirical gains on the main benchmark. In particular, the improvement on the challenging 20× subset is substantial, which supports the authors’ claim that the method is especially helpful in difficult low-magnification settings. However, the evaluation is limited to one dataset and the practical implications of using SAM3-based mask priors are not fully analyzed.
