reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces a multitask framework for ischemic stroke lesion segmentation on NCCT scans, utilizing a DINOv3 foundation model as the backbone for a dual-head UNet to segment the infarct core and total ischemic tissue. To refine these predictions, the model undergoes joint optimization driven by three objectives: a standard segmentation loss, an auxiliary task using an MLP to predict the mismatch ratio (IschemicArea / CoreArea), and a conditional denoising diffusion model tasked with approximating Tmax perfusion maps.
reviews.text_strengths: The research addresses a highly relevant, but challenging problem: predicting stroke penumbra and core from NCCT. The methodology is innovative, particularly in its use of a modern foundation model (DINOv3) and the attempt to derive physiological perfusion information (Tmax) from non-functional imaging. Qualitatively, the generated Tmax maps show promise in identifying blood flow abnormalities despite the limited signal in NCCT. The integration of auxiliary tasks to provide a “physiology constraint” is a conceptually sound approach to improving segmentation performance.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The manuscript suffers from significant technical and presentation issues. There are apparent circular dependencies in the proposed pipeline, where the encoder seems to require outputs from modules that have not yet been executed. The terminology is often misleading, specifically the use of “collaborative framework” to describe what is essentially a multitask learning setup. Furthermore, the experimental validation is hindered by a lack of transparency regarding the dataset (missing inclusion criteria, specifications from the scanners, distribution of lesion characteristics) and a weak quantitative analysis. The ablation study shows marginal improvements (e.g., 0.002 in Dice) when adding the high-complexity Diffusion module, which lacks statistical significance testing and calls into question the trade-off between model parameters and performance gains.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
General Concerns
The term “collaborative framework” is misleading. In the context of medical imaging and AI, this often refers to Federated Learning. The proposed approach is more accurately described as a multitask learning framework or a segmentation model with auxiliary optimization objectives.
Introduction
The second paragraph provides a highly superficial overview of related work. Several relevant state-of-the-art studies that attempt to predict infarct core from NCCT are missing. Authors could also consider mentioning efforts to predict penumbra from other modalities non-functional modalities.
The authors must expand the literature review to include specific state-of-the-art baselines for NCCT stroke segmentation to better contextualize their proposed method and results. For example, a more detailed comparison with the I2PC-Net model could be helpful.
Methodology and Pipeline
There are multiple typos in Figure 1: “regin” instead of “region”, “folw” instead of “flow”, and “Supervied” instead of “supervised”.
Section 2.2 and the Overview are inconsistent. Section 2.2 mentions a dual-head module for probabilistic masks of the core and penumbra, while the Overview states the penumbra and core.
Regarding the 1.8 mismatch ratio (Section 2.3): In clinical practice, this ratio is calculated using total volumes. Please clarify how this was adapted for 2D axial slices and if this introduces bias.
In Section 2.4, map “M” is mentioned but not labeled in Figure 1.Additionally, clarify why the output of the Diffusion Decoder is called a “Generative Attention Map” if it is intended to be an estimate of Tmax (noted as Tmax Hat).
Datasets and Implementation
Section 3.1 lacks essential details regarding the patient cohort. Please provide inclusion/exclusion criteria, study nature (retrospective/prospective), imaging equipment (NCCT/CTP) specifications, image dimensions, lesion characteristics (size, location), and any other relevant information.
In the Implementation subsection, there is confusion regarding Lambda parameters. The authors mention Lambda 2 increases to prioritize latent representation, but the description suggests they may be referring to Lambda 3 (reconstruction space). Please clarify this.
The 2D re-implementation of I2PC-Net for a “fair comparison” is questionable. Reducing a 3D method to 2D may strip it of its inherent advantages, potentially biasing the comparison and diminishing the novelty of the proposed method.
Clarify how the baseline models were adapted to output two maps (infarct and ischemic tissue) for the evaluation.
Results and Discussion
The description of the ablation study results is vague. Phrases stating that modules “help improve performance” should be replaced with specific quantitative measurements.
The quantitative gain from adding the Diffusion module is extremely low (e.g., 0.002 in infarct core) and actually results in performance loss in other metrics. Given the massive parameter overhead of a Diffusion model, this requires a much more rigorous justification or a statistical significance analysis to prove the differences are real.
While the qualitative Tmax maps are interesting, the authors should discuss and justify why the model is being burdened with such a complex module for such marginal quantitative gains.

While the core idea of using Foundation Models and Diffusion-based auxiliary tasks for stroke segmentation is novel and addresses a critical clinical need, the current version of the manuscript has significant flaws. The introduction provides a highly superficial presentation of state-of-the-art works, failing to adequately contextualize the proposed method against existing baselines for NCCT stroke segmentation. Furthermore, the dataset description is insufficient for reproducibility, and the quantitative results do not currently justify the high complexity of the proposed architecture. The marginal improvements observed in the ablation study, coupled with the lack of statistical significance testing and missing baseline comparisons in the evaluation, suggest that the paper requires a major revision and more rigorous validation before it is ready for publication.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors provided clarification on terminology, corrected several typos, and shared additional details regarding the method and dataset. While they did not provide a response for the state-of-the-art contextualization, the proposed methodology presents a novel and promising approach to a high-impact clinical problem.
Because the technical contribution is significant and addresses a critical area in medical imaging, I have decided to increase my score. However, I strongly recommend that the authors take this opportunity to refine the final version of the manuscript. Properly situating this work within the current landscape of NCCT analysis is essential for the scientific community to fully appreciate its value and novelty. Ensuring a more rigorous contextualization will significantly improve the paper’s presentation and long-term impact.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper proposes a multitask framework for infarct core and penumbra segmentation on NCCT using auxiliary physiological constraints and diffusion-based modeling.
Reviewers agree the problem is clinically relevant with a well-structured and potentially innovative approach, but raise concerns about unclear methodological details, weak justification of some design choices, limited transparency in data and preprocessing, and insufficiently supported performance gains. I suggest that the authors address these raised issues in the rebuttal.

There is consensus that the paper addresses a clinically important problem and proposes a technically promising multitask framework for infarct core and ischemic tissue segmentation from NCCT. The main concerns have been reasonably clarified in the rebuttal, and I therefore recommend acceptance.
However, there is a valid concern about the limited contextualization against state-of-the-art NCCT stroke analysis methods. I encourage the authors to address this as much as possible in the camera-ready.

The rebuttal does not address point-by-point the detailed observations from Reviewer 3, but the paper nevertheless makes a valuable and clinically-relevant contribution to the field of analysing non-contrast CT scans in patients presenting with stroke to clinics. Several methods are already commercially available for similar tasks, and this work does not seem to greatly improve their performance, but it does opens the avenue of research on the theme using the breadth of CT scans from multiple databases by giving the possibility to researchers worldwide of differentially identifying the core/penumbra infarcted regions, to be able to refine strategies to reduce the area affected by the stroke. In the final version, to carefully address point-by-point the suggestions of Reviewer 3 will be expected.
The rebuttal has sufficiently addressed the major concerns of the reviewers. The general core methodology is novel and addresses a critical clinical need.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank all reviewers for their thorough and insightful comments. Below we address the methodological and presentation concerns raised. 
Clarification of terminology and implementation: “Collaborative framework” refers to a standard end-to-end multitask framework in this paper. The segmentation branch predicts infarct core and ischemic tissue; the use of “core and penumbra” in Sec. 2.2 was a typo. The map “M” denotes the attention map derived from segmentation outputs for attention gating. In Sec. 2.3, the statement that mismatch is predicted “from segmentation outputs” is inaccurate; as shown in Fig. 1, mismatch is predicted by an MLP from encoder features. In Sec. 3.1, λ2 should be λ3, corresponding to the diffusion loss. These corrections clarify the intended implementation without changing the methodology.
For data concern, the dataset is a LVO dataset of 310 retrospective AIS patients, with following detailed inclusion criteria in [1]. Perfusion maps were affine-registered to NCCT space after skull stripping. Intensities were clipped to [0,100] HU for NCCT and [0,30] s for Tmax following [1]. Infarct core and ischemic tissue labels were obtained by standard thresholds (rCBF < 0.3, Tmax > 6s) and clinically reviewed. 
[1] Cai, Y. et al. CT perfusion map generation from multiphase CTA using a generative adversarial model for acute ischemic stroke. American Journal of Neuroradiology, 46(12), 2535–2544.Fig.1 may have caused confusion. The arrows returning to the DINOv3 encoder indicate gradient propagation during joint optimization rather than recursive execution. The diffusion branch uses segmentation outputs only as conditioning signals, while denoising is performed by an independent diffusion network. The framework follows sequential multitask optimization, and inference requires only NCCT input.
For mismatch branch, threshold of 1.8 follows the DEFUSE-3 criterion. The MLP predicts mismatch status from pooled latent features, providing a global structural constraint complementary to pixel-wise supervision, reducing the influence of small lesion fluctuations on ratio estimation and improving robustness in small infarct cases. Although mismatch is clinically volumetric, we adopt a slice-level approximation, where consistently derived 2D annotations serve as region-level supervision.
For diffusion branch, it is designed as a physiology-aware auxiliary constraint rather than a Dice-optimization module. Under Tmax supervision, it learns perfusion-related features and generates pseudo-perfusion representations (generative attention map) from NCCT. The modest Dice gain under 1.8 threshold suggests that the segmentation backbone already captures substantial lesion information, while the diffusion branch contributes through representation regularization and physiological interpretability. Although the Dice differences are modest, we note consistent trends across multiple experiments (Table 2, for threshold 0.8 and 2.8, infarct dice gain are 0.016 and 0.009, Ischemic tissue dice gain are 0.010 and 0.008), suggesting the improvements are systematic rather than random. Furthermore, this framework may provide a promising direction in our future work by mismatch-aware regional structural priors within denoising, which may further improve both pseudo-Tmax quality and Dice gain.
For fairness, all baselines, 2D or 3D methods, were adapted into the same dual-head 2D setting while preserving their core architectural components, which ensures that performance differences mainly reflect architectural design rather than dimensionality differences. The 2D formulation was adopted due to NCCT characteristics, including anisotropic resolution, ~5 mm slice thickness, limited through-plane continuity, and variable slice counts. Under these conditions, slice-wise 2D modeling is a practical and widely adopted strategy for NCCT lesion analysis. Code will be released upon acceptance.

title: PET-Adapter: Test-Time Domain Adaptation for Full and Limited-Angle PET Image Reconstruction
abstract: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) image reconstruction is inherently challenged by Poisson noise and physical degradation factors, which are further exacerbated in limited-angle acquisitions. While deep learning methods demonstrate promising performance, their generalization to unseen clinical data distributions remains limited without extensive retraining. We propose PET-Adapter, a test-time domain adaptation framework for generative PET reconstruction models pretrained solely on phantom data. Our method enables adaptation to clinical datasets with varying anatomies, tracers, and scanner configurations without requiring paired ground truth. PET-Adapter introduces layer-wise low-rank anatomical conditioning during adaptation and Ordered Subset Expectation Maximization-based warm-starting that initializes the generation from physics-informed reconstructions, reducing diffusion steps from 50 to 2 without compromising quality. Experiments across multiple clinical datasets demonstrate superior 3D reconstruction performance in both full-angle and limited-angle settings, highlighting the clinical feasibility and computational efficiency of the proposed approach. The code base for PET-Adapter will be made publicly available under https://github.com/ruveydayilmaz0/PetAdapter.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Synthetic Data / Data-centric AI

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a test-time domain adaptation framework for diffusion-based PET reconstruction, enabling models trained on phantom data to generalize to clinical datasets. It incorporates MR-guided conditioning through layer-wise modulation to introduce anatomical priors, and employs an OSEM-based warm-start strategy to significantly reduce diffusion sampling steps while preserving reconstruction quality.
reviews.text_strengths:
A key strength of this work is the comprehensive comparison with multiple state-of-the-art methods, including both classical reconstruction approaches (e. g. , OSEM, Bowsher) and recent diffusion-based techniques. The experimental evaluation spans several datasets with varying domain shifts, which strengthens the empirical validation. 
In addition, the proposed framework is relatively simple to train, as it relies on a pretrained model on phantom data and performs lightweight adaptation at test time without requiring paired ground truth data. This makes the approach practically appealing.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The overall methodological novelty is limited, as the proposed framework mainly combines existing components (diffusion models, low-rank adaptation, and MR-guided conditioning) in an incremental manner rather than introducing fundamentally new techniques. 
Moreover, the effectiveness of the warm-starting (WS) strategy is not fully convincing. As shown in the ablation study, the configuration without WS but with more sampling steps (T = 50) achieves comparable or even better performance than the proposed WS with T = 2 . This raises questions about whether WS truly improves reconstruction quality or mainly serves as a computational trade-off.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1.Clarification of the benefit of warm-starting (WS):
The ablation results suggest that WS does not outperform the configuration without WS when sufficient diffusion steps are used (e. g. , T = 50). The authors should clarify whether WS improves reconstruction quality or only reduces computational cost, and provide a more balanced discussion. 
2.Fairness of comparison with baseline methods:
The proposed method leverages both test-time adaptation and warm-start initialization, while baseline methods appear to use standard settings. This may lead to an unfair comparison. It would be helpful to include stronger baselines (e. g. , with similar initialization or adaptation) for a more rigorous evaluation. 
3.Evaluation protocol and ground truth definition:
For some clinical datasets, the ground truth is derived from MRI-based regional averaging rather than true PET measurements. This may bias the evaluation toward anatomically smooth reconstructions. The authors should discuss the limitations of this evaluation setup and its impact on the reported metrics. 
4.Lack of qualitative evaluation in limited-angle (LA) setting:
The paper does not provide qualitative reconstruction results for the LA experiments. Without visual inspection, it is difficult to assess whether the method introduces artifacts, such as MR-induced over-smoothing or sensitivity-related artifacts due to missing angular coverage. Including qualitative comparisons for LA cases would significantly strengthen the evaluation.

This paper addresses a relevant and practical problem in PET image reconstruction and provides a well-engineered framework with strong empirical results across multiple datasets. Although the methodological contribution is somewhat incremental and certain design choices (e.g., warm-starting) are not fully justified, the work demonstrates reasonable technical quality and potential practical impact.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose a new test-time fine-tuning method for diffusion model-based PET image reconstruction on out-of-distribution data. The core is low-rank MR-guided adaptation to enable fine-tuning and injection of MR prior. The authors also propose OSEM warm-starting to substantially shorten the sampling path of a DDPM. The idea of test-time domain adaptation for PET reconstruction, especially from phantom-only pretraining to diverse clinical datasets, is novel and practically relevant.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) Test-time fine-tuning based on LoRA and the injection of MR image prior. Since PET data have significant variation across different datasets, test-time fine-tuning for diffusion samplers is a potential solution for OOD data. This topic remains novel in PET. The authors also propose the LoRA module that injects MR image as the prior, which is a flexible way of incorporating prior information.
2) Warm-start is a feasible solution for acceleration. Typical diffusion samplers usually suffer from high computation cost. Another benefit, as the authors claim, is the feasibility of applying a pure 2D score function on the warm-started image without losing slice consistency across axial slices. This opens a new path for real 3D reconstruction under the memory limit.
3) The experiment design is bold. Although this is a general framework for OOD reconstruction, the authors train the score function on phantom images and apply it to simulated datasets, where there is a large domain mismatch between the training set and the testing data. The results demonstrate the strong adaptation capability of the proposed method.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) Unclear fine-tuning objective. I am not clear about \hat{x}^MAP at the beginning of p5.Is it Tweedie’s estimate \hat{x}_0? I suggest the fine-tuning objective be formulated more clearly.
2) This paper assumes that MR image is available; however, MR image prior is not guaranteed for many PET datasets. Could the authors comment on the method’s performance using plain LoRA without MR as the prior?
3) Only reconstruction on simulated data has been reported, which could be sufficient for a conference paper. Information on the simulation is not complete, such as the simulated scanner.
4) It is not very clear how the slice consistency is achieved. The author essentially claim a new way of circumventing direct 3D reconstruction. Is it true that the slice consistency is realized solely by a warm start and without further constraint in the sampling?
5) Potential unfairness when compared with baselines. Are the baselines implemented with the warm start? Could authors comment on the portion of the performance gain that is contributed to the warm start?
6) I suggest this work be referred to as well: Hashimoto et al., PET Image Reconstruction Using Deep Diffusion Image Prior, TMI, 2026
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The topic and the proposed method (LoRA fine-tuning) are relatively new in PET. The preliminary results are promising.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes PET-Adapter, an unsupervised test-time domain adaptation framework intended to reduce the generalization gap between generative PET reconstruction models trained on synthetic phantom data and unseen clinical data. The main contribution is a multi-component adaptation pipeline that combines low-rank anatomical conditioning based on MRI, an unsupervised adaptation objective that includes both measurement fidelity and anatomical regularization, and a physics-informed warm-start strategy based on OSEM reconstruction to reduce the computational cost of diffusion sampling.
reviews.text_strengths:
A major strength of the work is the warm-starting strategy. Instead of initializing diffusion sampling from pure Gaussian noise, the method starts from a perturbed OSEM reconstruction. This is a sensible design choice, since OSEM can already recover the low-frequency image structure efficiently, allowing the diffusion model to focus on refinement. In practice, this appears to reduce the number of sampling steps substantially, from 50 to 2, without an obvious loss in reconstruction quality.
Another strength is the use of layer-wise low-rank adaptation blocks to condition a pretrained unconditional score model on MR information at test time. This provides a practical way to inject anatomical guidance without retraining the full model. The experimental evaluation is also fairly broad, with comparisons across multiple datasets and methods.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Some aspects of the experimental setup are unclear. For example, it is not clear where the NX data come from, and the definition of the anatomical loss La should be stated more explicitly.
Although the experiments use clinical image volumes, the PET measurements y are still simulated using the Parallelproj framework. A stronger clinical validation would require raw scanner-acquired sinogram data. Even with realistic physics and noise modeling, simulated data may not fully capture scanner-specific effects such as detector-dependent artifacts, calibration imperfections, or more complex scatter behavior, which are precisely the kinds of domain shifts that test-time adaptation is meant to address.
In addition, while the overall integration is effective, the individual components are not fundamentally new. The conditioning mechanism based on low-rank adaptation and the broader idea of steerable conditional diffusion for test-time adaptation in medical imaging have both been explored in closely related settings.
Finally, while the paper includes ablations on warm-starting and TTDA, it does not separately ablate the anatomical guidance term La from the measurement fidelity term Lp. That makes it difficult to assess the specific contribution of the anatomical prior to the final performance.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

My overall score was mainly driven by the paper’s practical contribution and clear presentation. The paper is well written, and the proposed framework is easy to follow. Together with the fairly broad experimental evaluation, these strengths made the paper a positive submission overall.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper presents a test-time adaptation method for brain PET reconstruction to adapt to different clinical domain data with a phantom pre-trained diffusion model. An MR-guided conditioning via layer-wise adaptation blocks and a warm start through OSEM reconstruction prior are introduced. The experiments cover multiple centers and multiple vendors, including both FA and LA conditions, and the results reached an optimal performance compared with SOTA methods.
The authors have reached a consensus on the acceptance of the paper. While the technical novelty is incremental, the reviewers find the integration of LoRA and warm-starting for PET reconstruction to be a sound and well-engineered contribution. Its reduced computation load (T=2) could further enhance its potential for practical application.
Though an early acceptance is recommended, the authors should still provide feedback regarding (1) the benefit of warm starting beyond reduced computation cost, given that similar performance was achieved with more inference steps; (2) the requirement of MR conditioning since the MR prior is not always available; (3) results are on simulated data only; (4) the pre-training phantom dataset is relatively small containing only 20 scans; and (5) further implementation details as asked by R2 and R3.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their valuable and constructive feedback. We provide clarifications below regarding the main points raised in the reviews. We do not include additional experimental results, as new experiments cannot be added at this stage.
Effectiveness of warm-starting (WS): The main benefit of WS is computational efficiency rather than a direct improvement in reconstruction quality. As shown in Table 2, PET-Adapter with WS and T=2 diffusion steps achieves reconstruction quality comparable to the no-WS setting with T=50, while substantially reducing the number of sampling steps.
Fairness of comparison with baseline methods: To clarify the contribution of WS and TTDA, we included ablations of our method without WS and without TTDA in Table 2.The “w/o WS, T=50” setting corresponds most closely to the sampling regime used by the other methods, which also use T=50 diffusion steps in our experiments. We did not modify the baseline non-adaptive methods to include our adaptation mechanism, since doing so would change the original methods. Our goal was to compare against these methods as established non-adaptive baselines. That said, PET-Adapter could potentially be combined with other diffusion-based PET reconstruction methods to make them adaptable.
MRI-based regional averaging: For CERMEP and AGIEF, the provided PET images are relatively low-quality and blurry; therefore, we generated high-SNR reference volumes by averaging PET values within MRI-defined brain regions, as described in the paper. We agree that this evaluation protocol has limitations, we also tested the use of the original PET measurements as reference images and observed consistent results with the regional-averaging. We reported the regional-averaging results because they make anatomical and reconstruction details easier to inspect. For the NX dataset, we use the provided PET images directly as reference images, since they are already high-quality.
Qualitative LA reconstructions: We agree that qualitative LA examples would help readers better assess possible artifacts. Due to space limitations, the paper only includes qualitative results for the FA setting, while the LA results are reported quantitatively in the tables.
Availability of MR images: PET-Adapter still improves reconstruction quality when MR images are not available. However, performance is lower than in the MRI-guided setting, which is expected since MR images provide useful anatomical guidance during adaptation.
The simulated scanner: The CERMEP and AGIEF datasets were originally acquired using a Siemens Biograph mMR scanner, which is the scanner geometry we modeled in Parallelproj. For the NX dataset, the exact scanner acquisition model was not provided, so we could not reproduce the exact scanner geometry in our simulations. We acknowledge that this is a limitation.

title: PETFlux: Taming Natural Foundation Models for Accurate MRI-to-PET Synthesis
abstract: Synthesizing PET from MRI offers a radiation-free route to functional biomarkers but remains fundamentally ill-posed due to the weak coupling between anatomy and metabolism. Existing medical generative models trained on limited molecular imaging data often overfit or generate artifacts, while natural-image foundation models cannot be directly transferred because their priors and semantics are misaligned with radiological domains. We introduce PETFlux, a task-aligned adaptation framework that repurposes a pretrained natural-image backbone for the specific demands of MRI-to-PET synthesis. The framework addresses the key barriers of domain mismatch, structural-functional ambiguity, and spatial over-smoothing through three synergistic strategies: (i) Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) via rectified flow matching to realign natural priors with PET distributions; (ii) LLM-augmented prefix tuning grounded in an evidence-based clinical knowledge base to inject patient-specific metabolic semantics; and (iii) a log-scale focal frequency loss to preserve clinically critical functional detail. Experiments on the ADNI dataset demonstrate that PETFlux achieves state-of-the-art synthesis fidelity and yields substantial gains in downstream diagnostic classification, highlighting a principled pathway for repurposing natural foundation models in molecular imaging by effectively integrating anatomical constraints and patient metadata.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs
dataset_urls: We use paired MRI/PET data from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), including 18F-FDG PET and 18F-AV45 PET scans for MRI-to-PET synthesis. Data are available to approved researchers through the ADNI/LONI Image and Data Archive: https://adni.loni.usc.edu/data-samples/adni-data/

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposed a framework for MRI-to-PET synthesis that adapts a large pretrained natural-image foundation model to a clinically important but highly ill-posed medical imaging problem. Relative to prior MRI-to-PET work that mainly relies on GANs, Transformers, state-space models, or standard diffusion models trained on limited medical data, the paper proposes a more principled way to transfer foundation-model priors into this domain. It shows how to combine foundation models, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and clinically grounded metadata to improve MRI-to-PET synthesis.
reviews.text_strengths: This paper has several major strengths. First, it tackles a clinically important problem, since MRI-to-PET synthesis could reduce radiation exposure, cost, and limited access associated with PET while still providing useful functional information for diseases such as Alzheimer’s. Second, the paper presents a clever adaptation strategy that repurposes multiple pretrained foundation models for this downstream medical imaging task, instead of training a large model from scratch on limited paired data. Third, the use of LoRA-based fine-tuning is practically appealing, as it enables effective adaptation of a large backbone with much lower computational cost. Fourth, the proposed conditioning mechanism is particularly interesting: the paper transforms clinical metadata into semantic guidance that the generative model can better understand, which is a novel and well-motivated way to address the ambiguity of MRI-to-PET synthesis. Finally, the overall evaluation is strong, including multiple baselines, two tracers, ablation studies, and downstream diagnostic utility, which makes the empirical results convincing.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.2D Slice-based Limitation:​ The method operates on 2D slices, which fundamentally limits its ability to capture volumetric context. Given the paper’s own emphasis on the ill-posed nature of MRI-to-PET synthesis and its dependence on complex structural-functional relationships, this is a critical weakness. It is unclear how the model can faithfully synthesize global metabolic patterns (e. g. , distributed across the whole brain) when it only processes information slice-by-slice, potentially losing vital inter-slice dependencies.
2.Lack of Technical Detail and Validation for the LLM/Clinical Knowledge Base:​ The manuscript attributes the synthesis success to LLM-guided clinical descriptions derived from a knowledge base, yet provides insufficient detail on its curation, validation, and handling of conflicting guidelines. This lack of transparency severely hinders reproducibility. Furthermore, the integration of explicit, clinically informative metadata (e. g. , MMSE, CDR-SB) as narrative text makes it difficult to disentangle the contribution of true image translation from the injection of strong disease priors. A robustness analysis against noisy or missing metadata is required to substantiate the claims.
3.Insufficient Framework Generalization and Versatility Validation:​ While proposing a novel adaptation framework for foundation models, the evaluation is confined to a single dataset (ADNI). Validation on external datasets with different protocols is essential to demonstrate real-world generalizability. Additionally, the ablation studies do not fully isolate the contribution of the proposed adaptation strategy itself. Applying the complete pipeline to another foundation model of comparable scale would more fairly evaluate the framework’s core versatility, separating it from the benefits of the specific pre-trained priors used.
4.Incomplete Clinical Validation and Proof of Equivalence:​ Although downstream classification results are promising, a noticeable performance gap remains between synthetic and real PET, failing to establish clinical equivalence. The current quantitative metrics (SUVR, AUC) lack depth. A more comprehensive clinical validation is needed, including qualitative expert assessment (e. g. , blinded scoring of image quality and diagnostic confidence) to rigorously verify the claimed resolution of “clinically misleading textures” and prove the clinical utility of the generated images.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The overall score reflects several major concerns that collectively impact the paper’s technical rigor, generalizability, and demonstrated clinical utility. The primary factors leading to this assessment are as follows:
1.Lack of Technical Detail and Validation for the LLM/Clinical Knowledge Base:​ The manuscript attributes the synthesis success to LLM-guided clinical descriptions derived from a curated knowledge base. However, insufficient detail is provided regarding the construction, validation, and handling of potentially conflicting guidelines within this base. This lack of transparency severely hinders reproducibility. More critically, the integration of explicit, clinically informative metadata (e.g., MMSE, CDR-SB) as narrative text makes it difficult to disentangle the contribution of genuine image translation from the model’s reliance on injected, strong disease priors. A robustness analysis against noisy or missing metadata is required to substantiate the core claim that the model learns the true MRI-to-PET mapping.
2.Insufficient Framework Generalization and Versatility Validation:​ While proposing a novel adaptation framework for foundation models, the evaluation is confined to a single dataset (ADNI). Validation on external datasets with different imaging protocols is essential to demonstrate real-world generalizability. Furthermore, the presented ablation studies do not fully isolate the contribution of the proposed adaptation strategy itself. Applying the complete pipeline to another foundation model of comparable scale would provide a fairer evaluation of the framework’s core versatility, separating its benefits from those inherent to the specific pre-trained priors of the model used in this study.
3.Incomplete Clinical Validation and Proof of Equivalence:​ Although downstream classification results are promising, a noticeable performance gap persists between synthetic and real PET images, failing to establish clinical equivalence. The current reliance on quantitative metrics like SUVR and AUC lacks depth. A more comprehensive clinical validation is needed, incorporating qualitative expert assessment (e.g., blinded scoring of image quality and diagnostic confidence). This is necessary to rigorously verify the claimed resolution of “clinically misleading textures” and to ultimately prove the clinical utility of the generated images.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes PETFlux, a framework for MRI-to-PET synthesis that adapts a pretrained natural-image foundation model to medical imaging. The method combines LoRA-based rectified flow adaptation, LLM-guided conditioning from clinical metadata, and a spectral loss to improve fine metabolic detail. Experiments on ADNI with both AV45 and FDG PET show better synthesis metrics and stronger downstream classification performance than the compared baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper addresses MRI-to-PET synthesis problem with a timely foundation-model adaptation approach.
Method is technically interesting and combines the main components in a coherent way.
Evaluation includes both image synthesis metrics and downstream diagnostic utility.
The method is tested on two tracers, and the gains appear consistent across both AV45 and FDG.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
My main concern is that the method combines several ideas at once, so the true source of improvement is still a bit hard to isolate.
The ablation showed only trend plots, and it does not fully separate how much comes from LoRA adaptation, the LLM-based conditioning, and the spectral loss.
I also think the paper needs stronger statistical support. The results in Table 1 are promising, but only single values are reported. There are no confidence intervals, repeated runs, or significance tests, so it is hard to know whether the improvements are stable and clearly meaningful.
Only one dataset ADNI was evaluated.
It suggests to compare a metadata-only conditioning baseline without LLM-generated narrative text to show that this component is necessary beyond simpler metadata conditioning.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The paper is interesting and generally well written. To make it stronger, I suggest few improvements:
Make the novelty claim more precise in the introduction and discussion, and explain clearly what is new beyond combining existing components.
Improve the result section by adding uncertainty information such as standard deviation, confidence intervals, or significance testing.
Increase fontsize for numbers in Figure 3.

I think this paper is slightly above the acceptance threshold. The problem is important, the method is technically solid, and the empirical results are consistently strong across two PET tracers. My main concerns are that the novelty is more in the overall combination than in a single clearly new method, and the paper does not provide statistical testing or uncertainty estimates to show how reliable the improvements are.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal addressed most of my main concerns. I think the paper is acceptable and would be suitable as a highlighted poster.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of this paper is to perform MRI-PET tasks using a tuned Flux backbone. Two other innovations are the introduction of LLM as a condition and a frequency domain loss.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The charts are clear and easy to understand.
2.I greatly appreciate that the authors provided ACC/AUC metrics in addition to PSNR/SSIM, which enhances the persuasiveness of the experiments.
3.The ablation experiments are excellent.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.I would like to see a comparison of training and inference costs (GPU memory and time). I completely understand that the authors don’t need to worry that their current method is inferior to pix2pix, etc., and I would appreciate it if they could report some realistic metrics. It’s normal for methods based on Flux-like generative models to have such issues.
2.In fact, if PETFlux works in the latent space, I think it would be more reasonable for the comparison methods to also be trained in the latent space. If the authors could provide training results for 1-2 comparison methods in the latent space (if time is limited, providing only the pix2pix method would suffice, and the comparison results could be named pix2pix-latent), I would appreciate it. In my experience, VAE compression will result in some loss of accuracy, and PSNR/SSIM may decrease. However, this is not absolute, and I would prefer to see the authors’ practical application on this task.
3.In Figure 1, the encoder and decoder are generally VAEs, right? I understand that FLUX has strong VAE capabilities, but if the authors fine-tune the VAE on in-domain images, is it possible to further improve the metrics? Two additional experiments can be added here: (1) Changes in SSIM/PSNR after fine-tuning VAE (input x, decoded x after VAE) (2) Changes in SSIM/PSNR of generation task (x->y) after fine-tuning VAE.
4.Regarding the introduction of LLM. I feel it is very similar to some recent works [1][2]. Could you please add a discussion about them in the final version? Also, how would the effect change if the LLM embedding were replaced with the embedding extracted by sigLIP/DINO as the condition? This is the experimental addition I most want to see (sigLIP may be better aligned with the language; I am more concerned about the performance of DINO. If time permits, I suggest providing the effects of both DINOV2 and DINOV3.If resources are limited, only DINOV3 can be provided).
5.Other minor issues: (1) Line break issues in 3.1.Dataset. has no line break, while LLM Prompting, etc., have line breaks. (2) Many paragraphs have orphaned lines, which is not aesthetically pleasing. I suggest correcting this in the final version.

IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging, 2024, 44(3): 1218-1229.[2] Yang S, Zhou H, Yang Y, et al. LCM-Net: LLM-driven Cross-Modality MoE Feature Fusion Network for Cancer Survival Analysis[J]. IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging, 2026.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Considering the rebuttal limitations of MICCAI, the authors could prioritize answering question 4; further answers to questions 1-3 would be even better. Based on the rebuttal, I would consider further increasing the score from 4 to 5.

The motivation is quite good, and the charts are clear and easy to understand. It would be even better if my questions were answered.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
After reading the rebuttals, I recommend accepting the paper. The authors have reasonably addressed my main concerns, resolving most issues, including computational cost, potential spatial baseline settings, and VAE tuning. The reported efficiency data clarifies the trade-offs of PETFlux, and the explanations regarding pix2pix-latent and Flux VAE tuning are acceptable. I believe the discussion of computational and time costs is sincere; FLUX-like networks have faced similar issues in my own research, and efficiency optimization could be an important direction for future research, especially considering potential clinical applications.
In conclusion, this paper demonstrates a meaningful application, clear experimental results, robust ablation studies, and practical clinical indicators. I encourage the authors to further refine the final version, discuss the relevant LLM conditionalization work I mentioned in the original comment, and add the corresponding references. Therefore, I support the acceptance of this paper.

meta_reviews.text:
The reviewers appreciate the timely and principled adaptation of natural-image foundation models to the clinically vital task of MRI-to-PET synthesis. Strengths include the clever use of LoRA for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, the consistent performance gains across multiple tracers (AV45 and FDG), and the inclusion of downstream diagnostic metrics (ACC/AUC) to validate clinical utility. However, the reviewers raised several concerns that must be addressed in the rebuttal. Primary among these is the lack of transparency and validation for the LLM-guided conditioning; authors need to clarify how clinical metadata is curated. Reviewers also highlighted the limitations of the 2D slice-based approach in capturing 3D metabolic patterns and requested a robustness analysis against missing or noisy metadata to ensure the model isn’t simply memorizing disease priors. Furthermore, the rebuttal could include a comparison of computational costs (GPU memory/time), and a discussion on how the framework generalizes to external datasets beyond ADNI.

All reviewers were satistfied with the rebuttal. The authors should address the remaining concerns in the camera-ready version.

R1 is the only reviewer to not respond, and had the most concerns about the manuscript. The authors make it clear that there was significant minunderstanding on the contribution of the LLM module in the proposed method. R1 major points 2 and 3 are similar critiques on the limitations on dataset validation and reliance on only quantitative measures without the inclusion of clinically relevant metrics. Both of these are not addressed, however there are similar methods in the literature that rely on the quantitative metrics with only ADNI as a dataset. R2 and R3 are happy to accept and state their questions have mostly been addressed.

The authors did sufficiently address the concerns of the reviewers in the rebuttal. The work represents a clinically important contribution that is technically sound and clearly presented with robust ablation studies.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback and for recognizing the clinical importance (R1/R2/R3), technical soundness (R1/R2), downstream diagnostic utility (R1/R2/R3), and clear presentation(R2/R3) of our work. We address the main concerns below.
LLM/Clinical Knowledge Base Details (R1Q2)
We clarify that the LLM is not used to infer subject-specific diagnoses or PET findings. Our knowledge base follows fixed, auditable rules: MMSE/CDR-SB are mapped to coarse severity levels for each tracer. The LLM only rewrites these rule-selected profiles into standardized visual descriptions. The prompts contain no subject labels or PET data, ensuring no information leakage.
We will release the mapping rules, dictionaries, prompt templates, construction scripts, and LLM query scripts.
To address shortcut concerns, we evaluate missing/noisy metadata at inference: generic instruction with zero prefix (missing) and mismatched prompts/metadata (noisy). PSNR drops from 26.43/27.37 (full) to 25.01/26.99 and 25.48/27.08 (AV45/FDG), showing degradation but no collapse. Metadata remains useful as auxiliary guidance, and metadata-prefix-only is worse than full PETFlux.
2D Limitation (R1Q1)
We acknowledge this limitation. PETFlux uses slice-wise generation because Flux is native 2D, while full-resolution 3D generation remains memory-demanding and often relies on memory-saving approximations. Nevertheless, our evaluation is not limited to slice-level metrics: we reconstruct PET volumes via regional SUVR error and downstream 3D diagnostic AUC, which assess whether clinically relevant metabolic information is preserved at the volume level. 3D adaptation will be discussed as future work.
Generalization/clinical validation (R1Q3/R2Q4)
We agree that external cohorts and blinded expert assessment are needed before clinical translation. PETFlux improves synthetic PET quality and diagnostic utility, but remains a research-stage framework, not a replacement for real PET. 
ADNI is a large, longitudinal, multi-center benchmark (e.g., ResDM IJCAI 2024; DIReCT IPMI 2025, no clinical validation). Evaluation on 2,600+ AV45/FDG pairs supports first-stage validation. External validation, protocol-shift analysis, and blinded reader studies are important next steps.
Ablation Study (R2Q1/Q2/Q5/R1Q2)
Our ablation study is component-wise, not incremental. Each module—baseline, Log-FFT, LLM text, metadata prefix, and full PETFlux—is evaluated independently to isolate its contribution to performance. The caption of Fig. 3 will be revised to clarify this and avoid confusion.
Statistical reliability (R2Q3)
Table 1 reports mean values due to space constraints, but we agree that uncertainty is important. Representative PSNR improvements are statistically significant: AV45 PSNR 26.43 with 95% CI [25.82, 27.03], p = 5.60 × 10^-13; FDG PSNR 27.37 with 95% CI [26.87, 27.68], p = 2.51 × 10^-10.
References and formatting (R3Q4/Q5)
We thank the reviewer for the helpful references and will include cited works and fix formatting. Alternative visual embeddings (DINO/SigLIP) will be discussed as future comparison; performance with DINOV2/3 is a valuable extension.
Computational cost (R3Q1)
PETFlux is more expensive than lightweight GANs, but LoRA updates only 2.45% of parameters. At batch size 1, inference requires 36.86GB/4.87 s/slice; Pix2pix is 0.31GB/0.0052s/slice; Pix2pix-turbo is 6.42GB/0.3751s/slice.
Latent-space baseline (R3Q2)
Pix2pix is a lightweight image-space translation model; forcing it into the same VAE latent space mainly tests VAE compression rather than standard pix2pix. Our table already includes latent generative baselines, SD v1.5 and pix2pix-turbo, while pix2pix-latent is a useful future control.
VAE tuning (R3Q3)
Our preliminary VAE-tuning trials did not improve synthesis quality, likely because modifying the pretrained Flux VAE shifts the latent manifold expected by the DiT backbone and weakens LoRA adaptation.

title: PhaseAT: Fourier Phase Adversarial Training for Medical Image Domain Generalization
abstract: Reliable clinical deployment of deep medical image models is hindered by distribution shifts across scanners, sites, and acquisition protocols. Existing domain generalization (DG) methods often focus on style or intensity diversification, but they can still leave networks dependent on domain-specific texture correlations. Inspired by evidence that Fourier phase encodes semantic structure, we introduce \textsc{PhaseAT}, a phase-aware adversarial training framework for medical DG. \textsc{PhaseAT} forms phase-perturbed training views in the Fourier domain by iteratively updating a bounded phase perturbation while keeping the amplitude spectrum unchanged, thereby stressing spatial organization under matched appearance statistics. Perturbations are applied only to the luminance channel in YCbCr color space to avoid chromatic artifacts. Additionally, a simple phase-saliency mask concentrates updates on the most influential frequencies. The model is trained with a weighted combination of losses on clean and phase-perturbed samples, supporting both single-source and multi-source DG. We validate our method on two challenging medical datasets and demonstrate that \textsc{PhaseAT} achieves over 20\% improvement in single-source domain generalization, outperforming several state-of-the-art DG methods. The code implementation is available at:

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces PhaseAT, a phase-aware adversarial training framework that operates in the Fourier domain to enhance the model’s generalization ablities. The core idea is to adversarially perturb the Fourier phase of the luminance channel while most previous works are primarily focused on the intensity distribution. Evaluation on two medical datasets shows that PhaseAT can achieve over 20% improvement under single source DG settings.
reviews.text_strengths:

Adversarial attack on the phase domain can provide one novel insight for enhancing the model’s robustness. 
2.Strong single-source DG results with large margins: Table 1 show substantial and consistent improvements across all source domains on both datasets. 
3.Comprehensive ablation study: Table 3(b) systematically isolates each design choice — phase-only vs. amplitude-only vs. both, with/without saliency mask, RGB vs. YCbCr vs. luminance-only, adversarial vs. random perturbation.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The authors propose PhaseAT, an adversarial training scheme designed to improve robustness to domain shift through the generation of adversarial image examples during training.
To generate the adversarial samples, PhaseAT decomposes the image into its Fourier phase and amplitude components, and applies perturbations to the Fourier phase only. The adversarial example generated from this process is input into the model alongside the original image, and the model is trained to minimize the cross entropy loss on both images.
The authors evaluate their method in two image domains. The histopathology dataset Camelyon17-WILDS already has data from multiple acquisition sites. The authors also compile a diabetic retinopathy dataset from four existing datasets, each acting as a unique “site”.
PhaseAT is evaluated in single domain (the model is trained on one domain and tested on all others) and in multi-domain (model is tested on all domains except one and the left-out domain is used for testing) settings and compared with several recent examples from literature. Consistently, PhaseAT demonstrates strong performance compared to baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
Clearly motivated and well-structured: The authors clearly motivate their paper with a detailed discussion of the background literature and related works. The paper is structured sensibly in a way that is easy to follow. Figures are all clear and easy to understand.
Commitment to reproducibility: the authors have included an anonymized link to their source code and extensive details regarding their implementation and experimental set up, as well as full details of their algorithm in pseudocode.
Robust experimental validation: the authors evaluate their method across both single-domain and multi-source domain generalization tasks, following similar processes to other literature. They also include robust validations investigating sensitivity across various hyper parameters, generalization across architectures, and the importance of the various components of their proposed methodology. Such exhaustive experimentation is encouraging to see.
Ablations provide clarity on the importance of the individual decisions made: Table 3 (b), in particular, investigates the contribution of each component of the proposed methodology, as well as a discussion as to why removing/changing each component leads to a drop in efficacy. This kind of interrogation of design choices in the method is really nice to see and provides a clear justification for all choices.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Incorrect “best model” highlighted in Tables: Tables 1 and 2 both highlight the best performing model in bold text. Across all test cases, PhaseAT is highlighted as being the best, even when it is not. This is likely just a LaTEX formatting mistake. For example, in Table 1 (a) under source domain C4, PhaseAT isn’t the best performing model in 2 of the 4 test cases (C1 and C3) nor on average, yet it is highlighted in bold.
Missing statistical significance: Tables 1 and 2 report whether the best performing model shows a statistically significant performance improvement over other methods. Including statistical significance of the results would strengthen the claims around performance improvements as it would show that these are not simply due to noise in the results.
No examples of adversarial images: The paper doesn’t show an example of an adversarial image generated by PhaseAT. I appreciate that page limits are tight, and the perturbations are learned during training, but the inclusion of an example would help to illustrate the image features that the Fourier phase perturbation changes in an image.
Causes of differences in source domain performance are not discussed: Table 1, the chosen source domain has a significant impact on the model’s generalization (for example, with source domain C4 in the Camelyon1-WILDS dataset, the model struggles to generalize to all other domains). Do the authors have a theory for the reason behind this? Is this domain comprised of more challenging examples? Or does it represent a more extreme domain shift from the other sources?
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
In Table 3 (b) it would be nice to see a “baseline” row to compare to, to avoid comparing with models in other tables. This would help to make the value of each individual component even clearer.
For future work, it would be interesting to see how this approach might apply in contexts of shortcut learning, for example. This is mentioned in the introduction, and is out of the scope of this work, but I would be very interested to see how this approach might help address such problems.

The authors have proposed an interesting and well motivated method for adversarial model training to improve generalization to new distributions. The paper is clearly motivated and well-written. I would have liked to see measures of statistical significance over other methods that the authors compare to, particularly in cases where the performance gains are only modest, as well an example of a perturbed image feature that highlights specifically what image features the proposed method alters.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
After reading the authors’ rebuttal, I am pleased to see their commitment to addressing the issues raised by the other reviewers and me.
I am particularly pleased to see the reviewers confirm that they will include statistical significance tests in their results tables. As they mention in their review, the results demonstrate low variability across random seeds, but the gap between best and second-best is, on occasion, small. For example, the authors give the example in their rebuttal: “in Table 1(a) (Source C0), Phase-AT achieves 71.30±1.3 vs. 69.06±1.9 for RAS⁴DG”; these results are within a few percent of one another and show overlap in their deviations. The inclusion of, for example, t-tests can help show whether this improvement is significant.
Considering the author’s commitment to addressing the concerns and the relatively small scale of these corrections, I am happy to recommend acceptance.
However, I would like to comment on one point in the rebuttal. The authors claim: “The ‘Ours’ row was bolded for formatting consistency rather than to indicate per-cell superiority”. This is in direct contrast to the table captions in the paper, which explicitly state that the bold text highlights the best-performing model. Additionally, in Table 2, the authors appear to underline the worst-performing model (except in cases where they have incorrectly applied the bold text to their own model to indicate best performance). I would suggest adding text to the table captions to make this clear, and adding it to Table 1 as well for consistency.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a phase-perturbed training method for medical domain generalization (DG). The approach aims to improve out-of-distribution generalization by introducing adversarial perturbations during training. Experiments are conducted on two medical image classification datasets.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The overall narrative and logical flow of the paper are clear.
2.Research in medical domain generalization (DG) is of high practical importance.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The proposed phase perturbation as a data augmentation strategy contradicts prior insights and is internally inconsistent with the authors’ own claims. The paper states: “Since standard CNNs are biased toward texture cues [9], they frequently overfit to these unstable amplitude-driven correlations…”. If overfitting to amplitude-driven information is the issue, a more reasonable approach would be to introduce amplitude perturbations to improve robustness to cross-domain variations. Instead, the method perturbs the phase, which directly disrupts semantic structure. This may be unreliable, especially for medical tasks that heavily rely on structural information, such as segmentation and detection.
2.The novelty of the method is limited. Essentially, the approach applies Fourier-based data augmentation, which has already been widely explored in domain generalization literature. The only difference is that the perturbation is applied to the phase component rather than amplitude [1][2][3].
3.The experimental scope is too limited. Medical image analysis typically involves more segmentation and detection tasks, and evaluating only classification datasets is insufficient to validate the effectiveness of the method. Broader experimental validation is needed.
4.Regarding the claim: “This not only improves computational efficiency but also produces more structured perturbations with fewer color artifacts,” the improvement in computational efficiency is unclear. What is the additional computational cost introduced by the learnable phase perturbation compared to the baseline?
References:
[1] Xu Q, Zhang R, Zhang Y, et al. A Fourier-based framework for domain generalization. CVPR 2021.[2] Xu Q, Zhang R, Fan Z, et al. Fourier-based augmentation with applications to domain generalization. Pattern Recognition, 2023.[3] Wang X, Zhao Q, Zhang C, et al. Enhanced dynamic feature representation learning framework by Fourier transform for domain generalization. Information Sciences, 2023.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The overall score is mainly influenced by the limited novelty of the proposed method and the insufficient experimental validation. The approach is closely related to existing Fourier-based augmentation techniques, with only a minor variation in perturbing the phase component. In addition, the theoretical motivation is not fully convincing, and there are inconsistencies in the reasoning behind the method design. The experimental evaluation is also limited in scope, lacking validation on more diverse medical tasks such as segmentation or detection.
These factors together weaken the overall contribution and impact of the work.

meta_reviews.text:
Reviewers (scores 4, 4, 3) overall acknowledge that the paper has merit but have several concerns that the authors are encouraged to address in a rebuttal where possible. In particular:
statistical testing
details on computational complexity / runtime
general clarifications and a discussion of differences in source domain performances (R2)
Those seem addressable in a rebuttal.
Concerns centered around the selection of baseline methods and performance on dense prediction tasks are further shared concerns among reviewers, that however, are likely challenging to address without additional experiments.

All three reviewers are positive post-rebuttal suggesting to Accept this paper.
Reviewers appreciate the clarity and motivation of this work, as well as a comprehensive evaluation including ablation studies. Overall results and method are convincing. The authors submitted an effective rebuttal. Overall, I support the reviewers’ recommendation to accept this work.

PhaseAT introduces a novel adversarial training approach in the Fourier phase domain, moving beyond conventional amplitude based or style based domain generalization methods. The method is well validated through extensive ablations and multi domain experiments, showing consistent and substantial improvements. Reviewer #1 turned to Accept after rebuttal, and the theoretical concerns raised by Reviewer #4 were adequately addressed by ablation evidence (amplitude only 77.89% vs. PhaseAT 85.7%).

The paper proposes PhaseAT, a phase-aware adversarial training framework for medical domain generalization. All three active reviewers converged on acceptance after the rebuttal, consistently recognizing the novelty and performance gains. The authors should prepare the final version to incorporate the promised significance tests, formatting corrections, and discussion on Fourier-based DG works.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer. The reviews confirm PhaseAT’s key advantages: a novel, well-motivated DG formulation that moves beyond style perturbations to adversarial Fourier-phase perturbations; strong and consistent gains, especially in single-source DG; and robust validation via multi-domain experiments, ablations, clear presentation, and reproducibility. We address all concerns below:
Statistical Significance [R2, Meta] 
Tables 1–2 report mean ± std over 5 seeds, showing low variance and consistent performance across runs. The improvements over the strongest baselines are stable; e.g., in Table 1(a) (Source C0), Phase-AT achieves 71.30±1.3 vs. 69.06±1.9 for RAS⁴DG, and in Table 1(b) (Source Aptos), 44.99±1.9 vs. 41.50±2.3.We will report detailed paired t-test across the same 5 seeds and include 95% confidence intervals of the performance difference in the revision.
Computational Cost [R4, Meta] 
PhaseAT, like other adversarial training methods, uses K inner maximization steps and is therefore more expensive than ERM; our efficiency claim is only relative to adversarial variants perturbing all RGB or all YCbCr channels. By restricting perturbations to luminance (Y), PhaseAT reduces the inner-maximization dimensionality by 3×. We acknowledge this does not directly translate to wall-clock savings and add training time and memory in the revision.
Baselines (FedDG, DeepAug) [R1, Meta] 
Our evaluation covers three SOTA directions: style/intensity (AdverIN), disentanglement (ConDiSR), and Fourier-based methods (RAS⁴DG). FedDG and DeepAug are complementary but not directly aligned: FedDG focuses on cross-client amplitude mixing, while DeepAug uses pixel-space augmentations that emphasize texture cues. In contrast, PhaseAT operates in the Fourier domain with fixed amplitude and adversarial phase perturbations.
Dense Prediction [R1, R4, Meta] 
We thank the reviewers for the suggestion. PhaseAT is currently scoped to medical classification DG. Due to space constraints, dense prediction tasks are left as future work.
Source Domain Variability [R2] 
We agree that source-domain choice strongly affects SDG performance, as Camelyon17 centers differ in staining, scanners, and preparation, inducing different shortcut correlations. PhaseAT consistently improves over ERM across all sources, though gains vary (e.g., large for C2: 52.08→74.31, smaller for C4: 55.64→58.64), suggesting it is most effective when ERM relies more on domain-specific shortcuts. We will add this discussion and include a quantitative domain-distance analysis to better explain this variability.
Bold Formatting [R2] 
The “Ours” row was bolded for formatting consistency rather than to indicate per-cell superiority. In the revision, we will highlight only the best value in each column.
Adversarial Examples [R2] 
We appreciate the reviewers’ recognition of space constraints. We will make visualizations of adversarial examples available in the accompanying GitHub repository.
Phase vs Amplitude Perturbation [R4] 
PhaseAT complements, rather than replaces, amplitude-based DG by enforcing robustness under fixed amplitude (appearance) via small, bounded phase perturbations. To preserve semantics, perturbations are constrained, saliency-masked, and applied only to luminance. Table 3(b) shows amplitude-only (77.89%) and phase+amplitude (78.50%) underperform PhaseAT (85.7%), indicating constrained, gradient-guided phase perturbation is more effective in our setting.
Novelty [R4] 
PhaseAT’s novelty is not generic Fourier augmentation, but a constrained phase-adversarial objective: (i) inner maximization instead of stochastic mixing, (ii) phase-only perturbation with fixed amplitude, (iii) Wirtinger-style phase gradients, and (iv) saliency-masked, luminance-only perturbations for stability. Ablations show each is critical: random phase is weaker (81.90 vs. 85.7), removing the mask drops to 56.47, and RGB/YCbCr perturbations underperform.

title: PhaseGen: A Diffusion-Based Approach for Complex-Valued MRI Data Generation
abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) raw data (k-Space) contains valuable magnitude and phase information, yet clinical AI methods typically discard phase data. To address this, we introduce a magnitude-conditioned generative phase modeling framework that enables synthesis of complex-valued k-Space data from widely available magnitude-only MRI datasets. Pretraining with PhaseGen significantly improves k-Space skullstripping accuracy (from 40.1% to 80.1%) and enhances MRI reconstruction. This approach successfully bridges the gap between abundant magnitude-only datasets and information-rich complex-valued MRI data, enabling more accurate diagnostic tasks.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Synthetic Data / Data-centric AI

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This manuscript introduces a magnitude-conditioned generative model that is capable of simulating or generating complex-valued k-Space data.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.overall, the manuscript is clearly presented and easy to follow. 
2.the proposed magntude-guided phase generation model demonstrated the best performances for most experiments.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.There is not any simulated or generated phase images presented in the manuscript (only the PSNR / SSIM metrics showed), making the overall generation results doubtful. 
2.In table 1, Naive [209k] demonstrated the best PSNR at 8x acceleration instead of the proposed PhaseGen, and an SSIM of <56% is also at a very low level. 
3.No sequence details for the data involved were described, which is very important for this applicatio. 
4.It is not clear whethter the output of the complex-valued network in the proposed model is the complex-valued data or phase images directly in the current version. please clarify. 
5.The phase generation task presented in this manuscript is just a toy model instead of a realistic project in MRI reconstruction / acquisiitons, because one never acquire a “magntiude” image, only the “raw complex-valued kspace” data will be acquired in the forms of real + imaginary components instead of magnitude + phase. So it is just a click of the saving button in the scanner system to direct generate real phase data by just a fast fourier transform. 
6.The authors are correct that the phase information is very important; however, this is not ture for all types of MRI images (acquired using different sequences), and unfortunately, I do not think the phase is important in fastMRI dataset (for most of them are acquired using FSE sequence). In addition, the downstream tasks are also too simple. Taking the most famous MRI phase-based sequence (Susceptibility Weighted Imaging, SWI) as an example, the most important or foundamental informaiton is hidden in a background part, whos signal / intensity is usually much higher than the true information, and thus formulating the well known phase wraps.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Overall, the phase generation task presented in this manuscript is just a toy model instead of a realistic project in MRI reconstruction / acquisiitons for majorly two reasons: 
1.MRI scanners never acquire a “magnitude” image; only the “raw complex-valued kspace” data will be acquired in the form of real + imaginary components instead of magnitude + phase. So it is just a click of the saving-data button in the scanner system to directly generate real phase data by just a fast Fourier transform. 
2.Indeed, the phase information is not always very important for all types of MRI images (acquired using different sequences), and that is why there are only magnitude images in most previous public datasets. A realistic MRI phase-based application is SWI or more recent QSM (quantitative susceptibility mapping), and in these two sequences, the “phase” data (different from magnitude data) is much more complicated because a background signal should also be formulated and considered (this is because of the non-locality nature of phase components and partly the reason for phase wraps). 
These two points make this manuscript a toy-model-level work.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors argued, “Regarding the absence of qualitative phase visualizations: raw MRI phase maps are inherently non-interpretable to human observers, as their appearance is dominated by background field contributions unrelated to tissue structure”. However, this is not always the case, especially when multi-echo GRE sequences are used, and we can observe the obscure fine structures in tissues. The case is also true for FSE data, because they reflect the information of B0 field in the scanner. So, it is very important to “see” the phase images because they are meaningful in many important applications.
I agree that the complex-valued data should be beneficial for improving the results of the classification and cardiac segmentation tasks, as reported in recent works mentioned by the authors, but it does not mean that the “synthesized” phase data will also improve the performance of models on real-world applications. Indeed, estimating phase data from magnitude should be a very ill-conditioned problem, because they represent information from different dimensions/aspects, respectively. It is nearly impossible to complete this task without strong assumptions or priors. For example, knowing a complex number z’s magnitude is 1 only identifies a unit circle in complex space, instead of the exact phase. If this task is feasible, then the authors should discuss the reason and formulate the process.
As for the downstream brain extraction task shown in this work, the improvements in numeric metrics like DSC do not mean that you have got better brain extraction results, which can only be identified by visualizing the original brain images and the brain extraction/segmentation maps. Besides, the BET task itself is too simple; the authors should at least conduct a “realistic” segmentation work to demonstrate the effectiveness of their model, although in my opinion, the role of the model is not learning the “phase”, it is more like a high-level latent information beneficial for brain segmentation.
It will be better to conduct background removal to remove the background field from the synthesized phases using existing algorithms to see if they really synthesized useful information from the magnitude data, which will be a much more meaningful and persuasive downstream experiment compared to the BET experiment.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduced a magnitude conditioned generative phase modeling framework that enables synthesis of complex-valued k-Space data from widely available magnitude-only MRI datasets. Using the proposed method to generate complex training data and train for downstream tasks can significantly improves k-Space skullstripping accuracy and enhances MRI reconstruction.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper targets a very practical and important issue in MRI deep learning community: The lack of complex data for training and the performance degradation of magnitude-data-trained network on real-world application. It provides a novel way to generate complex dataset using diffusion model and shows its benefits on downstream tasks.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Lack of qualitative results
The paper does not include example phase images generated by the diffusion model or comparisons with ground truth. Such visualizations are important for assessing reconstruction quality in medical imaging and should be included.
2.Writing and organization
The writing can be improved for clarity. In Material and Methods section, I would suggest use separate sections to introduce methods/dataset for proposed phase generation method and downstream validation methods, which can benefit readers. In Results, avoid repeating table values in the text and instead focus on summarizing key findings and insights.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper targets a very practical and important issue in MRI deep learning community: The lack of complex data for training and the performance degradation of magnitude-data-trained network on real-world application. It provides a novel way to generate complex dataset using diffusion model and shows its benefits on downstream tasks.
