It extends LoRA/SineLoRA by using input-derived prior features to modulate the sinusoidal low-rank update, aiming to improve expressivity while keeping the adaptation parameter-efficient. The paper received consistent positive reviews, with all three reviewers recommending Weak Accept. Reviewers appreciated the clear motivation, simple formulation, good writing, and broad evaluation across multiple medical imaging tasks, including generation, segmentation, classification, and CT reconstruction. The main concerns are about the limited analysis of the learned modulation parameters, some unclear design choices, and reproducibility details. Overall, I recommend acceptance. The contribution is somewhat incremental relative to LoRA/SineLoRA, but the method is well motivated, technically sound, and evaluated across a reasonably broad set of medical imaging scenarios. The remaining issues can likely be addressed in the final version.

title: Prior-Anchored Debiasing for Long-Tailed Multi-Organ Pathology Report Generation
abstract: Automated pathology report generation from Whole Slide Images (WSIs) has attracted increasing attention in digital pathology. However, existing methods are predominantly developed under single-organ settings, overlooking the multi-organ scenarios encountered in clinical practice, where organ types typically follow a long-tailed distribution. To address this gap, we identify two critical biases: (1) visual representation bias, where the encoder favors head-class patterns over tail-class discriminative features, and (2) textual decoding bias, where the decoder overfits to head-class narrative patterns, yielding diagnostically unreliable outputs for tail-class organs. To mitigate these two biases, we propose a novel Prior-anchored multi-Organ pathology report Generation framework (PriOrGen). Specifically, a Visual-Prototype Anchored Bottleneck module leverages the information bottleneck principle with learnable anchor representations to selectively retain diagnostically relevant visual information while filtering out head-biased redundancy. Secondly, a Meta-Report Anchored Bank module constructs an organ-specific meta-report anchored bank and retrieves organ-faithful textual priors to steer the decoder away from head-class narrative patterns. Extensive experiments on a multi-organ pathology dataset demonstrate that our method effectively mitigates long-tail biases and achieves superior report generation performance across both head and tail organ categories compared to state-of-the-art methods.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The proposed methodology, PriOrGen, investigates a prototype-based approach for generating reports from Whole Slide Images (WSIs). The authors claim that by utilizing a meta-report bank and a query mechanism, they have effectively improved the generation performance for tail classes, addressing the challenges inherent in long-tail distributions.
reviews.text_strengths:
The proposed method is supported by a rigorous evaluation across 11 different cancer types.
The paper includes a thoroughly designed ablation study that clearly isolates and justifies the contribution of each individual component.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The necessity of the “meta-report” concept is questionable. Since pathology reports often follow standardized formats, it is unclear if this meta-report is a simple template or a structured representation of specific findings (e. g. , organ-specific mentions, staging). If it aims for the latter, an ontology-based graph approach might be more effective.
While prototypes are efficient, they risk losing fine-grained details. Using only 4 prototypes seems insufficient for pathology, where micro-scale patterns (e. g. , Lymphovascular Invasion, LVI) are critical for diagnosis. Compared to methods like PANTHER (using 16 or 32 prototypes), the proposed approach may only capture macro-patterns, which is a significant concern for clinical utility.
It is unclear whether the prototypes are organ-specific or universal. If the model relies on organ-specific learning, the claim of addressing “long-tail distributions” across a universal scale may be exaggerated. The authors should clarify the scope and implementation of these prototypes.
The authors used a mix of UNI and PLIP. For better consistency and to isolate the contribution of the proposed method, using a single backbone (e. g. , PLIP) throughout the experiments would have been more appropriate.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Although the methodology is well-executed and the results are promising, the paper tends to over-interpret the significance of certain components. Some of the high-level claims lack direct empirical support within the provided results.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: After reading the authors’ rebuttal, I find that the authors have responded thoroughly and in good faith, resolving many of the concerns I raised. The clarifications provided are convincing, and I expect that the promised revisions will lead to a meaningfully improved final manuscript. I therefore maintain my original decision to Accept.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper targets pathology report generation in a multi-organ setting where organ types follow a long-tailed distribution, a scenario that has received little attention compared with single-organ report generation. The authors identify two biases induced by the long tail, visual representation bias on the encoder side and textual decoding bias on the decoder side, and propose PriOrGen, a dual-prior framework that addresses both. Experiments covering 11 TCGA cancer types show gains over several baselines, particularly on tail-class organs.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The motivation is clear and clinically meaningful. Moving from single-organ to multi-organ pathology report generation is a realistic direction, and the observation that a long-tailed organ distribution induces both visual and textual biases is a reasonable framing that has not been explicitly studied before in this task.
2.The decomposition of the problem into two complementary bias sources is clean, and the proposed dual-prior design is conceptually aligned with these two sources.
3.The paper is clearly written and the figures communicate the proposed pipeline effectively.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Evaluation in the experiments relies only on BLEU-Mean, METEOR and ROUGE-L. However, these surface n-gram metrics have been shown to correlate poorly with clinical correctness in medical report generation. Since the central claim of the paper is improved diagnostic reliability on tail-class organs, the absence of any clinical or entity-level metric, and the absence of pathologist evaluation, makes it hard to verify that the method actually mitigates the “linguistically fluent but diagnostically erroneous” failure mode that it explicitly targets.
2.The reported improvements are small and their statistical reliability is not well established. Tail-class absolute gains are also modest and come from very small test sets. Results are reported from a single run without standard deviations, and the significance test uses n=11 organs as independent units rather than repeated runs, which provides limited statistical power. Under this protocol the improvements are not convincingly above noise.
3.No comparison against long-tail learning methods is included.
4.The capacity of VPAB appears insufficient and is not analyzed. Only K=4 prototypes are used to cover diagnostic patterns across 11 histologically heterogeneous organ types, and no sensitivity analysis on K is reported.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses a clinically relevant and under-explored problem, and the bias decomposition together with the corresponding dual-prior design is well motivated. However, the empirical support for the main claims is weak in its current form.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Although my concerns have not been fully addressed, given that the overall completeness of this paper is relatively high and the author has made efforts to supplement necessary experimental results in the rebuttal, I am inclined to accept it.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposed the PriOrGen, a novel pathological image report generation model that addresses the long-tail distribution issue. The proposed method first uses a visual-prototype anchored bottleneck module to filter redundant pathological patches and reduce the influence of long-tailed visual distribution. It then uses a Meta-Report Anchored Bank module to retrieve organ-level meta-report templates. The organ-level meta report ensures the model is not biased to the text distribution of the major organ classes. PriOrGen is evaluated on the ML-Path dataset with 11 different cancer types and an extremely biased distribution. The proposed method shows a uniform improvement in both head and tail classes and demonstrates balanced behavior across different organs and cancer types.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The proposed method is reasonable and well-validated. The PriOrGen addresses the distribution bias issue from both visual and text aspects. VPAB successfully compensates for scarce tail-class visual representations, while MRAB independently guards against textual overfitting during the decoding phase.
2.The ablation experiment is well organized and helpful. The paper not only evaluated the contribution of the VPAB and MRAB module, but also demonstrated the influence of hyperparameters like $\rho$ and $\mu$.
3.Code is provided with an anonymous link in the paper.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The proposed method is largely built on existing methods, such as LLMs like Gemini3-Pro and PLIP. While these methods are well-recognized in the field and are generally considered standard, it is still possible that these methods are not reliable in some aspects. A discussion about such influence should be included.
2.While the paper has evaluated the proposed method against multiple baselines, it would still be great if the proposed method were compared with a long-tail distribution-oriented method. Even simply comparing against a vanilla baseline trained with organ-wise balanced sampling can further highlight the contribution of the proposed method.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The reviewer is curious about the model size and training cost (in terms of GPU-hours) for the proposed method. Providing this information can help improve understanding of the model’s behavior.

Overall, this is a solid paper with clear writing, detailed evaluation, and non-trivial contribution. The paper’s arguments are properly discussed and validated through the experiments. Thus, the reviewer would like to recommend direct accept for this work.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal has largely addressed my concerns. I would encourage the authors to update the paper in the camera-ready version to reflect these new results.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper targets multi-organ report generation, which is quite uniquely position compared to single-organ. Specifically, the authors try to solve report generation for multi-organ settings, where organ type follows a long-tailed distribution. The authors propose PriorGen - a dual-prior framework that addresses biases introduced by long tail (visual and textual biases). The authors have evaluated and benchmark on 11 TCGA cancer types.
All the reviewers have agreed that this is an important problem setting that has been overlooked before and is well motivated clinically. The paper is also clearly written and easy to follow, with a rigorous evaluation across 11 cancer subtypes and detailed ablation studies.
Before making a final decision, certain questions require clarification, and I suggest the authors to lay particular emphasis on the below comments from the reviewers.
1.Meta-report concept (R#1): Whether this is really necessary? Why not do an ontology-guided report?
2.Number and nature of prototypes (R#1, R#2): Only 4 prototypes are required? Does it only capture macro-level structures? Were more prototypes tried or was there a sensitivity study done? And what did these prototypes actually learn? Were they organ-specific?
3.Consistent backbone (R#1): The authors should have used consistent UNI or PLIP throughout the experiments? Any reason why two different backbones were tried?
4.Text evaluation metrics (R#2): BLEU, METEOR don’t provide the best correlation with clinical correctness. Did the authors try any other metrics or qualitative interpretation?
5.Benchmarking with long-tailed (R#2,R#4): Standard long-tailed benchmarking is missing.

This paper proposes PriorGen which performs report generation for multi-organ settings, where organ type follows a long-tailed distribution.
All the reviewers agreed that this is an important problem setting that has been overlooked before and is well motivated clinically during the first round of review. Certain clarifications and comments were raised regarding the inconsistency of backbones, selection of prototypes, and meta-report concepts.
The authors have clarified during their rebuttal, although albeit by also adding additional experiments, which should not be taken into consideration for decision-making. Nevertheless, the authors have argued convincingly about their choice of backbones, meta-reports, long-tailed benchmarks and other issues that were raised. This is a nice contribution to the field of histopathology analysis.

The paper addresses an important and clinically relevant problem of multi-organ pathology report generation under long-tail distributions. Reviewers appreciated the clear motivation, the well-structured dual-prior design, and the practical formulation of mitigating both visual and textual bias in long-tail settings. The proposed framework is technically sound and supported by comprehensive experiments. Several concerns were initially raised regarding the interpretation of the meta-report representation, the limited number of prototypes, the lack of clinical evaluation metrics, and missing comparisons with long-tail learning methods. However, the rebuttal provided additional clarifications and supplementary experimental evidence that adequately addressed the reviewers’ main concerns. Multiple reviewers noted that the revised explanations and additional analyses substantially improved the paper and supported acceptance. Overall, I support acceptance.

This paper initially received divergent scores from reviewers. Following the rebuttal, however, the reviewers reached a consensus in favor of acceptance. 
Given the reviewers’ unanimous support for acceptance after the rebuttal, I recommend this paper be accepted.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the meta-reviewer and reviewers for recognizing the clinical importance, clear presentation, comprehensive evaluation, and ablations. We conducted additional analyses for major concerns below:
Meta-reports concept (R1Q1/MetaQ1). As shown in Fig. 2, meta-reports are designed at the organ level. They summarize recurring report templates and common organ-specific expressions in training reports, including diagnostic terminology, lesion descriptions, staging/margin phrases, and report-style context. Thus, they provide the decoder with an organ-faithful textual prior rather than a rigid output template. An ontology graph is complementary, but it mainly encodes predefined concepts and relations; it does not directly capture the empirical language distribution needed to mitigate textual decoding bias.
Prototype number (R1Q2/R1Q3/R2Q4/MetaQ2). VPAB prototypes are learned across organs. VPAB employ these prototypes to guide patch filtering rather than replacing fine-grained evidence. After prototype scoring, 40% of WSI patches are retained for decoding. We will further clarify these. Here, we further conduct K-sensitivity: 
Prototype_K / BLEU-MEAN / ROUGH-L / METEOR
2: 0.265 / 0.175 / 0.294
4: 0.273 / 0.181 / 0.305
6: 0.258 / 0.173 / 0.293
8: 0.254 / 0.168 / 0.286
K=4 is empirically optimal. Larger K adds redundant anchors rather than improving micro-pattern capture.
Backbone consistency (R1Q4/MetaQ3). UNI and PLIP play different roles. UNI is the main histology visual encoder for VPAB because of its strong pathology representation. PLIP is used only as the vision-language retrieval index in MRAB, matching selected patches to PLIP-encoded meta-reports. We added PLIP-only experiment here: 
Backbone / BLEU-MEAN / ROUGH-L / METEOR
PLIP-only: 0.257 / 0.170 / 0.288
Clinical correctness/statistics (R2Q1/R2Q2/MetaQ4). We further added clinical metrics comparing with second best baseline:
Method/ FactENT [1] / DocLens recall [2] / DocLens precision [2]
Ours: 0.514 / 0.3626 / 0.4522
BiGen: 0.501 / 0.3519 / 0.4011
These support better diagnostic content beyond surface overlap. 
For reliability, we conduct report-level tests vs BiGen: B-M p=0.0153 and METEOR p=2.52e-05 are significant; ROUGE-L p=0.1929 is not significant, which is same as Table 1.[1] Miura Y, Zhang Y, Tsai E, et al. Improving factual completeness and consistency of image-to-text radiology report generation[C]//Proceedings of the 2021 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies. 2021: 5288-5304.[2] Xie Y, Zhang S, Cheng H, et al. Doclens: Multi-aspect fine-grained medical text evaluation[C]//Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024: 649-679.
Long-tail benchmarking (R2Q3/R4Q2/MetaQ5). Since other long-tail learning methods are not designed for generation task, we added organ-wise balanced sampling (OWBS) as a standard long-tail baseline. 
Methods / BLEU-MEAN / ROUGH-L / METEOR
OWBS: 0.249 / 0.175 / 0.289
Ours: 0.273 / 0.181 / 0.305
This suggests simple resampling is insufficient, and the dual visual/text priors are needed.
Reliability/cost (R4Q1). Gemini-3 Pro is only used offline to construct the meta-report bank and does not participate in training or inference; potential unreliability is filtered through manual verification. PLIP is a mature pathology vision-language model validated on multiple benchmarks.
We will add these experiments/clarifications to strengthen the evidence for PriOrGen’s claims.

title: Prior-Guided Hierarchical Vector Quantized-VAE for Digital Subtraction Angiography Generation
abstract: Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA) is the clinical gold standard for vascular imaging but is frequently degraded by motion artifacts due to patient physiological movement. While deep learning offers a potential alternative to traditional subtraction, existing models often fail to handle cases with severe motion artifacts and frequently yield incomplete vessel reconstructions. To address these challenges, we propose a Prior-guided Hierarchical Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder (PH-VQVAE). First, our model features a dual-branch encoder that extracts features from both the pre-contrast mask and contrast images at multiple scales. We introduce a window-based cross-attention mechanism at each level to efficiently capture local contrast differences and fuse anatomical priors, enabling precise “soft subtraction” robust to local misalignments. Second, we abandon the continuous latent representations used in conventional generative models in favor of a hierarchical discrete modeling approach. By mapping multi-scale features to learned discrete codebooks, our method effectively filters out background noise and motion inconsistencies, which lack compact representations in the discrete space, while preserving the topological integrity of vessels. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly reduces motion artifacts and achieves superior reconstruction accuracy compared to the state-of-the-art generative models, offering a promising tool for safer and more efficient interventional imaging.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors present a method to remove the pre-bolus background signals from raw DSA images with robustness against motion artifact. The method is a modified VAE which integrates with hierarchical, limited-span attention and vector quantisation to suppress background noise while preserving signals from fine vessels.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper is well written, with a clear structure and a smooth, logical flow. The motivation is effectively presented, and the design is described and explained in a clear and coherent manner. The results provide convincing evidence that the proposed method achieves higher reconstruction accuracy compared to the referenced approaches.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
While the paper is generally well articulated, the clarity of several arguments could be improved. For example, (1) in the Introduction, the limitations of existing methods are presented as factual statements but are not supported by references. These sentences should be revised to clarify whether they reflect established findings or the authors’ own interpretations, and appropriate citations should be added where necessary. (2) Similarly, in the Methods section, the statement “Continuous latent spaces often encode stochastic motion artifacts and high-frequency noise indistinguishably from the vascular signal” should be supported with relevant references.
How to justify the use of SSIM and RMAE as quantitative metrics, when the referenced “ground truth” image contain motion artifacts? The authors should perhaps dicuss.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Overall, this work is well presented and the performance of the proposed method surpasses existing methods according to the evidence.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have addressed the key concerns. Therefore, I recommend acceptance.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
1) Hierarchical Discrete Modeling (VQ-VAE)
The authors pivot away from standard continuous latent representations toward a Hierarchical Vector Quantized-Variational Autoencoder (PH-VQVAE)
2) Prior-Guided Dual-Branch Architecture
Instead of treating the DSA task as a single-image translation, the authors utilize a dual-branch encoder to process the pre-contrast mask and the contrast image simultaneously.
3) Multi-Scale Window-based Cross-Attention (MWCA)
The core intelligence of the model lies in its fusion mechanism. Using window-based cross-attention at different resolutions allows the model to perform soft subtraction.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) The work makes a significant departure from standard single-scale continuous latent representations. By introducing the first hierarchical VQ-VAE specifically for the DSA task, the authors effectively resolve the feature averaging problem common in global compression. This multi-scale approach ensures that high-fidelity details of tiny collateral vessels are preserved, even at high compression ratios that typically cause loss of signal in conventional models.
2) The integration of a multi-scale window-based cross-attention mechanism provides a sophisticated framework for soft subtraction. Unlike traditional rigid subtraction, this localized attention allows the model to remain highly robust to the non-rigid local misalignments and physiological motion that typically degrade the clinical gold standard. This ensures a cleaner vascular reconstruction without the ghosting artifacts common in manual or simple automated methods.
3) An extensive comparative analysis against a wide array of state-of-the-art baselines supports the paper. By evaluating the PH-VQVAE using a diverse set of metrics, including PSNR, SSIM, RMAE, and LPIPS, the authors provide comprehensive quantitative proof that their hierarchical discrete modeling outperforms existing continuous generative approaches in both mathematical accuracy and perceptual realism.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) Limited Generalizability and Domain Robustness: The study relies exclusively on a single dataset for both training and testing, which fails to account for domain shift. In clinical practice, performance can vary significantly across different X-ray hardware, imaging protocols (e.g., varying kVp or dose levels), and patient populations. Without cross-dataset validation, it remains unclear whether the PH-VQVAE can maintain its accuracy when deployed in diverse clinical environments.
2) Constraints of Discrete Codebook Representation: While the hierarchical discrete codebook effectively filters noise, it introduces a risk of quantization error. Because the model forces the reconstruction to match a finite set of learned patterns, there is a potential clinical risk of pathology smoothing. Rare vascular structures might be incorrectly mapped to “normal” vessel prototypes in the codebook, leading to the loss of critical diagnostic details.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

1) The authors provide what is the first application of a Hierarchical VQ-VAE to the Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA) task.
2) The overall score was heavily influenced by the extensive experimental validation. The authors did not rely on a narrow set of metrics; instead, they conducted a comprehensive benchmarking exercise against a wide array of SOTA baselines.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes an improved version of VQVAE for digital subtraction angiography generation. The major contributions are a dual-branch encoder with cross attention for prior incorporation and hierarchical vector quantization for structural filtering. The experiments demonstrate the superiority of the proposed model in terms of reconstruction accuracy.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) The proposed model is overall a sound design, as the employed strategies, such as cross-attention and vector quantization, have been successfully employed for many medical image analysis areas. The overall methodology and illustration are straightforward to understand.
2) The experiments include an ablation study and a comparative study and are thus relatively comprehensive. The ablation study is detailed and clear, successfully validating the components of the proposed model. The qualitative results are nicely visualized and presented.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) The positioning of the proposed method is a bit unclear. Although VQVAE can be regarded as a generative model, its usage in this paper is more similar to a discriminative model. In fact, the proposed model is similar to a U-Net with a modified encoder and regularized latents. From this perspective, some of the compared approaches, such as the diffusion model, might not be appropriate for comparison. Besides, AaDSA, one of the state-of-the-art methods, does not use the mask image, not because the authors did not realize its importance, but because the research objective of AaDSA was to achieve subtraction-free DSA generation. However, the proposed model in this paper employs the mask image, leading to a potentially unfair experimental setup and comparison, and weakening the merit of the proposed model.
2) The motivation for the conducted improvements is insufficiently illustrated. For instance, the paper claims that the employed window-based cross-attention can perform a soft subtraction in the feature space. However, cross-attention is a general computational technique for representation learning that is widely used in deep learning. The connection between it and the soft subtraction in the feature space is unclear, and the paper shows no evidence to validate this argument. Besides, the cross-attention involves nothing like subtraction within it. To sum up, the utilization of techniques such as cross-attention and vector quantization is too general and optimized little with respect to the properties of the DSA generation task.
3) Some arguments are vague and a bit exaggerated. For instance, the paper claims, “Continuous latent spaces often encode stochastic motion artifacts and high-frequency noise indistinguishably from the vascular signal” on page 4.This is a very strong claim, and the paper does not give any theoretical or intuitive explanations to support it. In fact, most state-of-the-art research works related to vascular image analysis employ regular continuous latent representations instead of discrete ones. The paper seems to directly associate the performance improvements with some assumed functionalities of the employed techniques, which can hardly be convincing.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The proposed model is basically sound and achieves a good performance. However, the motivation of the employed techniques is not sufficiently aligned with the characteristics of DSA generation. The motivation contains unclear and exaggerated arguments, making the method less convincing. Besides, the potentially problematic comparative experiment setup weakens the quality of the proposed method.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have sought to address some of the concerns through new experimental results. From an effectiveness perspective, the new experimental results and accompanying explanations support the arguments of the authors to some extent. However, adding new experimental results to support arguments does not comply with the rebuttal guidelines. It is unfair to other authors who comply with the guidelines and thus do not add new results. Based on the original manuscript, the decision remains a rejection.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper proposes a prior-guided hierarchical VQ-VAE framework for DSA generation that aims to improve background suppression and vessel preservation.
Reviewers agree the method is well designed with strong empirical performance and clear presentation. I suggest that the authors clarify the raised concerns about 1) unclear motivation and positioning, 2) potentially unfair comparisons, and 3) limited validation of key claims.

The reviewers generally agree that the paper is well presented and proposes a sound prior-guided hierarchical VQ-VAE framework for DSA generation. The rebuttal clarifies several concerns regarding the motivation, positioning, and role of the proposed components. Overall, I would recommend acceptance.

This paper proposes a dual-branch encoder with cross-attention between reference and contrast images, coupled with a hierarchical VQ-VAE, for DSA reconstruction. The reviewers’ majority opinion is positive. R2 is strongly positive, viewing the hierarchical discrete representation as a meaningful departure from single-scale continuous latents and crediting the extensive benchmarking against SOTA baselines. R3 is negative, judging that the method is positioned as generative but functions more like a discriminative U-Net, and that several claims are made without evidence or are overconfident.
My view is that the design is well suited to the DSA task and the empirical results are convincing enough to merit acceptance. That said, R3’s concerns are valid and partly echoed by R1, and the authors are strongly encouraged to add the missing citations and to temper or substantiate the soft-subtraction and continuous-latent claims in the final version.
Finally, regarding the additional results in the rebuttal, which are in violation of the ‘no new results’ policy, R3 rightfully does not sway their opinion, and the other reviewers are already positive, and thus the rebuttal did not influence my final recommendation.
There are concerns of adding new experimental results to support arguments which does not comply with the rebuttal guidelines.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback (R1/R2: 5, R3: 3). We address the major concerns below.
1.More Fair Comparison (R3)
We added a comparison with the latest DSA imaging method, VCC-DSA, which was published online in MIA in April after our submission [Ge et al. MIA2026]. VCC-DSA also uses the mask image as an auxiliary input. After careful reproduction, VCC-DSA achieved PSNR 30.26, SSIM 0.899, and LPIPS 0.269, while our method performs better, especially in perceptual quality (LPIPS 0.085 vs. 0.269).
For AaDSA, we agree that the input discrepancy should be addressed. In the original manuscript, we had already compared AaDSA with our contrast-only variant, where both methods use only the contrast image. Under this fair setting, our method improves PSNR 27.35 → 28.11, RMAE 2.26 → 2.00, and LPIPS 0.231 → 0.181, with comparable SSIM.
We further added a dual-input comparison by upgrading AaDSA with a mask+contrast dual-branch encoder, termed AaDSA-Mask, and comparing it with our dual-branch concatenation baseline without cross-attention. Our model still performs better: SSIM 0.936 vs. 0.926, PSNR 32.33 vs. 31.90, and LPIPS 0.102 vs. 0.115.These results show that the improvement is not simply due to using the mask image, but comes from the proposed task-specific design.
2.Unclear Claims and Motivations (R1&R2&R3)
a) Claims on continuous spaces. 
Our statement was grounded in prior work. Specifically, prior studies have reported that continuous representations can be vulnerable to error accumulation [CVPR 2022], while VQ latent space can prevent input interference, such as noise and artifacts[MICCAI 2024]. We will soften the claims in the revision and add missing citations.
b) Task-specific design and quantization risks. 
Our cross-attention and VQ are not generic plug-ins but are specifically designed for DSA: 
i. The key challenge of DSA generation is to remove background structures shared by the mask image and contrast image while preserving contrast-enhanced vessels that only appear in the contrast image. Therefore, we separately encode the mask and contrast images, then perform cross-attention between their latent features. This allows the model to suppress shared background structures, e.g., bone and soft tissue, while enhancing contrast-filled vessels. 
In this sense, the module performs soft subtraction in latent space, avoiding artifacts caused by pixel-wise hard subtraction under mask–contrast misregistration. Thus, the dual-branch encoding with cross-attention is a task-specific design for DSA rather than a generic attention module. The ablation also supports its effectiveness: Concatenation / Ours — SSIM: 0.936 / 0.940, PSNR: 32.33 / 33.07, LPIPS: 0.102 / 0.095.
ii. To avoid the fine-detail loss of standard single-scale VQ, we adopt a hierarchical VQ design to mitigate the quantization risks. With tri-scale VQ, coarse levels preserve global topology while finer levels retain vessel details. Thus, VQ is also tailored to DSA’s need for both artifact suppression and fine-vessel fidelity.
3.Generalizability and Dataset Diversity (R1 & R2)
Although our data were collected from a single institution, the dataset is clinically diverse. It spans 6 years of acquisition, includes images from GE and Siemens scanners, and covers different artifact severities as well as both Anteroposterior (AP) and Lateral (LAT) projection views. To further assess generalizability, we evaluated the model separately on AP and LAT views. The results were consistent across views: AP / LAT — SSIM: 0.939 / 0.941, PSNR: 33.01 / 33.11, RMAE: 1.18 / 1.17, LPIPS: 0.100 / 0.089.These results indicate that the model maintains robust performance across different projection views.
Reference:
1.Gu et al., CVPR 2022, Vector Quantized Diffusion Model for Text-to-Image Synthesis
2.Han et al., MICCAI 2024, Non-Adversarial Learning: Vector-Quantized Common Latent Space for Multi-Sequence MRI
3.Ge et al. MIA 2026, VCC-DSA

title: PRISM: Differentiable Analysis-by-Synthesis for Fixel Recovery in Diffusion MRI
abstract: Diffusion MRI microstructure fitting is nonconvex and often performed voxelwise, which limits fiber peak recovery in narrow crossings. This work introduces PRISM, a differentiable analysis-by-synthesis framework that fits an explicit multi-compartment forward model end-to-end over spatial patches. The model combines cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), gray matter, up to K white-matter fiber compartments (stick-and-zeppelin), and a restricted compartment, with explicit fiber directions and soft model selection via repulsion and sparsity priors. PRISM supports a fast MSE objective and a Rician negative log-likelihood (NLL) that jointly learns σ without oracle information. A lightweight nuisance calibration module (smooth bias field and per-measurement scale/offset) is included for robustness and regularized to identity in clean-data tests. On synthetic crossing-fiber data (SNR=30; five methods, 16 crossing angles), PRISM achieves 3.5° best-match angular error with 95% recall, which is 1.9× lower than the best baseline (MSMT-CSD, 6.8°, 83% recall); in NLL mode with learned σ, error drops to 2.3° with 99% recall, resolving crossings down to 20°. On the DiSCo1 phantom (NLL mode), PRISM improves connectivity correlation over CSD baselines at all four tracking angles (best r=.934 at 25° vs. .920 for MSMT-CSD). Whole-brain HCP fitting (~741k voxels, MSE mode) completes in ~12 min on a single GPU with near-identical results across random seeds.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning
Machine Learning -> Synthetic Data / Data-centric AI

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The work proposes a methodology for joint inversion of multi-compartment stick and zepplin models and nuisance bias field, for both Gaussian and Rician noise models. The microstructure parameters, multiplicative bias field and noise model parameters are estimated jointly using gradient based optimization, along with spatially prior to promote smoothness in fiber directions and compartment volume fractions.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) This reviewer found the methodology novel, ambitious and well motivated. Particularly the integration of components typically considered “pre-processing” directly into the microstructure inverse problem is a good direction.
2) The quantitative results are promising in comparison to standard techniques, if not state of the art techniques at this point (see item 3 on weaknesses).
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) A key component of the method is spatial regularization. Particularly, the authors mention several priors used to regularize the peaks, including a “direction continuity”. What is this penalty function? How it handle/associate multiple peaks? More explanation would be helpful.
2) How are the prior regularizer penalties (the lambdas) set? Presumably, these will depend on acquisition parameters and SNR. Can the authors provide guidance on how to tune/set them in practice for different datasets. How sensitive is the method to their values?
3) There are a variety of recent (deep) learning-based approaches to FOD estimation which have reported to largely surpass the performance over CSD family of methods (see Section 4.5 of [1] for a non exhaustive list). The numerical experiments would be improved by comparing with one (or several) representative examples from this class of methods.
4) The method fixes the diffusivities. This can lead to bias in peak identification when microstructure differs significantly from nominal values [2]. This should at least be acknowledged, and ideally evaluated via simulation.
5) Some visual comparison of the recovered FOD fields between the methods would be a very helpful supplement to the quantitative results for evaluation.
[1] Davood Karimi, Simon K. Warfield; Diffusion MRI with machine learning. Imaging Neuroscience 2024.
[2] Guo F, et. al. Fiber orientation distribution from diffusion MRI: Effects of inaccurate response function calibration. J Neuroimaging. 2021.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Paper is borderline. Method is well motivated and novel and results are promising. Concerns remain about the number of tuning parameters and the sensitivity of the methods performance to them, as well as lack of qualitative results on the FOD reconstructions, particularly in crossing fiber regions, to supplement the quantitative results (see weaknesses for more details);
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Promising paper on the borderline. Main cited weakness of original submission were lack proper evaluation of sensitivity to model hyper-parameters/clear guidance for choosing them across different datasets, lack of qualitative evaluation on real data, and questionable relevance of comparisons/omissions. These issues are not adequately addressed by rebuttal. Paper would benefit from larger revision.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes PRISM, a fitting framework for diffusion MRI microstructure that combines an explicit multi-compartment analytic signal model (CSF, GM, K white-matter stick-and-zeppelin fibers, and a restricted compartment) with a nuisance calibration module (bias field, per-measurement affine correction, learned noise level). All parameters are optimized jointly end-to-end using Rprop. The method supports two data-fidelity modes: MSE and a Rician NLL that also learns the noise level self-supervised. It is evaluated on synthetic crossing-fiber data, the DiSCo1 phantom, and an HCP subject against CSD, MSMT-CSD, and ODF-FP.
reviews.text_strengths:
The end-to-end joint optimization of tissue parameters together with nuisance calibration (bias field, per-measurement affine, noise level) is a clean and to my knowledge novel reformulation of a pipeline that is typically split into separate preprocessing and fitting stages.
The Rician NLL formulation with self-supervised sigma recovery is a useful addition and produces a meaningful improvement over MSE.
The crossing-fiber benchmark is designed to be in the author’s disfavor: PRISM uses a deliberately mismatched D_perp (0.4 versus the true 0.3), while CSD and MSMT-CSD receive oracle response functions. Outperforming oracle-initialized baselines under this setup is a strong result.
The related work section is quite thorough and detailed to my knowledge and correctly situates PRISM against voxelwise classical fitters, learning-based voxelwise mappings, mesh-based differentiable simulators, and dictionary approaches.
Evaluation is quite through since it spans synthetic, phantom, and in-vivo data with multiple metrics.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The forward model and the source of differentiability are not clearly specified. Equations 3-5 define a closed-form analytic signal, so “differentiability” here appears to mean standard autodiff over analytic compartments rather than a custom differentiable solver. The term “differentiable” often implies a custom solver in related work, so stating explicitly that the forward model is closed-form with gradients from autodiff (and naming the framework such as PyTorch, Julia or JAX) would resolve the ambiguity and distinguish the contribution from differentiable simulator-based methods.
The DiSCo1 ablation shows the restricted compartment drops r by 9.4 pp when removed, versus 1.9 pp for topology and 0.7 pp for spatial priors. Without the restricted compartment PRISM scores r = 0.840, below MSMT-CSD at 0.920.Since the baselines do not include this compartment, part of the headline gain is model capacity, not the analysis-by-synthesis framework. Either give MSMT-CSD an equivalent compartment or report PRISM without the restricted compartment alongside baselines.
No sensitivity analysis for regularization. The method uses at least six tissue regularizers (spatial smoothness, direction repulsion, sparsity, orphan-WM, directional continuity, fiber ordering) plus calibration L2 and Total Variation, all with fixed global weights. It is not clear which are load-bearing, and the calibration regularizer weights and the 8^3 bias-field grid size are not justified or discussed.
No qualitative results. Only quantitative metrics are reported. Visualizations of fiber orientations, ODFs, or tractography on the phantom or HCP against baselines would support the numbers better and show failure modes.
The “differentiable analysis-by-synthesis” framing somewhat overclaims. In practice this is gradient-based fitting of an analytic multi-compartment model with joint nuisance estimation, which is close to what the NODDI or SANDI toolbox already do. Comparing against those methods, not only simulator-based ones, would make the actual difference (joint nuisance calibration, Rician NLL with learned sigma, patch-based spatial regularization) clearer.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Visualizations:
No qualitative figures are provided. Fiber orientation overlays on synthetic crossings, ODFs or tractograms on DiSCo1, and tissue fraction maps on HCP would support the quantitative claims and expose failure modes. A recovered bias field on HCP would also show the calibration module is doing real work rather than self-regularizing to identity.
Regularizer values, their usage and effects:
Six tissue regularizers plus calibration L2 and TV are used with fixed global weights and no sweep. A short sensitivity analysis on the main weights (lambda_sp, lambda_rep, lambda_sparse, calibration L2, bias-field grid size) would clarify which terms are load-bearing.

The paper presents a framework with joint tissue and nuisance calibration, Rician NLL with self-supervised sigma, and solid results across synthetic, phantom, and in-vivo data. The handicapped-but-winning synthetic benchmark supports the accuracy claim, and the Rician NLL with learned sigma is broadly applicable beyond this setting and thus a good contribution. That said, the method is closer to prior analytical fitters like NODDI than the paper makes it sound, the DiSCo1 gain largely comes from the restricted compartment the baselines lack, the source of differentiability is not stated, and there are no qualitative results or regularizer sensitivity analysis. A clearer positioning against NODDI, a compartment-matched ablation, and qualitative visualizations would address the main concerns.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
I recommend accept with revisions, contingent on how many of the points below can be addressed in the camera-ready.
Point 1: I agree with the clarification, but the mode of differentiability should be stated explicitly in the paper. Without naming the framework (PyTorch autograd in this case), a reader cannot tell whether gradients come from autodiff over the analytic compartments, a dedicated backward pass, or a differentiable simulator component. Stating this also addresses the “differentiable analysis-by-synthesis” framing, which otherwise reads as ambiguous.
Point 3: The rebuttal acknowledges the issue and revises the framing, which partially addresses my concern. The fact remains that PRISM without the restricted compartment scores 0.840 versus MSMT-CSD at 0.920 on DiSCo1, so part of the headline gain comes from added model capacity rather than from the analysis-by-synthesis framework itself. I would like to see the camera-ready be explicit about this in Sec. 4 and the discussion, or include a short study isolating the restricted-compartment effect in an extended version. A short discussion contrasting restricted versus unrestricted diffusion behavior would also help.
Point 6: This answers most of my questions about regularizer weights and their fixed values across datasets. For the extended version, I would like to see a proper sweep over regularizer effects, which terms each setting is sensitive to, and which are load-bearing.
Point 7: Qualitative figures within the camera-ready additional page would substantially support the quantitative claims. I recognize space is limited, so a fuller set in the extended version would be appropriate.
The idea is novel, and the joint nuisance calibration together with the Rician NLL formulation make this a good contribution. My recommendation is contingent on the differentiability clarification, an explicit acknowledgment of the restricted-compartment capacity effect in the camera-ready, and at least some qualitative figures being included.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The authors introduce PRISM, a method for fiber recovery in voxels of diffusion MRI data. It performs a global, rather than voxel-wise, fitting of the multi-compartment forward model. PRISM also estimates nuisance parameters (due to spatial bias field, signal intensity variation due to gradient direction, noise standard deviation). By being fully differentiable, the microstructure and nuisance parameters are estimated in one end-to-end optimisation.
The forward model includes up to K white matter fiber compartments, and includes soft model selection for the their number. This is done by incorporating a direction repulsion penalty term as well as a sparsity penalty term on minor fiber fractions.
Authors validate their method using simulated, digital phantom and in-vivo data. In simulated data, PRISM outperforms the baselines in terms of fiber detection and best-match angular error. In phantom data, they improve connectivity correlation.
reviews.text_strengths:
The novelty of this paper mainly resides in the optimisation of the nuisance calibration parameters simultaneously to the microstructure parameters, correcting for nuisances that may survive preprocessing.
The forward model includes many compartments (CSF, gray matter, up to K white matter fiber compartments and a restricted compartment), which enables to capture many different microstructural environments.
Experiments to evaluate the benefits of the calibration module are performed, showing it reduces angular error in the presence of intensity nuisance factors, but also that it does not affect microstructure parameter estimation in unperturbed data.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
PRISM performs global rather than voxel-wise optimisation, but its performance is compared solely against voxel-wise methods. A comparison with other global optimisation algorithms should be made. (e.g. Daducci A, Dal Palù A, Lemkaddem A, Thiran JP. COMMIT: Convex optimization modeling for microstructure informed tractography. IEEE Trans Med Imaging. 2015 Jan;34(1):246-57.doi: 10.1109/TMI.2014.2352414.)
Furthermore, spatial information via regularisation has previously been employed, but no comparisons have been made.
(e.g. A. Ramirez-Manzanares, M. Rivera, B. C. Vemuri, P. Carney and T. Mareci, “Diffusion Basis Functions Decomposition for Estimating White Matter Intravoxel Fiber Geometry,” in IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging, vol. 26, no. 8, pp. 1091-1102, Aug. 2007, doi: 10.1109/TMI.2007.900461.)
Qualitative results are not presented, impeding visual verification of the reported improvements to fiber recovery.
No comparisons to other methods are made for the real data experiment.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
There seems to be a typo in the first term of the sum in equation 9.

The experiments performed in this paper do not compare performance against other global optimisation methods, or methods that also employ spatial information. Furthermore, qualitative results are not present.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors addressed my concerns and have stated that qualitative figures will be included.

meta_reviews.text:
All three reviewers recognize the clear motivation, the novel joint nuisance-calibration framework, and the promising quantitative results of the proposed PRISM method, yet persistent critical concerns place the paper near the acceptance threshold. The authors must prioritize addressing these core points in their rebuttal. 1) Clarify the concrete formulation of spatial regularizers (especially direction continuity penalty) and provide sensitivity analysis plus practical tuning guidance for regularization weights; 2) Reframe the claimed “differentiable analysis-by-synthesis” contribution to avoid overstatement and clarify technical distinctions from prior arts; 3) Extend experimental comparisons with learning-based FOD estimation methods, global optimization baselines, and classic analytical models like NODDI; 4) Justify fixed diffusivity settings, explain unbalanced multi-compartment designs against baseline methods, and specify the implementation of differentiable optimization.

After careful review of the initial assessments, the author’s rebuttal, and post-rebuttal responses, I recommend rejecting this paper for several reasons. The primary concern is the lack of sensitivity analysis for the numerous regularization parameters, raising doubts about the method’s applicability to new datasets with varying characteristics. The authors’ claim that weights are fixed globally is problematic, as it does not provide guidance for practitioners. Additionally, the paper fails to compare PRISM with relevant state-of-the-art learning-based FOD estimation techniques, which are vital for contextualizing its performance. The absence of qualitative results also hinders the assessment of the recovered fiber orientations. Although reviewers expressed willingness to accept based on proposed changes, acceptance should rely solely on the current manuscript, which lacks essential components for a complete scientific contribution. The reviewer, confident in their assessment, maintained a Reject recommendation, highlighting substantive concerns about hyperparameter sensitivity and incomplete evaluations. The framing of “differentiable analysis-by-synthesis” remains overstated; the method is more of a gradient-based fitting approach similar to existing models like NODDI and SANDI. While the joint nuisance calibration is a valuable contribution, it does not represent a significant paradigm shift in the field.

The reviewers are generally positive after rebuttal, with two recommending acceptance and one maintaining a borderline rejection. The remaining concerns mainly relate to clearer reporting of differentiability, hyperparameter sensitivity, qualitative examples, and acknowledging the restricted-compartment capacity effect. Since these issues appear addressable in the camera-ready rather than fatal to the contribution, I recommend Accept.

Even though reviewer 1 is not wrong in suggesting that this paper would benefit from a larger revision, assuming that all the changes that have been promised in the rebuttal will be made to the final version, and code will be released, the paper is clearly among the stronger ones in my rebuttal batch already. Some of the suggested additional experiments might not fit within the MICCAI page limit anyway, and might thus be left for future work.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers and area chair for their constructive feedback.
1.Differentiability and positioning (R2, meta). The forward model (Eqs. 2-5) is a closed-form analytic multi-compartment expression; “differentiable” refers to gradient propagation via PyTorch autograd, not a custom solver, distinguishing PRISM from FEM-based simulators. In contrast to voxelwise fitters (CSD, NODDI, SANDI), PRISM jointly estimates bias field, per-measurement affine correction and noise level with microstructure; optimises 3-D slabs with neighbour-aware regularisation; and supports Rician NLL with self-supervised sigma.
2.Direction-continuity penalty (R1, meta). The summed term is K-permutation-invariant and avoids explicit cross-voxel peak matching: for each fiber k we sample its own fraction along its own direction and penalise along-fiber changes,
L_dc = (1/K) sum_k E_x f_k(x) (|f_k(x) - f_k(x + e d_k(x))| + |f_k(x) - f_k(x - e d_k(x))|), with e=0.5 voxel and trilinear interpolation. The f_k weighting localises the penalty to voxels carrying that fiber; +/- handles antipodal symmetry. This formula will replace the vague description. Thank you for pointing this out.
3.Restricted-compartment (R2, meta). R2 is right that part of the DiSCo1 gain reflects model capacity. Sec. 4 ablation reports PRISM without the restricted compartment at r=0.840 (full 0.934), below MSMT-CSD (0.920). PRISM’s contribution is enabling this compartment with nuisance calibration in one optimisation; we will temper Sec. 4/Discussion.
4.Fixed diffusivities (R1). Kernel diffusivities are fixed by design, following NODDI/SANDI/MSMT-CSD practice: joint estimation of diffusivities, fractions and directions is ill-conditioned at clinical SNR/shell counts (Jelescu 2016). PRISM still learns per voxel S_0, all K+3 fractions, K fiber directions and f_intra (Sec. 2). The synthetic benchmark probes this: PRISM uses D_perp=0.4 (Eq. 5) while baselines receive oracle/ground-truth-derived response functions (Sec. 3); despite this mismatch PRISM achieves 1.9x lower angular error at SNR=30 (Table 1). We will acknowledge in the revised version that a larger mismatch can bias peaks.
5.Missing comparisons (R1, R3, meta). (a) Many learning-based FOD methods (Karimi & Warfield 2024) need labelled training/protocol matching; PRISM is training-free. (b) COMMIT (Daducci 2015) weights streamlines from a precomputed tractogram, complementary to local FOD/fixel recovery. (c) DBF (Ramirez-Manzanares 2007) is relevant prior work on intra-voxel basis-function FOD; differs in scope from PRISM’s multi-compartment setting. (d) NODDI/SANDI are voxelwise analytic fitters, not K-crossing FOD baselines. Positioning will be revised.
6.Regularisation sensitivity (R1, R2, meta). Because signals are b0-normalised, all tissue weights are fixed when enabled (lambda_sp = lambda_rep = 0.01, lambda_sparse = 0.02; orphan/order = 0.01, dc = 0.005; Sec. 2), with no per-dataset tuning. Per Sec. 3, synthetic uses repulsion only, DiSCo1 adds topology, HCP the full suite; weights do not change. Sec. 4 ablation isolates each block: spatial 0.7 pp, topology 1.9 pp, restricted 9.4 pp. Calibration weights and the 8^3 bias-field grid were also fixed; the grid limits bias to low spatial frequencies. A systematic sweep is future work.
7.Qualitative figures and HCP scope (all reviewers, R3). HCP lacks ground-truth fiber orientations, so it is not claimed as a ground-truth fiber benchmark; head-to-head comparisons use synthetic and DiSCo1 data because they provide ground truth. If accepted, the camera-ready will add fiber-peak overlays from existing fits, within the additional page.
8.Eq. 9 typo (R3). The -log y term was dropped in transcription; it is a data-only constant independent of all optimised parameters, so gradients, fits and reported numbers are unaffected. We will correct it.
We commit to releasing source code upon acceptance. Thank you again for these thoughtful suggestions.

title: Privacy-Preserving Video-Based Facial Palsy Recognition via Dynamic Facial Action Modeling
abstract:
Rapid stroke screening is crucial in remote and resource-limited settings where timely medical expertise may be unavailable. Facial palsy, a visible and early indicator of stroke, oﬀers a practical and non-invasive basis for assessment, motivating the need for automated and reliable recognition methods. To address this need, we propose DP-Face, a video-based deep learning framework that captures dynamic facial asymmetry while preserving patient privacy. Rather than relying on raw RGB appearance, DP-Face integrates structural cues derived from facial landmarks and wrinkle patterns with temporal muscle dynamics modeled through facial Action Units. To promote reproducibility, we also construct Palsy-330, the largest publicly available video dataset to date for facial palsy classification, comprising 330 subjects. Evaluated under a patient-independent protocol, DP-Face outperforms existing baselines, demonstrating the promise of dynamic, privacy-preserving facial analysis for rapid stroke screening. The source code and dataset are available at
https://github.com/ChangYuance/DP-Face.
subject_areas: Special Topic -> AI for Population Health, Public Health & Epidemiology

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a video-based deep learning framework, DP-Face, for the recognition of facial palsy. The method generates privacy-preserving images by combining facial keypoint connections and wrinkle features, while leveraging facial action units to capture dynamic sequences of muscle movements. In the feature fusion stage, the model adopts a FiLM-based modulation mechanism to integrate AU dynamic features into appearance features. Furthermore, this paper constructs Palsy-330, currently the largest video-level facial palsy classification dataset, which includes 330 subjects.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Introduces Palsy-330, the largest video-level dataset (330 subjects) to date for facial palsy classification. 
2.The proposed PP images effectively eliminate identity-discriminative information. 
3.Utilizes the FiLM mechanism for multimodal modulation, which is empirically proven by ablation experiments to be superior to standard concatenation and attention strategies.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Lack of innovation: The DP-Face framework is essentially an assembly of standard visual and sequential modules. 
2.Typographical error in Table 3: In Table 3, the Specificity (Spec. ) value 52.5 of for DP-Face is incorrectly bolded. The highest value in this column is 70.0, achieved by the FP-VGGFace.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Due to a lack of innovation and rigor in data presentation, I recommend a Weak Reject.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors’ rebuttal can partially solve my concerns. While I understand the clinical trade-off of prioritizing high recall over specificity for early stroke screening, a specificity of 52.5% still poses a risk of introducing too many false positives in real-world clinical workflows. However, the application-driven motivation is clear, and the integration of privacy-preserving features for screening shows good clinical novelty and practical value. The evaluation on a real multi-center dataset is also appreciated. In summary, considering the overall contribution, I decide to update my rating to Weak Accept.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents DP-Face, a video-based framework for facial palsy recognition aimed at early stroke screening. The method combines privacy-preserving facial representations derived from landmarks and wrinkle patterns with temporal modeling of facial dynamics using Action Units (AUs). A multimodal fusion strategy based on FiLM integrates appearance and motion cues. Additionally, the authors introduce Palsy-330, a new dataset of 330 participants collected across multiple hospitals. Experimental results show moderate improvements over existing baselines and some generalization capability on an external dataset.
reviews.text_strengths:
-) The paper addresses a clinically relevant and impactful problem: early stroke screening through facial palsy detection in resource-limited settings.
-) The introduction of the Palsy-330 dataset is a valuable contribution, as it is relatively large for this task and collected in real clinical environments.
-) The use of participant-independent cross-validation is appropriate and avoids identity leakage during evaluation.
-) The proposed framework combines structural and temporal information in a reasonable way, leveraging both geometric representations and Action Units.
-) The idea of privacy-preserving representations is relevant, especially in medical applications involving sensitive patient data.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
-) The dataset description lacks important details, such as the distribution of samples per participant and more comprehensive statistics, making it difficult to assess potential biases.
-) The decision on using [27] for facial features detection is not justified. Why are you selecting this method and not others? And do you have any clous on how it can affect the overall pipeline?
-) The annotation protocol is insufficiently described, with no information about the number of clinicians, inter-rater agreement, or precise criteria for labeling facial palsy.
-) The temporal modeling design is not well justified, particularly the choice of sampling only 16 frames from sequences that are significantly longer, and it is unclear how temporal coverage is ensured. If you change this parameter, how does it affect the performance? And is there overlap between consecutive time windows?
-) The privacy-preserving claim is weakly supported, as identity recognition accuracy remains relatively high and no formal privacy evaluation or comparison to standard anonymization techniques is provided.
-) The performance improvements over prior methods are relatively modest and lack statistical significance analysis.
-) The evaluation does not fully address clinical relevance, as it focuses only on binary classification without considering severity levels or comparison with expert assessments.
-) Some implementation and preprocessing details are unclear, including specifics of AU extraction reliability and aspects of the training pipeline.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Overall, the paper addresses a clinically relevant problem and introduces a potentially valuable dataset together with a privacy-aware video-based framework. The integration of structural and temporal features is reasonable and supported by experimental results. However, several important aspects limit the strength of the contribution, including insufficient details about the dataset and annotation protocol, limited validation of the privacy claims, and relatively modest performance gains over existing methods. Additionally, the methodological novelty is incremental. Addressing these issues, particularly improving the clarity and rigor of the dataset description and providing stronger validation, would significantly strengthen the work.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal addresses my concerns by clarifying the dataset structure and emphasizing the reproducibility effort; however, the methodological contribution remains relatively limited and the lack of stronger baselines and annotation reliability analysis still weakens the overall impact.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents DP-Face, a video-based framework for facial palsy recognition aimed at enabling rapid stroke screening.
reviews.text_strengths: DP-Face combines a) a privacy-preserving structural representation (facial landmarks + wrinkle maps) with b) temporal facial Action Unit (AU) modeling, followed by multimodal fusion using FiLM. In addition, the authors introduce Palsy-330, a 330-subject dataset collected under clinical conditions with a standardized smile task. Experimental results show moderate improvements over prior image- and video-based baselines under a subject-independent protocol
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Incremental novelty in modeling despite reasonable integration. The core modeling components—AU-based representation, wrinkle/nasolabial modeling, and temporal dynamics—have all been explored in prior work. For example, AU-based facial palsy analysis and wrinkle-based asymmetry quantification have been previously studied, and recent works already combine structured facial representations with learned features. As such, the main contribution lies in the integration of privacy-preserving structural features with temporal AU modeling, rather than a fundamentally new modeling paradigm. This is still a reasonable contribution for MICCAI given the application context, but the paper would benefit from more precise positioning relative to prior work and a clearer articulation of what is novel.
2.The proposed “privacy-preserving” representation reduces identity classification accuracy from 99% to 57.6%, but this is still far above chance, suggesting residual identity leakage. There is no formal privacy framework (e.g., differential privacy, re-identification risk) used, and no comparison to alternative anonymization techniques (e.g., face de-identification, GAN-based anonymization). Some recent work (e.g., https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-96625-5_26) also performs explicit de-identification via motion transfer to synthetic identities and evaluates privacy–utility tradeoffs more rigorously; the current evaluation is relatively limited.
3.Clinical framing (stroke screening) is somewhat overstated. The paper is motivated by stroke screening, but the task evaluated is facial palsy classification (present vs. absent). While facial palsy is an important indicator, real-world stroke triage involves multiple symptoms and differential diagnoses (e.g., Bell’s palsy). The absence of evaluation in a true stroke or triage setting limits the strength of the clinical claims. This does not invalidate the work, but the paper would benefit from more cautious positioning, framing the contribution as facial palsy detection toward stroke screening rather than a direct solution.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper provides a useful and well-executed contribution to video-based facial palsy analysis, particularly through the release of a relatively large public dataset and a practical privacy-aware modeling pipeline. While the methodological novelty is incremental and the privacy/clinical claims could be better substantiated, the work is technically sound, reproducible, and relevant to the MICCAI community. With improved positioning and discussion of related work, this paper would make a valuable, application-oriented contribution.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Some, but not all, of my concerns were addressed. Still leaning slightly towards the accept side, considering the privacy-preserving domain is relatively underexplored for neurological diagnoses

meta_reviews.text:
The paper addresses a clinically relevant problem in video-based facial palsy recognition and introduces Palsy-330, a valuable multi-subject dataset collected under clinical conditions. Reviewers appreciated the practical motivation, dataset contribution, subject-independent evaluation protocol, privacy-aware representation, and integration of structural facial cues with temporal AU modeling. However, several concerns should be addressed in rebuttal. The reviewers consistently noted that the methodological novelty is incremental, as many components are based on existing facial representation and temporal modeling ideas. They also raised concerns about incomplete dataset and annotation details, limited validation of the privacy-preserving claim given residual identity leakage, modest performance gains, and somewhat overstated clinical framing as stroke screening rather than facial palsy detection. A focused rebuttal clarifying these and other points raised by reviewers would help reassess the paper’s contribution.

DP-Face targets a clinically relevant problem — privacy-preserving, video-based facial palsy recognition toward stroke screening — and its main strengths are the application-driven framing and Palsy-330, a large multi-hospital video dataset collected under real clinical conditions, evaluated under a subject-independent protocol. Reviewers consistently valued the dataset and practical motivation, while noting the methodological novelty is incremental (an integration of known components). The rebuttal clarified dataset/annotation details, strengthened the privacy validation, and appropriately tempered the clinical framing. Two reviewers moved to Accept. For camera-ready, authors should incorporate the rebuttal clarifications, soften the clinical claim, correct the Table 3 error, and release the dataset and code as committed.

After the rebuttal, two reviewers recommended acceptance, while one reviewer maintained a Reject recommendation. While the paper has some limitations regarding technical contribution, it also demonstrates several strengths, including a valuable public clinical video dataset and a practical framework design. Therefore, the paper is recommended for acceptance to MICCAI 2026.The authors are encouraged to incorporate the necessary changes discussed during the rebuttal process into the final camera-ready version.

The rebuttal addressed several concerns in a useful way. It clarified the dataset structure, sampling strategy, hospital distribution, annotation workflow, AU extraction, choice of landmark detector, and the intended clinical framing as “facial palsy detection towards stroke screening” rather than direct stroke screening. It also acknowledged the specificity issue on MEEI and the typo in Table 3.The additional ReID analysis described in the rebuttal helps support the authors’ interpretation that the privacy-preserving representation reduces re-identification risk, although this remains less strong than a formal privacy evaluation and was not part of the original manuscript.
The reviewer opinions after rebuttal remain mixed. R1 moved from Weak Reject to Accept, while still noting that low specificity may create many false positives in a practical screening workflow. R4 remained on the accept side, emphasizing the relevance of privacy-preserving neurological video analysis despite only partial resolution of concerns. R3 maintained a Reject recommendation, mainly because the methodological contribution remains limited and because stronger baselines and annotation reliability analysis are still missing. I weigh these points as follows: the unresolved weaknesses are real and should be discussed more carefully in the camera-ready version, but they do not fully outweigh the dataset contribution, the subject-independent evaluation, the practical privacy-aware formulation, and the reasonable empirical evidence.
Overall, the paper is recommended for acceptance as a marginal but acceptable MICCAI contribution.

author_feedback_text:
Q1: Methodological Innovation and Contribution (R1, R3, R4)
A: Our contribution is application-driven (MICCAI-oriented) rather than proposing a new backbone. The novelty lies in integrating existing components to address a real clinical problem: privacy-preserving video analysis for fast, early stroke screening. We are the first to combine PP images (de-identified geometry) with AU temporal dynamics for palsy detection. PP images remove identity cues (see Q3). As Table 2 shows, DP-Face achieves 75.1% accuracy on real data from ten Chinese hospitals, demonstrating strong potential for both home and clinical screening, even when compared to methods that directly use raw RGB images.
Q2: Dataset Details (R3)
A: Sampling: Each subject recorded one 4s smiling video (20 fps, ~80 frames). We apply 5 temporal offsets for uniform sampling, generating 4~5 samples per subject (mean±std in Table 1).
Annotation: Primary labels were provided by the collecting physicians, verified locally before uploading. The entire dataset was reviewed by a Chief Physician (15+ years experience) for consistency.
Other Details: Data were collected from 10 hospitals across central and western China, each contributing 2–101 subjects (mean 33.4, std 30.7). The top 3 hospitals contribute 65.9%, the last 4 less than 6%, reflecting real-world imbalance and providing a natural non-IID setting for further research topics such as domain adaptation and federated learning. The above metadata, along with additional information (e.g., age, gender), will be released together with the dataset to support the community.
Q3: Privacy-Preserving Validation (R3, R4)
A: We update the privacy-preserving validation experiment. We instead report ReID performance to provide stronger evidence. We extract features from RGB and PP images using separate ResNet-50 networks and train them with a triplet loss. For comparison, we also run the same experiment with RGB images only. Rank-1 accuracy drops from 100% (RGB-only) to 5.11% (PP→RGB, 100-person gallery, chance 1%), showing PP features prevent re-identification while retaining diagnostic utility. This also indicates the previous 57.6% classification result reflects memorization of “line structures” rather than identity.
Q4: Stroke Screening vs. Palsy Detection (R3, R4)
A: Facial palsy is a key BEFAST indicator for early stroke screening, but our model detects symptoms only. A positive result indicates the need for further medical consultation, not a definitive stroke diagnosis. We agree and will revise the description as “Facial Palsy Detection towards Stroke Screening”.
Q5: Choice of STAR (R3)
A: Accurate facial landmark detection is critical for reliable structural cues in facial palsy analysis. MediaPipe [2] is widely used but often produces overly symmetric 3D landmarks under severe asymmetry, reducing reliability. In contrast, STAR employs Self-adapTive Ambiguity Reduction (STAR) loss to reduce annotation ambiguity and produce more robust landmark features. It runs >20 fps on GPU, enabling real-time clinical application.
Q6: Spec. and Table 3 Error (R1)
