reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes Prompt and Probe (P²), a unified framework for adapting frozen, API-served foundation models (FMs) to both classification and segmentation in clinical imaging, while simultaneously performing annotation-efficient active learning—all using only input–output queries with no access to model weights, gradients, or internal representations.The framework operates in two stages. In the Prompt stage, a lightweight Visual Prompt Decoder (VIPD, ~2.1M parameters) is trained via zeroth-order optimization (SPSA) to generate task-aware input-space perturbations: global additive prompts for classification and spatial channel-concatenated maps for segmentation, derived from fused image (MAE ViT-B/16) and anatomical (Uformer) embeddings. In the Probe stage, the trained VIPD is repurposed as an uncertainty instrument: multi-scale perturbations applied to unlabeled samples produce prediction instability scores quantified at both image level (prompt-shift cosine dissimilarity, finite-difference sensitivity) and pixel level (boundary disagreement, volumetric change, pixel entropy). A rank-based fusion criterion with a task-emphasis parameter γ unifies acquisition across classification and segmentation tasks.The paper claims three principal contributions: (1) a unified VIPD producing both prompt types from a shared backbone; (2) multi-scale instability-driven acquisition within a single policy; and (3) a dynamically weighted cross-task training objective. Evaluated on seven public datasets across six clinical modalities, P² claims 40–60% label reduction while matching or exceeding fully supervised baselines. The central empirical finding is that spatial boundary instability signals—designed for segmentation—improve classification sample selection by up to 24.5 AUROC points, suggesting task-unified acquisition is fundamentally superior to task-specific alternatives.
reviews.text_strengths: S1.Well-scoped compound problem formulation. The simultaneous constraints of API opacity and annotation scarcity are genuine deployment bottlenecks in clinical AI. The gap analysis in Section 1 is specific and accurate, clearly positioning P² against VALIANT, BAPS, ZIP, and BlackVIP along three dimensions: black-box compatibility, annotation efficiency, and cross-task unification. No prior work satisfies all three simultaneously, and the paper makes a credible case for this gap.S2.Dual-use of VIPD as both prompt generator and uncertainty instrument. Repurposing a trained prompt decoder for informativeness estimation, without additional parameters or a separate acquisition module ,is an architecturally elegant economy. This avoids the common pitfall of bolting an independent uncertainty estimator onto a prompting framework, and the design consequence (sensitivity to input characteristics is exactly what is needed for sample selection) is intellectually compelling.S3.The cross-task signal transfer finding is scientifically significant. A 24.5-point AUROC drop on CheXpert,a classification-only dataset,from removing boundary disagreement signals alone is the paper’s most striking result. If reproducible and mechanistically validated, this implies that spatial boundary uncertainty is a domain-general proxy for diagnostic ambiguity in medical images, with implications extending well beyond this framework.S4.Breadth and realism of evaluation. Eight benchmarks across six modalities with API-constraint simulation using open-source FMs with all internal access explicitly disabled (BioViL, MedCLIP, MedSAM) is methodologically responsible and unusually broad for this class of paper. This exceeds the evaluation scope of any individual prior method in this space.S5.Practical deployability signal. Reporting convergence within 0.9 pts of FSL at ~50K queries (<1h at 1K queries/min) gives practitioners concrete, actionable guidance on real-world deployment feasibility, a type of analysis absent from most AL papers in medical imaging.
reviews.text_weaknesses: W1 [Critical]. The feature consistency loss Lfeat = ||F(X+P) − F(X)||² requires evaluation of intermediate representations F(·). Under the strict black-box constraint that defines the paper’s central premise, no access to weights, gradients, or activations, this loss cannot be computed on FM features. If F(·) refers to VIPD-internal features rather than FM features, the loss must be reframed as decoder self-regularization rather than FM feature drift constraint. As written, this is a direct contradiction of the paper’s core claim and must be explicitly resolved.W2 [Critical]. The rank fusion in Eq. 5 (RankFinal = γ·ICls + (1−γ)·ISeg) is a weighted sum of raw scores, not ranks. The abstract and body both use “rank-based fusion,” which is misleading. More substantively, ICls and ISeg are derived from different quantities (cosine dissimilarity + finite-difference sensitivity vs. pixel entropy + boundary Dice + volumetric change) and have different scales and distributions. Without normalization prior to fusion, the combined score will be dominated by the larger-magnitude component in an unpredictable, dataset-dependent manner. No normalization step is described.W3 [Significant]. The diversity loss Ldiv = −D_KL(y_prob || y^p_prob) maximizes KL divergence between original and perturbed outputs without a stabilization bound. Its interaction with the entropy term Lent which penalizes entropy proportional to prompt similarity S ,is not analyzed. When S takes intermediate values, both losses may partially oppose each other, creating unstable gradients. No loss interaction analysis or training stability curves are provided.W4 [Significant]. SPSA optimization at ~2.1M parameters raises unaddressed convergence concerns. The SPSA gradient estimator variance scales as O(d) in parameter dimensionality, making convergence noisier as parameter count grows. No variance analysis, adaptive perturbation schedule, or comparison to alternative zeroth-order methods (e.g., CMA-ES) is provided. Without convergence curves or stability analysis, the claim that zeroth-order training is “practical” at this parameter scale is asserted rather than demonstrated.W5 [Significant]. Baseline selection is inconsistent with the paper’s own threat model. Entropy Sampling is included as a black-box baseline, despite Section 1 explicitly arguing that API-served models do not expose calibrated softmax distributions. Genuinely black-box-compatible alternatives—margin sampling, least-confidence sampling, or diversity-based k-center clustering on image features requiring no FM interaction—are absent from the comparison.W6 [Significant]. The headline result (24.5 AUROC from ωb=0 on CheXpert) rests on a single dataset and single ablation condition. No sample-level analysis establishes what samples are uniquely selected by boundary disagreement, making it impossible to validate the anatomical ambiguity hypothesis against simpler explanations (e.g., CheXpert pathologies such as cardiomegaly and pleural effusion inherently involve complex organ boundaries, which may be a dataset-specific rather than universal phenomenon).W7 [Significant]. Dataset-specific tuning of 10 hyperparameters per dataset (Table 1) using a 3% stratified seed is a substantial methodological concern. The tuning procedure, whether a separate validation split was used, and whether hyperparameter selection consumed annotation budget are not described.W8 [Minor]. An unresolved “Fig. ??” cross-reference appears in Section 3.The abstract cites 92.8% AUROC on CheXpert with 60% labels, but the body reports 91.8% at 50% and 97.6% at 100%—the 92.8% figure is not traceable to any table or figure in the main text. Reference [3] (VALIANT, AAAI 2026, cited anonymously) appears to be prior work from the same group; the incremental technical contribution over VALIANT is not clearly delineated.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The cross-task signal transfer finding is genuinely interesting and could constitute the paper’s most significant contribution if properly validated. The authors are encouraged to provide: (1) a sample-level analysis showing which CheXpert images are uniquely selected by boundary disagreement, ideally with their pathology labels—to test the anatomical ambiguity hypothesis; (2) resolution of the Lfeat black-box contradiction, which is the most urgent revision needed; (3) normalization of ICls and ISeg before score fusion in Eq. 5; and (4) error bands on Figure 3 learning curves over the 10 reported runs. The VALIANT relationship should be explicitly addressed with a technical delta statement, as this is relevant to the novelty assessment.

P² addresses a well-motivated compound problem and the dual-use VIPD architecture is conceptually elegant. The evaluation breadth is commendable and the cross-task signal transfer finding could be impactful if validated. However, three issues prevent acceptance in current form: (1) the Lfeat feature consistency loss directly contradicts the black-box premise and must be resolved—this is not a minor clarification but a fundamental inconsistency that undermines the paper’s core claim; (2) the score fusion in Eq. 5 lacks normalization, making results unpredictable and dataset-dependent; (3) the VALIANT prior-work relationship is inadequately disclosed, creating uncertainty about the true incremental contribution. The weak baseline selection and missing statistical error bands on learning curves further weaken the experimental case. The paper is closer to acceptance than rejection; targeted revisions addressing items (1) and (2) would substantially strengthen it for resubmission.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors engaged with every single concern I raised — including providing concrete data for W4 (convergence curves, CMA-ES comparison), a sample-level analysis for W6, the min-max normalization specification for W2, and the critical L_self rename for W1.No concern was left completely unaddressed or dismissed.
The two critical concerns are both resolved. W1 is resolved by the L_self reframing — the fix is technically correct and eliminates the logical contradiction. W2 is resolved with concrete normalization specification and quantitative evidence that the choice matters but the method is robust. These were the highest bars, and both were cleared.
The significant concerns are mostly resolved or substantially mitigated. W4 receives the strongest response — detailed variance reduction mechanisms, monotonically contracting convergence curves, and a direct CMA-ES comparison all provided from what appears to be already-run experiments. W6’s sample-level evidence (62% vs. 31% base rate) combined with cross-dataset replication across four modalities provides reasonable support for the paper’s central finding. W7’s protocol is now clearly described.
Two residual concerns remain but do not warrant rejection. W3’s theoretical interaction analysis remains incomplete — the empirical stability evidence is acceptable for a conference paper but the theoretical claim is asserted. W5’s threat model tension — using open-source models that expose probabilities while motivating the work with proprietary APIs that don’t — requires careful revision of the framing, not just a caveat. Both of these can be addressed in the camera-ready without new experiments.

meta_reviews.text:
I am weighing the R2 accept with a lesser coefficient, and, thus, sending paper for the rebuttal.
Some of the issues from the reviews:
Iinternal model activations for the feature consistency loss, which directly goes against the black-box assumption the whole paper is built on.
The acquisition score combines different signals without normalizing them first, so the authors need to show generalizability across datasets.
Convergence analysis for the large model is needed.
Contradiction on the entropy sampling black-box regime?

The authors delivered a clear and convincing rebuttal; this paper is ready for MICCAI, provided the updates from the rebuttal round are implemented and explained in the paper.

The paper presents Prompt and Probe, a framework for adapting frozen or API-serve foundation models (FMs) to classification or segmentation in medical imaging. The reviewers acknowledged the novelty and practical motivation for the proposed framework, and found the evaluation quite rigorous, given the high number of models and datasets explored in the paper. Several weaknesses were pointed out, such as i) scale/coefficients of loss terms, ii) design choices, especially for hyperparameter tuning, and iii) inconsistencies between the namings of components (e.g., Lfeat or rank-based fusion) and their actual behavior. During the rebuttal, the authors addressed each reviewer’s points in detail and proposed appropriate changes to the manuscript as needed. I recommend acceptance.

This submission proposes a unified active visual prompting framework. R2 and R3 liked the approach and dual architecture. R1 noted missing details on hyperparameters. The rebuttal addressed most concerns, and provided missing details. One concern from my side is readibility of figures (zoom in and out multiple times made me dizzy - suggesting enlarging text size for increased visibility and impact). For all these reasons, and with respect to the other submissions, the recommendation is towards Acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We thank reviewers for recognizing P2’s compound-problem framing, the dual-use VIPD design, evaluation breadth, and the cross-task transfer finding.
[R1.1/R3.6] CheXpert +24.5 AUROC mechanism. Critical clarification: I_bnd uses NO segmentation GT. At probe time, MedSAM produces predicted boundary maps for the unlabeled CXR (original and perturbed); I_bnd = 1 - Dice(boundary_orig, boundary_pert) measures instability of MedSAM’s own predictions. Mechanism: CheXpert pathologies (cardiomegaly, effusion, atelectasis) have diagnostically informative contours; unstable boundaries indicate ambiguous anatomy, correlated with classification ambiguity. ~62% of I_bnd-uniquely-selected samples carry one of these labels (vs. ~31% base rate) — real cross-task transfer, not supervision leakage.
[R1.2/R2.3] L_unified weighting. Each term is naturally bounded — L_task is CE/Dice; L_div, L_ent in ~[0, log K]; L_feat is Lipschitz-bounded on the small VIPD trunk. All four stay within 1.5x of each other through training; no manual coefficient needed (curves added).
[R1.3] FSL ceiling. FSL 92.4% uses ViT-B/16 with matched preprocessing and 5-finding eval — within the 0.92-0.94 ViT range. DenseNet-121 is a textual reference, not the FSL backbone.
[R1.4/R3.7] Hyperparameter protocol. The 3% stratified seed is the validation split; tuning is random search over 30 trials per dataset, held out from the labeled pool — selection does NOT consume annotation budget.
[R1.5] “Fundamentally” overstated. Agreed — replaced with “consistently superior in the medical-imaging setting evaluated”.
[R1.6] Statistical test. Paired t-test over 10 runs with Bonferroni correction across all comparisons.
[R1.7] Tab.2 ACDC inconsistency. “Ours” uses dataset-specific weights (Tab.1) on top of (alpha_1, gamma); “Equal” fixes ALL weights uniformly. Caption clarified.
[R1.8/R3.8] Fig.??/Ref.[3]/ abstract. Cross-refs fixed; abstract 92.8% is P2 at 60% labels (Fig.3). VALIANT delta: it is classification-only black-box AL; P2 adds unified global+spatial prompting from one decoder, segmentation, and cross-task acquisition.
[R3.1] L_feat black-box consistency. Wording bug: F(.) is the VIPD’s OWN MLP-trunk feature (shared 1024-d activation), not FM features. L_feat = ||F_VIPD(X+P) - F_VIPD(X)||^2 is decoder self-regularization; no FM internals accessed. Renamed to L_self.
[R3.2] Score normalization. Per-batch min-max (“rank-based” = the resulting ranking): I_hat = (I - min_B)/(max_B - min_B + eps); Rank = gamma
I_hat_Cls + (1-gamma)
I_hat_Seg. Kvasir@10% Dice / CheXpert@50% AUROC: raw 56.8 / 90.6; min-max 58.5 / 91.8 (reported); Borda-rank 58.2 / 91.7.Eq. 5 corrected.
[R3.3] L_div / L_ent interaction. L_div’s KL is bounded by the supervised-loss-anchored perturbation; L_ent’s S-weighting routes entropy to whichever output matches current prompt similarity—complementary, not opposed. Training-loss std < 0.03 after epoch 20.[R3.4] SPSA convergence at 2.1M params. Variance controlled via Rademacher perturbations, Spall decay c_t=c_0/t^0.101, Polyak-Ruppert momentum, and n=8 SPSA/step (~8x reduction). CheXpert (queries/AUROC/std over 10 seeds):
5K : 71.3 / 2.1
10K : 82.4 / 1.4
20K : 88.1 / 0.8
50K : 91.5 / 0.5
100K : 91.8 / 0.4
Std contracts monotonically. CMA-ES at matched budget: 3-5 AUROC worse, ~3x memory.
[R3.5] Baselines under strict black-box. Entropy Sampling assumes returned probabilities (open-source FMs comply); caveat stated. Added strictly black-box baselines (CheXpert@50% / Kvasir@10%):
Random : 84.2 / 45.0
K-Center : 85.7 / 47.3
Coreset(CLIP) : 87.1 / 49.8
Margin : 88.4 / 51.2
Entropy : 88.9 / 52.6
P2 (Ours) : 91.8 / 58.5
[R2.1] Sec. 2 will be tightened with a notation table.
[R2.2] Add vs. concat. Classification uses additive prompts because z_I is a fixed-dim semantic vector—additive fusion preserves geometry without expanding FM input. Segmentation needs spatial alignment, so the spatial prompt is channel-concatenated.

title: Prompt Group-Aware Training for Robust Text-Guided Nuclei Segmentation
abstract: Foundation models such as Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM3) enable flexible text-guided medical image segmentation, yet their predictions remain highly sensitive to prompt formulation. Even semantically equivalent descriptions can yield inconsistent masks, limiting reliability in clinical and pathology workflows.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper tackles the sensitivity of text-guided segmentation to prompt variations by viewing semantically similar prompts as a group and enforcing consistent predictions across them. Based on this idea, it introduces a simple group-aware training framework that combines quality-based weighting of prompts and a logit-level consistency constraint. The method does not modify the model architecture and can be easily applied to existing text-conditioned segmentation models. Experiments show improved robustness to prompt variations and better cross-dataset generalization.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper addresses an important and practical problem in text-guided medical image segmentation, namely the sensitivity to prompt variations, which is particularly relevant in real clinical settings.
2.The key idea of modeling semantically equivalent prompts as groups and enforcing consistency is simple, intuitive, and well-motivated.
3.The proposed method is lightweight and easy to apply, as it does not require any architectural modification and only introduces additional training objectives.
4.The experimental setup is well-designed, including cross-dataset generalization and prompt quality variation, and the results consistently show improved robustness and reduced performance variance.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.assuming semantic equivalence, which, while effective in controlled settings, may be less representative of real-world scenarios where prompt meanings are ambiguous or partially overlapping.
2.Prompt quality is defined based on segmentation loss using ground-truth masks, which is not available at inference time, raising questions about how prompt reliability is handled in practice.
3.Although the ablation study shows the benefit of the proposed design, it would be helpful to further disentangle how much of the gain comes from the group-aware objectives versus the use of multiple prompts during training.
4.The approach enforces output-level consistency while keeping the text encoder fixed, and therefore does not fundamentally improve the semantic understanding of prompts.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses an important and practical problem in text-guided medical segmentation, namely sensitivity to prompt variations. The proposed group-wise consistency formulation is simple and intuitive, and the method is easy to apply without architectural changes. The experiments are solid, showing consistent improvements across prompt quality levels and cross-dataset settings.
However, the methodological novelty is moderate, and the approach relies on predefined prompt grouping and ground-truth-based quality estimation, which may limit its applicability in more realistic scenarios. Overall, the paper is clearly presented and empirically well-supported, making it suitable for acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper reformulates prompt sensitivity in text-guided segmentation as a group-wise consistency problem and proposes a training-time framework to improve prompt robustness for nuclei segmentation.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The mapping from prompts to masks is a key clinical challenge in pathology, where different textual descriptions legitimately refer to the same target structure. The motivation of this work is therefore well-grounded.
2.The zero-shot generalization results are inspiring. The method achieves improvements on 5 out of 6 external datasets and reaches competitive performance with SAMPO using only text prompts.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The optimization of L_group contradicts the stated motivation. The paper aims to make the model robust to low-quality prompts. However, L_group encourages the model to focus on high-quality prompts while relaxing on low-quality ones, effectively widening the gap. This directly conflicts with the goal of prompt invariance. The authors should explain how L_group and L_cons can work together when their optimization objectives are opposing.
2.A critical configuration is missing: removing only L_group while retaining L_cons. The current ablation cannot disentangle the independent contribution of L_group.
The paper states that both q̃_i (Eq. 5) and the weights w_i (Eq. 6) are computed with stopped gradients. If both are detached from the computational graph, L_group contributes zero gradient to the model optimization. The authors should clarify precisely which quantities retain gradients and how L_group provides a training signal.
4.The paper layout needs refinement. Tables 3, 4, and 5 are placed after the Conclusion section, making them hard to follow when reading the main text.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

See the above strengths and weaknesses.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a prompt group-aware training framework for text-guided nuclei segmentation. It models prompt variability by grouping semantically equivalent prompts and introduces quality-guided weighting and consistency regularization.
reviews.text_strengths: This paper suggest that modeling variability as a population consistency problem is both simple and well-motivated.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The paper relates to consistent learning and multi-view training. It focuses solely on prompt robustness and does not address the broader challenges in medical segmentation. It is currently unclear how cue groups are constructed in practice and whether the process is scalable. I’d like to know how sensitive this method is to misclassification. Can this method be extended to other modalities? What performance can this method achieve without a prompt? Moreover, some writing details to note: For example, it is not necessary to write the abstract in paragraphs.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The score is based on a clear and well-motivated idea with consistent empirical gains. The method is simple and effective, improving robustness to prompt variations. However, the novelty is moderate and the scope is relatively limited. Overall, this leads to a weak accept recommendation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text: I recommend provisional acceptance. The paper addresses a practical and timely problem in text-guided medical segmentation: robustness to prompt variation. The proposed group-aware training strategy is simple, lightweight, and easy to apply to existing models, and the experiments show consistent gains in prompt robustness and cross-dataset generalization. While the novelty is moderate and one reviewer raised important questions about the formulation of the group loss, gradient flow, and prompt-group construction, these issues appear clarifiable rather than fatal. Overall, the paper is well motivated and empirically convincing enough for acceptance, provided the authors address the methodological clarifications in the rebuttal or revision.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the reviewers and Area Chair for their careful evaluation of our manuscript and for the encouraging decision (Early Accepted). We are grateful for the recognition of the practical importance of prompt robustness in text-guided medical segmentation, and for the constructive suggestions that will help us further improve the final version. Below we summarize the main revisions we will make.
1.Scope and clinical relevance. 
Our work focuses on a controlled yet practically meaningful setting: multiple prompts that are intended to refer to the same segmentation target and therefore share the same supervision mask. We chose this setting to isolate a concrete reliability issue in text-guided segmentation, namely inconsistent predictions under alternative but clinically plausible phrasings. In the final version, we will state this scope more explicitly in the Introduction and Conclusion, and position broader prompt ambiguity as future work.
2.Training-only use of prompt quality. 
As noted by Reviewer 1, prompt quality is defined using segmentation loss with ground truth. We clarify that this signal is used only during training as a relative cue within each prompt group and introduces no extra requirement at inference time. Our inference procedure is unchanged: all methods are tested with a single prompt, without ensembling or online quality estimation. We will revise the method section to make this explicit.
3.Roles of
L_group
and
L_cons
. 
We agree that the relationship between these two losses needs clearer explanation. They are complementary rather than contradictory.
L_group
provides a relative optimization signal within a prompt group, allowing clearer prompts to serve as stronger anchors under the same supervision target, while
L_cons
directly encourages consistent predictions across prompts so that the model becomes less sensitive to wording variation. 
4.Additional ablation and separation from multi-prompt training. 
We agree that it is important to distinguish the benefit of using multiple prompts from the benefit of the proposed group-aware objectives. The current results (table 2) already suggest that increasing prompt number (K) alone does not monotonically improve performance, and that grouped multi-prompt training without the proposed objectives is insufficient. Following Reviewer 2’s suggestion, we will add the missing ablation that removes only
L_group
while retaining
L_cons
, so the individual contributions of the two losses can be isolated more cleanly.
5.Gradient-flow clarification. 
Reviewer 2 correctly identified an inconsistency in the manuscript description: if both the quality signal and weights were detached,
L_group
would yield no gradient. This is a writing error rather than an implementation issue. In the actual implementation, gradients are stopped only for the quality-derived ranking signal, while the weighting path remains differentiable. We will correct the equations and text so that the optimization description matches the implementation.
6.Prompt-group construction and extensibility. 
Prompt groups are constructed around the same image-target pair and shared mask, with prompts generated in a controlled manner by varying prompt type and prompt quality. This design does not require new mask annotations, only multiple semantically aligned descriptions for an existing target, which makes it practically scalable. We will make this pipeline clearer in the final version and release the code and prompt-construction details for reproducibility. We will also describe extension beyond pathology as a plausible future direction rather than a demonstrated result.
We again sincerely thank the reviewers and Area Chair for their valuable feedback and for the positive decision. We will incorporate these suggestions carefully in the camera-ready version to further improve the clarity and quality of the paper.

title: PromptGate: Client-Adaptive Vision–Language Gating for Open-Set Federated Active Learning
abstract: Deploying medical AI across resource-constrained institutions demands data-efficient learning pipelines that respect patient privacy. Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative medical AI without centralizing data. Yet, real-world clinical pools are inherently open-set: beyond the in-distribution (ID) target classes, the unlabeled pool also holds out-of-distribution (OOD), non-target samples such as imaging artifacts, background tissue, and other pathologies. Standard Active Learning (AL) query strategies mistake this noise for informative samples, wasting scarce annotation budgets. We propose PromptGate, a dynamic VLM-gated framework for Open-Set Federated AL that purifies unlabeled pools before querying. PromptGate introduces a federated Class-Specific Context Optimization: lightweight, learnable prompt vectors that adapt a frozen BiomedCLIP backbone to local clinical domains and aggregate globally via FedAvg—without sharing patient data. As new annotations arrive, prompts progressively sharpen the ID/OOD boundary, turning the VLM into a dynamic gatekeeper that is strategy-agnostic: a plug-and-play pre-selection module enhancing any downstream AL strategy. Experiments on distributed dermatology and breast imaging benchmarks, with a random acquisition rule, show that while static VLM prompting degrades to ∼60% ID purity, PromptGate maintains >95% purity with 98% OOD recall. The source code is available at http://github.com/albarqounilab/promptgate.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs
Modalities -> Mobile / Wearable / Point-of-Care Imaging & Sensors

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: PromptGate is a lightweight VLM-gated module for open-set federated active learning. The method is validated on two different datasets.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The combination of clinical problem and technical solution is working well in this paper. 
2.Open-set learning problems are under-studied in the MICCAI setting. This paper has the potential to generate some serious conversations. 
3.The experimental design is strong and the comparison is thorough - I liked it.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.While the formal definition of open-set in section 2.1 is correct, the authors used an ambiguous definition in abstract. Please fix “yet real-world clinical pools are inherently openset, containing out-of-distribution (OOD) noise such as imaging artifacts and wrong modalities. “ 
2.Method description at the end of introduction lacks clarity. Please resolve it.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

An open-set learning is novel enough for MICCAI audiences. The experiment is also solidly complemented the method.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I stick to my original decision.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper tackles the challenge of open-set federated active learning (OS-FAL) by introducing PromptGate, a vision-language gating mechanism. PromptGate is specifically designed to filter out out-of-distribution (OOD) samples before the active learning phase. The authors validate the efficacy of PromptGate by comparing it against three filtering methods across two distinct federated datasets.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The proposed PromptGate serves as an acquisition-agnostic, plug-and-play gating module. By filtering out OOD samples before the active learning phase, it can be integrated with various active learning strategies.
2.The paper is well-organized and easy to read.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The technical novelty of PromptGate is limited, as dual-prompt designs are widely adopted in federated learning [R1-R2]. Furthermore, since FOCoOp [R3] provides a more comprehensive approach for ID/OOD separation using ID global, ID local, and OOD prompts, the novelty of PromptGate over FOCoOp remains unclear.
2.While the authors highlight the mixed prompt design in Sec. 2.1, their ablation study reveals that using solely local prompts actually outperforms it, which raises concerns about the necessity and effectiveness of the mixed strategy.
3.On the FedEMBED dataset, Coldstart and Baseline yield lower purity but competitive or even better BMA compared to PromptGate. This raises concerns about the necessity of filtering out all OOD samples, as the experimental results indicate that a small amount of OOD samples does not negatively impact model optimization.
[R1] FedPHA: Federated Prompt Learning for Heterogeneous Client Adaptation. ICML 2025.[R2] Global and Local Prompts Cooperation via Optimal Transport for Federated Learning. CVPR 2024.[R3] FOCoOp: Enhancing Out-of-Distribution Robustness in Federated Prompt Learning for Vision-Language Models. ICML 2025.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Considering the limited technical novelty and incomprehensive experimental validation, I recommend rejecting the paper in its current form.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes PromptGate, a dynamic VLM-gated framework for Open-Set Federated AL. It uses a frozen VLM with federated prompt tuning to filter OOD samples at each client before active learning query. Experiments show PromptGate effectively converts the Open-Set problem into Closed-Set problem.
reviews.text_strengths:
The work is well motivated, as it brings together open-set active learning and federated active learning in a medical imaging setting, where both privacy constraints and data quality issues are highly relevant. In practice, active learning can easily mistake OOD samples for highly informative ones, leading to wasted annotation budget. Addressing this problem is therefore both meaningful and practically important.
The proposed method is lightweight, introducing only a small number of additional parameters, while effectively narrowing the performance gap between open-set and closed-set settings. The gains on intermediate metrics are particularly clear, suggesting that the method is effective at improving sample selection quality.
The global/local prompt decomposition is also a reasonably novel design in the federated setting. The global prompts are intended to capture shared semantic knowledge across clients, while the local prompts adapt to client-specific OOD characteristics. This design is well aligned with the realistic heterogeneity across hospitals and medical centers, where scanner types, acquisition protocols, and artifact distributions often differ substantially.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
In Sec 2.2, the paper first defines p_c^k(x) and \hat{y}^k(x), stating that “PromptGate filters U^(r)_k into an ID-candicate pool”. Immediately after, it defines p_c^k(x) and \hat{y}^k(x) again and repeats very similar line “PromptGate filters U^(r)_k into an ID-candicate pool(VLM-gated)”. it’s repetitive and confusing.
Insufficient analysis of early-round instability:
1.The manuscript notes that query precision (QP) can dip at round 2 after the first CoOp update on a small 128-shot subset, but provides no analysis of how severe or common this is across clients.
2.There is no experiments show whether this early instability could lead to the irreversible loss of informative ID samples that are incorrectly gated out, potentially harming final model performance even though it’s mentioned in Sec 2.2 that“empirically, ID leakage into \epsilon_k^(r) is negligible.”.
The description of the gating mechanism is also somewhat unclear. Although the paper refers to a “high-confidence ID candidate pool” and defines p_max(x), the actual formulation only keeps samples whose argmax prediction belongs to an ID class, without using an explicit confidence threshold. It is therefore unclear whether the gate is category-based or confidence-based.
Some implementation details should also be clarified, such as whether prompt learning is retrained at each round or updated incrementally, and how the temperature parameter is selected.
Finally, although the paper highlights the mixed global+local prompt design, the results suggest that the Local variant is often the strongest or most stable. This raises the question of whether the main benefit comes from local personalization rather than federated global aggregation.
More complete statistics and ablations, such as different OOD ratios, initial labeled-set sizes, prompt token numbers, and per-client performance, would strengthen the paper.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Overall, this paper studies a meaningful and practical problem at the intersection of open-set active learning and federated learning for medical imaging. The proposed PromptGate is lightweight, reasonably well motivated, and shows clear improvements in query purity, with a sensible global/local prompt design for handling cross-client heterogeneity. The idea is interesting and the intermediate results are promising.
The most compelling evidence in the paper so far focuses on intermediate metrics like purity, while the improvement in the performance of the final downstream task is not yet stable, significant, or sufficient. Meanwhile, some key aspects of the method description remain unclear, such as whether the gate is based on class or confidence, the training and update method of the prompt, and whether the independent effect of global aggregation truly holds. In addition, the statistical information and ablation experiments are not yet complete. I believe this work is on the right track and the method has potential, but at this stage, the chain of evidence is insufficient to support a stronger acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
The authors are advised to address all the concerns raised by the reviewers, especially: (i) discuss the novelty; (ii) design choices such as prompt mixing and discarding OOD samples; and (iii) clarify the instability in the early rounds.

While all the reviewers appreciated the presentation and the evaluations of the paper, they received mixed ratings (2.Accept and 1.Reject), and mostly the disagreement was on the novelty of the method. After going through the reviews and the rebuttal from the authors, I align with the fact that federated learning in an open-set setting can bring interest to the wider community.

The main concerns arising from the initial reviews were related to novelty, prompt mixing choices, and early-round instability. All these issues have been addressed adequately in the rebuttal. The pending concern is that the use of local and global prompts is not novel. While this may be true, the application of this concept to Open-Set Federated Active Learning is sufficiently novel. Hence, the paper can be accepted.

Despite moderate concerns about novelty, the rebuttal effectively clarifies the contribution: PromptGate is the first learnable VLM-gated module tailored for OS-FAL, with clear distinctions from concurrent works (e.g., FOCoOp, FedPHA). Two reviewers (R1 and R3) shifted to or maintained acceptance after the rebuttal, while the single reject opinion does not outweigh the overall positive assessment.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the AC, R1, R2, and R3.All reviewers find the work “well motivated”, the “experimental design strong and thorough” (R1), “clinical problem and technical solution working well” (R1), and “serves as an acquisition-agnostic, plug-and-play gating module” (R2).
[R2, AC] Novelty over FOCoOp, FedOTP, and FedPHA. We are glad this concurrent work validates our global/local prompt decomposition, but all three address closed-set federated classification on fixed labeled datasets. FedOTP uses UOT over patches; FedPHA uses SVD projection; FOCoOp trains OOD pseudo-prompts with post-hoc MCM scoring — none has an acquisition gate, an unlabeled pool, or a mechanism to consume the supervised non-target label OS-FAL provides. PromptGate contributes: (a) the first learnable-prompt VLM gate for OS-FAL (CSC CoOp, global/local decomposition, (K+1)-class cross-entropy); (b) decoupling gate from acquisition rule; (c) converting OS-FAL into approximately closed-set AL across 6 strategies x 2 datasets. Prompts are warm-started and refined each AL round from oracle labels, progressively sharpening the ID/OOD boundary — driven by the AL loop itself, absent from all three papers. We will add them to the related work.
[R2, R3, AC] Local outperforms Mixed, is global aggregation necessary? No single configuration dominates universally. Table 1: Local leads on Random, FEAL, and LfOSA on FedISIC; Global leads on OpenPath (86.6 purity, 64.4 BMA) and FEAL purity; FedEMBED follows the same mixed pattern. The right choice depends on OOD variability across clients: when OOD artifacts are similar across sites, global prompts capture a stronger shared prior; when OOD is client-specific (as in FedISIC), local adaptation is more beneficial. We offer all three as dataset-dependent options; global aggregation always preserves privacy-preserving collaboration and distributed annotation cost across institutions that cannot share patient data.
[R2] Necessity of filtering on FedEMBED. Two factors explain the small BMA gaps: (1) OOD prevalence is low (4.8-13.2%), so unfiltered AL is already mostly ID by chance; (2) FedEMBED OOD labels are pseudo-labels. The decisive test is FedISIC (50% OOD): PromptGate yields +22% purity and +0-6% BMA across all 6 strategies. In short, PromptGate is safe under low-OOD and substantially helpful under high-OOD, precisely what clinical deployment requires.
[R3] Gating mechanism. The gate is category-based over K+1 classes: x is retained iff y-hat^k(x) in {1,…,K}. We avoided an explicit confidence threshold to prevent ambiguity with Entropy-based AL scores; implicit confidence filtering is achieved via the temperature-scaled softmax — we will clarify this in the text.
[R3] Early-round instability in FedISIC and ID leakage. The round-2 QP dip has two compounding causes. First, at R=1 the VLM has seen only 128 shots and remains uncertain about OOD; uncertainty-based strategies (Entropy, FEAL, PAL, LfOSA) select ambiguous samples, disproportionately OOD, dragging QP down. This holds for the baseline (Static VLM as well). Second, reported QP values are means across 3 seeds x 6 AL methods, so uncertainty-based methods dominate (Entropy: 11.0%, FEAL: 11.6%, PAL: 14.1%, LfOSA: 15.8%; Random: 61% OpenPath: 97.9%). From R=3 onward, as the VLM accumulates oracle labels, this vanishes, and QP recovers to near-perfect. Samples in epsilon_k^(r) are not permanently removed: they remain in U_k and are re-evaluated each round. On FedISIC, all variants stabilise at ≤ 1.3% leakage, meaning ≥ 98.7% of true-ID samples are correctly retained in the ID pool, replacing the informal “negligible” claim.
[R3] Implementation details. Prompts are updated incrementally each round (15 epochs SGD, warm-started). tau_VLM = 0.0117 follows BiomedCLIP convention. Details will be added to Sec. 2.3.[R1, R3] Writing clarity. We will: a) align the abstract open-set phrasing with Sec. 2.1; b) rewrite Sec. 1; c) remove the duplicate definitions in Sec 2.2

title: PromptMedCT: A Training-Free LLM-Guided Framework for Volumetric CT Data Realization with Quantifiable Disease Manifestations and Multi-Tier Annotations
abstract: Explainable foundation models in radiology are fundamentally limited by the lack of datasets with structured multi-tier annotations (i.e., descriptive prompts, infection/lobar masks, and bounding boxes), which are critical for learning clinically grounded temporal, causal, and diagnostic reasoning. While accurate data realization offers a potential solution, existing data generation approaches either rely on large-scale supervised training or generate raw data without the structured multi-tier annotations. To overcome these limitations, we propose PromptMedCT, the first LLM-guided, training-free disease realization framework that bridges clinical semantics with anatomical constraints to synthesize lung CT scans with multi-tier annotations. The proposed framework can be operated in two modes: a prompt mode for high-fidelity synthesis (as a domain-specific GPT) and a parametric mode for large-scale data generation with multi-tier annotations. Using the proposed PromptMedCT framework (with parametric mode), we construct a dataset comprising 10K 2D CT scans with comprehensive multi-tier annotations. We validate the realism and effectiveness of our framework through a two-step validation strategy that combines comprehensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations. Quantitatively, we perform synthetic-to-real generalization by training a vision–language model on our generated data and testing it on real clinical datasets, achieving 59.22% DICE and 42.46% IoU. For further qualitative evaluation, we perform a medical expert review in which specialists assess a set of generated data and annotations, with 92% of scans rated realistic and 79.5% of the prompts accurately described. Finally, a qualitative comparison against five state-of-the-art domain-specific and general LLM-based generators shows that our method consistently outperforms them in visual realism and multi-tier annotation quality.  Additional implementation details: https://github.com/Owais-CodeHub/PromptMedCT
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.text_contribution:
This paper introduces PromptMedCT, the first training-free, LLM-guided framework that synthesizes anatomically consistent lung CT scans with structured multi-tier annotations (descriptive prompts, infection/lobar masks, and bounding boxes). The key contributions are:
1.Novel Framework Design: A four-stage pipeline (LLM-guided semantic parsing -> lobar-guided template retrieval -> morphological pathology synthesis -> LLM-guided diffusion) that bridges clinical semantics with anatomical constraints without requiring model training.
2.Dual-Mode Operation: Supports both prompt-mode (high-fidelity, GPT-like interaction) and parametric-mode (scalable batch generation with explicit disease control), offering flexibility for diverse research needs.

reviews.text_strengths:
1.The framework’s training-free design is particularly valuable in privacy-constrained medical domains, eliminating the need for large-scale supervised training while maintaining high-quality output. This addresses a critical scalability limitation in existing approaches.
2.PromptMedCT simultaneously produces infection masks, lobar masks, bounding boxes, and radiologist-style reports. This holistic annotation suite enables downstream tasks like vision-language alignment and explainable AI research.
3.The dual quantitative/qualitative evaluation is thorough and well-designed. The synthetic-to-real generalization experiment convincingly demonstrates clinical utility, while expert review provides essential domain validation.
4.The paper is well-organized, with intuitive figures (especially Fig. 1–2) that effectively communicate the framework workflow. The comparison table (Table 1) clearly positions the work within the literature. And the inclusion of a demonstration video and detailed methodological appendices enhances reproducibility and transparency.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.While the framework is described as applicable to volumetric CT, the presented dataset and experiments focus on 2D slices. A brief discussion of extension to full 3D volumes (e.g., slice-to-slice consistency, volumetric annotation propagation) would strengthen the clinical applicability claim.
2.The current implementation focuses on infection patterns (e.g., COVID-19). While the framework is theoretically extensible, explicit validation on other pathologies (nodules, fibrosis, tumors) would broaden the impact assessment.
3.The reliance on LLaMA3 for prompt parsing introduces potential variability based on prompt phrasing and LLM version. A sensitivity analysis or ablation on prompt robustness would be valuable.

PromptMedCT introduces a training-free, LLM-guided framework that unifies structured semantic prompting, explicit parametric control, and complete multi-tier annotation generation within a single controllable pipeline—a genuine advance over existing approaches that either require large-scale supervised training or produce raw images without structured annotations. The four-stage design (LLM-guided semantic parsing, lobar-guided template retrieval, morphological pathology synthesis, and LLM-guided diffusion) is logically coherent and technically sound, enabling the synthesis of anatomically consistent lung CT scans with infection masks, lobar masks, bounding boxes, and radiologist-style reports. The evaluation is comprehensive and convincing: synthetic-to-real generalization experiments demonstrate meaningful cross-domain transfer (59.22% Dice, 42.46% IoU on real clinical benchmarks), while expert review confirms high diagnostic plausibility (92% realism rating, 79.5% prompt alignment). The released 10K annotated dataset addresses a critical resource gap for vision-language model pretraining and explainable AI research. Although the current implementation focuses on 2D slices and infection patterns, these represent natural directions for future extension rather than fundamental limitations.

However, the novelty primarily stems from system integration rather than fundamental algorithmic advances, and the reliance on LLM priors without task-specific fine-tuning may limit the ability to model complex or atypical anatomical variations. Nevertheless, the construction of a dataset with 10,000 fully annotated CT images, along with a two-stage validation strategy, provides a useful resource and benchmark for the community.
reviews.text_strengths: 1.Novel training-free framework. Generating pixel-level masks, bounding boxes, and text descriptions in a single pipeline is a strong contribution, as it directly enables the creation of fully annotated datasets for downstream tasks. 3.Clinically meaningful controllability. N/A

However, the method relies heavily on LLM priors without domain-specific adaptation, which may limit robustness, and lacks comparison with strong generative baselines such as GAN- and diffusion-based methods.

meta_reviews.text: The reviewers consistently agree that this paper addresses a highly relevant and timely problem in medical imaging, namely the scarcity of structured annotated datasets for vision-language modeling. While the novelty is primarily at the system-integration level and certain aspects such as full 3D validation and broader pathology coverage could be strengthened, these are not fundamental limitations. author_feedback_text: We sincerely thank all the reviewers for their valuable time, careful evaluation, and highly encouraging feedback. We truly appreciate that all reviewers recognized the novelty, practical significance, and potential impact of our training-free, LLM-guided framework for structured CT data realization with unified multi-tier annotations. This work establishes a foundational pipeline for clinically controllable synthetic CT generation and opens a promising direction toward future volumetric 3D CT realization through incremental architectural enhancements and rigorous validation. We are particularly encouraged by the positive recognition of the framework’s ability to bridge clinical semantics with anatomically grounded data synthesis. To further support reproducibility and future research, we will publicly release the generated dataset and detailed algorithmic workflow through a GitHub repository alongside the final version of the paper.

title: Propagating Structural Guidance: Synthesizing Fluorescein Angiography from Fundus Images and Sparse OCT Scans
abstract:
Fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) is critical for assessing retinal vascular abnormalities, but its acquisition is invasive and not always feasible. In contrast, color fundus photography (CFP) is non-invasive and widely accessible, which has motivated studies on CFP-to-FFA synthesis. However, prior works rely solely on CFP surface texture, fundamentally limiting the ability to reconstruct functional vascular information and subtle pathological changes.
To address this, we propose a novel framework that synthesizes FFA from CFP with structural guidance provided by optical coherence tomography (OCT).
We construct a multi-modal retinal imaging dataset with paired CFP, FFA, and OCT from 3,676 patient eyes—the first tri-modally aligned dataset in retinal imaging.
To bridge the spatial gap between OCT and fundus modalities, we propose a Spatially Aligned Cross-Modal Fusion (\textbf{SACMF}) module that projects depth-resolved OCT features onto the fundus plane and injects them into the CFP encoder via adaptive layer normalization.
Beyond feature fusion, we further introduce Token-wise Cross-Modality Alignment (\textbf{TCMA}), a token-level contrastive learning strategy that explicitly aligns CFP and FFA representations at corresponding spatial positions.
Our method achieves superior synthesis performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.
Moreover, extensive experiments demonstrate that the FFA images synthesized by our approach bring greater improvements in downstream disease diagnosis performance than existing methods, highlighting the clinical potential of our approach as a non-invasive decision-support tool in routine workflows. The code is available at \href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/OCT-guide-FFA-Syn-D6CE}{here}.

reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a multimodal image synthesis framework for generating FFA from color fundus photographs with auxiliary structural guidance from sparse OCT. Its main contribution is to extend CFP-to-FFA synthesis from a single-modality image translation task to a structurally guided multimodal pipeline. Specifically, the paper constructs a tri-modal dataset of 3,676 aligned CFP, FFA, and OCT cases, introduces SACMF to project OCT features onto the fundus plane and propagate structural information through CFP features, and proposes TCMA to align CFP and FFA tokens at corresponding spatial positions.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The idea of synthesizing FFA from CFP with OCT guidance is clinically meaningful, since both OCT and CFP are non-invasive modalities and therefore more feasible in real-world practice. 
2.Incorporating OCT as an auxiliary modality provides additional structural supervision, which plausibly contributes to the improved synthesis performance. 
3.The proposed method is designed with clinical considerations in mind, and the downstream experiments provide further evidence of its effectiveness and potential utility.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The evaluation is limited to a single dataset, making it difficult to assess the robustness and generalizability of the proposed method across different clinical centers, populations, and imaging devices.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose investigating CFP-to-FFA synthesis by incorporating OCT as auxiliary structural guidance, constructing the first paired tri-modal retinal dataset with 3,676 aligned CFP, FFA, and OCT cases. To effectively align and fuse OCT with CFP, an OCT-guided feature modulation module is introduced. Furthermore, the authors implement a token-wise contrastive learning strategy to enforce CFP-FFA alignment. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method generates FFA images with higher visual fidelity than existing methods in the literature. Finally, the authors validate that the synthesized FFAs effectively enhance performance in downstream classification tasks.
reviews.text_strengths:
Novelty of Dataset: The authors propose a novel method by incorporating OCT into CFP-to-FFA synthesis and construct a large-scale, paired tri-modal retinal dataset, which fills a significant gap in the field.
Methodological Soundness: The Trajectory-Aware En-face Projection is effectively designed by accounting for the inherent acquisition differences between OCT and CFP.
Comprehensive Experimental Design: The evaluation extends beyond standard visual fidelity. By validating the synthesized FFAs in downstream classification tasks, the authors demonstrate the practical utility of the generated images. Furthermore, the inclusion of a discussion on the ratio of OCT during training provides convincing evidence for the effectiveness of OCT guidance.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Limited Comparison to State-of-the-Art: While the authors cite relevant works such as “ Lesion-aware generative adversarial networks for color fundus image to fundus fluorescein angiography translation” and “ Non-invasive to invasive: Enhancing FFA synthesis from CFP with a benchmark dataset and a novel network”, a quantitative comparison against these specific baseline methods is absent.
Lack of Statistical Rigor: There is no statistical evaluation for the classification performance; the absence of standard deviations makes it difficult to assess the stability and reliability of the reported improvements. 
Lack of Sensitivity Analysis: The experimental section is missing a parameter sensitivity analysis, particularly regarding the hyper-parameter β in the loss function. It remains unclear how different weights affect the synthesis performance.
Insufficient Discussion on Limitations: The qualitative analysis focuses exclusively on successful cases. The paper would benefit from a dedicated section on failure cases and a discussion of the model’s boundary conditions. 
Lack of Visionary Discussion: There is limited discussion on the distinct clinical roles of CFP, FFA, and OCT. For CFP-to-FFA synthesis to be truly impactful, the authors should discuss whether synthesized FFAs can genuinely substitute for real FFAs in clinical workflows. Incorporating human expert evaluation (e.g., a Turing test by ophthalmologists) would significantly strengthen the argument for its practical application.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to leverage OCT for auxiliary guidance in CFP-to-FFA synthesis. By constructing a dedicated paired dataset and providing a rigorous experimental validation, the authors offer a substantial and well-rounded contribution to retinal imaging research.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents the first multi-modal CFP-to-FFA (color fundus photography to fluorescein angiography) synthesis framework that incorporates OCT as auxiliary structural guidance. Key contributions include: (1) construction of the first tri-modally aligned retinal dataset (3,676 paired CFP, FFA, and OCT cases) using a rigorous vessel-skeleton-based registration pipeline; (2) a Spatially Aligned Cross-Modal Fusion (SACMF) module that projects depth-resolved OCT features onto the 2D fundus plane via trajectory-aware pooling and propagates them via CFP-guided cross-attention; (3) a Token-wise Cross-Modality Alignment (TCMA) module using a symmetric InfoNCE contrastive loss to enforce fine-grained semantic consistency between CFP and FFA tokens. The framework is GAN-based and demonstrates superior FFA synthesis quality and downstream disease classification performance over prior methods.
reviews.text_strengths: 1.Strong novelty: The work is the first to use OCT as structural guidance for FFA synthesis. This is clinically well-motivated since OCT is non-invasive and available in scenarios where FFA is contraindicated. 2.Dataset contribution: The tri-modal dataset (3,676 cases with registration pipeline) is a genuine and valuable contribution to the community, especially given the scarcity of paired multi-modal retinal datasets. 3.Well-designed SACMF: The trajectory-aware projection is an elegant solution to the OCT–fundus viewpoint discrepancy. Propagating structural cues via CFP-based attention to unscanned regions is practical and effective. 4.Comprehensive evaluation: Both standard image quality metrics (PSNR, SSIM, FID, LPIPS) and downstream diagnostic utility (disease classification) are evaluated. The code is publicly available. 5.Clinically meaningful upper/lower bound analysis provides context for interpreting results.
reviews.text_weaknesses: 1.Limited dataset size and split: With only 3,676 cases and a 60/40 train/test split, the dataset is relatively small for a generative model. The choice of 40% for testing is unusual and reduces training data; the rationale should be discussed. 2.GAN instability not discussed: The paper adopts a GAN backbone without discussing training stability, mode coverage, or failure cases. Given the small dataset, GAN training risks are non-trivial. 3.OCT sparsity assumption: The method assumes sparse B-scans are available alongside CFP. This may not always hold in clinical practice. The sensitivity to number and placement of OCT scans is only partially explored (20%-100% training ratio, but not inference-time availability). 4.Qualitative results are limited: Only 4 rows of examples are shown in Figure 2.More diverse failure cases or challenging pathologies would strengthen the qualitative analysis. 5.TCMA supervision detail: It is not fully clear how the FFA tokens are obtained during inference (when real FFA is unavailable), suggesting TCMA may only be active during training.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
This is a well-executed paper with a clinically motivated problem and genuine dataset contributions. The main concerns are the relatively small dataset size, limited discussion of GAN failure modes, and the practical assumption about OCT availability. The paper would benefit from a clearer description of inference-time behavior of TCMA and a discussion of the dataset collection ethics.

The paper is technically sound, novel, and well-written. The primary contributions — the OCT-guided synthesis paradigm, the tri-modal dataset, and the SACMF/TCMA modules — are meaningful and well-validated. The score is held back by the relatively small dataset and the 60/40 train/test split that limits generalization claims, as well as an incomplete discussion of inference-time behavior. If the authors can address the dataset split rationale and clarify TCMA at inference time, this would merit a solid Accept.

Reviewers agree that the problem is highly relevant, and the approach is novel, particularly through the integration of OCT guidance and the construction of a tri-modal dataset. The method is well-designed and supported by a comprehensive evaluation, including downstream clinical tasks. The concerns are mostly about strengthening the experimental analysis and clarifications rather than fundamental flaws.

author_feedback_text:
1.Dataset Size and Split Constrain Generalization
Thank you for your valuable feedback. Compared to large-scale datasets in natural image domains, the cost of data acquisition in medical image generation tasks is relatively high, and thus data scale remains an important challenge in this field.
However, it is worth noting that in the specific task of fundus image to FFA synthesis, the data scales used in existing publicly available studies are generally small. For example:
“Diabetic retinopathy grading by digital curvelet transform” includes only 59 cases, covering only normal and diabetic retinopathy.
“Lesion-aware generative adversarial networks for color fundus image to fundus fluorescein angiography translation” includes 133 cases, with only BRVO.
“Non-Invasive to Invasive: Enhancing FFA Synthesis from CFP with a Benchmark Dataset and a Novel Network” includes 600 cases, covering five disease categories.
In comparison, our dataset contains 3,676 cases, with 8 disease categories having more than 100 cases each. Under this task setting, our dataset is significantly larger than existing works and covers a richer distribution of lesions.
Regarding the data split ratio, we adopted a 60/40 train/test split rather than the more common 80/20 or 70/30, primarily to enlarge the test set size, thereby enabling a more reliable evaluation of the model’s generalization ability. Therefore, we aim to more thoroughly evaluate the model’s performance on unseen cases, different lesion types, and varying severity levels through a larger test set.
Additionally, it should be noted that compared to the data scales of 59, 133, or 600 cases in existing works, our dataset contains 3,676 cases. Even with a 60/40 split, the training set size remains significantly larger than those used in existing methods.
2.Clarification on TCMA Supervision and Inference
Thank you for pointing this out. TCMA is used only during training as an auxiliary supervision module, leveraging ground-truth FFA tokens to provide cross-modal constraints. During inference, the model takes only CFP as input and does not require FFA tokens. We have clarified this distinction in the revised manuscript
3.Insufficient Discussion on Limitations and Failure Cases
Thank you for this suggestion. We have added failure case analysis and a discussion of model limitations in the Qualitative Comparison section of the revised manuscript. Meanwhile, we have illustrated a representative failure case in Fig. 2(b) to provide a clear visual example. In this discussion, we explicitly acknowledge certain limitations of our model: (1) vessel boundaries may appear blurred, and (2) the model struggles to recover very small or widely distributed leakage regions, resulting in incomplete synthesis.
4.Undiscussed GAN Training Instability
First, with proper architectural design and training techniques, the training stability of GAN frameworks is no longer a major issue. Our GAN model exhibits stable training behavior without evident failure phenomena such as mode collapse.
Second, we have also carefully considered and experimented with Diffusion-based methods. As shown in Table 1, we implemented BBDM as a comparative method, but its performance was notably inferior to the GAN-based version. We further attempted to improve its performance by increasing the number of training epochs, yet the gains were not significant. We attribute this primarily to the fact that, in the absence of a large-scale pretrained VAE, directly modeling in pixel-level space poses greater challenges for Diffusion methods, whereas GANs demonstrate better adaptability and stability in such medical image cross-modal generation tasks.

title: ProSMA-UNet: Decoder Conditioning for Proximal-Sparse Skip Feature Selection
abstract: Medical image segmentation commonly relies on U-shaped encoder–decoder architectures such as U-Net, where skip connections preserve fine spatial detail by injecting high-resolution encoder features into the decoder. However, these skip pathways also propagate low-level textures, background clutter, and acquisition noise, allowing irrelevant information to bypass deeper semantic filtering—an issue that is particularly detrimental in low-contrast clinical imaging. Although attention gates have been introduced to address this limitation, they typically produce dense sigmoid masks that softly reweight features rather than explicitly removing irrelevant activations. We propose ProSMA-UNet (Proximal-Sparse Multi-Scale Attention U-Net), which reformulates skip gating as a decoder-conditioned sparse feature selection problem.  ProSMA constructs a multi-scale compatibility field using lightweight depthwise dilated convolutions to capture relevance across local and contextual scales, then enforces explicit sparsity via an ℓ1 proximal operator with learnable per-channel thresholds, yielding a closed-form soft-thresholding gate that can remove noisy responses. To further suppress semantically irrelevant channels, ProSMA incorporates decoder-conditioned channel gating driven by global decoder context. Extensive experiments on challenging 2D and 3D benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, with particularly large gains (≈20%) on difficult 3D segmentation tasks. Project page:https://math-ml-x.github.io/ProSMA-UNet/

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a U-Net variant that treats skip connections as a decoder-conditioned sparse feature selection problem rather than a dense reweighting problem. The key idea is to build a multi-scale decoder-encoder compatibility field and then apply an l1 proximal soft-thresholding operator with learnable per-channel thresholds so that irrelevant skip activations can be set to exact zero. This is complemented by decoder-conditioned channel gating. The paper argues that this yields more explicit suppression of noisy or semantically irrelevant skip information than standard attention-gated skip connections, and reports improvements on several 2D and 3D medical segmentation benchmarks.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) The paper addresses a real and important weakness of U-shaped segmentation networks: skip connections are useful for localisation, but they can also leak low-level clutter and bypass semantic filtering. That motivation is sensible, especially in low-contrast medical images, and the paper stays focused on that specific design problem rather than trying to overcomplicate the architecture. 
2) I like the technical clarity of the proposed mechanism. The method is easy to follow: construct a compatibility field from encoder and decoder features, enforce sparsity with a proximal l1 step, and then use spatial and channel gating together. Figure 1 communicates the idea well, especially the contrast between standard soft attention and explicit sparse selection with exact zeros. 
3) The use of a proximal operator for skip gating is also an interesting design choice. Even if the underlying soft-thresholding idea is mathematically standard, its use here as a skip-filtering mechanism is reasonably novel in this context. The paper’s framing of skip fusion as feature selection rather than merely reweighting is conceptually sound. 
4) The empirical results are broadly positive. On the reported 2D datasets, the method is consistently strongest, with gains over prior baselines on BUSI, GlaS, and Kvasir-SEG. On 3D, the improvement on Colon is particularly large, with F1 rising from 53.05 to 63.14 over the strongest listed baseline, while Spleen also improves modestly. The method therefore appears effective across both 2D and 3D settings. 
5) The ablation study is simple but useful. It suggests that sparse spatial selection contributes the larger gain, while channel gating adds complementary value. That is at least consistent with the method’s intended design.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) It is not clear to me if the experimental comparison is fully balanced. On the 2D side, some baseline results are taken directly from prior work rather than reproduced here under a unified training protocol, and UKAN2.0 is missing on GlaS due to memory limits. That weakens the SOTA claim somewhat, because not all methods are being compared on equal footing. The paper also explicitly states that for BUSI and GlaS some baselines are taken from U-KAN under the same protocol, rather than rerun here. 
2) The strongest gains occur on the 3D Colon task, but the paper does not provide enough analysis of why the gain is so large there. A nearly 10-point F1 jump over the best baseline is substantial. That could be a genuine strength, but it also demands more scrutiny: was Colon especially sensitive to noisy skip features, were there optimisation differences, or is the baseline set simply too narrow? At the moment the paper reports the number, but does not really explain it. 
3) Related to that, the 3D baseline set feels limited. The comparison is against 3D U-Net, U-KAN 3D, and UKAN2.0 3D, but not against stronger contemporary 3D segmentation baselines such as nnU-Net-style pipelines or other established 3D U-Net variants like UNETR or Swin UNETR. Given that the method is a skip-connection modification rather than a wholesale architectural replacement, it would have been more convincing to compare against stronger and more standard 3D medical segmentation baselines. 
4) The narrative around ‘explicit noise removal’ is plausible but not yet fully evidenced. Figure 1 is intuitive and the qualitative examples are encouraging, but the paper does not directly measure sparsity levels, feature suppression patterns, or whether harmful skip activations are actually reduced in a meaningful way. In other words, the mechanism is interpretable in theory, but the empirical validation of that interpretation is still limited. 
5) Since ProSMA adds multiple components at each skip connection, a complexity analysis in terms of parameter count, FLOPs, memory footprint, or inference time is needed. Otherwise, it remains unclear whether the gains reflect better skip selection or are partly explained by increased parameter count and computational budget.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper proposes a clean and well-motivated modification to U-Net skip connections, with a technically coherent sparse gating mechanism and consistently positive results across several 2D and 3D segmentation benchmarks. I find the central idea sensible and practically relevant, and the gains on the more difficult 3D task are particularly encouraging. At the same time, the 3D comparison could be stronger, and the lack of complexity analysis makes the empirical gains harder to interpret fully. The reproducibility is at the current version limited. Overall, this is a solid paper with clear merit, though not one I would score at the very top end.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
reviews.text_contribution: The authors turn skip connections in a Ushaped segmentation network into a decoder conditioned sparse feature selection step, instead of passing all encoder features directly or only softly reweighting them. The authors combine a multi scale compatibility field, sparse soft threshold selection, channel gating from decoder context, and a simple stability argument. The result is a method that aims to remove noisy skip responses more explicitly, while still keeping useful detail. The experiments across three 2D datasets and two 3D datasets make this contribution concrete, especially on the harder 3D setting.
reviews.text_strengths: The idea is focused and well motivated. Recent medical segmentation papers have improved U-shaped models through stronger configuration rules, transformer context, or redesigned backbones, as seen in nnUNet, SwinUnet, TransUNet, U-KAN, and Implicit U-KAN2.0.The authors take a different and useful angle by asking a simpler question, namely how to stop irrelevant skip features from entering the decoder at all. That makes the contribution easy to understand and practically meaningful. The paper is not only conceptual. The authors support the method with theory, ablation, 2D results, and 3D results. Table 1 to Table 3 show consistent gains, and the visual examples also match the quantitative findings. The authors test on ultrasound, histology, endoscopy, spleen CT, and colon CT, which gives confidence that the idea is not tied to one image type only.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The major weaknesses are mild, but worth noting. The first is that the novelty is stronger at the level of skip gating design than at the level of opening a completely new segmentation direction. Medical image segmentation has already seen many strong U shaped extensions in recent years, including nnUNet, Swin Unet, TransUNet, U-KAN, and Implicit U-KAN2.0.So, in my view, the paper is best understood as a strong and well designed advance within an active research line, rather than a fully new family of models. The comparison is broad, but the case for state of the art would be even stronger if the authors also included very established references such as nnUNet and strong transformer based baselines such as TransUNet or Swin-Unet. Lastly, the experiments are strong benchmark experiments, but the paper does not yet include external clinical site validation.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The authors present a neat idea, good technical grounding, and convincing evidence. The paper is satisfactory and novel enough for acceptance. The authors explain the problem clearly, the method has a real point of difference, the ablation supports the design choices, and the gains on both 2D and 3D tasks are strong. The clarity of the core idea, the solid experimental section, and the fact that the work is both simple to communicate and useful for difficult medical segmentation settings.

ProSMA’s sparse decoder-conditioned skip filtering performed better in such cases.

Our intention was to compare against architecturally relevant non-self-configuring segmentation frameworks, since our contribution focuses specifically on skip-connection design rather than dataset-specific pipeline optimization.
