Q4.The proposed proximal operator is guaranteed by its L1 formulation to produce exact zeros, which is a mathematical property, not a tunable effect. The segmentation gains across all datasets (especially the large improvement on Colon) serve as the functional evidence that harmful skip activations are meaningfully suppressed. title: ProSyn-Net: A Reliable Prototypical Synergy Network for Imbalanced Dermatologic Multimodal Ultrasound Diagnosis
abstract: Multimodal ultrasound, combining B-mode and color Doppler, is vital for the early screening of skin lesions. However, its automated clinical application is severely hindered by modality quality disparities, incidence-driven data imbalance, and model over-confidence. To this end, we propose ProSyn-Net, a unified multimodal diagnostic framework comprising three synergistic modules. First, a dynamic cross-attention fusion module adaptively aligns morphological and hemodynamic features while suppressing modality noise. The fused representations are then processed by a non-linear prototypical mapping module, which effectively disentangles complex, non-convex minority samples from majority clusters in a high-dimensional space. Finally, an uncertainty-aware manifold ensemble leverages the geometric diversity of these prototypes to yield reliable predictions and extract predictive uncertainty. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ProSyn-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance on the primary in-house imbalanced 6-class dataset (78.60% Macro F1 and 96.66% AUC), while showing promising transferability on a complementary independent public binary dataset (87.80% accuracy). We further analyze uncertainty-guided selective deferral for ambiguous cases. Code is available at https://github.com/EdualcLin/ProSyn-Net.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes ProSyn-Net, a multimodal dermatologic ultrasound framework that combines dynamic cross-attention fusion for B-mode and Doppler images, a non-linear prototypical mapping module for long-tailed classification, and an uncertainty-aware manifold ensemble with selective deferral. The method is evaluated on a 917-pair in-house 6-class dataset with an independent hold-out test set and on an independent public binary dataset.
reviews.text_strengths: This is a well-focused submission that addresses three real deployment problems at once: multimodal quality disparity, incidence-driven class imbalance, and over-confident predictions in a clinical setting. The method is technically coherent. Dynamic cross-attention is used to adaptively suppress low-quality modality evidence, the non-linear prototypical mapping is a meaningful response to minority-class manifold distortion, and the uncertainty-aware ensemble gives the reliability story a clear operational interpretation rather than treating uncertainty as an afterthought. The experimental section is stronger than average: the internal study uses an explicit hold-out test set after an 85/15 split, the baselines are described with attention to fairness, the paper reports minority-class gains (for example on SK), and the submission includes ablations, a public external evaluation, runtime trade-offs, and a clinically relevant deferral analysis.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The main limitation is that the external validation does not match the primary task. The internal benchmark is a 6-class problem, whereas the external public cohort is binary, so the paper should be more careful when framing this as broad cross-dataset generalization. A second limitation is deployment cost: the strongest setting uses a 5-fold ensemble with 50 MC-dropout passes, and the paper reports about 1.25 s per sample for the full ensemble. That is acceptable for research, but less lightweight than the narrative sometimes suggests. Third, the deferral story is promising but should be contextualized more carefully: the autonomous accuracy exceeds 91% at a 50% deferral rate, which is potentially useful but only if such a referral burden is acceptable in the intended workflow. Finally, the fairness claim is mostly strong but not perfectly uniform, because some baselines are reconfigured with the authors’ preferred ConvNeXt-Tiny plus focal-loss recipe while others retain their original designs.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
For rebuttal, I would focus more on calibrating claims than on adding many new experiments. Please state explicitly that the public external validation is binary rather than 6-class, explain how that should and should not be interpreted, and contextualize the clinical meaning of the 50% deferral result. It would also strengthen the paper to summarize the performance-latency trade-off between single-pass inference and the full ensemble, and to briefly justify why the chosen baseline adaptations are fair.

I am positive on this submission because it offers a coherent methodological contribution tied to real clinical failure modes, and the empirical evidence is broadly convincing. The paper does not only optimize a closed-set score; it also shows minority-class improvements, examines uncertainty estimation, and discusses selective deferral in a way that is relevant for deployment. My score is not higher because the external validation is not on the same 6-class task and the strongest inference setting is somewhat heavy. Even with those caveats, I view this as clearly above threshold.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contributions of the paper present the ProSyn-Net framework: It constructs a unified multimodal diagnostic architecture, using a dynamic cross-attention fusion mechanism to adaptively align morphological and hemodynamic features, effectively suppressing the noise interference from low-quality modalities. A nonlinear prototype mapping module is designed: It proposes to transform the Euclidean distance distribution into a discriminative subspace through nonlinear mapping, successfully separating the non-convex and irregular feature manifolds of minority classes (such as SK) from the majority classes, directly addressing the extreme imbalance problem of data driven by incidence rates. A manifold integration and safety rejection mechanism for perceiving uncertainty is introduced: By leveraging the geometric prototype topological diversity brought about by different data partitions in cross-validation, prediction uncertainty indicators are extracted. By handing over high-uncertainty samples to human experts for processing, the autonomous diagnostic accuracy of the system is increased to over 91%.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Strong clinical motivation: The problem definition is accurate and precisely targets the actual pain points in real clinical scenarios such as the absence of Doppler blood flow signals, the scarcity of rare lesion samples, and the “overconfidence” of AI models.
2.Solid experimental data: Rigorous comparative tests were conducted on the real clinical 6-class dataset (917 pairs, with a maximum imbalance ratio of 4.7:1) and an independent public binary dataset, proving its excellent generalization ability.
3.Significant performance improvement: In extremely rare classes (such as Seborrheic Keratosis, SK), the Macro F1 reached 80.79%, which was a significant leap compared to the baseline model CMX (62.14%), effectively demonstrating the effectiveness of the nonlinear mapping module.
4.Detailed ablation experiments: Detailed module ablation analysis and t-SNE visualization were provided, clearly showing the intuitive differences in feature decoupling between the linear Voronoi boundary and the nonlinear prototype manifold.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Limitations of the dataset: Although an open dataset was included for generalization testing, the core 6-class imbalanced dataset originated from a single institution (in-house, specialized hospital). The lack of multi-center (Multi-center) external independent validation has weakened the robustness persuasiveness of the model under different ultrasound devices and acquisition protocols to a certain extent.
2.The generation logic of fusion weights is relatively weak: The dynamic weight generator merely uses feature concatenation followed by MLP and Softmax to calculate the weights. Compared to the highly complex prototype mapping in the subsequent stage, this design of the fusion depth is slightly simple and may not be able to fully capture the fine-grained spatial dependencies across modalities.
3.Computational Overhead: The model inference stage combines 5-fold ensemble and 50 times of Monte Carlo random forward propagation (M=50 MC Dropout). This means that a single sample requires 250 forward propagations, and the total time consumption is approximately 1.25 seconds. For edge ultrasound devices, this delay is too high, limiting their possibility of real-time deployment.
4.Lack of visual interpretability: For dermatologists, in addition to the “uncertainty score”, if the model can provide visual attributions for the lesion area through methods such as CAM (Class Activation Map), the clinical acceptance will be higher.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

1.The use of cross-attn for fusion in B-ultrasound + Doppler color ultrasound is already a highly saturated routine operation. The dynamic weight generation merely outputs two global scalar weights through a simple MLP, which cannot achieve pixel-level or channel-level fine noise suppression. The claim of “suppressing low-quality modalities” lacks persuasiveness.
2.The greatest advantage of the classic prototype network lies in its interpretability - it directly obtains classification probabilities through strict Euclidean distance. In the paper, it is sent to a two-layer MLP with batchnorm and dropout for nonlinear mapping. Essentially, it is no different from the MLP’s decision-making for classification. There is a suspicion of packaging concepts.
3.Model integration based on 5-fold cross-validation (deep ensembles) and Monte Carlo random sampling (mc dropout) are very classic and ready-to-use techniques in the field of Bayesian deep learning. However, sacrificing inference time to obtain an uncertainty indicator for devices with limited computing resources on the clinical edge ultrasound equipment is not of practical value for such integration.
4.Although the authors did not provide open-source code, the description of the experiments is still relatively detailed. The comparison experiments and ablation experiments are also quite complete. The t-sne method is used to visually compare the non-linear mapping and pure distance in the paper to explain the reason for the improvement of the F1 index from 72.19% to 78.6%.
5.The framework diagram drawn by the authors is very professional. It decomposes the complex network structure into three subsystems using dotted lines and stage1-3 labels, and draws a three-dimensional scatter diagram of “discriminative manifold”.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces ProSyn-Net, a framework designed for reliable skin lesion detection using multimodal ultrasound data (morphological and hemodynamic features). The work addresses three critical barriers to clinical deployment: uncertainty estimation, high class imbalance, and multimodal data integration. The authors propose a dynamic cross-modal attention fusion to suppress noise from low-quality modalities, a non-linear prototypical mapping for imbalance handling, and an uncertainty-aware manifold ensemble to estimate predictive uncertainty.
reviews.text_strengths:
Major Strengths:
The approach is highly innovative and the “ProSyn” concept is both well-explained and easy to understand. That can be easily translate to other task and further enhance the handling of imbalanced dataset issues inherent to medical application.
The manuscript includes a clear ablation study to demonstrate the impact of each component and provides statistical analysis to verify the significance of the performance improvements.
The experiments are well-detailed, featuring comparisons against numerous baselines and utilizing rejection plots to validate the effectiveness of the chosen uncertainty measure U(x)
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Major Weaknesses:
The study mentions a second dataset with similar characteristics but does not utilize it for external validation (i.e., training on the larger in-house dataset and directly validating on the publicly available one). Given the importance of generalizability in clinical contexts, this is a missed opportunity to further demonstrate the robustness and clinical readiness of this very well-designed model.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
While the rejection plot is useful, the analysis would be significantly strengthened by including metrics such as Area Under the Risk Curve (AURC) or Excess AURC. These metrics would provide a more direct and standardized measure of the quality of the uncertainty-based ranking.

This is an exceptional and timely paper that addresses core challenges in medical AI, including uncertainty estimation and class imbalance. The proposed ProSyn-Net is innovative. The framework is supported by comprehensive experiments, a clear ablation study, and rigorous statistical analysis. The technical quality and potential for clinical impact make this a standout contribution.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text: After reviewing this manuscript alongside the expert evaluations, I note that the reviews are mixed but overall lean positive, with strong support highlighting the paper’s coherent methodological design, clinical relevance, and solid experimental validation, including ablations and uncertainty analysis. The main concerns—such as the mismatch between internal and external validation tasks, computational overhead, and the need for clearer justification of certain components—are valid but appear addressable through clarification and minor revision. Given the strength of the contribution and its relevance to reliable medical AI, I recommend a Provisional Accept, contingent on the authors adequately addressing these points in the rebuttal and final revision.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the reviewers and the meta-reviewer for their careful evaluation and constructive comments. We appreciate the recognition of the clinical relevance and overall methodological design of our work.
External validation scope. We will further clarify that the public dataset used in this work is an independent binary dermatologic ultrasound cohort, while our primary in-house task is 6-class imbalanced classification. Accordingly, we view this experiment as complementary evidence of transferability on an independent public cohort, rather than as a strictly matched external 6-class validation. Given the current scarcity of publicly available multimodal dermatologic ultrasound datasets closely aligned with our task setting, we used this cohort as complementary external evidence and will make this scope and limitation more explicit in the camera-ready version.
Deferral interpretation. We will also clarify that the uncertainty-guided deferral analysis is intended to illustrate a tunable, risk-aware human-AI collaboration setting, not to advocate a fixed clinical referral rate.
Prototype rationale. In addition, the prototype-based component is intended primarily to provide a structured class-distance representation for imbalanced, limited-sample learning, especially for irregular minority-class manifolds, rather than to make a standalone interpretability claim. Empirically, its value is reflected in the improvement over the pure-distance variant and in the stronger cross-fold ensemble gain observed in our ablation study.
Baseline fairness and efficiency. For fairness, we will clarify that the adaptations applied to architecturally flexible baselines were intended to place them in a more consistent and task-appropriate setting under a unified backbone and training recipe, while highly specialized methods retained their original designs. We also acknowledge that the full 5-fold ensemble with MC Dropout is a higher-performance but computationally heavier inference configuration, and we will make the corresponding runtime-performance trade-off more explicit in the final version.
We greatly appreciate these suggestions and will reflect them in the camera-ready revision to further improve clarity and calibrated presentation.

title: Proto-CAP: Prototype Memory Fusion and Curriculum-Adaptive Loss for Pediatric Myopia Visual Question Answering
abstract: Medical Visual Question Answering (Med-VQA) is pivotal for assisting clinical decision-making and automated diagnosis. While deep learning has achieved remarkable success in general VQA tasks, Med-VQA research targeting specific diseases—particularly pediatric myopia involving multimodal data—remains largely underexplored, primarily due to the scarcity of publicly available, expert-annotated datasets. In this paper, we present the Pediatric Myopia VQA dataset (PM-VQA). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first publicly available Med-VQA dataset dedicated to pediatric myopia. It comprises 2,741 multimodal images (CFP and OCT), totaling 14,781 expert-verified question-answer pairs(QA pairs). Furthermore, we propose an enhanced framework named Proto-CAP, designed to address the semantic gap and overfitting issues inherent in medical small-scale data. Within Proto-CAP, we introduce a Question-Guided Prototype Fusion mechanism and a Curriculum-Adaptive Poly-2 Loss to enhance prior knowledge injection and dynamically balance training difficulty. Experiments on PM-VQA demonstrate that our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance, reaching an accuracy of 79.19% and an F1-score of 78.74%, which outperforms existing methods by 2.10% in accuracy and 2.14% in F1-score.Code and dataset will be available at https://github.com/PixelOptic-Dev/Proto-CAP.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses medical visual question answering for pediatric myopia, which is a clinically relevant but relatively underexplored setting. The main contribution is two-fold. First, the authors introduce PM-VQA, a multimodal pediatric myopia VQA dataset built from clinical data and expert-verified question-answer pairs. Second, they propose Proto-CAP, an MMQL-based framework that augments visual representations with question-guided prototype memory fusion and uses a curriculum-adaptive Poly-2 loss to adjust optimization emphasis during training. The paper reports improved performance over several Med-VQA baselines on the proposed dataset and provides ablation results supporting the contribution of both proposed components.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper studies a clinically meaningful problem. Pediatric myopia is important in practice, and the Med-VQA setting is relevant and well-motivated.
The dataset effort is valuable. PM-VQA appears to be a carefully curated multimodal dataset with expert-verified QA pairs collected from clinical data.
The proposed method is reasonably matched to the task. Both the prototype-based fusion and the adaptive loss are motivated by the challenges of small-scale medical VQA.
The paper includes comparisons with several baselines, ablation studies, and qualitative examples.
The writing is generally clear. The overall pipeline is clear, and the qualitative visualizations help illustrate the intuition behind the method.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
My main concern is the data split protocol. The paper says the data are split into train/validate/test QA pairs, but it is unclear whether the split is image-based or patient-based. Since multiple QA pairs may come from the same image, this should be clarified carefully.
Table 2 needs stronger justification. Some compared methods are not sufficiently introduced, and it is therefore unclear why these baselines were selected. It would also strengthen the paper to compare with a more recent Med-VQA method, or at least discuss the difference more explicitly.
There are two issues about Table 3.First, why are Accuracy and Recall exactly the same for every row? If this is expected due to the metric definition, please explain it clearly. Second, Precision drops when either Proto or CAP is added alone, but improves when both are combined. The paper should give a clearer explanation of this interaction.
The contribution of the proposed loss needs to be clarified further. Its formulation appears closely related to PolyLoss [1], but the current presentation does not make it clear what the substantive difference is and why the proposed variant is necessary in this setting.
The paper would benefit from more details on the dataset and implementation. For example, it would be helpful to report the number of patients, the distribution of question types, whether all samples contain all modalities, and several missing training details needed to fully understand the setup. 
[1]. Leng, Z. , Tan, M. , Liu, C. , Cubuk, E. D. , Shi, X. , Cheng, S. , & Anguelov, D. (2022). PolyLoss: A polynomial expansion perspective of classification loss functions [Preprint]. arXiv. doi:10.48550/arXiv. 2204.12511
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper has several strengths, including a clinically relevant problem setting, a potentially useful pediatric myopia VQA dataset, and a method that shows consistent gains over multiple baselines. In particular, the combination of a clinically grounded multimodal dataset and a task-specific Med-VQA framework makes the work potentially valuable to the community. ButI still have some important concerns. The main issue is that the evaluation protocol is not fully convincing in its current form, since the paper states that the data were split into training, validation, and testing QA pairs, but does not clearly establish an image-disjoint or patient-disjoint split. Because multiple QA pairs can come from the same image, there is a possible leakage concern and it should be clarified. In addition, the methodological novelty is moderate, the validation is limited to a single internal dataset, and several details relevant to reproducibility are missing. Overall, I think the strengths slightly outweigh the weaknesses at this stage, and I am therefore placing the paper marginally above the acceptance threshold, while still expecting the authors to clarify the evaluation protocol and strengthen the presentation in rebuttal.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal addressed most of my concerns.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper makes two main contributions. First, it introduces PM-VQA, which is presented as the first expert-verified multimodal pediatric myopia Med-VQA dataset, built from CFP, OCT, and clinical records. This is potentially valuable because disease-specific ophthalmic VQA benchmarks are still scarce.
Second, the paper proposes Proto-CAP, an extension of MMQL with a Prototype Memory Fusion module and a Curriculum-Adaptive Poly-2 Loss. The method aims to improve semantic alignment and reduce overfitting in small-scale medical VQA. Overall, the dataset contribution is, in my opinion, the more important part of the paper.
reviews.text_strengths:
Important application setting. Pediatric myopia is clinically relevant, and Med-VQA for this disease is underexplored. The paper addresses a meaningful real-world problem.
Potentially useful dataset contribution. PM-VQA fills a gap in multimodal ophthalmic Med-VQA. If publicly released with clear protocols, it could become a useful benchmark for future work.
Reasonable method design. The prototype fusion and adaptive loss are both well motivated for small-scale medical data, and the method is easy to understand.
Clear empirical presentation. The paper includes baseline comparisons, ablations, and qualitative examples, which make the proposed improvements easy to follow.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The method novelty is limited.
The proposed Prototype Memory Fusion mainly combines prototype/memory learning, question-guided attention, and gated fusion, which are all familiar ideas in vision-language and medical multimodal learning. The paper does not clearly explain what is fundamentally new beyond adapting these components to this task.
A similar concern applies to the Curriculum-Adaptive Poly-2 Loss. Dynamic reweighting, curriculum learning, and hard-sample emphasis have all been widely studied, so the current loss design appears incremental rather than conceptually novel.
The paper should better position itself relative to prior work on memory/prototype learning and adaptive losses. Relevant references include Bengio et al. (2009), Santoro et al. (2016), Snell et al. (2017), Sukhbaatar et al. (2015), Lin et al. (2017), and Leng et al. (2022).
The experimental validation is still limited.
The reported gains over MMQL are promising but relatively modest, and all results are shown only on the newly introduced PM-VQA dataset. There is no external validation on another Med-VQA benchmark.
The paper also does not report variance, confidence intervals, or repeated runs with different random seeds. On a relatively small medical dataset, such reporting is important to show that the improvements are stable.
In addition, comparisons are mainly against prior Med-VQA baselines, but there is limited discussion of stronger modern multimodal baselines or pretrained vision-language models. This makes the “state-of-the-art” claim somewhat less convincing.
The paper’s value depends heavily on whether the dataset will be released.
In my view, the dataset is the most impactful part of the submission. However, the paper is not sufficiently clear about whether PM-VQA will be publicly released, and if so, under what access conditions.

N/A

This paper studies an important and underexplored problem, and I appreciate the effort to build a pediatric myopia multimodal Med-VQA dataset. The method is reasonable, the paper is clearly written, and the results are promising.
However, I am less convinced by the level of technical novelty, as both the prototype-based fusion and adaptive loss seem to be incremental extensions of existing ideas. The experimental validation is also somewhat limited, since it is restricted to the new dataset and lacks stronger robustness analysis.
Overall, my recommendation is cautious at this stage. That said, if the authors commit to publicly releasing PM-VQA with the benchmark split and evaluation code, I would be willing to raise my score to weak accept, because the dataset contribution would then provide clear community value.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper makes three contributions to medical visual question answering (Med-VQA) targeting pediatric myopia:
1- PM-VQA dataset. The authors construct what they claim to be the first publicly-oriented, expert-verified Med-VQA dataset dedicated to pediatric myopia. It comprises 2,741 multimodal images (Color Fundus Photography and Optical Coherence Tomography) collected from a collaborating hospital, with 14,781 question–answer pairs formulated by two ophthalmologists and validated by a senior expert. The data is partitioned into 10,271 / 2,287 / 2,223 train/val/test QA pairs.
2- Prototype Memory Fusion (Proto). A learnable memory bank M ∈ R^{K×D} of medical concept prototypes is queried by a global text representation (mean-pooled BERT embeddings) via attention; the retrieved concept vector C is fused with Swin-Transformer visual features V through a learned sigmoid gate, V_enhanced = LayerNorm(g·V + (1−g)·C). The aim is to inject domain priors and bridge the visual–language semantic gap.
3- Curriculum-Adaptive Poly-2 Loss (CAP). An extension of Poly-Loss (Leng et al., 2022) where the polynomial coefficients e₁ and e₂ are no longer static but scheduled with respect to current training accuracy: e₁ follows a cosine decay (fast early convergence) while e₂ increases linearly (late-stage hard-example mining). The aim is self-paced curriculum learning.
The two modules are integrated on top of the MMQL multi-question backbone (Chen et al., 2024), and their combination yields 79.19% accuracy and 78.74% F1 on PM-VQA, +2.10 / +2.14 points over MMQL.
reviews.text_strengths:
1- Pediatric myopia is a major public-health issue (cited prevalence of ~50% of the world’s population by 2050). Existing Med-VQA benchmarks (VQA-RAD [7], SLAKE [12]) are radiology-centric, while existing ophthalmology VQA datasets (DME-VQA [19], INSEGCAT-VQA [20], OphthalWeChat [22]) are largely repurposed from public datasets, single-modality, or lack QA verification (Table 1). PM-VQA is the only entry that is simultaneously clinical-source, multimodal (CFP+OCT) and QA-verified, which is a real value-add for the community.
2- QA pairs are formulated by two ophthalmologists and re-validated by a senior expert, with explicit quality control and de-identification stages (Fig. 1). Ethics committee approval is reported. This is stronger annotation governance than most ophthalmology VQA datasets.
3- The Prototype Memory Fusion is a sensible inductive bias for small-scale medical data: parameterising medical concepts as a learnable memory addresses the well-known data-scarcity problem cited in the introduction. The gating mechanism preserves the original visual stream, mitigating the risk that the prototype path overrides image evidence — a nice design choice.
The Curriculum-Adaptive Poly-2 Loss is a clean, lightweight extension of Poly-Loss [8] that ties coefficient scheduling to a model-state signal (accuracy). The cosine-decay / linear-increase schedule for e₁ / e₂ is consistent with the easy-to-hard curriculum intuition.
4- Seven Med-VQA baselines are compared (CMSA, M-Mixup, M2I2, MUMC, MEVF-BAN, Surgical-VQA, MMQL). The improvement over the closest baseline (MMQL) is non-trivial (+2.10% accuracy, +2.14% F1).
5- Table 3 ablates Proto and CAP independently and jointly, supporting the claim that the two modules are complementary (each adds something on its own; the combination is super-additive in F1: +0.98 + +0.74 individually vs +2.14 jointly).
6- The qualitative attention-map comparison in Fig. 3 (right panel) shows visibly more focal attention for Proto-CAP than for MMQL, lending some plausibility to the ‘medical-prior injection’ interpretation.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1- Each component is a thin variation on prior art:
The Prototype Memory Fusion is structurally a memory-augmented attention bank with a sigmoid gate. Memory networks for medical image analysis and gated text-conditioned visual fusion are well-established (e.g., dynamic memory networks for VQA, gated multimodal units of Arevalo et al. 2017, conditional reasoning of MEVF-BAN [23] which is itself a baseline here). The paper does not articulate what is fundamentally new beyond combining a learnable memory bank with a BERT-pooled query and a sigmoid gate.
The Curriculum-Adaptive Poly-2 Loss is a parameter-scheduling modification of Poly-Loss [8]. The schedules for e₁ (cosine decay) and e₂ (linear increase) are not formally specified (no equations, no hyperparameters, no sensitivity analysis). Tying loss weights to training accuracy is a small step beyond [8], and self-paced / curriculum-driven loss-shaping has a long history (Kumar et al. 2010; Bengio et al. 2009; focal-loss family). Without an explicit comparison against vanilla Poly-Loss with tuned static (e₁,e₂), the added value of the
adaptive
aspect is not isolated.
Overall the framework is MMQL [1] + memory bank + scheduled Poly-Loss; the +2.10% gain is real but modest and may largely come from the prototype module rather than from a conceptual breakthrough.
2- Table 1 advertises PM-VQA as multimodal (CFP and OCT), and the introduction motivates the work by the need for joint CFP/OCT analysis. However, Section 3 describes only a single image I processed by one Swin Transformer, with no explanation of how CFP and OCT are jointly fed to the model, aligned per-patient, or fused across modalities. Are CFP and OCT treated as independent samples (in which case the model is monomodal at inference time)? Are they concatenated, encoded by separate branches, or paired per patient? This is the most important methodological gap of the paper given that multimodality is an explicit selling point. Without clarification, the ‘multimodal’ claim is not supported by the method.
3- All experiments are run on the authors’ own PM-VQA. There is no evaluation on existing ophthalmology VQA datasets (DME-VQA, INSEGCAT-VQA, OphthalWeChat) nor on radiology benchmarks (VQA-RAD, SLAKE) to demonstrate that the Proto and CAP modules generalise. Given the reliance on a domain-specific memory bank, it is particularly important to show whether the gains transfer or whether they are tied to PM-VQA-specific concepts.
4- Tables 2 and 3 report single-point estimates with no standard deviation, no confidence interval, no multi-seed runs and no statistical test. With +2.10% accuracy on a 2,223-QA test set, the naive 95% Wilson CI for a binomial proportion is roughly ±1.7%, so the claimed gain over MMQL is barely outside the noise floor. For the Proto-only variant (+1.18%) and CAP-only variant (+0.65%) the claim is statistically not supported by the evidence shown.
5- The dataset section omits information that is essential to assess scientific value and risk of bias:
Number of unique patients (vs. number of images).
Patient demographics (age range, sex distribution, ethnicity, spherical-equivalent distribution, axial-length distribution).
Question type taxonomy and answer space (open vs. closed; answer-vocabulary size; class imbalance).
Inter-annotator agreement between the two ophthalmologists and the senior expert (Cohen’s κ or analogous).
Image-level metadata (device manufacturer, resolution, OCT scan pattern), which affects external validity.
How CFP and OCT are paired per patient and per QA pair.
Train/val/test split protocol is it patient-level (no leakage) or QA-pair-level (likely leakage)? This is critical because many QA pairs share an image; QA-level random splitting would let the model see the same image at train and test time.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

PM-VQA is a real and currently missing resource pediatric myopia is a high-impact public-health topic and existing ophthalmic VQA datasets are either monomodal, public-source or unverified. Releasing a clinical, multimodal, expert-verified dataset would be a valuable community contribution.
The proposed modules are well-motivated, simple to integrate, and the ablation supports their complementarity.
Empirical gains over a strong recent backbone (MMQL [1]) are consistent across all four reported metrics.
Methodological novelty is incremental: a memory bank with gated fusion + a scheduled Poly-Loss on top of an existing backbone. None of the three contributions is individually MICCAI-strong; the dataset is the strongest item but its size (2,741 images) and the missing description of the multimodal pipeline limit its standing.
The ‘multimodal’ claim central to the paper’s differentiation from existing eye-VQA datasets is not demonstrated in the method or experiments. The model as described in Section 3 is a single-image pipeline.
Single-dataset evaluation, no significance testing, no multi-seed variance, and a +0.65/+1.18% per-module gain that is below the binomial-CI noise floor for a 2,223-sample test set, jointly weaken the empirical evidence.
Reproducibility is poor: no code, no data link, no commitment to release, and several hyperparameters are unstated.
Several clarifications are needed regarding ethics on paediatric data and the rationale for demographic-prediction QA items.
Issues that should be addressed in rebuttal:
Clarify how CFP and OCT are jointly used (per-patient pairing, encoder topology, fusion stage). If the model is in fact monomodal, soften the multimodal claim.
Provide multi-seed mean ± std and a statistical test (McNemar or paired bootstrap) for Tables 2 and 3.- Describe the train/val/test split protocol (patient-level vs QA-level) and confirm absence of image-level leakage.
Specify K, p, and the closed-form schedules for e₁ and e₂; include a sensitivity analysis on K.
Add at least one cross-dataset experiment (e.g., DME-VQA or VQA-RAD) demonstrating that the Proto and CAP modules are not specific to PM-VQA.
Commit explicitly to releasing code, prototypes, and the PM-VQA dataset under a documented licence.
Discuss the inclusion of demographic-prediction QA items (e.g., gender) and report performance broken down by question type.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper introduces a pediatric myopia medical VQA benchmark (PM-VQA) and a Proto-CAP framework that combines prototype memory fusion with a curriculum-adaptive loss to improve multimodal reasoning performance. The work addresses a clinically meaningful and underexplored problem, and the curated, expert-verified dataset together with consistent empirical improvements over prior Med-VQA baselines make it potentially valuable to the community.
On the other side, the reviewers also raise main concerns. First, the evaluation protocol needs clarification: the current QA-level split raises potential leakage issues, and the absence of multi-seed results, statistical testing, and robustness analysis makes the reported gains hard to judge. Second, the “multimodal” aspect is unclear, as the paper does not explain how CFP and OCT are jointly modeled or fused. Third, the novelty appears limited, with both the prototype memory and adaptive loss being incremental extensions without clear differentiation from prior work. Fourth, the empirical validation is somewhat limited: it relies on a single internal dataset, includes insufficient comparison to stronger or more recent baselines, lacks robustness and statistical analysis, and does not demonstrate whether the proposed modules generalize beyond PM-VQA. Finally, key dataset and reproducibility details are missing, weakening transparency and rigor.

This paper proposes Proto-CAP, a pediatric myopia Med-VQA framework with prototype memory fusion and curriculum-adaptive loss, together with PM-VQA, an expert-verified pediatric myopia dataset from CFP and OCT images. The main strength of the work lies in the dataset contribution: pediatric myopia Med-VQA is clinically meaningful and underexplored, and PM-VQA could provide a valuable community benchmark. The rebuttal strengthens this aspect by committing to release the dataset and code upon acceptance. However, several concerns remain only partially resolved. The methodological contribution appears moderate, with prototype memory fusion and curriculum-adaptive loss representing incremental extensions of existing ideas, while validation is limited to a single internal benchmark with modest gains. In addition, the rebuttal clarification weakens the multimodal framing, as CFP and OCT are treated as separate Med-VQA tasks rather than jointly modeled at inference. Overall, my assessment is mixed: with the promised dataset release, I lean toward acceptance because the potential community value outweighs the remaining concerns. However, the methodological contribution alone would not, in my view, be sufficient without public release of the dataset, and I strongly encourage the authors to follow through on this commitment.

After reviewing the manuscript, the reviews, and the authors’ rebuttal, I recommend acceptance.
The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem in pediatric myopia assessment and introduces a clinically meaningful multimodal Med-VQA dataset. While the methodological novelty is moderate, the combination of a new benchmark, a well-motivated task setting, and consistent empirical improvements provides a valuable contribution to the community.
The main concerns raised during review related to the evaluation protocol, potential data leakage, reproducibility, and the scope of validation. In my view, the rebuttal adequately clarifies these issues and strengthens confidence in the reported results. This is reflected in the updated recommendations from Reviewers 1 and 2.
Overall, I believe the dataset contribution, clinical relevance, and experimental results outweigh the remaining limitations. The paper represents a useful contribution and I therefore recommend acceptance.

The paper addresses a clinically relevant and underexplored problem in pediatric myopia VQA, introducing the PM-VQA dataset and the Proto-CAP framework. The dataset appears to be a valuable contribution, with expert-verified annotations and multimodal ophthalmic data. The proposed method demonstrates consistent improvements over established Med-VQA baselines, and the rebuttal satisfactorily clarifies several key concerns, including confirmation of patient-level data splitting to prevent leakage, justification of baseline selection, clarification of multimodal dataset construction, and additional details regarding the prototype memory and curriculum-adaptive loss design. While the methodological novelty remains somewhat incremental and external validation is limited, the reviewers generally agree that the dataset contribution is significant and that the reported gains are meaningful in this specialized setting. Given the positive reviews, satisfactory rebuttal, and community value of the benchmark, I recommend the paper for acceptance.

author_feedback_text: Our CAP loss mimics the clinical training process. In the early stage, when accuracy is low, e1 promotes rapid convergence, allowing the model to quickly learn fundamental and typical ophthalmic anatomical structures. The cosine schedule provides slow initial decay, accelerated mid-stage adjustment, and smooth final convergence, preventing premature or overly rapid gradient decay and reducing training instability. In the later stage, as model proficiency improves, e2 increases linearly, suppressing redundant gradients from easy samples while amplifying attention to difficult clinical cases. Unlike PolyLoss, which usually provides only marginal gains on large-scale datasets, our dynamic curriculum plays a critical role in preventing overfitting in small-scale medical data. Proto provides clinically informative high-dimensional features, while CAP offers a dynamic learning path to fully exploit these features. CAP can therefore be regarded as an enhancement to Proto, and their combination significantly outperforms either module alone.

title: Protocol-Manifold Coverage Learning (PMCL): Source-Free Active Adaptation for Multi-Center Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma MRI Segmentation
abstract:
The cross-center deployment of primary gross tumor volume
(GTV) segmentation models for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) on CE-T1 MRI is frequently compromised by protocol mixture. This induces systemic domain shifts, primarily manifesting as boundary drift—severe
inflation of the 95% Hausdorff Distance (HD95) despite stable Dice scores.To address this, we introduce Protocol-Manifold Coverage Learning (PMCL), a source-free active adaptation framework. Operating within a minimal slice budget, PMCL selects target queries independently of source data or pseudo-labels. It quantifies protocol variation via a compact signature, isolates boundary-band Protocol Disagreement (PD) using
protocol-aware perturbations, and enforces Group Prior Coverage to prevent sampling collapse. Evaluated on 1,289 volumes across six centers under a 10% annotation budget, PMCL outperforms state-of-the-art methods, improving average Dice by ∼0.10 and reducing mean HD95 by∼3.9mm.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper addresses the issue of source-free active domain adaptation (SFADA) for tumour segmentation in T1 MR images. The problem is similar to source-free domain adaptation (SFDA), the goal of which is to use a network trained on a source domain and to fine-tune it on a target domain without any labelled data. In the SFADA case, however, the objective is to select a small subset of data for expert annotation prior to model fine-tuning. More generally, domain adaptation is a crucial challenge in medical image analysis because networks are typically specific to the underlying data distribution of their training/source dataset and may perform poorly on test/target data during deployment. Furthermore, the source dataset may be unavailable due to data privacy concerns, and the budget for target domain annotation may be limited. SFADA appears to be a suitable approach for addressing each of these challenges.
The authors propose selecting a subset of the target data based on hand-crafted features and the disagreement/uncertainty of the segmentation boundaries. In particular, hand-crafted features enable the selection of data representative of the target domain, while segmentation boundary uncertainty allows challenging cases to be detected and included for manual annotation and fine-tuning. The authors claim that by selecting cases with high boundary uncertainty, this improves the accuracy of the segmentation boundaries produced by the fine-tuned network.
Experiments were conducted on a multi-centre dataset with a 10% annotation budget. The dataset from each of the 6 centres was defined by specific acquisition parameters, hence the need for domain adaptation. The proposed method outperformed all other domain adaptation approaches.
reviews.text_strengths:
This paper addresses an important issue of interest to the medical imaging community. The proposed SFADA approach is not limited to tumour segmentation alone; it could also be adapted for other segmentation tasks. The paper is well written and organised. The methods and experiments are straightforward to follow, and the mathematical notation is clear and consistent. Despite the simplicity of the proposed approach, the extensive experiments indicate improved performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches.
Overall, the problem setting is relevant and the experimental scope is reasonable.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper is closely related to references [ref13] and [ref14], with similar SFADA setups and datasets. Unlike [ref13] and [ref14], which use features from the final layer of the segmentation network to generate a latent space for selecting target domain images, the proposed approach relies on basic handcrafted features (voxel size and Fourier transform statistics). It is unclear what criteria led to this selection of features and whether alternatives were tested. Notably, these features do not incorporate any information relating to anatomical shape. Therefore, it is unclear whether the selected target data for annotation are representative of the underlying shape distribution.
The ablation study does not clarify whether using boundary segmentation uncertainty for target data selection leads to more accurate delineation, as the Dice and HD95 scores are similar (with overlapping standard deviations) between the PMCL (full), w/o Protocol Perturb. And w/o Boundary Band rows. The lack of statistical analysis is also problematic.
The results show that the method achieves Dice scores in the range 64–78% and HD95 scores between 3.9 and 15.5 mm across all datasets. It is unclear whether this performance is adequate in a real-world scenario; the HD95 scores are particularly high.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Methods:
It is unclear why the raw probability maps are not used to compute boundary uncertainty directly.
The authors use an intensity-based transformation to create multiple views for evaluating boundary uncertainty, but is the network trained using intensity-based data augmentation?
In equation 4, the symbol ⊮ is not explicitly defined.
Experiments:
Is the target-only network trained on 10% or 100% of the target domain data? This should be clarified.
Results:
The authors claim ‘statistically significant increases in boundary deviation’, but the statistical test used is unclear (Student’s t-test?).

The paper is closely related to references [ref13] and [ref14], featuring similar SFADA setups and datasets. Even if the results indicate improved performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches, the methodological contribution remains incremental. The paper would benefit from a clearer justification of the handcrafted feature selection, stronger ablation evidence for the boundary uncertainty contribution, and statistical validation of the results.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have addressed my concerns, I recommend accepting the paper.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes PMCL, a source-free active adaptation framework that effectively addresses boundary shift in multi-center nasopharyngeal carcinoma segmentation under low annotation budgets by explicitly quantifying protocol disparities via compact signatures and targeting boundary drift with protocol-aware perturbations.
reviews.text_strengths: Overall, this paper addresses an important issue in active learning by proposing a dedicated sample screening strategy. The motivation is clear, the method is reasonably designed, and the experimental results show improvements over the entropy-based baseline. The work is generally well-organized and can be accepted with minor revisions.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Why are the comparison experiments only conducted under the 10% annotation budget? How does the proposed method perform under other budget settings such as 5%, 15%, and 20%? Can the superiority of the proposed method be maintained across different annotation budgets?
2.Although the proposed strategy outperforms conventional sampling, a more detailed analysis of selected samples, for example, sample difficulty, distribution, or visualization, would help readers better understand why the strategy works.
3.Related works on query based active learning could be briefly discussed to better position the contribution of this paper.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper targets an important and practical problem in active learning, with a clear and well-founded research motivation. The proposed sample selection strategy is logically designed and well integrated into the overall framework. The experimental results validate the effectiveness of the method, showing consistent improvements over the entropy-based baseline. The manuscript is well organized and clearly written, making it easy to follow and understand.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: In this paper, the authors address the domain shift problem in NPC GTV segmentation caused by protocol mixture across different centers. To tackle this challenge, the authors propose a source-free active domain adaptation framework, namely Protocol-Manifold Coverage Learning (PMCL). The framework consists of three key components: (1) representing each imaging volume with a compact protocol signature, (2) quantifying boundary uncertainty via Protocol Disagreement (PD) computed from a protocol-aware perturbation bank, and (3) introducing Group Prior Coverage to balance informative sample selection and protocol diversity. Experimental results demonstrate that PMCL achieves strong domain adaptation performance, particularly in improving boundary robustness under protocol variations.
reviews.text_strengths:
(1) The paper addresses a clinically meaningful problem and provides insightful observations with real-world impact. Shifting the focus in GTV segmentation from volumetric overlap to boundary drift is particularly important for radiotherapy planning. Moreover, the source-free setting aligns well with realistic clinical data governance constraints, where access to source data or features is often restricted. 
(2) The three core components in this work including Group Prior Coverage, Protocol Perturbation, and Boundary Band, are logically well-designed. The experimental evaluations are clear and interpretable, effectively demonstrating the contribution and necessity of each component. 
(3) The method is evaluated on a large multi-center dataset consisting of 1,289 volumes from six centers, across ten transfer tasks. The scale of evaluation is extensive, and the consistency in fine-tuning and testing across tasks, as well as the selection of baseline methods, is appropriate and well-justified.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(1) All comparative experiments are conducted only under a 10% annotation budget. The lack of performance curves across different budget levels (e.g., 5%, 10%, 20%) limits the practical insight for real-world deployment. In addition, although the paper compares with UDA methods that use source data (e.g., ADVENT, AdaptSeg), it does not provide an upper-bound result such as full supervision on the target domain (100%), making it difficult to assess the remaining performance gap. 
(2) Figure 3 presents qualitative results only for CenterA. It would be more informative to include examples from the most challenging target domain (e.g., CenterFS with the largest protocol gap) to better demonstrate the effectiveness of domain adaptation. 
(3) The current protocol signature uses only voxel area and frequency sharpness, which capture resolution and blur but ignore other important acquisition factors such as field strength, contrast agent, and reconstruction kernel. It remains unclear whether the proposed framework can effectively handle these variations, and thus its robustness across broader protocol differences is not fully validated.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper makes a valuable contribution to a clinically meaningful problem. The three core components are well-designed and effectively achieve domain adaptation while preventing sampling collapse. The main limitations lies in the lack of annotation budget sensitivity analysis, limited coverage of protocol-related factors, and insufficient qualitative visualization. Hope the authors can address these issues in revision. Therefore, I give a weak accept recommendation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors’ rebuttal addresses my main concerns. It clarifies the novelty of the paper compared with prior SOTA methods, justifies the compact protocol signature, clarifies the role of boundary protocol disagreement, and revises unsupported statistical significance claims. The explanation of the 10% active budget setting and the target-only upper bound also resolves ambiguity in the experimental protocol. Although budget sensitivity analysis and richer acquisition metadata remain limitations, partly due to page constraints, I maintain my recommendation for acceptance.

meta_reviews.text:
The reviewers provide somewhat mixed assessments of this paper (scores: 3, 4, 4), with overall positive feedback on the problem setting, experimental scale, and practical relevance, but concerns regarding limited novelty, insufficient ablation evidence, and missing analysis of key design choices . In particular, questions remain about the justification of handcrafted feature design, the effectiveness of boundary uncertainty for sample selection, and the lack of evaluation across different annotation budgets. Given these points, I encourage the authors to address the raised concerns in the rebuttal—especially by clarifying methodological choices, strengthening experimental analysis, and providing additional evidence where possible. A clear and detailed response will be important for the final decision.

After carefully reviewing the rebuttal and the post-rebuttal reviewer comments, my recommendation is to accept the paper. The paper addresses a clinically meaningful and practically important problem of source-free active domain adaptation for multi-center nasopharyngeal carcinoma tumor segmentation under limited annotation budgets. The proposed PMCL framework is well motivated, combining protocol signatures, boundary protocol disagreement, and group prior coverage to select informative and diverse target-domain samples. Although the methodological contribution is somewhat incremental and concerns remain regarding budget sensitivity analysis, statistical validation, and the limited protocol factors captured by the compact signature, the reviewers generally agreed that the rebuttal adequately addressed the main concerns. The evaluation on a large multi-center dataset across multiple transfer tasks is convincing, and the method shows consistent improvements over relevant baselines. Therefore, I recommend acceptance, with the expectation that the authors will clarify the remaining experimental details and limitations in the final version.
I recommend accept: post-rebuttal unanimous Accept.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and AC for the constructive comments. We focus on novelty, protocol-signature design, boundary-uncertainty evidence, budget, and reproducibility.
Novelty vs. prior SFADA (R1/AC). PMCL shares the SFADA setting with STDR/Versatile-SFADA, but addresses a different query problem. Prior methods mainly select samples via latent/reference representations for representativeness or calibration.PMCL does not perform latent-space clustering/reference-star selection and requires no source images, source features, or source-derived reference vectors during query selection. Its novelty is not replacing deep features with handcrafted ones, but selecting queries for protocol-induced boundary drift by coupling acquisition-protocol coverage with boundary-band disagreement under protocol-aware perturbations.
Protocol signature and uncertainty design (R1/R3/AC). The compact signature is not an anatomical-shape descriptor. log(dx·dy) captures in-plane sampling resolution, and log(FFT_H/FFT_L) captures frequency response/sharpness. We retained this 2-D signature because it is stable, interpretable, consistently available, and tied to resolution/blur shifts; richer metadata are often missing or center-specific. Shape/segmentation difficulty is handled separately by boundary-band PD. Unlike raw single-view probability uncertainty, PMCL probes prediction stability under protocol-aware perturbations and aggregates disagreement only in the predicted boundary band. Field-strength/reconstruction metadata were not consistently available, but can be incorporated when available.
Statistics and ablations (R1/AC). We agree that our statistical wording was unclear. The unsupported “statistically significant” wording in the ablation/boundary-deviation discussion will be removed. We will present Table 3 as directional component evidence rather than component-level significance claims. In the reported ablation tasks, full PMCL gives the best HD95 and best/tied-best Dice, but overlapping mean±std values make isolated component significance difficult to claim. Evidence that PMCL is not merely single-view uncertainty sampling comes from Entropy under the same target pool, 10% budget, source checkpoint, and fine-tuning/evaluation. Across the ten Table-2 tasks, PMCL improves Dice and reduces HD95 versus Entropy in all tasks; two-sided paired Wilcoxon tests on task-level summaries give p<0.005 for both metrics.
Experimental setting (R1/R3). Target-only is the upper bound trained with 100% labeled target data, not the 10% active budget. All query methods use the same target pool, budget, source checkpoint, fine-tuning schedule, test split, and metrics. The perturbation bank is used only for frozen-model query scoring, not as PMCL-specific training augmentation. Eq. 4 will replace the indicator symbol with 1[·].
Budget, visualization, and clinical interpretation (R1/R2/R3/AC). The 10% budget was chosen a priori as a low-annotation SFADA setting and applied identically to all query methods; thus, our claims are limited to this fixed-budget regime. We agree that 5/15/20% curves would provide useful deployment insight and will state budget sensitivity as a limitation rather than introduce new budget results. The omitted protocol-space visualization re-plots existing signatures/selection lists; if space permits, we will restore a compact version. CenterA was a conservative example, and following R3 we will replace or complement it with a compact CenterFS example from existing predictions. PMCL reduces limited-budget adaptation error but does not claim autonomous clinical deployment.
Reproducibility and related work (R1/R2/R3). We will clarify implementation and data/code availability. Center1/2 are private; CenterA/B/C follow M-NPC/STDR access; CenterFS is public. Upon acceptance, we will release cleaned code for PMCL query selection, PD/boundary scoring, baselines, and finetuning/evaluation with documented formats/commands.

title: PROTON: Prototype-Based Test-Time Online OOD Detection for Medical VLMs
abstract:
Medical vision-language models (VLMs) enable zero-shot clin-
ical image classification, yet reliably detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs at deployment remains an open problem. No static scoring method works across all shift types: Maximum Concept Matching (MCM) on FLAIR achieves 76.4% AUROC for far-OOD but only 42.4% for covariate shifts such as ultra-wide-field fundus images —effectively random. We trace this to a structural mismatch: covariate-shifted inputs are indistinguishable from in-distribution samples in softmax space, yet occupy distinct regions in the VLM’s embedding space. To exploit this untappe signal, we propose PROTON (PROtotype-based Test-time ONline
OOD detection), a lightweight post-hoc module that maintains an online prototype bank from high-confidence test predictions and adaptively fuses prototype distance with MCM scoring via stream-level variance statistics, requiring no model modification, training data, or prompt engineering. On the ophthalmology benchmark (FLAIR + FIVES), PROTON improves MCM by +23.9 AUROC on covariate shift, +8.8 on semantic, and +8.1 on far-OOD —the only zero-shot method to improve all three without hierarchical prompts or labeled data.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The work identifies that existing OOD detection methods in probability space (e. g. , MCM ), using contrastive VLMs as the backbone, mainly target semantic shift. However, in the medical domain, detecting covariate shift is equally important. To address this, it incorporates feature-space information via an online-updated memory bank.
The prototype bank is initially constructed using confidence scores from the softmax outputs. After processing multiple data streams, class prototypes are formed by averaging class embeddings, and the distance to these prototypes is used as the OOD score. The final OOD score is a weighted combination of the MCM score and the proposed embedding-based score.
reviews.text_strengths:
Strengths:
The paper is well-written and the identified problem (\i. e. , detecting both semantic-shift and covariate-shift) is interesting to the community.
Extensive experiments have been done to valid the effectiveness of the proposed framework.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Weaknesses:
It is true the the proposed framework is free from accessing the training data, however, it necessities to access test samples. Meanwhile, the construction of the prototype bank initially relies on the reliability of confidence score (\i. e. , MCM), however, one of motivations of this work is that MCM is unreliable to detect the covariate-shift OOD samples. Imagine that if the beginning sampels are mostly covariate-shift OOD samples, then the quality of prototype bank might be degraded.
I believe the authors miss one important work TAG [1], which does not rely on the model modification, training data, and prompt engineering. The authors are encouraged to incorporate the results of OOD detection using TAG as one of baselines.
[1] TAG: Text Prompt Augmentation for Zero-Shot Out-of-Distribution Detection, ECCV, 2024.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

See weaknesses.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
Thanks for conducting the suggested experiments. 
Q1: The authors evaluate PROTON across various ID_fraction settings, showing consistent improved performance compared to MCM. 
Q2: The authors add suggested baseline.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes PROTON, a lightweight prototype-based test-time online OOD detection framework for medical vision-language models. Its main contribution is to exploit the embedding-space structure of test samples by maintaining an online prototype bank and combining prototype distance with MCM scoring through adaptive variance-based fusion. This allows the method to improve OOD detection across covariate, semantic, and far-OOD shifts without requiring training data, prompt engineering, or model updates.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The proposed online prototype bank does not require access to training data, which is particularly valuable in medical applications where data privacy and restricted data sharing are major practical concerns.
2.The method shows clear empirical gains over strong baseline methods, with especially significant improvements on covariate shift while also consistently improving semantic and far-OOD detection.
3.The ablation and sensitivity studies suggest that the method is robust to hyperparameter choices, which strengthens its practicality for real deployment settings.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.A limitation of the paper is that the method is mainly validated on top of MCM. The authors claim that PROTON is compatible with other scoring functions, but they do not provide enough empirical evidence to show that it can reliably improve non-MCM scores as well.
2.The empirical comparison is not sufficiently broad. In particular, only a small number of non-MCM-style baselines are considered, and these are relatively old methods, which weakens the strength of the experimental validation.
3.The method strongly depends on high classification accuracy of the base model. If the model makes incorrect predictions, the prototype bank can be contaminated and may even fail completely. However, the paper does not discuss this sensitivity or analyze performance when the classifier is weak.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

My recommendation is based on limited confidence in the paper’s broader impact. The proposed method appears to be mainly an improvement over MCM, so it is unclear whether the idea has more general value beyond that specific setting. In addition, the set of baselines is relatively limited, which makes it harder to judge the true strength of the method against a broader range of alternatives. Finally, the experimental analysis is not thorough enough, and several important questions about robustness and applicability remain insufficiently explored.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes PROTON which is a lightweight post-hoc module for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection in medical vision-language models (VLMs). The core insight is that covariate-shifted inputs (e.g., ultra-wide-field fundus images) produce high softmax confidence indistinguishable from in-distribution samples, yet are geometrically separable in the VLM’s embedding space. PROTON maintains an online prototype bank built from high-confidence test predictions via FIFO queues, computes a prototype distance score, and adaptively fuses it with MCM scoring using Welford’s online variance estimation. The method requires no model modification, training data, or prompt engineering. On the FLAIR + FIVES ophthalmology benchmark, PROTON improves MCM by +23.9 AUROC on covariate shift, +8.8 on semantic shift, and +8.1 on far-OOD.
reviews.text_strengths:
I think the paper identifies a clear and well-characterized failure mode. The observation that covariate-shifted inputs are indistinguishable in softmax space but separable in embedding space (Figure 1) is compelling. The t-SNE plots, MCM score overlap analysis, and 2D scatter of MCM vs. prototype distance all provide direct evidence, which I find convincing. This is not just a hand-wavy motivation.
The method design is also elegant. PROTON adds no learnable parameters, requires a single forward pass, and uses O(1) memory per update via Welford’s algorithm. The confidence gate to prevent OOD contamination of prototypes is a small but important detail. I think the idea of using MCM variance to automatically detect when softmax confidence becomes unreliable (Eq. 3-4) is clever. The sigmoid interpolation avoids hard switching, and the behavior analysis showing αt dropping when covariate samples enter demonstrates the mechanism works as intended.
When I look at the ablation (Table 2), I appreciate that it systematically decomposes contributions: prototype distance (+15.5 covariate AUROC), adaptive fusion (+4.8), and confidence gate (+3.6). The γ × M sensitivity analysis across three medical domains (Figure 3b) also shows the method is robust across a wide range of hyperparameters, which is reassuring for practical deployment.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
My main concern is that the full evaluation is conducted on a single benchmark (FLAIR + FIVES) for the main results. The ID set contains only 300 samples (150 Normal + 150 DR) and OOD sets are similarly small. For a method that relies on online prototype accumulation, the stream length matters. The γ × M heatmaps in Figure 3b show results on radiology and pathology, but only as ∆AUROC without absolute numbers or dataset details. I would have liked to see full Table 1-style results on at least one additional domain.
Also, the method assumes the test stream contains a sufficient proportion of in-distribution samples to build meaningful prototypes. In deployment scenarios where most incoming samples are OOD (e.g., a screening system receiving many misrouted images), the prototype bank could be contaminated despite the confidence gate. The paper does not analyze sensitivity to the ID/OOD ratio in the stream, and I am curious about how the method degrades in such scenarios.
Another point I think is that hierarchical MCM (L=5) achieves 87.7% covariate AUROC versus PROTON’s 66.3%, which is a gap of over 20 points. While the authors note this requires domain-expert prompt trees, the performance difference is substantial and I think should be discussed more openly. The prototype convergence analysis (Figure 3a) is also shown only for radiology and pathology, not for the primary ophthalmology benchmark, which is an odd choice.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The paper is clearly structured. I find the “shift-type triage” idea mentioned in the Discussion (using the two-score decomposition to distinguish covariate vs. semantic vs. far-OOD) interesting but underdeveloped. Even a simple proof-of-concept would strengthen the paper. The σ²₀ reference threshold (set to 0.02) is described as “nominal ID-only variance” but how this value is chosen and whether it is sensitive to VLM architecture or dataset should be clarified.

I think the idea is new and fresh. Using online prototypes in the VLM’s embedding space to catch covariate shifts that softmax-based methods completely miss is a well-motivated contribution. The method is simple, parameter-free, and immediately deployable, which I find practically valuable. The core insight is convincingly demonstrated and the ablations are clean. The main limitations are the single-benchmark evaluation and the notable gap with hierarchical MCM, but these do not undermine the core contribution. I lean toward weak accept since the idea is sound and the direction is promising for the medical imaging community.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: After reading the rebuttal, I think my questions were mostly addressed. I would remain my score as weak accept. Thanks. Also, please make this work reproducible regarding the code and the model.

meta_reviews.text: This paper presents a well-motivated and elegant, parameter-free framework for online test-time OOD detection in medical vision-language models, effectively addressing both semantic and covariate shifts. In the post-rebuttal phase, the authors comprehensively resolved the core technical critiques by demonstrating robust performance across six distinct base scoring functions and multiple clinical modalities, earning the clear support of the majority of the panel. Although one reviewer maintained a negative recommendation regarding broader impact, the strong empirical gains, thorough validation, and consensus among the other experts lean firmly toward acceptance.

The paper presents PROTON, a framework for OOD detection with contrastive VLMs that addresses an important limitation of existing works where they focus on semantic shift while ignoring covariate shift, which is highly relevant in medical settings. By incorporating feature-space information through an online-updated memory bank, the method offers a clinically meaningful and technically useful extension. During the review process, reviewers identified an important baseline comparison, which the authors incorporated in the rebuttal. The updated results further demonstrate the strength of the PROTON framework, and reviewers also acknowledged these improvements, shifting toward acceptance. Given the method’s contribution, clinical relevance, and comprehensive analysis, this work represents a solid contribution to MICCAI, and I recommend acceptance.

Two reviewers recommend acceptance, and R2 recommends rejection. R2 points out that the proposed method has limited impact beyond the MCM method. R2 also points out limited baselines. However, MCM is usually indeed a strong baseline. Also, the number of comparative methods is limited in the online scenario without training data. Finally, R3 points out the limited experimental evaluations; however, the authors explore various medical VLMs and modalities, which, in my opinion, suffice for a conference version. Based on the above, despite their validity, I do not believe the remaining concerns invalidate the work, which is an interesting, practical contribution to OOD detection using VLMs. Therefore, I recommend acceptance.
Note: The FLAIR reference appears to be incorrect. It points out to a natural image VLM, not a medical VLM. Please correct this issue.

author_feedback_text:
We thank reviewers for recognizing PROTON’s novelty, motivation, and clean ablations. We address all the comments below.
[R2.1] Beyond MCM. PROTON needs only a scalar base score S_b and embedding e_t: S_PROTON^b = a_t
S_b_hat + (1-a_t)
S_proto_hat; MCM is one instantiation. Across six base scores, PROTON improves every one on all shifts (mean +11-15 AUROC). Cov AUROC (base->+PROTON):
MaxLogit 42.8->62.5; GL-MCM 43.5->65.8; Energy 43.8->62.0;
MCM 42.4->66.3; Entropy 44.1->63.1; TAG-MCM 45.7->67.1.Semantic and far-OOD follow the same pattern. The contribution is image-embedding geometry — a complement to any softmax/logit score, not an MCM trick.
[R2.2] Broader baselines. We add TAG-MCM (ECCV’24), Hier.MCM(L=5), and privileged ID-feature banks. Cov AUROC: TAG-MCM 45.7; kNN-ID 70.8, Mahalanobis-ID 68.6 (labeled ID features); Hier.MCM(L=5) 87.7 (LLM prompts); PROTON 66.3 (no train, no prompts); Hier.MCM+PROTON 88.4.PROTON matches privileged feature-bank methods without training data or prompts, and composes with Hier.MCM.
[R2.3] Sensitivity to classifier accuracy. Under forced misrouting, PROTON stays above MCM through 30% misrouting (65.5 vs 57.6 mean). The confidence gate (g=0.7) alone adds +3.6 cov-AUROC (Tab.2) by blocking OOD contamination; pure-MCM fallback (Alg.1) holds before K_min. We will add a conservative gate (confidence+margin+prototype-consistency) with base-score fallback when unstable.
[R1.1] Cold-start and online setting. PROTON is strictly online: x_t is scored using the bank from past accepted samples; the bank updates only after (B_t = Update(B_{t-1}, e_t) iff max_c p_{t,c} >= g). No labels, transduction, or model updates. Before all classes reach K_min, PROTON falls back to pure MCM (Alg. 1). The score is a fusion S_PROTON = a_t
S_MCM + (1-a_t)
S_proto — MCM only gates which samples enter the bank; the OOD decision uses S_proto, capturing the embedding separation MCM misses.
Stream ID-fraction (Sem/Cov/Far AUROC):
rho=90%: 63.2/67.4/84.8; rho=70%: 62.7/66.3/84.5 (default)
rho=30%: 58.8/58.5/80.4; rho=10%: 55.1/50.9/77.2; MCM: 53.9/42.4/76.4
PROTON stays above MCM down to 10% ID. Stream-order CIs (5 perms): 62.7+-1.1 / 66.3+-1.8 / 84.5+-0.9 (order-stable). The non-zero ID-fraction assumption will be stated explicitly.
[R1.2] TAG baseline. Added — see [R2.2]. TAG-MCM (45.7 cov-AUROC) underperforms PROTON (66.3) and is orthogonal: TAG augments text prompts, PROTON exploits image-embedding geometry. Using TAG-MCM as PROTON’s base score yields 67.1.
