[R3.1] Cross-domain / cross-VLM. We replace dAUROC heatmaps with absolute Table 1-style numbers across three VLMs/domains. Cov AUROC (MCM->PROTON): Ophth. (FLAIR) 42.4->66.3; Radio. (UniMedCLIP) 44.7->90.4; Patho. (QuiltNet) 45.3->84.2.Gains are largest on covariate shift; semantic and far-OOD also improve everywhere (full metrics in appendix). Datasets: Radio. = Normal/Pneumonia (RSNA, 300 ea.); Patho. = Benign/Malignant (PCam-derived, 300 ea.).
[R3.2] ID/OOD stream-ratio. See [R1.1]- PROTON stays above MCM down to 10% ID. In low-ID screening, the confidence gate+K_min fallback keep prototypes uncontaminated; pure-MCM is recovered in the worst case, so PROTON never degrades below baseline.
[R3.3] Hier.MCM gap and FLAIR convergence. The 21-point cov-AUROC gap is real: Hier.MCM uses LLM-generated prompt trees, PROTON uses none. They are complementary — Hier.MCM+PROTON reaches 88.4 cov-AUROC, and PROTON exceeds Hier.MCM on far-OOD (84.5 vs 82.4). PROTON’s distinct value: zero training data, prompt trees, or expert input. The FLAIR convergence plot will be added (cos to final prototype >0.99 within ~55 samples; parallels Fig.3a).
[R3.4] sigma_0^2 and shift-type triage. sigma_0^2 is not tuned per-VLM: sweeping {0.005-0.08} gives flat mean AUROC 69.8-71.2 (sigmoid saturation). 0.02 corresponds to early-stream ID variance from a brief warm-up. The (S_MCM, S_proto) decomposition supports shift-type triage with macro-F1 = 0.70 on 3-way Cov/Sem/Far classification.

title: ProtoReg: Prototype Guidance and Dual-Level Uncertainty-Weighted Consistency for Semi-supervised Pulmonary Perfusion Regression
abstract: Pulmonary perfusion imaging is clinically important, but paired 3D CT-perfusion annotations are difficult to obtain. Semi-supervised learning (SSL) can exploit abundant unlabeled CT volumes, yet existing SSL methods are less effective for voxel-wise dense regression because continuous pseudo-labels lack reliable confidence estimates and strong consistency may amplify teacher noise. To address this, we propose ProtoReg, a semi-supervised framework for 3D non-contrast CT-to-perfusion regression with prototype-guided uncertainty modeling and sub-unit-aware learning. ProtoReg adopts a teacher–student framework with weak-to-strong consistency and maintains a learnable functional prototype bank to estimate uncertainty via prototype-induced entropy. Based on this uncertainty, we introduce a Dual-level Uncertainty-weighted Consistency Loss (DUW-CL), which re-weights consistency at both voxel and lung sub-unit levels to suppress noisy pseudo-label propagation. We further incorporate 1,000 external unlabeled CT volumes from public datasets to improve generalization without additional perfusion annotations. Experiments on two independent CT-perfusion cohorts show consistent improvements over strong SSL baselines, and ablations validate the effectiveness of prototype guidance, DUW-CL, and supervoxel-aware modeling. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/johnhamtom/ProtoReg_main.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes ProtoReg, a semi-supervised framework for 3D pulmonary perfusion regression from non-contrast CT. Its core contribution is adapting prototype-based learning (typically used for discrete segmentation) to a continuous dense regression task by quantizing perfusion values into functional bins. It further introduces a Dual-level Uncertainty-weighted Consistency Loss that leverages prototype-induced entropy at both voxel and lung sub-unit levels to mitigate noise in pseudo-labels.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.It effectively bridges the gap between discrete prototype learning and continuous voxel-wise regression.
2.The evaluation includes very recent and competitive SSL baselines like UniMatch v2 (2025).
3.The method is validated on both private and public datasets, showing feasibility for inferring lung function without radioactive tracers.
4.Using lung sub-units (supervoxels) to provide regional consistency is a well-motivated approach for 3D medical volumes.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.While the authors compare against UniMatch V2, they omit discussion or comparison with prior prototype-based SSL methods like CPCL (Xu et al. , 2022) or UPCOL (Lu et al. , 2023). These are highly relevant as they also utilize prototype consistency in medical imaging.
2.The framework appears to be a combination of prototype learning and the DyCON strategy. Since the uncertainty weighting (Eq. 8–10) follows DyCON closely, the authors should clarify their specific technical innovations beyond this combination. A direct experimental comparison with DyCON is also missing.
3.In Equation 8, the parameter β is used without a clear definition or initial explanation in the preceding text.
[1] Xu Z, Wang Y, Lu D, et al. All-around real label supervision: Cyclic prototype consistency learning for semi-supervised medical image segmentation[J]. IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics, 2022, 26(7): 3174-3184.
[2] Lu W, Lei J, Qiu P, et al. Upcol: Uncertainty-informed prototype consistency learning for semi-supervised medical image segmentation[C]//International conference on medical image computing and computer-assisted intervention. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland, 2023: 662-672.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses a challenging and clinically valuable task. I appreciate the inclusion of 2025 baselines. However, the lack of comparison with more specialized prototype-based SSL methods and the strong reliance on the DyCON formulation without a direct comparison are concerning. If the authors can clarify their specific technical contributions over DyCON and discuss/compare against the aforementioned prototype methods in the rebuttal, I would be open to increasing my score.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors have successfully addressed my concerns in the rebuttal. The authors provided a clear theoretical distinction from DyCON regarding continuous 3D regression. They also properly clarified the notation of β and the omission of CPCL/UPCOL due to task differences. I maintain my positive recommendation to
Accept
.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
1.This paper proposes a semi-supervised framework for CT-to-perfusion synthesis, named ProtoReg, that addresses the paired CT–perfusion acquisition problem.
2.This paper tackles the continuous pseudo-label prediction problem by using prototype-induced entropy.
3.The results show consistent improvements across all datasets.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.This paper introduces a framework for a semi-supervised CT-to-perfusion task. This topic is novel and clinically meaningful.
2.The incorporation of dual-level (voxel-level and sub-unit-level) is reasonable and validated to improve the overall performance.
3.The experiment results demonstrate robust performance across both cohort datasets, and the evaluation metrics employed are appropriate for assessing perfusion data.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The notations in the method are sometimes difficult to follow (e.g., v first appears in sec. 2.2, but is first defined in sec. 2.3). The manuscript would benefit from clarity in notation.
2.The authors state that the model initially focuses on low-uncertainty regions and later shifts to refinement with milder entropy-guided weighting. However, in Eqs. (8) and (9), the notation w continues to assign higher weights to low-entropy predictions throughout training. Please clarify what is meant by “shifts to refinement with milder entropy-guided weighting” and justify the use of the geometric decay schedule.
3.The proposed DUW-CL appears closely related to UnCL in DyCON, with the main difference being a dual-level formulation. The authors should more clearly articulate the novelty and distinction of their approach.
4.Prototype-induced entropy for reliability assessment may not be entirely novel, as similar ideas have been explored in prior works such as [1,2]. Nevertheless, this might be the first work to introduce such a reliability assessment strategy in the CT-to-Perfusion synthesis task. 
[1] A unified uncertainty network for tumor segmentation using uncertainty cross entropy loss and prototype similarity (Diao et al., 2022)
[2] Comprehensive Evaluation of Prototype Neural Networks (Schlinge et al., 2025)
5.The original volumetric sizes of the datasets are not specified. Is it appropriate to uniformly resize all data to 128
128
128? Please provide details on the preprocessing pipeline and discuss whether interpolation affects the integrity of CT and perfusion data.
6.The authors claim consistent improvements on both private and public CT-perfusion datasets. However, the reported results only include private datasets (Cohorts A and B). Please clarify whether experiments were conducted on public datasets or only for training.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper addresses a clinically meaningful challenge in CT-to-perfusion synthesis. However, several issues remain unresolved in the manuscript. In particular, the overall method design appears to be largely adapted from prior work in other domains, and the originality and domain-specific contributions of this study should be more clearly articulated.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Lack of ablation studies, but agree with the clinical practice and the statistical analysis results.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes ProtoReg, a semi-supervised framework for 3D CT-to-perfusion regression (predicting SPECT-like perfusion maps from non-contrast CT). The framework uses a teacher-student setup with weak-to-strong consistency on a 3D U-Net backbone. The main contributions are: (1) a prototype bank where K functional prototypes are learned from labeled data by quantizing perfusion values into bins, (2) prototype-induced entropy as a confidence signal for continuous pseudo-labels (since regression has no natural confidence score), and (3) DUW-CL, a Dual-level Uncertainty-weighted Consistency Loss that re-weights voxel-wise consistency using both voxel-level and lung sub-unit (supervoxel) uncertainty. They also incorporate 1,000 external unlabeled CT volumes from public datasets. Experiments on a private cohort (233 patients) and a public cohort (100 studies) show improvements over MT-Reg, FixMatch-Reg, UniMatch-Reg, and UniMatchV2-Reg.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Underexplored problem: Semi-supervised learning for dense regression in 3D medical volumes is a real gap in the literature, most SSL work focuses on classification or segmentation. CT-to-perfusion synthesis is also clinically meaningful since SPECT acquisition is expensive. The application is well-motivated.
2.Solid baseline selection: The paper compares against MT-Reg, FixMatch-Reg, UniMatch-Reg, and UniMatchV2-Reg, all adapted to dense regression with the same backbone and protocol. Including UniMatch V2 as a baseline is the right call and reflects awareness of the latest work.
3.Ablations included: Table 3 covers prototype bin count (K=2,5,10), comparison against fixed-threshold filtering (th_consist=0.90/0.95), and the contribution of LSV-level weighting. This breaks down the design choices reasonably well.
4.External unlabeled data scaling: Adding 1,000 external CT volumes from public datasets and showing it still works is a practical demonstration. The 100% labeled + 1000 external CT setting is realistic for clinical scenarios where unlabeled CTs are abundant.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Improvements are very small relative to standard deviations. On Cohort A 100%, ProtoReg gets ρ=0.800±0.090 vs UniMatchV2-Reg at 0.797±0.100, a 0.003 difference with std devs of ≈ 0.1.On Cohort A 20%, ProtoReg is 0.778±0.110 vs UniMatchV2 at 0.776±0.110, essentially identical. The margins are well within run-to-run variance. No paired statistical tests are reported, so it’s impossible to know if these differences are meaningful.
2.Semi-supervised methods sometimes hurt performance. On Cohort B with 100% labels + 1000 unlabeled CT, MT-Reg (ρ=0.802), FixMatch-Reg (0.797), and UniMatch-Reg (0.801) all perform worse than the fully supervised baseline (ρ=0.810). ProtoReg only barely beats Sup-only (0.814 vs 0.810). The paper doesn’t address this finding, if external unlabeled data hurts most SSL methods on this cohort, that’s a significant negative result that needs to be addressed.
3.Method complexity vs gains. The full pipeline includes: teacher-student EMA + prototype bank + prototype classification loss + prototype-induced entropy + voxel-level uncertainty + LSV (supervoxel) uncertainty + dual-level consistency weighting + entropy regularization + geometric decay schedule. That’s a lot of moving parts for ~0.3% Spearman improvement over UniMatchV2.The ablation shows the LSV-level weighting helps (0.778 vs 0.774), but again the margin is small relative to noise.
4.Limited ablation scope. Ablations are only on Cohort A under the 20% labeled setting. The 100% labeled setting and Cohort B are not ablated. So we don’t know if the same components matter when labels are abundant or on a different cohort. This makes it harder to argue the design generalizes.
5.Some experimental details are unclear. It’s not clear if results are from single runs or averaged across multiple seeds. The train/val/test split protocol isn’t fully specified. The number of test cases per cohort isn’t stated explicitly.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1.Are the reported numbers from single runs or averaged over multiple seeds? Can you provide paired statistical tests between ProtoReg and UniMatchV2-Reg?
2.On Cohort B with 100% labels, why do most SSL methods underperform the supervised baseline? Does this suggest the unlabeled data is hurting more than helping in some settings?
3.Can you provide ablations on Cohort B and on the 100% labeled setting to confirm the design choices generalize?

The paper tackles a meaningful underexplored problem (semi-supervised dense regression for CT-to-perfusion) and the baseline selection is appropriate, including the latest UniMatch V2.However, the improvements over the strongest baseline are very small relative to standard deviations, often a fraction of a percent on Spearman ρ with std devs around 0.1 and no statistical significance tests are reported. The Cohort B results show that most SSL methods actually hurt performance compared to the supervised baseline at full label budget, which is a notable finding the paper doesn’t engage with. The method has many components but the ablation is limited to one cohort and one labeling ratio, so the generalization of the design choices is unclear. The core contributions are reasonable but heavily inspired by DyCON. On balance, the application is interesting and the experimental setup is thoughtful, but the small margins, lack of statistical tests, and unaddressed negative result tip this toward rejection. Statistical significance testing, broader ablations, and a discussion of the Cohort B finding would substantially strengthen the paper.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: My pre-rebuttal recommendation was Weak Reject. The rebuttal engaged with my concerns thoughtfully and clarified the DyCON distinction, but the substantive issues remain: (a) statistical significance on the primary metric is not established even with the new tests, (b) the core mismatch between method complexity and effect size persists. The application is interesting and the work is competent, but the contribution as evidenced doesn’t clear the MICCAI bar. I maintain my recommendation to reject.

meta_reviews.text:
All reviewers are inclined to finalize their decisions following the rebuttal. The authors are advised to address the concerns raised by Reviewers 3 and 4.

Two reviewers found the rebuttal fully addressed their concerns and recommend acceptance. One reviewer remains concerned that the gains over strong baselines are modest and may not justify the added complexity. While these concerns are valid, the work addresses an important problem, includes competitive comparisons against recent methods, and the rebuttal clarified the methodological contribution and provided additional statistical analysis. On balance, the positive assessments outweigh the remaining concerns.

After the rebuttal, two of the reviewers are satisfied with the authors’ answers and recommend acceptance. The third reviewer remains concerned about the low improvement achieved by the method for its added complexity. After reviewing the paper and rebuttal, the AC feels that the positive points of the paper outweigh the negative ones, and recommends acceptance. However, the authors are strongly encouraged to update their paper following reviewers’ comments and suggestions, in particular, regarding the statistical significance of results.

After the rebuttal, one reviewer raised the score to acceptance, and most reviewers are positive. The main contribution lies in the clinical importance of the semi-supervised regression task and the sound solution proposed for linking discrete prototypes with continuous voxels. The authors also clarified the differences from the DyCON model. Overall, this work is potentially beneficial to the relevant community. The authors are encouraged to improve the manuscript in the camera-ready version further, and acceptance is recommended.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and AC for their comments. We will release the code and provide the public dataset (Cohort B) download link upon acceptance. Below are our responses.
A. Method novelty/description.
[R2-W1, R3-W4] Related methods. Resp: We thank the reviewers for pointing out CPCL, UPCoL, DyCON, and related uncertainty-estimation methods. These studies mainly rely on discrete category-level signals, e.g., class predictions or probability maps. Our task is continuous voxel-wise regression, where pseudo-targets have no categorical confidence scores. Their uncertainty formulations are therefore not directly applicable as baselines. We will cite these works and clarify differences from ProtoReg.
[R2-W2, R3-W3] Difference from DyCON. Resp: ProtoReg differs from DyCON in two key aspects. First, DyCON estimates uncertainty from discrete segmentation probabilities, while ProtoReg models uncertainty from continuous functional values through functional prototypes. This bridges discrete prototype learning and continuous voxel-wise regression, providing reliability signals for pseudo-targets without class probabilities. Second, DyCON performs voxel/pixel-level uncertainty weighting, while DUW-CL computes reliability-weighted consistency at both voxel and anatomically meaningful lung-sub-unit levels. This captures regional functional continuity and suppresses fragmented pseudo-label noise. We will add these clarifications.
[R2-W3, R3-W1, W2] Notation and weighting schedule. Resp: We will check all notations and further define β before Eq. (8), clarifying its role in DUW-CL. In DUW-CL, w always gives higher weights to low-entropy predictions, while β controls entropy-weighting strength. As β decays, the gap between low- and high-entropy weights becomes smaller, smoothly expanding training from highly reliable regions to broader consistency refinement.
B. Data/preprocessing clarification.
[R3-W5, R3-W6, R5-W5] Preprocessing and dataset split. Resp: We will further add preprocessing and split details. Paired volumes were pre-registered and processed using a standardized pipeline [16,17]. Original CT/SPECT sizes are approximately 512×512×200 and 128^3.Only the pre-segmented lung ROI was resampled to 128^3, preserving CT–SPECT spatial correspondence and minimizing task-relevant information loss. Cohorts A/B use separate fixed 80/20 train/test splits; 25% of training is used for validation, and labeled/unlabeled splits are applied only to the remaining training data. Test sets contain 48/20 cases, and results are per-case mean±SD.
C. Results/statistics clarification.
[R5-W1, A1] Statistical Significance. Resp: We have conducted metric-wise paired statistical tests against UniMatchV2-Reg and will report p-values in the revision. ProtoReg achieves statistically significant improvements (p<0.05) over UniMatchV2-Reg on most metrics under most settings. Under Cohort A 20%, ProtoReg reaches p<0.05 on SSIM, MAE, and FL20.On Cohort B, most metrics also reach p<0.05 under both 100% and 20% settings. 
[R5-A2, W2] SSL performance on Cohort B. Resp: We will clarify this in the revision. Several SSL baselines underperform Sup-only in Cohort B 100%, likely due to domain shift or pseudo-label noise when full-label supervision is strong. ProtoReg mitigates this through prototype-induced uncertainty and dual-level weighting.
[R5-W3, W4, A3] Ablation. Resp: We will clarify the ablation findings. LSV-level weighting achieves statistically significant improvements in MAE, SSIM, and FL20.These metrics better reflect functional-region consistency and clinically relevant spatial fidelity, while Spearman ρ mainly measures global rank correlation and is less sensitive to local structural improvements. Due to page limits, we reported Cohort A 20% ablations, which best reflect the low-label reliability problem. We also conducted 100%-label ablations with consistent component benefits, and will include them with broader Cohort B analyses in an extended version.

title: Prototype Instance-Semantic Disentanglement with Low-Rank Regularized Subspace Clustering for WSIs Explainable Recognition
abstract: The tumor region plays a key role in pathological diagnosis. Tumor tissues are highly similar to precancerous lesions and non-tumor instances often greatly exceed tumor instances in whole-slide images (WSIs). These issues cause instance-semantic entanglement in multi-instance learning frameworks, degrading both model representation capability and interpretability. To address this, we propose an end-to-end prototype instance-semantic disentanglement framework with low-rank regularized subspace clustering, namely PID-LRSC, in two aspects. First, we use secondary instance-subspace learning to construct low-rank regularized subspace clustering (LRSC), addressing instance entanglement caused by an excessive proportion of non-tumor instances. Second, we employ enhanced contrastive learning to design prototype instance‒semantic disentanglement (PID), resolving semantic entanglement caused by the high similarity between tumor and precancerous tissues. We conduct extensive experiments on multicentre pathology datasets, implying that PID-LRSC outperforms other state-of-the-art methods. Overall, PID-LRSC provides clearer instance semantics during decision-making and significantly enhances the reliability of auxiliary diagnostic outcomes. Code and datasets are available at https://github.com/Prince-Lee-PathAI/PID-LRSC.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes PID-LRSC, a MIL framework for WSI classification that aims to disentangle instance and semantic entanglement between sparse tumor regions and abundant non-tumor/background patches. Experiments on two private SCC datasets and two public datasets show consistent improvements over recent MIL baselines, with visualizations suggesting clearer instance-level interpretability.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The low-rank metric-learning scheme is a simple but effective way to bias clustering toward discriminative, low-redundancy subspaces under extreme instance imbalance. 
2.The integration of prototype-based semantic anchoring with subspace clustering addresses both instance-level redundancy and tumor/precancerous ambiguity within a single training loop. 
3.Addressing sparse tumor signal dilution and semantic confusion with precancerous regions is highly relevant to real-world WSI use and clinical interpretability. Broad comparisons against strong MIL baselines on four datasets, including two from an external center, show consistent gains in ACC and AUC.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Inconsistent naming (CDF vs CFD), and some notational/typographical glitches that make sections harder to parse. The supplementary documents lack crucial information, such as a description of the private dataset. 
2.The current evaluation provides a limited ablation analysis; specifically, it lacks a detailed investigation into how the model’s performance fluctuates with changes to $r$, $\gamma_{1/2/3}$, the number of clusters, or specific prototype configurations. 
3.The success of PID critically depends on the prototypes, but their provenance, number, selection, and maintenance are insufficiently specified; robustness to prototype noise is not studied. 
4.Although Table 1 specifies the use of ‘Swin-T pretrained features’, it remains unclear whether this ViT encoder is fine-tuned during the end-to-end training process or strictly frozen as an offline feature extractor. This ambiguity regarding the exact source of the trainable parameters, combined with a lack of comprehensive training protocol details, significantly hampers the reproducibility of the proposed method.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The research motivation is clear and well-articulated, and the experimental results across the four datasets are highly encouraging. However, there are a few notable shortcomings regarding the presentation of the datasets and implementation details, which currently make it difficult to fully assess the rigor and reproducibility of the study. Additionally, the description of the prototype construction and its robustness is insufficient. If the authors can enhance the clarity of the methodology (particularly concerning the handling and formulation of the prototypes) and expand upon the ablation and sensitivity analyses, this work will represent a significant contribution to the field.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I have been satisfied with authors’ rebuttal responses.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes an interpretable WSI classification framework, PID-LRSC, that aims to address what the authors call “instance-semantic entanglement” in MIL-based pathology analysis. The method combines two main ingredients. First, it introduces a two-phase low-rank regularized subspace clustering module to separate sparse tumor-related instances from abundant non-tumor/background regions in a learned subspace. Second, it introduces a prototype-guided disentanglement module that uses prototype-to-subspace discrepancy to assign semantic roles to clustered groups and refine the final WSI representation. The paper further claims that this design improves both classification performance and interpretability on multicentre pathology datasets. These central claims and the two-stage decomposition of the method are described in the main submission.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper tackles a genuinely important and clinically relevant problem in computational pathology. Specifically, it addresses a well-known weakness of multiple instance learning (MIL) approaches applied to whole-slide images (WSIs): the extreme sparsity of diagnostically informative tumor regions amidst an overwhelming majority of non-tumor tissue, compounded by the semantic ambiguity between malignant and precancerous regions under weak supervision. The authors’ framing of this challenge as an “entanglement” problem—both at the instance and semantic levels—is intuitive, well-motivated, and particularly pertinent for developing explainable pathology models. This motivation is clearly articulated in the introduction and effectively illustrated in Figure 1 of the main paper.
Notably, the proposed method attempts to jointly advance representation learning and interpretability, rather than treating interpretability as a post hoc add-on. Instead of merely generating attention-based heatmaps after the fact, the authors seek to inject structural priors directly into the learned representation through clustering and prototype-guided refinement. This constitutes a more principled design choice compared to standard attention visualization strategies commonly adopted in the WSI literature.
The low-rank metric perspective introduced in the method is potentially interesting. In particular, the use of a learned positive semi-definite metric with enforced low-rank structure to guide subspace clustering offers a reasonable mechanism for suppressing redundant non-tumor variation. The coarse-to-fine formulation is conceptually sound, although certain technical aspects—such as the precise construction of prototype instance subspaces and the sensitivity to the fixed number of clusters—remain underspecified.
The empirical evaluation appears reasonably comprehensive at first glance. The authors compare their approach against a substantial set of recent WSI MIL baselines and report both accuracy (ACC) and area under the curve (AUC) across multiple datasets. The inclusion of ablation studies (Tables 1–3) and qualitative visualizations further suggests a concerted effort to substantiate their claims beyond performance on a single benchmark.
Importantly, interpretability is treated as a first-class objective—not just as a secondary benefit. The manuscript goes beyond claiming improved classification performance and actively attempts to align the disentangled, model-identified regions with pathologist-annotated ground truth boundaries. While this alignment is not yet fully quantified with rigorous metrics, the fact that the authors are explicitly engaging with this critical question sets their work apart from many WSI-focused papers that overlook clinical interpretability altogether.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper is built around an intuitively appealing idea, but in its current form, the main weakness is that several of its most important design choices are asserted rather than convincingly established. In particular, the decision to fix the clustering structure at three groups is insufficiently justified. Because this choice sits at the core of the proposed semantic decomposition, it cannot be treated as a minor implementation detail. The paper offers only a brief heuristic explanation: tumor, non-tumor, and background are common categories in WSI analysis. This does not amount to a principled argument that three clusters are appropriate for all datasets studied, nor does it show that performance is robust to alternative cluster numbers. As a result, the method risks looking partially tailored to a presupposed semantic partition rather than learning that structure from data. This concern is reinforced by the lack of a stronger sensitivity analysis around this design decision.
A second major weakness is that the prototype component, which is essential to the paper’s semantic disentanglement story, is not described with enough precision. The method repeatedly relies on a prototype instance subspace and even uses it directly in the loss formulation and semantic assignment process, yet the manuscript never makes fully clear how these prototypes are obtained, initialized, updated, or supervised. From the figures and wording, one can infer that domain knowledge may be involved, but it remains ambiguous whether the prototypes are externally provided, weakly selected, learned jointly, or derived from some additional annotations. This is not a minor omission: without a transparent description of prototype construction, it becomes difficult to assess whether the method is truly reproducible and whether it operates under the same supervision assumptions as the baselines. In a paper whose central claim is that prototypes resolve semantic ambiguity, the provenance of those prototypes should be explicit and technically complete.
Another serious issue is the inconsistency between the main submission and the supplementary material. The main paper presents PID-LRSC, whereas the uploaded supplementary file appears to describe a different method, with a different title, different terminology, different equations, and even a different dataset configuration. At present, the relationship between these two documents is not explained. This creates a practical problem for the reviewer because some details missing from the main paper are said to be deferred to the supplement, yet the supplement does not read as a direct extension of the submitted manuscript. More importantly, it creates a procedural concern: I could not determine whether this was an upload mistake, an earlier version of the work, or a separate, related submission that should have been explicitly contextualized. In any case, it weakens confidence in the submission package and substantially limits the paper’s reproducibility.
The paper is also somewhat weaker than it appears at first glance in the alignment between its conceptual narrative and its actual formulation. For example, the manuscript describes the method as involving enhanced contrastive learning, but the technical section mainly develops a discrepancy-based comparison between clustered subspaces and prototype representations, followed by rank-based semantic assignment and refinement. I did not find a clearly defined contrastive objective that matches the framing in the introduction. More broadly, the paper often uses strong interpretive language about disentanglement, causality, and semantic clarity, but the underlying optimization remains closer to a structured clustering-and-reweighting pipeline than a rigorously demonstrated disentanglement framework. This does not mean the method is ineffective, but it does mean that some of the claims are currently stronger than the evidence provided.
Finally, while the empirical results are promising, the interpretability claims are still supported more by selected qualitative examples than by a sufficiently rigorous quantitative evaluation. The visualization results are suggestive, and the alignment with annotated regions is encouraging, but for a paper that places explainability at the center of its contribution, I would have expected stronger evidence, such as systematic localization metrics, agreement analysis, or a more structured clinical validation of the highlighted regions. The writing and presentation also need polishing, as inconsistencies in notation, formatting, and phrasing occasionally make it harder than necessary to follow the technical argument. Taken together, these issues do not erase the potential of the work, but they do make the current version feel methodologically under-specified and not yet fully mature for acceptance.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The paper presents a compelling intuition: in WSI MIL, both weak performance and limited interpretability may originate from a fundamental mismatch between pathological structures and the latent organization induced by bag-level supervision. This represents a valuable and worthwhile perspective. However, the current version falls short of establishing a sufficiently complete “evidence chain” that connects the initial assumption through the proposed method to comprehensive validation.
Two critical revisions are essential for strengthening the manuscript. First, the authors must clearly articulate how prototypes are obtained and specify the supervision mechanisms they rely on. Second, the inconsistency between the main manuscript and supplementary material requires resolution to ensure methodological coherence throughout the paper.
Additionally, I would strongly encourage the authors to incorporate a sensitivity analysis of the number of clusters, ideally comparing the fixed k=3 setting against adaptive or larger-k configurations. Currently, the three-group decomposition appears more assumed than empirically demonstrated. Furthermore, the interpretability claims would benefit significantly from quantitative localization metrics or a more systematic reader study, rather than relying solely on qualitative examples, thereby substantially strengthening the paper’s contributions to the field.

My assessment is shaped less by the headline results and more by the opportunity to strengthen the methodological exposition. The paper presents a promising idea that addresses an important challenge in WSI MIL, and the reported empirical gains are nontrivial and encouraging. The core intuition—that weak performance and interpretability may stem from a mismatch between pathological structure and bag-level supervision—is insightful and warrants further exploration.
That said, several aspects would benefit from clarification to fully realize the paper’s potential. The source and learning mechanism of the prototypes could be articulated more explicitly, and the rationale behind the fixed three-cluster design would be strengthened with additional justification or sensitivity analysis. Similarly, clarifying the precise correspondence between the narrative claims and the optimization objective would enhance the methodological transparency.
Despite these points for improvement, the work makes a valuable contribution to the field, and I believe it merits acceptance with the expectation that the authors will address these methodological clarifications in the final version. The foundational idea is sound, the empirical results are promising, and with modest refinements to the exposition, this could become a well-regarded contribution to WSI MIL research.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: After carefully reading the rebuttal and re-evaluating the submission, I am willing to support acceptance, although I still believe several aspects of the paper could be strengthened in the camera-ready version. My original concerns mainly focused on whether some of the core methodological choices were sufficiently justified and whether the paper provided enough technical transparency for reproducibility. The rebuttal substantially improved clarity on these issues. In particular, the authors clarified that the three-cluster design is intended as a coarse pathological prior rather than a claim about exact biological subtypes, which makes the formulation more reasonable in the context of WSI semantic decomposition. While I still think a broader sensitivity analysis over different values of K would further strengthen the work, the explanation that the groups correspond to lesion-related tissue, microenvironment/non-lesion tissue, and background/artifacts provides a coherent pathological interpretation that is consistent across datasets and aligns with common practice in WSI analysis. More importantly, the rebuttal clarified the prototype construction process in significantly greater detail. The authors now explicitly state that prototypes are annotated by five experts using unions of tumor regions and are only class-specific during training, with variability intentionally incorporated to improve robustness. This clarification addresses my earlier concern that the provenance and supervision assumptions behind the prototypes were under-specified. Although these details should ideally appear more explicitly in the main manuscript, the methodological pipeline is now sufficiently understandable and reproducible.
reviews.text_ethics: Although I do not have enough information to conclude that there is a definite ethics violation, I note a procedural/research-integrity concern regarding the supplementary material. The uploaded supplement appears to contain a separate full manuscript with a different title, method description, and experimental setup, rather than a conventional appendix directly supporting the submitted paper. However, the submission does not explain the relationship between the main paper and this supplementary manuscript, nor does it clarify whether this is an earlier version, a related concurrent submission, or another work on the same topic. If this supplementary document is indeed a different paper on a closely related topic, the authors should explicitly disclose and justify the distinction. In its current form, the lack of such clarification creates uncertainty about submission consistency and compliance with conference policy.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes PID-LRSC, an end-to-end multiple-instance learning framework for explainable whole-slide image recognition. The method targets two issues in WSI classification: instance entanglement caused by the dominance of non-tumor regions, and semantic entanglement caused by visual similarity between precancerous and tumor tissue.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper addresses an important computational pathology problem: making MIL-based WSI recognition both accurate and interpretable. The motivation around sparse tumor regions, redundant non-tumor regions, and ambiguous precancerous/tumor morphology is clinically plausible.
The proposed decomposition into instance-level subspace clustering and semantic prototype disentanglement is interesting. The method attempts to move beyond attention heatmaps by assigning instances to tumor, non-tumor, and background-like subspaces, which could improve interpretability if validated.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The method is difficult to fully understand and reproduce from the current manuscript. Many important dataset and implementation details are deferred to supplementary material, including dataset sizes, train/test splits, patch extraction, magnification, prototype construction, and exact feature-extractor settings. Since two key datasets are private, the public-dataset protocol and release details become especially important.
The mathematical presentation has several ambiguities. The learned metric matrix dimensions are not always clear. The derivation that the nuclear norm equals the trace only holds under positive semidefinite assumptions, which should be stated carefully. The KMeans step is not differentiable, yet the paper repeatedly describes the full method as end-to-end; the actual gradient path through clustering should be clarified. The characteristic function discrepancy formulation is also underexplained, including how the sampling distribution and kernel are implemented.
The role and construction of prototypes are insufficiently specified. The method relies on prototype instances as semantic anchors, but it is unclear how many prototypes are used, whether they require pathologist annotation, whether they are class-specific, whether they come from training slides only, and how sensitive the method is to prototype quality.
The interpretability claims are promising but not quantitatively validated. The paper shows qualitative alignment with pathologist boundaries, but it does not report localization metrics against annotations, such as tumor-region Dice, pointing-game accuracy, overlap with annotated tumor regions, or correlation with expert ROI labels.
Statistical reliability is not sufficiently reported. The tables give point estimates but no confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests. This is important for WSI datasets, where slide counts may be limited and patient-level split variance can be high.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper tackles a relevant and challenging pathology problem and reports strong results against many MIL baselines. However, the current manuscript has significant clarity, reproducibility, and methodological-validation issues. The interpretability claims need stronger quantitative evidence, and the prototype/clustering mechanisms require clearer specification.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper proposes a MIL framework for WSI classification that combines low‑rank regularized subspace clustering to separate sparse tumor instances from abundant non‑tumor/background regions and prototype‑guided semantic disentanglement to resolve ambiguity between precancerous and malignant tissue. The reviewers agree that the paper addresses a well‑known challenge in computational pathology and show consistent and encouraging performance improvements (ACC/AUC) over a broad set of recent MIL baselines on four datasets. The reviewers raised question about the insufficient specification of prototype construction and learning, lack of clarity and details influencing the reproducibility, and oversimplified fixed clustering assumption (K=3) without justification. Please respond to the main concerns of the reviewers, including the following ones: How are prototypes obtained, initialized, updated, and supervised?What is the exact training setup regarding the feature extractor?How is the non‑differentiable K‑means step handled in the claimed “end‑to‑end” training?Provide a full description of the private datasets.

The paper receive an average score of 4, and one reviewer raised the score after rebuttal. Though the reviewer with negative score did not update the post-rebuttal score, most of his/her concerns have been addressed in the rebuttal. The author should incorporate the substantive informatoin in the rebuttal into the final version of the paper.

This paper was initially invited for rebuttal following the primary review period, where reviewers raised several concerns regarding insufficient specification of prototype construction and learning, and missing details. After carefully evaluating the authors’ rebuttal, the reviewers’ revised feedback, and re-examining the paper, I conclude that the authors have effectively addressed the key concerns raised, and the work now meets MICCAI’s publication standards.

After rebuttal, the paper has received generally favorable reviews, with one reviewer not providing an update to their score. While some concerns with respect to the experimental setting have been answered, concerns on methodological choices, sensitivity analysis, and in-depth description regarding the provenance behind the prototype construction persist. Unless other concerns regarding the supplementary information in the code repository prevent acceptance, the paper is in my opinion slightly above the acceptance threshold.

author_feedback_text:
For Meta Reviewer:
Please kindly refer to R2.1 R3.1, R3.2 and R3.3 for your concerns.
Reviewer #1:
R1.1 ‘CDF’ was a typo and has been revised. Critical details like private datasets are in abstract link because of double-blind. For Prototype construction, please kindly refer to the same response of R3.3.
R1.2 In Fig 2, PID-LRSC uses pretrained Swin-T fully open for end-to-end training. All compared models use frozen features extracted by Swin-T in two stages. They were trained by RMSprop with fixed random seed 0 for reproducibility. (See abstract link: section2 for details)
Reviewer #2:
R2.1The choice K=3 is a coarse pathological prior rather than exactly three biological subtypes. The three groups correspond to factors: lesion/tumor-related tissue, microenvironment or non-lesion tissue, and background/artifacts such as blur, bubbles or staining artifacts.. This coarse partition is common across WSI analysis and generalizes across datasets.
R2.2 For Prototype constructions, please kindly refer to the same response of R3.3.
R2.3 The main paper and supplementary one are to comply with the MICCAI dual-submission policy for similar topics (see official guidelines).
R2.4 Enhanced contrastive learning is not formulated instance-wise but at subspace level. Specifically, c_min and c_max minimize/maximize the discrepancy between clustered subspaces and prototypes, achieving spatial-level disentanglement. And the final aggregation Z_WSI employs semantic-guided feature refinement with ranked prototype discrepancies, which alleviates semantic entanglement.
R2.5 Based on ground truth, heatmap and semantic clustering, we randomly selected WSIs to compute two average Dice scores. They are CSCC (0.4605, 0.4424), LSCC (0.7096, 0.2210), Lung (0.6198, 0.3341), and Kidney (0.6988, 0.4981).
Reviewer #3:
R3.1 Critical details are in the abstract link. For example, two private datasets are CSCC (262 WSIs3) and LSCC (342 WSIs), split into the same 6:4 train/test ratio as public DHMC-Kidney and Lung; Patches per WSI are at 10x magnification; Prototype construction refers to R3.3; and ImageNet-pretrained Swin Transformer is used to extract frozen features for compared model training and fully open for end-to-end PID-LRSC training.
R3.2 (1) The learned matrix W is in shape [r,n]. Here n=768 is the output of ViT encoder and r=384 is a trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness. Matrix (W^T)W leads to a positive semi-definite matrix A. It completes the nuclear norm derivation. (2) Although K-means is non-differentiable, c_min, c_max and trace(A) are computed in the low-rank subspace parameterized by W, whose printed gradients are showed in the computational graph. So it can be propagated through via ‘autograd’. Thus, PID-LRSC enables end-to-end deep-clustering paradigm rather than isolated clustering. (3) For CFD: Given feature input Z and sampled frequency t=4096, define Phi_z(t)=E[cos(t^T Z)+isin(t^T Z)]. Then we can compute the phase function and amplitude function. See details and codes in abstract link.
R3.3 Prototype are given by 5 experts with double-blind using the union of tumor regions. 64 prototypes per WSI are included in CSCC , 81 for LSCC and 5 for public datasets. The prototype instances are class-specific only for training stage. Because of the multi-expert unions, they have large annotation variability to reduce subjectivity and improve training robustness. Also, enough quantity of prototype from different pathologists alleviates sensitivity to prototype quality. (Data and details see abstract link: section2)
R3.4 Based on ground truth, heatmap and semantic clustering, we randomly selected WSIs to compute two average Dice scores. They are CSCC (0.4605, 0.4424), LSCC (0.7096, 0.2210), Lung (0.6198, 0.3341), and Kidney (0.6988, 0.4981).
R3.5 We fixed seed=0 across all stages to ensure reproducibility and reduce variation caused by initialization and sampling. And our model focuses on slide-level representation capability.

title: Prototype Learning for Visual Field Estimation from Fundus Photography in High Myopia
abstract: Visual field (VF) sensitivity assessment is critical for quantifying functional impairment in high myopia (HM), yet conventional perimetry is subjective, time-consuming, and affected by substantial testretest variability. Deep learning-based estimation of VF sensitivity from fundus photography has emerged as a promising alternative; however, most existing approaches directly regress all 52 pointwise sensitivities and do not explicitly consider latent defect patterns. In this work, we propose ProtoVF, a prototype-based framework for fundus-to-VF estimation in HM. ProtoVF explores the underlying low-dimensional prototypes of VF patterns and predicts their combination coefficients from fundus images to estimate the full 52-point VF sensitivity map. By reformulating VF estimation as a prototype-learning problem, ProtoVF imposes an explicit prior over plausible VF patterns and decomposes predictions into clinically interpretable prototype patterns. In five-fold cross-validation on a large real-world HM cohort, ProtoVF achieved 2.55 MAE and 4.09 RMSE, outperforming the regression baseline, particularly in eyes with severe VF loss (MD ≤ −6 dB). These findings demonstrate that this prototype-based learning enables a more accurate, robust, and interpretable solution for fundus photography-based VF estimation in HM. Our code is available at https://github.com/OptometryAI/ProtoVF.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This manuscript proposes ProtoVF, a prototype learning framework for estimating 52-point visual field sensitivity from fundus photography in high myopia. The core idea is to replace direct pointwise regression with prediction of coefficients over a compact set of learned visual field prototypes, with the goal of improving robustness and interpretability in a limited and noisy-label setting.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper addresses a clinically meaningful problem. Functional assessment in high myopia is important, and the motivation for reducing dependence on subjective perimetry is well stated. 
The prototype-based formulation is conceptually interesting. Recasting VF estimation as coefficient prediction over a lower-dimensional prototype space is a reasonable way to impose structure and may improve interpretability. 
The manuscript includes both quantitative and qualitative evaluation, as well as an ablation over prototype generation methods and prototype number. That is helpful for understanding the method’s internal design choices.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1-The novelty is somewhat incremental relative to prior fundus-to-VF estimation work in high myopia. 
2-The experimental comparison is limited. The main baseline is a generic regression model, and stronger recent high-myopia-specific methods are cited but not clearly compared in a fair, detailed way. 
3- (important) I couldn’t understand how the prototypes and coefficients from the fundus images are computed. Providing pseudocode for both the training and testing phases would help clarify this. 
4-Clinical validation is modest. The study is single-center, from a relatively homogeneous population, and restricted to non-glaucomatous HM (i think), which narrows the clinical significance and generalizability of the findings.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
I coudn’t figure out how the proptptypes and coeffeficnets from fundus are computed. Having a pseudo code for training steps and testing phase is needed.

The paper is clinically relevant, generally well organized, and contains an interesting, structured prediction idea.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a new method for predicting visual field sensitivity based on fundus photographs. Unlike traditional approaches that directly predict a 52-dimensional vector from fundus photographs, this method treats the visual field sensitivity to be predicted as a linear combination of different visual field patterns. First, a prototype matrix basis is extracted from all visual field reports using algorithms such as PCA. Subsequently, deep learning methods are employed to learn the weights of the different prototype matrices, thereby predicting the sensitivity map.
reviews.text_strengths:
The advantage of this approach lies in transforming the parameter learning of 52 distinct point locations into the learning of lower-dimensional and more interpretable weights associated with classical visual field sensitivity distribution patterns.
A particularly interesting aspect of the paper is the detailed ablation study regarding the number prototypes for visual field reports. It clearly and intuitively demonstrates the relationship between the number of prototypes and the Mean Squared Error (MSE) across different methods for generating prototypes.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
a. In the visualization of prototypes, this paper utilizes AA instead of PCA, which demonstrates superior comprehensive performance. This weakens the credibility of the conclusions.
b. Neural network learning is also a crucial component. The paper lacks a theoretical justification for the network selection. It is recommended to supplement with ablation studies to elaborate on this choice.
c. The conclusions related to visualization should not be placed in Section 3.4 ablation study.
d. The ablation study section in Figure 3 shows that for most methods (e.g., PCA), the model accuracy improves as the number of prototypes increases. A sufficient justification is not provided for the selection of k = 10 (the paper mentions this configuration provided a favorable balance between representational capacity and generalization. But this only applies to the AA method ).
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

In summary, this paper proposes a new method for predicting visual field sensitivity based on fundus photographs, which possesses a certain degree of interpretability and holds innovative significance in the medical field. However, there is still room for refinement regarding the algorithm details and experimental setup.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
Four specific concerns were raised in Q7.After careful evaluation of the authors’ rebuttal, I conclude that none of them undermines the core contribution or validity of the paper.
Concern a (visualization used AA instead of the best‑performing PCA). The authors clarified that visualization serves clinical pattern interpretation, not model selection. AA produces archetypes at the convex hull of the VF distribution, which resemble real, interpretable defect patterns (e.g., blind‑spot enlargement, arcuate defects). PCA components are orthogonal variance directions and are less naturally read as standalone VF maps. This explanation is fully reasonable; the paper already reports PCA as the best performer in Table 1.No credibility issue remains.
Concern b (lack of justification for network choice / ablation). While the paper does not provide an ablation on the backbone, the choice of ResNet‑34 is standard and widely adopted.
Concern c (visualization placed in Sec. 3.4 Ablation Study). This is a purely structural/editorial issue. It does not alter any scientific claim or result. The content itself is valuable and can be moved to a more appropriate section (e.g., Results or a separate interpretation subsection).
Concern d (k=10 chosen without sufficient justification, seemingly only for AA). The authors correctly pointed out that Fig. 3 shows VF reconstruction error, not final fundus‑to‑VF estimation error. Increasing k reduces reconstruction error for PCA/NMF/SVD but also makes coefficient learning harder and may overfit label noise. Selecting k=10 as a compact operating point balances representational capacity and learnability. This justification applies to all methods, not only AA. The concern is resolved.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors proposed a deep learning model that uses a ResNet-34 to encode color fundus images into coefficient representations of visual field (VF) prototypes. These coefficients are then used to predict all 52 test locations in the 24-2 Humphrey visual field for patients with high myopia. To construct the VF prototypes, the study explores several dimensionality reduction techniques, including archetypal analysis (AA), principal component analysis (PCA), nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF), and truncated singular value decomposition (Truncated SVD). The central motivation of this work is to leverage the relative stability and objectivity of color fundus imaging to predict visual field measurements, which are inherently subjective. This study aims to establish a relationship between structural features observed in fundus images and functional visual outcomes.
reviews.text_strengths: The authors clearly stated that the training and test datasets are separated at the subject level during cross-validation. This is an important methodological practice in machine learning, as it helps prevent information leakage caused by strong correlations between paired eyes from the same individual.
reviews.text_weaknesses: Predicting HVF outcomes from color fundus photographs in highly myopic eyes is inherently challenging. Unlike glaucoma, high myopia often lacks clearly localized or easily interpretable retinal nerve fiber bundle defects in fundus images that can be directly associated with VF loss. In this context, OCT may provide more direct and informative structural indicators of optic nerve damage to support structure–function modeling and VF prediction. [However, high myopia can introduce substantial retinal curvature, which may degrade OCT image quality and lead to unreliable RNFL segmentation and thickness measurements, creating an additional source of uncertainty.] Anyway, relying solely on color fundus images represents a difficult problem setting and may limit the achievable prediction performance. In addition, the neural network architecture appears relatively conventional and may not reflect more recent advances in model design. Finally, some of the clinical background statements, such as ‘Deep learning-based estimation of VF sensitivity from fundus photography has emerged as a promising alternative; …’ appear somewhat overstated given the current limitations and variability in this task.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

While the study addresses an important and challenging problem, the proposed approach is limited by both the choice of imaging modality and the model design. Predicting HVF outcomes from color fundus photographs in highly myopic eyes presents inherent clinical and technical challenges, which may restrict the achievable performance. In addition, the methodological novelty appears limited, and some of the clinical claims are not sufficiently supported. These concerns reduce the overall impact and strength of this submission.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I thank the authors for their efforts in addressing the reviewers’ comments and questions. Humphrey visual field (HVF) testing is inherently subjective and noisy, and fundus photographs acquired using different camera systems, settings, and imaging protocols may substantially affect image quality. Although the revised manuscript provides additional clarification, I remain uncertain about the robustness and generalizability of this fundus-based VF estimation approach (ProtoVFs) for highly myopic eyes in broader real-world clinical settings, particularly because the current evaluation appears to rely on images obtained from a single camera at a single center with a relatively limited number of images. Additionally, it remains unclear whether the performance differences between the linear regression model and ProtoVFs were statistically significant.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper presents a prototype-based framework for estimating visual field sensitivity from fundus photographs in high myopia. The problem is clinically relevant, and the prototype formulation is a potentially interesting way to impose structure and improve interpretability. However, the current submission still has several important limitations. In particular, the methodological novelty appears somewhat incremental, the experimental comparisons are not sufficiently strong or comprehensive, and the description of how prototypes and coefficients are learned from fundus images is not yet sufficiently clear. In addition, the clinical validation is limited by the single-center setting and the restricted study population, which weakens the generalizability of the conclusions. The authors are encouraged to address these concerns in the rebuttal.

After considering the reviews and the rebuttal, I recommend acceptance. The paper addresses a clinically relevant problem and proposes a prototype-based output formulation for estimating visual field sensitivity from fundus photographs in high myopia. The rebuttal clarifies the prototype and coefficient learning process, the choice of prototype visualization, and the selection of prototype number. The work provides a focused and interpretable proof of concept with reasonable experimental support. I therefore recommend acceptance.

ProtoVF reframes fundus-to-VF estimation in high myopia as coefficient prediction over a learned visual-field prototype basis rather than direct 52-point regression — a formulation reviewers found “conceptually interesting” and a reasonable way to impose structure and improve interpretability. The clinical motivation (a low-cost, accessible screening signal) is well stated, and subject-level data separation supports methodological rigor. The rebuttal clarified that prototypes are learned only from training VF data, resolving the central point of confusion. Remaining concerns — fundus-only limitations, single-center/single-camera evaluation, and unclear statistical significance — are fair cautions on generalizability rather than fatal flaws. On balance, a useful, reproducible, and interpretable contribution.
For camera-ready, the authors should fold in the rebuttal clarifications (particularly that prototypes are learned only from training VF data) and the committed code release, add the training/testing pseudocode requested in review, and report statistical testing of the reported gains alongside an explicit discussion of the single-center generalizability limitations.

After considering the reviews and the authors’ rebuttal, I recommend acceptance.
The paper tackles a clinically relevant problem and proposes an interpretable framework for visual field estimation from fundus images. The methodology is sound and the experimental results are generally convincing.
Most of the concerns raised during the review process have been adequately addressed in the rebuttal. While questions remain regarding broader generalizability and the lack of statistical significance analysis, these are limitations of the current study rather than fundamental weaknesses of the work.
Overall, I believe the paper makes a useful contribution to the field and will be of interest to the community.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for recognizing the value of our work:
clinical relevance, described as a “clinically meaningful problem” (R1) and an “important and challenging problem” (R3) with “innovative significance” (R2).
methodological value, including a “conceptually interesting” prototype formulation to “impose structure and improve interpretability” (MR/R1), “more interpretable weights” (R2), and “quantitative and qualitative evaluation” (R1) with a “detailed ablation study” (R2).
Q1: We have released anonymized GitHub code and implementation details following MICCAI reproducibility guidance.
Q2 (MR/R1/R2/R3): Novelty, comparisons, and network choice
ProtoVF is the first prototype-based method for VF estimation. Instead of directly regressing 52 VF sensitivities, ProtoVF predicts coefficients over a compact VF basis learned from real VF data, constraining outputs to empirically observed patterns. Thus, the contribution of ProtoVF is not a new backbone, but a structured output-space formulation for VF estimation.
Our primary baseline uses the same image encoder (widely used ResNet) and training protocol, differing only in output formulation, which isolates the effect of the proposed prototype parameterization. Broader network selection is complementary to ProtoVF and does not undermine this controlled conclusion.
Our results also show favorable performance relative to previous myopia-specific AI studies (Ref. 26, 27).
Q3 (MR/R1): Prototype and coefficient learning
We clarify that ProtoVF does not extract prototypes from fundus images. Prototypes are learned only from the training VF data. As described in Section 2.2, the prototype generator derives a fixed VF basis that provides an empirically constrained output space, while the ResNet learns image-derived coefficients over this basis.
Q4 (R2): Prototype visualization and number selection
Among all ProtoVFs, ProtoVF-PCA achieved the best predictive performance. The visualization, however, was intended for disease-related VF pattern analysis rather than model selection. We visualized AA because its archetypes represent boundary patterns in the VF distribution and resemble realistic, interpretable VF maps. By contrast, PCA components represent orthogonal directions of variance and are less naturally interpreted as standalone VF maps.
Fig. 3 reports VF reconstruction accuracy, not final fundus-to-VF estimation accuracy. Larger k (more prototypes) reduces reconstruction error for NMF/PCA/SVD, but also requires the image encoder to infer more coefficients and may capture VF label noise. Thus, k = 10 was used as a compact operating point balancing representation and learnability.
Q5 (MR/R1/R3): Imaging modality and study population
R3’s concern reflects the challenge of fundus-based VF estimation in high myopia, but this does not mean fundus images lack VF-relevant structural signal. Prior clinical studies (Ref. 21, 24) reported associations between fundus morphology and VF in myopia, and previous AI studies (Ref. 26, 27) also support the feasibility of modeling this relationship. Our results provide further evidence that this signal can be learned.
OCT may provide more direct structural measurements, but it is complementary rather than a replacement for our fundus-based model. Fundus photography is relatively low-cost, fast, accessible, and widely used in screening and primary-care settings. Therefore, the fundus-only setting is clinically relevant, especially for preliminary VF-risk estimation where perimetry or OCT may be unavailable.
Our study is intentionally focused on high myopia, an emerging vision-threatening condition for which VF assessment is important yet often unmet and challenging (Ref. 8). However, the prototype-based output formulation is not inherently limited to high myopia and could be investigated in other diseases with structured VF loss in future work, such as glaucoma, for which characteristic VF patterns have been well documented.

title: Prototype Memory-Guided Training-Free Anomaly Classification and Localization in Prenatal Ultrasound
abstract:
Prenatal anomaly classification and localization is of critical importance for fetal health and pregnancy management.
Although ultrasound (US) is the primary modality for prenatal screening, accurate diagnosis remains challenging due to the low prevalence and high heterogeneity of anomalies. Existing deep learning methods for prenatal tasks rely on large-scale annotated datasets, which are difficult to obtain in practice.
Although few-shot learning alleviates data scarcity, it typically requires fine-tuning for new categories, limiting its practicality in resource-limited clinical settings.
To address these challenges, we propose a training-free framework for multi-class prenatal US anomaly classification and localization that operates with only a few reference images per class, representing the first exploration of this setting.
Our framework comprises three key components:
(1) a memory bank with multi-granular prototypes that explicitly models both class-level semantics and anomaly characteristics;
(2) a prototype-driven soft merging mechanism that aggregates discriminative features to detect the anomaly region; and 
(3) a class-aware refinement strategy that leverages prototype consistency to improve category prediction.
Extensively validated on a multi-center prenatal US dataset containing 1,149 cases, with a total of 2,357 images and 9 categories, our proposed method outperforms the competitors.
subject_areas: Special Topic -> AI for Neglected Diseases & Limited-Resource Settings

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose a training-free framework for multi-class prenatal ultrasound anomaly detection. In the proposed method, a memory bank is constructed of multiple granularities. First, they use the CLS token to understand the coarse class identity of the disease. Then they extract embeddings of the bounding box where the anomaly lies and store it in their memory bank. They use DINOv3 as the backbone to extract features. Using this memory bank, the authors first shortlist top-M disease classes by comparing the CLS token of the new image with the feature vector of each class in their memory bank. For each of these shortlisted disease classes, the anomaly features are retrieved and slides against the new image to find patches with highest similarity. Top-S highest similarity patches are then taken and they are averaged out to get a centroid. Using this centroid, the authors re-score the entire image. Their intuition behind this is that rescoring with centroid helps aggregate the neighbouring patches that share features and suppress noise. The authors finally draw a bounding box around the patches lying in the top 5% anomaly scores. The proposed method outperforms known training-free methods as well as few shot object detection methods achieving mAP of 60.67.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper proposes a training-free method, which outperforms FSOD methods by a large margin (TRR-CCM generates mAP of 49.26, which is the second-best result after the authors’ proposed framework, which achieves an mAP of 60.67). The idea of having multi-granular memory bank is reasonable and intuitive. Scaling this method with more data can potentially provide better results and can be employed in a clinical setting.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The authors do not talk about the value of M and S in top-M and top-S selection for disease class and anomaly embeddings, respectively. The authors do not use a public dataset either. This makes it difficult to reproduce the results. The choice of M and S is extremely important since these are the driving hyperparameters in a training-free setting. I would encourage authors to discuss the methodological or empirical decision of choosing a particular value for M and S.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper provides a training-free framework - which makes it easier to deploy in resource-constrained environments. Moreover, this does not come at a cost of accuracy, the authors achieve a drastic improvement over traditional methods. However, the choice of hyperparameters is not sufficiently discussed. That, along with not using a public dataset makes reproducibility rather limited.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a training-free framework for multi-class prenatal ultrasound anomaly detection that requires no task-specific fine-tuning and operates with only a few annotated reference images per category.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The training-free, few-shot approach directly addresses the real-world bottleneck of scarce annotated prenatal anomaly data, making it clinically practical.
Class-level prototypes for coarse-grained recognition and anomaly-specific prototypes for fine-grained localization naturally align with the clinical “classify-then-localize” diagnostic workflow.
3.The multi-center dataset spanning 9 categories across three anatomical regions, combined with five random splits reporting mean and standard deviation, provides good diversity and statistical rigor.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The proposed method uses a frozen DINOv3 foundation model while competing FSOD methods use weaker backbones (e.g., ResNet-101). Without re-running baselines with the same backbone or ablating the backbone choice, the reported gains cannot be attributed to the proposed framework itself.
2.The 95th-percentile thresholding always highlights top-responding regions regardless of whether an anomaly exists, inevitably producing false detections on normal images (~29% of the dataset). The paper reports no false positive rate or specificity, which is a critical omission for a clinical screening tool.
3.The stated split (1,440 reference + 1,017 test) does not sum to the reported total (2,357), leaving 100 images unexplained. Additionally, it is unclear whether splits are constructed at the patient level; categories with few patients but many images per patient (e.g., single ventricle: 29 patients, 197 images) pose a high risk of data leakage that could inflate results.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses a clinically meaningful problem with an intuitive framework, but concerns regarding the fairness of backbone comparison, handling of normal cases, and dataset partitioning consistency need to be clarified before stronger endorsement can be given.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have addressed my concerns well. It would be even better if the dataset could be made publicly available in the future.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of the paper is a training-free multi-class prenatal ultrasound anomaly detection framework that operates with only a small number of reference images per class. The method builds a multi-granular prototype memory bank using DINOv3 features, combining class-wise prototypes and anomaly-related prototypes, then performs candidate retrieval, anomaly-aware soft merging, and class-aware refinement to localize anomalies and predict their categories. The paper further validates the approach on a multi-center prenatal US dataset with 9 categories.
reviews.text_strengths:
First, the paper addresses a highly important clinical problem. Prenatal ultrasound anomaly analysis is a low-incidence, high-heterogeneity setting in which large supervised datasets are difficult to build, so the few-reference training-free direction is practically relevant.
Second, the dataset is a real strength. A multi-center, 9-category, 1,149-case prenatal US benchmark spanning brain, heart, and abdomen is meaningful and clinically diverse.
