reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The author did not answer all the questions very well.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This manuscript tackles a persistent issue in medical image analysis: the opacity of end-to-end classification models. By orchestrating collaborative agents to follow BI-RADS clinical guidelines, the authors achieve commendable diagnostic traceability. The three-stage evidence-grounded framework is well-motivated, and the interpretability figures are compelling. However, relying on a complex cascade of foundational models demands a deeper investigation into error propagation, memory dynamics, and algorithmic efficiency before clinical adoption.
reviews.text_strengths: Integrating BI-RADS guidelines into a multi-agent framework beautifully bridges the persistent gap between black-box deep learning and strict clinical diagnostic workflows.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The pipeline heavily relies on upstream models like YOLO and nnU-Net. If the initial ROI extraction completely fails or isolates severe acoustic artifacts, downstream agents might confidently process garbage. Please provide an explicit failure-case analysis demonstrating how the risk modeling agent handles catastrophically wrong bounding boxes.
2.Employing a vision-language model for semantic parsing is interesting but risky. The manuscript lacks detail on the specific VLM used and the exact prompting strategy. Medical VLMs often hallucinate features. Detail how these hallucinations are tightly constrained before reaching the auditable diagnostic-attribute fusion agent.
3.Equation 1 introduces critical constants regulating temperature, instability scaling, and consistency penalization. A method claiming stable rule-based alignment must demonstrate that its clinical interpretability does not heavily rely on dataset-specific tuning. Omitting a sensitivity analysis for these hyperparameters weakens the generalizability claim.
4.The critic-guided calibration relies on a memory retrieval mechanism. I question how the size, quality, and diversity of this memory bank affect the final calibration. Please evaluate how the calibration agent behaves if the memory bank is drastically reduced or contains highly imbalanced prior cases.
5.Running multiple agents, a VLM, and hybrid segmenters introduces massive computational overhead compared to typical monolithic networks. For a system aiming at real-world clinical workflow integration, you need to report the end-to-end inference latency per image and discuss the pipeline’s hardware deployment requirements.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The conceptual shift from direct image-to-label mapping to structured evidence aggregation fundamentally improves the trustworthiness of automated medical image diagnosis.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper presents a multi-agentic framework for strcutred evidence aggregation and traceable/interpretable breast ultrasound diagnosis, showing promising performance. Several concerns, espeically those regarding technical novelty (especially from the AI agent perspective), system sensitivity to key upstream models, and computational complexity, should be addressed.

An interesting paper with the novelty of multi-agent design. Overall, the authors rebuttal could address most concerns regarding technical and evaluation details.
R2 and R4 recommended Accept. Although R3 recommended Reject, the weaknesses mentioned appear to be relatively minor and could likely be addressed in the camera-ready version.

The authors have clarified most of the concerns raised by reviewers. The manuscript proposes a quite interesting and novel agentic framework for medical image analysis, of which the merit is well acknowledged.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank ACs, PCs, and reviewers for the constructive comments. We appreciate the recognition of our well-structured multi-agent design, strong clinical interpretability and traceability, and comprehensive validation. We provide point-by-point responses below. Code will be released upon acceptance.
R2-Q1: Agent Novelty.
Unlike general medical-agent frameworks (e.g., MedAgents) that rely on free-form collaboration and lack clinical-rule alignment and decision traceability, our method encodes BUS clinical rules as executable constraints by learning structured diagnostic evidence, estimating rule-aligned risk and performing critic-guided calibration, improving interpretability and traceability.
R2-Q2: Memory Calibration.
Our calibration is a rule-constrained retrieval and verification step, not heuristic post-processing. Specifically, the calibration agent generates candidate updates, and a rule-constrained selection policy chooses among them and the initial prediction, avoiding arbitrary label flips. Memory bank is built from validation cases, and retrieval keys are diagnostic-state embeddings (e.g., lesion shape) rather than raw images or labels.
R2-Q3: Rule-Constrained Autonomy.
Our agents perform rule-constrained coordination, not open-ended autonomy. Unlike fixed pipelines, each agent updates shared diagnostic states when reliability/consistency checks pass, e.g., the risk agent updates only when evidence confidence is sufficient, the critic revises only under rule-aligned retrieval agreement. This ensures clinically auditable decisions in high-risk BUS diagnosis.
R2-Q4: Diagram Readability.
In the final version, we will simplify Fig.1 by reducing visual clutter (e.g., arrows/text), grouping 3 stages clearly and enlarging labels for readability.
R3-Q1: Presentation. 
Fig. 1 was manually designed in PowerPoint. See R2-Q4 for revision details.
R3-Q2: Formatting.
Larger font size and whitespace will be applied to Tab. 3 and Fig. 2 in the final version.
R3-Q3: Reference Completeness.
We will carefully re-examine the references to ensure completeness.
R3-Q4: Dataset Size.
Sec. 3 cited the public datasets. Final version will add specific dataset sizes.
R3-Q5: Novelty.
Please see R2-Q1 for novelty details: rule-aligned design, evidence-grounded methodology and traceable clinical workflow. R2 further noted our ‘well-structured multi-agent system design,’ which supports the contribution.
R4-Q1: ROI.
Our model mitigates poor-ROI impact by complementing ROI-based structural cues with image-level semantic cues. In a poor-ROI case, low ROI reliability down-weights unreliable structural cues (e.g., edge strength) and suppresses malignant trigger, while semantic cues (e.g. indistinct margin) still support malignancy. As a result, RACA still predicts malignant correctly, showing robustness to poor ROIs.
R4-Q2: Hallucination.
We use Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct with a fixed JSON-only prompt (released with codes). The prompt restricts VLM outputs to four controlled diagnostic slots with confidence, evidence, and uncertainty fields. Before fusion, outputs pass parsing, vocabulary validation, and rule-based consistency checks. Unsupported claims are mapped to “unknown” or low-confidence, preventing hallucinations from entering diagnosis.
R4-Q3: Parameter.
Parameters in Eq. 1 were fixed across all three datasets without per-dataset tuning, yet RACA achieves consistent performance gains, indicating robustness rather than reliance on hyperparameter search. A full sensitivity analysis will be in future work.
R4-Q4: Memory Robustness.
Reducing the memory bank from 100→50% caused only a small ACC drop of ≤5%, while further reducing it from 50→0% led to a 5-10% ACC drop, indicating graceful degradation. Our memory banks are class-imbalanced (BUSI 64/48, BUV 33/10, BUSBRA 113/55 benign/malignant), supporting robustness to memory imbalance. 
R4-Q5: Latency. 
Runtime is 31.40 s/image on one RTX 4090 24GB GPU, with most latency from VLM (31.38 s/image).

title: RADAR: A Multimodal Benchmark for 3D Image-Based Radiology Report Review
abstract: Radiology reports for the same patient examination may contain clinically meaningful discrepancies arising from interpretation differences, reporting variability, or evolving assessments. Systematic analysis of such discrepancies is important for quality assurance, clinical decision support, and multimodal model development, yet remains limited by the lack of standardized benchmarks. We present RADAR, a multimodal benchmark for radiology report discrepancy analysis that pairs 3D medical images with a preliminary report and corresponding candidate edits for the same study. The dataset reflects a standard clinical workflow in which trainee radiologists author preliminary reports that are subsequently reviewed and revised by attending radiologists. RADAR defines a structured discrepancy assessment task requiring models to evaluate proposed edits by determining image-level agreement, assessing clinical severity, and classifying edit type (correction, addition, or clarification). In contrast to prior work emphasizing binary error detection or comparison against fully independent reference reports, RADAR targets fine-grained clinical reasoning and image–text alignment at the report review stage. The benchmark consists of expert-annotated abdominal CT examinations and is accompanied by standardized evaluation protocols to support systematic comparison of multimodal models. RADAR provides a clinically grounded testbed for evaluating multimodal systems as reviewers of radiology report edits.
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers
Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs
Special Topic -> AI for Neglected Diseases & Limited-Resource Settings

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces RADAR, a multimodal benchmark for image-grounded radiology report revision. The task is formulated to evaluate whether candidate report edits are supported by 3D CT images, along with assessing their clinical severity and categorizing edit types. The dataset is constructed from real-world preliminary-to-attending report revisions, aiming to reflect realistic clinical workflows.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper targets radiology report discrepancy analysis in a realistic workflow (resident-to-attending revision), which is highly relevant to clinical quality assurance and patient safety. This problem setting goes beyond traditional report generation or error detection tasks.
The benchmark provides useful empirical insights into the limitations of current multimodal models, particularly in image-grounded reasoning and clinically nuanced decision-making (e. g. , severity assessment), which is valuable for the community.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The dataset is relatively small and restricted to a single institution and a single anatomical region (abdominal CT), which raises concerns about statistical robustness and generalizability.
The dataset is not publicly released and requires a data usage agreement. While understandable due to clinical constraints, the lack of a clear and accessible release plan may limit reproducibility and broader community adoption of the benchmark.
Despite the strong clinical motivation, the evaluation is limited to comparisons among foundation models. There is no comparison with radiologists, existing clinical QA workflows, or prior methods, making it difficult to assess real-world clinical impact.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The paper presents a promising direction toward discrepancy-aware evaluation in radiology. To strengthen the work, the authors are encouraged to (1) expand the dataset across institutions and anatomical regions, (2) improve dataset accessibility (e. g. , partial release, benchmark server, or evaluation API), and (3) include comparisons with human experts or existing clinical practices to better demonstrate practical impact.

This score is based on the above strengths and weaknesses.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
Although I initially had concerns about the limited dataset scale and accessibility, the rebuttal convincingly clarifies that the main contribution is a clinically meaningful task formulation and an initial benchmark for image-grounded verification of report revisions.
The authors also commit to releasing the benchmark through a community challenge platform under a DUA, which improves my confidence in the work’s value and reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution is RADAR, a benchmark for evaluating whether candidate radiology report edits are justified by 3D CT evidence in a real report review workflow. By combining agreement detection, severity assessment, and edit type classification, the benchmark captures a more realistic and clinically relevant form of multimodal reasoning than prior setups based mainly on binary error detection or report comparison.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper’s strongest point is the task design. It frames radiology report review as judging whether proposed edits are supported by the scan, how important they are, and what kind of change they make. This is more clinically meaningful than simpler benchmark tasks.
The benchmark is also grounded in a real review workflow, using preliminary reports that are later revised by attending radiologists. This makes the setup more realistic and gives the benchmark more credibility. The evaluation is also useful in practice because it reports runtime and compares different input settings.
Finally, the results clearly show that the task is hard for current models. That is a strength of the benchmark, because it shows that the problem is meaningful and not already solved.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Benchmark scale: The dataset size is the main concern. For a paper whose main contribution is a benchmark, the scale should support reliable evaluation. Here, the benchmark is still too small for that standard. This is especially clear in the Natural test set, which contains only five real disagree cases, making disagreement detection on real examples statistically hard to interpret. The results section also misses important supporting analyses, such as stronger significance testing and more detailed breakdowns.
Annotation validity: All annotations come from a single radiologist, and the paper does not report inter-rater agreement for any of the three labels. That makes it difficult to judge how stable or reproducible the benchmark labels are, especially for more subjective dimensions such as severity.
Synthetic data reliance: The benchmark depends heavily on synthetic disagree edits to balance the evaluation set. This design choice is understandable, but its effect on benchmark validity should be discussed more clearly. In particular, the paper should better explain why one model was used for generating synthetic edits and another for evaluation, and what risks this creates for bias or mismatch.
Pilot study scope: Because the benchmark is small, based on a single institution, the current version feels closer to a pilot study than a fully established benchmark. This narrow scope is not necessarily a flaw for an early resource, but it should be discussed more directly in the limitations, especially when considering how well the setup may transfer to other modalities, body regions, or reporting workflows.
Missing analysis: The paper also lacks analysis of what makes cases difficult or what separates model success from failure. More error analysis would make the benchmark much more informative. It would also help to first test how well the models understand the CT images themselves before evaluating the full discrepancy task.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Minor suggestions:
1) I would bring to the title that it is about discrepancies assessment
2) Use hyperlinks for your references, that if I click on [1] I get to [1]
3) Not sure if both links are needed under [16]
4) Consider using et al for some papers with a million authors. But be consistent.
5) PDF rendering: “meaningful testbed” goes over the line
6) Instead of having Discussion and Conclusion, maybe combine and instead have limitations separate, this would make it easier to distinguish
7) In table 2, just for readability, I would maybe separate Mixed and Natural a bit more or shade the Comp column aggregated view or the main row of the four models you think is most important to compare. Now it takes a bit to understand what I exactly should compare.

The paper addresses an important and still underexplored problem: checking whether suggested edits to radiology reports are actually supported by the imaging data. Its strongest contribution is the task itself, and the three-part annotation setup is well thought out. If this is expanded and validated more carefully, it could become a useful resource for the community.
At the same time, the current study feels too limited to fully support the benchmark claim. The dataset is very small, uses only one annotator, and does not report inter-rater agreement. The evaluation of disagreement detection also relies mostly on synthetic examples instead of real clinical cases. There is also no error analysis, no confidence intervals, and no subgroup breakdown.
Overall, I think the paper has a strong and worthwhile idea, but the evidence is not yet strong enough for this to work as a benchmark paper in its current form. Right now, it reads more like a promising pilot study than a fully established benchmark. The paper would be much stronger if the authors could show agreement between annotators, clarify why some important baselines were not included, and report statistical uncertainty more clearly.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper presents RADAR, a novel multimodal benchmark for evaluating image-grounded verification of radiology report edits, based on real clinical revisions and designed to assess fine-grained discrepancy reasoning.
reviews.text_strengths:
The proposed benchmark is well grounded in a realistic clinical workflow.
The paper introduces a novel and well-motivated task formulation, a new multimodal task of image-grounded verification of report edits, moving beyond prior work on report generation or synthetic error detection.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The dataset is relatively small (50 CT studies), which raises concerns about statistical robustness and limits the reliability of the empirical comparisons as well as the generalizability of the findings.
The task assumes the availability of candidate edits and focuses only on their verification, bypassing the more challenging and clinically relevant step of discrepancy detection. This assumption limits the applicability of the approach to real-world deployment scenarios.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
To further strengthen the impact, it would be helpful to expand the dataset in scale and diversity, e.g., including more institutions, imaging modalities, or anatomical regions, to better support generalizability.
The current baselines are relatively limited. It would be valuable to explore stronger or task-adapted approaches, and more importantly, to consider integrating discrepancy detection and verification into a unified framework, which would better reflect real-world clinical settings.
It would improve clarity to provide representative examples illustrating each label category (agreement, severity, edit type), helping readers better understand the annotation criteria and task definition.
Since the annotations are performed by experts, including a human baseline or inter-annotator agreement would help contextualize model performance and provide a clearer sense of the intrinsic difficulty of the task.

Despite the relatively small dataset size, the paper proposes a clinically meaningful and novel task formulation for image-grounded radiology report review. The benchmark is well-motivated and offers a valuable direction for evaluating multimodal models.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: While the benchmark still has limitations in scale and completeness, the paper presents a novel and clinically meaningful problem setting for multimodal radiology reasoning. The proposed evaluation paradigm is realistic and valuable for future research directions. Overall, I view the paper as a borderline accept / weak accept.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper proposes methodology to assess agreement between an abdominal CT scan and its radiology report and suggest edits. Weaknesses (in evaluation) include a small dataset of 50 abdominal CT studies from a single institution and annotations for training by a single radiologist.

The authors have satisfactorily addressed key concerns raised in the reviews.
The reviewers unanimously agree this work passes the bar for acceptance and presentation at the conference.

The authors provided a valid rebuttal and the major concerns seem to be all addressed. The dataset is a bit small though, looking forward to seeing the extension of the benchmark at a better publication platform. Good luck.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and Area Chair for the thoughtful feedback and encouraging assessment of RADAR’s clinical relevance and novelty. We are pleased that all reviewers recognized the importance of the task formulation and its grounding in a realistic radiology workflow. Below we address the major concerns.
1.Benchmark scale, single institution, and “pilot study” framing (R1/R2/R3).
We agree that the current benchmark is limited in scale and diversity. Our goal was not to claim that RADAR provides broad benchmark coverage, but to introduce a new multimodal task formulation: image-grounded verification of report revisions derived from real preliminary-to-attending workflows. We will clarify this positioning and strengthen the limitations discussion regarding single-institution abdominal CT data and limited natural disagreement cases. The core contribution is the task setting itself. Existing multimodal radiology benchmarks mainly focus on report generation or synthetic error detection, whereas RADAR introduces a clinically grounded discrepancy-review setting. We believe this distinction supports the work’s value beyond dataset scale, and we will make this framing clearer in the revision.
2.Annotation validity and lack of inter-rater agreement (R2/R3).
We appreciate the suggestion regarding additional expert validation and inter-rater agreement analysis, and agree that these additions would strengthen the benchmark. The annotations were performed by an experienced abdominal radiologist using structured guidelines designed to reflect the clinical review workflow. In the revision, we will clarify the annotation protocol in greater detail and include inter-annotator agreement analysis to better quantify annotation consistency. We also recognize that severity assessment contains inherent subjectivity and will discuss this more in limitation.
3.Reliance on synthetic disagreement edits (R2).
The scarcity of naturally occurring incorrect edits reflects the clinical workflow: most attending revisions are correct refinements or clarifications, while incorrect edits are rare and often limited to unnecessary wording changes. We introduced synthetic disagreement edits to create a more balanced evaluation setting for image-grounded verification. To maintain transparency, we report “Mixed” and “Natural” evaluations separately. We will further clarify this rationale and discuss the limitations of synthetic augmentation. The “Natural” dataset remains fully composed of real clinical revisions and is intended to reflect real-world performance.
4.Missing baselines, human comparison, and additional analyses (R1/R2/R3).
This paper is primarily a benchmark and task definition contribution rather than a system development paper. Accordingly, we evaluated representative multimodal foundation models under consistent input conditions to establish baseline performance on the proposed task. We agree that radiologist-level comparison, subgroup/error analyses, and unified detection + verification pipelines would be valuable, and we position them as future work. The task is designed to isolate image-grounded verification as a foundational subproblem. This is an intentional scoping decision: before addressing full end-to-end discrepancy discovery, it is important to establish whether current multimodal models can determine whether a given report revision is supported by the image. The end-to-end setting is harder because candidate edits are not provided and the model must identify discrepancies without guidance. Demonstrating model limitations in this constrained setting already provides meaningful evidence of the challenges ahead.
5.Reproducibility and accessibility (R1/R2/R3).
The benchmark is being released through an established community challenge platform and will be made publicly available upon approval of a Data Use Agreement (DUA). Further details about the data and code will be made available upon publication.

title: RadHiera: Semantic Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Medical Report Generation
abstract: Vision-language models have shown promising results in radiology report generation. However, most existing methods generate reports as flat text and do not explicitly model the semantic dependency between the Findings and Impression sections, which can lead to inconsistencies between clinical observations and diagnostic conclusions. In this paper, we propose RadHiera, a semantic hierarchical reinforcement learning framework for radiology report generation. RadHiera follows the semantic organization of radiology reports by first optimizing overall report quality, then improving the diagnostic accuracy of the Impression section, and finally enforcing consistency between Findings and Impression so that diagnostic conclusions are supported by clinical evidence. Specifically, we begin with a base reward that combines linguistic quality and medical factuality to provide supervision on the whole report. On this basis, we introduce a severity-aware reward for the Impression section that places greater emphasis on errors involving clinically critical conditions, thereby reducing both missed diagnoses and overstatement. We further enforce cross-section consistency using Expert Model-derived label sets, with subset constraints and hallucination penalties to ensure that impressions remain faithful to the findings. Experiments on three public chest X-ray benchmarks show that RadHiera consistently improves diagnostic accuracy and inter-section consistency over state-of-the-art methods, while also demonstrating good adaptability to ultrasound report generation.  The source code is available at https://github.com/xmed-lab/RadHiera.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes RadHiera, a semantic hierarchical reinforcement learning framework for radiology report generation. The core idea is a multi-level reward mechanism for GRPO-based RL training: (1) a base reward combining linguistic fluency and clinical correctness at the whole-report level, (2) a severity-aware reward for the Impression section that weights clinically critical conditions more heavily, and (3) a cross-sectional consistency reward enforcing that Impression labels form a subset of Findings labels. Experiments are conducted on three public chest X-ray datasets and one private ultrasound dataset.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The motivation is clinically well-grounded. Radiology reports have an inherent hierarchical structure (Findings → Impression), and explicitly modeling this dependency in the optimization objective is a reasonable and meaningful direction.
The evaluation covers four datasets spanning two imaging modalities (chest X-ray and carotid ultrasound).
The ablation study (Table 3) provides some evidence that each reward component contributes, showing that the full hierarchical reward yields synergistic improvements over partial configurations.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.UniRG (Liu et al. , arXiv 2601.17151, Jan 2026) adopts a very similar paradigm, SFT on a vision-language model followed by GRPO with composite rewards, and has achieved state-of-the-art on the RexRank leaderboard. RadHiera and UniRG share the same RL algorithm (GRPO), similar reward decomposition philosophy (combining linguistic, clinical, and model-based signals), and overlapping evaluation datasets. The paper does not cite, discuss, or compare with UniRG in any form.
2.The paper claims to follow the RexRank evaluation protocol (citing [24]) and uses RexRank-associated datasets (MIMIC-CXR, IU-Xray, ReXGradient), yet does not submit to the public leaderboard for standardized evaluation. The results on the private test set used by rexrank is worth reporting.
3.The consistency reward (Eq. 9) is a hard binary signal (1 if I⊆F, else 0). It also only penalizes hallucinated Impression labels but ignores omissions (conditions present in Findings but absent from Impression).
4.The three rewards in Eq. 4 are summed without weighting coefficients. No justification for direct addition is given, nor is there a discussion of potential conflicts between rewards.
5.All clinical rewards depend on CheXbert for label extraction (Eqs. 6, 8), yet CheXbert covers only 14 conditions and may have reduced accuracy on generated (vs. human-written) text. This creates a risk of reward hacking. The model could learn to produce text that maximizes CheXbert label agreement without genuinely improving clinical quality. This limitation is not discussed.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses a clinically motivated problem, enforcing hierarchical consistency in radiology report generation, and the high-level idea of a multi-level reward aligning with report structure is appealing. However, I have several concerns as mentioned in the weaknesses section. I would consider increasing my score if those concerns are adequately addressed in the rebuttal.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes to explicitly model the consistency between Findings and Impression section in a radiology report generation and optimize clinical metrics directly and not only word likelihood. To achieve this they propose to train report generation using RL (GRPO) with a multi-level reward formulation targeting both clinical correctness and consistency.
reviews.text_strengths:
three level reward design covers important aspect of radiology reporting, such as the general correctness, emphazised caution with critical conditions and internal consistency
generalization to US report generation, which is generally a harder and less researched task compared to Xray reporting
the ablation study in Table 3 is informative and helps understanding the contributions of the different reward parts
comprehensive evaluation on three X-ray datasets and one internal Ultrasound dataset
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The set of methods the paper compares to is relatively small. Rexrank includes models which achieve better results in some of the metrics than the models, one especially good excluded model being UniRG-CXR which outperforms on multiple metrics on multiple dataset (e.g. in RadCliQ and SembScore on MIMIC-CXR, in RadCliQ, RadGraph, SembScore and BertScore on IUXray and in RadCliQ, SembScore and RadGraph on ReXGradient). It would strengthen the paper to either explain why this model was excluded or include it in the comparison.
The reported IU-Xray and ReXGradient scores for models such as MedGemma and MedVersa differ from the results reported in ReXRank. It would be helpful if the authors could clarify whether these differences come from changed evaluation settings, different checkpoints, prompt/template choices, or their own fine-tuning setup.
The consistency reward is rather simple. It is set to 1 if Impression labels are a subset of Findings labels, else 0.That could potentially encourage overly conservative impressions and would ignore deviations in e.g. severity or findings going beyond the 14 chexbert labels.
The evaluation metric for consistency follows the same subset logic, so consistency issues outside that paradigm would also be missed during evaluation.
Some techinical details are missing:
How is the syntax reward calculated, which measurements are used to reward fluency and semantic similarity?
How is the clinical reward calculated, what is used to “extract clinical entities” and how is the comparison defined?
Which clinical label calssifier is used for both the severity and the consistency reward? (impression reward)
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The general idea and motivation of the paper is well-grounded and the proposed reward design covers important aspects of report generation. Further, the evaluation is extensive, spanning multiple datasets and ablations. However, in its current form their are important points, which I would need to see clarified in the rebuttal before I can justify recommending acceptance. The most important points are clarifying the evaluation results with respect to the official ReXRank leaderboard and adding the missing technical details. I would also like to see the current limitations of the consistency reward discussed.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors clarified my main concerns regarding the comparison to UniRG and other leaderboard models, the rational for the subset constraint and missing technical details. I would ask the authors to include all these new information in the final version of the paper.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses the inconsistency between the Findings and Impression sections in radiology report generation and proposes a reinforcement learning framework that incorporates explicit cross-sectional constraints into the training objective.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper addresses a well-known issue in radiology report generation—cross-sectional inconsistency—and proposes a simple subset-based constraint that is easy to implement and empirically effective.
The consistency reward is clearly formulated and supported by ablation, where most of the gains can be attributed to this component.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The method relies heavily on a frozen classifier to define both supervision and reward, effectively reducing the problem to optimizing agreement with the classifier rather than improving report generation.
Since evaluation is also based on classifier-derived metrics (e.g., CheXbert-F1), the reported improvements may largely reflect metric alignment rather than genuine gains in clinical quality.
The severity-aware component is not convincingly validated, and its contribution appears marginal.
The hard subset constraint is overly restrictive and does not reflect real clinical reporting, where impressions may reasonably extend beyond explicitly stated findings.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The paper addresses an important problem and proposes a simple and effective constraint. However, the contribution appears to rely heavily on classifier-based supervision, and it remains unclear whether the gains reflect true report quality improvement or metric alignment. Clarifying this point would significantly strengthen the paper.

The paper addresses an important issue in report generation and proposes a simple consistency constraint that is clearly formulated and empirically effective. However, the method relies heavily on classifier-derived labels for both reward and evaluation, making it unclear whether the gains reflect true improvements in report quality or better alignment with the evaluation metrics. In addition, the severity-aware component is not convincingly validated. Overall, the idea is reasonable but the contribution appears limited, leading to a borderline recommendation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The rebuttal satisfactorily addressed several of my main concerns. In particular, the authors clarified that the subset constraint is not an arbitrary heuristic but reflects the dominant structure observed in real reports, with approximately 93% of samples satisfying the Findings-Impression subset relation. This substantially strengthens the motivation for the proposed consistency reward.
The additional CheXbert-only baseline was also helpful in addressing my concern regarding simple metric optimization. The results suggest that optimizing only classifier-derived agreement does not recover the broader improvements observed with the proposed hierarchical reward formulation, particularly in consistency and report structure.
I still believe the overall contribution is more engineering-oriented than fundamentally methodological, and the approach remains heavily dependent on classifier-derived supervision. In addition, the severity-aware component appears weaker than the consistency reward and contributes relatively modest gains overall. However, the rebuttal provides reasonable clarification for these points, including class-wise improvements on clinically important findings.
Overall, the paper presents a simple but practically meaningful approach to improving cross-sectional consistency in radiology report generation, and the empirical evidence is sufficient to place the paper slightly above the acceptance threshold.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper addresses the structural dependency between the “Findings” and “Impression” sections of radiology reports through a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework. The model optimizes a composite reward function that balances linguistic quality, diagnostic severity, and cross-section consistency. The core contribution is a hierarchical supervision strategy that ensures the diagnostic conclusions in the Impression section are logically supported by the clinical evidence described in the Findings.
While the paper presents good contributions, its recommendation for acceptance is contingent upon the authors clarifying the following points during the rebuttal phase:
1.Comment on the technical difference between the proposed method and UniRG (Liu et al., 2026).
2.The “Consistency Reward” (Eq. 9) is criticized for its simplistic. Address the “subset” flaw. Explain how the model avoids being overly conservative or missing findings, and discuss why a soft or more nuanced consistency metric wasn’t used.
3.The framework relies almost entirely on CheXbert for clinical rewards, severity mapping, and final evaluation. This creates a circularity where the model is essentially trained to “hack” the CheXbert classifier. Improvements in CheXbert-F1 may simply reflect the model’s ability to mimic the classifier’s biases rather than a genuine increase in clinical accuracy or reporting quality. Comment on the evidence that clinical improvements are genuine and not just the result of metric alignment with the CheXbert classifier.
4.The paper omits several crucial details necessary for reproducibility: (1) the three primary rewards are summed without weights, with no justification for how potential conflicts between fluency and clinical accuracy are resolved; (2) The specific calculations for “syntax reward” and the mechanism for “extracting clinical entities” are not sufficiently explained; (3) Results for MedGemma and MedVersa differ from published RexRank scores, and it is unclear if this is due to re-training, different checkpoints, or altered evaluation settings.

The authors have addressed the reviewers’ comments well. All reviewers have now agreed on acceptance of the paper.

The paper proposes RadHiera, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework for medical report generation that enforces consistency between Findings and Impression sections via a multi-level reward function. Reviewers raised several concerns: (1) lack of comparison to the concurrent UniRG work; (2) the simplistic binary subset constraint for consistency reward; (3) potential reward hacking due to heavy reliance on CheXbert for both training and evaluation; and (4) missing implementation details affecting reproducibility. The rebuttal successfully clarified the paper’s novelty relative to UniRG, empirically validated the subset constraint, and provided a strong counterexample to the reward-hacking critique. Reviewers acknowledged these points, with R2 and R3 raising their scores from weak reject to accept. Given the thorough rebuttal and the clinical relevance of enforcing Findings-Impression consistency, the paper meets the acceptance threshold. The authors should incorporate the rebuttal clarifications (UniRG comparison, subset statistics, CheXbert-only baseline results) into the final manuscript in the revision.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the Meta-Reviewer (AC) and reviewers (R1-R3) for their feedback. Key responses below:
1.UniRG comparison (R1, R2, AC-Q1): We will cite/discuss UniRG. Both use SFT+GRPO, but optimize different objects: UniRG is a large-scale RL system using an 8B backbone and 550k+ studies, optimized with report-level metrics. RadHiera instead targets the Findings-Impression dependency: with a 3B backbone and 200k+ studies, we design a novel semantic hierarchy reward that grounds Impression conclusions in Findings evidence. We reproduced a UniRG-style recipe under the same 3B/200k+ setting on MIMIC-CXR:
Method | BLEU2 | BERTS | SembS | RadG | 1/RadC
————-+——-+——-+——-+——-+——-
UniRG-3B | 0.188 | 0.402 | 0.421 | 0.255 | 0.901
RadHiera-3B | 0.206 | 0.421 | 0.442 | 0.282 | 0.939
UniRG-8B | 0.205 | 0.419 | 0.491 | 0.266 | 1.006
Under the same scale, RadHiera (ours) outperforms UniRG-3B and remains competitive with UniRG-8B.
2.Consistency reward (R1-R3, AC-Q2): The subset constraint reflects the dominant report structure, not an arbitrary simplification. It enforces a subset relation: Impression diagnoses should be supported by Findings. Under the same label space, 93.0% of MIMIC-CXR samples satisfy this relation: 31.0% equal and 62.0% strict subset; extension cases account for only 7.0%. Similar patterns are observed in other datasets.
Although the consistency reward cannot penalize omissions, omissions are handled by the severity-aware reward, which penalizes missed critical diagnoses. Its overall gain is modest due to sparsity of severity labels, but class-wise results improve clinically important findings: pneumothorax F1 0.5191->0.5560 and pulmonary edema 0.4892->0.5278, supporting its role in mitigating omissions.
We did not use soft overlap metrics because they may penalize valid concise subsets, encourage copying Findings into Impression, and introduce noisy reward. Also, we acknowledge the limitation from finite label space and labeler noise.
3.CheXbert hacking concern (R1, R3, AC-Q3): We directly test a CheXbert-only plus base reward baseline that optimizes classifier-derived label agreement without our hierarchy design:
Method | BLEU2 | BERTS | SembS | RadG | 1/RadC | F1 | Consis
————–+——-+——-+——-+——-+——–+——-+——-
CheXbert-only | 0.191 | 0.409 | 0.381 | 0.211 | 0.901 | 0.401 | 0.781
RadHiera | 0.206 | 0.421 | 0.442 | 0.282 | 0.939 | 0.394 | 0.851
CheXbert-only obtains slightly higher CheXbert-F1 but underperforms on NLG quality, RadGraph, RadCliQ, and Findings-Impression consistency. This shows classifier-only optimization can cause narrow metric alignment, whereas RadHiera’s semantic hierarchy reward improves broader report quality and consistency. CheXbert-F1 alone is not definitive clinical validation; the pattern indicates RadHiera is not simply exploiting CheXbert-specific biases. Future: multi-labeler/uncertainty-aware rewards and blinded radiologist evaluation.
4.Implementation, reproducibility, and baselines (R1, R2, AC-Q4): We will add missing details. (1) Rewards are summed equally (1:1:1), selected by hyperparameter search; nearby weights were stable. (2) Syntax/fluency uses BLEU and ROUGE-L; semantic similarity uses BERTScore/SembScore. Clinical entity reward uses RadGraph-style extraction: generated/reference reports are converted into normalized tuples covering observations, anatomy, negation/uncertainty, and relations; micro-F1 is computed. CXR severity/consistency rewards use CheXbert 14-class labels; ultrasound uses a modality-specific labeler trained on privately annotated reports. (3) MedGemma/MedVersa differ from ReXRank because we fine-tuned/evaluated them under the same splits, prompts, decoding, and scripts as RadHiera to ensure fair comparison rather than directly copying leaderboard numbers. We will release code/checkpoints/scripts and submit/report ReXRank private-test results when available.

title: RADIANT-PET: Reasoning-Augmented PET/CT Lesion Segmentation with Large Language Models and Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Accurate lesion segmentation in PET/CT is critical for oncology, yet remains challenging because physiologic tracer uptake and artifacts can mimic malignant signal. We present RADIANT-PET, a reasoning-augmented framework that couples a high-sensitivity voxel-level segmentation model with lesion-level large language model (LLM) adjudication. Candidate uptake regions are generated with a deliberately permissive segmentation stage, then converted into structured textual descriptions that summarize uptake intensity, morphology, and regional and global anatomical context. An LLM classifies each candidate as true lesion vs. false positive, optionally leveraging the radiology report as additional clinical context. To strengthen lesion-level reasoning, we further optimize a local LLM via reinforcement learning using Group Relative Policy Optimization, with rewards that encourage anatomically plausible decisions. Across AutoPET and an institutional test cohort, RADIANT-PET consistently outperforms strong image-only baselines, with the largest improvements observed when radiology reports are provided. Overall, these results demonstrate that LLM-based lesion-level reasoning adds a novel reasoning layer beyond conventional segmentation, suppressing physiologic false positives and aligning voxel-level predictions with clinical interpretation.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Reinforcement Learning / Control / Decision-Making

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents a framework that use a language model with RL fine-tuning to improve the segmentation performance of a high-sensitivity U-Net model.
reviews.text_strengths:
This framework incorporate free-text radiology reports as additional clinical context for lesion segmentation. 
Additionally, the proposed method improves the classification accuracy of the LLM using reinforcement learning.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
My main concerns are about the rl fine tuning. 
1.The reward design is discrete and sparse, which leads to weak ranking signals within groups. This makes it harder for the model to learn meaningful distinctions and capture variance within the groups. 
2.The anatomical reward design is overly strict, as it only assigns credit for exact matches. This raises the question of how near correct predictions that are close to the ground truth are handled. 
3.RL significantly improves performance over the baseline; however, only GRPO was evaluated. Consider comparing it with other LLM fine-tuning methods.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The authors propose a novel methodology, and the Threshold + loss-RL approach significantly improves performance across all metrics. However, the manuscript lacks a clear description of GRPO, comparisons with other fine-tuning methods, and justification for the choice of reward function.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a reasoning-augmented framework for PET/CT lesion segmentation, which combines a high-sensitivity candidate generation stage with LLM-based lesion-level adjudication. The main contribution is the introduction of an explicit reasoning layer that filters false-positive uptake candidates using structured lesion descriptions, anatomical context, and optionally radiology reports. The paper further incorporates GRPO to improve the local LLM’s candidate classification ability, and reports improved performance over strong image-only baselines on both public and institutional datasets.
reviews.text_strengths:
(1) Novel framework design. The idea of converting segmentation outputs into structured text and using an LLM to adjudicate each candidate lesion is a reasonable and interesting approach. It draws on how radiologists incorporate anatomical and clinical context into their decisions, which gives the framework a sensible motivation beyond purely image-based processing.
(2) Practical reinforcement learning application. Using GRPO to fine-tune a local LLM is a pragmatic choice given privacy constraints in clinical deployment. The results show that the method provides measurable improvements over the base model, making the contribution practically credible for real-world clinical settings.
(3) Clear presentation and well-organized paper. The paper is logically structured and easy to follow. Figure 1 directly exposes raw JSON code as part of the main pipeline illustration, which make visual clarity for readers familiar with the implementation details. Figure 2 more effectively illustrates the qualitative impact of RL on the model’s reasoning trace. Overall the writing is clear, the motivation is well-stated, and the progression from candidate generation to LLM adjudication to final segmentation is communicated in a coherent and readable way.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(1) Training details are not sufficiently clear. The description of the training setup is not detailed enough. Important implementation details, such as the GRPO group size, are missing or only briefly mentioned. This makes it difficult to assess the robustness of the method and limits reproducibility.
(2) The experimental design involving report-conditioned input is not explained clearly enough. It is unclear why the radiology report should be used in this setting, especially since the report itself may already contain direct or indirect information about whether a candidate uptake is true or false. If the report already includes clinician interpretation, then part of the reported gain may come from access to the answer rather than from better lesion-level reasoning. The paper should explain the clinical purpose of this setting more carefully and clarify what information from the report is actually used.
(3) Although the paper tries to address the false-positive lesion problem, the clinical value of the task is not well reflected in the method design or experimental evaluation. First, false-positive uptake in PET is not limited to normal physiologic uptake; inflammatory uptake is also an important source of false positives, but this is not clearly discussed or evaluated in the paper. Second, in real clinical practice, clinicians are often more concerned with false-positive lesions in regions such as the abdomen, where interpretation cannot be resolved by simple anatomical plausibility or symmetric patterns alone. The paper does not provide targeted evaluation on these more challenging local regions, which limits its practical clinical value. Third, the method relies heavily on structured information derived from high-sensitivity lesion segmentation, organ segmentation, and hand-crafted features. The paper does not sufficiently discuss whether these inputs are reliable enough, or whether they already encode enough fixed clinical or anatomical knowledge to account for much of the false-positive filtering.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

My score is mainly based on the gap between the methodological interest of the paper and its currently limited demonstrated clinical value. The proposed framework is technically interesting, especially the use of structured lesion descriptions for LLM-based candidate adjudication. However, the paper does not yet convincingly show that the method addresses the most clinically meaningful false-positive scenarios, and some parts of the experimental design, especially the report-conditioned setting, remain insufficiently justified.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: After reading the rebuttal and considering the other reviewers’ concerns, I recommend Reject. While the paper shows some novelty, the rebuttal does not sufficiently address my concern that the overall contribution remains limited. Therefore, I do not think it is strong enough for acceptance.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
In their manuscript “RADIANT-PET: Reasoning-Augmented
PET/CT Lesion Segmentation with Large
Language Models and Reinforcement Learning” the authors describe an automated framework for automated lesion segmentation in PET/CT imaging. They address a common challenge in PET/CT lesion segmentation: How to find an optimal balance between sensitivity and minimization of false positives.
To this end they propose a two-stage framework: (1) permissive candidate lesion generation (threshold or UNet) and (2) lesion-level classification by an LLM using structured region descriptions and radiology reports, enhanced by GRPO RL.
The authors describe improved performance using this method as compared to direct UNet-based lesion segmentation alone.
reviews.text_strengths: The main strength and novelty of this work is the introduction of a per-lesion reasoning process for classification of PET lesions. The underlying idea of using structured lesion descriptors allows the introduction of novel training mechanisms like reinforcement learning into this field of application. In addition, the proposed method is inherently interpretable since it is based on natural language descriptors and reasoning chains.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
This work has major limitations:
Baselines: The authors only compare their method to internal ablations but do not use SOTA baselines for automated PET lesion segmentations. Suitable baselines exist publicly (e.g. high performing methods of prior MICCAI challenges such as the autoPET challenge). The used baseline, which is the highest performing model from the autoPET 3 challenge was designed for multi-tracer applications and is thus not a specialized SOTA model for FDG-PET segmentation. Comparison to SOTA baselines is an important prerequisite for the assessment of method performance
The LLM-based classification method only uses high level text descriptors of a lesion derived e.g. from organ locations segmented with Total Segmentator or PET lesion properties. Such concepts do not capture image information directly and are this limited in their contribution to lesion classification. Using a multimodal VLM would be a much more suitable approach. In addition, the authors should compare this LLM-based classifier to simple baselines such as per lesion patch CNN-based classifier.
Related to the point above, an LLM classifier cannot improve per lesion segmentation accuracy. It is thus unclear how a threshold-based baseline can be suitable for such a method. How was the threshold determined? Was it a global SUV, per lesion? Per study? “We chose 2.5 because it is the standard cutoff for defining
metabolically active lymphoma” - this not a clinically accurate statement - there is not threshold for metabolically active lymphoma.
The clinical application, training and evaluation is exclusively done on Lymphoma cases using FDG-PET images. This limits the generalizability of presented results.
Data and results are described superficially. The authors do not provide information on the type of lymphoma, stage, tumor burden, patient cohort characteristics. Also, results are only presented at a high level with global statistics. It is also unclear how model performance was measured. Are the provided metrics per lesion? Per volume? What is the variation (only mean values are presented). Where were most errors observed? etc..
It is unclear how accurate the institutional baseline is (“candidate regions were manually labeled by a hematologist and a radiologist”, an expert Nuclear Medicine Physician or specialized Radiologist would be more appropriate for this task). What software was used? Was this also threshold based? Or purely manual? How many lesions were segmented in how many organs?
Providing more image examples would be helpful to allow the reader to have a better understanding of model performance
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Strengths:
Novel Method in the field of PET lesion segmentation introducing LLM-based reasoning and reinforcement learning.
Weaknesses:
Baselines and generalizability: The study compares mainly internal ablations and a non-applicable autoPET baseline, with no evaluation against state-of-the-art, modality-specific baselines (e.g., top FDG-PET methods from MICCAI challenges). Evaluation is limited to lymphoma FDG-PET/CT, raising concerns about generalizability to other cancers, tracers, and multi-center settings.
Reproducibility gaps: No public release of code. Critical details (cohort characteristics, lesion counts, software/tools used for manual labeling, thresholding choices) are insufficient for replication.
Evaluation details missing: Results are presented at a high level (mean values) without lesion-level breakdowns, uncertainty estimates, or statistical significance tests. Lacking are per-lesion/per-volume metrics, subgroup analyses, and error analyses to understand failure modes.
Methodological concerns: The LLM-based per-lesion classifier relies on high-level text descriptors rather than direct multimodal image features. There is no comparison to multimodal baselines (e.g., VLM or patch-CNN classifiers).
Threshold and clinical claims: Some statements (e.g., “2.5 is the standard cutoff for defining metabolically active lymphoma”) appear clinically inaccurate.
Dataset and deployment specifics: Institutional baseline labeling by “an expert hematologist and a radiologist” lacks detail on expertise, workflow, and number of lesions; no description of imaging protocols, scanner types, or patient-level attributes (stage, tumor burden) provided.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors responded to major concerns and provided helpful context. 
While major open questions remain about the approach and performance of presented methodology, it can be reasonable to address these in future work.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper was evaluated by reviewers with expertise in the field who identified limitations resulting in mixed enthusiasm for this work. Questions were raised regarding clinical impact, appropriate comparisons to state-of-the-art, and unclear methodological details.

The reviewers showed some enthusiasm for this work being presented at the conference. Several concerns remain but the overall contributions are strong enough to justify acceptance.

This paper presents an interesting framework that combines lesion-level reasoning with large language models and reinforcement learning for PET/CT lesion segmentation. Reviewers appreciated the originality of incorporating structured lesion descriptions and reasoning-based candidate adjudication, as well as the clinical motivation of reducing false positive findings.
However, concerns remained regarding the strength of experimental validation, choice and breadth of baselines, clinical impact, and overall evidence supporting the proposed design choices. While the rebuttal clarified several methodological and implementation details, it did not fully resolve these concerns. Given the mixed reviews and remaining questions regarding validation and significance, I think the paper remains marginally below the acceptance threshold for MICCAI this year.

Overall, the rebuttal clarified several important methodological and reproducibility details, but significant concerns remain regarding baseline adequacy, generalizability, and the strength of evidence for clinical value. I therefore recommend rejection.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for the constructive comments.
*Reproducibility [All]. We commit to release all code, HS-UNet weights, GRPO scripts, and LoRA adapters upon acceptance.
*SOTA baselines [R3]. Our baseline, nnUNet-v2, won autoPET III and ranked first on the FDG sub-track. It outperforms earlier autoPET I/II winners, while autoPET IV reformulated the task as interactive click-prompted segmentation and is therefore not directly comparable. nnUNet-v2 is thus the appropriate SOTA.
*Thresholding [R3]. We used fixed-SUV thresholding because it reflects how lymphoma metabolic tumor burden is calculated in multicenter clinical trials. Prespecified thresholds reduce reader- and site-dependent variability, and international TMTV harmonization efforts recommend threshold-based approaches (SUV ≥2.5, SUV ≥4.0, or 41% SUVmax) as standards for delineating active lesions. Thus, per-lesion voxel-level delineation is not the limiting factor in PET lymphoma segmentation; the central challenge, which RADIANT-PET targets, is distinguishing true tumor uptake from false positives at the lesion level.
*GRPO details and reward design [R1,R2]. Sec. 2.4 was condensed due to page limits; the final version will include full implementation details. We fine-tuned gpt-oss-20b in BF16 using Unsloth + TRL GRPOTrainer with LoRA on all attention and MLP projections: q/k/v/o and gate/up/down. LoRA rank was 8 with α = 16.GRPO used 4 completions per prompt, temperature 1.0, and 2,048-token limits for prompts and completions. Optimization used AdamW-8bit with LR 5e-5, linear decay, 10% warmup, weight decay 1e-3, per-device batch size 4, and gradient accumulation 4.The reward summed three terms: (i) binary correctness, with +1 for the correct physiological-site versus lesion-site label and −1 if both labels appeared; (ii) anatomical-site accuracy, with +2 for exact matches and +1.5 for curated equivalence groups, such as bone/bone marrow or GI subregions; and (iii) a reasoning trace regularizer, with −0.5 if certain key words were not referenced. Reward weights were selected by ablation, and this configuration achieved the best validation F1.We chose GRPO over SFT because candidate labels and anatomical sites provide verifiable ground truth, a rare opportunity in clinical AI, where labels are often subjective or incompletely specified.
*Clinical impact and cohort description [R2,R3]. The project was motivated by our clinical experience treating lymphoma patients, where accurate baseline PET/CT tumor burden is crucial for precision risk stratification, treatment selection, and outcome prediction across modern therapies, including CAR T-cell therapy. All patients in our cohort underwent CAR T-cell therapy, and most had large B-cell lymphoma. We will add cohort and annotation details truncated for space. These are presentation clarifications of existing analyses, not new experiments.
*LLM vs VLM/patch-CNN [R3]. During development, we evaluated a medical VLM, MedGemma, and observed weak lesion-level classification, likely due to limited PET/CT data in open-source medical VLM pretraining; effective fine-tuning would require larger datasets, which we note as future work. We agree that a per-lesion CNN classifier would be a valuable baseline; however, a CNN cannot natively incorporate the radiology report as a conditioning signal, which is central to our framework.
*Annotation [R1,R3]. Institutional labels were generated by a visiting radiologist with >10 years of experience in general radiology, including nuclear medicine, and finalized by two board-certified clinicians: a hematologist with 8 years of lymphoma and routine PET/CT experience, and a radiation oncologist with 8 years of expertise in tumor-target delineation. Annotation was performed in 3D Slicer. Candidate lesions were manually selected and refined by region expansion or shrinkage to an SUV threshold of 2.5.The framework was also evaluated on the external autoPET dataset to assess generalizability.

title: Radiogenomics-Driven Hierarchical Multimodal Stacking for Non-invasive Triage of High-Risk PKD1-Truncating Genotypes in ADPKD
abstract: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) exhibits a pronounced genotype-phenotype gap and substantial radiological “biological mimicry” across mutation classes, which together hinder early risk stratification. Height-adjusted total kidney volume (htTKV) is the current gold-standard imaging biomarker for disease progression, yet its ability to resolve underlying genetic subtypes is limited by extensive phenotype overlap. In particular, high-risk PKD1-truncating (PKD1-T) mutations are often radiologically indistinguishable from milder PKD1 non-truncation (PKD1-NT), PKD2, or  no-mutation-detected cases on routine MRI. This work introduces a radiogenomics-driven, two-stage hierarchical stacking framework that integrates 3D MRI radiomics with clinical profiles for non-invasive triage of PKD1-T genotypes. First, handcrafted radiomic features are extracted from automatically segmented total kidney volume masks on T2-weighted MRI and compressed into out-of-fold (OOF) probabilistic representations using multiple base classifiers under strictly nested cross-validation. These compact radiomics-derived signatures are then fused with clinical variables (age, htTKV) in a meta-learning stage designed to capture non-linear imaging-clinical interactions while rigorously preventing data leakage. On a multi-institutional cohort of 414 genetically confirmed ADPKD patients, the proposed hierarchical multimodal framework achieves an AUC of 0.722 ± 0.060 and an accuracy of 0.725 ± 0.058 for discriminating PKD1-T from a heterogeneous “Other PKD” group, significantly outperforming both radiomics-only (AUC 0.677 ± 0.061) and clinical-only (AUC 0.664 ± 0.081) baselines. These findings highlight the complementary value of 3D MR-based radiomic texture heterogeneity and tabular clinical profiles for non-invasive radiogenomic triage of high-risk PKD1-truncating genotypes, particularly where comprehensive genetic testing is limited by cost or availability.
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
1.The paper addresses non-invasive genotype triage of high-risk PKD1-truncating ADPKD using T2-weighted MRI, radiomics, and basic clinical variables. 
2.The main contribution is a two-stage hierarchical stacking design that compresses radiomics into out-of-fold probabilistic signatures and fuses them with age and htTKV in a meta-learning stage. 
3.The paper claims to improve over unimodal imaging-only or clinical-only approaches by modeling complementary non-linear imaging-clinical interactions while controlling leakage through nested cross-validation. 
4.The evidence presented includes a multi-institutional cohort of 414 genetically confirmed patients, repeated nested cross-validation, calibration analysis, decision-curve analysis, and SHAP-based interpretation. 
5.The practical implication is a potentially useful triage tool for prioritizing genetic testing or closer surveillance when sequencing resources are limited.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The clinical question is important and harder than many prior ADPKD imaging tasks because it targets intra-PKD1 heterogeneity rather than simpler PKD1-vs-PKD2 discrimination. 
2.The cohort is substantial for this disease setting: 414 genetically confirmed patients after quality control, drawn from multiple institutions. 
3.The evaluation pipeline is careful about leakage: scaling, LASSO selection, SMOTE, and out-of-fold prediction generation are all nested within the training folds. 
4.The paper goes beyond AUC and includes calibration, decision-curve analysis, and SHAP, which is useful for a translational paper. 
5.The multimodal model significantly outperforms the radiomics-only and clinical-only baselines, reaching AUC 0.722 versus 0.677 and 0.664, respectively.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.There is no true external hold-out validation; repeated cross-validation on the same multi-institutional cohort is useful but does not establish transportability. 
2.The methodological novelty is moderate: hierarchical stacking with out-of-fold features is a careful application of known ensemble ideas more than a genuinely new technical concept. 
3.Performance remains only moderate, and the absolute gain over unimodal baselines is modest, so the practical utility of the model as a triage tool is still uncertain. 
4.The clinical baseline is fairly narrow, using only age and htTKV; stronger non-imaging comparators are missing. 
5.The “Other PKD” label combines several biologically different subgroups, which may obscure where the method truly helps or fails. 
6.The framework depends on automated kidney segmentation, but the sensitivity of the radiomics pipeline to segmentation errors is not analyzed.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
This paper would be strengthened by:
1.Adding an institution-held-out or temporally held-out external test set. 
2.Comparing against stronger clinical baselines beyond age and htTKV. 
3.Reporting subgroup analyses, especially for PKD1-NT versus PKD2 versus NMD cases, and sensitivity to segmentation quality.

My score is based on the importance of the clinical task, the moderate novelty of the multimodal stacking strategy, and the reasonably careful validation. The main positives are the strong attention to leakage prevention and the multi-institutional cohort for a difficult radiogenomic problem. The main concerns are the lack of an external hold-out test and the only moderate discrimination, with fairly modest gains over the unimodal baselines.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a two-stage hierarchical stacking framework for non-invasive radiogenomic triage of high-risk PKD1-truncating (PKD1-T) genotypes in ADPKD. The objective is to discriminate PKD1-T mutations from a heterogeneous “Other PKD” group (PKD1-NT, PKD2-T, PKD2-NT, no-mutation-detected) using 3D MRI radiomics fused with routine clinical variables (age, htTKV), without requiring genetic testing. This goes beyond the binary PKD1 vs. PKD2 classification or Mayo Imaging Classification stratification that prior ADPKD radiomics work has addressed. The central claim is that high-dimensional radiomic features, compressed into OOF probability representations and fused with clinical variables in a meta-learner, capture non-linear imaging-clinical interactions that unimodal models miss. The multimodal model achieves AUC 0.722 ± 0.060 on a multi-institutional cohort of 414 genetically confirmed patients, with improvements in calibration and decision curve analysis over both unimodal baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper addresses an underexplored clinical problem. Most radiomics work in ADPKD targets PKD1 vs. PKD2 discrimination or Mayo Imaging Classification risk stratification. The intra-PKD1 problem, specifically isolating high-risk truncating variants from a heterogeneous “Other PKD” group, is harder and more clinically relevant. Where genetic testing is unavailable or cost-prohibitive, an imaging-based triage tool has potential to prioritize who gets sequenced.
The dataset is a strength. A multi-institutional cohort of 414 genetically confirmed ADPKD patients is large for a rare hereditary disease, and genetic confirmation is the right ground truth standard.
Methodological rigor is above average for a radiomics paper. Nested cross-validation with SMOTE applied exclusively within training folds is correctly implemented; LASSO selection is also fold-wise. Many radiomics publications leak information by applying SMOTE before splitting or selecting features on the full dataset. This paper avoids both mistakes.
The evaluation goes beyond AUC. ECE and DCA provide a more honest picture of clinical utility, and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on paired fold results are statistically appropriate for the repeated CV design.
SHAP findings are biologically plausible. Age as the dominant clinical predictor aligns with established genotype-phenotype relationships in ADPKD. Texture descriptors (GLCM inverse difference, GLSZM small area emphasis) reflect cystic structure heterogeneity consistent with known PKD1-T phenotypic signatures. The two signals are complementary, not redundant.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
No ethics statement appears in the manuscript. The paper uses multi-institutional retrospective patient MRI data and genetic profiles. No IRB/ethics committee approval, informed consent, or data governance arrangements are mentioned.
Age confounding is not addressed. SHAP identifies age as the dominant predictor. The PKD1-T group (mean age 33.6 ± 8.3 years) is four years younger on average than the “Other PKD” group (37.6 ± 7.8 years). The model may be discriminating on age rather than on genotype-linked imaging features. The paper does not report performance with age removed, nor does it discuss whether this age gap reflects a genuine genotype-phenotype relationship or a sampling artefact.
No external validation. All data are pooled under nested CV. The performance reported (AUC 0.722) may not generalize beyond this specific cohort. A held-out external institution is needed before any clinical deployment argument can stand.
Sensitivity-specificity imbalance in radiomics-only models. Radiomics-only RF achieves sensitivity 0.764 but specificity 0.602.This indicates systematic bias toward predicting PKD1-T. The paper does not discuss whether SMOTE amplifies this bias or how threshold calibration addresses it.
LASSO selection stability not reported. Across 30 outer folds, feature selection instability is a known issue. Reporting the distribution of selected feature counts and the most consistently selected features would strengthen reproducibility.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The clinical question is well-motivated. Non-invasive genotype prediction in ADPKD fills a real gap: genetic testing is costly, not universally available, and a validated imaging biomarker would improve risk stratification before kidney function declines. The 414 patients multi-institutional cohort is a genuine asset, and the statistical execution is careful and above average for radiomics papers.
Two concerns reduce confidence. First, age confounding is not addressed. The PKD1-T group is approximately four years younger, and age is the top SHAP predictor. An ablation removing age from the feature set would clarify whether the model captures genotype-specific texture or a demographic proxy. Second, validation is internal only. The deployment framing in the Discussion overstates what a single-cohort repeated CV result supports.
Neither concern invalidates the work. Both are addressable: the first potentially in rebuttal, the second by scoping the conclusions. The missing ethics statement should be corrected before publication. On balance, the clinical novelty and execution quality warrant acceptance contingent on addressing these points.

N/A
