On the other hand, the discussion of clinical use cases, comparative analysis of methods and conditions, and the interpretation of features are insufficient and should be strengthened.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
The reviews are consistently positive, with three weak-accept recommendations. The paper addresses a clinically relevant and challenging problem: non-invasive triage of high-risk PKD1-truncating genotypes in ADPKD using MRI radiomics and routine clinical variables. The reviewers recognize several strengths, including the multi-institutional genetically confirmed cohort, careful nested cross-validation to reduce leakage, multimodal stacking of radiomics and clinical profiles, and evaluation beyond AUC through calibration, decision-curve analysis, and SHAP interpretation.
The main concerns are the lack of a true external hold-out validation set, moderate methodological novelty, only moderate discrimination with modest gains over unimodal baselines, and the need to address possible age confounding given that age is the dominant SHAP predictor. The authors should also clarify clinical use cases, subgroup performance within the heterogeneous “Other PKD” group, segmentation sensitivity, and the missing ethics statement. These issues are important but appear addressable in revision and do not substantially undermine the contribution.

title: RaD-Seg: Region-Aware Disentangled Learning for Plan-Guided Longitudinal Tumor Segmentation in Head-and-Neck Adaptive Radiotherapy
abstract: Adaptive radiotherapy (ART) for head-and-neck (H&N) cancer requires reliable longitudinal delineation of primary and nodal gross tumor volumes (GTVp/GTVn) to update treatment plans under evolving anatomy. Clinically, mid-treatment (midRT) contouring anchors to stable anatomical landmarks while interpreting deviations in tumor-bearing regions as treatment response; however, many learning-based methods either decouple pre-treatment (preRT) from midRT or impose overly global temporal consistency, thereby under-modeling the heterogeneous, target-dependent evolution of GTVp/GTVn. We propose RaD-Seg, a clinically grounded framework that mirrors the plan–verify–adapt workflow via three modules: (i) Region-Aware Dual-Stream Contrastive Learning uses region prototypes to disentangle stable anatomical anchors from response-sensitive features, maintaining spatial reliability and sensitivity to regression; (ii) Temporal-Difference Response Encoding encodes cumulative radiation effects as an explicit preRT–midRT residual code to modulate midRT representations, rather than conflating response with incidental appearance variation; and (iii) Plan-Guided Asymmetric Regularization anchors midRT semantics to the preRT planning definition in anatomically stable regions while permitting clinically plausible target evolution. Patient-level cross-validation on HNTS-MRG 2024 shows significant gains in midRT GTVp/GTVn delineation over strong baselines.
subject_areas: Special Topic -> AI for Population Health, Public Health & Epidemiology

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: In this paper, the authors introduce a three-module approach called RaD-Seg for GTVp/GTVn longitudinal segmentation in head-and-neck adaptive radiotherapy treatment planning. These modules are inspired from the clinical paradigm of plan-verify-adapt and are validated on the HNTS-MRG 2024 dataset (N=150). In this study, RaD-Seg has been found to outperform five baseline approaches significantly. Although the clinical rationale behind the work is quite obvious and the ablation study is fairly thorough, the current version of this manuscript lacks in technical accuracy, experimental validation, and methodology.
reviews.text_strengths:
One of the most valuable strengths of the paper is the association between specific technical modules and individual workflow phases of ART. Asymmetric focus on stable and regressing anatomy is highly justified.
Evaluating all modules and module pair combinations listed in Table 1 and conducting statistical significance tests is highly responsible research-wise. That each module works in addressing a different type of failure mode is an evident conclusion.
Although the Dice score improvements compared to the best existing solution (Dual Flow UNet) are relatively small (+0.20% for GTVp and +1.31% for GTVn), the Hausdorff distance reductions are impressive: GTVp from 6.45 to 4.25 mm, and GTVn from 9.81 to 7.55 mm. The boundary accuracy matters clinically much more than volume overlap in contouring tasks.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper fails to mention τ (contrastive temperature in Equation 2), m (margin in Equation 4), r (dilation radius in Equation 10), and any of the loss weighting factors in the compound objective function (Equation 13). These parameters are crucial and significantly influence the learning process and how the different losses interact with each other. Their absence makes the replication and fair comparison of the method impossible. As a multi-objective training is the primary contribution of the paper, this is a significant gap. There is no sensitivity analysis performed on these factors.
The anchor mask Ω_anc is derived from the ground-truth preRT label Y_pre using equation (10). It has been stated in the paper that “Inference requires only (I_pre, I_mid). “ This suggests that Y_pre cannot be obtained during inference. In the case where the anchor mask Ω_anc is defined using the predicted preRT label map, it should be stated clearly. This is because an error in estimating the anchor mask will affect the plan constraint. In addition, in the case where PGAR only performs during training but not at inference time, then this is very significant information that should be stated clearly, since it shows that plan-guided constraints do not incorporate boundary awareness at inference time.
Using a single encoder E for both preRT and midRT assumes the two timepoints live in a shared feature space, despite known appearance differences due to radiation-induced edema, tumor regression, and weight loss. The lack of an ablation study or comparison with a dual encoder approach leaves us wondering about their impact.
VoxelMorph is a registration algorithm and not a segmentation technique. It is listed in Table 2 without further description on how the midRT segmentations are created based on VoxelMorph (for example, deform the preRT label maps using the deformation fields computed). The comparison itself is not flawed. However, without this information, it is impossible to determine if the baseline is unfairly treated or disadvantaged.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This manuscript offers a highly clinically motivated approach with HD95 improvements compared to the best baseline being significant and relevant. In addition, the three proposed modules complement each other and exhibit strong ablative results. However, there are two reasons why I cannot confidently accept this work. First, all important hyperparameters such as contrastive temperature τ, margin m, dilation radius r, and composite loss coefficients are not specified, meaning that the work is not reproducible without them, and it remains unknown whether its performance is stable for different parameter values. Second, the role of PGAR during inference is unclear since Ω_anc is calculated based on Y_pre during training, while the authors claim that no labels are required during inference.

reviews.text_contribution:
The authors present a clinically grounded framework that mirrors the plan–verify–adapt workflow in head-and-neck tumor segmentation targeting adaptive radiotherapy. They encode pre-RT MR and mid-RT MR images using a shared encoder into anatomy and response features, respectively, and enhance segmentation performance using three modules and corresponding losses:
L_ana: To enforce temporal consistency of background prototypes
L_resp: To encourage low temporal drift for background anchors and temporal signatures for target structures (i.e., GTVp and GTVn)
L_plan: To anchor midRT prediction masks to preRT prediction masks (i.e., plan semantics in stable anatomy) without forcing preRT features to explain midRT changes.
The authors evaluate their method called RaD-Seg on the HNTS-MRG 2024 cohort (MICCAI Challenge 2024) for midRT segmentation of GTVp and GTVn, achieving statistically significant improvements over SOTA baselines.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for their constructive assessment and for recognizing the clinical motivation, ablation design, and boundary improvements of RaD-Seg. We address the main concerns below.
-Reproducibility and hyperparameters. We agree that these details should be explicit. In our implementation, the contrastive temperature in Eq. (2) was τ=0.1, the response-margin in Eq. (4) was m=1.0, and the dilation radius in Eq. (10) was r=5 voxels after resampling to 1-mm isotropic spacing. The full objective in Eq. (13) used equal weights of 1.0 for all four terms, i.e., L=Lseg+Lana+Lresp+Lplan, with Lseg=CE+Dice. These values were fixed for all folds, ablations, and comparisons, with no test-set tuning. The choice of r corresponds to a 5-mm exclusion margin around preRT targets, avoiding excessive plan consistency near potentially regressing boundaries; m=1.0 encourages non-trivial response separation without over-enforcing temporal divergence. We will add these details, the backbone/channel configuration, training protocol, and the value for τ, m, r, and loss weights.
-Role of PGAR and use of labels. PGAR is a training-time regularizer. Ωanc is derived from the preRT planning label only during training to define reliable non-target regions and avoid using midRT labels for the plan constraint. At inference, neither Ypre, Ωanc, Ymid, nor the frozen plan teacher is required; the trained student directly predicts the midRT mask from (Ipre, Imid). Thus, the plan prior is distilled into the representation and decoder during optimization, while deployment follows the stated image-only input setting. We will explicitly state this distinction.
-Baseline and backbone clarification. The “Baseline” in Table 1 is not an external method; it is the same encoder-decoder backbone as RaD-Seg, trained with concatenated preRT–midRT input and only Lseg, without RDC, TDRE, or PGAR. Therefore, the ablation isolates the proposed modules rather than model size. Its stronger performance than nnU-Net mainly comes from paired longitudinal input and the same task-specific training setup, not from additional RaD-Seg losses. We will introduce this baseline clearly and report the exact encoder type.
-Shared encoder. We agree that a dual-encoder design is a meaningful alternative. We chose a shared encoder to maintain longitudinal feature comparability between preRT and midRT and avoid extra capacity that could confound the ablation. Since the scans are from the same MRI sequence and ART workflow, a shared feature basis is appropriate, while regression, edema, and deformation are explicitly modeled by the response stream and TDRE rather than forced to be invariant. We will clarify this rationale.
-VoxelMorph comparison. VoxelMorph was used as a registration-based contour-propagation baseline: the preRT image was registered to the midRT image, the deformation field was applied to the preRT GTVp/GTVn labels, and the warped labels were evaluated as midRT segmentations. We will add this description to clarify that VoxelMorph is not treated as a direct segmentation network.
-Figures and presentation. We will correct “TDME” to “TDRE” and clarify that preRT images are only longitudinal references, while predictions target midRT. Green denotes predicted GTVn to highlight false-positive nodal over-delineation near prior/preRT GTVp; RaD-Seg suppresses this implausible leakage. We will revise captions/legends, align slices, enlarge panels, and declutter t-SNE plots.
-Clinical interpretation. We will strengthen the discussion by emphasizing that the main clinical benefit is improved boundary fidelity, reflected by HD_95 reductions for both GTVp and GTVn. Although dose-distribution analysis is beyond this study, more accurate midRT boundaries are directly relevant to target coverage, margin adaptation, and sparing of nearby organs-at-risk.

title: RadSLDP: Selective Local Differential Privacy for Radiology Vision-Language Models
abstract:
Medical Vision–Language Models (VLMs) for radiology report generation are often fine-tuned by external developers due to hospitals’ limited computational infrastructure. It requires sensitive patient data to be transmitted to untrusted training environments, which creates privacy risks. Standard Differential Privacy protects the trained model but assumes trusted access to raw data, making it unsuitable for untrusted external training. Local Differential Privacy (LDP) enables privacy-preserving training in untrusted settings by perturbing all text token embeddings before transmission but significantly degrading clinical utility. We observe that clinical reports contain both image-inferable and non-inferable content and define the non-inferable portion as non-visual clinical context (NVCC), such as demographics and medical history, which constitutes the primary privacy risk. To preserve privacy while maintaining utility, we propose RadSLDP, a selective LDP mechanism that perturbs only expert-validated NVCC token embeddings, with each protected embedding satisfying formal (ε, δ)-LDP via the Gaussian mechanism. As a result, RadSLDP matches or outperforms uniform LDP in 94% of comparisons. It improves BLEU-4 by 24–77% and CheXbert Micro-F1 by 87–108% on ReXGradient dataset. RadSLDP also exhibits lower performance variability across privacy budgets, enabling practical
privacy-preserving VLM fine-tuning in untrusted settings.
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers
Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose RadSLDP, a selective embedding-level Local Differential Privacy (LDP) mechanism designed for training radiology vision-language models in untrusted environments. The method is model-agnostic and selectively perturbs only the embeddings corresponding to Non-Visual Clinical Context (NVCC) tokens, providing formal (ε,δ)-LDP guarantees via the Gaussian mechanism. The effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated on three large-scale datasets, showing substantial utility improvements, including notable gains in BLEU-4 and Micro-F1 scores.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper presents a strong problem motivation by clearly identifying a realistic and important challenge: training medical vision-language models in untrusted external environments. It also effectively highlights the limitations of existing approaches, such as DP-SGD, which rely on trusted access to raw data and are therefore not suitable for this setting.
2.The authors introduce the concept of Non-Visual Clinical Context (NVCC), focusing on non-inferable components such as demographics and medical history. By selectively protecting these tokens and ensuring formal (ε,δ)-LDP guarantees via the Gaussian mechanism, the approach is both clinically meaningful and well-aligned with privacy risks, contributing to improved model utility.
3.The proposed RadSLDP method extends selective local differential privacy to multimodal vision-language models. Unlike prior approaches that apply uniform noise or focus only on text-based settings, this method selectively perturbs sensitive tokens, making it a simple, model-agnostic, and computationally efficient solution suitable for real-world deployment.
4.The paper includes strong experimental validation using three large-scale datasets—ReXGradient, CheXpert Plus, and MIMIC-CXR—across multiple model architectures. The results consistently demonstrate substantial improvements over baseline LDP, including significant gains in BLEU-4 and Micro-F1 scores across different privacy budgets.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The paper presents limited clinical evaluation, as the results are primarily reported using standard NLP metrics such as BLEU and Micro-F1.There is no validation or assessment from clinical experts (e. g. , radiologists), making it unclear how well the generated reports perform in real clinical settings or whether they are reliable for practical use.
2.The proposed approach relies on a multi-stage pipeline involving clustering, LLM-based labeling, and expert validation to identify NVCC-related sensitive tokens. This raises concerns about the method’s generalizability to new datasets, as the process for adapting or extending the annotation pipeline is neither clearly described nor validated.
3.Although experiments are conducted on three datasets, the comparison is limited. The method is primarily evaluated against uniform LDP, without including stronger or more relevant baselines such as DP-SGD adaptations or other selective DP approaches (e. g. , “Just Fine-tune Twice”). This limits the strength of the empirical validation.
4.Some experimental results require further clarification. For example, in Table 3, certain models (e. g. , LLaVA-7B and Qwen2-7B) do not show consistent improvements in BLEU scores across privacy budgets. The paper would benefit from a more detailed analysis explaining these trends.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper addresses an important and timely problem related to privacy-preserving training of medical vision-language models in untrusted environments and proposes a reasonable solution using selective local differential privacy. However, several key limitations prevent the paper from meeting the acceptance threshold.
The evaluation lacks clinical validation, as the performance of the proposed method is assessed only using NLP-based metrics without input from clinical experts. Additionally, the experimental comparison is limited, as the method is primarily evaluated against uniform LDP without including stronger or more relevant baselines. The paper also does not clearly address the generalizability of the approach to new data samples, despite being evaluated on three datasets, particularly given its reliance on a complex annotation pipeline.
Furthermore, the experimental results require deeper analysis. For instance, as noted in Table 3, certain models do not show improvement in BLEU scores as the privacy budget (ε) increases, which is counterintuitive and not sufficiently explained. This raises concerns about the robustness and consistency of the proposed method.
Overall, while the paper attempts to address important limitations of existing privacy-preserving approaches, the lack of clinical validation, limited comparisons, and concerns regarding generalizability and result analysis lead to a weak reject recommendation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors provide a selection framework of NVCC tokens that require privacy protection and facilitate selective LDP on this set of tokens to reduce the aggregate data pertubation in the LDP setting.
reviews.text_strengths:
The motivation for focusing privacy protection on NVCC tokens in the ChestXrays domain is well-articulated and convincing.
The paper provides adequate background on differential privacy, enabling readers to understand the contribution, and includes a thoughtful discussion of the limitations inherent to embedding-level LDP.
The proposed approach appropriately incorporates expert validation to ensure the correctness of LLM-based NVCC token selection.
The experimental evaluation is comprehensive, spanning three datasets and multiple privacy configurations.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Major:
The authors should specify the δ values used across all experimental settings for reproducibility and clarity.
Minor:
It would strengthen the analysis to include a correlation study between dataset-level NVCC token proportions and the magnitude of benchmark score improvements. This would help explain why certain datasets (e.g., ReXGradient) show more substantial improvements compared to others.

N/A

Well presented and self-contained paper that provides an application focussed solution.

reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Delta claim was resolved, stays accept

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes RadSLDP, a selective Local Differential Privacy method for fine-tuning radiology VLMs when training is outsourced to untrusted parties. The key idea: clinical text has two parts — image-inferable findings (not private) and Non-Visual Clinical Context (NVCC) like demographics and history (private). Only NVCC token embeddings are clipped and perturbed with Gaussian noise; the rest pass through unchanged. Authors build a taxonomy of 347 subcategories from 141K clinical indications (PubMedBERT + HDBSCAN + GPT labels + physicist validation). Experiments on 3 datasets (ReXGradient, CheXpert Plus, MIMIC-CXR) with 3 VLMs (LLaVA-7B, Qwen2-7B, Qwen2-2B) show RadSLDP beats uniform LDP in 34/36 cases at ε=8.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper addresses a realistic and underexplored problem: hospitals without sufficient compute must outsource VLM fine-tuning to untrusted parties, a setting where DP-SGD’s trusted-curator assumption does not hold, making uniform LDP the correct baseline. The core insight — that clinical indication text separates into image-inferable content (not privacy-critical) and Non-Visual Clinical Context such as demographics and history (privacy-critical) — is intuitive and well-motivated. The taxonomy itself is the paper’s most substantive contribution: 347 expert-validated subcategories derived from 141,129 clinical indications pooled across three large datasets, built through a sensible pipeline of PubMedBERT embedding, HDBSCAN clustering, GPT labeling, and physicist review, with transparent reporting of the 5 corrections made. The formal privacy analysis is clean — Theorem 1 and the ∆₂ ≤ 2C sensitivity derivation are correct, and Remark 1 honestly lays out sequential, advanced, and Rényi composition rather than hiding the record-level question. Empirical evaluation is solid for an 8-page paper: three datasets, three VLM backbones, four complementary metrics, and the inclusion of DP-SGD and non-private results clearly marked “for reference only” reflects good scientific practice. The stability analysis in Table 3, showing lower BLEU-4 variance across ε values, is a nice touch that supports the selective-perturbation intuition.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Privacy claim is weaker than it reads. The guarantee is per-token (ε,δ)-LDP. With ~10.6 NVCC tokens per record, record-level ε at per-token ε=8 becomes ~85 under sequential composition — not meaningful privacy. The abstract and intro present ε=8 as if it were a record-level claim. This is the core issue.
Baseline comparison is not fair. Uniform LDP perturbs all 28.7 tokens; RadSLDP perturbs only 10.6.At the same per-token ε, RadSLDP consumes a much smaller record-level budget. So “beats LDP in 94% of cases” partly just reflects fewer tokens being noised. A matched record-level comparison is missing.
“Image-inferable = not sensitive” is informal. Tokens like “status post mastectomy” or “evaluation for TB” may be inferable from the X-ray but are still stigmatized medical info. Releasing them unperturbed confirms a condition an attacker could otherwise only guess. No formal leakage analysis is given.
Policy function relies on cluster-level LLM labels. HDBSCAN clusters are assumed to be semantically pure for inferability. Only 5/347 corrections reported; no phrase-level audit, no inter-annotator agreement, no handling of out-of-cluster phrases at inference.
Limited novelty. Selective DP for text already exists (Shi et al. NAACL’22, Just Fine-tune Twice, Wang et al. 2024, Yu et al. 2025, Mai et al. ICML’24). The mechanism (clip + Gaussian on selected embeddings) is standard. Real novelty is the NVCC taxonomy, not the method.
Missing experiments. No ablation separating demographic-regex vs. cluster labels. No empirical privacy attack (membership/attribute inference). ε sweep stops at 4 — no results at ε ≤ 1 where privacy is meaningful. No comparison to JFT [25] or [30] adapted to VLMs. No ablation over clipping norm C.
Minor issues. Fig. 1 typos (“Thread Model” → “Threat Model”, “Ouput” → “Output”). Abstract says 94% but 29/36 outperform + 5/36 match. “GPT-5.2” [21] cites a generic OpenAI URL — looks like a placeholder.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Real problem, sensible approach, useful taxonomy. But the privacy claim is per-token and the comparison to uniform LDP is not at matched record-level privacy, which makes the headline numbers misleading. The mechanism itself is a straightforward application of standard Gaussian LDP. The “image-inferable = safe” claim is informal and not empirically tested. I would raise to Weak Accept if the rebuttal provides (i) matched record-level comparisons, or (ii) an empirical privacy-attack evaluation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: All major concerns have been addressed during the rebuttal process.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper has mixed reviews. The review strongly recommending acceptance has not provided enough technical justification. Hence, this review cannot be trusted. The other two reviewers have raised valid concerns, especially regarding the clinical validation and experimental results as well as on the issue of record-level differential privacy. These issues must be addressed clearly in the rebuttal.

The main issues regarding record-level differential privacy clinically-oriented metrics have been clarified satisfactorily. This has also been acknowledged by two of the reviewers. Hence, the paper can be accepted.

All reviewers highlighted the importance of the paper and found the proposed method to be novel. Two reviewers recommended acceptance, while the reviewer recommending weak rejection raised concerns regarding the clinical evaluation. In the rebuttal, the authors clarified that the method was also evaluated using clinically relevant metrics.

The paper proposes RadSLDP, a selective embedding-level Local Differential Privacy (LDP) mechanism for fine-tuning radiology vision-language models in untrusted environments.
Based on the reviewers’ feedback and the authors’ rebuttal, I recommend accepting this manuscript. All three reviewers converged to accept post-rebuttal, 
The final version should clearly clarify the distinction between per-token and record-level privacy guarantees, provide matched record-level comparisons with uniform LDP, and address the minor presentation issues such as figure typos.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and MR for the feedback and for recognizing the motivation, NVCC taxonomy, formal privacy analysis, and evaluations. We address each below.
R1.1 Clinical evaluation: beyond BLEU/ROUGE we report CheXbert Micro-F1 and RadGraph F1 which are clinically oriented metrics, standard for clinical-content fidelity.
R1.2 Generalizability: the taxonomy pools indications from three datasets (500K+ studies, 141K units). Sec 2.2 describes that new indications are embedded and assigned to existing subcategories or grouped into new clusters. We will acknowledge that OOD will need additional annotation.
R1.3 Baselines: DP-SGD and JFT do not match our threat model. DP-SGD requires access to raw samples which JFT operates internally. RadSLDP privatizes inputs locally before transmission, so uniform embedding-LDP is the direct baseline. DP-SGD is a non-applicable reference (Tab 2).
R1.4 Tab 3: the near-flat RadSLDP behavior across ε is the stability property claimed. Since RadSLDP perturbs only 11 NVCC tokens on average, compared with 27 tokens for uniform LDP, changes in the Gaussian noise scale affect only a small fraction of the input. As ε grows and σ shrinks, the marginal effect on BLEU is then small.
R2.1 δ: δ=1/n where n is the training set size. With C=1.0 and ε, σ follows Thm.1 Eq.4. 
R2.2 NVCC% vs gain: NVCC proportion is similar across datasets (MIMIC 37.2%, CheX 36.6%, ReX 37.1%), so proportion does not explain the gap. ReXGradient has the shortest indications (24 vs 28 vs 30 tokens), so each preserved image-inferable token contributes more to the signal. LDP also has lower scores on ReXGradient, giving more headroom.
R3.1 Privacy claim: We clarify we state “each protected embedding satisfying formal (ε,δ)-LDP” not record-level. We acknowledge in Remark 1 that sequential composition gives (kε,kδ). However, our claim is RadSLDP outperforms uniform LDP at any matched ε. Under this bound, RadSLDP’s record-level budget (kε=11ε) is strictly smaller than uniform LDP’s (Lε=27ε) at higher utility. The privacy budget is tunable (e.g per-token ε=0.8 gives composed=8.5), and the same qualitative trend holds across settings as shown in Tab 3. 
R3.2 Fairness: both methods use the same mechanism, clipping norm, ε, δ per perturbed token, differing only in sensitivity policy. Fewer perturbed tokens is the intended benefit of the NVCC policy, not a confound. A record-level-matched comparison would change the per-token guarantee and answer a different threat model.
R3.3 Image-inferable: by “image-inferable”, we mean lower incremental leakage under the outsourced threat model, not absolute non-sensitivity. The trainer receives the de-identified radiograph, so image-inferable text adds less marginal information than NVCC. The framework is also extensible: in settings where image-inferable findings must be hidden, those tokens can be added to the protected set without changing the mechanism.
R3.4 Cluster labels: clustering is necessary at 141K units. New phrases go to the nearest cluster. Like spaCy-based detectors in prior selective-DP work [24,25,30,33], we acknowledge possible policy noise: false positives reduce utility, false negatives are residual privacy risk. Neither affects the LDP guarantee on selected tokens.
R3.5/3.6 Novelty: we do not claim novelty in the Gaussian mechanism. Our contribution is selective LDP for radiology VLM fine-tuning under an untrusted trainer plus the NVCC taxonomy. Prior selective DP only targets unimodal text. SLDP-FT[30] uses sequence-level S-SeqLDP, a different privacy unit from per-token (ε,δ)-LDP, and a privacy-forward-weight tied to BERT encoder layers for classification. Adapting to VLMs requires redesigning the privacy unit, sensitivity bound, and noise placement, constituting a new method.
MR: We thank the MR for the priorities. Priority concerns are addressed as follows. Clinical validation: R1.1.Experimental results: R1.3, 1.4, 3.2, 3.5/3.6.Record-level DP: R3.1.

title: RaLMPH: Reliability-Aware Learning for Multi-Pathologist Harmonization in Whole-Slide Image Classification
abstract: Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) is a standard paradigm for Whole-Slide Image (WSI) analysis and has achieved strong results in computational pathology. However, most MIL pipelines assume a single “gold” label per slide, which conflicts with clinical practice where substantial inter-pathologist variability is common. Existing multi-annotator learning and label-refinement methods typically estimate global annotator reliability or rely on single-instance assumptions, making them poorly suited to MIL and to localized diagnostic contexts where experts disagree. We propose RaLMPH (Reliability-aware Learning for Multi-Pathologist Harmonization), a MIL-based label reconciliation framework for WSIs annotated by multiple pathologists. RaLMPH introduces a reliability field that jointly models (i) local neighborhood structure in WSI feature space and (ii) expert uncertainty (entropy), enabling per-sample identification of trustworthy reference neighborhoods. Leveraging this field, RaLMPH performs sample-wise local annotator ranking to select reliable opinions per slide and applies an adaptive gating mechanism to fuse labels conditioned on local reliability. Experiments on a clinical WSI dataset with labels from six pathologists, as well as controlled simulated benchmarks, show that RaLMPH consistently outperforms existing approaches. Further analyses clarify how our reliability-aware mechanism improves label reconciliation and downstream MIL performance.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose RaLMPH, a Multiple Instance Learning framework for Whole Slide Image classification under multi-annotator disagreement. The core idea is to model the local feature-space neighborhood jointly with annotator-specific trust estimates in order to derive reliable pseudo-labels for ambiguous samples. These labels are then used to supervise two alternative MIL backbones. The method is evaluated on an in-house dataset annotated by six pathology experts at the WSI level, and on a public dataset with synthetically generated multi-rater labels. Competitive performance is reported against several baselines from the label-noise and crowdsourcing literature.
reviews.text_strengths:
Clinically relevant dataset and problem formulation. The use of a real-world WSI dataset with labels from 6 independent pathology experts is a notable contribution. Such datasets are difficult to obtain in the computational pathology literature because of the high burden for pathologists.
Robustness to reduced annotator count. Figure 3 demonstrates that model performance does not degrade dramatically when fewer annotators are available. This is an important practical property to better understand the framework’s applicability in realistic annotation scenarios.
Thorough ablation study. The ablation analysis is comprehensive and provides meaningful insight into the contribution of individual components. The authors adequately justify the empirical value of each design choice, which strengthens confidence in the method.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Incomplete comparison with SoTA learning from crowds methods. The evaluation does not include recent end-to-end learning from crowds baselines based on transition matrices. Methods such as those learning annotator confusion matrices jointly with the classifier (e. g. , [1],[2],[3]) would provide a more informative comparison. The current set of baselines does not allow the reader to disentangle how much benefit comes from the preprocessing of labels versus the MIL backbone itself. Including these baselines is essential to properly contextualize the contribution and assess whether a fully end-to-end approach would be competitive.
Insufficient theoretical motivation for the diagonal structure of the reliability field. In Eq. (1), the weight matrix M_nm is constrained to be diagonal. This effectively reduces the distance modulation to a per-feature rescaling and ignores all inter-feature correlations. The authors do not provide a principled justification for this choice. A diagonal approximation may be computationally convenient, but it requires explicit motivation. Without this, the reliability field as formulated appears to be an ad hoc design decision.
The “pushing ambiguous samples further apart” inductive bias is not well-justified. The reliability field Phi is designed to increase distances between samples with high label entropy or feature variance. The implicit assumption is that ambiguous samples should be separated in the clustering step. However, ambiguous samples may naturally occupy a fuzzy intermediate region of the feature space — precisely because the underlying biology is genuinely borderline — and artificially inflating distances between them could fragment meaningful clusters or distort the neighborhood structure.
Sparse annotation setting not fully explored. While the experiment with fewer annotators (second strength above) partially addresses annotation efficiency, it still assumes that all available annotators have labeled all samples. In practice, a more realistic and economically motivated scenario is one where annotation effort is distributed across the crowd, so that each sample is only labeled by a subset of annotators. It would substantially strengthen the paper to include an experiment where labels are sparsely assigned — simulating a crowdsourcing protocol — and to evaluate whether the framework remains effective in this setting. This would directly speak to the practical utility of the proposed approach in real annotation pipelines.
References
[1] Li, S. , Xia, X. , Deng, J. , Ge, S. , & Liu, T. (2024). Transferring annotator-and instance-dependent transition matrix for learning from crowds.  IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence, 46(11), 7377-7391. 
[2] Chu, Z. , Ma, J. , & Wang, H. (2021, May). Learning from crowds by modeling common confusions. In Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (Vol. 35, No. 7, pp. 5832-5840).  
[3] Gil-González, J. , Daza-Santacoloma, G. , Cárdenas-Peña, D. , Orozco-Gutiérrez, A. , & Álvarez-Meza, A. (2025). Generalized cross-entropy for learning from crowds based on correlated chained Gaussian processes.  Results in Engineering, 25, 103863.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses a clinically relevant and underexplored problem, presents a genuinely multi-annotator WSI dataset, which is difficult to encounter in the literature, and provides a thorough ablation study. However, several technical design choices lack sufficient theoretical justification, the comparison against state-of-the-art learning-from-crowds methods is incomplete (it misses confusion matrices methods as the one I suggested to the authors in my review), and a key practical scenario — sparse, non-exhaustive annotation — is only partially explored, which is of clear importance for posterior deployment.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors have not adequately addressed my concerns.
Regarding the lack of baselines, the authors do not clarify why they did not compare their method with the cited literature, nor do they discuss how this absence of comparison affects the validity and positioning of the present study.
Regarding the theoretical rationale, the authors reiterate the model workflow instead of providing a clear argument for the conceptual and methodological foundations of the work.
I believe this work has potential; however, in its current form, I do not consider it suitable for publication at MICCAI. Nevertheless, I encourage the authors to carefully consider the feedback and further strengthen the work for future submissions.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a label reconciliation framework for MIL-based WSI classification with multiple pathologist annotations. It introduces a reliability field that couples bag-level feature variance with label entropy to identify trustworthy neighborhoods, combined with a sample-wise local expert ranking and an adaptive gating mechanism for label fusion. Unlike prior multi-annotator methods that assume global annotator reliability or single-instance data, RaLMPH specifically targets the localized nature of diagnostic authority in clinical pathology.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The motivation is well grounded. Inter-pathologist disagreement on WSI labels is a real bottleneck in clinical pipelines, and existing multi-annotator literature almost exclusively targets single-instance data, leaving the MIL setting unaddressed. The paper’s framing, that pathologist disagreement reflects locally varying expertise rather than global noise, matches how diagnostic workflows actually operate.
2.The empirical comparison is fairly thorough. RaLMPH is benchmarked against a reasonable set of baselines across two MIL backbones and three datasets, including one real multi-expert clinical cohort.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The method defines an expert’s local reliability based on the cosine similarity between their individual label and the local mean label. However, relying on the mean/consensus to evaluate reliability contradicts the paper’s core motivation that simple consensus is often insufficient or misleading in ambiguous WSI regions. This formulation risks simply upweighting experts who conform to the majority, rather than identifying true specialized diagnostic authority in cases of high disagreement.
2.According to Sec 3.1, the test set ground truth is determined through “experts’ agreement” from the same cohort. Evaluating a multi-annotator reconciliation method against a consensus generated by the same annotator pool may introduce bias. A more objective evaluation of clinical utility would require an external gold standard, such as IHC results, patient clinical outcomes, or a completely independent panel of senior pathologists.
3.Table 1 reports the mean and standard deviation for Accuracy and AUC. However, given the relatively small margins of improvement and overlapping standard deviations between RaLMPH and strong baselines, statistical significance tests are necessary to confirm the validity of the performance gains.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper addresses a highly practical problem in computational pathology of handling inter-pathologist variability in MIL, and the proposed reliability-aware framework demonstrates consistent empirical improvements across multiple datasets.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The motivation of this paper is reasonable, and the experimental validation is quite sufficient, so I recommend acceptance.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses multi-pathologist label variability in whole-slide image (WSI) classification under Multiple Instance Learning (MIL). The authors propose RaLMPH, a reliability-aware label reconciliation framework that builds a reliability field combining bag-level feature variance and annotator entropy to define a neighborhood metric, ranks locally reliable experts per sample, and fuses opinions via an adaptive gating mechanism. Experiments on a real clinical dataset with six pathologists and on public datasets with synthesized experts show consistent improvements over strong baselines and recent multi-annotator methods.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper introduces a technically novel framework that incorporates a reliability field, local expert sorting, and adaptive gating, enabling more precise modeling of annotator reliability and label fusion at the sample level.
2.It demonstrates solid experimental rigor, with consistent improvements across multiple MIL backbones, well-designed ablations, and evaluations on both real multi-expert datasets and controlled synthetic settings.
3.The presentation is clear and well-motivated, with an intuitive pipeline and effective use of figures to illustrate the key components.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The authors cited ‘CONCH’[14] and ‘Madeleine’[9] as two pre-trained feature encoders in the training setting part. But there is no comparison experiments on how they performed differently towards the task.
2.While the reliability field is a novel concept, its formulation (combining entropy and variance in a Mahalanobis-like metric) may be difficult to interpret clinically or theoretically. How does this concept related to pathological understanding?
3.While the reported improvements are generally consistent, the experimental evaluation lacks statistical significance testing. The multi-annotator setting primarily relies on synthetic annotators, which raises concerns about real-world applicability. Is it applicable in the clinical scenario?
4.Is it possible to test on more backbones and compare the performance?
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper tackles an important and underexplored problem in computational pathology, and it is conceptually well-aligned with clinical realities of localized expertise and ambiguous cases. The work would benefit from clearer mathematical/execution details, statistical significance reporting, and broader comparisons to probabilistic multi-annotator fusion adapted to MIL. Nonetheless, the contributions are original and practically relevant, with thorough ablations and useful analyses. I view this as a solid and valuable contribution for MICCAI.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Although the authors’ response has partially solved my concerns, the proposed method is a novel trial to this area. Therefore, I made my final decision to accept this paper.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper received mixed reviews, including two weak accepts and one weak reject. The work addresses a clinically important and relatively underexplored problem: handling multi-pathologist disagreement in MIL-based WSI classification. The positive reviews recognize the strong motivation, the value of using a real multi-expert clinical cohort, and the promise of the proposed reliability-aware label reconciliation framework, with empirical improvements and ablation studies providing some support for the main design choices. However, the reviewers also raise important concerns regarding incomplete comparison with recent learning-from-crowds methods, insufficient theoretical or clinical justification for the reliability-field formulation, and potential bias in the evaluation protocol due to the use of consensus labels from the same annotator pool as the test reference. The paper would also benefit from statistical significance testing and further analysis under realistic sparse annotation settings where not every annotator labels every sample. Overall, the paper has meaningful clinical motivation, a valuable problem setting, and encouraging results, but several aspects of the formulation and evaluation remain insufficiently justified; therefore, the authors are invited to submit a rebuttal before a final decision is made.

After rebuttal, this paper receives two accept recommendations and one rejection. The AC acknowledges that RaLMPH addresses an important and underexplored problem in computational pathology: reconciling multi-pathologist disagreement for MIL-based WSI classification. The paper is clinically well motivated, uses a valuable real-world cohort annotated by six pathologists, and proposes a reliability-aware framework that models local expert reliability rather than relying on simple consensus. The rebuttal addresses several key concerns by clarifying the comparison with learning-from-crowds methods, the rationale for the reliability field, the evaluation protocol, statistical testing, and the scope of sparse-annotation settings. Although some concerns remain regarding theoretical justification and broader comparison with recent annotator-confusion models, the majority of reviewers agree that the method is novel, practically relevant, and empirically validated across multiple datasets and MIL backbones. Therefore, the AC recommends acceptance.

Overall, the reviewers acknowledge the strong clinical motivation, novel formulation, and generally solid empirical performance, with two reviewers supporting acceptance after rebuttal. While some concerns remain regarding incomplete comparisons, limited theoretical justification, and potential evaluation bias, the rebuttal partially addressed these issues and strengthened confidence in the methodology.

The paper proposes RaLMPH, a reliability-aware multiple-instance learning framework for WSI classification under multi-pathologist disagreement. The method models local feature-space neighborhoods together with annotator-specific reliability estimates to derive reliable pseudo-labels or harmonized labels for ambiguous samples, and evaluates the approach on a real WSI dataset annotated by six pathology experts as well as public datasets with synthetic multi-rater labels.
The initial reviews were mixed but overall close to positive, with scores of 3 / 4 / 4.Reviewers appreciated the clinical relevance of the problem, the use of a real multi-pathologist WSI dataset, the attempt to model localized diagnostic reliability rather than global annotator reliability, the empirical improvements across MIL backbones/datasets, and the ablation analyses. The main concerns were incomplete comparison to recent learning-from-crowds baselines, insufficient theoretical justification for the reliability-field formulation and its diagonal/metric structure, possible bias in using expert agreement from the same cohort as ground truth, lack of sparse-annotation evaluation, limited statistical significance reporting, and incomplete comparison of pretrained feature encoders.
The rebuttal addressed several of these concerns. The authors clarified that GLAD was included as a comparison, explained the design rationale for the reliability field and channel-wise feature rescaling, emphasized that expert entropy reflects biological ambiguity, clarified that the method targets a fixed expert cohort rather than generic crowdsourcing, and provided additional explanation regarding statistical testing and feature extractor usage. They also noted that the in-house dataset contains 1,382 WSIs annotated by six experts and argued that results on public datasets support generalization.
Some concerns remain. Reviewer 1 was not persuaded that the rebuttal adequately addressed the missing learning-from-crowds comparisons or the conceptual justification of the reliability-field formulation. The evaluation protocol still relies partly on expert agreement as the target and does not fully resolve the concern about an independent gold standard. The sparse-annotation setting is also left largely as future work. Thus, the paper remains somewhat borderline.
After rebuttal, the reviewer opinions are R / A / A. Reviewer 1 maintained reject due to unresolved concerns about baselines and theoretical rationale. Reviewers 2 and 3 recommend accept, emphasizing that the problem is clinically relevant, the motivation is reasonable, the experimental validation is generally sufficient, and the method is a novel attempt in an important area. I place slightly greater weight on the two positive post-rebuttal assessments and the practical relevance of the real multi-pathologist WSI setting, while acknowledging the unresolved conceptual and evaluation limitations.
I recommend Accept. The paper addresses an important and clinically realistic problem, and the use of real multi-expert pathology annotations is valuable. Although the theoretical justification and comparison to recent learning-from-crowds approaches should be strengthened, the reviewer consensus after rebuttal is moderately positive, and the remaining issues appear to be limitations rather than fatal flaws. The camera-ready version should clearly discuss the assumptions behind the reliability field, the limitations of using expert agreement as reference, the lack of sparse-label evaluation, and the scope of comparison to learning-from-crowds methods.

author_feedback_text:
We appreciate the constructive comments. We also appreciate that the reviewers recognized the clinical relevance(R1-3,M) and empirical rigor(R1,R3,M) of RaLMPH.
[R1]
We fully concur with your feedback. As noted in the 3rd Para. of the Intro., we cited the recommended [2] as citation [3], with GLAD[25]. Viewing them as a hidden-state approach, we included GLAD for comparison, which utilizes an EM-algorithm for end-to-end training. RaLMPH consistently outperformed GLAD across experiments. We will certainly consider your valuable recommendations in our future work.
This design was to enable parallelized feature rescaling while modulating channel-wise operation. Label entropy H acts as a slide-level scalar factor across all channels of z_n, while sigma is computed per channel via feature D.O.[18]. Since [18] is applied to dropped z_n, using WSI encoder[9], the inherent inter-channel correlations captured by the [9] are relevant rather than ignored. We will clarify it in the revised manuscript to address your valuable feedback.
We would like to emphasize that the annotations were provided by certified pathologists, whose H captures biological ambiguity. Fig.2 demonstrates that RaLMPH achieves meaningful alignment by integrating both ambiguous WSI features and experts H into the construction of Phi. Our quantitative analysis also confirms this synergy enhanced WSI comprehension.
RaLMPH demonstrated robustness in the Sec. 3.3, even when J'<<J. Our study targets clinical expert cohorts where a fixed group of specialists collaborates, which differs from a crowdsourcing where sparse labels from unknown workers are common. We appreciate and concur with your comment. Accordingly, we will reflect this to limitation section and plan to investigate it the furture work.
[R2]
We appreciate your concern and would like to clarify the following. The reliability field Phi, which precedes the Local Reliable Expert Sorting, incorporates the multiple experts opinions via label entropy H. Consequently, prior to identifying a specific diagnostic authority, Phi determines cluster assignments by comprehensively integrating the insights of all experts.
Involving a consistent cohort across the entire splits reflects actual clinical practice, where the goal of clinical MIL is to emulate expert judgment[22]. We also agree with your concern and we proactively evaluated RaLMPH on two public dataset. The consistent performance gains across these benchmarks demonstrate that RaLMPH’s utility is generalizable.
We appreciate your suggestion to strengthen our study. We have confirmed a significant improvement p<.05(.01) on the BCNB, While the margins in some metrics of In-house and BRACS may appear small, the consistency of improvement across all 3 datasets and 2 diverse backbones underscores the superiority of RaLMPH. We will add these statistical results to Tab.1 and describe them faithfully in the manuscript.
[R3]
We apologize for the confusing description. CONCH[14] is a patch-level extractor, while Madeleine[9] is a WSI-level extractor trained on CONCH features. The citation error in Sec. 2.1 (citing [14] instead of [9]) caused the misunderstanding in the experimental description. We have corrected this in the manuscript.
Pathologists' opinions on a WSI can vary significantly[24], with levels of disagreement differing across cases[6]. Motivated by this, we developed Phi to jointly consider expert opnions and sample representations. Please see responses to R1-Q2 and Q3 for additional details.
Please refer to response to R2-Q3 regarding the statistical test.
The In-house dataset (1,382 WSIs, annotated by 6 experts) serves as a real-world validation of RaLMPH, proving its efficacy in meeting actual clinical requirements beyond benchmarks.
In this study, we focused on widely-validated MIL frameworks to ensure a reliable comparison. We agree with your suggestion and will actively consider it for follow-up studies.

title: RAM-Missing: Retrieval-Augmented Missing-Aware Fusion for Robust Lung Cancer Subtyping
abstract: In real-world clinical settings, multimodal medical data are often characterized by severe modality imbalance and structured missingness. In our tri-modal lung cancer cohort (WSI, CT, RNA), 75.4% of patients lack CT scans. Most existing multimodal learning methods implicitly assume complete modality availability or rely on naive imputation, leading to catastrophic performance collapse when applied to highly incomplete deployment data. To address this challenge, we propose RAM-Missing, a Retrieval-Augmented Missing-aware fusion framework designed for robust lung cancer subtyping under severe missingness. Specifically, our framework introduces three key components: (1) We design a Retrieval-Augmented Proxy Generator that constructs proxy embeddings for missing CTs by querying a historical memory bank. (2) We introduce a Retrieval Uncertainty Quantifier that mathematically estimates retrieval entropy to gauge the reliability of these proxies. (3) We propose an Uncertainty-Guided Conditional Router that dynamically allocates fusion experts based on the modality mask and uncertainty signal, effectively preventing the model from over-trusting low-quality imputed features. Extensive experiments using patient-level 5-fold cross-validation demonstrate that RAM-Missing consistently mitigates catastrophic degradation under extreme missing ratios, achieving superior prevalence-weighted AUROC and cross-fold stability compared to conventional fusion strategies. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Flliin/RAMMissing.
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers
Applications -> Outcome Prediction / Prognosis / Longitudinal Modeling
Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This work presents a retrieval-augmented framework for dealing with missing modality in lung cancer subtyping. Specifically, the authors consider the missing of CT scans while WSI and RNA are available. Missing CT is dealt with embedding-based cross-modality retrieval, and then the three modalities are fused by an uncertainty-guided conditional router. The method was validated on the TCGA lung cancer dataset, showing that the proposed method could achieve robust performance under high missing ratios.
reviews.text_strengths:
1, the authors deal with a practical problem in cancer subtyping, where missing modality affect the performance of AI systems 
2, the design of MoE fusion can deal with multi-modality and fuse them adaptively
3, The method show stable performance under different CT missing ratio
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1, The authors assume that Eq. 1 can retrieval similar cross modality cases. However, this assumption may not hold when the three encoders are not aligned during pretraining. It seems that the three encoders are pretrained separately (WSI encoder is ResNet50 pretrained on ImageNet, while 3D ResNet is trained on CT). As they are not well aligned, one cannot ensure that the feature similarity-based retrieval works. Therefore, the rational of the method is limited. In addition, the authors did not report the performance of cross-modality retrieval, so it is unclear how this step is reliable.
2, The missing modality problem setting does not match clinical practice. The author said that “High-cost imaging modalities such as CT are often available only for a subset of patients, whereas pathology and transcriptomic data are more routinely collected”. This is not correct in most clinical environment. CT scanning is much cheaper than WSI and transcriptomic data. For lung cancer patient, CT scanning is usually first obtained for preliminary diagnosis, if the patient is suspicious of cancer, then WSI is obtained for further diagnosis. Especially in underdeveloped regions, patients may not have WSI and RNA information, but CT scans are more available. It is more practical to consider the missing of WSI/RNA rather than the missing of CT.
3, The method was only validated on one dataset, which makes it generalizability to other datasets unknown. The author also did not consider the missing of WSI and RNA.
4, The experimental results are unconvincing. Table 1 shows that only using WSI or RNA leads to an AUROC of 0.68 and 0.64, respectively. When CT is missing, a baseline method combining WSI and RNA is expected to achieve AUROC higher than 0.68.However, the authors’ method only has an AUROC of 0.509, which is much lower than the baseline and single modality prediction.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The problem setting does not match clinical practice, and the method rationale is weak, with unconvincing experimental results
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Due to the unrealistic problem setting, poor alignment between the encoders of different modalities and unconvincing results, I keep my score for the review. Though the authors tried to explain these issues, the reply does address the concerns.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes RAM-Missing, a retrieval-augmented missing-aware fusion framework for multimodal lung cancer subtyping under severe modality imbalance. The method addresses a realistic clinical setting where CT scans are frequently missing by constructing proxy CT embeddings through a memory-based retrieval mechanism. It further introduces an entropy-based uncertainty quantification to estimate the reliability of retrieved proxies and integrates this signal into a mixture-of-experts (MoE) fusion module via a conditional routing mechanism. The framework is evaluated on a tri-modal TCGA cohort (WSI, CT, RNA) and demonstrates improved robustness and stability under high missingness scenarios compared to standard multimodal fusion approaches.
reviews.text_strengths:
Clinically relevant problem formulation: The paper explicitly addresses severe modality missingness (e.g., 75.4% CT missing), which is highly realistic in clinical practice and often overlooked in multimodal learning .
Well-structured and interpretable framework: The proposed architecture (Fig. 1) clearly separates modality encoding, retrieval-based proxy generation, uncertainty estimation, and adaptive fusion, making the design easy to follow and interpret .
Uncertainty-aware fusion mechanism: Incorporating entropy-based uncertainty into the routing decision is a meaningful contribution that helps mitigate over-reliance on potentially noisy imputed modalities.
Demonstration of catastrophic failure in baselines: The paper provides strong evidence that standard fusion methods collapse under missing modalities (Table 1), which is an important and valuable insight.
Comprehensive ablation studies: The contribution of each module (retrieval, router, uncertainty) is systematically evaluated (Table 2), strengthening the validity of the design.
Robustness analysis: Evaluation across varying missingness levels (Table 3) provides useful insight into model stability under realistic deployment conditions.
Use of prevalence-weighted metrics: The adoption of weighted AUC aligned with real-world modality distribution is appropriate and improves evaluation realism.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Outdated WSI backbone choice:
The WSI encoder relies on a ResNet-50 pretrained on ImageNet with global average pooling (p.3) . However, recent work in computational pathology has demonstrated the superiority of self-supervised and transformer-based models (e.g., DINO/ViT variants) for capturing fine-grained morphological features. The authors do not justify this design choice, which may limit performance.
Suboptimal pooling strategy:
The use of global average pooling for slide-level aggregation may dilute discriminative signals in heterogeneous WSIs. Alternative approaches such as max pooling or attention-based pooling are often more effective but are not explored or discussed.
Retrieval proxy validity is not validated:
The framework critically depends on retrieval-based proxy CT embeddings (p.4) , yet there is no direct evaluation of whether these proxies meaningfully approximate true CT features. This raises uncertainty about whether performance gains stem from meaningful reconstruction or architectural regularization.
Limited performance gains:
The improvement in weighted AUC (e.g., ~0.546 to 0.564 in Table 1) is relatively modest , and the clinical significance of this gain is not clearly justified.
Incomplete evaluation metrics:
The paper reports AUC-based metrics but does not include F1-score or other threshold-dependent metrics, which are important for evaluating classification performance in imbalanced clinical settings.
Limited dataset diversity:
The evaluation is restricted to a single TCGA cohort without external validation, raising concerns about generalizability.
No clinical/expert validation:
There is no assessment of whether retrieved proxies or predictions align with clinically meaningful patterns.
Simplistic uncertainty estimation:
The entropy-based uncertainty formulation may not fully capture the reliability of retrieved proxies and lacks deeper validation.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The paper addresses an important and practical challenge in multimodal medical AI. To further strengthen the work, the authors are encouraged to:
Justify the choice of ResNet-50 as the WSI backbone, or compare with modern self-supervised/pathology-specific encoders (e.g., DINO-based models).
Explore alternative feature aggregation strategies (e.g., max pooling or attention-based pooling).
Provide additional evaluation metrics such as F1-score for better clinical interpretability.
Validate the quality of retrieval-based proxy embeddings (e.g., similarity to ground-truth CT features).
Clarify the practical significance of the observed performance gains.
Provide external validation or cross-dataset evaluation.
Include clinical or expert-based assessment if possible.
Addressing these points would significantly strengthen the contribution.

This paper addresses a highly relevant problem in multimodal medical learning—robust performance under severe modality missingness—and proposes a well-motivated retrieval-augmented fusion framework with uncertainty-aware routing. The approach is technically sound and demonstrates improved robustness compared to standard baselines, particularly in preventing catastrophic performance degradation.
However, several limitations reduce the overall impact. The method relies on relatively simple unimodal encoders (e.g., ResNet-50 for WSI) and basic pooling strategies, which may not fully exploit available data. The evaluation lacks important metrics such as F1-score, and the observed improvements in AUC are relatively modest, raising questions about practical significance. Additionally, the key component of retrieval-based proxy generation is not sufficiently validated.
Overall, the paper presents a solid contribution with meaningful insights but would benefit from stronger validation, improved modeling choices, and more comprehensive evaluation.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper proposes RAM-Missing, a retrieval-augmented missing-aware fusion framework for multimodal lung cancer subtyping (LUAD vs. LUSC) under severe structured modality missingness. The setting involves tri-modal data (WSI, CT, RNA), where CT is missing in 75.4% of patients, reflecting a realistic and clinically relevant deployment scenario.
The method introduces three key components: (1) a retrieval-based CT proxy generator using a memory bank of complete cases, (2) an entropy-based uncertainty estimator for retrieval reliability, and (3) a conditional Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) fusion mechanism that dynamically routes information based on modality availability and uncertainty signals. Extensive experiments on TCGA with patient-level cross-validation and realistic missingness patterns demonstrate strong robustness and significant mitigation of catastrophic performance degradation.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Strong clinical relevance and realistic problem setting
The paper addresses an important and practically relevant problem: multimodal cancer diagnosis under severe and structured missingness. The reported CT missing rate (75.4%) reflects real-world clinical constraints rather than artificially simulated missing patterns, significantly increasing the practical value of the study.
2.Well-motivated robustness objective
Unlike many multimodal learning works that focus solely on average-case performance, this paper explicitly targets worst-case robustness and failure prevention under missing modalities. The use of prevalence-weighted AUROC and stress testing under varying missing ratios is appropriate and clinically meaningful.
3.Clear and coherent methodological design
The proposed framework is well-structured and logically consistent:
Retrieval-based proxy construction effectively addresses missing CT modalities.
Uncertainty estimation via entropy provides a principled signal for reliability assessment.
Conditional MoE routing enables adaptive fusion and mitigates the risk of relying on noisy imputed features.
The overall architecture is well-motivated and easy to follow.
4.Strong robustness and stability analysis
The experimental results demonstrate consistent improvements in missing-CT scenarios and, more importantly, significant reduction in catastrophic performance collapse (AUC < 0.5 cases). The stress test under increasing missingness ratios further strengthens the claim of robustness.
5.Potential clinical impact
The emphasis on avoiding failure cases rather than solely improving average performance is particularly important for medical applications. The proposed uncertainty-aware routing mechanism improves interpretability and may increase clinician trust in multimodal AI systems.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Moderate methodological novelty
While the overall framework is well-designed, the individual components (retrieval-based imputation, entropy-based uncertainty, and MoE routing) are relatively well-established. The novelty lies primarily in their integration and application to a realistic missing-modality clinical setting.
However, given the strong motivation and careful system design, this does not significantly reduce the contribution.
2.Limited external validation
The evaluation is restricted to TCGA data. Although the missingness simulation is realistic, cross-institutional validation would further strengthen claims regarding generalizability.
3.Heuristic nature of uncertainty modeling
The uncertainty estimation is based on Shannon entropy of retrieval weights, which is intuitive but relatively simple. A more principled probabilistic calibration analysis could further improve methodological rigor.
