reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents a study that predicts long-term visual acuity following anti-VEGF therapy for diabetic macular edema by combining OCT images with clinical data. By integrating large-scale models for each modality—such as RETFound ViT-Large and T2G-Former—with techniques like LoRA, Cross-Attention, and Temporal Learner, the authors have successfully improved prediction performance. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that using information from two visits in a complementary manner improves accuracy compared to simple single-time-point predictions. It effectively combines state-of-the-art methods, and the role and effectiveness of each method are clearly illustrated through ablation studies. The text is well-structured and easy to understand.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.By effectively utilizing foundation models, the authors achieve high-accuracy visual acuity prognosis predictions using a relatively small dataset. Given the limited availability of labeled data in prognosis prediction, this approach is expected to become the standard practice.
2.The approach of combining information from multiple visits is reasonable from a clinical perspective, and the authors also explain the clinical rationale for incorporating other methods.
3.Comprehensive benchmarking against previous methods has been conducted, and ablation studies have been performed appropriately.
4.The challenge of long-term visual acuity prediction is of high clinical importance, and the clinical significance of the improved prediction accuracy achieved by this method is discussed accurately.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The authors combine multiple deep learning methods, and ReVA is a framework with a very large number of parameters. It is unclear which of these parameters were fixed and which were learned from the data in this study. Since the model was trained on a small number of cases, it is believed that the number of parameters used for training should be reduced as much as possible to avoid overfitting.
2.In the abstract, the authors claim that a key advantage of this model is its ability to predict visual prognosis not only at 24 months but also at 3, 6, 12, and 18 months; however, the accuracy of these predictions at 3, 6, 12, and 18 months is not presented in the results or discussion sections, nor is the impact of these predictions on the 24-month prediction examined.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This is an excellent paper that effectively combines appropriate methods and provides clear clinical interpretation, and it appears that most of the validation was conducted appropriately. It is also interesting that the study demonstrates improved predictive accuracy with longitudinal data. This research would be of even greater value if the parameters trained using the data from this case series and the handling of the multiple endpoints highlighted as key features in the abstract were clarified.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper addresses an important and clinically meaningful problem: long-term visual acuity forecasting after anti-VEGF treatment using early OCT and clinical information. The proposed ReVA framework is practically motivated and shows promising performance, especially for 24-month visual acuity prediction. However, several key claims require stronger evidence. In particular, the paper frames the task as multi-horizon forecasting, but detailed per-horizon results for 3, 6, 12, and 18 months are not sufficiently reported. The role of auxiliary supervision from intermediate follow-up outcomes also needs to be validated through ablation. In addition, the reported performance gains are relatively modest, and the paper should provide stronger statistical testing against all major baselines. Since the tabular-only model is already close to the full multimodal model, simple clinical baselines based on baseline and month-1 VA should be included to justify the added architectural complexity. The authors should also clarify OCT alignment across visits, explain the heatmap visualization in Fig. 2 more rigorously, and provide a clearer release plan for code, pretrained models, and data.

All reviewers who provided explicit post-rebuttal opinions support acceptance. Reviewer #1 states that the authors addressed the raised questions, and Reviewer #3 indicates that the work was already acceptable before rebuttal and that the heatmap-related concern was resolved. The rebuttal also addresses the main meta-review concerns by providing per-horizon results, auxiliary-supervision ablation, a VA-only clinical baseline, paired Wilcoxon significance testing, cohort statistics, model-complexity clarification, and a clearer release plan for code and pretrained models. Remaining limitations, including single-center validation and modest dataset size, should be acknowledged in the final version, but they do not outweigh the paper’s clinical relevance and overall positive post-rebuttal consensus. The authors should provide the full open-source implementation to improve the reproducibility and broader impact of the paper.

All reviewers recommended acceptance for this paper. The authors should commit to addressing the remaining concerns in the camera-ready version. 1) more clearly report performance across all VA forecast horizons, not only the main 24-month. 2) clarify the incremental value of imaging over tabular-only predictors. 3) provide the statistical testing and uncertainty analysis. 4) provide a clear release plan for code, pretrained models, and data splits.

The paper addresses a clinically important problem and presents a practical multimodal framework for forecasting long-term visual acuity after anti-VEGF treatment. The use of baseline and month-1 OCT together with clinical variables is well motivated, and the overall framework is technically coherent. The experimental results, benchmarking, ablations, and interpretability analysis are solid.
The rebuttal addressed the main concerns convincingly. In particular, the authors clarified the response-aware modeling design, provided detailed per-horizon results, explained the handling of missing labels and auxiliary supervision, added statistical significance testing, and reported cohort statistics. They also clarified that only a small fraction of parameters are trainable, which helps address concerns about overfitting despite the large backbone.
Some limitations remain, especially the single-center dataset and the moderate methodological novelty, but these do not outweigh the strengths of the work.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for recognizing ReVA’s clinical importance, clear formulation, benchmarking, ablations, and interpretability analysis. We address the main concerns below.
[Meta/R1/R2: Novelty and response-aware modeling] Many prior VA prediction studies focus on single-endpoint prediction or short-term treatment response, whereas ReVA targets forecasting VA at 3/6/12/18/24 months from only baseline and month-1 data. Rather than naively concatenating the two visit representations, ReVA extracts visit-level OCT/clinical features and explicitly models early treatment response via a gated delta module applied to the feature difference between month-1 and baseline. Since this delta is computed in feature space, pixel-level OCT registration is not required. Fixed scan/view ordering ensures corresponding view-level features are compared, while gating and delta dropout reduce sensitivity to noisy visit-to-visit changes. The aggregation ablations in Table 2c support the benefit of this response-aware design.
[Meta/R1/R2/R4: Multi-horizon results, missing labels, and auxiliary supervision] We will add detailed per-horizon results. Under identical patient-level 5-fold CV, ReVA achieved MAE/RMSE/R² of 0.1135±0.0019/0.1495±0.0114/0.6687±0.0429, 0.1261±0.0118/0.1640±0.0228/0.5846±0.1042, 0.1218±0.0087/0.1556±0.0175/0.6420±0.1005, 0.1283±0.0105/0.1631±0.0111/0.5914±0.0851, and 0.1246±0.0066/0.1621±0.0056/0.6064±0.0727 at 3/6/12/18/24 months, respectively. Compared with other methods, ReVA ranks second at 3 months and first at all horizons from 6 to 24 months. Patients with complete labels at all five horizons were used to ensure comparable per-horizon evaluation; the observation mask is included to support future incomplete-label settings. Removing intermediate-horizon supervision degraded 24-month performance to 0.1341±0.0057/0.1667±0.0099/0.5829±0.0827, supporting the value of trajectory-level supervision.
[Meta/R2: Clinical baseline and added architectural value] A VA-only baseline using baseline/month-1 VA obtained MAE/RMSE/R² = 0.1396±0.0122/0.1763±0.0103/0.5368±0.0742 at 24 months; ReVA reduced MAE/RMSE by 10.7%/8.1%, showing added value beyond early VA alone.
[Meta/R2/R4: Statistical testing] We performed one-sided paired Wilcoxon tests on out-of-fold patient-level absolute errors using identical 5-fold splits (α=0.05). ReVA significantly outperformed compared methods at 12/18/24 months, and the 24-month improvement over the variant without auxiliary supervision was also significant. We will report the exact p-values in the revision.
[Meta/R1/R2/R4: Dataset statistics, generalization, and sharing] We will add cohort statistics: age 61.7±11.6 years; 98 female/90 male; 97 left/91 right eyes. Baseline VA/CST are 0.499±0.248 logMAR and 425.5±97.8 μm; month-1 VA/CST are 0.583±0.263 and 339.3±73.3 μm. Lesion prevalence is IRF/SRF/PED: 176/73/3 of 188.Mean VA at 3/6/12/18/24 months is 0.572±0.262/0.577±0.263/0.566±0.266/0.545±0.259/0.562±0.262 logMAR. Although modest, the cohort spans heterogeneous DME presentations across demographics, VA/CST, and lesion, making it clinically nontrivial. However, we acknowledge the single-center limitation and will state external/multicenter validation as future work. We will release code and pretrained models; de-identified data may be shared upon reasonable academic request, subject to institutional approval.
[R2/R4: Model complexity] Although ReVA has 310.4M total parameters, only 7.1M (2.3%) are trainable. RETFound is frozen; only LoRA layers, tabular encoder, fusion module, and temporal prediction head are optimized. Thus, ReVA is parameter-efficient rather than fully fine-tuned, reducing overfitting risk in this modest cohort.
[Meta/R1/R3: Presentation and interpretability] We will define all abbreviations at first use and in Fig. 1, and revise Fig. 2 to include OCT context without and with heatmaps, with a clearer explanation of how the highlighted regions should be interpreted.

title: Rest2Visual: Predicting Visually Evoked fMRI from Resting-State Scans
abstract: Understanding how intrinsic brain activity constrains stimulus-evoked responses is a central challenge in cognitive neuroscience. Task-based fMRI measures localized evoked activation but is costly and difficult to scale, whereas resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) is easier to acquire yet lacks direct stimulus interpretability. We study resting-conditioned synthesis of visually evoked fMRI (ve-fMRI): given an rs-derived intrinsic functional prior and a visual stimulus image, we predict the corresponding trial-wise activation volume. We propose Rest2Visual, a 3D encoder–decoder network that encodes the resting prior into hierarchical volumetric features and injects stimulus embeddings into the decoder via adaptive group normalization to produce stimulus-specific maps. Using large-scale rs–stimulus–evoked triplets, Rest2Visual improves voxel-wise and representational agreement over stimulus-agnostic and modality-ablated baselines, and preserves subject-specific response structure. We further use image reconstruction as a downstream probe to assess whether the synthesized activations retain stimulus information. The results suggest that individualized intrinsic organization can be transformed into stimulus-aligned activation patterns for scalable functional modeling.
subject_areas: Applications -> Digital Twins / Simulation / Synthetic Data
Machine Learning -> Synthetic Data / Data-centric AI

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper studies the synthesis of visually evoked fMRI, where a subject-specific intrinsic prior derived from resting-state fMRI is combined with a visual stimulus to predict trial-wise evoked activation maps. To address this problem, the authors propose Rest2Visual, a conditional 3D encoder-decoder that preserves volumetric resting-state structure while injecting stimulus information through bottleneck conditioning and AdaGN-based decoder modulation. The paper further contributes a practical triplet-construction pipeline on the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), pairing resting-state priors, visual stimuli, and evoked task-fMRI scans, as well as an empirical study showing that the synthesized maps improve voxel-wise and representational agreement over simple baselines, preserve subject-specific response structure, and remain informative for downstream image reconstruction. Overall, the paper’s contribution lies in showing that individualized resting-state organization can be transformed into stimulus-aligned task responses through a multimodal conditional generation framework.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper proposes an interesting multimodal formulation that combines resting-state priors and visual stimuli to synthesize trial-wise visually evoked fMRI, which is a meaningful extension beyond standard stimulus-to-brain encoding alone. The model design is well aligned with this goal, using a 3D conditional architecture that preserves volumetric structure while modulating predictions with image-derived features. The evaluation is also reasonably comprehensive, covering voxel-wise accuracy, representational structure, regional analysis, ablations, qualitative inspection, subject-specificity, and downstream reconstruction. Altogether, these elements make the work a convincing proof of concept.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The experimental evaluation has several important limitations:
i). Although the full model outperforms random prediction, the resting-state-only baseline, and noise-based ablations, these comparisons are relatively weak and do not establish that the method is competitive with more realistic learned alternatives.
ii). The results suggest limited cross-subject generalization. As shown in Table 3, performance on an unseen subject drops substantially in terms of Pearson correlation, RSA, and MAE relative to the standard setting. This indicates that the method relies heavily on subject-specific patterns observed during training and does not yet learn a robust subject-agnostic mapping. Because one of the paper’s motivations is to reduce the burden of task-fMRI acquisition, weak generalization to new subjects significantly limits the practical utility of the approach.
iii). Although, the model improves voxel-wise and representational metrics, the downstream reconstruction results remain noticeably worse than those obtained from ground-truth fMRI. As shown in Table 2, reconstructions from the predicted maps lose information relative to reconstructions from real NSD beta maps, both in low-level similarity and in higher-level semantic measures. This weakens the claim that the synthesized activations can serve as a close substitute for true task-evoked fMRI. They are clearly useful, but they still remain meaningfully inferior to actual measured responses.
iv). The empirical evidence remains largely proof of concept on a small and highly controlled dataset. The study is based on only eight NSD subjects, all collected under a high-quality experimental protocol. While the in-distribution results are promising, this is not sufficient to support stronger claims about robustness, scalability, or clinical relevance. The weak performance on unseen subjects further reinforces this concern.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The experimental section would be stronger with more competitive baselines. While comparisons to random prediction, resting-only prediction, and modality-noise ablations are useful sanity checks, they do not show how the method performs relative to stronger learned alternatives.
Generalization is another important issue. Although results on unseen stimuli are encouraging, the substantial drop on unseen subjects suggests that the method still depends heavily on subject-specific patterns seen during training. Since one motivation is to reduce the burden of task-fMRI acquisition, improving robustness to new subjects seems important.
The discussion of practical or clinical relevance should also be more cautious. Because the experiments are conducted on a small, highly controlled NSD cohort of healthy participants, the work is better interpreted as a proof of concept than as evidence of clinical feasibility.

While the proposed idea is interesting and technically feasible, the experimental results highlight several limitations that weaken the overall empirical case and prevent a clear recommendation for acceptance. Nevertheless, as an initial proof of concept, the work explores a promising direction and may therefore warrant a weak accept.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes Rest2Visual, a method to predict visually evoked fMRI beta maps using intrinsic functional priors from resting-state fMRI and external visual stimuli. The model outperforms baseline methods, enables meaningful visual image reconstruction from predicted brain activity, and generalizes well to novel stimuli. By linking resting-state brain organization to task-driven responses, the work provides a new way to estimate task activations without explicit task scanning, which is valuable for clinical and neuroscientific applications. This multi-level evaluation supports the effectiveness of the proposed method and rules out explanations based on noise or intrinsic topology alone.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper introduces a novel paradigm of resting-conditioned prediction of visually evoked fMRI activity, which aims to synthesize single-trial beta maps using only a resting-state fMRI intrinsic prior and a visual stimulus. This is conceptually interesting and practically valuable because it connects the brain’s intrinsic functional architecture (from rs-fMRI) to stimulus-driven responses, potentially reducing the need for lengthy task fMRI scans. The idea of using resting-state as an individual prior for task prediction is under-explored and represents a clear conceptual advance. The authors compare against two strong non-parametric baselines (Random and Resting), assess performance at both voxel-wise and representational similarity levels, and further validate results using a downstream image reconstruction model (MindEye2).
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Some experimental details require further clarification, including key parameters such as Ds, Hs, Ws, as well as the number of training samples.
2.The paper uses only 8 participants, a small sample size that may limit the reliability of the reported performance and the generalizability of the proposed method.
3.The results in Table 3 show very poor cross-subject generalization, which largely reduces the ability of model. As shown in Table 3, the model exhibits substantially poor cross-subject generalization, which considerably weakens its practical utility and reliability.
4.The fMRI signal of the PCC region already reflects the BOLD hemodynamic response; convolving it with a canonical HRF during seed-based GLM analysis appears redundant and physiologically unjustified.
5.While predicted activation maps are qualitatively similar to ground truth, noticeable inconsistencies exist in Figure 2.The feasibility of replacing real task-fMRI with predicted data has not been sufficiently established.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper presents a novel and well-motivated framework to predict visually evoked fMRI from resting-state priors and visual stimuli, with a rigorous multi-level evaluation including strong baselines and image reconstruction. It offers clear conceptual value and potential for clinical applications. However, the score is limited by notable weaknesses: a small sample size of 8 subjects, very poor cross-subject generalization, unclear experimental parameters, a physiologically redundant HRF convolution step, and visible inconsistencies in predicted activation maps. These issues restrict practical applicability but do not invalidate the core contribution, resulting in a solid but not outstanding paper.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces a new fMRI analysis pipeline for visual stimuli. This new pipeline, called Rest2Visual, uses resting-state fMRI data to extract subject-specific priors that, when paired with the stimulation image, allow for the extraction of statistical parametric maps for the task (what the authors call “predicted fMRI”). This predicted fMRI is then validated against the maps yielded by a GLM-based analysis. This paper is particularly interesting as it demonstrates that resting-state fMRI data may be used to supplement task fMRI analyses, for example by establishing priors.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper is well grounded and the methods are solid. It explores an interesting approach of using data from rs-fMRI to establish priors that are then used to estimate GLM-based maps for task-fMRI. The paper also explores both a full brain analysis and an analysis restricted to only the visual cortex.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Firstly, in my opinion it is important to underscore that this method is not estimating actual BOLD signal measured in a fMRI acquisition but rather the statistical parametric maps that are the output of a GLM-based analysis. This confusion is accentuated by the authors calling the output of their pipeline “predicted fMRI”. This distinction is important as the fMRI signal is much more complex as it shows variations in oxygenated blood in the brain rather than statistical linear correlations between this signal and the paradigm design. Although the contribution of this work is still valid, estimating GLM-based statistical maps and estimating whole-brain BOLD signal are different challenges.
Secondly, I think the paper could be improved by using a simple quantitative measure of the overlap between the predictions and the NSD-provided ground truth beta maps. In Fig. 2 there could be a common simple metric (overlap, Jaccard, Dice-Sørensen, etc.) that allows readers to quickly understand how much the predicted maps overlap with to the ground truth.
Lastly, I understand that the paper is already on the limit of the allowed length, but I think the issue of limited subject diversity, and, thus, generalization. Particularly when the pipeline showed such poor performance for the unseen subject test (which may have been expected), I believe this requires further explanation (i.e. why the priors are so subject-specific).
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper is overall well grounded and built upon solid methods. It tackles a relevant challenge. However, in my opinion, the three main points raised in the weaknesses section (estimating GLM-based maps and not fMRI signal, not having a simple measure of overlap between estimated and ground-truth maps, and not exploring the poor performance from the unseen subject test) hold it back from an “Accept”.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text: The reviewers were uniformly enthusiastic about the paper. However, they did note a few areas of clarification that the authors should address in the final version.

title: Rethinking RAG: Mitigating Text-Driven Hallucinations via Feature-Level Retrieval Integration in Medical LVLMs
abstract: Medical Large Vision-Language Models (Med-LVLMs) achieve strong capability but remain prone to hallucinations that pose serious diagnostic risks. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has been explored to mitigate this issue. However, existing approaches append retrieved evidence as text to the language input, which shifts the model’s focus toward textual cues instead of visual reasoning and increases the risk of copying retrieved reports. To address this, we propose a RAG framework that leverages retrieved image–text pairs to enhance the visual representation of a query image through modified cross-attention. We incorporate a novel training objective into this module to prevent over-reliance on a few references and promote semantically faithful alignment. In addition, we observe that commonly used CLIP-based retrieval often assigns high similarity to negated and non-negated sentences with contradictory clinical meanings, resulting in mismatched references and potential hallucinations. To mitigate this, we design a negation-aware retrieval strategy that filters clinically inconsistent cases prior to feature fusion. Experiments on three benchmarks in radiology and ophthalmology demonstrate consistent improvements over the base model and text-prompt RAG baselines, by reducing language shortcuts and reinforcing visual evidence utilization. Source code will be released upon publication.
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers
Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a medical RAG framework that integrates retrieved image-text pairs at the feature level rather than appending retrieved reports as text prompts. The core idea is to inject retrieved evidence into the vision encoder through gated cross-attention, so retrieval can improve visual grounding without encouraging direct text copying. The paper also introduces a grounding loss to prevent attention collapse onto only a few retrieved references and a negation-aware retrieval strategy to filter clinically contradictory cases before fusion. Compared with standard text-prompt RAG, this is an interesting reformulation because it explicitly targets the language-shortcut problem in Med-LVLMs. Overall, the main contribution is a more visually grounded retrieval integration strategy for reducing text-driven hallucinations in medical LVLMs.
reviews.text_strengths: First, the paper addresses a meaningful and timely problem, namely that conventional medical RAG may unintentionally increase hallucinations by biasing generation toward retrieved text instead of image evidence. Second, the proposed feature-level retrieval integration is technically interesting and reasonably novel in the medical LVLM setting, especially when combined with the attention grounding loss and the negation-aware filtering module. Third, the method is supported by a fairly comprehensive evaluation across three benchmarks spanning both radiology and ophthalmology, where it consistently outperforms the base model and several strong RAG baselines such as FactMM-RAG, RULE, and MMed-RAG. Fourth, the ablation study is useful and shows that both the grounding loss and negation-aware retrieval contribute substantially to performance. Finally, the attention-ratio analysis is a particularly strong aspect of the paper because it provides mechanistic evidence that the method indeed increases reliance on visual tokens rather than only improving final metrics.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The main weakness is that the novelty is moderate rather than fully groundbreaking, since the work still builds on the broader medical RAG, while the cross-attention style fusion is also conceptually related to prior multimodal architectures. In particular, the negation-aware retrieval module is effective but somewhat heuristic, and simple sign inversion of embeddings, and the paper does not compare this against stronger learned semantic contradiction modeling. A second weakness is that the evaluation still relies mainly on VQA metrics and ROUGE/METEOR, without a stronger clinical factuality analysis or expert reader study to directly verify hallucination reduction in practice. In addition, the VQA benchmark is constructed from GPT-4-generated yes/no pairs, which introduces an additional synthetic layer and may not fully reflect real clinical questioning settings. Overall, these limitations keep the paper at a weak accept level for me rather than a clear accept, but the idea is still promising and the empirical evidence is solid enough to merit positive consideration.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I give a weak accept / borderline accept recommendation because the paper addresses an important limitation of current medical RAG systems and proposes a well-motivated feature-level retrieval integration strategy that is supported by consistent improvements across multiple benchmarks. The method is not fully groundbreaking, as it builds on an already active line of medical RAG research, and the clinical validation could be stronger, but the technical idea is clear, the analysis is thoughtful, and the empirical results are strong enough to make the paper a worthwhile contribution.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors present a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework designed to mitigate “text-driven hallucinations” in Medical Large Vision-Language Models (Med-LVLMs). Recognizing that standard RAG methods append retrieved reports as text—thereby causing models to bypass visual reasoning in favor of copying textual cues—the proposed method fuses retrieved image-text pairs directly into the visual representation via a gated cross-attention mechanism inserted into the vision encoder. To support this, the authors introduce a correspondence-based grounding loss that prevents attention collapse, and a negation-aware retrieval strategy that inverts the CLIP embeddings of negated sentences to filter out clinically contradictory cases. Evaluated on IU X-ray, MIMIC-CXR, and Harvard-Fair VLMed, the method demonstrates superior VQA and report generation performance while empirically increasing the model’s reliance on visual tokens.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The proposed method is generally well-motivated and properly validated. Instead of directly appending the retrieved reference pairs as raw images/texts, the paper fused them into the original query image token using a properly designed cross-attention mechanism before entering the LLM. The experimental results in Table 4 further support the argument, where the proposed method indeed aligns the LLM’s attention to the image tokens.
2.The idea of using the gated fusion mechanism and grounding loss is quite elegant and intuitive. The gated fusion mechanism ensures that the fused features are combined with the raw ViT feature adaptively and ensures the worst-case performance. And the grounding loss aligns the local correlation between the query patches and reference images with their semantical similarity.
3.The evaluation in the paper is very detailed and robust. It not only demonstrates a uniform performance improvement on three different datasets with two different modalities but also provides a thorough ablation that analyzes the contribution of each building component.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.One of the reviewer’s major concerns is the design of negation-aware retrieval. Using negation detection to avoid contradictory retrieved pairs is intuitively convincing. Directly negating the feature embedding is not that straightforward. “Mass presented” and “Mass not presented” are not opposite in terms of high-dimensional geometry. Additionally, naive negation detection may also confuse cases like “Mass presented” and “Mass free”, where both are affirmative sentences but their meaning are completely different.
2.The complexity of the proposed method is quite concerning, given its marginal performance improvements. The proposed method introduces multiple new hyperparameters like $alpha$ and $K$. However, the sensitivity with respect to these hyperparameters is not properly evaluated in the paper (limited by the paper length). On the other hand, the performance improvements in Table 1 compared with the baselines are not very significant as well. Most of the improvements are only ~1.5% to the second-best method.
3.The base model used here is relatively outdated. The paper uses LLaVA-Med-1.5 as the base model, but this is a model that was released 3 years ago, and there are more robust base models like Lingshu, MedGemma, and HuatuoGPT-V. It would be more helpful to evaluate the proposed method on more recent baselines.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1.The proposed method helps to shift the VLM’s attention towards the vision tokens according to Table 4.But is there any theoretical explanation for this? The proposed method should have the same token length as the raw LLaVA-Med baseline, but why does the proposed method give a much higher visual-token attention score?

Overall, this is a solid paper with enough contribution to the field. While there are still some issues to be answered, it does not harm its quality to pass the acceptance bar.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
A Multimodal RAG framework for Med-VLMs that integrates retrieved image–report pairs directly into the vision encoder via gated cross-attention, rather than appending retrieved evidence as additional text context to the LLM, to prevent language shortcuts and encourage more visual grounding.
A negation-aware sentence-level retrieval strategy that addresses the well-known insensitivity of CLIP-based similarity to fine-grained clinical semantics, particularly negated findings, by inverting embeddings of negated sentences and applying consistency-based filtering to exclude clinically contradictory cases.
A correspondence-based attention grounding loss that supervises cross-attention weights using patch-level visual similarity to prevent attention collapse onto a narrow subset of retrieved items.
reviews.text_strengths:
The authors clearly identify a fundamental structural limitation in existing text-prompt RAG approaches, language bias and shortcut copying, and address it through a principled feature-level integration. The attention ratio analysis provides convincing empirical support for this motivation.
The proposed method achieves SOTA results across all benchmarks. This suggests the framework generalizes well across imaging modalities.
Addressing CLIP’s insensitivity to negated clinical findings is a clinically meaningful and underexplored contribution. The embedding polarity-flip is an elegant and lightweight solution, and the qualitative example effectively illustrates its practical impact in filtering diagnostically contradictory cases.
Each proposed component is individually validated, and the results demonstrate that all components contribute meaningfully, with the grounding loss and negation-aware retrieval showing the largest individual impact.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Relying solely on NLP metrics (ROUGE-L, METEOR) is inadequate for medical report generation. These metrics measure lexical overlap rather than clinical accuracy. Incorporating clinical efficacy metrics would more convincingly demonstrate the medical validity of generated reports. Currently, you can’t conclude from the report generation table.
Restricting VQA evaluation to binary yes/no questions risks inflating performance gains due to class imbalance or decision boundary biases. More fine-grained question types (e.g., open-ended, multiple-choice) would provide a more rigorous and clinically meaningful assessment of the method’s diagnostic reasoning capability.
All experiments are conducted solely on LLaVA-Med. Given that different VLMs exhibit varying sensitivities to additional context, evaluating on at least one additional backbone would strengthen the generalizability claims of the framework.
Table 3 does not specify which dataset the ablation results correspond to, making it difficult to contextualize the reported numbers.
Limited architectural novelty: using cross-attention for multimodal feature fusion is a well-established paradigm. In recent multimodal RAG literature (e.g., read Abootorabi et al., Ask in Any Modality, 2025), cross-attention-based fusion has been widely adopted. The contribution is therefore more of a careful domain adaptation than a fundamentally novel architecture, though the specific design choices are well-suited to the medical setting.
A qualitative visualization of attention patterns, both with and without the loss, is necessary to assess whether the model is attending to semantically meaningful regions.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Section 2.3 could be written more clearly.
Try to make the tables more self‑explanatory.

The paper addresses a well-motivated limitation of text-prompt RAG in medical VLMs, and the proposed components, particularly negation-aware retrieval and the grounding loss, are clinically informed with consistent empirical improvements. However, architectural novelty is limited, as cross-attention-based multimodal fusion is well-established in the broader literature. Evaluation credibility is further weakened by reliance on lexical metrics alone, binary-only VQA, and single backbone testing. However, the contribution remains valuable to the MICCAI community for its practical insights and design choices. They need some important revisions for the camera-ready if this paper is accepted.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text:
All three reviewers independently assigned a score of 4, showing clear consensus. 
The paper addresses a well-motivated problem—language shortcuts in text-prompt RAG for medical VLMs—and proposes a coherent feature-level integration via gated cross-attention, a negation-aware retrieval strategy, and a correspondence-based grounding loss. Empirical results are consistent across three benchmarks and two modalities, and the attention-ratio analysis provides mechanistic support for the core claim. 
Common concerns across reviews include reliance on lexical metrics (ROUGE/METEOR) without clinical efficacy measures, binary-only VQA evaluation, and experiments limited to a single and outdated backbone LLaVA-Med. Authors should address these issues in the camera-ready version.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely appreciate the reviewers for their constructive comments, and appreciate the opportunity to clarify several points raised in the reviews.
(R1) Negation-aware retrieval is heuristic, just a sign inversion of embeddings: Sign inversion in cosine-similarity space was chosen as a deliberate lightweight and training-free design, broadly compatible with any CLIP-based retriever and free of additional supervision. A fully learned semantic-contradiction model could in principle capture finer cases such as “mass present” vs. “mass free”, but would introduce training overhead and dataset-specific supervision. Combined with the symmetric sentence-level matching (Eq. 1) and the consistency score (Eq. 2), our filtering helps filter clinically contradictory cases in practice, as shown in Fig. 2 (left) and the +5.36pp Acc contribution in Table 3.(R1, R3) Reliance on lexical metrics and binary VQA: These protocols were adopted to align exactly with the medical-RAG baselines we compare against (RULE, MMed-RAG, FactMM-RAG), which all use the same metrics and yes/no VQA, so a controlled comparison required following the same setup. To complement these protocols, we additionally report the attention-decomposition analysis (Table 4), which provides mechanistic evidence that our gains stem from increased visual grounding rather than text copying. Incorporating clinical-efficacy metrics and open-ended VQA would offer complementary evidence in subsequent studies.
(R2) Why does the proposed method give a much higher visual-token attention score, even though the input token length is the same as raw LLaVA-Med: The input token sequence to the LLM (system prompt + visual tokens + question) is indeed identical to the raw LLaVA-Med-1.5, so the increase in Vision ratio is not due to changes in token composition. Rather, retrieved evidence is injected into the ViT hidden states via gated cross-attention before the projection, so the visual tokens entering the LLM carry higher task-relevant signal density while their length remains unchanged. As the LLM finds more diagnostically useful information within the visual segment, attention shifts toward it, as shown in Table 4 where the Vision ratio rises from 0.06 to 0.27 on MIMIC-CXR. In contrast, text-prompt RAG appends retrieved evidence as post-vision text tokens, which inflate Post-Vision and further suppress the Vision ratio below the base model.
(R2, R3) Experiments are limited to a single and outdated backbone (LLaVA-Med-1.5): The choice of LLaVA-Med-1.5 was intentional, since all medical-RAG baselines we compare against (FactMM-RAG, RULE, MMed-RAG) use the same backbone, which is necessary to isolate the contribution of our retrieval-integration design. Extending the framework to more recent Med-LVLM backbones is a meaningful direction for follow-up work.
(R3) Section 2.3 clarity, Table 3 dataset, and table readability: We appreciate these suggestions and agree that these aspects could be presented more clearly. For reference, the Table 3 ablation results are on MIMIC-CXR (the Full model row matches the corresponding row in Table 1).

title: Rethinking the Adaptation of Vision Foundation Models for Efficient Cell Segmentation
abstract: Cell segmentation is critical for computational pathology and biomedical discovery. While recent Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) have demonstrated remarkable universal feature representations, unlocking their full potential for cellular imaging is currently bottlenecked by resource-intensive adaptation paradigms. Existing methods typically rely on fine-tuning heavy visual encoders, leading to extensive computational overhead and a dependency on large-scale annotations. To address this, we propose the EffiCell-Seg framework for highly efficient cell segmentation without re-training the visual encoder. Our core insight is that pretrained VFMs intrinsically encode complementary structural priors: global saliency for localizing potential cells, and local morphological patterns for delineating cellular structures. To harness these priors, we devise a Cell Structure Prompt Encoder (CSP-Encoder) that synthesizes semantic-aware saliency and principal morphological features from frozen VFM representations into explicit structural prior maps. Moreover, we propose a Synergistic Mask Decoder (SM-Decoder) that enforces contextual consistency by jointly predicting geometric distance fields and semantic maps via mutual cross-guidance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EffiCell-Seg outperforms state-of-the-art methods across diverse cell imaging modalities while requiring only 5M trainable parameters, over 130 fewer than fully fine-tuned VFM counterparts. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EffiCell-Seg.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper proposes a parameter-efficient cell segmentation framework that leverages the structural knowledge of Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) without requiring backbone fine-tuning.
This paper introduces a CSP-Encoder, which utilizes the saliency map between spatial tokens and the CLS token, alongside the PCA principal components of the spatial tokens, to effectively bridge pretrained knowledge with cellular structures.
SM-Decoder is proposed to jointly predict geometric distance fields and semantic maps via interactions between structure-aware prompt embeddings and spatial tokens.
The proposed method, EffiCell-Seg, achieves strong performance while using substantially fewer trainable parameters than prior approaches.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.This paper achieves highly competitive performance while requiring significantly fewer trainable parameters compared to existing baseline approaches.
The ablation results are informative and support the claim that both the CSP-Encoder and the SM-Decoder play meaningful roles in the observed performance gains. 
3.Since the proposed framework operates on frozen VFM features rather than relying on backbone-specific fine-tuning, it appears potentially extensible to other VFM architectures.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The paper emphasizes computational efficiency, yet the evidence is limited to trainable parameter counts. Reporting latency, GPU memory, or throughput under the same hardware would substantially strengthen this claim. 
2.The paper states that PCA is applied to the spatial tokens and that the top-K components are retained, but it does not report the actual value of K and analyze the sensitivity to this hyperparameter. Since PCA-based morphology is a central part of the method, an ablation over K would improve both clarity and reproducibility. 
3.It remains unclear how much of the reported superiority comes from the proposed design versus the use of a strong frozen DINOv3 backbone. 
4.The paper identifies reliance on large-scale annotated data as a major limitation of prior work; however, the proposed method also appears to require considerable annotated supervision, given that it is trained with ground-truth.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper proposes an interesting parameter-efficient framework for cell segmentation by leveraging the structural knowledge of frozen Vision Foundation Models (VFMs). However, the claim regarding computational efficiency is insufficiently supported, as it relies solely on trainable parameter counts without providing practical metrics such as latency or GPU memory usage. Furthermore, while the authors identify the dependency on large-scale annotations as a major limitation of prior work, the proposed method itself still requires dense pixel-level ground-truth masks for training.

reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have addressed my concerns in the rebuttal. I am changing my recommendation to Accept.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes EffiCell-Seg, an efficient cell segmentation framework that leverages frozen visual foundation models (VFM) without fine-tuning the visual encoder. The method is motivated by the observation that pretrained VFM contains useful structural priors, including global saliency cues for cell localization and local morphological patterns for boundary delineation. To exploit these cues, the authors propose Cell Structure Prompt Encoder (CSP-Encoder) to extract the structural prior maps from frozen VFM features and a Synergistic Mask Decoder (SM-Decoder) to jointly predict semantic maps and geometric distance fields through cross-guidance. Experimental results on the CellSeg and DSB datasets show that the method achieves strong performance in both binary and instance segmentation with smaller parameter count.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) This method is motivated by a sensible and potentially useful observation. The authors identify that despite the domain gap, pretrained VFM models may remain useful for cell segmentation since cell instances also exhibit structured boundaries and locally coherent regions. The qualitative evidence in Figure 1 strengthens this motivation. In addition, the use of a frozen image encoder is practically appealing, as it substantially reduces computational cost during training.
2) The reported results show promising results against prior methods on both binary and instance segmentation, while maintaining a much smaller parameter count.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) Some implementation details could be described more clearly, particularly the neck layer and its role.
2) The construction of geometric and semantic queries is not fully explained, and additional detail would improve the clarity and reproducibility of the method.
3) Since the proposed framework relies heavily on pretrained VFM features, an additional comparison or ablation across different types of pretrained VFMs, such as SAM, would help clarify how sensitive the method is to the choice of foundation model and would provide a better understanding of how much the performance depends on the selected pretrained backbone.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper is overall well-motivated. My concerns are relatively minor and mainly related to the clarity of several architectural details and supporting ablations.

Although one of my concern is left for future work, it overlaps with a point raised by R3 that was adequately addresses in the rebuttal. Overall, i maintain my recommendation for acceptance.

reviews.text_contribution: EffiCell-Seg adapts a frozen VFM for cell segmentation by extracting structural priors from DINOv3 features using CLS-token cosine similarity and PCA of spatial tokens, fusing them into structural prior maps via a lightweight CSP-Encoder. A Synergistic Mask Decoder then jointly predicts geometric distance fields and semantic maps through bidirectional cross-attention, with watershed post-processing for instance separation. Only ~5M parameters are trained.
reviews.text_strengths: The core idea is clean: frozen VFM features already encode global saliency and local morphology, and re-aligning these is sufficient without any encoder fine-tuning. The 130x parameter reduction over CellSAM while still outperforming it is compelling. The ablation honestly isolates each component, and the gains are consistent across both datasets and both task types.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The method is only tested with DINOv3 as the backbone and never ablates whether the claimed structural priors generalize to other VFMs like SAM or CLIP. The two datasets are small and familiar; results on PanNuke or CoNIC would strengthen generalization claims. Performance margins over the second-best method are modest, and no variance across runs is considered. Minor: The DINOv3 citation points to an August 2025 arXiv preprint, which raises questions about which model version was actually used!
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The frozen-encoder angle is interesting, and the efficiency part is strong, but the single-backbone dependency without ablation and limited dataset diversity leaves many open questions.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper received mixed feedback, and the reviewers raised concerns that I believe can be (partially) resolved. In particular, the two rejection scores raised concerns regarding missing implementation details and insufficient ablation justification, which are well-suited for clarification in a rebuttal. Also, the reviewers appreciate the novelty and strong performances. Thus, I believe this submission deserves an opportunity to rebut.

The reviewers appreciate the novelty and strong performances, and the initial concerns have been fully addressed during the rebuttal. I recommend accepting this submission.

The paper presents a novel and practical approach to efficient cell segmentation by re-aligning structural priors from a frozen VFM using the proposed CSP-Encoder and SM-Decoder, achieving strong semantic and instance segmentation results with only ~5M trainable parameters. Although initial concerns were raised about implementation details, efficiency evidence, backbone dependence, and ablations, the rebuttal satisfactorily clarified most key points, and two reviewers updated or maintained accept recommendations; remaining limitations do not outweigh the paper’s novelty, efficiency, and empirical strength.
All reviewers recommended acceptance, and I see no compelling reason to recommend otherwise.

author_feedback_text:
R1Q1: Computational efficiency. 
A: On a single NVIDIA H20 GPU at 512×512 resolution, EffiCell-Seg achieves 54 ms latency, 18.5 FPS throughput, and 3.5 GB GPU memory. In contrast, all SAM-based methods in Tab 1-2 using heavier SAM-ViT-H require 115-178 ms latency, 5.6-8.7 FPS throughput, and 6.4-8.7 GB memory. This confirms that EffiCell-Seg is not only parameter-efficient but also achieves superior inference efficiency over existing methods.
R1Q2: PCA hyperparameter K.
A: Ablation with K=1/2/3 yields Dice 87.70/87.71/87.76 on CellSeg and 93.14/93.17/93.21 on DSB, with corresponding latency of 54/57/61 ms. Performance differences are within 0.1% while latency grows linearly with K. We therefore adopt K=1 as the best trade-off between performance and computational cost.
R1Q3: Source of superiority. 
A: As illustrated in Tab 3, directly decoding frozen DINOv3 features yields only 83.52/89.74 Dice on CellSeg/DSB. Adding our CSP-Encoder and SM-Decoder brings 4.18/3.40 Dice gains to 87.70/93.14, outperforming all baselines. This confirms that the reported superiority primarily stems from our proposed design.
R1Q4: Annotation requirement.
A: EffiCell-Seg does not require considerable annotated supervision. By freezing the VFM encoder and only optimizing the lightweight CSP-Encoder and SM-Decoder (~5M parameters), our method achieves superior performance with only a few hundred training samples. In contrast, methods like CellSAM [16] fully fine-tune heavy encoders on more than 10K annotated cell images. Our design greatly reduces the labeled samples required for adapting VFMs to cell segmentation.
R2Q1: Neck layer.
A: The neck layer consists of a 1×1 convolution, LayerNorm, 3×3 convolution, and LayerNorm, which projects frozen VFM spatial tokens into a unified feature space aligned with the prompt embedding dimension for subsequent fusion in the SM-Decoder (Eq. 4).
R2Q2: Geometric and semantic queries. 
A: As shown in Fig. 2 and Eq. 4-5, q_g and q_s are randomly-initialized learnable tensors optimized end-to-end: q_g captures spatial organization for distance field prediction, while q_s encodes category-aware features for semantic mapping. They are first grounded via two-way attention with VFM features and the prompt embedding (Eq. 4), then mutually refined through bidirectional cross-attention (Eq. 5).
R2Q3: Comparison across VFMs.
A: We agree that exploring our framework with other VFMs would further strengthen the generality, and will explore this in future work.
R3Q1: Empirical VFM comparison.
A: Replacing DINOv3 with SAM and CLIP as the frozen backbone, EffiCell-Seg achieves 87.02/92.48 and 85.93/91.37 Dice on CellSeg/DSB, respectively, compared to 87.70/93.14 with DINOv3.DINOv3 provides the best structural priors for cell segmentation, while the framework remains effective across different VFMs.
R3Q2: Dataset diversity.
A: Our CellSeg and DSB datasets cover fluorescence, brightfield, DIC, and H&E modalities with multiple cell types. In contrast, the suggested PanNuke and CoNIC are both restricted to H&E only. Our datasets exhibit greater modality diversity.
R3Q3: Performance margins and variance.
A: Although the PQ gains over the second-best SAC are 1.27-1.38 on the two datasets, paired t-tests across test samples confirm strong statistical significance with p-values < 0.001 on both CellSeg and DSB. Moreover, the consistency across all four metrics (Dice, mIoU, PQ, F1) demonstrates that our improvements are robust rather than attributable to run-to-run variance.
R3Q4: DINOv3 version.
A: We confirm that we use the August 2025 arXiv preprint version of DINOv3 [22] (the first official release), which is also the version publicly available on the official repository.

title: Retinopathy of Prematurity Staging via Prototype-Evidential Learning
abstract:
Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) staging via fundus imaging is critical for timely screening and treatment planning in premature infants. However, automated diagnosis is frequently impeded by low image quality and the high visual similarity between adjacent disease stages, both of which introduce significant diagnostic ambiguity. To address this, we propose ProtoEvi-ROP, an interpretable and uncertainty-aware framework designed to enhance the reliability of early-stage ROP staging. 
Our approach synergizes a prototype-based reasoning mechanism for feature-level interpretability with evidential uncertainty modeling to explicitly quantify decision confidence. Additionally, we introduce a region-focused regularization strategy to stabilize prototype geometry, preventing feature drift.
Extensive experiments on two ROP fundus datasets demonstrate that ProtoEvi-ROP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Crucially, the estimated uncertainty serves as a robust reliability indicator, effectively filtering incorrect predictions. Selective prediction experiments reveal a clear accuracy-coverage trade-off, confirming that high uncertainty correlates with increased diagnostic risk, while decision space visualizations elucidate the synergy between interpretable prototype reasoning and uncertainty quantification.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper addresses the diagnostic ambiguity in Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP) staging caused by low image quality and high visual similarity between adjacent stages. It proposes a dual-stream framework named ProtoEvi-ROP. Its main contributions include:
Integrating interpretable prototype learning with uncertainty-quantifying evidential learning. The prototype branch learns stage-specific morphological prototypes via distance metrics to handle “conflicting evidence” (features resembling multiple stages). The evidence branch models evidence strength via the Dirichlet distribution to handle “insufficient evidence” (ambiguous features). 
A “Region-Focusing Regularization” strategy is proposed, applying a central region mask to the prototype branch’s input to force the model to focus on peripheral vascular-avascular junction pathologies, stabilizing prototype learning. 
An improved Dempster-Shafer evidence theory rule is employed to fuse the belief masses from the two branches, better handling conflicts between them. 
Experiments on two ROP datasets show the method outperforms existing methods in metrics like accuracy. Furthermore, its estimated uncertainty effectively distinguishes correct from incorrect predictions, enabling risk-aware decision-making.
reviews.text_strengths:
​ Accurately identifies the core challenge in automated ROP staging—visual ambiguity and diagnostic uncertainty—and explicitly categorizes uncertainty into “conflicting evidence” and “insufficient evidence,” providing a clear motivation. 
The proposed ProtoEvi-ROP framework is well-designed, innovatively and systematically integrating prototype learning (providing geometric interpretability) and evidential learning (providing uncertainty quantification) within a single model. 
Conducts extensive experiments on two datasets, including comparisons with various SOTA methods, thorough ablation studies (validating the dual-branch and masking strategies), and calibration analysis of uncertainty (accuracy-coverage curve). Results show consistent performance gains. 
Goes beyond reporting performance numbers by providing in-depth analysis through feature space visualizations and uncertainty distribution statistics, explaining whythe model works and howits uncertainty estimates correlate with prediction errors, enhancing the work’s credibility.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
（1）The core idea of combining “prototype learning” and “evidential learning” is not novel in medical image analysis or general machine learning. Prior works have explored integrating evidential uncertainty into prototype networks for open-set recognition or handling out-of-distribution samples. The paper fails to sufficiently argue the fundamental distinction​ and significant advantage​ of its “prototype-evidence” dual-stream design compared to existing hybrid approaches. The “novelty” lies more in the application task (ROP staging) and specific component design (e. g. , regional masking), not in a core paradigm shift. 
（2）The forced masking of the central 1/3 region as a “hard inductive bias” raises concerns about its generalizability. While ROP pathologies often occur in the periphery, the location and size of central structures like the optic disc are not absolutely constant​ across different devices or imaging conditions. This hard masking may discard potentially informative central features (e. g. , optic disc morphology, vascular arcade) and could harm model robustness with changing data distributions. The authors do not discuss the limitations of this design. 
﻿
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
（1） In the introduction or related work section, please provide a more in-depth discussion differentiating your work from existing “prototype + uncertainty” hybrid approaches, explicitly stating the unique contributions of your work in terms of problem-driven​ (addressing specific types of diagnostic ambiguity) and technical implementation​ (e. g. , asymmetric masking, improved DS fusion rule). 
（2）​ Please supplement the discussion with the potential limitations and applicability boundaries of the regional masking strategy. Also, consider adding an analysis of computational complexity and inference time to assess the method’s practicality. 
（3） It is strongly advised to add comparative experiments with specialized uncertainty estimation and interpretability methods, particularly using uncertainty calibration metrics​ and prototype quality/interpretability​ for quantitative comparison. This would more powerfully demonstrate the dual advantages of the proposed framework.

（1）Insufficient Novelty:​ The core of this paper is combining prototype learning and evidential learning. This idea itself is not novel, and the paper fails to sufficiently articulate its fundamental innovation compared to existing hybrid approaches. Its contribution lies more in the engineering implementation for the specific task of ROP (e.g., regional masking) rather than proposing a new methodology with broad impact.
（2）The reliance on “Region-Focusing Regularization” as a strong prior lacks thorough validation and discussion regarding its generalizability and robustness. In real-world clinical settings with significant data variance, this hard masking could lead to information loss and performance degradation.
﻿
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors have carefully addressed the reviewers’ concerns and provided detailed clarifications regarding the motivation, architectural design, uncertainty modeling, clinical relevance, computational complexity, and dataset limitations of the proposed method. In particular, the revised manuscript now better explains the rationale behind the asymmetric uncertainty decoupling framework, the clinically motivated hard masking strategy, and the practical role of uncertainty-aware screening in reducing diagnostic risk.
The additional analyses on uncertainty mechanisms, computational efficiency, and ablation studies further strengthen the technical validity of the work. The authors also clarified the dataset construction process and committed to publicly releasing the dataset, which improves the reproducibility and potential impact of the study.
Overall, the manuscript presents a meaningful and technically sound contribution to uncertainty-aware ROP screening, with clear clinical significance and strong experimental support. Therefore, I recommend acceptance of the paper.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces ProtoEvi-ROP, an interpretable and uncertainty-aware framework tailored for the staging of Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP). The core contribution lies in the integration of a prototype-based branch for feature-level interpretability and an evidential learning branch to quantify uncertainty. A coordination consistency loss is further employed to align the dual branches. Experimental results on two ROP datasets demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches. The ablation studies and uncertainty analyses suggest that the framework provides a reliable mechanism for risk-aware clinical predictions.
reviews.text_strengths:
Methodological Novelty: The synergy between prototype-based learning and evidential deep learning is well-motivated, offering a dual perspective on both “why a decision was made” and “how confident the model is.”
Clarity of Presentation: The methodology is logically structured and the technical components are well-articulated.
Insightful Evaluation: The authors provide comprehensive analyses (e.g., Fig. 4) to substantiate the effectiveness of the uncertainty estimation and its alignment with interpretability, which is crucial for medical applications.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Redundancy in Presentation: In Section 2.1 Evidential Branch part, the opening two sentences description appear redundant, as they essentially convey the same concept in slightly different phrasing. 
Parameter Sensitivity: The paper lacks a sensitivity analysis for several key hyperparameters, specifically the temperature \tau in Eq. (1) and the balancing coefficients \lambda_{evi} and \lambda_{cc} in Eq. (7). Exploring how these parameters influence model performance and uncertainty calibration would strengthen the technical depth.
Clinical Impact of Uncertainty Filtering: While the authors show that filtering out high-uncertainty samples improves accuracy in Fig.4(d), this “rejection” mechanism may lead to a decrease in Recall, which is a critical metric in ROP screening to avoid missed diagnoses.The authors should discuss the clinical implications of these “rejected” cases.It would be highly beneficial to analyze the class distribution of these high-uncertainty samples. Are they predominantly from minority classes or borderline stages? Is there a correlation between model uncertainty and the difficulty levels perceived by human experts? An in-depth analysis of these limitation cases is needed to ensure the model’s reliability in a real-world clinical workflow.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I recommend an Accept for this manuscript as it presents a well-engineered and conceptually sound framework, ProtoEvi-ROP, which effectively addresses the critical need for interpretability and reliability in medical AI. The integration of prototype-based feature learning with evidential uncertainty estimation is both technically innovative and clinically relevant. The authors have demonstrated superior performance across multiple ROP datasets, and the ablation studies provide strong evidence for the necessity of each component. While the sensitivity of certain hyperparameters and the potential impact of uncertainty-based filtering on Recall are areas for future discussion, the current work establishes a robust baseline for risk-aware clinical staging. The ability to quantify decision confidence significantly enhances the potential for human-AI collaboration in real-world screening workflows. Overall, this paper offers a complete and insightful contribution that is likely to be of high interest to the medical imaging community.

The paper proposes ProtoEvi-ROP, a dual-stream framework for ROP staging that integrates:
Prototype-based learning for interpretable geometric reasoning
Evidential deep learning for uncertainty estimation
The key novelty lies in:

Combination of interpretability + uncertainty is meaningful and important in medical imaging.
The dual-branch design (prototype + evidential) is conceptually sound and well justified.

The method mainly combines existing ideas:
prototype learning
evidential deep learning
Dempster–Shafer fusion

2.Lack of comparison with recent uncertainty-aware medical models:

4.Generalization not validated:

reviews.text_detailed_comments:
This is a well-structured and solid paper addressing an important clinical problem. The integration of interpretability and uncertainty is valuable, particularly for safety-critical applications like ROP screening.
However, the paper would benefit from:
stronger novelty justification beyond combining existing methods,
broader comparisons with uncertainty modeling approaches,
and more rigorous validation on external datasets.
Clarifying these aspects would significantly strengthen the contribution.

The paper addresses an important problem and proposes a well-designed framework that combines interpretability and uncertainty estimation in a meaningful way. The experimental results are strong and consistent across datasets, and the analysis of uncertainty is particularly valuable for clinical applications.
However, the methodological novelty is somewhat limited, as the approach mainly integrates existing techniques rather than introducing fundamentally new components. Additionally, the evaluation lacks comparisons with standard uncertainty baselines and does not include external validation, which is important for medical imaging applications.
Overall, improvements in novelty justification and evaluation would strengthen it further.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors addressed most of my major concerns in the rebuttal. In particular, they provided a clearer justification for the architectural novelty by explaining the asymmetric decomposition between prototype-based geometric ambiguity modeling and evidential reliability estimation. The clarification regarding the clinical motivation of the masking strategy and the uncertainty-driven human-in-the-loop workflow was also helpful.
The additional discussion on computational complexity and inference speed further strengthens the practical relevance of the method for real-world screening settings.
While some limitations still remain, particularly the lack of comparisons with standard uncertainty baselines such as MC Dropout and Deep Ensembles, as well as the absence of external validation, I believe the overall contribution is sufficiently strong for acceptance. The paper presents a well-structured and experimentally comprehensive framework with meaningful clinical motivation, strong quantitative results, uncertainty analysis, interpretability studies, and ablation experiments.
Overall the rebuttal adequately clarified the main concerns that motivated my initial weak reject score.

meta_reviews.text:
The reviewers raise concerns that the methodological novelty is mainly integrative, combining prototype learning, evidential learning, and Dempster–Shafer fusion without sufficiently distinguishing the proposed design from prior uncertainty-aware prototype-based methods.
The authors should address the robustness and justification of key design choices, especially the central-region masking strategy, hyperparameter sensitivity, uncertainty filtering mechanism, and potential impact on recall and minority/borderline ROP stages.
The rebuttal should also clarify generalizability and reproducibility concerns by discussing dataset limitations, external or cross-dataset validation, comparisons with standard uncertainty baselines such as MC Dropout, Bayesian methods and deep ensembles, and computational complexity.

The paper is accepted. The rebuttal addressed most major concerns, especially the motivation of the asymmetric uncertainty design, masking strategy, computational cost, and dataset limitations. Although the novelty is somewhat integration-oriented and external validation remains limited, the method is clinically meaningful, experimentally solid, and provides useful uncertainty-aware support for ROP screening.
Overall, a well motivated paper, and the authors’ rebuttal addressed most reviewers’ concerns.

The rebuttal substantially strengthened the case for acceptance. In particular, the authors clarified the motivation for the asymmetric dual-branch design, justified the central masking strategy using the clinical staging criteria, discussed computational efficiency, and explained the intended human-in-the-loop role of uncertainty filtering. They also committed to releasing the private dataset, which improves reproducibility and impact.

author_feedback_text:
1.Novelty（R1 & 3）
Our framework is not a mere concatenation of existing tools, but a problem-driven architectural paradigm tailored to early-stage ROP. Standard prototypes overconfidently force geometric fits on weak evidence (Fig.3, Ablation II), while standard EDL lacks interpretability (Fig.3, Ablation I). Our fundamental innovation asymmetrically decouples uncertainty types. Mirroring clinical reasoning, our asymmetric architecture explicitly decouples functions into two parallel pathways: one pathway a morphological expert isolating conflicting evidence, and a global reliability gatekeeper isolating insufficient evidence. Rather than artificially averaging divergent predictions, our integration strategy explicitly preserves this inter-stream conflict. This transforms uncertainty into an actionable indicator of diagnostic risk, demonstrating a cohesive, structural innovation that resolves geometric confusion and evidence insufficiency far beyond a simple plug-and-play hybrid model
2.1/3 central hard mask （R1 & 3）
The 1/3 spatial mask is not an arbitrary heuristic, but a principled anatomical prior based on ICROP-3 guidelines [3]. Clinically, ROP staging is strictly defined by morphological changes at the peripheral vascular-avascular junction. The central region (optic disc and macula) is highly salient but diagnostically irrelevant. Without the mask, prototype networks suffer from severe shortcut learning on these central features. Masking explicitly forces the prototype branch to align with clinical diagnostic criteria. This asymmetric design is empirically validated (Fig. 3, Ablation II), improving accuracy by 1.2% (SZ-ROP) and 1.3% (PEFI-ROP) over the unmasked baseline.
3.Computational Complexity (R1 & 3)
ProtoEvi-ROP estimates uncertainty with a single deterministic forward pass, avoiding the N-fold inference overhead of MC Dropout and deep ensembles. Although slightly more costly than a single-stream baseline, it delivers improved performance. The final model (47.02M parameters, 8.26 GFLOPs) achieves 7.88 ms/image and 126.94 FPS on an RTX 5090 GPU. This favorable trade-off between performance, reliability, and efficiency makes the system ideal for real-time screening applications.
4.Uncertainty baselines (R1 & 3)
We agree that MC Dropout and Deep Ensembles are standard uncertainty baselines. We have evaluated our internal uncertainty mechanisms in the current version of the manuscript (Fig. 3, Ablation I; Fig. 4c,d). We systematically compared standard softmax, prototype entropy, Dirichlet evidence, and our Reduced DS fusion, which consistently achieved the highest Accuracy, F1-score, and AUC. We will also make a comprehensive quantitative comparison against the suggested baselines in the camera-ready supplementary material.
5.Clinical Impact of Uncertainty Filtering & presentation (R2)
We agree that maximizing Recall is critical in ROP screening. However, our uncertainty filtering does not discard samples, it serves as a Human-in-the-Loop triage mechanism. Forcing a deterministic prediction on highly ambiguous images risks dangerous false negatives. By flagging high-uncertainty cases for senior expert review, the system actively protects diagnostic safety. We will emphasize this workflow in the revision. Additionally, we thank the reviewer for identifying the textual redundancy in Section 2.1, which we will streamline for better flow.
6.Dataset limitation (R3)
Acquiring high-quality fundus images from infants is notoriously difficult due to poor pupil dilation and eye movement. We respectfully clarify that the used datasets are substantial given the extreme challenges of neonatal ophthalmic imaging. Our study utilizes SZ-ROP (756 images), the largest publicly accessible ROP staging dataset, while our PEFI-ROP dataset (858 images) exceeds this benchmark. To resolve the concern about reproducibility, we formally commit to publicly releasing our dataset upon acceptance.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Anatomical Guidance for Text-to-CT Generation
abstract: Text-conditioned generative models for volumetric medical imaging provide semantic control but lack explicit anatomical guidance, often resulting in outputs that are spatially ambiguous or anatomically inconsistent. In contrast, structure-driven methods ensure strong anatomical consistency but typically assume access to ground-truth annotations, which are unavailable when the target image is to be synthesized. We propose a retrieval-augmented approach for Text-to-CT generation that integrates semantic and anatomical information under a realistic inference setting. Given a radiology report, our method retrieves a semantically related clinical case using a 3D vision-language encoder and leverages its associated anatomical annotation as a structural proxy. This proxy is injected into a text-conditioned latent diffusion model via a ControlNet branch, providing coarse anatomical guidance while maintaining semantic flexibility. Experiments on the CT-RATE dataset show that retrieval-augmented generation improves image fidelity and clinical consistency compared to text-only baselines, while additionally enabling explicit spatial controllability, a capability inherently absent in such approaches. Further analysis highlights the importance of retrieval quality, with semantically aligned proxies yielding consistent gains across all evaluation axes. This work introduces a principled and scalable mechanism to bridge semantic conditioning and anatomical plausibility in volumetric medical image synthesis.
