Code is available at https://github.com/arco-group/RAGText2CT.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Synthetic Data / Data-centric AI

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper tackles the problem of synthesising three‑dimensional CT volumes from free‑form radiology reports while ensuring anatomical plausibility. Purely text‑conditioned models capture semantics but produce anatomically inconsistent volumes because reports lack spatial information, whereas mask‑conditioned methods require segmentation labels at inference and are therefore impractical.
The authors propose a retrieval‑augmented framework: a three‑dimensional vision‑language encoder retrieves the most semantically similar case from a training corpus, uses the retrieved case’s segmentation mask as a structural proxy, and injects this proxy into a frozen report‑conditioned latent diffusion model via a ControlNet branch. This design retains the flexibility of text conditioning, approximates anatomical structure without requiring ground‑truth masks at inference, and preserves the pretrained generative backbone.
The contributions include (1) framing report‑conditioned CT generation as a retrieval‑augmented problem where anatomy is treated as a latent proxy, (2) integrating this proxy with a latent diffusion backbone through a separate ControlNet branch while keeping the backbone frozen, and (3) empirically evaluating the approach on the CT‑RATE dataset against text‑only baselines, mask‑conditioned upper bounds and retrieval‑quality ablations.
The work therefore represents an engineering combination of retrieval‑augmented generation and existing diffusion architectures.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The method addresses a clinically relevant gap: synthesising CT volumes from reports without relying on segmentation masks at inference. Retrieving a semantically similar case and using its mask approximates anatomical structure while preserving the flexibility of text conditioning.
2.The approach leverages a pretrained latent diffusion model and adds a ControlNet branch to inject the proxy mask through zero‑initialised residual connections, so only the control branch is trained. This preserves the existing generative capabilities, simplifies optimisation and makes the system modular.
Experiments report image fidelity using two‑dimensional and three‑dimensional FID, clinical consistency via a pretrained CT‑Net classifier, and spatial controllability via Dice and HD95 after segmenting generated volumes. Baselines include multi‑stage pipelines (GenerateCT, MedSyn), diffusion‑based report models (Text‑to‑CT, Report2CT), a mask‑conditioned upper bound (MAISI) and ablations on retrieval quality. An ablation comparing nearest, farthest and random retrieval demonstrates that semantically aligned proxies improve FID, classification AUC and Dice scores, whereas poor retrieval degrades performance. Statistical tests (paired Wilcoxon) are reported.
4.The paper clearly formulates the problem, retrieval mechanism and ControlNet integration with equations and describes training and inference procedures. Dataset splits, preprocessing and hyper‑parameters are provided, and code release upon acceptance is promised.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The proposed method uses known components: a three‑dimensional vision‑language encoder, nearest‑neighbour retrieval and ControlNet conditioning and applies them to CT generation. MAISI already uses ControlNet with segmentation masks; here the mask is replaced by a retrieved proxy. The contribution is therefore incremental and primarily combines existing tools rather than introducing a fundamentally new generative mechanism.
2.The method relies on retrieving a single nearest neighbour based on report embeddings. There is no quantitative analysis of how often the retrieved mask matches the target anatomy. Failure modes where the nearest neighbour is anatomically dissimilar for example, different pathology or organ size are not examined. Using multiple neighbours or alternative retrieval strategies is not explored.
Experiments are conducted only on the CT‑RATE dataset using automated metrics. Clinical consistency is measured via CT‑Net classification on real CTs, which tests recognisability rather than whether the generated image reflects the described pathology. Moreover, spatial controllability compares generated masks to the retrieved proxy rather than ground‑truth anatomy, thus high Dice scores may reflect copying the proxy rather than generating correct anatomy. FID is known to correlate poorly with clinical plausibility. There is no external validation by radiologists, no pathology‑specific breakdown, and no tests on other body regions or report styles.
4.The paper compares to several baselines but does not discuss or evaluate alternative controllable text‑to‑CT strategies, such as models guided by pseudo‑masks, landmarks or multiple proxies. Retrieval‑based generative models outside medical imaging are not cited. A comparison against a simpler structural prior without retrieval would help isolate the contribution of the retrieval step.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses a real limitation of report-conditioned 3D CT generation by introducing a practical mechanism for adding anatomical guidance without requiring target masks at inference time. The central idea: retrieving a semantically related case and using its annotation as a structural proxy is reasonable and better aligned with realistic deployment than methods that assume direct access to anatomical labels at generation time. The experimental results also support the claim that structural guidance improves over text-only conditioning. At the same time, the contribution is incremental rather than fundamental, since it mainly modifies how structural conditioning is obtained within an already active line of work. In addition, the validation would be more convincing with stronger evidence on generalization, failure modes, and anatomy-faithfulness beyond adherence to the retrieved proxy.
Overall, I find the paper worthy of acceptance, but with a moderate confidence level and mainly on the basis of a useful methodological refinement rather than a major conceptual advance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: While the rebuttal effectively clarifies the method’s implementation and design choices, there remain opportunities for strengthening the validation narrative in future work. On retrieval validation, the authors cite strong MAP metrics from prior work on their encoder, which is reassuring, though providing direct quantitative evidence of retrieval success on their own generated test cases would further support the core assumption that semantic similarity reliably yields anatomically coherent proxies. The ablation comparing nearest, random, and farthest retrieval is valuable empirical evidence, and the authors might consider extending this with documented examples of cases where semantic misalignment occurred, to help readers understand the method’s failure modes and boundaries. The evaluation design, comparing Dice scores to the retrieved proxy rather than ground truth is sensible given that reports underspecify anatomy, and the authors make a fair point that high AUC alongside high Dice suggests the method achieves both structural coherence and clinical plausibility. That said, future work might explore whether validation on out-of-distribution cases or cross-dataset experiments would demonstrate robust generalization beyond CT-RATE. On novelty, the authors reasonably position their contribution as addressing a systematic limitation of text-to-CT methods through retrieval-augmented conditioning; while the individual components are established, the framing as solving the spatial underspecification problem in reports is a valid contribution. A radiologist reader study remains an important next step to validate clinical utility, which the authors acknowledge. Overall, the work makes a solid methodological contribution with clear practical motivation, and these directions would strengthen its impact.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a retrieval-augmented framework for report-conditioned 3D CT generation, where anatomical structure is approximated via a retrieved proxy rather than requiring ground-truth annotations at inference time. Specifically, given a radiology report, a semantically similar case is retrieved using a 3D vision-language encoder, and its associated segmentation mask is used as a structural prior injected into a latent diffusion model via ControlNet. The method aims to bridge semantic conditioning and anatomical consistency under a realistic inference setting.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) Well-motivated problem: addresses the gap between semantic-only and structure-driven generation.
2) Interesting use of retrieval to approximate anatomical priors without requiring annotations at inference.
3) Technically sound integration with latent diffusion + ControlNet.
4) Multi-axis evaluation (FID, CT-Net, Dice/HD95).
5) Ablation on retrieval strategies (nearest/random/farthest) is useful.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) Lack of validation of the core retrieval assumption:
The method critically depends on retrieving a “semantically related clinical case using a 3D vision-language encoder” (Abstract, p.1), yet there is no rigorous quantitative or qualitative validation that the retrieved cases are indeed semantically or anatomically aligned with the input reports. The paper does not provide retrieval metrics (e.g., recall@k, similarity distributions) or qualitative retrieval examples beyond limited illustration (Fig. 2, p.8).
2) Unclear training and domain alignment of the vision-language encoder:
On page 3, the authors state that “text conditioning is implemented through embeddings extracted from a vision-language model based on the CLIP paradigm [24], extended with a 3D image encoder.” However, it is unclear whether this encoder is sufficiently pretrained or fine-tuned on radiology-specific data(in this case CT). Without strong modality-specific alignment, the reliability of semantic retrieval from radiology reports is questionable.
3) No radiologist or expert evaluation:
Despite operating in a clinically sensitive domain, the paper lacks any expert (radiologist) validation. This is particularly important given that the method assumes that retrieved reports and their associated anatomy are clinically meaningful proxies.
4) Assumption that radiology reports fully represent image content is not validated:
The approach assumes that the input report provides a sufficiently complete and accurate semantic description of the underlying CT volume. However, radiology reports are often incomplete, variable, and focused on salient findings rather than full anatomical description. The paper does not analyze how this limitation affects retrieval or generation.
5) Evaluation of spatial controllability is proxy-based:
Dice and HD95 are computed against retrieved masks rather than ground truth (p.7), which may overestimate anatomical correctness and does not confirm true alignment with the intended anatomy.
6) Moderate methodological novelty:
The framework is primarily a combination of existing components (retrieval + latent diffusion + ControlNet), with limited fundamentally new modeling contributions.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The proposed idea of using retrieval to approximate anatomical priors is interesting and potentially impactful. However, the paper would significantly benefit from:
1) Explicit evaluation of retrieval quality (e.g., retrieval accuracy, qualitative case studies across multiple examples)
2) Clarification of the training and domain adaptation of the 3D vision-language encoder
3) Expert (radiologist) validation of generated outputs and retrieved cases
4) Analysis of failure modes when retrieval is semantically incorrect or anatomically mismatched
Addressing these points would strengthen confidence in the central claim that retrieval provides meaningful anatomical guidance.

While the paper addresses an important problem and proposes a conceptually interesting retrieval-augmented framework for text-to-CT generation, the central assumption of the method—that semantically meaningful anatomical proxies can be reliably retrieved from a vision-language embedding space—is insufficiently validated. The paper claims that “a semantically related clinical case is retrieved using a 3D vision-language encoder” (p.1), yet provides no rigorous quantitative or qualitative evidence supporting the quality or reliability of this retrieval process.
Furthermore, it is unclear whether the underlying vision-language model is adequately pretrained or adapted to the radiology domain (p.3), raising concerns about the semantic alignment between reports and CT volumes. The absence of radiologist evaluation further limits confidence in the clinical validity of both retrieved proxies and generated images.
While the experimental results show improvements across several metrics, these gains may be partially driven by proxy-based evaluation and do not fully establish anatomical correctness or clinical realism. Given that the core contribution relies heavily on retrieval quality, the lack of thorough validation in this component is a significant limitation.
Overall, the paper presents a promising direction but requires stronger validation and analysis to support its central claims.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
Thank you to the authors for the detailed rebuttal. I appreciate the additional clarification regarding the retrieval mechanism, particularly the retrieval ablation analysis (Nearest vs Random vs Farthest) and the inclusion of retrieval statistics from the underlying encoder framework. These additions strengthen confidence that the retrieved proxies contain meaningful phenotype-level information rather than arbitrary anatomical guidance.
I also appreciate the clarification that the goal is not exact anatomical reconstruction, but structurally coherent conditioning aligned with report semantics. While concerns regarding the absence of radiologist evaluation and the indirect nature of some evaluation components remain, the rebuttal substantially improves the technical justification of the central retrieval assumption. I therefore revise my assessment toward a borderline positive recommendation.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes augmenting a text-conditioned 3D CT synthesis framework with a retrieval-based anatomical proxy. Given a radiology report at inference time, the method retrieves the most semantically similar case from the training corpus using a shared 3D vision-language embedding space, and uses its segmentation mask as a structural prior. This proxy is injected into a frozen latent diffusion model via a ControlNet branch. The main claim is that this enables anatomically coherent generation without requiring any annotations at inference time, bridging the gap between purely text-conditioned generation and structure-conditioned methods.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The clinical motivation is strong. Text-only CT synthesis often produces spatially inconsistent outputs, and requiring a ground-truth segmentation mask at inference is unrealistic in most deployment settings. Framing anatomy as a “retrievable proxy” is a natural and promising solution to this tension.
2.The retrieval quality ablation is clean and directly supports the paper’s central message. It cleanly isolates the contribution of semantic alignment from the structural conditioning mechanism itself.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The framework is quite incremental over Text-to-CT [22]. The proposed method essentially adds a ControlNet branch to that prior model, with the mask sourced from retrieval rather than ground truth. This is fine, but the framing overstates the architectural novelty.
2.The paper positions MAISI as an upper bound that “assumes access to ground-truth annotations at inference time,” but this is not fully accurate. MAISI itself supports inference with TotalSegmentator-predicted masks rather than ground-truth masks, the same tool used here to generate training proxies.
Comparing FID between systems with different training distributions is problematic and is not acknowledged anywhere. MAISI was trained on ~10K multi-site CT volumes from diverse datasets; this system and all text-conditioned baselines train on CT-RATE (~27K chest CTs).
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper tackles a real problem and the three-axis evaluation is well-designed. The method is however incremental over Text-to-CT [22]. The MAISI comparison is also unfair, as MAISI already supports TotalSegmentator-predicted masks at inference, the same tool used here, making the annotation-free claim overstated.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
After reading the authors’ rebuttal and the discussion, I would like to update my recommendation from Weak Reject (3) to Weak Accept (4).
The rebuttal addressed my main concerns about the MAISI comparison and the FID evaluation. In particular, the clarification that MAISI uses the target case’s own mask as an oracle condition, while the proposed method retrieves a proxy from the report, makes the comparison clearer. The authors also clarified that all methods were retrained on CT-RATE, which helps address my concern about the FID comparison.
I still think the method is somewhat incremental, and the lack of radiologist evaluation and more detailed failure analysis remains a limitation. However, after the rebuttal, I think the paper is reasonably strong for a marginal acceptance.

meta_reviews.text:
This is borderline. One weak accept and two weak rejects, but all three reviewers agree the problem is important and that the retrieval-based anatomical proxy is a sensible idea.
The main issue is that the core retrieval assumption is not validated strongly enough. Multiple reviewers point out that the whole method depends on retrieving anatomically and semantically meaningful neighbours, yet the paper does not provide enough direct evidence that this actually happens. This is the most important point for rebuttal.
There are also concerns that the contribution is more incremental than the paper claims, essentially adding retrieval-based proxy conditioning to an existing text-to-CT and ControlNet setup. In addition, Reviewer 3 raises a specific concern that the positioning against MAISI may be overstated, since MAISI can also operate with predicted masks rather than true masks at inference.
The evaluation is generally solid, but several parts remain indirect. Spatial controllability is measured against the retrieved proxy rather than true anatomy, and there is no expert validation or deeper analysis of retrieval failures and pathology-specific behaviour.
The authors should focus on validating retrieval quality more directly, clarifying the training and domain alignment of the vision-language encoder, moderating or justifying the novelty claims, and addressing the fairness of the MAISI comparison. If these points are answered convincingly, the paper could still move into the accept range.

The central claim depends on the retrieved proxy being anatomically and semantically meaningful for the input report, but the submitted paper does not provide sufficient direct validation of retrieval quality. The rebuttal clarifies that some retrieval metrics come from prior work rather than the present experiments. The nearest, random, and farthest ablation is useful, but it remains indirect evidence: it shows that better embedding similarity improves generation metrics, not that the retrieved masks are anatomically appropriate for the intended target case.
The method is incremental over an existing text-to-CT model and ControlNet-style conditioning. Spatial controllability is evaluated against the retrieved proxy rather than true anatomy, so it primarily measures adherence to the proxy, not anatomical correctness. There is no expert validation, no pathology-specific failure analysis, and the MAISI comparison still requires careful qualification as an oracle or upper-bound comparison.

The rebuttal successfully addresses the core concerns: the retrieval ablation and encoder clarification confirm that semantic retrieval yields anatomically meaningful proxies, satisfying Reviewers #1 and #2.Reviewer #3’s novelty and MAISI comparison concerns are acknowledged but do not undermine the practical contribution of annotation-free anatomical conditioning.
The paper is a solid, well-motivated methodological refinement with clear clinical relevance, though future work should include radiologist validation and direct retrieval metrics.

This paper was reviewed by three experts in the field. The initial recommendations were one Weak Accept and two Weak Rejects. After the rebuttal, reviewers updated their recommendations to Accept. Based on the authors’ rebuttal and the reviewers’ post-rebuttal feedback, I believe the authors have adequately addressed the key concerns, including retrieval validation, novelty, and comparison with MAISI. Therefore, the paper is recommended for acceptance to MICCAI 2026.The authors are encouraged to incorporate the necessary changes discussed during the rebuttal process into the final camera-ready version.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers and the AC for the constructive feedback.
[R1,R2,R3] Retrieval Validation: We clarify that our ablation was designed to validate the core retrieval assumption. Comparing RAG-Nearest, Random, and Farthest under identical generative conditions directly isolates retrieval quality: the monotonic, statistically significant degradation from Nearest→Random→Farthest across all evaluation axes (paired Wilcoxon p<0.05) is direct empirical evidence that semantic similarity correlates with anatomically and clinically meaningful proxies. Regarding explicit retrieval metrics: our system uses the 3D encoder of [22], the following numbers are from that paper, not new results from our experiments. [22] evaluates the encoder retrieval on CT-RATE achieving Re@5=0.041, Re@10=0.072, Re@50=0.229, Re@100=0.368 and MAP@1=0.987, MAP@5=0.848.MAP@K is the most informative metric for our task: the proxy does not need to replicate the target anatomy, but to provide a structurally coherent scaffold aligned with the report pathological content. MAP@1 confirms the nearest neighbor shares the same pathological class in nearly all cases. 
[R1,R2,R3] Novelty: No prior work addresses annotation-free anatomical conditioning for text-to-CT generation. We agree the individual components are not new in isolation, and that architecturally we build on [22], a deliberate choice, as it ranks as SOTA on the VLM3D Challenge [12], the MICCAI benchmark for this task. Our core contribution is identifying and addressing a systematic limitation of text-to-CT methods: radiology reports are inherently underspecified with respect to spatial structure, and this limitation propagates directly into anatomically inconsistent outputs, with consequences in real deployment scenarios (Morrison et al., “A Human-centered approach to identifying promises, risks & challenges of text-to-image generative AI in radiology”, AIES 2025). We propose retrieval-augmented anatomical proxy conditioning to counter this flaw, achieving statistically significant improvements across all three evaluation axes.
[R1,R2] Spatial Controllability: Dice and HD95 are intentionally computed against the retrieved proxy, measuring the model’s ability to follow the provided scaffold, which is the relevant capability in our setting. Evaluating against the GT would be misleading, as the report does not describe individual anatomy. In addition, a model trivially copying the proxy would score high here but degrade on AUC (Table 2); RAG-Nearest achieves both the highest Dice and highest AUC, confirming the two axes are complementary and that structural guidance does not come at the cost of semantic quality. 
[R2] Encoder Domain Alignment: We apologise for the ambiguity. The encoder used for retrieval is pre-trained on CT-RATE, not a generic CLIP encoder. This will be stated explicitly in the final version.
[R3] MAISI Comparison: R3 correctly notes that MAISI supports predicted masks at inference, however the key distinction is not the mask source, but whose mask is used: MAISI conditions on the target volume’s own mask, giving it direct structural access to the case being synthesized, making it an oracle upper bound. Our method requires no mask at inference; the proxy is obtained purely via retrieval from the input report. MAISI has no mechanism to obtain a structural proxy from a report alone, nor can it leverage the report for conditioning. MAISI’s oracle status will be stated more explicitly in the final version.
[R3] FID comparability: All methods were retrained on CT-RATE following official repositories, ensuring uniform training distribution, shape, and preprocessing. This was necessary since FID is a distributional metric sensitive to data shape and CT-Net would otherwise operate on heterogeneous inputs. This will be further acknowledged in the final version.
[R1,R2] Radiologist Evaluation: We acknowledge the absence of a reader study as a limitation and consider it a priority for future work

title: Retrieval-Based Mixture-of-Experts for Patient-Specific Cancer Survival Prediction with Incomplete Multimodal Data
abstract: Survival prediction is crucial in clinical oncology for cancer prognosis and treatment planning. Recent survival prediction models have shown that integrating pathology whole-slide images (WSIs) and gene expression data effectively improves performance by leveraging complementary morphological and molecular information. However, in clinical practice, complete multimodal data are often unavailable due to high costs, privacy concerns, and workflow constraints, resulting in substantial modality missingness. In such settings, existing methods typically (i) rely on modality-specific or modality-common information shared across patients, often overlooking patient-specific cross-modal dependencies, and (ii) adopt a single static prediction pathway, which limits their ability to adapt to diverse missingness patterns. To address these challenges, we propose Retrieval-based Mixture-of-Experts (RMoE) for robust cancer survival prediction with incomplete multimodal data. To explicitly capture patient-specific cross-modal dependencies, RMoE utilizes bidirectional cross-modal retrieval, identifying phenotypically similar patients and enabling patient-adaptive imputation through biologically relevant neighbors. Furthermore, we introduce a reliability-aware Mixture-of-Experts architecture, where a router dynamically weights specialized experts by assessing retrieval confidence and modality availability, ensuring stable predictions regardless of diverse missing modality settings. Experiments on three public cancer datasets with 60% missingness show that RMoE consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art methods.
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper is well written, clearly structured, and easy to follow. The methodology is thoughtfully designed and introduces a novel approach to handling incomplete multimodal data through the integration of retrieval-based imputation and a reliability-aware mixture-of-experts framework. The overall idea is both interesting and relevant, particularly in realistic clinical settings where missing modalities are common. The proposed method is technically sound, and the motivation is well aligned with practical challenges in multimodal survival prediction.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper has several strong aspects. First, it proposes a novel formulation for handling incomplete multimodal data through a retrieval-based paradigm, where missing modalities are imputed using patient-specific neighbors rather than global statistics or generative models; this is particularly interesting because it explicitly models patient-level cross-modal dependencies, which are often overlooked in prior work. Second, the integration of a reliability-aware Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is well-motivated and technically sound, enabling the model to dynamically adapt to different missingness scenarios by weighting unimodal and multimodal experts based on retrieval confidence, which improves robustness in realistic settings. Third, the approach demonstrates strong clinical relevance, as it directly addresses the common issue of missing data in real-world oncology workflows and does not rely on complete multimodal inputs. Fourth, the evaluation is comprehensive, including multiple TCGA cohorts, different modality availability settings, and comparisons with both unimodal and multimodal baselines, showing consistent improvements even under high missingness. Finally, the paper provides supporting analyses such as ablations, retrieval visualization (e. g. , t-SNE), and generalization experiments with alternative backbones, which help validate the effectiveness and flexibility of the proposed framework.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Despite the strengths of the paper, there are several important limitations.
First, the degree of interpretability and biological insight is limited. While the proposed retrieval mechanism is motivated by identifying phenotypically similar patients, the paper does not provide sufficient analysis to explain what specific histopathological or genomic features are driving the predictions. The provided t-SNE visualization offers only a high-level view of the embedding space and does not yield clinically actionable insights. In addition, the behavior of the reliability-aware Mixture-of-Experts (e. g. , expert selection patterns and their clinical meaning) is not analyzed, which further limits interpretability.
Second, the paper does not include clinicopathologic variables such as age, tumor stage, or grade, which are well-established prognostic factors. As a result, it is unclear whether the proposed model captures truly novel multimodal information or whether it is implicitly learning patterns correlated with these clinical variables. This limits the ability to assess the independence and added clinical value of the learned representations. Including such features or providing an analysis/discussion on their potential impact would strengthen the paper’s clinical relevance.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Please see the weakness section.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: In my view, this manuscript can be accepted.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: They propose a bidirectional cross-modal retrieval mechanism that uses the available modality to retrieve phenotypically similar patients from a memory bank in a shared embedding space, and imputes the missing modality via similarity-weighted aggregation of top-k neighbors, with retrieval restricted to the same risk group. They also introduce a reliability-aware MoE architecture, where a router dynamically interpolates between unimodal and multimodal experts based on retrieval confidence, so that the model can fall back to the unimodal expert when retrieval is unreliable. The method is evaluated on three TCGA datasets (BLCA, BRCA, UCEC) under 60% missing.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The problem is practical. In real clinical workflows, a missing modality is common. The paper targets this relevant practical issue.
2.Compared to prototype-based or shared-representation methods, using patient-specific neighbors to impute missing modalities directly addresses the patient-level heterogeneity argument the authors make in the intro. This idea is well-motivated.
3.RMoE achieves the best performance in most setting, and the observation that genomics-only RMoE on BRCA outperforms the multimodal results of several competing methods is interesting.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Lack of baseline. This paper should compare with SOTA methods, such as [1]
[1] Zhou, Junjie, et al. “Robust multimodal survival prediction with the latent differentiation conditional variational autoencoder.” CVPR 2025.2.The paper reports results only on BLCA, BRCA, and UCEC. Given that TCGA covers a large number of cancer types and that prior multimodal survival works commonly evaluate on 5 or more cohorts, limiting evaluation to three cohorts makes it difficult to assess whether the method generalizes across cancer types with different tumor biology and survival characteristics. A broader evaluation is needed to substantiate the generality claim.
3.The paper’s core claim is robustness to missing modalities, yet the experiments cover only one missing rate. How does performance change at 30%, 50%, or 80% missingness? Without this, the robustness claim is not fully supported.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses a clinically important problem with a reasonably well-motivated design. However, evaluation is limited to only three TCGA cohorts and a single missingness rate. If the authors can extend evaluation to more TCGA cohorts and report results under multiple missingness rates I would be willing to raise the score.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors argue that three cohorts suffice because results are consistent across them. However, the comparison methods they cite (DisPro, ProSurv) themselves evaluate on 5+ TCGA cohorts. Given substantial differences in tumor biology and modality informativeness across cancer types, three cohorts cannot rule out cohort-specific behavior. 
For missing rates, there is an internal tension in the authors’ defense. They justify the single 60% setting by “following prior methods for fair benchmarking,” yet frame robustness to missing modalities as the paper’s core contribution. These positions conflict: if the protocol just mirrors prior work, the robustness claim cannot exceed what that protocol demonstrates. Substantiating robustness as a headline contribution requires a performance curve across varied missing rates.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper’s main contribution is a survival prediction framework for incomplete WSI+genomics data that combines two components:
Bidirectional cross-modal retrieval to impute the missing modality by retrieving similar patients from a multimodal memory bank using cosine similarity in a learned shared space.
Reliability-aware MoE routing that adaptively mixes unimodal and multimodal experts according to a confidence score derived from retrieval similarity.
A secondary contribution is the use of a risk-aware cross-modal contrastive loss, where patients in the same discretized survival-risk group are treated as positives when learning the retrieval space.
reviews.text_strengths:
The problem is important and clinically relevant. The paper directly addresses incomplete multimodal data, which is a real issue in pathology and genomics workflows, rather than assuming full modality availability. This is also a trending topic in multimodal medical learning at the moment.
The method is conceptually clean and does not rely on generative imputation. The idea is kind of similar to finding a “digital twin” given that we can not reliably get image counterfactuals.
Analysis is intuitive and supports the authors’ story that both retrieval and reliability-aware expert routing matter.
The empirical results are quite strong and I do believe these are generalizable gains (as opposed to generative imputation methods).
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Great work, but really need to stress the clinical contribution better (maybe you can’t change a whole lot this submission, but if you get accepted/later present this work elsewhere, u need to think again about the story logic). My understanding of your greatest contribution is that you get rid of the prevalent generative imputation methods, which real clinicians will without doubt discard in real diagnostics workflows. Your method is not only novel in the technical sense, it is well-motivated by real-life clinical practice (the doctors look at similar patients, and would ideally desire a “ digital twin “ when they think of AI for missing modalities. As someone who work with patients, doctors would buy your method a lot more than a “diffusion for missing data imputation” paper.
MICCAI doesnt encourage more experiments. But I believe a small experiment that is not MCAR could greatly strengthen the story. Missingness often depends on site, workflow, indication, or patient subgroup. 
If you read the other recent MoE and missingness type of work, which I highly encourage you to compare with (not actually running them , just talkin about it ) and discuss in the related works, you would find out that they are treating different missing patterns as different groups. By doing so, my understanding is that they implicitly encode MNAR subgroup information, although they are not perfect – even within the same subgroup, there could be different missing reasons and the missing modalities could be of high or little clinical value. Therefore it would be really great for you to run something that isnt MCAR and is well controlled and see how it goes.
Two papers that leverages the “missingness subgroup” mindset that I mentioned above:
nips 24 Flex-MoE: Modeling Arbitrary Modality Combination via the Flexible Mixture-of-Experts
cvpr 26 REMIND: Rethinking Medical High-Modality Learning under Missingness–A Long-Tailed Distribution Perspective
3.A potential concern about outcome-informed retrieval space design is that the retrieval learning explicitly uses discretized survival-risk labels to define positives, and training-time retrieval is restricted to same-risk-group entries. Can you talk more about whether this creates optimism?
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The multimodal fusion with missingness subfield literally needs papers like this that gets rid of fancy imputations. There is a irreducible information gap for missing modalities and imputation of modalities will literally just inject more noises. This work does the opposite and is well motivated by clinical reality that doctors look for “patient twins” given we can never get the counterfactual data of tests not done.
Authors also manage to combine this intricately with recent moe architectures elegantly.
I gave a 4 instead of 5 or 6, because this work can be truly impactful if the not MCAR setting can be discussed more (this is also what other recent missingness works have shifted towards explicitly or implicitly).
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: authors have addressed my comments fully, thus I recommend for accept

meta_reviews.text:
Due to the mixed reviews, I recommend inviting the paper for rebuttal. The authors are encouraged to address the major concerns raised by the reviewers. If these issues can be adequately resolved during the rebuttal process, I would consider acceptance, even if the reviewers may not update their scores afterward.

This paper presents a retrieval-based mixture-of-experts framework for survival prediction with incomplete multimodal data. I agree with Reviewers #1 and #3 that the problem is clinically important, the proposed retrieval-based design is well motivated, and the experimental results are consistently strong across multiple settings. While Reviewer #2 raised concerns regarding the limited number of cohorts and missingness-rate evaluations, I view these as opportunities for future work rather than issues that undermine the main contribution. Overall, the paper provides a novel and practically relevant solution to multimodal missingness and I recommend acceptance.

The reviewers agreed that the paper addresses an important and clinically realistic problem, namely survival prediction with incomplete multimodal data, and appreciated the retrieval-based “patient twin” formulation together with the reliability-aware MoE design. The method was viewed as technically sound, clinically well motivated, and empirically strong, particularly because it avoids potentially unreliable generative imputation and instead leverages patient-specific retrieval for missing modality handling. Although concerns remain regarding broader evaluation across additional cohorts, varying missingness settings, and non-MCAR scenarios, the post-rebuttal discussion overall supports the novelty, practical relevance, and potential impact of the work. I therefore recommend acceptance.

The paper tackles a clinically important incomplete multimodal survival prediction problem and proposes a reasonable retrieval-based MoE framework. Two reviewers support acceptance after rebuttal. Although evaluation is limited to three TCGA cohorts and one main missingness rate, the method is well motivated, technically sound, and shows consistent improvements. The final version should tone down broad robustness claims and discuss missingness assumptions and clinical-variable integration more clearly.

author_feedback_text:
We greatly appreciate the constructive feedback from the AC & Reviewers. We respond to all concerns below.
R1: ADDITIONAL INTERPRETABILITY ANALYSIS.
– We note that analyses of our main component were prioritized. Since our primary goal is to compensate for missing modalities through retrieval, we focus on verifying retrieval effectiveness through t-SNE. Our MoE is interpretable by design, as gating weights reflect confidence in each expert according to retrieval quality, providing transparent decision-making. Additional analyses (e.g., WSI heatmaps and genomic importance scores) were omitted due to limited space.
R1: INTEGRATION OF CLINICAL VARIABLES.
– Since our framework is modality-agnostic, clinical variables can be naturally incorporated as auxiliary metadata. We agree that this integration may further improve predictive performance. We will discuss it as a potential extension in the final version.
R2: ADDITIONAL BASELINES & DATASETS.
– We included 8 competitive baselines spanning unimodal, multimodal, and 5 recent methods handling missing modalities during both training and test.
– We appreciate suggesting LD-CVAE. While LD-CVAE assumes complete multimodal data at training and specifically addresses missing genomics at test, our RMoE considers a more challenging setting where either WSI or genomics may be missing during both training and test. Therefore, we prioritized methods more closely aligned with our challenging setting. Notably, DisPro (CVPR2025) and ProSurv (MICCAI2025) target survival prediction under all possible missing settings.
– We evaluated our RMoE on widely used BLCA, BRCA, and UCEC datasets, which represent diverse cancer types with different cross-modal characteristics. Consistent improvements across all cohorts support the generalizability of our approach. As noted in the Conclusion, we are extending our method to larger external clinical cohorts.
R2: MISSING RATES.
– Our robustness claim refers to maintaining strong performance under severe missing modality settings during both training and test, unlike many previous methods that only consider test-time missingness.
– In this work, we adopt the 60% missingness setting in training, following comparative methods for fair benchmarking. DisPro explicitly evaluates under 60% missingness, while ProSurv reports 60% as the most severe setting in its ablation study. We adopt this severe missing rate during training, expecting that superior performance under such severe conditions would generalize to less challenging missing rates. Moreover, we evaluate extreme missing settings during test (i.e., WSI-only and genomics-only), and our RMoE consistently achieves the best performance across all settings.
– While our experiments consider such highly challenging missing settings, we will further investigate diverse missing rates for a more comprehensive robustness analysis.
R3: HIGHLIGHTING CLINICAL MOTIVATION.
– Thanks for recognizing the clinical relevance of our RMoE. Our method performs retrieval-based reasoning using clinically similar patients, which better aligns with real-world clinical workflows. We will emphasize this clinical motivation in the final version.
R3: MNAR SETTING.
– While this study focuses on standard MAR/MCAR benchmark settings, our retrieval-based completion strategy is potentially more robust to MNAR settings than purely generative approaches because it leverages biological similarity among clinically related patients. We will evaluate realistic MNAR settings where missingness correlates with clinical covariates in future work.
R3: CLARIFICATION ON RETRIEVAL SPACE DESIGN.
– We clarify that our design does not introduce optimistic bias or label leakage. Risk-group labels are used only as a coarse auxiliary signal to stabilize the retrieval process and organize clinically meaningful neighborhoods during training. Retrieved features provide contextual support for modality completion but never serve as surrogate labels.

title: Retrieval-Guided Semi-supervised Federated Learning for Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Semi-supervised federated learning (SSFL) has emerged as a promising approach for medical image segmentation, enabling collaborative learning across institutions using both limited labeled and abundant unlabeled data without sharing sensitive patient information. However, existing methods utilize publicly available labeled data merely as a generic training pool for knowledge transfer, failing to exploit the fine-grained semantic information embedded in individual public samples that could directly inform the segmentation of unlabeled local data. To overcome this limitation, we propose a Retrieved Reference-guided Semi-Supervised Federated segmentation framework (R2S2Fed) that explicitly leverages public labeled data as contextual references rather than a generic knowledge source. During local training, our method dynamically retrieves semantically relevant public references for each unlabeled local sample based on feature similarity, and leverages their representations to generate query-specific segmentation parameters through a dynamic segmentation head. This provides explicit supervision for unlabeled local data, enabling each client to perform adaptive segmentation tailored to its local data characteristics. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed method consistently outperforms existing SSFL approaches in both IID and Non-IID settings.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes R2S2Fed for the labels-for-public semi-supervised federated segmentation setting, where clients have unlabeled private data and a public labeled dataset is available. The main idea is to treat the public dataset not merely as a source of global supervision, but as a query-conditioned reference memory. For each unlabeled local query, the method retrieves semantically similar public samples and uses their representations to generate a dynamic segmentation head tailored to that query. The paper further proposes Query-Adaptive Retrieval (QAR), which periodically refreshes retrieval based on the evolving encoder, and evaluates the method on IID ISIC2018 and non-IID polyp segmentation settings.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The labels-for-public SSFL setting is practical and relevant, and the paper addresses it with a clearly motivated retrieval-based perspective. 
2.Using public labeled data as query-specific references, rather than only as a source of global model supervision, is the most novel and interesting part of the paper. 
3.The gains on the heterogeneous polyp setting are substantial, which suggests that the retrieval-guided formulation may indeed be particularly useful under domain shift. 
4.The paper includes qualitative examples and some ablation analysis, which is appreciated for a method that aims to exploit sample-level semantics.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Regarding the dynamic head formulation in Section 2.2: The authors state that the cross-attention output omega in R^{2 x C} directly defines the parameters, with the ‘background channel’ serving as the bias. However, for a standard 1x1 convolution layer mapping from C input channels to 1 or 2 output channels (binary segmentation), the Bias should be a scalar or a vector of size 1 or 2, not a vector of size C. This is important because it is central to the proposed method. 
2.Table 2b is incomplete or at least very hard to interpret. The ‘retrieval on train and test’ ablation appears to show only three configurations instead of a full 2 x 2 design, which makes it difficult to disentangle the contribution of retrieval during training versus inference. 
3.The training pipeline is somewhat inconsistent with the paper’s main narrative. After federated aggregation, the server performs additional training on the public dataset using randomly selected references rather than retrieval-based references. This makes it harder to isolate how much of the gain comes from the proposed QAR mechanism itself. 
4.There are several notation and presentation issues that reduce precision, such as the mixed use of R and S in the reference-supervision equation and the brief explanation of randomly reversed masks.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Overall, I find the paper promising. The retrieval-guided use of public labeled data is a meaningful step beyond treating public data as a generic knowledge source, and the empirical gains in the heterogeneous setting are noteworthy. But several important technical details remain unclear and some experimental choices or ablations are not yet fully convincing.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have adequately addressed several of my concerns. Having considered the complete rebuttal and the other reviews, I keep my initial rating as weak accept.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The author proposed a retrieval-based method for semi-supervised federated learning for medical image segmentation. The core idea is to retrieve top-k samples from a publicly available dataset for each client image, use them to generate dynamic heads for segmentation networks, and employ fixmatch semi-supervised training at the client level using these retrieved samples.
reviews.text_strengths:
The idea of using a public dataset as a reference for queries (unlabeled client images) is novel in the context of semi-supervised FL for medical image segmentation. 
Good performance, as seen in Table 1, and includes appropriate baselines required in labels for public settings.
Ablation Studies are particularly informative. It shows that even when the retrieved sample size is small, the model still performs well [Table 2(a)].
reviews.text_weaknesses:
One major weakness of the approach is the need for a reference dataset at test time. In an ablation study (Table 2(b)), when retrieval is omitted, random references are assigned instead of zero-filling or random noise filling. Which means during test-time inferences, we still need a reference to make a prediction, which is impractical in an offline scenario.
Section 2.2 training strategy, last para, mentions random selection of references rather than semantic selection for diversity? What’s the justification for needing diversity here (assuming this is for server training)? There is no evidence (cited work or experiments) to support this claim.
The number of clients in the non-IID setup is very low compared to the prior study[1]. It utilizes 4 clients in non-IID instead of 3 clients.
[1] Ma, Y., Wang, J., Yang, J., Wang, L.: Model-heterogeneous semi-supervised federated learning for medical image segmentation. IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging 43(5), 1804–1815 (2024)
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
What was happening in local client training when K =1? As per section 2.2 training strategy, one image in the retrieved set is strongly augmented, and the remaining are used as references for supervised training. When K=1, there are no other references. In such a scenario, how does the model predict the output?
The labels in Figure 3 are wrong. The top row is ISIC, and the bottom row is Polyp.

The method is interesting and fairly novel (establishing references), and they outperformed the baselines by quite a large margin compared to existing baselines in non-iid. This will help in future work to pursue a similar avenue of retrieval-based method in semiFL.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: While i still have my concerns in test-time requirements of reference, I recommend acceptance, based on the strong performance of proposed method and overall contribution to the community to pursue retrieval based SemiFL.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a retrieval-guided SSFL framework that retrieves similar public labeled samples for each unlabeled client image and uses them to generate query-specific segmentation parameters, aiming to improve federated medical image segmentation, especially under heterogeneity.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Solid empirical gains in the heterogeneous setting. On the non-IID polyp benchmark, the reported improvements are substantial: R2S2Fed achieves 67.15 Dice / 57.43 IoU on average, compared with 59.66 / 47.83 for the strongest baseline LSSL. 
2.Useful ablation on retrieval. The paper does include ablations on the number of retrieved references and on whether retrieval is used during training and/or inference. These studies provide some evidence that retrieval during training is more important than retrieval only at test time. 
3.Qualitative examples are consistent with the quantitative trend. The visual comparisons in Fig. 2 and the retrieval visualization in Fig. 3 help illustrate the authors’ intuition that semantically relevant public references may be more beneficial under heterogeneity.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Limited methodological novelty. The main concern is that the paper does not appear to introduce a sufficiently new algorithmic contribution. The proposed framework combines several familiar components: public-sample retrieval, cross-attention-based reference conditioning, dynamic/query-specific segmentation parameters, FixMatch-style semi-supervised training, and standard FedAvg aggregation. The paper itself states that the framework is inspired by prior hypernetwork/context-dependent segmentation approaches, which further weakens the novelty claim. As a result, the contribution feels more like an application-specific integration than a distinctly new method. 
2.The federated learning component is fairly standard. On the FL side, the method relies on conventional FedAvg, and the server additionally trains on the public dataset after aggregation, as commonly done in prior SSFL works. There is no new federated optimization strategy, no communication-efficient mechanism, no privacy analysis, and no explicit treatment of client heterogeneity beyond reference retrieval. This makes the “federated” contribution less compelling. 
3.Experimental scope is too narrow for the claimed generality. The experimental validation is limited to two 2D segmentation tasks: skin lesion segmentation on ISIC2018 and polyp segmentation across four datasets. The backbone is a relatively standard ResNet34 encoder-decoder. There is no validation on more diverse medical segmentation settings, no 3D benchmark, no stronger modern backbone, and no comparison to more recent segmentation paradigms. For a MICCAI paper claiming a generally useful framework, this scope feels insufficient. 
4.The improvement in the IID setting is modest. On ISIC, the average Dice improves only from 84.71 ((FL)2) to 85.26, which is a rather small margin. This weakens the claim that the proposed mechanism provides broad and consistent gains beyond a more specialized heterogeneous setting. 
5.Ablations do not fully support the strongest paper narrative. The paper emphasizes query-adaptive retrieval and query-specific adaptation at inference time, but Table 2b indicates that retrieval during training is the main source of gain, while retrieval at inference provides only marginal improvement. This suggests that the true benefit may come more from retrieval-enhanced training than from the claimed adaptive inference behavior. The paper should reconcile this observation more carefully.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

My recommendation is mainly based on limited novelty and insufficient experimental breadth. Although the idea is reasonable, the method largely combines existing ingredients—retrieval from public data, dynamic/query-conditioned segmentation, FixMatch-style training, and standard FedAvg—while the paper itself notes inspiration from prior hypernetwork/context-conditioned segmentation frameworks.
In addition, the evaluation is relatively narrow for MICCAI: it uses only two 2D tasks with a standard ResNet34 encoder-decoder, the gain in the IID setting is modest (85.26 vs. 84.71 Dice), and the ablation suggests that retrieval helps mainly during training rather than strongly supporting the claimed adaptive inference story.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I have read the rebuttal carefully. While the authors clarified several technical details, my main concerns remain unresolved. The methodological novelty still appears limited, as the rebuttal does not substantially change my assessment that the proposed framework is mainly an integration of existing ideas rather than a clearly new algorithmic contribution. The FL component also remains standard, with no new optimization, communication, privacy, or heterogeneity-specific mechanism beyond the proposed retrieval strategy. Finally, the experimental scope remains narrow, being limited to two 2D segmentation settings with a standard backbone; the claim that the method is extendable to 3D or other backbones does not provide additional evidence. Therefore, I do not think the rebuttal changes the core assessment, and I will maintain my score of 2.

meta_reviews.text:
I invite a rebuttal despite one “Reject” and two “Weak Accept” scores. The method is promising, but key concerns must be clarified: (1) the dynamic head formulation and bias dimension (R1), (2) the incomplete ablation in Table 2b and the need for a reference at test time (R1,R2), (3) the limited novelty and narrow experimental scope (R3). The rebuttal should focus on these technical clarifications and provide additional ablations or analysis to strengthen the claimed contributions.

After carefully considering the initial reviews, the authors’ rebuttal, and the final post-rebuttal opinions of reviewers, I recommend Accept. While Reviewer #3 raised valid concerns about novelty and experimental breadth, the rebuttal convincingly clarified the key technical issues (e.g., bias formulation, test-time reference dependency, and the role of random server-side selection). Reviewers #1 and #2, who initially rated the paper as Weak Accept, both upgraded to Accept after the rebuttal, acknowledging that the major concerns were adequately addressed.

Despite the authors’ efforts, several critical technical and empirical concerns raised by the reviewers and the AC panel remain insufficiently addressed:
1.Incomplete Ablation Studies and Over-simplification (Table 2b): The reviewers pointed out that the ablation experiment was incomplete. Though the authors provided the missing configuration, the justification for the experimental setup remains overly brief and over-simplified. The authors primarily stated that they followed existing literature without providing the specific, explicit details of the experimental settings required to make the ablation self-contained and convincing.
2.Test-time Reference Dependency and Practical Constraints: A major concern is that the framework requires reference samples during the inference/testing phase. Although the authors argued that the model can achieve comparable performance with random references or a small shipped reference set, this dependency inherently restricts the model’s flexibility, offline applicability, and deployment capability.
Overall, while the core idea is noted, the combination of a constrained inference paradigm and insufficient depth in the ablation/experimental verification prevents the paper from meeting the acceptance threshold of the conference.

The paper proposes R2S2Fed, a retrieval-guided semi-supervised federated learning method for medical image segmentation in the labels-for-public setting, where clients have unlabeled private data and a labeled public dataset is available.
After considering the reviews and rebuttal, my recommendation is accept.
While some concerns remain regarding the methodology novelty and test-time inference, the retrieval-conditioned use of public labeled data is a useful and timely direction for semi-supervised federated medical segmentation. Reviewers generally agree that the retrieval-based use of public samples is interesting, and two reviewers support acceptance after rebuttal.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for constructive feedback. We address the major concerns as below.
1 (R3.1, R3.2) Limited methodological novelty and FL contribution
We propose a fundamentally new SSFL paradigm that reframes public labeled data from a generalized supervisory source into a sample-level semantic resource. Prior methods compress public labeled data into model parameters or pseudo-labels, inevitably losing sample-level semantics. We are the first to repurpose public data as a per-query reference. For each unlabeled client image, QAR dynamically retrieves the reference set as the encoder evolves, and a dynamic head transforms the retrieved references via cross-attention into query-adaptive parameters. These coupled mechanisms preserve sample-level semantics throughout federated training, enabling sample-level adaptation that differs from aggregation-based approaches.
To demonstrate our framework, we intentionally use the simplest baselines. Our method still achieves the highest performance in both IID and Non-IID, maintaining strong results with FedAvg alone even under severe heterogeneity. Furthermore, our framework is compatible with optimization-based FL methods, expecting further gains when combined with them.
2 (R3.3) Narrow experimental scope
We follow the experimental setting of Ma et al. (IEEE TMI 2024) for fair comparison. Our framework is backbone-agnostic and can be extended to 3D segmentation.
3 (R3.4) Small ISIC gain weakens the consistent-gains claim
We achieve the best performance in both IID and non-IID settings. IID is a relatively easier benchmark where most methods are already saturated. Despite this, our method maintains stable performance across all clients, whereas competing methods exhibit drops on certain clients.
4 (R1.3, R2.2) Random selection for server-side training contradict QAR
Random server selection and client QAR play complementary roles: random ensures global model stability, while QAR enables query-specific adaptation. With query and reference from the same public dataset, server retrieval selects near-identical samples, hindering generalization to the client-public gap. Replacing random with retrieval drops polyp dice to 18.45.5 (R1.2, R3.5) Incomplete Table 2b and weak inference-time gain undermine the adaptive inference claim.
Completing the 2x2 ablation, the (training retrieval, no test retrieval) configuration shows only a 0.02 difference from the full setting, consistent with the trend when training retrieval is omitted. Regarding R3’s concern, QAR improves training by providing the dynamic head with better supervision through semantically relevant references, as evidenced by the ~5% drop shown in Table 2b. when training retrieval is removed. Consequently, the marginal inference-time gain is expected. We will revise Contribution 1 to “retrieval-guided training enabling reference-aligned inference” and update Table 2b. 
6 (R2.1) Test-time reference dependency limits offline applicability
Our framework achieves comparable performance with random references at inference (cf. Q5), showing representations are robust to the reference choice. A small reference set shipped with the model suffices for offline deployment.
7 (R2.3) Fewer clients in non-IID setup than prior work
Although we follow Ma et al., CVC-ClinicDB and CVC-300 are derived from the same source data (EndoScene, CVC Barcelona), making them a single split rather than independent federated clients. We therefore conduct our experiments under a stronger heterogeneous setting with three datasets from truly distinct institutions.
8 (R1.1) Background channel as bias inconsistent with scalar bias of 1x1 conv
The background channel of w is averaged across the channel dimension to yield a scalar bias. We will clarify Section 2.2.9 (R1.4, R2 Optional): Minor presentation and clarity issues.
We thank the reviewers and will address these in the final version.

title: REVEAL++: Differentiable Phenotypic Grouping for Vision–Language Retinal Modeling of Alzheimer’s Disease Risk
abstract:
The retina offers a noninvasive window into neurodegenerative disease, capturing subtle structural patterns associated with a risk of future cognitive decline. Vision–language alignment frameworks such as REVEAL have shown that pairing retinal fundus images with structured clinical risk narratives improves early prediction of Alzheimer’s disease (AD).
A key design choice in these approaches is the use of phenotypic grouping, where individuals with similar risk profiles are treated as multi-positive pairs during contrastive learning. 
However, existing methods operationalize phenotypic similarity as a discrete construct, relying on hard group assignments that impose rigid supervision and decouple group formation from representation learning. 
We propose a continuous formulation of phenotypic structure within contrastive learning. Rather than assigning samples to fixed clusters, we model inter-subject similarity as a differentiable weighting function derived from intra-modality embedding similarities in both retinal images and risk profiles. These weights define soft multi-positive relationships through a continuous aggregation operator, enabling graded supervision that reflects the spectrum nature of disease risk. We further introduce a soft-target contrastive objective that jointly learns cross-modal alignment and phenotypic structure in an end-to-end manner. Evaluated on UK Biobank retinal imaging data for incident AD prediction, the proposed framework consistently outperforms discrete group-based contrastive learning and standard vision–language baselines. By treating phenotypic similarity as a learnable, continuous signal rather than a fixed grouping rule, our approach provides a principled and robust foundation for population-scale neurodegenerative risk modeling from multi-modal retinal and clinical data. Code is available at: .
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers
Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a soft Differentiable Phenotypic Grouping method within a contrastive learning framework and applies it to the published REVEAL for Alzheimer’s disease (AD) risk prediction. Results show that the proposed method achieved the best performance
reviews.text_strengths: 1.The proposed method extends the REVEAL with a soft Phenotypic Grouping within contrastive learning and shows an advantage in AD risk prediction
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Clarity of the overall framework: The overall framework is not clearly presented. The proposed method appears to be built upon REVEAL, but this prior work is not properly cited in the main text. Although the REVEAL paper is included in the reference list, it is not explicitly referenced where relevant, which affects clarity and attribution. 
2.Task definition: The task is not clearly defined. In particular, it is unclear what form the Alzheimer’s disease (AD) risk prediction takes (e. g. , classification, regression, or risk score estimation). 
3.Clarity of notation: The definition of symbols needs to be clarified. For example, the meaning of \tau in Section 2.3 is not clearly explained, which may lead to confusion.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Clarity of writing, Completeness of the Paper
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Although the authors claim to have corrected some errors and revised certain definitions, I do not think these changes adequately address the overall concerns through a minor revision, especially those related to the overall framework. Therefore, I maintain my final recommendation of rejection.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper proposes REVEAL++, a vision-language alignment framework for Alzheimer’s disease (AD) risk prediction. Based on the prior work REVEAL, REVEAL++ introduces a key innovation of substituting the original hard threshold-based phenotypic grouping with continuous phenotypic weighting in the group-aware contrastive learning framework. REVEAL++ applies a soft-target contrastive objective based on phenotypic similarity to enable multi-positive contrastive supervision so as to reflect the spectrum-like nature of AD risk and improve the prediction performance.
The method is evaluated on a clinical Alzheimer’s dataset and is compared with traditional SVM baselines and vision-language baselines. AUROC, balanced accuracy, F1-score and MCC are reported in the results to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The proposed REVEAL++ consistently outperforms baseline methods in all the reported metrics and achieves new state-of-the-art performance.
reviews.text_strengths:
(1) The paper presents a clear and well-motivated improvement over the prior method, where the hard threshold-based phenotypic grouping strategy in REVEAL is effectively redesigned into continuous phenotypic weighting considering the limitations of introducing hard artificial boundaries, resulting in improved performance. 
(2) The proposed modifications are clearly described, and implementation details and hyperparameter settings are sufficiently documented, facilitating reproducibility.
(3) The experimental results show consistent performance gains over a range of visual-language baselines and the prior method REVEAL, indicating that the proposed modifications are practically effective.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(1) The overall methodological novelty is somewhat limited, as the proposed method (REVEAL++) is only an modification of the prior work (REVEAL), with relatively minor changes to the original design.
(2) The paper only reports performance of the modified model compared to the prior work with a single additional result without more comprehensive analysis. The lack of deeper experimental studies, for example, including comparisons with image-based CNN/Transformer baselines or studies on the contribution of each modality, may limit the overall novelty and the strength of the empirical evidence supporting the proposed improvement.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

REVEAL++ presents a well-motivated improvement over REVEAL by replacing a hard threshold-based phenotypic grouping strategy with continuous phenotypic weighting, which is intuitive and empirically effective. The method is clearly described with sufficient implementation details, and shows consistent performance gains over several visual-language baselines and REVEAL, suggesting practical usefulness.
However, the overall novelty is incremental, and the experimental evaluation is limited in scope, lacking deeper comprehensive comparisons and ablation studies.
Overall, despite these limitations, the method demonstrates consistent empirical improvements and reasonable design clarity. With additional analysis and clearer justification, the paper would meet the criteria for acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The paper presents REVEAL++, a well-motivated extension of REVEAL that improves retinal image-based AD risk prediction by replacing discrete group assignments with a differentiable phenotypic weighting mechanism. This modification better captures the continuous nature of preclinical AD progression and consistently improves performance over REVEAL and multiple vision-language baselines. While the novelty builds on prior work, the authors distinguish inherited components from new contributions and provide thorough ablation analyses within the page limit. Additional clarifications, including task definition, notation, and evaluation protocol, further strengthen understanding and reproducibility will be supported via code release. Overall, the paper makes a significant methodological contribution to early AD prediction from retinal data and meets the standard for MICCAI acceptance.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper introduces a differentiable phenotypic weighting framework for vision–language modelling of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) risk from retinal images and associated clinical narratives. Building on prior work (REVEAL) the key idea is to replace hard phenotypic group assignments with a continuous, learnable formulation that captures inter-subject similarity.
The method constructs a soft phenotypic weighting matrix that encodes pairwise similarity between subjects using sigmoid-based gating functions with learnable sharpness. This matrix is then incorporated into a multi-positive contrastive learning objective, allowing sampled pairs to contribute to the loss as positives or negatives with varying degrees of strength, rather than through hard assignment.
The approach is evaluated on a large-scale UK Biobank cohort (~40k subjects), where it demonstrates improved AD risk prediction performance over prior vision–language baselines, including REVEAL, achieving state-of-the-art results within this setting.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper presents a clear and conceptually sound methodological contribution. The proposed approach is well motivated and addresses a genuine limitation of the GACL approach. The formulation is elegant, integrates naturally into standard contrastive objectives, and appears novel in this context.
The paper is nicely structured and the methodology is easy to follow, supported by a strong visual overview in Fig. 1.The combination of intra-modality similarity to define phenotypic relationships and cross-modality similarity for alignment is well thought through.
The experimental evaluation is thorough and convincing. The use of a large-scale dataset (UK Biobank) strengthens the empirical claims, and the inclusion of strong baselines, including prior work from the same line of research, provides a fair comparison. Running experiments across multiple random seeds further supports the robustness of the results.
Empirically, the method consistently outperforms baselines and improves upon the prior REVEAL framework, suggesting that the proposed weighting mechanism provides meaningful gains.
Finally, the paper is generally well written and clearly structured, with only minor issues in notation and clarity.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed reading this paper. I think it could be a strong contribution that would attract interest from the MICCAI community, subject to concerns being addressed about the reproducibility of the methodology.

The methodological contribution is both elegant and well-motivated, and addresses a clear limitation in prior work. The paper is also clearly presented, with a coherent narrative and a method that is easy to follow despite its novelty. Furthermore, the experimental evaluation is rigorous and lends credibility to the claims of SOTA performance. I have erred towards weak acceptance due to the lack of anonymised source code (or a commitment to release it upon acceptance) and lack of detail about the AD prediction task.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I am satisfied that the authors rebuttal satisfactorily addresses my minor concerns with the presentation of the paper. Having already felt the paper was worthy of acceptance, my decision to accept remains the same.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper proposes a soft differentiable phenotypic grouping strategy for vision-language AD risk prediction.
