reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces the Evidence Attribution Score (EAS), a simple behavior-based metric to detect “visual confabulation” in multi-image medical vision-language models. It measures the overlap between images a model actually depends on (via leave-one-out ablation to build the Behavioral Evidence Set, BES) and images the model claims to use (via repeated prompting to build the Claimed Evidence Set, CES). Applied to 200 questions from MedFrameQA across eight VLMs, it shows that 40–79% of correct answers rely on wrong or no visual evidence. It also highlights a clear difference: chain-of-thought prompting strongly improves EAS in open-source models but barely affects closed-source ones. The work argues that accuracy alone is misleading for clinical reliability and proposes EAS as a complementary metric.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The core idea is timely and valuable. Many people are now discussing how VLMs can give correct answers for the wrong reasons, especially in medicine where justification matters. Defining visual confabulation clearly and separating it from regular hallucination is helpful.
2.The EAS formulation is straightforward yet insightful. Using leave-one-out ablation for behavioral dependence is model-agnostic and works for both open- and closed-source models, which is practical. The three causal validations (evidence swap, perturbation fragility, and Shapley agreement) give decent support that EAS tracks real grounding rather than just correlation.
3.The chain-of-thought finding is striking and potentially useful: it suggests open-source models have latent visual capabilities that default prompting fails to engage. This behavioral divide between model families is something accuracy metrics completely miss. The paper is clearly written, the figures are helpful, and the discussion on limitations is honest.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The main limitation is the small evaluation scale. The authors use only 200 questions from MedFrameQA, even though the full benchmark has over 2,800 pairs. While they argue that the computational cost (thousands of forward passes) makes larger tests difficult, 200 examples feel thin when drawing broad conclusions about systematic differences between all open-source and closed-source models, or about confabulation rates in general. More questions, or at least a clearer justification for why this subset is representative, would strengthen the claims.
2.Another concern is the Claimed Evidence Set (CES). Asking the model three times “which images are important” and taking a 2/3 majority is a reasonable heuristic, but it still relies on the model’s own verbal reporting. It may not reliably reflect what the model actually attends to during inference. The authors could have strengthened this by comparing CES against internal signals (e.g., attention weights or activation patterns in open-source models) or by benchmarking EAS against other grounding metrics from prior work on VLM faithfulness. Without such cross-validation, it is harder to be fully convinced that low EAS always means true visual confabulation rather than limitations in how CES is elicited.
3.The paper could also discuss more explicitly how well leave-one-out captures distributed or redundant visual information across images, even though they provide Shapley results as support.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Overall I found the topic engaging and the proposed EAS a useful step toward more trustworthy evaluation of medical VLMs. The distinction between behavioral dependence and claimed evidence is worth exploring further. Addressing the scale of the study and providing more direct validation of the CES component (perhaps on open models where internal signals are accessible) would make the conclusions more robust. Minor suggestion: consider reporting results on a larger random subset if computationally feasible, or at least include an ablation on subset size.

I recommend weak accept mainly because the problem is interesting and relevant to the MICCAI community, and the EAS idea offers a clean, actionable way to look beyond accuracy in multi-image medical VQA. The CoT results add a nice behavioral insight that could influence how people prompt models in practice.
That said, the relatively small test set (200 questions) limits how strongly we can interpret the broad claims about open- vs closed-source models and overall confabulation prevalence. The CES elicitation also feels a bit indirect. These are fixable issues, and I think the paper sits right around the acceptance borderline. A solid rebuttal addressing the sample size concern or adding supporting analyses would likely push it higher for me.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors provided a targeted rebuttal that addressed my primary concerns, though I remain cautious about the limitations of their evaluation scale.
Their statistical defense of the 200 question subset is mathematically sound. The tight bootstrap confidence intervals and strong p values indicate that the sample size is adequate to support their specific empirical claims. However, it is undeniable that 200 questions serve as a bare minimum proof of concept. While sufficient for a methodological contribution, the community will eventually need larger scale validation to confirm whether these confabulation rates generalize across broader medical tasks.
Regarding the CES heuristic, their clarification that the Jaccard similarity operates purely on discrete image IDs rather than text tokens resolves the verbosity bias concern. The most robust technical point in the rebuttal is the evidence that CoT prompting structurally alters the Behavioral Evidence Set. Proving that the actual behavioral dependency shifts, rather than just the text output, is a highly valuable finding for prompt engineering.
While Reviewer 1 is correct that the lack of clinician adjudicated ground truth is a severe limitation, I accept the authors’ concession that EAS is strictly a behavioral proxy. Developing rigorous, annotation free evaluation protocols to test evidence utilization and visual reasoning is practically necessary for auditing modern multi-image VLMs. The proposed black box framework is genuinely novel and pushes the boundary of how we evaluate medical AI beyond simple accuracy. I am raising my score to Accept, conditional on the authors strictly avoiding any overclaims regarding clinical correctness in the final manuscript.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper studies whether multi-image medical vision-language models arrive at correct answers using the correct visual evidence, rather than relying on shortcuts such as textual priors. 
It claims to introduce the Evidence Attribution Score (EAS), which compares an ablation-based Behavioral Evidence Set (BES) with a prompt-based Claimed Evidence Set (CES). It uses their overlap to quantify alignment between actual and claimed evidence. 
The paper evaluates this framework on a multi-image medical VQA benchmark across several open- and closed-source models, reports high rates of “visual confabulation” among correct answers, and presents additional analyses including chain-of-thought prompting and several causal-style validation experiments.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The empirical effort is substantial. The paper evaluates several model families, compares open- and closed-source systems, studies the effect of image count, and includes additional validation experiments beyond the main metric.
2.The chain-of-thought result is interesting. The observation that CoT substantially increases EAS in open-source models while leaving closed-source models largely unchanged is potentially useful for future work on inference-time safeguards and model auditing.
3.The paper addresses an important and practically relevant problem. In medical multi-image settings, answer accuracy alone is not sufficient if the model does not rely on the appropriate visual evidence. This is a worthwhile evaluation question for clinically motivated AI systems.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.My primary concern is not that the paper applies ideas to medical imaging. That is entirely reasonable for MICCAI. My concern is that the paper presents the broader methodological idea as more novel than it is, while failing to properly acknowledge closely related prior work from ML/CV/xAI and VQA faithfulness. In particular, the paper does not cite (or talk about) important works on models being right for the wrong reasons, shortcut learning, faithful explanations, and faithful/plausible grounding, including Right for the Right Reasons [R1], Unmasking Clever Hans Predictors [R2], ERASER [R3], Taking a HINT [R4], and Measuring Faithful and Plausible Visual Grounding in VQA [R5]. These are not peripheral citations. They are directly relevant to the paper’s central framing.
As a result, the paper’s contribution is not positioned accurately enough relative to prior work. The contribution would be much more convincing if framed as an application and adaptation of these ideas to the setting of multi-image medical VLMs, rather than as if the broader conceptual gap were largely unaddressed. In its current form, the paper risks presenting a community’s existing ideas as if they were substantially new in this manuscript.
2.There are also several critical citation errors or misuses, which weaken the credibility of the technical framing:
(a) The paper gives the wrong arXiv identifier for MedVH; the cited identifier does not match the MedVH paper [R6].
(b) The paper states that its threshold choice is analogous to slight-to-fair agreement in Cohen’s kappa, but cites Pearl’s Causality for this claim. That is not an appropriate citation for a kappa-interpretation statement. If the paper wants to use that language, it should cite a standard agreement-interpretation reference such as [R7].
References:
[R1] Ross, A.S., Hughes, M.C. and Doshi-Velez, F., 2017, August. Right for the right reasons: training differentiable models by constraining their explanations. In Proceedings of the 26th International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (pp. 2662-2670).
[R2] Lapuschkin, S., Wäldchen, S., Binder, A., Montavon, G., Samek, W. and Müller, K.R., 2019.Unmasking Clever Hans predictors and assessing what machines really learn. Nature Communications, 10(1), p.1096.
[R3] DeYoung, J., Jain, S., Rajani, N.F., Lehman, E., Xiong, C., Socher, R. and Wallace, B.C., 2020, July. ERASER: A benchmark to evaluate rationalized NLP models. In Proceedings of the 58th annual meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (pp. 4443-4458).
[R4] Selvaraju, R.R., Lee, S., Shen, Y., Jin, H., Ghosh, S., Heck, L., Batra, D. and Parikh, D., 2019.Taking a hint: Leveraging explanations to make vision and language models more grounded. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (pp. 2591-2600).
[R5] Reich, D., Putze, F. and Schultz, T., 2023, December. Measuring faithful and plausible visual grounding in VQA. In Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2023 (pp. 3129-3144).
[R6] Gu, Z., Chen, J., Liu, F., Yin, C. and Zhang, P., 2026.MedVH: Toward systematic evaluation of hallucination for large vision language models in the medical context. Advanced Intelligent Systems, 8(1), p.2500255.
[R7] Landis, J Richard and Gary G. Koch. “The measurement of observer agreement for categorical data.” Biometrics 33 1 (1977): 159-74 .
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The paper would be significantly stronger if it were reframed more modestly and more accurately. In particular, I encourage positioning the work as an application and adaptation of evidence-faithfulness ideas to the multi-image medical VLM setting, rather than as if the broader methodological idea were largely missing from prior work. A careful revision of the related work and several key references is necessary.

I find the empirical study interesting and the application worthwhile, but the paper currently does not meet the standard I would expect for scholarly positioning. The related work and citation practice need substantial correction.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: After reading the rebuttal, I maintain my recommendation to reject. The rebuttal acknowledges the missing related work and citation issues, but these are only promised for the camera-ready version, and I cannot assess whether the paper will be properly reframed without seeing the revised discussion and related-work text. More importantly, my concern is not only missing citations, but that the paper’s central claims remain stronger than what the metric supports. EAS is still an agreement score between two model-derived proxies, not evidence that the model used clinically appropriate visual information. BES remains a coarse leave-one-out proxy, CES remains prompt-dependent, the thresholding choices remain heuristic, and the evaluation is still limited to 200 questions without clinician-labeled evidence or a stronger benchmark-bias analysis. The rebuttal improves the framing in principle, but it does not sufficiently resolve the core validity and overclaiming concerns. Therefore, I do not think the paper is ready for acceptance in its current form.

meta_reviews.text:
As both the merits (relevance, model-agnostic design, interesting empirical findings) and limitations (failure to acknowledge/compare existing works in the general ML domain, lack of justification for key experimental design choices) stand out, as mentioned by reviewers, the authors are invited to submit a rebuttal.

The paper received mixed reactions after the rebuttal. Reviewers agree on the relevance of the question and the reasonable clarification regarding the sample size, while having remaining concerns over the over-simplified approach (the overlap between leave-one-out results and self-reported importance) when positioned against the more complex inconsistency/hallucination detection contexts. Taking the reviews, responses, and follow-up comments together, it is reasonable to say that the proposed approach (more like for behavioral consistency under simplified settings) does not fully support the claimed contributions toward addressing the complex mirage + hallucination problem.

Personally I like this paper. It makes a highly important conceptual contribution, separates “getting the answer right” from “using the right evidence,” which is directly relevant for clinical trust. The finding that 40–79% of correct answers are confabulated is striking. I recommend the acceptance of this work.

The paper is accepted as a borderline but meaningful contribution. The reviewers generally agreed that the work addresses an important and underexplored problem in evaluating evidence grounding and visual confabulation in multimodal medical AI, particularly for closed-source multi-image VLMs. The rebuttal successfully addressed several major concerns, including additional analyses on CoT impact, statistical clarification for the small dataset setting, and improved transparency regarding the evaluation protocol.
At the same time, some limitations remain. In particular, the current EAS/BES/CES metrics should be framed more carefully as heuristic proxies for evidence alignment rather than direct measures of clinical validity, and the paper should avoid overstating causal or clinical conclusions. The final version should also incorporate the missing explainability and faithfulness-related citations raised during review and further clarify the limitations of the proposed evaluation framework. Despite these remaining concerns, the benchmark and auditing protocol provide a practical and novel evaluation perspective that is likely to be valuable for the community.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the Reviewers and ACs for recognizing our clinical relevance, practical protocol, and impactful CoT findings. Major concerns are addressed below.
1) Novelty & Literature (Reviewers 1 & 3): Our main contribution is the BES/CES framework and the resulting Evidence Attribution Score (EAS), which together provide a practical black-box auditing protocol for testing whether multi-image medical VLMs arrive at correct answers for the right visual reasons when gradient access is unavailable. We thank Reviewer 3 for highlighting relevant prior work. While [R1] and [R3] rely on gradient access or token-level rationales, and [R4]-[R5] focus on single-image VQA grounding, our setting is annotation-free and uses image-level evidence across multiple medical images. We agree that [R1]-[R5] provide important conceptual foundations and will cite and discuss them in the Introduction and Related Work. We will also correct the MedVH citation [R6] and replace the Pearl citation with Landis & Koch (1977) [R7] in the camera-ready version.
2) Evaluation Scale (Reviewers 1 & 2): Due to computational cost, we sampled a balanced subset of 200 MedFrameQA questions (50 each for 2-5 images). Unlike standard VQA benchmarking, each EAS evaluation requires repeated CES prompting alongside leave-one-out causal ablations across all images. Evaluating the full benchmark across 8 models requires >200,000 forward passes and ~700,000 API calls/prompts, making exhaustive auditing prohibitive. Our stratified subset (Sec 4) yielded tight 95% bootstrap CIs (width 0.06-0.12) and achieved p<0.001 for all primary findings, providing sufficient statistical precision.
3) Clinical Ground Truth & BES Limitations (Reviewers 1 & 2): EAS is a behavioral proxy, not a clinician-adjudicated ground-truth metric (Sec 6). While high EAS does not guarantee clinical correctness, low EAS on a correct answer conservatively signals potential confabulation and text-prior reliance. Reviewer 1 asks if low EAS reflects benchmark-level text answerability. If low EAS were purely a dataset artifact, we would expect similar BES=∅ rates across models. Instead, substantial model-specific variation (e.g., open-source vs. closed-source) supports that EAS captures genuine visual dependence differences. While leave-one-out ablation may miss synergistic dependencies, our Shapley analysis demonstrated moderate-to-strong agreement (0.393) with LOO BES, supporting LOO as a computationally feasible lower bound.
4) CES Heuristics & Verbosity Bias (Reviewers 1 & 2): The EAS threshold (τ) is a tunable hyperparameter. While findings are robust across τ∈[0.1,0.5], we intentionally set a lenient baseline (τ=0.3) to avoid artificially inflating failure rates from redundant slices. Under even higher evaluated thresholds (e.g., τ=0.7), confabulation predictably soars to 70-90%. Yet, our low baseline still exposes very high rates of confabulation. During pilots, 5 and 7 CES prompts yielded no major shift in decisions. Since 3 prompts already cost 48k queries, scaling further wastes compute without improving results. Jaccard sets contain discrete image IDs (e.g., {Img1, Img3}), not text tokens. A verbose model claiming Img1 in a paragraph has a CES size of 1, identical to a concise model.
5) CoT Gains & Cross-Model Comparisons (Reviewer 1): The strongest evidence that CoT changes visual behavior, not just explanation style, is that BES itself changes. BES is measured entirely through ablation and does not depend on explanation text. Under default prompting, open-source models frequently exhibit text-prior dependency (BES=∅). Under CoT, these cases drop substantially across models, meaning image removal changes the answer more often. This supports the interpretation that CoT increases genuine visual dependence rather than merely changing reporting style. Finally, on the strict intersection of correctly answered questions across all models, rankings and conclusions remain consistent with the main text.

title: R-MSA: Rhythm-Conditioned Surgical Video Skill Assessment via Morphology Synchronization and Uncertainty Calibration
abstract: Automated video-based surgical skill assessment enables objective feedback for training, especially in resource-limited settings. However, most existing methods rely on generic spatiotemporal modeling (e.g., absolute positional encoding or simple temporal aggregation) and overlook large execution rhythm variability across surgeons. For instance, experts tend to operate smoothly and efficiently, whereas novices exhibit slower and irregular patterns, which ultimately limits skill discrimination. To address this, we propose R-MSA (Rhythm–Morphology Synchronous Assessment), a rhythm-aware framework that explicitly models execution rhythm differences. Specifically, a Rhythm Morphology Encoder performs duration-conditioned rhythm encoding to generate rhythm-adaptive representations for variable-length videos. A Morphology-Synchronous Decoder with learnable queries aligns latent morphology primitives (e.g., needle driving, knot tying) across rhythm-normalized sequences. To refine procedural correspondence, a Surgical Sequence Alignment Module integrates a Gaussian temporal prior into co-attention for localized temporal alignment. Finally, an Uncertainty-Calibrated Interpretable Tree produces relative skill scores with calibrated uncertainty through reparameterized prediction. Experiments on JIGSAWS, HeiChole, and our proposed Kangduo datasets show that R-MSA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in ranking correlation and error metrics. Code will be released upon acceptance.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes R-MSA, a video-based surgical skill assessment framework built around the idea that execution rhythm is an important but under-modeled source of variation in surgical performance. The method combines four parts: pairwise sequence alignment with a Gaussian temporal prior, duration-conditioned rhythm encoding to normalize videos with different execution tempos, a learnable-query decoder intended to extract rhythm-invariant morphology primitives, and a soft decision tree that outputs relative skill scores with uncertainty estimates. Besides, the paper introduces a new Kangduo dataset, consisting of 104 HD robotic suturing videos with expert scores.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The central observation that skill is reflected not only in what actions occur but also in how rhythmically and regularly they unfold is well motivated. The expert/novice contrast shown on page 2 is intuitive and clinically plausible: experts tend to be smoother and more regular, whereas novices are slower and more erratic. This is a sensible perspective for surgical skill assessment and a useful framing contribution.
2.The overall pipeline on page 4 is coherent: first align videos, then inject rhythm conditioning, then extract synchronized morphology primitives, then predict with uncertainty. Even if some components are incremental individually, the paper presents a clear systems-level design rather than a loose collection of tricks.
3.The reported performance is good. On JIGSAWS, the method achieves the best average SROCC across LOSO, LOUO, and 4-fold protocols, and competitive-to-best MAE. On HeiChole and Kangduo, it also reports the strongest SRCC and lowest MAE among compared methods.
4.A new dataset with 104 HD robotic suturing videos and larger duration variability is potentially important, especially since the paper argues that older benchmarks such as JIGSAWS do not sufficiently stress rhythm-aware modeling. I recommend releasing this dataset publicly if possible, as it could be a useful resource for the community.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Some claimed novelty is overstated, and several modules are adaptations of familiar ideas. While the overall combination is interesting, the paper does not clearly establish a strong leap over recent surgical skill assessment baselines such as ViSA, MT-ViT, Contra-Sformer, T2CR, and RICA² cited in the paper. In particular, the move from generic video temporal modeling to rhythm-aware conditioning is the main conceptual novelty, but the implementation feels somewhat heuristic.
2.The paper claims rhythm is distinct from absolute duration or speed, but the actual rhythm encoding appears to be based on binning videos into 4 groups according to execution duration, then scaling sinusoidal frequencies by the bin index. That makes the practical definition of rhythm quite close to coarse duration conditioning, not a richer measurement of rhythm regularity, periodicity, pauses, or local tempo variation. This mismatch between concept and implementation weakens the core claim.
3.The method regresses relative skill scores from video pairs, using target-exemplar representations. That can work, but the paper does not explain enough about how exemplars are selected, how inference behaves under different exemplar choices, whether performance is sensitive to the reference pool, and how this compares to direct absolute score regression.
4.Kangduo dataset may be a strong contribution, but the paper gives only limited details on the scoring rubric, inter-rater reliability, participant expertise distribution, acquisition conditions, train/test subject separation, and whether the dataset will actually be released.
5.The paper says it uses an I3D backbone and compares with prior methods, but for some baselines it is not completely clear whether results were reproduced under the same preprocessing, splits, and supervision conditions (or instead copied from prior publications). Also, Table 1 mixes methods using video only, video + kinematics, and sometimes extra annotations, which makes the comparison not perfectly clean.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This is an interesting work overall. The paper addresses an important problem, proposes a coherent rhythm-aware framework, and reports very good results across three datasets. The ablations are meaningful, the qualitative visualizations support the technical claims, and the new Kangduo dataset could be a practical contribution for the community.
However, my concerns are mostly about overclaiming. The paper’s core concept of rhythm is interesting, but the actual implementation looks closer to duration-conditioned encoding than a deep model of rhythm. Likewise, the uncertainty calibration and interpretability claims are not fully validated. Several components are also adapted from familiar ideas.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes R-MSA, a rhythm-aware framework for pairwise surgical video skill assessment that aligns two videos, conditions features on execution rhythm/duration, extracts morphology primitives, and predicts a relative skill score with an uncertainty-aware tree. The authors report improved results over prior methods on JIGSAWS, HeiChole, and Kangduo (their newly proposed dataset).
reviews.text_strengths:
Strong methodological novelty
Strong experimental design and results
Good presentation
Contribution of a new dataset (will it be released?)
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The notation needs to be clarified. In Section 2.1, Vk and Vl appear to denote the two input videos, but it is not stated explicitly whether these correspond to the target and exemplar/reference videos. Likewise, N is introduced in the feature tensor shapes but is never defined.
There seems to be a conceptual disagreement between Sections 2.1 and 2.2.Authors write, “Surgical videos of the same task exhibit large duration variance due to differing
execution rhythms”. If that is the case, wouldn’t it contradict what you said about “comparable procedural phases tend to appear in temporally neighboring segments after uniform sampling”?
The loss formulation is underspecified and difficult to follow. Please define L_ranking, L_uncertainty, L_DAE, and L_var explicitly, including all terms and supervision signals. It is also unclear whether mu denotes the relative skill score and whether sigma is directly optimized.
The inference procedure is currently too vague. The paper says that mu is used as the skill estimate at inference, but the full test-time setup is missing: is prediction performed against a single exemplar/reference video or multiple exemplars, and how is a final absolute or per-video score obtained from pairwise predictions?
The uncertainty interpretation is unclear. As defined, sigma appears to quantify uncertainty of the pairwise relative prediction, rather than uncertainty intrinsic to the target video itself. This seems closer to data uncertainty for the pair, so the manuscript should explain this distinction more carefully and justify the interpretability claims.
Also, the practical use of uncertainty for interpretability is not sufficiently demonstrated. It is unclear how these uncertainty estimates would actually be used by clinicians or trainees in practice.
For consistency, it would be preferable to report multiple-seed results on JIGSAWS as well, not only on HeiChole and Kangduo. The current experimental section states that multiple random seeds are used for the latter two datasets, but not for JIGSAWS.
The paper would benefit from stating some limitations.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Nice work and I appreciate that some omissions are because of space limitations. Please try to address my comments, I believe they will make the paper stronger - in particular, the comments on the loss functions, inference, and uncertainty.

See major weaknesses

The proposed framework is technically well motivated. The paper is clearly written, although the methodological pipeline is a bit complex to follow easily. The empirical results are strong. Overall, I found this to be a solid and well-executed contribution.
reviews.text_strengths: The manuscript has several major strengths. First, the proposed framework appears technically well designed and well motivated. Second, the empirical results are strong, with high performance metrics that suggest the proposed approach is effective for the task.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper has received 3 positive reviews with all reviewers suggesting acceptance. I broadly agree with their assessment but I find the weaknesses listed by Rev #1 and #2 very accurate and these undoubtledly diminish the contribution of the work in the its relevant area (surgical skill asssessment).
My recommendation is for the paper to be accepted but the authors are strongly advised to address the comments by Rev #1 and #2.

author_feedback_text:
Dear Area Chairs and Reviewers,
We sincerely thank you for the positive feedback, constructive comments, and Early Accept recommendation. Your insights will significantly improve our camera-ready version. We address the main concerns below:
1.Dataset Ethics and Availability (R1, R2, R3) We apologize for the missing dataset details. The Kangduo suturing tasks were performed on surgical phantoms (simulated tissue), not human patients, thus involving no human subjects or privacy/ethical concerns. Regarding availability, while raw videos are restricted by our collaborating institution’s IP policies, we are committed to reproducibility. Upon publication, we will publicly release the extracted I3D visual features, expert annotations, and the complete R-MSA source code to allow full reproduction of our results.
2.Baselines and Input Modalities (R1, R2) We appreciate the reviewers noting the mixed input modalities (video-only vs. video+kinematics) in Table 1.Including baselines with extra kinematic data actually highlights R-MSA’s competitiveness. Achieving superior performance using only video data demonstrates that effectively modeling execution rhythm bridges (and even surpasses) the performance gap with models relying on privileged multi-modal sensors. We will explicitly clarify these modalities in the revised table.
3.Concept of “Rhythm” & Inference Procedure (R1, R2) We agree with R1 that our duration-binning is a heuristic proxy for surgical rhythm. We will refine our novelty claims and explicitly discuss this in the Limitations, noting future work will model continuous, fine-grained spatiotemporal dependencies to capture local rhythm variations beyond discrete duration groups.
Regarding inference (R1, R2): Following established pairwise assessment protocols (e.g., CoRe, T2CR), a target video is compared against a fixed pool of expert exemplars from the training set. The absolute score is obtained by adding the predicted relative skill differences (mu) to the exemplars’ ground-truth scores. This pipeline will be detailed in the revision.
4.Notation, Loss Formulation, & Uncertainty (R2)We thank R2 for the meticulous check. We will explicitly define variables (Vk, Vl, N) and expand the loss formulations. We completely agree with R2 regarding uncertainty: our learned sigma primarily quantifies the pairwise predictive (data) uncertainty between target and exemplar, rather than the intrinsic absolute cognitive uncertainty of the target video alone. We will refine our interpretability claims to accurately reflect this critical distinction.
5.Additional Clarifications and Corrections All other minor issues will be carefully addressed in the camera-ready version. Specifically, we will clarify the temporal sampling strategy to resolve the apparent discrepancy between Sec. 2.1 and 2.2 (R2), define acronyms like LOSO/LOUO (R3), report multiple-seed variance results on JIGSAWS (R2), and expand our comprehensive discussion of limitations. We are fully committed to polishing the manuscript to meet MICCAI’s highest standards.
Thank you again for your time and the recognition of our work.

title: Robotic Ultrasound Makes CBCT Alive
abstract: Intraoperative Cone Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) provides a reliable 3D anatomical context essential for interventional planning. However, its static nature fails to provide continuous monitoring of soft-tissue deformations induced by respiration, probe pressure, and surgical manipulation, leading to navigation discrepancies. We propose a deformation-aware CBCT updating framework that leverages robotic ultrasound as a dynamic proxy to infer tissue motion and update static CBCT slices in real time. Starting from calibration-initialized alignment with linear correlation of linear combination (LC2)-based rigid refinement, our method establishes accurate multimodal correspondence. To capture intraoperative dynamics, we introduce the ultrasound correlation UNet (USCorUNet), a lightweight network trained with optical flow-guided supervision to learn deformation-aware correlation representations, enabling accurate, real-time dense deformation field estimation from ultrasound streams. The inferred deformation is spatially regularized and transferred to the CBCT reference to produce deformation-consistent visualizations without repeated radiation exposure. We validate the proposed approach through deformation estimation and ultrasound-guided CBCT updating experiments. Results demonstrate real-time end-to-end CBCT slice updating and physically plausible deformation estimation, enabling dynamic refinement of static CBCT guidance during robotic ultrasound-assisted interventions. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ziyuan-li/robotic-us-cbct-updating.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents a deformation-aware updating framework for static Cone Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) images using real-time robotic ultrasound (US). To address the critical issue of intraoperative soft tissue deformation that compromises surgical navigation, the authors propose USCorUNet. This network estimates the real-time deformation field directly from the US stream, allowing for the dynamic updating of preoperative/intraoperative CBCT slices without subjecting the patient to additional radiation.
reviews.text_strengths: The introduction of the USCorUNet to continuously estimate deformation fields from US streams is technically sound. It elegantly bridges the gap between the high refresh rate of US and the static nature of CBCT. The integration of calibrated alignment with deep learning-based deformation estimation demonstrates a comprehensive understanding of robotic ultrasound-guided surgical systems. The achieved real-time performance is crucial for intraoperative deployment.
reviews.text_weaknesses: Ultrasound imaging is notoriously susceptible to artifacts such as acoustic shadowing, speckle noise, and signal dropouts. The paper lacks a detailed discussion or specific experiments on how USCorUNet handles sudden drops in US image quality. The description of the validation dataset in the current manuscript could be more detailed. It is not entirely clear to what extent the framework was validated on highly realistic in-vivo data versus idealized phantoms. Phantom studies, while valuable for baseline metrics, often fail to replicate the complex non-rigid deformations and heterogeneous textures of real human tissue.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This is a solid paper with a compelling clinical application and a well-designed technical pipeline. I am inclined to recommend acceptance, provided the authors can adequately address the concerns regarding robustness to US artifacts and clarify the validation dataset details during the rebuttal phase.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper presents a deformation-aware CBCT updating framework that uses robotic ultrasound as a dynamic proxy. The main contributions are: (1) an end-to-end workflow from calibration/registration to real-time CBCT slice updating, (2) a lightweight network USCorUNet that estimates dense deformation fields from adjacent ultrasound frames without ground-truth deformation labels, leveraging RAFT-derived pseudo-labels combined with self-supervised photometric and regularization losses, and (3) a practical system integrating a KUKA robot, Siemens ultrasound, and CBCT, demonstrated on phantoms and in vivo arm data.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The authors provide a full pipeline from hand-eye calibration, LC2-based rigid refinement, deformation estimation, to CBCT slice updating. This is a valuable engineering contribution for robotic ultrasound-guided interventions.
2.Since ground-truth deformation fields are unavailable for ultrasound, the method distills pseudo-labels from RAFT optical flow, then refines them with confidence-weighted photometric loss and Jacobian-based folding regularization. This semi-supervised + self-supervised approach is sensible and well-motivated.
3.USCorUNet runs at ~11ms end-to-end, enabling real-time intraoperative use. The local correlation volume and 1/8-resolution decoding strike a reasonable trade-off between accuracy and speed.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The authors state that LC2 searches “within a constrained range” after calibration initialization, but no numerical values (e.g., translation/rotation limits) or validation of convergence range are provided.
2.Although a Gaussian correction profile is introduced for probe compression, the paper does not quantify the relationship between applied force and deformation estimation error. The model assumes a symmetric convex profile, which may not hold for heterogeneous tissues or off-center indentation.
3.All metrics are indirect (photometric consistency, forward-backward error, folding ratio, bone mask Dice). No validation against physical markers, finite-element simulations, or ex vivo tracked targets is provided. The clinical plausibility of the estimated deformation fields still remains partially unverified.
4.If I understand correctly, the method updates only the single CBCT slice coplanar with the ultrasound plane, not the full 3D volume. This restricts applicability for true 3D navigation.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a complete, real-time deformation-aware CBCT updating framework with a lightweight network trained without ground-truth deformation labels, achieving strong results on phantoms and in vivo data. Limitations include unclear capture range, indirect validation, and limited clinical scenarios, but these do not detract from the clear technical contribution and reproducibility.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I still hold the same view that the paper can be accepted.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a workflow for updating CBCT images with live ultrasound during image-guided interventions. The framework includes ultrasound calibration, registration, and CBCT deformation, and introduces USCorUNet for ultrasound-to-ultrasound deformation field estimation. Overall, the topic is highly relevant to the MICCAI community, as it addresses an important challenge in image-guided intervention and aims to improve the integration of complementary intraoperative imaging modalities.
reviews.text_strengths:
The manuscript has several strengths.
It presents a complete workflow rather than an isolated methodological component, which enhances the translational value of the work and makes the proposed approach more compelling from an application perspective.
The idea of leveraging a RAFT-inspired optical flow strategy to capture deformations between consecutive ultrasound frames is interesting and well aligned with the dynamic nature of deformation induced in ultrasound imaging.
The validation is also supported by a relatively diverse dataset, including phantom data, and the comparison against other U-Net-based approaches is appreciated. These elements together make the study relevant and potentially impactful.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The methodological contribution would benefit from clearer positioning. Several of the key building blocks of the framework appear related to existing work, including LC2-based multimodal registration, deformable registration approaches, and CBCT updating strategies. My understanding is that the contribution is focused on USCorUNet. As currently presented, the statement of contributions is somewhat misleading. A clearer articulation of what is fundamentally novel in the proposed framework would help the reader better understand the scope.
The central problem appears to be the ultrasound-to-ultrasound deformation estimation. However, it is not yet clear how the proposed solution compares with more classical frame-to-frame ultrasound registration strategies, such as a simple NCC-based approaches. This comparison seems particularly important, as it would help establish rationale to whether the proposed method provides a meaningful advantage over simpler and more established alternatives.
Another point that would benefit from clarification is how out-of-plane deformation is handled. In addition, the video examples appear to show some discrepancy in the out-of-field ultrasound deformation. It would therefore be helpful for the manuscript to discuss how such deformations are modeled, and more generally, how robust the method is when out-of-plane or out-of-field motion occurs.
There are also some concerns regarding the experimental setup and evaluation. The study mentions scans of in vivo forearm and upper-arm ultrasound (Dataset A), but no ethics approval or related statement appears to be provided.
The results presented in Table 2 are difficult to interpret without a clear understanding of the force-stratified evaluation protocol. A concise explanation of this protocol would greatly improve the readability and interpretability of the results.
The fine-tuning strategy also raises some questions. The manuscript indicates that fine-tuning was performed on different datasets while keeping the train, validation, and test ratios unchanged. As presented, Table 3 seems to report mean results on test sets drawn from datasets that were also used during training or adaptation. This makes it difficult to judge whether the reported improvements reflect true generalization or are partly driven by dataset-specific adaptation. Clarifying this point would be important, particularly for understanding how the method is expected to perform in clinical practice, where the deformation source is not known in advance. Also a discussion of the anticipated robustness and expected performance under such realistic conditions would substantially strengthen the work.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Overall, this is a relevant and promising paper that addresses an important translational problem. The proposed workflow is comprehensive, and the technical implementation appears strong. The manuscript would be significantly strengthened by a clearer and more precise articulation of its methodological novelty, as the current framing tends to overstate the contributions. In particular, stronger justification for the ultrasound-to-ultrasound registration approach, along with a clearer description of the evaluation and its implications for clinical generalization, would help better support the paper’s claims and impact.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have addressed most of my comments. I recommend acceptance, provided that the justifications and discussions included in the response are incorporated into the final version of the paper.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper presents a clinically relevant framework for deformation-aware CBCT updating using real-time robotic ultrasound, integrating calibration, registration, deformation estimation, and CBCT slice updating into a complete workflow. Reviewers generally agree that the system-level contribution is strong, the real-time performance is promising, and USCorUNet is a technically sound component for ultrasound-based deformation estimation without ground-truth deformation labels. However, concerns remain regarding the precise methodological novelty, the lack of comparison with simpler ultrasound registration baselines, the use of indirect validation metrics, robustness to ultrasound artifacts and out-of-plane motion, and the clarity of dataset/evaluation protocols.

The rebuttal effectively addressed the reviewers’ concerns, providing sufficient clarification and additional evidence where requested. Following the rebuttal, all reviewers expressed support for acceptance, indicating a clear consensus that the paper meets the standard for acceptance at MICCAI.

The main concerns (R3) appear resolved after rebuttal, namely clarification of novelty and methodological details. The authors are encouraged to incorporate rebuttal clarifications in the camera ready version of their paper.
I recommend this submission is accepted

All 3 reviewers are overall satisfied with the rebuttal and recommend acceptance.
The authors have done a good job in the rebuttal clarifying all criticism. However, since it is not explicitly stated the authors must incorporate all major points in their rebuttal in the final manuscript.
I recommend acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and AC for their careful assessment and summary. We appreciate R1/R2’s encouraging evaluations (recommended Accept) of our full pipeline, USCorUNet design, and accuracy–speed trade-off, R3’s constructive suggestions and recognition of the complete workflow, RAFT-inspired deformation modeling, diverse validation, and translational value, as well as the AC’s summary.
Methodology (R3): 
The reviews highlight our core contributions: (i) a pipeline from hand-eye calibration and LC2 refinement to deformation estimation and CBCT slice updating; (ii) USCorUNet, a lightweight bidirectional network estimating dense deformation without ground-truth labels via RAFT-derived pseudo-labels and semi-/self-supervised losses, running at ~11 ms; (iii) real-time CBCT updating for probe- and externally induced deformations, bridging high-refresh-rate US and static CBCT; and (iv) validation on in vivo and three phantom datasets. As suggested, we will clarify the distinction between established building blocks and our task-specific integration, USCorUNet, and CBCT-updating contributions.
Baselines (R3): 
NCC/block matching (BM) is a useful local patch-tracking reference, but mainly measures local similarity rather than dense, physically plausible deformation. Prior works (Che et al., “Ultrasound Registration …”, Methods 2017; Sotiras et al., “Deformable Medical …”, TMI 2013; Alessandrini et al., “Detailed Evaluation …”, TMI 2016) show that US registration is sensitive to noise/artifacts/decorrelation, and BM can have larger bias/errors than flow-based methods. Thus, we used task-level baselines: RAFT [18] for dense US-US motion, DefCor-Net [9] for force-stratified comparison, and LC2-FFD [4] for CBCT updating. Together with forward-backward (FB) consistency, folding ratio, Dice, and CBCT-update metrics, they assess motion quality, anatomical/physical plausibility, and downstream utility beyond patch similarity.
Validation metrics (R1/R2): 
We use MAE/NCC for alignment, FB residual for inverse consistency, folding ratio for physical plausibility, bone-mask Dice for anatomical marker correctness, and CBCT-update metrics. For shadowing/dropout/speckle decorrelation, the confidence-weighted photometric loss [10] downweights unreliable regions, while Jacobian regularization suppresses implausible folding; Table 1 ablations show worse FB/Dice/folding scores when either confidence or regularization is removed. We agree that FEM/ex vivo tracked targets would further strengthen validation and will state this point; our current evidence combines multi-dataset evaluation with task-level CBCT updating.
Scope/out-of-plane motion (R2/R3): 
The method updates the 2D CBCT slice corresponding to the active 2D US plane; full 3D volume updating is not claimed. Out-of-plane motion is not directly observed by 2D US. Thus, EDT/Gaussian spatial weighting lets deformation decay away from the observed US window, rather than inferring out-of-plane deformation without additional image evidence.
Dataset/protocol (R1/R3): 
Dataset A uses data from DefCor-Net [9], which was collected under IRB approval No. 2022-87-S-KK. Table 2 follows the force-stratified protocol of DefCor-Net: force between robot and probe is synchronized with B-mode frames and grouped into 1–6 N. Table 3 reports regime-level adaptation, not per-test fitting: the probe-adapted model uses only training splits pooled from Datasets B–D, and the external-adapted model only uses the Dataset B training split; all test splits are held out.
LC2/Gaussian details (R2): 
LC2 searches in-plane translations within ±10 CBCT pixels (0.655 mm/pixel) around the projected US position; slice/orientation are fixed by calibrated geometry. The Gaussian profile is a spatial prior for transferring local US motion to the CBCT ROI, not a calibrated force-to-error model. We will clarify this in the camera-ready version.
We appreciate all constructive feedback and recognition of our contributions.

title: Robust automatic brain vessel segmentation in 3D CTA scans using dynamic 4D-CTA data
abstract: Existing datasets for brain vessel segmentation in CTA are limited in scale and largely restricted to major vessels, leaving peripheral vasculature underrepresented. We address this data-level bottleneck by introducing DynaVessel, a richly annotated dynamic 4D-CTA dataset, alongside a novel annotation pipeline that exploits multi-phase contrast enhancement and background subtraction to reduce the effort required for expert manual annotation of vessels. This not only enlarges our dataset by 5-6 fold, but also provides a novel data-driven method for training deep learning models to detect arteries and veins despite the wide variation in vessel contrast encountered in single-phase CTA scans. DynaVessel comprises 110 training volumes from 29 patients and 165 test volumes from 14 patients. By comparing with two similarly-sized datasets for brain vessel segmentation in CTA, we demonstrate that DynaVessel-trained nnUNet models produce superior segmentations compared to the same model trained on single phase data, with an average mDC of 0.846/0.957 for arteries/veins, shorter average directed Hausdorff distance (0.304 mm/0.08 mm for arteries/veins) and improved topology sensitivity (0.877/0.974 for arteries/veins) in the TopBrain dataset. Code, model weights, and instructions to access the dataset are available online: https://github.com/alceballosa/robust-vessel-segmentation.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Synthetic Data / Data-centric AI

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper presents a data-centric approach for intracranial vessel segmentation in CTA by leveraging dynamic 4D-CTA acquisitions. It introduces a semi-automatic pipeline that uses phase-specific contrast differences and image registration to separate arteries and veins, enabling efficient annotation with reduced manual effort. Using this pipeline, the authors construct the DynaVessel dataset, which includes multi-phase CTA volumes with artery and vein labels. They demonstrate that training a standard nnU-Net on this multi-phase data improves robustness to contrast variability and yields improved segmentation performance, particularly for vein detection, compared to models trained on conventional single-phase datasets.
reviews.text_strengths:
Effective use of dynamic 4D-CTA for annotation efficiency:
The paper proposes a practical and well-motivated pipeline that leverages temporal contrast dynamics to separate arteries and veins. By reusing annotations across multiple phases, the approach reduces manual labeling effort, which is a major bottleneck in vascular segmentation tasks.
Data-centric contribution with multi-phase diversity:
The introduction of the DynaVessel dataset, containing multi-phase CTA volumes with artery and vein labels, is valuable. In particular, the inclusion of multiple contrast phases per patient provides richer supervision and exposes models to a broader range of intensity variations, which is often missing in existing CTA datasets.
Improved robustness to contrast variability:
The experimental results demonstrate that training on multi-phase data improves robustness across different contrast phases. The analysis of performance across phases (e. g. , Fig. 4–5) provides useful insight into how contrast timing affects segmentation quality.
Clear and interpretable preprocessing pipeline:
The artery/vein separation method based on registration and intensity comparison is simple, interpretable, and grounded in physiological contrast differences, making it easy to understand and potentially reproduce.
Use of standard and well-established backbone (nnU-Net):
By building on nnU-Net, the paper isolates the contribution of the data and preprocessing pipeline rather than architectural changes, which strengthens the claim that performance gains are driven by improved data quality and diversity.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Limited methodological novelty:
The paper does not introduce a new segmentation model or learning framework, but instead relies on a standard nnU-Net backbone. The main contribution lies in the data curation and preprocessing pipeline.
Limited validation of annotation quality:
The ground truth is generated via a semi-automatic pipeline (iCafe + thresholding) and validated by a single neuroradiologist. There is no assessment of inter-observer variability or annotation uncertainty. Given the difficulty of artery–vein separation and distal vessel labeling, the reliability of the annotations is not sufficiently established.
Evaluation limitations and metric choice:
The paper emphasizes a modified Dice coefficient (mDC) that measures sensitivity but does not penalize false positives. This is non-standard and may bias results toward higher scores. Standard Dice, precision-recall analysis, or statistical significance testing are not sufficiently reported, making it harder to fully assess performance improvements.
Limited evidence for generalization across scanners and sites:
All data appears to be acquired from a single scanner and institution. Despite claims of robustness to real-world variability, there is no evaluation on multi-center or multi-scanner datasets, which limits confidence in clinical applicability.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The paper addresses an important and practical problem in CTA vessel segmentation and presents a thoughtful data-centric approach. The idea of leveraging dynamic 4D-CTA to reduce annotation burden and improve robustness across contrast phases is well-motivated and has clear potential impact. The empirical gains, particularly for vein segmentation, are promising.
To further strengthen the work, the authors may consider clarifying and reinforcing several aspects:
Annotation quality and validation: Since the dataset is a key contribution, additional discussion on annotation reliability (e. g. , inter-observer variability or quality control procedures) would improve confidence in the results. 
Evaluation metrics and reporting: Including standard Dice scores alongside the proposed mDC metric, as well as additional analysis of false positives/precision, would provide a more complete picture of segmentation performance. 
Generalization: The paper would benefit from a more cautious discussion of generalization, especially given the single-center data source. Clarifying this limitation explicitly would strengthen the overall presentation. 
Positioning of contributions: The paper would be clearer if it explicitly frames itself as a data-centric contribution (dataset + annotation pipeline) rather than a methodological advance, which would better align expectations with the presented results.
Overall, this is a solid and practically relevant contribution, and addressing the points above would further improve its clarity and impact.

The paper presents a well-motivated and practically relevant data-centric contribution, introducing a semi-automatic annotation pipeline that leverages dynamic 4D-CTA to efficiently generate artery and vein labels. The resulting multi-phase dataset is valuable, and the experiments demonstrate clear improvements in robustness to contrast variability, with particularly strong gains in vein segmentation. The analysis of performance across contrast phases is also insightful and highlights an important challenge in CTA-based segmentation.
While the methodological novelty is limited and some concerns remain regarding dataset size (in terms of unique patients), the overall contribution, especially the combination of annotation strategy, dataset, and demonstrated impact on robustness, is meaningful for the MICCAI community. The work provides useful insights and a practical direction for improving vessel segmentation.
Overall, the paper is slightly above the acceptance threshold, and I would support acceptance provided the authors clarify the evaluation setup and better position their contribution.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This work introduces a dynamic CTA dataset with whole brain paired arterial and vein annotations, including an annotation protocole for the dynamic modality. Authors show that training segmentation models dervied from such dynamic data can improve vasculature segmentation performance, even in out-of-domain datasets.
reviews.text_strengths:
The provided dataset is very relevant for the community and unique; to my knowledge, no other dynamic CTA datasets are available.
Authors show that models derived from such dataset outperform vasculature segmentation when compared to prior datasets.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Novelty: While the dataset + protocol is definitely a contribution in the field, the derivation of a vasculature segmentation model is limited and weakly evaluated. Authors make use of an nnUnet model -as were used in prior works in diverse tastes, e.g. TopCow/TopBrain- with limited baseline comparisons and ablations. Beyond the dataset, it is not clear what is the ‘methodological contribution’ of this work.
Labels: While authors could have obtained a timepoint-specific vessel mask for each CTA timepoint in a series; instead, a single arterial / vein mask is annotated from the Peak arterial/venous phases. Given that the dataset is the main novelty in this work, this represents a limitation, since no single timepoint enhances the whole brain vasculature so that it the labels can be considered as a ground-truth for all the timepoints in the series. Such differences are even strengthened in some pathologies (e.g. stroke), where delayed bolus arrival to the ipsilateral brain hemisphere creates larger bolus arrival delays.
The work is not easy to read. Please check below my comments about it.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Are images defaced/skull-struppied for full patient anonymization purposes?
The abstract is not easy to read, unless someone is expert in this field. There is no background nor introduction: why this topic is important to be addressed? what are the problems with current models/datasets?
Also abstract: “ (…) models trained on our dataset produce superior segmentations compared to the same models (…)” –> but then, only results of the proposed model are mentioned. Authors could summarize here how “much better” these results are.
Can you briefly include what is icafe? It is mentioned along the text; but note that not everyone reading this work will know about it.
Introduction: “(…) because of the abscence of interphase motion (…)” –> What is interphase motion in this context? Does it refer to patient motion? Then, this is not 100% guaranteed.
Did you compensate for patient head motion? How?
Algorithm: is very hard to follow without any context. What is Sa, Sv, Xa, Xv? Please define.

The novelty of this work lies exclusively in the labelled dataset, as models derived from it have been widely explored in previous works, with more extensive validations and analysis (which are mostly missing here). Being the dataset the most relevant contribution here, the annotation protocol still derives labels from single timepoints rather than separate masks for each of the.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of this paper is the collection and annotation of a large-scale 4D-CTA brain vessel dataset with arterial and venous labels. By leveraging dynamic 4D-CTA acquisitions, the authors efficiently generate multi-phase CTA volumes for each patient and reuse annotations across phases, effectively increasing the dataset size by a factor of five to six. The paper demonstrates through experiments that training deep learning models on this large, multi-phase dataset improves the robustness and accuracy of brain artery–vein segmentation, particularly under varying contrast conditions.
reviews.text_strengths:
-Novel and valuable dataset:
The most significant contribution lies in the construction of a relatively large 4D-CTA dataset for brain vessel segmentation, which is rare in this domain. The use of dynamic CTA allows efficient annotation reuse across phases and provides rich temporal contrast information.
-Clear empirical benefit of data scale:
The experiments convincingly show that increasing the amount and diversity of training data leads to improved artery and vein segmentation performance, including better topology-related metrics.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
-Restricted impact on the broader community:
Although code and models are promised to be released, the dataset itself does not appear to be publicly distributable. This limits the potential impact of the work on the broader research community and its reuse in follow-up studies.
-Limited methodological novelty:
While the dataset itself is novel, the technical approach is not. The segmentation models and training strategy rely entirely on established deep learning frameworks (e.g., nnU-Net) and standard loss functions. No new network architecture, learning strategy, or theory is introduced.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a valuable and well-curated 4D-CTA dataset and clearly demonstrates the benefits of large-scale, multi-phase data for brain vessel segmentation. However, the lack of methodological novelty and the limited accessibility of the dataset reduce its impact. Thus, this is considered to a borderline submission for MICCAI.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The construction of a large-scale 4D dataset is a valuable and novel contribution. This effort goes beyond the typical scope seen in prior work. Overall, I believe the paper meets the acceptance threshold.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper presents a data-centric approach for brain vessel segmentation in CTA by leveraging dynamic 4D-CTA to construct a multi-phase annotated dataset and improve robustness to contrast variability.
Reviewers agree that the dataset and annotation pipeline are valuable and practically relevant, but raise major concerns about limited methodological novelty, unclear validation of annotation quality, and limitations in evaluation metrics and generalization claims. I suggest that the authors address these concerns in the rebuttal.

The paper presents limited methodological innovation, but reviewers agree that the data contribution could be valuable for the community. I could recommend provisional acceptance, but strictly conditioned on the authors making the dataset publicly available. If the dataset and annotations cannot ultimately be made publicly available, the paper should not be accepted.

The rebuttal did not address all the reviewers’ concerns, being the main concern the lack of methodological novelty of the work presented. Certainly the preparation of the dataset and the dataset per se are valuable, but without being able to access the whole dataset, and without accompanying it with relevant disease-related clinical information, its impact and usefulness may be limited. Suggest this paper being more appropriate for one of the workshops of the conference rather than for the mainstream track. In addition, in the rebuttal it is stated that statistical significance could be added, but it does not specify which tests of statistical significance authors are referring to or whether they already have done these analyses.

The paper receives mixed reviews (2 positives and 1 negative). Although this work does not provide a new method, however, it provides a valuable and well-curated 4D-CTA dataset and demonstrates the benefits of large-scale, multi-phase data for brain vessel segmentation. Authors promise to open-source this dataset, which will be valuable for the MICCAI community. I recommend acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their insightful feedback, which will significantly improve our manuscript:
Generalization (R1): To clarify, DynaVessel (DV) comes from one hospital using a Canon-Toshiba scanner, and we evaluate the model on O.O.D. datasets from 2 countries in another continent (Europe): 1) a subset of ISLES, 2) TopCoW (+derived datasets), which was acquired with a Siemens scanner. Covering more scanners/hospitals would be ideal, but the fact a model trained on N=29 patients with multi-phase CTA can achieve SOTA performance on O.O.D. data suggests strong generalization
Data availability/Anonymization (R2,R3): Due to changing federal government and institutional mandates, our institutional IRB, compliance and data security administrators have instituted stricter oversight procedures for data sharing, which we have been working through for the last 3 months. We preclude reidentification by removing patient information from DICOM headers and removing facial bones/soft tissue from all scans (no skull stripping). We’re optimistic this will satisfy our new compliance responsibilities and allow us to release DV before the paper is published
Methodological novelty (R1,R2,R3): while we don’t propose a new architecture/loss function, DV is the largest CTA dataset for brain vessel segmentation and the first to use Dynamic 4D-CTA to simplify & scale up the annotation process. We appreciate R1’s encouragement to position our contribution as data-centric and will increase the emphasis on this in the revised version
Limited ablations (R2): we did dataset-level ablations: Figs. 4 & 5 show ablations of the impact of contrast at inference (tested on all phases) and the impact of training on a single image per patient (at peak vein/peak arterial contrast). We hope these results will address R2’s concerns about ablations
Metrics (R1): R1 is right: mDC can be “gamed” by over-segmenting a scan. However, the adHD metric will severely penalize cases where the boundaries of the predictions are far from the targets, as it sums minimum distances from each GT-surface point to the nearest predicted surface point. Our annotations cover more vessels than existing datasets, so traditional metrics wouldn’t convey the impact of our approach on the O.O.D. data. Still, we present extra metrics for binary vessel segmentation with the DV model on 3 datasets:
Metric DVtest VVerse TopBrain
Dice 0.64 0.20 0.30
Precision 0.55 0.12 0.18
Recall 0.79 0.65 0.90
Qualitative analysis reveals that FNs are infrequent while FPs mostly comprise very distal/scalp vessels (Fig 7c) and bright background objects that can be removed with a brain mask. In addition, we will add statistical significance tests comparing the DV model to all baselines in the revised version
Data quality assurance (R1,R2):The 16cm detector used for the Dynamic-4D-CTA protocol means the patient experiences little motion during the 60 second data acquisition, minimizing inter-phase patient motion. We also use intra-patient rigid registration (validated by a radiologist) between the peak arterial phase and other phases to ensure all images are properly aligned (Sec 2.2). We’ll detail the radiologist’s quality verification procedure for vessel annotations and discuss the limitations due to the lack of inter-rater agreement metrics in the camera ready
Single-phase annotations (R2): Dynamic-4D-CTA acquires data for all vascular phases, allowing retrospective selection of optimal peak phases per patient. We ensure all relevant vasculature parts are highlighted in the peak phases by including only healthy patients with symmetric vascular trees and no occlusions. Evaluation on cases from TopCoW (e.g., ct_001) that have partly occluded or non-opacified arteries confirmed that DV nnUNet segmentation accuracy is robust to such artifacts and pathologies
Clarity (R3):We will improve clarity and accuracy in the abstract (incl. task relevance), the description of iCafe, and variable definitions

title: Robust Colonoscopy Video Polyp Segmentation via Quality-Aware Memory and Prototype Alignment
abstract: In colonoscopy video polyp segmentation, degradations such as motion blur, specular reflections, and occlusions often render single-frame features incomplete and unreliable. However, most existing methods rely heavily on current-frame features to construct queries for cross-frame retrieval and alignment, leading to performance drops under such degradations. To address this, we propose a query-enhanced cascaded memory framework integrating Quality Awareness (QA) and Prototype Alignment (PA). Specifically, (1) to construct stable query representations for robust retrieval, we propose a quality-aware sensory memory mechanism that adaptively gates memory updates based on observation reliability and state consistency; (2) to mitigate appearance drift, we propose a prototype alignment mechanism that maintains appearance prototypes as long-term anchors. By leveraging stable queries to retrieve relevant prototypes, our framework enables reliable cross-frame association. On the most challenging Unseen-Hard subset of SUN-SEG, our method improves the best baseline by 2.9% in Dice and 4.2% in Sensitivity (Sen), demonstrating superior robustness under degraded conditions.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a query-enhanced cascaded memory framework for video polyp segmentation under degraded imaging conditions. Its key idea is to construct more reliable temporal queries using a Quality Awareness (QA) module with gated sensory memory, and then use these stable queries to retrieve long-term appearance anchors through a Prototype Alignment (PA) module. The method is designed to reduce reliance on noisy current-frame features and to mitigate appearance drift across video frames.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper is well motivated by realistic failure modes in colonoscopy videos, such as motion blur, specular reflections, occlusions, and large inter-frame displacement. The overall method is coherent: QA stabilizes short-term memory updates using reliability and consistency signals, while PA introduces long-term prototype anchors to counter appearance drift. This decomposition is intuitive and well matched to the task. Another strength is that the empirical gains are concentrated on the hardest evaluation setting: the method improves the best baseline by 2.9% Dice and 4.2% Sensitivity on SUN-SEG Unseen-Hard, and the ablation study shows that QA and PA provide complementary gains.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The main weakness is limited evaluation breadth. All experiments are conducted on SUN-SEG, so it is difficult to judge how well the method generalizes beyond this benchmark. A second weakness is that the technical novelty, while solid, is moderate: the paper combines ideas related to memory gating, dynamic memory, and prototype/feature-bank style retrieval that are related to prior works such as quality-aware dynamic memory, adaptive feature bank methods, space-time memory networks, and SALI. The contribution lies more in the task-specific integration than in a fundamentally new temporal modeling formulation. Finally, some implementation details that matter for reproducibility and robustness are not fully analyzed, such as initialization of the prototype bank and sensitivity to design choices like prototype-bank size, top-K retrieval, and update interval.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

My overall recommendation is Accept. The paper addresses an important and realistic problem in video polyp segmentation, the method is well aligned with the failure mode it targets, and the experimental improvements on the hardest split are meaningful. The work is not highly groundbreaking, and the evaluation is limited to a single dataset, but overall the paper is technically sound, clearly motivated, and empirically convincing enough to merit acceptance.

reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose a query-enhanced cascaded memory framework for robust colonoscopy video polyp segmentation under degraded conditions. The framework includes a Quality Awareness (QA) module that filters unreliable short-term observations through gated sensory memory, and a Prototype Alignment (PA) module that uses stabilized queries to retrieve long-term appearance prototypes to alleviate appearance drift.
reviews.text_strengths:
(1) The paper addresses the degradation of single-frame queries and the subsequent noise propagation in colonoscopy video analysis. 
(2) The Quality-Guided Network presents a well-structured design.
(3) The proposed method demonstrates quantitative improvements.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(1) Real-time performance is crucial for clinical deployment. However, the manuscript does not report inference speed (FPS), computational cost (FLOPs), or model parameters. Given the cascaded architecture with multiple attention modules, the practical feasibility remains unclear.
(2) In Section 2.2, Eq. (4) extracts candidate prototypes using the current predicted mask. Unlike the QA module, this step does not apply a quality gate. As a result, high-confidence false positives may be added to the prototype bank. Under the LFU replacement strategy, frequently queried errors could persist in memory and potentially worsen the appearance drift the module aims to address.
(3) The paper does not provide a code repository or dataset availability statement, which makes it difficult to verify implementation details or computational cost.

N/A

This paper presents a structured framework for robust video polyp segmentation, and the QA module offers a reasonable strategy to filter degraded observations. The method also shows clear experimental improvements.
