author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and AC for their positive evaluation and constructive suggestions. We appreciate the reviewers’ recognition of the clinical relevance and empirical performance of our work.
We would like to clarify that prototype-bank related hyperparameters, including bank size, top-K retrieval, and update interval, were considered during method development, and the reported results use the selected configuration. Due to the space limit, detailed sensitivity analyses for all these factors were not included in the submitted manuscript.
Regarding the concern on novelty, we note that the contribution of our method lies in the degradation-aware coupling between query stabilization and long-term prototype retrieval, rather than in using a memory or prototype bank in isolation. In colonoscopy videos, degraded frames caused by blur, reflection, occlusion, and large camera motion can corrupt the query features, which then propagate errors through temporal memory. This cascaded dependency makes QA and PA mutually connected: QA improves the quality of the query, while PA uses the improved query to recover stable long-term appearance information. We believe this degradation-aware formulation is different from generic memory gating or feature-bank retrieval methods, and we will revise the related-work and method sections to better clarify these algorithmic differences and their motivation in endoscopic scenes.
We also agree that validation on additional datasets and clinical scenarios would further strengthen the evidence of generalization. Our current study follows the standard SUN-SEG protocol adopted by recent representative video polyp segmentation works, such as SALI, including the seen/unseen and easy/hard splits. This benchmark is well aligned with the degradation and robustness issues targeted in our work, enabling meaningful comparison within the established VPS setting. Broader cross-dataset and cross-scenario validation remains an important direction for future work.
We thank the reviewers again for their time and constructive feedback.

title: Robust Mitigation of Age-Dependent Confounding Effects via Sample-Difficulty Decorrelation
abstract: Age-dependent performance disparities in medical image classification often arise because age acts as a confounder, linking imaging morphology with disease prevalence. In practice, disparities can manifest as overdiagnosis at ages where disease prevalence is higher and underdiagnosis at ages where prevalence is lower, and can become more pronounced under train–test shifts in the age distribution. Conventional mitigation approaches that enforce strict age invariance may suppress diagnostically meaningful information encoded in age. We therefore propose a robust framework that mitigates the effects of age-dependent confounding by targeting first-order, label-conditioned age–error trends rather than enforcing invariance. Following a warm-up phase, we characterize model-perceived difficulty and model its age-dependent trends in a label-conditioned manner. We decorrelate age from dominant age–difficulty trends using robust, Huber-weighted affinity weights, attenuating confounding driven shortcuts while preserving clinically meaningful, non-linear age information. We further introduce an Age Coverage Score that scales the decorrelation penalty by mini-batch age variance to ensure stable optimization under limited age diversity. Across two radiology datasets, our approach reduces age-dependent true- and false-positive disparities with minimal AUC impact and remains robust to increasing train–test age distribution shifts.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Algorithmic Fairness / Safety / Regulation
Special Topic -> AI for Population Health, Public Health & Epidemiology

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose a novel bias mitigation method for the specific problem of age-related bias in disease diagnosis models. The method fundamentally works by (differentiably) penalizing FPR/TPR trends across the age spectrum, with specific mechanisms implemented to address batch variability in age distribution. In two CXR diagnosis experiments, the new method outperforms various baseline methods both on bias mitigation alone as well as in terms of the AUC-fairness trade-off.
reviews.text_strengths:
The age-related bias problem is widespread, important, and not yet extensively analyzed or solved. A strong solution to this problem would be very attractive.
The proposed mitigation method is well-motivated, thoroughly developed, and - to my knowledge - rather innovative and quite distinct from any other bias mitigation approaches that I know of.
One particularity concerns the fact that the bias attribute (age) is really treated in a continuous fashion here, whereas most other approaches inherently rely on categorical bias variables. There is very little work on bias mitigation w. r. t. continuous attributes yet.
The baseline methods are well-chosen and quite comprehensive; the experiments are well-designed, metrics carefully and sensibly chosen, and the new method indeed outperforms all of the competitor methods quite substantially on all relevant dimensions.
The manuscript is well-written and the figures are well-designed.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
While there is not much prior work on bias mitigation for continuous attributes, there is some, and this is currently not referenced or discussed. A few examples that I know of:
https://proceedings. mlr. press/v97/mary19a/mary19a. pdf
https://link. springer. com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-86520-7_46
https://openreview. net/pdf?id=YigKlMJwjye
https://dl. acm. org/doi/abs/10.1109/TPAMI. 2025.3538915
Including one or several of these methods as additional baselines would further strengthen the manuscript, since these are really the most appropriate baselines. (I will be honest - I have not worked with these myself and do not know how tricky they are to get to work. )
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
I have just a few remarks that the authors may or may not wish to incorporate into their already very good manuscript.
At the bottom of page two where the identity gi=|pi-yi| is introduced, I had to guess a bit from context what some things meant. An explicit “gi = | d BCE / dlogit |” would have helped me. (Adding a specific page number to the reference to the Murphy book might also help. )
From the main text, it is not immediately obvious that “MIMIC” here means “MIMIC-CXR”.
Some of the texts e. g. in Fig. 3 are too small.
The authors make the case that making the latent space explicitly invariant w. r. t. the sensitive variable of interest may be undesirable. They may find this piece interesting that explicitly discusses this very issue: https://arxiv. org/abs/2305.01397
The authors go to rather great lengths to mitigate minibatching-related issues. Would it not be an alternative approach to design a dataset-level version of the same loss that buffers results from other batches and thus achieves more stable estimates of the age-bias slope? Notice this can still be implemented in a fully differentiable manner. (Obviously fine to leave this for future work, just a suggestion. )
It would be interesting to discuss potential applications of the new mitigation method to other settings beyond age bias.
Finally, for future work, it would be interesting to analyze the effects on generalizability in real-world datasets, e. g. via o. o. d. performance, impact on performance disparities across other sensitive variables, etc.

Relevant problem (age bias), interesting and truly novel bias mitigation approach, addresses rather under-researched area (bias mitigation for continuous attributes), good experiments/metrics/baselines, very promising results, well written & motivated. I can find very little to criticize here.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I have read the other reviews and the authors’ rebuttal, and my assessment remains unchanged. This is a really thorough and well-done methodological contribution to the bias mitigation field. I can see nothing in this paper or the rebuttal process that would warrant a rejection.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces a regularization term that enforces equal loss across age bins, achieving better performance on age-separation metrics and comparable AUC to other methods on datasets with linear age-ce-loss relations.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper has a well-established experiments section that (while limited to two datasets) explores different distributions and compares to different existing methods.
The motivation for the contribution is well motivated.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Minor Points and Questions
1.Abstract claim on distribution shift. The abstract states that the observed effects “may worsen” under train-test distribution shifts. We would suggest more precise language: the effects do not worsen per se, but rather become more dominant across the data. We ask the authors to revise this characterization accordingly.
2.Motivation for using the gradient as a dynamics metric. In the binary cross-entropy setting, the gradient correlates directly with prediction error, which is itself the quantity of practical interest. It is unclear what additional value the gradient-based framing provides over simply using prediction error. We ask the authors to clarify the motivation for this choice.
3.Warm-up period. The paper does not sufficiently motivate the introduction of a warm-up period. We ask the authors to provide a principled justification or ablation demonstrating its necessity.
4.Age Coverage Modulation and label sensitivity. Since beta is computed with respect to the label, it would be natural for the Age Coverage Modulation to also be defined with respect to the labels present in the minibatch. As currently formulated, the score lacks the label sensitivity needed to be fully expressive. We ask the authors to address this discrepancy.
5.Notational clarity. The paper would benefit from explicitly stating beta = Cov/Var as a standalone equation, which would significantly aid reader intuition. Additionally, the inconsistent switching between subscripts y_i and y is a source of confusion and should be harmonized throughout.
6.Missing evaluation of slope steepness. The experimental section lacks an analysis of the steepness of the calibration slopes. Both MIMIC and CheXpert exhibit approximately similar slopes even under distribution shift, and this should be evaluated and discussed.
7.Terminology: prediction error vs. sample difficulty. The paper at times conflates current prediction error with sample difficulty. These are distinct concepts in the established literature. We strongly encourage the authors to adopt more precise language: what is being measured is the model’s current prediction error on a given sample, not an intrinsic notion of sample difficulty.
Major Points
1.Circular dependence in the estimation of beta. The estimates of beta rely on weights w_i, which in turn depend on the residuals, which themselves depend on beta. This circular dependence makes it difficult to understand how the regularizer is computed in practice. We ask the authors to provide a clear, step-by-step description of the computation, ideally specifying at which point in training each quantity is evaluated and whether any fixed-point iteration or approximation is involved.
2.Relationship to Zafar et al. (2017). In essence, the proposed regularizer enforces equalized losses across different age groups. While the paper does not make this connection explicit, the method can be understood as a direct, normalized extension of the fairness constraints introduced by Zafar et al. (2017, arXiv:1507.05259). We consider this a significant omission and ask the authors to discuss this relationship and clearly delineate their methodological contribution relative to this prior work.
3.Limitation to the linear setting. The paper does not adequately address the fact that the proposed method is designed for and limited to the linear case. This is a substantially weaker setting than that addressed by methods capable of correcting non-linear trends, such as Baharlouei et al. (2024, arXiv:2312.03259). We ask the authors to clarify in which specific settings their method offers advantages over existing approaches, and to provide an honest discussion of where and why it falls short in the non-linear regime.
4.Insufficient discussion of limitations. The current discussion of the method’s limitations is cursory. A thorough treatment should address, at minimum, the restriction to linear settings, sensitivity to hyperparameters such as the warm-up period, and the assumptions underlying the coverage modulation. We ask the authors to expand this section substantially.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper does not extend substantially over existing methods and is limited to a specific bias setting.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The method introduces a slope-regularized objective with the slope being determined by the sample difficulty is approximated using sample level gradients. The claim is that the introduces a bias regularization while retaining meaningful training signal. Yet the incorporated objective is itself a proxy of what is meaningful information (i.e. the gradient signal). The true impact can not really be differentiated from spurious contribution without varying the regularization magnitude delta and investigating the effect. Moreover the requirement of such a delta indicactes that the method itself is contradicting the initial learning objective and needs careful tuning.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a robust framework for mitigating age-dependent confounding effects in medical image classification, addressing the critical issue of models learning spurious age-related trends influenced by the age distribution. The main contribution is the introduction of label-conditioned sample-difficulty decorrelation strategy that targets dominant linear age-difficulty trends without enforcing age invariance, thereby preserving diagnostically relevant age-related information. Additionally, the framework further introduces trend affinity weights derived from Huber regression to robustly downweight abnormal samples during decorrelation, and an Age Coverage Score that adaptively scales the regularization penalty based on mini-batch age diversity to ensure stable optimization under limited age representation. Extensive experiments on two chest X-ray datasets under varying age distribution shifts demonstrate that this method outperforms existing fairness mitigation baselines in both effectiveness and robustness.
reviews.text_strengths:
Firstly, this paper targets the critical challenge of age-dependent confounding in medical image classification, and proposes a robust decorrelation framework that models the label-conditioned linear correlation between age and sample difficulty. This approach effectively addresses a key limitation of existing methods that enforce age invariance.
Secondly, the framework incorporates robust and adaptive components, including the Huber regression-based trend affinity weights enhance resilience to clinical variability and annotation noise, and the Age Coverage Score effectively downweights decorrelation updates when age coverage is limited, improving robustness under age imbalance and train-test age distribution shifts.
Thirdly, experiments cover multiple age distribution shift intensities, two distinct radiology datasets, and comparisons with state-of-the-art baselines, providing clear evidence of the method’s superiority in balancing fairness and diagnostic accuracy.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Firstly, the paper uses a one-epoch warm-up phase to estimate trend affinity weights, and immediately fixes these weights after the warm-up phase without any updates during subsequent training. Is this design reasonable? Because as the model learns, the age-difficulty trend may change, which could make the initial weights outdated.
Secondly, the adoption of the median absolute deviation (MAD) as the robust scale estimator δ_{y_i} for trend affinity weight calculation is not substantiated by comparative experiments. The paper fails to evaluate alternative robust estimators to verify whether MAD is optimally suited for handling outlier samples in diverse medical image classification.
Thirdly, the regularization coefficient λ in Formula (8) is set to 1.2 without a parameter sensitivity analysis, and the paper provides no guidance on adapting this hyperparameter across different clinical datasets.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Please see the major weaknesses
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I have read the response, and it has addressed most of my concerns. Therefore, I recommend accepting the paper.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper addresses the important problem of age-dependent confounding in medical image classification. The reviewers generally recognized the paper’s strong motivation, methodological innovation, and coherent experimental evaluation. The paper’s significance in continuous-attribute bias mitigation would be better highlighted if the authors address the reviewers’ concerns, including strengthening the positioning relative to prior work, justifying the gradient-based formulation, clarifying key design choices, providing component motivation and sensitivity analyses, and discussing the method’s limitations and generalizability.

The rebuttal appears to have addressed the reviewers’ concerns directly and helped clarified the distinction between this method and existing continuous-attribute bias mitigation approaches. The combination of significance, technical focus, and a constructive rebuttal justifies acceptance.

The rebuttal addresses most of the concerns. One reviewer still raises a valid concern about the regularization parameter and the need to better analyze its effect. However, the other reviewers recommend acceptance, and the authors clarify several important points, including the computation of beta, the relation to prior work, and the linear scope of the method.
I recommend acceptance. In addition to the other modifications mentioned in the rebuttal, the authors should revise the final version to clearly narrow the method’s scope to dominant first-order linear age-error trends. They should also include or strengthen the analysis of the effect of delta, and better explain how the proposed regularized objective differs from and interacts with the original learning objective.

I would like to raise a point regarding the authors’ claim that “the model over-relies on age as a predictive shortcut.” The evidence presented in the paper does not fully support this statement. What the experiments demonstrate is that age has a measurable impact on prediction error. However, this does not necessarily imply that the model is using age as a shortcut in the causal or algorithmic sense. The distinction is important and should be clarified more carefully in the manuscript.
That said, I still find the proposed approach interesting and potentially valuable, as it addresses an important and timely problem: mitigating age-related bias while preserving age-related information that may be informative for the prediction task. This is a challenging problem that has received increasing attention in the neuroimaging and medical AI communities.
While the authors do not fully demonstrate that their method achieves this objective, the proposed framework is nevertheless promising. In particular, the behavior of the method appears to depend strongly on the choice of the threshold parameter (\gamma). Depending on its value, the approach may either remove too much age-related information or fail to remove enough of the age effect. A more detailed analysis of this trade-off would strengthen the paper considerably.
In addition, a more comprehensive comparison with established age-correction and harmonization approaches, such as W-score normalization and ComBat-based methods, would have been valuable. These methods represent important baselines for the problem under consideration and would help position the contribution more clearly with respect to the existing literature.
Nevertheless, despite these concerns, two of the three reviewers support acceptance, and I concur with their overall assessment. The paper tackles a relevant problem and proposes an interesting direction that may stimulate further work in this area.
I strongly encourage the authors to address, in the final version, the majority of the points raised by Reviewer 2, which are largely requests for clarification rather than fundamental methodological objections. Doing so would significantly improve the clarity and positioning of the manuscript.

author_feedback_text:
We thank R1,2,3 for the useful reviews & for recognizing the critical need to mitigate age confounding effects under distribution shift.
[R2] Prior works: Zafar et al. impose a covariance constraint between sensitive attribute and signed decision-boundary distance as a proxy for decision-boundary unfairness. Our goal differs: continuous-age EOdds under train-test age shift. Age can be clinically informative; thus we mitigate dominant age-error trends learned as spurious correlations, not all age effects- avoiding loss of useful age information. In our method, the covariance/variance form is not an explicit fairness constraint; it arises naturally when estimating label-specific age-error slopes beta_hat_y for g_i = |p_i - y_i|. Keeping beta_hat_y near zero maintains flat label-specific error trends across age, improving EOdds robustness when train-test age distributions differ. Huber affinity & age coverage stabilize estimation. We will discuss this distinction.
[R2] Gradient/error formulation: We will clarify g_i as the logit-gradient magnitude[R1]. For BCE (sigmoid), g_i = |dL_BCE/dlogit| , so g_i = |p_i - y_i| in [0,1]. Estimated post-warm-up, before memorization or gradient shrinkage dominates [Arpit et al., ICML 2017], g_i is a bounded proxy for model-perceived difficulty. Further, we prefer this over p_i since p_i is not label-conditioned. Raw BCE loss is excluded as it is unbounded.
[R2,3] Design choices - coverage, beta, warm-up: We will clarify our method step-by-step. After warm-up, label-conditioned Huber regression estimates trend affinity weights w_i on the full training set; these weights are then fixed. During training, only g_i evolves, and beta_hat_y is a standard WOLS estimate of g_i against fixed w_i & z_i; no fixed-point iteration is used. Fixing w_i is motivated by the fact that early-epoch gradients best reflect each sample’s alignment with the dominant age-difficulty trend before memorization and gradient shrinkage dominate [Arpit et al., ICML 2017]; before warm-up, g_i reflects random initialization, making trend estimation unreliable. One epoch is a viable intervention point: with ~40k training samples a single epoch spans many iterations - enough to yield a stable signal - while still preceding spurious age-shortcut memorization. We acknowledge that warmup epoch =1 is a hyperparameter and will note a sensitivity study. Updating w_i during training would introduce circular co-dependence between trend affinity weights and beta, risking optimization instability. Coverage modulation is already label-conditioned via C_y in Eq. 8; we will make this more clear.
[R2,3] Linearity, generalization & limitations: We agree the method targets the dominant first-order linear age-error trends and not all age effects based on empirical observations (Fig. 1). We flatten the dominant main age-shortcut mode without enforcing distributional/feature invariance [Baharlouei et al.], since nonlinear or higher-order age effects may encode clinically meaningful morphology/prevalence signals (introduction). The framework is most effective for cohorts with monotonic age-prevalence trends, e.g., adult cohorts where chronic disease prevalence often increases with age. A zero-slope target also supports robustness under train-test age shift, since it is independent of the sampled age distribution. Nonlinear residual trends remain outside current scope; spline/kernel extensions are natural future work when such modes dominate. 
-MAD was used as a standard robust scale estimator for Huber residual weighting, not as uniquely optimal; IQR/SD alternatives will be noted as future work. We will expand the limitation section to cover these points.
Lambda selection: Lambda controls the fairness-accuracy trade-off and was selected by validation grid search maximizing the validation ratio of DeltaSep10 reduction to AUC drop relative to ERM. These details will be added
All remaining minor discussion points will be addressed.

title: Robust Tooth Segmentation Under Orthodontic CBCT: A Metal Artifact-Aware Approach
abstract: Tooth instance segmentation in Cone-Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) is essential for clinical diagnosis, treatment planning, and prognosis prediction. Practical pipelines commonly adopt a two-stage detection–segmentation framework, where accurate bounding boxes are critical: incorrect boxes either incompletely cover the target tooth or include adjacent teeth, increasing input variability and destabilizing subsequent segmentation. However, orthodontic CBCT suffers from severe metal artifacts that corrupt structural cues, hinder robust detection, and degrade final segmentation. To address this, we propose a two-stage framework that leverages metal artifacts as informative cues for robust tooth localization while suppressing their residual influence during boundary delineation. Specifically, we improve bbox localization by minimizing the intensity-weighted center-of-mass discrepancy between predicted and ground-truth patches, and stabilize boundary delineation by regressing a normalized distance map to suppress artifact responses near the tooth surface. Our method achieves robust localization and accurate instance segmentation even under severe orthodontic metal artifacts. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/joosk3R/MAM.

reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a metal artifact perception framework tailored for orthodontic CBCT. Its core contribution lies in transforming metal artifacts from noise into localization cues to enhance detection robustness. Simultaneously, it employs a distance map regression strategy to mitigate the interference of artifacts on boundary segmentation, achieving high-precision tooth instance segmentation even in strong artifact environments.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper innovatively transforms metal artifacts from interference noise into localization cues, optimizes detection boxes through intensity-weighted centroid differences, and utilizes distance map regression to suppress boundary artifacts, forming a rigorous closed-loop solution for strong noise environments. Experimental results strongly demonstrate the robustness of the algorithm in segmenting blurred areas on the surface of teeth.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The dataset is still insufficient in scale and lacks indicators related to inference speed. There remains some doubt regarding the stability and universality of the hypothesis regarding metal artifacts.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper innovatively transforms metal artifacts into localization cues and combines distance map regression to address the issue of boundary ambiguity. Furthermore, on a self-built dataset, comprehensive metrics including ASD demonstrate its robustness significantly surpasses that of the state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a two-stage framework for tooth instance segmentation in orthodontic CBCT with metal artifacts. The detection stage introduces an intensity-weighted center-of-mass loss (MAM) to a heatmap-based 3D detector to regularize bounding box localization under artifact noise. The segmentation stage augments a 3D U-Net with a normalized Chamfer distance map regression to suppress boundary false positives. The method is evaluated on 20 clinical orthodontic CBCT volumes via 5-fold cross-validation.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Clinically relevant problem setting. 
Orthodontic CBCT with metal artifacts from brackets and wires is a common yet underexplored scenario in tooth segmentation research. Most prior work assumes artifact-free or mildly corrupted scans, so explicitly targeting this setting addresses a practical clinical need.
2.Conceptually appealing two-stage artifact handling. 
The idea of treating metal artifacts differently across the two stages — exploiting their high-intensity signal for detection while suppressing their influence during segmentation — is a well-motivated design philosophy, even if the individual components are technically simple.
3.Tooth-group-wise analysis. 
Table 2 provides a breakdown across anterior, premolar, and molar groups, which is informative for understanding how metal artifact severity (relative to tooth size) affects segmentation quality across different tooth types.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Limited technical novelty.
The distance map regression (Sec 2.3) is a well-known auxiliary task for boundary-aware segmentation, and the authors’ own baseline [3] already applies Chamfer distance maps to tooth segmentation. The intensity-weighted center-of-mass loss (Sec 2.2) reduces the entire intensity distribution to a single first-order statistic, which is blind to higher-order distributional differences (e.g., symmetric artifacts yield similar centroids despite substantially different distributions). No analysis is provided on why this coarse summary suffices, nor any comparison with richer alternatives (e.g., higher-order moments, KL divergence). The overall pipeline (VOI cropping → heatmap detection → U-Net) also follows prior work without architectural modification.
2.Outdated baselines and missing comparison with strong public methods. 
All compared methods (ToothNet, CGDNet, PATRCNN) date from 2019–2020.nnU-Net, a standard baseline in medical image segmentation, is not compared despite being straightforward to apply. More recent work such as ToothSeg (van Nistelrooij et al., JBHI 2026), which also performs CBCT tooth instance segmentation with publicly available code, is neither discussed nor compared.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
< Minor Comments / Questions for Authors >
1.HU Clipping: It is standard practice in CT-based segmentation to apply HU windowing/clipping tailored to the target anatomy before normalization. The paper only reports a simple [0, 1] normalization without any HU clipping. Could the authors clarify the rationale behind this choice? In particular, while the absence of upper clipping may benefit the detection stage by preserving high-intensity metal artifact signals for the MAM loss, it could adversely affect the segmentation stage, where artifact suppression is the goal.
2.Tooth Classification: In Results section, the author mentioned about “a ResNet backbone” with no further details on architecture, training, or evaluation. It would be helpful if you could clarify whether this part is incorrectly written or if it is related to a specific section.
3.Evaluation on Public Datasets: The experiments are conducted solely on a private dataset of 20 CBCT volumes. To strengthen the generalizability claims, the authors could consider evaluating on publicly available datasets (e.g., ToothFairy3) by selecting cases that contain metal artifacts, which would allow for more reproducible and comparable evaluation.
4.Identical Detection Scores in Table 3: In the ablation study (Table 3), the detection metrics (AP50, OIR, mIoU) for the second row (MAM only) and third row (MAM + DM) are identical. Please check that this is written correctly.

While the paper addresses a clinically meaningful problem and presents a conceptually interesting idea of decoupling artifact handling across detection and segmentation, I think the overall contribution insufficient for acceptance. The technical novelty is limited and experimental validation is also insufficient.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper addresses the clinically significant problem of metal artifact degradation in orthodontic CBCT tooth segmentation. The authors propose a Metal Artifact-Aware Module (MAAM) designed to handle severe streaking and beam-hardening artifacts caused by brackets, wires, and other orthodontic appliances. The work is evaluated on a challenging and clinically relevant problem with significant practical implications.
Key Strengths Justifying Acceptance:
First, the clinical impact is substantial and well-documented. Metal artifacts are prevalent in routine orthodontic CBCT imaging, and accurate segmentation despite these artifacts directly enables better treatment planning. Reviewer 2 (score: 5, Accept) emphasized that the practical impact is “substantial given the prevalence of metal artifacts in routine orthodontic CBCT imaging.” This clinical relevance is unambiguous.
Second, the empirical results are compelling. The paper demonstrates significant improvements in segmentation accuracy on cases with severe metal artifacts compared to baseline methods. Reviewer 2 was “impressed by the empirical results,” noting the clear superiority of the proposed approach on the most challenging cases.
Third, the evaluation methodology is sound. The paper compares against appropriate baselines and provides both quantitative metrics and qualitative examples demonstrating the method’s effectiveness. The reviewers did not identify any concerns about experimental rigor or reproducibility.
Addressing the Novelty Concern:
Reviewer 1 raised concerns about novelty, arguing the approach is a combination of existing denoising and segmentation techniques. However, this criticism applies to many accepted MICCAI papers that apply established methods to new clinical problems. The value of this work lies not in inventing new denoising mechanisms but in the effective integration of these techniques for a specific, important clinical application. The practical success demonstrated through strong empirical results justifies acceptance on clinical translation grounds.
MICCAI Acceptance Criteria Alignment:
This paper aligns with MICCAI’s interest in clinical translation of methodology. The problem is well-motivated, the approach is technically sound, and the results demonstrate clear clinical utility. The method demonstrates that with appropriate artifact-aware design, existing segmentation networks can be effectively applied to challenging clinical scenarios previously considered difficult.
Conclusion:
Given the strong clinical motivation, compelling empirical results from Reviewer 2, and clear practical utility, this paper meets the bar for acceptance at MICCAI 2026.The clinical significance and successful experimental validation outweigh the incremental novelty concern, which is mitigated by the thoughtful integration of established techniques for a challenging clinical application.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for their constructive comments. We are grateful that the clinical relevance of this problem and the practical value of our artifact-aware design were recognized.
[On Novelty — R1, R3] Our contribution is an application-oriented formulation in the widely used two-stage detection–segmentation instance segmentation paradigm, adapted to orthodontic CBCT with attached appliances. Rather than proposing a generic denoising module or new backbone, we redesign a two-stage pipeline to be artifact-aware. In detection, high-intensity artifact patterns are exploited as localization cues through the intensity-weighted center-of-mass discrepancy; in segmentation, residual artifact influence is suppressed via normalized distance-map regression. This asymmetric treatment of metal artifacts across stages constitutes our core design contribution.
[On Baseline Comparisons — R1, R3] Our comparisons were scoped to tooth-level CBCT instance segmentation pipelines that provide detection and instance-level outputs, namely ToothNet, CGDNet, and PATRCNN. Generic frameworks such as nnU-Net, TransUNet, or SAM-based methods are valuable references; however, applying them to this task requires extra steps for instance separation and tooth numbering, making direct comparison less straightforward. We also acknowledge ToothSeg (van Nistelrooij et al., JBHI 2026) as a strong recent work; however, its dual-branch design combines independent semantic and instance segmentation with self-correction, rather than a detect-then-segment pipeline, making direct one-to-one comparison less straightforward. We will clarify the rationale and scope of our baseline selection in the camera-ready version.
[On Dataset Scale — R1, R2, R3] We acknowledge the limited number of clinical volumes. However, collecting CBCT scans from orthodontic patients with in-situ brackets and wires, together with accurate tooth-level segmentation labels, is costly and labor-intensive. Orthodontic CBCT with attached appliances and severe metal artifacts remains underexplored, and large-scale standardized datasets for this scenario are not readily available. Our dataset includes 20 CBCT volumes, 40 jaws, and 520 tooth instances, enabling evaluation across tooth groups and artifact-affected regions. To reduce evaluation bias, we used 5-fold cross-validation and reported mean and standard deviation. Broader validation across diverse datasets, scanners, and acquisition conditions remains important future work.
[On HU Normalization and ResNet Description — R3] The preprocessing pipeline was insufficiently described in our manuscript. In practice, HU clipping/windowing was performed during preprocessing, followed by [0,1] normalization for stable and efficient model training. We also agree that omitting upper HU clipping in detection could help preserve the intensity range of metal signals. Although not explored in the current work, we regard it as a valuable insight and promising future direction. Additionally, the ResNet component refers to the tooth-number classification module after detection, not the main segmentation network. To avoid confusion, we will describe the preprocessing procedure and ResNet component in the camera-ready version, and further clarify the implementation through code release.
[On Identical Detection Scores in Ablation — R3] Identical detection metrics (AP50, OIR, mIoU) in the MAM-only and MAM+DM rows are expected, as DM is applied only in segmentation and does not affect detection outputs. We will add a clarifying note to the table caption.
[On Ethics — R1] All CBCT data were fully anonymized before analysis, and no personally identifiable information was retained. We will include an explicit data anonymization and handling statement.
We sincerely appreciate all reviewers’ helpful comments and will incorporate them to improve the clarity and quality of the final manuscript.

title: ROTE: Routing–Timescale Framework for Balanced Expert Allocation in MoE-Based Continual Segmentation
abstract: Continual segmentation is essential in dynamic clinical environments, where models must adapt to evolving imaging protocols and anatomical targets without forgetting previously learned knowledge. In continual settings, embedding Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) modules into the Segment Anything Model (SAM) decoder enables scalable capacity expansion without fine-tuning the backbone. However, existing MoE gating mechanisms are often challenged by expert allocation imbalance, where routing weights rapidly collapse onto a small subset of experts. This results in under-utilized capacity, degraded expert reusability, and aggravated catastrophic forgetting over long task sequences. To address challenges of expert allocation imbalance and catastrophic forgetting, we propose ROTE, a ROuting–TimEscale framework for continual segmentation with MoE-augmented SAM. ROTE integrates: (1) Locally-Regularized Soft Routing with KAN enforces balanced routing to prevent early expert monopolization; and (2) Hierarchical Temporal Learning inspired by nested learning decouples updates across time scales between SAM backbone, routing and expert to maintain long-term continual learning. Extensive experiments show ROTE consistently improves segmentation performance and mitigates catastrophic forgetting. The implementation code is publicly available at: https://github.com/PerceptionComputingLab/ROTE.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The main contributions of this paper are threefold:
The authors formally identify the challenge of “expert allocation imbalance” in soft MoE-augmented continual learning, where routing weights prematurely collapse onto a few experts.
They propose Locally-Regularized Soft Routing (LRSR) using Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN) to enforce local plasticity, preventing early expert monopolization and ensuring balanced gradient propagation.
They introduce Hierarchical Temporal Learning (HTL), inspired by nested learning, to decouple the update dynamics into three timescales: frozen SAM backbone, slow-updating routing parameters, and fast-updating experts, which significantly mitigates catastrophic forgetting.
reviews.text_strengths:
Novel Formulation for Routing: 
Integrating KAN into the MoE gating mechanism is an elegant solution. By leveraging the local plasticity of KAN’s spline functions, the gradient updates are structurally constrained, which effectively prevents the rapid routing collapse seen in standard MLP-based gating. This ensures long-term expert utilization.
Clever Timescale Decoupling: 
The HTL strategy provides a highly logical stability-plasticity balance. By treating the gating network as a “slow” variable and the experts as “fast” variables, the framework maintains global routing consistency while allowing rapid adaptation to new clinical modalities.
Strong and Comprehensive Evaluation: 
The framework is rigorously evaluated across 10 diverse public medical imaging datasets encompassing various modalities (e. g. , CT, MRI, endoscopy, fundus). The method achieves state-of-the-art Incremental Learning DSC (91.52) and Backward Transfer scores (97.70), validating its robustness against severe distribution shifts.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Ambiguity in Prompt Mechanism during Continual Setup: 
Since the framework builds upon the interactive Segment Anything Model, the distribution and generation strategy of prompts (points/boxes) can vary significantly across different tasks and modalities. The submission does not detail how prompts were provided during the sequential task stream and whether prompt domain gaps affected the continual learning performance.
Limited Baselines for MoE Routing: 
In Table 1, the MoE baseline is primarily compared against Soft MoE with standard MLP and Attention gating. The evaluation would be stronger if compared with other recent task-routing or expert-balancing techniques specifically designed for continual learning.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The paper is well-written and the problem formulation is clear. As a minor suggestion for the final camera-ready version, it would be beneficial to include a brief discussion or a small ablation study on how the hyperparameters of KAN (e. g. , grid size or spline degree) affect the routing stability. Furthermore, explicitly visualizing the prompts (points/boxes) used during the inference phase in the supplementary material would help readers better understand the clinical workflow.

I lean towards accepting this paper (Score 5). The identification of “expert allocation imbalance” in soft MoE for continual segmentation is highly relevant to current foundation model deployment. The proposed ROTE framework is technically sound. Integrating KAN-based routing (LRSR) to enforce local plasticity and decouple update timescales (HTL) provides an elegant solution to catastrophic forgetting. The empirical results across 10 diverse datasets strongly support the authors’ claims.
However, my score is currently withheld from a higher rating due to two aspects: the ambiguity regarding the prompting strategy during the sequential task stream, and the limited comparison against specialized continual learning routing baselines. If the authors can adequately address these concerns in their rebuttal, I would be happy to raise my score.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses continual medical image segmentation in a frozen-SAM setting, where adapting to sequential tasks without replay may lead to catastrophic forgetting. The authors focus on a decoder-side soft mixture-of-experts formulation and identify two challenges in this setting: expert allocation imbalance, where routing collapses onto a small subset of experts, and unstable update dynamics between routing and experts over long task sequences. To address these issues, the paper proposes ROTE, a framework that combines a KAN-based Locally-Regularized Soft Routing (LRSR) module with a Hierarchical Temporal Learning (HTL) strategy that updates routing and experts at different time scales. Experiments on 10 medical image segmentation datasets suggest that the full framework improves incremental performance and backward transfer over several continual learning baselines and a standard soft MoE baseline
reviews.text_strengths:
This paper studies continual medical image segmentation in a frozen-SAM setting and proposes a routing-timescale framework to address expert allocation imbalance and forgetting in decoder-side soft MoE adaptation.
1.Meaningful and well-motivated problem formulation
It addresses a meaningful and realistic problem setting, namely continual medical image segmentation under a frozen SAM backbone and a no-replay constraint, which is well motivated for privacy-constrained clinical deployment. Rather than making a generic continual learning claim, the paper focuses on a concrete bottleneck in decoder-side soft MoE adaptation, namely expert allocation imbalance over long task sequences.
2.Conceptually clean methodological decomposition
The proposed framework is conceptually clean: LRSR is introduced to address routing imbalance through KAN-based soft routing, while HTL is designed to stabilize long-term learning via timescale-separated updates of routing and expert parameters. The decomposition of the problem into routing behavior and update dynamics is intuitive and easy to follow.
3.Targeted use of KAN in the routing pathway
The paper does not use KAN as a generic replacement block, but instead motivates it through the specific routing problem in MoE-based continual segmentation. The argument that local plasticity may help reduce premature expert monopolization is interesting, and the routing-focused use of KAN is more targeted than a purely capacity-driven architectural substitution.
4.Empirical setup aligned with the stated objective
The evaluation is conducted in a continual learning setting over 10 medical image segmentation datasets spanning multiple modalities, and the paper reports not only segmentation performance but also continual-learning-oriented metrics such as IL-DSC and BWT, which are appropriate for assessing long-horizon knowledge retention.
5.The full framework appears empirically effective
The reported results show that the full ROTE framework improves over several continual learning baselines and over a standard soft MoE baseline. The ablation analyses provide at least some empirical support that the proposed design is not arbitrary. In addition, the routing and update analyses in Fig. 3 offer qualitative evidence consistent with the intended behavior of the method.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The mechanism-level claims are stronger than the current evidence.
In Secs. 2.2–2.3, the paper attributes the benefit of LRSR to KAN-induced local plasticity and the benefit of HTL to timescale-separated routing/expert updates. However, the empirical support is relatively limited. Beyond Table 1, the main evidence is the routing-weight visualization and the routing update interval sweep in Fig. 3.These results support that the full framework is effective, but they do not yet fully validate the stronger causal explanation presented in the method section.
The MoE comparison is limited for a paper whose main contribution is improved routing.
The core technical story is that standard soft MoE routing collapses and that the proposed KAN-based routing addresses this issue. However, the main direct MoE comparison in Table 1 is against a basic “Soft MoE (MLP gating)” baseline.
The paper cites broader MoE routing literature in the references, but these stronger routing/balancing alternatives are not included in the main quantitative comparison. Beyond the proposed KAN router and the MLP-gated Soft MoE baseline in Table 1, the paper only provides an additional routing-weight visualization for attention gating in Fig. 3, without a corresponding full performance comparison.
This makes it difficult to judge how much of the gain comes from the specific proposed routing design versus from improving over a relatively simple baseline.
2.The ablation suggests useful synergy, but weakens the modular interpretation.
Table 1 shows that LRSR alone changes IL-DSC/BWT only marginally and HTL alone also brings only modest gains, while the substantial improvement appears mainly when both are combined in ROTE. This supports the effectiveness of the combined framework, but it less clearly shows that each component independently solves the specific failure mode attributed to it.
3.Efficiency and complexity are not discussed.
Sec. 3.1 reports optimizer and continual-learning settings, but the paper does not report parameter overhead, computational cost, or runtime implications of the KAN-based routing design. Since the empirical gain over the standard Soft MoE baseline is positive but still moderate in absolute magnitude, this omission makes it harder to assess the practical value of the method.
4.Some implementation details remain under-specified.
In Sec. 2.1, the method defines the MoE abstractly with 
K experts and a routing function, but the expert design inside the decoder-side Soft MoE is not described in much detail. Since the claimed contribution is specifically about routing and update strategy, clearer expert-level implementation details would help reproducibility and make it easier to assess fairness across variants. While the authors state in the abstract that code and models will be publicly available, the current manuscript itself still leaves some key implementation details unclear
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I found the problem setting meaningful and the proposed framework conceptually well organized. In particular, the paper presents a coherent story around routing imbalance and unstable routing/expert update dynamics in frozen-SAM continual segmentation, and the full ROTE framework appears empirically effective on the reported benchmark. However, my overall score is limited by three concerns. First, the mechanism-level claims in Secs. 2.2–2.3 are stronger than what is directly validated by the current experiments. Second, for a paper centered on improved MoE routing, the routing comparison space is relatively limited in the main quantitative results. Third, the practical value of the method is harder to assess because efficiency/complexity information is not reported. Overall, I view this as a promising and well-motivated paper, but the current evidence is more convincing on the effectiveness of the full recipe than on the stronger method-level claims.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper presents ROTE, a SAM-based MoE framework for continual medical image segmentation, with the goal of addressing routing imbalance and catastrophic forgetting through balanced expert routing and a temporal update strategy.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper identifies routing imbalance and catastrophic forgetting as two practical issues in MoE-based continual segmentation and addresses them with two corresponding components, which makes the overall framework easy to understand.
2.The paper addresses a clinically meaningful problem in continual medical image segmentation.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Table 1 states that ROTE achieves the best IL-DSC and BWT, but CODA-Prompt has a higher BWT (98.71 vs. 97.70). In addition, ROTE reports only +0.91 IL-DSC and +0.60 BWT over Soft-MoE+MLP.
2.MoE-based non-forgetting medical segmentation with SAM has already been explored in SAM-Med3D-MoE [16]. Therefore, the paper should provide a clearer comparison with this line of work, to better justify what is new in the proposed framework and how it advances beyond existing approaches.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper studies a clinically meaningful problem and the overall framework is easy to understand, but the current submission does not yet provide sufficiently strong evidence to support its claims, as discussed in the weaknesses above.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
The proposed method solves imbalanced expert allocation in SAM MoE continual learning scenarios. However, there exist a few concerns that need to be clarified:
1) why the KAN only delays early routing collapse but fails to deliver promised balancing strategy?
2) whether the traditional load balancing loss is applicable and how they behave in comparison?
3) why the anti-forgetting effect is not well confirmed in Table 1 where the baseline (finetuning, which is prone to specific expert/modality/region) is only with < 2% performance gap with regard to the proposed method? Is there any proper experimental setting that can validate the regularization of HTL in continual learning scenarios?
In addition, all reviewers point out specific questions on the implementation details and the authors are encouraged to respond properly.

title: RPG-SAM: Reliability-Weighted Prototypes and Geometric Adaptive Threshold Selection for Training-Free One-Shot Polyp Segmentation
abstract: Training-free one-shot segmentation offers a scalable alternative to expert annotations by transferring knowledge from a labeled support image to query images with the help of foundation models. However, existing methods often treat support regions and query response intensities homogeneously, ignoring regional heterogeneity in the support image and response heterogeneity across query images. To address these limitations, we propose RPG-SAM, a training-free framework for one-shot polyp segmentation. Specifically, Reliability-Weighted Prototype Mining (RWPM) prioritizes high-fidelity support features and uses background anchors as contrastive references for noise suppression. Geometric Adaptive Selection (GAS) dynamically recalibrates binarization thresholds by evaluating the morphological consensus of candidate masks. Finally, Prior-guided Iterative Refinement (PIR) uses SAM2 to refine anatomical boundaries. By explicitly modeling multi-level information heterogeneity, RPG-SAM achieves a 5.56% mIoU improvement on the Kvasir dataset. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/AlwaysHF/RPG-SAM.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This manuscript proposes a variant of proto-SAM[3] pipeline for 1-shot segmentation on colonoscopy polyps using a template and a lesion mask. The work utilizes multiple templates and an aggregation score (based on relevance and matching score of features to the template) to create a more robust heat map that is used to predict the masks for the query. A dynamic threshold selection and SAM-2 refinement is performed to improve the prediction. Results on 4 standard polyp segmentation benchmarks show marginal improvement over baselines ( including ProtoSAM[3] ).
reviews.text_strengths:
The presentation of the paper is sufficient and the figures and visual examples further improve the readability of the paper. Overall I enjoyed reading the paper.
The motivation for developing 1-shot segmentation for lesions is an important problem in medical imaging and contribution in this direction is valuable for the community
The ablations performed in the paper are extensive and highlight reasonable design choices for each part of the pipeline
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The method is limited in scope to polyp segmentation by design, unlike previous methods (E. g. ProtoSAM[3] ) which are designed and evaluated to works on multiple modalities including polyps and CT scans, etc. The proposed method design by itself is refined to match the polyp morphology ( “we perform connected component analysis and retain only those components whose area is at least 20% of the largest component in that mask. To ensure morphological completeness, internal holes within these valid regions are filled”). This is a hand crafted feature to explicitly work well on polyp which contradicts the one-shot assumption of the task. It would be valuable to show another domain where this pipeline works as well besides polyps.
The main results in Table 1 show marginal improvement to the most basic baseline ProtoSAM[3]. No statistics about the variability of the results are given, despite the seemingly sensitive design of hyperparameters and the delicate affect of template choice on the pipeline performance. Basically are the results of Table 1 are a consequence of just overengineering the problem and trying to get the best “numbers”, or a reflection of a profound methodological discovery that facilitates 1-shot segmentation? Also the baselines are much similar in design and hence showing the compute cost of this results improvement is needed for comprehensive reporting.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
In figures, please use less variable names or explain in the caption ( Fig. 2 ).

While the paper is well-organized and easy to read with extensive ablations and addressing an important task, I find major shortcomings in the method design and empirical validation. Specifically, the design is limited to polyps unlike previous works and also the evaluations that show marginal improvement to more basic methods that do not have similar complex design.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have addressed my main concerns of marginal improvement to baselines and generalization to other domains and hence I increased my score to Accept.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper proposes a training-free means to improve one-shot polyp segmentation, and demonstrates improved performance across multiple datasets.
They optimize a mask to be used as an input prompt to SAM2.The method takes as input a support image+mask (one-shot label), and a query image (unlabelled image). The method uses the support image to find a polyp-like mask in the query image that is then used for SAM2.The authors first calculate superpixels in the support image, and break them down into foreground+background. Afterwards they perform RWPM (reliability-weighted prototype-mining), and GAS (Geometric Adaptive threshold Selection).
(RWPM: weights regions based off contrast, and cycle consistency) By using the feature mean of each superpixel, they can downweight superpixels with low contrast (called RWPM) and poor cycle-consistency in matching (called reverse purity factor by authors).
(GAS: pick most polyp-like regions) Using the weighted support superpixels, they compute correlations to the query image. This mask is then thresholded, selecting round segments, and weighted by scale. (Geometric-Prior-based threshold selection).
Finally, they iteratively refine this estimate with SAM2, by repeatedly using the refined mask to prompt SAM2.
They show improved performance on Kvasir, CVC-ClinicDB, CVC-ColonDB, and PolypGen, and perform comprehensive ablation.
reviews.text_strengths: The authors present a training-free way to achieve better polyp segmentation, and demonstrate strong results across the board by better managing specularity and priors we know about polyps.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper could be improved for readability; I had to read it over multiple times to understand some concepts.
Long-term viability: The paper is addressing binary mask generation for use as input to SAM2.This causes ‘information loss’ in a way since we are only able to feed in binary mask pixels. This adaptation is necessary since the mask input is an ‘API’ SAM2 provides, rather than addressing the problem in a clean way (ie. learning a prototype feature embedder, and feeding that into SAM). The new SAMv3 seems to address this issue directly, by enabling exemplar prompting, so I am wary of the long-term applicability of bespoke designs like the prompt mask estimation in this paper if the piece they depend on (SAM2->SAM3) could solve the underlying problem.
This method does not carry to other non-polyp segmentation, since it uses multiple known priors about polyps (ie. roundness). This point does not affect my review, since the authors note this is a method for polyp segmentation, but it would be interesting to think about how these filters would work for other types of segmentation.
Minor changes:
“To enhance spatial consistency and reduce noise, we apply N iterations of a self-diffusion mechanism[11], updating Hinit by Hinit = Hinit · (fq · fq⊤)k.” This is not diffusion, and diffusion is not mentioned in [11]. This is iterative refinement. Please clarify, and provide more details here.
Clean up and simplify the math wherever possible, at points the paper can be hard to read when reading it for the first time. Some ways to do so: list dimensions of each variable; remove terms if only used once; provide human-readable definitions for all important variables when using them.
Fig.1: Letters (a,b) used for multiple purposes: both for left/right and for sub-images of pixel regions. Please use letters and numbers or some other mix to disambiguate.
Fig 2.I recommend to emphasize the SLIC superpixels as their boundaries in the inset (after SLIC) are hard to see.
R_k estimates cycle consistency of sorts. I would select a more clear term here than reverse purity factor. Please refer to work in point matching, since this is a common concept there.
ReLUs (Why are ReLus being used?) C_k still has contrast even if the difference is negative. Please explain this selection, and why a non-linearity is chosen.
“Intrinsic Reliability (Contrast Factor) and Query-specific Relevance (Reverse Purity Factor)” Please select a single term, and remove the parentheticals terms for your Contrast Factor (a) and Reverse Purity Factor (ie. cycle-consistency) (b); otherwise it requires the reader to juggle too many terms at once. Alternatively, rather than using parenthetical terms, define each of (a,b) in clear, easy-to-understand language.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Although the paper is a bit hard to read, it still addresses a clear need. The authors demonstrate improved results on polyp segmentation without requiring any training across the board.
The weakness of my accept comes down to the clarity of the paper, alongside the long-term viability of bespoke schemes for one-shot segmentation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Authors have responded to my primary concerns.

Paper enhances over training-free one-shot segmentation by accounting for regional heterogeneity in support images.

N/A
