meta_reviews.text:
This paper proposes RPG-SAM, a training-free one-shot segmentation framework for polyp detection using foundation models, specifically SAM2.The motivation is to address limitations in existing SAM-based one-shot pipelines, which rely on uniform assumptions about support features and fixed thresholding for prompt generation.
This is a solid, well-engineered system with meaningful improvements in a practical setting. However, novelty is incremental and theoretical depth is limited.
Also, the paper has many unclear points and concerns that can be discussed during a rebuttal period.

concerns were addressed, reviewers all agree with the acceptance.

RPG-SAM presents a well-engineered, training-free, one-shot segmentation framework that leverages SAM2 to successfully resolve regional and response feature heterogeneities in polyp detection. The authors’ rebuttal successfully countered the initial concerns regarding limited domain generalizability and marginal baseline improvements by introducing out-of-domain evaluation on the CHAOS-CT dataset ($+6.3\%$ IoU gain over ProtoSAM) and validating strong statistical significance ($p < 0.001$) alongside reduced computational latency ($0.18$s vs. $0.89$s).
three accept after rebuttal, i agree.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank all reviewers and the AC for their constructive comments. We are encouraged that the reviewers recognized the importance of training-free one-shot medical segmentation, the clarity of our motivation, and the effectiveness of our ablation studies. We address the major concerns below.
1)@R1 @R2: Generalization beyond polyp segmentation.
Although motivated by polyp segmentation, RPG-SAM’s core modules (reliability-weighted prototype mining, background suppression, adaptive thresholding, and iterative SAM refinement) are not limited to colonoscopy. On non-polyp CHAOS-CT, using 20 slices sequentially as one-shot supports with unchanged hyperparameters, RPG-SAM achieves Dice 77.63±5.74 and IoU 71.41±6.14, outperforming ProtoSAM (71.33±4.45 / 65.41±5.82; both p<0.001). This supports cross-domain generalization beyond polyp-specific morphology.
2)@R1: Marginal improvement, statistical significance, overengineering, and computational cost.
We respectfully argue the gain is not marginal. Across Table 1 datasets, RPG-SAM averages 74.61±8.14 Dice and 67.87±7.77 IoU, compared with ProtoSAM’s 70.07±8.65 and 62.44±8.42 (+4.54 Dice and +5.43 IoU). Under a 30-support-slice Kvasir setting, RPG-SAM obtains 75.84±11.33 Dice and 68.90±11.08 IoU, versus ProtoSAM’s 59.21±13.37 and 50.59±13.64 (both p<0.001), showing robustness to support choice. RPG-SAM is also more efficient: 3.5 GB and 0.18 s per prediction versus 6.9 GB and 0.89 s for ProtoSAM.
3)@R2: Long-term viability in the context of SAMv3.Training-free methods remain valuable in medical imaging because they avoid task-specific optimization, large annotations, and retraining across datasets. Although learning a dedicated prototype embedder may be cleaner, it requires training and thus falls outside our training-free one-shot setting. We agree SAMv3 exemplar prompting is relevant; on Kvasir, SAMv3 reaches Dice 75.26 and IoU 69.77, still below RPG-SAM (85.65 and 78.65), suggesting that medical-specific reliability modeling and query-adaptive priors remain useful.
4)@R2: Clarification of “self-diffusion”
We agree the term is misleading. This step is not generative diffusion but affinity-based iterative heatmap refinement. After Hinit is obtained, a query-query affinity matrix is computed from DINOv2 features, and Hinit is propagated over this graph so feature-similar pixels reinforce each other while isolated activations are suppressed. We will revise “self-diffusion mechanism” to “affinity-based iterative heatmap refinement”.
5) @R2: Why ReLU is used in the contrast and reverse-purity terms.
ReLU acts as a reliability gate. For C_k, a negative value means the foreground prototype is closer to support background than foreground; keeping it would introduce unstable negative weights. For R_k, a negative value means reverse matches fall inside the support foreground less often than expected by the foreground area ratio, i.e., no better than chance. ReLU thus suppresses unreliable/non-consistent prototypes.
5)@R1 @R2: Readability, variables, figures, and minor changes.
We will simplify notation, reduce variables, list key tensor dimensions, clarify Fig. 1 and Fig. 2, and use clearer terminology.
6)@R3: Detection and classification under clinical uncertainty.
Our work focuses on training-free one-shot binary segmentation to reduce annotation dependence. It’s an important task, as also pursued by recent works such as OPSAM [11] . The reviewer’s suggestion on image quality, bowel preparation, polyp type, morphology, and size is highly valuable, and we will consider these factors in future stratified analyses and joint detection-segmentation-classification workflows.

title: RT-Super: Learning Tumor Segmentation from Longitudinal Images and Reports
abstract: Multi-tumor segmentation is important for early cancer detection and allows radiologists to visualize, verify, and understand AI predictions. However, tumor segmentation masks are expensive, time-consuming, and unavailable for many tumor types in public data. Instead, hospitals have vast, readily-available data that can guide segmentation: radiology reports and longitudinal images with multiple contrast phases. We use this readily-available data to substitute for tumor masks in training AI for tumor segmentation. To this end, we propose a new architecture, RT-Super. It has a teacher network, which analyzes the patient’s longitudinal images and reports to create high-quality tumor masks. These masks train a student network, which sees a single image and no report. In inference, when longitudinal images and reports are unavailable, we use the student. RT-Super uses a new CNN-Transformer architecture and novel Consistency Losses that exploit tumors location consistency across longitudinal images. We train RT-Super to segment esophagus, uterus and spleen tumors, which have few or no public masks. Even without training masks, RT-Super can segment these tumors and surpass public AI models. Overall, we demonstrate that learning from longitudinal images, multi-phase images, and reports can overcome mask scarcity and advance multi-cancer detection and segmentation. Code: https://github.com/MrGiovanni/RT-Super

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes TR-Distillation, a teacher-student/self-distillation framework for multi-cancer tumor detection and segmentation under severe mask scarcity. The teacher uses radiology/pathology report attributes together with longitudinal and multi-phase CT scans, while the student is trained to infer from a single image without reports, which is the clinically practical deployment setting. The work also introduces a report-aware transformer that generates convolutional kernels, inter-image cross-attention across scans, and a longitudinal consistency loss. In addition, the paper assembles a sizable internal dataset of 5,000 CT scans with reports focused on tumor types that lack public segmentation masks: esophagus, spleen, and uterus tumors.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper addresses a highly relevant and practical problem: most hospitals have abundant reports and serial imaging but very limited voxel-wise tumor masks. The proposed training/inference asymmetry is therefore well motivated clinically: rich context is used only at training time, while inference remains feasible from a single scan. 
2.The paper presents strong internal empirical results. In Table 1, the full TR-Distillation model achieves the best overall detection F1 among methods trained on the authors’ dataset and clearly outperforms the public baselines reported in the paper. The ablation labeled “non-longitudinal” also suggests that the longitudinal/multi-phase training signal contributes measurably beyond report supervision alone. 
3.The work has clear translational value because it targets tumor types for which public segmentation resources are scarce, and it explicitly studies both the no-mask and few-mask regimes. That makes the contribution more meaningful than a purely incremental accuracy improvement on an already saturated benchmark.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The main novelty is somewhat integrative rather than foundational. Report-based supervision for segmentation is already present in R-Super [2], report/image representation learning is already explored through CLIP-style and vision-language approaches [7,18], the student backbone is MedFormer [11], dynamic kernel selection is explicitly inspired by Dynamic Convolution [10], and registration is built on UniGradIcon [20]. The paper’s real novelty is the combination of these ideas with longitudinal/multi-phase information, which is meaningful, but the manuscript occasionally presents the advance more broadly than the evidence supports. 
2.The ablation study is not deep enough to isolate where the gains actually come from. The paper shows a non-longitudinal ablation, but it does not disentangle the impact of: report-aware kernel generation, inter-image cross-attention, consistency loss, LLM-extracted attributes, and the use of pathology information. Without such decomposition, it is difficult to judge which proposed component is essential and which is incidental. 
3.The evaluation section lacks critical detail, especially for segmentation. The manuscript reports Dice scores, but the description of the test set emphasizes detection labels from reports/pathology and does not clearly explain how the segmentation ground truth on the test cohort was obtained, how many test masks exist, who annotated them, or whether there was any quality control or inter-rater assessment. This is an important omission for a segmentation paper. 
4.The paper is also limited by single-system internal validation. All training and testing data come from the same hospital system/state, so the claims of robustness and broad clinical applicability remain unproven. Given that reporting style, scanner protocols, contrast timing, and follow-up practices can vary substantially across institutions, an external validation set would materially strengthen the work. 
5.Some of the public-model comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples. For example, Merlin and MedGemma are used through report generation for tumor detection rather than through a segmentation setting aligned with the proposed task. These comparisons are still interesting, but they are less convincing than the same-data comparisons against R-Super, segmentation, CLIP, and related baselines.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

My overall score is driven by the combination of strong practical motivation, a well-designed and clinically plausible training/inference setup, and convincing internal gains over the baselines presented in the manuscript. I find the idea of using longitudinal scans and reports as training-only supervision for a single-image student to be both useful and timely. At the same time, I am holding the paper back from a stronger accept because the novelty is partly integrative, the ablations are not sufficiently granular, and the experimental section leaves important questions unanswered about segmentation ground truth and external generalization. On balance, I think the paper is above the bar, but only marginally so, and I would expect the rebuttal to clarify the evaluation protocol and novelty positioning.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I am changing my recommendation to Reject after the rebuttal. The author response contains multiple new/additional experimental results, which are explicitly not allowed by the MICCAI rebuttal rules.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents TR-Distillation, a self-distillation framework for multi-tumor CT segmentation that replaces expensive voxel-level tumor masks with readily available hospital data—radiology reports, pathology reports, longitudinal images, and multi-phase contrast images. The teacher network is a hybrid CNN-Transformer that ingests all available patient data (reports and longitudinal/multi-phase scans) to produce pseudo-masks via a report-aware cross-attention mechanism and a dynamic convolutional kernel bank (soft mixture-of-experts style). The student network, which is embedded as a subnetwork of the teacher (self-distillation), operates on a single image without reports at inference. A novel Consistency Loss enforces spatial alignment of tumor predictions across longitudinal scans. The framework is trained on 5,000 CT scans with reports covering esophagus, spleen, and uterus tumors—three types that lack public segmentation masks—and demonstrates substantial improvements over public AI models (MedGemma, Merlin, ULS) and several weakly/semi-supervised baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Clinically grounded motivation and problem formulation. The observation that radiologists routinely consult longitudinal scans, multi-phase images, and prior reports when delineating tumors is compelling. The paper translates this clinical workflow into a principled teacher-student framework where the teacher mimics the radiologist’s information-rich setting and the student mimics the information-poor setting at first diagnosis. The focus on esophagus, spleen, and uterus tumors—which currently lack public segmentation masks—addresses a genuine gap in the field.
2.Novel and technically interesting architecture. The report-aware transformer that dynamically generates convolutional kernels is a creative design. Specifically, the use of a learnable bank of M = 16 candidate 3×3×3 kernels combined via softmax-weighted mixture (Sec. 2.1, page 5) avoids the computational cost of directly generating large kernels, while still allowing report-conditioned feature refinement. The self-distillation design—where the student is physically embedded within the teacher—is efficient and avoids maintaining two separate networks.
3.Comprehensive comparison against public models. The evaluation includes public foundation models (MedGemma, Merlin) and a dedicated lesion segmentation model (ULS), in addition to multiple training paradigms (CLIP, multi-task learning, Models Genesis, Report Supervision, standard supervised segmentation). The +49% average F1-score improvement over the best public model (Table 1) is substantial.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Vague and ambiguous dataset description.
The dataset description in Section 3 is insufficiently precise for a methodological paper and raises several unresolved questions. The text states: “5,000 CT scans paired radiology reports and pathology reports, including esophagus, spleen and uterus tumors, 100 longitudinal CT scans.” It is unclear whether the 100 longitudinal CT scans are a subset of the 5,000 or an additional set, yielding 5,100 total scans. Similarly, the paper mentions “100 multi-phase scans” on page 2 but does not clarify their relationship to the 5,000.The two training variants are described as: TR-Distillation† using 5,000 image–report pairs, and TR-Distillation using 5,000 image–report pairs plus 100 image-mask pairs. But how exactly are the 100 longitudinal scans incorporated during training? Are they always included in both variants? How many of the 5,000 scans contain tumors versus being non-tumor controls? What is the per-organ breakdown of the training set? Without these details, it is difficult to assess the experimental setup or reproduce the work.
2.Unclear and potentially unfair baseline training settings.
Closely related to the vague dataset description, the training conditions for baseline methods are not clearly specified, making it difficult to assess whether comparisons are fair. Table 1 marks each method’s use of “longi.” (longitudinal), “report,” and “mask” columns, but the actual number of training samples used by each baseline is never stated explicitly. For instance, it appears from context that methods marked with “report” and “mask” (e.g., R-Super, CLIP, Multi-task learning) may use reports and 100 masks, but do they all have access to the same 5,000 image–report pairs? Methods like Models Genesis and the supervised segmentation baseline appear to use only 100 masks without reports—but do they also train on the remaining ~4,900 unlabeled images in any capacity (e.g., self-supervised pre-training)? The classification baseline is marked only with “report” but its training procedure is barely described. Without explicit, per-baseline specification of how many images, reports, and masks each method uses, the reader cannot determine whether performance differences are attributable to the proposed architecture or to differences in data volume and supervision type. This is especially concerning because TR-Distillation leverages 5,000 reports plus longitudinal data plus multi-phase data—potentially a much richer supervisory signal than what baselines receive. The authors should provide a clear table specifying the exact training data (number of images, reports, masks, longitudinal pairs) used by each method.
3.Dice scores reported only in the table caption, not in the body text.
The table caption for Table 1 reports Dice scores: “TR-Distillation: 35 average; 37 spleen; 68 esophagus; 71 uterus. TR-Distillation†: 17 average; 7 spleen; 27 esophagus; 25 uterus. R-Super (best baseline): 30 average, 36 spleen, 21 esophagus, 34 uterus.” However, these Dice scores do not appear anywhere in the body text of Section 3 or elsewhere in the paper. They are also absent from Table 1 itself, which only shows sensitivity (Se), specificity (Sp), and F1-score columns. This is problematic for several reasons. Dice is the standard metric for segmentation quality, and yet it is relegated to a caption with no discussion, no statistical analysis, and no comparison against all baselines. The Dice values themselves are notably low (e.g., 35 average for TR-Distillation, 7 spleen Dice for TR-Distillation†), which warrants discussion. Are these values computed only on true-positive cases? Over all cases including non-tumor controls? The omission of Dice from both the main table and the body text is a significant gap for a segmentation paper.
4.Insufficient ablation study.
The paper presents a single ablation that removes longitudinal/multi-phase training entirely (Table 1, bottom row). For an architecture with at least five novel or adapted components—(i) the Consistency Loss, (ii) report cross-attention, (iii) inter-image cross-attention, (iv) dynamic kernel generation via the soft MoE bank, and (v) soft vs. hard distillation targets—a single ablation is inadequate. Without isolating each component, we cannot determine whether the Consistency Loss actually helps, whether the dynamic kernel bank outperforms standard convolutions, or whether soft distillation targets contribute meaningfully. A systematic ablation table (removing one component at a time) is standard for multi-component methodological papers and is essential here.
W5.Teacher performance is never reported.
The entire framework rests on the premise that the teacher, with access to reports and longitudinal data, produces high-quality pseudo-masks that effectively train the student. Yet the teacher’s segmentation performance is never evaluated anywhere in the paper. This is a significant omission for two reasons: (1) it is impossible to assess the quality of the pseudo-masks that drive learning, and (2) the “distillation gap” (teacher performance minus student performance) remains unknown. If the teacher’s masks are poor, the student cannot be expected to learn well; if the teacher significantly outperforms the student, there may be room for improvement in the distillation mechanism. Reporting teacher Dice scores alongside student scores is essential for validating the core mechanism.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses a well-motivated and important problem—learning tumor segmentation from readily available hospital data rather than expensive masks—and proposes a technically interesting architecture. However, several fundamental issues prevent confident acceptance: (1) the dataset description is too vague to fully understand the experimental setup; (2) the training conditions for baselines are unclear, raising concerns about fairness of comparisons; (3) Dice scores—the primary segmentation metric—appear only in a table caption with no discussion or full reporting; (4) the ablation study is too coarse to attribute performance to specific components of a multi-component system; and (5) the teacher’s performance is never reported, leaving the core distillation mechanism unvalidated. Addressing these issues—by providing precise dataset and training details, equalizing and documenting data access across baselines, fully reporting and discussing Dice scores, adding component-wise ablations, and reporting teacher performance—would substantially strengthen the paper.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Although I still have concerns about the paper’s clarity, its motivation and methodology are quite attractive, and my major concerns about the dataset description and ablation studies have been addressed. So I move towards an accept.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: In clinical practice, diagnostic and treatment decisions are typically based on longitudinal imaging, culminating in radiology and pathology reports rather than the availability of precise 3D segmentation masks. This paper demonstrates that such realistically available outputs can be effectively leveraged to train improved models, compared to approaches that do not utilize this information.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper is clearly motivated by real clinical practice. It designs experiments that demonstrate the value of leveraging additional data sources that are often more readily available than clean segmentation masks or classification labels. This is valuable for guiding data curation strategies, as the proposed setting better reflects real clinical conditions, including longitudinal imaging, radiology reports, and pathology reports at the patient level.
2.The paper provides clear explanations at each step and is transparent about its core technical components, such as the loss functions used, how ground-truth labels are handled when available, and the use of MedFormer as the backbone. The technical details are also well motivated, including what information is extracted from existing reports and how it is incorporated into the model.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The overall Dice scores remain relatively low (ranging from 30–70 in Table 1), which raises concerns about practical performance. In addition, the presentation is somewhat unclear, as the Dice metric is only described in the table caption rather than being explicitly labeled within the table itself.
2.The segmentation baselines and comparisons appear limited. The evaluation includes only three methods, two of which are based on TR-Distillation, resulting in a lack of diversity in comparison. It would strengthen the paper to include more established baselines, such as MedFormer and nnU-Net trained with the full set of 100 labeled samples.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The concerns raised in the weaknesses do not diminish the overall value of the paper. However, addressing and clarifying these points would strengthen the work and could justify a higher rating. The paper is particularly compelling in terms of its motivation and the results it demonstrates; the narrative is well connected and largely convincing. Moreover, it offers an insightful perspective on how to mitigate the challenges of curating segmentation masks in real-world clinical settings.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I will keep my decision as accept, since the authors added additional results using nn-UNet, which was previously missing as an important segmentation baseline. They also improved the presentation of the results by moving the Dice scores into the table, making the comparisons clearer and more effective.

meta_reviews.text:
Please answer the concerns raised by the three reviewers in the rebuttal, especially on training settings, ablation study, segmentation performance and more baselines, and dataset description.

The paper presents a valuable method to learn tumor segmentation from longitudinal CT and radiology reports. The authors’ rebuttal further added important baselines, ablation studies, dataset, method and experimental clarifications. Two reviewers recommended acceptance. Although R1 pointed out that MICCAI does not allow new results in rebuttal, I think the paper represents a contribution that is attractive to the MICCAI community.

The core idea of teacher-student distillation to address the problem of severe label scarcity for segmentation was seen as interesting by all three reviewers. The authors addressed most of reviewers’ concerns although concerns regarding the clarity of the dataset and completeness of experiments. Authors added new experiments, which are not allowed according to the MICCAI rules. It would be better if the authors kept the additional experiments to bare minimum needed (e.g. nnU-Net) and instead address concerns in the discussion.

After reviewing the comments and the authors’ responses, I find that most concerns have been addressed. Overall, the paper is in good shape for acceptance. I recommend accepting the submission, while encouraging the authors to incorporate the reviewers’ suggestions carefully when preparing the final version.

title: S2DLight: Single Step Diffusion Network via Degradation-Aware Adaptation for Surgical Endoscopic Image Low-Light Enhancement
abstract: Surgical endoscopy inherently involves constrained lighting conditions, which can obscure fine anatomical structures. Consequently, low-light image enhancement (LLIE) is crucial for improving visual clarity and structural discernibility. Recent diffusion-based methods improve restoration quality but are typically trained from scratch on small medical datasets, limiting their ability to exploit broader visual priors. Large-scale pretrained text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models encode powerful generative knowledge, yet directly applying them to surgical LLIE suffers from mismatched visual characteristics and high inference cost. We propose S2DLight, a single-step latent restoration framework built on a Stable Diffusion backbone for endoscopic LLIE. We introduce Degradation-Aware Adaptation to provide image-specific low-light guidance via contrastive degradation representations, and reformulate iterative sampling into one forward latent prediction to improve efficiency. To compensate for removing progressive refinement, we incorporate Latent Structural Augmentation, and further mitigate training-inference prompt mismatch using Training-Time Semantic Alignment. Experiments on public endoscopic benchmarks demonstrate that S2DLight achieves state-of-the-art performance while reducing the computational burden associated with large-scale diffusion inference.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: S2DLight introduces a single-step diffusion framework specifically tailored for surgical endoscopic image enhancement. By integrating Stable Diffusion pre-trained priors into the medical imaging domain, it systematically addresses the bottlenecks of conventional diffusion models in surgical contexts, such as slow inference, mismatched visual features, and the absence of semantic guidance.
reviews.text_strengths: The core strength of S2DLight lies in its systematic adaptation of large-scale pre-trained T2I diffusion models (Stable Diffusion) for surgical endoscopic enhancement. It ingeniously addresses the clinical bottleneck of slow inference through single-step reformulation, while integrating degradation-aware adaptation and semantic alignment to bridge the domain gap between medical and natural imagery. This framework provides a practical and efficient solution for deploying diffusion models within real-time surgical workflows.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The manuscript does not explicitly explain the rationale for why using a trained degradation estimation network is more effective at capturing low-light characteristics. 
2.Regarding the training of the Degradation Estimation Network, the paper utilizes two patches from the same low-light image as positive pairs and patches from other images as negative samples for contrastive training. However, there is no explanation justifying this specific approach. What is the underlying rationale for this contrastive learning method? What specific problem is it intended to address, and how or why does this training enable the model to resolve such issues?
3.The single-step diffusion mentioned in the paper appears to resemble the DDIM (Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models) algorithm. Could the authors clarify the distinctions between the proposed method and DDIM, as well as its specific advantages?
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

While the paper demonstrates a substantial amount of work, several modules are insufficiently explained.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The modules still lack interpretability and innovation.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose S2DLight, a low-light image enhancement (LLIE) method for restoring surgical endoscopic images that reuses a pre-trained text-to-image Stable Diffusion model, introducing intermediate adaptations and LoRA-based tuning. The experiments show clear quantitative improvements over the state of the art (SOTA) while maintaining competitive inference times for near-real-time applications.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper is very well written, featuring a clearly explained methodology, excellent visualizations of the processing pipeline, and thorough qualitative evaluations and comparisons. The method addresses a real-world problem with well-posed motivation, the ablation study effectively justifies the pipeline’s design choices, and the authors commendably retrain a non-surgical LLIE method to ensure a fair comparison.
reviews.text_weaknesses: While the quantitative results show a significant improvement over SOTA, the qualitative evaluation doesn’t really show differences or improvements over existing methods, such as LighTDiff or DiffLL, raising the question whether the additional computational costs and longer inference time are justified for the visual quality improvements. Reusing a pre-trained diffusion model but adapting it for single-pass inference raises the question of why a simpler, inherently non-diffusion-based approach was not used instead. Additionally, while the ablation study shows that Latent Structural Augmentation successfully bypasses the need for iterative refinement and improves performance, the paper does not demonstrate the performance difference between using standard diffusion refinement versus relying solely on this augmentation.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1.What is the primary motivation for using a diffusion model if inference is ultimately performed in a single iteration?
2.Since generating training data via [6] alters colors, how does the model perform in real-world settings where colors are not distorted by gamma transformations?
3.Finally, how would the model perform if the degradation embedding branch (DENet) were removed or replaced with a fixed embedding?

While the method is well-motivated and demonstrates quantitative improvements, the lack of noticeable qualitative enhancements over existing methods does not currently justify the increased computational cost of a diffusion-based approach, making the overall benefit marginal.

With Degradation-Aware Adaptation, Single-Step Reformulation, and Training-Time Semantic Alignment, it improves enhancement quality while significantly cutting inference cost.
reviews.text_strengths: This paper addresses surgical endoscopic low-light image enhancement, a task with clear clinical relevance, by proposing S2DLight, a single-step diffusion framework. The overall framework is well designed and clearly problem-driven, and it effectively tackles several key challenges in adapting pretrained text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models to the medical domain, including domain discrepancy, inference efficiency, and semantic-conditioning inconsistency. The comparative experiments and ablation studies on public datasets are sufficiently thorough and provide solid evidence for the effectiveness of the proposed method. Particularly commendable is the Single-Step Reformulation, which significantly reduces inference cost while largely preserving enhancement quality, making the method not only technically interesting but also promising for practical applications.
reviews.text_weaknesses: Although the paper reports strong quantitative results on the relevant datasets, it still has several limitations. First, the method is evaluated only on EndoVis17/18 and has not been validated in real clinical low-light scenarios. Second, no downstream tasks are included, which makes the clinical applicability of the method less convincing.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper proposes a single step Stable Diffusion based framework for low light enhancement of surgical endoscopic images, using degradation aware conditioning, latent structural augmentation, and training time semantic alignment to improve quality and speed. The reviewers noted the promising performance but raised several important limitations. First, the methodological motivation remains unclear, particularly the rationale for the degradation estimation network, the contrastive learning design, and the distinction between the proposed single step formulation and existing DDIM style diffusion methods. Second, there is a disconnect between the strong quantitative gains and the qualitative examples, making it unclear whether the improvements translate into visibly meaningful enhancement or justify the computational complexity of a large diffusion backbone. Third, the experimental validation is limited to synthetic low light degradation on EndoVis17 and EndoVis18, without evaluation on real clinical low light scenarios or downstream surgical tasks, which weakens the practical and clinical claims. Decision is rebuttal.

After rebuttal, I recommend accept decision. The reviewers agree that the paper addresses a relevant surgical image enhancement problem with strong quantitative results, fair comparisons, and useful ablation studies. The main concerns relate to novelty, interpretability of individual modules, qualitative improvement over existing LLIE methods, and limited clinical/downstream validation. The rebuttal provides reasonable clarification of the distinction from DDIM, the motivation for transferring Stable Diffusion priors rather than using iterative sampling, and the role of DENet and contrastive degradation learning. While the lack of real clinical low-light validation and downstream task evaluation remains as limitations, these issues are adequately acknowledged and do not outweigh the methodological contribution and experimental evidence. As a result, the decision is accept.

Orignally 4-4-3.where the 3 was the only reviewer with post-rebuttal interaction, and remained the reject. Having carefully looked at the reviews, the rebuttal and the paper, I feel that this is the most borderline case I have seen so far. Reviewers rightfully point out the lack of thorough clinical evaluation, but also see the technical merit. I would give this paper the benefit of the doubt.

After the rebuttal, R1 maintained a Reject recommendation, R3 maintained an Accept recommendation, while R2, who initially provided a Weak Accept recommendation, did not provide an updated review. Although the paper demonstrates some strengths, including promising experimental results, it also exhibits several fundamental limitations.
First, as noted by both R1 and R3, the proposed model was evaluated only on synthetic low-light data, leaving its real-world clinical utility unclear. While collecting paired low-light and normal-light clinical data may be challenging, it would still be feasible to collect low-light clinical data and provide qualitative or quantitative results to better assess the model’s practical performance.
Second, the rebuttal does not fully address R2’s concern regarding the necessity of the diffusion-based design. As stated in the rebuttal, the proposed framework neither starts from Gaussian noise nor recursively denoises latent representations, but instead operates as a single-step latent restoration framework using Stable Diffusion priors. This raises the question of whether a simpler denoising autoencoder, initialized with pretrained Stable Diffusion components, could achieve similar performance with a more straightforward design and justification.
Considering these concerns, the paper is not recommended for acceptance. The authors are encouraged to address the reviewers’ comments when revising the paper for submission elsewhere.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank all reviewers for their constructive and insightful comments. We appreciate their recognition of the relevance, motivation, and experimental quality of S2DLight. The comments are valuable for improving the clarity of our manuscript. For clarity, W denotes weakness items and C denotes optional comments.
[Common questions]
[R1-W3, R2-W2/C1] Motivation for diffusion and difference from DDIM
R: Our goal is not iterative sampling, but transferring pretrained Stable Diffusion priors to surgical LLIE, where medical data are limited. S2DLight differs from DDIM. DDIM follows a scheduled reverse trajectory. In contrast, S2DLight treats the encoded low-light latent as a degraded state at a fixed timestep and restores it in one forward pass. It neither starts from Gaussian noise nor recursively denoises the latent. Thus, S2DLight is a single-step latent restoration framework using SD priors, not a DDIM sampler.
[R1-W1/W2, R2-C3] DENet and contrastive degradation learning
R: DENet provides image-specific degradation guidance. Low-light degradation varies across frames due to illumination, exposure, noise, and tissue appearance; thus a fixed embedding cannot adapt to different degradation severity. In contrastive learning, patches from the same low-light image are positives because they share similar degradation, while patches from different images are negatives because their degradation statistics usually differ. This encourages degradation-related cues and suppresses local anatomy-specific information. Removing DENet or using fixed embedding would reduce the model to a generic prompt-conditioned enhancer.
[R2-C2, R3-W1/W2] Synthetic degradation, clinical validation, and downstream tasks
R: We agree that real clinical low-light data and downstream evaluation would further strengthen the evidence. However, paired real low-light/normal-light surgical data are difficult to obtain, since collecting well-aligned pairs under different illumination settings in real procedures is challenging. Thus, synthetic paired protocols are commonly used in surgical LLIE for training and fair comparison. We will state this limitation, avoid over-claiming clinical deployment, and discuss real-data collection, unpaired/semi-supervised adaptation, and downstream tasks as future work.
[Reviewer-specific questions]
[R1] Modules insufficiently explained
R: We appreciate this comment and will better explain the modules: DENet provides image-specific degradation conditioning; contrastive learning separates degradation cues from anatomy; Single-Step Reformulation transfers SD priors without iterative sampling; and Latent Structural Augmentation compensates for reduced progressive refinement.
[R2-W3] Standard diffusion refinement vs proposed single-step design
R: The submitted manuscript includes 1/4/50-step comparisons, directly evaluating iterative refinement against our single-step design. Results show that S2DLight achieves better overall accuracy with much lower inference cost. This suggests that directly restoring the encoded low-light latent is more effective for surgical LLIE than repeated diffusion refinement, which may cause over-refinement or distribution drift.
[R2-W1] Limited qualitative improvement
R: We understand this concern. Differences between strong LLIE methods can be hard to observe due to limited figure size and fine endoscopic structures. We will add enlarged local regions. The consistent gains in PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS further support improved fidelity, structure preservation, and perceptual quality.
[R3-W2] Lack of downstream task evaluation
R: We agree that downstream tasks such as segmentation or instrument recognition would provide additional clinical evidence. This work focuses on surgical LLIE, and our experiments evaluate paired enhancement quality, efficiency, and component effectiveness. We will avoid over-claiming clinical deployment and include downstream validation as future work.

title: S2GAIN: Spatio-Spectral Guided Affinity Imputation Network for Alzheimer’s Disease Diagnosis with Incomplete Modality
abstract: Multimodal neuroimaging provides complementary information for early computer-aided diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). However, in clinical practice, modalities such as PET are often missing due to cost and accessibility constraints, hindering stable cross-modal inference. Existing approaches either synthesize the missing modality in the image domain, which may introduce artifacts and noise that interfere with classification, or perform feature-domain alignment and completion while emphasizing spatial consistency, making it difficult to handle MRI-PET heterogeneity in texture patterns and frequency components. Moreover, forcing unpredictable cross-modal components to fit can inject noise and degrade diagnosis. To address these issues, this paper proposes the Spatio-Spectral Guided Affinity Imputation Network (S²GAIN), which employs a cascaded dual-stream cross-modal interaction backbone and multi-stage lightweight imputers to infer missing PET features layer by layer. A spatio-spectral joint alignment strategy is introduced to apply contrastive constraints in both the spatial domain and the frequency-domain magnitude spectrum, improving heterogeneous representation alignment. An affinity-guided reliability-weighting mechanism is further designed to suppress noise propagation from uninferable components. Finally, image-domain reconstruction regularization is employed to improve consistency between imputed metabolic representations and PET. Experimental results on ADNI demonstrate that S²GAIN achieves superior and consistent performance under missing-modality settings.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The main contributions of this study are as follows.
First, to address missing PET data in Alzheimer’s disease diagnosis, the authors propose S²GAIN, a novel incomplete multimodal learning framework that progressively recovers PET representations from MRI in feature space, enabling stable diagnosis when PET is unavailable at inference.
Second, they introduce S²JA, a spatio-spectral joint alignment strategy that improves cross-modal representation alignment by enforcing consistency in both the spatial and frequency domains.
Third, an affinity-guided reliability weighting mechanism, AGRW, is developed to emphasize reliably predictable components while suppressing non-inferable noise from modality heterogeneity, thereby reducing noise propagation and enhancing robustness.
Finally, the method incorporates image-domain reconstruction regularization via a PET reconstruction branch to preserve spatial and metabolic texture consistency of deep metabolic features, making the completed representations both diagnostically informative and structurally consistent with real PET.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The methodological innovation is well targeted. The authors identify two critical limitations in existing missing-modality approaches and design corresponding solutions accordingly. First, most feature completion methods focus only on spatial-domain alignment, even though the discrepancy between MRI and PET lies not only in spatial structure but also in texture patterns and frequency components. Second, many studies implicitly assume that MRI can recover the full spectrum of PET information, whereas part of the metabolic information in PET is not reliably predictable from MRI; forcing such components to be fitted may introduce noise and further blur the classification boundary. To address these issues, the authors propose S2JA and AGRW. S2JA extends alignment from the spatial domain to a joint spatial-frequency framework by incorporating amplitude-spectrum constraints, while AGRW uses affinity to estimate the reliability of cross-modal completion, emphasizing more trustworthy correspondences and suppressing noise from inherently unpredictable components. The main novelty lies not merely in the use of FFT or weighting, but in a more refined modeling perspective: distinguishing how modality differences should be aligned and which components should not be forced to be learned. 
2.The experimental evaluation is convincing, particularly the cross-cohort validation. This is another major strength of the study. Many related works rely solely on splits within a single dataset, which may yield strong performance but provide limited evidence of robustness under distribution shift. In contrast, this study conducts a bidirectional cross-cohort evaluation on ADNI-1 and ADNI-2, training on one cohort and testing on the other, and then reversing the setting. This design is substantially more rigorous than conventional random splits and offers stronger evidence of generalization. The stronger experimental protocol, together with results that closely match the methodological motivation, makes the overall empirical support more compelling.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The applicability of the proposed method remains relatively narrow. Although the title claims to address the general problem of incomplete modalities, the study focuses primarily on a single missing-pattern setting, namely the availability of MRI with missing PET, and all experiments are conducted under this assumption. While this scenario is clinically meaningful, the paper does not establish whether the method would remain effective in more complex incomplete multimodal settings, such as simultaneous absence of multiple modalities or varying missing rates. The authors do acknowledge in the conclusion that future work should extend the framework to more challenging missing-modality scenarios. 
2.The reliability weighting mechanism still depends on supervision from real PET data. The idea of AGRW is reasonable, yet during training it requires the affinity between completed features and ground-truth PET features to generate reliability weights. In essence, this means that the mechanism still relies on the availability of true PET supervision at the training stage. Therefore, although effective under the current experimental setting, the paper does not clarify whether this module would retain the same advantage in scenarios where paired PET data are scarcer and supervision is weaker. 
3.The validation of completion quality is still not sufficiently direct. A central goal of this study is to recover PET representations from MRI, and the authors further introduce image-domain reconstruction regularization to encourage the completed representations to better approximate the metabolic distribution and structural consistency of real PET images. However, the experiments mainly report downstream classification results, together with ablation studies and parameter sensitivity analyses, without providing more direct evidence of completion quality, such as quantitative similarity metrics between completed and real PET or visual comparisons of representative cases. As a result, the current findings demonstrate more clearly that the method benefits classification, while offering less direct support for the claim that it produces more faithful PET representations. 
4.Although the paper compares the proposed method with several advanced missing-modality imputation approaches, it omits a particularly important baseline: a strong MRI-only classifier. Without reporting the performance of a model trained directly on MRI alone, using either a standard backbone such as ResNet or the paper’s own 3D Dense Block, it is difficult for readers to assess the absolute performance gain brought by the proposed cross-modal completion framework over a single-modality MRI setting.
5.Some writing issues are also present in the manuscript. On page 3, in Contribution 1, there is a missing space before “spectrum”. In Contribution 2, the ending period is missing. On page 6, after DfpetL, there should be a space following the period.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The primary reason for my Weak Accept recommendation is that this work proposes a relatively comprehensive and well-targeted solution to the practically important problem of missing PET data in Alzheimer’s disease diagnosis. Rather than simply combining existing modules, the method is designed to address two critical limitations of current missing-modality approaches. First, it extends cross-modal alignment from the spatial domain alone to a joint spatial-frequency modeling framework. Second, it introduces a reliability weighting mechanism to explicitly suppress noise propagation caused by components that are inherently difficult to infer from MRI. These designs show clear novelty and are well aligned with the problem setting. Furthermore, the paper adopts a bidirectional cross-cohort evaluation between ADNI-1 and ADNI-2.Compared with the common practice of using only within-dataset train/test splits, this setting provides stronger evidence of generalizability, making the experimental protocol itself more convincing.
However, I do not think the current evidence is sufficient to justify a stronger recommendation. First, the method is mainly validated under a single missing-modality pattern, namely MRI available and PET missing. Although the title suggests a broader incomplete-modality setting, the manuscript does not yet demonstrate the effectiveness of the method in more complex missing scenarios. Second, AGRW still relies on ground-truth PET supervision during training, and the paper does not clarify whether this mechanism would remain effective when paired PET data are more limited. Third, although the paper emphasizes that the proposed method can recover representations that are closer to real PET, the experiments mainly report downstream classification performance. More direct evidence on the quality of modality completion is still missing, such as similarity analysis against ground-truth PET, representative visualizations, or comparison with a stronger MRI-only baseline.
As a result, while the paper provides reasonably strong evidence that the proposed method improves classification performance, it offers less direct empirical support for the claim that it more faithfully recovers PET representations. In addition, the manuscript contains several minor writing and formatting issues, suggesting that the overall presentation could be further improved.
Overall, I believe this work shows promising novelty and potential practical value, and it is worthy of publication. However, since the experimental validation and supporting arguments are not yet fully comprehensive, Weak Accept is the most appropriate recommendation at this stage.

author_feedback_text:
Reviewer 1.Thank you for the suggestion. We selected λ1, λ2, λ3, α, and β for sensitivity analysis because they directly correspond to the three core objectives of S²GAIN, i.e., S²JA, AGRW, and R², and control the balance between spatial and spectral alignment. Thus, they are the most relevant objective-level hyperparameters. We agree that other factors, such as temperature τ, stage number L, imputer capacity, and PET decoder configuration, are also worth studying. However, they are mostly internal or structural hyperparameters, and changing them would affect model capacity, computation, and memory simultaneously. Due to the page limit, we prioritized the loss-related parameters and will study more settings in future extended work. We also thank the reviewer for pointing out the layout issue of Table 2.
Reviewer 2.Thank you for the comments. We agree that this work focuses on the clinically common setting where MRI is available but PET is missing. MRI is generally more accessible and less costly, whereas PET is more likely to be absent due to cost, equipment requirements, and radioactive tracers. Thus, our goal is to impute PET-related latent representations from MRI for PET-missing AD diagnosis. More complex cases, such as multiple missing modalities, different missing patterns, or varying missing rates, are not covered here. We will explore them in future extended work, e.g., missing both fMRI and PET after introducing additional modalities.
Regarding AGRW, we agree that it uses real PET features during training. Our method follows a supervised cross-modal imputation setting: paired MRI-PET data are used to learn the MRI-to-PET mapping, while only MRI is required during PET-missing inference. AGRW does not remove PET supervision; instead, it uses the affinity between imputed and real PET features as a reliability weight to emphasize predictable cross-modal associations and suppress non-inferable components.
Regarding completion quality, we agree that similarity metrics or visual comparisons would provide more direct evidence. However, our goal is not PET image synthesis for visual inspection, but PET-related feature imputation for diagnosis. Thus, the current evaluation focuses on diagnostic performance, cross-cohort generalization, and module ablation. R² is an auxiliary regularizer rather than a standalone synthesis module; Table 3 shows that removing R² decreases performance, suggesting its benefit for structural consistency and diagnostic usefulness. The current results mainly support diagnostic effectiveness rather than pixel-level PET recovery. We will study direct completion metrics and visual comparisons in future extended work.
Regarding the MRI-only baseline, we agree that it is important. The current comparisons focus on incomplete-modality learning and imputation methods under a similar setting. Table 3 shows that removing S²JA, AGRW, or R² degrades performance, indicating that the gain is not solely from the backbone. Still, these ablations cannot replace a direct MRI-only baseline. Due to the page limit, this comparison is not included, and we will add it in future extended work. We also thank the reviewer for pointing out the writing issues.
Reviewer 3.Thank you for the important comment. We agree that diagnostic performance alone cannot fully demonstrate interpretability or modality-specific validity. In S²GAIN, S²JA constrains MRI/PET features in spatial and frequency domains; AGRW uses feature affinity to focus on PET-related components inferable from MRI; and R² encourages deep PET-related features to preserve image-domain spatial structure. These designs encourage PET-consistent representations, but do not fully establish interpretability or target-modality validity. The current experiments mainly show diagnostic usefulness, and we will further study interpretability and modality-specific validation in future extended work.

title: S3H-Net: Injecting Hybrid Semantic-Spatial Guidance via Superpixel Hypergraphs for Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Accurate segmentation of medical images remains a intricate challenge due to the complex geometry of target structures and their blurred boundaries. While recent approaches leverage topological and semantic information by introducing graph or hypergraph, they face two critical limitations: i) ﬁxed patch nodes inherently ignore object boundaries, causing semantic ambiguity by mixing heterogeneous features; and ii) restricting reasoning to bottlenecks or skip connections fails to fully inject global contexts for ﬁne-grained segmentation. To address these issues, we propose S3H-Net, a novel architecture that integrates Superpixel-based Semantic-Spatial Hypergraphs. Speciﬁcally, distinct from patch-based methods, we utilize a boundary-aware Simple Linear Iterative Clustering (SLIC) algorithm for node construction, encouraging contour-aware regional grouping and alleviating heterogeneous feature mixing. Furthermore, we design Hybrid Semantic-Spatial Hypergraph (HSSH) blocks to construct a parallel Semantic Encoder, which captures multi-scale high-order semantic guidance continuously. To explicitly bridge the semantic gap between the non-local hypergraph topology and local convolutional features, we introduce a Cross-Covariance Semantic Injection (CCSI) module. By exploiting inter-channel attention, this module eﬀectively injects the reasoned global context into local features for comprehensive semantic awareness. Extensive experiments on ﬁve medical imaging modalities demonstrate that S3H-Net signiﬁcantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Our code is available on GitHub.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper tackles the limitation of fixed patch-based nodes (e. g. , in hypergraph networks), which do not adequately account for object boundaries. It also addresses the issue of modeling global context only at bottlenecks or through skip connections. 
To this end, the authors propose an architecture that utilizes superpixel-based hypergraphs, where nodes are constructed using the boundary-aware SLIC superpixels algorithm. In addition, they introduce hybrid hypergraph blocks (HSSH) to build an encoder that continuously captures multi-scale, high-order semantic information. 
To bridge the semantic gap between hypergraph (global) and convolutional (local) features, the authors propose a CCSI module. The proposed architecture is evaluated across five medical imaging modalities and achieves strong performance.
reviews.text_strengths:
The authors effectively integrate multiple concepts and improvements to address several key challenges: (1) the complex geometry of target structures and their blurred boundaries, (2) the limitation of fixed patch-based nodes, which inherently ignore object boundaries, and (3) the restriction of global reasoning to bottlenecks or skip connections. 
To tackle these issues, they propose a set of complementary enhancements. Specifically, the architecture employs a dual-encoder design, where a CNN captures local features while a hypergraph encoder models global, high-order relationships. For node construction, the method leverages a boundary-aware and differentiable superpixel algorithm, enabling better alignment with object boundaries. Furthermore, the authors introduce an injection module to effectively fuse features from the two encoders. The authors also provide a link to the code.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The authors do not report the model complexity in terms of the number of parameters or FLOPs. This is particularly important given that the architecture employs two encoders, one of which is a hypergraph module that is typically computationally expensive.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

There are relatively few papers on hypergraph-based segmentation, and this work provides multiple contributions: (1) a dual-encoder architecture, including a hypergraph encoder; (2) a method that utilizes a boundary-aware node construction algorithm; and (3) a mechanism to fuse the two encoders while reducing the semantic gap.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The paper has a good contribution.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents a well-motivated and technically model that achieves strong empirical results across diverse medical imaging modalities. The main contributions are threefold: a boundary-aware SLIC algorithm that generates semantically pure nodes aligned with anatomical contours, a Hybrid Semantic-Spatial Hypergraph (HSSH) that captures high-order correlations through complementary semantic and spatial hyperedges, and a Cross-Covariance Semantic Injection (CCSI) module that bridges the gap between non-local topological reasoning and local spatial representations.
reviews.text_strengths:
(1) The boundary-aware SLIC is the most original contribution of the paper. Formulating the edge probability as a barrier integral (Eq. 1–2) yields an elegant and fully differentiable design that enforces strict boundary adherence at the node construction stage.
(2) The hybrid hypergraph construction, which combines FCM-based semantic hyperedges with dilated spatial hyperedges, is well-motivated and reasonable, albeit somewhat incremental relative to prior hypergraph designs.
(3) Comprehensive experiments across five medical imaging modalities demonstrate that S³H-Net consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with statistical significance testing further supporting the reliability of the improvements.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1)While the proposed framework demonstrates a certain degree of novelty as a whole, each of its major components is either an existing method or a straightforward extension thereof. In the superpixel module, although the introduction of boundary constraints via a composite-trapezoidal approximation of an edge-aware line-integral barrier shows some innovation, the overall architecture still follows the SSN framework. In the hypergraph reasoning module, the construction strategy is essentially a combination of two existing approaches (FCM-based semantic edges and dilated-window spatial edges). Similarly, the CCSI module closely resembles channel-wise co-attention, which has already been explored in existing works such as DuSFE[1], MA-Neck[2].
[1] “DuSFE: Dual-channel squeeze-fusion-excitation co-attention for cross-modality registration of cardiac SPECT and CT.” Medical image analysis 88 (2023): 102840.[2] “MA-Neck: Mutual attention-based feature enhancement for lightweight object detection.” Pattern Recognition (2025): 112254.
2) The choice of hyperparameters in the implementation section warrants further justification. In particular, the values λ_xy = 0.17 (SLIC compactness) and λ_b=0.5 (boundary sensitivity) are stated to be “set empirically” but without supporting evidence. It is unclear whether these values were determined through grid search, ablation studies, or simply adopted from prior work. A sensitivity analysis would strengthen the reproducibility of the method and help readers understand the robustness of performance to these settings. Relatedly, the number of sampled points K used in the trapezoidal approximation of the barrier integral (Eq. 2) is never specified.
3) The experiments section lacks a sensitivity analysis for the scale factor λ in the hybrid incidence matrix H=[H_sem||λ*H_spa]. Although the authors report λ=5 as an empirical choice, no evidence is provided to justify this value, and it is unclear how sensitive the model is to this balance between semantic and spatial hyperedges.
4) The paper would benefit from visualizations of the generated superpixels and the constructed hypergraphs overlayed on medical images. Such qualitative evidence is needed to substantiate the motivation presented in Fig. 1 that superpixels of anatomical boundaries are more faithfully than grid patches, and that the learned hyperedges capture meaningful high-order semantic correlations.
5) The overall presentation of the manuscript requires significant refinement. The writing style feels somewhat non-standard and repetitive, characterized by an over-reliance on “We”-led sentences. The authors are encouraged to revise the manuscript to achieve more varied sentence structures and to adopt more precise academic terminology. On the of Page 5 “Hypergraph Construction” reads: “…we employ the Fuzzy C-Means (FCM) algorithm inspired by [9]…”. References should not be used as grammatical components of the sentence. Phrasings such as “…in [1]…” or “Reference [1] states…” are not acceptable. The authors should rephrase such sentences and ensure proper reference formatting throughout the manuscript. A careful pass for English constructions, grammatical errors, and formatting inconsistencies is strongly recommended to improve overall presentation quality.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The proposed method appears to build mainly upon a combination of existing techniques. I will reconsider my evaluation based on the authors’ response.

2.The paper addresses a relevant problem in medical image segmentation. This is a challenging task with practical significance and a reasonable motivation, namely to handle the complex geometric shapes of the target structure and the ambiguous boundaries of these shapes.
3.The proposed network is logically designed. The experimental section is reasonably complete. The paper reports results on multiple public datasets and includes both ablation studies and a cross-dataset generalization experiment, which strengthens the empirical evaluation.
4.The method shows competitive performance against recent baselines, with consistent gains on the reported benchmarks. This suggests that the proposed design is effective in practice, even if the margins are not always large.
5.The contribution is presented in a fairly clear way. The roles of the main components are distinguishable, and the paper makes a concrete engineering contribution to biomedical image segmentation.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The overall methodological novelty appears somewhat limited. The motivations behind some modules are not discussed in much depth.
2.The main weakness is limited novelty. The proposed method is a combination of several familiar ideas. The integration is reasonable, but the methodological contribution feels incremental rather than fundamentally new. The work does not introduce fundamentally new modeling principles or theoretical insights.
3.Although the reported results are competitive, the margins over the strongest baselines are not always large. In some cases, the improvements are quite modest, raising questions about whether the improvements justify the additional architectural complexity, which makes it harder to judge how meaningful the gains are in practice.
4.The paper emphasizes segmentation accuracy but does not provide much information about model complexity, inference speed, or computational cost. Since the proposed framework introduces additional modules, it would be useful to report efficiency-related metrics such as the number of parameters, FLOPs, or inference time.

N/A

The paper addresses a relevant problem in medical segmentation and presents a technically reasonable model. The overall framework is coherent, and the results are generally competitive. However, the contribution is fairly incremental. The method combines several familiar ideas, and the paper does not fully show that the overall design represents a clear methodological advance rather than a careful integration of existing components.
The experimental section is adequate but not fully convincing. Although the paper includes ablations and cross-dataset evaluation, the improvements over strong baselines are sometimes small, and there is no reporting of variance, repeated runs, or statistical significance. This makes it difficult to judge the robustness of the claimed gains.
