reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces two structure-aware pre-evaluation metrics, SAM-Cluster and SAM-LP, for ranking WSI feature extractors (FEs) without running full MIL training. The central idea is to use SAM-derived region masks as pseudo-structural priors so that representation quality is assessed at the region/bag level rather than through global pooling or i. i. d. patch assumptions. SAM-Cluster evaluates unsupervised separability as a ratio of intra-region cohesion to relaxed inter-region separability, while SAM-LP mitigates signal dilution in supervised evaluation by reweighting structural prototypes through an EM procedure. The paper validates the approach on 8 public WSI datasets against 10 candidate FEs, with a ground-truth ranking constructed from 9 MIL aggregators × 5 seeds, and reports that the proposed metrics correlate substantially better with downstream MIL performance than several generic transferability baselines, making FE screening considerably more practical.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.FE selection for WSI pipelines is expensive, yet highly consequential for downstream performance — the paper reports a 20+ percentage-point swing on Camelyon16 between ResNet50 (76.59%) and Virchow2 (97.98%). This is a meaningful problem with clear real-world impact that has been largely underexplored compared to aggregator design.
2.The methodological intuition is well-motivated. Using SAM masks as pseudo-structural regions is a sensible way to move beyond global statistics and incorporate tissue organization into FE evaluation. The SAM-Cluster metric is simple and interpretable, and SAM-LP provides a reasonable mechanism to counter signal dilution under bag-level supervision by reweighting structural prototypes.
3.The experimental scope is a major strength. The study spans 8 diverse public datasets, 10 candidate feature extractors, 9 MIL aggregators, and 5 random seeds per configuration, which gives the downstream “ground-truth” ranking a credible basis and makes the Spearman correlations meaningful.
4.The paper evaluates both unsupervised and supervised settings, and supplements the main results with analyses on sample efficiency (N from 5 to 100), top-k screening, and hyperparameter sensitivity (τ and β). These additional experiments substantively strengthen the practical value of the work.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The empirical gains are meaningful but not uniformly dominant across all datasets. For the supervised metric, Linear Probing ties SAM-LP exactly on UBC-OCEAN (both 0.8303), SAM-LP is actually slightly lower than LP on TCGA-GLIOMA (0.4424 vs. 0.4545), and LogME is the strongest metric on PANDA (0.7430 vs. SAM-LP’s 0.5879). The paper would benefit from an explicit discussion of these failure/near-tie cases and from a characterization of when the SAM-based prior is most beneficial (e. g. , in terms of structural heterogeneity, tumor-to-background ratio, or bag size).
2.The contribution of SAM is not fully isolated experimentally. Prior work such as SAM-MIL [6] has already established that SAM-derived structural priors are useful in WSI analysis — the novelty here is repurposing such priors as a pre-evaluation signal for FE selection rather than as an aggregator component. This repositioning is reasonable, but the paper does not compare against simpler spatial or regionalization alternatives (e. g. , coordinate-based grouping, superpixels, Otsu-based tissue components, or random region prototypes of matched size). Such ablations are necessary to show that the gains are specific to SAM rather than to any form of region-level grouping.
3.The “ground-truth” FE ranking is defined as the average downstream performance across 9 MIL aggregators. This is reasonable as a broad benchmark, but in practice many users select an FE for a fixed downstream aggregator. Correlations with per-aggregator rankings — or at least a stratified comparison between attention-based aggregators (e. g. , ABMIL, TransMIL) and simpler pooling aggregators — would substantially strengthen the practical claim.
4.Several implementation details remain under-specified for exact reproducibility: the SAM variant and backbone used, the WSI magnification/resolution at which masks are generated, the patch-to-mask assignment rule, any mask filtering or merging step, class balancing in the sampled 30-WSI subsets, and the EM stopping criterion.
5.The computational-efficiency argument is largely qualitative. The paper states that metric computation reduces evaluation time from “weeks” to “minutes” and scales O(1) in |Φ|, but provides no concrete wall-clock runtime, GPU/memory usage, or hardware-based comparison for SAM preprocessing versus even a limited MIL search. A simple table quantifying these savings would directly support one of the paper’s main selling points.
6.The EM formulation in SAM-LP (Eq. 7) reweights each prototype by its isolated predictive likelihood P(Y_i | c_{i,k}; θ), while the prototype embeddings c_{i,k} themselves remain fixed throughout the EM loop (only the weights α and the classifier θ are updated). This is structurally closer to a static attention model than to the context-dependent weighting learned by attention-based MIL aggregators. It is therefore unclear whether SAM-LP is most predictive of attention-based downstream behavior, mean-pooling behavior, or both — a targeted per-aggregator analysis would clarify what class of downstream models SAM-LP is actually forecasting.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I lean Weak Accept because the paper tackles an important and under-studied problem in WSI learning, proposes a sensible structure-aware solution, and supports it with a broad empirical study. The practical value is tangible: even moderately reliable top-k screening of feature extractors could save substantial computation in real MIL pipelines, and the reported correlations (average ρ = 0.5348 for SAM-Cluster and ρ = 0.6258 for SAM-LP) are non-trivial given the difficulty of the task.
I do not rate the paper higher for several reasons. The computational advantage, which is one of the paper’s headline claims, is argued qualitatively rather than quantitatively. The role of SAM itself is not fully disentangled from simpler regionalization alternatives, leaving open whether the gains stem from SAM specifically or from any region-level grouping. The ground-truth ranking is averaged across 9 aggregators, which may overstate the metrics’ utility for practitioners who have already committed to a particular aggregator, and SAM-LP’s EM formulation (with fixed prototypes and isolated per-prototype likelihoods) may be better aligned with some downstream aggregators than others.
Overall I find the contribution useful and promising, with the final judgment depending meaningfully on the rebuttal.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal substantively addresses four of my six concerns. Most importantly, the per-aggregator stratification (W3, W6) directly confirms my hypothesis that SAM-LP’s EM formulation aligns most closely with mean pooling (ρ = 0.6078) while remaining stable across pooling and attention-based aggregators (0.5688 ± 0.0226), and shows the averaged ground-truth ranking is well-represented at the per-aggregator level (mean ρ = 0.8205). The structural-complexity characterization (W1) gives actionable guidance on when SAM-LP helps over LP, and the FLOPs-level breakdown for SAM versus FE extraction (W5) makes the efficiency claim concrete rather than rhetorical. The main residual gap is the SAM-versus-simpler-regionalization ablation (W2), which is deferred to a journal extension; the arguments against Otsu, grid, and SLIC are defensible, but a matched random-region-prototype control would still have strengthened the methodological isolation of SAM’s contribution. On balance, the rebuttal converts the qualitative claims into quantitative evidence and engages directly with the methodological critiques, so I am now comfortable above the acceptance threshold.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses the problem of feature extractor (FE) selection for WSI-based MIL pipelines, which currently requires exhaustively training hundreds of model configurations to identify the best-performing FE for a given dataset. The authors propose a pre-evaluation framework that ranks candidate FEs without any MIL training, using only pre-extracted embeddings from a small slide subset. The core contribution is two WSI-aware suitability metrics: SAM-Cluster, an unsupervised metric that evaluates intra-region feature cohesion and inter-region separability using SAM-derived segmentation masks as structural pseudo-labels; and SAM-LP, a supervised metric that replaces naive mean-pooling with an EM-based prototype weighting scheme to address signal dilution from non-diagnostic background patches. The framework is evaluated across 8 public datasets covering diverse cancer types, reporting Spearman rank correlations against ground-truth MIL performance derived from 90 fully trained configurations per dataset.
reviews.text_strengths:
The problem formulation is practically motivated and well-scoped. The observation that no single FE dominates across datasets, combined with the scaling argument (10 FEs × 9 aggregators × 5 seeds = 450 runs per dataset), makes a compelling case for a cheaper pre-selection step. This is a real bottleneck in computational pathology research that has not received much direct attention.
The use of SAM as a source of structural pseudo-labels is a reasonable design choice. Rather than relying on pathology-specific annotations, the authors leverage SAM’s zero-shot segmentation to approximate histological boundaries, and Fig. 2 provides at least qualitative evidence that the resulting masks are meaningful. The decoupling of SAM inference from the candidate FEs means the segmentation cost is paid once per WSI regardless of how many FEs are being evaluated, which is a practical advantage.
The experimental setup is unusually thorough for this type of paper. Grounding the evaluation in 90 fully trained configurations per dataset (10 FEs × 9 aggregators × 5 seeds) across 8 diverse datasets provides a fairly robust reference ranking and makes the reported Spearman correlations more credible than if they were based on a single aggregator or a much smaller experimental grid.
The sample size analysis is a useful practical contribution. Showing that SAM-LP approaches near-peak correlation at N = 30 while conventional LP requires substantially more samples directly supports the claim that the framework can reduce selection cost without severely sacrificing reliability.
The hyperparameter sensitivity results are also helpful. The fact that τ and β can be fixed globally without dataset-specific tuning is important for a method intended to be used before committing to a full downstream training pipeline.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The performance gains of SAM-LP over standard Linear Probing are not uniformly strong across datasets. In Table 1, SAM-LP underperforms LP on TCGA-GLIOMA and PANDA, and only modestly improves over it on several others. The average improvement is partly driven by large gains on a few datasets, especially TCGA-NSCLC, while the advantage is smaller or absent on some others. The paper does not really discuss when SAM-based prototyping helps most and when it does not. That limits interpretability of the metric in practice.
SAM’s suitability as a structural prior for pathology images is asserted more than systematically validated. Fig. 2 shows a single qualitative example on colorectal tissue, which is visually convincing, but it remains unclear how well SAM masks capture meaningful boundaries in more difficult settings such as diffuse tumors, necrosis, artifacts, or highly heterogeneous slides. Some broader analysis of SAM mask quality or failure modes across the included datasets would strengthen this assumption.
The EM optimization in SAM-LP requires slide-level labels, so SAM-LP is still a supervised metric. This is not a flaw by itself, but the paper should be clearer about the practical label requirements and where SAM-LP is applicable versus where only SAM-Cluster can be used. Relatedly, it would help to know how many labeled slides are needed before SAM-LP becomes reliable in practice.
The paper does not report the actual wall-clock time or computational cost of running the proposed framework end-to-end. The claim that evaluation is reduced “from weeks to minutes” is plausible, but it is not backed by concrete timing numbers. Since efficiency is a major motivation for the work, a simple runtime table would make this part of the argument much more convincing.
The Top-k analysis is useful, but Top-5 is a relatively loose criterion given that there are only 10 candidate FEs in total. Reporting per-dataset Top-1 and Top-2 selection accuracy more explicitly would make the practical selection value easier to judge.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper tackles a practical and underaddressed problem in computational pathology with a reasonable technical approach. The experimental foundation is solid: the reference ranking is derived from an unusually large number of trained configurations, and the evaluation spans 8 diverse datasets. The proposed metrics improve over the main baselines in aggregate, and the sample-size analysis supports the claim that the method can be useful in low-cost FE pre-selection. My main reservations are that the benefits of SAM-LP are not equally strong on all datasets, the efficiency claim is not backed by concrete timing numbers, and the Top-k analysis is not as strong as it could be given the relatively small candidate pool. These are meaningful but addressable concerns rather than fundamental flaws, so overall I lean weak accept.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have responded substantively to all major concerns. The computational cost analysis with concrete FLOPs figures clarifies the efficiency advantage over exhaustive MIL training. The explanation of when SAM-LP outperforms LP — specifically on datasets with high structural complexity such as TCGA-NSCLC and BRACS — provides useful and actionable guidance that was missing from the original submission. The aggregator bias concern is addressed by showing that the averaged GT ranking correlates strongly with per-aggregator rankings (mean ρ = 0.8205), confirming the robustness of the ground truth. The justification for using SAM over simpler alternatives is also reasonable. I am raising my score to 5.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a MIL-free framework for selecting WSI feature extractors on a target dataset. Its key contribution is two structure-aware metrics, SAM-Cluster and SAM-LP, which use SAM-derived regions to evaluate feature quality at the bag level and better reflect WSI spatial heterogeneity than standard global metrics.
reviews.text_strengths:
(1) The paper addresses a practically important problem: feature extractor choice clearly affects downstream MIL performance and currently requires expensive trial-and-error training.
(2) The proposed metrics are well motivated for WSI data, especially by incorporating region-level structure instead of relying on naive global pooling or patch-wise i.i.d. assumptions.
(3) The empirical study is relatively broad, with multiple datasets, feature extractors, and MIL aggregators, which increases the practical relevance of the findings.
(4) The supervised variant, SAM-LP, is a sensible attempt to reduce signal dilution from irrelevant tissue regions.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(1) The ground-truth FE ranking is defined by averaging performance across multiple MIL aggregators, which may obscure important FE–aggregator interactions and does not fully reflect real-world model selection for a fixed downstream pipeline.
(2) Although the reported rank correlations are promising, the improvements over baselines are not always large or consistent across datasets, and statistical uncertainty (e.g., variance, confidence intervals, significance tests) is missing.
(3) The efficiency claim is insufficiently quantified: the paper argues for major computational savings, but does not provide concrete runtime, GPU-hour, or memory comparisons.
(4) It remains unclear whether the gain comes specifically from SAM-based structural priors or more generally from any region-based grouping, since no ablation with simpler alternatives is provided.
(5) The supervised protocol needs a clearer description, especially regarding label usage, subset construction, and separation from downstream evaluation to rule out potential leakage.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper addresses a relevant and practical problem in computational pathology and presents a well-motivated, empirically promising solution. However, the current evidence is not yet fully convincing due to limited statistical analysis, insufficient efficiency quantification, and missing ablations on the role of SAM.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I think the idea is very interesting.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper studies the practical problem of selecting WSI feature extractors before full MIL training and proposes a structure-aware pre-evaluation framework based on SAM-derived regional information. The reviewers find the problem practical and the empirical study reasonably broad. However, several concerns remain about the methodological justification, the consistency of the empirical findings, and the practical strength of the efficiency claim, etc. The authors are encouraged to address the concerns in the rebuttal.

The rebuttal addresses most concerns such as clarifying the efficiency analysis, aggregator-specific behavior, dataset-dependent performance patterns, label usage, and implementation details. The revision should incorporate these clarifications and quantitative analyses into the manuscript.

All three reviewers raised their scores to accept after rebuttal. The idea and the methodology novelty are recognized by the reviewers. The rebuttal addressed most of the concerns raised in the first round of review.
clear accept for this paper.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback and recognition of the problem’s practical importance (R1, R2, R4) and our extensive experimental setup (R1, R2, R4). We deeply value your insightful suggestions and address the main concerns below.
1.Computational efficiency quantification (R1, R2, R4)
We will add a table reporting parameters, GPU memory, FLOPs, and wall-clock runtime for each component (FE, SAM, MIL aggregator, SAM-LP, SAM-Cluster), along with the following analysis.
Exhaustive search costs: C_exhaustive = N × |Φ| × (K × C_FE + M × C_aggregator), where N is total WSIs, |Φ| candidate FEs, K average patches per WSI, M aggregators (9 in our study).
Our framework costs: C_ours = n × [|Φ| × (K × C_FE + α) + C_SAM], using only n ≪ N WSIs and no MIL training.
On Camelyon16 (RTX A6000, FE avg. 341M params, K = 4,090): K × C_FE ≈ 327 TFLOPs per WSI, while C_SAM ≈ 3.2 TFLOPs (<1% of single-FE extraction, run once on thumbnails) and α ≈ 3.7 MFLOPs (no backprop). Therefore C_ours / C_exhaustive ≈ n / N, with further savings from avoided aggregator training.
2.SAM vs. simpler regionalization alternatives (R1, R2, R4)
We excluded simpler alternatives by design:
Otsu: Our pipeline (Trident) already removes background, so Otsu cannot capture intra-tissue heterogeneity.
Grid grouping: Ignores biological boundaries entirely.
SLIC superpixels: Requires dataset-specific tuning (segment count, compactness), which contradicts our framework’s “zero-shot, out-of-the-box” philosophy — users would need to tune segmentation hyperparameters before they can even select an FE.
However, we fully understand the necessity of quantitatively demonstrating that SAM’s regionalization outperforms other alternatives. We will address this point and include a detailed quantitative comparison in the subsequent journal extension.
3.When SAM-LP outperforms LP (R1, R2, R4)
SAM-LP gains correlate with structural complexity (avg. patches and SAM regions per WSI):
High complexity (SAM-LP > LP): TCGA-NSCLC (3,834 patches, 90.3 regions): ρ improves 0.6364 → 0.9515.BRACS (3,617 patches, 128.6 regions) shows similar gains.
Low complexity (SAM-LP ≤ LP): PANDA is the smallest (200 patches, 19.7 regions), where LP/LogME suffices. TCGA-GLIOMA and UBC-OCEAN have many patches but limited structural separation (53–70 regions), yielding comparable performance.
This provides actionable guidance: SAM-LP is most beneficial on large, structurally heterogeneous slides where signal dilution is severe.
4.Aggregator bias and ground-truth robustness (R1, R4)
We averaged across 9 aggregators × 5 seeds to assess general FE transferability. To address the fixed-pipeline concern, our per-aggregator breakdown shows:
The averaged GT ranking correlates strongly with individual aggregator rankings (mean ρ = 0.8205) and especially with the best-performing aggregator per dataset (ρ = 0.9299), confirming its representativeness.
Per-aggregator stratification: SAM-LP correlates highest with Mean Pooling (0.6078) and RRT-MIL (0.5955), lowest with WiKG (0.5448), averaging 0.5688 ± 0.0226 across 9 aggregators. As R1 hypothesized, the linear-probing-based formulation aligns most closely with mean pooling. SAM-Cluster correlates highest with CLAM (0.5260) without a clear architectural pattern.
Predictive power remains stable across pooling and attention-based aggregators.
5.Missing implementation details (R1, R4)
Hardware specs, SAM configuration, and EM stopping criteria will be added to the manuscript and released code. Supervised label usage is documented in the code: patient-level train/val/test splits prevent leakage, and pre-evaluation metrics are computed only on training-set subsets (5 random samplings of n WSIs). All baseline results are averaged over 5 seeds. We will add variance to Table 1 and report significance tests for main results.
6.Other points (R2)
Top-k: Fig. 4(c) reports Top-1 through Top-5.- Sample size: Fig. 4(a, b) analyzes n.

title: SAMoCo: A Learning-Initialized and Physics-Refined Framework for Sampling-Agnostic Motion Correction in MRI
abstract: Patient motion during magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) acquisition leads to severe artifacts that degrade diagnostic quality. End-to-end deep learning (DL)-based motion correction methods are prone to structural hallucinations and often exhibit limited generalizability across different image contrasts. While some studies instead estimate motion parameters and perform model-based reconstruction to avoid hallucinations, they are typically restricted to specific k-space sampling patterns. To address these challenges, we present a novel retrospective motion correction framework that synergistically integrates DL-based motion estimation with model-based optimization and reconstruction. Our hybrid approach consists of two key components: (1) A pre-trained neural network that explicitly processes both undersampled k-space data and sampling patterns to infer motion parameters, enabling flexible adaption to variable numbers of shots and phase-encoding lines; specifically, this network combines convolutional neural network with gated recurrent unit, and is trained on a diverse simulated dataset encompassing varying image contrasts, anatomical orientations, and sampling patterns; (2) An instance-wise autofocusing algorithm that jointly refines the initial motion parameters and updates coil sensitivity maps, ultimately yielding artifact-free images. The proposed framework generalizes well across different image contrasts, k-space sampling patterns, and acceleration factors. Validations on fastMRI dataset and in-house MRI data demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in motion artifact suppression, while preserving strict physical fidelity and strong cross-protocol generalization capability. These results highlight the potential of our approach for robust clinical deployment.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents SAMoCo, a hybrid framework for retrospective MRI motion correction that combines learning-based motion initialization with physics-based refinement. Specifically, the method first uses a sampling-pattern-aware network to estimate shot-wise motion parameters from undersampled k-space, and then refines these parameters jointly with coil sensitivity maps through an autofocusing-based model-driven reconstruction process. Experiments on fastMRI and in-house data show consistent improvements over several representative baselines under different acceleration settings.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The sampling mask is used as a dynamic routing mechanism to extract per-shot PE lines before Bi-GRU temporal modeling, allowing a single trained network to generalize across varying shots, ACS lines, and acceleration factors without retraining — directly addressing the fixed-trajectory limitation of prior methods. 
2.Most existing methods assume perfectly known sensitivity maps, which is unrealistic under simultaneous undersampling and motion corruption. SAMoCo incorporates sensitivity estimation into an alternating inner-outer optimization loop alongside motion refinement, treating the two as a principled coupled estimation problem. 
3.The ablation quantifies motion parameter MAE directly (>70% reduction after autofocusing), disentangling each component’s contribution beyond image metrics alone. Testing on unseen FLAIR contrast and a different-vendor scanner further supports cross-contrast and cross-site generalization.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Major Concerns:
1.It is unclear how well the motion estimation network generalizes beyond the training shot-number distribution. Since the method emphasizes sampling-agnostic motion estimation, it would be important to evaluate whether the network remains stable when the number of shots at test time exceeds or differs from the training range. 
2.The sensitivity of the full pipeline to initialization quality is not sufficiently analyzed. Since the method is explicitly learning-initialized and physics-refined, the paper should better clarify how robust the final reconstruction is to different qualities of initial motion estimates. 
3.The contribution of joint sensitivity-map updating is not sufficiently isolated. In particular, it would be helpful to show how much performance is lost if the method refines only motion parameters while keeping the sensitivity maps fixed. 
Minor Concerns:
4.The paper should describe the sampling-pattern-guided shot-wise feature extraction more clearly. In particular, the aggregation operation used to form shot-wise feature vectors is not sufficiently specified. 
5.The computational cost of the iterative refinement is not clearly reported. Since the method relies on inner/outer optimization loops, reporting the number of iterations, convergence behavior, and runtime overhead relative to the baselines would improve the practical assessment. 
6.The motion-correction evaluation remains relatively limited in scale, especially given the strong claims on generalization.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The work is physically grounded, the ablation is more rigorous than typical, and the cross-site generalization results are encouraging. However, each individual component has clear precedent and the contribution is primarily their combination, which reads as incremental. The evaluation is modest (60 slices, 6 subjects), all motion is simulated with no real-motion validation, inference time is never reported, and the sensitivity map modeling choice is neither ablated nor compared against standard alternatives such as ESPIRiT.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This work presents a retrospective motion correction framework that is a hybrid of deep learning and model-based methods. A deep learning model estimates motion parameters from undersampled k-space data and k-space sampling patterns, and the model-based algorithm and framework update coil-sensitivity maps and reconstruct artifact-free images. This method demonstrates SOTA performance on one publicly available and one in-house datasets.
reviews.text_strengths:
The work is relevant, well-motivated and well-organized, and free of grammatical errors and typos
Figures are neat and legible
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The motion simulation method is not explained in sufficient detail.
Non-cartesian sampling patterns are not considered, and no justification for exclusion is presented.
Robustness of the method on pathological data is not evaluated.
Downstream performance evaluations are not considered. For example, does segmentation performance on the motion-corrected data approach that of the ground truth?
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
SAMoCo is never expanded anywhere in the text

While the work is relevant and presented clearly, it is not easily reproducible. Further, the scope of the work is limited to cartesian trajectories and healthy data, making it difficult to assess the value and impact of the motion-correction method in real-world settings.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: A hybrid retrospective motion-correction framework is proposed that performs a DL–based motion estimation coupled with a physics-driven optimization and reconstruction framework. The DL model is pre-trained to estimate rigid body motion parameters such as translation and rotation from each k-space shots. A pre-training stage is utilized where rigid motion is simulated with random motion parameters for multiple contrasts, anatomical orientations etc. to predict motion parameters from k-space shots. The pre-trained network is simply used for initialization after which it has no role. An iterative model based reconstruction (physics driven autofocus method) is used to jointly refine the motion parameters and estimate the coil sensitivity maps. The outer loop updates the coil sensitivities and the inner loop updates the motion parameters. The method is tested using retrospective under sampling experiments and simulated motion on IXI datasets, fastMRI datasets and in-house datasets. The method is compared to AF+ and JSMoCo in addition to other baseline methods with no motion compensation and is shown to outperform those methods at acceleration factors of 2 and 3.
reviews.text_strengths: The DL-part is only used as an initialization for motion parameter estimation. The motion corrected reconstruction is performed using physics-based formulations such as autofocus. Thus there is no hallucination risk, which could be a real risk if it were an end-to-end DL approach. The DL-network for motion estimation uses a spatial-temporal framework which may aid to estimate reasonable motion parameters in a temporally consistent manner from the retrospective measurements (although this aspect is not described in the paper). The method is shown to work on more than one contrast (eg: simulated multi-shot T1 and T2 datasets).
reviews.text_weaknesses: The proposed method is fundamentally limited to multi‑shot or segmented MRI acquisitions where motion is approximately rigid and constant within each shot. The standard T1/T2 datasets are not multi-shot acquisitions, where the key assumptions of this paper breaks down. What the paper demonstrates on T1/T2 are simulated cases where a single shot acquisition is split into a multi-shot acquisition retrospectively and does not reflect a standard MRI acquisition. More realistic multi-shot methods would have been multi-shot EPI or non-Cartesian methods (eg: multi-shot spiral, radial), where the feasibility of the method is not demonstrated. The method is stated to be sampling agnostic, however the description makes it clear that the method is sampling aware and is a strict constraint. It is not clear how multiple contrasts or orientations will recast the method as sampling-agnostic.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a principled method for retrospective motion correction is a well-defined but limited regime of multi-shot acquisitions where the rigid, inter-shot model assumptions hold. The method is tested in those settings using synthetic datasets and analytically simulated motion and is shown to work well. However, neither the standard clinical T1/T2 nor the fastMRI T1/T2 datasets are multi-shot datasets, rather they are single-shot methods where the assumptions do not hold. The method is not validated in a true multi-shot dataset where the acquisition itself was performed in a multi-shot fashion. Moreover the sampling-agnostic claim is not supported in the experiments.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text: The reviewers agree that the paper presents a well-motivated and technically sound hybrid framework that combines learning-based initialization with physics-driven refinement for MRI motion correction. The method is clearly described, shows consistent improvements over strong baselines, and demonstrates promising generalization across datasets and acquisition settings. While concerns remain regarding evaluation scale, realism of motion settings, and some claims (e.g., sampling-agnostic behavior), these are viewed as limitations that can be addressed in future work rather than fundamental flaws. Overall, given the solid methodology, empirical gains, and potential clinical relevance, I recommend acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank all reviewers and the meta-reviewer for their positive reviews and constructive feedback, which have been very helpful in improving the quality of our work. Below, we address their main comments as follows:
(1) We agree with R3 that our proposed method is limited to multi-shot or segmented MRI. However, we would like to clarify that the term “multi-shot” in our work includes segmented acquisitions in which multiple k-space lines are acquired within one TR, such as T1-weighted MPRAGE, T2-weighted TSE, and FLAIR sequences. These sequences are widely used in standard clinical scans. In fact, the T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and PD-weighted images from the IXI dataset were acquired in a multi-shot manner, with echo-train-lengths of 208, 16, and 16, respectively. We have added the following text to the revised paper to clarify this point: “Notably, all images were acquired in a multi-shot manner with varying echo-train-lengths.” Additionally, we revised the opening sentence of Section 2.1: “We focus on the retrospective motion correction problem in 2D multi-shot MRI, such as in common sequences like fast spin echo.”
(2) We agree with R3 that the term “sampling-agnostic” may be imprecise, as the initial motion estimation takes sampling patterns as input, making the method “sampling-aware”. Our intended meaning was that SAMoCo is not limited to a single fixed sampling pattern; the same trained network can handle variable shot numbers, ACS lines, and acceleration factors without retraining. In future publications, we will replace “sampling-agnostic” with more precise terminology, such as “sampling-flexible”, to better describe the ability of the framework to generalize across different sampling schemes.
(3) We thank R1 and R2 for their valuable suggestions regarding real-motion validation, generalization to shot numbers beyond the training distribution, non-Cartesian sampling, pathological data, and downstream clinical tasks. We plan to investigate these issues in our future work. In addition, we will follow R1’s suggestion to further analyze the influence of initial motion estimation and joint sensitivity map updating through additional ablation studies.

title: SANT-CBM: Structurally-Aware and Noise-Tolerant Semi-supervised Concept Bottleneck Models
abstract:
Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) have emerged as a promising direction for interpretable medical image analysis by grounding predictions on human-understandable concepts. However, training effective CBMs typically requires dense concept annotations by clinical experts, which is prohibitively expensive and scarce. While semi-supervised CBMs attempt to leverage unlabeled data, they often suffer from label noise inherent in pseudo-labeling and fail to preserve the pathological correlations between concepts (e.g., symptom co-occurrences). In this paper, we propose a novel Structurally-Aware and Noise-Tolerant
CBM (SANT-CBM) framework for semi-supervised medical image
classification. To address the unreliability of pseudo-labels, we introduce a GMM-based Dynamic Weighting mechanism that models the loss distribution of unlabeled samples to separate clean supervision from noise, effectively “denoising” the training process. Furthermore, we propose a Structural Consistency Loss that aligns the correlation matrix of predicted concepts on unlabeled data with the reference correlation derived from clinical priors. This ensures that the model learns biologically plausible concept combinations rather than independent features. Extensive experiments on two public dermatology datasets (Fitzpatrick17k and 7-point) demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art semi-supervised CBM baselines. Specifically, our approach achieves diagnostic accuracies of 77.83% (vs. 71.52%) on Fitzpatrick17k and 73.27% (vs. 67.52%) on 7-point (based on 10% labeled), establishing a new benchmark for label-efficient and interpretable medical diagnosis.
Keywords: Concept Bottleneck Models · Semi-supervised Learning ·Medical Image Classification.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses a practically important problem in concept bottleneck models, namely how to train interpretable CBMs under sparse concept annotations in a semi-supervised medical setting. The paper identifies two limitations of existing semi-supervised CBMs: noisy pseudo-labels on unlabeled data and the lack of structural constraints over concept co-occurrence. To address these issues, the authors propose SANT-CBM, which combines a GMM-based dynamic weighting mechanism to down-weight unreliable pseudo concept supervision and a structural consistency loss to align predicted concept correlations with a reference correlation matrix derived from labeled clinical concepts. Experiments on two dermatology datasets show improved task accuracy over prior semi-supervised CBM baselines, especially in the low-label regime.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper tackles an important bottleneck in CBMs, namely the heavy reliance on dense concept annotations, which is especially costly in medical imaging. Extending CBMs to the semi-supervised setting is highly relevant. 
2.The discussion of pseudo-label noise and the neglect of concept-to-concept pathological structure is well motivated, particularly for medical diagnosis where concepts are often correlated rather than independent. 
3.The two main components—GMM-based denoising and structural consistency regularization—are intuitive, and well integrated into the CBM pipeline. 
4.The reported gains over SSCBM in task accuracy are substantial, especially with 10% labeled data, suggesting that the proposed regularization is useful for label-efficient diagnosis.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.A notable issue is that task accuracy improves clearly, but concept accuracy does not consistently improve across datasets and settings, compared to SSCBM (Table 1) . This makes it unclear whether the method truly improves the bottleneck concepts themselves, or mainly benefits the final classifier downstream of the concepts.
2.The paper does not sufficiently compare with or discuss recent label-free CBM methods, such as:
Label-Free Concept Bottleneck Models
Explain via Any Concept: Concept Bottleneck Models with Open-Vocabulary Concepts
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I lean weak accept. The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem in semi-supervised CBMs for medical imaging. The proposed method is well motivated, technically clear, and demonstrates meaningful gains in task accuracy under limited concept supervision. However, the evidence for improved concept quality is not yet fully convincing.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a semi-supervised concept bottleneck model that leverages unlabeled data by generating pseudo-concept labels via kNN retrieval from a labeled feature bank, followed by per-concept Gaussian mixture model (GMM)–based denoising using agreement between pseudo-labels and model predictions. To further improve reliability, the method introduces a structure-aware regularization that aligns predicted concept correlations with a reference correlation matrix computed from labeled data. The approach aims to learn concept representations that are both noise-tolerant and structurally consistent, thereby improving downstream task performance under limited concept supervision.
reviews.text_strengths:
Methodology. Effectively combines psuedo-label denoising (GMM) with structure aware learning, addressing key challenges in semi-supervised CBMs. And Uses per-concept reliabiilty weighting leveraging noisy pseudo labels effectively instead of discarding them.
Demonstrates improved task performance in low-label regimes showing practical value when concept annotations are scarce .
reviews.text_weaknesses: Concept accuracy remains largely uncahnged, suggesting tha t improvements stem from enforcing structured interactions ratehr than improving individual concept predictions, which raises questions about interpretability benefits typically what CBMs are motivating.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
-A brief discussion clarifying why task performance improves despite minimal gains in concept accuracy would bring more clarity to the results, particularly in relation to the limitations of standard concept evaluation metrics not capturing the structural consistency in combinations, but can still help improve task accuracy?

The paper addresses an important limitation of concept bottleneck models, scaling to limited concept supervision through a combination of denoising and structural constraints. The approach is promising and well-motivated, however further analysis can help understand the relationship between concept quality and downstream performance, as well as the robustness of the learned structure.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors response clarifies that the proposed structured objective is intended to improve relationships among concepts that helps improve downstream task classification rather than independendt concept prediction accuracy. This helps explain the observed discrepancy between steady concept performance and improved task performance. While some uncertainty remains regarding the learned concept correlations estimated from relatively sparse labeled datasets (10-20%) consistently reflect clinically meaningful structure, I believe the paper presents a meaningful contribution to semi-supervised concept bottleneck learning.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes SANT-CBM, a semi-supervised concept bottleneck model for medical image classification that aims to improve both robustness and plausibility of concept learning under scarce concept annotations. The method combines two components on unlabeled data: (1) a GMM-based dynamic weighting strategy that down-weights potentially noisy pseudo-label supervision at the concept level, and (2) a structural consistency loss that aligns the batch-wise correlation matrix of predicted concepts with a reference correlation matrix computed from labeled concept annotations. Experiments on Fitzpatrick17k and the 7-point Checklist dataset show improved diagnostic accuracy over prior semi-supervised CBM baselines, especially in the low-label regime.
reviews.text_strengths:
This paper studies an important problem how to make concept bottleneck models more label-efficient while preserving interpretability in medical image classification. The motivation is well aligned with clinical deployment scenarios.
The core strength of this research lies in its highly effective, label-efficient framework that synergizes probabilistic denoising with clinical priors to establish a new state-of-the-art in medical diagnosis. By introducing a GMM-based Dynamic Weighting mechanism, the model robustly filters noise from unlabeled data, while a novel Structural Consistency Loss explicitly forces the network to learn biologically plausible concept combinations rather than isolated features. This dual innovation enables SANT-CBM to significantly outperform existing methods, achieving remarkable diagnostic accuracy improvements of 6.31% and 5.75% on the Fitzpatrick17k and 7-point datasets, respectively, using only 10% labeled data.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.While the motivation to introduce clinical constraints is commendable, the proposed Formula (7) is fundamentally a standard feature correlation matrix alignment, a highly common approach for consistency loss. Shifting the computation target to a batch-wise predicted concept Pearson correlation matrix ($\hat{R}_{batch}$) lacks substantial theoretical novelty.
2.The use of the term “Clinical Priors” is heavily exaggerated. In the current methodology, the reference matrix is derived purely from the Pearson correlation of concept annotations within the labeled training set, rather than integrating external clinical knowledge graphs or expert-defined ontological structures. Consequently, this mechanism is essentially dataset-level concept correlation regularization, not an independent clinical prior.
3.Section 4.1 specifies a batch size of merely 16.Computing a Pearson correlation matrix on such a remarkably small batch size is statistically prone to extreme variance and instability. The authors do not address how calculating sample-to-sample correlations within such small batches avoids introducing highly noisy gradients during training.
4.The paper motivates the method partly through “noise tolerance,” but it is not always clear whether the targeted noise is pseudo-label noise (inherent in the semi-supervised learning process) or challenging real-world dermatology image quality. This distinction matters significantly because the proposed GMM weighting method operates on pseudo-supervision loss distributions rather than directly modeling or addressing physical image corruption.
5.Figure 1 is not provided in a vector graphics format. It exhibits significant blurring and pixelation when zoomed in, which fails to meet the standard publication quality of top-tier journals/conferences.
6.The visual representation of the “Clinical Priors” in Figure 1 only displays three features (Asymmetry, Color, Blue-Gray Veil). Given that the experiments utilize 22 and 19 concepts for the Fitzpatrick17k and 7-point datasets respectively, this excessive simplification prevents readers from intuitively grasping the actual computational complexity of the high-dimensional matrix alignment.
7.In the “Reference Matrix” portion of Figure 1, there is a complete absence of a legend or colorbar. Furthermore, it is never explicitly explained what the irregularly darkened areas within the orange boxes actually represent, leaving the visualization visually ambiguous.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
he paper addresses a relevant and interesting problem, and I appreciate the attempt to combine robustness and structural plausibility in semi-supervised CBMs. For the rebuttal, I would especially appreciate clarification on three points: (1) why the reference correlation matrix is described as a “clinical prior” when it appears to be estimated from the labeled training set, (2) how the structural consistency term on unlabeled data should be interpreted relative to more standard consistency-style regularization, and (3) several implementation details that are currently hard to infer from the manuscript. Improving the explanation of Figure 1 would also make the paper easier to follow.

The paper studies an important problem, namely semi-supervised concept bottleneck models for medical diagnosis under scarce concept annotations. The empirical results are encouraging: in the 10% labeled setting, SANT-CBM achieves clear task-level improvements over SSCBM on both Fitzpatrick17k and 7-point, which suggests that the proposed framework has practical value for label-efficient interpretable learning.
However, I currently rate the paper as a Weak Reject because I am not yet fully convinced by the strength of the methodological contribution and by several aspects of the presentation and experimental justification. First, while the motivation for introducing “clinical priors” is appreciated, the proposed structural consistency loss in Eq. (7) appears, in essence, to be a standard correlation-alignment regularizer applied to the batch-wise Pearson correlation matrix of predicted concepts. Relative to prior semi-supervised CBM work, this is a meaningful extension, but the degree of theoretical novelty seems moderate.
Second, the term “clinical prior” appears somewhat overstated in the current manuscript. The reference matrix is computed from concept correlations within the labeled training set, rather than derived from an external clinical knowledge source or expert-defined prior structure. As a result, the method seems closer to dataset-level concept correlation regularization than to the incorporation of an independent clinical prior.
Third, I also have some concern about the stability of estimating a batch-wise Pearson correlation matrix with the reported batch size of 16, especially early in training when concept predictions on unlabeled data may themselves be noisy. This issue is not sufficiently discussed. 
In addition, Figure 1 is low-resolution and difficult to parse, and its simplified visualization does not clearly convey the actual high-dimensional matrix alignment used in the experiments. The lack of clear legend/color explanation further affects readability.
Overall, I think the paper has promising empirical performance, but the current version still has important weaknesses in novelty calibration, conceptual framing, and clarity. For the rebuttal, I would particularly appreciate clarification on the exact type of “noise” the method is intended to address, the intended interpretation of the “clinical prior,” and the authors’ perspective on the stability of the batch-wise structural loss.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
I thank the authors for their rebuttal. However, after considering the response, I would still recommend rejection.
The rebuttal clarifies that the proposed GMM module targets pseudo-label noise in unlabeled concept supervision rather than directly modeling physical image corruption or real-world dermatology image artifacts. This clarification is useful, but it also weakens the original “noise-tolerant” framing. In the submitted manuscript, the GMM branch is described as “denoising” the training process, but technically it is a small-loss / loss-distribution based reweighting mechanism applied to pseudo-concept supervision. I therefore still find the denoising claim somewhat overstated.
Similarly, the rebuttal acknowledges that the so-called “clinical prior” is not derived from external clinical knowledge, expert-defined ontology, or a medical knowledge graph, but from concept correlations in the labeled training set. This supports my original concern that the manuscript overstates the clinical-prior aspect. The method is more accurately described as labeled-set concept correlation regularization rather than the incorporation of an independent clinical prior.
I also remain unconvinced by the methodological novelty of the Structural Consistency Loss. As formulated in the paper, it computes a batch-wise Pearson correlation matrix of predicted concepts on unlabeled data and aligns it with a reference correlation matrix using a Frobenius-norm penalty. While this may be a reasonable regularizer, the operation itself is relatively simple and closely resembles standard correlation-alignment or consistency regularization. The rebuttal reframes the contribution as concept-level structure regularization for unlabeled predictions in semi-supervised CBMs, but I still view this as an incremental extension rather than a sufficiently strong methodological contribution.
The response regarding batch stability is also only partially convincing. The authors mention epsilon normalization, a moderate structural-loss weight, and three independent runs, but they do not provide direct evidence that estimating a concept correlation matrix from a batch size of 16 is statistically stable, especially early in training when pseudo-concept predictions may be noisy.
Finally, the concerns about the figures remain. The submitted Figure 1 is low-resolution, visually ambiguous, lacks adequate legends/color explanation, and does not clearly convey the actual high-dimensional concept-correlation alignment used in the experiments. The authors promise to improve the figure in the final version, but the current decision should be based on the submitted manuscript and rebuttal rather than promised future revisions.
Overall, although the empirical gains are interesting, the rebuttal does not sufficiently resolve my concerns regarding overstated terminology, limited methodological novelty, insufficient stability justification, and presentation quality. I therefore maintain a reject recommendation.

meta_reviews.text:
Reviewers feedback is mixed. However, the novelty contribution is recoganized by all. The authors are encouraged to address the common concerns raised by the reviewers, like “why task performance improves despite minimal gains in concept accuracy”, and clarify the points like “the exact type of ‘noise’”, in the final version.

The authors addressed several main concerns raised by the reviewers, and are strongly encouraged to avoid overclaiming as per Reviewer #3’s comments.

Started with diverse comments and concerns and diverging ratings, the rebuttal is with limited effectiveness in addressing the major concerns, including but not limited to issues over novelty concern, over-claims of clinical prior and others, and presentation concerns. 
Overall it requires significant revision efforts that goes beyond minor nature to get into MICCAI in this round.

This is a borderline paper with mixed reviews. Reviewers agreed that the work addresses an important and under-explored problem—extending Concept Bottleneck Models to semi-supervised and label-scarce medical imaging settings—and that the integration of GMM-based pseudo-label denoising with structural consistency regularization is well motivated and yields substantial gains in task accuracy under low-label regimes. However, they also raised serious concerns about the paper’s soundness and significance: first, concept accuracy did not consistently improve alongside task accuracy, raising questions about whether the method enhances interpretability or merely optimizes downstream classification; second, reviewers highlighted overstated claims regarding “denoising” and “clinical priors,” noting that these are more accurately described as standard loss reweighting and dataset-derived correlation regularization rather than genuine noise modeling or external clinical knowledge integration; third, the methodological novelty of the structural consistency loss was viewed as limited, with close resemblance to existing correlation-alignment techniques, and concerns were raised about statistical instability due to small batch sizes and inadequate empirical justification. The rebuttal addressed some, but not all, concerns—clarifying design choices while falling short of resolving issues around terminology, novelty, and robustness. After careful deliberation, I lean towards accepting this manuscript.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for their recognition of our work. We address the common concerns below.
(1) Why task accuracy improves more than concept accuracy. We agree that SANT-CBM should not be interpreted as uniformly improving every marginal concept AUC. Our claim is more specific: under sparse concept labels, bottleneck quality has both an individual-concept aspect and a joint-configuration aspect. Standard concept accuracy evaluates each concept independently, whereas the downstream classifier also depends on whether the concept vector forms plausible co-occurrence patterns. Table 2 separates these effects. On Fitzpatrick17k with 10% labels, GMM denoising improves concept AUC from 86.31 to 87.81 and task accuracy from 71.51 to 74.38.Structural loss alone changes marginal concept AUC only slightly (86.47) but improves task accuracy to 75.13, indicating that it helps mainly through joint concept structure. Combining both gives the best reported pair, 88.84/77.83.We also note that under the low-label regime, further improving marginal concept AUC is inherently challenging, as even sota semi-supervised CBMs (SSCBM) achieve only moderate gains beyond the supervised baseline. In this context, the improvement from 86.31 to 87.81 (GMM alone) is non-trivial. More importantly, as shown in Table 2, the structural loss alone yields a substantial task gain (71.51 → 75.13) with almost no change in marginal concept AUC, confirming that task improvement primarily comes from better concept co-occurrence structure rather than from isolated concept accuracy. We will revise the discussion to state this distinction explicitly rather than implying that all gains come from marginal concept accuracy.
(2）Noise type and batch stability. The noise targeted by the GMM is pseudo-label noise in unlabeled concept supervision. Image artifacts may induce unreliable pseudo-label losses, but the method does not claim to directly model physical image corruption. The GMM models per-concept pseudo-supervision loss distributions and down-weights unreliable pseudo-concept targets. For the batch-wise structural loss, the batch correlation is used as a stochastic training regularizer rather than as a one-shot estimate of clinical statistics. The Pearson denominator includes epsilon normalization, the structural term is weighted moderately (lambda_s=0.3), and the reported results are means of 3 independent runs. The structural-loss-only ablation improves task accuracy from 71.51 to 75.13, suggesting that the signal is useful rather than destabilizing in this setting. (3) “Clinical prior” and novelty. We agree with R3 that the current wording can overstate the source of the prior. The reference matrix is computed from labeled clinical concept annotations in the training set; it is not an external knowledge graph or expert ontology. We will rename it as an “empirical clinical-concept correlation prior” or “labeled-set concept reference matrix” throughout the final version. Our novelty claim is not Pearson correlation alignment itself is new. The contribution is concept-level structure regularization on unlabeled predictions in a semi-supervised CBM, complementing SSCBM’s local visual alignment and the GMM denoising branch. This is the mechanism behind the low-label task gains recognized by the reviewers.
For R1’s label-free/open-vocabulary CBM concern, these methods address a different setting: discovering or naming concepts without a fixed clinically annotated concept set. SANT-CBM instead assumes a small labeled set of clinically defined concepts and a larger unlabeled pool.
For R3’s Figure 1 concerns, we agree and will improve the final version with vector-quality artwork and a legend explaining the matrix values and highlighted regions.

title: SAR-Net: Sample-Agnostic Retrieval Network for Robust Brain Tumor Segmentation with Missing Modalities
abstract: Incomplete multi-modal MRI data severely degrades clinical brain tumor segmentation. Existing solutions utilizing generative synthesis or implicit disentanglement often suffer from hallucinated artifacts or weak feature discriminability. To address these limitations, we propose a novel Sample-Agnostic Retrieval Network (SAR-Net), shifting the paradigm from “fabricating’’ missing features to “retrieving’’ latent style prototypes from a global distribution. We explicitly disentangle images into modality-agnostic “content’’ and sample-agnostic “styles’’, utilizing a Dynamic Style Memory Bank optimized via Momentum Contrastive Learning to ensure high discriminability. To impute missing modalities, a Global Consensus Voting mechanism retrieves compatible style prototypes, which are then fused with structural content via adaptive modulation. Extensive evaluations on BraTS 2020, together with ablation studies on BraTS 2018, demonstrate that our framework outperforms state-of-the-art methods under diverse missing-modality settings. The code is available at https://github.com/CoCodeRepo/FS2R.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs
Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces the SAR-Net framework for brain tumor segmentation under missing MRI modalities. Instead of synthesizing missing modalities or relying on modality-invariant representations, the method reconstructs missing modality features by retrieving style prototypes from a memory bank. The reconstructed features are then integrated into a segmentation network with transformer-based fusion.
reviews.text_strengths:
The use of Gram matrices to represent style and the separation between structural and statistical components are well-motivated, and the integration with contrastive learning is reasonable.
The component-wise and loss-wise ablations support the contribution of each module, and the incremental gains from retrieval and contrastive learning are demonstrated.
The experiments consider all missing-modality combinations.
Gains in more challenging regions (TC/ET) are more than those of WT, suggesting the method may indeed improve boundary precision.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The method largely combines existing ideas (Gram matrix-based style transfer, memory banks with MoCo-like contrastive learning, and feature modulation via AdaIN).
The assumption that Gram matrices capture modality-specific style independent of anatomy is borrowed from natural image literature. However, in MRI, intensity distributions are not just stylistic, and scanner/protocol variability, as well as pathology, may be entangled.
The selected baselines are reasonable, but recent studies in diffusion-based imputation or foundation models with multimodal learning are not addressed.
Given the added architectural complexity (memory bank, contrastive learning, retrieval, transformer), the improvements achieved over the baseline are relatively small.
The paper criticizes generative models for being computationally expensive, but does not provide runtime comparisons, memory consumption, or training stability discussion.
No cross-dataset evaluation is provided to show how well this generalizes to unseen distributions or whether performance depends on dataset-specific factors.
The paper argues that retrieval avoids hallucination, but does not provide qualitative evidence (e. g. , failure cases, visual comparisons).
The paper lacks implementation details to ensure reproducibility. Several aspects are missing, including training hyperparameters (learning rate schedule, batch size, number of epochs), memory bank configuration (size, update frequency, queue length per modality), momentum coefficient, and temperature in contrastive learning, details of data preprocessing and augmentation, and architectural specifics (e. g. , encoder backbone, feature dimensions, transformer configuration).
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The method seems stable and yields consistent improvements in clinically relevant regions. However, implementation details are missing, and the claimed novelty or general impact is not convincing. The framework builds on established components, and the gains over prior work are relatively incremental.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
After considering the rebuttal, I am moving my score to Accept for the following reasons:
The authors provided full implementation details.
The authors acknowledged the limitation of the Gram matrix/style analogy in the MRI context, conceding that intensity distributions are entangled with scanner, protocol, and pathology effects, and committing to moderating the relevant language in revision.
The hallucination concern is adequately reframed: since SAR-Net operates at the feature level rather than synthesizing missing-modality images, image-level hallucination is not applicable, and the original claim is a definitional rather than empirical one.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: Addressing the prevalent clinical challenge of missing modalities in multi-modal MRI, this paper proposes SAR-Net, a method designed to effectively enhance inference accuracy under incomplete data conditions. Distinguishing itself from generative synthesis and representation learning approaches, this method innovatively introduces a retrieval-based paradigm. It imputes missing modality features via similarity retrieval, thereby circumventing the generation of hallucinated artifacts. Architecturally, the authors innovatively decouple structural information and explicitly disentangle latent styles from spatial structures. Furthermore, they employ momentum updates and contrastive learning to efficiently maintain a memory bank, ultimately achieving high-performance inference in missing-modality scenarios.
reviews.text_strengths:
This paper demonstrates several key strengths. 
1.First, it proposes an innovative retrieval-based approach to solve the missing modality problem, designing specialized feature extraction and retrieval methods tailored to the specific challenges of missing modalities in medical segmentation tasks. 
2.Furthermore, in the context of multi-modal medical image segmentation, the authors accurately identify the distinction between structural information and modality-specific styles, developing a corresponding disentanglement module. To efficiently maintain the memory bank, the study introduces contrastive learning to further enhance the separability and distinctiveness of different modality styles. 
3.Finally, the paper is well-structured and logically coherent, and the experimental results robustly demonstrate the excellent performance of the proposed model.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
However, the manuscript still has several weaknesses that warrant further clarification. 
1.Missing Loss Function Weights: The paper does not specify the weighting coefficients for the various loss functions. The authors should discuss how different weighting ratios might affect the model’s performance. 
2.Inconsistent Dataset Usage: There is a discrepancy in the datasets used for evaluation: the ablation study is conducted on the BraTS 2018 dataset, while the SOTA comparison uses the BraTS 2020 dataset. Even though these datasets share some overlapping cases and exhibit domain similarity, this experimental design choice lacks a proper justification. 
3.Limited Reproducibility: The paper lacks comprehensive implementation details and does not provide reproducible source code, which hinders the overall reproducibility of the method.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I recommend this manuscript for direct acceptance. Addressing the prevalent clinical challenge of missing modalities in multi-modal segmentation, this paper innovatively introduces a retrieval-based paradigm. To tackle the core challenges of feature extraction and memory bank maintenance inherent in retrieval systems, the authors propose highly targeted designs: explicitly disentangling features into structural content and modality-specific styles, and employing contrastive learning to maintain the dynamic memory bank. These innovations enable the model to efficiently retrieve and impute missing features. Comprehensive experimental results robustly demonstrate that SAR-Net consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods across various missing-modality scenarios, particularly under severe missingness, highlighting its significant potential for real-world clinical applications. Furthermore, the manuscript is well-structured, logically coherent, and supported by thorough experiments. It is a highly meritorious work worthy of acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Thanks to the author for the additional response, which addressed some of my concerns.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: SAR-Net proposes a “Disentangle-Contrast-Retrieve” paradigm for brain tumor segmentation under missing MRI modalities. It decouples images into modality-agnostic structural content and sample-agnostic styles (via Gram matrices), maintains a momentum-updated Dynamic Style Memory Bank optimized with contrastive learning, and retrieves missing modality styles via Global Consensus Voting across available modalities. Retrieved styles modulate structural content via AdaIN-inspired adaptive feature modulation for final segmentation.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Methodological contribution is novel. Framing missing modality imputation as style retrieval rather than generation is well-motivated.
2.Disentanglement with Gram matrix is more explicit than adversarial or implicit alignment methods. Visualizations confirm that.
3.Comprehensive evaluation reported. All 15 missing modality combinations were reported with both DSC and HD95 showing consistent gains in clinically critical TC and ET regions.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The authors claim to have tested on BraTS 2024, but there is no result shared in the paper.
2.TMFormer [24], KMD [9], and CCSD [18] are cited but not compared against despite being directly relevant and recent. (citation indexes from paper).
3.Table 1 is the BraTS 2020 results. But ablation is on BraTS 2018.The standard convention is to share results across all datasets and to show ablation results on a subset. That is not followed here, and the claim that it surpasses all BraTS 2018, 2020, and 2024 is not supported.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The retrieval paradigm is novel and the ablations are thorough, but the missing BraTS 2024 results, absent recent baselines, and inconsistent experimental evaluation (not supporting all the claims) make this paper incomplete.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
While Reviewer 2 strongly recommends acceptance, Reviewers 1 and 3 raise significant concerns regarding the inconsistency of experimental datasets, missing results for BraTS 2024, and lack of comparison with recent relevant baselines. The authors should clarify these experimental discrepancies, provide the missing BraTS 2024 results, and justify their methodological novelty against existing style-transfer and retrieval methods to secure acceptance.

All reviewers suggest to accept this submission.

The paper introduces an innovative retrieval-based paradigm (SAR-Net) to address missing modalities in multi-modal brain tumor segmentation, a contribution recognized by the panel as clinically valuable and methodologically well-motivated. During the rebuttal phase, the authors successfully clarified key technical implementation settings, refined the conceptual framing of feature-level style retrieval, and resolved major concerns regarding reproducibility, resulting in a strong positive consensus. While minor reservations remain regarding evaluation dataset consistency across the ablation studies, the overall methodological merits and robust performance gains warrant acceptance, provided that all promised clarifications are meticulously integrated into the camera-ready version.

The model’s approach is novel: framing missing modality imputation as style retrieval.
Moreover, authors successfully address reviewers’ comments, I therefore recommend acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for your valuable comments to improve our work.
To Meta Reviewer: Below we have provided clarify experimental discrepancies, BraTS 2024 results, and methodological novelty.
BraTS dataset inconsistency (R1,R2,R3): (1) using BraTS 2020 for SOTA comparison and BraTS 2018 for ablation is aimed to show more datasets results within limited space. (2)The mention of BraTS 2024 in the abstract was an editing error, for fine-grained six-label BraTS 2024, we have additional evidence: in a large-scale six-region evaluation, SAR-Net improves over M2FTrans, with DSC gains of +0.5/+0.9/+0.4/+1.0/+0.5/+0.8 for WT/TC/ET/NETC/SNFH/RC and mean HD95 reduced from 7.78 to 6.58 mm. Following rebuttal policy, we do not provide more results here..
Reproducibility and code (R1,R2): Key settings are Adam, lr=2e-4, weight decay=1e-4, poly LR decay, batch size 1, 1000 epochs, seed 1024, and 128^3 crop with rotation/intensity/flip augmentation. Memory bank uses 250 entries per modality-layer, 10 warm-up epochs, momentum 0.995, and 4/128 positive/negative samples. Gram-layer temperatures are 0.5/0.45/0.4/0.35/0.3, with weights 0.3/0.25/0.2/0.15/0.1.Total loss is unit-weighted Lcon+Lrec+Lreg+Lds+Lseg. Code will available after accept.
Novelty and Gram/style statistics (R1): Our approach is not a mere heuristic but a genuine innovation grounded in a deep understanding of the missing modality segmentation problem. SAR-Net uses mature components, but not as a simple stack: Gram prototypes summarize modality statistics, contrastive learning organizes the bank, retrieval selects sample-agnostic prototypes for missing modalities, and feature modulation injects them into segmentation features. We agree MRI intensity distributions are entangled with scanner/protocol variations and pathology, and are not “style” in the natural-image sense. Here, “style” is a proxy for modality-specific statistical cues, including modality appearance, protocol-related intensity variations, and distributional information. We do not claim perfect anatomy-independent disentanglement; because complete disentanglement remains difficult, SAR-Net uses Gram prototypes to aggregate these statistics as feature-level compensation cues, rather than reconstructing images or treating prototypes as anatomical representations. We will weaken “style” wording to avoid equating MRI intensity differences with natural-image style, and discuss limitations.
Complexity, efficiency, and hallucination (R1): Although average gains may appear moderate, the results highlight robustness in extreme missing-modality cases and difficult tumor regions, the focus of clinical missing-modality scenarios. SAR-Net is slower than lightweight CNN/fusion baselines due to memory bank, retrieval, and Transformer modules, but avoids iterative image-level synthesis and is algorithmically more efficient than diffusion-style imputation. At inference, it uses one feature extraction pass and compact Gram-memory lookup, without generating missing MRI images. Thus, this is a cost-benefit/algorithmic-efficiency argument, not a runtime benchmark. We will clarify this tradeoff. Here, “mitigating unreliable feature hallucination” refers to avoiding image-level hallucination from synthesized missing-modality images; SAR-Net performs feature-level retrieval/compensation, so there is no image-level hallucination issue.
Uncompared related works (R3): We thank R3 for noting TMFormer, KMD, and CCSD. Our baselines focus on reproducible representative methods from different paradigms under comparable missing-modality settings. KMD is a plug-and-play Koopman module, TMFormer refines Transformer via token merging, and CCSD appeared very recently and was not included. SAR-Net focuses on retrieval-based training/architecture using sample-agnostic style prototypes. Fair comparison requires unified implementation/protocol, which cannot be added in rebuttal.
We thank the reviewers again and will incorporate these clarifications.

title: SAVer: Structure-Aware Validation of Standard Fetal Head Planes via Clinically Grounded Anatomical Completeness
abstract:
Standard fetal head plane identification in ultrasound is es-sential for accurate biometric measurements and early detection of neurodevelopmental abnormalities. Automating the identification of these planes can optimize diagnostic workflows. Existing approaches predominantly treat plane identification as a global image-level classification task, often relying on superficial visual features rather than clinically defined anatomical criteria.
