The paper never states how D_val is constructed, which is a critical missing experimental detail.
4.No ablation studies on any component. There is no ablation isolating the contribution of EMA smoothing, IQR penalization and the FSM stabilizer. The contribution of these components is crucial since they are claimed as one of the main contributions of the paper.
5.The “no manual configuration” claim is overstated.SEA-PEFT still requires setting many parameters and the entire audit space design including which topologies and rank values to include. These are presented as inherited defaults from prior work, but a clinical user who is “not an AI engineer” would still need guidance on these choices, and no sensitivity analysis is provided to justify that they transfer reliably across new datasets or modalities.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses a genuinely important and well-motivated problem — automating PEFT configuration for few-shot 3D medical image segmentation — and the core idea of on/off perturbation-based utility estimation is intuitive, elegant, and computationally practical. The experimental results are consistent and encouraging across multiple datasets, backbones, and shot regimes, and the practical efficiency of the method aligns well with the clinical deployment scenario the paper targets.
There are couple of weaknesses I see as mentioned in the weaknesses section. I think the most critical ones among all are the followings:
1- Missing ablation studies (W4). EMA smoothing, IQR penalization, and the FSM stabilizer are all presented as key contributions of the paper, yet none of them are individually validated. Without ablations, it is impossible to know whether these components are genuinely necessary or whether a much simpler design — for example plain moving average smoothing without IQR, or no FSM at all — would perform comparably.
2- The validation set construction is never clarified (W3). This is particularly damaging in the 1-shot regime, which is one of the paper’s headline experimental settings. If a separate labeled scan is used for validation, the effective annotation budget is doubled, making the 1-shot claim misleading. If the single training scan is split, training quality is compromised. Either way the experimental setup needs to be explicitly described — as it stands, the 1-shot results cannot be properly interpreted.
In general I am positive about the paper. However, I think the weaknesses are major enough to suggest rejection. My initial rating is weak reject but I would be happy to increase my score after rebuttal.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal addresses some of my concerns, especially by clarifying the validation set construction and providing high-level ablation results for EMA/IQR and FSM. I also understand that the authors had limited space to respond to all reviewers’ comments, and I appreciate their efforts. However, I still find the response insufficient to raise my score because several critical points remain unresolved. First, the authors do not provide the actual standard deviations, confidence intervals, or per-seed results in the rebuttal, so the robustness of the reported gains remains unclear. This is particularly important because the improvements over the strongest baselines are modest in some settings. Second, the selected adapter configurations are only described qualitatively, without concrete per-dataset, per-shot, or per-layer details, which weakens the central claim that SEA-PEFT discovers meaningful dataset-specific configurations. Finally, although the authors clarify that D_{val} is a fixed public validation partition and is used consistently across methods, I remain concerned that excluding this labeled validation set from the annotation budget may make the “1-shot” setting less realistic from a clinical few-shot adaptation perspective. I acknowledge that this may be less problematic if the same validation protocol is applied fairly to all methods. Overall, while the rebuttal improves clarity, I still consider these remaining issues substantial and suggest reject.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors formulate a 3D medical image few-shot PEFT configuration as an online resource allocation problem, bypassing computationally prohibitive offline architecture searches. It introduces an “on/off perturbation” auditing mechanism coupled with EMA+IQR smoothing and a Finite-State Machine (FSM) to dynamically select optimal adapter topologies during training.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.This paper focuses on an important and practical topic.
2.The paper is generally well-structured and relatively easy to understand and follow.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The core “on/off perturbation” scoring relies on a strong, unverified assumption of independent adapter utility. This fundamentally ignores potential synergistic or antagonistic effects between different layers and adapter types, risking severely sub-optimal greedy allocations.
2.The omission of current automated or dynamic PEFT baselines (e.g., NOAH, AutoPEFT, AdaLoRA) is unacceptable. Dismissing these comparisons due to 3D computational costs without providing even a proxy 2D benchmark leaves the claimed optimality completely unverified. Moreover, AdaLoRA is not constrained by few-shot settings, and the authors themselves mention it in the text; why was it not included in the comparison?
3.Crucial empirical ablations for the heavily emphasized EMA+IQR tracker and FSM stabilizer are entirely missing. Readers cannot isolate or verify the actual performance impact of these specific engineering components versus the overarching framework.
4.The framework’s heavy reliance on a robust validation set D_val for high-frequency utility auditing contradicts the premise of a strict few-shot clinical setting. The authors fail to define the size of D_val or address the severe risk of architectural overfitting when validation data is critically scarce.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The primary reasons for recommending a weak rejection are the complete absence of comparisons against state-of-the-art dynamic or search-based baselines, an unverified assumption regarding the independent utility of adapters, and a lack of necessary ablation studies for the proposed stabilization mechanisms.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal has addressed most of my concerns. Although AdaLoRA still achieves performance comparable to the proposed method, which was my main remaining concern, I am convinced by the authors’ response and would like to update my recommendation to accept.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper received mixed reviews, specifically one strong accept and two weak reject, one of whom remains positive and open to increasing the score. During the rebuttal, I would be especially interested in the authors’ feedback on the following points:
(1) The omission of current automated or dynamic PEFT baselines in the quantitative evaluation. In particular, please clarify what is meant by “not feasible for high-resolution 3D segmentation at 1–10 shots,” for example, in terms of compute time, GPU usage, or parameters compared to the results in Table 3.Please also elaborate on the exclusion of AdaLoRA from the comparisons. (2) Clarify what is used as the validation set in the few-shot regime. (3) Regarding the missing ablation studies, while new experiments are not allowed during rebuttal, these components involve a few hyperparameters. Please clarify whether they are fixed across all experiments or per task, and in the latter case, how this is handled in few-shot regimes.
Please also address other important concerns raised by the reviewers.

After the rebuttal, the paper received 2 “Accept” and 1 “Reject” recommendations. One of the initial reviewers increased the initial score.
The rebuttal successfully clarified the exclusion of dynamic PEFT baseline methods due to their computational cost and provided positive comparisons with AdaLoRA. Also, the additional high-level results on the stability of performance under hyperparameter modifications are encouraging. The remaining concerns from R2 to recommend rejection point out: (1) Not providing standard deviation in performance; (2) Missing detailed analysis on selected configuration; and (3) The consideration of the validation set on the few-shot budget. These are all valid comments.
For (1-2), in my opinion, these comments are not invalidating and might be justified by space constraints. For (1), although performance gains may be tight in a specific scenario, the proposed SEA-PEFT procedure is motivated not only by performance but also by the practical utility of automatically selecting the PEFT configuration in a stable way across data regimes, backbones, and datasets.
Regarding (3), I find this concern more problematic. The validation data is used to guide the audit phase by computing the Dice score. Therefore, as R2 argues, it requires annotation and should, accordingly, be considered part of the annotation budget. At least, it should be acknowledged that a few-shot validation set is required for SEA-PEFT. According to the repository, the authors appear to use K=2 for validation. Results with SEA-PEFT (1 train shot + 2 validation shots) are positive compared to non-dynamic baselines using 5 shots (e.g., in Table 1). Therefore, results suggest an efficient profit from such validation data. The authors should revise the manuscript to make the validation set design more explicit.
Based on the above, the remaining concerns do not invalidate the manuscript’s strengths, which cover a timely, practical topic on the more automated adaptation of medical foundation models and propose an original adaptation procedure with positive empirical validation across backbones and datasets. I recommend acceptance.

This paper introduces SEA-PEFT, an online allocation framework designed to automate parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) configurations for few-shot 3D medical image segmentation. By utilizing a search-audit-allocate loop during training, the framework estimates task-level adapter utility through model-agnostic on/off perturbations, bypassing the need for computationally prohibitive offline architectural searches. The paper received split post-rebuttal recommendations consisting of one Strong Accept, one Accept, and one Reject. Reviewers highly praised the clinical practicality of automating site-specific adaptation without dedicated AI engineers, the conceptual soundness of the online knapsack formulation, and the rare inclusion of theoretical convergence bounds within length constraints. Furthermore, extensive multi-organ evaluation on TotalSegmentator and FLARE datasets demonstrates noticeable gains of 2.4–2.8 mean Dice points over competitive fixed-topology baselines within highly reasonable GPU execution timeframes.

Good paper with interesting idea on search–
audit–allocate loop for PEFT in 3D fewshot segmentation. The rebuttal resolves most of the concerns and therefore I recommend acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their careful feedback. Per MICCAI 2026 guidelines, PDF supplementary is prohibited, so all requested ablations and clarifications are included inline below and will be incorporated in the camera-ready.
[Fair comparisons and Meta-Q2] All baseline numbers follow published configurations of [1] (MICCAI 2025) and [18] (MICCAI 2023). SEA-PEFT uses the identical backbone, D_train, D_val, D_test, random seeds, training protocol, and matched parameter budget across all experiments. D_val is the fixed public validation partition, entirely separate from the K training shots.
In the 1-shot setting, 1 labeled volume is used for gradient updates; D_val is not counted toward the few-shot budget (annotation cost is exactly K volumes). Three random seeds were used for both the search phase and the final retraining; results are on the held-out test set, never D_val. Mean+-std will be included in the camera-ready.
[Meta-Q1] Why NOAH/AutoPEFT are infeasible here. Both [32] and [33] require one complete end-to-end training run per candidate. Our audit space covers 120+ configurations; at 1-shot, one run takes 2.5h on V100 (Table 3), so a full sweep exceeds 300 GPU-hours per organ per shot setting, prohibitive for the per-site adaptation scenario we target, whereas SEA-PEFT explores the same space in one run.
AdaLoRA (new comparison; LoRA-only audit space, ranks {2,4,8,16,32}; identical protocol). 5-shot: SEA-PEFT avg. 77.60 vs. AdaLoRA 75.57 (Gall: 81.03 vs. 78.11; Eso: 48.62 vs. 43.76). 10-shot: 79.84 vs. 76.57 (Gall: 84.58 vs. 80.01; Eso: 52.46 vs. 45.72). SEA-PEFT wins by 2.0-3.3 Dice points because direct perturbation-based utility is more reliable than SVD-based saliency when gradient signals are noisy at 5-10 shots.
[Meta-Q3 and R#2-W5] Hyperparameters are fixed across all experiments, organs, datasets, and backbones (no per-task tuning): K=200, M=0.2N, beta=0.95, lambda_S=0.5, tau_act=tau_rank=3, Pmax=1%.
We swept K={100,500, 800,1000}, M={0.1N,0.5N,0.8N,1.0N}, and beta={0.90,0.925,0.975,0.999} individually. On TotalSeg (1/5-shot): mean absolute Delta Dice change relative to the default across all conditions is 0.12 (K), 0.64 (M), 0.31 (beta); worst-case degradation is -0.82, -0.55, -0.59.On FLARE (1/5/10-shot): 0.12, 0.14, 0.24 mean; -0.54, -0.53, -0.47 worst. Performance is bounded and stable across all sweeps without per-task tuning. We will revise “engineer-free” to “toward engineer-free” throughout.
[R#2-W1] Selected configurations. SA dominates across layer depths (PA secondary; SAPA selective); LoRA leads unit-type choice (AdaptFormer next; Affine-LN sparse). Allocations are layer-non-uniform and dataset-dependent, confirming the search discovers structured, dataset-specific configurations rather than a fixed pattern. Per-dataset breakdown will be added in the camera-ready.
[R2-W4 and R4-W3] Ablation results (DeltaDice vs. no component, TotalSeg).
EMA+IQR: avg. +2.83 (1-shot), +3.60 (5-shot) across 9 organs; largest gains on Aor +12.08 (1-shot) and +9.88 (5-shot), Gall +5.47 and +9.93.
FSM: avg. +2.15 (1-shot), +1.74 (5-shot), +1.58 (10-shot); largest gains on Gall +5.29, Eso +4.60, Sto +3.31 (1-shot). Both components are individually necessary. Full tables will be added in the camera-ready.
[R#4-W1] Adapter utility is not assumed independent. The on/off audit measures each adapter’s marginal Dice conditioned on the current active set, capturing co-adapter synergy and antagonism. The greedy allocator treats these as additive, bounded by the epsilon term in Eq. 8 and refined by repeated audit cycles. SEA-PEFT outperforming AdaLoRA across every organ and shot setting confirms the approximation is tight in practice.
[R#1-W1] FLARE gains are smaller because joint multi-class (9 organs) Dice is a noisier per-adapter signal than binary per-organ Dice, inflating the epsilon term in Eq. 8.The same pattern appears in [1] and [18]. We will add this discussion.

title: Self-Supervised Implicit CEST Reconstruction via Physics-Informed Lorentz Encoding
abstract: Multi-Pool Chemical Exchange Saturation Transfer (CEST) MRI provides valuable metabolic information but is clinically limited by long acquisi-tion times. Although sparse sampling reduces scanning time, reconstructing high-resolution Z-spectra from limited data remains an ill-posed inverse problem. Conventional interpolation and generic Implicit Neural Rep-resentations (INRs) often lack physical constraints, leading to spectral artifacts and physically invalid signals. To address this, we propose Lorentz Encoding (LE), a physics-informed framework that formulates CEST recon-struction as a self-supervised reconstruction task via implicit continuous coordinate learning. Unlike generic positional encodings, LE regularizes the continuous spectral mapping by projecting sparse coordinates into a physically constrained space governed by a combination of parametric Lorentzian profiles with learnable basis functions. This mechanism effectively reduces noise and enforces consistency with physical models. Experiments on in vivo human brain data demonstrate that LE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, under a 39-point sampling strategy, LE achieves a PSNR of 57.58 dB and an SSIM of 0.9994. Furthermore, the learned physics-informed encodings form a continuous, geometrically or-dered trajectory in the latent space, ensuring accurate quantitative metabo-lite mapping (APT, NOE, MT).
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose Lorentz Encoding, a physics-informed framework that formulates CEST reconstruction as a manifold-constrained inverse problem.
reviews.text_strengths: By replacing generic positional encodings with Lorentz Encoding, the method explicitly incorporates the underlying CEST physics into the reconstruction process. This mechanism effectively reduces noise, promotes consistency with the physical model, and achieves superior performance over state-of-the-art methods across multiple metabolite maps, including APT, NOE, and MT.
reviews.text_weaknesses: There are two major concerns. First, the training details are insufficiently described. For the 18 subjects, the manuscript should clarify the criteria used to split the data into training, validation, and testing sets. It should also report the image dimensions and the number of slices included in the analysis. For the 2D model, it remains unclear whether all slices were used for training or whether a selection strategy was adopted, such as restricting training to middle slices or slices with higher image quality. Second, it would strengthen the paper to include an ablation study that evaluates the two parallel encoding modules separately. Such an analysis would better illustrate the contribution of each module and help clarify whether spatial or spectral feature is more critical to the overall model performance.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The use of spectral features to construct a physics-informed model is innovative. However, the validation requires further improvement to more clearly demonstrate the effectiveness of incorporating spectral features into the framework.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: In this work the authors propose a new method for fitting Lorentzian’s to Z-spectra in chemical exchange saturation transfer MRI. This method is based on a Implicit Neural Representation method in which however the authors decouple the spatial and spectral parts of the problem by performing an encoding process separately for the spatial coordinates (Through Hash Encoding) and for spectral parts through an Lorentz Encoding in which the spectras are projected onto a manifold of Lorentzian functions.
reviews.text_strengths:
The proposed Lorentz Encoding method is clearly novel for this application, also the concept with the decoupling of the spectral and spatial appears to be novel in approach for CEST MRI.
Overall the presented work is well described and in a very understandable language. The description of the method has enough details and at the same time is not very convoluted that is can be understood by a person with a bit of experience in CEST MRI. The presented experiments are well designed, easy to follow and to understand what is going on in the results themselves.
The limitation section identifies correctly issues of the method.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
There are a few weaknesses of this work. 
My biggest concern is about the reference which the authors use for the calculation of the PSNR/SSIM metrics in their Table 2.Based on the desciption in the text above I would understand that the calucations are performed against the maps/results from the Direct MPLF applied to the undersampled spectra. Such an approach would be wrong as the observed effects would be affected by the decreasing performance of the MPLF on the undersampled spectra.
However in the Figure 3 the authors provide reference maps which are clearly obtained from direct MPLF on the fully sampled spectra. As such it’s not clear to me what is the final set up in these results. Please clarify this aspect of the results.
Also a missing aspect of the work is how was the training performed and how were the testing cohorts created.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I believe the authors should be able to address all of the weaknesses of the work in the rebuttal phase and at the same time the presented quality of the work as well as novelty of the approach deem it fair to me to recommend a weak accept rate
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a physics-informed INR framework for CEST reconstruction. The key idea is to treat spatial and spectral coordinates differently: spatial coordinates are encoded with hash encoding, while the frequency coordinate is encoded with a set of learnable Lorentzian basis functions. The combined representation is then decoded by an MLP to recover dense Z-spectra.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in CEST MRI, namely reducing acquisition burden while preserving spectral fidelity. The proposed Lorentzian encoding of the frequency dimension is a reasonable way to introduce CEST specific prior knowledge into an INR framework, and this is the most interesting part of the method. The reported results against the baselines included in the paper are consistently strong across the three sampling settings, both for reconstructed spectra and for the derived APT, NOE, and MT maps. The manuscript is also generally readable, and the overall motivation is clear.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The technically new part is the Lorentzian encoding of the frequency dimension. The broader ideas of using INR for CEST reconstruction, or of treating spatial and spectral dimensions differently, are not new. More importantly, closely related CEST papers have already addressed recovery or quantification from sparsely sampled data using deep learning, including Chen et al., MRM, 2024, and Cheema et al., MRM, 2025.These are more relevant comparisons than several baselines currently included in the paper, yet no direct comparison is provided.
Terms such as “Lorentzian manifold,” “physical subspace,” and “manifold-constrained optimization” are stronger than what is actually defined. What the paper clearly specifies is a learnable Lorentzian feature map for the frequency coordinate, followed by a general INR decoder. I think the paper would be stronger and more precise if it described the method as a physics-informed spectral encoding rather than a fully constrained manifold model.
The learning objective and optimization problem are not stated clearly enough for a methodological paper. The paper gives the forward mapping and an (L_2) loss over the sampled set, but it remains unclear how the training is organized in practice, what exactly is optimized, and how the slice-by-slice optimization mentioned later relates to the earlier mathematical description.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
This is a thoughtful paper on an important CEST problem, and I found the idea of using a Lorentzian encoding for the frequency dimension interesting. My main suggestion is to narrow and sharpen the claims. In my view, the specific contribution is not INR for CEST reconstruction in general, but the use of a learnable Lorentzian spectral encoding inside that framework. I would encourage the authors to explain this point more directly, to define the learning objective and optimization problem more clearly, and to moderate the language around “manifold-constrained optimization.” I also think the paper would be substantially stronger with a direct comparison to the closest recent CEST papers on sparse sampling already cited in the manuscript.

I found the paper technically sound at a high level, and the central idea is more meaningful than a generic INR variant. However, I think the contribution is still somewhat incremental for a MICCAI methodological paper. The strongest aspect is the Lorentzian encoding of the frequency dimension, but the paper does not compare directly with the most relevant CEST-specific prior work, and the validation remains limited to retrospective experiments on healthy subjects. The formulation also needs to be stated more clearly. For these reasons, I currently place the paper slightly below the acceptance threshold.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
After considering the rebuttal, my final recommendation is to accept. The rebuttal clarified several points that were central to my initial concerns, particularly the reference used for the quantitative metrics, the subject-specific INR optimization protocol, and the pointwise L2 objective over the acquired sparse Z-spectra. These clarifications make the experimental setup and optimization procedure sufficiently clear.
My view of the contribution remains measured. The strongest contribution is the Lorentzian physics-informed encoding of the spectral coordinate for CEST reconstruction, rather than INR for CEST in general or a fully established manifold-constrained optimization framework. I still think the manuscript would benefit from more precise language around “manifold-constrained optimization” and a clearer framing of the method as a physics-informed spectral encoding within a subject-specific INR framework.
The submitted work contains a meaningful methodological idea, the CEST-specific spectral encoding is technically reasonable, and the reported results are promising. On balance, I view the paper as slightly above the acceptance threshold.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper received multiple positive reviews with some key concerns that should be addressed in rebuttal. All three reviewers agree that the contribution of Lorentzian spectral encoding is a novel and meaningful way to contribute CEST-specific features into INR frameworks. Novelty and limitations are recognized and appropriate. This rebuttal should focus on a few key concerns that reviewers highlighted:
1) clarify the reference used in Table 2
2) provide data splitting and training details
3) moderating the language specific such as “Lorentzian manifold” to better reflect theory that is substantiated in the results (R3)

The authors have addressed the reviewers’ concerns to my satisfaction. The paper makes a solid methodological contribution with a strong technical foundation and promising results. These reviews put it above the acceptance threshold in my mind.

This paper proposes a physics-informed INR framework for CEST reconstruction that decouples spatial and spectral coordinates, encoding the frequency dimension through learnable Lorentzian basis functions to inject CEST-specific prior knowledge. All reviewers agree that the Lorentzian spectral encoding is a novel and meaningful way to incorporate CEST physics into an INR framework, that the method is clearly described, and that the reported gains across sampling settings and metabolite maps are consistent. The rebuttal clarified the points central to the reviewers’ concerns, including the reference maps used for the Table 2 metrics, the subject-specific INR optimization protocol and data split, and the point-wise L2 objective over the acquired sparse Z-spectra, and the reviewer who had initially placed the paper below the threshold confirmed these resolved the central ambiguities and moved to acceptance. The main remaining reservation is that the terminology around “manifold-constrained optimization” is stronger than what the formulation establishes, and the authors are encouraged to moderate this language toward a physics-informed spectral encoding within a subject-specific INR framework, as committed.

This submission proposes a physics-based encoding for CEST MRI reconstruction. R1 and R2 liked the explicit integration of CEST physics with spectral approach. R3 disliked missing baseline comparisons and clarity issues. The rebuttal addressed these concerns. Consensus is on acceptance. For all these reasons, and with respect to others submissions, the recomemdnation is towards Acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
GENERAL RESPONSE TO ALL REVIEWERS
We thank the reviewers for recognizing our Lorentzian spectral encoding as a novel, meaningful contribution to INR frameworks. We prioritize addressing every clarification below. All conceptual clarifications will be incorporated into the final manuscript to ensure theoretical completeness.
1.COMMON MAJOR CONCERNS:
1.1 TABLE 2 REFERENCE METRICS (ADDRESSES R2-Q1)
All quantitative metrics in Table 2 are computed against the reference maps derived from the FULLY SAMPLED (97-offset) spectra, matching the reference maps in Figure 3.The “Direct MPLF” (fitted directly on under-sampled data) is included purely as a minimum baseline. It serves as a lower bound to guarantee that all evaluated interpolation methods yield positive improvements over direct sparse fitting, preventing any negative degradation. We have modified the manuscript to clarify this rationale.
1.2 TRAINING DETAILS AND DATA SPLIT (ADDRESSES R1-Q1, R2-Q2)
Regarding the data split, our framework follows the subject-specific optimization paradigm inherent to Implicit Neural Representations (INR). An independent continuous mapping f(x, y, ∆ω)→I is trained from scratch for each individual subject.
DATA: For all 18 participants, magnetic resonance images were acquired in the axial plane, with the field of view (FOV) specifically positioned to cover the midbrain region. A single 128x128 slice with matrix of 128x128 and 97 frequency offsets was acquired per patient.
SPLIT: Models are trained independently per subject using sparse offsets (21, 29, or 39 points; Fig. 2). A 21-offset strategy provides 344,064 training pairs (128x128x21). Remaining offsets form the test set.
OPTIMIZATION: Training involves 10,000 epochs and the final epoch model is used for evaluation.
2.SPECIFIC REVIEWER CONCERNS:
REVIEWER 1
ABLATION STUDY: To clarify module contributions while adhering to MICCAI policy, we performed an internal check on a randomly selected single case under the 29-offset sampling condition. Ablating Spatial MHE (using Fourier PE+LE) degraded boundaries and caused PSNR to drop to 52.20 dB. Conversely, ablating Spectral LE (replacing it with generic MHE + Fourier) dropped PSNR to 42.03 dB. Our proposed joint MHE+LE approach achieves the highest fidelity (54.44 dB) on this case. These empirical findings validate our decoupled design, and we will explicitly discuss the orthogonal contributions of both modules in the revised text.
REVIEWER 3
COMPARISON WITH PRIOR WORK: We compared our approach with previous works using a 5-fold cross-validation on an 18-subject dataset with 29-offset acquisition. First, Cheema’s 2D U-Net struggled on our single-slice data (PSNRs ~20 dB vs ours >31 dB) without their larger cross-slice training cohorts. Second, to evaluate Chen’s 1D spectral U-Net, we heavily augmented our data to match their massive training pool. While this fully-supervised U-Net achieved slightly higher Z-spectra interpolation fidelity (PSNR 57.94 dB vs our 56.53 dB), our strictly unsupervised approach generated highly competitive parameter maps (APT PSNR 31.60 vs 31.54 dB) without requiring any external training data or ground-truth labels. Importantly, the parameter maps produced by the 1D U-Net are quite noisy, whereas our unsupervised Lorentzian prior acts as a natural physical regularizer to effectively denoise the output. We will explicitly highlight this paradigm contrast in the revised text.
OPTIMIZATION OBJECTIVE: The objective minimizes the point-wise L_2‭‬ loss between the INR prediction and acquired sparse Z-spectra. For our slice-by-slice 2D implementation, the network takes 2D spatial coordinates (x, y) and frequency offset ∆ω ‭‬‭‬as inputs. The weights are optimized exclusively over the acquired sparse coordinates of that specific slice. The explicit loss equation and step-by-step training process will be added.‬‬‬‬‬‬

title: Self-supervised Learning on Lingual Ultrasound Video Encodes Clinically Meaningful Articulatory Structure of Rhotic Production in Residual Speech Sound Disorder
abstract: Speech sound disorder (SSD) affects many school-aged children and can lead to long-term academic, social, and mental health difficulties. Speech-language pathologists use ultrasound, a non-invasive imaging modality, to visualize tongue motion during speech and provide biofeedback treatment. The American English rhotic (r sound) is particularly challenging, as distinct articulatory strategies can produce the same perceived sound. Label-efficient self-supervised learning systems are increasingly being developed to automate scalable and objective SSD assessment. However, existing work has primarily focused on phoneme-level classification and provides limited insight into within-phoneme articulatory variations. In this paper, we present the first self-supervised learning framework that focuses on within-phoneme articulatory structure of American English rhotic production from lingual ultrasound video of children with residual SSD. We further introduce speaker adversarial regularization to reduce inter-speaker variability while preserving articulatory structure in the learned representations. Our results on the recently curated PERCEPT-US multimodal corpus demonstrate that self-supervised learning without task specific fine-tuning yields embeddings that accurately discriminate between perceptually accurate and inaccurate rhotic productions (mean ACC = 0.974; mean MCC = 0.941) and between articulatory subtypes of perceptually accurate rhotics, namely retroflex and bunched configurations (mean ACC = 0.961; mean MCC = 0.897). Code is available at https://github.com/kimtae55/BYOL-VS.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper addresses the challenge of learning articulatory representations from lingual ultrasound videos for children with speech sound disorders (SSD), specifically focusing on the complex American English rhotic sound. The authors propose BYOL-VS, a joint embedding self-supervised learning (SSL) framework that integrates a video vision transformer and a speaker adversarial network. The adversarial component uses a gradient reversal layer to suppress inter speaker variability, which is a major confounding factor in ultrasound analysis. The method is evaluated on the PERCEPT-US dataset without task specific finetuning. It demonstrates superior performance over existing SSL baselines in classifying both perceptual accuracy and within-rhotic tongue shapes.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The integration of an adversarial speaker classifier into a BYOL framework is a practical and highly effective strategy to explicitly handle the high inter speaker variability inherent in pediatric ultrasound data.
2.The quantitative results are impressive. The proposed BYOL-VS significantly outperforms strong SOTA baselines like VideoMAE and RESA on both downstream classification tasks using a simple k-NN probe.
3.The qualitative analysis is a strong point, particularly the extraction of mean tongue contours from the learned clusters (Figure 3). This provides excellent clinical interpretability, validating that the representations capture true, recognizable articulatory geometry.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The downstream evaluation relies entirely on k-NN probing of the frozen representations. Providing results with standard linear probing or end-to-end finetuning would give a more comprehensive picture of the embeddings utility for standard clinical pipelines.
2.The ablation study primarily focuses on the adversarial weight (\lambda_{grl}). Additional ablations on the choice of the spatiotemporal encoder itself (e. g. , comparing ViViT against standard 3D CNNs) would help isolate the specific contributions of the transformer backbone.
While the PERCEPT-US dataset is large for this specific domain, the paper does not extensively detail the demographic distribution of the 70 child speakers. It remains somewhat unclear how well the model might generalize to different age groups (e. g. , adults) or more diverse clinical populations.
4.As the authors briefly acknowledge in the conclusion, speech production is inherently multimodal. The current framework relies solely on ultrasound video, missing out on synchronized acoustic signals that could provide strong supervisory signals for disambiguating articulatory shapes.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a clinically meaningful problem with a well-designed and effective method, achieving strong and interpretable results. While evaluation and ablation scope are somewhat limited, the core contribution is solid and relevant to MICCAI. With expanded validation, this would be a clear accept.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: As stated in the response, most weakness points proposed by are due to the page limitation of MICCAI. I keep my weak accept decision and hope the authors can release a full version journal points to address the weakness points.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors introduce BYOL-VS, a joint-embedding self-supervised learning (SSL) framework applied to lingual ultrasound video for evaluating residual speech sound disorders. The framework combines Bootstrap Your Own Latent (BYOL), a Video Vision Transformer (ViViT) for spatiotemporal encoding, and an adversarial speaker classifier to suppress inter-speaker variability. The method evaluates within-phoneme articulatory structure (rhotic production) without relying on task-specific fine-tuning.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper targets a highly specific and valuable clinical application: evaluating distinct articulatory strategies (e.g., retroflex vs. bunched) that produce perceptually equivalent rhotic sounds, which is notoriously difficult in clinical practice. The use of the PERCEPT-US corpus represents a strong empirical foundation, as it provides a large-scale, expert-labeled resource for within-rhotic child ultrasound analysis. The proposed method achieved high classification accuracy (mean 0.974 for accuracy, 0.961 for rhotic subtype) purely through a k-nearest neighbor probe without task-specific encoder fine-tuning, demonstrating the quality of learned representations.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.From a methodological standpoint, the paper is primarily an application-driven integration of existing techniques. It concatenates BYOL, ViViT, and a standard gradient reversal layer for domain adaptation (speaker adversarial network). It lacks a fundamental algorithmic innovation specifically tailored to the physics or dynamics of tongue ultrasound imaging. 
2.The abstract highlights the ability to perform downstream tasks without task-specific fine-tuning. However, the Method section (Section 2) completely omits how the downstream classification is technically executed. The reader only discovers in the Experiments section (Section 3) that a kNN probe is utilized. This disrupts the logical flow and clarity of the proposed framework.
3.The experimental setup reveals critical inconsistencies in hyperparameter tuning across the compared state-of-the-art (SOTA) models. For instance, VideoMAE uses a batch size of 32, while BYOL and BYOL-VS use 16.Learning rates also vary significantly ($1 \times 10^{-4}$ vs $2 \times 10^{-4}$). These discrepancies severely undermine the fairness of the benchmark comparisons.
4.The evaluation is restricted to only two SSL baselines (VideoMAE and RESA). A broader comparison with other contemporary temporal/video SSL frameworks would better substantiate the superiority of BYOL-VS.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

While the application domain is highly relevant and the empirical results on the PERCEPT-US dataset are impressive, the paper currently falls short on methodological novelty and experimental rigor. The core architecture is a direct pipeline of established methods (BYOL + ViViT + GRL) without domain-specific algorithmic modifications. More importantly, the unfair hyperparameter configurations across baselines cast doubt on the comparative superiority claimed by the authors. A clear justification for the baseline settings and a restructuring of the method section to include the kNN downstream protocol are required before acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The author’s response has largely addressed my concerns, yet further comparisons with state-of-the-art methods are still needed in future work.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose a self-supervised approach to analyze tongue ultrasound videos to track articulatory movements during speech production, particularly for analyzing rhotic sounds produced by children with residual speech disorder. As I understood, the main contribution is including a speaker adversarial module in a self-supervised method.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper is well-written and technically solid. The authors clearly explain their methods and the experimental setup appears to be correct. The inclusion of the speaker adversarial approach seems to yield considerable performance gains on the downstream task and also demonstrates how it improves the embedding space.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The medical application is unclear or not properly motivated. I’m not an expert in linguistics, so I can’t comprehend how important rhotic analysis is, but it seems the proposed approach addresses a very specific component of the English language, even though speech development also concerns the correct production of plosives and even vowels. Although I believe the same architecture could be easily extended to other phonemic groups.
To me, it is still unclear why speaker-dependent information should be suppressed. If the idea is to build a system that ultimately would support speech therapy, so shouldn’t the model be adapted to the speaker? The ablation study shows that suppressing some of the information improves performance in the downstream tasks. I think some clarification is needed.
It’s not explained in the paper in what context the rothic sounds are analyzed. I suppose there is a specific speech elicitation task, and rhotics are extracted from specific words, but the paper doesn’t clarify where. I’m asking because the context of the frames is 12, so I wonder if you actually catch enough articulatory movement in such a short context to properly analyze articulatory problems.
Regarding the methods, I wonder why the authors did not try to incorporate other methods such as MoCo, SimCLR, or DINO? Also, I wonder if the speaker adversarial actually improves the performance so much, wouldn’t this also improve the performance of the other methods?
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I think the paper is missing a comparison with more SSL methods to show that including this speaker adversarial approach boosts the performance of the SSL model. There are also some minor details about the data used and how the articulatory movement is actually evaluated that are not properly described in the paper. It is of particular importance because not many people in the community have knowledge of linguistics.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

meta_reviews.text:
I recommend rebuttal, broadly consistent with the reviewer signal (4, 4, 3 — two Weak Accepts and one Weak Reject). Per MICCAI guidelines, the strict “all ≥4” rule for early accept is not satisfied (R3 = 3), so rebuttal is the appropriate choice rather than early accept. The paper proposes BYOL-VS, a self-supervised framework for lingual ultrasound video built from BYOL + ViViT spatiotemporal encoder + a gradient-reversal speaker-adversarial branch, and evaluated on PERCEPT-US for two clinically meaningful tasks: rhotic perceptual accuracy (correct vs incorrect) and within-rhotic subtype (retroflex vs bunched). Speaker-disjoint 5-fold CV is correctly enforced. Paper-level inspection confirms two real strengths that justify reconsideration after rebuttal:
(1) The empirical gains are unusually large. 
(2) The qualitative validation is genuinely interpretable. Spectral clustering of frozen embeddings yields cluster-mean tongue contours that match expert-traced ground truth (Fig. 3 right) with low RMSE.
However, the paper has two issues that the rebuttal must address before acceptance:
(a) Methodological novelty is integrative. BYOL + ViViT + GRL are all standard, off-the-shelf components; there is no domain-specific algorithmic modification.
(b) Only VideoMAE and RESA are compared as video-SSL baselines. There is no MoCo/SimCLR/DINO comparison and no apples-to-apples test where the speaker-adversarial GRL branch is added to a baseline.

I recommend accept. In essence, BYOL-VS (BYOL + ViViT + speaker-adversarial GRL) achieves unusually strong empirical results on lingual ultrasound video for residual speech sound disorder, with interpretable cluster-mean tongue contours that match expert tracings and a complete ablation study supporting the design, justifying acceptance over R3’s lowest-confidence concern on novelty/baseline breadth,

Although the technical contribution of the paper is limited, it targets a clinically important problem of articulatory structure learning from lingual ultrasound videos for children with speech sound disorders. The paper presents a BYOL style SSL approach, making it label efficient and generalizable. The paper should be of interest to the MICCAI community.

I recommend Accept. The paper studies a narrow but well-defined clinical problem: learning ultrasound video representations for rhotic production in children with residual speech sound disorder. The method is not a new SSL objective. It combines BYOL, a video transformer encoder, and a speaker-adversarial branch. The value of the paper is that this combination matches a real structure in the data: tongue motion should be retained, while speaker-specific ultrasound variation should be reduced.
The empirical results support this design. BYOL-VS performs well with a frozen encoder and a simple kNN probe, which suggests that the representation itself carries useful articulatory information. The cluster analysis is also helpful. The recovered mean tongue contours are not just performance numbers; they show that the embedding separates recognizable rhotic tongue shapes. This makes the result easier to interpret clinically.
The original concerns were fair. The method has limited algorithmic novelty, the first version did not describe the downstream kNN protocol clearly enough, and the baseline comparison needed more explanation because the training settings differed across methods. The rebuttal addresses these points sufficiently for me. Broader SSL baselines and linear-probe or finetuning results would still make the paper stronger, but they are not necessary for acceptance here.
I therefore support acceptance. The paper is application-driven, but the application is specific, the nuisance factor is handled in a direct way, and the learned representations show both quantitative and anatomical evidence of usefulness.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their feedback and respond as follows. The addressed points will be clarified in the final version.
Meta C1, Novelty: Our core contribution is meaningful to MICCAI. Although BYOL, ViViT, and GRL are established components, our integration of them is tailored to lingual ultrasound via spatiotemporal modeling, anatomically constrained augmentations, speaker-adversarial regularization, and speaker-disjoint evaluation to assess generalization. The careful design outperforms existing methods and recovers clinically interpretable embeddings. This is the first SSL study for within-rhotic articulatory structure and for using the newly curated PERCEPT-US, the largest American English child speech corpus. Our work contributes to the translational goal of an accessible, take-home speech therapy system.
Meta C2, Benchmark: Based on our initial experiments, GRL is not BYOL-specific: adding GRL to VideoMAE and RESA improves mean ACC by 2–3% and mean MCC by 7–9%. The paper only reported BYOL-VS not VideoMAE/RESA + GRL, because it gives the best results, and its BYOL backbone has already beaten VideoMAE and RESA on our data. We only consider VideoMAE/RESA/BYOL as baselines rather than MoCo/SimCLR/DINO because pair construction for contrastive methods (MoCo/SimCLR) is hard for sensitive articulatory data (papers [4][11]), and RESA is already a SOTA baseline that outperforms MoCo, DINO, SimCLR, and 8 others in clustering and downstream classification (paper [21]).
R1 C1, Probing: We only reported kNN due to page limit. In our initial experiments, linear probing result is directionally consistent but smaller in values, where BYOL-VS is still the best in both tasks (mean ACC = 0.793 & 0.753, mean MCC = 0.657 & 0.558; cf. Table 1). Finetuning is excluded as our goal tests whether SSL yields clinically useful, annotation-free representations.
R1 C2, Ablation: Due to page limit, we only include the key ablation: whether adversarial regularization encourages interpretable embeddings. We use ViViT as vision transformers have shown better performance than CNN-based models in literature (paper [2]).
R1 C3, Scope: PERCEPT-US targets the children population central to RSSD therapy: ages 8–17, sampled from CT/NJ/NY and balanced by sex and age (see paper [5]). It is the largest child speech corpus with ultrasound data for this clinical aim. Thus, findings should generalize to the target children population, while extension to adults requires further validation.
R1 C4, Multimodal: Multimodal alignment with acoustics is the next step. An ultrasound-only model is the necessary first step to confirm that the learned representations encode tongue-shape structure needed for visual biofeedback.
R2 C1, Novelty: See Meta C1.
R2 C2, Protocol: We will revise Section 2 to explicitly describe the downstream evaluation protocol.
R2 C3, Fairness: All models used the same 5-fold CV protocol and comprehensive search space (e.g. LR 0.0001–0.0005; BS 2–256). Reported settings are each model’s best validation configuration.
R2 C4, Benchmark: See Meta C2.
R3 C1, Motivation: In the U.S., the American English rhotic sound is the highest prevalence therapy target in older children (Farquharson et al, 2026, CLP). This combined with SLP staffing shortages and heavy caseloads (ASHA 2024 Schools Survey) motivates our project.
R3 C2, Speaker: The motivation is to prevent models from exploiting speaker-specific artifacts over articulatory subtypes. The ablation study shows that moderate regularization improves performance and embedding separability, but excessive suppression leads to degradation.
R3 C3, Context: The task is syllable repetition: 15 syllables, repeated 3 times, spanning consonantal r (e.g. ‘ru’), coda/vocalic r (e.g. ‘ear’), syllabic r (e.g. ‘er’), and vowel contexts. Productions are 50–60ms; 12 frames capture suffice rhotic movement while limiting neighboring coarticulatory influence (paper [5]).
R3 C4, Benchmark: See Meta C2.

title: Self-supervised Longitudinal Neuroimaging Augmentation for Continuous Staging of Alzheimer’s Disease
abstract: Traditional diagnostic groups in Alzheimer’s disease provide only a coarse estimate of disease progression, limiting their utility for early detection and disease monitoring. Recent efforts have sought to learn continuous disease staging from longitudinal neuroimaging biomarkers. However, such data are often limited in practice, as most subjects in typical cohorts have only one single visit. To address this challenge, we propose a self-supervised data augmentation framework based on a residual generative adversarial network (GAN) to synthesize follow-up visits for baseline-only subjects. The model incorporates a monotonic brain change constraint to generate biologically plausible follow-up visits. The synthesized visits showed overall good agreement with real longitudinal follow-up visits in terms of direction of change. When combined with real longitudinal observations, the augmented data lead to consistent and measurable improvements in downstream continuous staging, as evidenced by significantly enhanced temporal preservation across real follow-up visits in held-out test data.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The primary contribution of this work is the introduction of SLOPE, a method designed to generate plausible PET images specifically for data augmentation tasks in machine learning applications within neuroimaging.
reviews.text_strengths: A key strength of the paper lies in its use of real PET data for training and validation, supported by a well-designed experimental setup that includes a dedicated holdout set.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The main weakness of the paper is that the longitudinal constraints embedded in the model introduce a strong bias toward disease progression in the generated images. As the reported results highlight, the generated images exhibit an unrealistic association that is not present in the real holdout data.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper could be strengthened by stratifying the results into MCI-AD converters versus MCI-stable subjects. If the proposed data augmentation algorithm improves conversion recall on the holdout dataset, this would provide strong evidence that the approach offers potential benefits for real-world clinical applications.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses the scarcity of longitudinal data in Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) studies by proposing a self-supervised data augmentation framework. The authors use a Residual Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to synthesize follow-up amyloid PET scans for subjects who only have a single baseline visit. The generator is constrained by a monotonicity assumption (amyloid accumulation is irreversible). The synthesized data is then used to train SLOPE, a continuous staging model. The authors report that this augmentation reduces the “violation ratio” (temporal inconsistency) in the staging scores on a held-out test set.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The problem of sparse longitudinal data in AD cohorts is clinically relevant.
2.The idea of incorporating biological priors (monotonicity) into generative models is interesting.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Biologically Invalid Assumption of Strict Monotonicity: The core innovation of this paper—enforcing a strict non-negative residual to ensure monotonic amyloid increase—is biologically flawed. While amyloid burden generally increases over the course of AD, it is not strictly monotonic at the individual voxel or regional level
2.Insufficient Validation of Generated Data Fidelity: The paper relies heavily on Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and cosine similarity of change vectors. FID is known to be insensitive to local structural changes and can be misleading in medical imaging. Cosine similarity measures direction but not magnitude or anatomical plausibility. There is no qualitative assessment (visual inspection by neuroradiologists) provided to confirm that the generated “follow-up” scans look like realistic AD progression. Without demonstrating that the synthetic images preserve anatomical integrity and realistic pathology spread, the claim of “biologically plausible” generation is unsupported.
3.Methodological Ambiguities: The description of the discriminator’s role is unclear. How does the discriminator distinguish between “real” follow-ups and “generated” follow-ups if the generated ones are forced to be monotonic while real ones contain noise? If the discriminator learns to reject noisy real samples in favor of clean synthetic ones, the model may be discarding valuable information about data variability.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Limited Novelty and Incremental Contribution:
1.Generative augmentation for medical imaging is a well-explored field. The combination of GANs with monotonic constraints has been explored in other contexts. The application to SLOPE is incremental. Furthermore, the paper does not adequately address why other, more robust methods for handling missing longitudinal data (such as mixed-effects models, multiple imputation, or trajectory modeling techniques specifically designed for sparse data) were not considered or compared. The proposed solution adds significant complexity (training a GAN) for a marginal gain in a specific metric (violation ratio) that may not translate to clinical utility (e.g., prediction of conversion to dementia). 
2.The proposed method imposes a rigid biological constraint (strict monotonicity) that does not align with the complexities of neuroimaging data and AD pathology. The resulting improvements in downstream staging appear to be artifacts of this constraint rather than genuine enhancements in disease modeling. Without validation against clinical endpoints or more robust baselines
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper describes a generative model for longitudinal amyloid PET data from people with Alzheimer’s disease. The motivation is to use the generative model to augment training data for a staging model. Experiments demonstrate viability of the generator and improvements in a learned staging model after including synthetic data in training.
reviews.text_strengths:
Well motivated and of high relevance.
A simple idea that seems to work reasonably well.
Results show a positive impact on the downstream model.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The technique (SLOPE) that motivates the work in the submission, and is used in the experiments to demonstrate benefit, it so far only published on biorxiv, so it is yet to be fully verified via peer review. It sounds sensible enough from the description in the paper, but it rather limits the demonstration of the power of the proposed generative model. The synthetic data the model produces would certainly be useful for other models like SLOPE. The paper would be substantially stronger if it showed performance improvements in other methods as well.
I found the experiment in section 4.1 a little difficult to appreciate. Unclear what we’re supposed to conclude from figure 2. How does this show that the generative model is doing something sensible when both baselines are flawed?
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Overall this is a reasonable submission. It is not a major contribution, but is a fairly standard data generation method that demonstrably improves training of a potentially useful model.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text: Reviewers are generally positive. It addresses a clinically relevant problem with methodologically interesting and novel approach and is well motivated. While Reviewer #2 mentions weaknesses and reviewer #3 finds the experiment in 4.1 not well enough explained, the work overall has added value to the MICCAI audience

author_feedback_text:
Monotonicity Constraint and Realism of Generated PET Data (R1, R2): We thank the reviewers for raising this important point. We agree that real longitudinal amyloid PET measurements are inherently noisy and may exhibit local or regional fluctuations across visits. Together with the limited number of MCI conversion cases, this presents a major challenge for robust staging of disease progression and may appear to conflict with the monotonicity constraint. In our framework, however, the goal is not to exactly reproduce noisy subject-specific future PET observations. Instead, we aim to generate future amyloid states that are biologically plausible, progression-consistent, and still close to the empirical PET distribution. As a result, the generated samples may deviate slightly from individual noisy observations, which is expected. These cleaner synthetic progression signals are intended to better guide the downstream staging model, helping it learn the underlying biological trajectory of amyloid accumulation rather than overfitting to noises or irregular fluctuations.
Additional Downstream Validation (R1, R3): We thank the reviewers for this valuable suggestion. In the current study, we focused on evaluating whether the proposed augmentation improves longitudinal consistency in continuous amyloid staging using SLOPE as the downstream model. We agree that additional validation across downstream tasks and models would provide a more comprehensive assessment of the framework. As the next step of this project, we will extend the evaluation to clinically relevant tasks such as MCI-to-AD conversion prediction and more downstream models beyond SLOPE.

title: Self-supervised Spline Autoencoder for Smooth Latent Dynamics in Echocardiography
abstract: Cardiac phase identification is important for assessing heart function in echocardiography, yet existing automatic approaches typically rely on supervised learning or strong structural assumptions. We show that self-supervised learning of smooth latent dynamics can enable phase-conditioned geometric analysis of cardiac motion. In this work, we present a Spline Autoencoder that learns temporally smooth and consistent evolutions of latent embeddings, capturing cardiac motion as low-rank dynamical structures. We discover a cardiac phase variable using a label-agnostic algorithm based on the spectral embedding of normalized latent trajectory velocities, enabling precise temporal localization of end-diastole (ED) and end-systole (ES) events. Evaluated on the EchoNet-Dynamic dataset, our method achieves a localization mean absolute error (MAE) of 2.3 frames (ED/ES MAEs of 2.7/3.6 frames after label-informed semantic assignment with 94.0% accuracy), which is competitive with supervised methods. Zero-shot evaluation on the EchoNet-Pediatric dataset demonstrates robust generalization across populations and imaging views, with a localization MAE of 3.0 frames. These results suggest that temporal smoothness and consistency are effective inductive priors for learning cardiac motion dynamics, yielding a latent geometry that supports precise phase-event localization, with lightweight calibration for semantic ED/ES assignment. Our code is available at https://github.com/LCJKwan/SplineAE-Cardiac.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes an unsupervised framework for cardiac phase discovery in echocardiography based on smooth latent dynamics. Its main contribution is a spline-based autoencoder that learns temporally smooth and consistent latent trajectories from echo videos without phase labels, combined with a dynamical phase discovery method that uses normalized latent velocities, spectral embedding, and phase-aligned projection to localize ED and ES.
reviews.text_strengths: The main strengths of the paper are the relevance of the problem, the coherent methodological pipeline, and the zero-shot evaluation on pediatric echocardiography. In particular, the idea of combining smooth spline-based latent trajectories with a dynamical phase discovery procedure is conceptually clear and reasonably well motivated. The zero-shot transfer results across populations and views are also a positive aspect of the experimental evaluation.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
While the latent trajectory learning and phase discovery stages are unsupervised, the final ED/ES semantic assignment uses a global ED–ES alignment axis computed from training-set ED and ES embeddings, which relies on label information.
The paper’s technical description could also be improved. For example, the encoder architecture is not described clearly enough in the main text, which weakens reproducibility.
Finally, although the results are competitive, the gain over the strongest prior unsupervised baseline is limited. On EchoNet-Dynamic, the pooled localization MAE improves only modestly over LMP, and the ES result is in fact clearly worse than LMP (3.6 vs. 2.0 frames), even though the overall pooled metric is slightly better. This makes the practical advantage less convincing than the headline result suggests.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The idea of learning smooth latent trajectories for phase discovery is reasonable, and the zero-shot pediatric evaluation is a positive aspect, but the overall contribution feels closer to an incremental refinement of existing unsupervised phase-analysis approaches than to a clearly new formulation.
A major factor in my score is that the “unsupervised” claim should be stated more carefully. Although the representation learning and phase discovery stages are unsupervised, the final ED/ES semantic assignment relies on a global ED–ES alignment axis computed from training-set ED and ES embeddings, which uses label information. In my view, this weakens the end-to-end unsupervised framing that is central to the paper’s positioning. 
I was also not fully convinced by the experimental margin over the strongest prior unsupervised baseline. On EchoNet-Dynamic, the pooled localization MAE is only modestly better than LMP, and the ES error is substantially worse than LMP, even though the headline localization number is slightly stronger. This makes the practical improvement less compelling than the overall presentation suggests. In addition, some parts of the technical description, such as the encoder design, are not described clearly enough, which further reduced my confidence.
Overall, I found the paper promising, but in its current form I see it as slightly below the acceptance threshold.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a Spline AutoEncoder framework for the unsupervised identification of end-diastole and end-systole in echocardiography videos. By fitting a spline to the latent space, authors enforcing temporal smoothness through a second-order finite-difference penalty. A novel dynamical phase discovery algorithm is introduced, which uses spectral embedding of normalized latent velocities to recover a circular phase variable. Event localization is then performed by identifying the peak and valley of the projected latent trajectory onto a 2D plane using Partial Least Squares and an a SVD decomposition. The method was evaluated using and internal and external dataset (EchoNet-Dynamic and EchoNet-Pediatric). Authors perform a small ablation analysis.
reviews.text_strengths:
— The method shows some degree of novelty by enforcing temporal smoothness through fitting a spline to the latent trajectory. Additional, authors propose to use the normalized velocities in the tangent space for spectral embedding to handle cyclic dynamics in high-dimensional latent spaces while remaining more stable than position-based methods.
— The zero-shot evaluation on pediatric data (both A4CH and PSAX views) demonstrates that the model captures fundamental cardiac motion geometry rather than just dataset-specific appearance.
— Competitive Unsupervised Performance
— The spline-based formulation combined with the cross-reconstruction provides a mathematically grounded way to enforce temporal consistency without requiring periodic assumptions.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
— As noted by the authors, the recovered phase is invariant to global rotation. The reliance on a post-training calibration using a global average vector to distinguish ED from ES introduces a small supervised component (or at least a requirement for a labeled reference set) to achieve final labeling which goes against the main goal of the paper. It is not well explained how the authors achieve this lightweight post-training.
— While localization is stable, the labeling accuracy drops significantly (from 93.8% to 83.2%) when moving from A4CH to PSAX views in the pediatric dataset. This suggests the “global ED-ES axis” is not entirely view-invariant.
— While λ spline is ablated, there is limited discussion on the impact of the number of control points (n_ctrl =16) or the spline degree (p=3). It is unclear how these choices affect the capture of high-frequency motion details or arrhythmias.
— Results should include 95% confidence intervals (for example using bootstrap), especially for the pediatric zero-shot results in the errors (Table 1 and 2).
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Constructive Comments:
— Include 95% CI.
— A brief analysis of the inference time per video would be beneficial, as solving the normal equations for splines is efficient but spectral embedding can be computationally intensive for very long sequences.
— In Figure 3, the authors show a label assignment error. A more detailed discussion or a confusion matrix on which types of heart rates or pathologies (e.g., tachycardia) lead to these flips would be clinically valuable.
— It would be interesting to see an ablation comparing the PLS-based projection (Step 3 in Algorithm 1) against a standard PCA projection to further justify the “phase-conditioned” aspect.
— In Fig 1, clarify if the partitions are mutually exclusive or if they can overlap in time, as this affects the difficulty of the cross-reconstruction task

The method proposed shows competitive Unsupervised Performance and some novelty

The paper tackles a phase detection problem with an interesting idea. However, it is critically undermined by an inaccurate central premise: the unsupervised claim is technically incorrect for the end-task. The quantitative advantage is marginal, and in a key metric, it is worse. The paper falls below the acceptance threshold due to a flawed central claim and insufficient performance advantage.

The authors address well previous concerns and all reviewers agreed to accept this paper.
The rebuttal addressed reviewers’ concerns and all three reviewers moved to accept post-rebuttal.

The paper presents an interesting self-supervised representation-learning approach for cardiac phase analysis in echocardiography. The main concern was that the original “unsupervised” framing was overstated because the final ED/ES semantic assignment uses a training-set ED/ES alignment axis. The rebuttal addresses this issue constructively and after the rebuttal, all reviewers moved to acceptance. The evidence support accept. Congratulations!

author_feedback_text:
We are grateful for the valuable feedback from all reviewers. We respond to the suggestions and concerns below:
(R1/R2/R3) Unsupervised claim and paper positioning
We agree that wording around “unsupervised” should be framed more cautiously. While SplineAE training and localizing trajectory extrema are label-free, resolving the semantic ambiguity of ED/ES on detected extrema requires label information. We clarify that there is no fine-tuning or gradient-based optimization on labels. Instead, we compute the sign of the dot product between the extrema axis and the training-set global ED/ES axis, as described in Section 2.3.
Our intended contribution is primarily representational, as described in Section 1: Our self-supervised SplineAE discovers low-rank loop-like latent dynamics from echocardiography. Moreover, instead of enforcing a fixed 2D latent bottleneck [15] or explicit periodicity constraints [6], we rely only on temporal smoothness and consistency. Label-free latent geometry discovery of cardiac phase is supported by topology analysis, qualitative observation of latent loops, cardiac event localization, and zero-shot pediatric transfer.
ED/ES detection is a downstream task to evaluate clinical relevance of learnt representations. To reflect this positioning, we will rephrase the title to: “Self-supervised Spline Autoencoder for Smooth Latent Dynamics in Echocardiography”. We will revise the wording of manuscript content accordingly, to clearly explain self-supervised training, label-agnostic phase extraction with event localization, and label-informed ED/ES semantic assignment.
(R1) Performance margin and ES error
In addition to relaxed constraints during representation learning, our label-free localization performance is competitive. Localization error is equal to pooled error with perfect ED/ES labelling. Meanwhile, ED/ES MAE degradation are caused by semantic label flips after otherwise accurate localization, where errors are as large as the ED-ES interval.
(R2/R3) Failure case
We observe localization failure when a coherent latent loop does not emerge, often in low-quality videos with chambers moving out of view. Pediatric PSAX ED/ES MAE rises due to the 10% reduction in label assignment accuracy from A4C, as semantic directions in latent space may shift with view. However, the label-agnostic localization derived from trajectory geometry remains stable, as the MAE remains at 3.0 frames.
(R2/R3) Hyperparameter choices
Cubic splines balance smoothness and expressivity, while nctrl=16 for 64-frame partitions, approximately 1 control point per 4 frames, captures curvature without fitting frame-level noise. K=15 empirically balances preserving cross-cycle semantic neighbours against over-connecting temporally adjacent samples, which depends partly on frame rate. We clarify that splines are only used in training; inference uses encoder embeddings directly in Algorithm 1.
(R1) Reproducibility
The full architecture and implementation will be included in the code repository release. Briefly, the encoder uses residual blocks [3×3 conv, GroupNorm, GELU, 3×3 conv], with 2 residual blocks before each downsampling stage, and 5 such stages before average pooling.
(R2) Nearest-hit localization
The reviewer’s interpretation is correct. This protocol follows LMP [15] for EchoNet Dynamic under the same sparse-label limitation, so the comparison is like-to-like. Qualitative inspection of videos and Fig.3 suggest that our method aligns trajectory extrema to ED/ES events without dense over-prediction.
(R3) Other concerns
We reported mean±SD, that could be reported as 95CI for clarity. Cross-partitions are mutually exclusive if the video is longer than 127 frames, but may randomly overlap if the video is too short. We also hypothesize that model errors or geometry irregularities may correlate with clinical pathologies. However, the EchoNet datasets lack pathology labels. We believe this is an important direction for future work.

title: Self-supervised Temporal Regularization for Landmark-Based Cardiac Segmentation with Automatic AHA Regional Mapping
abstract: Graph-based cardiac segmentation with implicit anatomical correspondences provides topological guarantees and population-level analysis capabilities, but models trained on independent frames of image sequences exhibit temporal discontinuities that affect reliable clinical measurements, particularly in cardiac ultrasound. In this work, we introduce self-supervised temporal regularization as a post-training refinement stage that exploits the temporal coherence in image sequences to enforce consistent cardiac segmentation and motion estimation over time, without requiring per-frame annotations. By penalizing velocity and acceleration discontinuities across consecutive frames, our method achieves temporally consistent segmentations while maintaining the learned anatomical correspondences. We further leverage these correspondences to automatically map landmarks to the AHA 17-segment clinical standard, enabling standardized regional assessment and detection of pathological myocardial motion patterns. Validation on CAMUS dataset demonstrates the clinical utility of combining temporal consistency with automatic regional mapping. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/david-montalvoo/MaskHybridGNet-TempReg.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents work based on the segmentation algorithm proposed in Reference [6]. A self-supervised temporal regularization is introduced as a post-training refinement stage that uses temporal coherence in image sequences to ensure consistent cardiac segmentation and motion estimation over time without requiring annotations for each frame. The proposed method produces temporally consistent segmentations while preserving learned anatomical correspondences. These correspondences are then leveraged to automatically map landmarks to the AHA’s 17-segment clinical standard, which enables a standardized assessment of regional cardiac function.
