reviews.text_strengths: The paper is well-written. The proposed method is well-described and appears as reasonably novel, maybe even as pioneering, regarding work along the “skin-brain axis”. Experiments and ablations are extensive, results look convincing.
reviews.text_weaknesses: Apart from the fact that authors don’t mention their intended publication of the method’s code, I only see one major weakness in the authors’ work: It is not immediately clear to me why the steps from transforming tabular skin reports to textual skin reports to text embeddings are really necessary. Since the authors use XGBoost as a tabular, text-only baseline and since the results appear quite competitive with the textual, text-only baselines, couldn’t they likewise have used XGBoost outputs as the inputs to an adapter, similar to how they currently use the text model outputs? Maybe this could have provided a more lightweight alternative, and maybe this could be discussed as an alternative approach.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Abstract: Though admittedly pretty common, the abbreviation “AUC” should be introduced somewhere.
Method (Sect. 2): What is the size (in pixels) of the input images?
Method (Sect. 2): Did the authors consider alternative outputs other than binary (“at risk”/”not at risk”)? While I understand the use of a binary classifier for introducing the method, I doubt the output’s clinical relevance. Maybe classifications or regressions regarding more fine-grained clinical conditions could be an alternative here? This is by all means a question that I just ask out of curiosity, still maybe the authors could consider it for their Discussion or their potential future work.
Residual fusion (Sect. 2.2):
– The text introduces f_uv as a “linear projection”, while, if I understand correctly, the corresponding blue box in Fig. 2 is labeled “MLP”. An MLP, however, is in general not a linear projection (e. g. through its activation functions). So which one is it, a linear projection or an MLP? Same for P_t. 
– z_text, z_fused: Since “text” and “fused” are not variables themselves, they should not be italicized.
Implementation details (Sect. 3.1):
– What activation function is used in the MLP?
– an
initial
learning rate is given for the optimizer, which implies to me a learning rate schedule (i. e. an adjusted learning rate over time). So either the used learning rate schedule should be added (together with its remaining choice of parameters) or the word “initial” should be dropped.
Baseline comparisons (Sect. 3.2):
– “Encoding … with LLMs consistently outperforms … XGBoost” – I think “consistently” is an overstatement here, given that only 2 out of 6 LLMs (w. r. t. F1) or 4 out of 6 LLMs (w. r. t. AUC) actually outperform XGBoost (see Table 1). Authors should consider rephrasing. 
– “Statistical differences are primarily observed in AUC rather than F1, suggesting differences in ranking rather than fixed-threshold performance. “ – I do not understand this sentence. In particular, how does AUC reflect “differences in ranking” (what is the latter supposed to mean in the first place), while F1 should reflect “fixed-threshold performance” (again, what is the latter supposed to mean in the first place)? Authors should perhaps consider rephrasing. 
– “The advantage of multimodal integration lies in … computational efficiency. “ – How does multimodal integration provide efficiency; in particular, as compared to what? Authors should consider a clarification. 
– “Compared with end-to-end VLMs such as Qwen2.5-VL (AUC std ± 10.20%), HARF demonstrates more stable behavior (AUC std ± 4.32%)” – Did the authors intentionally not mention Qwen3-VL here, which to my understanding of the authors’ definition of stability, actually shows a
more stable
behavior than HARF (AUC std ± 3.86%)? If so, what was the reason for this nonmention? Authors should consider adapting their corresponding observation.

As already mentioned above, I think the method is reasonably novel (even pioneering perhaps), the evaluation is sound and extensive, and the results are convincing. I am pretty positive that authors can refute my only major concern via an extended discussion or, if necessary, via rebuttal.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose Skin2Mind, which they position as the first multimodal framework for mental health risk screening based on facial skin images and structured skin reports. The method combines modern domain-specific dermatology foundation models for image representation learning with LLM-based encoding of structured skin reports. To integrate the multimodal embeddings, the authors introduce a Hierarchical Anchor Residual Fusion (HARF) strategy, which aims to reduce inter-modal redundancy and stabilize fusion by treating UV facial images as the anchor modality and incorporating the remaining modalities through gated residual pathways.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) the paper explores a novel and unconventional application setting. The use of facial skin phenotypes and structured skin reports for mental health risk screening is, to my knowledge, highly original and makes the paper stand out from more conventional multimodal medical AI studies. The work is interesting because it attempts to test whether current foundation models can capture the relationship between objective facial skin phenotypes and individual-level mental health risk.
2) the paper proposes a new multimodal fusion mechanism, HARF, which is a meaningful technical contribution. The hierarchical anchor-residual design is well motivated by the fact that the modalities are partially redundant, since the images and reports are derived from the same acquisition pipeline. 
3) the paper makes good use of modern pretrained backbones and includes a reasonably broad comparison of unimodal and multimodal baselines, including vision-only, text-only, and VLM-based approaches. The inclusion of ablation studies across fusion strategies and modality choices strengthens the empirical section.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
A major weakness is that the biological and clinical justification of the core hypothesis remains somewhat limited. The paper makes an ambitious claim about the relationship between skin phenotypes and mental health risk, but the supporting biological motivation is not yet fully convincing. In my view, this type of claim would benefit from stronger support from more established biomedical and clinical literature.
A second weakness is the small and imbalanced dataset. The study is conducted on only 192 subjects, with a substantial class imbalance, which raises concerns about the robustness and generalizability of the findings. Given the novelty and sensitivity of the proposed application, stronger validation on a larger and more diverse cohort would be important.
Another concern is that the paper criticizes conventional mental health screening for relying on self-reported questionnaires and clinical interviews as subjective tools, but the proposed labels are themselves based on DSM-5-derived questionnaires. This weakens the claim that the method provides a substantially more objective alternative, since the supervisory signal still originates from questionnaire-based assessment.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I rate this paper 4/6 because it is novel, ambitious, and methodologically interesting, and it presents a creative use of modern foundation models to test a new hypothesis in medicine. In particular, the paper is strong in its use of multimodal learning, its proposed fusion mechanism, and its comparison with several relevant baselines. The ablation studies are also helpful and suggest that the proposed fusion design contributes meaningfully beyond simpler alternatives.
At the same time, I do not score it higher because the paper makes a relatively strong clinical and biological claim on the basis of a small, imbalanced cohort and labels that are still questionnaire-derived. Thus, while the technical contribution is interesting and the experimental study is promising, the current evidence is not yet sufficient to fully support the broader implications suggested by the paper. I would have liked to see stronger biological grounding, validation on a larger dataset, and a more clinically detailed evaluation setting.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
