author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and Area Chairs for their constructive feedback and for recognizing the novelty and interdisciplinary potential of Skin2Mind. We have carefully revised the camera-ready version to improve clarity, reproducibility, and alignment between the manuscript text and the implemented framework, while keeping all experiments, numerical results, and conclusions unchanged.
First, following reviewer suggestions regarding framing and interpretation [R2], we refined several statements throughout the manuscript to avoid overstating “objectivity” in mental health assessment. We clarified that DSM-5 labels remain questionnaire-derived clinical measures and revised the Introduction and Abstract to position Skin2Mind as a complementary computational screening framework based on quantitative facial skin phenotypes rather than a replacement for standard psychiatric assessment. We also refined the discussion comparing AUC and F1 to clarify the distinction between ranking performance and fixed-threshold classification behaviour [R1].
Second, we improved methodological clarity in Section 2.Reviewer comments correctly noted that several textual descriptions were inconsistent with the architecture illustrated in Fig. 1 [R1]. We therefore updated the manuscript so that the written description precisely matches the implementation used during training and evaluation. Specifically, projection and gate components previously described as “linear layers” are now correctly described as two-layer MLP modules, consistent with the implemented method shown in Fig. 1.Additionally, the description of the text-side fusion component has been clarified for consistency with the implementation. We also added a brief rationale for using Qwen2.5-7B instead of the DermLIP text encoder and conventional tabular models such as XGBoost for long structured reports [R1, R3]. Our skin reports contain more than 400 heterogeneous descriptors with compositional semantic relationships across pigmentation, structural aging, barrier sensitivity, and pilosebaceous activity. These reports exceed the short-caption scope of CLIP-style text encoders, while tabular models treat features largely independently and cannot fully capture higher-order semantic interactions across descriptors. We therefore used frozen LLM embeddings to obtain richer semantic representations of the structured reports. These are documentation clarifications only: no code, hyperparameters, datasets, or experiments were modified, and all reported results (including the headline AUC of 81.66%) remain identical to the accepted version.
Third, we addressed reproducibility and presentation concerns raised by the reviewers [R1, R3]. We added the public code repository, clarified implementation details (e.g., constant learning rate, ReLU activations), corrected several notation inconsistencies and figure labels, and revised parts of the baseline discussion to make comparisons more precise and balanced. We also added the required ethics approval, informed consent, acknowledgments, disclosure statements, and final de-anonymized author information in accordance with the Springer LNCS camera-ready guidelines.
Overall, all revisions are minor clarifications, wording refinements, or mandatory camera-ready updates. No new experiments were added, no results were changed, and the scientific conclusions of the paper remain unchanged.
Thank you again for the valuable feedback and for supporting this interdisciplinary direction at the intersection of multimodal AI, dermatology, and mental health screening.

title: SLICE-MIL: Counterfactual Semantic Anchoring of Disentangled Evidence for Child-Pugh Grading
abstract: Child-Pugh (CP) grading, a widely used clinical standard for therapeutic decision-making in hepatocellular carcinoma, integrates biochemical and clinical markers to assess hepatic reserve. Estimating CP grade from routinely acquired contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) may provide opportunistic, complementary imaging evidence and facilitate investigation of associations between structural imaging phenotypes and clinically assessed hepatic reserve. However, inferring CP-related functional status from structural imaging requires overcoming a fundamental structure-function semantic gap. Because CP grade is determined by multiple biochemical and clinical factors, its imaging manifestations are heterogeneous and deeply entangled. Conventional Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) architectures do not explicitly decouple these complex representations, making them susceptible to associative shortcut learning rather than capturing stage-relevant pathological patterns. To explicitly model this structure-function mapping, we propose SLICE-MIL, a spatial-logical framework for ordinal evidence disentanglement. Structurally, an anatomical mask-guided mechanism explicitly decouples the entangled intra- and extra-hepatic features. Functionally, a hierarchical evidence disentanglement module employs representation-level counterfactual ablations to anchor stage-specific semantics, encouraging the decoupled representations to align with the progression logic of CP deterioration. Multicenter validation demonstrates that explicitly bridging this semantic gap mitigates reliance on spurious correlations, substantially improving cross-domain robustness and interpretability.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Causal Inference / Counterfactual Reasoning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: SLICE‑MIL addresses the structure‑function semantic gap and feature entanglement issues that exist in assessing Child‑Pugh grade from CT images. Through anatomy‑guided spatial decoupling, orthogonal decomposition, residual routing, and counterfactual semantic anchoring, it achieves explicit decoupling and causal regularization of ordered pathological evidence, thereby improving cross‑domain generalization and interpretability.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Separate intra/extra-hepatic features via anatomy-gated queries to reduce cross-regional confounding. 
2.Orthogonal decomposition, residual routing, and counterfactual semantic anchoring achieve causal regularization of ordered pathological evidence
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.anatomical disentanglement only separate the lesion and liver parenchyma, maybe more detailed anatomical disentanglement (liver segements, portal vein and so on). 
2.It’s hard to understand the Logical Dependency Graph. what is difference compare with SCM?
3.Through counterfactual intervention, the model transform the CP classifier to a binary classify task. What’s more, the three manually defined classification rules directly hard-coded clinical priors into the loss, rather than the true causal relationships learned by the model.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Despite some methodological issues, the overall approach is sound. The implemention of DO operation method is novel, and the experiments are thorough.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose SLICE-MIL, a spatial-logical framework based on Multiple Instance Learning for the assessment of Child-Pugh grading using contrast-enhanced CT scans. The method introduces an Anatomy-Driven Dual-Query Attention for spatial disentanglement. Overall the method appears novel, but I have some major comments.
reviews.text_strengths:
(1) The authors framed the clinical challenge as a “tructure-function semantic gap and try to solve the issue of shortcut learning prevalent in standard MIL architectures.
(2) The proposed ADDA used clinical priors to separate feature extraction, preventing the early cross-contamination of visual signals. They also applied counterfactual masking to guide the model, which is novel.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(1) The authors justify the use of an MIL architecture by stating that 2D CNNs suffer from label noise and 3D CNNs face a strict resolution-context trade-off. However, these claims are not empirically validated in the manuscript. In Table 1, the proposed SLICE-MIL is exclusively compared against other generic MIL frameworks. To convincingly demonstrate the necessity of this complex MIL approach, the authors must include standard non-MIL baselines, such as a 3D ResNet or a 2.5D CNN taking the abdominal/liver region (or dual-stream inputs) as data. Without these, the superiority of the MIL paradigm for this specific task remains unproven.
(2) In the abstract, the authors claim that deriving the CP grade directly from CECT enables “opportunistic, non-invasive profiling of hepatic reserve.” I think this claim is overstated and misrepresents the clinical reality of the Child-Pugh score. The CP grade is a multi-source metric heavily reliant on biochemical blood biomarker, and neurological assessment. CECT can only capture morphological changes. Predicting systemic biochemical functional deficits solely from morphological features relies on correlation rather than direct measurement. The clinical utility claims should be toned down, acknowledging the fundamental information gap between imaging morphology and blood-based biomarkers.
(3) The propsoed spatial disentanglement module heavily relies on the upstream extraction of binary liver and extrahepatic masks, presumably generated by TotalSegmentator. In my experiments of such models, I found in real-world clinical scenarios involving advanced cirrhosis or massive hepatocellular carcinoma (conditions frequently seen in patients assessed with the CP score), the liver and spleen are often severely deformed, leading to high failure or inaccuracy rates in automated segmentation tools. The authors should address how sensitive the downstream orthogonal decomposition and routing mechanisms are to upstream mask inaccuracies. An ablation study or a robustness analysis is necessary.
(4) The authors use terms like do-calculus, causal grounding, and counterfactual interventions to describe the proposed semantic anchoring. In my opionin, they were rfeature masking combined with label modification. While this is a highly effective and good regularization technique, it may not constitute strong causal inference. Could the authors clarify the terminology to better reflect the mathematical nature of the operations, in order to avoid over-claiming causal discoveries?
(5) Minor points: In Section 2.1, the definition of Q assumes the masks are quasi-disjoint. A brief statistical summary would strengthen this assumption; Please clarify the computational overhead introduced by the QR decomposition and dynamic routing; In Fig.1 their is Anatomy-Driven Differential Attention, but it should be Anatomy-Driven Dual-Query Attention; ‘Consequently, Current’, C should be c.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I keep open in raising my score if the concerns are explained.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
Thank you for the authors’ response. I appreciate that the authors have partially addressed my concerns; however, several issues remained.
I agree that patient-level Child-Pugh labels fit a weakly supervised MIL formulation. I also acknowledge the practical challenges of training 3D models under heterogeneous CT acquisition protocols. However, I do not think this fully resolves the concern regarding missing non-MIL baselines. Standard 2.5D or 3D models can still be trained with patient-level supervision, for example through scan-level aggregation, liver/abdomen cropping, or volume-level classification. I understand that the MICCAI rebuttal policy does not allow additional experiments at this stage, but similar liver fibrosis staging studies have included broader baseline comparisons, including single-view, whole-image, and multi-view methods [1,2]. Therefore, the current rebuttal justifies the motivation for using MIL, but does not empirically establish that MIL is superior to reasonable non-MIL alternatives.
Regarding segmentation robustness, the response is partially convincing but still limited. The use of downsampled masks may reduce sensitivity to minor boundary errors, but the rebuttal does not provide direct evidence of robustness against systematic segmentation failures. This limitation should be explicitly acknowledged in the final manuscript, preferably in the discussion or conclusion.
[1] Gao, Z., Liu, Y., Wu, F., Shi, N., Shi, Y., & Zhuang, X. (2023). A reliable and interpretable framework of multi-view learning for liver fibrosis staging. In International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention (pp. 178–188).
[2] Liu, Y., Gao, Z., Shi, N., Wu, F., Shi, Y., Chen, Q., & Zhuang, X. (2025). MERIT: Multi-view evidential learning for reliable and interpretable liver fibrosis staging. Medical Image Analysis, 102, 103507.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper proposes a Slice-MIL framework for predicting Child-Pugh grade from contrast-enhanced CT scans, aiming to enable non-invasive estimation of hepatic functional reserve in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma. The authors highlight that Child-Pugh scoring is clinically important for treatment planning but is traditionally based on both biochemical and clinical parameters, making direct imaging-based prediction challenging.
To address this, the method treats each CT scan as a bag of slices and applies a multiple-instance learning framework with anatomy-guided feature disentanglement and counterfactual reasoning. The proposed approach separates intrahepatic and extrahepatic features using anatomical masks and further applies mechanisms intended to reduce shortcut learning and enforce more clinically meaningful representations. The model is evaluated on a multicenter dataset with internal and external validation, showing improved performance and robustness compared to baseline approaches.
reviews.text_strengths:
The study addresses a clinically important problem, as Child-Pugh scoring is central to management decisions in hepatocellular carcinoma.
The attempt to derive systemic hepatic function from CT imaging is innovative and clinically relevant, particularly for opportunistic assessment.
Use of a multicenter dataset with external validation improves the strength of evidence for generalizability.
The anatomical masking and slice-level learning approach is consistent with clinical interpretation, where radiologists assess both parenchymal changes and signs of portal hypertension.
The focus on reducing shortcut learning and improving robustness is appropriate for real-world deployment scenarios.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The study lacks clear clinical validation of predictions against standard Child-Pugh scoring components, particularly biochemical and clinical parameters.
It is not fully clear how well the model performs in clinically ambiguous or borderline cases, where grading is subjective.
The reliance on CT-only inference may limit applicability, since Child-Pugh grading is inherently a multimodal clinical construct.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
How does the model perform in borderline or mixed presentations, where clinical scoring is less definitive?
Can the model distinguish between hepatic parenchymal dysfunction and extrahepatic causes of ascites or portal hypertension?
How robust is the method to variations in CT acquisition protocols across centers?

The paper addresses an important clinical problem of predicting Child-Pugh grade from CT scans, which has strong relevance for treatment planning in liver cancer patients. The proposed Slice-MIL framework is well motivated and aligns with clinical reasoning by separating liver-related and extrahepatic features and using anatomical guidance for prediction. The use of a multicenter dataset with external validation adds strength to the results and suggests good generalizability. Overall, the work is clinically meaningful, methodologically sound, and shows clear improvement over baseline approaches, making it suitable for acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
The three reviewers gave two weak reject recommendations and one accept. Given the split opinions and some rather valid concerns raised, the paper would benefit from a rebuttal (clarify the missing baseline comparisons, rephrase the causal claims, and address segmentation robustness).

One reviewer has increased their scores and one reviewer has lowered their score. My impression from the paper also remains somewhat mixed. Given the importance of the clinical application, I will still recommend an accept given the authors pay close attention to R2 post-rebuttal comment and implement the requested clarifications in the camera-ready (if ultimately accepted).

The decision is to accept the paper. It addresses a clinically relevant problem by proposing a novel framework to map structural imaging to functional clinical scores. In the rebuttal, the authors effectively justified their architectural choices, clarified their terminology, and resolved concerns regarding segmentation robustness.

After rebuttal, the reviewer opinions lean positive but remain mixed. Reviewer #1 changed to Accept, and Reviewer #3 already recommended acceptance, emphasizing the clinical relevance, multicenter evaluation, external validation, and reasonable anatomy-guided MIL design. However, Reviewer #2 maintains Reject because the rebuttal does not fully resolve the lack of non-MIL baselines, such as 2.5D/3D or scan-level aggregation models trained with patient-level supervision, and provides limited direct evidence for robustness against systematic segmentation failures.
Overall, the paper is clinically meaningful and methodologically interesting, but still has unresolved limitations in baseline completeness, segmentation robustness, and the clinical scope of CT-only Child-Pugh prediction. I therefore recommend acceptance, provided that these limitations and overclaims are clearly addressed in the final version. The authors should provide the full open-source implementation to improve the reproducibility and broader impact of the paper.

author_feedback_text:
Thanks for the valuable feedback. We are encouraged by the recognition of the clinical relevance(R3), methodological novelty(R1,R2)and thorough evaluation(R1,R3).Below we address the main concerns.
Q1(MR,R2):Rationale for MIL
We agree that including systematic 2D/2.5D/3D baselines could make the argument more complete, but we didn’t include because they are not suitable to this task:
1.2D/2.5D models lack slice-level gold-standard labels; individual slices often contain only partial evidence.
2.3D models face computational trade-offs and are sensitive to variations in slice thickness, spacing, and sequence length, making them less suitable for CT scans with heterogeneous protocols.
In early exploration, we ran systematic 2D/2.5D/3D experiments. The results confirmed these principles. MIL performs weakly supervised learning at the patient level, matching CP grading’s multi-source nature and enabling interpretable slice aggregation. Additionally, our proposed SLICE-MIL is lightweight, with only 1.26M additional parameters (+4.5%) and 0.087G extra FLOPs (+1.9%).); QR decomposition adds no inference overhead once the projection is fixed; dynamic routing uses linear-complexity gating.
Q2(MR,R1,R2):Causal claims and Logical Dependency Graph(LDG)
R1 referred to Structural Causal Model (SCM), which is a mathematical framework that represents causal relationships between variables using structural equations and a directed acyclic graph (DAG). SCM assumes that the true variables are observable with clearly defined causal paths, but for Child-Pugh grading these variables cannot be directly observed from imaging, making it impossible to define explicit causal paths or structural equations. The LDG in SLICE-MIL is a visualization of the latent embedding’s logical disentanglement, not a DAG. Instead, we construct a latent-space representation to stage-specific CP increments, using counterfactual ablations to functional deterioration logic, maintaining three-class classification. Due to the multi-source nature of CP assessment, the model would struggle to learn the progression logic directly from CT-only data without these constraints. 
R2 mentioned “do-calculus” and “counterfactual interventions,” which in our method correspond to latent-space ablations that guide stage-specific progression. This implements a form of weak causal inference, regularizing stage-specific progression and reducing shortcut learning, rather than performing strong causal inference on the specific clinical variables. We treat these rules as weak causal priors with clinical guidance, rather than strict causal discoveries. This design aims to help bridge the structure–function semantic gap in CP grading. We apologize for the Fig.1 labeling error-“Causal grounding”,it will be corrected to “semantic anchoring”, consistent with the Fig.1 caption and the manuscript.
Q3(MR,R1,R2):Segmentation robustness
Our original intention is to design the model without relying on fine anatomical structures. Simply distinguishing body regions and liver parenchyma is sufficient. TotalSegmentator achieves a Dice score of ~0.94 for liver segmentation, and minor boundary errors in malignant cirrhosis or small tumors do not affect downstream processing, as the model incorporates all regions. We designed ADDA uses the masks only as regional guidance at a downsampled 7×7 resolution without pixel-level constraints. Experiments show downstream modules performed independently.
Q4(R2,R3):Clinical scope
As R3 noted, CP grading indeed relies on multiple modalities, but our work is limited to exploring CECT features related to CP, not as a substitute for standard assessment. We thank R3 for highlighting borderline cases, CP components, and etiology, and will include these clinical considerations in the discussion of the final manuscript. Further experimental exploration will be addressed in future work.
The final manuscript will incorporate these revisions.The code will be released upon acceptance.

title: SlideGuard: WSI Artifact Detection Benchmark
abstract: To ensure the highest quality in cancer research and computer aided diagnostics in computational pathology, Whole Slide Image (WSI) quality should be carefully monitored. While several open-source Quality Control (QC) tools exist, their comparative performance remains largely unaudited. In this work, we present the first independent, cross-species benchmark for WSI QC solutions focused on the critical task of automated artifact detection. Recognizing that model generalization is often hindered by narrow training data, we curated a diverse artifact-centric dataset featuring 11 distinct artifact types across 6 tissue types, 2 species, and 4 independent data sources. We evaluate both pixel-level segmentation and patch-level classification methods, normalizing their outputs and comparing them to expert-annotated WSIs. Performance is quantified using Dice score, accuracy, precision, and recall within tissue containing region. Our results reveal a substantial performance gap; average artifact detection Dice scores do not exceed 0.6, with significant performance variability across dataset subcategories. To support ongoing development, we release our dataset at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20339462 and our benchmarking tool at https://www.codabench.org/competitions/16457.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces a novel H&E-stained WSI dataset designed to investigate the performance of artifact detection methods, benchmarks several existing methods, and provides a comprehensive analysis of the results.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper is very well written and easy to follow. Its organization is sound.
The authors designed the first (soon to-be) publicly available dataset for artifact detection, filling an important gap in the highly unstandardized digital pathology ecosystem. Furthermore, the dataset covers multiple organs (and indications) and species, with data originating from three sources for human WSIs and one source for mouse WSIs. This enables the benchmarking of artifact detection methods in a non-trivial and realistic setting. In addition to slides containing artifacts, the authors also included near-perfect slides, as negative controls.
The benchmark itself is convincing; the authors evaluate the main relevant methods, and account for the many discrepancies between existing methods (e. g. pixel-level segmentation of artifacts versus patch-level classification, or inconsistencies in artifact-type labels). The chosen metrics are relevant, and the results section includes comments on the limitations of these metrics in the context of the benchmark.
The discussion section is thorough, suggests guidelines to drive the community forward and addresses the limitations of the work (e. g. partial annotation subjectivity).
reviews.text_weaknesses:
While the paper does not suffer from major weaknesses, we believe it could benefit from the following clarifications:
The central claim that artifacts « impair the performance of automated algorithms » is currently backed by a single citation from 2021.Given the significant progress of computational pathology in the last 5 years (e. g. the paper cited by the authors does not use any pathology foundation models, which are now the backbone of most modern methods), it would be valuable to include more recent studies. Recent artifact detection methods, for instance, may provide more information on this topic.
How the Dice score and other metrics are computed across settings is partially unclear.
For instance, the authors state « Artifact detection performance was quantified using class-specific Dice scores, accuracy, precision, and recall.  » but accuracy is not computed, and the following sentence can be found slightly below « Due to divergent artifact taxonomies among the benchmarked methods, class-specific precision and Dice score calculations were infeasible.  ». This discrepancy likely stems from the fact that « class » equates to artifact type in the second statement, and « class » equates to artifact or not in the first, but this is initially confusing for the reader. Likewise, the subsequent sentence uses the term « label-agnostic recall » to indicate the recall for the artifact class. Standardizing the nomenclature would make the paper easier to read.
The authors state « To compare methods producing artifact masks (pixel-level) and those calculating per-patch predictions, ground truth was discretized to each patch-level method’s native grid; a patch was labeled as an artifact if annotation coverage exceeded 25%.  » Does this mean that segmentation methods are evaluated with a Dice score computed pixel-wise over the full WSI (or is there a per-patch computation averaged across the slide ?) and that the Dice is computed patch-wise across the full WSI for patch-level classification methods ? Likewise, how was the 25% cut-off chosen ?
If possible, given the constrained MICCAI format and available information, it would be interesting to include the magnification used for all benchmarked methods and the sets of classes in the comparison table (Table 1). Additionally (again, if possible), it would be helpful to indicate explicitly the training sources of each of the methods (as opposed to only providing the number) as to enable the detection of a possible over-fitting to the training set artifacts. This would also better contextualize the discussion subsection around the fuzzy mapping between nominal magnification and resolution in MPP.
The authors state « High recall for artifact categories not included in a model’s native label set indicates either cross-class false positives or a generalized sensitivity to morphological deviations from artifact-free tissue.  ». Having the sets of classes for each method explicitly stated or via an asterisk added to the per-artifact recall table for instance (for the cases where the artifact type does not exist for a given method) would enable the reader to understand the situations in this actually happens compared to situations where the method is successfully able to point-out the specific artifact type.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I recommend an Accept for this submission.
The authors present a valuable contribution to the computational pathology community by introducing the first publicly available dataset for WSI artifact detection. The dataset covers a comprehensive range of tissue types and centers across two species, providing a realistic setting for QA methods. The subsequent benchmarking study is rigorous.
Although there are a few minor points that could benefit from clarifications, the paper does not suffer from any major weaknesses.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: In this paper, the authors curated a novel benchmark dataset focused on the task of automated WSI artifact detection, comprising of 6 tissue types, 2 species, and 4 independent data sources. This data also contains pixel-level annotations of the artifacts. Additionally, they also evaluated pixel-level segmentation, and patch-level classification with this dataset and compared them to expert annotated WSIs.
reviews.text_strengths:
Motivation: This paper addresses a major challenge in the field of digital pathology. Artifacts are often found in WSIs and there are several automated QC methods (histoQC, pathprofiler, DKL, TCNN, etc.), each with its own limitations. Such a curated dataset would aid in the development of robust artifact-detection and quantification algorithms.
Rich dataset: Multi-source, multi-species dataset encompassing 11 artifact categories across 6 tissue types, 2 species, 6 organs, and 4 datasets. 
Rich pixel-level annotations: 2,116 detailed pixel level annotations for the eleven artifact classes
Table 3 highlights variations in performance of different automated QC methods, warranting the need for such a dataset that might help build better QC methods
reviews.text_weaknesses:
o Fig 1 is unclear. The ground truth artifact mask shows the tissue as foreground and the rest as background. In this example, is the entire foreground an artifact? Or does the black region in the center of the mask represent the artifact?
o The annotations were performed by a single reader. This may add subjectivity and bias to the dataset.
o Although the dataset is valuable, the algorithms developed for evaluation i.e., to segment the tissue or to label the patches we not optimal. This may affect the results:
o The tissue detection steps involve basic methods like “intensity thresholding at 200”, which is not a robust approach and the performance can vary with respect to staining variations.
o “a patch was labeled as an artifact if annotation coverage exceeded 25%”. The algorithm outputs are at patch level although the annotations are at pixel level leading to loss of information.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

In this paper, the authors curated a novel benchmark dataset focused on the task of automated WSI artifact detection. This seems to be an extensive dataset that may be useful for the digital pathology community to develop stronger, more robust automated QC methods. The results in the paper show that the performance of existing QC methods vary quite a bit compared to manual annotations, thereby highlighting the need to build a method that’s more robust and this dataset may be helpful.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: In this paper the authors present a third-party independent benchmark dataset and pipeline to evaluate existing WSI Quality Control methods for artifact detection. Their experiments and comparison span across 5 segmentation models and 2 patch classifiers (7 distinct methods), evaluated on 53 H&E WSIs. With these comparisons, the authors provide insights into current limitations of QC solutions and establish a standardized clinical evaluation framework to help the community developing deployable and robust models for artifact detection.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) First Independent third-party benchmark dataset for WSI artifact detection, from multiple sources (4 centers), species (human/mice), tissue types (6), and broad artifact taxonomy (11 artifacts). While annotated from a single expert, this is in line with practices of previous benchmarks for WSI QC quantification (GrandQC, Weng et al., Nature Communications 2024).
2) Breadth of method comparison, with evaluation spanning 7 methods from 2019 to 2024, 5 segmentation models and 2 patch classifiers (TCNN and PathProfiler), with these methods trained on varying data scales and domains. This is a valuable comparison for the community on existing tools, showcasing out-of-the box performance on a real world dataset.
3) Release of a practical standardized benchmarking tool for future QC method evaluation, promising to lower the barrier for future developers to situate their work within a common framework.
4) Importance of findings, that while methods reliably preserve artifact-free tissue, they do not perform consistently in artifact localization tasks across different sources and taxonomies.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) “The first benchmark to test WSI QC methods” claim is overstated and misleading. GrandQC (Weng et al.) already provides a publicly released annotated test dataset of 318 WSIs across 4 organ types with pixel-level ground truth and a head-to-head comparison of multiple QC tools, making it a de facto benchmark for this task. SlideGuard’s genuine and significant novelty is that it is the first independent benchmark for this task, with a broader diversity of samples (multi-species, multi-center, 11 artifact classes). The authors need to reframe this contribution precisely along these lines, independence and diversity versus scale, and additionally verify and disclose whether any overlap exists between SlideGuard’s TCGA slides and GrandQC’s training set, as this would directly affect the validity of GrandQC’s evaluation within this benchmark.
2) Annotator subjectivity described in the ‘Detection Asymmetry’ paragraph and Conclusions section undermines the reliability of the dataset’s ground truth. This statement directly contradicts the single-annotator protocol: if boundary subjectivity is significant enough to alter or explain systematic performance gaps across all evaluated methods, then the absence of an extra annotator and inter-rater agreement analysis is a critical methodological gap, not a mere limitation. This is especially consequential for a benchmark paper, whose primary contribution is the ground truth itself. While GrandQC also relied on a primary single annotator for the test set, authors explicitly argue on the peer review process file, that inter-rater agreement is less critical for artifact detection due to its relatively objective nature. SlideGuard takes the opposite position by acknowledging annotation subjectivity as a key driver of performance variability, making the absence of inter-rater analysis a self-inflicted and particularly consequential contradiction that the authors must address.
3) At 53 WSIs, the dataset is substantially smaller than comparable benchmarks (GrandQC test set: 318 WSIs). No per-class annotation statistics are reported, making it impossible to assess class imbalance or evaluate whether rare artifact categories are sufficiently represented (should be reported in both table 2 and 3). Given this limited scale, the absence of uncertainty estimates, no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests, makes it difficult to quantify how different performance between methods is.
4) The inference resolution is never specified: the MPP or nominal magnification at which each method processes WSIs is not reported or standardized across the benchmark, despite the authors themselves identifying MPP inconsistency as a key practical limitation in the Discussion. This is a direct internal contradiction that must be resolved. The authors should explicitly state the extraction MPP for each method, clarify whether this is fixed or method-dependent, and discuss how resolution differences across methods may confound the reported performance comparisons. Furthermore, the recommendation to shift from nominal magnification to MPP in the Discussion is presented as a practical requirement but is entirely unsupported by the benchmark itself, no ablation or sensitivity analysis is performed comparing method performance across different MPP values (under the same nominal magnification), which would be the natural way to empirically ground this claim.
5) How sensitive is the performance of patch classifiers to the discretization threshold? An ablation on 10%, 15%, 20%, 25%, 50% and 75% might explain how reliable are current results for TCNN and PathProfiler. The choice on 25% is not empirically validated.
6) Table 2 reports Dice scores for all methods without distinguishing between pixel-level spatial overlap Dice for segmentation methods and patch-level F1 score for TCNN and PathProfiler, which is what Dice mathematically reduces to when a single binary label is assigned per patch. These quantities should be clearly and distinctly presented. The authors must explicitly state what metric is being reported for each method type and clearly flag the weaknesses of cross-paradigm comparison.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Minor weaknesses:
1) Table 1 has column alignment issues; namely, the ‘Backbone’ and ‘Dataset Characteristics’ columns appear not centered, making this table visually aesthetically weird.
2) Table 3 has some results bold without being the best for example ‘Precipitates’ and ‘Ink’ performance of Path profiler. In this table it would be useful to have the actual dataset percentage next to the artifact to show how meaningful current comparison are based on annotated size.

This paper provides the community with a valuable benchmark dataset for QC evaluation. However, current score is justified by four distinct issues: the novelty claim requires reframing as GrandQC already provides a public benchmark; the paper self-contradicts by invoking annotation subjectivity to explain performance gaps which, if significant, requires a second annotator and inter-rater agreement analysis; critical dataset characterization is missing including per category annotation distributions, uncertainty estimates in metrics, and inference resolution; and the MPP recommendation in the discussion section is unsupported by sensitivity analysis.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text: SlideGuard proposes a heterogeneous multi-source artifact dataset and harmonized evaluation of segmentation- vs patch-QC detectors. The reviewers appreciated the clarity, community needs for standardized quality control benchmarking, and richness of taxonomy/sources. Conscientious limitation discussion on metrics, and partial subjectivity (R2–4). Raised issues include sharpening evidence that artifacts degrade modern pipelines versus a single dated citation plus clarifying Dice/accuracy nomenclature and patch-threshold derivation (R2), overstated “first benchmark” claim versus GrandQC and questions on overlap/train contamination (R4), interplay of annotation subjectivity with single-reader protocol lacking inter-rater study (R4), comparatively small corpus vs some benchmarks lacking uncertainty/per-class prevalence detail (R4), and presentation issues in comparative tables noted as minor polish (R4). The AC read the paper, reviewed it, and agrees that the paper has merit and that the benchmark with the dataset would be of interest to the community. The authors should address the raised concerns in their revised version.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their thoughtful and constructive feedback. We are encouraged by the reviewers’ positive feedback on SlideGuard’s relevance and have carefully considered each suggestion to improve the manuscript. Below, we address the technical and editorial points raised.
Regarding annotator subjectivity: We distinguish between semantic agreement and geometric precision. Artifact classification is an objective task for experienced histotechnicians. However, for artifacts like dust (soft edges) or ink (complex structures), manual polygons lack the pixel-level granularity of machine segmentation. This inherent spatial ambiguity, rather than annotator bias, may limit attainable Dice scores.
Addressing magnification used by models: To ensure a fair comparison, models were evaluated using their native resolution requirements. Forcing an incorrect scale would inherently compromise the benchmark. Patch-level methods were provided with their exact requested MPP, whereas pixel-level methods processed the WSIs directly to manage resolution internally. Running tools ‘off-the-shelf’ this way exposes how they handle physical scale inconsistencies across centers, providing a realistic sensitivity analysis.
In regard to the comparison modes: Pixel-level methods were evaluated pixel-wise and patch-level methods were evaluated patch-wise using their native output grids. The 25% discretization threshold was chosen empirically based on previous works, and we acknowledge the importance of a sensitivity study in future works. We also acknowledge that patch-level methods benefit from this task simplification, and we explicitly flag the weaknesses of this cross-paradigm comparison in the Results. To further address this, Tables 2 and 3 have been updated in the camera-ready version to group methods by output type to clearly distinguish these evaluation modes.
As to the intensity masks: They were manually verified to ensure accurate ROIs. This step solely excludes background, focusing analysis on artifact localization rather than the models’ internal tissue detection. Large-scale datasets in the future will adopt more robust segmentation. We are thankful to the reviewer for pointing it out as a future direction.
To address the “first benchmark” phrasing: We have reformulated the claim to more accurately reflect SlideGuard’s contribution as the first independent, cross-species benchmark. SlideGuard’s value lies in its high taxonomic granularity (11 artifact classes) and its inclusion of non-TCGA human and animal samples, providing a guarantee of unseen data samples.
As to the expansion of tables: Thank you for the constructive suggestions to expand the comparison in Table 1 (including magnification and artifact types) and to provide a broader analysis of the annotation dataset. However, due to strict page constraints and the inability to include supplementary material, we are unable to accommodate these additions. Furthermore, presenting raw annotation metrics or dataset percentage alone, as a mere numerical addition to Table 3, would be misleading without a thorough contextual discussion of the variations in artifact sizes that we unfortunately cannot fit within the current space limits. Relevant information will, however, be included on the Grand Challenge page of the project.
Regarding presentation and editorial clarity: We have expanded the literature review on the downstream impact of artifacts, unified our terminology (consistently using ‘class’, ‘label’, and ‘category’), and improved mask visibility in Figure 1.In Table 3, we also identified the bolding errors post-submission and have corrected the table along with the relevant commentary in the Results to accurately reflect the model rankings. These refinements, along with all other formatting suggestions, will be incorporated into the camera-ready version.

title: Slim nnU-Net: Revisiting nnU-Net Self Configuration from an Optimization Angle
abstract: nnU-Net is the de facto standard for medical image segmentation, yet its architectures remain computationally expensive. We revisit nnU-Net self-configuration from an optimization angle: instead of heuristic architecture design or post-hoc pruning, we reformulate nnU-Net training as a proximal optimization problem with non-smooth regularizations on network structures. We design the reguarlization as a mixed L1 and group L2 loss. Using proximal optimization for this mixed loss enables safe removal of entire channels without harming the segmentation loss. It unifies weight and structure learning in a single, integral training process; and ``slim” nnU-Net architectures emerge as the result of optimization. We carry out experiments on both 2D cardiac MRI (ACDC) and 3D brain tumor segmentation (BraTS 2023) datasets, and benchmarked our method against a range of established baselines. We show that for both 2D and 3D nnU-Net, our method removes >99% of the weights structurally, while preserving near-baseline Dice performance. We further show that the reconfigured nnU-Nets deliver substantial run-time gains, with up to 96% FLOP reduction for 2D and 86% for 3D. Compared to baselines, slim nnU-Net achieves the best accuracy–efficiency trade-off. Our method enables more efficient inference and reduced hardware requirements for broad applications of nnU-Net.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper revisits nnU-Net self-configuration from an optimization perspective rather than heuristic architecture design. It formulates nnU-Net training as a proximal optimization problem and introduces a sparse group lasso regularization, enabling the removal of entire channels without degrading segmentation performance. 
The authors evaluate their method on two datasets, ACDC and BraTS 2023, and demonstrate that it can remove more than 99% of the weights while preserving near-baseline Dice performance.
reviews.text_strengths:
Revisiting nnU-Net self-configuration from an optimization perspective is novel, given that nnU-Net is a widely used segmentation model.
Using proximal optimization for a mixed loss enables the removal of entire channels without degrading segmentation performance.
The experiments in the paper are comprehensive.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The authors neither provide a link to the source code nor indicate whether it will be released, which affects reproducibility.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Mainly because revisiting nnU-Net self-configuration from an optimization perspective is novel, given that nnU-Net is a widely used segmentation model.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The contribution is good and nnU-Net might benefit from this paper.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper revisits nnU-Net self-configuration from an optimization perspective. Instead of using heuristic pruning or post-hoc architecture redesign, it formulates nnU-Net training as a proximal optimization problem with mixed element-wise ℓ1 and group-wise ℓ2 regularization. This encourages both weight sparsity and structured channel sparsity during a single training process, allowing entire channels to be removed after training. The method is evaluated on 2D cardiac MRI segmentation (ACDC) and 3D brain tumor segmentation (BraTS 2023), where it reportedly achieves extreme compression with strong accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs relative to several pruning baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
A major strength is that the paper tackles a very relevant practical problem: nnU-Net is effective but often computationally heavy, especially in 3D. The motivation is clear and important for broader deployment. The paper frames this not as generic pruning, but as an extension of nnU-Net’s self-configuration philosophy toward optimization-based structure learning, which is a clean and appealing idea.
The formulation is simple and principled: sparse-group regularization is introduced directly into the training objective, and proximal updates are used because the regularizer is non-smooth. The derivation in the methods section is easy to follow, and Figure 1 on page 3 clearly illustrates how sparse weights and channels emerge and lead to a compact slimmed model.
The paper does more than report parameter counts: it shows Dice-vs-FLOP tradeoffs in Figure 2, optimization dynamics in Figure 3, layer-wise retention patterns in Figure 4, and actual CPU/GPU timing in Table 1.This gives a more convincing picture than reporting sparsity alone. In particular, the results on page 8 suggest that prox-mix reaches very strong compression regimes while keeping Dice close to the original nnU-Net.
The 3D results are particularly important because that is where nnU-Net’s computational burden is often most restrictive.
reviews.text_weaknesses: My main concern is novelty relative to existing pruning literature. Sparse-group regularization, proximal optimization, and structured pruning are all established ideas, and the manuscript itself cites prior work on proximal training and structured sparsity. The main novelty here seems to be the adaptation of these ideas to nnU-Net and the framing as “self-configuration from an optimization angle.” That is interesting, but the conceptual advance over existing structured pruning/proximal methods feels somewhat incremental.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
This is a solid and well-presented paper with a nice optimization perspective on nnU-Net compression. I think it would become stronger with three additions:
(1) include a reduced-width / reduced-capacity nnU-Net baseline trained from scratch at similar compute;
(2) expand the experimental validation to more datasets or at least provide stronger discussion of generality; and
(3) clarify hyperparameter and threshold selection so the reported Pareto frontier is easier to interpret from a model-selection standpoint.

I am slightly positive on this paper. The problem is relevant, the method is principled, and the results are strong enough to be interesting. In particular, the combination of very high structural compression and near-baseline Dice on both ACDC and BraTS is compelling, and the inclusion of real runtime measurements is a plus.
My reservation is that the paper does not yet fully prove that this is the best way to obtain efficient nnU-Nets, rather than one reasonable pruning-based route. The novelty over prior structured pruning and proximal sparsity work is moderate, and the missing smaller-model baseline leaves an important question unanswered. That keeps me at weak accept rather than a stronger score.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This work formulates nnU Net training as a proximal optimization problem with mixed ℓ₁ and group ℓ₂ regularization to encourage structural sparsity. The approach removes entire channels during training, unifying weight and structure learning into a single process, resulting in slim nnU Net architectures.
reviews.text_strengths:
The manuscript is well-structured.
The motivation is clearly explained.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Pruning is a well-established technique for network compression. Both single-granularity (e.g., unstructured, semi-structured, structured) and mixed-granularity pruning have been extensively studied. 
(1) The related work would benefit from including a discussion of other mixed granularity pruning techniques.
(2) The reviewer is not fully convinced why the proposed method is specifically investigated on nnU Net, as both the addressed problem and the proposed approach appear general and applicable to other networks and tasks as well.
(3) A comparison with state of the art mixed granularity pruning methods should be provided in Section 3.
2.The use of L1/L2 regularization in the loss function to encourage unstructured or structured sparsity, as well as channel level coarse grained pruning, has already been explored in prior works. Consequently, the novelty of the proposed method appears somewhat limited.
3.The experiments are limited to nnU‑Net. It is recommended to evaluate it on more SOTA networks. In addition, the method should be compared with other leading pruning approaches, including mixed‑granularity methods.
4.More implementation details such as training hyperparameters and pre-processing strategies should be provided to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The major concerns include 1) the relatively limited novelty of the proposed approach, 2) the narrow experimental scope, restricted to nnU-Net without comparison to SOTA pruning methods, and 3) the insufficient implementation details.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Thank you for the response. After reading the rebuttal and other reviews, I would like to keep my current rate.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper makes nnUNet more efficient and the empirical. The results are strong, especially the large structured compression, FLOP reduction, and actual runtime gains while keeping Dice close to the original nnUNet.
However there still exist some concern: sparse group regularization, proximal optimization, and structured pruning are established ideas, and the paper’s contribution is mainly adapting and framing them for nnUNet. 
For rebuttal, the authors should clarify the novelty over prior structured/proximal pruning, justify the contribution, explain hyperparameter and pruning-threshold selection.

This paper proposes Slim nnU-Net, which formulates nnU-Net compression as a proximal optimization problem with mixed element-wise and group-wise sparsity regularization. The problem is practically relevant, since nnU-Net remains widely used but can be computationally expensive, especially in 3D segmentation.
The main strength of the submission is its empirical evaluation. The method is tested on both 2D cardiac MRI segmentation and 3D brain tumor segmentation, and the submitted manuscript reports strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs, with substantial reductions in model size and FLOPs while maintaining near-baseline Dice performance. The reported CPU and GPU inference measurements further support the practical value of structured compression.
I agree with the reviewers that the methodological novelty is moderate, since proximal optimization and structured sparsity are established techniques, and broader comparison with alternative compact nnU-Net designs would strengthen the work. Nevertheless, the adaptation to nnU-Net is well motivated, technically sound, and experimentally convincing. Overall, I consider the paper above the acceptance threshold.

As pointed out by the reviewers, combining nnU-Net with network pruning is an interesting idea with practical importance. Although I agree with Reviewer #3 that the theoretical contribution of the pruning component is relatively weak, the integration of nnU-Net with pruning appears to be novel, and its practical advantages could be substantial. Considering the rebuttal as well, I recommend accepting this paper.

The paper received mixed reviews, with both positive and negative opinions. After carefully reading the rebuttal and the reviewers’ comments, I believe that the authors have addressed most of the concerns raised during the review process. Although some issues remain not fully resolved, I find the work interesting and the remaining weaknesses do not constitute sufficient grounds for rejection. Therefore, I recommend accepting the paper, and I encourage the authors to further improve the manuscript in the final version.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback. We are encouraged by the positive remarks that the optimization perspective is novel (R1) and clean (R2), nnU-Net reconfiguration is high relevant and practical (R2), and that our results are strong and comprehensive (AC) by including FLOP and runtime gains. We address the main concerns below.
Novelty of the work: We appreciate R1’s comment that reformulation of nnU-Net configuration from an optimization angle is a major novelty. nnU-Net is the cornerstone of medical image segmentation, but its computational cost is high. Optimization of nnU-Net configuration is meaningful from both theoretical and practical angles, but not well studied. In standard nnU-Net, self-configuration is rule-based, while existing pruning works were not compatible with nnU-Net: they typically adopt training-pruning-retraining pipelines, which are heuristic-driven, iterative, and sub-optimal from the optimization angle. In contrast, our work is built on the proximal optimization theories, and the pruning is done in one training trajectory (Fig. 1). It is theoretically grounded, and practically keeps the nnU-Net-v2 framework intact: no dynamic topology changes, pruning-retraining cycles, or ad hoc feature-analysis are needed; only a proximal step is inserted after the standard gradient update. This offers both theoretical and practical advantages over existing work.
Smaller-model baseline: We thank R2 for this important remark. We address it from two angles: first, without the proposed proximal optimization, we could not reach the specific configuration; the work would then change to expensive neural architecture search (NAS); second, over-parametrization is crucial for DL training to find good solutions, and prior work has shown that starting from small networks cannot match the results of starting from large networks and then pruning. We have done additional experiments that confirmed this: a randomly initialized small nnU-Net with matched FLOPs showed Dice drops of 1.91% on ACDC and 1.68% on BraTS. The difference is significant in medical image segmentation benchmarks. We will add this discussion to revision.
Reproducibility and implementation details: We will release the code upon acceptance.
Hyperparameter and pruning-threshold selection (Meta, R2, R3): The sparsity weights λg and λ1 can be selected on the validation set according to the desired Dice-FLOP trade-off. In our experiments, favorable settings were consistent: both ACDC and BraTS worked well around λg = 1e-3, with λ1 in the range of 5e-4 to 1e-3.The pruning threshold τ is selected after training as an operating point. Sweeping τ gives the validation Dice-FLOP Pareto curve, from which one can choose a compact model according to the acceptable Dice drop. The final operating point can be chosen from the validation Dice-FLOP Pareto curve to achieve strong FLOP reduction with minimal Dice drop; in our experiments, this typically corresponded to τ in the range of 0.05–0.1 relative to the layer-wise maximum group norm. We will add the details to the revision.
Focus on nnU-Net and benchmarking (R3): The paper indeed focuses on nnU-Net self-configuration, rather than generic pruning of architecture. This is a deliberate choice: despite rapid developments, nnU-Net remains the de facto framework for medical segmentation. Therefore, making nnU-Net more efficient, while keeping the original implementation intact, has broad practical impact, especially for 3D cases. For benchmarking, we included state-of-the-art baselines for U-Net and ablation studies: LTH, STAMP, Sauron, GD-mix, and prox-group within nnU-Net-v2 framework. It covered unstructured, structured, feature-based pruning, and variants of proximal sparsity. We showed that prox-mix achieved the best accuracy-efficiency tradeoff (Fig.2), providing a simple, principled, and nnU-Net-compatible way for boosting efficiency without losing performance.

title: SMART-KNEE: Sparse-Morphology Based Anatomical Reconstruction Using Topology-Aware Networks for Imageless Total Knee Arthroplasty
abstract:
Imageless Total Knee Arthroplasty (ITKA) requires real-
time acquisition of patient-specific anatomical landmarks without pre-
operative CT or MRI, posing a significant challenge for intraoperative
planning. Despite utilising 3D knee reconstruction algorithms, modern
ITKA systems continue to struggle with accurate knee shape estimation
and the anatomical axis alignment - both prerequisites for reliable ITKA
planning. We present SMART-KNEE, a cascaded anatomy-aware recon-
struction framework that generates patient-specific Femoral (F) and Tib-
ial(T) bone morphology from a minimal set of intraoperatively collected
anatomical landmarks, without preoperative imaging. In the first stage,
a Topology-Aware Equivariant Graph Neural Network (EGNN) predicts
the complete anatomical landmark set from four intraoperative anchor
landmarks, enforcing topological consistency and anatomical plausibility
under under E(3)-equivariance (invariance to 3D euclidean transforma-
tions). In the second stage, an Anatomy-Aware GAN reconstructs com-
plete patient-specific bone surfaces by fusing the EGNN-predicted land-
marks with partial intraoperative surface point clouds. SMART-KNEE
achieves precise landmark localization error (F: 2.28 mm ± 1.68 mm; T:
1.65 mm ± 0.83 mm). Test cohort surface reconstruction yields Dice F-
87%, T-92.477%, Hausdorff Distance F-5, T-4.3 mm and ground truth

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The study presents SMART-KNEE, a cascaded DL framework for reconstructing 3D patient-specific femoral and tibial models during imageless total knee arthroplasty. There are two steps in the pipeline: first, an E(3)-equivariant 
graph neural network predicts a full set of anatomical landmarks from four intraoperative anchor points; second, an anatomy-aware GAN fuses these landmarks with a sparse intraoperative point cloud to reconstruct the dense bone surface. The authors validate the method on a physical phantom, achieving sub-3mm accuracy, and contribute a new dataset of 361 annotated bone models
reviews.text_strengths:
The technical formulation is sophisticated and well tailored to the surgical usecase. Using an E(3)-equivariant graph neural network is a strong design choice, as it ensures the network can accurately predict landmarks regardless of the arbitrary coordinate frame transformations inherent to intraoperative optical tracking. 
The system demonstrates impressive accuracy, significantly outperforming baselines like VN-EGNN in landmark prediction, and achieving surface reconstruction errors well below the 3 mm threshold generally accepted for clinical viability in TKA. 
Splitting the pipeline into a sparse structural prediction and dense morphological generatio elegantly constrains the generative model, ensuring anatomical plausibility.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The study predicates its clinical narrative heavily on the assumption that robotic or highly navigated systems (which require 3D models) are the definitive standard of care. However, conventional TKA remains the standard in many regions, making the clinical motivation somewhat unstable. Framing this as a mandatory solution for the “standard” workflow is slightly overstated. 
While the methodology is great, the validation is restricted to in-silico metrics and a pristine physical phantom. In a real world intraoperative setting, acquiring the anchor points and sparse point clouds is complicated by soft tissue, cartilage thickness, blood, and surgeon variability. It remains unclear how robust the system is to noisy input data derivd from a real patient
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The study presents a great and novel methodology (combining EGNNs and GANs for a distinct clinical problem) and provides a potentially valuable dataset. The rating is currently a weak accept due to the gap between the mathematical/phantom validation and the realities of the clinical workflow, as well as the somewhat overstated clinical motivation. If the authors can adequately clarify the system’s robustness to realistic intraoperative noise and inference times in the rebuttal, this paper would be a good addition to the MICCAI program.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: My recommendation for acceptance is justified by the authors’ comprehensive and convincing rebuttal, which directly resolved the most critical concerns raised during the initial review. A key factor was the clarification that the validation was conducted on physical 3D printed phantoms using clinical-grade optical tracking rather than being purely in-silico, which effectively proves the system’s robustness against realistic intraoperative noise and operator variability. Additionally, the authors provided a strong technical argument regarding why traditional baselines like NeRF or diffusion models are unsuitable for the extreme sparsity of surgical point clouds, while simultaneously demonstrating that their approach significantly outperforms traditional statistical shape models by requiring fewer landmarks and avoiding mean-biased outputs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes SMART-KNEE, a cascaded framework for reconstructing patient-specific knee anatomy in imageless total knee arthroplasty (ITKA) from sparse intraoperative data. The method consists of: 1) A topology-aware E(3)-equivariant graph neural network (EGNN) that completes the full anatomical landmark set from only four intraoperative anchor points, enforcing geometric consistency and anatomical plausibility; 2) An anatomy-aware generative adversarial network (GAN) that reconstructs complete femoral and tibial bone surfaces by fusing predicted landmarks with sparse intraoperative surface point clouds. The framework eliminates the need for preoperative CT/MRI while achieving clinically acceptable accuracy, enabling real-time intraoperative planning. Additionally, the authors release a dataset of 361 annotated knee models.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Structured decomposition via anatomy-aware intermediate representation. The primary strength of this work lies in its formulation of imageless reconstruction as a structured two-stage problem, where anatomical landmark completion serves as an explicit intermediate representation between sparse intraoperative observations and dense surface reconstruction. This design is conceptually meaningful and non-trivial, as it introduces a clinically interpretable and geometrically constrained representation that reduces ambiguity in downstream generation. Unlike end-to-end implicit reconstruction approaches, this decomposition leverages anatomical priors in a modular manner, improving both stability and interpretability.
2.Topology-aware E(3)-equivariant modeling for landmark completion. A key methodological novelty is the integration of topology-aware graph modeling with E(3)-equivariant neural networks for anatomical landmark prediction. By explicitly encoding anatomical structure as a graph and enforcing equivariance under rigid transformations, the method ensures geometric consistency across varying poses and sparse inputs. This approach goes beyond conventional regression or statistical shape models by enabling structured propagation of anatomical constraints, which is particularly effective for recovering unobserved or geometrically distant landmarks.
3.Dual-conditioned generative reconstruction with anatomical constraints. The proposed reconstruction framework introduces a dual-conditioning mechanism that integrates local geometric evidence (partial point clouds) with global anatomical structure (predicted landmarks). This design provides a more controlled and anatomically grounded generative process compared to purely data-driven shape completion methods. Additionally, constraining the generator within a pretrained latent geometry manifold enhances realism and stability, representing a meaningful step toward reliable patient-specific reconstruction in clinical environments.
4.High clinical relevance with imageless and low-input requirements. The work demonstrates strong translational potential by achieving clinically acceptable reconstruction accuracy without reliance on preoperative CT or MRI. This significantly reduces the dependency on imaging resources while maintaining geometric fidelity, addressing a critical limitation in current ITKA systems. The ability to operate under minimal intraoperative input, combined with end-to-end validation, highlights the practical value of the approach for real-world surgical navigation scenarios.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Moderate level of methodological novelty with room for clearer differentiation. The methodological novelty of the framework is moderate and could be better articulated. While the integration of a topology-aware EGNN with an anatomy-aware GAN is well-motivated and tailored to the ITKA scenario, the core components themselves are based on established architectures. As such, the contribution is primarily reflected in the system-level design and problem formulation rather than in fundamentally new modeling techniques. To strengthen the novelty claim, the authors could more explicitly highlight what new capabilities emerge from this integration, for example through targeted ablation studies demonstrating the necessity of topology-aware modeling, or by providing theoretical or empirical analysis showing advantages over alternative architectural combinations.
2.Implicit reliance on learned statistical priors. Despite being framed as an imageless reconstruction approach, the method still relies on implicit statistical priors learned from data. The GAN-based reconstruction stage encodes population-level anatomical distributions within its latent space, effectively replacing explicit statistical shape models (SSMs) with learned priors. This raises a conceptual concern regarding whether the method truly overcomes the limitations of SSM-based approaches or simply shifts the dependency to a different representation. The authors could address this by providing experiments that evaluate generalization beyond the training distribution, such as testing on out-of-distribution anatomies or reduced training data settings, and by explicitly comparing the behavior of the model with classical SSM-based methods in terms of adaptability and bias.
3.Idealized assumptions on intraoperative input quality. The method relies on assumptions about the quality and distribution of intraoperative inputs that may be optimistic in practice. It assumes the availability of well-distributed anchor landmarks and relatively structured sparse surface point clouds, whereas real surgical data may be significantly noisier, incomplete, or unevenly distributed due to occlusion and acquisition constraints. This limits confidence in the robustness of the approach under realistic conditions. To improve this aspect, the authors could include robustness experiments by simulating noise, missing landmarks, or partial point clouds, and analyze performance degradation under such conditions to better reflect clinical applicability.
4.Lack of comparison with stronger or more recent baselines. The experimental evaluation lacks comparisons with several strong and relevant baselines from recent literature. In particular, methods based on diffusion models, implicit neural representations (e.g., NeRF, occupancy networks), or modern shape completion frameworks are not considered. Without such comparisons, it is difficult to assess the relative advantage of the proposed approach in the broader context of contemporary 3D reconstruction methods.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

1.Moderate level of methodological novelty with room for clearer differentiation.
2.Idealized assumptions on intraoperative input quality.
3.Lack of comparison with stronger or more recent baselines.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: After reading the rebuttal, I maintain a reject recommendation. The response does not sufficiently resolve my main concerns regarding clinical validity, novelty, and evaluation rigor. Although the authors clarify that the phantom evaluation was performed on 3D-printed CT-derived bone models with optical tracking, this remains a pre-clinical phantom study rather than evidence of robustness in real intraoperative, cadaveric, or patient-specific TKA settings. The claimed “clinical readiness” therefore remains overstated. Methodologically, the rebuttal argues for system-level novelty, but the framework is still mainly a combination of known components (EGNN-based landmark completion and GAN-based shape reconstruction) with limited evidence that each design choice is essential. The baseline comparison also remains insufficient: comparisons are made mainly against generic EGNN variants, while direct and fair comparisons with established statistical shape modeling, sparse point-cloud reconstruction, or recent implicit/generative reconstruction methods are not convincingly provided. Finally, several key concerns are deferred to future work, including systematic noise injection, missing-landmark analysis, partial-occlusion robustness, and broader validation. Thus, the rebuttal improves clarification but does not materially strengthen the submitted evidence to meet MICCAI acceptance standards.
