meta_reviews.text: All 3 reviewers see merit in the paper, particularly highlighting the methodological contributions and the clear way this paper is organized. SVR is applied to the pancreas, a very interesting application with the methodology adapted and made bespoke. 2 recommend clear acceptance, 1 is between weak accept and pending rebuttal - clarifies however that they tend towards accept (this review is also the shortest and rated as not confident).

author_feedback_text:
Dear Area Chair and Reviewers,
We sincerely thank you for your time, the constructive feedback, and the recommendation for acceptance. We are thrilled that you recognized the clinical value of addressing low-redundancy pancreatic SVR and the methodological strengths of SRPAN. We would like to address the main points raised in the reviews for the public record:
1.Reproducibility and Source Code (Reviewers 1 & 3)
We agree that reproducibility is vital. The full source code for SRPAN is being made open-source, and a link to the GitHub repository will be included in the camera-ready manuscript.
2.Evaluation Metrics and Downstream Validation (Reviewers 1 & 3)
We agree that reprojection fidelity is an indirect metric. However, acquiring true isotropic ground-truth MRI is highly challenging, as it is not part of standard clinical care for pancreatic surveillance. We are actively working on obtaining such data for future validation. As noted, evaluating the impact of these reconstructions on downstream clinical and AI tasks is our immediate next step.
3.Rigid Motion Assumption (Reviewer 2)
Our dataset was acquired using strict respiratory-triggered and breath-hold protocols. Upon careful inspection of the imaging, we did not observe severe non-rigid artifacts. For this first proposed method, we deliberately chose to keep the registration component simpler and more robust. We agree, however, that extending the framework to handle non-rigid deformations is a valuable future outlook for less strictly controlled acquisitions.
4.Asymmetric Gating Strategy (Reviewers 1 & 2)
We agree that fixing the axial stack as the reference could be problematic if it were of poorer quality. While we could manually inspect each case to select the best reference, we fixed the axial stack to ensure the framework remains fully automatic. This choice is grounded in our data’s specific artifact profile: while both scans are highly consistent in the coronal view around the pancreas, the coronal scan exhibits clear image degradations in its out-of-plane (axial) view. Therefore, the axial scan consistently serves as the more reliable reference in our clinical protocol.
Thank you again for your time and expertise.

title: SS-IoSR: Self-supervised Intraoral Scans Repair
abstract:
Intraoral 3D scans are fundamental in digital dentistry but
often contain geometric artifacts such as holes and non-manifold structures due to acquisition constraints and complex dental anatomy. We introduce SS-IoSR, a self-supervised hybrid framework for intraoral scan repair that combines masked autoencoder-based geometric representation learning with a hybrid explicit–implicit reconstruction strategy. The model operates on localized point cloud patches guided by clinicianselected seed points, enabling anatomically consistent reconstruction of missing regions. A differentiable Poisson-based refinement module further improves surface continuity and geometric fidelity. Experimental evaluations on public and in-house intraoral scan datasets show that SS-IoSR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art completion methods across multiple metrics, demonstrating improved reconstruction accuracy
and higher structural similarity for clinically relevant dental regions.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a self-supervised point cloud completion method for intraoral 3D scans. The approach consists of two stages: in the first stage, a Masked Autoencoder (MAE) is pre-trained by masking parts of the point cloud and reconstructing them; in the second stage, the pre-trained network is further utilized to refine the reconstruction of input point clouds. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
reviews.text_strengths: The main contribution of this work lies in demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed framework for intraoral 3D scans.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper has the following limitations:
The overall level of novelty is limited. The adopted framework has already been applied in self-supervised point cloud completion for general scenarios, and the authors do not provide sufficient task-specific improvements, making the novelty unclear. 
There are several unclear aspects in the method description. For example, in the first stage, it is not specified whether the masked point cloud is fed into the MAE as a whole or processed patch-by-patch. The concept of the masked token in Figure 1 is not clearly explained. Additionally, when the input point cloud contains missing regions, it is unclear how the seed points are selected. 
The writing quality needs improvement, as the paper contains several issues such as improper paragraph organization and grammatical errors.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper has issues in method design, writing quality, and novelty. Therefore, I recommend rejection.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors’ clarification regarding the novelty of the work has convinced me. Therefore, I have decided to raise my score to Accept.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose a two-stage model training method to learn detailed completions of partial intraoral scans. The first stage is fully self-supervised, as they train transformer-based encoders and decoders on uniformly distributed patches of the scan, of which ca. 65% are masked out. The second stage then uses clinically chosen landmarks around which a fixed-radius region is masked out, completed with the model pre-trained in the first stage. The completed point cloud is then refined with an implicit representation to remove noise and to extract a watertight mesh.
reviews.text_strengths: The authors show convincing results, and the application is quite relevant in the dental field. I have just very recently taken an intraoral scan myself and can confirm that it can be quite difficult to always get an accurate surface reconstruction of all teeth. Hence, a prior-based completion model could prove beneficial.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
There is a big overlap in the proposed method with the prior work “IoSR: End-to-End Intraoral Scans Repairing”. The authors don’t try to hide this, since they cite this previous work and since the naming is also a clear extension. However, it is not quite obvious to me what the exact innovation is in this work compared to this prior work. If I’m not mistaken, the authors propose to use a PointNet instead of a DGCNN in the pre-training, but I fail to see how this is any more self supervised (as suggested by the added “SS” in front of IoSR) than the previous work. The authors should describe in more detail how exactly they improved upon the prior work instead of describing their method as if it was completely new.
The authors don’t mention any plans to make their code or trained model public. Since the methodology does not seem to be very original, but their results indeed show some improvement and potential for actual clinical implementation, I strongly suggest the authors consider publishing of their code and their trained model.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The authors include a short subsection about implicit models in their related work section. They include DeepSDF, which is quite a famous and relevant work, but if I’m not mistaken, the implicit representation the authors employ is optimized on each case, not a pre-trained shape model like DeepSDF. The other work on implicit representations that the authors mention seems a bit random to me. Additionally, the authors state that “most existing implicit reconstruction approaches are formulated for supervised global shape completion, aiming to recover overall object geometry from partial observations. In contrast, intraoral scan repair targets localized geometric defects on otherwise complete meshes, requiring spatially localized reasoning and tighter integration with explicit surface representations rather than purely global volumetric modeling.” I do think there’s some truth in that, but there are definitely some more recent implicit models, like NPHM, which use localized models in addition to the global model and together with a geometric initialization of the model weights, this allows such models to capture a lot of geometric details. Another highly relevant work would be “An Implicit Parametric Morphable Dental Model” which is not cited by the authors. The authors could argue here that these two works would require manual preprocessing for identifying the individual teeth, but otherwise, I fail to see why their method should perform any better, at least there’s no comparison in the results.

Although the results look promising, I cannot confirm their validity without the authors sharing their trained model, and the authors fail to describe their exact contribution compared to the prior work “IoSR: End-to-End Intraoral Scans Repairing”.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors further specified some key differences between their approach and prior work. I encourage them to specify this appropriately in the paper as well. 
Furthermore, the authors promise to release source code, models, and even the dataset upon acceptance, which makes their contribution considerably stronger.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents SS-IoSR, a self-supervised framework for repairing defective 3D intraoral scans. The method first pre-trains a masked autoencoder on point cloud patches, then uses it with an implicit refinement module and differentiable Poisson surface reconstruction to complete missing regions. A sees point was provided by a clinician to indicate the defect location. The method is evaluated on public Teeth3DS and an in-house dataset, showing improvements over existing baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The problem is clinically relevant. 
2.The framework design is reasonable and well-motivated.
3.The paper is well-written, and the improvement is considerable.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The semi-automatic setting requires a clinician to select a seed point and a fixed radius. The sensitivity to seed point placement and radius choice is not analyzed.
2.The in-house dataset is used for evaluation but will only be released upon acceptance. Reproducibility is currently not possible.
3.The paper lacks discussion on failure cases or limitations of the method.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses a clinically relevant problem with a reasonable hybrid design, and the experimental results show clear improvements over baselines.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text:
While the paper demonstrates strong applicability and compelling results in the dental field, its technical novelty is currently unclear, as the framework appears to be a direct application of general self-supervised point cloud completion methods. The authors must clarify the specific task-based contributions that distinguish this work. Additionally, several methodological details require clarification. The authors are encouraged to address these technical and presentation concerns in their response.

This paper introduces a self-supervised framework named SS-IoSR for repairing defective three-dimensional intraoral scans. The method is highly innovative and the experimental results on the public Teeth3DS and internal datasets demonstrate significant improvements over the baseline.

There are 3 Accepts after rebuttal. Reviewers agreed that the application is clinically relevant and the results are promising. The main initial concerns were novelty, relation to prior IoSR work, and reproducibility.
The rebuttal clarified the differences from prior work and the self-supervised/local repair setting, and the authors also committed to releasing code, models and data. Some details should still be made clearer in the final version, but the main concerns seem addressed. I recommend acceptance.
Great work

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback and are encouraged that R3 recognizes the clinical relevance and effectiveness of our results. This rebuttal addresses concerns regarding novelty, methodology, and reproducibility.
#Novelty & IoSR Comparison (R1, R2): 
SS-IoSR introduces a novel Self-Supervised paradigm for intraoral scan repair, addressing fundamental limitations in existing literature:
Data & Learning Novelty: Unlike supervised frameworks relying on paired “clean/defective” scans, our Phase 1 Masked Autoencoder (MAE) learns the dental geometry manifold directly from raw, unlabeled clinical data. Unlike MAE frameworks for general 3D shapes, our method is specifically adapted to intraoral scans, where highly non-uniform densities and complex structures make standard KNN-based patching unreliable. We introduce a density-aware fixed-radius patch strategy to preserve anatomical coherence across irregular surfaces. This eliminates synthetic defect bias and demonstrates that self-supervised priors, when tailored to dental topology, outperform supervised synthetic training.
Conceptual & Architectural Shift: While IoSR uses a global strategy, SS-IoSR focuses on localized repair to preserve high-frequency details (e.g., incisal edges) that global methods oversmooth. We leverage a Transformer-based MAE for long-range geometric reasoning across patches. Crucially, our ablation studies show that self-supervised methods without implicit geometric modeling are insufficient; thus, we introduce a DPSR-based implicit refinement block (IRB) to recover fine-grained inter-dental details and maintain surface continuity, ensuring clinical fidelity where explicit reconstructions fail.
#Methodological Details (R1, R3):
Patch-wise Processing: In Stage 1, the point cloud is processed patch-by-patch. We utilize a fixed-radius strategy (3mm) rather than KNN to ensure a consistent geometric scale, critical for dental scans where point density varies significantly based on scanner hardware.
Masked Tokens: Masked tokens are learnable geometric placeholders. Combined with positional embeddings, they serve as spatial queries that allow the decoder to identify the locations of missing regions and reconstruct their coordinates based on the surrounding anatomical context.
Seed Point Selection: Seed points are clinician-selected to indicate the centroid of a defect (e.g., the centroid of a hole’s boundary polyline). This human-in-the-loop (HITL) paradigm is the most effective strategy for clinical safety; it ensures repairs are targeted and avoids “hallucinations” common in fully autonomous models. This is vital as real-world defects are typically limited in scale; repairing massive gaps is often unnecessary and lacks patient-specific anatomical reference. Our sensitivity analysis confirms robustness to selection variability up to 1mm.
#Literature & Implicit Models (R2):
We thank R2 for the citations (e.g., NPHM, Zhang et al.), which we will include. Unlike DeepSDF, our implicit module performs per-case optimization to preserve clinical fidelity rather than global class-based modeling. Unlike Zhang et al., which requires explicit tooth-level identification and occupancy vectors, SS-IoSR operates on raw, arbitrary surfaces, bypassing the need for prior segmentation or tooth-level labeling.
#Sensitivity, Limitations, & Reproducibility (R1, R2, R3):
The 3mm radius was defined with dental experts to balance context and precision. We will add a dedicated section on limitations: SS-IoSR may struggle with extensive structural loss (e.g., missing an entire crown) where local context is insufficient. Future work could integrate global shape priors as a guide. Finally, we officially commit to releasing the source code, models, and our paired dataset upon acceptance. This will establish the first standardized benchmark for dental scan restoration. A professional linguistic revision (R1) will be performed to clarify Stage 1/2 transitions.

title: SSPT: Spiking Serialized Point Transformer for Couinaud Segmentation in 3D Medical Data
abstract: Couinaud segmentation is a fundamental step in surgical planning for anatomical liver resection. Anatomically, Couinaud liver segments are defined by the vascular system. However, in medical imaging, the critical issue is that the defining landmarks, i.e., vessels, are extremely sparse within the vast liver parenchyma. Current methods employ handcrafted dense sampling strategies to exploit more vascular data points, leading to high energy consumption and a heavy dependency on manual data rebalancing. We propose Spiking Serialized Point Transformer (SSPT), a Spiking Neural Network (SNN) architecture, to tackle these challenges efficiently and effectively. In particular, SSPT devises Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons to enable a 3D transformer framework, serializing unordered point cloud data into structured temporal spike trains. This spike-based design enables temporally consistent aggregation of critical anatomy (e.g., vessels) context from sparse medical imaging data, while avoiding manually designed sampling strategies and their associated biases. Experimental results on MSD8 and LiTS datasets demonstrate that SSPT delivers high-fidelity segmentation (up to 92.14% Dice) and robust boundary precision (down to 2.24 mm ASD) with a minimal energy footprint of 10.97mJ. Moreover, our experimental results demonstrate that spiking dynamics can inherently capture sparse anatomical topologies, presenting a robust and energy-efficient solution for offline preoperative liver surgery planning. Code is available at https://github.com/Yan0918/SSPT.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents SSPT, a spiking neural network (SNN) point transformer for Couinaud liver segmentation. The key idea is to take the 3D liver point cloud and lay it out as a 1D sequence using a Z-order curve that keeps nearby points close together, then feed chunks of this sequence to the network over a few time steps like a rhythmic signal (with TSD: Temporal Scanning Dispatcher). Attention is then restricted to local windows, and the expensive multiplications in the attention computation are replaced with simple additions driven by binary spikes (SSA). Evaluated on LiTS and MSD8, SSPT achieves 92.14% Dice at 10.97 mJ, which beats the SOTA (APVN) and allows a 98% energy reduction versus the PTv3 counterpart at equal parameter count (12M).
reviews.text_strengths:
Novel and well-scoped contribution: it seems to be the first transformer-based SNN for 3D Couinaud point-cloud segmentation. The energy-efficiency narrative is clean and quantitative (45nm CMOS model, per-layer firing rates reported).
The PTv3 comparison at equal parameter count is the right experiment. It isolates spiking dynamics from capacity effects.
TSD is a well-motivated solution to the spatio-temporal mismatch problem in SNN point processing. The ablation Table 2 Cat. III is convincing.
Serialization ablation (Z-order vs. random vs. k-NN) and time-step analysis (T=1/2/3) are informative and support the design choice made.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Dataset labels are undocumented. Neither LiTS nor MSD8 ships with Couinaud annotations. The paper never states where they come from.
Preprocessing details for voxel baselines are not given.
Table 2 Cat. III contradicts Table 1.The Scanning Wave row reports LiTS ASD=2.24 / MSD8 ASD=2.44, but Table 1 and the abstract report LiTS=2.44 / MSD8=2.24.The columns appear transposed.
No statistical testing performed, the tables lack standard deviations.
The claim “the binary gating mechanism of LIF neurons serves as a dynamic threshold, prioritizing high-entropy structural regions such as vessel bifurcations” is not verified. No spike-activity visualization is provided, only segmentation outputs are shown.
The “Real-time intraoperative” claim in the conclusion is unsupported. No wall-clock latency or neuromorphic hardware deployment is reported. The energy estimate is theoretical.
The theoretical energy model (versus actual neuromorphic hardware measurement) and the single-dataset / single-split evaluation for both MSD8 and LiTS are limitations that should be stated more explicitly.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
I would appreciate if the authors publish the code if the paper gets accepted.

The core idea is to show that an SNN point transformer can match ANN accuracy on a clinically relevant 3D medical task at a fraction of the energy: this is interesting and novel. The TSD mechanism and the point-specific PTv3 comparison are well-executed. However, the undocumented Couinaud labels, the internal table inconsistency, the likely under-tuned nnU-Net and the unsupported intraoperative claim prevent me from giving a strong accept. With fixes to these issues, this would be a solid contribution.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have tried to answer the main concerns raised by the reviewers. Also code will be released which makes their approach at least reproduceable for the scientific community.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes SSPT, a spiking neural network for Couinaud liver segmentation from point cloud representations of 3D medical images. Its main design includes a Temporal Scanning Dispatcher (TSD), which organizes 3D points along a space-filling curve and feeds them over time steps to Leaky Integrate-and-Fire neurons, and a Spiking Serialized Attention (SSA) module, which uses binary spike-gated queries within local windows to reduce arithmetic complexity. Experimental results on LiTS and MSD8 suggest that the method is competitive with existing voxel-based, hybrid, and point-based approaches in segmentation accuracy, and may offer advantages in theoretical energy efficiency.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Introduces a principled spatio-temporal serialization (TSD) of unordered point clouds to create coherent spike trains, addressing the common mismatch between static 3D geometry and SNN temporal dynamics.
2.Designs a spiking self-attention variant (SSA) that uses binary query spikes with localized windows to approach linear complexity while replacing much of QK multiplications with additions, a compelling hardware-aware rethinking of attention for point clouds.
3.Incorporates a spiking conditional positional encoding (SCPE) with parallel sparse 3D convolutions to compensate spatial information loss due to serialization; the end-to-end hierarchical U-Net-like spiking transformer is well-motivated.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Major concerns:
1.The energy analysis is theoretical (45 nm CMOS model) and not hardware-measured; it does not include memory movement costs or GPU/CPU runtime, which can dominate in practice for point-cloud pipelines.
2.SSA still performs floating-point softmax/value aggregation; the overall fraction of operations actually reduced to additions versus multiplications is not fully quantified per layer, making the magnitude of energy savings somewhat assumption-sensitive.
3.The gating granularity and stability of spike generation (per-channel/per-head) and its impact on attention quality are under-specified; no sensitivity analysis for spike threshold or membrane dynamics is provided.
4.The most serious issue is the unclear source of the Couinaud ground truth. LiTS and MSD8 do not provide Couinaud annotations by default, yet the manuscript does not explain how these labels were obtained, generated, or validated. This is not a minor omission but a fundamental problem that undermines the rigor and credibility of the entire study. 
5.The evaluation is incomplete and insufficiently convincing. The paper reports only overall metrics, without segment-wise Dice results for each Couinaud region, especially for anatomically challenging segments such as Segment I (caudate lobe). This makes it difficult to judge the actual clinical usefulness of the method. 
6.The computation of ASD is unclear and lacks reproducibility. Since the predictions are point-wise, the paper should clearly describe how point labels are converted into surfaces or volumes before boundary distances are measured. Without these details, the reported ASD values are difficult to interpret. 
7.The fairness of the comparisons is questionable. Voxel-based methods are evaluated on dense full-resolution volumes, while the proposed method uses sampled point clouds. The energy comparison is therefore not fully fair, and the paper does not provide runtime or peak memory results to support its practical efficiency claims. 
8.Important baselines are missing. The manuscript does not compare against recent Couinaud-specific, vessel-guided, or clinically relevant methods. In particular, Couinaud segmentation in CT has already been addressed in mature frameworks such as TotalSegmentator v2, yet no comparison is provided. This makes the practical contribution unclear. 
9.The qualitative results do not convincingly support the claimed advantages. Even in the visual examples, the proposed method still shows noticeable boundary offsets and inaccurate delineations. This weakens the claim that point-cloud-based modeling is particularly advantageous for this task.
10.Several table entries appear duplicated or inconsistent (e.g., identical Dice/ASD in ablation for different serialization settings; some text/table typos), which undermines confidence in reported numbers.
11.Data preprocessing and feature composition are under-specified (e.g., what per-point features are used beyond coordinates/intensity? any normalization, augmentation?).
12.Training/validation/test splits, case counts per split, and cross-validation protocols are not reported; reproducibility is limited without code or detailed settings (e.g., window size w, neighborhood/window overlap, spike thresholds).
13.Does not discuss or compare to recent Couinaud-specific methods that incorporate vascular priors or registration-based augmentations. Given the paper’s focus on topology-aware segmentation and boundary precision, omitting these is a notable gap.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper introduces a creative and potentially impactful SNN-based framework for 3D point-cloud liver segmentation, with principled serialization and a hardware-conscious attention design. The methodological novelty is credible and the energy-efficiency narrative is compelling. However, serious concerns about experimental validity and reproducibility remain: most critically, the provenance of Couinaud labels on LiTS and MSD8 is not explained, undermining confidence in the central claims; the boundary metric computation pipeline is unspecified; and energy/runtimes are presented largely as theoretical estimates without corroborating system-level measurements. The omission of direct comparisons to recent Couinaud- or vessel-guided methods further weakens contextualization. With detailed clarification of labels, reconstruction steps, and practical runtime/memory measurements—and with stronger contextual baselines—this work could be a valuable contribution. In its current form, I recommend rejection, primarily due to dataset/labeling ambiguity and incomplete experimental reporting, despite the promising technical ideas.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper presents a spiking neural network (SNN) architecture called Pulse Sequence-Encoded Point Cloud Transformer (SSPT) for Couinaud liver segmentation of 3D medical point clouds. By introducing a time scanning scheduler (TSD), the 3D spatial topology is serialized into one-dimensional time pulses, and the pulse-encoding attention (SSA) is utilized to convert floating-point multiply-add operations into low-power accumulation operations. This model demonstrates excellent performance in terms of theoretical energy consumption. 
Introducing the low-power characteristic of SNN into 3D medical point cloud processing is an inspiring and highly promising research direction. However, the current manuscript has significant flaws in data preprocessing as a black box, the fairness of cross-modal baseline comparison, the reproducibility of experiments, and the consistency of clinical motivation. These issues directly affect the validity and credibility of the experimental results. Therefore, I currently give a preliminary evaluation of “Weak Reject”. But I am very much looking forward to seeing the authors’ strong responses to the following core issues in the Rebuttal stage.
reviews.text_strengths:
Major Strength 1
The paper presents a novel and well-motivated architecture adaptation by elegantly combining the Z-order space-filling curve with the sliding window mechanism (TSD). This design effectively resolves the critical spatiotemporal mismatch between static 3D geometric point clouds and the continuous spike dynamics of spiking neural networks (SNNs). Such a cross-paradigm alignment is non-trivial and represents an original way to bridge discrete geometric representations with event-based, continuous-time computation, making the work technically innovative and conceptually interesting.
Major Strength 2 
A key strength lies in the extremely high theoretical energy efficiency enabled by the proposed SSA module. The module maintains linear complexity while drastically reducing floating-point operations. Compared with traditional artificial neural networks, the work reports a remarkable 98.1% reduction in theoretical energy consumption, which is outstanding and highly relevant to resource-constrained medical imaging and clinical deployment scenarios. This strong efficiency advantage significantly enhances the practical value of the method.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Major Weakness 1 
The paper is primarily motivated by real-time intraoperative surgical planning and ultra-low-power constraints to justify the use of SNNs. However, Couinaud segmentation is clinically a preoperative offline planning task, where energy consumption and millisecond-level latency are generally less critical than absolute segmentation accuracy. This makes the core motivation less convincing. 
Major Weakness 2 
The paper lacks critical details regarding 3D point cloud extraction from raw CT/MRI volumes. The authors state that data are converted to 3D point clouds via windowing/cropping and then sampled to 60,000 points using FPS. However, how the initial point cloud is generated from the 3D volume is completely unclear, whether by intensity thresholding, uniform grid sampling, or another strategy. This missing step is essential for reproducibility, because segmentation performance strongly depends on the initial point distribution, especially when extracting sparse vascular structures.
Major Weakness 3
The claimed energy efficiency is based on theoretical calculations under a 45nm CMOS process, which is acceptable for conceptual validation but incomplete for SNN research. Standard evaluation in this field also requires practical runtime metrics independent of custom ASIC hardware. The authors should supplement their results with actual inference speed (ms/volume or FPS) and peak GPU memory usage (MB) on a commodity GPU such as RTX 3090 to complement the theoretical energy claims and enable fairer comparison with existing ANN methods.
Major Weakness 4 
To ensure full reproducibility of the proposed method, the authors are strongly encouraged to release the source code (including data preprocessing, model implementation, and evaluation scripts). Without accessible code, it is difficult for the community to verify, reproduce, or build upon the presented approach, which limits the impact and transparency of the work.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

My recommendation of a ‘Weak Reject’ reflects a careful balance between the paper’s highly original methodological contributions and its shortcomings in clinical motivation, reproducibility, and practical evaluation.
Major factors favoring acceptance:
The paper presents a highly innovative cross-paradigm alignment by adapting Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) for 3D unstructured medical point clouds. The elegant combination of the Z-order space-filling curve with the sliding window mechanism (TSD) successfully resolves the spatiotemporal mismatch between static geometry and continuous spike dynamics. Furthermore, the theoretical 98.1% reduction in energy consumption achieved by the SSA module is an outstanding technical achievement that highlights the potential of SNNs in resource-constrained scenarios.
Major factors driving the ‘Weak Reject’:
Despite the strong technical core, the current manuscript falls marginally below the acceptance threshold due to four critical issues:
Misaligned Clinical Motivation: The paper justifies the use of SNNs by citing “real-time intraoperative” constraints. However, Couinaud segmentation is standardly a preoperative offline planning task where absolute accuracy far outweighs energy efficiency or millisecond latency.
Critical Reproducibility Gap (Data Preprocessing): The exact pipeline for extracting the initial 3D point cloud from dense raw CT/MRI volumes (before applying FPS to reach 60k points) is opaque. Because vascular structures are sparse, blind sampling on raw voxels is physically problematic. This missing step makes the results impossible to replicate.
Lack of Practical Evaluation Metrics: Relying solely on theoretical ASIC energy calculations (45nm CMOS) is insufficient. To fairly compare with ANN baselines, practical runtime metrics, specifically inference speed (ms/volume) and peak memory usage (MB) on standard commodity GPUs (like the RTX 3090 used)—must be reported.
Closed Source Code: The absence of source code further exacerbates the reproducibility issues, limiting the community’s ability to verify the data pipeline and the SNN implementation.
Condition for Acceptance:
I “would not mind if accepted” and am very open to raising my score to an ‘Accept’ if the authors can use the rebuttal to: 1) transparently detail the raw-volume-to-point-cloud preprocessing pipeline, 2) provide practical GPU-based inference latency and memory metrics, and 3) explicitly commit to releasing their source code.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper has some technical merit on 3D medical point cloud segmentation. The reviewers has concern on the evaluation and datasets, lack of metrics of claims. Unequal comparison, etc.

For this paper, i found some reviewers’ comments and opinions are less informative or purely AI-generated; therefore, a complete re-review is conducted by AC. Based on AC’s addition review, the major concern of this paper is the evaluation and datasets; this paper seems to have only evaluated several old datasets, which may already be saturated and cannot fully reflect the real effectiveness of this proposed method.

Given the author’s rebuttal which addresses the main criticisms of the paper, my recommendation would be to accept the paper given the points for rejection raised by reviewers could be be addressed fairly easily in the revised version.

The rebuttal substantially clarifies the dataset labels, CT-to-point-cloud preprocessing, ASD computation, practical GPU efficiency, and clinical scope, and although some concerns about baseline breadth, statistical reporting, and reproducibility remain, the technical novelty and addressed core ambiguities support acceptance with these details incorporated in the camera-ready version.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the reviewers for recognizing the design of our SSPT model. We will release the full source code, including the model implementation, preprocessing, augmentation, evaluation, and energy-estimation scripts, upon publication.
1.[R1,R2,R3] Preprocessing pipeline from CT to point clouds
We follow APVN (TMI 2024) for raw-volume preprocessing: from paired CT/label volumes, we crop and retain the liver regions covered by Couinaud annotations, apply CT windowing and normalization, and convert the retained voxels into point samples with coordinates, intensity, and labels; training uses controlled point sampling and testing uses full-point chunked inference, while voxel baselines directly use the same ROI-constrained normalized volumes. All methods are consistent in terms of data source, anatomical scope, intensity normalization, and spatial preprocessing. We will detail the pipeline in the revision.
2.[R1,R2,R3] Dataset labels
For LiTS, we use the Couinaud annotations released by APVN (TMI 2024), for MSD8, we use the Couinaud annotations released by GLC-UNet (MLMI 2019). We will add the reference in the revised manuscript.
3.[R1,R2,R3] Practical efficiency (peak GPU memory and inference speed)
We thank the reviewers for noting this issue. Regarding the efficiency comparison, we report measured efficiency on a single RTX 3090 (24 GB). On the MSD8 test set, SSPT achieves 3.79 s/volume and 6.47 GB peak GPU memory, compared with 6.933 s/volume and 5.91 GB for PTv3, and 4.438 s/volume and 6.08 GB for APVN. Peak memory is reported using maximum memory allocated. Thus, SSPTachieves an inference speed 45.3% faster than PTv3 and 14.6% than APVN, while consuming moderately more GPU memory. We will add the measured results to Table 1.
4.[R1,R2] Energy calculation
We thank the reviewers for raising the fairness concern. In our experiment, to fairly evaluate the computational cost of point-based and voxel-based representations, we designed point and voxel inputs with equivalent input sizes (point 65,000, voxel (16* 64 *64)).
As stated in the manuscript, we estimate the theoretical compute energy of each forward pass. Following widely adopted protocols of SPT (AAAI 2025) and SDT (NeurIPS 2023), we estimate theoretical compute energy under the 45 nm CMOS model, where ANN energy is computed from total MACs, while SNN energy is computed from first-layer MACs plus firing-rate-weighted ACs in subsequent spiking layers.
5.[R1,R3] Clarifying the clinical scope: offline Couinaud segmentation.
We agree that Couinaud segmentation should be positioned as an offline preoperative planning task. We will revise any wording that could be interpreted as claiming demonstrated real-time or intraoperative deployment. Thank you for reminding.
6.[R2] ASD computation and reproducibility.
Following the evaluation protocol of the APVN (TMI 2024), We map the point-wise predictions back to the NIfTI label volume using the stored voxel-index coordinates, evaluate them only within the annotated foreground mask, and then compute ASD for labels 1–8 with the surface-distance library using the physical spacing from the reference NIfTI header. We will add the details in the revised manuscript.
7.[R2] Evaluation against SOTA baselines and qualitative analysis
In the submitted experiments, we selected APVN (TMI 2024), which is currently the state-of-the-art Couinaud segmentation model with publicly available source code and data.
8.[R1,R2] Table typo and inconsistency correction
We thank the reviewers for carefully checking the reported results. We will correct all identified table/text inconsistencies in the revised manuscript.
9.[R1,R2] Statistical robustness and reporting completeness
In the revised manuscript, we will report results as mean ± standard deviation, and provide segment-wise Dice. We will also extend spike-activity visualization to support the discussion of binary gating behavior.

title: Stabilizing Temporal Inference Dynamics for Online Surgical Phase Recognition
abstract:
Online Surgical Phase Recognition (SPR) models can reach high frame-wise accuracy, yet their predictions often lack temporal stability, fragmenting workflow understanding and reducing the reliability of downstream assistance. We show that this instability is not random noise but arises from two mechanisms: early misclassifications corrupt temporal feature states and propagate forward to form error cascades, and phase transitions follow evidence-accumulation dynamics whereas most online SPR systems rely on memoryless frame-wise decisions, making them sensitive to transient confidence fluctuations. We propose a unified Train–Inference–Evaluation framework that explicitly stabilizes temporal inference dynamics using model-agnostic, plug-and-play components. For training, the Temporal Error-Cascade (TEC) loss suppresses error onset and mitigates forward error propagation by stabilizing temporal feature evolution. For inference, the Evidence-Gated Transition Predictor (EGTP) enforces evidence-driven state transitions, allowing phase changes only when accumulated evidence exceeds a confidence boundary. For evaluation, we introduce the Temporal Fragmentation Index (TFI), a
reliability-aware metric that quantifies instability-induced temporal disagreement beyond conventional frame-wise and token-based measures. Experiments on Cholec80 and AutoLaparo across three representative backbones show that the proposed framework substantially improves temporal stability and reduces prediction fragmentation, while maintaining or modestly improving frame-wise performance. Code is available at https://github.com/MRUIL/StableSPR.
subject_areas: Surgery -> Surgical Skills, Workflow & Team Dynamics

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors present an approach to stabilize temporal inference dynamics in surgical phase recognition by a) introducing a novel loss for training SPR backbones that penalizes frequent phase switching, and b) including an evidence-gated transition predictor that prevents frequent phase switching. In addition, the authors introduce a novel metric to accurately capture the instability of SPR across entire video segments.
reviews.text_strengths: The authors address an important issue: stability in SPR which is relevant to the community. The proposed modules for stabilization, the loss function and the evidence based gate, are well motivated and methodologically sound. The introduction of a novel metric to better capture temporal inference instability is an important addition which benefits the community. The experiments using two different data sets and three different state-of-the-art SPR backbones, and their results illustrate the validity of the proposed contributions. The results clearly show that temporal stability has been drastically improved.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The main weakness is that improvements obtained with the proposed approach with respect to Accuracy and Precision are modest. This is however not the main claim of the manuscript. The temporal stability is indeed improved significantly.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The legibility of the labels in some figures should be improved. In Fig. 2a, EGHS probably refers to EGTP.

The relevance to the community, the novelty of the proposed elements and the convincing experiments and results.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a framework for dealing temporal instability in surgical phase recognition in surgical videos. It includes a loss function for learning, an additional step for inference and a metric for validation. It has been tested on two publicly available data sets with ablation studies and shown improvements in several metrics.
reviews.text_strengths:
The objective of the paper is relevant.
However, temporal instability is on issue between other ones in surgical workflow recognition from surgical videos
The proposed solution is generic and can be used within several architectures as shown in the paper.
The proposed solution includes a coherent framework covering training, inference and validation.
Quantitative validation performed with several metrics on two publicly available datasets show the added value of the approach.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper is based ont the statement that “true surgical phase transitions are inherently evidence-accumulation processes”. It is true but it is not the only reason. Instability can simply come from a wrong or ambiguous definition of a phase or since the information is not available in the video: something happens out of the field of the surgical video.
In the Metrics section and in the introduction section, one of the first (if not the first) publications mentioning this issue and suggesting corresponding new metrics is not cited: Dergachyova, O., Bouget, D., Huaulme, A., Morandi, X., & Jannin, P. (2016). Automatic data-driven real-time segmentation and recognition of surgical workflow. Int J Comput Assist Radiol Surg, 11(6), 1081-1089.Results: Analysis without standard deviation and without statistical analysis is not acceptable. The statement of order of magnitude improvements is oversold.
Extension: And what about step recognition ? Is there the same issue ? Is your solution compatible ? Will it provide the same improvements ?

N/A

A well written paper but could be improved especially as regards to the results section.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses an important problem in online surgical phase recognition, predictions may be frame-wise accurate but temporally unstable, which can fragment workflow understanding and reduce the reliability of downstream assistance systems. To address this, the authors propose a unified train–inference–evaluation framework consisting of: (i) the Temporal Error-Cascade (TEC) loss, which emphasizes the onset of consecutive errors during training to reduce forward error propagation; (ii) the Evidence-Gated Transition Predictor (EGTP), which models phase changes as an evidence-accumulation process during inference rather than relying on instantaneous argmax decisions; and (iii) the Temporal Fragmentation Index (TFI), a new metric intended to quantify instability-induced temporal disagreement beyond frame-wise accuracy and Edit Score. The framework is presented as model-agnostic and plug-and-play, and experiments on Cholec80 and AutoLaparo with three backbones suggest improved temporal stability. The combined addage of TEC and EGTP to each of the three backbones resulted in higher performance and stability across both datasets.
reviews.text_strengths: A major strength of the paper is that it focuses directly on temporal stability, which is a clinically relevant perspective for online surgical workflow recognition. The proposed framework is also conceptually clean, with separate components for training, inference, and evaluation, and the methods themselves are easy to understand and appear broadly applicable across several representative SPR backbones, including Trans-SVNet, SKiT, and Surgformer. The introduction of the TFI metric further strengthens the paper, as it highlights a real limitation of Edit Score by distinguishing between predictions that may have similar compressed token sequences but very different temporal fragmentation. The qualitative and quantitative results consistently show that EGTP strongly reduces flickering and rapid phase switching across datasets.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Experimental protocol and reporting: It is currently difficult to assess how reliable the reported gains actually are. In particular, the paper states that Cholec80 is split into 40 training and 40 testing videos, but it does not explain how hyperparameters such as alpha and k are selected in the absence of a validation split. In addition, the paper reports only single-run numbers without standard deviations or multiple-seed experiments, even though many of the reported gains in accuracy-related metrics are small and may not be statistically meaningful; this is especially important because some prior work in this area (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.13961) has reported variances on Cholec80 which might suggest that several of the perfomance metrics reported could be statistically indistinguishable. This also goes in line with recent findings regarding overclaiming model accuracy when statistical variability is not considered (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.04720) which in particular affects the validity of the “improved accuracy” claim in this study.
2.Benefit of EGTP architecture: The empirical comparisons do not fully compare EGTP against simpler or more established temporal smoothing alternatives. Since EGTP functions as a post-processing comparison to standard temporal smoothing or structured prediction methods, such as transition constraints or probabilistic sequence smoothing approaches, would be important to show that the benefit comes from the proposed mechanism rather than from generic temporal regularization alone. Furthermore, because surgical workflows follow a strict procedural order, the authors should evaluate whether simply restricting impossible phase transitions (e.g., using a transition prior matrix derived from the training set) would achieve similar stability improvements. Without this baseline, it is unclear if the dynamic evidence accumulation of EGTP is truly necessary or if a simpler transition constraint would suffice.
3.Interpretation of results: The results reveal trade-offs that are not discussed clearly enough. While EGTP strongly improves TFI and Edit Score, some precision, recall, and Jaccard results on Cholec80 are better without EGTP, suggesting that stronger temporal smoothing may suppress true transitions or harm class-wise performance in some settings. Similarly, in the EGTP versus E-Const comparison, the proposed method is argued to be better mainly due to slightly higher accuracy and more consistent threshold scaling, but in some cases E-Const yields substantially lower TFI, so the paper should better justify why the chosen balance between marginal accuracy gains and much larger stability differences is preferable for practical deployment.
4.Missing discussion: A major structural weakness is the absence of a discussion section which is necessary to bring the achieved results into perspective of related work and discuss shortcomings and future work. A summarizing conclusion is not sufficient for this. Furthermore, the experiment section should be renamed to Experiments and Results to highlight where the results are presented in the paper.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
All figures and tables should be self-explanatory. In particular in the caption of figure 1 the terms p, P, E, y^, M should be introduced
The authors claim that “On AutoLaparo of Surgformer, EGTP reduces TFI from 10.67 to 0.48” while table 1 only shows a reduction from 10.67 to 0.96.- While the newly introduced TFI metric conceptually addresses the temporal disagreement within segments compared to Edit Score, its benefit doesn’t seem to show in the performed validation in which Edit Score features a similar “nearly one order of magnitude” change. It would be good to discuss / highlight scenarios in the context of SPR where TFI is beneficial.

This paper addresses a highly relevant clinical problem by proposing an elegant, model-agnostic framework (TEC, EGTP, and TFI) to explicitly tackle temporal instability in online surgical phase recognition. However, the experimental methodology currently lacks the rigor required to fully support the authors’ claims. Most critically, the paper does not define a validation split for the Cholec80 dataset or generally clarify the subsets used, raising significant concerns about hyperparameter tuning (such as alpha and k) and potential data leakage on the test set. Additionally, the absence of variance estimates or standard deviations across multiple random seeds makes it impossible to verify the statistical significance of the reported marginal accuracy gains, which is a known issue in this field. Finally, EGTP operates as a temporal post-processing decision policy but fails to compare against established temporal smoothing baselines, such as Hidden Markov Models (HMMs), Conditional Random Fields (CRFs), or basic surgical workflow transition priors. While the core ideas and the new TFI metric are strong, the authors must clarify their data splitting protocol, provide variance estimates, and include standard baselines in the rebuttal for this work to confidently cross the acceptance threshold.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text: This paper tackles a clinically important problem. Reviewers consistently agree on the relevance, soundness, and generality of the approach. The key contributions are well-motivated and practically impactful, with clear and consistent improvements in temporal stability across multiple datasets and backbones. The introduction of TFI is also a valuable addition for the community. While minor concerns remain (e.g., statistical reporting and additional baselines), they do not undermine the strength of the core contributions. Overall, the paper shows clear novelty, solid validation, and high practical relevance. Therefore, I would suggest early acceptance.

title: Stage-Aware Adaptive Reaction–Diffusion Framework for Modeling Alzheimer’s Disease Progression with Tau and Amyloid-β PET Scans
abstract:
Longitudinal PET enables regional quantification of amyloid-
β (Aβ) and tau burden in Alzheimer’s disease, yet long-horizon forecasting is challenging due to sparse, irregular follow-up and strong heterogeneity in disease stage and pace of the progression. Mechanistic progression models are interpretable but often rigid, while generic neural ODE regressors handle irregular sampling at the cost of mechanistic transparency and stability. We propose a lightweight, stage-aware mechanistic neural ODE that couples a connectome-constrained diffusion–reaction backbone with structured local residual dynamics. The model includes state-dependent diffusion modulation on a fixed structural connectome, an explicit negative-feedback channel, and a logistic-shaped residual gain, routed by a simple gating module over latent disease time and global burden with subject-specific affine time alignment. On ADNI tau-PET and amyloid-PET cohorts, we improve ROI-level forecasting on held-out subjects setting and reveal stage- and biomarker-dependent patterns in effective coupling and component contributions.
subject_areas: Applications -> Outcome Prediction / Prognosis / Longitudinal Modeling

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper proposes STARD, a stage-aware and interpretable mechanistic neural ODE framework for modeling Alzheimer’s disease progression from sparse longitudinal tau- and amyloid-PET data. The main contribution lies in bridging mechanistic modeling and data-driven flexibility while preserving interpretability. 
Extensive experiments on ADNI tau- and Aβ-PET datasets demonstrate improved ROI-level forecasting accuracy over both mechanistic and neural ODE baselines. Moreover, the model enables interpretable decomposition of disease dynamics, revealing stage-dependent shifts in diffusion strength and component contributions across biomarkers.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper effectively combines a connectome-constrained reaction–diffusion model with neural ODE flexibility, achieving a good balance between interpretability and predictive power. 
2.The introduction of latent disease-time alignment and stage-aware gating allows the model to explicitly account for inter-subject heterogeneity in disease stage and progression speed, which is highly relevant for Alzheimer’s disease modeling. 
3.The proposed dynamic, ROI-wise diffusion modulation (dmod) significantly extends classical diffusion models by allowing disease-dependent connectivity effects rather than assuming globally fixed diffusion. 
4.The decomposition into mechanistic backbone and structured local residual provides clear physiological interpretability and enables meaningful post-hoc analysis.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Although the paper integrates several components, most of the underlying ideas are based on well-established prior work. For example, connectome-based reaction–diffusion models have been widely studied [1], and neural ODEs for irregular time-series modeling are already quite mature [2]. Latent disease-time modeling and temporal alignment have also been explored in neurodegenerative disease progression [3], and more recently, hybrid approaches combining mechanistic models with neural networks have been proposed [4]. As a result, the current work feels more like an integration and refinement of existing techniques rather than introducing a fundamentally new modeling paradigm. This also suggests that the related work discussion could be strengthened, as some recent developments are not fully covered. 
2.Some key components, such as the structured local residual term, the negative-feedback mechanism, and the gating design, are not sufficiently motivated or explained. In particular, the connection between these components and the underlying biological processes is not clearly established, and there is limited support from prior literature. This makes the claim of interpretability less convincing. 
3.The method is the main contribution of the paper and is presented in a heavily formula-driven way. However, the large number of symbols and equations makes it somewhat difficult to follow. It would help to include a short preliminaries section or a table summarizing the notations, so that readers can more easily understand the formulation. 
4.Further, the paper does not provide an open-source implementation or a clear reproducibility pathway, which raises concerns about the reliability and reproducibility of the experimental results.
[1] Chaggar, Pavanjit, Jacob W. Vogel, Alexa Pichet Binette, Travis B. Thompson, Olof Strandberg, Niklas Mattsson-Carlgren, Linda Karlsson et al. “Personalised regional modelling predicts tau progression in the human brain. “ PLoS Biology 23, no. 7 (2025): e3003241.
[2] Kidger, Patrick, James Morrill, James Foster, and Terry Lyons. “Neural controlled differential equations for irregular time series. “ Advances in neural information processing systems 33 (2020): 6696-6707.
[3] Young, Alexandra L. , Neil P. Oxtoby, Sara Garbarino, Nick C. Fox, Frederik Barkhof, Jonathan M. Schott, and Daniel C. Alexander. “Data-driven modelling of neurodegenerative disease progression: thinking outside the black box. “ Nature Reviews Neuroscience 25, no. 2 (2024): 111-130.
[4] Wen, Zheyu, George Biros, and Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI. “Aligning personalized biomarker trajectories onto a common time axis: a connectome-based ODE model for Tau–Amyloid beta dynamics. “ Medical Image Analysis (2025): 103757.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Overall, I lean towards a weak accept. The paper addresses an important problem in Alzheimer’s disease progression modeling and proposes a reasonably well-designed framework that combines mechanistic modeling with neural ODEs. The stage-aware formulation and the integration of diffusion–reaction dynamics with adaptive components are meaningful and lead to consistent improvements over several baselines. In addition, the model provides some level of interpretability, and the experimental results are fairly comprehensive.
However, I do have concerns regarding the level of novelty, as many components build upon existing ideas and the contribution is more incremental. Some parts of the method are not sufficiently motivated or clearly explained, particularly in terms of their biological interpretation. The writing could also be improved for better clarity, and the lack of an open-source implementation raises minor concerns about reproducibility.
Despite these issues, I believe the paper has solid technical value and could be of interest to the community, especially for researchers working on disease progression modeling and interpretable continuous-time methods. With improved clarity and stronger positioning with respect to prior work, the paper would be further strengthened.

1.The authors include many features that are characteristic of pathological aging and Alzheimer’s disease. This includes features from imaging modalities that are traditionally used to understand disease progression in research. 
2.The authors are able to show exciting results that lead to imaging features dominating the prediction since imaging metrics are generally objective features. 
3.The authors use open source data which is accessible to the public. This adds to the reproducibility of the work.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
There are a few weaknesses, but only in terms of presentation. 
1.Some of your figures include the “red squiggly misspell” lines in the names of the models.
2.Inside the text, there are words that are separated by dashes that should not be such as “models”. In the author’s text it has “mod-els”.

reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Great work. I believe that, for future studies, you may want to include white matter hyperintensities (WMH) detected on T2FLAIR images (or Proton Density + T1w). WMH has been shown to be a better predictor of AD, even over hippocampal size alone. It may be worth exploring this biomarker.

I believe researchers in the AD space have been looking for a model like this to help predict AD early so that they can help figure out treatment or lifestyle modifications that stop or slow progression. I believe the researchers still have a ways to go, but this is in the correct direction.

meta_reviews.text: This paper presents a well-designed and clinically meaningful framework for modeling Alzheimer’s disease progression, with reviewers highlighting strong motivation, solid experimental validation, and useful interpretability. While the approach is largely an integration of existing ideas and thus somewhat incremental in novelty, it is technically sound and demonstrates consistent improvements over relevant baselines. Some components would benefit from clearer motivation and explanation, and the manuscript could be improved in terms of clarity and reproducibility details. Overall, the work makes a valuable contribution, and with these revisions, it meets the bar for acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the reviewers and the AC for their careful reading, constructive comments, and positive assessment of our work.
We agree that STARD builds upon several established lines of research, including reaction–diffusion modeling, continuous-time neural models, and latent disease-time alignment. Our intended novelty is not to introduce these ideas as isolated components, but to integrate them into a constrained mechanistic-neural ODE formulation tailored to sparse longitudinal tau- and Aβ-PET progression modeling. Unlike generic neural ODE models, STARD preserves an explicitly decomposable disease-dynamics structure, thereby reducing the black-box nature of continuous-time forecasting. In addition, the state-dependent diffusion modulation and structured local residual provide controlled flexibility beyond conventional reaction–diffusion models, leading to improved forecasting performance while retaining mechanistic interpretability.
We also appreciate the reviewer’s concern regarding the biological motivation of the structured local residual, negative-feedback term, and gating mechanism. We clarify that these terms are not intended to identify independent, directly observable biological mechanisms at this stage. Rather, they are structured phenomenological channels designed to separate net local suppressive or clearance-like effects from local amplification effects, and to adapt their relative contribution across latent disease stages. In future work, we aim to further refine these modules to better disentangle heterogeneous and potentially confounded processes involved in Alzheimer’s disease progression.
We agree that, within the limited page length, presenting all mathematical details clearly is challenging. To improve readability and reproducibility, we will also release the model implementation, configuration files, and necessary preprocessing/reproducibility instructions at the camera-ready stage, subject to ADNI data-use restrictions.
We thank the reviewer for pointing out presentation issues. We will carefully correct all typographical and formatting errors in the camera-ready version, including spell-check underlines in figures, unintended word hyphenations, and equation formatting problems.
Finally, we appreciate the suggestion regarding white matter hyperintensities. While the current study focuses on modeling tau- and Aβ-PET progression, we agree that WMH and even regional brain atrophy could provide complementary information for disease progression modeling. Together, the cognition test could also be incorporated. Incorporating these additional biomarkers, while carefully handling their noise and modality-specific uncertainty, is our important direction for extending this work into a more comprehensive journal-level study.

title: STAMP: Subtype-Aware Spatio-Temporal Atlases for Personalized Prediction of Longitudinal Alzheimer’s Disease Progression
abstract: Automatic disentanglement of progression subtypes in neurodegenerative disorders is critical for patient stratification in clinical management and trial enrichment. Existing disease subtyping methods operate exclusively on low-dimensional scalar biomarkers, discarding the fine-grained spatial patterns necessary for biologically meaningful subtype discovery and patient-level personalization. Conversely, continuous-time models that directly operate on longitudinal 3D brain MRI recover a single shared population trajectory and perform no subtyping, critically limiting personalized prediction and clinical interpretability. To fill this gap, we present STAMP, a longitudinal progression subtyping framework that, integrates automatic subtype discovery directly into the optimization of a continuous-time spatio-temporal atlas from longitudinal 3D T1 brain MRI. STAMP jointly learns subtype-specific temporal placements, dense image deformation fields, and region-wise progression functions, enabling probabilistic subtype assignment and personalized trajectory prediction for new subjects. Evaluated on longitudinal ADNI-1/GO/2 data, STAMP achieves the lowest forecasting error in 16 of 18 anatomical regions and statistically significant improvements in 11 regions compared to single-trajectory and post-hoc subtyping baselines, while recovering clinically interpretable subtype structure.
subject_areas: Applications -> Outcome Prediction / Prognosis / Longitudinal Modeling

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a longitudinal progression subtyping framework named STAMP that integrates automatic subtype discovery into the optimization of a continuous-time spatio-temporal atlas from longitudinal 3D brain MRI for personalized trajectory prediction.
reviews.text_strengths:
1 The overall research topic is highly valuable because longitudinal analysis and the generation of disease trajectories represent crucial frontiers in the medical imaging community. 
2 The method reasonably incorporates neurological priors to guide regional progression analysis, resulting in a clinically meaningful contribution that should be extended to broader disease categories and morphological topics in future studies. 
3 The writing is clear, and the figure is well presented.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1 While the modeling is logical, real-world brain disease evolution is highly non-linear, and the sequential process of first analyzing subtype progression to subsequently drive the deformation backbone might introduce overly strong linear assumptions and error accumulation, which the authors need to clarify again. 
2 The authors are encouraged to explore advanced medical world model architectures like Brain-WM [1] to utilize a unified multimodal framework that can collaboratively process subtype discovery and spatio-temporal deformation, allowing the two tasks to mutually align and promote each other end-to-end. 
3The study lacks validation on independent external longitudinal cohorts, making it difficult to confirm whether the discovered subtypes are generalizable neurodegenerative patterns or merely overfitted to the specific data distribution of the ADNI dataset.
[1] Brain-WM: Brain Glioblastoma World Model, arxiv, 2026.

reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a subtype-aware longitudinal disease progression model that jointly learns the subtype structure and continuous-time spatio-temporal atlas directly using 3D T1 brain MRI scans. The method can infer the subtype membership and personalized future trajectory simultaneously for given subjects. Experimental results on longitudinal ADNI-1/GO/2 data showcase lower predicting errors in majority of regions and also statistically significant improvements compared to single-trajectory baselines, while providing with interpretable subtypes.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper overcomes the limitations of the existing subtyping work which utilize scalar biomarkers such as the SuStaIn framework, and also improves upon imaging-based disease progression modeling without tackling the heterogeneity, therefore this paper is well-positioned to bridge the gap and potentially contribute to the field of neurogenerative disease modeling and subtyping
The key contribution of the paper is the novel integration of subtyping framework with continuous-time atlas modeling, which is conceptually strong as the subtype assignment is embedded in an end-to-end fashion within the model by a joint learning scheme
Besides the combination of several technical components such as Neural ODE-based progression functions, the authors further apply regularization to avoid all subjects collapse into trivial solutions, as this is a critical issue for subtyping in this domain

The current experiment lacks the comparison to subtyping methods in the domain, as the paper is somewhat positioned against methods like SuStaIn
There is limited discussion on cases where the subtype assignment fails or the uncertainty in the subtyping, as well as the sensitivity to the number of subtypes
All the experiments are only conducted on ADNI dataset, without external validation dataset such as BLSA, AIBL, OASIS, etc., which limits the generalizability and robustness of the proposed method

reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces a spatiotemporal disease progression model, designed for brain MRI and neurodegenerative disease, that accounts for distinct disease subtypes. This fills a clear hole in current disease progression modelling technology, where current subtype models do not consider the whole image or continuous temporal change and current spatiotemporal models do not consider subtypes. Results are encouraging showing improved prediction of longitudinal morphological change over a well-chosen set of contemporary baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
Fills a clear gap in disease progression modelling technology

reviews.text_weaknesses:
These preliminary results don’t really show disease subtypes but rather seem to separate out people on a trajectory of normal aging (subtype 1) from those on a genuine dementia trajectory (subtype 2). This is evidenced by the fact that most of the CN cases get assigned to subtype 1 while all of the dementia cases get assigned to subtype 2. This does have some value, but does not quite achieve what the authors intend the method to achieve. Perhaps some further tuning of the parameters might reveal actual disease subtypes, as found using e.g. SuStaIn on the same data set.
Figure 2 isn’t particularly useful as presented. It is hard to distinguish the subtypes by eye. More useful would be to show a visual comparison with SuStaIn subtypes to highlight whether the STAMP subtypes align at corresponding disease/model stages
