3.The paper reports mean and standard deviation metrics but does not include statistical significance testing. Given the small performance margins, such analysis is important to validate whether the improvements are meaningful.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses an important problem and proposes a well-motivated framework, including the contrast encoder and structure feature masking. The method is clearly presented and supported by ablation studies. However, the main factors leading to my decision are the limited novelty relative to prior works on multi-contrast MRI and INR-based methods, and the modest qualitative and quantitative improvements over existing methods. The reported gains are small and not supported by statistical significance analysis, making it unclear whether they are meaningful in practice.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have addressed my comments, and I have no further major concerns.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper proposes an INR-based framework for accelerated multi-contrast MRI reconstruction that disentangles a shared structural latent from a contrast-specific latent space. The reviewers agree on several strengths: the problem is well motivated, the architecture is technically sound, the structure feature masking is an interesting idea supported by ablations, and the experimental protocol includes both single- and multi-contrast baselines.
The AC found reviewers split (4/4/3) on three main points. The first is novelty. R2 views the motivation and idea as novel, whereas R3 argues that shared structure/contrast representations have already been explored in multi-contrast MRI reconstruction (citing Niessen et al., NeRP, and IMJENSE) and that the paper needs clearer positioning of what is fundamentally new beyond porting disentanglement into INR. R1 takes a middle position, treating the contribution as incremental but meaningful. The second concern is whether the modest quantitative gains (~0.2–0.3 dB PSNR, ~0.005–0.007 SSIM over MC-IMJENSE) are sufficient; R1 and R2 accept them as part of an incremental contribution, while R3 views them as too small to justify acceptance without statistical significance testing. The third weakness is the sole use of the 0.3T M4RAW dataset, which R3 frames as a strength (low-field, clinically relevant) but R1 and R2 view as a limitation on generalizability.
The AC views these points primarily clarification issues, rather than fundamental flaws in the experiments/comparisons. Given the split scores and the tractable nature of the concerns, I recommend inviting the authors to respond in rebuttal before a final decision. Please carefully read reviewers’ comments and MICCAI rebuttal guidelines while preparing the rebuttal.

This paper proposes a structure-contrast disentangled INR for multi-contrast MRI reconstruction, and while the quantitative gains over MC-IMJENSE are admittedly modest, the rebuttal confirmed they’re statistically significant across all settings and gave a reasonable justification for the single-dataset evaluation, with R3 moving to accept and R1 holding a positive score. The core idea is interesting and the disentanglement design is supported by ablations, so I’m recommending acceptance. The camera-ready should include the corrected Fig. 4b interpretation the authors acknowledged during rebuttal.

The authors have addressed the reviewers’ concerns in their rebuttal. Specifically, they have addressed the novelty of the method and provided statistical tests to show that, while modest, the improvements described are statistically significant. I believe that this paper represents a solid contribution that should be recommended for acceptance.

The authors clarified their novelty and well addressed the concerns of R3 who rated the submission as weak reject before rebuttal. I vote for accept and feel this is a timely paper using INR and enforcing structural disentenglement. It would raise discussion at MICCAI 2026.

author_feedback_text:
We thank reviewers and meta-reviewer for their valuable feedback. We have summarized the points and provide our response as follows.
1.R3 views the core idea of structure / contrast disentanglement as not entirely new. To the best of our knowledge, Niessen et al. [12] is the only MRI reconstruction method that jointly models multiple contrasts with an INR, and this work did not explore structure/contrast disentanglement. R3 views NeRP [14] and IMJENSE [5] as having leveraged shared representation across contrasts; however, both methods have only explored single contrast reconstruction. We believe that our proposed framework for inter-contrast information sharing remains an entirely new concept in the field of zero-shot reconstruction.
2.R1,R2 view the evaluation solely on the M4RAW dataset as a weakness. To the best of our knowledge, M4RAW is the only publicly available raw MRI dataset consistently collected with paired contrasts. R2 proposes fastMRI, and while subsets of the dataset do contain subjects with multiple contrasts, they are inconsistent and exhibit mismatched resolution, alignment, and matrix sizes, making them not directly suitable for multi-contrast INR reconstruction. We note that because our method is subject-specific (i.e. zero-shot) we do not face the same domain-shift challenges common to supervised methods; therefore, we strongly believe that our method will generalize well to clinical field strengths.
3.R1 comments that our method may be sensitive to inter-contrast misalignment. We do not view this limitation to be insurmountable within our proposed framework. We expect that confounds such as motion can be addressed by transforming the co-ordinate inputs to align the internal continuous representations without any other modifications to the image models. Leveraging this, we are actively working on extending our method to handle misalignment and other sources of heterogeneity that would be encountered in real-world settings.
4.R2 suggests that the contrast branch of the network is too compact, and could be replaced with something more expressive. Our fundamental hypothesis is that the majority of information within a set of matched contrast images is contained within the shared anatomical structure, and that the contrast differences relative to the shared structure can be encoded with far less complexity; therefore, we believe that the limited expressivity of the contrast branch is key for our proposed structure/contrast separation. However, it may be interesting to explore contrast encoder complexity in the future.
5.R1,R2,R3 view the quantitative improvements as modest, additionally R3 notes that no statistical significance testing was performed. Firstly, we can confirm that the originally presented PSNR/SSIM improvements of our method relative to the next best performing model MC-IMJENSE are statistically significant across all contrasts and acceleration factors (p < 1e-4 in all cases). Additionally, we note that the M4RAW dataset represents an extremely noisy reconstruction context, where the baseline quality of the data likely confounds efficient information sharing between contrasts. Given this, we believe that the consistent performance gains of 0.2-0.3dB across all tested acceleration rates demonstrates the strong theoretical basis for our idea of structure contrast disentanglement.
Additionally, we wish to correct a mistake that was made in our proposed interpretation of the learned contrast embeddings (Fig. 4 b). We originally claimed that they are generalizable between subjects despite entirely independent and uniquely initialized training runs. This is inaccurate, as the existing figure was made with identically-initialized training runs. With full random initialization, the contrast embeddings are not aligned across subjects, as each subject specific training run learns the structure/contrast separation in a unique way. An updated figure would be included in the final paper.

title: Subject- and Task-Aware EEG Foundation Model
abstract: Recent advances in EEG foundation models have predomi nantly relied on self-supervised learning to extract generalizable representations from large-scale datasets. However, this paradigm overlooks the rich semantic information such as subject identities and task labels available in pre-training datasets. Therefore, it limits the model’s ability to consider inter-subject variability and task heterogeneity in EEG datasets, often resulting in suboptimal generalization to unseen subjects and adaptation to various tasks. In this paper, we propose a novel Subject- and Task-Aware EEG Foundation Model (STEM) that fully leverages available semantic information. This method disentangles feature representations into subject-aware and task-aware components by integrating a metric-based meta-learning with contrastive self-supervision. This maximizes the utility of semantic labels to guide the learning of robust features. Extensive experiments across three down- stream benchmarks demonstrate that incorporating semantic supervision significantly enhances adaptation capability for various tasks and new subjects. Our findings suggest that actively utilizing subject and task information during pre-training is crucial for building robust EEG foundation models. The code is available at https://github.com/SionAn/MICCAI2026STEM.
subject_areas: Modalities -> EEG / MEG / ECG / Physiological Signals

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a novel Subject- and Task-Aware EEG Foundation Model (STEM) that moves beyond conventional self-supervised pretraining by explicitly incorporating semantic information such as subject identities and task labels into the learning process. The framework includes a shared encoder, a decomposer module, and specialized decoders, jointly optimized to learn robust and adaptable representations, leading to improved performance across multiple downstream EEG benchmarks and few-shot adaptation scenarios.
reviews.text_strengths:
Introduces a novel paradigm by integrating semantic supervision into EEG foundation models. 
Effectively disentangles subject-aware and task-aware representations. 
Combines self-supervised learning with metric-based meta-learning in a unified framework. 
Addresses key challenges of inter-subject variability and task heterogeneity. 
Demonstrates strong performance across multiple downstream tasks and datasets. 
Includes comprehensive evaluation on both task-related and state-related EEG benchmarks. 
Shows superior efficiency compared to larger foundation models (e. g. , fewer parameters than EEG-DINO). 
Provides ablation studies validating the contribution of each component. 
Demonstrates strong few-shot adaptation capability for new subjects. 
Well-aligned with emerging trends in foundation models for biomedical signals.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The improvement over strong baselines is relatively modest in some benchmarks (e. g. , Table 2 on page 6). 
The novelty is partly incremental, as contrastive learning and meta-learning have been previously explored in EEG and representation learning. 
The disentanglement mechanism lacks deeper theoretical justification or analysis. 
Limited discussion on computational cost and scalability for large-scale deployment. 
Generalization across highly diverse real-world datasets is not extensively validated.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Overall, the approach is promising and aligns well with current trends in foundation model research.

The paper presents a well-motivated and technically strong contribution by introducing a subject- and task-aware framework for EEG foundation models. The integration of semantic supervision with contrastive learning and meta-learning is both meaningful, addressing key limitations of existing self-supervised approaches. The method is well-designed and supported by comprehensive experiments, including multiple benchmarks, ablation studies, and few-shot adaptation analysis, demonstrating consistent improvements and strong generalization capabilities. While some aspects of the methodology build upon existing techniques and the performance gains are comparable in certain cases, the overall contribution is significant and advances the direction of EEG foundation models.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a novel framework called STEM for learning generalizable EEG representations. The authors argue that existing EEG self-supervised learning paradigms overlook valuable semantic information such as subject identity and task labels, leading to poor model performance when dealing with inter-subject variability and task heterogeneity. To address this, STEM combines contrastive self-supervised learning with a metric-based meta-learning strategy. The model employs a shared encoder and a Decomposer to disentangle latent features into subject-aware and task-aware components. The authors evaluate STEM on three downstream datasets, demonstrating competitive performance compared to existing baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
(1) The research motivation aligns well with a key point in the field, addressing the problem of existing EEG foundation models neglecting semantic information, and is practically oriented.
(2) The model architecture is well-designed and complete, with basic experimental validation carried out, achieving performance improvements on certain downstream datasets.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(1) The feature Decomposer is designed using only simple 1D convolutions, and the theoretical justification for the disentanglement mechanism is insufficient. It is not demonstrated why this architecture can effectively separate subject-specific and task-specific features. The model lacks explicit mathematical constraints to prevent task features from still being entangled with subject information, such as orthogonality loss, adversarial feature learning, or mutual information minimization
(2) The related work only surveys self-supervised EEG foundation models, without adequate coverage of related areas such as semantics-aware representation learning, meta-learning-based feature disentanglement, and cross-subject biosignal modeling. The paper fails to clearly differentiate its contributions from existing work on semantics-aware representation learning and cross-subject EEG modeling, resulting in low discriminability of its claimed novelty.
(3) The total loss function is a weighted sum of three components, but no justification is provided for the choice of loss weights, and no ablation study is conducted on them. The training stability and reasonableness of this design remain unvalidated.
(4) There are no qualitative visualization experiments for representation disentanglement, making it impossible to intuitively verify the actual separation between subject-specific and task-specific features. The validation of the core design is thus insufficient.
(5) Since the authors integrate multi-task datasets during pre-training, what is the scaling law of the model after incorporating the proposed feature disentanglement mechanism, and how does performance change accordingly?
(6) As a “foundation model,” the experiments must cover a broader range of downstream tasks, such as LOSO emotion recognition or LOSO epilepsy detection.
(7) Statistical significance tests are absent from the ablation results tables. The performance gaps between the full STEM model and its ablated variants (w/o Subject and w/o Task) are very small, which further undermines the significance of the proposed feature disentanglement design.
(8) Can the authors provide more in-depth empirical analysis to explicitly demonstrate that task representations are fully independent of subject identity and that subject representations are insensitive to task? For example, t-SNE visualizations of features colored separately by subject and by task, or cross-classification accuracy tests.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Although the motivation of this paper to address EEG signal heterogeneity is clearly articulated, and the work demonstrates solid performance on certain benchmarks, the methodology lacks sufficient depth and constraint mechanisms to substantiate the core claim of “feature disentanglement.” Furthermore, the relatively small model scale and the limited scope of downstream experimental evaluation are insufficient to support the ambitious positioning of this work as a general-purpose “foundation model.” I therefore recommend a weak rejection, and encourage the authors to strengthen the mechanistic design of feature disentanglement and substantially expand the breadth of empirical evaluation in future submissions.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes STEM, an EEG foundation model that augments self-supervised contrastive pretraining with metric-based meta-learning over subject IDs and task labels. A shared encoder feeds three decoders (self-supervised, subject, task), and a decomposer disentangles latent features into subject-aware and task-aware components. Patch embedding combines a 1D CNN tokenizer with Fourier, 3D-electrode, and sinusoidal position embeddings. Pretraining uses 18 public EEG datasets; evaluation is on PhysioNet-MI, SHU-MI, and ISRUC, including a few-shot adaptation setting.
reviews.text_strengths:
Clear motivation: Using subject and task labels during foundation-model pretraining, rather than treating EEG as unlabeled, is a sensible direction given inter-subject and task variability.
The combination of SSL contrastive pretraining with episodic metric-based meta-learning for subject/task disentanglement is not something directly covered by the major EEG foundation models (LaBraM, CBraMod, CSBrain, EEG-DINO), which rely on masked reconstruction or distillation.
Parameter-efficient: STEM reports 3.1M parameters vs. up to 201M for EEG-DINO.
Few-shot adaptation analysis is a relevant addition given the personalization motivation.
Competitive with BIOT and LaBraM-Base on the reported benchmarks.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Benchmark claims overstated.
Under the standard CBraMod/CSBrain evaluation protocol, the published numbers on these same datasets are: PhysioNet-MI BAcc — CBraMod 0.6174–0.6417, CSBrain 0.6304; SHU-MI BAcc — CBraMod 0.6370, CSBrain 0.6417; ISRUC BAcc — CBraMod 0.7865, CSBrain 0.7925.STEM’s numbers (0.6242 / 0.6226 / 0.7863) sit in the BIOT–LaBraM-Base band and are generally below CBraMod and CSBrain, yet the paper frames STEM as SOTA. The authors should clarify whether splits and metrics match the CBraMod protocol, and temper SOTA claims accordingly.
Novelty of disentanglement is overstated.
Subject-invariant / task-relevant EEG disentanglement has substantial prior art not discussed: Özdenizci et al. (IEEE Access 2020, adversarial subject-invariant EEG), Han et al. (arXiv 2008.11426, disentangled adversarial AE) and PTSM (arXiv 2508.11357, 2025, dual-branch task/subject orthogonality). The specific combination with foundation-model pretraining is the real novelty and should be framed as such.
Missing EEG meta-learning baselines.
The central methodological ingredient is meta-learning, yet no EEG meta-learning method is compared — not even the four An et al. works the paper itself cites, nor Ng & Guan 2024 (Neural Networks, subject-as-task meta-learning), SSML (Neural Networks 2023), or MAgML (2025).
3D electrode-coordinate embedding is not properly positioned.
[2510.21585] REVE: A Foundation Model for EEG – Adapting to Any Setup with Large-Scale Pretraining on 25,000 Subjects
already proposes 3D-coordinate-based positional encoding for EEG foundation models and is pretrained at a larger scale; it should be cited and contrasted. Also
CoordConformer: Heterogenous EEG datasets decoding using Transformers | OpenReview
is another example of coordinate-based positional encoding.
Anomalous ablation number.
In Table 4, “w/ MAE” reports AUC-PR = 0.2204 on SHU-MI, well below the 0.5 chance floor for balanced binary classification and ~0.45 below the other variants. This is almost certainly a reporting error (label inversion or metric bug), since MAE-style EEG SSL (MAEEG, EEGViT-MAE, CBraMod’s own pretext) consistently yields competitive numbers. Please re-verify and additionally report AUROC / BAcc for this cell.
Undeclared inconsistency.
Section 3 mentions “two state-related EEG analysis [14, 19]”, but reference [19] (Mumtaz depression) does not appear in Table 1 or the results.
EEG-DINO comparison unclear.
EEG-DINO does not report PhysioNet-MI / SHU-MI / ISRUC in its MICCAI 2025 paper, so STEM’s EEG-DINO numbers on ISRUC must be from a re-implementation, this should be stated.
No variance reporting.
Gains over the closest baselines are small (e.g., +0.0017 Acc over CBraMod on PhysioNet-MI) with no error bars or significance testing.
Design choices unjustified.
Asymmetric sampling for subjects vs. symmetric for tasks, K=3, and patch length 40 are not ablated.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The method is clearly described and the motivation to use subject/task semantics in EEG foundation model pretraining is reasonable. However, the contribution as presented has issues: (1) the SOTA claim is not supported when STEM’s numbers are compared against the CBraMod/CSBrain protocol, on which those models outperform STEM on all three target datasets
(2) both the disentanglement idea and the 3D-coordinate embedding have direct prior art (Özdenizci, Jeon, Han, PTSM; REVE) that is not engaged with. 
The core idea of combining SSL pretraining with metric-based meta-learning is worthwhile and should be surfaced more carefully; with clearer benchmarking and reporting of results, better positioning against prior disentanglement / meta-learning work, and corrected ablations.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper proposes a subject- and task-aware EEG foundation model that integrates semantic supervision with contrastive self-supervised learning and meta-learning. The motivation is well aligned with challenges in EEG representation learning, particularly inter-subject variability and task heterogeneity. The method is evaluated across multiple datasets and includes few-shot adaptation experiments, which are relevant and valuable contributions.
The reviewers raised several concerns regarding the positioning and validation of the contribution. In particular, the claim of state-of-the-art performance appears overstated, as the reported results are not consistently stronger than existing methods under comparable evaluation protocols. The novelty of the disentanglement mechanism is also partially incremental, with related prior work not sufficiently discussed or differentiated. Also, some inconsistencies in reported results and experimental details further reduce confidence in the claims.
However, the core idea is promising, and the paper presents a meaningful direction by combining semantic supervision with foundation model pretraining. The concerns raised primarily relate to positioning, validation, and clarity rather than fundamental flaws.
Given the above, the paper is invited for rebuttal.
The authors are encouraged to:
-Clarify benchmarking protocols and moderate claims of state-of-the-art performance.
-Strengthen comparison with relevant prior work, particularly in disentanglement and meta-learning.
-Include additional baselines or justify their absence.
-Provide statistical validation such as variance and significance testing.
-Resolve inconsistencies in reported results.

The rebuttal addressed the major concerns reasonably well by clarifying that the main contribution is the integration of semantic supervision and meta-learning within a multi-task EEG foundation model setting, rather than proposing disentanglement itself as a novel concept. The authors also clarified benchmarking details, corrected inconsistencies in the reported results, and addressed the absence of statistical significance reporting.
While some limitations remain, particularly regarding broader validation and deeper theoretical analysis, I believe the major concerns were sufficiently addressed and the paper is above the acceptance threshold.
The authors have sufficiently addressed the major concerns from the reviewers. EEG foundation models can an interesting topic for the MICCAI community.
The authors have addressed most of the concerns raised by the reviewers.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank all reviewers and the meta-reviewer for their valuable feedback. We address each concern below, grouped by topic.
1.Novelty (R1.2). While contrastive learning and meta-learning have been used in EEG analysis, existing studies have focused on a single task/dataset setting, without considering generalizability. Moreover, current EEG foundation models solely rely on self-supervised learning without leveraging semantic information. Our contribution lies in leveraging semantic information for EEG foundation model to learn more generalizable EEG representations.
2.Disentanglement (R1.3, R2.1, R2.4, R2.7, R2.8, R3.2). Disentanglement itself is not new in EEG analysis. We adopt the design of [3], but our novelty lies in being the first to integrate disentanglement into an EEG foundation model trained across multiple tasks/datasets via meta-learning, boosting performance and generalizability. For R2’s concerns, all variants in Table 4 show statistically significant improvements (p<0.05). The t-SNE on ISRUC demonstrates that task-dependent features form class-wise clusters across subjects, while subject-dependent features are well separated regardless of class.
3.Comparison (R1.1, R3.1, R3.7, R3.8). We followed the same experimental settings as previous works. Reproducibility issues have been reported on the official baseline GitHub repos; thus, we reproduced baselines with a large gap using official code. EEG-DINO was reproduced as it was not validated on our settings. For R1 and R3’s concerns, the gaps over baselines are statistically significant (p<0.05). We will state this, soften SOTA to consistent improvements, and clarify that some scores come from reproducing with official code.
4.Evaluation scope (R1.5, R2.6, R3.6). We agree that broader validation would further strengthen the work. Notably, we found that STEM also shows similar performance trends on the Mumtaz dataset, supporting the generalizability.
5.Missing baselines (R3.3). Existing EEG meta-learning methods focus on formulating each subject as an individual task to mitigate inter-subject variability, and target single-task few-shot scenarios. In contrast, STEM leverages multiple task labels alongside subject IDs via meta-learning. Due to these different setups, direct comparison is not entirely straightforward. We will clarify these differences in the revised paper.
6.Corrections (R3.5). The correct scores were AUCPR = 0.5231 and AUROC = 0.5827.7.Related work (R2.2, R3.4). We primarily focused on EEG foundation models due to space limitations. We will expand it to cover related studies suggested by R2 and R3.Importantly, while prior works have been conducted on a single task/dataset, our work extends these to a multi-task/dataset setting. 3D-coordinate encoding is not intended as a primary contribution, but rather shares a similar purpose to the related approaches mentioned by R3.8.Additional ablations (R1.4, R2.3, R2.5, R3.9). Pretraining takes ~2 weeks, making ablations such as scalability, loss weights, scaling law, and design choices difficult to complete within the rebuttal period. However, regarding (R2.3) and (R2.5), we verified the effect of loss weights and the scale of training samples during fine-tuning. For (R2.3), task loss weight showed larger variance than subject loss weight, and deviating from the default values led to performance degradation, particularly when weights exceeded 1, as they interfere with the primary objective. For (R2.5), STEM achieves comparable results to the baselines even when fine-tuned with half of the training samples, suggesting the effectiveness of meta-learning in enabling data-efficient fine-tuning. Regarding (R1.4), STEM requires significantly fewer MACs than EEG-DINO, though more than others due to 5× more patches from our smaller patch size. We believe this can be improved through exploration of optimal patch sizes. We agree these analyses would strengthen the work and will discuss them.

title: Subject-Specific Low-Field MRI Synthesis via a Neural Operator
abstract: Low-field (LF) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) improves accessibility and reduces costs but generally has lower signal-to-noise ratios and degraded contrast compared to high field (HF) MRI, limiting its clinical utility. Simulating LF MRI from HF MRI enables virtually evaluating novel imaging devices and developing LF algorithms. Existing low field simulators rely on noise injections and smoothing, which fails to capture the contrast degradation seen in LF acquisitions. To this end, we introduce an end-to-end LF-MRI synthesis framework that learns HF to LF image degradation directly from a small number of paired HF-LF MRIs. Specifically, we introduce a novel \textbf{H}F to \textbf{L}F coordinate–image decoupled neural \textbf{O}perator (H2LO) to model the underlying degradation process, and tailor it to capture high-frequency noise textures and dedicated image structure. Experimental results in T1- and T2-weighted MRI demonstrate that H2LO produces more faithful simulated low-field images than existing parameterized noise synthesis model and popular image-to-image translation models. Furthermore, it improves performance in downstream image enhancement tasks, showcasing its potential to enhance LF MRI diagnostic capabilities.
subject_areas: Applications -> Digital Twins / Simulation / Synthetic Data

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
Authors propose a model that synthesizes ULF images from HF images using a neural‑operator–based network that models the underlying degradation process and captures high‑frequency noise textures and relevant image structure. Their approach employs a branch–trunk architecture optimized with pointwise intensity fidelity and gradient‑based regularization.
They also evaluate a downstream image‑enhancement task, using the synthesized images as augmentation to assess whether the method improves performance on real ULF data.
reviews.text_strengths:
The application of neural operators to image synthesis is a key novelty of this work.
The authors claim that their model addresses limitations of prior pixel‑wise image‑to‑image translation methods, which often fail to capture realistic textures and accurately model contrast changes. By explicitly modeling the degradation process, the proposed approach provides a more principled way to approximate ULF acquisition characteristics.
reviews.text_weaknesses: While the proposed approach introduces a novel use of neural operators for ULF synthesis, the empirical improvements over existing state‑of‑the‑art methods are relatively marginal. This limits the current impact of the work and suggests that the method requires further refinement to demonstrate clear advantages in real‑world settings.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Figure 2 is referenced in the Introduction, but the figure itself is primarily presented in the Results section. In addition, the authors could include a dedicated discussion section to address the limitations of current state‑of‑the‑art methods in comparison to their approach. The manuscript would benefit from reorganizing these elements to ensure a more consistent and coherent reading experience.
Why do you compare only the results of Arnold’s work in Figure. 2? Is it due to lowest parameters (=4) used in the model?

Given the strengths and weaknesses outlined above, I believe the manuscript should be accepted for a poster presentation. Authors provided comprehensive experimental evaluations, and a poster format will allow them to present their ideas, receive targeted feedback, and further refine this new direction for the field.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a neural operator-based framework (H2LO) for subject-specific low-field MRI synthesis, reformulating HF-to-LF translation as a continuous operator learning problem. By combining a coordinate-aware neural operator with high-frequency-preserving design, the method captures both contrast shifts and noise characteristics more effectively than conventional simulators and image-to-image models, while also demonstrating utility for downstream enhancement tasks. Personally I appreciate the idea, from HF to LF, which I believe is under-explored and valuable.
reviews.text_strengths:
First, the paper presents a novel and well-motivated formulation by modeling HF-to-LF MRI synthesis as a continuous operator learning problem, rather than a conventional voxel-wise image translation task. This perspective is aligned with MRI physics, where field strength affects the underlying signal formation and frequency characteristics, making the formulation both principled and meaningful. 
Second, the proposed H2LO architecture is technically elegant and well-designed, combining a CNN-based branch network with a coordinate-based SIREN trunk to capture both spatial context and high-frequency details. The introduction of spatially varying operator coefficients allows the model to adapt locally to tissue-specific contrast changes, which is particularly important for realistic LF simulation.
Third, the paper demonstrates practical relevance and downstream utility, showing that the synthesized LF images can effectively augment training data and improve LF MRI enhancement performance. The evaluation is relatively comprehensive, including both reconstruction metrics and histogram-based measures, and shows consistent improvements over traditional simulators and image-to-image baselines
reviews.text_weaknesses:
First, while the operator-based formulation is well motivated, the methodological novelty over INR and operator-learning works is somewhat limited. The proposed H2LO builds upon existing frameworks such as DeepONet and coordinate-based representations (e.g., SIREN, LIIF-style extensions ), and the contribution mainly lies in adapting these components to the HF to LF MRI setting rather than introducing a fundamentally new architecture.
Second, the study relies on a very limited dataset (23 subjects) for learning the HF-to-LF mapping, which raises concerns about generalization and robustness. Although 5-fold cross-validation is used, the model may still overfit to scanner-specific characteristics or acquisition protocols, and the paper does not provide evaluation on external datasets or across different scanners/field strengths .
Third, the baseline comparison, while reasonable, is not fully comprehensive, particularly with respect to recent medical imaging methods. The evaluation focuses on general I2I models (Pix2Pix, diffusion) and a classical simulator, but lacks comparison with more recent physics-informed or diffusion-based MRI translation/enhancement approaches (e.g., works such as ref 8,9,11 cited in the paper but not included as baselines), which may limit the strength of the empirical claims.
Fourth, the paper does not fully establish clinical validity or realism of the synthesized LF images, beyond standard image similarity and histogram-based metrics. There is no expert evaluation or task-based assessment (e.g., diagnostic performance), making it unclear whether the generated images faithfully reflect clinically relevant LF characteristics rather than metric-level similarity.
Finally, the method assumes perfect spatial alignment between HF and LF scans, which may not hold in real-world scenarios. The reliance on registered paired data simplifies the problem and may limit applicability to settings where such precise alignment is unavailable or difficult to obtain.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper presents a technically sound and well-motivated approach to HF to LF MRI synthesis, with a formulation that is aligned with MRI physics and a clean neural operator design. The idea of modeling cross-field transformation as an operator is both conceptually meaningful and practically useful, especially given its demonstrated benefit for downstream tasks like LF enhancement.
However, the contribution is somewhat incremental in methodology, as it builds on existing neural operator and implicit representation frameworks, and the evaluation is limited by a small dataset and lack of clinical validation. These issues prevent it from being a strong accept, but the overall clarity, technical consistency, and relevance make it worthy of acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper proposes an end-to-end framework for synthesizing low-field (LF) MRI from high-field (HF) MRI by formulating the problem as a mapping between function spaces rather than fixed-grid voxel regression.
Specifically, the authors model the HF-to-LF transformation as a neural operator. The proposed architecture consists of a 3D CNN-based branch network that encodes the input HF volume, and a sinusoidal implicit neural representation (SIREN) trunk network that takes output spatial coordinates as input. The outputs of the branch and trunk networks are combined to predict the LF image intensity at a given location.
The method demonstrates improved performance over conventional image-to-image translation approaches while using fewer parameters.
reviews.text_strengths:
Novelty: This is the first paper proposing an end-to-end framework for HF-to-LF MRI image synthesis
Performance: The method generally outperforms all baselines both quantitatively and qualitatively, while using the least number of parameters.
Elegant: The formulation of HF-to-LF synthesis as a function to function mapping constraints the model to mathematically backed good solutions compared to pixel-to-pixel methods.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Requires paired HF-LF images to train which can be challenging to obtain in practice.
It is unclear whether the proposed method can generalize to unseen HF-to-LF scenarios i.e. if a model is trained on HF dataset A, can it equally synthesis LF images from a new dataset B. Dataset B could be from a different anatomy or device.
The proposed SIREN trunk is inferior to the w/o SIREN setting based on the quantitative results and ablations, and its justification is based on subjective qualitative analysis. Also, it is not clear what w/o SIREN setting exactly is.
The method was only evaluated on a single dataset of healthy subjects and it remains to be seen how the method generalizes to large popultations, different devices, sites, and pathological cases.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Minor comments:
Histogram metrics: the metrics are computed on the foreground (IHF > 0.01). This could potentially explain why the metrics show Pix2Pix to be better than the proposed method as T2W images are mostly dark. Perhaps, for future work, you want to modify the definition of the background to mean the entire interior of the skull.
“…,our method achieves the best performance across almost all metrics for both T1 and T2 contrasts”: The method achieves the best results across all metrics only on T1.Please correct.
What does the arrow from the branch output to the trunk input represent? My understanding is that the trunk only expects x as the input.

The proposed method is novel and adopts DeepONet to a new medical problem of low-field MRI image synthesis, a largely underexplored domain.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text: Given that all three reviewers have recommended acceptance, I am pleased to congratulate the authors on the acceptance of their paper at this phase.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers and the meta-reviewer for the efforts in reviewing this paper and providing constructive and positive feedback. We are very encouraged by the fact that reviewers found both the methodology, neural operator, and the application venue, LF MRI synthesis, reasonable and interesting.
We would like to answer some of the reviewers’ points of confusion.
R1 12, paragraph 2: In histogram visualization, we compare against Arnold et al.’s method because their model is explicitly optimized for histogram-statistic matching. In contrast, our model and the other comparison models are trained with pixel-wise consistency objectives. Therefore, we considered it more appropriate to visualize Arnold et al.’s method using histogram-level consistency, which better aligns with the objective it optimizes. We will clarify this point in the camera-ready version.
R3 12, paragraph 3: We apologize for drawing the arrow in the wrong direction and causing confusion. Yes, the trunk only expects coordinates, and the coordinate lookup is the information flow from the trunk to the branch. We will correct this in the camera-ready version.
For the rest of the constructive feedback, we will incorporate it into our future work to further improve the method and clinical utility. Thanks again for your kind reviews.

title: Sub-Resolution Monocyte Detection in Time-Lapse MRI: A Benchmark
abstract: Detecting individual immune cells in time-lapse magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables the non-invasive study of inflammatory processes. However, automated detection of contrast-enhanced monocytes remains highly challenging due to their extremely small spatial footprint (2–6 pixels), heterogeneous appearance, temporal variability, and ambiguity with confounding phenomena such as micro-bleeding. In this work, we introduce the first publicly available time-lapse MRI dataset for contrastive monocyte detection. The dataset contains carefully annotated sequences capturing substantial appearance variability and realistic clinical artifacts. We establish baseline performance using state-of-the-art object detection architectures and demonstrate that standard detectors perform suboptimally in the sub-resolution regime, especially under domain shift. Furthermore, we systematically analyze the contribution of key components of the YOLO architecture by progressively pruning its detection heads, feature pyramid levels, and loss terms. Our results reveal which architectural elements are essential for reliable detection of ultra-small objects, with a focus on domain generalization. We believe this dataset and analysis provide a benchmark for future research in microscopic structure detection in medical imaging.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper introduces the first publicly available 4D time-lapse MRI dataset for sub-resolution monocyte detection, comprising 124 recordings and over 115,000 annotations. The authors establish a standardized benchmark protocol, including fixed data splits, a distance-based AUC evaluation metric, and baseline results using multiple YOLO variants and Faster-RCNN. On this basis, the authors conduct systematic ablation experiments on the detection heads, feature pyramid levels, and loss functions of the YOLO architecture, analyzing which components are essential for detecting 2–6 pixel objects. 
The dataset is of significant value to the field, with a clearly defined task and practical application background (inflammation and cancer research). However, this paper has notable shortcomings in annotation quality validation, domain shift analysis, temporal information utilization, and experimental design.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) Clear dataset contribution: The first publicly available MRI dataset for sub-resolution immune cell detection, containing realistic clinical artifacts and diverse object appearances. 
2) Clear problem definition: Reasonably distinguishes sub-resolution detection (SRD) from conventional small object detection and cell tracking tasks. 
3) Comprehensive baseline experiments: Compares multiple YOLO variants and Faster-RCNN, evaluating domain shift on both k-fold cross-validation and an independent test set. 
4) Insightful ablation study: Prunes detection heads, backbone depth, pooling operations, and loss terms, providing practical guidance for future method design.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) Rows 2 and 3 in Table 1 have identical data. Is this because the experimental results are truly consistent, or is there a data duplication error?
2) The authors propose using a 4-pixel matching threshold for computing AUC, claiming that this threshold is based on “AUC stability and annotation uncertainty. ” However, no data or figures are provided in the paper to support this claim. 
3) The specific sources of “domain shift” need to be clarified: individual mouse differences, scanning parameters, magnetic field inhomogeneity, artifact types, etc. It is recommended to add a simple comparison of domain adaptation methods. 
4) The ground-truth bounding boxes use a fixed 10×10 size, which is much larger than the actual 2–6 pixel monocytes. This may cause the network to learn background patterns rather than the target signal, and indirectly leads to redundancy of coarse detection heads and degraded generalization of the CIoU loss. It is recommended to use tighter bounding boxes and supplement with a receptive field analysis.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper addresses a clinically important and technically challenging task with a novel, valuable dataset and a complete benchmark. The overall work is solid and meaningful to the community. However, several issues in experimental design, result presentation, and validation need to be carefully revised. The paper is slightly above the acceptance threshold and can be accepted after proper revision.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces the first publicly available 4D time-lapse MRI dataset for sub-resolution monocyte detection, along with a standardized benchmark protocol. The dataset includes 124 recordings and over 115k annotations capturing immune cells at extreme small scales (2–6 pixels). The authors establish baseline performance using modern object detectors (YOLO variants, Faster R-CNN) and propose a distance-based evaluation metric tailored to sub-resolution detection. Additionally, they perform a systematic ablation study on YOLO architecture components to identify key factors influencing detection performance and domain generalization.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Important dataset contribution
First publicly available dataset for this problem, addressing a clear gap in reproducibility and benchmarking.
2.Well-motivated problem
Sub-resolution detection (2–6 pixels) is a genuinely hard and underexplored regime in medical imaging.
3.Comprehensive dataset analysis
Strong statistical characterization (e.g., distribution of annotations and trajectories on page 4), which adds credibility and insight.
4.Appropriate evaluation redesign
Replacing IoU with a distance-based matching metric is well-justified for this regime.
5.Systematic benchmarking
Evaluation across multiple detectors and controlled experiments (Table 1, page 6) provides a solid baseline.
Insightful ablation study
The architectural analysis (Table 2, page 7) offers useful insights into what matters for ultra-small object detection.
6.Practical relevance
Potential impact on non-invasive immune monitoring and inflammation research.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Limited methodological novelty
The paper mainly evaluates existing architectures rather than proposing a new detection method.
2.Baseline-focused rather than solution-oriented
While the benchmark is valuable, there is no strong new algorithm addressing the problem.
3.Generalization discussion is limited
Domain shift is observed (Table 1), but deeper analysis or mitigation strategies are lacking.
4.No comparison to specialized small-object methods
Missing comparisons to methods from IR small target detection or point detection literature.
5.Annotation quality concerns
The authors acknowledge possible labeling noise but do not quantify its impact.
6.Clinical translation is indirect
The work is preclinical (mouse data) and lacks discussion on human applicability.
7.No temporal modeling baseline
Despite time-lapse data, models are mostly slice-wise; temporal models (e.g., RNN/transformers) are not explored.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1.Consider adding temporal modeling baselines, since the dataset is inherently time lapse.
2.Include comparison with specialized small-object detection methods beyond YOLO variants.
3.Provide quantitative analysis of annotation noise impact.
4.Expand discussion on domain adaptation strategies, given strong domain shift.
5.Clarify how this approach may translate to human MRI data.

This paper provides a valuable dataset and benchmark, which is highly relevant for the community and fills a clear gap. The experimental analysis is thorough and offers useful insights into sub resolution detection challenges.
However, the work is primarily benchmark oriented with limited methodological novelty, and the absence of new algorithms or deeper modeling innovations reduces its impact compared to stronger MICCAI contributions.
Overall, the dataset contribution and careful evaluation justify acceptance, but the paper sits near the threshold due to limited novelty.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: Detecting cells on MRI is challenging as MRI does not provide cellular-level resolution. The paper presents a “4D time-lapse MRI dataset for sub-resolution for monocyte detection” and evaluates Faster RCNN and YOLO variants. The paper further evaluates YOLO v8n with different loss and architectural changes (e.g. backbone down-steps, neck up-sampling, etc).
reviews.text_strengths: The task is interesting, given the extreme scale of the target objects. The paper notes that the standard small object detection typically involves 32x32 pixel targets, whereas the monocytes on MRI span 2-6 pixels. The connection to the Infrared Small Target Detection and Segmentation and the reference to successful YOLOv8-P2 variants set up the paper well. Public datasets in medical imaging are always valuable.
reviews.text_weaknesses: Ferucarbotran is mentioned as the contrast agent but the annotation process could be more clearly described. (e.g. It is unclear who performed the 115,570 annotations or whether any inter-observer variability analysis was done.) If the paper followed the protocol from reference [15] Maška et al. it would be helpful to state this explicitly, and clarify annotator expertise (e.g. radiologists/trained annotators). Considering the 4-pixel tolerance (assuming in all directions) is relatively lenient given the image size and the target size (2-6 pixels), inter-operator analysis could help justify this choice. It would be helpful to see other metrics (e.g. percentage of correctly predicted cells) aside from AUC.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a very difficult task and a valuable dataset. The paper highlights some valuable insights on YOLOv8n’s performance on their task (e.g. default setup vs different loss, upsampling layer, etc) and their dataset (e.g. ringing artifacts). The annotation process could be more detailed and the evaluation is mainly limited to AUC. Overall, the paper is promising but somewhat limited in terms of methodological depth and evaluation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper presents a benchmark dataset for sub-resolution monocyte detection in time-lapse MRI, along with a standardized evaluation protocol and comprehensive baseline experiments.
The reviewers’ scores are 4, 4, and 4, indicating a clear consensus toward acceptance.
The reviewers agree that the dataset is valuable and the experimental analysis provides useful insights for this challenging task, although the methodological novelty is limited.
The AC therefore recommends early accept.
For the camera-ready version, the AC suggests addressing minor clarity issues noted by the reviewers, such as providing more detailed descriptions of the annotation process, clarifying the evaluation protocol and metrics, and improving the readability and presentation of figures and results.
Please refer to the reviewers’ comments for more detailed suggestions.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all the reviewers for their constructive feedback. As we find no major misunderstandings or inaccuracies in the reviews, we focus on addressing some concerns and questions.
1.Annotation Methodology and Threshold Justification (Reviewers 1 and 3):
The reviewers questioned the 4-pixel matching threshold used for computing the AUC and the fixed 10×10 bounding box size. We empirically determined the threshold by evaluating multiple trained networks under varying distance tolerances. Improvements beyond a radius of 4 were negligible, indicating AUC stability. Regarding the bounding box size, we tested smaller boxes and observed significantly worse performance. We hypothesize that background patterns are essential for distinguishing monocytes from similar phenomena, particularly in uncharacteristic regions. The acquisition and detection protocol follows the established procedures from [15] Masthoff et al. All annotations for this study were performed by a single experienced biologist. Given this setup and the considerable size of the dataset, a full interobserver analysis was infeasible. We therefore prioritized rigorous quality assurance through protocol standardization and expert-led consistency checks. The manuscript has been revised to clarify these points.
2.Domain Shift and Generalization (Reviewers 1 & 2):
The reviewers noted the limited discussion of sources of domain shift and the lack of domain adaptation methods. We clarify that the only source of variation in our dataset is natural biological variability among individual mice (e.g., healthy, tumor-bearing, or treated animals), which affects cell counts but not monocyte appearance or MRI characteristics. All scanning parameters and the measurement protocol were kept constant across acquisitions. While magnetic field inhomogeneities and artifacts cannot be fully excluded, they are comparable across all data. The observed domain shift is therefore attributable solely to expected biological variation. Due to page constraints, we could not include a detailed analysis or comparison of domain adaptation methods. We plan to address these techniques, including normalization methods and data augmentation, in a journal extension.
3.Comparison to Specialized Small-Object Methods (Reviewer 2):
The reviewer requested comparisons to the literature on IR small target detection. This paper is intended as a baseline to compare current state-of-the-art generic detection networks and establish a foundation for future work. Specialized small-object methods are a natural next step.
4.Clinical Translation (Reviewer 2):
We acknowledge the preclinical nature of this work. Time-lapse MRI is a versatile tool in preclinical research and can offer great insights into immune cell dynamics upon varying inflammatory stimuli. However, to the best of our knowledge, it is not yet feasible to track single cells in humans. Achieving clinical translation would require further development of MRI hardware to achieve sufficient spatial resolution, adjusting contrast agent dosing, and validating the pipeline in larger animal or human cohorts, alongside standard regulatory considerations.
Nevertheless, we anticipate that methods developed on this mouse dataset will serve as a foundation for monocyte detection in human MRI, as the appearance of single cells in humans will likely be similar, thereby enabling scalable applications in human immune system research.
5.Temporal Modeling (Reviewer 2):
Temporal models (RNN/transformers) are beyond the scope of this paper, which focuses on dataset release and baseline performance. We agree that temporal methods are promising and plan to explore them in follow-up work.
6.Additional Metrics (Reviewer 3):
Beyond the area under the curve (AUC), we intend to report additional metrics in a journal extension, as the page limit of the current manuscript does not permit their inclusion.

title: Sulcus-Aware Hippocampal Surface Modeling with Training-Time Sulcus-Guided Learning
abstract:
Analyzing hippocampal structure is important for characterizing localized geometry that is poorly captured by volumetric summaries. Yet existing surface reconstruction pipelines often suppress the hippocampal sulcus—a thin internal indentation—because it is under-resolved by partial-volume effects or introduce incorrect topology. Deformation based methods have a risk of self-intersections.
We present a sulcus-aware, topology-consistent surface reconstruction framework that anchors subjects to a sulcus-preserving template and learns a smooth template-to-subject deformation to transfer the surface with vertex-wise correspondence. Sulcus masks are used only in training to encourage sulcal alignment in a training-time auxiliary manner. Inference hence uses only standard structural volume and hippocampus masks without requiring sulcus masks. 
Experimental results show improved sulcus fidelity while maintaining competitive overall boundary agreement and stable meshes with minimal geometric failures. The resulting topology-consistent and sulcus-preserved surfaces enable surface-based sulcus morphometry; in a pilot downstream task, we show the proposed method captures sulcus-related surface statistics in cognitively normal (CN) and Alzheimer’s disease (AD) cohorts. The software is available at https://github.com/Shape-Lab/Sulcus-Aware-Hippo-Surface.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose a method for hippocampal surface modeling that takes into account the hippocampal sulcus in the image and shape model. They construct a sulcus-aware template by iterative registration by incorporating a signed distance field term. The sulcal indentation is computed from the difference of the sulcal mask from the hippocampus shape mask. In order to learn the deformation field, they use two complementary methods, i) compute a low-resolution sulcus probability map for voxel-wise soft supervision, and ii) extract a boundary point cloud from the sulcus masks used only to compute surface-distance penalty (using the Chamfer distance) against the deformed template surface. The template-to-subject deformation is represetned by a diffeormophic transformation by integrating stationary velocity fields. The template based deformation approach guarantees topology consistency across registrations. In the experimental results, the authors show a pilot study of AD vs CN group differences.
reviews.text_strengths:
Few papers have explicitly tackled sulcal-based modelling in hippocampal shape analysis. Thus this paper highlights a unique and commonly overlooked problem.
In formulating this problem, the authors have generated a dataset of 0.33 mm isotropic sulcus masks, intially automated and then refined manually by hippocampal experts. This is a valuable dataset by itself, used for training by the authors but may also be generally useful to the community.
The authors present a thorough evaluation of their idea across multiple methods.
The use of signed distance fields instead of binary masks also ensures topological correctness.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
While the paper primarily tackles sulcus indentation aware modeling, it does not explicitly visualize the indentation. This is a major weakness. Figure 2(a) shows small lateral-view thumbnails with yellow arrows pointing to surface curvature variations, but the hippocampal sulcus is absent from these views. Thus it was harder to visualize what exactly was modeled and represented here.
The sulcal mask did not explicitly directly feature in the mathematical formulation. The sulcus masks are defined in terms of soft occupancy maps, which in turn are not defined explicitly. The authors refer to the paper by Hwang et al. but omit the definition of the sulcus map from this paper. Instead they just denote these maps using the symbol P_S and P_T. Similarly the boundary point cloud B_S is not formally defined. The authors state that these maps are obtained using the block-averaging operator, but this operator is not defined either. This made the paper difficult to follow.
The sulcus shape is not explicitly modeled. The main geometric features of a sulcus are it’s depth, curvature, concave/convex nature etc. are not directly represented in the formulation. One would expect a sulcus-aware method to be represented by explicit geometric features such as sulcal depth fields, curvature-based losses, or medial axis constraints that represent the shape information instead of global appearance based measures.
Since the formulation of the occupancy maps was not specified, it was not clear if the signed distance fields were only used for the purpse of extraction of point clouds, or was it also passed through the alignment network?
There were several weaknesses in the the experimental results.
in Figure 3(b), the SPHARM-PDM representation computes alignment using a spherical harmonic parameterization while the proposed method uses template deformation. It is not clear what is being compared when calculating group differences. Is it the magnitude of the deformation field or is it vertex wise displacement to the template?
Why is the ODC+smooth that yields a better hippocampal distance (Table 1) absent from the results in Figure 3(b)?
An ablation study that includes the proposed method without the sulcus-aware modeling is missing. This is because for experimental purposes, a sulcus-aware template is already constructed along with the sulcal indentation information. Thus it is not clear how much gain is obtained from the sulcus-aware template itself and whether incorporating sulcal constraints later during hte semi-supervised alignment stage does make a significant difference. Thus it was not clear whether the sulcus mask supervision during training actually did anything. Similarly voxel occupancy maps or the boundary extraction step could also undergo ablation to determine the performance of the proposed method.
Important papers such as HippUnfold (DeKraker, J. , Haast, R. A. , Yousif, M. D. , Karat, B. , Lau, J. C. , Köhler, S. , & Khan, A. R. (2022). Automated hippocampal unfolding for morphometry and subfield segmentation with HippUnfold. elife, 11, e77945.) are not cited. While subfield segmentation is out of scope of the proposed work, the above paper does explicitly model the SRLM (stratum radiatum lacunosum moleculare) landmarks for the hippocampal sulcus. Thus it will be useful to compare the proposed method with their work.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper tackles an important problem in the field. There has been a general lack of extensive studies that have undertaken hippocampal modeling with sulcal-aware methods. Thus the paper tries to address an important gap. However, aspects of the sulcal representation are not adequately described as that’s one of the main contributions of the paper. Further the reliance on masks that capture the global features instead of local features such as sulcal depth, curvature, geometry etc, weakens the explicit shape constraints that are important for hippocampal modeling. The experimental results have limitations in terms of lack of ablation studies, while the statistical results were unconvincing.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The author’s response clarified my doubts and explained certain methodological details.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
A sulcus-aware hippocampal surface reconstruction framework that preserves the thin hippocampal sulcus — typically washed out by mask-based extraction and smoothing — while enforcing a fixed topology.
A template-based diffeomorphic deformation that jointly warps a sulcus-preserving template volume and mesh to each subject, yielding topology-consistent surfaces with vertex-wise correspondence and propagating the template sulcus to obtain subject-specific sulci.
Experiement results showing improved sulcus fidelity and stable meshes with competitive boundary agreement, plus a pilot downstream application to surface-based sulcus morphometry in CN and AD cohorts.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper tackles a well-motivated and technically challenging problem: preserving the hippocampal sulcus in surface reconstruction. The sulcus is narrow, highly susceptible to partial-volume effects, and routinely washed out by conventional mask-based pipelines, yet it carries morphometric signal relevant to aging and Alzheimer’s disease. Addressing this gap is of clear interest to dementia researchers.
The template-based diffeomorphic deformation design is well suited to the problem, simultaneously delivering fixed topology, vertex-wise inter-subject correspondence, and stable meshes with minimal self-intersections — directly addressing a known limitation of deformation-based surface methods.
The evaluation is comprehensive, combining surface-distance-based measures, mesh quality metrics, and a pilot downstream morphometry analysis in CN and AD cohorts, and demonstrates improved sulcus fidelity over state-of-the-art baselines such as SPHARM-PDM.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
There is a concern that the method may attenuate clinically meaningful disease effects to fit the sulcus. In Figure 3, disease effects in the hippocampal head appear diminished relative to SPHARM-PDM and prior literature, where AD-related atrophy is consistently reported across the entire hippocampus. This raises the possibility that the template-to-subject deformation establishes noisy correspondences in the hippocampal head as a by-product of prioritizing sulcal alignment.
The “semi-supervised” framing is unclear. Semi-supervised learning typically means training with a small amount of labeled data alongside a large volume of unlabeled data. If only a subset of subjects have sulcus annotations, the number of labeled versus unlabeled subjects and how they are combined during training should be explicitly reported.
Important neural network details are missing, including the architecture and network hyperparameters, which limits reproducibility.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Figure 2(b): the meaning of the color map should be clarified. If it represents the Jacobian determinant of the deformation field, the striped pattern observed in the hippocampal head is concerning, as it may indicate that the proposed method establishes noisy or locally unstable correspondences in this region — potentially as a side effect of prioritizing sulcal alignment.

The paper addresses a well-motivated problem and the template-based diffeomorphic design delivers topology-consistent surfaces with improved sulcus fidelity. However, the possibility that prioritizing sulcal alignment introduces noisy correspondences in the hippocampal head and attenuates well-established AD effects is a significant concern, compounded by the unclear semi-supervised framing and missing network details. A convincing rebuttal on these points could move the paper above the acceptance threshold.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have successfully addressed all my concerns in the rebuttal.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors present a hippocampus surface reconstruction pipeline that is sulcus-aware, improving the geometric accuracy of hippocampal surface analyses. First, the authors construct a sulcus-aware template consisting of an intensity image, hippocampus soft mask, and sulcus soft mask defined on a 64×64×64 voxel grid. A spatial transform is then learned (VoxelMorph) using supervision from the hippocampal SDF and MRI, and applied to the template surface generated via marching cubes. During training, sulcal labels are used to supervise the spatial transformation, upsampled to increase their gradient weighting, along with the transformed boundary point cloud. The method is evaluated on 1mm isotropic T1-weighted MRI and compared against SPHARM-PDM and PTSD as baseline methods, as well as generic reconstruction approaches, using 120 cases for training and 15 for evaluation (across both hemispheres). The authors also conduct a clinical study demonstrating that their method produces more sulcus-localized statistical clusters than both baselines when comparing AD and CN groups.
reviews.text_strengths: Clinical evaluation: The authors perform a preliminary clinical study, comparing vertex-wise analyses comparing AD-CN patient groups on surfaces reconstructed using different methods. While these results need further validation, they illustrate the importance of handing surface geometry on downstream analyses.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The reconstructed mesh is dependent on the quality of the sulcus-aware template
While the proposed method minimizes topological errors, the registration does not guarantee no self-intersections.
Fig 2c, the plots are missing axes labels on the x-axis.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The authors address a clinically meaningful problem of reconstructing hippocampal sulcal geometry. The proposed framework is well-motivated and validated against established baselines, demonstrating improved sulcal fidelity without sacrificing overall geometric accuracy. The downstream morphometry result further confirms that these improvements translate into meaningful clinical findings.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text:
The reviewers have provided valuable feedback on the paper, which proposes a novel sulcus-aware hippocampal surface modeling framework. Given the mixed reviews (two Weak Reject, one Accept), the authors must address the lack of clarity in formulation explicitly defining the sulcal mask’s soft occupancy maps and the role of signed distance fields. The most crucial experiment is to show the gain only to the sulcus-aware components.

The authors addressed the main concerns of the reviewers and thus warrants an acceptance.

Reviewers summarized strengths of your work such as potential clinical relevance and novel aspects related to methodological changes in view of the relatively new domain of postmortem MRI. However, they also detailed significant weaknesses and shortcomings of concept, methodology and descriptions. There is no doubt that the application area is an emerging field that requires adaptation and of known segmentation and modeling concepts but also new approaches – also facing challenges regarding validation and comparison. However, balancing pros and cons and MICCAI’s high bar, your paper may be considered not to be mature enough and thus not fully ready to be accepted at MICCAI.

This submisson proposes a sulcus-aware hippocampal surface modeling using template-based diffeomorphic deformation. R3 liked clinical relevance. R1 and R2 noted mathematical inconsistencies, minor. The rebuttal has clarified all concerns. The consensus is acceptance and novelty in method. For all these reaons, and with respect to other submissions, recommendation is towards acceptnace.

author_feedback_text:
We appreciate the reviewers for providing insightful comments that help us improve the quality of our paper. Please see our responses below.
Sulcus representation and equations (R1).
Geometric descriptors such as sulcal depth, curvature, and medial axis may benefit sulcus-aware modeling. However, reliable extraction of these features typically requires an explicit surface mesh generated by a specific surface reconstruction procedure. As a result, our model may be biased toward reproducing the characteristics of that reconstruction protocol. We instead use expert-validated high-resolution sulcus labels and convert them into two explicit supervision signals: sulcus occupancy maps and sulcal boundary points.
The sulcus occupancy maps (P_S) and (P_T) are obtained by applying standard 3X3X3 average pooling (block averaging in Sec. 2.4) to the binary sulcus masks (L_S) and (L_T). The boundary points (B_S) are extracted from the SDF of the sulcus-aware mask (Y~), whereas the alignment network receives the SDF of the whole hippocampal mask (Y). Thus, Y~ is used only for boundary point extraction and is not fed into the network. We will explicitly state their math notations in Sec. 2.4.
Necessity of the sulcus-aware template and sulcus-guided components (R1, R3).
Since subject meshes deform from the template, its quality is central (Sec. 2.2). During method development, we found that a simple template often failed to preserve sulcal folding as smoothness and mesh-regularity constraints tended to suppress the indentation. This motivates our unique sulcus-aware template construction. Also, as discussed in Sec. 1, the sulcus is often under-resolved at typical clinical resolution (~1 mm^3). Thus, we use a “soft” sulcus occupancy map for learning since the sulcus tends to be occluded in the hippocampal hard label. The boundary points provide explicit supervision of surface geometry. In Eq. (7), the Chamfer loss computed in Euclidean domain for finer level of supervision for deformation. Resulting in over 32% reduced sulcus distance than existing methods (Table 1).
Shape correspondence and clinical analysis (R1, R2).
We appreciate the concern regarding possible correspondence issues. Since ground-truth landmarks are unavailable in our dataset, directly evaluating regional correspondence errors was infeasible. In Fig. 2(c), we instead evaluated correspondence using PCA-based generalization and specificity following [31]; our method achieved the lowest reconstruction errors, suggesting stable shape correspondence. We note that the improved correspondence quality influences the observed statistical differences in Fig. 3.We apologize for the confusion. The colormap in Fig. 2(b) represents Koenderink’s curvedness but not the Jacobian determinant; the striped patterns do not indicate deformation instability.
The per-vertex surface-area analysis requires inter-subject shape correspondence. Thus, ODC-based methods were excluded in area analysis as shape correspondence is not provided during their surface reconstruction.
Surface visualization (R1): The sulcal indentation is visible in the surface-volume overlay in Fig. 2(a). However, it is less apparent in the surface rendering due to the selected viewpoint and limited panel size. We will update the figure to better highlight the existing sulcal structure using enlarged slice-based overlays and transparent or cut-away renderings that expose the indentation.
Terminology (R2): We agree that the term “semi-supervised” is ambiguous. We used this to indicate that sulcus labels are used only as auxiliary training supervision and are not required at inference. To avoid confusion, we will rename this component as training-time sulcus supervision.
Minor fixes (R1, R2, R3): We will correct typos and add the missing axis labels as well as missing citations. To further support reproducibility, we will add implementation details about the U-Net architecture and release the code as stated in the abstract.

title: SuRe-Flow: Surface-to-CT Synthesis via Retrieval-Augmented Rectified Flow for CT-Free Superficial Radiotherapy
abstract: Background: Superficial radiotherapy still relies on CT simulation for dose calculation, adding resource burden and imaging radiation for benign or shallow disease. Optical surface scanning is non-ionizing, but surface-to-CT synthesis is ill-posed because one surface can match multiple internal anatomies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes SuRe-Flow, a retrieval-augmented rectified flow framework that enables CT-free superficial radiotherapy by synthesizing volumetric CT from optical surface scans. The core contributions are: (1) a contrastive representation learning module that retrieves topologically matched anatomical priors from a large database to resolve the ill-posed 1-to-N mapping ambiguity inherent in surface-to-CT synthesis; (2) a retrieval-conditioned flow mechanism that injects these priors via ControlNet to disentangle conflicting ODE trajectories in rectified flow; and (3) a dose-aware frequency penalty that explicitly regularizes high-frequency boundaries to preserve tissue interfaces critical for electron beam dosimetry. The work demonstrates clinical feasibility through large-scale validation (20,022 training/1,000 test patients) and clinical TPS evaluation, achieving 5.0 HU MAE in the 0–20mm therapeutic zone and 96.7% Gamma Index passing rate.
reviews.text_strengths:
