meta_reviews.text:
The rebuttal should address three decision-affecting concerns. First, methodological positioning: the method is built on the LiveCC streaming backbone, with the main contributions being hierarchical supervision, state-transition tokens, and dataset curation; the rebuttal should clarify the differentiation from the LiveCC formulation and from prior hierarchical surgical video-language work such as HecVL. Second, the evaluation relies primarily on a GPT-4o pairwise win rate, with no standard captioning metrics and no objective workflow metrics such as phase or step accuracy or transition localization; the rebuttal should add these. Third, the real-time and streaming claim is not currently substantiated by latency, throughput, memory, or FLOPs analysis, and the LLaVA-Video and Qwen2.5-VL baselines are evaluated zero-shot rather than fine-tuned on SurgOnAir-11K, which weakens the comparison.

The paper proposes a streaming vision-language model for real-time surgical narration, built on the LiveCC backbone and incorporating hierarchical supervision, state-transition tokens, and a new SurgOnAir-11K dataset. The reviewers split evenly after the rebuttal. The principal concerns are methodological novelty, reliance on a pairwise LLM-as-a-judge metric without standard captioning or workflow metrics, and the streaming claim, which is not currently substantiated by efficiency reporting. The rebuttal addresses these concerns by introducing a temporal alignment metric, clarifying that phase labels come from expert metadata while only step labels are LLM-assisted, and committing to latency and FLOPs analysis. The dataset, the explicit framing of real-time narration as a research problem in surgery, and the integration of phase and step supervision with state tokens together constitute a recognizable contribution. The two post-rebuttal Accepts are well argued. The camera-ready version must include the efficiency analysis, at least one standard captioning metric, and the LLM-as-a-judge results.

Overall, I believe the paper’s strengths (timely real-time surgical narration problem, substantial dataset curation, and hierarchy-aware streaming formulation with state-transition tokens) outweigh its limitations (moderate architectural novelty, dependence on LLM-as-judge evaluation). Although, the latter critique is rather serious, to my mind. Given the solid rebuttal, I think this borderline case could become a good poster at the main track and I recommend acceptance.
After the rebuttal, reviewer’s recommendation remain mixed with some key concerns unresolved.

author_feedback_text:
We thank reviewers for the positive feedback. We appreciate reviewers recognizing the importance of surgical video streaming. We also appreciate that R1 recognize our SurgOnAir-11K dataset as “substantial,” and that R2 note its potential as “a useful resource for future work.” Moreover, R1, R3, and R4 acknowledge our hierarchical design. Finally, we thank R1, R2, and R4 for positively noting our experiments and ablations.
Contribution clarification(R1/R2/R3/R4):
Our contributions are threefold. Application: We present the first real-time surgical narration framework for intraoperative assistance, enabling online responses instead of retrospective full-video analysis (e.g., LLaVA-Surg, SurgVidLM). Methodology: We unify continuous narration and discrete hierarchical state transition via special state tokens. This achieves simultaneous narration and workflow recognition, unlike prior works (e.g., LiveCC, HecVL) that address them separately. Dataset: We introduce SurgOnAir-11K, the first real-time narration dataset, providing temporally aligned supervision for streaming surgical video narration.
State token for hierarchical modeling(R2/R3/R4):
As R1 notes, surgical workflows are inherently hierarchical. Unlike HecVL’s discriminative vision-language alignment, our generative model targets live narration (R3). Flat narration may produce locally plausible but globally inconsistent descriptions over long streams. To address this, we formulate phase/step transition prediction as an auxiliary task. This injects hierarchical knowledge to boost narration coherence, yielding 20% gains over the flat baseline.
Caption metrics(R3):
In surgical narration, both semantic correctness and temporal alignment are critical. To assess narration quality, we employ an LLM-as-a-judge evaluation. This approach serves as a robust alternative to metrics like BLEU, as it accommodates greater expressive diversity while better capturing clinical semantics. An analysis of our temporal alignment performance is shown below.
Temporal alignment evaluation (R1/R3): 
We analyze 421 evaluation clips containing tool and action transitions. A prediction is temporally correct if the new tool or action appears in the generated narration within 1.5 seconds after the transition. Under this criterion, SurgOnAir correctly identifies 68.4% of clips, compared with 27.3% for HuluMed-7B [7], which also tends to produce less specific narrations during transitions. These results suggest that hierarchy-aware modeling improves temporal adaptation by providing procedural context during streaming generation.
Fine-tune baseline models (R3) :
We thank the reviewer for the suggestion. We clarify that LLaVA-Video-7B and Qwen2.5-VL are included only as reference general-purpose offline MLLMs, not as direct baselines. They are used to show that general models struggle with surgical video understanding. Since they are offline captioning models, fine-tuning them would not demonstrate live narration ability or causal streaming understanding.
LLM-Generated labels (R2):
The phase annotations are from expert-provided video metadata, while only the step-level labels are LLM-generated. To provide the requested evaluation on the generated step annotations, we report high cross-model agreement rates, including 82.69% agreement with Claude Sonnet 4 and 90.5% agreement with Gemini 3.1 Pro. The generated hierarchy therefore provides higher-level procedural context for temporally grounded narration, rather than workflow labels.
Latency(R4):
Under the 2 FPS streaming setting, HuluMed-7B [7] requires on average 1.94 seconds to process and generate narration for 1 second of video, whereas SurgOnAir requires only 0.95 seconds, making it substantially better aligned with real-time streaming requirements.
We will also add procedural distributions, curation prompts, and fix citation inconsistencies (R3) in revised manuscript. To our knowledge, this is the first work on real-time surgical narration.

title: SurgRFO: Foundation Model Based Compositional Synthesis of Critical Retained Foreign Objects in Intraoperative Chest X-Rays
abstract:
Critical retained foreign objects (RFOs) on intraoperative
Chest radiographs are rare but high-risk events, and their scarcity limits robust automated detection model training and generalization. We introduce SurgRFO, a two-stage synthesis framework for generating realistic RFO-present intraoperative chest X-rays. In Stage 1, a Roentgen chest X-ray foundation model is fine-tuned on surgical-domain images to generate realistic, RFO-free backgrounds that preserve anatomy, indwelling lines and tubes, and intraoperative imaging characteristics. In Stage 2, a lightweight generator trained on localized RFO patches from limited positive cases synthesizes diverse RFO instances, which are composited onto backgrounds using conditional Poisson fusion for photometric consistency. We evaluate SurgRFO through (i) a blinded clinician study assessing realism and clinical plausibility, and (ii) downstream detection performances when augmenting Faster R-CNN, YOLOv8, and Retina with synthesized data. SurgRFO consistently improves sensitivity at low false-positive-per-image (FPPI) operating points on internal and external test sets. Clinician ratings indicate realism comparable to real intraoperative images. Ablation analyses examine fusion strategies and synthesis scale, and ethical safeguards for synthetic surgical data are discussed. The code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/Yuanyun936/SurgRFO/.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Algorithmic Fairness / Safety / Regulation
Machine Learning -> Synthetic Data / Data-centric AI
Special Topic -> AI for Neglected Diseases & Limited-Resource Settings

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose SurgRFO, which synthesizes intraoperative chest X-rays with “critical” retained foreign objects (RFOs) to improve downstream detection of these RFOs. The framework comprises two stages: first, a fine-tuned foundation model that generates chest radiographs, and second, a model that adds critical RFOs to the images through a blending mechanism. The authors claim they will release a benchmark dataset of 144 annotated intraoperative chest radiographs with critical RFOs (although this claim is refuted in the GitHub).
reviews.text_strengths:
Significance of clinical application. Detecting RFOs is an important clinical problem (https://www. cureus. com/articles/320644-retained-foreign-object-signals-a-dangerous-atmosphere-in-the-operating-room#!/; https://www. sciencedirect. com/science/article/pii/S0039606025003654). While various safeguards have been explored to facilitate the detection of RFOs, RFOs continue to go undetected due to the complexity of the task.
Use and release of clinical radiographs with critical RFOs. 
Due to the rarity of these objects, evaluating on these images and sharing them with the public is a significant contribution.
Robust evaluation of synthetic image quality, including a blinded clinician study, quantitative distribution measures, and a downstream classification performance analysis across three classification models.
External validation was performed.
The code was made publicly available.
The first figure is an informative graphical abstract.
The proposed framework splits synthesis into two parts (radiograph then RFO) to strengthen the fidelity of the RFOs. The synthetic images improve downstream classification across three classification models
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Lack of downstream performance comparison with other synthetic generation models/augmentation strategies. The work does not compare its downstream detection results against closely related prior methods, such as https://link. springer. com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-032-08009-7_15 that similarly applies synthetic data augmentation for detecting critical RFOs. In addition, the paper does not provide downstream performance comparisons against alternative generative models or augmentation strategies. As a result, it remains unclear whether the observed gains are attributable to the specific generative methodology proposed, or simply to increasing the effective training set size. Would we see similar performance gains with RoentGen? What about if we just injected RFO patterns into otherwise negative images?
Substantial overlap with earlier work, limiting novelty. The work does not consider a 2025 MICCAI workshop paper (https://link. springer. com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-032-08009-7_15), which similarly employs synthetic data augmentation to improve downstream critical RFO detection and releases a synthetically generated dataset of chest radiographs with critical RFOs. The submission should have referred to and contextualized this work (i. e. compared model performance), clearly distinguishing the submission’s contributions from this prior work. Especially when making claims such as “no public dataset dedicated to critical RFOs exists” and “the first publicly available dataset dedicated to critical RFOs. ”
The two contributions of using synthetic data augmentation to improve downstream critical RFO detection and the release of a chest radiograph dataset of critical RFOs were again repeated in an arXiv preprint (https://arxiv. org/abs/2507.06937v1) that the submission cited as a work with “high-fidelity and diverse X-ray synthesis”. While the preprint cannot limit the novelty of the submission under consideration as it is not published, it should at least be properly contextualized if cited.
Conflicting information on the dataset release. The authors state in the manuscript that they are publicly releasing their dataset (no link is provided), but on GitHub, they state that they cannot release the data due to privacy constraints. As this dataset release is arguably one of the greatest contributions of the work, the GitHub message is concerning.
Missing dataset details that are important for contextualizing the results and public release. How many patients were there? With a 6:1:3 patient-level split, how many radiographs did that put in the test dataset? What were the class ratios in the test dataset? It is important for the reader to know the number of scans in the test dataset, how many contained critical RFOs, and how many patients those scans were sourced from. 
In addition, how many radiologists labeled the images? Were multiple perspectives considered during this labeling process? If so, how were disagreements between radiologist labels managed, especially when it comes to bounding boxes? What were the criteria for differentiating between critical and non-critical RFOs? 
Was it truly only the training images that were preprocessed? Shouldn’t all images go through the same preprocessing pipeline?
Was the same training dataset used for the synthesis network and the classification network? If so, for synthesis network training, I assume all the negatives in the training dataset constituted D_bg and the positives D_rfo? 
How was Stage-1 synthesis evaluated on 5k images when there were only 944+144 in the dataset?
What radiographs were the external cohort compared to, as all reported external images had critical RFOs?
Downstream detection performance measures were not reported with measures of uncertainty or confidence. Additionally, the authors did not perform a statistical analysis of the downstream performance gains. Both of which reviewers were supposed to look for in the official MICCAI guidelines (https://conferences. miccai. org/2026/en/REVIEWER-GUIDELINES. html). This is especially concerning as the reader does not know how small of a sample size is being tested, nor the class balance of that sample. Having said that, the proposed model has obvious enough performance gains over the baseline.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The abstract says, “ethical safeguards for synthetic surgical data are discussed”, but this is not actually an aspect of the work.
The introduction contains duplicate sentences: “Two fundamental challenges dominate. Two major challenges arise. “
In the introduction, “low hundreds of images” doesn’t make much sense.
Figure 1 introduces inconsistencies that can easily be misinterpreted. For example, it implies that data was sourced from three institutions, even though it was sourced from two. Furthermore, it implies radiologists looked through >50,000 images to locate RFOs, when really this is a retrospective study where the authors used reports to identify RFOs. The actual 5-point Likert scale would be more useful to see than the specified “Image Rating Rubric”. Was the question truly, “Which one is real?” Because the metric “Syn->Real” implies the question was “Is this image synthetic or real”.
In 2.1, “Patient-level splits into training, validation, and test sets were applied consistently across cohorts to prevent information leakage” is redundant with 3, which makes much more sense “split into training, validation, and test sets with a 6:1:3 patient-level ratio. ”
In 3.1, I would take a moment to discuss how adapted Roent-Gen worsened diversity performance (MS-SSIM) and why that’s okay.
In Section 3.1, when discussing Table 2, the justification for treating FID as the primary metric and MS‑SSIM as secondary on the grounds that MS‑SSIM would be dominated by preserved backgrounds is unconvincing. FID is similarly sensitive to large‑scale structural similarity and would also be dominated by background preservation in this setting. As such, this distinction does not meaningfully address the underlying evaluation issue. It would be preferable to state the results directly and acknowledge the observed performance differences, rather than providing a rationale that does not apply consistently across metrics.
In Table 3, I would bold both 0.394 for YOLOv81 because bolding one while underlining the other seems arbitrary
The radiologist-driven Turing test would make more sense before the downstream evaluation, as it is evaluating synthetic image quality, which is directly related to section 3.1.
Briefly describing the training of classification models would be helpful. Was hyperparameter tuning performed on the validation dataset for each model?
I know that MICCAI has limited space, but seeing the actual results for external validation would be helpful.
How was confidence measured for ConfAUC? How many images were in Turing test?

I would have recommended acceptance this paper, if not for Weakness 1.As the main purpose of this paper was to improve downstream classification performance, I would have liked to see the paper prove to me that the proposed methodology outperformed other forms of augmentation. I really loved the idea of a two-step framework, but the results didn’t demonstrate to me that it was necessary. All the results really say is that synthetic augmentation improves classification performance, which is widely well-known.
While I would not like to see these additional experiments in a rebuttal, I would like to see that the authors appropriately contextualize past works, explicitly stating the contributions of their paper over the past works. I would also like to see confirmation that the radiological images with critical RFOs will be released (which would be the largest contribution of the work). And finally, I would want to see that the missing information has been added in, and that the erroneous sentence in the abstract claiming ablation analyses and ethical considerations was deleted.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
My greatest hesitation is the lack of comparison to other augmentation strategies. A reader cannot know if the proposed methodology outperforms contemporary augmentation techniques.
Other than that, the work seeks to solve an important clinical problem and proposes an innovative solution for improving synthetic augmentation for cases with rare pathologies/objects. The public release of real-world RFOs will also be of great interest to the community.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces SurgRFO, a two-stage synthetic augmentation pipeline that generates realistic RFO-positive surgical chest radiographs and shows that these synthesised positives improve downstream object detection performance, including evaluation on an external site.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Detecting critical RFOs is a safety-critical task where real positive data are rare; focusing on improving sensitivity/robustness is well aligned with clinical needs.
2.The proposed synthetic positives are used to improve multiple mainstream detectors, suggesting good practical utility and ease of adoption in existing clinical/engineering pipelines.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The paper does not clearly state whether the data used to train the synthesis models (Stage 1/Stage 2) come strictly from the Site 1 training split, or whether Site 1 validation/test cases might be used during synthetic data generation. If the synthesis model is trained on test-patient images and then used to generate data for downstream evaluation, this would compromise the fairness of the internal assessment.
2.In the downstream detection experiments (Sec. 3.2), multiple metrics are reported (e.g., mAP, FROC, FNR, FOR, ACC), but their exact definitions and computation protocols in the detection setting are not clearly specified. Moreover, the overall experimental setup and evaluation procedure in this section are not sufficiently clear.
3.The data section states that Site 2 provides “An additional 20 critical RFO-positive cases,” yet the external results include metrics that depend on false positives (e.g., FROC). The authors should clarify whether the Site 2 external test set includes negative samples, and provide its size and class composition. If no negative cases are included, the paper should explain how these metrics are defined and computed for the external evaluation.
4.Table 4 reveals an interesting gap: in (a), clinicians give comparable quality/realism scores to real and synthetic images, yet in (b), they can still distinguish synthetic images with an accuracy of ~75%. Could the authors explain why the images receive similar quality/realism ratings despite being distinguishable?

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper presents a two-stage compositional synthesis framework (SurgRFO) for generating intraoperative chest X-rays with critical retained foreign objects (RFOs) to address the scarcity of positive training data. Specifically, it decouples global background modeling using a diffusion-based foundation model from localized RFO synthesis via patch-based generation and conditional Poisson blending. In addition, the authors introduce the Intraoperative RFO Bench, a curated dataset of annotated surgical radiographs, and demonstrate that synthetic data augmentation improves downstream detection performance across multiple models.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Clinical relevance and problem importance
The paper addresses the detection of critical retained foreign objects (RFOs), which are rare but high-risk events in intraoperative settings. This problem is highly relevant to patient safety and remains underexplored due to extreme data scarcity and subtle visual characteristics. The focus on such a clinically meaningful and challenging task significantly strengthens the impact of the work.
2.Well-motivated compositional synthesis framework
The proposed two-stage framework separates global background generation from localized object synthesis, which aligns well with the inherent structure of intraoperative radiographs. This design enables better modeling of rare and small objects that are difficult to capture in fully end-to-end generative approaches. The use of conditional Poisson blending further ensures photometric consistency between synthesized objects and background, improving visual coherence .
3.Performance improvements across downstream task models
The experimental results show that augmenting training data with synthesized samples leads to consistent improvements across multiple detection architectures, including Faster R-CNN, RetinaNet, and YOLOv8.
4.Inclusion of clinician-centered evaluation
The incorporation of a radiologist-driven Turing-style evaluation adds a clinically meaningful validation of the generated images. The comparable quality ratings between synthetic and real images under blinded assessment support the plausibility of the synthesis results and enhance the translational relevance of the study .
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Limited integration between stages
The proposed method adopts a two-stage pipeline in which background generation and object synthesis are trained independently and combined through a post-hoc optimization process. However, this design prevents joint feature learning between the background (normal chest radiographs) and the synthesized objects (RFOs). As a result, the model is unable to capture globally consistent representations, which may limit both visual coherence and scalability of the framework.
2.Limited dataset size and insufficient generalization validation
The dataset contains only 144 positive cases, and the external test set is very small (20 cases). While it is understandable that positive cases are inherently scarce, there exists a large amount of publicly available negative data. Incorporating external public datasets, particularly for downstream evaluation and Turing test analysis, would strengthen the conclusions and provide more convincing evidence of generalization.
3.Incomplete baseline comparisons
The experimental comparisons are limited to RoentGen and DreamBooth, which do not fully represent the current state of the art. The absence of more recent and competitive baselines makes it difficult to assess the true advantage of the proposed method. Including stronger and more up-to-date generative models would provide a more comprehensive evaluation.
4.Evaluation metrics are not fully aligned with the task characteristics
The use of FID and MS-SSIM for evaluating medical X-ray synthesis is debatable, as these metrics do not necessarily reflect clinical fidelity or the realism of localized lesions. The paper itself acknowledges that MS-SSIM is largely dominated by background similarity. More task-specific metrics would provide a more meaningful and clinically relevant evaluation.
5.Limited analysis of downstream task improvements
The downstream evaluation aims to demonstrate that incorporating synthetic data improves detection performance. However, the analysis lacks depth. In addition to accuracy, aspects such as stability and robustness should be considered, for example by reporting standard deviations across multiple runs. Furthermore, evaluating performance under reduced base data (data ablation) could provide stronger evidence of the effectiveness of the synthesized data. Relevant related studies have demonstrated such evaluation strategies and could be referenced for comparison.
Layer Separation: Towards Adjustable Joint Space Width Images Synthesis (ACM MM 2025)
https://doi.org/10.1145/3746027.3755407
Towards Generalizable Tumor Synthesis (CVPR 2024)
https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2024/papers/Chen_Towards_Generalizable_Tumor_Synthesis_CVPR_2024_paper.pdf
6.Lack of discussion on X-ray imaging physics
X-ray image synthesis differs fundamentally from natural image synthesis, as it is governed by specific imaging physics. The current approach, which relies on a “copy-paste”-style compositional strategy, may not fully respect the physical formation process of X-ray images (e.g., attenuation and projection). A more detailed discussion or justification of how the proposed method aligns with or approximates these physical principles would strengthen the work.

This paper addresses a clinically important and challenging problem, namely the detection of rare critical retained foreign objects (RFOs) in intraoperative radiographs. The work is well-motivated, and the proposed framework provides a practical solution to the issue of extreme data scarcity by leveraging synthetic data generation. The introduction of a curated dataset and the consistent improvements observed across multiple detection models suggest that the approach has meaningful potential and practical value.
While the methodological novelty is somewhat limited, as the framework mainly combines existing techniques in a structured manner, the design is reasonable and tailored to the characteristics of the problem. The inclusion of clinician-based evaluation further strengthens the relevance of the work from a translational perspective.
There are, however, several aspects that could be further improved, including stronger baseline comparisons, more comprehensive validation, and more task-specific evaluation metrics. Addressing these points would make the contribution more convincing and robust.
Overall, despite some limitations in novelty and experimental depth, the paper presents a meaningful application with practical impact and a reasonably solid experimental demonstration. With further refinement, it has the potential to make a useful contribution to the field, and I consider it suitable for borderline acceptance.

reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The paper is overall well-structured and addresses a meaningful research problem with clinical relevance. The rebuttal addressed several important concerns raised during review. Therefore, I believe the revised paper is marginally above the acceptance threshold for MICCAI.

meta_reviews.text:
Paper summary: This paper introduces SurgRFO, a two-stage synthetic augmentation pipeline that generates realistic RFO-positive surgical chest radiographs and shows that these synthesised positives improve downstream object detection performance, including evaluation on an external site.
Strengths: This work addresses a clinically important and safety-critical problem. A key strength is the introduction and public release of a rare clinical radiograph dataset containing critical RFO cases, which represents a valuable contribution to the field. The proposed well-motivated compositional synthesis framework, which separates radiograph generation from localized RFO synthesis, is technically sound and improves the fidelity and realism of synthesized objects. This is further supported by robust evaluation of synthetic image quality through blinded clinician assessment, quantitative distribution analysis, and external validation. Importantly, the synthetic data consistently improve downstream detection performance across multiple mainstream architectures (e.g., Faster R-CNN, RetinaNet, YOLOv8), demonstrating strong practical utility, ease of adoption in existing clinical pipelines, and alignment with the clinical need to improve sensitivity and robustness in rare-event detection.
Weaknesses:
First, the novelty is somewhat weakened by substantial overlap with prior work on synthetic augmentation for critical RFO detection, yet the manuscript does not adequately contextualize or compare against these closely related methods.
In addition, the downstream detection gains are not compared against alternative synthetic generation or simpler augmentation strategies, leaving it unclear whether the improvements stem from the proposed method itself or simply from increased training data.
The paper also lacks important dataset and experimental details, including cohort composition, labeling protocols, train/test separation for synthesis, preprocessing consistency, and external cohort setup - which raises concerns about reproducibility and evaluation fairness.
Furthermore, downstream performance is reported without statistical significance analysis or measures of uncertainty, despite relatively small positive sample sizes, limiting confidence in the robustness of the reported gains.
Decision Rationale: The paper has clear strengths, but several substantive concerns remain unresolved, particularly regarding the limitations above. These points appear addressable through author clarification. I therefore recommend Invite for Rebuttal.

Thank you for the constructive rebuttal for addressing the reviewers’ concerns. The discussion improved confidence in both the technical contribution and the clinical relevance of the work.
The Reviewers acknowledged that the paper tackles an important clinical problem and proposes an innovative approach for synthetic augmentation in the setting of rare pathologies and objects. This is an interesting contribution for the MICCAI community.
One remaining concern is the limited comparison against other contemporary augmentation strategies, which makes it difficult to fully position the proposed method within the broader augmentation literature. While this limitation should be acknowledged more clearly, the current evidence is sufficient to support the paper’s main claims. The planned public release of real-world RFO data is also expected to provide meaningful value to the community.
For the camera-ready version, I recommend authors to strengthen discussion of related augmentation approaches and clarify the scope of claims accordingly.
I support the acceptance of this paper.

This manuscript presents a method to generate synthetic XRay images with foreign objects to aid in the development of a method to recognise foreign objects XRay images. This addresses a clinically important dataset and the authors will also release this dataset.
The reviewers found the method to be technically sound and interesting. The limitations were limited novelty, and no comparison with other augmentation strategies.
Although there is some overlap in methodology with prior works, this manuscript is evaluated on real images with foreign objects whereas other methods generated synthetic evaluation image.
I am accepting this manuscript because on balance I find the novelty an important step change the other weaknesses (lack of comparison with other data augmentation methods) are counter balanced by the strengths of the work.
The reviewers’ concerns have been successfully addressed in the rebuttal, making the work a solid contribution especially for what concerns methodological applications in MIC.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for their constructive comments. All reviewers (R1–R3) acknowledged the clinical importance of rare, safety-critical RFO detection. R2, R3 recognized SurgRFO as a meaningful two-stage synthetic augmentation framework, noting its downstream detection gains (R2, R3), robust synthetic image evaluation including clinician assessment (R1, R3), external validation (R1, R2), code release, and planned release of intraoperative RFO dataset (R1, R3). Below, we address the reviewers’ concerns. 
R1, Meta-R (Relation to prior RFO synthesis work and novelty): We agree that Zhou et al. (MICCAI DEMI 2026) is relevant and should be contextualized. That work releases CT-based physically synthesized RFO images, rather than real intraoperative radiographs with critical RFOs. Its pipeline inserts RFO meshes into relatively clean CT volumes from normal patients and projects them to X-rays, which is valuable but differs from our target setting: cluttered surgical chest radiographs acquired during real intraoperative workflows. SurgRFO is designed around this domain gap. We curate and release, to our knowledge, the first publicly available real de-identified intraoperative surgical chest radiograph dataset dedicated to critical RFO detection with bounding-box annotations, distinguishing it from prior physically synthesized CT-projection datasets. In the revision, we will add this work to the Introduction, clarify this distinction, and include a contextual comparison. 
R1, Meta-R (Dataset release): We confirm that, upon acceptance, our public release will include de-identified intraoperative RFO radiographs, annotations, and all synthetic SurgRFO images used in the paper. The earlier GitHub statement was imprecise and has been corrected. We also provided example real and synthetic images in the earlier repository to demonstrate the data format and visual quality. 
R1, R2, Meta-R (Cohort details, preprocessing, and leakage prevention): We will add a dedicated paragraph detailing cohort composition, labeling, and experimental protocols. The Site-1 cohort contains 144 critical RFO-positive cases and 944 RFO-negative cases, with one case per patient. Positive and negative cohorts were split at the patient level using the same 6:1:3 train/validation/test protocol, ensuring no patient overlap. We will report exact positive/negative counts for each split. All synthesis components, including background adaptation, RFO appearance modeling, placement-prior estimation, and blending-parameter selection, used only the training split; validation/test images were never used for synthesis training or tuning. Detectors were trained on the training split, selected using validation data, and evaluated only on held-out internal and external cohorts. All images followed the same preprocessing pipeline. We will also clarify labeling criteria/workflow, detector training details, and hyperparameters; implementation details are available in the earlier released code. 
R1, R3, Meta-R (Compare with simpler augmentations): We agree that stronger augmentation comparisons are important. Both real-only and SurgRFO-augmented detector training used the same standard data augmentations, including random flipping and intensity normalization. Thus, the reported gains are not due to basic augmentation being applied only to SurgRFO. To further isolate the contribution of the proposed synthesis strategy, we will add a simple RFO copy-paste/injection baseline using the same number of synthetic-positive samples, allowing direct comparison between SurgRFO and increased synthetic sample count alone. We will clarify the full augmentation protocol. 
R1, R3, Meta-R (Statistical analysis): We agree that uncertainty analysis is important in this rare-event setting. We will add patient-level bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for the primary downstream metrics using fixed held-out test predictions. These intervals will be reported in the main tables.

title: SurgVLA-Bench: Towards Evaluating Vision-Language-Action Models for Laparoscopic Surgical Robotics
abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models represent a promising direction for embodied intelligence in surgical robotics. Despite the prevalence of VLA benchmarks for general robotics, standardized evaluation platforms specifically designed for surgical contexts remain absent. 
To address this limitation, we present SurgVLA-Bench, the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating VLA models in laparoscopic surgical robotics. Leveraging the SurRoL simulation platform, we construct a hierarchical task taxonomy ranging from atomic actions to complete surgical procedures, complemented by a multi-dimensional evaluation framework assessing action accuracy and semantic consistency. We then systematically evaluate two representative paradigms, including autoregressive models such as OpenVLA, and flow matching models such as , , and SmolVLA. Our experiments show that autoregressive models tend to excel in semantic understanding, while flow matching models often achieve higher task precision but may face generalization trade-offs. However, even the best-performing models remain far from satisfactory, as the constrained endoscopic field of view, restricted viewing angles, and frequent occlusions persist as fundamental physical bottlenecks. The code and data are available at https://github.com/VCL-HNU/SurgVLA .

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces SurgVLA-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models in laparoscopic surgical robotics. Built on the SurRoL simulation platform, the benchmark defines a hierarchical task taxonomy spanning three difficulty levels and eight tasks ( from atomic actions to the hemostatic procedure involving sequential steps). The paper constructs a dataset of ~800 trajectories and evaluate four representative VLA models (OpenVLA, pi0, pi0.5, SmolVLA).
reviews.text_strengths:
Hierarchical task design: The three-level taxonomy is well-structured, with each level targeting distinct capability dimensions.
Model coverage: Evaluating autoregressive and flow matching paradigms provides insights about trade-offs between semantic understanding and action precision.
Beyond success rate analysis: Additional experiments on prompt robustness and cross-level generalization provide useful insights about the limitations of state-of-the-art models in the surgical domain.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The paper’s primary contribution is the benchmark itself rather than a novel method. The dataset construction, simulation environment, and evaluation protocol rely on existing platforms (SurRoL, LoRA fine-tuning) without architectural or methodological innovation. This is acceptable for a benchmarking paper, but the paper should clarify what the expected technical contribution of future work building on SurgVLA-Bench would be.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Despite limited technical novelty, the benchmark is a useful resource for VLAs in surgical environments with a well-designed evaluation framework.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The paper presents an integrated vision-language-action framework in surgery in a simulated environment. Even though there is a clear sim-to-real gap, it is a useful resource for early surgical VLA benchmarking in a practical and reproducible manner, allowing the community to advance in the field and compare new methods against available baselines with the hierarchical tasks and metrics proposed in this work. Additionally, the benchmarking study and analysis of existing general-domain VLAs adapted to this scenario is valuable to understand strengths and weaknesses of existing models regarding transferability. Therefore, my recommendation is to accept this paper as it represents a contribution to the surgical data science community.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents SurgVLA-Bench, the first benchmark specifically designed for evaluating Vision-Language-Action models in surgical robotics. Built upon the SurRoL simulation platform, it introduces a hierarchical evaluation framework spanning three difficulty levels and eight tasks, covering a wide range of capabilities from atomic actions to complete surgical procedures. The authors also construct a standardized surgical VLA dataset, provided in multiple formats including LeRobot, RLDS, and 3D point cloud, facilitating direct adoption and future extension by the research community. Four representative VLA models are evaluated across several dimensions including success rate, prompt robustness, and cross-task generalization. Experimental results reveal that autoregressive models tend to excel at semantic understanding, while flow matching models demonstrate superior precision in task execution, yet none of the evaluated models achieve satisfactory performance under multi-task training and testing conditions.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Hierarchical Evaluation Framework.
The paper introduces a three-level hierarchical benchmark that progressively increases in complexity, ranging from atomic actions to multi-step surgical procedures. This design enables fine-grained assessment of surgical VLA models at different difficulty stages, providing richer diagnostic insights than a single overall performance metric.
2.Dedicated Dataset with Extensibility and Multi-format Support.
The authors construct a surgical task dataset from scratch, collecting over 800 manually verified trajectories across eight tasks, addressing the lack of surgical data for VLA research. The dataset will be released in three mainstream formats (LeRobot, RLDS, and 3D point cloud), and an integrated data collection pipeline is provided to support future dataset scaling.
3.Evaluation of Representative VLA Models.
Four representative VLA models covering two mainstream paradigms are evaluated not only on success rate, but also across prompt robustness, instruction informativeness utilization, and cross-task generalization.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Lack of Zero-shot Baseline.
In the introduction, the authors claim that VLA models trained on general domains lack applicability to surgical contexts. However, in the experimental section, all four VLA models are evaluated only after LoRA fine-tuning on the SurgVLA-Bench dataset. No zero-shot performance is reported as a baseline, leaving the claim insufficiently supported by quantitative evidence.
2.Inconsistency in SmolVLA Performance Reporting.
In Table 2, SmolVLA achieves a success rate (SR) of 0% on task T1-1.However, in the Analysis of Success Rate section, the authors report that SmolVLA achieves 82% SR on T1-1 under single-task training. Please clarify this inconsistency.
3.Insufficient Explanation for Generalization Results
In the Analysis of Generalization section, the authors attribute OpenVLA’s notable performance gain on T1-1 after transfer to the cleaner training signal in Level 1, where interference from other objects is absent. However, this explanation is unconvincing, since T2-1 (the corresponding gauze grasping task in Level 2) also involves only the gauze object without distractor objects, yet a slight performance degradation is observed after transfer. This contradicts the proposed explanation.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

1.Insufficient Baseline Comparisons.
Without zero-shot performance as a reference, it is difficult to determine whether the observed low performance stems from the inherent difficulty of the surgical tasks or from the intrinsic limitations of the selected models, leaving the central claim that general-domain VLA models lack applicability to surgical contexts insufficiently supported.
2.Inconsistency Between Reported Results and Analysis.
There are discrepancies between the numerical results presented in the tables and the descriptions provided in the analysis section. The inconsistency undermines the reliability of the reported findings.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors addressed all my concerns. Overall, the benchmark proposed in this paper makes a meaningful contribution to the surgical VLA community.

meta_reviews.text:
SurgVLA-Bench is a benchmark framework for surgical VLA models. While timely, this work is limited to simulation, with associated issues of sim-to-real transfer, tissue deformation, etc. Further lack of a zero-shot baseline, inconsistency in reporting, and the lack of clarity around generalization prevent acceptance.

The rebuttal clarifies many of the reviewers’ concerns (data diversity, tissue realism, zero-shot baselines, etc.)
While R1 raises valid concerns about sim-to-real transfer not being validated within this work, the rebuttal points out that Surrol has been shown to have good sim-to-real transfer in prior work. Moreover, with the potential for future work to separate surgical perception from surgical decision control, as in self-driving, this work provides a valuable benchmark for surgical decision control, which is arguably the more critical component for surgical autonomy.
R1 also characterizes the work as a limited extension from Surrol. Unfortunately, the authors have no opportunity to respond to this point, which was not raised in the initial review, but I believe they would argue for the value of hierarchical task decomposition specifically suited for VLA evaluation, whereas Surrol focuses on atomic tasks.

I recommend acceptance. The paper presents SurgVLA-Bench, a timely benchmark for evaluating vision-language-action models in surgical robotics. Although the work is primarily a benchmark rather than a new VLA architecture, it addresses a clear gap in the surgical robotics community by providing hierarchical tasks, standardized datasets, and evaluation of representative VLA models.
The rebuttal addressed the main technical concerns raised by the reviewers. In particular, the authors clarified the scope of the simulator-based benchmark, the relevance and limitations of sim-to-real transfer, the current exclusion of deformable tissue tasks, the zero-shot baseline behavior, and inconsistencies in the reported SmolVLA results. Reviewers #2 and #4 support acceptance after rebuttal. Reviewer #1 remains concerned about simulation realism and clinical transfer, which is a valid limitation, but I view this as acceptable for an early benchmark contribution rather than a fatal weakness.

After reviewing the rebuttal letter and reviewers’ post-rebuttal comments, I recommend the paper for acceptance. Even though the technical novelty is limited, the proposed benchmark and evaluated baselines are suitable contributions.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback. We address each concern below.
Reviewer 1:
Q1&3: Domain Gap and Sim-to-Real Feasibility
R1&3: We acknowledge the visual gap between simulation and clinical settings. However:
1)Prior work[1] has demonstrated successful sim-to-real transfer for this setup, confirming the practical relevance of our findings. Due to the difficulty of obtaining consistent real-world surgical data, simulation platforms such as SurRoL are increasingly serving as a key infrastructure for benchmarking surgical models.
2) Our simulation replicates real-world 7-DOF robotic kinematics and task success criteria, which are the decisive factors for task performance.
3) The visual gap can be effectively mitigated via style transfer.
[1] Long Y, et al. Surgical embodied intelligence for generalized task autonomy in laparoscopic robot-assisted surgery. Science Robotics, 2025.Q2: Framework Flexibility and Data Diversity
R2: SurgVLA-Bench covers atomic operations (grasp, place, reach) that form the basis of most surgical procedures. The framework’s modular design allows researchers to easily integrate new tasks by replacing anatomical models or adjusting trajectories. This capability to efficiently generate diverse datasets addresses the dual evaluation needs of assessing both task-specific proficiency and cross-scenario generalization.
Q4: Realism of Deformable Tissue
R4: We acknowledge certain surgical tasks, such as retraction and dissection, inherently require realistic tissue deformation. However, our current tasks can be completed without tissue deformation, so the evaluation remains valid. Realistic modeling of tissue deformation for complex maneuvers is a key focus of our future work.
Reviewer 2:
Q1: Platform Innovation and Future Work
R1: Our work focuses on benchmarking rather than VLA architectural innovation. Our core contributions are:
1) We provide the first open-source (after acceptance), reproducible, multi-level evaluation platform for surgical VLA models, establishing a standardized pipeline that the community currently lacks.
2) The multi-layered task design systematically uncovers capability bottlenecks that single-task setups cannot reveal, providing clear directions for future surgical VLA research.
Based on these contributions, we will expand the framework with more diverse tasks and multi-dimensional metrics to offer a comprehensive baseline for comparison.
Reviewer 4:
Q1: Lack of Zero-shot Baseline
R1: Initial zero-shot tests yielded 0% success across all tasks, so we did not report them as a separate baseline. The reasons are:
1)General VLAs lack exposure to surgical instruments and anatomy.
2)Surgical kinematics differ from industrial settings.
Therefore, zero-shot evaluation is not necessary, and we performed domain-specific fine-tuning and then conducted comparison.
A full explanation and analysis will be included in the final version.
Q2: Inconsistency in SmolVLA Performance Reporting
R2: The 0% success rate in Table 2 comes from a multi-task training setup where task interference occurs. The 82% success rate mentioned in the text is from a single-task training setup.
This stark gap shows that lightweight models like SmolVLA suffer from severe interference during multi-task learning, highlighting the need for more robust multi-task architectures in surgical scenarios.
Q3: Insufficient Explanation for Generalization Results
R3: T2-1 is not a distractor-free environment; it is a multi-object scene where instruments such as needles act as deliberate distractors. The performance drop compared to distractor-free T1-1 is therefore expected.
Architecturally, unlike models such as π0.5 that employ explicit vision-language alignment, OpenVLA fuses image and language embeddings directly within the LLM. This leads to biases in understanding similar language tokens and a tendency to overfit to the scene, impairing the model’s ability to handle multi-object scenarios.

title: SurgZSD: Zero-Shot Surgical Action Triplet Detection via Attribute Composition and Clinical Feasibility Inference
abstract: While traditional surgical action triplet detection has achieved remarkable progress, these closed-set models often fail in highly variable, real-world clinical environments where completely novel instruments, anatomical structures, and actions frequently emerge. To address these limitations, we introduce SurgZSD, a novel framework that leverages medical priors to facilitate attribute composition and joint inference for surgical triplets. Specifically, we initially fine-tune Grounding DINO to establish the precise spatial grounding of the surgical instruments. Following this localization stage, we introduce the Medical Knowledge-Guided Attribute Composition (MKAC) module. Guided by medical priors, this module leverages a pretrained Vision-Language Model (VLM) to parse the localized bounding box regions into structured semantic attributes, thereby composing unseen surgical instruments, targets, and verbs. Subsequently, to accomplish comprehensive surgical triplet recognition, we introduce the Clinical Feasibility-Constrained Joint Inference (CFCJI) module. This module introduces clinical feasibility matrices constructed based on medical priors. By formulating a Top- joint inference objective function, it globally integrates the visual parsing scores with a clinical compatibility penalty term to yield the final surgical action triplets. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SurgZSD not only achieves state-of-the-art performance in zero-shot scenarios but also retains competitive performance under closed-set settings.The source code is available at https://github.com/DengNova/SurgZSD.

Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses the problem of zero-shot detection of surgical action triples and proposes a framework called SurgZSD. The proposed framework introduces a Medically Knowledge-Guided Attribute Combination (MKAC) module, which decomposes entities into structured attributes and performs combinatorial reasoning using a visual-language model. Additionally, it includes a Clinical Feasibility Constraint Joint Inference (CFCJI) module, which integrates prior medical knowledge to enforce compatibility constraints among the elements of the triples. Experiments demonstrate that the method achieves good performance in zero-shot scenarios.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.This paper addresses a significant and practical challenge in surgical scene understanding—the ability to generalize to unseen instruments, targets, and actions—which is of great importance for real-world applications in various surgical procedures.
2.Rather than performing direct classification, the method utilizes VLMs to extract structured attribute representations, thereby enabling compositional generalization.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.To my knowledge, both the ITG-Trip and MCIT-IG methods pre-trained the object detection model Deformable DETR on Cholec80.In contrast, this paper fine-tunes Grounding DINO on the CholecTrack20 dataset. The authors did not conduct ablation experiments for Stage A, which raises doubts as to whether the model’s performance gains are primarily attributable to Stage A.
2.This method does not perform training or inference at the frame level, thereby neglecting the temporal dependencies that are crucial for understanding surgical actions—a factor that is critical for contextual inference in surgical procedures.
3.The proposed framework consists of decoupled components across multiple stages, which limits end-to-end optimization and hinders clinical deployment.
4.As shown in Figure 2, after Stage 2, the instrument has already obtained a unique predicted probability. Why is it necessary to perform a Top-K operation on the instrument in Stage 3?

N/A

This paper addresses the challenge of zero-shot surgical action triplet detection and demonstrates a degree of innovation. However, I have serious concerns regarding the fairness of the comparisons and the model’s effectiveness.

reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The author has addressed some of my concerns, but I remain worried about the fairness of the Stage A and the clinical applicability of this model.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: (1) The paper introduces SurgZSD, the first framework proposed for zero-shot surgical action triplet detection. (2) It proposes the Medical Knowledge-Guided Attribute Composition (MKAC) module, which uses a Vision-Language Model to parse localized regions into structured attributes based on medical prototypes to recognize unseen entities. (3) It introduces the Clinical Feasibility-Constrained Joint Inference (CFCJI) module, which formulates a joint inference objective constrained by clinical feasibility matrices to globally integrate visual scores and output coherent surgical action triplets.
reviews.text_strengths: (1) This paper formulates a novel and challenging problem by introducing a strict zero-shot paradigm to surgical scene understanding, where training and testing classes are completely disjoint. （2）The framework innovatively synergizes an open-set object detector with a VLM and an LLM to bridge the domain gap without requiring fully annotated fine-grained surgical data for novel classes.
reviews.text_weaknesses: (1) The topic shares conceptual similarities with a recent ICLR submission, “Cognitive-Awakening Chain-of-Surgery for Compositional Zero-Shot Surgical Triplet Recognition.” Although that work focuses on triplet recognition rather than detection, the underlying compositional zero-shot motivation is highly related. The authors should cite and explicitly discuss the differences and relative advantages of their proposed framework compared to this work. (2) The framework currently infers actions based purely on spatial interactions within isolated frames. Since surgical actions are inherently continuous and dynamic, have the authors considered incorporating temporal information in VLMs to further enhance triplet detection accuracy? (3) To ensure strict reproducibility, the promised code release must guarantee that all dependencies, the exact structured prompt templates used for the VLM, and the fully generated Knowledge Base are open-sourced alongside clear, step-by-step documentation.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a highly original and clinically relevant approach to surgical scene understanding by addressing the inevitable presence of novel instruments and anatomies in real-world deployments. The proposed integration of medical prior knowledge for attribute composition and clinical feasibility inference is logically sound and well-justified. Furthermore, the zero-shot evaluation on 1377 manually annotated images clearly demonstrates that SurgZSD significantly outperforms baseline models, which struggle with spatial localization or domain gaps. Although the proposed method is quite straightforward, I find it to be highly simple and effective.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I maintain my original opinion based on the concerns and evaluation provided in my previous review.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a framework for zero detection of surgical action triplets from images with the help of object detectors, VLM for describing the instruments and then a clinically constructed knowledge base to identify the instruments based on description followed by identification of actions and anatomy.
reviews.text_strengths: 1.The paper is well presented and structured, stating clearly the focus on each component of the method.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The VLM questionnaire for action and anatomy are not clearly stated in the paper. Fig 2 could be modified to show the questions for each of I,V,T.
2.A curious question is does 3 questions with 4 options each sufficient to represent all laparoscopic surgical tools? Any reference / proof to support this i.e., some kind of graph or visual representation showing the known surgical tools to mapping to the questions and options in one-on-one manner. This kind of representation would strengthen the completeness of the proposed method.
3.What data is the VLM pretrained on? Is it a general purpose VLM or surgically trained VLM? If it is general purpose VLM then, in the extended version of this work it would be better to show an ablation with different off the shelf VLMs such that the effectiveness of the framework is portrayed.
4.Does the knowledge base contain information generic to all surgeries and triplets? If it contains information related to the triplets in evaluation then the zero-shot concept applies only to detecting the instruments and the title need modifications accordingly.

N/A

The concept of the work is novel, however there are few aspects which need further clarifications and the paper could be accepted if those issues are addressed.
