meta_reviews.text:
SurgZSD presents an approach to zero-shot surgical triplet detection combining open-set Grounding DINO with a Medical-Knowledge-Guided Attribute Composition module and a Clinical Feasibility Constraint. Two key issues require response before a final decision: (1) Fair-comparison concern - prior triplet-detection baselines (ITG-Trip, MCIT-IG) pretrain Deformable DETR on Cholec80 training data, while this work fine-tunes Grounding DINO on CholecTrack20 (2) Scope of the VLM attribute-query scheme — the 3-question/4-option protocol has not been validated to cover the full instrument space. The authors should address these issues thoroughly in the rebuttal.

After reviewing the rebuttal letter and reviewers’ post-rebuttal comments, I recommend acceptance.
All reviewers were satistfied with the rebuttal. The authors should address the remaining concerns in the camera-ready version.

The rebuttal clarifies key points such as the detector setup, attribute-query scheme, and design choices, but does not fully resolve concerns about fair comparison, coverage of the attribute space, and lack of temporal modelling. Overall, the reviewers in general lean toward acceptance due to the novelty of the problem and approach, but evaluation limitations remain.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and AC for constructive comments and recognition of novelty and clinical relevance. Our responses are provided below.
1.Fairness and Stage A (R1, R3, AC). We understand the reviewer’s concern about fairness. The comparison with ITG-Trip and MCIT-IG is intended to show that a zero-shot-oriented framework can still retain reasonable capability under the closed-set setting. CholecTrack20 is derived from Cholec80 and provides instrument localization, making it a reasonable source for detector fine-tuning. Deformable DETR is a closed-set detector, whereas the zero-shot setting may contain unseen instruments, thus Grounding DINO is used as an open-vocabulary model. SurgZSD is detector-agnostic: any reliable open-set instrument detector can serve as Stage A. We agree that detector-level ablations would strengthen the analysis and will include them as future work. Stage A provides localization proposals, while the main methodological contribution lies in the MKAC and CFCJI modules. The ablation studies in the manuscript demonstrate the effectiveness of these two modules.
2.VLM attribute-query scheme (R3, AC). We apologize that Fig. 2 simplified the query design and caused misunderstanding. “3 questions with 4 options” is only a compact illustrative example, not the full attribute vocabulary. In our work, the attribute dimensions are fixed for interpretability, but the candidate options are expandable. Thus, the method does not assume that four options can cover all instruments. A new entity can be added by defining its attribute prototype in the attribute space, without additional visual samples. We will revise Fig. 2 and provide the prompts and attribute vocabularies.
3.Temporal information, optimization, and deployment (R1, R2). We agree temporal context is important, especially for verb recognition. This work focuses on frame-level zero-shot triplet detection, temporal information is complementary to the framework. A natural extension is to replace the frame-level VLM parser with a video-aware parser that can incorporate motion and temporal context. This will be considered as future work. SurgZSD is intentionally modular: the detector, VLM attribute parser, and feasibility inference layer can each be independently inspected and optimized. Although this sacrifices part of the end-to-end optimization capability, it improves the transparency required for clinical review.
4.Top-K operation in Stage C (R1). Although Stage B scores instrument candidates, the top-1 prediction is only used for the instrument detection comparison experiment. For complete triplet prediction, relying solely on the top-1 prediction may be unreliable, because unseen instruments can share similar attributes. Stage C is designed to avoid locally confident but clinically implausible combinations. Therefore, Top-K serves global triplet optimization, rather than redundant prediction. We will clarify this in the revision.
5.Knowledge base and VLM usage (R3). The knowledge base contains no triplet-level information, such as triplet labels or frequency statistics, avoiding data leakage. It is built separately for instruments, targets, and verbs using general medical prior knowledge and semantic attribute prototypes generated with GPT-5.2.The VLM reasoning module in Stage B and Stage C is Qwen3VL-Plus, a general purpose VLM without surgical-domain training or fine-tuning. Thank you for the valuable suggestion. We will evaluate different off-the-shelf VLMs and further explore fine-tuning domain-specific surgical VLMs in the extended version.
6.CoCoS Comparison (R2). First, CoCoS recognizes unseen combinations of seen components, whereas SurgZSD detects unseen instruments, targets, and verbs. Next, SurgZSD relies on medical attributes and clinical feasibility constraints, while CoCoS leverages temporal Glance-Gaze-Think reasoning. Thus, they are complementary. 
7.Reproducibility (R2). Upon acceptance, we will immediately release the code.

title: SurvTTA: Order-Aware Test-Time Adaptation for Heterogeneous Domain Shifts in Multi-modal Survival Analysis
abstract: Multi-modal survival analysis enables patient risk stratification and clinical decision-making in oncological prognosis. However, existing methods often suffer from heterogeneous domain shifts in real-world cross-site deployment, which refer to data discrepancies from inter-center equipment and modality-specific protocol variations. We observe that survival ordinal characteristics remain invariant across clinical sites and modalities. Leveraging this insight, we propose SurvTTA, the first test-time adaptation framework for accurate multi-modal survival analysis under heterogeneous domain shifts. SurvTTA bridges multi-modal domain gaps by maintaining reliable topological risk-order consistency and modality-wise aligned representation, enabling stable adaptation of pretrained models across different clinical sites with only unlabeled data. Specifically, a novel order-aware regularization is well-designed to account for the ordinal characteristic of survival prediction, enforcing stable risk ordering across data shifts. Meanwhile, modality-decoupled adaptation is proposed to balance modal-wise adaptation across multi-modal data distributions. Additionally, An uncertainty-aware gradient correction is introduced to stabilize optimization. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of SurvTTA in multi-modal survival analysis, enabling stable test-time adaptation and remarkable performance.
subject_areas: Applications -> Outcome Prediction / Prognosis / Longitudinal Modeling
Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes SurvTTA, a Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) framework designed specifically for multi-modal survival analysis in oncological prognosis. The authors address the critical challenge of heterogeneous domain shifts encountered when deploying models across different clinical sites. SurvTTA innovatively leverages the ordinal nature of survival risk by introducing a Topological Consistency module, a Decoupled Geometric Alignment module, and an Uncertainty-aware Gradient Correction module. Experiments on Head-Neck-PET-CT and HECKTOR datasets demonstrate that SurvTTA outperforms existing regression TTA methods by effectively maintaining risk-order consistency without requiring source data or target labels.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The work addresses the critical issue of domain shifts in multi-center medical deployments. By focusing on TTA without needing source data or target labels, it offers a practical solution for real-world clinical settings where data privacy and accessibility are major constraints.
2.The core insight to leverage the ordinal nature of survival risk (rather than absolute values) is strong. The Topological Consistency module, which maintains both node-wise risks and edge-wise pairwise orderings, is a sophisticated method to preserve the survival structure under distribution shifts.
3.The integration of Decoupled Geometric Alignment (handling modality-specific shifts) and Uncertainty-aware Gradient Correction (resolving optimization conflicts) demonstrates a comprehensive understanding of the instability issues in TTA, making the framework well-suited for complex heterogeneous data.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Contradiction in Online Setting: Section 3.1 mentions an “online setting” with data discarded post-inference, yet the method runs “3 epochs” with rollback. Suggestion: Clarify how rollback works without stored data. Is a buffer used? This is crucial for reproducibility.
2.The paper only compares against two specific regression TTA methods. Suggestion: Discuss or test against standard UDA/TTA classification methods (e. g. , adversarial learning, TENT) to better justify why existing general methods fail for survival analysis.
3.The ablation study lacks analysis on key hyperparameters and augmentation strength. Suggestion: Add a brief sensitivity analysis, especially regarding 3D rotations, to ensure anatomical integrity isn’t compromised.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Equation (4), the derivation from the constrained optimization is dense. Suggestion: Briefly explain how the Lagrangian solution translates to the per-sample update and justify why prediction variance directly indicates objective conflict.

It requires mandatory revision to fix the methodological description, clarify the online setting, and clean up the text. If these issues are not addressed, it could easily tip into rejection territory.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper proposes SurvTTA, a novel test-time adaptation (TTA) framework for multi-modal survival analysis under heterogeneous domain shifts .
The key insight is that survival prediction is inherently ordinal, and that risk ordering remains invariant across domains, even under significant distribution shifts. Based on this observation, the authors introduce:
a topological consistency module to preserve risk ordering structure,
a modality-decoupled alignment strategy to handle heterogeneous shifts across modalities, and
an uncertainty-aware gradient correction mechanism to stabilize test-time optimization.
The method enables adaptation without access to source data or target labels, and demonstrates strong improvements in cross-domain survival prediction across multiple datasets.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper addresses a highly relevant and challenging problem: cross-site generalization in multi-modal survival analysis under heterogeneous domain shifts. Unlike standard classification tasks, survival prediction has intrinsic ordinal structure, and the paper explicitly leverages this property. This is a well-grounded and insightful formulation.
2.A key strength is the idea of modeling survival prediction through risk ordering invariance, rather than absolute score matching. The proposed topological consistency formulation (node-wise + edge-wise constraints) provides a principled way to encode ordinal structure in test-time adaptation. This perspective is both novel and well aligned with survival analysis theory, and represents a meaningful contribution beyond existing TTA methods.
3.The experimental section is thorough and convincing. The use of risk ranking (rather than absolute prediction) and evaluation via Kaplan–Meier curves strengthens the clinical relevance of the work.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Although the paper compares with several TTA methods, the baselines are relatively limited. It would strengthen the paper to include comparisons with:
more recent or stronger domain generalization / adaptation methods, or alternative survival-specific adaptation strategies.
2.The framework introduces multiple components (topology, alignment, gradient correction), which may increase computational overhead and optimization complexity. A discussion on efficiency and scalability would be helpful.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The idea of leveraging ordinal structure in survival analysis for TTA is particularly interesting and could be further explored in future work.
It would be valuable to investigate how the framework performs under more extreme domain shifts or with missing modalities.
A discussion on runtime cost and deployment considerations would further strengthen the practical relevance.

This paper presents a novel and well-motivated approach to test-time adaptation in multi-modal survival analysis, addressing a challenging and clinically important problem. The key strengths include a clear and insightful formulation based on survival ordering, strong methodological contributions, and convincing experimental validation.
While there are minor limitations in baseline comparisons and analysis depth, these do not detract from the overall contribution.
Overall, I find this work to be technically sound, novel, and impactful, and I would recommend acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes SurvTTA, a test-time adaptation (TTA) framework for multi-modal survival analysis under heterogeneous cross-site domain shifts. The core observation is that survival risk ordering is invariant across clinical sites and modalities, which is leveraged to adapt pretrained models using only unlabeled target data. The method is evaluated on two multi-site PET/CT datasets (Head-Neck-PET-CT and HECKTOR).
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Clinically well-motivated problem. TTA for survival analysis under heterogeneous multi-modal domain shifts is a genuinely underexplored problem with practical relevance for cross-site deployment. The paper is the first to address this combination.
2.The insight that survival risk ordering (rather than absolute scores) is site-invariant is well-motivated and directly informs the TC module design. Framing this as a topological graph with node- and edge-level consistency losses is technically coherent.
3.The DGA module’s per-modality treatment is a sensible and important design choice given that different imaging modalities (CT vs. PET) exhibit different degrees of domain shift. This is often overlooked in unified TTA approaches.
4.The failure of SSA on HMR and instability of ST variants highlight a real practical gap, and SurvTTA’s robustness across target sites is a meaningful result.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The HECKTOR target sets appear to have on the order of 20–30 patients each based on dataset sizes and splits. No confidence intervals or statistical significance tests are reported for any of the main results
2.The paper compares against only two regression TTA methods (CASP, SSA) and self-training variants. CASP is from sentiment analysis (AAAI 2025) and SSA from ICLR 2025 — neither is designed for survival prediction. Stronger baseline comparison is needed
3.ResNet-18 with cross-attention or Concat-MLP fusion is a fairly shallow source architecture. It is unclear whether performance gains reflect TTA effectiveness or compensating for a weak source model.
4.Table 2(b) shows that +T+G (mean 70.28%) underperforms +G alone (70.46%). This is a notable finding that contradicts the narrative and is dismissed in a single sentence. A thorough analysis of why these objectives conflict and why UGC resolves them is necessary to validate the design.
5.Presenting post-TTA significance (P=0.036) without confidence intervals or sample size . λ1, λ2, τ, c, and γ govern all three modules and their interactions, how is the hyperparameter selection done.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The problem is well-motivated, and the core idea of leveraging rank-order invariance for survival TTA is interesting. However, the evaluation is critically underpowered, target sets of ~20–30 patients produce C-index estimates with very high variance, and no uncertainty quantification is provided for any result. The ablation reveals an internal inconsistency (TC+DGA < DGA alone) that is not adequately addressed. The baseline comparison is narrow and uses methods not designed for survival prediction. The UGC module has substantial overlap with CAGrad, but lacks sufficient differentiation. Significant additional experiments, baselines, and addressing queries are needed before the paper is ready for publication.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text: The paper presents a test time adaptation (TTA) technique for survival analysis across different sites. The reviewers have acknowledged the importance of the problem and the soundness and practicality of the solution. They highlight three newly introduced components that were well described: a module to preserve the risk order, a modality alignment module, and an uncertainty-based stabilizer. Strengths include the relevance of the addressed problem (survival across sites), the evaluation done on two public datasets, and the improvement over a choice of baselines. Some issues were raised about the choice of baselines, as they rely on simple architectures and/or focus on natural image regression (instead of survival analysis). Another weakness is the lack of confidence intervals or a statistical significance test. Consider upgrading the paper to overcome these.

title: SutureFormer: Learning Surgical Trajectories via Goal-Conditioned Offline RL in Pixel Space
abstract: Predicting surgical needle trajectories from endoscopic video is critical for robot-assisted suturing, enabling anticipatory planning, real-time guidance, and safer motion execution. However, most surgical recordings lack synchronized robot kinematics, and dense frame-level annotations are prohibitively expensive to obtain from clinical experts. To address these challenges, we propose SutureFormer, a goal-conditioned offline reinforcement learning framework that reformulates trajectory prediction as visual navigation in pixel space. SutureFormer operates solely on raw image sequences under sparse supervision, eliminating the need for kinematic signals or dense annotations. It encodes variable-length video observations using a Spatial CNN and Transformer architecture to capture both local spatial cues and long-range temporal dependencies. It then autoregressively predicts future waypoints within an action space comprising discrete directions and continuous magnitudes. A guidance channel constructed from nine sparse keyframe waypoints provides goal conditioning. To enable stable offline training from expert demonstrations, we adopt Conservative Q-Learning with confidence-weighted rewards and behavioral cloning regularization. We evaluate SutureFormer on a new kidney wound suturing dataset comprising 1,158 trajectories from 50 patients, where it reduces Average Displacement Error by 56.8% compared to the strongest baseline, demonstrating the effectiveness of pixel-level sequential action modeling and the offline RL formulation for surgical trajectory prediction.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Reinforcement Learning / Control / Decision-Making

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes SutureFormer, a surgical trajectory prediction framework that uses endoscopic video, sparse keyframe supervision, and a goal-conditioned offline RL formulation in pixel space. A Spatial CNN + Transformer encoder processes observed frames and coordinates, and a CQL-based policy predicts future waypoints via discrete directions and continuous magnitudes. The method is evaluated on a kidney wound suturing dataset with around 1k trajectories from many patients.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper targets a relevant CAI problem, namely surgical trajectory prediction for suturing, and tries to reduce reliance on robot kinematics. It also uses a real clinical dataset with patient-level split, and the reported quantitative improvements over the chosen baselines are large
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The main weakness is limited algorithmic novelty. Most of the technical ingredients appear to be standard and assembled from existing components: CNN/Transformer visual encoding, goal conditioning, discrete direction plus magnitude prediction, CQL for offline RL, behavior cloning regularization, and spline interpolation for dense pseudo-labels. The paper’s main novelty seems to lie more in the task reformulation and engineering combination than in a genuinely new method.
A second weakness is that the paper does not convincingly show that the offline RL formulation itself is the source of the gain. There is no ablation isolating CQL versus simpler supervised trajectory prediction or imitation-learning variants under the same architecture and inputs. As a result, it is hard to tell whether the improvements come from RL, from the goal-guidance design, or simply from a stronger architecture and preprocessing pipeline.
On the other hand, the experimental validation is limited. The evaluation is restricted to one dataset, one procedure type, and 50 patients, with no external validation, no robustness study, and no statistical significance testing. This makes it difficult to assess generalization and clinical impact. Not sure if this is the standard in the surgical robots domain.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I do not find the paper sufficiently strong in methodological innovation for MICCAI, however, the problem itself could be interesting. The application is relevant and the reported results are promising, while the method is largely a combination of existing ideas rather than a clearly new algorithmic contribution. So it is a weak accept.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper proposes a goal-conditioned offline reinforcement learning framework that reformulates surgical needle trajectory prediction as navigation in pixel space.
Reviewers highlight the novelty of formulating surgical trajectory prediction as RL in pixel space, the methodological choice of conservative Q-learning with confidence-weighted rewards, the reliance only on sparse keyframe annotations, and substantial quantitative improvements with patient-level splits.
Concerns include limited algorithmic novelty since most components are off-the-shelf, missing ablations isolating the offline-RL formulation from simpler imitation variants, evaluation restricted to a single procedure without generalisation, unclear dataset provenance, and questions about the inference-time pseudo-guidance, etc.
Reviews are mixed, and the authors may respond to the concerns in the rebuttal.

After the rebuttal, all reviewers uniformly recommend acceptance.

There is consensus on accepting this paper after rebuttal.
I do highlight that the rebuttal includes new experiments (requested by a reviewer) and that this is not within MICCAI rebuttal guidelines.
My accept assessment is on the basis that the present paper (without considering new experiments or code/dataset promises) is of enough good quality for MICCAI.
I would urge the authors NOT to make substantial changes to the main submitted paper, such as creating whole new subsections (and having to make other non-peer reviewed changes to fit within page limit).
Given that MICCAI reviews & rebuttal will be public after publication, that should be enough for full transparency.
Minor fixes/clarifications as suggested are still welcome, of course.
The author provides detailed feedback, and the rebuttal has addressed most of the concerns raised by the reviewers. All the reviewers have agreed to accept it.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers and will revise paper as follows.
Novelty. CNNs, Transformers, and CQL are established. Novelty lies not in these modules individually, but, to our knowledge, in the first framework formulating vision-based surgical trajectory prediction as pixel-space visual navigation. This differs from prior ESD studies [1,2]. Renal suturing has distinct dynamics and constraints: speed varies with tissue handling and stitch planning, while prolonged dwelling at a cutting site in ESD or dissection may increase tissue damage risk and disrupt the procedure. They therefore generalize poorly to our dataset. Our results suggest visual navigation is effective for suturing trajectory prediction and motivate surgical AI.
Related work and baselines. We will cover surgical trajectory prediction, kinematics-based motion prediction, and video-based imitation learning. Given sparse surgical video trajectory literature, we include general baselines following the closest endoscopic dissection works [1,2], and will separate and justify surgical and general baselines.
Ablation study. We will better isolate offline RL. We conducted a CQL ablation by removing only CQL versus simpler supervised trajectory prediction, but omitted it due to page limit. Removing CQL causes 23.5%, 18.6%, and 18.1% degradation in ADE, FDE, and FD. This shows the gain is not merely from architecture or preprocessing, but is substantially supported by conservative offline RL. We will add this ablation as a new subsection.
Pseudo-guidance. We apologize for the ambiguous phrase polynomial extrapolation from observed frames. Pseudo-guidance is not extracted from image pixels; it is generated by fitting a low-degree polynomial to historical trajectory points, using 10 points in our implementation. Early inference is dominated by observed coordinates. During rollout, predicted coordinates are appended and guidance is recomputed, gradually transitioning to the model-inferred trajectory. It is only a weak, low-latency prior; the policy still predicts direction and magnitude from visual context, current position, and offline RL.
Generalization and clinical development. SutureFormer is not purely appearance based. Although this dataset uses clinical keyframe annotations and interpolation to obtain observed needle-tip coordinates, the framework is source-agnostic for coordinates and guidance, and can use priors from a detector or tracker. First validating the method in a well-defined instrument and tissue setting is reasonable for clinical technology development, since reliable annotations validate the core framework before manual inputs are replaced by automated perception modules and broader-domain evaluation.
Dataset and validation. We will state external validation as a limitation. Still, private clinical datasets are common in MICCAI surgical video and robotics because of collection, annotation, and privacy constraints; examples include [1,3,4]. Our dataset contains 1,158 trajectories from 50 patients, with patient-level 35/8/7 train/val/test splits and 861/151/146 trajectories, preventing same-patient leakage. We will add raw frame distribution (89.47±74.74, median 64, range 10–501), data source, model size, runtime and implementation details. We plan to release code upon acceptance. The dataset is part of a comprehensive dataset and will be released once the dataset paper is accepted.
Discussion and limitations. We will correct Qualitative Results to Quantitative Results, expand comparison discussion, discuss Fig. 2 corner cases, and add Limitations on single-procedure and single-center validation, reliance on observed coordinates, and decision-support rather than autonomous execution.
[1] Imitation learning for dissection trajectory prediction. MICCAI 2023.[2] Learning dissection trajectories via equivariant diffusion. Medical Image Analysis 2025.[3] Dia-LLaMA. MICCAI 2025.[4] Geometric-Guided Few-Shot Dental Landmark Detection. MICCAI 2025.

title: SwallowReg: SAM-Assisted Deformable Registration with Adaptive Global-Local Features for Cine-MRI Swallowing Function Quantification
abstract: Although medical image registration is an effective tool for quantifying organ motion, its application in assessing postoperative swallowing function in tongue cancer remains limited. Recognizing that existing methods often fail to fully exploit the semantic priors from segmentation tasks, we propose an end-to-end joint learning framework for segmentation and registration on dynamic cine-MRI sequences. By leveraging semantic priors from the Segment Anything Model to guide the registration, it becomes possible to precisely model the complex post‑operative motion of the tongue. Our contributions can be generalized into three aspects:(1) We construct a deeply supervised SAM feature adaptor, where the U-Net encoder generates a multi-scale semantic feature pyramid to provide hierarchical anatomical priors for the registration task. (2) We design a novel convolutional unit combining DCNv3 and Swin-transformer to capture local-to-global features; a bidirectional coordinate attention fusion module is further introduced to adaptively fuse multi-scale features from both the SAM feature adaptor and registration encoder. (3) To directly enhance registration accuracy along anatomical boundaries, we propose an EdgeWeightedIoU loss that employs a Laplacian operator to extract and refine these boundaries from the segmentation output. Ablation studies show that our SAM scheme achieves a 7.55% Dice improve-ment on the sagittal tongue MRI dataset. In SOTA experiments on the coronal tongue MRI dataset, VoxelMorph, TransMorph, and our Baseline gain 3.93%, 35.22%, and 3.32% in Dice respectively after integrating our SAM scheme. Con-sistent improvements are also observed on the ACDC cardiac MRI da-taset .  Our code is available at: https://github.com/FFigo/SwallowReg.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes an end-to-end joint segmentation and registration framework for tongue motion analysis in cine-MRI, integrating SAM-based semantic priors with a hybrid CNN–Transformer architecture to improve anatomical alignment and motion estimation.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper addresses a clinically relevant problem, namely tongue motion analysis for swallowing assessment using cine-MRI.
The proposed method introduces a joint segmentation and registration framework, leveraging SAM-based semantic priors, which is a meaningful and relatively novel integration for improving region-specific alignment.
The model design is technically comprehensive, combining CNN and Transformer components with multi-scale supervision, and is supported by an ablation study to analyze different modules.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The performance improvements over existing methods are relatively small, and no statistical analysis is provided, making it difficult to assess their significance.
The use of the ACDC cardiac MRI dataset is not well justified, and the stronger improvements on this dataset raise concerns about the relevance of the evaluation to the targeted clinical application.
Parts of the methodology and result interpretation lack clarity and sufficient support, which affects readability, reproducibility, and the strength of the conclusions.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1.Introduction:
The claim that “Current tongue movement quantification often relies on manual annotation of tongue structures and subsequent estimation of movement parameters by clinicians, which is time-consuming, inefficient, and associated with inter-observer variability. “ is not supported by references. Please cite relevant literature.
II recomment to briefly discuss existing semi-automatic or automatic approaches for tongue motion analysis to clarify how the proposed method advances beyond them.
2.Methodology:
The methodology is technically rich and appears well-structured. However, parts of the description are difficult to follow, particularly regarding the interaction between the different modules (e. g. , SAM Feature Adaptor, Swin-Intern block, and BCAF). I recommend a more explicit description of the data flow to improve readability and reproducibility.
3.Experiments:
3.1.Dataset and Criteria:
The inclusion of the ACDC cardiac MRI dataset is not sufficiently justified. Since the proposed method is designed for tongue motion analysis, it is unclear why a cardiac dataset with different anatomical and motion characteristics is used. The authors should clarify the motivation for this choice and explain how it supports the evaluation of the proposed approach.
3.2.Ablation Experiments:
The ablation study is comprehensive and shows consistent performance improvements. However, some explanations (e. g. , why SAM performs better on coronal data or the trade-off between Dice and GNCC/SSIM) are not well supported and seem speculative. More evidence or clearer justification would strengthen this part.
3.3.Performance Comparisons with SOTA
The reported performance improvements over existing methods are relatively small (differences are often around ~1%), but are described with very strong claims (e. g. , “most significant gains” and “optimal performance”). A more balanced discussion is needed, and statistical analysis should be provided to show whether these improvements are meaningful.
The relevance of the ACDC cardiac dataset to the targeted tongue motion task remains unclear and should be better justified. In addition, the main performance improvements appear more pronounced on the ACDC dataset than on the tongue MRI data, which raises concerns about how well the proposed method addresses the intended clinical application.

The paper presents an interesting methodological approach and addresses a relevant clinical problem. However, the overall performance improvements over existing methods are relatively small and lack statistical validation, making it difficult to assess their significance. In addition, the use of an unrelated dataset (ACDC) is not well justified, and the stronger results on this dataset raise concerns about the relevance of the evaluation to the intended application. Finally, the clinical feasibility and impact of the proposed method are not sufficiently discussed, which limits the practical significance of the work.

The authors propose a framework for jointly learning segmentation and registration on dynamic cine-MRI sequences of moving tongues. By leveraging a pre-trained SAM encoder, the feature extractor generates multi-scale

meta_reviews.text:
Critical concerns have been raised by all the reviewers about limited improvement, unclear theoretical justification and presentation, insufficient details, and missing experimental comparisons.
The authors are invited for rebuttal about the concerns raised by the reviewers.

After carefully evaluating the authors’ rebuttal, the reviewers’ revised feedback, and re-examining the paper, I conclude that the authors have effectively addressed the key concerns raised, and the work now meets MICCAI’s publication standards.

The rebuttal does not adequately address reviewers’ concerns. I agree with R1.The paper still lacks methodological clarity and substantial improvements over existing methods. More empirical evidence is required; with the reported results, it’s hard to justify the methodological superiority.

Reviewers recognized the clinical relevance of swallowing function quantification and appreciated the integration of SAM-derived semantic priors with global-local feature modeling. Following the rebuttal, two reviewers were satisfied and maintained or changed to Accept, noting that the authors clarified the data flow, module contributions, use of the ACDC dataset, and ablation results. However, one reviewer remained unconvinced, emphasizing that the paper still lacks sufficient methodological clarity, substantial performance improvements over existing methods, and appropriate statistical validation. Overall, the rebuttal addressed several presentation and interpretation concerns and strengthened the case for the proposed modules, but some limitations remain regarding statistical evidence, reproducibility details, and the modest scale of demonstrated improvements. Given the post-rebuttal reviewer balance and the clarified methodological contribution, I recommend acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for the critical comments and ratings (3,5,4) with detailed responses below. 
To clarify the Data Flow, the framework takes moving and fixed images as input. (1) They respectively enter the SAM Adaptor, where a frozen ViT-B encoder produces embeddings fed into a U-Net to yield four-scale features and segmentation masks. (2) In parallel, their concatenation enters the Registration Encoder (Swin-Intern Blocks), yielding same-scale features. (3) Both enter BCAF, yielding two mutually enhanced feature types per scale. (4) The Decoder uses these as skip connections to produce the deformation filed φ to warp moving images by STN.
[R1; R3] On novelty and module design. (1) Paradigm: using SAM features to boost registration is a novel cross-task knowledge transfer. (2) Module/loss: BCAF bidirectionally fuses SAM and encoder features per scale; the edge-weighted IoU loss uses SAM boundary cues via adaptive weighting. Both are SAM-distilled components. Table 1 ablates each component (Row 1=our Baseline: a Swin-Intern four-scale encoder with skip connections progressively decoded to displacement field with no SAM; Row 6=full model). Sagittal: edge-weighted IoU loss +2.32% Dice (Rows 1→3); BCAF vs. concat. +2.98% (Rows 5→6); full +7.55% over Baseline (35.17→42.72), confirming necessity of each module.
[R1; R3] On limited SOTA comparison and marginal gains. Rows 1–3 in Table 2 are SOTA methods (CNN/VM (2019), Transformer/TM (2022), Diffusion-assisted/LDM (2025)); Row 4 is our Baseline(separately trained). Rows 5–7 (+SAM) only replace the Registration Net with our framework. Taking VM as an example, coronal Dice+3.93%,GNCC+7.37%,SSIM+6.92%; same for TM and Baseline, confirming gains across different registration networks.[R1; R3] On the ACDC dataset and data scale. (1) ACDC records cardiac ED-ES Cine-MRI; Xiao et al. (2023) also used it for registration and cross-organ generalization. (2) However, ACDC is cardiac-only where tongue MRI spans the whole head with complex moving tissues. In the last row of Table 2, tongue Dice shows +4.75% over pre-registration (91.26→96.01), comparable to ACDC’s +5.95%. (3) Our dataset requires specialized equipment and privacy consent, with very few public dataset.
[R1] On missing citations on annotation costs and tongue motion methods. Sun et al. (2024) noted substantial annotation labor in tongue Cine-MRI; Lee et al. (2014) proposed a semi-auto approach with user seeds on a few slices via random walker and deformable registration for motion analysis; Yang et al. (2020) proposed a fully auto approach using TPS robust-point-matching to register contours across Cine-MRI frames and extract deformation fields for motion quantification. They will be added to the final manuscript.
[R1] On speculative explanations in the ablation study. (1) On SAM features’ coronal advantage, rows 1 vs. 2 in Table 1: SAM features surpass encoder features on all coronal metrics (Dice +0.17%, GNCC +0.36%, SSIM +1.58%) while encoder features surpass on all sagittal metrics (Dice +1.49%, GNCC +1.35%, SSIM +2.29%), showing complementarity. (2) On the Dice vs. GNCC/SSIM trade-off. BCAF boosts sagittal Dice (+2.98%, Rows 5→6) while GNCC (−0.17) and SSIM (−0.46) drop, reflecting different metric sensitivities. Dice benefits from BCAF’s boundary refinement; GNCC and SSIM measure global intensity correlation and local structural consistency-both more sensitive to boundary deformation gradients. As the primary motion axis with larger deformations, the sagittal plane amplifies these gradient effects, marginally impacting GNCC/SSIM but substantially boosting Dice. In the coronal plane (Dice +0.42%, GNCC +0.03%, SSIM +0.20%), all improve, confirming a sagittal-complexity trade-off, not a BCAF deficiency.
[R1; R2; R3] Additional points. (1) Reproducibility: code/data will be released on GitHub if accepted. (2) GT contours in Figs. 3–4 are unlabeled and labels will be added. (3) Writing quality: will be carefully revised.

title: SWoMo: Neuro-Symbolic World Model for Cataract Surgery Simulation
abstract: Realistic surgical simulation plays a crucial role in training novice surgeons and in the development of autonomous agents. World models can scale such simulation environments to realistic and diverse procedures by predicting future patient states conditioned on current observations and surgical actions. However, current state-of-the-art approaches often fail to satisfy key criteria required for clinical applicability, including visual realism, physically grounded interactions, and the ability to simulate scenarios beyond the training distribution. Hence, we introduce SWoMo, a neuro-symbolic world model for cataract surgery simulation that decouples motion generation from visual realism. The symbolic component, consisting of a rule-based simulator and scene graph representations, models motion dynamics and tool-tissue interactions, while a diffusion model produces realistic visual appearance, including textures and tissue deformations. We propose an inverse pairing strategy that reconstructs real surgical videos in the simulator to obtain paired simulated and real videos, which are then used to train our video diffusion model for the reverse objective of sim-to-real translation. Our experiments show both qualitative and quantitative improvements over prior work. We demonstrate that our simulator further satisfies the key criteria, including generalisation to unseen interaction geometries, improvements in downstream phase detection, and unsupervised video style transfer. The code, data, and model weights are available at: .
subject_areas: Applications -> Digital Twins / Simulation / Synthetic Data
Machine Learning -> Synthetic Data / Data-centric AI
Surgery -> Surgical Skills, Workflow & Team Dynamics

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The authors propose a surgical simulation environment (world model) which decouples the simulation (performed in a 3D rendering engine) from the video-translation (diffusion model). A key part of the method is that paired image data is generated automatically from the input video, by segmenting the video data and reconstructing the same scene and motion in the simulation environment. The translation (diffusion) models are conditioned on input images and graph representations of the scene to control
Evaluation shows that novel co-occurance is handled well by the model, downstream tasks benefit from the generated data and style-transfer works well.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper is very well-written and clear. Though not all components can be explained in depth in the limited space, the core components are clearly described and the authors mention they want to release code.
I especially liked the clear definition of three key criteria in the introduction. If more space is allowed in the rebuttal, I could imagine that the conclusion could more specifically re-iterate how these are addressed by the method, especially criteria II (physical plausibility) is not explicitly addressed, I think (But is probably fullfilled because the simulation is derived from real data?).
reviews.text_weaknesses:
I don’t fully understand what the Symbolic Scene Graph adds, or why. If I understand correctly, the Graphs are created from the simulation, so they effectively encode the same information as the scene and its segmentation mask. This means that the “misalignents” and “conflicting signals” between the segmentation maps and the real images that are quoted as an issue would also exist in these graphs, and passing them to the network has no conceptual advantage? I understand why the misalignment between segmentation maps and real images causes issues during the training, but I believe the reasoning “by providing explicit structural relationships” doesn’t quite explain the solution - after all, the segmentation maps also contain this information (and, I would argue, in a more explicit manner than the graph). 
This may be difficult to do (because it’s a deep model), but maybe the authors can explain why they think this helps in practice? 
(Note: I didn’t follow reference [28], maybe this would have contained the explanation)
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
In “Video Diffusion Model with Graph-Image-Video Conditioning”, the terms “x_t” and “x_{t-1}” are used to, I think, represent the various noisy versions of an image. However, since x_{t} is aready “the image for frame t” above, I suggest to use a different parameter here. For example, “x_{t,\omega}” and “x_{t,\omega-1}”.
I don’t think I’ve ever seen the term “world model” used when the world representation is so explicit. Most work on world models I’ve seen have an implicit/hidden/deep model of the world rather than using a simulation. While I like the approach a lot and see the benefits of an explicit representation, maybe this distinction should be clarified more. In a way, the method could be considered a simulation with a video-to-video translation component, which are usually not framed as “world models”. Note: I think it might be enough to more explicitly state that, given the current state and past of the simulation, your full method only needs an tool movement, to fully predict the next state and output video frame?
At the end of the methods section, the description of the “second stage” is in large parts describing the ControlNet method. This is acknoledged correctly in the Introduction, but I think the citation should be repeated here for clarification, i. e. for readers who don’t know ControlNet.
Is the batching into 16 frames also used at inference? This might hinder usage in a real-time “training” setting.
I think Fig. 2 is not referenced in the text
I think a common problem with world models is that they only model what they’ve seen. The OOD test is interesting, but if this is for training: What happens if the user or agent makes a mistake? Do the CATARACT datasets contain “negative” examples, issues, complications?
“seqeunce” -> sequence
Because the authors identify border-regions between segmented structures as critical and difficult, perhaps the comparison via “bounding boxes” is not ideal. Why not use a pixel-level segmentation?
According to Table 1, SG2VID performs second-best in most metrics. From the introduction, I could not quite understand what the advantage of the current method is compared to SG2VID - is it mainly that the segmentation method is used directly?

I only have two issues with the paper: The graph-component may be motivated even better and the usage of the term “world-model” is (albeit probably correct) somewhat different from how it’s usually used in most state-of-the-art methods. Both issues could probably be fixed by adding a few sentence or slight rewording.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes SWoMo, a neuro-symbolic world model for cataract surgery simulation that explicitly decouples interaction dynamics from visual realism. The method combines a rule-based simulator and scene graph representation to model tool motion and tool–tissue interactions, while a diffusion model translates simulated sequences into realistic surgical videos. To bridge simulation and real data, the paper introduces an inverse pairing strategy that reconstructs real surgical videos in the simulator and uses the resulting paired data for sim-to-real video generation. The approach further demonstrates generalization to unseen interaction geometries and supports applications such as unsupervised video style transfer and downstream phase recognition improvement. Overall, the main contribution is a structured and controllable framework for interactive surgical simulation that integrates symbolic dynamics with high-fidelity video synthesis.
reviews.text_strengths:
Well-motivated neuro-symbolic design: The paper presents a clear and technically meaningful decomposition between symbolic dynamics and neural visual synthesis, which makes the framework more controllable and interpretable than purely generative approaches.
Strong practical relevance for surgical simulation: By combining a rule-based simulator with sim-to-real video generation, the method targets an important real-world problem and offers a plausible path toward more realistic and interactive surgical training environments.
Comprehensive empirical validation: The paper evaluates the method from multiple angles, including visual quality, conditioning fidelity, out-of-distribution generalization, style transfer, and downstream phase recognition, which strengthens the overall experimental support.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The world model claim is somewhat overstated: The core dynamics are largely governed by a rule-based simulator rather than being learned end-to-end, which makes the method closer to a neuro-symbolic simulation pipeline than a fully learned world model.
The downstream benefit is relatively limited: Although the method improves phase recognition performance, the gains are modest, especially on the larger dataset, which weakens the practical impact of the claimed utility for task model training.
The evaluation scope remains narrow: The experiments are restricted to cataract surgery and a limited set of phases, with no closed-loop policy learning or interactive control evaluation, so the broader usefulness of the proposed framework is not yet fully demonstrated.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a clear and well-motivated neuro-symbolic framework that combines structured simulation with high-fidelity video synthesis, and the overall idea is both technically interesting and relevant to surgical simulation. Its strengths lie in controllability, interpretability, and fairly broad empirical evaluation across synthesis quality, conditioning fidelity, OOD generalization, and downstream utility. However, the work also has notable limitations: the “world model” formulation is somewhat overstated given the rule-based dynamics, the downstream gains are modest, and the evaluation remains limited to a narrow surgical setting without closed-loop decision-making experiments. Overall, despite these weaknesses, I think the paper offers sufficient novelty and practical value to merit acceptance.

reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes SWoMo, a neuro-symbolic world model for cataract surgery simulation that decouples interaction dynamics from visual appearance. It uses an inverse pairing strategy to generate paired sim-real data, which can better generalize to unseen surgical scenes.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The key innovation of decomposing the motion/geometry and visual appearance is interesting, compared with previous legacy of generative modelling that lacks physical grounding.
2, The experiments and evaluation are extensive and well-executed. This work has multiple evaluation metrics, comprehensive ablation studies and downstream task (phase recognition) validation.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The utilization of rule-based simulator may be limited for physical realism in complex tissue deformation or force interactions. As indicated by PhysWorld [34], modelling deformable physics is a better option in this scenario.
2.Lack of performance comparison of other strong baseline, including physWorld [34] that models deformable objects and Surgical-CD [32] that achieve sim-to-real translation via diffusion models.
3.This work lacks novelty in algorithm. It is more of a combination of prior works (including SG2VID, PhysWorld, Surgical-CD), with application on cataract surgery. It also relies on many preprocessing modules, for example, the segmentation model, motion module, SAM2 for tool masks, etc. Such complicated framework increase the probability of error accumulation and limited robustness.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a coherent system that addresses an important gap in surgical simulation. However, the score is not high because the core novelty is incremental at the algorithm level.
