meta_reviews.text:
This paper introduces a model for cataract surgery simulation that combines a rule-based simulator and a scene-graph representation with a video diffusion model.
Reviewers consistently praise the well-motivated neuro-symbolic design, the clarity of writing, the strong practical relevance to surgical training, and the comprehensive empirical validation.
Concerns include the somewhat overstated framing as a true world model given the rule-based core, modest downstream gains, evaluation confined to a single surgical domain, missing comparisons to closely related prior work, and unclear added value of the symbolic scene graph beyond segmentation maps.
Reviews are consistent in supporting acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We would like to sincerely thank all the reviewers for their positive comments. We greatly appreciate your recognition of SWoMo’s attempt to address the three key requirements for practically relevant surgical world models: high visual realism, physically grounded interactions, and dynamic world representations that generalize beyond the training distribution, which current state-of-the-art methods do not jointly address. We also appreciate your recognition of the motivation behind our neuro-symbolic design, which decomposes symbolic dynamics from neural visual synthesis. Furthermore, we sincerely thank the reviewers for acknowledging our effort on the extensive empirical validation. We have addressed the main comments below and will gladly incorporate all suggested revisions into the final manuscript.
(R1) Added value of symbolic scene graph (SG): As shown by the ablation in Table 1 (SWoMo-✗SG), the inclusion of SGs leads to significant improvements in both visual fidelity (up to 56.6% reduction in FVD and 43.4% reduction in FID) and conditional adherence (up to 38.5% increase in BB IoU and 39.2% increase in F1). However, we agree that the explanation for the improvements introduced by the SG is currently brief, and we will clarify this further in the final manuscript. The SG is constructed such that each node represents a connected component from the segmentation map and contains only high-level information about its component, including centroid, spatial spreading, average depth, and average optical flow within the region. As a result, the SG abstracts away local pixel-level misalignments between the segmentation and video frames, especially near tool-tissue boundaries where segmentation-only conditioning can introduce smoothing artifacts and reduce synthesis quality. Since small boundary shifts or noisy pixels have limited effect on component-level attributes such as centroid, spreading, average depth and flow, the SG extracted from the predicted segmentation can remain closer to the real scene structure and the true SG, despite local segmentation errors. By incorporating SG conditioning, the model is also not constrained to strictly follow potentially misaligned pixel-level segmentation boundaries. Instead, the SG provides higher-level structural guidance, giving the generator flexibility to decide where the visual boundary should realistically appear based on the image context, leading to sharper and more coherent tool-tissue interactions.
(R2) Framing as a true world model: We thank R1 for already helping us to highlight that our approach is still considered as a world model, but with a more explicit world representation. As R1 noted, most existing world models rely on implicit or latent representations, whereas our approach explicitly models scene dynamics, which is particularly important for physically grounded interactions and improved generalisation beyond the training distribution, where purely implicit world models will struggle. In particular, given the current simulation state together with the action input, SWoMo still predicts the next state and generates the corresponding future video frame. We will clarify this distinction more clearly in the manuscript.
(R3) Comparison to prior work: We have extensively benchmarked SWoMo against multiple baselines with publicly available implementations. The baselines mentioned by R3, such as PhysWorld and Surgical-CD, unfortunately, either do not provide publicly available code or are image-based generative models designed for unpaired datasets.

title: SymmDiff: Symmetry-Guided Diffusion for Fracture Localization in Pelvic Radiographs
abstract: Unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) offers a promising direction for fracture analysis where abnormal annotations are scarce, yet pelvic X-ray fracture detection remains exceptionally challenging due to overlapping anatomy, projection artifacts, and the inherently asymmetric presentation of fracture patterns. We introduce SymmDiff, a symmetry-aware diffusion framework that embeds contralateral anatomical consistency directly into the generative correction process, mirroring the clinical practice of bilateral comparison. By pairing anatomically corresponding left–right regions and enforcing symmetry-consistent reconstruction during diffusion, SymmDiff generates a normal-corrected radiograph that selectively suppresses fracture-induced asymmetries while preserving global anatomical structure, enabling precise fracture localization through residual discrepancies between the input image and its symmetry-corrected counterpart. Extensive evaluations on pelvic radiographs spanning subtle to severe fractures show that SymmDiff consistently outperforms existing anomaly-detection baselines, highlighting the effectiveness of symmetry-guided generative modeling for reliable fracture localization in clinical imaging. Code is available at https://itsabdulrahman.github.io/symmdiff.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: In this paper, the authors introduce a novel symmetry-guided diffusion model for fracture localization in pelvic radiographs. Specifically, the method embeds contralateral anatomical information into the model to detect fractures.
reviews.text_strengths: The proposed method is novel. The idea of using symmetry-corrected generated images to identify fracture locations is interesting.
reviews.text_weaknesses: While the proposed method achieves good performance compared with other state-of-the-art generative models, it would be better if the authors also compared it with commonly used detection methods, such as YOLO. Fracture detection may not necessarily require generative models like DDPM for this task. In addition, the paper lacks evaluation metrics for image quality, such as the FID score. It would also be beneficial to include radiologists to assess the quality of the generated images.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a novel and interesting approach by introducing a symmetry-guided diffusion model for fracture localization in pelvic radiographs. The idea of leveraging contralateral anatomical symmetry and using symmetry-corrected generated images to highlight fracture regions is both intuitive and technically interesting. This formulation provides a new perspective on incorporating anatomical priors into generative modeling for medical imaging tasks, which could inspire further research in this direction.
The experimental results demonstrate competitive performance compared to other state-of-the-art generative models, suggesting that the proposed approach is effective for the task. Despite some limitations—such as the lack of comparison with standard detection methods (e.g., YOLO), absence of image quality metrics like FID, and missing human expert evaluation—the core idea is novel and shows clear potential impact.
Overall, while the experimental validation could be strengthened, the methodological contribution and innovation justify a weak accept, as the work is likely to stimulate further research and improvements in symmetry-aware medical image analysis.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces a generative framework for unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) in pelvic X-rays. It addresses the difficulty of identifying fractures amidst complex overlapping anatomy and projection artifacts by mimicking the clinical practice of side-to-side comparison. The model uses a symmetry-conditioned latent diffusion process that establishes a patient-specific representation of normal anatomy through contralateral correspondence.
reviews.text_strengths: The method is clinically relevent and the Symmetry-Diffusion appoarch is innovative. By embedding contralateral consistency directly into the denoising process, the model suppresses asymmetries caused by normal anatomical variation or projection tilt.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.While the pelvis is generally symmetric, true biological asymmetry and variations in patient positioning (tilt/rotation) during X-ray acquisition are common. Although the authors suggest that latent encoding provides robustness to ‘minor projection mismatch’, the paper would benefit from a more detailed analysis or a ‘stress test’ showing how the model performs under significant pelvic tilt or in patients with pre-existing non-fracture asymmetries.
2.A primary concern for any symmetry-guided model is the occurrence of bilateral fractures. If both sides of the pelvis are fractured, the ‘structural prior’ from the contralateral side may itself be abnormal. While the authors mention using identity constraints and population-level atlases as future work, the current manuscript lacks a clear demonstration of how the model fails or adapts when symmetry is violated on both sides simultaneously.
3.The qualitative results show some fractures that appear relatively obvious visually. To better justify the necessity of this complex generative framework, the authors may provide a more focused evaluation on ‘subtle’ or ‘occult’ fractures where standard radiological interpretation often fails. Quantifying performance specifically on these ‘difficult’ cases would more clearly highlight the clinical value of the SymmDiff approach.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The framework relies heavily on an assumption of anatomical symmetry, which may fail in cases of bilateral fractures or significant physiological asymmetry. Furthermore, while the method performs well on “normal-to-normal” completion, its effectiveness in correcting actual severe clinical deformities remains unproven. The reliance on a “black box” transformer also lacks the interpretability of traditional statistical models, and the current evaluation lacks a comparison against a version of itself guided by a general healthy atlas rather than patient-specific symmetry, making it difficult to fully isolate the unique value of the symmetry-inductive bias.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper introduces SymmDiff, a symmetry-guided latent diffusion framework for unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) in pelvic radiographs. The core idea is to embed contralateral anatomical consistency directly into the reverse diffusion process, mirroring the clinical practice of bilateral comparison. The input image and its horizontally flipped counterpart are encoded into a shared latent space via a fine-tuned VAE. During inference, an ROI mask derived from bilateral discrepancy identifies suspicious regions, a latent swap initializes those regions toward the contralateral reference, and symmetry-conditioned DDIM denoising reconstructs a pseudo-healthy image with reverse updates constrained to the ROI. Anomalies are localized through a multi-scale fusion of pixel, gradient, perceptual, and latent residuals between the input and reconstruction. Evaluation on a single-center pelvic X-ray dataset (1,268 normal training cases, 534 abnormal test cases) shows consistent improvements over four diffusion-based UAD baselines at both image and pixel levels, and ablations demonstrate that each component contributes to performance.
The overall method appears innovative; however, the authors do not describe in sufficient detail several parts of the proposed architecture that are essential for reproducing the results, such as the type of VAE encoder used and the architecture of the U-Net network.
reviews.text_strengths:
The central methodological idea — conditioning each reverse diffusion step on a patient-specific contralateral reference — is novel within the diffusion-based UAD literature. Prior methods either treat denoising as anatomy-agnostic or apply bilateral comparison post-hoc or in discriminative settings. Embedding symmetry into the reverse trajectory dynamics is a genuinely new contribution that is well-motivated by established clinical reading practice for pelvic radiographs.
The clinical rationale is strong. The pelvis is one of the clearest anatomical cases for bilateral comparison, and the paper connects this practice to the technical design in a coherent way. The choice of application domain is not arbitrary — it is one where the proposed inductive bias is most naturally justified.
The ablation study is thorough and informative. Five ablations each isolate a specific component, and all show consistent degradation. Importantly, the removal of symmetry conditioning causes the largest performance drop, which confirms that the core mechanism is driving the results rather than ancillary design choices. This is the most convincing evidence in the paper.
The ROI-constrained reverse diffusion (Eq. 9) is cleanly formulated with a verifiable identity preservation property outside the ROI. This targeted correction strategy is a sensible design choice that reduces the risk of global structural drift during reconstruction, addressing a known failure mode of diffusion-based UAD.
The performance gains over the strongest baseline (THOR) are substantial, particularly at the pixel level (AUPRC 36.2 –> 43.9, F1max 37.2 –> 42.7), suggesting the method provides meaningfully better localization rather than marginal improvement.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The comparison set is narrow and limited exclusively to diffusion-based UAD methods. There is no comparison with feature-based anomaly detection approaches such as PatchCore, which is cited (ref [4]) but not benchmarked. More critically, there is no comparison with a simpler symmetry baseline — for instance, left-right subtraction with alignment and thresholding. Without this, it is impossible to disentangle how much of the performance gain comes from the diffusion framework versus the symmetry prior itself. This is a significant omission that weakens the empirical contribution.
The evaluation is conducted on a single anonymized dataset from one institution with no external validation. Pelvic radiographs vary considerably across institutions due to equipment, positioning protocols, and patient demographics. The symmetry assumption can degrade under oblique projections, rotated patients, or bilateral pathology. The authors acknowledge cross-site generalization as future work, but the absence of any robustness analysis on these factors limits confidence in the method’s generalizability. There is no stratification of results by fracture severity, location, or type. With 534 abnormal cases, meaningful subgroup analysis is feasible. This matters because the clinical value proposition differs substantially for subtle versus severe fractures — if the aggregate numbers are driven primarily by severe cases that radiologists would not miss, the practical utility is limited. Five qualitative examples do not substitute for systematic analysis.
The latent swap claim (Eq. 8) rests on an unstated assumption that the contralateral latent is closer to the true normal latent than the original input within ROI regions. This is plausible for unilateral fractures but could fail for bilateral pathology, symmetric normal variants, or significant projection asymmetry. The paper does not acknowledge or bound this assumption.
No confidence intervals, standard deviations, or statistical significance tests are reported for results. Given the dataset size, some estimate of variance would strengthen the claims considerably.
The authors do not describe in sufficient detail several architectural components that are critical for reproducibility. Specifically, the type of VAE encoder and the architecture of the U-Net network are not specified, making it challenging to independently reimplement the method even with access to the described training hyperparameters.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The most impactful improvement would be the inclusion of non-diffusion baselines. A feature-based method such as PatchCore and a simple symmetry-difference baseline would substantially strengthen the evaluation by clarifying what the diffusion framework contributes beyond the symmetry prior. This is not a request for additional experiments, but rather an observation about what would make the empirical story complete.
A stratified analysis by fracture severity would significantly strengthen the clinical relevance argument. Even a coarse split into minor, moderate, and severe categories with per-group metrics would help readers assess where the method adds value.
The bilateral pathology case deserves more than a passing mention in the conclusion. Since the entire framework rests on the assumption that the contralateral side provides a reliable normal reference, the failure mode when both sides are abnormal is fundamental. Some analysis or at least explicit discussion of how the method behaves in this scenario would be valuable.

The paper presents a well-motivated and technically coherent idea — embedding pelvic symmetry directly into the reverse diffusion process — and the ablation study provides credible evidence that this mechanism is the primary driver of performance. The gains over the strongest diffusion-based baseline are non-trivial, and the clinical framing is appropriate.
However, several issues, collectively, prevent a higher score. The empirical evaluation is narrow: the absence of non-diffusion baselines (e.g., PatchCore) and, more critically, the absence of a simple symmetry-difference baseline make it difficult to isolate the contribution of the diffusion framework from that of the symmetry prior alone. The single-center evaluation without external validation or robustness analysis limits confidence in generalisability. The lack of subgroup analysis by fracture severity leaves the clinical utility of the method unclear. No statistical measures of uncertainty are reported for the results given.
Reproducibility appears to be an issue. The VAE encoder type and U-Net architecture — both fundamental to the proposed framework — are not specified. The ROI scoring function, binarization threshold, fusion weights, and patch masking details are either vague or absent. This is a key shortcoming for a methods contribution, and it is the primary factor limiting the score. Much of this may be addressed by the authors’ planned code release, but is difficult to understand if this is true from the paper alone.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text: All three reviewers recommend weak accept. The core idea of embedding contralateral symmetry directly into the reverse diffusion trajectory is clinically well-motivated and technically novel within the diffusion-based UAD literature, and the ablation credibly demonstrates that symmetry conditioning is the primary performance driver. The authors should address in the final version the absence of a simple left-right subtraction baseline and the missing architecture details, which are critical for reproducibility.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and AC for their insightful feedback and for recognizing the novelty of embedding contralateral consistency directly into the diffusion trajectory. Below we address the major concerns raised by the reviewers.
Choice of baselines (R1, R3): SymmDiff is designed for unsupervised anomaly Detection (UAD), motivated by the scarcity of fine-grained fracture annotations and the difficulty of predefining fracture morphologies. Supervised detectors such as YOLO require annotated abnormal cases for training and therefore address a different setting from the proposed UAD formulation. We agree that PatchCore [4] is a strong feature-memory method. Our current evaluation focused on reconstruction-based diffusion methods to isolate the contribution of symmetry-guided correction within a comparable paradigm, as PatchCore takes a fundamentally different approach, scoring anomalies against a memory bank of normal patches rather than via reconstruction discrepancy. A thorough cross-paradigm comparison would meaningfully complement our evaluation and is an important direction we plan to pursue.
Contribution of symmetry vs. diffusion (R3): We agree that simple left-right difference is an important conceptual baseline. The submitted ablations help isolate this point. The ROI is derived from bilateral discrepancy, but removing ROI-constrained denoising reduces performance (pixel AUROC 83.2 vs. 88.4), indicating that raw symmetry discrepancy alone is insufficient. Conversely, removing symmetry conditioning degrades the model toward an anatomy-agnostic diffusion baseline (79.9 vs. 76.5), showing that the improvement comes from embedding the contralateral prior into the reverse trajectory, not merely from using diffusion. Direct subtraction compares sides; SymmDiff uses the contralateral side to synthesize a pseudo-healthy correction while preserving non-ROI anatomy.
Robustness to symmetry violations (R2, R3): Two failure modes were raised: projection tilt and bilateral fractures. The method does not assume perfect pixel-wise symmetry. The use of latent space rather than pixel space abstracts local textures into higher level features, which improves robustness to minor projection tilt and rotation. For bilateral fractures, the ROI gating with identity constraints (Eq. 9) provides a stabilizing bias: regions outside the ROI mask remain unchanged, so when both sides are abnormal the global anatomy is preserved rather than corrupted by a degraded contralateral prior. Population level healthy atlases could serve as a secondary anchor for bilateral fracture cases, which is a key area for future work.
Reproducibility (R3): The VAE is the pre-trained perceptual-compression autoencoder from [12], trained with a perceptual loss, patch-based adversarial objective, and KL regularization, with a down sampling factor of 8, we fine-tune it on pelvic radiographs. The denoiser is an attention U-Net with timestep embedding and a squared-cosine-beta noise schedule, with z_sym incorporated via channel-wise concatenation as described in Sec. 3.2.Configuration files and training scripts will be released with the code.

title: Synergistic Information Disentanglement for Omni-Modal Slide Representation Learning in Computational Pathology
abstract: In computational pathology (CPath), developing omni-modal self-supervised learning (SSL) models that integrate histology, genomics, and clinical reports enables transferable representation learning for whole slide images (WSIs). Existing approaches implicitly force heterogeneous modalities into a uniform latent space by contrastive alignment, causing modality collapse where unique, synergistic diagnostic signals (termed as Φ) are discarded in favor of trivial redundancy. We hypothesize that the strongest task-agnostic SSL training signal stems from distilling the synergistic interactions over merely aligning shared redundancy. To this end, we introduce Φ-OMNI, a synergistic information disentanglement framework grounded in Partial Information Decomposition (PID) theory for slide representation learning. Unlike standard contrastive approaches, Φ-OMNI employs a Synergistic Information Bottleneck (SIB) regulated by the proposed ΦID objective, which explicitly suppresses marginal redundancy while maximizing irreducible synergy, thereby distilling high-order cross-modal interactions. Following pretraining on breast (n=1031) and lung (n=919) cohorts, Φ-OMNI demonstrates superior few-shot performance across five independent external datasets spanning eight tasks compared to supervised and SSL baselines. Source code is available.
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers
Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper addresses an important limitation in multimodal pathology pretraining: existing methods often rely on cross-modal alignment in a way that may wash out complementary, modality-specific information. To tackle this, the authors propose \Phi-Omni, an omni-modal self-supervised framework that uses histology, transcriptomics, and pathology reports during pretraining, but only needs WSI input at test time. The main idea is to replace redundancy-driven alignment with a synergy-oriented objective, implemented through a Synergistic Information Bottleneck (SIB) and a \PhiID loss inspired by Partial Information Decomposition. The method is evaluated on breast and lung cohorts and obtains strong few-shot transfer results across subtyping and mutation prediction tasks against MIL baselines and recent pathology foundation models.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper tackles a genuinely important problem for multimodal pathology pretraining, and the deployment setup is practical since inference can still be unimodal. 
2.The comparison study is reasonably solid, including both standard MIL baselines and several recent pathology foundation models. The gains are also fairly consistent across the few-shot settings. 
3.The ablation studies are helpful and make it easier to see that both the architectural choices and the full loss design matter.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The pathology report pipeline deserves a more careful leakage analysis. Even if explicit diagnostic labels are removed, reports can still contain subtype-related wording, biomarker mentions, or other highly label-proximal cues.

reviews.text_contribution: In this paper, the authors proposed a synergistic information disentanglement framework grounded in Partial Information Decomposition theory for slide representation learning. The proposed model includes a Synergistic Information Bottleneck (SIB) regulated via the designed objective, which minimizing redundancy while maximizing synergy, thereby distilling high-order cross-modality interactions.
reviews.text_strengths:
(1) The manuscript is clearly articulated and accessible. The figures and visualizations are both high-quality and illustrative. Furthermore, the study is underpinned by a thorough review of existing literature and a well-justified rationale for the proposed approach.
(2) The authors perform extensive benchmark few-shot learning experiments on multiple cancer cohorts; the results validate its superiority for downstream analysis in comparison with an excellent choice of state-of-the-art supervised and self-supervised baselines. Detailed ablation studies are well-conducted for demonstrating the effect of each module and strategy design in the proposed method.
(3) The design of maximizing the synergistic information of multimodal representation by mutual information is quite interesting, such a design is transferable to multiple scenarios in multimodal representation alignment and fusion.
(4) The methodology is presented with clarity and appears reproducible. A significant strength of this work is the exclusive use of public datasets for experimental validation.
reviews.text_weaknesses: I have identified no significant weaknesses in this work. However, I have provided several comments regarding the literature review, methodology details, and experimental settings in (12) to help improve the paper’s quality.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
(1) The literature review is comprehensive, covering most state-of-the-art methods like TANGLE, MADELEINE, and MIRROR. However, the recent work on [1,2,3] might provide additional context. The authors are encouraged to briefly discuss how Φ-Omni differs from these specific theoretical perspectives in the introduction.
(2) The composite loss function defined in Section 2.4 introduces a hyperparameter γ to balance the contrastive alignment and the synergistic disentanglement. While the chosen value of γ=0.2 yields strong results, the manuscript would benefit from a brief discussion or citation regarding the selection strategy for this weight. For instance, was it tuned based on a specific validation set, or does it follow the common practice from similar works? A short explanation would enhance the reproducibility of the method.
(3) The Section 2.1 text encoding pipeline mentions an ‘OCR-based pipeline with text cleaning.’ For the sake of completeness and reproducibility, it would be helpful if the authors could briefly describe the specific rules used for the ‘text cleaning’ step.
[1] Ming Y Lu et al. A visual-language foundation model for computational pathology [J]. Nature Medicine, 2024.[2] Tristan Lazard et al. Giga-SSL: Self-supervised learning for gigapixel images [C]. CVPR, 2023.[3] Yilan Zhang et al. Prototypical information bottlenecking and disentangling for multimodal cancer survival prediction, ICLR, 2024.

The manuscript demonstrates exceptional quality and clarity. Each component of the proposed framework is well-justified and has been empirically validated to enhance multimodal data alignment through self-supervised learning, as evidenced by extensive experiments on public datasets.

reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes Φ-Omni, a self-supervised learning framework for omni-modal WSI representation learning in computational pathology. The central contribution is a paradigm shift in multimodal pretraining, moving away from redundancy-driven contrastive alignment toward synergistic information disentanglement. Grounded in PID theory, the authors decompose the mutual information between the fused representation and the three modalities into three atoms: Redundancy, Uniqueness, and Synergy. Building on this decomposition, the author introduced the SIB module and GCP with ΦID objective. The authors validate Φ-Omni across eight diagnostic tasks on five public independent cohorts, demonstrating superior few-shot generalizabillity over SOTA supervised MIL and SSL baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Clear motivation: The paper rightly points out that standard contrastive learning forces different modalities together, which keeps redundant info but loses complementary signals. Using PID theory makes perfect clinical sense, since diagnosis relies on how modalities combine, not just what they share.
2.Most slide-level SSL papers only do two modalities. This paper jointly integrates WSI, RNA-seq, and pathology reports.
3.The experimental setup strictly follows the TANGLE (k-shot linear probing, 10 random seeds, macro-AUC). The evaluation spans 8 tasks across 5 external cohorts, and the performance is robust.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Mirror[1] also uses a similar idea to fix modality collapse. This paper needs to explain exactly why your PID approach is fundamentally better and add an experimental comparison with Mirror.
[1] Wang, T., Fan, J., Zhang, D., Liu, D., Xia, Y., Huang, H., Cai, W.: Mirror: Multi-modal pathological self-supervised representation learning via modality alignment and retention. arXiv preprint arXiv:2503.00374 (2025)
2.Training on around 2,000 TCGA slides is small compared to recent foundation models. Also, testing TCGA-trained models on CPTAC often suffers from site-specific biases.
3.Lack of ablation, please add Image+Gene only and Image+Text only to isolate the contribution of text reports.

N/A

The main strength of this work is bringing PID into multimodal representation learning for computational pathology. However, this work lack of comparasion from Mirror and the pretaining datastets are small and limited in TCGA. My current recommendation is Weak Accept.

meta_reviews.text: he reviewers are overall positive about this submission, which proposes a synergistic information disentanglement framework for omni-modal slide representation learning using WSI, transcriptomics, and pathology reports during pretraining while requiring only WSI at inference. The work addresses an important problem in multimodal computational pathology, is clearly presented, and shows strong few-shot performance across multiple cancer cohorts with useful ablation studies and comparisons to several MIL and pathology foundation model baselines. The main remaining concerns are the need for a more careful leakage analysis of pathology reports, clearer positioning and ideally comparison against the closely related MIRROR method, additional modality-combination ablations such as Image+Gene and Image+Text, and more details on text cleaning and hyperparameter selection. Overall, despite these limitations, the methodological idea is interesting, the experimental evidence is reasonably strong, and the paper is likely to make a valuable contribution if the authors adequately address these issues in the final version.

title: Synergistic Perception-Reasoning Governance: Grounding Medical MLLMs with Verifiable Anatomical Evidence
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) show strong promise for clinical VQA and radiology report generation, yet inference-time hallucinations still undermine trustworthy use: models can produce fluent conclusions that conflict with imaging evidence. Existing mitigation strategies typically rely on additional training, external retrieval/knowledge bases, or multi-stage post-hoc verification, which increases cost and pipeline complexity and often generalizes poorly across models and tasks. To address this, we propose a holistic, training-free evidence-injection framework that systematically mitigates hallucinations through dual-side evidence injection. By leveraging ROI priors acquired using MedSAM in our implementation, we recalibrate the visual perception trajectory via ROI-guided activation modulation while anchoring the textual reasoning trajectory by mapping anatomical coordinates into discrete semantic tokens as verifiable external memory. Then we introduce a task-aware dynamic router to select modality-specific interventions based on task semantics, balancing perceptual grounding and linguistic fluency. We conduct systematic evaluations on 2 tasks and 5 datasets using LLaVA-1.5-7B, LLaVA-Med-1.5-7B, Qwen3-VL-8B/32B, and InternVL-3.5-8B/38B. Controlled ablations and visualizations further validate the framework, which consistently outperforms baselines across medical benchmarks, improving close-ended accuracy by up to ~6%↑ and reducing open-ended hallucinations by ~35%↓. The code has been made available on GitHub: https://github.com/Henry991115/SPRG.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Algorithmic Fairness / Safety / Regulation

Is such a categorization reasonable? If a question involves multiple categories, which evidence-injection strategy should be used?
Furthermore, as shown in Table 1, errors made by the classifier in the dynamic router may lead to performance that is even worse than the original MLLMs. However, the authors do not provide any evaluation of the classifier’s performance.
3.Organizing the bounding boxes into structured descriptions may introduce redundancy. Compared to directly injecting labels and bounding boxes into the prompt, structured descriptions result in a longer context.
4.The author does not address how the accuracy of the mask/bbox affects both text and vision-side. According to the qualitative analysis presented in the paper, vision-side injection directly influences the model’s attention, and inaccurate masks may lead to more hallucinations. However, the authors neither conduct experiments to evaluate mask accuracy nor discuss how it impacts the experimental results.

a) Unclear of the source of the initial bounding box(bbox) for medSAM. As we known, MedSAM is a promptable segmentation model that requires the input bboxes. But the paper not mentioned that where these bboxes came from during inference time. Since the “training-free” claim will be substantially weakened if the bounding box need the manually annotated or provided by other detection network. 
b) Missing of the training detailed of question classifier. The Task-aware Router rely on the classifier h(q) but the paper did not mention how to train the question classifier. If the supervised data is need, that will be conflict to the claim of “Training-free” 
c) The methodological novelty is moderate. As mentioned in paper, there are many prior work such as VCD, DoLa, OPERA, AVISC, DAMRO, PAI, and M3ID has already explored for the inference-time hallucination. Relative to these works, the present paper more like a medical-domain integration.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
I encourage the authors to clearly explain the source of the candidate bounding boxes and provide more detail on the task-aware router in the rebuttal.

It is well-motivated and evaluates the approach across comprehensive models, datasets, and task settings with reasonably consistent positive gains. meta_reviews.text:
Paper summary: This paper introduces a training-free framework to address visual misinterpretation hallucinations in medical MLLMs. The authors conducted a comprehensive evaluation across 6 MLLMs and 5 datasets, with reported consistent improvement over diverse baselines.
Strengths The reviewers identified several strengths, including:
The plug-and-play design of the proposed method is a good advantage, which has real deployment value.
The reasonable interpretability of the method.
Comprehensive evaluation and consistent improvement over diverse prior baselines.
Weaknesses: The main concerns raised by reviewers include: My major concern is the lack of clarity about how ROI labels are obtained, and the missing training details of the question classifier. The paper also lacks detailed descriptions of the experimental settings, such as the specific architecture of the task-aware dynamic router.
Review Reconciliation: Reviewer opinions are largely consistent regarding the contributions of this work.
Decision: After considering the reviews and manuscript, I believe the paper is technically sound, addresses an important problem in addressing visual misinterpretation hallucinations in medical MLLMs, and presents a meaningful contribution beyond existing work. The empirical validation is convincing. I therefore recommend Provisional Accept.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the Area Chair (AC) for the recommendation and for recognizing that our work is technically rigorous, addresses visual misinterpretation hallucinations in medical MLLMs, makes meaningful contributions beyond prior studies, and provides convincing empirical validation. We also thank R2, R3, and R4 for their feedback. We address the main concerns below.
(1) R3&R4 - ROI/bbox source and MedSAM. We apologize for the unclear ROI acquisition description. Our contribution is not a new ROI proposal or detection algorithm, but an evidence-injection mechanism using reliable anatomical ROI evidence to mitigate visual misinterpretation hallucinations without updating MLLM parameters. The framework is not tied to MedSAM; MedSAM is only one medium for acquiring ROI masks, and any reliable ROI source, such as annotations, detectors, segmentation models, or other promptable models, can be incorporated.
(2) R2&R4 - Router and training-free claim. The router is not a separately trained classifier. We use a zero-shot LLM-based router with a fixed classification prompt to map each question into four categories. It trains no router parameters and does not update the medical MLLM backbone; thus, the framework remains training-free with respect to the medical MLLM. Routing accuracies were 91.25% for GPT-4o, 95.54% for GPT-5, 89.67% for Qwen3-0.6B, and 93.64% for Qwen3-1.7B.
(3) R2 - Multi-attribute questions and routing issues. We acknowledge that clinical questions may involve multiple attributes; e.g., “whether the left atrium is enlarged” involves both localization and measurement. The current router selects the intervention according to the dominant semantic risk; finer multi-label routing is future work. Routing errors may select a suboptimal intervention and partly explain category-level drops. However, the router does not generate the final answer; it only selects the evidence-injection strategy, so errors mainly affect the intervention path rather than directly injecting incorrect answers.
(4) R2&R3 - Inaccurate masks/bboxes. ROI evidence does not provide diagnostic conclusions or finding labels. It only provides approximate anatomical location and region extent, indicating “where the model should pay more attention,” rather than “what answer the model should produce.” The final judgment is still made by the MLLM based on the original image, question, and vision-language reasoning. Severely inaccurate ROIs may weaken grounding or introduce misleading visual priors. However, most ROI evidence obtained in our experiments is reasonably accurate; under such conditions, our evidence-injection method is robust and consistently reduces visual misinterpretation hallucinations.
(5) R2 - Structured ROI description. The structured ROI description is not simply used to lengthen the prompt. It converts raw coordinates into semantically interpretable anatomical evidence, including anatomical label, spatial location, bbox extent, and relative area. Compared with raw coordinates alone, this representation is better aligned with the MLLM language interface.
(6) R4 - Novelty. Prior works have studied inference-time hallucination mitigation from decoding, contrastive decoding, or attention calibration perspectives. Our novelty lies in using ROI-level verifiable anatomical evidence as a grounding anchor to jointly constrain visual perception and textual reasoning in medical MLLMs. Thus, our contribution is coordinated visual-perceptual and text-reasoning guidance for medical visual misinterpretation hallucinations, rather than another generic decoding heuristic.
(7) R3 - Scope and reproducibility. We chose radiology tasks because visual misinterpretation hallucinations are clinically important and quantitatively evaluable. In principle, the framework is not limited to radiology, as it only requires reliable anatomical ROI evidence; validation on other modalities remains future work. The code is released on GitHub: https://github.com/Henry991115/SPRG.

title: SynHydro: Biomechanics-Driven Domain Randomization for Hydrocephalus-Agnostic, Generalizable Tissue-Ventricle Segmentation Across Age, Modality, and Resolution
abstract: Early diagnosis and quantitative assessment of pediatric hydrocephalus are critical, yet automated segmentation remains challenging due to severe anatomical deformation and substantial appearance variation across early neurodevelopment, imaging modalities, and resolutions. Current deep learning approaches are often limited to ventricle-only segmentation and tailored to specific acquisition protocols, hindering their clinical utility for comprehensive joint tissue analysis and longitudinal evaluation. We propose SynHydro, a novel biomechanics-driven simulation and domain-randomized augmentation framework. SynHydro synthesizes diverse hydrocephalus anatomies from readily available healthy tissue labels and generates corresponding MRIs with randomized image characteristics. This creates a large-scale, synthetic training dataset encompassing a wide spectrum of disease severity, MRI contrast, noise, resolution, and artifacts for joint tissue-ventricle segmentation. Extensive experiments on in-house and public datasets demonstrate that a segmentation model trained exclusively on this pure synthetic data achieves performance comparable to models trained with real hydrocephalus annotations. More importantly, SynHydro-trained models exhibit superior cross-modality and cross-resolution robustness, and reliably preserve pre-/post-operative volumetric trends. By eliminating the dependency on labor-intensive pathological annotations, SynHydro provides a powerful and practical solution for building robust, generalizable segmentation tools for pediatric hydrocephalus monitoring across the clinical imaging landscape.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Synthetic Data / Data-centric AI

reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a three stage method for robust and accurate pediatric image segmentation with hydrocephalus, using only healthy images. The method comprises of three stages: (1) creation of realistic hydrocephalus maps with bio mechanical deformations from healthy label maps, (2) creation of images with domain randomization, and (3) training a segmentation model using both normal and the created synthetic dataset. The paper claims to segment hydrocephalus images robustly among different modalities, ages and resolutions.
reviews.text_strengths:
-The paper presents a simple method to utilize healthy images to create a model that is robust to large anomalies in the brain. 
-The writing is clear and understandable.
-The idea of synthesizing images with hydrocephalus anatomy with the described bio mechanical driven method is novel, and performing well (Dice score of ~0.85) to segment white matter, gray matter and ventricles in pediatric T1w MRI.
-
reviews.text_weaknesses:
“Real-Augmented: Trained on 1400 augmented data synthesized from all available training labels (both longitudinal and control), representing a strong data-augmentation baseline with real pathological labels”, “Real-Augmented achieves the best performance on T1w, serving as an approximate upper bound” The usage of baseline and upper bound interchangeably is confusing. Could they consider changing this description?
What is the reason for selecting only T1w sequences for testing quantitatively? The results lack the cross modality segmentation robustness.
In datasets, the authors mention they have 132 longitudinal sessions and 131 control scans. Then in the implementation section, they mention having 125 longitudinal and 47 control 3D images. How did they select these subjects for annotating, is it random?
HyKid dataset has ground truth segmentations available for gray matter, white matter, cerebrospinal fluid, the choroid plexus, and the lateral ventricles. What do the authors imply when they say “ground-truth labels consistent with the purpose of this study is not available” ?
Both the qualitative and quantitative results show similar performance to the “Real augmented” case. The augmentations seem to capture modality differences & the resolution difference and seem to be useful looking at the qualitative improvement from real paired to real augmented. This generalization raises the question of applying augmentations to the baseline (control only) model. I believe the setting with strong spatial and intensity augmentation to control set, without explicitly creating the hydrocephalus images should be included in the results as well for a fair comparison.
The results lack comparisons with segmentation methods similarly trained with domain randomization and have shown good performance over various anatomical changes [1,2]. The authors have cited the first paper yet have not included any results. I believe it would be useful to compare with the existing methods, as they are known to not fail in cases of such large enlargement of ventricles (see the results in a similar work dealing with abnormalities [3]).
The title and the motivation suggests that the method is age, modality and resolution. I do not think the results are supportive of this claim. It would be useful to show results on different modalities, ages and resolutions separately to be able to claim this. Figure 3 if helpful for understanding the consistency over modalities yet it just shows “a” representative subject, which is not convincing. Table 2 shows correlation among different modalities, but without GT labels on different modalities it’s hard to judge. I could suggest using a tool like SynthSR [4] to be able to map all sequences and resolutions into the same space for evaluation purposes, and then you can compare your method with those obtained labels for example.
The proposed model’s advantage is not using the labeled images with pathologies. To highlight the need for the method, it could be useful to do the ablation study at different number of labeled subjects with the pathology (i.e. does 50% control, 50% pathological subjects in the real augmented setting perform considerably worse than the real augmented upper bound presented in results?).
[1] B Billot, DN Greve, O Puonti, A Thielscher, K Van Leemput, B Fischl, AV Dalca, JE Iglesias. SynthSeg: Segmentation of brain MRI scans of any contrast and resolution without retraining. Medical Image Analysis, 83, 102789 (2023). 
[2] B. Billot, C. Magdamo, Y. Cheng, S.E. Arnold, S. Das, & J.E. Iglesias, Robust machine learning segmentation for large-scale analysis of heterogeneous clinical brain MRI datasets, Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 120 (9) e2216399120, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2216399120 (2023). 
[3] Z. Shang et al. Towards contrast- and pathology-agnostic clinical fetal brain MRI segmentation using SynthSeg, NeuroImage, Volume 327, 2026, 121729, ISSN 1053-8119, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroimage.2026.121729.[4] JE Iglesias, B Billot, Y Balbastre, C Magdamo, S Arnold, S Das, B Edlow, D Alexander, P Golland, B Fischl.

. Science Advances, 9(5), eadd3607 (2023).
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The idea of synthesizing images for specific structural changes in brain is a useful idea and the authors show a method that shows good performance for segmenting ventricle, gray matter and white matter structures under modality and resolution changes. However, the results lack comparison with very similar methods, a trivial baseline of control images with train-time augmentation, the appropriate semi supervised ablation and the evaluation on different sequences, ages and resolutions (unlike what’s claimed). Quantitative evaluation of one of two datasets is missing.
