meta_reviews.text:
The reviewers provide mixed evaluations of this paper (scores: 3, 4, 5), with strengths noted in the problem motivation, methodological formulation, and empirical evaluation, but also concerns regarding limited novelty, clarity of presentation, and depth of experimental analysis . In particular, reviewers highlight missing statistical validation, insufficient analysis of hyperparameters and sensitivity, and unclear differentiation from closely related prior work. Given these differences, I invite the authors to address these concerns in the rebuttal—especially by clarifying methodological distinctions, strengthening experimental evidence, and improving clarity where needed. A clear and comprehensive response will be important for the final decision.

After carefully reviewing the rebuttal and the post-rebuttal reviewer comments, my recommendation is to accept the paper. The paper addresses an important and clinically relevant problem in test-time adaptation for pelvic bone segmentation under domain shift. The proposed ReGA framework, including the SICE-based reliability estimation and feature refinement strategy, is well motivated and evaluated on multiple datasets. While concerns remain regarding the degree of novelty relative to existing TTA/SFDA methods such as TEGDA, the majority of reviewers considered the rebuttal sufficient and supported acceptance. The work is clearly presented, provides useful empirical validation, and offers a practical contribution for improving segmentation reliability and anatomical consistency in unseen clinical domains. Therefore, I recommend acceptance, with the expectation that the authors will further clarify the distinction from closely related methods, add missing statistical and hyperparameter analyses where possible, and temper overstated novelty claims in the final version.
The authors have addressed the reviewers’ comments well. Two reviewers acknowledged the novelty and significance of the work. Therefore acceptance of the paper is concluded.

I recommend accept: post-rebuttal R1 raised to Accept and R3 maintained Accept (recommending Highlighted Poster), outweighing R2’s downgrade to Reject on TEGDA-similarity and workshop-venue assessments.

author_feedback_text:
R1Q1, Q3, Q4: Terminology, Notation, and Technical Details. We have added relevant citations and refined the statements. Specifically, the teacher-student schemes refer to TTA methods where an EMA-updated teacher generates pseudo-labels for supervising the student on target domain data. We clarify that θᵗ denotes the source-trained PBS model parameters, while f(θᵗ) denotes the corresponding segmentation model. Ambiguous expressions are corrected, and θᵗ is now defined at its first occurrence in Sec. 2.During TTA, dropout is kept active, and each target sample is forwarded K times to obtain stochastic predictions P̂ᵢₖ, where k indexes the stochastic forward pass. Following [7], we analyze K=1,5,10,15 and set K=5 in all experiments.
R1Q2: Evidence and Literature Support for Claims. The prior TS schemes with pseudo-label supervision have shown that unreliable predictions can be propagated and accumulated under domain shifts in the cited works [15,25]. Table 1 shows that these methods suffer from poor HD95, indicating notable boundary delineation errors. We apologize for missing citations and included works (e.g., AdaMI [Bateson et al., 2022] and EDCP [Liu et al., 2026]) showing that enforcing anatomical consistency is crucial for reliable adaptation. Cited works [14,16] and TestFit [Zhang et al., 2025] show that self-supervised learning has been widely explored in TTA, but its explicit use for enforcing target-domain anatomical consistency remains underexplored.
R1Q5, Q6, Q7: Strengthening Experimental Evidence. We agree that ReGA is positioned as an application-focused TTA framework for PBS. PBS is sensitive to boundary ambiguity and anatomical inconsistency under domain shifts; ReGA is designed to suppress unreliable boundary predictions and to promote anatomical consistency across pelvic regions. 
Further, in a new MSD_T10 → CLINIC setting, ReGA is also superior to source-only models and other TTA baselines, i.e., TENT, InTEnt, VPTTA, CoTTA, and TEGDA. Specifically, it improves Dice by 8.8 over the source-only model while reducing HD95/ASD by 18.8/4.7 and outperforms other TTA baselines by 3.3 - 4.8 Dice, with 16.8 - 26.7/3.5 - 4.1 reductions in HD95/ASD. Paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests show that ReGA improves Dice (p≤0.008), HD95 (p≤0.001), and ASD (p≤0.002) over TTA baselines in CLINIC → KITS19, and achieves notable HD95/ASD gains (p≤0.05) with comparable Dice in CLINIC → MSD_T10.
We conduct sensitivity analysis on key hyperparameters. ReGA is robust to M when M＞10, with Dice variations within 0.3.K=5 is selected as significant computation overhead would occur for K＞5 with a marginal gain of 0.1 in Dice. ReGA performs best at β=0.01 (range 0.005 - 0.020), other values degrade Dice minimally (0.6 max). Dropout rate of 0.5 (range 0.1 – 1.0) provides a balanced stochastic perturbation, yet the worst dropout rate results in only 0.6 degradation in Dice.
R2Q1, Q2: Methodological Distinctions. While ReGA is partially inspired by the general adaptation philosophy of TEGDA, it targets a different task, i.e., TTA of PBS models, where boundary ambiguity and anatomical consistency are critical under domain shifts. To this end, we introduce a new metric SICE for optimization that jointly considers region overlap and boundary deviation and further uses Lrc for confidence- and SICE-weighted RCL. Thus, Lrc not only reduces computation but also promotes reliable anatomical-region feature. In Table 2, the variant w/o Lrc performs worse, especially in HD95, indicating the contribution of Lrc to preserving anatomical integrity.
R3Q1: Choice of Dataset. TTA aims to adapt a source pre-trained model to the test data during inference in a source-free and online manner. Following this, the PBS model is trained on limited labeled 3D CT volumes from one institution and then adapted to unlabeled data from another institution. In the future, we aim to build a larger standardized multi-center 3D pelvic CT datasets.

title: Text as a Compass: Semantic-Navigated 3D Bone Collapse Prediction via Orthogonal Micro-volume Primitives
abstract: Accurate collapse prediction is pivotal for joint-preserving treatment in osteonecrosis of the femoral head (ONFH). However, mainstream 3D-CNN-based methods struggle to capture decisive fine-grained pathological signs due to the intrinsic global receptive field dilution effect, where volumetric isotropic aggregation diffuses sparse pathological singularities. Conversely, clinical reports explicitly document key regional features indicative of collapse, providing critical semantic cues to guide visual focus and enhance prediction. Driven by this clinical insight and the critical need to mitigate the volumetric signal dilution effect, we propose COMPASS (Clinical Orthogonal Micro-volume Primitive Aligned Semantic Search), a novel text-guided fine-grained evidence identification framework for ONFH collapse prediction. First, we introduce the tri-planar orthogonal micro-volume primitive (OMVP), a topological manifold representation that concentrates singularity energy onto orthogonal bases to counteract volumetric smoothing. Second, we devise a dual-stage optimization strategy. It begins with semantic space alignment to proactively navigate from macro-ROIs to micro-lesions using textual priors. Furthermore, it incorporates counterfactual causal verification to eliminate spurious correlations via hybrid supervision. Independent evaluations across diverse clinical scenarios confirm COMPASS’s state-of-the-art accuracy, yielding 97.01% AUC on a cohort with fine-grained lesion masks and 84.91% on a public dataset relying solely on coarse regional annotations, alongside causally verified localization.
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers
Applications -> Outcome Prediction / Prognosis / Longitudinal Modeling
Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper presents a framework for ONFH collapse prediction that formulates the task as language-guided local evidence identification. Instead of predicting collapse directly from global 3D image features, the method uses clinical text to guide the model toward local image regions that may contain predictive pathological signs. 
To support this formulation, the paper introduces OMVP, which represents each local 3D neighborhood using three orthogonal planar views, and a two-stage training scheme that first aligns local image features with clinical text and then uses counterfactual text supervision to suppress mismatched text-image responses.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper formulates ONFH collapse prediction as a language-guided local evidence identification problem, instead of a standard global 3D classification problem. This is an interesting formulation because it is well matched to the clinical motivation that predictive signs of collapse may appear as subtle local structural changes rather than only as global volumetric patterns. 
2.Another strength of the paper is the counterfactual text constraint to refine the selection of informative local tokens. Rather than relying only on positive image-text alignment, the method also uses mismatched or semantically contradictory text to suppress responses from regions that are visually salient but not supported by the queried semantics. 
3.Results demonstrate that the proposed method improves performance
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The paper presents OMVP as a projection-based representation, but from the figure and formulation it seems closer to extracting three orthogonal slices from a local 3D region. The manuscript does explain whether this operation is simple slice extraction or a more general projection process. 
2.The counterfactual text constraint is an important part of the proposed framework, but limited detail on the counterfactual text generation makes it difficult to understand. Its unclear if the texts are created by template replacement, manual editing, or mismatching with other samples. 
3.The paper states that a sparse loss is used when fine-grained masks are unavailable, but it does not provide the explicit form of this loss or explain how the sparsity is enforced. 
4.The main novelty is the use language models but at the same time, using text priors are now routinely applied, and there is no innovation in the language model.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper makes a meaningful contribution by formulating ONFH collapse prediction as a language-guided local evidence identification task. Overall, the paper presents a coherent method with a clear motivation and a empirical study.
However, the description of the OMVP operation is not clear and the construction of the counterfactual text is not described in sufficient detail.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_ethics: This paper uses a private datasets, the authors should provide clinical trial registration number or acknowledge waiver consent.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper’s contributions lie in its clinically grounded integration of textual and imaging data, using report-derived semantic cues to guide fine-grained visual evidence identification. Introducing orthogonal micro-volume primitive (OMVP) is a technically innovative contribution that directly addresses a known limitation, the dilution of sparse pathological signals. The dual-stage optimization strategy, combining semantic alignment with counterfactual causal verification, further strengthens the framework by improving both localization and robustness against false correlations. Additionally, the method demonstrates strong performance across datasets with varying annotation granularity, highlighting its practical applicability. Overall, the approach is both conceptually novel and well-aligned with clinical reasoning, which enhances its potential impact.
reviews.text_strengths:
Evaluation of generalizability: The method is evaluated on a public dataset in addition to the internal cohort, providing some assessment of generalization beyond the training distribution.
Well-justified problem formulation: The paper addresses a clearly motivated problem, particularly the challenges of detecting and localizing micro-lesions within volumetric data.
Methodological novelty: The introduction of the tri-planar orthogonal micro-volume primitive (OMVP) offers an interesting topological manifold representation that aims to concentrate singularity energy along orthogonal bases, addressing issues related to volumetric smoothing. Additionally, the proposed dual-stage optimization strategy, combining semantic space alignment with textual priors to guide the transition from macro-regions of interest to micro-lesions is a novel design.
Good empirical performance: The model achieves high performance, with an AUC of 97.01% on a cohort with fine-grained lesion annotations and 84.91% on a public dataset with coarse regional labels, along with reported causally verified localization.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
While the authors include text-only and vision-language baselines, in addition to label tokenization, the comparison remains limited, as other relevant multimodal fusion and geometry-aware approaches are not considered.
Clinical reports are often heterogeneous and inconsistently structured; however, the paper does not discuss how variability in the clinical reports affects the robustness of the proposed approach and how they have addressed .
The authors use BioBERT for textual embedding extraction. However, more recent approaches such as BioLinkBERT leverages links between documents, enabling a more comprehensive semantic finding across different reports, outperforming BERT. I recommend the authors to also consider this approach.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper presents a well-motivated approach for integrating clinical reports with imaging data through semantic-guided modeling, addressing an important challenge in this application area. The idea of using clinical report semantics as a form of guidance signal represents a promising direction for improving performance. The experimental results demonstrate consistent improvements over baseline methods, including text-only and vision-language approaches, suggesting that the proposed framework effectively captures complementary information across modalities. The inclusion of interpretability components further strengthens the contribution by providing insight into how textual cues influence model behavior. While there are some limitations, such as a relatively limited comparison with other multimodal fusion and geometry-aware methods, lack of discussion on variability in clinical report structure, and the use of BioBERT instead of more recent alternatives like BioLinkBERT, these do not override the overall contribution. Overall, the paper introduces a compelling and impactful idea with solid empirical support.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
1.The paper proposes a text-guided framework for ONFH collapse prediction from CT, using a two-stage vision-language optimization strategy.
2.The paper introduces a tri-planar representation of 3D volumes—Orthogonal Micro-Volume Primitives (OMVP)—to mitigate the receptive field dilution effect in 3D CNNs.
3.The paper incorporates counterfactual reasoning by constructing mismatched vision-language pairs to suppress inconsistent semantic activations.
4.Experiments on both a private dataset (175 cases) and a public dataset (191 cases) demonstrate improved performance over conventional methods.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Overall, the paper is generally well-written.
2.The use of tri-planar representations to alleviate volumetric dilution is well-motivated and effective for capturing sparse lesions.
3.The semantic alignment framework with MIL-based attention for selecting relevant OMVPs is novel and technically interesting.
4.The proposed method uses text input to guide the evidence identification and adds counterfactual grounding to reduce hallucinations. The results are qualitatively evaluated in Fig. 3.
5.The ablation study confirmed the positive effects of each component proposed.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Overstatement of OMVP novelty.
OMVP is essentially a tri-planar (multi-planar) representation of a 3D volume, which has been widely used in prior works [*1, *2, *3, *4]. 
The novelty appears to lie more in the attention-based aggregation and top-k selection, and the use of tri-planar representation rather than the representation itself.
I recommend revising the claims regarding the novelty of OMVP to better reflect this distinction.
2.Unclear use of 2D U-Net on OMVP for segmentation.
The OMVP representation (H,W,3) consists of three orthogonal planes that are not spatially aligned. 
It is therefore unclear how a single 2D U-Net can produce a meaningful spatial output (e.g., a segmentation map) from such input. 
In standard practice, U-Net output channels correspond to aligned spatial features or segmentation classes, whereas in OMVP the channels represent different planes rather than consistent spatial locations.
While using a 2D model may be reasonable for regression tasks (e.g., Stage I), where features are ultimately pooled into a vector, this design is questionable for segmentation. Segmentation requires pixel-wise spatial consistency, which OMVP does not provide.
A more natural approach would be to process each plane independently with separate segmentation models (or at least forward passes) and aggregate the results afterward [*2, *3, *4]. 
The paper should clarify how the proposed U-Net handles OMVP inputs and produces spatially meaningful outputs.
3.The heuristic sparsity loss L_sarse in Eq (6) is not clearly defined, and its formulation or source is missing.
4.The parameter k used in Stage II is not specified, and the method for choosing it is unclear.
[
1] A. Parsoon et al.: Deep Feature Learning for Knee Cartilage Segmentation Using a Triplanar Convolutional Neural Network. MICCAI 2013.[
2] A. Mortazi et al.: Multi-Planar Deep Segmentation Networks for Cardiac Substructures from MRI and CT. STACOM 2017.[
3] V. Sundaresan et al.: Triplanar ensemble U-Net model for white matter hyperintensities segmentation on MR images. Medical Image Analysis. (2021)
[
4] T. Chen et al.: 2.5D Multi-view Averaging Diffusion Model for 3D Medical Image Translation: Application to Low-count PET Reconstruction with CT-less Attenuation Correction. IEEE TMI. (2025)
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The figure 2 Stage 2 losses can be confusing.
It’s not clear how the “Consistency loss”, “Suppression loss”, and “Heuristic constraint” correspond to equations in section 2.4.I recommend explicitly labeling the loss terms (e.g., L_dice, L_cf, and L_sparse) in the figure for clarity.

Overall, this is a strong paper with solid motivation and promising results.
However, the claims regarding OMVP novelty and the unclear handling of tri-planar inputs in the 2D U-Net raise important concerns.
Therefore, I recommend weak acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
The three reviewers are all in favor of this work. This paper aims to predict bone collapse by using text from clinical reports to guide the model toward looking at the right spots in 3D CT scans, rather than just feeding the whole scan into a classifier. The idea is clever and deserves the accept.
Minor: my personal view is that the paper has some unclear parts and overclaims that could use some fixing (clarify the OMVP and U-Net implementation details, define the missing parameters as suggested by reviewers, and explain the text generation part).
Lastly, please address some ethics concern: regarding the use of private dataset (mention waiver or IRB, etc.).

title: Text as Illumination: Spatial Contrastive Retinex Learning for Language-Guided Medical Image Segmentation
abstract:
Language-guided Medical Image Segmentation (LMIS) has shown great potential to improve the delineation of anatomical struc-tures and lesions by integrating clinical textual information. Existing methods generally rely on either implicit interaction between textual and visual features or auxiliary coarse-grained supervision for cross-modal alignment. However, these methods lack explicit and fine-grained constraints to ensure semantic consistency, causing a mismatch between language and the segmentation outputs. To address this issue, we propose Text-as-Illumination Retinex Network (TIRNet), a novel Retinex-inspired framework that treats text embeddings as semantic illumination for feature modulation, thereby improving semantic consistency in LMIS. TIRNet introduces two key blocks integrated at each decoder stage: (1) the Retinex-inspired Text Modulation Block (RTMB), which employs positive and negative illumination maps to enhance text-relevant foreground features and suppress background interference; and (2) the Consistent Detail Compensation Block (CDCB), which selectively recovers high-frequency details via a consistency-gated mechanism conditioned
on illumination reliability. Furthermore, we propose a Multi-Scale Illumination Supervision Loss (MSIS-Loss), comprising a Region-Grounded Contrastive Loss (RGC-Loss) that enforces cross-modal similarity to be concentrated in text-relevant foreground regions and suppressed in background regions, and a Background Suppression Loss (BS-Loss) that provides pixel-level supervision for negative illumination maps, jointly ensuring a precise cross-modal alignment at each decoder stage. Extensive experiments on the MosMedData+ and QaTa-COV19 datasets demonstrate that TIRNet achieves state-of-the-art performance in LMIS. The code is available at: https://github.com/anaanaa/TIRNet.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper presents TIRNet (Text‑as‑Illumination Retinex Network) for language‑guided medical image segmentation. The core idea is to treat text embeddings as semantic illumination that modulates visual decoder features. y. Four main contributions are claimed:
1.RTMB (Retinex‑based Text Modulation Block) – Derives positive and negative illumination maps from cross‑modal similarity to explicitly enhance text‑relevant foregrounds and suppress backgrounds. 
2.CDCB (Consistent Detail Compensation Block) – Recovers high‑frequency details from encoder features via a consistency‑gated mechanism conditioned on illumination reliability. 
3.MSIS‑Loss (Multi‑Scale Illumination Supervision Losses) – Combines a Region‑Grounded Contrastive loss that enlarges foreground‑background margins and a Background Suppression loss that provides pixel‑level supervision for negative illumination maps. 
4.Experiments on MosMedData+ and QaTa‑COV19 show state‑of‑the‑art performance compared to both unimodal and multimodal methods, including LViT and TeViA.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Mapping Retinex theory to cross‑modal segmentation is creative and well‑motivated. The idea of using text as “illumination” that positively/negatively modulates features is elegant. 
2.Unlike prior implicit or coarse‑grained alignment methods, the proposed RTMB produces per‑pixel similarity maps and two complementary illumination maps, enabling explicit foreground amplification and background suppression at each decoder stage.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The text encoder is a frozen CLIP model pre‑trained on general natural images and captions. Medical reports contain highly specialised terminology and different linguistic structure. No analysis or mitigation (e. g. , fine‑tuning, prompt engineering, or medical‑specific text encoder) is provided. 
2.The evaluation lacks empirical efficiency profiling; while architectural complexity is quantified via parameters and FLOPs, clinically critical metrics including inference latency and memory footprint remain unreported. 
3.The comparative evaluation in Table 1 exhibits methodological inconsistency in metric reporting. Specifically, some baselines (e. g. , U-Net, nnU-Net) report solely sample-level metrics (m-Dice, m-IoU), whereas certain multi-modal competitors (e. g. , TeViA) provide only global metrics (g-Dice, g-IoU). Notably, TIRNet is the sole method presenting all four metrics, precluding direct and equitable comparison across the complete metric suite. To ensure fair and transparent benchmarking, we strongly recommend that the authors compute and report the missing metrics for all comparative methods through standardized re-implementation.

N/A

The paper offers notable strengths, including a novel Retinex-inspired cross-modal segmentation framework, explicit spatial alignment with complementary illumination maps, and thorough ablation studies.
However, several unresolved weaknesses limit its overall impact: (1) lack of discussion on CLIP’s domain adaptation to medical terminology; (2) missing clinically critical metrics such as inference latency and memory footprint; (3) inconsistent metric reporting in Table 1 (mixed sample-level vs. global metrics), preventing fair comparison across baselines.
Given the novelty and solid technical core, the paper merits acceptance, but addressing the above issues—especially metric consistency and efficiency profiling—is strongly recommended before final publication.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes TIRNet, a language-guided medical image segmentation (LMIS) framework inspired by Retinex theory. It treats text embeddings as “semantic illumination” to modulate visual features via a Retinex-based Text Modulation Block (RTMB) and a Consistent Detail Compensation Block (CDCB). Additionally, a Multi-Scale Illumination Supervision Loss (MSIS-Loss) is introduced to enforce cross-modal alignment through region-grounded contrastive learning and background suppression.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Innovative Perspective: Mapping Retinex theory from low-level vision enhancement to cross-modal feature modulation provides a novel conceptual framework for LMIS.
2.Architecture Design: The explicit decoupling of foreground enhancement (L+) and background suppression (L−) is a well-structured engineering approach to handle multi-modal interference.
3.Empirical Results: The method demonstrates competitive performance on MosMedData and QaTa-COV19 datasets compared to several recent baselines.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Logical Conflict Between Local Receptive Fields and Global Spatial Semantics: The proposed TIRNet relies on a CNN-based U-Net architecture. While the text embeddings provide global semantic information, the visual features in the decoder stages are inherently local due to the translational invariance of convolutional kernels. The manuscript does not mention the use of explicit Positional Encodings. I am concerned about how the model manages to achieve precise spatial alignment for directional or lateral clinical instructions (e.g., “lower left lung” vs. “lower right lung” ). In the absence of a global coordinate system or positional embeddings, local features in anatomically symmetric regions may yield nearly identical similarity responses to the same global text vector, potentially leading to cross-lateral false positives. The authors should clarify how the architecture maintains global spatial consistency without explicit positional information.
2.Anomalous Performance of MSIS-Loss and Hyperparameter Sensitivity: In Table 3, the sensitivity analysis reveals a concerning trend regarding the proposed losses. The baseline model (λ_cl=0, λ_bg=0) achieves an m-Dice of 84.36.However, adding the Background Suppression Loss (BS-Loss) independently (λ_cl=0, λ_bg=0.5) results in a performance degradation to 84.20.Furthermore, when λ_cl and λ_bg are set to 0.5, the result (84.35) remains inferior to the baseline. It appears the proposed losses only provide a marginal gain at a very specific hyperparameter setting (λ_cl=1, λ_bg=0.5). This suggests that the pixel-level hard constraint of BS-Loss may conflict with the mixed-semantic nature of deep-stage features (large receptive fields), leading to optimization instability. The authors need to provide a deeper mechanistic explanation for why these losses act as negative optimizers in several parameter configurations.
3.Conceptual Overstatement of Retinex Formulation:
While the “Text-as-Illumination” metaphor is inspiring, the mathematical implementation in Equation 5 is effectively a sophisticated dual-path spatial attention or feature-gating mechanism. Unlike traditional Retinex theory, which addresses an ill-posed inverse problem (decomposing unknown illumination from a single image), this framework uses feed-forward gating signals derived directly from text. Referring to this as a strict “extension of Retinex theory” feels like a conceptual overstatement. A more rigorous description would frame it as a Retinex-inspired decoupled attention mechanism.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I recommend a Weak Reject. The core idea of using text as a modulation signal via a decoupled positive/negative illumination scheme is interesting and shows promise. However, I have major concerns regarding the architectural logic of spatial alignment in a pure CNN framework without positional embeddings (Weakness 1). More importantly, the ablation and sensitivity studies (Table 3) show that the proposed loss functions often perform worse than the baseline unless tuned to a very specific point, raising questions about the robustness and the underlying synergy of the MSIS-Loss components (Weakness 2). I invite the authors to address these logical and experimental inconsistencies in their rebuttal.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors’ rebuttal addressed the specific questions raised in my review. My final evaluation is based on the following responses:
1.Spatial Alignment: Addressed. The provided CoordConv ablation experiment answered my empirical question. The authors clarified that the model relies on zero-padding for spatial awareness rather than explicit spatial grounding.
2.MSIS-Loss Anomaly: Addressed. The authors explained that BS-Loss causes “over-conservatism” on deep-stage mixed-semantic features. This explanation accounts for the hyperparameter sensitivity observed in the original ablation study.
3.Retinex Metaphor: Addressed. The authors confirmed the framework is a structural inspiration rather than a strict Retinex decomposition, aligning with the critique regarding the terminology.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of this paper is proposing an innovative cross-modal fusion framework for language-guided medical image segmentation. The core of this framework is the Retinex-based Text Modulation Block (RTMB), which dynamically modulates visual features via a dual-path gating mechanism using text embeddings. Secondary contributions include the Consistent Detail Compensation Block (CDCB) for recovering high-frequency structural details guided by illumination reliability, and multi-scale illumination supervision losses (RGC-Loss and BS-Loss) to enforce structured foreground-background contrast and alignment.
reviews.text_strengths: The major strength is the Retinex-based Text Modulation Block (RTMB), which utilizes text embeddings as condition vectors to dynamically modulate visual features via a dual-path gating mechanism. This spatial weighting approach is mathematically sound and demonstrates a strong capability to selectively enhance foreground targets while suppressing complex backgrounds, offering an inspiring and practically valuable perspective for multimodal feature alignment in medical imaging.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
In Section 2.1, the Retinex formulation is introduced into a cross-modal setting, interpreting the visual decoder feature as reflectance and the text embedding as illumination. While the dual-path modulation effectively separates foreground and background, the underlying physical analogy appears conceptually forced. Retinex is inherently a low-level physical model for illumination-reflectance decomposition, whereas the proposed method operates entirely in a high-level semantic space as a form of text-guided feature modulation. In the rebuttal, I would appreciate it if the authors could clarify their justification for this strict physical analogy. Moving forward, it would be more appropriate to reframe this design as a “Retinex-inspired modulation mechanism” to improve conceptual rigor.
The current ablation studies mainly demonstrate the incremental benefit of the RTMB module, which largely reflects the inherent advantage of simply incorporating cross-modal information. However, this alone does not sufficiently justify the necessity of the proposed architectural complexity. Specifically, why did the authors not explore or discuss comparisons with alternative, standard modules that serve a similar purpose, such as a standard cross-attention mechanism? Without such a de facto baseline, it is difficult to determine whether the proposed dual-path modulation offers meaningful performance or efficiency advantages over conventional cross-modal fusion methods. I look forward to the authors’ discussion and insights on this architectural choice during the rebuttal.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Overall, I lean towards a weak accept for this paper. The major positive factor is the clever design of the RTMB module, which provides an effective and interesting way to disentangle foreground and background in medical images. However, my score is held back by two main issues: the conceptually forced Retinex physical analogy, and the lack of alternative fusion modules in the ablation studies. In the rebuttal, I look forward to the authors’ clarification on the conceptual rationale and their discussion/insights regarding why alternative fusion modules were not considered.
