meta_reviews.text:
This submission proposes TIRNet, a Retinex-inspired language-guided medical image segmentation framework using text-derived positive/ negative modulation maps, detail compensation, and multi-scale illumination supervision. Reviewers generally found the core idea interesting and technically promising, with competitive results on MosMedData+ and QaTa-COV19 and useful ablations supporting the RTMB/CDCB design. However, several important concerns should be addressed in rebuttal: whether the Retinex framing is conceptually justified versus a standard text-guided attention/gating mechanism; whether the method offers advantages over conventional cross-attention or alternative fusion baselines and how spatially specific text cues are handled in a CNN-based architecture without explicit positional encoding.

The rebuttal addresses reviewers’ concerns reasonably well. Overall, I recommend acceptance. The contribution is technically interesting and the rebuttal substantially reduces the main doubts about architectural necessity, spatial alignment, efficiency, and evaluation fairness.

The proposed Retinex-inspired text modulation framework is recognized as an innovative and effective approach to language-guided medical image segmentation. While initial concerns were raised regarding the forced physical Retinex analogy, spatial alignment logic in CNNs, and the optimization sensitivity of the loss functions, consensus among reviewers post-rebuttal highlights that the authors have successfully resolved these issues through comprehensive empirical clarifications.
three accepts, i agree.

author_feedback_text:
To All:
Q1: Retinex Rationale (MR, R2, R3)
A1: In fact, our TIRNet is not a strict Retinex decomposition to solve the illumination-reflectance inverse problem. We instead use Retinex as a structural inspiration: text embeddings provide semantic illumination-like signals to modulate visual decoder features. It enhances text-relevant foregrounds and suppresses irrelevant backgrounds. In the revised version, we will clarify the above facts and provide more motivations about using the dual-path spatial gating mechanism in Eq. 5.Q2: RTMB vs. Other Fusion Methods (MR, R3):
A2: To verify the effectiveness of RTMB, we replace it with two standard alternatives, i.e., concatenation fusion and cross-attention fusion. On QaTa-COV19, they achieve 82.40/73.44 and 82.88/73.90 in m-Dice/m-IoU, respectively. They are consistently lower than the ones (83.13/74.45) achieved by RTMB. These results verify that the improvement is not merely from introducing textual information, but from the proposed RTMB.
Q3: Spatial Alignment w/o PE (MR, R2):
A3: Indeed, explicit PE is not used in TIRNet. However, visual features of our framework are not position-agnostic. This is fully supported by three facts: (1) zero-padding can provide implicit absolute-coordinate cues (Islam et al., ICLR 2020); (2) hierarchical down-sampling and skip connections help preserve and propagate relative spatial information; and (3) deep decoder stages have a large effective receptive field, enabling them to capture holistic organ layouts rather than only local textures.
In addition, TIRNet introduces explicit spatial grounding through MSIS-Loss. At each decoder stage, down-sampled masks supervise the illumination maps, thereby penalizing activations outside the text-relevant ground-truth regions. More importantly, adding normalized 2D CoordConv/PE before RTMB results in negligible gains across all metrics [84.50/76.17/91.37/84.11 (QaTa-COV19)] compared to TIRNet. It confirms that explicit PE is unnecessary here. We will add more representative visualizations to show the effect of the localization-aware text.
To R1:
Q1: CLIP Domain Gap
A1: We further evaluate the text encoder adaptation. On QaTa-COV19, replacing frozen CLIP with BioMedCLIP and MedCLIP-ResNet50 achieves 83.57/75.00/90.58/82.79 and 83.77/75.23/90.79/83.14, respectively. They are both below the frozen CLIP setting. Besides, the prompt engineering with “A medical image showing {Text}.” yields lower results (83.82/75.25/90.80/83.15). Fine-tuning the CLIP produces comparable results (84.48/76.06/91.31/84.01). This suggests that text encoding is not the primary bottleneck in our structured-text setting.
Q2: Efficiency
A2: Under the same evaluation setting, TIRNet takes 115.46 ms/case with 1426 MiB peak GPU memory. While not the fastest, it remains practical and is more efficient than several LMIS baselines, e.g., LViT (378.59 ms, 17518 MiB) and LGA (117.03 ms, 4338 MiB). We will include the latency/memory and discuss the accuracy-efficiency trade-off in the revision.
Q3: Metric Consistency
A3: The original table followed the metrics reported in prior works. We agree that standardized evaluation is preferable. We therefore re-evaluated all compared methods under a unified protocol, which enables full comparisons, e.g., [TeViA: 84.12/75.69/90.96/83.41; U-Net: 78.46/68.59/86.66/76.47 (QaTa-COV19)]. We will update Table 1 accordingly in the revision. Note that the main conclusion remains unchanged.
To R2:
Q1: MSIS-Loss
A1: In fact, BS-Loss is an auxiliary regularizer. With (0, 0.5), MSIS-Loss suppresses backgrounds, making the model over-conservative around small lesions, ambiguous boundaries, or deep-stage mixed-semantic features. When both weights are 0.5, the highlighted foreground remains insufficient to balance this suppression. Thus, the weights (1, 0.5) better match our design: RGC-Loss provides the main semantic alignment, while BS-Loss offers moderate background regularization.
To R3:
See General Response A1/A2.

title: Text as the Sieve: Information Bottleneck Guided Prototype Sieving for Text-Guided Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Accurate pulmonary lesion segmentation is vital for clinical diagnosis, yet conventional single-modal models often struggle to leverage the rich semantic priors available in diagnostic reports. While multimodal approaches have emerged to bridge this gap, recent research has transitioned from dense additive fusion to redundancy-reduction strategies such as token pruning. However, existing pruning-based methods remain suboptimal due to a mismatch in Token Scale—pruning concise text instead of redundant visual tokens—and a Delayed Interaction paradigm that allows background noise to propagate through the encoder. To address these limitations, we propose Text-driven Semantic Information-sieve (TeSi), an Information Bottleneck (IB) guided framework that shifts the focus to early encoder-side sieving. Specifically, to resolve the scale mismatch, an IB-Sieve mechanism treats text as a semantic filter to rank and hard-select informative visual prototypes; and to reform the interaction paradigm, our framework performs early visual sieving in the encoder, followed by an asymmetric decoder with adaptive context fusion that selectively refines textual guidance for precise boundary recovery without re-introducing noise. Extensive experiments on the QaTa-COV19-v2 and MosMedData+ datasets demonstrate that TeSi achieves competitive performance compared to current state-of-the-arts. Moreover, our method provides improved clinical interpretability through explicit prototype-to-report alignment, validating the effectiveness of the proposed sieving paradigm.
subject_areas: Applications -> Multimodal Integration with Clinical / Genomic / Biomarkers
Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper addresses two key issues in text-guided medical image segmentation: Token Scale Mismatch (where existing methods prune concise text rather than redundant visual tokens) and the Delayed Interaction Paradigm (where text guidance is introduced only at the decoding stage). To this end, the TeSi framework is proposed. Its core components include:
1.IB-Sieve Mechanism: Utilizes text semantics to rank and perform hard selection on visual prototypes, filtering out visual redundancy early at the encoder stage. 
2.Asymmetric Decoder: Incorporates adaptive text fusion to prevent semantic drift. 
3.Axial Prototype Generation: Compresses the sequence length from H x W to H+W . 
The method achieves competitive results (91.37% Dice) on the QaTa-COV19-v2 and MosMedData+ datasets.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Accurate and Insightful Problem Formulation: The observation that existing token pruning methods target the wrong object (pruning concise text tokens instead of redundant visual ones) is valuable, with a clear motivation. The formulation of “Token Scale Mismatch” and “Interaction Paradigm” is precise. 
2.Sound IB-Sieve Design: Using text as a semantic sieve to rank and hard-select visual prototypes integrates the Information Bottleneck principle with cross-modal interaction naturally. The design of aggregating residual prototypes into a background token also thoughtfully addresses information preservation. 
3.Effective Axial Prototype Compression: The axial decomposition compressing H×W to H+W is a practical engineering design that balances efficiency and representational power. 
4.Rationale for Asymmetric Decoder: The design of bypassing SPI to use original text embeddings directly to prevent semantic drift is logical, and ablation studies verify its superiority over symmetric designs. 
5.Interpretability Analysis (Spatial Semantic Maps): The multi-scale semantic maps in Fig. 3 provide intuitive visualization of text-visual alignment, enhancing the method’s interpretability. 
6.Well-Structured Ablation Studies: Table 2 covers core components such as interaction paradigms, screening mechanisms, and decoder designs, clearly showing the contribution of each module.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Marginal Performance Gains and Lack of Statistical Significance: On QaTa-COV19-v2, TeSi (91.37%) is only 0.16% higher than FMISeg (91.21%) and 0.34% higher than ABP (91.03%). On MosMedData+, TeSi (77.96%) is notably lower than FMISeg (79.30%). Such minute differences are unconvincing without reporting standard deviations from multiple runs. The paper fails to report any statistical significance tests or variance information. 
2.Narrow Dataset Coverage Limited to COVID-19 Lung Scenarios: Both datasets are COVID-19 lung images (one X-ray, one CT), making the claim of “medical image segmentation” overly broad. The lack of validation on other organs, diseases, or modalities makes it difficult to assess generalization capability. Specifically, it is unclear if the effectiveness of IB-Sieve relies on the relatively uniform background of lung images. 
3.Sub-SOTA Results on MosMedData+ with Inadequate Explanation: On MosMedData+, TeSi’s Dice (77.96%) and mIoU (63.87%) are lower than FMISeg (79.30%/65.71%) and TGCAM (where mIoU is lower than TeSi). The paper attributes this to “limited training data hinders Transformer-based generalization,” yet TeSi uses a ConvNeXt backbone, not a Transformer. This explanation is self-contradictory. 
4.Weak Connection to Information Bottleneck Theory: While the paper claims inspiration from the IB principle, the connection is largely intuitive. There is no formal analysis or experimental validation regarding the minimization of I(Z;X) and maximization of I(Z;Y) . IB-Sieve is essentially a similarity-based top-k selection; branding it as “Information Bottleneck” feels like over-packaging. 
5.Lack of Analysis on Fixed Selection Ratio ( k=0.5 ): IB-Sieve uses a fixed 50% selection ratio, but the paper does not analyze the impact of different k values. The optimal k likely varies with lesion size and modality, making this a key hyperparameter that requires discussion. 
6.Missing Computational Efficiency Comparison: The paper emphasizes reducing computational redundancy as a core motivation but fails to report efficiency metrics (FLOPs, parameter count, inference time) compared to baselines. It is impossible to judge the actual efficiency gains from axial prototype compression and IB-Sieve. 
7.Negligible Contribution Differences in Ablation Studies: In Table 2, the Dice scores for Rows 2-7 range from 91.02% to 91.37%, a maximum difference of only 0.35%. This undermines the claim of “necessity” for each component—the differences may well be within the noise range. 
8.Incomplete Baseline Comparisons: AT and ABP lack results on MosMedData+ (marked as “-“), weakening the completeness of cross-dataset comparisons. If this is due to unavailable code, it should be stated.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper proposes a reasonable framework for text-guided medical image segmentation. The core insight—that visual redundancy rather than text tokens should be pruned—is valuable. The design of the IB-Sieve mechanism and the asymmetric decoder is clear, and ablation studies cover major design decisions.
However, the performance gains on the primary dataset are very marginal (+0.16% Dice) and lack statistical significance verification. The dataset coverage is narrow, the connection to IB theory is weak, and the results/explanation for MosMedData+ are contradictory.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The paper sits directly on the threshold. Ultimately, the balance tilts slightly toward acceptance due to the following considerations:
Practical Engineering Value: The rebuttal successfully demonstrates that the architectural components do exactly what they were designed to do—reduce computational complexity (25.7 GFLOPs vs. up to 54.2 GFLOPs in baselines) while maintaining highly competitive segmentation accuracy. The Axial Prototype Generator’s sequence length compression (H×W→H+W) is a useful engineering contribution.
Statistical Validity Established: By providing multi-run statistics (std<0.04), the authors have proven that their architectural improvements are genuine developments and not random seed noise. This satisfies a critical requirement from the Meta-Reviewer and Reviewer #1.
Interpretability Gains: As highlighted by multiple reviewers, the generation of intuitive, text-aligned spatial semantic maps provides strong clinical explainability that bridges the gap between black-box models and clinician adoption.
Condition for Final Camera-Ready Upload:
The authors must explicitly temper their claims in the final manuscript. They must substitute the over-packaged language of “Information Bottleneck Optimization” with “IB-inspired structural capacity constraints” as specified in their response. Furthermore, they must include the newly cited GFLOPs/parameter counts, add the standard deviations, correct the self-contradictory Transformer/CNN text, and clearly document the uniform-background lung dataset limitation in the discussion section.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper identifies two main weaknesses in current text-guided medical image segmentation. First, there is a token scale mismatch, which focuses on text pruning instead of removing redundant images. Second, there is a suboptimal interaction paradigm, where late-stage fusion allows noise to spread. To tackle these issues, the authors propose TeSi, which is based on the Information Bottleneck (IB) principle for early visual redundancy suppression. The key components are the IB-Sieve mechanism, which uses text as a semantic filter to choose informative visual prototypes, and the asymmetric decoder, which prevents semantic drift by using text as a steady anchor during boundary refinement.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.This work successfully uses the information bottleneck principle in medical multimodal learning to tackle visual redundancy. This is novel.
2.The Axial Prototype Generator effectively reduces sequence length from quadratic to linear, making the computation manageable and representing a technical innovation.
3.Unlike black-box fusion models, TeSi provides spatial semantic maps that clearly indicate which parts of the image the model focuses on based on specific text cues, such as “lower right lung.” This shows superior interpretability compared to previous works.
4.The method used achieved a high 91.37% Dice score on the QaTa-COV19-v2 dataset and demonstrates robustness on the smaller MosMedData+ dataset, outperforming recent benchmarks like ABP and FMISeg.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The study mainly focuses on X-ray and CT for pulmonary infections. It is not clear how the “axial prototype” approach would work with 3D volumetric data or other imaging methods like MRI, where textures are more intricate.
2.The IB-Sieve has a fixed selection ratio of k=0.5.The paper does not examine the impact of varying ratios on performance across different lesion sizes.
3.Although the results are robust, the COVID-19 datasets are somewhat specialized. Testing on a wider range of pulmonary diseases would better confirm clinical generalizability.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
None

The article deals with an important and frequently neglected problem in multimodal medical imaging: the enormous discrepancy between succinct textual descriptions and the redundant visual information. The use of preventive sieving in the early stages rather than remedial fusion in the late stages is both logical and empirically valid. The spatial semantic maps’ interpretability is especially useful to clinical adoption.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Having carefully read the authors’ rebuttal, I maintain and strengthen my recommendation to accept this paper. The three concerns I originally raised, sieving ratio, limited dataset generalization, and 3D/MRI applicability, are each addressed satisfactorily: the authors report ablations across k ∈ {0.3–0.7} supporting k=0.5 as a principled choice, honestly acknowledge the COVID-19 scope limitation while clarifying that the design is not lung-specific, and appropriately scope volumetric extension as future work. The IB formalization is further clarified through an explicit variable mapping (X→Z→Y) with a credible justification for preferring structural over explicit variational optimization. The additional stability data (Dice std < 0.04 pp, ablation gaps of 0.12–0.35%) reinforces confidence in the reported improvements within the high-performance regime. The rebuttal demonstrates thorough command of the method’s theoretical grounding and empirical behavior, and the core contributions of IB-inspired early visual sieving, linear-complexity axial prototype generation, and interpretable spatial semantic maps remain compelling and well-supported.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes TeSi, a text-guided medical image segmentation framework that uses text as a semantic sieve to select informative visual prototypes early in the encoder. The method is motivated by two claimed limitations of prior work: Token Scale mismatch and Delayed Interaction. Concretely, the paper introduces axial prototype generation, a Semantic Prototype Interaction (SPI) module, an IB-Sieve mechanism for text-guided prototype selection, and an Asymmetric Decoder with adaptive text fusion. Experiments are conducted on QaTa-COV19-v2 and MosMedData+, with ablation studies and qualitative interpretability analysis. The overall paper is well organized and the motivation is understandable.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper identifies two intuitively meaningful issues in prior text-guided segmentation methods: pruning text rather than visual redundancy, and introducing text too late in the pipeline. This provides a coherent rationale for encoder-side semantic filtering.
2.The method is not merely a stack of unrelated modules. The prototype compression, SPI alignment, early prototype sieving, and asymmetric decoding form a consistent design narrative.
3.The paper provides component ablations and spatial semantic map visualizations.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.In section 2.3, the paper frames the method as information bottleneck guided and minimizing I(Z;X) while maximizing I(Z;Y). The manuscript does not clearly define what the X, Y and Z actually represents in this problem settings. Moreover, the implementation is text-visual similarity ranking followed by top-k selection, trained only with CE and Dice loss, without an explitic information-bottleneck objective, variational formulation or mutual-information-based optimization. The IB appears largely conceptual rather than methodologically rigorous. Can the authors clarify in what precise sense the method is an Information Bottleneck method.
2.The paper states that it reports Dice, mIoU and Accuracy, but the tables only show Dice and mIoU. Why are Accuracy results not shown?
3.In Table 2, nearly all multimodal variants outperform the uni-modal baseline by roughly 4 points in both Dice and mIoU, while the differences among the proposed components themselves are relatively small. This makes it difficult to determine the specific effect size of each design choice. The ablation mainly shows that introducing the overall multimodal framework is beneficial, but does not convincingly disentangle how much of the gain comes from IB-Sieve, SPI, the spatial map recovery, or the asymmetric decoder individually. Can the authors clarify what conclusions can be drawn from Table 2?
4.In section 2.1 and 2.2, the paper claims reducing redundancy and improving efficiency. however, these efficiency benefits are not quantitatively validated in the experiments.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper addresses an interesting problem and proposes a coherent multimodal segmentation framework. However, I recommend rejection because the main claims are not sufficiently supported by rigorous evidence. The experimental comparison does not appear to be based on a clearly unified reproduction of baselines, which weakens the claimed performance advantage. Moreover, the Information Bottleneck interpretation is insufficiently defined, and the ablation study does not clearly isolate the effect of each proposed component. As a result, the paper’s central contributions remain only partially validated.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: After reading the authors’ rebuttal, I appreciate their detailed responses, which have addressed most of my concerns. I am therefore willing to raise my score to WR. However, I remain unconvinced by the explanation of the IB component, particularly the interpretation of minimizing I(Z;X). Overall, the rebuttal improves my confidence in the work, but this remaining conceptual concern prevents me from assigning a more positive score.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper studies text-guided medical image segmentation and proposes the TeSi framework to address two limitations of existing methods: the scale mismatch between concise textual tokens and redundant visual tokens, and the delayed interaction caused by introducing textual information only at the decoding stage. Overall, the topic is relevant and meaningful, the motivation is reasonably clear, and the framework is coherently structured.
However, the reviews show considerable divergence, as several central claims of the paper still require stronger experimental evidence and more rigorous theoretical justification. In the rebuttal, the authors should clearly explain the precise relationship between IB-Sieve and the Information Bottleneck principle; provide or justify the absence of standard deviations over multiple runs and statistical significance analysis; clarify the actual contribution of each proposed module; report efficiency-related metrics to verify whether axial prototype compression and visual prototype sieving indeed bring computational benefits; discuss the effect of different sieving ratios across lesion sizes and datasets; clarify whether baseline comparisons were conducted under a unified experimental setting, and explain the missing Accuracy results and incomplete baseline results; and discuss the potential applicability and limitations of the method beyond COVID-19 lung datasets, including other organs, MRI, and 3D volumetric data.

The paper addresses a meaningful problem in text-guided medical image segmentation by focusing on visual-token redundancy and the delayed use of textual guidance in existing methods. The proposed TeSi framework is coherent, with axial prototype generation, text-guided visual sieving, and an asymmetric decoder forming a clear design around early semantic filtering. The initial concerns about marginal gains, weak connection to the Information Bottleneck principle, missing efficiency evidence, fixed sieving ratio, and limited dataset scope were valid. However, the rebuttal addresses these issues in a reasonably convincing way. In particular, the authors clarify that the method is IB-inspired rather than a formal variational IB optimization, provide multi-run stability results, report computational cost showing meaningful efficiency advantages, and add analysis of the sieving ratio. Although the evaluation remains limited to COVID-19 lung datasets and the MosMedData+ results are not uniformly superior to all baselines, the method is technically sound, interpretable, and practically useful. Overall, I believe the paper makes a solid contribution to text-guided medical segmentation and would support acceptance, with the expectation that the final version clearly tempers the IB claim and discusses the dataset-scope limitation.

The paper proposes TeSi, a text-guided segmentation framework that performs early visual prototype sieving using textual semantics, combined with axial prototype compression and an asymmetric decoder. Reviewers agreed that the motivation is clear and that the method forms a coherent design addressing visual redundancy and late text interaction. Initial concerns included marginal gains, lack of variance/efficiency reporting, weak formal connection to Information Bottleneck theory, fixed sieving ratio, and limited validation on COVID lung datasets. Limitations remain: the MosMedData+ result is competitive but not best, and generalization beyond pulmonary datasets is unproven. Nevertheless, the method is technically sound, interpretable, and sufficiently validated for acceptance.

The paper presents a useful framework for text-guided medical image segmentation, with meaningful early visual sieving and interpretable spatial semantic maps. However, the newly added results cannot be considered during rebuttal per MICCAI policy.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the reviewers for their constructive comments. Our responses are below:
Q1 IB formalization (R1, R3)
We appreciate this critical comment. Our method follows an IB-inspired structural bottleneck design rather than explicit variational IB optimization.
Using our paper’s notation, the IB variables correspond as:
X: multi-scale features {Xi}
Z: sieved high-semantic prototypes Z_sem
Y: segmentation mask (E_text as a semantic proxy for Y)
A structural IB approximation is induced via capacity constraints on Z (see Q4), jointly promoting:
Min I(Z;X): Axial compression reduces token capacity (↓H(Z)); IB-Sieve further prunes P_v to Z_sem, discarding task-irrelevant regions into the p_bg token.
Max I(Z;Y): SPI aligns prototypes across modalities, ensuring Z remains predictive of Y, further reinforced by Dice/CE objectives. Our early trials with explicit IB loss led to instability with marginal gains, suggesting the structural design is sufficient in practice.
Q2 Model effectiveness and module contributions (R1, R3)
We respectfully clarify that the modest improvements reflect a high-performance region (>91% Dice), where only incremental gains are expected. Similar patterns also appear in prior works[16,23], including their ablations.
We agree that reporting standard deviations would strengthen the results. Across 8 runs, our TeSi shows stable performance with Dice std < 0.04 pp on QaTa, while ablation gaps (0.12%–0.35%) exceed this variation range, suggesting reliable improvements.
Table 2 isolates each module via targeted substitutions to disentangle specific contributions:
IB-Sieve: removing sieving (Row 4) leads to the lowest performance, indicating its importance.
SPI: replacing with MHCA (Row 5) results in a consistent drop, supporting the shared alignment design.
Spatial map: Row 6 shows a similar decreasing trend.
Decoder: Rows 2/3/7 support the asymmetric fusion design; a decoder-only variant reduces to a late-fusion scheme akin to ABP[16].
Q3 Missing Accuracy and incomplete baselines (R1, R3)
We apologize for the confusion. The mention of ACC was a typo. ACC is near ceiling on this task (e.g., >97% on QaTa) and omitted in recent works[11,16,23], making it less informative for comparison. We will correct this.
All baseline results are taken from original papers under their reported settings with identical dataset splits, following standard practice. ABP and AT lack MosMedData+ results due to unavailable code or missing task configurations; we avoid potentially unfair re-implementation and will clarify this in the final version.
Q4 Computational efficiency (R1, R3)
By compressing encoder tokens from 4165 to 147 (~28×), our design drastically cuts cross-modal encoder cost, achieving improved results with only 25.7 GFLOPs (vs. 54.2/17.7/34.3 for [9,10,23]) and ~75% of FMISeg[23]’s parameters (text encoder excluded).
Q5 Sieving Ratio (R1, R2)
We explored k ∈ {0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7}. Early checks suggested no clear advantage of lesion/dataset-specific tuning, so k=0.5 was chosen as a fixed midpoint to avoid overfitting. Adaptive ratios are interesting for future work.
Q6 MosMedData+ results (R1)
We clarify that TeSi slightly outperforms TGCAM but remains below FMISeg on MosMedData+, and our claim is therefore “competitive”, not SOTA.
The confusing wording refers to the attention-based SPI module rather than the CNN backbone, and will be revised.
Following prior work[10], we used mild augmentation, while FMISeg adopts heavier strategies (e.g., rotation, noise) according to its code, which may partly explain the performance gap.
Q7 Dataset scope and Generalization (R1, R2)
We acknowledge the current limitation to COVID-19 lung datasets, due to limited availability of public datasets with paired reports. The core design—text-driven visual sieving—does not assume lung-specific properties. The strategy can in principle be extended to 2.5D/3D prototypes, but validation on MRI and volumetric data remains future work.

title: Text Guidance and Distance Gating Improve Detection and Segmentation of Focal Cortical Dysplasia
abstract: Focal Cortical Dysplasia (FCD) is a leading cause of drug-resistant focal epilepsy, and its identification on MRI can enable potentially curative surgical treatment. FCD features are often subtle and heterogeneous and current deep learning models for automated detection exhibit limited sensitivity. In clinical workflows, prior knowledge about the suspected localization of seizure onset can guide lesion search. We hypothesize that this prior knowledge can similarly guide a deep learning model in the presence of ambiguous imaging features. We propose a text-guided graph neural network that incorporates prior knowledge to guide FCD detection on cortical features derived from MRI. We further introduce a cluster-wise distance-based gating mechanism that leverages the per-vertex distance regression head at inference to suppress false-positive predictions. Experimental results demonstrate that hemisphere- and lobe-level localization information improves sensitivity and segmentation quality, while the gating mechanism substantially increases specificity.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses the challenging task of automated detection and segmentation of Focal Cortical Dysplasia (FCD) from MRI, a leading cause of drug-resistant focal epilepsy. The authors build upon the state-of-the-art MELD framework, which uses surface-based graph neural networks. The core novelty is the integration of textual prior knowledge about the suspected anatomical localization of the lesion (e. g. , hemisphere or lobe) to guide the model’s attention. The proposed framework employs a frozen vision encoder (MELD) and a frozen text encoder (RadBERT), with fusion achieved via a GuideDecoder architecture adapted for cortical surface meshes. Additionally, the authors introduce a cluster-wise distance-based gating mechanism at inference time, leveraging the existing distance regression head of MELD to suppress false-positive predictions, thereby significantly improving specificity. Experiments on the large, multi-center MELD dataset demonstrate that incorporating coarse localization cues improves sensitivity and segmentation IoU, while the gating mechanism effectively restores specificity compromised by the text-guided model.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) The paper makes a compelling clinical argument: in presurgical epilepsy evaluation, prior knowledge about seizure onset zone localization is routinely available (from semiology, EEG, PET, etc. ). Leveraging this non-imaging information to guide a deep learning model is a logical and underexplored direction in FCD detection. This bridges the gap between purely data-driven methods and clinical workflow. 
2) The adaptation of the GuideDecoder fusion mechanism from 2D vision to cortical surface meshes (using HexUnpool and SpiralConv) is a non-trivial technical contribution. It demonstrates a careful handling of irregular graph-structured data. The distance-based gating is a simple yet highly effective inference-time post-processing step. It cleverly re-purposes an existing auxiliary output (distance regression) to address the specific failure mode (increased false positives on healthy controls) of the text-conditioned model. The quantitative impact on specificity is substantial (from ~27% to ~93% on the main cohort). 
3) The evaluation strictly follows the established MELD protocol, using a large multi-center dataset with a held-out independent test cohort (Bonn). This ensures a fair comparison and assesses generalizability. The use of multiple text conditioning variants (hemisphere only, lobe only, hemisphere+lobe) and the robustness strategy of random sampling during training (including “unclear” prompts) is a thoughtful experimental design that explores the granularity of required prior information.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) The text prompts are derived from atlas-based overlap with the ground-truth lesion. In a real clinical scenario, the prior information would be provided as free text by a clinician (e. g. , “suspected left temporal lesion”). The current evaluation uses structured, clean atlas labels. The authors correctly note this as a future direction (free-form radiological narratives). It would strengthen the discussion to explicitly state that performance may degrade with noisy or imprecise clinical text and that this evaluation represents an upper-bound or “oracle” setting for text guidance. 
2) The ablation in Table 4 focuses on gating aggregation rules, but does not isolate the effect of the text guidance itself versus the modified decoder architecture. The baseline is MELD. The Vision+LM model introduces both text fusion and the GuideDecoder with HexUnpool/SpiralConv. Could some of the gain be attributed solely to architectural changes?
3) The text mentions replacing standard 2D upsampling with HexUnpool and standard convolution with SpiralConv. A brief justification for why HexUnpool was chosen over simpler interpolation on the mesh would be helpful for readers unfamiliar with spherical surface processing. 
4) In the References section, reference [8] (Park et al. ) appears to be duplicated or mis-cited. It is listed as a narrative review on AI for FCD, but the citation in text is for RadBERT. The actual RadBERT citation is missing. The authors should ensure the RadBERT model is properly cited. 
5) The dice metirc should be used in the experiments to evaluate the performance of the proposed method.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper presents a well-motivated, technically sound, and rigorously evaluated extension to the state-of-the-art MELD framework for FCD detection. The integration of clinically available prior knowledge via text guidance is both novel and practical. The proposed distance-based gating mechanism is an elegant solution to the specificity degradation introduced by the text conditioning.
The manuscript is clearly written, and the experimental design adheres to high standards (multi-center data, independent test cohort, bootstrap confidence intervals). The identified weaknesses primarily concern presentation clarity, citation accuracy, and a more explicit discussion of limitations regarding text prompt realism.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have explained the issues that I am conerned. I have no other questions.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The authors propose a novel method for automated FCD detection in focal epilepsy from MRI, that combines the MELD graph neural network of cortical surface features with a text encoder of prior knowledge of FCD location. To deal with increased detection of false-positive clusters, the authors further introduce a gating mechanism of aggregated distance within each cluster to its boundary.
The model is trained and evaluated on participants of the MELD project. Performance of the model using different levels of coarseness in text input and gating mechanisms is compared to the standard MELD model in test and validation cohorts.
reviews.text_strengths: The main strength of the paper is its potential in focal epilepsy to combine imaging-based input with other clinical information, such as radiology notes, which tend to be available for surgical candidates, but are currently not incorporated in automated lesion detection tools. In practice, pre-surgical evaluation considers a variety of sources of information, and the paper demonstrates that incorporating some of these into imaging-based localisation tools could substantially improve performance.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The authors motivate the incorporation of text-based information of lesion localisation with the typical availability of prior clinical knowledge. However, in their analysis the authors generate the text input by using the MELD pipeline to predict a lesion localisation, which is then mapped to an anatomical template to generate textual descriptions. This appears to be a circular way of generating input, which is then used alongside the MELD surface features to refine localisation. What is the conceptual justification for generating text input using a model based on MRI cortical surface features, only then to combine the text input with the same model of cortical features? Instead, why not use input independent of the MELD pipeline, e.g. notes of a radiologist, or findings of EEG?
2.Another methodological consideration is the gating mechanism. Does applying a median (min/max) threshold of the distance of vertices within a cluster to its boundary not bias towards detecting small and, in particular, narrow lesions? What is the justification for using this mechanisms specifically?
3.Further, table 4 compares the novel method with all gating mechanisms to MELD with the same gating options. However, the discussion of this is very limited, e.g. the authors do not discuss that MELD with added gating mechanism outperforms their model in three out of five metrics. It is also unclear why these results are only show for the main cohort, and not the independent validation cohort.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper makes a novel and interesting contribution. Whilst the choice of some analysis steps are unclear, the results are convincing, and the method has clinical relevance with potential further development in the future.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: My concern regarding the apparent circularity of using MELD-derived predictions as text input has been clarified, in that the text descriptions are derived from ground-truth lesion masks, not model output. The authors also address the gating mechanism concern convincingly, noting true-positive clusters are preserved regardless of lesion size. The point about MELD+gating outperforming Vision+LM on some specificity metrics is reasonably framed as a sensitivity-specificity trade-off.

reviews.recommendation_label: Strong Reject — must be rejected due to major flaws
reviews.text_contribution: The work proposes a multimodal segmentation framework that integrates surface-based visual features with text descriptions that encode prior knowledge on anatomical localization of the seizure onset to guide Focal Cortical Dysplasia (FCD) detection.
reviews.text_strengths: The work tries to combine surface-based and textual data to segment lesions in the brain
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The work is not clear organized. It is hard to follow and the motivation is not clear. What advantage does the text adds to the segmentation?
The authors call it segmentation but it should rather be parcellation as it is surface-based.
These text-based inputs are very primitive and does not provide enough information as the results are quite inferior in general; huge portions of the legions are missed.
Why was surfaces used? Can we use volumetric segmentations (without the graph-based framework) and then check the results with that; perhaps an ablation study might be good?
The gating mechanism lacks technical grounding what is the use of computing the SDF?
The different loss functions need ablation studies to see what is the true effect of each loss.
The results are poor as the overlap is very small (red vs black outline)
The work needs to be evaluated on different domains.
You only show segmentation in one limited region
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Limited evaluation on only one dataset in a very localized region and lack of clear technical description
It is not clear merely integrating two modalities can produce any improvements in the segmentation
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal still doesn’t address the main issues. The evaluation is very limited and the concern regarding the simplicity or the lack of adequate text prompts have not been addressed. The concern regarding the overlap of the segmentation is not addressed: the red and black overlap between the prediction and the groundtruth is way too off.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper proposes the ingenious idea to combine text and images for the detection of FCD. The experimental design is performed on a multi-centre dataset with efforts to assess generalisability. There are certain aspects that would benefit from better clarification / justification in a rebuttal especially with respect to the text input and its generation as well as the gating mechanism. Choices for the evaluation in terms of independent cohort and ablation investigations should also be discussed and justified if possible.

The authors have well addressed all comments and clarified important points yielding a much stronger submission that should have its place in the conference.

After rebuttal, R1 and R2 remained Accept, while R3 maintained Reject, due to that the evaluation remained limited, the text prompts were overly simplistic and unrealistic, and the proposed method offered limited methodological novelty beyond integrating text guidance into the existing MELD framework. While incorporating clinical prior knowledge is an interesting direction, the current evidence is insufficient to demonstrate a substantial technical advance or broad generalizability, leading to my recommendation of Reject.

This has been a difficult choice as I have some mixed feelings after reading the paper and checking all comments post-rebuttal. On the positive side, I think the main inspiration for the proposal is sound and interesting. If for pre-operative scans there is prior knowledge from a radiology report, why not use it? On the negative side (and this is mostly highlighted by reviewer #3 in their original comments and post-rebuttal), the evaluation has some issues and the final implementation of “texts prompts” is questionable. I am not entirely convinced by the rebuttal, especially on the “text prompt” part and that may be caused by the fact that I have seen other papers with LLMs that suffer from similar issues. The advantage of model for radiological reports is their ability to extract meaningful information from unstructured text reports. The “text prompt” here are simple and essentially amount to categorical variables (could just be one-hot encoded vectors). The use of a LLM for the current implementation is not well justified.
However, and this is where my final decision comes from, the authors agreed to contextualise their work and explain that the results might not be representative to a real setup with text reports and for this paper in particular I think the strengths and novel-ish idea is good enough for acceptance. I would still advise the authors to extend their current work with real radiological reports for a more impactful work.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer. The meta-review highlights three themes (text generation, gating, evaluation choices), grouped below.
[1] Text input: source and realism (R1, R2, MR) R2 raises a concern that the text appears circular (MELD predictions
re-fed into MELD). We respectfully clarify this is not the case: textual descriptions are derived from ground-truth lesion masks registered to template space via AtlasReader (Sec. 3.1), following MELD’s localization procedure but using GT, not model output. The goal is a methodological proof of concept that text representations of coarse anatomical priors can guide detection. We agree this setup is an upper-bound evaluation, performance may degrade with noisy clinical text, and radiology notes or EEG findings are the natural next step. Such data was not consistently available across the 23-center MELD cohort. This is discussed in Sec. 5 and we will make it more explicit, as requested by R1.
[2] Distance gating: rationale and bias (R2, R3, MR)
The gating uses the existing MELD signed-distance head (Sec. 2.3): inside lesions distances are negative, outside they are positive and grow with distance from the boundary. FP clusters in healthy cortex retain high positive distances and are filtered, while true-lesion clusters contain near-/negative-distance vertices and are kept. The Youden’s J threshold is positive on our data; therefore, as long as distance predictions are accurate, true-positive clusters are not filtered regardless of lesion size. Empirically, sensitivity is largely preserved on both cohorts (Tables 2-3) while specificity rises from 27.5% to 93.3% (main) and 37.3% to 94.0% (Bonn).
[3] Evaluation choices and ablations (R1, R2, R3, MR) R3 states evaluation is on a single dataset. We respectfully note Sec. 3.1 describes two cohorts: the multi-center MELD cohort (23 centers, 1.5T/3T) and the independent Bonn cohort as external test set. Improvements over MELD are consistent on both, supporting generalizability. 
R2 notes MELD+gating outperforms Vision+LM on some specificity metrics (Table 4). Our objective is improved sensitivity, the clinical bottleneck in FCD detection. Vision+LM detects more lesions and yields higher IoU, particularly on Bonn (sensitivity 78.0% vs 69.5%, IoU 0.306 vs 0.218); we view this as a sensitivity-specificity trade-off and will frame it as such in the revision.
R1 asks whether gains stem from text or from the modified decoder. In an unreported ablation, Vision+LM with “unclear” prompts at inference (no localization content) shows no consistent gains over MELD; gains appear only with informative prompts, indicating the contribution is not purely architectural. If permitted, we will add a note on this ablation to the final version.
Reviewer-specific points
R1: HexUnpool preserves the icosphere mesh correspondence during upsampling, ensuring consistent feature propagation across resolutions and integrating naturally with SpiralConv, unlike generic interpolation.
The RadBERT citation was a preparation error and will be corrected.
IoU and Dice are monotonically related (Dice = 2*IoU/(1+IoU)); we used IoU per the MELD protocol for direct comparability.
R3: The surface formulation follows MELD and is motivated by FCD manifesting as subtle cortical morphological/signal changes along the cortical sheet; the model performs vertex-wise lesion prediction, a segmentation task in surface-based neuroimaging, not parcellation. The loss exactly follows MELD (Sec. 3.2) for fair comparison. IoU values are in line with published MELD on this challenging task; the relevant signal is consistent improvement on both cohorts. We will improve methods clarity and will release code upon acceptance.

title: Text-Deficient Multimodal Stroke Segmentation with Lesion-Grounded Self-Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract:
Acute ischemic stroke requires rapid delineation of infarct
core on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) to guide time-critical decisions. Clinical urgency yields preliminary reporting as an early workflow summary centered on lesion location and extent, which enables report-conditioned multimodal segmentation. Paradoxically, the same urgency also makes preliminary reports frequently missing or inconsistently archived in retrospective cohorts, creating a key bottleneck for multimodal stroke segmentation. To address this gap, we present (i) Lesion-Grounded Self-Retrieval-Augmented Generation (LeG-RAG), a training pipeline that retrieves lesion-concordant reports using atlas-normalized lesion masks and synthesizes missing reports with a multimodal large language model without additional training, and (ii) LLMSwin, a report-conditioned multimodal segmentation architecture for brain MRI that extracts text features by combining the report with learnable prompts and feeding them into a frozen Llama-3-8B-Instruct model, and fuses these representations with multi-scale features from a SwinUNETR 3D backbone via two-way transformers. Experiments on a multi-institutional 3D stroke MRI dataset show that LeG-RAG achieves superior retrieval performance compared with state-of-the-art image-embedding methods across text-deficiency regimes, while remaining diagnostically consistent under ASPECTS-based reliability checks. LLMSwin achieves state-of-the-art segmentation across text-availability settings, outperforming image-only and prior multimodal segmentation baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/HeeseongEom/LeG-RAG.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs
Machine Learning -> Synthetic Data / Data-centric AI

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
this paper presented a pipeline for handling text-deficient multimodal stroke segmentation. To do so, the authors proposed LEG-RAG to retrieve lesion-matched reports and synthesize missing ones, and then use these reports in a report-conditioned segmentation model, LLMSwin. 
The experiments are fairly complete as well, with evaluations on report quality, segmentation performance and ablation studies.
reviews.text_strengths:
this is a meaningful problem to study. the paper targeted a practical clinical problem rather than an artificial benchmark setting, where missing or inconsistently stored reports are common in retrospective datasets.
the paper does not just add text as an auxiliary input, but builds a full framework for retrieving, generating, and using missing reports. The lesion-grounded retrieval idea is also well motivated, since it uses atlas-aligned lesion information to find more clinically relevant examples than generic embedding similarity.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.the technical novelty is not extremely strong at the component level. Most of the main ingredients, such as retrieval-augmented generation, frozen LLM-based text encoding, prompt tuning, and transformer-based multimodal fusion, are already established ideas. So the contribution feels more like a well-designed integration of existing methods than a fundamentally new methodological innovation. 
2 In addition, since the retrieval process depends on atlas-space lesion masks, the broader applicability of the framework to other settings may need more discussion.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

this is a solid paper with a well-motivated problem setting and a complete system design. I think the work is interesting and useful, especially from an application perspective. However, the innovation is more moderate, since much of the framework is built by adapting and combining existing techniques. In that sense, the paper is stronger as a problem-driven multimodal system paper than as a fundamentally new method paper.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses the common issue of missing reports in stroke imaging cohorts by proposing the LeG-RAG framework. This framework uses lesion mask-driven retrieval and large model synthesis to fill in textual gaps. Simultaneously, the LLMSwin architecture is designed, utilizing frozen Llama-3 data to extract textual features and fusing them with the SwinUNETR 3D backbone network for segmentation.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The proposed LeG-RAG framework attempts to inversely complete the clinical context using atlas-normalized masks. This approach, which utilizes large language models (LLM) to achieve a closed loop in clinical reasoning, has practical application potential.
2.LLMSwin employs a dual-path Transformer to effectively align 3D spatial features with LLM semantics, achieving a good balance between parameter efficiency and segmentation performance.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The MLLM and LLM models used in this article are general-purpose models, and neither is easily considered state-of-the-art, as they generally perform poorly on medical data. Also the BiomedCLIP. Consider using LLM models fine-tuned for medical data, such as Medgemma and Fleming-R1, and also consider more advanced general-purpose LLM models such as ChatGPT/Gemini/DeepSeek (if available), or open-source models like Llama4/Qwen3.5.Similarly, consider MLLM models such as MediX-R1/MedMO/Fleming-VL.
2.In spatial key-value retrieval, a cosine similarity threshold of delta = 0 is set. Due to the sparsity of 3D space, delta = 0 almost loses its filtering significance, which may lead to excessive load on the subsequent clinical context retrieval system and the introduction of a large number of noisy cases. Supplementary sensitivity experiments on delta (e.g., delta in [0, 0.05, 0.1]) are required to analyze its impact on retrieval efficiency and final segmentation accuracy.
3.The final testing phase inputs images and corresponding reports to output the final segmentation results, similar to Sam3.Furthermore, there are existing methods to fine-tune Sam3 on medical data (https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2511.19046), and a comparison of these methods is requested.
4.In Table 1, LLMSwin achieves a segmentation accuracy (DSC) that matches the upper limit of 80% of real text when the text availability is only 20%. Please check and report the specific components of the dataset used in Stage/Laterality/Territory/Middle Cerebral Artery/HemorrhagicTransformation and analyze whether overfitting exists in the synthesized text.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper has clinical application potential and a reasonable structural design, but it lacks professionalism in model medicine, lacks comparison with advanced models, and suffers from insufficient interpretability of its abnormally high performance conclusions. Furthermore, the experimental rigor has not yet reached the acceptable threshold.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The main contributions of this paper are:
1.LeG-RAG - a lesion-grounded retrieval-andsynthesis framework for text-deficient stroke training.
2.LLMSwin - a reportconditioned volumetric multimodal segmentation architecture.
3.Comprehensive evaluation showing improved synthesized-report quality and robust segmentation under text deficiency.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Strong Performance: LLMSwin achieves state-of-the-art results across various text-availability settings.
2.Ablation Studies: The paper includes clear ablations showing that the combination of DSC and HD95 in the retrieval process is superior to using either metric alone.
3.Generalizability: Testing on two held-out sets (Test A and Test B) from multiple institutions suggests the model is robust.
reviews.text_weaknesses: 1.Inference Efficiency: While the performance is strong, the use of a Llama-3-8B model—even when frozen—introduces significant computational overhead. A brief discussion on inference latency compared to traditional U-Net architectures would be beneficial.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

1.Clinical Relevance and Impact: The paper addresses a highly practical bottleneck in clinical AI: the missing or inconsistent archiving of preliminary reports in retrospective stroke cohorts. By enabling report-conditioned segmentation even when text is missing, the work aligns well with real-world clinical workflows.
2.Methodological Innovation: The LeG-RAG pipeline introduces a clever, spatially grounded retrieval strategy. Instead of relying on generic image embeddings, it uses atlas-normalized lesion masks to retrieve contextually relevant reports. The inclusion of the Clinical Context Score (CCS), combining Dice similarity and Hausdorff distance, is a well-motivated technical contribution for medical imaging.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text: I align with the overall consensus reached by the reviewers

title: Text-Guided Multi-frequency Latent Diffusion for Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: In latent diffusion-based segmentation, the model is trained to recover anatomically consistent regions from noisy latent mask representations conditioned on the input image. Recent diffusion-based approaches provide strong generative priors, but their conditioning is often limited to image or latent features, without explicit structural or semantic guidance. This may lead to unstable predictions and imprecise boundary delineation. In this work, we propose a text-guided multi-frequency latent diffusion framework for medical image segmentation, termed TMF-Seg. The model introduces an Image–Text Conditional Fusion module that encodes image and text conditions and integrates them through cross-attention to obtain a semantically informed representation. We further design a Text-Guided Multi-Frequency Enhancement module that decomposes the fused features into high-, mid-, and low-frequency components and adaptively reweights them according to the textual context, providing complementary semantic and structural priors for the diffusion process. The enhanced conditional features are then fed into a latent diffusion U-Net for efficient single-step segmentation. Experiments on three public datasets, Kvasir-SEG, MosMedData+, and QaTa-COV19, show that TMF-Seg consistently improves segmentation accuracy over several strong baselines. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/qczggaoqiang/TMF-Seg.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper proposes TMF-Seg, a latent diffusion framework for medical image segmentation that strengthens the conditioning pathway rather than modifying the diffusion backbone itself. The method adds two main components:
an Image–Text Conditional Fusion (ITCF) module that uses cross-attention to fuse image latents with text embeddings from Bio-ClinicalBERT, and
a Text-Guided Multi-Frequency Enhancement (TGME) module that decomposes fused features into high-, mid-, and low-frequency components and adaptively reweights them according to text-derived semantic context.
The authors keep the autoencoder and diffusion model frozen and train only the proposed condition encoder. They evaluate the approach on three public datasets—Kvasir-SEG, MosMedData+, and QaTa-COV19—and report consistent gains over CNN, CNN-transformer, and latent-diffusion baselines, with additional ablation evidence supporting the contribution of the ITCF and TGME modules.
reviews.text_strengths:
Clear methodological idea. The paper has a focused contribution: improving latent diffusion segmentation by enriching the conditioning signal with both semantic guidance from text and structural guidance from frequency-aware enhancement. This is more coherent than papers that combine many loosely connected modules. 
Well-motivated design. The paper argues that latent diffusion segmentation quality depends strongly on conditioning, and that image-only conditioning may not provide enough semantic or structural guidance in hard regions. The proposed ITCF and TGME directly target this motivation. 
Architectural modularity. A practical strength is that the method leaves the autoencoder and diffusion backbone frozen and only redesigns the condition encoder. This makes the contribution relatively modular and easier to integrate into existing latent diffusion segmentation pipelines. 
Reasonable empirical coverage. The method is tested on three public datasets spanning colonoscopy, CT, and chest X-ray segmentation, which is better than validating on only a single dataset or modality. 
Consistent quantitative improvements. The paper reports that TMF-Seg outperforms all listed baselines across the three datasets. Compared with SDSeg, the gains are modest but consistent:
Kvasir-SEG Dice: 91.03 → 92.63
MosMedData+ Dice: 80.97 → 81.34
QaTa-COV19 Dice: 89.92 → 91.42.
Ablation study supports both modules. On QaTa-COV19, adding ITCF or TGME individually improves over SDSeg, and the full model performs best, supporting complementarity between the two components. 
Paper organization is straightforward. The framework diagram and module descriptions are reasonably easy to follow, and the method-to-experiment flow is logical. The figures on pages 3–4 help clarify the overall pipeline and the TGME design.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Novelty appears incremental rather than strong. The paper combines known ingredients—latent diffusion segmentation, image-text fusion via cross-attention, and frequency-based feature decomposition/reweighting. The contribution is a sensible integration of these ideas, but based on the paper alone it does not yet read as a fundamentally new segmentation paradigm. The closest prior art cited by the paper already includes text-guided segmentation/diffusion and texture/semantic enhancement, so the novelty margin over existing latent diffusion conditioning approaches seems moderate. The paper should position itself more sharply against recent text-guided and semantics-enhanced segmentation works, especially SDSeg, TSLDeg, LViT, STPNet, and the cited text-guided diffusion literature. 
Text supervision is insufficiently specified. A central claim is that the method benefits from textual descriptions, but the paper does not clearly explain where these text descriptions come from, how they are constructed for each dataset, whether they are standardized templates, whether they are manually curated, and what information they contain relative to the mask labels. This is important because performance may depend substantially on prompt design and text quality. Without this detail, both fairness and reproducibility are weakened. The method section states that the input consists of an image and its textual description, but the dataset section does not explain the source of the text. 
Limited analysis of the text contribution. Although the ablation shows ITCF helps, there is no deeper study of text robustness: e. g. , different prompt templates, noisy/incorrect text, empty text, generic text, or prompt sensitivity across datasets. Because the paper’s main claim is text-guided segmentation, this missing analysis is noticeable. 
Ablation scope is narrow. The ablation is conducted only on QaTa-COV19.Stronger support would come from at least one additional dataset, and ideally from analysis of frequency-band weights, DCT design choices, or alternative fusion baselines. 
No statistical analysis or variance reporting. The reported gains on some datasets are fairly small, especially on MosMedData+. The paper does not report standard deviations, confidence intervals, or multi-seed results, so it is hard to judge whether the improvements are robust. 
Limited efficiency discussion. The paper states training hardware and basic settings, but does not quantify added computational overhead, parameter increase, or inference-time cost relative to SDSeg. Since the method adds text encoding and multi-frequency branches, such analysis would strengthen the practical case. 
Clinical impact remains indirect. The datasets are public and diverse, but there is no validation on a clinical workflow, no expert reader study, and no downstream task analysis. So the work is best viewed as a methodological paper rather than a clinically translated contribution
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The paper addresses an interesting direction for diffusion-based segmentation by enriching the conditioning pathway with language and frequency-aware structure modeling. The overall framework is coherent and the empirical results are promising. To strengthen the paper, I encourage the authors to clarify the provenance and construction of the text descriptions for all datasets, add a more comprehensive comparison to closely related text-guided/semantic-enhanced segmentation methods, and include stronger robustness analysis around prompt quality and statistical significance. A runtime/parameter comparison against SDSeg would also improve the practical evaluation

I lean Weak Accept because the paper presents a coherent and technically sound improvement to latent diffusion segmentation, supported by consistent gains on three public datasets and a reasonable ablation showing the benefit of both proposed modules. The idea of strengthening diffusion conditioning using image-text fusion and text-guided multi-frequency enhancement is sensible and appears effective in practice.
At the same time, I do not view the novelty as especially high. The work appears more like a careful combination of existing ideas than a major conceptual advance, and the paper does not yet analyze several important issues deeply enough—especially the origin and role of the text descriptions, robustness to prompt design, statistical significance of the gains, and computational overhead. The ablation is also limited to one dataset. These limitations prevent me from scoring it as a clear accept. Still, the method is well motivated, the empirical results are positive, and the contribution seems above the rejection threshold for a methodological MICCAI paper

reviews.text_contribution:
This paper proposes TMF-Seg, a text-guided multi-frequency latent diffusion framework for medical image segmentation. The core contributions are:
1.Propose an Image-Text Conditional Fusion (ITCF) module that fuses image latent features and medical text embeddings via cross-attention to inject semantic guidance into diffusion-based segmentation.
2.Design a Text-Guided Multi-Frequency Enhancement (TGME) module that decomposes fused features into high/mid/low frequency components via DCT and adaptively weights them using text semantics to strengthen structural and boundary priors.
3.Enhance the conditioning of a frozen latent diffusion model to achieve more accurate and stable segmentation, validated on three public datasets (Kvasir-SEG, MosMedData+, QaTa-COV19).
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Compared to prior works, this work innovatively integrates textual semantics and multi-frequency structural modeling into the diffusion conditioning, which is well justified for medical images with ambiguous boundaries and low contrast.
2.The TGME module uses DCT-based frequency decomposition and text-guided adaptive weighting. It allows the model to dynamically emphasize high-frequency details (boundaries), mid-frequency structures, or low-frequency global context based on textual prompts. This is biologically plausible and practically beneficial for medical segmentation. 
3.The experiments are complete, and the evaluated datasets are diverse. 
4.The paper is well organized, with intuitive figures and reasonable explanations. The motivation, method, and logic are easy to follow.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The training loss was not descripted in the whole paper. Please add this content.
2.Can you ensure the alignment between image and text features? How to verify if text and images are aligned? Please provide corresponding attention map.
3.The novelty in core technical components is limited, for example, the ITCF module uses standard cross-attention for image-text fusion.
4.The paper does not provide examples or details of the text prompts used for each dataset. Please provide the details of the text prompts. 
5.No robustness testing on noisy, low-quality, or pathological images.
6.Please provide detailed training strategy, such as loss functions.

The novelty is relatively limited, and its clinical application will be evaluated.

reviews.text_contribution:
1.The main novelty is the DCT-based multi-frequency design. The model splits the fused feature into high-, mid-, and low-frequency parts. This lets the model handle fine details, boundaries, and global structure in a more explicit way.
2.The text feature is used to predict the weight of each frequency branch. This means the model can adaptively decide which frequency information is more important for the current image.
reviews.text_strengths: A major strength of the paper is the method design. The model decomposes the fused feature into different frequency components, which gives a more fine-grained way to model details, boundaries, and global structure. It then uses a weighting module to adaptively combine these frequency branches, so the text signal can provide more effective guidance during segmentation. This module provides a new angle for fusing text features and image features.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) A major weakness is that the ablation study is limited to module-level comparisons. It only shows that the proposed module is useful as a whole, but it does not verify whether the high-, mid-, and low-frequency branches actually capture the different types of information claimed by the authors, such as fine details, boundaries, and global structure. Therefore, the current experiments do not fully support the interpretation of the proposed frequency decomposition design. 
2) In addition, the paper does not provide enough analysis of the adaptive weighting process, for example how the weights are distributed across different frequency branches in practice. More experimental evidence would be helpful to clarify the contribution of the frequency decomposition design to the fusion of text and image features.
3) The related work discussion is not sufficient, author/s should discuss existing works that adopt Multi-Frequency in greater domain and differentiate the contribution against them.

N/A

The paper has a clear idea, and the method is interesting. In particular, the frequency decomposition design gives a new way to fuse text and image features, and the results are better than several baselines. However, the current evidence is not strong enough to fully support the main claim of the paper. The ablation study is limited to module-level comparisons, so it does not show whether the high-, mid-, and low-frequency branches really capture different types of information, as claimed by the authors. The paper also lacks an analysis of the adaptive weighting process, for example, how the weights are distributed across the three frequency branches.
