reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Although the paper does not introduce a fundamentally new methodological idea, it presents a meaningful application that demonstrates the feasibility and practical value of applying the multi-frequency concept in this setting. The rebuttal has clarified several of my concerns. Given the limited space of the MICCAI format, the paper is acceptable.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper introduces TMF-Seg, a text-guided multi-frequency latent diffusion framework that enhances medical image segmentation via image-text fusion and adaptive frequency feature reweighting. Reviewers commend the modular design, consistent performance gains across three diverse public datasets, and intuitive integration of clinical text semantics and structural frequency information. There are some limitations which include incremental technical novelty, incomplete text prompt documentation, and narrow ablation studies that fail to fully validate frequency branch functionality and cross-modal alignment.

Most of concerns have been addressed or clearified adequately.

Overall, the work appears above the acceptance threshold. The contribution is not a major conceptual breakthrough, and several analyses would still strengthen the paper, but the method is well motivated, the reported improvements are consistent, and the rebuttal resolves enough of the key methodological and reproducibility concerns to support acceptance.
three accept, i agree.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their positive feedback on the novel method design (R1, R2, R4), effective experimental results (R1, R2), clear organization (R1, R2), and ablation study (R1), and thank the AC for acknowledging these strengths. Following the rebuttal guidelines, we address remaining concerns below without new experiments.
Q1: Frequency branch validation (R4)
We clarify that the three frequency branches are defined by pre-defined, non-overlapping DCT coefficient index sets registered as fixed buffers (not learned): high-freq uses top-16 DCT indices (capturing fine-grained details and boundaries), mid-freq uses low-8 indices (structural transitions), and low-freq uses bottom-8 indices (global anatomical context). These index sets are mathematically disjoint by construction, guaranteeing spectral separation. The DCT filters are fixed (register_buffer), so each branch provably receives distinct frequency content.
Q2: Adaptive weight distribution analysis (R4)
The text-to-frequency mapping is a two-layer MLP (768→128→3) followed by Softmax, producing per-sample weights α_h+α_m+α_l=1 conditioned on each sample’s textual description via mean-pooled Bio-ClinicalBERT embeddings. For example, “Bilateral pulmonary infection, two infected areas, all left lung and all right lung.” and “one medium white round polyp, located in center of the image” encode very different semantic signals, leading to different frequency weight distributions. The Grad-CAM results in Fig. 4 further confirm that TGME shifts attention toward structure-aware regions, consistent with text-driven frequency modulation.
Q3: Text prompt details (R1, R2)
Text descriptions are publicly available clinical annotations. For QaTa-COV19 and MosMedData+, they are released by LViT [10] authors as structured annotations (.xlsx format) and described with specific lesion characteristics per image (e.g., for one QaTa-COV19 sample: “Bilateral pulmonary infection, three infected areas, upper middle lower left lung and upper middle lower right lung”). For Kvasir-SEG, descriptions were obtained from corresponding paper authors upon request and will be released with our code upon acceptance. All prompts are per-image clinical descriptions providing inherent semantic diversity rather than generic templates. Text robustness analysis is feasible and will be explored.
Q4: Training loss and variance reporting (R2,R1)
Following SDSeg [12], we adopt L = L_noise + λL_latent, where L_noise predicts Gaussian noise and L_latent minimizes latent estimation error (λ=1, both MAE). Only the condition encoder (ITCF+TGME) is trained; Diffusion backbone and autoencoder remain frozen. Variance reporting and statistical analysis will be included in the revised paper.
Q5: Related work on multi-frequency methods (R4)
Our TGME differs from prior multi-frequency works (e.g., [15]) in two key aspects: (1) frequency decomposition is applied in the latent conditioning space rather than image space, which is novel for diffusion-based segmentation; (2) frequency reweighting is dynamically text-guided per sample, rather than statically learned. We will expand the related work discussion to highlight these distinctions.
Q6: Cross-modal fusion design and alignment (R2)
Cross-attention in ITCF computes attention scores between each spatial image position (query) and text tokens (key/value), enabling image features to selectively attend to semantically relevant textual cues. Grad-CAM improvements in Fig. 4 support that meaningful semantic alignment is learned. We will include explicit cross-attention map visualizations upon acceptance.
Q7: Novelty (R1, R2)
The contribution lies in the principled integration of text-guided semantic conditioning and frequency-domain structural priors within latent diffusion conditioning, unexplored for medical image segmentation. Consistent gains over SDSeg, TSLDeg, and LViT (Table 1) support its practical value.

title: TGBD-Net: Tumor-Guided Bridging Distillation for Joint EGFR Mutation and Survival Prediction in Lung Cancer from CT Imaging
abstract: Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutation prediction and progression-free survival (PFS) prediction are critical tasks for targeted therapy planning in lung cancer and can be jointly modeled from the same chest CT scan. In real-world clinical datasets, supervision is often inconsistent across patients: not all patients have labels for both tasks and tumor region annotations, leading to heterogeneous supervision across different patient subsets. However, most existing multi-task learning methods leverage a single shared representation across tasks, with limited consideration of representation consistency during training on these differently supervised patient subsets. In this study, we propose the Tumor-Guided Bridging Distillation Network (TGBD-Net), a unified framework for stabilizing representation learning under heterogeneous supervision, enabling joint EGFR mutation and PFS prediction. The proposed Tumor-Guided Feature Extraction (TGF) module regularizes feature learning using available tumor region annotations, while maintaining consistent behavior when such annotations are unavailable. In addition, a Bridging Distillation (BD) module enables cross-task knowledge transfer, allowing patients with single-task labels to contribute to joint representation learning. Experiments on a cohort of 7,348 patients with lung cancer demonstrate that TGBD-Net achieves an AUC of 0.823 for EGFR mutation prediction and a C-index of 0.743 for PFS prediction, highlighting its effectiveness in real clinical settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/MenchYoung/TGBD-Net.
subject_areas: Applications -> Outcome Prediction / Prognosis / Longitudinal Modeling

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose a Tumor-Guided Bridging Distillation Network (TGBD-Net), a unified framework designed to enable stable feature representation learning under heterogeneous supervision, while simultaneously supporting EGFR mutation prediction and PFS estimation.
reviews.text_strengths: The main contributions are summarized as follows: (1) a unified framework that incorporates patients with single-task labels into joint learning; (2) two complementary representation-level mechanisms that regularize feature formation without requiring tumor annotations for all patients, and enable knowledge transfer across patient subsets with different task labels in a shared representation space; (3) extensive experiments on 7,348 patients demonstrating the robustness of TGBD-Net across multiple tasks.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Methodology:
1、The organization and input pipeline of data for different tasks are not clearly described (i. e. , how different tasks are constructed). For each task, what do the classification and regression heads specifically output? 
2、 How is qtg obtained and trained? 
3、 Compared with other cross-attention mechanisms, what are the key innovations of the TGF module? 
4、 How are the teacher and student models explicitly defined in the bridging distillation process?
Experiments:
1、 The authors do not explain why TGBD-Net does not achieve the best performance in terms of sensitivity and specificity. 
2、Although extensive comparative experiments are conducted, the paper does not present the detection performance of single-task learning under different supervision settings.

N/A

The authors present a notable and innovative idea that effectively addresses a challenging problem in this domain.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes TGBD-Net, a multi-task learning framework for joint EGFR mutation status classification and progression-free survival (PFS) prediction from chest CT scans . The key idea is that real-world clinical datasets include patients with varying label availability and partial tumor-region annotations. Two complementary modules are proposed: (1) a Tumor-Guided Feature Extraction (TGF) module that uses cross-attention to incorporate tumor region information when bounding box annotations are available, and (2) a Bridging Distillation (BD) module that transfers cross-task supervision through a set of periodically updated anchor prototypes, enabling partially labeled patients to contribute to joint representation learning.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Clinically motivated problem formulation. Heterogeneous supervision (partial labels, partial annotations) is a genuine, under-addressed challenge in real-world clinical ML. Framing MTL under this constraint is practically relevant.
2.Well-designed BD module. The anchor-based bidirectional distillation mechanism is technically interesting; using K-means prototypes with Hungarian matching to preserve identity across updates is a thoughtful design choice. The two-stage (attribute update → soft label distillation) formulation is clean and clearly explained.
3.Large-scale evaluation. 7,348 patients are a large cohort for this task domain, lending credibility to the reported performance figures.
4.Thorough ablations. The three ablation studies — module combinations, alignment strategies/feature choices, and anchor parameterization strategies — are well-structured and provide meaningful insight into each design decision.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Single-institution data, no external validation. All 7,348 patients are from one hospital. Without external validation, it is unclear whether the learned representations generalize across scanners, protocols, or institutions.
2.Severe label imbalance in the joint set. Only 383 patients have both EGFR and PFS labels, versus 6,484 with EGFR-only. The BD module is designed to exploit partially labeled samples, but with such an extreme imbalance, the learned anchor attributes for survival may be unreliable. The paper does not analyze sensitivity to this imbalance.
3.PFS test set is very small. The test set contains 735 patients total, but only a fraction have PFS labels (roughly ~96 based on the 8:1:1 split of 481 PFS patients). KM curves show only 86 patients. 
4.TGF module design has limited novelty. The tumor-guided cross-attention with conditional alignment is a reasonable engineering choice, but cross-attention with partial supervision is well-established. The claim of novelty here should be more carefully scoped relative to existing tumor-region attention methods in the CT radiogenomics literature (e.g., the MICCAI 2025 paper by Huang et al. (Feature copy paste) on EGFR prediction is cited but not compared against).
5.No comparison against the most relevant prior work on heterogeneous MTL for medical imaging. JTR-MTL (Nishi et al., CVPR 2024) is the closest baseline and was designed specifically for partially labeled MTL, yet the paper does not discuss why TGBD-Net’s BD mechanism is preferable; the analysis remains quantitative only.
6.Hyperparameter sensitivity not analyzed. K=4 anchors, τ=0.2, α=0.9, β=0.5 are set without any sensitivity analysis. Given that these govern the distillation quality, this is an important omission.
7.Model selection criterion is asymmetric. The best model is chosen based on validation AUC (EGFR), and the same checkpoint is used for PFS evaluation. This may systematically favor EGFR performance; a joint validation criterion would be more principled.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses a real clinical problem, and the BD mechanism is technically novel. If the authors address the weakness, I can think about improving the score.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes TGBD-Net for joint EGFR mutation and PFS prediction from chest CT with heterogeneous supervision. I think the main contribution is that the authors combine anchor-based task memory, task-specific attribute accumulation, and similarity-weighted soft label distillation in a quite nice way. Because of this design, cases with only one task label can still provide some information for joint training. The tumor-guided feature module is another helpful part, since it uses available tumor annotations to guide the shared representation, but does not require annotation for every patient. Overall, the contribution is mainly this combined framework for partially labeled multi-task learning.
reviews.text_strengths:
A main strength of the paper is the BD design. I think the way the authors connect anchor-based task memory, task-specific attribute accumulation, and similarity-weighted soft label distillation is quite nice. This makes the framework more than a standard shared-backbone multi-task model, and it gives a reasonable way for partially labeled cases to still contribute across tasks through the shared anchors.
Another strength is that this design may help the model capture EGFR-associated radiographic patterns in a more structured way, instead of only relying on a single global shared feature. Together with the tumor-guided feature module, the method tries to organize phenotype-related information in the shared representation while still handling missing labels and missing tumor annotations.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The survival part is still a weakness. PFS is one of the main endpoints, but the paper does not clearly explain the PFS definition, censoring details, or treatment background. Also, the number of PFS cases is much smaller than the EGFR cohort, so the survival results need stronger support.
Another weakness is that some interpretation is a bit too strong. TGF alone improves EGFR prediction, but it does not improve the C-index over the baseline, and the tumor-guided feature is much worse than the final fused feature for PFS. So while the full model works better overall, the role of TGF should be discussed more carefully.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I gave this paper a weak accept because I think the idea is interesting and the overall method is reasonably well designed. In particular, the BD part is a nice way to connect partially labeled cases across tasks, and the full model gives the best overall results in both EGFR prediction and PFS prediction. The ablation study also supports that the full design is better than the simpler variants. I still have some concerns about the survival part and a few claims that could be written more carefully, but overall I think the paper has enough technical value and practical relevance to be accepted.

meta_reviews.text: All positive reviews

author_feedback_text:
1.TGF novelty and methodological role
Re to R1-C3, R2-C4: The key contribution of TGF is enabling tumor-guided representation regularization under partially available annotations, where attention patterns learned from annotated samples can be implicitly transferred to unannotated patients. Our work primarily focuses on joint EGFR/PFS learning with partially available labels and annotations, which differs from FCP-Net (MICCAI 2025 Huang et al.), which addresses slice-thickness variability through feature copy-paste for EGFR prediction. Re to R3-C2: TGF mainly enhances tumor-focused features, which is more beneficial for EGFR prediction due to tumor morphological patterns in CT, while PFS prediction may require broader surrounding tissue environment. Therefore, the full TGF+BD framework achieves the best overall PFS performance.
2.BD Module and difference from existing MTL methods
Re to R1-C4: In BD, anchor-level attributes accumulated from labeled patients serve as teacher signals, while partially labeled patients act as students through bidirectional soft distillation (Sec. 2.2). Re to R2-C5: Compared with JTR-MTL and other optimization-level MTL approaches that mainly address task conflicts or dynamic weighting, BD performs representation-level regularization through bridging anchors in a shared semantic space.
3.Survival cohort, heterogeneous supervision and generalization
Re to R2-C1/3, R3-C1: PFS was defined as the time from the initiation of treatment (EGFR-TKI) to the progression of the disease with regular follow-up; 18.5% cases were censored. External multicenter validation will be explored in future work. The PFS cohort is smaller than the EGFR cohort due to the limited availability of longitudinal follow-up data in real-world clinical settings. Nevertheless, the cohort includes heterogeneous acquisition conditions (e.g., varying CT slice thicknesses of 3–8 mm), partially mitigating overfitting to a single acquisition condition. Additionally, compared with many imaging-based survival studies, the current cohort remains relatively large-scale for PFS modeling. Re to R2-C2: To alleviate label imbalance, we adopted a weighted sampling strategy to increase the exposure of PFS samples during training (Sec.3.2). The motivation of BD is to improve PFS learning through joint supervision from the larger EGFR cohort under heterogeneous labeling. Despite limited PFS labels, TGBD-Net achieved the best survival performance among all baselines, supporting the effectiveness of the learned anchor attributes. 
4.Experiments and evaluation
Re to R1-Exp1/2: Regarding sensitivity/specificity, TGBD-Net achieves the best overall balance between the two metrics while also obtaining the best AUC and C-index. Table 1 includes corresponding single-task baselines (e.g., ResNet, Swin Transformer, DeepSurv), while Sup.-MTL demonstrates that simple joint learning improves over separate single-task modeling. Heterogeneous supervision is only defined in the joint multi-task setting. Re to R2-C7: Since the EGFR cohort is larger, validation AUC provides a relatively more stable selection criterion. All methods were evaluated under the same selection protocol to ensure fair comparison, and TGBD-Net still achieved the best survival performance, suggesting that the learned shared representation does not overfit to EGFR alone.
5.Additional clarifications
Re to R1-C1/2: The dataset can be divided according to task labels (EGFR-only/PFS-only/both) and annotation availability, which are unified through the loss routing in Eq. (5). The EGFR head outputs classification logits, while the PFS head outputs a survival risk score. qtg is a learnable token with the same feature dimension as fg in TGF, acting as a tumor-guided prior optimized end-to-end (Sec 2.1). Re to R2-C6: Hyperparameter sensitivity experiments were conducted for K=2/3/4/6, α=0.8/0.9, β=0.5/1.0.The best-performing settings were selected. Due to page limitations, complete results were omitted.

title: TGH-DB: Template-Guided Heteroscedastic Diffusion Bridge for Brain MRI-to-PET Synthesis
abstract: Amyloid Positron Emission Tomography (PET) plays a critical role in the early diagnosis and staging of neurodegenerative disorders; however, its widespread clinical use is constrained by high costs, radiation exposure, and limited accessibility. Synthesizing amyloid PET from routine structural Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) represents a promising alternative, yet existing methods often yield unreliable, physiologically inconsistent results due to the lack of prior knowledge about amyloid plaque distribution. To address the problem, this work explores population-level amyloid pathology priors with explicit modeling of spatially varying voxel-wise variability and proposes a fully 3D Template-Guided Heteroscedastic Diffusion Bridge (TGH-DB) for brain MRI-to-PET synthesis. The proposed framework introduces a population-level amyloid pathology template, defined by voxel-wise mean and standard deviation estimated from the training cohort, to steer the diffusion process toward an empirically plausible target distribution. Unlike conventional diffusion models that drift toward an isotropic Gaussian prior, our forward process progressively guides PET signals toward the population-level amyloid pathology template with injection of spatially adaptive, heteroscedastic noise, thereby explicitly modeling regional variability in amyloid uptake. To effectively leverage structural information from various MRI modalities, we further develop the Time-Aware Evolutionary Denoiser (TAED) that integrates multimodal MRI information. TAED comprises parallel encoders, Time-Aware Fusion (TAF) modules, and a time-modulated decoding pathway so that different types of MRI information are adaptively exploited during the diffusion process. Extensive experiments on two public datasets demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms representative existing approaches in both quantitative metrics and qualitative visual evaluations.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a template-guided diffusion framework for MRI-to-PET synthesis, where the conventional isotropic Gaussian endpoint is replaced by a population-level amyloid pathology template characterized by voxel-wise mean and standard deviation maps. It further introduces heteroscedastic noise to encode spatially varying population variability and a TAED-based time-aware multimodal MRI fusion mechanism for denoising.
reviews.text_strengths: The work is conceptually coherent and addresses a real weakness of standard diffusion formulations for medical image synthesis, namely the lack of anatomy- and pathology-aware priors. The proposed template-guided endpoint is the most interesting aspect of the paper and gives the method a clearer medical motivation than simply scaling up the denoiser. The methodology is well structured, the paper is generally easy to follow, and the experimental results are reasonably consistent across datasets and tracers. The ablation studies also suggest that the main components contribute meaningfully.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The paper’s strongest claims are somewhat ahead of the evidence: the experiments show improved synthesis quality, but do not directly validate the claimed physiological plausibility of the generated PET images. 
2.The proposed heteroscedastic design appears to capture cohort-level spatial variability rather than truly calibrated subject-level uncertainty, so the uncertainty-related claim may be overstated. 
3.A key assumption of the method—that voxel-wise SUVR distributions approximately follow Gaussian patterns—is asserted but not sufficiently supported by direct statistical evidence. 
4.Because the pathology template is derived from the training cohort, the method may introduce cohort-prior bias, potentially pulling rare but real individual abnormalities toward the population mean. 
5.Although the paper compares against several methods, it does not clearly include some of the most recent and most closely related MRI-to-PET or distribution-guided baselines, which weakens the strength of the SOTA claim.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I lean Weak Accept because the paper is logically sound, the main idea is meaningful, and the code release is a positive factor. However, the manuscript currently over-claims some findings, and the SOTA claim is weakened by missing strong recent baselines. So this is only marginally above the acceptance threshold and depends on the rebuttal. These are important but fixable issues, and if the authors address them well in the rebuttal or revision, I would be quite supportive of acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes 3D diffusion bridge framework for synthesizing brain amyloid PET images from multimodal MRI. Unlike conventional diffusion models that target Gaussian noise, TGH-DB guides the diffusion process toward a population-level amyloid pathology template derived from training data statistics.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Using template-based priors instead of standard Gaussian priors is an effective and novel method to reduce the search space in medical image synthesis.
2.The author proposed voxel-wise variance to capture local variations in amyloid uptake.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The proposed method relies on a population-level template (μ_tpl, σ_tpl) estimated from the training cohort. However, the paper lacks an analysis of how this model performs on completely independent external datasets where the PET intensity distributions might differ. Specifically, I would like to see the distribution gap between the training and test splits within the current datasets.
2.The Time-Aware Fusion (TAF) module and the multi-encoder design add significant complexity compared to simple channel-wise concatenation. While the ablation study shows a drop in performance without TAED, the architectural rationale specifically why individual Swin Transformer encoders are necessary for each modality is not sufficiently detailed.
3.While amyloid-positive/negative classification was performed for the A4 dataset, it was omitted for the HABS-HD dataset, which reportedly includes MCI and AD subjects. Furthermore, classification performance is not reported in the Ablation Study.
4.The paper states that the template is estimated from the training cohort but does not clarify the composition of this cohort. Since amyloid distribution differs significantly between cognitively normal individuals and those with Alzheimer’s disease, using a single unified template might be suboptimal. It is unclear if the authors used only healthy controls for the template or a mixture of subjects.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The idea of Template-Guided diffusion is a significant contribution to the field. However, there are concerns regarding the statistical robustness of the template and the motivation for architectural design choices. If the authors can address the concerns regarding external validation and the impact of disease-specific distributions on the template, I would be willing to increase my score.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have partially addressed my concerns. While the paper is on the borderline, the idea and contributions are strong. I recommend Accept. I hope the remaining concerns raised by the reviewers are addressed in the camera-ready version.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This work explores brain MRI-to-PET synthesis and introduces a population-level amyloid pathology prior, characterized by the mean and standard deviation estimated from the training cohort, to modify the zero-mean, homoscedastic variance setting in the original diffusion process. The method is validated on two public datasets and demonstrates clear improvements in quantitative metrics compared with competing methods.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Redefining the mean and variance of the forward noising process is a novel and interesting design, which differentiates this work from conventional diffusion-based synthesis methods.
2.The experimental comparison is relatively comprehensive, and the proposed method shows clear improvements in quantitative metrics over competing approaches. The inclusion of downstream-task validation further strengthens the evaluation.
3.The ablation study is comprehensive and clearly demonstrates the contribution of each component to the overall performance improvement.
4.The paper is well organized and clearly written, with a logical presentation of the motivation, method, and experiments.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The term “Diffusion bridge” seems not fully appropriate here. The proposed method is still essentially a conditional diffusion model with MRI as the conditioning input. Its main modification lies in redefining the mean and variance of the forward noising process, rather than constructing a bridge process that interpolates between two endpoint distributions, as in diffusion bridge formulations.
2.Public datasets used in this study may exhibit bias in the distribution of amyloid PET phenotypes. For example, the A4 cohort mainly includes cognitively unimpaired individuals with amyloid-positive PET, whereas LEARN and HABS-HD include amyloid-negative subjects and/or participants with different cognitive statuses. The authors should further clarify the proportions of amyloid-positive and amyloid-negative subjects in each training and testing subset, and assess whether such distributional bias may cause the model to favor synthesized PET images with elevated cortical uptake or SUVR. In particular, for MRI inputs from amyloid-negative or non-AD individuals, additional quantitative evaluations are recommended, such as SUVR bias in the negative group, specificity, and false-positive rate, to verify that the model does not systematically generate falsely “positive-like” PET patterns.
3.Normalizing PET images to a standard space facilitates the construction of a population-level template and enables cross-subject comparability of µ_tpl and σ_tpl. However, the required affine and nonlinear transformations may alter individual anatomy. As such, standard-space results are more appropriate for population-level modeling than for direct individual-case presentation. The authors should clarify whether the final output can be mapped back to the original space to support interpretability and practical usability at the subject level.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses a meaningful problem and presents a reasonably novel method. The overall results are promising, and the main idea is well supported. However, a few aspects still require further clarification or additional experiments.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: After reading the authors’ rebuttal, my final recommendation is Accept. The rebuttal has sufficiently addressed my main concerns.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper received 2 weak accept and 1 weak reject. Reviewers agree that this is a novel and well-motivated idea, particularly in introducing pathology-aware priors into diffusion modelling, and the method shows consistent quantitative improvements with solid ablation studies.
Key issues to address in rebuttal include: (1) over-claimed conclusions about physiological plausibility and uncertainty modeling (R1); (2) template bias and generalization concerns, including cohort composition and robustness to distribution shifts (R1, R2, R3); (3) discussion on the limited validation (R2, R3); and (4) method clarity and justification, statistical assumptions (e.g., Gaussian SUVR)(R1, R2, R3).
The authors are encouraged to provide a detailed response to reviewers’ concerns.

This is a strong retuttal. Reviewers’ main concerns are fully addressed.

The rebuttal addressed the main concerns about template bias, architectural motivation, and terminology, and both initially borderline reviewers updated their recommendations to accept. The paper now has a clear consensus toward acceptance, with a novel and well-motivated template-guided diffusion formulation and solid empirical results, while some limitations in physiological interpretation and external validation remain to be refined in future work.

The submission proposes a novel and well-motivated diffusion framework for MRI-to-PET synthesis. Following the rebuttal phase, the initial skepticism has been successfully resolved, leading to a clear consensus for acceptance from all reviewers. In their response, the authors effectively mitigated concerns from the reviewers. The authors must ensure that all clarifications provided in the rebuttal are fully integrated into the final camera-ready version.

author_feedback_text:
Over-claimed physiological plausibility and uncertainty modeling (AC, R1)
We will clarify “physiological plausibility” as empirical spatial distributions and “uncertainty” as voxel-wise variability.
Template bias and generalization (AC, R1, R2, R3)
Our template is used as priors to stabilize ill-posed estimation problems. It is not the sole factor determining the estimation result, where observed data also plays a substantial role in the estimation. Moreover, we used a large number of PET images for template construction, which better represents the population with reduced bias. Finally, we confirm that templates constructed from different cohorts are consistent. The two templates estimated from A4 and HABS-HD show highly similar patterns, with elevated values in posterior cingulate/precuneus, frontal, lateral temporal, and parietal cortices, and lower values in the cerebellar cortex. This suggests that the template captures a stable amyloid-related spatial pattern rather than dataset-specific artifacts.
Template cohort composition (AC, R2)
The template is estimated from all training subjects. In future work, we will construct separate normal and abnormal templates and enable their adaptive integration.
Classification validation and ablation (AC, R2)
We performed amyloid-positive/negative classification on A4 because it is directly aligned with the goal of amyloid PET synthesis. In contrast, MCI/AD is a broader clinical diagnostic task influenced by multiple factors. The classification task was not included in the ablation study because its performance is affected by the classification method, making it harder to attribute performance changes specifically to the ablated component. We will clarify this.
Amyloid status bias (AC, R3)
In A4, the positive proportions in training/validation/test sets are 69.52%/73.03%/68.63%, respectively. TGH-DB achieves PSNR of 31.51/31.63 and SSIM of 92.88/93.19 for amyloid-positive/negative subjects, respectively, indicating stable performance for both subgroups. Moreover, the downstream classification results support that the model does not systematically generate false positive PET patterns.
Gaussian SUVR assumption (AC, R1)
In our preliminary analysis, we randomly sampled a large number of voxels and confirmed that their SUVR distributions show Gaussian patterns. We agree that this should be interpreted as an approximation rather than a strict distributional claim.
Baselines and SOTA claim (R1)
Some recent methods were not included because their task settings differ from ours or code is unavailable. For example, [13] relies on cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers, while [29] synthesizes multi-tracer PET images. We will soften the SOTA claim and state that our method outperforms representative existing methods.
TAF and multi-encoder design (AC, R2)
The multi-encoder and TAF designs are motivated by the complementary roles of T1W and FLAIR. T1W provides structural contrast and FLAIR is sensitive to anomalies. Independent encoders allow the model to preserve modality-specific representations before fusion. Besides, different diffusion time steps require different MRI cues. Therefore, TAF uses time embedding to adaptively modulate the contribution of each modality. The ablation results indicate the benefits of the design.
Diffusion Bridge (R3)
We agree that our method is not a classical diffusion bridge in the strict sense. We use the term “bridge” because the forward process introduces a mean drift term and a heteroscedastic noise term to connect PET images with the template. This directed transition and reverse interpolation among the current latent state, the predicted clean PET, and the template make our formulation resemble a bridge-like diffusion process. We will clarify that our method is bridge-like.
Native-space usability (AC, R3)
The spatial transformation is saved for each subject, and synthesized PET can be mapped back to the native space accordingly.

title: TG-OT: Topology-Guided CCTA-IVUS Registration via Optimal Transport Matching
abstract: Registering coronary CT angiography (CCTA) and intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) enables comprehensive coronary analysis that neither modality can provide alone, yet their fusion remains challenging due to differences in imaging geometry, resolution, and artifact profiles. Existing methods depend on pre-computed lumen or vessel wall segmentations that are unreliable under IVUS acoustic shadowing from calcifications, limiting their clinical applicability. We propose TG-OT, a fully automatic CCTA-IVUS registration framework that eliminates this dependency by integrating trained feature detectors directly into the registration pipeline. Lightweight CNNs are trained to predict calcifications, bifurcations, and lumen radii on the topological (theta, z) cylinder, encouraging topologically coherent detections without requiring explicit segmentation. Registration is formulated as an optimization over centerline warping parameters, driven by an unbalanced Sinkhorn optimal transport loss on the cylindrical geometry that provides spatially informative gradients even for spatially disjoint predictions, complemented by a lumen matching term. Evaluated on N=47 paired CCTA-IVUS cases in a 5-fold cross-validation setup, TG-OT achieves strong longitudinal (Dice_ctl = 0.99), rotational (S_=0.96), and lumen alignment (Dice_L=0.69) without manual interaction or prior segmentation, marking a meaningful step toward clinical integration of automatic CCTA-IVUS fusion.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper describes a novel approach to aligning pullback IVUS images of the coronary arteries with CCTA images. To achieve this, the paper uses unbalanced optimal transport to align segmentation masks in both modalities. The identified transform is then used to locally deform the centerline and rotate cross-sectional views. The method is developed and validated using a unique dataset of IVUS + CCTA images of 47 patients.
reviews.text_strengths:
Using optimal transport for registration is very interesting, in particular in scenarios where little overlap is expected between two masks.
The paper shows good results on challenging data.
The paper is of very high quality, explains all concepts clearly and understandably, and presents a clear ablation study. Figures illustrate the method well.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
While the method is interesting, results do not entirely convincingly show superiority over alternative approaches. Authors compare their OT scheme (the main contribution) with a Dice-based optimization scheme in Table 2.Results indicate that registration with a Dice loss leads to very similar results. In fact, there’s a bit of a mismatch between the single result shown in Fig. 3 and the aggregate results shown in Table 2.In Table 2, I barely see a difference between Dice and OT (also not in terms of Sc), while in Fig. 3, Dice demonstrates an Sc of 0.12 and OT an Sc of 0.96.This example seems to be an outlier.
The Discussion is a bit confusing. It says that ‘the dependency on error-prone intermediate segmentations’ is removed, but as far as I can see, the method directly depends on intermediate segmentations. The difference is not clear to me.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The feature-extraction CNNs are frozen (Fig. 1), but the abstract states that feature detection is integrated directly into the registration pipeline.
One of the parameters optimized is the per-frame local rotation \theta_p. I can imagine there is a strong correlation between this parameter across adjacent slices. Is this exploited?
Why was the guidewire not used to mask the OT loss, but only the image losses?

This is a high-quality paper that solves a clinically and technically challenging problem using a technically sound method, and it would definitely be of interest to the community. The paper is very well-prepared.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The few concerns I had were adequately addressed in the rebuttal. I remain of the opinion that this paper is of high quality and will be of interest to the MICCAI community.

reviews.recommendation_label: Strong Reject — must be rejected due to major flaws
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses the registration problem between coronary intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) and coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA). The proposed method integrates feature detection directly into the registration workflow. The authors formulate the registration task as a centerline deformation parameter estimation problem and solve it using optimal transport. The method is validated on 47 paired datasets.
reviews.text_strengths: The primary strength of this work is the introduction of a novel approach to coronary image registration.
reviews.text_weaknesses: However, a key limitation is the lack of clarity in the methodological description, particularly regarding notation. Many symbols used in the solution process are not explicitly defined. For instance, the parameters \theta and z, which appear in the abstract, are never introduced. Similarly, the meanings of M and F in Equation (2), presumably denoting the moving and fixed images, are left to the reader’s inference. It is also unclear what A represents in Equation (2), and the bold symbols \boldsymbol{\mu} and \boldsymbol{v} in Equation (9) are not explained.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
All equations in this paper should be revised and clarified; otherwise, they are difficult for readers to understand.

The methodological desription is confusing for readers to understand.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
M_w (warped moving) and F (fixed) are introduced at the start of Sec. 2.2.->I mean M and F in the first term of Eq.(2) instead of M_w and F in the second term of Eq.(2), they are confusing.
(θ, z) are angular and longitudinal coordinates on the unwound cylinder (Sec. 2.1, Fig. 2 caption).->The term “polar coordinates” is too general, and the authors do not explicitly state here that these are “angular and longitudinal coordinates”.
A in Eq. 2 is the lumen cross-sectional area, described directly after the equation.-> The readers can not find “A” directly after the equation. The authors should check the submitted version.
In Eq. 8, μ and ν are the marginal probability vectors from Eq. 4, where u and v are the Sinkhorn scaling vectors described after Eq. 7.->The term “marginal probability vectors” does not appear where the author mentions it, and explicit definitions of μ and ν are not found around Eq. 4.The authors should check the submitted version.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: Registration of coronary CCTA and IVUS images is a crucial step in coronary artery disease assessment. This work presents a novel topology-guided CCTA-IVUS registration approach, termed TG-OT. Method: We incorporate feature detection into the registration framework. An unbalanced Sinkhorn optimal transport loss is utilized to regularize the feature matching. The architecture inherently enforces topological coherency, thus enabling robust registration even for CCTA images suffering from severe geometric deformation, calcifications, and poor lumen segmentation. The TF-OT framework is evaluated on 47 pairs of CCTA-IVUS cases. Results: Comparable or better Dice scores for both lumen and calcification segmentation are obtained in comparison to other state-of-the-art methods. The fully automatic approach achieves results without manual intervention or prior CCTA segmentation.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Novelty in Registration Framework / Method: Novel methodology that integrates feature detection within a registration framework. Specifically, novelty is found in using an unbalanced Sinkhorn optimal transport loss to enable registration under large spatial displacement and extensive topological change between modalities.
2.Multimodal Integration: addressing the challenging task of image co-registration of CCTA and IVUS. Integrating information from both modality improves the ability to assess and diagnose coronary artery disease; and allows for a more complete analysis of both vessel morphology and plaque characteristics.
3.Robustness to Challenges: The method addresses challenges in CCTA-IVUS registration, specifically geometric deformation, calcifications, and lumen segmentation. The framework leverages topology-guided constraints and an optimal transport loss to enhance robustness in dealing with these inherently difficult aspects, which traditional registration approaches often struggle with.
4.Clinical Relevance: This improved registration accuracy and robustness has direct clinical relevance for CCTA-IVUS fusion images.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Limited Generalizability of Dataset: Although results were quantitatively validated on 47 pairs of CCTA-IVUS images, it would be highly desirable to validate results on a much larger, more diverse dataset from various centers. The number and the dataset of the images used in the study, although sufficient for the proof-of-concept study, may not cover all possible clinical scenarios in real clinical practice.
2.Computational Complexity and Efficiency: The optimization of the algorithm for multi-RTX 2080 Ti GPU calculations resulted in the method taking approximately 90 seconds per case on a single RTX 2080 Ti GPU, which, while feasible for research purposes, does not represent real-time clinical efficiency.
3.Lack of Ablation Studies on Specific Components: Although the full pipeline is described, it would give more strength to the paper if more extensive ablation studies could be performed to quantify the contribution of individual components such as the topology-guided constraints and unbalanced Sinkhorn optimal transport loss.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

1.A highly novel and methodically sound approach to a critical problem in medical image analysis.
2.The results are also supported by robust qualitative results on CC and LAD coronary arteries. 
3.Though there is room for improvement, particularly regarding the diversity of the training datasets and runtime efficiency, the strength of this work lies in its contributions. 
4.The paper is written clearly, and the algorithm is thoroughly explained.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I believe the rebuttal of this article can solve my problem, so I accept it.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper proposes TG-OT, a topology-guided framework for CCTA–IVUS registration that formulates cross-modality alignment as an optimal transport problem, integrating feature detection and using an unbalanced Sinkhorn formulation to handle large spatial discrepancies and topological variations. Reviewers agree that the paper tackles an important and clinically relevant problem, and that the use of optimal transport for this challenging multimodal registration task is novel and technically interesting, with promising results demonstrated on a paired dataset of 47 patients. However, the reviews are highly conflicting. While one reviewer finds the paper to be high quality and clearly presented, another raises serious concerns about the clarity of the methodological description, particularly incomplete or undefined notation and insufficient explanation of key equations, which significantly limits readability and reproducibility. Additional concerns include limited evidence of clear superiority over simpler alternatives (e.g., Dice-based alignment), modest dataset size, lack of detailed ablation studies, and relatively high computational cost.

The author’s response still failed to address the reviewers’ concerns.

The three reviewers have acknowledged a highly novel approach and a challenging multi-modal registration problem. The method relies on an optimal transport formulation for registration, which I find worth discussing at MICCAI. The main remarks on R2 concern clarity. The authors should make an effort to ensure all clarity remarks are addressed in a revised version of the paper.

After carefully read the original submission, concerns from all reviewers, I share the opinion that this paper is of high quality and will be of interest to the MICCAI community. The I credited no new experiment, and the authors correctly declined the extra ablation R3 wanted, citing the rebuttal limit.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and AC for their constructive feedback, and are encouraged that all reviewers recognize the novelty and clinical relevance of TG-OT. Concerns are grouped below.
1.Apparent similarity of OT and Dice in Table 2 (R1, AC)
R1 correctly notes that medians appear close in Table 2, while Fig. 3 shows a large gap. Aggregated metrics mask the relevant signal as cosine similarity has a heavily skewed distribution, and OT’s benefit is concentrated in outlier cases with severe rotational drift. Once predicted plaque/bifurcation locations stop overlapping, Dice’s gradient vanishes, and alignment cannot recover. OT supplies spatially informed gradients via the cylindrical geodesic cost (Eq. 6). This is reflected in (i) Wilcoxon signed-rank significance p<0.01 (Sec. 4), (ii) the Sc Q1 shift (0.92 vs. 0.90), and (iii) Fig. 3, which is a representative drift case.
2.”Removing dependency on intermediate segmentations” (R1)
We thank R1 for catching this ambiguity. We refer to volumetric lumen/wall segmentations in the 3D MPR domain, which prior methods (Kadry et al., Li et al.) rely on and which are unreliable under IVUS acoustic shadowing. Our CNN instead predicts only feature presence along radial rays on the (θ, z) cylinder, a well-posed task even under shadowing, and a strictly weaker form of supervision than full volumetric segmentation. We will clarify this in the Discussion.
3.Notation and equation clarity (R2, AC)
We note that the highlighted symbols are defined in the following places in the manuscript:
M_w (warped moving) and F (fixed) are introduced at the start of Sec. 2.2.(θ, z) are angular and longitudinal coordinates on the unwound cylinder (Sec. 2.1, Fig. 2 caption).
A in Eq. 2 is the lumen cross-sectional area, described directly after the equation.
In Eq. 8, μ and ν are the marginal probability vectors from Eq. 4, where u and v are the Sinkhorn scaling vectors described after Eq. 7.We agree that A should be labeled explicitly and the kernel iteration made fully self-contained. We thank R2 for their notes on clarity and are committed to improving these passages in a camera-ready version.
4.Reproducibility (R2, R3)
Code availability is noted in Sec. 2 of the manuscript. The reference appears as plain text rather than a hyperlink, which may have caused confusion. We will highlight this.
5.Dataset, runtime, ablations (R3)
Dataset: We agree that the cohort is relatively small, and we aim to evaluate performance on a larger scale in future work. Nonetheless, the dataset contained considerable variation in plaque burden, pullback length and rotational drift, which motivated our OT formulation.
Runtime: Our hardware resources were unfortunately limited to an RTX 2080Ti GPU. Modern hardware would yield runtime speedups, increasing feasibility of time-critical interventions. We would also like to note that for coronary analysis, CCTA-IVUS fusion is typically diagnostic-only with a longer time horizon, allowing for more processing time.
Ablations: During method development, sanity checks on synthetic data with non-overlapping and mismatched topologies motivated the unbalanced OT formulation. The 8-page limit led us to prioritize comparison against established baselines on real data. Although we agree that a comprehensive ablation on this would benefit the paper, it cannot be included per the MICCAI rebuttal guidelines.
Optional concerns (R1)
Frozen CNNs: CNNs are indeed pre-trained, and subsequently employed during the registration phase, which is why we note that feature detection is ‘integrated’ into the registration pipeline. We will gladly make this more explicit.
Per-frame rotation correlation: This is exploited via a cumulative B-spline parameterization of θ (Sec. 2.2, Transformation model), enforcing smooth pullback twist informed by global rotational accumulation.
Guidewire masking: Feature presence on (θ, z) remains detectable under shadowing, whereas NCC/NMI require pixel-level reliability.

title: The Learnability Gap in Medical Latent Diffusion
abstract:
Generative data augmentation with latent diffusion models is a promising strategy for addressing class imbalance in medical imaging, yet current approaches focus on perceptual fidelity and domain-specific autoencoder fine-tuning while neglecting a more fundamental bottleneck. We identify and formalize the learnability gap: large-scale pretrained autoencoders faithfully encode discriminative features for medical classification, as evidenced by near-lossless performance in reconstruction space, yet their latent representations are structured in ways that are difficult for classifiers to learn from. Across five autoencoder families and four medical benchmarks spanning chest radiography, dermatoscopy, computed tomography, and echocardiography, we show that this gap persists regardless of architecture, initialization strategy, or hyperparameter tuning, and that medical-domain fine-tuning of the autoencoder does not close it.
To probe and partially narrow the gap, we introduce noise-conditioned latent classifiers with FiLM layers and image-space distillation, deploying them as diagnostic instruments and initial mitigations to evaluate latent space quality.
These models offer 64x throughput and 120x memory gains over image-space models while serving as diagnostic tools for latent space quality. Our analysis provides a new framework for evaluating autoencoder latent spaces and identifies their structure, rather than their fidelity or domain specificity, as the primary obstacle to closing the performance gap between real and synthetic medical training data.
Model and code made available at https://github.com/MischaD/LearnabilityGap.git.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper identifies and studies what the authors call the learnability gap in medical latent diffusion pipelines. The key observation is that pretrained autoencoders can preserve class-discriminative information well enough for reconstruction-space classifiers to perform similarly to image-space classifiers, yet the corresponding latent representations remain much harder for downstream classifiers to learn from directly. To support this claim, the paper presents a broad empirical study across five autoencoder families and four long-tailed medical imaging benchmarks spanning chest X-ray, dermatoscopy, CT, and echocardiography. The paper also introduces noise-conditioned latent classifiers with FiLM conditioning and image-space distillation, which partially reduce the gap while being computationally efficient.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The question of whether latent diffusion models truly preserve clinically useful class information is highly relevant, especially for long-tailed medical datasets where synthetic augmentation is often proposed as a practical solution.
2.The notion of a “learnability gap” is easy to understand and practically meaningful. The distinction between information being preserved and information being easy to learn from is an important one, and the paper makes this point effectively.
3.The analyses of reconstruction fidelity, medical-domain fine-tuning, distillation, and noise conditioning help support the claim that the issue is structural rather than simply due to poor reconstruction quality or insufficient tuning.
4.The presentation is clear, and the main message comes across well.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The diagnosis of the problem is interesting and well supported, but the proposed latent classifier only narrows the gap partially. As a result, the methodological contribution feels more incremental than the analytical one.
2.The paper argues that the problem comes from the structure of the latent space rather than information loss, which is plausible and largely supported by the experiments. However, the more specific explanation involving high-frequency patterns and inter-channel correlations remains a hypothesis rather than something directly demonstrated.
3.A major motivation of the paper is that this learnability gap may limit the usefulness of synthetic data for rare-class medical learning. However, the paper does not directly test whether a larger gap actually leads to worse downstream augmentation performance, weaker rare-class gains, or poorer class-conditional generation.
4.The paper makes a convincing case that latent-space classification is harder, but it would be more compelling to show the downstream effect on diffusion-based data generation itself.
5.Since the work is positioned in the medical imaging domain, it would be helpful to include stronger evidence that the identified issue matters for clinically meaningful pathology preservation, rather than mainly for benchmark classification performance.
6.The results strongly suggest that reconstruction fidelity alone is not the main issue, but some of the wording makes the causal interpretation sound more definitive than the current evidence fully supports.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper makes a useful point: latent spaces can preserve class information while still being hard for downstream classifiers to learn from. This is a relevant observation for medical generative modeling, and the experiments are broad enough to make the finding credible. At the same time, I found the paper more convincing as an analysis paper than as a solution paper. The proposed method only partially reduces the gap, and the paper does not directly show how this issue affects downstream generative augmentation performance. Because of that, I see the work as promising, but not yet strong enough for acceptance in its current form.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Based on the rebuttal, I find that most of my major concerns have been adequately addressed. There are still a small number of remaining issues, but overall, I am willing to recommend Accept.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: Main Contribution: The paper introduces a discrepancy between the information preserved in latent spaces and the information in image/reconstruction space, the learnability gap. The paper proceeds to quantify it across different autoencoders and datasets, offering solutions for how the gap can be closed.
reviews.text_strengths: Major Strengths: The paper does a great job in identifying and formalizing a problem and then suggesting solutions (distillation from image space, FiLM layers). It also offers a great discussion (e.g., Why does the gap exist?). The choice of datasets for evaluation is also solid and diverse. The motivation of performing this research to explain why generative data augmentation is lacking is clear and well established. The idea is novel and interesting to the audience of MICCAI. Clever use of the Wilcoxon test to quantify the gap.
reviews.text_weaknesses: Major Weaknesses; Weak writing; equations are not clear (e.g. FiLM related equations are introduced without context), and notation is often not explained, while bold values on tables are occasionally incorrect. Figures are also not very intuitive and comprehensive. The paper is poorly organized, and there is more breadth than depth. Documenting the image space extensively is unnecessary since it is similar to the reconstruction space. Similarly, the computational efficiency advantage of latent space inference is well-established in the literature and does not require extensive investigation. This space would be better used for developing the theoretical justification for the gap. It would be interesting to mathematically explain the decomposition/compression of images in latent space and justify why discriminative information is missing. The paper has a very applied approach to a theoretical problem. Finally, I believe contrastive learning and its performance in classification tasks should also be investigated.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Additional comments to authors: The paper is very interesting, but it seems rushed. It took multiple readings to understand the goal of the paper, and some of the writing is messy. Relevant formulas should be noted, the right values should be set in bold in tables, and a directional arrow can help the reader understand what values are better (higher vs lower). Equations should be better explained. Some questions:
1) Do you believe contrastive learning is important to check for its performance in classification tasks? Is it because they are not used in data augmentation that they were skipped?
2) Why do you think that both image/reconstruction space should both be checked in detail?
3) How exactly are you planning to evaluate with a radiologist? What are the questions and answers you would be expecting?
4) The motivation is data augmentation, do you think that evaluating latent vs image space on classification tasks is an accurate way to establish this gap in distinctive feature preservation?

Weak Accept Justification: The paper is interesting and relevant to the MICCAI audience. It’s a novel idea that many people would benefit of learning from. The contributions are twofold; an alternative way of leveraging and understanding the effectiveness of the latent space and a solution to ensuring latent space preserves information necessary for classification tasks.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: My question about the value of image vs reconstruction was answered, and the generative utility was well explained as well. I still believe the paper is a bit rushed and can benefit from more focused writing, but I appreciate and value the novelty and potential discussion that it can bring to the MICCAI audience.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper identifies a “learnability gap” in the latent space of variational auto encoders (VAEs) for medical classification tasks. The gap is identified by comparing the performance of classifiers in the direct image space, reconstructed (by the VAE) image space and the VAE’s latent space. The paper shows significant performance degradation when the classifier is trained on latent space features compared to reconstructed and image space features, indicating a learnability gap in the VAE’s latent space. The paper proposes a few methods to reduce the effects of the learnability gap (hyper parameter optimization, noise conditioned classifier).
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The approach of the paper is methodical and sound.
2.The identified learnability gap can have a major impact on using latent generative models for data generation, for the classification task.
3.The paper investigates a few approaches to mitigate the learnability gap.
4.The paper is well written and easy to follow.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.A core motivation of the paper is that synthetic data generated from latent generative models have non-discriminative features in the latent space. This leads to the learnability gap found by the paper. However, the learnability gap only shows that a classifier trained in the latent space performs poorly compared to a classifier trained in the image space. But the motivation seems to claim that this learnability gap can affect the performance of a classifier trained in pixel-space on data generated from latent generative models. This claim is not justified by the paper.
2.Limited novelty from the perspective of the concept: Prior work already suggests that standard VAE/latent-diffusion latent spaces may be poorly aligned with discriminative objectives [1, 2, 3]. This work extends this concept for the medical domain.
3.Can the authors provide evidence for their hypothesis that the reason for the learnability gap is “the pixel-wise reconstruction distributes class-discriminative features across high-frequency spatial patterns and inter-channel correlations that convolutional classifiers struggle to exploit”?
[1] Kouzelis, Theodoros, et al. “Eq-vae: Equivariance regularized latent space for improved generative image modeling.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2502.09509 (2025).
[2] Leng, Xingjian, et al. “Repa-e: Unlocking vae for end-to-end tuning of latent diffusion transformers.” Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision. 2025.
[3] Dillon, Barry M., et al. “Better latent spaces for better autoencoders.” SciPost Physics 11.3 (2021): 061.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper requires additional justifications on the reasons for its motivation and positioning with respect to prior work. If these concerns are well addressed, I am willing to raise my score.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The rebuttal clarified many of my concerns. However, I am still not convinced why the learnability gap can affect the performance of a classifier trained in pixel-space on data generated from latent generative models. The rebuttal by the authors argues very strongly that the if the latent-space is “unlearnable” for classification, “synthetic data will suffer from feature collapse regardless of diffusion training”. This is a very strong claim with no experiments supporting its validation. Moreover, many works ([4], [5]]) have shown significant gains in classification performance when trained on pixel-level data generated through latent generative models. As per the author’s claims, adding synthetic data should not have aided performance or should have worsened it due to the “feature collapse”.
Nevertheless, the rest of the paper still provides valuable insights into latent-space classification and probing for the medical domain. For these reasons I lean towards acceptance. However, I suggest the authors to avoid such strong wording in the final version.
[4] Morís, Daniel I., et al. “Adapted generative latent diffusion models for accurate pathological analysis in chest X-ray images.” Medical & Biological Engineering & Computing 62.7 (2024): 2189-2212.
[5] Akrout, Mohamed, et al. “Diffusion-based data augmentation for skin disease classification: Impact across original medical datasets to fully synthetic images.” International conference on medical image computing and computer-assisted intervention. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland, 2023.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper focuses on the difficulty of downstream classification from the latent representations of autoencoders and proposes a solution to partially address this challenge. The paper presents useful analysis, however there are several concerns raised by the reviewers, including limited novelty, clinical impact, and insufficient support for the claims.

The authors have made convincing efforts in their rebuttal especially positioning the paper as finding-and-analysis work. It formalizes the observation of difficulty in learning from latent representations of pretrained autoencoders for the downstream tasks like classification. Although the proposed solution is not very effective, it shows a possible direction to mitigate the observed issues. The paper has some strong claims which authors have agreed to reword and reframe in the final version. Overall the paper has valuable insights, especially in terms of latent space probing and analysis.

This paper was reviewed by three experts in the field. Based on the reviewers’ post-rebuttal feedback, the paper is recommended for acceptance to MICCAI 2026.The authors are encouraged to incorporate the necessary changes discussed during the rebuttal process into the final camera-ready version.
After rebuttal, all reviewers decide to accept the paper, the author successfully adderss the problems , and I recommend the acceptance of the paper.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and AC. R1, R2 and R3 all recognized the originality and clinical relevance of the learnability gap, the methodical analysis (R3), the diverse benchmarks across five autoencoder families (R2), the clear presentation (R1, R3), and the statistical rigour (R2).
[A] POSITIONING: FINDING vs. METHOD (R1, R3)
The paper is primarily a finding-and-analysis submission. The core contribution is revealing an intrinsic structural bottleneck in medical latent spaces. That the gap remains highly significant (p=9.5e-7 across 20 autoencoder x dataset pairs) even after extensive hyperparameter optimization (HPO), distillation, and noise conditioning is itself the key finding: misalignment between reconstruction fidelity and latent learnability is a fundamental architectural challenge that cannot be tuned away. FiLM and distillation are presented as initial mitigations and diagnostic instruments, not as the contribution. We will revise the framing to emphasize the discovery over the mitigation.
[B] PROBING AS A PRINCIPLED LOWER BOUND ON GENERATIVE UTILITY (R1, R2, R3, R3.1)
All three reviewers asked about downstream generative augmentation results. Our probing framework is a controlled lower-bound test for that exact question, and we argue it is the more rigorous diagnostic. A class-conditional generator p(z|y) must place mass on the class-conditional manifold in latent space. If a high-capacity HPO-tuned classifier p(y|z), tasked only with finding a decision boundary, cannot reliably extract discriminative features from the latents even with noise conditioning and image-space distillation, then no diffusion model trained with denoising losses on the same latents can be expected to allocate density to features it cannot itself separate. Probing isolates the diagnosis from the well-known confounders of generative training, such as schedule choice, classifier-free guidance scale, sample budget, and the FID vs downstream-bACC reporting mismatch. By identifying this gap at the autoencoder stage we provide a diagnostic tool, i.e., high reconstruction fidelity is a deceptive metric, and if the latent space is unlearnable, synthetic data will suffer from feature collapse regardless of diffusion training. This directly addresses R3.1.
[C] CLINICAL PATHOLOGY PRESERVATION (R1.5)
bACC, AUC and MCC are computed on clinical labels including pneumothorax, melanoma, AVSD and the CT-RATE findings, which are the pathologies that synthetic augmentation is intended to enrich. The gap is therefore measured on the clinical task that motivates the pipeline.
R1.2, R3.3 Causal language around the decoder reassembling features.
We agree this should be nuanced. We will frame the CNN-unfriendly latent format as the most plausible structural explanation consistent with our failure-to-learn results, rather than a proven cause.
R2.2 Image vs Reconstruction space, purpose of the comparison.
Comparing Image vs Reconstruction tests whether the autoencoder retains information; comparing Reconstruction vs Latent tests whether that information is accessible. This triangulation is essential to prove the gap is a learnability issue and not simple information loss. We will state this explicitly.
R3.2 Novelty relative to cited prior work.
We will cite Dillon and expand the discussion of Kouzelis and Leng, which are already cited as refs 20 and 21.Beyond demonstrating that this gap persists in medical imaging, we investigate it using probing, which unlike prior natural-image work does not rely on the confounding generative training and sampling process. The empirical finding that medical-domain autoencoder fine-tuning (MedVAE vs MedVAE-FT) does not close the gap and in fact widens it relative to RS is a direct counter to the prevailing assumption in the medical generative literature that domain-specific autoencoders solve the problem.
We respectfully ask to be evaluated on the diagnosis and the framework, both of which we believe the evidence supports.

title: The Neuro-Developing Engine: a Surrogate Longitudinal Model for Infant Brain Dynamics Via Causal Distillation
abstract: Understanding how individual infant brain function evolves over development requires models that capture personalized longitudinal changes in functional dynamics, rather than static connectivity estimates. However, existing data-driven approaches largely focus on longitudinal functional connectivity (FC) prediction, leaving a significant gap in mechanistic interpretability, causal analysis, and grounded support for targeted intervention in atypical brain development. To address this challenge, we propose the first Neuro-Developing Engine (NDE), a novel surrogate longitudinal model of infant brain dynamics utilizing resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) data. By learning age-dependent transitions between individualized surrogate brains at the individual level, NDE not only predicts the evolution of surrogate brain dynamics across continuous ages but also identifies brain regions exhibiting strong modulatory effects during development. Specifically, 1) leveraging individualized Neural Perturbational Inference (NPI) surrogate models that capture subject-specific brain dynamics, we design a developmental residual model equipped with FiLM-conditioned generators to distill explicit age-driven modulation between younger and older brain dynamics, conditioned on graph-embedded individual identity and ages. 2) To enhance causal and age-sensitive representations, we combine causal distillation and Jacobian spectrum objectives with a soft-label contrastive loss that enforces alignment between predicted residual dynamics and age gaps. 3) To enable inverse-control analysis, we introduce region-level “counterfactual developmental knobs” that modulate residual dynamics, allowing the quantification of how age-dependent perturbations reshape FC over development. Extensive experiments demonstrate NDE’s ability to model individualized developmental dynamics, predict connectivity changes, and support counterfactual inverse-control simulation, highlighting its potential for mechanistic understanding and guiding early intervention in typical and atypical neurodevelopment.
subject_areas: Applications -> Digital Twins / Simulation / Synthetic Data

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents a highly innovative and methodologically sophisticated framework, the Neuro-Developing Engine (NDE), for modeling longitudinal brain dynamics in infancy. The core idea of learning age-conditioned transitions between individualized neural surrogates represents a significant conceptual leap beyond static or predictive connectivity modeling. The work is exceptionally well-structured, with clear motivations, a comprehensive methodological presentation, and rigorous experimental validation on two independent cohorts. The introduction of “counterfactual developmental knobs” for in-silico interventional analysis is a particularly compelling contribution that enhances the mechanistic interpretability of the model. The results are convincing, demonstrating superior performance against ablated variants and the model’s utility in identifying divergent trajectories in an at-risk population.
reviews.text_strengths:
The primary innovation is the formulation of neurodevelopment as a process of transitioning between subject-specific dynamic models, rather than predicting static functional connectivity (FC) or learning a population-average trajectory. This approach inherently captures individual differences and the evolution of dynamics, not just correlations.
The combination of FiLM-conditioned residual dynamics, age-gap-aware gating, and causal distillation (behavior + EC + Jacobian spectrum) is well-designed and empirically validated.
The PDE cohort demonstrates real-world utility—identifying divergent connections and proposing counterfactual interventions.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper compares NDE with RNN/CNN variants of the surrogate architecture and ablations, but does not compare with other longitudinal FC prediction methods.
Section 2.2 describes counterfactual generation from random noise, but the free-rollout FC used in evaluations (Table 1) is not fully explained. How many steps? Is the model unrolled autoregressively from an initial noise vector? The authors should clarify the procedure for generating FC_free, perhaps in a dedicated paragraph or supplementary note.
