Table 1 reports means and standard deviations, but no p-values or statistical tests are provided to confirm that NDE’s improvements over baselines (e. g. , NDE w/o C, NDE-FC) are significant.
The “developmental knobs” are described as modulating residual dynamics (Eq. 9). However, the paper does not explain how the intervention vector g is optimized or selected for the results in Fig. 3c-e. Is g learned via gradient descent to minimize divergence? Or is it a fixed perturbation? The methodology for identifying “top FC drivers” should be detailed.
The model trained on BCP is fine-tuned on 50% of TD infants from the PDE dataset (Fig. 3a caption says “fine-tuned on 50% TD infants”). However, the PDE dataset has only 35 TD controls. Fine-tuning on 50% of those (≈17-18 subjects) may lead to overfitting. The authors should report the number of TD subjects used and consider cross-validation or a more robust fine-tuning strategy.
The conclusion is brief and does not discuss limitations.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This is a high-quality paper that introduces a novel and impactful framework for modeling longitudinal brain development.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of the paper is that their proposed method, NDE, unlike existing methods, models continuous developmental changes rather static connectivity.
reviews.text_strengths: The major strength of the paper is the fact that the proposed method allows longitudinal modeling, unlike cross-sectional approaches of the past. Furthermore, the way that the method was developed allows it to simulate transitions between ages, rather than disconnected timepoints. The model does so while preserving subject-level individual properties.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The model makes assumptions about certain neurodevelopmental patterns for the sake of stability and implementation of model, such as the fact that the brain development takes on a monotonic, plateauing curve pattern. While this may be accurate for healthy infant aging, if the model were to be adopted for other patterns such as aging across human life span, such as events that may lead to regression or nonlinear shifts, such assumption may become a limitation of the model.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I believe the conceptual novelty of proposing a longitudinal, continuous model serves as a strong selling point of the work. Additional external validation and biological/clinical findings that further validate the predictions of the model would make the model more interpretable. Finally, some of the assumptions of the model may make it more stable and good at reproducing expected patterns, but may limit what it can accurately model.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces a NDE framework that models how infant brain dynamics evolve over time using resting state fMRI data where the connectivity evolves dynamically as opposed to treating it as a static measurement. It builds subject-specific surrogate brain models and learns age-driven transitions between them, while also allowingcausal analysis and counterfactual simulations on brain regions.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The formulation is technically sound, especially the FiLM-conditioned residual transition module that models how brain dynamics evolve with age while preserving subject identity. This is a nice way to separate subject-specific structure from developmental effects.
2.The paper goes beyond prediction and explicitly targets causal interpretability, using Jacobian-based effective connectivity and causal distillation. This makes the model more aligned with neuroscience questions.
3.The counterfactual developmental knobs is a strong idea, as it allows simulation of how perturbing specific regions affects future connectivity.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The whole framework depends on training separate surrogate models per (subject, age) and then learn transitions between them, but from a computational perspective, it seems that it is data inefficient and could scale poorly. There is no discussion of how stable these surrogates are with limited timepoints.
2.The comparisons are weak with respect to other competing methods, since Table 1 only compares against standard models like (baseline surrogate, RNN, CNN, ablations) rather than established longitudinal models like [1]. Given that [1] is already discussed in the introduction, it would have been more convincing to include it in the evaluation.
3.The FiLM-based residual transition in the paper assumes that the developmental changes are additive corrections from the source surrogate (Eq. 4–5), which is a fairly strong assumption? In early brain development where dynamics could change nonlinearly, this residual formulation might be too restrictive but this is not discussed.
[1] A few-shot learning graph multi-trajectory evolution network for forecasting multimodal baby connectivity development from a baseline timepoint, MICCAI 2021
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper has an interesting idea of modeling longitudinal brain dynamics with surrogate models and causal transitions, which is quite different from standard FC prediction approaches. However, the method raises some concerns around scalability, lacks comparisons with stronger longitudinal baselines, and makes restrictive modeling assumptions.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Thank you to the authors for addressing my comments. Therefore, I recommend accepting the paper. Great work!

meta_reviews.text:
The reviewers agree that the paper presents a novel and promising framework for modeling longitudinal brain dynamics with strong methodological contributions, particularly in its causal and individualized formulation. However, concerns remain regarding missing comparisons to established longitudinal baselines, unclear methodological details (e.g., rollout and intervention procedures), limited statistical validation, small sample size, and unclear assumptions.

The authors provides a strong rebuttal that successfully addresses the reviewers’ concerns. Overall the proposed method is novel and has uniquely interesting utility. This strength outweighs the potential drawback of missing relevant longitudinal baseline comparisons.

I think that the idea is interesting. Although some weaknesses still remain, I thought that authors have provided a good discussion on this early-stage but interesting research, and have provided some convincing responses to specific critiques. I strongly encourage authors to include better clarifications and revisions as suggested by reviewers to strengthen the final version. I would argue for accept.

Despite some lingering concerns, the authors have done a good job addressing the main critiques to extent allowed by MICCAI (i.e., no new experiments). This work would be of interest to the community.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the Area Chair and reviewers (R) for their constructive comments and for recognizing NDE as a “novel and promising framework” with “strong methodological contributions,” including its “causal/individualized formulation”, “rigorous validation”, and counterfactual developmental knobs as a “strong idea”. Below, we clarify the main concerns.
Comparison with longitudinal FC prediction methods (R1, R4): 
We agree that longitudinal FC prediction methods are relevant. However, they are not directly target-matched to NDE: existing methods primarily forecast FC matrices, whereas NDE can model developmental transitions as a causal surrogate system. In NDE, effective connectivity (EC) and counterfactual sensitivity are primary outputs, while FC only serves as a static summary of the generated dynamics. To test whether NDE’s performance can be explained by optimizing FC matching alone, we included NDE-FC, a within-framework variant trained with FC-similarity loss. Table 1 shows that although NDE-FC achieves reasonable FC prediction, it degrades EC preservation and developmental fidelity, supporting our central claim that NDE captures causal surrogate dynamics beyond conventional FC matching. We will clarify this scope distinction and discuss direct FC-forecasting comparisons as a future extension in the revision.
Assumption on residual formulation and developmental pattern (R3, R4): 
We would like to clarify that NDE does not impose monotonic, plateauing, linear, or additive developmental trajectories on FC edges. Eqs. 4-5 operate at fMRI signal level rather than directly on FC. Specifically, Eq. 4 adds an age-conditioned signal residual to the source-age neural surrogate to predict target-age fMRI state evolution, while FC is derived afterward from the generated time series. Thus, the residual formulation does not constrain FC trajectories. Moreover, the residual is produced by nonlinear FiLM-conditioned networks, allowing nonlinear transitions. Similarly, the age-gap gate in Eq. 5 regularizes the residual magnitude at signal level to stabilize training, without forcing FC to be monotonic or plateauing. We will clarify this distinction between signal- and FC-level constraints, while noting that the age-gap gate may reduce sensitivity to abrupt dynamical shifts.
Details on FC_free generation and developmental knob (R1): 
We will better define FC_free and developmental knob in the revision. As stated in Sec. 3.2, FC_free in Table 1 is computed from BOLD dynamics generated by autoregressive “free rollouts span 200 steps across four random seeds”. Regarding the developmental knob g, it is not optimized. As introduced in Sec. 2.2 through Eq. 9 and the leverage score (Imp_k) definition, g is inserted into the trained NDE with fixed parameters, and the leverage score of each region k on a targeted FC edge is computed via automatic differentiation. Top FC drivers in Fig. 3c-e are ranked by |Imp_k|, while the sign of Imp_k indicates modulation direction.
Scalability, surrogate stability, PDE fine-tuning, and statistics (R1, R4):
Regarding scalability, the individualized surrogates are lightweight and trained independently, making this stage parallelizable. Although this design preserves scan-specific dynamics, we will acknowledge surrogate stability under limited timepoints as a limitation. For PDE fine-tuning, we understand the concern that limited TD samples may increase the overfitting risk. We have mitigated the risk by 1) matching scan protocol and age range between BCP and PDE data; 2) using 68 longitudinal scans from 18 TD infants; and 3) conservative fine-tuning with the identity encoder frozen and a reduced learning rate. We will clarify these and acknowledge the need for larger TD samples in the revision. Moreover, using the existing cross-validation outputs, a paired permutation test confirmed that NDE significantly outperformed competing methods across tasks (p < 0.001). We will include this in the revision.

title: The Paper Has a GitHub, the GitHub Has a README, the README Has Nothing: Reproducibility Signals for Review Support
abstract: Reproducibility policies promise “checkable” medical-imaging science, yet many submissions still ship unverifiable artifacts. Our analysis of 3722 MICCAI papers shows code-linking rising from 51.8% (2021) to 72.5% (2025), but ~13% of linked repositories are inaccessible or empty. We present paper-snitch, a reviewer-facing decision-support tool that turns these signals into an evidence-grounded report. Paper-snitch parses PDFs, resolves and sanity-checks repositories, and applies policy-aware checklists aligned with MICCAI expectations, producing a review-time verifiability score decomposed into interpretable sub-scores plus criterion-linked excerpts and artifacts reviewers can inspect. It never executes untrusted code or attempts GPU-heavy reproduction, focusing instead on bounded, verifiable checks. We compare paper-snitch on 100 randomly sampled MICCAI 2025 papers with human annotators using shared evaluation criteria, indicating that automated, bounded checks can scale reproducibility screening while keeping final decisions with reviewers.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a tool to analyze papers in support of peer-review. While it doesn’t fall within the traditional scope of MICCAI contributions, it addresses the important problem of reliability and thoroughness of reproducibility reviews during the peer-review process.
reviews.text_strengths:
Open a discussion on the sustainability and quality of peer review
Propose a LLM-based tool to analyze papers and associated code repositories, with acceptable performance compared to human reference
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Casual writing tone
Lack of comparison with other LLM-based reviewing tools
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses an important topic: the reliability of reproducibility evaluations during peer review. It describes and evaluates a LLM-based tool to produce reproducibility checklists, dataset and code analyses.
The paper doesn’t compare the proposed system to any baseline, nor does it reference related tools on LLM-based reviews. For instance, it would be important to understand the specific relevance of the tool presented compared to existing AI agents/companions such as Claude Code, Gemini CLI or Open AI Codex, and a reference to previous literature on LLM-assisted peer review (e.g., https://aclanthology.org/2024.emnlp-main.70).
Relatedly, LLM-assisted peer review raises a number of questions that are not discussed by the authors, including:
Privacy of the authors’ submissions;
Biases in human and LLM evaluations;
Prompt injections in submissions.
Given that the main contribution of the paper isn’t directly in the MIC or CAI domains, it would be important to discuss the broader implications of using such technical solutions in the review process.
The tone of the writing is slightly casual, including phrases such as “Let us start by lowering our blood pressure”, which I think should be avoided. Similarly, the name of the tool, paper “snitch”, suggests a confrontational approach to peer review, which may raise questions.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors present Paper-Snitch, a decision-support framework designed for reproducibility screening during the peer-review process for conferences. Unlike automated filters, the system focuses on artifact verifiability through three core pillars: (i) evidence-grounded outputs traceable to specific PDF spans or repository files, (ii) review-time safety via static inspection (avoiding untrusted code execution or heavy GPU training), and (iii) a scalable, auditable workflow for conference-level deployments. The system elegantly separates probabilistic LLM-based fact-detection from a deterministic mathematical scoring module, providing both a numerical grade and actionable recommendations for authors.
reviews.text_strengths:
Targeted Utility: The paper addresses a critical, growing need in the MICCAI and broader academic community for standardized, scalable reproducibility checks during conference reviews.
Deterministic Actionable Outputs: The framework’s decision to use LLMs only for finding evidence while leaving the actual scoring to fixed mathematical formulas is an elegant solution to the problem of LLM non-determinism. Moreover, by generating specific recommendations (e.g., flagging missing checkpoints or dataset links), the tool moves beyond a simple “pass/fail” gate and can serve as a constructive feedback mechanism for authors.
Static Safety: The reliance on static inspection rather than code execution ensures the tool is secure and computationally efficient enough to be feasible for large-scale conference use.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
LLM Specification Ambiguity: There is a lack of clarity regarding which models were used. While Section 4 and the code repository mention GPT-5, Table 1 suggests GPT-4o performed better. The paper would benefit from clarifying which model was ultimately used and referencing the choice in LLM earlier than Section 4.* Fragility of Code Analysis: The “Code Embeddings” section appears highly dependent on specific file-naming conventions (e.g., “train/test”). The authors acknowledge this fragility, but the current implementation may fail on repositories with non-standard structures or unclear naming, which may be equally likely at conferences. Furthermore, how does Paper-Snitch handle Jupyter notebooks?
Free/Open-Source Alternatives: The paper does not address why proprietary models (OpenAI) were chosen over open-source alternatives (e.g., Ollama).
Nitpick: There appears to be an overuse of italics for serving different functions throughout the paper.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
It would be useful to clarify the LLM notation in the paper and what it refers to and the other comments brought up in the “Weaknesses” section

The recommendation is primarily driven by the framework’s ability to successfully address an urgent gap in standardized reviewing criteria for conference-level reproducibility. By focusing on artifact verifiability, the authors provide a scalable, “review-time safe” solution that is critically needed in the MICCAI community.
A key contribution lies in its deterministic scoring logic, which resolves LLM non-determinism by restricting the model to evidence-gathering via a structured checklist. Moreover, the authors not only address a reproducibility concern, but make their code and a working demo readily available.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces a tool called Paper-Snitch for assessing reproducibility and verifiability in medical imaging papers, especially MICCAI. Instead of trying to fully reproduce results, the tool performs bounded checks that are feasible during peer review: it parses the paper, identifies the paper type, inspects linked repositories without executing code, evaluates paper/code/dataset artifacts against policy-aligned criteria, and produces a verifiability report with scores, evidence snippets, and qualitative summaries. The authors motivate the work with an analysis of 3722 MICCAI papers showing that although code sharing has increased, a large fraction of linked repositories remain empty. They evaluate the system on 100 MICCAI-2025 papers against experienced human annotators and report high percentage of machine-human agreement.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.This paper addresses an important problem and has a clear scope. It is important to check reproducibility during peer review, but artificially checking the code is difficult and time-costing for reviewers.
2.The overall system design is thoughtful and well structured since it separates paper analysis, code analysis, dataset analysis, and final aggregation into interpretable components, and it grounds its outputs in inspectable artifacts.
3.The paper is well written and generally easy to follow. The authors do a good job explaining what the system is supposed to do. The figures and diagrams are clearly presented.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Several parts of the pipeline rely heavily on LLM-based decisions, including classification, criterion assessment, and repository file selection. Although the paper is transparent about it in the limitations section, it is still a concern whether the proposed system can be implemented in a trustworthy way that ensures privacy, which is important in peer-review process.
2.The evaluation is somewhat limited since it is conducted on 100 papers from a single venue (MICCAI-2025). This leaves some uncertainty about robustness and generalizability.
3.It would strengthen the paper if the authors included a self-case-study showing how Paper-Snitch evaluates this submission itself and its accompanying repository, since this would help readers understand the form and usefulness of the generated report in a concrete end-to-end example. (This is not a weakness, but something interesting to see.)
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper studies an important problem, has a reasonable idea and implementation, and is well written. My only concern is practicality (generalizability, privacy, etc.) of using it in peer-review.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper addresses a timely and important topic: assessing the reproducibility of papers during conference review periods. The authors propose an interpretable framework, largely based on LLMs and paid services, to analyze various aspects of papers and compute mathematical scores aligned with standard reproducibility checklists in conference review forms. 
The reviewers agreed on the paper’s main strengths: it opens a discussion on the sustainability and quality of peer review, and the framework provides acceptable performance compared to human reference. However, R#1 and R#3 pointed out important points that should be addressed in the rebuttal:
The proposed framework is based on online tools, which can raise concerns about privacy issues. During conference reviews, confidentiality prevents reviewers from feeding the full PDF paper to any AI Agent. How does the proposed framework tackle this issue?
Even if the authors demonstrated a strong agreement between human & LLM evaluations, it is important to discuss the potential biases that could arise from the use of LLM: i) How could we incorporate such a framework for peer-review without introducing biases in the evaluation process? ii) How could we ensure its robustness towards prompt injection or AI-generated papers?
The evaluation of the proposed framework is limited to 100 papers, randomly sampled from MICCAI 2025 across 3 categories. Could you clarify the distribution of reproducibility scores across these papers? Did you use any form of stratification for sampling these papers?
In addition, only two architectures for the LLM have been compared (GPT4-o and GPT5). Comparison with existing AI agents such as Claude Code, Gemini CLI or Open AI Codex, and a reference to previous literature on LLM-assisted peer review would be needed.
As a minor point, the authors should clarify the provenance of the results shown in Fig. 1.Do these metrics come from a previous study, or is it part of this study? If so, the authors should give more precisions about it.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for their constructive feedback. We are encouraged that they identified several strengths: the paper addresses a timely problem for MICCAI, opens discussion on the sustainability and quality of peer review, and proposes a practical reproducibility-screening framework. Reviewers appreciated that Paper-Snitch is not an automated reviewer, but an auxiliary tool for verifiability. They also highlighted evidence-grounded design, static inspection without executing untrusted code, interpretable analyses, deterministic scoring, actionable recommendations, human agreement, and available code/demo resources.
Scope and role in peer review.
Paper-Snitch is intended only to support reviewers or chairs with auditable checks of objective artifact signals; final judgment remains human. We will strengthen this framing.
Privacy.
Submissions cannot be sent to external AI services without policy, consent, and processing guarantees. The current implementation is a proof-of-concept; the framework is model-agnostic. There are multiple options to evaluate when moving to production: running the pipeline in a controlled environment, disabling external web search during double-blind review, using local/open-weight models, storing minimal audit artifacts, or ensuring that manuscripts and repositories are not used for model training with a specific contract signed with service providers.
Regarding bias, prompt injection, and robustness
, LLM-assisted peer review can introduce risks. Paper-Snitch mitigates some of them by restricting LLMs to evidence retrieval and structured criterion assessment, while scores are computed deterministically. This does not eliminate bias, but provides tools for mitigation. Like medical imaging tools that assist expert clinicians and surgeons in daily clinical workflows—supporting, standardizing, and accelerating specific tasks without replacing professional judgment—Paper-Snitch is designed to play an analogous role in the peer-review process. It provides reviewers and chairs with structured, evidence-grounded reproducibility checks, helping them identify missing or unverifiable artifacts more consistently while leaving all scientific and acceptance decisions to human experts. For prompt injection, schema-constrained outputs and deterministic tree checks are used. We avoid executing untrusted code.
Evaluation.
100 MICCAI 2025 papers are an initial validation rather than definitive evidence of generalizability. We will clarify that the papers were randomly sampled and stratified by method, dataset, and both.
Model choice and baselines.
Both GPT-4o and GPT-5 were evaluated under the same embeddings and scoring code. Notably, the demo is designed with extensibility in mind, and models powering the tool can be configured at runtime. Future extensions will include a thorough evaluation of open-source and local alternatives, including Ollama-served models, alongside agentic tools such as Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and OpenAI Codex.
Regarding code-analysis fragility,
non-standard repositories may challenge file selection. We will clarify this limitation and note that repository templates or required entry points would improve reliability. Jupyter notebooks are handled statically as JSON/text artifacts: markdown, imports, cells, commands, and outputs can be inspected, but notebooks are not executed.
Finally, we clarify the provenance of Fig. 1.
The MICCAI code-availability statistics are part of this study and are produced by the code-availability node applied to the analyzed MICCAI corpus.

title: Think Global, Look Focal: Dual-Stream Retrieval-Augmented Pathology Report Generation for Whole Slide Images
abstract: Automatically generating pathology reports from gigapixel Whole Slide Images (WSIs) is essential for reducing pathologist workload and improving clinical efficiency. However, the gigapixel resolution and semantic complexity of WSIs expose two critical limitations in existing methods: (1) Visual dilution: Predominant approaches treat WSIs as single-granularity patch sequences, causing fine-grained focal details to be overwhelmed by background noise; (2) Retrieval noise: Existing methods rely on raw corpora with non-diagnostic redundancy, and their fusion mechanisms fail to suppress interference from low-similarity evidence, leading to factual hallucinations. To address these issues, we propose DR-Gen, a Dual-Stream Retrieval-Augmented Pathology Report Generation framework. Inspired by pathologists’ workflow, DR-Gen decouples global tissue context from focal cellular details via two visual streams: a global stream for slide-level architecture and a focal stream for diagnostic regions. A Visual Priming Adapter leverages these decoupled features as visual anchors, grounding generation in slide morphology. To safeguard medical validity, we construct a CAP-protocol-guided diagnostic knowledge bank and propose an Adaptive Confidence Gating module that dynamically reweights evidence by retrieval confidence. Experiments on the PathText (BRCA) benchmark show that DR-Gen consistently outperforms existing methods in both report quality and subtype classification, achieving a relative improvement of 10.4% in BLEU-4. Ablation studies further validate each proposed component. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/jasonlightx/DR-Gen.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes DR-Gen, a novel Dual-Stream Retrieval-Augmented Pathology Report Generation framework for gigapixel Whole Slide Images (WSIs). To combat visual dilution and semantic sparsity, the authors design a global-focal visual extraction mechanism that mimics the “think global, look focal” workflow of pathologists, anchored by a Visual Priming Adapter (VPA). Furthermore, to address retrieval noise and factual hallucinations common in existing RAG methods, the paper introduces a College of American Pathologists (CAP)-guided knowledge bank and an Adaptive Confidence Gating (ACG) module to dynamically filter and reweight retrieved medical evidence.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The architectural design is highly intuitive and aligns seamlessly with real-world clinical workflows. Decoupling the visual processing into a global stream (for tissue architecture) and a focal stream (for cellular details) is an elegant solution to the unique challenges posed by gigapixel WSIs.
2.The transition from unstructured raw corpora to a structured, CAP-protocol-guided atomic knowledge bank significantly reduces non-diagnostic redundancy. Coupled with the ACG module, which uses temperature-scaled softmax to calibrate confidence, the model effectively filters out irrelevant priors and curbs factual hallucinations.
3.The experimental results are convincing. The model achieves state-of-the-art performance not only on traditional NLP metrics (e. g. , a 10.4% relative improvement in BLEU-4) but also on clinical classification metrics (F1 score of 0.926 for subtype prediction) and factual correctness ($Fact_{ent}$). The ablation studies clearly isolate and validate the individual contributions of the dual-stream architecture, VPA, and ACG components.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The evaluation is exclusively conducted on the PathText (BRCA) benchmark, which focuses solely on breast cancer. Because morphological features and diagnostic complexities vary drastically across different organs and cancer types (e. g. , lung or prostate cancer), the lack of multi-center or multi-organ cross-validation makes it difficult to assess the true generalizability of the framework.
2.The retention ratio ($\kappa$) for the focal stream is fixed at 0.6.Given that the proportion of diagnostically relevant tissue—such as tumor bed size—fluctuates wildly from slide to slide, a fixed ratio might discard critical micro-morphological details in slides with extensive lesions, or conversely, introduce background noise in slides with extremely localized focal points. An adaptive retention mechanism would make the methodology more robust.
3.The reliance on the CAP protocol to construct the diagnostic memory bank is effective here, but it poses scalability challenges. The authors do not adequately discuss how this approach would translate to rare diseases or pathologies that lack standardized, well-documented reporting templates, which could result in high manual construction costs in broader clinical applications.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The authors have identified a critical bottleneck in computational pathology—the paradigm mismatch when applying standard radiological vision-language models to semantically sparse, gigapixel WSIs. The proposed DR-Gen framework addresses this with a logically sound, clinically inspired dual-stream design and a robust confidence-gated retrieval mechanism. The methodology is sound, and the experimental results demonstrate meaningful improvements in both linguistic fluency and clinical accuracy. The score is held back from being higher primarily due to the limitation of validating the model on only a single, organ-specific dataset, and the lack of provided source code for immediate peer verification.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper presents two main contributions. First, it proposes a dual-stream visual modeling framework that integrates global and focal representations to address the visual dilution problem in gigapixel Whole Slide Images (WSIs). By explicitly decoupling slide-level tissue structure from fine-grained diagnostic regions, the approach enables more effective multi-scale modeling and reduces the risk of diagnostically relevant cues being overwhelmed by background noise. Second, it introduces a structured knowledge-enhanced retrieval mechanism together with a confidence-aware fusion module. A CAP-guided atomic diagnostic knowledge bank is constructed to provide higher-quality medical priors, and an Adaptive Confidence Gating (ACG) module is designed to dynamically reweight retrieved evidence based on confidence scores, thereby mitigating retrieval noise and improving the factual consistency of the generated reports.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The motivation is well-grounded and clearly articulated. Given the gigapixel scale and extreme semantic sparsity of Whole Slide Images (WSIs), the need to jointly model global tissue structure and focal diagnostic regions is both intuitive and clinically meaningful. The proposed dual-stream design aligns well with the real diagnostic workflow of pathologists (i.e., “global overview followed by focal inspection”), making the formulation both principled and practically relevant.
2.The experimental evaluation is thorough and convincing. The paper includes comprehensive ablation studies that systematically validate the contribution of each component, including the dual-stream decomposition, VPA, and ACG modules. In addition, the authors provide hyperparameter analyses that offer further insight into the robustness and sensitivity of the method, strengthening the empirical credibility of the approach.
3.the paper is well-written and clearly structured. The technical design is presented in a logical and coherent manner, and the connection between motivation, method, and experimental validation is easy to follow. This clarity helps readers understand both the intuition and the implementation details of the proposed framework.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The proposed framework is relatively complex, involving multiple components such as dual-stream modeling, VPA, and ACG. While each module is justified, the overall design introduces additional implementation and computational overhead, and it is unclear whether the performance gains warrant this level of complexity.
2.The experimental evaluation is limited to a single dataset (PathText-BRCA). This raises concerns about the generalizability of the method to other pathology domains, where data distributions and reporting styles may differ significantly.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Overall, this paper presents a well-motivated and thoughtfully designed approach to pathology report generation. The proposed dual-stream framework aligns well with the characteristics of gigapixel WSIs, and the integration of a confidence-aware retrieval mechanism is both intuitive and practically meaningful. The experimental evaluation is reasonably thorough, with ablation studies and hyperparameter analyses that help validate the effectiveness of the individual components. The paper is also clearly written and easy to follow.
That said, there are still some limitations. The overall framework is relatively complex, involving multiple interacting modules, and it is not entirely clear whether the performance gains fully justify this level of design complexity. In addition, the evaluation is limited to a single dataset, leaving questions about generalizability to other pathology domains.
Despite these concerns, the paper provides a solid contribution with a reasonable level of novelty and empirical support, and therefore is slightly above the acceptance threshold.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes DR-Gen, a dual-stream retrieval-augmented framework for pathology report generation. The core innovation lies in decoupling visual processing into global (tissue architecture) and focal (diagnostic cellular details) streams, combined with a confidence-gated retrieval mechanism to suppress non-diagnostic noise.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Clear motivation
The identification of Visual dilution and Retrieval noise is clear and convincing.
2.Dual-Stream mechanism
To deal with the visual dillution, this paper proposed a dual-stream mechanism, emulating the ‘think global, look focal’ clinial practice of pathologists.
3.Strong results
The Factent metric (0.519) and high classification F1 indicate that the model preserves factual medical entities, which is critical for clinical utility. The qualitative example (Fig. 2) effectively illustrates the reduction of hallucinations compared to baseline.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The CAP-protocol-guided knowledge bank is mentioned as constructed from “atomic diagnostic statements,” but the paper lacks details about the bank construction.

Clear and strong motivation. The dual-stream mechanism significantly improves the model’s performance.

The paper addresses a well-motivated problem with a clinically inspired dual-stream design and demonstrates solid empirical gains. No major consensus concerns.

title: Through the Schrödinger Bridge: Benchmarking Antemortem Image Restoration from Postmortem Autolysis to Enhance Forensic Diagnostics
abstract: Forensic histopathology, essential for determining cause of death and disease diagnosis, is severely impeded by postmortem autolysis, i.e., an irreversible, stochastic degradation process that distorts tissue morphology and introduces diagnostic subjectivity, thereby underscoring the value of restoring autolyzed images to a diagnostically plausible, pre-autolysis state for improving objectivity in forensic practice. This restoration task is fundamentally challenging due to the large, non-deterministic morphological changes caused by autolysis and the infeasibility of pixel-wise paired data, which invalidates assumptions underlying supervised and cycle/structure-consistent unpaired translation methods. To address this, we formalize forensic histopathology autolysis restoration as a new task: under unpaired supervision, transform postmortem images with severe autolysis into diagnostically meaningful ``antemortem’’ representations. We contribute AutoPath, the first homologous yet unpaired dataset for this problem, constructed by splitting specimens into adjacent tissue blocks—one processed immediately, the other exposed to induce autolysis—yielding nearly ten thousand  patches from 69 cases with varying liver conditions. We fruther frame the problem as a Schrödinger Bridge between the autolyzed and non-autolyzed distributions, offering a principled approach to modeling stochastic, severe morphological degradation. Critically, we demonstrate the misalignment of generic image-level generative metrics (e.g., FID) with diagnostic utility and propose a forensically grounded, slide-level diagnostic distribution consistency evaluation. Overall, this work establishes a reproducible benchmark (encompassing task definition, a real-world dataset, and an evaluation methodology) toward rigorous and practically meaningful progress in autolysis restoration for forensic pathology.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Synthetic Data / Data-centric AI

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper introduces a new and clinically meaningful task in computational pathology: restoring severely autolyzed postmortem histopathology images toward diagnostically plausible antemortem representations under unpaired supervision.
The authors make three key contributions:
Task and Dataset: They formalize forensic autolysis restoration as a new problem and introduce AutoPath, the first homologous yet unpaired dataset constructed by splitting adjacent tissue blocks from the same specimen, enabling medically meaningful supervision despite the absence of pixel-wise pairing. 
Methodology: They formulate the problem as a Schrödinger Bridge (SB) stochastic transport between autolyzed and non-autolyzed distributions, which is conceptually well-aligned with the irreversible and stochastic nature of autolysis. The model avoids structural consistency constraints and instead focuses on distribution-level alignment. 
Evaluation Framework: They propose a slide-level diagnostic distribution consistency metric, demonstrating that commonly used generative metrics (e. g. , FID) are misaligned with forensic diagnostic utility, and advocate for clinically grounded evaluation.
Overall, the paper establishes a new benchmark for this underexplored problem and provides a framework for evaluating restoration quality in a clinically meaningful way.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Novel and clinically relevant problem formulation
The paper addresses an important and underexplored challenge in forensic histopathology. The distinction between autolysis restoration and conventional image translation is clearly articulated and well-motivated. 
2.Well-designed dataset with strong practical grounding
The AutoPath dataset is a significant contribution. The use of spatially adjacent tissue blocks to construct homologous yet unpaired samples is a thoughtful and realistic solution to the lack of paired data. 
3.Conceptually appropriate modeling choice
The use of Schrödinger Bridge to model stochastic, irreversible degradation is well aligned with the problem characteristics. The decision to remove structural consistency constraints is also justified and differentiates this work from standard unpaired translation methods. 
4.Clinically meaningful evaluation beyond FID
The paper convincingly shows that lower FID does not correspond to better diagnostic quality. The proposed slide-level diagnostic distribution consistency is a strong contribution and more aligned with real-world forensic practice. 
5.Comprehensive evaluation (quantitative + human + case-level)
The combination of patch-level metrics, expert validation, and slide-level consistency provides a more holistic evaluation than typical generative modeling papers.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Limited methodological novelty beyond adaptation of SB framework
While the formulation is well motivated, the model itself appears to be an adaptation of existing neural Schrödinger Bridge approaches with adversarial alignment. The primary novelty lies more in task formulation and evaluation rather than algorithmic innovation. 
2.Insufficient implementation details and reproducibility concerns
Key aspects of the method are under-specified, including model architecture, training schedule, SB loss implementation, and hyperparameters. This limits reproducibility. 
3.Evaluation relies on a potentially weak intermediate classifier
The slide-level evaluation depends on a classifier trained with ~300 annotated patches. The robustness and calibration of this classifier are not sufficiently validated, raising concerns about the reliability of WSDC/WKL metrics. 
4.Limited statistical rigor in expert evaluation
The expert validation results are promising but lack statistical analysis (e. g. , inter-rater agreement, confidence intervals, significance testing). The evaluation protocol may also introduce forced-choice bias. 
5.Risk of hallucination and clinical misinterpretation not fully addressed
Since the task does not enforce structural fidelity, the model may generate plausible but incorrect morphology. The paper does not sufficiently discuss the potential risks of such hallucinations in forensic diagnosis. 
6.Limited dataset scope and generalization
The dataset is restricted to liver tissue and a relatively small cohort (69 cases). It is unclear how well the method generalizes to other organs, magnifications, or varying degrees of autolysis. 
Baselines may not be sufficiently strong or recent
7.Comparisons are mainly against GAN-based unpaired methods. Stronger diffusion-based or medical-specific baselines would strengthen the claims.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
This is an interesting and well-motivated work addressing a clinically meaningful problem. I particularly appreciate the effort to go beyond standard generative metrics and propose a more domain-relevant evaluation framework.
To further strengthen the paper, I suggest:
Providing more detailed methodological descriptions to improve reproducibility. 
Adding statistical analysis to expert validation (e. g. , agreement metrics, significance testing). 
Evaluating the robustness and calibration of the slide-level classifier. 
Including failure cases and analyzing when the model produces unrealistic or misleading structures. 
Expanding discussion on clinical applicability and risks of hallucination. 
Considering stronger or more recent baselines.
Overall, the work has strong potential as a benchmark and problem-defining contribution.

The paper addresses a novel and clinically relevant problem and introduces a valuable dataset and evaluation framework. The experimental results provide useful insights, particularly regarding the limitations of standard generative metrics in medical contexts.
However, the methodological novelty is moderate, and there are concerns regarding reproducibility, evaluation rigor, and potential clinical risks (e.g., hallucination). The work is still promising and likely to stimulate further research in this area, but some aspects require clarification and strengthening.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_ethics:
The proposed method raises potential concerns regarding hallucination of non-existent pathological structures. Since the model aims to generate diagnostically plausible “restored” images without enforcing structural consistency, it may introduce artificial morphology that does not correspond to the true underlying tissue.
In forensic settings, such hallucinated features could potentially mislead diagnosis or interpretation. The paper would benefit from a clearer discussion of intended use (e. g. , visualization vs. diagnostic support) and safeguards against misuse.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a highly novel computational pathology task: utilizing a deep generative model (Schrödinger Bridge) to restore severely autolyzed H&E-stained slides to a state closely resembling fresh tissue. To overcome the physical impossibility of obtaining pixel-level ground truth, the authors cleverly construct a “homologous yet unpaired” liver tissue dataset. Overall, the paper has an excellent entry point, clear motivation, and holds significant practical value for forensic and clinical pathology. However, the manuscript currently exhibits noticeable shortcomings in the comprehensiveness of its quantitative evaluation, the validation of its downstream clinical utility, and its cross-organ generalizability, which require further improvement.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.High Novelty and Forensic/Clinical Significance:
Unlike previous “bypass” strategies that rely on specialized equipment (e.g., virtual staining via autofluorescence microscopy), this paper tackles the most challenging and common issue head-on: restoring routine H&E slides that have suffered from autolytic degradation. The introduction of this task fills a critical gap in the field and has immense practical application value.
2.Clever Dataset Design:
The “homologous yet unpaired” data collection strategy elegantly addresses the impossibility of acquiring paired Ground Truth due to the destructive nature of tissue preparation. This provides an excellent and rigorous experimental paradigm for future research in this domain.
3.Reasonable Methodological Choice:
Given that autolysis inherently destroys cellular structures, traditional unpaired translation methods relying on cycle consistency (e.g., CycleGAN) are fundamentally unsuitable. The authors’ choice to utilize the Schrödinger Bridge to model the stochastic dynamics between complex, structurally disparate distributions is logically sound and perfectly tailored to the task’s characteristics.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Insufficient Quantitative Metrics:
The current evaluation lacks standard distribution-level metrics for generative models (e.g., FID, KID) to objectively measure image quality. Furthermore, a subjective evaluation by professional pathologists (e.g., Mean Opinion Score or a Turing Test) is missing, which is crucial for assessing morphological fidelity and the presence of generative artifacts.
2.Lack of Downstream Validation:
The paper does not evaluate whether the restored images actually recover diagnostic value. Including a standard computational pathology task—such as nuclei instance segmentation or lesion classification—on the restored images is essential to prove the practical and clinical utility of the proposed method.
3.Limited Scope (Liver Tissue Only):
The experiments are exclusively conducted on liver tissue. Since different organs (e.g., kidney, brain, heart) exhibit vastly different autolysis mechanisms and morphological changes, the generalizability of the proposed framework to other tissue types remains unverified.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The conceptualization of this paper is outstanding, but the depth and breadth of the experiments do not yet fully support its ambitious task setting. If the authors can supplement the Rebuttal/Revision phase with downstream task validation and richer quantitative metrics, this will be a highly impactful and excellent piece of work.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces a new task of forensic histopathology autolysis restoration, aiming to transform postmortem autolyzed tissue images into diagnostically plausible antemortem representations under unpaired supervision. The authors contribute a novel dataset (AutoPath) constructed using adjacent tissue blocks to approximate correspondence between autolyzed and non-autolyzed samples, and formulate the restoration problem as a Schrödinger Bridge to model stochastic morphological degradation. Additionally, the paper proposes a clinically motivated evaluation framework based on slide-level diagnostic distribution consistency, highlighting limitations of conventional generative metrics such as FID.
reviews.text_strengths:
Novel problem formulation: The paper defines an important and underexplored task in computational pathology—autolysis restoration for forensic diagnostics—which is both clinically relevant and technically challenging.
Dataset contribution: The AutoPath dataset is a valuable contribution. The use of adjacent tissue blocks to approximate homologous but unpaired samples is a thoughtful and practical design that reflects real-world constraints.
Principled modeling approach: Framing the problem as a Schrödinger Bridge is theoretically well-motivated for modeling stochastic, irreversible morphological degradation. This is a strong methodological choice for unpaired translation with large domain shifts.
Clinically aligned evaluation: The paper correctly identifies limitations of FID and introduces a slide-level diagnostic distribution consistency framework, which is more meaningful for clinical applications.
Inclusion of expert evaluation: The use of board-certified forensic pathologists for blinded evaluation adds credibility and relevance to the results.
Comprehensive evaluation pipeline: The combination of patch-level metrics, expert validation, and slide-level consistency provides a multi-faceted evaluation strategy.
Overall, the combination of a new task, dataset, and clinically motivated evaluation makes this a meaningful contribution to the field.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Limited dataset scale and diversity: The dataset consists of 69 cases from a single organ (liver), which may limit generalizability across tissues, disease types, and forensic scenarios.
Weak supervision and label dependency in evaluation: The slide-level evaluation relies on a classifier trained on a relatively small number of annotated patches (~300), which may introduce bias and affect the reliability of the diagnostic distribution consistency metric.
Lack of strong quantitative improvement: The method does not achieve the best FID score and the improvement in expert preference (23.81%) is relatively modest, raising questions about the magnitude of practical gains.
Ambiguity in restoration validity: Since autolysis is irreversible, there is no ground truth for restored images. While the authors acknowledge this, the framework still assumes that generated images are diagnostically meaningful without rigorous validation beyond preference-based evaluation.
Risk of hallucination in generative model: The Schrödinger Bridge model may introduce plausible but incorrect morphological structures, which could mislead downstream diagnosis. This risk is not deeply analyzed.
Evaluation depends on downstream classifier: Slide-level consistency metrics rely on a trained classifier, making the evaluation indirect and dependent on classifier performance rather than purely on restoration quality.
More importantly, the absence of ground truth for restoration combined with reliance on indirect evaluation metrics makes it difficult to assess whether the generated images are diagnostically correct or merely visually plausible.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
This paper presents an interesting and important direction for forensic pathology, combining dataset creation, modeling, and evaluation. However, stronger validation of restoration correctness and broader evaluation across datasets would improve confidence in the approach. Additionally, clearer discussion of ethical considerations and potential risks of generative hallucination would strengthen the work.

This paper introduces a novel and clinically meaningful problem in forensic histopathology and provides a well-designed dataset and principled modeling approach. The use of a Schrödinger Bridge for modeling stochastic degradation is technically sound, and the evaluation framework appropriately emphasizes clinical relevance over traditional generative metrics.
However, several limitations reduce confidence in the results. The dataset is relatively small and limited in scope, and the evaluation relies on indirect measures such as expert preference and classifier-based distribution consistency. Additionally, the inherent ambiguity of the restoration task, combined with the risk of hallucinated structures, raises concerns about whether the generated images are clinically reliable or potentially misleading.
Overall, the paper is slightly above the acceptance threshold due to its novelty and practical importance, but would benefit from stronger validation and broader evaluation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper’s main strengths are its novel and clinically important formulation of autolysis restoration in forensic histopathology, the carefully designed AutoPath dataset using homologous yet unpaired adjacent tissue blocks, and the well-motivated use of Schrödinger Bridge to model stochastic and irreversible degradation. The evaluation is also clinically meaningful, combining patch-level metrics, expert assessment, and slide-level diagnostic consistency beyond standard FID.
However, the reviewers also noted several weaknesses. The model has limited methodological novelty, as it largely adapts existing Schrödinger Bridge approaches, and the dataset is restricted to a relatively small liver cohort, leaving generalization unclear. More importantly, the evaluation has key limitations: the slide-level metrics rely on a weakly validated classifier, expert evaluation lacks stronger statistical analysis, and there is no ground truth to confirm whether the restored images are diagnostically correct rather than merely visually plausible. The paper also insufficiently addresses hallucination risks, downstream diagnostic validation, and comparisons with stronger recent baselines.
Having said this, I find that the paper balances between strong and weak aspects, leaning towards the positive side. I believe the main strength lies in its strong clinical usefulness for restoring degraded slides, an important problem that has not yet been actively studied. I also note that all three reviewers unanimously agree that the paper is acceptable and highly praise its clinical usefulness and practical value. Based on this assessment, I recommend acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their valuable comments and positive feedback. We are encouraged that reviewers consistently recognized the novelty and forensic significance of the task, the value of the AutoPath dataset, the suitability of the Schrödinger Bridge (SB) formulation, and the importance of clinically grounded evaluation beyond FID.
We emphasize that this work is primarily intended as a benchmark-defining and clinically grounded formulation for forensic autolysis restoration, rather than a purely architecture-driven generative modeling paper.
R2Q1&R2Q7: Method novelty and baselines
The main novelty lies in:
(1) formalizing forensic autolysis restoration as a new computational pathology task
(2) constructing the first homologous-yet-unpaired benchmark (AutoPath)
(3) introducing clinically grounded evaluation beyond conventional perceptual metrics.
SB is adopted as a principled framework for modeling irreversible and stochastic autolysis. Since severe autolysis physically destroys tissue structures, strong structural consistency assumptions are unsuitable for this task. Thus, we focus on distribution-level restoration rather than architectural novelty alone.
We used representative unpaired translation methods as baselines and agree that stronger diffusion/pathology-specific baselines would be valuable future extensions.
R2Q2: Reproducibility
In the camera-ready version, we will further provide implementation details, training settings, and hyperparameters. We also plan to publicly release the code and AutoPath dataset.
R2Q3&R5Q2&R5Q6: Reliability of the classifier
The classifier is intended as a proxy for slide-level diagnostic distribution consistency rather than an absolute diagnostic oracle. We adopt CONCH pretrained weights, which are extensively validated in computational pathology.
Although only ~300 annotated patches were used, we only fine-tuned a lightweight MLP head while keeping the encoder fixed, resulting in stable convergence. The downstream categories also correspond to relatively standard histopathological patterns.
R2Q4&R3Q1&R5Q3: Evaluation and quantitative metrics
A key motivation of this work is to demonstrate that conventional perceptual metrics such as FID may not align with clinically meaningful restoration quality. Besides FID, we additionally included blinded expert evaluation and slide-level diagnostic consistency evaluation.
The discrepancy between FID and slide-/expert-level evaluations further supports the need for clinically grounded evaluation.
R2Q5&R5Q4&R5Q5&R5Q7: Hallucination and restoration validity
Our goal is not pixel-wise reconstruction of the original tissue, which is physically impossible under irreversible autolysis and destructive tissue processing. Instead, we aim to restore diagnostically plausible distributional representations.
This is also why we avoid enforcing strict structural consistency constraints. Under severe autolysis, forcing strong structural alignment often produces anatomically implausible artifacts because many cellular structures are irreversibly destroyed.
To address the lack of direct ground truth, we employ clinically grounded indirect evaluations, including patch-level analysis, slide-level diagnostic consistency, and expert assessment. We position this framework as a visualization and decision-support tool under expert supervision rather than an autonomous forensic diagnostic system.
R2Q6&R3Q3&R5Q1: Dataset scope and downstream validation
Liver tissue is one of the most important organs routinely sampled in forensic autopsy and is particularly suitable for studying autolytic degradation. We agree that broader multi-organ validation would further strengthen the benchmark and are currently expanding the dataset scale and diversity.
We also agree that downstream validation is important. Our slide-level diagnostic consistency evaluation itself serves as a clinically motivated downstream task focuing on disease distribution consistency after restoration.

title: Through-Plane Attention for Anisotropic CT Super-Resolution Improves Quantitative Lung Cancer Analysis
abstract: Volumetric computed tomography (CT) often exhibits severe through-plane anisotropy due to thick-slice acquisition, disrupting structural continuity and degrading downstream lung cancer analysis. We propose TVSRN-V2, a volumetric super-resolution (SR) framework with an anisotropy-aware Through-Plane Attention Block (TAB) that models inter-slice dependencies by factoring attention into orthogonal sagittal and coronal planes. To broaden the degradation distribution during training, we use hybrid pseudo-low-resolution (pseudo-LR) augmentation combining real paired scans with synthetic degradations. Clinical utility is evaluated across pulmonary lobe and bronchi segmentation, histology classification, and survival prediction in 742 patients (539 from three independent external cohorts). TVSRN-V2 achieves PSNR 39.16 dB and SSIM 0.946, and yields an absolute Dice improvement of 0.16 for bronchi over bicubic interpolation on real low-resolution CT. SR features improve histology classification (F1 +0.03–0.07, ) and internal survival prediction (C-index +0.06, ), with smaller non-significant external prognosis gains.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduced an improved version of super resolution for volumetric CT. The proposed TVSRN-v2 is an asmmetric encoder decoder SR built on top of swin v2.the main contribution the paper claimed is it’s dual attention branch through plane attention block. Another part is a hybrid pseudo low res aug strategy. the evaluation contains common PSNR SSIM, also pulmonary lobe/bronchi segmentation, histology classification, survival prediction on large internal and external cohorts.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.I’m very familiar with the SR works and examined many approaches, this field in general is very challenging because the current benchmarks are extremely high and hard to beat so I welcome the authors effort to improve on top existing methods. The TAB is actual less impressive than hybrid pseudo LR aug. it’s a good approach to mitigate the data size limitation and homogeneity of real paired SR data. 
2.the evaluation that improves downstream task is valuable empirical evidence on the importance of SR with a variety of task types. the paper reports consistent imporvements over original TVSRN in several settings, and the segmnetation gain on real low res CT is noticable. 
3.the inclusion of extra large external validation is a strength
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.the novelty of the v2 is relatively low compare to previous work. the paper highlighted TAB as central new contribution, but TVSRN already has a TAB inside the decoder’s FIM, with two parallel branches on coronal and sagittal view. the difference is just very minor. 
2.the main competition method shouldn’t be TVSRN, it should eb CTHNet which is an improved version of TVSRN and the performance is really good on the CTHNet with several substantial redesign of the architecture. 
3.the empirical gains are mixed relative to the strength of the claims. The improvement over the original TVSRN in PSNR is modest, and the downstream gains, while directionally positive, are not uniformly strong across all external prognosis settings. This makes the novelty issue harder to overlook, because the paper is not paired with a clearly empirical jump
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Overall, the paper’s positioning is not clear enough about its relationship to prior works. Because TAB, the RPLHR-CT setting, the asymmetric encoder-decoder formulation, and the general thick-slice-to-downstream-analysis story are all strongly tied to earlier work, the manuscript needs much clearer attribution and framing.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The response is constructive and honest, the main concern is still the central framework novelty is weak. the response narrows the difference to adaptive gating, swin v2 modernization, and hybrid pseudo-lr training. those are good engineering efforts, just it’s very incremental. that said, it’s still is a valuable work because of the clinical validation, but not around TAB novelty.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a transformer-based volumetric super-resolution framework (TVSRN-V2) for anisotropic CT, introducing a through-plane attention mechanism to explicitly model inter-slice dependencies and demonstrating its impact on downstream lung cancer analysis tasks.
reviews.text_strengths:
The problem is important, common in clinical practice, and well-motivated.
The method is well-designed with a clear focus on through-plane modeling.
The evaluation is comprehensive, including multi-center validation and multiple downstream tasks.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The comparisons are not fully sufficient to establish the necessity and uniqueness of the proposed design, lacking stronger 3D or inter-slice modeling baselines.
The paper provides limited analysis on why downstream improvements are achieved beyond reporting performance gains.
The presentation can be improved, e.g., Figure 1 is unclear and Table 3 is difficult to read due to small font.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The score is based on the above strengths and weaknesses.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Although the response clarifies some architectural differences from TVSRN, it does not adequately address my core concern regarding the necessity of the proposed design, especially why TAB is preferable to other plausible 3D or inter-slice modeling strategies and how it leads to the reported downstream improvements.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of this work is the introduction of the TAB module, which restores structural continuity by employing two orthogonal attention pathways. A secondary contribution is the use of pseudo-low-resolution (pseudo-LR) augmentations during training. Combined with real paired data, this strategy aims to improve generalization across scanners while minimizing domain gaps. Finally, the approach is evaluated extensively on multiple datasets, including ablation studies, to assess both performance and potential clinical utility.
reviews.text_strengths:
(S1) The paper provides an extensive evaluation of clinical utility across multiple downstream tasks, covering five acquisition protocols and three distinct tasks. The results of the proposed model are promising compared to the two alternative approaches evaluated.
(S2) The authors address the scarcity of high-quality paired super-resolution (SR) datasets by incorporating pseudo-low-resolution (pseudo-LR) images during training, which is a well-motivated strategy to improve generalization.
(S3) Statistical testing is performed, and confidence intervals are provided, supporting the reliability of the reported results.
(S4) The manuscript includes a discussion of the limitations of the proposed approach, providing context for the scope and applicability of the method.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(W1) The related work is limited, with only a single reference ([13]) cited for existing CT super-resolution (SR) approaches. Several recent methods, including publications from the last few years at MICCAI and other venues, are not discussed or compared. I recommend performing a focused literature search for recent CT SR approaches and citing them appropriately. Including these references would provide a more complete context and support claims made in, for example, the final sentences of Subsection 2.2.
(W2) While downstream task performance is reported, a qualitative assessment of the SR outputs is missing. No visual comparisons between SR and high-resolution (HR) images are provided, making it difficult to evaluate structural consistency and the potential for hallucinated features.
(W3) The manuscript does not report inference speed, which is an important factor for assessing clinical feasibility in real-world settings.
(W4) No systematic or controlled hyperparameter optimization is reported, limiting confidence in whether the results reflect an optimized configuration.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
(C1) Abbreviations are not consistently introduced and used throughout the manuscript. Each abbreviation, including common ones such as CT and LR, should be defined upon first use in both the abstract and main text, and then used consistently thereafter.
(C2) Several variables are not properly defined, which reduces clarity and makes some equations harder to follow.
(C3) Some statements and components lack references (e.g., Section 2.2). Each method, claim, or component should be properly cited.
(C4) Headings should not appear consecutively without intervening text (e.g., Section 2 followed directly by Subsection 2.1). It would also improve readability to include a brief introductory sentence at the start of Subsection 2.1.
(C5) There are undesirable line breaks in several places (e.g., page 3: “[…] LUNA16 dataset (<= LINEBREAK 3 mm) […]” and page 5 before “(C-Index)”). These could be corrected using non-breaking spaces to improve formatting and readability.
(C6) Variables in the text and equations should be written in italics (e.g., p in the abstract).
(C7) References should be ordered numerically when multiple are cited together (e.g., page 1 [1, 2] instead of [2, 1]).
(C8) Equations should be properly integrated into the text with correct punctuation and formatting to improve readability.
(C9) The number of GPUs used for training is not explicitly stated and should be reported.
(C10) The orange text in Figure 1 is difficult to read; adjusting the color or contrast would improve visibility.
(C11) As a suggestion, considering the Gradient SSIM (G-SSIM) metric may provide a more sensitive evaluation for SR tasks in addition to standard SSIM.

The paper introduces a novel architectural component within an existing model and validates it through extensive ablation studies. The reported results are statistically significant and indicate promising performance. However, several recent related works are not discussed or compared, which limits the contextualization of the contribution. In addition, there are stylistic and formatting issues that should be addressed to improve clarity and presentation.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors addressed most of the weaknesses identified in my original review, with the exception of (W4), which remains unresolved. In particular, the rebuttal provided additional clarification regarding the TAB module, the role of the hybrid pseudo-LR strategy, and the planned qualitative evaluation of structural consistency. Assuming that the improvements and corrections outlined in the rebuttal, including the addressed comments, are incorporated into the final manuscript, I would support acceptance of the paper.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper had mixed reviews that would be improved by a rebuttal. The reviewers noted a large external validation, multiple downstream tasks, and statistical testing as positives in the study, but the main uncertainty was whether the claimed architectural novelty is real relative to prior TVSRN/CTHNet-style methods. The paper presents TAB as the central contribution, but the original TVSRN already appears to contain a related through-plane attention block inside its decoder/FIM with parallel coronal and sagittal branches. If true, the architectural novelty is minor. Notes were also made that recent CT SR literature was missing from the related work and comparisons. The rebuttal should focus on: 1) explaining precisely how TAB differs from prior TVSRN/FIM and whether CTHNet is included, unavailable, or not comparable, 2) cite and contextualize recent CT SR methods, especially those with 3D or inter-slice modeling, and 3) include qualitative SR/HR comparisons, if available.

The authors were straightforward and clear in their rebuttal, but there are still remaining concerns that were not (or could not) be addressed at this stage. In particular, there is a need to evaluate stronger baselines and to compare the TAB module against other similar methodologies. While this remains unaddressed, the reviewers highlight the careful rebuttal of their concerns and the powerful clinical validation. In the end, the contribution is solid and well-positioned in clinical validation, if incremental. I recommend acceptance of this article, but in remains borderline.

The key contribution is the component introduced for super resolution – novelty of TAB component must be clarified and explained in terms of other prior works as to how it improves super resolution accuracy. All reviewers were concerned regarding the engineering focus of the innovation so it is important to really clarify and frame the contribution in relation to prior works better.

Concerns regarding the technical novelty and justification of the proposed design were not fully addressed, but reviewers agreed that it is a valuable work, provided the improvements are incorporated into the final version.

author_feedback_text:
Relationship to TVSRN
We agree that TVSRN-V2 is an evolutionary rather than paradigmatic advance. Our contribution is a clinically oriented redesign targeting through-plane structural recovery in anisotropic CT, combined with a robust training strategy and evaluated across multiple real-world tasks and institutions.
TAB Design and Distinction from TVSRN (R2)
The original TVSRN uses Feature Interaction Modules (FIMs) for cross-scale fusion, with coronal and sagittal interactions appearing only during local decoder refinement. TAB, described in Section 2.2, is architecturally distinct: it reshapes intermediate features into orthogonal (D,H) and (D,W) representations, applies shifted-window self-attention independently in each plane, and fuses the results via adaptive learned gating:
F_TAB = σ(W_g ⋅ [F_sag; F_cor]) ⊙ F_sag + (1 − σ(W_g ⋅ [F_sag; F_cor])) ⊙ F_cor
This differs from implicit inter-slice aggregation by decomposing volumetric attention into orthogonal pathways before adaptively recombining them. The ablation in Section 3.1 (Table 1) supports this design: TAB removal produced the largest single-component degradation (−1.34 dB PSNR, −0.026 SSIM), and the largest downstream gains occurred in anatomies most sensitive to through-plane averaging — bronchi and lobes.
CTHNet and Related Work (R1)
We thank R1 for identifying the convolutional-transformer hybrid of Yu et al. (npj Digital Medicine, 2024) as a relevant baseline. The T-CTH block similarly processes coronal and sagittal pathways in parallel, but fuses them via element-wise summation. TVSRN-V2 uses adaptive channel-wise gating instead, allowing the network to weight orthogonal evidence dynamically according to local anatomy. Importantly, Yu et al. identify training data homogeneity as a primary limitation of their framework — a bottleneck our hybrid pseudo-LR strategy is designed to address directly. Per MICCAI guidelines, we cannot introduce new empirical comparisons during rebuttal, but we will revise the related work section to contextualize CTHNet fully and address the runtime considerations raised by R3.
Hybrid Pseudo-LR Augmentation (R1)
As described in Section 2.1, the hybrid pseudo-LR strategy is a core component of the framework, combining real paired RPLHR-CT data with synthetic degradations spanning heterogeneous slice thicknesses to improve robustness across scanners and acquisition protocols. We will revise the manuscript to foreground this contribution more explicitly alongside the TAB design, clarifying that the two together constitute the primary methodological advance.
Structural Consistency and Qualitative Evaluation (R3, AC)
Given the text-only rebuttal format, we cannot include figures here.
