author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for appreciating AID’s clinical importance and methodological grounding. The central contribution is a semantic-aware pre-training formulation that treats structured clinical variables as supervision signals for image-tabular medical representation learning. We address concerns below.
Q1: Novelty beyond TIP and relation to TP-BERTa (R2, R3).
In contrast to TIP/MMCL/CITab’s semantic-agnostic flat-vector treatment with uniform masking and continuous regression, AID models inter-feature diagnostic hierarchy via a label-free importance curriculum and intra-feature ordinal-continuous structure via soft-label discretized reconstruction. We thank R3 for pointing to TP-BERTa, whose goal is orthogonal: it encodes ordinality at the input-tokenization level for a unimodal tabular LM, while AID enforces it at the reconstruction-objective level inside image-tabular multimodal pre-training, where visual evidence reconstructs masked clinical semantics. Empirically (Tab.1), AID’s linear probing exceeds prior SSL baselines’ full fine-tuning (incl. TIP, 0.984 vs 0.971), with OOD 0.944 vs 0.911 showing gains from semantic-aware design, not scaling. TP-BERTa will be cited and contrasted in camera-ready.
Q2: TabPFN role, aggregation, masking stability (R1, R2, R3).
TabPFN serves only as an offline label-free meta-prior for dataset-level feature hierarchy. Designed for small-scale tabular data, it is applied once offline rather than as a backbone for 400K cohorts. For aggregation (R2), each layer averages multi-head weights; feature saliency from query (row sum, outgoing influence), key (column sum, incoming relevance) and self-attention (diagonal, self-relevance) is summed across layers, L1-normalized and min-max scaled, yielding a closed-form heuristic, not Attention Rollout. Formal notation will be added to §2.2.For row heterogeneity (R2), TabPFN’s in-context inference uses a single PCA-pseudo-label across rows, producing a dataset-level vector by construction. By design, it serves as a cohort-level masking prior, not a patient-specific explanation; patient-level heterogeneity is modeled by the multimodal encoder during representation learning. We clarify that s_i is fixed by design as the label-free curriculum; the representation evolves under it (Fig.3(e,f)). The per-feature cap α=r_max=0.7 (R1) applies only to top-importance features; the dataset-level expected ratio stays ~0.3, so adaptive masking targets clinically salient features rather than masking more. On joint training (R3), a jointly trained visual prior captures image-token saliency from multimodal optimization, whereas TabPFN supplies a tabular bias before pre-training (future work).
Q3: Soft-label discretized reconstruction (R1, R3).
On bin sensitivity (R1), B∈{20,50,100} shows an inverted-U with B=50 consistently best (smaller B over-smooths intervals; larger B approaches noisy regression). Unlike hard quantile discretization, the triangle-kernel preserves ordinal neighborhood structure; unlike Gaussian smoothing it avoids over-smoothing while distinguishing near-bin from far-bin errors. The DR loss notation in Eq.2 will be refined to clarify summation over samples, features and bins (R2).
Q4: Statistical reliability and three-head protocol (R1, R2).
Due to space, fold-wise std was omitted; in our 5-fold protocol AID’s std (≈0.5%) stays below TIP’s (≈1%), placing the OOD margin well outside fold-to-fold variation. The three-head ensemble averages image-only, tabular-only and multimodal logits, applied uniformly to AID and baselines (per TIP/CITab), giving no AID-specific advantage; representation quality is evidenced by linear probing surpassing prior baselines’ full fine-tuning.
Minor.
DINOv3 is self-supervised in pre-training but grouped with supervised methods because we fine-tuned its weights with labels; we will relabel it as “SSL”. More implementation details and full results will be made publicly available.

title: Unsupervised and Segmentation-Free Phase Unwrapping for 4D Flow MRI Using Deep Image Prior
abstract: 4D flow MRI provides rich hemodynamic information by encoding blood-flow velocities in the image phase; however, image quality highly depends on the velocity-encoding (venc) setting—high venc reduces the velocity-to-noise ratio (VNR), whereas low venc improves VNR but increases the risk of phase wrapping, potentially introducing substantial bias in downstream flow quantification. We propose PUDIP-Flow, an unsupervised and segmentation-free phase-unwrapping method for aortic 4D flow MRI based on the deep image prior (DIP). The method formulates phase unwrapping as an optimization problem that enforces consistency with wrapped spatiotemporal phase gradients, and solves it by fitting a 3D U-Net to a single scan without paired training data. To reduce reliance on manual segmentation of regions of interest, we further introduce an automated weighting mask derived from phase-contrast MR angiography features and temporal variance, thereby suppressing contributions from stationary background tissue. Experiments on retrospective and prospective aortic datasets show that PUDIP-Flow improves unwrapping accuracy and robustness compared with established baselines, with particularly strong performance when manual segmentations are unavailable.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This manuscript proposes PUDIP-Flow, an unsupervised phase-unwrapping method for aortic 4D flow MRI using the Deep Image Prior (DIP). The authors formulate unwrapping as a gradient-domain optimization problem, fitting a 3D U-Net to a single scan to enforce spatiotemporal continuity. Comparative studies were conducted to compare PUDIP-Flow with LAP, NRPS, and PUMA algorithms, and the results demonstrated that the proposed method led to desirable results.
reviews.text_strengths: Overall, the logic flow of this manuscript is clear, and it is well-organized and easy to follow. The results is also desirable compared the other traditional comparative algorithms.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The proposed PUDIP-flow is merely an application of the well-established DIP algorithms to the MRI phase unwrapping problem, and the innovation in the methodological point of view is low for MICCAI, considering that DIP has already been applied to MRI phase unwrapping, e. g. , DIP-UP method https://www. mdpi. com/2078-2489/16/7/592.
The authors showed a limited literature review in the manuscript about the more recently proposed phase unwrapping algorithms, especially the deep learning ones, like PHU-Net, Phase-Net, PhaseNet2.0, PU-GAN, et al.
Although the proposed PUDIP-Flow is oriented to the 4D flow data; however, there are no special or innovative designs for catering to the 4D spatial-temporal nature of the data. Instead, the authors only used a multi-channel U-net, which is basically still a 3D algorithm.
There are also some efficiency concerns for the proposed method, which is nearly 8 minutes per scan, which is much longer than traditional Laplacian or path-based algorithms, and should also be much longer than the above-mentioned deep learning-based algorithms, especially the supervised learning ones.
The loss function (eq. 6) design is also too simple. As the authors described in the manuscript, Itoh’s condition is only valid when the gradient of flow is limited; however, they did not show this is the case for their applications. In addition, this theory is pretty out-of-date (proposed in 1982); indeed, there are many state-of-the-art equations building relationships between the wrapped phase and the potential unwrapped solutions (some of them are also the basis for the Laplacian unwrapping).
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

My major concerns are about the technical novelty of the manuscript. DIP is a well-established technique in CV and has been successfully applied to many areas in the medical imaging field already. I do not think the “A+B” type of innovations is good enough for MICCAI. Specifically, the DIP-UP / PHU-Net / PhaseNet papers I recommended to the authors are just an arbitrary search on Google Scholar using the keywords “DIP” + “Phase Unwrapping” + “MRI”, while the authors did not present any introductions, comparisons, or discussions. More detailed commnets can be found in the above “drawback” part.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The DIP-UP method I mentioned in my previous comment is just a quick search on Google Scholar using “DIP + phase unwrapping”, and there is also some other good fully unsupervised phase unwrapping method: “Robust Phase Unwrapping via Deep Image Prior for Quantitative Phase Imaging” (QPI) published at IEEE Transactions on Image Processing 2021 (DOI: 10.1109/TIP.2021.3099956), which is nearly the same topic as this manuscript from the methodological point of view. So, this work is definitely not the first fully unsupervised, segmentation-free DIP pipeline for phase unwrapping.
In addition, it is really easy to transfer DIP-UP / QPI to 4D flow data, since the major methodological improvement is a 4D loss, while the model for iterative tuning is still a 3D conventional U-net, as used in DIP-UP and QPI.
So, the novelty of this manuscript is just marginal and limited, and their literature review work is not enough as well, without comparing to any deep learning-based comparative methods, considering it is very easy to transfer these methods for 4D flow data (e.g., conduct phase unwrapping for each time point one by one).

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces a phase unwrapping approach for 4D flow MRI data based on the Unet and a loss function which formulates Itohs condition combined with a weighting which considers the temporal variation of flow velocities. The authors evaluate their approach against other state-of-the-art methods with regard to noise and the amount of voxels with phase wrap.
reviews.text_strengths: The authors present a deep learning based approach which implements concepts from earlier segmentation and optimization-based phase unwrapping approaches. The concepts are well motivated clearly described and compared to the state of the art.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The authors do not present an ablation study to assess the benefit of the suggested weighting concept.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a well motivated approach for a clinically relevant problem. The implementation is described in such a way that it can be reproduced and compared against the state of the art.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes an unsupervised and segmentation-free phase-unwrapping method for aortic 4D flow MRI based on the deep image prior. This method adopts a 3D U-Net to generate unwrapped phases corresponding to the 4D flow MRI via an unsupervised training manner. Retrospective and prospective experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
reviews.text_strengths: The major strength of this paper is the idea of using the unsupervised and automatic segmentation mask to generate the unwrapped phases of 4D flow MRI.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The rationality and novelty of using a 3D U-Net to generate the unwrapped phases should be further clarified. 
2.The compared methods, i.e., Refs. [1], [5], and [9] were proposed more than 10 years ago. As a result, the current experimental results are partially convincing. The comparison should be performed with more up-to-date methods.
3.The unsupervised training, validation, and test details of the proposed method are missing. These details are important for further understanding of this method.

N/A

Please refer to the listed major weaknesses of this paper.

meta_reviews.text:
The manuscript presents a clinically relevant unsupervised phase-unwrapping method for 4D flow MRI, with promising results especially in the segmentation-free setting. However, the novelty over existing DIP-based and deep-learning phase-unwrapping methods is not clearly established, and the comparison to recent MRI phase-unwrapping methods appears incomplete. The rebuttal should focus on clarifying the specific methodological novelty, justifying the choice of baselines, and providing missing implementation details needed for reproducibility.

The reviewers found the problem clinically relevant and the results promising, especially for phase unwrapping without manual segmentation. The rebuttal clarified the main concerns about novelty, baseline choices, the weighting-mask ablation, and implementation details.

This paper received after rebuttal two “accept” and one “reject” recommendation from the reviewers. One reviewer keeps having significant reservations regarding novelty and performed literature review that could not be sufficiently resolved in the rebuttal.
While the topic is certainly important and - as pointed out by one of the reviewers - has relevance for other areas relying on phase processing, search for similar literature indeed reveals some closely connected studies that make the current paper appear incremental in nature.
Reviewers raised concerns on its novelty since simiilar ideas has been published somewhere else. However, it is still worthy of exploring its usage in a new clinical scenario

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and AC. We address the major concerns below.
Q1.Novelty vs. DIP-UP and recent DL phase-unwrapping methods (R1, R3, Meta).
4D flow phase unwrapping differs structurally from prior settings: the target is a phase-difference Φ = ∠(I_FE · I^*_FC) (Eq. 1) — stationary tissue gives Φ ≈ 0, air is pure noise, and signal concentrates in vessels — unlike static GRE field-map unwrapping where every brain voxel encodes B0.The problem also spans three velocity-encoding directions and cardiac frames.
Despite the name, DIP-UP [Zhu 2025] REQUIRES supervised pre-training (PHU-Net3D/PhaseNet3D on ~28,800 paired patches with synthetic GT) before DIP refinement, uses a Laplacian loss, and targets static 3D brain GRE for QSM with no temporal or velocity-encoding component. PUDIP-Flow is unsupervised, uses a 4D spatiotemporal gradient-domain L1 loss, and targets the 4D flow phase difference. PHU-Net/PhaseNet 2.0/PU-GAN are likewise supervised, for 2D optical phase or static MRI.
Our contributions therefore stand: (i) the first fully unsupervised, segmentation-free DIP pipeline for 4D flow phase unwrapping with a 4D spatiotemporal gradient objective (Eq. 6); (ii) an automated PCMRA × temporal-std weighting mask (Eq. 8) exploiting the phase-difference structure; (iii) systematic validation across vencs and SNRs.
Q2.Baselines and uncompared recent methods (R1, R3, Meta).
LAP [9], NPRS [1], PUMA [5] are the standard 4D-flow baselines, forming the public 4DFlow-unwrap benchmark [6] whose reference implementations we use. Two 4D-flow-specific recent methods are not included: (a) Berhane et al. [4] is supervised, requiring large paired wrapped/unwrapped data — the gap our method addresses; (b) CWLS [Ref. 19] is neither open-sourced nor reproducible from the paper. The 2D networks R1 lists target a different problem and need paired 4D flow data to retrain.
Q3.”Just a 3D U-Net” — the 4D design (R1, R3).
Stacking temporal frames as output channels of a 3D U-Net is deliberate: the architecture stays lightweight while temporal continuity is imposed by the 4D finite-difference operator ∇ : R^N → R^4N in the loss (Sec. 2.2). Table 2 confirms this is load-bearing — replacing spatiotemporal TV with spatial-only TV raises nRMSE. Temporal information also drives the mask via std_t(P) (Eq. 8), most robust in Table 3.
Q4.Ablation of the weighting concept (R2).
Tables 2 and 3 include the relevant ablations: width Nc, L1 vs. L2, spatial-only vs. spatiotemporal TV, and four weighting masks (Pstd, P, mean-P, all-ones). Pstd is the most robust across vencs.
Q5.Computation time (R1).
The ~8 min figure is on a single GPU without ROI cropping; both factors dominate. The three velocity-encoding directions are independent and can parallelize across GPUs. This post-processing is offline; a few minutes per scan fits clinical workflow and does not affect bedside use.
Q6.Reproducibility (R3, Meta).
Sec. 2.3 lists the experimental settings; baselines use the public 4DFlow-unwrap repo [6]. Code will be released upon acceptance.
Q7.Itoh’s condition (R1).
We acknowledge |∇Ψ| ≤ π is not formally proven, and under very severe wrapping it can fail locally and degrade accuracy — visible as the rising nRMSE at the lowest vencs in Tables 1–2.For our experimental range (30–90 cm/s), however, the condition holds in the vascular ROI on physical grounds: aortic flow follows viscous incompressible Navier–Stokes, yielding fields smooth in space and time at our scales, so discrete gradients of Ψ stay below π.
On “outdated” alternatives: Eq. (4) underpins LAP [9, 2016], Poisson [14, 1995], WLS [19, 2021] — methods spanning three decades, including R1’s own suggested baselines; the Schofield–Zhu Laplacian identity R1 alludes to (basis of LAP, already our baseline) is a reformulation of the same local-smoothness premise, more noise-sensitive (second-order). Local violations are absorbed by the L1 loss (Table 2), DIP prior, std_t mask, and congruence step (Eq. 9)

title: Unsupervised Brain Anomaly Detection as a Bayesian Inverse Problem with Diffusion Prior
abstract:
Unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) aims to localize abnormal regions in medical scans without pixel-level annotations. A typical strategy seeks to reconstruct a pseudo-healthy image  that preserves subject-specific anatomy. Recently, diffusion models have been proposed to perform UAD. However, these methods rely on heuristic noise schedules or synthetic corruptions to balance subject-specificity and anomaly removal.
In this work, we propose an alternative formulation of UAD as a Bayesian inverse problem under a diffusion prior. First, we introduce a latent spatial anomaly mask that models pixel-wise consistency between a test image and its latent corresponding pseudo-healthy image. Then, we propose an approximation of the unknown generation process that links healthy anatomy, anomalies, and the observed image, enabling a well-defined likelihood within the Bayesian framework. Building on recent advances in diffusion-based inverse problem methods, we jointly infer the pseudo-healthy image and the anomaly mask via annealed posterior sampling. We evaluate our approach on FDG PET (ADNI) and FLAIR MRI (BraTS 2021), demonstrating improved anomaly localization performance compared to other diffusion-based approaches and validating the contribution of our introduced model. Our code is available at https://github.com/HuguesRoy/UAD_DAPS

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes an inverse-problem formulation of anomaly detection, where a diffusion model is used to describe the prior distribution over images and the latent clean image and anomaly mask are inferred via an annealed posterior sampling algorithm. This is demonstrated in 2D PET and MRI benchmarks and shows competitive performance.
reviews.text_strengths: A novel probabilistic algorithm for mask inference is introduced, which seems mathematically principled and well justified. The procedure is described clearly with a good level of mathematical detail. The results indicate a good level of performance, both quantitatively and qualitatively and is competitive with other works.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
It’s a bit unclear why only the best possible Dice is reported? (with standard deviation across subjects/slices?) without including mean, and std-dev across samples? In practice we don’t have access to an oracle to select so it would be good to understand the average, and worst case scenario. It would also be instructive to see the performance on some anomaly free slices. Some information about the diversity of inferred masks would be interesting.
[1] should also be referenced and compared against.
[1] Beizaee, Farzad, et al. “Mad-ad: Masked diffusion for unsupervised brain anomaly detection. “ International Conference on Information Processing in Medical Imaging. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Page 6: [Dice] rather than a citation.
It would be good to understand whether the DAPS algorithm was a required component, or if the mask inference procedure is partially agnostic to the form of diffusion based inverse problem method.
In the graphical model in Fig 1, it would be beneficial to denote y in a different format to make it obvious that it’s the only variable that is observed, and everything else is latent.

The algorithm is novel (to the best of my understanding), well principled and achieves good performance. The paper is also clearly presented. I have some reservations about only reporting the max Dice, but this should be straightforward to resolve, and there is a paper to cite.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This work’s main contribution is to recast unsupervised brain anomaly detection as explicit Bayesian posterior inference under a diffusion prior. In particular, they introduced a latent anomaly mask and an approximate likelihood using them that links the image to a pseudo-healthy image. The samples of the pseudo heathy image, mask, and the anomaly are derived using Langevin dynamics using DAPS.
reviews.text_strengths:
Current diffusion-based UAD methods methods (e.g. THOR, AutoDDPM) also use anomaly maps derived during inference diffusion inference. The main distinction of this work is to pose the recovery of the mask and pseudo-healthy image as a single Bayesian inference rather than a heuristic combinations of mask and diffusion inference. This is a much more elegant approach, and it translates to improved performance as shown by their results.
The qualitative results in Fig. 2 are impressive and clearly demonstrate the benefits of the proposed method.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The paper summarizes current diffusion-based UAD methods in one sentence without providing any details on their mechanisms and the distinction with their formulation. I think describing how they work, and how they differ from the proposed scheme would help the readers appreciate the methodological contributions.
2.The focus is on having a single elegant formulation, which is a clear strength. However, the authors make several heuristic choices, which are not well motivated. In particular, the authors vary the weightings and contributions of different terms arbitrarily during the annealing process, which are not theoretically justified. For example
a. Why do they choose the likelihood variance to vary depending on the scale (k). I understand the prior variance could vary depending on the scale, but it is not common to vary the likelihood variance. Why would this be justified, and what solution will the algorithm converge to.
b. They mention that the prior weight is tuned depending on the scale. They should make the exact dependence more explicit. This again seems to be a deviation from the “true Bayesian formulation”.
c. The step sizes in (6) and (7) are selected at each step based on gradient magnitudes. Please state the exact formula used for the step sizes.
3.It would have been helpful to include a figure showing the evolution of the mask and the pseudo-healthy image as a function of annealing steps.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper builds upon the existing diffusion approaches for anomaly detection by introducing a combined Bayesian formulation that is less heuristic. Their results clearly show the benefit of the combined formulation. While they also make some heuristic choices in the implementation, I think the overall contribution merits acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a novel formulation of unsupervised anomaly detection as a Bayesian inverse problem with a diffusion prior. A latent spatial anomaly mask is introduced to model pixel-wise consistency between the observed image and its pseudo-healthy reconstruction, and the unknown forward model is approximated via a mask-weighted likelihood. Joint inference of the healthy image and anomaly mask is performed via annealed posterior sampling with Langevin dynamics, building on the DAPS framework. The method is evaluated on brain MRI (BraTS 2021) and FDG PET (ADNI) and compared against a range of reconstruction-based and diffusion-based UAD baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
The Bayesian inverse problem formulation is principled and well-motivated, addressing a genuine limitation of existing diffusion-based UAD methods. The theoretical grounding is clearly presented.
The posterior factorisation cleanly disentangles anomaly information from healthy anatomy by separately modelling a healthy image prior and an anomaly mask, which is a conceptually appealing and novel contribution.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Small anomalies are entirely excluded from the BraTS evaluation, with only medium and large lesions considered. This is a significant omission, as detection of subtle anomalies is arguably the most clinically relevant and challenging regime, and precisely the setting where the generative approach and global mask modelling are most likely to struggle. Without this evaluation, the practical utility of the method remains unclear.
BraTS T1 and T2 modalities are not included, limiting the evaluation to FLAIR only and neglecting low-contrast anomaly settings where the method may behave differently.
The approximate forward model assumes that anomalies correspond to high-variance Gaussian deviations from healthy samples (Eq. 3), which is generally not true in practice where anomalies are structured. While acknowledged in the conclusion, this is a fundamental modelling limitation that deserves more prominent discussion and, if possible, empirical analysis of its impact.
The independence assumption between xt and m in the intermediate posteriors (Eq. 2) is not justified. Unlike x0, xt may carry anomaly localisation information, and assuming independence here could introduce a non-trivial approximation error that is not discussed.
Slice-level anomaly scoring is not discussed and is omitted from the evaluation entirely, despite being a clinically relevant and commonly reported metric in the UAD literature.
The baseline comparison is limited to diffusion-based UAD methods and a small number of reconstruction-based approaches. Established feature-distribution-based (self-supervised) methods such as PaDiM [1], PatchCore [2] or PII/NSA [3-4], which have shown strong performance in anomaly detection tasks, are not included. Without these comparisons it is difficult to assess where the proposed method truly stands relative to the broader UAD landscape.
The method involves numerous hyperparameters (λ0, λc, μ, c, step sizes ηx and ηa, number of Langevin iterations, number of intermediate posterior steps), and no sensitivity analysis is provided. The description of how ηx and ηa are updated is particularly limited, raising reproducibility concerns.
The ablation study is conducted only on BraTS large lesions, leaving open whether the relative contributions of each component hold across lesion sizes, modalities, and the excluded small anomaly regime.
The PET anomalies are entirely synthetic, which limits the clinical validity of that part of the evaluation. This is not sufficiently discussed.
The method is evaluated on 2D slices only, and the extension to 3D is deferred to future work, which is a notable practical limitation given that most clinical use cases involve volumetric data.
[1] Defard, T., Setkov, A., Loesch, A., & Audigier, R. (2021, January). Padim: a patch distribution modeling framework for anomaly detection and localization. In International conference on pattern recognition (pp. 475-489). Cham: Springer International Publishing.
[2] Roth, K., Pemula, L., Zepeda, J., Schölkopf, B., Brox, T., & Gehler, P. (2022). Towards total recall in industrial anomaly detection. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF conference on computer vision and pattern recognition (pp. 14318-14328).
[3] Tan, J., Hou, B., Day, T., Simpson, J., Rueckert, D., & Kainz, B. (2021, September). Detecting outliers with poisson image interpolation. In International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention (pp. 581-591). Cham: Springer International Publishing.
[4] Schlüter, H. M., Tan, J., Hou, B., & Kainz, B. (2022, October). Natural synthetic anomalies for self-supervised anomaly detection and localization. In European Conference on Computer Vision (pp. 474-489). Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Including small anomalies in the BraTS evaluation is strongly encouraged, as this is the regime most relevant to assessing the practical limitations of the approach.
Extending the baseline comparison to include feature-distribution-based methods would provide a more complete and informative evaluation of the proposed approach relative to the broader state of the art.
Extending the evaluation to additional BraTS modalities (T1, T2) would provide a more complete picture of the method’s robustness to anomaly contrast.
A more thorough discussion and ideally empirical analysis of the Gaussian anomaly assumption and the independence assumption in Eq. 2 would strengthen the theoretical transparency of the paper.
A sensitivity analysis of the number of intermediate sampling steps and Langevin iterations, given their linear impact on inference time, would be informative and practically useful.
Including slice-level scoring would bring the evaluation in line with standard practice in the UAD literature.
An interesting direction worth exploring would be to use the posterior probability of an approximately empty mask (m ≈ 1) as a normality score, which flows naturally from the proposed framework and could provide a principled image-level detection metric.

The methodology is novel, rigorously derived, and the probabilistic perspective on UAD is a genuinely valuable contribution that could inspire future work. However, the evaluation has crucial gaps, most notably the exclusion of small anomalies, slice-level scoring and only sparse comparison to SOTA UAD methods, that prevent a confident assessment of the method’s practical utility. These gaps are addressable without fundamental changes to the method.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

meta_reviews.text: Two reviewers were strongly positive. R4 is weakly negative, but raises issues that may be addressed. However, I also agree that R4’s raised issues limit scope and impact.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback. Since the paper has been provisionally accepted, we will use the revision to clarify the following modeling choices and limitations.
[R4] Independence between $x_{t_k}$ and $m$. 
We agree that $x_{t_k}$ may retain residual information about anomalies. However, following DAPS, the noisy diffusion state $x_{t_k}$ is only introduced as an auxiliary variable to approximate the intractable image prior $p(x_0)$ via the conditional diffusion prior $p_k(x_0 \mid x_{t_k})$. We additionally assume independence from $m$ as a tractable approximation. The empirical performance across both datasets suggests this approximation does not critically impair the method in practice. We have made this approximation explicit in the revised manuscript.
[R4] Approximate the forward model. 
We would like to clarify the distinct roles of the two components of our forward model. While Eq. 3 utilizes an isotropic Gaussian likelihood, this is only one component of our model. The spatial structure of anomalies is explicitly captured by the random Gaussian field prior on the mask $m$. As shown by the ablation without spatial regularization in the mask prior (Table 3-(C)), the isotropic Gaussian likelihood alone struggles to capture structured anomalies, highlighting the importance of the structured prior.
[R3] Annealed likelihood variance. 
Unlike standard inverse problems with a known forward model, both the reconstruction and the anomaly mask are uncertain in our setting. Inspired by DAPS, we use a sequence of intermediate likelihoods whose variance evolves jointly with the conditional diffusion prior across scales. A larger variance in early iterations allows broader exploration of reconstruction-mask pairs, while a smaller variance later enforces closer consistency with the measurement. The algorithm targets the final annealed approximate posterior associated with the last variance level. The fixed-variance ablation in Table 3-(B) supports the usefulness of this annealing.
[R3] Scale-dependent $\lambda_0$. 
Since the likelihood term scales as $1/r_k^2$, keeping $\lambda_0$ fixed would change the relative strength of the likelihood and mask regularization during annealing. We adapt $\lambda_0(k)$ across scales to maintain a consistent balance between these terms in the intermediate posteriors. This is part of the annealed approximation used for sampling, rather than a claim that the underlying Bayesian prior itself is scale-dependent.
[R3-R4] Langevin step sizes. 
As in DAPS, the effective step size decreases as the intermediate posteriors become sharper. Since the energy gradients with respect to the healthy image $x_0$ and the mask unconstrained logits $a$ can have different scales, we adapt the step sizes $\eta_x$ and $\eta_a$ inversely to the gradient of the energies $|\nabla x_0 U_k|2^2$ and $|\nabla a U_k|_2^2$, respectively, with clipping for numerical stability.
[R4] PET evaluation and additional MRI sequences. 
We agree that synthetic PET anomalies do not capture the full clinical variability of real disease. However, our goal was to complement the BraTS FLAIR tumor experiments with a different modality and disease pattern: FDG PET with Alzheimer-like hypometabolism. The synthetic setting provides ground truth and enables quantitative comparison, while still revealing differences between methods.

title: Unsupervised Domain Adaptation for Pelvic Landmark Localization in CT and MR Using Landmark-Conditioned Synthesis
abstract: Accurate 3D pelvic landmark localization is essential for hip morphology assessment and surgical planning. However, most models are trained on a single modality and therefore suffer substantial performance degradation when applied to a different modality due to severe domain shift. To alleviate this performance drop, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) methods based on image synthesis have been explored. Nevertheless, sparse landmark annotations make it difficult for existing synthesis methods to enforce semantic consistency between translated and real images, which limits the effectiveness of UDA. To address this limitation, we propose a UDA framework for 3D pelvic landmark localization using semantically consistent landmark-conditioned synthesis. Specifically, building on a CycleGAN backbone, we introduce landmark-conditioned adversarial learning (LCAL), which incorporates class- and laterality-conditioned local discriminators to promote semantically consistent image synthesis in regions surrounding each landmark. For localization, we employ modality-specific detectors to encourage consistent localization predictions across synthesized images of the same subject with different styles. Additionally, we propose a pseudo-label ensembling mechanism (PLEM) that produces reliable pseudo-labels by jointly considering localization confidence and cross-prediction spatial consistency, providing effective supervision in the target domain. Experiments on an unpaired hip CT-MR dataset demonstrate that our method outperforms other state-of-the-art UDA approaches on both CT-to-MR and MR-to-CT adaptation tasks. The code is available at https://github.com/KangqingYe/LCS-UDA.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Synthetic Data / Data-centric AI

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a UDA framework for 3D pelvic landmark localization that combines CycleGAN-based image synthesis with landmark-conditioned local adversarial learning (LCAL) and a pseudo-label ensembling mechanism (PLEM) to improve cross-modality robustness between CT and MRI without requiring target annotations.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper addresses a clinically relevant problem: cross-modality 3D anatomical landmark localization under limited annotations. 
2.The proposed LCAL introduces landmark-aware local discrimination, which incorporates anatomical priors into GAN-based synthesis and improves local structural realism beyond standard CycleGAN. 
3.The PLEM strategy effectively combines prediction confidence and spatial consistency to generate more reliable pseudo-labels for unsupervised target-domain supervision. 
4.Experimental results show consistent improvements over baseline UDA methods on CT-to-MR and MR-to-CT tasks.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The LCAL module assumes that rigid alignment to a common coordinate system makes landmark locations broadly comparable across CT and MR. However, rigid registration does not guarantee anatomical correspondence at the local level, and inter-subject variability may still lead to spatial mismatch. It is unclear whether such weak alignment is sufficient to support reliable “semantically consistent” local adversarial training, and whether this introduces noisy or biased supervision in LCAL. 
2.For style transfer in UDA, beyond CycleGAN-based methods, there are also recent diffusion-based approaches, such as “Reliable Source Approximation: Source-free Unsupervised Domain Adaptation for Vestibular Schwannoma MRI Segmentation”, “Training-free image style alignment for domain shift on handheld ultrasound devices”, and “Zero-shot Medical Image Translation via Frequency-guided Diffusion Models”. It would be beneficial to briefly discuss and compare these methods to position the proposed work better. 
3.The dataset is relatively small (70 CT and 68 MR images), and only 47 MR images are used for training. Given the reported fully supervised upper bound (MRE 3.36 mm) using 47 labeled MR images, it is unclear whether the proposed complex UDA framework is necessary compared to simply annotating few MR data and training a supervised model. 
4.Relevant references of evaluation metrics (MRE and SDR) choice should be provided. 
5.As shown in Fig. 3d, CycleGAN-based synthesis appears already visually plausible and close to the proposed method. A more detailed analysis or explanation is needed to support the claimed improvements.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a reasonably well-designed UDA framework combining synthesis and pseudo-label learning. Although some components (e.g., LCAL and spatial alignment assumptions) are incremental and rely on strong implicit assumptions, the overall pipeline is technically sound and demonstrates consistent empirical improvements over existing baselines.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes an Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) framework built upon a CycleGAN backbone to address performance degradation in 3D pelvic landmark localization across CT and MR modalities. The core methodological contribution involves Landmark-Conditioned Adversarial Learning (LCAL), which introduces class- and laterality-conditioned local discriminators to enforce semantic consistency specifically around anatomical landmarks during image synthesis, addressing limitations of standard global adversarial learning in sparse annotation scenarios. Additionally, the framework incorporates a Pseudo-label Ensembling Mechanism (PLEM) for target supervision without manual annotations. The evaluation shows effectiveness on an unpaired hip CT-MR dataset across bidirectional adaptation tasks, with quantitative improvements over existing SOTA UDA approaches in localization accuracy.
reviews.text_strengths:
The problem of cross-modality landmark localization is highly relevant in clinical practice, particularly given the cost and difficulty of annotating MR images compared to CT. The proposed approach addresses a realistic need in surgical planning and morphological assessment.
The LCAL module represents a thoughtful extension of CycleGAN by incorporating landmark-aware local discriminators. Conditioning on class and laterality to guide adversarial learning is a meaningful attempt to improve semantic consistency in anatomically critical regions.
The paper is generally well-structured, and the experimental section includes comparisons with state-of-the-art UDA methods (e.g., CycleGAN, ICMSC, UMSCS). Results are reported for both adaptation directions (CT→MR and MR→CT), strengthening the empirical validation.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The dataset is relatively small (70 CT and 68 MR scans). To ensure robustness, the method should be validated using a more rigorous cross-validation protocol to demonstrate generalizability across different cohorts.
The method relies on the assumption that “anatomical structures are approximately consistent” after global registration. This is a strong assumption that requires quantitative or statistical justification, particularly given the variability in pelvic anatomy due to pathology or patient-specific factors.
The paper does not include a sensitivity analysis for key hyperparameters (e.g., lambda weights in cycle-consistency and LCAL losses and thresholds in PLEM)​. This limits the understanding of how robust the method is and how easily it can be tuned in practice.
The claim that LCAL improves semantic consistency is primarily supported by qualitative visual results. Including quantitative metrics (e.g., SSIM, perceptual similarity, or region-specific evaluation around landmarks) would strengthen the evidence for the effectiveness of the proposed module.
The description of the three-stage training strategy is not fully clear. In particular, it is not specified how the initial pseudo-labels are obtained in Stage 1 prior to the activation of PLEM. Since LCAL relies on these pseudo-labels to define local regions, this introduces a potential circular dependency between pseudo-label generation and discriminator training. Clarifying this initialization step and the interaction between LCAL crop selection and PLEM would improve the clarity of the method.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Some figures could benefit from clearer annotations. In particular, Figure 3(d) should explicitly highlight the landmark regions in the synthesized images to make the qualitative comparison more interpretable.

This paper presents a methodologically sound approach to a clinically relevant problem in medical imaging. The proposed LCAL and PLEM mechanisms show promise in addressing domain shift challenges in landmark localization. However, the current submission has significant concerns regarding the robustness of the experimental validation, insufficient justification of key assumptions (e.g., anatomical consistency), and lack of clarity in critical methodological components such as pseudo-label initialization. These issues, along with missing quantitative analysis of synthesis quality and hyperparameter sensitivity, weaken the overall strength of the empirical evidence.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have addressed my specific technical objections through quantitative justification and clarifications. They provided evidence validating the anatomical consistency assumption and clarified that Stage 1 training avoids circular dependencies, resolving my primary concerns; furthermore, they committed to releasing the code. Regarding hyperparameters, while a more comprehensive ablation study would be preferable, the current explanation clearly justifies their selection criteria and demonstrates robustness to perturbations. While I acknowledge that a more rigorous evaluation protocol (e.g., cross-validation or multi-center data) would further strengthen claims regarding generalizability, these limitations do not undermine the methodological soundness of the proposed framework.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper proposes a synthesis-based UDA framework for cross-modality 3D landmark localization, combining image translation and localization learning in a unified pipeline.
It introduces landmark-conditioned adversarial learning (LCAL) to improve semantic consistency in local regions around landmarks during image synthesis.
A pseudo-label ensembling mechanism (PLEM) is designed to refine target-domain supervision by leveraging confidence and cross-style prediction consistency.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper tackles a meaningful and underexplored problem (cross-modality landmark localization), which is harder than segmentation due to sparse supervision.
The idea of enforcing local semantic consistency around landmarks is intuitive and well-motivated.
The pseudo-label ensembling strategy is simple but effective, and aligns well with the overall framework.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The core of the image synthesis still heavily relies on a standard CycleGAN, and the landmark detector (SCN) is a pre-existing architecture. The technical contribution is largely incremental, focusing on specific conditioning rather than a fundamental shift in UDA strategy.
2.The success of the PLEM and LCAL modules depends on several empirically set thresholds and loss weights. There is a lack of discussion regarding how sensitive the performance is to these values across different datasets or anatomies.
3.The method depends on anatomical priors (e.g., proxy landmark assignment), which may limit applicability in more diverse or less structured scenarios.
4.While the results are promising, the study is validated on a relatively small dataset of 70 CT and 68 MR images. More extensive testing on diverse, multi-center data would be necessary to prove the model’s robustness against varying imaging protocols.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

My recommendation is based on a balance between the relevance of the problem and the current limitations of the approach. The paper addresses an important and challenging task in cross-modality landmark localization and proposes a reasonable framework with some well-motivated components.
However, the overall novelty appears incremental, as the method mainly builds on existing synthesis-based UDA pipelines with additional refinements. In addition, the evaluation is relatively limited and does not fully demonstrate generalization or robustness across datasets and settings.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
This manuscript introduces a CycleGAN-based unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) method for 3D landmark detection in pelvic CT/MRI images. Specifically, it uses landmark-conditioned adversarial learning (LCAL) to promote semantically consistent image synthesis and adopts a pseudo-label ensembling mechanism to provide target-domain supervision. The method is evaluated on an unpaired hip CT-MR image dataset, and it produces better landmark detection performance than some other GAN-based models. However, the reviewers have raised several significant concerns as follows:
1.The technical contribution is incremental, because the proposed method is built on existing architectures such as CycleGAN [25] and SCN [15]. It would be helpful to clarify the technical contributions.
2.The method relies on a strong assumption, i.e., anatomical structures are approximately consistent after performing rigid registration. However, this assumption may not hold in practice because rigid registration does not guarantee anatomical correspondence at the local level.
3.The method is evaluated on a single, small dataset with 70 CT and 68 MR volumes. Please clarify whether this dataset is sufficient to justify the effectiveness and the generalizability of the proposed method. In addition, given that fully supervised learning with a small set of images can provide much better landmark detection performance (in 3mm and 5mm SDR) in Table 1, it is not clear whether using a complex UAD framework is necessary.
4.The method is not compared with recent diffusion-based approaches, which produce very impressive image synthesis performance. Although the authors should not provide additional experimental results in the rebuttal, it would be helpful to clarify what the advantages of the proposed GAN-based approach are in this landmark detection application, in comparison with diffusion-based models.
5.There is no sensitivity analysis for important hyperparameters in the proposed method, such as the thresholds in Eq. (6) and the \lambda parameters in Eq. (8). Please clarify whether the proposed method is robust with respect to different hyperparameter values.
6.The three-stage training strategy is not clearly explained. Please add more details.
Please consider addressing the reviewers’ concerns in the rebuttal.

This manuscript introduces a CycleGAN-based unsupervised domain adaptation method for 3D landmark detection in pelvic CT/MRI images. It adopts landmark-conditioned adversarial learning (LCAL) to promote semantically consistent image synthesis and a pseudo-label ensembling mechanism to provide target-domain supervision. The method outperforms several other GAN-based approaches on CT -> MR and MR -> CT domain adaptation directions. The rebuttal has addressed most of the reviewers’ concerns, including technical contributions, anatomical consistency assumption, training details, dataset size, and hyperparameter sensitivity. Therefore, the manuscript is recommended for acceptance.

Majority of reviewers are in favor of this work after rebuttal. Some concerns regarding methodology and experimental evaluation have been addressed convincingly according to two reviewers, and I agree with this assessment. While a larger evaluation would be beneficial, the idea is interesting and addresses an interesting problem area, intermodality landmark localization with few annotations. Although the methodological contribution might be a bit incremental, I still see this as interesting work to spark discussion at the conference.

This is a borderline paper with mixed reviews. Reviewers agreed that the work addresses a clinically relevant and technically challenging problem—cross-modality 3D anatomical landmark localization under limited annotations—and that the proposed LCAL and PLEM strategies offer meaningful improvements over standard UDA baselines. However, they also raised serious concerns about the paper’s significance and soundness: first, the technical contribution is largely incremental, building on standard CycleGAN and existing detector architectures without introducing a fundamentally new UDA paradigm; second, the evaluation is limited to a relatively small single-center dataset, with insufficient validation of robustness, generalizability, and sensitivity to hyperparameters; third, key methodological assumptions—such as reliable anatomical alignment across subjects and the stability of pseudo-label generation—lack strong quantitative justification, and the dependence on empirically tuned thresholds and anatomical priors may limit broader applicability. The rebuttal clarified certain design choices and provided additional quantitative support, but it did not fully resolve concerns regarding limited novelty, dataset scale, or robustness analysis. After careful deliberation, I lean towards rejecting this manuscript.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their comments.
R4 Incremental contribution. Unlike segmentation UDA, landmark UDA remains underexplored, and prior work [6] fails on the large CT-MR gap (Table 1). It is also intrinsically harder: segmentation UDA [19,21] preserves semantic consistency via dense masks, unavailable for sparse landmarks. LCAL addresses this through conditioned local adversarial learning, while PLEM improves pseudo-label quality based on confidence and spatial consistency.
R1,2&4 Anatomical consistency assumption. 1) LCAL does not require voxel-wise correspondence. Conditioned on the landmark class, the discriminator only requires both patches to contain the neighborhood of the same landmark, so modest misalignments do not bias the supervision, as GAN-based methods are known to tolerate such misalignment [RegGAN]. 2) The assumption is needed only when valid pseudo-labels are unavailable, mainly for early-stage stability. Once PLEM yields valid pseudo-labels, LCAL crops are driven by them. 3) Quantitatively, the pairwise distances between same-class landmarks across all training CT-MR subjects have a mean of 9 voxels, with 97.6% below 20 voxels. With a patch side length of s_c=40 voxels, the proxy-label-based patch reliably covers the same landmark. 4) Rigid alignment is a standard preprocessing step in unpaired 3D cross-modality synthesis, already applied to anatomies such as the abdomen and heart [19], and the brain [20].
R2 Three-stage training. Stage 1: only the synthesis networks are trained, while the detectors are not updated. Thus, no pseudo-labels are produced and all LCAL crop centers are set to y^s, eliminating any circular dependency. Stage 2: the synthesis networks are frozen and the detectors are trained with L_sup and L_PLEM. Stage 3: all networks are trained jointly, with LCAL crops following Eq. (1). We will release the source code.
R1 UDA necessity. For hip morphology, our 3.53 mm is comparable to the 3.36 mm upper bound, within inter-observer variability for 3D landmark annotation. Reaching it requires 47 MR volumes × 54 landmarks, exactly the burden UDA eliminates, especially as MR labeling is harder than CT [13].
R1,2&4 Dataset size & generalization. Our dataset size and splitting strategy are similar to those of prior UDA studies [19, 21] and 3D landmark detection work [8] (e.g., 100 images). Validation in both directions indicates that the effectiveness is not direction-specific. We acknowledge that cross-validation and multi-center evaluation would further validate robustness.
R1&2 Synthesis quality. Since synthesis serves localization rather than being the final goal, image quality is not our evaluation criterion. LCAL targets local semantic consistency, which global appearance metrics do not directly measure. SSIM requires voxel-aligned pairs, which are unavailable. We therefore evaluate LCAL via localization (Table 2, Fig.3(b)). Fig.3(d) shows CycleGAN distorting the acetabular-notch boundary while our method preserves it.
R1 Diffusion-based comparison. Our GAN-based method enables single-pass generation, allowing end-to-end joint training with the detector. However, diffusion-based methods have been largely restricted to 2D slices due to computational cost (e.g., TISA, RSA, FGDM). The few 3D extensions require paired data [MC-IDDPM] or segmentations [Diffuse-UDA], neither applicable to our setting.
R2&4 Hyperparameter sensitivity. All hyperparameters are set by design, not by extensive tuning: λ_cyc=10 follows CycleGAN [25]; λ_LCAL=0.5 keeps LCAL below the global adversarial term; τ_c=0.9 selects high-confidence predictions; τ_d=3 voxels (4.5 mm) matches the SDR@5mm scale. Even extreme perturbations τ_c→0/τ_d→∞ yield 3.61/3.62 mm MRE (only +0.1 mm vs. 3.53 mm; Fig.3(c)). Table 2 further shows that removing LCAL/PLEM entirely degrades MRE by only ~0.5 mm.
R1 Evaluation metrics. MRE and SDR are commonly used metrics [6,8].

title: Unveiling Brain-Body Axis Interactions in Psychiatric-Endocrine Disorder with Deep Graph Causal Neural Network
abstract: Understanding the role of the brain-body axis in the causal relationship between psychiatric disorders and endocrine disorders is crucial for advancing multi-organ disease modeling and precision medicine. Despite the importance of understanding these interactions, the development of a mature framework has been hindered by traditional models’ inability to move beyond mere statistical associations to uncover true causal directionality in high-dimensional, population-scale data. In this study, we proposed a graph neural network (GNN)-based framework to construct causal graphs capturing interactions among brain imaging features, organ-level physiological indicators, and disease outcomes. Leveraging the directed acyclic graph (DAG)-GNN model, we perform causal structure learning on the comprehensive UK Biobank cohort, enabling the discovery of DAGs that reflect potential causal dependencies. Experimental results demonstrate that our method effectively uncovers interpretable brain-body-disease pathways, revealing shared white-matter vulnerabilities across distinct disorders and highlighting how intermediate physiological systems mediate these interactions, providing insights into psychiatric and endocrine conditions. Our code is available at https://github.com/NIMGroup/UKBCausal.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Causal Inference / Counterfactual Reasoning
Special Topic -> AI for Population Health, Public Health & Epidemiology

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper addresses an important problem with an interesting technical framework. The integration of MAE for missing data, PCA for dimensionality alignment, and DAG-GNN for structure learning is well-motivated. However, the causal claims are substantially overstated given the cross-sectional observational design, and the lack of any quantitative validation of the learned causal graph is a significant gap. With more careful framing of what the method can and cannot establish, this could become a strong contribution.
reviews.text_strengths:
This paper proposes a GNN-based causal discovery framework to model directed interactions among 27 white matter tracts, 5 organ systems, and 11 psychiatric/endocrine disorders using UK Biobank data. The authors adopted a masked autoencoder handles missing organ-level features, PCA compresses brain dMRI features, and DAG-GNN learns a directed acyclic graph representing putative causal relationships. They report interpretable brain-body-disease pathways, including convergent white matter vulnerabilities and mediated systemic cascades.
The brain-body axis is becoming important more and more for both psychiatric and endocrine diseases. The paper addresses a genuine gap: most prior work examines brain-body links in isolated pairs or uses purely correlational methods. Modeling the full multi-organ, multi-disease interaction network simultaneously is a valuable direction for precision psychiatry and computational medicine. 
The organ-specific masked autoencoder is a brilient solution to use with UK Biobank analyses. Training on complete cases with synthetic masking, reconstructing only masked entries, and using the learned latent space (rather than imputed values) for downstream analysis is methodologically cleaner than standard mean imputation or deletion approaches. The comparison against Mean+PCA and SoftImpute baselines provides empirical support. 
The paper carefully ensures that brain (PCA), organ (MAE latent), and disease (embedding) nodes share a consistent feature dimensionality before graph construction. This is a necessary and non-trivial design choice.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Since the entire framework learns from cross-sectional data, argument of causal structure is severely limited. The authors should clearly mention this limitation, and future plan or suggestion for followup study to overcome this. 
Importantly, due to same reason, the “causal directions” should be carefully re-addressed, otherwise it is well-validated (and known) direction. 
The discovered DAG is not validated against any external ground truth, alternative causal discovery methods (PC algorithm, GES, FCI, NOTEARS), or known causal relationships from randomized trials or Mendelian randomization studies. Without any form of validation. Although the UKB provides relatively comprehensive data, the sample is not still representative for our species. So, if external validation is not feasible, clearly mention limitation to prevent the over-interpretation of the finding.
Minor issues
The sample size reduction from 501,000 to 11,628 (due to requiring both imaging and complete organ data) may introduce selection bias that is not discussed.
The threshold values for edge filtering (0.5 and 0.2) appear arbitrary; sensitivity analysis would be informative.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The approach is novel, the data and analysis is straightforward. But need some ‘tone down’ to prevent potential ‘causal’ misunderstanding.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper proposes a unified causal-discovery pipeline to jointly model brain microstructure, organ-level physiology, and psychiatric/endocrine disease outcomes from the UK Biobank.
The pipeline has three stages: 
1- Masked autoencoder (MAE) that learns a compact latent representation robust to missing physiological entries.
2- PCA-based alignment step that projects each brain ROI’s high-dimensional dMRI features to the same latent dimensionality (d = 3) as the organ embeddings, so brain, organ, and disease nodes can share a unified node-feature tensor. 
3- DAG-GNN variational graph model with a NOTEARS-style differentiable acyclicity constraint and an augmented-Lagrangian objective that learns a weighted adjacency matrix over 27 JHU white-matter tracts, 5 organ systems, and 11 diseases.
The application contribution is a post-hoc inspection of the learned DAG at two edge thresholds (w > 0.5, w > 0.2), describing: 
1- Convergent transdiagnostic vulnerability of the cingulum of the cingulate gyrus and the posterior limb of the internal capsule. 
2- Mediated cascades such as overweight → metabolic → cingulum and hypothyroidism → depression → superior cerebellar peduncle.
reviews.text_strengths:
1- The author proposed that a directed representation of joint brain–microstructure, organ, and disease relations is an underexplored and clinically meaningful direction, rather than relying on pairwise correlational brain–body studies.
2- The study leverages a large-scale, multimodal dataset such as the UK Biobank, combining diffusion metrics across 27 JHU white matter bundles with organ-level phenotypes spanning musculoskeletal, immune, metabolic, renal, and hepatic systems, along with 11 disease labels derived from ICD-10 and self-report records.
3- Rather than using mean or low-rank imputation, the author used a masked autoencoder for organ-level representation learning to handle missing or zero values.
4- The author shared an anonymized code link (https://anonymous.4open.science/r/UKBCausal) for reproducibility.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1- The paper does not propose a new loss, architecture, or theoretical result. The contribution is largely a pipeline assembly, indicating limited methodological novelty.
2- The author used random thresholds for edges (w > 0.5 for the most essential and w > 0.2 for the second most important) with no sensitivity analysis or justification for these cutoffs.
3- The author did not take into account basic confounders such as age, sex, and head motion. Could you please justify this?
4- Temporal misalignment between brain and organ phenotypes (critical): Section 2.3 explicitly states that brain dMRI features are taken from UK Biobank imaging instance 2.In contrast, Section 2.1 does not specify which instance the organ-level phenotypes (HbA1c, C-reactive protein levels, creatinine, albumin, etc.) come from. Most UK Biobank data for these variables are available only in instances 0 and 1, not the imaging instance. e.g: https://biobank.ndph.ox.ac.uk/showcase/field.cgi?id=30600
In the UK Biobank dataset, there are four instances:
Instance 0: Initial assessment visit
Instance 1: First repeat assessment visit
Instance 2: Imaging visit
Instance 3: First repeat imaging visit
5- The author reports a sample size of 11,628 subjects, but does not provide detailed sample sizes for individual phenotypes after filtering and intersection, making it difficult to assess the effective sample size.
6- The graph is trained and tested on the same dataset (UK Biobank). It would be beneficial to evaluate it on an external cohort as well.
7- All three figures have only one-line titles instead of proper captions. Additionally, in Figure 2 (right), the y-axis is labeled “Number of ROIs (CSV files)”; what does “CSV files” mean in this context?
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses an interesting integrative question, and the UK Biobank application is ambitious; however:
1- The methodological contribution is a straightforward pipeline of published components (MAE, PCA, and DAG-GNN).
2- The causal graph is evaluated only qualitatively, without structural metrics, stability analysis, baselines, or confounder control.
3- Brain and organ phenotypes are selected from different UK Biobank visit instances, which structurally undermines the interpretation of causal directionality.
With quantitative DAG evaluation, a clarified disease-node specification, and instance-aligned phenotypes, this could become a clear accept.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper presents a causal graph learning framework to uncover interactions between brain white-matter microstructure, body organ systems, and psychiatric diseases using large-scale observational data.
The motivation is significant since most of analyses mainly identify statistical associations, while this paper focuses on a casual relationship which is crucial for mechanistic insights into psychiatric disorders.
reviews.text_strengths: It is an interesting interdisciplinary problem where it integrates brain imaging, organ physiology and disease. It uses large-scale dataset like UK Biobank to provide strong statistical power. The idea of integrating brain + body + disease nodes is novel and it can handle missing organ features y using masked autoencoder. It identifies shared white-matter vulnerability hubs for potential biological insights.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Causal interpretation is weak. The paper claims causal discovery, but data is purely observational cross-sectional. No temporal ordering was mentioned. No mention of potential confouding variables like age, sex. No interventin or instrumental variables were used. DAG-GNN may infer statistical correlation, but interpreting edges as causal mechanism is risky. The authors should clarify assumptions (causual sufficiency, no hidden confouders)and discuss limitations more carefully.
2.Evaluation is weak. The paper mainly evaluates the reconstruction error of MAE, but no quantiative validation of causal structure. It worths doing some prediction evalution or even do some statistical enrichment anlaysis or replication in another dataset. It also lacks comparison with other causal models.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The causal validity and evaluation needs to be further improved.
