reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a DAG-GNN-based framework that integrates a masked autoencoder (MAE) for missing value imputation and PCA for dimensionality alignment to uncover interpretable causal brain-body-disease interactions from incomplete observational data.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper tackles a clinically important problem: causal inference in brain body axis interactions. Unlike traditional correlation based studies, this work explicitly models directed dependencies. The combination of MAE for missing data, PCA for feature alignment, and DAG GNN for graph learning is sensible and technically sound.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Experimental details are insufficient for reproducibility. “Repeated 5 times” is not specified (e.g., 5-fold cross-validation or 5 random splits). The MAE training mask ratio is not reported, while only the test-time 30% masking is described. Key sample statistics, including total participant count, disease-positive numbers per condition, and final organ-specific sample sizes after 70% filtering, are missing from the method section.
2.Figure 2 has poor readability: font sizes are too small, only a subset of the 27 ROIs are shown without selection criteria, and the y-axis label of the third subplot contains a “CSV” artifact, suggesting the figure was generated without proper post-processing.
3.Sensitivity analyses are lacking. There is no investigation of different MAE training mask ratios, no justification for choosing the 70% observed feature threshold for subject filtering, and no explanation for setting the edge weight thresholds (w > 0.5 for “most essential” and w > 0.2 for “second essential”) in the causal graph.
4.The baseline methods “Mean+PCA” and “SoftImpute” are mentioned without any description of their implementation details or the rationale for their inclusion, making the comparison less transparent.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The core idea and framework are novel and clinically promising. However, the paper requires major clarifications in experimental protocols, sensitivity analyses, and figure quality to ensure reproducibility and scientific rigor.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

meta_reviews.text:
The study proposes a method that probes brain-body association with a wide array of non-imaging phenotypes, validates on a large-scale dataset, and aims to provide mechanistic insights beyond simple association. These are major strengths, timely, and will be of great interests to medical AI researchers. However, reviewers also raise concerns on missing details on methodological and experimental design. A major concern is that whether it is possible to better validate the derived causal structure.

The reviewers’ concerns were mainly about clarity of methodological and experimental design, which were large resolved in the rebuttal and will likely be resolved in the final version. The causal claim indeed needs to use caution, but findings are still causally insightful as long as the authors can clarify assumptions and when the causal claims can become invalid. I believe MICCAI should put more emphasis on multi-modal medical data investigation beyond imaging and single-organ analysis, so I believe the study will potentially become a valuable asset to the community.

After considering the reviews and rebuttal, I recommend acceptance. The paper addresses an interesting brain–body–disease interaction problem using UK Biobank data, and proposes a useful integrated framework combining missingness-aware organ representation learning, imaging feature alignment, and DAG-based graph modeling.
The rebuttal appropriately acknowledges that the causal interpretation should be toned down, and that the learned graph should be framed as hypothesis-generating candidate directed dependencies rather than validated causal mechanisms. My acceptance recommendation assumes that the final version will clearly reflect this more cautious framing.

Three of four reviewers originally assigned Weak Accept, while one reviewer (R2) rejected the submission during the review phase based on concerns about methodological depth, comparison to existing causal discovery methods, and insufficient ablation studies.
No reviewer submitted a post-rebuttal opinion, and specifically, the absence of a post-rebuttal opinion from R2 means I cannot assess whether the authors’ clarifications were satisfying. From what I can see, the rebuttal was substantive and specifically addressed several of R2’s points, including clarifying the causal modelling assumptions and the distinction between their approach and standard GNNs.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback, which has improved the rigor and clarity of our work.
Response to R#1: We agree that the causal interpretation from observational UKB data should be treated with substantial caution. We will tone down strong causal wording and describe the learned DAG as candidate-directed dependencies/hypothesis-generating brain–body–disease pathways, rather than as confirmed biological causality. Since ground-truth brain–body causal graphs are unavailable, longitudinal cohorts, MR, interventional studies, and independent datasets are needed for confirmation. We will also discuss potential UKB selection bias arising from cohort overlap.
Response to R#2: We agree that methodological contribution is more accurately framed as an integrated, missingness-aware brain–body–disease framework rather than a new loss, architecture, or theory. Importantly, the integration is not a sequential assembly: MAE, ROI-wise PCA, and DAG-GNN are coupled to build modality-aligned node features for one heterogeneous graph, enabling joint brain–organ–disease structure learning [1,8,23]. Regarding confounders and UKB instances, age, sex, head motion, and temporal differences are important limitations. Organ biomarkers were taken from instance 0, while dMRI features were from imaging instance 2; thus, although organ measures generally precede imaging, edges should not be interpreted as definitive temporal or interventional causal effects. Instead, they represent candidate-directed dependencies requiring further validation. Phenotype-specific sample sizes, filtering steps, and effective sample counts should be reported more transparently, and external-cohort validation remains an important area for future work.
Response to R#3: We agree that the causal interpretation from cross-sectional observational data should be handled cautiously. DAG-based structure learning relies on assumptions such as causal sufficiency, the Markov condition, and faithfulness [23], while hidden confounding from age, sex, head motion, medication, lifestyle, and selection effects may remain. Thus, the learned edges should be interpreted as candidate-directed dependencies for hypothesis generation rather than validated causal mechanisms. The MAE reconstruction primarily evaluates the missing-data representation module rather than the causal graph itself; this limitation should be stated more clearly to avoid overclaiming graph validity. Additional prediction tasks, enrichment analysis, external replication, and comparisons with other causal discovery methods would be valuable avenues for future work to validate the inferred structure quantitatively.
Response to R#4: We agree with R#4 that several experimental and reproducibility details require clarification. Repeated 5 times means five independent random masking trials for held-out reconstruction evaluation. MAE training used random masking ratios from 10% to 40%, while 30% was used for evaluation as the most common organ-missingness level. The 70% observed-feature threshold was used to balance organ-feature reliability and retained sample size [12]. The mask protocol, disease counts, and organ-specific sample sizes should be stated more explicitly. Our initial bootstrap analysis showed stable recovery of the main pathways, suggesting robustness beyond a single split or threshold. These results were omitted for space because they are supporting rather than central evidence, but can be included in the camera-ready version. Mean+PCA and SoftImpute were included as common linear and low-rank missing-data baselines; their implementation and rationale will be clarified.
Minor issues: Figure/caption/ROI issues and the “CSV files” artifact will be corrected in the camera-ready. The thresholds w>0.5 and w>0.2 were used solely to visualize the learned continuous adjacency matrix, and threshold-dependent findings will be interpreted with greater caution in the discussion.

title: U-ReLSE: Voxel-Wise Evidential Uncertainty-Regularized MIL for Vertebral Metastasis Detection with Hybrid Supervision
abstract: Detecting vertebral metastases on CT in real-world practice is challenging because high-quality lesion masks are scarce, while vertebra-level labels mined from radiology reports are plentiful but noisy. We propose U-ReLSE, an uncertainty-regularized log-sum-exp pooling method for multiple instance learning (MIL) that converts voxel-wise lesion predictions into vertebra-level malignancy probabilities. The key idea is to let the model “trust” voxels it is confident about and “down-weight” voxels it finds ambiguous: we learn voxel-wise evidential (Dirichlet) certainty under segmentation supervision and use it as deterministic weights inside a mask-aware pooling operator, softly suppressing unreliable regions while preserving interpretable lesion localization and uncertainty maps. We train a 3D vertebra ROI model with a shared encoder and segmentation/evidential heads using a unified hybrid objective (Dice loss, evidential losses, and vertebra-level BCE) that integrates strong voxel-level supervision and weak report-derived labels. On multi-institutional in-house data with two cross-national external test cohorts, U-ReLSE consistently improves vertebra-level detection over standard pooling baselines, including Spine-Mets-CT-SEG (AUC 0.861 vs. 0.838–0.839; DeLong p<0.05) and a US-private cohort (AUC 0.907 vs. 0.871–0.903), with favorable recall–false-positive trade-offs. Because U-ReLSE only replaces the pooling layer, it can be readily applied to other strong–weak supervised detection problems under label noise and domain shift.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

The model was trained using multi-center, single-nation data and evaluated on an external, multi-national, multi-center cohort. reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a framework for vertebra-level metastasis detection from CT that combines heterogeneous supervision sources, including both voxel-level and vertebra-level labels of varying reliability (e.g., manually verified versus report-derived). The key methodological component is an uncertainty-aware aggregation mechanism, Uncertainty-Regularized Log-Sum-Exp (U-ReLSE) pooling, which incorporates evidential uncertainty estimates into a mask-restricted pooling operation over vertebral regions. This allows the model to aggregate voxel-level predictions into vertebra-level decisions while accounting for uncertainty. The approach is evaluated on multiple datasets, including external cross-national cohorts, and demonstrates improved performance compared to evaluated baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
*The paper addresses vertebra-level metastasis detection from CT, which is of clear clinical importance. The formulation at the vertebra level aligns well with clinical workflows and reporting.
*The framework combines voxel-level and vertebra-level annotations with different levels of reliability (e.g., manually verified versus report-derived labels). This is a realistic setting, and the ability to leverage such heterogeneous supervision is a strong aspect of the work.
*The proposed U-ReLSE pooling integrates evidential uncertainty estimates into a log-sum-exp aggregation over anatomically constrained regions. While conceptually related to existing weighted pooling and attention-based MIL approaches, incorporating uncertainty to modulate the aggregation is a reasonable extension in the presence of noisy labels.
*The method is evaluated on multiple datasets, including cross-national cohorts, which is a significant strength. External validation beyond a single in-house dataset increases confidence in generalization. The paper compares against multiple baselines and demonstrates improvements, supporting the proposed design.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
*Some of the main claims are stronger than what is directly supported by the experiments. The abstract states that the method stabilizes learning under label noise and domain shift while retaining interpretable localization and uncertainty cues. While the external validation does provide some evidence of cross-dataset generalization, I did not find direct evidence for improved robustness to label noise, nor a quantitative validation of the interpretability of the localization/uncertainty outputs. Thus, these aspects seem more suggested than demonstrated.
*The distinction from the evaluated baselines is not explained clearly enough, and the comparison to nGWP pooling, Attention MIL pooling, and ReLSE would benefit from more intuition. At present, it is hard to to understand what specific limitation of each baseline is being addressed and what is contributed by U-ReLSE. A clearer comparison would also help the reader better judge the degree of novelty.
*The supervision terminology is confusing. The paper appears to use “strong” and “weak” supervision primarily to refer to label reliability, rather than the more common usage based on annotation granularity such as voxel-level versus vertebra-level labels. Since the method also mixes supervision at different spatial levels, this terminology makes parts of the method (e.g. the loss design) harder to follow than necessary. Clearer definitions early in the paper would improve readability and reduce ambiguity.
*The notation around the losses is not fully clear. In particular, the transition from vertebra-level labels to notation of the form y_{v,i,c} (voxel-level labels?) is not introduced. This matters because it affects the interpretation of how the evidential head is supervised and how the claimed uncertainty mechanism is learned.
*The method may be sensitive to the quality of the vertebra segmentation used in preprocessing. Since pooling is restricted to voxels inside the vertebra mask, errors in this mask could directly affect the final vertebra-level predictions. This is particularly relevant in a paper that emphasizes generalization under domain shift, because robustness may then partly depend on the cross-domain robustness of the preprocessing segmentation model. I would prefer to see an analysis of this dependency.
*Some design choices would benefit from additional justification. For example, constraining the learnable γ to a fixed range may be reasonable, but the paper does not make it fully clear why this interval was chosen and how sensitive performance is to it. Since γ controls the pooling behavior (mean-like vs max-like aggregation), this choice is not entirely trivial.
*A few formulations are unnecessarily vague. For example, phrases such as “reliable validation and test sets” are not fully explained. It would be helpful to clarify whether “reliable” refers to annotation quality, curation, or simply the use of fixed splits. This clarity is important in a paper that discusses noisy supervision.
*The external validation is a strength, but some wording around it could be toned down. Referring to the evaluation as “benchmark-style external validation” seems overstated when one of the cohorts is private, since this limits direct comparison by future work. The external validation itself is valuable, but the framing could be more toned down.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses a clinically relevant problem and proposes a well-motivated framework that combines heterogeneous supervision sources. The use of uncertainty-aware pooling to incorporate voxel-level evidential estimates into vertebra-level predictions is a reasonable design, and the method is evaluated on multiple datasets, including external cohorts. At the same time, some of the central claims, particularly regarding robustness to label noise and interpretability, are only partially supported by the experiments, and certain aspects of the method and notation could be clarified further. Overall, the paper presents a solid contribution with convincing empirical results, but with some limitations in presentation and clarity. These factors place it above the acceptance threshold, but not among the strongest submissions. Releasing the source code would strengthen the reproducibility of the work.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal clarified several methodological and presentation-related issues, including the positioning relative prior approaches. I remain somewhat concerned that my comments W1 and W8 were not addressed, i.e. “Some of the main claims are stronger than what is directly supported by the experiments…” and “(…) Referring to the evaluation as ““benchmark-style external validation”” seems overstated when one of the cohorts is private, (…) the framing could be more toned down.” My concern was not merely about wording, but about ensuring that central claims are aligned with the empirical support provided. I still find some of the framing around robustness, interpretability, and external validation stronger than what is demonstrated. Nevertheless, I acknowledge the limited rebuttal space and appreciate the authors’ engagement with the broader set of comments. I therefore retain my recommendation, but would strongly encourage the authors, should the paper be accepted, to align the framing of their claims with the supporting evidence in the final manuscript.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper studies a practical supervision regime for vertebral metastasis detection, where voxel-level lesion masks are limited but report-derived vertebra-level labels are more abundant and noisy. Its main technical contribution is U-ReLSE, which uses voxel-wise evidential certainty learned from strongly labeled cases to improve vertebra-level aggregation. The external validation on two cohorts is also a meaningful strength.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) The problem setting is clinically relevant and practically motivated.
2) The method is technically coherent in how it transfers information from strong voxel supervision to weak vertebra-level prediction.
3) The paper includes external validation rather than relying only on an internal split.
4) The model retains lesion-level interpretability instead of reducing the task to a purely black-box vertebra classifier.
5) The gains appear reasonably consistent across datasets.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) The novelty is practically useful, though somewhat incremental, and reads more as a careful extension of existing ideas than as a fundamentally new MIL framework.
2) The MIL comparison is reasonable but still somewhat limited; comparison against a broader set of more recent MIL variants would help clarify the robustness of the gain.
3) Vertebra localization/indexing is understandably not the main focus of the paper, but the downstream pipeline depends on it, so a brief discussion of how indexing errors might affect supervision and evaluation would strengthen the manuscript.
4) The weak-label construction could be described more clearly, especially for negatives, unmentioned vertebrae, and ambiguous reports.
5) Table 3 is informative, but it is not a fully matched supervision-only ablation because supervision type is partially entangled with differences in training data composition.
6) An additional controlled comparison that derives weaker vertebra-level labels from the same strongly annotated cases could help isolate the effect of supervision type more clearly.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper addresses a clinically meaningful problem and presents a technically coherent approach for a realistic hybrid-supervision setting. I also view the external validation on two cohorts as a notable strength, and the empirical improvements are generally consistent. My reservations are mainly about experimental clarity rather than the overall direction: the comparison in Table 2 is largely fair but not a strictly pooling-isolated ablation, Table 3 is informative but not fully disentangled from differences in training data composition, and the manuscript would benefit from clearer discussion of the upstream vertebra localization/indexing dependency and the report-label generation procedure. Overall, I find the paper promising and practically relevant, but at present I remain slightly below the acceptance line.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors reasonably addressed my main concerns regarding weak-label construction, ablation interpretation, and the dependency on vertebra preprocessing. I still view the novelty as moderate, and Table 3 should be interpreted as a comparison of realistic annotation regimes rather than a fully disentangled supervision-only ablation. However, the paper addresses a clinically relevant problem, presents a coherent method, and provides external validation with generally consistent gains.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper addresses a relevant clinical problem. The use of uncertainty-aware pooling and external validation are strengths. However, the novelty over prior work is not fully clear, and some key claims are not well supported. There are also concerns about clarity and aspects of the evaluation. These points need to be clarified in the rebuttal.

The paper includes evaluation on external cohorts and addresses a practically meaningful application. Reviewers raised questions regarding novelty, evaluation setup, and presentation clarity, and the rebuttal clarified several of these points. Based on the reviewer discussion and updated feedback, the paper is above the acceptance threshold.

R2 and R3 were satisfied with the rebuttals and revised their recommendations (R2: Weak Accept to Accept, R3: Weak Reject to Accept). However, both reviewers suggested further clarification on certain parts of the paper that should be addressed in the final camera-ready version.
The rebuttal addressed most key concerns, clarifying methodology and experimental design. The strengths outweigh the weaknesses, supporting acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers and the AC. We address the main concerns: novelty, ablation, clarity, and preprocessing dependency.
1.Novelty over prior work (R2-W2, R3-W1).
Our novelty lies in using voxel-level certainty, learned primarily from a small set of voxel masks, as MIL aggregation weights, enabling more robust incorporation of noisy vertebra-level weak labels. Prior uncertainty-aware MIL methods learn instance uncertainty only from bag-level weak supervision, where uncertainty may reflect both incorrect vertebra labels and visual ambiguity between normal and abnormal structures. In contrast, U-ReLSE uses an evidential head trained with voxel mask supervision to estimate voxel-level lesion certainty that directly weights vertebra-level aggregation. This prevents BCE gradients driven by noisy vertebra labels from reinforcing uncertain voxels as lesions, thereby mitigating overfitting to label noise. The improvement from Hybrid ReLSE to U-ReLSE in Table 3 (AUC 0.831->0.861) supports this design. Thus, U-ReLSE does not merely add an uncertainty component to MIL. It uses voxel-mask-supervised lesion certainty to gate the local evidence that contributes to vertebra-level weak label aggregation and its back-propagated gradients.
2.Ablation design (R3-W5/W6, R1-W1).
R3 notes that ablations are “entangled.” However, comparisons of nGWP, Attention MIL, and U-ReLSE in Table 2, and of Hybrid ReLSE vs. U-ReLSE in Table 3, are pooling-isolated ablations: training data, supervision, and encoder are held constant while only pooling varies. Notably, Hybrid ReLSE and U-ReLSE share the same LSE formulation, differing solely in uncertainty weighting, directly showing that certainty-weighted aggregation improves robustness under noisy supervision. Regarding supervision-type isolation (R3-W6): Table 3 was designed to compare realistic annotation scenarios. We did examine the suggested setting as part of our ablation design: on Spine-Mets, AUC was 0.742 (Verified-Vertebra-only) and 0.821 (Verified+Report-Vertebra), both well below Hybrid U-ReLSE (0.861); this was omitted for space. We will clarify comparison levels in the final manuscript. R1’s concern about missing quantitative results and ablations is addressed by Tables 2 and 3, which provide quantitative external validation and ablations.
3.Clarity.
Terminology (R2-W3/W7): Our use of “strong/weak” for label reliability and “voxel/vertebra” for granularity caused confusion. We will adopt three categories: (a) Verified-Voxel (multimodality-confirmed masks), (b) Verified-Vertebra (confirmed vertebra labels), (c) Report-Vertebra (noisy vertebra labels). “Reliable validation and test sets” refers to annotation quality; we will clarify this.
Notation (R2-W4): y_{v,i,c} denotes voxel-level labels, defined only for Verified-Voxel data. L_edl and L_kd apply exclusively to these.
γ range (R2-W6): γ is constrained to [4,16], interpolating between average and max pooling. This range was selected via validation, within which performance was stable. The learned γ converged to 8.17.Weak-label construction (R3-W4): Only vertebrae explicitly named in reports were labeled as weak positives. Unmentioned vertebrae were excluded from BCE (not labeled negative) to avoid false-negative risk. Negatives were defined as vertebrae without positive masks in mask-annotated cases. Ambiguous or non-vertebra-specific reports were excluded. We will clarify in the final manuscript.
4.Preprocessing dependency (R2-W5, R3-W3).
Vertebra segmentation [13] is a fixed model shared by all methods and does not affect relative comparisons. ROIs include margins around centroids, and pooling masks use dilation to mitigate boundary errors. Evaluation-set vertebra indices were curated by radiologists. Consistent gains on two distributionally distinct external cohorts support generalization of the pipeline.
5.Ethics (R3). This study is IRB-approved. All data were obtained with opt-out consent and anonymization per ethical guidelines.

title: URLCF: Universal Representation Learning for Cross-Domain Few-Shot Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection
abstract: Developing generalizable predictive models for brain disease detection critically depends on the availability of a large amount of fMRI data. To enable large-scale analysis, it is often necessary to aggregate data from multiple acquisition sites/domains. However, differences in scanners and acquisition protocols across sites lead to unfavorable heterogeneity in data distribution, which hinders reliable biomarker identification and undermines the generalizability of predictive models. In this paper, we propose URLCF, a novel few-shot learning framework that learns a set of universal representations by distilling knowledge from multiple separately trained models for cross-domain autism detection. Specifically, we first train multiple domain-specific networks to serve as teacher models for guiding the universal model. Subsequently, domain-specific data are simultaneously fed into both the universal and teacher models. By randomly masking the output features of the universal model and employing domain-specific generators to reconstruct these masked features, we align the learned representations of the universal model with those of the teachers. Concurrently, a domain discriminator is introduced to perform domain alignment, jointly facilitating the learning of universal representations. Finally, few-shot fine-tuning is conducted on the unseen domain to enable rapid adaptation to the unseen distribution. Experimental results on the ABIDE dataset demonstrate that URLCF achieves superior performance in autism detection under both zero-shot and five-shot settings, confirming its effectiveness in generalizing to unseen domains with limited data. The code is available at https://github.com/dwd111/URLCF.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper proposes a two-stage framework (URLCF) for cross-domain few-shot ASD detection from rs-fMRI functional connectivity. The method first distills knowledge from multiple site-specific teacher models into a universal student representation through masked feature reconstruction, logit distillation, and domain discrimination, and then performs lightweight few-shot adaptation on unseen sites. The experiments are conducted on the ABIDE dataset under a leave-one-site-out setting with both zero-shot and five-shot evaluation. ￼ ￼
I view this as a clinically motivated engineering paper with moderate novelty. The problem is important and realistic, but the technical contribution is largely a combination of existing ingredients, including multi-teacher distillation, masking-based reconstruction, adversarial/domain alignment, and lightweight target adaptation, rather than a fundamentally new representation-learning method. The manuscript somewhat over-packages this as “universal representation learning. ”
reviews.text_strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem in multi-site neuroimaging, and the evaluation protocol is well aligned with the motivation. The leave-one-site-out setting is appropriate for studying unseen-site generalization, and the additional five-shot setting is also clinically relevant. The overall framework is coherent and the reported empirical gains over the included baselines are encouraging. The paper is also generally well organized and includes ablation analysis and qualitative visualization.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Global limitation:
The paper does not truly establish “universal” representations in a strong scientific sense; it mainly shows improved performance on the ABIDE benchmark. The biological and interpretability claims are also overstated. The presented FC visualization, t-tests, and t-SNE plots are post-hoc and correlational, and do not justify claims about reliable biomarkers or mechanistic interpretability. ￼
Method-induced limitation:
The main concern is limited novelty. Once unpacked, the method is a relatively standard combination of teacher-student distillation, masked reconstruction, domain discrimination, and a lightweight adapter. In addition, the framework is fairly heavy, requiring multiple teacher models, generators, and a discriminator, yet the paper provides little analysis of computational cost, hyperparameter sensitivity, or training stability. The ablation study is useful but still not enough to show why this specific combination is necessary. ￼
Dataset-induced limitation:
The empirical validation is restricted to ABIDE only. Although leave-one-site-out is stronger than random splitting, it is still internal validation on a single benchmark. This is not sufficient to support strong claims about robust cross-domain generalization. In addition, the five-shot setting is inherently fragile in medical imaging due to substantial subject-level and site-level heterogeneity. ￼
Another concern is reproducibility. Although the paper provides an anonymized code link, the anonymous repository does not yet appear sufficiently complete for full verification. These missing details should be explicitly addressed in the rebuttal. In particular, the authors should clarify what exactly is included, whether the full training and evaluation pipeline can be reproduced, and whether all implementation details, scripts, and dependencies needed for leave-one-site-out and few-shot experiments are available.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
This is a technically competent paper on an important problem, but the claims should be better calibrated. In particular, the authors should tone down the language around “universal representation” and “reliable biomarkers,” better position the work as an integration of existing techniques, and clarify the completeness of the anonymous repository in the rebuttal.

Overall, I find this paper borderline but positive. It addresses a meaningful practical problem, uses a suitable evaluation protocol, and reports consistent gains over the listed baselines on ABIDE. However, the novelty is moderate, the biological and interpretability claims are overstated, and the evidence for broader generalizability remains limited because the validation is confined to a single benchmark. In addition, although the submission provides an anonymized code link, the current repository content does not yet appear sufficient for full reproducibility, and this should be clarified and completed in the rebuttal.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Thank you for your response. I understand that some raised issues are difficult to sufficiently address during the rebuttal stage. As no additional supportive evidence can be provided, I will keep my original rating.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: In this work, a novel few-shot learning framework is introduced for ASD detection. The framework follows the student-teacher design to obtain a universal student model from datasets across multiple domains. In addition, a masked generation and a discriminator are integrated to promote universal learning. The proposed model, URLCF, demonstrates superior performance.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The URLCF effectively addresses the multi-site deployment bottleneck by utilizing a Teacher-Student distillation strategy, which extracts and transfers knowledge from multiple domain-specific models into a single, unified student network to mitigate fMRI data heterogeneity.
2.The authors introduce a highly robust alignment mechanism that combines masked generative reconstruction with a conditional domain discriminator, actively forcing the network to learn generalized, universal representations rather than site-specific artifacts.
3.The framework’s efficacy is rigorously validated through extensive comparative experiments on the ABIDE dataset against diverse baselines, while a detailed ablation study successfully demonstrates the critical contribution of each individual module to the model’s overall zero-shot and five-shot performance.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.How is the performance score ( s_i ) computed? If it relies on training accuracy, how do you prevent overfitted teacher models—especially those trained on small ABIDE sites—from being given overly large weights?
2.Were the baseline models (especially MAML, Prototypical Networks, and the domain-invariant approaches) built using the same 3-layer MLP architecture as your feature extractor?
3.Minor: a missing citation on page 6 (ComBat[?]).
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Even though the methodology’s novelty is limited, the proposed method offers a practical solution to few-shot autism spectrum disorder detection, highlighting promising performance together with an ablation study. Therefore, I suggest a weak accept.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: All my concerns have been addressed, and I believe the added revisions will greatly improve the clarity of the manuscript. I therefore recommend accepting this paper.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
1.The authors introduce a few-shot learning framework that distills knowledge from multiple domain-specific teacher models into a single universal student model to alleviate multi-site fMRI heterogeneity.
2.It uses masked generative alignment combined with a conditional domain discriminator to align feature distributions.
3.Extensive experiments on the ABIDE dataset demonstrate model effectiveness.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The manuscript is well-structured, logically organized, and clearly written.
2.It provides biological interpretability for evaluation.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.A shallow MLP is inadequate for capturing the complex topological features of FC networks, lagging behind current SOTA methods that favor GNNs or Transformers.
2.Does masking 1D latent features differ fundamentally from standard dropout? Furthermore, what is the specific advantage of masking in the latent space rather than directly on the raw FC matrices?
3.Relying exclusively on the ABIDE dataset is insufficient to prove generalizability. The authors are strongly encouraged to validate URLCF on additional multi-site datasets, such as REST-meta-MDD. 
4.The selected baselines and reference list are notably outdated (mostly pre-2022). Excluding recent SOTA methods [1-2] significantly weakens the persuasiveness of the results.
[1] Yang Y, Ye C, Su G, et al. Brainmass: Advancing brain network analysis for diagnosis with large-scale self-supervised learning[J]. IEEE transactions on medical imaging, 2024, 43(11): 4004-4016.[2] Yu S, Jin S, Li M, et al. Long-range brain graph transformer[J]. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 2024, 37: 24472-24495.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The methodological innovation is insufficient, and the comparative experiments rely on outdated baselines. Furthermore, evaluating on a single dataset significantly weakens the overall persuasiveness of the results.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have adequately addressed my primary concerns regarding the backbone architecture, masking strategy, and model generalizability.

meta_reviews.text:
Based on the three reviews, the paper addresses an important practical problem and uses a reasonable evaluation protocol. However, all reviewers raise substantial concerns. R1 notes limited novelty and the claim of “universal” representations. R2 questions the weighting mechanism and baseline comparisons. R3 delivers a strong critique: the shallow MLP backbone is inadequate compared to current GNN/Transformer methods, masking in latent space lacks clear advantage, the validation is restricted to a single dataset (ABIDE), and the baselines are notably outdated. Given these issues, the authors must reply the concerns regarding architectural limitations, dataset generalizability, baseline recency, and reproducibility.

The rebuttal does a good job in clarifying the “universal” representations in the paper. The reviewers and I agree that the paper merits acceptance to MICCAI in its current form.

After carefully reviewing the authors’ rebuttal, I have revised my initial assessment to Accept. The authors directly addressed key concerns including clarifying the intended meaning of “universal representation,” explaining the principled integration of modules with ablation evidence, justifying MLP choice for stable optimization under limited data, distinguishing latent masking from dropout, and committing to expanded validation on additional multi-site datasets.

This paper is recommended for acceptance. The reviewers converged positively after rebuttal, and the authors adequately addressed the main concerns regarding the backbone choice, masking strategy, few-shot setting, and generalizability.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their comments and enthusiasm for our work.
R#1 
Q1: Global limitation A1: In this work, the term “universal representation” is intended to describe representations that are transferable across heterogeneous imaging domains, rather than biologically universal representations in a strict neuroscientific sense. We will revise the manuscript to avoid overly broad interpretations. Also, we agree that the current visualization analyses are post-hoc and correlational. These analyses were used to provide qualitative insight into the learned feature structure and cross-domain consistency. We will revise the manuscript to present these findings as preliminary observations that may motivate future neuroscientific validation.
Q2: Method limitation A2: Although the individual modules are inspired by existing techniques, the main contribution of this work lies in the principled integration of these modules into a unified framework for cross-domain few-shot fMRI representation learning under severe site heterogeneity. Importantly, ablation results indicate that these components play complementary roles within the framework, as removing any individual module leads to degraded unseen-domain generalization performance. Regarding computational costs, we would like to mention that multi-teacher training is performed only once in an offline stage. During inference and target domain adaptation, only the student model and a lightweight adapter are used, making the framework computationally efficient for few-shot fine-tuning.
Q3: Generalization A3: The current study primarily focuses on ASD-related analysis and evaluation. We will further validate our method on additional multi-site datasets (e.g., MDD and ADHD) in future work. 
Q4: Reproducibility A4: As suggested, we have updated the anonymized repository to clearly present the full training and testing pipeline, ensuring the reproducibility of our implementation. 
R#2 
Q1: Calculating of performance score A1: For each non-held-out site, we split the data into training and validation sets, and compute the validation accuracy as the performance score using a single fully connected layer. To prevent overfitted teacher models, we apply a temperature scaling parameter τ in Eq. (1), which smooths the weight distribution, ensuring that no single teacher model dominates the distillation process.
Q2: Architecture of baselines A2: For a fair comparison, all few-shot learning and domain-invariant methods were implemented using the same three-layer MLP architecture as our feature extractor.
Q3: Missing citation A3: We apologize for the typo error, and will revise it in the revised version. 
R#3 
Q1: Deficiencies of MLP A1: We agree that shallow MLPs are insufficient to fully capture the complex topological structure of FCs. In this study, we use shallow MLPs to avoid over-parameterization and ensure stable optimization, especially under limited neuroimaging data. This lightweight backbone also allows us to better evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed framework itself, independent of sophisticated network architectures.
Q2: Masking A2: Masking is a feature corruption strategy that hides parts of the input to promote robust representation learning, whereas dropout is a regularization technique that randomly drops neural activations during training to reduce co-adaptation and prevent overfitting. Compared with directly masking raw FC matrices, masking semantically enriched high-level latent representations enables more robust feature learning and improves downstream clinical prediction performance.
Q3: Generalization A3: A similar concern was also raised by R#1.A detailed response is provided in our reply to Q#3 of R#1.Q4: Comparison methods A4: We have already compared against 3 categories and 9 baseline methods. In future work, we will further expand the comparisons by incorporating additional SOTA methods to provide a more comprehensive evaluation.

title: UT-MIL: Uncertainty-Rectified and TME-Decoupling Dual-Stream Aggregation for Robust WSI Survival Prediction
abstract: Survival analysis using Whole Slide Images (WSIs) is often challenged by histological artifacts and ambiguous tissue morphology within the tumor microenvironment (TME). While Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) has become a standard paradigm for this task, existing methods frequently overlook feature-level reliability, leading to overconfident yet erroneous prognostic stratifications. For advanced prognostic modeling, explicitly managing uncertainty is imperative to reduce out-of-distribution noise and refine ambiguous signals. To this end, we propose UT-MIL, an uncertainty-aware TME-decoupling framework that integrates clinical prognostic logic through two synergistic phases. First, we introduce the Uncertainty-Guided Feature Rectifier (UGFR) to estimate feature-level uncertainty using perturbation sensitivity and a Histomorphological Memory Bank. Unlike passive estimation, UGFR performs active feature intervention via a tri-branch routing mechanism: removing highly uncertain features, preserving reliable features, and refining ambiguous representations via prototype retrieval. Second, to aggregate the resulting purified manifold, we design the TME-Decoupling Contextual Aggregator (TDCA). TDCA employs a dual-stream architecture comprising a Critical Stream to highlight high-risk malignant foci and a Context Stream that utilizes learnable latent queries to decouple multifaceted TME patterns. Comprehensive evaluations across five TCGA benchmarks demonstrate that UT-MIL achieves superior prognostic performance over representative MIL baselines. Beyond empirical gains, our framework yields high-fidelity, noise-resilient spatial interpretability that integrates localized risk determinants with global histological contexts. Our code is available at https://github.com/hutaiyuan/UTMIL.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors proposed an uncertainty-rectified multi-instance learning framework, which models the noise injection-based aleatoric uncertainty term, along with a clustering-based epistemic uncertainty term. Moreover, instead of traditional soft attention in ABMIL, a tri-branch hard routing mechanism was introduced to handle the high, intermediate, and low uncertainty patches.
reviews.text_strengths: The idea to decouple and explicitly formulate the aleatoric and epistemic terms with noise injection and clustering is intriguing and seems to be effective. The authors also performed extensive evaluation on the pancancer datasets, showing superior performance against existing SotA ABMIL approaches in survival prediction in both c-index and KM-curve/logrank test for risk prediction and stratification. The authors also conducted ablation studies to identify the impact of handling aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty individually.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Rather than showing the mean/std of c-index across k-fold cross-validation, it may be more concise to simply compute the “global” c-index of all out-of-fold predictions. Moreover, the authors should perform statistical tests such as paired permutation tests, or at least bootstrap CI of the c-index difference, to demonstrate that the c-index improvement is consistent/significant. It is also easier for readers if the authors directly address the relative c-index improvement in percentage.
Moreover, while the authors already showcase the clinical interpretation of regions with various uncertainty identified by the model, it is important to know whether the uncertainty modeling is inflated because of the existence of abundant of artifacts, or that the model can still identify the most aggressive patterns only within high image quality tissue patches.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
(1) As author stated, the signal of survival trajectory may reside beyond the most aggressive tumor pattern. So to this end, if we limit the bag of patches to only those without artifacts through quality control, do these regions discarded during the routing phase really not informative to survival prediction? This may need an explicit quantitative answer. 
(2) It can be interesting to know the impact of # of histomorphological phenotypes as well as the threshold of uncertainty.

The study is shipped with relatively comprehensive experimental design and sufficient size of cohort in the scope of a conference publication. However, the authors should at least provide the statistical test or bootstrap CI of c-index as the evidence to show the improvement is significant. The relevant tests involve no model training and can be trivially added to Table 1 and Table 2 so it poses no time/space constraint.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution is an uncertainty-aware MIL framework that explicitly disentangles and rectifies aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties at the feature level. It further introduces a TME-decoupling aggregation mechanism to jointly model local risk regions and global histological context, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper presents a relatively comprehensive experimental evaluation under multiple settings, which helps to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method to some extent.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The Introduction does not sufficiently summarize or analyze the current research landscape. While several related works are mentioned, there is a lack of structured discussion on existing limitations and how the proposed method is fundamentally different from prior MIL-based survival models. Strengthening this part would help clarify the motivation and novelty of the work. 
2.In Section 2.1 (Tri-Branch Dynamic Routing), the paper introduces a hard-routing mechanism based on uncertainty quantiles. However, the rationale behind choosing hard routing over conventional soft-attention-based masking is not clearly justified. Given that soft attention is widely adopted in MIL frameworks, a more detailed explanation (e.g., theoretical intuition or empirical motivation) is necessary to support this design choice. 
3.The paper lacks sufficient theoretical grounding in the Dual-Uncertainty Estimation module. The two proposed uncertainty measures appear to be heuristic constructs rather than principled probabilistic formulations.
Specifically, the so-called aleatoric uncertainty is derived from feature perturbations induced by externally injected noise 
𝜖, which is independent of the true data-generating process. This formulation seems to reflect perturbation sensitivity or representation instability, rather than intrinsic data uncertainty.
Likewise, the epistemic uncertainty, defined as the distance to the nearest prototype, is more aligned with an OOD or novelty measure. Such a distance-based metric does not directly quantify uncertainty in the model’s predictive function 
𝑓, and therefore may not faithfully capture epistemic uncertainty.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

While the paper demonstrates novelty, the overall presentation and technical explanations need to be more thorough. Certain essential components are insufficiently described and should be further clarified.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose UT-MIL, an uncertainty-aware TME-decoupling MIL framework designed to address morphological ambiguity in the Tumor Microenvironment (TME) for WSI-based survival analysis. By explicitly modeling uncertainty, the framework prevents over-confident predictions in ambiguous regions, thereby enhancing the clinical reliability and robustness of AI-driven prognostic decision-making.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper introduces an Uncertainty-Rectified Group Aggregator (URGA) that calculates and sums aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties. This allows for a sophisticated tri-branch routing system (keep, refine, drop), ensuring that only high-quality or appropriately adjusted features contribute to the final prediction.
The proposed TME-Decoupling Contextual Aggregator effectively separates features into a Critical Stream for isolating key individual patch features and a Latent Query Context Stream for capturing diverse histological patterns. This dual-stream approach provides a more nuanced representation of the complex TME landscape.
The use of t-SNE visualizations to demonstrate the separation of ambiguous and reliable features in the manifold provides strong qualitative support for the effectiveness of the uncertainty-based filtering.
The study successfully demonstrates that high-level feature engineering—leveraging uncertainty-based routing and contextual decoupling—leads to meaningful performance improvements in WSI survival analysis across multiple benchmarks.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
While the proposed modules contribute to performance, the framework relies on a highly explicit and hand-crafted architecture. This design choice deviates from the current trend in representation learning, which favors end-to-end, data-driven architectures over manually engineered routing logic.
The current implementation requires manual tuning of uncertainty routing thresholds for each specific task. The framework would be more robust and scalable if these thresholds were implemented as trainable parameters rather than fixed hyperparameters requiring manual intervention.
The paper lacks a thorough sensitivity analysis regarding the uncertainty thresholds. There is insufficient justification for the chosen values, and it remains unclear how sensitive the final survival predictions are to fluctuations in these parameters.
Despite the claim of “TME-decoupling,” the qualitative evidence in Figure 4 primarily highlights the severe tumor core. There is a lack of detailed clinical explanation or evidence demonstrating how the model specifically distinguishes and decouples the broader TME components.
In Figure 2, the Kaplan-Meier survival curves are presented without a direct comparison to existing baseline methods. To demonstrate superior prognostic stratification, it is necessary to show that the proposed method yields more distinct and statistically significant survival separations compared to previous models.
The manuscript contains inconsistent terminology, such as the use of “Uncertainty-Rectified Feature Frontend (URGA).” The application of terms like “Frontend” and “Backend” feels somewhat unconventional in this architectural context and may lead to confusion for the reader.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a technically sound framework that enhances clinical reliability by integrating uncertainty-aware routing with TME-decoupling. By filtering for reliable features and diversifying task-specific branches into critical and contextual streams, the authors demonstrate meaningful performance gains in WSI survival prediction.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

meta_reviews.text: The paper introduces a new framework for WSI survival prediction by rectifying uncertainty. The proposed mehtod is evaluated on five public datasets and show performance improvements over a series strong baselines. All three reviewers give positive scores. Though quite a few weakness points are listed by the reviewers, most issues can be resolved given enough space and time.

title: VA-Adapter: Adapting Ultrasound Foundation Model to Echocardiography Probe Guidance
abstract: Echocardiography is a critical tool for detecting heart diseases, yet its steep operational difficulty causes a shortage of skilled personnel. Probe guidance systems, which assist in acquiring high-quality images, offer a promising solution to lower this operational barrier. However, robust probe guidance remains challenging due to significant individual variability. This variability manifests as differences in low-level features within two-dimensional (2D) images, which complicates image feature understanding, and differences in individual three-dimensional (3D) structures, which poses challenges for precise navigation. To address these challenges, we first propose leveraging the robust image representations learned by ultrasound foundation models from vast datasets. Yet, applying these models to probe navigation is non-trivial due to their lack of understanding of individual 3D structures. To this end, we meticulously design a Vision-Action Adapter (VA-Adapter) to online inject the capability of understanding individual 3D structures. Specifically, by embedding the VA-Adapter into the foundation model’s image encoder, the model can infer cardiac anatomy from historical vision-action sequences, mimicking the cognitive process of a sonographer. Extensive experiments on a dataset with over 1.31M samples demonstrate that the VA-Adapter outperforms strong probe guidance models while requiring approximately 33 times fewer trained parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/LeapLabTHU/VA-Adapter.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces VA-Adapter, an efficient module that equips pre‑trained ultrasound foundation models with probe‑guidance capability for echocardiography. By inserting the adapter into deep layers of a frozen image encoder and modelling historical vision‑action sequences with a transformer‑based interaction module, the method learns subject‑specific 3D cardiac anatomy. Experiments on a large dataset show that VA-Adapter reduces navigation error.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The idea of repurposing diagnostic foundation models for probe guidance via a lightweight adapter that explicitly models vision‑action sequences is novel. Most prior work trains guidance models from scratch or uses clinician’s statistical experience with visual guidance.
2.With only 2.6M trainable parameters, the method achieves strong performance, making it attractive for resource‑constrained clinical settings.
3.The paper incorporates a large dataset with image‑action pairs and trajectories obtained from robot teleoperation, which is substantial and also covers ten standard echocardiographic planes.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The evaluation is mainlu metric‑based. There is no user study to measure success rate, time to target plane, or image quality. Without such validation, the real‑world impact remains unclear.
2.The model uses only L=4 frames. The effect of longer histories or adaptive sampling is not explored, and the paper does not discuss how robust the method is to different temporal granularities.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper introduces a novel and parameter‑efficient VA‑Adapter that successfully adapts ultrasound foundation models for probe guidance, achieving strong accuracy with only 2.6M trainable parameters. The evaluation is thorough, including comparisons with strong baselines, extensive ablations, and real‑time latency analysis on a large dataset. While dataset diversity and clinical validation are limited, the core technical contribution is significant, well‑validated, and clearly presented.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes VA-Adapter, a task-specific parameter-efficient module that adapts ultrasound foundation models such as EchoCLIP, USFM, and BiomedCLIP for echocardiography probe guidance. The method keeps the pretrained image encoder frozen, inserts VA-Adapters into its deeper layers, and processes short history sequences of sampled images and relative probe motions by interleaving visual and action tokens in a bottleneck space. These are updated through a vision-action interaction module, then aggregated by a GRU and mapped to 10 target-specific heads that predict 6-DoF motion from the current frame to each one of the 10 standard cardiac views. On a dataset of 356 expert scans from 178 adults (1.31M image-pose pairs), the method reduces translation and rotation MAE compared with strong single-frame and sequential baselines while using about 33× fewer trainable parameters and adding only minimal inference latency.
reviews.text_strengths:
The vision–action adapter design that injects interleaved action tokens into deeper layers of a frozen foundation model is innovative and well-motivated for capturing patient-specific 3D structure from 2D sequences.
The residual mapping of adapted visual tokens back to the backbone feature space and progressive propagation of action tokens across adapter layers is a thoughtful architectural choice that balances adaptation and preservation of pre-trained knowledge.
Segmental sampling of histories encourages larger inter-frame motion and richer anatomical variation compared to consecutive frames, which is well aligned with the goal of structure inference.
The paper evaluates across three different ultrasound foundation backbones and compares PEFT strategies (LoRA, Prefix Tuning, vanilla adapters) with consistent gains for VA-Adapter.
Ablations on the interaction module and adapter dimension provide insight into where improvements come from and how capacity impacts performance/efficiency.
Inference-time profiling shows the proposed adapters add marginal latency and meet real-time needs on commodity GPUs.
The overall method is clearly described, with a coherent forward pass across interleaved vision–action tokens and a clean training strategy (frozen backbone, tuned adapters).
Dataset acquisition and label formation (relative action to standard views via recorded poses) are explained in a reproducible way.
Tackling operator dependence in echocardiography via learning 3D structure from 2D sequences is a clinically relevant problem.
Demonstrating that ultrasound foundation models can be efficiently adapted to probe guidance meaningfully connects two active research directions (diagnosis and acquisition/navigation).
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper argues that VA-Adapter enables the model to infer patient-specific 3D cardiac structure from vision-action history, but the evidence is entirely downstream: lower action-prediction error. There is no intermediate analysis showing that the learned representation actually encodes anatomy, spatial state, or geometric consistency better than the alternatives. So the structural-reasoning interpretation is plausible, but not really proven by the presented experiments.
The metric is purely MAE on 6-DoF action vectors; there is no closed-loop evaluation (e.g., success rate to reach target plane, steps-to-target) or user study to establish clinical relevance of the observed error reductions.
The rotation parameterization and associated MAE in degrees are not specified (Euler vs. axis–angle), raising concerns about discontinuities and comparability across poses.
The equal weighting of translation (mm) and rotation (deg) by normalization may not reflect their differential impact on view quality and acquisition success.
No external validation: single-center, single scanner/probe, two experts. Generalization to different vendors, probes, operators, and patient populations (e.g., high BMI) is untested.
Absence of per-plane results and dispersion measures (e.g., SD/CI) makes it difficult to assess robustness and whether gains are uniform across views.
The sequential baselines’ configurations are not fully specified (where/how sequence fusion occurs, whether encoders are frozen, and whether parameter counts are matched), complicating fairness assessments.
Limited ablations: no study of sequence length L, history sampling strategies (segmental vs. consecutive), or adapter placement depth.
While general baselines are covered, related ultrasound guidance works using quality assessment signals or robotic autonomy (e.g., QA-NET-style guidance, recent compact autonomous liver US systems) are not discussed, and clinical navigation success metrics commonly used in robotic US are absent.
Fig. 1(c) is too small and should be enlarged to ensure the details are clearly visible. Additionally, Fig. 1(a) and (b) do not need to be presented as figures; the statistics of the public FM dataset and the private dataset could be more effectively conveyed in the text or summarized in a table.
Fig. 2 should present the architecture more clearly. It is currently unclear whether each pair of consecutive red layers is connected via one green linear layer and one VA-Adapter; if that is the intended design, it should be shown explicitly in the figure. Additionally, the indexing of the red layers is inconsistent (k in the left panel vs. i in the right) and should be unified. If the right panel is intended as a zoomed-in view of the left, this relationship should be clearly observable.
The figures would benefit from more detailed and informative captions that better explain their components and relationships.
Fig. 2 appears incomplete, as the final output of the model is not shown. For completeness, consider including the predictor head, the model’s final output, and the associated loss functions in the diagram.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
This is a strong submission with a real technical idea and a clinically meaningful target task. The strongest evidence in the paper is the ablation against the vanilla adapter and the matched-backbone comparison against full fine-tuning. Those experiments make a convincing case that the gain is coming from the proposed vision-action interaction design rather than from a generic PEFT effect.
My main recommendation is to tighten the framing of what the paper has shown. The experiments support that VA-Adapter improves offline sequential action prediction for target-plane guidance. They do not yet fully establish robust closed-loop guidance, nor do they directly verify the stronger claim that the model has learned an individualized 3D structure. I would therefore encourage the authors to present that interpretation a bit more cautiously.
The paper would also benefit from a more explicit acknowledgment that MAE is only a proxy for guidance success. Even a short discussion of what level of translation/rotation error is likely clinically acceptable would help the reader interpret the reported gains. Finally, since the dataset is one of the important parts of this work, more details on subject diversity and hard cases would strengthen the paper.
Questions for Authors
What exact blocks/layers receive adapters for each backbone (EchoCLIP CNN, USFM/BiomedCLIP Transformers)? Please provide a schematic/table so others can reproduce your insertion strategy.
How were the sequential baselines configured (fusion point, frozen vs. fine-tuned encoders, GRU settings)? Can you clarify why “sequential fully tuning” sometimes underperforms freezing?
Did you evaluate different sequence lengths L or compare segmental sampling against consecutive frames quantitatively? How sensitive is performance to L and the sampling scheme?
How many standard-plane annotations per subject are available, and how do you compute targets when some planes are missing or sparsely visited?
Can you provide any closed-loop proxy evaluation (e.g., iterative application of predicted actions with pose retrieval, steps-to-target, success rate) or phantom tests to link MAE to navigational success?
How does the model generalize across operators, scanners, and probes? Any evidence from leave-one-operator-out or cross-vendor splits?
How are translation and rotation scales normalized for the loss? Did you explore alternative weighting or a multi-task uncertainty weighting scheme?

This paper presents a timely and well-executed approach to adapt ultrasound foundation models for echocardiography probe guidance via a novel vision-action adapter. The method is conceptually elegant, computationally efficient, and empirically strong on a sizable in-house dataset, with consistent gains over solid baselines and PEFT alternatives. However, the evaluation focuses on pose MAE without closed-loop navigation metrics or external validation, and baseline configurations need clearer specification to establish fairness fully. The work’s potential impact is high, but additional evidence, per-plane robustness, sequence-length/sampling sensitivity, rotation handling, and some form of closed-loop or prospective validation, would substantially strengthen the case for clinical relevance. I view this as a strong, innovative contribution, provided the authors address the key concerns and clarify experimental details.
Also, please remove the last part of your introduction regarding your other anonymized related manuscript (Ultrastar), and also remove it from the references, as it is not cited in this paper.
“We also submit an anonymized related manuscript [2] (in the supplementary material) that investigates sequence modeling for probe guidance. The two submissions are complementary and non-trivially different in methodological focus and experimental emphasis.”
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces a VA-adapter module that can be combined with previously developed foundation models for echocardiography for the probe guidance task. Probe guidance data collection is challenging because it must be acquired prospectively, but foundation models for ultrasound were trained on millions of retrospective images, so this paper explores if we can utilize them as a transfer learning technique. VA-adapter is added in the deep layers of foundation models, and is trained to encode images together with timestep embeddings and the action pairs. Image encoder takes in a current frames and samples 4 past frames and produces latent vectors for each 5 frames, they are subsequently fed into a GRU head which predicts 10 different heads denoting 10 different views and how to move the probe to get to them. As a result, they show that their sequential approach combined with transfer learning from previous foundation models outperform single-frame-no-transfer-learning approaches, and that adapter fine-tuning for this task is superior to PEFT fine-tuning strategies.
reviews.text_strengths:
Innovative adaptation of ultrasound foundation models for the task of probe guidance
Strong ablations and comparison between different foundation models and different PEFT strategies
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Visualizations of ‘Retrieved Plane’ in Figure 6 is a bit misleading because your search space is limited to only the sampled frames (you take KNN neighbor to retrieve the plane). You should provide how big of a difference was between a predicted Trans and Rot and a nearest neighbor.
Outdated sources, no source is from 2025.Please add a comparison metrics or discussion with EchoWorld https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13065 and Cardiac Copilot https://arxiv.org/html/2406.13165v1
The paper argues that the main benefit is using pre-trained weights from previous foundation models. To support this argument, the authors should present an ablation where the same architectures are used but weights are initialized either at random or from ImageNet.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper would be of interests to the community because it describes an effective adaptation of previously developed foundation models for a new task - probe guidance. However, the authors need to provide more evidence (as explained above) in their rebuttal to strengthen main claims.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_ethics: It actually makes the most sense to do only USFM because it’s trained as masked autoencoder, for CLIP (EchoCLIP, BioMedCLIP) they are trained to learn concepts not necessarily structures visible so potentially they don’t see the structure.

meta_reviews.text:
The reviews are consistently positive, with scores of 5, 4, and 4.The paper presents VA-Adapter, a parameter-efficient approach for adapting ultrasound foundation models to echocardiography probe guidance. The strengths are the clear technical contribution, strong empirical performance on a sizable robotic echocardiography dataset, comparisons across multiple foundation backbones and PEFT methods, useful ablations, and low trainable-parameter/runtime cost.
The main weaknesses are the lack of closed-loop or user-study validation, the absence of external validation, reliance on offline translation/rotation MAE as a proxy for guidance success, and limited analysis of robustness across views, sequence lengths, and acquisition settings. These are important limitations, but they do not outweigh the technical contribution and positive reviewer consensus. I recommend acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
Thanks for the reviewers’ constructive comments and suggestions. We have carefully revised the manuscript and address the main concerns below.
<R1,R2: Offline MAE Metric and Clinical Relevance> In the field of ultrasound probe navigation, evaluating model performance via offline proxy metrics is a prevalent practice [1-3]. As a practical metric, offline MAE strongly correlates with navigation quality and serves as a prerequisite for closed-loop success. For a study focused on methodological innovation, this metric directly and rigorously quantifies the model’s decision-making precision at the algorithmic level. We agree that closed-loop validation is an excellent suggestion to further enhance clinical impact. We are actively overcoming hardware and ethical barriers to evaluate real-world closed-loop performance for a future journal extension. Regarding the clinical relevance of the observed error reductions, key cardiac anatomical landmarks are on the millimeter scale, even minor mm/° improvements are clinically meaningful. As a clinical reference, the average expert repositioning error is reported to be 5.7° [2]. By reducing the rotation error from approximately 7.8° to 6.7°, our method significantly narrows the gap to expert-level proficiency.
<R1,R2: Sequence Length and Sampling Strategy> To ensure real-time clinical navigation, we set L=4 as a practical trade-off between capturing sufficient context and maintaining low inference latency. We adopted segmental sampling over consecutive sampling because the latter causes minimal inter-frame motion and high redundancy, hindering 3D structural understanding. By dividing the history into equal segments and randomly sampling one frame per segment, we effectively mitigate redundancy and capture richer cardiac information. Regarding robustness to temporal granularities, our sampling mechanism exposes the model to highly diverse temporal granularities and large spatial spans during training. Furthermore, our model relies on the actual relative probe motion between sampled frames rather than temporal indices, which intrinsically guarantees its robustness to temporal granularities.
<R2: Generalization> To assess patient-level generalization, we evaluated our method on a large validation cohort composed entirely of unseen subjects, including male and female subjects, ages ranging from 18 to 69, BMIs ranging from 19.0 to 34.6, and diverse cardiac pathologies. This setting provides a direct evaluation of patient-level generalization. For device-level generalization, the main impact of different ultrasound systems is typically reflected in low-level image appearance. During our data acquisition, sonographers adjusted imaging settings adaptively for individual patients, which introduced substantial appearance diversity into the training data. In addition, recent work [4] has shown that a navigation model trained on 247,000 images from a single device can generalize to other ultrasound devices; in comparison, our model is trained on over one million images. We will add multi-center external validation to future work.
<R2: Robustness across views> In our original experiments, we performed a comprehensive evaluation across each individual view to ensure the system’s reliability. While the manuscript reported averaged metrics to provide a more concise overview, our internal data from the initial assessment confirms that the performance gains are indeed uniform: the VA-Adapter consistently outperforms the baselines across all 10 standard views in both translation and rotation dimensions. We will add a detailed explanation in the revision.
Due to space constraints, we cannot address every minor comment here. However, we sincerely value all remaining suggestions and will meticulously incorporate them into the camera-ready version.
[1] Pose-GuideNet, MICCAI’24 [2] Real-world Visual Navigation for Cardiac Ultrasound View Planning, MICCAI’24 [3] EchoWorld, CVPR’25 [4] UltraBot, Nat. Commun.’25

title: Validation of simulation-based evaluation by inclusion of unlabeled data and meta-ablation
abstract: Lack of adequate ground truth data is a common issue in various medical image processing tasks. Especially in non-uniform image registration and image reconstruction, dense manual labeling of data is both infeasible and insufficient in terms of accuracy, which prevents the use of a manually-labeled test set. In contrast, simulation can offer unlimited data with exact ground truth. However, since simulations are based on models that are limited themselves, the evaluated algorithm could be overfitted to the limited simulation model, and therefore perform worse in real data (the “realism gap”). In this paper, we use combinations of simulated and real data to quantitatively reveal the gap: additional degrees of variation in real data worsen the compensation of the simulated data, introducing a mismatch with its ground truth. Next, we present meta-ablation, a concept to match the simulation to the real data. Inspired by ablation studies, this is achieved by joint variation of the simulation and the compensation method while observing and ideally closing the mismatch.
