reviews.text_strengths:
First, this article design the method by introducing the correlation of multichambered correlations and the they can captures the motion correlation between each part of the heart.
Second, this article focus on the complete inputs and 3d+t generations and it seems reasonable to me to include these tasks since this is related to an issues that sometimes might encounter.
Third, this article have some graphs to help understanding the detail of the articles as well.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
First, in [Table 2] there is a systematic gap in validation. Author only reports the synthetic SAX and LAX reconstruction results of LA and RA, however for its “Real Dataset”, it didn’t show the results of LA and RA. This will inevitably leads to a validation error since synthetic LAX usually use displacement algorithm. Usually in real LAX and SAX dataset, there is always breath noises and image quality issue in LAX images, so I think using only synthetic LAX is lack of solid validation of model performance. 
Second, the way author used to get ground-truth meshes are likely to may lead to proxy reference. In the article they stated that “we register and fit a Statistic Shape Model to segmentation masks predicted by a publicly available method to generate ground-truth cardiac meshes.”
However, this leads to inherent biases that ground-truth meshes uses the SSM model, which is a statistical model that will introduce model-based proxy. The SSM model has a potential generating bias that ground-truth meshes might be embedded in template-like anatomy. The results of using these generated ground-truth meshes lead to weakening this article’s statement of model results comparison. 
Third, in the ablation study, the article ablation still have a validation gap between their results and their conclusions. In the article, the authors states that “ VecHeart outperforms the baselines in both complete and missing data scenarios, validating our HPT and ACM designs”.However, the ablation experiment in “Table 1” and “Table 2” does not contain the design ablation for “HPT”, “ACM”. If the author still simultaneously contains these three parts together in the ablation study, then it will be difficult to see whether individual module are effective enough. 
Fourth, In the quantitative analysis part (Figure 2) the author only provide results for 1 or 2 samples. However, usually for the quantitative analysis it is important to provide the worst, medium, best result to demonstrate the generalizability of the model. It is especially in this type of missing part and SAX-only conditions, since the model received sparse information input. If the author only demonstrated selected cases, then there is a potential of cherry-picking result, which leads to gaps in validation examinations. 
Fifth, for the (3D+t) tasks, there is a validation gap of using only two metrics (vFID and Cycle-CD). The first reaons is that these metrics is indirect to clinical application, some more clinical-related metrics should be used such as ejection fraction and volume curve of the heart. Furthermore, the author should also compared with other published 3D+t reconstruction pipeline.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
First, I am not sure how Table 1 is coded in the original Latex file, but the MICCAI 2026 template states that “If you have tables, the smallest font size allowed is 8pt.” I compared this against the front size produced using the 8pts in the templated, and the numerical number in the Table 1 appears to be much smaller compared to 8pts. I am therefore unsure whether the authors are following the MICCAI 2026 formatting requirements. If not, this may be unfair to other authors who strictly adhered to the formatting rules, as they would be more constrained by space and therefore unable to include some extra amount of their data or numerical results. In addition, the extremely small font size makes reading and comparing much more difficult as number are dense and compact.

This article provide the VecHeart this new model and focus on a reasonable clinical issue. Key factor for this score is that the ablation experiments still have a experimental gap and also the ground-truth meshes still embedded with potential proxy bias. Furthermore, there is a lack of the independent ablation of each innovative components and sensitive experiments of different loss component in their result.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text:
I totally agree with the reviewer #2 that the motivation/fomulation of this study is not quite convincing. The authors should explain this clearly in the rebuttal stage.

The motivation is still not fully convincing to me. The paper claims that multi-part latent representation improves clinical utility, but the link between reconstruction accuracy and downstream clinical tasks such as index analysis or cardiac simulation is not sufficiently demonstrated. Therefore, the work appears more like an incremental improvement over existing implicit/shape-prior methods rather than a clearly motivated methodological advance.

The rebuttal clarified the motivation and intended use as a multi-part latent representation rather than a clinical end-application, reframed the missingness study as a probe of new capabilities, and resolved the evaluation concerns, leading R2 to move from a reject to accept while R1 maintained acceptance. On balance, the methodological contribution is good enough, and I therefore recommend acceptance.

Reviewers generally agreed that the proposed VecHeart framework provides meaningful methodological contributions, particularly in modeling multi-part cardiac structures under sparse and incomplete input settings, and achieves strong performance across multiple reconstruction and generation benchmarks. The main concerns were related to the clinical motivation and interpretation of the missingness experiments, the evaluation of anatomically unobserved regions, and the clarity of the intended downstream use case. The rebuttal clarified that the missingness setting is primarily designed to evaluate representation robustness and conditional completion ability rather than immediate clinical deployment, and also addressed concerns regarding proxy bias, ablation design, and the role of anatomical priors.

author_feedback_text:
[R1] We appreciate the advice and will explore it.
[R2] Formulation, motivation: Our motivation, as detailed in the first two paragraphs of the Intro, is to propose a better multi-part 3D latent representation to address the limitations of prior implicit methods: restriction to single-part modeling or reliance on complete surface and slow test-time optimization. Accurate multi-part modeling is important and a prerequisite for downstream tasks like index analysis and cardiac simulation. By introducing HPT, ACM, MA, VecHeart achieves SOTA performance across widely studied benchmarks, including better representation capacity with faster inference (Tab 1 Top) and better visible part reconstruction from sparse slices (Tab 2). “limit their clinical utility” means prior implicit methods’ performance and speed limitations on the fundamental shape representation problem. Regarding the learned prior: even standard SAX MRI is sparse and necessitates anatomical priors. Incorporating prior is common in SOTA methods [19,32,33,34,37].
[R2] Missingness Evaluation: The missingness experiment is designed to probe the model’s ability in extreme scenarios without requiring architecture modification, rather than to show immediate clinical relevance. This evaluation highlights the model’s ability to produce plausible outputs on unobserved parts under severe data constraints, rather than representing its only intended use. We acknowledge the reconstruction of unobserved anatomy is not perfect, but this shows VecHeart’s potential for application like conditioned generation (e.g., via volume or pathology). The model’s SOTA reconstruction performance on visible parts, which is a well-established and standard setting, shouldn’t be overshadowed by its currently imperfect handling of extreme tasks, where it shows potential despite not being fully mature. We shouldn’t be penalized for exhibiting new abilities absent in previous methods. Regarding “usable”: CD is computed as the standard sum of pred-to-gt and gt-to-pred squared L2 distances, and is thus not directly comparable to the 2mm threshold. Using the comparable mean surface distance instead yields 3.02/2.51 mm, indicating strong potential despite these parts being completely missing.
[R2] Literature: Requiring comparison with unpublished preprints is inappropriate, especially HeartFormer was released only 3 months before deadline. Moreover, given the fact that we do things these unpublished methods do not fully cover, we don’t see how they diminish our work’s novelty.
[R2,R3] 3D+t Generation Experiment: We clarify that this experiment evaluates mesh sequence generation via diffusion model, not reconstruction (3D+t reconstruction is in Tab 2, Real SAX). Following the setting of CardiacFlow, the current SOTA for 3D+t generation, VecHeart shows better volume preservation and periodic consistency. We agree by including analysis with clinical-related distributions and metrics can further strengthen the evaluation.
[R3] Real Evaluation of LA/RA: It’s impossible to evaluate 3D LA/RA quality as we can’t get 3D GT from LAX, which is just a 2D image. Also, the real dataset we use only has SAX. Thus synthetic evaluation is the only viable proxy for 3D LA/RA accuracy.
[R3] GT mesh: 1060 shapes are directly derived from expert CT annotations, ensuring no proxy bias. SSM is only used to obtain bi-ventricle GT for real SAX MRI. Our evaluation against SSM GT is zero-shot (no SSM bias during training), yet we still achieve SOTA. Ours-finetune proves adapting to SSM bias indeed improves metrics.
[R3] Ablation Study: Ours-Sep serves as an ablation for HPT, proving modeling inter-part relationship is beneficial. Excluding ACM can keep performance on visible parts, but it won’t produce any meaningful results on missing parts, which we mention in the main text as: “cant extend to missing-input”. We will clarify.
[R3] Visual Results: Due to space limit, more visualization will be provided in a possible journal extension.

title: VEGA: Vision Enhanced Generative Augmentation for Cross-Subject Electrocardiogram Generalization
abstract: Electrocardiogram (ECG) signals are critical physiological indicators for assessing human health status and diagnosing cardiovascular diseases. However, substantial inter-subject feature variability poses a major challenge to cross-subject generalization in ECG analysis. Existing methods primarily rely on domain adaptation and subject-invariant feature learning, which are often task-specific and may introduce potential data leakage. To address these issues, we propose Vision Enhanced Generative Augmentation (VEGA), a novel paradigm that enables models to quickly adapt to different subjects through data generation without introducing any data leakage. Specifically, VEGA leverages rich semantic priors from a generative model pre-trained on natural images to guide the synthesis of realistic and diverse ECG signals. To adapt to the visual generator, one-dimensional (1D) ECG signals are first converted into two-dimensional (2D) visual representation. Then, to align the numerical distributions between the visualized ECG signals and natural images, VEGA adopts a lightweight domain adaptation strategy by fine-tuning only the normalization layers of the generator with a small amount of external ECG data. Through augmented ECG data generation, VEGA effectively bridges the feature distribution gap between training and testing subjects. We evaluate VEGA on multiple ECG tasks, including fatigue detection, ventricular premature beat (VPB) detection, and generative heartbeat prediction. Across all tasks and datasets, VEGA consistently improves cross-subject generalization performance, demonstrating its effectiveness as a unified generative augmentation paradigm for ECG analysis. Our code is available at https://github.com/Yuyun1011/VEGA-release.
subject_areas: Applications -> Digital Twins / Simulation / Synthetic Data
Applications -> Outcome Prediction / Prognosis / Longitudinal Modeling
Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs
Machine Learning -> Synthetic Data / Data-centric AI
Modalities -> EEG / MEG / ECG / Physiological Signals

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The core contribution of this paper is the proposal of VEGA (Vision Enhanced Generative Augmentation), a novel cross-modal data augmentation framework specifically designed to tackle the challenge of cross-subject generalization in Electrocardiogram (ECG) analysis. 
Due to the significant morphological variability of ECG signals across different subjects, deep learning models often overfit to subject-specific identity cues rather than task-relevant features. To address this, VEGA innovatively transforms 1D ECG signals into 2D visual representations and leverages the rich structural priors from a natural-image pre-trained Masked Autoencoder (MAE) to synthesize diverse and realistic ECG samples. To align the natural image modality with the ECG modality, the authors introduce a parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategy coupled with a novel Frequency Adapter. By augmenting the training set with these generated samples, VEGA acts as a module that explicitly bridges the salient feature distribution gap between training and testing subjects, thereby significantly boosting the robustness of downstream tasks such as fatigue and VPB detection.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper directly tackles a well-known challenge in ECG analysis: severe inter-subject variability that leads to poor generalization on testing patients. Instead of relying on traditional fine-tuning techniques, which may risk data leakage, VEGA solves the distribution gap from a data generation perspective. By enriching the training manifold with diverse, generated cross-subject samples, it forces the downstream networks to focus on task-relevant discriminative features rather than memorizing patient-specific backgrounds. The latent space visualization (Fig. 3) provides convincing evidence that VEGA effectively aligns the training and testing distributions.
2.The methodological highlight of this work is the highly creative cross-modal adaptation. Training high-fidelity generative models (such as Diffusion) from scratch typically requires massive amounts of ECG data, which is clinically impractical. VEGA elegantly bypasses this by exploiting the spatial/structural similarities between natural images and the periodic waveforms of ECGs. The strategy of dividing 1D ECGs into segments and stacking them column-wise into a 2D matrix successfully preserves both intra-cycle morphology and inter-cycle dynamics.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.While the authors position VEGA primarily as a generative augmentation framework, the empirical validation lacks comprehensive comparisons with existing time-series data augmentation techniques. In the generative heartbeat prediction task (Table 2), VEGA is only compared against NF and DDPM For the core clinical downstream tasks, the experiments only compare the baseline models against themselves with VEGA augmentation (i. e. , Model vs. Model + VEGA). Without more baselines, it is difficult to determine whether the performance gains are uniquely attributed to VEGA or merely the general benefit of having more training data.
2.The assumption of ‘label preservation’ during the generative augmentation process. The authors utilize a MAE that masks a certain proportion of the input and reconstructs it, claiming that ‘the original task labels are preserved for the generated outputs. However, this claim lacks validation. In cardiovascular diagnostics, diseases like VPB are often characterized by highly localized, subtle morphological anomalies. If the random masking mechanism happens to obscure these critical pathological regions, the MAE might utilize its learned priors to reconstruct a morphologically ‘normal’ waveform. Assigning the original pathological label to this smoothed or normalized reconstruction would inadvertently introduce noisy labels into the training set, potentially confusing the downstream classifier.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The major factors driving my recommendation are the highly innovative cross-modal methodology and its strong practical implications for ECG analysis. While I have noted a few areas for improvement in my detailed comments, the need for 1) broader comparisons with traditional data augmentation baselines, and 2) a verification regarding how localized pathological features are needed.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: i’m good with the rebuttal, partially address my concerns.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: VEGA is a generative augmentation method for cross-subject ECG generalization. It proposes parameter-efficient fine-tuning, updating only layer normalization parameters to adapt the 2D model to ECG morphology with minimal data. The generated ECG samples augment the training distribution, reducing the feature gap between training and test subjects.
reviews.text_strengths:
Strong few-shot efficiency results. Table 2 shows that VEGA with only 10% training data outperforms DDPM and normalizing flows.
Task-agnostic design. VEGA is applied across multiple downstream architectures and distinct tasks without task-specific modification.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Missing baselines for the generative component and the adaptation component. The prior works (Chen et al. and Yoon et al.) are cited in related work but absent from comparison.
The inference-time sampling procedure is not clearly described. It is ambiguous whether generation proceeds by masking a contiguous future segment of an existing training sample and reconstructing it, or by generating from scratch?
The paper motivates 2D conversion, but providees no comparison against 1D-based generative baselines. Without this comparison.
The paper repeatedly claims that VEGA produces “diverse” augmented samples, but provides no quantitative evidence of diversity.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

While the paper presents a clever parameter-efficient adaptation module (Frequency Adapter) and demonstrates solid empirical improvements in few-shot scenarios, the core methodological contribution—converting 1D ECGs to 2D to exploit natural image priors—is insufficiently validated. The complete absence of 1D generative baselines and missing comparisons against directly related works (Chen et al., Yoon et al.) leaves a major gap in proving the necessity of the proposed pipeline. Furthermore, the lack of clarity regarding the sampling procedure and unsubstantiated claims of generation diversity push the paper below the acceptance threshold in its current state. A strong rebuttal addressing the baseline comparisons is required.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal clarifies the sampling process, but my main concern remains. The key claim is that VEGA improves downstream cross-subject generalization, but the paper does not compare against baselines on the downstream tasks. I also remain unconvinced by the diversity evidence, since figure 3 appears to use more reference/training samples in the right panel, making the visual comparison difficult to interpret. Therefore, I keep my score unchanged.
reviews.text_ethics: All datasets used are established public benchmarks with no privacy issues raised.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes AURORA to address the limitation of existing learning-based approaches for reconstructing standard 12-lead ECG from a single-lead measurement, which often fail to adequately reflect the intrinsic physiological principles of ECG signals. The proposed method first reconstructs one additional limb lead using a learning-based model, and then computes the remaining limb leads based on the Einthoven and Goldberger equations. Subsequently, the full limb leads are used as conditions to reconstruct the precordial leads. Experimental results on the PTB-XL and CUSPH datasets demonstrate improvements in RMSE, DTW, and PCC metrics. The paper also reports both reconstruction performance and downstream disease prediction results. However, the proposed approach appears to be a hybrid extension of existing lead reconstruction frameworks with the incorporation of ECG-related equations, resulting in limited methodological novelty. Furthermore, the potential issue of error propagation in the staged reconstruction pipeline is not sufficiently analyzed. Overall, while the study direction is meaningful, several aspects require further refinement at the current stage.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper formulates the ECG reconstruction problem not as a purely end-to-end generation task, but as a structured problem leveraging ECG vector relationships. It introduces a hybrid strategy in which only one limb lead is reconstructed via learning, while the remaining limb leads are derived analytically using physiological equations. The proposed IGUANA framework combines a lead representation learner with an AdaIN-based 1D U-Net generator and incorporates both source reconstruction and representation consistency in the training process. Comprehensive experiments are conducted on both PTB-XL and CUSPH datasets, including comparisons with competing methods, claim validation, and loss ablation studies. The reconstructed 12-lead ECG achieves AUROC and AUPRC performance close to that of the original ECG in downstream disease prediction tasks.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The method largely resembles an integration of existing lead reconstruction architectures with ECG-based analytical relationships, and thus does not strongly highlight methodological novelty. The experimental setting fixes the input lead to Lead I and the auxiliary lead to Lead II, but lacks sufficient validation of generalization across different lead configurations. The rationale for adopting the current 6-to-6 conditioning scheme in precordial lead reconstruction is not sufficiently compared with alternative design choices. Since the proposed approach follows a staged reconstruction pipeline, further analysis is required to examine the potential accumulation of reconstruction errors across stages. Some competing methods rely on the authors’ own implementations, leaving potential bias due to differences in reproduction settings.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I selected Weak Accept because the paper presents a technically coherent framework and reports consistent improvements across multiple evaluation settings, which supports the practical relevance of the proposed approach. In particular, the combination of learning-based lead reconstruction with ECG-related analytical relationships is well motivated, and the empirical results on PTB-XL and CUSPH suggest that the method is effective in both reconstruction quality and downstream utility. At the same time, the methodological novelty is somewhat limited, as the overall design remains close to a hybrid extension of existing reconstruction pipelines, and several design choices would benefit from stronger validation. In addition, the staged reconstruction process raises questions about possible error propagation, and the current experiments do not fully resolve these concerns. Overall, I consider the paper to be slightly above the acceptance threshold because it offers a meaningful contribution with reasonable experimental support, although it still leaves room for further clarification and refinement.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
After reading the authors’ rebuttal, I maintain my Accept recommendation.
The rebuttal provides clarifications on the role of visual priors, the necessity of the Frequency Adapter, the inference-time sampling procedure, label preservation, and generation diversity. The authors also explain that the generation process is based on single-step parallel decoding rather than long-horizon autoregressive generation. This explanation partially alleviates my concern about error accumulation.
The experimental results show performance improvements and reduced variance after applying VEGA in fatigue detection, VPB detection, and generative heartbeat prediction. These results support the view that the proposed method provides a practical contribution to cross-subject ECG generalization.
However, some concerns remain. The connection between natural image structures and ECG waveforms is still not sufficiently justified. The comparison with simple 1D augmentation baselines is also limited, as it does not include methods such as Gaussian noise injection, temporal shifting, or scaling. The use of a Vision Transformer backbone requires further discussion in terms of computational cost. More analysis of the external ECG adaptation process and its effect would also strengthen the paper.
Overall, I believe that the rebuttal addresses some of my concerns, but it does not fully resolve all remaining issues. Nevertheless, given the observed performance improvements across multiple tasks, I consider the paper to be slightly above the acceptance threshold and therefore recommend Accept.

meta_reviews.text:
While reviewers agreed that the paper addresses important challenges in ECG analysis and features innovative design elements, they also raised serious concerns about the paper’s evaluation rigor, methodological clarity, and novelty: First, the empirical validation lacks comprehensive baselines, and relevant prior works are absent from comparisons, making it hard to attribute performance gains to the proposed methods. Second, key claims and procedures lack validation or clarity. Third, methodological novelty is not strongly highlighted, with one method resembling an integration of existing architectures and insufficient justification for design choices. Since the reviews are mixed, we would like to invite the authors to provide a rebuttal. In addition to clarify other concerns, please try to address the following points during rebuttal: include comprehensive comparisons with existing time-series augmentation techniques, 1D-based generative baselines, and relevant prior works; validate the “label preservation” claim and clarify the inference-time sampling procedure; highlight methodological novelty, justify key design choices, and address potential reconstruction error accumulation.

This is a borderline paper with mixed reviews. While reviewers agreed that VEGA effectively addresses a critical challenge in ECG analysis—poor cross-subject generalization—by creatively adapting 2D generative models to enrich the training manifold and align distributions, they also raised serious concerns about the paper’s soundness and significance: first, the empirical validation lacks comprehensive baselines, particularly comparisons with existing time-series augmentation techniques and alternative generative approaches, making it difficult to isolate VEGA’s unique contribution versus generic data expansion benefits; second, the assumption of label preservation during masked reconstruction is insufficiently validated, raising the risk of introducing noisy labels when critical pathological features are obscured; third, the evidence for generated sample diversity is purely qualitative and unsubstantiated, while the experimental design omits key comparisons, such as 1D generative baselines and alternative lead configurations. The rebuttal clarified certain procedural details but did not fully resolve concerns regarding novelty, baseline comparisons, diversity quantification, or label preservation validation. After careful deliberation, I lean a bit towards rejecting this manuscript.

The rebuttal clarifies several key aspects of the method, particularly the sampling procedure, the role of the Frequency Adapter, and the rationale behind the cross-modal design.
However, some limitations remain only partially resolved. In particular, the lack of direct comparisons with standard time-series augmentation techniques and 1D generative baselines in downstream tasks is still an important gap, and the evidence supporting generation diversity and label preservation remains somewhat indirect.
Given the novelty of the cross-modal augmentation strategy and the consistent empirical improvements across tasks, the rebuttal sufficiently strengthens the paper.

The rebuttal clarifies several methodological details and partially addresses concerns regarding model design, label preservation, and baseline comparisons. I appreciate the interesting idea of leveraging visual generative priors for ECG augmentation, and the reported empirical improvements suggest potential value. However, I still have some reservations about the core motivation: ECG is inherently a 1D periodic physiological signal with strong cycle- and morphology-specific constraints, and it remains insufficiently justified why a vision generative model should be more suitable than signal-specific generative models for this task. Overall, while this concern remains, I am willing to support acceptance given the novelty of the cross-modal formulation and the promising experimental results.

author_feedback_text:
We thank AC and all reviewers for their efforts and constructive feedback. All your constructive comments are considered.
1.The novelty, integration concern and error accumulation (MR[3])
(1) Novelty of the Paradigm: VEGA is the first systematic framework that bridges visual priors and 1D ECG generation to enable cross-subject augmentation without data leakage. Its tailored frequency adapter freezes self-attention to preserve spatial priors learned from images, while explicitly injecting global spectral information to model ECG’s periodic nature. The design effectively disentangles spatial and spectral features, and its superiority is quantitatively validated in Table 2.
(2) Integration Innovation: All model components are elaborately designed rather than arbitrarily assembled, forming a minimal yet indispensable architecture. Specifically, the MAE captures reconstructive visual priors, instance normalization enables amplitude bridging, frozen self-attention preserves pre-trained prior knowledge under limited data, and the Frequency Adapter achieves spectral alignment. Our contribution lies in the synergistic combination of these modules, instead of their isolated individual functions.
(3) Error Accumulation Issue: Unlike conventional autoregression, VEGA adopts single-step parallel decoding for future ECG segments, thereby inherently avoiding long-horizon error accumulation—a deliberate architectural design to enhance model robustness.
2.Label preservation and inference-time sampling procedure (MR[2]/R1[2]/R2[2])
During inference, VEGA converts the ECG into a 2D representation and maps it to the left image half via bilinear interpolation without masking, so no information is lost. The right half is fully masked and reconstructed by the MAE. For augmentation, the alignment loss targets the original sequence; for prediction, it targets the future sequence. The substantial Recall and F1-score improvements after VEGA augmentation (Fig. 4) confirm that sensitivity to positive samples is preserved without distorting pathological waveforms. Predictive generation visualizations (Fig. 5) further verify that VEGA faithfully reconstructs key waveform morphologies under varying conditions.
3.Diversity issue (R2[4])
Regarding generation diversity, we provide both mechanistic explanations and visual evidence.
(1) Source of diversity: Diversity is inherent in our design. First, bilinear interpolation during 2D resizing introduces sub-patch shifts (hyper-parameter η). Second, the MAE’s stochastic masking naturally produces varying outputs from the same input, since different visible patch mosaics yield distinct completions.
(2) Latent space evidence (Fig. 3): Latent feature visualization shows that VEGA substantially broadens the training distribution toward the test set, directly evidencing the generation of diverse, subject-variant features that bridge the generalization gap.
4.Lack of comprehensive baselines (MR[1]/R1[1]/R2[3]/R2[1])
As clarified in Q1, VEGA is the first framework bridging visual priors and 1D ECG generation for cross-subject augmentation. It adopts a cross-modal paradigm of visual pre-training and fine-tuning on a small external ECG dataset. In contrast, diffusion models and normalizing flows typically require large amounts of data; fine-tuned on the same limited data as VEGA, they would suffer mode collapse, produce nearly pure noise, and cause a sharp performance drop. To demonstrate VEGA’s few-shot generative capability, we employ conditional generation (i.e., predictive generation), which effectively alleviates the mode collapse problem prevalent in diffusion and other mainstream methods. As Table 2 shows, VEGA achieves better generative performance with far fewer training samples than other 1D generative methods. In the revised version, we will rigorously add more baseline comparisons under fair experimental settings to validate the advantages of the proposed method.

title: VesselSim: learning 3D blood vessel segmentation without expert annotations
abstract: Blood vessel segmentation is a core task in medical image analysis for the care of vascular diseases and surgical planning, yet the challenges of providing expert vascular annotations pose a major obstacle for the progress of related deep learning techniques. To address this, we propose \texttt{VesselSim}, a two-stage framework for universal 3D blood vessel segmentation that eliminates the need for real annotated data during training. First, we introduce a stochastic, geometry-driven vascular simulation framework that models recursive branching, curvature-controlled growth, and collision-aware topology, followed by domain-randomized intensity synthesis to generate 16,500 anatomically plausible 3D angiographic volumes. Second, a 3D U-Net is trained solely on this synthetic data. To bridge the domain gap from synthetic to real images at inference time, we introduce a test-time adaptation strategy via a self-supervised mask reconstruction decoder, enabling adaptation to unseen clinical scans without prior domain knowledge. We evaluate \texttt{VesselSim} in a zero-shot setting on multiple real-world datasets spanning MR and CT across several anatomical regions, including the brain and kidneys. Despite being trained exclusively on synthetic data, \texttt{VesselSim} achieves performance competitive with state-of-the-art vascular segmentation foundation models. These findings suggest that learning vessel geometry from synthetic tubular structures is effective for robust cross-domain generalization, substantially reducing the reliance on acquired medical imaging data and more importantly, expert annotations.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of the paper is the proposal of VesselSim, a 3D blood vessel segmentation framework based on synthetic-only training plus annotation-free test-time adaptation. The method first introduces a vascular simulation pipeline that combines recursive branching, curvature-controlled random walks, collision-aware topology, and physiologically motivated radius decay to generate vessel geometries with varied tortuosity and scale. These masks are then converted into angiography-like volumes through domain randomization. A 3D U-Net is trained entirely on this synthetic data, with cbDice added to encourage tubular continuity and topology preservation. At inference time, the model is further adapted to unseen real scans through a self-supervised mask reconstruction objective, updating only the encoder’s instance-normalization parameters. The key message of the paper is that strong geometry-driven priors, combined with test-time adaptation, can substantially reduce or even remove the need for real expert annotations in 3D vascular segmentation while remaining competitive with recent foundation models.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper has three main strengths. First, it addresses an important practical problem: the high cost of vessel annotation. Second, the framework is coherent, with synthetic geometry, domain randomization, cbDice, and TTA fitting together well. Third, the results are notable: despite synthetic-only training, the method clearly outperforms VesselFM on TopCoW MRA and is also competitive on clDice for TopCoW CTA and HiP-CT, suggesting strong topology preservation.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat integrative rather than fundamentally new. The synthetic vessel generation clearly builds on prior lines of work such as VascuSynth (Hamarneh & Jassi, 2010), stochastic L-system-based 3D vessel synthesis (Galarreta Valverde et al. , 2013), and more recent vessel generation models such as VesselVAE, VesselGPT, and VesselDiffusion. The current simulator appears to extend prior rule-based generation with curvature-controlled random walks, collision checking, and QC heuristics, but the paper does not directly quantify how much these additions matter compared with existing simulators. Likewise, the reconstruction-based TTA is close in spirit to prior self-supervised or reconstruction-driven test-time adaptation methods such as Context Encoders, Rec-TTT, and TopoTTA. Overall, the contribution feels more like a strong systems paper than a clearly novel methodological leap.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper addresses an important and practical problem, 3D blood vessel segmentation without expert annotations, and presents a technically coherent solution. The proposed framework combines a geometry-driven synthetic vessel generator with annotation-free test-time adaptation, which is a meaningful direction for reducing dependence on costly real vascular labels. What mainly pushed the paper above the acceptance threshold for me is the empirical evidence: as shown in Table 1 (page 6), VesselSim, despite being trained only on synthetic data, achieves the best clDice on all three benchmarks and is especially strong on TopCoW MRA (71.8 Dice / 76.2 clDice). The comparison is particularly compelling because the paper states that VesselFM was pretrained on TopCoW and HiP-CT, whereas VesselSim uses no real annotated training data. I also found the ablation study reasonably supportive of the paper’s claims, showing that cbDice improves structural/topological consistency while the reconstruction branch and TTA improve cross-domain robustness. I do have reservations—mainly that the individual components are somewhat incremental and that the TTA protocol could be described more clearly, but overall I believe the practical significance, strong synthetic-only results, and solid experimental validation make this paper marginally above the acceptance threshold.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose a multi-stage framework, VesselSim to enable robust, zero-shot blood vessel segmentation on 3D medical image data. Particularly, VesselSim builds on a Unet architecture trained purely on multi-scale, synthetically generated 3D angiographic data and augmented with test-time adaptation of segmentations. Synthetic generation is based on an extended stochastic braching framework aimed at generating high-tortuosity samples. The full synthetic training dataset comprises from synthetic images from previously published framworks, augmented with the authors’ high-tortuosity samples. A classical composite training objective is extended with an auxiliary mask reconstruction loss through in-painting random vessel segments. The reconstruction decoder is also utilized to update instance normalization layers of the encoder in a single test-time adaptation epoch. Compared to vessel-foundation models (vesselFM, SAM-Med3D, UniverSeg), VesselSim shows superior Dice and superior center-line Dice performance on two and three out of three real vascular datasets (HiP-CT, TopCow-CTA/MRA, respectively.
reviews.text_strengths:
Accessibility: synthetic-only training enables valuable zero-shot segmentations that can highly boost efficiency of clinical research in neurovascular disease. Even if used as initial annotation to be refined, this can save significant time in the model prototyping process, enable teaching and involving of junior clinical raters and ultimately lead to more precise annotations and models.
Focus on real clinical challenge: Vessel tortuosity is a highly relevant clinical challenge in blood vessel assessment. The natural variation of human vasuclature and specifically the complex shapes and curvature of vessels make not only interpretation but intervention (e.g. intra-arterial thrombectomy) challenging and in many cases potentially harmful. Thus, extending research, datasets and models that better depict tortuosity of vessels is of high clinical relevance.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Limited methodological novelty: While the authors present a unique combination of approaches, synthesis methodology is largely based on published literature [13]. Most importantly in my opinion, only half of the used synthetic vessel data is generated with the proposed method (i.e. high-tortousity vessels), thus results might show general benefit of the stochastic branching framework (i.e. solely application of it and no extension), regardless of the proposed extension. On the other hand, test-time adaptation does count as a novel contribution.
Limited demonstration of performance: While the included datasets are important benchmarks, they are limited in anatomical representation. TopCoW-CTA and TopCoW-MRA essentially comprise of paired imaging of the same subject/anatomy, thus from a structural vessel heterogeneity perspective, does not necessarily count as two distinct datasets. On the other hand, kidney blood vessels are naturally less tortuous (as the authors’ figures also show), thus further blood vessel segmentation datasets (e.g. ) should be included to reliably support the presented conclusions.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Could the authors clarify if the ablation presents cummulative methodology?
Does “Base Unet + recon” also include “cbDice”? Does “+recon” also imply TTA?
This is an important detail to justify the interpretation of performance improvement yielding from these methods alone or via their combination
Did the authors test training a low-tortuosity-only baseline within your framework?
Since high-tortuosity synthetic vessels only take up half of the training data (apart from skull and background samples) the authors cannot surely claim that the improvement on top of vessel-foundation models originates exclusively from their proposed approach of extending the referenced and used stochastic branching framework.
The following result mentioned in the Discussion cannot be found in the current Results, to the best of my knowledge:
“Notably, with the additional skull simulation, the mean Dice score was improved from 0.61 to 0.72 before TTA
for the TopCow MRA dataset”
If the authors have conducted experiments with and without skull simulation, it would be valuable to include in the presentation of Results for the relevant datasets (TopCow).

The authors present an important direction of research, however the work as is has multiple limitations that might prevent justification of the authors’ conclusions. Part of the stated novel contribution (i.e. high-tortuosity vessel generation) is applied in parallel to existing generation methodology and not tested in isolation, thus reliability of the seen performance improvements might be questionable.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
VesselSim proposes a two-stage annotation-free methodological framework for 3D blood vessel segmentation. Firstly it used a process of stochastic branching simulation that generates 16,500 anatomically similar vascular patches spanning both low- and high-tortuosity morphologies, incorporating physiologically informed parameters (Murray’s law for radius scaling, breadth-first growth, collision avoidance). Secondly, it trains a 3D U-Net exclusively on this synthetic data using a composite loss that includes a centerline boundary Dice term, augmented by a self-supervised mask reconstruction auxiliary task designed to enable test-time adaptation (TTA) to unseen real clinical scans.
The framework is then evaluated zero-shot across three real-world datasets covering brain (CTA, MRA) and kidney (HiP-CT) vasculature and compared against vascular and general foundation models.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Zero-shot generalization without any real annotations
Variability of geometry driven synthetic pretraining is supported with competitive performance across foundational models(FM) . VesselSim matches or is similar to FM despite training only on synthetic data and across three datasets (TopCoW CTA and HiP-CT)
2.Vascular simulation framework: Paper extends prior rule-based methods by incorporating curvature-controlled biased random walks, Murray’s law radius scaling, collision avoidance, and a quality control pipeline.
3.Lightweight and targeted test-time adaptation: Paper presents restricting TTA updates to instance normalization parameters with empirical validation. 
4.Well-structured ablation study and evaluation across diverse imaging modalities and anatomical regions.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The paper acknowledges that both TopCoW and HiP-CT are included in VesselFM’s training corpus, which confers a potentially large advantage to that baseline. A more detailed discussion of this asymmetry in the results section would be benefited.
2.Given the high variance (e.g., HiP-CT VesselSim: 31.6 ± 21.5 Dice), differences between methods may not be statistically significant.
3.Major vessels (carotid arteries, vertebral arteries, main renal arteries) are clinically important and their omission may limit applicability in certain downstream tasks
4.The abstract and introduction consistently spell the method name as “VessselSim” (three s’s) in the Conclusion section, while the rest of the paper uses “VesselSim.” This should be corrected.
5.Unreadably small parameter legend in Figure 1 and the absence of SAM-Med3D from the qualitative comparison.
6.Include at least one figure showing example synthetic vascular patches alongside their corresponding real-domain counterparts to visually ground the domain gap discussion.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Improvement of images with increase font size and separate images for more resolution and clarity.

VesselSim designed synthetic data generation framework, combined with a lightweight TTA strategy, can match specialized vascular foundation models trained on large real-data which makes it well- above thresholds of acceptance but also presents with modifiable areas namely asymmetric comparison with overlapping training data, lack of clarity with TTA setup and high variance which prevents clinical adoption.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

meta_reviews.text: All three reviewers independently scored your paper a “Weak Accept,” recognizing the practical significance and clinical relevance of your work. The consensus is that VesselSim provides a highly compelling framework. Achieving zero-shot performance that matches or even exceeds foundation models (like VesselFM), especially considering that VesselFM had the asymmetrical advantage of being pretrained on the evaluation datasets, is a notable accomplishment for the community. The reviewers also praised your integration of physiologically informed synthetic generation (e.g., Murray’s law, collision avoidance) to model challenging, high-tortuosity vessels. However, the reviewers have raised several important points regarding clarity, methodological details, and presentation. You are suggested to address the raised issues in your final version.

title: VigilSAM3: Reinforcement-Optimized Memory Gating for Ultra-Long Surgical Video Segmentation
abstract:
Laparoscopic hepatectomy demands real-time identification of critical vascular structures, including Glisson’s pedicle, hepatic veins, and transient bleeding points, to enable pre-emptive vessel clamping and prevent life-threatening haemorrhage. These targets are frequently obscured and deformable, and in ultra-long procedures spanning thousands of frames they further suffer extreme scale imbalance and intermittent visibility, making memory-based propagation prone to temporal drift where a single corrupted entry cascades forward irreversibly.
Memory-based propagation dominates long-range video segmentation, yet existing methods treat all predictions equally when updating the memory. 
Moreover, efficient intraoperative guidance demands minimal surgeon-model interaction, making autonomous quality control indispensable.
We present VigilSAM3, built on SAM3’s dual-system architecture, which introduces a hierarchical memory firewall that guards memory quality at pixel, class, and frame levels. A causal-Transformer scheduling agent selects among Trust, Correct, and Reset actions, with its policy refined via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using class-aware rewards.
We further introduce Hepa-Vein, the first multi-class large-scale hepatectomy surgical video semantic segmentation dataset. Experiments on Hepa-Vein and DSAD demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, with pronounced gains on small, transient vascular structures.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Reinforcement Learning / Control / Decision-Making

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents VigilSAM3, a reinforcement-learning-optimized framework for long-horizon surgical video segmentation, specifically targeting laparoscopic hepatectomy. The authors address the critical problem of “temporal drift” in ultra-long surgical videos by introducing a hierarchical Memory Firewall and a GRPO-based scheduling agent that dynamically chooses between Trust, Correct, and Reset actions. Furthermore, the paper introduces Hepa-Vein, a large-scale dataset with 21,734 annotated frames focused on critical vascular structures
reviews.text_strengths:
Technical Innovation: Using reinforcement learning (GRPO) to solve the sequential decision-making problem of “when to update memory” is a principled and effective approach to mitigating temporal drift. 
Clinical Relevance: The focus on small, transient structures like “Blood Points” (<0.1% of frame area) is highly relevant to surgical safety. 
Dataset Contribution: Hepa-Vein appears to be a high-quality, expertly annotated dataset that fills a gap in hepatectomy benchmarks. 
Strong Empirical Results: The model achieves state-of-the-art performance on both Hepa-Vein and DSAD datasets, particularly showing significant gains in challenging small-target classes.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Fairness of Baselines (Model Versioning): The proposed method is built upon SAM3, while many compared SOTA methods (e. g. , ReSurgSAM2, MedSAM2) are based on the older SAM2 architecture. It is unclear how much of the performance gain is attributed to the SAM3 backbone vs. the proposed RL-scheduling and Memory Firewall. 
Question: Can the authors provide results where the baseline models (like ReSurgSAM2) are implemented using the same SAM3 backbone for a fairer comparison?
Baseline Performance Discrepancy: In Table 1, the performance of MedSAM3 on “Blood Point” (39.32 Dice) is significantly lower than the proposed method (66.73 Dice). 
Question: Was MedSAM3 specifically fine-tuned for small-target detection on this dataset? Such a large gap suggests the baseline might not have been fully optimized.
Real-time Latency Peaks: While the average FPS (22.53) is reported , the system involves a heavy “System 2” detector for corrections. 
Question: What is the peak latency when the “Correct” or “Reset” actions are triggered? For real-time surgical guidance, the consistency of the frame rate is as important as the average speed.
There are minor typographical errors in some table labels (e. g. , “Glison” instead of “Glisson”)
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
no

VigilSAM3 is a technically sound paper with a clear clinical application and a strong new dataset. However, the lack of architectural parity in comparisons and the unaddressed latency peaks prevent a higher recommendation. I recommend a Weak Accept, pending the authors’ clarification of these points during the rebuttal.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: Long-range video segmentation usually depends on memory-based propagation methods like SAM2 and SAM3, but the memory can, over time, become corrupted through inaccurate predictions, causing drift in future frames. This paper proposes a way to tackle this drifting problem through memory gating, which observes the quality of predictions at the pixel, class, and entire frame levels before updating the memory. A scheduling agent based on a transformer continuously observes the quality of the memory and takes three different actions, and can even evict already stored memories from the tracker and reset if the quality worsens. The policy of the agent is refined through GRPO.
reviews.text_strengths:
The motivation of the paper is clear. It shows a strong attempt to solve the limitations of current video segmentation methods when applied to ultra-long videos, especially in the surgical context.
The paper is somewhat easy to follow, with good overall structure and organization.
All components of the method seem to complement each other and appear necessary, with clear and justified explanations for their inclusion.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Major: Overall lack of related work on long-term surgical segmentation methods. Also, no mention of other works that address memory drift and memory management in video segmentation.
Major: The evaluation is selective: the paper reports class-wise scores but omits an overall (full-image) metric. Furthermore, on the DSAD dataset, only 2 out of 8 classes are reported, raising concerns about fairness of the comparison.
Comparison methods were also not optimised for rare classes. E.g. nnunet can be trained with class-weighted CE for improved performance on rare classes
Needs clarification how video segmentation performance is being evaluated with datasets where annotation is not on complete video
The evaluated domain is very limited especially for general segmentation task. Need additional surgical domains (e.g., Cataract-1k, AutoLaparo, ,..)
How is temporal continuity handled during the reset action? It would be helpful to also report temporal continuity/smoothness metrics.

N/A

Weak accept. Even though the motivation and methodology of the paper are strong, the selective evaluation, specified in weakness, raises concerns
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposed the VigilSAM3 Framework which introduce a hierarchical memory mechanism to control the quality of memory in SAM3.VigilSAM3 uses a Reinforcement Learning-based method to decide the actions of the memory control. This paper also propose a dataset for laparoscopic hepatectomy which consist of 39 videos.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.This approach introduces excessive computational overhead by deploying expensive RL and detection modules to tackle visibility issues that classical methods solve more efficiently. For instance, kinematic priors provide a more elegant solution for occlusions, and the ByteTrack philosophy demonstrates that low-confidence detections still hold valuable temporal information. A more fundamental flaw lies in the handling of endoscopic camera ego-motion. Without Global Motion Compensation (GMC), treating corrected frames as persistent Anchored Memory creates a spatial mismatch as the lens moves, leading to catastrophic drift rather than stability.
2.The core of the “Hierarchical Memory Firewall” essentially reduces to standard residual fusion and MLP-based gating, offering limited novelty in spatiotemporal modeling. Given that recent medical imaging tasks have shown that Confidence-based Reset mechanisms can effectively mitigate memory drift in occluded scenarios, the complexity of the RL-based approach must be justified. A training-free baseline utilizing simple confidence-triggered resets is mandatory. This would prove that the GRPO agent’s performance stems from genuine causal reasoning over long sequences, rather than simply mimicking a static decision threshold. 
3.A critical concern in the proposed architecture is its over-reliance on the perceived authority of System 2.By designating System 2 outputs as persistent anchor, the authors overlook the reality that detectors frequently produce false positives in noisy endoscopic environments. This design creates a positive feedback loop of errors; a single misdetection becomes a permanent reference point, ensuring that the memory remains permanently polluted. Without a verification or aging mechanism for these anchors, the system’s long-term stability is fundamentally compromised.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The clinical motivation of this work is commendable, and the Hepa-Vein dataset constitutes a substantial contribution to the MICCAI community. However, as a methodology-focused paper, the core logic appears increasingly fragile under rigorous scrutiny.
I hope the authors can address these issues in the rebuttal:
1.Provide some training-free baseline using simple confidence-threshold resets to justify the indispensability of the RL agent. For examples, BoT-Sort, ByteTrack, and the other training-free methods like https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.19380.2.Explain or implement a Global Motion Compensation (GMC) mechanism to resolve the failure of static anchors caused by camera ego-motion.
3.Demonstrate that the Hierarchical Firewall and RL scheduling yield significant performance gains even when stripped of the parameter advantage of SAM3.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: In the rebuttal, the authors provided helpful textual clarifications, particularly regarding the low false-anchor rate, which partially alleviates my concerns about long-term error accumulation.

meta_reviews.text:
The reviewers generally found the paper clinically meaningful and technically promising, and all current recommendations are in the weak-accept range. At the same time, several important concerns were raised that should be addressed carefully in the rebuttal, as they may materially affect the final assessment.
First, the rebuttal should clarify the fairness of the experimental comparisons, especially the extent to which the reported gains come from the proposed memory-gating and scheduling design versus the use of a SAM3-based backbone while several competing methods are built on earlier SAM variants. In particular, the comparison to MedSAM3 and other strong baselines would benefit from clearer discussion of whether they were fully optimized under matched settings, especially for the rare and small Blood Point class.
Second, the necessity of the RL-based scheduling component should be more convincingly justified. One reviewer explicitly questioned whether simpler non-RL alternatives, such as confidence-threshold-based correction or reset rules, could already recover much of the benefit. A strong rebuttal should therefore clarify whether the gains of the GRPO agent go beyond what can be achieved by straightforward heuristic scheduling, and why the additional complexity is warranted.
Third, the evaluation protocol should be clarified and, if possible, strengthened. Concerns were raised regarding selective reporting, including the fact that only two classes are reported on DSAD and that no more global or overall metric is shown. The authors should explain the rationale for this reporting choice, clarify how evaluation is performed when annotations are not available for complete videos, and address whether the conclusions remain consistent under broader reporting.
Fourth, the real-time and deployment-oriented claims would benefit from a more detailed runtime analysis. Reporting only average FPS is likely insufficient when the method includes heavier Correct and Reset actions. It would help to clarify the latency associated with each action type, the frequency of these actions during inference, and whether occasional correction steps introduce problematic latency spikes.
In addition, the rebuttal should address the stability of the anchored-memory design. Reviewers raised concerns about whether treating “System 2” outputs as persistent anchors could create long-term error accumulation when the detector is wrong, and whether camera ego-motion may undermine the validity of persistent anchors in endoscopic videos. Even if these issues are already implicitly handled by the architecture, they should be explained more explicitly and convincingly.
Finally, the reviewers also noted some issues related to positioning and completeness, including limited discussion of prior work on memory drift and memory management in long surgical video segmentation, the need to clarify rare-class optimization in baselines, and several minor presentation issues.
Overall, the paper remains competitive, but the rebuttal should focus on demonstrating that the observed gains are genuinely attributable to the proposed method, that the RL component is necessary beyond simple heuristics, and that the evaluation and deployment claims are both fair and sufficiently substantiated.

The authors’ rebuttal includes excessive new experimental results, which is a direct violation of the rebuttal guidelines. As the guidelines state, such a violation should lead to rejection.
The responses addressed the main concerns about fairness issue of evaluation setting and baselines. Yet, new results on new dataset should not be added.

The reviewers generally consider the paper clinically meaningful and technically promising, and they also recognize the value of the dataset contribution. The rebuttal clarified several concerns regarding memory stability and parts of the evaluation protocol. Although there are some concerns are partially solve, considering the reviews and response the paper is slightly above the acceptance threshold.

author_feedback_text:
Thanks for kind advice.
R1
(1) To isolate the SAM3-backbone effect, we built a SAM3-backed ReSurgSAM2-style baseline by preserving credible initialization and diversity-driven memory selection on the official SAM3 detector/tracker. It obtains Dice/IoU 68.14/55.93, while VigilSAM3 obtains 69.18/57.22, suggesting the gain is not merely from SAM3.(2) MedSAM3 releases image-level SAM3 LoRA training but no video memory-propagation recipe. We adapted it with the same first-frame prompt/tracking protocol as our SFT stage, without MF or Correct/Reset. At shorter clip length, MedSAM3 reaches Blood Pt. Dice/IOU of 57.79/46.29.The remaining gap is because pure tracking cannot recover once tiny Blood Points are missed or written inaccurately into memory. In VigilSAM3, Correct/Reset invokes System 2 to generate dense logits S_t conditioned on the existing prompt and draft D_t; S_t refines output and memory. No manual prompt or GT mask is used at inference.
(3) On A800, forced Trust/Correct/Reset peaks at 36.3/154.9/143.5 ms. The latter two are sparse, so latency still controllable.
(4) We will correct “Glison” to “Glisson”.
R2
(1) We will expand related work: STCN/AOT establish memory-based VOS; XMem designs sensory/working/long-term memory; SAM2Long/DAM4SAM address SAM2 error accumulation, distractors, and memory selection; SurgSAM2/ReSurgSAM2 study surgical SAM2 via frame pruning, credible initialization, and diversity-driven memory. We position VigilSAM3 as complementary: it learns Trust/Correct/Reset and gates writes at pixel/class/frame levels.
(2) The two DSAD classes originally reported are vascular structures, matching Hepa-Vein’s goal; this was for vascular generalization rather than cherry-picking. We further evaluated 11 DSAD classes: mesenteric artery 74.65, intestinal veins 64.71, abdominal wall 84.21, colon 68.35, pancreas 41.53, spleen 68.99, stomach 82.58, small intestine 65.59, ureter 31.65, vesicular glands 45.74, liver 76.07, with overall Dice/IoU 63.14/52.68, which is competitive with SOTA methods.
(3) VigilSAM3 uses no class-weighted segmentation loss; rare-class handling comes from class-aware GRPO reward and per-class memory gating. U-Net/nnU-Net with class-weighted loss obtain Blood Point Dice/IoU 26.05/19.74 and 28.32/21.97.(4) Hepa-Vein is extracted from long raw videos, but all retained benchmark frames are densely annotated; every evaluated frame has a GT mask, with no unlabeled/interpolated/pseudo-labeled frames.
(5) For domain breadth, AutoLaparo gives Dice/IoU 87.26/80.91, close to LMS-Net (88/82), supporting generalization beyond hepatectomy and DSAD.
(6) For temporal continuity, VigilSAM3 outperforms ReSurgSAM2 on Contour Jitter↓/t-IoU↑: 11.13 vs. 14.47, and 71.65 vs. 65.96; Reset does not introduce discontinuity.
R3
(1) The agent is lightweight; main overhead is occasional System-2 invocation, whose latency is bounded. We thank the reviewer for GMC. By adding lightweight GMC variant in the dense-prompt path: for an anchor at frame a, its dense logits are warped to frame t using H_{a->t} before memory conditioning, without changing SAM3 detector/tracker. This improves Dice/IoU from 69.18/57.22 to 69.77/57.69.We will consider this direction for extension.
(2) Table 3 isolates SA, MF, and GRPO under the same SAM3 backbone. We added training-free Periodic Correct, Confidence Correct, and Confidence Reset baselines with the same SAM3 detector/tracker and prompt protocol. The best rule baseline is Confidence Reset, but is still 4.48/3.51 lower than VigilSAM3 in Dice/IoU, supporting that GRPO is not mimicking a static threshold and simple non-learning scheduling cannot replace the learned policy.
(3) To test false anchors, promoted anchors have mean Dice 92.79 and false-anchor rate 1.63% (Dice<0.3). After anchor promotion, t-IoU is 74.39 and Contour Jitter is 7.08, showing no persistent error feedback loop. We will clarify that Reset removes recent contaminated memory and re-initializes the current state.

title: VIHD: Visual Intervention-Based Hallucination Detection for Medical Visual Question Answering
abstract: While medical Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown promise in assisting diagnosis, they still frequently generate hallucinated responses that appear linguistically plausible but lack visual evidence. Such hallucinations pose risks to clinical decision-making and necessitate effective detection. Existing introspective detection methods primarily perform uncertainty estimation or logical verification by analyzing model responses conditioned on original or perturbed inputs. However, such external perturbations are often heuristic and context-agnostic, which overlooks the internal cross-modal dependency between generated tokens and related visual tokens during decoding. To address this issue, we propose VIHD, a Visual Intervention-based Hallucination Detection method that leverages targeted visual token masking to calibrate semantic entropy for more effective hallucination detection. VIHD locates visually dominant decoder layers via Visual Dependency Probing (VDP), executes Visual Intervention Decoding (VID) via token masking to calibrate the semantic distribution, and quantifies the resulting Calibrated Semantic Entropy (CSE) as a reliable hallucination signal. Extensive experiments on three medical VQA benchmarks with two medical MLLMs demonstrate that VIHD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, underscoring the importance of fine-grained visual dependency for hallucination detection. The code will be available at https://github.com/Jiayi-Chen-AU/VIHD
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents a training-free hallucination detection method for medical VQA called VIHD. The method first identifies decoder layers with strong visual dependency, then masks highly attended visual tokens during decoding to generate intervened responses, and finally fuses the original and intervened semantic distributions into a calibrated semantic entropy score for hallucination detection. The main contribution is therefore a targeted visual intervention framework for introspective hallucination detection, together with an adaptive entropy calibration scheme and empirical validation on three medical VQA benchmarks and two medical MLLMs.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Clear methodological novelty. The paper explicitly identifies visually dominant decoder layers, performs attention-guided token masking to produce intervened responses, and uses the resulting response shift to calibrate semantic entropy.
2.Strong empirical performance. The method consistently outperforms all compared baselines across three datasets, two backbones, and two metrics.
3.Useful ablation and analysis. The paper studies the contribution of each component (VDI, VID, CSE), compares different layer-selection and masking strategies, analyzes sliding-window width and masking ratio, and shows robustness under a different sampling strategy (Top-K).
4.Good fit to the medical MLLM setting. The motivation is clinically relevant: hallucinated but fluent answers are a real concern in medical VQA. The method is training-free and does not rely on external verifiers at inference time, which makes it attractive compared with heavier verification pipelines.
5.Generally clear presentation. The pipeline is easy to follow, Fig. 1 is helpful, and the equations map cleanly to the algorithmic components.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Detection requires repeated stochastic decoding (M=10 for normal responses and M=10 for intervened responses), semantic clustering with DeBERTa-Large-MNLI, and access to internal attention and visual tokens. This may limit practical deployment. A runtime or memory analysis is missing.
2.Novelty is meaningful but somewhat incremental relative to recent introspective/perturbation-based work. The paper is clearly related to prior semantic-uncertainty and intervention-style methods. The contribution is a well-designed refinement rather than a completely new paradigm, so the paper should position this distinction a bit more explicitly.
3.Some analyses are still missing. I would have liked to see statistical significance or variance over runs, dedicated close-ended results rather than only open-ended/all, qualitative examples of true positives/false positives, and failure-case analysis. These would help readers understand when the intervention signal is most reliable.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I lean toward weak accept because the paper addresses an important problem in medical MLLMs, proposes a technically sound and reasonably novel method, and demonstrates consistent improvements over strong baselines across multiple datasets and backbones. However, I do not rate it more highly because the novelty, while meaningful, is somewhat incremental relative to recent work, and the computational overhead of the detector is not analyzed.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes the VIHD framework, a novel method for hallucination detection in medical MLLMs. The approach introduces VDI to identify key layers with significant visual dependency, enabling partial visual token masking during the decoding process to perturb visual representations. Additionally, the authors propose calibrated semantic entropy to measure semantic dispersion between normal responses and visual-intervened responses. Comprehensive experiments on three distinct datasets and two medical MLLMs demonstrate the effectiveness of the VIHD method. Furthermore, detailed ablation studies validate the necessity and contribution of each key component in the framework.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper provides a clear and detailed introduction to existing hallucination detection methods, offering readers a comprehensive overview of the current landscape.
2.The proposed method is innovative, introducing VDI and VID to inject perturbations into key visual tokens of critical latent layers. Additionally, CSE effectively evaluates semantic dispersion, providing a reliable and robust indicator for hallucination detection.
3.The experimental evaluation is thorough. The main results demonstrate significant performance gains compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the detailed ablation studies and parameter sensitivity analyses reveal the stability and robustness of the VIHD framework.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Minor comment: 
1.The names VDI and VID are very similar, which may easily confuse readers. The authors might consider using more distinctive names for these designs to enhance readability.
2.The authors can consider reporting the time cost of the proposed method, as computational efficiency is an important factor in evaluating methods for hallucination detection.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This work addresses hallucination detection, a critical challenge in MLLMs. The authors present VIHD, a novel and effective approach that combines key visual token perturbation with semantic entropy computation for identifying hallucinations. The experimental results are robust and thoroughly validated. Therefore, I recommend accepting this paper.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes VIHD, a training-free, introspective pipeline for detecting hallucinations produced by medical multimodal LLMs in VQA. Rather than treating the MLLM as a black box and perturbing its inputs, VIHD reaches inside the decoder with three coupled stages. Visual Dependency Identification (VDI) aggregates cross-modal attention from generated tokens to visual tokens layer by layer and selects a sliding window of w consecutive layers whose cumulative visual attention is maximal. Visual Intervention Decoding (VID) then re-runs generation while masking the top-ρ highest-attention visual tokens inside those visually dominant layers, producing an “intervened” response. Finally, Calibrated Semantic Entropy (CSE) draws M normal and M intervened responses, clusters them into semantic equivalence classes with DeBERTa-MNLI, and fuses the two distributions either complementarily (when the cosine similarity ≥ τ) or contrastively (otherwise); the entropy of the fused distribution is the hallucination score. On VQA-RAD, SLAKE, and VQA-Med-2019 with Hulu-4B and Lingshu-7B, VIHD improves AUC over the strongest prior method (VASE) by 1.68–12.00 points.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The conceptual pitch is clear and genuinely distinct from existing introspective detectors: VASE and Semantic Entropy rely on heuristic input-level perturbations, whereas VIHD performs a targeted internal intervention on the very visual tokens the model is attending to, which is a cleaner operationalisation of “is the answer actually supported by visual evidence.”
2.The empirical study is broad— three benchmarks, two recent medical MLLMs, seven baselines, two metrics (AUC and AUG), and a sampling-strategy robustness check
reviews.text_weaknesses: The originality of the approach is weak. The central mechanism — masking high-attention visual tokens and contrasting the resulting distribution with the original — is close in spirit to Visual Contrastive Decoding (Leng et al., CVPR 2024 [14]) and Self-Introspective Decoding (Huo et al., ICLR 2024 [9]), both of which the paper cites but does not compare against as detection methods.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

VIHD proposes a clean, training-free internal-intervention pipeline (VDI + VID + CSE) that consistently outperforms seven strong baselines across three medical VQA datasets and two MLLMs with well-structured ablations, but its novelty is incremental over VASE / Semantic Entropy / Visual Contrastive Decoding and its key hyperparameters appear tuned on the test splits without a held-out validation set, placing it just above the acceptance bar — hence weak accept.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

meta_reviews.text: While the reviewers note some concerns regarding incremental novelty and computational overhead, there is a consistent positive consensus that the paper addresses a critical and timely problem in medical multimodal LLMs and proposes a technically sound, well-motivated, and practically useful solution.
