For the camera-ready version, the authors must: (1) incorporate the isolated ablation studies for the injection block and the loss design (BCE, Dice, Focal, and their combinations) to disentangle optimization gains from architectural gains, as requested by Reviewer #2; (2) add statistical significance analysis across multiple runs to confirm the robustness of the reported improvements; (3) explicitly discuss the efficiency trade-off (parameters, FLOPs, latency vs. accuracy) and justify when the added cost is clinically warranted; and (4) integrate all clarifications and analyses from the rebuttal into the main text.

author_feedback_text:
Thank the AC and reviewers.Our point-by-point responses follow.
1.Clarification of Novelty & Addressing Unsupported Claims (R1, R2, Meta)
Regarding the concern that our work is merely simple architectural assembly:
We clarify our work is far from trivial assembly.Our core innovations include three aspects: first,synergistic ConvNeXT-Mamba dual-encoder fusion,where Injection Block and bottleneck cross-attention enable inter-branch interaction, preventing heterogeneous feature misalignment; second,we devise a multi-scale enhanced decoder with our Multi-Scale VSS Block,addressing single-scale limitations and improving multi-scale anatomical segmentation;third, we adopt Focal Loss replacing cross-entropy,alleviating class imbalance and improving hard sample performance.
Regarding the core motivational claims in our introduction — including ViT Limitation and four inherent limitations of Mamba-UNet — lack sufficient literature support, we cite references to validate each claim explicitly:
a.ViT Limitation:TransUNet[Chen et al.,2021] shows patch-based embedding impairs localization and boundary accuracy.
b.Mamba Limitation:LocalMamba[Huang et al.,2024] indicates 2D-to-1D scanning weakens local detail modeling without CNN compensation.
c.Skip Connection Limitation:U-Net V2[Peng et al.,2024] verifies naive skip fusion introduces semantic noise, motivating CSAG design.
d.Loss Limitation:Focal Dice Loss-based V-Net[Prencipe et al.,2022] confirms standard losses perform poorly on hard samples,justifying our Dice+Focal Loss adoption.
2.Efficiency & Dual-Encoder Cost Justification (R1, R2, R3, Meta)
Regarding concerns on model efficiency and computational overhead of the dual-encoder design, we present computational metrics under the same test conditions(Batch Size 1,224×224 input,1×RTX5090,8-class segmentation):
Original Mamba-UNet: Params 35.86M | GFLOPs 9.12 | Latency 14.01ms
Our VM-NeXT UNet: Params 72.46M | GFLOPs 16.51 | Latency 21.76ms
Although parameters increase,GFLOPs remain competitive.21.76ms latency meets clinical real-time requirements(>30 FPS),and this slight tradeoff is worthwhile for a 3.23% DSC improvement from architectural optimization,excluding gains from loss function adjustment.
3.Targeted Ablations (R2, Meta)
Regarding the lack of ablation experiments for InjectionBlock and the rationality of loss function selection in ablation studies:
a.Injection Block:Isolated ablation results show that without it,the dual-encoder achieves DSC 83.24%,HD95 24.31mm;with it,DSC improves to 83.81% and HD95 decreases to 18.52mm,confirming no redundancy.
b.Loss Design:All intermediate ablations adopt Dice+CE Loss,with architecture alone boosting DSC from 82.38% to 85.61%.The final Dice+Focal Loss further improves performance to 86.21%.
4.Response to Inconsistency Between High-Resolution Claim and 224×224 Setup (R2, Meta)
Regarding the concern that Mamba’s high-resolution advantage conflicts with our 224×224 input setup:
We use 224×224 for fair comparison with TransUNet/SwinUNet.Mamba’s linear complexity supports high-resolution processing without OOM. VMamba [Liu et al.,2024] and VM-UNet [Ruan et al.,2024] confirm SSMs remain competitive at 224×224,with global receptive fields capturing long-range dependencies,validating our claim.
5.Baselines & Visualization (R1, R2, R3)
Regarding missing CNN baselines in our evaluation:
We have compared our method with CNNs(UNet),recent SOTAs(MERIT, ScaleFormer) and previous MICCAI networks(Reseg-UNet).
Regarding incomplete qualitative visuals and missing CNN visual comparisons:
Pure CNNs are well-established baselines,so we focus visuals on advanced models to highlight fusion advantages,while the CNN baseline is included quantitatively.Due to 6-page limit,we only present Synapse visuals;results on Synapse and ACDC verify cross-dataset robustness.
Regarding Synapse dataset configuration:
Adopting 8 anatomical categories on Synapse follows standard benchmarks;we will clarify the principle.

title: VOGeo-Gaze: Calibration-Free, Geometry-Aware Deep Learning for Real-Time Gaze Tracking in Clinical Video-Oculography
abstract: Quantitative eye movement analysis is important for neurological diagnostics, yet existing video-oculography (VOG) systems typically require calibration, device-specific settings, or accurate gaze labels. We present VOGeo-Gaze, a real-time, calibration-free, geometry-aware neural network that estimates gaze by reconstructing anatomically meaningful eyeball parameters from image features. Trained only on the public TEyeD dataset with weak gaze supervision, the method was evaluated on 116 clinical recordings from 17 patients and 19 healthy subjects using EyeSeeCam, a clinical gold-standard VOG system. VOGeo-Gaze achieved median absolute angular errors of 0.33° horizontally and 0.35° vertically, with nearly 92% of recordings below 1° error while operating at >300 FPS. These results demonstrate sub-degree clinical gaze estimation without subject-specific calibration, camera intrinsics, accurate gaze labels providing a scalable and interpretable alternative to conventional VOG pipelines. Code is available at https://github.com/DSGZ-MotionLab/VOGeo-Gaze
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
reviews.text_contribution: The novelty in this work lies in a novel method for estimating eye gaze from VOG video, without the requirement for patient-specific calibration or the provision of camera properties. This is achieved through an end-to-end model that minimises a custom loss function during training. The model learns eyeball parameters, corrects for refraction and provides temporal stabilisation. The estimation of refraction correction and temporal stabilisation are shown to be significant factors in the competitive level of accuracy obtained by the system.
reviews.text_strengths:
The approach developed achieves comparable results to the best-performing benchmark system (3DeepVOG), but without the requirement for patient calibration or the provision of additional parameters, such as camera properties. The level of accuracy ultimately obtained for gaze estimation is < 1 degree for horizontal and vertical gaze. 
The system developed is shown to be robust to adverse conditions, such as low-lighting. 
The work presents a novel approach involving the estimation of eyeball parameters rather than the estimation of gaze directly. 
The system is shown to be computationally efficient enough to allow for realtime processing of VOG data, which is an additional advantage over some poorer performing techniques and suggests that this system could have clinical applicability.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The approach is shown to work not quite as well as the best-performing system tested (3DeepVOG).
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents the methods developed very thoroughly and clearly, and the system developed is evaluated comprehensively. The system is shown to work very well and appears to overcome a severe limitation of conventional systems, i.e. patient-specific calibration. In my opinion, this work is novel, technically interesting, practically useful and it is well described and presented.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
reviews.text_contribution:
The authors propose VOGeo-Gaze, a calibration-free geometry-constrained framework. The contributions of this paper as far as I can tell:
1) awareness of corneal refraction, 
2) sub-degree clinical gaze, 
3) model based recovery of gaze
reviews.text_strengths: Well written paper with highly promising results.
reviews.text_weaknesses: I did not have any major issues with this paper.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
What is the advantage of a differentiable reformulation ?

Very good and convincing presentation
Good results comparable to gold standard
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This work reformulates VOG gaze estimation from angular regression to anatomical parameter reconstruction, enabling physically interpretable optimization via a differentiable refractive eye model.
reviews.text_strengths: Compared with existing methods, VOGeo-Gaze requires no calibration, no camera intrinsics, and no precise gaze labels, replacing direct angle regression with geometry-aware anatomical parameter reconstruction.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Quantitative and qualitative comparisons with state-of-the-art methods are insufficiently comprehensive. The current evaluation only includes a limited set of baselines on a single clinical dataset, lacking comparisons with recent calibration-free gaze estimation, geometry-aware eye modeling, and real-time VOG tracking approaches published in the past 2–3 years. Meanwhile, qualitative results only demonstrate one failure case of calibration-based methods, without systematic visualization on diverse clinical scenarios (e.g., occlusion, low-amplitude eye movement, headset misalignment), making it difficult to fully verify the robustness and generalization of the proposed method.
2.The justification of novelty and contribution lacks clear reasoning grounded in prior work and experimental evidence. The authors do not explicitly highlight the critical limitations of existing clinical VOG pipelines and learning-based gaze estimators. In addition, the connection between the experimental results and the claimed advantages (e.g., calibration-free, geometry-aware, interpretable) is not sufficiently elaborated.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This assessment is mainly based on prior studies, the method proposed in this work, and its experimental results.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
1.The paper presents VOGeo-Gaze, a calibration-free, geometry-aware neural network for gaze estimation in clinical video-oculography (VOG). The framework integrates a corneal refraction corrector (Fref), a prior gaze estimator (Fdir), and a temporal stabilization module (Ftem). 
2.The core idea is to shift optimization from angular gaze space to anatomical parameter space: instead of directly regressing gaze angles (θH, θV), the model reconstructs latent eyeball parameters (eyeball center ceye, optic axis n, pupil radius r_pup) via a differentiable, refraction-aware reformulation of the two-sphere eye model.
3.Supervision relies on segmentation labels and weak directional constraints derived from the TEyeD dataset, requiring neither subject-specific calibration, camera intrinsics, nor accurate gaze annotations. 
4.Clinical evaluation on 116 EyeSeeCam recordings from 17 patients and 19 healthy subjects reports 0.33°/0.35° median absolute angular error, with >91% of recordings below 1° error, at real-time throughput (>300 FPS).
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Novel paradigm with physically grounded design: By explicitly modeling corneal refraction in a differentiable manner, VOGeo-Gaze addresses a known limitation of prior geometry-free and refraction-neglecting methods. The three-contribution structure is clearly articulated.
2.Clinically meaningful and rigorous evaluation: The evaluation is conducted on real EyeSeeCam recordings spanning multiple oculomotor protocols across both patient and healthy subject populations. The use of median MAE with interquartile ranges, together with the <1° threshold percentage, provides a clinically interpretable performance characterization. The Wilcoxon paired test for geometric consistency adds statistical rigor.
3.Comprehensive ablation study: Table 4 systematically isolates the contribution of each module. The large performance gap when removing Fref provides strong evidence that explicit refraction modeling is the critical driver of accuracy.
4.Efficiency and real-time capability: At 2.3M parameters and 9.2 GFLOPs per forward pass, VOGeo-Gaze is computationally competitive with 3DeepVOG while achieving >300 FPS. This is practically relevant for clinical deployment.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Fixed anatomical priors may limit clinical generalizability: The method relies on population-average anatomical constants. In a neuro-otology clinic, patients may present with conditions affecting ocular anatomy. The authors do not analyze sensitivity to anatomical prior mismatch or report per-pathology performance.
2.Missing relevant baselines: The paper cites De²Gaze and CVL but only includes CVL in Table 3 and does not include De²Gaze in the comparison. De²Gaze is a geometry-aware learning method and would represent a more directly comparable Type B baseline. The authors should either include De²Gaze in the comparison or provide an explicit justification for its exclusion.
3.The “device-independent” claim is not experimentally validated: The abstract and introduction claim device independence, but the model is trained on TEyeD and evaluated exclusively on EyeSeeCam. No cross-device experiment is presented.
4.Architecture description and Figure 2 readability: The architectural overview is extremely dense and contains overlapping notation (e.g., Epup, Ê_pup, E^pup_R, E^pup_PD appearing in close proximity with subtly different superscripts). A cleaner schematic and more self-contained method description would significantly improve readability and reproducibility.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

VOGeo-Gaze addresses a genuine clinical need, such as calibration-free, interpretable gaze estimation, with a technically sound and well-evaluated approach. The core idea of anatomical parameter space reconstruction with explicit corneal refraction is novel and the clinical results are compelling.
The main factors preventing a stronger recommendation are: (1) the missing De²Gaze baseline; and (2) the device-independence claim lacking empirical support.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper provides an eye gaze tracking algorithm that exploits geometric constraints grounded on eye anatomy to improve accuracy without relying on camera calibration. The method’s purpose is to assist in video oculography measurements. The method is tested on an in-house dataset, showing the proposed algorithm achieves similar accuracy to prior work, with the advantage of not requiring calibration.
The paper received a consensus of “accept/weak accept” reviews. There is broad agreement on the novelty of the approach and that the reported results are meaningful and relevant.
Some reviewers would like to see the method compared against more baselines, although it is recognised that utilised baseline 3DeepVOG is also recognised as good representative of the state-of-the-art. I believe that the current experiments are justifiable in the context of the short MICCAI format and provide enough evidence that this is a strong enough paper for MICCAI.

title: VolDiT: Controllable Volumetric Medical Image Synthesis with Diffusion Transformers
abstract: Diffusion models have become a leading approach for high-fidelity medical image synthesis. However, most existing methods for 3D medical image generation rely on convolutional U-Net backbones within latent diffusion frameworks. While effective, these architectures impose strong locality biases and limited receptive fields, which may constrain scalability, global context integration, and flexible conditioning. In this work, we introduce VolDiT, the first purely transformer-based 3D Diffusion Transformer for volumetric medical image synthesis. Our approach extends diffusion transformers to native 3D data via volumetric patch embeddings and global self-attention that operates directly over 3D tokens. To enable structured control, we propose a timestep-gated control adapter that maps segmentation masks to learnable control tokens, which modulate transformer layers during denoising. This token-level conditioning mechanism allows precise spatial guidance while preserving the modeling advantages of transformer architectures. We evaluate our model on high-resolution 3D medical image synthesis tasks and compare it to state-of-the-art 3D latent diffusion models based on U-Nets. Results demonstrate improved global coherence, superior generative fidelity, and enhanced controllability. Our findings suggest that fully transformer-based diffusion models provide a flexible foundation for volumetric medical image synthesis. The code and models trained on public data are available at https://github.com/Cardio-AI/voldit.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
1) Fully Transformer-Based 3D Diffusion Model 
Proposes VolDiT, the first purely transformer-based architecture for 3D medical image synthesis, replacing conventional U-Net backbones.
2) 3D Tokenization for Volumetric Data 
Introduces 3D patch embedding to convert volumetric latents into tokens, enabling global self-attention across entire volumes.
3) Timestep-Gated Control Adapter (TGCA) 
Develops a conditioning mechanism that injects segmentation-based control tokens with adaptive timestep-dependent gating for stable and precise generation.
4) Improved Controllability and Anatomical Alignment 
Achieves better spatial control and anatomical consistency compared to existing diffusion-based methods.
5) Comprehensive Experimental Validation 
Shows superior performance on LUNA16 and TaviCT datasets in terms of fidelity, diversity, and conditional accuracy.
6) Establishes Transformers for 3D Medical Generation 
Shows that global attention-based models scale effectively to volumetric medical data, providing a foundation for future research.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) Strong Novelty 
Introduces the first fully transformer-based 3D diffusion model for medical image synthesis, removing convolutional locality bias.
2) Effective Global Modeling 
Uses global self-attention over 3D tokens, improving anatomical consistency and long-range dependencies.
3) Novel Conditioning Mechanism (TGCA) 
Proposes timestep-gated control tokens for adaptive and stable conditioning, enabling precise spatial control.
4) Improved Controllability 
Achieves better segmentation-aligned generation with improved Dice and boundary accuracy.
5) Comprehensive Evaluation 
Extensive experiments on multiple datasets with fidelity, diversity, and conditional metrics, including strong baselines.
6) Fair and Rigorous Comparisons 
Uses consistent training settings and includes ablations (model size, patch size, gating).
7) Scalable and Forward-Looking Design 
Transformer-based framework is extensible to multimodal and higher-dimensional settings.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1) Limited Novelty 
Primarily extends existing Diffusion Transformers to 3D; conceptual innovation is incremental.
2) Dependence on Latent Diffusion 
Relies on VQ-GAN latent space, similar to prior LDM-based approaches.
3) Small-Scale Evaluation 
Experiments are limited to relatively small datasets (LUNA16, TaviCT), raising generalization concerns.
4) No Clinical Validation 
Lacks expert evaluation or demonstration in real clinical workflows.
5) Evaluation Limitations 
Uses FID and generic feature extractors, which may not fully reflect medical image quality.
6) Limited Baseline Comparisons 
Does not compare against more recent large-scale or foundation-model-based methods.
7) Missing Efficiency Analysis 
No detailed discussion of computational cost or scalability of 3D transformers.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1) Strong work overall: Novel transformer-based design with effective conditioning and solid results.
2) Clarify novelty: Better position against recent transformer/diffusion methods in medical imaging.
3) Stronger comparisons: Include more recent state-of-the-art or foundation-model baselines.
4) Evaluation improvement: Consider more medical-specific metrics beyond FID.
5) Efficiency discussion: Add analysis of computational cost and scalability.
6) Clinical relevance: Briefly discuss or demonstrate downstream utility.

The paper presents a solid methodological contribution by introducing a fully transformer-based diffusion model for 3D medical image synthesis. The proposed architecture is well-motivated, and the use of global self-attention for volumetric data is both timely and relevant. In particular, the timestep-gated control adapter is a meaningful addition that enables improved controllability in conditional generation settings. The experimental results are generally strong, showing consistent improvements in fidelity, diversity, and segmentation-aligned synthesis across multiple datasets.
The score is moderated by several limitations. The novelty is somewhat incremental, as the work primarily extends existing Diffusion Transformer frameworks to 3D medical imaging. Additionally, the evaluation, while comprehensive in terms of metrics, relies heavily on generic measures and lacks more domain-specific or clinically meaningful validation. The comparisons are also somewhat limited, as more recent large-scale or foundation-model-based approaches are not included. Furthermore, the paper does not sufficiently discuss computational cost and scalability, which are important considerations for transformer-based models in 3D settings.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes CardioDiT, a unified 4D latent diffusion transformer framework for cine CMR synthesis. Unlike previous works that factorize space and time (2D+t), CardioDiT treats the 3D+t volume as a single 4D tensor. It utilizes 4D positional encodings and a spatiotemporal VQ-VAE to model global spatiotemporal dependencies, ensuring inter-slice consistency and physiologically plausible cardiac motion.
reviews.text_strengths:
Unified 4D Modeling: The move away from architectural factorization (e.g., temporal modules) towards a “native” 4D Transformer is a significant methodological step forward.
Consistency Metrics: The introduction of d-SSIM and AR_{ED} provides a rigorous way to measure through-plane anatomical alignment, which is often neglected in synthesis papers.
Physiological Fidelity: Validating the model via Ejection Fraction (EF) distributions and W2 distance shows a deep understanding of the clinical requirements of cardiac imaging.
Scalability Analysis: The study of model size (S, B, L) and the use of FlashAttention demonstrates the framework’s readiness for large-scale training.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Standardization via Cyclic Repetition: Standardizing sequences to 32 frames via repetition may introduce artificial periodicity. The authors mention this as a limitation, but it does weaken the claim of “truly continuous” dynamics slightly.
Dataset Size for Evaluation: While the FID and Precision/Recall are reported, they are calculated on only N=50 synthetic samples. This is a very small sample size for stable FID estimation (standard is usually 2k-50k), which might lead to high variance in reported scores.
Temporal Resolution: The model uses a patch size of p_t =2 in the temporal dimension. Discussing how this affects the capture of rapid valve movements or early diastolic filling would be valuable.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

CardioDiT represents the state-of-the-art in 4D medical image synthesis, demonstrating a clear path toward “foundation models” for dynamic medical imaging.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) framework for 3D medical image synthesis with volumetric semantic mask conditioning. A VQ-GAN compresses input volumes into latents with an 8× downsampling factor per spatial dimension. A two-stage training strategy is adopted: (i) unconditional DiT training using cosine noise scheduling and smooth L1 loss, and (ii) conditional training where the frozen DiT backbone is guided by segmentation-derived control tokens encoded via a 3D CNN. The method aims to address spatial inconsistency issues observed in 3D latent diffusion models (LDMs).
reviews.text_strengths:
Introduces a transformer-based denoising architecture for volumetric diffusion, moving beyond 3D U-Net–based LDMs.
Clearly motivates the spatial inconsistency limitations of 3D LDMs and demonstrates that mask-conditioned DiTs can partially mitigate these issues.
The two-stage training strategy is well-aligned with large-scale diffusion model design principles and allows effective conditioning without retraining the full backbone.
Patch-based tokenization with 3D sine–cosine positional embeddings is a reasonable and scalable design choice for volumetric data.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Inconsistent dataset splits are used across evaluations (90/5/5 for Lung CT vs. 60/20/20 for the in-house dataset) without justification, which affects comparability and reproducibility.
The evaluation protocol lacks consistency: 
o TaviCT uses an ImageNet-pretrained 2.5D feature extractor,
o LUNA16 uses MedicalNet-pretrained 3D ResNet-50.This results in FID scores differing by orders of magnitude (≈0.005 vs. ≈3.1), making cross-dataset interpretation difficult.
Comparisons are limited to 3D LDM baselines. Other relevant 3D diffusion approaches (e.g., wavelet-based or hierarchical CNN diffusion models) are missing.
Implementation and system details are insufficient, particularly for a transformer-based volumetric model: 
o No discussion of hardware, memory consumption, batch sizes, or inference-time constraints.
o This is critical given the reported resolutions (e.g., 512×512×256 → 128×128×64 latent volumes).
Qualitative analysis is limited: 
o Figure 3 uses lower-resolution TaviCT volumes (192³) without including corresponding ground-truth images.
o It is unclear whether similar inconsistencies persist at higher resolutions such as Lung CT (512×512×256).
Tables and figures do not clearly distinguish conditional vs. unconditional generation results, reducing clarity.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a promising and relevant direction for 3D medical image synthesis using Diffusion Transformers with semantic mask control. However, evaluation inconsistencies, missing baselines, and limited reproducibility details substantially weaken the empirical claims. Addressing these issues—particularly by unifying evaluation metrics, adding stronger 3D baselines, and clarifying computational constraints—would significantly strengthen the submission.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

meta_reviews.text: This paper was reviewed by three experts in the field. Based on the reviewers’ feedback, the paper is recommended for provisional acceptance. While the reviewers agree on the contribution of the proposed framework and the promising experimental results, they also raised several valuable concerns that should be addressed in the final camera-ready version, including insufficient implementation details and a lack of efficiency analysis. The authors are encouraged to address these issues to the best of their ability.

title: Volume-Fused Super-Resolution OCT Reveals Cellular-Level Structures in the Outer Segment Across Wider Fields Without Adaptive Optics
abstract: Due to its historic limitations in imaging speed, for a long time, ophthalmic Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) image analysis focused on features such as retinal layer thickness or fluids, which are visible in 2D B-scans. Although OCT angiography raised interest in en face (C-scan) images to visualize vascular layers, analysis of structural en face features like nerve fibers or photoreceptors was limited by transverse resolution, shot noise, and eye motion creating non-uniform displacements and distortion in raster-scanned volume images. Imaging of these structures is limited to much more complex adaptive optics imaging devices, which place a major hurdle for clinical translation, and complicate imaging by requiring pupil dilation. In this contribution, we integrate computational methods for motion, distortion and illumination compensation of repeated OCT volumes with orthogonally alternating fast scan directions, resulting in a consistent 3D point cloud, and apply the first fully-automatic inverse model for reconstructing 3D (multi-frame) super-resolved ophthalmic OCT images with higher sample density and reduced blur. In particular, we visualize reflections from individual cones in the outer segment with visible-light OCT across a 3 x 3 mm^2 field. Our method is unique in its comprehensive description of confounders of the imaging process, unlocks a novel paradigm of widefield OCT acquisition, and significantly broadens access to features of high clinical interest.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The central contribution is a comprehensive, model-based 3D super-resolution pipeline for ophthalmic OCT that unifies motion, distortion, illumination, and artifact compensation into a single inverse-problem framework. By formulating the image formation process explicitly and inverting it through non-iterative fusion followed by iterative deblurring with Tikhonov regularization, the method achieves cellular-level imaging of photoreceptor cone reflections in the outer segment over a widefield, without requiring adaptive optics hardware or pupil dilation. This broadens access to clinically relevant retinal microstructures that were previously observable only with significantly more complex and expensive AO systems.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The imaging model in Eq. (1) is notably comprehensive: it jointly accounts for non-uniform motion (via spatiotemporal displacement parameterization), illumination bias (via per-A-scan coefficients with foreground masking), optical distortion (shearing and curvature), and noise. This level of completeness is uncommon in prior OCT super-resolution work and is well motivated by the practical confounders in ophthalmic imaging. 
2.The method is purely computational and does not require hardware modifications, pupil dilation, or real-time eye tracking. This represents a significant practical advantage for clinical translation compared to AO-OCT, which demands expensive additional hardware and is restricted to small imaging fields. 
3.The reproducibility experiment in Figure 3, where the super-resolution pipeline is applied independently to two disjoint subsets of five volumes each, is a convincing and well-designed validation strategy. It demonstrates that the observed cone reflections are consistent across independent data splits rather than artifacts introduced by the reconstruction. 
4.The paper provides a clear and well-structured ablation across intermediate processing stages (single input, fused, supersampled, super-resolved) in Figure 2, which allows the reader to appreciate the incremental contribution of each component. The visual improvements in contrast, sharpness, and separability of cone reflections are substantial. 
5.The clinical relevance is clearly articulated: S-cones, which are the likely source of the observed reflections, are known to be more vulnerable in diseases such as retinitis pigmentosa, diabetes, and glaucoma, making them valuable as early biomarkers.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The evaluation is limited to eight healthy volunteers from a single imaging site using a single prototype device. No pathological data are included, which leaves unclear whether the pipeline generalizes to diseased retinas where tissue geometry, reflectivity, and motion patterns may differ substantially. Even a preliminary case or discussion of expected failure modes in pathology would strengthen the paper. 
2.The paper lacks quantitative evaluation metrics. All results are presented qualitatively through visual inspection of en face images and B-scans. No resolution measurements (e. g. , Fourier ring correlation, point source analysis), no quantitative comparison against AO-OCT references, and no SNR or contrast-to-noise ratio analysis are reported. This makes it difficult to objectively assess the magnitude of the improvement or compare with other methods. 
3.The choice of key hyperparameters, including the upsampling factor (3x), deconvolution sigma_tv = 2.9 um, regularizer weights lambda = 0.2 and gamma = 0.1, and step size delta = 0.12, appears to be fixed without justification or sensitivity analysis. The paper does not discuss how performance varies with these settings or how they should be adapted for different devices, wavelengths, or imaging fields.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

While the proposed pipeline is comprehensive in its modeling of imaging confounders and demonstrates visually compelling results, the lack of any quantitative evaluation metrics makes it difficult to objectively assess the claimed resolution improvement or compare with existing methods. In addition, the evaluation is restricted to eight healthy subjects from a single site with no sensitivity analysis on key hyperparameters, leaving the generalizability and robustness of the approach insufficiently demonstrated for a venue of this caliber.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose an approach to the reconstruction of super-resolution OCT scans using computational methods without the use of adaptive optics. The concept of replacing adaptive optics with computational aberration correction methods has been around for a long time. However, this work presents a more comprehensive approach by integrating all elements of the distortions (motion correction, distortions, and super-resolution) into a single mathematical model. This mathematical model contributes to the development of the super-resolution OCT field. Elaborating on all the details and components of this approach more thoroughly, and linking them to specific examples of algorithmic implementations, would make this a highly valuable contribution to the field.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper presents a comprehensive approach to the reconstruction of super-resolution images in OCT. The strength of this work lies in the fact that motion artifacts, aberration correction, and resolution enhancement are all addressed within unified mathematical procedures. The authors attempt to provide a comprehensive mathematical description of these procedures. I consider this part to be important, albeit highly abstract.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Major:
The authors claim: “This work describes a computational method for reconstructing higher resolution 3D images from repeated (non-AO) retinal OCT volumes by inverting a uniquely comprehensive imaging model.” and describe some sophisticated math in Section 2.However, there is a lack of clarity on how this actually works. My experience with numerical aberration correction using numerical wavefront reforming (e.g., with Zernike polynomial expansion) without adaptive optics demonstrates that achieving super-resolution requires numerical aberration correction with digital beam refocusing to a spot tighter than the initial probing beam. I know this is possible if one locks onto reference points on the retina, corrects the distortions for them to make them sharp structures, and then refocuses more narrowly than the initial beam width. However, the algorithm proposed by the authors is described in highly dense mathematical language, without revealing the physical principles behind such correction and refocusing processes. I would like to see a more detailed explanation in the paper connecting the math to the physical processes, clarifying how and through which operations on physical fields and wavefronts it is possible to compensate, correct, and refocus the beams to achieve super-resolution.
I have some doubts regarding reproducibility: there is no mention in the paper whether the data and code are either already hosted somewhere or will be released upon publication so that the community can verify their functionality as described. Most of the operations remain described too abstractly for me, and it is not obvious how they are actually implemented in the algorithms. Personally, I would prefer to recommend such a complex paper for publication only if the code implementation of this algorithm, along with the provided test data, is made openly available for verification, as I do not have full confidence in the reproducibility of these results.
Minor:
In the mathematical representations, for example in formula (3), the operations should clearly have the meaning of spatial spectrum filtering, represented explicitly as a convolution, or in the Fourier domain as operations on the spectrum. One way or another, distortions and aberrations that occur in OCT arise in k-space, and are usually corrected in this domain, either explicitly (Fourier domain) or in the spatial representation via convolutional functions. This physical meaning should be explicitly stated and described to improve the understanding of the presented algorithm.
I would extract the initial parameters of the OCT system and describe them in a separate Methods section. The Methods section currently starts immediately with the algorithm, although it would be great to indicate at the beginning what exactly this is being applied to. Perhaps it would be useful to clearly add this in your response in the rebuttal thread.
The following comment is also related to the description of the device and the process: the scanning pattern should be described and illustrated more clearly. It is currently not very clear how the information was acquired and accumulated. The point cloud panel in Fig. 1 does not look informative to me.
The citations are not in the correct numerical order based on their appearance in the text (e.g., they jump from 9 to 6, then 25, etc.). Please renumber them sequentially.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Lack of clarity. See comments in the list the major weaknesses of the paper. Major: The mathematical description of the processes, which fundamentally deal with physical distortions, is too abstract. There is a weak connection in the description to the underlying physics and aperture effects. I do not believe the super-resolution together with aberration correction are a purely algorithmic problem where physics can be ignored, especially considering that the proposed approach replaces adaptive optics with computational operations. 
Furthermore, there is no mention of whether the source code will be provided to clarify how this actually works explicitly in practice. 
Adding clearer descriptions to the some appendix will help me better understand the method during the rebuttal and allow me to raise my score from a “weak accept” to an “accept.”
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Although the topic could be explored from a physics perspective rather than solely a computer science one, the paper is interesting and merits acceptance. My remaining questions can be discussed with the authors in person at the conference or addressed in a future extended publication.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper presents a computational framework for reconstructing super-resolved 3D retinal OCT volumes from repeated non-adaptive optics scans by combining motion correction, distortion compensation, illumination normalization, and inverse-model-based reconstruction. Its main contribution is enabling visualization of outer segment cellular structures over wider fields without adaptive optics hardware.
reviews.text_strengths: 1.This paper achieves cellular-level OCT enhancement without adaptive optics, which improves clinical feasibility. The proposed pipeline is technically comprehensive and addresses multiple acquisition confounders in a unified framework. The qualitative results are also convincing, with clear improvements in sharpness and reproducibility shown in Figures 2 and 3.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Limited methodological novelty. Several major components in this paper are built directly on the prior work, especially motion correction, illumination compensation, and distortion modeling. 
2.The super-resolution stage mainly relies on a classical weighted least-squares formulation related to prior multi-frame super-resolution methods. 
3.Evaluation is mostly qualitative and limited to eight healthy-subject datasets.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
It would strengthen the paper to include quantitative metrics for evaluating the reported improvements in image quality and structural visibility.

The paper presents meaningful results with clear practical relevance. However, the methodological novelty should be stated more explicitly, and quantitative metrics should be added to better support the reported improvements.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The paper quality is good. Just two concerns, as I mentioned: 1.data, and 2.quantitative metrics. The authors mentioned the size limitation of not having quantitative metrics. This does not sound reasonable to me. But I still lean towards accepting.

meta_reviews.text:
The authors are expected to provide reasonable explanations for the quantitative analysis and hyperparameter selection to address the reviewers’ concerns. In addition, some reviewers raised concerns regarding the reproducibility of the proposed method.

After reading the rebuttal and other reviewers’ comments, I think the authors have provided reasonable clarifications to the reviewers’ concerns.

This paper proposes a computational 3D super-resolution OCT reconstruction framework for repeated non-adaptive-optics retinal OCT volumes, aiming to reveal cellular-level outer-segment structures over wider fields without adaptive optics hardware or pupil dilation.
The reviewers recognized the practical and clinical significance of the work, especially its unified model-based treatment of motion correction, distortion compensation, illumination normalization, and inverse reconstruction. They also appreciated the visually compelling improvement in cone-reflection visibility and the reproducibility experiment using independent data splits.
The reviewers raised concerns about the limited quantitative evaluation, small healthy-subject cohort, lack of pathological cases, hyperparameter justification, and reproducibility. In the rebuttal, the authors clarified the rationale behind key hyperparameters, discussed prior experience on a larger set of clinical OCT data, and explained that the current work focuses on computational super-resolution rather than digital aberration correction. Reviewers were satisfied overall, and all post-rebuttal recommendations support acceptance.
Although quantitative metrics and broader pathological validation would strengthen an extended version, the paper presents a meaningful and practically relevant framework with convincing qualitative evidence. Therefore, I recommend acceptance.

The paper presents a computational framework for reconstructing super-resolved 3D retinal OCT volumes from repeated non-AO scans, aiming to reveal cellular-level outer segment structures over wider fields without adaptive optics. Reviewers agreed that the problem is important and that the practical clinical motivation is strong, especially given the potential to broaden access to microstructural retinal imaging without additional hardware. The unified treatment of motion correction, distortion compensation, illumination normalization, and inverse-model-based reconstruction was also viewed positively.
Before rebuttal, the main concerns were the lack of quantitative evaluation, limited validation on only eight healthy subjects from a single site, and insufficient clarity on some methodological and physical aspects of the reconstruction process. The rebuttal addressed these points partially but meaningfully. In particular, the authors clarified the intended scope of the work, explained why paired AO-OCT ground truth and direct quantitative comparisons are not realistically available, provided additional justification for hyperparameter choices, and clarified that core preprocessing steps have already been applied more broadly in their larger clinical experience, even though the present study focuses on a limited vis-OCT dataset for the outer-segment cone application. They also clarified that the method does not rely on digital aberration correction, which helps sharpen the framing of the contribution.
The paper still has limitations. Quantitative evaluation remains limited, pathology cases are not included in the current study, and reproducibility would be stronger with public code or more implementation detail. Some of the claims would also benefit from a clearer distinction between what is already validated in the manuscript and what is supported mainly by broader prior experience.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their careful feedback and positive comments, including “significant practical advantage for clinical translation”, “visual improvements in contrast, sharpness, and separability of cone reflections are substantial”, “a convincing and well-designed evaluation” (Fig. 3, qualitative), “clear and well-structured ablation”, “The clinical relevance is clearly articulated”, “cone reflections are consistent across independent data splits”, “well motivated by the practical confounders”.
(Quotes from Reviewer #1.)
Subsequently, we focus on major critique, and Reviewer #1, because he provided the worst rating (weak reject).
Qualitative Evaluation [Meta,R1,R3]
We agree that an extended journal article should include quantitative evaluation. Here, due to the page limit, we prioritized the in our view most tangible and convincing evaluation
Our qualitative evaluation (Fig. 3) provides an immediate and intuitive impression of the improvement, and demonstrates its consistency in independent data splits. Multiple instances of each individual improvement (gaps/doubling, cone undistortion, contrast/separability of cone reflections) can be pointed out in a single, small crop.
Quantitative evaluation would mix these effects into a single abstract number. It is often chosen to prove subtle/non-obvious improvements, and to compare to prior methods. However, our improvement is visually “substantial”, and since this is a fundamentally novel approach, no directly comparable method exists.
The mentioned AO-OCT ground truth only exists in a handful places on earth; we do not have access to paired data. An unpaired comparison image is referenced on p. 7 [16, Fig. 5].
Hyperparameter selection [Meta,R1]
2D-upsampling-factor (3^2=9) should scale with volume repeats (10); sigma_tv was chosen as transverse resolution (9um) / 1D-upsampling-factor 3; regularizer weight controls denoising/blur and should be small; anisotropy factor gamma: small to not blur layers; step size: safe margin below divergence. Added.
Limitation to 8 datasets [R1,R3]
Core processing steps (motion, illumination, distortion compensation) have been applied to >1000 clinical high-resolution 850nm SD-OCT datasets across diverse pathologies, incl Parkinson’s disease (severe motion) and elderly patients (severe opacities/vignetting). Failure modes are opacities (low illumination) or strong mirror artifacts, if a large portion of the dataset is affected. However, such data is not usable for clinical quantification; compensation is meaningless. Only a handful of the >1000 cases failed due to motion. Added.
For our application (OS cones), we wanted to maximize resolution of the initial data, motivating our transition to vis-OCT despite limited data. We expect similar processing behavior in vis-OCT with somewhat increased illumination issues due to a higher sensitivity to opacity of shorter wavelength light.
Reproducibility [R3,Meta]
Our contribution is an extensive framework that unifies several prior works (motion, illumination & distortion compensation) and adds super-resolution processing. We carefully summarized key ideas of all prior work, but comprehensive reiteration is infeasible in an 8p paper (@R2: there is no appendix anymore); we have to refer to prior papers for implementation details.
Reproducibility concern on aberration correction (ACor) [R2]
Digital ACor methods use large beam diameters to increase SNR & allow very fast scanning. This scales up aberration effects substantially, but temporal closeness makes them locally consistent, allowing estimation & compensation.
Our novel approach: commercial beam diameter & scanning speed, SNR enhancement via averaging, digital super-resolution.
Challenges: motion, illumination, distortion.
We don’t describe ACor because it is less needed & we are not doing it.
Our key message: We achieve substantial improvement without it.
Finally, we revised the manuscript for clarity regarding all related comments

title: VoxShield: Protecting 3D Medical Datasets from Unauthorized Training via Frequency-Aware Inter-Slice Disruption
abstract: The release of public 3D medical image segmentation (MIS) datasets accelerates clinical research but simultaneously heightens risks of unauthorized AI model training. While Unlearnable Examples (UE) offer protection by injecting imperceptible perturbations to prevent effective model learning, existing methods primarily target 2D scenarios. They neglect the volumetric spatial correlations and inter-slice anatomical consistency inherent in 3D medical volumes, which serve as critical learning priors for 3D segmentation networks. To bridge this gap, we propose VoxShield, a UE framework that explicitly targets the volumetric inductive biases of 3D networks. Our core insight is that by systematically dismantling the cross-slice continuity that 3D architectures rely on, we can fundamentally impair their spatial aggregation process. Specifically, we introduce an Inter-Slice Frequency Consistency Disruption mechanism that maximizes the spectral divergence between adjacent slices, injecting structural incoherence along the z-axis.Complementing this structural attack, a Semantic Prediction Disruption module is incorporated. By maximizing the L1 divergence between clean and perturbed logits, it forces the injected noise to penetrate the entire network and corrupt the final semantic mapping. Experiments on BraTS19 and FLARE21 demonstrate that VoxShield successfully degrades 3D segmentation performance, reducing the DSC from 80.0% to near 0.0% and from 88.6% to 6.8%, respectively. All protections are achieved with minimal perturbation (epsilon = 4/255) while preserving high visual fidelity. The code is available at https://github.com/KK266299/VoxShield

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper introduces VoxShield, a novel framework for generating unlearnable examples (UE) specifically designed for 3D medical image segmentation, addressing a gap where prior UE methods only work well for 2D data. Its main contribution is that 3D segmentation models rely heavily on cross-slice (volumetric) consistency, and that disrupting this property can effectively prevent models from learning.
1.Inter-Slice Frequency Consistency Disruption perturbs adjacent slices to break their spectral continuity, undermining the spatial coherence that 3D models depend on. 
2.Semantic Prediction Disruption forces divergence between predictions on clean vs. perturbed data, ensuring the perturbation propagates through the network and corrupts semantic learning.
reviews.text_strengths:
a lot of baselines considered for evaluations, which are strong baselines.
the method is well motivated and easy to read and the equations are clear.
targets the problem of un-learnable examples for 3d data for which there is gaps in research.
anonymized code is shared which is much appreciated.
good ablation on the different components of the proposed loss.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The work does not mention the use of augmentations used during training. Can the authors please share the augmentation used if any? If no augmentation were used can you please comment, either from your own experiments or previous work in the field, on the effectiveness of your method (and compared baselines) when augmentations are used [3, 4, 5]. I am mostly gearing this question towards the idea that augmentation can be seen as a “defence” against the attacked dataset just like in adversarial learning. As a simple test, does mean / median filtering make the examples learnable again (even if at a lower performance) or perhaps using a 3D nnUNet instead [5].
The work is quite related to the field of analysis computer vision models through frequency sensitivity [1]. The work essentially utilises this failure mode for their method which is great. However, there has been a lot of work in making models less frequency sensitive too. Have you considered performance with such models / training [2]? Can you share your intuition of how effective it will be?
The proposed method explicitly uses the segmentation masks of the training data. This opens up two questions:
a. Is it a simple reversible process to make the dataset learnable again? For instance, if I suspect the data is made unlearnable, can I analyse the mask areas in the training images and since I would likely see a different frequency profile than the rest of the image (hypothetically), can I somehow remove these additional frequency response areas?
b. Do you have any intuition or results for only a subset of classes has VoxShield applied to them and some subset does not? Does it make the overall image unlearnable or only the specific classes on which the VoxShield was applied.

reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes VoxShield, a novel approach to guard against unauthorized learning from 3D medical image segmentation data via the injection of imperceptible perturbations. The method optimizes for Inter-Slice Frequency Consistency Disruption and Semantic Prediction Disruption to prevent unauthorized models from extracting useful knowledge from a protected dataset. Evaluation on BraTS19 and FLARE21 demonstrates protection efficacy and cross-architecture transferability.
reviews.text_strengths:
(1) The methodology is well-motivated and sound. The inter-slice frequency consistency disruption module maximizes spectral divergence between adjacent slices, directly targeting the volumetric continuity prior assumed by most 3D segmentation models. This is complemented by a semantic prediction disruption module that maximizes the ℓ1 distance between clean and perturbed logits. The two components address distinct and complementary vulnerabilities, and their individual contributions are validated by the ablation study. 
(2) Evaluation on BraTS19 and FLARE21 confirms strong protective efficacy.
(3) Cross-architecture transferability is demonstrated across common architectures (3D-UNet, Attention UNet, UNet++, and TransUNet). Ablations are clean and sufficient, clearly isolating the contribution of each loss component.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(1) It would strengthen the evaluation to include experiments against purification-based defenses (e.g., Invisible Image Watermarks Are Provably Removable Using Generative AI). 
Even if attack efficacy is not fully preserved after purification (which is fine and does not negate this work’s contribution), characterizing the method’s behavior under naive filtering or generative purification defenses would deepen understanding of its failure modes and help inform future defense-aware design.
(2) It would be interesting to explore whether the perturbations transfer to tasks beyond segmentation, such as classification, detection, registration, reconstruction, or clinical regression (e.g., age prediction). I understand that the method is explicitly designed around segmentation, but the semantic disruption component may transfer well to other tasks, and the inter-slice frequency consistency disruption component may offer advantages in other volumetric learning settings as well.
(3) It would be worth examining whether protection efficacy differs between normal anatomy / body parts segmentation and abnormality/lesion segmentation, as these tasks differ substantially in the nature of the learned features. The authors may also consider extending evaluation to additional imaging modalities or body regions to assess generalizability.
(4) Would there be benefits from replacing logit divergence with divergence at intermediate feature layers?

reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes VoxShield, an Unlearnable Examples (UE) framework designed explicitly to target the volumetric inductive biases of 3D networks.It introduces an Inter-Slice Frequency Consistency Disruption mechanism that maximizes the spectral divergence between adjacent slices to inject structural incoherence along the z-axis.It incorporates a Semantic Prediction Disruption module that maximizes the L1 divergence between clean and perturbed logits to corrupt the final semantic mapping.
reviews.text_strengths:
Novel approach to 3D data protection: The methodology addresses a critical gap by explicitly targeting the volumetric spatial correlations and inter-slice anatomical consistency inherent in 3D medical volumes. Existing methods primarily target 2D scenarios and neglect these 3D priors.
Strong empirical performance: The experiments clearly demonstrate that VoxShield successfully degrades 3D segmentation performance, dropping the DSC from 80.0% to near 0.0% on BraTS19 and from 88.6% to 6.8% on FLARE21.
Cross-architecture transferability: The protective perturbations transfer effectively across various victim architectures. Protection successfully generalizes from a UNet surrogate to Attention UNet, UNet++, and TransUNet models.
Preserved visual fidelity: The protection is achieved using a minimal perturbation budget of 4/255, ensuring that the visual quality of the medical scans is maintained.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Reliance on a single surrogate architecture: The study strictly uses a 3D UNet implemented in MONAI for both the surrogate model and the noise generator. The paper does not investigate whether using a different surrogate architecture (such as a Transformer-based model) during the generation phase would yield stronger or weaker cross-architecture transferability.
Lack of perturbation budget ablation: The evaluation employs a strict, fixed perturbation budget set to 4/255.The submission lacks a sensitivity analysis to demonstrate how varying this threshold impacts the trade-off between imperceptibility and the degradation of segmentation performance.
Limited loss weight justification: The optimization relies on fixed loss weights set to 0.2 and 0.05.The paper does not provide an ablation or explanation on how these specific hyperparameters were chosen or how sensitive the framework is to them.

The paper tackles a highly relevant and growing issue concerning the unauthorized AI model training on publicly released 3D medical image datasets.
VoxShield provides a well-motivated and technically sound solution by systematically dismantling the cross-slice continuity that 3D architectures rely on.
The results strongly support the claims, showing drastic performance drops on victim models while retaining high image quality.
But there exists incomplete ablation of the noise generation pipeline: The study lacks essential experiments justifying its generation setup. It relies on fixed hyperparameters (e.g., a 4/255 perturbation budget and rigid loss weights) without providing a sensitivity analysis, and exclusively uses a single 3D-UNet surrogate without exploring how different surrogate architectures (such as Transformers) might influence the effectiveness and cross-architecture transferability of the generated noise.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the meta reviewer and the reviewers for their time and constructive comments. We are committed to revising our manuscript according to the suggestions, which we believe will significantly improve the quality and clarity of our work. Below we address the main concerns.
1.Defenses and robustness (Meta-R#2, R#2, R#3, R#5). In our experiments, we evaluated mean/median filtering as a potential defense; these results were omitted due to page constraints. Filtering acts locally and cannot reconstruct the spectral coherence between adjacent slices that VoxShield deliberately destroys, and VoxShield maintained strong protection under these conditions. Due to page constraints, we were unable to include a more comprehensive defense evaluation; a broader assessment covering frequency augmentation during training and generative purification is an important direction we plan to pursue in future work.
2.Surrogate architecture and hyperparameters (R#4). We chose 3D UNet as the surrogate as it is a classic and well-performing architecture widely adopted in 3D medical segmentation. In addition, we conducted cross-architecture experiments, and the results show that perturbations transfer effectively to Attention UNet, UNet++, and TransUNet, showing that the attack targets the inter-slice continuity prior shared across all 3D architectures rather than any UNet-specific feature. Most existing UE methods operate at ε = 8/255, whereas VoxShield achieves strong protection at the stricter ε = 4/255, reflecting higher perturbation efficiency. The loss weights were determined via grid search, and Table 3 confirms both components contribute meaningfully.
3.Reversibility and partial-class protection (R#2). Regarding reversibility, we implemented a simple filtering-based defense and found it did not meaningfully restore the protected data, as filtering cannot reconstruct the inter-slice spectral coherence VoxShield destroys. We acknowledge that generative purification methods represent a more fundamental challenge and plan to investigate this in future work. Regarding partial-class protection, we thank the reviewer for raising this interesting point and view it as a worthwhile direction to explore in future work.
4.ROI mask and label shortcuts (R#5). We agree that the annotation-derived ROI mask may introduce label-correlated perturbation locations and that this deserves clarification. In our threat model, the ROI mask is used only by the data owner to concentrate the perturbation budget on anatomically meaningful regions, while the exploiter evaluates on clean test images without perturbations. Thus, such a perturbation-location cue cannot be directly relied upon at test time.
5.UnSeg comparison (R#5). We appreciate this suggestion. UnSeg is designed for 2D segmentation and relies heavily on SAM, making a faithful reimplementation for 3D volumetric segmentation non-trivial as it would require substantial architectural modifications. We believe the existing baseline suite including UMed, which is specifically designed for medical segmentation, already provides a representative comparison. That said, we agree that a comparison with UnSeg would further strengthen the evaluation and look forward to including it in future work.
We are genuinely grateful for the additional suggestions. On per-slice analysis, we conducted cross-slice comparisons and noise visualizations; per-slice performance differences were modest and inter-slice spectral variation was not visually prominent, consistent with the disruption operating at the volumetric feature level. We thank all reviewers once more for their constructive engagement.

title: VRUGA: Visual and Reasoning Uncertainty Guided Active Learning for Medical MLLM Post-training
abstract: Medical Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) hold significant potential for clinical visual question answering (VQA), yet their reliability is often compromised by unstable visual grounding and flawed reasoning logic. While reinforcement learning-based post-training, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), offers a path to steer model behavior, its efficacy is severely constrained by the high cost of expert supervision. To address this, we propose VRUGA, an active learning framework designed to maximize GRPO post-training efficiency under a constrained expert budget. Specifically, we introduce Dual-Uncertainty Quantification (DUQ) to identify high-risk failure modes by jointly evaluating visual grounding stability and reasoning trajectory consistency. Logic-Aware Diversity Sampling (LADS) is subsequently employed to select a representative active set by leveraging decoder hidden-state embeddings to capture a diverse spectrum of latent reasoning patterns. Finally, a Cross-Threshold Pseudo-Labeling (CTPL) mechanism stabilizes the alignment process through tiered supervision, integrating expert-corrected samples with majority-voted pseudo-label anchors to mitigate policy overfitting. Extensive evaluations on VQA-RAD, SLAKE, and PathVQA benchmarks demonstrate that VRUGA achieves a 75.2% average accuracy, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art active learning baselines while requiring only a 10% expert annotation budget.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs
Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning
Machine Learning -> Synthetic Data / Data-centric AI

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes VRUGA, an active learning framework for GRPO-based post-training of medical MLLMs under limited expert annotation budget. The framework has three modules: (1) DUQ measures visual attention consistency and CoT token entropy as dual uncertainty, (2) LADS performs diversity sampling in decoder hidden-state space using farthest point sampling, and (3) CTPL combines expert labels with pseudo-label anchors to stabilize RL post-training. Experiments on VQA-RAD, SLAKE, and PathVQA show 75.2% average accuracy with 10% expert budget.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Budget-efficient post-training of medical MLLMs is a practical bottleneck. The connection between active learning and RL alignment is clearly motivated.
2.Separating visual grounding instability (U_vis) from reasoning trajectory uncertainty (U_rsn) goes beyond simple logit entropy.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.No standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. As a result, the robustness of the reported gains cannot be confidently assessed from the current submission alone.
2.The strongest reported result, 75.2%, uses 10% expert data plus 50% unlabeled anchors, whereas the main baselines in Table 1 are reported under 10% expert data only. The paper does disclose this and also reports VRUGA (w/o Unl. ) at 73.0%, which is the fairer direct comparison. However, the headline gain should be framed more carefully. I would encourage the authors either to reframe the headline claim or to add a matched ‘baseline + pseudo-label anchor’ (e. g. , “DEUCE + CTPL”) comparison.
3.The paper motivates DUQ using visual grounding instability and reasoning trajectory uncertainty, but evaluation is limited to exact-match accuracy on closed-ended VQA. This is a standard metric for the benchmark, yet insufficient to directly validate claims about reasoning quality or grounding faithfulness.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1.Please clarify the exact GRPO reward function for both expert-labeled and pseudo-labeled samples. Is it exact match only, or does it include format/CoT quality components?
2.How is the train/test split constructed? Is the standard split from each benchmark used, or is there a custom split for the active learning pool?
3.What is the computational overhead of DUQ (K=8 stochastic runs with attention extraction) compared to standard baselines?

The paper sits at a useful intersection of AL and GRPO post-training that has received little prior attention in the medical VQA literature. However, several issues prevent acceptance in the current form. First, the absence of statistical evidence makes the reported gains difficult to assess with confidence, particularly on VQA-RAD where the margin is very small. Second, the headline comparison involves asymmetric data usage between VRUGA and baselines. These are important issues that the authors would need to address before acceptance can be considered.

Experiments on VQA-RAD, SLAKE, and PathVQA show improved accuracy under a 10% expert annotation budget, with the full method reaching 75.2% average accuracy.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes VRUGA, an active learning framework that enhances reinforcement-learning-based post-training (GRPO) for medical multimodal LLMs, making them more label-efficient for clinical VQA. It introduces Dual-Uncertainty Quantification (DUQ) by combining visual grounding instability and reasoning uncertainty, Logic-Aware Diversity Sampling (LADS) for reasoning trajectory sampling in the decoder hidden-state space, and Cross-Threshold Pseudo-Labeling (CTPL) to stabilize GRPO with expert-labeled hard cases and majority-voted pseudolabel anchors. The framework achieves state-of-the-art accuracy under a limited expert budget across multiple VQA datasets.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper proposes a dual-view uncertainty framework that combines visual grounding instability with reasoning-trajectory entropy. This design is interesting as it explicitly models uncertainty in both visual grounding and reasoning processes for generative multimodal VQA.
2.The proposed LADS strategy leverages decoder hidden states of CoT tokens and applies farthest-point sampling weighted by the dual-uncertainty score. This provides a logic-aware way to capture diverse reasoning patterns during sample selection.
3.The CTPL module incorporates high-confidence unlabeled samples into GRPO via majority-voted pseudo-labels, thereby improving data efficiency and stabilizing training under limited labeled data.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The method relies on attention maps as proxies for visual grounding stability (Uvis). However, the reliability of attention as an explanation mechanism is debated, and the paper does not clearly specify how attention is extracted (e.g., layers/heads, aggregation scheme, or the top-m token selection).
2.DUQ requires multiple stochastic decodes for each sample across the unlabeled pool, which could be computationally expensive for large datasets. The paper does not discuss runtime or scalability.
3.The framework assumes the availability and usefulness of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning in medical VQA, but the potential mismatch between generated CoT and the model’s actual reasoning process is not analyzed.
4.The main comparison (Table 1) uses additional unlabeled data for the proposed method, while the baselines appear to rely only on labeled data. Including semi-supervised or self-training counterparts for baselines would make the comparison fairer.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Q1.How exactly are attention maps extracted for Uvis (e.g., which layers/heads and aggregation strategy)? What is the value of m for top-m visual tokens?
Q2.Are the reported results averaged over multiple random seeds for DUQ sampling, LADS selection, and GRPO training? If not, could variance or error bars be reported?
Q3.What is the computational overhead of DUQ (K stochastic decodes per sample)? It would be helpful to report runtime or GPU cost.
Q4.Do Uvis and Ursn correlate with actual error likelihood? Correlation or calibration analysis would help validate the uncertainty formulation.

The paper proposes an interesting framework that combines dual-uncertainty estimation with logic-aware diversity sampling and pseudo-labeling for data-efficient multimodal VQA. The idea is promising and addresses an important challenge in reducing expert annotation requirements for medical VQA tasks. While several aspects could be better analyzed—such as the reliance on attention maps for grounding estimation, the computational cost of DUQ, and the assumptions regarding Chain-of-Thought reasoning—these issues mainly relate to missing analysis or experimental validation rather than fundamental flaws in the approach. Additional experiments, clearer methodological details, and fairer comparisons with semi-supervised baselines would further strengthen the work. Overall, the proposed ideas are interesting and potentially useful, and with some clarifications and stronger empirical analysis, the paper could make a meaningful contribution.

Considering such practical value, I recommend acceptance.

title: WaCT-US: Cyclic-Alignment Scaled Contour Tubes for Efficient, Calibrated Uncertainty in Echocardiography
abstract:
Uncertainty in echocardiography segmentation is predominantly geometric: speckle, shadowing, and inter-scanner variation create boundary ambiguity that propagates to clinical measurements.
We propose WaCT-US, a contour-native uncertainty representation that outputs a calibrated prediction set (``contour tube’’) around a single predicted boundary.
Cyclic landmark alignment resolves closed-curve indexing, and a learned heteroscedastic scale profile specifies where the boundary is intrinsically ambiguous.
Split conformal calibration on held-out data yields one global scalar that meets a user-chosen coverage level with finite-sample, distribution-free marginal validity.
Inference requires one forward pass with light post-processing.
We evaluate on CAMUS and EchoNet-Dynamic across three seeds at nominal  conformal coverage.
While matching Dice, WaCT-US achieves the best mean calibrated uncertainty scale (representing conformal efficiency and tube thickness) while holding comparable coverage and improving uncertainty-guided error localization. This information can estimate how wrong the underlying segmentation model is on each input image.  The code will be publicly available at  .

A contour tube is estimated around a single contour with varying thickness indicating uncertainty. Cyclic alignment is performed to have a consistent indexing of the contour. The method is evaluated on public data with comparison to alternatives and promising results.

It is unclear how this method could generalize to 3D surfaces.
No discussion of the sensitivity to distribution shift.

reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose WaCT-US, a contour-native uncertainty representation that outputs a conformal calibrated prediction set (“contour tube”) around a predicted boundary. They introduce a second prediction head to predict the local scale for the confidence region around the predicted landmark, driven by a pinball loss. The authors evaluate on CAMUS and EchoNet-Dynamic.
reviews.text_strengths:
The methodology is novel and addresses an important problem (deriving efficient confidence regions around predictions with adequate coverage of the ground truth).
The framework is sound.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
I am not certain that the paper conclusively demonstrates the superiority of the method over the SOTA. The methods seem to all have very similar performance with respect to all metrics, with a slight edge for the proposed method w.r.t. Scale, that may only be statistically significant for one of the two datasets (no direct significance test is performed).
Part of my unease comes from the fact that the methods to derive the Scale metric for the proposed method and for the baselines might be fairly diverse and this might impact the reported numbers. I would be grateful if the authors can comment on this.
One weakness is that despite deriving confidence sets that are geometrically more constrained (as contour tubes), the main segmentation head itself is unchanged. As in, it is still based on predicting a mask, trained with Dice+BCE, which for echo data will often lead to predictions that are both topologically incorrect and geometrically unconstrained. In my opinion this is a strong limitation for the practical usefulness of the work.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
I am unsure why all metrics are bolded for the WaCT-US lines in Table 1.
The Dice performance of the trained networks seems to be a bit below standard numbers reported for CAMUS. Although this is not the main aim of the paper, I would be more at ease analyzing confidence estimates on baselines that are fully on par with the literature.
Baselines specific to echocardiography could be relevant additions, for instance 
Judge et al., Asymmetric Contour Uncertainty Estimation for Medical Image Segmentation, MICCAI 2023
My understanding is that there is no particularly beneficial interaction between the segmentation head and the scale head during training. Is that correct?

At this point of time, it seems to me the weaknesses of the paper slightly outweigh its strengths, but I am willing to adjust my rating after the rebuttal.
