reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
Many thanks to the authors for taking the time to respond to the reviewers’ comments and questions.
Final assessment: For me, the paper is entirely borderline. Given a choice between accept and reject, I am choosing accept because I believe the paper could be interesting to the UQ community.

a boundary-centric conformal approach with good novelty
Weaknesses:
Limited evidence for the relevance and effectiveness of the approach, given limited improvement across datasets with no statistical significance test
One could have favored exactly the opposite approach of demonstrating the relevance of the framework by demonstrating its applicability on a natively contour-based segmentation method, and demonstrating both superior segmentation quality and sharper uncertainties.
The benefit of having calibrated prediction sets is reduced when the returned contour is as likely to be topologically and geometrically incorrect.

Please prioritize responding on comparisons with more recent and relevant baselines and clarify whether the observed performance differences are statistically significant. Additionally, address concerns regarding the evaluation of the Scale metric and ensure fair comparability across methods. Finally, respond to limitations and generalizability concerns, including applicability to 3D settings, robustness to distribution shift, and evidence of the practical advantages of the proposed approach.

The paper presents WaCT-US, a contour-native uncertainty representation that outputs a conformally calibrated prediction set. The strengths and limitations of the work were both clearly discussed during the review process, and the benefits appear to outweigh the weaknesses. In particular, the boundary-centric conformal formulation is novel and practically appealing, especially given the significant speedup reported by the authors. The questions regarding relevant baselines were also adequately addressed in the rebuttal. Overall, the paper is recommended for acceptance.

All reviewers agreed that this paper is well prepared and of interest to MICCAI. R2 originally recommended borderline reject, but raised their score to accept after authors’ rebuttal. AC recommends acceptance.

This paper proposes a novel efficient uncertainty quantification in echocardiography segmentation around boundaries through scaled contour tubes. It adopts cyclic landmark alignment to address index inconsistency and split conformal calibration to ensure marginal coverage. Although there are some shortcomings in terms of generalizability, sensitivity analysis, and performance advantages, these do not undermine the contributions and potential impact of this paper’s methodological innovation. The method will provide a new perspective on uncertainty quantification in medical image segmentation and is expected to enhance the reliability and accuracy of diagnoses in clinical practice.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer (MR) for constructive feedback. We focus on fair comparison/statistical interpretation, recent echo baselines, and scope/practicality.
Fair comparison, Scale, significance (R2/R3/MR). We do not claim Dice/HD superiority; the segmentation protocol is intentionally kept standard/comparable to isolate UQ. Bolding WaCT-US rows in Table 1 was intended only to mark the proposed method, not metric-wise dominance. The claim is coverage-efficiency: at nominal 0.9 conformal coverage, WaCT-US gives the smallest calibrated tube scale with one forward pass. Scale is comparable because all methods are converted to the same tube family: sample the method’s local uncertainty on the predicted contour, compute the same Eq.(3) score, calibrate a method-specific λ̂ by the same quantile rule on the same validation split, evaluate on the same test frames, and report Scale=mean_i[λ̂ mean_j s_ij]. Raw entropy/vacuity/std units are not compared; a global rescaling of any raw map is absorbed by λ̂, leaving λ̂s and Scale unchanged. Table 1 reports comparable coverage with exact 95% CIs; WaCT-US has the lowest mean Scale (CAMUS 8.09 vs 8.98 next; EchoNet 5.10 vs 5.27 next). We did not include a direct Scale significance test, and the EchoNet gap is modest; thus the claim is an observed Pareto advantage in Scale and compute, not formal statistical dominance.
Recent/relevant baselines (R2/R3/MR). The baselines cover UQ regimes under protocol parity: post-hoc deterministic maps, evidential/temperature maps, and sampling/Bayesian approximations (MC dropout, Laplace, SWAG), all conformalized identically. Judge et al. is relevant and cited; however, it produces asymmetric contour-regression uncertainty, whereas WaCT-US produces a split-conformal prediction set around a standard segmenter with finite-sample marginal coverage. A fair comparison would require an adapter/conformalized contour-set variant, so we do not claim dominance over that line. Similarly, recent conformal segmentation works cited in the paper are mask/morphology based or contour objects in another setting; they do not evaluate the same closed-contour, learned-local-scaling, single-pass echo setting.
Segmentation/topology and scale head (R2). We agree topology-constrained echo segmenters are valuable. WaCT-US is architecture-agnostic (Sec.2.3) and can wrap stronger/topology-aware backbones. The Dice+BCE U-Net keeps the center-contour model unchanged across UQ methods. R2 is correct that the scale head is not designed to improve Dice/topology or feed back to correct the center contour; it learns residual-dependent local scale so the output reports where/how much the contour may be wrong. Limitations of the chosen segmenter, including the CAMUS Dice concern, therefore affect absolute segmentation quality, but not the within-paper UQ comparison: WaCT-US is not given a stronger center-contour model than the baselines.
Shift, 3D, practical advantage, reproducibility (R1/MR). The paper states the exchangeability requirement: Theorem 1 gives P_te(d_s≤λ̂)≥1−α−δ under TV shift δ, so we do not claim robustness to arbitrary shift; weighted conformal alternatives are noted for drift. In 3D, split-conformal validity could apply to a chosen surface score under exchangeability, but cyclic shift would need surface correspondence/alignment; our empirical claim is limited to 2D echo contours. Practical value is shown in Fig.2: WaCT-US has the lowest AURC and deferring the top 20% most uncertain CAMUS samples reduces retained contour MAE by 15.7%; Fig.2b shows contour-tube overlays where uncertainty tracks image quality/contour mismatch. For reproducibility, Secs.2.3/3.1-3.3 specify public datasets/splits, preprocessing, model, losses, optimizer/epochs, M=64, τ=0.9, scale weight, calibration quantile, baselines, and metrics; we intend to release code after acceptance.

title: Wasserstein-Aligned Localisation for VLM-Based Distributional OOD Detection in Medical Imaging
abstract: Zero-shot anomaly localisation via vision-language models (VLMs) offers a compelling approach for rare pathology detection, yet current methods suffer from a lack of healthy reference context, high prediction variance, and suboptimal reference selection. We introduce WALDO, a training-free framework grounded in optimal transport theory that addresses these limitations through: (i) entropy-weighted Sliced Wasserstein distance for anatomically-aware reference selection from DINOv3 patch distributions, (ii) Goldilocks zone sampling exploiting the non-monotonic relationship between reference similarity and localisation accuracy, and (iii) self-consistency aggregation via weighted non-maximum suppression. On the NOVA brain MRI benchmark, WALDO with Qwen2.5-VL-72B achieves 43.5 ± 1.6% mAP@30 (95% CI: [40.4, 46.7]), representing a 19% relative improvement over zero-shot baselines. Cross-model evaluation shows consistent gains: GPT-4o achieves 32.0 ± 6.5% and Qwen3-VL-32B achieves 32.0 ± 6.6% mAP@30. Paired McNemar tests confirm statistical significance for the primary pair (p = 1.8 × 10⁻⁶, hit@30). We provide theoretical analysis of the Goldilocks effect through distributional divergence, demonstrating why moderate-similarity references optimise the bias-variance tradeoff in comparative visual reasoning. Code: https://github.com/bkainz/WALDO_MICCAI26_demo
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs
Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

The approach show competitive and remarked results.

reviews.text_strengths:

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The authors propose WALDO - a training-free framework utilizing optimal transport theory to localise pathologies in brain MRI and chest X-ray images. The framework processes a query image and a healthy reference pool with DINOv2, extracting patch embeddings and measuring distributional similarity through an entropy-weighted Sliced Wasserstein distance. References from the “Goldilocks zone” are selected via DPP for diversity. Performance is evaluated on two datasets; for the NOVA brain MRI benchmark, the authors also reproduced the benchmark’s baseline results. WALDO significantly outperforms the baselines, achieving improvements of more than +19% mAP@30 on both brain MRI and chest X-ray images.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The proposed framework is training-free, allowing VLMs to perform in a zero-shot regime.
2.The authors provide a theoretical analysis of the non-monotonic relationship between reference similarity (needed to correctly identify a healthy reference image based on anatomical consistency) and localization accuracy (needed to correctly localise the pathology).
3.The paper is well-written and the code in the repository is well-organised, reflecting a strong commitment to reproducibility. Notably, the authors reproduced the results from the benchmark and provided a thorough ablation study evaluating the contribution of every component of the method (Table 3).
4.The sensitivity analysis of hyperparameters is a valuable addition, demonstrating that the authors are aware of the importance of robustness to parameter choices.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Page 2, “Limitations of Current Approaches.” In L3, the authors state that stochastic sampling causes high prediction variance with standard deviations exceeding 5% mAP — it is unclear how this value was obtained. A reference or derivation should be provided.
2.Page 4, “Implementation Details.” The authors mention that images were resized to 512×512, but the initial image resolution is never stated. Additionally, λ = 0.1 is used, whereas intuitively a value of 0.5 might seem more natural. A more detailed justification of how these values were chosen would strengthen the paper.
3.It is unclear why only 200 samples were selected from the VinDr-CXR dataset. A justification for this choice should be provided, as it may affect the reliability of the evaluation.
4.In Table 1, Qwen3-VL-235B (MoE) outperforms WALDO. While the authors attribute this to the model’s expert routing mechanism conflating reference and query contexts, it remains unclear whether the performance gap is simply attributable to the significantly larger model size. This leaves an important comparison underexplained. 
5.In Table 1, five models are considered; however, Qwen3-VL-235B (MoE) and Gemini-2.0-Flash are absent from further experiments, such as Table 2.The rationale for this inconsistent model selection should be clarified.
6.Page 5, “Experiments. Models.” The authors mention that ablation experiments were also conducted with DINOv3, but the corresponding results are nowhere to be found in the paper or in the repository. These should either be included or the reference should be removed.
7.Page 6, “Experiments. Models.” The paper states that Table 2 shows chest X-ray performance in the range of 24–35% mAP@30, whereas the actual values in Table 2 range from 10.9 to 34.1.This inconsistency should be corrected. Furthermore, the claim that heart size and shape vary substantially among healthy individuals is used to explain lower chest X-ray performance, but it is not discussed whether similar variability exists in brain MRI, which would undermine this explanation.
8.Page 7, “Experiments. Sensitivity Analysis.” The sensitivity analysis covers only hyperparameter values in the vicinity of the chosen ones. It remains unclear whether other, more distant values could yield better performance, which limits the conclusions that can be drawn from this analysis.
9.The authors mention VLM hallucinations, but the frequency and impact of them in the experiments is never discussed. Given that the framework relies on VLMs, this is a notable omission that should be addressed.
10.The paper lacks any comparison with supervised methods on the same tasks, or at least an explanation of why such a comparison would be impossible or inappropriate. Including such a comparison, even indicatively, would help contextualise the achieved performance and provide a clearer picture of the remaining gap between training-free and fully supervised approaches.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
1.The VinDr-CXR dataset is not mentioned in the abstract, despite being used in the evaluation. It would be worth at least briefly noting its inclusion.
2.The title of Table 3 should specify that Qwen2.5-VL-72B was used, to avoid ambiguity.
3.Page 6, “Experiments. Goldilocks Effect Analysis.” It should be explicitly noted that the results discussed in this section correspond to Table 1, to help the reader follow the analysis more easily.

The paper presents WALDO, a training-free framework for unsupervised pathology localisation in medical images that operates in a zero-shot regime, removing the need for annotated training data - a significant bottleneck in medical imaging. The experimental results demonstrate strong performance, with improvements exceeding +19% mAP@30 over the baselines on both brain MRI and chest X-ray images.
While several weaknesses were identified - including small inconsistencies in reported metrics and underexplained design choices - these are largely addressable through revisions and do not undermine the core contributions of the work. The major weaknesses raised should be addressed before finalisation, but none of them represent fundamental flaws. Overall, the strengths of the paper outweigh its weaknesses, and I recommend acceptance subject to the authors addressing the comments provided.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper introduces a zero-shot method for finding anomalies in medical images with vision-language models and without the need for labeled training data . The idea of using Wasserstein distance to compare image patches and picking healthy references that are moderately similar to the query is clever and deserves a pass.
Despite my provisional accept recommendation, I agree that the main hypothesis appears to lack rigorous statistical testing and feels more like a qualitative story than a proven theory (which is fine, but the paper needs to be presented accordingly). Also, the paper needs to compare against a simple CLIP-based baseline or a standard sampling strategy. Lastly, the authors should address the latency increase and make some clarification to experimental details (3D MRI data handing, etc., Also: why only 200 samples from the chest X-ray dataset?

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and AC for the constructive feedback. The camera-ready paper addresses every point compatible with the “no new experiments / no number changes” rule. We summarise the updates and clarify a few misinterpretations.
Statistical robustness (R1.W2, R3.W9, AC). The criterion is now stated explicitly: paired McNemar tests on the binary hit@30 (IoU>=0.3) indicator at alpha=0.05.The Qwen2.5-VL-72B NOVA pair p-value is tightened from “p<0.01” to the exact p=1.8e-6 (same paired test, same sample size). §Error Analysis adds a hallucination quantification (R3.W9): 27-47% of WALDO predictions on VinDr-CXR are false positives (IoU=0), yet WALDO reduces the per-image no-correct-localisation rate by 22-55 percentage points compared to zero-shot, so the recall gain dominates the false-positive volume.
Backbone naming (R3.W6, R2.W4). The submitted text inconsistently referred to “DINOv2”; all experiments were in fact run with DINOv3-ViT-B/16 (facebook/dinov3-vitb16-pretrain-lvd1689m). Abstract, Figure 1 caption, and §Models are corrected. No reported numbers change. Post-hoc analysis revealed that there is no measureable difference between v2 and v3 for our method.
Factual corrections (R3.W3, R3.W7, INT). §Implementation now states n=949 for VinDr-CXR (the “n=200” sentence was a stale leftover; Table 2 was already n=949). The CXR mAP@30 prose range “24-35%” is corrected to “10.9-34.1%” to match Table 2.NOVA sample count is corrected from 907 to 906.Image resolutions (NOVA 480x480, VinDr-CXR up to 1024x1024 DICOM) and the lambda=0.1 grid-search rationale are now stated (R3.W2). The +360% relative-gain figure for GPT-4o on CXR was a derived-number typo and is corrected to +230% (recomputed from Table 2; (10.9-3.3)/3.3).
Qwen3-VL-235B regression (R2.W1, R3.W4). §Results now explicitly rules out model scale: Qwen2.5-VL-72B is ~3x smaller yet has comparable zero-shot performance (36.4%) and benefits strongly from WALDO (+19.5%). The regression appears MoE-specific.
Clarifications.
(i) (R2.W2) The Goldilocks effect is distinct from identity-mapping prevention: we operate on patch-level feature distributions via Sliced Wasserstein at prompt time, exploiting a bias-variance tradeoff in differential VLM reasoning. The mechanism and granularity differ from latent-replay / regularisation strategies in atlas-based or generative methods.
(ii) (R3.W7) §Results now states explicitly that brain-MRI variability exists, but focal pathologies produce contrast changes absent in healthy tissue, making healthy references more discriminative for MRI than for CXR.
(iii) (R2.W6, AC) NOVA provides pre-extracted 2D axial slices; the reported experiments do not require volumetric handling.
(iv) (R3.W10) §Limitations explains the absence of supervised baselines: WALDO targets the setting where labelled training data is absent, which is the norm for rare diseases.
Items deferred to the post-publication extended version. Under the no-new-experiments rule, the following could not be added to the camera-ready and are flagged for an extended arXiv and journal version: a WinCLIP / CLIP-based reference baseline (R1.W3, R2.W3, AC); K-Means / Coreset reference-selection ablations (R2.W5); CXR runs of Qwen3-VL-235B and Gemini-2.0-Flash (R3.W5); a wider hyperparameter sweep beyond the chosen-vicinity (R3.W8); and a more formal information-theoretic treatment of the Goldilocks bound (R1.W1). We thank the reviewers for these strong directions.

title: WaveDE: Wavelet-Routed Dual-Expert Network for Fundus Photograph Enhancement
abstract:
Fundus photography is essential for retinal disease screening and diagnosis, yet low-quality images are common in clinical practice, undermining both clinical reading and automated analysis. Fundus image enhancement faces two key challenges: (i) real degradations are often compound, causing enhancement models trained under single-degradation settings to generalize poorly; and (ii) restoring low- and high-frequency components involves conflicting objectives, making it difficult to jointly achieve global consistency, fine-detail recovery, and noise suppression. We propose WaveDE, a wavelet-routed dual-expert network for fundus photograph enhancement. Discrete wavelet transform-based band routing decomposes decoder features into low- and high-frequency subbands processed by two specialized experts: the low-frequency expert performs global correction and provides structural priors, while the high-frequency expert leverages them to enhance textures and suppress noise. A high-frequency-injected VAE decoder further recovers fine details lost to latent compression, and an anatomical consistency regularization enforces structural fidelity of vessels and the optic disc. On multiple public datasets, WaveDE achieves the best PSNR (39.02, 95% CI: 38.90–39.16)
and SSIM (0.98, 95% CI: 0.97–0.98) among 12 state-of-the-art methods, with consistent gains across 2 classification and 4 segmentation datasets; out-of-distribution evaluations further confirm cross-domain robustness.The code and model are available at https://github.com/CowboyH/WaveDE.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes WaveDE, a wavelet-routed dual-expert network for fundus image enhancement.
reviews.text_strengths:
1) Large-scale experiments and comprehensive evaluation framework.
2) Explicitly decomposing composite degradations into low-frequency global degradations and high-frequency local artifacts has a solid signal processing foundation. The structural guidance map G introduces meaningful interaction between experts rather than independent processing.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.Training relies entirely on programmatically synthesized degradations (brightness, contrast, saturation, halo, dark spots, noise, blur, and combinations). However, real clinical degradations are more complex (e. g. , optical aberrations, cataracts, vitreous opacity, tear film instability). Although the paper acknowledges this gap, it provides limited validation on real unpaired low-quality images (only MR-ART). Downstream evaluations (Table 2) still rely on synthetic degradations, failing to demonstrate effectiveness on real data. This is a critical limitation for clinical translation.
2.WaveDE combines SD v1.5 U-Net, FD-Block (VMamba + asymmetric convolutions), HFI-VAE decoder, and two teacher networks (U-Net++, PraNet). However, the paper does not report model size, training time, inference latency, or GPU memory usage. Training is conducted on RTX PRO 6000 (96 GB), which exceeds typical clinical deployment conditions. Efficiency analysis is essential for practical applicability.
3.The structural guidance map (G) is claimed to enable meaningful interaction between experts. However, ablation only evaluates the presence/absence of FD-Block as a whole, without isolating the contribution of (G). A variant without guidance would strengthen this claim.
4.VMamba is used for long-range modeling, but no comparison is provided with alternatives such as Transformers or CNNs. The choice appears driven by complexity rather than task-specific necessity.
5.Datasets such as RFMiD and FIVES are included in both training and downstream evaluation. Although training uses synthetic pairs, exposure to high-quality images may bias results. This issue is not discussed.
6.The use of PraNet for optic disc detection lacks justification. Fixed weights ((\lambda_v), (\lambda_{od})) and spatial coefficients (Eq. 7) are not analyzed.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Reference to list the major weaknesses of the paper.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
While the rebuttal clarifies several implementation details, it does not sufficiently resolve my main concerns regarding the paper’s empirical validity and practical significance.
The most critical issue remains the heavy reliance on synthetically generated degradations. Although the authors argue that the synthesis pipeline is physically motivated, the paper still lacks convincing validation on real low-quality clinical fundus images. Importantly, both the restoration benchmarks and downstream evaluations are primarily conducted on synthetic degradations, so the reported gains do not adequately demonstrate real-world robustness or clinical applicability.
In addition, the method is also considerably complex, combining SD v1.5, VMamba-based FD-Blocks, HFI-VAE, and multiple anatomical teacher networks. However, efficiency and deployment analysis remain limited. Reporting ~100 ms inference on RTX 4090 after rebuttal is helpful, but practical resource trade-offs, parameter counts, and memory/runtime comparisons against baselines are still missing.
Overall, I find the engineering effort substantial and the experimental performance competitive. However, the current evidence is still insufficient to support the paper’s broader claims regarding robustness, generalization, and practical clinical applicability.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper studies the problem of fundus image enhancement, with a particular focus on compound degradations commonly encountered in clinical acquisition, such as uneven illumination, blur, noise, and local artefacts occurring simultaneously. The authors propose WaveDE, whose core idea is to decompose features into different frequency components using the discrete wavelet transform and process low- and high-frequency information with two dedicated experts: the low-frequency expert is responsible for global correction and provides structural priors, while the high-frequency expert restores texture details and suppresses noise under its guidance. In addition, the paper introduces a high-frequency-injected VAE decoder to compensate for the loss of high-frequency details caused by latent-space compression, and an anatomical consistency regularization term that uses vessel and optic disc teacher networks to constrain anatomical consistency. Experiments on multiple public datasets show that the proposed method achieves strong performance in image enhancement metrics as well as downstream classification and segmentation tasks.
reviews.text_strengths:
In real-world fundus image acquisition, multiple degradations often co-occur, whereas many existing methods are still designed around single-degradation settings. Therefore, the two core challenges identified by the authors, namely compound degradations and the conflict between global correction and fine-detail recovery, are well motivated. The problem formulation is clear, the application background is realistic, and the overall motivation is sound.
The proposed method is built around the central idea of frequency decoupling. DWT is used to separate frequency bands, which are then processed by dedicated low- and high-frequency experts. The high-frequency-injected VAE decoder and anatomical regularization further strengthen detail recovery and structural fidelity.
The authors report not only PSNR and SSIM for image restoration, but also evaluate the effect of the enhanced images on downstream classification and segmentation tasks, and further include OOD evaluation on PAPILA and ARIA. This goes beyond showing that the images merely “look better” and attempts to demonstrate that the enhancement is beneficial for downstream medical image analysis. In particular, in Table 1, the proposed method achieves clearly better PSNR and SSIM than the compared methods on both the full test set and the different subsets, indicating strong overall performance.
The emphasis on anatomical consistency is also well aligned with the requirements of medical imaging tasks. Rather than focusing only on visual quality, the authors additionally use vessel and optic disc priors to constrain the enhancement results, which can help reduce structural artefacts and hallucinated content to some extent. This is meaningful in the medical imaging context.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Although the improvements in classification and segmentation are a strength of the paper, the main text does not provide sufficiently detailed descriptions of the downstream models, including their specific architectures, training procedures, and whether exactly the same training and evaluation protocol is used for all enhancement methods. Since the downstream results are an important part of the paper’s empirical support, insufficient detail here weakens both the persuasiveness and the reproducibility of the work.
The selection of baselines and the fairness of the comparisons could also be improved. In addition to fundus enhancement methods, the paper includes methods originating from other tasks such as super-resolution, image inpainting, and ultrasound imaging. However, not all of these baselines are necessarily the most appropriate or strongest competitors for the specific problem studied here. A comparison more focused on directly relevant fundus or medical image enhancement methods would make the conclusions more convincing.
One of the central assumptions of the paper is that different degradations mainly reside in different frequency bands, and can therefore be disentangled through deterministic frequency-band routing. This intuition is reasonable, but at present it is supported mainly indirectly through overall performance and ablation results. The paper lacks more direct analysis showing what the low-frequency and high-frequency experts actually learn, and which types of degradations benefit most from this design.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

My score is based on the paper’s clear motivation, targeted method design, and strong experimental results. The proposed frequency-decoupled dual-expert framework is well matched to the problem of compound degradations in fundus images, and the paper evaluates the method not only on restoration metrics but also on downstream classification and segmentation tasks, which strengthens its practical relevance. I lean toward a positive recommendation because the method appears effective and the results are consistently strong. However, I remain somewhat cautious because the downstream evaluation setup is not fully described, some baselines are not the most directly relevant, and the paper lacks deeper analysis of the proposed frequency-decoupling mechanism.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
After reading the authors’ rebuttal, my final opinion is Accept.
The submitted paper addresses an important and practical problem in fundus image enhancement, especially compound degradations and the tension between global correction and fine-detail recovery. The proposed frequency-decoupled dual-expert design is coherent and well matched to the problem setting. The original paper already provides strong empirical evidence, including image restoration metrics, ablation studies, downstream classification and segmentation evaluation, and OOD evaluation.
The authors’ rebuttal is also helpful in clarifying several major concerns raised in the reviews. In particular, the response clarifies the synthetic-data rationale, the training/deployment distinction, the downstream evaluation protocol, the disjointness of data splits, the datasets used for anatomical teacher models, and the baseline selection. These clarifications alleviate my main concerns about experimental fairness and reproducibility.
I still think the paper has limitations. The reliance on synthetic degradations leaves a remaining synthetic-to-real gap, and the analysis of some methodological components, such as the structural guidance map and the LF/HF experts, is still not fully isolated. I also agree that failure cases and more detailed discussion of real clinical degradations would strengthen the paper. I do not rely on promised future ablations or future extensions as new evidence for the decision.
Nevertheless, based on the submitted paper and the clarifications in the rebuttal, I think the strengths outweigh the remaining weaknesses. The method is well motivated, the empirical results are strong, and the paper is likely to be useful to the fundus image enhancement and medical image restoration communities. Therefore, I support acceptance.

reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes WaveDE, a wavelet-routed dual-expert network for fundus photograph enhancement. The method combines a frequency-decoupled dual-expert block, a high-frequency-injected VAE decoder, and an anatomical consistency regularization term based on frozen vessel and optic disc teachers. Experiments on multiple public fundus datasets show strong PSNR/SSIM and improvements on several downstream classification and segmentation benchmarks.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper addresses an important problem in retinal imaging, as low-quality fundus photographs are common in practice and can affect both clinical reading and automated analysis.
2.The overall framework is well structured. The separation between low-frequency global correction and high-frequency detail restoration is reasonable and clearly presented.

3.What datasets were used to train the anatomical teacher networks, and is there any overlap with the current experimental datasets?
4.Failure cases are not discussed.
