reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: WaveDE addresses a clinically relevant fundus enhancement problem with a coherent wavelet-routed dual-expert design. The rebuttal reasonably clarifies data leakage, synthetic data, efficiency, and downstream protocols. Strong PSNR/SSIM, OOD, and downstream classification/segmentation results outweigh missing fine-grained ablations.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper tackles an important problem and presents a technically solid solution with strong empirical results. The reviewers are generally positive, but several issues need to be clarified before the work can be fully assessed.
The main concern is limited validation on real-world degradations. The model is trained on synthetic corruptions, while real clinical degradations are more complex. Current evaluation relies largely on synthetic settings, with only limited real-data validation. The authors should better justify the clinical applicability and, if possible, provide additional analysis on real degraded images.
Second, experimental protocol and fairness need clarification. There is potential overlap between training and downstream datasets, and it is unclear whether splits are strictly disjoint. The downstream evaluation setup (e.g., retraining vs. direct inference) is also not clearly described. Baseline selection could be more focused on relevant fundus enhancement methods.
Third, methodological analysis is incomplete. Key components (e.g., structural guidance, frequency decoupling, VMamba choice) are not sufficiently isolated or justified through ablations. More insight into what each module contributes would strengthen the claims.
Finally, efficiency and reproducibility are underreported, including model size, runtime, and training details.
Addressing these points would significantly strengthen the paper.

After considering the reviews and the authors’ rebuttal, I recommend acceptance.
The paper addresses an important problem in fundus image enhancement and presents a coherent framework supported by strong empirical results across restoration, downstream analysis, and out-of-distribution evaluation. The rebuttal adequately addresses most of the major concerns regarding experimental protocols, reproducibility, and evaluation fairness.
While concerns remain regarding the reliance on synthetic degradations and the need for broader real-world validation, these limitations do not undermine the main findings of the paper. Overall, I believe the contribution is technically sound, practically relevant, and sufficiently supported by the presented evidence.
Recommendation: Accept.

The reviewers generally viewed the problem as important and the design as coherent, and two reviewers supported acceptance after the rebuttal. I also recommend acceptance, while noting that the paper should be framed carefully around its synthetic-degradation setting.
WaveDE addresses a practical problem in fundus image enhancement, where compound degradations can harm both visual quality and downstream analysis. The proposed wavelet-routed dual-expert design is well matched to this setting: low-frequency correction, high-frequency restoration, high-frequency injection in the VAE decoder, and anatomical consistency regularization form a coherent framework. The empirical results are strong, including PSNR/SSIM, ablations, downstream classification/segmentation, and OOD evaluation. The rebuttal also clarifies several important points about data splits, downstream protocols, teacher datasets, and deployment cost.
The main limitation is that training and much of the evaluation rely on synthetic degradations, so claims about real clinical robustness should be stated with caution. For the camera-ready version, the authors should incorporate the rebuttal clarifications on split disjointness, downstream evaluation protocol, teacher-network training data, inference cost, and baseline selection. They should also clearly discuss the synthetic-to-real gap, the limited real-degradation validation, and the remaining failure mode on color-related degradations.
After reading the rebuttal and other reviewers’ comments, I think the authors have reasonably addressed the main concerns.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for recognizing the problem as “important” (R3), the application background as “realistic” (R2), our “coherent” (R3) and “targeted” (R2) design, the “comprehensive” (R1) and “broad” (R3) evaluation, and the “consistently strong” (R2) performance. Key details below will be added in the camera-ready.
1.R1-W1: Synthetic data. Since paired real LQ–HQ samples are scarce, we generate synthetic data via [23]. It is widely adopted in fundus enhancement, including recent SOTA models MDA [5] and GFE [16]. [23] is physically grounded, explicitly modelling the ophthalmoscope imaging system and real degradation factors. Our synthesis thus approaches the real degradations induced by cataract haze (e.g., brightness/contrast/halo) and vitreous opacity (dark hole + blur). Real paired data are future work.
2.R1-W2: Efficiency & reproducibility. Training and deployment costs differ: 96 GB is for training only; deployment uses ~10 GB on a 24 GB RTX 4090, ~100 ms per image. This is because WaveDE needs only one forward pass (Sec. 2), not iterative diffusion, and the two teachers are dropped at inference (Sec. 2.3). Training details: Sec. 3.1.3.R1-W3: Ablation of G. We agree this would help. The closest existing evidence is w/o FD in Tab. 1 (which removes G together with FD-Block), giving ~2 dB PSNR drops across all subsets. A w/o G ablation is left for future work.
4.R1-W4: VMamba choice. VMamba is task-specific. The LF expert’s global corrections need long-range modelling with preserved spatial structure. CNNs lack long-range capacity; Transformers have weak inductive bias for local structure; VMamba’s 2D selective scan provides both, fitting the task.
5.R1-W5, R3-W1, R3-W3: Data leakage & HQ-exposure bias. Two measures: (i) strictly disjoint splits with no overlap between any training stage (enhancement, ACR teachers, downstream evaluators) and any test split; (ii) WaveDE still ranks first on OOD sets whose HQ images were unseen in training, indicating no HQ-exposure bias. The OD teacher uses Chákṣu/SMDG from the enhancement training split only; the vessel teacher uses DRIVE, LES-AV, TREND, DRHAGIS, all disjoint from our experimental datasets.
6.R1-W6: PraNet, weights, and coefficients. PraNet’s reverse attention refines weak boundaries, matching our OD-preservation goal. The spatial coefficients (1+10σ for vessels, 1+5σ for OD; Eq. 7) are task-aware: higher for sparse vessels, lower for the compact OD. Global weights λ_v=0.01, λ_od=0.04 (Eq. 8) were tuned on the validation set. 
7.R2-W1, R3-W2: Downstream protocol. Downstream models — classification: ConvNeXt-Tiny; segmentation: U-Net++ (vessels), PraNet (OD). All trained with AdamW (lr=1e-4, cosine annealing, 100 epochs) using each model’s official loss. Segmentation models reuse ACR teachers’ architectures but train on disjoint data (R1-W5). Identical protocol across methods: each downstream model is trained once on HQ and frozen; enhanced outputs from all methods are tested on the same frozen model—no retraining.
8.R2-W2: Baseline selection. Our baselines cover both SOTA fundus enhancement methods (MDA, OTE, GFE) and methods from related fields whose algorithms are suitable for fundus enhancement; methods relying on modality-specific mechanisms (e.g., algorithms targeting CT/MRI-specific noise) are excluded. Against SOTA fundus methods alone, WaveDE still leads by 4.66–9.24 dB PSNR (Tab. 1).
9.R2-W3: Direct analysis of LF/HF experts. We agree this would help. As indirect evidence, Tab. 1 (w/o FD) shows Local artifact and Blur benefit most, and Fig. 2 shows our model attains the smallest LF and HF residuals. An LF/HF discussion will be added in the camera-ready. We will explore w/o LF and w/o HF ablations in future work.
10.R3-W4: Failure cases. We acknowledge this omission. From Tab. 1, the most apparent relative weakness is the colour subset, where WaveDE’s PSNR (33.73 dB) trails other subsets (39+ dB). This failure mode will be discussed in camera-ready.

title: WaveDiT: Distribution-Aware Wavelet Flow Matching for Efficient 3D Brain MRI Synthesis
abstract:
Large and demographically balanced datasets are essential for reliable neuroimaging biomarkers. Full-resolution 3D brain MRI synthesis can support data augmentation in this setting, but existing approaches either incur prohibitive computational cost at volumetric scale or rely on lossy latent compression that may compromise anatomical detail. As a result, practical 3D generative augmentation often requires specialized compute infrastructure.
We propose WaveDiT, a conditional flow matching framework operating in the coefficient space of a 3D Haar Discrete Wavelet Transform. The model combines factorized spatio-depth attention with band-wise heteroscedastic uncertainty modeling derived from higher-order wavelet statistics. Predicted log-variance is integrated directly into both the flow objective and conditioning pathway, enabling adaptive precision consistent with the heavy-tailed and input-dependent variance structure of anatomical detail. This formulation supports full-resolution 3D synthesis under practical memory and time constraints on a single modern GPU.
Evaluation on a multi-site cohort demonstrates improved alignment between generated and real MRI distributions, together with enhanced downstream brain age prediction and region-level anatomical agreement relative to diffusion, latent, and wavelet-based baselines.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper studies 3D medical image generation with a wavelet-based DiT under a flow matching formulation. The authors make three main contributions. First, they introduce a 3D WaveDiT framework that models volumetric data in the wavelet domain. The design is motivated by an empirical analysis showing that different wavelet bands exhibit highly different energy distributions and statistical evolution during flow matching. Based on this observation, the method is designed to handle low-frequency and high-frequency components in a more adaptive way. Second, following this, the paper proposes an uncertainty-aware Morpheus module, to estimate band-wise uncertainty. The module conditions on frequency statistical features of the current state xt​ to adaptively adapt their Bayesian heteroscedastic objective. Third, to further make transformer modeling practical for 3D volumes, the paper adopts an efficient slice attention design. In shallow layers, they use window attention to capture local high-frequency structures, while deeper layers combine intra-slice attention and cross-slice attention to preserve both details and anatomical consistency across slices. They evaluate their model, termed WaveDiT-CFM, on image generation, brain age prediction using the generated volumes, and ROI analysis, and the results consistently demonstrate its strong performance.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper is generally well written and easy to follow. The motivation is clear, and the overall framework is reasonably presented. 
2.The paper studies a meaningful problem in 3D medical image generation, i. e. , how to generate high-quality 3D volumes efficiently while keeping the training complexity manageable. The overall design, combining wavelet modeling, uncertainty-aware optimization, and efficient attention, is thoughtful and well motivated. 
3.The method contains some interesting technical designs. In particular, the analysis of wavelet-band statistics during flow matching provides reasonable support for the band-aware design, and the uncertainty-aware conditioning is also a novel part of the framework. 
4.The experimental evaluation is fairly comprehensive. In addition to image generation results, the paper also includes brain age prediction and ROI analysis on generated volumes, which makes the evaluation more convincing.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The overall framework contains several components, so it is sometimes not easy to fully understand the contribution of each individual design choice. In addition, the introduction of several advanced modules makes the paper a bit harder to follow in some parts. These aspects could be further clarified with more detailed analysis if possible. 
2.The uncertainty-aware formulation is interesting, but its role could be better discussed. In particular, it would be helpful to further explain how the learned uncertainty contributes to the final improvement.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper is well written and studies a meaningful problem in 3D medical image generation, namely how to generate high-quality 3D volumes efficiently while keeping the training complexity manageable. The overall framework is technically sound, and the combination of wavelet modeling, uncertainty-aware optimization, and efficient attention design is thoughtful and well motivated. The experimental evaluation is also fairly comprehensive, covering not only image generation quality, but also brain age prediction and ROI analysis on the generated volumes.
My main concerns are relatively minor. Since the framework contains several components, it is sometimes difficult to fully disentangle the contribution of each design choice, and some parts could be explained more clearly. I also think the role of the uncertainty modeling could be further analyzed.
Overall, I am positive about the paper and think it is worthy of acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The paper presents
WaveDiT
, a generative framework for efficient full-resolution
3D brain MRI synthesis
that operates in the coefficient space of a
single-level 3D Haar discrete wavelet transform (DWT)
. The central motivation is that existing 3D MRI generative approaches face a trade-off between fidelity and computational efficiency: pixel-space diffusion models are costly for volumetric data, while latent diffusion methods reduce cost at the expense of lossy compression that may compromise anatomical detail. Wavelet-domain methods avoid learned compression artifacts, but previous works generally treat all wavelet subbands uniformly, despite their markedly different statistics.
The main methodological contribution has two tightly coupled parts:
1.
Wavelet-domain conditional flow matching for 3D MRI synthesis.
The model uses a conditional flow matching formulation in wavelet space rather than diffusion in voxel space or latent space. The use of wavelets preserves invertibility while reducing spatial resolution, allowing the model to synthesize full-resolution 3D MRI under practical memory and runtime constraints. The paper further extends the Hourglass Diffusion Transformer (HDiT) design to volumetric data by introducing a computationally efficient
factorized spatio-depth attention
mechanism. The volume is processed as a sequence of 2D slices for spatial modeling, and inter-slice consistency is restored by explicit depth attention. This avoids the prohibitive cost of full 3D global self-attention while preserving volumetric coherence.
2.
Morpheus: state-aware uncertainty modeling in the wavelet domain.
A key novelty is the observation that wavelet subbands exhibit strongly different and time-varying distributions along the generative trajectory: the approximation band remains relatively close to Gaussian, whereas high-frequency bands are sparse, heavy-tailed, and highly heteroscedastic. To exploit this, the authors propose
Morpheus
, a lightweight auxiliary network that predicts
band-wise log-variance
from higher-order wavelet statistics of the current noisy sample state, including mean, standard deviation, max absolute value, L2 norm, skewness, and kurtosis. The predicted uncertainty is used in two ways: 1) to define a
Bayesian heteroscedastic flow objective
that adaptively reweights errors according to predicted precision, instead of applying uniform MSE across all bands and locations; 2) to provide
frequency-aware conditioning
to the backbone, enabling the model to adapt its predictions to the current reliability and complexity of each wavelet band during both training and inference.
Experimentally, the paper shows that this combination improves both
efficiency
and
quality
. WaveDiT generates full 3D MRI in about
1 second with 10 steps
on a single modern GPU, while outperforming diffusion, latent diffusion, and prior wavelet/flow baselines in:
global distribution metrics (FID, MMD),
downstream
brain age prediction
when synthetic data are used for augmentation,
and
ROI-level anatomical fidelity
measured by region-wise intensity error, KL divergence, and Dice overlap.
Overall, the paper’s main contribution is a
distribution-aware, wavelet-domain flow matching framework for practical and anatomically faithful 3D brain MRI synthesis
, with explicit modeling of the heteroscedastic and heavy-tailed structure of wavelet coefficients.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.
Well-justified use of the wavelet domain.
The paper makes a convincing case for why wavelets are attractive for 3D MRI synthesis: they reduce spatial dimensionality while preserving invertibility and avoiding learned compression artifacts. This is especially relevant in neuroimaging, where subtle cortical and anatomical details matter. The empirical analysis showing that the approximation band contains most energy, while high-frequency bands are sparse and heavy-tailed, provides a solid statistical basis for the proposed design.
2.
Efficient architecture for full-resolution 3D synthesis.
The proposed factorized spatio-depth attention is practically important. Full 3D self-attention at this resolution would be infeasible, and the paper provides a concrete complexity analysis demonstrating large computational savings. The design—local 2D neighborhood attention at higher resolution and deeper factorized spatial/depth attention—appears sensible and aligned with volumetric anatomy.
3.
Strong practical efficiency.
A notable strength is that the method supports
full-resolution 3D generation on a single H100 GPU
, with training in about
26 hours
and inference in about
1 second for 10 steps
. In this problem domain, practical accessibility is a meaningful contribution, since many high-quality 3D generative methods remain difficult to use outside highly specialized compute settings.
4.
Comprehensive evaluation beyond standard generative metrics.
The evaluation is stronger than many generative imaging papers because it does not rely only on FID-like metrics. The authors follow a
multi-level evaluation protocol
:
global distributional alignment (FID, MMD, MS-SSIM),
a clinically relevant downstream task (
brain age prediction
),
and
ROI-level anatomical analysis
using segmentation-based metrics.
This is important because global image metrics can miss anatomically meaningful errors. The ROI and downstream analyses make the empirical case substantially more convincing.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.
The uncertainty model is relatively coarse.
Morpheus predicts
band-wise
log-variance from global summary statistics per channel rather than finer-grained spatial uncertainty. Given that heteroscedasticity is argued to vary strongly across space, especially near tissue boundaries, a spatially resolved uncertainty model might be more faithful to the stated motivation. The current design is elegant and lightweight, but potentially limited. The paper does not deeply analyze whether band-wise uncertainty is sufficient compared with more localized alternatives.
2.
Evaluation remains limited to one modality and one task setting.
The study focuses only on
T1-weighted brain MRI
. This is a reasonable starting point, but it limits generalizability. It is unclear whether the gains would transfer to:
other MRI contrasts,
pathological populations,
or other 3D medical imaging modalities such as CT.
The authors acknowledge this limitation.
3.
Potential concern about downstream evaluation interpretation.
The brain age prediction improvement is interesting, but the causal interpretation should be made carefully. Better augmentation performance does not necessarily imply that the generated images are clinically realistic in all relevant respects; it may partly reflect task-specific regularization or data balancing effects. The paper is reasonably cautious, but this point is worth emphasizing.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses an important and practical problem: efficient, anatomically faithful
full-resolution 3D brain MRI synthesis
. Its strongest aspects are:
a well-motivated
wavelet-domain formulation
,
a novel
state-aware uncertainty module (Morpheus)
that is integrated into both the loss and conditioning,
an efficient
factorized spatio-depth transformer architecture
,
and a
strong empirical evaluation
that goes beyond standard image-generation metrics by including brain age prediction and ROI-level anatomical analysis.
I found the paper technically solid and empirically convincing. The method appears to deliver a meaningful improvement in the quality-efficiency trade-off, especially under a low-step sampling regime and practical single-GPU constraints. The ablations also support the central design choices.
The main reasons I do not score it higher are:
some aspects are
incremental relative to recent wavelet-based MRI generation papers
, especially WDM [Friedrich et al., 2024] and FlowLet [Danese et al., 2025];
several building blocks are adapted from prior work, so the novelty is more in the integration and domain-specific design than in a fundamentally new generative principle;
the validation is currently limited to
T1-weighted brain MRI
, without expert human assessment of realism.
Overall, however, I think the paper makes a useful and timely contribution to medical image generation, and the empirical evidence is strong enough to justify acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes WaveDiT, a conditional flow-matching framework for efficient full-resolution 3D brain MRI synthesis in the wavelet domain. The method combines a 3D Haar DWT representation, a factorized spatio-depth DiT backbone, and a Morpheus module for state-aware heteroscedastic uncertainty modeling. The goal is to improve full-volume 3D MRI synthesis under practical memory and inference constraints.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in scalable 3D brain MRI synthesis, where voxel-space diffusion is expensive and latent compression may lose anatomical detail. The wavelet-domain formulation is well motivated, and the analysis of band-wise statistics provides a reasonable basis for the Morpheus uncertainty module. The paper also includes many relevant baselines, ablations, efficiency comparisons, and downstream evaluations such as brain age prediction and ROI-level anatomical analysis.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The main weakness is the evaluation protocol. Although the paper is framed as a 3D medical image synthesis method, it does not report commonly used image synthesis metrics such as PSNR, SSIM, or LPIPS, making it difficult to assess voxel-level fidelity and perceptual image quality. The authors argue that global volumetric metrics can be biased by background voxels, but this does not fully justify omitting foreground-masked or ROI-based PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS comparisons. In addition, the downstream brain age prediction result may not directly reflect synthesis fidelity, since improved BAP performance could come from distributional or demographic augmentation rather than anatomically accurate image generation. Finally, the model is still relatively large, around 142M parameters, and requires an H100 for training, which somewhat weakens the claim of broad accessibility despite its faster inference.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This work presents a technically interesting and reasonably well-motivated framework for efficient 3D brain MRI synthesis. The wavelet-domain modeling, factorized spatio-depth attention, and heteroscedastic uncertainty module are coherent, and the comparisons with diffusion, latent, and flow-based baselines are fairly strong. However, I am not fully convinced by the evaluation protocol. For a medical image synthesis paper, the absence of standard image-quality metrics such as PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS is a significant limitation, even if additional distributional and downstream metrics are provided. Overall, the method is promising, but the evaluation should be more complete and the claims about synthesis quality should be better supported.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

meta_reviews.text: This paper presents a technically interesting and well-motivated framework for efficient 3D brain MRI synthesis. The problem is meaningful, and the proposed combination of an HDiT backbone with the Morpheus state-aware uncertainty scheduler is promising. Also, the paper is well-written, and the evaluation is fairly comprehensive. The main concerns are the absence of standard image-quality metrics, such as PSNR, and the need for a more detailed analysis of the individual model components. The authors should carefully address these points, along with the other concerns raised by the reviewers, in the final version.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their thoughtful and constructive feedback.
R2
(W1) “Several components … difficult to disentangle individual contributions.”
Each component corresponds to a distinct design axis isolated in the ablations: Voxel-space (representation), w/o Morpheus (uncertainty), RFM/OTFM/CFM (flow objective). The architecture mirrors two distinct observations: local HF structure (neighborhood attention) and cross-slice consistency (spatio-depth attention). We will make this mapping explicit.
(W2) “Role of uncertainty.”
Morpheus contributes through both loss reweighting (Eq.1) and conditioning, introducing band-wise precision aligned with the heteroscedastic statistics of wavelet subbands. Its removal degrades global (FID, MMD), downstream (BAP), and ROI metrics simultaneously (Tables 2b, 3), indicating a structural rather than cosmetic contribution.
R3
(W1) “Band-wise uncertainty is coarse.”
The dominant heteroscedasticity is between bands (Table 1), spanning up to 90x in kurtosis, which motivates a band-wise formulation. Dense voxel-wise uncertainty at 224^3 would require a decoder comparable to the backbone, undermining efficiency. Spatial selectivity is nonetheless captured implicitly through:
conditioning on higher-order moments,
local neighborhood attention focusing on high-frequency regions,
AdaRMSNorm modulation, which translates band-wise signals into spatially adaptive activations.
(W2) “Evaluation limited to T1w brain MRI.”
We agree, and this is explicitly acknowledged in Sec. 4.T1 is the standard benchmark in the existing 3D MRI generative literature, enabling direct comparison with prior work. We will extend the framework to other modalities.
(W3) “BAP gains may reflect distributional effects rather than anatomical realism.”
The ROI metrics in Table 3 are designed for exactly this concern. Unlike BAP, iMAE, KLD, and Dice are computed on independently segmented regions and are insensitive to demographic balancing. WaveDiT-CFM is best across all ROI metrics together with BAP.
R4
(W1) “Absence of PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS is a limitation.”
We appreciate this point and clarify our methodological position. WaveDiT addresses age-conditional synthesis, not reconstruction: each sample is drawn from p(x|age) with no one-to-one correspondence to any real volume, so paired PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, are not well-defined in our setting. The closest paired analogue already in Table 2 is intra-set MS-SSIM, designed precisely to avoid this issue.
To engage the concern directly, we conducted an intra-cohort, age-matched study over 500 within-cohort pairs. The real reference is PSNR 15.93 ± 1.48 dB, SSIM 0.715 ± 0.030, LPIPS 0.204 ± 0.035.The aim is not to maximise these metrics but to match the real cohort’s own intra-similarity distribution, so deviations acquire a diagnostic interpretation: positive ΔPSNR with negative ΔLPIPS signals mode collapse (pairs too self-similar); negative ΔPSNR with stable SSIM/LPIPS points to additive noise or artefacts; strongly negative ΔLPIPS with otherwise normal PSNR/SSIM indicates perceptual collapse.
WaveDiT-CFM is closest to the real reference on all three metrics: ΔPSNR = +0.76 dB, ΔSSIM = +0.004, ΔLPIPS = −0.020.By contrast, MOTFM exhibits mode collapse (ΔPSNR = +5.10, ΔLPIPS = −0.077), MD homogeneous collapse (ΔPSNR = +4.13, ΔLPIPS = −0.044), and MLDM perceptual collapse (ΔLPIPS = −0.105) despite a “normal” PSNR/SSIM.
(W2) “BAP improvement may not reflect synthesis fidelity.”
See R3(W3): ROI metrics (Table 3) measure anatomical consistency independently of demographic effects, and WaveDiT-CFM leads across all of them.
(W3) “142M parameters and H100 weaken accessibility.”
WaveDiT runs in ~12 GB VRAM at batch size 1 (e.g., 4060ti). The H100 was used only for hardware parity across baselines, since WDM, MLDM, and BS exceed 24-48 GB at full resolution. At 142M parameters WaveDiT is the lightest full-resolution 3D MRI generator among the compared models.

title: Wavelet-Enhanced Coarse-to-Fine Radiology Report Generation with Large Language Models
abstract: Automatic chest X-ray report generation requires models to capture fine-grained visual evidence and describe findings within clinical context. Existing approaches often entangle global structure and local details, making subtle cues prone to attenuation during compression and cross-modal alignment. Most frameworks also rely on single-image inputs and underuse patient priors, limiting their ability to reflect diagnostic intent and disease evolution. We propose Wavelet-Enhanced Radiology Report Generation (WERG), a clinically motivated coarse-to-fine framework built on a multimodal large language model that supports joint conditioning on clinical context and prior images. WERG generates an initial draft, retrieves observation-aligned report snippets as textual priors, and refines the report with enhanced visual evidence. Moreover, we introduce a wavelet-based frequency-domain detail enhancement module to emphasize subtle abnormalities while preserving global semantics, and a diagnosis-guided calibration branch trained with weak observation labels. Experiments on MIMIC-CXR and IU X-Ray show consistent gains on NLG and clinical metrics, producing more detailed and clinically consistent reports.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces WERG, a framework for radiology report generation that utilizes wavelet transforms to enhance high-frequency visual details and a retrieval mechanism to inject clinical priors. The method aims to solve the problem of subtle detail loss during feature compression. Experiments show it achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MIMIC-CXR dataset in both language generation and clinical accuracy metrics.
reviews.text_strengths:
(1) The use of wavelet transforms to explicitly separate and amplify high-frequency visual details is a technically solution to the common problem of “detail attenuation” in medical image analysis. 
(2) The combination of visual enhancement with the RRKE retrieval module creates a strong coarse-to-fine generation pipeline that logically aligns with clinical diagnostic reasoning. 
(3) The results are impressive, setting a new benchmark on the MIMIC-CXR dataset with significant gains in clinically relevant metrics.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
(1) The “Related Work” is insufficient. The introduction fails to adequately contrast WERG with recent LLM-based medical generators. Please explicitly discuss how your wavelet method differs from other visual enhancement techniques in recent literature. 
(2) The ablation study is confusing. Since DGVFC depends on FDE, testing “FDE alone” is misleading. Please restructure the ablation to test the combined visual enhancement block (FDE+DGVFC) against the baseline for clarity. 
(3) The IU X-Ray evaluation is weak. Testing in a zero-shot setting without fine-tuning makes comparison difficult. Please either fine-tune on IU X-Ray or provide a stronger justification for the zero-shot approach. 
(4) Figure 2 lacks visual proof. The qualitative examples need bounding boxes or zoomed insets on the X-rays to prove the model is actually detecting the “subtle cues” mentioned in the text.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
There are grammatical issues. For example, “phrase findings under clinical context” in the abstract is awkward. A thorough language edit is recommended.

The manuscript requires significant revisions to strengthen the ablation studies, clarify the methodological dependencies, and improve the presentation of qualitative results before it can be considered for publication.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: After reading the rebuttal, I think the authors addressed most of the major concerns reasonably well. In particular, they clarified the motivation and role of the FDE+DGVFC modules, explained the ablation design more clearly, and acknowledged the issue with inconsistent clinical metrics in the comparison table. The response on the IU X-Ray zero-shot setting was also reasonable and consistent with prior work.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper focuses on the automatic report generation of the chest X-ray. It proposes a coarse-to-fine framework WERG which is built on the multimodal LLM. In the framework, it combines four important parts: retrieval-augmented text priors (RRKE), wavelet-based frequency-domain visual enhancement (FDE), and diagnosis-guided feature calibration (DGVFC). Most of the experiments on MIMIC-CXR and IU X-Ray show consistent and relatively improved performance, while gains on n-gram overlap metrics such as BLEU-1 and ROUGE-L are relatively modest.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.Clinical Relavance: This paper focus on the automatic generation of the X-ray report. The framework it proposes tries to generate finer reports with consistency and accuracy. And this application can truly reduce the radiologists’ documentation burden and make the radiology workflow more consistent.
2.Methodological novelty: The framework it proposes is different from the one-pass methods of LLM generation in the past. It adds three components in the architecture: report retrieval, wavelet-based frequency-domain detail enhancement, and diagnosis-guided visual feature calibration.
3.Experimental effort: The paper finishes experiments on two public chest X-ray benchmarks, MIMIC-CXR and IU X-Ray. The baselines /competitive models it chooses are all reasonable and proper. The ablation study design is also complete to prove every new components’ contributions.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The paper is of generally good quality, but several aspects would benefit from further clarification and discussion.
1.The combination of RRKE, FDE, DGVFC is reasonable, but the components are not particularly novel in isolation. Wavelet decomposition for feature enhancement has been explored in visual representation learning (like Wave-ViT, ECCV 2022), and retrieval-augmented report generation has been studied in the work like PromptMRG (AAAI 2024). The contribution therefore lies primarily in their integration, which could be positioned more explicitly and justified more carefully. 
2.The cross-dataset results on IU X-Ray are a little bit mixed. WERG achieves the best MTR and R-L but falls below the strongest baselines on B-4, and the authors’ explanation that prior-guided refinement introduces paraphrasing and sentence reordering is qualitative and not empirically verified. This makes the generalization benefit less convincing, especially since IU X-Ray is used in a zero-shot setting and only a limited set of metrics is reported there. A more systematic analysis of when and why the refinement stage degrades n-gram precision would strengthen the paper.
3.Clinical Usability: The sensitivity of retrieval quality to the size and domain of this database, as well as potential data privacy concerns in clinical settings, are not addressed. (But this point is relatively less important in the weakness considering the limitation of the paper pages.)
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I think this paper is relevant and technically reasonable, especially it tries to integrate wavelet-based visual enhancement with retrieval-augmented generation into a multimodal LLM. The experiment results on MIMIC-CXR are good, and the ablation study provides evidence for the proposed modules. 
However, my overall score is mainly limited by concerns regarding the limited novelty of individual components, the mixed performance on IU X-Ray. But I still look forward to authors’ feedback and would like to give higher scores if I can receive more detailed explanation from the authors.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I support acceptance. The paper is technically reasonable and clinically relevant, although some concerns remain. In the final version, the authors should make the novelty claim more modest, discuss the IU X-Ray metric inconsistency more carefully, and add a clearer limitation/privacy discussion for the retrieval module.

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper proposes WERG, a coarse-to-fine multimodal-LLM framework for chest X-ray report generation. The model conditions on the current CXR, optional clinical context, and prior images, then refines an initial draft using retrieved report priors (RRKE), a wavelet-based frequency-domain detail enhancement module (FDE), and diagnosis-guided visual feature calibration (DGVFC). The main intended contribution is to improve fine-grained finding coverage and clinical consistency, especially for subtle abnormalities and comparison-aware reporting.
reviews.text_strengths:
S1.Clinically meaningful problem setting.
The paper addresses a clinically meaningful problem setting by incorporating the current image, optional clinical context, and prior studies, which are relevant for comparison-aware chest X-ray reporting.
S2.The main technical novelty is in FDE/DGVFC.
The most distinctive part of the paper is the visual-side design in Sec. 2.3–2.4: frequency-domain detail enhancement (FDE) and diagnosis-guided visual feature calibration (DGVFC). This is the clearest novel aspect of the submission. 
S3.The paper includes a reasonably complete evaluation package.
The submission reports results on MIMIC-CXR and zero-shot IU X-Ray, includes ablations, and provides qualitative examples.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
W1.The paper has some novelty in FDE/DGVFC, but the overall methodological novelty is limited.
From Sec. 1 and Sec. 2.1–2.2, WERG is presented as a broad coarse-to-fine, diagnosis-aware, retrieval-augmented multimodal-LLM framework, but the paper does not clearly separate inherited ideas from the actual new contribution. Diagnosis-aware prompting already appears in PromptMRG [1], retrieval/knowledge-augmented LLM report generation is already explored in KACL [2] and RADAR [3], and knowledge-enhanced LLM report generation is already explored in KARGEN [4]. After a strict reading, the part that appears genuinely new is mainly FDE/DGVFC, and that novelty does not feel strong enough to support the broader novelty claim of the full pipeline. Also, RADAR [3] is cited in the introduction but omitted from the comparison table despite being one of the closest baselines. 
W2.The experimental comparison could be strengthened; the comparison set is incomplete, the criteria for ensuring a fair evaluation are not explicitly defined, and some clinical metrics appear non-comparable.
WERG’s Table 1 presents its MIMIC-CXR METEOR = 0.347 as the highest among the listed baselines, but the paper does not explain that several strong recent MLLM baselines with substantially higher METEOR are omitted. In RADAR [3], the MIMIC-CXR comparison includes LLaVA-Med [5] (0.353), MAIRA-1 [6] (0.333), MAIRA-2 [7] (0.420), Libra [8] (0.489), and RADAR [3] itself (0.450). Without discussing such baselines, the current table gives an incomplete picture of the recent literature. In addition, the paper does not state that baselines were re-run under a unified protocol, so preprocessing, report-section choice, tokenization, and evaluation details may differ across papers. A further concern is the KARGEN 0.203 entry: KARGEN reports 0.203 as RadGraph F1 [9], whereas WERG labels the clinical columns as CheXbert-style Precision/Recall/F1 [10]. Ultimately, the use of disparate metrics in the same comparison prevents a fair assessment of the results, thereby limiting the overall credibility and interpretability of the clinical validation section.
W3.The ablation study is not strong enough to support the claimed contribution.
In Table 3, DGVFC is only evaluated together with FDE, so its individual contribution is not isolated. There is also no comparison against a simpler enhancement baseline. As a result, the paper shows that the full stack helps, but not that the specific wavelet-based design is necessary. 
W4.Reproducibility is weak.
The paper does not provide code, and the method description is not detailed enough for reliable reproduction. In Sec. 2.1–2.4, the exact instantiated vision backbone/LLM is not clearly specified, and key details remain vague, including the retrieval classifier g(⋅), the label space used in RRKE/DGVFC, the rule for “relatively less emphasized” sentence selection, and the training/loss details for the full model. This makes the results difficult to audit and hard to reproduce. 
References
[1] Jin, H., Che, H., Lin, Y., Chen, H.: PromptMRG: Diagnosis-Driven Prompts for Medical Report Generation. In: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, pp. 2607–2615 (2024).
[2] Sha, Y., Pan, H., Meng, W., Li, K.: Contrastive Knowledge-Guided Large Language Models for Medical Report Generation. In: Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention – MICCAI 2025, LNCS, pp. 111–120.Springer, Cham (2025).
[3] Hou, W., Cheng, Y., Xu, K., Li, H., Hu, Y., Li, W., Liu, J.: RADAR: Enhancing Radiology Report Generation with Supplementary Knowledge Injection. In: Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, pp. 26366–26381 (2025).
[4] Li, Y., Wang, Z., Liu, Y., Wang, L., Liu, L., Zhou, L.: KARGEN: Knowledge-enhanced Automated Radiology Report Generation Using Large Language Models. In: Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention – MICCAI 2024, LNCS, vol. 15005, pp. 382–392.Springer, Cham (2024).
[5] Li, C., Wong, C., Zhang, S., Usuyama, N., Liu, H., Yang, J., Naumann, T., Poon, H., Gao, J.: LLaVA-Med: Training a Large Language-and-Vision Assistant for Biomedicine in One Day. In: NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks (2023).
[6] Hyland, S.L., Bannur, S., Bouzid, K., Castro, D.C., et al.: MAIRA-1: A Specialised Large Multimodal Model for Radiology Report Generation. arXiv preprint arXiv:2311.13668 (2023).
[7] Bannur, S., Bouzid, K., Castro, D.C., et al.: MAIRA-2: Grounded Radiology Report Generation. arXiv preprint arXiv:2406.04449 (2024).
[8] Zhang, X., Meng, Z., Lever, J., Ho, E.S.L.: Libra: Leveraging Temporal Images for Biomedical Radiology Analysis. Findings of ACL, pp. 17275–17303 (2025).
[9] Jain, S., Agrawal, A., Saporta, A., Truong, S.Q.H., Duong, D.N., Bui, T., Chambon, P., Zhang, Y., Lungren, M.P., Ng, A.Y., Langlotz, C.P., Rajpurkar, P.: RadGraph: Extracting Clinical Entities and Relations from Radiology Reports. In: NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks (2021).
[10] Smit, A., Jain, S., Rajpurkar, P., Pareek, A., Ng, A.Y., Lungren, M.P.: Combining Automatic Labelers and Expert Annotations for Accurate Radiology Report Labeling Using BERT. In: Proceedings of EMNLP, pp. 1500–1519 (2020).
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

While the paper introduces some technical novelty via FDE/DGVFC, the overall contribution feels thin compared to recent work, and the empirical results aren’t robust enough to support acceptance.
1.Limited Novelty
The high-level pipeline is very similar to existing diagnosis-aware and retrieval-augmented frameworks like PromptMRG, KACL, RADAR, and KARGEN. Once you look past the standard coarse-to-fine MLLM setup, the only truly new component is the visual enhancement/calibration module.
2.Experimental Flaws
Missing Baselines: The authors claim a METEOR advantage but ignore several top-tier MLLM baselines (like LLaVA-Med, MAIRA-1/2, and Libra) that actually report much higher scores on MIMIC-CXR.
Unfair Comparison: There’s no mention of a unified protocol for the baselines. Without knowing if the preprocessing, tokenization, and metric computation were standardized, the comparison isn’t reliable.
Metric Confusion: The clinical table seems to mix apples and oranges—listing RadGraph F1 for KARGEN alongside CheXbert metrics for WERG. These aren’t interchangeable.
3.Reproducibility
The paper is quite hard to follow from an implementation standpoint. There’s no code, the specific LLM backbone isn’t named, and key details—like the retrieval classifier, the RRKE/DGVFC label space, and the specific loss functions—are left vague.
Because the novelty is limited and the evaluation is inconsistent, I don’t believe the paper is ready for publication in its current state.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
The reviewers recognize the clinical importance of automating radiology report generation and find the technical approach—specifically the use of wavelet transforms for detail enhancement—to be a promising direction. However, there are significant concerns regarding the fairness of the experimental comparisons and the clarity of the paper’s specific contributions.
The authors must provide direct and data-driven responses to the following points to avoid a rejection:
Completeness of Literature and Baselines: Reviewers noted that several recent, high-performing models (e.g., RADAR, MAIRA-1/2, Libra) were omitted from Table 1.You must explain these omissions or update your comparison to include these state-of-the-art results to prove the superiority of WERG.
Inconsistent Metrics: Clarify the clinical evaluation metrics. Reviewer #3 pointed out a potential “apples-to-oranges” comparison where CheXbert metrics were compared against RadGraph F1 scores from other papers. Please provide a unified metric comparison.
IU X-Ray Evaluation: Address why the IU X-Ray results were presented in a zero-shot setting and why certain n-gram metrics (like B-4) dropped compared to baselines.

The authors have clearly clarified the issues raised by the reviewers. The explanations in the rebuttal look reasonable and correct to me.

The reviewers agree that the paper has clinical relevance and technical merit, with promising integration of wavelet-based visual enhancement and retrieval-augmented generation in multimodal LLMs. Some concerns were raised about the limited novelty of individual components, experimental inconsistencies, and insufficient implementation details, which are addressed in the rebuttal.

The paper is recommended for acceptance after considering the rebuttal and discussion among Reviewers.
The rebuttal successfully addressed several major concerns, particularly regarding the metric inconsistency and experimental settings, which improved reviewer confidence in the results. While some questions remain regarding the degree of methodological novelty, the consensus is that these concerns are not sufficient to outweigh the paper’s contributions and empirical validation.
For the final version, the authors are encouraged to moderate the novelty claims, provide a clearer discussion of the IU X-Ray metric issue, and expand the discussion of limitations, particularly regarding the retrieval module and potential privacy considerations.
I recommend Accept. I also suggest that the authors revise the novelty discussion and limitations section in the camera-ready version.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the Meta-Reviewer (MetaR) and all reviewers (R) for their constructive feedback. We respond below organized by key themes. 
1.Contribution & Methodological Novelty (R2W1, R3W1) WERG formulates radiology report refinement as jointly constrained by textual priors and fine-grained visual evidence. Existing methods provide textual guidance but lack precise visual support. WERG unifies textual priors, frequency-domain visual enhancement, and diagnostic semantic calibration, enabling observation-level priors and enhanced visual cues to jointly guide report refinement. We introduce wavelet-based enhancement (FDE) to explicitly separate low-frequency structure and high-frequency details, enhancing boundaries, textures, and local density cues before LLM decoding. DGVFC aligns these enhanced features with diagnostic semantics, improving grounding for report refinement. This integration addresses weak synergy in prior RRG pipelines, forming a targeted, clinically relevant solution rather than a simple stack of modules. 
2.Ablation & Module Justification (R1W2, R3W3, R1W1) Ablation analyses clarify each module’s contribution. Table 3 compares the baseline, FDE-alone, and FDE+DGVFC. FDE+DGVFC consistently improves BLEU-4/METEOR/ROUGE-L (+0.008/+0.013/+0.003) and CE Precision/Recall/F1 (+0.010/+0.128/+0.075) over the baseline. FDE-alone serves as a control to ensure wavelet enhancement preserves base visual representation. Compared to FDE-alone, DGVFC further improves recall by 0.108 without reducing precision, indicating enhanced coverage of positive observations. Wavelet decomposition is necessary: CXR report generation requires both global structure and high-frequency details, which are more controllably enhanced than with unconstrained feature learning. FDE is not generic frequency decomposition: high-frequency sub-bands are fused as residuals and low-frequency components modulate channels, preserving global semantics while enhancing fine-grained evidence for LLM refinement. 
3.Experimental Protocol & Dataset Settings (MetaR, R1W3, R2W2, R3W1, R3W2) We follow prior work for zero-shot IU X-Ray evaluation (PromptMRG AAAI’24; DDaTR TMI’25), noting that the standard IU test split may be unsuitable for disease-aware metrics. Comparisons use example-based CE; consistent with top-tier papers (HSA MICCAI’24; DCL CVPR’23), we cite and fairly compare recent methods. For KARGEN, we acknowledge an oversight and will remove its clinical entry while keeping NLG metrics. Reported IU X-Ray performance differences (e.g., lower BLEU-4) can arise from wording variability despite correct diagnostic predictions, as noted in prior work. Higher METEOR/ROUGE-L indicates improved semantic coverage and robustness to distribution shift.Missing comparisons (MAIRA-1/2, Libra) were excluded due to clear differences in model scale(7B vs our 3.8B). RADAR reproduction under controlled settings did not outperform WERG, making direct inclusion unfair. 
4.Clinical Significance & Qualitative Visualization (R3W1, R1W4) WERG targets real intrapartum CXR scenarios, supporting observation-level report refinement and clinically relevant measurements. We will enhance Figure 2 with bounding boxes to improve interpretability. The method’s alignment of textual priors and fine-grained visual evidence ensures outputs are semantically and diagnostically coherent, supporting clinical applicability. 
5.Reproducibility, Related Work, & Language (R3W4, R1W1, R1) We will release full implementation details, code, and model weights upon acceptance to facilitate reproducibility. Due to space, not all recent LLM-based RRG models are compared in the main paper, but we will include discussion of LLaVA-Med, MAIRA-1/2, and Libra in the final version. We will thoroughly polish the manuscript language for clarity. 
6.Data Privacy & Retrieval (R2W3) We acknowledge the concern regarding retrieval and data privacy and will add discussion of privacy-aware retrieval in the final version.

title: Wavelet-Guided Spectral–Spatial Learning for Medical Hyperspectral Image Segmentation
abstract: Medical Hyperspectral Imaging (MHSI) provides rich pixel-level biochemical information and has demonstrated strong potential in computational pathology. However, the high spectral dimensionality and strong inter-band redundancy make effective spectral–spatial representation learning challenging. Most existing methods encode spectra as flat channel-wise features or tokenized sequences, without explicitly modeling their intrinsic multi-scale structure. To address this limitation, we propose a wavelet-guided spectral–spatial segmentation framework for MHSI. By performing one-dimensional wavelet decomposition along the spectral dimension, we explicitly separate global biochemical trends and local spectral variations. Instead of replacing the original spectrum, the low-frequency component is incorporated as a structural prior via a per-pixel adaptive scalar gate, stabilizing deep spectral learning. Furthermore, we introduce Band-Aware Aggregation and Spectral-Enhanced Skip Connections to enhance spectral–spatial interaction in the decoding process. Extensive experiments on public medical hyperspectral datasets demonstrate that our method consistently improves segmentation performance compared with state-of-the-art methods. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Junya99/Wavelet-Guided-MHSI.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a novel wavelet-guided framework for spectral-spatial segmentation of medical hyperspectral images. Instead of using the wavelet transform as a preprocessing step, the model reparameterizes spectral representations in the wavelet domain and incorporates a gated low-frequency structural prior for spectral modeling.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper is highly relevant, is well-written and easy to follow.
The proposed pipeline is evaluated against the state-of-the-art on two different medical hyperspectral image segmentation datasets through quantitative benchmarking and shows superior performance.
A detailed ablation study reveals the contribution of the different components of the design to the performance of the framework.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The following are not major weaknesses as such, but are still worth addressing.
The font size of the text in the figures is too small and makes interpretation on A4/letter paper (almost) impossible.
The “additional boundary supervision term” is mentioned for the training loss without further specification. A clarification would be appropriate.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper is well-motivated, is detailed and clearly written, and presents convincing experimental results. I think this is a valuable contribution to the field.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors convincingly addresses major concerns in their rebuttal.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes a wavelet-guided spectral-spatial framework for medical hyperspectral image segmentation. Its main contribution is to use low-frequency wavelet components as an adaptive structural prior for spectral modeling, together with Band-Aware Aggregation and Spectral-Enhanced Skip Connections to improve spectral-spatial interaction during decoding.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper addresses an important representation issue in medical hyperspectral image segmentation, namely that spectral signatures are multi-scale but are often modeled as flat channel-wise features or tokenized sequences. This motivation is clear and relevant.
The wavelet-guided design is interesting. Using the low-frequency wavelet component as an adaptive structural prior, rather than as a simple preprocessing step or full replacement of the spectrum, is a reasonable and technically meaningful contribution.
The experimental results are solid. The method is evaluated on two public medical hyperspectral datasets and shows consistent improvement over strong CNN, Mamba and Transformer-based baselines.
The ablation study is a strength. It supports the choice of residual LF integration, the db2 basis, and the proposed decoding modules, which makes the paper more convincing.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The methodological novelty is moderate. The paper combines wavelet decomposition, attention-based spectral modeling, and U-Net-like decoding modules, and the main novelty is in how these components are integrated rather than in a fundamentally new formulation. The paper itself cites prior wavelet-based MHSI work and recent wavelet-guided hyperspectral deep models.
The empirical gains are relatively modest. This is especially true on the MOD dataset, where the improvement over the strongest baseline is small.
The paper does not provide enough analysis of computational cost or scalability. Since medical hyperspectral data are high-dimensional, runtime, memory use, and comparison of efficiency would strengthen the practical value of the method.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper is technically sound, well organized, and shows improvement on medical hyperspectral segmentation benchmarks with a reasonable methodological contribution. However, the novelty is moderate, the gains are not large, and the clinical validation remains limited.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal addresses my points reasonably. The authors clarify that the novelty is the use of the LF component as a pixel-adaptive gated structural prior inside the network. They also explain the smaller gain on MOD by its lower spectral richness, and provide useful efficiency clarifications, including parameter count and the small runtime contribution of the 1D wavelet operation. The rebuttal addresses Reviewer #1’s questions about figure readability and the boundary supervision term, and it addresses Reviewer #3’s concerns about fair baseline retraining and inference latency. Some limitations remain, especially the incremental nature of the contribution and limited clinical validation. However, the method is technically sound, the evaluation on MDC and MOD is solid, and the ablation study supports the roles of residual LF guidance, db2, BAA, and SESC.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper introduces a method to decompose hyperspectral signatures using 1D wavelet transform, separating low-frequency (global biochemical trends) and high-frequency (local spectral variations), rather than treating spectra as flat channels or tokens. The obtained low-frequency part is used as a per-pixel gated structural prior to guide and stabilize deep spectral feature learning. In addition, Spectral-Enhanced Skip Connections and Band-Aware Aggregation modules have been explored to improve how spectral information is propagated and fused, enabling adaptive band-wise feature reweighting during reconstruction. Experiments on public datasets demonstrate that the proposed method improves segmentation performance compared with SoTA methods.
reviews.text_strengths:
The paper proposes to use 1D wavelet transform to decompose hyperspectral signatures instead of treating spectra as flat tokens, aiming to physically separate global biochemical trends from local variations, mimicking professional signal processing.
The employment of low-frequency components as a per-pixel gated structural prior potentially anchors the deep learning process, providing stability and reducing noise interference.
The used Spectral-Enhanced Skip Connections and Band-Aware Aggregation possibely addresses the specific challenges of hyperspectral data, such as inter-band redundancy and the need for adaptive feature reweighting.
The proposed model outperforms State-of-the-Art (SoTA) benchmarks, proving that modeling the intrinsic multi-scale structure of spectra yields measurable performance gains.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
While the paper frames the use of 1D wavelet transforms as a key contribution, the decomposition of hyperspectral signatures into multi-scale components (low vs. high frequency) is a long-standing technique in the field.
The paper claims superiority over State-of-the-Art (SoTA) methods, but it leaves several critical questions unanswered regarding the experimental setup. There is no indication if the SoTA models were retrained from scratch using the same hardware, optimizer, and data splits. If the authors compared their results against the reported numbers in original papers, the comparison is likely invalid due to differences in preprocessing, spectral calibration, and augmentation strategies. It is unclear if the SoTA models were given the same level of hyperparameter optimization as the proposed method, which often leads to baseline bias.
The introduction of specialized modules like Band-Aware Aggregation (BAA) and Spectral-Enhanced Skip Connections (SESC) inevitably increases the network’s parameter count and operations. Without reporting MACs, Parameters (M), and Throughput (FPS), it is impossible to determine if the performance gains are due to the wavelet-guided intelligence or simply because the model is significantly larger/deeper than the SoTA baselines.
For medical applications (especially real-time pathology), latency is a critical constraint. The 1D wavelet transform adds a preprocessing step that, while mathematically simple, must be accounted for in the total inference pipeline.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper presents a technically sound wavelet-guided framework for MHSI segmentation, effectively utilizing 1D wavelet decomposition to separate global biochemical trends from local spectral noise. The inclusion of specialized modules like Band-Aware Aggregation demonstrates a sophisticated approach to handling inter-band redundancy.
However, the technical novelty is incremental, wavelet transforms are long-established in HSI, and the evaluation lacks critical transparency. Specifically, the absence of computational cost metrics (MACs/throughput) and confirmation of fair baseline retraining leaves the practical clinical utility unverified.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: While the technical novelty is somewhat incremental, the paper presents a solid and well-designed framework for MHSI segmentation with effective integration of wavelet decomposition and band-aware modeling. Overall, the work provides meaningful empirical and application value to the medical HSI community.

This submission proposes a wavelet-based segmentation of MHI images. The reviews are found constructive and converges on concerns on moderate novelty (integrating established components), on modest gains to chosen baselines, serious readibility issues (sizes in figures), but note a solid validation. For these reasons, the recommendation is towards requesting a rebuttal.

The reviewers has reached a consensus on recommending acceptance. The rebuttal has resolved the initial concerns about novelty and computational efficiency.
While the technical novelty is somewhat incremental, the paper presents a solid and well-designed framework. All reviewers recommended acceptance.

All three reviewers now recommend acceptance after rebuttal. The rebuttal effectively clarifies the core novelty, addresses efficiency and fairness concerns, and resolves minor clarity issues. Some limitations remain, mainly the incremental nature of the contribution and limited clinical validation, but the method is technically sound, empirically well supported, and of clear interest to the medical HSI community.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank all reviewers and the AC for their constructive and detailed feedback. We appreciate the following encouraging comments: “well-written and easy to follow…convincing experimental results” [R1]; “The wavelet-guided design is interesting…is a reasonable and technically meaningful contribution” [R2]; “sophisticated approach to handling inter-band redundancy” [R3].
R1Q1 (Clarity) 
A: We acknowledge the readability issue and will increase the font size of all figures in the revised version to ensure clarity.
R1Q2 (Boundary supervision term)
A: The boundary supervision term is an auxiliary loss applied to the predicted edge map and combined with the segmentation loss. The boundary target is automatically generated from the ground-truth mask and requires no additional annotations.
R2Q1 & R3Q1 (Novelty)
A: We respectfully clarify that we do not claim the wavelet decomposition itself as the novelty. The key contribution is how the LF spectral component is used inside the network. Here, we integrate the LF component into the network as a pixel-adaptive gated structural prior for spectral representation learning, which is significantly different from prior MHSI wavelet work only used as external preprocessing for denoising or compression. The ablation study (Table 2) further suggests that this improvement does not arise from a naive combination of components, since directly using LF features or simple LF+HF fusion yields weaker performance than the proposed residual LF guidance design. The final improvement comes from the specific residual LF guidance together with decoder-side spectral propagation through BAA and SESC. Thus, the novelty lies in spectral representation learning for clinical MHSI segmentation.
R2Q2 (Performance on the MOD)
A: We agree that the gain on MOD is relatively modest compared to MDC, which is reasonable given their characteristics: MOD contains only 16 spectral bands and 138 imaging scenes, while MDC has 60 spectral bands and 538 scenes. Since our method is designed to exploit structured spectral information, the advantage is naturally more visible on the richer MDC dataset. Nevertheless, the method still obtains the best IoU, DSC, and HD on MOD (Table 1), indicating robustness of the method rather than dataset-specific overfitting. To our knowledge, this is also one of the first dense segmentation studies on the recently released MOD dataset (2024).
R2Q3 & R3Q3 (Efficiency and scalability)
A: Although explicit efficiency metrics were not reported, Table 2 (row 6) already shows that the proposed framework outperforms strong baselines even before BAA and SESC are introduced, indicating that the primary gain comes from the wavelet-guided LF prior rather than increased model complexity alone. In fact, the proposed model has slightly fewer parameters (26.61M) than the original baseline (FSS, 27.06M), since the heavier low-rank module is replaced by lightweight feature refinement modules (BAA/SESC) operating on grouped features and skip pathways, rather than introducing additional heavy global modeling modules.
R3Q2 (Fair baseline comparison)
A: We’d like to confirm that all compared methods were re-implemented and retrained from scratch under an identical experimental protocol, including the same data splits, preprocessing pipeline, and data augmentation strategies. All methods were given comparable hyperparameter tuning effort to ensure a fair comparison. All trained model weights are stored, and the reported results can be consistently reproduced under our implementation.
R3Q4 (Inference latency)
A: We’d like to clarify that the wavelet transform in our framework is not an external preprocessing step, but an internal differentiable operation integrated into the network forward pass. Runtime profiling shows that the proposed 1D wavelet operation contributes only 1.1% of the total forward time. The transform itself uses fixed spectral filters and introduces negligible additional overhead.

title: wBCAM: Windowed Bi-directional Cross-Attention with Mamba for Enhanced 3D Vascular Reconstruction in Free-Hand Photoacoustic and Ultrasound Imaging
abstract:
Integrated photoacoustic and ultrasound (PAUS) imaging has significant potential in clinical applications due to its ability to provide complementary pathological information. By integrating a standard 1D-array US transducer with laser fibers, PA images can be acquired for vascular disease assessment. However, reconstructing 3D vascular structures remains challenging due to intrinsic limitations. While additional hardware, such as a motorized stage or motion tracker, can sequentially align image frames in 3D space, these approaches introduce additional costs and operational constraints.
To overcome this limitation, we propose a free-hand PAUS framework based on windowed Bi-directional Cross-Attention with Mamba (wBCAM) for scan motion estimation and 3D US volume reconstruction. Given sequential PAUS frames, the model first encodes adjacent frame pairs into temporal local tokens. Using overlapping sliding windows, wBCAM performs local-to-global cross-attention that writes spatial evidence from local tokens into a set of learnable global tokens. The global tokens are then updated across windows using a Mamba-based selective state-space module, enabling sequential motion memory and long-range temporal reasoning. Subsequently, global-to-local cross-attention feeds back the updated global context to refine local representations within each window.
The proposed method is validated on dynamic in-vivo datasets acquired from the human forearm. Both quantitative and qualitative results demonstrate accurate motion estimation and high-resolution 3D reconstruction of vascular structures. The source code of this study is publicly available at (https://**.).

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The main contribution is a sensor-free free-hand 3D PAUS reconstruction framework that adapts recent sensorless freehand US trajectory-estimation ideas to the PAUS setting, where stable long-range motion estimation is especially important because small trajectory errors visibly break vascular continuity. The paper’s specific technical contribution is the proposed wBCAM architecture: consecutive B-mode frame pairs are encoded with a ViT-style encoder, processed in overlapping temporal windows, written into learnable global tokens through local-to-global cross-attention, updated with a Mamba state-space module, and then fed back to local tokens via global-to-local cross-attention before relative/window/sequence-level motion regression. This is meant to explicitly model long-range dependencies and reduce accumulated drift. 
A second contribution is the application framing: unlike earlier sensorless work focused mainly on freehand 3D ultrasound reconstruction, this paper targets 3D PA vascular reconstruction from free-hand PAUS without external tracking during inference, which is clinically interesting because PA is more sensitive to motion inconsistency in thin vascular structures. The paper also contributes an in-vivo human forearm evaluation with both PAUS and US datasets, using EM-sensor trajectories as supervision during training/testing.
reviews.text_strengths:
The strongest aspect is the good problem choice. Free-hand 3D PAUS without external tracking is clinically meaningful and technically harder than ordinary freehand US reconstruction because broken trajectory consistency directly degrades 3D vessel continuity. The paper explains this motivation clearly and the qualitative figures on page 8 support that the task matters. 
A second strength is that the method is reasonably well matched to the stated failure mode. The paper argues that frame-to-frame/local methods drift over long sequences, then proposes a design that explicitly couples local evidence with global memory. That architectural logic is coherent: local frame-pair tokens preserve discriminative short-range motion cues, while global tokens plus Mamba provide a mechanism for longer-range temporal consistency. The multi-level heads for relative, window, and full-sequence motion are also sensible for this task. 
A third strength is the empirical pattern of results, especially on absolute metrics. On the US dataset, wBCAM is best on all absolute metrics; on the PAUS dataset it is again best on all absolute metrics, even though it is not best on relative metrics. That pattern is consistent with the paper’s central claim that the method mainly helps by suppressing accumulated drift rather than by maximizing short-range alignment. The ablation also supports that global tokens, windowing, and token regularization each contribute incrementally. 
A fourth strength is the translation toward PAUS rather than only ultrasound. Prior sensorless freehand 3D reconstruction literature is mostly ultrasound-focused, including early deep learning approaches by Prevost et al. and DCL-Net, later online/self-supervised variants, IMU-assisted models, and more recent local+global or Mamba-based US reconstructions. Extending this line into free-hand PAUS and showing actual reconstructed vascular volumes is valuable.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The biggest weakness is limited methodological novelty relative to recent freehand US reconstruction literature. The paper’s individual ingredients are close to existing trends:
sensorless freehand 3D reconstruction itself is not new, going back at least to Prevost et al. 2018 and DCL-Net 2020.
explicit local/global context for sensorless 3D ultrasound is already central in DualTrack (2025).
Mamba/state-space modeling for long-range freehand 3D ultrasound reconstruction was already used in FiMA (MICCAI 2024), which explicitly argues for SSMs to mine long-range spatiotemporal information.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I would place this paper at Weak Accept because it addresses a meaningful translational problem, proposes a technically coherent architecture, and shows a convincing empirical advantage on the metrics that matter most for long-sequence 3D reconstruction, namely the absolute drift-sensitive metrics and qualitative vascular continuity. The PAUS application angle is also a real plus.
What prevents a higher score is that the contribution feels incremental relative to very recent sensorless freehand US literature. FiMA already introduced Mamba/SSM-based long-range modeling for freehand 3D reconstruction, and DualTrack already emphasized joint local/global context. So the paper’s novelty lies more in the exact architectural synthesis and the PAUS use case than in a fundamentally new idea.
Also, the validation is still limited to forearm data and does not yet fully demonstrate robust clinical generalization. So overall I see this as a solid and relevant paper, but not yet a top-tier standout.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors addressed well to the comments

This work builds upon previous work by first extending the participant pool to 19 volunteers, second by training a network to incorporate both US and PA images to improve on the 3D registration, and third by introducing a new framework wBCAM offering greater robustness across both short- and long-distance motion inaccuracy.
reviews.text_strengths: The methods are described clearly, and the results are compelling. Combined with the code that will be released digitally, I have no doubt others could reproduce the work. In a limited number of places, the text is a little short on detail. Specifically:
Section 2.1, the beamformer algorithms for both US and PA have not been described or defined
The PA acquisition was stated at 10 FPS, but what was the acquisition rate for US? The text confirms this was higher, allowing for more accurate pose estimation, but not HOW much higher.

reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors’ rebuttal addresses the primary concerns raised in my initial review.
They provided a technically justification for the discrepancy between the relative and absolute metrics. In continuous trajectory estimation, prioritizing long-range stability (absolute metrics) over myopic frame-to-frame alignment (relative metrics) is indeed the correct approach to minimize cumulative drift. Since 3D vascular topology is highly sensitive to this accumulated drift, their design trade-off is well-justified.
The rebuttal also clarified the architectural novelty, differentiating wBCAM from FiMA and DualTrack. Using Mamba strictly to propagate compact global-memory tokens across windows while preserving attention-based local motion estimation demonstrates a thoughtful, problem-specific design rather than a naive “plug-and-play” backbone replacement.
Since the authors have logically defended their design choices and clarified the methodological distinctions, I am upgrading my score to recommend acceptance.

All reviews are positive after rebuttal, and the remaining concerns have been adequately addressed. The authors clarified the key methodological points, provided useful implementation details, and the reviewers’ final opinions now support acceptance.
