author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for their constructive comments. We address the main concerns below.
Method novelty (R1,R4)
Prior sensor-free freehand 3D reconstruction exists (Prevost’18, DCLNet’20). Our contribution is a long-range trajectory modeling mechanism for drift-sensitive 3D PAUS vascular reconstruction. Unlike DualTrack (separate local/global streams + fusion), wBCAM uses learnable global tokens as structured motion memory, iteratively written/read via windowed bi-directional cross-attention (L2G/G2L), enabling unified local/global modeling and drift suppression. Unlike FiMA (SSM on backbone features), wBCAM uses Mamba only to propagate compact global-memory tokens across windows while preserving attention-based local motion estimation. This design explicitly targets cumulative trajectory inconsistency that degrades long-range vascular continuity in freehand 3D PAUS reconstruction.
Relative vs. absolute motion (R3,R4)
We do not regress absolute poses independently. We compose predicted relative transforms to obtain the trajectory and compute absolute metrics against EM-tracker-derived ground truth. Better frame-to-frame metrics do not guarantee long-range stability: small but temporally biased/inconsistent step errors accumulate into drift. wBCAM enforces long-range consistency via windowed global-memory propagation, yielding better absolute metrics and more coherent 3D vascular reconstruction. This is particularly important in long freehand scans, where small but biased local errors accumulate and distort reconstructed vascular topology.
Fig. clarity / qualitative comparison (R2,R3,R4)
Fig. 3 overlays trajectories from multiple methods for space-efficient qualitative comparison; the legend was unintentionally omitted. In the US panels, the grayscale volume is the EM-tracker reference (“truth”) and colored curves are estimated scan trajectories. In Fig. 3, yellow, purple, blue, green, and red trajectories correspond to DCL-Net, MoGLo-Net, DualTrack, FiMA, and the proposed wBCAM, respectively. We will add legends/scale bars in Fig. 3 and clarify arrow numbers (processing order) in Fig. 2.
Acquisition/beamforming details (R2)
US/PA images use delay-and-sum (DAS) beamforming; US additionally uses envelope detection and log compression for B-mode, whereas PA is reconstructed as initial-pressure maps without log compression. The PAUS sequence operates at 10 Hz (20 Hz laser PRF with interleaved full-aperture acquisition). The US-only dataset was acquired at 20 Hz (no laser).
Split / bias (R2)
The 12:3:4 ratio is subject-level (12/3/4 subjects out of 19). All scans from a subject belong to a single split; test subjects are disjoint from train/val, so within-subject similarity cannot bias test performance.
EM tracker comparison (R2)
Quantitative evaluation against EM ground truth is reported in Table 1, and Fig. 3 provides a trajectory-overlay comparison; we will make the EM reference and legend explicit.
Missing citations (R3)
We will add representative citations for DL-based frame-to-frame motion estimation/registration.
Method details (R3)
Temporally enhanced tokens V are produced by temporal self-attention applied after GAP (GAP → temporal self-attention → V); we will label this block and V in Fig. 2/caption. ViT encodes adjacent frame pairs (not the full sequence as channels). We will explicitly state hyperparameters (M=16, N=65 with random sub-sequences of length 64, w=16) and loss weights (λ1, λ2, λ3).
3D vascular metrics & code (R3,R4)
We agree there is no dedicated quantitative metric on 3D vasculature; since 3D continuity is primarily governed by accumulated pose error, EM-GT motion metrics serve as a surrogate and are supported by consistent trajectory overlays and preserved vascular continuity in Fig. 3.Future work will validate geometry using external 3D references (e.g., CTA/MRA). The URL was redacted for double-blind review; we will expand implementation details and release code upon publication.

title: Weakly-Supervised Coronary Artery Segmentation from DSA Sequence via Motion-Aware Modeling
abstract:
Accurate coronary artery segmentation from Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA) is critical for computer-aided cardiovascular diagnosis and intervention.
In DSA, contrast wash-in provides characteristic temporal perfusion cues, i.e., vessels progressively enhance over time, which can help distinguish true vessels from dark non-vessel tubular structures and improve recognition under low-contrast conditions by comparing neighboring frames.
However, exploiting such cues is non-trivial, as cardiac motion introduces non-rigid vessel deformation and misalignment across frames.
Clinically, radiologists typically review the entire dynamic injection process, but measure only a single key frame where the vessel is maximally opacified.
Based on this observation, we present \textbf{MACOS}, a \textbf{M}otion-\textbf{A}ware \textbf{CO}ronary \textbf{S}egmentation framework that leverages long-range temporal injection context to supervise segmentation only on a key frame with maximal opacification.
Specifically, we first propose a Motion-Aware Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) module to explicitly estimate inter-frame displacement fields to align features before aggregation, thus enabling robust spatiotemporal modeling under cardiac motion.
Then, to leverage unlabeled intermediate frames, we further introduce a Physics-Informed Vessel Loss to enforce monotonic vessel growth driven by contrast wash-in, for providing effective regularization without requiring dense annotations.
Experiments on 971 DSA sequences demonstrate that MACOS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, improving robustness on typical challenging cases.
To the best of our knowledge, MACOS is the first framework to exploit long coronary DSA sequences for weakly-supervised vessel segmentation with only key-frame annotation, and is validated on the largest coronary DSA video dataset to date.
Code is available at .
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents a weakly supervised framework for coronary artery segmentation in digital subtraction angiography (DSA). The method leverages temporal information from DSA sequences to improve segmentation performance without requiring additional annotations. Specifically, the framework uses preceding frames in the sequence to guide the segmentation of the final frame. The authors introduce a Motion-Aware Gated Recurrent Unit that models inter-frame misalignment caused by cardiac motion by estimating displacement fields, which are then used to align frames during segmentation. In addition, the method incorporates a physics-informed loss that penalizes the disappearance of vessel regions after alignment, thereby promoting more consistent vessel representation across frames. The contribution is supported by component-wise ablation studies and evaluation on a relatively large dataset of 971 angiography sequences, with comparisons against state-of-the-art methods demonstrating improved segmentation performance.
reviews.text_strengths:
Clear: The paper is well structured, with a clear presentation of the motivation, method, and results.
-Methodological contribution: The proposed weakly supervised framework leverages temporal information in DSA sequences, with well-motivated components to address motion and vessel consistency without requiring additional annotations. It is evaluated on a large dataset, outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, and is supported by an ablation study demonstrating the contribution of its main components.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Novelty positioning: The claim that this is the first work to explore long-sequence modeling for DSA vessel segmentation appears overstated, as Zhang et al. (2025, DOI: 10.1109/TMI. 2025.3540886) also proposed a spatio-temporal approach that leverages temporal information for this task. Authors should provide a discussion of this prior work and a more precise explanation of how the present method differs from it.
Limited discussion: Some parts of the paper would benefit from clearer explanation, particularly how the displacement fields are derived from the feature maps. Additionally, clarify why T=6 frames was selected, and include information on ethical approval.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
This paper is clear and well-structured. It introduces a weakly supervised framework for coronary artery segmentation in DSA, with a well-motivated use of temporal information to address motion and vessel consistency without requiring additional annotations. The evaluation is well described, using a large dataset, comparisons with state-of-the-art methods, and an ablation study that supports the contribution of the main components.
The paper would be strengthened by a more precise positioning of its novelty, particularly in relation to prior spatio-temporal work such as Zhang et al. (2025). In addition, some methodological details would benefit from clearer explanation, especially how the displacement fields are derived and why T=6 frames was selected. Including information on the ethical approval of the dataset would also be important for the completeness of the manuscript.

The paper introduces a weakly supervised framework for coronary artery segmentation in DSA. The use of temporal information is well justified, effectively addressing motion artifacts and ensuring vessel consistency without the need for additional annotations. The approach is technically sound, and the evaluation is robust, featuring a large dataset, thorough comparisons with state-of-the-art methods, and an ablation study that demonstrates the value of the main components.
While the paper would benefit from a more precise positioning of its novelty relative to prior spatio-temporal work and a clearer explanation of some methodological details, these issues do not outweigh the overall strengths of the submission.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_ethics: There is no information on the ethical review board for the dataset.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents a weakly supervised coronary artery segmentation framework for DSA sequences, where only the maximally opacified key frame is annotated while the full sequence is used for learning. The main contribution is a motion-aware long-sequence modeling framework (MACOS) that explicitly estimates inter-frame displacement fields for feature alignment before temporal aggregation, together with a physics-informed vessel loss that exploits monotonic vessel enhancement during contrast wash-in to regularize unlabeled intermediate frames. The method is validated on a relatively large DSA dataset and shows consistent improvements over strong single-frame and sequence-based baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper addresses a clinically meaningful and practically relevant setting: in DSA, clinicians inspect the whole injection sequence but annotations are typically available only on a key frame.
2.The method is well motivated. Explicit motion compensation is appropriate for coronary DSA, where cardiac motion causes non-rigid deformation and simple temporal aggregation can blur vessel structures.
3.The physics-informed vessel loss is intuitive and tailored to the imaging process, leveraging contrast wash-in dynamics without requiring dense frame annotations.
4.The experimental study is reasonably comprehensive, including comparisons with CNN, Transformer, Mamba, and sequence-based baselines, as well as component ablations and temporal configuration analysis.
5.The reported results are strong and consistent across multiple metrics, and the qualitative examples suggest improved robustness on challenging low-contrast and motion-affected cases.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The methodological novelty is moderate rather than truly substantial. The core design combines motion estimation/warping with recurrent temporal aggregation and a monotonicity-based regularization term; while effective, the individual components are conceptually incremental.
2.The physics-informed monotonic vessel growth assumption may not always strictly hold in real clinical DSA due to varying injection dynamics, local contrast propagation patterns, catheter/view changes, or severe motion/artifacts. The paper would benefit from a more careful discussion of failure cases and assumption violations.
3.Although the paper reports strong segmentation metrics, it provides limited analysis of the motion module itself. For example, there is no quantitative evaluation of alignment quality, no visualization of estimated motion fields in difficult cases, and no comparison with stronger motion-aware/video segmentation alternatives.
4.The experimental validation could be strengthened by reporting cross-center generalization more explicitly, clarifying whether data from the two centers differ substantially in acquisition protocol, and showing stratified performance or leave-one-center-out results.
5.Reproducibility is currently limited in the manuscript. Important implementation details such as exact sampling strategy, sequence normalization/preprocessing, model complexity/inference cost, and code availability are not yet sufficiently detailed for full reproducibility.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper addresses a clinically relevant and practically meaningful weakly supervised setting for coronary DSA segmentation. The proposed framework is technically sound, the motivation for motion-aware long-sequence modeling is clear, and the empirical results are consistently better than strong baselines. In particular, the gains over both single-frame and prior temporal models suggest that explicit motion compensation is useful in this setting.
My main reservations are about the level of novelty and the depth of validation. The technical contribution is somewhat incremental, and the paper would be stronger with more detailed analysis of failure cases, motion estimation quality, and cross-center generalization. Nevertheless, I find the work solid overall, and the combination of clinical relevance, method-task alignment, and strong experimental performance makes it worthy of acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The paper proposes MACOS, which leverages long-range temporal information from complete DSA injection sequences for weakly supervised coronary artery segmentation. The core contributions include MA-GRU and a Physics-Informed Vessel Loss. The problem setting is clinically motivated and the experimental scale is relatively large.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The temporal information during the contrast agent wash-in phase in DSA has indeed been largely overlooked by existing methods. Meanwhile, cardiac motion alignment represents a real and practical challenge, making the motivation well justified.
2.The dataset is relatively large in scale, which enhances the credibility of the results.
3.The experimental section employs a clear incremental ablation design, where components are progressively added, making the contributions of each module easy to interpret.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The dice improvement of MACOS over nnUNet is only 1.40%, with also overlapping standard deviations. But there’s no statistical test (e.g. Wilcoxon test) provided in the paper, so it is hard to determine whether the improvement is statistically significant or simply due to randomness.
2.The current monotonicity assumption only holds for the wash-in phase. How should violations of this assumption be handled during the wash-out phase (e.g., at the end of the sequence)?
3.MA-GRU is essentially a combination of ConvGRU, optical flow estimation and feature warping. There is already substantial similar work in video object segmentation (e.g., DEVA, Cutie). The paper lacks review or discussion of related work and does not clarify the differences from general motion-compensation approaches in video segmentation. The monotonicity constraint in the Physics-Informed Vessel Loss is conceptually simple and lacks comparison with temporal consistency losses from other domains. Also, the motion estimation network consists of only three 3x3 convolutional layers, which may be insufficient for handling non-rigid cardiac motion. The work provides no quantitative evaluation or visualization of motion estimation quality.
4.There are writing issues and inconsistent terminology: Contribution 2 refers to Global Motion Loss + Physics-Informed Vessel Loss, and Fig. 1 caption labels (b) Global Motion Loss. However, Section 2.5 defines the total loss L_total using only L_mot and L_phy, and Global Motion Loss is never formally defined. It is unclear whether these terms are equivalent.
5.In Table 1, “SVS-Net [15]” actually corresponds to reference [5] (Hao et al., 2020), not [15] (Yang et al., 2019), which is a single-frame method.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper proposes the MACOS framework for coronary artery segmentation from DSA, combining long-range temporal modeling with explicit motion compensation. The clinical motivation is well grounded, the dataset is among the largest for this task, and the ablation design is clear. These strengths support that the work has potential publication value. However, the main conclusions lack statistical testing, making it unclear whether the reported improvements are significant. Some technical details are insufficiently specified, although the authors state that the code will be released.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text:
This paper presents a weakly supervised framework for coronary artery segmentation in DSA that leverages temporal information and a physics-informed loss.
Reviewers agree the problem is clinically relevant and the proposed method is well-motivated and developed on a relatively large dataset, but note moderate novelty and missing validation details.
I suggest that the authors address the raised concerns, including 1) better position novelty against prior work, 2) provide statistical significance and stronger analysis, 3) clarify methods and fix inconsistencies, and 4) release code and models for reproducibility. Please also provide the necessary information on the ethical review board for the dataset.

title: Weakly-Supervised Temporal Decomposition with Graph Neural Networks for Parkinsonian Turning Assessment
abstract: Turning difficulty is an early and clinically significant indicator of Parkinson’s disease (PD). Skeleton-based approaches are already widely used in clinical movement analysis, as they offer a markerless and privacy-preserving representation of human motion from ordinary video. However, automated turning assessment from skeleton sequences remains challenging due to the temporal complexity of turning movements. Existing skeleton-based methods either treat the entire sequence globally, ignoring its inherent temporal structure, or require expensive frame-level phase annotations. We propose a weakly-supervised temporal decomposition framework that discovers discriminative temporal patterns from video-level diagnostic labels alone. The framework integrates a transition detector operating on motion gradients with spatial-temporal graph convolutional networks via learned soft masks, decomposing the turning sequence into multiple temporal instances with diagnostic relevance learned through attention aggregation. A learnable adjacency mechanism further adapts the skeleton graph to emphasize clinically relevant body connections. Decoupling boundary detection from the classification objective allows the learned phase structure to serve as an independent clinical interpretation, unbiased by diagnostic labels. Evaluated on the clinical PD dataset, our method achieves an AUC-ROC of 91.05% under 5-fold subject-level cross-validation, while providing interpretable outputs including instance-level importance weights and anatomical relevance maps consistent with clinical knowledge of Parkinsonian turning symptoms. The code is available at https://github.com/jieming1113/TempoDecompGCN-PD
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning
Special Topic -> Telemedicine & Mobile Health Imaging

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
Main contributions are:
1) weakly-supervised temporal decomposition framework
2) a dual-branch architecture
3) evaluation on a clinical dataset
reviews.text_strengths: The main strength of this paper is the proposed architecture, which introduces a novel and well-motivated approach to Parkinsonian turning assessment. The ablation study is clearly demonstrates the contribution of each component. The comparison with existing methods is also convincing, with the proposed method outperforming all baselines across all reported metrics.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Several comments on the text:
1) The terms task-specific and phase-specific temporal structure are central to the paper but never explicitly defined. Adding a short definition in the Introduction would help readers coming from a general ML background.
2) The term ‘phase boundaries’ is used in the Introduction before being formally defined in Section 3.2.I would suggest either adding a brief informal definition at first use in the Introduction, or at minimum a forward reference to Section 3.2.
3) In the Introduction, two consecutive sentences essentially say the same thing: ‘learning phase boundaries directly from video-level diagnostic labels alone’ and ‘without any frame-level supervision’ convey the same idea. I’d suggest merging these into one sentence to avoid repetition.
4) The claim that frame-level annotations are impractical in clinical settings is made in Related Work and then repeated again in Section 3.2.
5) The limitation of fixed skeleton topology (treating all joint connections equally) is only introduced in Section 3.3, but I think it would fit better in the Introduction alongside the global pooling limitation. This way readers understand from the beginning that the paper addresses both temporal and spatial rigidity in existing methods, which better reflects the full scope of the contribution.
More broadly, some motivational points are repeated across sections in slightly different wording. A careful pass to either consolidate or use forward/backward references would tighten the paper considerably.
6) What is the difference between the ST-GCN baseline in Table 1 (which achieves 61.71% AUC) and the ST-GCN method in Table 3 (69.94% AUC)? Should they be identical?

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses automated assessment of turning in Parkinson’s disease (PD) patients using 2D skeleton sequences extracted from video. The core challenge is that turning exhibits an inherent temporal structure that is clinically relevant, yet most existing methods either process the sequence globally or require expensive frame-level annotations of movement phases. The authors propose a weakly-supervised framework that decomposes the sequence into temporal instances via learned boundary scores derived from motion gradients. A diagnostic branch based on ST-GCN with adaptive adjacency and MIL-style gated attention aggregates instance-level representations into a video-level prediction. Evaluated on the REMAP clinical dataset with 1,294 sequences and 5-fold subject-level cross-validation, the method achieves 81.54% accuracy and 91.05% AUC-ROC, outperforming several baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The paper tackles a clinically relevant and well-motivated problem. Turning is a meaningful indicator in PD assessment, and skeleton-based analysis provides a practical and privacy-preserving representation.
The methodological contribution is clear and reasonably novel. The approach goes beyond standard temporal attention by explicitly discovering ordered temporal instances in a weakly-supervised manner and integrating them with GCN-based modeling. The decoupling of boundary learning from classification is conceptually interesting and supports interpretability.
3.The experimental evaluation is solid within scope. The paper includes meaningful ablations, comparisons with relevant baselines, and interpretability analysis. Performance improvements, especially in AUC-ROC, are substantial.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The interpretation of the discovered temporal instances as clinically meaningful phases is somewhat overstated. Boundary detection is driven only by sparsity and smoothness constraints, and classification loss does not influence boundary learning. While this supports interpretability claims, it does not strongly validate that the learned segments correspond to true biomechanical phases.
2.Reproducibility is moderate. While several experimental details are provided, important aspects remain unclear, including some hyperparameters, such as the weighting coefficients (λₛ and λₘ) of the auxiliary loss terms.
3.Evaluation is limited to a single clinical dataset. The authors acknowledge this limitation, but it still restricts the strength of conclusions regarding real-world clinical applicability and generalization.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Strengths include a clear methodological contribution and strong experimental performance. Weaknesses include limited validation scope, moderate reproducibility, and somewhat overstated interpretability claims. Overall, the strengths outweigh the weaknesses.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
After reading the rebuttal, I consider that the authors have satisfactorily addressed most of my main concerns. In particular, they clarified that the learned temporal segments should not be interpreted as validated biomechanical phases, but rather as soft temporal transition candidates/instances. This substantially mitigates my concern that the interpretability claims were overstated. The authors also addressed the reproducibility concern by providing the missing auxiliary loss weights, and they clarified the apparent discrepancy between the lightweight ST-GCN ablation baseline and the full ST-GCN architecture. These clarifications are satisfactory.
The main remaining limitation is the evaluation scope. Although the dataset contains a relatively large number of sequences, the rebuttal clarifies that these correspond to only 12 PD and 12 HC participants. The use of subject-level 5-fold cross-validation is appropriate and helps avoid data leakage, but the small number of subjects and the lack of severity-stratified analysis still limit the strength of the clinical generalization claims.
Overall, I consider that the rebuttal resolves the main methodological and presentation concerns, while the remaining limitations are acceptable.

meta_reviews.text:
There are some discrepancies among the three reviewers, consisting of one weak reject, one weak accept, and one accept. The main contributions of the paper include the proposed dual-branch weakly supervised temporal decomposition framework, that is evaluated on a clinical dataset with promising results. Meanwhile, there are a number of aspects of the work that raise concerns. It would be beneficial if the authors provide further input and clarifications in the areas specifically brought out by the reviewers, including but not limited to, how to ensure constrained training process in current system esp. by engaging the current loss functions, empirical studies of the statistical robustness aspect; details of the empirical evaluations; possibly overstated claims; reproducibility; improvement of the current presentation.

Most of the major concerns have been addressed by the rebuttal. That said, there remain concerns such as the limited number of subjects in dataset. The authors are encouraged to carefully follow the reviews and revise the draft accordingly, if it is eventually accepted by this MICCAI.

The paper deals with the automated analysis of the Parkinson’s disease turning assessment, which is a clinically well-motivated problem. Specifically, the authors have proposed a dual-branch architecture based on skeleton-based processing backbones.
The reviewers identified that this is an important and clinically motivated problem to be solved and appreciate the dual-branch architecture. However, several concerns were raised regarding the choice of the loss functions and how they relate to the main goal of the paper and most importantly the limited size of the dataset especially in terms of the number of subjects (only limited to 12PD and 12 healthy controls), which questions the generalzability and robustness and experimental validation of the claims of the proposed framework. Moreover, I also think that several major baselines in the general skeleton-based human activity understanding domain are missing - for instance HyperGCN (modeling skeleton sequences as a hypergraph). The authors built on the very old baselines of skeleton-based GCN processing where ST-GCN was one of the first baselines, but have not explored how more recent approaches compare to it. Thus, the gains presented by the authors may be due to the inherent incapability of methods like ST-GCN to extract relevant features necessary for this task.

After rebuttal, two reviewers are satisfied with the rebuttal. The authors have properly addressed most major concerns including interpretability, reproducibility and architectural discrepancy. Yet limited participant count and absence of severity-stratified analysis weaken clinical generalization. Overall, this is a good paper and the recommendation is Accept.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their thorough and constructive feedback. We address the major concerns below.
[Q1] Presentation suggestions (R1-W1–W5)
All five presentation suggestions will be addressed in the revision.
[Q2] Baseline vs full model of ST-GCN: Table 1 and Table 3 (R1-W6)
The “ST-GCN baseline” in Table 1 is our lightweight 2-block encoder, serving as the minimal ablation baseline (61.71% AUC). The “ST-GCN [27]” in Table 3 is the full Yan et al. architecture, trained under the same protocol (69.94% AUC). The 8.23% gap reflects this capacity difference, not an inconsistency; a clarifying footnote will be added.
[Q3] Training constraints and link between losses and motion saliency (R2-W1,W2)
The decomposition branch is architecturally decoupled, but its boundary estimates remain explicitly constrained. Boundary scores s(t) are computed from [f(t);Δf(t)], capturing motor state and motion change, and are constrained by a learnable position prior, temporally ordered K=3 masks, and L_sparse/L_smooth. The auxiliary losses suppress dense or fragmented detections. By design, non-differentiable boundary selection prevents L_cls from directly biasing boundary locations, preserving label independent transition discovery, while the resulting masks still serve as weights in mask-weighted pooling and ultimately determine the sequence representation used for classification. We will clarify this path and describe the learned regions as soft temporal transition candidates, not ground truth phases. The +5.93% AUC gain over fixed decomposition (Table 1, (p<0.01)) supports this design.
[Q4] Adaptive adjacency design (R2-W3)
Physical skeleton topology serves as an anatomically informed architectural prior, constraining learnable adjacency to anatomically valid connections, limiting parameter space on clinical-scale data and preserving interpretability of learned edge weights. We agree that non-local dynamics carry clinical value; capturing such interactions is a natural direction for future work.
[Q5] Statistical robustness (R2-W4)
All tables report mean±standard deviation across the same subject-level 5-fold CV. Table 1 already includes paired t-tests (
*p<0.01, **
p<0.001), confirming each component is statistically significant; the last row of Tables 2–3 is also statistically significant over all other configurations; significance notes will be added in the revision.
[Q6] Clinical characterization (R2)
Our evaluation uses the REMAP dataset. PD diagnosis followed the UK Brain Bank Criteria. The 1,294 sequences (773 PD, 521 HC) derive from 12 PD and 12 HC participants. H&Y=2.3±0.8 (entry criterion ≤3, mild-to-moderate PD); per-H&Y-stage breakdown is not reported. MDS-UPDRS III=36.8±23.0.A clinical summary will be added to Section 4.1.Subject-level 5-fold CV prevents data leakage; fold assignment was not stratified by severity score, as our framework operates solely on video-level diagnostic label; severity-stratified analysis remains future work.
[Q7] Interpretability claims (R3-W1)
We agree that the learned segments should not be interpreted as validated biomechanical phases. “Early/Mid/Late-Turn” are temporal-ordering names for soft instances, not frame-level phase annotations. Fig. 2 provides qualitative interpretation only: PD shows higher late-instance attention than HC (α₃=0.51 vs 0.36), and the anatomical map emphasizes lower-limb connections, consistent with prior PD turning/gait findings. We will replace “clinically meaningful phase boundaries” with “soft temporal transition candidates/instances” and state that direct frame-level phase validation remains future work.
[Q8] Reproducibility: missing hyperparameters (R3-W2)
Missing λ_s=0.05 and λ_m=0.1 will be added to Section 4.1; others are already reported. Code will be released upon acceptance.
[Q9] Single-dataset (R3-W3)
We acknowledge this limitation. REMAP is among the few public labeled datasets for PD turning assessment, and cross-cohort generalization remains future work.

title: When Brains Disagree: Biological Ambiguity Underlies the Challenge of Amyloid PET Synthesis from Structural MRI
abstract:
Structural MRI-to-amyloid PET synthesis has been proposed as a non-invasive alternative for amyloid assessment in Alzheimer’s disease (AD). However, reported performance of identical models varies widely across studies, and increasingly complex architectures have not led to consistent gains. This inconsistency is thought to be caused by a fundamental biological ambiguity: MRI captures neurodegeneration, while PET measures amyloid pathology - two processes that are often temporally decoupled in AD. As a result, similar MRI patterns may correspond to different amyloid states, creating ambiguous one-to-many mappings. MRI-to-amyloid PET synthesis may therefore be intrinsically ill-posed; however, this idea has yet to be tested scientifically.
The aim of this work is to test this hypothesis through two controlled experiments.
We first control the training distribution by stratifying paired MRI-PET data by amyloid and neurodegeneration status. Using two standard synthesis models under a controlled design, we show that biologically unambiguous mappings are learnable in isolation, but performance collapses when data ambiguity is introduced. This demonstrates that ambiguity in the data distribution, rather than architectural capacity, constrains performance.
Second, we show that introducing orthogonal biological information in the form of plasma biomarkers resolves this ambiguity. When multimodal inputs are incorporated, performance improves and stability is restored.
Together, these findings suggest that limited and inconsistent performance in MRI-to-amyloid PET synthesis is explained by intrinsic biological ambiguity, and that stable, meaningful progress requires multimodal integration rather than architectural complexity.

reviews.recommendation_label: Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
reviews.text_contribution: The paper uses controlled experiments to explore the extent to which an established medical image analysis problem—synthesis of amyloid PET scans from corresponding structural MRI scans—is actually solvable. Starting with a matched MRI-PET data set, they identify ambiguities, i. e. cases where similar MRI scans correspond to quite different PET scans. They show that removing such ambiguities from the training set improves synthesis performance by a lot. They then show that when you take the full data set with all of its ambiguities and then add relevant side information to the training process (i. e. , an alternative measure of amyloid status), effectively removing ambiguities in a different way, you improve synthesis performance. The conclusion is that in some sense this particular problem is fundamentally difficult to solve due to biological ambiguity, and therefore we are unlikely to make much progress on it simply by throwing ever-more-elaborate deep learners at the problem.
reviews.text_strengths: This is exactly the kind of paper MICCAI needs more of. We are forever formulating new problems and publishing a solution to that problem; leading to a cascade of other people trying to publish better solutions later on. No one seems to ask whether the problem was ever solvable to begin with; what the upper bounds of performance are. Answering the solvability question would tell us when new attempts to squeeze better performance out of a new algorithm are unlikely to be fruitful. Because the solvability question is rarely addressed, we waste untold person-hours on algorithms that are unlikely to push the field forward. This paper addresses solvability and that is commendable.
reviews.text_weaknesses: The only weakness I see is that the presentation of plasma Alzheimer biomarkers as “complementary” information to the amyloid PET scans is confusing. Blood and PET are different, that is true, but both of them are estimates of the same underlying biological construct which is brain amyloid burden. I would prefer the blood markers to be presented as a second measurement of amyloid rather than something that is truly “complementary. ”
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Sometimes the right work to do is the work that generates discussion. This paper does that, which is great. Keep up this kind of work please.

This is quite different from 90+% of submitted papers, almost all of which propose a specific algorithm to solve a specific problem. This paper is likely to generate significant discussion, and some pushback no doubt, because it is asking whether it is a waste of time to try to solve an established problem at all. We need that kind of discussion.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper investigates why MRI-to-amyloid PET synthesis has yielded inconsistent and often poor results across the literature. The primary hypothesis is that the fundamental problem is biological ambiguity: MRI captures neurodegeneration while amyloid PET measures amyloid pathology, and these two processes are temporally decoupled in Alzheimer’s disease, creating ill-posed one-to-many mappings.
To experiments conducted using ADNI data where
In experiment 1 the data is stratified by amyloid (A) and neurodegeneration (N) into concordant (A+/N+, A-/N-) and discordant (A+/N-, A-/N+) subsets. Two distinct architecture models (pix2pix GAN and latent diffusion) trained on these subsets achieved strong in-distribution performance but struggled with others.
In experiment 2, the imaging information was conditioned on the plasm biomarkers via FiLM modulation which show performance improvement in both models. This demonstrates that the synthesis limitation can be attributed to missing biological information rather than model architecture.
reviews.text_strengths:
This paper present an important, hypothesis-driven analysis of a popular neuroimaging problem of interest. Rather than proposing yet another synthesis model, it asks a fundamental question about why existing approaches fail and designs controlled experiments to answer it. The hypothesis is clearly stated, biologically grounded in established AD progression models, and testable.
The stratification into concordant and discordant training subsets cleanly isolates the effect of biological ambiguity. The two distinct model architecture further strengthen the argument for architecture-independence.
The large test set (n=1,720) with bootstrap confidence intervals provides statistically reliable estimates.
The concordant/discordant models achieving ~82–85% balanced accuracy in-distribution but collapsing out-of-distribution is strong evidence for the ambiguity hypothesis.
The paper is well-written with a logical flow from motivation to hypothesis to experiments to conclusions.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The N-intermediate cases, which likely constitute a substantial fraction of the data, are excluded from the stratified analysis but presumably included in the Baseline. How many subjects fall in the N-intermediate category?
For an apples to apples comparison in Experiment 2, it would be helpful to train/test the MRI-only model on exactly the same 589 pairs that have the plasma biomarkers and compare the results.
Similarly, the work would also benefit from training a plasma-only prediction model from completeness.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper provides a principled explanation for the wide performance variability reported across MRI-to-PET synthesis studies and offers a constructive path forward (multimodal integration rather than architectural complexity). This has practical value for researchers working in this space.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The content of this work focus on the usage of image generator, including GANs and diffusion models, to derive PET-amyloid images. The authors demonstrate that brain MR images are limited in generating synthetic PET-amyloid images, since some patients do not display visible anatomical neurodegeneration (detectable by MRI) associated with the deposition of amyloid plaques. 
To overcome this, they showed that by combing plasma markers related to amyloid plaques, it is possible to derive more accurate and reliable synthetic PET-amyloid. 
The experimental setup planned by the authors proves the point that spatial information derived from MRI may not be sufficient to derive accumulation of amyloid where neurodegeneration is not visible, regardless of the architecture and methods used.
reviews.text_strengths: The authors presented a well-organized experimental setup to prove their research questions. The concept of combining biomarkers and MRI images is not novel but it serves well the purpose of directing image generator to derive accurate images.
reviews.text_weaknesses: Some concepts presented are a little redundant. It is a bit questionable whether it is then needed to synthesize PET images when, maybe your information can be maybe derived by the blood markers already.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The setup of expriments presented by authors and prove their research question. The use of image generator while combing biomarkers is an interesting approach to obtain surrogate of anatomical and molecular information, but require further investigations.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.

meta_reviews.text: I will follow the decision of all the reviewers. R1 recommended a strong acceptance, while R2 and R3 recommended acceptance. Except of some minor fixable weaknesses the reviewers state that the the work is well-executed and statistically credible.

author_feedback_text:
We sincerely thank the reviewers for their very positive and constructive feedback. We are particularly pleased that the reviewers found the hypothesis and experimental design regarding the solvability of MRI-to-amyloid PET synthesis meaningful and well-supported. We also appreciate the reviewers’ valuable suggestions. We summarise our responses below.
R1: “the presentation of plasma Alzheimer biomarkers as “complementary” information to the amyloid PET scans is confusing”
Response: We agree that the wording could be clarified. Our intention was not to describe plasma biomarkers as complementary to amyloid PET, since both reflect the same underlying biological process. Rather, we meant that plasma biomarkers provide information complementary to structural MRI. We will revise the wording accordingly.
R2.1: “How many subjects fall in the N-intermediate category?” 
Response: A total of 447 subjects (36%) in the Baseline training and 672 subjects (39%) in the full test set fell into the N-intermediate category. These cases lie between the two neurodegeneration extremes and therefore contribute to ambiguity in a more continuous manner than our defined N-/N+. We verified that including or excluding these cases does not change the overall behaviour or conclusions of the study. Nevertheless, we retained them because they represent a substantial and clinically realistic portion of the data.
R2.2: “in Experiment 2, it would be helpful to train/test the MRI-only model on exactly the same 589 pairs that have the plasma biomarkers and compare the results” 
Response: We agree this would provide a more direct comparison and will consider it in future work, though it would substantially reduce sample size and may affect statistical power and stability.
R2.3: “the work would also benefit from training a plasma-only prediction model from completeness”
Response: We appreciate this suggestion and agree that such an experiment would be informative. Our primary goal with Experiment II was not to demonstrate the superiority of multimodal prediction in itself, but rather to test whether it could reduce ambiguity. However, we agree that a plasma-only model would generally help to directly quantify the relative contributions of MRI versus molecular biomarker information. We will explore this in future work.
R3: “It is a bit questionable whether it is then needed to synthesize PET images when, maybe your information can be maybe derived by the blood markers already.”
Response: This is an important point, and we agree that plasma biomarkers raise a broader question regarding the utility of PET synthesis. In this work, however, the primary role of plasma biomarkers was to test the biological ambiguity hypothesis, rather than to justify the clinical necessity of PET synthesis itself. 
At the same time, we believe PET synthesis may still provide clinically useful spatial information that is not directly available from plasma alone, and hence remain valuable from an interpretability perspective
Once again, we sincerely thank all reviewers for their valuable feedback and encouraging comments.

title: When Does Uncertainty Become Meaningful in Medical Vision-Language Models? Alignment Enables Disease-wise Uncertainty and Risk-Aware Prediction
abstract: Recent Vision–Language Models (VLMs) have shown strong zero-shot performance for chest X-ray interpretation, yet they lack reliable uncertainty estimation, particularly in multi-label clinical settings requiring disease-wise confidence. Existing similarity-based uncertainty methods are largely designed for single-label OOD detection and become unreliable when affirmative and negated disease hypotheses are not semantically aligned, causing uncertainty to reflect representation ambiguity rather than clinical decision uncertainty. We introduce Bi-EDL, a fine-tuning framework that combines bidirectional multiple-choice questioning with evidential deep learning (EDL) to estimate disease-wise uncertainty on aligned image–disease representations. By reinterpreting hypothesis-level similarities as evidence and modeling them as the parameters of a Beta distribution under an evidential deep learning framework, the proposed method mitigates overconfidence inherent in similarity-based scoring and enables pathology-specific uncertainty estimation. Experiments demonstrate improved selective risk controllability under both normal and covariate-perturbed conditions, achieving performance beyond that of the baseline model. Our findings suggest that meaningful uncertainty in medical VLMs emerges when disease hypotheses are semantically aligned, highlighting alignment as a key condition for reliable risk-aware prediction in clinical settings.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The authors propose a different uncertainty framework for multilabel xray classification using VLMs. They argue existing “similarity-based” approaches are not adequate for the multilabel reality of most X-ray classification tasks, given that embedding similarity is often global and not disease-wise. The authors propose to extend similarity-based uncertainty using special prompts that convey specific diseases, including negation of their presence, and use the similarity results as parameters for an Evidential Deep Learning classification approach.
Moreover, the authors explore whether their proposed approach can mitigate overconfidence, a very real problem in these types of models.
reviews.text_strengths:
The proposed method addresses a very current problem in the field: the variability of performance for VLMs dealing with rare/underrepresented diseases vs more common ailments, and how this creates a coverage-risk. The proposal to mitigate these problems through additional contrastive prompting fine-tuning and evidence-based deep learning is sound, leveraging recent proposals of deviating from cross-entropy-based classifications in these types of models.
Evaluation (in the context of ablation of the same model) is extensive, exploring metrics beyond simple classification performance and going into failure detection and overconfidence evidence, a topic of high interest currently with more and more VLMs being tested in the field.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
In my opinion, the data and the prompts used in the research should be better explained in the manuscript. What is local and global text in the formulations? How does that relate to the used dataset? Also, not everybody will know about the common 14 findings in multilabel x-ray datasets.
The work focuses on a single model and data source, where there are multiple multilabel datasets available publicly, such as CheXpert, MIMIC-CXR, and BRAX, to name a few.
I understand the reasoning to focus on a single model, but I believe including baseline results from a different medical VLM would enrich the paper significantly, such as MedGemma 1.5 for example. This recommendation is grounded on it being a commonly used model for real deployments currently.
AUROC is a poor performance metric for this problem. Classes are often unbalanced and over (pleural effusion) or under represented (pneumonia). I recommend including PR-AUC. In addition regarding metrics, a visualization or table per class would be very important for this problem, instead of aggregating.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Minor comments:
Formatting and presentation of equations in section 2.1 can be improved.
Figure two should have all plots on the same y scale
Authors assume knowledge about the existing methodology they are adapting, but a brief explanation of the difference between the global and local representations for text and images would be welcome in the manuscript, since there are many ways to attempt to represent locally and globally.

The proposal is very interesting, with a lot of potential, but I believe evidence for the proposed techniques is insufficient, mainly due to the use of a single dataset and focusing on ablation of the same model.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I accept the rebuttal arguments and, after a reread, understand the authors’ focus on aspects beyond classification performance.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal

1) Method section is not easy to understand without significant background on this topic. I would suggest explaining the core ideas with more plain language examples;
2) The proposed method is tested on a single dataset. Even though it is a large dataset, it is always better to evaluate on more diverse datasets to demonstrate method robustness.

N/A

Good motivation. Reasonably novel method. Evaluation shows real performance improvement on a large dataset.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This work expands the uncertainty estimation task to VLM-based multi-label classification. Specifically, the authors introduce Bi-EDL, which combines bidirectional alignment (between images and text) and deep evidential learning. Experimental results demonstrate that Bi-EDL achieves improvements in uncertainty estimation.
reviews.text_strengths: The proposed method is a new paradigm to estimate the uncertainty based on evidential learning.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Main: The paper is difficult to follow due to the lack of explanatory diagrams and unclear definitions of notations.
Major 1: The bidirectional method is very similar to CLIP’s contrastive learning, where the model learns to distinguish paired images and text. How does your Bi-MCQ method differ from CLIP?
Major 2: Figure 1(a) uses circles, triangles of different colors, and arrows, which are poorly understandable. The authors should adopt an intuitive way to present their motivation. Besides, the left subfigure in Fig. 1(b) exhibits the same uncertainty measurements in both correct and incorrect cases, which is also confusing.
Major 3: For better comprehension, an architectural diagram should be provided to illustrate the details of the models and the plug-in attribute of the proposed Bi-EDL. Moreover, the training and inference processes of Bi-EDL should be clearly marked for intuitiveness.
Major 4: Positive and negated prompts/descriptions for individual diseases are critical elements of the proposed Bi-EDL. Considering that the used ChestXray-14 dataset is a classification dataset, which is not equivalent to a multi-choice question dataset, it is necessary to introduce the details of constructing the multi-choice question dataset and provide examples.
Major 5: Many notations are not explained, such as S^{I2T}, y^{I2T}, \tau^{I2T}, K, y_{k}.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Despite the innovation in proposing the paradigm of uncertainty estimation based on evidential learning, the article is hard to follow due to the lack of explanatory diagrams and unclear definitions of notations.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: Despite the innovation in proposing the paradigm of uncertainty estimation based on evidential learning, the article is hard to follow due to the lack of explanatory diagrams and unclear definitions of notations.

meta_reviews.text:
The reviewers request rebuttal on clarity and methodological positioning, especially explaining the Bi-MCQ/Bi-EDL formulation in plain language, defining all notations, clarifying local/global text and prompt construction, and explicitly distinguishing the method from CLIP-style contrastive learning.
The authors should strengthen the experimental evidence by adding PR-AUC and per-class results, evaluating on additional chest X-ray datasets such as CheXpert, MIMIC-CXR or BRAX if feasible, and comparing with at least one other medical VLM such as MedGemma.
The rebuttal should also address presentation issues by improving Figure 1, adding an architecture diagram showing the plug-in training/inference workflow, and providing concrete examples of the positive/negated multi-choice prompts used to convert ChestXray-14 into the proposed task format.

The paper is accepted. Two reviewers support acceptance after rebuttal, citing good motivation, reasonable novelty, real performance improvements on a large dataset, and satisfactory clarification of the dataset and broader evaluation focus. One reviewer maintained rejection due to clarity issues, including missing explanatory diagrams and unclear notation, but this reviewer had lower confidence and even identified the paper as suitable for a highlighted poster. Overall, the remaining concerns are mainly presentation-related and can be addressed in the final version, while the technical contribution and empirical results are above the acceptance threshold.

The reviewers highlighted the novelty of the method and its clinical relevance. Some of the concerns related to novelty were clarified in the rebuttal, which convinced the reviewers. The authors are advised to address the issues related to presentation in the final version.

The paper presents an uncertainty framework for multilabel X-ray classification using VLMs, focusing on the variability of VLM performance across rare or underrepresented diseases versus more common conditions, and the resulting coverage-risk tradeoff. The proposed mitigation strategy, based on contrastive prompting fine-tuning and evidence-based deep learning, is sound and well motivated. The work also includes an extensive evaluation, which supports its practical relevance. Some concerns were raised regarding the limited scope of the analysis, particularly its focus on a single dataset. The authors reasonably clarified that this was an intentional controlled design choice: the goal was not to compare architectures, but to isolate how disease-wise calibrated alignment reshapes uncertainty structure under a fixed backbone. While generalization across additional datasets and VLM backbones remains important future work, such expansion cannot reasonably be expected during the rebuttal stage. Considering the merits of the work, I find the paper interesting and recommend acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers for the constructive feedback. The core contribution of this work is not merely a new uncertainty score, but the observation that disease-wise hypothesis alignment reshapes uncertainty semantics in multi-label clinical settings, enabling more reliable selective prediction.
(R1, R2) Concern regarding single-dataset evaluation: This was an intentional controlled design. The aim is not architectural comparison, but to isolate how disease-wise calibrated alignment reshapes uncertainty structure under a fixed backbone setting, since architectural variation itself can substantially alter uncertainty behavior. Generalization across diverse datasets and VLM backbones remains an important direction for future work.
(R1) PR-AUC and evaluation metrics: We agree that PR-AUC is more robust than AUROC under severe class imbalance. However, the primary objective of this work is not classification optimization, but evaluating whether uncertainty meaningfully ranks high-risk predictions for selective prediction. Accordingly, the core metrics are AURC and Risk@90, which directly assess uncertainty-based risk ordering rather than class-wise classification performance. AUROC is reported only as an auxiliary metric to confirm that the proposed alignment strategy does not degrade predictive performance.
(R1) Per-class analysis and disease prevalence: The 14 findings correspond to the standard ChestXray14 disease labels, which exhibit substantial prevalence imbalance across diseases. Rather than performing exhaustive per-class benchmarking, Fig. 2 was designed to illustrate how disease-wise uncertainty behavior changes under differing prevalence conditions, highlighting the relationship between semantic alignment and uncertainty structure in both common and rare disease settings.
(R1, R2, R3) Clarification of representations and notation: Global representations denote [CLS]-level embeddings, while local representations correspond to patch/token-level features. Bi-MCQ applies bidirectional cross-attention to explicitly discriminate affirmative and negated disease hypotheses using both global and local image-text representations.
(R3) Difference from CLIP: Bi-MCQ differs from CLIP primarily at the objective level. Under a CLIP-style contrastive objective, negation prompts can lead to trivial convergence under severe disease imbalance, as negated descriptions become positive pairs for most samples. In contrast, the MCQ formulation forces the model to identify a single correct answer among competing affirmative and negated disease hypotheses, enabling disease-wise uncertainty formation rather than global similarity matching. This process is further supported through bidirectional cross-attention over both global and local representations.
(R3) Clarification of Fig. 1: Fig. 1(a) is intended to illustrate that global contrastive alignment alone has structural limitations for disease-wise uncertainty estimation, as similarity separation does not necessarily yield meaningful uncertainty ordering under multi-label settings. Combining contrastive alignment with EDL reshapes the uncertainty distribution to better separate high-risk and low-risk predictions. In Fig. 1(b), uncertainty is derived from the similarity difference between affirmative and negated disease prompts, where smaller differences correspond to higher uncertainty.
(R3) MCQ construction details: The MCQ structure is constructed directly from existing binary labels without additional annotation, using symmetric I2T/T2I formulations for disease-wise candidate discrimination.

title: When Tissue Speaks: Vibroacoustic Monitoring of Tissue Response During Electrosurgery
abstract: Electrosurgical coagulation is widely used in laparoscopic surgery; however, intraoperative assessment of tissue response remains indirect and largely reliant on visual cues, increasing the risk of insufficient coagulation or excessive thermal damage. In this work, we investigate vibroacoustic (VA) sensing as a non-invasive modality for monitoring electrosurgical coagulation. VA sensing captures structure-borne mechanical vibrations generated at the tool-tissue interaction point without requiring modifications to standard surgical instruments or workflows. Using a bipolar electrosurgical setup, VA signals were acquired under two complementary scenarios: prolonged coagulation of ex vivo porcine liver tissue to analyze temporal signal evolution, and coagulation of ex vivo porcine liver, muscle, and fat to investigate tissue-specific responses. The signals were analyzed using time- and time-frequency-domain signal processing methods. Results show that VA signals evolve systematically throughout coagulation, revealing distinct phases up to carbonization. In addition, tissue-specific analyses demonstrate reproducible differences in temporal dynamics and spectral content, enabling clear separation of tissue types in a non-linear embedding space. These findings indicate that VA sensing captures reproducible state-dependent and tissue-specific characteristics during electrosurgical energy delivery, highlighting its potential to address the clinical challenge of perceiving and controlling tissue response during electrosurgery.
subject_areas: Modalities -> Mobile / Wearable / Point-of-Care Imaging & Sensors

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents the first use of vibroacoustic (VA) sensing for non-invasively monitoring electrosurgical coagulation of tissue. To accomplish this, the authors propose the combination of standard surgical instruments with a small VA sensing unit using existing standardized connectors and thus not negatively affecting the surgical workflow. In an ex vivo setting, prolonged coagulation as well as coagulation of different tissue types showed distinct coagulation phases along the coagulation procedure and differences in temporal dynamics and spectral content promising to allow separation of different tissue types.
reviews.text_strengths:
Clinical relevance: Proposing and analyzing a method for tissue response monitoring, the paper addresses a real and important limitation of conventional electrosurgery which is especially relevant in laparoscopic and robotic settings where perception is limited. This is a clinically well motivated sensing problem that can matter in CAI.
Hardware setup and workflow: The hardware setup and sensing workflow provides an elegant solution how to integrate tissue response measurements into electrosurgical applications without disturbing the conventional surgical workflow. Mounting the vibroacoustic sensor proximally on standard instruments allows direct tissue response sensing without requiring custom tool tips or increasing the invasiveness of the intervention.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Phase transition claim: From the experiments performed for scenario I, the claim that the observed phase-dependent changes appear consistent with thermally induced tissue transformations is hard to verify from the performed experiments as no real indicators (e. g. tissue temperature) of the transition from one tissue transformation phase into the other is provided. This leaves this part of the paper in the speculative, a more thorough investigation including real-world reference measures would be required.
Tissue differentiation claim: While the performed analysis provide some indication that tissue differentiation can be possible with this method, a proper analysis should include a hold out test set to establish differentiation performance
Methodological reproducibility: The methodological description lacks detail to allow for straightforward reproduction of the method. In particular, the description of the implementation and parametrization of the individual processing steps remains rather vague.
Statistical rigor: The authors claim statistical significance for their results shown in Fig. 3e but do not provide statistical tests, confidence intervals or similar to support this claim.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Detailed comments on the paper can be found in the following:
1.It remains unclear how the frequency-dependent noise threshold was determined. 
2.The visual inspection “to identify frequency bands showing consistent dynamical changes” is currently not described in sufficient detail for reproduction. 
3.How were the homomorphic envelope, the low-pass filter and the moving average filter parameterized to determine the indicators?
4.How were the peaks in the signal detected? Which method has been used for this?
5.Why are there gaps between the pseudo-frequency regions? 200-250 Hz between LF and MF? 3000-5000 Hz between MF und HF?
6.For the sentence “Fig. 3(b–d) show the instantaneous band-energy contribution indicator (%) of the identified LF, MF, and HF
bands. “, “LF, MF, and HF” should be reordered such that it reflects the same order as Fig. 3(b-d). 
7.How were the phase transition points determined exactly?
8.While the dominant MF activity is visible in the example given in Figure 3a-d, the aggregated statistical result do not seem to show such a clear peaking in Ph2.

The paper addresses a clinically relevant problem and proposes an elegant, surgical workflow-compatible sensing approach with promising early results shown on ex-vivo tissue. However, the current evidence remains preliminary. The main claims on tissue-state phases and tissue differentiation are not sufficiently supported by objective reference measurements, held-out validation, or rigorous statistics. Together with missing implementation details, this limits confidence in the robustness and reproducibility of the findings.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: I appreciate the authors’ clarification with respect to the transition point determination, the UMAP/kNN analysis and the exploratory character of the performed study. I still believe that this is a very interesting and clinically valuable research direction. However, the rebuttal does not fully address my main concerns about the current level of validation. In particular, I would still recommend extending the analysis to include objective reference measurements of tissue state such as temperature or other thermal/tissue-damage indicators, a more comprehensive validation of tissue differentiation beyond exploratory visualization, and a complete description of the methodological details. In its current form, I therefore maintain my original assessment, but believe that a revised and resubmitted version could become a valuable contribution to the field.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces vibroacoustic (VA) sensing as a way to monitor electrosurgical bipolar coagulation. The tissue heating during the procedure generates vibrations throught the tool that get picked up by a sensor that is clipped on, allowing the monitoring of tissue responses and upgrading already existing tools in a cost effective way.
reviews.text_strengths:
S1 : Electrosurgical tissue state monitoring is an open clinical problem. The VA sensing solution is not invasive, tool agnostic and addresses a gap not covered by existing systems (impedance or acoustic based methods)
S2 : Scenario 1 (temporal evolution) and Scenario 2 (tissue type differentiation) address two clinically relevant and separate questions, providing a more complete picture.
S3 : Signal analyisis choice: four indicators (homomorphic envelope, peak density, stationary CWT, normalized stationary CWT) capture complementary elements of the signal.
S4 : No instrument modification is a strong practical contribution.
S5 : Data and code will be released on acceptance, bolstering reproducibility.
S6 : Experiment performed by an experienced surgeon with a standardized protocol.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
W1 : Boxplots for phase wise band energy contributions (Fig. 3e, 3f) reported but have no p-values, confidence intervals, nor statistical tests. Paired Wilcoxon tests or similar would be expected with N=15 in Scenario 1.The lack of quantitative significance data is a big methodological gap.
W2 : Phase transitions (~2.3 s, ~7.5 s) are identified from a representative single trial, then used to segment all 15 trials, then boxplots are computed. The method does not verify if transitions occur at consistent times across trials or if data driven phase detection phase detection would yield the same structure.
W3 : All tissue is ex vivo porcine. In vivo involves perfusion, blood oozing, varying tissue hydration etc… Extension to in vivo scenarios is entirely unexplored.
W4 : N=15 for S1 and N=10 per tissue for S2 : with small sample sizes, overfitting becomes an issue when using UMAP (https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.03426, Section 6)
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
Q1 : The phase transitions (~2.3 s, ~7.5 s) were identified visually from a single representative trial before being applied to segment all 15 trials for quantitative analysis. What is the inter trial variability of these transition times? A formal change point detection analysis would bolster reproducibility claims.
Q2 : The UMAP embedding in Fig. 4e uses n=3, seems far below typical dataset sizes. Could you report a leave on out cross validation or similar on the four indicator vectors?

This is a solid proof of concept demonstrating that vibroacoustic sensing can capture tissue-state information during electrosurgical coagulation. The application is novel and sound yet some methodological concerns are significant warranting a revision.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
Clarified two main concerns that I had.
UMAP/kNN confirmed as descriptive visualization and not a predictive classifier.
Phase transitions clarified as per-trial manual annotation and not transferred from one representative trial, needs to be stated explicitely in the final paper.
Statistical rigor and R1 reproducibility concerns remain unsatisfied.
Sensing concept is genuinely novel. Clip-on + tool-agnostic hardware is an elegant and cost-effective contribution.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of this paper is showing that vibrations made when using electrosurgery can give us useful information about the tissue. The researchers found that these vibrations change in predictable ways as the tissue is heated and even show differences between different types of tissue (like liver, muscle, and fat). This could help surgeons better control the process and avoid damaging tissue.
reviews.text_strengths:
This paper is the first to use vibrations (called “vibroacoustics”) to learn more about tissue during electrosurgery. It’s a new way to get information, going beyond just looking and measuring electricity.
The sensor is designed to easily attach to existing surgical tools without needing any changes to how surgeons work or putting anything inside the patient’s body
The experiments were designed very well to test different aspects of the technique (how vibrations change over time and how they differ between tissues). They followed a clear plan and were done consistently.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
-The authors should clarify whether the UMAP + kNN analysis is intended as descriptive visualization or as a predictive classifier. If the former, the classifier framing and claims of ‘complete separability’ and ‘robust differentiation’ should be softened. If the latter, a proper cross-validation (e.g., leave-one-out given n=30) should be reported with accuracy metrics.”
Another potential limitation is the extremely small sample size (only 30 total samples across all tissue types). With so few data points, it’s difficult to draw firm conclusions about the technique’s reliability and generalizability. A larger sample size would provide more confidence in the findings.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The paper introduces vibroacoustic sensing as a genuinely novel monitoring modality for electrosurgery, an application not previously explored. The proposed clip-on sensor is tool-agnostic, non-invasive, and translationally attractive, and the two-scenario experimental design is clean and well-structured. The results are visually compelling.
However, enthusiasm is tempered by several concerns. The authors should clarify whether the UMAP + kNN analysis is intended as descriptive visualization or as a predictive classifier: if the former, the classifier framing and claims of “complete separability” and “robust differentiation” should be softened; if the latter, a proper cross-validation (e.g., leave-one-out given n=30) should be reported with accuracy metrics. Another limitation is the extremely small sample size (only 30 samples across all tissue types), which makes it difficult to draw firm conclusions about reliability and generalizability.
Overall, the paper introduces a promising new sensing direction and provides preliminary yet suggestive evidence, which I believe will benefit the community, provided that the authors address the concerns mentioned above in the revision.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The rebuttal adequately addresses my main concerns on the UMAP framing and sample size. I maintain my Weak Accept.

meta_reviews.text:
Given the mixed but generally borderline-positive reviews, I recommend inviting a rebuttal.
Several key concerns: (1) provide stronger statistical support for the reported phase differences; (2) clarify how phase transitions were determined and whether they are consistent across trials; (3) clarify whether UMAP/kNN is descriptive or predictive, and provide proper cross-validation if predictive claims are made; (4) temper claims about tissue differentiation given the small ex vivo sample size; and (5) improve methodological detail for reproducibility.

Reviewers recognized the novelty, clinical relevance, and translational appeal of the proposed sensing concept. Following the rebuttal, two reviewers were satisfied with the clarification that the UMAP/kNN analysis is descriptive rather than predictive, and that phase transitions were annotated independently per trial rather than transferred from a single representative example. However, one reviewer still has concerns regarding the validation and lack of objective reference measurements of tissue state, such as temperature or tissue-damage indicators. Overall, the rebuttal appropriately tempered some claims and clarified the exploratory nature of the work, but concerns remain regarding statistical rigor and biological validation. Given the novelty and potential impact of the sensing approach, I recommend acceptance.
The rebuttal has not addressed the validation questions raised by the first reviewer, which are important in understanding the value of the proposed work.
The reviewers’ concerns have been successfully addressed in the rebuttal, making the work a solid contribution especially for what concerns clinical applications in CAI.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for the constructive feedback. All reviewers recognized the clinical relevance, novelty, and translational potential of the proposed vibroacoustic (VA) sensing approach for electrosurgery. 
Regarding the concern about statistical support for the reported phase differences, Scenario I aims to show that VA signals evolve systematically during electrosurgical coagulation, revealing reproducible signal changes up to tissue carbonization. Fig. 3(a–d) illustrates the temporal evolution of the VA signal, while Fig. 3(e,f) was intended to generalize these observations across the 15 independently analyzed VA data from a signal perspective, rather than to provide statistical validation of tissue-state transitions. Across VA signals, consistent redistribution of energy between LF/MF/HF bands and reduced total spectral energy in the late phase were observed. We apologize if some wording suggested stronger statistical claims.
