The interpretation of these behaviors as thermally induced tissue transformations was intended as hypothesis-driven, consistent with established thermal tissue literature and the manuscript conclusion that the biological interpretation is based on indirect evidence and requires validation.
Regarding the clarification on how phase transitions were determined and their consistency across trials, we apologize if the methodological description was not sufficiently clear. In the manuscript, signals were described as segmented according to transition points identified during the qualitative analysis. However, the manual annotation procedure was not described explicitly enough. The transition points shown in the representative example were not transferred to all signals. Instead, phase transitions were independently identified for each VA signal through manual annotation based on changes observed in the CWT spectrum and band-energy indicators. The goal was to characterize systematic changes in VA signal behavior during coagulation. The temporal duration of the phases naturally varied across signals. The reproducible aspect was therefore not fixed transition timing, but the consistent evolution of VA signal behavior during coagulation.
Regarding the descriptive or predictive role of the UMAP/kNN analysis, Scenario II was intended as a descriptive exploratory analysis rather than a predictive classification framework. UMAP was used as an unsupervised visualization of the extracted VA indicators without tissue labels, while the kNN boundaries were included only to illustrate local label consistency. Therefore, the observed grouping reflects structure inherently present in the extracted signal features rather than supervised optimization toward tissue classes.
Regarding tempering claims about tissue differentiation given the small dataset, we agree that the current ex vivo dataset is limited and does not support strong claims regarding generalizability. Scenario II should therefore be interpreted as exploratory evidence that different tissues exhibit distinguishable VA behaviors in this controlled setting.
Regarding reproducibility, the methodology combines standard signal-processing methods with the proposed VA sensing framework. Therefore, the manuscript focused primarily on the sensing concept and signal behaviors rather than low-level implementation details. For clarification, the pseudo-frequency bands were identified from recurrent spectral activity patterns consistently observed across signals, and all processing steps were applied using fixed parameters. The planned release of code and data will allow full reproducibility and inspection of the processing pipeline.
Overall, we believe the work fits well within the MICCAI scope and evaluation criteria. The paper addresses a clinically relevant CAI problem, introduces a novel sensing concept with translational potential, and presents systematic exploratory experiments supporting the feasibility of the proposed approach.

title: When Views Disagree: Conflict-Aware Evidential Inference for Multi-view Mammography
abstract: Multi-view mammography benefits from complementary craniocaudal and mediolateral oblique projections, yet differences in acquisition quality and anatomical coverage often lead to conflicting diagnostic evidence between views. Most existing multi-view learning approaches address this variability through deterministic feature fusion, implicitly assuming that disagreement can be resolved by stronger representations, an assumption that can yield brittle or overconfident predictions in safety-critical screening settings. We present Conflict–Evidential Inference Network (CEI-Net), an uncertainty-aware framework that reframes multi-view mammography classification as evidential reasoning under disagreement. Rather than enforcing consensus at the feature level, CEI-Net represents each view as a source of uncertain evidence and performs fusion by selectively moderating class hypotheses that are unsupported across views. This design allows disagreement to manifest as calibrated uncertainty when appropriate while still enabling confident decisions when reliable evidence is available from a single view. Empirical evaluation of the CBIS-DDSM and VinDr-Mammo benchmarks shows that this conflict-aware inference paradigm yields consistent improvements in discrimination and calibration over deterministic fusion methods, without adding auxiliary routing/quality networks. These findings suggest that explicitly reasoning about disagreement, rather than absorbing it, is critical for robust and interpretable multi-view decision-making in clinical screening. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/rayhan-ahmed91/CEI-Net.
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper addresses a clinically important problem in multi-view mammography: inter-view conflict and overconfident deterministic fusion. The proposed CEI-Net introduces a novel uncertainty-aware framework based on evidential deep learning and class-conditional conflict gating, which explicitly models disagreement rather than simply absorbing it. The work is technically sound and well-motivated. It achieves better performance than existing CNN, Transformer, and Mamba-based methods in both discrimination and calibration.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The work correctly identifies a critical limitation of existing multi-view fusion methods: they ignore view disagreement and produce overconfident, poorly calibrated predictions. The problem is clinically relevant. 
2.The method is novel. 
3.The paper is well-organized.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The paper is motivated by conflicting evidence between CC and MLO views, but the quantitative analysis mainly reports dataset-level AUROC, ECE, and NLL improvements, without stratifying performance by clinically important disagreement regimes such as low-quality views, partial breast coverage, dense breasts, subtle lesions, or artifact-heavy cases. As a result, the manuscript does not clearly demonstrate in which concrete clinical scenarios the proposed conflict-aware evidential inference is most beneficial, rather than simply improving average benchmark performance. 
2.The whole framework relies on the assumption that inter-view disagreement can be adequately characterized by class-wise Jensen-Shannon divergence between per-view Dirichlet means and then moderated by a scalar conflict gate. However, the paper does not analyze whether this design remains reliable in harder cases such as severe asymmetry of lesion visibility, view-specific false positives, very weak evidence in both views, or anatomically inconsistent but still clinically meaningful complementary findings. Thus, the robustness of the core conflict-modeling assumption is still not fully demonstrated. 
3.The method assumes consistent paired CC/MLO views and standard preprocessing, and although the paper includes a missing-view test-time ablation, it does not evaluate real-world issues such as view mispairing, acquisition mismatch, corrupted views, variable compression quality, or imperfect preprocessing and breast cropping. Since such factors are common in practical mammography workflows, the real clinical robustness and deployability of the framework remain unclear.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The problem is clinically relevant and important, and the method is novel. However, the validation requires further improvement.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: The authors have made a satisfactory rebuttal that can address my comments.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of this paper is the proposal of the Conflict-Evidential Inference Network (CEI-Net). By leveraging evidential deep learning, CEI-Net provides an uncertainty-aware framework specifically tailored to the multi-view nature of mammography, effectively incorporating inter-view disagreement.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper is driven by a strong motivation, as effectively leveraging the multi-view nature of mammography is of clinically relevant. The proposed method cleverly learns from incorporating two types of uncertainty by extracting view-specific features via an encoder and tokenization, computing Dirichlet evidence for each view, and applying class-wise conflict weighting. Furthermore, a major strength of this work is its comprehensive evaluation, successfully demonstrating improved AUROC and statistical significance compared to various recent SOTA models.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The major weaknesses of this paper are as follows:
Baselines for Uncertainty: The baseline models used for comparison are deterministic and rely solely on simple temperature scaling, which may not provide a sufficiently rigorous baseline for evaluating uncertainty estimation.
Visualizations: In the lower section of Figure 2, the clinical focus is somewhat ambiguous. It is unclear which specific regions or features within the mammogram the reader is expected to observe.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
While using 224x224 images is an understandable concession to computational constraints and aligns with the strongest baseline (Mammo-Clustering), mammograms are inherently ultra-high-resolution. This aggressive downsampling inevitably causes significant information loss. I would appreciate the authors’ perspective on this limitation.
2.Edge Cases: The proposed framework appears highly conservative, penalizing weights first for uncertainty and then again for inter-view disagreement. I am curious about the model’s robustness and reliability when handling complex edge cases, such as early-stage malignancies with ambiguous margins in dense breasts.

I believe this is a good EDL study that effectively leverages the unique characteristics of mammography. Rather than simply adopting existing methodologies, the authors propose an architecture specifically tailored for this domain. My recommendation is based on their rigorous evaluation, which includes validation on two distinct open datasets, extensive comparisons with various baselines, and thorough ablation studies that clearly demonstrate the effectiveness of each component.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The authors claimed to release the source code and/or dataset upon acceptance of the submission.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: This study is driven by a strong motivation, cleverly redefining multi-view disagreement as epistemic uncertainty to formulate and train EDL. The authors have successfully addressed my previous concerns. They provided a sufficient explanation of how the deterministic baseline was adapted for the EDL comparison and committed to improving the visualizations. As pointed out by myself and other reviewers, including an analysis of vulnerable edge cases related to false negatives would certainly strengthen the paper. However, since the authors have already demonstrated clear performance improvements over various SOTA baselines and provided a solid ablation study, I consider the current evaluation to be sufficient for MICCAI.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
The main contribution of this manuscript lies in its conceptual reframing of multi-view mammography classification, shifting the paradigm from deterministic feature fusion to an uncertainty-aware evidential reasoning framework. Specifically, author make three methodological contributions:
1.Reframing Inter-View Conflict as Epistemic Uncertainty
Unlike conventional methods that tend to absorb or average out disagreements between views , the proposed CEI-Net models each mammographic view as an uncertain evidence source via Dirichlet distributions. This approach successfully translates multi-view inconsistencies into interpretable epistemic uncertainty, which is highly valuable for preventing overconfident and potentially brittle predictions in ambiguous clinical scenarios.
2.Class-Conditional Conflict Gating
To intelligently aggregate conflicting evidence, the authors introduce a novel gating mechanism driven by Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence. Rather than applying a uniform penalty across an entire view, this mechanism quantifies conflict at the level of individual diagnostic hypotheses. This allows the model to selectively attenuate evidence only for highly disputed classes, offering a more nuanced and interpretable fusion strategy.
3.Uncertainty-Derived Reliability Weighting
The framework dynamically computes a reliability score for each view based on the strength of its accumulated Dirichlet evidence. This design not only enables adaptive weighting during view fusion but also elegantly accommodates common clinical “missing-view” scenarios by naturally assigning zero weight to absent inputs without requiring architectural modifications.
reviews.text_strengths:
The manuscript presents a well-motivated and methodologically sound approach to multi-view mammography classification. The major strengths of this work include:
1.Novel Problem Formulation (Evidential Reasoning under Disagreement): The paper elegantly reframes multi-view mammography from a standard deterministic feature fusion problem to an uncertainty-aware evidential reasoning paradigm. Instead of forcing a consensus at the feature level—which can lead to overconfident predictions —the CEI-Net models each view as a source of uncertain evidence via Dirichlet distributions. This appropriately translates inter-view diagnostic conflict into calibrated epistemic uncertainty, which is highly valuable for safety-critical clinical screening.
2.Methodological Elegance (Class-Conditional Conflict Gating): The proposed fusion mechanism uses Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence to quantify conflict at the class hypothesis level. This is particularly innovative because it selectively attenuates only the disputed diagnostic hypotheses, rather than indiscriminately penalizing the entire view. Furthermore, the model achieves this directly in the evidence space without relying on auxiliary routing or image-quality sub-networks, ensuring high parameter efficiency.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Q1: Risk of False Negatives Induced by the JS Gating Mechanism.
The authors employ a Jensen-Shannon (JS) gating mechanism, defined as $g_k = \exp(-\gamma JS_k)$, to attenuate evidence when the CC and MLO views disagree. However, in clinical practice, it is common for a lesion to be visible in only one view (e.g., deep in the breast, captured only by MLO) due to anatomical occlusion. In this scenario, the CC view might confidently predict “benign” (seeing only normal tissue), while the MLO view confidently predicts “malignant.” This creates a high JS divergence, triggering the gating mechanism to strongly attenuate the “malignant” evidence, which could lead to a fatal false negative. How does the proposed method distinguish between “true asymmetric lesion visibility” and “spurious conflict caused by noise” to prevent the model from compromising and missing the diagnosis?
Q2: Limited Spatial Interpretability of the Conflict Mechanism.
While Figure 2 effectively demonstrates the interpretability of the JS gating mechanism at the mathematical and predictive level (showing how uncertainty increases in high-conflict cases like Fig. 2e), it lacks spatial/clinical interpretability. Since CEI-Net relies on extracting “Top-M salient spatial tokens” from each view, the model inherently possesses spatial information about where the evidence originates. Could the authors expand their qualitative analysis to visualize which specific spatial tokens or anatomical regions are driving the high JS divergence? Providing token-level heatmaps or spatial overlays alongside the probability charts would significantly bridge the gap between mathematical conflict resolution and actionable clinical interpretability.
Q3: Dataset Discrepancy and Potential View Dominance.
Could the authors explain why the proposed method achieves a significantly higher performance gain on CBIS-DDSM compared to VinDr-Mammo (whereas baseline methods perform relatively consistently across both)? Furthermore, in Table 2, the
Deterministic Prob-Avg
achieves an AUROC almost identical to the missing-MLO (
CC only
) setting. Does this suggest that the model’s decisions heavily rely on the CC view? Additionally, the Expected Calibration Error (ECE) for
CC only
is lower than that of
MLO only
, which seems to contradict the textual claim regarding the higher discriminative value of the MLO view.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper presents a novel uncertainty-aware evidential reasoning framework (CEI-Net) for multi-view mammography classification. The transition from deterministic feature fusion to epistemic uncertainty modeling is a strong conceptual contribution. However, critical concerns regarding clinical safety and empirical interpretability preclude a higher initial score.
Key Strengths (Driving the Accept):
Evidential Reframing: Effectively models inter-view conflict as epistemic uncertainty via Dirichlet distributions, mitigating overconfident predictions in ambiguous cases.
Class-Conditional Gating: The JS divergence-based gate provides a mathematically elegant, hypothesis-level conflict resolution mechanism, offering more nuanced fusion than global pooling approaches.
Inherent Robustness: Uncertainty-derived reliability weighting naturally handles missing clinical views without requiring architectural modifications.
Major Reservations (Driving the “Weak” modifier):
Clinical Safety (False Negatives): The conflict gating mechanism risks treating true asymmetric lesion visibility (e.g., a tumor visible only in MLO due to depth) as “conflict,” potentially suppressing critical malignant evidence and causing fatal false negatives.
View Dominance: Ablation results (Deterministic Prob-Avg vs. CC only) strongly suggest the model’s decision-making is overwhelmingly biased toward the CC view, contradicting text assertions regarding the higher discriminative value of the MLO view.
The methodological innovation is sound. I am open to raising my score if the authors can adequately address the false-negative edge cases and provide spatial evidence of interpretability during the rebuttal.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text:
The motivation and novelty of this work are consistently recognized; while, some concerns (especially those regarding empirical evaluations under typpical situations) should be addressed.

Overall, a strongly motivated paper, and the authors provided a solid rebuttal, which addressed major concerns rasied by the reviwers.

The three reviewers recognize a novel formulation of multi-view disagreement in terms of epistemic uncertainty, and note an elegant method and a strong contribution. Several of the issues raised by the reviewers were adressed in the rebuttal through an enriching discussion. This clarifications should be also included in the paper.

The paper presents a novel method for handling multi-view conflict in breast mammography, a particularly relevant and frequent clinical case. To do so, the authors model this conflict as a source of epistemic uncertainty using Dirichlet distributions and propose a gating mechanism based on Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence. Experiments are conducted on two large-scale mammography datasets and demonstrate the framework’s benefits in managing conflicting cases. In the first round of reviews, the reviewers’ main concerns were: i) management of asymmetric visibility cases (when a lesion is not visible on a view), disagreement regimes, and treatment of single-view cases; ii) uncertainty baselines and interpretation; and iii) view dominance and potential bias. The authors clearly responded to all the reviewers’ points, promising to better clarify asymmetric visibility, single-view, and robustness to acquisition features in the camera-ready paper. In addition, the authors revised Fig. 2 to address R2 and R3 concerns about the spatial interpretability of tokens. 
R1 and R2 were satisfied with these answers and recommended acceptance. While R3 did not provide an updated recommendation, I believe the authors addressed his questions in the rebuttal and therefore also recommend acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We thank the reviewers and AC for recognizing the clinical motivation, novelty, clarity, and empirical evaluation of CEI-Net. We revised Fig. 2 and related text to clarify conflict behavior and spatial evidence.
Safety under asymmetric visibility (R1/R2/R3). A lesion visible in only one view is an important safety case. CEI-Net does not force CC/MLO consensus or convert disagreement into a benign decision. Each view first contributes evidence according to its Dirichlet strength, r(v)=S(v)/(S(v)+K). The JS gate is then applied to reliability-weighted evidence, not directly to class probabilities or to an entire view. Thus, when one view is confident and the other is weak or uncertain, the confident view can still dominate. When two confident views disagree, the gate reduces Dirichlet concentration for the disputed hypothesis and increases epistemic uncertainty rather than suppressing malignancy. We now clarify that such cases are uncertain/high-risk for review/triage. For single-view inference, JS is set to zero, so no artificial conflict is introduced. Missing-view results support this: CC-only and MLO-only remain functional, while full model performs best.
Disagreement regimes and robustness (R1/R2/R3). Dense breasts, partial coverage, artifacts, mismatch, corrupted views, and view-pairing errors matter in deployment. We do not claim full prospective robustness to all acquisition failures, and the conclusion now clarifies this limitation. The current evidence tests the central claim that conflict modeling improves inference under disagreement or shift. Fig. 2 stratifies cases by JS disagreement and shows that stronger disagreement is associated with higher error and NLL. Table 2 evaluates missing-view inference without retraining, and cross-dataset results show improved calibration and NLL under domain shift. We will study view mispairing, corruption, imperfect cropping, and dense/subtle-lesion cases in future robustness tests.
Uncertainty baselines and ablations (R2). To separate temperature scaling from uncertainty modeling, we compare CEI-Net with evidential variants using the same backbone and tokenization, including equal-weight fusion, reliability-only fusion, JS-gating-only fusion, and removal of tokenized evidence. Temperature scaling is applied only for evaluation calibration, while the actual uncertainty mechanism is the Dirichlet evidence strength plus JS-based conflict modulation. We now state this explicitly. 
Spatial interpretability and revised Fig. 2 (R2/R3). The previous figure made belief-level conflict clearer than clinical localization. We revised Fig. 2 to overlay selected Top-M spatial tokens and distinguish malignant, benign, and disputed tokens in specific regions. The revised panels connect image regions selected by CEI-Net with per-view belief, JS disagreement, and class-wise gates, which links conflict to spatial evidence.s
View dominance and dataset discrepancy (R3). The similarity between deterministic probability avg. and CC-only, especially on CBIS-DDSM, reflects naive averaging, not CEI-Net collapsing to CC. Full model outperforms CC-only, MLO-only, and deterministic avg. on both datasets. Compared with CC-only, full CEI-Net improves AUROC from 0.796 to 0.855 on CBIS-DDSM and from 0.804 to 0.829 on VinDr-Mammo, while reducing ECE from 0.135 to 0.109 and from 0.300 to 0.073.This indicates that fusion uses complementary information from both views. We corrected the wording about MLO being generally more discriminative: in these splits, CC has stronger standalone signal, while full CEI-Net remains best.
Image resolution (R2). 224x224 downsampling can remove subtle findings. We used this resolution for controlled comparison with baselines and feasible multi-run evaluation. Since all methods use the same preprocessing, gains reflect conflict-aware evidential inference rather than a resolution advantage. We now state this limitation and will explore high-resolution patch or multi-scale extensions.

title: When, Where, and How: Adaptive Binning for Tabular Self-supervised Learning
abstract: Medical tabular data are ubiquitous in clinical research, but deep learning for tables remains underexplored because reliable labels often require costly expert adjudication, even though structured clinical variables are routinely available in tabular form.  Self-supervised learning can leverage these unlabeled tables, and recent binning-based pretexts offer a promising inductive bias, but existing objectives fix a single global quantile discretization and apply feature-agnostic supervision. We propose Adaptive Binning, a training-adaptive discretization pretext for tabular SSL that couples discretization to learning through a feature-wise coarse-to-fine curriculum. Motivated by the spectral bias of neural networks and the principles of curriculum learning, our method progressively refines discretization per feature upon plateau detection and selects representation-aware splits to jointly improve value-space concentration and representation-space coherence. A heterogeneity-aware objective unifies categorical reconstruction with ordinal supervision for numerical features, and experiments on public medical tabular datasets under unified evaluation protocols show consistent gains for linear probing and fine-tuning without dataset-specific discretization tuning. We further introduce a medical tabular SSL benchmark with standardized protocols to support reproducible progress in this underexplored domain. Our code is available at https://github.com/labhai/Adaptive-Binning.
subject_areas: Applications -> Outcome Prediction / Prognosis / Longitudinal Modeling
Machine Learning -> Semi- / Weakly- / Self-supervised Learning

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: Proposes an Adaptive Binning framework that replaces the conventional fixed global binning used in SSL for medical tabular data with a per-feature, coarse-to-fine discretization that evolves adaptively during training. The framework comprises three modules (FPT, DIGS, HORD) and is accompanied by a unified benchmark over eight public medical tabular datasets.
reviews.text_strengths:
Intuitive and clean framing
The problem is structured around three questions — When / Where / How — so the role and motivation of each module are clearly articulated.
Novelty
A tabular SSL method that adaptively adjusts discretization during pretraining, with a representation-space-based criterion for bin splitting.
Generality across encoders
Table 4 evaluates fine-tuning on five encoders (MLP, ResNet, TabNet, FT-Transformer, T2G-Former), confirming an encoder-agnostic effect.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Poor clarity and readability (major concern)
The formulation and overall presentation are difficult to follow. The paper should present the method more clearly, with concise explanations of each component and its role.
Insufficient empirical evidence for the core adaptive binning claim
Although adaptive binning is the central contribution, the paper does not provide direct evidence of how the binning evolves (e. g. , no bin-schedule visualization or bin statistics).
Ambiguity in ablation design
FPT and DIGS appear mutually dependent, yet the ablation study does not clearly describe how components are removed or substituted. This makes it difficult to interpret the contribution of each module.
Incomplete and inconsistent evaluation
Fine-tuning is reported on only a subset of datasets (4/8) without justification, and model design choices (e. g. , MLP variants) vary across datasets without explanation. This limits the reliability of the evaluation.
Missing analysis of computational overhead
The additional cost introduced by DIGS is not discussed, leaving the practical efficiency of the method unclear.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

Positive factors:
Clear and well-motivated When/Where/How framing; novel adaptive, representation-aware discretization for tabular SSL; broad hyperparameter robustness sweep; encoder-agnostic effectiveness across five architectures; unified benchmark over eight public medical tabular datasets.
Negative factors: 
Core adaptive claim is not empirically visualized (no bin-schedule evolution; bin counts unspecified for both method and baselines); ambiguous ablation protocol due to mutual dependence between FPT and DIGS; fine-tuning reported on only 4 of 8 datasets without justification; no computational-overhead analysis for DIGS; per-dataset MLP design choices left unexplained.
Overall:
The paper offers genuine novelty and a reasonable formulation, but suffers from insufficient empirical support for its core claim and a shallow interpretation of the experimental results. Adding bin-schedule visualizations, clarifying the ablation substitutions, and running consistent fine-tuning across all 8 datasets with corresponding analysis would justify an upgrade in score.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification: My concerns have been adequately addressed in the rebuttal. I find the proposed method meaningful and novel.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper proposes Adaptive Binning, a training-adaptive discretization pretext task for tabular self-supervised learning. It is designed to address the limitation of using a single global quantile discretization in prior work. The method progressively refines feature-wise discretization when training plateaus and performs representation-aware split selection. The paper also introduces a heterogeneity-aware objective that combines categorical reconstruction with ordinal supervision.
The method is evaluated on multiple tabular datasets and reports favorable improvements over prior SOTA baselines.
reviews.text_strengths:
S1: The paper studies tabular representation learning, which is an important topic for medical AI applications.
S2: The adaptive discretization design is well motivated and technically reasonable.
S3: The reported performance gains are meaningful, and the experimental section is relatively comprehensive.
S4: The manuscript is generally clear, well organized, and easy to follow.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
W1: Some existing SSL approaches model heterogeneous tabular features separately with regression/classification objectives (e.g., MSE for numerical features and cross-entropy for categorical features) [R1, R2], without relying on discretization. The paper should provide a clearer conceptual or empirical comparison against this line of methods, including when adaptive binning is preferable.
W2: There are also methods with learnable discretization/tokenization mechanisms that aim to preserve ordinal information [R3]. The novelty and practical advantage of Adaptive Binning over such approaches are not yet fully clarified.
[R1] Du, Siyi, et al. “TIP: Tabular-image pre-training for multimodal classification with incomplete data.” European Conference on Computer Vision. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland, 2024.
[R2] Somepalli, Gowthami, et al. “SAINT: Improved Neural Networks for Tabular Data via Row Attention and Contrastive Pre-Training.” NeurIPS 2022 First Table Representation Workshop.
[R3] Yan, Jiahuan, et al. “Making Pre-trained Language Models Great on Tabular Prediction.” The Twelfth International Conference on Learning Representations.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

I find the problem important and the proposed idea interesting, and the empirical results are promising. However, the current draft does not yet provide sufficiently clear positioning against some closely related directions. Clarifying these differences through more direct comparisons and discussion would make the paper better.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
I find the rebuttal convincing overall. The authors have largely addressed my main concerns by clarifying the distinction from prior methods, and by adding empirical comparisons with SAINT and tree-based baselines.
I also find the responses to the other reviewers’ concerns helpful. In particular, the added bin evolution statistics addresses the main concern about whether adaptive binning actually occurs during training. I agree that clinical tabular data is a valid and important medical data modality for MICCAI. While broader transfer experiments and additional discussion would further strengthen the paper, I do not view the absence of imaging integration as a fundamental relevance issue.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
Feature-wise plateau trigger (FPT) for training-adaptive, per-feature discretization refinement in tabular SSL
Dispersion-Informed Gain-based Splitting (DIGS) coupling value-space variance reduction with representation-space coherence for split selection
Heterogeneity-aware ordinal loss (HORD) unifying categorical cross-entropy with soft ordinal supervision for numerical features
Medical tabular SSL benchmark with standardized protocols across 8 datasets and 4 task types
reviews.text_strengths:
Well-structured method with clear, orthogonal components validated by strong ablations
Rigorous hyperparameter analysis with statistical significance across datasets
Consistent transfer gains across multiple downstream architectures
Useful benchmark with standardized protocols improving reproducibility
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Limited relevance to MICCAI, as the work is purely tabular with no imaging or clinical workflow integration
Missing comparisons with strong tabular baselines (both SSL methods and tree-based models like XGBoost/CatBoost)
SSL motivation is weak, given the small dataset sizes
Evaluation is restricted to in-dataset pretraining without demonstrating transfer learning benefits
The practical advantage over standard tabular methods is not clearly established
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The paper’s strongest contribution for a clinical AI venue is the benchmark (Table 1) with standardized protocols — this alone could support a workshop paper but is insufficient as the primary MICCAI contribution.
The spectral bias motivation for coarse-to-fine curriculum is conceptually appealing but never empirically verified — no experiment shows that coarser bins are learned first or that refinement timing correlates with spectral learning dynamics.
Results on HFC (299 samples) consistently show no benefit from FPT/DIGS (Table 3 w/o FPT: same as Ours on HFC) — this suggests the method degrades gracefully on small datasets but also raises the question of whether the improvements on larger datasets are driven by dataset scale rather than the adaptive mechanism itself.

Technically sound with clear design and strong empirical analysis, but limited MICCAI relevance and incomplete baseline comparisons weaken the overall impact. The SSL motivation and evaluation setup are not fully convincing, making the contribution insufficient for acceptance.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.

meta_reviews.text:
A further rebuttal is required for the reviewers to reach a consensus.

Great work.

While the reviews are still mixed, the overall consensus ultimately favors acceptance. The authors provided a comprehensive rebuttal that effectively addressed the core technical critiques by expanding baseline comparisons and clarifying the underlying mechanics of the method. Ultimately, the robust empirical validation and the practical value of the proposed framework represent a good contribution to the community.

The presented work is novel and provides a valuable benchmark for future research in medical tabular self-supervised learning. Its adaptive discretization design is well motivated and technically reasonable, with several strengths broad hyperparameter robustness analysis, encoder-agnostic effectiveness across five architectures, and a unified benchmark over eight public medical tabular datasets.
The concerns raised during review were well addressed by the authors in the rebuttal. One remaining concern relates to MICCAI relevance, since the paper focuses on non-imaging medical tabular data. While the authors argue that MICCAI does consider non-imaging data, my understanding is that such cases are typically strongest in multimodal settings where at least one modality is medical imaging. Nevertheless, aside from this scope concern, the paper is technically solid and valuable. Therefore, I recommend acceptance.

author_feedback_text:
We thank all reviewers for their constructive comments and recognition of our novel training-adaptive binning pretext, unified medical tabular SSL benchmark, clear When/Where/How design, and strong, encoder-agnostic gains.
R#1
Clarity: We will add Sec.2.2 pseudocode to reduce text-heavy presentation, with concise explanations of each component and its role.
Bin evolution: Refinement occurs in 7/8 datasets; median per-dataset mean bin count increases 5.54→17.44.Adaptation is thus observed, and we will add bin-schedule visualizations/statistics, including BR’s fixed T.
Ablation: FPT & DIGS are not mutually dependent (Tab.3): w/o-FPT and w/o-DIGS each correspond to When & Where. w/o-FPT keeps DIGS with fixed-epoch refinement; w/o-DIGS keeps FPT with value-space variance reduction only. Tab.3 caption will be revised for clarity.
overhead: DIGS affects pretraining only, not fine-tuning/inference; mean wall-clock overhead across pretraining is 7.48%.
Fine-tuning coverage: Tab.4 was task-stratified, not performance-selected, with one dataset per task (BC/NMC/OMC/Reg) due to space; we will expand it to all datasets/encoders. MLP fine-tuning on omitted datasets gives Ours 1st on ILPD↑, CTG↑, PT↓, and 2nd on MHR↑: 74.9 vs Sup 74.5; 87.6 vs BR 87.3; 13.0 vs BR 13.3; 63.0 vs BR 63.9.Design choices for MLP variants (Tab.1) are set per dataset via supervised validation and fixed across Tabs.2-4 for reliability; non-MLP encoders use defaults.
R#2&3
Baselines: Adaptive Binning is training-adaptive SSL, not discretization alone. Unlike [R1-2 by R#2] heterogeneous-feature regression/classification or [R3] learnable discretization/tokenization, it creates label-free ordinal targets, uses HORD, and refines them via FPT/DIGS. As requested, we compare on Tab.4 datasets against strong tabular baselines—tabular SSL (SAINT [R2]) and tree-based models—with Ours’ best encoder per dataset. SAINT-Sup/SAINT-SSL/XGBoost/CatBoost/Ours: HFC↑ 92.3/92.5/92.2/92.4/94.2; ESR↑ 71.8/74.7/70.7/67.1/76.9; EOL↑ 95.5/94.9/95.0/91.7/97.1; BFP↓ 4.40/4.51/4.86/4.85/4.77.Ours is best on 3/4 vs SAINT, 4/4 vs trees. Its practical role is SSL initialization for numerical and graded clinical variables, not replacing supervised tabular learners.
R#3
MICCAI relevance: Purely tabular focus does not limit MICCAI relevance. We do not claim current imaging/clinical workflow integration; we target label-scarce, workflow-native clinical tables, not generic tabular data. Because medical SSL remains imaging/language-centric, label-efficient SSL for this modality is a clinical need, not a convenience. Our contribution is twofold, coupling Adaptive Binning, the primary methodological advance for clinical tabular SSL, with a new benchmark for reproducible evaluation. This scope is consistent with MICCAI’s call for papers on integration of imaging/non-imaging and multimodal data, instantiated at MICCAI’25 by ≥6 non-imaging papers, e.g., ProCDS (Tan et al.) and MVP-LLMs (Hao et al.).
Motivation/transfer: For small-dataset SSL motivation and in-dataset-only evaluation, we provide semantically matched EOL→BFP transfer with reinitialized input/head: unlabeled EOL pretraining improves BFP↓ at all fractions. Sup/Transfer at 25, 50, 75, 100%: 5.69/5.39, 5.92/5.47, 5.61/5.19, 5.50/5.07—transfer beyond in-dataset pretraining; broader transfer is Sec.4 future work.
Spectral bias: Two EOL analyses test whether coarser bins are learned first and refinement timing follows the coarse-to-fine curriculum. (i) To reach 95% final performance, coarse targets (2/4 bins) needed ≤10 epochs and fine targets (8/16 bins) 400/500 epochs. (ii) Refinement was first accepted at epoch 18, consistent with this ordering.
HFC/scale: HFC is a no-refinement case, not evidence of scale-driven gains. Because refinement never triggers, Ours matches w/o FWA/FPT/DIGS in Tab.3.The smaller BFP (n=252) did refine, and w/o FWA/FPT/DIGS worsened RMSE; gains reflect the adaptive mechanism, not scale alone.

title: Where Is the Needle Tip? VA Sensing Reveals Hidden Needle-Tissue Transitions During US Guidance
abstract: Reliable identification of tissue transitions during ultrasound-guided needle insertion remains challenging, particularly when needle-tip visibility is degraded by imaging geometry or acoustic artifacts. Most prior work focuses on spatial localization, while fewer approaches address mechanically meaningful events such as boundary crossing between adjacent tissues. This study investigates whether proximal vibroacoustic (VA) sensing can detect tissue transitions during insertion. VA signals recorded at the needle hub were analyzed using a time–frequency representation, and statistical similarity to tissue-specific reference segments was quantified using the first-order Wasserstein distance. Transition time was derived from a log-distance ratio signal indicating regime change. Experiments were conducted on 42 controlled insertions in a layered ex-vivo biological phantom with synchronized ultrasound (US) video. Results show consistent regime shifts at tissue boundaries and temporal agreement with US-based annotations across different visibility conditions. These findings indicate that proximal VA sensing captures mechanical interaction changes associated with tissue transitions and may provide complementary feedback during US-guided procedures.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper presents Vibroacoustic Analysis (VA) to supplement US-guided needle tracking, where different environments cause different vibrations in the needle that can then be unmixed via signal processing and yield exact timings of when the needle traversed from one medium to the next. This is an extension of previously presented work where only VA was performed during initial insertion, not during tissue-to-tissue transition as now explored by the authors. The paper presents an initial demonstration using ex vivo tissue samples embedded in gelatin.
reviews.text_strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of US-guided needle guidance, which is a known challenge. By adding VA, the authors demonstrate for the first time that tissue-to-tissue needle transitions could be detected even in cases where the needle was poorly visualized under US imaging. The authors use reasonably realistic phantoms and perform 42 seperate insertions, giving great confidence in the presented data being reproducible. The signal processing steps are reasonably well described.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Some key parameters are missing, making it impossible for readers to reproduce the work:
specifications of the VA sensor are absent: what is its bandwidth, sampling rate, and in which direction(s) does it sense? How many DoFs, if more than one?
Neither the figures nor the video show scale bars, so as reader I am left guessing at the scale of the tissue layers, imaging depths, needle insertion velocities etc. Figs. 3+4 do not have units (fig 4) or any labels (fig 3).
42 needle insertions were performed, but it is not stated whether these were performed at different positions, phantoms, velocities, insertion angles, etc. How diverse were these repeat measurements? What was (approximately) the insertion velocity?
In addition, the signal processing could have been described r motivated in greater detail:
Why was Wasserstein distance chosen as key metric, what is special about it? Would there have been alternatives or superior options?
“an interactionsensitive frequency band is extracted” is insufficiently clear - the authors do not specify the values of this band here, and only mention it on page 6 “in passing”. Similar choices (e. g. the window length of the moving window, and the exact choice of reference window(s)) should also be clarified.
Finally, the paper is in my opinion too light on the clinical implications:
a ca. 1s difference between US and VA transition times (Fig. 5) is significant and would arguably make any kind of guidance meaningless. What was the needle insertion speed, i. e. , what were the depth uncertainties corresponding to these timing differences? What precision is required? Arguably, the centimetre-regime (I assume; no scale bars provided) demonstrated here is of limited value, as that level of accuracy is certainly attainable using US imaging - or even markings on the needle. Image guidance becomes crucial at the (sub) millimetre scales; how would the method perform here?
The video is a useful addition, but mostly casts “doubt” on the accuracy of the extraction of t_tc. I appreciate your algorithms specify this is the true time, but looking at the Wasserstein distance, arguably the regime change occurs BEFORE the software-determined t_tc in all three (high/mid/low visibility) cases. Especially when mm-scale scenarios are targeted, this could cause significant issues.
The text does not specify, but the video suggests all needle insertions were performed at constant velocity, which is not representative of actual needle placement, where image guidance informs repositioning and motion is often non-uniform. How will the VA method hold up in these cases, as vibrations due to “jagged” motion could well mask the VA signals?
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The work as presented is of interest and timely. However, without any discussion on future clinical relevance and translational aspects, it is at risk of becoming “white noise”, especially of some of the choices made when designing the algorithms are, presently, a bit ad hoc.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: This paper describes the use of vibroacoustic (VA) sensing to detect tissue interfaces in a benchtop experiment of 42 needle insertions into a beef liver-chicken breast phantom and is used to complement ultrasound imaging. The study demonstrates the utility of VA signals for identifying the transition despite poor ultrasound visualization and stability within tissues coupled with changes at the boundary.
reviews.text_strengths:
Major strengths:
1.This paper addresses a persistent need in ultrasound imaging to localize needle tips even under variable visibility conditions and presents an approach without the need for burdensome hardware and workflow changes.
2.The evaluation is generally comprehensive within the space constraints of the paper and strongly supports the validity of the proposed approach.
3.The paper is well-written and logical, with attractive, easily interpreted figures.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
Major weaknesses:
1.The primary weakness of this paper is the incremental novelty of the work. Although the paper well-done and does not overstate the impact, the contributions represent only small advancements over previous works and there appears to be missing relevant works on similar topics that are not acknowledged. For example, Sühn et al. (Vibro-acoustic sensing of tissue-instrument-interactions allows a differentiation of biological tissue in computerised palpation. Comput Biol Med. 2023 Sep;164:107272.doi: 10.1016/j.compbiomed.2023.107272) has previously described the intra-tissue stability listed in this paper as a main contribution but this work is not referenced or differences elucidated.
2.I would have liked to have seen a better ground truth used for comparison of the boundary timing as opposed to the US recording, given that one of the best use cases for this technology is when US visibility is poor. The authors acknowledge “timing differences between VA detection and US annotation increased under low-visibility conditions, this is consistent with greater uncertainty in manual tip identification” suggesting that an external verification method is necessary to assess true agreement.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
The major revisions are already described in the weaknesses section above. A few additional minor items:
1.In the Introduction, a more comprehensive description of the limitations of embedded force sensing approaches would be beneficial, as this is a more similar approach to the one proposed than the image-based methodologies.
2.There are some minor grammatical errors. The first paragraph of 2.2 contains multiple errors impacting the readability and clarity of this section.
3.Limitations are only superficially mentioned in the Discussion but should be more specifically identified and expressed.

Overall, this paper is well-written and interesting on a long-standing challenging topic in the image-guidance space. It provides promising results using techniques that would be of interest to the MICCAI community; however, has limited novel additions to the field and some methodological improvements in the evaluation scheme would improve the work.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: The main contribution of this paper is a needle-guided interventional system that detects tissue boundaries using vibro-acoustic signal analysis. This feature can be particularly helpful during US-guided interventions where the needle tip may be difficult or impossible to see directly, or when the needle needs to be placed within a tissue region defined by fascial boundaries. This project proposes a transducer placed at the needle’s distal end (external to the patient) to record vibrations generated as the needle penetrates fascial boundaries. The two main contributions include demonstrating that tissue-to-tissue transitions can be identified from proximal VA measurements, even when needle visibility is limited, and that the VA signal is stable within tissue type but shows distinct changes at boundary crossings. These findings support proximal VA sensing as a complementary perception channel and provide a rationale for interaction-based tissue characterization. This approach is significant because it adds an inexpensive sensor to the proximal end of the needle via a standard Luer lock connection, without otherwise changing the needle-guidance configuration.
reviews.text_strengths:
This is a compelling example of how multi-sensor input can complement a widely used procedure to address a perennial problem! It relies on capturing information (sound produced by the interaction of a needle with tissue) that is inherently present for every procedure, but is not captured.
This approach requires a simple, inexpensive attachment to a standard needle guidance setup that causes minimal disruption to the standard workflow. It is readily implementable in the clinic.
The system is entirely passive.
It clearly complements the visualization of needle position relative to tissue boundaries when ultrasound does not provide this information.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The current display modality is somewhat non-intuitive. A sentence indicating how this might actually be used in the clinic – what the user interface to this additional information might look like - would be helpful.
The rationale for using CWT and the Wasserstein distance framework. is not immediately clear. A brief discussion would be appreciated.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

It is innovative.
Provides useful clinically relevant information;
Has the potential to streamline needle-guided interventions.
A company already exists to manufacture the sensor device – so it can be readily deployed.
It is non-invasive and subject to minimal regulatory requirements.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not provide sufficient information for reproducibility.

meta_reviews.text: This submission proposes a needle tip tracking methodology in the context of US-guided interventions where the target may not always be visible. The authors propose to track surrounding tissue motions as a proxy for needle motion whenever this structure is not visible. The method is validated in repeated phantom trials under different levels of visibility.

title: WHO-CXRBench: A CXR Benchmark for Diagnostic Rule Retrieval in CLIP-Style MedVLMs
abstract: Medical vision-language models (MedVLMs) have progressed rapidly and demonstrate strong performance across a broad range of clinical tasks, including report generation, disease classification, and cross-modal retrieval. The success can be attributed to contrastive language-image pretraining (CLIP), which holistically aligns image and text into a shared embedding space, thereby unifying visual and linguistic representations. While these models excel on coarse-grained medical tasks, where global image-level semantics are sufficient for success, such as modality recognition, disease classification, and standard image-report retrieval, it remains challenging for them to succeed in fine-grained and evidence-driven clinical scenarios. In those settings, models are supposed to identify and retrieve specific diagnostic evidence and align it to clinically applicable criteria. Otherwise, misidentifying or overlooking diagnostic evidence may lead to clinically contradictory errors and weaken the reliability and interpretability of the final diagnoses. Therefore, rigorously quantifying CLIP’s fine-grained retrieval capability in realistic clinical settings is essential. In this paper, we introduce WHO-CXRBench, a benchmark grounded in WHO chest X-ray (CXR) diagnostic guidelines for fine-grained diagnostic rule retrieval. We curate an evaluation set of 6{,}115 patient-level samples, resulting in 29{,}375 patient-rule pairs. We quantify the retrieval performance by Recall@K, Precision@K, nDCG, and mAP. Experiments show that even the best-performing baseline achieves only 14.23\% Recall@10 and 13.06\% nDCG@10, indicating that current CLIP-style MedVLMs still have space for improvement in fine-grained diagnostic rule retrieval. We believe that WHO-CXRBench builds a valuable foundation for evaluating MedVLMs’ performance under realistic clinical settings. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/LyxDLiI/WHO-CXRBench
subject_areas: Machine Learning -> Multimodal Models / LLMs / VLMs

reviews.recommendation_label: Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution: Deciphered request for structured English summary frameworkMajor Contributions. WHO-CXRBench introduces the first WHO-guideline-grounded benchmark specifically designed for fine-grained diagnostic rule retrieval in chest X-rays, filling a clear gap left by existing coarse-grained MedVLM evaluations. The paper proposes a three-stage automated construction pipeline — Prior-Guided Content RAG for hierarchical guideline extraction, GRADE-RA for quality-controlled rule filtering, and report-based personalized rule alignment — that reduces a noisy 1,154-rule corpus to a curated 300-rule set while preserving all 37 disease categories. Additionally, a VQA rationality check demonstrates that the extracted personalized rules serve as meaningful clinical context, improving downstream diagnostic performance.
reviews.text_strengths: Strengths. The problem motivation is compelling and clinically grounded: the “clinical contradiction” failure mode in existing CLIP-style retrieval is illustrated concretely and resonates with real-world radiology practice. The benchmark pipeline is principled and largely reproducible, with GRADE-RA offering a transparent, deterministic quality scoring mechanism. The evaluation is comprehensive, covering 12 state-of-the-art CLIP-style MedVLMs across both general-purpose and CXR-specialist categories, and the finding that broader medical-domain pretraining (UniMed-CLIP) outperforms CXR-specialist models is a genuinely interesting and actionable insight for the community.
reviews.text_weaknesses: Weaknesses. The most critical concern is that the core task assumption — that image-to-rule retrieval is a valid proxy for clinical reasoning — is never substantively justified with clinical or cognitive science evidence. Methodologically, the LLM judge used for positive label construction is never identified or ablated, creating a reproducibility gap and potential circular validation risk; the τ = 0.5 alignment threshold lacks task-specific sensitivity analysis; and the manual audit’s 92.7% precision figure is inflated by cherry-picking top-confidence rules rather than random sampling. Beyond methodology, the paper’s analysis is shallow: it reports that all models perform poorly but offers almost no explanation of why — no failure case analysis, no breakdown by disease category or rule frequency, and no discussion of what architectural changes would actually improve performance on this benchmark.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The overall score reflects a paper with a genuinely valuable research direction that is, at this stage, insufficiently substantiated to merit acceptance. The benchmark addresses a real and underexplored problem — the disconnect between semantic similarity optimization in CLIP-style MedVLMs and the evidence-driven, guideline-grounded nature of clinical radiology — and the three-stage construction pipeline demonstrates meaningful engineering effort. However, two factors weigh heavily against acceptance in the current form. First, the foundational assumption that retrieval of WHO diagnostic rules is a clinically valid proxy for radiological reasoning is never defended beyond intuition; without this justification, the entire benchmark’s clinical relevance remains an assertion rather than an established fact. Second, the methodological transparency is inadequate for a benchmark paper, where reproducibility is paramount: the undisclosed LLM judge, the unjustified threshold τ, and the biased manual audit collectively undermine confidence in the quality of the ground-truth labels — which are, after all, the benchmark’s most critical artifact. On top of these concerns, the experimental analysis stops at reporting numbers rather than generating insight, which limits the paper’s contribution to the field. A strong benchmark paper should not only reveal that models fail, but explain the structure of that failure well enough to guide future model design. With substantial revisions addressing these points, the work has clear potential; in its current state, it falls short of the standard expected for MICCAI publication.Sonnet 4.6Extended
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission does not mention open access to source code or data, but provides a clear and detailed description of the algorithm to ensure reproducibility.

reviews.recommendation_label: Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviews.text_contribution:
This paper introduces WHO-CXRBench, a benchmark grounded in WHO chest X-ray (CXR) diagnostic guidelines for fine-grained diagnostic rule retrieval. Experiments indicate that current CLIP
style MedVLMs still have space for improvement in fine-grained diagnostic rule retrieval. The proposed WHO-CXRBench builds a valuable foundation for evaluating MedVLMs’ performance under realistic clinical settings.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The proposed WHO-CXRBench addresses a clear gap in existing evaluation protocols by focusing on diagnostic rule retrieval rather than standard image–report matching or classification. This shift toward knowledge-grounded evaluation is conceptually valuable and could encourage more clinically relevant model development.
2.The benchmark is constructed based on WHO diagnostic guidelines, which enhances its clinical credibility. The inclusion of structured diagnostic rules and patient-level alignment provides a more interpretable and verifiable evaluation target compared to conventional free-text retrieval tasks.
3.The experimental results reveal that existing CLIP-style MedVLMs perform poorly on fine-grained diagnostic rule retrieval (e.g., low Recall@K and nDCG), providing useful evidence that current models are insufficient for evidence-level reasoning. This diagnostic insight is valuable for the community.
4.The inclusion of VQA-based validation and manual inspection of rule alignment strengthens confidence in the constructed benchmark and supports its practical relevance.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
1.The reported poor performance of existing models is a central claim of the paper; however, it is unclear whether this is primarily due to model limitations or the intrinsic difficulty and potential noise of the proposed benchmark. In particular, errors introduced during rule construction and report–rule alignment may contribute to the observed performance degradation. The paper does not sufficiently disentangle these factors, making it difficult to draw definitive conclusions.
2.Several key steps in the pipeline—including rule extraction, quality assessment, and report–rule alignment—depend heavily on LLM-based processing. This raises concerns regarding:
reproducibility,
potential hidden biases,
error propagation across stages.
While the authors provide some validation (e.g., manual audit), a more systematic analysis of noise sensitivity and robustness would strengthen the credibility of the benchmark.
3.The inclusion of MRM in Table 3 is questionable, as it is not a CLIP-based method, unlike the other compared approaches. This inconsistency may lead to unfair or less meaningful comparisons and should be clarified or revised to ensure methodological alignment across baselines.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

The proposed WHO-CXRBench provides a challenging evaluation setting for both general-purpose and CXR-specialized CLIP-style models, highlighting an important gap in fine-grained, evidence-based retrieval. However, the paper lacks sufficient clarity regarding several key aspects of the benchmark design and experimental settings, which makes it difficult to fully assess the validity and fairness of the evaluation. These points should be carefully addressed in the rebuttal.
Overall, the work is well-motivated and potentially valuable, but further clarification is needed to strengthen its credibility.

reviews.text_contribution: This paper introduces WHO-CXRBench, a new benchmark designed to evaluate medical vision-language models (MedVLMs) on the task of fine-grained diagnostic rule retrieval. Motivated by the gap between coarse-grained semantic alignment evaluation and the actual evidence-driven workflow of clinicians, the authors construct a dataset based on the WHO chest radiography manual and MIMIC-CXR.
reviews.text_strengths:
1.The authors provide a comprehensive comparison of 12 state-of-the-art CLIP-style MedVLMs, spanning both general-purpose models and CXR-specialist models. 
2.The inclusion of a Visual Question Answering (VQA) rationality check proves that the retrieved rules actually serve as useful contextual evidence, significantly improving Qwen2.5-VL-7B’s performance.
3.The paper identifies a weakness in current AI models. The results demonstrate that contrastive learning optimized for image-report similarity fails to capture localized evidence-to-rule grounding.
reviews.text_weaknesses:
The LLM generates conf(r,g) to define \mathcal{G}_\mathcal{S}^+. LLM-based relevance judgment introduces semantic bias into ground truth, skewing evaluation toward biased models.
2.GRADE-RA boosts quality but sharply reduces data scale. The final corpus \mathcal{G} has only 300 rules across 37 diseases (8.1 per disease), too limited to capture real radiological complexity.
3.Personalized golden rules use a fixed threshold \tau=0.5.Diverse, nuanced clinical language makes this rigid cutoff exclude valid low-confidence matches or admit marginal false positives.
reviews.text_detailed_comments:
N/A

This paper proposes a valuable WHO-CXRBench for fine-grained diagnostic rule retrieval in medical vision-language models, with comprehensive SOTA model comparisons, valid VQA rationality verification, and insightful findings on the flaws of current contrastive learning designs. However, critical limitations remain: LLM-based ground truth introduces semantic bias, the final rule dataset is overly small to reflect real radiological complexity, and the fixed threshold for golden rules is rigid for nuanced clinical language. These merits support acceptance while the non-trivial flaws prevent a higher score, leading to my overall recommendation of Weak Accept.
reviews.text_reproducibility: The submission has provided an anonymized link to the source code, dataset, or any other dependencies.
reviews.text_post_rebuttal_justification:
The authors have partially responded to reviewer concerns in the rebuttal but failed to resolve all core critical issues. Solved points include supplementing LLM model information, $\tau$ threshold ablation analysis, partial failure case analysis, architectural ablation results, removing inconsistent baseline MRM, and clarifying that VQA results do not cause circular validation.
Nevertheless, several fundamental flaws remain unaddressed. First, systematic analysis of LLM-induced semantic bias and error propagation is incomplete, and full-scale human verification is unfinished, leaving reproducibility and ground-truth credibility concerns unresolved. Second, the limited rule corpus size still cannot fully reflect real radiological complexity, and sufficient justification for its adequacy is lacking. Third, the core assumption that image-to-rule retrieval serves as clinical reasoning proxy still lacks solid clinical and cognitive evidence, only with wording revision. Fourth, it still cannot clearly disentangle performance degradation caused by model limitations or benchmark inherent noise. Besides, the inflated manual audit precision issue is not explained at all.

meta_reviews.text:
The paper presents WHO-CXRBench, a WHO-guideline-grounded benchmark for fine-grained diagnostic rule retrieval from chest X-rays, evaluating 12 CLIP-style MedVLMs. The benchmark addresses a critical gap in coarse-grained MedVLM evaluation, is clinically grounded in WHO guidelines, and includes a comprehensive comparison of models plus a VQA rationality check showing retrieved rules improve downstream performance. However, all reviewers highlight heavy LLM dependence for rule extraction, quality filtering, and ground-truth alignment—raising semantic bias, reproducibility, and error-propagation concerns without sufficient sensitivity analysis. The final rule set is too small (300 rules across 37 diseases, ~8 per disease) to capture real radiological complexity. Analysis remains shallow: no failure-case breakdown by disease category or rule frequency, and the paper does not disentangle whether poor performance stems from model limitations versus benchmark noise.
Issues to be addressed in rebuttal:
LLM-based ground-truth construction: identify the LLM, analyze bias/error propagation, and justify its use without circular validation.
Small rule set size: discuss whether 8.1 rules per disease is sufficient for fine-grained retrieval; consider sensitivity to data scale.
Shallow analysis: add failure case examination, performance breakdown by disease/rule frequency, and architectural insights.
Provide clinical/cognitive justification: core assumption that image-to-rule retrieval proxies clinical reasoning.

The authors’ rebuttal partially addresses several methodological concerns raised by the reviewers, including disclosing the LLM details, providing τ threshold sensitivity analysis, adding preliminary failure case breakdowns, reporting architectural ablation results, removing the inconsistent MRM baseline, and clarifying that the VQA experiment does not constitute circular validation. However, critical issues identified in the original reviews remain insufficiently resolved. Most significantly, the rebuttal does not provide a systematic analysis of LLM‑induced semantic bias and error propagation across the three‑stage pipeline; the human verification of report‑rule matches is reported as incomplete. Whether the rule corpus size (300 rules, ~8.1 per disease) is limited continues to lack adequate justification for capturing real‑world radiological complexity, with only a promise to add rule‑length statistics rather than substantive evidence. Finally, the rebuttal does not disentangle whether poor model performance stems from benchmark noise versus genuine model limitations. Given these foundational concerns, the paper does not meet the standards for acceptance.
A particularly controversial issue, raised by Reviewer #1 and echoed here, is that the authors implicitly assume that image‑to‑rule retrieval proxies clinical reasoning without clinical or cognitive validation. The ground‑truth rules are aligned and derived directly from the report (the final diagnosis), and any intermediate diagnostic evidence not mentioned in the report would be excluded from the positive set. Consequently, the retrieval task is reduced to predicting a subset of the final diagnosis rather than capturing an independent intermediate reasoning step. This conflation means the benchmark does not truly assess whether a model can retrieve clinically meaningful intermediate evidence; it simply tests alignment with the documented diagnosis. The authors have not provided any clinical validation that the retrieved rule set, constructed in this report‑dependent manner, corresponds to actual clinician reasoning or guideline‑application steps. Without such validation, the benchmark’s claimed clinical grounding is undermined. Combined with the incomplete human verification and unresolved bias from LLM‑based label construction, the benchmark is not ready for publication.

The paper presents retrieval of relevant guideline as a proxy for correct interpretation of chest X-rays in preliminary reads provided by VLM models. The reviews are a bit mixed (appears to have some automation in some of the reviews) and the authors appear to be responding to some of the concerns.

author_feedback_text:
Q1.LLM construction (reproducibility, bias, and error propagation) [R1&R2-2&R3-1]. We agree that LLM-assisted construction raises risks. For reproducibility, the omitted LLM construction details are now provided in the anonymized repository. Code and benchmark will be released upon acceptance. For hidden bias, we used a rule-matching strategy that feeds the LLM one report and one rule at a time to judge whether they match, rather than having it select a rule from a preset set. This trades computational cost for accuracy via semantic understanding. Experiments confirmed that different LLMs make stable decisions in most cases. A cross-LLM report-rule matching check between DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct achieved 86.8% binary agreement, suggesting that most report-rule support decisions are stable across LLMs. For error propagation evaluation, following MedR-Bench (NC, 2025), we have started human verification of the LLM-extracted rule corpus. Manual auditing of all report-rule matches is being expedited, with 1543/6513 cases completed. We will add stage-wise analysis for rule extraction, GRADE-RA filtering, and report-rule alignment in the final version.
Q2.τ sensitivity [R1&R2-2&R3-3]. This analysis was omitted due to space limits. τ=0.3 gives broader coverage but adds 37013 low-confidence pairs in the 0.3–0.5 range, reaching 73448 total pairs and 10.8 rules per case. τ=0.5 offers a relatively balanced trade-off, with 5.8 rules per case and 36435 pairs. τ=0.7 yields higher confidence but reduces rule diversity, with 3.0 rules per case and 14283 pairs. The VQA task performed best at τ=0.5.Combining these results with clinicians’ qualitative feedback, we selected τ=0.5.This is also consistent with recent LLM ranking works using 0.5 as the relevance-score threshold, e.g., G-RAG (arXiv, 2025) and Synthetic-Data Reranking (RANLP, 2025).
Q3.Size and failure analysis [R1&R2-1&R3-2]. Given our focus on high-precision, image-verifiable rules and LLM hallucination risks, our strict filtering trades diversity for reliability. Meanwhile, rule count alone does not fully capture benchmark diversity, as a single rule may encompass multiple findings, locations, and conditions. We will add rule-length statistics to clarify this point. Failure analysis on UniMed-CLIP reveals non-uniform errors. Disease-level failures are more frequent in categories with overlapping CXR patterns (e.g., pneumonia and lung neoplasms), where opacities, consolidation, or infiltrates overlap, making qualifiers like laterality and distribution critical. At the rule level, longer and more compositional rules are harder; rules in the upper length quartile (≥23 words) achieve only 7.3% Recall@10, compared to 18.2% for shorter rules.
Q4.Architecture and MRM [R1&R2-3]. For architecture, stronger visual encoders improve performance. MedCLIP improved from ResNet50 to ViT, increasing Recall@10 from 1.85% to 8.27%, and UniMed-CLIP improved from ViT-Base to ViT-Large, increasing Recall@10 from 9.62% to 14.23%. In contrast, enlarging UniMed-CLIP’s text encoder decreased Recall@10 to 9.35%, suggesting that visual grounding matters more than generic text-side scaling. For MRM, we agree with R2-3 and will remove it from the comparison.
Q5.Circular validation and VQA utility [R1]. VQA is not used to validate ground-truth correctness. Instead, it only tests whether retrieved rules provide useful downstream context to an independent VLM, Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Ground-truth quality is assessed separately by manual audit against CXR and report evidence, with a full audit ongoing. Thus, construction, VQA testing, and quality audit are separated.
Q6.Clinical and cognitive scope [R1]. We apologize for any lack of clarity in our original description. As shown in Fig. 1, our goal is to evaluate an intermediate step in clinical diagnosis; specifically, whether models can map raw CXR images to guideline-based diagnostic criteria. We will revise the wording accordingly.

title: Wrist Camera Pose-Guided Multi-view Fusion for Occlusion Reconstruction in Robot-Assisted Microsurgical Anastomosis
abstract: Precise visual perception is a cornerstone of safety and efficacy in embodied robot-assisted surgery. However, the intricate operations of microsurgical anastomosis are often plagued by severe occlusions of frequent instrument-tissue interactions, which severely hinder the visibility of micro-scale structures like suturing threads. To mitigate this challenge, we introduce the Camera Pose-Guided Geometry-Aware Transformer, a novel framework for occlusion-aware reconstruction by leveraging a wrist-mounted camera configuration for surgical robots. Specifically, we curate a multi-view dataset with well-calibrated wrist camera poses. By introducing an implicit camera pose encoding mechanism, our proposed method effectively fuses geometric priors into the framework, facilitating robust cross-view alignment and feature aggregation. Furthermore, our architecture exhibits superior robustness to diverse occlusion ratios and numbers of multi-view inputs, enabling reconstruction with complementary wrist perspectives. Our method establishes a new multi-view benchmark for suturing thread recognition in microsurgical anastomosis and significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art approaches. This work emphasises the importance of the wrist-camera pose in multi-view fusion, providing a transformative approach to occlusion recovery and fine-grained visual perception for surgical robotics.
